**COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL LIBRARY, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONICAL, OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III; A CHRONOLOGICAL REPRINTING OF ALL EXTANT MONUMENTS OF CATHOLIC TRADITION DURING THE FIRST TWELVE CENTURIES OF THE CHURCH, CAREFULLY CORRECTED ACCORDING TO THE MOST ACCURATE EDITIONS, COMPARED WITH ONE ANOTHER AND WITH CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES; CONTINUALLY ILLUSTRATED WITH DISSERTATIONS, COMMENTARIES, AND VARIANT READINGS; ENLARGED BY ALL WORKS DISCOVERED AFTER THE MOST EXTENSIVE EDITIONS COMPLETED DURING THE LAST THREE CENTURIES; FURNISHED WITH PARTICULAR ANALYTICAL INDEXES FOLLOWING INDIVIDUAL VOLUMES OR AUTHORS OF SOME IMPORTANCE; ARRANGED WITH CHAPTERS PROPERLY DISTRIBUTED WITHIN THE TEXT ITSELF, AND WITH HEADINGS DISTINGUISHING THE UPPER MARGIN OF EACH PAGE AND INDICATING THE SUBJECT TREATED; AMPLIFIED WITH WORKS BOTH DOUBTFUL AND APOCRYPHAL WHICH NEVERTHELESS POSSESS SOME AUTHORITY IN RELATION TO ecclesiastical tradition; ENRICHED WITH TWO GENERAL INDEXES: ONE OF SUBJECTS, SO THAT, UPON CONSULTING IT, WHATEVER ANY ONE OF THE FATHERS WROTE ON ANY SUBJECT MAY BE SEEN AT A GLANCE; THE OTHER OF HOLY SCRIPTURE, FROM WHICH THE READER MAY READILY DISCOVER WHICH FATHERS, AND IN WHAT PLACES IN THEIR WORKS, COMMENTED UPON THE INDIVIDUAL TEXTS OF THE INDIVIDUAL BOOKS OF SCRIPTURE.**

A most accurate edition, readily to be preferred to all others if the following are considered: the clearness of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the completeness of its correction, both the variety and number of works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, constantly uniform throughout the course of the entire work, the low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and small treatises hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE**

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine monks, vol. XII, p. 86.)

There are few ancient writers whose history has supplied more material for satires and apologies than the famous Abaelard. The censors of his writings represent him as a rash philosopher who wished, through the subtleties of a false dialectic, to corrupt the majestic simplicity of our dogmas. His defenders, on the contrary, maintain that, supported by the rules of sound logic, he introduced order and method into theology; that he purified its principles and sounded its depths through refinements beyond the reach of his adversaries’ penetration. Others, attending only to his morals, portray him as a worldly philosopher, the victim of sensuality, whose barren impression and disgraceful marks, they say, he bore even into the sacred retreats in which shame and despair had compelled him to confine himself. These too have their opponents, who, while admitting Abaelard’s earlier disorders, maintain that he repaired them through a striking and sincere conversion. Our duty is to examine these different opinions impartially and, in the light of fair criticism, to draw from them what seems most conformable to truth. That is what we propose to do in this article.

### § I.—History of Abaelard’s Life

Peter Abélard, or Abaelard, [Note: [Col. 0009] On the different ways of pronouncing his name, see the notes on the *Judgments of the Learned*, vol. I, p. 326, and Fr. Niceron, vol. IV, p. 1 ff.], son of Berengar and Lucia, both distinguished by nobility, was born in 1079 at Le Pallet [Note: [Col. 0009] In Latin, *Palatium*. Hence he was often called *Petrus Palatinus*, or the “Palatine Peripatetic.”], in the county of Nantes. His father, who had acquired some literary cultivation before embracing the profession of arms, regulated the education of his children according to this plan, placing the cultivation of the mind before the military exercises for which he destined them. Abaelard, the eldest [Note: [Col. 0009] M. Joli, in his remarks on Bayle’s *Dictionary* (p. 10), has made completely evident Abaelard’s seniority, disputed by certain critics.], received a token of special affection in the particular care devoted to his studies; he advanced rapidly in the course of letters. When he came to dialectic, the thorny labyrinth of that science captivated a mind naturally fond of intricacies and subtleties. The charm went so far that, as he himself says, he sacrificed Mars to Minerva, and the glory he might have gained by arms to the desire of making a name for himself in the disputes of the Lyceum. Filled with this idea, he left his country at about sixteen years of age and began to travel through different regions, stopping wherever dialecticians were to be found, entering the lists against them, and always leaving behind proofs of his ability. After five years these philosophical travels brought him to Paris, where he found champions against whom he at first did not dare measure himself. The most celebrated among them was William of Champeaux, master of the principal school.

When Abaelard presented himself to obtain permission to hear him, he displayed on that occasion a merit which dazzled and delighted the professor. Not only did William consent to admit him as a disciple in his school; he even wished to have him as a friend in his own house.

So much favor, which the calmness of philosophy ought, it seems, to have moderated, inflamed the young man’s heart and soon made him overstep the bounds of subordination. He undertook to make himself the equal of his master and openly attacked his opinions. This ungrateful and rash conduct having angered William of Champeaux, they had to separate. Dismissed, Abaelard departed for Melun, then one of the residences of the court, intending to open there a school of philosophy of his own. He succeeded despite the obstacles raised against him. Having there declared himself the antagonist of the Parisian philosopher, he made it his business to undermine both his doctrine and his reputation. To this end, he sent his students from time to time to challenge Champeaux’s students to disputation; and, if he is to be believed, these skirmishes always ended to the advantage of his own side. But because the distance between the two schools caused the contest to languish, he moved his school to Corbeil, in order to make the encounters livelier and more frequent.

In the midst of these exploits, an illness caused by excessive work compelled him to go and breathe his native air. On his return he found William of Champeaux teaching in the cloister of the new monastery of Saint-Victor, wearing the habit of a regular canon. This unexpected transformation surprised and affected him. He went to find his master, asked him to forget his excesses, and, although about thirty years old, did not hesitate to place himself again under his discipline. But the difference in their opinions, from which neither wished to depart, soon caused a new rupture. William maintained the *universal a parte rei*, which Bayle [Note: [Col. 0009] Bayle’s accusation against Champeaux’s opinion is very well refuted in the *Mémoires de Trévoux*, year 1758, p. 2248.] groundlessly calls an undeveloped Spinozism. Abaelard, an ardent nominalist, revived his earlier objections, strengthened by new syllogisms. Then, he says, he pressed his [Col. 0011] adversary so hard that he compelled him to recant. It is obvious that, to be believed, this fact would require an authority less suspect than that of the interested party who publicized it. In any case, weary of the humble status of a student, Abaelard wished to begin lecturing again. His name had already made him formidable in the schools of Paris. The successor whom William of Champeaux had appointed when he withdrew to Saint-Victor, informed of Abaelard’s designs and fearing to have him as a rival, came of his own accord to offer him the exercise of his chair. He did more: he did not disdain to take his place among the hearers of the man to whom he lent his authority to teach. If this generosity greatly pleased Abaelard, it no less displeased the Victorine [Note: [Col. 0011] The learned and judicious author of the new *History of the University* says that Abaelard preferred another school offered to him to that which William of Champeaux had occupied. Accordingly, he applies to a professor other than William’s successor the removal from office which followed this offer. But Abaelard’s text seems to state quite positively the opposite. It is too long to reproduce in a note. Those who judge the matter worthy of examination may consult the source.]. The latter found a way to make it ineffectual, by having the titular professor removed on serious charges and appointing another of his disciples, very devoted to his wishes, to replace him.

After this setback, Abaelard returned to Melun, where he restored his chair with the same success as before. At about the same time William of Champeaux, for his part, left Saint-Victor with his community to establish himself in the country. Our philosopher, seeing that the man who had supplanted him was then without support, hurried back with the intention of dislodging him. He brought with him his school from Melun, which he regarded as a small army under whose leadership he was to fight. With this troop he went to lodge—that is, to give his lectures—on Mont Sainte-Geneviève, whose position, he says, seemed favorable for besieging his enemy and battering his defenses. This kind of philosophical camp soon received new reinforcements. A great number of volunteers flocked there, and the opposing party suffered great desertions from which Abaelard’s party benefited. William did not hear these reports tranquilly from the depths of his retreat. He immediately set out and hastened to Paris. But his presence could not restore courage to the man whom he had come to relieve. That weak and timid spirit preferred to abandon the contest and fled in shame to a monastery. Thus the battlefield remained to the two former rivals, each supported by his adherents. The dispute only became more animated. Arguments were launched on both sides with new ardor, and the bitterness of the two parties was such that its noise resounded through all the provinces. Abaelard, whom we are here merely copying, ends his account of this adventure by saying that, without exaggeration, and indeed falling short of the truth, he may apply to himself the verse which the poet puts in Ajax’s mouth:

> If you ask the outcome of this battle,  
> I was not defeated by him.  
> (*Ovid, Metamorphoses*, XIII.)

Yet a contemporary author very worthy of trust relates an anecdote on this point that somewhat tarnishes our philosopher’s triumph. Can one believe that, while he was fencing with such success against an old man practiced in all the artifices of dialectic, a young logician succeeded in putting him to flight [Note: [Col. 0011] *Life of St. Goswin*, I.18.]? This new champion was Goswin, later abbot of Anchin in Flanders, then a disciple of Joscelin, who was teaching at the same time on another part of Mont Sainte-Geneviève. Offended by Abaelard’s swaggering and by several bold propositions that he advanced, Goswin dared to challenge him to disputation and pressed him so hard that he put him, as the saying goes, with his back against the wall. The defeated man was careful not to add this incident to his own account.

Hostilities were suspended by a second journey that Abaelard was obliged to make to Brittany, summoned by his mother, who wished, following her husband’s example, to enter religious life. His desire to resume the war made him settle his family affairs promptly. But upon his return he learned that William of Champeaux had just been made bishop of Châlons-sur-Marne. This promotion, which deprived him of the only rival he judged worthy of himself, disturbed his plans and suggested new ones. He abandoned Paris and philosophy in order to study theology at Laon under the famous schoolmaster Anselm, whose reputation drew students from every side. The favorable opinion he had formed of this professor did not withstand experience. After hearing him for some time, he found, he says [Note: [Col. 0011] Here is the portrait he gives of this professor: “He was indeed admirable in the eyes of his hearers, but insignificant in the sight of questioners. His command of words was remarkable, but his meaning contemptible and devoid of reasoning. When he kindled a fire, he filled his house with smoke, not illuminated it with light. His tree appeared wholly covered with leaves and conspicuous to those viewing it from afar; but when people approached and examined it more carefully, they found it fruitless.” “One cannot restrain one’s indignation,” says a capable modern writer (*History of the University of Paris*, vol. I, p. 25), “on seeing a man treated thus who, during the forty years in which he taught theology, was regarded as the light and oracle of the Latin Church; who was called the Doctor of Doctors; and in whose school were formed great theologians and learned, pious prelates who brought renown not only to France but to England, Germany, and Italy.”], his ability far below the celebrity of his name. Since theology then consisted only in exposition of Holy Scripture, it occurred to him that by reading some good commentary at home he would advance much more than by attending Anselm’s school. He had pursued this method for some time with satisfaction when, by a sort of challenge, he found himself obliged to give public proof of the advantage he had derived from it. The text he selected for this trial was the first chapter of Ezekiel, one of the most difficult passages, as is known, in Holy Scripture. He acquitted himself so successfully, to his audience’s satisfaction, that they asked him to continue on the following days. He readily consented and undertook to follow the prophecy through to the end. But the schoolmaster, without whose permission this was occurring, gave him no time to do so. Urged by two of his disciples, Alberic and Lotulf, he silenced the new professor and thus stopped the kind of assault which he was committing against his authority.

Unable either to receive or give lessons at Laon, Abaelard returned to try his fortune once more at Paris. On his arrival, he found that the principal chair, the great object of his ambition, was vacant. His friends and protectors worked for him in such a way that they secured it for him. To this office, [Col. 0013] whose duties embraced philosophy and theology, a canonry was probably then attached. What is certain is that Abaelard became [Note: [Col. 0013] How could it have been denied that Abaelard was a canon, when Heloise, wishing to dissuade him from marriage, speaks to him thus: “But if laymen and pagans lived as celibates in this way, what ought you, a cleric and canon, to do?”] a canon at the same time as the chair was conferred on him. His wishes, so long frustrated, seemed at last fulfilled: no rival capable of obstructing him, no superior in the schools with whom he feared to compromise himself. His first lectures, in which he resumed the exposition of Ezekiel begun at Laon, won him the greatest reputation. There was talk of no one but Professor Abaelard, not only in France but in every foreign country. Anjou, Brittany, Flanders, England, and Germany hastened to send their young men to Paris to be trained in the sciences under so renowned a doctor. In a word, no school had ever been so brilliant as his; and since every student then paid fees, profit kept pace with glory.

Abaelard did not possess only one kind of merit, nor did he shine only in the exercise of his profession. A pleasing appearance, great liveliness of mind, a melodious voice, and a thousand other agreeable qualities had gained him great favor in fashionable society, especially among women. To bear so many advantages in a Christian manner required more than ordinary virtue, and unfortunately he did not possess it. Intoxicated by his prosperity, Providence permitted him to fall into an error which poisoned the whole remainder of his days. We refer to his well-known affair with Heloise, whom he seduced under the pretext of philosophy, which he had undertaken to teach her. It is known that the fruit of their love was a son named Astralabe. It is also known what cruel and cowardly vengeance Heloise’s relatives inflicted upon the seducer, despite the care he had taken to repair their daughter’s honor by marrying her.

Nothing could console him: neither the expressions of sympathy which all ranks of the city gave him on this occasion, nor the retaliatory punishment inflicted upon some of the guilty persons. His despair allowed him to see no refuge other than a cloister in which to bury his shame. He chose that of Saint-Denis and bound himself there by solemn vows about the year 1119, after compelling his wife to do the same in the abbey of nuns at Argenteuil. His restless and biting temper followed him into his retreat.

Under Abbot Adam, the monks of Saint-Denis departed in several respects from the strict observance of the Rule, though they were much [Note: [Col. 0013] See the apology of Abbot Adam and his house in Duchesne’s notes on Abaelard’s first letter, and in the *Mémoires de Trévoux*, year 1738, p. 2248.] less depraved than Abaelard portrays them in the *History of His Misfortunes*. The new professed monk, without office or commission, wished to set himself up as a reformer. His indiscretion brought upon him the humiliations it seemed to deserve. He soon found himself abandoned by all his brethren. In this extreme solitude, a delegation of his students arrived most opportunely to end his troubles. Its object was to persuade him to resume his lectures. If he is to be believed, he yielded to this proposal only with difficulty. The abbot and his community were of a different mind: all readily consented. A priory near the lands of the count of Champagne was assigned to him for his school. He left Saint-Denis, and was seen to depart without regret.

It was then that he began to distinguish himself by the singularity of his opinions. Since the end of the preceding century, questions concerning the Trinity had furnished the most ordinary subject of disputes among theologians. Abaelard, who prided himself on accounting for everything, undertook to explain this mystery by the lights of philosophy alone. Not content to set forth his system orally, he committed it to writing, thereby arousing the most capable doctors against himself. Roscelin was the first to denounce him to the bishop of Paris. But the disgrace Roscelin had previously brought upon himself through his own errors saved his adversary on this occasion. His denunciation was attributed, perhaps too lightly, to ignorance or ill will. Nevertheless, Abaelard did not escape this assault unscathed. Alberic and Lotulf, his two former rivals, then professors at Rheims, returned to the attack and chose to denounce him before the council assembled at Soissons in 1121 by Conon, the pope’s legate. The accused appeared in response to the summons, not without having run the risk, he says, of being stoned as a heretic when entering the city. He disputed with his adversaries [Note: [Col. 0013] Besides the accusation of heresy, he was reproached with teaching without a master, *sine magistro*. A learned man, following Duboulay (*History of the University of Paris*, vol. I, pp. 135–136), maintains that the true sense of this expression—ambiguous, according to him—is to be drawn from the practice of later centuries, in which it was not enough to have attended a master’s lectures for a certain time in order to receive permission or a license to teach; one also had to give one or more courses of public lectures under the direction of a doctor. Abaelard, it is added, had not satisfied this rule, established in his time as to the substance of the matter; therefore he could be reproached with teaching without a master, when he ought to have had one above him and to have taught only in a subordinate capacity. But those who speak thus have not observed that Abaelard had formerly occupied the principal chair at Paris—that of the episcopal school, and properly speaking the theological chair—with the approval of all ranks. How can one maintain after this that, when later teaching in the countryside, he needed to be supervised by a master? It therefore seems simpler and truer to say with Dom Rivet (*Literary History*, vol. IX, p. 82) that the reproach that he taught without a master meant that he gave lectures in theology without having obtained the permission then required for teaching in private schools—a permission granted by the chancellors or schoolmasters of episcopal churches.], preached, and explained his doctrine publicly and privately during the council; in short, he omitted nothing in his defense. But all was in vain. At the final session, the Fathers summoned him, had a brazier brought in, and ordered him to throw his book into it. This done, they compelled him to recite aloud the creed called that of Saint Athanasius, as a profession of faith—a terrible sentence which, by his own admission, he carried out only while shedding many tears, which were anything but signs of repentance. Nor was this all. To crown his ignominy, he was confined as a seducer in the monastery of Saint-Médard at Soissons.

Fortunately, the abbot and monks of Saint-Médard were people who prided themselves on humanity. Moved by their prisoner’s calamity, they omitted no care to soften his captivity. It did not last long. When the legate left France, he granted Abaelard’s release, though with the order that he return [Col. 0015] to Saint-Denis. The memory of the unfavorable impressions he had left there against himself, and the stigma he had just received, warned him in every way to adopt feelings, a tone, and manners capable of winning minds back in his favor. But an irresistible itch to speak and contradict soon brought him fresh troubles. Reading Bede, he found that Saint Dionysius the Areopagite had been bishop of Corinth, not Athens; from which it followed that he was not the same person as the apostle of Gaul, as was then believed. This text seemed to him to open too fine a field for disputation to be neglected. He therefore dared to oppose the received opinion—an opinion upon which, in a sense, the safety of the kingdom and the glory of the Gallican Church were thought to depend. His brethren, scandalized, brought their complaints to the abbot, who handled the matter according to the prejudices of the time. Abaelard was summoned before the chapter and severely reprimanded for his rashness. They even went so far as to threaten to denounce him to the king as guilty of high treason. Since the threat was serious, or appeared so to him, he did not think he ought to wait for its effect. One night, therefore, he escaped from the cloister and took refuge on the lands of the count of Champagne. This prince, who knew him, placed him in the monastery of Saint-Ayoul at Provins. Despite this powerful protection, Adam continued to pursue him in his refuge. He complained to the religious of Saint-Ayoul about the shelter they gave him, and had Abaelard himself ordered to return by a fixed date under pain of excommunication. Death did not allow the rigorous superior time to carry his resentment further. Suger, who succeeded him, at first wished to follow his predecessor’s final course against the fugitive; but overcome by entreaties, he eventually allowed Abaelard to go wherever he wished, provided that he promised stability in no monastery.

Master of his choice of dwelling, Abaelard went to settle on the banks of the river Ardusson, in a deserted place near the town of Nogent-sur-Seine. His disciples did not delay in coming to find him there. Neither the horror of the place nor the difficulty of obtaining the necessities of life discouraged this multitude of young men, most of them delicately brought up. Eager as they were for his lessons, the company of their master stood in place of everything for them. To leave him no cause for distraction, they undertook to provide for his maintenance. The manner in which they discharged this duty testifies to their generosity.

Content to live themselves in huts of reeds, they built him a stone dwelling and transformed the little oratory that he had constructed with his own hands into a spacious and well-adorned church. This building was dedicated to the Paraclete, a title at which certain people murmured as an innovation. “Never,” they said, “has one seen a church consecrated to one divine Person alone.” Likewise censured, perhaps with more reason, was a statue which he had devised to represent the mystery of the Trinity: it was a stone group composed of three figures joined back to back, with perfectly identical faces. These complaints affected him all the more because their authors were reported to be [Note: [Col. 0015] It appears that Abaelard was ill informed, especially in regard to Saint Bernard, for Bernard clearly declares (*Epistle* 377) that he had no knowledge whatever of Abaelard’s doctrine before it was denounced to him by William of Saint-Thierry; this, as will be stated below, did not occur until 1139.], Saint Bernard and Saint Norbert, two of the most influential figures of their time. Fear seized him to such a degree that he believed every day that he was on the point of being brought before another council to be condemned once more. While he was in these perplexities, two deputies from the monastery of Saint-Gildas of Rhuys in Lower Brittany came to announce that their chapter had elected him abbot. They bore the decree of election and had taken the precaution of obtaining the consent of the abbot of Saint-Denis. No occurrence ever seemed happier to him. He departed joyfully, about the year 1126, for his abbey, persuaded that his enemies would lose sight of him in so remote a country. But his unhappy fate caused him to avoid one misfortune only to plunge into another. The monks of Saint-Gildas lived disorderly lives, and the lord of Rhuys took the opportunity to seize the monastery’s goods. The new abbot wished to reform the monks and restrain the tyrant’s usurpations. His zeal failed on both sides and served only to make him enemies within and without. In the midst of these conflicts, he learned that the nuns of Argenteuil, of whom Heloise was then prioress, had been expelled in 1127 to make room for the religious of Saint-Denis. This news revived conjugal tenderness in his heart. He immediately set out, took his former wife, and led her, together with those of her sisters who wished to follow her, to the wilderness of the Paraclete. Through the benefactions of neighboring lords and with the permission of the ordinary—the venerable Atton, bishop of Troyes—this place was erected into an abbey, governed by Heloise. Abaelard, who regarded this foundation as his own work, devoted all his care to perfecting it. Yet people spoke of his frequent journeys to the Paraclete, and interpreted their motives maliciously. To put an end to these evil reports, he chose to withdraw from this beloved place, resolving never to return.

On returning to his abbey, he found there, as he had expected, nothing but vexations and persecutions. Matters even went beyond what he had foreseen, if it be true that his monks, as he relates, were wicked enough to attempt his life. However that may be, it is certain that the disgusts he endured finally led him to resign his dignity; this occurred at the latest in the year 1136. We in fact see him in that year [Note: [Col. 0015] Here is the passage from John of Salisbury (*Metalogicon*, book II, chapter 10) which informs us of this fact and the following one: “When, still very young, I had first migrated to the Gauls for the sake of study, in the second year after the illustrious King Henry, the Lion of Justice, had departed from human affairs, I betook myself to the Peripatetic, who at that time presided as a renowned teacher on Mount Saint Geneviève, admired by all. . . . Then, after his departure, which seemed to me too hasty, I attached myself to Master Alberic.” Dom Rivet (*Histoire littéraire*, vol. IX, p. 66), assuming with all critics that John of Salisbury was born in 1110, finds a contradiction in the first part of this text. Indeed, on that hypothesis John of Salisbury, one year after the death of Henry I, king of England—for it is unquestionably this prince who is meant here—must have been twenty-six years old, Henry having died in 1135. How then could he say that he was still in the earliest years of adolescence, *adolescens admodum* (“quite a youth”)? But the contradiction disappears as soon as one calls into question the date which supplies its basis, namely the year 1110 assigned as the year of John of Salisbury’s birth—a date which in fact, as we shall show in our treatment of this author, has no certain foundation.] again giving lectures on Mount Saint Geneviève at Paris, and eclipsing all his colleagues by the brilliance of his intellect and the crowd of those who came to hear him. But he abandoned his chair—why is not known—the following year; and no document enables us to know [Col. 0017] the place to which he withdrew. [Note: [Col. 0017] M. Joli (*Remarks on Bayle*, p. 15) says that he returned to the Paraclete; but what is the proof?]

Wherever it was, Abelard did not remain idle. He used the leisure of his retreat to revise the works he had composed up to that time and to put them in a condition to appear before the public. As soon as they came into the public’s hands, they made a great stir and gave rise to diverse judgments. The author’s new method—proceeding in theology, as in dialectic, by way of demonstration—dazzled the greater number. People admired the power of this genius, who had made for himself a path to reach mysteries hitherto believed inaccessible to the human mind. Others, on the contrary, saw in this undertaking only presumption, rashness, and delusion. Among the latter was William [Note: [Col. 0017] Peter of Cluny, book IV, letter 4. Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick*, book I, p. 48.], formerly Benedictine abbot of Saint-Thierry, whose surname he retained, who had become a monk of Cîteaux at the abbey of Signy. From Abelard’s two principal books he drew the propositions that seemed to him most offensive, and refuted them in a writing which he sent to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and to Saint Bernard. [Note: [Col. 0017] Bernard, letter 326.] The sending was accompanied by two letters in which he asked these weighty persons to tell him what they thought both of the extracts and of the refutation. We do not possess the bishop of Chartres’s reply. That of the abbot of Clairvaux bears the stamp of the most exact circumspection. [Note: [Col. 0017] Bernard, letter 325.] He praises William for his zeal against novelties and approves his work in general; “but,” he adds, “the matter being of the utmost importance, it is necessary, before I can decide, that we confer together somewhere. This can take place only after Easter, considering the circumstance—for it was then Lent—which does not permit us to violate our retreat or to attend to concerns other than prayer.” The holy abbot’s prudence did not stop at this precaution.

He went in person to the accused. [Note: [Col. 0017] Bernard, letter 189.] He pointed out to him the scandal aroused by his books, and handled that lively and haughty spirit so skillfully that he obtained more than he had hoped; for Abelard carried his compliance so far as himself to choose Bernard as judge of his doctrine, promising to submit to whatever decision he might make. [Note: [Col. 0017] Bernard, letter 337.] If these dispositions of our theologian were sincere, they did not have the merit of perseverance. Treacherous friends reproached him with them as cowardice and succeeded in making him disavow them. The most vehement of all was the famous Arnold of Brescia, once his disciple, who, expelled from Italy for his seditious declamations against the pope and clergy, had taken refuge in France. This dangerous man represented the intentions of the abbot of Clairvaux toward him in such odious colors that he induced him to enter into open warfare with him.

To this end Abelard went to the archbishop of Sens, [Note: [Col. 0017] Bernard, letters 189 and 190.] Henry Sanglier, and asked him to convene an assembly in which he might engage in a formal disputation with that abbot upon the articles in his doctrine which the latter found objectionable. The prelate consented and wrote to Saint Bernard to attend the council which he was to hold at Sens during the octave of Pentecost in the year 1140. Unaccustomed to the battles of the schools, the holy man at first refused the challenge, fearing, he said, to measure himself against a man bristling with all the points of dialectic. [Note: [Col. 0017] The same, letter 90.] Moreover, it seemed dangerous to him—these again are his words—to commit wholly divine truths to the outcome of a wholly human disputation. He accordingly replied to the archbishop that he would not go to the council, since the matter for which he was summoned was not his own private cause but that of the whole Church.

Such were the abbot of Clairvaux’s first thoughts. Better advised afterward, he presented himself for the contest. [Note: [Col. 0017] The same, letter 189.] The assembly at Sens was among the most numerous. King Louis the Younger was present, with the counts of Champagne and Nevers. All the bishops of the province, except two—Samson, archbishop of Reims, together with three of his suffragans—formed the tribunal which was to pronounce judgment. Besides these prelates, a multitude of learned men had come, attracted by the importance of the case and the reputation of the contestants. Abelard’s supporters did not doubt that he would easily win the victory over an adversary whom they said fear had already half defeated. On both sides people expected to see him deploy all the resources of his art, in order to expose his opponent’s weakness and perplex his judges.

But his conduct at the very first step caused these fine hopes to vanish. Saint Bernard [Note: [Col. 0017] Geoffrey, *Life of Saint Bernard*, book III, chapter 5.], after the propositions extracted from Abelard’s books had been read, summoned him, without further preamble, to declare whether they were his or not and, if they were, to defend or retract them. Abelard was disturbed by this abrupt opening. Instead of replying categorically, he said that he appealed to the pope, and immediately departed, leaving the assembly in the greatest astonishment. The council was undoubtedly entitled to disregard so frivolous an appeal. Yet fear of compromising itself with the Holy See suggested a middle course. It was agreed to separate the doctrines from the person of their author and reserve the latter issue for the pope. On the former point, after comparing the denounced extracts with the authorities alleged by Saint Bernard, all the Fathers united in censuring them. They contented themselves with stigmatizing them collectively, and the judgment was drafted in the final session.

It remained to give an account of these proceedings to the Holy See. The abbot of Clairvaux, entrusted with this commission, performed it by two letters: one written in the name of the province of Sens, the other on behalf of the archbishop of Reims and the three suffragans who had accompanied him. In both, after recounting what had passed between Abelard and the abbot of Clairvaux from the beginning of the affair, they beg the pope to examine the articles sent to him, to weigh carefully the sentence condemning them, and to stamp it with the seal of his authority. Besides these synodical letters, Saint Bernard wrote several in his own name, both to the pope and to the cardinals, especially to those who, having been Abelard’s disciples, were thought likely to take a more particular interest in his fate. Here is how he represented him to the pope; the other letters are in much the same tone. [Note: [Col. 0017] Letter 189.]

“Abelard is a dragon laying snares in secret. What am I saying? Today he no longer fears to show himself. And would to God that his writings were shut up in chests instead of being circulated and read in public places! Alas, these pestilent fruits [Col. 0019] of error fly through the world, taking for darkness the light which they hate. Their deadly poison has penetrated castles and cities. They have passed from nation to nation, from one kingdom to another. To what times have we come! Another Gospel is being manufactured; a new faith is proposed to the peoples; another foundation is laid than that which has been laid. Virtues and vices are treated contrary to the rules of sound morality; the sacraments in a manner far from safe; the mystery of one God in three persons with rash curiosity. Abelard, a new Goliath, advances with all his martial equipment, preceded by his armor-bearer, Arnold of Brescia. The union of these two men could not be closer, like that of the two shells of an oyster, which leaves no opening for air to enter and separate them. Imitators of him who transforms himself into an angel of light, they display outward appearances of piety without possessing either its spirit or its reality. By means of this imposing exterior they deceive the religious faith of those who securely lend an ear to their discourses. . . . Judge now, O successor of Peter, whether he who attacks the faith of this prince of the apostles ought to find asylum near his see.”

While the abbot of Clairvaux was preparing his adversary’s ruin with such care and activity, the latter, full of blind confidence, was proceeding slowly toward the tribunal which he himself had demanded. [Note: [Col. 0019] Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick*, book I, chapter 48.] But scarcely had he reached the gates of Lyons when fatal news undeceived him. It was there that he learned how Rome had received his appeal, [Note: [Col. 0019] *Life of Abelard*, vol. II, p. 141.] so unfavorably that, without waiting for his arrival, the pope had confirmed the sentence of Sens, ordered the books burned, and sent instructions into France that he and Arnold of Brescia be arrested and each confined separately in a monastery. Then, struck as by a thunderbolt, he did not know what to do. Fear and shame held him in suspense and permitted him neither to advance nor to retreat. In this distress he resolved to turn aside to Cluny, to consult Abbot Peter the Venerable, who knew him.

Peter, after drying his tears, gave him very sound advice, which he followed: [Note: [Col. 0019] Peter of Cluny, book IV, letter 4.] he should remain at Cluny instead of going to pursue his affair at Rome, where there was nothing more to hope for. The charitable abbot himself undertook to obtain his absolution from the pope. But because peace with Saint Bernard was a necessary preliminary, Peter and Rainald, abbot of Cîteaux, who happened then to be at Cluny, persuaded him to go to the saint at Clairvaux. Never did a reconciliation between theologians, after a most bitter war, encounter fewer difficulties. The abbot of Clairvaux, who, like the bee, had only a sting without venom, laid aside all animosity as soon as Abelard assured him of the orthodoxy of his sentiments. On his return, the abbot of Cluny hastened to report this news to the Holy Father, at the same time asking him to restore the penitent to the communion of the Church. Although the pope’s reply has not come down to us, there is no doubt that he readily consented to so just a request.

Freed from every anxiety, Abelard spent the remainder of his days in a calm proportionate to the disturbances which had hitherto agitated them. All his free time was divided among prayer, study, and conferences which the abbot charged him to deliver from time to time to the community. In the course of these exercises, an illness which befell him made it necessary to send him, for a change of air, to the priory of Saint-Marcel at Chalon-sur-Saône. At first he appeared better there; but the illness having returned, carried him off on 21 April 1142, in the sixty-third year of his age. The religious buried him in the church beneath [Note: [Col. 0019] It has disappeared for a century.] a tomb upon which they had engraved the following two verses:

> It is enough for the tomb: here lies Peter Abelard,  
> To whom alone lay open whatever was knowable.

*Est satis in tumulo, Petrus hic jacet Abaelardus,  
Cui soli patuit scibile quidquid erat.*

Peter the Venerable, announcing his death to Héloïse, does not hesitate to compare him to Saint Martin and Saint Germanus, two models whom, he says, Abelard equaled: the one in profound humility, the other in extreme poverty—“so that, to one who judges rightly, neither did Germanus appear more abject, nor Martin himself poorer”: *In tantum ut nec Germanus abjectior, nec ipse Martinus bene discernenti pauperior appareret.* His mind, he adds, contemplated, his tongue uttered, and his conduct proclaimed only things divine, philosophical, learned: *Mens ejus, lingua ejus, opus ejus semper divina, semper philosophica, semper eruditoria meditabatur, docebat, fatebatur*—“His mind, his tongue, and his work always meditated upon, taught, and professed divine, philosophical, and learned things.”

Héloïse, affected, as may readily be imagined, by the loss announced to her, neglected nothing that she owed to the memory of her husband. She requested that his body be transferred to the Paraclete, as he had desired. This was granted her despite the opposition of the religious of Saint-Marcel. She further requested absolution for the deceased, a formality then believed important both for this world and the next. The abbot of Cluny caused it to be issued to her in these terms: [Note: [Col. 0019] Book IV, letter 345.]

> I, Peter, abbot of Cluny, who received Peter Abelard as a monk and granted his body, secretly brought, to Abbess Héloïse and the nuns of the Paraclete, by the authority of almighty God and of all the saints absolve him, in respect of my office, from all sins.

*Ego Petrus Cluniacencis abbas, qui Petrum Abaelardum in monachum recepi, et corpus ejus furtim delatum Heloisae abbatissae et monialibus Paracleti concessi, auctoritate omnipotentis Dei et omnium sanctorum absolvo eum pro officio ab omnibus peccatis.*

This formula, according to the usage of the time, was attached to Abelard’s tomb.

Men of letters shared Héloïse’s grief. We possess five epitaphs [Note: [Col. 0019] The first is by Peter the Venerable. The second, believed to be by the same author, follows the first in Damboise’s *Apology for Abelard*, toward the end. The third, by an unknown author, was published by Dom Bernard Pez, p. 22 of the preface to the third volume of his *Anecdotes*. The fourth, composed by Philip of Harvengt, is on p. 801 of his works; it is entitled *Epitaph of Master Peter* and begins with the verse: “The light-bearer has set; the lesser stars shine forth.” *Lucifer occubuit, stellae radiate minores.* There can be no doubt that it concerns Abelard, from all the great qualities it attributes to its hero. The fifth, without an author’s name, is reported by Rawlinson at the beginning of his edition of Abelard’s letters.] which they composed in Abelard’s honor. [Note: [Col. 0019] Nicéron, vol. IV, p. 19.]

## § II.—His printed works

Abelard’s entire life was that of a scholar continually occupied in disputing, teaching, or [Col. 0021] writing. As he prided himself on universal learning, there was no branch of literature esteemed in his time in which he did not seek distinction. The diversity of works produced by this kind of polymathy would, if all had reached us, furnish seven or eight classes. We shall make five from those which the public possesses.

The first will include his letters to Héloïse and to the nuns of the Paraclete, together with that which occasioned this correspondence. The second, his other letters to various persons; the third, his sermons; the fourth, his commentaries on Scripture; the fifth, his theological works.

**I.** After returning to Saint-Gildas, having consolidated the establishment of the community at the Paraclete, Abelard conceived the idea of writing, in the form of a letter to a friend, the history of his misfortunes. There he recounts the principal events of his life from his birth down to the real or supposed persecutions which he was then suffering from his monks. It is a kind of apology in which praise of the author, insults, and calumnies against his adversaries are spread with equal profusion. If, for want of a better source, we have drawn from it the principal facts concerning him, we have carefully avoided admitting most of the circumstances with which he accompanies them, unless supported by more certain records.

**II.** Héloïse was too predisposed in Abelard’s favor to protect herself from the impressions made by such a writing. Chance having brought it into her hands, she read it with the tenderness and credulity that blind devotion can inspire. Until then, having received no letter from Abelard, she had not dared to anticipate him. But as soon as she learned that his life was in danger, she hastened to break silence in order to show the lively interest she took in his condition. Her letter began by complaining that, knowing the extent of her attachment, he had neglected, since their first separation, to use toward her the sole means of representing absent friends. What followed was an outpouring of heart concerning her husband’s present and past misfortunes.

In his reply, Abelard assures her that his silence was not the effect of negligence, still less of forgetfulness, but rather of his firm persuasion that she could readily dispense with his counsel. He thanks her for the new proof of friendship which she gives him by joining, in the sentiments of her heart, in his afflictions. But he asks her not to confine her compassion to sterile groans. He exhorts her to implore divine aid for him; and on this occasion he gives a fairly fine encomium of prayer. In particular, by examples drawn from the Old and New Testaments, he demonstrates the efficacy of women’s prayers for persons dear to them, and of wives’ prayers for their husbands. Finally he begs Héloïse and her daughters, when they learn of his death—which he lets them see is near—to take care that his body be conveyed to the Paraclete: “that,” he says, “our daughters—indeed, our sisters in Christ—often seeing our tomb, may be the more stirred to pour forth prayers to the Lord for me.” *Ut filiae nostrae, imo in Christo sorores, sepulcrum nostrum saepius videntes, ad preces pro me Domino fundendas amplius invitentur.*

**III.** This letter was intended to console Héloïse; the words ending it only embittered her grief. Believing herself near the moment of widowhood, this desolate wife addressed to the object of her affection new complaints still more intense and moving than the first. There she lays bare the condition of her soul. But, touching here only what may help us understand our author’s reply, we shall merely indicate the four points around which this lamentable writing turns.

First, she complains that her superior and master had named her first in the superscription of his reply. It was indeed then the custom to place first the name of the more highly qualified person in formulas of this sort. The formula of which Héloïse complains ran as follows: *Heloissae dilectissimae sorori suae in Christo P. Abaelardus frater ejus in Christo*—“P. Abelard, her brother in Christ, to Héloïse, his most beloved sister in Christ.” Second, she reproaches him for taking pleasure in overwhelming her not only by the account of the evils he was presently enduring, but also by the announcement of a future misfortune, the very thought of which was unbearable to her. Third, she rejects the praise he gives her as unworthy of it, confessing that all her conduct is merely dissimulation and hides a disordered heart beneath the appearances of virtue. Finally, recalling, under the fourth point, the catastrophe that ended their love, she dares accuse heaven in this respect of a double injustice: first, for having punished the crime of two guilty persons upon one alone; second, for having exacted that vengeance at the time when the crime had been repaired by the most complete satisfaction.

**IV.** In his second letter Abelard seeks to apply remedies to these four wounds in Héloïse’s heart. First, he justifies the superscription of which she complained by the sublime rank she has attained in passing from the arms of a wretched mortal to the bridal bed of the Monarch of heaven. He tells her that the black clothing in which she is arrayed, far from disfiguring her in that bridegroom’s eyes, makes her resemble the Ethiopian woman of the Song of Songs, whose dusky color had attracted the king’s gaze and fixed his affections. He piles up mystical and even physical reasons to explain this comparison. Yet among the latter there are some in which this zealous spiritual director reveals traces of his former worldly ideas.

He answers the second reproach by reminding Héloïse that she herself had begged him not to conceal from her anything concerning his present condition. “Why then,” he says, “make it a crime in me that I declared my sufferings to you, after the urgent prayers you made to me not to hide them from you? Would it become you, besides, to pass your days in joy while mine are exposed to the greatest dangers? Do you wish to share with me only pleasure and leave the whole of sadness to me? No: nothing distinguishes true friends from false ones better than the eagerness of the former to share our misfortunes, whereas the latter wish to share only our prosperity. Therefore suppress these frivolous speeches and put an end to reproaches which do not proceed from the bowels of charity.”

On the third point Abelard congratulates Héloïse on esteeming herself unworthy of praise, provided that she speaks sincerely and does not truly seek contradiction. In answering the fourth, he shows that the penalty for his incontinence was just, as proportioned to the crime, and salutary because of the benefits resulting from it. He acknowledges that, being the more guilty of the two, he deserved that vengeance should fall upon himself alone. He begs Héloïse not to fail to recognize the grace which God had granted to her herself, by preserving her from the effects of His justice in order to make her feel only those of His mercy.

“Remember,” he says to her, “my dearest sister, what nets divine goodness used to catch us in the stormy sea of the world in which we were submerged; what holy violence it did us in withdrawing us from the depths of the abyss which had swallowed us up. Then you will see that, far from complaining, each of us ought especially to apply to himself that word of the Prophet: ‘The Lord cares for me; the salvation of my soul is dear to him.’ Can you indeed think of the danger from which we have been delivered—and you ought [Col. 0023] to think of it continually—without being penetrated by the liveliest gratitude? Ah, never forget, and never cease to proclaim, with the most public thanksgivings, the wonders which God has performed in our favor. Thus console by our example sinners who despair of pardon, and teach all what they ought to promise themselves from humble and fervent prayer, seeing two hardened sinners who were, as it were, compelled to receive such great benefits. Enter still further into the depth of God’s adorable designs concerning us. Consider with what paternal charity He made His chastisements serve for our correction; with what wisdom He used even the hands of wicked men to make us abandon impiety; with what marvelous ingenuity He effected, through the wound of one part of my body, the cure of both our souls. Compare the miserable state in which we were with the manner in which we emerged from it; the disease with the remedy. See what we deserved, and admire in the pardon we received the ineffable goodness from which it proceeded.”

He ends by begging her no longer to trouble him with such complaints unless she wishes to renounce his friendship.

Héloïse, checked rather than convinced by these remonstrances, did not dare reply. Being even less able to remain silent, she chose subjects more suited to Abelard’s taste and at the same time more useful and edifying, on which to write to him. In the letter immediately following this one, she requested of him, in the name of her community, two things. The first was to instruct them concerning the origin of religious women and the authority of their profession; the second, to compose for them a rule proper and particular to their sex, since that of Saint Benedict, she said, had not been made for women and contained several matters suitable only for men. Abelard was extremely flattered by these requests, which gave him an opportunity, in the one case, to display his learning and, in the other, to give proof of his wisdom and experience in the direction of souls. He gave Héloïse two successive answers, separately satisfying the two objects of her letter.

**V.** The first is a kind of dissertation in which he traces the origin of the monastic state back to the birth of Christianity and gives Christ himself as its founder. He first says that an outline of it is found in the life of the prophets, in that of the Rechabites, and in the large number of widows who lived in the Temple, wholly separated from the world, consecrated to the Lord, occupied day and night in His worship, devoted to fasting, prayer, and all the exercises that constitute a holy life. But leaving the age of the Law, which produces nothing perfect, he pauses at the age of grace to show there, as soon as it began, the establishment of religious life in its final perfection.

“It is then,” he says, “that we see Jesus Christ gather around himself persons of both sexes, so that under his direction they might observe the essential practices of monastic life. This divine master wished himself to lay down the plan of so holy a manner of life, so that men and women who might later wish to dedicate themselves to it could find in his institution both the supreme authority and the perfect model of their profession. There, united with the community of apostles and disciples, holy women, having the Mother of the Lord at their head, after renouncing all property in order to possess only Jesus Christ, exactly fulfilled what he prescribes to all who would enter a religious society: ‘If anyone does not renounce all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple.’”

After the publication of the Gospel, our author sees the monastic institute following the progress of the Christian religion. The Church of Jerusalem is, according to him, nothing but a great society of monks of both sexes. The Therapeutae of Egypt represent them, he says, still more vividly. From there he descends to the time of the first Christian emperors and shows, under their reigns, numerous colonies of religious women established even in the most dreadful deserts. Throughout this very long letter, Abelard lavishly scatters praises of pious women, and especially of virgins, whose merit he extols by the prerogatives they received from Jesus Christ, the praises bestowed on them by the Fathers, and a large number of historical anecdotes gathered from ecclesiastical authors and even from pagan writers.

**VI.** The nuns of the Paraclete undoubtedly read with pleasure a work in which everything most magnificent that had hitherto been said in honor of their sex and condition was surpassed. Abelard brought their satisfaction to its height by sending them shortly afterward the rule they had requested. The Rule of Saint Benedict and the Constitutions of Fontevraud form the basis of this writing, which contains many excellent things along with some peculiarities. Following the model of Fontevraud, the author wishes there to be a monastery of men near that of the women, to attend to their external affairs and provide them spiritual assistance. He limits the number of women officers to seven and specifies their functions in detail.

Speaking of the portress, he says: “She shall not grant men entrance into the monastery without the abbess’s permission. As for women, she shall make no difficulty for them.” The abbess, or another sister acting on her behalf, shall wash the feet of poor persons who need it. This practice, then, was still in use in the twelfth century.

Abelard forbids the placing in the church of any sculpted or relief image. He permits only a wooden cross to be placed upon the altar, adorned, if desired, with the figure of the Savior. He prescribes three communions a year for the sisters: at Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas. To fulfill worthily, he says, this important obligation, they shall prepare themselves by three days of fasting on bread and water; from the first of these days they shall take care to cleanse their conscience by humble and thorough confession.

With regard to food, he permits the use of meat three times a week and attempts to prove that this indulgence in favor of the sex is not contrary to the ancient rules. From the autumnal equinox until Easter, the sisters, because of the shortness of the days, shall have only one meal; but they shall not change their food, except on the days of abstinence appointed by the Church.

Their clothing shall conform to the humility of their profession. There shall be a distinction for virgins after they have received consecration from the bishop’s hand. It shall be a cross which they shall wear embroidered upon the veil at the top of the head, so that at sight of this venerable mark men may be deterred from casting upon them any overly free gaze.

Finally, the article with which this rule ends concerns Holy Scripture, the reading of which is recommended—not hasty and superficial reading, but serious and profound study.

Seventh. Our author had this last point so much at heart that he made it the particular subject of a new letter addressed to the nuns of the Paraclete. There, following Saint Jerome, he sets out the method to be followed in this kind of study. Along with Latin, he wished, like that Father, that they should acquire Greek and Hebrew, in order to understand the sacred text in its original purity. He cites the examples of the Paulas, Eustochiums, Asellas, and so many other Roman ladies who, by practising what he proposed, became so [Col. 0025] famous for their learning. “It is not only Christian virgins and widows,” he says, “but even women involved in the encumbrances of marriage whom I offer you as models. Why then should you not practise, in the leisure and tranquillity of your solitude, what others knew how to combine with the intercourse and turbulent occupations of the world? You have all the less ground for excusing yourselves from it because none of the facilities necessary for success is lacking to you. For, besides the help of books, you have in your superior a mistress capable of teaching and guiding you through her knowledge of the three languages. Make use, I urge you, of the treasure in your hands. Hasten to draw from it riches which men have allowed to be lost, and ensure that through your care there may revive, to the glory of your sex, the science, so important and now so neglected, of sacred letters.”

Eighth. However difficult what Abelard proposed might have seemed to women, his letter met with no opposition. The nuns of the Paraclete applied themselves with remarkable zeal to making use of his advice. They succeeded beyond his expectations. In the following year they testified to their progress by a collection of the most difficult passages of Holy Scripture, which they sent him under the title *Problems*, asking for their solution. These difficulties number forty-two. Abelard did not delay in answering them. The merit of his solutions may be judged from the following two examples.

The nuns asked how one should understand the statement of the Apostle Saint James that whoever violates the law in one point is guilty of all. Abelard replies that what constitutes the law is the whole body of commandments taken together; thus, one who had kept the whole law except for a single commandment is guilty of not having kept all the commandments, which, joined together, form what is called the law.

Again they asked: why, when instituting the sacrament of the Eucharist, did the Saviour not say, “This is my body, the body of the New Testament,” as he said, “This is my blood, the blood of the New Testament”? Does he not thereby seem to attribute more merit to his blood than to his flesh? The body which we receive in the sacrament, Abelard replies, is the humanity which Jesus Christ took in the Virgin’s womb. Now humanity in itself did not seal the New Testament. For a testament, as Saint Paul says, comes into force only after death, being without force as long as the testator lives. It was therefore the passion of Jesus Christ—the shedding of his blood, by which he ended his mortal life—that set the irrevocable seal upon the testament he made in our favour. Thus what he said of his blood he ought not to say of his body, lest he confuse the beginning with the consummation of our salvation.

Ninth. Finally, Abelard’s last letter to Heloise contains a profession of faith concerning the errors imputed to him at the Council of Sens. At the same time he addressed to the public another similar work, of which we shall speak later.

Tenth. Among his other letters addressed to different persons, the first in chronological order is that which he wrote to the Bishop of Paris in response to the accusations made against his doctrine by the famous Roscelin. The accuser’s name is not stated; but he is easily recognized from the traits by which Abelard describes him. In print, the author and the bishop are designated only by the initials P. and G. On this point Dom Rivet (*Hist. lit.*, vol. VIII, p. 464), following Du Boulay, Father Pagi, and Dom Mabillon, maintains that the former cannot mean Peter Abelard, and that the latter denotes neither Galon nor Girbert, who successively held the see of Paris from 1104 until 1124. But the reasons offered by these critics disappear when one sees the King’s manuscript, no. 2923, where this letter bears the title: “Letter of Peter Abelard” (*Poetri Abaelardi epistola*). Once the author’s name is known, the bishop to whom it is addressed is no longer an enigma. It is plainly Girbert, who was in fact bishop when Abelard’s first work on the Trinity appeared.

Here is the substance of the letter. “I learn,” says Abelard, “that a man known for his errors concerning the Trinity—whom he does not fear to make three gods—and for the disgrace which those errors have deservedly brought upon him, is preparing to denounce to you as heretical the work I composed on the same subject, principally with the intention of refuting his opinions. If this is so, and if he carries it out, I beg you to appoint for me a suitable time and place for a formal disputation before you and in the presence of learned persons, with my accuser.”

He then recalls some odious incidents in the latter’s life: that he had been expelled from England for calumnies advanced against Saint Anselm; that in France he had drawn upon himself the hatred of good men by a letter in which he attacked the blessed Robert of Arbrissel; and that he had received corporal discipline in the chapter of Saint-Martin of Tours for other equally intemperate remarks. He concludes by saying that he is not at all surprised to hear errors from the mouth of a man who had carried extravagance so far as to maintain this proposition: when it is said that Jesus Christ ate part of a fish, this must be understood as a part not of the thing but of the word used to express it.

Eleventh. After his escape from Saint-Denis, Abelard wrote from Provins to his abbot to retract the opinion he had ventured concerning the Apostle of the Gauls. In this letter he seeks to prove that Bede, who had previously guided him, was mistaken in confusing Saint Denis the Areopagite with Saint Denis of Corinth. This is evident, he says, because the latter did not die until the reign of Marcus Aurelius—that is, about the middle of the second century—which he demonstrates by various authorities. He further maintains, but without foundation, that Bede afterwards withdrew this opinion in his Commentary on the Acts of the Apostles. This is the sum of the letter, whose success did not answer the author’s expectations. Abbot Adam remained no less angry with him, nor less firm in demanding that he return to Saint-Denis.

Twelfth. Abelard’s zeal for the honour of his profession appears in a letter written to a regular canon who wished to exalt his order above the monastic state. We have nothing indicating the precise date of this work or the name of the adversary to whom it was addressed. Some [Note: [Col. 0025] Nicer., vol. IV, p. 13.] think that the author is attacking Saint Norbert; but they offer no proof. Be that as it may, Abelard had already spent some years in religious profession when he repelled the regular canon’s attacks. As for the arguments he employs, since the public takes only a very moderate interest in this dispute, we shall simply refer those who wish to know them to the work itself. Let us only observe that there would be no plausibility in saying that the Benedictines drew from it, in recent [Col. 0027] times, their strongest arguments in their memoirs against the regular canons concerning precedence in the Estates of Burgundy. A modern writer [Note: [Col. 0027] Gerv., *Vie d’Abel.*, vol. I, p. 271.], to whose eyes nothing in Abelard’s productions is mediocre, has nevertheless dared to assert it. Yet inspection of the documents readily proves the contrary.

Thirteenth. Abelard defended the interests of his beloved dialectic no less warmly against those who decried that art as a source of illusions. His fourth letter is intended to refute one of these censors. He compares him to the fox in the fable, which, unable to climb a cherry tree, professed disgust for cherries and contempt for those who ate them. Then, taking a serious tone, he endeavours to make felt the difference between true and false dialectic. He exalts the former as much as he depreciates the latter; but he maintains that a good theologian should possess both, so as, he says, to be able to reason soundly and resolve the sophisms of the enemies of truth.

Fourteenth. A rather slight matter, whose triviality was scarcely worth disputing, aroused Abelard’s anger against the Abbot of Clairvaux several years before the great quarrel that divided them. The facts are these. Saint Bernard, having come to the Paraclete during Abelard’s absence, noticed that the abbess altered a word in the Lord’s Prayer when reciting it at the end of Vespers, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. For instead of saying, in the ordinary manner, *panem nostrum quotidianum*—“our daily bread”—she said *panem nostrum supersubstantialem*—“our supersubstantial bread.” The saint mildly rebuked her for this singularity. Heloise and her nuns did not fail to inform their spiritual father upon his return. Abelard immediately wrote Saint Bernard a very sharp letter in defence of the alteration which he himself had suggested.

His defence consists in maintaining that the word *supersubstantialem*, used by Saint Matthew, ought to be preferred to *quotidianum*, employed by Saint Luke, for two reasons: first, because the authority of the former, who had learned the Lord’s Prayer from the Saviour’s own mouth, outweighs that of the latter, who received it only from the Apostles; secondly, because the term ἐπιούσιον (*epiousion*), read in the disputed passage in the Greek text of both Evangelists, is rendered better by *supersubstantialem* than by *quotidianum*. But since this does not answer the charge of innovation, he has recourse to recrimination in order to clear himself. He in turn accuses the Cistercian Order of having introduced into the celebration of the Divine Office several customs peculiar to itself: singing at Nocturns at all times, without distinction of feasts, the same hymn, *Aeterne rerum conditor* (“Eternal Creator of things”); suppressing commemorations of the saints at the end of Lauds and Vespers; almost entirely abolishing processions; singing the Alleluia from Septuagesima until the beginning of Lent; and saying at Nocturns the Invitatory with the doxology during the final three days of Holy Week—practices, in his view, ridiculous and much less excusable than the small change he had made in the Lord’s Prayer. Abelard’s historian [Note: [Col. 0027] Id., ibid., vol. II, bk. IV, no. 8.] does not hesitate to decide in his favour in this dispute, to which Saint Bernard does not appear to have judged it proper to reply. Nevertheless, it is certain that the nuns of the Paraclete, better advised, later abandoned a singularity which displayed more affectation than genuine piety.

Fifteenth. We shall divide Abelard’s sermons, or monastic conferences, into two parts. The first will include the thirty-two discourses he delivered for the Paraclete, together with a sermon on Saint Stephen which the editors have placed among his letters. The second will contain three other works which he also seems to have delivered orally.

1. In a prologue Abelard tells Heloise that, after completing the book of Hymns and Sequences which she had requested, he hastened to give her a new token of his affection by composing sermons for the edification of her daughters on the principal feasts of the year; that in this work, instead of attempting to scatter the flowers of rhetoric over the subjects he treats, he had thought only of giving a clear and simple explanation of sacred Scripture; and that this method seemed to him more suited to the spirit of true eloquence, which requires the speaker always to adapt himself to the capacity of his hearers.

The idea Abelard gives of his sermons is accurate. They are indeed very simple, though rather solid, homilies, in which he applies himself to unfolding the meaning of various passages of Scripture, without troubling much about the sequence and connection of the discourse. In several he addresses his brethren, which shows that he delivered them at Saint-Gildas. Yet he attacks none there of those enormous vices with which he charges them in the history of his misfortunes. Was this charitable restraint? Was it fear of calumniating the innocent to their faces? One may think as one wishes. But here is a striking example of his boldness in disparaging his most irreproachable adversaries when he thought he could do so with impunity.

“We recently saw,” he says in the thirty-first sermon, “with astonishment mingled with indignation and contempt, Norbert and Farsit, his companion in apostolic work, making useless efforts to perform the great miracle of resurrection. After prostrating themselves and praying a long time in that posture, we saw them rise no further advanced than before. Then, filled with impudence, far from blushing at their failure, they dared blame the bystanders, whose unbelief, they said, had prevented the effect of their lively and unshaken faith. A worn-out artifice of all those who rashly undertake such enterprises! A pitiful evasion for persons who have no valid excuse to offer! It is true that by this means they sometimes succeed in deceiving the simple. But, according to the testimony of Truth, nothing is so hidden that it is not discovered at last. As for us, the tricks of these charlatans will never impose upon us. We know them all; and, to cite only one example, we know how they go about curing slight fevers and other mild ailments. Their skill in this consists in subtly mixing into the food given to the sick certain remedies suited to their condition, and then offering prayers and blessings over them. Whatever happens, they are then safe. If recovery follows, it is not omitted to attribute it to their merits. If the attempt fails, the sick persons’ lack of faith is the cause.” Thus Abelard avenged himself for Saint Norbert’s care in warning the faithful against the danger of his doctrine.

2. Three expositions form the second part of his Conferences. One concerns the Lord’s Prayer, another the Apostles’ Creed, and the last the creed which bears the name of Saint Athanasius. It is certain that the second was preached on the octave day of Easter. The other two were probably delivered on other occasions.

[Col. 0029] Sixteenth. Of the great number of commentaries which Abelard composed on Holy Scripture, only two are in the hands of the public. The first, divided into five books, concerns the Epistle to the Romans; it is at once literal, theological, and moral. The author follows his text step by step, explains every phrase, and often every part of a phrase separately; then shows, or attempts to show—for he is far from always successful in his glosses—the relation of one phrase to another, the order of the Apostle’s discourse, and the progress and connection of his proofs. From time to time he discusses questions of dogma and morals arising from the passages he examines. These are ordinarily the most hazardous parts of the work. In his decisions one discovers traces of most of the opinions which later served as grounds for his condemnation. Other opinions appear there which, though they did not incur censure, are scarcely less remarkable for their singularity. We shall give only the following example.

On the occasion of the Apostle’s words, “The law is holy; the commandment is good,” he digresses upon the essential character of charity. “The name of charity,” he says, “does not suit a love which would look to our own interest and to the enjoyment of eternal happiness in God—a love from which it would follow that our final end lay in ourselves and not in the supreme Being. Those who love in this manner deserve the name of friends of fortune, and serve God from a principle of cupidity rather than from a movement of grace. To be true and sincere, love, according to Saint Augustine, must be gratuitous; that is, it must seek its object for its own sake. Therefore God is not to be loved because he gives us tokens of his love by doing us good, but because, whatever he does to us, he deserves to be loved above all things. For Truth itself tells us that, if we love only those who love us, we shall receive no reward . . . . . Yet such is the error of almost all Christians that they are not ashamed to admit that, if God promised them no reward, they would then cease to love him. A humiliating confession—a mercenary disposition! As though even in punishing God were not always equally lovable, since his punishments rest only upon our demerits or upon some other reasonable cause which, precisely because it is just, ought to please everyone.”

He then objects to himself the authority of David, who says that he inclined his heart to keep the Lord’s commandments in view of a reward, and that of Jesus Christ, who declares blessed those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. But regarding the first text he answers that it concerns only the beginning, not the perfection, of the good life. One begins, he says, with fear and hope, but ends with charity, which is the summit of perfection. Regarding the Saviour’s words, he adds, they do not mean, in his opinion, that those who keep continence ought to do so out of desire for the kingdom of heaven, but that by living thus they will deserve to be admitted there. Those who accept this doctrine must at least concede, according to the author, that it was not common in his time; it was opposed by Hugh of Saint-Victor.

The chronological place of this Commentary among Abelard’s works is easy to determine. It comes after his *Introduction to Theology*, which is cited in it, and before his *Moral Theology*, which he announces as forthcoming and in which he promises to elucidate several questions which here he only touches upon in passing. It was therefore composed, at the earliest, while Abelard was teaching at the Paraclete.

Seventeenth. The second Commentary which has been published is on Genesis. It forms part of the fifth volume of the *Anecdotes* of Dom Martène and Dom Durand (p. 1363), under the title *Hexaemeron*, which it bears in the manuscript of Mont-Saint-Michel from which it was published. The work is incomplete and extends only to the seventeenth chapter of the sacred text that it treats. It is dedicated to Heloise, at whose request Abelard says he undertook it. The editors regard it as the last fruit of his pen, basing this judgment on the correctness of its doctrine and expressions, especially with regard to the errors of which he was accused at the Council of Sens. The author follows the same method in this commentary as in the preceding one, except that in this he makes more frequent use of allegory. Several fine questions concerning the creation of the various beings are treated with considerable clarity and precision. Yet not everything in it is beyond criticism.

It is time to proceed to his purely theological works.

Eighteenth. The *Introduction* [Note: [Col. 0029] This work bore different titles. It is the same work that Saint Bernard calls the *Book of Sentences* in his letter 188: *Legite, si placet, librum quem dicit Sententiarum*—“Read, if you please, the book which he calls the Sentences.” Dom Mabillon, in his *Iter Germanicum*, says that he saw in the library of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg a manuscript containing Abelard’s *Sentences*, in which he is called “Bajolard,” divided into thirty-seven chapters; these are nothing other than his *Introduction to Theology*.] to Theology was, according to Abelard himself, his first attempt in matters of religion. Until then, he says, his studies had been confined within the limits of philosophy; but the entreaties of his disciples made him take flight. They represented to him that, after filling his own mind and sufficiently imbuing them with the knowledge presupposed by theology, after putting into their hands the key to the sanctuary of truth, it was just and suitable to his profession that he should direct his studies to loftier objects and initiate them into that science for which he had prepared the way by his precepts on the art of reasoning. “It was to yield,” he adds, “to the importunity rather than to the fairness of these remonstrances that I undertook to carry out, according to my ability and with divine assistance, what I was continually asked to do. Besides, let no one be mistaken: I do not undertake to set forth here the exact truth. My purpose is merely to follow the intention of those whom I obey, by sincerely expounding my own opinions: *Non tam veritatem promittentes, quam opinionis nostrae sensum, quem efflagitant, exponentes*—‘not so much promising truth as setting forth the meaning of our opinion, which they demand.’”

This *Introduction* is divided into three books, the first of which contains a summary of the whole treatise. The author makes the entire economy of religion consist in three things: faith, charity, and the sacraments.
