He promises to treat each of these points separately; but he keeps his word only with respect to the first—or at least we possess only what concerns that subject. All the truths embraced by faith, he says, concern either God’s nature or his conduct toward creatures. There is only one divine nature, which subsists in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Although perfectly equal, none of these three persons is the same as either of the other two, because, with one and the same nature, which makes them perfectly equal, they have properties that characterize and distinguish them. The Father’s proper characteristic is to be unbegotten, that is, to derive his origin from himself alone; the Son’s is to be begotten of the Father; and the Holy Spirit’s is to proceed from both, although neither this generation nor this procession includes any idea of temporal formation or creation. Now, since it is one thing to be unbegotten, another to be begotten, and a third distinct condition simply to proceed from a begotten principle and an unbegotten principle, it necessarily follows that there is a real distinction among the persons distinguished by these three properties. Such is the summary of faith concerning the Trinity. Let us now try, he continues, to make this mystery intelligible, if not by direct and evident reasons, at least by examples and comparisons.

Two questions arise on this subject. The first is what this distinction of persons in one divine nature means, and why the same God is called Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The second is to define precisely the Trinity of Persons in one unique, indivisible substance, and to shield this doctrine from the violent assaults continually directed against it by philosophers. Here is our view. It seems to us that the names of the three persons perfectly express the fullness of the supreme good. For God’s omnipotence, which gives him the power to do all that he wills, is denoted by the name Father; the wisdom by which he infallibly discerns all things is denoted by the name Son; and his goodness toward creatures, the source of the beautiful order reigning in the universe, is made known by the name Holy Spirit. A being is not supremely perfect when its power is defective in any respect; it is not happy in every sense when it can in certain respects err; it is not absolutely good when it does not will that all things should occur in the best possible way. But the conjunction in the highest degree of these three things—power, wisdom, and goodness—forms the complete assemblage of all goods.

Nevertheless, the attributes by which we designate each of the three persons are not so proper to one as not truly to belong to the others according to unity of nature. The same must be said of certain actions which we refer to one of the three persons because of the properties distinguishing them. Thus power, wisdom, and goodness, with all the works proceeding from them, are common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, without its following that all three exist in the same manner. For only the Father can be Father—that is, unbegotten; only the Son has the property of being begotten; and only the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. The development of these truths opens a broad field for disputation and enables us to explain more clearly the distinction of the three persons of the Trinity.

For, considering the Father as unbegotten, we find that omnipotence belongs to him in a special manner, since not only can he do all things with the cooperation of the other two persons, but he derives his existence and power from himself alone, while he communicates both to the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Son, as begotten, represents a portion of that power which he received from his Father. We may indeed rightly say that the Father begot through his omnipotence; this means that wisdom was born of omnipotence, because wisdom itself is a species of power—namely, the power of discernment—but not the fullness and totality of supreme power. This is precisely how the Father and Son differ. After producing several passages from the holy doctors to show that power is attributed to the Father and wisdom to the Son, the author proceeds to the Holy Spirit and likewise seeks to show that goodness and the gifts flowing from it are used to characterize him. Having thus sketched his system, he postpones putting the finishing touches to it until the following books.

The rest of this book—that is, about two-thirds of it—is occupied by a digression in which the author tries to prove that all nations before the Messiah knew the mystery of the Trinity. For this purpose he heaps up the authorities of the most celebrated pagan philosophers. Since one might object that God, according to Scripture, had confounded the wisdom of the wise of the world, he forestalls the objection by maintaining that the anathema just mentioned admits exceptions; that, in fact, several philosophers held very reasonable opinions concerning the Divinity, taught and practised the maxims of the purest morality, and finally believed in the Messiah on the testimony of their Sibyls and of oracles disseminated throughout the world. It would therefore be contrary to reason to despair of their salvation. [Note: [Col. 0031] Those wishing to know how futile proofs of this sort, and other similar proofs produced since then, are may read the second part of the fine preface at the head of the new edition of Saint Justin.]

Abelard’s contemporaries were as little disposed as we are to relish the display of secular learning in a subject apparently so little suited to it. He himself foresaw this. Consequently, he employs nearly half of his second book in justifying himself on this point. He calls Saint Jerome, Saint Augustine, and other ecclesiastical writers as guarantees, recounting their examples and testimonies to show the esteem in which they held, and the use they made of, pagan books in religious disputes. “That is conceded,” someone will say to me, he adds; “but what is the point of writing new works on our doctrines?” What is the point? This is his answer: “Has there ever been a more pressing necessity than now to write, attacked as we are not only by Jews and pagans, but also by domestic enemies occupied in combating the Church’s doctrine?”

Among the latter he identifies four, without naming them, who, in his opinion, presided over as many distinct sects. “The first,” he says, “who dogmatizes in France has the audacity to teach that before the Incarnation faith in the Messiah was not necessary to salvation; that the body of Jesus Christ was formed in the Virgin’s womb in the ordinary manner, except that no man took part in it; and that, since the Father begot his Son, who is consubstantial with him, it follows that he begot himself. The second, who spreads his errors in Burgundy, maintains that the three properties distinguishing the divine persons are three essences distinct not only from the divine nature, but also from the persons.” This was probably a disciple of Roscelin, though not Roscelin himself, as Duchesne supposes [Note: [Col. 0031] *Abael. Op.*, notes.], for Roscelin is not known to have taught in Burgundy.

“The third,” he continues, “holds his pestilential chair in Anjou. He goes further than the second, daring to affirm that even the absolute properties, such as justice and mercy, are distinct from the divine nature, so that there would be as many distinct things in God as there are [Col. 0033] perfections.” This is the error later taught by Gilbert of Poitiers; he was therefore not its author.

“Finally, the fourth, who infects Berry, carries madness so far as to say that God can be mistaken, on the principle that things can happen otherwise than he foresaw them. It is now for those who object to further writing on religious subjects to see whether all these heresies do not require one to take up the pen in order to refute them.”

After this kind of justification, Abelard resumes the subject he had begun in the first book. He first says that, since we lack proper terms to express the divine nature and perfections—too exalted for the human mind to comprehend—we can answer questions put to us on this matter only by tropes and comparisons. Now, of all comparisons, the following seems to him best suited to make the mystery of the Trinity perceptible. In a piece of copper, he says, on which the image of a prince is engraved in order to impress it upon wax, two things are distinguished whose properties differ, though they have but one essence: namely, the material and the form composing one and the same seal. Apply this example to the first two persons of the Trinity. As the seal is in a sense born from the copper, so the Son derives his being from the substance of the Father, and in this sense is said to be begotten. Now we have said above that the name Father expresses omnipotence, and that of Son wisdom, which is only one kind of power. Likewise, the seal of copper is not the whole mass of copper, but only a portion of that material; in this it corresponds to the imperfect power of the Son. This seal also provides us with the idea of the procession of the Holy Spirit; and, to understand this properly, first note the difference between proceeding and being begotten. It consists in this: the one who is begotten shares in the Father’s substance, whereas one who simply proceeds does not share in it. Now goodness, which constitutes the character of the Holy Spirit, contains the idea of no power, but expresses only the movement and effects of love. This third person, therefore, is not of the Father’s substance, and consequently does not derive its origin from him by generation; rather, it proceeds from the Father and the Son, because love proceeds from power and wisdom.

This granted, I now perceive in the copper seal a third property, distinct from material and form: the action of sealing, or of impressing upon another, softer material the figure and image that it bears—an action which proceeds from the seal but is nevertheless not of its substance. The first of these three properties begets the second, and the concurrence of the one and the other produces the third. Thus the Son is born from the Father, of whom he is called in Scripture the form, image, and figure of his substance; and both together produce the Holy Spirit, their common action. The particular effect of this action is to engrave in us the imprint of divine power and wisdom, and, through the graces of which the Holy Spirit is the dispenser, to restore the features effaced by sin. This explanation seems to our author equally suited to confound heretics and to bring back the schismatic Greeks, who refer the procession of the Holy Spirit to the Father alone. After a rather long dispute against the latter, he ends his second book and crowns the proofs of his system with the authority of the philosophers, striving to persuade his readers that all they said concerning the soul of the world must be understood of the Holy Spirit.

The third book is entirely devoted to the essential and absolute attributes of the Godhead. “Concerning omnipotence,” says our author, “the usual question is whether God can do something other than what he does, and whether he can do it better than it is.”

Abelard declares for the negative, supporting it with the following reasons.

1. Since every kind of good is equally possible to God, who needs only his word in order to exercise his power, he would necessarily be guilty either of injustice or jealousy if he did not do all the good that he can do.

2. He does and omits nothing without a sufficient and very good reason. Therefore, whatever he does, he does because it was fitting that he should do it; and whatever he does not do, he omits because there was some impropriety in doing it. One will object to me, he says, that it was equally fitting for God to do or not do what he has done. But one fails to notice that between reasonable and unreasonable there is the same contradiction as between doing and not doing. Therefore, if he has reason to do a thing, it is contrary to reason that he should refrain from it.

Abelard proposes a second objection, from which he admits it is more difficult to extricate himself. “A reprobate,” he says, “can be saved; now this cannot happen except by God’s will. Consequently God can do something that he does not do.” “I answer,” he says, “that the proposition, ‘a reprobate can be saved,’ is true only with respect to the creature, which, being mutable by nature, is equally capable of salvation and damnation. But the proposition is false with respect to God, because it is incompatible with his nature to do anything derogating from his infinite perfection, and consequently to do what it would not be fitting for him to do.”

This can be clarified by examples. A voice can be heard even if there were no one to hear it, or if all human beings were deprived of hearing. A field is capable of cultivation even on the supposition that there were no hands to cultivate it. Some, nevertheless, admitting that God always chooses the most perfect means to attain his end, imagine that he may do things at a time other than that at which he does them. But this is absurd in a being who must always act in the most fitting manner and bring about, on every occasion, what is most appropriate. Nor should it be said that, if God cannot at every time do everything that he does, it follows that he has not always the same power and is not at every time almighty. For it is certain that the determination of time concerns the act and not the power. It is one thing indeed to say, “I can do this at such a time,” and another to do it actually. At the moment when I speak, I have the power to be silent. Yet speaking and being silent are two acts that I cannot combine or exercise at the same time. Thus, in order to know whether someone has the power to do a thing, it is unnecessary to suppose that he performs it actually; it suffices to be assured that he will perform it when he wills. Now it is certain that God can do all that he wills, since nothing resists his will. This is why, according to Saint Augustine, he is called almighty. But because he is infinitely wise, he can will nothing out of season; whence it follows that he places every event at the moment most fitting to the perfection of the universe.”

Here is the optimism for which some would claim credit for modern philosophy, set out by our author with the greatest possible art of persuasion. Abelard does not even claim to have invented it; rather, he acknowledges that he drew it from the writings of the Platonists. He also has the sincerity to admit that neither the Fathers nor the doctors of his own time favored this opinion: “Although this opinion of ours has few or no adherents, and appears to disagree greatly with the sayings of the saints and somewhat with reason” (*Licet haec nostra opinio, paucos aut nullos habeat assentatores, et plurimum dictis sanctorum, et aliquantulum a ratione dissentire videatur*). As has been seen, Hugh of Saint-Victor was one of his principal opponents on this point; and we have described the means employed by that writer to pulverize this system, as false in itself as it is harmful in its consequences.

[Col. 0035] Abelard then speaks of God’s immortality, wisdom, and knowledge. What he says concerning each of these attributes offers nothing inconsistent with the analogy of faith. He proves very well that what is called chance enters into the designs of Providence. On the compatibility of divine foreknowledge with the creature’s freedom, he raises two objections; but he answers only the first, and the printed work stops there. Dom Martène [Note: [Col. 0035] *Anecd.* vol. V, p. 1363.] testifies that he encountered no continuation in any manuscript. But Oudin [Note: [Col. 0035] *Script.* vol. II, p. 1169.] assures us that one exists in the Bodleian Library under this title: *Supplement to the Third Book of Peter Abelard’s Introduction to Theology* (*Petri Abaelardi Introductionis ad Theologiam libri tertii supplementum*).

**XIX.** Since the *Introduction to Theology* had been condemned in the manner described above at the Council of Soissons, Abelard, without abandoning its principles, chose to recast it and to make his system appear again under another title. This he did in the treatise entitled *Christian Theology*. It is divided into five books. The first is the same, in different terms, as the first book of the *Introduction*. In the second, the author attacks Christians who disapprove of employing the authority of pagan sages in matters of religion. The third contains:

1. An invective against sophists who admit into our mysteries only what accords with reason;
2. A summary of faith concerning the Trinity;
3. Objections to this mystery;
4. Observations on all the senses which may belong to the terms “similar,” “different,” and “persons.”

In the fourth, the author employs all the resources of his dialectic to resolve the objections he had proposed in the preceding book. The fifth and last is merely a repetition of the third book of the *Introduction*.

After this account, there can be no doubt that it was one of these two writings—or rather both together—that fell into the hands of William of Saint-Thierry, and whose only difference, as he wrote to Saint Bernard [Note: [Col. 0035] Bernard, *Works*, vol. III, epistle 326.], was that one sometimes compressed what the other had expanded, or expanded what it had compressed: “There were then two little books containing almost the same things, except that sometimes more was found in one, less in the other” (*Duo autem tunc erant libelli idem pene continentes, nisi quod in altero plus, in altero minus aliquando inveniretur*).

As for the time when the latter was composed, we conjecture that Abelard began it in his abbey of Saint-Gildas and did not make it public until after his resignation. For then, as the same William observes [Note: [Col. 0035] “For when nearly all the masters of ecclesiastical teaching had died, the enemy of the Church’s household, rushing as it were into an empty commonwealth, seized for himself a unique mastery within it, doing in Holy Scripture what he had been accustomed to do in dialectic” (*Emortuis quippe omnibus pene doctrinae ecclesiasticae magistris, quasi in vacuam rempublicam Ecclesiae domesticus irruens inimicus singulare sibi in ea magisterium arripuit, agens in Scriptura divina quod agere solebat in dialectica*).], freed from his most formidable adversaries whom death had taken away, he thought he found the field clear in which to disseminate his opinions with impunity [Note: [Col. 0035] *Ibid.*].

**XX.** The moral treatise entitled *Know Thyself* (*Scito teipsum*) [Note: [Col. 0035] Pez, *Anecdota*, vol. III, p. 673.] followed closely upon the *Christian Theology*, which it cites and of which it may be regarded as the continuation and culmination. Abelard (ch. 1) divides moral dispositions into virtues and vices. He distinguishes sin from vice in that vice is an inclination toward evil, while sin is consent given to that inclination. The soul, he says (ch. 3), is the seat of sin. There sin is consummated, and outward action adds nothing to it; so that, when one has consented to evil in one’s heart, it is equally sinful to do it or not do it. Sensual pleasures are in themselves indifferent. The known prohibition against using them makes up all their evil. The divine eye is unlike ours (ch. 7), which attends only to works and neglects the inward acts of the will. God, on the contrary, regards only intention in his rewards and punishments, because intention is like the touchstone of all our actions, which, in themselves and apart from intention, may be common to the good and the wicked.

That being so, it is of the utmost importance for us to know whence the malice and goodness of intention arise. To resolve this question, the author gives the following definition of sin (chs. 12, 13, 14). Sin, he says, consists in doing what we judge to be contrary to the divine will, and consequently includes a formal contempt of God. Therefore everything done against the light of conscience is vicious, and conversely whatever conforms to that same light is free from sin. Yet Jesus Christ on the cross prayed his Father to forgive the Jews because they did not know what they were doing; and Saint Stephen likewise asked, concerning his persecutors, that his martyrdom should not be imputed to them as sin.

Abelard tries to evade the force of this objection by distinguishing various meanings of the term “sin.” Sometimes, he says, it means the victim offered for sin, as when Christ is said to have been made sin for us. It is also used for the punishment due to sin. Thus Christ is said to have borne our sins because he underwent their punishment. Finally, the name “sin” applies to sinful works. Now it should be noted that punishment is not always the consequence and proof of sin properly so called. This is seen in the example of the prophet who, having been sent to preach against Bethel, was killed on his return by a lion because he had violated the prohibition God had given him against eating on his journey. For what could have been his fault in believing, on the word of another prophet like himself, that God had revoked that purely arbitrary prohibition? One may therefore be innocent and nevertheless deserve a temporal punishment for having committed, through ignorance, the work of sin.

On this principle we do not hesitate to maintain that those who, through ignorance and in good faith, persecuted Jesus Christ and his followers committed only the work of sin; they would have been much more guilty in this respect if, resisting the movements of their own conscience, they had spared them: “Thus we say that those whom they believed ought to be persecuted sinned in the performance of the act; yet they would have committed a more serious fault if, against conscience, they had spared them” (*Sic et eos quos persequendos credebant, per operationem peccasse dicimus; qui tamen gravius culpam peccassent, si contra conscientiam eis parcerent*). This is philosophical sin.

Abelard, however, alarmed by the consequences of this doctrine, seems to wish to retrace his steps. He does not wish it inferred from his principles that unbelief does not always shut the entrance to heaven; and the reason he gives is that, in order to be damned, it is enough not to believe in Jesus Christ, even though this should arise, he says, rather from ignorance than from deliberate malice.

Such are the wounds of our soul. The author next examines their remedy, which he makes to consist in three things: penance, contrition, and satisfaction. He treats each separately, but more as a declaimer than as a theologian. Speaking of the signs of repentance [Col. 0037] given by usurers and extortioners at the hour of death, he inveighs against the avarice of confessors who, instead of urging them to restore ill-gotten goods, advised them to buy Masses. I say “buy,” he repeats, for they make a disgraceful trade of the holiest thing. The price is fixed as for an ordinary commodity. One pays a denarius for one Mass, and forty for an annual Mass: “In this commerce it is clear that a fixed price is established among them: namely, a denarius for one Mass and forty for an annual [Mass]” (*In quo quidem mercimonio praefixum apud eos pretium esse constat, pro una scilicet missa denarium, et pro annuali quadraginta*). This remark, apart from what may be blamed in it, proves the antiquity of Mass stipends and the care already taken to fix them in order to prevent the abuse that might arise from them.

On the occasion of indulgences, whose overly frequent use he censures, he treats of the power of the keys. At first he seems to deny this power to bad prelates; but, following the thread of his argument, one sees that he speaks only of the power of discernment and not of jurisdiction. It must nevertheless be admitted that he is neither exact in his expressions nor firm in his principles. This is the dominant defect of the whole work, in which one perceives an author continually embarrassed, feeling his way, and often falling into contradiction with himself, for lack of having sufficiently studied the subject he treats.

**XXI.** As Abelard’s final theological writing, we shall give his *Confession of Faith*, drawn up after the Council of Sens in order to dispel the clouds which that assembly’s judgment had cast upon his doctrine. This piece, like the last letter to Héloïse, is merely a simple exposition of the author’s views concerning the articles alleged against him, without invectives or arguments. Concerning some of these articles, he denies ever having taught them. Concerning the others, he tacitly accuses himself by limiting himself to professing doctrine diametrically opposed to them. At the beginning and end he beseeches the faithful not to allow themselves to be prejudiced by false reports and to regard him as the most submissive of the Church’s children. This writing has wrongly been confused with his *Apology*. We shall show the difference between them when speaking of those lost writings.

### § III.—His Manuscript Works

It is far from the case—and perhaps not to be desired—that all Abelard’s writings should be in the hands of the public. A great part of them, without mentioning those that are lost, has remained in manuscript in various repositories, both domestic and foreign. Strictly speaking, all that may be required of us is a simple but exact enumeration of these obscure monuments. Nevertheless, we shall not adhere so scrupulously to this duty as to refrain from adding, from time to time, a few observations when the matter is worth the trouble.

These productions fall into four classes: philosophical works, commentaries on Scripture, theological treatises, and verse.

In the first class are:

**I.** A commentary on Aristotle’s *Topics*, existing in the King’s Library (no. 7493) under the title: *Glosses of Abelard on the Topics* (*Glossae Abaelardi in Topica*).

**II.** Four works preserved in the Library of Saint-Victor, the first entitled: *The Four Books of Peter the Peripatetic on the Categories, or on Aristotle’s Predicaments* (*Petri Peripatetici libri quatuor Categoriarum, sive super praedicamenta Aristotelis*). The second: *The First and Second Books of Peter the Peripatetic on the Analytics* (*Petri Peripatetici Analyticorum liber primus et secundus*). The third: *The Book of Divisions of Peter the Peripatetic* (*Petri Peripatetici liber Divisionum*). This same book is in the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. The fourth: *The Book of Definitions of Peter the Peripatetic* (*Petri Peripatetici liber Definitionum*).

**III.** A manuscript in the Library of Mont-Saint-Michel contains the following two works:

1. *Treatise of Abelard on Intellects* (*Tractatus Abaillardi de intellectibus*);
2. *The Physics of Aristotle by the Same Abelard* (*Ejusdem Abaillardi Physica Aristotelis*).

**IV.** In another manuscript of the same library are found: *A discourse of Peter Abelard on generation and corruption. Also, on intellects and speculations* (*Petri Abailardi sermo de generatione et corruptione. Item de intellectibus et speculationibus*). But this last work is the same as the first in the preceding manuscript.

**V.** In the Ambrosian Library at Milan may be seen: *Peter Abelard on Porphyry’s universals, on the predicaments, and on the books On Interpretation* (*Petri Abailardi in Porphyrii universalia, in predicamenta, in libros Perihermenias*).

**VI.** The work listed as *Peter Abelard the Scholar* (*Petri Abaelardi Scholarius*) is kept in that of the King of England, among the manuscripts of the Jacobean Library [Note: [Col. 0037] *Catalogue of English Manuscripts*, p. 4, no. 8670.].

**VII.** Dom Martène says [Note: [Col. 0037] *Literary Journey*, p. 244.] that he saw at the abbey of Tamié in Savoy a manuscript bearing this inscription: *Treatise of Peter Abelard on universals and singulars, addressed to Oliver, his son* (*Petri Abaelardi de universalibus et singularibus ad Olivarium filium suum tractatus*). This work does not appear to differ from our author’s *Logic*, since John of Salisbury testifies that the philosophers of the twelfth century included all logic in the *Treatise on Universals*. It would be sought in vain today at Tamié. Nothing more is seen there than its title in an old catalogue. Nor is it in the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, although Oudin [Note: [Col. 0037] *Script.* vol. II, p. 1172.] and Dom Montfaucon place among that library’s manuscripts a *Logic* or *Dialectic* of Abelard. But it must occur in some other repository, since Duchesne had promised to publish this treatise, which he had in his hands.

**VIII.** The philosophical moral treatise entitled *Peter Abelard’s Ethics* (*Petri Abaelardi Ethica*) forms part of the manuscripts of the Englishman Thomas Gale [Note: [Col. 0037] *Catalogue of English Manuscripts*, p. 4, no. 6087.]. It is divided into two books, of which a fragment of the second is found among the manuscripts of Anthony Wood [Note: [Col. 0037] *Ibid.*, no. 8615.].

**IX.** Our author had composed a treatise on arithmetic entitled *Peter Abelard’s Rithmomachy* (*Petri Abaelardi Rhythmomachia*). M. Le Beuf [Note: [Col. 0037] *Dissertation on Paris*, vol. II, p. 87.] says that this treatise, known to him only from a catalogue of Richard de Fournival dated to the thirteenth century, is no longer found, unless it be the Saint-Victor manuscript numbered 620.

Abelard’s unpublished commentaries on Holy Scripture make up two volumes in the King’s Library. The first contains an explanation of the Psalms; the second, elucidations of all Saint Paul’s epistles.

His theological works are:

[Col. 0039] **1.** The famous work entitled *Yes and No* (*Sic et non*), one of the three writings that gave his adversaries the greatest advantage against him. It is seen in the Library of Mont-Saint-Michel and in that of Marmoutier. Dom Montfaucon and Dom Martène [Note: [Col. 0039] *Anecdota*, vol. V, p. 1362.] had also seen it among the manuscripts of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. The latter even asserts that he examined it carefully with the intention of publishing it, an intention which he abandoned, he says, after recognizing that the book was more likely to scandalize the faithful than to edify them. But that copy has since disappeared, unless it is either the Marmoutier copy or the Mont-Saint-Michel copy, which was then deposited at Saint-Germain and was subsequently returned. The work is too important not to deserve at least a brief notice.

Dom Gervaise, who never knew it except by its title, speaks of it with the assurance of a man who had read it from end to end, and with the prejudice of a declared partisan of Abelard.

In a long prologue, in which the design and purpose of the treatise are explained, the author begins by saying that, although many contradictions are encountered in the writings of the Fathers, it is nevertheless not permitted rashly to judge them, despise them, still less condemn them. “Let us not be surprised,” he says, “if, lacking the spirit that guided their pen, we do not possess the key to many of their expressions, whose usage has been abolished or changed. Besides, the same term often has various meanings; and, as each abounds in his own sense, so each also has his particular manner of expression.”

He then gives rules of criticism for discerning the source of the contradictions sometimes found in sacred writers, and even more so in ecclesiastical authors. These rules are judicious and exact. Abelard cites various passages of the Fathers in which, humbly acknowledging that they may be mistaken, they ask readers to excuse them. Saint Augustine’s *Retractations* are not forgotten. Abelard ends his prologue with these words:

> “Having set these matters forth beforehand, it pleases us, as we have undertaken, to collect the various sayings of the holy Fathers as they occur to memory, containing questions arising from the disagreement which they appear to have, so that they may provoke tender readers to the greatest zeal for the investigation of truth and make them more acute in carrying it out. For this is defined as the first key of wisdom: namely, constant or frequent questioning. The most penetrating of all philosophers earnestly exhorts us, in the category of relation, to embrace it with our whole desire, saying: ‘Perhaps it is difficult to declare confidently concerning such matters unless they have been thoroughly examined. But it will not be useless to doubt concerning each point. By doubting, moreover, we come to inquiry . . .’ Hence it pleased us to prefix to this work of ours, which we compiled from the sayings of the saints gathered into one volume, the decree of Gelasius concerning authentic books, in order that it may be known that we have introduced nothing here from apocryphal works. We have also appended excerpts from the *Retractations* of Blessed Augustine, from which it may appear that nothing has been placed here from those things which he himself corrected by retracting them.”
>
> (*His itaque praelibatis, placet, ut instituimus, diversa sanctorum Patrum dicta colligere, prout occurrerint memoriae, aliqua ex dissonantia quam habere videntur, quaestionem continentia quae teneros lectores ad maximum inquirendae veritatis studium provocent et acutiores in executione reddant. Haec quippe primae sapientiae clavis definitur, assidua scilicet seu frequens interrogatio; ad quam quidem toto desiderio amplectendam philosophus ille omnium perspicacissimus in praedicamento ad aliquid studiose adhortatur, dicens: Fortasse autem difficile est de hujusmodi rebus confitenter declarare, nisi pertractatae sint. Dubitare autem de singulis non erit inutile. Dubitando autem ad inquisitionem venimus . . . Unde placuit huic operi nostro, quod ex sanctorum dictis compilavimus, in unum volumen congregatis, decretum Gelasii de authenticis libris praescribere, quo videlicet sciatur nihil nos hic ex apocryphis induxisse. Excerpta etiam Retractationum B. Augustini adjunximus, ex quibus appareat nihil hic ex his quae ipse retractando correxit, positum esse.*)

This prologue is rather good proof of Abelard’s learning. One might wish that, faithful to the rules he had just established, he had applied himself throughout the work to fulfilling the commitments he had undertaken. But instead of sound criticism suited to resolve the apparent contradictions of the Fathers, one sees only a tissue of their respective passages, which seem to oppose one another either in substance of opinion or in expression. These passages concern faith, the Trinity, the Incarnation, and the sacraments. Each article displays several Fathers as if engaged in conflict with one another. One might say that Abelard himself doubted their unanimity on matters so essential and wished to lead his readers to doubt it. But let us set aside so injurious a suspicion and believe rather that his only aim was to make a vain display of his erudition.

**2.** Two conferences, or disputations: one between a philosopher and a Jew, the other between a philosopher and a Christian. These two pieces form part of the manuscripts of Thomas Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln [Note: [Col. 0039] *Catalogue of English Manuscripts*, p. 2, no. 2392.], and of those of Thomas Gale [Note: [Col. 0039] *Ibid.*, p. 4, no. 6086.]. The second is also found in the Jacobean Library [Note: [Col. 0039] *Ibid.*, p. 4, no. 8206.].

**3.** *Abelard’s Doctrine* (*Abaelardi doctrina*). Only those who have had access to Henry Langley’s library [Note: [Col. 0039] *Ibid.*, p. 4, no. 6954.], where this treatise occurs, can say whether it differs from the *Introduction to Theology* and the *Christian Theology*.

**4.** *Peter Abelard on the True Essence of God and on the Catholic Faith* (*Petrus Abaelardus de vera essentia Dei et de fide catholica*). The same must be said of this work, which is entered in the catalogue of the manuscripts of the same Henry Langley and in that of York Cathedral [Note: [Col. 0039] *Ibid.*, p. 4, no. 42.].

**5.** *Peter the Peripatetic on the Sacrament of the Altar* (*Petri Peripatetici de sacramento altaris*). It is mentioned in the catalogue of the manuscripts of the King of Sardinia [Note: [Col. 0039] p. 281, cod. 884]; and that of York Cathedral likewise records it [Note: [Col. 0039] *English Manuscripts*, p. 4, no. 6954.].

**6.** *Peter Abelard’s Elucidarius*. Under the article on Saint Anselm we spoke of a work entitled *Elucidarium*, found in the Appendix to the latest edition of his works. Dom Martène [Note: [Col. 0039] *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. V, p. 1362.] had seen this same work in the Abbey of Fontaines, in the diocese of Tours, bearing Abelard’s name; and in another manuscript at Clairvaux Abbey, according to the testimony of the same critic, it is attributed to Angeld of Montléon. We have proved that it belongs to Honorius of Autun. Yet it remains to be known whether it is the same as the *Elucidarius* entered under our author’s name in the inventory of the Jacobean Library (no. 8207). We are not in a position to decide this.

**7.** A discourse on the conception of the Blessed Virgin, preserved in the Jesuit Library at Bordeaux, according to Possevin’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0039] *Script.* vol. II, p. 232.]: “His discourse on the conception of the Blessed Virgin exists at Bordeaux among our people, obtained from the monastery of La Sauve-Majeure in that district. Yet it is doubted whether it is the same as that which Rescius published at Louvain many years ago under the name of Peter Comestor. For we have not been able to compare them together” (*Ejus oratio, de conceptione B. Virginis exstat Burdigalae apud nostros e monasterio Sylvae-majoris in eo tractu obtenta. Dubitatur tamen num sit eadem quam multos ante annos Lovanii edidit Rescius Petro Comestori ascripta. Nec enim simul eas conferre potuimus*).

The poetic works of our author which escaped the shipwreck of time without yet seeing the light are:

[Col. 0041] **I.** Verses to his son Astralabe under the title: *Elegiac Verses of Peter Abelard to Astralabe, His Son, on Morals and a Pious and Upright Life* (*Petri Abaelardi versus elegiaci ad Astralabium filium suum de moribus et vita pia ac proba*). Mr. Richard Widmore, keeper of the Cottonian Library, where they are preserved in the Vitellius class, has kindly sent us the first twelve, which we shall in turn communicate to the public.

> Astralabe, my son, sweetness of a father’s life,  
> I leave you a few words for your pursuit of learning.  
> Let your care for learning be greater than your care for teaching;  
> for by the one you benefit others, by the other yourself.  
> When there is nothing left for you to learn, cease learning;  
> nor think you should cease before then.  
> Learn for a long time, and teach firmly and slowly;  
> and do not rush too quickly into writing.  
> Let your concern be not who speaks, but what is said:  
> well-spoken words give a name to their author.  
> Do not swear by the words of a beloved master,  
> nor let a teacher hold you captive through his own affection.

**II.** A prose lament on the misfortune of Dinah, daughter of Jacob. This piece is in the Vatican Library in a thirteenth-century manuscript. Here is its beginning, which His Eminence Cardinal Passione kindly had copied for us:

> Offspring of Abraham, Israel-born, illustrious in the blood of the patriarchs,  
> by the ravishing of an uncircumcised man I have become the prey of a defiled man;  
> the supreme stain of a holy race, mocked in the games of an alien people.  
>
> Woe to me, miserable woman, betrayed by myself!  
> What advantage was it to me to look upon foreigners?  
> How grievously have I been known, desiring to know these women!  
> Woe to me, miserable woman, betrayed by myself!

It is noteworthy that in the manuscript this prose, or sequence intended for singing in church, is notated according to the manner of the time: that is, in round dots, without lines or clefs, and with square or lozenge-shaped notes like ours.

### § IV.—His Lost, Doubtful, and Spurious Writings

The most considerable work of Abelard that has fallen prey to time is his *Apology*. All critics until now have wrongly confused it with his *Confession of Faith*, of which we gave an account above. To be convinced of the difference between these two pieces, one need only compare them in light of what contemporary authors tell us concerning the former. First, according to the testimony of Otto of Freising [Note: [Col. 0041] *Deeds of Frederick*, ch. 49.], the former began with these words: “Lest, according to that saying of Boethius, time be wasted on preambles that contribute nothing, we must come to the matter itself, so that the truth of the facts may excuse my innocence rather than the prolixity of words” (*Ne juxta Boetianum illud proaemiis nihil afferentibus tempus teratur, ad rem ipsam veniendum est, ut innocentiam meam ipsa rerum veritas potius quam verborum excuset prolixitas*). The other, on the contrary, begins: “It is a well-known proverb: Nothing is so well said that it cannot be distorted” (*Notum proverbium est: Nihil tam bene dictum, quod non possit depravari*).

Moreover, the latter is orthodox, as we have shown, and full of moderation; whereas the *Apology*, according to the account given by William of Saint-Thierry [Note: [Col. 0041] *Cistercian Library*, vol. IV, p. 239.] in his refutation of it, was equally blameworthy both for the tone of bitterness and insolence which the author adopted against his adversaries and for the substance of its contents, which was anything but consistent with the analogy of faith.

No trace remains of the commentary on Ezekiel that our author had begun at Laon, when he took it upon himself there to give lectures in theology, and later dictated in the school at Paris. If the admiration this work aroused in Abelard’s own time could serve us as a rule, we should have just cause to regret its loss.

Certain people today are much more sensitive to the loss of his poems, especially his songs, whose most usual subject was his beloved Héloïse. There is no need here to recall the arguments previously used to show that these songs were in the vernacular, or Romance language, rather than in Latin. The other fruits of Abelard’s poetic vein of which knowledge has reached us were a book of hymns and sequences that he had composed for the Paraclete [Note: [Col. 0041] Abelard, *Works*, p. 1136.].

Duchesne published, as having formerly formed part of this book, a rhymed prose on the mystery of the Incarnation. He nevertheless admits that it occurs separately and anonymously in the manuscripts. His authority for attributing it to Abelard is Doctor Josse Clicthou [Note: [Col. 0041] *Elucid. eccles.*, c. 5.]. But Clicthou speaks only on the authority of Demochares [Note: [Col. 0041] *Observ. Missae celebr.*, c. 15.] and Antoine Bellote [Note: [Col. 0041] Ant. Bellote, *Observ. ad rit. Eccles. Laud.*, p. 414, no. 6.], who bring forward no proof for their opinion other than public report, which ascribed it to our author. It must be admitted that the piece is not unworthy of him. It was formerly sung in several churches. It begins thus:

> He sends to the Virgin  
> Not just any angel,  
> But Might itself,  
> His archangel,  
> The lover of humankind.

One might perhaps have still better grounds for assigning to him another prose which we previously counted among Hildebert’s works (*Hist. lit.*, vol. XI, p. 389), following its latest editor, Father Hommei [Col. 0043], and the Magdeburg Centuriators. It concerns the mystery of the Trinity and bears Abelard’s name in an old manuscript from the Abbey of Bec, from which Father Martène extracted it for insertion in the ninth volume of his great Collection (pp. 1092–1097). Add that, after explaining the faith of the mystery of the Trinity in a very clear and precise manner, the author protests the sincerity of his belief, like a man who had given occasion for its being doubted. This seems much more fitting for our author than for Hildebert, who had never made himself vulnerable on this point. In any event, these are his words:

> This is the orthodox faith;  
> Here is no error or harm.  
> As I speak, so too I believe;  
> Nor do I yield to the perverse side.

The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* [Note: [Col. 0043] Vol. VII, p. 595.] likewise produce, under Abelard’s name, a distich whose subject might have furnished material for a fairly long poem. Alphonsus of Goulaine, they say, a powerful lord of Brittany, having secured peace between Philip I, King of France, and William II, King of England, these two monarchs, in gratitude, granted him the privilege of uniting their arms in his shield. On this occasion, they add, Abelard composed the following two verses:

> This arbiter joined both kings in love;  
> And the illustrious house bears its arms from each of them.

But we are not told from where this distich was taken. Besides [Note: [Col. 0043] See *Nouv. Trait. de Dipl.*, vol. IV, p. 378 ff.], is it really certain that the arms of the Kings of France and England go back beyond the twelfth century, as would have to be assumed if the authenticity of these two verses and of the event they state were accepted?

We agree with the Parisian theologians, authors of the censure placed at the head of Abelard’s works, concerning the treatise against heresies which Duchesne inserted in his edition. This book, they say, besides not bearing Abelard’s name in the manuscripts, exhibits neither his manner of expression, style, nor subtlety: “As this book does not display Abelard’s name in the manuscript codex, so neither does it savour of his manner of speech, style, and acuteness.” It is a treatise against the Albigensians, in which one finds a writer far better informed about the various opinions and practices of those heretics than anyone was in Abelard’s time. Its style is harsh, dry, and negligent; it has neither ornament nor variety of expression. The author’s way of disputing is simply to set specific passages of Scripture against every error which he reviews, without adding any reasoning. All seventeen chapters begin either with the words *Haeretici dicunt*—“The heretics say”—or with these: *Sunt quidam haeretici qui asserunt*—“There are certain heretics who maintain.” This proves that the book concerns existing heresies, and not, as Dom Gervaise thinks, ancient heresies having no relation whatever to the time when the author wrote.

During his lifetime Abelard was accused of being the author of a bad book entitled *Sentences*. We acknowledge his disclaimer of it in his Confession of Faith. It is true that his *Introduction to Theology*, as we have said, sometimes bore that title. But in his day there was another work entitled *Sententiae divinitatis* (“Theological Sentences”), which circulated under his name. Gautier of Saint-Victor, one of those who attribute this work to him [Note: [Col. 0043] Egass. Bul., vol. II, p. 200.], has preserved for us its opening words, which are all that remain of it. They are these: “All you who thirst, come to the waters; drink, my friends, and be made drunk, my dearest ones.”

We shall not pause to prove that the *Roman de la Rose* is a work formerly attributed to Abelard wholly without grounds. Everyone now knows that Guillaume de Lorris [Note: [Col. 0043] *Abael. apologia.*] and Jean de Meun are its true authors. D’Amboise guessed very badly when he said that Abelard’s and Heloise’s love was the subject of this work. It does not even have the appearance of plausibility.

## § V.—His doctrine

From the account we have just given of Abelard’s works, it is sufficiently apparent that it is impossible to clear his doctrine in every respect of the censures with which it has been branded. It remains, therefore, to make known in detail the points on which he truly erred, and to characterize the conduct of his judges. Was Abelard guilty of all the errors attributed to him? Was the procedure followed in judging him regular? These are the two matters now to be examined.

To answer the first question, let us take up the fourteen articles censured by the Council of Sens, adding Saint Bernard’s refutation of these same articles [Note: [Col. 0043] Bern., *Op.*, pp. 640–657.]. These two documents, placed together as may be seen in the new edition of this Father, shed mutual light upon one another and make the decision easier to understand.

The first proposition which the Abbot of Clairvaux reproves in our theologian provides, according to this holy doctor, the key to his system and reveals the foundation upon which he built his opinions. “Faith,” Bernard makes him say, “must be guided by natural light; for it is the mark of a frivolous mind to believe too readily. Now the person who believes too readily is one who makes faith precede reason. For what use is it to profess what one cannot explain, and to teach a doctrine which one is unable to make intelligible to those who hear us?” These are not exactly Abelard’s expressions; but he uses equivalent ones [Note: [Col. 0043] “He who believes too readily is one who, without discrimination and forethought concerning what is said, assents before he investigates, so far as he can, with the reason still unknown, what is being urged upon him. What benefit is there in soundness of speech when the hearer’s understanding does not follow it?”]—and even stronger ones, going so far as to maintain that a truth should not [Col. 0045] be believed because God has said it, but accepted because one is convinced that it is so: *Nec quia Deus hoc dixerat, creditur; sed quia hoc sic esse convincitur, recipitur*—“It is believed not because God has said it, but accepted because it is proved to be so.” This is a principle that must lead far; the same is true of the following.

“Faith,” says Abelard, “is an estimation of things which do not fall under the senses. It is, according to the Apostle, the argument of things not apparent. Now an argument is the reason that leads us to believe a thing doubtful in itself” [Note: [Col. 0045] “For faith is an estimation of things not apparent, that is, not subject to the bodily senses. Faith is the argument of things not apparent . . . an argument is a reason that establishes belief in a doubtful thing.”]. From this Saint Bernard infers that Abelard permits reason to rise up against revelation; that he authorizes it to reconsider what Scripture has decided; that he at least makes doubt compatible with faith. These consequences are natural, and this cannot be denied. Yet, far from having consistently admitted them, the author is seen sometimes to have combated them, even successfully. But what he could not disavow in any case, without undermining his new method at its foundation, was that faith is not absolutely above reason; that the former proposes nothing which the latter is unable to explain; and that both may alike pronounce, the one upon the reality and the other upon the nature, of our mysteries.

By these principles Abelard prepared his readers to accept his new explanations of the Trinity. We have reported them above; it remains only to assess them.

The comparisons which our theologian uses to explain the distinction of the divine persons have two equally disadvantageous aspects. Under one, one believes one perceives Sabellianism; under the other, Arianism seems to appear. We gladly persuade ourselves—and not without evidence—that he was free from both errors. But what cannot be excused in him is that he truly confused all theological notions concerning the Trinity. For what becomes of theology when the Father is represented as producing only a certain power, namely wisdom, in the generation of the Son; and the two together as producing only a goodness devoid of power in the procession of the Holy Spirit? Is it not even a sin against the rules of reasoning to restrict omnipotence to the Father, on the ground that he alone holds his existence and power from himself? As Saint Bernard very judiciously says, by the same reasoning wisdom and goodness would equally be the Father’s distinctive properties, since he possesses them on the same title. Moreover, Abelard contradicted himself in terms concerning the Holy Spirit, confessing on the one hand that he is consubstantial with the Father and Son, while denying on the other that he is their substance. “Then,” Saint Bernard replies, “do the Father and the Son proceed from the substance of the Holy Spirit? But if neither can be said, what becomes of consubstantiality?” Finally, without intending it, he made this third person a contingent being by giving him, as his specific attribute, the goodness which he communicates to creatures, and by representing him [Note: [Col. 0045] “Plato appropriately set the Holy Spirit as the soul of the world, as it were the life of the universe.”] as the soul of the world—which suggests that he exists only insofar as created beings exist. Whatever Dom Gervaise may say [Note: [Col. 0045] *Vie d’Abail.*, vol. II, p. 181.], no minor or major distinction can save such absurdities.

Modern theologians are embarrassed to determine the meaning of the following proposition: “Although we grant that Jesus Christ is a third person in the Trinity, we nevertheless do not say that this person, who is Christ, is a third person of the Trinity.” Father Alexandre [Note: [Col. 0045] *Hist. Eccl.*, saec. XII, diss. 7, art. 6.], followed by most writers, finds in it only a dialectical subtlety expressed in terms favorable to Nestorianism. But Dom Martène [Note: [Col. 0045] *Thes. anecd.*, vol. V, p. 656.] sees in it, with better reason, the error of the Nihilists, of whom Abelard was the leader according to Gautier of Saint-Victor’s testimony: namely, the error of saying that Jesus Christ, insofar as he is man, was not something.

Here is an article which bears novelty upon its face. “All our doctors,” Abelard says, “agree that the devil, before Jesus Christ, had absolute power over man and possessed him by right of conquest, just as a conqueror possesses one whom he has conquered. But it seems to me that this is not so. I say, on the contrary, that the devil had real power over man only by divine permission, in the manner of a jailer, and that the Son of God did not come to deliver us from the devil’s captivity.” Saint Bernard observes upon this: “All our doctors agree on one thing, and you dare to affirm the contrary. New Ishmael, in raising your hands in this way against all, do you not see that you arm everyone’s hands against yourself? But, finally, what better thing do you bring? What more subtle thing have you devised? What more secret thing have you discovered than what the saints and wise men have perceived until our day?” Passing from this to the substance of the proposition, he proves that the devil had a real and legitimate power over the human race: a power prefigured by that of the various conquerors of Judaea; a power similar to Pilate’s over Jesus Christ; a power expressed by that of the armed strong man, who is none other than the devil, whose goods are human beings; hence a power quite different from that of a jailer over prisoners committed to his charge. “Moreover,” adds this Father, “while maintaining that the devil’s dominion was just, let us not confuse dominion with will. Neither the will of this tyrant nor that of the man who deserved to be enslaved to him was just; only the will of God, who permitted this subjection, was just. For justice is derived from will, not from power.” From this faithful summary of Saint Bernard’s doctrine on the point under examination, one may properly ask our author’s apologists what they find objectionable in it. Abelard, to hear them [Note: [Col. 0045] Gerv., *Vie d’Abail.*, p. 182.], did not say enough, while Saint Bernard said too much.

Certainly the former did not say enough in treating of man’s captivity, and consequently he also necessarily diminished the work of his deliverance. Was it in fact to represent the full efficacy of the mystery of our redemption—or rather, was it not to annihilate it—to confine it, as he does, to example and instruction? “I hold,” he says, “that the singular grace of our justification and reconciliation with God through the blood of Jesus Christ consists in this: that his Son, having assumed our nature, did not cease until his death to instruct us by his examples and words, and that he intensified [Col. 0047] our attachment to him by the bonds of love, so that, inflamed at the sight of so great a benefit, our charity may be ready to endure everything in order to please him. I do not doubt that, just as people in this time of grace, the ancient Fathers, who awaited in faith that remarkable favor, were, in contemplating it, inflamed with the most ardent charity. Our [Note: [Col. 0047] In the original, the first member of this final sentence is: *Redemptio itaque nostra est illa summa in nobis per passionem Christi dilectio*—“Therefore our redemption is that supreme love in us through Christ’s passion.” Dom Gervaise translates it thus (*Vie d’Abail.*, vol. II, p. 158): “Our redemption therefore consists in that supreme love which Jesus Christ showed us by his death and passion”; that is, he substitutes the supreme love which Jesus Christ showed us by his death and passion for the great love inspired in us by Christ’s passion. This writer commits another infidelity in translating the final member of the same sentence, which reads: *Quae (dilectio) non solum nos a servitute peccati liberat, sed veram nobis filiorum Dei libertatem acquirit*—“Which love not only frees us from the slavery of sin, but obtains for us the true freedom of the children of God.” In Dom Gervaise’s version: “A love which not only delivered us from the slavery of sin, but acquired for us the freedom of the children of God.” The verbs *liberat* and *acquirit* are here rendered in the past in order forcibly to make Abelard’s text say that it is Jesus Christ’s love for us which delivered us from slavery and acquired true freedom for us. This bad faith in the translator has already been noted before us (*Journ. de Trév.*, 1739, p. 1766).] redemption, therefore, is that great love which Christ’s passion inspires in us: a love which not only frees us from the slavery of sin, but also obtains for us the freedom of God’s children.” If these expressions do not contain pure Pelagianism, one does not know where it can be found.

To attack Christ’s satisfaction is at the same time to derogate from his grace. These two dogmas are inseparable, and one always receives the rebound of attacks directed at the other. Now this is how Abelard, after directly attacking the first, reasons regarding the second: “If it were true that man could not prepare himself for grace without the assistance of another grace, he would be beyond blame in sinning, because then the lack of grace would fall back upon him from whom it proceeds. But this is not so, and truth teaches us to reason otherwise. Therefore we must say that, by means of the reason which man has received from God, he can adhere (*cohaerere*) to the grace offered to him; so that the person who is saved is no more favored by heaven, before he adheres to grace, than the person who is not saved. Such, indeed, is the conduct of the supreme Being toward all persons in the order of salvation. Like a jeweler who displays precious stones for sale and makes them shine before the public’s eyes in order to excite the desire to acquire them, God presents his grace to all people, exhorts them through his Scriptures, and invites them by examples to adhere to it by making good use of their freedom.” There must be no mistake: according to our author, this grace which God offers to all people is not actual grace, but habitual or sanctifying grace; and the comparison he uses allows no other sense to be given to his expressions. With respect to actual aids, the same comparison shows that, with Pelagius, he admitted no others than reason aided by doctrine and law.

It remained only for our author, in order to be a complete Pelagian, to deny original sin. This he did not fail to do in these terms: “When we say that people are born with original sin and contract it from the first father, this should be understood rather of the penalty of sin to which they are born subject than of an actual fault of the soul and a real contempt for divinity. For one who does not yet have the use of reason or freedom cannot be guilty of any transgression or neglect, and consequently has nothing in himself that can deserve either punishment or reward.”

In the order of nature, Abelard gives scarcely less ground for censure than in that of grace. The optimism of which he was the restorer produced two paradoxes under his pen. The first, already mentioned, was that God cannot do what he does either in another manner or at another time; the second, that he cannot prevent evil. It is appropriate to transcribe here the proof by which he supports this latter proposition. “To be the cause of evil,” he says, “presupposes the power or the duty to prevent it. For if one ought to obstruct it without being able to do so, or if one can do so without being obliged to do so, one is equally free from blame in permitting it. Now the second case is precisely that in which God finds himself. His goodness dispenses him from, and his wisdom renders him unable, to oppose evil. As good, it befits him to permit things to occur in the best possible manner; as wise, he is unable to prefer a lesser good to the most perfect, and consequently to cut off evil, which is the source of the greatest advantages.” It is unnecessary to reflect upon the danger of this doctrine. A wise and enlightened reader will anticipate the reflections.

The propositions of our author which form the foundation of his *Treatise on Morals* offend right reason and piety so visibly that there is no honorable person who should not be scandalized by them. For what becomes of moral teaching when sins of ignorance and even deicide are justified; when all that is criminal in our actions is reduced to formal contempt of God alone; when divine justice is accused of punishing innocent persons even with eternal torment? Abelard, convicted of having advanced all these horrors, has nevertheless found apologists among persons who profess to detest them [Note: [Col. 0047] Gerv., *Vie d’Abail.*, vol. II, p. 221.]. This is because everything changes its appearance in an author when he is read through the eyes of prejudice.

We have seen that Abelard did not understand himself when treating of the authority of pastors, for lack of knowing how properly to distinguish the power of jurisdiction from the power of discernment. The censure properly struck what he says on this important point, as being at least capable, through its confusion, of leading the faithful into error.

We have finally reached an article in which even impartial critics have perceived nothing relating to faith and, consequently, nothing that could be the object of an ecclesiastical censure. It is the article concerning the Eucharist. Abelard maintains two things there [Note: [Col. 0047] Bern., *Opp.*, p. 642.]: first, that absolute accidents remain in the air; second, that the body of Our Lord does not fall to the ground. The first is indeed quite irrelevant to the integrity of dogma. It is the only one these persons have considered; but the attention of the [Col. 0049] Fathers of Sens was directed to the second, as is apparent from the title they gave this article: *Quod corpus Domini non cadit in terram*—“That the Lord’s body does not fall to the ground.”

We shall pursue Abelard no further in his wanderings. Limited by our plan to examining the charges brought against him at the Council of Sens and subsequently before the Holy See, we believe we have put our readers in a position to assess the substance of this great controversy. Let us now turn our eyes to the conduct of his judges and see whether they faithfully discharged the duties attached to their office. This is the second part of the undertaking we have assumed.

Whether Abelard was subject to the jurisdiction of the Council of Sens by reason of his residence or not, it is certain that he became so by choosing that assembly to judge his dispute with Saint Bernard. For to say with Dom Gervaise that he had chosen the prelates of Sens as witnesses rather than arbiters of his dispute is gratuitously to ascribe to him an extravagance without example in history. What civil or ecclesiastical tribunal has ever had a cause voluntarily brought before it without an intention to submit to its decision?

The manner in which the council used its authority seems at first to offer rather more ground for criticism. To judge, it is said, fourteen doctrinal articles in a single session, without preliminary examination, without taking the trouble to compare them with the books from which they were drawn, without weighing the arguments for and against: such was the conduct of the Fathers of Sens, and no canonical assembly had furnished them a model for it. But in truth, upon what do Abelard’s apologists base these assertions? Are they not even formally contradicted by the synodal letters of the prelates of Sens and those of Saint Bernard, the only documents which can take the place of the acts of the council that time has withheld from us? Indeed, far from having hastened their decision as is supposed, Abelard’s judges testify that they [Note: [Col. 0049] “Moreover, we condemned, on the day before the appeal made to you, his propositions of perverse doctrine . . . often read and reread in public hearing, and shown most evidently to be not only false but heretical, both by the truest arguments and by authorities of Blessed Augustine and other holy Fathers introduced by the lord of Clairvaux.” Bernard, Ep. 337. This *pridie ante factam ad vos appellationem*—“on the day before the appeal made to you”—incidentally gives reason to think that, after appealing orally to the pope, Abelard subsequently had his appeal notified in writing to the council when he learned that his first step had not suspended that assembly’s proceedings.] read and reread the articles of his doctrine often in public hearings before pronouncing; far from neglecting to consult tradition, they declare that they rendered judgment only after questioning the holy Fathers, especially Saint Augustine; far from omitting verification of the accused man’s views in his own books, everything leads us to believe that they carried it out carefully, since of the seventeen articles brought forward by Saint Bernard, they limited their censure to fourteen—no doubt because the erroneous sense of the other three seemed to them to disappear in the original. Let us nevertheless acknowledge it: although the prelates of Sens did anything but judge, as the saying goes, upon mere assertion, there is no doubt that the learning, influence, and activity of the man of God, as has already been observed, greatly helped to shorten their proceedings and likewise influenced their decision.

With regard to Pope Innocent, the power of the Abbot of Clairvaux over his mind is even more perceptible in the course which he adopted toward our theologian. Without an adversary so formidable, there is every appearance that, through the friends Abelard had at Rome, his appeal would have been favorably received there; that the pope, instead of forestalling his arrival by a sentence more severe than the first, would have granted him the time necessary to come and cast himself at his feet; and that, upon a profession of faith like the one which he had circulated in France before his departure, he would have spared his person and, if not reformed, at least mitigated the judgment of Sens. But God, who had merciful designs toward this proud spirit, cast him down by the very means which seemed destined to make him triumph. Moreover, for the security of the deposit of faith, it was important that writings strewn with bold assertions, filled with improper expressions, directed according to a method unknown to all antiquity—not to mention the gross errors with which they were infected—should remain forever branded along with their author’s name. By this means future ages were taught not to cut out new paths for themselves in order to find chimerical solutions to incomprehensible truths. Happy would theology schools have been if this lesson had always been deeply engraved upon the hearts of masters and disciples!

## § VI.—His genius, learning, and manner of writing

If, without regard for truth, we had resolved to portray in Abelard’s person a finished model of learning, nothing would better suit that purpose than the abbreviated account of his talents with which Dom Gervaise concludes the history of his life. This incomparable man, he says, was grammarian, orator, poet, musician, philosopher, theologian, mathematician, astronomer, and jurist. He played instruments, knew five or six languages, and was ignorant of nothing in sacred or profane history. What century has produced a man who knew so many things? But far from blindly subscribing to this praise, we make it our duty to subject it to the crucible of criticism, in order to separate what is hyperbolical and contrary to truth.

First, since his Treatise on Grammar has not come down to us, the degree of his knowledge of that art can be judged only from the use he made of it in his other writings. Now his style reveals anything but a man thoroughly acquainted with the principles and rules of expression. It is easy but uncorrected, clear but inelegant; it has several of the bad qualities of twelfth-century Latinity and not all its good ones.

To do full justice to his poetic vein, we shall not hesitate to acknowledge that he rivalled the most able versifiers of his time, such as Hildebert, Marbode, and so forth; but nothing in his verse places him above them.

Heloise’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0049] *Abael. Op.*, p. 46.] leads us to believe that he had a taste for vocal music and that nature had endowed him with an excellent voice for performance. As for instrumental music, it is a talent attributed to him without foundation. It would not have cost Dom Gervaise much more to tell us which instruments his hero could play.

Discourses in which neither art nor genius makes itself felt, and whose entire value lies in their soundness, cannot secure their author a distinguished rank among orators. Such, nevertheless, are those sermons of Abelard on which his talent for the pulpit is praised. Placed beside those of Saint Bernard, they could not sustain the comparison.

Of all branches of philosophy, the one Abelard knew best was dialectic; yet what proves that he knew it badly is that he never had the art of simplifying it, abbreviating it, and reducing it to the small number of useful precepts which it contains. Through a depraved taste for empty subtleties, he gave preference to the least important questions, treated universals with the most tedious prolixity, and disputed for the honor of victory rather than from love of truth.

His theological learning may be praised as much as one likes; his authority will never carry weight in religious matters. It is evident that he wrote on theological subjects from himself and without troubling himself about tradition. Hence those improper expressions, dangerous principles, dubious arguments, and the other deviations which we have previously noted in his writings.

Are we to be believed when he is represented as a man ignorant of nothing in sacred or profane history? One would scarcely dare say as much even of the Scaligers, Saumaise, and Petau. Yet the reading of these great men extended far beyond the *Tripartite History*, that of the Venerable Bede, the *Lives of the Desert Fathers*, and a few chronicles, which are almost the only sources from which our author drew what he knew of antiquity.

There is scarcely less exaggeration in making him speak five or six languages. He knew Latin, French, and, if one wishes, Lower Breton. But he scarcely understood Greek, and Hebrew even less. The few traces found of these latter two languages in his writings—where he nevertheless had so often occasion to employ them—prove that they were anything but familiar to him.

Geometry, arithmetic, and astronomy were sciences as common as they were little developed in the twelfth century. People then contented themselves with learning their elements. Our author does not appear to have carried his investigations further.

As for the title of jurist, it rests solely upon an equivocation of names. The passage from Accursius which is cited concerns a professor of law, something which no one will show that our author ever was. Indeed, were there such professors in his day? Here are Accursius’s words from his commentary on the law *Quinque pedum* [Note: [Col. 0051] Bayle, art. “Abailard.”]: “And Peter Bailard, who boasted that from any writing, however difficult, he could draw a sound understanding, said here: ‘I do not know.’” It is doubtful whether Accursius correctly gave this professor’s name, since Crinitus calls him John Balard [Note: [Col. 0051] Nicer., vol. IV, p. 32.].

Let us conclude from these observations that Abelard was a man of much intelligence, capable of making great progress in the sciences, had he been more receptive to the advice of the wise and learned persons of his time, more attentive to the subjects he treated, and less passionately devoted to novelties. For want of these dispositions, he became only a proud sophist, a poor reasoner, a mediocre poet, a feeble orator, a superficial scholar, and a rejected theologian.

## § VII.—Editions and translations of his works
Two men of letters, François d’Amboise, Councillor of State, and André Duchesne, agreed at the beginning of the last century to publish a collection of Abailard’s Works. This edition, which appeared at Paris in 1616, in a large quarto volume, from Nicolas Buon, is noteworthy on three grounds. First, instead of an approbation, it has at its head a censure by the theologians of Paris upon all passages in the author’s writings which they had judged blameworthy. Secondly, despite this precaution, Rome had it placed on the Index. The third circumstance gives rise to a kind of typographical problem: on the title page of some copies the edition is attributed to the care of André Duchesne; in others it bears the name of François d’Amboise, Councillor of State. The former are adorned with: 1. a dedicatory epistle composed by Duchesne; 2. a preface by the same, in which he gives an account of his work and names François d’Amboise among those who communicated manuscripts to him; 3. a collection of ancient testimonies in Abailard’s favour. All this is lacking in the latter copies, and is replaced by an apology for the author, composed by the Councillor of State. There is, moreover, a difference in the privilege: Duchesne is named in the copies which attribute the edition to him, whereas in the others the editor’s name is suppressed. We shall not pause to investigate the causes of this diversity, upon which Bayle has discoursed at great length. It is enough to be assured that it does not indicate different editions; and the perfect conformity of the copies in every other respect leaves no room for doubt.

With regard to the pieces included in the body of this collection, and the order observed in it, the reciprocal letters of Abailard and Héloïse first appear, preceded by the letter concerned with the history of the former’s misfortunes. Then come his letters to various persons, together with those written to him or composed on his account. His three expositions—of the Lord’s Prayer, the Apostles’ Creed, and that which bears the name of St Athanasius—the Problems of Héloïse, and the book against heresies, of which we spoke in examining his spurious works, form, as it were, a third part. His sermons follow, and are followed by his Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans. Finally, his Introduction to Theology, together with the Prose in honour of the Virgin, concludes this collection of his writings. Duchesne further enriched it with learned notes upon the history of the author’s misfortunes, notes which d’Amboise retained in his copies.

We nevertheless observe several defects in this edition. Besides the fact that insufficient attention was paid, in arranging the pieces, to their relations with one another and to the order of their subjects, it is full of errors. Some arise from the inaccuracy and mutilation of the manuscripts on which it was based; others must be laid to the printer’s account. The latter carried his carelessness so far as to place different printing dates in different copies. For in some one sees the year 1606, in others 1616, which is the true date, and finally in others 1626. This, joined to the other variations we have noted, strengthens the error concerning a multiplicity of editions.

Our author’s *Christian Theology* was published, from a manuscript of the abbey of Marmoutiers, by Dom Martène in the fifth volume of his *Anecdota* (p. 1140). The notice which the editor placed before this work is full of prudent reflections and very well-selected learning.

[Col. 0053] His *Hexameron*, or Commentary on Genesis, taken from a manuscript of Mont-Saint-Michel, is found in the same volume (p. 1363), with preliminary observations which likewise ought not to be neglected.

We owe to the care of Dom Bernard Pez the moral treatise entitled *Know Thyself* (*Scito teipsum*). Having discovered it in the abbey of St Emmeram, this learned man included it in the third volume of his *Anecdota* (p. 673). One may see in the general preface to that volume what he thinks of the doctrine of this writing.

Abailard’s letter to the Bishop of Paris against Roscelin has been put into print three times, subsequent to and from the edition of Duchesne and d’Amboise: namely, by Du Boulay in the second volume of his *History of the University* (p. 492), by Father Labbe in the tenth volume of the *Councils* (p. 487), and by Father Dubois in the eleventh book of his *History of the Church of Paris*. The second unhesitatingly assigns it to our author. The other two, as has already been said, regard it as the work of an unknown writer.

The four letters of Abailard to Héloïse, and the three which he received from her, have twice been republished in this century. The first time was at London in 1718, in an octavo volume by Mr Rawlinson, with a great number of variants which have made all the idioms and less correct expressions formerly observed in the style of these letters disappear. The editor tells us in his preface that for this purpose he used the manuscript of a friend who did not wish to be named. But one need know the public only slightly to persuade oneself that so vague an assurance will find credit with it. It has long since recovered from the deception of these alleged secret manuscripts whose age and repository are never disclosed. Thus Rawlinson’s corrections deserve no consideration, having no mark of authenticity.

Dom Gervaise, the other editor, not content with republishing these letters, added a translation; the whole was contained in two duodecimo volumes published in 1723 at Paris by Barrois.
