In giving an account of his work, he says: 1. that he carefully revised the text of his authors from the best manuscripts (yet no difference can be perceived between this edition and that of 1616); 2. that what led him to provide a translation of these letters was the equally unfaithful and obscene paraphrases by which attempts had been made to disfigure the noble and Christian sentiments which they contain. But if he carefully observed the laws of decorum, it cannot be said that he equally fulfilled the duty of an exact translator. He often renders his original into French with the expansiveness and freedom of a paraphrast.

Dom Gervaise was not the first translator of these letters. Jean de Meun had put them into French as early as the fourteenth century. [Note: [Col. 0053] *Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions*, vol. XVII, p. 754.] He himself informs us of this at the beginning of his translation of Boethius’s *On the Consolation*. But his work has not come down to us.

With regard to these paraphrases of which the modern translator complains, and others which followed them, we shall refrain from enumerating them, because they bear no relation to the object of this history.

[Col. 0053]

## SECOND NOTICE

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. V, p. 232.)

[Col. 0053A] Let us be permitted to borrow an account of Peter Abaelard from Louis Jacob, to which I shall add my own annotations. Thus he writes in Book III, *On the Writers of Chalon*, p. 139:

Peter Abaelard, or Abelard, surnamed the Dialectician—[Note: [Col. 0053A] By Bergomensis, *Baliardus*; by Alciatus, *Baylardus*; in Bernard, Epistle 180, as if *Abeillardus*; called “the bee of France”; by John of Salisbury, the Palatine Peripatetic, from his birthplace, where in A.D. 1079 he was brought into the light at Palais, a town in Lesser Brittany, not from a royal palace, as seems to be implied in the *Selected Halle Observations*, vol. VI, observation 20. His teacher in dialectic was Roscelin; in philosophy, William of Champeaux; in logic, Anselm of Laon, the standard-bearer of the Nominalists. His pupil was Arnold of Brescia, etc.] an Armorican by nation, head of the theological school at Paris, a philosopher and theologian celebrated throughout the world, a singular prodigy of learning, both divine and human, lived for some time a not very honourable life [Note: [Col. 0053B] He called the son conceived in a clandestine love-affair Astralabe. He himself was afterwards made a eunuch, while asleep and thinking of no such thing, by Fulbert, Héloïse’s guardian and kinsman, in indignation. See Edmund Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. V, p. 1140 ff.; Boëllius’s *Lexicon*, under “Abelard”; and the writers of lives: Jacob Thomasius in the *History of Wisdom and Folly* by his son Christian Thomasius, vol. I, p. 75 ff.; Étienne Pasquier in the celebrated work *Researches into France*, Book VI, ch. 17; and Gervaise in his *Life of Abaelard*, carefully composed in six books in French, [Col. 0054B] Paris, 1720, 12mo, two volumes; *Acta Eruditorum*, 1721, p. 263; *Mémoires de Trévoux*, 1721, p. 941; *Journal littéraire*, vol. XI, p. 255; C. A. Heumann, *Acta philosophorum*, part XVI, p. 529 ff.] with Héloïse of Montmorency, second to none in birth and learning. But shortly thereafter they repented; she became a nun and then, in 1130, superior of the monastery of the Paraclete, of the Order of St Benedict, in the diocese of Troyes; [Col. 0054A] while he became a monk of Saint-Denis near Paris, and was afterwards appointed abbot of Rhuys.

He became entangled in various errors, for which he was condemned at the Council of Soissons in A.D. 1121 [Note: [Col. 0054B] See Pagi, under A.D. 1121, no. 14 ff.] and at Sens in A.D. 1140 by the most holy men Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, and Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny. But, having come to a better mind [Note: [Col. 0054B] He also testified, in a written Apology, to the injury done him by his more vehement adversaries. Compare d’Amboise’s prolegomena to Abaelard’s Works, Duchesne’s notes on Abaelard’s *History of Calamities*, and the aforementioned Gervaise.] he proved a great ornament of monastic life in the monastery of Cluny until the end of his life. [Note: [Col. 0054B] He died at Chalon in A.D. 1142.] He wrote a very great many works, published in one volume [Note: [Col. 0054B] Paris, 1616, quarto.] through the labour and zeal of the most illustrious François d’Amboise, knight, councillor to the king in his most sacred council, Baron of Chartraine, etc., containing:

[Col. 0055A] The Letters [Note: [Col. 0055C] Héloïse, renowned for intellect and learning, niece of Fulbert, canon of Paris, Abaelard’s pupil, beloved, and wife; a nun at Argenteuil; and finally, formerly prioress of that monastery of the Benedictine Order, abbess of the Oratory of the Paraclete, which Abaelard had founded in a district of the diocese of Troyes or Tricasses and had given to her with the approval of Innocent II. Héloïse, skilled in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin letters, died in 1162. See Duchesne’s notes to the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 146 ff., and Miraeus on Henry of Ghent, ch. 16; on the excessively free French paraphrases of the reciprocal letters of Héloïse and Abaelard, published either by Bussy-Rabutin, Cologne, 1695, or by Father F. G. de Beauchamps, Paris, 1714 and 1721, 12mo; and the praiseworthy work of Gervaise, who published at Paris in 1723, 12mo, in two volumes, the three Latin letters of Héloïse to Abaelard and the four of Abaelard to Héloïse, together with a prose French translation and occasional historical notes. The third, vol. II, p. 209, contains extensive praises of the order of nuns and of the female sex; the fourth prescribes a Rule for nuns, pp. 212, 595. On the more corrected Latin edition of these letters by Richard Rawlinson, London, 1718, quarto, see *Journal littéraire*, vol. IV, p. 375; *Bibliothèque ancienne et moderne*, vol. IX, p. 348; *Journal des Savants*, November 1718, [Col. 0056C] p. 239.] of Peter Abaelard and Héloïse: some of them contain the *History of Abaelard’s Calamities*, p. 3; some the origin of the religious order of nuns, p. 94; and the institution, or Rule, of the same, p. 130.

He prefixed learned prolegomena concerning Abaelard, his errors, [Note: [Col. 0056D] Abaelard’s opponents: William, Abbot of St Thierry (above, vol. III, p. 168); the Anonymous Writer (Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, on whom see above, vol. III, pp. 6 and 8); Walter of Laon and of St Victor; but above all St Bernard. See John Caramuel of Lobkowitz, *St Bernard Triumphing over Peter Abaelard*, Louvain, 1644, quarto; Jean Mabillon on Bernard’s articles concerning the Abaelardian heresies, etc.; *Literary Voyage of Two Benedictines*, vol. I, part II, p. 213.] and adversaries. Much in this work is the same as in the books *On Faith in the Holy Trinity*; nor could John of Cornwall deny [Note: [Col. 0056D] In his eulogy addressed to Pope Alexander III. See André Duchesne’s notes on Abaelard, p. 1159; Pagi, under A.D. 1113, no. 13.] that Peter Lombard, his master, had frequently had these books before his eyes and followed them in the celebrated work of the *Sentences*.

IX, pp. 1092–1097; Paris, 1733, folio. But Jacques Hommey had published the same under the name of Hildebert of Le Mans in the *Spicilegium of the Fathers*, p. 446; Paris, 1684, octavo.

It appeared in C. V. Bernard Pez’s *Anecdota*, vol. III, part II, pp. 927–988.

The *Elucidarium*, which in an old manuscript codex of the monastery of St Mary of Fontaines in the diocese of Tours [Col. 0057A] bears Abaelard’s name, while in a Clairvaux manuscript is attributed to Angelus of Mont-Leon, according to Martène, vol. V of the *Anecdota*, p. 1362; there he also observes that it was published among the spurious works of St Anselm of Canterbury.

Peter Abaelard’s *Logic, or Dialectic*, which André Duchesne promised to publish, p. 1160, has not yet seen the light. Nor has the *Book of Sentences*, *Yes and No*, manuscript in English libraries—unless it is the same [Note: [Col. 0057B] Such was the opinion of Jean Mabillon in his *German Journey*, p. 64, in the edition prepared by me, where he testifies that he found in a codex of the monastery of St Emmeram the Sentences of Bajolard, contained in thirty-seven chapters, and adds that it is Abaelard’s *Introduction to Theology*. Similarly Trithemius, ch. 381, calls Abaelard’s *Theology* “a volume shadowed by dialectical obscurity and varied by many Sentences.”] as the *Introduction to Theology* which I mentioned above among the published works. Nor have the Hymns which he composed in metrical style to be sung in the monastery called the Paraclete [Note: [Col. 0057B] Appendix to Henry of Ghent, ch. 3.]; nor the Expositions on Genesis (if Cave means works distinct from the Commentary on the Hexameron), on the Psalter, or on Paul’s Epistles mentioned by Cave, whereas among published works only the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans is read; nor the glosses on Ezekiel; nor finally the elegiac verses to his son Astralabe, concerning morals and a pious and upright life, manuscript in the Cottonian Library, p. 86.

[Col. 0057B] Abaelard himself was ordered to commit his book *On Unity and Trinity* to the flames at the Synod of Soissons in 1121.

Bernard Pez (Dissertation prefixed to vol. III of the *Anecdota*, p. XXII) says that in a Tegernsee codex he found this note:

> Peter, who is Abaelard, called Bajolard by most people, [Col. 0058A] [Note: [Col. 0057B] By others, incorrectly, also Beliardus, Baliardus, Biliardus. See Daniel Zwicker, *A New Confirmation of the Peaceful Peacemakers*, p. 502; in Alberic, p. 296, [Col. 0058B] Abulardus; in Ptolemy of Lucca under A.D. 1134, Baalardus.] an Englishman by nation [Note: [Col. 0058B] Abaelard himself declares that he was not English by nation but French, and this has been demonstrated by the writers of his Life.] first devoted himself to grammar and dialectic, then to theology. But, being of inestimable subtlety and possessed of an unheard-of capacity of memory beyond the human measure, he was at one time a pupil of Master Roscius [Note: [Col. 0058B] Read Roscelin, or Rucelin.] and began to listen to him with a certain “picking of splinters” from his opinions. [Note: [Col. 0058B] That is, as if marking and condemning the splinters in the eye of his teaching. See Du Cange under *festuca*.] Nevertheless, he imposed upon himself the duty of attending his lectures for a year. Soon he began to have companions and to give public lectures at Paris on Dialectic and Theology; and in a short time he readily surpassed all the masters of France. Since he had heard nothing of the Quadrivium [Note: [Col. 0058B] The Quadrivium consists of the four mathematical disciplines—arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and music—as the Trivium consists of grammar, logic, and rhetoric.] he secretly attended some mathematical lectures, against the will of his master Theodoric. [Note: [Col. 0058B] Theodoric.] In these, his understanding as a hearer recoiled, because of their difficulty, beyond what he expected. Once, when he was distressed and indignant, Master Theodoric said jokingly: “What is a full dog accustomed to carry but bacon?” Now *bajare* means “to lick.” From that time he began to be called Bajolard. Since he rejected that name as imposed upon him from a certain defect, he caused himself to be called Habaelard under a spelling not unlike it, [Col. 0058B] as though he had the whole and the fatness of the arts in himself.

Among the unpublished works should likewise be counted a small work *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, preserved in manuscript Latin Codex 884 of the Library of the University of Turin. Mansi.

[Col. 0057]

## DISSERTATION ON THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF PETER ABAELARD

(Oudin, *Ecclesiastical Writers*, II, 1161.)

[Col. 0057C] Peter Abaelard was born in a certain town situated at the entrance to Lesser Brittany, about eight miles east of the city of Nantes, called Palais, to pious parents, Berengar and Lucia. His father, distinguished by a military belt but no less inclined to literary pursuits, took care that his sons should be instructed in letters before arms.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Life of Peter Abaelard

Peter Abaelard, endowed with a natural aptitude for letters, left the pomp of military glory, together with his inheritance, to his elder brothers. He renounced Mars in order to be nurtured in Minerva’s bosom. To be formed in humane and philosophical disciplines, he went to Paris, the greatest city of France and most celebrated for the study of letters. There he was a pupil of William of Champeaux, Archdeacon of the Church of Paris and professor of Peripatetic philosophy. At first pleasing to him, he later became exceedingly troublesome because of his power in disputation, by which he seemed often to overcome him in the schools.

In theology he had as master Anselm, dean of the Church of Laon; there [Col. 0058C] he had as fellow pupils Alberic of Rheims and Lothulf the Lombard, rivals of his glory and perpetual detractors from his reputation. Not long after returning from Laon to Paris, Abaelard, still a young man, became a master of a school from being its pupil. While teaching, he fell in love with Héloïse, as he himself testifies in chapters 6 and 7 of his *History of Calamities*, p. 10: she was the most accomplished young woman, niece of Fulbert, Canon of Paris. By clandestine concubinage he had by her a son named Peter Astralabe.

It is easy to imagine how greatly Canon Fulbert’s anger blazed against Abaelard because of his niece’s secret seduction and lost chastity. He could not appease him except by making the beloved woman his wife. Abaelard therefore married Héloïse; yet she publicly denied that she was Abaelard’s wife, lest she injure his prospects—a fact which caused her uncle Fulbert no small grief. Accordingly, while Héloïse was shut up with nuns at Argenteuil, Abaelard, unwary and alone, slept in the house of the exasperated Canon Fulbert. Héloïse’s kinsmen suddenly burst by night into his chamber and bed, and cut off his male parts. Abaelard, ashamed because of the infamy of the wound inflicted upon him, withdrew into the concealment of monastic cloisters, prompted, as he himself testifies, more by shame than by devotion. [Col. 0059A] He took the monastic habit in the abbey of St Denis. Héloïse, meanwhile, received the veil blessed by the bishop in the monastery of Argenteuil, where she was subsequently prioress.

Abaelard suffered the gravest persecutions from false brethren and from his rivals Alberic and Lothulf, which he sets forth in a sorrowful style in his *History of Calamities*. At about this time, around 1118 or 1119, they wasted away with envy at the reputation which Master Peter had gained by a book composed by him *On Theology*, and everywhere defamed him as a heretic and an advocate of three gods. This rumour, spread widely and far concerning him, gave occasion for councils assembled against him.

He also had the monks of St Denis as enemies, because he censured too freely their secular way of life and irreligious morals. He inflamed their envy still further by vindicating, in a private discussion, the opinion of the Venerable Bede: Dionysius the Areopagite, he maintained, had been Bishop of Corinth rather than of Athens. From this it seemed to follow that the Dionysius called Apostle of the Gauls was not the Areopagite, whom the Acts testify was Bishop of Athens. Hence arose a grave tumult against Abaelard. Hence the monks loudly proclaimed him an enemy of the monastery of St Denis—indeed, of the kingdom of France—because he took away from it the honour in which it gloried uniquely, namely the apostolate of St Dionysius the Areopagite.

He excuses his contention against the ill-affected monks, declares that he had by no means denied the Areopagite, and vainly asks that regular discipline be imposed on him if he had committed any fault. The abbot, having assembled the elders, though himself a man of no observance and of a most lukewarm spirit, threatens—as if the whole of Christian faith were at stake—that he will send at once to the king, who will exact vengeance upon Abaelard as one taking from him the glory and crown of his kingdom. Meanwhile Abbot Adam orders Master Peter to be carefully watched until he can hand him over to the king.

Abaelard therefore takes refuge in flight. Entering the territory of Count Theobald, he stays near the castle of Provins in a certain cell of the monks of Troyes. Hence great outcries were raised against him, and not a single charge of heresy was omitted from those brought against him. His rivals Alberic and Lothulf, masters of the schools of Rheims, denounced Peter Abaelard before the tribunal of the Church as guilty of multiple errors against the Catholic faith, and stirred up Ralph, Archbishop of that city, against his novelties. Having communicated the matter to the Bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Apostolic See in Gaul, Ralph caused a council to be convened at Soissons in 1121 for the hearing of the case. A day was appointed for Abaelard, and he was ordered to produce for the synod his book *On the Trinity*, or *On Theology*, which was the source of offence.

Abaelard appeared before the Apostolic legate and gave him the book to be examined and judged, professing himself most ready to correct or make satisfaction for anything he might have written deviating from Catholic faith. Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, favoured him and strongly urged that his writings should be produced, that he should be questioned, and that he should be granted free opportunity to answer, lest a man celebrated for his intellectual and learned reputation should seem oppressed by prejudice. Geoffrey then advised that he be sent back to the abbey of St Denis, and that there the cause should be examined before a larger gathering of bishops and learned men.

But the wiser course was thought to be to impose silence on a dialectician furnished with sophisms, moreover an innovator and sufficiently convicted from his book of manifold error; to compel him to make a profession of faith and publicly burn his book. This was done by decree of the synod. After several disputes with his rivals, Abaelard was summoned to the council and compelled by decree of the Fathers to hand over the book to the flames [Col. 0060A] and to set forth his faith before all. When he wished to profess it in his own words, the Fathers ordered him to recite from writing the Creed of St Athanasius, in order more fully to curb the pride of an innovating man excessively confident in dialectic. He was then handed over to the Abbot of St Medard, to be confined in his cloister as in a prison. After he had been brought out, however, the Apostolic legate sent him back to the monastery of St Denis.

We learn the history of this council from St Bernard’s Epistle 193 to Cardinal Ivo; from Otto of Freising, Book I, chapter 47, of *The Deeds of Frederick*; and most fully from Abaelard’s own letter to a friend *On His Calamities*, chapter 10—although a witness in his own cause is highly suspect. That the council considered it sufficient ground for condemning the book that it had been published without approval from the Roman pontiff and the Church may be inferred from Abaelard’s own testimony. “They said,” he writes, [Col. 0060B] “that this should suffice for the condemnation of the little book: that I had presumed publicly to read it when it was commended by neither the authority of the Roman pontiff nor that of the Church, and that I had already made it available to many persons for copying. It would be very beneficial to Christian faith if the presumption of many should be prevented by my example.”

Having returned to the abbey of St Denis, Abaelard obtained from the abbot, with the consent of the Most Christian King, permission to withdraw into some solitude where he might live as a monk. He went to a most pleasant wilderness in the bishopric of Troyes. There, on land generously granted him by certain persons with the assent of the Bishop of Troyes, he first built, of reeds and straw, an oratory in the name of the Holy Trinity. When scholars learned of this, they began to flock to him from every direction. Leaving cities and castles, they made their dwelling in the wilderness; instead of houses they constructed little huts; instead of delicate foods they subsisted on wild herbs and common bread; instead of soft beds they procured straw and litter for themselves; and finally, instead of tables, they placed clods of earth beneath them. When the said oratory could not contain their immense multitude, they enlarged it and, constructing it of stones and timbers, gave it a better form.

From the Oratory of the Paraclete he was chosen, by the unanimous election of the brethren, for the abbey of St Gildas of Rhuys in the diocese of Vannes in Lesser Brittany. In that monastic office he endured many labours and many dangers. The pious man was especially distressed because he knew that if he attempted to compel the undisciplined monks to a regular life, he could not live in safety; but if he did not do so to the best of his ability, he would, as he himself says, incur the danger of eternal damnation.

Besides this, he was continually harassed by the prince—or rather petty tyrant—of that region. Taking advantage of the monks’ disorder, this man had appropriated for his own use all the places adjoining the monastery [Col. 0060D] and oppressed the monks themselves with exactions harsher than those imposed upon tributary Jews. But how much Abaelard endured from the unbridled monks—how often he was attacked when poison was put even into the sacred cup and during the very sacrifice of the altar; how often he was terrified by a threatening sword—no one will readily believe unless he has heard his complaints in the first Letter to a Friend, chapter 13. There, after much else, he writes:

> Each day I behold, as it were, a sword hanging over my neck, so that I can scarcely breathe during meals. It is as is related of the man who, when he accounted the power and amassed wealth of the tyrant Dionysius the greatest happiness, looked at the sword suspended above him by a hidden thread and learned what happiness attends earthly power. This I too, now raised from a poor monk to an abbot, experience without ceasing: I am so much the more miserable as I have become richer, so that by my example also the ambition of those who seek such a position voluntarily may be restrained.

When he repeatedly returned to the monastery of the Paraclete, which he had relinquished and granted to his beloved Héloïse, in order to assist her and her sisters with his counsel, his most malicious detractors turned this against him as a crime. They ascribed to desire for former pleasure and to carnal love what he did solely at the prompting of charity. On this matter he complains bitterly near the end of his first letter to a friend, where he also indicates that he derived the greatest consolation from these words of St Jerome in Letter 99 to Asella:

> Nothing is objected to me except my sex; and even this would never have been objected, had not Paula been setting out for Jerusalem. Before I knew the house of holy Paula, the whole city’s sentiments were harmonious in my favour; by the judgment of nearly everyone I was deemed worthy of the highest priesthood. But I know that through good report and evil report one comes to the kingdoms of heaven.

We learn these things from Abaelard himself in his historical letter to a friend concerning his calamities.

Accordingly, after abandoning the government of the abbey of Saint-Gildas, it is not sufficiently clear to what place he withdrew; but wherever Abelard was, [Col. 0061B] the storm of envy raised against him everywhere battered the man with extraordinary assaults. Some think that Abelard, thus made an exile and driven out, resumed teaching at Paris toward the end of his life. John of Salisbury seems to lend credence to this view: having entered the Parisian schools in 1136, he says that he attached himself to the Palatine Peripatetic, a name by which they suppose Peter Abelard to be indicated—indeed it is almost certain from the Victorine manuscripts and others, which we shall immediately cite verbatim. Finally, John of Salisbury expressly calls him so in Book II, chapter 17 of the *Metalogicon*, where, speaking of logical universals, he says: “In this opinion our Palatine Peripatetic Abelard was caught, and he left many followers and witnesses of this profession, and still has others.” Yet Abelard nowhere himself writes that he resumed the Parisian schools after the Paraclete. But however this may be, after enduring various calamities, he was at last regarded as a heretic at the Council of Sens in 1140.

Indeed, this wound inflicted anew by Bernard against Peter [Col. 0061C] Abelard would not have been renewed unless he had then reopened his schools. This seems to be suggested by Peter, abbot of Cluny, in his letter to Innocent II, Roman pontiff, where he says that Peter Abelard had left behind schools and studies when he withdrew to remain at the monastery of Cluny. Hence I conclude that before that time he had kept his schools open down to that year, 1140; their reopening gave Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, the occasion for renewed agitation against him. “Meanwhile, admonished by us, but more especially, as we believe, inspired by God, he chose for himself a perpetual dwelling at your Cluny, having abandoned the tumults of schools and studies.”

When, therefore, after leaving Brittany, Peter Abelard had reopened his schools, he again stirred up against himself no small tempest among the new orders, to which he was hostile—I mean the Cistercians and Premonstratensians—whom he mocked and derided in public schools. Accordingly, after the schism of Peter Leonis had been extinguished, in 1140, chiefly at the urging of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, a council was held at Sens in the case of Peter Abelard. Summoned before the archbishop of Sens by his adversaries, and widely denounced as an upholder of heresies, he asked that he might set forth his teaching and be permitted, in a public assembly, to defend himself against the slanders and objections of his enemies. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, attended the synod to refute Abelard’s errors. On the appointed day bishops and learned and most distinguished men of every order were present, and Louis VII, the Most Christian king, was to witness the assembly. While Abelard stood before the synod, articles extracted from his own books were produced; while these were being read, he is said to have withdrawn from the council, appealing to the Roman pontiff. This seems incredible. Otto of Freising writes that he made the appeal from fear of a popular riot; but that is wholly implausible, since, with the king of France, Count Theobald, and many noble [Col. 0062A] men present, there was nothing to fear from the people.

Out of reverence for the Apostolic See, Abelard was reserved for the judgment of the supreme pontiff, and the Fathers decreed nothing against his person. Yet, notwithstanding the appeal, they condemned the doctrines which they deemed unsound, and sent Innocent II a report of everything, urging him, by virtue of the office of his primacy, likewise to condemn the errors and, by confirming the sentence of the synod, to restrain this innovating man. These facts are attested by Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, in Book III, chapter 5 of the *Life of St Bernard*, and by Otto of Freising, Book I, chapter 48 of *The Deeds of Emperor Frederick*. There Otto also supplies the letter to Innocent II from Samson, archbishop of Reims; Josselin of Soissons; Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons; and Alvisus, bishop of Arras. It contains a brief exposition of Abelard’s case and of the synod’s proceedings, and they say in it:

“Peter Abelard strives to empty Christian faith of its worth, since he thinks that, by human reason, he can comprehend all that God is. He ascends to heaven and descends into the abysses. Nothing is hidden from him, whether in the depths of hell or in the heights above. He is great in his own eyes, disputing against faith concerning faith, walking in matters great and wondrous beyond him, an investigator of Majesty, a fabricator of heresies. Long ago he made a book *On the Holy Trinity*, but under the Roman Church’s legate it was tested by fire, because iniquity was found in it. Cursed is he who rebuilds the ruins of Jericho. That book has risen from the dead, and with it many heresies that had slept have risen and appeared to many. At last he has extended his branches even to the sea and his shoots even to Rome. This is that man’s boast: that his book has, in the Roman curia, where to lay its head; from this his error has been strengthened and confirmed. Accordingly, with confidence he preaches everywhere the word of iniquity.

“Therefore, when the abbot of Clairvaux, armed with zeal for justice and faith, rebuked him before the bishops concerning these matters, [Col. 0062C] he was neither confounded nor did he deny them; but, from the day, place, and judge whom he himself had chosen, without injury, without burden, in order to prolong his iniquity, he appealed to the Apostolic See. The bishops who had assembled for this purpose, deferring to Your Reverence, did nothing against his person; but solely, from medicinal necessity lest the disease prevail, they rejected the articles formerly condemned by the holy Fathers. Since, therefore, that man draws a multitude after himself and has a people who believe him, it is necessary that you meet this disease with a speedy remedy, etc. We have proceeded in this matter as far as we dared. It remains, most blessed Father, for you henceforth to provide that no stain of heretical depravity may contaminate the beauty of the Church. To you the Bride of Christ has been entrusted, O friend of the Bridegroom! It is yours to present her as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ.”

Its style shows that this letter was written by Bernard, Abelard’s adversary.

[Col. 0062D] Condemned again in 1140 at the Council of Sens, having lodged an appeal to the Apostolic See, Peter Abelard passed through Cluny on his way to Rome. There, by chance, the Cistercian abbot arrived with Peter the Venerable. Thus negotiations were undertaken there to procure peace between Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and Peter Abelard. At the urging of these mediators, Peter returned to concord with Bernard; and, although he had once and again been condemned for heresy in councils, he was nevertheless gladly and willingly admitted into fellowship at the Cluniac monastery.

I cite as witness to this matter Peter himself, abbot of Cluny, in his letter to Innocent II on behalf of Peter Abelard. Its wording is as follows:

“Master Peter, as I believe, very well known to your wisdom, recently came from France and passed through Cluny. We asked where he was going. He replied that, oppressed by the vexations of certain persons who, to his great abhorrence, laid upon him the name of heretic, he had appealed to Apostolic Majesty and wished to take refuge with it. We praised his purpose and advised him to flee to that well-known and common refuge. We said that apostolic justice, which has failed no stranger or pilgrim, would not fail him; we promised that mercy itself would come to his aid wherever reason required it.

“Meanwhile the lord abbot of Cîteaux arrived, and with us and with him alike dealt concerning peace between him and the lord of Clairvaux, on whose account he had appealed. We too laboured for his peace and urged him to go with the Cistercian abbot to Bernard. We added this to our admonitions: if he had either written or said anything offensive to Catholic ears, he should, at Bernard’s urging and that of other good and wise men, remove it from his utterances and erase it from his books. And so it was done. He went; he returned; and, mediated by the lord of Cîteaux, he reported that, their former complaints having been silenced, he had peacefully come to an agreement with the lord of Clairvaux.

“Meanwhile, admonished by us, but more especially, as we believe, inspired by God, he chose for himself a perpetual residence at your Cluny, having abandoned the tumults of schools and studies. Thinking this suitable to his old age, his weakness, and his religious profession, and believing that his learning—by no means wholly unknown to you—could benefit the great multitude of our brethren, we assented to his wish; and, if it should thus please your kindness, we graciously and joyfully permitted him to remain with us as your own in every respect, as you know.

“Therefore I, however insignificant, yet yours, beseech you; the most devoted community of Cluny beseeches you; he himself beseeches you through himself, through us, through the bearers of this letter, your sons, and through these letters which he asked me to write: command him to spend at Cluny the remaining days of his life and old age, perhaps not many, [Col. 0063B] and lest through anyone’s insistence he be expelled or removed from the house which, like a sparrow, and from the nest which, like a dove, he rejoices to have found, protect him with the shield of apostolic defence, according to the manner in which you cherish all good men and have also loved this one.”

He was called the Dialectician of his age, because of his extraordinary power of argument, by which he was especially effective in disputations. He was accused by Saint Bernard of many errors—errors which many persons of our own times, having weighed the arguments on both sides, think and affirm were never proved against him. It is not our purpose to determine anything concerning this matter. According to the varying party interests, he was accused and acquitted, condemned and praised, by authors of his own time.

## CHAPTER II. On the extant printed and manuscript works of Peter Abelard.

The highly worthy works of Peter Abelard and his wife Heloise were printed at Paris in quarto in 1626, in this order: four letters to Heloise, which may be considered treatises rather than letters. In the penultimate he discusses learnedly the origin of nuns and monastic religion; in the last he gives Heloise and the nuns of the Paraclete their Institution or Rule.

Seven other letters to various persons. A letter to a friend, or *History of His Misfortunes*, illustrated with learned notes by André Duchesne. An *Apology*, or *Confession of Faith*, also printed in Bertrand Tissier’s *Library of Writers, or Fathers, of the Cistercian Order*, vol. IV, p. 254, among the works of William of Saint-Thierry. An exposition of the Lord’s Prayer. An exposition of the Apostles’ Creed. An exposition of the Creed of Saint Athanasius. One book of solutions to problems, dedicated to Heloise. A book against heresies. Five books of commentaries on the Epistle to the Romans. Thirty-two sermons to be read on the feasts throughout the year, addressed to Heloise and her virgins of the Paraclete.

[Col. 0064A] Three books of an *Introduction to Theology*, the third of which is incomplete in the printed editions. Or, as he himself calls it in Letter 21 to Geoffrey of Paris, p. 334, a “little work on faith in the Holy Trinity,” which produced very many enemies for him and against which Abbot Bernard rages. Yet Peter Lombard, the Master of the Sentences, habitually handled this work and kept it almost continually before his eyes while writing his *Books of Sentences*, as John of Cornwall, Lombard’s disciple, acknowledges in André Duchesne’s notes on Abelard, p. 1159. Among the manuscripts of the Bodleian Library, MS 8615; in Langbaine’s miscellanies, MS 2, no. 6: a supplement to the third book of Peter Abelard’s *Introduction to Theology*, p. 148; no. 7: a fragment of the second book of Peter Abelard’s *Ethics*, p. 180; no. 8: an excerpt from the same Abelard’s *Dialogues*, pp. 182–213; no. 10: extracts from certain manuscripts of Peter Abelard in the Balliol Library, [Col. 0064B] p. 247. These items complete the list of Abelard’s works.

He also wrote a commentary on the prophet Ezekiel, begun at Laon while he was hearing Anselm and later completed at Paris, where he had opened his schools; Abelard himself, I think, speaks of it in his first letter to a friend, the one concerning his misfortunes.

The same author wrote a book of *Sentences* and another entitled *Know Thyself*, which he calls his *Ethics*. Saint Bernard speaks of these latter works in his letters, and Peter himself in his *Apology*. This work of Peter Abelard’s *Sentences* is commonly entitled *Sic et Non* (“Yes and No”) in old manuscripts, because it reconciles apparent contradictions in Scripture. It thus exists in manuscript in the public library of Cambridge, MS 168, no. 8, and at the College of Saint Benedict there, MS 391. The library of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea preserves these manuscripts also, together with the *Commentary on Genesis* dedicated to his Heloise, according to Jean Mabillon, in his edition of the works of Saint Bernard, when appending notes to Letter 188.

Indeed, the lengthy treatise of Peter Abelard’s *Sentences*, called *Sic et Non*, which reconciles apparent conflicts among passages of Holy Scripture, is held there under pressmark E. I, beginning: “Since amid so great a multitude of words, etc.” Abelard’s *Hexameron*, mutilated at its end, is kept in the said library of Saint Michael together with Alan’s *On the Art of Preaching*, under pressmark M. I; it begins: “Three passages are taken from the Old Testament, etc.” An exposition by the same Peter Abelard on the Epistles of Paul and on the Psalter is in manuscript in the Colbert Library, MS 4334. These things concern his theological writings. As for philosophical treatises, Francis de Amboise, royal counsellor, who investigated and published Abelard’s works, promised to bring to public light the Logic of the same Peter which he possessed in manuscript; [Col. 0064D] whether he fulfilled this promise is doubtful to me, since I have never heard anything of it, even after making inquiry.

That Peter Abelard, who is also called Peter the Peripatetic in manuscript codices, wrote many theological works is certain; individual little works by him also lie hidden in manuscript in English libraries.

Among the Bodleian manuscripts, no. 8622; in the manuscripts of Anthony à Wood, MS 9: verses of Peter Abelard to his son Astralabe. And in the Cottonian Library, under the image of Vitellius, C. VIII, no. 3: elegiac verses of Peter Abelard to his son Astralabe, *On Morals and a Pious and Upright Life*.

Among the Oxford University manuscripts, no. 458; in the Balliol College manuscripts, R. 5: three books of Peter Abelard’s *Theology*, of which the third is complete, not mutilated and incomplete as in the printed editions; one book of *Ethics*; a commentary on the Epistle to [Col. 0065A] the Romans; two *Dialogues*: the first a dialogue of a philosopher with a Jew, the second a dialogue of a philosopher with a Christian. Likewise, no. 2392, in the manuscripts of Thomas Barlow at Queen’s College, MS 20: two dialogues of Peter Abelard: first, of a philosopher with a Jew; second, of a philosopher with a Christian. Among the manuscripts of England’s cathedral churches and other celebrated libraries, nos. 6086 and 6087; in the manuscripts of Thomas Gale, MSS 252 and 253: Peter Abelard’s *Dialogues*; Peter Abelard’s *Ethics*, rare writings, never printed. Likewise, no. 8206, in the manuscripts of the Jacobaean Library, MS 484: Peter Abelard’s *Sic et Non*, but the opening “Sic” is lacking; a dialogue of the same author between a Christian and a philosopher, whose beginning is missing. Likewise no. 8207, in the manuscripts of the Jacobaean Library, MS 485: his *Elucidarius*, in octavo. Among the manuscripts of the same churches, no. 42, in the manuscripts of the metropolitan church of Saint Peter at York, MS 42, no. 10: Peter Abelard, *On the True Essence of God and on the Catholic Faith*; no. 11: Peter the Peripatetic, *On the Sacrament of the Altar*. Likewise no. 6434, in the manuscripts of Charles Thynne, MS 64: chapters by Peter Abelard and his letters. Likewise no. 6954, in the manuscripts of Sir Henry Langley, MS 1: Peter Abelard’s *Doctrine*, in folio. Finally, in the Cottonian Library under the image of Otto, C. XIV, no. 15: a letter of Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, to Pope Innocent concerning the heresies of Master Peter Abelard; no. 16: a letter of the same on the same subject to the cardinals; no. 17: Peter Abelard’s reply against the calumnies of the articles brought against him. Among the manuscripts of England’s cathedral churches and other celebrated libraries, no. 8670, in the manuscripts of the Jacobaean Library, MS 948: Peter Abelard’s *Scholarius*. We leave it to the English to investigate what is denoted by titles of this kind.

Let us now speak of Peter Abelard’s philosophical works, [Col. 0065C] all of which still survive and have been seen by us in manuscript in Parisian libraries. For in the Victorine library of the Regular Canons of Saint Augustine there is an outstanding codex, marked M.M.M. 6, in which are nearly all the philosophical works of Peter Abelard, the Palatine Peripatetic. In this manuscript codex the logical works of the said Abelard occur in the following order:

On Aristotle’s *Categories*, fol. 117. The commentary begins: “But one thing must universally be understood concerning the kinds of substances, etc.” By the same author: *On Modes of Signification*, fol. 127: “The text unfolded above, for the discernment of the signification of names and things, carefully explained, according to the distinction of the ten categories, the natures designated by words, etc.” Likewise, fol. 132: Book I of Peter Abelard, the Palatine Peripatetic, on the *Prior Analytics*. It begins: “The proper and due sequence required by the text demands that, after the treatment of individual expressions, etc.” [Col. 0065D] Fol. 137: Book I ends; Book II of the same work begins, that is, of the *Categoricals*: “Having carefully treated, therefore, the parts or members of categorical propositions of which they are composed, etc.” Fol. 143: Book II ends; Book III begins: “Since we have shown the natures of propositions in these statements, etc.” Fol. 149: Book I of the *Topics* of Peter Abelard, the Palatine Peripatetic: “Just as before the construction of categorical syllogisms their material had to be prepared in categorical propositions, etc.” Fol. 183: the book of the *Topics* of Peter Abelard, the Palatine Peripatetic, ends; Book I of the *Posterior Analytics* of Peter Abelard, the Palatine Peripatetic, begins: “My rivals have most recently devised a new slanderous charge against me as I write on the art of dialectic, asserting that it is not lawful for a Christian to treat matters that do not concern faith, etc.” [Col. 0066A] Fol. 187: Book I of the *Hypotheticals* ends; Book II begins: “Having carefully treated the nature of all hypothetical propositions, let us proceed to their syllogisms, etc.” Fol. 191: Book II of the *Posterior Analytics* of Peter Abelard, the Palatine Peripatetic, ends; *On Divisions* by Peter Abelard, the Palatine Peripatetic: “Not only the necessity of learning itself commends expertise in dividing or defining.” Fol. 199: by the same author, *On Definitions*: “Thus far we have treated divisions, of which enough has been said; now it follows that we turn to definitions, because, as has been said, definitions arise from divisions.”

In the Royal Library, MS 5492, fol. 168, the glosses of Peter Abelard on the *Topics* begin. Thus: “The purpose of the *Topics*, as Boethius is going to say later, is to demonstrate the force of similar arguments, that is, an abundance of probable arguments, etc.”

In the library of Fleury, pressmark A. 4, there is a *Logic* of Peter Abelard, together with the *Logic* of Rabanus.

In the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, MS 635: the *Dialectic* of Peter Abelard, the divine Peripatetic. A few words after the title having been eaten away by decay, it reads: “the purpose concerning the single categorical proposition suitable for a regular categorical syllogism, etc.” This codex perhaps agrees with others; for no leisure was afforded us to examine and compare it with them.

In the library of Saint Michael in Peril of the Sea, pressmark P. H. 12: Peter Abelard’s *Treatise on Understandings*. It begins: “Concerning speculations, therefore, etc.” It is mutilated at the end.

> **Note:** On Abelard’s manuscript philosophical works, see the highly learned preface by M. V. Cousin to the book edited by him, entitled *Unpublished Works of Abelard, Contributing to the History of Scholastic Philosophy in France*, quarto, Paris, 1846. —ED. PATR.

## CHAPTER III. The remainder of Peter Abelard’s life, down to his death.

[Col. 0066C] Not knowing where to turn, he found refuge at Cluny with Peter the Venerable. There, two years later, having become a Cluniac monk, he died at the priory of Saint-Marcel near Chalon, of that order, in 1142, on 21 April, at the age of sixty-three. Heloise, formerly his beloved and afterwards his wife, converted after Peter’s conversion and made abbess of the Paraclete in the diocese of Troyes, died in 1163, on 17 May.

We have as a witness beyond all exception to Peter’s holy life and death Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, in his letter to Heloise, abbess of the Paraclete. After proclaiming and extolling him as truly a philosopher of Christ, he adds:

“I do not remember ever seeing anyone like him in humility of dress and manner, so much so that not even a German appeared more abject, nor Martin himself poorer, to a discerning observer. And though, at my command, he held a higher rank in that great throng of our brethren, he seemed the lowliest of all, in clothing most unkempt. I often marvelled and, when, in processions, I preceded him with the rest according to custom, almost stood amazed that a man of such great and famous name could despise and abase himself so. And whereas certain professed religious, who wear a religious habit, are excessively eager that it should be costly, he was entirely moderate in such things; content with a simple garment of whatever kind, he sought nothing further. He observed the same principle in food, in drink, and in every care of his body. And I do not say that he condemned only superfluities: in word and life alike, he condemned all things in himself and in everyone else unless they were very necessary. Reading was continual for him, prayer frequent, silence unbroken, unless either familiar conversation with the brethren or public discourse about divine things to them in the assembly compelled him to speak.

[Col. 0067A] “He frequented, as he was able, the heavenly sacraments, offering to God the sacrifice of the immortal Lamb. Indeed, after he had been restored to apostolic favour through my letters and labour, he almost celebrated them continually. Why say more? His mind, tongue, and work always meditated upon, taught, and professed divine, philosophical, and learned things. Such a man—simple and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil—having for some time consecrated to God the last days of his life by this manner of living, was sent by me to Chalon for rest, since he was troubled more than usual by scabies and certain bodily ailments. For, on account of its pleasant air, by which it surpasses almost every part of our Burgundy, I had provided him a suitable place, near the city indeed, but separated from it by the Saône.

“There, as far as his infirmity permitted, he returned to his former studies and was always occupied with books. Nor, as is said of Gregory the Great, did he let a single moment pass without always praying, reading, writing, or dictating. While engaged in these sacred pursuits, he was found by the coming of that Gospel Visitor; and He found him not sleeping, as He finds many, but awake. He found him truly awake and called him to the nuptials of eternity, not as a foolish virgin but as a wise one. For he brought with him a lamp full of oil: that is, a conscience filled with the testimony of a holy life. Struck by illness in order to pay the common debt of mortals, and as it grew worse, he was in a short time brought to his end.

[Col. 0067B] “Then how holily, devoutly, and catholically he made first a confession of faith and then a confession of sins; with what eager affection of heart he received the viaticum—the pledge of pilgrimage and eternal life, namely the body of the Lord Redeemer; how faithfully he commended his body and soul, here and unto eternity, to Him—of these things the religious brethren and the entire community of that monastery in which lies the body of the holy martyr Marcellus are witnesses. Master Peter ended his days in this manner. And he who, through his singular mastery of learning, had been known and famous almost throughout the whole world, persevering gentle and humble in discipleship to Him who said, ‘Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart,’ thus, as it is worthy to believe, passed to Him.

[Col. 0067C] “Therefore this man, venerable and dearest sister in the Lord—you who, after carnal union, clung to him by the bond of divine charity, so much stronger as it is better, and with whom and under whom you served the Lord for a long time—this man, I say, God cherishes in His bosom in your place, as though he were another you, and reserves him to be restored to you through His grace at the Lord’s coming, at the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God descending from heaven.”

The Chronicle of Cluny speaks thus of the same matter under Peter the Venerable:

“Peter Abelard by name, recalled from errors of faith by our venerable abbot Peter and Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, abjuring the impious doctrines which he had previously taught concerning the faith, became a Cluniac monk. Thereafter his mind, tongue, and work were always occupied with divine things. He died in 1142, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [21 April], aged sixty-three. His body, granted by Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, to Abbess Heloise, was conveyed to the monastery of the Paraclete.”

The venerable abbot sent to that same religious heroine [Col. 0068B] Master Peter’s absolution, to be hung upon his tomb. It was composed in these words:

“I, Peter, abbot of Cluny, who received Peter Abelard as a Cluniac monk and granted his body, secretly brought away, to Abbess Heloise and the nuns of the Paraclete, by the authority of almighty God and of all the saints absolve him, by virtue of my office, from all his sins.”

We have said these somewhat more copious things in favour of Peter Abelard, whose calamities and shattered reputation have aroused our compassion, and whose genius and power of speech we admire. They are drawn chiefly from the fourth century of the *History of the University of Paris*, both from the catalogue of illustrious academicians, p. 758 and following, where there is more in his praise, and from the *History* passim, where there is very much on Abelard’s fortunes and doctrine. See Noël Alexandre, *Selected Chapters of Ecclesiastical History*, twelfth century, Part III, Dissertation 7, where he sets forth Abelard’s varying fortunes at great length in a work devoted exclusively to that subject. Nor did William Cave omit him in his *History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 1120, pp. 650 and following, 651 and 652.

[Col. 0067]

# ON ABELARD’S DOCTRINE

*(Dom Edmond Martène, Preface to* Anecdota, *vol. V, part II.)*

Learned men had hitherto desired Peter Abelard’s *Christian Theology* in order to clarify certain difficulties and settle the questions debated in the schools concerning his doctrine. Learned reader, you have it in this volume, edited from a manuscript codex of Marmoutier, together with a preliminary notice in which we have recorded many observations that seemed to us worthy of attention. We were not unaware, however, that in our own age Peter Abelard has had defenders who, seeking to exculpate him, have not feared to accuse Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux—a most holy and gentle man—of rash judgment. Whether Abelard is rightly defended and Bernard condemned must be investigated briefly.

For a clearer view of the matter, Abelard’s defenders should not labour so much to show that in his writings he set forth the Catholic Church’s teaching on the distinction of three persons in God and unity of substance, as to determine whether, by writing, he taught nothing contrary to that doctrine. For it can happen, and not infrequently happens, that authors truly Catholic and firm in the Church’s faith, whether through carelessness or the precipitancy of a keen intellect, mingle doubtful and erroneous propositions with true ones—propositions properly subject to continual censure. Bernard did not deny the first point concerning Abelard; he maintained the second.

And certainly, among others, such are the following propositions: “In God, the Father is omnipotence, the Son some power, the Holy Spirit no power”; “Every human being naturally possesses faith in the Holy Trinity.” To every Catholic these present an obvious erroneous and heretical meaning. “But,” you will say, “learned men today turn these propositions toward a Catholic meaning.” Precisely so; but if that is the case, scarcely any proposition in heretical writers exists to which a subtle person cannot attach a Catholic meaning. Just as, conversely, no Catholic writer, however devout, exists in whom contentious men cannot twist certain propositions, sound and devout in themselves, into a perverse meaning.

For example, these propositions are heretical: “Christ did not die for all”; “God does not will to save all.” Yet some can interpret these propositions in a Catholic sense. But grant that Abelard’s aforementioned propositions can be bent toward an orthodox sense: is he therefore to be exculpated, and Saint [Col. 0069A] Bernard condemned, when Bernard brought propositions extracted from Abelard’s own writings before the Apostolic See? Or does the Apostolic See itself, which censured them, deserve less reverence? Certainly not. I demonstrate this by the following arguments.

Whenever an author in writing puts forward some doubtful propositions which can receive an adverse meaning, and, when canonically summoned, refuses to explain them before lawful judges, he certainly ought not to be cleared of suspected error; nor ought those who accuse the author of error to be condemned. Now, after Peter Abelard had summoned even a reluctant Bernard to the Council of Sens, and when, before lawful judges whom he himself had chosen as arbiters of his doctrine, Bernard asked him either to deny or confess the propositions extracted from his writings, or at least to explain them and, if possible, attach a Catholic meaning to them, he was unwilling to do either. What fair judge of the facts, then, can excuse him, or condemn Bernard without rashness?

Moreover, whenever some propositions slip from an author’s pen which, in their obvious sense, offend pious ears, and the author, accused of the manifest error contained in his propositions, denies that he ever uttered those propositions and condemns them as heretical wherever they are found—if those propositions do in fact occur in his writings, must it not be admitted that he wrote them in an erroneous sense, one condemned by all? And can those who condemn the author then be blamed without rashness? But this happened to Abelard. Hear what he himself says in his retraction:

“As for the allegation maliciously laid against me, that I wrote: ‘The Father is full power, the Son a certain power, the Holy Spirit no power’: I therefore shun, detest, and condemn these words together with their author, as is most just; they are not so much heretical as diabolical. If anyone finds them in my [Col. 0069C] writings, I declare myself not merely a heretic but a heresiarch.”

By these words Abelard seems to cut his own throat with his own sword and to applaud Bernard, the censor of his writings, since it is absolutely certain that those words are found in Book IV of his *Theology*.

Indeed, anyone who has once recognized Peter Abelard’s cast of mind will readily observe that the man was so constituted by nature that he could without difficulty teach propositions opposed to one another. We possess a book by the same Abelard in which, indulging his natural bent, he turns all the mysteries of the Christian religion to either side, denying what he had asserted and asserting what he had denied. Our Achéry once considered publishing this work, but, after serious examination and on the advice of learned men, judged it more worthy of eternal darkness than of light. Anyone who considers these things attentively will not find it difficult to judge that Peter Abelard could in one place attribute the same power to the three persons in the Trinity and in another assign omnipotence to the Father, some power to the Son, and no [Col. 0069D] power to the Holy Spirit; nor, therefore, that Bernard is to be blamed for reproving these propositions in Abelard.

[Col. 0070A] Certainly, although the mystery of the Trinity has hitherto appeared incomprehensible even to the most learned theologians, so great a light had shone upon Peter Abelard that he maintained it could be known by reason itself. Indeed, his disciples themselves proclaimed such subtlety in him that, having searched out the deep mysteries of the Holy Trinity, he knew *perfectly and completely* how three persons exist in one divine essence and how, amid the plurality of persons, there is unity of the divine essence. For this Walter—who, after Bartholomew, became bishop of Laon—rebukes him in a letter written to him, *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 473. In it he also refutes Abelard’s way of explaining God’s omnipotence, and sharply charges him with promising, in composing an introduction to Holy Scripture, not so much to teach truth as to set forth the meaning of his own opinion. “For who,” he says, “being orthodox and intending to treat of the Catholic faith, would promise to expound not the **TRUTH** but the **MEANING OF HIS OWN OPINION**? Who, moreover, hearing that not **TRUTH** but **OPINION** is promised, would dare place faith in what follows?”

At the end of his letter he addresses him thus: “By your letters I wish to know whether you believe yourself imperfect in the knowledge of God, or whether you are confident that already in this life you have attained its utmost increase. For this is what your disciples boast, to which your writings seem to testify. Further, inform me whether you still believe that God is not essentially in the world or elsewhere, and that angels and souls are nowhere; for, if I remember rightly, I heard you acknowledge this when we last conferred together concerning certain propositions. Further, among us it has been discussed that your wisdom affirms that Christ, by preaching, laboring, and finally dying, merited nothing; and that no one ought to be rewarded or punished for good or evil works except on account of will alone.”

Yet, though we do not approve Abelard’s license in writing, we judge Gerard of Auvergne’s censure of him far less tolerable. For in the Cluniac manuscript chronicle preserved in the royal library, he writes under Peter the Venerable:

> At that time Peter Abelard was most famous for his reputation for learning, but he taught perfidy concerning the faith. He was also a necromancer and familiar with a demon.

[Col. 0070C] The published Cluniac Chronicle judges him far more fairly, in these words:

> Abelard, named Peter, having been recalled from errors of faith by our abbot Peter the Venerable and Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, retracted what he had formerly taught perfidiously concerning the faith, became a monk of Cluny, and thereafter his mind, his tongue, and his work were always occupied with divine, philosophical, and learned meditation, teaching, and confession. And, as is read of Gregory the Great, he permitted not even a moment to pass without always either praying, reading, writing, or dictating. His reading was unceasing, his prayer frequent, his silence continual—unless familiar conversation with the brethren or a public discourse concerning divine matters before them in the assembly required otherwise.

Accordingly Peter the Venerable, earnestly commending him, wrote such an epitaph concerning him: “The Socrates of the Gauls,” etc.

[Col. 0071]

## APOLOGETIC PREFACE FOR PETER ABELARD

To the most illustrious and most wise lord, Lord Nicolas Brulart, knight, lord of Sillery, baron of Marines, Chancellor of France and Navarre. By François d’Amboise, knight, councillor of the king in the more sacred council.

(*The Works of Peter Abelard, philosopher [sic] and theologian, abbot of Ruys, and of Héloïse, his wife, first abbess of the Paraclete; now first published from the manuscript codices of the illustrious François d’Amboise, knight, councillor of the king in the more sacred council, baron of Chartraine, etc.; with his apologetic preface and the censure of the Doctors of Paris.—Paris: at the expense of Nicolas Buon, 1616, quarto, with royal privilege.*)

[Col. 0071A] Since students have very often lacked living teachers of instruction, or have not readily and conveniently had such highly learned teachers as they wished, libraries came to be founded by nobles or by distinguished and wealthy men. In them books of the best and ancient authors were stored and preserved, as provisions are placed in a storehouse; and from them, as from a rich larder, those eager for learning might in due season draw the choicest treasures of knowledge.

Thus Pisistratus of Athens, Eumenes of Pergamum, and Ptolemy Philadelphus, because at great expense they caused almost two hundred thousand books to be copied from autograph originals, deserved well of posterity and consecrated their names to immortality. Nor did Lucius Lucullus, Asinius Pollio, Trajan, Gaius Pliny, and Tacitus attain less praise for splendor and magnificence among the Romans through forming richly furnished libraries of numerous volumes.

[Note: [Col. 0071C] Thus the author of the Preface writes everywhere, using *f* for *ph*, which we have not wished to alter. The Patristic Editors.]

[Col. 0071B] If those still profane, entangled in the errors of blindness and the foul darkness and deceptions of demons, applied such care to seeking and collecting the remains merely of poets, philosophers, and historians, what should we think of the pious concern of the heroes of the nascent Church in a not dissimilar matter? How much more just is their praise, because they devoted themselves eagerly to this care after the seeds of the divine word had been scattered throughout the world: so that first the prophetic and canonical Scriptures, then the sermons and interpretations of orthodox writers, might be copied with due care and placed in the inner sanctuaries and shrines of churches, like arsenals from which the surest weapons could be prepared against the assaults of rising heresies.

In his own age Constantine the Great strove with great diligence and burning zeal, and by his authority brought it about that authentic copies were sought again from the very sources: that the Hebrew records of the prophets and the Greek writings of the apostles should be reproduced in the languages in which they had first been written for the world; that apocryphal books should be distinguished from canonical books—which Melito and Origen had reckoned as numbering twenty-two—so that the proper honor of each might remain inviolate, and counterfeit wares not be substituted for genuine ones, coals for treasures.

[Col. 0071C] From this, certainly, we see that the purity, unity, antiquity, and universality of doctrine admitted no novelties and allowed itself to be divided piecemeal into fragments. Peter’s *protocathedria* [primacy of the first seat] at Lérins indicates that these are the sure marks of the Church. Thus what Marcion and men of like stamp attempted by corrupting the most sacred writings ultimately met with no success; those writings remained unharmed amid public and cedar tablets, safe from every snare of impostors, so that nothing was found in them by which Arius, Eutyches, or Nestorius could support his cause.

[Col. 0072A] And when certain misguided men dared to foist the canons of Sardica upon the Church as Nicene canons, the entire deception was exposed by the incorrupt manuscript copies of the Nicene canons found in libraries at Constantinople, Alexandria, and Antioch. Eusebius also mentions the libraries of Jerusalem and Caesarea. In imitation of all these, Western churches too established public and private libraries, so that those preparing themselves for sacred orders might use and enjoy them by wholly devoting themselves to the reading of the Bible and the Fathers. Bishops took care that everyone should possess faithfully copied books at home and handle them by night and day.

For this purpose diligent scribes, skilled in signs and abbreviations, were trained. When Irenaeus of Lyons and other sound teachers published books, they often adjured them by all things sacred to copy faithfully what was in the archetypal exemplar and neither subtract, add, nor alter anything.

[Col. 0072B] But the barbarism of later times caused harm. It employed unlearned and ignorant scribes, often even monks, whom their abbots compelled, lest they waste away in idleness, to spend certain hours copying books. Indeed, little women and girls hired out their services for this work, to the great injury and disgrace of learning, until, by the singular favor of God, the art of printing was invented before the beginning of the fifteenth century.

Thus, of the writings left by the ancients—many of which might have aided the right ordering of life and the knowledge of very many arts—few were preserved; and these so corrupted and mutilated that they could scarcely be read or understood. In a short time there burst into print, through engravers, a stupendous indiscriminate mass of authors who had long struggled with cockroaches and moths. Yet far more authors lay hidden, by the fate of books, in that dust and decay of manuscripts, until they were gradually brought forth through the diligent ingenuity of the curious.

[Col. 0072C] If anyone has always had at heart the searching, examining, and investigating of those ancient libraries, I certainly have always professed that purpose from youth: whether following the example of my contemporaries, to raise as far as I could the fallen renown of learning by cleansing its stains; whether because I may have loved textual criticism more than was fitting; or because I delight in that varied and miscellaneous reading.

Thus several letters of the most learned Peter Abelard and of Héloïse, [Col. 0073A] his wife, came into my hands. At first they pleased me, and when reread they pleased me exceedingly. I also began seeking this author’s other works. Some I found written on parchment in extremely minute and most difficult characters, and I corrected them by comparison with various copies; after correction, I repeatedly had a single exemplar copied. But the pleasure of reading and the public and private benefit which those willing to devote themselves to their reading will gain overcame the labor.

For Abelard—or Bailard, if I speak with Accursius and Alciato; or Balard, with Genebrard; or, if you prefer, Abailard, from the French name for a little bee; or Ab Abailard, for this latter form I found in the chronicle of Jean Crispin—was Peter, a young man, lord of a castle-palace at Saint-Nazaire in the diocese of Nantes on the Loire, son of the knight Berengar and of Lucia. Among us it is common to use *ab* for *de* in gentile names, just as I, who am vernacularly called “of Amboise,” might be named Abamboesius.

[Col. 0073B] Both his parents were born of noble forebears. After bearing several children and educating Peter Abelard, whom they had entrusted to be formed by Roscelin’s instruction, they gave themselves over to the bonds of religion. Their son, sent by their command to Paris, grew in the bosom of that celebrated academy, as Erichthonius was reared in Minerva’s lap, into a great man: not only a polymath, furnished with an encyclopedia of every science and knowing all things, but also leader of philosophers and theologians, foremost in his kind, and reputed the first author of scholastic or disputational theology. Hence arose, according to Vignier, the sects of Nominalists and Realists.

Samson, archbishop of Reims, with his suffragans, reporting him to the pope, declared that nothing escaped him, whether in the depths of the sea or in the heights above; that he could readily answer on universal philosophy, mathematics, and any question whatsoever.

[Col. 0073C] When his fellow students invited him to display his ability by interpreting Ezekiel’s most obscure prophecy, he obtained the interval of a brief night and made himself an object of wonder to the whole academy. Our jurists also exercised him in the rough places of Justinian’s law, so that the above-mentioned glossator, on the law *Quinque pedum praescriptione*, of the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, *Code, on the settlement of boundaries*, under the word *praescriptione*, wrote thus concerning him:

> But Peter Bailard, who boasted that he could derive a sound understanding from any text, however difficult, here said: “I DO NOT KNOW.”

What wonder if Azo and Accursius himself, who thought that nothing appeared in the law which they had not thoroughly understood, should have erred so greatly that the great Andreas Alciato, in his treatise on the five-foot prescription, after praising Peter Bailard as a professor famous in his age because he candidly confessed that he did not understand that law, himself mocks and reproves his doctors’ interpretation and their followers Baldus, Paulus, and Salicetus? They try to infer from it the rule that in ancient times no action was customarily brought over five feet—that is, over a most trivial thing—though various actions were established concerning a small acorn, a fish, and an egg: *Digest*, law 1, *On the Action concerning an Acorn*; *Institutes*, *On the Division of Things*, § “Of Hens”; *Digest*, law *Si proprietarius*, *On Threatened Damage*.

[Col. 0073D] The truer interpretation, however, ought to have been drawn from the Law of the Twelve Tables, which provided that, boundaries being fixed between neighboring estates, a space of five feet should be left, through which each owner might go and drive; and the Law of Mamilia prohibited prescription by use over this space, as appears in Cicero, *On the Laws*, book I, and in the *Agrimensor Urbicus*, *On Boundaries*.

From these proofs I judge that Abelard possessed such quickness and dexterity of intellect that he could make great progress in a short time in any science—especially in that called the queen of the others—and reach the goal sooner than another could leave the starting-gates. But later there will be a fuller field for speaking of him.

[Col. 0074A] Héloïse, however—like another Susanna or Esther, beautiful and fearing God, connected by legitimate descent with that most ancient family of Montmorency, not the illegitimate daughter but the niece of a canon of Paris—had been taught from infancy to chant the Psalms in Hebrew. She was the bright star and ornament of her sex; instructed by her husband in the three languages, as well as mathematics, philosophy, and theology, she was inferior to him alone. So great a chorus of gifts of intellect, prudence, patience, humility, every virtue, and chastity adorned her. She revered her husband religiously after the brief and clandestine use, for a few months, of their lawful marriage; she was the most loving wife of a husband unjustly emasculated and absent. One may doubt whether she benefited married women more by example, or virgins, whether while she presided over the nuns of Argenteuil or those of the Paraclete.

If you look to marital dignity and knowledge of languages or Scripture, you would think you saw another Paula; [Col. 0074B] if to the observance of perpetual chastity and the austerity of her conduct, another Eustochium—she whom bishops loved as a daughter, abbots as a sister, and laypeople as a mother. She was so revered and admired by all that, when her husband was pressed by the arrows of envy and calumny, malice found in her and her conduct nothing which it could bite with its “Theonine” tooth (*dente Theonino*).

I examined the eloquence of her letters and thereby recognized and approved the mark of fidelity. Her keenness of mind and her great progress in reading Holy Scripture and the Fathers are sufficiently shown by those problems or doubts which she set down in writing for her lord, teacher, and husband to resolve. Whoever reads them attentively will acknowledge the truth of Aristotle’s celebrated saying: it is no less difficult to formulate a question well than to solve it well.

I pass over how subtly this heroine satisfied Saint Bernard, who was lodging at the monastery of the Paraclete, when he—though he thought rather unfairly of Abelard—asked why, in the public recitation of the Lord’s Prayer, she used the words “our supersubstantial bread,” whereas the other churches commonly said “daily.” Supported in reply by the distinction of the Greeks, whose authority, as Ambrose says, is greater, she adduced the text of Matthew alone: **τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν τὸν ἐπούσιον**, “our supersubstantial bread.” She preferred a translation from Hebrew to the wording of her own language, as may be seen in the fifth letter of the second book, addressed to that same Lord Bernard.

[Col. 0074C] Happy—oh, exceedingly happy—pair of spouses, and marriage well united amid unequal fortunes, not divided even in death, if he could have avoided the assaults of envy as successfully as she did in the weaker sex! O divinely gifted husband and wife, most highly cultivated in every branch of learning, whom neither the preceding age nor any following age produced as equals!

Yet although Héloïse possessed such gentleness that no one ever dared hurl the darts of malevolence against her or oppose her gentleness, how many grievous things to recount and harsh things to endure must we think rushed upon her! For she was often attacked, struck, and, as it were, pierced through the side of the husband whom she loved with her whole heart. In her own heart she often endured whatever the ill will and cruelty of the envious and hostile could inflict upon the reputation and body of her earthly bridegroom.

[Col. 0074D] Despising this world’s enticements, she consecrated herself wholly to Jesus, her heavenly bridegroom, and of her own accord crucified her own flesh: a woman truly strong, like the prudent women mentioned in the Gospel who provided themselves with many works of piety lest oil fail in their lamps.

The Batavian Siren wrote to the virgins of Cologne consecrated under the name of the Maccabees a comparison between virgin and martyr. She maintains that a truly continent person falls little short of a martyr: the martyr suffers his flesh to be cut by the executioner, while the virgin or continent person daily mortifies her flesh and is, in a sense, her own executioner. The martyr delivers up her body; the virgin or widow subdues, reduces, and tames it into the service of the spirit.

[Col. 0075A] These words may certainly be applied to our Héloïse, who renounced in this life lusts, riches, pleasures, pride, luxury, gems, purple garments, and enjoyments; loving nothing in this age, dead to the world, and living for Christ alone. To be held fast in his embraces, she uttered dove-like groans, and by prayers, psalmody, sacred reading, silence, fasts, and pious occupations reduced her body to servitude. This is no less praiseworthy in a continent woman than in a virgin, since it is a greater virtue to abstain from things pleasing though good. Jerome, however, thinks differently, judging the preservation of chastity more difficult in a virgin, who imagines that what she has not experienced is greater and sweeter.

Peter himself, in the letter which we have placed before the whole work, speaks briefly and modestly of his beloved wife and sister. He recounts the history of his own life, his miseries and afflictions—indeed, even his deaths: how, while sleeping, he was made a eunuch by the uncle and kinsmen of his wife in a most savage and shameful act of vengeance; how, after taking the monastic habit in the monastery of Saint Denis, he was ill-treated by the brethren because, from Bede’s second writing on the Acts of the Apostles, he had raised that controversy concerning the two Dionysiuses, one the Areopagite, the other the Corinthian.

[Col. 0075B] On this point we set out our judgment in the preface placed before the histories of Gregory of Tours, and in our defense of him against Flacius’s calumnies: we followed Cardinal Baronius rather than Gregory of Tours.

He also recounts how he presented at Soissons before the legate his treatise *On Divine Unity and Trinity*, composed for the benefit of his students, who demanded human and philosophical reasons, and was compelled, without any examination of the matter, to throw it into the fire with his own hand. How grievous this was let those judge who know that authors love their books no less than fathers love their children.

The other matters he recounts in this letter concerning his calamities, not without the keenest feeling of pain and evidence of patience—his retreat into solitude, the first foundations laid in the wilderness of the Paraclete, the depraved conduct of the monks of Ruys over whom he presided, and the oppression of a tyrannical neighbor—can be repeated better by the author himself than by me. My purpose is rather to defend my Abelard, if not from error, which may befall a worthy man, at least from the falsely alleged bondage of heresy.

[Col. 0075C] These most just causes impelled me to seek, collect, read, and reread all the copies I could obtain in various provinces, assuredly copies of the best quality and not devoid of value, and to form the plan of publishing them: both in order to benefit the republic of sacred learning and to defend our France from the impostures of those who deny the perpetual truth of what Saint Jerome, citing Pliny, affirms: that she alone lacks monsters.

For what better could I do than rescue from the flames the name, even in his last days, of an utterly innocent monk, and dedicate to our own age and to posterity the works of a most learned writer, elaborated through great sweat and sleepless labor?

Accordingly, I obtained one copy of the letters in Armorica, where as a young man I first entered upon the duties of the broad-striped gown and my senatorial rank; a second from Philip de la Porte, abbot of Tiron, an excellent poet and my closest friend, who affirmed that he had received it from the heirs of Stephen Gormelain of Corseul; a third from the monastery of the Paraclete. I went there so that I might gather for public use whatever of Abelard’s works I could find there. I was received courteously and, through the graciousness of the reverend Lady Marie de Rochefoucauld, my most wise kinswoman, was led by the hand to the adjoining tombs of the founder and foundress.
