[Col. 0075D] For her paternal grandmother, Antoinette d’Amboise, who married the knight Torquato Barbesius, only daughter of Vidi d’Amboise and niece and heiress of Charles de Calvimont, lord and marshal of France, increased the whole most ancient family and transferred our eldest line to the Rochefoucaulds.

She also shared with me homilies for the divine office, to be read throughout the whole course of the year, written in Abelard’s style, together with collects and hymns. In them a great light of Catholic piety shines forth, whether one reads or sings them.

[Col. 0076A] I obtained various short works from the library of Navarre; homilies from the celebrated College of the Sorbonne; five books of commentary on the Epistle to the Romans from the monastery of Saint Michael of the Mount, or “in peril of the sea,” which the most learned Father Jacques Sirmond, theologian of the Society of Jesus, gave for use to Antoine du Chesne; and three books of the *Introduction to Theology*, of more recondite learning, from a manuscript codex of the library of the Canons Regular of Saint Victor near our walls. Other items came from elsewhere, as I have indicated in their proper places.

Unless those Fathers had known these works to be useful to professors of the Catholic, apostolic, and Roman faith, they surely would have consigned them to avenging flames to be burned. Instead, they gave us works preserved by God with such care, to be copied and brought into public view.

I devoted no small labor to examining and correcting them by collation, in order to fulfil a vow by which I had long been bound, when I allowed my booklet on the council to be published. If I found anything difficult, I shared it with my brother, the Right Reverend Adrien d’Amboise, bishop of Tréguier, eminent among theologians, and with other friends as well. Neither they nor I found in these works anything whose reading could be unfruitful.

[Col. 0076B] Nevertheless, lest I should be lashed by a silent or open reproach of tongue or thought, I resolved first to publish the accusations against Abelard and the defenses and refutations on his behalf, and to examine them strictly by the weights and measures of arguments, lest anyone accuse me of acting rashly or wrongly.

Athletes—indeed, most valiant warriors—are brought into the arena, whose powers of intellect, reputation, and more than life itself are put at stake:

> For no light or sportive prizes are sought,  
> But they contend, like Turnus, for life and blood.

[Col. 0076C] And as the poet says of Hector in the twentieth book of the *Iliad*:

> **Πρόσθε μὲν ἐσθλὸς ἔφευγε, δίωκε δέ μιν μέγ᾽ ἀμείνων,**  
> **Καρπαλίμως, ἐπεὶ οὐχ ἱερήιον οὐδὲ βοείην**  
> **Ἀρνύσθην, ἅ τε ποσσὶν ἀέθλια γίνεται ἀνδρῶν,**  
> **Ἀλλὰ περὶ ψυχῆς θέον Ἕκτορος ἱπποδάμοιο.**

> Before this, the brave man fled, but a far better man pursued him swiftly; for they were not contending for a sacrificial beast or an ox-hide, such as become prizes for men in foot-races, but they ran for the life of horse-taming Hector.

The accompanying Latin verses read:

> Here, then, borne on in the race, one fled while the other pressed hard;  
> the good and brave man sped ahead on swift foot;  
> the better followed. For the contest was not for a bull’s hide,  
> nor for an ox—such prizes as are wont to be given in races—  
> but for the life and soul of great Hector.

Therefore this unhappy doctor, numbered among the accused and proscribed, must be brought, most illustrious and consummate guardian of the laws, to the tribunal of your dignity—most august throughout all Europe—the court of the governor of the Gauls, from whose judgment appeal is forbidden, before whom judges of all other supreme senates and provincial courts lower their fasces; to the balance of your divine Themis. There he may plead his cause as though from chains and answer the heads of the gravest charges brought by great informers—or rather accusers—not so much intimidated as relying on the justice of his case and on the innocence of his life and morals.

[Col. 0076D] By this innocence he was not condemned in person by the legate of the Apostolic See in the province subject to the archbishops of Reims; rather, his blind obedience was proved by his burning his writing. From those assembled at Sens he received nothing other than the condemnation of propositions he did not acknowledge as his own; he himself was not heard, and appealed to the most holy Apostolic See.

From Pope Innocent, the best and greatest, to whom the whole matter had been referred, he deserved the token of full absolution and the honorable refuge at Cluny which he had requested. From your most equitable judgments and decrees he will also obtain restoration in full, together with the lawful freedom of advocacy, so that, borne by the breath of your favor, he may be:

[Col. 0077A]

> Praised, flourish, please, be reread, and be loved

through every mouth, through the famous academies of the whole world, and through the libraries of scholars. And, just as an edict of the Divine Augustus was issued for retaining the *Aeneid*, so let an edict of Lord Brulart be published, decreeing that Abelard’s learned works are not to be destroyed.

For your Excellency can easily heal, by your glance alone, the impaired reputation of a philosopher and theologian who to this day has languished no less than those displayed for passers-by to see at the shrine of Aesculapius. For you are Brulart of Sillery, in whose hand lies every power of enacting and repealing laws; you preside in the lofty, star-filled, illustrious, and shining summit and zenith, so to speak, of magistracies and every honor. As the sun displays splendor to the world, so you display it to this kingdom. From that most brilliant circle, shining amid flames, you offer yourself from an exalted watchtower as a Cynosure to honorable studies.

You have healed, to the applause of all good people, the wounds inflicted on France by the injustice of former times. You have, if not uprooted, at least in large measure cut back and removed the seeds of quarrels and lawsuits, especially courtly ones, than which there could be no more deadly plague. You have strengthened the French state when it often wavered under adverse fortune; when at times it was almost extinguished and overthrown by dissensions, you alone not only restored it but also greatly increased it. Publicly you have always cultivated justice, and privately temperance and self-restraint, from your earliest years. By your three embassies—to Navarre, Switzerland, and Rome—you demonstrated that you were born for the public good, and matched good fortune to great virtues.

[Col. 0077B] To omit other merits, extraordinary not merely toward kings but toward your country and individuals: it is no wonder that, born of so great a father, resplendent in the ancient pedigrees of a most ancient house, and moved by such illustrious domestic examples, you have conceived and performed nothing that was not excellent, great, and worthy of knightly and patrician forebears.

Because you command silence concerning your father when speaking of you, I shall say only this: by the order of fate and hereditary right, the royal signet-office came to you. On account of the outstanding and heroic virtues of the lord president de Berny, all good people cried out that its administration was owed to that parent of yours, the most upright Cato of our age. Those who knew his wisdom and constancy, and admired them, confess that he surpassed by far those two Romans—or three hundred Socrateses. He will live in their memory as long as goodness, judgment, innocence, and wisdom have a place.

[Col. 0077C] To virtue, which he always held as his guide, he joined good reputation as its companion—without which life would be unpleasant to a wise man. I therefore think you especially to be congratulated, most worthy guardian of justice, because you so willingly take possession of this true and solid inheritance of paternal praise. You steadfastly retain the ancient custom of your ancestors of meriting well of all, enriched by heroic virtues, eloquence, learning, skill, and experience in the greatest affairs. I entreat you again and again to leave this custom attested also by your customary favor toward this author.

O then, Abelard, how fortunate you are! Once struck with cruel blows, you were brought to that most wretched state in which, hearing yourself abused by very many people, all who did not know you well believed you to have been spewed out of the order of things by the vomiting of a nauseated Fortune. But that great Brulart came to meet you, a saving and protecting genius. You have fled to his sacred anchor, beneath which you need think no waves, however mountainous, and no storms or tempests are to be feared. See how little you ought to fear with so great a judge; see what a light of clemency and equity rises before your eyes.

[Col. 0077D] Let your rivals, adversaries, and mockers come, then, and contend with you by charges—yes, even by insults. For what insult is more severe than to be called a heretic, when envy will always find you wherever you hide?

For here I do not choose to relate what was done through envy at Soissons, while Abelard was still serving among the brethren of the royal monastery of Saint Denis. There he showed himself an obedient son of the Church, proving his case to the legate of the Apostolic See. At the legate’s bidding, he chose to burn with his own hand his commentary on the Trinity—though he believed it contained nothing contrary to the faith—rather than furnish an occasion for scandal.

There will be a mighty contest in the ancient city of Sens. The battle-line will be led by a most valiant chief centurion, both witness and author above every exception: Saint Bernard, son of Tesselin, first abbot of Clairvaux, light and pillar of his order. A disciple of the woods, he was called a doctor of the Church truly taught by God; he was renowned for miracles before and after his death, and was enrolled among the heavenly host by Alexander III. His fame and authority were so great, and still flourish now, that no one could rightly use concerning him the formula, “I do not want this man; he is timid,” without immediately seeming foolish not to agree; and to wish to oppose him in any respect or detract from his credibility would seem close to impiety.

[Col. 0078A] When Bernard heard that Abelard had returned from the monastery of Saint-Gildas—which he had renounced—and that several little works, partly truly and partly falsely attributed to him, were being read, he conceived indignation which he judged fitting. He stirred and summoned the leaders of the Church to the Synod of Sens, brought Abelard before them as accused of violating religion, and sent the principal heads of his grave accusation to the cardinals and Pope Innocent.

Many were roused to spiritual arms by this trumpet-call. But it is better to hear the blast of the trumpet itself: namely, the letter numbered 187 among Bernard’s letters, bearing the title “To summon the bishops to Sens”:

> A report has gone out among many, and we believe it has reached you, how indeed at Sens, in the octave of Pentecost, we are summoned and challenged to a contest for the defense of the faith—although the servant of God ought not to quarrel, but to be patient toward all.

I refrain from the following words, which the reader may find in book II of this work. It was not enough unless this man of God, endowed for eloquence by nature rather than art, had awakened by this cockcrow the bishops and cardinals resident in the Roman court through another letter, beginning: “No one doubts that it belongs to you to remove scandals from the kingdom of God.” There, in book II, you will find these barbs directed against Peter:

> Read, if you please, the book which he calls *Theology*; read also the other which they call his *Sentences*, and likewise that entitled *Know Thyself*; and observe how great a crop of sacrileges and errors runs wild there.

Peace to the matter; I shall add no more. Rather I am inclined to cry:

> …Are there such great angers in heavenly minds?

[Col. 0078C] For with the same tenor—indeed, the same fervor—Bernard sends through his servant and messenger Nicholas a letter to Innocent II, beginning: “It is necessary that scandals come. Necessary, but not pleasant.” After securing goodwill in the opening, he briefly narrates the events at Sens before King Louis VII in an assembly of bishops, abbots, and very many religious and clerics.

From this one may infer that Abelard was not heard while standing to make his defense, but that certain matters began to be read; unwilling to hear them, he departed and appealed to the Apostolic See. Bernard thinks this was not permitted to him and applies the torches of conflagration in order to extort his condemnation: “We have escaped the lion,” he says, “but have fallen upon the dragon.”

Not content with this, he collects articles of heresies, sweeps up trifles from every quarter out of papers, lectures, and writings—some of which were Abelard’s, some circulated under his name—and, having received certain things even from ill-wishers, he—a holy man indeed, but one who, while in prison, could be deceived—sent them to Innocent as true and established facts. Although these are not found in the letters published under Bernard’s name, yet because I discovered them in a certain manuscript (that I may conceal nothing), I have taken care to transcribe them in good faith. This is not because I suppose that Abelard, or anyone else, was of so perverse a mind as to wish to rave in such absurd and impious propositions; rather, the more discordant and impious those doctrines are, the more they ought to be judged alien from, and many parasangs distant from, the mind and understanding of so pious and well-conducted a monk, who never acknowledged the books from which the greater and more dangerous part of these articles was excerpted.

But if certain charges are made from his genuine writings, one must have recourse to his real meaning, and not turn against him words that have been cut short. For there is nothing which cannot be corrupted by reporting it badly; and it often happens that, if some teacher treats a question problematically and on both sides, an ill-employed smatterer takes the arguments for doubt as arguments for decision. We have often seen this happen, and lately at the castle of Fontainebleau in a disputation before the king and the most celebrated assembly of French nobles. For who could refrain from laughing—or rather, from indignation—if he read in the *Summa Theologiae* of that angelic Thomas Aquinas, question 3, article 1, these words:

> Whether God is a body: it seems that he is. For a body is that which has three dimensions. But Sacred Scripture attributes this to God; for it is said: “He is higher than heaven, deeper than hell” (Job 11); therefore God is a body.

If someone thrust these words upon us as Thomas’s doctrine, would he not mingle heaven with earth and sea with heaven? Yet the conclusion of that same doctor—which the impostor would have suppressed—is diametrically opposed. It is as follows:

> Since God is the first unmoved mover, the first being, and the noblest of all, it is impossible that he should be a body. To the first objection, therefore, it must be said that Sacred Scripture conveys spiritual and divine things to us under bodily likenesses, etc.

Let us therefore come to the aforesaid articles, which that great man, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, is said to have sent to Pope Innocent II, having been found—if it is lawful to believe it—partly in the book *Theology*, partly in the book *Sentences*, partly in the book entitled *Know Thyself* (*Scito teipsum*). Abelard denied having written the latter two books. Concerning these detestable errors anyone may use the words:

> Alas! Can so great a crime fall upon anyone?

[Col. 0079C]

That the Father is full power, the Son a certain power, and the Holy Spirit no power.

That the Holy Spirit is not of the substance of the Father or the Son.

That Christ did not assume flesh in order to free us from the yoke of the devil.

That neither God and man, nor this person who is Christ, is the third person in the Trinity.

That free will by itself suffices for some good.

That God can do or omit only those things which he does, only in the manner in which he does them, and only at the time when he does them—and not otherwise.

That God neither can nor ought to prevent evils.

That we have not contracted guilt from Adam, but punishment only.

That those who crucified Christ in ignorance did not sin, and that whatever is done through ignorance ought not to be imputed as guilt.

That in Christ there was no spirit of the fear of the Lord.

That the power of binding and loosing was given only to the apostles, not to their successors.

That through works a man becomes neither better nor worse.

That operation properly or specially belongs to the Father, who is not from the mind, and not wisdom and goodness as well.

That the devil introduces suggestions through the operation of stones or herbs.

That the coming at the end of the world can be attributed to the Father.

[Col. 0080A]

That Christ’s soul did not itself descend into hell, but only by power.

That neither an act, nor a will, nor concupiscence, nor pleasure when it moves the soul, is sin; nor ought we to wish it extinguished.

I do not believe there is anyone washed in the water of baptism and, as they say, endowed with a rich Minerva—that is, thoroughly instructed in the mysteries of faith—who could think of defending and maintaining propositions so absurd, so foreign to the creeds of faith, so horrible. Nor do I think one must labour excessively to weaken this opinion, since Abelard’s life, spent piously and in the fear of God, gives no scent of any doctrine except one holy, harmonious and consonant with the interpretations of Sacred Scripture and the Fathers. If it is true that faith is shown and reveals itself in works, he himself undertook a singular struggle to combat heresies; and if perhaps any otherwise expressed statements are found in his book *Theology*, he retracted them in a public confession of faith issued by himself, corrected either by the force of reason or by the authority of Scripture.

There follows another letter of the same Bernard to the same pope Innocent, of the same subject as the preceding letters—except that it is more lengthy in accusation and argument—whose opening is: “It is necessary that this be referred to your apostolate.” “You have,” he says, “in France a new theologian from an old master, who from his earliest age played at dialectic and now raves in the sacred Scriptures. While, of all things that are in heaven above and on earth below, he deigns to be ignorant of nothing save, I know not what, himself alone, he sets his mouth in heaven.”

Since the remainder contains nothing except what is rehearsed in the articles written above, I prefer that the fair-minded and curious reader seek it in the letter itself, which is long and learned. Whoever has read it all should not give a definitive judgment until he has first read the brief reply:

> He who decides when the other side has not been heard,  
> Though he has decided rightly, has not been fair.

[Col. 0080C]

Nor was that eminent head of a monastery content to issue, in his own person, a pamphlet of fitting magnitude, and to draw his pen against Abelard with so many, such great, and such bitter barbs, unless he also stirred up Samson, archbishop of Rheims, and three of his suffragans, as though to extinguish a common conflagration. For he dictated letters in their names to the pope, so that through them the accusation might have greater weight. Two commendatory letters are added as an appendix: one to Cardinal Guido of Castello, who had heard Peter in theology and was later elected pope, taking the name Celestine; the other to Cardinal Ivo also, of the same tenor.

In the former he continually objects that little book, *Γνῶθι σεαυτόν*—“Know Thyself”—which Peter emphatically denied having written. With this vast opening of accusation, that accuser of great renown forestalled every resource that might serve the defendant. But what proofs does he then adduce? None, or almost none; for the letters are brief. Whatever he has said verbatim, Scaurus denies in a word. For if accusation sufficed, who would ever be innocent? There is also the worn saying: “As one man is no man, so one witness is no witness.” And if anyone asks what was the fruit and outcome of so many writings and so much voluntary labour, it was certainly twofold.

For Innocent, Christ’s vicar and supreme judge in matters of faith—whom no orthodox person dared oppose or even mutter against—by his rescript condemned outright, and before the other side had yet been heard, the heads of the doctrines sent to him and ascribed to Peter Abelard, though not Peter’s own person for heresy. If Abelard, appearing before the court at Rome to refute the objections, had been granted some hours, a few days, or adjournments, perhaps the die would have fallen otherwise. But the most powerful accusers, triumphing as though in white chariots, sang a joyful paean and spread abroad their victory throughout the world. Thus that unhappy man, unheard, was ill-spoken of among very many honourable people; and copies of his works, which had illuminated Gaul and Italy by their splendour, were handed over as poems of a dreadful crime either to be burned in devouring pyres, or to rot hidden amid the damp, grime, and ashes of old libraries. They were no longer entrusted to Tryphon and other copyists—their true physicians—for correction; indeed, they would have perished utterly, unless some good genius and divine impulse had stirred us to seek them out, raise them from the dust, emend them, and publish them.

This is especially confirmed by the testimony of those whom we shall show below to have thought and written well of them, and to have held his various writings in delight and admiration. Their unanimous voice was that Abelard did not intend to write anything against the received faith of the Church; and that, if anything of the kind had crept in, it should be believed to have come from elsewhere, or perhaps through the fault of copyists. Nor ought the reader, where much shines in a work, to be offended by a few blemishes:

> … which negligence has poured forth,  
> Or human nature has insufficiently guarded against.

[Col. 0081B]

For neither a great good is spoiled by a small evil, nor what is useful by what is useless:

> Evils lie near to goods; under error itself,  
> Virtue has often borne accusations in place of vice.

Yet we must not proceed to such rashness as to dare assert that he never erred. Rather, if he erred in anything, he did so not through heretical perversity—for only obstinacy resisting the Church’s doctrine and authority makes a man a heretic—but through the weakness of human nature, or perhaps through excessive powers of intellect. And if there was any fault, he made amends for it, so that he might defend himself under the law of the Twelve Tables: “The same law for the sound as for the strong.” [The reading is uncertain.]

Meanwhile, it pleases Bernard, that strong warrior, as it were to bring forward some writers of those and subsequent times as reinforcements, who supported his opinion, as though they depended on his mouth or writings, lest anyone suppose that I either did not know them or wished to hide them in silence. Let the company therefore be led by Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, most eloquent writer of Bernard’s life and most ardent defender of his master’s reputation. These are his words, Book III, chapter 5:

> In those days there was Peter Abelard, a distinguished master and most famous in the repute of learning, but treacherously teaching doctrine concerning the faith. When writings full of most grievous blasphemies of his began to fly about everywhere, learned and faithful men brought these profane novelties of words and meanings to the man of God, St Bernard. He, desiring in his customary goodness and kindness that the error be corrected and the man not confounded, approached him with private admonition. He dealt with him so modestly and reasonably that Abelard too, moved to compunction, promised to correct everything according to Bernard’s judgment.
>
> But after this Peter had withdrawn from him, urged by wicked counsels and trusting unhappily in the powers of his own intellect and in his abundant practice of disputation, he recoiled from the sounder purpose. Finally, he sought the metropolitan of Sens, since a great council was soon to be held in his church, and accused the abbot of Clairvaux of secretly disparaging his books. He further stated that he was prepared publicly to defend his writings, requesting that the aforesaid abbot should be summoned to the council if he had anything to say. It was done as he requested. But the summoned abbot utterly refused to come, declaring that it was not his affair.
>
> Afterwards, however, persuaded by the counsels of great men—lest through his absence scandal should arise among the people and his adversary’s horns should grow—he at last consented to go, agreeing sadly and not without tears, as he himself testifies in his letter to Pope Innocent, in which he pursues the whole matter more fully and clearly. The day came, and a great multitude assembled in the church, where the writings of that Peter were produced in the midst by the servant of God, and the articles of error identified. Finally, Abelard was given the choice either of denying that they were his, or humbly correcting the error, or, if he could, answering the arguments and testimonies of the holy Fathers brought against him.
>
> But he, neither willing to come to his senses nor able to withstand the wisdom and Spirit that spoke, appealed to the Apostolic See in order to gain time. Yet afterwards, admonished by that eminent advocate of the Catholic faith, and now knowing that nothing would be done against his person, that he would answer as freely as securely, would only be heard, and would be borne with in all patience—not struck by any sentence—he refused this also by every means. For he afterwards confessed to his own people, as they say, that at that hour his memory had in great measure been troubled, his reason clouded, and his inward understanding fled. Nonetheless, the church that had assembled dismissed the man, punished the abomination, abstaining from his person but condemning the depraved doctrines. But when would that Peter find refuge in the see of Peter, being so far at variance with the faith of Peter? Therefore the apostolic bishop, involving the author himself in the same sentence with his errors, condemned his writings to fire and the writer to silence.

If Abelard were asked, “What do you say to this?” perhaps he would reply: “I do not want this man; I reject him; he is one of the household.”

In the second rank advances one second to none, Vincent of Beauvais, who nevertheless derives what he writes from his predecessors. In the *Mirror of History*, Book XXVII, chapter 13, he says:

> At that time there was Peter Abelard, a distinguished master, most famous in the repute of learning, but treacherously teaching doctrine concerning the faith. Pope Innocent condemned his writings to fire and the writer to silence. Blessed Bernard noted the reprehensible articles in his books in a letter.

Antonius Floretus, who recounted in detail the life and miracles of St Bernard, follows Vincent in every respect. With a few changes, omissions, or additions, the same matters are transcribed in the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, in the continuation of Sigebert, in Antonius Sabellicus, *Enneads* IX, in Bergamo, and in Blessed Platina. I make nothing of these recent, plebeian packers of annals, especially manuscript ones; all taught in the same school, they have fished the same hair-splittings from the same pools to be reported in their chronicles, and in the same words. Thus they must now be regarded as no more than one witness—not eyewitnesses, but merely hearers—and therefore excluded by the same perpetual objection.

[Col. 0082C]

From this one may gather how variously different men relate things. For our man, after lodging his appeal from the assembly at Sens, prepared for a journey to Rome in order to be admitted to kiss the feet of the Apostolic See. But he was anticipated by reconciliation and blessing, and allowed to remain in peace at the monastery of Cluny. There he lived with Peter the Venerable, appointed over the scholastic chair and ordered to sit in the first place after the abbot; yet in humility he was an outstanding observer of silence, except when commanded either to interpret the Scriptures or to preach, as will appear below from the letters of that same Peter. At last, as illness and disease grew worse, he was sent to Chalon, to St Marcellus the martyr, and rendered up his pious soul to God.

Aventinus says that Roscelin and Abelard were founders of a new school, who established the science of words or expressions and discovered a new way of philosophizing. Under their influence two kinds of Peripatetics began to exist: the old kind, rich in producing things, which claims for itself the science of things, whence its followers are called Realists; and the new kind, which draws that science to names, whence these are called Nominalists, because, avaricious of things and lavish of names and notions, they seem to be defenders of words. These matters come from Book VI of his *Annals*, which Vigner has transcribed in his historical library.

John, monk of St Victor near and outside the walls of Paris, says:

> At Sens, by command of King Louis, there was held against Peter Abelard an assembly of bishops and abbots of the whole kingdom. He was producing scandal in the Church by a certain profane novelty of words and meanings. Therefore, in the presence of King Louis and St Bernard, he was questioned concerning many things; and when he was about to answer, fearing justice and truth, he appealed for a hearing before the Apostolic See. Having thus escaped, not long afterward he died at Chalon, at St Marcellus. In the county of Champagne he founded the conventual church of nuns at the Paraclete.
>
> This Peter was a subtle and famous master, most celebrated in the repute of learning, but treacherously teaching doctrine concerning the faith. Pope Innocent condemned his writings to fire and the writer to silence. St Bernard noted the reprehensible articles in his books in the letter which he wrote concerning him to Pope Innocent. Yet his books are possessed by many. “I myself,” says Helinand, “have found many reprehensible things in them.”

Geoffrey of Auxerre had once been this Peter’s disciple, and for a long time was St Bernard’s secretary, etc. And because Helinand has been mentioned, I shall say in passing that he was a Belgian Picard, the subtlest French poet of his time. He composed an elegant treatise *On Death* in vernacular verse; at last, weary of the vanity of this world, he chose the solitary life in the monastery of Froidmont, of the Cistercian order, under the bishop of Beauvais, and was exceedingly dear to that bishop and to the bishop of Senlis, his neighbours. You will find more concerning him in Trithemius’s catalogue of the Benedictine race and the families under it.

The mention of Trithemius draws from us extracts from his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> Peter, a Parisian dialectician called Abelard, French by nation, most learned in secular philosophy and nobly instructed in the divine Scriptures, delighting in novelty of terms and attempting to investigate matters too high for him, was overcome by glory and fell into many errors. Through the action of the holy abbot Bernard, he was condemned with his depraved doctrines at the Council of Sens. From this time secular philosophy began, through its useless curiosity, to defile sacred theology. This Peter wrote several little works which, if he had not mixed errors into them, might have benefited posterity. Among them survives a volume, shadowed by dialectical obscurity and varied with many opinions, which he wished to entitle his *Theology*, Book I, and certain other works. He flourished under Emperor Conrad III, in the year of the Lord 1140.

Conrad’s two bibliographers, Gesner and Lycosthenes, give the same words word for word.

John Naucletus, Volume III, from Christ’s birth, generation 39:

> Under Innocent, Peter Abelard is condemned, as Vincent relates in the *Mirror*, concerning whom St Bernard says to Innocent: “We have in France a new theologian from an old master.”

I shall add no more, since that chronographer himself admits that he took his material from Bernard and Geoffrey cited above. In the same column he recounts a great miracle, which he affirms happened in Speyer Cathedral before Emperor Conrad and a great multitude and concourse of people: St Bernard greeted the Virgin Mother three times, in the hearing of many, and was greeted in return by her once.

[Col. 0083D]

Paulus Aemilius of Verona, most celebrated historian of the French, Book V under Louis the Younger:

> Peter Abelard, a Breton, had most numerous gatherings of disciples, who emulated the studies of all the liberal arts. People flocked to him from every quarter; nor was he content with the glory and learning of his own age. Disputing about God and the Christian religion, he departed from other schools and opinions. Above all, he gave offence because, in defining holy faith, he asserted things contrary to the tradition of the holy Fathers, so that he seemed to hold that theological faith consists of false persuasion and doubtful opinion. If this were admitted, the firmness and certain, unassailable conviction of our piety would be undone.
>
> He joined the force of words, which he called the discipline of names, to theological studies in such a way that, while in his conception of words he proclaimed God, best and greatest, as three and yet one, he seemed in fact to attack and refute this. At Sens an assembly of the Gallican Fathers was held against his doctrines. He was compelled to give his writings to the fire. Yet the young men who emulated learning did not therefore desert him. When a day was again appointed, the question renewed, and he was condemned, he appealed to the supreme pontiff. The latter both condemned that sect and imposed silence upon the man.

Vigner in his historical library offers nothing else concerning Abelard except what he admits receiving from others, among whom he praises Gilbert Génébrard—later archbishop of Aix—as his principal authority.

Bernard Girard du Haillan of Bordeaux, who elegantly committed French history to writing by command and at the expense of Charles IX, says the following about our man under Louis the Younger:

> Abelard—or Abbayelard—an Armorican, was considered a supreme master in dialectic and the most learned man of his time. He had very many disciples and followers who hung upon his lips in order to learn the liberal disciplines; people flocked to him from every side. Not content with these things, he penetrated into the hidden places of theology, disputing obstinately concerning religion and misusing the signification of names.

And shortly thereafter:

> Condemned in a provincial synod, he appealed to the supreme pontiff, who imposed silence upon him.

The historian of French affairs then adds the entire narrative of Abelard’s and Heloise’s love, flight, childbirth, and marriage; then how she took the three vows at Argenteuil and he at St Denis on the Seine; how he built the monastery of the Paraclete near Nogent and afterward placed his wife over it; and how he himself moved back to his homeland, became head of St Gildas of Rhuys, and renounced that abbey in order to enjoy a more tranquil way of life. Girard himself, within our memory, was commendatory abbot of that community of Rhuys; when I was a young man, he counted me among his especial friends in his old age, and I praised him in a panegyric poem.

[Col. 0084C]

Francis Belleforest of Comminges, likewise my acquaintance, Girard’s contemporary and rival, whom I also celebrated in verse, in Book III, chapter 47 of his large two-part work of *Annals*, is copious and Asiatic—indeed, not to say redundant. He heaps up much concerning our man, partly established and partly unknown: namely, that Abelard, swollen with an exquisite knowledge of humane letters and more hidden philosophy, advanced so far in arrogance that, following his own sense rather than that of the Church, he dared to distort many things in Sacred Scripture, introduce new doctrines, and maintain a new and most pernicious opinion for Christians concerning the fate of Stoics and poets. I pass over the other errors which he recounts as pierced through by Blessed Bernard with the sword of the divine word, lest he seem to do a thing already done.

But I cannot accept as established what he asserts under the pontificate of Lucius: that Abelard, before King Louis and a national council, sang a recantation, recognized and abjured his errors. It is sufficiently and more than sufficiently proved that something of this sort occurred under Innocent. He is also mistaken in saying that Abelard passed to monastic life after that vomit; for it is clear from what has been written above that, still young, he entered the Benedictine order immediately after he was made a gelding or eunuch. If it were as Belleforest says, late repentance would not for that reason be blameworthy. Seneca rightly says:

> The road to good morals is never late;  
> He who repents of having sinned is almost innocent.

Concerning Heloise, his wife and afterward abbess, he candidly admits that she was distinguished by the holiness of her life and death. Yet he perversely misuses style and intellect when he criticizes the final clause of the epitaph: namely, that Abelard was boldly shameless and arrogant in boasting that all things which could be known lay open to him alone. As though Abelard, while alive, had composed for himself an epitaph whose author Peter the Venerable acknowledges himself to be—Peter, the constant hearer of Abelard’s most learned sermons, witness to his pious conduct and his death in Christ.

What is altogether intolerable is this: although Belleforest acknowledges that Abelard was reconciled to the Church, passed from a son of wrath to a son of love, was acceptable to the supreme pontiff, and rendered his soul to the Lord in a most steadfast profession of faith, he nevertheless invents that his bones were, long afterward, taken from the tomb and burned and consumed by fire. He cites and has no author for this opinion, unless perhaps Argentré. It can easily be refuted and disproved by the necrology of the Paraclete and by the letters of Peter of Mauriac himself. These testify that Abelard breathed out his soul at Chalon among the hands of the Cluniacs, that his body was laid in an honourable sarcophagus at St Marcellus, and was afterwards sent back to Heloise, who arranged for her husband to be buried in the church or chapel of the Paraclete and, after she herself had died, wished to be joined to him as his inseparable companion in death as in life.

Even today their tomb, dedicated by a common inscription, is seen in the Paraclete oratory, with a record of their anniversary days. At their recurrence memorial rites are performed for the two founders: for the doctor, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [21 April], the day on which he passed to the Lord in the climacteric sixty-third year of his life; and for the deaconess and truly most devoted mother, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June [17 May].

[Col. 0085B]

Thus far we have measured out—and indeed patiently endured—the method of accusation, scarcely confined even in a longer time to the dripping of water; we are thirsty enough to say, “water poured out beyond measure.” It was fair, since the defendant’s case has the more favourable side, to add four water-clocks to the three, as in Pliny. Yet we shall collect the defences more briefly than so great a matter may properly be told, producing a number of witnesses by whom this cause is supported and Abelard acquitted. We have indeed admitted that he was a man and could slip, be deceived, and err in some things—not in all the things imputed to him. But he was not therefore a heretic: he always acknowledged the sacred hierarchy of the Church, submitted himself and his vows to the supreme pontiff, God’s vicar, and gave such clear proofs of repentance.

For these matters I shall cite very many witnesses, not inferior to the foregoing in learning and faith. I always except St Bernard, comparable to none in holiness and the phoenix of his age. When he had not yet passed out of youth, he migrated from his father’s house into the Cistercian wilderness with thirty companions. Hidden among huts and thickets, instructed by none but God, he was believed to be *Theodidaktos* (θεοδίδακτος), “taught by God.” He gained more favour in humility than Solomon in all his glory. By most learned commentaries on the darkest enigmas of Scripture, by most eloquent sermons, and by meditations of profound meaning, he drew all men into admiration of himself, to the renown of his name, love, and reverence. The desires of the whole world flocked to him; the entire monastic and ecclesiastical order seemed to depend on his admonitions and example; bishops, princes, and peoples sought counsel from his oracles, recognized him as arbiter of truce and peace, and all ranks desired to be commended to his prayers.

Moreover, in that self-denial and austerity of the wilderness, many signs and wonders of divine power shone forth while he was still living on earth. By his prayers and merits a boy was healed by a kiss, a lame man made upright, a paralytic cured, lepers cleansed, demoniacs freed, schismatics restored to sacred communion, many monasteries founded, and seven hundred souls and more won for God. Many things also later came to pass which he had foreseen and foretold in the prophetic spirit, especially at his blessed death. Moved by these things, Pope Alexander III, eleven years after St Bernard’s death, enrolled him in the catalogue of saints—what they customarily call “canonizing.” For saints of this kind, after inquiry, are judged by the Church worthy to be inserted within the Roman canon customarily recited in consecration; just as jurists note that some law of the *Digest* or the *Code* has been “canonized” because Gratian inserted it into the body of decrees and canons.

[Col. 0086A]

It is fitting for all Catholics to submit to the judgment of the Holy Roman Church. But this holiness and, so to speak, canonization—which I gladly embrace, seeking his intercessions with Christ—does not necessarily establish as valid everything which St Bernard said, did, disputed, or wrote while he lived on earth; any more than it establishes all the writings of the venerable Fathers of antiquity, such as St Hilary. Although he was a scourge of the Arians, St Jerome nevertheless warns that his writings should be read with suspended judgment. For Hilary, defender of faith in the Trinity, made two statements in which the Church does not follow him: first, that Christ felt no pain in the Passion; second, that he held no created thing to be incorporeal. Claudian of Lyons drew his sword against these errors. Yet for that reason the learning and holiness of this Gallican doctor did not lose the merit of a confessor, whom his mother [the Church] spared as a good son.

Augustine and Jerome attack one another with mutual bites. Jerome, from the words, “It is good not to touch a woman,” and from the Apostle’s words, *κρεῖττον γαμεῖν ἢ πυροῦσθαι*—“it is better to marry than to burn”—tries to infer that it is evil to touch a woman, and argues too harshly about marriage; Senator Pammachius directs his sword against him. This opinion was condemned at the Council of Gangra. Augustine, with Innocent I, declares in many places that the Eucharist is no less necessary for infants than baptism; the Church rejects this. Yet it is enough that the holy man himself did not favour his own errors, and therefore published his books of *Retractions*, wiser second thoughts.

Not even the angelic doctor, St Thomas Aquinas, though he surpassed all philosophers and theologians by long distances and first reached the goal of learning and wisdom from the prisons [of study], could find any disciple or follower willing to swear so absolutely by his words that they could not be contradicted. Many things are found in his very laborious volumes which many do not approve—indeed, things which are not held as certain and established either by the College of Navarre, the Sorbonne, or even the order of Preachers itself, in which he served.

[Col. 0086C]

With the holy abbot’s permission, therefore, let it be lawful to say what his disciple, once a monk of Clairvaux and later abbot of Morimond, Otto, bishop of Freising, dared to record in his *Annals*. Otto was son of Leopold the Pious, margrave of Austria, and uncle of Frederick I Barbarossa, whose life he wrote. Although he held his abbot in great veneration, he writes that Bernard burned with zeal for the Christian religion and, through habitual gentleness—this is Otto’s own expression—was in some measure credulous: he detested masters who relied too confidently upon human reasoning and secular wisdom, and readily lent his ear to anyone reporting something adverse about such men, according to the saying of Festus:

> Much learning turns men to madness.

It could thus have happened that Bernard persuaded himself that Abelard had said or written certain things which he had not, or which ought not to have been understood in the worse sense. Here is our Teucer protected beneath Ajax’s sevenfold shield.

Nor are other defenders lacking, among whom Peter of Mauriac—otherwise called Mauritianus—ninth abbot of Cluny, takes the lead. Although among his own he acquired the title of saint, in the Roman Martyrology he was content with the surname “Venerable.” This is he whom St Bernard did not hesitate to prick, along with his whole order, with the goad of his anger, as may be seen in his Letter 1. Because of Bernard’s nephew through his brother, who had been taken away from him and Clairvaux and made over to the Cluniacs, he says that certain of them came in sheep’s clothing but were inwardly ravening wolves.

Therefore the testimony of this great Father and doctor, joined with Otto’s, will stand the test in Critolaus’s balance with not greater but certainly equal weight. The common saying is: “Papinian defeats men singly, but is defeated by two”—especially since Bernard may seem here to have put his sickle into another man’s harvest.

For our Benedictine, consecrated with the abbatial ring, was in no way subject to Cistercian jurisdiction. Aegina did not overhang the Piraeus: that worthy Burgundian presided over his flock by the little river Aube at the furthest limits of Champagne, while our Breton likewise presided over his own on the coast of the Armorican Ocean. Nor did equal have authority over equal, abbot over head of a monastery; nor did danger arise for our Breton from any cause other than great rather than bad repute.

But if St Bernard, an ecclesiastical man, thought nothing ecclesiastical alien to himself; if our man had to be resisted to his face because he appeared blameworthy, then that Roman judicial procedure concerning the choice of a suitable accuser should certainly have been exercised: the prosecutor ought to have been selected from the province of Tours, not from the province of Sens, and still less from the province of Lyons. For Clairvaux lies near and is subject to Langres, which is under the archiepiscopal jurisdiction of the primate of Lyons. Our forefathers placed him in a higher rank above the bishops of the Celts because Lyons, under the Roman emperors, had been the seat of the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, conveniently situated and accessible for Gauls, Spaniards, and Britons. That dignity still survives today in the primacy of Lyons over the provinces of Sens, Tours, and Rouen, excluding and exempting Rheims and the Belgians. Yet this was not always so. Under Charlemagne, his son, and his grandsons, Sens was distinguished by the title “Primate of the Gauls and the Germans.”

Grant this, nevertheless, to the most ardent zeal and conspicuous integrity of the holy Father: that, being a prelate in the Church of God and the third in that numerous offspring of Cistercian archimandrites, often summoned to the courts of kings and princes for counsel, and having, among the distinguished journeys which he undertook for religion’s sake, accomplished this with William, duke of Aquitaine and count of Poitou—that he brought him back from the wicked conspiracy of the antipope Anacletus to obedience to the true Father of Fathers [Col. 0087C] and to repentance—grant, I say, that he was permitted in this matter to discharge an embassy for Christ. Grant also that, while the dogs appointed to guard the flock were silent and unable to bark, he was allowed by his own blast to summon and awaken the guardians of the Capitol.

Certainly this is to be proclaimed in his praise: that he did not shrink either from Abaelard’s golden stream of speech or from the thunderbolt of his tongue; that, with lofty and unbroken spirit, after Arnold of Brescia and Peter of Bruys, he summoned to examination Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, denounced by his own archdeacons and believed to introduce certain novelties concerning faith in the Trinity; and that he was even prepared to pronounce an anathema upon him before Pope Eugenius III, then residing at Paris. By his supreme authority Eugenius referred the entire matter to his council at Rheims, as Otto himself relates in several chapters of Book I of *The Deeds of Frederick*.

This was indeed that puppy whom his mother Aletha, [Col. 0087D] wife of Tesselin, while carrying him in her womb, saw in a dream as a sign of the future birth: namely, that she would bear a little dog wholly white, reddish on its back, and barking loudly. Troubled by this alarming vision and asking its meaning, she received this answer from a certain religious man inspired by the breath of prophecy: “You shall be the mother of an excellent little dog, who will become the guardian of God’s house and will utter mighty barks against the enemies of the faith on its behalf.” Thus William in Book I of his *Life*. The outcome confirmed the prophecy. For he spared no one, not even the fathers and magnates who held power in the Roman curia; nor did he seek the favor of any very powerful person by even the slightest flattery. Yet he did not have a heart of horn, nor a Vatinian hatred for anyone, nor lasting enmities, knowing that anger might indeed be indulged briefly, but that one must not sin, and that the spur of anger should be used only as a whetstone for Christian courage.

He was quick to anger, yet capable of being appeased. [Col. 0088A] For, like that Roman dictator, he allowed this Peter and that Gilbert, when for God’s sake they sought reconciliation with him and begged forgiveness for human errors, to be restored to the communion of the Church from which they had been cast out, as it were by the edict of a praetor. Most wisely says the great Augustine: “The Catholic Church, in a mother’s bosom, received back very many of her children—like Peter after the tears of his denial and the warning of the cockcrow, or like that same Peter after his wrongful dissimulation had been corrected by Paul’s voice.” And elsewhere: “Peter is placed in authority after he has been tested, because Peter denied; it profited him, because he amended himself.” And St Ambrose: “Even the fall of saints is useful; nor did it harm them to be stained by a lapse.”

There is nothing in human affairs so pure, so holy, or so firm that it cannot sometimes be defiled, shaken, or overthrown—unless the providence of God, best and greatest, which is never absent from its own people in their hour, should suddenly call back, lead back, and draw back through the Holy Spirit valiant soldiers and leaders in the battle line from bypaths into the true way. [Col. 0088B] For, to say nothing of that Adamantius, Origen, who, in order to avoid the disgrace of an Ethiopian—which he was not to commit but to suffer—burned incense to idols and washed away that faint-hearted act by long streams of tears: how many incongruous and absurd things are found in his golden writings, which nevertheless are read and retained, although this is said of him: “Where Origen is wrong, no one is worse; where he is right, no one is better.” Thus Basil, bishop and teacher of the Greek Church, father of so many monks throughout the East, was not approved even by his own followers in every respect. And Tertullian, though in the full bloom of his powers he had won countless triumphs over heretics, did he not, when the evening of life was already declining, fall into the heresy of the Cataphrygians, mixing many poisonous and deadly herbs—as Homer sang of Egypt—with remedies salutary to the soul?

What need is there to speak of Pope and martyr Marcellinus, except that God permitted him, frightened by repeated tortures, to fall for a time [Col. 0088C] and to stagger for an hour, yet not to be broken: after his transgression, having summoned his brother bishops, he pronounced upon himself a sentence of deposition? What need also to recall Hosius and Lucifer, who by their falls provided lessons in human frailty and in an inscrutable mystery?

It would be pointless if I wished to linger longer on this theme, since Liberius himself, successor to Peter’s see, imitated him in weakness: at the beginning of his pontificate he sent his legates to Alexandria against Athanasius, condemned him as refusing judgment, and, although acquitted by so many judgments, barred him from sacred communion. Indeed, afterwards, worn down by exile and by a desperate desire to recover his see, he subscribed to the letter sent from Sirmium by the synod to the Easterners; for this Hilary, carried away by the heat of faith, wished to strike him with an anathema.

[Col. 0088D] Was not the pseudo-council of Rimini compelled under the Emperor Constantius, at the urging of Ursacius and Valens, contrary to the formula of the Nicene declaration and the decree of the three hundred and eighteen bishops, concerning *ousia* and *homoousios* [Greek: οὐσίας καὶ ὁμοουσίου, “substance and consubstantiality”], so that the whole world groaned and, in Jerome’s phrase, was astonished to find itself almost Arian? Yet the Nicene faith was restored and established anew, and the world was snatched from Satan’s jaws through that same Liberius, who, returning to a sounder mind, thereafter rendered outstanding service in restoring, strengthening, and preserving the ancient and orthodox faith—both personally and through those three triumvirs of the Christian commonwealth returned from exile: Athanasius of Alexandria, Hilary of Poitiers, and Eusebius of Vercelli, “the greatest stewards of souls” [Greek: μεγίστους τῶν ψυχῶν οἰκονόμους]. Nor did God permit merely one or two, but many sitting at the summit of the Catholic Church, to stray for a time from the path of virtues, so that, made better, they might learn that true fathers ought neither proudly to insult sinful sons nor to be slow in forgiving those who desire to return.

But to return to our Abaelard: we ought to give God immense and never-ceasing thanks that, because of those storms and disturbances at Sens arising from every side, and because of the appeal to the apostolic tribunal, the little vessel of St Peter was neither gravely nor long endangered. [Col. 0089A] It quickly regained serene calm through Abaelard’s repentance; and God, according to the foreknowledge of the ages, as Hermas the Shepherd says, turns all things—even the worst—toward good. That this may become more readily known, I ask you who have heard testimonies against Abaelard also to hear the authoritative encomia and benevolent judgments of eminent men of his own and the following century concerning his amendment, vindication, or innocence.

Let Otto, bishop of Freising, sometime of the Cistercian order, lead the whole host in repelling the charge. Although he possessed imperial lineage, he spent the first years of his youth under the discipline of St Bernard. Let Father Maurice, a truly venerable abbot, serve as Otto’s supporting cohort. I have therefore taken care to transcribe here Otto’s words from Book I [Col. 0089B] of his *History of the Deeds of Frederick I*, chapters 47, 48, and 49, so that they may carry greater weight.

**Chapter 47.** Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, was so zealous through the fervor of Christian religion and, through habitual gentleness, in a sense so credulous, that he both disliked masters who relied too much upon human arguments and secular wisdom, and readily lent an ear if anything discordant with the Christian faith was said to him of such men. Hence it came about that not many days before this, on his instigation, silence was first imposed upon Peter Abaelard by the bishops of Gaul and afterwards by the Roman pontiff.

This Peter drew his origin from that province of Gaul which is now called Brittany by its inhabitants. For the aforesaid land is fruitful in clerics of acute intellects and skilled in arts, but almost foolish in other affairs, such as the two brothers Bernard and Theodoric, most learned men, were. This man, I say, was devoted from early age to literary studies and other intellectual accomplishments, but was so [Col. 0089C] arrogant and so trusting solely in his own intellect that he scarcely condescended, from the height of his mind, to listen humbly to masters. Yet he first had as teacher one Roscelin, who first in our times established in logic the doctrine of words; and afterwards, moving on to the most eminent men Anselm of Laon and William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons, he judged the weight of their sayings empty of subtle keenness and did not endure them long.

Thereupon, assuming the role of a master, he came to Paris, possessing great power in the subtlety of inventions useful not only for philosophy but also for moving people’s minds to laughter. There, on a well-known occasion, having been badly treated, he became a monk in the monastery of St Denis. There, applying himself day and night to reading and meditation, he became, from keen, keener; from learned, more learned. After some time he was released from obedience to his abbot, appeared again in public, and resumed the office of teaching. Holding, therefore, the doctrine of words or names in natural philosophy, [Col. 0089D] he rashly mixed it with theology. Thus, teaching and writing concerning the Holy Trinity, he excessively attenuated the three Persons, whom the holy Church had hitherto both piously believed and faithfully taught to be not merely empty names but distinct realities differentiated by their own properties. Among other things, using unsuitable examples, he said: “Just as the same discourse is proposition, assumption, and conclusion, so the same essence is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

For this reason, at the provincial synod convened against him at Soissons in the presence of the legate of the Roman see, he was judged a Sabellian heretic by eminent men and renowned masters, Alberic of Rheims and Leutald of Novara, and was compelled by the bishops to cast into the fire with his own hand the books he had published. He was granted no opportunity to answer, because his skill in disputation was suspected by all. These things took place under Louis the Elder, king of the Franks.

**Chapter 48.** Afterwards, while he was again lecturing for many days [Col. 0090A] and drawing after him a very great multitude of followers, when Innocent was seated in the city of Rome and Louis, son of the former Louis, was reigning in France, he was again summoned by the bishops and Abbot Bernard to a hearing at Sens. King Louis, Count Theobald Palatine, other nobles, and an innumerable multitude of people were present. There, while his faith was being examined, fearing a popular disturbance, he appealed to the presence of the apostolic see. The bishops, together with the abbot, sent an embassy to the Roman Church and brought back in letters a sentence of condemnation upon him concerning the articles for which he was accused. A copy of these letters begins: “To the most reverend lord and beloved Father, Innocent, by the grace of God supreme pontiff,” etc.; see them in full in the Appendix. Innocent’s rescript begins: “Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers Henry, archbishop of Sens, and Renaud, archbishop of Rheims,” etc.; seek this also in full below, in the same place.

[Col. 0090B] **Chapter 49.** Peter, learning that the condemnation of his doctrine had been confirmed by the Roman Church, withdrew to the monastery of Cluny, writing an apology in which he denied in part the wording, but wholly the meaning, of the aforesaid articles.

Here, then, is Abaelard praised by a praiseworthy man for his natural ability and philosophical learning; here is that Alexander among learned men portrayed and fashioned by an Apelles and a Lysippus, even with his blemishes. For we possess three letters of the abbot of Cluny, inserted among his works, which make up the greater part of the substantial volume of the Cluniac library recently collected and published by the learned André Duchesne. I do not deny that he also assisted me in collating, correcting, and publishing these copies. Since the reader may easily find those letters in the Appendix, I shall not dwell upon them, but shall merely point toward the sources.

In the first letter, namely that addressed to Pope Innocent II, he says that Abaelard, whom he calls Master Peter, burdened by the persecutions of certain men wishing to impose upon him the name of heretic—[Col. 0090C] which he greatly abhorred—appealed to the apostolic majesty. He says that the Cistercian abbot had negotiated peace between Abaelard and Clairvaux; that they had met and ratified friendship through mutual and brotherly embraces; and that it was agreed between them that, if anything offensive to Catholic ears should afterwards be found in Abaelard’s writings, it should be erased with a sponge. This was done. Master Peter himself, inspired by God, left behind the tumults of the schools and freely chose Cluny as his permanent residence. The abbot therefore asks, both on Peter’s behalf and that of the brothers of Cluny, that he be permitted to spend the remaining days of his old age at Cluny and be protected by the shield of apostolic defense.

In the second letter, addressed to Heloise, the abbot spends several pages in praise of that most wise deaconess. In enumerating her remarkable virtues, he pauses to explain several words of the holy language—Hebrew—which he does not deny were very well known to that eminent [Col. 0090D] woman, as were Greek and Latin. Yet he praises her in such a way that anyone can readily see that he does not wish ignorantly to flatter her, but to show that she was most worthy of marriage with Abaelard, always to be named with honor: a truly Christian philosopher, whom he believes divine providence had brought to the houses of Cluny in order to enrich them in him and through him with a gift dearer than all gold and topaz.

For he declares that he had never seen anyone comparable to Abaelard in humble dress and bearing, so that neither Blessed Germanus appeared more lowly nor Blessed Martin himself poorer. A little later he writes: “His reading was continuous, his prayer to God frequent, his silence unbroken, unless either familiar conversation with the brothers or public discourse to them on divine matters compelled him to speak. As far as he was able, he frequently offered to God the heavenly sacraments, the sacrifice of the immortal Lamb. Indeed, after he had been restored to apostolic favor through my letters and labor, he almost performed this without interruption. And why say more? His mind, his tongue, and his work always meditated, taught, and professed things divine, things [Col. 0091A] philosophical, things ever more learned.” Such a man—simple, upright, fearing God and departing from evil—consecrated the last days of his life to God in his manner of life among us.

Because he was burdened by bodily infirmities, he was sent by me to Chalon. There he was always occupied with books and, as is written of Gregory, never let a moment pass without always either praying, reading, writing, or dictating. In these exercises of sacred work, the arrival of that evangelical visitor found him. He brought with him a lamp full of oil, possessing a conscience filled with the testimony of a holy life. Then, indeed, how holily, devoutly, and catholicly he first made confession of faith and then confession of sins; with what yearning affection of heart he received the viaticum of his pilgrimage and the pledge of eternal life, namely the body of the Lord Redeemer; how faithfully he commended his body and soul, here and for eternity, to him—of these matters the religious brothers and the whole convent of that monastery in which the body [Col. 0091B] of St Marcellus the martyr lies are witnesses.

Thus the master completed his days: he who, by the mastership of singular learning, was known and famous almost throughout the whole world, persevered meek and humble in the discipleship of him who said, “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart”; and thus, as it is fitting to believe, passed to him. At the end of the letter the abbot appends the epitaphs of his friend.

Let anyone now go, if he wishes to deny credence to so weighty a witness; let anyone go, if he wishes to retain the opinion once conceived and vainly spread concerning Peter; let anyone go, if he wishes to deter students from reading the sacred works of so Catholic a monk. But, since mention has been made of the martyr Marcellus, I shall say in passing that he is the one who, bound by arms and hands to four trees, was torn into pieces as their branches sprang upward again, and mutilated limb by limb for Christ. A church was erected to him, which we have venerated, at Chalon in the most delightful district of all Burgundy, near the city indeed but with the Saône flowing between; it [Col. 0091C] is richly endowed and possessed by the brethren of Cluny. On Marcellus and his miracles, see Gregory of Tours, Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*.

In the third letter the abbot promises Heloise that he will arrange for provision to be made for Astralabe, Abaelard’s son, from a prebend in one of the noble churches; concerning this he afterwards also wrote to the pope. He sends the master’s absolution, written upon a charter and secured with seals, in this form:

> I, Peter, abbot of Cluny, who received Peter Abaelard as a monk of Cluny and granted his body, secretly conveyed, to Abbess Heloise and the nuns of the Paraclete, by the authority of almighty God and of all the saints absolve him from all his sins by virtue of my office.

If it is most certain that we are to be judged in the state in which we are found—that is, in which we die—who would not hope and trust with unfeigned charity that our Peter, after the aforesaid profession [Col. 0091D] and confession, was absolved and received into Abraham’s bosom, having heard at the last that sweet voice: “Today you shall be with me in Paradise” [Greek: Σήμερον μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ]. For it was said to the disciples: “Whatever you loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 18); and: “Whose sins you forgive” (John 20), etc. And St Augustine, that is, in *On Christian Doctrine*: “Christ gave these keys to his Church, so that what it should loose on earth might be loosed in heaven, and what it should bind on earth might be bound in heaven: namely, so that whoever should believe in the Church and, corrected from sins, should turn back, being established in the bosom of the Church, might finally be healed by faith and amendment.”

But lest we suppose that the Venerable One was alone among many in adorning Abaelard with the epithet of holiness, there are others near to those times who reported miracles in addition to his reputation for holiness. I shall produce the words of the manuscript Chronicle of Tours:

> “Peter Abaelard had built a monastery in the territory of Troyes, in a certain meadow where he had been accustomed [Col. 0092A] to teach, which he called the Paraclete. There he assembled many nuns and set over them as abbess a certain religious woman, once his wife, learned in Latin and Hebrew letters. She, truly his friend, kept great faith with him after his death in continual prayers, and transferred his body from the place where he died to the aforesaid monastery. In whose tomb this epitaph is inserted:
>
> Here Peter Abaelard lies; the inscription tells enough.
>
> To him alone was open whatever was knowable.”

For, as is said, when she lay in her final illness, she commanded that after death she should be placed beneath her husband’s tomb. And so, when she had died and was carried to the opened tomb, her husband, who had died many days before her, raised his arms to receive her and, embracing her, clasped his arms about her.

[Col. 0092B] Here one is moved to exclaim: “O the depth of the riches of the knowledge and wisdom of God!” Behold, he who had in some manner been reckoned among the wicked after death gives manifest signs of divine mercy, so that where perhaps transgression had abounded, grace might abound. It is surely remarkable that he himself received his dead wife approaching him with outstretched arms and, having taken his beloved into his embrace, gave by compressing those same arms a sign that the covenant of marriage had not died. Whether God wished this as a reward for strict repentance, to show that he does not recoil from those who return to their senses; or whether it was granted to our heroic woman, whom all, with absolutely no dissent, proclaim to have surpassed all the women of her age in faith, example, and learning, and who certainly ought to be numbered among the blessed.

I remember reading something similar in Gregory of Tours concerning the chastity and burial of the Two Lovers, in Book I of the *History of the Franks* and in *The Glory of the Confessors*. Though married, they lived for many years in one bed with marvelous virginity. When the virgin [Col. 0092C] had gone first to Christ and her bridegroom was placing her in the grave, he exclaimed in astonishment: “I give you thanks, eternal Lord, because, as I received this treasure entrusted by you, so I restore it unstained to your loving-kindness.” At this she smiled and said: “Why do you speak when you have not been questioned?” The historian, a native of Auvergne, adds that this husband followed his wife not long afterwards. But when the tombs of the two had been placed by different walls, there appeared a new marvel revealing their holy chastity: when people came to the place in the morning, they found the bodies joined together in the same coffin, though they had left them far apart. Thus the monument of their buried bodies might not separate those whom heaven holds united as companions.

To this day the inhabitants of the place customarily call these two saints “the Lovers” and venerate them with the highest honor. Churches in Auvergne, dedicated to God under an unknown name, [Col. 0092D] stand in their honor; and we ourselves have seen one consecrated to the Two Lovers on the bank of the Seine, not far from Rouen. The same Gregory of Tours relates a similar story of the senator Hilary near the castle of Dijon. He had received a son by his wife and, in accordance with the Apostle, had preserved marriage honorable and the marriage-bed undefiled. He died and was committed to burial in Parian marble; after the course of a year his wife was placed in the same tomb beside her husband, who raised his right hand and embraced his wife’s neck.

But if some, deaf to these mighty works of God and hardening their hearts, hold the writings of the Fathers not in mockery but in contempt, and profess to believe nothing except what they find recorded in the most explicit documentary writings on the pages of both the Old and New Testaments, behold, I offer the text (4 Kings 13): “Elisha died, and they buried him. But certain men burying a man threw the body into Elisha’s tomb; and when it [Col. 0093A] touched the prophet’s bones, the man came to life and stood upon his feet.”

What greater miracles do you suppose there are? The supreme Author of both is present:

> … namely, God, the eternal maker of the world, older than its beginning, more enduring than its end, whose hand has never been shortened, who said (John 14): “He who believes in me shall do the works that I do, and shall do greater than these.”

Let us proceed to the remaining testimonies, on the understanding that we are not obliged to follow strictly the law and order of chronology.

Let us see what is in the Chronicle of Robert, monk of Auxerre:

> “In the year of the Lord 1140, at Sens, in the presence of King Louis, a gathering of bishops and religious abbots was held against Peter Abaelard. He was most subtle in intellect and a remarkable philosopher. He had built a monastery in the territory of Troyes, in a certain meadow where he had been accustomed to teach, and there, [Col. 0093B] by episcopal authority, gathered many nuns. He called it the Paraclete. Over these nuns he set as abbess Heloise, once his wife, a religious woman most thoroughly learned in both Hebrew and Latin letters. She, truly his friend, kept great faith with him after his death in continual prayers, and transferred his body from the place where he died to the aforesaid monastery.”

The *Supplement to the Supplement of Chronicles* of Friar James Philip, hermit:

> “Baliard [Abaelard], born in France, a Peripatetic and most learned in all sciences, flourished in those times in the city of Paris and composed many works most worthy of reading. Since he seemed to waver on certain articles of faith, he was compelled in the presence of Louis the Younger and a gathering of most learned prelates to recant. Thus he not only showed himself free from those doubts or errors, but continued for the remainder of his life in true monasticism with strict devotion. Remaining in a desert place with several disciples, [Col. 0093C] he lived and died in great holiness.”

I shall also add the following historians, who, since they charge Abaelard with no crime, seem to have supported him. The *Annals of the Monastery of Morigny*, Book II: “Peter Abaelard, monk and abbot, was a religious man, an outstanding master of schools, to which learned men flocked from almost all Latin Christendom.” Nearly the same is found in the manuscript of St Peter in the Place—wrongly called St Peter the Living—which records the year of his death together with the epitaph.

Henry of Ghent, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, mentions our Peter in two places and calls him a master of dialectical skill—indeed, of all the liberal arts—and of the theological school.

Likewise, the manuscript Chronicle of the Archbishops of Sens says: “In the year 1142 Master Peter Abaelard, otherwise Abailard, formerly a canon of the major church of Sens, died. He reformed monasteries of nuns, especially the abbey of the Paraclete, which he himself founded and in which he is buried with his wife. For he had first [Col. 0093D] been married and afterwards was a canon.”

It rightly says that he reformed monasteries of virgins, because, asked by Heloise to write on the origin and dignity of nuns and to lay down for her and her companions a rule for serving God religiously, he elegantly accomplished both tasks in two letters. In the former, which is seventh in order, he traces monastic profession from the cradle of the primitive Church, indeed from the sacred college of the Messiah himself and from the earliest ascetics; and he surveys at great length the praises of the female sex and of virginity. In the latter, which is the eighth and deserves rather the name of a book compiled from the sayings of the Fathers than that of a letter, he prescribed a rule for the virgins of the Paraclete. In its threefold treatise *On Continence*, *On Poverty*, and *On Silence*, he gives most salutary precepts and most wisely orders the other duties belonging to the rule of monastic life.

All nuns ought truly to keep this golden little book constantly in hand by night and day; and we have caused it to be translated into the French language. [Col. 0094A] For it yields nothing to the rules handed down by St Basil, St Augustine, and St Benedict, which Erasmus, Melanchthon, and the Centuriators do not deny are genuine and written by those authors. Caesarius, bishop of Arles—as Gregory of Tours reports—wrote rules for men, and his sister Caesaria for virgins, which for some time flourished in Gaul in vigorous observance. But St Maurus, sent by St Benedict into Gaul to reform monasteries of those serving God, substituted for those older rules the new and strict rule of his master. Almost all persons of both sexes use it to this day, except the canons of St Augustine, the brethren in the desert, and the followers of both Francis of Assisi and Francis of Paola.

Francis Petrarch of Florence, restorer, after the injury of the ages, of reviving literature that had been corrupted, in Book II of *The Solitary Life*, counts Abaelard among illustrious and wise philosophers beloved by God, in these words: “I shall join to so many ancient philosophers one [Col. 0094B] more recent, not very far removed from our own age, Peter, called Abaelard—of what faith I do not rightly know, but, as I hear, regarded by some with suspicion, and certainly not of humble intellect. As he himself recalls in a long account in the *History of My Calamities*, yielding to envy he penetrated the remote places of Troyesan solitude, though not without a great gathering of students from every side. The fame of his celebrated teaching had drawn to him as a solitary man disciples from many cities; nevertheless, he lacked the desired rest, which stubborn envy and hatred had uprooted for him at the very root.”

Platina—whether Bartholomew or Baptista—formerly abbreviator of the Roman chancery and afterwards the celebrated compiler of papal history, transfers to the pontificate of Lucius II what others report concerning our Abaelard under Innocent II. Yet he speaks sufficiently candidly about Abaelard: “With Lucius’s consent, a synod of certain bishops and abbots was assembled in Gaul against Peter Abaelard, [Col. 0094C] a Peripatetic philosopher, a man of much learning, not thinking rightly in certain matters in accordance with our faith. Defeated by arguments in the presence also of King Louis, he not only changed his opinion but also assumed monastic life and religion, and thereafter lived most holily in a deserted place with certain disciples.”

Severinus Binius—or some other learned and diligent editor of that great Cologne edition of the councils of 1606—fell into this error of Platina, or *mnēmonikon hamartēma* [Greek: μνημονικὸν ἁμάρτημα, “an error of memory”].
