He writes that the council of Sens was held under Lucius, little mindful that shortly before he had assigned it to Innocent. For Lucius’s pontificate, if we believe Abbot of Ursberg and Onofrio, lasted scarcely seven months, or at most eleven, and extended into the year 1144. But Innocent sat for about thirteen years and travelled in Gaul.

Yet there follows another anachronism by the same Binius, in volume III, part II, of his *Councils*, when he says that the two councils which he calls private—the council of Soissons and that of Sens against [Col. 0094D] Abaelard—were held in the same year, 1140. For the succession and reckoning of dates prove that twenty years intervened between the two. In this I wonder that the learned Gilbert Genebrard, royal professor, also erred by placing only one year between them.

That gathering at Soissons was convened, as Abaelard himself relates in Letter 1, through the agency of Ralph, archbishop of Rheims, at the request of his rivals. The occasion was that Conon, bishop of Palestrina and legate of the Holy Roman Church, was then in Gaul on account of other councils and affairs; he was asked not to refuse to preside. Abaelard says in that letter—the complete report of this whole affair—that Conon had endeavored to favor him. This Conon acted three times or more as legate for the supreme pontiff in the assembly of our bishops, and departed from Gaul around the year 1120, never returning to us after that time.

At that time Abaelard was still under the discipline of the abbot of Saint-Denis, ardent in flourishing youth, [Col. 0095A] and had not yet gone to Count Theobald Palatine of Champagne and Brie to obtain from him a few acres of land and meadow on which to lay the foundations of the cell of the Paraclete. All of this occurred before he was summoned to govern the abbey of Rhuys. But when he was summoned to that assembly at Sens, advancing age could already have sprinkled him with gray hairs—though this is denied of eunuchs—and he had already reached sixty years. Let that diligent investigator of the antiquity of councils be excused by me, if a light sleep stole over him in the course of a long and difficult work.

As for the Centuriators of Magdeburg, although in various places they have made honorable mention of our subject and omitted none of the diligence and ingenuity found in authors of that age in praising him, I gladly pass them by because they corrupted the ancient and excellent body of ecclesiastical history with their new leaven. Nor do I think anything should here be excerpted from the most truthful *Annals* of that great Cardinal Baronius, [Col. 0095B] for whose soul all should pray well because of the vigils and labors which he willingly endured for so many years for the Church’s sake. He recounts at length many matters concerning our Peter and his happy death in volume XII, nearly transcribing them himself from the passages stated above, especially from Peter, abbot of Cluny.

The most distinguished Bertrand d’Argentré, president at Rennes, a most acute jurist and most eloquent historian of Celtic Brittany—who loved me when he was old and seasoned, while I, a Neoptolemus, was undergoing my first apprenticeship in public office in the senate of that province, and whom I uniquely cherished and revered as a father—honourably mentions this Breton and his genius in two places in his *Annals*. First, in Book I, chapter 10, where he lists the great and celebrated men born in, or originating from, Armorica, and assigns Abelard the foremost place in philosophy and theology. And in Book III, chapter 9, in the Life of Conan III, where he adorns him with the title “universal,” that is, “all-knowing.” He means this to be understood not as though Abelard knew everything—which cannot befall any man—but in comparison with all the rest, whom he surpassed by a great distance; trusting in his learning, he wished to establish the foundations of holy faith upon human demonstrations.

Such are d’Argentré’s words. After pursuing this whole history, he complains that Abelard was not heard at the council convened against him, because all—even the learned and subtle—had dreaded the keenness of his intellect, the ready fluency of his agile tongue, the golden river, or rather the fiery, three-forked thunderbolt, of his eloquence, and the griffins of his syllogisms and twisted enthymemes. He says that St Bernard, through excessive zeal and solitude, was inclined to credulity and anger, and carried on a most bitter quarrel with him, writing letters full of acrimony to various persons in opposition to him. He says, “the abbot,” whom he incorrectly calls William; for that abbot, a disciple of Peter, was called not William but Peter Berengar, and he defended our Breton under conspicuous patronage.

Finally, he says that Abelard brought so clear an interpretation to his propositions that matters which at first sight occasioned an anxious uncertainty in thought were, once his interpretation had been understood, afterwards judged true, plain, certain, and consonant with orthodox faith. In that faith, d’Argentré testifies, Abelard died and received Christian burial with his most learned wife, a woman accomplished in Greek and Hebrew letters and never sufficiently praised.

Almost the same things are related by my intimate friend Jean Papire Masson, a most trustworthy historian, in *Annals*, Book III, under Louis the Younger. He recounts Abelard’s Armorican origin; his studies in logic and then theology at Paris; his love affair with Heloise; how she conceived, fled, bore a child, and secretly married Peter after returning; how her father or uncle avenged the injury by castration; how Abelard hid under a monk’s habit in the monastery of St Denis and she under a nun’s at Argenteuil; how he became a most accomplished theologian and she a most learned and modest deaconess; how, compelled to resume teaching, he later yielded to envy and withdrew into the solitude of Nogent, where he built the Paraclete oratory for hermits rather than cenobites, and afterwards set the companion of his bed over its virgins; and how, having been placed over hard-necked monks on the shores of the Ocean and in the Venetian inlets, he voluntarily laid down that burden.

Masson adds the council held against him at Sens; his appeal to Innocent when he was not heard; his humane reception at Cluny by the Mauriacian, general of the order, who reconciled him with St Bernard and the most holy Roman See; and he bears witness to the strict penitence that Abelard underwent and to his truly Christian death. These matters, and many more in favour of this doctor, may be read amid the rough-hewn and broken materials—or ruins—of that architect Masson, who is not to be regretted; they sufficiently show how great a man he was, how dear to God, and how humbly and sincerely obedient to the Church.

But two very ancient poets of our country pull my ear. One is anonymous, living about the year 1360, who poured forth these rhymes, from which it appears that Abelard thought and believed concerning human free will as did the universal Church. Erminius—who has lately departed from us—renewed this doctrine of free will in several towns of Batavia, especially in Rotterdam, the city from which Erasmus sprang:

> Pierre Abelard, in a chapter  
> Where he speaks of free will,  
> Tells us truly  
> That it is an aptitude  
> Of a rational will,  
> Capable of being directed to good or evil;  
> By grace it inclines toward doing good,  
> And toward evil when it falls away.

On this most difficult question one should consult Dr Erasmus’s *Diatribe against Luther’s Bondage of the Will*.

Guillaume de Lorris, somewhat earlier, but the foremost poet of his age, embraced Abelard’s history in that poem, epic according to the usage of those times, to which he gave the title *The Romance of the Rose*. This work, filled with varied and miscellaneous learning but not yet brought to completion, was finished forty years later by Jean de Meun on the Loire, called Clopinel—“the limping one”—an outstanding mathematician. I would not dare add verses in praise of both.

Since Abelard, when young, poured forth many vernacular rhymes in an oratorical style, as it were hybrids, for his Heloise, I wish that I had been permitted to insert in these encomia similar rhymes in that same old language, which may be called rustic among us. In them a true poet tries to draw men away from the desire for the marriage bond, warning them not to submit their necks to the marital halter unless they wish to suffer the loss of liberty.

To prove this assertion, he adduces a memorable saying of Heloise, whom he praises as a learned and wise woman. Though she loved and adored her husband ardently, and had borne him a son who resembled his father in face, she nevertheless did all she could, with urgent entreaties to the man whom she revered after God, to prevent him, for the honour of the woman who had given birth, from making her his wife out of his mistress by solemn rite and nuptial blessing. She kept saying that it was enough for her, preserving mutual love within the depths of her heart, if she saw him adorned with the mitre and episcopal insignia of which he was worthy.

But the poet twists this into another sense, as if she had meant that the embraces of lovers are sweeter than those of persons bound by marriage laws. This must not be taken to mean that she had a mind estranged from and averse to the rights of marriage, or that she wished to prefer the freedom of concubinage to the conditions, however ample and splendid, of royal marriage. Rather, she pursued her lord with such love and reverence that she did not hesitate to choose and vow monastic severity, perpetual continence, and obedience for his sake, rather than, through the obstacle and intervention of their marriage, hinder Abelard, once made a husband, from receiving the reward of his outstanding genius and admirable learning—namely, the purple and the cardinal’s hat. At that time only men eminent in learning were adorned with these, and only by these degrees were raised to the heights of ecclesiastical honours.

But learning availed little without celibacy. For this reason Jason Mainus, the jurist, when at Pavia that Frenchman was publicly expounding from the lectern, before King Louis XII of France, five cardinals, and a hundred nobles filling the benches, the law *Gallus*, Digest, “On the Freeing of Children,” dressed in a golden robe, said that he had never married—although others regarded this as blessed—so that, on the recommendation of the king, who was triumphing over the Ligurians after the conquest of Genoa, Pope Julius II might know him to be eligible for the purple hat. So says Jovius.

Hence Heloise confesses in her second letter that, while still a young woman, she was first drawn to the austerity of monastic life not so much by religious devotion as for Abelard’s sake. Thus these words of hers ought not to be pressed too hard against her:

> “If the emperor Augustus of the world sought me as his wife, I would rather,” she says, “be your prostitute than empress of the world.”

This was spoken figuratively and poetically, as in Catullus:

> My woman says that she would prefer to marry no one  
> Rather than me—not even if Jupiter himself desired her.

For she burst out with these words from contempt for wealth, honours, and things dependent on fortune, and from an overflowing marital love and matronly chastity. Further, they came from the reverence and devotion which admiration for his divine genius, incomparable learning, faith, integrity, and constancy had produced in the woman’s mind. If an immediate death for her husband were necessary, she would readily have surpassed Evadne, Penelope, Alcestis, Brutus’s Porcia, or Paetus’s Arria in devotion—or all those women of whom Propertius wrote these elegiac lines:

> Happy is the single law of death for Eastern husbands,  
> Whom red Dawn colours with her own horses.  
>
> For whenever the final torch is joined to the death-bearing bed,  
> A pious throng of wives stands with hair unbound.  
>
> The wives compete: which living woman shall follow  
> Her husband? It is shame not to have been allowed to die.  
>
> The victors burn and offer their breasts to the flames,  
> And lay their scorched faces upon their husbands’.

I had almost omitted the encomium of both by that excellent old man, a person of the highest distinction and in every respect most learned, my teacher Étienne Pasquier. While I was writing this, he died peacefully in God at almost ninety years of age, to the great grief of all. That other Varro and diligent investigator of antiquities devoted the nineteenth chapter of Book V of his *French Investigations* entirely to describing the loves, sufferings, and miseries of Abelard and Heloise, and to composing their praises—for constancy and other virtues, and, above all, for learning worthy of admiration. By these they won great celebrity and glory; Abelard also won from it the fiercest flames of envy, from which he was delivered by divine assistance.

In the continuous and varied narration of these events, that wondrous encomiast deployed every sinew of his eloquence. The succession of Abelard’s misfortunes, the variety of times, and the changes of fortune bring the reader great delight, if not joined with pain, at least with compassion, when the matter is presented as though before one’s eyes; they inspire admiration, astonishment, joy, and hope—especially since the entire subject concludes with a remarkable end: namely, Abelard’s pious falling asleep in Christ after bitter repentance, and his burial, which he received in the bosom of his beloved, as he himself had greatly desired and directed in his last testament.

Of Heloise Pasquier speaks in such a way as neither to take away her true praise nor to attach a false one. In sum, he grants her only as much glory as is due to a noble and leading woman, highly cultivated in every kind of learning, most loving toward her husband, most steadfast in his adversity, most constant in her vows—especially chastity—and most watchful as a deaconess. Whoever desires more on this subject may pluck it, not from these little gardens of Adonis of mine, but from the most pleasant and sweet-scented beds, arbours, rose-gardens, nurseries, and orchards of Pasquier’s various *Investigations*. I have placed him last here as my strongest witness, because I have always kept his virtues stored in the deepest recesses of my heart; thus it came to pass that, newly received into heaven, he emerged from the innermost cabinet of my breast.

With such great testimonies and illustrious encomia, who would not rejoice that the writings of so excellent a doctor and so holy and learned a woman—writings destined to live after the centuries—have been rescued and preserved from fires by our labour, and defended against every kind of destruction?

But if anyone objects that Abelard erred on certain articles and was condemned in the synod of the province of Sens, and that therefore the adjudicated matter must be accepted as truth, let him have this answer: Abelard was indeed received as an accused person, but no trial was carried through. Moreover, when he appealed to the supreme pontiff in defence of his innocence, that judicial appeal suspended the judgment, if there was any.

But that all may better understand what was done in that assembly at Sens, let them read the *Apology* inserted in this work, reproduced from the Royal Library under the names of Letters 17 and 18 of Book II, by Peter Berengar, scholastic of Poitiers. As Abelard’s disciple, he painted in varied colours certain men among those who, judging before the time, were not ashamed to set a black theta—θ, the mark of death—against their unheard master.

“For,” he says, “it commonly happens that he who judges quickly condemns willingly.” Let whoever wishes read the entire *Apology*; I shall excerpt only these passages.

> Walking in Christ’s way, coming forth in secret, he was stripped of his seamless tunic. After dinner a book was brought, and a certain young man was ordered to declaim Peter’s little works in a loud voice. But that young man, animated by hatred of Peter, shouted more loudly than had been required. After a while you might see his rivals from the crowd jeering, stamping foot against foot, laughing, and making sport. They were scattered in their hearts; they gnashed their teeth at Peter, having the eyes of a mole. “Should we let this philosopher live?” they said.
>
> And a little later: “The eyes of many relaxed into lethargic sleep. Amid this the reader sounds out the text, the hearer snores. One leans on his elbow to give his eyes sleep; another contrives sleep for his eyelids upon a soft cushion; another, bowing his head over his knees, dozes. Whenever the reader found any sufficiently thorny passage in Peter, he cried out to deaf ears: ‘Do you condemn it?’ Then some of the common people, awakened at the final syllable, said in sleepy voices and with drooping heads: ‘We condemn it.’ Others, awakened by the uproar of condemnation, cut off the first syllable and said: ‘We swim’ (*namus*).”
>
> Amid these things Peter prayed: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips and from a deceitful tongue.”

Among so many and such great straits Abelard fled to the refuge of Roman examination. “I am a son,” he said, “of the Roman Church. I wish my cause, as if I were impious, to be judged; I appeal to the Caesar of the Church.” Yet notwithstanding his appeal, the proceedings were reported to the Apostolic See, and letters of condemnation against Peter immediately flew from the Roman See through the Gallican Church.

Thus was condemned that mouth, storehouse of reason, trumpet of faith, dwelling-place of the Trinity. Condemned—alas!—in his absence, unheard and unconvicted. “Whose fault, good Jesus,” he says, “had such judges in heaven that the sides of the cause were not examined on both sides?” “But,” they say, “they wished to correct Peter.” Why then did they brand him before the people with the mark of mutual blasphemy? Again, if they took away Peter’s popular affection, how did they intend to correct him? The Prophet spoke excellently: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy” [Psalm 140]. “Spare him, illustrious warrior; he does not attack Peter’s faith who affirms Peter’s faith. Allow him to be with you a Christian and Catholic.”

Let us consider Abelard’s faith in part of his letter to Heloise:

> “My sister Heloise, once dear to me in the world, now most dear in Christ: logic has made me hateful to the world. The perverse say that in it I am most excellent, but that I limp in Paul. I do not wish to be a philosopher in such a way as to kick against Paul, nor to be an Aristotle in such a way as to be separated from Christ.”
>
> And a little later: “I believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God by nature and in truth. I so affirm the Trinity in the persons that I always preserve unity in the substance. I believe the Son to be equal to the Father in all things—in eternity, power, will, and work—and I do not listen to Arius, who places before and after in the Trinity. I also testify that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial and coequal in every respect with the Father and the Son. I believe also that the Son of God became the Son of Man, and that he subsists as one person from two and in two natures; that he suffered, died, rose again, ascended to heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead. I also affirm that sins are remitted in baptism, that we need grace by which both to begin good and to bring it to completion, and that those who have fallen are restored through repentance. What need is there to speak of the resurrection of the flesh, when I boast in vain that I am a Christian if I do not believe that I shall rise again?”

These are excerpts from Peter’s letter, most of which we have inserted below, in order to make it clear and evident to all that Abelard did not attack Peter’s faith.

Berengar then adds that he saw a little catalogue compiled by Abelard’s enemies, in which were read not Abelard’s doctrines, as they falsely boasted, but articles of an abominable fabrication. Some of these he denies outright; others he considers must be refuted, although he acknowledges that Peter could have erred. He also ventures to accuse a writing, which he believed came from the Cistercian household, of error concerning the origin of souls. That opinion of Origen, smelling of I know not what Pythagorean and Platonic doctrine, must be cut off by the sword of orthodox truth. For the holy Catholic Church holds that souls newly created are daily infused into bodies newly created, according to Christ’s saying: “My Father works until now, and I work” [John 5].

Concerning this Berengar, while he was defending his teacher’s fame and name, Petrarch says in his *Apology* that he was eloquent, not of great bodily stature but of immense acuteness; he later excused himself because the holiness of so great a man had not yet filled the entire world. “When Abelard,” he says, “was slipping into sleep or error, he ought gently to have shown him the way; if he had been wounded, it was right to place him upon the beast, pour wine and oil into his wounds, and bring him back to the innkeeper of the universal Church—that is, the supreme pontiff. Whoever recognizes him as Christ’s vicar, Peter’s successor, and primate of bishops, and is prepared to conform himself to his command, cannot be called reprobate.”

Berengar turns these and many other trifles to the reader’s weariness through excessive reverence for his teacher—if reverence could be excessive in one who knew Juvenal’s words:

> May the gods grant the shades of our great men light earth free from dust,  
> Crocuses breathing fragrance, and perpetual spring in their urn,  
> Who wished a teacher to stand  
> In the place of a holy parent. . . .

What then? Was Berengar the boldest of them all? By no means. But he was much more dutiful toward his teacher than the other fellow-students. Yet he was not so eager even for this praise that he wished to snatch it from others said to have drawn their pens for their master. For he seems to have been chosen alone by his companions, as one who could speak with the greatest talent and the least danger to his reputation, since he had scarcely passed beyond adolescence.

Thus, invited to a rich harvest of reply, he gathered only stalks and immediately abandoned the undertaking. In this first struggle he asked, in a way, to be excused because, burning with excessive zeal for his teacher, he vomited forth a book against his most holy adversary. He could not afterwards retrieve it like a stone once thrown, because copies of it had immediately flown through France and Italy. In another letter to the bishop of Mende he excuses himself in these words:

> “Is he not a man? Does he not sail with us upon this great and wide sea, among creeping things without number? Though his ship may be borne along by a more favourable voyage, the security of the deep is uncertain. For even the south wind has not yet given him assurance, according to Augustine’s saying: ‘While a man lives, he does not know whether he is worthy of wrath or hatred.’”
>
> And a little later: “He is not yet fixed in the firmament, though in my judgment he is the Martin of our times. I think this of the abbot: that he is a burning and shining lamp; but he is nevertheless in an earthen vessel. He had condemned Abelard, my teacher, the trumpet of faith, the armoury of the law, walking with straight foot in the path of morals. He had condemned him, I say, and had strangled his voice without a hearing. I was a young man at that time. I set my breast to cleanse Abelard. ‘But,’ they say, ‘such a theologian ought not to be criticized by you.’ In what does the abbot dare? He dares in letters; I dare also. He dares in theology; I dare also. He dares in holiness; here I do not dare.”

This is Berengar’s excuse for his *Apology*, with which he concludes: “In the field of philosophy it has always been permitted that one should rebuke another for just causes, while truth is the greater friend.”

For Bernard’s enrolment among the saints, which followed ten years after St Bernard’s death, is indeed a witness to his holiness, but it does not approve all the aforementioned statements, deeds, or writings of his. St Bernard was truly a good and holy man, truly he shone as a kind of constellation of Orion in his age. Even those who departed from the Catholic Church could neither injure the purity of his rays nor cast darkness upon them; some of these keep Bernard constantly at hand and delight in him. Among them may be named that man of outstanding talent, François Hotman, jurist. Though hostile in disposition to monks, he regarded this author in old age as weighty and this doctor as pre-eminent, confessing that he advanced through constant reading of him and drew pure meanings from Holy Scripture.

It remains, therefore, since you have calmly heard others speaking for Abelard, that you should not refuse an ear to him speaking a few words for himself. Against the various reproaches brought against him, he was satisfied with a very short apology or confession, scarcely exceeding three pages. In it he detests as diabolical, together with their authors and fabricators, the articles of the above-mentioned catalogue, and denies that anything of the kind is found in his volumes.

He professes that both the Son and the Holy Spirit are from the Father, so that they are of the same substance, utterly the same will and power, as the Father. He affirms and, affirming, believes that Jesus Christ alone was incarnate: the only and true Son of God the Father, begotten from the Father’s substance before the ages. He likewise believes and asserts that the Holy Spirit, the third person in the Trinity, proceeds from both the Son himself and the Father. He maintains that God’s grace is necessary for all, so that neither natural capacity nor freedom of will can suffice for salvation without it. He confesses that Christ’s crucifiers committed a most grievous sin in the very act of crucifixion. He recognizes that the power of binding and loosing was given to all successors of the apostles, as to the apostles themselves, to worthy and unworthy bishops alike.

Why say more? Since he replies modestly and briefly to each objection, denies that he wrote the book of *Sentences* from which the chapters published against him were excerpted, whether through ignorance or malice, and thus defends his innocence that he asks, through the mercies of Jesus Christ, that anything seeming doubtful be fraternally taken in the better sense—who can further doubt that this was Peter’s true faith? From it he drew firmness of hope. Speaking in it wholesomely, as he himself said, he did not fear Scylla’s barking, mocked the whirlpools of Charybdis, scorned deadly strains with a deaf ear, did not shudder at rocks, was not shaken by rushing storms, and was not moved from his place. For he was founded upon firm rock; and therefore he deservedly found refuge at the See of St Peter, with which he was reconciled through the Mauriacian. But I shall restrain myself. For, as Cicero says, a reconciliation ought not to be called a favour which never ceased.

Therefore we ought to be of good courage and hope well that no labours undertaken for the honour and reputation of piety and holiness in our doctor have been in vain. As for the sound and outstanding learning which remains, in every kind of letters, nothing more need be added except this: in that age, most fertile in distinguished talents, there was no one in any respect comparable with him.

That this may be more readily known, I shall hastily name some of the more eminent men flourishing about that time. I think St Bernard, Peter of Mauriac, Otto of Freising, William of Châlons, Anselm of Laon, John Roscelin, Albert of Rheims, and Gratian of Bologna have been sufficiently mentioned above. I hesitate to count Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, as the sun of theologians among the stars: great as he was, he emerged, with many others, from the school and scholarly retreats of our Abelard, as from the Trojan horse.

Let Robert, bishop of Salisbury; Ivo, bishop of Chartres; another Robert, abbot of Marmoutier; Baldwin, archbishop of Dol; Marbod, bishop of Rennes; John of Arras, bishop of Thérouanne; William the Armorican and Ralph Niger, epic poets; the two Williams, one abbot of Saint-Thierry at Rheims and the other of Newburgh; Lotulf of Novara; Geoffrey of Auxerre; Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis; Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans; Honorius, bishop of Autun; Peter the Chanter of Paris; another Peter of Roissy; Hugh, Richard, Adam, and Andrew, monks of St Victor; the two Ruperts, of Deutz and Bologna; Aubert and Peter of Rheims; Geoffrey, archdeacon of Bordeaux; Boso the Englishman; Bruno of Cologne; Vicerius Trustinus of York; Peter of Blois, bishop of Bath; Walter of Coutances, from the royal stock of the Bretons; Alfred, priest and historian; Hugh the Carthusian, historian; John of Oxford, historian; Herbert Losinga; Bartholomew of Iscanus; Turgot, abbot of Durham; Oderisius and Peter of Monte Cassino; Joachim, abbot of Fiore; Gilbert, Laurence, and Ralph of Westminster; Nicholas of Wacton; William of Somerset; Walter, Daniel, and Robert of Budlington; William and Robert of Fécamp; Sterlo and Osbert of Gloucester; Gilbert of Holland; Vignomus, homilist; Peter of Pisa, jurist; Roger, mathematician; Thebit and al-Farghani, astronomers; William Sturdus and Guido, poets; Caradoc, historian; Odo of Kent; William, archbishop of Tyre; Rudolf, Lucas, and Frank, German abbots; Robert the Pole; Adalbert of Spalding; Richard de Pratellis; and others, whose enumeration would take too long.

To these must deservedly be added that great Gilbert of Poitiers, bishop of Poitiers, if not the Romulus of his academy, then at least its Camillus. Accused by Adam of the Little Bridge and Hugh of Campo Florido, chancellor of King Louis VII, he was brought before the tribunal of the supreme pontiff, then travelling through Gaul, and encountered a danger equal to Abelard’s. So powerful was the inveterate opinion inherited from unlearned ancient ages that anyone who surpassed the common crowd in perfected genius and learning was immediately believed alien from the faith.

I acknowledge that learning without fear of God and piety is of little use. But where these meet in one subject, more benefit flows to the Church from these two sisterly qualities than from either alone. And what of our man? Did he not leave behind all those named above in learning and piety? Finally, he surpassed many even in holiness, if St Bernard and the archbishops Thomas of Canterbury and Malachy of Ireland are excepted, whose merits placed them in heaven.

What then? Did not the twelfth century shine also with illustrious and learned women? Among these our Heloise glitters as the moon among the lesser fires. Among them I am pleased to reckon Hildegard, Matilda, Sophia with her daughter, and Elizabeth, who left it uncertain whether they were more commendable for learning or for austerity of life.

All acknowledge as wholly true what the Mauriacian wrote to our Heloise in Book V: “Not only in religion, but in honourable and praiseworthy studies and in secular wisdom, her fame became known to the whole world; she surpassed all women and almost exceeded all men.” “But soon,” he says, “when it pleased him who separated you from your mother’s womb, by his grace you transformed your studies of learning to something far better: instead of logic you chose the Gospel; instead of physics, the Apostle; instead of Plato, Christ; instead of the academy, the cloister—now wholly and truly a philosophical woman.”

What wonder, since under the reign of Louis the Younger—whom William of Tyre, Book XXII, calls a most pious and Christian king—studies of all liberal and mathematical arts flourished at Paris, as did philosophy, medicine, and theology? According to Rigord, the king rewarded their professors with honours, fees, prizes, and—what has fallen out of use—the revenues of ecclesiastical benefices, together with worthy recompenses. Thus he preferred that Peter, Lombard by name and origin and author of the *Book of Sentences*, should be elected bishop of Paris rather than Louis the Fat’s own brother, who was then archdeacon of Paris; nor did he take it bitterly or resent that a doctor who was a foreigner and born elsewhere should be preferred to him. For the same must be said of the Parisian academy as of Rome: it is the common homeland of the inhabitants of the world.

Nor did studies of languages and divine learning flourish only among Christians at Paris, but also among Jews. Benjamin the Hebrew, born in Spain, bears witness to this. In his *Itinerary* he writes that he came to Paris under that king, and calls it the capital of the kingdom: “There are in it disciples of all the wise men now living in every region, most learned men who apply themselves night and day to the study of the Law.”

This is sufficiently clear from the doctors named above. To them I shall add Peter Alfonsi, who became a Christian from Judaism and had as sponsor at baptism Alfonso, excellent king of Castile, a most learned mathematician. But other persons falsely called learned I think should be wrapped in silence: Peter of Bruys; the Petrobrusians, Henricians, Adamites, Marlenses, Cathars, Jacobites—all unworthy of mention; the Marrucini and the Fools. Abusing letters, they infected diverse regions of the world with perverse heresies. Yet Gaul remained free from them through the aid of Doctor Abelard, who set forth the creed of his sincere faith in a separate book published against heresies.

It therefore seems all the more unworthy that Abelard’s books, not properly recognized, have remained placed among prohibited books to this day, while their author’s name has been impaled on a stake—he who professed himself the most vigorous enemy of heretics. Indeed, his eighth letter alone sufficiently shows how piously and Catholicly he thought concerning the Eucharist and the other articles of faith. If any of his works had come into the hands of those who compiled the Index of books suspected of faith, they would certainly either have removed from it Abelard’s name, concerning whom they had seen and discovered nothing bad, or allowed his works, cleansed by doctors, to appear publicly—as we now give them to the Christian and Catholic commonwealth, polished and smoothed by the pumice stone of the theologians of Paris. Since they are senators of keen judgment, they decided that nothing in them was to be expunged; but whatever seemed somewhat harsh was either to be tempered by a gentler interpretation or prudently guarded against.

The case is concluded. You see, most wise guardian of the laws, that the reading of Abelard is useful and beneficial to the Church; that he was a good and learned monk, cleansed of suspicion of error, rendered more illustrious by adversity, to be honoured more greatly after death, numbered among the orthodox, and adorned with every praise, proclamation, writing, and monument.

And since amid those many and great affairs of the realm which you uphold as Atlas upholds the sky, we observe that you always devote several hours of your leisure to reflection and the reading of ancient authors, please include him among those whom you have resolved to esteem, read, and love especially. Accept kindly these studies and services of mine, which, as is my duty, I have desired to contribute to your honour and adornment. Be persuaded that, among those who admire, love, and honour your virtues—whose number is great in proportion to your eminence—I shall yield to none.

[Col. 0103B] The funeral rites and obsequies of Abelard, and likewise of his wife, shall place a colophon upon this *Apology for Abelard*. For Euripides’ Ulysses, wishing to persuade the Greeks that Polyxena must be slaughtered at Achilles’ hands, declares that so long as he enjoys this light he is content with moderate honours; but he desires that his burial be seen as most splendidly adorned, “for favour endures long” (*διὰ μακροῦ γὰρ ἡ χάρις*).

This highest culmination of good fortune befell Abelard as Cornelius Tacitus befell Verginius in Pliny: he had an eloquent panegyrist, namely Peter the Venerable, and the most desired mourner—or funeral lament—that decorated his tomb with her tears was the most excellent Heloise, who left it uncertain whether she loved or revered her husband more.

A sixfold epitaph of Abelard may be seen below.

That great doctor died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May [21 April] 1142, in his climacteric year. Heloise died on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June [17 May] 1163, for she is believed to have survived her husband by twenty-two years and more. Her epitaph, contained in four verses, is not by the author of the preceding ones. Yet I have wished to add it, although she was worthy of greater praises, being eloquent beyond the measure of her sex:

> In this tomb lies the prudent abbess Heloise.  
> She founded the Paraclete; with the Paraclete she rests.  
> Her joys are above the lofty heavens of the saints.  
> By her merits and prayers may she raise us from the depths.

Hail and farewell, my Abelard restored to life: phoenix both to yourself and to your ashes, brought forth into the light by truth, the daughter of time. Take this saying to yourself in remembrance:

> What the envious crowd had taken from me while I lived,  
> Honour will repay twofold after my death.

[Col. 0103]

# Epitaphs of Abelard

## I. By Peter the Venerable, as is also the following.  
(*Works of Abelard*, p. 342.)

[Col. 0103C]

> Socrates of the Gauls, greatest Plato of the Western lands,  
> Our Aristotle—whatever logicians there have been,  
> Either his equal or better—acknowledged prince  
> Of the world of learning; varied, subtle, and keen in genius;  
> Abelard, overcoming all things by the power of reason  
> And by the art of speech, was such a man; yet he conquered all things more  
> When, professing the monastic life and rule of Cluny,  
> He passed over to the true philosophy of Christ.  
>
> In that philosophy, happily completing the last stage of a long life,  
> He gave hope that he would one day be numbered among the good philosophers,  
> When May recalled the eleventh day before the Kalends.

## II.

(*Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, V, 235.)

> Peter lies hidden in this rock, whom the world called Homer;  
> But now the stars—a star...
they have.

The sun to the Gauls was here, but now fate has taken him away:

Therefore the land of Gaul lacks its own sun.

He, knowing whatever was knowable by anyone, surpassed

The masters, teaching the arts without a teacher.

The eleventh day before the Kalends of May carried Peter away,

Depriving the halls of logic of their king.

The tomb is enough: here lies Peter Abelard,

To whom alone was open whatever was knowable.

III.

(Rawlinson, edition of *The Letters of Peter Abelard*, p. III, from an Oxford manuscript.)

Peter has died; with his death every philosopher falls,

All philosophy perishes,

The garment of philosophy is now torn into pieces.

Gaul, once abundant in studies and philosophy,

Mourns Peter, dead to philosophy;

Its gem withdrawn, it laments, made solitary.

[Col. 0104C] Logic laments Aristotle, lately taken from it;

Ethics, grieving, laments Socrates taken from it;

Physics, Plato; eloquence, likewise Cicero.

The arts lament that their craftsman has died,

Who set forth what they thought, because he understood it.

Peter himself was Aristotle—or another Aristotle and his heir—

The only one who discovered the limits of Aristotle’s arts.

He taught that words signify together with things,

And taught that words mark things by signifying them.

He corrected the errors concerning genera, and likewise species;

He placed genus and species in the word alone,

And observed that genus and species are utterances.

What is significative, what is signified,

What it is to signify—he wisely distinguished.

What things were, and what words signified,

He disclosed more clearly than the other experts in the art.

Thus both “animal” and “no animal” are shown to be genera;

Likewise “man,” but “no man,” is called a species.

Relying on his intellect, Peter taught subtle

Doctrines which earlier teachers had not taught.

[Col. 0104D] As the arts are difficult for all others,

So they were easy for Peter, and, as Peter expounded them, clear.

Peter worthy of praise, Peter to be mourned even by an enemy,

Died; envious fate snatched him away by sudden death.

Mists of errors rise as you, Peter, fall;

Had you stood, they would have fallen; and, as you rose, they would have lain low.

Glory made you renowned; your fame made you everlasting;

Nor could death erase your titles.

Death itself envied you, who were a cause

Of envy to all: death was your enemy.

Now your doctrine of the vocal has become real:

Death is the argument; thus the tomb is your place.

Teaching these matters in words, you learned them in things,

And by dying you prove that man is mortal.

IV.

(Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus anecdotorum novissimus*, vol. III, *Dissertatio Isagogica*, p. XXII.)

Peter, beloved of the clergy; Peter, seeker of truth,

[Col. 0105A] A saving tongue and lamp of the scholarly throng,

Skill in argument, abundance of speech—

After the wars of the world, a new star shines in heaven.

From the fragile world he is summoned in the month of April:

Flower of eloquence, dew of counsel, whetstone of intellect,

Fountain of grammar, bridge of rhetoric, and mountain of logic,

Light of the Church, guide of justice among the wicked,

Torch of the school, peace of the pupil, righteous and innocent.

He departed hence, but did not die, nor did he cease to be.

He passed away, but did not perish; he passed into being.

A harsh people, acting violently, plotted against him;

Christ gladdened him above the ethereal radiance.

V.

(*Works of Philip, Abbot of Bonne-Espérance*, p. 801.)

Lucifer has set; shine forth, lesser stars,

Whose ray had dimmed you as inferior stars.

[Col. 0106A] At his setting you at last came to your rising,

And the anchor of your ship reached port through shipwreck.

Mature, teachable, pious: he accomplished, preferred, purchased

His course, right, heaven—by time, law, faith.

VI.

(*Writers of Gallic and Frankish Affairs*, vol. XII, p. 415, from the chronicle of Richard of Poitiers.)

Peter Abelard, greater than the greatest,

Has died; one immense grief has come upon all.

Gaul possessed nothing greater or more brilliant than he.

No one’s death brings so great a ruin upon the Latin world.

As far as the fame of the Roman name extends,

The fame of his genius and learning flew.

For he was born of a Poitevin father and Breton mother;

He studied among the French, and died a monk at Chalon.

[Col. 0105]

# PETER ABELARD’S APOLOGY, OR CONFESSION OF FAITH

Peter Abelard, one of all the children of holy Church, but the least among them, to all the children of holy Church.

It is a well-known proverb: “Nothing is so well said that it cannot be corrupted”; and, as blessed Jerome observes: “He who writes many books takes on many judges.” I too, although I have written few small works—or, compared with others, none at all—have not been able to escape the mark of reproach. Yet in those matters concerning which I am seriously accused, I recognize no fault of my own—God knows this!—nor, if there has been any, will I defend it insolently. Perhaps [variant: *fortassis*, “perhaps”] I have written some things in error which ought not to have been written; but I call God, witness and judge, upon my soul, that in the matters of which I am accused I presumed nothing out of malice or pride.

I have spoken much in many schools, and my teaching has never dealt in stolen waters or hidden bread. Openly, for the edification of faith or morals, I have spoken what seemed salutary to me; and whatever I wrote I willingly set before all, that I might have them as judges, not disciples. If anywhere I have gone too far through much speaking—as it is written, “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. 10:19)—an importunate defence has never made me a heretic. I have always been ready to make satisfaction by correcting or deleting what I have said wrongly; and I shall certainly persevere in that purpose to the end.

But just as it is mine to wish to correct my evil statements, if there are any, so it is fitting for me to repel charges wrongly brought against me. For blessed Augustine says: “He is cruel who neglects his reputation” [Note: [Col. 0105] Augustine, Sermon 52, *To the Brothers in the Desert*]; and, according to Tully, “Silence resembles confession.” I have therefore judged it fair to answer point by point the things written against me, following the principle by which blessed Gregory instructs the faithful against the tongues of detractors in these words:

> We must know that, just as by our own effort we ought not to provoke the tongues of slanderers, lest they perish, so, when they have been provoked by their own malice, we ought to endure them with equanimity, that merit may increase for us. Yet sometimes we must also restrain them, lest, while they spread evil reports about us, they corrupt the innocent hearts of those who might have heard us to good effect.

[Note: [Col. 0105] Homily 9, book I on Ezekiel.]

Let brotherly charity therefore recognize me, however I may be, as a son of the Church: receiving whole and entire all that she receives, rejecting all that she rejects; and let it recognize that I have never torn apart the unity of faith, although I am inferior to others in moral character.

Accordingly, as for the charge maliciously made against me that I wrote, “The Father is full power, the Son a certain power, the Holy Spirit no power”: I abhor, detest, and condemn those words together with their author, as is most just, as not merely heretical but devilish. If anyone finds them in my writings, I acknowledge myself not only a heretic but even a heresiarch.

I profess that both the Son and the Holy Spirit are from the Father, so that they are of the same substance as the Father and altogether of the same will and power. Where substance or essence is wholly identical, there can be neither diversity of will nor inequality of power. Whoever asserts that I wrote that the Holy Spirit is not also of the substance of the Father does so from great malice or ignorance.

I profess that the Son of God alone was incarnate, in order to free us from the slavery of sin and from the yoke of the devil, and by his death to open for us the entrance to the heavenly life.

[Col. 0107] I believe and affirm—and, affirming, believe—that Jesus Christ is the true and only Son of God, begotten from the substance of the Father before the ages; and that the third person in the Trinity, the Holy Spirit, proceeds both from the Son himself and from the Father.

I hold the grace of God to be so necessary for all that neither natural capacity nor freedom of choice can suffice for salvation without it. That grace goes before us, that we may will; follows us, that we may be able; and joins itself to us, that we may persevere.

I believe that God can do only those things which it is fitting for him to do, and that he can do many things which he will never do.

Evils [variant: *Multa quoque*, “Many things also”] done through ignorance must be reckoned as faults, especially when, through our negligence, we happen not to know what it was necessary for us to know beforehand. Such was the man of whom the Psalmist says: “He was unwilling to understand, that he might act well” (Ps. 35:4).

I confess that God frequently hinders evils, because he not only forestalls the effect of the malicious, so that they cannot do what they wish, but also changes their wills, so that they wholly turn away from the evil which they had devised.

I affirm that from Adam, in whom we all sinned, we have contracted both guilt and punishment, because his sin was the origin and cause of all our sins also.

I confess that Christ’s crucifiers committed a most grievous sin in the crucifixion itself.

Many things are said of Christ which should be understood not so much according to his head as according to his body, which is the Church: for example, that spirit of fear which is the beginning of wisdom—the fear which perfect charity casts out (1 John 4:19). Therefore it must be believed that this spirit of fear was never in the soul of Christ, which possessed most perfect charity, though it is not absent from the lower members. For that soul, through the union with the Word itself, possessed such perfection and such security that it knew itself wholly unable to commit anything by which it might incur punishment or offend God.

Yet I acknowledge that chaste fear, enduring for ever and ever, which is properly called the reverence of charity, is always present both in Christ’s own soul and in the elect angels and human beings. Thus it is also written of the heavenly spirits:

> Dominions adore; Powers tremble.

I profess that the power of binding and loosing was granted to all successors of the apostles as equally as to the apostles themselves, and to bishops both unworthy and worthy, so long as the Church receives them.

I confess that all who are equal in love of God and neighbour are equally good and equal in merits; and that no merit before God is lost if the disposition of a good will is hindered from its effect. For an angel, having been sent by God, ought not to be reckoned better because he accomplishes what he wishes to do; nor should the soul of Christ be reckoned better because it added accomplishment to its will. Rather, every good person remains equally good whether he has time for acting or not, provided that he retains an equal will to act well and does not remain inactive in what he does not do.

I profess that God the Father is equally wise and the Son equally benevolent with the Holy Spirit, because in no fullness of goodness and in no glory of dignity can one of the persons differ from another.

That the coming of the Son at the end of the age could be attributed to the Father has never—God knows it!—entered my mind, nor did it find its way into my words.

Likewise, that Christ’s soul did not descend to hell in its own substance but only by its power is wholly remote from both my words and my thought.

The final chapter also, which I am accused of having written—namely, that neither an act, nor a will, nor concupiscence, nor the pleasure which moves [variant: “which move”] it, is sin; and that we ought not to wish these things extinguished—is no less foreign to both my spoken and written statements.

But I received with the greatest astonishment our friend’s conclusion to the articles written against me, where he said: “These articles have been found partly in Master Peter’s book *Theology*, partly in his book *Sentences*, and partly in the book entitled *Know Thyself*.” For no book called *Sentences* is found to have been written by me. Yet, like the other articles against me, this too was put forward through malice or ignorance.

If, then, there is any consolation in Christ Jesus, if there are any bowels of compassion, I beseech your brotherly mercy: let no one sin by besprinkling with venom [variant: *nemo*, “no one”] my innocence, which truth frees from blame. For it belongs to charity not to accept a reproach against one’s neighbour (Ps. 14:3), to interpret doubtful matters in the better sense, and always to heed that sentence of the Lord’s mercy: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Matt. 7:1).

[Col. 0109]

# CENSURE OF THE DOCTORS OF PARIS

[NOTE.]

The works of Peter Abelard, exceedingly pious and learned, were committed to print with their blemishes—as commonly happens in ancient writings. In order that anyone may read through them without stumbling, besides the disposition which the author displays in his *Apology*, assenting in all things to the Church, certain Parisian theologians have carefully noted and indicated what might be rough or hazardous in each passage of his works; and a ready remedy has been applied to each of the more dangerous statements. If, however, anyone with sharper eyes should later observe further matters, he will render a most welcome service to all who are truly Catholic.

Those things which have not been weighed in a sufficiently even balance of truth in the letters of Abelard, Heloise, and certain others.

[Col. 0109A] Col. 163, ch. 12 of the *History of Calamities*. Abelard complains somewhat too bitterly—though without naming them—of Doctors Bernard and Norbert, who were hostile more to his errors than to himself.

Col. 181, Letter 2. Heloise attacks the same holy men under the name of false apostles, and sharply satirizes certain others along with them.

Col. 185, same letter. Heloise imprudently recounts what harmful love extorted from her.

Col. 256, Letter 7. Abelard judges, contrary to Catholic truth, that a dead catechumen can attain glory. Yet this is consonant with faith, if he died contrite and would not have refused baptism had anyone been willing to bestow this grace on him.

Col. 288, middle, Letter 8. He does not make fulfilment of the conjugal debt wholly free from sin. But this must by no means be granted in the case of those who observe uprightness and propriety.

Col. 375. Fulco, in his letter to Abelard, rashly and venomously attacks the holy apostolic see.

Col. 353. When Abelard accuses of presumption the person who substitutes *daily* for *supersubstantial* in the Lord’s Prayer, he gives little weight to the Church’s received custom of reciting it thus.

Appendix. The apology of Berengar the schoolman for his master Abelard, being insulting toward St Bernard and the Council of Sens, did not deserve publication; neither did the following two letters by the same author. In the first of them he washes away the stains of his *Apology* but brands himself with others; in the latter he crudely mocks the Carthusians.

## In the Exposition of the Creed

Col. 622. [Col. 0109C] Abelard explains God’s omnipotence meagrely, perhaps mindful of his own error, by which he had asserted that God can do only those things which he at some time does. But he erased this error in the *Apology*.

Col. 627. He appears to deny that the soul of Christ the Lord descended to hell according to its own substance. But in the *Apology* he thinks otherwise.

Col. 628. Because he asserts that no increase of blessedness accrued to Christ’s body through its ascension into heaven, he unduly diminishes even the additional happiness of the heavenly dwelling, which all receive.

## In Heloise’s Problems

Col. 682. In the answer to Problem IV, Abelard attributes doubt in faith to the Virgin Mary at the death of her Son, on the authority of St Augustine in the book *Questions of the Old and New Testaments*; but that book is entirely spurious.

Col. 694, in the solution of Problem XIII. He condemns as sin that which is done from invincible ignorance. In the *Apology*, however, he defends the contrary opinion.

Col. 695. [Col. 0110A] He falsely attributes invincible ignorance to those for whom the Lord prayed during his Passion, and St Stephen likewise; or to the person who, according to the Gospel, spoke a word against the Son of Man.

Col. 703, in the solution of Problem XV. Abelard departs from truth in holding that the Law of Moses neither teaches that sin is completed in the mind, nor holds anyone guilty for coveting another’s property, nor defines anyone other than a Jew as one to be loved as a neighbour.

Col. 704, in the solution of Problem XVI. He thinks that the command to love one’s neighbour, recalled by Christ the Lord, binds Jews alone; nor does he see that the commandments of the Decalogue, because they belong to natural law, bind every person.

Col. 710, in the solution of Problem XXIV. He thinks that the Jews did not judge evils or goods from intention itself; this should be admitted only concerning some cases.

Ibid. Abelard contends that it has nothing to do with sin that we take forbidden food into our mouth. But in this way he entirely removes the greater gravity of sin arising from the accompanying external act.

Col. 711, in the solution of Problem XXV. Understand grace as withdrawn from Esau in the sense of a more abundant grace, not all grace.

## In the Book against Heresies

Just as this book bears no name of Abelard in the manuscript, so it has neither his manner of expression, style, nor keenness of mind.

Appendix, col. 1834. The author says that the apostles imposed hands only on those whom they appointed as preachers, presbyters, or deacons, and that Holy Scripture establishes nothing concerning others. But the divine utterances show sufficiently clearly that the same practice was used in the consecration of bishops and in the sacrament of confirmation.

## In the Commentary on St Paul’s Letter to the Romans

Col. 832. Abelard understands these words of St Paul, “the showing of his righteousness,” as charity and righteousness infused into us, whereas they ought chiefly to be understood of Christ’s charity and the righteousness by which he made satisfaction for us.

Col. 833. To Abelard’s words, “when he freed the elect alone,” apply this caution: Christ frees the elect because they alone actually attain the glory which the others too could have merited through Christ, had it not depended upon themselves.

Col. 834. He judges that the devil acquired no right over the person whom he deceived, although by the most just right a human being becomes, through sin, subject to eternal punishment and to the tormenting devil. Accordingly, Abelard, having examined the matter more closely, professes in the *Apology* that Christ by his death freed humankind from the devil’s yoke.

Same column. Understand that sin was forgiven to the Blessed Virgin Mary only insofar as she sinned in Adam, not that she ever personally incurred it.

Col. 835. Read cautiously the statement that the divine Word assumed a human being: that is, he took human nature to himself.

Ibid. Abelard indeed explains well our justification and redemption in Christ’s blood and death: through the immeasurable love which he displayed in suffering and dying, Christ redeemed us from slavery to sin and vindicated us into the freedom of the children of God. But because he either did not recognize, or passed over in silence, the Passion and death proceeding from love as a work of infinite justice and satisfaction, adequate for removing all sins and punishments, he either did not follow or did not attain the Catholic Church’s genuine understanding of our redemption. Since St Bernard rightly rebuked this in Letter 190, he elicited from Abelard the testimony of a Christian mind in his *Apology*: “I profess that the Son of God alone was incarnate, in order to free us from the slavery of sin and from the yoke of the devil, and by his death to open for us the entrance to the heavenly life.”

Col. 836 and 837. [Col. 0111B] He errs in two respects. First, he thinks that, for one who is righteous before baptism, sins have not yet been forgiven in baptism; for that person, by the desire for baptism, has already received forgiveness of sins. Secondly, he interprets sins not yet forgiven as punishment not yet paid.

Col. 837. Understand that baptized infants are not yet capable of charity or righteousness through elicited acts.

Col. 858. By “the sins which Christ removed by dying,” Abelard wrongly explains that only their punishment was removed. Thus he strikes against the same rock elsewhere as well.

Col. 861. He refers St Paul’s words, “in whom all sinned,” only to punishment, omitting the very guilt of original sin, which all incurred. Elsewhere he wavers on the same slippery ground, but he overturns all these passages in the *Apology* by this single support: “From Adam, in whom we all sinned, I affirm that we have contracted both guilt and punishment.”

Col. 864. He asserts that Christ was compelled by a divine command to pray for us. But an erroneous mode of expression underlies this opinion.

Ibid. and col. 865. Abelard considers sins to be forgiven in the same way as their punishment is remitted; and elsewhere he considers that for someone to “have sin,” apart from the past action of sin, means nothing other than to remain liable to punishment. But Catholic doctrine rejects this opinion of his.

Col. 869. He declares that only those infants who die with the stain of origin are such as, had they lived, would have been destined to be most wicked. But this seems wholly rash.

Ibid. He asserts that infants are damned for the sins of others, but does not observe that the stain of origin which they possess properly closes to them the entrance of life.

Col. 870. He draws the conclusion somewhat ineptly that the abstinence of Lent or Friday was not instituted or confirmed in apostolic times in the form now observed, because certain neophytes in St Paul’s day distinguished no one day from another in eating.

## In the Sermons

[Col. 0112B] Col. 417. In the sermon on the Purification of Blessed Mary, he persuades himself that the Jews received no reward in the heavenly promises for their obedience. This is true only of works of the law considered apart from faith and charity.

Col. 450. He judges that Peter did not make as much satisfaction for his threefold denial as Marcellinus did for offering incense to idols. A dangerous comparison.

Ibid. He counts it a fault that St Paul, according to the custom of the Nazarenes, consecrated himself to God, and that he circumcised Timothy, although he did not sin at all in these matters.

Col. 471. He writes that no one should presume to pray thus: “All holy clerics, bishops, or canons, pray for us.” But he ought to have remembered that the verses of the Litanies, “all holy pontiffs, all holy priests and Levites,” carry almost the same meaning.

Col. 474. He accuses Norbert of a vain attempt to raise a certain dead man, perhaps because he found him opposed to his doctrines.

## In the Introduction to Theology

Col. 979. Abelard’s opinion that charity alone is worthy of reward departs from the truth. For faith, hope, and the other virtues, accompanied by charity, also obtain eternal rewards. Elsewhere he ran into the same stumbling-block.

The remaining points in this little work, the *Introduction*, which seem worthy of notice are those criticized by St Bernard in Letter 190. Abelard answers them by his public profession of Catholic faith and by an anathema against error, in the letter addressed to all the children of the Church. Let the reader consult both in this volume.

[Col. 0113]

# FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF PETER ABAELARD—LETTERS

[Note: [Col. 0113A] **Abaelardi.** The ancient writers are not consistent with themselves concerning this surname. St Bernard, Otto of Freising, Geoffrey, Robert of Auxerre, and others call him *Abailardus*; the author of the *Chronicle of the Archbishops of Sens* calls him *Abaulardus*; the anonymous canon of Tours, *Abaielardus*; and Vincent of Beauvais, *Abelardus*. Nor is there greater agreement among French writers. John Clopinel of Meung, a contemporary of King Philip the Fair, calls him *Abayelart*; another unidentified poet, who wrote in 1377, calls him *Abulart*; and the French calendar of the Paraclete, *Abaalarz*. Notwithstanding this variety, we have retained the reading of the ancient manuscripts and, with William of Nangis, John, regular canon of Saint-Victor, and certain others, have called him *Abaelardus*.]

## FIRST LETTER, WHICH IS THE HISTORY OF CALAMITIES

[Note: [Col. 0113B] **History of Calamities.** This is the genuine title of the letter, prefixed by the author himself, as Petrarch—a grave and eloquent writer—informs us in book II of *The Solitary Life*, in these words: “To so many ancient philosophers I shall add one more recent, not very remote from our own age, a man whose standing I do not know precisely, but who, as I hear, is suspected of unsound faith by some, yet certainly not of low intellect: that Peter surnamed Abailard. As he himself recalls at length in the *History of his Calamities*, yielding to envy, he penetrated the hidden places of the solitude of Troyes,” etc. John of Meung, who had read them, asserts in the following verses that this and the other letters were divided into definite chapters:

> “A marvellous saying,
> Written in the letters,
> Which one who searched well would find in the chapters.”]

Written by Abelard to a friend.

**SUMMARY.**—From the monastery of Saint Gildas in Lesser Brittany, of which Peter Abelard was then abbot, he writes this letter to a friend whose name neither he discloses anywhere in the letter, although it is long, nor Heloise when she mentions this letter in the second. It is a narrative. Throughout the whole text of the letter he carefully recounts his previous life from childhood to the time at which he wrote it. Yet he makes no mention of John Roscelin, that most learned philosopher whom Otto, bishop of Freising, a weighty writer living at the same time, affirms was his teacher.

Moreover, he vividly describes what he did or wrote, in what spirit he did so, what he suffered, and how fiercely his rivals burned with envy against him; and he gives a brief, pointed, and shrewd answer, as occasion arises, to his detractors. Finally, he seems to have written this letter more for his own consolation than his friend’s: namely, so that he might endure present misfortunes more lightly through recollection of former ones, and more easily dispel fear of imminent dangers. For he does not compare his friend’s troubles with his own in order that the latter may appear more serious.

[Col. 0113A] Examples often stir or mitigate human emotions more strongly than words. Therefore, after offering some consolation in speech to one present, I have resolved to write to one absent a consolation drawn from the very experiences of my own misfortunes, so that, in comparison with mine, you may recognize your trials as either none at all or slight, and bear them more tolerably.

### CHAPTER I. On the birthplace of Peter Abelard and his parents

I therefore [Note: [Col. 0114B] **Born in a certain town, called . . . Palatium.** Hence in his dialectical writings, which are in my possession, he calls himself *Palatinus*. This town, as he says, lies at the entrance to Lesser Brittany, about three leagues from the city of Nantes, and is commonly called *Palais*.] was born in a certain town [Col. 0114A], built at the entrance to Lesser Brittany, about eight miles, I think, east of the city of Nantes, which is called by the proper name Palatium.

[Note: [Col. 0114B] **As was the nature of my land, etc.** Otto, bishop of Freising, says not very differently, in book I, chapter 47, of *The Deeds of the Emperor Frederick I*: “For that aforesaid land—namely Brittany—is productive of clerics of keen intellect, devoted to the arts, but nearly foolish in other affairs; such were the two brothers Bernard and Theodoric, most learned men.” Moreover, the Breton people are those whom Henry, monk of Auxerre, describes as:

> … most famously enclosed between twin rivers,  
> Formerly called Armorican by its ancient name.

There is no need here to report what Pliny, the Venerable Bede, and others wrote about the Bretons of Gaul, since these matters are well known to everyone.]

As the nature of my country or people was light in temper, so I proved apt in intellect for literary learning.

[Note: [Col. 0114C] **But I had a father.** His name was Berengar; as Peter himself writes below, he later converted to the monastic profession.]

But I had a father somewhat educated in letters before he was distinguished with the military belt. Thereafter he embraced letters with so great a love that he determined to have every son he might have educated in letters before arms. And so it was indeed done. Therefore, since he held me, his first-born son, the dearer, [Col. 0115A] he took the greater care that I should be educated.

[Note: [Col. 0115C] **Therefore I, etc.** This passage was restored from manuscripts 2544, 2545, 2993, and the manuscript of Troyes by the distinguished Victor Cousin (*Works of Abelard*, Paris, 1849, quarto, p. 4). It was previously read: “Thus the first-born,” etc. Patristic Edition.]

But the more and more readily I advanced in literary study, the more ardently I devoted myself to it and was so enticed by my great love of letters that, leaving the pomp of military glory, together with the inheritance and prerogative of my first-born status, to my brothers, I wholly renounced the court of Mars in order to be nurtured in Minerva’s lap.

And because [Note: [Col. 0115C] **The armour of dialectical reasoning, etc.** He omitted the name of his first teacher in dialectic. Otto of Freising nevertheless testifies that he was a certain Roscelin, while Aventinus calls him Rucelin. Otto’s words are: “He had first, however, as teacher a certain Roscelin, who first in our times established in logic the doctrine of words.” And Aventinus, book VI of the *Bavarian Annals*: “I find that there lived in these times also Rucelin the Breton, master of Peter Abelard, founder of a new academy, who first established the science of words or terms and found a new way of philosophizing.” Yet this man, a Breton according to Aventinus, is called a man of Compiègne by that ancient anonymous historian of the Franks and is asserted to have been a disciple of a certain John, a powerful sophist in dialectic. For the historian who wrote a fragment of Frankish history from Robert to King Philip I says:

> “In dialectic also these were powerful sophists: John, who maintained that the same sophistic art was vocal; Robert of Paris; Roscelin of Compiègne; Arnulf of Laon. These were followers of John, and they too had very many hearers.”

Yet one should not therefore suppose that this contradicts Aventinus. Roscelin may have been born in Brittany and later been a cleric in the church of Compiègne. Certainly Anselm, abbot of Bec, who flourished at that time, calls him a cleric in his letter to Fulco, bishop of Beauvais, in these words:

> “I hear—though I cannot believe it without reservation—that the cleric Roscelin says that in God the three persons are three things separated from one another, as are three angels, though their will and power are one; or that the Father and the Holy Spirit were incarnate, and that three gods may truly be said to exist if usage allowed it.”

From this one may in some degree infer why our Peter does not mention him among his teachers. For Ivo, bishop of Chartres, also suggests in Letter 7 that Roscelin defended certain insane opinions on articles of the Christian faith, although he does not state what they were. But more will be said on this matter before the Council of Soissons.

For now I add from Aventinus that: “By the authorship of Roscelin himself, two schools of Aristotelians and Peripatetics began to exist: the one old, rich in producing things, which claims for itself the knowledge of things and is therefore called the Realists; the other new, which disperses this knowledge and is therefore called the Nominalists, because they seem to be miserly of things but prodigal of names and notions, defenders of words. Between these two schools there is dissension and civil war. The standard-bearers of the former are the Italian Thomas Aquinas and John Duns Scotus; of the latter, the Englishman William of Ockham.”]

I preferred the armour of dialectical reasoning to all the teachings of philosophy, exchanged the other weapons for these arms, and preferred the trophies of disputations to the conflicts of wars. Therefore, travelling through various provinces in disputation, wherever I had heard that the study of this art was flourishing, I became an emulator [variant: *ambulator*, “wanderer”] of the Peripatetics.

## Chapter II. On the persecution by his master William; on his teaching at Melun, Corbeil, and Paris; on his departure from Paris to Melun, return to Mont Sainte-Geneviève, and return home

At last I came to Paris, where this discipline had customarily flourished most greatly, namely to William of Champeaux, my teacher, then pre-eminent in this field both in achievement and reputation.

> [Note: Col. 116C. Namely, to William of Champeaux.—William was first archdeacon of the Church of Paris, later a regular canon, and finally bishop of Châlons, as we shall see below. Otto of Freising likewise states that Abelard studied under him: *On the Deeds of Emperor Frederick I*, book I, chapter 47, Col. 116D.]

After remaining with him for a while, and being at first acceptable to him, I later became most troublesome to him. I attempted to refute certain of his opinions; I often undertook arguments against him; and sometimes I seemed the superior in disputation. Those of our fellow students who were considered foremost bore this with all the greater indignation, since I was regarded as later both in age and in the time I had devoted to study.

Here began the origins of my misfortunes, which persist even now; and the more widely my reputation spread, the more other people’s envy was inflamed against me. At last, presuming upon my ability beyond the strength of my years, I aspired, while still a youth, to direct schools myself, and I secured a place in which to do so: the fortress of Melun [variant: “the fortress at Melun”], then a distinguished royal residence.

> [Note: Col. 116D. The fortress of Melun and royal residence.—King Hugh of the Franks granted the fortress and county of Melun, or Meldun, as a fief to Burchard the Old, count of Vendôme and lord of Lavarzin. Later Renaud, Burchard’s son, chancellor of France and bishop of Paris, was count of Melun under King Robert, as is evident from the documents of the church of Saint-Denis-de-la-Chartre. But upon his death the county returned to Henry I, Robert’s son, who appointed a viscount there. For in the charter of Philip confirming his father’s foundation of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, “Urso, viscount of Melun,” subscribed among the other knights of the royal court. Finally Philip himself, Henry’s son, established his royal residence at Melun, where he also died in our Abelard’s lifetime, as Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, testifies in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, son of Philip:
>
> “When he was nearly sixty years old, having laid aside the kingship at the fortress of Melun on the river Seine, in the presence of Lord Louis, he closed his last day.”]

My aforesaid master perceived this; and, seeking to place our schools as far as possible from his own, he secretly contrived by every means available to him to deprive me, before I had left his school, both of our proposed school and of the place secured for me [Col. 117A]. But because he had certain enemies there among the powerful men of the land, I attained my wish through their support; and his manifest envy won me the approval of very many people.

From the beginning [variant: apprenticeship] of our school, my name began to spread so widely in dialectic that the reputation not only of my fellow students but even of my master himself gradually dwindled and was extinguished. Thus, becoming still more confident in myself, I transferred our schools as quickly as possible to the fortress of Corbeil, which lies nearer to Paris, so that from there our opportunity might provide more frequent assaults in disputation.

> [Note: Cols. 117A–118C. Concerning the fortress of Corbeil.—This too is an ancient fortress and, if not a residence of kings, at least of queens. To clarify this, I shall also note the old counts of Corbeil, Corboil, or Curboil.
>
> Certainly the most ancient count of Corbeil of whom I have read was Haimo, said to have lived in the year of Christ 963. For John, monk of Saint-Victor, writes of him under that year:
>
> “At the same time the body of blessed Guenailus, abbot, was transferred from Brittany into Gaul because of fear of the Normans; and, by God’s ordering, it was received in the fortress of Corbeil by Count Haimo and honorably deposited in a church built by that Haimo in his honor.”
>
> And the Calendar of Saint Guenailus, under 21 May:
>
> “The solemn anniversary of Count Haimo, founder of Blessed Guenailus of Corbeil, who gave that church the tenants whom we possess beyond the bridge over the Seine.”
>
> But if this is so, the long interval of years suggests that this Haimo was different from that Count Haimo of Corbeil who, as Odo, monk of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, reports, “journeying to Rome to pray at the shrines of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, met the end of his life there on the journey.” For this occurred near the beginning of Hugh’s reign.
>
> After his death, “Burchard, count of Vendôme, joined in marriage his wife, named Elizabeth, herself born of noble lineage; and in the bridal chamber of that union King Hugh gave him the fortress of Melun and Corbeil and the county of the city of Paris.” Thereafter Burchard too styled himself count of Corbeil. Or, if this latter Haimo is the one who built the church of Saint Guenailus, or Guenaldus, the body of that saint must have been brought to Corbeil later than the aforesaid John recorded.
>
> This latter opinion pleases me all the more because Burchard, husband of his wife Elizabeth, mentions in a charter issued for Saint Guenaldus the grant which Haimo had made to the aforesaid church:
>
> “We wish all faithful clerics and laypeople to know that I, Burchard, count of Corbeil, for the remedy of my soul and of those of my ancestors and successors, and at the request also of Guillaud, canon of the same place, and of my son Master Renaud, have granted to Saint Guenailus the little lands which Count Haimo had formerly given to that saint, etc.”
>
> Further, this Burchard, count of Corbeil, is mentioned also in the Calendar of Saint Guenailus:
>
> “Likewise, the anniversary of Count Burchard, who gave the same church certain tenants at Mundeville.”
>
> Afterwards William became count of Corbeil; he subscribed to the discovery of the bodies of Saint Denis and his companions in the reign of King Henry I. I would not affirm that he was the son of Elizabeth and her first husband Haimo.
>
> After William, Renaud held the county and attended the confirmation of King Philip I’s foundation of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, about the year of Christ 1067. Burchard II succeeded Renaud and, in 1071, granted the cloister of Saint Exuperius to the canons of Corbeil. He had a son Odo, likewise after him count of the fortress of Corbeil, concerning whom the documents of Saint-Martin-des-Champs speak under the year 1097.
>
> Suger relates in the *Life of Louis the Fat* that he was a cousin of Guy the Red and died when struck by the spear of Count Stephen. After this, his kinsman Hugh of Crécy, son of Guy the Red, was compelled by Louis the Fat, son of Philip, to “renounce the fortress of Corbeil, of which he claimed to be heir, together with all forced services, tallages, and possessions.”
>
> Finally Louis the Younger, son of Louis the Fat, or Louis the Elder, left the land of Corbeil to his wife Adela as a dower. This is shown by the charter of King Philip II, Adela’s son, issued at Corbeil in 1180:
>
