> “Philip, by the grace of God king of the Franks, etc. Let all present and future persons know that, while our mother Adela held the land of Corbeil as her dower, she gave to Peter, her cleric and a canon of Blessed Exuperius, in recognition of his service, the house which Isabella and Bertran her son had sold to Elias the Jew,” etc.
>
> Thus it is clear how the fortress of Corbeil also became a royal residence. Indeed, from this time kings appointed viscounts there, as at Melun. The documents of Blessed Mary of Gournay mention “Pagan, viscount of Corbeil,” in 1205.]

Not long afterward, however, worn down by excessive application to study, I fell ill and was compelled to return home. Separated, as it were, from France for several years, I was sought with still greater eagerness by those whom the teaching of dialectic interested.

When a few years had passed and I had long since recovered from my illness, my teacher William, archdeacon of Paris, changed his former dress and entered the order of regular clerics. He did so, people said [Col. 119A], in the hope that the more religious he was considered, the higher he might be promoted in rank of office—as shortly afterward happened, when he became bishop of Châlons.

> [Note: Cols. 118C–119A. My teacher William.—Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, admirably praises this change of dress in William in Letter 1, addressed to him:
>
> “My soul rejoices and exults at your conversion and manner of life, offering thanks to him whose gift it is that you have at last resolved to practise philosophy. For you did not yet have the savor of a philosopher when, from the acquired doctrine of philosophers, you did not display the beauty of moral knowledge,” etc.
>
> He entered the regular order in a certain chapel of Saint Victor outside Paris; there, with several disciples, he began to build the monastery which King Louis the Fat afterwards magnificently completed and endowed with great and rich revenues. This is attested first by an anonymous but ancient author who collected the beginnings of various abbeys and noted their founders:
>
> “At the same time Master William of Champeaux, formerly archdeacon of Paris, a man exceedingly learned and religious, having assumed the habit of a regular canon, began, with several of his disciples outside the city of Paris, on the site where there was a chapel of Saint Victor the martyr, to build a monastery for clerics. When he had been raised to the bishopric of Châlons, the venerable Gilduin, his disciple, became the first abbot there.”
>
> This also explains what Abelard says shortly afterward: “Yet the habit of his conversion did not withdraw him either from the city of Paris or from his customary philosophical study; rather, in the very monastery to which he had retired for religion’s sake, he immediately conducted public schools in his usual manner.” We say more elsewhere about him after he had become bishop of Châlons.]

Yet this habit of conversion did not withdraw him either from the city of Paris or from his customary study of philosophy. Rather, in the very monastery to which he had withdrawn for religion’s sake, he immediately conducted public schools in his usual way.

Then I returned to him in order to hear rhetoric from him. Among the other contests of our disputations, I compelled him, by the clearest argumentative disputations, to alter—indeed, to abandon—his old position on universals. In that theory of the common nature of universals, he maintained that one and the same thing in its entirety was present essentially and simultaneously in each of its individual instances [Col. 119B]; these had no diversity in essence, but only variety through a multiplicity of accidents. He corrected this view so as thereafter to say that the same thing was present not essentially but indifferently.

Since the question of universals is always the principal question among dialecticians, and so important that Porphyry himself, writing of universals in his *Isagoge*, did not venture to decide it, saying, “For such a matter is most profound,” once William had corrected [variant: corrected]—indeed, had been compelled to abandon [variant: had abandoned]—that opinion, his teaching fell into such neglect that he was scarcely admitted any longer to lectures on dialectic [variant: to the other subjects of dialectic], as though the entire substance of the art consisted in this very doctrine of universals [Col. 119C].

Hence our teaching acquired such strength and authority that those who had formerly adhered most strongly to our master and most fiercely attacked our instruction flocked to our schools. The very man who had succeeded our master in the schools of Paris offered me his place, so that there, with the others, he might submit himself to my instruction—precisely where our former master, his and mine, had once flourished.

During the few days in which I directed the study of dialectic there, it is not easy to express how our master began to waste away with envy and burn with grief. Unable long to bear the heat of his conceived misery, he cunningly undertook once more to remove me. Since he had nothing he could openly do against me, he sought to take away the schools from the man who had granted me his teaching post. He brought the most disgraceful charges against him and installed another, an enemy of mine, in his place [variant: in his office].

Then I returned to Melun [variant: Melidun] [Col. 120B] and established our schools there as before. The more openly his envy persecuted me, the more authority it gave me, in accordance with that poetic line:

> Envy aims at the highest things; the winds blow about the loftiest peaks.

(Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, I.369.)

Not long afterwards, when he realized that almost all his disciples [variant: the discerning ones] had grave doubts about his religious profession and were murmuring vehemently about his conversion—because, namely, he had not withdrawn from the city at all—he moved himself, his community of brethren, and his schools to an estate some distance from the city.

I immediately returned from Melun to Paris [Col. 120C], hoping thenceforward for peace from him. But because, as I have said, he had caused our place to be occupied by my enemy, I set up the camp of our schools outside the city on Mont Sainte-Geneviève, as though to besiege the man who had occupied our place.

> [Note: Cols. 119C–122C. Outside the city on Mont Sainte-Geneviève.—This hill, formerly called Lecutitius or Locotitius, lay outside the walls of Paris until 1211, when Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, “enclosed the entire city in a circuit on the southern side as far as the river Seine,” as Rigord relates, “including within the circuit of the walls a very great expanse of land on both sides and compelling owners of fields and vineyards either to lease those fields and vineyards for inhabitants to build new houses upon them or themselves to establish new houses there, so that the whole city as far as the walls might appear full of houses.”
>
> Accordingly Eugenius III, in a letter to Odo, abbot of Sainte-Geneviève, says that the church was still outside Paris in 1150: “Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Odo, first abbot of the church of Sainte-Geneviève, which is beside Paris.” Alexander III repeats the same in another letter to Abbot Alberic, issued in 1163.
>
> That this church was a centre of literary and public schools—even before the secular canons were changed into a regular order through the aid and efforts of Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, at the command of Pope Eugenius III and the illustrious King Louis VII of France, father of Philip Augustus—is indicated both by our Peter’s statement that he pitched the camp of his schools there and by the earlier Hulbodus. As an ancient inscription in the church of Saint John the Baptist at Liège records:
>
> “While still a young man, having fled Paris from scholastic instruction, he attached himself to the canons of Sainte-Geneviève in the reign of Robert, king of France; and in a short time became the instructor of many schools. When for some time he was unknown to Lord Notger, bishop of Liège, he was finally compelled by execution of an episcopal canonical sentence to return, leaving behind many marks of learning and moral discipline.”
>
> Therefore, in memory and, as it were, in honorable testimony of this fact, for a long time afterward the chancellor of the University of Paris was chosen solely from the community of canons of Sainte-Geneviève, until the pontificate of Pope Benedict XI, who first granted authority and power equal to those of the chancellor of the Church of the Blessed Virgin Mary.
>
> The anonymous writer of the *Life of Abelard* says:
>
> “At that time Master Peter Abelard, having gathered many pupils about himself, held a public school in the cloister of Sainte-Geneviève. He was indeed a man of proven learning and exalted eloquence, but an inventor and defender of unheard-of novelties; seeking to establish his own opinions, he rejected other opinions that had been approved. Hence he had incurred the hatred of those of sounder judgment; and as his hand was against all, so all hands were armed against him. He said things no one had dared to say before, so that all might marvel at him.
>
> “When the absurdity of his inventions came to the attention of those who were staying at Paris for the sake of learning, they first stood astonished; then, led by a certain zeal for refuting falsehood, they began to ask among themselves who would undertake the task of disputing against him. It was surely disgraceful that, among so many learned persons, the speaker of such trifles should have no opponent; that one barking in this manner should not be driven off by the staff of truth; that he would invent still more and declaim more freely if there were no critic of his unhappy undertakings.
>
> “Since the venerable young man Goswin possessed both effective eloquence and a keen intellect, they urged him to confront Abelard on such foolishness. This was not difficult to obtain, for he burned and longed intensely for it, and it would have been labor to restrain one so willing, had he not feared incurring the reproach of presumption.
>
> “Master Joscelin, who later held the see of Soissons, loved Goswin greatly and forbade the undertaking, dissuading him from such a contest. He said that ‘Master Peter’ was ‘not a disputant but a quibbler; that he played the role of a jester more than of a teacher; that, like Hercules, he would not lightly cast aside the club once seized’—that is, that he was obstinate in error; that unless a matter went according to his own view, he would never yield to truth; that whoever attempted to teach a mocker injured himself; that it was enough to understand Abelard’s tricks and not be drawn into his vanities.’
>
> “The learned man and teacher dismissed these and similar discouraging words, since eloquence and a rich vein of wisdom enabled him to direct his speech wherever he wished. But Goswin, paying no attention to his warnings and arguments, though otherwise he greatly revered him, and not considering that he was still a novice scarcely reaching manhood while that master was a most warlike man accustomed to victories, took several companions and went up Mont Sainte-Geneviève, like David about to meet Goliath in single combat. There Abelard thundered forth to his listeners wonderful and unheard-of opinions, mocking, as it were, the battle-lines of soundly wise men.
>
> “When Goswin reached the place of contest, that is, entered Abelard’s school, he found him lecturing and inculcating his novelties upon his pupils. As soon as the newcomer began to speak, Abelard turned a grim look upon him. Knowing himself to be a man trained for battle from youth, and seeing the other just beginning adolescence, he despised him in his heart—perhaps no less than the uncircumcised Philistine despised holy David. For Goswin was fair and handsome in appearance, but slight in body and not tall in stature.
>
> “When that proud man was compelled to answer and Goswin pressed his attack vigorously, he said, ‘See that you keep silent, and beware of disturbing the course of my lecture.’ But Goswin had not come to be silent and pressed sharply, while his adversary, in turn, despising him, paid no heed to the words of his little sheep, judging it unworthy that so great a teacher should answer so very small a youth. He judged by outward appearance, which seemed contemptible to him because of its shortness, but did not attend to the heart, which sees keenly.
>
> “When his own students, who knew the youth well enough, urged him not to omit an answer—saying that he was a sharp disputant, greatly supported by learning; that it was not unbecoming to undertake disputation with such a person, but most unbecoming to scorn him further—he said, ‘Let him speak, if he has anything to say.’
>
> “Having received permission to speak, Goswin formed, from the points that moved him, a proposition so apt that it gave no impression whatever of trivial and chattering wordiness, but won the attention of all by its seriousness. As Goswin made his assumptions and Abelard affirmed them, and Abelard could not contradict those affirmations, every avenue of evasion was wholly closed. Finally, by Goswin, who was not ignorant of Abelard’s devices, Abelard was convicted of maintaining something inconsistent with reason.
>
> “Thus the strong man had been bound by the one who entered his house; and he came down from the mountain after one who had bound Proteus, changing form, with the indissoluble knot of truth. When they came to those who had been staying apart in the tents of the schools, they burst into cries of exultation and joy: the tower of pride had been humbled, the wall of obstinacy had fallen, the mocker of Israel had failed, the anvil of the hammerer and the hammer forging lies had been broken, and, finally, the engine of falsehood had been destroyed. This had been accomplished not by a weighty crowd, not by assistance begged from outside, not by the premeditated ingenuity of sophisms, nor by extraordinary personal authority overpowering the opponent, but by a humble, steadfast, learned, and powerful defender of truth.”  
> (*Patristic Edition.*)]

When he heard of this, our master immediately and shamelessly returned to the city, bringing back to the former monastery the schools he was then able to maintain and the community of brethren, as though to release from our siege the soldier whom he had abandoned [variant: dismissed].

But while he intended to benefit that man, he harmed him most severely. He had previously had some pupils of whatever quality, especially because of the lecture in which [variant: because of Priscian’s lectures, in which] he was believed to be very capable. But after the master’s arrival he lost every one of them and was thus compelled to cease directing the schools. Not long afterwards, as though now despairing further of worldly glory, he too entered [variant: was compelled to enter] monastic life.

After our master’s return to the city, what conflicts of disputation our pupils had both with him and with his disciples, and what results fortune gave in these wars to our side—indeed, to myself in them—you too have long since learned from the event itself. But I shall speak more moderately in Ajax’s words, and say boldly:

> …if you ask the outcome  
> of this battle, I was not defeated by him.

(Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, XIII.89.)

If I were silent, the event itself cries aloud, and the issue of the affair makes it known.

While these things were happening, my dearest mother Lucia compelled me to return home.

> [Note: Col. 122C. My dearest mother Lucia …—The Calendar of the Paraclete: “On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November died Lucia, mother of our master Peter.”]

After my father Berengar had entered the monastic profession, she intended to do the same. When this had been accomplished, I returned to France, chiefly in order to learn more of theology, since [variant: because] our often-mentioned master William was now flourishing in the bishopric of Châlons [Col. 122B].

> [Note: Cols. 122D–123C. William in the bishopric of Châlons …—William, or Wuillelmus, now bishop of Châlons, is mentioned by Ivo of Chartres, Letter 268; Saint Bernard, Letter 3; and Otto of Freising, *On the Deeds of Frederick I*, book I, chapter 47. He was raised from being a regular canon of Saint-Victor to the bishopric in the year of Christ 1112, as may be inferred from the election of his disciple Gilduin as first abbot of the church of Saint-Victor in 1113. He bore the episcopal office for seven years and six months. Thus the manuscript list of bishops of Châlons says: “The venerable William governed the Church for seven years and six months.” When these had been completed, he finally yielded to fate in 1119, on 25 January, as is learned from these words of the Victorine Calendar: “The eighth day before the Kalends of February: anniversary of Wuillelmus, bishop of Châlons [Col. 123B], and our canon [Col. 123C].”]

In this branch of study, his teacher Anselm of Laon then held the greatest authority by reason of his long standing.

> [Note: Cols. 123C–124D. Master … Anselm of Laon …—There were several Anselms of Laon at nearly the same time. The history of the restoration of the Church of Laon, written by a canon of that church, mentions Anselm, abbot of Saint-Vincent at Laon, who “had presided over his monastery for almost seventeen years and, having gone to Rome for the benefit of that monastery, was found there, by a remarkable event and God’s ordering, by the clerics of Tournai, who had lacked their own bishop for four hundred years. He was chosen bishop, and was consecrated pontiff by Pope Eugenius, bound unwillingly and resistingly by the bond of obedience. Thus through him the ancient dignity was restored to the Church of Tournai in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1145.” [See *Patrology*, vol. CLVI, col. 1003 ff., Patristic Edition.]
>
> It also mentions another, earlier Anselm, surnamed Beessi, “who, by pretending to be religious, was greatly praised and honored by all. Therefore the treasury of the Church of Laon was entrusted to him, along with other guardians, because it was the ancient custom of that church to entrust its treasury to seven guardians, four clerics and three laymen. But, as became evident from the outcome, he was far different in heart from what people saw outwardly. Seeing that everyone trusted him greatly, he secretly tore off no small part of the gold and precious stones with which crosses to be placed on the altar on feast days had been covered, and gave it to a goldsmith for sale.”
>
> Finally, it mentions a third Anselm of Laon, consulted after this theft from the treasury was discovered by the other canons of Laon and by the citizens, as the lamp and light of the whole city. The same author says of him [see above, col. 1011]:
>
> “A general assembly of canons and citizens was immediately called; they debated what ought to be done; and, before all others, Master Anselm, then the lamp of the whole city, was consulted. As one most skilled in divine law, he immediately recalled the history of Joshua: how the Lord commanded that the theft committed in Jericho, though no one knew of it, be sought by lot—first through the tribes, then through families and households, and finally man by man. Following the example of this most careful investigation, Master Anselm advised that the perpetrator of so great a crime should be sought by the ordeal of water: one innocent child from each parish of the city should be placed in a vessel filled with blessed water; whichever parish was found guilty by lot, one child from every house in that parish should be put into the water; and, if any house were detected, all men and women belonging to it should be compelled to clear themselves by the ordeal of water.”
>
> From this it is clear that this later Anselm was the very Master Anselm of Laon whom Peter Abelard says then possessed the greatest authority through antiquity. He was a canon and dean of the Church of Laon, not a bishop, as some have written quite thoughtlessly. The writer already cited teaches this above all in these words:
>
> “Master Anselm, a most wise man, then canon and dean of our Church, was renowned throughout nearly the whole Latin world for the fame of his learning and eloquence.”
>
> Among other hearers and disciples of his lectures were Master William of Champeaux, archdeacon of the Church of Paris, discussed above; our Peter Abelard, himself later a most celebrated master; Alberic of Reims; Lotulf of Novara, or Lombard; and especially William, archbishop of Canterbury. The aforesaid historian of the Church of Laon testifies to this when he says:
>
> “We therefore took up the bier and relics of our lady and came to Canterbury, where Lord William, very well known to us, was then archbishop; for he had long before gone to Laon to hear Master Anselm’s lectures, had remained many days in the bishop’s house, and had taught there the sons of Ralph, chancellor of the king of England.”
>
> From these words it may be inferred that the Church of Laon was then like a great gathering-place for students from every direction, whom the celebrated fame of Master Anselm’s teaching drew from many cities and regions. In what year he died and where he was buried will be stated below.—See the *Notice on Anselm of Laon* prefixed to his works, *Patrology*, vol. CLXII, Patristic Edition.]

## Chapter III. How he came to Laon to Master Anselm

I therefore approached this old man, whose name had been gained more through long use than through ability or memory. Anyone who came to him uncertain, seeking an answer on some question, returned still more uncertain. He was admirable in the eyes of his hearers, but of no worth before those who asked questions. He possessed an astonishing command of words, but one contemptible in meaning and empty of reason.

When he kindled a fire, he filled his house with smoke, not with illuminating light. His tree, wholly covered with leaves, seemed conspicuous to observers from afar; but to those who approached and examined it more carefully [Col. 123B], it proved fruitless. When, therefore, I came to it to gather fruit, I discovered it to be the fig tree which the Lord cursed (Matthew 21:19; Mark 11:13), or that ancient oak to which Lucan compares Pompey, saying:

> …there stands the shadow of a great name,  
> like a lofty oak in a fruitful field.

(Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book IV.135.)

Having learned this, I did not lie idle for many days in his shade. But when I gradually began to attend his lectures less frequently, some men then prominent among his disciples took this very badly, as though I had become a despiser of so great a master. They therefore secretly stirred him too against me and, through malicious insinuations, made me odious to him.

One day, after some comparisons of opinions, we students were joking with one another. When one of them, seeking to provoke me, asked what I thought of the reading of sacred books—since I had as yet studied only secular learning—I answered that this study was surely most salutary, since in it the salvation of the soul is known [Col. 124B]. Yet I was greatly astonished that, for educated people to understand the expositions of the holy fathers, their writings themselves or the glosses did not suffice, so that they needed another instruction [variant: another teacher].

Most of those present laughed and asked whether I could do this and dared undertake it. I answered that I was prepared to put it to the test, if they wished. Then they shouted [variant: cried out] and laughed still more: “Certainly,” they said, “we agree.”

“Let a commentator on some unfamiliar Scripture,” I said [variant: therefore], “be sought and given to us [variant: to you], and let us test what you promise.”

All agreed upon the most obscure prophecy of Ezekiel. Having obtained the commentator’s exposition, I immediately invited them to a lecture on the following day. They gave me unsolicited advice, saying that one should not hurry into so great a matter, but that I, inexperienced as I was, ought to spend longer in investigating and establishing the exposition. Indignantly I replied that it was not my custom to make progress by practice, but by natural ability; and I added that either I would abandon the matter entirely, or they must not delay attending the lecture at my discretion.

Only a few attended our first lecture [Col. 125B], because all thought it ridiculous that I, still apparently wholly inexperienced in sacred learning [variant: inexperienced], should undertake such a thing so hastily. Yet the lecture proved so pleasing to all who were present that they exalted it with exceptional praise and pressed me, following this pattern of our lecture, to compose glosses.

When those who had not attended heard this, they began eagerly to come [variant: to contend and flock] to the second and third lectures, and everyone alike became exceedingly anxious from the very beginning to copy the glosses which I had begun on the first day.

### Chapter IV. On Master Anselm’s Persecution of Him

Accordingly, the aforesaid old man, violently stirred by envy [Col. 0125C], and, as I mentioned above, from that time incited against me by the persuasions of certain persons, began to persecute me in sacred study no less than our William had formerly done in philosophy. Now there were then in this old man’s schools two men who seemed to excel the rest: Alberic of Rheims, namely, and Loculphus [al. Lotulfus; but in Otto of Freising, Leutaldus of Novara] the Lombard. The more highly these men thought of themselves, the more fiercely were they inflamed against me.

Thus, chiefly through their instigations, as was afterwards discovered, that old man, disturbed by them, shamelessly forbade me any longer to carry on the work of glossing which I had begun in the place where he was master. He alleged this reason: that if perhaps [Col. 0125D], being still inexperienced in this field of study, I should write anything mistakenly in that work, it might be imputed to him. When this reached the ears of the students, they were stirred with the greatest indignation at so obvious a calumny of envy—something which had never before happened to anyone. The more evident it was, the more it brought me honour; and, by persecuting [al. having persecuted] me, it made me more renowned.

[Col. 0126A]

### Chapter V. How, Having Returned to Paris, He Completed His Glosses Which He Had Begun to Teach at Laon

After a few days—

> [Note: [Col. 0125D] “Having returned to Paris,” etc.—Otto of Freising, *On the Deeds of Frederick I*, book I, ch. 47: “Afterwards,” he says, speaking of Abelard, “going to very eminent men—Anselm of Laon and William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons—and judging the weight of their words to be empty of subtlety’s keen edge, he did not endure them for long. Thereupon assuming the role of a master [Col. 0126D], he came to Paris, powerful in a great subtlety of invention, useful not only for philosophy but also for moving men’s minds to amusement and jest.”

—having returned to Paris, I peacefully held for some years the schools which had long been assigned and offered to me, from which I had first been driven out. There, at the very beginning of my teaching, I strove to complete those glosses on Ezekiel which I had begun at Laon. These proved so acceptable to their readers that they believed I had now gained no less favour [al. glory] in sacred study than they had seen me gain in philosophy.

Hence our schools increased greatly through enthusiasm for both kinds of teaching; and how much profit they brought me in money, and how much renown, could not have escaped even you through common report. But prosperity always puffs up fools [Col. 0126B], worldly tranquillity weakens the vigour of the mind, and it is easily dissolved through carnal allurements. When I judged myself to be the sole surviving [al. superior] philosopher in the world and feared no further disturbance, I began to loosen the reins for lust, though I had formerly lived most chastely. And the more I advanced in philosophy or sacred study, the farther I departed, in the uncleanness of my life, from philosophers and divines.

For it is agreed that philosophers—let alone divines, that is, persons devoted to the exhortations of sacred study—have especially excelled in the beauty of continence. Since, therefore, I laboured wholly in pride and luxury, divine grace bestowed on me, though unwilling, a remedy for both diseases: first for luxury, then for pride. For luxury, by depriving me of the means with which I practised it; for pride, which sprang up in me chiefly from knowledge of letters, by humbling me through the burning of that book in which I chiefly gloried, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1).

[Col. 0126C] I now wish you to know both histories of this event more truly from the event itself than from hearsay, and in the order in which they occurred. Since I had always abhorred the uncleanness of prostitutes, and was kept from excess and from frequenting noblewomen by the continual occupation of scholarly study, and knew little of the society of laywomen, perverse fortune, as the saying goes, flattering me, found a more convenient opportunity by which more easily to cast me down from this pinnacle of eminence; or rather, by which divine mercy might claim for itself one who was most proud and unmindful of the grace received [Col. 0126D], once he had been humbled.

### Chapter VI. How, Falling in Love with Heloise, He Received From It a Wound Both of Mind and Body

For there was in the city of Paris—

> [Note: [Col. 0126D] “A certain young girl named Heloise.”—The learned man Papyrius Masson, book III of his *Annals*, says that this Heloise, a girl of outstanding intelligence and beauty, was the natural daughter of some John, a Parisian canon. But it is not evident whence he drew this claim; nor does it agree with Abelard’s own words or even with the Calendar of the Paraclete, which records the death of the canon Fulbert—Heloise’s uncle—though corruptly under the name Hubert, in these words: “7 Kalends of January: Hubert, canon and uncle of Lady Heloise, died.”

> Indeed, Fulbert, canon of Paris, is also mentioned by Orderic Vitalis, monk, in book VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*. The chronology especially leads me to believe that he too was the same uncle of Heloise: “In the reign of King Louis,” he says, “there was at Paris a canon named Fulbert, who possessed an entire bone from Saint Ebrulf’s spine. A chaplain from the chapel of Henry, king of the Franks, had taken it away and long before given it to him as a pledge of affection. Fearing, for various reasons, to retain it, he summoned, through the mediation of Fulk, priest of Maule, William of Montreuil, prior of Maule, and handed over the relics to be carried to the Church of Ouche.”]

—a certain young girl named Heloise, niece of a canon called Fulbert. The more he loved her, the more diligently he had endeavoured to advance her in every branch of literary learning that he could [Col. 0127A]. Though she was not of the least beauty in face, she was supreme in abundance of learning. For the more unusual this good thing—literary learning—is among women, the more it commends a girl and makes her famous throughout the whole kingdom.

Having considered all the circumstances which usually attract lovers, I judged her the most suitable person with whom to enter into a love affair, and I believed I could do this most easily. For at that time I was of such great reputation, and excelled in youth and physical attractiveness, that I feared no rejection from any woman whom I might deem worthy of my love. I believed this girl would consent all the more readily, because I knew that she both possessed and loved literary learning; and because, even when absent, we could make ourselves present to each other by written messengers [Col. 0127B], write many things more boldly than we could say them in speech, and thus always enjoy delightful conversation.

Wholly inflamed with love for this young woman, I sought an opportunity to make her familiar to me through domestic and daily intercourse, and so more easily draw her to consent. To accomplish this, I dealt with the aforesaid uncle of the girl through the intervention of some of his friends, asking that he receive me into his house, which was near our schools, for whatever payment for board he might require. I pretended that my studies were greatly hindered by domestic care for my household and that the expense burdened me excessively.

Now he was very greedy [Col. 0127C], and was extremely eager that his niece should make continual progress in literary instruction. By these two means I easily obtained his agreement and got what I desired, since he was wholly intent upon money and believed that his niece would gain something from my teaching. In this matter, by earnestly entreating me beyond what I would have dared to hope, he furthered my wishes and served my love. For he placed her wholly under my instruction, so that whenever I was free after returning from the schools, by day or night, I might devote myself to teaching her; and, if I found her negligent, I might discipline her severely.

I was greatly amazed by the extent of his simplicity: I was no less astonished within myself than if he had entrusted a tender lamb [Col. 0127D] to a hungry wolf. For, in giving her to me not only to be taught but also to be severely disciplined, what else did he do but grant my wishes complete licence and offer an opportunity—even had we not wished it—so that, if I could not bend her by caresses, I might more easily bend her by threats and blows? But two things especially turned him away from shameful suspicion: his love for his niece, and the reputation for continence which I had formerly enjoyed.

Why say more? First we were joined in one house, afterwards in heart. Under the pretext of instruction we gave ourselves wholly to love, and study supplied the secret retreats [al. recesses] which love desired. With books opened before us, more words of love than of reading entered our conversation; there were more kisses than reasoned sentences. Hands were more often drawn to bosoms than to books; love more often turned our eyes upon each other than reading directed them to the written page. To lessen suspicion, love sometimes gave blows—not anger, but affection; not wrath, but tenderness, sweeter than all perfumes [Col. 0128B].

What more? No stage of love was omitted by us in our desire; and if love could devise anything unusual, it was added. The less we had experienced these delights, the more ardently we pursued them, and the less readily did they turn to disgust. The more this pleasure possessed me, the less I was able to attend to philosophy and devote myself to the schools. It became intensely wearisome to me to go to the schools or remain there, and equally burdensome, since I had to preserve nights awake for love and days for study.

My teaching had then become so negligent and lukewarm that I produced everything not from intellectual power but from habit. I had become merely a reciter of my former discoveries; and if I could compose any poems, they were love poems, not philosophical doctrines. Many of these poems, as you yourself know, are still widely circulated and sung in many regions, especially by those whom a similar life delights [al. whom a similar life delights]. What grief, what groans, what lamentations our students raised over this, once they perceived this occupation—or rather disturbance—of my mind [Col. 0128C], it is not easy even to imagine.

For so manifest a matter could now deceive only few, and no one, I think, except the very man to whose disgrace it chiefly pertained: the girl’s uncle himself. Although some persons had occasionally reported it to him, he could not believe it—both because, as I mentioned above, of his excessive affection for his niece, and because he knew the continence of my past life [Col. 0128D]. For we do not readily suspect shamefulness in those whom we love greatly; nor can the stain of shameful suspicion exist in intense love.

Thus blessed Jerome says in his letter to Sabinianus (letter 48):

> “We are usually the last to know the evils of our own household, and, while neighbours sing of them, remain ignorant of the faults of our children and wives. But what is known last nevertheless at some point comes to be known; and what everyone discovers cannot easily remain hidden from one person.”

[Col. 0129A] So, after several months had passed, this also happened to us. Oh, how great was the uncle’s pain when he learned it! How great the lovers’ pain at their separation! How overwhelmed was I with shame! With what anguish was I afflicted at the girl’s distress! What surges of sorrow did she endure because of my disgrace! Neither complained about what had happened to himself or herself, but about what had happened to the other. Neither bewailed personal troubles, but the troubles of the other.

Yet this separation of bodies was the greatest union of souls. Denial of physical access kindled love more fiercely; and the pain of shame, once undergone, made us more shameless. The less acute the pain of shame became, the more fitting the action seemed. Thus there happened to us what poetic fable tells of Mars and Venus when they were discovered.

> [Note: [Col. 0129D] Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book XIV, and Homer, *Odyssey*, book VIII.]

Not long afterwards the girl discovered that she had conceived, and immediately wrote to me about it with the greatest joy, asking what course I thought should be taken. One night, while her uncle was absent, as we had arranged, I secretly took her from her uncle’s house and promptly sent her to my homeland.

> [Note: [Col. 0129D] “There she stayed with my sister . . .”—The name of this sister of Abelard was Dionysia; I find that she died “on the second Nones of December.” Thus the Calendar of the monastery of the Paraclete: “2 Nones of December: Dionysia, full sister of our master Peter, died.”]

There she stayed with my sister—

> [Note: [Col. 0129D] “Until she bore a son, whom she called Astralabe.”—Heloise herself, writing to Peter, abbot of Cluny, says: “Remember, for God’s sake and ours, your Astralabe, that you may obtain for him a prebend from either the bishop of Paris [Col. 0130D] or any other bishop.” Peter replied to Heloise: “For your Astralabe, and ours on your account, as soon as the opportunity is given, I shall gladly endeavour to obtain a prebend in one of the distinguished churches.” That this Astralabe, or Astrolabe, also bore the name Peter is shown by the necrology of the Paraclete in these words: “4 Kalends of November: Peter Astralabe, son of our master Peter, died.”]

—until she bore a son, whom she named Astrolabe.

After her departure, her uncle was, as it were, driven mad. No one could know except by experience how he burned with grief and how he was afflicted by shame. He did not know what he should do to me, or what snares he should lay for me. If he killed me or mutilated my body in some way, he feared especially that his dearest niece might suffer for this in my homeland. He was utterly unable to seize me and keep me somewhere against my will, especially because I took great precautions against this, since I did not doubt that, if he were able or dared to act, I would attack him sooner.

At last, greatly sympathizing with his excessive anguish, and bitterly accusing myself, as for the greatest treachery, of the wrong that love had done, I approached the man [Col. 0129D] with entreaties and promises of whatever satisfaction he himself might prescribe. I maintained that no one who had experienced the force of love could find this surprising, if he remembered into what great ruin women had cast even the greatest men from the very beginning of the human race [Col. 0130A].

In order to appease him beyond what he could have hoped, I offered to make satisfaction by joining in marriage to myself the woman whom I had seduced, provided it was done secretly, lest I suffer injury to my reputation. He agreed; and, by his own pledges and those of his people, and with kisses, he made the peace I requested with me, the more easily to betray me.

### Chapter VII. The Aforesaid Girl’s Discouragement of Marriage; Yet He Marries Her

I immediately returned to my homeland and brought back my beloved in order to make her my wife. But she did not approve of this at all; indeed, she strongly dissuaded me for two reasons, namely danger and disgrace to me. She swore that no satisfaction of this kind could ever appease her uncle, as was afterwards discovered [Col. 0130B].

She also asked what glory she would gain from me if she made me inglorious and humiliated both herself and me together. What punishments the world ought to exact from her if it deprived the world of so great a light; what curses, what losses to the Church, what tears of philosophers would follow this marriage. How improper and lamentable it would be that I, whom nature had created for all, should be devoted to one woman and subjected to such shame. She vehemently denounced this marriage as altogether disgraceful and burdensome [al. dishonourable] to me.

She set before me both my loss of reputation and the difficulties of marriage. In urging us to avoid these, the Apostle says:

> “Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she will not sin. Yet such people will have tribulation in the flesh; but I spare you” (1 Cor. 7:27).

And again:

> “I want you to be free from anxieties” (ibid., 32).

If I would not accept either the Apostle’s counsel or the exhortations of the saints concerning so great a yoke of marriage, then, she said, I should at least consult philosophers and consider what they have written on the subject, or what has been written about them. Even the saints often do this carefully in rebuking us.

Such is the passage of blessed Jerome in the first book *Against Jovinianus*, where, after carefully setting forth in considerable detail Theophrastus’s intolerable burdens of marriage and continual anxieties, he establishes by most evident arguments that a wise man should not take a wife; and Jerome himself concludes those philosophical arguments of exhortation thus:

> “When Theophrastus argues these and similar points, which of the Christians is not put to shame?”

[Col. 0131A] The same writer says in the same work:

> “Cicero, when Hirtius asked him, after he had repudiated Terentia, to marry her sister, wholly refrained from doing so, saying that he could not give attention both to a wife and to philosophy. He did not simply say ‘give attention,’ but added ‘at the same time,’ unwilling to do anything that might be made equal to the pursuit of philosophy.”

But, leaving aside for the moment this hindrance to philosophical study, consider the condition required by honourable living itself. What concord is there between students and maidservants; between writing desks and cradles; between books or tablets and distaffs; between styli or pens and spindles? Who, intent upon sacred or philosophical meditations, can endure the crying of children, the lullabies of nurses soothing them, and the noisy crowd of a household, men and women alike? [Col. 0131B] Who can bear the continual filthy messes of little children?

You will say that the rich can do this: those whose palaces or spacious houses contain separate quarters, whose wealth does not feel expenses, and who are not tormented by daily concerns. But, I say, this is not the condition of philosophers, but of rich persons; nor will those who pursue wealth or are entangled in worldly cares have leisure for divine or philosophical duties. Therefore the distinguished philosophers of old, who most greatly despised the world—not so much abandoning secular life as fleeing it—denied themselves every pleasure, in order to rest in the embrace of philosophy alone.

One of them, indeed the greatest, Seneca, instructing Lucilius, says (*Letters*, 73):

> “One must not philosophize only when one has leisure; everything must be neglected, in order that we may devote ourselves to this pursuit, for which no amount of time is sufficiently great. It matters little whether you abandon philosophy or merely interrupt it. For it does not remain where it was interrupted. We must resist occupations; they must not be unravelled, but removed.”

What those who are truly called monks now endure among us for the love of God, those who were noble among the nations—the philosophers—endured for the desire of philosophy. For among every people, whether gentile, Jewish, or Christian, there have always been some who excelled others in faith or uprightness of life, separating themselves from the people by some exceptional continence or abstinence.

Among the Jews in ancient times there were the Nazirite men, who consecrated themselves to the Lord according to the Law; or the sons of the prophets, followers of Elijah or Elisha, whom, as blessed Jerome attests [Col. 0131D] (letters 4 and 13), we read of as monks in the Old Testament. Finally there were those three sects of philosophy which Josephus, distinguishing them in book XVIII of the *Antiquities* (ch. 2), calls Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes.

Among us are monks, who imitate either the common life of the Apostles or that earlier solitary life of John. Among the gentiles, as has been said, there were philosophers. For they referred the name of wisdom or philosophy not so much to the acquisition of knowledge as to the religious discipline of life, as we have learned from the very origin of the name itself, on the testimony also of the saints.

Thus blessed Augustine says in book VIII of *The City of God*, distinguishing the schools of philosophers:

> “The Italian school had Pythagoras of Samos as its founder, and from him the very name of philosophy is said to have arisen. For whereas those who seemed to surpass others in a certain kind of praiseworthy life were formerly called wise men, when this man was asked what he professed, he replied that he was a philosopher—that is, a student or lover of wisdom—because to profess oneself wise seemed excessively arrogant.”

[Col. 0132B] When, therefore, it says here, “those who seemed to surpass others in a certain kind of praiseworthy life,” it plainly shows that the wise men of the gentiles—that is, philosophers—were so named rather for the praise of their life than for knowledge. How soberly and chastely they lived, it is not for us now to collect by examples, lest I seem to teach Minerva herself.

But if laymen and gentiles lived thus, bound by no profession of religion—

> [Note: [Col. 0131D] “What ought you, a cleric and canon, to do . . .?”—I find nowhere of what church Abelard was a canon, unless perhaps he was of Sens. For a manuscript chronicle of the archbishops of Sens has this: “In the year 1142,” it says, “Master Peter Abaelard, canon first of the greater Church of Sens, died . . . He was a canon, and afterwards married.” Yet some suspect that the provincial council later convened against him at Sens gave rise to this opinion. However this may be, it must not be doubted, even on the testimony of his own wife, that he was a cleric or canon before he married.]

—what ought you, a cleric and canon, to do, lest you prefer shameful pleasures to divine offices; lest this Charybdis swallow you headlong; lest you plunge yourself shamelessly and irretrievably into these obscenities? If you do not care for the prerogative of a cleric, at least defend the dignity of a philosopher. If reverence for God is despised, let at least love of honour restrain your shamelessness.

Remember that Socrates was married, and by what shameful misfortune he first paid the penalty for this blot on philosophy, so that others thereafter might be made more cautious by his example. Jerome himself does not omit this, writing in the first book *Against Jovinianus* as follows concerning Socrates:

> “On one occasion, when he had resisted the endless insults which Xanthippe hurled down at him from above, she poured filthy water over him. He made no further reply than, after wiping [al. lowering] his head: ‘I knew that rain would follow that thunder.’”

She further added how dangerous it would be for me to take her back, and how much dearer to her, and more honourable for me, it would be to be called my beloved rather than my wife: so that I might keep her by grace alone, rather than be constrained by any force of the marriage bond [Col. 0132D]. And, if we were separated for a time, we would receive more delightful pleasures from our meeting in proportion as such meetings were rarer.

By arguments such as these, urging and dissuading, when she could not turn aside my folly and could not bear to offend me, she ended her speech with deep sighs and tears:

> “One thing remains at the end: in the destruction of us both, the grief which follows will be no less than the love which has preceded it.”

[Col. 0133A] In this she did not lack the spirit of prophecy, as the whole world afterwards recognized. After our little son was born and entrusted to my sister, we returned secretly to Paris. A few days later, after private night vigils of prayer had been celebrated in a certain church, we were joined there at dawn by the nuptial blessing, with her uncle and certain friends of mine and hers present. Immediately afterwards we departed separately in secret, and thereafter saw one another only seldom and covertly, concealing as far as possible what we had done.

But her uncle and his household, seeking consolation for their disgrace, began to make public the marriage which had been contracted and to violate the pledge given to me concerning it. She, on the contrary, cursed them and swore that it was utterly false. Therefore he was violently enraged and assailed her with frequent insults. When I learned this—

> [Note: [Col. 0133B] “I sent her to the abbey called Argenteuil.”—The abbey of Argenteuil, Argentolium, or, as the ancients call it, Argentogilum, was founded in the district of Paris on the River Seine by Hermenricus and his wife Mummana, who first established monks there. But after its destruction by Norman raids, Queen Adelaide, wife of King Hugh and mother of King Robert, rebuilt it from the foundations and assigned it to nuns serving God under the Rule of Saint Benedict, as Helgaud, monk of Fleury, teaches in his *Life of King Robert*:

> “His mother also, Adelaide, a queen greatly admirable in holy devotion, built a monastery in the Parisian territory, at the estate called Argenteuil, where she assembled a considerable number of handmaids of God prepared to live under the rule of Saint Benedict, in praise and glory of the inspirer of all good things; and she wished it to be dedicated and consecrated to the almighty Lord under the honour of holy Mary, Mother of God and perpetual Virgin.”

> Moreover, she obtained from King Robert confirmation of the churches and estates, very many of which she granted to that monastery. For in the manuscript cartulary of Saint-Denis, preserved in his very richly furnished library by Jacques-Auguste de Thou, a man most distinguished for manifold nobility and learning, I have found the following charter issued by her son, the king.

#### Gift Made by King Robert to the Nuns of Argenteuil

> “By the will of the King of kings, Robert, king of the Franks, we wish this to be publicly known to all our faithful Catholics. Since we are unwilling in any way to depart from the practice of our predecessors concerning the ordinances of sacred religion, we exhort all who tend toward blessedness to help us most earnestly by their vigilance in strengthening the privileges concerning the possessions of God and of His saints [Col. 0133D], so that they may receive with us remission of sins for worthily carrying out such a work.
>
> Moved by the prayers of our most distinguished mother, Queen Adelaide—to whom we ought to deny nothing whatever, but rather to serve most devotedly in every respect—regarding the confirmation by charter of certain churches and estates which [read: which] she gave to the nuns serving God in the monastery of Saint Mary at Argenteuil, for the repose of her own soul, that of our father Hugh of blessed memory, and ours, we have willingly complied with her desire and, favouring her requests, have taken care to fulfil her petition on proper grounds.
>
> The possessions granted are these. First, those which King Hugh possessed at Argenteuil, giving them to those consecrated to God and dwelling there. Also Cavenoilus, where thirty *mansi* are reckoned to be held, with a church in honour of Saint Peter. Likewise the estate of Montiliacus, with seven *mansi* and a church in honour of Saint Martin. In the village of Aconiacus, two *mansi*. In Otrevilla likewise, two and a half *mansi*. Between Alnedum and Lisivilla, one *mansus*. At Villena, therefore, one *mansus*. At Satrovilla, twenty *mansi* with two fisheries. On the island of Berliseia, and in the estate itself of Cornella, another fishery. At Argenteuil, the market, the wheel-toll, and the wine tax. At Lupocurte, five *mansi*. The estate of Trapas also, with all belonging to it and its church. The estate of Anilecortis, with all belonging to it and its church. The estate of Burduneium likewise, with all belonging to it and its church. The estate of Monsterolum with its church. The estate of Saint Loanium [read: Saint Soanius], with its church, one mill, and twelve arpents of meadow. The estate of Brathelas [Col. 0134C], with all its appurtenances and churches; likewise the estate of Merlant; likewise the estate of Carisius, with three mills and meadows.
>
> We confirm by our authority all the aforesaid possessions, given to the aforesaid nuns for love of God and reverence for the most blessed Mary, Mother of God, so that they may always remain valid under the fullest protection and safeguard of immunity. Thus, no one henceforth, in our time or that of our successors, shall dare to enter in order to exact legal claims, fines or tributes, lodgings or provisions, to take sureties, unjustly to distrain either free persons or slaves of that Church dwelling upon their lands, or to demand any revenues or unlawful exactions; nor shall anyone presume to exact the things mentioned above.
>
> Rather, let it be permitted to those nuns to possess the aforesaid things peacefully under the protection of this guarantee, for the support of those who serve God there until the end. And so that this charter may be held firmer in God’s name and more diligently preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own faithful, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our seal.
>
> Done at Easter at Saint-Denis, in the twelfth year of the reign of Robert, most glorious king of the Franks, indiction 1. Franco, chancellor, at the king’s command, have examined and subscribed it.”

> How, after those nuns had been expelled, the monastery of Argenteuil returned again to monks will be noted more fully below.]

—I sent her to a certain abbey of nuns near Paris, called Argenteuil, where she herself had once been raised and educated as a little girl. I also had garments suitable for the religious life [al. monastic way of life], except for the veil, made for her, and clothed her in them.

When her uncle and her relatives and connections heard this, they thought that I had now cruelly deceived [al. mocked] them, and that, by making her a nun, I would easily rid myself of her. Therefore, greatly angered, they conspired against me. One night, while I was resting and sleeping in the private chamber of my lodging, with one of my servants bribed by money, they inflicted upon me a most cruel and shameful punishment, one received by the world with the utmost astonishment [Col. 0134B]:

> [Note: [Col. 0134D] “That is, by cutting off those parts of my body . . .”—How Abelard was castrated at night, how all ranks of the city of Paris gathered to him in the morning in astonishment, and with how great lamentation they afflicted themselves in mourning for the wound in his body—especially the women—is very well described by Fulk, prior of Deuil, in the letter which he then sent him for consolation: “You had given your limbs to rest and sleep,” etc. See this letter below.]

That is, they cut off those parts of my body by which I had committed the deed they lamented. [Col. 0135A] When they immediately fled, the two who could be caught were deprived of their eyes and genitals. One of them was the aforesaid servant, who, though he remained with me in my service, had been led by greed into betrayal.

### Chapter VIII. On the Wounding of His Body. He Becomes a Monk in the Monastery of Saint-Denis; Heloise a Nun at Argenteuil

When morning came, it is difficult—indeed, impossible—to express with what astonishment the whole city gathered around me, with what lamentation it afflicted itself, with what cries it tormented me, and with what weeping it disturbed me. Above all, the clerics, and especially our scholars, tortured me with intolerable lamentations and wailings, so that I was wounded far more by their compassion than by the suffering of my injury, [Col. 0135B] and felt shame more than the wound, and was afflicted more by humiliation than by pain.

There came to my mind how great was the glory in which I had lately flourished; how, by an easy and momentary blow, it had been humbled—or rather utterly extinguished. How justly, by God’s judgment, I was punished in that part of my body in which I had sinned. How justly the man whom I had formerly betrayed had repaid me in kind by betraying me. With what praise my enemies would exalt so manifest an act of justice. What lasting anguish this wound would bring upon my parents and friends. How widely this singular disgrace would spread throughout the whole world. What path would thereafter lie open to me; with what face could I appear in public, pointed at by every finger [variant: “marked out”], gnawed at by every tongue, and made a monstrous spectacle to all? [Col. 0135C]

Nor did it cause me little shame that, according to the literal sense of the Old Law, eunuchs are held in such abomination before God that men made eunuchs by the removal or crushing of their testicles are forbidden to enter the Church as foul and unclean; and that animals of this sort are likewise wholly rejected in sacrifice. Leviticus 22:24: “You shall not offer to the Lord any animal whose testicles are bruised, crushed, cut, or removed.” Deuteronomy 23:1: “A eunuch [Col. 0136A] whose testicles have been bruised or cut off, and whose member has been severed, shall not enter the assembly of God.”

In this condition of such miserable ruin, I confess that shame rather than the devotion of conversion drove me into the hiding places of monastic cloisters. Yet she first, of her own accord, took the veil at my command and entered a monastery.

> **Note: [Col. 0135D] “Both therefore,” etc.**—The abbey of Saint-Denis at Paris, renowned as it is, needs no explanatory notes. That Peter Abelard assumed the monastic habit there is attested by William of Nangis in his *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 1141, and before him by Otto, bishop of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick I*, book I, chapter 47, in these words: “There [that is, at Paris], having been badly treated on a sufficiently well-known occasion, he became a monk in the monastery of Saint-Denis. There, devoting himself day and night to reading and meditation, he became keener from being keen, and more learned from being learned.”

Thus we both received the sacred habit at the same time: I in the abbey of Saint-Denis, she in the aforesaid monastery of Argenteuil. I remember that, when many people compassionately but vainly sought to deter her in her youth from the yoke of the monastic rule as from an intolerable punishment, she broke forth, as best she could, amid tears and sobs into Cornelia’s lament:

> … O greatest husband!  
>
> [Col. 0136B] O husband unworthy of my bridal chamber! Had Fortune  
> Such power over your head? Why did I, impious woman, marry,  
> If I was to make you wretched? Now receive the penalty—  
> Yet one which I shall willingly pay.
>
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book VIII, 94.)

With these words she immediately hurried to the altar; at once she took from the altar the veil blessed by the bishop and, before all, bound herself by monastic profession.

Scarcely had I yet recovered from my wound when clerics flocking to me earnestly entreated, with continual petitions both our abbot and myself, that I should now devote myself to study for the love of God, rather than for the desire of money or praise, as I had done hitherto; that I should consider that the talent entrusted to me by the Lord (Matthew 25:15) would be demanded back by him with interest; and that I who had until then chiefly attended to the rich [Col. 0136C] should henceforth devote myself to teaching the poor. They urged me especially to recognize that I had now been touched by the Lord’s hand so that, withdrawn more freely from carnal enticements and from the tumultuous life of the world, I might give myself to literary study—and might become truly a philosopher not so much of the world as of God.

> **Note: [Col. 0135D] “But that abbey of ours … was exceedingly secular and disgraceful in its life.”**—Yet not very long before, Kings Hugh and Robert had procured its reform through the agency of the venerable Odilo, abbot of Cluny, whom Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, calls an archangel. This is stated first by Ademar, monk of Limoges, in his *Chronicle* [*Patrologia*, vol. CXLI, col. 46]:
>
> “The monastery of Blessed Denis, which had already corrupted its former monastic rule, King Hugh restored more honorably, as was fitting in the churches of the Lord, to regular discipline through the agency of the venerable Abbot Odilo; and he recalled several other monasteries of saints to the beauty of their former discipline.”
>
> Jotsald, monk of Cluny, also states it in the *Life of Saint Odilo* [*Patrologia*, vol. CXLII], book II, chapter 9:
>
> “Near Paris is the monastery of Saint Denis the martyr, illustrious through the honor of his glorious body. This place had been entrusted by the Frankish kings Hugh and Robert to Odilo, man of God, that it might be improved through monastic order and the teaching of a regular life. At one time, while God’s servant was staying in that monastery, he supplied nourishment of life and the draught of salvation to his hearers with eloquent speech. The elder Ivo, an amiable man, then held the office of provost, and he strove to observe and honor the worthy father,” etc.

But the abbey to which I had withdrawn was exceedingly secular and utterly disgraceful in its way of life.

> **Note: [Col. 0136D] “Its abbot himself, in proportion as he surpassed the others in rank, was worse in life …”**—The abbot of Saint-Denis in question was named Adam. He began to govern the monastery in [Col. 0137A] 1094; but whether his life was as infamous as Abelard here writes may reasonably be doubted. For it is clear from the following document provided by the records of Saint-Denis that he took great care of Christ’s poor.
>
> [Col. 0137B] **On five measures of grain given by the almoner to the poor**
>
> “In the name of God, I Adam, by God’s grace abbot of the monastery of Christ’s martyr Denis, wish it to be made known to the whole body of the faithful that, in the thirteenth year of our rule, famine grew so severe in our land that grain, though purchasable at a dear price, could scarcely be found. Afflicted and almost lifeless through this scarcity, the poor crowded in many ways upon our workshops. Countless numbers rushed daily to the doors of the alms-house. Moved by compassion for their distress, my brethren and I assembled in chapter and began to deliberate how we might relieve their want and need.
>
> “While we were considering this, Brother John, to whom we had entrusted the alms-house, rose in the midst and said that, if we granted that the alms-house and its adjoining property should be free from every exaction by the officials of Saint-Denis and from every evil custom, he himself would procure five measures of grain [Col. 0137C] and give them for the support of the poor. Therefore, with the consent of the entire chapter, I granted what he asked, etc. Witnesses to this act are, first, I Adam, abbot, who ordered this charter to be made; then Lord Theobald, abbot of Fosses; Allelmus, prior; etc. Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1111, indiction IV, epact IX, 206 [concurrent VI?], cycle X, golden number XIV, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, Easter Day, the fourth day before the Nones of April, its twentieth lunar day, in the reign of Lord Louis, son of King Philip; in the fourth year of his reign, in the month of May.”
>
> There are, moreover, other documents in the same place in which his piety and concern for the honor and increase of divine worship appear, as follows:
>
> **Gift of Adam, abbot of Blessed Denis, and of the whole convent, concerning the church of Saint Peter, to the church of Saint Paul**
>
> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Father, [Col. 0137D] Son, and Holy Spirit. Amen. Adam, by the grace of God abbot of the monastery of Christ’s martyrs Denis, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, to all children of the holy and universal Church, present and future. I wish it to be known to the charity of you all that I and our chapter—that is, the church of Blessed Denis—by common decree and favor have given—and, by our own hand, through the keys of the church [which?] we shall have placed upon the altar as the endowment of the church when it is to be dedicated, have given, I say—to the basilica of Saint Paul the church of Saint Peter situated beside it, free and unencumbered.
>
> “We have also given it authority to appoint and remove a priest there, saving the honor of our Church. The reason for this gift is that each year, on the night of the feast of Blessed Denis, the canons of Saint Paul shall come in procession to the church in which his body rests and there festively sing Matins before our community. To the priest Ralph, surnamed ‘of Fosses,’ who held the aforesaid church of Saint Peter from us, we have given a full prebend in the refectory at the first table, so that [Col. 0138A] he may possess it in full for as long as he lives. We have also granted that the prebend of bread and wine which those canons received in the storehouse may be received in the refectory. Whoever takes away this endowment of the Church, or withdraws from the aforesaid Ralph during his lifetime the prebend granted him by us, shall be subject to divine vengeance and to our [Col. 0138B] anathema. Done, given, and confirmed in the chapter of Saint-Denis in the year of the Incarnate Word 1114, indiction VII, epact XXIII, concurrent IV, the seventh year of King Louis. The sign of Adam, abbot; of Saint Alelmus, prior,” etc.
>
> Therefore I cannot sufficiently wonder why Abelard should also assert that, by frequently and vehemently reproving, sometimes privately and sometimes publicly, the “intolerable filthiness” of that abbot and the monks of Saint-Denis, he had made himself excessively burdensome and hateful to all—unless perhaps he wished to return something of equal favor, at least in sharpness of language, to men whom he later found most hostile. See Saint Bernard’s letter 78, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII.

Its abbot himself, in proportion as he surpassed the others in preeminence, was worse in life and more notorious in infamy. By frequently and vigorously rebuking their intolerable foulness, sometimes privately and sometimes publicly, I made myself excessively burdensome and hateful to all. Greatly pleased by the daily insistence of our pupils, they found an opportunity to remove me from their midst. Thus, after they had pressed and importuned for a long time, with our abbot and brethren likewise intervening, [Col. 0138A] I withdrew to a certain cell, intending to continue my teaching as usual.

> **Note: [Col. 0138B] “To this place such a multitude of scholars flocked …”**—No one has expressed more briefly Abelard’s innumerable multitude of pupils than the author of the *Chronicle of Maurigny*, who says [*Patrologia*, vol. [Col. 0138C] CLXXX]:
>
> “Peter Abelard, monk and abbot, was a religious man, a most excellent master of schools, to whom learned men flocked from almost the whole Latin world.”
>
> What that author contained in summary and almost in a single word, Fulk, prior of Deuil, had earlier set out more clearly and in greater detail. In the letter in which he consoled Abelard after his castration, he speaks thus of pupils and hearers flocking to his schools from Italy, Germany, Spain, England, Flanders, and every province of France:
>
> “Rome sent you her own pupils to be taught; and she who formerly used to pour the knowledge of every art into her hearers showed herself wiser than her wise self by sending you her scholars. No extent of land, no mountain summits, no hollow valleys, no road, however beset by difficult danger and by robbers, held them back from hastening to you. The sea lying between and the terrible storm of the waves did not frighten the throng of English youths; despising every danger, they flocked to you upon hearing your name. Distant Brittany sent its creatures to be trained. The people of Anjou, their savagery tamed, served you among their own. Poitevins, Gascons, Iberians, Normandy, Flanders, Germans, and Swabians continually strove to cultivate, praise, and proclaim your genius. I pass over all those dwelling in the city of Paris, and in the nearest and most distant regions of Gaul, who thirsted to be taught by you as though no branch of learning could be found except with you. Moved by the brilliance of your intellect, the charm of your speech, the ease of your most fluent tongue, and the subtlety of your knowledge, they hastened on their way as if toward the clearest fountain of philosophy.”
>
> Lest anyone should doubt that there were Roman pupils among the rest, Saint Bernard himself, although somewhat hostile to our Abelard, attests the same thing in letter 193: “He”—namely Peter Abelard—“is nevertheless confident because he boasts that he has had cardinals and clerics of the Curia as his pupils.” Elsewhere he indicates that Guy of Castello, cardinal priest, later Pope Celestine II, [Col. 0139B] was likewise Abelard’s hearer [letter 92, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII].
>
> To associate with supreme pontiffs and cardinals certain more learned bishops as well, Peter of Novara—called Lombard from his native Lombardy, afterward bishop of Paris and Master of the Sentences—embraced Abelard’s lectures above all others. Finally, it is clearer than proof requires that Geoffrey of Auxerre and Berengar of Poitiers, of whose writings and learning something will be said elsewhere, were his pupils.

To this place such a multitude of scholars flocked that neither the place sufficed for lodging nor the land for provisions. There, giving my chief attention, as suited my profession, to sacred reading, I did not entirely abandon the discipline of secular arts, to which I had been especially accustomed and which they eagerly demanded from me. Rather, from these I made [Col. 0139A] a kind of hook, in order that, baited with the savor of philosophy, I might draw them toward the reading of true philosophy—as ecclesiastical history recalls that Origen, the greatest of Christian philosophers, was accustomed to do.

When the Lord seemed to have bestowed on me no less grace in divine Scripture than in secular learning, our schools began to increase greatly from both kinds of study, while all the others greatly declined. This stirred up especially the envy and hatred of the masters against me. Seeking in every possible way to disparage me, they continually objected two things in particular [Col. 0140A] while I was absent: namely, that it was very contrary to the purpose of a monk to occupy himself with the study of secular books; and that I had presumed, without a teacher, to undertake the office of teaching divine learning. Thus they sought to forbid me every exercise of scholarly teaching, continually inciting bishops, archbishops, abbots, and every person of religious standing whom they could influence.

### Chapter IX. On His Book of Theology and the Persecution He Endured from His Fellow Students. A Council against Him

> **Note: [Col. 0139B] “It happened,” etc.**—Abelard himself gives this treatise various names in different places. In his letter to Geoffrey, bishop of Paris, he calls it a *Little Work on Faith in the Holy Trinity*; in his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, he frequently calls it his *Theology*; and in the preface to the work, the *Sum of Sacred Learning*, or an *Introduction to Divine Scripture*.
>
> He says that he composed the work in order to satisfy the request of scholars who demanded that the Trinity, the foundation of the Christian faith, should be explained through human and philosophical arguments and analogies, and who sought things that could be understood rather than merely spoken. Yet these were not the only reasons for writing, as may be inferred from book II, article 4, where he teaches that heresies had not in his age been so repressed that no foundation of faith was any longer needed; indeed, no heretics of former times had broken forth into such madness as certain of his contemporaries had raged.
>
> More explicitly, in the preceding article, he says:
>
> “Whatever any of these men may maintain, I wonder with what face anyone can blame me if he praises the foresight of others who have written on these matters. Unless perhaps he says that our present treatise is wholly superfluous because their teachings suffice, no heresies which need resistance spring up any longer, and no doubts about our faith remain which seem to require some arguments either for its instruction [Col. 0139D] or for its defense. Would that it were so! But, passing over the innumerable multitude of unbelievers outside the Church—both Jews and pagans—who would dare profess that all heresies have been so repressed that there are now no schisms of faith among us and that no dissensions will arise hereafter?”
>
> Accordingly, he composed that book both for his scholars and to repress heretical teachers of the divine books who in his own day not only held but also taught many things contrary to Catholic faith and holy doctrine. “One of them,” he says in article 5, “held a chair of pestilence in France, another in Burgundy, a third in the region of Anjou, a fourth in the territory of Bourges.”
>
> Indeed, he wrote principally against the heresy of one of them, as he himself declares in the already cited letter to Geoffrey, bishop of Paris:
>
> “It has been reported to us by certain of our pupils who have come here that that ancient enemy of the Catholic faith, proud and ever puffed up, whose detestable heresy—of confessing, indeed even preaching, three gods—was convicted by the Fathers at the Council of Soissons [Col. 0140B] and in addition punished with exile, has poured forth many insults and threats against me, having seen a certain little work of ours on faith in the Holy Trinity, written especially against the aforesaid heresy by which he himself is notorious.”
>
> In book II of that work, article 7, he says:
>
> “Another man, likewise entangled in the same errors, posits in God three properties, according to which three persons are distinguished, as three essences distinct both from the persons themselves and from the very nature of divinity—so that God’s fatherhood or sonship, or certain processions, may be things distinct both from the persons themselves and from God himself.”
>
> Who this heretic was need not be sought long if we consider what Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, wrote to Fulk, bishop of Beauvais, about Roscelin, the first teacher of our Abelard. Speaking among other things of Roscelin’s perverse errors concerning the Trinity, which were to be condemned by Rainald, archbishop of Reims, Anselm says:
>
> “I hear—though I cannot believe it without doubt—that the cleric Roscelin says that the three persons in God are three things separated from one another, as three angels are; yet that there is one will and power; or that the Father and the Holy Spirit became incarnate, and that three gods may truly be called such if usage admitted it. He asserts that Archbishop Lanfranc, of venerable memory, held this opinion, and that I do also. Accordingly, it has been said that a council is shortly to be assembled by the venerable Rainald, archbishop of Reims. Since I think that your reverence will be present there, I wish you to be instructed as to what answer you should make on my behalf, should reason require it.”
>
> A little later:
>
> “Whoever asserts as truth the blasphemy which I have set forth above as something I heard Roscelin say—whether man or angel—is anathema; and, to confirm this, I say that, as long as he persists in this obstinacy, let him be anathema. For he is not a Christian at all.”
>
> What could be said more fitting or closer to Abelard’s words? Yet Anselm’s addition that this Roscelin asserted that Lanfranc and Anselm himself shared his opinion proves still more plainly that this was the very man against whom our Peter wrote. For Abelard says in the aforesaid letter to Geoffrey:
>
> “This man dared to forge a defiant letter against that eminent herald of Christ, Robert of Arbrissel; and he blazed so fiercely with insults against that magnificent doctor of the Church, Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury, that by the command of the king of England his shameless obstinacy was disgracefully driven from England, and he scarcely then escaped with his life. He wishes that Anselm should share in his disgrace, so that he may console his own disgrace through the disgrace of good men; he hates nothing except goodness, because he cannot endure being good. Because of the excess of his arrogance, he was expelled with the greatest dishonor from both kingdoms in which he had lived, England and France; and in the church of Blessed Martin itself, of which he is said to have been a canon, he was, as they say, at times [the printed text has *nunquam*, “never”; read perhaps *nonnunquam*, “sometimes”] beaten by the canons, [Col. 0141A] and maintained his customary behavior.”
>
> These words also help interpret another passage of the same Anselm. Writing to Pope Urban II, he reports that, while he governed the monastery of Bec, a certain cleric in France had presumed to make this assertion:
>
> “If there are three persons in God, one thing only, and not three things, then the Father, together with the Son and Holy Spirit, became incarnate.”
>
> He adds that this man was compelled at a council by the venerable Rainald, archbishop of Reims, to abjure his error. [Col. 0141B] Anselm nevertheless says that he afterward heard the author of this novelty, persisting in his opinion, declare “that he had abjured what he said for no other reason than that he feared being killed by the people.”
>
