> Further, everything Peter Abelard says about the council held at Soissons, and Anselm about the defense of the opinion after the abjuration, is likewise attributed to Roscelin by Ivo, bishop of Chartres, in letter 7:
>
> “Ivo, by the grace of God humble bishop of Chartres, to Roscelin. Do not think more highly than you ought to think, but think soberly. If you were the hundredth sheep, lost in the wilderness but now restored to the flock, then, just as my zeal burned against you while I understood you to be turned away and opposed, so my spirit would rest in you if I knew you converted and returned to sound doctrine. But because I know that, after the Council of Soissons, you most diligently defended your former opinion in secret disputations in the hearing of certain persons whom you know well along with me, and wished to persuade them of the same opinion which you had abjured, and of other opinions no less mad, it cannot enter into my heart that you have yet corrected your faith or changed your conduct for the better.”
>
> Finally, what Aventinus writes of Ruscelin, or Roscelin—that he was the founder of the Nominalists, “who, greedy for things and lavish with names and notions, seemed to be defenders of words”—does not wholly disagree with this further objection which Abelard levels against his opponent:
>
> “This man, a pseudo-dialectician as well as a pseudo-Christian, holds in his dialectic that no thing has parts; and he so shamelessly distorts the divine text that, where it says that the Lord ate part of a broiled fish, he is compelled to understand not a part of the thing but a part of the phrase ‘broiled fish.’”
>
> It is therefore unsurprising that Abelard thought it superfluous to identify this man by name, since so many distinctive marks made him uniquely conspicuous. Let this suffice concerning [Col. 0141D] the occasion for composing the treatise *On the Trinity*.

It happened that I first set myself to discuss the very foundation of our faith through analogies drawn from human reason, [Col. 0141A] and composed for our scholars a theological treatise, *On Divine Unity and Trinity*. They demanded human and philosophical arguments, and sought things that could be understood rather than merely spoken. For they said that utterance was superfluous when understanding did not follow it; that nothing could be believed unless first understood; and that it was ridiculous for anyone to preach to others what neither he himself nor those whom he taught could grasp by the intellect. In this, the Lord himself rebukes them as “blind guides of the blind” (Matthew 15:14).

> **Note: [Col. 0141D] “That treatise,” etc.**—The esteem in which this book was held can be shown by the testimony of Saint Bernard alone. Writing to the bishops and cardinals of the Roman Curia [letter 88, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII], he says:
>
> “Read, if you please, the book of Peter Abelard which he calls *Theology*. It is readily available, for, as he boasts, it is much read in the Curia.”
>
> And in letter 191 [same source]:
>
> “That book has risen from the dead; it has already extended its branches to the sea and its shoots even to Rome. This man’s boast is that his book has a place in the Roman Curia where it may lay its head.”
>
> But because the *Books of Sentences* of Peter Lombard, bishop of Paris, attained such standing that they alone eventually deserved to be read in public schools of theology, even from ancient times onward, I shall seem to have commended Abelard’s *Theology* greatly enough if I can openly show that the said Lombard drew chiefly upon it in composing those books. This will be neither difficult nor, perhaps, unwelcome to some.
>
> It is learned from the *Eulogy* of John of Cornwall, a pupil of Lombard himself. After saying, “Master Peter Abelard argues thus in his *Theology*: ‘What is it to say that God becomes man, except that the divine substance, which is spiritual, [Col. 0142B] unites the human substance, which is bodily, to itself in one person?’” he adds, after several intervening lines:
>
> “I have all the more suspected that Master Peter Lombard received this opinion from Master Peter Abelard because he often had that book in his hands; and perhaps, examining each point less diligently—as one whose skill in disputation rested more on practice than art—he could be deceived.”
>
> Thus Saint Bernard ignorantly attributes the book of *Sentences* to Abelard himself in letter 189. For, as Abelard declares in his *Confession of Faith*, “no book entitled *Sentences* will ever be found to have been written by me.”
>
> But before passing to other matters, it will be worthwhile here to undertake a more extensive examination of all this Abelard’s works and writings, especially since Trithemius and others who have spoken of him enumerate only the few works touched upon by Saint Bernard.

[Col. 0142C] **List of the Works of Peter Abelard**

Abelard first composed a work on dialectic, mentioned at the beginning of this letter and in book III of his *Theology*. For in that place the manuscript wrongly has *grammar* for *dialectic*, in these words:

> “That a spirit cannot be moved from place to place is taught us by the testimony both of philosophers and saints, as we showed when treating of quantity while writing our grammar.”

This dialectic, or logic, will shortly, God willing, be printed separately for the benefit of candidates for philosophy.

Moreover, he wrote glosses on the prophet Ezekiel, and love songs, many of which, as he himself says in this very letter, were commonly performed and sung in many regions in his time, especially by persons pleased by a similar way of life.

He also wrote the treatise or book of *Theology* already discussed above; likewise, a *Commentary on [Col. 0142D] the Epistle to the Romans*, which Saint Bernard mentions in his letters to Pope Innocent; and another book which, as the same Bernard says, he entitled *Know Thyself*. This appears to be the *Ethics* to which Abelard himself refers certain questions in the aforesaid commentary. William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, confirms this near the end of book III of his *Disputation*, dedicated to Hugh, archbishop of Rouen:

> “The same Peter also wrote another little work which he entitled *Know Thyself*, and called, if I am not mistaken, his *Ethics*.”

That is, because in it he discussed at length matters of morals—or, to use Saint Bernard’s words, he dealt morally with virtues and vices.

Nor do I doubt that the anonymous poet who wrote in 1376 had read this book. For, since Abelard had promised in his aforesaid *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans* [Col. 0143A] that he would treat free choice in the *Ethics*, the poet cited the following definition of free choice from Abelard:

> Pierre Abelard, in a chapter  
> in which he speaks of free choice,  
> tells us truly  
> that it is a capacity  
> of a rational will,  
> capable of good or evil,  
> and by grace inclined to do good,
And to evil when it declines. [Col. 0143B] But this Ethics, although most diligently sought, has not yet been found or recovered. Finally, Abaelard composed a *History of His Misfortunes*, mentioned by Petrarch; several letters to Heloise and others, some of which are mentioned by Jean Clopinel of Meung; a Rule and ordinances for nuns; expositions of the Lord’s Prayer, the Apostles’ Creed, and the Athanasian Creed; solutions to Heloise’s problems; sermons for the course of the year, addressed to the virgins of the Paraclete; and certain other little works which we have now published for the first time; likewise ecclesiastical hymns, found in the Breviary of the Paraclete; and also an *Apologetic* in defence of his innocence. I am inclined to believe this to be distinct from the *Apology*, or *Confession of Faith*, which he addressed to all the children of the Church; the following words of Otto, Book I of *The Deeds of Frederick I*, chapter 49, move me to this conclusion:

“After the condemnation,” he says, “of his doctrine”—of which we shall speak later [Col. 0143C]—“he withdrew to the monastery of Cluny, writing an *Apologetic*, in which he denied in part the words, and wholly the meaning, of the aforesaid chapters; and it begins thus: ‘That, according to Boethius’s saying, no time may be wasted on prefaces that contribute nothing, we must come to the matter itself, so that the abundance of the facts rather than of words may excuse my innocence.’”

These words, I say, move me because they are not found in the aforementioned *Confession of Faith*, which we inserted on page 330 of this work [see Ambrosian edition]; nor is it inconceivable that he also composed a second and still more extensive apology in defence of his Theology. This also appears to be confirmed by William, Abbot of Saint-Thierry, in Book I of his *Disputation*, when he says: “By his *Apology* he makes his Theology worse; he adds new errors to old ones and strives stubbornly and contentiously to defend them.” And a little before: “First I ask why he falsely charges the abbot, a man of holy religion and great renown, with having fabricated the claim that in [Col. 0143D] his Theology he wrote that the Son is a certain power, and the Holy Spirit no power at all. For in his *Apology*, which Peter himself directs against the abbot, he denies having said this; but he declares that he said that divine Wisdom is a certain power of the Father, not the Son; and that the love of the Father and Son is some power, not the Holy Spirit; and he stubbornly maintains that this is true.” Yet I have not hitherto been able to see this *Apology*. And these, unless I am mistaken, are all the works which Peter Abaelard wrote.]

When very many people had seen and read this treatise [Col. 0143A], it began to please everyone greatly, since it seemed to satisfy all alike concerning these questions. And because these questions seemed more difficult than all others, the greater their gravity had proved to be, [Col. 0144A] the greater was thought to be the subtlety of their solution. Hence my rivals, violently inflamed, assembled a council against me—especially [Note: [Col. 0143D] **Those two old plotters.**—Both were pupils of Anselm of Laon and pre-eminent above the rest in his schools; Heloise also mentions them in Letter 2, and Otto, Bishop of Freising, in Book I of *The Deeds of Frederick I*, chapter 47, where he calls them “distinguished men and renowned masters.” By then they themselves were conducting schools at Rheims. But the one whom our Abaelard calls Lotulf the Lombard, Otto calls Leutald of Novara. Alberic, surnamed of Rheims, [Col. 0144A] is also praised by Saint Bernard in Letter 13 to Pope Honorius, in which he is said to have been elected Bishop of Châlons after the death of William of Champeaux. For the words of Saint Bernard, petitioning Honorius for confirmation of his election, are as follows:

“Concerning the Church of Châlons, my lord, I say that, so far as lies in me, I neither ought nor can conceal its danger. We who are nearby see, indeed we already feel, that the peace of the aforesaid Church will soon be gravely disturbed, unless they can obtain the assent of Your Piety to the election of that distinguished man, Master Alberic—an election in which the entire clergy and people [Col. 0144B] have agreed and do agree with one vote and voice.”

Yet although he prayed as a suppliant, he did not obtain his request, as is clear both from the lists of Bishops of Châlons and from Abaelard, and from Letter 58 of the same Saint Bernard, which plainly teaches that Ebalus succeeded William. Master Alberic, however, shortly afterward became a canon of Liège, as is clear from the calendar of Saint-Victor at Paris; and at last, while already growing old in his office as schoolmaster, he obtained the archbishopric of Bourges. For the chronicler of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens notes this under the year 1139: “In this year,” he says, “Ulgrin, Archbishop of Bourges, died. Alberic of Rheims succeeds.” And still more explicitly: “In the year 1141 Peter of La Châtre is ordained Archbishop of Bourges, upon the death of Alberic of Rheims, the master.”]

those two old plotters, namely Alberic and Lotulf, who, after [Note: [Col. 0144B] **After the deaths of their masters . . .**—William [Col. 0144C] of Champeaux, bishop, died in 1119, as has already been noted above; Anselm of Laon, however, died in 1116, as John, a regular canon of Saint-Victor, writes in his *Chronicle*: “In this year,” he says, “there died the venerable man Anselm, dean of Laon, a most famous master, illustrious for his learning, venerable for the uprightness of his conduct and the maturity of his counsel; among his other works he arranged marginal and interlinear glosses on the Psalter.”

Another manuscript chronicle adds to these words: “He also expounded the Epistles of Paul and other writings of both Testaments in the same manner, by outlining them; and in expounding and glossing them according to the writings of the ancient Fathers, he laboured until old age. Pope Eugenius is reported to have said of him that God had stirred up his spirit lest Scripture perish. Though repeatedly called to episcopal sees, he never consented.” He died at Laon and was buried in the church of Saint Vincent, where one of his [Col. 0144D] disciples adorned his tomb with the following epitaph, fitting to his character and merits:

> In this tomb sleeps that most celebrated master,  
> Anselm, who throughout the regions of the wide world  
> Drew renown from every quarter, and praise from every quarter.  
> Sound faith, abundant learning, reverence in conduct,  
> A splendid life, a generous hand, prudent action,  
> Gracious speech, vigorous discipline, gentle correction,  
> Wise counsel, a provident, sober, and merciful mind.  
> But the gifts which God’s generous grace bestowed  
> Black July dissolved on the accursed Ides.  
> May the grace by which he flourished in life attend him in death.

He had a brother named Ralph, likewise outstanding in no ordinary wisdom. “For through these brothers,” as is still read in the aforementioned *Chronicle*, “but especially through Anselm, the glory of literal learning and the understanding of the Scriptures was in large measure revived.” This is confirmed by that contemporary canon of [Col. 0145A] Laon who described the ruin and restoration of the cathedral church, in these words:

“Just as formerly the Lord destroyed the city of Jerusalem and permitted the children of Israel to be led captive, yet, for the consolation of the few who remained, left the prophet Jeremiah there with them [Col. 0145B], so, when we were placed amid so great a calamity, He mercifully preserved for us two most wise men—namely the aforesaid Master Anselm and his own brother Master Ralph. Sweetly consoling both clergy and laity, refreshing them with diverse sayings of Scripture, they exhorted them not to fail under the adversities of tribulations.” [See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXII.]]

the masters of both them and us, namely William and Anselm, had died, desired to reign alone, as it were, after them, and even to succeed them as heirs. Since both were conducting schools at Rheims, by persistent instigations they stirred up [Note: [Col. 0145B] **Their archbishop, Ralph.**—Ivo of Chartres, Letter 190; Abbot Robert under the year 1114; Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, Book II of *Miracles*, chapter 5; and very many others call this Ralph Archbishop of Rheims. Suger, however, in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, and the continuator of Aimoin, Book V, chapter 50, call him Rodolph together with our Abaelard; Lisiard, in the *Life of Saint Arnulf, Bishop of Soissons*, chapter 36, and the monk Nicholas, in Book III, chapter 24 of the *Life of Saint Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens*, call him Rudolph.

He had formerly been treasurer of the Church of Rheims and was surnamed “the Green,” as can be learned even from this single passage of Peter, Abbot of Cluny (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXIX): “Among these,” he says in Book II of *Miracles*, chapter 5, “Matthew chose a cleric of rather exemplary life, then treasurer of the Church of Rheims, who was named Ralph and surnamed the Green; this man devoted himself to Matthew in a special bond of religious fellowship. Thereafter, when the same Ralph was taken away and raised to the archbishopric of Rheims, he did not desert the man whom he had chosen.”

He was raised to the archbishopric after Manasses, the maternal uncle of Bartholomew, Bishop of Laon. Thus the *History of the Church of Laon* reads: “Accordingly, when he [namely Bartholomew] had been elected to the bishopric of the city of Laon with the unanimous assent of the entire clergy and people, he was presented to Lord Ralph, Archbishop of Rheims, who had succeeded the aforesaid Manasses, his mother’s uncle; and he was consecrated with great solemnity by him and many other bishops in the time [Col. 0145D] of Pope Paschal and Louis, King of the Franks, and was sent as a new shepherd to the desolate sheep.” And Robert of Torigni states briefly: “In the year 1114, in the metropolitan see of Rheims, after the distinguished Manasses, when Gervase had been expelled, Ralph succeeded; he bore the surname the Green.”]

their Archbishop Rodolph against me, so that, [Note: [Col. 0145D] **Having summoned Conon, Bishop of Palestrina.**—This Conon, or Cuno, legate of Pope Paschal II, is mentioned by the monk Nicholas in Book IV, chapter 9 of the *Life of Saint Godfrey, Bishop of Amiens*; by Suger in the *Life of Louis the Fat* (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI); by Robert of Auxerre under the year 1115; by William of Malmesbury, Book I of *The Deeds of the Bishops of England* (*Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX); and by others. Several letters addressed to him by Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, and Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, also survive. The Chronicle of the Abbot of Ursberg calls him Cuno, and another writer calls him Cono. Perhaps this name is no different from Conrad; for the Chronicle of Vézelay has, under the year 1024: “Cono, who is also Conrad, [Col. 0146A] emperor at Rome . . .”

This Bishop of Palestrina served twice as legate of the Apostolic See in Gaul: once under Paschal, in 1115, when he held three councils at Beauvais, Rheims, and Châlons. The old Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens teaches us this: “In the year 1115,” it says, [Col. 0146B] “a council was held at Rheims, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April [27 March]. Another had been held at Beauvais by Conon, Bishop of Palestrina, legate of the Roman Church. Again in the same year another was held at Châlons, on the fifth day before the Ides of April [9 April].”

The second time was about the year 1120, under Pope Calixtus II, as is evident from King Louis the Elder’s charter concerning the church of Cergy and the possessions belonging to it:

“Having taken counsel with our palatines, we hastened with our consort to that basilica of the most holy martyrs—namely Dionysius and his companions—and, in the presence of the venerable Bishop Lord Conon, legate of the Apostolic See, because by the right and custom of departing kings of the Franks the insignia of the realm are rendered to that holy martyr as to their leader and protector, we restored to him our father’s crown, made satisfaction for delaying its restoration, and, restoring to the Church the church at Cergy which we freely possessed, with tithes and all things belonging to that church, bestowed it upon those holy martyrs, both for the salvation of our soul and for the governance of the kingdom and the preservation of our consort and offspring.”

And below: “Publicly enacted in the year 1120 from the Incarnation of the Word, the twelfth of the reign, and the fifth of Queen Adelaide, our son Philip consenting.” This is confirmed by the aforementioned chronicler of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif, who also reports that Conon then held another council at Beauvais: “In the year eleven hundred and twenty,” he says, “a council was held on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November [18 October] by Lord Conon of Palestrina, legate of three provinces—Rouen, Sens, and Rheims. Daimbert the archbishop, with his suffragans and abbots, was summoned to this council at Beauvais.”

There can therefore be no doubt that the lists of Arras err when they state that this Conon died in 1117, on the fifth day before the Ides of August [9 August]. It is no less clear that what Abaelard writes must be referred not to Conon’s first but to his second legation. For he has already mentioned the death of William of Champeaux, who died in 1119, and a little later he refers to Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, who is known to have succeeded Ivo only in 1116.] having summoned Conon, Bishop of Palestrina, who was then acting as legate in Gaul, they held a certain gathering [Note: [Col. 0146D] **Under the name of a council in the city of Soissons.**—At about the same time two councils were convened at Soissons. The first, against Roscelin, was summoned by Rainald, Archbishop of Rheims, in 1095; it is mentioned by Ivo in Letter 7, by Anselm, Abbot of Bec, in his letter to Fulco, Bishop of Beauvais, and by our Abaelard in his letter to Geoffrey, Bishop of Paris, as we have already shown. The second was this council, in 1120, presided over by Conon, legate of the Apostolic See, against the aforesaid Abaelard’s book *On the Trinity*. Therein it was burned, without any opportunity being granted him to reply. For this is stated both later by Abaelard himself and by Otto, Bishop of Freising, Book I, chapter XLVII, of *The Deeds of Frederick I*, in these words:

> “When a provincial synod had been assembled at Soissons in the presence of the legate of the Roman [Col. 0147D] See, he was judged a Sabellian heretic by the distinguished men and renowned masters Alberic of Rheims and Leutald of Novara, and was compelled by the bishops to commit with his own hand to the fire the books which he had published, no opportunity being granted him to reply because all suspected his skill in disputation.”

Hence Bernard states succinctly in a letter to Cardinal Ivo concerning the same Abaelard: “He was condemned at Soissons [Col. 0148D] together with his work, in the presence of the legate of the Roman Church.”]

under the name of a council [Col. 0146A] in the city of Soissons; and they invited me to bring with me that celebrated work which I had composed on the Trinity. And so it happened. But before I arrived there, those two aforesaid rivals of ours had so slandered me among clergy and people that, on the first day of my arrival, the people and a few of our disciples who had come there nearly stoned me, saying, as they had been persuaded, that I preached and had written that there are three gods. As soon as I came to the city, I went to the legate and gave him my little book to inspect and judge. I offered that, if I had written anything dissenting from the Catholic faith, I was ready for correction [variant: “rebuke”] or satisfaction. But he immediately ordered me to take the book itself to the archbishop and to those rivals of mine, so that those who accused me in this matter might judge me—thus fulfilling in me also the saying: “Our enemies are judges” (Deut. 32:31).

Although they repeatedly inspected and turned over the book, finding nothing which they dared bring forward against me in the hearing, they postponed until the end of the council the condemnation of the book for which they were longing. [Col. 0147B] Before the council sat [variant: “withdrew”] each day, however, I publicly expounded to everyone the Catholic faith as I had written it; and all who heard it, with great admiration, commended both the clarity of the words and our meaning. When people and clergy observed this, they began saying to one another: “See, now he speaks openly, and no one says anything against him.” Yet the council hastens to its conclusion, having, as we heard, been assembled chiefly against him. Have the judges discovered that they, rather than he, are in error? Because of this, our rivals were daily more and more inflamed.

One day Alberic came to me with hostile intent [variant: “with the intention of attacking”], accompanied by certain of his disciples. After some flattering conversation [Col. 0147C], he said that he was surprised by a point which he had noted in that book: namely, that although God begot God and yet there is only one God, I nevertheless denied that God had begotten himself. I replied at once: “On this point, if you wish, I shall give a reason.” “We do not care,” he said, “for human reasoning or our own understanding in such matters, but only for words of authority.” I said to him: “Turn the page of the book, and you will find an authority.” The book which he himself had brought with him was at hand. I turned to the passage, which I knew but which he had not found, since he was seeking only material that could harm me. God willed that what I wanted should quickly present itself. It was a passage entitled Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book I [Col. 0147D] (chapter 1):

> “Whoever thinks that God has such power that he himself begets himself is all the more mistaken because not only is God not so constituted, but neither is a spiritual nor a bodily creature. For there is absolutely no thing that begets itself.”

When his disciples who were present heard this, they stood aghast and blushed. But he, seeking somehow [Col. 0148A] to protect himself, said: “Well, it must be understood properly.” I added [variant: “joined thereto”] that this was not a novelty, but irrelevant to the present issue, since he had demanded words only, not meaning. Yet if he wished to attend to meaning and reason, I said that I was prepared to show him, on the basis of his own proposition, that he had fallen into the heresy according to which he who is father is the son of himself. On hearing this, he immediately became, as it were, furious and turned to threats, declaring that neither my reasons nor authorities would avail me in this case. And so he departed.

On the last day of the council, before they reassembled, the legate and archbishop began a long deliberation with my rivals and certain persons as to what should be decided concerning myself and [Col. 0148B] my book, for which matter they had chiefly been summoned. Since they had nothing from my words or from the writing then before them which they could allege against me, and since all had become somewhat silent or were now criticizing me less openly, [Note: [Col. 0148D] **Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres.**—The second of that name, successor to Ivo and later legate of the Apostolic See; much is said of him by Saint Bernard and by another Bernard, Abbot of Bonneval, who wrote his life. Several letters from Geoffrey, Abbot of Vendôme, to him also survive.]

Geoffrey, Bishop of Chartres, who surpassed the other bishops both in the renown of his religious character and in the dignity of his see, began as follows:

“You all know, lords present here, this man’s teaching—whatever it may be—and his talent: in every pursuit to which he has applied himself he has had many admirers [variant: “flatterers”] and followers; he has greatly eclipsed the reputation of both his own masters and ours; and, as it were, has extended the branches of his vine from sea to sea. If you burden him with a prejudgment—which I do not think you will—although you know that you will rightly offend many, many will not be lacking who will wish to defend him; especially since in the writing presently before us we see nothing that can sustain an open accusation. And because, according to Jerome’s saying, ‘Strength that stands in the open always has rivals’ [Note: Jerome, *Prologue to the Hebrew Questions on Genesis*], and ‘lightnings strike the highest mountains’ [Note: Horace, *Odes*, Book II, 10], take care lest, by acting violently, you confer more renown upon him and incur more guilt for ourselves through envy than he incurs through justice.

“For false report, as the aforementioned teacher observes (Letter 10), is quickly crushed, and the later life judges the earlier. But if you intend to proceed canonically against him, let his doctrine or writing be brought forward, and let him be questioned and freely permitted to answer, so that, convicted or having confessed [variant: “confounded”], [Col. 0148D] he may be utterly silenced. At least follow the judgment of blessed Nicodemus, who, wishing to deliver the Lord himself, said: ‘Does our law judge a man unless it first hears from him and knows what he does?’ (John 7:51).”

At this, my rivals immediately raised a noisy outcry: [Col. 0149A] “What wise [variant: “of a wise man”] counsel—to contend against the verbosity of one whose arguments or sophistries the whole world could not withstand!” But it was surely much more difficult to contend with Christ himself, whom Nicodemus nevertheless invited them to hear according to the ordinance of the law.

When the bishop could not induce their minds to accept what he had proposed, he attempted to restrain their envy by another route. He said that the few present could not suffice for examining so great a matter, and that this case required a more extensive investigation. He offered the further counsel that my abbot, who was present, should take me back to my abbey—that is, the monastery of Saint-Denis—and that there, after more and more learned persons had been assembled, it should be determined through a more diligent [Col. 0149B] examination what ought to be done concerning this matter. The legate agreed to this final proposal, as did all the rest. The legate then immediately rose to celebrate Mass before entering the council, and through that bishop he conveyed to me the permission which had been settled: namely, that I should return to our monastery and wait there for what had been agreed.

Then my rivals, reflecting that they had achieved nothing if the affair were handled outside their diocese, where they would have little power to exercise judgment—since they had little confidence in justice—persuaded the archbishop that it would be highly dishonourable to him if this case were transferred to another hearing, and that it would be dangerous should I thus escape. They at once ran to the legate, changed his decision, and dragged him against his will [Col. 0149C] into condemning the book without any examination, immediately burning it before everyone’s eyes, and confining me in perpetual enclosure in a foreign monastery.

For they said that this ought to be sufficient for condemnation of the book: that I had presumed to read it publicly without its having been approved by the authority either of the Roman pontiff or of the Church, and had already supplied it myself to many persons for copying. It would also be very beneficial to the Christian faith if, through my example, similar presumption in many others were forestalled. Since the legate was less learned than was necessary, he relied heavily on the archbishop’s counsel [variant: “made much use of it”], just as the archbishop relied on theirs. When the Bishop of Chartres perceived [Col. 0149D] this, he immediately reported these machinations to me and strongly urged me to endure this more patiently the more plainly their violent conduct was apparent to everyone. I should not doubt that the violence of such manifest envy would greatly harm them and benefit me. Nor should I be at all disturbed about confinement in a monastery, since I could be certain that the legate himself, compelled to do this, would completely set me free a few days after leaving this place. Thus, as best he could, weeping himself, he consoled me as I wept.

## Chapter X. On the Burning of the Book Itself; on the Persecution of Him by His Abbot and the Brethren

Accordingly, when I was at once summoned to the council, they compelled me, without any examination by disputation, to throw my own aforementioned book into the fire with my own hand. And so it was burned. Yet, when they appeared to have nothing to say, one of my adversaries muttered that he had found written in the book that God the Father alone is omnipotent. When the legate caught the implication, he replied in great astonishment that this should not be believed even of some boy [variant: “little child”], that he could err so grossly: [Col. 0150B] “For the common faith,” he said, “both holds and professes that there are three omnipotents.”

On hearing this, a certain Theodoric, a master of the schools, mockingly introduced that saying of Athanasius (*in the Creed*): “And yet not three omnipotents, but one omnipotent.” When his bishop began to rebuke and restrain him as though he were guilty of speaking against majesty, he boldly resisted; and, recalling as it were Daniel’s words (Dan. 13:48), he said: “Thus, foolish sons of Israel, without judging or recognizing what is true, you have condemned a daughter of Israel. Return to judgment, and judge the judge himself, whom you have appointed as such a judge for the instruction of the faith and correction of error [variant: “errors”], [Col. 0150C] and who, when he ought to judge, has condemned himself by his own mouth. May divine mercy today openly deliver the innocent man, as it once delivered Susanna from false accusers.”

Then the archbishop rose and, altering the wording as occasion required, confirmed the legate’s assertion: “Indeed, my lord,” he said, “the Father is omnipotent, the Son omnipotent, and the Holy Spirit omnipotent. Whoever dissents from this is plainly astray and ought not to be heard. And now, if it pleases you, it is good that this brother should set forth his faith before everyone, so that it may, as necessary, either be approved or disapproved and corrected.”

But when I rose to profess and explain my faith, in order to express in my own words what I believed, my adversaries said that [Col. 0150D] [variant: “necessary”] nothing else was required of me except to recite the Athanasian Creed, which any boy could do equally well. And lest I should plead ignorance in excuse, as though I did not have those words in use, they had a written copy brought for me to read. I read, amid sighs, sobs, and tears, as best I could. [Note: [Col. 0149D] **Thereafter, as though guilty and convicted.**—This abbot was perhaps that Anselm who, about the year of Christ 1128, was Abbot of Saint-Vincent at Laon and finally became Bishop of Tournai in 1145; concerning him we have already spoken above from the *History of the Church of Laon*.

The monastery of Saint Medard was begun by Chlothar I, king of the Franks, at Soissons, and completed and endowed by his son Sigebert, as Gregory, Archbishop of Tours, teaches in Book IV, chapter 22 of the *History of the Franks*, in these words: “Also in the time of King Chlothar, Saint Medard, bishop of God, having completed the course of good work and being full of days, pre-eminent in holiness, died. King Chlothar buried him with the highest honour in the city of Soissons and began to build a basilica over him, which his son Sigebert afterward completed and furnished.” Saint Gregory, the supreme pontiff, further reports that this monastery had been made by John III, his predecessor, the head of all the monasteries and abbeys of France.

But because the letters which assert this are highly suspect and are also charged with forgery by many, it is fitting to insert here the entire constitution of John III; although it too is not free from the fault of fabrication, or at least alteration. For among other things it mentions the title “archbishops,” which was not in use before the age of Pippin and Charlemagne. Its style also does not appear consistent with papal letters of that century. Indeed, confirmations of monastic foundations were not sought from the Roman See, nor were years from the Lord’s Incarnation appended to public instruments, until much later, as the most learned and illustrious Cardinal Baronius teaches somewhere. The constitution or privilege of John III is as follows:

**Privilege of Pope John III, granted to the Monastery of Saint Medard at Soissons.**
> “To the rulers of the whole world, governing the fabric of the world under Christ the ruler—to those present, namely, and those to come—John, least in the quality of his merits, but, by the grace of Christ, prelate of the holy Roman see. It is evident that those whom the religion of divine faith and apostolic majesty ennobles ought to demonstrate their faithful service by the fruit of their works and the devotion of their acts. Therefore, by divine grace inspiring us and at the persuasion of the clemency of the most eminent King Chlothar, we grant in every respect this privilege to the monastery of Saint Mary and Blessed Peter, situated outside the city of Soissons, where Lord Medard is seen to rest and Abbot Daniel to preside: namely, that they may hold and possess in their entirety the lands which our son Chlothar gave for the salvation of his soul—Cromacum, Attipiacum, and his estate of Aluvit in the district of Metz—together with the wood commonly called Patella Salis; and that they may have, hold, and possess them with lands, houses, buildings, and altars.
>
> “We also decree, by the authority of the holy Trinity and inseparable Unity, in the place of the blessed apostle Peter, before King Chlothar and all the common people of the Franks—that is, archbishops, [Col. 0151D] bishops, judges, and all the people of the Christian Roman rulers—that no king, prelate, or judge shall exact from the lands of Saint Mary and Lord Medard, or from their churches or altars, tolls, tithes, new exactions, bans, or freda. Nor is this done to the unjust prejudice of the author of laws or canons, since nothing is diminished from canonical authority by whatever is granted to the places of venerable saints for the tranquillity of peace and the service of God.
>
> “We further establish that, just as this see of blessed Peter is known to be free from every service owed to kings and to all powerful persons, so, with every evil custom of all kings, archbishops, bishops, archdeacons, and judges removed, the monks of the aforesaid basilica may freely devote themselves to God and obey in all things the practices of the Rule of Saint Benedict without any disturbance. By the present privilege we also grant them permission that, upon an abbot’s death, they may summon for the purpose of ordaining an abbot whichever archbishop [Col. 0152A] or bishop they wish. They shall act similarly in the ordinations of priests, levites, and the other orders which they celebrate in their monastery, if they wish, without any opposition from the archbishop of Rheims or the bishop of Soissons.
>
> “To the present abbot and all [Col. 0152B] his successors we grant the power, during the solemnities of Mass, to pronounce blessings and to preach to the people, in reverence of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Stephen, Christ’s protomartyr, and Lord Medard, by whose honour and merits that consecrated place shines. To their venerable and chief altar we grant, by royal command and apostolic authority and for the sake of honour, all churches and altars from all lands which have been or shall be bestowed. The consecration of fonts and the mysteries of the scrutiny shall always be celebrated in this monastery. Let them also seek the blessing of chrism and oil wherever they please; and let so great an honour never be withheld by any ruler on any pretext or necessity, lest a place of such high dignity be debased—a place which we have constituted the head of all monasteries in the whole of Gaul, and which we permit to be subject to no one’s dominion. Rather, being always placed under royal protection, [Col. 0152C] it shall have, by the authority of the bishops of this holy Roman see, the advocacy of blessed Peter.
>
> “Let all successors of the holy Church of God and governors of the realm beware of rendering void this privilege, which has been sanctioned by apostolic authority, truly confirmed by the hands of kings, made with the consent of Baudarius, bishop of Soissons, and moreover strengthened by the following anathema of seventy bishops. Whoever, in the name of authority, becomes an opponent of this decree; or disturbs the brothers in the aforesaid basilica; or removes anything from all things granted or to be granted to that place; or orders otherwise: on the day of the Lord’s revelation let him be *anathema maranatha*, cut off from the fellowship of Christianity and estranged from the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Whatever his eminence or rank, let him be deprived of his honour in this present age and banished into exile; and in the age to come let him be condemned with Judas, betrayer of the Lord, to eternal punishments, [Col. 0152D] and let him be plunged with the devil and his angels into the lowest hell, never to rise again—unless he appeases the minds of the holy congregation and is reconciled to the ministers of the holy Church of God.
>
> “I, Simplicius, notary of the holy Roman see, have subscribed and sealed. Given in the Church of Saint Sylvester, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the year 562 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth indiction.”

Moreover, how highly other Frankish kings after Chlothar valued that distinguished basilica of Saint Medard is shown especially by what Andrew, monk of Marchiennes, writes:

> “In the eleventh year of his empire, Emperor Louis obtained from Pope Eugenius the body of Saint Sebastian the martyr and placed it at Soissons in the basilica of Saint Medard; at its arrival God performed many miracles.”

Then, as if guilty and convicted, I was handed over to the abbot of Saint Medard, who [Col. 0151A] was present, and was dragged to his cloister as to a prison. The council was immediately dissolved. The abbot and monks of that monastery, supposing that I would remain with them thereafter, received me with the greatest rejoicing and, treating me with every care, vainly tried to console me.

O God, who judgest righteousness, with how much gall of spirit and bitterness of mind did I then shamefully accuse you; how furiously did I charge you, repeatedly uttering that complaint of blessed Antony: “Good Jesus, where were you?”

> [Note: Col. 0152D. St Jerome, *Life of Blessed Antony*.]

How fiercely I burned with grief, how shame overwhelmed me, how despair disturbed me, I could then feel but cannot express. I compared what I was now enduring with what I had formerly suffered in the body, and judged myself the most miserable of all men. I considered that former betrayal a slight thing in comparison with this injury, and lamented damage to my reputation far more than to my body. [Col. 0153A] For I had come to the former through some fault—[variant: “an old fault”]—whereas the utterly sincere intention and love of our faith, which had compelled me to write, had brought me to this open violence.

When all to whom the report had reached strongly condemned this deed as so cruel and inconsiderate, each of those present shifted the blame from himself onto others; so much so that even our enemies denied that it had been done by their counsel, and the legate publicly declared above all his detestation of the Franks’ malice in this affair. Soon afterward, moved by repentance, when for a time he had been compelled to satisfy their envy, he brought me out of the other monastery and restored me to my own. There I found almost all, as I have mentioned above, still hostile to me, since the foulness of their life and their shameless conduct made them wholly suspicious of me—[variant: “which”]—because they bitterly endured my rebukes.

A few months [Col. 0154A] later fortune gave them an opportunity by which they contrived to destroy me. For one day, while reading, I happened upon a statement of Bede’s in which, in his exposition of the Acts of the Apostles, he maintains that Dionysius the Areopagite was bishop of Corinth rather than of Athens.

> [Note: Col. 0153B. “Dionysius the Areopagite,” etc.—This judgment of Bede concerning Dionysius the Areopagite is still displeasing to many today, who maintain that Dionysius, bishop of Paris, was that Areopagite. But what they cite concerning Innocent III—who gave the body of Saint Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, to the monks of Saint-Denis at Paris—seems neither to favour their opinion greatly nor wholly to prove Abelard’s view, supported by Bede’s authority. An anonymous author who wrote about the relics of the abbey of Saint-Denis recounts the matter thus:
>
> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1215, Innocent III, pope of the holy [Col. 0153C] Roman Church, summoned a general council to the City from every nation under heaven. There were present shepherds and prelates of holy mother Church—namely patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and abbots—and innumerable other persons of lower rank and order. Kings and princes of diverse peoples were also present, either in person or through envoys. But the venerable abbot of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite, named Henry, could not attend with the others, because the weakness of advanced age did not permit it. He therefore sent in his own place and on behalf of his church the religious and honourable man Master Hemeric, prior, with other persons of the same church, to present themselves as fittingly as possible before the lord pope.
>
> “That great council was accordingly held, in which there was discussion of the Catholic faith, morals, the condition of the universal Church, and other matters which it would be lengthy and unnecessary to relate here. When the council was dissolved, each was permitted to depart. But the lord pope, not wishing publicly to reveal to all the goodwill, favour, and loving affection which he then bore, and had always borne, toward the venerable monastery of blessed Dionysius, summoned the aforesaid Hemeric and his companions to himself and, as a pledge of perpetual charity, gave them an inestimable treasure: namely, the body of the most holy Dionysius the confessor, bishop of Corinth. He ordered them to convey it with them honourably into France and, on his behalf, to present it with all reverence to the church of blessed Dionysius. He further gave them letters testifying to his grant, strengthened with the seal of the holy apostolic see. They, with fitting thanksgivings, received this noble, holy, and venerable deposit; rejoicing in the free generosity of the supreme pontiff, they returned to France as swiftly as possible.”
>
> The testimonial letters of Innocent were drawn up there in the following terms:
>
> **[Col. 0154B] Authentic Letter of Pope Innocent**
>
> “INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of Saint-Denis at Paris: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “Whether the glorious martyr and bishop Dionysius, whose venerable body rests in your church, is to be considered that man called the Areopagite who was converted by the apostle Paul, various persons hold varying opinions. Some confess that Dionysius the Areopagite died and was buried in Greece, and that another Dionysius preached Christ’s faith to the peoples of the Franks. Others maintain [Col. 0154C] that he came to Rome after the death of blessed Paul and was sent into Gaul by Saint Clement, pope; and that another was the man who died and was buried in Greece—yet that both were outstanding in deed and illustrious in speech.
>
> “We, wishing to prejudice neither view but desiring to honour your monastery, which belongs immediately to the Roman Church, devoutly send you, through our beloved son Hemeric the prior and certain other envoys from your monastery sent to the general council, the sacred pledge of blessed Dionysius which P., cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, of good memory, then legate of the apostolic see, brought from Greece to the City. Thus, when you possess both relics, no doubt may henceforth remain that the sacred relics of blessed Dionysius the Areopagite are held in your monastery.
>
> “Receive them therefore reverently, repaying us in return by ensuring that special remembrance of us is always made to God in your prayers [Col. 0154D] and that, according to the offering of those same envoys of yours, the anniversary of our death is solemnly observed. To all who devoutly gather to venerate these sacred relics, we remit by apostolic authority forty days of the penances imposed upon them. Therefore let absolutely no one infringe this document of our grant and remission, or rashly oppose it. But if anyone presumes to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.
>
> “Given at the Lateran, on the day before the Nones of January, in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.”
>
> But as regards Abelard: when his brothers gravely threatened him and wished to take vengeance upon him because he had denied that their patron had been the Areopagite, he was at length compelled to sing a recantation. For he addressed a letter to Abbot Adam, his abbot, “Against those who, on the authority of Bede [Col. 0155C] the presbyter, tried to prove that Dionysius the Areopagite was Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, and not rather bishop of the Athenians.” Yet he ended it uncertainly in these words:
>
> “Finally, that we may be able altogether to allay this dispute of conflicting opinions by a most peaceful conclusion, perhaps we may easily preserve Bede’s truthfulness and accept nothing merely by conjecture, if we suppose that there were two Dionysiuses, bishops of Corinth: so that one of the Dionysiuses, bishops of Corinth, was the same as Dionysius the Areopagite of whom Bede writes, and at different times presided as bishop at both Athens and [Col. 0155D] Corinth, and afterward was ordained apostle of the Gauls by Saint Clement; while the other of the Dionysiuses, bishops of Corinth, was that Dionysius of whom ecclesiastical History and Jerome make mention.”
>
> Whatever the case, as Abelard himself says, it need not concern us greatly whether Dionysius, bishop of Paris, was himself the Areopagite or came from elsewhere, provided that he attained so great a crown with God.]

That Dionysius the Areopagite had been bishop of Corinth rather than of Athens appeared very contrary to those who boasted that their Dionysius was that Areopagite, whom his *Acts* themselves declare to have been bishop of Athens. Having found this, I showed it, almost jokingly, to certain brothers who were standing nearby: namely, that testimony of Bede which was brought against us. They became greatly indignant and called Bede a most mendacious writer, declaring that they held their Abbot Huldoin—[variant: “Hilduin, and rightly so”]—to be a truer witness, since he had travelled throughout Greece for a long time to investigate this matter and, having learned the truth, had in the *Acts* of Dionysius which he wrote truthfully removed this doubt.

When one of them pressed me with persistent questioning as to what I thought of this controversy—Bede’s, that is, and Huldoin’s—I replied that Bede’s authority seemed preferable to me, since churches throughout the Latin world read his writings. At this they were violently inflamed and began to cry out that I had now openly shown what they had always claimed: that I had been hostile to our monastery, and that I had now especially insulted the whole kingdom by taking away the honour in which it particularly gloried, when I denied that their patron was the Areopagite.

But I replied that I had not denied this, and that it was not a matter of great concern whether he was himself the Areopagite or from elsewhere, provided that he had attained so great a crown with God. They immediately ran to the abbot and reported what they had charged me with—[variant: “were about to charge me with”]. [Col. 0155B] He gladly heard it, rejoicing that he had obtained some opportunity to crush me, for the more shamefully he lived than the rest, the more he feared me.

Then, having assembled his council and the brothers, he gravely threatened me and said that he would hasten to send to the king so that vengeance might be taken upon me, as though I were depriving him of the glory and crown of his realm. He ordered that I meanwhile be kept securely until he delivered me to the king. In vain I offered to submit to regular discipline, if I had committed any offence.

Then, appalled by their wickedness, since I had for so long endured such adverse fortune, wholly despairing as though the entire world had conspired against me, I secretly fled by night, with the consent of certain brothers who pitied me and with the assistance of some [Col. 0155C] of our students. I went to the nearby land of Count Theobald, where I had previously lived in a cell.

> [Note: Col. 0155D. “To the land of Count Theobald.”—This Theobald, or Theobaldus, was Theobald II of that name, count of Troyes and Provins; he died in 1151.]

He knew me somewhat, and deeply sympathized with the oppressions of which he had heard. There [Col. 0156A] I began to live in the castle of Provins—[variant: “Pruvins”]—in a certain cell belonging to the monks of Troyes. Its prior had formerly been familiar with me and had loved me greatly; he rejoiced very much at my arrival and cared for me with every diligence.

> [Note: Col. 0155D. “I began to live in the castle of Provins, namely in a certain cell of the monks of Troyes.”—He means the cell of Saint Aigulf, founded by Theobald I at Provins, where in 1048 he placed monks of Saint Peter of Troyes, as is clear from a diploma of King Henry:
>
> “A count of the highest nobility, named Theobald, came before our serene majesty, asking and earnestly petitioning that he might be permitted to place monks from the monastery of Lord Peter of Troyes, called Cellensis, in a certain church of Saint Aigulf situated beneath the town of Provins, which he held from us as a benefice, and appoint them perpetually and continuously to administer God’s service there, which had previously been performed negligently,” etc.
>
> Furthermore, the records of Saint Geneviève at Paris also mention the fair of Saint Aigulf at Provins in the year 1220. Nor are other documents of the cartulary of the Paraclete irrelevant, in which “Brother Felix, humble abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Cella at Troyes, and Guichard, prior of Saint Aigulf at Provins,” are mentioned about the year 1271.]

One day it happened that our abbot came to that castle to see the aforesaid count on some business of his own. When I learned this, I approached the count with that prior and asked him to intercede for me with our abbot, that he might absolve me and grant me leave to live monastically wherever a suitable place might be found for me. The abbot and those with him submitted the matter to deliberation, promising to answer the count about it that very day before their departure.

When they had deliberated, it seemed to them that I wished to transfer to another abbey and that this would be an immense disgrace to them. For they attributed to themselves the greatest glory because, at my conversion, I had turned aside to them, as though I had despised every other abbey; and they said that the greatest reproach would now fall upon them if, rejecting them, I passed over to others. Therefore they would listen neither to me nor to the count on this subject. Instead, they immediately threatened that unless I returned swiftly, they would excommunicate me. They strictly forbade the prior to whom I had fled ever again to keep me, unless he were willing to share in the excommunication. [Col. 0156C]

At this both the prior and I were greatly troubled.

> [Note: Col. 0156D. “But the abbot,” etc.—That is, Adam or Adamus, abbot of Saint-Denis, discussed above. He died in 1123, as will shortly appear from the election of his successor.]

But the abbot departed in this obstinacy and died a few days later.

> [Note: Col. 0156D. “When another had succeeded him . . .”—Adam’s successor was Suger, who was then absent. For he was staying with Pope Calixtus II, sent by King Louis the Fat on matters concerning the realm of France. He himself relates this in his *Life of King Louis*:
>
> “Suddenly there came a young household servant who recognized me and my people and, with joy and sadness, announced the death of our lord, Abbot Adam of good memory, my predecessor, and the election of our person, made by the whole convent.”
>
> Elsewhere he also indicates that he was elected in the same year in which his predecessor Adam died, namely 1123. In a decree concerning the men of the village of Saint-Denis, whom he later set free, he counts the year 1125 as the third of his administration:
>
> “Done in the monastery of blessed Dionysius in general assembly, Lord Suger, venerable abbot of the same monastery, presiding, in the third year of his administration, in the year 1125 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on Sunday, the Ides of March, the seventh lunar day, third indiction, fourteenth epact, third concurrent, while Louis, glorious and illustrious king of the Franks, reigned in the seventeenth year of his rule and confirmed the present grant. I, Abbot Suger, have subscribed.”
>
> And below: “I, Gregory, chancellor of Lord Abbot Suger, have reread and subscribed.”]

When [Col. 0157A] another had succeeded him, I met with him in the presence of the bishop of Meaux, asking him to grant what I had requested from his predecessor.

> [Note: Col. 0157B. “I met with him in the presence of the bishop of Meaux.”—I do not yet know with certainty who this bishop of Meaux was. Yet I can affirm that he was either Burchard or his successor Manasses. For in the records of Saint-Martin-des-Champs I find Burchard still alive in 1122, the third year of his episcopate; but Manasses had already begun to govern the church of Meaux in 1125, when he “gave the church of Choisy to Saint Martin, with candles for the feast of Blessed Mary, with little cakes for the feast of Saint Stephen, with eighteen denarii to be paid by the priest within twelve days after Christmas, with both greater and lesser tithes belonging to the same church and to the chapel of Marolles; and, by the counsel also of Lord Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, with forty solidi to be paid every year by the priest from the benefices of the same church.”]

Although at first he did not assent, afterward, through the intervention of some of our friends, I appealed to the king and his council about it, and thus obtained what I wanted.

> [Note: Col. 0157B. “Stephen, then the king’s steward . . .”—No more precise determination of that date can certainly be drawn from this. For Stephen the steward is found to have subscribed charters of King Louis also in 1120 and 1122 in the archives of Saint-Denis. Setting aside this inquiry, we should rather now examine who this Stephen, steward or seneschal, was. Hugh of Cléry, in his commentary on the chief stewardship and seneschalship of France, formerly hereditary in the counts of Anjou, teaches that he was Stephen of Garlande, successor to William of Garlande as steward:
>
> “William of Garlande, then seneschal of France, acknowledged in that conference that he owed homage to Count Fulk for the seneschalship of France, and he was thereafter at the count’s disposal. After William came Stephen of Garlande as seneschal, who paid homage to the count.”
>
> But what that author does not reveal, I learned elsewhere: namely, that this Stephen was brother of William of Garlande, as well as of Ansel, or Anselm, the steward, and Gilbert the cupbearer. This is stated in a charter of Louis the Fat confirming the foundation of Blessed Mary of Gournay. Although lengthy, it may suitably be included here, especially because it is highly relevant to explaining our author’s passage. It reads as follows:
>
> **Charter of Louis the Fat**
>
> “I, Louis, raised by God’s merciful dispensation to be king of the Franks, wish all the faithful, both future and present, to know that Guy the Red and his wife Adelaide, with equal devotion, built from the foundation the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, and Saint John the Evangelist, situated on the river Marne near the castle of Gournay. Having bestowed many benefices upon it, they granted it, with all that belonged to it, to the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs to possess in perpetuity.
>
> “That we may distinguish their gifts, which they gave to the aforesaid church, from other benefices, we order those gifts to be set down by name. Their first gift bestowed, as stated, upon the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs is this: the aforesaid church with its enclosures and all the adjoining precinct; the chapel of Gournay; the land of Luabum; the mill at Gournay; and at Roussy, the church with its cemetery and a third part of the same village. These are specifically the gifts of Guy and his wife Adelaide, bestowed by them upon the aforesaid monks.
>
> “We further wish all to know that Ansel of Garlande, our steward, gave to the aforesaid monastery two parts of the village at Roussy and thus granted the monks the whole village, except the wood; and he gave that wood to the same monks and their guests for burning, lodging, and their own necessary use. He likewise gave them Nuisel—the church, that is, and all that belongs to it—with tenants, lands, meadows, vineyards, wood, and mill, as the monks possess these things; and also the tithe of Bercorelles and two parts of the tithe of Berchères. Baldwin of Clacy gave the remaining third part with the cemetery to the monks, with the assent of our steward Ansel.
>
> “Ansel also bestowed upon the same monastery the entire tithe of Pontoise, half the tithe at Torcy called that of Saint Martin, and the church of Essonnes with its cemetery and tithe. Stephen, [Col. 0158C] Ansel’s brother, granted to the monastery the tenants dwelling in that same cemetery. At Cannoil, whatever Albert of Brie—the church with its tithe, meadows, land, and wood—gave to the monks of the aforesaid monastery, he gave with Ansel’s consent, since he held it from Ansel’s fief. Ansel, of good memory, enriched the aforesaid monastery with these and other benefices and made Christ its heir, with the consent of his brothers Stephen, William, and Gilbert.
>
> “At Vodo, which is between Gournay and Cale, they possess fifteen arpents of meadow: five by our gift, seven by the gift of Alberic of Montfermeil, and three by the beneficence of other faithful persons. We approve and will, and so far as pertains to our majesty confirm forever, all these aforesaid gifts: those of Guy the Red and his wife, of our steward Ansel, of Stephen his brother, of Baldwin of Clacy, and of Alberic of Montfermeil. We also confirm to the same church the land and wood of Champ Moulu, which Arnulf of Corquerelles gave to the aforesaid monks with the assent of Payen of Montjay. We likewise confirm to that church the land and wood called Raimund’s.
>
> “Done at Paris in the year 1124 of the Incarnate Word, the seventh year of Queen Adelaide. Sign of Stephen the steward; sign of Gilbert the cupbearer; sign of Hugh the constable; sign of Alberic the chamberlain. Given through the hand of Stephen the chancellor.”
>
> But this charter raises a difficulty which must be examined somewhat more carefully. For it has Stephen the steward and Stephen the chancellor subscribing at the same time, although the annals of the monastery of Morigny, written by Theulf and several monks of that place, make Stephen of Garlande, the steward, identical with Stephen the king’s chancellor. The words of Theulf in Book II of the *Annals* (*Patrology*, vol. 180) are:
>
> “When William, brother of Ansel the steward, died, Stephen the chancellor, brother of both, became chief of the royal household. In past generations it had been unheard of for a man who exercised the office of deacon to hold at once, after the king, the foremost rank in military affairs. This capable man, endowed with worldly wisdom and flourishing in our time above other mortals in temporal prosperity through the revenues of many ecclesiastical benefices and through intimacy with the king—such that some said he ruled the king rather than served him—gave his niece in marriage to Amaury of Montfort together with the honour of Rochefort which had come to the girl by marriage. Swollen with pride and forgetful of himself, he made Queen Adelaide hostile to him through very frequent annoyances. As their hatreds increased and the king was disturbed, he was deprived of his office and expelled from court. Seized, as it were, by a kind of madness, he strove with all his strength to disturb the kingdom; relying on the aid of a valiant man-at-arms, Amaury, he set this country aflame with wars. But when he could not bring his desires to effect, he returned to himself, relinquished the seneschalship which he claimed to possess by hereditary right, and was reconciled with King Louis through the intervention of Queen Adelaide.”
>
> From this it may very easily be judged how great and what sort of man Stephen of Garlande the steward was. But I cannot be persuaded that he was Stephen the chancellor who afterward became bishop of Paris. For many things occurring in ancient and trustworthy records seem to prove the contrary.
>
> First, the records of Saint Martin relate that Stephen, bishop of Paris, “gave in perpetuity to Saint-Martin-des-Champs, in the year 1133, the church of Saint-Denis called ‘of the Prison,’ which secular hands had long unjustly seized and which had also in his time reverted to the royal hand; it was restored into his own hands with the assent, request, and will of King Louis, with Queen Adelaide agreeing and Henry, abbot of that church, consenting.” But letters of Henry, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, mention “the servants of Stephen of Garlande,” who as late as 1138 “held the castle of Gournay with its dependencies in wardship for Amaury, count of Évreux, son of his niece, to whom that castle had devolved by hereditary right.”
>
> Secondly, the tomb of Stephen, bishop of Paris, who died in 1140, shows that he was first chancellor and afterward bishop, making no mention whatever of steward or seneschal:
>
> “Here lies the reverend father and lord Stephen of blessed memory, once chancellor of France, afterward bishop of Paris,” etc.
>
> Finally, [Col. 0160B] what is clearer than the noonday sun is that the records of Blessed Mary of Gournay mention at once “Stephen, bishop of Paris, and Stephen the steward holding Gournay.” The doubt thus removed, it remains to add that Ralph, count of Péronne or Vermandois, succeeded Stephen of Garlande in the seneschalship. Hugh of Cléry expressly testifies to this when he says:
>
> “After Stephen came Ralph, count of Péronne, as seneschal, who likewise rendered homages and service.”
>
> After Ralph, Theobald the Great, count of Blois, exercised the office of steward under Louis the Younger. After Theobald the Great, another Theobald, his son and likewise count of Blois, was seneschal of Philip Augustus. And so with the rest.]

For Stephen, then the king’s steward, having summoned the abbot and his household apart, asked [Col. 0158A] them why they wished to keep me against my will, when they could easily incur scandal and gain no benefit, since my manner of life and theirs could in no way agree—[variant: “be compatible”]. I knew, however, that this was the view of the royal council: that the less regular that abbey was, the more subject and useful it was to the king, namely in regard to temporal profits. I therefore believed that I would readily obtain the assent of the king and his advisers.

[Col. 0159A] And so it happened. But lest the monastery lose the boast which it had in me, they allowed me to withdraw into whatever solitude I wished, provided that I did not subject myself to any abbey. This was agreed and confirmed by both sides in the presence of the king and his advisers.

Accordingly I withdrew to a certain solitude in the district of Troyes, known to me beforehand. There, when some land had been given to me by certain persons, with the consent of the bishop of the region, I first built a small oratory in the name of the holy Trinity out of reeds and straw.

> [Note: Col. 0160B. “With the consent of the bishop of the region.”—That is, Hatto, bishop of Troyes and afterward a monk of Cluny, concerning whom Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, Saint Bernard, and other writers of that age wrote much in their letters.]
>
> [Note: Col. 0160C. “I built a certain oratory in the name of the holy Trinity . . .”—Here he does not mention what he relates elsewhere and repeatedly: although that oratory had been founded and dedicated in the name of the holy Trinity, because there, as an exile and a man already in despair, he had received some relief through the consolation of divine grace, he called it the Paraclete, or Paraclit, in memory of this benefit. Robert of Auxerre, the Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens, and others affirm this also.
>
> He built it in the district of Troyes, above the river Arduson or Ardicon, in the parish of Quincey, near Nogent-sur-Seine. William of Nangis, in his *Chronicle*: “For he had built a monastery in the bishopric of Troyes near Nogent-sur-Seine, in a certain meadow where he had been accustomed to read.” Innocent II, in a letter to Heloise: “To Heloise, abbess, and the other sisters in the oratory situated in the district of Troyes, in the parish of Quincey, above the river Arducon.” The Roman pontiffs call it “the abbey of the Paraclete,” “the oratory of the Holy Trinity,” “the Paraclete,” and “the oratory of the Holy Spirit.” But more concerning it follows later.—See Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. VI, p. 85. Editor.]

There, while lying hidden with one of our clerics, I could truly sing to the Lord:

> “Behold, I fled afar off, and remained in solitude” (Psalm 54:8).

### CHAPTER XI. When the students learned this

[Note: [Col. 0160D] *When the students learned this*, etc. Francis Petrarch, Book II of *On the Solitary Life*: “This Peter Abelard, yielding to envy, penetrated the hidden places of the wilderness of Troyes, though not without a great gathering of students from every side, whom the fame of his celebrated learning had drawn to that solitary man as disciples from many cities; yet he did not obtain the rest he desired, which stubborn envy and hatred had uprooted for him from its very foundation.”]

When the students learned this, they began to flock together from every direction. Leaving cities and towns, they inhabited the wilderness; instead of spacious houses they built themselves small huts; instead of delicate foods they lived on wild herbs and coarse bread; instead of soft beds they procured reeds and straw; and instead of tables they raised clods of earth.

Truly, you would have thought that they were imitating those ancient philosophers of whom Jerome, in the second book against Jovinianus, speaks in these words:

> “Through the senses, as through certain windows, vices gain entrance into the soul. The citadel and stronghold of the mind cannot be taken unless the hostile army has burst in through its gates. If someone delights in circus spectacles, in contests of athletes, in the movements of actors, in women’s beauty, in the brilliance of gems and garments, and in other things of this sort, the soul’s freedom has been taken captive through the windows of the eyes, and that prophetic saying is fulfilled: ‘Death has entered through our windows’ [Jer. 9:21]. Therefore, when through these gates, as it were, certain wedges of disturbances have entered the citadel of our mind, where will its freedom be? Where its strength? Where its thought of God? Especially since touch also paints for itself former pleasures, compels the soul to share in the recollection of vices, and in some fashion to perform what it does not perform.
>
> “For these reasons many philosophers, being so persuaded, abandoned crowded cities and suburban gardens, where there are irrigated fields, leafy trees, the murmuring of birds, the mirror of a spring, a babbling brook, and many enticements for eyes and ears, lest through luxury and abundance of resources the soul’s strength should grow soft and its chastity be violated. For it is useless often to see the things by which you were once captured and to expose yourself to the experience of things from which you can with difficulty abstain. Thus the Pythagoreans also, avoiding gatherings of this kind, were accustomed to dwell in solitude and desert places.”

But Plato himself, though rich, and though Diogenes trampled his bed with muddy feet, chose, so that he might devote himself to philosophy, an Academy estate far from the city, not merely deserted but even unhealthy, so that by the care and constant pressure of disease the assaults of lust might be broken, and his pupils might feel no pleasure other than that of the subjects they were learning.

Such a life is also reported to have been led by the sons of the prophets who adhered to Elisha [4 Kings 6]. Jerome likewise, as though speaking of the monks of that time, writes among other things to the monk Rusticus (Epistle IV):

> “The sons of the prophets, whom we read of as monks in the Old [Col. 0161C] Testament, built themselves little cells beside the streams of the Jordan; and, abandoning crowds and cities, lived on gruel and wild herbs.”

Such were our students there, building their little huts above the river Arduzon: they seemed more like hermits than students. And the greater the gathering of students there, and the harsher the life they endured in our instruction, the more my rivals thought it glorious for me and shameful for themselves. When they had done against me all that they could [variant: *had been able*], they were grieved that all things worked together for my good. Thus, according to Jerome’s saying, though I was far removed from cities, the forum, lawsuits, and crowds, envy nevertheless found me in hiding, as Quintilian says.

For [variant: *who*], silently complaining and groaning among themselves, they said: “Behold, the whole world has gone after him. We have gained nothing by persecuting him; rather, we have made him more famous. We strove to extinguish his name, but we have only kindled it more. Behold, in the cities students have every necessity at hand; yet, despising civic pleasures, they flock to the poverty of the wilderness and voluntarily make themselves miserable.”

At that time intolerable poverty especially compelled me to undertake the direction of a school, since I was unable to dig and ashamed to beg. I therefore returned [variant: *turned back*] to the art that I knew, and was compelled, instead of manual labor, to perform the service of my tongue. The students, moreover, freely provided me with every necessity, whether food, clothing, cultivation of the fields, or building expenses, so that no domestic concern might hold me back from study.

Since our oratory could not contain even a small part of them, they necessarily enlarged it; and, building it of stone and timber, improved it [variant: *inhabited it*]. Since it had been founded and later dedicated in the name [variant: *honor*] of the Holy Trinity, yet because, when a fugitive and so despairing, I had there taken a little breath of consolation from divine grace, I named it the Paraclete [variant: *Paraclitum*, and so everywhere], in remembrance of this benefit.

Many who heard this received it with great astonishment; and some vehemently criticized it, saying that no church might be assigned specially to the Holy Spirit rather than to God the Father, but only to the Son alone, or to the whole Trinity together, according to ancient custom. They were led into this criticism chiefly by the error of thinking that there was no difference between “Paraclete” and “the Paraclete Spirit.”

For although the Trinity itself, and each person in the Trinity, is called God and helper, each may also rightly be called Paraclete—that is, comforter—according to the Apostle’s words: “Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our tribulation” [2 Cor. 1:3]. And according to what Truth says: “He will give you another Paraclete” [John 14:16].

What, moreover, prevents the house of the Lord from being ascribed to the Father or to the Holy Spirit just as it is to the Son, when every church is alike consecrated in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and there is no distinct [variant: *divided*] possession among them in anything? Who would presume to erase from the front of the entrance the title of him to whom the house itself belongs?

Or, since the Son offered himself in sacrifice to the Father, and consequently prayers in the celebrations of Mass are directed especially to the Father and the sacrifice is offered to him, why should the altar not appear especially to be his to whom supplication and sacrifice are chiefly made? Is it more correct to call it the altar of him to whom sacrifice is made than of him who is sacrificed? Or would anyone rather acknowledge it to be the altar of the Lord’s cross or sepulchre, or of blessed Michael, John, Peter, or any saint—though neither are they sacrificed there, nor is sacrifice made to them, nor are supplications addressed to them?

Certainly, not even among idolaters were altars or temples called the altars or temples of any except those to whom they intended to render sacrifice and worship. But perhaps someone will say that churches or altars ought not to be dedicated to the Father because there is no deed [variant: *feast*] of his which grants him a special solemnity. Yet this reasoning surely takes this away from the Trinity itself and does not take it away from the Holy Spirit. For the Spirit himself has, by reason of his coming, his own solemnity of Pentecost, just as the Son has the feast of his Nativity by reason of his own coming. For as the Son was sent into the world, so the Holy Spirit was sent upon the disciples and claims a solemnity as his own.

Indeed, if we attend more carefully to apostolic authority and to the operation of the Spirit himself, a temple seems more reasonably to be ascribed to him than to any of the other persons. For the Apostle assigns a special [variant: *spiritual*] temple specifically to no one of the three persons except the Holy Spirit. He does not say “temple of the Father” or “temple of the Son” as he says “temple of the Holy Spirit,” writing thus in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” [1 Cor. 6:17]. And again: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own?” [ibid., 19].

Who also does not know that the sacraments of divine benefits performed in the Church are specially ascribed to the operation of divine grace, by which the Holy Spirit is understood? For from water and the Holy Spirit we are reborn in baptism, and then for the first time are constituted, as it were, a special temple for God. At confirmation too, the grace of the sevenfold Spirit is bestowed, by which God’s very temple is adorned and dedicated.

What wonder, then, if we assign a bodily temple to that person to whom the Apostle especially assigns a spiritual temple? Or to whose person is a church more properly said to belong than to his operation to which all the benefits administered in the Church are specially assigned?
