Yet we do not maintain this in such a way [variant: *conduct this matter*] as to admit that, when we first called our oratory the Paraclete, we dedicated it to one person alone; rather, we did so for the reason given above, namely, in remembrance of our consolation. And yet, even if we had done so in the manner supposed, it would not have been contrary to reason, though unknown to custom.

### CHAPTER XII. The persecution of him by certain men as though they were new apostles

While I was hiding there in body, but my fame was then traversing the whole world and wholly echoing, like that poetic fiction called Echo [Note: [Col. 0163C] Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book III, 358.], which indeed has much voice but no substance beneath it—my former rivals, now less able to prevail by themselves, stirred up against me certain new apostles in whom the world placed great trust.

[Note: [Col. 0163C] *The one*, etc. He means Saints Norbert, founder of the canonical congregation of Prémontré, and Bernard, the chief promoter of the Cistercian monastic order. The latter, the first abbot of the monastery of Clairvaux, was blessed by William of Champeaux, bishop of Châlons, about the year 1114, while the bishopric of Langres was vacant, as is recorded in the Victorine Chronicle; and afterward he deserved to become the father of more than three hundred monks.

The former, according to an ancient canon of the Church of Laon, was, “after a few years, the new discoverer and initiator of new light and new conversion, not only inward but outward brightness as well—namely Lord Norbert—who came from Lorraine into France. Divine grace going before and accompanying him, he planted in the bishopric of Laon that first vine which, rooted and grounded in charity, has now sent forth its shoots and has abundantly made drunk many princes and young men, virgins, old men together with the young, with the wine of its strength that gladdens the heart of man; so that, powerfully intoxicated, they seek nothing but to praise the name of the Lord and sing to him a new song.”

Nor does the following passage, which the author of the Chronicle of Limoges reports under the year 1130, seem altogether ill suited to this place:

> “In these times the canonical order of Prémontré and the monastic order of Cîteaux, like two olive trees before God, supplied the world with the light of piety and the richness of devotion; and, like fruitful vines, propagated the branches of religion on every side. Gradually spreading the fragrance of their good repute throughout almost all the boundaries of the Christian world, they built new abbeys where the worship of God had not existed before. Thus brothers of both orders were sent to Syria and Palestine, where they built several abbeys. In those times the Church had a beautiful and splendid appearance, surrounded by the variety of different orders and professions: here Prémonstratensians, there Cistercian monks, and elsewhere women devoted to God—of various habits and professions—living regularly in chastity and poverty under the yoke of obedience. They stirred one another up by religious fervor and competed in founding new monasteries in different places.”

Yet both propagators of these two orders were full of bitterness and hostility toward our Abelard, as is clear even from a few letters Bernard wrote against him to Pope Innocent and to the cardinals.]

One of these boasted that he had revived the life of regular canons, the other that of monks. Traveling through the world in preaching and shamelessly attacking me as much as they could, they made me for a time quite contemptible both to certain ecclesiastical and secular authorities. They spread such malicious reports concerning both my faith and my life that they even turned away from me the chief of our friends; and those who still retained anything of their former affection for me concealed it in every way through fear of them.

God himself is my witness how often, whenever I knew a gathering of ecclesiastical persons was being assembled, I believed it was being done for my condemnation. Immediately, stunned as by the blow of an approaching thunderbolt, I awaited being dragged as a heretic or profane person before councils or synagogues. And, to compare a flea with a lion, an ant with an elephant, my rivals persecuted me with no gentler spirit than the heretics once persecuted blessed Athanasius.

Often—as God knows—I fell into such despair that I planned, leaving Christian lands, to go among the heathen and there live as a Christian in peace among Christ’s enemies under whatever terms of tribute. I believed that they would be entirely more favorable to me in proportion as they suspected me, because of the charge laid against me, of being less Christian; and that for this reason they would believe I could more easily be inclined to their sect.

### CHAPTER XIII. The abbey to which he was appointed, and the persecution of him by both his sons—that is, the monks—and a tyrant

While I was being continually afflicted by such disturbances, and this final course remained to me—namely, to flee to Christ among Christ’s enemies—I found an opportunity by which I thought to avoid these snares for a little while; but I fell among Christians and monks far more savage and worse than heathens.

[Note: [Col. 0165C] It was in Lesser Brittany, etc. This abbey was the most ancient of all the abbeys of Brittany. For Saint Gildasius, or Gildas, surnamed the Wise, born in Great Britain, laid its first foundations in the time of King Childeric, son of Merovech. Lest I seem to have said this with insufficient probability, I shall produce the testimony of an anonymous but ancient and trustworthy author, who wrote the life and deeds of Saint Gildas:

> “When, by God’s command, Gildas came to Armorica, formerly a region of Gaul—then called Brittany by the Britons, who possessed it—he was honorably received by them with great joy.”

And a little later:

> “Coming, therefore, to a certain fortress on Mount Reuvysius, situated in view of the sea, he there built a monastery of superior construction and completed in it cloisters according to the cenobitic rule.”

And again:

> “The body of the holy man was placed in the church which he himself had built in the ancient fortress of Reusium. There it was preserved through many courses of years and reverently honored by the whole Breton people, because innumerable miracles were performed there.”

It is therefore clear why that monastery acquired the name of Saint Gildas of Rhuys. But later, when wars arose in Brittany and Solomon, the devout count of the Bretons, was cruelly killed by impious men, not only was that place itself, together with another named Lochmenech, wholly deserted and destroyed, but their inhabitants too were compelled to seek foreign regions. Choosing new settlements in the district of Bourges, they carried with them the precious body of Saint Gildas and placed it in the monastery of Déols, where Ebbo, prince of Bourges, kindly received them.

This is explicitly confirmed by the author of the Chronicle of Limoges in these words:

> “At the same time,” namely about the year of Christ 907, “there was founded in Berry, in the fortress of Déols, the noble monastery called Déols, by Ebbo, an illustrious man and lord of the aforesaid fortress. Shortly afterward this devout man religiously received from Brittany many monks fleeing with many relics of saints, who had escaped the fury of the Normans through fear of death. They brought the body of blessed Gildas, abbot, to the monastery of Déols. The same chosen servant of God, Ebbo, built for it a monastery of his own beside his castle on the other side of the water, where the venerable body of that saint, honorably deposited with the relics of many saints, rests.”

Nevertheless, when it pleased almighty God that the monastery of Rhuys should be restored, it did not thereafter rejoice any less in the name of Saint Gildas. For at last Count Geoffrey, having obtained lordship over all Brittany, as the aforementioned writer of the Life of Saint Gildas relates, “asked Goslin, then abbot of the monastery of Fleury and afterward archbishop of the Church of Bourges, to send him the monk Felix to restore the monasteries in his region that had been destroyed to the ground. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1008, Felix was therefore sent by the aforesaid abbot to Count Geoffrey, who received him honorably and gave him the aforesaid monasteries”—namely Rhuys and Lochmenech—“with all their appurtenances; and he commended him to his brother Judicael, bishop of Vannes, in whose diocese those monasteries were situated.”

And some time afterward:

> “When he doubted which of the two places he ought to establish as the seat of the abbey, he consulted Duke Alan and the bishop of Vannes about the matter. Having summoned noblemen, and some bishops as well, they established the place of Saint Gildas, because it was more ancient and more abundant in the fertility of its soil, in grain and wine, and in fruit-bearing trees; and, in their seasons, more plentiful in its various kinds of large fish.”

Perhaps I have related these matters at greater length than was proper; but this was chiefly on account of Peter Abelard, who was himself a Breton and was eventually called, by the unanimous election of the brothers and with the assent of the ruler of the land, to that abbey of Saint Gildas, as he declares in his own words. William of Nangis also testifies that he was an abbot in Brittany, though he does not name the abbey, when he says: “Peter Abelard, a distinguished and most celebrated master of dialectic, first married, then a monk of Saint-Denis in France, afterward appointed abbot in Brittany, where he had been born.”]

There was in Lesser Brittany, in the bishopric of Vannes, a certain abbey of Saint Gildas of Rhuys [variant: *Ruiensis*, better; commonly “of Rhuys”], which had been left desolate by the death of its pastor. The unanimous election of the brothers, with the consent of the ruler of the land, called me to it, and easily obtained this from our abbot and brothers. Thus the envy of the Franks drove me westward, as the envy of the Romans had driven Jerome eastward.

Never, God knows, would I have consented to this except in order somehow to escape, as I have said, the oppressions that I was continually suffering. For the country was barbarous, its language unknown to me; the vile and ungovernable life of those monks was notorious to almost everyone; and the people of that land were inhuman and disorderly.

Thus, as a man terrified by a sword hanging over him throws himself over a precipice, and, in order to defer one death for a moment, incurs another, so I knowingly transferred myself from one danger to another. There, beside the roaring waves of the Ocean, since the farthest limit of the land afforded me no further means of escape, I often turned over in my prayers the words: “From the ends of the earth I cried to you, when my heart was distressed” [Ps. 60:3].

I think that by now it can escape no one's notice with what anxiety that undisciplined congregation of brothers, whose government I had undertaken, tormented my heart night and day, when I considered the dangers to both my soul and body. For I knew with certainty that, if I tried to compel them to the regular life which they had professed, I could not remain alive; and that, if I did not do this as far as I could, I should be condemned [variant: *damaged*].

A certain tyrant, most powerful in that land, had long since subjected the abbey itself to himself, having found an opportunity in the disorder of the monastery. He had turned all the lands adjoining the monastery to his own uses and oppressed the monks with more severe exactions than tributary Jews.

The monks pressed me for their daily needs, though they had nothing in common from which I could provide for them. Each had formerly sustained himself, his concubines, and his sons and daughters from his own purse. They rejoiced in my distress about this; they too stole and carried off whatever they could, so that, when I failed in the administration itself, I might be compelled [variant: *they might compel me*] either to abandon discipline or to leave altogether.

Since the entire barbarism of that country was alike lawless and undisciplined, there was no one whose help I could seek, since I differed from all alike in my habits. Outside, that tyrant and his retainers continually oppressed me; within, the brothers incessantly plotted against me. Thus the fact itself showed that the Apostle’s saying was spoken especially of me: “Fightings without, fears within” [2 Cor. 7:5].

I considered and lamented how useless and miserable a life I led, how fruitlessly I lived both for myself and for others, how much I had formerly benefited clerics, and how, having now abandoned them because of the monks, I bore no fruit either among them or among the monks. In all my undertakings and efforts I had become so ineffective that the following reproach could most rightly be applied to me in every respect: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” [Luke 14:30].

I fell wholly into despair when I recalled what I had fled and considered what I had encountered. Counting my former troubles as though they were now nothing, I frequently groaned within myself and said: “I suffer these things deservedly, for, abandoning the Paraclete—that is, the Comforter—I thrust myself into certain desolation; and, wishing to avoid threats, I fled to certain dangers.”

But what tormented me most was that, having left our oratory, I could not provide for the celebration of the divine office as I ought, because the extreme poverty of the place scarcely sufficed for the necessities of one man. Yet the true Paraclete himself brought true consolation to me in this great desolation and provided, as he should, for his own oratory.

[Note: [Col. 0167B] *It happened … that the abbot … of Saint-Denis*, etc. The monastery of Argenteuil had been subject to the abbey of Saint-Denis from its very founders. Later, however, Charlemagne entrusted it to his daughter Theodrada. Having gathered nuns there, she held it on the condition that, after her death, it should return to the use of the church of Saint-Denis. This is clearly demonstrated by the following charter of the emperors Louis and Lothair, taken from the cartulary of Saint-Denis:

**Confirmation of the Emperors Louis and Lothair concerning the church of Argenteuil, which Hermenricus and his wife Mumma [read: Nummana] gave to Saint-Denis.**]

[Col. 0167C] “In the name of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ: Louis and Lothair, emperors Augustus by the ordering of divine providence. If things which God-fearing people have bestowed or granted by solemn donation upon places dedicated to divine worship are afterwards known to have been alienated from them on any pretext, and if we restore them by our authority to their former condition and confirm them anew by the decree of our command, we confidently believe that this undoubtedly pertains both to our attaining eternal blessedness and to strengthening the stability of our empire.

Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future alike, know that the illustrious woman, our sister Theodrada, consecrated to God, represented to our clemency that she had learned that the monastery called Argenteuil, situated in the district of Paris on the river Seine—which she had first held by the benefaction of our lord and [Col. 0167D] father Charles, most serene emperor, and afterwards by our own grant—ought to belong to the monastery of the blessed and glorious martyr of Christ, Dionysius, where at present the venerable man Hilduin, abbot and archchaplain of our sacred palace, is seen to preside as ruler. She requested that, for the increase of our reward, we should cause it to be restored to its former condition: namely, that after her departure from this light, unless another monastery should first have been given her by us in exchange for it, or unless she should choose of her own will to relinquish it, the said monastery should be received into the authority of the monastery of Saint-Denis without any opposition or challenge by anyone.

Having heard her salutary and religious petition, we questioned the aforesaid venerable man Hilduin, who was present, whether he knew anything concerning this matter. He immediately [apparently presented] the donation of a certain God-fearing and religious man named Ermenric and of his wife Nummana, who had built the aforesaid monastery upon their own property [Col. 0168B] and had transferred it by a testamentary document to the monastery of the blessed martyr of Christ Dionysius through a solemn donation; likewise, the charter of confirmation of Lothair, formerly king, which he had ordered drawn up concerning that same donation. These induced us to grant the petition of our beloved sister Theodrada and, as she requested, to restore by our authority the aforesaid monastery of Argenteuil to the authority of Saint-Denis, the most precious martyr of Christ.

Accordingly, we order that this confirmation of our authority be made, by which we decree and command in every respect that, after the departure of our beloved sister from this life, the aforesaid monastery of Argenteuil shall be received into the monastery and authority of the most blessed martyr of Christ Dionysius. It is known that it was originally delivered or granted to that monastery by the aforesaid faithful servants of God, for the love of God and out of reverence for those saints and their pious intercession. It shall be so received without the contradiction of any person and without inquiry by us or by our successors; and whatever is presently seen to belong there, with all its integrity and appurtenances, shall be restored to the right and lordship of that monastery.

And if it should happen that our sister should wish, before the end of her life, to relinquish that monastery either voluntarily, as we have said, or in exchange for another monastery, then nonetheless, without any opposition or awaiting any formal conveyance, it shall be received permanently for possession by the monastery of the aforesaid most blessed martyr of Christ Dionysius, as stated above. Thereafter, no person, under any dignity or power whatsoever, shall ever presume to make any claim against, or bring any suit against, the rulers of the monastery of the aforesaid most blessed martyr of Christ Dionysius. Rather, they may peacefully possess and administer the aforesaid monastery of Argenteuil, without anyone’s unjust challenge, just as they possess and administer the other properties granted in like manner to, and belonging to, the authority of Saint-Denis. They shall have full freedom in all matters to do whatever they judge desirable for the need and benefit of that Church, according to the rule of the Christian religion.

And so that this charter of confirmation or restoration by our authority may retain inviolable and unshaken force in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hands and ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.

—The sign of Louis, most serene emperor; the sign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus. Durand, deacon, authenticated it in place of Fridugis.”

But when the Normans had destroyed that religious house, Adelaide, wife of King Hugh, restored it and again established nuns there; they remained there until the time of Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis. How he expelled them and reclaimed the abbey for the ancient right of his monastery in the year of Christ 1127, he himself relates thus in his little book *On the Things Done by Him*:

[Col. 0169A] “When, in the teachable age of my youth, I was turning over the old charters in the archive concerning our possessions, and consulting the books of immunities because of the malice of many litigants, there frequently came into my hands the charter of the foundation of the monastery of Argenteuil by Ermenric and [Col. 0169B] his wife Numma. It contained the statement that the place had belonged to the abbey of Saint-Denis from the time of King Pippin, but had been alienated on account of an unfortunate arrangement in the time of his son Charlemagne. For that emperor had established there as abbess of nuns a daughter of his who refused human marriage, on the condition that, after her death, it should return to the use of the Church. But, owing to the disturbance of the kingdom under the sons of his son—that is, the strife among the sons of the Pious One—this could not be accomplished while she survived.

“Since our predecessors had often laboured over this matter with little result, after taking counsel with our brethren, we sent our messengers and the ancient charters of foundation and donation, with the privileges of confirmation, to Rome to Pope Honorius of blessed memory, requesting that he investigate and restore our right by canonical examination. Being a man of judgment and guardian of justice, he restored to us the place itself with its appurtenances, both because of our right and because of the outrageous misconduct of the nuns [Col. 0169C] living badly there, so that religious order might be reformed in it. King Louis, beloved son of Philip, our lord and friend, confirmed the same restoration and, by the authority of royal majesty, granted to the Church whatever regalian rights he had there.”

And in the *Life of Louis the Fat*:

“Pope Honorius, a grave and stern man, had learned our right concerning the monastery of Argenteuil, disgraced by the most wretched conduct of its young women, both through the testimony of his legate Matthew, bishop of Albano, and of the lords of Chartres, Paris, Soissons, and also of Renaud, lord archbishop of Reims, and of many other men. After reading the commands of the ancient kings Pippin, Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and others concerning the right to the place, presented by our aforesaid messengers, he, with the agreement of the entire curia, restored and confirmed it to Saint-Denis, both on account of our right and because of their foul enormities.”

It happened that our abbot of Saint-Denis acquired in some fashion the aforesaid abbey of Argenteuil [variant: *Argentolii*], as belonging from ancient times to the right of his monastery. In it that woman, now our sister in Christ rather than our wife, Heloise, had received the religious habit [Col. 0168B]; he violently expelled the community of nuns from it [Col. 0169A], among whom our companion held the priorship.

[Note: “When ... the exiles were dispersed ...,” etc.—Some of the nuns of Argenteuil, thus expelled from their monastery, were transferred to the convent of Blessed Mary of Foitel, or of the Wood, as may be gathered from these letters of Henry, abbot of Saint-Denis:

“Henry, by God’s grace abbot, and the convent of Saint-Denis, greet in the Lord all who shall see these present letters. We make known that, whereas a dispute was pending between us on the one side and the abbess and nuns of Foitel on the other, concerning both the possession and the ownership of the church of Blessed Mary of Argenteuil, which [read: *quae*?] is a priory with its appurtenances, by apostolic authority, before the lord prior of Saint-Victor of Paris, the holy precentor of Senlis, and Master R. of Orson, canon of Noyon, for the sake of peace we promised the said nuns that we would give and assign them, from our lands in the territory of Tremblay, a tithe worth ten pounds annually, within fifteen days after the agreement was made, etc. Done in the year of the Lord 1207.”

For that convent had been restored to the former right of the abbot of Saint-Denis on the condition that he provide the nuns with places where they might save their souls. But Peter Abelard invited Heloise, who held the priorship of the community, together with certain others from [Col. 0170B] the same congregation who adhered to her, to his oratory of the Paraclete, and there made her abbess over the rest. William of Nangis also testifies to this, saying: “But there he caused Heloise to come with certain religious nuns, after she had subsequently been expelled in France through the agency of Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis. There she became abbess.” Before him Robert of Auxerre says: “This most subtle and remarkable philosopher Abelard had built a convent in the territory of Troyes, in a certain meadow where he had been accustomed to read; there, by episcopal authority, he gathered many nuns and named it the Paraclete. Over those nuns he set as abbess Heloise, his former wife, a religious woman and one very thoroughly educated in both Hebrew and Latin letters.”]

Accordingly, when they were being scattered as exiles to various places, I understood that an opportunity had been offered me by the Lord to provide for our oratory. Returning there, I invited her, with certain others of the same congregation who adhered to her, to the aforesaid oratory. When I had brought them there, I granted and gave her the oratory itself with all that belonged to it. Subsequently Pope Innocent II, with the assent and intervention of [Col. 0170A] the bishop of the district, confirmed our donation in perpetuity by a privilege for them and their followers.

[Note: “Pope Innocent II ...”—See this privilege among the *Registers of Innocent II*, no. 70, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX, col. 114.]

At first they endured there a poor life and for a time great desolation; but the regard of divine mercy, whom they served devoutly, soon consoled them, showed itself to them also as the true Paraclete, and made the surrounding peoples merciful and favourable toward them.

[Note: “More ... than I suppose.”—The surrounding peoples, being merciful and favourable toward them, bestowed many gifts. But before all others, “Milo, lord of Nogent,” as is read in the records of the Paraclete, “in whose territory the oratory of the Paraclete was built, gave to that place three cultivated fields: one between Bruslet and the road, another beside Carma, and a third beside the road to Triagnel, on the left. He further granted to the aforesaid place whatever his men might give it from his entire fief. He also gave the use-right of his wood of Mont-Morvé for all time, for every necessity of that place; likewise, the entire marsh adjoining that place on the bank of the Ardution, both for making gardens and for other necessities.

“He placed all these things—at the dedication of the oratory itself or blessing of the cemetery—and the complete immunity of the entire place, before all the people present, into the hand of the lord bishop of Troyes, and thus confirmed them for ever, Hilduin the dean, [Col. 0170D] Hilduin the Great, Stephen Ridel, and Renaud Carnail being present. Moreover, on the day when the nuns entered and took possession of the oratory, he gave them the entire fishery of the little river Ardution, wholly exempt, from Saint-Aubin to Quincey. He also, on behalf of his niece, the countess, who was received as a nun, gave the oven of Saint-Aubin with the use-right of the wood that he had at Furmies, Ansel of Triagnel, holy Milo, and his brother Peter being present. For the soul of his son Hugh, buried there, he gave the cultivated field at Noereth with a third part of Guamnoveries, those who were present at the burial being present.

“Simon of Nogent likewise gave from his allod two cultivated fields: namely, one upon which the oratory itself was built, and another on Mount Limars, in the presence of Hilduin the dean and Milo of Nogent. Hubert of Nogent gave two acres of land before the oratory itself, through the hand of Milo of Nogent.”

Somewhat later Theobald, count of Troyes, confirmed all these things, namely in 1146, “with the approval of Isabel, daughter of the aforesaid Milo, and of her son-in-law Girard, and of Freer, Josfrid, Gaucher, and Stephen, his nephews.” He himself also gave those nuns a measure of grain every year and the entire fishery at his mills near Ponts, as is contained in the letters of Pope Eugenius III, cited above.

Further, “Galo and his wife Adelaudis, sister of Ermelina, who gave herself to God and to the church of the Paraclete as a nun, approved and granted to God and to the said church of the Paraclete and to the nuns serving God there one half of the mill of Crèvecœur, the vineyards of Crèvecœur, and forty solidi of rent. From this rent the nuns of the Paraclete received the rent of Provins, and what remained to be received from the forty solidi they received at Les Essarts. This grant was made at Provins in the presence of Count Theobald and his wife Countess Matilda, and through the hand of the count himself. So that it might remain firm and unshaken, the count ordered it to be confirmed by the authority of his seal, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1133, when Louis was reigning king of the Franks, Henry was seated in the archiepiscopal chair of Sens, [Col. 0171C] and Hato was bishop of Troyes.”

King Louis of the Franks likewise granted in perpetuity to the same “nuns of the Paraclete that they, or their servants, should never pay him or his successors any customary due throughout all his land on any goods which they bought for their own use or which they sold from their own property for their needs. In order that this might remain ratified and inviolate, he ordered it committed to writing and, lest it be broken by posterity, publicly confirmed it by the authority of his seal at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, in the year of the Incarnate Word 1135, the twenty-seventh of his reign, and the third year since his son Louis had been raised to kingship.”

Moreover, Countess Matilda, wife of Theobald, willed that the abbey built by her at Pomeraye should be subject to the convent of the Paraclete. For the grant of the aforesaid place, which Heloise herself, first abbess of the Paraclete, had given her for its construction through the intervention of religious men, [Col. 0171D] “the countess gave to the church of the Paraclete three measures of grain yearly from her mill at Provins below Crèvecœur, with the approval of her sons, Counts Henry, Theobald, and Stephen,” as appears in the letters of Hugh, archbishop of Sens, drawn up concerning this matter. We have also reproduced these letters above in full with the rescripts of the Roman pontiffs. [See the appendix at the end of this volume.]

She further confirmed the tithe of Saint-Martin-des-Champs and of Boal, which her clerk William gave after his death to the church of the Paraclete and to the nuns serving God there, in the year 1154, when Louis was reigning king of the Franks and Hugh was archbishop of Sens. She also bestowed many other goods on the same convent, which it would be tedious and tiresome to recount.

Finally, “Hato himself, bishop of Troyes, gave one half of the entire tithe of Saint-Aubin and one half of the candles at the Purification of the Blessed Mary. Milo of Quincey, knight, with the assent of [Col. 0172A] his wife Petronilla, his son Garnerius, and his daughter Isabel, [gave] whatever he possessed in the tithe of Quincey. Ansel, lord of Triangel, [gave] the conventual priory of Blessed Mary of Triangel in the diocese of Troyes; likewise Ansel his son [gave] one half of the entire wood called Couldroy, in the territory of Marcilly. Others, whose names I have not found, [gave] the priories of La Vallée in the same diocese, Neufort in the diocese of Meaux, and Saint-Martin of Beaurain in the diocese of Beauvais.

“Manasses, bishop of Meaux, [gave] one eighth part of both the great and the small tithe of Melun, one half of the small tithe of Tilly, and one quarter of the small tithe of Saint-Maxime. Beucelina, wife of Guerric of Ponts, who entered the Paraclete as a nun, [gave] a house with a cellar situated at Sesamie. The noblewoman Helia of Villamauro, widow of Milo of Provins, formerly marshal of Champagne, [gave] ten pounds of annual revenue from her own patrimony. Mary, countess of Troyes, [gave] her street at Provins. Finally, Agnes of Marigny, upon her admission, [gave] two thirds of the small tithe of the village of Marigny; her nephew Manasses, one third; and Theobald, his son, one third, with the approval of his wife Letuisa.”

These are the chief benefactors of the monastery of the Paraclete, to whom I could add several others. But my pen hastens on to matters still needing notice.]

They were increased, in temporal resources [variant: estates], more in one year—God knows, as I suppose—than I could have increased them in a hundred years had I remained there. For the weaker women’s sex is, the more pitiable is their poverty, and the more readily it moves human hearts; and their virtue is more pleasing both to God and to human beings.

[Note: “To that sister of ours who was over the others.”—He means Heloise, first abbess of the Paraclete. Concerning her learning and religious life Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, writes briefly to her:

“I had not yet passed the bounds of adolescence, nor yet entered upon youth, when report made known to me not yet the name of your religious profession, but nonetheless that of your honourable and praiseworthy studies. I heard at that time that a woman, though not yet freed from worldly bonds, was giving the utmost devotion to literary learning and to the study of secular wisdom. By pursuing this lofty study, you surpassed all women and almost surpassed all men. Soon thereafter, in accordance with the words of the Apostle, when it pleased him who set you apart from your mother’s womb by his grace, you changed the pursuit of learning for something far better: in place of logic, the Gospel; in place of natural philosophy, the Apostle; in place of Plato, Christ; in place of the Academy, the cloister—now wholly and truly a philosophical woman.”

The monk of Auxerre likewise testifies that she was a religious woman, very thoroughly educated in both Hebrew and Latin letters; and the French calendar of the Paraclete itself says: “Heloise, mother and first abbess of this place, most radiant in learning and religious life.”

Abelard himself makes this still clearer in the letters which he wrote to her. In his *Exhortation on the Study of Letters to the Virgins of the Paraclete*, he says: “In your mother you have instruction sufficient for everything: both as an example of virtues and as teaching in letters. Not only is she acquainted with Latin learning, but also with Hebrew and Greek; she alone at this time appears to have attained that mastery of the three languages which all praise as a singular grace in blessed Jerome.”

—We have transferred to the appendix to Abelard’s works the succession of abbesses of the monastery of the Paraclete which André Duchesne had inserted here. EDITOR.]

But so that these Notes, which began with Abelard, may similarly end with him, we must add briefly what he himself omitted in his *History of My Calamities*: namely, the second condemnation of his book on the Trinity, carried out at Sens. Otto of Freising relates this among others in book I of *The Deeds of Frederick I*, chapter 48:

[Col. 0173B] “While Innocent sat in the city of Rome and Louis, son of the elder Louis, reigned in France, Peter Abelard was again summoned by bishops and Abbot Bernard to a hearing at Sens, King Louis, Count Palatine Theobald, other nobles, and countless people being present. When his faith was being examined, fearing an uprising of the people, he appealed to the presence of the Apostolic See. But the bishops and abbot sent an embassy to the Roman Church and brought back in letters a sentence of condemnation upon him and the articles for which he was accused.”

The continuator of Sigebert, Robert of Auxerre, William of Nangis, Vincent of Beauvais, John, canon of Saint-Victor, the author of the *Chronicle of Tours*, and others tell the same story. But Geoffrey, monk of Clairvaux, gives a different account, and with sharper feeling, in book III, chapter 5, of the *Life of Saint Bernard* [*Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII]:

[Col. 0173C] “In those days there was Peter Abelard, an eminent master, most celebrated for his reputation for learning, but treacherously teaching doctrines concerning the faith. When writings full of his most grievous blasphemies began to circulate everywhere, learned and faithful men brought the profane novelties of his words and ideas to the man of God, Saint Bernard. Desiring, with his customary goodness and kindness, that the error be corrected but the man not confounded, Bernard approached him with a private admonition. He dealt with him so moderately and reasonably that Abelard, struck with compunction, promised to correct everything according to Bernard’s judgment.

“But after Peter had left him, stimulated by wicked counsels and relying disastrously upon his intellectual powers and his extensive practice in disputation, he recoiled from his sounder intention. He then sought out the metropolitan of Sens, because a great council was soon to be held in his church, and accused [Col. 0173D] the abbot of Clairvaux of secretly disparaging his books. He further declared himself ready to defend his writings publicly and requested that the aforesaid abbot be summoned to the council, to say whatever he might have to say. It was done as he requested. But the summoned abbot wholly refused to come, declaring that this was not his affair.

“Later, however, moved by the advice of great men, lest his absence cause scandal among the people and increase the adversary’s arrogance, he at last consented to go—sadly indeed, and not without tears, as he himself testifies in his letter to Pope Innocent, in which he recounts the whole matter more fully and clearly. The day arrived and a large assembly gathered in the church. There the writings of Peter were brought forward by the servant of God, and the articles of error were identified. Finally Abelard was given the choice of denying that they were his, humbly correcting the error, or, if he could, answering the arguments and the testimonies of the holy Fathers brought against him. But he neither wished to recover his senses nor was able to resist the wisdom and Spirit speaking through Bernard; to gain time, he appealed to the Apostolic See.

“Even after he had been urged by that outstanding advocate of the Catholic faith—or perhaps then knew that nothing was to be done against his person—to answer freely and securely, merely to be heard and borne with in all patience, not struck by any sentence, he altogether refused this too. For he afterwards confessed to his own people, they say, that at that hour his memory had been greatly disturbed, his reason clouded, and his inward understanding fled. Nevertheless the assembled Church dismissed the man, punished the abomination, abstaining from the person but condemning the perverse doctrines. For where would that Peter find refuge in the See of Peter, being so far removed from Peter’s faith? The apostolic bishop therefore embraced the author himself, together with his errors, in the same sentence: he condemned the writings to fire and the writer to silence.”

Whatever the case may be, Berengar of Poitiers, once Abelard’s pupil, seeing these things, dared at that time to defend against everyone the name and reputation of his teacher and master. He wrote on his behalf that *Apology*, [Col. 0174C] which we have now also arranged to be printed among Abelard’s works from the library of the Most Christian King [see the Appendix, at the end of the volume], though it is full of immense bitterness against Saint Bernard. Afterwards, for this reason also rebuked by many, he excused himself by saying that he had written it as a young man, more in jest than in earnest. He himself testifies to this in a letter to the bishop of Mende; and Petrarch cites it in the *Apology*, calling him “a man not without eloquence,” in these words:

“Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, condemned Peter Abelard, once a learned man. Angered by this, Berengar of Poitiers—himself a man not without eloquence and Peter’s disciple—wrote one book against Bernard, not indeed large in bulk but immense in bitterness. Later, rebuked by many for it, he excused himself by saying that he had written it as a young man and that the saintliness of the man was not yet fully known to him.”

When that council, held in [Col. 0174D] 1140, had been dissolved, the unhappy Abelard, uncertain what to do, went to Cluny. There he was kindly received by Peter, called the Venerable; shortly afterwards, through the efforts of Peter and the Cistercian abbot, he and Saint Bernard also conferred and laid aside their enmities. The abbot of Cluny himself informed Innocent II of this.

Abelard nevertheless did not cease to write an *Apologeticus* in defense of his innocence. When this became known to William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, who loved Saint Bernard with deep affection and had transferred himself to the Cistercian order at Signy, where he died happily, William abandoned his exposition of the *Song of Songs* in order to direct the sharpness of his pen against Abelard. William himself declares this in a letter to the brethren of Mont-Dieu:

“Besides, there are other little works of ours: a book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*; *Meditations* not wholly useless for forming the spirits of novices in prayer; and an exposition of the *Song of Songs* down to the passage, ‘A little while after I had passed them by, I found him whom my soul loves.’ But Peter Abelard prevented me from completing the last-named work. For I did not think I could enjoy such delicate inner leisure while he outside was, as they say, so cruelly laying waste the boundaries of our faith with a naked sword.” [Col. 0175B]

He composed three books under the title *Disputation of the Catholic Fathers against the Doctrines of Peter Abelard*, which he dedicated to the most wise prelate Hugh, archbishop of Rouen. These are undoubtedly the books of which Geoffrey, a Cistercian monk, speaks in a letter addressed to Henry, cardinal of Albano. Knowing that Henry had attended the Council of Reims, where Pope Eugenius III had rather absolved than condemned Bishop Gilbert of Poitiers, Geoffrey writes:

“I have also heard that, concerning the condemnation of Peter Abelard, Your Diligence desires more fully to know the truth: his little books were publicly burned by Pope Innocent II of pious memory in the city of Rome and in the church of Saint Peter, the pope declaring him a heretic by apostolic authority. [Col. 0175C] Indeed, many years earlier, a venerable cardinal and legate of the Roman Church named Cono, formerly a regular canon of the church of Saint Nicholas of Arrouaise, had likewise burned his theology while holding a council at Soissons; he accused Peter in person and, after convicting him of heretical perversity, condemned him.

“Therefore, if it please your desire, satisfaction will be given through the little book on the *Life of Saint Bernard* and through Bernard’s letters sent to the curia. Yet I found at Clairvaux a little book by an abbot of black monks in which the errors of that same Peter are marked; I also remember seeing it long ago. But although it has been diligently sought for many years, the first quire could not be found, as the keepers of the books assert. Therefore it is our intention to send into France, to the monastery of which the author of that book was abbot; and, if I can recover it, to have the whole codex copied and sent to you. For I believe that this should suffice for your investigation: that you may learn what things have been condemned, in what manner, and why.”

And lest anyone wonder why he speaks of the first quire of that book, I now possess the very copy itself, given me by the learned and courteous Nicholas Camusat, canon of the church of Troyes. At its beginning is still written: “One quire is missing; whoever has retained the obedience of the scribes, let him seek it.”

—The writings of William of Saint-Thierry are extant in the *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXX. EDITOR.

But that same Geoffrey, first Abelard’s pupil and afterwards a Cistercian monk, commonly surnamed of Auxerre, also wrote against his former master Abelard. Helinand, another monk at Froidmont, asserts this before all others; he himself quotes certain words of Geoffrey as follows [*Scriptores rerum Gallicarum*, vol. XIV, p. 370]:

“This Geoffrey of Auxerre had once been a disciple of Peter and for a long [Col. 0176B] time was notary to Saint Bernard. Among other things he said of that same Peter: ‘I remember that he was once my master, who, emptying our redemption of its price, commended nothing else in the sacrifice of the Lord’s Passion but an example of virtue and an incentive to love. For what the Scriptures testify concerning the devil’s power—that the human race was redeemed by that precious blood—he maintained consisted solely in this: that an example was given us of striving unto death for truth and justice, and that, as it were, an incentive to love was supplied, since an occasion for loving in return was given by the love bestowed.

“‘These things indeed are great and true, but they are not the only things. Blessed be God, who afterwards gave both me and you a better master, through whom he rebuked the former master’s ignorance and refuted his presumption. According to this latter master, Christ displayed three special things for us in his Passion: an example of virtue, an incentive to love, and the sacrifice [Col. 0176C] of redemption. Since the heretic who nullified the third could derive no benefit from the other three.’ Geoffrey wrote these and many other things strongly and Catholicly against Peter, his master.”

Vincent of Beauvais repeats the same words in book XXI, chapter 17, of the *Historical Mirror*, as does John, monk of Saint-Victor, in his *Chronicle* under the year of Christ 1140.

Meanwhile Abelard fell ill and, sent by his abbot Peter to Chalon for the sake of his health, died there in the monastery of Saint-Marcellinus of the Cluniac order on 21 April in the year of Christ 1142, in the sixty-third year of his age. For the old calendar of the Paraclete, written in French, records: “Master Peter Abelard, founder of this place and institutor of its holy religious life, died on 21 April, aged sixty-three years.”

There is no need to recount with how much austerity, penitence, and devotion he closed that last end [Col. 0176D] of his life. Peter the Venerable himself, his abbot, described it excellently and at length in his letter to Heloise, abbess of the Paraclete, which we also include below among Abelard’s letters. But it should not be passed over that Robert of Auxerre, William of Nangis, and others testify with Peter himself that Heloise, once Abelard’s wife, “after his death kept great faith with him in continual prayers and transferred his body from the place where he died to the aforesaid monastery of the Paraclete.”

Finally, as is read in the *Chronicle of Tours*, she herself, “when laid low by illness, ordered that when dead she should be placed within her husband’s tomb. When she died and was brought to the tomb, her husband, who had died many days before her, raised his arms, received her, and, embracing her, clasped her with his arms.”

The Lord granted such favour in the eyes of all to that sister [Col. 0173A] of ours who presided over the others, that bishops loved her as a daughter, abbots as a sister, and laypeople as a mother; and all alike admired her religious devotion, prudence, and incomparable gentleness of patience in every circumstance. The more rarely she allowed herself to be seen—so that, shut within her cell, she might devote herself more purely to sacred meditation and prayer—the more ardently those outside sought her presence and the counsels of her spiritual conversation.

### CHAPTER XIV. On the Defamation of Shameful Conduct

But since all their neighbors vehemently blamed me because I provided less for their poverty than I could and ought to have done—and because I could easily have done so, at least by our preaching—I began to return to them more frequently, in order to assist them in whatever way I could. Yet in this matter I was not without the muttering of envy; and the habitual perversity of detractors most shamelessly accused what sincere charity compelled me to do, saying that I was still held by some pleasure of carnal desire, since I could scarcely, or never, endure the absence of my former beloved.

Frequently reflecting upon that complaint of blessed Jerome, who, writing to Asella concerning false friends (Letter 99), says: “Nothing is charged against me except my sex; and this would never have been charged unless Paula were setting out for Jerusalem,” and again: “Before,” he says, “I knew the house of holy Paula, the whole city was united in its enthusiasm for me; by the judgment of almost everyone I was declared worthy of the highest priesthood. But I know that through good report and evil report one comes to the kingdom of heaven”—when, I say, I recalled this injury of detraction inflicted upon so great a man, I drew no small consolation from it, saying: “Oh, if my enemies found in me so great a ground for suspicion, with what detraction would they oppress me! But now that divine mercy has freed me from this suspicion, how does suspicion remain when the means of committing such shameful conduct has been taken away? What, moreover, is this latest accusation, so shameless?”

For this condition so completely removes every suspicion of such shamefulness in the eyes of all that those who are especially careful in guarding women employ eunuchs for them, as sacred history relates concerning Esther and the other maidens of King Ahasuerus (Esther 2:3). We also read that the powerful eunuch of Queen Candace was set over all her treasures (Acts 8:27); Philip the Apostle was sent by an angel to convert and baptize him. Such men have always attained greater dignity and familiarity among modest and honorable women, precisely because they stood farther from this suspicion.

Indeed, in order wholly to remove that suspicion, Ecclesiastical History, Book VI, records that the great Christian philosopher Origen, when he too devoted himself to the sacred instruction of women, laid hands upon himself.

> [Note: Col. 0177D. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 7.]

Yet I thought that divine mercy had been more favorable to me in this than to him: what he is believed to have done with insufficient foresight, and thereby incurred no small blame for, was done to me through another’s fault, so as to prepare me, unburdened, for a similar work; and with so much the lighter a penalty because it was briefer and sudden, so that, overcome by sleep when they laid hands upon me, I scarcely felt any pain. But what I perhaps suffered less from the wound then, I now suffer more severely—perhaps “for longer”—from detraction; and I am tormented more by the loss of reputation than by the mutilation of my body. For, as it is written: “A good name is better than great riches” (Prov. 22:1).

And, as blessed Augustine recalls in a sermon, *On the Life and Conduct of Clerics*:

> [Note: Col. 0177D. Sermon 52, *To the Brothers in the Desert*.]

“He who, trusting in his own conscience, neglects his reputation, is cruel.” And above he says: “We provide,” he says, “good things, as the Apostle says, not only before God but also before men” (Rom. 12:17). “For our own sake, our conscience within us suffices. For our neighbor’s sake, our reputation ought not to be defiled, but to have force among us. There are two things: conscience and reputation. Conscience is for you; reputation for your neighbor.”

But what would envy have charged against Christ himself, or his members—namely, the prophets, apostles, or other holy Fathers—if it had existed in their times, when it saw them, bodily whole, especially associated with women in such familiar intercourse? Thus blessed Augustine, in his book *On the Work of Monks*, shows that women themselves clung to the Lord Jesus Christ and the apostles as companions so inseparable that they even went out with them to preach (chapter 4):

> “For this reason faithful women who possessed earthly means went with them and ministered to them from their own resources, so that they might lack none of those things which pertain to the support of this life. And whoever does not think that the apostles acted so that women of holy conduct went about with them wherever they preached the Gospel, let him hear the Gospel and learn how they did this by the example of the Lord himself. For it is written in the Gospel: ‘Afterward he went on a journey through cities and villages, preaching the kingdom of God; and the twelve were with him, and certain women who had been healed of unclean [or, evil] spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene, and Joanna, wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward, and Susanna, and many others who ministered to him from their resources’” (Luke 8:1).

And Leo IX [or, Leo the Great], in his work against the letter of Parmenian [or, Parmenius] concerning monastic observance, says:

> “We profess altogether that it is not lawful for a bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon to cast off his own wife, under the pretext of religion, from his care, so as not to provide her food and clothing; but he is not to lie carnally with her. Thus we read that the holy apostles acted, blessed Paul saying: ‘Do we not have the right to take about with us a woman who is a sister, as also the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?’ (1 Cor. 9:5). See, foolish man, that he did not say, ‘Do we not have the right to embrace a woman who is a sister?’ but ‘to take her about with us’; namely, that they might be supported by them as the recompense of preaching, while there was no longer carnal marriage between them.”

Certainly that Pharisee who said within himself concerning the Lord, “This man, if he were a prophet, would surely know who and what kind of woman it is who touches him, because she is a sinner” (Luke 7:39), could have formed a much more plausible conjecture of shameful conduct concerning the Lord, as far as human judgment is concerned, than these men can concerning us. Likewise, one who saw his mother entrusted to a young man (John 19:27), or prophets lodging and associating especially with widows (3 Kings [1 Kings] 17:10), might have drawn from this a far more likely suspicion.

What, too, would these our detractors have said if they had seen that captive monk Malchus, of whom blessed Jerome writes, living in the same dwelling with his wife?

> [Note: Col. 0178D. In the *Life of Malchus*.]

How greatly would they have counted this as a crime! Yet when that outstanding teacher saw it, he highly commended it, saying:

> “There was there an old man named Malchus, a native of the same place, and also an old woman in his dwelling. Both were devoted to religion, and so constantly attended the threshold of the church that you would have believed them to be Zacharias and Elizabeth of the Gospel, except that John was not between them.”

Why, finally, do they refrain from slandering the holy Fathers, whom we frequently read—and have even seen—establishing women’s monasteries and ministering to them, following the example of the seven deacons whom the apostles appointed for themselves over the tables and the provision for women? (Acts 6:5). For the weaker sex so greatly needs the aid of the stronger that the Apostle establishes the man as head over the woman. As a sign of this, he also commands her always to have her head veiled (1 Cor. 20:5).

Hence I am not a little astonished that these customs have long prevailed in monasteries: that, just as abbots are set over men, so abbesses are set over women, and that women as well as men bind themselves by the profession of the same Rule. Yet that Rule contains many things which women, whether superiors or subjects, cannot possibly fulfill.

Moreover, in many places, with the natural order overturned, we see abbesses and nuns themselves exercising lordship even over clerics to whom people are subject; and they can induce them to evil desires all the more easily because they have greater authority over them and impose upon them that most grievous yoke. Considering this, that satirist said:

> Nothing is more intolerable than a wealthy woman.

> (Juvenal, *Satires* VI.459.)

### CHAPTER XV

Often considering these things within myself, I had resolved, so far as it was permitted me, to provide for those sisters and undertake their care; and, that they might reverence me more, also to watch over them by my bodily presence. And since a persecution more frequent and greater than formerly afflicted me—not from brothers now, but from sons—I might flee to them from the heat of this storm as to a certain harbor of calm, and there breathe a little; and, since I gained no fruit among monks, might gain at least some among them. This would be all the more salutary for me because it was more necessary for their weakness.

But now Satan has so hindered me that I find no place where I can rest, or even live; rather, I am carried about everywhere as a wanderer and fugitive, like the cursed Cain (Gen. 4:14). As I have mentioned above, “fights without, fears within” (2 Cor. 7:5) torment me unceasingly—indeed, fears both without and within, and likewise fights and fears. A far more dangerous and frequent persecution rages against me from my sons than from enemies. For I always have these men present, and continually endure their snares. I see the violence of enemies threatening my body if I leave the cloister. But within the cloister I constantly endure the violent as well as deceitful schemes of sons—that is, monks committed to me as to an abbot, that is, a father.

How often they tried to destroy me by poison, as was done to blessed Benedict!

> [Note: Col. 0179D. St. Gregory, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 3.]

It was as though the very reason for which he abandoned his perverse sons openly exhorted me, by the example of so great a Father, to do the same: lest, deliberately exposing myself to certain danger, I be found a rash tempter of God rather than his lover—indeed, my own destroyer.

While I protected myself as far as I could against their daily snares in the administration of food and drink, they attempted to poison me in the very sacrifice of the altar, by putting poison into the chalice. And one day, when I had come to Nantes to visit the count in his illness, they planned to kill me by poison through a servant who was in our company, while I was lodging in the house there of a certain blood-brother; for there they believed that I would be less on guard against such a plot.

But by divine ordering it happened then that, while I paid no attention to the food prepared for me, a brother of the monks whom I had brought with me ate this food unknowingly and fell dead on the spot; and the servant who had attempted this fled, terrified alike by his conscience and by the evidence of the deed itself.

From then on, their wickedness being manifest to all, I began openly, as far as I could, to avoid their snares; I even withdrew myself from the abbey’s community and lived in cells with a few men. If they learned that I was going anywhere, they set corrupt brigands, bought with money, on roads or paths to kill me. While I labored amid these dangers, perhaps on some day the hand of the Lord struck me heavily when I fell from our horse, breaking the channel of my neck. This fracture afflicted and weakened me far more than the earlier wound.

Sometimes, restraining their untamed rebellion by excommunication, I compelled certain of them whom I feared most publicly to promise me upon their faith or oath that they would thereafter depart wholly from the abbey and trouble me no longer in any matter. Publicly and most shamelessly violating both their given pledge and their oaths, they were at last compelled, by the authority of Pope Innocent of Rome—who sent his own legate for this purpose—to swear to this very thing in the presence of the count and bishops, along with many other matters. Nor did they rest even then.

Recently, when those whom I have mentioned had been expelled and I returned to the abbey community, entrusting myself to the remaining brothers, whom I suspected less, I found them much worse than the former. I escaped them only with difficulty when, no longer plotting poison but drawing the sword against my throat, they were hired by a certain nobleman of the region. I still labor under this danger; every day I seem to see a sword hanging over my neck, so that I can scarcely breathe even at meals. It is like the man of whom we read that, when he reckoned the power and acquired wealth of the tyrant Dionysius to be the height of happiness, he saw a sword secretly suspended over himself by a thread [or, “power”], and thereby learned what happiness accompanies earthly power (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, V).

I too now experience this unceasingly, raised from a poor monk to an abbot: I have become more wretched in proportion as I have become richer, so that by our example the ambition of those who seek this office willingly may be restrained.

Let this account, dearest brother in Christ and most intimate companion through long association, which I have written to you concerning the history of my calamities—amid which I have labored continually, as it were from my cradle—suffice for your desolation and the injury done to you. Thus, as I declared in the opening of my letter, you may judge your oppression, in comparison with mine, to be either none at all or slight, and bear it the more patiently because you see it to be smaller.

Always take this for consolation, which the Lord foretold to his members concerning the members of the devil: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also. If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you. If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own” (John 15:20). And the Apostle says: “All who desire to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). Elsewhere: “I do not seek to please men. If I were still pleasing men, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1:10). And the Psalmist: “They are put to shame who please men, because God has rejected them” (Ps. 52:6).

Blessed Jerome, carefully considering this—whose heir I especially see myself to be in the reproaches of detraction—writes to Nepotian (Letter 2): “If,” says the Apostle, “I were still pleasing men, I would not be Christ’s servant. He ceases to please men, and becomes Christ’s servant.” To Asella concerning false friends (Letter 99), he says: “I give thanks to my God that I am worthy for the world to hate me.” And to the monk Heliodorus (Letter 1): “You are mistaken, brother, you are mistaken, if you think that a Christian ever suffers no persecution. Our adversary goes about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour, and you think there is peace? (1 Pet. 5:8). He sits in ambush with the rich” (Ps. 9:10).

Strengthened, then, by these teachings and examples, let us bear these things all the more securely because they happen more unjustly. Let us not doubt that, if they do not profit us for merit, they at least profit us for some cleansing. And because all things are governed by divine ordering [or, dispensation], let each of the faithful at least console himself in every affliction with this: the supreme goodness of God never permits anything to occur in disorder, and whatever is done perversely, he himself brings to the best end.

Therefore it is rightly said to him in all things: “Your will be done” (Matt. 6:26). How great, finally, is that consolation for those who love God, on apostolic authority: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8:28). That wisest man carefully considered this when he said in Proverbs: “Whatever happens to him shall not make the righteous man sorrowful” (Prov. 12:21). From this he plainly shows that all who become angry over any burden of their own—at things which they do not doubt are done to them by divine ordering—depart from righteousness; they subject themselves more to their own will than to the divine will, and inwardly oppose the words they utter, “Your will be done,” preferring their own will to the divine. Farewell.

## LETTER II. Heloise’s Petitionary Letter to Peter

[Col. 0181]

### ARGUMENT

When Heloise, formerly Abelard’s beloved, afterwards his wife, and finally placed by him at the head of the monastery of the Paraclete—which he had founded from its foundations out of the resources of his disciples—read his letter to a friend, she writes this letter to him, begging him to write to her concerning his dangers or deliverance, so that she may share either his sorrow or his joy. She also protests that he has not written to her since taking monastic vows, although formerly he sent her many love letters. Finally, she describes her love for him, both the shameful and carnal love of the past and the chaste and spiritual love of the present; and she bitterly complains that he is not loved in return in the same way. The letter is richly full of many emotions and plaintive lamentations in a womanly manner, and permits one to behold a woman’s heart overflowing with much learning.

### Heloise to Abelard

To her lord—or rather, father; to her husband—or rather, brother; his handmaid—or rather, daughter; his wife—or rather, sister—Heloise, to Abelard.

A certain person recently happened to bring me, beloved one, your letter sent to a friend for consolation. Recognizing from the very heading of its title that it was yours, I began to read it all the more eagerly because I embrace its author himself more dearly; so that, though I have lost the thing itself, I may at least be refreshed by his words as by some image of him.

I remember that nearly everything in that letter was full of gall and wormwood, recounting the pitiful history of our conversion and your continual crosses, my unique one. You truly fulfilled in that letter what you had promised your friend at its beginning: that he should judge his own troubles, in comparison with yours, to be none or small.

First you set forth the persecutions directed against you by your teachers; then the outrage of the supreme betrayal inflicted upon your body. You next turned your pen to the execrable envy and excessive hostility of your own fellow students, namely Alberic of Rheims and Lotulf the Lombard. You did not omit what, at their instigation, was done concerning that glorious work of your theology, nor what was done to yourself when you were condemned as if in prison. You then came to the schemes of your abbot and false brothers; to those most grievous slanders against you stirred up by the aforesaid rivals, those two pseudo-apostles; to the scandal that arose among many because the oratory had been given the unprecedented name of the Paraclete; and finally you completed the pitiable history with the intolerable and still continuing persecutions of your life—those of that most cruel exacter and of the wicked monks whom you call your sons.

Since I judge that no one can read or hear these things with dry eyes, they renewed my griefs all the more because they set forth every point more carefully; and they increased them the more because you reported that the dangers threatening you were still growing. Thus we are all compelled to despair of your life, and our trembling hearts and palpitating breasts daily await those final tidings of your death.

Therefore, by Christ, who still in some way protects you for himself, we entreat you to deign to inform his and your little handmaids by frequent letters concerning the shipwrecks [or, “you as shipwrecked”] amid which you still struggle, so that you may have us—at least we who alone remain to you—as companions in sorrow or joy. For those who suffer with one who suffers usually bring some consolation to the afflicted, and any burden laid upon several persons is carried, or borne away, more lightly.

And if this storm should subside a little, the more quickly must letters be sent, because they will be more welcome. Whatever you write to us, you will confer no small remedy upon us, if only by this one thing: that you show yourself mindful of us.

Seneca himself teaches us by his own example how delightful are letters from absent friends, writing somewhere to his friend Lucilius (Letter 48): “I give thanks because you write to me often. For by the one means possible you show yourself to me. I never receive your letter without our immediately being together.”

If portraits of absent friends delight us, renewing memory and alleviating the pain of absence with a false and empty consolation, how much more delightful are letters, which bring true marks of an absent friend! Thanks be to God that no envy prevents you from restoring your presence to us at least in this manner, that no difficulty hinders you, and—I beg you—that no negligence delays you.

You wrote a lengthy letter of consolation to your friend: for his adversities indeed, but concerning your own. Carefully recounting these yours, while you directed yourself to his consolation, you greatly increased our desolation; and while you wished to heal his wounds, you inflicted certain new wounds of sorrow upon us and enlarged the old ones. Heal, I beg you, what you have done, you who strive to cure what others have done.

You showed kindness to a friend and companion, and paid the debt both of friendship and companionship; but you have bound yourself to us by a greater debt. We ought to be called not merely friends, but dearest friends; not merely companions, but daughters—or by whatever sweeter and holier title may be imagined. How greatly you have obligated yourself toward them needs no arguments or testimonies to establish what is not uncertain; even if all were silent, the fact itself cries aloud.

For after God you alone are the founder of this place; you alone built this oratory; you alone established this congregation. Here you built nothing upon another’s foundation. Everything here is your creation. This wilderness, occupied only by wild beasts or robbers, had known no human habitation and had had no house. In the very dens of wild beasts, in the very hiding-places of robbers, where God was not even accustomed to be named, you erected the divine tabernacle and dedicated a temple belonging to the Holy Spirit.

You brought no resources of kings or princes to construct it, although you could have brought much and very great wealth, so that whatever was done might be attributed to you alone. Clerics or scholars flocking here competitively for your teaching supplied all necessities. Those who lived from ecclesiastical benefices—who had not known how to make offerings but only to receive them, whose hands were made for receiving, not giving—here became lavish and importunate in making offerings.

Therefore this is yours—truly yours—your own new plantation in a holy purpose. Its plants are still especially tender, and frequent watering is necessary for their growth. This plantation is sufficiently weak from the very nature of the female sex; it is frail even if it were not new. Hence it requires more diligent and more frequent cultivation, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the increase” (2 Cor. 3:6).

The Apostle had planted and founded in faith, through the teaching of his preaching, the Corinthians to whom he wrote. Afterwards Apollo, the disciple of that Apostle, watered them with sacred exhortations; and thus divine grace bestowed upon them an increase of virtues.

You cultivate by frequent but fruitless admonitions, and sacred discourses in vain, the vineyard of another which you did not plant and which has turned bitter to you. You teach and admonish rebels, and make no progress. In vain you scatter the pearls of divine speech before swine (Matt. 7:6). Consider what you owe to the obedient, you who devote so much to the obstinate. Consider what you owe to daughters, you who grant so much to enemies.

And, omitting the others, weigh how great a debt you have bound yourself by toward me, so that you may render more devotedly to your one woman what you owe in common to devout women. How many and how great treatises the holy Fathers composed for the instruction, exhortation, and consolation of holy women, and with what diligence they composed them, your excellence knows better than our smallness.

Thus I have long been moved by no slight amazement that oblivion has already seized the tender beginnings of our conversion: that, admonished neither by reverence for God, nor by love for us, nor by the examples of the holy Fathers, you have not tried to console me—wavering and already worn away by long sorrow—either by speech when present or by letter when absent.

Know that you are bound to me by so much greater a debt because it is certain that you are more closely bound by the sacramental bond of marriage; and you are all the more answerable to me because, as is plain to all, I have always embraced you with immoderate love. All who knew us know, dearest one, how much I lost in you, and how, by a miserable disaster, that supreme and universally known betrayal took you away from me and took myself away from myself with you; and how the grief caused by the manner of the loss is incomparably greater than that caused by the loss itself.

But the greater the cause for grief, the greater remedies of consolation must be applied—not by another, certainly, but by you yourself, so that you who alone are the cause of grief may alone be the agent of consolation. For you alone can make me sad, make me glad, or console me. And you alone owe this to me most greatly, especially because I fulfilled all your commands so completely that, when I could not offend you in any way, I was willing to destroy myself at your command. And what is greater and astonishing to say: love has turned to such madness that it took from itself, without hope of recovery, the very thing it alone desired.

At your immediate command I changed both my dress and my mind, showing you to be the sole possessor of both my body and my soul. Never—God knows—did I seek anything in you except you; desiring you purely, not what was yours. I waited for neither marriage bonds nor any dowry; nor did I strive to fulfill my own pleasures or wishes, but yours, as you yourself know.

And if the name of wife seems holier and stronger, the title of beloved has always seemed sweeter to me; or, if you are not offended, that of concubine or whore. For the more I humbled myself for your sake, the greater favor I might obtain with you, and the less I might injure the glory of your excellence.

You yourself, for your own sake, had by no means entirely forgotten this in the letter sent to a friend for consolation which I mentioned above. In it you did not disdain to set forth certain reasons by which I had tried to draw you back from our unlucky marriage-bed; though you kept silent concerning many reasons by which I preferred love to marriage, freedom to bondage.

I call God as witness: if Augustus, ruling over the whole world, had deemed me worthy of the honor of marriage and had confirmed the entire world to be ruled by me forever, it would seem dearer and more honorable to me to be called your whore than his empress. For one is not better because one is richer or more powerful: the former belongs to fortune, the latter to virtue. Nor should she think herself at all beyond price who marries a richer man rather than a poor one more willingly, and desires more in her husband what is his than himself.

Certainly, whatever woman is led to marriage by this desire deserves payment rather than favor. For it is certain that she follows possessions, not the man, and, if she could, would wish to prostitute herself to one richer.

This is plainly demonstrated by that argument of the philosopher Aspasia, related by the Socratic Aeschines concerning Xenophon and his wife. When the aforesaid philosopher had proposed this argument to reconcile them, she concluded it thus: “When you have achieved this, so that no man may be better and no woman happier upon earth, you will surely seek with greatest eagerness what you think best: that you may be the husband of the best possible wife, and she married to the best possible husband.”

This is indeed a holy and more-than-philosophical saying, one to be called the utterance of wisdom itself rather than of philosophy. Holy is this error, and blessed this deception among married persons: that perfect love may preserve the marriage bond uninjured, not so much through continence of bodies as through chastity of minds.

But what was error to others had granted me manifest truth. For what those women merely judged concerning their husbands, the same concerning you did I—and did the entire world—not merely believe, but know. My love for you was therefore all the truer because it stood farther from error.

For what king or philosopher could equal your renown? What land, city, or village did not burn to see you? Who, I ask, did not hurry to behold you when you went forth in public, and, as you departed, pursue you with uplifted neck and fixed eyes? What married woman, what virgin, did not desire you when absent and burn for you when present? What queen or powerful woman did not envy my joys or my marriage-bed?

I confess that two qualities especially belonged to you, by which you could immediately draw to yourself the hearts of any women: skill in composing and singing—gifts which we know no other philosophers attained. Using these almost as a game to refresh yourself from the labor of philosophical study, you left many poems composed in amorous meter or rhythm. Owing to the excessive sweetness both of their composition and their melody, they were often sung, and kept your name constantly upon everyone’s lips, so that the sweetness of the melody did not allow even the unlettered to forget you.

For this reason women above all sighed in love for you. And since the greater part of these songs celebrated our love, they quickly made me known in many regions and kindled many women’s envy against me. For what excellence of mind or body did not adorn your youth?

What woman who then envied me is not now compelled by my calamity to pity me, deprived of such great delights? Whom, male or female, even if an enemy, does the compassion owed to me not now soften at once? Although most guilty, as you know, I am most innocent. For guilt lies not in the outcome of the act but in the intention of the agent; equity weighs not what is done, but the spirit in which it is done. What disposition I have always held toward you, you alone who experienced it can judge. I submit all things to your examination; I yield entirely to your testimony.

Say one thing, if you can: after our conversion—which you alone resolved to bring about—have I become so neglected and forgotten by you that I am refreshed neither by your conversation when present nor consoled by your letter when absent? Say it, I say, if you can; or I shall say what I feel—indeed, what everyone suspects.

Desire, rather than friendship, joined you to me; the heat of lust, rather than love. Once what you desired ceased, whatever you displayed for its sake vanished likewise. This, beloved one, is not so much my conjecture as everyone’s; not so much private as public; not so much particular as common. Would that it seemed so to me alone, and that your love could find some excuses by which my grief might subside a little!
