Would that I could invent occasions through which, by excusing you, I might in some fashion conceal my own worthlessness.

Consider, I beg you, what I ask; you will see these things small and very easy for you. Since I am deprived of your presence, grant to my longing for words [or, “written marks”], of which you have abundance, the sweetness of the image of you before me. In vain do I expect you to be generous in deeds if I endure you to be miserly in words.

I had believed that I had deserved much from you, since I have done everything for your sake, now most of all persevering in your service. It was not devotion to religion, but your command alone, that brought this young woman to the harshness of monastic life. If I earn nothing from you in this, judge how vainly I labor. I have no reward to expect from God for this, since it is evident that I have as yet done nothing from love for him.

I followed you in dress as you hastened to God—indeed, I went before you. For, as though mindful of Lot’s wife who looked back (Gen. 19:26), you first made me God’s servant by sacred garments and monastic profession, before making yourself so. In this one matter, I confess, I grieved and blushed deeply that you had so little confidence in me.

Yet, God knows, I would not hesitate at your command to go before or follow you into Vulcan’s places. For my soul was not with me but with you. And even now, especially if it is not with you, it is nowhere. Yet it cannot be without you.

But act, I beg you, so that it may be well with you. It will be well with you if you find it kindly disposed, if you return favor for favor, small things for great, words for deeds. Would that, beloved one, its love had less confidence in you, so that it might be more anxious! But the more secure I have now made you, the more negligent I find you.

Remember, I beseech you, what I have done, and consider how much you owe. While I enjoyed carnal pleasure with you, it was uncertain to many whether I acted from love or lust. But now the end shows from what beginning I undertook it. In short, I have forbidden myself every pleasure in order to obey your will. I have reserved nothing for myself except to become yours, especially now.

Consider, then, what injustice is yours, if you repay less—indeed, absolutely nothing—to one who deserves more, especially when what is asked is small and very easy for you. Therefore, by the God to whom you offered yourself, I entreat you to restore your presence to me in whatever way you can, namely by writing me some consolation. Thus refreshed, I may devote myself more eagerly to divine service.

When you formerly sought me for temporal pleasures, you visited me with frequent letters and made your Heloise a constant subject in everyone’s mouth by frequent song. Every street and every house resounded with me. How much more rightly should you now stir me toward God than you then stirred me toward lust!

Consider, I beg you, what you owe; attend to what I request. And I conclude a long letter with a short ending. Farewell, my unique one.

## LETTER III. Peter’s Reply to Heloise
[Col. 0187]

**SUMMARY.**—In the preceding letter Abelard replies to Heloise and frankly explains that his failure to write to her for so long did not arise from neglect of her, but from his confidence in her prudence, learning, piety, and religious devotion: he believed that she required neither exhortation nor consolation. He asks her to write back, saying what divine exhortation or consolation she wishes him to send; he will satisfy her desire. He asks her, together with her sacred choir of virgins and widows, to assist him before God by their prayers, lucidly discussing from Scriptural authority how great is the efficacy before God of prayer—especially that of wives for their husbands. Recalling the prayers hitherto offered for him in that monastery by holy women at each canonical hour, he likewise prescribes others to be said for the safety of one absent. Furthermore, he asks that, wherever or in whatever manner it should happen that he departs this life, they should arrange for his dead body to be brought to the convent of the Paraclete and buried there.

[Col. 0187B] ABAELARD, her brother in Christ, to Heloise, his most beloved sister in the same Christ.

That I have not yet written you anything of consolation or exhortation since our conversion from the world to God must be attributed, not to my neglect, but to your prudence, in which I have always placed the fullest confidence. For I did not think that one to whom divine grace had abundantly bestowed what is necessary—so that by both words and example you are able to teach those who err, console the faint-hearted, and exhort the lukewarm—needed such things. Indeed, you had long been accustomed to do this when, under the abbess, you held the office of prioress. If now you provide for your daughters with as much diligence as you then did for your sisters, we believe it sufficient, and therefore judge our instruction or exhortation altogether superfluous.

[Col. 0187C] But if your humility sees the matter otherwise, and if even in matters pertaining to God you need my teaching and writings, write to me concerning what you desire, so that I may answer as the Lord grants me to do. Thanks be to God, who, inspiring concern for my very grave and continual dangers into your hearts, has made you sharers in my affliction, so that divine mercy may protect me through the aid of your prayers and swiftly crush Satan beneath our feet.

For this purpose especially I hastened to send the Psalter which you earnestly requested of me, sister once dear in the world and now dearest in Christ: namely, that for our great and many transgressions and for the daily urgency of my dangers, you may offer to the Lord an unceasing sacrifice of prayers.

[Col. 0188B] Many testimonies and examples occur to us concerning the great place that the prayers of the faithful hold with God and his saints, especially those of women for their loved ones and of wives for their husbands. Attending carefully to this, the Apostle exhorts us to “pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17). We read that the Lord said to Moses: “Let me alone, that my wrath may burn” (Exod. 32:10). And to Jeremiah: “But you, do not pray for this people, and do not stand in my way” (Jer. 7:16).

From these words the Lord himself plainly declares that the prayers of the saints put, as it were, a bridle upon his wrath, restraining it so that it may not rage against sinners as much as their merits demand.

[Col. 0188C] Thus the one whom justice leads, as though freely, toward vengeance may be turned aside by the pleading of friends and held back, as though unwillingly, by a certain force. Accordingly, the words addressed to one praying or about to pray are: “Let me alone,” and, “Do not stand in my way.” The Lord commands that prayer not be made for the wicked. Yet the righteous man prays despite the Lord’s prohibition, obtains from him what he asks, and changes the sentence of the angry Judge. Thus it was added concerning Moses: “And the Lord relented from the evil which he said he would do to his people” (Exod. 32:14).

Elsewhere it is written of all God’s works: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 148:5). Yet in this place he is recorded both as having said what the people deserved in affliction and, forestalled by the power of prayer, as not fulfilling what he had said.

[Col. 0189A] Consider, then, how great is the power of prayer, if, when we pray what we are commanded to pray, the prophet nevertheless obtained by praying that very thing for which God had forbidden him to pray, and turned God away from what he had said. To him another prophet also says: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. 3:2).

Let earthly rulers hear and heed this—those who, under the pretext of justice proposed and decreed, are found more obstinate than just; who are ashamed to seem yielding if they become merciful, and false if they alter their decree or do not carry out what they established with insufficient foresight, even though they correct their words by their deeds. Such men, I would rightly say, should be compared with Jephthah, who, more foolishly fulfilling what he had foolishly vowed, killed his only daughter (Judg. 11:39).

[Col. 0189B] But one who wishes to be a member of God says with the Psalmist: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 101:1). “Mercy,” as it is written, “triumphs over judgment,” mindful that Scripture elsewhere threatens “judgment without mercy to one who has shown no mercy” (Jas. 2:13).

The Psalmist himself, carefully considering this, annulled in mercy, at the entreaty of the wife of Nabal the Carmelite, the oath which in justice he had made concerning the destruction of her husband and his household (1 Kings 25:3). He preferred prayer to justice, and the wife’s entreaty wiped away the husband’s offence.

[Col. 0189C] In this, sister, an example and assurance are set before you: if that woman’s prayer prevailed with a mere human being, you are taught what your prayer for me may dare before God. For God, who is our Father, loves his children more than David loved a woman making supplication. David indeed was regarded as pious and merciful; but piety and mercy itself is God. The woman then pleading was secular and a laywoman, not joined to the Lord by a profession of holy devotion.

And if you alone are insufficient to obtain your request, the holy community of virgins and widows that is with you will obtain what you cannot obtain alone. For when Truth says to the disciples, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” (Matt. 18:20), and again, “If two of you agree concerning anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father” (ibid., 19),

[Col. 0189D] who cannot see how great is the power before God of the frequent prayer of a holy congregation? If, as the Apostle declares, “the persistent prayer of a righteous person is very powerful” (Jas. 5:16), what must be hoped from the multitude of a holy community?

You know, dearest sister, from the twenty-eighth homily of blessed Gregory, how great an aid the prayer of brethren brought by nature [variant: “in due course”] to a brother who was unwilling or opposed. Your prudence is by no means unaware of what is carefully written there: when he had already been brought to the end, with what anxiety of peril his wretched soul suffered, and with what despair and weariness of life he tried to call the brethren back from prayer.

Would that this might invite you and the assembly of holy sisters more confidently to prayer, so that he through whom, as Paul testifies, women received even their dead back through resurrection might preserve me alive for you.

[Col. 0190A] For if you turn over the pages of the Old and New Testaments, you will find that the greatest miracles of resurrection were displayed principally, indeed almost exclusively, to women—performed either for them or through them. The Old Testament records two dead persons raised at maternal entreaties: one through Elijah (1 Kings 17:17), the other through his disciple Elisha (2 Kings 4:34). The Gospel, however, contains only three resurrections performed by the Lord; these were granted to women and notably confirm by their events the apostolic saying mentioned above: “Women received their dead by resurrection” (Heb. 11:35).

[Col. 0190B] Moved by compassion for her, he restored to his mother the son of the widow, raised at the gate of the city of Nain (Luke 7:15). He also raised his friend Lazarus at the entreaty of his sisters, Mary and Martha (John 11:44). And since the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue received this same grace at her father’s request (Mark 5:42), “women received their dead by resurrection,” because, having been raised, she received her own body back from death, just as those women received the bodies of their own people.

These resurrections took place after only a few intervening circumstances. But the manifold prayer of your devotion will readily obtain the preservation of my life. The more pleasing to God your abstinence and chastity, consecrated to him, are held to be, the more propitious you will find him. Perhaps many of those who were raised were not even believers, just as the widow mentioned above was not read to have been a believer—she who did not ask, yet whose son the Lord raised.

[Col. 0190C] But we are bound together not only by the integrity of faith; we are also joined by the profession of the same religious life. Yet, to omit for the moment the most holy congregation of your community, in which the devotion of very many virgins and widows continually serves the Lord, I shall come to you alone. I do not at all doubt the power of your holiness before God; and you are especially able—and, above all in the crisis of such adversity under which I labour, especially bound—to act for me.

Therefore always remember in your prayers him who is particularly yours; and watch in prayer with all the more confidence because you recognize that this is more justly yours to do and therefore more acceptable to him who is to be prayed to. Hear, I beg you, with the ear of your heart what you have often heard with the ear of your body.

[Col. 0190D] It is written in Proverbs: “A diligent woman is the crown of her husband” (Prov. 12:4). Again: “He who finds a good woman finds a good thing and will draw delight from the Lord” (Prov. 18:22). And again: “House and riches are given by parents, but a prudent wife properly comes from the Lord” (Prov. 19:14). And in Ecclesiasticus: “Blessed is the husband of a good woman” (Sir. 26:1); and, shortly afterwards: “A good woman is a good portion” (ibid., 3). And according to apostolic authority: “The unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife” (1 Cor. 7:14).

[Col. 0191A] Divine grace especially displayed the truth of this in our own kingdom, that is, the kingdom of the Franks. For when King Clovis was converted to the faith of Christ, it was in response to his wife’s prayer more than to the preaching of the saints that they subjected the whole kingdom to divine laws; and chiefly by the example of those above, those below were urged to persistence in prayer.

The Lord’s parable strongly invites us to such persistence: “If he persists in knocking, I tell you that, even if he will not give him anything because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as much as he needs” (Luke 11:8). By this, so to speak, importunity in prayer Moses, as I have mentioned above, weakened the severity of divine justice (Exod. 32:14) and changed the sentence.

[Col. 0191B] You know, beloved, how much loving concern your community formerly showed in prayer for my presence. At the completion of each daily canonical hour it was accustomed to offer the Lord this special supplication for me, first reciting and chanting the response and its verse, and then adding these petitions and this collect:

Response: “Do not forsake me, nor depart from me, O Lord” (Ps. 38:22).

Verse: “Always give heed to help me, O Lord” (Ps. 70:1).

Petitions: “Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you. Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you” (Ps. 102:2).

Prayer [variant: “Let us pray”]: “O God, who through your little servant have deigned to gather your handmaids in your name, we beseech you to grant that both they and we may persevere in your will. Through the Lord,” etc.

[Col. 0191C] But now, absent from you, I need the aid of your prayers all the more because I am constrained by the anxiety of greater danger. Therefore, begging I ask, and asking I beg, that I may especially now, in my absence, learn how true your love toward one absent has been, by your adding the following form of special prayer at the completion of every hour:

Response: “Do not abandon me, O Lord, Father and Master of my life, lest I fall before my adversaries and my enemy rejoice over me” (Sir. 23:1).

Verse: “Take up weapons and shield, and arise to help me. Let him not rejoice” (Ps. 35:2).

[Col. 0192A] Petitions: “Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you. Send him help, O Lord, from the sanctuary, and defend him from Zion. Be for him, O Lord, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy. Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you” (Ps. 102:2).

Prayer [variant: “Let us pray”]: “O God, who through your servant have deigned to gather your handmaids in your name, we beseech you to protect him from every adversity and restore him unharmed to your handmaids. Through the Lord,” etc.

But if the Lord delivers me into the hands of enemies, so that they prevail and kill me, or if, through any event, I enter the way of all flesh while absent from you, I beg that you arrange for our body, wherever it may lie, whether buried or exposed, to be carried to your cemetery,

[Col. 0192B] where our daughters [variant: “your daughters”]—indeed, sisters in Christ—may be more strongly prompted, by frequently seeing our tomb, to pour out prayers to the Lord for me. For I judge no place safer or more salutary for a soul desolated and sorrowing over the error of its sins than one properly consecrated to the true Paraclete, that is, the Consoler, and specially marked by his name.

Nor do I think any place of Christian burial is more fitting among believers than among women devoted to Christ. Concerned for the burial of the Lord Jesus Christ (Mark 16:1), they both preceded it and followed it with precious ointments; and, diligently watching beside his tomb and tearfully mourning the death of the Bridegroom, they fulfilled what is written:

[Col. 0192C] “The women sitting by the tomb mourned, weeping for the Lord” (Matt. 27:61). There first, through angelic appearance and speech, they were consoled concerning his resurrection; and immediately they deserved to receive the joys of that resurrection, when he appeared to them twice, and to touch him with their hands.

Finally, above all things I ask this: you who now suffer excessive anxiety about the danger to my body should then, especially concerned for the salvation of my soul, show to me dead how much you loved me alive, by the special and particular aid of your prayers.

Live, farewell; and may your sisters live and fare well.

Live—but, I beg, in Christ [variant: “in the Lord”], mindful of me.

**LETTER IV. Heloise’s reply to Peter.**

[Col. 0191]

**SUMMARY.**—The letter is full of lamentation and grief. Heloise laments her own wretched condition, that of her nuns, and that of Abelard himself, taking the occasion for her lament from the final portion of the preceding letter, in which Abelard mentions his departure from this life. She employs many expressions of feeling to move the reader to compassion for herself and Abelard, perhaps even to draw tears. She laments Abelard’s wound as well. She complains much about the carnal desires once inflamed within their bodies, which she had experienced with Abelard. Accordingly, she not unfittingly diminishes the importance of her outward and visible religious profession, attributing it to pretence rather than piety; she asks to be aided by the prayers of her Abelard, and humbly rejects praise of herself.

[Col. 0191D] To her one alone after Christ, from his one alone in Christ.

My one alone, I am astonished that, contrary to the usual custom of letters—indeed, contrary to the natural order of things itself—you presumed in the very opening of your epistolary greeting to place me before yourself: a woman before a man, a wife before her husband, a handmaid before her master, a nun before a monk and priest, a deaconess before an abbot.

[Col. 0192D] For it is the proper and honourable order that those who write to their superiors or equals should place before their own names the names of those to whom they write.

[Col. 0193A] But if they write to inferiors, those who precede in dignity precede in the order of writing as well.

We also received with no small astonishment the fact that, while you ought to have brought a remedy of consolation to those whom you have desolated, you increased their desolation; and that you stirred up tears in those whom you ought to have soothed. For which of us could hear with dry eyes what you placed near the end of your letter, saying: “If the Lord should deliver me into the hands of enemies, so that they may prevail and kill me,” and so forth?

O dearest one, with what heart did you conceive this? With what mouth could you bear to say it? May God never so forget his handmaids as to preserve them alive after you. May he never grant us that life which is more grievous than every kind of death. It is fitting that you celebrate our funeral rites, that you commend our souls to God, and that you send before yourself to him those whom you have gathered for God, so that you may no longer be troubled by any concern for them and may follow us with greater joy because you are then more secure concerning our salvation.

[Col. 0193B] Spare us, I beg you, master; spare us such words, by which you make wretches most wretched. Do not take from us before death even that little life which we may have. “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6:34); and that day will bring enough anxiety, wrapped in every bitterness, to all whom it finds.

“For what need,” says Seneca, “is there to summon evils and lose life before death?” My one alone, you ask that, if absent from us you end this life by whatever misfortune, we should have your body brought to our cemetery, so that you may receive a fuller benefit from our prayers through continual remembrance of you. But how can you suppose that remembrance of you could slip away from us? Or when will there then be a suitable time for prayer, when the greatest disturbance will permit nothing to remain tranquil?

[Col. 0193C] When the soul will retain neither the faculty of reason nor the tongue the use of speech? When the frantic mind, if I may put it so, more angry than at peace even with God himself, will not so much appease him by prayers as provoke him by complaints? Then wretches will have leisure only to weep, not permission to pray; and we must hasten rather to follow you than to bury you, so that we are more likely to be buried with you than able to bury you.

When we have lost our life in you, we shall not be able to live after your departure. Would that we might not even be able to survive until then! The mention of your death is a kind of death to us. What then will the reality of this death be when it finds us? May God never permit that, surviving you, we should render you this service owed to you or offer you this aid which we wholly expect from you. Would that we might precede you rather than follow you!

[Col. 0193D] Spare us, therefore, I beg you; at least spare your one alone, by refraining from words of this sort, which pierce our souls like swords of death, so that what comes before death is more grievous than death itself. A spirit consumed by grief is not at peace, and a mind occupied by disturbances cannot devote itself sincerely to God.

Do not, I beg you, hinder the divine service to which you have especially devoted us. Every unavoidable event which, when it occurs, will bring with it the greatest grief ought to come suddenly, lest it torture us long beforehand with useless fear—an event against which no foresight can provide help. This the poet also rightly considered when he prayed to God, saying:

> Let whatever you prepare come suddenly; blind is  
> The human mind to future fate. Let the fearful be allowed to hope.

(Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book II, 14–15.)

What hope remains to me if I lose you? Or what reason remains for staying in this pilgrimage, where I have no remedy but you, and in you no other consolation than this alone—that you live—while every other delight in you is forbidden me, and I am not even granted the enjoyment of your presence, so that I might someday be restored to myself? Oh, if it may lawfully be said: God has been cruel to me in every respect! Oh merciless mercy! Oh unfortunate fortune, which has now spent upon me all the weapons of its attack so completely that it has none left with which to rage against others; it has emptied its whole quiver upon me, so that others now need fear its wars in vain. Nor, if any missile still remained to it, would it find in me a place to wound. Amid so many wounds it fears one thing only: that death may end my punishments. And though it never ceases to destroy me, it nevertheless fears the destruction it hastens. Oh, most miserable of all miserable women! Most unhappy of all unhappy women! The more I attained, raised above all other women, to a lofty rank through you, the more grievous was the fall which, cast down from it, I suffered both in you and in myself! For the higher the step of one ascending, the heavier the fall of one collapsing. What fortune of noble and powerful women could ever be set before mine or equalled with it? And what woman, finally, has fortune cast down so utterly or been able to crush with such grief? What glory did it confer upon me in you [variant: “in life”]? What ruin did it bring upon me in you? How vehement was it toward me in either direction, so that it observed no measure either in good things or in evil! In order to make me more miserable than all others, it had made me happier than all before them. Thus, as I reflected upon how much I had lost, griefs consumed me all the more greatly in proportion as greater losses overwhelmed me; and pain at what was lost succeeded all the more greatly in proportion as love for what had been possessed had preceded more greatly, and the joys of highest delight were brought to an end by the sadness of highest sorrow.

And, so that greater indignation might arise from the injustice, every rule of equity in our case has together been overturned. For while we enjoyed the delights of anxious love and—if I may use a more shameful but more explicit term—gave ourselves to fornication, divine severity spared us. But when we corrected what was unlawful by what was lawful, and covered the shamefulness of fornication with the honour of marriage, the wrath of the Lord laid its hand heavily upon us, and did not endure the undefiled marriage-bed which it had long before tolerated when polluted. For men caught in any adultery, the punishment you suffered would have been more than sufficient vengeance. What others deserve through adultery, you incurred through marriage, by which you had thought that you had already made satisfaction for every injury. What an adulteress gives to her adulterous lovers, your own wife gave to you. Nor did this happen when we were occupied with our former pleasures, but when we were already living more chastely, separated for a time: you presiding over the schools at Paris, and I, at your command, living among the nuns at Argenteuil. Thus, separated from one another [variant: “from each other”], so that you might devote yourself more diligently to the schools and I more freely to prayer or meditation upon sacred reading, and living more holily in proportion as we lived more chastely, you alone in your body paid the penalty for what we both had committed together. You alone bore the punishment; two were guilty. And you, who ought to have borne less, endured all of it. For the more you had made satisfaction for me by humbling yourself, and had exalted both me and all my family, the less liable had you made yourself to punishment, both before God and before those traitors.

Oh, wretch that I am, born to be the cause of so great a crime! Oh, supreme ruin of great men, the customary bane wrought by women! Thus it is written in Proverbs concerning the woman against whom one must beware: “Now therefore, my son, listen to me, and attend to the words of my mouth. Let not your mind be drawn aside into her ways, nor be deceived by her paths. For she has cast down many wounded men, and all the strongest have been slain by her. Her house is a way to hell, penetrating into the depths of death” (Prov. 7:24). And in Ecclesiastes: “I surveyed all things in my mind, and found woman more bitter than death: she is the snare of hunters, and her heart a net. Her hands are chains. He who pleases God will escape her; but the sinner will be taken by her” (Eccl. 7:26).

The first woman immediately took the man captive out of Paradise (Gen. 3:6), and she who had been created for him by the Lord as a help became his supreme destruction. Delilah alone overcame that strongest Nazirite of the Lord, whose conception had been announced by an angel; and, after he had been betrayed to his enemies and deprived of his eyes, grief finally drove him to crush himself together with the ruin of his enemies (Judg. 16:4). Solomon, wisest of all men, was made foolish by the woman whom he had joined to himself; she forced him into such madness that she cast him down into idolatry until the end of his life—him whom the Lord had chosen to build His temple, after rejecting his father David, who had been righteous—when he had forsaken that divine worship which he proclaimed and taught both in speech and writing (3 Kings 11:7). Most holy Job endured in his wife his final and most grievous contest, for she urged him to curse God (Job 2:9). And the most cunning Tempter knew this very well, having often found by experience that the downfall of men is easiest through their wives. Finally, extending his customary malice even to us, he tempted through marriage the man whom he had not been able to overthrow through fornication; and he used a good thing badly, though he had not been allowed to use an evil thing badly.

At least I give thanks to God for this: that he did not draw me, like the women mentioned above, into guilt through mutual consent, although through affection he made me the cause of the evil committed. But even if innocence cleanses my mind and the consent does not incur the guilt of this crime, many sins nevertheless went before, which do not allow me to be wholly free from guilt in this crime. For by long serving the pleasures of carnal allurements, I then deserved what I now suffer; and what followed rightly became a punishment in me for my preceding sins. A perverse end must be imputed even to evil beginnings. Would that I might be able to perform worthy penance especially for this sin, so that by the prolonged contrition of penance I might somehow repay the penalty for the wound inflicted upon you; and that what you suffered in your body for an hour, I might, as is just, undergo throughout my life in contrition of mind, and thus at least make satisfaction to you, if not to God.

For, if I confess the weakness of my most wretched soul truly, I cannot discover by what penance I may appease God, whom I continually accuse of the utmost cruelty in this injury; and by indignation at His dispensation I offend Him more by opposing it than I soften Him by satisfaction in penance. How, moreover, can there be said to be repentance for sins, however great the bodily affliction, if the mind still retains the will to sin and burns with its former desires? It is easy enough for anyone to accuse himself by confessing sins, or even to afflict the body through outward satisfaction. But it is exceedingly difficult to tear the mind away from desires for the greatest pleasures. Hence holy Job, after he had said, “I will let loose my speech against myself” (Job 10:1)—that is, “I will loosen my tongue and open my mouth, through confession, to accuse my sins”—immediately added: “I will speak in the bitterness of my soul” (ibid.).

Blessed Gregory, explaining this, says: “There are some who confess their faults in open words, yet do not know how to groan in confession, and recount with delight the things that should be mourned” (*Morals* IX, ch. 23). Therefore one who speaks in detestation of his sins must speak of them in bitterness of soul, so that this very bitterness may punish whatever the tongue accuses through the judgment of the mind. But how rare this bitterness of true repentance is, blessed Ambrose carefully observes: “I have found more easily those who preserved innocence than those who performed repentance” (*On Penance*, ch. 10).

Those lovers’ pleasures which we shared were so sweet to me that they cannot displease me, nor can they scarcely slip from my memory. Wherever I turn, they continually present themselves to my eyes together with their desires. They do not spare me even in sleep with their illusions. Amid the very solemnities of Mass, where prayer ought to be purest, the obscene phantoms of those pleasures so utterly take my wretched soul captive that I occupy myself more with those shameful things than with prayer. When I ought to groan for what I have done, I sigh rather for what I have lost. And not merely the acts we performed, but also the places and times in which we performed them, are so fixed with you in my mind that in them I do everything with you, and even while sleeping I do not rest from them. At times the very movement of my body reveals the thoughts of my mind, and I cannot restrain unbidden words.

Oh, truly wretched am I, and most worthy of that lamentation of the groaning soul: “Unhappy man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). Would that I could also truthfully add what follows: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid., 25). This grace, dearest one, forestalled you; by healing with one wound of the body, it cured you of many such stings in the soul. And in that in which God is thought to have opposed you more, He is found more favourable: in the manner of a most faithful physician, who does not spare pain in order to provide for health.

But in me, these stings of the flesh and inducements to lust are inflamed most strongly by the youthful heat of my age and by experience of the most delightful pleasures; and they crush me by their assault all the more because the nature they attack is weaker. Those who have not detected the hypocrite proclaim me chaste. They reckon bodily purity a virtue, though it is a virtue not of the body but of the mind. Having some praise among men, I merit nothing before God, who tests heart and reins and sees what is hidden. At this time I am judged religious [variant: “in heart”], when now no small part of religious life is hypocrisy, and when the person who does not offend human judgment is extolled with the greatest praises.

Perhaps this too seems in some way praiseworthy and somehow acceptable to God: if someone, by the example of an outward work and under whatever intention, does not become a scandal to the Church, so that through him the Lord’s name is no longer blasphemed among unbelievers nor the order of his profession defamed among the carnal. This too is no small gift of divine grace, through whose gift one comes not only to do good but also to abstain from evil. But this comes first in vain where the other does not follow, as it is written: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. 36:27). And both are done in vain if they are not done from love of God.

Yet in every condition of my life—God knows—I fear offending you more than God; I seek to please you more than Him. Your command drew me to the religious habit, not divine love. See what an unhappy life, more pitiable than all others, I lead, if I endure so much here in vain and shall have no reward in the future. For a long time my pretence deceived you, as it deceived many, so that you imputed hypocrisy to religious devotion; and therefore, commending yourself especially to our prayers, you ask of me what I await from you. Do not, I beg you, presume so much concerning me that you cease to help me by prayer. Do not judge me healthy, lest you withdraw the grace of medicine. Do not believe me free from need, lest you delay helping in my necessity. Do not suppose that I am well [variant: “health”], lest I fall before you sustain me as I am collapsing. Feigned praise of oneself has harmed many and deprived them of the aid they needed.

The Lord cries through Isaiah: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you, and destroy the way of your steps” (Isa. 3:12). And through Ezekiel: “Woe,” He says, “to you who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand, and pillows beneath the head of every age, to deceive souls” (Ezek. 13:18). Conversely, Solomon says: “The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails driven deep,” for they do not know how to stroke wounds but to pierce them (Eccl. 12:11). Cease, I beg you, from praising me, lest you incur the shameful mark of flattery and the crime of falsehood; or lest whatever good you suppose to be in me be puffed about by the wind of vanity through being praised. No physician skilled in medicine judges an inward illness by inspection of outward appearance. No things possess any merit before God which are common alike to the reprobate and the elect. Such are the things done outwardly—things which no saints perform with such zeal as hypocrites do. “The heart of man is perverse and inscrutable; who shall know it?” (Jer. 17:9). And there are ways of a man which seem right, but their end leads to death (Prov. 14:12). Human judgment concerning that which is reserved to divine examination alone is rash. Hence it is written: “Do not praise a man in his lifetime” (Ecclus. 11:30)—that is, do not praise a person while by praising him you may make him not praiseworthy.

Your praise of me is the more dangerous to me because it is more pleasing; and I am all the more captivated and delighted by it because I strive more earnestly to please you in every respect. I beg you, always fear for me rather than trust in me, so that I may always be helped by your concern. But now above all there is cause for fear, when no remedy for my incontinence remains in you. Do not, in exhorting me to virtue and summoning me to battle, say: “For virtue is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9), and: “He shall not be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5). I do not seek the crown of victory. It is enough for me to avoid danger. It is safer to avoid danger than to undertake war. In whatever corner of heaven God places me, He will satisfy me. There no one will envy another, since what each possesses will suffice for each.

To strengthen this counsel of ours also by authority, let us hear blessed Jerome [Note: Col. 0197D, *Against Vigilantius*]: “I confess my weakness: I do not wish to fight in hope of victory, lest I someday lose the victory.” What need is there to abandon what is certain and pursue what is uncertain?

## LETTER V. Peter’s reply, again, to Heloise

[Col. 0199]

**SUMMARY.**—Abelard says, with ingenuity, that the whole of Heloise’s latest letter consists of four principal points, and he answers each in turn, not so much in order to excuse himself as to instruct, exhort, and console Heloise. First, he gives the reason why, in his last letter, he placed her name before his own. Second, he explains that he had mentioned his dangers and death because she had adjured him to do so. Third, he approves her rejection of his praise, provided that it is sincere and not motivated by desire for praise. Fourth, he discusses at greater length the occasion of each of their conversions to monastic life. He so minimizes the wound in the shameful part of his body, which she lamented, as to declare it most salutary for them both and the cause of many good things, by comparison with the shameful acts of that same private part; and for this reason he extols divine wisdom and mercy. Finally, many things are set down throughout for Heloise’s instruction, exhortation, and consolation. A brief prayer is also included, by which the nuns of the Paraclete might make God favourable to Abelard and Heloise.

[Col. 0199A] The servant of Christ to the bride of the same.

I remember that you expressed your troubled resentment concerning four matters which form the substance of your latest letter. First, you complain that, contrary to the customary form of letters—indeed, contrary even to the natural order of things—our letter directed to you placed you before me in its salutation. Second, though I ought rather to have brought you a remedy of consolation, I increased your desolation and stirred up tears which I should have calmed, by adding there: “But if the Lord should deliver me into the hands of my enemies, so that, prevailing, they may kill me,” etc. Third, you added that old and continual complaint of yours against God concerning the manner of our conversion [variant: “way of life”] toward God, and the cruelty of that betrayal committed against me. Finally, you set against my praise of you your own accusation of yourself, with no slight entreaty that I should not presume to do this hereafter.

I have resolved to reply to each of these points, not so much for my own excuse as for your instruction or exhortation: so that you may assent the more willingly to my requests in proportion as you understand them to have been made more reasonably; and may heed me the more in your own matters in proportion as you find less to blame in mine; and may fear all the more to despise me in proportion as I seem less deserving of blame.

But concerning the inverted order of our salutation, as you call it, this was done also according to your own judgment, if you consider carefully. For you yourself stated what is obvious to everyone: when one writes to superiors, their names are placed first. Understand, then, that from the time when you began to be my lady, having become the bride of my Lord, you were made superior to me, according to what blessed Jerome wrote to Eustochium (Letter 22): “For this reason, my lady Eustochium, I write these things. For I ought to call the bride of my Lord ‘lady.’” Happy exchange of such marriages: once the wife of a wretched little man, you are now exalted in the chambers of the highest King. Nor are you raised through the privilege of this honour above merely your former husband, but above all the servants of that same King.

Do not wonder, therefore, if both living and dead I especially commend myself to your prayers, since it is established by public law that, with their lords, their brides have greater power in interceding than their households, and ladies more than servants. In their figure, that queen and bride of the highest King is carefully described when the psalm says: “The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. 44:10). It is as though it plainly said: she clings most intimately to her bridegroom at his joined side and walks with him, while all others stand at a distance [variant: “stand by”] or follow behind.

Exulting in the excellence of this prerogative, the bride in the Song of Songs—that Ethiopian woman, so to speak, whom Moses took as wife (Num. 12:1)—says: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem. Therefore the king loved me and brought me into his chamber” (Song 1:4). And again: “Do not consider me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me” (ibid., 5). Though in these words the contemplative soul is described generally, which is specially called the bride of Christ, nevertheless your outward dress itself speaks more expressly of their application to you. For the outward garb of black or coarse clothing, like the mourning attire of good widows grieving for husbands whom they loved and who have died, shows you truly to be widows and desolate women in this world, according to the Apostle, to be supported by the resources of the Church (1 Tim. 5:16). Scripture also recalls the mourning of these widows over their slain bridegroom, saying: “The women sitting at the tomb mourned, weeping for the Lord” (Matt. 27:61).

The Ethiopian woman has outward blackness of flesh and, as regards externals, appears uglier than other women; yet inwardly she is not unlike them, but in many respects even more beautiful and fairer, as in her bones or teeth. The whiteness of those teeth is praised even in the bridegroom himself, when it is said: “And his teeth are whiter than milk” (Gen. 49:12). Thus she is black in outward things but beautiful in inward things (Song 1:4), because, afflicted bodily in this life by frequent adversities and tribulations, she is outwardly made dark, as it were, in the flesh, according to the Apostle: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer tribulation” (2 Tim. 3:12). For just as white signifies prosperity, so black not inappropriately signifies adversity.

But inwardly she is white, as it were, in her bones, because her soul is strong in virtues, as it is written: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is from within” (Ps. 44:14). For bones, being inward parts covered by the outer flesh, are the strength and firmness of the flesh which they bear or support; they fittingly represent the soul, which gives life to, supports, moves, and governs the flesh in which it dwells, and supplies it with all health. Its whiteness or beauty consists in the very virtues with which it is adorned. She is also black in outward things because, while still in exile in this pilgrimage, she holds herself cheap and lowly in this life, so that she may be exalted in that life which is hidden with Christ in God, having now attained her homeland.

The true Sun thus discolours her, because the heavenly love of her bridegroom humbles her in this way or torments her with tribulations, lest prosperity exalt her. He discolours her—that is, makes her unlike others who long for earthly things and seek the glory of the world—so that she may truly become a lily of the valleys through humility: not a lily of the mountains, like those foolish virgins who, puffed up within themselves by bodily purity or outward abstinence, withered in the heat of temptation. Therefore, speaking to the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, to the more imperfect faithful, who are worthy rather of the name daughters than sons—she rightly says: “Do not consider me because I am dark, because the sun has discoloured me” (Song 1:5). It is as if she said more plainly: that I so humble myself or endure adversities so manfully is not from my own strength, but from the grace of Him whom I serve.

Heretics and hypocrites behave otherwise: as far as the eyes of men are concerned, they humble themselves greatly in hope of earthly glory or endure many things uselessly. Their abasement or tribulation is greatly to be wondered at, since they are more miserable than all people, enjoying neither the goods of the present life nor those of the future. The bride, carefully considering this, says: “Do not wonder why I do this.” Rather, those people are to be wondered at who, burning with desire for earthly praise to no purpose, deprive themselves of earthly advantages and are miserable both here and in the future. Such is the continence of the foolish virgins, who were excluded from the door (Matt. 25:1).

And because, as we have said, she is black and beautiful, she rightly says that she has been loved and brought into the king’s chamber: that is, into the secret place or repose of contemplation, and into that bed of which she says elsewhere: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:1). The very ugliness of blackness loves what is hidden rather than what is manifest, and secrecy more than publicity. Such a wife desires the secret delights of her husband rather than the public ones, and wishes to be felt in bed rather than seen at table. And it frequently happens that the flesh of black women, the more unattractive it is to the eye, is the more pleasant to the touch; and therefore their pleasure is more pleasing and fitting in secret delights than in public ones, and their husbands, to delight in them, bring them into the chamber rather than lead them out in public.

In accordance with this metaphor, the spiritual bride, after saying, “I am black, but beautiful” (Song 1:4), immediately added: “Therefore the king loved me and brought me into his chamber” (ibid., 3), assigning each thing to its corresponding reason. That is: because she is beautiful, he loved her; because she is black, he brought her in. Beautiful inwardly, as I have said, through the virtues the bridegroom loves; black outwardly through the adversities of bodily tribulations. This blackness—namely, bodily tribulations—readily tears the minds of the faithful away from love of earthly things, suspends them upon desires for eternal life, and often draws them from the tumultuous life of the world into the secrecy of contemplation. Blessed Jerome writes that this happened in the case of that Paul who was, as it were, the beginning of our—that is, the monastic—life [Note: Col. 0201D, St Jerome, *Life of Paul the Hermit*].

This lowliness of coarse garments likewise seeks secrecy more than publicity; and it must be carefully preserved through the great usefulness [variant: “humility”] of the more secluded place, which especially suits our profession. Precious clothing above all invites one to appear in public. Blessed Gregory proves from this that no one seeks it except for empty glory and worldly display (*Homily* 40 on Luke 16): “For no one adorns himself with these things in secret, but where he may be seen.”

The chamber of the bride mentioned above is that to which the bridegroom himself invites one at prayer in the Gospel, saying: “But when you pray, enter into your chamber, and, having shut the door, pray to your Father” (Matt. 6:6). It is as though He said: not in streets or public places, as hypocrites do. By “chamber,” therefore, He means a place secluded from the tumults and sight of the world, where prayer may be offered more quietly and purely: namely, such places as the secluded spaces of monastic solitudes. There we are commanded to shut the door—that is, to block every entrance, lest the purity of prayer be hindered by some occurrence and our eye plunder our unhappy soul.

We still suffer grievously from many despisers of this habit of ours, who, when they celebrate the divine offices with their cloisters or choirs thrown open, shamelessly expose themselves to the public gaze of women and men alike; and especially at the solemn festivals, when they pollute themselves with costly ornaments, like the worldly people to whom they display themselves. In their judgment, a feast is more celebrated in proportion as it is richer in outward finery and more abundant in banquets. It is more honourable to be silent about their most wretched blindness, so utterly opposed to the religious life of Christ’s poor, in proportion as it is shameful to speak of it. Completely Judaizing, they follow custom as their rule and have made God’s commandment void by their traditions, considering not what ought to be done but what is customary.

Yet, as blessed Augustine also recalls [Note: Col. 0203D, Book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, ch. 3; Distinction 8, chapter *Qui contempta*], the Lord said: “I am the truth” (John 14:16), not, “I am custom.” Let whoever wishes commend himself to the prayers of those whose door is open. But you, brought by the heavenly King Himself into His chamber and resting in His embraces, always with the door shut and wholly devoted to Him—inasmuch as you cling to Him more familiarly, according to the Apostle’s saying, “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17)—we trust have a purer and more effective prayer. For this reason we urgently request their aid, believing that you will offer them for me with all the greater devotion because we are bound together by greater mutual love.

That you were disturbed by my mention of the danger in which I labour, or of the death I fear, was also done in accordance with your own exhortation—indeed, your adjuration. For your first letter to me contains this passage: “Therefore, by Christ Himself, who still in some way protects you for Himself, we beseech you that you may deign to inform His and your handmaidens by frequent letters about the shipwrecks in which you still toss, so that you may have us at least, who alone remain to you, as companions in sorrow or joy. For those who share another’s sorrow usually bring some consolation to one who suffers; and any burden laid upon several is borne or carried more lightly.”

Why, then, do you reproach me for making you sharers in my anxiety, when by adjuring me you compelled me to do so? Is it fitting that you should rejoice in so great a despair of the life by which I am tormented? Do you wish to be companions only in joy, not in sorrow—neither to weep with those who weep nor to rejoice with those who rejoice? There is no greater difference between true and false friends than that true friends join themselves to adversity, false ones to prosperity. Cease, I beg you, from these words and restrain complaints of this sort, which are far removed from the inwardness of love.

Or if you are still offended by these things, nevertheless, since I stand at so critical a point of danger and in daily despair of life, it is fitting that I should be concerned for the salvation of my soul and provide for it while I can. If you truly love me, you will not hate this provision. Indeed, if you had any hope of divine mercy toward me, you would desire all the more that I be freed from the miseries of this life, in proportion as you see them to be more intolerable. For you know certainly that whoever frees me from this life will rescue me from the greatest punishments. What I may incur afterwards is uncertain; but there is no doubt from how great evils I shall be released.

Every miserable life has a pleasant ending, and all who truly sympathize and grieve with the anxieties of others desire them to end. Even at their own loss, if they truly love those whom they see distressed, they attend not so much to their own advantage as to that of the afflicted persons. Thus a mother desires even that death may end the protracted illness of a son, which she herself cannot bear; and she accepts being deprived of him rather than having him as a companion in misery. And whoever is greatly delighted by a friend’s presence nevertheless prefers that friend’s absence be happy rather than his presence miserable, because he cannot bear miseries which he is unable to relieve.

But you are not permitted to enjoy even my miserable presence. Nor do I see why, when you have no opportunity to provide anything for your own advantage in me, you should prefer that I live most miserably rather than die more happily. If you desire our miseries to be prolonged for your own advantage, you prove yourself an enemy rather than a friend. Since you shrink from appearing so, I beg you, as I have said, cease from these complaints.

I approve your rejection of praise, for in that very thing you show yourself more praiseworthy. For it is written: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17), and: “He who humbles himself exalts himself” (Luke 18:14). Would that it may be so in your mind as it is in your writing! If it is, your humility is true, lest it vanish because of our words. But take care, I beg you, lest in that very way you seek the praise which you seem to flee, and reject with your mouth what you desire in your heart.

Of this blessed Jerome writes, among other things, to the virgin Eustochium (Letter 22): “We are led by a natural evil. We gladly favour our flatterers; and although we answer that we are unworthy, and a more cunning blush spreads over our faces, nevertheless the soul rejoices inwardly at its own praise.” Virgil describes the same cunning wantonness in Galatea: she sought by fleeing what she wanted, and through the pretence of refusal more strongly incited her lover toward herself:

> “And she flees to the willows,” he says, “and wishes first to be seen.”
>
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* III.21.)

Before she hides, she wishes to be seen fleeing, so that the very flight by which she seems to reject the young man’s company may obtain it more fully. So too, while we seem to flee human praise, we stir it up more strongly toward ourselves; and when we pretend to wish to remain hidden, so that no one may recognize what to praise in us, we unwittingly [variant: “shamelessly”] give more attention [variant: “inflame more strongly”] to our own praise, because we seem more worthy of praise for that reason.

We say this because such things often happen, not because we suspect such things of you, concerning whose humility we do not hesitate. But we also wish you to refrain from such words, lest to those who know you less well you seem, as Jerome says (Letter 22), to seek glory by fleeing from it. My praise will never puff you up; rather, it will urge you toward better things, and you will embrace more diligently whatever I praise, in proportion as you strive more to please me. Our praise is not testimony to your religious devotion, from which you might take any ground for pride. Nor should one believe friends because of anyone’s commendation, any more than enemies because of their disparagement.

At last it remains for us to come to that ancient and, as we have said, constant complaint of yours: namely, that concerning the manner of our conversion you presume rather to accuse God than, as is right, to glorify him. I had long believed that this bitterness of your mind [Col. 0205A] had vanished through the manifest counsel of divine mercy. The more dangerous it is for you, crushing body and soul alike, the more pitiable it is and the more grievous to me. Since, as you profess, you strive in every respect to please me, lay it aside at least in this one matter, so that you may not torment me—indeed, so that you may please me above all. With it you cannot please me, nor can you attain blessedness with me. Will you endure that I should go there without you—you who profess that you wish to follow me even to Vulcan’s realm? Seek religion at least for this one reason: lest you be separated from me as I hasten, as you believe, to God. And do so all the more gladly because the place to which we must come is happier, so that our fellowship may be more pleasing in proportion as it is more blessed.

Remember what you said. Recall [Col. 0205B] what you wrote: that in this manner of our conversion, in which God is thought to have been more opposed to me, he has, as is plain, proved more favorable to me. Let this disposition of his please you at least in this one respect: that it is most salutary for me—indeed, for you as well, if you will admit the reason for your grief. Do not grieve that you were the cause of so great a good, for you should not doubt that you were created by God chiefly for this. And do not lament that I suffered this, unless the benefits of the martyrs’ sufferings and of the Lord’s own death will also make you sad. Would you bear it more tolerably, and would it offend you less, if it had happened to me justly? Certainly, if it had happened thus, it would have occurred in a way more shameful to me and more creditable to my enemies: justice would have won praise for them, and guilt contempt for me. Nor then [Col. 0205C] would anyone blame what was done, moved by compassion for me.

Yet, that we may soften the bitterness of this pain even in this way, we shall show that this happened to us both justly and beneficially, and that God more rightly took vengeance upon those joined in marriage than upon fornicators. You know that after the making of our marriage compact, when you were living at Argenteuil among the nuns in the cloister, I once came privately to visit you; and you know what the intemperance of my lust did there with you, even in a part of the refectory itself, since we had nowhere else to withdraw. You know, I say, that this was then done most shamelessly in a place so reverend and consecrated to the supreme Virgin. Even if all other crimes were absent, this alone would deserve a far heavier punishment. Why should I recount the former [Col. 0205D] acts of fornication and most shameless defilements which preceded the marriage? Why, finally, should I recount my supreme betrayal, by which I so shamefully seduced your own uncle away from you, with whom I was constantly a guest in his house? Who would not judge that I was justly betrayed by him whom I myself had so shamelessly betrayed before? Do you think that the momentary pain of that wound suffices as vengeance for crimes so great? Or rather, that so great a benefit is owed for evils so great? What wound do you think sufficient for divine justice in response to so great a defilement, as we have said, of the most sacred place of his mother?

Certainly, unless I am greatly mistaken, not so much that most salutary wound was turned into punishment for these things as are the sufferings which I endure daily without ceasing [Col. 0206A]. You also know that when I sent you, pregnant, into my native country, you put on the sacred habit and pretended to be a nun; and by such a pretense you irreverently mocked the religion which you now possess. Consider, then, how fittingly divine justice—or rather grace—drew you unwillingly to this religion, at which you did not fear to mock: so that in the very habit you might pay the penalty for sinning against it; so that the truth of the thing itself might provide a remedy for the falsehood of the pretense and correct it. But if you wish to join our benefit to divine justice in our case, you may call what God then did for us not so much justice as grace.

Consider therefore, consider, dearest one, by what nets of his mercy the Lord [Col. 0206B] fished us out from the depth of this most perilous sea, and from what a Charybdis-like gulf he drew us out, shipwrecked though unwillingly, so that each of us may rightly seem able to burst forth [variant: “break forth”] into that cry: “The Lord is concerned for me” (Ps. 39:18). Think and think again in how many dangers we stood, and from how many the Lord delivered us. Always recount, with the fullest thanksgiving, the great things the Lord has done for our soul (Ps. 65); and comfort by our example all wicked persons who despair of the Lord’s goodness, so that all may observe what happens to those who entreat and ask, when benefits so great are bestowed upon sinners [variant: “now sinners”] and unwilling persons.

Ponder the most profound counsel of divine mercy in us: how mercifully the Lord turned his judgment into correction [Col. 0206C], how wisely he used even evils themselves, and how devoutly he put away impiety, so that the most just wound to one part of my body might heal two souls. Compare the danger with the manner of deliverance; compare the sickness with the medicine. Examine the causes of our deserts, and marvel at the disposition of mercy. You know to how many shameful acts my unrestrained lust had enslaved our bodies, so that no reverence for decency or for God, not even on the days of the Lord’s Passion or of any solemn feasts, could call me back from the rolling mire of this filth. And although you were unwilling and resisted and dissuaded as best you could, being by nature the weaker, I often dragged you into consent by threats and blows. For I was joined to you by such ardor of desire [Col. 0206D] that I preferred those wretched and obscene pleasures—which we blush even to name—to God and to myself; nor did divine mercy seem able to provide otherwise, except by altogether denying [variant: “cutting off”] me these pleasures without any hope.

Thus, most justly and mercifully, although through the utter betrayal by your uncle, I was diminished in that part of my body in which the dominion of lust was situated and in which the entire cause of this desire consisted, so that the member which had committed everything in us might justly be punished; that by suffering it might expiate what it had sinned by delighting; that it might circumcise me, in mind and body alike, from those impurities in which I had immersed myself wholly as in mud; and [Col. 0207A] that it might make me more fit even for sacred altars, in proportion as no contagion of carnal defilement could thereafter draw me back. How mercifully, too, he willed that I should suffer only in that member, whose loss would provide for the soul’s salvation without disfiguring the body or hindering [variant: “impeding”] any ministry of offices. Indeed, it made me readier for all honorable duties in proportion as it freed me further from this greatest yoke of desire.

Therefore, when divine grace cleansed me rather than deprived me of these most worthless members, which are called “shameful parts” because they serve the exercise of extreme shamefulness and do not even bear their proper name, what else did it do but remove filth [Col. 0207B] and vices in order to preserve the purity of cleanness? We have heard that some philosophers, vehemently desiring this purity of cleanness, even laid hands upon themselves in order wholly to remove from themselves this disgrace of desire. For the removal of this “thorn in the flesh” the Apostle too is said to have begged the Lord, and not to have been heard (1 Cor. 12:7).

An example is that great Christian philosopher Origen (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VI.7), who, in order wholly to extinguish this flame within himself, did not shrink from laying hands upon himself. It was as though he understood literally that those are truly blessed who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven (Matt. 19:12); as though he believed that such persons truly fulfilled what the Lord commands concerning members that cause us to stumble—namely, that we cut them off from ourselves [Col. 0207C] and cast them away (Matt. 18:9); and as though he took Isaiah’s prophecy more historically than mystically, by which the Lord prefers eunuchs to other faithful persons, saying:

> “If eunuchs keep my Sabbaths and choose what I have willed, I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name which shall not perish” (Isa. 56:4).

Yet Origen incurred no small guilt when he sought a remedy for sin through bodily punishment. For, possessing zeal for God but not according to knowledge, he incurred the guilt of homicide by laying hands upon himself. It is certain that what he did by diabolical suggestion or by the gravest error was done to me by another through the mercy [Col. 0207D] of God. I avoid guilt; I do not incur it. I deserve death and obtain life. I am called, and I resist. I press on in crimes, and am drawn unwillingly to pardon. The Apostle prays and is not heard (1 Cor. 12:8); he persists in prayers and does not obtain. Truly, “the Lord is concerned for me” (Ps. 39:18). I will therefore go and recount the great things the Lord has done for my soul (Ps. 65:16).

Come too, inseparable companion, in a single act of thanksgiving—you who have become a partner both in guilt and in grace. For the Lord has not forgotten your salvation; indeed, he has been greatly mindful of you, since by a certain holy omen in your name he foretold especially that you would be his own when he marked you with the name Heloise, from his own name, which is *Heloim* [Hebrew: “God”]. He himself, I say, mercifully arranged to provide in one event [Col. 0208A] for two persons whom the devil strove in one event to destroy. For a little before this happened, he had bound us to one another by the indissoluble law of the sacrament of marriage, because I wished to retain you, whom I loved beyond measure, forever—or rather because he himself was already planning by this occasion to convert us both to himself.

For if you had not first been joined to me in marriage, you might easily, when I withdrew from the world, have clung to the world either through the promptings of relatives or through the carnal delights of pleasures. See, therefore, how concerned the Lord was for us, as though he were reserving us for some great uses, and as though he were angered or grieved that the talents of literary learning entrusted to us both were not being administered for the honor of his name; or as though he feared even in his most incontinent [Col. 0208B] servant what is written: “For women cause even the wise to apostatize” (Ecclus. 19:2), as is certain in the case of Solomon, the wisest of men (3 Kings 11:1).

But how great a return your talent of wisdom daily brings to the Lord! You have already borne many spiritual daughters for the Lord, while I remain wholly barren and labor vainly among children of perdition. O how detestable a loss! How lamentable an evil, if, occupied with the filth of carnal pleasures, you bore a few children for the world in pain—you who now bring forth a manifold offspring for heaven in exultation! You would have been no more than a woman, whereas now you surpass even men; you have turned Eve’s curse into Mary’s blessing. O how unseemly it would have been for those sacred hands, which now even turn over divine [Col. 0208C] volumes, to serve the indecencies of womanly care!

He deigned to raise [variant: “rescue”] us from the contagions of this mire and the delights of this mud, and to draw us to himself by a certain force—the force by which he willed to convert Paul when struck down—and perhaps by this very example of ours to deter other learned people from such presumption. Therefore, sister, I beg you, do not let this disturb you, and do not be troublesome to our Father as he corrects us fatherly. Rather heed what is written: “Those whom God loves, he corrects” (Prov. 3:12); and, “He chastises [variant: ‘scourges’] every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). And elsewhere: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Prov. 13:24). This punishment is momentary, not eternal; it is for cleansing, not [Col. 0208D] condemnation. Hear the prophet and be strengthened: “The Lord will not judge the same thing twice, and a double tribulation shall not arise” (Num. 1:9). Consider that supreme and greatest exhortation of Truth: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). Hence Solomon also says: “The patient man is better than the strong man, and he who rules his own spirit than the conqueror of cities” (Prov. 16:32).

Does not the only-begotten Son of God, innocent, seized for you and for all by utterly wicked men, torn apart, scourged, mocked with his face veiled, struck with fists, covered with spittle, crowned with thorns, and finally suspended between thieves upon that cross—then so shameful an instrument—and put to death by that then horrible and accursed kind of death [Col. 0209A], move you to tears or compunction? Sister, always keep before your eyes and bear in your mind this true bridegroom of yours and of the whole Church. Look upon him going out to be crucified for you and carrying his cross for himself. Be among the people and women who wept and lamented him, as Luke recounts in these words: “And a great multitude of people and women followed him, who wept and lamented him” (Luke 23:27).

Turning kindly toward them, he mercifully foretold the destruction that would come in vengeance for his death, a destruction from which, if they were wise, they could thereby protect themselves:

> “Daughters of Jerusalem,” he said, “do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children. For behold, days are coming in which they will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts [Col. 0209B] that have not nursed.’ Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’ For if they do these things in the green wood, what shall be done in the dry?” (ibid., 28)

Suffer compassionately with him who willingly suffers for your redemption, and feel compunction over him crucified for you. Be always present in mind at his tomb, and lament and mourn with the faithful women. Of them, as I have already mentioned above, it is written: “The women sitting by the tomb lamented, weeping for the Lord” (Luke 23:27). Prepare with them ointments for his burial—but better ones, spiritual rather than bodily. For he who did not receive those bodily spices asks for these. Over these feel compunction with your whole devotion. He himself, through Jeremiah, exhorts the faithful to this compunction of compassion, saying:

> “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Jer. 1:12).

That is: whether anyone who suffers ought to be grieved over through compassion as I ought, since I alone without guilt pay the penalty for what others have sinned. He himself is the way by which the faithful pass from exile to their homeland. He also raised for us, for this purpose, the cross concerning which he so cries out as a ladder. Here the only-begotten Son of God was slain for you; he was offered because he willed it (Isa. 53:7). Grieve by compassion over this one thing; by grieving, suffer compassionately. Fulfil what was foretold through the prophet Zechariah concerning devout souls:

> “They shall mourn for him as for an only-begotten son, and shall grieve over him as one is accustomed to grieve [Col. 0209D] at the death of a firstborn” (Zech. 12:10).

See, sister, how great must be the mourning of those who love the king over the death of his firstborn and only-begotten son. Consider with what mourning the household, with what grief the entire court is consumed; and when you come to the bride of the only-begotten who has died, you will not be able to endure her intolerable wailings. This, sister, must be your mourning; this your wailing—you who have been joined to this bridegroom in a blessed marriage. He purchased you, not with things belonging to himself, but with himself. He purchased and redeemed you with his own blood. See how great a right he has over you, and consider how precious you are.

The Apostle, considering this price of his, considering in this price how great is the one for whom it is given, and adding what return he makes for such great grace, says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord [Col. 0210A] Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). You are greater than heaven, greater than the world, for your price was the very Creator of the world. What, I ask, did he see in you—he who lacks nothing—that he should contend for acquiring you even unto the agonies of a death so horrible and shameful? What, I say, does he seek in you except yourself? A true friend desires yourself, not your possessions. A true friend, who was to die for you, said: “No one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

He loved you truly; I did not. My love, which involved us both in sins, should be called desire, not love. I fulfilled my wretched pleasures in you, and this was all that I loved. [Col. 0210B] “I suffered for you,” you say, and perhaps that is true; but more through you, and that against my will. It was not from love of you, but under compulsion of myself; not for your salvation, but for pain. He, however, suffered beneficially and freely for you—he who by his Passion heals every sickness and removes every suffering.

I beg you: let all your devotion, all your compassion, all your compunction be directed to this, not to me. Grieve over the injustice of such great cruelty committed against one so innocent; do not grieve over the just vengeance of equity upon me—indeed, as has been said, the greatest grace granted to us both. For you are unjust if you do not love justice; and most unjust if knowingly you oppose the will—indeed, the grace so great—of God. Weep for your restorer, not your corrupter; your redeemer, not your seducer; the Lord who died for you, [Col. 0210C] not the servant who lives, or rather who has only now truly been freed from death.

Take care, I beg you, lest what Pompey said to the mourning Cornelia be most shamefully reproached to you:

> Great Pompey lives after the battles;  
> But fortune has perished: what you weep for is what you loved.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, VIII.84–85)

Consider this, I pray, and blush, unless you approve the most shameless acts you committed. Therefore, sister, receive—receive, I beg you—patiently what mercifully happened to us. This is a father’s rod, not a persecutor’s sword. A father strikes in order to correct; an enemy strikes [variant: “strikes”] in order to kill. By a wound he forestalls death, rather than inflicts it; he applies the knife in order [Col. 0210D] to cut away disease. He wounds the body and heals the soul. He ought to have killed, yet gives life. He cuts away uncleanness in order to leave what is clean. He punishes once so that he may not punish always; one suffers from the wound so that two may be spared death. Two were involved in guilt; one in punishment.

This too is granted to the weakness of your nature by divine mercy, and in a certain way justly. For in proportion as you were naturally weaker in sex and stronger in continence, you were less liable to punishment. I give thanks to the Lord for this: he then both freed you from punishment and reserved you for a crown. And whereas by one bodily suffering he once cooled me from all the heat of this desire, in which I was wholly occupied through excessive incontinence, so that I might not fall, he reserved for you many greater sufferings of the mind during your youth, arising from the constant [Col. 0211A] prompting of the flesh, for the crown of martyrdom.

Although it may weary you to hear this and you may forbid it to be said, the manifest truth speaks it. For wherever there is always a battle, there also remains a crown; because no one will be crowned unless he has contended lawfully (1 Tim. 2:5). But for me no crown remains, because no cause for contest remains. The material for battle is lacking to one from whom the spur of desire has been taken away. Yet I consider it something if, though I receive no crown from this, I nevertheless avoid some punishment, and if perhaps many eternal punishments are remitted through the pain of one momentary punishment. For it is written concerning the men—indeed, the beasts—of this most wretched life: “The beasts rotted in their dung” (Job 1:17). I do not complain that my merit is lessened, while I do not doubt that yours [Col. 0211B] increases.

For we are one in Christ, one flesh through the law of marriage. Whatever is yours, I do not regard as foreign to me. But Christ is yours, because you have become his bride. And now, as I mentioned above, you have me as a servant, whom you once recognized as master; yet I am now joined to you more by spiritual love than subjected by fear. Thus we have greater confidence in your advocacy for us before him, that through you I may obtain what I cannot obtain through my own prayer—especially now, when the daily pressure of dangers or disturbances permits me neither to live nor to devote myself to prayer.

Nor am I able to imitate that most blessed powerful official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasures and had come from so [Col. 0211C] far away to worship in Jerusalem (Acts 8:29). As he was returning, Philip the Apostle was sent by an angel to convert him to the faith; and he had already merited this through prayer or assiduous sacred reading. So that, though rich and a Gentile, he might not be idle from this even on the road, it was accomplished by the great benefit of divine providence that a passage of Scripture came before him which gave the Apostle a most fitting occasion for his conversion.

And so that nothing may impede or delay the fulfillment of this petition of ours, I have hastened to compose and send you the prayer itself which you are to say as suppliants to the Lord for us.
