God, who from the very beginning of human creation formed woman from the rib of man and established the great sacrament of the marriage bond; who with immeasurable honors exalted marriage both by being born of one betrothed and by beginning miracles at a wedding; and who, as it once pleased you, granted this remedy even to the incontinence of my weakness: do not despise the prayers of your little handmaid, which I pour forth as a suppliant before the presence of your majesty for the transgressions of myself and of my beloved [variant: “as my own”]. Forgive, O most gracious one—indeed, graciousness itself; forgive our sins, however great, and let the immensity of our offenses [Col. 0212B] experience the multitude of your ineffable mercy. I beg you, punish the guilty in the present, so that you may spare them in the future. Punish for an hour, lest you punish eternally. Receive the rod of correction against your servants, not the sword of wrath. Afflict the flesh so that you may preserve the souls. Be present as purifier, not avenger; more kind than just; a merciful Father, not a harsh Lord.

Test us, Lord, and try us, as the Prophet asks concerning himself (Ps. 25:2)—as though he openly said: First examine our strength, and then moderate the burdens of temptations according to it. Blessed Paul too promises this to your faithful, saying: “For God is able, and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also make a way out [Col. 0212C] so that you may be able to endure” (1 Cor. 10:13). You joined us, Lord, and divided us when it pleased you and in the manner it pleased you. Now [variant: “This which”], Lord, what you have mercifully begun, most mercifully complete. Join eternally to yourself in heaven those whom you once divided from one another in the world. Our hope, our portion, our expectation, our consolation, Lord, who are blessed for ever. Amen.

Farewell in Christ, bride of Christ; farewell in Christ, and live for Christ. Amen.

## LETTER VI. Heloise’s Letter to the Same Peter

[Col. 0211]

[Col. 0211C] **Summary.**—In this letter Heloise chiefly asks Abelard to write two things for herself and her nuns. The first is that he teach them from where the order of nuns took its beginning. The second is that he write them some rule and prescribe a definite pattern of life suitable to women alone—something no holy Father had previously attempted. She appears to have been led to make this request by certain chapters of the Benedictine Rule, which women can scarcely, or not at all, fulfill without the greatest danger. She discusses them so learnedly that she seems to prove that the holy founder wrote the Rule for men alone, not women. Therefore she judges it improper that burdens so heavy should be laid upon the weaker female sex as upon the stronger male sex.

She also offers her own opinion as to why the holy Fathers did not prescribe rules for nuns, maintaining that it is enough for women not to be inferior in continence and abstinence to clerics and secular churchmen, or to monks called regular canons. She also discusses at length the moderate dispensation and prudent consideration by which blessed Benedict tempered his Rule, as well as the observance of the Rule itself—especially the prohibition of meat and the permitted use of wine. She treats more fully of external works, diminishing their importance and preferring inward ones. Finally, she urges Abelard to order everything concerning fasts and divine observance with such discretion that he may wish to provide for the weakness of the female sex. Here you may observe a woman’s learning and a mind filled with every kind of doctrine. For what precious commodity could you fail to find in so rich a storehouse, whether you seek philosophy, theology, or even eloquence? O happy age, which beheld such a woman, in whom you would hesitate what to admire first and what last!

[Col. 0213A] To him who is specially her lord, from her who is uniquely his.

Lest you perhaps be able to accuse me of disobedience in anything, even the immoderate grief expressed in my words has had a bridle imposed upon it by your command, so that at least in writing I may restrain myself from those things against which it is not merely difficult but impossible to guard in speech. For nothing is less within our power than the mind, and we are compelled more to obey it than able to command it. Thus, when its affections spur us on, no one can so repel their sudden impulses that they do not easily break forth into effects and pour themselves out more easily through words, which are the readier signs of the soul’s passions. As it is written: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12:34).

I shall therefore withdraw my hand from writing those things in which I cannot restrain my tongue from speaking [Col. 0213B]. Would that the grieving mind were as ready to obey as the writing right hand. Yet you can provide some remedy for grief, even if you cannot remove it altogether. For as one nail drives out another which has been inserted, so a new thought excludes the former one. When the mind is occupied with another matter, it is compelled to let go of or suspend its memory of prior things. And the more honorable the matter thought about is judged to be, and the more necessary that to which we direct the mind appears, the more every thought occupies the mind and draws it away from other things.

Therefore all of us, handmaids of Christ and your daughters in Christ, now humbly ask two things from your fatherhood, which we see to be very necessary for us. The first is that [Col. 0213C] you would instruct us concerning the origin of the order of nuns and the authority of our profession. The second is that you establish and send us some written rule, one proper to women, fully describing the state and habit of our manner of life [variant: “conversion and profession”]. We have seen that this has not yet been done by the holy Fathers.

Because of the lack and need for such a rule, men and women are now received in monasteries to the profession of the same Rule, and the same yoke of monastic institution is laid upon the weak sex just as upon the strong. Among the Latins women now profess the one Rule of blessed Benedict just as men do. Yet it is evident that it was written for men alone, and that it can be fulfilled only by them, subjects and superiors alike. To pass over the other chapters of the Rule, what relevance for women has what is written there concerning cowls, drawers, and scapulars (ch. 55)? What relevance has it for them to prescribe tunics or woolen garments worn next to the flesh, when their monthly purgations of superfluous moisture wholly reject such things? What relevance for them has the ordinance concerning the abbot (ch. 11), that he himself read the Gospel lesson and begin the hymn after it? What relevance [Col. 0214A] has the provision (ch. 56) that the abbot’s table be set apart with pilgrims and guests?

Does it suit our religious life either never to offer hospitality to men, or for an abbess to eat with men whom she has received? O how easily the cohabitation of men and women leads to the ruin of souls! Especially at table, where gluttony and drunkenness rule, and wine is drunk sweetly, “in which is debauchery.” Blessed Jerome, guarding against this very thing, recalled it in writing to a mother and daughter (Ep. 47): “Chastity is difficult to preserve amid feasts.” The poet too, a teacher of lust and shamefulness, in the book entitled *The Art of Love*, carefully sets forth how greatly banquets especially provide an occasion for fornication, saying:

[Col. 0214B]

> And when wines have sprinkled Cupid’s thirsty wings,  
> he remains, and stands heavily in the place where he began . . .  
>
> Then laughter comes; then the poor man grows horns;  
> then grief and cares, and the wrinkle of the brow, depart . . .  
>
> There girls have often carried off the minds of young men.

And Venus rages in the veins, fire in fire. (OVID, *The Art of Love*, book I, 233.)

But even if they admit to table women alone who have been received as guests, does no danger lie hidden there? Certainly, nothing is so effective in seducing a woman as feminine pandering. Nor does a woman so readily entrust the shamefulness of a corrupted mind to anyone as to another woman. Hence the aforesaid Jerome (*Epistles* 13 and 22) especially urges women of holy purpose to avoid the company of worldly women.

Finally, if, excluding men from our hospitality, we admit women alone [Col. 0214C], who does not see how greatly we offend men, upon whose benefactions monasteries of the weaker sex depend—especially if those from whom they receive more appear to bestow little or nothing in return? But if the tenor of the aforesaid Rule cannot be fulfilled by us, I fear that the saying of the Apostle James may also be spoken to our condemnation: “Whoever keeps the whole law, but stumbles in one point, has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2:10). That is to say: a person is judged guilty precisely in this respect—that, though he performs many things, he does not fulfil all things. And he becomes a transgressor of the law through one point, unless he has fulfilled all its commands in their entirety.

The Apostle himself immediately and carefully explains this, adding: [Col. 0214D] “For he who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill.’ But if you do not commit adultery, yet kill, you have become a transgressor of the law” (ibid., 11). It is as though he said openly: Therefore anyone becomes guilty through the transgression of any one commandment, because the Lord himself, who commands one thing, commands the other also. And whichever commandment of the law is violated, he himself is despised—the one who established the law not in one commandment but jointly in all its commands.

But, to pass over the provisions of that Rule which we cannot observe at all, or cannot observe [Col. 0215A] without danger: when has a community of nuns ever been accustomed to go out to gather harvests, or to undertake agricultural labours? Or when has it tested the steadfastness of women seeking admission for one year, and in the third year instructed them, after the Rule has been read aloud, as the Rule itself commands (chap. 48)? Again, what is more foolish than to undertake a road unknown and not yet shown? What is more presumptuous than to choose and profess a life which you do not know, or to make a vow which you cannot fulfil?

But since discernment is the mother of all virtues, and reason is the mediator [variant: *moderatrix*, “governess”] of all goods, who would judge to be either virtue or good that which seems to depart from these? For virtues themselves, when they exceed due measure and proportion, ought, as Jerome declares (*Epistle* 8), to be reckoned among vices. And who does not see that it is wholly divorced from [Col. 0215B] reason and discernment if, before burdens are imposed, the capacities of those upon whom they are imposed are not first examined, so that human effort may follow the constitution of nature? Who [perhaps “loads,” or something similar, is missing] an ass with a burden so great as he judges fitting for an elephant? Who imposes upon boys or old men burdens as great as those imposed upon men? Upon the weak, that is, as great as upon the strong; upon the infirm, as great as upon the healthy; upon women, as great as upon males? Upon the weaker sex, plainly, as great burdens as upon the strong?

Pope Gregory the Blessed, carefully observing this point, thus distinguished in chapter 14 of his *Pastoral Rule* [part III, admonition 1] between persons to be admonished and persons to be commanded: “Men, therefore, are to be admonished in one way, women in another; for heavier things are to be imposed upon the former, lighter upon the latter: let great things exercise the one, while gentle things win over the other by soothing them.”

Certainly those who wrote rules for monks did not merely remain altogether silent concerning women; rather, by establishing things which they knew could in no way suit them, they sufficiently and fittingly indicated that the necks of bulls and heifers ought not to be pressed under the same yoke of rule, because those whom nature has made unlike ought not to be made equal in labour. Yet Benedict the Blessed, not forgetful of this discernment [Col. 0215C], and as if filled with the spirit of all the righteous, so regulates everything in his Rule according to the condition of persons and times (chap. 2), that all things, as he himself concludes in one place, may be done with measure.

Beginning therefore with the abbot himself, he commands (chap. 64) that he preside over those subject to him in such a way that, according to the character or understanding of each one, he conforms and adapts himself to all; so that he may not only suffer no loss in the flock entrusted to him, but rejoice in the increase of the good flock. He must always suspect his own frailty, and remember that the bruised reed is not to be broken (Isa. 42:3). Let him also distinguish the times, reflecting on the discernment of holy Jacob, who says: “If I make my flocks labour too much in travelling, they will all die in one day” (Gen. 33:13).

Taking, therefore, these and other testimonies of discernment, the mother of virtues (chaps. 37, 38, 39), he so tempers everything that the strong may have what they desire, and the weak may not flee away. To this moderation [Col. 0216A] of administration belongs indulgence toward boys, old men, and all who are weak; the giving of a meal before the others to the reader or the weekly servers; and, even within the community itself, provision concerning the quality or quantity of food and drink according to the differences among persons. Concerning each of these matters, moreover, it is written there with care (chap. 41). He likewise relaxes the appointed times of fasting according to the character of the season or the amount of labour, as the infirmity of nature requires.

What, I ask, would this man—who so regulates everything according to the condition of persons and times, that the things instituted may be borne [variant: *profiteri*, “professed”] by all without murmuring—what, I say, would he have provided for women, had he also established a Rule for them equally with men? For if in certain matters he is compelled to soften [Col. 0216B] the strictness of the Rule for boys, old men, and the weak because of nature’s very weakness or infirmity, what would he have provided for the fragile sex, whose nature is known to be especially weak and infirm?

Consider, then, how far it is from every rational discernment that women and men should be bound by profession of the same Rule, and that the weak and the strong should be laden with the same burden. I think it enough for our weakness, and something that should be counted very great, if the virtue of our continence and abstinence equals that of the rulers of the Church themselves and of clerics established in sacred orders. Especially since Truth says: “Everyone will be perfect if he is like his teacher” (Luke 6:40). For them too, it would be a great thing if we could equal religious laypeople. For what we regard as small in the strong we admire in the weak. And according to the Apostle’s saying: “Power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

Lest the religious life of laypeople be held cheap, Chrysostom meets us in his seventh homily on the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying of the kind of religious life found in Abraham, David, and Job [variant: Jacob], though married men (chap. 4): [Col. 0216C] “There are many things in which he may labour in order to charm that beast. What are they? Labours, readings, vigils. But what have these to do with us, you say, who are not monks? Do you tell me this? Tell Paul, when he says: ‘Watchful in all patience and prayer’ [cf. Rom. 13:14]; when he says: ‘Make no provision for the flesh in its desires.’ For he was not writing these things only to monks, but to all who were in cities. A secular person ought not to have anything more than a monk except intercourse with his wife alone. In this he has pardon, but in all other matters not at all; rather, he ought to do everything equally with monks. For even the beatitudes spoken by Christ (Matt. 5:3) were not spoken only to monks. Otherwise the whole world will perish, and he has confined the things of virtue to a narrow space. And how can marriage be honourable, if it merely hinders us?”

From these words it is plainly gathered that whoever adds the virtue of continence to evangelical precepts will fulfil monastic perfection. And would that our religious life could rise to this: to fulfil the Gospel, not to exceed it, lest we seek to be more than [Col. 0217A] Christian.

For this reason, I believe, the holy Fathers decreed not to lay upon us, as upon men, some general Rule as though it were a new law, nor to burden our weakness with the magnitude of vows, observing the Apostle’s saying: “For the law produces wrath; for where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). And again: “But the law entered in, so that sin might abound” (Rom. 5:20).

The same supreme preacher of continence, having great confidence in our weakness and, as it were, urging younger widows to second marriages, says: “I wish younger women to marry, bear children, be mistresses of households, and give no occasion to the adversary” (1 Tim. 5:14). Recognizing this to be most salutary, Jerome counsels Eustochium concerning women’s rash vows in these words (*Epistle* 22): “But if even those who are virgins are not freed on account of other faults, what will become of those who have prostituted the members of Christ and changed the temple of the Holy Spirit into a brothel? It would have been better for a person to enter marriage, to walk upon level ground, than, aiming at higher things, to fall into the depths of hell.”

Augustine also, advising against their rash profession, writes to Julian in his book *On Widowed Continence* (chap. 9): [Col. 0217B] “Let her who has not begun deliberate; let her who has undertaken it persevere. Let no opportunity be given to the adversary; let no offering be withdrawn from Christ.”

For this reason too, the canons, providing for our weakness, decreed that deaconesses ought not to be ordained before the age of forty, and this only after careful testing, whereas deacons may be promoted from the age of twenty. There are also in monasteries those called regular canons of blessed Augustine, professing, as they say, a certain rule; and they do not consider themselves in any respect inferior to monks, though we see them both eat meat and wear linen. If our weakness could equal [variant: *adaequare*, “make equal to”] their virtue, would it be considered a small thing?

Moreover, for a safer and gentler concession concerning all foods, nature itself has provided, furnishing our sex with a greater virtue of sobriety. For it is established that women can be sustained by much more sparing expenditure and less nourishment than men, and physical science declares that they are not so readily made drunk. Hence Macrobius Theodosius, in book VII of the *Saturnalia*, records these words (chap. 5): [Col. 0217C] “Aristotle says that women are rarely drunk, old men frequently. A woman’s body is very moist. Its smoothness and brightness of skin demonstrate this. Above all, the regular purgings, which relieve the body of superfluous moisture, demonstrate it. Therefore, when wine drunk falls into so great an abundance of moisture, it loses its force and does not easily strike the seat of the brain, its strength having been extinguished.”

Again (ibid.): “The female body, assigned to frequent purgings, is furnished with many openings, so as to stand open to channels and furnish pathways for moisture flowing toward its outlet in evacuation. Through these openings the vapour of wine quickly evaporates. By contrast, the body of old men is dry, as the roughness and squalor of their skin proves.”

From these considerations, then, reflect how much more safely and justly any food [variant: “any food whatsoever”] and drink may be allowed to our nature and weakness, since our hearts cannot easily be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness: from the former, sparingness in food protects us; from the latter, as has been said, the nature of the female body. [Col. 0218A] It ought to be enough for our weakness, and counted a very great thing, if, living chastely and without private possession, and occupied with divine offices, we equal in food either the leaders of the Church themselves or religious laypeople—or, finally, those called regular canons, who especially profess to follow the apostolic life.

Finally, it is a matter of great prudence for those who bind themselves to God by a vow to vow less and perform more, so that grace may always add something beyond what is owed. For Truth himself says: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done’” (Luke 17:10). It is as though he said openly: We are to be counted unprofitable and, as it were, of no account and without merits, because, content with paying only what we owed, we have added nothing beyond it through grace.

Concerning such gratuitous additions, the Lord himself also speaks elsewhere in a parable: “And whatever you spend besides, when I return I will repay you” (Luke 10:35). If many rash professors of monastic religion in this time considered this more carefully, observed the profession to which they swore, and diligently investigated the tenor of the Rule itself, they would offend less through ignorance and sin less through negligence. But now, almost all alike run indiscriminately toward monastic life [variant: conversion]; having been admitted without order, they live more disorderly still; and with the same ease with which they profess an unknown Rule, they despise it and establish as law whatever customs they wish. [Col. 0218B]

We must therefore take care not to presume to lay upon women a burden under which we see almost all men already succumbing—indeed, failing. We see that the world has grown old, and that human beings themselves, together with the other things of the world, have lost their former vigour of nature; and, according to the saying of Truth, that love has grown cold not merely in many but in almost all (Matt. 24:12). Thus it is necessary, according to the condition of persons, that Rules written for persons themselves either be changed [Col. 0218C] or softened.

Benedict the Blessed himself, not forgetful of this discernment, admits that he so moderated the severity of monastic discipline that he considered the Rule composed by him, in comparison with earlier institutes, to be nothing more than a kind of instruction in decency and a beginning of religious life. He says (final chapter): “We have written this Rule so that, by observing it, we may show that we possess at least some decency of conduct or a beginning of religious life. But for one who hastens to the perfection of religious life, there are the teachings of the holy Fathers, the observance of which brings a person to the heights of perfection.”

Again (ibid.): “Therefore, whoever you are who hasten to the heavenly homeland, fulfil, with Christ’s help, this very small Rule for beginners; and then at last, under God’s protection, you will attain the greater heights of teaching and virtue.”

Although, as he himself says (chap. 18), we read that the holy Fathers formerly used to complete the Psalter in one day, he moderated the psalmody for the lukewarm so that, even in the weekly distribution of psalms, monks were content with a smaller number than clerics [variant: “were”].

What, moreover, is so contrary to religion and monastic quiet as that which above all provides fuel for lust, excites disturbances, and destroys in us the very image of God by which we excel other creatures—that is, reason? This is wine, which Scripture declares more harmful than all things pertaining to food and urges us to avoid. The greatest of sages also speaks of it in Proverbs, saying: [Col. 0219A] “Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness tumultuous. Whoever delights in them will not be wise” (Prov. 20:1). “Who has woe? Whose father has woe? Who has quarrels? Who has pits? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Is it not those who linger over wine and devote themselves to draining cups? Do not look upon wine when it is yellow, when its colour shines in the glass. It enters smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a serpent and pour out poison like a basilisk. Your eyes will see strange women, and your heart will speak perverse things. And you will be like one sleeping in the midst of the sea, and like a drowsy helmsman whose rudder has been lost; and you will say: ‘They struck me, but I did not hurt; they dragged me, and I did not feel it. When shall I awake and find wines again?’” (Prov. 23:29).

Again: “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel, do not give wine to kings, because there is no secret where drunkenness reigns; lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments, and alter the cause of the children of the poor” (Prov. 31:4). And it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Wine and women cause even the wise to apostatize, and rebuke the sensible” (Ecclus. 19:2).

Jerome himself, writing to Nepotian (*Epistle* 2) concerning the life of clerics, and indignantly complaining, as it were, that priests of the Law, who abstained from everything capable of intoxication, surpass our clergy in this abstinence, says: [Col. 0219B] “Let your breath not smell of wine, lest you hear that saying of the philosopher: ‘This is not offering a kiss, but offering wine.’ The Apostle condemns drunken priests (1 Tim. 3:3), and the Old Law forbids them: ‘Those who serve at the altar shall not drink wine or strong drink’ (Lev. 10:9). In the Hebrew language *sicera* is the name for every drink capable of intoxication: whether it is made by fermentation, from the juice of fruits, or from honeycomb boiled down into sweetness; whether the drink of herbs is pressed out, the fruit of palms is expressed into liquid, or a richer water is strained from cooked grains. Flee everything that intoxicates and overturns the state of the mind just as you flee wine.”

Behold: what is prohibited to the pleasures of kings is wholly denied to priests, and is known to be more dangerous than all foods. Yet Benedict the Blessed, so spiritual a man, is compelled by a certain accommodation to allow it to monks in his own age (chap. 40). “Although,” he says, “we read that wine is absolutely not for monks, yet because in our times this cannot be persuaded to monks,” etc.

He had read, I believe, what is written in the *Lives of the Fathers* in these words (part II): “Some told Abbot Pastor of a certain monk that he did not drink wine, and he said to them: ‘Wine is absolutely not for monks.’” Again, after some intervening material: [Col. 0219C] “A celebration of the masses once took place on the mountain of Abbot Antony, and a jar of wine was found there. One of the elders took up a small vessel, carried a cup to Abbot Sisoes, and gave it to him. He drank once, and a second time he took it and drank. He offered it to him a third time, but he did not take it, saying: ‘Stop, brother; do you not know that this is Satan?’”

And again, concerning Abbot Sisoes (ibid.): “Abraham therefore said to his disciples: ‘If one comes to church on Saturday and Sunday and drinks three cups, is that not much?’ And the old man said: ‘If Satan were not present, it would not be much.’”

Where, I ask, have meats ever been condemned by God or forbidden to monks? See, I beg you, and observe by what necessity he softens the Rule even in that matter which is more dangerous for monks and which he knows not to belong to them: namely, because abstinence from it could no longer be persuaded to monks in his day. Would that the same accommodation were exercised in this age too: that, in matters called intermediate between good and evil and indifferent, such moderation might be made that profession would not demand what can no longer be persuaded; and that, when all indifferent things were permitted without scandal, it would suffice to forbid sins alone. [Col. 0220A] Thus also in food, as in clothing, provision should be made so that what could be obtained more cheaply should be supplied, and in all things need rather than superfluity should be considered.

For the things which do not prepare us for the kingdom of God, or do not commend us to God, are not to be greatly valued. Such are all things done outwardly, common equally to the reprobate and the abject, equally to hypocrites and the religious. For nothing so separates Jews from Christians as the distinction between outward acts and inward ones—especially since between children of God and children of the devil love alone distinguishes, which the Apostle calls the fulfilment of the law and the end of the commandment (Rom. 13:10).

Therefore, diminishing this glory of works altogether in order to prefer the righteousness of faith, he addresses Judaea thus: “Where is your boasting? It is excluded. By what law? By the law of works? No, but by the law of faith. We hold that a person is justified by faith without works of the law” (Rom. 3:27). Again: “For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God. For what does Scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:2; Gen. 15:6). And again: “To the one,” he says, “who does not work, but believes in God who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace” (Rom. 4:5).

The same Apostle, allowing Christians the eating of every food and distinguishing it from those things which justify, says: [Col. 0220B] “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 14:17). “All things indeed are clean, but it is evil for the person who eats with offence. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine, nor anything by which your brother is offended, or scandalized, or made weak.”

For in this passage no eating of food is forbidden, but the offence caused by eating—by which certain Jews who had converted were scandalized when they saw even the things eaten which the Law had forbidden. The Apostle Peter, wishing also to avoid this scandal, was sharply rebuked by him and beneficially corrected, as Paul himself recalls in writing to the Galatians (Gal. XIV, 11 [an erroneous reference as printed]). Writing again to the Corinthians: “Food does not commend us to God” (1 Cor. 8:8). And again: “Eat whatever is sold in the market” (1 Cor. 10:25). “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1). And to the Colossians: “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink” (Col. 2:16). And after some intervening material: “If you have died with Christ from the elements of this world, why do you still make decrees as though living in the world? ‘Do not touch, do not taste, do not handle’—all of which perish by their very use, according to human commands and teachings” (ibid., 20).

He calls “the elements of this world” the first rudiments of the Law according to carnal observances, in the teaching of which the world—that is, the people still carnal—was first exercised as though in learning the elements of letters. From these elements, that is, from carnal observances, both Christ’s people and Paul’s own people have died, since they owe nothing to them and no longer live in this world; that is, they do not attend to and establish distinctions among carnal persons concerned with figures, distinguishing certain foods or any things from others and thus saying: [Col. 0220C] “Do not touch these or those things” (ibid., 21).

Those things touched, tasted, or handled, the Apostle says, perish to the soul by their very use—by which we use them even for a certain humiliation [variants: *vilitatem*, “lowliness,” and in another manuscript *utilitatem*, “usefulness”]—according, I say, to the commands and teachings of human beings, that is, carnal people who understand the Law carnally, rather than according to Christ or his own followers. For when Christ sent the Apostles themselves out to preach, when they needed especially to guard against every scandal, he nevertheless so allowed them to eat all foods that, wherever they were received as guests, they should live as their hosts did, eating and drinking what was set before them (Luke 10:8).

Paul himself, by the Spirit, already foresaw that they would depart from this teaching of the Lord and of himself. Concerning them he writes to Timothy: “But the Spirit plainly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, attending to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy, forbidding marriage, commanding abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who know the truth; because every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer. By setting these things before the brethren, you will be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and the good doctrine which you have followed” (1 Tim. 4:1). [Col. 0220D]

Finally, if one fixes one’s bodily eye on the outward display of abstinence, who would not prefer John and his disciples, wasting themselves by excessive abstinence, to Christ himself and his disciples in religious devotion? John’s own disciples, murmuring against Christ and his followers as people still Judaizing in outward things, asked the Lord himself: “Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?” (Mark 2:18).

Augustine the Blessed, carefully considering this and considering the difference between virtue and the display of virtue, so assesses outward actions that works add nothing to merits. Thus he says in his book *On the Good of Marriage* (chap. 21): “Continence is a virtue not of the body but of the soul. Now virtues of the soul are sometimes manifested in the body, sometimes in a disposition, as the virtue of martyrs appeared in their enduring of sufferings.”

Again (ibid.): “For patience was already in Job, which the Lord knew and to which he bore witness (Job 1:8), but it became known to human beings by the test of temptation.”

Again: “But that it may be understood more clearly how virtue can exist in a disposition even when it is not present in an act, I shall speak from an example of which no Catholic doubts. No one faithful to Christ’s Gospel doubts that the Lord Jesus, in the reality of flesh, hungered, thirsted, ate, and drank. Was there then not in him the virtue [Col. 0221A] of continence from food and drink, as great as it was in John the Baptist? For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they said, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they said, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners’” (Matt. 11:19).

Again: “Then, after he had said those things about John and himself, he added: ‘Wisdom has been justified by her children’ (ibid.), who see that the virtue of continence ought always to exist in the disposition of the soul, but ought to be manifested in act according to the suitability of circumstances and times, just as the virtue of the holy martyrs’ patience.”

Accordingly, just as the merit of patience is not unequal in Peter, who suffered, and John, who did not suffer, so the merit of continence is not unequal in John, who experienced no marriage, and Abraham, who begot children. For both John’s celibacy and Abraham’s marriage served Christ according to the distribution of times. John therefore possessed continence both in act, while Abraham possessed it in disposition alone. For at that time, when the Law following the days of the patriarchs pronounced accursed the one who did not raise up seed in Israel (Deut. 25:7), the one who could not act did not yet act, though he possessed the virtue. But when the fullness of time came (Gal. 4:4), it could be said: “Let one who can receive it, receive it; let one who possesses it, put it into practice; let one who is unwilling to put it into practice not falsely claim to possess it” (Matt. 19:12).

From these clear words it is gathered that virtues alone obtain merits before God, and that all who are equal in virtues, however much [Col. 0221B] they differ in their acts, equally earn favour from him. Hence all who are truly Christians are so wholly occupied with the inner person—adorning that person with virtues and cleansing it from vices—that they take no, or very little, concern for the outward person.

Thus we read that the Apostles themselves behaved so rustically and, as it were, improperly even in the Lord’s own company that, as though forgetful of every reverence and propriety, when passing through fields they were not ashamed to pluck ears of grain, rub them together (Matt. 12:1), and eat them like children. Nor were they concerned about washing their hands when they were about to take food. When some persons accused them, as it were, of impurity, the Lord excused them: “To eat with unwashed hands,” he said, “does not defile a person” (Matt. 15:18).

There he immediately added in general that the soul is defiled by no outward things, but only by those which proceed from the heart: “namely,” he says, “evil thoughts, adulteries, murders” (ibid., 19), and so forth. For unless the mind is first corrupted by a wicked will, whatever is outwardly done in the body cannot be sin. Hence he rightly says that adulteries and murders themselves proceed from the heart, since they are committed even without bodily contact [variant: *contactu*], according to the saying: “Whoever looks upon a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28); and, “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

Nor are they necessarily committed when bodies are touched or injured: for example, when someone is oppressed by violence, or when a judge, compelled by justice, puts a guilty person to death. For “every murderer,” as it is written, “has no part in the kingdom of God” (ibid.). [Col. 0221C] Therefore, we must not greatly assess what things are done, but with what intention they are done, if we strive to please him who tests heart and reins, sees in secret, and will judge the hidden things of human beings. Paul says, “according to my Gospel” (Rom. 2:16), that is, according to the doctrine of my preaching.

Thus the widow’s small offering, which was two coins—that is, a quadrans (Mark 12:42)—was preferred over the abundant offerings of all the rich by him to whom it is said: “You have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2); for the offering pleases him more because of the giver than the giver because of the offering, as it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel and upon his gifts” (Gen. 4:4). That is, he first examined the devotion of the offerer, and then regarded the gift offered by him [variant: *ipsa*, “by her”] as pleasing. This devotion of the mind is considered greater before God insofar as we place less confidence in outward things that are done.

Accordingly, after the general permission of foods, concerning which, as we have recalled above, he writes to Timothy, the Apostle adds also concerning the exercise of bodily labour: “But train yourself for godliness. For bodily exercise is moderately useful, but godliness is useful for all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4:7); because a devout disposition of the mind toward God earns from him both what is necessary here and what is everlasting in the future.

What else, then, are we taught by these teachings [Col. 0221D] than to think as Christians, and, with Jacob, to provide the father’s refreshment from domestic animals—not, with Esau, to take trouble over wild animals (Gen. 27:6), and to Judaize in outward things? Hence also comes the Psalmist’s saying: “In me, O God, are your vows, which [variant: *quas*, feminine] I shall render to you as praises” (Ps. 55:12).

To this, add also the poetic saying:

Do not seek yourself outside yourself. (Persius, *Satires* I.7.)

There are many and innumerable testimonies, both from secular and ecclesiastical teachers, by which we are taught that things which are called external and indifferent [variant: “from indifferent matters”] are not to be given great concern. Otherwise the works of the Law and its slavery—as Peter says, an unbearable yoke—would be preferred to evangelical freedom, [Col. 0224B] and to Christ’s sweet yoke and light burden. Christ himself invites us to this sweet yoke and light burden: “Come,” he says, “you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28).

Accordingly, the aforesaid apostle sharply rebuked certain persons already converted to Christ, but who still thought that the works of the Law should be retained. As is written in the Acts of the Apostles, he says: “Men and brethren, why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? Rather, we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus we shall be saved, just as they also” (Acts 15:10).

And you yourself, I beg you, as an imitator not only of Christ but also of this apostle, moderate the commands concerning works, in discrimination as well as in name, as befits [Col. 0224C] a weak nature and so that we may be able to devote ourselves as fully as possible to the offices of divine praise. Commending this sacrifice, after rejecting all external sacrifices, the Lord says: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you; for the world and its fullness are mine. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats? Offer to God a sacrifice of praise; render your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I shall deliver you, and you shall honor me” (Ps. 49:12).

Nor do we say this in order to reject the labor of bodily works when necessity requires it. But we should not regard as great those things which serve the body and hinder [variant: impede] the celebration of the divine office—especially since, on apostolic authority, devout women have been granted in particular that they should be supported by the services of another’s provision rather than by the work of their own labor. Thus Paul writes to Timothy: “If any believing woman has widows, let her provide for them, and let not the Church be burdened, so that it may suffice for those who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:16).

By “true widows” he means all those devoted to Christ, for whom not only has their husband died, but the world also has been crucified, and they to the world. It is fitting that they should be supported at the Church’s expense, as though from the revenues of their own bridegroom. Thus the Lord himself provided [variant: foresaw] for his mother an apostle as guardian rather than her husband (John 19:26); and the apostles appointed seven deacons (Acts 6:5), that is, ministers of the Church, to minister to devout [Col. 0225A] women.

We know indeed that the Apostle, writing to the Thessalonians, so strictly restrained certain persons living idly or meddlesomely that he commanded: “If anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat” (2 Thess. 3:10); and that blessed Benedict, especially in order to avoid idleness, prescribed manual labor (chapter 48). But was Mary sitting idle when she listened to Christ’s words? (Luke 10:39.) Was Martha laboring both for her sister and for the Lord, and murmuring enviously about her sister’s repose, as though she alone had borne the burden and heat of the day?

Thus even today we frequently see those who labor in external matters complain when they provide earthly things for persons occupied with divine offices. Often they complain less of what tyrants seize than of what they are compelled to pay to these, as they call them, lazy [Col. 0225B] and idle people. Yet they see that these persons are occupied not merely in hearing Christ’s words, but continually in reading and chanting them. They do not observe that, as the Apostle says, it is no great thing for them to share material things with those from whom they expect spiritual things (1 Cor. 9:11). Nor is it unfitting that those intent upon earthly matters should serve those occupied with spiritual ones.

For this wholesome freedom from labor was granted, even by the ordinance of the Law itself, to the ministers of the Church: the tribe of Levi was to receive no earthly inheritance, so that it might serve the Lord more freely, but was to receive tithes and offerings from the labor of others (Num. 18:21).

Concerning also the abstinence of fasts, which Christians seek more as abstinence from vices than from food, if you decide that anything ought to be added [Col. 0225C] to the institution of the Church, it must be considered [Col. 0226A] and established according to what is expedient for us. Above all, however, provision must be made concerning the ecclesiastical offices and the arrangement of the psalms, so that at least in this matter, if you please, you may relieve our weakness: lest, when we complete the Psalter in a week, we must necessarily repeat the same psalms.

Blessed Benedict also, when he had arranged it according to his own judgment, left this admonition in his Rule for the practice of others: that, if another arrangement seemed better to anyone, he should order the psalms differently (chapter 18). For he observed that, with the succession of times, the adornment of the Church had increased, and that what had first received a rough foundation afterwards acquired the ornament of a building.

But above all we wish you to determine what we are to do concerning the Gospel reading at the night vigils. For it seems dangerous at that time to admit priests or deacons among us to recite this reading—women who ought especially to be separated from every approach and sight of men—both so that we may devote ourselves more purely to God and that we may be safer from temptation.

It is now yours, lord, while you live, to establish concerning us what we must observe forever. For after God you are the founder of this place; through God you are the planter of our congregation; with God you are the institutor of our religious life. Perhaps after you we shall have another teacher, one who builds upon another’s [variant: other] foundation. We therefore fear that he will be less solicitous concerning us, or less heeded by us; and, finally, one who, even if he wishes equally, cannot do equally.

Speak [Col. 0226C] to us, and we shall listen. Farewell.

## LETTER VII. A Further Letter from Peter to Heloise, Concerning the Origin of Nuns

[Col. 0225]

[Col. 0225C] **SUMMARY.**—Having been asked by Heloise in the preceding letter to write to her and her companions concerning the origin of the order of nuns, Abelard responds in this letter most fully to her wish and theirs. He derives that order from the primitive Church—indeed, from the sacred company of the Lord and Savior himself—and recounts what Philo the Jew and the *Tripartite History* relate about the earliest ascetics. He extols the female sex with marvelous praises in each of its ranks; and, not only among Christian or Jewish women, but also among Gentile or pagan women, he surveys at great length the praises of virginity. Indeed, almost the entire letter contains nothing but a most elegant encomium of the female sex; yet he treats more extensively the praise of virginity, whose marvelous deeds are recorded even among pagans.

[Col. 0225D] To your charity, dearest sister, which has stirred up in both yourself and your spiritual daughters a concern regarding the order of your profession—namely, whence the religious life of nuns began—I shall reply briefly and concisely, if I can.

For the order of monks or nuns derived the fullest pattern of its religious life from our Lord Jesus Christ. Yet even before his Incarnation there had been some beginnings of this vocation, among both men and women. Hence Jerome, writing to Eustochium (Letter 4), says: “The sons of the prophets, whom we read of as monks in the Old Testament,” etc. The Evangelist also mentions the widow Anna, constant in the Temple and divine worship, who together with Simeon deserved to receive the Lord in the Temple [Col. 0226D] (Luke 2:25) and to be filled with prophecy.

Therefore Christ, the end of justice and the consummation of all good things, came in the fullness of time in order to perfect the good things that had been begun, or to reveal those unknown; and, as he had come to call and redeem both sexes, so he deigned to unite both sexes in the true monasticism of his own community, so that from it authority for this profession might be given alike to men and women, and a perfection of life might be set before all for imitation.

For there, with the apostles and the other disciples, we read that there was an assembly of holy women together with his mother (Luke 8:2). Renouncing the world and abandoning every possession, in order to possess Christ alone—as it is written, [Col. 0227A] “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15:5)—they devoutly fulfilled that by which all who are converted from the world are initiated, according to the rule handed down by the Lord, into the community of this life: “Unless one renounces all that one possesses, one cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33).

How devoutly these most blessed women, and true nuns, followed Christ; and how great a favour and honour both Christ himself and afterwards the apostles showed toward their devotion, the sacred histories carefully relate. In the Gospel we read that the Pharisee who had received the Lord as a guest, when he murmured, was rebuked by him; and that the service rendered by the sinful woman was far preferred to his hospitality (Luke 7:37). We also read that, when Lazarus had already been raised and was reclining with the others, his sister Martha alone served at table, while Mary poured a pound of costly ointment over the Lord’s feet and wiped them with her own hair; the house was filled with the fragrance of that rich ointment; and Judas was moved to covetousness at its price, because it seemed to be so wastefully used, while the disciples were indignant (John 12:3).

Thus, while Martha busied herself with food, Mary provided ointments: the former refreshes him inwardly, while the latter revives him outwardly in his weariness. Nor does the Gospel record that anyone except women ministered to the Lord (Luke 8:2). They had devoted even their own resources to his daily sustenance and especially supplied him with the necessities of this life. He himself showed himself the humblest servant to his disciples [Col. 0227C] at table and in the washing of feet (John 13:5). But we do not know that he received this service from any disciples or other men; rather, as we have said, women alone rendered such service to him in these and other acts of human care.

And as in that instance there was Martha’s service, so in this we know there was Mary’s service (Mark 14:3). In rendering it she was the more devout because she had previously been the more sinful. The Lord, pouring water into a basin, performed the office of washing. But she rendered this service to him with the tears of inward compunction, not with outward water. The Lord wiped the washed feet of his disciples with a towel. She used her hair in place of a towel. She further added the soothing applications of ointments, [Col. 0227D] which we do not read that the Lord employed.

Who, moreover, does not know that a woman was so bold through trust in his grace as even to anoint his head by pouring ointment over it? This ointment is remembered as poured out not from an alabaster vessel merely opened, but from one broken, so that the vehement desire of her excessive devotion might be expressed: she judged that it was to be reserved for some far greater use, and used it in so great a service. In this she also showed by her deed the very cessation of anointing which Daniel had foretold would come after the Holy of Holies had been anointed (Dan. 9:24). Behold, a woman anoints the Holy of Holies; and by the act itself she proclaims both that he is the one whom she believes him to be and that he is the one whom the prophet’s words had foreshadowed.

What, I ask, is this kindness of the Lord, or what this dignity of women, that he offered both his head and his feet to be anointed by women alone? What, I beseech you, is this prerogative of the weaker sex: that a woman should also anoint the supreme Christ, who from his conception had been anointed with every ointment of the Holy Spirit (Isa. 11:2), and, as it were by bodily sacraments, consecrate him as king and priest, making him Christ—that is, “anointed”—in bodily fashion?

We know that the patriarch Jacob first anointed a stone as a type of the Lord. Afterwards it was permitted only to men to perform the anointings of kings or priests, or any sacramental rites of anointing, although women sometimes presume to baptize. Formerly the patriarch sanctified the stone that was a temple; now the bishop sanctifies the altar with oil [Col. 0228B]. Thus men impress sacraments by figures; but the woman acted in the very truth itself, as Truth himself testifies, saying: “She has done a good work upon me” (Mark 14:6).

Christ himself is anointed by a woman; Christians by men. The head itself, that is, by a woman; the members, by men. And it is fittingly remembered that the woman poured out the ointment, rather than dripped it upon his head. Thus the bride sings beforehand of him in the Song of Songs: “Your name is ointment poured out” (Song 1:2). The Psalmist also mystically prefigures the abundance of this ointment by that which flowed [variant: “flows”] from the head down to the hem of the garment, saying: “Like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, which descends to the hem of his garment” [Col. 0228C] (Ps. 133:2).

We read that David received a threefold anointing, as Jerome also mentions in his commentary on Psalm 25; so too did Christ and Christians. For the Lord’s feet and his head received a woman’s ointment. But Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus, as John relates, buried him when dead with spices. Christians too are sanctified by a threefold anointing: one takes place in baptism, another in confirmation, and the third is for the sick.

Consider, therefore, the dignity of the woman through whom the living Christ was twice anointed, namely in feet and head, and received the sacraments of king and priest. The ointment of myrrh and aloes, however, used for preserving dead bodies, prefigured the future incorruption of the Lord’s body, which every one of the elect has obtained [variant: “will obtain”] in the resurrection. The earlier ointments applied by women reveal his singular dignity in both kingship and priesthood: the anointing of the head, the higher dignity; that of the feet, the lower.

Behold, he receives even the sacrament of a king from a woman, though he refused the kingdom offered him by men and fled when they wished to seize him and make him king (John 6:15). A woman performs the sacrament of the heavenly, not the earthly, king—of him, I say, who afterwards said of himself: “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Bishops glory in anointing earthly kings amid the applause of the people; they consecrate mortal [Col. 0229A] priests, adorned in splendid garments embroidered with gold. And they often bless those whom the Lord curses.

A humble woman, without changing her dress or preparing ceremonial adornment, performs these sacraments upon Christ, even while the apostles themselves are indignant—not by the office of pre-eminence, but through the merit of reverence [variant: “love”; Paris manuscript: “devotion”]. O great constancy of faith! O inestimable ardour of charity, which believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things! The Pharisee murmurs while the Lord’s feet are anointed by a sinful woman; the apostles openly take offence because the woman has presumed even to anoint his head. Yet the woman’s faith remains unwavering everywhere [variant: “certainly”], trusting in the Lord’s goodness; and in each case she does not lack the Lord’s support in commendation.

How welcome and pleasing the Lord found her ointments he himself declares when, asking that this ointment be kept for him, he said to the indignant Judas: “Let her keep it for the day of my burial” (John 12:7). It is as if he said: Do not reject this service of hers to one living, lest you also deprive one dead of the manifestation of her devotion in this matter. For it is certain that holy women prepared spices also for the Lord’s burial. She would surely have been less diligent then had she now been repulsed and endured shame.

When the disciples were indignant at so great a woman’s boldness and, as Mark recounts, were even raging against her, the Lord subdued them with his gentlest reply. He so highly exalted this benefaction that he judged it should be included in the Gospel and foretold that it would everywhere be preached together with it [Col. 0229C] (Mark 14:9), in remembrance and praise of the woman who did what was accused of no slight presumption. We do not read that the Lord’s authority so commended and ordained the services of any other persons. Likewise, when he preferred the alms of the poor widow to all the offerings of the Temple (Mark 12:43), he clearly showed how acceptable women’s devotion was to him.

Peter indeed dared to profess that he himself and his fellow apostles had left all things for Christ. Zacchaeus, receiving the coming of the Lord whom he had longed for, gave half his goods to the poor and restored fourfold whatever he had extorted (Luke 19:8). Many others made greater expenditures for Christ or in Christ, offered far more precious things for divine service, or left them for Christ. Yet they did not attain such praise from the Lord’s commendation as did women.

How great their devotion to him always was, the end of the Lord’s earthly life itself plainly shows. For when the chief of the apostles denied him, the Lord’s beloved disciple fled, and the other apostles were scattered, these women stood fearless; no fear or despair could separate them from Christ either in his Passion or in death. Thus the Apostle’s words seem especially applicable to them: “Who shall separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress?” (Rom. 8:35).

Therefore Matthew, after reporting concerning himself and the others alike, “Then all the disciples left him and fled” (Matt. 26:56), subsequently adds the perseverance of the women, who stood by him even while he was crucified, as far as they were permitted: [Col. 0230A] “There were there many women at a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him” (Matt. 27:55). The same Evangelist carefully describes them as clinging immovably even to his tomb: “Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting opposite the tomb” (ibid., 61).

Mark too, referring to these women, says: “There were also women looking on from a distance, among whom were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome. When he was in Galilee, they followed him and ministered to him; and many other women came up with him to Jerusalem” (Mark 15:40). John, who had earlier fled, relates that he stood near the cross and stood by the crucified one; but he first presents the perseverance of the women, as if he had been encouraged and recalled by their example: “There stood by the cross of Jesus his mother, and his mother’s sister Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalene. Therefore when Jesus saw his mother, and the disciple standing” (John 19:35), etc.

Long before, blessed Job prophesied in the person of the Lord of this constancy of the holy women and failure of the disciples: “With my flesh consumed, my bone has clung to my skin, and only lips have been left around [Col. 0230C] my teeth” (Job 19:20). In the bone, which supports and carries the flesh and skin, resides the strength of the body. Therefore in Christ’s body, which is the Church, “his bone” signifies the stable foundation of Christian faith, or that ardour of charity of which it is sung: “Many waters cannot quench charity” (Song 8:7), and of which the Apostle says: “It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:7).

Flesh is the inward part of the body, and skin the outward. The apostles, therefore, who devoted themselves to preaching the food of the inner soul, and the women, who supplied bodily necessities, are compared respectively to flesh and skin. Thus, when the flesh was consumed—that is, when the apostles were scandalized at the Lord’s Passion and despaired of his death—the devotion of the holy [Col. 0230D] women remained immovable and did not depart at all from Christ’s bone. For they retained such constancy of faith, hope, and charity that they were not separated from him, though dead, either in mind or in body.

Men are naturally stronger than women both in mind and body. Therefore masculine nature is rightly signified by flesh, which is nearer to bone; feminine weakness by skin. The apostles themselves, whose role it is to bite by reproving the failings of others, are called the Lord’s teeth. For them only lips—that is, words rather than deeds—remained, when, despairing of Christ, they spoke more than they acted for Christ.

Such indeed were those disciples to whom he appeared as they went to the village of Emmaus and spoke with one another [Col. 0231A] about all that had happened; there he corrected their despair. What, finally, did Peter or the other disciples possess then beyond words, when the Lord’s Passion arrived and the Lord himself foretold their coming scandal at his Passion? Peter said: “Even if all are scandalized in you, I shall never be scandalized” (Matt. 26:33). And again: “Even if I must die with you, I shall not deny you. And all the disciples said likewise” (ibid., 35). They spoke, I say, rather than acted.

For he who was first and greatest of the apostles, who had shown such constancy in words that he said to the Lord, “I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke 22:33), and to whom the Lord had then specially entrusted his Church, saying, “And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers” (ibid., 32), was not ashamed to deny him at the voice of a single maidservant. Nor did he do so once only: a third time he still denied him while he was living; and all the disciples together took flight from the living Lord in a single instant. Yet women were not separated from him in death either in mind or body.

That blessed sinner among them, even seeking him when dead and confessing him as her Lord, said: “They have taken the Lord from the tomb” (John 20:2). And again: “If you have taken him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away” (ibid., 15). The rams—indeed, even the shepherds—of the Lord’s flock flee; the sheep remain fearless.

The Lord rebukes these men as weak flesh because at the very hour [Col. 0231C] of his Passion they could not watch with him even for one hour. The women spent a sleepless night at his tomb in tears and deserved to be the first to see the glory of his resurrection. How faithfully they had loved him living, even unto death, they showed not so much in words as in deeds. And because of the concern which they showed for his Passion and death, they were the first to be gladdened by his risen life.

For when, according to John, Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus buried the Lord’s body, wrapping it in linen cloths with spices, Mark recounts their care: Mary Magdalene and Mary of Joses watched where he was laid. Luke also refers to them: “The women who had come with Jesus from Galilee followed; [Col. 0231D] they saw the tomb and how his body was laid; and, returning, they prepared spices” (Luke 23:55). Apparently the spices of Nicodemus did not suffice them unless they added their own. On the Sabbath they were indeed silent, according to the commandment. But according to Mark, after the Sabbath had passed, very early in the morning on the day of the Resurrection, Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome came to the tomb.

Now that we have shown their devotion, let us describe the honour they deserved. First they were consoled by an angelic vision concerning the Lord’s resurrection, now accomplished; then they were the first to see and touch the Lord himself. Mary Magdalene came first, as she was more fervent than the others. Afterwards she and the other women together, of whom it is written that after the angelic vision, “they went out from the tomb, running to announce the Lord’s resurrection to the disciples. And behold, Jesus met them, saying: ‘Hail.’ They came near, took hold of his feet, and worshipped him. Then Jesus said: ‘Go, announce to my brothers that they are to go into Galilee. There they will see me’” [Col. 0232A] (Matt. 28:8).

Luke also continues concerning this: “It was Magdalene, and Joanna, and Mary of James, and the others who were with them, who told these things to the apostles” (Luke 20:10). Nor does Mark omit that they were first sent by an angel to announce these things to the apostles, where it is written, as the angel speaks to the women: “He has risen; he is not here. But go, tell his disciples, and Peter, that he goes before you into Galilee” (Mark 16:6). The Lord himself, appearing first to Mary Magdalene, said to her: “Go to my brothers and tell them: I ascend to my Father” (John 20:17).

From these things we gather that these holy women were, as it were, made apostles over the apostles. Sent to the apostles either by the Lord or by angels, they announced that supreme joy of the Resurrection, awaited by all, so that through them the apostles might first learn what they would afterwards preach to the whole world. The Evangelist above also mentions that the Lord greeted them when he met them after the Resurrection, showing by both his meeting and his greeting how much care and favour he had for them. For we do not read that he uttered to others the distinctive word of greeting, “Hail”; indeed, he had previously forbidden the disciples this greeting when he said to them: “Greet no one on the road” [Col. 0232C] (Luke 10:4). It is as though, now that he had obtained the glory of immortality, he reserved this privilege for devout women, to render it to them in person.

Moreover, when the Acts of the Apostles relate that, immediately after the Lord’s Ascension, the apostles returned from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem and carefully describe the religious life of that most holy assembly, they do not pass over the persevering devotion of the holy women: “These all persevered with one accord in prayers, with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus” (Acts 1:14).

But, leaving aside the Hebrew women who were the first to be converted to faith while the Lord was still living and preaching in the flesh, and who began the pattern of this religious life, let us consider also the widows of the Greeks who were afterwards received by the apostles. With what diligence and care the apostles treated them is shown by the fact that Stephen, the most glorious standard-bearer of Christian warfare and the first martyr, together with certain other spiritual men, was appointed by the apostles themselves to minister to them.

Thus it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “As the number of disciples increased, a murmur arose among the Greeks against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministry. Then the Twelve apostles summoned the multitude of the disciples and said: ‘It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve [Col. 0233A] tables. Therefore, brothers, choose from among you seven men of good testimony, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this work. But we shall devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.’ The saying pleased the whole multitude; and they chose Stephen, full of faith and the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timothy, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch. They set these before the apostles, and, having prayed, they laid hands upon them” (Acts 6:1).

Accordingly, Stephen’s self-restraint is greatly commended, because he was assigned to the ministry and service of holy women. How excellent this ministry and service was, and how acceptable both to God and to the apostles, the apostles themselves declared by their own prayer and laying on of hands, as if adjuring those whom they appointed to this work to act faithfully, and helping them by both blessing and prayer so that they might be able to do so.

Paul too claims this administration for himself as part of the fullness of his apostolate: “Do we not have the right,” he says, “to lead about a sister, a woman, as also the other apostles do?” (1 Cor. 9:5). It is as though he said openly: Are we permitted, like the other apostles, to have assemblies of holy women and take them with us in preaching, so that they may provide from their own resources the necessities needed by the apostles in their preaching?

Accordingly Augustine says in *On the Work of Monks*, chapter 4: “For this purpose believing women who possessed earthly resources [Col. 0233C] went with them and ministered to them from their own resources, so that they might lack none of the things belonging to the support of this life.” Again, in the same work: “Anyone who does not think that the apostles did this, namely that women of holy conduct travelled about with them wherever they preached the Gospel, should hear the Gospel and learn how they did this by the example of the Lord himself.”

For it is written in the Gospel: “After this he himself went on a journey through cities and villages, preaching the kingdom of God; and the Twelve were with him, and certain women who had been healed of unclean spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene; Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward; Susanna; and many others, [Col. 0233D] who ministered to him from their resources” (Luke 8:1). Hence it is also clear that the Lord, as he travelled in his preaching, was bodily sustained by women’s service, and that they clung to him together with the apostles as inseparable companions.

Then, as the religious life of this profession multiplied among women no less than among men, at the very beginning of the newborn Church women, like men, possessed dwellings of their own monasteries. Thus Ecclesiastical History, recording among other things in Book II, chapter 16, the praise which the most eloquent Jew Philo not only spoke but also magnificently wrote concerning the Alexandrian Church under Mark, says: “This kind of people exists in many parts of the world.” And after some intervening material: “In every place there is a house consecrated to prayer, called *Senivor*, or a monastery.” Again, in the same chapter: “Therefore they not only understand the subtle hymns of the ancients, but themselves compose new ones to God, setting them in every kind of metre and melody with a sufficiently worthy and sweet harmony.”

After he had set forth many things concerning abstinence and the offices of divine worship, he added, in the same place: “With the men whom we have mentioned are also women, of whom many are now elderly virgins, preserving bodily integrity and chastity not from any necessity but through devotion. Eager to consecrate themselves to the pursuits of wisdom not only in soul but also in body, they judge it unworthy to enslave to lust a vessel prepared for receiving wisdom; and they refuse to bear mortal offspring, since they seek the most holy and immortal union with the divine Word, from which may be left a posterity in no way subject to the corruption of mortality.”

Again, in the same place, concerning Philo: “He also writes about their assemblies: the men gather separately, and likewise the women separately in the same places; and they keep vigils as is customary among us.”

From this arises what the Tripartite History records in praise of Christian philosophy—that is, the prerogative of monastic life—embraced no less by women than by men. For it says in Book I, chapter 11: “The founder of this most elegant philosophy was, as some say, the prophet Elijah and John the Baptist.” But Philo the Pythagorean reports that in his time distinguished Hebrews from every quarter practiced philosophy on an estate situated on a hill beside Lake Maria [Col. 0234C]. He describes their dwellings, food, and manner of life as such as we now see among Egyptian monks. He writes that they took no food before sunset; always abstained from wine and blood; had bread, salt, and hyssop as food, and water as drink. Elderly virgins lived with them, abstaining from marriage of their own free will for love of philosophy.

Hence too comes Jerome’s statement in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 8, in praise of Mark and the Church: “First proclaiming Christ at Alexandria, he established a Church of such teaching and continence of life that he compelled all followers of Christ to follow his example.” Finally, when the most eloquent Philo among the Jews saw the earliest Church at Alexandria, still observing Jewish practices, he wrote a book in praise of his people concerning their conversion; and, just as Luke relates that the believers at Jerusalem had all things in common (Acts 2:44), so Philo recorded for posterity what he saw being done at Alexandria under Mark as teacher.

Again, chapter 11: “Philo the Jew, an Alexandrian by nation and of priestly descent, is for this reason numbered by us among ecclesiastical writers: in writing about the first Church of Mark the Evangelist at Alexandria, he was engaged in praise of our people, recording that they existed not only there but also in many provinces, and calling their dwellings [Col. 0235A] monasteries.” From this it appears that the first Church of believers in Christ was such as monks now imitate and desire to be: nothing belonged to anyone as private property; no one among them was rich and no one poor; estates were divided among the needy; they devoted themselves to prayer and psalms, as well as teaching and continence. Such, Luke relates, were the first believers at Jerusalem (Acts 4:32).

If we examine the ancient histories, we shall find that women were not separated from men in matters pertaining to God or to any distinctive form of religious life. Sacred histories also relate that, together with men, women not only sang divine songs but composed them. The first song concerning the deliverance of the Israelite people was sung to the Lord not only by men but also by women; from this they immediately received authority for celebrating in the Church the offices of divine worship.

For it is written: “Miriam the prophetess, sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and dances. She led them in song, saying: ‘Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified’” (Exod. 15:20). Moses is not there called a prophet, nor is he said to have led the singing as Miriam did; nor are men reported to have possessed timbrel or dance as women did. Since, therefore, Miriam is called a prophetess as she led the singing, she seems to have uttered this song not so much by dictating or reciting it as by prophesying. Her being described as leading the others in song shows how orderly and harmonious their psalmody was.

That they sang not only with voice but also with timbrels and dances indicates not only their very great devotion, but also mystically expresses the form of spiritual song in monastic communities. The Psalmist exhorts us to this when he says: “Praise him with timbrel and dance” [Col. 0235C] (Ps. 150:4), that is, with the mortification of the flesh and with that harmony of charity of which it is written: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

Nor is what they are reported to have done in singing devoid of mystery: in it the jubilations of contemplative souls are figured. When such a soul raises itself toward heavenly things, it leaves, as it were, the fortress of its earthly dwelling; and from the inmost sweetness of its contemplation it renders to the Lord a spiritual hymn with the highest exultation.

There too we have songs of Deborah [variant: “Delbora”], of Anna, and likewise of the widow Judith, as also in the Gospel of Mary the Lord’s mother. Anna, namely, in offering her little son Samuel to the tabernacle of the Lord (1 Sam. 1:25), gave monasteries authority to receive children. Hence Isidore, in chapter 5 of his rule for brothers established in the Honorian [variant: Honoriac] coenobium, says: “Whoever was entrusted to the monastery by his parents should know that he is to remain there permanently. For Anna offered Samuel as a boy to God. He remained in the service of the Temple to which his mother had assigned him, and served where he had been placed.”

It is also established that Aaron’s daughters, together with their brothers, belonged so fully to the sanctuary and the hereditary portion of Levi that the Lord thereby provided food for them too. Thus it is written in the Book of Numbers, where the Lord himself says to Aaron: “All the first-fruits of the sanctuary, which the children of Israel offer to the Lord, I have given to you, and to your sons and daughters, by a perpetual right” [Col. 0236A] (Num. 18:19). Hence women’s religious life does not seem separated even from the clerical order. They are evidently joined to it even in name, since we call them both deaconesses and deacons—as though we recognized in both the tribe of Levi, and, as it were, Levites.

In the same book we also have that greatest vow and consecration of the Lord’s Nazirites established alike for women and men, the Lord himself saying to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When a man or a woman makes a vow to be sanctified and wishes to consecrate himself or herself to the Lord, they shall abstain from wine and everything that can intoxicate. They shall not drink vinegar made from wine or from any other beverage, nor anything pressed from grapes. They shall not eat fresh or dried grapes during all the days in which they are consecrated to the Lord by vow. Whatever comes from the vine, from the dried grape to the seed, they shall not eat during the whole time of their separation” (Num. 6:2).

I think that the women keeping watch at the entrance of the tabernacle belonged to this religious order. From their mirrors Moses made the vessel in which Aaron and his sons were to wash, as it is written: “Moses placed the bronze basin in which Aaron and his sons were to wash; [Col. 0236C] he made it from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle” (Exod. 28:8).

The ardour of their great devotion is carefully described: even when the tabernacle had been closed, they clung to its doors and kept the watches of holy vigils, spending the night itself in prayer and, while the men rested, not ceasing from divine service.
