That the tabernacle is said to have been closed to them aptly signifies the life of penitents, who are separated from others so that they may afflict themselves more harshly with the laments of penitence. This life, indeed, is said to belong especially to the monastic profession, whose order is described as nothing other than a certain more sparing form of penitence.

The tabernacle at whose entrance they kept watch is to be mystically understood as that of which the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat” (Heb. 13:10)—that is, those who devote voluptuous service to their body, in which they serve here as in a camp, are not worthy to partake of it. The entrance of the tabernacle is the end of the present life, when the soul leaves the body here and enters the life to come. Those keep watch at this entrance who are concerned about the departure from this life and entry into the future one, and who arrange their departure through penitence so as to deserve that entry.

Concerning this daily entrance and departure of the holy Church, the Psalmist offers this prayer: “May the Lord guard your entrance and your departure” [Col. 0236D] (Ps. 121:8). For he guards our entrance and departure together when, as we depart from here and have already been purified through penitence, he immediately brings us in there. He fittingly named entrance before departure, attending not so much to their order as to their dignity: for this departure from mortal life is painful, but that entrance into eternal life is the highest exultation.

Their mirrors are outward works, from which the soul’s ugliness or beauty is judged, just as the quality of a human face is judged from a bodily mirror. From these mirrors a vessel is made in which Aaron and his sons may wash themselves when the works of holy women and so great a constancy in God on the part of the weaker sex strongly rebuke the negligence of bishops and priests, and especially move them to tears of compunction. And if the bishops and priests themselves exercise due care for them, these women’s works prepare for their sins the forgiveness by which they may be washed.

From such mirrors blessed Gregory surely made for himself a vessel of compunction when, marvelling at the virtue of holy women and the victory of the weaker sex in martyrdom, he sighed and asked: “What will barbarian men say, when such delicate girls endure so much for Christ, and the frail sex triumphs in so great a contest that it itself more often, with the double crown of virginity and martyrdom—[source breaks off]”

“...we may know them to be strong?” Among these, as has been said, keeping watch at the door of the tabernacle, and who had now, as though Nazarites of the Lord, consecrated their widowhood to him, I do not doubt that blessed Anna was numbered: she deserved, together with holy Simeon, to receive in the Temple the Lord Jesus Christ, the unique Nazarite of the Lord; and, becoming more than a prophet, in that same hour in which Simeon recognized him through the Spirit, she recognized, pointed him out as present, and publicly proclaimed him. The Evangelist, pursuing her praise more carefully, says:

> “And there was Anna, a prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Asher. She had advanced in many days and had lived with her husband seven years from her virginity. And she had been a widow until the age of eighty-four; she did not depart from the Temple, serving with fastings and prayers night and day. And coming in at that same hour, she gave thanks to the Lord and spoke of him to all who were awaiting the redemption of Jerusalem [variant: Israel]” (Luke 2:36).

Mark each statement and consider how intent the Evangelist was upon praising this widow, and by how many encomia he exalted her excellence. He carefully set forth the grace of prophecy which she customarily possessed; her parent and tribe; the long duration of her holy widowhood, after the seven years she had endured with her husband and in which she had devoted herself to the Lord; her constancy in the Temple; her persistence in fasting and prayer; her confession of praise, giving thanks to the Lord; and her public preaching concerning the promised and now-born Saviour. Simeon, however, the Evangelist had previously commended for righteousness, not prophecy; nor did he record in him such a virtue of continence or abstinence, nor such diligence in divine service, [Col. 0238A] nor did he add anything concerning his preaching to others.

Of this profession [variant: perfection] and purpose are the true widows of whom the Apostle, writing to Timothy, says: “Honour widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:3). Again: “But she who is truly a widow and desolate, let her hope in God and persist in supplications and prayers night and day. And this especially, that they may be blameless” (ibid., 5). And again: “If any of the faithful have widows, let them provide for them, and let not the Church be burdened, so that it may suffice for those who are truly widows” (ibid., 16).

He calls those true widows who have not dishonoured their widowhood by a second marriage, or who, persevering thus more through devotion than necessity, have dedicated themselves to the Lord. He calls desolate those who renounce all things in such a manner that they retain no support of earthly consolation, or have no one to take charge of them. He commands that these be honoured and judges that they should be supported from the revenues of the Church, as though from the proper income of Christ their bridegroom. He also carefully describes what kind of women should be chosen for the ministry of the diaconate:

> “Let a widow be chosen not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one man, having testimony in good works: if she has brought up children, if she has received strangers, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has ministered to those suffering tribulation, if she has followed every good work. But avoid younger widows” (ibid., 9).

Blessed Jerome, explaining this passage, says: “Avoid them in the ministry of the diaconate, lest a bad example be given in place of a good one—if, that is, younger women are chosen for this office, women more prone to temptation and naturally more frivolous; and lest, lacking the prudence acquired through the experience of advanced age, they provide a bad example to those to whom above all they ought to have given a good one.”

The Apostle openly acknowledges that he had already learned this danger among younger widows through definite experience, and moreover provides counsel against it. For after saying, “But avoid younger widows” (ibid., 11), he immediately added both the reason for this and the remedy of his counsel:

> “For when they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have made void their first faith. At the same time they learn to be idle, going about from house to house; and they are not only idle, but also talkative and meddlesome, speaking what they ought not. Therefore I wish younger women to marry, bear children, be mistresses of households, and give no occasion to the adversary for reproach. For already some have turned back after Satan.”

Blessed Gregory too, following this apostolic foresight concerning the selection of deaconesses, writes to Maximus, bishop of Syracuse, in these words (book III, epistle 11): “We most emphatically forbid young women to be made abbesses. Therefore let your Fraternity permit no bishop to veil any virgin unless she is sixty years old and her life and character have been examined.”

Those whom we now call abbesses were formerly called deaconesses—as ministers rather than mothers. For *deacon* means “minister,” and they considered that deaconesses should be named from service rather than from precedence, in accordance with the teaching of the Lord himself, both by example and word:

> “He who is greater among you shall be your minister” (Matt. 23:11).

And again:

> “Which is greater, he who reclines at table or he who ministers? But I am in the midst of you as one who ministers” (Luke 23:27).

And elsewhere:

> “Just as the Son of Man came not to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matt. 20:28).

Accordingly Jerome himself was not a little bold in censuring the very title of abbot, in which he knew that many already gloried, on the authority of the Lord himself. Explaining the passage where it is written [variant: which was written] in the fourth Epistle to the Galatians (book II), “crying, Abba, Father,” he says:

> “*Abba* is Hebrew and means exactly the same thing as ‘father.’ Since *Abba, Father* is said in the Hebrew and Syriac tongue, and since the Lord commands in the Gospel that no one should be called Father except God (Matt. 5:34), I do not know by what licence we either call others by this name in monasteries or consent to be called by it ourselves. And certainly he who said that one must not swear gave this command. If we do not swear, neither should we call anyone Father. If we interpret ‘Father’ one way and think differently concerning swearing, we shall be compelled to do so.”

It is clear that Phoebe belonged to these deaconesses. The Apostle, carefully commending her to the Romans and entreating them on her behalf, says:

> “I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is in the ministry of the Church which is at Cenchreae, that you may receive her in the Lord worthily of the saints and assist her in whatever matter she may need from you. For she herself also has assisted many, and myself as well” (Rom. 16:1).

Both Cassiodorus and Claudius, explaining this passage, declare that she was a deaconess of that Church. Cassiodorus says: “He indicates that she was a deaconess of mother Church. This is still done in the Greek regions, as though for the sake of military service. Nor is the use of baptizing denied to them in the Church.” Claudius says: “This passage teaches by apostolic authority that women too are appointed to the ministry of the Church. Phoebe, appointed to this office in the Church at Cenchreae, is commended by the Apostle with great praise and recommendation.”

Writing to Timothy, the Apostle likewise establishes the manner of their life by a similar instruction concerning character, joining them among the deacons themselves:

> “Deacons likewise must be modest, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not pursuing shameful gain, holding the mystery of faith in a pure conscience” (1 Tim. 3:8).

And:

> “Let these first be tested, and then let them minister, having no charge against them. Women likewise must be modest, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let deacons be the husbands of one wife, ruling their children and households well. For those who have ministered well acquire for themselves a good standing and great confidence in the faith which is in Christ Jesus” (ibid., 10).

[Col. 0240A] Therefore what he there says concerning deacons—“not double-tongued”—he says here of deaconesses—“not slanderers”; and what he says there, “not given to much wine,” he here calls “sober.” The remaining things which follow there he briefly includes here in the words “faithful in all things.” And just as he prohibits bishops and deacons from being twice-married [variant: bigamous], so he ordains that deaconesses too should be wives of one man, as we have already recalled:

> “Let a widow be chosen not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one man, having testimony in good works: if she has brought up children, if she has received strangers, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has ministered to those suffering tribulation, if she has followed every good work. But avoid younger widows” (1 Tim. 5:9).

How much more careful the Apostle was in this description or instruction of deaconesses than in the foregoing regulations for bishops and deacons is easy to show. For what he says—“having testimony in good works,” or “if she has received strangers”—he nowhere mentions regarding deacons. What he adds—“if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has ministered to those suffering tribulation,” and so forth—is left unspoken both of bishops and of deacons. He says that bishops and deacons must have no charge against them; but concerning these women he commands not merely that they be blameless, but declares also that they have followed every good work.

He prudently provided also for the maturity of their age, so that they might have authority in all things, saying, “not less than sixty years old”; and that reverence should be shown not only to their life but also to their age, proved over many years. Thus, although the Lord loved John exceedingly, he nevertheless placed Peter, who was older, before him and the rest. For all are less offended when an older person rather than a younger is preferred to them; and we obey an elder more willingly, one whom not only his life, but nature and the order of time as well, has made prior to us.

Hence Jerome, in the first book Against Jovinian, when mentioning Peter’s precedence, says: “One is chosen so that, a head being established, the occasion of schism may be removed. But why was John not chosen? Deference was paid to age, because Peter was older, lest one still an adolescent, almost a boy, should be placed before men of advanced age, and the good teacher—who ought to have removed occasion for quarrelling from his disciples—should seem to furnish, in the young man whom he loved, a cause for envy.”

That abbot considered this matter carefully who, as is written in the *Lives of the Fathers*, removed precedence from a younger brother who had come first to conversion and gave it to an older one, for this one reason alone: that the latter surpassed the former in age. He feared, indeed, that even a brother by flesh might take it ill to have a younger man preferred to him. He remembered also that the apostles themselves had been indignant with two of their number when they seemed, with the intervention of their mother, to seek a certain prerogative from Christ—especially since one of these two was younger than the other apostles: namely John himself, of whom we have just spoken.

Nor did apostolic care show great vigilance only in establishing deaconesses; it is evident how diligent it was generally concerning widows of holy profession, in order to remove every occasion of temptation. For after saying, “Honour widows who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:3), he immediately added: “But if any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to govern her own household and to render a return to her parents” (ibid., 4). And after some intervening words he says: “If anyone does not take care of his own, and especially of those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (ibid., 8).

In these words he provides at once for due humanity and for the religious purpose undertaken: lest little children be left destitute under the pretext of religion; lest natural compassion toward those in need disturb the widow’s holy purpose, force her to look back, and sometimes even draw her into sacrileges, so that she might give something to her own family which she has fraudulently taken from the common fund. Hence the counsel is plainly necessary: women entangled in the care of their household must, before passing to true widowhood and fully devoting themselves to divine service, render this return to their own parents, so that, just as they were reared under their parents’ care, they in turn may provide by the same law for their descendants.

Emphasizing also the religious life of widows, he commands them to persist in supplications and prayers night and day. Most solicitous also concerning their relatives, he says: “If any faithful person has widows, let that person provide for them, and let not the Church be burdened, so that it may suffice for those who are truly widows” (ibid., 16). It is as though he said plainly: if a widow has household members able to provide her necessities from their own means, let them provide for her in this matter, so that the public resources of the Church may suffice to support the others. This statement plainly shows that, if any are obstinate concerning widows of this kind who belong to them, they ought to be compelled to this duty by apostolic authority.

Providing not only for their need but for their honour also, he says: “Honour widows who are truly widows.” We believe that such were the women of whom Paul called one his mother and John the Evangelist called another his lady, out of reverence for their holy profession. Paul, writing to the Romans, says: “Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine” (Rom. 16:13). John, in the second Epistle which he writes, says: “The elder to the chosen lady and her children” (2 John 1:1), etc. Asking her also to love him, he adds below: “And now I ask you, lady, that we love one another” (ibid., 5).

Relying upon this authority, Jerome, writing to Eustochium, a virgin of your profession, was not ashamed to call her “lady”; indeed, he immediately added why he ought to do so, saying (epistle 22): “For this reason, my lady Eustochium: I ought indeed to call the bride of our Lord a lady,” etc. Later in the same letter, setting the prerogative of this holy purpose above every glory of earthly happiness, he says:

> “I do not want you to have the company [variant: companionship] of married women; I do not want you to go to the houses of nobles; I do not want you frequently to see what, in despising it, you chose to be a virgin. If the ambition of those offering greetings crowds about an emperor’s wife, why do you wrong your husband? Why do you, the bride of God, hasten to the wife of a man? Learn holy pride in this matter. Know that you are better than they.”

Writing also to a virgin dedicated to God concerning virgins consecrated to God, he begins by saying how great their blessedness in heaven and dignity on earth are (epistle 14):

> “How great a blessedness holy virginity possesses in heavenly things, we learn not only from the testimony of Scripture but also from the practice of the Church, by which we learn that a special merit belongs to those whose consecration is spiritual. For although every company of believers receives equal gifts of grace and all glory in the same blessings of the sacraments, these possess something proper above the rest, since from that holy and immaculate flock of the Church they are chosen by the Holy Spirit, according to the merit of their own will, as holier and purer victims, and are offered upon the altar through the high priest of God.”

Again (ibid.):

> “Virginity therefore possesses what others do not possess, since it both obtains a special grace and enjoys, so to speak, the special privilege of its consecration. For the consecration of virgins may not be celebrated, except when danger of death presses, at any other time than Epiphany, the Easter Octave, and the feasts of the apostles. Nor may the veils to be placed upon the sacred heads of the virgins themselves be consecrated except by the high priest, that is, the bishop.”

But monks, although they are of the same profession or order and of the more worthy sex, even if they are virgins, are permitted to receive a blessing on any day, from an abbot, both for themselves and for their own garments—that is, their cowls. Priests and the other clergy of lower rank may always be ordained at the fasts of the Four Seasons, and bishops on every Sunday. The consecration of virgins, however, in proportion as it is more precious, is rarer; it has claimed for itself the joy of the most eminent solemn feasts.

The whole Church rejoices especially over their admirable virtue, as the Psalmist foretold in these words: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her” (Ps. 44:15). And again: “They shall be brought in gladness and rejoicing; they shall be brought into the temple of the king” (ibid., 16). This consecration [variant: their consecration] is said to have been composed or dictated by Matthew, both Apostle and Evangelist, as is read in his Passion; there it is also recorded that he himself died a martyr for their consecration or for the defence of their virginal purpose. The apostles, on the other hand, left us no written blessing either for clerics or monks.

Their religious order alone has been marked by the very name of holiness, since they are called *sanctimoniales* from *sanctimonia*, that is, holiness. For the weaker women’s sex is, the more pleasing to God and more perfect is its virtue, according to the testimony of the Lord himself, who, exhorting the Apostle in his weakness toward the crown of combat, says: “My grace is sufficient for you; for power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

Speaking through the same Apostle of the members of his body, which is the Church, and as though especially commending the honour of such weak members, he adds in the same Epistle, namely the First to the Corinthians:

> “Rather, those members of the body which seem weaker are more necessary; and upon those members of the body which we think less honourable, we bestow more abundant honour; and our uncomely members have more abundant comeliness. But our comely members have no need. Yet God has tempered the body, giving more abundant honour to that which lacked it, so that there may be no schism in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another” (1 Cor. 12:22).

In whom could anyone say more fully that these things have been fulfilled through the dispensation of divine grace than in the weakness of the female sex itself, which both fault and nature had made contemptible? Consider each rank in this sex: not only virgins, widows, and married women, but even the abominations of prostitutes; and in them you will see Christ’s grace more abundant, so that, in accordance with the Lord’s and Apostle’s sayings, “the last shall be first, and the first last” (Matt. 20:16), and “where sin abounded, grace superabounded” (Rom. 5:20).

If we trace back from the very beginning of the world the benefits or honour conferred upon women by this divine grace, we shall find that woman’s creation at once excelled in a certain dignity, since she was created in Paradise while man was created outside it. Women are thus especially admonished to consider how Paradise is their natural homeland and how much more fitting it is for them to follow the celibate life of Paradise. Hence Ambrose, in his book *On Paradise*, says:

> “And God took the man whom he had made and placed him in Paradise. You see that he who already was is taken. He placed him in Paradise. Observe that man was made outside Paradise and woman within Paradise. The man is found better though made in the lower place, and she who was made in the better place is found inferior.”

Moreover, the Lord restored Eve, the source of all evil, in Mary before he repaired Adam in Christ. And just as fault began from a woman, so grace began from a woman, and the prerogative of virginity flowered anew. In Anna and Mary, widows and virgins, the pattern of holy profession was displayed before examples of monastic religion were proposed to men in John or the apostles.

If, after Eve, we consider the courage of Deborah, Judith, and Esther, we shall surely bring no slight shame upon the strength of the male sex. Deborah [variant: Delbora], judge of the Lord’s people, fought when the men failed; and, after defeating the enemies and liberating the Lord’s people, she triumphed mightily (Judg. 4:9). Judith, unarmed and accompanied by her maid Abra, attacked a terrifying army; cutting off the head of Holofernes with his own sword, she alone laid low all the enemies and delivered her desperate people (Judith 13:10). Esther, secretly prompted by the Spirit and joined to a Gentile king even against the decree of the law, forestalled the counsel of the utterly impious Haman and the king’s cruel edict; and she turned the decree established by royal deliberation to its opposite almost in a single instant of time (Esther 8:5).

It is reckoned a great act of courage that David attacked and defeated Goliath with sling and stone (1 Sam. 17:49). Judith the widow advances against the hostile army without sling and stone, about to fight without any aid of armour (Judith 9:16). Esther delivers her people by a word alone; and when the decree was turned against the enemies, they themselves fell into the snare which they had set. The memory of this distinguished deed deserved among the Jews a solemn annual celebration of joy—a distinction which no deeds of men, however splendid, obtained.

Who would not marvel at the incomparable constancy of the mother of seven sons? As the history of the Maccabees relates (2 Macc. 7:1), the most impious King Antiochus vainly tried to compel the sons, seized together with their mother, to eat pork contrary to the law (Deut. 14:7). Forgetful of her own nature and heedless of human affection, having only the Lord before her eyes, this mother sent her sons beforehand to the crown by as many sacred exhortations as she herself triumphed through martyrdoms, being at last consummated by her own martyrdom. If we review the entire sequence of the Old Testament, what can we compare with the constancy of this woman?

That vehement tempter of blessed Job, considering the weakness of human nature in the face of death, said: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job 2:4). For we naturally shrink so greatly from every distress of death that we often oppose one limb to defend another and fear no inconveniences in preserving this life. But she endured to lose not only her own soul but also the souls of her sons, lest she incur a single offence against the law. What, I ask, was this transgression to which she was being compelled? Was she required to renounce God or burn incense to idols? Nothing, I say, was demanded of them except that they eat meats forbidden them by the law.

O brothers and fellow monks, who so shamelessly crave meat every day against the rule’s institution and our profession, what will you say to the constancy of this woman? Are you so unashamed that, when you hear these things, you are not confounded by shame? Know, brothers, that just as the Lord reproaches unbelievers with the queen of the south, saying, “The queen of the south shall rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it” (Matt. 12:42), so you deserve still more to be reproached by the constancy of this woman: she did far greater things, and you are bound more tightly to religious observance by the vow of your profession.

Her virtue, tested in so great a contest, deserved to obtain this privilege in the Church: that her martyrdom should have solemn readings and a Mass, a distinction granted to none of the ancient saints who died before the Lord’s coming, although in the history of the Maccabees that venerable old man Eleazar, one of the chief scribes, is related to have already been crowned with martyrdom for the same cause (2 Macc. 6:18). But because, as we have said, the female sex is naturally weaker and its virtue therefore more acceptable to God and worthier of honour, that martyrdom in which no woman took part did not deserve commemoration in a feast—as though it were not considered a great matter for the stronger sex to endure stronger sufferings.

Accordingly Scripture, overflowing more fully in praise of the aforesaid woman, says:

> “But the mother was beyond measure wonderful and worthy of blessed memory. Seeing her seven sons perish within the course of one day, she bore it with good courage because of the hope which she had in the Lord. She exhorted each of them bravely, filled with wisdom and infusing a manly spirit into her womanly thought” (2 Macc. 7:20).

Who would not judge that Jephthah’s daughter ought to be taken as a model for the praise of virgins? (Judg. 11:39.) Lest her father be held guilty of even an imprudent vow, and lest the promised sacrifice defraud divine grace of its benefit, she encouraged her victorious father to strike her own throat. What, I ask, would she have done in the contest of martyrs if perhaps unbelievers had compelled her to apostatize by denying God? Would she, when questioned concerning Christ, have said with that prince of the apostles: “I do not know him”? (Luke 22:57.) Released freely by her father for two months, when these were completed she returned to her father to be killed. She voluntarily gives herself up to death and challenges it rather than fears it. Her father’s foolish vow is punished, and the greatest lover of truth redeems her father’s command. How greatly must she have abhorred in herself the lapse which she would not tolerate in her father? How great is this virgin’s ardour toward both her earthly and heavenly Father! By her death she determined at once to free the former from falsehood and preserve the promise made to the latter.

Hence this great fortitude of a maiden’s spirit deserved by a certain prerogative to obtain that, every year, the daughters of Israel should assemble together and celebrate the virgin’s festive funeral with certain solemn hymns, and, moved by the virgin’s suffering, sympathize with pious lamentations. But, to pass over everything else, what was more necessary for our redemption and the salvation of the whole world than the female sex, which bore for us the Saviour himself? The singularity of this honour was put before blessed Hilarion by the woman who first dared to break in upon him, as he marvelled, saying: “Why do you turn your eyes away? Why do you flee one who asks? Do not look upon me as a woman, but as wretched. This sex gave birth to the Saviour.”

What glory could be compared with that which this sex attained in the Lord’s mother? Our Redeemer could certainly, had he wished, have assumed a body from a man, just as he chose to form the first woman from the body of a man (Gen. 2:22). But he transferred this singular grace of his humility to the honour of the weaker sex. He could also have been born from another, more dignified part of a woman’s body than that utterly lowly part through which other human beings, conceived in the same way, are born. Yet, for the incomparable honour of the weaker body, he consecrated its generative part far more by his birth than he had consecrated that of man by circumcision.

[Col. 0246A] But, leaving aside for the moment this singular honour of virgins, let us, as we proposed, turn our pen to the other women. Consider, therefore, how great a grace Christ’s coming immediately bestowed on Elizabeth, a married woman, and how great on Anna, a widow. Zachariah, Elizabeth’s husband and a great priest of the Lord, was still held mute by the distrust of unbelief; but at Mary’s arrival and greeting, Elizabeth was immediately filled with the Holy Spirit, felt the child leap in her womb, and, being the first to utter prophecy concerning Mary’s now-accomplished conception, became more than a prophet (Luke 1:5). For she immediately announced the virgin’s present conception and stirred up the mother of the Lord herself to magnify the Lord for this very thing.

The gift of prophecy seems to have been fulfilled more excellently in Elizabeth, in recognizing the Son of God as soon as he was conceived, than in John, in pointing him out when he had long since been born. Therefore, just as we call Mary Magdalene the apostle of the apostles, so let us not hesitate to call this woman the prophet of the prophets, or likewise blessed Anna the widow, of whom we have spoken more fully above.

And if we extend this grace of prophecy even to the Gentiles, let the prophetess Sibyl come forward and bring forth what was revealed to her concerning Christ. If we compare with her all the prophets, even Isaiah himself—who, as Jerome maintains (epistle 117), ought to be called not so much a prophet as an evangelist—we shall see that in this grace too a woman far surpasses men. Augustine, giving testimony concerning her against heresies, says (chapter 3): “Let us hear what their prophetess Sibyl also says concerning him: ‘The Lord has given another to faithful men to worship.’” Again (ibid.): “Recognize him [variant: recognize it] as your Lord, the Son of God.” Elsewhere she calls the Son of God a *symbolum*, that is, a counsellor. And the prophet says: “They shall call his name Wonderful, Counsellor” (Isa. 9:6).

Again, the same Father Augustine, in book XVIII of *The City of God* (chapter 23), says concerning her: “At that time some report that the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied, though some rather believe her to be the Cumaean. And there are twenty-seven verses of hers which, as someone translated them into Latin verse, contain this:”

“The earth will be wet with the sweat of judgment;

From heaven a king will come, who is to be for all ages,

[Col. 0246D] namely, present in the flesh in order to judge the world.” The first letters of these verses, joined together in Greek, signify: “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.”

Lactantius likewise adduces certain Sibylline prophecies concerning Christ (Institutions, book IV, ch. 18): “Afterward he will come into the hands of unbelievers. With unclean hands they will strike God on the face, and with their defiled [variant: unclean] mouths they will spit out venomous spittle. Yet he will submissively give his holy back to the blows; and, receiving fists, he will remain silent, lest anyone recognize what Word, or whence he has come, speaks to those below; and he will be crowned with a crown of thorns. For food they gave him gall, and for thirst vinegar. They will display this table in hospitality. For this foolish nation did not understand your God, worthy of praise in the minds of mortals, but crowned him with thorns and mixed gall for him. The veil of the Temple will be torn; and in the middle of the day there will be night for three hours; and he will die, having undergone sleep for three days; and then, returning from the lower world, he will come to the light, shown first in the beginning of the resurrection.”

Surely, unless I am mistaken, Virgil, that greatest of our poets, had heard and considered this prophecy of the Sibyl when, in his Fourth Eclogue, he foretold that in the near future, under Caesar Augustus, in the consulship of Pollio, there would be the marvelous birth of a certain boy sent from heaven to earth, who would also take away the sins of the world and would wondrously establish, as it were, a new age in the world. He was prompted, as he himself says, by the prophecy of the Cumaean song—that is, of the Sibyl who is called Cumaean [variant: Cumaean]. For he speaks thus, as though exhorting everyone to rejoice with him and to sing or write about this great boy who was to be born; in comparison with him, he reckons all other subjects as quite lowly [variant: weak] and worthless:

> Sicilian Muses, let us sing of matters somewhat greater;  
> Not all delight in shrubs and humble tamarisks.  
> Now comes the final age foretold by the Cumaean song.  
> A great order of ages is born anew from the beginning.  
> Now the virgin too returns; Saturn’s kingdoms return.  
> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven, etc.  
> (VIRGIL, *Eclogue* IV, 1.)

Consider each utterance of the Sibyl, and how fully and plainly it comprises the sum of the Christian faith concerning Christ. In prophesying or writing, she omitted neither his divinity nor his humanity, neither of his comings nor either of his judgments: first, the judgment by which he was unjustly judged in the Passion; and second, that by which he will justly judge the world in majesty. Omitting neither his descent into the lower world nor the glory of his resurrection, she seems to have surpassed not merely the prophets but even the Evangelists themselves, who wrote nothing whatever of that descent.

Who would not also marvel at that familiar and lengthy conversation in which he alone deigned so carefully to instruct that lone Gentile and Samaritan woman—a matter at which even the Apostles were greatly astonished? He wished to ask a drink from an unbelieving woman, reproached for the number of her husbands, though we know that he sought no further sustenance from anyone. The Apostles arrive and offer him food which they had bought, saying, “Rabbi, eat” (John 4:31). Yet we do not see him receive what was offered, but rather put forward, as though by way of excuse: “I have food to eat which you do not know” (ibid., 32).

He asks the woman for drink. Excusing herself from granting him this favor, she says: “How is it that you, being a Jew, ask a drink from me, who am a Samaritan woman? For Jews do not associate with Samaritans” (ibid., 9). And again: “You have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep” (ibid., 11). Thus he desires a drink from an unbelieving woman who refuses it, while he does not care for the food offered by the Apostles. What grace, I ask, is this which he displays toward the weaker sex: that he should ask water of [Col. 0248A] this woman who gives life to all? What is it, I say, except that he openly indicates that women’s virtue is so much dearer to him as their nature is known to be weaker, and that he thirsts all the more ardently for their salvation as their virtue is known to be more wonderful? Hence, when he asks drink from a woman, he indicates especially that he wishes his thirst to be satisfied through the salvation of women.

Calling that drink also food, he says: “I have food to eat which you do not know.” Later, explaining this food, he adds: “My food is to do the will of my Father.” He thereby indicates that this is, as it were, the singular will of his Father where the salvation of the weaker sex is concerned.

We also read that the Lord had a familiar conversation with Nicodemus, that ruler of the Jews, in which he instructed him concerning his salvation when he came secretly to him (John 3:1); but that conversation did not then obtain so great a fruit [variant: this fruit]. For this Samaritan woman, indeed, was then filled with the spirit of prophecy, inasmuch as she professed both that Christ had already come to the Jews and that he was to come to the Gentiles, when she said: “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ. When he comes, he will announce all things to us” (John 4:25). And many from that city ran to Christ because of the woman’s word and believed in him; and he himself remained with them for two days—though elsewhere he says to the disciples: “Do not go into the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans” (Matt. 10:5).

Elsewhere John relates that certain Gentiles who had gone up to Jerusalem to worship on the feast day announced through Philip and Andrew to Christ that they wished to see him. Yet he does not record that they were admitted, nor that such abundant access to Christ was granted to them when they asked it as was granted to this Samaritan woman, who did not ask it at all. His preaching among the Gentiles seems to have begun with her: he not only converted her, but through her, as has been said, gained many. The Magi, immediately enlightened by the star and converted to Christ, are said to have drawn many to him by their exhortation or teaching; but they alone came in person. From this too it is clear how great a grace a woman obtained from Christ among the Gentiles: going ahead, announcing his arrival to the city, and preaching what she had heard, she herself so swiftly won many from her people.

And if we turn over the pages of the Old Testament or of Gospel Scripture, we shall see that, in those supreme benefits of the raising of the dead, divine grace was bestowed especially upon women, and that these miracles were performed only for them or because of them. For first we read that, through Elijah and Elisha, at the intercession of mothers their sons were raised (3 Kings 17:22; 4 Kings 4:22). And the Lord himself, raising the son of a certain widow, the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue (Mark 5:42), and Lazarus at the request of his sisters (John 11:44), bestowed the benefit of this immeasurable miracle chiefly upon women. Hence the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: “Women received their dead by resurrection” (Heb. 11:35). For the girl who was raised received back her dead body, and the other women received, for their consolation, those dead persons whom they mourned, raised to life.

From this too it is clear how great a grace he always showed women: first making them glad by the resurrection both of themselves and of those dear to them, and at last greatly exalting them by his own resurrection, since, as has been said, he appeared to them first (Matt. 28:5; Mark 16:5). This sex too seems, amid the persecuting people, to have earned favor through a certain natural affection of compassion toward the Lord. For, as Luke recalls, when the men led him away to crucify him, their women followed, weeping and lamenting him. [Col. 0249B] Turning to them, and mercifully repaying, as it were, the return due for this piety at the very moment of his Passion, he foretells the doom [variant: destruction] so that they might guard against it: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me; but weep over yourselves and over your children. For behold, days are coming in which they will say: Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne” (Luke 23:28).

Matthew also records that the wife of the most unjust judge had previously worked faithfully for his deliverance, saying: “While he was sitting on the judgment seat, his wife sent to him, saying: Have nothing to do with that righteous man. For today I have suffered much in a dream because of him” (Matt. 27:19). While he was preaching, we read that one woman alone from the whole crowd raised her voice in such great praise of him as to cry blessed the womb that bore him and the breasts that suckled him. From him she immediately deserved to hear a merciful correction of her confession, though it was most true; for he promptly answered her: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11:28).

John alone among Christ’s Apostles obtained this privilege of love, to be called the Lord’s beloved. But concerning Martha and Mary, John himself writes “that Jesus loved Martha, and her sister Mary, and Lazarus” (John 11:5). This same Apostle, who records that by the privilege of love, as has been said, he alone was loved by the Lord, distinguished women with this very privilege, which he did not ascribe to any of the other Apostles. And although in this honor he associated their brother with them, he nevertheless placed them before him, whom he believed to excel in love.

Finally, to return to faithful or Christian women, I delight to proclaim—and in proclaiming to marvel at—the regard of divine mercy even in the abjection of public prostitutes, which is astonishing. What was more abject than Mary Magdalene or Mary of Egypt, according to the condition of their former lives? Yet whom did divine grace afterwards exalt more highly either in honor or in merit? The former remained, as we have already recalled (*Lives of the Fathers*), as it were in an apostolic community; the latter, as it is written, contended in an anchorite’s struggle above human strength. Thus, in the vocation of each kind of monk, the virtue of holy women may excel, and the saying of the Lord to unbelievers, “Prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21:31), may seem a reproach even to faithful men; and according to the difference of sex and manner of life, the last may become first and the first last (Matt. 20:16).

Who, finally, does not know that women embraced Christ’s exhortation and the Apostle’s counsel with such zeal for chastity that, to preserve alike the integrity of body and mind, they offered themselves to God as a holocaust through martyrdom, and, triumphing with a double crown, strove to follow the Lamb, the spouse of virgins, wherever he goes? (Rev. 14:4.) This perfection of virtue we have found rare among men, frequent among women. We also read that some women had such zeal for this prerogative of the flesh that they did not hesitate to lay hands upon themselves, lest they lose the incorruption they had vowed to God and so fail to come as virgins to the virgin Bridegroom.

He also showed the devotion of holy virgins to be so pleasing to him that, when a multitude of Gentile people ran to the aid of blessed Agatha, he set her veil against the terrible fire of boiling Etna and thereby delivered them from the conflagration of both body and soul. We know of no monk’s cowl that obtained the grace of so great a benefit. We read indeed that, at the touch of Elijah’s cloak, the Jordan was divided and gave a passage on dry ground both to him and to Elisha (4 Kings 2:8); but through a virgin’s veil an immense multitude of people, still unbelieving, were saved in mind as well as body, and thus, once converted, the way to heaven lay open to them.

This also commendably attests the dignity of holy women: they are consecrated in their own words, saying, “He has pledged me with his ring; I am betrothed to him” (AMBROSE, sermon 90). These are indeed the words of blessed Agnes, by which virgins making their profession are betrothed to Christ.

If anyone should wish to learn the form and dignity of your religious life among the Gentiles, and to introduce from there also certain examples for your exhortation, he will readily discover that even among them some institution of this purpose preceded yours—excepting what pertains to the rule of faith—and that many things among them, as among the Jews, preceded what the Church, gathered from both, retained but transformed for the better. Who does not know that the Church adopted from the Synagogue all ranks of clergy from doorkeeper to bishop; the ecclesiastical use of tonsure by which clerics are made; the fasts of the Four Seasons; the offering of unleavened bread; the adornment of priestly vestments; and certain rites of dedication or other sacraments?

Who also does not know that, by a most useful dispensation, God retained among converted Gentiles not only the grades of secular dignities in kings and other princes, certain decrees of laws, and the teachings of philosophical discipline, but also received from them certain grades of ecclesiastical dignities, a form of continence, and the religious observance of bodily purity? For it is established that bishops or archbishops now preside where flamens or archflamens formerly stood; that temples once established for demons were afterward consecrated to the Lord and made illustrious by memorials of saints.

We know also that among the Gentiles especially the prerogative of virginity flourished, whereas the curse of the Law constrained the Jews to marriage (Deut. 25:5); and this virtue, or purity of flesh, was so acceptable to the Gentiles that great communities of women in their temples dedicated themselves to a celibate life. Hence Jerome, in his Commentary on Galatians, book III, chapter 6: “What ought we to do, in whose condemnation even Juno has women married only once, Vesta women virgins only once, and other chaste idols?”

By *univirae* (“women of one husband”) and *univirgines* (“women virgins only once”), he means, as it were, nuns of one husband, who had known husbands, and virgin nuns. For *monos*, from which *monachus*, “monk,” is called—that is, “solitary”—means “one.” In book I *Against Jovinianus*, after introducing many examples concerning the chastity or continence of Gentile women, Jerome says: “I know that I have said much in the catalogue of women, so that those who despise faith in Christian modesty may learn chastity at least from pagans.”

In the same work he commended that virtue of continence so highly that the Lord seems especially to have approved this purity of flesh in every people, and to have exalted it even in certain unbelievers, whether by a comparison of merits or by the performance of miracles. “Why,” he says, “should I mention the Erythraean and Cumaean Sibyl, and the other eight? For Varro thinks there were ten, whose distinction was virginity, and the reward of virginity, divination.” Again: “When Claudia, a Vestal virgin, came under suspicion of unchastity, she is said to have drawn by her girdle a ship which thousands of men had been unable to pull.”

And Synodius, bishop of Clermont, speaks thus in the prefatory poem to his little book:

> Such was neither Tanaquil, nor she  
> Whom you, Tricipitinus, begot;  
> Nor such she who, consecrated to Phrygian Vesta,  
> Beside the swelling Albula’s waters,  
> Drew a ship with her virgin hair.  
> (*Poems*, XXIV, 39.—See *Patrology*, vol. LVIII, col. 746.)

Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 11: “Now, if we come to those miracles which they set against our martyrs as performed by their gods, will not even these be found entirely to serve and benefit us? For among the great miracles of their gods, surely great is that which Varro recounts: that a Vestal virgin, when she was endangered by a false suspicion of unchastity, filled a sieve with water from the Tiber and carried it to her judges without any part of it dripping away. Who held back the weight of the water despite all those openings? Then will almighty God be unable to remove a heavy weight from an earthly body, so that a body made alive may dwell in the same element in which the life-giving Spirit wills?”

Nor is it surprising if God exalted even the chastity of unbelievers by these or other miracles, or permitted it to be exalted through the ministry of demons, so that believers might now be all the more encouraged toward it, as they learned that it was more highly honored even in unbelievers. We know that grace was bestowed upon the office of Caiaphas, not upon his person, and that false Apostles likewise sometimes shone with miracles; and these were granted not to their persons but to their office.

What wonder, then, if the Lord granted this not to the persons of unbelieving women but to their virtue of continence, at least in order to free an innocent virgin and crush the wickedness of a false accusation? For the love of continence is certainly good even in unbelievers, just as the observance of the marriage covenant is God’s gift among all people. Therefore it should not seem remarkable if God honors his gifts, not the error of unbelief, by signs performed for unbelievers, not believers—especially when, through these signs, as has been said, innocence is set free, the malice of perverse people is restrained, and people are more strongly urged toward that good which is thus magnified; and through this good, unbelievers themselves sin less, the more they withdraw from the pleasures of the flesh.

This is why the blessed Jerome, together with many other arguments, properly introduced these examples against the aforementioned incontinent heretic: that one who does not marvel at such things in Christians may blush at them among pagans.

Who likewise would deny that the power even of unbelieving rulers is a gift of God, although they use it perversely; or that their love of justice, their gentleness, instructed by the natural law, or their other qualities appropriate to princes, are gifts of God? Who would deny that these are good because they are mixed with evils, especially since, as blessed Augustine maintains and evident reason proves, evils cannot exist except in a good nature? Who would not approve the poetic saying:

> The good hate to sin out of love of virtue.  
> (HORACE, *Epistles*, book I, epistle 15.)

Who would not rather approve than deny the miracle of Vespasian, not yet emperor, which Suetonius relates (*Vespasian*, ch. 7), namely that a blind man and a lame man were cured by him, so that princes may wish more eagerly to emulate his virtue? Or the story that blessed Gregory acted on behalf of Trajan’s soul (JOHN THE DEACON, book II of the *Life of St. Gregory*, ch. 44)? People know how to gather a pearl from the mud and distinguish grains from chaff. God cannot fail to recognize his gifts joined to unbelief, nor can he hate anything that he has made. The more these shine with signs, the more clearly he shows them to be his own; they cannot be defiled by human wickedness; and they show believers what kind of God they should behold, since he displays himself so to unbelievers.

How great a dignity that chastity devoted to temples attained among unbelievers is shown by the punishment for its violation. Juvenal, recalling this punishment in Satire IV against Crispinus, says of him:

> . . . . . with whom a violated priestess had lately lain,  
> While her blood was still warm, about to go beneath the earth.

[Col. 0253A] Hence Augustine, *City of God*, book III: “For the ancient Romans themselves buried alive the priestesses of Vesta when they were detected in unchastity. But adulterous women, although punished by some penalty, they did not punish with death.” So much more severely did they avenge what they regarded as hidden divine chambers than human beds.

But among us the care of Christian rulers has provided all the more for our [variant: your] chastity, because it is beyond doubt holier. Hence Emperor Justinian says: “If anyone should dare—not, I say, to abduct, but even merely to attempt—to marry sacred virgins, let him be struck with capital punishment.” The sanction of ecclesiastical discipline also, which seeks remedies of penance rather than penalties of death, unquestionably forestalls your falls with a severe judgment. Hence Pope Innocent’s statement to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, chapter 13: “Women who are spiritually married to Christ and veiled by a priest, if they afterwards either marry publicly or are secretly corrupted, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless he to whom they had joined themselves has departed this life.”

But those women who, though not yet covered by the sacred veil, nevertheless have always professed that they remain in a virginal purpose—although they were not veiled—must perform penance for some period, because their pledge was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a contract of good faith is not ordinarily dissolved for any reason, how much more can this promise, which they have contracted with God, not be dissolved without punishment? For if the Apostle Paul said that women who had departed from their purpose of widowhood incurred condemnation because they had made void their first faith (1 Tim. 5:12), how much more so virgins who have not kept faith with their earlier profession?

Hence that notable Pelagius says to the daughter of Mauritius: “The adulteress of Christ is more criminal than the adulteress of a husband. Therefore the Roman Church recently established so severe a sentence regarding such women that it scarcely judged them worthy even of penance, if they had violated a body sanctified to God by lustful defilement.”

And if we should investigate how much care, diligence, and love holy teachers, inspired by the examples of the Lord himself and the Apostles, always showed toward devout women, we shall find that they embraced and fostered their devotion with the utmost zeal of love, and continually instructed and enlarged their religious life with manifold efforts of teaching and exhortation.

And, to pass over the rest, let the chief teachers of the Church be brought forward: Origen, Ambrose, and Jerome. The first of these, that greatest philosopher among Christians, embraced women’s religious life with such zeal that he laid hands upon himself, as Ecclesiastical History reports (book VI, ch. 7), lest any suspicion turn him away from teaching or exhorting women.

Who does not also know what a great harvest of divine books blessed Jerome left to the Church at the request of Paula and Eustochium? Writing them, among other things, a discourse on the Assumption of the Lord’s Mother according to their petition, he himself declares this, saying (epistle 10): “But because I cannot refuse anything you command, bound by your excessive love, I shall attempt what you urge.” Yet we know that certain very great teachers, eminent in both rank and holiness of life, sometimes wrote to him from afar to request small writings and did not obtain them.

Hence blessed Augustine says in the second book of his *Retractations*, chapter 41: “I wrote two books to the priest Jerome while he was living at Bethlehem: one on the origin of the soul, the other on the saying of the Apostle James where he says, ‘Whoever keeps the whole Law but offends in one point has become guilty of all’ (James 2:10), consulting him concerning both. But in the former he did not solve the question I proposed. In the latter I did not conceal what seemed to me concerning its solution; but I consulted him whether he approved it. He replied [variant: wrote back], praising this consultation of mine, but answered that he did not have leisure to respond. I, however, did not wish to publish these books while he was in the body, lest perhaps he should answer at some time and they might rather be published with his response itself. But after he died, I published them.”

Behold, so great a man waited for so long a time for a few small replies from the aforementioned man and did not receive them. Yet we know that Jerome labored, at the request of the aforementioned women, in translating or dictating so many and such great volumes, showing them in this matter far greater reverence than he showed a bishop. Perhaps he embraces their virtue with so much more zeal, and cannot bear to grieve them, as he considers their nature more fragile.

Thus sometimes the zeal of his love toward women of this kind is found to be so great that in their praises he seems somewhat to exceed the path of truth, as though he had experienced in himself what he mentions elsewhere: “Love,” he says, “has no measure” (epistle 17). At the very beginning of the *Life of Saint Paula*, wishing, as it were, to prepare his reader’s attention, he says (epistle 27): “If all the limbs of my body were turned into tongues, and all my members resounded with human speech, I should say nothing worthy of the virtues of holy and venerable Paula.”

He described also the venerable and miracle-shining lives of certain holy Fathers, in which far more marvelous things are recounted. Yet he seems to have extolled none of them with as great praise of words as he commended this widow. Writing also to the virgin Demetrias, he adorned the opening of his letter with such great praise of her that he seems to fall into no slight flattery (epistle 8): “Among all the subjects which, from childhood to this age, I have written either in my own hand or that of secretaries, nothing is more difficult than the present work. For in writing to Demetrias, a virgin of Christ who is first in nobility and wealth in the city of Rome, if I say everything fitting to her virtues, I shall be thought to flatter.”

For it was sweetest to this holy man to advance fragile nature toward the arduous pursuits of virtue by whatever art of words he could employ. But so that deeds may give us surer arguments in this matter than words, he cultivated women of this kind with such great love that his immense holiness impressed upon itself a blemish upon its own reputation. He himself recalls this, writing to Asella about false friends and those who slandered him, among other things saying (epistle 99): “Although some think me wicked and overwhelmed with every disgrace, you do well in judging even evil people good according to your own mind. For it is dangerous to judge another’s servant, and there is no easy pardon for having spoken perversely of the upright. Some kissed my hands and slandered me with a viperous mouth. They grieved with their lips but rejoiced in heart. Let them say what they ever thought differently in me from what became a Christian. Nothing is alleged against me except my sex. And even this would never be alleged unless Paula were setting out for Jerusalem.”

Again (ibid.): “Before I knew the house of holy Paula, the whole city’s enthusiasm resounded in my favor. In the judgment of almost all, I was considered worthy of the highest priesthood. But after I began, according to her merit of holiness, to venerate, honor, receive [perhaps: esteem] her, all virtues immediately deserted me.” And after some further words (ibid.): “Greet Paula and Eustochium, whether they will it or not, mine in Christ.”

We likewise read that the Lord himself showed such familiarity to the blessed prostitute that the Pharisee who had invited him now entirely distrusted him, saying within himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would certainly know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him” (Luke 7:39). What wonder, then, if, for the gain of such souls, members of Christ, stirred by his example, do not flee damage to their own reputation? Origen, as has been said (EUSEBIUS, book VI, ch. 7), when he wished to avoid this, endured inflicting a graver injury upon his body.

And the remarkable love of the holy Fathers became known not only in their teaching or exhortation of women, but also sometimes proved so vehement in their consolation of them that their astonishing compassion seems to promise certain things contrary to faith in order to soothe their grief. Such, indeed, is the consolation of blessed Ambrose, which he dared to write to the sisters of Emperor Valentinian upon his death, maintaining the salvation of one who died a catechumen. This seems far removed from Catholic faith and Gospel truth.

For they were not unaware how acceptable the virtue of the weaker sex had always been to God. Hence, although we see countless virgins following the Lord’s Mother in this purpose of excellence, we recognize few men who have obtained the grace of this virtue, by which they could follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14:4). And when some women, through zeal for this virtue, laid hands upon themselves so that they might preserve even bodily integrity which they had vowed to God, not only was this not reproved in them, but among many their martyrdoms earned the distinction of churches bearing their names.

Betrothed virgins too, if before they are carnally joined to their husbands they decide to choose a monastery and, rejecting a human being, make God their spouse, have freedom to do so—a freedom which we do not read was granted at all to men. Many of them were also so inflamed with zeal for chastity that they not only assumed male dress against the decree of the Law in order to guard their chastity (Deut. 22:5), but also so excelled among monks in great virtues that they deserved to become abbots. Thus we read of blessed Eugenia (*Lives of the Fathers*), who, with Saint Helenus the bishop aware of it—indeed, at his command—put on male clothing and, baptized by him, was joined to the company of monks.

I think, dearest sister in Christ, that I have written enough in reply to the first of your latest [variant: petition of your latest] requests: namely, concerning the authority of your order and, in addition, the commendation of its particular dignity, so that you may embrace the purpose of your profession all the more zealously as you better know its excellence. Now, that I may complete the second also, with the Lord’s consent, may I obtain this through your merits and prayers. Farewell.

## LETTER VIII, Which Is of the Same Peter to Heloise. An Institution or Rule for Nuns.

[Col. 0255]

**SUMMARY.—**Abelard, having been asked by Heloise for two things, answered one of them in the preceding letter and now carries out the other. For the second part of Heloise’s petition had been that he should write a rule for the nuns of the Paraclete; and he accomplishes this clearly in the present book rather than in a letter, gathering together, like flowers, the sayings of many holy Fathers. He calls the treatise threefold because it deals chiefly with three principal monastic virtues: continence, voluntary poverty, and silence. He appoints seven sister-officials over their entire community, prudently to preside over the others both in matters concerning souls and in those concerning temporal or bodily affairs. He permits them meat on three days of each week and the moderate use of wine, and carefully and suitably arranges the remaining matters belonging to the order of monastic life.

[Col. 0255C] Having now, to the best of our ability, dealt with some part of your request, it remains, God granting, to apply ourselves to fulfilling the desires both of you and of your spiritual daughters concerning the part that remains. For, in accordance with the order of your aforesaid petition, it remains that some form of instruction—like a rule for your way of life—be written by us and given to you, so that you may know more certainly from a written text than from custom what course you ought to follow. Therefore, relying partly on good customs, partly on the testimonies of Scripture and the supports of reason, we have resolved to gather all these things into one, so that we may adorn the spiritual temple of God which you are (2 Cor. 6:16), as it were with certain excellent pictures, and, from many incomplete materials, complete one little work as best we can.

In this work, indeed, imitating the painter Zeuxis, we intend to do in the spiritual temple what he planned to do in a material one. For, as Tully recalls in his *Rhetoric* (book I), the people of Croton engaged him to adorn with the finest paintings a certain temple which they revered most devoutly. To do this more carefully, he selected for himself five most beautiful maidens from that people; while painting, he looked at them standing before him, so that he might imitate their beauty in his painting. This was plausibly done for two reasons: first, because, as the aforesaid teacher recalls (*ibid.*), that painter had acquired the greatest skill in portraying women; and also because a maidenly form is naturally judged more graceful and delicate than a masculine build [variant: “compactness”].

The aforementioned philosopher says that he chose several maidens because he did not believe that he could find in one girl all the limbs equally beautiful; nor did he think that nature had ever bestowed upon anyone so great a gift of beauty that all the limbs were equally beautiful, as though nature herself perfected nothing wholly in the composition of bodies, but conferred all advantages on one person in such a way that she had nothing left to grant to others.

So too, for depicting the beauty of the soul and describing the perfection of Christ’s bride—in whom, as in a kind of mirror of one spiritual virgin kept always before your eyes, you may discern your own beauty or ugliness—we have proposed to instruct your manner of life from many teachings of the holy Fathers [Col. 0257D] and the best monastic customs, selecting each item as it occurs to memory and gathering it, as it were, into one bundle, wherever I see it suited to the holiness of your vocation. Nor only those regulations which concern nuns, but also those concerning monks. For as you are joined to us by name and by the profession of continence, so nearly all our regulations apply to you as well.

Therefore, as we have said, plucking from these many things as if they were flowers, with which we may adorn the lilies of your chastity, we ought with far greater care to portray Christ’s virgin than Zeuxis did to paint the image of an idol. He thought five maidens, whose appearance he might imitate, sufficient. But we, possessing an abundant store of the teachings of many Fathers [Col. 0258A] and trusting in divine aid, do not despair of leaving you a more perfect little work, through which you may attain to the lot or description of those five prudent virgins whom the Lord sets before us in the Gospel for the portrayal of Christ’s virgin (Matt. 25:8). That we may accomplish this as we wish, may we obtain it through your prayers. Farewell in Christ, brides of Christ.

We have resolved to make this instruction of yours a threefold treatise: one concerning the description and safeguarding of your religious life, and the ordering of the celebration of divine service. In these things, I judge, the sum of monastic religion consists: namely, that one should live continently and without private property, and devote oneself especially to silence. [Col. 0258B] This is, according to the Lord’s discipline in the evangelical rule, to gird one’s loins (Luke 12:35), to renounce all things (Luke 14:33), and to avoid an idle word (Matt. 12:36).

The continence of chastity is that of which the Apostle speaks when urging it: “She who is unmarried, and the virgin, thinks of the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 7:34). “In body,” he says—throughout the whole body, not in one member—so that no limb may turn aside to any wantonness in deeds or words. She is holy “in spirit,” moreover, when neither consent defiles her mind nor pride inflates it, as happened to those five foolish virgins who, while they ran to the sellers of oil, remained outside the door. When, after the door had been shut, they knocked and cried in vain, “Lord, Lord, [Col. 0258C] open to us,” the bridegroom himself answered terribly: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:11).

But when, leaving all things, we naked follow the naked Christ, as the holy apostles did, then for his sake we set aside not only earthly possessions and the affections of fleshly kinship, but even our own wills; so that we may not live according to our own judgment, but be governed by the command of our superior, and submit ourselves entirely for Christ’s sake to the one who presides over us in Christ’s place, as to Christ himself. For he himself says to such persons: “He who hears you hears me; and he who rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16). Even if he should—God forbid—live badly, while commanding rightly, the judgment of God is nevertheless not to be despised because of the vice of the man. Concerning anyone at all he himself commands: “Whatever they tell you, keep and do; but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23:3).

He himself carefully describes this spiritual conversion to God from the world, saying: “Unless anyone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33). And again: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, or mother, and wife, and children, and brothers, and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple” (*ibid.* 14:26). To hate father or mother, then, means not to wish to follow the affections of fleshly kinship; just as to hate one’s own life means not to wish to follow one’s own will. Elsewhere too he commands this, [Col. 0259A] saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23).

For in this way, coming after him, we draw near to him; that is, we follow him chiefly by imitating him, who said: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38). It is as if he said: Do all things through obedience. For what does “let him deny himself” mean, except to set aside fleshly affections and one’s own will, and entrust oneself to be governed by another’s judgment, not one’s own? And in this way assuredly one receives one’s cross not from another, but takes it up oneself: that cross by which the world is crucified to one and one to the world, when by the voluntary vow of one’s own profession one forbids oneself worldly and earthly desires. This is not to follow one’s own will.

For what else do fleshly people seek except to accomplish what they wish? And what is earthly pleasure except the fulfillment of one’s own will, even when we do what we wish with the greatest labor or danger? Or what else is it to bear a cross—that is, to endure some suffering—except for something to be done against our will, however easy or useful it may appear to us? Hence another Jesus, far inferior, warns in Ecclesiasticus: “Do not go after your desires, and turn away from your own will. If you grant your soul its desires, it will make you a joy to your enemies” (Ecclus. 18:30).

But when we thus utterly renounce both our possessions and ourselves, then, truly casting away every form of private ownership, we enter upon that apostolic life [Col. 0259C] which brings all things into common, as it is written: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). “Nor did any of them call anything that he possessed his own; but all things were common to them. And distribution was made to each according as anyone had need.” For not all had equal needs; and therefore not all were given equal shares, but each according to need. They had one heart through faith, because one believes with the heart; one soul, because they had from charity the same mutual will, since each wished for another what he wished for himself and sought not his own advantage more than that of others; or because all things were referred by all to the common benefit, with no one seeking or desiring what was his own, but what was Jesus Christ’s.

Otherwise they would by no means live without private ownership, which consists more in ambition than in possession. An idle or superfluous word is the same thing as excessive speech. Hence Augustine says in the first book of his *Retractations* (preface): “Far be it from me to count speech excessive when necessary things are said, however great the number or length of the words.”

Hence Solomon says: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking; but he who restrains his lips is most prudent” (Prov. 10:19). Great care must therefore be taken concerning that in which sin is never absent; and this disease must be guarded against all the more diligently because it is avoided more dangerously and more difficultly. Foreseeing this, blessed Benedict says (ch. 42): “At all times monks ought to devote themselves [Col. 0260A] to silence.” For it is evidently more to devote oneself to silence than merely to keep silence. Devotion is the vehement application of the mind to accomplishing something. We do many things negligently or unwillingly; but we do nothing diligently except willingly and attentively.

How difficult and useful it is to restrain the tongue, the Apostle James carefully observes when he says: “We all offend in many things. If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2). Again: “Every nature of beasts, birds, serpents, and other creatures is tamed, and has been tamed, by human nature” (*ibid.* 3:7). Considering at once how great is the material for evil in the tongue and the destruction of all good, he says above and below: “The tongue indeed is a small member; what a great fire, how great a forest it sets ablaze; [it is] the whole world of iniquity, a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (*ibid.* 3:5).

What is more dangerous than poison, or what must be guarded against more? As poison extinguishes life, so talkativeness utterly overthrows religious life. Hence he says above: “If anyone thinks himself religious, not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, that person’s religion is vain” (James 1:26). And in Proverbs it is written: “Like a city lying open and without a circuit of walls is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Prov. 25:28).

This is what that elder carefully considered who, when Anthony said of talkative brothers traveling with him, “You have found good brothers with you, abba,” replied: “They are good indeed, [Col. 0260C] but their dwelling has no door. Whoever wishes enters the stable and looses the donkey” (*Lives of the Fathers*, part II, book *On Continence*). For our soul is, as it were, tied to the Lord’s manger, refreshing itself there by a certain rumination of holy meditation; but it is loosed from that manger and runs hither and thither through the whole world in thoughts unless the enclosure of silence restrains it.

Words introduce things understood into the mind of the soul, so that it attends to what it understands and clings to it in thought. By thought we speak with God, as by words with human beings. And while we attend here to human words, we must necessarily be drawn away from there. Nor are we able to attend simultaneously to God and to human beings. Not only idle words, but even those which seem to have some usefulness, must be avoided, because one easily passes from necessary words to idle ones, and from idle words to harmful ones.

“For the tongue,” as James says, “is a restless evil.” The smaller or subtler it is than the other members, the more mobile it is; and while other members are wearied by movement, it is wearied when it does not move, and rest itself becomes burdensome to it. And the subtler it is in us, and the more flexible from the softness of our bodies, the more mobile and prone to speech it is, and open as a seedbed of every wickedness.

The Apostle, observing this fault especially in you, wholly forbids women to speak in church, and does not permit them even in matters pertaining to God to ask questions except of their husbands at home. Even in learning these things or doing anything whatsoever, he subjects them especially to silence, writing thus to Timothy concerning them: [Col. 0261A] “Let a woman learn in silence with all subjection. But I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to exercise authority over a man, but to be in silence” (1 Tim. 2:11). If he thus provides for silence among lay and married women, what ought you to do?

Again, indicating to the same man why he had commanded this, he rebukes them as talkative and speaking when they ought not. Therefore, providing some remedy for so great a plague, let us at least utterly tame the tongue by continual silence in these places or at these times: namely, in prayer, in the cloister, dormitory, refectory, during every meal, and in the kitchen; and after Compline this should especially be observed by all from that point onward. In these places or at these times, let us use signs instead of words if necessary. Care must also be taken diligently to teach and learn these signs, through which, even if words are needed, one may be summoned for conversation to a fitting place designated for this purpose. When those necessary words have been briefly spoken, let one return to the previous practice, or let what is suitable be done.

An excess in words or signs must not be corrected lukewarmly, but especially an excess in words, in which the greater danger threatens. Blessed Gregory, eagerly desiring with great and grave concern to remedy this danger, thus instructs us in the seventh book of the *Moralia* (ch. 18): “When we neglect to avoid idle words, we come to harmful ones. Hence provocations are sown, quarrels arise, the torches of hatreds are kindled, and all peace of hearts is extinguished.” Therefore Solomon rightly says: “He who lets out water is the beginning of quarrels” (Prov. 17:[Col. 0261C]14). To let out water is to relax the tongue into a flood of speech. Conversely, and in a good sense, he says: “Deep water is from the mouth of a man” (Prov. 18:4).

Therefore, he who lets out water is the beginning of quarrels, because one who does not restrain the tongue destroys concord. Hence it is written: “He who imposes silence on a fool calms angers” (Prov. 26:10). By this he plainly warns us to apply the strictest discipline especially in correcting this fault, lest its punishment be deferred in any way and religious life thereby be chiefly endangered.
