For from it spring detractions, disputes, insults, and sometimes conspiracies and plots; these do not so much shake as overthrow the entire structure of religious life.

When this fault has been cut off, perhaps wicked thoughts are not wholly extinguished, but they will cease from corrupting others. Abbot Macarius considered the avoidance of this one fault sufficient, as it were, for religious life [variant: “having considered”], and gave the following warning, as it is written (*Lives of the Fathers*, part II, book *On Continence*): “Macarius the Great, abbot in Scetis, said to the brothers: ‘After the services, flee the churches, brothers.’ One of the brothers said to him: ‘Father, where else can we flee from this solitude?’ And he put his finger on his mouth, saying: ‘This is what I say must be fled.’ And so he entered his cell and, shutting the door, sat alone.”

This virtue of silence, which, as James says, makes a person perfect (James 3:2), and concerning which Isaiah foretold, “The work [Col. 0262A] of righteousness is silence” (Isa. 17:32), was embraced with such fervor by the holy Fathers that, as it is written (*Lives of the Fathers*, part II), Abbot Agatho put a stone in his mouth for three years until he learned silence.

Although a place does not save, it nevertheless affords many opportunities for observing religion more easily and safeguarding it more securely. Many aids and hindrances to religious life depend upon it. Thus the sons of the prophets—whom, as Jerome says (letter IV, 13), we read were monks in the Old Testament—transferred themselves to the secrecy of the wilderness, setting up their huts beside the streams of the Jordan.

John too and his disciples, whom we also regard as founders of our vocation, and thereafter Paul, Anthony, [Col. 0262B] Macarius, and those who flourished especially in our vocation, fled the tumult of the world and a world full of temptations, and brought the couch of their contemplation to the quiet of the wilderness, so that they might devote themselves more sincerely to God. The Lord himself, whom no movement of temptation could approach, teaching us by his own example, sought secret places when he especially wished to do anything, and avoided the crowds of the people.

Thus the Lord himself consecrated the wilderness for us by a fast of forty days; he fed the crowds in the wilderness; and, for purity of prayer, withdrew not only from crowds but even from the apostles. He also instructed and appointed the apostles apart on a mountain; he marked solitude with the glory of his transfiguration; by the manifestation of his resurrection he gladdened the disciples gathered together on a mountain; from a mountain he ascended into heaven; and he performed all his other mighty works in wildernesses or secluded places.

Appearing also to Moses and the ancient Fathers in wildernesses, leading the people through the wilderness to the promised land, giving them the law while they remained there long, raining manna, drawing water from the rock, consoling the people by frequent appearances, and working wonders, he plainly taught how greatly he, to whom we can devote ourselves more purely there, loves solitude for our sake.

Likewise, carefully describing and strongly approving the freedom of the wild ass, which loves solitude, he says to blessed Job: [Col. 0262D] “Who has sent the wild ass free, and who has loosed his bonds? To whom I gave a home in the wilderness, and his dwelling-places in the salt land. He despises the multitude of the city; he does not hear the cry of the taskmaster. He surveys the mountains as his pasture, and seeks out every green thing” (Job 39:5).

It is as if he plainly said: Who did this except I? For the wild ass, which we call the woodland ass, is the monk, who, freed from the bonds of secular things [variant: “men, and in some [reading] of vices”], has betaken himself to the tranquil freedom of solitary life and, fleeing the world, has not remained in the world. Hence he dwells in a salt land, when his limbs are dry and parched through abstinence. He does not hear the cry of the taskmaster, but [rather] the voice, because he gives his belly not superfluities but necessities.

For what taskmaster is so importunate and daily as the belly? It has its cry—that is, its immoderate demand—for superfluous and delicate foods, and in this it must not be heard. The mountains which are his pasture are the life or teaching of the exalted Fathers, by reading and meditating upon which we are refreshed. By “every green thing” he means all writings concerning heavenly and unfading life.

Urging us especially toward this, blessed Jerome writes thus to the monk Heliodorus (letter 1): “Interpret the word *monk*: it is your name. What are you doing in a crowd, you who are alone?” Again, distinguishing our life from that of clerics, he writes to the presbyter Paul (letter 15): “If you wish to perform the office of presbyter, if the work or perhaps burden of the episcopate delights you, live in cities and towns, and make the salvation of others the gain of your own soul. But if you desire to be what you are called, a monk—that is, one alone—what are you doing in cities, which surely are not dwellings for solitary persons but for many?”

Every vocation has its own leaders. To turn to our own: bishops and presbyters should have as their example the apostles and apostolic men, and, possessing their honor, should strive also to possess their merit. But let us have as leaders of our vocation Pauls, Anthonys, Hilarions, and Macariuses. And, to return to the material of Scripture, Elijah is our leader, Elisha is ours, and ours are the leaders and sons of the prophets, who lived in fields and solitude (4 Kings [2 Kings] 6:1) and made themselves huts beside the streams of the Jordan.

Among them too are those sons of Rechab [Col. 0263C] who drank neither wine nor strong drink, who dwelt in tents, and whom God praises through Jeremiah, declaring that a man from their line shall not fail to stand before the Lord (Jer. 35:19). Therefore let us too set up tents for ourselves in solitude, so that we may stand before the Lord and be better able to remain ready for his service; lest a crowd of people shake the couch of our rest, disturb our quiet, introduce temptations, and tear the mind away from its holy purpose.

Blessed Arsenius, guided by the Lord, was given to all as a clear example of this free tranquility of life. Hence it is written (*Lives of the Fathers*, part II, book *On Quiet*): “While Abbot Arsenius was still in the palace, he prayed to the Lord, saying: ‘Lord, direct me to salvation.’ And a voice came to him saying: ‘Arsenius, flee human beings, and you will be saved.’” Again: “When he departed for monastic life, he prayed the same prayer again, saying: ‘Lord, direct me to salvation.’ And he heard a voice saying to him: ‘Arsenius, flee, be silent, be at rest. For these are the roots of not sinning.’”

Thus instructed by this one rule of the divine command, he not only fled human beings but drove them away from himself. When his archbishop and a judge came to him one day and asked him for an edifying discourse, he said: “And if I tell you, will you keep it?” They promised that they would. He said to them: “Wherever you hear that Arsenius is, do not come near.”

On another occasion, when the archbishop came to visit him, he first sent to see whether Arsenius would open [Col. 0264A] the door. Arsenius sent him this message: “If you come, I will open to you; but if I open to you, I open to everyone, and then I shall no longer remain here.” Hearing this, the archbishop said: “If I go to persecute him, I shall never go to the holy man.”

He also said to a Roman matron who came to visit his holiness: “How did you dare undertake so great a voyage? Do you not know that you are a woman, and that you ought not go anywhere, lest you go to Rome and tell other women, ‘I saw Arsenius,’ and they make the sea a road for women coming to me?” But she said: “If the Lord wills that I return to Rome, I will not permit anyone to come here. But pray for me, and remember me always.” He replied: “I pray God to erase the memory of you from my heart.” Hearing this, she went away distressed.

This man too, when asked by Abbot Mark why he fled human beings, replied, as it is written (*Lives of the Fathers*, part IV, chapter *On Eternity*, and part II, *On Charity*): “God knows that I love human beings, but I cannot be with God and human beings at the same time.”

Indeed, the holy Fathers so abhorred human association and recognition that some of them, in order to remove people utterly from themselves, pretended to be insane and—even more astonishing to say—professed themselves heretics. Whoever wishes may read in the *Lives of the Fathers* concerning Abbot Simon (*ibid.*, part II, book *On Display*) how he prepared himself for the provincial judge who was coming to him: covering himself with a sack, taking bread and cheese in his hand, [Col. 0264C] he sat at the entrance of his cell and began to eat.

Let him also read concerning that anchorite (*ibid.*, §3, and part IV, *Against Vainglory*) who, sensing that certain people were coming to meet him with lamps, stripped off his clothes and threw them into the river; standing naked, he began to wash them. His attendant, seeing this, was ashamed and begged the people, saying: “Go back, because our elder has lost his mind.” When he came to the elder, he said: “What have you done here, abba? For all who saw you said that the elder has a demon.” But he replied: “That is what I wanted to hear.”

Let him read further concerning Abbot Moses (*Lives of the Fathers*, part II, book *On Display*), who, to remove the provincial judge utterly from himself, rose to flee into a marsh. That judge and his companions met him and asked: “Tell us, elder, where is the cell of Abbot Moses?” He said to them: “Why do you wish to seek him? He is a foolish man and a heretic.”

What also of Abbot Pastor [Shepherd] (*ibid.*), who did not even permit himself to be seen by the provincial judge, although his sister was pleading with him to free her son from prison? Behold: the powerful of the world seek the presence of the saints with great reverence and devotion, while the saints strive to repel them utterly, even at the cost of the greatest disgrace to themselves.

And that you may recognize the virtue of your own sex in this matter, who could sufficiently praise that virgin who rejected even a visit from the most blessed Martin in order to devote herself to contemplation? Thus Jerome writes to the monk Oceanus (letter 51): “In the *Life of the Blessed Martin*, [Col. 0265A] I think we mentioned Sulpicius’s account: as holy Martin was passing by and wished to greet a certain virgin eminent in character and chastity, she refused, but sent a gift [variant: *xenium*, ‘guest-gift’] and, looking through the window, said to the holy man: ‘Pray there, Father, for I have never been visited by a man.’ On hearing this, holy Martin gave thanks to God because she had, being imbued with such conduct, preserved a chaste will. He blessed her and departed full of joy.”

Truly, she disdained—or feared—to rise from the couch of her contemplation, and was ready to say to her friend knocking at the door: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5:3). O how great an injury would bishops or prelates of this age consider it done to themselves if they endured such a repulse from Arsenius or from this virgin!

Let those monks who now live in solitude be ashamed at these examples: they delight in the frequent company of bishops; they build houses of their own in which they may receive them; they do not merely fail to flee the powerful of the world, attended by crowds or attracting them, but invite them in, and, multiplying houses on the pretext of guests, turn the solitude which they sought into a city.

By this stratagem of the ancient and cunning tempter, nearly all monasteries of the present age—though first established in solitude so that people might be avoided—after the fervor of religion cooled, invited people in and, gathering male and female servants, built very large villages in monastic places. Thus they returned to the world, or rather drew the world to themselves. Entangling themselves in the greatest miseries and binding themselves to the greatest servitude, both to ecclesiastical and earthly powers, while seeking to live idly and subsist on others’ labor, they lost alike the name and life of monk—that is, of solitary person.

They are also often pressed by such great troubles that, while laboring to protect their dependents and their possessions, they lose their own, and the monasteries themselves are burned by the frequent fires of neighboring houses. Yet ambition is not restrained even then. Moreover, those who cannot endure whatever discipline the monastery possesses, scattering themselves through villages, castles, and cities, and living two or [Col. 0265D] three together, or even singly, without observance of any rule, are so much worse than secular people as they apostatize more completely from their profession.

Abusing their dwelling-places as they abuse themselves, they call their places “obediences,” where no rule is kept, where nothing is obeyed except belly and flesh, and where, dwelling with their relatives or intimates, they do what they wish all the more freely because they have less reverence for their own consciences. In these most shameless apostates, those transgressions which are venial in other people are beyond doubt criminal. May you endure neither to encounter nor even to hear of the life of such people.

Solitude is all the more necessary for your weakness because here we are less beset by the wars of fleshly temptations and wander less through the senses toward bodily things. Hence blessed Anthony says (*Lives of the Fathers*, part II, book *On Quiet*): “He who sits in solitude and remains at rest is delivered from three battles: those of hearing, speech, and sight; and he will have only one struggle, that of the heart.”

Jerome, the distinguished teacher of the Church, carefully considering these and the other advantages of the wilderness and vigorously exhorting the monk Heliodorus toward them, cries out (letter 1): “O wilderness, rejoicing in God as a familiar friend! What are you doing in the world, brother, you who are greater than the world?”

Now that we have discussed where monasteries should be built, let us show what the location of the place itself should be. In establishing the site of the monastery itself, care should be taken, as blessed Benedict also advises (ch. 66), that, if possible, those things especially necessary for monasteries should be contained within its enclosure: that is, a garden, water, a mill, a bakehouse with an oven, and places where the sisters may carry on their daily work, lest occasion be given for wandering outside.

As in the camps of the world, so in the camps of the Lord—that is, monastic congregations—there must be persons appointed to preside over the rest. For there one commander presides over all, at whose nod all things are done. According to the size of the army or the variety of offices, he shares his burdens with certain persons and employs subordinate officers who oversee different groups or duties. So it must also be done in monasteries: one matron must preside over all, [Col. 0266C] at whose consideration and judgment all the rest do everything; and no one may presume in any matter to oppose her or even to murmur against any command of hers.

For no human assembly, nor any household, however small, of a single family can stand unharmed unless unity is preserved in it, so that its whole realm rests under the authority [variant: “service”] of one person. Thus the ark, which bore the type of the Church, had many cubits both in length and breadth, yet was brought to completion in one point. And Proverbs says: “Because of the sins of a land, its princes are many” (Prov. 28:2). Thus too, after Alexander’s death, when kings multiplied, evils multiplied also. And Rome, when its rule was shared among several governors, could not maintain concord.

Hence Lucan recalls in his first book:

> … You, Rome made subject to three masters,  
> became the cause of evils; nor were the deadly compacts  
> of a divided sovereignty ever sent into a multitude.  
> (*Lucan*, book I)

And a little later:

> … While earth shall bear up sea, and air the earth,  
> while the long labors of Titan shall roll on,  
> and night in heaven shall follow day through as many signs,  
> there will be no loyalty among partners in rule, and every power  
> will be impatient of a sharer. …  
> (*Ibid.*)

Such indeed were those disciples of holy Abbot Frontonius, whom he had gathered in the city where he was born, to the number of seventy; and although he had obtained great favor there both with God and with human beings, he left the city monastery and drew them naked with their movable goods into the wilderness. Later, like the people of Israel complaining against Moses because he had led them from Egypt, leaving pots of meat and the abundance of the land, into the wilderness, they murmured vainly, saying: “Is chastity alone in the wilderness, and absent from cities? Why then do we not return to the city from which we departed for a time? Or will God hear those who pray only in the wilderness? Who can live on the food of angels? Whom does it please to become the companion of cattle and wild beasts? What necessity keeps us here? Why then, returning to the place in which we were born, do we not bless the Lord?”

Hence the Apostle James also warns: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you receive a greater judgment” (James 3:1). Jerome also writes to the monk Rusticus concerning the ordering of life (letter 4): “No art is learned without a master. Even dumb animals and herds of wild beasts follow their leaders. Among bees, the rest follow one that goes before. Cranes follow one in ordered formation. There is one commander, one judge of a province. From its foundation Rome could not have two brothers as kings at the same time, and it was dedicated by fratricide. In Rebekah’s womb Esau and Jacob waged war. Each church has one bishop, one archpresbyter, one archdeacon, and every ecclesiastical order depends upon its own rulers. One pilot is in a ship. One master is in a house. In an army, however great, the standard of one person is watched. Through all these things the argument tends to this: to teach you that you are not to be left to your own judgment, but ought to live in a monastery under the discipline of one Father and in the fellowship of many.”

Thus, in order that harmony may be preserved in all things, it is fitting that one woman preside over all, whom all obey in every respect. Under her, too, certain other persons should be appointed, as it were magistrates, according as she herself shall determine. She shall command what offices they are to hold and to what extent they are to preside, so that they may be, as it were, leaders or consuls in the army of the Lord; while all the rest, like soldiers or infantry, under their provident care, may freely fight against the Evil One and his satellites. We believe that seven persons from among you are necessary and sufficient for the whole administration of the monastery: namely, the portress, cellarer, wardrobe-keeper, infirmarian, chantress [elsewhere, *cantatricem* (“female singer”), but wrongly], sacristan, and finally the deaconess, whom they now call abbess. [Col. 0267D]

In these camps, therefore, and in this divine warfare, as it is written: “The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7:1); and elsewhere: “Terrible as an army arrayed in battle-order” (Song 6:3), the deaconess holds the place of an emperor, to whom all render obedience in every respect. The six others under her, whom we call officials, hold the places of commanders or consuls. All the remaining nuns, whom we call cloistered sisters, like soldiers promptly perform the divine service. The lay sisters, however, who, renouncing the world, have also devoted themselves to the service of the nuns, wear a religious but not monastic habit and, like infantry, hold a lower rank. [Col. 0268A]

Now it remains, by the Lord’s inspiration, to arrange the individual ranks of this warfare, so that against the assaults of demons it may truly be said, “an army arrayed in battle-order.” Beginning, I say, with that head itself, the deaconess, as was stated, let us first make provisions concerning her, through whom all things are to be ordered.

As we recalled in the preceding letter, the blessed Apostle Paul, writing to Timothy, carefully describes how eminent and tested her holiness ought to be, saying: “Let a widow be chosen who is not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one husband, having testimony in good works: if she has brought up children, if she has received strangers, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has ministered to those suffering tribulation, if she has followed every good work. But avoid younger widows” (1 Tim. 5:9). [Col. 0268B]

Above, too, when he was establishing the way of life of deaconesses together with that of deacons, he says: “Women likewise, modest, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things” (1 Tim. 3:11). What understanding or rationale all these requirements contain, we have, so far as we judge, sufficiently discussed in our preceding letter—especially why the Apostle wishes her to have been the wife of one husband and to be of advanced age.

We therefore wonder not a little how this pernicious custom has grown up in the Church: that virgins rather than women who have known husbands should be chosen for this office, and that younger women should frequently be set over older. [Col. 0268C] Yet Ecclesiastes says: “Woe to thee, O land, whose king is a child” (Eccl. 10:16); and we all alike approve that saying of blessed Job: “With the ancients is wisdom, and in long time prudence” (Job 12:12). Hence it is also written in Proverbs: “Old age is a crown of dignity, which shall be found in the ways of righteousness” (Prov. 16:31).

And in Ecclesiasticus: “How beautiful is the judgment of grey hair, and for elders to know counsel. How beautiful is the wisdom of veterans; understanding and counsel are the glorious crown of old men. Great experience and their glory is the fear of God” (Ecclus. 25:6). Again: “Speak, you who are older, for it becomes you. Young man, speak in your own cause only when there is need. If you are questioned twice, let your answer be concise. In many matters be as though ignorant; listen silently, while also inquiring. Do not presume to speak in the midst of magnates [elsewhere, *magnatum*, “of the great”]; and where elders are present, do not speak much” (Ecclus. 32:4). [Col. 0268D]

For this reason the presbyters who preside over the people in the Church are interpreted as “elders,” so that even by their name they may be taught what kind of persons they ought to be. And those who wrote the Lives of the Saints called “elders” those whom we now call abbots.

Thus every care must be taken that, in the election or consecration of a deaconess, the Apostle’s counsel may come first (1 Tim. 5:2): that is, that such a woman be chosen as ought to excel the others in life and teaching, who by her age also promises maturity of character; who has deserved to command through obeying; and who has learned and more firmly known the Rule by practice rather than by hearing it. [Col. 0269A]

If she is not educated in letters, let her know that she is not being appointed for philosophical schools or dialectical disputations, but for the teaching of life and the performance of works. Thus it is written of the Lord: “Who began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1)—first to do, afterward to teach. For teaching by deed is better and more perfect than teaching by speech; teaching by action than by word.

Let us carefully heed this, as it is written. Abbot Ipitius [Ipericius] said: “He is truly wise who teaches others by his deed, not by words.” Nor does this bring little consolation and confidence.

Consider also that argument of blessed Antony by which he confuted the verbose philosophers who mocked the teaching of a man whom they regarded as unlearned and illiterate: “Answer me,” he said, “which comes first, understanding or letters? And which is the origin of the other: does understanding arise from letters, or do letters arise from understanding?” When they asserted that understanding was the author and inventor of letters, he said: “Therefore, he whose understanding is sound does not require letters.” [Col. 0269B]

Let her also hear the Apostle’s saying and be strengthened in the Lord: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1 Cor. 1:20). And again: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the ignoble and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy things that are, so that no flesh may glory in his presence” (1 Cor. 4:20). [Col. 0269C]

For, as he himself says afterward, the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power.

If she judges that she must return to Scripture in order to know certain matters better, she should not be ashamed to seek and learn this from educated persons, nor despise instruction in letters in these matters; rather, she should receive it devoutly and diligently, since the chief of the apostles himself carefully accepted the public correction [elsewhere, *correptionem*, “rebuke”] of his fellow apostle Paul (Gal. 2:11). For, as blessed Benedict also observes, the Lord often reveals what is better to the lesser member. [Col. 0269D]

Moreover, in order that we may follow still more fully the Lord’s providence, which the Apostle also mentioned above, this election should never be made from among the noble or powerful of this world, except under the greatest necessity and for the most certain reason. Such women, easily trusting in or glorying in their lineage, become presumptuous or proud; and especially when they are natives of the place, their precedence becomes harmful to the monastery.

For one must fear that the proximity of their relatives may make them more presumptuous, that their frequent visits may burden or disturb the monastery, and that she herself may suffer harm to her religious life through her own people, or become an object of contempt to others, according to that saying of Truth: “A prophet is not without honour except in his own country” (Matt. 13:57).

Foreseeing this, blessed Jerome, writing to Heliodorus, after enumerating many things that hinder monks who remain in their native land, says: “From this reckoning arises that final conclusion: a monk cannot be perfect in his own country. But not to wish to be perfect is to sin.” [Col. 0270A]

How great, moreover, is the harm to souls if she who presides by the authority of religion is inferior in religious life? It is enough for each subject to display particular virtues. But in her the examples of all virtues ought to shine forth, so that she may anticipate by her own examples everything she commands others to do; lest she oppose by her conduct what she commands, destroy by her deeds what she builds by her words, and have the word of correction taken from her mouth because she blushes to correct in others what she is known to commit herself.

The Psalmist prays to the Lord that this may not happen to him, saying: “Take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth” (Ps. 148:43). For he had in view that most grave rebuke of the Lord, which he himself also mentions elsewhere, saying: “But God said to the sinner: Why do you declare my statutes and take my covenant in your mouth? Yet you hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Ps. 49:16). [Col. 0270B]

The Apostle carefully guarding against this says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should become reprobate” (2 Cor. 9:27). For when a person’s life is despised, it follows that his preaching or teaching also is held in contempt. And when someone ought to heal another, if he suffers from the same infirmity, the sick person rightly reproaches him: “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23).

Let whoever seems to preside over the Church carefully consider how great a ruin his fall brings about, when he draws those subject to him down with him into the precipice. [Col. 0270C] “Whoever,” says Truth, “shall break one of these least commandments and shall so teach men, shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19). He breaks the commandment who violates it by acting against it; and, corrupting others by his example, he sits as a teacher in the chair of pestilence.

If anyone who acts thus is to be considered least in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the present Church—how great a sinner must that worst superior be, from whose negligence the Lord requires the blood not only of her own soul but also of the souls of all her subjects?

Therefore Wisdom rightly threatens such persons: “Power was given you by the Lord, and strength by the Most High, who will examine your works and search out your thoughts. Since, being ministers of his kingdom, you have not judged rightly nor kept the law of justice, he will appear to you terribly and swiftly, because most severe judgment shall be made upon those who rule. Mercy is granted to the lowly; but the mighty shall suffer mighty torments, and a stronger punishment presses upon the stronger” (Wis. 6:4). [Col. 0270D]

It is enough for each of the subjects to guard against her own sin. But death threatens superiors even in the sins of others. For as gifts increase, so too the account to be rendered for gifts increases; and from one to whom more is entrusted, more is required.

We are especially warned in Proverbs to guard against so great a danger, where it says: “My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have pledged your hand to a stranger. You are ensnared by the words of your mouth and caught by your own sayings. Do, therefore, what I say, my son, and free yourself, because you have fallen into your neighbour’s hand. Run about, hasten, awaken your friend; do not give sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” (Prov. 6:1). [Col. 0271A]

For then we make ourselves surety for a friend when our charity receives someone into the way of life of our congregation. We promise that person the care of our oversight, just as that person promises us obedience. We likewise pledge our hand to that person when, by making this promise, we undertake the responsibility of our work on that person’s behalf. Then we fall into that person’s hand, because unless we provide for ourselves against that person, we shall find that person the destroyer of our soul.

Against this danger counsel is supplied when it continues: “Run about, hasten,” and so forth. Thus, walking now here, now there, after the manner of a provident and tireless commander, she should diligently go around and inspect her camp, lest through anyone’s negligence an entrance be opened to him who, “like a lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). [Col. 0271B]

Let her know first all the evils of her household, so that they may be corrected by her before they become known to others and are made an example. Let her beware of what blessed Jerome reproaches in foolish or negligent persons: “We are accustomed to be the last to know the evils of our own household and, while neighbours sing of them, to remain ignorant of the faults of our children and spouses.”

Let one who presides thus attend to the fact that she has undertaken the guardianship of bodies as well as souls. Concerning the guardianship of bodies she is admonished in Ecclesiasticus: “Do you have daughters? Guard their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful countenance” (Ecclus. 7:26). And again: “A daughter is a hidden care for her father; vigilance and anxiety concerning her take away sleep, lest she be defiled” (Ecclus. 42:9). [Col. 0271C]

We defile our bodies not only by fornication, but by performing in them anything indecent—whether with the tongue or another member—or by abusing any bodily faculty for some vanity. As it is written: “Death enters through our windows” (Jer. 9:12), that is, sin enters the soul through the instruments of the five senses.

But what death is more grievous, or what guardianship more perilous, than that of souls? “Do not fear,” says Truth, “those who kill the body but can do nothing to the soul” (Matt. 10:28; Luke 12:4). If anyone hears this counsel, who would not fear the death of the body more than that of the soul? Who does not beware the sword more than falsehood? Yet it is written: “A lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11). What can be killed more easily than the soul? What arrow can be fashioned more swiftly than sin? Who can guard even against a thought? Who is sufficient to guard against one’s own sins, much less those of others? What fleshly shepherd can sufficiently guard spiritual sheep against spiritual wolves, invisible sheep against invisible wolves? [Col. 0271D]

Who does not fear the ravager, who never ceases to assail us, whom no enclosure can exclude and no sword can kill or wound? Peter the Apostle exhorts us to beware of him, who constantly lies in wait and especially persecutes religious persons, according to Habakkuk: “His food is choice” (Hab. 1:16), saying: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8).

The Lord himself tells blessed Job how great is his presumption in devouring us: “He shall swallow up a river and not wonder; he trusts that Jordan may flow into his mouth” (Job 40:18). For what will he not presume to attack, who presumed even to attack and tempt the Lord himself? He who immediately captured the first parents from paradise, and from the apostolic company snatched away even the apostle whom the Lord had chosen? What place is safe from him, what enclosure is not penetrable by him? Who can guard against his snares, who can resist his strength? [Col. 0272A]

He is the one who, by one blow shaking the four corners of the house of the holy man Job, crushed and destroyed his innocent sons and daughters (Job 1:19). What can the weaker sex do against him? For whom is his deception to be feared as greatly as for a woman? For he first seduced her and, through her, likewise enslaved her husband and all their posterity.

Desire for a greater good deprived the woman of the possession of a lesser good. By this same art he will now easily seduce a woman when she desires to preside rather than to be of service, being driven thereto by ambition for possessions or honour. What of these motives came first will be proved by what follows.

If a superior lives more delicately than her subjects, or claims for herself some private possession beyond necessity, there can be no doubt that she desired this. If afterward she seeks more precious adornments than before, she surely swells with vain glory. What she formerly was will afterward become apparent. Whether what she formerly displayed was virtue or pretence will be shown by her elevation to office. [Col. 0272B]

Let her be drawn to office rather than come to it, the Lord saying: “All who come are thieves and robbers” (John 10:8). “They came,” says Jerome, “not those who were sent.” Let her be taken for honour rather than take honour for herself. For, says the Apostle, “No one takes honour to himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5:4). When called, let her mourn as one led to death; when rejected, let her rejoice as one delivered from death. [Col. 0272C]

We blush to say in words that we are better than others. Yet when this is shown in deeds by our election, we are shameless without shame. For who does not know that the better ought to be preferred to the rest? Hence in Book 24 of the *Moralia*, chapter 15: “He ought not to undertake the leadership of men who does not know how to rebuke men well by admonishing them. He who is chosen to correct the faults of others must not himself commit what should have been cut away.”

Yet in this election, if perhaps we refuse the offered dignity by some slight verbal repulse—though this shamelessness has been offered to our ears—we certainly bring this accusation against ourselves in order that we may appear more righteous and more worthy. [Col. 0272D]

Oh, how many have we seen weep bodily and laugh in heart at their election! They accuse themselves as unworthy, and thereby seek still more for themselves favour and human approval, observing what is written: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17).

Yet when it afterward happens that they are accused and an opportunity to withdraw is offered them, they strive most importunately and shamelessly to defend for themselves the superiority which they had represented, with feigned tears and genuine self-accusations, that they accepted unwillingly.

How many canons have we seen in churches resisting their bishops when they were compelled by them to sacred orders, professing themselves unworthy of such ministries and altogether unwilling to consent—yet when the clergy afterward perhaps chose them for the episcopate, how little or no refusal did they endure! [Col. 0273A]

And those who yesterday, as they said, fled the diaconate in order to avoid danger to their souls, now, as though made righteous in a single night, do not fear the precipice of a higher rank. Of such persons it is written in Proverbs: “A foolish man claps his hands when he has become surety for a friend” (Prov. 17:18).

For the miserable man then rejoices in what ought rather to make him mourn: when he comes to the governance of others, he is bound by his own profession to the care of his subjects, by whom he ought rather to be loved than feared.

Seeking, as far as we can, to guard against this plague, we absolutely forbid a superior to live more delicately or luxuriously than her subjects; to have private retreats for eating or sleeping; rather, she must carry out everything with the flock entrusted to her, and provide for them all the more because she is more constantly present among them. [Col. 0273B]

We know that blessed Benedict, being especially solicitous for pilgrims and guests, established the abbot’s table separately with them (chapter 56). Although this was piously established then, it was later changed, by a most useful arrangement of monasteries, so that the abbot should not withdraw from the community, but should appoint a faithful steward to provide for pilgrims.

For a fall is easy amid feasting, and then discipline requires more vigilant attention. Many are more indulgent to themselves than to their guests on the pretext of guests; hence those absent are gravely injured by suspicion and murmur. A superior’s authority is also lessened in proportion as his manner of life is less known to his own people.

Moreover, any want is more tolerable to all when it is equally shared by all, especially by superiors. We have learned this also in Cato. For he, as it is written, when the people thirsted with him, refused and poured out the little water offered to him; and it sufficed for all. [Col. 0273C–D]

Since, therefore, sobriety is especially necessary for superiors, they should live all the more sparingly because provision for the others must be made through them. And lest they turn God’s gift—that is, the office of superiority granted to them—into pride and especially use it to insult their subjects, let them hear what is written: “Do not be like a lion in your house, overthrowing your household and oppressing those subject to you” (Ecclus. 4:35). “Pride is hateful before God and men” (Ecclus. 10:7). “The Lord has overthrown the seats of proud rulers and caused the meek to sit in their place” (ibid., 17). “Have they made you ruler? Do not exalt yourself. Be among them as one of themselves” (Ecclus. 32:1). [Col. 0274A]

And the Apostle, instructing Timothy concerning those subject to him, says: “Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father; younger men as brothers; old women as mothers; younger women as sisters” (1 Tim. 5:1).

“You did not choose me,” says the Lord, “but I chose you” (John 15:16). All other superiors are elected by their subjects, and are created and appointed by them, because they are taken up not to lordship but to service. But he alone is truly Lord and has the right to choose subjects to serve him. Yet he did not present himself as lord but as minister; and, by his own example, he rebuked those already aspiring to the summit of rank, saying: “The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them, and those who have power over them are called benefactors. But you are not so” (Matt. 20:25). [Col. 0274B]

Therefore anyone imitates the kings of the Gentiles who seeks lordship over subjects rather than service; who labours to be feared rather than loved; and who, swelling with pride in the teaching authority of her office, loves the chief places at banquets, the first seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men.

To prevent us from glorying even in titles and to ensure humility in all things, the Lord says concerning the honour of that appellation: “But you are not to be called Rabbi, and call no man your father on earth” (Matt. 23:8). Finally, prohibiting all boasting, he says: “Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled” (ibid., 12).

Care must also be taken lest the flock be endangered through the absence of its shepherds, and lest discipline within grow slack while superiors wander abroad. We therefore decree that the deaconess, attending more to spiritual than bodily affairs, should not leave the monastery for any external business, but should be so much the more solicitous for her subjects as she is more constantly present among them. Her presence should also be more venerable to people in proportion as it is rarer, as it is written: “Withdraw from one more powerful than yourself; for this very reason he will invite you the more” (Ecclus. 13:12). [Col. 0274C]

If the monastery requires an embassy, monks or their lay brothers should undertake it. For men must always provide for women’s necessities. The greater women’s religious commitment, the more they are free for God and the more they require the protection of men.

Thus Joseph is admonished by the angel to care for the Mother of the Lord, though he is not permitted to know her. And when the Lord himself was dying, he provided, as it were, another son for his mother to care for her temporal needs. [Col. 0274D]

There can be no doubt how much care the Apostles bestowed upon devout women, as we have already recalled sufficiently elsewhere; indeed, because of their service they instituted seven deacons. Following this authority, and compelled also by the necessity of the matter itself, we have decreed that monks and their lay brothers, after the manner of the apostles and deacons, shall provide for women’s monasteries in matters belonging to external care. Monks are especially necessary to them for the Masses, and lay brothers for manual works.

It ought therefore to be done, as we read was done at Alexandria under Mark the Evangelist at the very beginning of the Church’s birth, that women’s monasteries should not lack monasteries of men, and that through men of the same religious profession all external matters should be administered for women. [Col. 0275A]

Then, indeed, we believe women’s monasteries will observe the religious commitment of their purpose more firmly if they are governed by the care of spiritual men, and if one and the same shepherd is appointed for both sheep and rams: so that he who presides over men may likewise preside over women, and so that, always in accordance with apostolic teaching, man may be the head of woman, as Christ is the head of man and God the head of Christ.

Hence the monastery of blessed Scholastica, situated on the property of the brethren’s monastery, was governed by her brother’s care and was instructed and consoled by his frequent visits or those of the brethren.

Blessed Basil’s Rule also instructs us in one place concerning the prudent conduct of this governance, as follows: “Question: Is it right for the superior to speak, apart from her who presides over the sisters, anything pertaining to the edification of the virgins? Answer: And how will that precept of the Apostle be observed which says: ‘Let all things be done honestly and in order’?” (1 Cor. 14:40). [Col. 0275B]

Again, in the following chapter: “Question: Is it suitable for the superior frequently to speak with her who presides over the sisters, especially if some of the brethren are harmed by this? Answer: Since the Apostle says, ‘Why is my liberty judged by another’s conscience?’ (1 Cor. 10:29), it is good to imitate him when he says, ‘I have not appeared to use my power, lest I should put any stumbling-block in the way of the Gospel of Christ’ (1 Cor. 9:12). And, so far as possible, they should be seen more rarely, and conversation should be concluded more briefly.” [Col. 0275C]

Hence also comes the decree of the Council of Seville: “By common consent we have decreed that monasteries of virgins in the province of Baetica shall be governed by the ministry and protection of monks. For we then provide wholesome measures for virgins consecrated to Christ when we choose for them spiritual fathers by whose guidance they may not only be protected but also built up by instruction.”

Yet this caution is to be observed regarding monks: kept apart from the women’s private quarters, they are not to have customary permission to approach even the vestibule. Neither the abbot nor the man set over them may, apart from her who presides, speak to Christ’s virgins anything concerning moral formation. Nor should he converse frequently with the superior alone, but only in the presence and witness of two or three sisters. Thus access is to be rare and speech brief. [Col. 0275D]

Far be it from us to wish that monks should be familiar with Christ’s virgins—a thing even to say is wicked. Rather, as the prescriptions of the Rule or the canons admonish, we assign the women to the monks’ governance alone, with the sexes kept distinctly and far apart; and we decree that one most approved monk be chosen, whose duty is to attend to their rural or urban estates, erect buildings, or provide whatever else is necessary for the monastery, so that Christ’s handmaids, concerned only for the benefit of their souls, may live solely in divine worship and devote themselves to their own works.

Indeed, he who is appointed over them by his abbot must be approved by the judgment of his bishop. Let the women make garments for those same communities from which they expect protection; and from the same communities, as stated above, they will in turn receive the fruits of labour and assistance in management. [Col. 0276A]

Following this arrangement, we wish women’s monasteries always to be subject to men’s monasteries in such a way that the brethren care for the sisters and one man presides over both as a father; both monasteries are to look to his oversight, and those of both sexes are to be, as it were, one flock and one shepherd in the Lord.

This fellowship of spiritual brotherhood will be more pleasing both to God and to people in proportion as it can more perfectly suffice for every sex coming to conversion: that monks may receive men and nuns women, and that it may give counsel to every soul considering its salvation. Whoever wishes to convert together with a mother, sister, daughter, or any woman whose care that person bears, may there find complete comfort. The two monasteries should be joined in a bond of greater charity and mutual concern in proportion as the persons in them are more closely united by kinship or affinity. [Col. 0276B]

We further wish the superior of the monks, whom they call abbot, to preside over the nuns in such a way that he recognizes those who are brides of the Lord—whose servant he himself is—as his own ladies; and that he rejoices not in ruling over them but in being of service to them.

Let him be like a steward in a royal household, who does not oppress the mistress with command but provides for her: promptly obeying her concerning necessities, not complying with her in harmful matters, administering everything external in such a way that he never enters the secret chamber unless commanded.

In this manner, therefore, we wish the servant of Christ to provide for Christ’s brides, faithfully to care for them for Christ’s sake, and to confer with the deaconess about all matters that ought to be discussed. Without consulting her, he may determine nothing concerning Christ’s handmaids or the matters that concern them; nor may he presume to command or speak anything to any of them except through her. [Col. 0276C]

Whenever the deaconess calls him, he must not delay in coming; and whatever she advises him concerning things needed by herself or those subject to her, he must not delay, insofar as he is able, to carry out. When summoned by the deaconess, however, he must never speak with her except openly and in the presence of approved witnesses; he must not sit close beside her or detain her in prolonged conversation.

All things pertaining to food or clothing, and any money as well, shall be collected or kept among Christ’s handmaids; from these things what is necessary shall be given to the brethren from what remains over to the sisters. Thus the brethren shall manage all exterior matters, while the sisters attend only to things which it is suitable for women to do within: namely, making and washing even the brothers’ garments; preparing bread, giving it for baking, and receiving it when baked. [Col. 0276D]

The care of milk and its products shall likewise belong to them, as well as the feeding of hens or geese, and whatever women can do more suitably than men.

When the superior himself has been appointed, he shall swear in the presence of the bishop and the sisters that he will be their faithful steward in the Lord and will diligently protect their bodies from carnal defilement. If, God forbid, the bishop should find him negligent in this, let him immediately depose him as guilty of perjury.

All the brethren also, in their professions, shall bind themselves to the sisters by this oath: that they will in no way consent to their being burdened and will, to the extent of their ability, provide for their bodily purity. No man, therefore, may have access to the sisters except with the superior’s permission; nor may anything sent to them be received unless transmitted through the superior. [Col. 0277A]

No sister may ever go beyond the enclosure of the monastery; rather, as stated, the brethren shall manage all exterior affairs and the strong shall labour at strenuous works.

No brother may ever enter this enclosure unless he has obtained the permission of the superior and deaconess, and some necessary or honourable cause requires it. If anyone should presume to act contrary to this, let him be expelled from the monastery without delay.

Yet lest the stronger men presume in any respect to oppress the women, we decree that they too presume nothing against the deaconess’s will, but carry out all things even at her direction; and that all alike, men as well as women, make profession to her and promise obedience, so that peace may be firmer and concord better preserved in proportion as less is permitted to the stronger; and so that the stronger may be less burdened by obeying the weaker in proportion as they fear their violence less. [Col. 0277B]

And the more one humbles oneself here before God, the more certain it is that one will be exalted. Let what has been said at present concerning the deaconess suffice. Let us now turn our pen to the officials.

The sacristan, who is also the treasurer, shall provide for the whole oratory and keep all the keys belonging to it, as well as the things necessary for it. She shall receive any offerings; she shall care for making or repairing whatever is necessary in the oratory and for its whole adornment. It is also her duty to provide the altar breads, altar vessels and books, the altar’s entire ornamentation, relics, incense, lamps, the clock, and the ringing of signals. [Col. 0277C]

If possible, virgins should make the altar breads, clean the grain from which they are made, and wash the altar cloths. But neither relics nor altar vessels may ever be touched by her or by any nun, nor even the altar cloths except when they have been handed to them for washing. Monks or their lay brothers are to be called and awaited for this purpose.

If necessary, some persons may be appointed under her to this office, worthy to touch these things when required; after the chests have been unlocked by her, they shall take them out or replace them there.

She who presides over the sanctuary ought to excel in purity of life and, if possible, be whole in mind as well as body; both her abstinence and continence must be proven. Above all, she must be instructed in the calculation of the moon, so that she may provide for the oratory according to the reckoning of times. [Col. 0277D]

The chantress shall provide for the whole choir, arrange the divine offices, have charge of instruction in singing and reading, and supervise matters pertaining to writing or dictation. She shall also keep the book-chest, issue and receive its books, and take charge of, or be diligent about, their copying and repair. [Col. 0278A]

She shall arrange how the choir is seated and assign seats; provide who is to read or sing; and compose the roster to be recited in chapter on Saturdays, in which all the weekly officials are recorded. For these reasons, she should especially be literate and should not be ignorant of music.

She shall also provide for the whole discipline after the deaconess; if the latter is occupied with other matters, she shall perform her duties in this respect.

The infirmary mistress shall minister to the sick and watch over them both against fault and against want. Whatever illness may require—food, baths, or anything else—must be granted them. For the proverb in such cases is well known: “No law is laid down for the sick.” Meat is by no means to be denied them, except on Friday, or on the principal vigils, or the fasts of the Ember Days or of Lent. Yet they should be restrained from sin all the more strictly, because they are under the greater obligation to think of their end. Above all, they must then cultivate silence, in which excess is especially common, and persevere in prayer, as it is written: “My child, in your sickness do not despise yourself, but pray to God, and he will heal you. Turn away from sin, direct your hands aright, and cleanse your heart from every sin” (Ecclus. 38:9).

A vigilant attendant must always be at hand for the sick, so that, when necessary, she may immediately help them; and the house must be furnished with everything required for that illness. Provision must also be made, according to the resources of the place, for medicines if needed. This can more easily be done if the woman in charge of the sick is not inexperienced in medicine. The care of matters that lessen the blood—that is, bloodletting—shall also belong to her. Someone must be skilled in phlebotomy, so that it may not be necessary for a man to enter among the women on this account. Provision must likewise be made for the offices of the hours and for Communion, so that the sick are not deprived of them: at least on the Lord’s Day they should receive Communion, preceded, as far as they are able, by confession and satisfaction. The teaching of the blessed apostle James concerning the anointing of the sick must also be carefully observed. For performing it, especially when there is despair of the sick person’s life, two senior priest-monks with a deacon, carrying consecrated oil with them (James 5:14), shall be brought in; and, with the community of sisters present but separated by a wall, they shall celebrate this sacrament. Similarly, when necessary, Communion shall be administered.

The house of the sick must therefore be so arranged that the monks may have easy entrance and exit for these rites, neither seeing the community nor being seen by it. At least once each day the deaconess and the cellarer shall visit the sick woman as though she were Christ, so that they may conscientiously provide for her needs, bodily as well as spiritual, and may deserve to hear from the Lord: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. 25:36).

If the sick woman approaches her end and enters the agony of death, a sister attending her shall immediately hasten to the community with a clapper, and, striking it, announce the sister’s death. Then the whole community, whatever the hour of day or night, shall hurry to the dying woman, unless prevented by the divine offices [variant: “impeded”]. If this occurs—since nothing is to be preferred to the work of God—it will suffice for the deaconess to hasten with such sisters as she chooses, and for the community to follow afterward. Whoever comes at the sound of this clapper shall immediately begin the litany, until the invocation of the holy men and women has been completed; then the psalms and the other things pertaining to the funeral rites shall follow.

How salutary it is to visit the sick or the dead, Ecclesiastes carefully observes when he says: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting; for there the end of all human beings is recalled, and the living person considers what he himself will become” (Ecclus. 7:3). Likewise: “The heart of the wise is where sorrow is” (ibid., 5).

The deceased sister’s little body shall immediately be washed by the sisters and, clothed in some cheap but clean undergarment and stockings, placed upon the bier, with her head wrapped in a veil. These garments shall be firmly sewn or tied to the body and shall not afterward be moved. The sisters shall carry the body into the church; when burial is required, the monks shall commit it to the grave, while the sisters meanwhile devote themselves attentively to psalmody or prayers in the oratory. The deaconess’s burial alone shall have this additional honor: her whole body shall be wrapped only in haircloth, and she shall be sewn up entirely within it as though in a sack.

The vestiarian shall provide for everything that concerns the care of clothing, namely footwear as well as all other things. She shall have the sheep shorn and receive hides for shoes. She shall prepare and collect flax and wool and have the entire care of the looms. She shall supply thread, needles, and shears to everyone. She shall have charge of the whole dormitory and provide bedding for all. She shall also care for tablecloths, hand-towels, and every kind of cloth: cutting, sewing, and washing them. To her above all belongs the saying: “She sought wool and flax, and worked according to the counsel of her hands” (Prov. 31:13). “She put her hand to the distaff, and her fingers grasped the spindle. She shall not fear for her household because of snowy cold, for all her household are clothed in double garments; and she shall laugh on the last day. She considered the paths of her household and did not eat the bread of idleness. Her children arose and proclaimed her most blessed” (Cant. 6:8 [an erroneous citation for Proverbs 31]). She shall possess the tools for these works and determine which tasks from her work she ought to assign to the sisters. She shall also have charge of the novices until they are received into the congregation.

The cellarer shall have charge of all things relating to food: the storeroom, refectory, kitchen, mill, bakehouse with its oven, gardens and orchards, and the entire cultivation of the fields; likewise bees, herds, all livestock, and necessary birds. [Col. 0280A] Whatever is needed for food shall be sought from her. Above all, she ought not to be avaricious, but ready and willing to distribute everything necessary. “For God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). We absolutely forbid her, in administering her charge, to be more indulgent to herself than to others; she must neither prepare special dishes for herself nor reserve for herself what she deprives others of. “The best steward,” Jerome says, “is one who reserves nothing for himself.” Judas, abusing the office of his stewardship, though he had the money-box, perished from the apostolic company. Ananias likewise, and Sapphira his wife, by withholding, incurred the sentence of death.

To the portress, or doorkeeper—for they are the same—belongs the reception of guests or any arrivals whatsoever, informing the appropriate persons about them or bringing them where necessary, and the care of hospitality. She should be discreet in age and mind, so that she knows how to receive and give an answer, and how to judge who should be received, and in what manner, or who should not. The religious character of the monastery ought especially to be adorned through her, as through the Lord’s vestibule, since knowledge of the monastery begins with her. Let her therefore be gentle in words and mild in speech, so that even in dealing with those whom she excludes, after giving an appropriate reason, she may endeavor to build up charity. For it is written: “A gentle answer breaks wrath, but a harsh word stirs up fury” (Prov. 15:1). And elsewhere: “A sweet word multiplies friends and softens enemies” (Ecclus. 6:5).

Since she sees the poor more often and knows them better, she shall distribute whatever food or clothing ought to be given to them. If she or the other officials need the assistance or relief of certain sisters, deputies shall be assigned to them by the deaconess. These should especially be selected from among the conversae, so that no nun may ever be absent from the divine offices, chapter, or refectory. The portress shall have a small house beside the gate, in which she or her deputy is always available to arrivals. There too they must not remain idle, and must cultivate silence all the more, since their talkativeness can more easily become known even to those outside. It is certainly her duty not only to keep away persons whom she ought to exclude, but also wholly to exclude rumors, lest they be heedlessly carried to the community; and she is to be held accountable for any excess in this matter. If she hears anything that ought to be known, she shall report it privately to the deaconess, so that the latter may deliberate about it as she sees fit.

As soon as there has been knocking or calling at the gate, the sister on duty shall ask the arrivals who they are and what they want, and, if appropriate, immediately open the gate to receive them. Only women may be lodged inside. Men shall be directed to the monks. No one, therefore, shall for any reason be admitted within without first consulting the deaconess and receiving her order. Women, however, shall immediately be given entry. The portress shall have received women, or men entering for any reason, wait in her cell until the deaconess or sisters, if necessary or expedient, come to meet them. The deaconess herself, or the sisters, shall also carefully render this service of hospitality to poor persons requiring the washing of feet. For the Apostle is especially called a deacon because of this service of humanity. Thus one of the Fathers in the Lives of the Fathers says: “For your sake the Savior, having become man, became a deacon; girding himself with a towel, he washed the disciples’ feet, commanding them to wash their brothers’ feet.” Hence the Apostle mentions a deaconess, saying: “If she has received strangers, if she has washed the feet of the saints” (1 Tim. 5:10). And the Lord himself says: “I was a stranger, and you gathered me in” (Matt. 25:35).

All officials except the chantress should, if suitable women can be found for this work, be appointed from among those who do not attend to letters, so that the others may devote themselves more freely to study.

[Col. 0281B] The necessary ornaments of the oratory shall be present, but not superfluous ones: clean rather than costly. Nothing of gold or silver shall be fashioned for it, except one silver chalice—or more, if necessary. No silk ornaments shall be used, except stoles or phanons. There shall be no carved images in it. Only a wooden cross shall be erected at the altar; if it is thought desirable that an image of the Savior be painted upon it, this is not forbidden. But the altars shall contain no other images. Let the monastery be content with two bells. A vessel of holy water shall be placed outside at the entrance of the oratory, so that those entering in the morning, or departing after Compline, may bless themselves with it.

No nun shall be absent from the canonical hours. As soon as the signal has sounded, setting aside everything else, they shall hasten to the divine office, though with modest gait. On entering the oratory quietly, they shall say, as far as they can: “I shall enter into your house; I shall worship toward your holy temple” (Ps. 5:8), etc. No book shall be kept in choir except one needed for the present office. The psalms shall be said openly and distinctly, so as to be understood; and the psalmody or chant shall be so moderate that those with weak voices may sustain it. Nothing shall be read or sung in church unless taken from authoritative Scripture, especially from the New or Old Testament. Both shall be divided through the readings so that they are read entire in church over the course of the year. Expositions upon them, sermons of the doctors, or any writings containing something edifying from Scripture shall be recited at table or in chapter; and reading shall be permitted to all wherever it is needed.

No one shall presume to read or sing anything she has not first reviewed. If one of them happens to pronounce something incorrectly in the oratory, she shall make satisfaction there, quietly, while prostrating herself before all, saying: “Forgive, Lord, even this time my negligence.”

At midnight, according to the prophetic institution, they must rise for the night vigils; therefore they must go to bed sufficiently early for weak nature to be able to bear these vigils. Everything belonging to the day should, where possible, be done in daylight, as blessed Benedict also prescribed. After the vigils they shall return to the dormitory before the hour of Matins is sounded. If any of the night remains, sleep must not be denied to weak nature. Sleep especially refreshes weary nature, makes it able to endure work, and preserves it sober and cheerful. Yet those who need to meditate upon the Psalter or certain readings, as blessed Benedict also mentions, must do so in such a way that they do not disturb those who are resting. He said “meditation” rather than “reading” in this place precisely so that one person’s reading might not impede another’s rest. And when he says, “by the brethren who need it,” he certainly did not compel them even to this meditation. Nevertheless, if instruction in chant is also needed, similar provision must be made for those who require it.

The morning hour shall be performed as soon as day begins to dawn; and, if it can be arranged, it shall be rung at the rising of the morning star. When it is completed, they shall return to the dormitory. If it is summer, however, because then the night-time is short and Matins long, we do not forbid them to sleep a little before Prime, until they are awakened by the signal. Blessed Gregory also mentions this rest after the morning Lauds in chapter 2 of the *Dialogues*, when speaking of the venerable man Libertinus: “On the following day a matter was appointed on account of the monastery’s benefit. Therefore, after the morning hymns had been completed, Libertinus came to the abbot’s bed and humbly asked him for a prayer.”

This morning rest shall not be denied from Easter until the autumnal equinox, after which the day begins to shorten. On leaving the dormitory, they shall wash and, taking books, sit in the cloister reading or singing until Prime is sounded. After Prime they shall go to chapter, and, when all are seated there, the reading of the Martyrology shall be given, the moon having first been announced. Afterward, either some edifying discourse shall be delivered, or something from the Rule shall be read and expounded. Then anything requiring correction or arrangement must be dealt with.

It must be understood that neither a monastery nor any house ought to be called disordered merely because disorderly things occur there, but only if, once they have occurred, they are not diligently corrected. For what place is wholly free from sin? Blessed Augustine, carefully considering this when instructing his clergy, says in one passage (Letter 137):

> However vigilantly the discipline of my household may be maintained, I am a human being and live among human beings. Nor do I dare arrogate to myself that my household is better than Noah’s ark, where nevertheless among eight persons one was found reprobate (Gen. 7:1); or better than Abraham’s household, where it was said, “Cast out the maidservant and her son” (Gen. 21:10); or better than Isaac’s household: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:3); or better than Jacob’s household (Gen. 25:22), where a son violated his father’s bed; or better than David’s household (2 Kings 13:1), in which one son lay with his sister and another rebelled against his father’s so holy gentleness; or better than the fellowship of the apostle Paul, who, if he had lived among good people, would not have said, “Without were conflicts, within were fears” (2 Cor. 7:5), nor spoken: “There is no one who is genuinely concerned for you. All seek their own interests”; or better than the fellowship of Christ himself, in which eleven good men endured Judas, the faithless traitor and thief; or finally better than heaven, from which angels fell.

He also strongly exhorts us to monastic discipline, adding:

> I confess before God that, since I began to serve God, I have found it difficult to experience persons better than those who have made progress in monasteries; so too I have found none worse than those who have fallen in monasteries.

Thus, I think, it is written in the Apocalypse: “Let the righteous become still more righteous, and let the filthy become still more filthy” (Rev. 22:11).

Discipline of correction must therefore be so strict that any sister who sees something in another that requires correction and conceals it shall be subject to a more severe discipline than the one who committed it. No one, therefore, shall delay to accuse either her own fault or another’s. But whoever accuses herself before another does so shall deserve a milder discipline, as it is written: “The righteous person is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17), if her negligence has ceased. No one shall presume to excuse another, unless perhaps the deaconess asks others about the truth of a matter unknown to her. No one shall ever presume to strike another for any fault unless the deaconess has assigned her to do so.

For it is written concerning corrective discipline: “My son, do not reject the discipline of the Lord; do not lose heart when you are corrected by him. For the Lord corrects the one whom he loves, and as a father he delights in a son” (Prov. 3:11). Likewise: “Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but whoever loves him diligently instructs him” (Prov. 13:24). “When a pestilent person is scourged, the fool will become wiser” (Prov. 19:25). “When a pestilent person is punished, the little one becomes wiser” (Prov. 21:11). “A whip for a horse, a bridle for an ass, and a rod for the back of the imprudent” (Prov. 26:23). “Whoever corrects a person shall afterward find favor with him more than one who deceives through the flatteries of the tongue” (Prov. 28:23). “All discipline indeed seems at present to be not a matter of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceable fruit of righteousness to those trained by it” (Heb. 12:21). “A father’s shame lies in an undisciplined son; but a foolish daughter will be diminished” (Ecclus. 22:3). “Whoever loves his son applies the lash to him continually, that he may rejoice in the end” (Ecclus. 30:1). “Whoever teaches his son shall be praised in him, and shall glory in him among his household. An untamed horse becomes stubborn, and an undisciplined son becomes reckless. Indulge your son, and he will make you afraid; play with him, and he will make you sad” (ibid., 8).

In deliberation, everyone may state her own opinion; but whatever seems right to all must be held as the unalterable decree of the deaconess, in whose judgment all things rest—even if, God forbid, she herself is mistaken and establishes what is worse. Hence this saying of blessed Augustine in the *Confessions*: “A person sins greatly who is disobedient to his superiors in anything, even if he chooses things better than those commanded him.” For it is far better for us to do something well than merely to do a good thing. One must consider not so much what is done as how, or with what disposition, it is done. Whatever is done in obedience is done well, even though what is done seems by no means good. Therefore superiors must be obeyed in all things, however great the loss of possessions, provided no danger to the soul is apparent. Let the superior take care to command rightly, for it is enough for subjects to obey rightly; they must follow not their own will, as they have professed, but that of their superiors.

We absolutely forbid [variant: “We forbid everyone”] that custom should ever be preferred to reason, or that anything should ever be defended because it is customary rather than because it is rational; not because it is usual, but because it is good. And it should be accepted all the more willingly the better it appears. Otherwise, like Judaizers, we would prefer the antiquity of the Law to the Gospel. Blessed Augustine, advancing many testimonies concerning Cyprian’s judgment, says in one place (Book III):

> Whoever, despising truth, presumes to follow custom is either envious and malicious toward brethren to whom truth is revealed, or ungrateful toward God, by whose inspiration his Church is instructed.

Likewise (Book VI):

> In the Gospel the Lord says, “I am the Truth” (John 14:6). He did not say, “I am custom.” Therefore, once truth has been made manifest, let custom yield to truth. Likewise, once truth has been revealed, let error yield to truth; for Peter also, who formerly circumcised, yielded to Paul preaching the truth.

The same author, Book IV, *On Baptism*:

> Those who are overcome by reason vainly set custom before us, as though custom were greater than truth, or as though in spiritual matters one ought not to follow what has been revealed for the better by the Holy Spirit.

This is plainly true: reason and truth must be preferred to custom. Gregory VII to Bishop Wimund [variant: Willimund], *Distinction* 8, chapter *Si consuet.*:

> And certainly, to use the judgment of blessed Cyprian, every custom, however ancient or widespread, must wholly yield to truth; and a practice contrary to truth must be abolished.

How greatly the truthfulness of words too should be embraced, we are admonished in Ecclesiasticus: “For your soul’s sake, do not be ashamed to speak the truth” (Ecclus. 4:24). Likewise: “Do not in any way contradict a word of truth” (ibid., 30). And again: “Before all your works let a truthful word go before you, and before every act a firm counsel” (Ecclus. 27:20).

Nothing should be regarded as authoritative because it is done by many, but because it is approved by the wise and good. “The number of fools,” Solomon says, “is infinite” (Eccles. 1:15). And according to the assertion of Truth: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14). Precious things are always rare; things abundant in number are diminished in value. In counsel no one should follow the greater part of people, but the better part. One should consider not a person’s age but wisdom; attend not to friendship but truth. Hence the poetic saying:

> “It is right to learn even from an enemy.”  
> —Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book IV

Whenever counsel is needed, it must not be delayed. If deliberation concerns important matters, the community shall be summoned. In considering lesser matters, it will suffice for the deaconess to summon to herself a few persons of the senior rank. It is also written concerning counsel: “Where there is no governor, the people fall; but safety lies where there are many counsels” (Prov. 11:14). “The way of a fool is right in his own eyes, but the wise person listens to counsels” (Prov. 12:15). “My child, do nothing without counsel, and after you have acted you will not repent” (Ecclus. 32:24).

If something undertaken without counsel happens to have a successful outcome, the benefit of fortune does not excuse human presumption. But if, after counsel, they sometimes err, the authority that sought counsel shall not be held guilty of presumption. The one who trusted is not so much to be blamed as those to whom he himself gave assent while they erred.

When they leave chapter, they shall attend to the work that ought to be done: reading, singing, or manual labor, until Terce. After Terce, Mass shall be said. For its celebration one of the monks, a priest assigned for the week, shall be appointed. He, indeed, if there is a sufficient number [variant: “present”], ought to come with a deacon and subdeacon, who may provide what is necessary for him or themselves perform their proper functions. Their entrance and departure shall be managed in such a way that they are never exposed to the community of sisters. If more ministers are necessary, provision shall also be made for them, always, if possible, in such a way that monks, because of the nuns’ Masses, are never absent from their own community’s divine offices.

If the sisters are to receive Communion, an elder priest shall be chosen to communicate them after Mass, after the deacon and subdeacon have first departed, in order to remove an occasion of temptation. At least three times each year the whole community shall communicate: at Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord, as the Fathers instituted even for laypeople. They shall prepare themselves for these Communions so that, on the third day beforehand, all come to confession and appropriate satisfaction, and purify themselves with a three-day fast of bread and water, frequent prayer, all humility, and trembling, repeatedly considering within themselves the Apostle’s fearful sentence:

> “Therefore, whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. Therefore many among you are sick and weak, and many sleep. But if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Cor. 11:27).

After Mass they shall return to their work until Sext and shall never live idly, but each shall perform what she can and ought. After Sext they shall eat, unless it is a fast day.
