Then None must be awaited, and in Lent Vespers as well. At no time shall the community be without reading. When the deaconess wishes to end it, she shall say, “It is enough,” and all shall immediately rise to give thanks to the Lord.

In summer, after the meal until None, they shall rest in the dormitory; after None they shall return to work until Vespers. After Vespers they shall either eat supper immediately or take drink, and then, according to the custom of the season, go to the conference reading. On Saturday, before the conference, acts of cleanliness shall be performed, namely washing the feet and hands. In this service the deaconess shall serve with the weekly sisters who have served in the kitchen. After the conference they shall come immediately to Compline, and afterward go to sleep.

Concerning food and clothing, the apostolic judgment is to be maintained, where it is said: “But having food and coverings, with these let us be content” (1 Tim. 6:8). That is, necessities should suffice; superfluities should not be sought. And whatever can be acquired more cheaply, obtained more easily, and consumed without scandal, should in fact be allowed. [Col. 0286B]

For the Apostle avoids, in matters of food, only the scandal of one’s own conscience or that of another, knowing that the fault lies not in food but in desire. “He who eats,” he says, “must not despise him who does not eat. And he who does not eat must not judge him who eats. Who are you to judge another’s servant? He who eats, eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who does not eat, does not eat for the Lord, and gives thanks to God. Therefore let us no longer judge one another; rather judge this: not to put a stumbling-block or scandal before a brother. I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean through him, except for the person who considers something unclean. The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. All things indeed are clean; but it is evil for the person who eats through a stumbling-block. It is good not to eat meat or drink wine, nor anything by which your brother is offended or scandalized” (Rom. 14:3).

After speaking of a brother’s scandal, he also adds the scandal of the person himself who eats contrary to his conscience, saying: “Blessed is he who does not judge himself in what he approves. But he who makes distinctions, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith. And everything that is not from faith is sin” (ibid., 22). For in everything we do against our conscience and against what we believe, we sin. And in what we approve—that is, by the law which we approve and accept—we judge and condemn ourselves, if we eat those foods which we distinguish, that is, exclude and separate by law [Col. 0286C] as unclean.

So great, indeed, is the testimony of our conscience that it especially accuses or excuses us before God. Hence John also recalls in his First Epistle: “Beloved, if our heart does not rebuke us, we have confidence before God. And whatever we ask, we receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do those things which are pleasing before him” (1 John 3:21).

Accordingly Paul also rightly says above that nothing is unclean through Christ except to the person who thinks something unclean (Rom. 14:23), that is, who believes it to be unclean and forbidden for himself. We call foods “common” which, according to the law, are called unclean, because the law excludes them from its own people as though they were outside the law, exposing and making them public. Hence common women are unclean, [Col. 0287A] and anything common or made public is cheap or less valued.

Therefore he declares that no food is common—that is, unclean—through Christ, because Christ’s law forbids none, except, as stated, in order to remove scandal, whether that of one’s own conscience or that of another. Concerning this he says elsewhere: “Therefore, if food scandalizes my brother, I shall never eat meat, lest I scandalize my brother” (1 Cor. 8:13). “Am I not free? Am I not an apostle?” (1 Cor. 9:1). As if he said: Do I not have that freedom which the Lord gave the apostles, namely, freedom to eat whatever foods they please or to receive sustenance from others? For when he sent the apostles, he said in one place: “Eating and drinking what they have” [Col. 0287B] (Luke 10:7), thus distinguishing no food from the rest.

The Apostle carefully considers this and diligently maintains that every kind of food, even if it is the food of unbelievers or food sacrificed to idols, is lawful for Christians—avoiding only, as we have said, scandal in food: “All things,” he says, “are lawful, but not all things are profitable. All things are lawful to me, but not all things edify. Let no one seek his own [another reading: seeks], but that of another. Eat whatever is sold in the market, asking no questions on account of conscience” (1 Cor. 10:22). “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Ps. 23:1). “If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions on account of conscience. But if anyone says, ‘This has been offered to idols,’ do not eat, because of him who pointed it out, and because of conscience—I mean not your conscience, but another’s. Give no offense to Jews, Greeks, or the Church of God.”

From these words of the Apostle it is plainly inferred that no food is forbidden to us which we can eat without offense to our own conscience or another’s. We act without offense to our own conscience when we are confident that we keep the plan of life by which we can be saved. We act without offense to another’s conscience when we are believed to live in the manner by which we may be saved. We shall indeed live in that manner if, while allowing all things necessary to nature, we avoid sins; and if, not presuming upon our own strength, we do not bind ourselves by profession to the yoke of a life beneath which we shall be overburdened [Col. 0287D] and fall—our fall being the graver, the higher the degree of our profession had been.

Forestalling this fall and the vow of a foolish profession, Ecclesiastes says: “If you have vowed anything to God, do not delay in paying it; for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeases him. But whatever you have vowed, pay it. It is better not to vow than, after a vow, not to fulfill what was promised” (Eccles. 5:2). The apostolic counsel likewise meets this danger: “I wish younger women to marry, bear children, manage households, and give the adversary no occasion for reproach. For already some have turned back after Satan” (1 Tim. 5:14). Considering the frailty of their age, he sets the remedy of a less strict life against the danger of a better one. He advises remaining at the bottom, lest one be cast headlong from a height. Blessed Jerome also follows this counsel when instructing the virgin Eustochium (Epistle 22): “But if even those who are virgins are not saved because of other faults, what will happen to those who have prostituted the members of Christ and turned the temple of the Holy Spirit into a brothel? It would have been better for a person to enter marriage and walk on level ground than, striving for higher things, to fall into the depths of hell.”

Even if we review all the Apostle’s sayings, we shall never find him permitting second marriages except to women. Yet especially exhorting men to continence, he says: “Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not seek to remove his circumcision” (1 Cor. 7:18). And again: “Are you released from a wife? Do not seek a wife” (ibid., 27). Moses, however, is more indulgent to men than to women: he permits one man several women at the same time, but not one woman several men; and he punishes women’s adultery more severely than men’s.

“A woman,” says the Apostle, “if her husband has died, is freed from the law of her husband, so that she is not an adulteress if she is with another man” (Rom. 7:37). And elsewhere: “But I say to the unmarried and widows: It is good for them if they remain as I am. But if they do not contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn” (1 Cor. 7:8). Again: “If her husband has fallen asleep, a woman is free. Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. But she will be happier if she remains thus, according to my counsel” (ibid., 39).

He grants second marriages not only to the weaker sex, but does not dare to limit them by any number; when their husbands have died, he permits them to marry others. [Col. 0288C] He fixes no number for their marriages, provided they escape the guilt of fornication. Let them marry repeatedly rather than commit fornication once, lest, if they prostitute themselves to one man, they pay to many the debt of carnal intercourse. Yet even that payment of the debt is not altogether free from sin; lesser sins are permitted in order that greater sins may be avoided.

What wonder, then, if that in which there is no sin whatsoever is allowed so that they do not incur sin—namely, any necessary foods, though not superfluous ones? For, as has been said, the fault lies not in food but in desire: when one takes pleasure in what is not permitted, desires what is forbidden, and sometimes consumes with shamelessness that from which the greatest scandal arises. But among all human foods, what is so dangerous, harmful, and opposed to our religion or holy tranquillity as wine? The great sage, observing this carefully, especially warns us away from it, saying: “Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness tumultuous. Whoever delights in them will not be wise” (Prov. 20:1). “Who has woe? Whose father has woe? Who has quarrels? Who has pits? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of the eyes? Is it not those who linger over wine and devote themselves to emptying cups? Do not look at wine when it grows yellow, when its color shines in the glass. It goes down smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a serpent and pour out venom like a basilisk. Your eyes will see strange women, and your heart will speak perverse things; [Col. 0289A] and you will be like one sleeping in the midst of the sea, and like a helmsman overcome by sleep after losing the rudder. And you will say: ‘They struck me, but I did not hurt; they dragged me, but I did not feel it. When shall I wake up and find wines again?’” (Prov. 23:29).

Likewise: “Do not give wine to kings, O Lemuel; do not give wine to kings, for there is no secret where drunkenness reigns, lest perhaps they drink and forget judgments, and dismiss the cause of the children of the poor” (Prov. 31:4). And it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “A drunken workman will not grow rich, and he who despises small things will gradually fall. Wine and women make wise men apostatize and rebuke the sensible” (Ecclus. 19:1).

Isaiah likewise, passing over every other food, mentions wine alone as the cause of the people’s captivity: “Woe,” he says, “to you who rise early to pursue drunkenness and continue drinking until evening, so that you burn with wine. Harp and lyre and drum and flute and wine are at your banquets, and you do not regard the work of the Lord. Therefore my people have been led captive because they had no knowledge. Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 5:11). Extending his complaint from the people even to priests and prophets, he says: “But these also have not known because of wine, and have gone astray because of drunkenness. Priest and prophet have not known because of drunkenness; they are swallowed up by wine, they have gone astray in drunkenness, they have not known the seer, they have ignored judgment. For all tables are filled with vomit and filth, [Col. 0289C] so that there is no place left. Whom will he teach knowledge, and whom will he make understand what is heard?” (Isa. 28:7).

The Lord says through Joel: “Wake up, you drunkards, and weep, you who drink wine in sweetness” (Joel 1:5). For he does not forbid the use of wine in necessity, as the Apostle advises Timothy concerning it “because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5:23)—not merely infirmities, but frequent ones. Noah first planted a vineyard (Gen. 9:20), perhaps not yet knowing the evil of drunkenness; and, becoming drunk, he uncovered his thighs, because the shamefulness of lust is joined to wine. When he was mocked by his son, he pronounced a curse upon him and bound him under a sentence of servitude—things which we know had not occurred before.

Lot’s daughters saw that the holy man could be drawn into incest only through drunkenness (Gen. 19:33). The blessed widow likewise believed that proud Holofernes could be deceived and overthrown only by this device (Judith 13:4). We read that angels appearing to the ancient fathers and received by them in hospitality ate meat, not wine (Gen. 18:1). Ravens brought to Elijah, that greatest and first of our princes, while he hid in the wilderness, sustenance of bread and meat morning and evening, not wine (3 Kings 17:6). The people of Israel also, nourished in the wilderness by the most delicate foods, especially quails, are read neither to have used wine nor to have desired it (Exod. 16:13). Those meals of bread and fish by which the people were sustained in the wilderness are likewise reported to have contained no wine.

Only weddings—where the intemperance of wine, in which there is lust, is indulged—received a miracle (John 2:8). But the wilderness, the proper dwelling of monks, knows the benefit of meat rather than wine. Even that supreme religious observance of the Nazarites under the Law, by which they consecrate themselves to the Lord, avoided only wine and whatever can intoxicate (Num. 6:3). What virtue, what good remains in drunkards? Hence we read that not wine alone, but also everything able to intoxicate, was forbidden even to the ancient priests.

Jerome, writing to Nepotian on the life of clerics (Epistle 2), indignantly complains that priests of the Law, abstaining from everything able to intoxicate, surpass our own priests in this abstinence: “By no means smell of wine, lest you hear the philosopher’s saying: ‘That is not offering a kiss, but offering a drink.’” The Apostle condemns drunken priests, and the old Law forbids them: “Those who serve the altar (1 Cor. 10:13) shall not drink wine or strong drink” (Luke 1:15). In Hebrew speech, *sicera* denotes every drink that can intoxicate: whether it is made by fermentation, or from the juice of fruits; whether honeycombs are boiled down into sweetness; whether a drink of herbs or fruits of palms is pressed into liquid; or whether water, made richer by cooked grain, is strained. Flee everything which intoxicates and overturns the mind’s stability just as you flee wine.

From the Rule of Saint Pachomius: “Let no one touch wine or sauce except in the place of the sick.” Who among you [another reading: among us] has not heard that wine does not belong to monks at all, and that monks of old so abhorred it that, earnestly warning against it, they called it Satan himself? Hence we read in the *Lives of the Fathers*: “Some told Abbot Pastor about a monk who did not drink wine; and he said to them: ‘Wine does not belong to monks at all.’” Likewise, further on: “A celebration of the masses was once held on the mountain of Abbot Antony, and a small jar of wine was found there. One of the elders took it, carried a little vessel—a cup—to Abbot Sisoes, gave it to him, and he drank once and a second time; he accepted it and drank. He offered it to him a third time, but he did not accept it, saying: ‘Stop, brother; do you not know that it is Satan?’”

Again, concerning Abbot Sisoes: “Then Abraham says to his disciples: ‘If he comes to church on Saturday and Sunday, and drinks three cups, is that not too much?’ And the old man said: ‘If Satan were not involved, it would not be too much.’” Therefore blessed Benedict also, not forgetting this, when he permitted wine to monks with a certain dispensation, says (ch. 46): “Although we read that wine does not belong to monks at all, nevertheless because in our times monks cannot be persuaded of this at all…”

What wonder, then, if that which ought not at all to be permitted to monks is wholly forbidden by blessed Jerome even to women, whose nature is weaker in itself and yet stronger against wine? For, instructing Eustochium, Christ’s virgin, in preserving virginity, he vehemently exhorts her, saying (Epistle 22): “If, therefore, there can be any counsel in me, if one believes the experienced, this is my first warning and entreaty: that the bride of Christ flee wine as poison. These are the demons’ first weapons against youth. Avarice does not so shake us, pride does not so inflate us, ambition does not so delight us. We easily do without other vices. This enemy is enclosed within us. Wherever we go, we carry the enemy with us. Wine and youth are a double fire of pleasure. Why do we add oil to the flame? Why do we furnish fuel for fires to a burning little body?” [Col. 0291A]

Yet it is established from the writings of those who have written on natural science that the force of wine can prevail much less over women than over men. Macrobius Theodosius, giving the reason for this in Book IV of the *Saturnalia*, says as follows (ch. 6): “Aristotle says that women are rarely intoxicated, old men frequently. A woman’s body is exceedingly moist. The smoothness and brightness of the skin demonstrate this; above all, the frequent purgations which relieve the body of superfluous moisture demonstrate it. Therefore, when wine that has been drunk falls into so great an abundance of moisture, it loses its force and does not easily strike the seat of the brain, its strength having been extinguished.” Likewise (ibid.): “The female body, cleansed by frequent purgations, is furnished with many openings, so that it lies open in channels and provides pathways for the moisture flowing toward its exit in evacuation. Through these openings the vapor of wine quickly evaporates.”

On what grounds, then, is granted to monks what is denied to the weaker sex? How great is the madness of allowing it to those whom it can harm more, and denying it to others? What, finally, is more foolish than for religion not to abhor what is more contrary to religion and causes people most greatly [Col. 0291C] to apostatize from God? What is more shameless than not to avoid—indeed, to take the greatest delight in—what is forbidden even to kings and priests under the Law (Prov. 31:5; Lev. 10:9), while claiming the abstinence of Christian perfection?

Who, indeed, does not know how much, in this age, the special concern of clerics and monks is occupied with storerooms, that they may fill them with different kinds of wine? They season it with herbs, honey, and spices, so that they may become drunk more easily as they drink more pleasantly; and may stir themselves to lust more intensely as they burn more with wine. What is this if not frenzy rather than error: that those who bind themselves most strictly by a profession of continence prepare themselves least for keeping their vow—or rather, arrange matters so that it can scarcely be kept? Although their bodies are confined within cloisters, their hearts are full of lust, and their minds burn toward fornication.

Writing to Timothy, the Apostle says: “Drink water no longer, but use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5:23). Since a little wine is granted to him because of illness, it is certainly clear that, if healthy, he would drink none. If we profess the apostolic life, especially vow a pattern of penitence, and undertake to flee the world, why do we especially delight in what we see to be most hostile to our purpose and more pleasant than all foods? Blessed Ambrose, a careful describer of penitence, finds fault with nothing in the diet of penitents except wine, saying (*On Penance*, Book II, ch. 20): “Does anyone suppose that penitence exists where there is ambition to acquire rank, where there is a pouring-out of wine, where there is the use of the marital union itself? One must renounce the world. I have found more easily those who have preserved innocence than those who have performed fitting penitence.” Likewise, in *On Flight from the World* (ch. 9): “You flee well if your eye flees cups and bowls, lest it become lustful while it lingers over wine.”

Of all foods he mentions wine alone in connection with flight from the world; and he declares that, if we flee wine, we flee the world well, as though all worldly pleasures depended upon this one [another reading: wine]. Nor does he even say, “if the palate avoids its taste,” but also, “if the eye avoids its sight,” lest it be captured by lust and pleasure in what it frequently beholds. Hence also comes Solomon’s saying, which we recalled above: “Do not look at wine when it grows yellow, when its color shines in the glass” (Prov. 23:31).

But what, I ask, shall we say here, who, so that we may delight both in its taste and in its sight, season it with honey, herbs, and various spices and insist that it be served in bowls? Blessed Benedict, compelled to make an allowance for wine, says (ch. 40): “At least let us agree on this: not to drink to satiety, but more sparingly; for wine makes even the wise apostatize” (Ecclus. 19:2). Would that drinking to satiety were sufficient, so that we might not be carried beyond this transgression into the excess of a greater offense.

Blessed Augustine also, arranging monasteries for clerics and writing them a rule, says (ch. 2): “Only on Saturday and Sunday, according to custom, let those who wish receive wine”—that is, both out of reverence for the Lord’s Day and its vigil, which is Saturday, and because the brothers then gathered together, having been dispersed through their cells. Thus blessed Jerome too recalls in the *Lives of the Fathers*, writing of the place he called Cellia, in these words (Part I): “They live separately in their cells. Yet on Saturday and Sunday they come together in one body at church, and there see one another as though restored to heaven.” It was therefore fitting that this concession be made, so that when gathered together they might rejoice jointly in some refreshment, not so much saying as feeling: “Behold, how good [Col. 0292D] and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1).

See how, if we abstain from meat, a great achievement is credited to us, however excessive our consumption of other things may be. If at great expense we procure diverse dishes of fish; if we mingle flavors of pepper and spices; if, when drunk with unmixed wine, we add cups of herb-flavored wine and bowls of spiced wine. All of this is excused by abstinence from cheap meat, provided we do not devour it publicly—as though the quality of foods rather than excessive consumption were culpable, when the Lord forbids us only gluttony and drunkenness (Luke 21:34), that is, the excess of both food and wine rather than their quality.

Blessed Augustine carefully observes this and, fearing nothing in foods except wine and distinguishing no quality of food, thought this sufficient in abstinence, as he briefly expressed it (Epistle 109): “Subdue your flesh by fasts and by abstinence from food or drink, as far as health permits.” He had read, unless I am mistaken, this saying of blessed Athanasius in his exhortation to monks: “Let there be no fixed measure of fasts for those who desire them, but only as far as ability allows, unless the person is laboring; let them always be solemn except on the Lord’s Day, not vowed.” As if he said: If they are undertaken by vow, let them be devoutly completed at every time except on Sundays. No fasts are prescribed here; only the limit permitted by health is established.

For it is said: “He considers only nature’s capacity and allows it to set its own measure for itself, knowing [Col. 0293B] that there is no fault in anything if measure is maintained in all things.” Thus we must neither dissolve ourselves in pleasures more loosely than is fitting, as is written of the people nourished on the marrow of wheat and the purest wine: “He grew fat, became broad, and kicked” (Deut. 32:15); nor, worn down or wholly overcome by excessive abstinence, fall, or lose our reward by murmuring, or glory in singularity.

Forestalling this, Ecclesiastes says: “The righteous man perishes in his righteousness. Do not be righteous overmuch, and do not be wiser than necessary, lest you be amazed and, as though admiring your own singularity, swell with pride” (Eccles. 7:17). Let discretion, the mother of all virtues, preside over this carefulness in such a way that it diligently considers what burdens to impose upon whom, following each person’s own strength [Col. 0293C] and nature rather than dragging them; that it removes not the use of satiety [another reading: fullness], but the abuse of excess. Thus vices are uprooted without injury to nature.

It is enough for the weak if they avoid sins, even if they do not ascend to the summit of perfection. It is enough also to sit in a corner of paradise, if you cannot sit with the martyrs. It is safe to vow small things, so that grace may add greater things to what is owed. Hence it is written: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to do’” (Luke 17:10).

“The law,” says the Apostle, “works wrath; for where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). And again: “For without the law sin was dead. But I once lived without the law. When the commandment came, sin revived; but I died, and the commandment which was for life was found to be for death to me. For sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and killed me through it, so that sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment” (Rom. 7:8). Augustine, *To Simplicianus*: “Because desire was increased by prohibition, it was made sweeter and therefore deceived.” The same, in Book II of the *Questions*, Question 83: “The persuasion of pleasure toward sin is more vehement when prohibition is present.”

“Always we strive toward what is forbidden and desire what is denied.” (Ovid, Book III.)

Let whoever wishes to bind himself, as it were under the yoke of a new law, by professing some rule, take heed of these things with trembling. Let him choose what he can do; let him fear what he cannot. No one becomes liable to a law unless he has first professed it. Deliberate before you profess; when you have professed, observe it. What is voluntary beforehand becomes necessary afterward. “In my Father’s house,” says Truth, “there are many dwelling-places” (John 14:2). Thus there are also many ways by which one may arrive there. Married people are not condemned, but the continent are saved more easily. The rules of the holy Fathers were added not so that we might be saved, but so that we might be saved more easily and might devote ourselves more purely to God. “If a virgin marries,” says the Apostle, “she does not sin; nevertheless such persons will have tribulation in the flesh. But I spare you” (1 Cor. 7:28). Likewise: “The unmarried woman and the virgin think upon the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in body and spirit. But she who is married thinks upon the things of the world, how she may please her husband. Now I say this for your advantage, not that I may cast a snare upon you, but for what is fitting and what affords the means of serving God without hindrance” (ibid., 34).

This is most easily accomplished when, withdrawing bodily also from the world, we shut ourselves within the enclosures of monasteries, lest secular tumults disturb us. Nor should only the one who receives a law take care: the one who imposes a law must also take care lest, by multiplying commands, he multiply transgressions. The Word of God, when He came, made a shortened word upon the earth. Moses spoke many things; yet, as the Apostle says, “the law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:19). Indeed, it spoke many things, and things so burdensome that the Apostle Peter declares that no one could bear its commands, saying: “Men and brethren, why do you test God by putting a yoke upon the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we shall be saved, even as they” (Acts 15:10).

In few words Christ instructed the apostles concerning the building up of character and holiness of life, and taught perfection. Removing harsh and heavy things, He commanded things sweet and light, in which He brought all religion to completion: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart; and you shall find rest for your souls. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light” (Matt. 11:28).

For often in good works it happens as it does in worldly business. Many indeed labor more in business and gain less. And many are outwardly afflicted more, yet advance less inwardly before God, who looks upon the heart rather than the work. The more they are occupied in outward matters, the less they can devote themselves to inward things; and the more they become known among people, who judge according to outward things, the greater glory they attain among them, and the more easily they are deceived through pride. Confronting this error, the Apostle strongly diminishes works and magnifies justification by faith, saying: “For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before the Lord. For what does Scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:2). And again: “What then shall we say? That the Gentiles, who did not pursue righteousness, attained righteousness—but the righteousness which is from faith—whereas Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness? Why? Because not from faith, but as though from works” (Gen. 15:6).

Those who cleanse the outside of the cup or dish take less care for inward cleanliness; watching over the flesh more than the soul, they are carnal rather than spiritual. But we, desiring Christ to dwell in the outward person through faith, account outward things of little importance—things common alike to reprobate and elect—attending to what is written: “In me, O God, are your vows, which I shall render to you as praises” (Ps. 56:12). Therefore we do not follow that outward abstinence of the Law, which clearly contributes nothing to righteousness. Nor does the Lord forbid us anything in food (Luke 21:34), except surfeiting and drunkenness—that is, excess. What He permitted us, He did not blush to display in Himself, though many were greatly scandalized thereby and reproached Him. Thus He speaks of Himself: “John came neither eating nor drinking, and they said, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they said, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine’” (Matt. 11:18).

And when He excused His own because they did not fast like the disciples of John (Matt. 9:14), nor, while eating, took great care for the bodily cleanliness of washing hands, He said: “The children of the bridegroom cannot mourn while the bridegroom is with them” (ibid., 15). And elsewhere: “Not what enters into the mouth defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth. But what proceeds from the mouth comes forth from the heart, and these things defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person” (Matt. 15:11).

Therefore no food defiles the soul, but the desire for forbidden food. For as the body is defiled only by bodily filth, so the soul is defiled only by spiritual filth. Whatever is done in the body need not be feared if the mind is not drawn to consent. Nor should one trust in bodily cleanliness if the mind is corrupted by its will. Thus the entire death and life of the soul lies in the heart. Hence Solomon says in Proverbs: “With all vigilance guard your heart, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. 5:23). And according to the aforesaid declaration of Truth, the things that defile a person proceed from the heart; for by good or evil desires the soul is condemned or saved.

But because there is a very great union of soul and flesh joined in one person, every care must be taken lest the pleasure of the flesh draw the soul into consent, and lest, while the flesh is indulged too much, it grow wanton and resist the spirit, beginning to rule when it ought to be subject. We can guard against this if, granting everything necessary, we cut away excess altogether, as has often been said, and deny the weaker sex no use of foods, but deny every abuse of them. Let all things be permitted for use, but let none be consumed immoderately.

“Every creature of God,” says the Apostle, “is good, and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. By setting these things before the brethren, you shall be a good minister of Christ Jesus, nourished by the words of faith and the good doctrine which you have followed” (1 Tim. 4:4). Therefore we too, following with Timothy this teaching of the Apostle, and according to the Lord’s sentence avoiding in food nothing except surfeiting and drunkenness (Luke 21:34), should so regulate all things that by them all we sustain weak nature, not nourish vices. And the more any particular thing can harm through its excess, the more moderation it should receive.

For it is greater and more praiseworthy to eat moderately than to abstain altogether. Hence blessed Augustine, in his book *On the Good of Marriage*, when speaking of bodily sustenance, says: “No one uses them well unless he can also refrain from using them. Many more easily abstain, so as not to use them, than moderate themselves so as to use them well. Yet no one can use them wisely unless he can also refrain from using them continently.” From this habit Paul also said: “I know both how to abound and how to suffer need” (Phil. 4:12). To suffer need belongs to people of every kind; but to know how to suffer need belongs to great persons. So also anyone can begin to abound; but to know how to abound belongs only to those whom abundance does not corrupt.

Concerning wine, therefore: because, as has been said, it is a luxurious and tumultuous thing, and is consequently most opposed both to continence and to silence, women should either abstain from it altogether for God’s sake—as the wives of Gentiles are forbidden it through fear of adultery—or temper it with water so that it may provide alike for thirst and health and have no power to harm. We believe this will be achieved if at least a fourth part of the mixture is water. Yet it is very difficult to observe the drink set before us in such a way that we do not drink from it to satiety, as blessed Benedict prescribes concerning wine (ch. 40). Therefore we judge it safer not to forbid satiety, lest we thereby incur danger [alternative reading: “danger to life”]. For, as we have often said, satiety is not culpable, but excess is.

That herb-infused wines be prepared as medicine, or even that pure wine be taken, is not to be forbidden. Yet the community must never use these; they are to be tasted separately by the sick. We likewise altogether prohibit the finest wheat flour, *similago*, from the inner kernel of wheat; but whenever they have wheat, let at least a third part of coarser grain be mixed with it. Let them never enjoy hot bread, but only bread baked at least one day beforehand.

The deaconess should so provide other foods that, as we have already said, she may assist the weaker sex with what can be bought more cheaply or obtained more readily. For what is more foolish than, when our own goods suffice, to buy those of others? When necessary things are at home, to seek superfluities outside? When things sufficient are at hand, to labor for what is superfluous? In this necessary moderation of discernment, instructed not so much by human as by angelic—even divine—example, let us know that, in passing through the necessities of this life, we should seek not so much the quality of foods as contentment with what is available.

Thus angels eat the meat Abraham prepared (Gen. 18:9), and the Lord Jesus refreshed a fasting multitude with fish found in the wilderness (Mark 8:8; John 6:10). From this we are plainly taught that the eating of meat and fish alike is not to be rejected indiscriminately; rather, that food should especially be eaten which is free from sinful offense, offers itself willingly and is easier to prepare, and requires less expense.

Thus Seneca, that great advocate of poverty and continence and greatest among all philosophers in the formation of morals, says (Letter 5 to Lucilius): “Our purpose is to live according to nature. It is contrary to nature to torture one’s body, to hate easy cleanliness, to desire squalor, and to use foods that are not merely cheap but selected and disgusting.” As it is luxury to desire delicate things, so it is madness to shun customary things that are not costly to procure. Philosophy demands frugality, not punishment. Yet frugality need not be unkempt; this is the measure that pleases me.

And Gregory, in Book XXX of the *Morals* (ch. 13), teaching that one must attend, in human habits, not so much to the character of foods as to that of minds, and distinguishing the temptations of gluttony, says: “Sometimes it seeks more sumptuous foods; sometimes it desires that whatever is to be consumed should be prepared more carefully. At other times what it desires is more lowly, and yet it sins through the very heat of its boundless desire.” The people brought out of Egypt perished in the wilderness because, despising manna, they demanded meats which they considered more sumptuous. And Esau lost the glory of the firstborn because with great heat of desire he coveted a cheap food, namely lentils; when he preferred them even to the sale of his birthright, he showed how eagerly he panted after them. For the fault lies not in the food but in the appetite.

Thus we often consume more sumptuous foods without fault, and taste cheaper foods not without guilt of conscience. Esau, of whom we have spoken, lost his primacy through lentils (Gen. 25:23), while Elijah in the wilderness preserved his bodily strength by eating meat (2 Kings 17:4). Thus the ancient enemy, understanding that the cause of condemnation lies not in food but in craving for food, subjected the first human being to himself not by meat but by an apple, and tempted the second not by meat but by bread. Hence Adam’s fault is often committed even when cheap and lowly things are consumed. Therefore those things should be eaten which necessity of nature requires, not those suggested by the lust of eating.

We desire with less longing things we see to be less precious, more abundant, and more cheaply bought: such as the common food of meat, which strengthens weak nature much more vigorously than fish, costs less, and is easier to prepare. The use of meat and wine, like marriage, is counted among things intermediate between good and evil—that is, indifferent things—although the use of marital intercourse is not altogether free from sin, and wine is held to be more dangerous than all foods.

If wine, when taken moderately, is not forbidden to religious life, what need have we to fear regarding other foods, provided measure is not exceeded in them? If blessed Benedict himself (ch. 40), though he declares it not to belong to monks, is nevertheless compelled by a certain dispensation to permit it to monks of his own time, because the fervor of former charity has already grown cold, why should we not permit to women other things which no profession yet forbids them? If bishops themselves and the rulers of the holy Church, and indeed monasteries of clerics, may eat meat without offense—because no profession binds them from it—who will blame its being allowed to women, especially if in other matters they endure a stricter discipline? “For it is enough for the disciple to be as his master” (Matt. 10:24).

And it seems a great inconsistency if what is allowed to monasteries of clerics should be forbidden to monasteries of women. Nor should it be considered a small thing if women, together with the rest of monastic discipline, are not inferior in this one allowance of meat to religious laypeople—especially since, according to Chrysostom (Homily 7, ch. 4), nothing is allowed to secular persons that is not allowed to monks, except intercourse with a wife alone. Blessed Jerome likewise, judging the religious life of clerics not inferior to that of monks, says (Letter 10): “As though whatever is said against monks did not redound upon clerics, who are the fathers of monks.”

Who, moreover, does not know that it is altogether contrary to discernment to impose the same burdens upon the weak as upon the strong, or the same abstinence upon women as upon men? If anyone demands authority for this besides the very teaching of nature, let him consult blessed Gregory on the matter as well. For this great ruler and teacher of the Church, diligently instructing the other doctors of the Church also in this matter, says in chapter 24 of the *Pastoral Rule* (Part III, Admonition 1): “Men, therefore, are to be admonished in one way, and women in another; for heavy things are to be enjoined upon the former, lighter things upon the latter. Great tasks should exercise the former; lighter things should convert the latter by gentle persuasion. For things that are small in the strong are considered great in the weak.”

Although this permission of cheap meat affords less pleasure than the flesh of fish or birds, which blessed Benedict nevertheless does not forbid us. The Apostle too, distinguishing the different kinds of flesh, says: “Not all flesh is the same flesh; but one is that of human beings, another that of cattle, another that of birds, another that of fish” (1 Cor. 15:39). The Law indeed places the flesh of cattle and birds in sacrifice to the Lord, but never fish, lest anyone believe the eating of fish to be cleaner before God than that of meat. Fish, moreover, are more burdensome or costly for poverty inasmuch as they are less plentiful than meat, and strengthen weak nature less: in one respect they burden more, in the other they help less.

We, therefore, providing alike for people’s circumstances and nature, forbid nothing in foods, as we have said, except excess. We moderate the eating of meat and of other things so that, with all things allowed, the abstinence of nuns may be greater than that of monks who are currently forbidden certain things. We therefore wish the eating of meat itself to be regulated thus: they may take it no more than once a day; different dishes from it are not to be prepared for the same person; no additional dishes are to be served separately; nor may anyone eat it more than three times a week—namely, on the first, third, and fifth feriae—whatever feasts may intervene. For the greater the solemnity, the more it ought to be celebrated with the devotion of greater abstinence.

Gregory Nazianzen, that eminent teacher, strongly exhorts us to this in Book III, *On the Lights, or the Second Epiphanies*: “Let us celebrate the feast day not by indulging the belly but by rejoicing in spirit.” The same author, in Book IV, *On Pentecost and the Holy Spirit*, says: “And this is our feast day: let us lay up in the treasures of the soul something enduring and perpetual, not things that pass away and dissolve. Its own evil is enough for the body; it does not need more abundant material, nor does the unruly beast need more abundant food in order to become more unruly and press more violently.”

Blessed Jerome, his disciple in this regard, likewise records in a certain place in his letter concerning gifts received (Letter 19) why solemnity should be observed more spiritually: “Therefore we must take greater care that we celebrate the solemn day not so much by abundance of food as by the rejoicing of the spirit; for it is very absurd to wish to honor with excessive satiety a martyr whom we know to have pleased God by fasts.” Augustine, *On the Medicine of Penance* (ch. 4): “Consider the countless thousands of martyrs. Why does it please you to celebrate their birthdays with disgraceful banquets, yet not please you to follow their lives with honorable conduct?”

Whenever meat is lacking, we allow them two dishes of whatever kind of cooked foods; nor do we prohibit fish from being added. But no costly flavors are to be added to foods in the community; they are to be content with the things that grow in the land in which they live. They may eat fruit only at supper. Yet for medicine, whenever there is need, we never forbid herbs, roots, certain fruits, or other such things to be placed upon the table.

If a visiting nun is received as a guest and takes part at table, let her experience the kindness of charity through some additional dish being served to her. If she wishes to distribute anything from it, she may do so. She, or they if there are several, shall sit at the larger table, and the deaconess shall serve them; afterward she shall eat with the others who serve at table.

If any sister wishes to tame her flesh by a sparer diet, she must by no means presume to do this except through obedience; and it must by no means be denied her if she appears to seek it not from frivolity but from virtue, and if her strength can bear it. Yet no one is ever to be permitted, on this account, to be absent from the community or to pass any day without food.

On Friday they must never use a seasoning of fat, but, content with Lenten food, should share by a certain abstinence in the suffering of their Bridegroom on that day. But the following practice is not merely to be forbidden but strongly abhorred: in many monasteries they customarily clean and wipe their hands and knives with some portion of bread left over from the meal, bread which ought to be reserved for the poor; and, to spare the tablecloths, they pollute the bread of the poor—indeed, the bread of Him who, considering Himself present in the poor, says: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40).

Let the general institution of the Church concerning abstinence in fasts suffice them. We do not presume to burden them in this respect beyond the religious practice of faithful laypeople, nor dare we prefer their weakness in this respect to the strength of men. But from the autumnal equinox until Easter, because of the shortness of the days, let us judge one meal a day sufficient. Since we say this not for the abstinence of religious observance but because of the shortness of the time, we shall distinguish no kinds of food here.

Let costly garments, which Scripture altogether condemns, be most carefully avoided. The Lord especially dissuades us from them, accusing by them the pride of the condemned rich man and, conversely, commending John’s humility. Blessed Gregory, carefully observing this, says in Homily 6 on the Gospels: “What does it mean to say, ‘Those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings’ (Matt. 11:8), except openly to demonstrate that those serve not a heavenly but an earthly kingdom who flee the hard things to be endured for God, but, devoted only to outward things, seek the softness and pleasure of this present life?”

The same author, in Homily 40, says: “There are some who do not think that the adornment of fine and costly garments is a sin. But if it were not a fault, the word of God would never so carefully state that the rich man who was tormented in hell had been clothed in linen and purple. For no one seeks outstanding garments except for vain glory, namely, in order to appear more honorable than others. A costly garment is sought for vain glory alone. The thing itself testifies that no one wishes to be clothed in costly garments where he cannot be seen by others” (1 Pet. 3).

The First Epistle of Peter, dissuading secular and married women from this, says: “Likewise let wives be subject to their husbands, so that, even if any do not believe the word, their wives may win them without a word through their conduct, observing your chaste conduct in fear. Let their adornment be not outward—arranging of hair, encircling with gold, or the adornment of garments—but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is rich in the sight of the Lord” (1 Pet. 3:1).

It was right to judge women rather than men to be especially warned away from this vanity, since their weaker minds desire it more, inasmuch as luxury may be more readily imitated through and in them. But if secular women must be restrained from it, what ought to be provided for women devoted to Christ, for whom their very adornment is that they are unadorned? Therefore whoever desires such adornment, or does not refuse it when offered, loses the testimony of chastity. And whoever is such should be thought not to be preparing herself for religion but for fornication, and should be regarded not so much as a nun as a prostitute. Her very adornment is like the advertisement of a pimp, betraying an unchaste mind, as it is written: “A person’s dress, the laughter of the teeth, and a person’s gait proclaim what he is” (Ecclus. 19:27).

We read in John, as we have mentioned above, that the Lord commended and praised the cheapness or roughness of clothing rather than food. “What did you go out into the wilderness to see?” He says. “A man clothed in soft garments?” (Matt. 11:8). The use of costly food can sometimes have some useful dispensation; that of costly garments has none. For the more costly garments are, the more carefully they are guarded; they profit less, burden the purchaser more, are more easily damaged because of their fineness, and provide less warmth to the body.

No cloth is more fitting for the mournful habit of penance than black, nor do any skins so suit brides of Christ as lambskins, so that, in their very habit, they may appear clothed in—or be admonished to clothe themselves in—the Lamb, the Bridegroom of virgins. Their veils, however, are to be made not of silk but of some dyed linen cloth. We wish there to be two kinds of veil: one for virgins already consecrated, the other for those not yet consecrated.

The veils of chaste virgins are to bear the impressed sign of a cross, so that they may show that through bodily integrity also they belong especially to Christ; and, just as in consecration they differ from the others, so they may be distinguished by this sign of their habit, so that all the faithful, awed thereby, may more strongly shrink from burning with desire for them. The virgin shall wear this sign of virginal purity at the crown of her head, worked in white threads; and she must by no means presume to wear it before she has been consecrated by a bishop. No other veils are to be marked with this sign.

They are to have clean undergarments next to the flesh, and are always to sleep girded in these. We do not deny their weak nature the softness of mattresses or the use of linen sheets. Each shall sleep and eat separately. Let no one presume to be angry if garments or anything else sent to her by someone is given to another sister who has greater need. Rather, let her then rejoice especially when she has gained the fruit of almsgiving in her sister’s necessity, or sees that she lives not for herself alone but also for others. Otherwise she does not belong to the fellowship of holy community and is not free from the sacrilege of private ownership.

For covering the body we believe an undergarment, a fur garment, and a gown sufficient; and, when the cold becomes very severe, a mantle over these. They may use this mantle also as a covering while lying down. But because of the infestation of vermin or the burden of washing away dirt, all these garments should be double, as Solomon says literally in praise of the strong and prudent woman: “She shall not fear for her household from the cold of snow; for all her household are clothed in double garments” (Prov. 31:21).

Their length is to be so moderated that they do not extend beyond the edge of the shoes, lest they stir up dust. The sleeves are not to extend beyond the reach of the arms and hands. Stockings, foot-wraps, and shoes are to protect the legs and feet. They must never go barefoot under the pretext of religion. For beds, one mattress, a pillow, a head-cushion, a blanket, and a sheet are sufficient. They are to cover the head with a white band, a black veil over it, and, in place of cutting off the hair, a lambskin cap is to be placed underneath when needed.

Nor should excess be avoided only in food or clothing, but also in buildings or in any possessions. In buildings this is plainly recognized if they are constructed larger or more beautiful than is necessary, or if, adorning them with carvings or paintings, we build not dwellings for the poor but raise palaces for kings. “The Son of Man,” says Jerome (Letter 1), “has nowhere to lay his head, and you measure out broad porticoes and vast expanses of roof?” When we take pleasure in costly or handsome mounts, not only excess but the vanity of pride becomes evident. But when we multiply herds of animals or earthly possessions, [Col. 0302C] ambition then expands itself toward outward things; and the more we possess on earth, the more we are compelled to think about them, and are recalled away from contemplation of heavenly things. And although we are enclosed bodily within cloisters, yet the mind is compelled to follow those things that are outside and that it loves; it spreads itself with them alike here and there. And the more things are possessed that can be lost, the greater the fear by which they torment us; and the more precious they are, the more they are loved, and the more wretchedly they ensnare the soul through ambition for them. Therefore every precaution must be taken that we set a fixed limit to our household and our expenses, and neither desire anything beyond necessities, nor accept what is offered, nor retain what has been received. For whatever exceeds necessity, we possess by robbery; [Col. 0302D] and we are guilty of the deaths of as many poor persons as we could have supported from it.

Accordingly, each year, when provisions have been gathered, care must be taken to determine how much is sufficient for the year; and if anything remains over, it is not so much to be given to the poor as restored to them. There are some who, ignorant of the proper measure of foresight, though they have small revenues, delight in maintaining a large household. Burdened by its upkeep, they shamelessly beg while seeking support for it, or violently extort from others what they do not possess. We now see even certain fathers of monasteries of this kind, who glory in the size of their community and strive to have not so much good sons as many; they seem great in their own eyes if they are counted among the greater men because of their numbers. In order to draw such men under their own [Col. 0303A] dominion, though they ought to preach hard things to them, they promise easy ones; and, receiving indiscriminately those whom they have not first tested by any examination, they lose them when they readily apostasize. As I see it, Truth reproached such people when he said: “Woe to you who traverse sea and land to make one proselyte; and when you have made him, you make him twice as much a child of Gehenna as yourselves” (Matt. 23:15). They would certainly glory less in numbers if they sought the salvation of souls more than numerical strength, and presumed less upon their own powers in the account they must render of their governance.

The Lord chose few apostles; and from among that very choice one apostatized so greatly that the Lord said of him: “Have not I [or: *Have I not*] chosen you twelve, and one of you is a devil?” [Col. 0303B] (John 6:71). As Judas perished from among the apostles, so Nicholas also perished from among the seven deacons. And when the apostles had as yet gathered only a few, Ananias and his wife Sapphira deserved to receive the sentence of death (Acts 5:5). Indeed, when many disciples had previously gone back from the Lord himself, few remained with him (John 18:6). For narrow is the way that leads to life, and few enter by it; whereas, on the contrary, broad and spacious is the way that leads to death, and many thrust themselves into it of their own accord (Matt. 7:14). For, as the Lord himself testifies elsewhere: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). And according to Solomon: “The number of fools is infinite” (Eccles. 1:15). Therefore let anyone who rejoices in a multitude of subjects fear [Col. 0303C] lest, according to the Lord’s declaration, few among them be found chosen; and lest, by multiplying his flock without measure, he prove less adequate to guard it, so that the prophetic saying may rightly be addressed to him by spiritual persons: “You have multiplied the nation; you have not increased the joy” (Isa. 9:3).

Such persons, indeed—those who glory in numbers—are frequently compelled to go out, return to the world, and run about begging for both their own needs and those of their dependents. They entangle themselves more in bodily than spiritual cares, and gain disgrace rather than glory. This is all the more shameful in women, since for them to run about through the world appears less safe. [Col. 0303D] Therefore whoever wishes to live quietly and honorably, to devote himself or herself to divine offices, and to be held dear both by God and by the world, must fear to gather people whom he or she cannot maintain; must not rely, for personal expenses, upon other people’s purses; and must be diligent not in requesting alms but in giving them.

That great Apostle, preacher of the Gospel, although he had authority to receive support from the Gospel, labored with his hands, lest he seem to burden anyone and make his glory void (1 Thess. 2; 1 Cor. 9). What rashness or shamelessness, then, is ours—whose task is not to preach but to bewail our sins—when we seek by begging? From what source can we support those whom we gather thoughtlessly? We often even break out into such madness that, though we do not know how to preach, we hire preachers and, taking pseudo-apostles about with us, [Col. 0304A] carry crosses and reliquary phylacteries, in order to sell these things, as well as the word of God—or even the fabrications of the devil—to simple and uneducated Christians, promising them whatever we think will help extract money. How much our order and the very preaching of the divine word have already been debased by this shameless greed, which seeks its own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, I think no one can now fail to know.

Thus abbots themselves, or those who appear to be the chief men in monasteries, by thrusting themselves importunately upon powerful people of the world and worldly courts, have now learned to be more carnal than cenobites. Hunting human favor by every artifice, they have grown accustomed to converse more often with people than to speak with God. [Col. 0304B] They frequently read in vain and neglect—or hear but do not heed—what blessed Anthony warns, saying (*Lives of the Fathers*, Part II, book “On Quiet”): “Just as fish die if they remain too long on dry land, so monks who linger outside their cell or remain with secular men are loosened from their purpose of quiet.” Therefore, as a fish returns to the sea, so we must return to the cell, lest by lingering outside we perhaps forget inward watchfulness.

Blessed Benedict himself, the writer of the monastic Rule, carefully observing this, plainly taught both by example and in writing, as though he wished abbots to be continually present in monasteries and to stand diligently over the care of their flock. For when he had gone out with the brethren to visit his most holy sister, [Col. 0304C] and she wished to keep him, for edification’s sake, at least one night, he openly declared that he could in no way remain outside his cell. Nor, indeed, did he say, as Gregory records (*Dialogues*, II.33), “We cannot,” but “I cannot,” because through him the brethren could do this, whereas he himself could not, unless the Lord, as later happened, revealed it. Thus, when he wrote the Rule, nowhere does he mention the abbot’s departure, but only that of the brethren.

He also provided so carefully for the abbot’s continual presence that at the vigils of Sundays and feast days he ordered the Gospel reading, together with what is joined to it, to be recited only by the abbot. Further, by establishing that the abbot’s table should always be with pilgrims and guests, and that whenever guests are fewer [Col. 0304D], he should summon whomever he wishes of the brethren to dine with him—leaving only one or two seniors with the brethren—he plainly indicates that the abbot ought never to be absent from the monastery at mealtime. He should not, having become accustomed to the luxurious dishes of princes, abandon to his dependents the monastery’s coarse bread; of such men Truth says: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them upon people’s shoulders, but they are unwilling to move them with their own finger” (Matt. 23:4). And elsewhere, concerning false preachers: “Beware of false prophets who come to you” (Matt. 7:15). “They come,” he says, “of themselves, not sent by God, nor waiting until they are summoned.”

John the Baptist, our chief, to whom the high priesthood came by hereditary right, once withdrew from the city into the wilderness, abandoning the high priesthood for monastic life and cities for solitude. [Col. 0305A] The people went out to him; he himself did not go in among the people. Though he was so great that he was believed to be Christ, and though he could correct nothing in the cities, he was already in that little bed from which he was ready to answer the knocking Beloved: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5:3).

Therefore whoever desires the hidden retreat of monastic quiet should rejoice in being a little bed rather than a bed. “For,” as Truth says, “from the bed one will be taken and the other left” (Luke 17:34). But the little bed, we read, belongs to the Bride—that is, to the contemplative soul more closely united to Christ and cleaving to him in highest desire. We read that no one who enters it is left behind. Of it she herself also speaks [Col. 0305B]: “Passing the night in my little bed, I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:1). And, disdaining or fearing to rise from that little bed, she answers the knocking Beloved as we recalled above. For she believes that dirt exists only outside her bed, by which she fears her feet may be defiled.

Dinah went out to see people of another nation and was corrupted. And as was foretold by his abbot to that captive monk Malchus, and as he afterward experienced himself, a sheep that leaves the sheepfold quickly lies exposed to the wolf’s bites. Therefore, lest we gather a multitude for which we seek an excuse to go out—or rather are compelled to go out—and make gain from others at our own loss, as lead is consumed in a furnace in order that silver may be preserved, [Col. 0305C] we should instead fear lest the fierce furnace of temptations consume both the lead and the silver alike.

“They say, ‘Truth says: “The one who comes to me I will not cast out”’” (John 8:37). Nor do we wish that those whom we have received should be cast out; rather, we wish to make provision concerning those to be received, lest, after receiving them within, we ourselves be cast outside on their account. For we read that the Lord did not cast out one whom he had received, but refused one who offered himself. To the man who said, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go,” he replied: “Foxes have dens” (Matt. 8:19), etc. He also carefully admonishes us, when we contemplate doing something, to provide beforehand for the resources required for it: “Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the expenses that are necessary, whether he has enough to finish it? Otherwise, after he has laid the foundation and is unable to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was unable to complete it’” (Luke 14:28).

It is a great thing if someone is sufficient even to save himself alone; and it is dangerous for one who can scarcely remain watchful enough for his own keeping to provide for many. No one is diligent in guarding unless he has been cautious in receiving. And no one perseveres in what he has begun as does the person who is slow and prudent in beginning. In this matter women’s foresight should be so much the greater because their weakness is less able to bear heavy burdens and needs especially to be nurtured in quiet.

[Col. 0306A] Sacred Scripture is a mirror of the soul, in which anyone who reads while living and progresses through understanding recognizes the beauty of his morals or detects their deformity, so that he may strive to increase the former and remove the latter. Recalling this mirror to us, blessed Gregory says in Book II of the *Morals* (chap. 1):

> “Sacred Scripture is set before the eyes of the mind like a kind of mirror, so that our inner countenance may be seen in it. There indeed we recognize what is foul in us; there we behold what is beautiful in us. There we perceive how much progress we make; there we perceive how far we are from progress. But one who looks upon Scripture without understanding it is like a blind man holding before his eyes that by which he cannot know what he is like. Nor does he seek the teaching in Scripture for which it was made; [Col. 0306B] and, like an ass put to a lyre, he sits idly over Scripture. He has, as it were, bread set before him, by which he is not refreshed though hungry, since, while the word of God neither penetrates him through understanding nor is broken for him by another’s teaching, he possesses food uselessly, which does him no good whatever.”

Hence the Apostle, generally exhorting us to the study of the Scriptures, says: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4). And elsewhere: “Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph. 5:18). For one speaks to oneself or with oneself who understands what one utters, or derives fruit from understanding [Col. 0306C] one’s words. The same Apostle says to Timothy: “Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching” (1 Tim. 4:13). And again:

> “But remain in those things which you have learned and which have been entrusted to you, knowing from whom you learned them; and that from childhood you have known the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you for salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus. All Scripture, inspired by God, is useful for teaching, for rebuking, for correcting, for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work” (2 Tim. 3:14).

Likewise, warning the Corinthians concerning understanding Scripture, so that they might be able to expound what others say from Scripture, he says:

> “Pursue charity; desire spiritual things, but especially [Col. 0306D] that you may prophesy [or, make progress]. For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God. But one who prophesies builds up the Church. Therefore, let one who speaks in a tongue pray that he may interpret. I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind. I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind. Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit, who will fill the place of the unlearned person? How will he say ‘Amen’ to your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying? For you indeed give thanks well, but the other is not built up. I thank God that I speak in the tongue of all of you; but in church I would rather speak five words with my understanding, so that I might instruct others also, than ten thousand words in a tongue. Brothers, do not become children in understanding; but be children in malice, and perfect in understanding” (1 Cor. 14:1 ff.).

[Col. 0307A] A person is said to “speak in a tongue” when he forms words only with his mouth and does not minister by expounding them through understanding. But one prophesies or interprets who, after the manner of the prophets—who are called seers, that is, persons of understanding—understands what he says, so that he may expound it. He prays with the spirit or sings psalms with the spirit who forms words merely with the breath of utterance and does not apply the understanding of his mind.

But when our spirit prays—that is, when the breath of our utterance alone forms words, and what is brought forth by the mouth is not conceived in the heart—our mind is without the fruit which it ought to have in prayer: namely, that by understanding the words it may be pierced and kindled toward God. Therefore he warns us to possess this perfection in words: not merely, after the fashion of the many, to know how to utter words, but [Col. 0307B] also to have in them the meaning of understanding; and he declares that otherwise we pray or sing psalms fruitlessly.

Blessed Benedict follows him in this, saying (Rule, chap. 19): “Let us so stand for psalmody that our mind may be in harmony with our voice.” The Psalmist also commands this, saying: “Sing psalms wisely” (Ps. 46:8), so that the savor and seasoning of understanding may not be lacking from the utterance of words, and that we may be able truly to say with the Lord himself: “How sweet are your words to my palate!” (Ps. 118:105). And elsewhere: “He takes no pleasure in a man’s pipe” (Ps. 146:10). For a pipe emits sound for the delight of pleasure, not for understanding of the mind. Hence those are rightly said to sing well on pipes yet not please God thereby, who are so delighted by the melody of their singing that [Col. 0307C] no understanding is built up through it.

For what reason, says the Apostle, when blessings are made in the Church, will “Amen” be answered if what is prayed in that blessing is not understood—namely, whether what the prayer asks is good or not? Thus we often see many unlearned persons, ignorant of the meaning of letters, mistakenly praying in church for things more harmful than useful to themselves; for example, when it is said, “May we so pass through temporal goods that we do not lose eternal ones.” The close resemblance of the words in the phrase easily deceives some, so that they say either, “that we may lose eternal things,” or utter it, “that we may not admit eternal things.”

Providing also against this danger, the Apostle says: “Otherwise, if you bless with the spirit” [Col. 0307D] (1 Cor. 14:16)—that is, if you form the words of blessing only with the breath of utterance and do not instruct the hearer’s mind by their meaning—“who shall fill the place of the unlearned person?” That is: who among those present, whose part it is to respond, will do by responding what the unlearned person cannot—and indeed ought not—to do? “How shall he say ‘Amen’?” since he does not know whether you are leading him into a curse rather than a blessing.

Finally, how will those who lack understanding of Scripture minister the edification of discourse to themselves, or expound or understand even the Rule, or correct faulty utterances? Hence we wonder greatly by what suggestion of the enemy this has come about in monasteries: that there is no study there of understanding the Scriptures, but only instruction in singing or in forming words—not understanding them—as though the bleating of sheep had more usefulness than pasture. For the food of the soul and its spiritual refreshment is understanding of divine Scripture itself. Thus, when the Lord sent the prophet Ezekiel to preach, he first fed him with a scroll, which immediately became sweet as honey in his mouth (Ezek. 3:13). Of this food it is also written in Jeremiah: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4). He breaks bread for little ones who opens the meaning of the letter to simpler people. These little ones ask for bread to be broken when they desire their souls to be nourished by understanding of Scripture, as the Lord testifies elsewhere: “I will send a famine upon the land—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord” (Amos 8:11).

[Col. 0308B] Conversely, the ancient enemy has brought into monastic cloisters a hunger and thirst for hearing human words and worldly rumors, so that, being occupied with idle talk, we despise divine utterances all the more insofar as they become tasteless to us, lacking the sweetness and seasoning of understanding. Therefore the Psalmist, as we mentioned above, says: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Ps. 118:103). He immediately added in what this sweetness consisted, saying: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (ibid., 109): that is, I have received understanding from your commandments rather than from human ones, being taught and instructed by them.

Nor did he omit the usefulness of this understanding, adding: “Therefore I hated every way of iniquity.” Many ways of iniquity are so [Col. 0308C] evident in themselves that they easily become hateful or contemptible to all; but we recognize every way of iniquity only through divine utterances, so that we may avoid them all. This is also the meaning of: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you” (ibid., 11). They are stored in the heart rather than merely sounding in the mouth when our meditation retains their understanding. The less diligently we pursue their understanding, the less we recognize and avoid these ways of iniquity, and the less able we are to guard ourselves against sin.

This negligence is to be reproved all the more in monks who aspire to perfection, because this instruction would be easier for them: they abound in sacred books and enjoy the leisure [Col. 0308D] of quiet. Rebuking those who boast of the multitude of their writings while being idle from their reading, that elder in the *Lives of the Fathers* says excellently (Part II, Book *On Discernment*):

> “The prophets wrote books; our Fathers came after them and worked much in them. Their successors indeed committed them to memory. But the generation which has now come has written them on paper and parchment and laid them away, idle, in windows.”

Abbot Palladius likewise strongly exhorts us both to learn and to teach, saying (ibid.): “A soul living according to the will of Christ ought either faithfully to learn what it does not know, or openly to teach what it knows.” But if it can do both and will not, it suffers from the sickness of madness. For the beginning [Col. 0309A] of departure from God is disgust with instruction; and when the soul does not desire that for which it always hungers, how does it love God?

Blessed Anastasius also, in his exhortation to monks, so commends zeal for learning or reading that he urges prayers themselves to be interrupted for it. “I shall proceed,” he says, “along the path of our way [or, life]. First there must be concern for abstinence, endurance of fasting, constancy in prayer, and desire for reading, or, if anyone is still unacquainted with letters, desire for hearing with eagerness to learn. For these are the first little ornaments, as it were, of infants’ cradles in the knowledge of God.” And after saying: “Prayer, however, must be pressed so earnestly that scarcely any time interrupts it,” he later adds: “If possible, let the interruption of reading alone break it.”

For otherwise the Apostle Peter would not admonish us: “Always be ready to give an answer to all who ask you concerning the word of your faith and hope” (1 Pet. 3:15). Nor would the Apostle say: “We do not cease praying for you, that you may be filled with the knowledge of him in all wisdom and spiritual understanding” (Col. 1:9); and again: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col. 3:16).

In the Old Testament too, the divine utterance impressed a similar concern for sacred instruction upon people. Thus David says: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of pestilence; but his delight is in the law of the Lord” (Ps. 1:1). And God says to Joshua [Col. 0309C] son of Nun: “This book shall not depart from your hands, and you shall meditate upon it day and night” (Josh. 1:18).

Slippery evil thoughts frequently intrude upon these occupations; and although such diligence keeps the mind fixed upon God, worldly care nevertheless makes it anxiously preoccupied with itself. One devoted to religious labor suffers this frequent and troublesome intrusion; surely an idle person will never be free from it. Blessed Pope Gregory says in Book XIX of the *Morals* (chap. 6):

> “We groan that the times have now begun in which we see many placed within the Church who do not wish to practice what they understand, or who despise even to understand and know sacred utterance itself. For, turning their hearing from truth, they turn to fables, while all seek their own things, not those of Jesus Christ. God’s writings are found and known everywhere; they are set before the eyes. If people disdain to know them, scarcely anyone seeks to know what he has believed.”

[Col. 0309D] Both the rule of their profession and the examples of the holy Fathers strongly exhort them to this. Benedict says nothing at all about instruction or the study of singing (Rule, chap. 48), although he gives many commands concerning reading and carefully assigns times for reading as for labor. He so provides even for the instruction of dictating or writing (Rule, chap. 55) that, among the necessities which monks ought to expect from the abbot, he does not omit tablets and a stylus. When he further commands (Rule, chap. 48) that at the beginning of Lent all [Col. 0310A] monks receive individual books from the library, which they are to read through completely in order, what could be more ridiculous than to devote oneself to reading without applying oneself to understanding?

For the saying of the Wise Man is well known: “To read and not understand is to neglect.” Such a reader rightly deserves the Greek reproach, ἀλλ’ ὄνος λύρας, “but an ass at a lyre.” For a reader holding a book is like an ass at a lyre, unable to do that for which the book was made. It would be far more beneficial for such readers to apply themselves elsewhere, where there would be some usefulness, rather than idly inspect the letters of Scripture or turn leaves. In these readers we plainly see fulfilled what Isaiah says:

> “The vision of all shall be to you like the words of a sealed book.
