When they give it to one who knows letters, they will say, ‘Read this’; and he will answer, ‘I cannot, for it is sealed.’ And the book shall be given to one who does not know letters, and he shall be told, ‘Read’; and he will answer, ‘I do not know letters.’ And the Lord said: Because this people draws near to me with its mouth and glorifies me with its lips, but its heart is far from me, and they have feared me by human command and teachings, therefore, behold, I shall proceed to work a great and astonishing wonder among this people. For the wisdom of its wise men shall perish, and the understanding of its prudent men shall be hidden” (Isa. 29:11–14).

[Col. 0310B] In cloisters, all who have learned to pronounce letters are said to “know letters.” Yet insofar as understanding is concerned, while professing that they do not know the law, they possess the book delivered to them as sealed just as much as those whom the passage there calls illiterate. Rebuking them, the Lord says that they draw near to him rather with mouth and lips than with heart, because they cannot at all understand what they can somehow manage to utter. Since they lack knowledge of divine utterances, they follow by obedience human custom rather than the usefulness of Scripture. For this reason the Lord also threatens that those who seem wise among them and sit as teachers shall be blinded.

Jerome, the greatest teacher of the Church and an honor to the monastic profession, exhorts us to love of letters, saying: “Love the knowledge of letters, and you will not love the vices of the flesh” (Epistle 4). By his own testimony we also learn how much labor and expense he expended upon their study. Among other matters which he himself writes about his own study, evidently to instruct us by his example, he recalls in one place to Pammachius and Oceanus:

> “While I was young, I burned with a wonderful love of learning. I did not teach myself, according to the presumption of some; I frequently heard Apollinaris at Antioch and attended him while he instructed me in the Holy Scriptures. Already my head was being sprinkled with gray hairs, and it was more fitting to be a teacher than a pupil. Yet I went to Alexandria. I heard Didymus, and I thank him in many matters because I learned what I did not know. People thought I had finished learning. Again, at Jerusalem and Bethlehem, with what labor and at what cost did I have Baranina the Hebrew as a night-time teacher?” (Epistle 65).

[Col. 0311A] For he feared the Jews and presented himself to me as another Nicodemus (John 3:1 ff.).

He had surely stored in a mindful heart what he had read in Ecclesiasticus (6:18): “My son, receive instruction from your youth, and until gray hairs you shall find wisdom.” Not only instructed by the words of Scripture, but also by examples of the holy Fathers, he added, among the other praises of that excellent monastery, this concerning its distinctive exercise in the divine Scriptures:

> “Never have we seen such great exercises in meditation upon, understanding of, and knowledge of the divine Scriptures, that you would almost believe every one of them to be an orator in divine wisdom.”

Holy Bede also, as he relates in his history of the English, having been received into a monastery from childhood, says: “From that time I spent the whole period of my life dwelling in the same monastery; I gave all my labor to meditation upon the Scriptures, and amid observance of regular discipline and the daily care of singing in church, I always found it sweet either to learn or to write.”

But those who are now educated in monasteries persist in such folly that, content with the sound of letters, they undertake no care for understanding and strive to instruct not the heart but the tongue. Solomon’s proverb openly rebukes them: “The heart of the wise seeks instruction, but the mouth of fools feeds upon ignorance” (Prov. 15:44), since it delights in words it does not understand. The less they can love God and be kindled toward him, the more they withdraw from understanding him and from the sense of Scripture which instructs us about him.

[Col. 0311C] We believe that this has occurred in monasteries chiefly for two reasons: either through the envy of lay brothers and sisters—that is, converts—or even of the superiors themselves; or through the idle talk to which we see monastic cloisters today given over in great measure. These, wishing us to attend to earthly rather than spiritual concerns with them, are those who, like the Philistines, pursue Isaac as he digs wells (Gen. 26:15); by filling them with a heap of earth they strive to prevent his water. Explaining this, blessed Gregory says in Book XVI of the *Morals*:

> “Often, when we apply ourselves to sacred utterances, we endure more grievously the snares of malignant spirits, because they sprinkle [or, scatter] the dust of earthly thoughts upon our mind in order to darken the eyes [Col. 0311D] of our attention from the light of inward vision” (chap. 8, on Job 24).

The Psalmist endured this greatly when he said: “Depart from me, you wicked, and I will search out the commandments of my God” (Ps. 118:115), clearly intimating that he could not investigate God’s commandments while enduring in his mind the snares of malignant spirits. We also recognize the same thing to be signified by the wickedness of the Philistines in the action concerning Isaac, who filled with heaps of earth the wells which Isaac had dug. For we indeed dig wells when we penetrate deeply into the hidden meanings of Sacred Scripture. Yet the Philistines secretly fill them when, as we strive toward the heights, unclean spirits suggest earthly thoughts to us and, as it were, take away the water of divine knowledge we have found.

But because no one overcomes these enemies by one’s own strength, Eliphaz says: “The Almighty shall be against your enemies, and silver shall be heaped up for you” (Job 22:25). As though he said: When the Lord drives malignant spirits away from you by his own power, the talent of divine utterance grows brighter in you.

This writer, unless I am mistaken, had read the homilies on Genesis by Origen, the great philosopher of Christians, and had drawn from his wells what he now says about these wells. For that zealous digger of spiritual wells, vigorously exhorting us not only to drink from them but also to dig them, speaks thus in Homily XII on the exposition mentioned above (chap. 26):

> [Col. 0312A] “Let us attempt also to do what wisdom warns us, saying: ‘Drink water from your own springs and from your own wells. Let your fountain be your own’ (Prov. 5:15). Therefore, you too, hearer, attempt to have your own well and your own fountain, so that, when you take hold of the book of the Scriptures, you may begin also to bring forth some understanding from your own sense, in accordance with what you have learned in the Church. Attempt also to drink from the fountain of your own understanding. Within you is the nature of living water; there are perennial veins and flowing streams of rational meaning—provided only that they are not filled with earth and rough debris. But labor to dig your earth and cleanse away the filth: that is, cultivate your understanding, put away sloth, and shake off the torpor of your heart. Hear what Scripture says: ‘Prick the eye, and bring forth a tear; prick the heart, and bring forth understanding’ (Ecclus. 22:19). Cleanse your understanding also, so that at some time you may drink from your own fountains and draw living water from your own wells. For if [Col. 0312B] you have received within yourself the word of God, if you have received living water from Jesus and have received it faithfully, there will come to be in you a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.”

In the following homily, concerning the aforesaid wells of Isaac, he says:

> “Those whom the Philistines had filled with earth are without doubt those who close off spiritual understanding, so that neither they themselves drink nor permit others to drink” (Homily XIII, chap. 26).

Hear the Lord saying: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and you did not permit those who wished to enter” (Luke 11:52). But let us never cease digging wells of living water, and, examining now old things and now new, let us become like that evangelical scribe of whom the Lord said: “Who brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matt. 13:52).

[Col. 0312D] Again, let us return to Isaac and dig wells of living water with him. Even if the Philistines oppose us, even if they quarrel, nevertheless let us persist with him in digging wells, so that it may also be said to us: “Drink water from your own vessels and from your own wells” (Prov. 5:15). Let us dig so much that the waters of the well overflow into our streets, so that knowledge of the Scriptures may not only suffice for us, but that we may teach and instruct others to drink. Let human beings drink, and cattle also, because the Prophet says: “You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 35:7).

And after some intervening matter he says: “Whoever is a Philistine and savors earthly things does not know how to find water in every land, how to find rational meaning. What does it profit you to possess learning and not know how to use it, to possess speech and not know how to speak?” [Col. 0313A] This belongs properly to Isaac’s children, who dig wells of living water in every land.

But you must not be so; rather, laying idle talk entirely aside, let all women who have attained the grace of learning strive to be instructed in those things which concern God. As it is written concerning the blessed man: “But his delight is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he shall meditate day and night” (Ps. 1:2). The usefulness which follows from this constant study of the law of the Lord is immediately joined to it: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of waters.” For a tree is dry and fruitless when it is not watered by the streams of divine utterances. Of these it is written: “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38).

These are those streams of which the bride sings in the *Song of Songs*, describing the bridegroom: “His eyes are like doves beside channels of water, washed with milk and sitting by most abundant streams” (Song 5:12). Therefore you also, washed with milk—that is, shining with the brightness of chastity—sit like doves beside these streams, so that, taking draughts of wisdom from them, you may be able not only to learn but also to teach, and, like eyes, show the way to others; and may be able not only to behold the bridegroom himself but also to describe him to others.

Concerning his unique bride, who deserved to conceive him in the ear of her heart, we know that it is written: “But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart” (Luke 2:19). Thus the Mother of the supreme Word, holding his words in [Col. 0314A] her heart rather than merely in her mouth, also carefully compared them, because she diligently examined each thing and compared them with one another—how fittingly all agreed among themselves.

She knew that, according to the mystery of the Law, every animal is called unclean unless it chews the cud and divides the hoof. For no soul is clean unless, by meditation, it chews over divine precepts as much as it can grasp, and has discernment in carrying them out, so that it does not merely do good things, but does them well—that is, with a right intention. The division of the hoof of the foot is discernment of the mind, concerning which it is written: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” “If anyone loves me,” Truth says, “he will keep my word” (John 14:23). But who can keep through obedience the words or precepts of his Lord [Col. 0314B] unless one has first understood them? No one will be zealous in carrying them out unless one has been attentive in hearing.

So too we read of that blessed woman who, setting all else aside, sat at the Lord’s feet and heard his word—namely, with those ears of understanding which he himself requires when he says: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 11:15). But if you cannot be kindled to such fervor of devotion, imitate at least in love and study of sacred letters those blessed disciples of Saint Jerome, Paula and Eustochium, at whose particular request the aforesaid teacher illumined the Church with so many volumes.

Thus far the Nantes manuscript, and likewise the Victorian manuscript. But in the Paraclete manuscript, which is also everywhere considerably fuller, we find the following; and these appear to be Heloise’s.

[Col. 0313]

[Col. 0313C] Our instructions take their beginning from the teaching of Christ, who preached and maintained poverty, humility, and obedience. We follow the footsteps of the apostles, who lived in common. In our clothing we preserve poverty and humility; in subjection, obedience; in our manner of life, because we live in common, we follow the apostles. Whatever the source from which temporal benefits may come, they are divided among individuals as far as possible; if there is not enough for all, more is given especially to those who are more needy. And since we renounce the world and serve God, let us remain steadfast in our purpose of chastity and, according to our strength and the measure of his gift, strive to please him.

## On the conformity of observances

[Col. 0313D] With the Lord watching over us and granting us some places, we have sent some of our number, in sufficient number, to maintain the religious life. We record the customs of our good purpose, so that what the mother has maintained unchangeably, the daughters may maintain uniformly.

## On clothing

Our clothing is cheap and simple: lambskins, linen garments, and woolen garments. In buying or making these, expensive things are not chosen, but whatever can be purchased or obtained more cheaply. Whatsoever ought to suffice would need to be specified; but we are far from sufficiency.

## On beds

[Col. 0314C] In our beds we have mattresses, pillows, and linen sheets, as these are distributed to each person. If each does not receive what is sufficient, it is ascribed to poverty.

## On food

We eat whatever bread there is: if there is wheat, wheat bread; if it is lacking, bread from any kind of grain. In our refectory the meatless foods are legumes and what the garden produces. Milk, eggs, cheese, and fish—if they have been given—are served more rarely. Wine is to be mixed with water. Two dishes are provided at the first meal. At supper there are greens, fruit, or some [Col. 0314D] such thing, if it can be had. We also endure the lack of these things without murmuring.

## On obedience

Due obedience is rendered to the abbess and prioress alone. No one presumes to leave the monastic enclosure without their permission. No one may speak, give or receive anything, or retain anything except what has been permitted. In other respects, we obey one another through the affection of charity.

## Whence necessities are supplied

It would accord with the religious life to live from cultivating the land and from our own labor, if we could. But because through weakness we are not sufficient for this, we admit lay brothers and lay sisters, so that what the rigor of religious life does not permit to be administered by us may be fulfilled through them. We also receive whatever alms the faithful give, according to the custom of other churches.

## When we go out

[Col. 0315A] We hold to the established rule that no veiled woman, for any necessity whatever, may go out for external business or enter the house of any secular person. But for domestic business and for the safeguarding of our goods, we send into our houses nuns and lay sisters who have been tested both by age and by manner of life.

## On those who come from afar

We do not permit a newcomer to remain with us for a long time; [Col. 0315B] but if she wishes to remain and reason permits her reception, within the first seven days she must either make profession or depart.

## When a lay sister becomes a nun

If any lay sister coming to us has been received into the lay sisters’ manner of life, she shall by no means afterward become a nun, but shall remain in the vocation in which she was called.

## On the night offices from the Kalends of October until Easter

When the signal is heard, we rise promptly for vigils and, encouraging ourselves with moderation, hasten to the work of God. When the signal has ceased, at the direction of the prioress we make the customary prayers: bowed on solemnities, prostrate on ordinary days. When the prayers are completed, we sign ourselves and enter our places. The weekly sister, whose office is “God, come to my assistance,” begins: “Come, Holy Spirit,” continuing with the verse and prayer. This too we do at the beginning of all the Hours: singing on the principal solemnities, without singing on other days. The weekly sister begins, “Lord, open my lips,” and we continue the divine office according to the custom of regular churches.

After vigils we all go out, and the oratory is secured if it is not daylight; and, with a light kindled, those who need reading or work sit in the chapter house. If it is daylight, Prime follows immediately. On feasts and Sundays, whether it is daylight or not, we all return to the dormitory, resting [Col. 0315D] in our beds until, when day shines more clearly, we come at the dormitory signal into the cloister. Prime is rung; and when the prioress gives the signal, we all enter the church, with the choir and the younger sisters preceding. Similarly, before all the Hours the signal of the prioress is awaited.

Before Prime, prayer is made between the forms, as before vigils. After Prime follows the morning Mass. Then we go to chapter, and accusations and corrections are made according to the measure of the faults, at the discretion of the one presiding over chapter. On certain solemnities the sisters come to chapter and their faults are corrected. Whenever the brothers commit grave offenses, they are summoned into chapter and corrected before the common chapter, so that they may be shamed by greater embarrassment. On the principal solemnities [Col. 0316A] there is a sermon in chapter.

After leaving chapter, we devote ourselves to reading until Terce, if the time permits. Terce and the greater Mass follow. Sext follows without an interval. After Sext we devote ourselves to reading until None. The ministers and the reader receive mixed wine. After None we enter the refectory; a reading is heard in the greatest silence, and in other matters we follow the order of regular communities. When “But thou, O Lord” has been said, we proceed in order, singing thanks, and enter the oratory. When the thanksgivings in church are finished, we enter the chapter house; the lay sisters assemble, and something for edification is expounded to the common audience by the sister to whom this has been assigned. If time remains, we sit in the cloister until Vespers. Vespers are sung. It should be known that no one leaves the choir without permission.

[Col. 0316B] After Vespers we sit in the cloister, serving meditation and praying in our hearts, entirely without signals and in the greatest silence. Before the conference we drink in the refectory. When the weekly sister gives the blessing, we immediately go to the conference, with no one turning aside anywhere. After the conference we sing Compline in church. When “May they rest in peace” has been said, we make prayer between the forms. At the signal of the abbess or prioress, standing upright, we sign ourselves; then, departing in order and beginning with the elders, we are sprinkled with holy water by the abbess or prioress. Going up to the dormitory, we turn to our beds and lie down clothed and girded.

## On Sundays

[Col. 0316C] On Sundays, after leaving chapter, we receive holy water from the abbess or prioress, and make a procession in the cloister, one carrying the cross and two carrying candles. After Sext we take our meal. Immediately after the meal comes None. After None something is expounded for edification, as stated above. After Vespers supper is held. Thereafter we conduct ourselves in the manner stated above.

On ordinary days, Prime is sung very early in the morning; afterward we sit in the cloister until Terce, reading, singing, and working. Prayer between the forms precedes, and Terce follows. After Terce comes the morning Mass. Then we go to chapter. After leaving chapter we sit in the cloister. The weaker sisters receive mixed wine according to the dispensation [Col. 0316D] of the abbess. No one may sit in the cloister without work or reading. After Sext follows the greater Mass, and None immediately follows. After None we enter the refectory. We continue the rest as stated above.

## On the summer season
From Easter until the aforesaid Kalends of October, after Lauds we return to our beds; and after some interval a signal is sounded in the dormitory. Rising, we come into the cloister and read and sing until Prime. Before Prime, both on feast days and on ordinary days, prayers are said between the rows of seats. After Prime follows the morning Mass. Then we go to chapter. On leaving chapter, we sit in the cloister, reading and working until Terce. [Col. 0317A] After Terce the principal Mass is celebrated. Then Sext; and we go to the refectory. After the thanksgiving, we go to the dormitory, and it is permitted to sleep, read, or work in our beds without anyone’s disturbance. At the first signal for None we rise and prepare ourselves, so that, when the second signal has sounded, we may enter the church in order at the signal of the abbess or prioress. After None we perform the office for the dead. Then we enter the refectory and drink water. Afterwards we sit in the cloister, reading and working. We also go out for work at whatever hour of the day we are necessarily summoned. After Vespers supper is served. Thereafter we follow the arrangement stated above. In the greater litany, on the three Rogation days, on Friday and Saturday, on the vigil of Saint John the Baptist, the vigil [Col. 0317B] of the Apostles Peter and Paul, the vigil of Saint Lawrence, the vigil of the Assumption, and from the Ides of September until Easter, we fast.

From the Council of Tribur, chapter 10.

Virgins who, before the age of twelve, have placed the sacred veil upon their heads without the knowledge of their *mundiburdus* [legal guardian], and whose guardians have consented by keeping silent for a year and a day, are to remain in their holy purpose. But if, within the said year and day, those guardians make a claim on their behalf, their petition is to be granted—unless perhaps the virgins, moved by the fear of God, persevere in the religious habit with the guardians’ permission.

On the consecration of nuns, from the Council of Carthage.

[Col. 0317C] When a virgin who is to become a nun is presented for consecration to her bishop, she is to be brought forward in such garments as she will always wear, suitable to her profession and holiness.

From the decree of Gelasius, chapter 12.

The sacred veil is by no means to be imposed upon devout virgins except at Epiphany, during the Easter octave, or on the feasts of the Apostles; nor before their twenty-fifth year, unless, as has been said concerning baptism, they have been seized by a grave illness. If they beg for it, lest they leave this world without this gift, it is not to be refused them.

From the decree of Pope Pius.

Virgins are not to be veiled before [Col. 0317D] twenty-five years of age, except perhaps because the preservation of virgin chastity is endangered; nor are they to be consecrated at any time other than Epiphany, the Easter octave, and the feasts of the Apostles, unless the urgency of death requires otherwise.

From the Council of Milevis, chapter 25.

Likewise it has been decided that, if any bishop veils a virgin under twenty-five years of age because her virgin chastity is endangered—whether a powerful abductor or ravisher is feared, or she has at some time been struck by a troubling apprehension of mortal danger—so that she may not die unveiled, whether at her parents’ request or at that of those to whose care she belongs, the council’s determination concerning that number of years shall not prejudice her.

[Col. 0318A] Jerome Against Jovinian.

If a virgin marries, she has not sinned—not that virgin who has dedicated herself to the service of God. For if any one of these marries, she will incur condemnation, because she has made void her first faith. But if they object that this was said concerning widows, how much more does it prevail concerning virgins, when even those are not permitted to marry who were once permitted to do so? Virgins who marry after consecration are not so much adulteresses as incestuous women.

From the Decree of Pope Eutychian, chapter 13.

Moreover, in certain places we have found an established practice full of folly and contrary to ecclesiastical authority: namely, that some abbesses and certain nuns presume, against right, to impose the veil upon widows and [Col. 0318B] virgin girls. Consequently, certain women unjustly veiled think that they can more freely serve their carnal desires and fulfil their own wishes. Therefore we decree that, if after this ruling an abbess or any nun breaks out into such audacity as to presume to veil either a widow or a virgin girl, she shall be subjected to canonical judgment until she makes satisfaction.

Boniface the martyr to Hilteribald, king of the English.

Among Greeks and Romans, one would be regarded as having brought something like blasphemy against God upon himself if, when specifically questioned before ordination about this sin and found guilty, he had lain with a veiled and consecrated [Col. 0318C] woman; such a person would be excluded from every rank of God’s priests. For this reason, dearest son, it must be carefully considered how weighty this sin appears in the eyes of the eternal Judge: it will place its perpetrator among the servants of idolatry and cast him out from the divine ministry of the altar, even though, after performing penance, he may have been reconciled to God.

From the Council of Rouen, chapter 9.

It has been determined that widows ought not to be veiled. Likewise it has been determined that, if henceforth any priest proves to be a contumacious transgressor of this rule—that is, presumes to veil any widows—he shall incur peril to his rank, since even bishops are not permitted to do this. Likewise it has been determined concerning [Col. 0318D] virgin girls, who are not to be veiled by priests, that anyone attempting this shall be condemned as a transgressor of the canons.

From the Council of Mainz, chapter 6.

Let no one attempt to veil widows, as has been determined in the decrees of Gelasius, chapter 13; for neither divine authority nor the form of the canons has granted this. If, however, a widow has of her own will professed continence, as is read in chapter 21 of the same Gelasius, let her intention render account to God on her behalf. For just as, according to the Apostle, she was by no means forbidden to marry if she could not contain herself, so, after deliberating with herself, she ought to preserve for God the pledged faith of chastity. Yet we, supported by the authority of the Fathers, decree and judge in this sacred assembly [Col. 0319A] that, if she has voluntarily put upon herself a veil, although not consecrated, and has offered an oblation to God in church among the veiled women, whether she wishes it or not she must thereafter retain the religious habit. This holds even if she wishes to confirm by oath that she put the veil upon herself with the intention and understanding that she could remove it again.

From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.

The holy synod has decreed that widows who receive the sacred veil from the altar of their own free will for a holy way of life shall remain in that same purpose. For we determine that it is unlawful, after they have consecrated themselves to God under the veil and made an offering among the veiled women, for them again to be permitted to lie to the Holy Spirit.

Pope Nicholas to Archbishop C. and his suffragans.

[Col. 0319B] A widow who has placed the sacred veil upon her head, prayed in church among the other veiled women, and made an offering with them, if she has professed that she will remain in that habit, pledging never to lay aside the veil of religion, must not presume to depart from religious observance.

Augustine, On the Gift of Widowhood.

Widows who do not practise continence should marry before they vow by profession to observe continence; if they do not fulfil what they have vowed, they are rightly condemned.

From the Council of Orange, chapter 6.

We decree that a profession to preserve widowhood, made before the bishop in the *secretarium*, with the widow’s garment put on before the bishop, is not to be violated; nevertheless, the woman who deserts that [Col. 0319C] profession is deservedly to be condemned.

From the Council of Toledo, chapter 5.

All women coming to the sacred religious life are to cover their heads with a mantle and make a written and ratified profession, after which they are no longer to be allowed to relapse into the audacity of transgression. But any among them found to have surrendered either mind or dress to transgression are to incur a sentence of excommunication; and, after again changing their habit, they are to remain confined in monasteries under the hardships of severe penance until they close their final day.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius sent to the bishops of Sicily, chapter 9.

[Col. 0319D] We do not allow widows to pass to marriage who have remained for a long period in a religious purpose and observance. Likewise, we forbid virgins to marry who have spent many years of their life in monasteries.

From a letter of Pope Gregory sent to Boniface.

Concerning widows who depart from their purpose of widowhood, about whom, dearest brother, your affection has wished to consult us: I believe you know from Saint Paul and many holy Fathers that, unless they return, they have long ago been condemned. We likewise judge, by apostolic authority, that they are to be condemned [Col. 0320A] and excluded from the communion of the faithful and from the thresholds of the Church, until they obey their bishops and return, willingly or unwillingly, to the good which they began. But concerning unveiled virgins, should they stray, we possess the following decree of our predecessor of holy memory, the pope:

Those, however, who, though not yet covered by the sacred veil, have nevertheless always professed to remain in a virginal purpose—although they have not been veiled—if they marry, must do penance for some time, because their promise was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a contract made in good faith is customarily dissolved for no reason, how much more can this promise, made by covenant with God, not be dissolved without punishment? For if virgins not yet veiled are thus [Col. 0320B] punished by public penance and excluded from the assembly of the faithful until they make satisfaction, how much more ought widows—who are of more mature age and sounder wisdom and judgment, who have often experienced the company of husbands, assumed the religious habit, and at last apostasized and returned to their former vomit—to be expelled by us and by all the faithful from the thresholds of the church and the assembly of the faithful until satisfaction, and handed over to prisons? In what manner is such a person, according to blessed Paul, to be delivered to Satan, that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord? (1 Cor. 5:5). Of such persons the Lord also speaks through Moses: “Remove the evil from your midst” (ibid., 13). Of them He also says through the Prophet: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees vengeance; [Col. 0320C] he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Ps. 57:11). For of such persons, their like, and those consenting with them, it is said that “not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are guilty” (Rom. 1:32).

From a letter of Pope Nicholas, chapter 5.

Nicholas, servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and most holy fellow-brother Adaberinus, archbishop of the holy church of Vivacum.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] F. To Aluinus of holy Januensis, to whom Distinction 34, chapter 1 is addressed. For Adaberinus is mentioned in none of Nicholas’s letters [Col. 0320D], nor have I yet been able to discover what the church of Vivacum is.]

Concerning the woman about whom you asked—who after her husband’s death placed the sacred veil upon her head and pretended to be a nun beneath that veil, but later returned to marriage—it seems good to me that, because through hypocrisy she wished to disturb the ecclesiastical rule [Col. 0320D] and did not lawfully persevere in her vow, she should do penance for her wicked deception, return to what she promised, and to the sacred ministry which she began. For if we consent that everyone may counterfeit, rather than truly perform, all ecclesiastical sacraments as he wishes, all ecclesiastical order will be thrown into confusion; the ordinances of the Catholic faith will not stand, nor will the sacred canons be duly observed. What good did it do Simon Magus to receive holy baptism hypocritically and pretend that he would remain in Christianity, when, after his fraud had been exposed by the Apostle, what was to befall him was pronounced? For he says: “May your penance be with you unto perdition. For your heart is not right before [Col. 0321A] God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours, and pray to God that perhaps the thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and the bond of iniquity” (Acts 8:20–23). Therefore we judge that such persons, unless they come to their senses, should be struck with the spiritual sword. For it is not lawful to lie to the Holy Spirit, as Ananias and Sapphira lied and immediately perished.

From the Council of Arles, chapter 7.

All should know that the bodies of women consecrated to God are, by the vow of their own promise and the words of the priest, consecrated temples of God, as is proved by the testimonies of Scripture. Their violators are therefore sacrilegious persons and, according to the Apostle, are known to be children of perdition.

[Col. 0321B] The Apostle says:

“Command,” he says, “that widows be irreproachable. Let a widow be chosen not less than forty [Vulgate: sixty] years old, having testimony in good works, if she has brought up children.” And: “Avoid younger widows. For when they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have made void their first faith; and at the same time they are idle, speaking what they ought not. Therefore I desire younger women to marry, bear children, manage households, and give the adversary no occasion for reproach. For already some have turned back after Satan” (1 Tim. 5:7–15).

From the Council of Mainz, chapter 13.

[Col. 0321C] We judge that abbesses, together with their nuns, ought in every respect to live rightly and justly. Those, however, who have made profession according to the Rule of Saint Benedict are to live separately. But if they live canonically, they are to be kept fully and under diligent supervision, remain in their cloisters, and have no exit abroad. The abbesses themselves also are to reside in their monasteries and not go out without the permission and counsel of their bishop.

From the Council of Mainz, chapter 26.

An abbess is by no means to leave her monastery except with the permission of her bishop. And whenever she goes abroad, she is to take the greatest care of the nuns whom she takes with her, so that no occasion [Col. 0321D] of sin may be given them.

From the Council of Gangra, chapter 9.

An abbess is to take diligent care of the community entrusted to her and see that the nuns are zealous in reading and the office, in the chanting of psalms, and in every good work. She is to provide them leadership, since she will render account for their souls before the Lord; and she is to provide the nuns with necessary allowances, lest want of food or drink perhaps compel them to sin.

From the Council of Mainz, chapter 14.

Nuns are by no means to leave the monastery, unless perhaps their abbess permits it because some necessity presses.

[Col. 0322A] From the Council of Gangra, chapter 13.

If any woman, for the sake of a supposed continence, changes her dress and, instead of the customary female clothing, adopts male attire, let her be anathema.

From the same council, chapter 14.

If any woman, as she supposes for divine worship, cuts off her hair, which God gave her as a reminder of subjection, let her be anathema, as one who dissolves the commandment of obedience.

From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3.

A bishop is to enter the monasteries of monks and nuns frequently and, sitting in their assembly with weighty and religious persons, diligently [Col. 0322B] examine the life and conduct of the men or women. If he finds anything blameworthy, he is to strive to correct it. He is also to investigate carefully the chastity of the nuns; and if any woman is found who, disregarding her purpose of chastity, shamelessly has intercourse with a cleric or layman, she is to be sternly restrained with beatings and confined in private custody, unless she worthily repents of the evil she has committed. By the authority of the sacred canons it is also to be forbidden that any layman or cleric have access to their cloisters and private dwellings; nor are priests to enter except solely for Mass. When Mass has been completed, they are to return to their own churches. Furthermore, the bishop is to announce publicly and privately to all how great a sin is committed by one who presumes to defile the bride of Christ. For if the man who violates another man’s bride is held guilty, how much more is he made guilty of affronting majesty who corrupts the bride [Col. 0322C] of almighty God?

On nuns.

Bishops are to take diligent care that nuns live without private property, so that they cannot excuse themselves under the pretext of any poverty.

On nuns.

We decree that abbesses, prioresses, and other holders of obediences shall render accounts in chapter of all income, revenues, and expenses every year, at least four times a year; and that, so the condition both of obediences and priories may be known to the cloistered community, an account be put in writing, in such a way that the convent retains one written copy and the abbess another. On account of scandals arising from the conduct of nuns, we decree concerning black-clad [Col. 0322D] nuns that they receive no deposit in their houses from any persons; above all, they are not to permit chests belonging to clerics or laypersons to be deposited with them for safekeeping. Boys and girls customarily reared and educated there are to be expelled altogether. All are to eat together in the refectory and sleep separately in the dormitory. All the nuns’ private chambers are to be destroyed, unless, after inspection by the bishop, one is retained as necessary for an infirmary or for another cause that appears just and necessary to the bishop. Likewise, nuns are in no way to be permitted to go out or stay overnight elsewhere, except perhaps for a grave cause and rarely; and the abbess is to be enjoined not to permit nuns to leave otherwise. If at any time the abbess permits one to go out for a just cause, she is to direct her to return without delay [Col. 0323A] and give her a companion—not according to her own preference, but one whom the abbess judges suitable. Suspicious and superfluous doors are to be blocked up. In this matter bishops are to exercise diligence and care, personally and through their officers, and so restrain the women’s lives and conduct that, through their diligence, the scandals now arising from their life may be suppressed.

On sisters not being sent out.

Our sisters are not to leave, unless perhaps they are sent from cloister to cloister to stay for at least one year. But if an evident necessity arises for which one must go out, this is to be done with the permission of the abbot of Prémontré, provided that his consent can be awaited without serious danger to her. If any [Col. 0323B] abbot sends one out otherwise, let him be punished according to the gravity of the offence, at the discretion of the general chapter—especially if scandal arises from the sister who has been sent out. In time of war, however, any abbot may transfer the sisters subject to him to safe places. If it is otherwise, the abbot under whom this occurs shall fast on bread and water every Friday for a full year.

On sisters not being received.

Because dangerous times press upon us and the Churches are burdened beyond measure, by the common counsel of the chapter we decree that henceforth no sister is to be received. But if anyone proves a transgressor of this statute, his abbess shall be punished without mercy.

[Col. 0323C] Likewise, on sisters not being received.

No sister is henceforth to be received into the order except in those places which from ancient times have been permanently assigned for receiving sisters.

On proof concerning sisters to be received.

If any women, by virtue of an old concession made to them before the promulgation of the ordinance concerning sisters not being received, wish to be received as sisters, they are in no way to be received unless they prove, either by documents or by a sufficient number of brethren—namely, four or five—that the concession was made to them before the prohibition of the order by the abbot or convent.

On women not being exchanged.

Women who from ancient times have places in [Col. 0323D] our houses so as to be received as sisters are not to transfer their places to any others; nor is any change of persons to be made concerning women.

On girls not being brought up in our houses.

Since we can scarcely suffice even for our own brothers and sisters with meagre fare, it would appear absurd if we nourished outsiders in luxury—especially such persons through whose association our brothers or sisters could be corrupted. Therefore, under strict prohibition, we have judged it necessary that, after all secular girls hitherto received to be brought up in the cloisters of our sisters have been dismissed, no other whatever is henceforth to be admitted for upbringing. If any girl already received wishes to leave, or if anyone is received for upbringing and forcibly intrudes herself, either personally or through others, [Col. 0324A] divine offices shall wholly cease in that place until she has departed.

That our sisters are not to have black tunics.

We have thought it proper to add the following to the foregoing, firmly decreeing under penalty of excommunication that our sisters are to be clothed only in white tunics and black surplices. In these surplices, indeed, no excess or finery is to be visible, lest their dress be conspicuous and seem to seek delights of clothing rather than virtues of character.

On sisters discovered in carnal lapse.

If any sister is discovered in a carnal lapse, she is immediately to be expelled from the house and is in no way, even if she obtains mercy, thereafter to return, unless [Col. 0324B] under this condition: that she be deprived of the veil forever and, wearing cheap clothing and living on scant food, serve as a slave without ever leaving the cloister. But if she commits the offence a second time, she is to be expelled and is thereafter to expect no right of readmission from the order. If any woman goes outside the sisters’ enclosure, she is to abstain on bread and water every Friday for a year. Moreover, if she goes outside the outer gate of the house and returns within eight days, she may be received as a fugitive; yet she is to undergo the penalty for a more serious fault for forty days and take her meal on bread and water every Friday for a year. If she returns after eight days, this is to be added to her penalty: until the next general chapter she is to be deprived of the veil and serve as a slave, but is not on that pretext [Col. 0324C] to leave the cloister.

On the going out of sisters.

We have heard that certain churches of our order are ill-spoken of because their sisters go out too readily. But because many dangers to souls may arise from this, and perhaps have arisen, we forbid them henceforth to go out for any business or work, or even in legal matters to give testimony.

On the common life of sisters.

The history in the Acts of the Apostles makes sufficiently clear and plain that Ananias and his wife Sapphira, after offering to the chief of the Apostles what they possessed only temporarily, but retaining part of the price of a field sold by them, were struck by sudden death. Therefore, because whatever things have been written have been written for our [Col. 0324D] instruction, so that the vice, or at least the appearance, of private ownership may be rooted out, we decree that every abbot of our order shall so provide for his sisters that they live from the common fund and in common, work together and for the common benefit, and are not permitted to possess private property. Rather, necessities are to be supplied them from the common fund according to the resources of the churches to which they belong. If anything is given to any one of them by anyone, she is immediately to bring it into the common stock, according to the precept of our father Augustine. But if she presumes to retain it and is discovered by the abbot or prioress, she is to be punished more severely according to the statutes of the order.

That sisters are not to be frequently visited.

Since, according to the Apostle, all Christ’s faithful, [Col. 0325A] and especially religious men, ought to abstain from every appearance of evil, we forbid both subjects and prelates to open the sisters’ door, even in other houses. We nevertheless allow that, if anyone comes to them for the purpose of preaching, he shall go no farther than the open door of the church; rather, sitting there, he shall pour forth the word of God to them as they listen, [Col. 0326A] and shall by no means allow chaplains or his companions to enter to them.

## LETTER IX. The same Peter’s letter to the virgins of the Paraclete. On the study of letters.

[Col. 0325]

[Col. 0325A] Blessed Jerome, greatly occupied with the education of Christ’s virgins, [Col. 0325B] among the other things which he writes for their edification, especially commends to them the study of sacred literature; and for this purpose he invites them not so much by words as by examples. Mindful, indeed, of the saying with which, while instructing Rusticus, he declares, “Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh,” he judged love of this study to be so much more necessary for women because he saw them to be naturally weaker and frailer in body. Nor does he introduce, for this exhortation of virgins, only an argument drawn from likeness to virgins; rather, to make a comparison from the lesser, he takes widows and married women as examples, in order the more to stimulate brides of Christ to this study by means of women of the world, and by the virtue of laywomen to rouse or [Col. 0325C] shame the sluggishness of nuns. And because, in accordance with the Gregorian saying, “everyone begins with small things in order to attain greater,” it is helpful first to set forth with what care he endeavoured to instruct little girls in sacred letters. Thus, to omit other matters, let us now bring forward what he sets down for Laeta concerning the education of her daughter Paula: this discipline of letters for the sake of moral instruction.

“She must be educated,” he says, “as a soul that is to become a temple of God. Let her have letters made of boxwood or ivory, and let them be called by their proper names. Let her play with them, so that play itself may be education. And let her not merely retain the order of the letters, so that the memory of their names passes into a chant; but let their arrangement also be often confused, with the last letters mixed among the middle and the [Col. 0325D] middle among the first, so that she knows them not by sound alone but by sight as well. When she begins to guide a stylus in wax with a trembling hand, either let another hand placed over hers guide and control her fingers, or let the letters be carved upon a tablet, so that her traces may be drawn in the same grooves enclosed by margins and cannot wander outside. Let her join syllables for a reward, and let her be enticed by the little gifts with which that age can be won over. Let her have companions in learning, whom she may envy and by whose praise she may be stung. She is not to be scolded if she is slower; rather, her ability must be aroused by praise, so that she rejoices when victorious and grieves when defeated. Above all, care must be taken that she does not come to hate study, lest the bitterness of lessons imposed in childhood remain beyond her unformed years. The very names through which she gradually becomes accustomed to weaving words together must not be random, but selected and deliberately amassed: namely, the names of prophets and apostles, and the whole succession of patriarchs [Col. 0326A] from Adam, as it descends in Matthew and Luke [Col. 0326B], so that, while she is doing one thing, preparation may be made for her future memory. A teacher of sound age, life, and learning must be chosen. Nor, I think, will a learned man be ashamed to do for a related or noble girl what Aristotle did for Philip’s son: namely, to give the beginnings of letters himself, despite the lowly work of writing-masters. Things are not to be despised as small, without which great things cannot stand. The sound of the letters themselves and the first instruction in learning are pronounced differently by the learned mouth and by the rustic. Nor should she learn in youth what she will later have to unlearn. What unformed minds have drunk in is uprooted only with difficulty.”

Greek history relates that Alexander, the most powerful king and conqueror of the world, could not rid himself, in either character or gait, of the faults of his tutor Leonidas, with which he had [Col. 0326C] been infected while still a little boy. In order, moreover, to commend memorization of Scripture recitation, Jerome himself wishes a fixed daily amount of reading to be prescribed, which she is to perform from memory. He directs that attention be given not only to Latin letters but also to Greek, since both languages were then common at Rome, especially because the Scriptures had been translated from Greek into Latin, so that she might know them better from their source and judge them more truly. For the Latin language did not yet employ a translation according to the Hebrew truth.

He therefore says: “Let her render to you each day a task gathered from the flowers of Scripture. Let her learn the metre of Greek verse. Let Latin education immediately follow; for unless it forms the tender mouth from the beginning, [Col. 0326D] the tongue is corrupted into a foreign sound and native speech is defiled by alien faults. Instead of jewels and silk, let her love the divine books, in which she is pleased not by embroidered decoration in gold and Babylonian dyed fabric, but by a corrected and learned text, clearly distinguished for the sake of faith. Let her first learn the Psalter; let her turn herself away through these songs; and in Solomon’s Proverbs let her be instructed for life. In Ecclesiastes let her become accustomed to despising worldly things. In Job let her pursue examples of virtue and patience. Let her proceed to the Gospels, never to lay them down from her hands. Let her drink in the Acts and Epistles of the Apostles with the whole desire of her heart. And when she has enriched the storehouse of her breast with these treasures, let her commit to memory the Prophets, the Heptateuch, the books of Kings and Chronicles, and also the volumes of Ezra and Esther. Finally, let her learn the Song of Songs without danger, lest, if she reads it at the beginning, she be wounded by not understanding, beneath its carnal words, the [Col. 0327A] epithalamium of spiritual marriage. Let her beware of all apocryphal writings; and if she should ever wish to read them, not for the truth of doctrines but out of reverence for their signs, let her know that they are not by those whose names they bear as titles, that many corrupt things have been mixed into them, and that it requires great prudence to seek gold in mud. Let her always keep Cyprian’s works in hand. Let her run through Athanasius’s Letters and Hilary’s books with unhindered step. Let her delight in the treatises and talents of those whose books show no wavering in piety. Let her read the others in such a way as to judge rather than follow them.

“You will reply: ‘How can I, a woman living in the world, observe all this amid such a throng of people in Rome?’ Do not then undertake a burden you cannot bear. Rather, after you have weaned her with Isaac and clothed her with [Col. 0327B] Samuel, send her to her grandmother and aunt. Return this most precious jewel to Mary’s chamber, and place her in the cradle of the infant Jesus. Let her be brought up in a monastery; let her be among choirs of virgins; let her not learn to swear; let her regard lying as sacrilege; let her not know the world; let her live like an angel; though in the flesh, let her be without flesh; let her think every human being like herself. And, to pass over other things, she would surely free you from the difficulty of guarding her and the danger attending that guardianship. It is better for you to long for her while absent than to be anxious at every point. Entrust the little girl to Eustochium; let her admire that woman from her earliest years, whose speech, walk, and dress are a lesson in virtues. Let her be in the lap of her grandmother, who by long experience has learned to nourish, guard, and teach virgins. Hannah, after offering in the tabernacle [Col. 0327C] the son whom she had vowed to God, never received him back. If you send Paula, I promise to be both her teacher and nurse: I will carry her on my shoulders and, though an old man, form her stammering words—far more gloriously than the philosopher of the world, who educated not a king of Macedonians destined to perish by Babylonian poison, but a handmaid and bride of Christ, to be offered to the heavenly kingdoms.”

Consider, dearest sisters in Christ and fellow-servants, what great care so eminent a doctor of the Church undertook in the education of one little girl; how diligently he distinguished everything that he judged necessary for instruction, beginning from the alphabet itself. He gives guidance not only concerning the pronunciation of syllables and the joining of letters, but also concerning writing; he also provides that companions be joined to her, by whose envy or [Col. 0327D] praise she may be strongly stirred. In order, moreover, to make her learning voluntary rather than forced, and to cause her to embrace study with a greater love, he advises that she be encouraged by caresses, praise, and little gifts. He also specifies that the very names are to be gathered from sacred Scripture, so that by first practising their utterance she may commit these things most fully to memory, in accordance with the poetic saying:

> What it has once been freshly imbued with, it will preserve the scent of.

…The vessel long . . . . . .

He also carefully describes what sort of teacher should be chosen for this purpose; nor does he omit that a fixed measure of reading ought to be prescribed, which she should faithfully complete every day and keep firmly in her heart. And because at that time the use of Greek letters was also widespread at Rome, he does not permit her to remain ignorant of Greek letters [Col. 0328A]—chiefly, I think, because the translation of the divine books has come down to us from the Greeks, so that she might discern what among us was lacking or different; and perhaps because the liberal arts afford some benefit to those striving toward perfection in learning. He also puts forward the condition of the Latin language, as though he were beginning our instruction from its very foundation.

But when she has advanced from the sound of words to their meaning, so that she wishes already to understand what she has learned to pronounce, he distinguishes for her various books: both those belonging to the canon of the two Testaments and the treatises of learned teachers, by whose instruction she may advance toward perfection. Among the canonical Scriptures he so strongly commends the Gospels to her [Col. 0328B] that he judges they should never leave a virgin’s hands; as though he lays a greater obligation of Gospel reading upon deaconesses than upon deacons. For the latter must read it aloud in church, whereas the former ought never to be free from its reading.

Then, writing to the mother concerning her daughter, lest the mother should plead any excuse that a secular woman in Rome, amid so great a multitude of people, could accomplish all these things, he advises her to free herself from this burden and entrust her daughter to a monastery of virgins, where she may be educated without danger and more perfectly trained in the matters he has mentioned. Finally, removing every possible occasion for anxiety lest the mother should be concerned about finding such a teacher as he himself had described, he offers himself as both teacher and nurse if the girl is sent from Rome to Jerusalem—to her holy grandmother Paula [Col. 0328C] and her aunt Eustochium.

Indeed, in a promise astonishing to relate, so great a doctor of the Church, though weakened by old age, declares that he would not disdain to carry the virgin on his shoulders, as though he were her bearer. Yet among the suspicious such a thing could scarcely occur without suspicion, nor among religious persons without scandal. Nevertheless, this man full of God, long known to all for the integrity of his life, confidently promised everything, provided only that he might so instruct one virgin as to leave her herself a teacher to others, and that Jerome might be read in her by one who had never seen Jerome.

But let us pass from little girls to older virgins, whom he constantly urges toward literary study, both by writing to them what they should read [Col. 0328D] and by praising them for their constancy in reading or speaking. Let us hear what he says, writing to the virgin Principia concerning Psalm 44:

> “I know, Principia, daughter in Christ, that many reproach me because I sometimes write to women and prefer the weaker sex to men. Therefore I ought first to answer my detractors, and then come to the little discussion you have requested. If men were asking about the Scriptures, I would not speak to women. If Barak had wished to go to battle, Deborah would not have triumphed over the defeated enemies.”

And after some intervening remarks:

> “Apollos, an apostolic man and most learned in the Law, is taught by Aquila and Priscilla, who instruct him in the way of the Lord. If it was not shameful for the Apostle to be taught by a woman [Col. 0329A], why should it be shameful for me, after men, to teach women also? These and similar matters, most venerable daughter (*semnotatē*), I have briefly touched upon, so that you may neither regret your sex nor men exalt their own name—men to whose condemnation the life of women in the Holy Scriptures is praised.”

After virgins, it is pleasing to consider widows, and how greatly they too advanced in the study of sacred letters by his testimony and praise. Thus the same doctor, writing to the same virgin Principia concerning the life of Saint Marcella, as she had requested, says among the marks of her virtues:

> “Her zeal for the divine Scriptures was incredible; and she always sang: ‘I have hidden your words in my heart, that I may not sin against you’ (Ps. 118:11). And that saying concerning the perfect man: ‘His delight is in the law of the Lord, and in his law he will meditate day and night’ [Col. 0329B] (Ps. 1:2); and: ‘From your commandments I have gained understanding’ (Ps. 118:104). Finally, when ecclesiastical necessity had brought me to Rome with the holy bishops Paulinus and Epiphanius, and I modestly avoided the eyes of noble women, she acted, according to the Apostle, ‘in season and out of season’ (2 Tim. 4:2), so that her diligence overcame my modesty. Since I was then thought to possess some reputation in the study of Scripture, she never met with me without asking something concerning the Scriptures. Nor did she immediately rest satisfied, but raised questions in opposition—not in order to dispute, but to learn through inquiry the solutions to objections which she understood might be raised.

> “I fear to say what virtues and what intelligence I found in her [Col. 0329C], lest I exceed the bounds of credibility and cause you greater grief as you remember how great a good you have lost. This alone I shall say: whatever had been accumulated in us through long study and prolonged meditation, as though transformed into nature itself, she tasted, learned, and possessed. Thus, after our own instruction, if any dispute arose over a Scriptural testimony, people would go to her as judge. And because she was very prudent, she answered questions in such a way that she called her own views not her own, but either mine or someone else’s, so that even in the very act of teaching she confessed herself a disciple. For she knew the Apostle’s saying: ‘But I do not permit a woman to teach’ (1 Tim. 2:12), lest she should seem to do an injury to the male [Col. 0329D] sex—and sometimes to priests—when they asked concerning obscure and ambiguous matters.

> “She comforted our absence through mutual conversation; what we could not render in the flesh, we rendered in spirit. She always met letters, surpassed us in attentions, and anticipated us with greetings. The absence did not cost much when continuous letters united us. In this tranquillity and service of the Lord, a storm of heresy arose in these provinces and disturbed everything. It advanced to such fury that it spared neither itself nor any good person. And, as though it were not enough to have spread its corruption here everywhere, it brought to the Roman harbour a ship full of blasphemies, once its poisonous and filthy teaching had found at Rome persons whom it could lead astray.

> “Then holy Marcella, who had long restrained herself lest she should seem to act from rivalry [Col. 0330A], after she perceived that the faith praised by an apostolic mouth was being violated by many—so that this teaching was drawing even priests, some monks, and especially worldly people into agreement with it, and deceiving the simplicity of the bishop, who judged others by his own character—resisted publicly, preferring to please God rather than men. This was the beginning of the heretics’ condemnation: she produced witnesses who had first been instructed by them and afterwards corrected from heretical error; she showed the multitude of those deceived; she brought forward the impious volumes *Peri Archōn* (‘On First Principles’), which were displayed as corrected by the hand of a scorpion; and, though summoned by frequent letters to defend themselves, the heretics did not dare to come. So great was the force of conscience that they preferred to be condemned in absence rather than refuted in person [Col. 0330B]. Marcella was the source of this most glorious victory.”

You see, dearest sisters, how much fruit the praiseworthy study of one matron, set at the head of all the faithful in the city, produced in suppressing heresies; and by what great lamp of learning one woman drove away even the darkness of the Church’s own teachers. Concerning her study of sacred letters, by which she deserved this victory, the same doctor recalls, for your exhortation, in the preface to Book I of his Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians:

> “I know indeed her zeal; I know her faith—what flame she always bears in her breast. She surpasses her sex, forgets mankind, and, while the drum of the divine volumes sounds, crosses the Red Sea of this world. Certainly, when I was in Rome, she never found me so hurried [Col. 0330C] that she did not ask something concerning the Scriptures. Nor, in the Pythagorean manner, did she consider whatever I answered correct; nor did authority prevail with her without reason or prior examination. Instead, she examined everything and weighed all things with a discerning mind, so that I felt I had not so much a pupil as a judge.”

At that time, learning flourished so ardently in holy women as well as men that they were by no means content with instruction in their own language, but sought the streams of Scripture that they possessed from the sources themselves; nor did they believe that the poverty of a single language was sufficient for them. Hence the above-mentioned doctor, writing to Paula on the death of her daughter Blesilla, says among other things in Blesilla’s special praise:

> “Who could pass without sobbing over her persistence in prayer, the refinement of her language, the strength of her memory, the keenness of her intelligence? Had you heard her speaking Greek, you would have thought that she knew no Latin. If she turned her tongue to Roman speech, her language had no trace whatever of foreignness. Moreover, what all Greece marvels at even in Origen, she conquered the difficulties of the Hebrew language—not, I say, in a few months, but in days—so that she competed with her mother in learning and chanting the psalms.” [Col. 0330D]

The same doctor also does not omit that her mother Paula herself, as well as Paula’s other daughter, the virgin Eustochium dedicated to God, were no less occupied with the same study of letters and languages. Thus, writing the life of Paula, he says of her:

[Col. 0331A]

> “Nothing was more teachable than her intelligence. She was slow to speak, swift to listen, mindful of that precept: ‘Hear, Job, and be silent’ (Job 33:31). She knew the Holy Scriptures by heart. Finally, she compelled me to read through the Old and New Testaments with her daughter while I expounded them. I at first refused through modesty; but because of her persistence and repeated requests, I granted it, teaching what I had learned. Whenever I hesitated and honestly confessed that I did not know, she would by no means accept this from me; rather, by continual questioning she compelled me to indicate, from among many and varied opinions, which seemed more probable to me.

> “I shall tell another thing which perhaps may seem incredible to the envious. She wished to learn Hebrew, which I myself learned in part from youth with much labour [Col. 0331B] and sweat, and which I do not abandon despite tireless practice lest it abandon me; and she succeeded, so that she sang the psalms in Hebrew and spoke without any Latin idiom whatever. This we still see today in her holy daughter Eustochium. For they knew that the learning contained in Latin books had proceeded from Hebrew and Greek writings, and that an interpreter cannot fully preserve in a foreign language the idiom of any language.

> “Both Hebrews and Greeks, glorying in perfection, have accordingly been accustomed sometimes to mock our translators as imperfect. They support this with the following comparison: any liquid repeatedly poured from one vessel into several necessarily diminishes in its fullness, and the quantity found in the later vessels cannot equal that which it had in the first [Col. 0331C]. Thus it often happens that, when we try to refute Jews by means of certain testimonies, they easily refute us, because we do not know Hebrew, by pointing out, as they say, the falsity of our translations.”

The aforementioned most wise women, carefully observing this, were by no means content with instruction in their native language, so that they might not only instruct their own people but also refute others, and might refresh their thirst from the clearest water of the fountain. To this, I think, Jerome himself, skilled in these languages, had especially urged them by his example. Writing to Pammachius and Oceanus, he describes in these terms the labour and expense by which he acquired the perfection of this skill:

> “While I was young, I was carried along by a marvellous zeal for learning; nor, contrary to the presumption of certain people, did I teach myself. At Antioch I frequently heard and attended Apollinaris of Laodicea; and although he instructed me in the Holy Scriptures, I never adopted his contentious doctrine concerning their meaning. My head was already sprinkled with grey hair, and it became me to be a teacher rather than a pupil. Yet I went to Alexandria and heard Didymus. I give him thanks in many matters: what I did not know, I learned; what I knew, I did not lose through his teaching. People thought I had finished learning; I came again to Jerusalem and Bethlehem. At what labour, at what price, did I have Barabbas as my nocturnal teacher? For he feared the Jews and presented himself to me as another Nicodemus [Col. 0332A]. I frequently mention all these persons in my works.”

Considering this zeal of so great a doctor and of holy women for the divine Scriptures, I have urged—and I desire you unceasingly to fulfil—that, while you can and have a mother skilled in the three languages, you should be carried toward this perfection of learning, so that whatever doubt arises from differing translations may be settled by your own examination. This seems not incongruously to have been prefigured by the title of the Lord’s cross, written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: namely, that in his Church, extended throughout the whole world, learning in these pre-eminent languages should abound, in whose letters the Scripture of both Testaments is contained.

You have no need of a long journey or great expense in order to learn these languages [Col. 0332B], as happened to blessed Jerome, since you have, as has been said, a mother sufficient for this study. After virgins and widows, let faithful married women also provide you with an incentive to learning, either rebuking your negligence or increasing your zeal. The venerable Celantia likewise offers you an example. Desiring to live rightly even in marriage, she earnestly requested that Jerome himself prescribe for her a rule of married life. Writing to her on this matter, he says:

> “Urged to write by your letter, I confess that for a long time I hesitated over my reply, modesty commanding me to be silent. For you ask—and ask earnestly and insistently—that I set before you a definite rule from the Holy Scriptures, according to which you may direct the course [Col. 0332C] of your life: so that, once you know the Lord’s will, amid worldly honours and the enticements of riches, you may love the furnishing of good character more, and may be able, though situated in marriage, to please not only your husband but also him who granted marriage itself. Not to satisfy so holy a request and so pious a desire—what else is that than not to love another’s progress? I shall therefore yield to your prayers and endeavour, by his own sayings, to encourage you, who are prepared to fulfil God’s will.”

Perhaps this matron had heard what Scripture records in praise of holy Susanna. After first saying that she was exceedingly beautiful and feared God, Scripture immediately adds the source of that fear and true adornment of the soul: “For her parents, being righteous, educated their daughter according to the law of Moses” [Col. 0332D] (Dan. 13:3). Susanna, not forgetting this education amid the troubles of marriage and the disturbances of worldly occupations, though condemned to death, deserved to condemn her own judges and elders.

Expounding this passage in Daniel, Jerome suitably uses the statement, “Her parents, being righteous, educated their daughter,” and so forth, as an occasion for exhortation:

> “This testimony should be used to exhort parents to teach, according to God’s law and divine word, not only their sons but also their daughters.”

And because such things are very often wont to impede the pursuit both of letters and of virtues, let that exceedingly wealthy queen of Sheba shake from you every sluggish torpor of negligence [Col. 0333A]. Despite the great labour imposed by her weaker sex, the fatigue and dangers of a long journey, and immense expense, she came from the ends of the earth to test Solomon’s wisdom and to compare with him what she knew concerning the things she did not know. Solomon so highly approved her study and labour that, as a reward, he gave her everything she asked, besides what he had voluntarily offered her in royal fashion.

Many powerful men came together to hear his wisdom, and many kings and rulers of the earth honoured his teaching with great gifts. Although he received many presents from them, we do not read that he rewarded any of them on this account except the aforementioned woman. By this he plainly showed how highly he approved a holy woman’s study and zeal [Col. 0333B] for learning, and how pleasing he judged it to be to the Lord. Later the Lord himself—true Solomon, indeed more than Solomon—did not omit to cite her for the condemnation of men who despise his teaching: “The queen of the south,” he says, “will rise at the judgment and condemn this generation” (Matt. 12:52).

Take care, dearest sisters, that your own negligence does not likewise condemn you in that generation. You have still less excuse because you need not undertake the fatigue of a long journey or provide for great expense. You have in your mother instruction sufficient for every purpose: both as an example of virtues and as instruction in letters. She is not only learned in Latin, but also not unacquainted with Hebrew and Greek [Col. 0333C] learning. In this age she alone seems to have acquired that skill in the three languages which everyone praises as a singular grace in blessed Jerome, and which he himself especially commends in the venerable women mentioned above.

For the two Testaments have reached our knowledge in these three principal languages. The title of the Lord’s cross, likewise inscribed in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, plainly indicates that the Lord’s teaching and the praises of Christ—indeed, the mystery of the Trinity itself—were to be proclaimed and hearts strengthened in these especially, throughout the threefold breadth of the world, just as the wood of the cross itself, upon which that title was placed, was threefold [Col. 0333D]. For it is written: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matt. 18:16).

Therefore, so that Holy Scripture might be established by the authority of three languages, and the learning of any one language confirmed by the testimony of the other two, divine providence decreed that the Old and New Testaments together should be contained in these three languages. It is also established that the New Testament itself, which surpasses the Old both in dignity and usefulness, was first written in these three languages, as though the title placed upon the cross had signified this beforehand. For certain parts of it were written in Hebrew because they were addressed to Hebrews; similarly, certain parts were necessarily written in Greek, and certain parts in Latin, in the proper languages of those to whom they were directed.

The first Gospel, according to Matthew, was first written in Hebrew, as it was written for Hebrews [Col. 0334A]. It is likewise established that Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, James’s Epistle to the twelve tribes now dispersed, Peter’s likewise, and perhaps some others, were written in Hebrew for the same reason. Who can doubt that the three Gospels were written in Greek for Greeks, together with whatever epistles of Paul and the others were directed to them, and also the Apocalypse sent to the seven churches of Asia? We know that Paul wrote one epistle to the Romans. Let us Latins therefore glory that we have little from ourselves, and reflect how necessary to us are the teachings of others. If we desire fully to know them, they must be sought at the fountainhead itself rather than in the streams of translations—especially [Col. 0334B] because their diverse translations produce ambiguity rather than certainty for the reader.

For it is not easy, as we have noted above, for a translation to preserve the idiom—that is, the distinctive character—of any language and provide a faithful rendering in every individual case, so that we can express in a foreign language all things just as they were said in their native language. Even within a single language, when we seek to explain one thing by another, we often fail because we do not possess a precise word that can express it more clearly. We know also that blessed Jerome, especially skilled in these three languages, often differs from himself in his translations and their commentaries. In his expositions he frequently says, “Thus it stands [Col. 0334C] in the Hebrew,” though the statement is not found in his translations made, as he himself asserts, according to the Hebrew. What wonder, then, if different translators differ from one another, when even one person is sometimes found to disagree with himself?

Whoever wishes to be certain in these matters should not be content with the water of a stream, but should seek and draw its purity from the fountain. For this reason Jerome’s translation, which was the latest and sought more carefully from Hebrew or Greek itself, as far as he could, as from the fountainhead, surpassed the older translations among us; and with new things arriving, the old things were cast away, as is written in the Law. Therefore Daniel says: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” [Col. 0334D] (Dan. 12:4).

Jerome did what he could in his own time, almost alone in a foreign language. Having not a trustworthy but a Jewish interpreter, on whose assistance he relied greatly, as he himself testifies, he displeased many because he did not think the existing translations sufficient. Yet because he persisted in his undertaking, he prevailed with God’s help, as though observing and fulfilling that saying of Ecclesiastes: “To the source from which rivers go forth they return, so that they may flow again” (Eccl. 1:7). Those Scriptures from which he drew are, as it were, the fountainhead of scriptural translations; and translations quickly fail when rejected as false if they are shown to depart from their source and not to return to it in agreement.

But lest we suppose this one translator sufficient for everything, as though he had attained perfection of skill in every matter—especially in Hebrew, in which he is said among us to excel—let us hear his own testimony on the subject, lest we presume to credit him with more than he possesses. Writing to Domnion and Rogatianus, and against an accuser, he says:
