> “We who have at least a small knowledge of the Hebrew language, and to whom Latin speech is not altogether lacking, can judge more readily concerning other matters and express in our own language what we ourselves understand.” [Col. 0335A]

Blessed is that soul which, meditating upon the law of the Lord day and night, endeavours to draw every Scripture at the very spring of its source as the purest water, lest through ignorance or impossibility it mistake for clear water the turbid streams that wander in different directions, and be forced to vomit up what it has drunk. This zealous study of foreign languages has long since declined; with neglect of letters, knowledge of them has perished. Let us recover in women what we have lost in men; and, for the condemnation and judgment of the stronger sex, let the queen of the south again seek in you the wisdom of the true Solomon.

You are able to devote yourselves to this all the more because nuns can labour less at manual work than monks, and, through the quiet of leisure and the weakness of their nature, can more easily fall into temptation. Hence the aforesaid doctor, pre-eminent for your instruction and exhortation, encourages your labour in the study of letters both by writings and examples—especially lest it should ever be necessary, under the pretext of learning, to summon strength, or lest the mind, vainly occupied with the body, wander abroad and, abandoning its bridegroom, commit fornication with the world [Col. 0336A].

## LETTER X. From Peter Abelard to Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux

[Col. 0335]

[Col. 0335B] To the venerable and most beloved brother in Christ, BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux: PETER, fellow-priest.

When recently I came to the Paraclete, compelled by certain business to be transacted there, your daughter in Christ and our sister, who is called abbess of that place, related to me with the greatest rejoicing that you had come there, long desired, for the sake of a holy visitation; and that, not as a man but as though an angel, you had strengthened both her and her sisters by sacred exhortations. But she confidentially informed me that you had been somewhat troubled, in the affection with which you especially embrace me, because in that oratory the Lord’s Prayer is not recited in the daily offices as it is customarily recited elsewhere. Since you believed this to have been done by me [Col. 0335C], I seemed to you noteworthy on this account, as though for some innovation.

When I heard this, I resolved to write to you whatever apology I can make on this matter, especially because, as is fitting, I grieve over your displeasure more than that of anyone else.

It is established, as you know, that we possess this Lord’s Prayer in writing only from Matthew and Luke. One of them, being both apostle and evangelist, was present when this prayer was delivered; hence there can be no doubt that he recorded it more fully and perfectly, just as he did the entire Sermon on the Mount into which it is inserted. Luke, however, Paul’s disciple, was present neither at that sermon nor when he heard things from the Lord’s own mouth; rather, he wrote what he learned chiefly from Paul’s report, though Paul too is not known to have been present at that sermon. [Col. 0335D] He records, moreover, not that more perfect discourse of the Lord which He delivered on the mountain with the apostles, but the one He gave to the crowds on the plain. For, as is written, when the Lord was about to choose the apostles, “he went up into the hill-country”; but when He was to teach the crowds, He returned to the level ground. There He ascended; here He descended—plainly showing how much loftier was that teaching by which He instructed the teachers [Col. 0336B] themselves.

Finally, on the testimony of blessed Jerome, as manifest truth itself confirms, we know that what is heard and what is seen are reported differently; and what we understand better, we also express better. Matthew drank from the spring itself, Luke from the stream flowing from that spring. We do not accuse Luke of falsehood, nor will he be angry with us if we prefer Matthew to him and prefer the Lord’s Prayer, delivered generally to all the apostles and written by an apostle, to that which was spoken to a single disciple—especially since Matthew’s version is plainly superior both in authority and in completeness. In order that we may judge better of each prayer, as though both lay before our eyes, it is useful to insert them here.

Accordingly, as Matthew writes, when He delivered the aforesaid prayer [Col. 0336C] to the apostles, He said: “Thus, therefore, you shall pray: Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us today our supersubstantial bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:9–13).

But Luke says: “It came to pass, when He was praying in a certain place, that when He ceased, one of His disciples said to Him: Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples. And He said to them: When you pray, say: Father, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive [Col. 0336D] us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation” (Luke 11:1–4).

It is therefore evident that Matthew wrote more perfectly than Luke, as we have recalled above: Matthew included seven petitions in it, Luke only five. The former was, as was fitting, delivered more perfectly to the apostles, and was arranged in that number of petitions by which the fullness of sevenfold [Col. 0337A] grace is signified—those primary and greater gifts which Paul confesses that the apostles received, saying: “But we, having the firstfruits of the Spirit,” etc. (Rom. 8:23). The latter prayer, which Luke reports as having been delivered by the Lord long after the Sermon on the Mount, at the request of one of the disciples, appropriately marks the type of that disciple’s imperfection by the number five of its petitions. There are five bodily senses, just as there are seven gifts of the Spirit. Thus that number suits those who are still, as it were, carnal and inferior to spiritual persons.

I think there can be no doubt that this applies to that one disciple who is known not to have been present with the apostles when the Lord delivered the New Testament to them on the mountain—a discourse into which, as we have said, He inserted the prayer itself, which that disciple had not yet heard. And when he says, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John [taught] his disciples,” by mentioning John, who was in every respect less than Christ and more imperfect, he indicates the imperfection of his own understanding as well.

It is also established that the Law, which consists of five books and was given to a carnal people, led more by the senses than by reason and desiring bodily rather than spiritual goods, is often represented by John. It was therefore not incongruous that one who asked Christ for such instruction in prayer as John had given should receive a less perfect prayer than the apostles received. Because of this imperfection in him, the holy Fathers rightly provided that the more perfect form written by Matthew should instead come into use and be frequently used in the Church’s [Col. 0337C] offices.

Who, then, can state what reason there was for retaining all Matthew’s other words yet changing this one alone—saying “daily” in place of “supersubstantial”—if indeed anyone can state it adequately? For the term “daily” does not seem to express the excellence of this bread as “supersubstantial” does; and it seems no slight presumption to correct an apostle’s words, and to make one prayer out of two evangelists in such a way that neither seems sufficient by himself, and to utter it as neither the Lord spoke it nor any evangelist wrote it. This is especially so since, in all other things read in the Church from their writings, their words remain unmixed, however they may differ in completeness or incompleteness.

If, therefore, anyone accuses me of innovation in this matter, let him consider whether the person more deserving of accusation is not the one who presumed to compose one new prayer from two prayers anciently written—one to be called not so much evangelical as his own. Finally, the Greeks’ discrimination—whose authority, as blessed Ambrose says, is greater—has adopted into customary use Matthew’s prayer alone, for the reasons, I think, stated above, saying: τὸν ἄρτον ἡμῶν, τὸν ἐπιούσιον, that is, “our supersubstantial bread.” Although Luke wrote in Greek and Matthew in Hebrew, the Greeks nevertheless determined to use more frequently the older and more perfect prayer in a foreign language, and to follow a translation rather than the text in their own language. [Col. 0338A]

Thus, unless I am mistaken, I seem to be liable to accusation for antiquity rather than novelty, both on grounds of reason and the authority of antiquity; and I am less to be judged presumptuous, since in this matter I follow above all the Lord, the apostles, and the manifest provision of the Greeks. For there can be no doubt that the apostles habitually used the prayer delivered to them by the Lord and first written down by an apostle in precisely those words in which they had received it from the Lord and in which the apostle had recorded it. For who would not judge that those who live in common, and thereby especially follow apostolic life, ought above all to adhere also to the apostles’ teaching?

Finally, when the Lord delivered this prayer either in Matthew’s words or in Luke’s, and commanded that it be said as He delivered it, who does not see that those who say it as it was never delivered by Him nor written by anyone are no moderately presumptuous? How great is the presumption, in this prayer, to follow no written text and retain no command of the Lord—indeed, to dare to correct both the written text and the Lord Himself, if such presumption can perhaps be called correction! Yet I command no one, and persuade no one, to follow me in this and depart from common use. Let each abound in his own understanding. Yet whoever he may be should consider that practice is not to be preferred to reason, nor custom to truth. Both secular laws and the teachings of the holy Fathers have been especially determined to commend this to us.

Code, book VIII, chapter 1: “The authority of long-established custom and usage is not slight; yet it does not prevail so absolutely by its own force as either to overcome reason or the law.” Augustine, book IV, *On Baptism*: “Those who are overcome by reason vainly object custom to us, as though custom were greater than truth, or as though in spiritual matters one should not follow what has been revealed for the better by the Holy Spirit. This is plainly true: reason and truth must be preferred to custom.” Gregory VII, to Wimund, bishop of Aversa: “If perhaps you object custom, it must be observed that the Lord says: ‘I am,’ he says, ‘the truth’ (John 14:6); he does not say: ‘I am custom.’”

Blessed Gregory also, writing to Augustine, bishop of the English, concerning the diverse customs of churches, leaves it to his prudence in divine offices or the celebration of Mass to choose from the various practices of others whatever he decides upon, and not to follow even the mother Church of Rome itself so much in such matters as what he judges ought to be maintained: “Your brotherhood knows the custom of the Roman Church, in which it remembers that it was reared; but it pleases me that, whether in the Roman, Gallican, or any other Church, you have found anything that may better please almighty God, you should carefully choose it and instill it into the Church of the English—still new in the faith—as a chief ordinance, gathering it from many churches. For things are not to be loved for the sake of places, but places for the sake of good things. Therefore choose from each and every Church what is devout, religious, [Col. 0339A] and right; and, having collected these as it were into a bundle, establish them as a custom in the minds of the English.”

But if in such matters we too may choose from the customs of churches, our choice does not seem blameworthy: it imitates in this point also the judgment of the Greeks, from whom we have received much teaching, so that the authority of custom is not lacking to such manifest reason. We see that you yourselves adhere so strongly to this reasoning, and are so vehement in it, that you dare to maintain and defend it in the divine offices against the custom of all churches.

For you, as though newly arisen and taking great delight in novelty, have instituted among yourselves, by certain new decrees, a different manner of performing the divine office, contrary to every custom of clerics and monks long observed and still continuing; yet you do not think yourselves to be accused on this account. If this novelty or singularity of yours departs from the antiquity of others—which you believe to agree especially with reason and with the tenor of the Rule—you do not care how greatly others may be astonished or murmur about it, provided you obey what you think is reason.

To mention a few matters, with your leave: you have rejected the customary hymns and introduced certain ones unheard among us, unknown to nearly all churches, and less adequate. Thus throughout the entire year, in vigils both of weekdays and festivals, you are content with one and the same hymn, whereas the Church uses different hymns according to the diversity of weekdays or festivals, just as it does different psalms and other things known to belong to these; and manifest reason requires this. Thus those who hear you chant always the same hymn on the Nativity, Easter, Pentecost, and other solemnities—namely, *Aeterne rerum conditor* (“Eternal Creator of all things”)—are struck dumb with utter amazement; they are moved not so much to admiration as to ridicule.

You have altogether forbidden among yourselves the prayers which are everywhere said in the Church after the supplication and the Lord’s Prayer, and those called the intercessions of the saints, as though either the world had less need of your prayers or you had less need of the saints’ intercessions. And, what is remarkable, though you establish all your oratories in memory of the Lord’s Mother, you make no commemoration of her there, any more than [Col. 0339D] of the other saints. You have excluded from among yourselves almost the whole observance of processions. You do not omit the Alleluia in Septuagesima according to the custom of the common Church, but retain it until Lent. The Creed called the Apostles’ Creed, which from ancient times is regularly recited by clerics and monks alike at Prime and Compline, has been removed from your practice; yet you have decreed that the Creed of Athanasius be recited only on Sundays.

You chant the *Gloria* with the responsories of the vigils only on the days of the Lord’s burial; you have entirely abolished the ancient [Col. 0340A] custom. On those days you have instituted the saying of the invitatory and hymn, with only three lessons and responsories with the *Gloria*, contrary to all Church custom and, as is said, to reason. For since this three-day period is observed in mourning as the Lord’s funeral, and since the vigils of these days are commonly called Tenebrae because the lights are extinguished there to express this grief, it seems by no means a little remarkable that the invitatory, the hymn, or the *Gloria*—which are rather voices of joy—should be sung there.

Although all these things arouse great astonishment in everyone—namely, why this novelty of yours should be preferred among you to the practice of the whole Church—you nevertheless do not on that account depart from your institution or heed what others murmur, because you are confident that you act reasonably. The institution of your Rule compels you to make a new work out of an old one, as Jerome recalls of himself. For the Apostle forbids not novelties of expression, but only those that are profane and contrary to faith. Otherwise we should not prefer the New Law to the Old, and, after the canonical Scriptures, should reject—after the manner of heretics—the many terms concerning the faith which have necessarily been devised.

For the refutation of a new heresy the new word ὁμοούσιον (*homoousion*, “of one substance”) was devised; nor are the terms *Trinity* and *person* inserted in the canonical Scriptures. Finally, who is unaware of the diverse and innumerable customs of churches in the divine offices, even among clerics themselves? Certainly the city of Rome itself does not observe the ancient custom of the Roman See; only the Lateran Church, mother of all, preserves the ancient office, while none of her daughter churches follows her in this. Nor does even the basilica of the Roman palace. The metropolitan church of Milan differs from all others so greatly in such matters that not even one of her suffragan churches imitates its mother’s observance. Likewise Lyons, the first see of Gaul, alone persists in its own office.

Though so great a variety has arisen in these matters, whenever one thing after another has been newly instituted, no charge of novelty arises, because there has been no opposition to the faith. This variety in divine worship provides a certain delight because, as Cicero observes, sameness in everything is the mother of satiety. Therefore He who willed to be proclaimed in every kind of language also decreed to be worshipped by diverse forms of office. [Col. 0340D] And since He composed the aforesaid prayer in different forms and commanded prayer in either form, how shall we fulfill His command if we presume to subtract a word and never utter it in the form in which He Himself spoke it?

Finally, to satisfy everyone, let each now, as I said above, abound in his own understanding; let him say it as he wishes and vary Christ’s words as he pleases. But I shall preserve them unchanged, so far as I can, just as I preserve their meaning.

## LETTER XI. Of Peter Abelard.—Against those who attempt, on the authority of the presbyter Bede, to argue that Dionysius the Areopagite was Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, rather than bishop of Athens.

[Col. 0341]

[Col. 0341A] To his most beloved father ADAM, by God’s grace abbot of the monastery of the most glorious martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, whose bodies rest there; and likewise to his dearest brothers and fellow monks: PETER, a monk in habit, a sinner in life, wishes you grace and peace, as the Apostle says, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

The error of one person often entangles many; and persons prone to evil are more easily drawn into falsehood by one person than into truth by many. I say this because many are accustomed to set against the truth which we maintain concerning Dionysius the Areopagite the authority of Bede alone, setting aside weightier authorities that favor us, whether through malice or perhaps ignorance. For Bede declares that Dionysius the Areopagite was bishop [Col. 0341B] of Corinth, whereas others, whose authority is far more substantial, maintain that he was rather bishop of Athens and prove by their assertions that Dionysius the Areopagite was altogether one person and Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, another.

Let us therefore set down the words of each and then consider whether they are not merely different but mutually opposed and wholly contradictory. If we find this, let us judge the authorities themselves, so that, since they cannot all be preserved, the one supported by lesser dignity may be placed in jeopardy.

Thus it is written of this matter in *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 23, in these words: “At last we must come to the commemoration of blessed Dionysius, bishop of the Church of Corinth, whose learning and grace in the word of God benefited not only the peoples whom he had undertaken to govern, but also those far away, to whom by letters he made his presence available. There survives, finally, his letter to the Lacedaemonians concerning the Catholic faith, as well as another to the Athenians, in which he invites and urges the elders to belief in the Gospel. In that same letter he indicates that Dionysius the Areopagite, who, instructed by the apostle Paul, believed in Christ according to what is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, was the first to be ordained bishop at Athens by that Apostle.”

Jerome too—that outstanding doctor of the Church, I mean—records the same matter in his book *On Illustrious Men*: “Dionysius, bishop of the Church of Corinth, possessed such eloquence and industry that he instructed by letters not only the peoples of his own city and province, but also those of other provinces and cities. Among these letters is one to the Lacedaemonians, one to the Athenians,” etc. And shortly afterward: “He flourished under the emperors Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus.”

Now let us set down Bede’s own words. In his exposition of the Acts [Col. 0342A] of the Apostles, namely at the place where it is said, “among whom also was Dionysius the Areopagite” (Acts 17:34), he says: “This is the Dionysius who, once ordained to the episcopate, gloriously governed the Church of Corinth and left many volumes of his own composition concerning matters useful to the Church, which remain to this day, taking his surname from the place over which he presided. For the Areopagus is the council of Athens, deriving its name from Mars; indeed Mars is called Ἄρης in Greek, and a hill πάγος.”

Having therefore introduced the authorities, as we proposed, let us consider, as we promised, their difference or contradiction. The two authorities cited above, which agree with each other, seem wholly contrary to Bede’s authority. For from them it is plainly demonstrated that Dionysius the Areopagite was one person and Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, another. According to the *Ecclesiastical History*, Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, is said to have written about Dionysius the Areopagite; and Dionysius the Areopagite is there identified as bishop of Athens.

No less clearly, from Jerome’s words, does this man appear to be different from the other, since Jerome says that Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, flourished under Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius. Dionysius the Areopagite, however, who was converted by Paul’s preaching, plainly lived in the time of Christ and the apostles and was already so much an adult that he is known to have had at that time a wife, Damaris, who is mentioned along with him in Acts. Hence it is there written that “certain men, joining themselves to [Col. 0342C] Paul, believed, among whom were Dionysius the Areopagite, and a woman named Damaris, and others with them” (Acts 17:34).

From the time of the Emperor Tiberius, under whom the Lord suffered, to the times of the aforesaid emperors, under whom Dionysius of Corinth is said to have flourished, chronologists calculate more than one hundred and sixty years—so that the life of the aforesaid man could in no way have sufficed for so great a span. For it is written in the Psalms: “And if [they are] eighty years in the strong, their further part is toil and sorrow” (Ps. 89:10 [Vulgate]). From this it is clearly inferred that Dionysius the Areopagite was one person and Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, another.

Thus, by the opinions of the aforesaid authors, [Col. 0342D] we refute Bede’s view, especially since their authority is far weightier and because the word ought rather to stand in the mouth of two than of one. For it is certain that Bede and the other ecclesiastical writers have recourse to the *Ecclesiastical History* as the first and greatest foundation of ecclesiastical events. What, then, do you think Bede could answer if you showed him that the writings whose authorities he frequently invokes stand against him? Nothing, surely, more fittingly than that verse of the wise man:

> No one will agree with a man who disagrees with himself.

Lest anyone take it heavily or recoil violently from the fact that Bede is sometimes deceived and has uttered certain things by his own spirit rather than the divine Spirit—merely because the Latin Church especially uses his expositions—let him call to mind the prophet Nathan, who was deceived concerning the building of the Temple; likewise the pernicious dissimulation of the Prince of the Apostles, corrected by his fellow apostle Paul, “because,” he says, “he was blameworthy” (Gal. 2:11); and also the venerable teacher Augustine, who was not ashamed voluntarily to correct his own errors and to revise nearly all his writings. Let him reflect as well on Elijah’s proverb: “For we are not better than our fathers.” Then, indeed, when he has recalled the errors of so great men, he will cease to marvel at Bede’s error.

For, as blessed Gregory states in the first homily on Ezekiel, the Holy Spirit sometimes withdraws Himself from the minds of the faithful in order to preserve humility and permits them to fall into error, so that they may recognize how useless they remain when the Holy Spirit departs. Even when He presides over the minds of saints, He reveals some things in such a way as to conceal others. We need not be greatly troubled if we concede that saints sometimes erred in histories or in matters that do not touch the peril of the Catholic faith, when Augustine can plainly be convicted by Jerome of having erred in the history of the seventh psalm, in whose title one reads, “For the words of Chusi, son of Jemini,” as being wholly without knowledge of Hebrew truth.

Yet if anyone relies upon Bede’s authority, it may perhaps be permissible, in order to satisfy everyone, to say that at this point Bede followed the opinion of others rather than established his own judgment. For we often refer what saints write to the opinion of others rather than to their own judgment, so that we may preserve the authorities of the saints unharmed. Thus let us say in this place also that Bede introduced the judgment of those who, deceived by the equivocation of the name, believed Dionysius the Areopagite and Dionysius of Corinth to be the same person.

For we see that even blessed Ambrose departed so far at one point from historical truth through an equivocation of the name that he asserted that James, the brother of John, whom the Lord took apart with his brother John and Peter at His Transfiguration, was that James who first ascended the [Col. 0344A] sacerdotal throne. This must, however, be understood of another James, the one called the Lord’s brother and first ordained to the Church of Jerusalem; it is he who must be understood to have first ascended the sacerdotal throne in this sense.

If, then, so great a teacher was permitted to depart from historical truth in his exposition of the Gospel through the equivocation of the name James, what wonder if the equivocation of the name Dionysius deceived Bede also, or very many others—especially in that exposition of Acts which Bede himself certainly revised afterward? In the little preface to that revision, to summarize his words briefly, he begins thus: “We know that the outstanding teacher Augustine made books of *Retractions* concerning certain of his own smaller works. We too were pleased to imitate his industry; thus, after the exposition of the Acts of the Apostles which we composed several years ago, we now prepare for the same volume a short booklet of Retractions, chiefly for the purpose of adding what was insufficiently said and correcting what seemed to have been said otherwise than it ought.”

In that same exposition Bede frequently introduced the verses of Aratus, whose errors we know in some respects; for Jerome plainly shows in the aforesaid book *On Illustrious Men* that Aratus erred concerning the very day on which Peter and Paul suffered. Aratus and Bede, relying on Aratus’s authority, take that day to be the same only in the yearly recurrence of the date, whereas Jerome declares that Peter and Paul suffered on precisely the same day, in the fourteenth year of Nero. [Col. 0344C]

Finally, that we may wholly settle this dispute of differing opinions by the most peaceable conclusion: perhaps we can easily both maintain Bede to be truthful and understand nothing as merely opinion, if we suppose that there were two Dionysii, bishops of Corinth. In that case one of the Dionysii, bishops of Corinth, would be identical with Dionysius the Areopagite, of whom Bede writes; he would have presided as bishop at Athens and Corinth at different times and afterwards have been ordained apostle of Gaul by Saint Clement. The other Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, would be the Dionysius of whom the *Ecclesiastical History* and Jerome speak. Thus, I think, the entire controversy can be resolved.

The sum of all that we have proposed for resolving the matter is therefore this: either we must concede that Bede was deceived; or that he presented to us the opinion of others; or that there were two bishops of Corinth. Farewell, beloved in the Lord.

## LETTER XII. Of Peter Abelard.—Against a certain regular canon who disparaged the monastic order and preferred his own to it.

[Col. 0343]

[Col. 0343D] By the report of many, it has reached our ears that you have repeatedly and seriously disparaged our order—that is, the monastic order—in the presence of many people. [Col. 0344D] We believe that you have presumed to do so for no other reason than that, by humbling ours, you might endeavor to exalt the clerics of your own profession, whom you call regular canons. We are astonished, if this is so; but we should be even more astonished if it is not so, since we can suspect no other cause.

You say, as people say, that our order is far inferior to yours and that monks fall greatly short of the dignity of clerics. First, in this matter, we wish to ask you what dignity you mean: dignity of precedence among human beings, or of religious devotion before God. If it is the latter, this is surely the truest dignity, which especially commends us to God, adorns us with virtues, and makes us correspondingly more glorious in heaven the humbler we are considered on earth.

But by what reason or authority clerics can claim this dignity for themselves—say, if you can; or add why you cannot. For who does not know, as daily experience teaches us, that even those clerics who excel in higher rank choose monastic life when they endeavor perfectly to correct what they have done wrongly in clerical life? Though they may pass from the clerical state to monasticism, they are in no way permitted to return from monasticism to the clerical state. Or, when ecclesiastical persons are sometimes chosen from monasteries because of their excellence in religious devotion and set over clerical offices, the monastic habit itself possesses such greater dignity that, once assumed, it ought not to be laid aside; for its sake not only secular dress but even clerical dress must be discarded.

What also is the reason why monks, when they are often made bishops, are set over clerics or assigned to whatever ecclesiastical offices? Why, conversely, are abbots not made from clerics in monasteries, or why do they not undertake the care of monastic offices? Why, I ask—why, I entreat you—unless because it is judged utterly unfitting that one of a more lax life should be placed over the governance of a life for whose sake even that former life must be despised and, as we have said, corrected?

Why also do you yourselves, and the whole Church, say in the supplication of the litanies: “All holy monks and hermits; all holy virgins; all holy widows and continent persons, pray for us,” and not, “All holy clerics,” or “holy priests,” or “holy bishops”? Surely because these names designate office rather than religious devotion, whereas the former designate religious devotion.

Why also is no mention made of your class, as there is of monks and virgins, in those hymns for the feast of All Saints in which both you and others seek the saints’ intercessions? For thus it is written:

> Choir of holy virgins,  
> And of all monks,  
> Together with all the saints,  
> Make us companions of Christ.

Likewise:

> May the intercessions of monks,  
> And all the citizens of heaven,  
> Grant the prayers of the suppliants,
And ask for the reward of life. Yet I hear that you are accustomed to raise against us that saying too of our Jerome: “If a monk falls, a priest will pray for him; but for the fall of a priest, who will pray?” [Col. 0346A] Certainly you could say this on whatever grounds only if monks could in no way happen to be priests. But when he says, “a monk is a priest,” he thereby distinguishes from the designation of priest a monk who is not a priest. Thus when we say “king and soldier,” or “bishop and priest,” or “priest and deacon,” although kings too are soldiers, bishops priests, and priests deacons, we understand a soldier who is not a king, a priest who is not a bishop, and an ordinary deacon. Likewise, when he says, “A priest will pray for him,” he means that special prayer of the Mass which belongs to the priest, not that prayer which is available to every righteous person. Commending this generally, the Apostle says: “For the persistent prayer of a righteous person avails much” [Col. 0346B] (James 5:16). For the more righteous anyone is, the more he deserves to be heard by Him who weighs deeds rather than words, and considers life rather than speech.

How greatly the same doctor prefers the monastic life to your own in respect of its perfection, he plainly indicates in writing these words to the monk Heliodorus: “Interpret the name ‘monk’: it is your very name. What are you doing in a crowd, you who are alone? What then? Are all who live in a city not Christians? Is your situation not the same as that of the rest? Listen to the Lord saying: ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me’ (Matt. 19:21). But you have promised to be perfect. For when, having abandoned worldly military service, you made yourself a eunuch for the kingdom of heaven, what [Col. 0346C] else did you do but follow the perfect life?” And, after some intervening remarks: “The calling of monks,” he says, “is one thing, that of clerics another,” that is, their profession and mode of life are far removed from each other, and their purpose tends toward different ends, “as,” he says, “I have outlined above.”

Where he did this cannot be identified except where he distinguished monastic perfection from the life of believers dwelling in cities, saying: “What then? Are all who live in a city not Christians?” Writing also to Paulinus, priest and monk together, he plainly indicates that clerics ought rather to live among people than to maintain the perfection of monastic solitude:

“Since, therefore, you ask me fraternally by what path you ought to proceed, I shall speak to you with unveiled [Col. 0346D] face. If you wish to exercise the office of priest, if either the work or perhaps the honor of the episcopate delights you, live in cities and towns, and make the salvation of others the gain of your own soul. But if you wish to be what you are called, a monk—that is, one alone—what are you doing in cities, which surely are not dwellings for those who are alone, but for many? Every vocation has its own leaders. And, to come to our own case: let bishops and priests have the apostles and apostolic men as their examples; possessing their honor, let them strive to possess their merit also. But let us have as leaders of our vocation Pauls, Antonys, Julians, Hilarions, and Macariuses; and, to return to the authority of Scripture, our leader is Elijah, our [Col. 0347A] Elisha, our guides are the sons of the prophets, who lived in fields and deserts and made themselves shelters near the streams of the Jordan.”

Among these too are the sons of Rechab, who drank neither wine nor strong drink, dwelt in tents, were praised by God’s voice through Jeremiah, and to whom it was promised that from their stock there should never fail a man standing before the Lord. Nor should you admire among our leaders only Elijah, who shone so greatly among the ancient people that he deserved to be taken alive into heaven; but also John, who came in his spirit and was, as it were, another Elijah. The Lord gave so great a testimony concerning him that, because of the excellence of his life, he called him an angel on the testimony of the prophet, and set him not only above the prophets but above all human beings.

Concerning him Chrysostom also says in the twenty-second homily on the Gospels, which begins: “Of John it is said: ‘There was a man sent from God, whose name was John’ (John 1:6).” Grace is comprehended in the man, for John is interpreted “God’s grace,” because he received a greater grace. Therefore he practises philosophy in the desert and reserves himself for Christ’s coming, because he was to announce Christ. At once he is nourished in the desert, at once he grows there; he does not wish to associate with people, but in the desert he practises philosophy with angels. Consider, monks, your dignity: John, himself a monk, is the leader of your doctrine. As soon as he is born, he lives in the desert; he is nourished in solitude; he awaits Christ in solitude. At the time when Jesus was born, he was [Col. 0347C] in the desert. This Temple which we see to have been destroyed—how great were its riches, how much gold, how much silver, how many gems, how much silk, how many priests, scribes, and offices of every kind it possessed—Josephus describes. Christ is unknown in the Temple and proclaimed in the desert. Why do I say all this? To teach that John the Baptist is the leader of your doctrine.”

You have heard, brothers, the leaders alike of our vocation and yours adduced above, so that the difference between the two orders may be clear. If you rejoice that the apostles too are numbered among your leaders, and that the pontiffs of both Old and New Testament, from Aaron himself down to Annas and Caiaphas, are yours, then, I beg you, do not resent that Elijah and John, greater than these, are the leaders of our vocation. There is no doubt that John exchanged the clerical estate [Col. 0347D] for monasticism. Though he was the son of a high priest, and at that time the pontifical dignity belonged to him by hereditary right, he preferred the wilderness to the city, the monk to the pontiff, and perfection of life to ecclesiastical pre-eminence.

Jerome also, writing to the monk Rusticus, says: “I hear that you have a devout mother, a widow of many years, who nursed and educated you as a child. John the Baptist too had a holy mother and was the son of a high priest; yet he was not overcome either by his mother’s affection or by his father’s wealth, so as to live in his parents’ house at peril to his chastity. He lived in the desert and, with eyes longing for Christ, deigned to look upon nothing else. The sons of the prophets, whom [Col. 0348A] we read of as monks in the Old Testament, built themselves huts beside the streams of the Jordan; abandoning the throngs of cities, they lived on porridge and wild herbs.”

Elsewhere he also mentions them: “Elijah was a virgin, Elisha a virgin, the sons of the prophets were virgins.” What is it, I ask, brother, that when the Lord chose apostles, he did not summon John from the desert, nor, when he himself was to be baptized by him, call him back from solitude even for an hour, but came to him like the rest of humankind, and among the rest was himself baptized by a monk, as it is written: “It came to pass, when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized,” etc.? What, I ask, except that, as he said, he judged Mary’s part preferable to Martha’s part: namely, the repose of contemplation to the cares and frequent disturbances [Col. 0348B] of the world?

Occupied with precisely these cares, the Apostle groans, saying: “Apart from those things which are external, there is my daily pressure, the care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:28–29). How difficult it is, amid such occupations and troubles, to preserve purity of mind and to travel earthly paths without some contagion of dust, the Lord himself plainly taught when he resolved to wash the apostles’ feet.

The Bride in the Song of Songs carefully observes this. When the Bridegroom knocks at her door and asks her to rise from her bed and open to him, she prudently excuses herself in these words: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” (Song 5:3). For what is the bride’s bed but the repose of the contemplative soul, withdrawn from the cares and concerns of the world? In the cloister, like a bride in her bridal chamber, it gives itself to God all the more fully and is bound to him more closely by its whole desire, the farther it is removed from worldly occupations; and already, by contemplation, it is so joined to him in the secret chambers of heaven that it is one spirit with God. Thus it is written of blessed Martin: “He compelled his failing limbs to serve the spirit; reclining on his bed, he no longer deigned to look upon earth, but was wholly intent upon heaven.”

When the Bridegroom comes to the such secret repose of contemplative bed, he asks that it be opened to him [Col. 0348D] when the Christian people entreat some contemplative soul to take up their governance and thus admit them to itself. Christ himself is also said to do this in his members, since it is by his inspiration that it is done, and under his name and authority that it is sought. But the perfect soul, ardently loving its repose, refuses to rise from its bed when it flees the labor lest, by benefiting others, it suffer loss in its own perfection; and to the insistent Bridegroom it says, as has been stated: “I have taken off my tunic”—that is, I have voluntarily laid aside the outward care of worldly actions. The inner and finer garment is the under-tunic; the outer and coarser one, the tunic. Thus the former attire is rightly assigned to the contemplative life, the latter habit to the active life.

Those who shut themselves within monastic cloisters contemplate the splendor of the highest light all the more subtly and perfectly [Col. 0349A] the further they are removed from external worldly cares. The Bride refuses to put on again this occupation with cares, which Martha expends upon the needs of her neighbor and which those who preside over the people exercise, when she refuses altogether to return from contemplation to action. Therefore, adding the reason, she says: “I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” Our affections, by which we are drawn to do anything whatsoever, are like feet by which we are led. Whoever withdraws the mind from worldly cares washes these feet; for when the spirit is scattered among diverse concerns, it is difficult that it should not at least be stained with some blemishes of thought or at times yield to temptations.

The Bride, considering this, fears to set her feet down from the bed onto the ground—that is, to involve herself again in cares—because she believes that no place outside her bed is free from defilement. At last, when the Bridegroom insists, she is compelled to rise from the bed and open to him as he asked; but when she wished to hold him and embrace him as she was accustomed, it is added: “But he had turned aside and passed on” (Song 5:6). God cannot be found in public as he can in secret; nor can Martha’s anxiety, troubled about many things, attend Christ continually, nor can a mind intent on worldly cares keep quiet watch in God.

Thus the Bridegroom himself, so that we may pray more devotedly, instructs us to shut the door [Col. 0349C] of the chamber. Otherwise he turns aside and passes from us, because the less we devote ourselves to him, the more we are forsaken by him and deprived of the gifts of his grace. Even his Bride, upon passing into public life from the secrecy of the bridal chamber, finds how much she diminishes her perfection for the profit of others; and danger grows proportionately as the greater remains the account she must render for those entrusted to her.

Consider, I beg you, brother, the dignity of your order and the condition of your office, in which merit is diminished and danger threatens. See what advancement in rank amounts to where perfection of religious life is taken away; where one becomes greater before the world and lesser before God, and bears a grave loss to oneself. You rejoice that Leah, whom you have married, is fruitful; but you grieve when you look upon her bleary eyes. [Col. 0349D] Leah’s marriage was nocturnal, as though such a union were not worthy of daylight. So long as Rachel remained barren, she lived unharmed; but after she became fruitful, she was destroyed in childbirth. From this it is clearly suggested how perilously that which you glory in is undertaken, and that this glory should be called ruin or downfall rather than exaltation.

Observing their easy fall and perilous ascent in accordance with the Psalmist’s words, “You cast them down when they were lifted up” (Ps. 72:18), blessed Jerome writes in one place to the monk Heliodorus: “But if the pious blandishments of the brothers urge you also toward the same order, I shall rejoice at your ascent, but fear for your fall.” The same Jerome, [Col. 0350A] commending the security of the solitary—that is, monastic—life against Vigilantius, says: “Why, you ask, are you going to the desert? Obviously so that I may neither hear nor see you; so that I may not be disturbed by your madness or endure your wars; lest the eye of a harlot capture me, lest a most beautiful form lead me to unlawful embraces. You will answer: This is not fighting but fleeing. Stand in the battle-line; armed, resist your adversaries, so that after conquering you may be crowned. I confess my weakness: I do not wish to fight in the hope of victory, lest at some time I lose the victory. If I flee, I have avoided the sword; if I stand, I must either conquer or fall. Why must I abandon what is certain and pursue what is uncertain? Death must be avoided either by shield or by feet. You who fight may be overcome and may conquer; when I have fled, I [Col. 0350B] do not conquer by what I flee, but flee in order not to be conquered. There is no security in sleeping beside a serpent. It may happen that it does not bite me; nevertheless, it may happen that it bites me at some time.”

The same writer says to Oceanus, on the death of Fabiola: “Let a religious person beware of living where it is necessary to perish or conquer every day. For it is safer to be unable to perish than not to perish while near danger.” The great philosopher of morals Seneca holds this same opinion, and, advising his Lucilius to philosophize thus, says in the fifty-third of the letters he wrote to him:

“We ought to choose a place healthy not only for the body but also for character. We ought to act so as to flee as far as possible from the incitements of vices. The mind must be hardened and drawn far away from the enticements of pleasures. [Col. 0350C] One winter-quarter undid Hannibal; the comforts of Campania enervated that man unconquered by snows and the Alps. He conquered by arms; he was conquered by vices. We too must serve as soldiers, and in a kind of military service in which leave is never granted. Pleasures must first be subdued; as you see, they have carried off even fierce natures. If anyone considers how great a task he has undertaken, he will know that nothing must be done delicately or softly.”

But perhaps you will answer these counsels of both the holy Fathers and the philosophers by saying that it is indeed dangerous to undertake ecclesiastical administration and exceedingly difficult to labor in it as one ought; but certainly [Col. 0350D] the rewards are greater in proportion as the difficulty imposed by this labor is greater. To this I first reply with Cicero: “If something is laborious, it is not immediately glorious.” Otherwise, in the Church of God those who are entangled in the daily troubles and continual anxieties of marriage would be preferred to those who lead a celibate life, are less burdened by worldly care, and on this account devote themselves to God more freely and purely, as persons who have attained the repose of the bed.

Finally, if you exalt as increased in merit those who, confident in their virtues, choose to endure rather than flee the conflicts of temptations and the enticements of the world, consider whether those who have vowed continence should be advised to preserve that virtue in brothels or wherever frequent fornications [Col. 0351A] occur.

> **[Note: Col. 0351D. Something seems to be missing.]**

Consider whether they should voluntarily expose themselves to dangers, paying more heed to angels than to human beings, and with such security about themselves presume to test God. Why are clerics also forbidden to have women living in their household, except such female relatives concerning whom no suspicion of impropriety can arise? Your own chief teacher, as you say, Augustine, resolved so completely to avoid even these that he would not permit even his most holy sister to live with him, saying: “Those who are with my sister are not my sisters.”

Why too do you yourselves, Regular Canons—as you have recently named yourselves, just as you have recently arisen—enclose your cloisters with a great circuit of walls and remain, in the manner of monks, separated from the enticements and temptations [Col. 0351B] of the world? Therefore, if, as you yourselves teach and as is evident to everyone, human weakness should rather be protected from dangers than voluntarily exposed to them, then surely it is prudent to avoid all temptations so far as we can, especially if we choose a life which has greater merit and is less exposed to temptation. This is shown both by the authority of the Fathers and by clear examples from reality.

It is agreed that the Lord preferred the contemplative life and its repose to the tumultuous activity of believers, and it is certain that Mary’s part, which he called the better, is preferred to Martha’s part. For although Martha refreshed the Lord, Mary was more happily refreshed by the Lord, and the Lord ministered a refreshment far better than Martha’s. [Col. 0351C] Martha’s service is to provide for bodily needs, dispense the word of preaching, and, by virtue of one’s particular office, care more for others than for oneself. For the shepherds of the Church, insofar as they are shepherds, ought to think not so much of their own pasture as of that of those subject to them, and in this they profit not so much themselves as others. Therefore, when the Lord appointed Peter to this office, he did not say, “Feed yourself,” but “Feed my sheep,” or “my lambs” (John 21:16), that is, instruct or strengthen them with the bread of spiritual teaching or exhortation. Of this bread of the divine word it is written elsewhere: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4).

If at this time you compare the labor and harshness of life of clerics with that of monks [Col. 0351D], this need not be examined by long disputation, since daily experience makes it plain. Compare bishops with abbots, archpriests of churches with priors of monasteries, clerics with monks; and let anyone judge which of them leads the harsher or more laborious life. If you weigh labor [Col. 0352A], you will find us far superior in merit, since you yourselves assign us no life other than that of penitents and call our cloisters not places of dignity but prisons of penance.

Blessed Jerome, distinguishing that life from the life of clerics, writes to Heliodorus on the death of Nepotianus: “If anyone, having abandoned the clerical office, gives himself over to the austerity of monks, let him be frequent in prayers, wakeful in praying, and offer tears to God, not to human beings.” Certainly, if the life of clerics were stricter, and those who preside in ecclesiastical dignity excelled also in austerity of life, monks would by no means desire the episcopate so greatly, nor would spiritual fathers invite clerics to monastic life with such concern.

Of the same kind is this support from the aforesaid doctor, exhorting a deacon: [Col. 0352B] “You say, ‘As a deacon I cannot safely leave the church. I fear that I shall incur sacrilege if I abandon the altars.’ But consider, I beg you, that it is difficult enough to fill Stephen’s place or Paul’s, to stand in angelic ministry and look down on the subject peoples from the shining garment above. A pearl is precious, but easily broken, and once broken it cannot be restored.”

Again: “When they tear a good life to pieces in cities, what will you do, brother, in the midst of them? Either you will pursue things contrary to continence, or, if you do not wish to do so, you yourself will be condemned. I pass over the various enticements by which even the most rigid minds are softened. Now I affirm this: even if things were not so, in comparison [Col. 0352C] with so great a good you ought to have abandoned lesser things. Add that you are a deacon, but the Church will not feel losses through your departure. Elijah lived in the desert. A company of prophets followed Elisha. John, the forerunner of the Lord, nourished in solitude, descended only so far as the banks of the Jordan in order to rebuke the crowds coming together, and, understanding the Pharisees to be the clerics of the Jews, to denounce them as a brood of vipers. You recently saw the deserts of Egypt; you beheld the angelic household. How many flowers are there! How the meadows bloom with spiritual gems! You saw the garlands with which the Lord is crowned.”

Again: “You will have a cell which holds you alone. Indeed, you will not be alone: an angelic throng will dwell with you. You will have as many companions as saints. You will read the Gospel; Jesus will converse with you. You will unfold the apostles or [Col. 0352D] prophets. Will you be able to have any such companion in your conversations?”

Let us at least follow little women; let the weaker sex teach us. How many women, powerful alike in wealth and nobility—I do not wish to name them, lest I seem to flatter—have abandoned their possessions and scorned their children, judging easy to do what you considered difficult out of your own fear?

## LETTER XIII. By Peter Abelard

### An invective against a certain man ignorant of dialectic, who nevertheless criticized its study and thought all its doctrines sophistries and deceptions.

[Col. 0351]

[Col. 0351D] A certain mysterious fable about a fox has been adopted [Col. 0352D] by common people as a proverb. A fox, they say, having seen cherries [Col. 0353A] on a tree, began to climb it in order to refresh himself from them. Since he could not reach them and fell back down, he said angrily: “I do not care for cherries; their taste is utterly vile.” So too certain teachers of our time, because they cannot attain the power of dialectical reasoning, curse it in such a way that they think all its doctrines sophistries and judge them deceptions rather than arguments. These blind guides of the blind, not knowing, as the Apostle says, either what they speak about or what they affirm, condemn what they do not know and accuse what they do not understand. They judge deadly a taste which they have never sampled. Whatever they do not understand, they call foolishness; whatever they cannot grasp, they consider madness.

Since we cannot refute these persons, devoid of reason, by arguments [Col. 0353B], let us at least restrain their presumption by the testimonies of Holy Scripture, upon which they profess especially to rely. Let them recognize how greatly ecclesiastical doctors commend the art they vehemently detest—namely dialectic—as supposedly opposed to sacred reading, and how necessary they judge it to Holy Scripture. Blessed Augustine dared to exalt this science with such praises that, in comparison with the other arts, he confesses that it alone knows how to make others know, as though it alone should be called a science. Hence in the second book *On Order* he says:

“The discipline of disciplines, which they call dialectic. It teaches teaching; it teaches learning. In it reason itself displays and reveals what it is and what it desires; it alone knows, [Col. 0353C] and not only wishes but is able to make others know.”

In the second book *On Christian Doctrine*, when he declares that among all arts dialectic and arithmetic are especially necessary to sacred reading—the former for resolving questions, the latter for investigating the mysteries of allegories, which we often explore in the natures of numbers—he extols dialectic all the more inasmuch as he declares it more necessary for settling every uncertainty of questions. He says:

“There remain the things which pertain not to the senses of the body but to the reasoning faculty of the mind, where the discipline of disputation and number rules.” But the discipline of disputation is of very great value for penetrating and resolving [Col. 0353D] every kind of question that occurs in Holy Scripture. Only the desire for wrangling and a certain childish display of deceiving one’s adversary must be avoided there. For there are many things called sophisms—false conclusions of arguments—and they often imitate true conclusions so closely that they deceive not only the slow-witted but even intelligent people who are insufficiently attentive. Scripture, I think, condemns this kind of deceptive conclusion in the place where it is said: “He who speaks sophistically will be hateful” (Ecclus. 37:23).

It is evident that dialectic and the sophistical art are greatly distinct from one another: the former consists in the truth of arguments, the latter in their resemblance; the latter supplies deceptive arguments, while the former resolves their fallacies and teaches [Col. 0354A] false arguments to be detected by distinguishing them from true ones. Yet both sciences, dialectic and sophistic alike, concern the discrimination of arguments. No one can be discerning in arguments unless able to distinguish false and deceptive arguments from true and fitting ones. Therefore writers on dialectic have not omitted a treatment of this art, since Aristotle himself, the leader of the Peripatetics, also taught it by writing the *Sophistical Refutations*.

For just as knowledge of evil too is necessary to a righteous person, not in order to do evil but in order to avoid evil when it is known, so mastery of sophisms cannot be lacking to the dialectician, so that he may thus guard himself against them. Nor will he be discerning in argumentative reasoning unless, knowing false and true arguments alike [Col. 0354B], he can carefully distinguish the latter from the former and judge both. Thus, as blessed Jerome attests, Solomon too strongly exhorts us to recognize false as well as true arguments. Writing against the slanders of the great orator of the city of Rome, as we now write against similar people, Jerome says among other things about that supreme wise man Solomon:

“At the beginning of Proverbs he warns us to understand sayings of prudence, subtleties of words, parables and obscure speech, sayings of the wise and riddles—things which properly belong to dialecticians and philosophers.”

For what does he understand by sayings of wisdom and subtleties of words except the distinction between true and deceptive arguments? [Col. 0354C] As we have said, these are so conjoined that no one can be discerning in them who does not know both, since knowledge of opposites is necessary for knowledge of anything at all. No one can carefully know virtues who is ignorant of vices, especially since some vices are so close to virtues that by their likeness they easily deceive many people, just as false arguments draw most people into error by their likeness to true arguments.

Thus diversity of views arises not only in dialectic but also a multiplicity of errors in the Christian faith, when verbose heretics draw many simple people into different sects by the snares of their assertions. Untrained in argumentation, they accept resemblance for truth and fallacy for reason. [Col. 0354D] Against this plague the ecclesiastical doctors themselves admonish us to exercise ourselves in disputations, so that what we do not understand in the Scriptures we may seek from the Lord not only through prayer but also by reciprocal inquiry through disputation. Hence Augustine says in his treatise *On Mercy*, when expounding the Lord’s words, “Ask and it shall be given you; seek and ye shall find; knock and it shall be opened unto you” (Matt. 7:7): “Ask by praying, seek by disputing, knock by requesting—that is, by questioning.”

We cannot refute the assaults of heretics or of any unbelievers unless we can resolve their arguments and refute their sophisms with true reasoning, so that falsehood yields to truth and dialecticians restrain sophists [Col. 0355A]; always ready, as blessed Peter admonishes, to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason concerning the hope or faith that is in us. In this disputation, when we have convicted those sophists, we shall show ourselves dialecticians and shall prove ourselves the more mindful disciples of Christ, who is Truth, the more richly we possess the truth of arguments.

Who, indeed, does not know that the art of disputation itself, by which both these and those are indiscriminately [Note: Col. 0355D. The passage is corrupt.] said to be named? For the Son of God himself, whom we call the Word, the Greeks call Λόγον (*Logon*), that is, the conception of the divine mind, or God’s wisdom, or reason. Hence Augustine, in chapter 44 of the book *Eighty-Three Questions*, says: “‘In the beginning was the Word,’ which in Greek is called λόγος (*logos*).” [Col. 0355B] The same writer, in the book *Against Five Heresies*: “‘In the beginning was the Word.’ The Greeks say it better: λόγος (*logos*). For λόγος signifies both ‘word’ and ‘reason.’” And Jerome, writing to Paulinus on the divine Scriptures: “‘In the beginning was the Word’: λόγος (*logos*) has many meanings in Greek. For it is ‘word,’ ‘reason,’ ‘calculation,’ and the cause of each thing by which the individual things that subsist do so. We rightly understand all these in Christ.”

Therefore, since the Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of the Father, is called λόγος (*logos*) in Greek, just as he is called the Father’s σοφία (*sophia*, “wisdom”), the science which is also joined to him in name, and which by a certain derivation is called *logic* from λόγος, seems especially to belong to him; and just as Christians are named from Christ, so logic properly appears [Col. 0355C] to be named from λόγος. Its lovers too are called philosophers all the more truly the truer lovers they are of that higher wisdom. When that highest wisdom of the supreme Father put on our nature in order to illumine us with the light of true wisdom and turn us from love of the world to love of himself, he made us at once Christians and true philosophers.

When he promised his disciples that power of wisdom by which they could refute the disputations of opponents, saying, “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom which your adversaries will not be able to resist” (Luke 21:15), he plainly promised them, after love of himself—which makes them rightly called philosophers—the armor of arguments by which they might become supreme [Col. 0355D] logicians in disputation. [Col. 0356A] The hymn for Pentecost, *Beata nobis gaudia* (“Blessed joys for us”), carefully distinguishes these two things—namely, his love and his teaching—by which they would become both philosophers and supreme logicians, when it says:

> That they might overflow in words,  
> And burn with charity.

For the coming of the heavenly Spirit, revealed to them in fiery tongues, bestowed especially these two things: through love, to make them philosophers; through the power of arguments, supreme logicians. Thus the Spirit was rightly displayed in the form of fire and tongues, since he bestowed upon them love and eloquence in every kind of language.

Who does not know that the Lord Jesus Christ himself frequently convicted the Jews in disputations and restrained their slanders by writing as well as by reasoning, establishing the faith not only by the power of miracles [Col. 0356B] but also greatly by the force of words? Why did he not use miracles alone to achieve these things, by which the Jews, who seek signs, would especially have been moved, unless he determined to teach us by his own example how we too should draw to faith by arguments those who seek wisdom? Distinguishing these two, the Apostle says: “For Jews ask for signs, and Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Cor. 1:22). That is, the latter are moved to faith especially by arguments, just as the former are principally moved by signs.

But since the signs of miracles have now ceased, one struggle alone remains to us against all opponents: to convince by words where we cannot do so by deeds. This is especially so because, among discerning people, arguments have greater force than miracles, concerning which it can easily be doubted whether a diabolical illusion has produced them. Thus Truth says: “False prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect” (Matt. 24:24).

“But,” you will say, “much error also intrudes into arguments, so that when argumentative reasons are offered, it is not easy to discern which should be accepted as arguments and which rejected as sophisms.” Yes, I say, this happens to those who have not acquired mastery of arguments. Lest this happen, one must devote oneself to the discipline of reasoning—that is, logic—which, as blessed Augustine observes, is highly valuable for penetrating every kind of question occurring in sacred writings. But it is certainly necessary for those teachers who, trusting that they are sufficient to resolve questions, do not evade them.

## LETTER XIV. From the Same Peter Abelard to G., Bishop of Paris

[Col. 0355]

[Col. 0355D] To G., by the grace of God bishop of the see of Paris, and at the same time to the venerable clergy of that same Church, P. offers perpetual submission of due reverence.

It was reported to us by certain of our disciples who came to us that that chosen [or: “erect,” perhaps a corrupt reading] [Col. 0356D] and ever puffed-up ancient enemy of the Catholic faith—whose detestable heresy, namely the confession, indeed the preaching, of three gods, was convicted by the Fathers at the Council of Soissons and moreover punished with exile—has vomited forth many insults and threats against me, having seen [Col. 0357A] a certain little work of ours, *On Faith in the Holy Trinity*, written especially against the aforesaid heresy by which he himself is disgraced. It was further reported to us by one of our disciples, to whom he spoke about this matter, that he was awaiting you while you were absent, in order to show you that I had inserted certain heresies into that work; and likewise to stir you against me, as he tries to stir all persons against me.

If this is so, and if he now persists in this as well, we beseech you, champions of the Lord and defenders of the sacred faith, to summon him and me at an appointed suitable place and time; and, before Catholic and discerning men whom you may provide with you, to hear what he mutters against me in my absence, and to subject to due correction either him for the imputation of so great a crime, [Col. 0357B] or me for such presumption in writing. Meanwhile I give thanks to God that, if I endure as an adversary in the faith the supreme enemy of God and destroyer of faith, I am compelled to contend for the faith in which we stand; and that, through his persecution, I now seem to be numbered among good men, since he is known always to be hostile only to good men, his life and teaching being manifest to all.

This man dared to concoct a defiant letter against that distinguished herald of Christ, Robert of Arbrissel; and he burned with such insults against that great doctor of the Church, Anselm, [Col. 0358A] Archbishop of Canterbury, that at the command of the king of England his shameless obstinacy was disgracefully expelled from England, and he then scarcely escaped with his life. He wishes him to share in his disgrace, so that he may console his own disgrace by the disgrace of good men. He hates nothing but what is good, because he cannot endure to be good himself. On account of his arrogance—[read perhaps: “intemperance”]—he was driven with the utmost dishonour from both kingdoms in which he had lived, namely those of the English and the French; and even in the church of Saint Martin, of which he is said to be a canon to its shame, he has, they say, never observed his usual custom without being beaten by the canons.

[Col. 0358B] I considered it superfluous to identify him by name, since the singular notoriety of his unbelief and manner of life makes him especially conspicuous. As he is a pseudo-dialectician, so also is he a pseudo-Christian. Since in his dialectic he thinks that no thing has parts, he shamelessly perverts the divine text so that, where the Lord is said to have eaten “part of a broiled fish,” he is forced to understand not a part of the thing, but a part of the expression “broiled fish.” Therefore do not wonder if one accustomed to set his mouth against heaven rages upon earth; if one who persecutes the Lord disparages His members; and if one spares no one who cannot spare even himself. Farewell.

[Col. 0357]

## LETTER XV. Roscelin’s Letter to P. Abelard

(Most recently edited by J. A. Schmeller, assistant librarian at Munich, *Proceedings of the First Class of the Royal Bavarian Academy of Sciences*, vol. V, part III.)

## NOTICE

While examining manuscript codices of the Royal Library at Munich, acquired from the former Benedictbeuern library, we came upon, in a small thirteenth-century volume now numbered 4643, among other treatises of very different subjects, a rather lengthy letter. Lacking both superscription and subscription, it indicates neither to whom nor by whom it was sent. Yet its wording proves that it was addressed to Peter Abelard. For a long time we remained uncertain from which contemporary—and indeed adversary—of this most celebrated man it had proceeded, until, examining his works, we found a certain letter by him (the twenty-first in the Paris edition of 1616). Since it extraordinarily illuminates the following letter, we rightly set it before it here.

“G., by the grace of God bishop of the see of Paris,” etc. Let the reader consult the preceding letter.

Those especially learned in literary antiquity, and particularly in French antiquity, may determine, by comparing this letter with the following one, whether it can be attributed to any author other than Roscelin of Compiègne, that notorious former standard-bearer of the philosophical sect of the Nominalists.

If our opinion finds favour, perhaps they too will judge that this sole monument, hitherto known, of a man most famous in his own age is not to be despised. But since we have neither the capacity nor leisure to dwell upon the controversies and heroes of ancient scholastic philosophy, it seemed necessary now to make available for examination by more learned persons the letter itself, plain and unvarnished, as we extracted it from manuscripts whose reading is in part not altogether easy; without repeating here what we mentioned concerning it in the proceedings of our Academy (*Gelehrte Anzeigen*, 1847, no. 253).

Roscelin, once the leader of the Nominalists in philosophy, to Peter Abelard: a letter hitherto unpublished.

[Col. 0357C] If you had tasted, even slightly, the sweetness of the Christian religion which you displayed in your outward bearing, you would certainly not, forgetful of your order and profession, and forgetful of the many and great benefits which from boyhood until youth I bestowed upon you under the name and in the office of a master, [Col. 0358C] have burst forth so violently into malicious words against my innocence as to wound brotherly peace with the sword of your tongue, according to the saying: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5); nor would you have despised the most health-giving and, in practice, easiest commandments of our Saviour.

[Col. 0359A] For when Truth says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone; but if he does not listen to you, bring witnesses; and if he does not listen even then, tell the Church” (Matt. 18:15), you trampled underfoot the first two commands in a sudden frenzy of anger, leapt improperly to the third, and sent to the illustrious and pre-eminent church of Saint Martin at Tours letters overflowing with detraction against me and reeking most foully from the vessels of your own uncleanness. In them, having portrayed my person with the many stains of disgrace as though with the varied colour of leprosy, you fell into an insult even against that most holy Church itself, when, your foot slipping from the path of decency, you called it a “pit.”

For in sacred speech a pit is always understood in an evil sense: “That he might dig a pit before my face” (Ps. 56:7); “a pit for [Col. 0359B] my soul” (Jer. 18:20); “If a blind man gives guidance to a blind man, both fall into a pit” (Matt. 15:14); and “He who prepares a pit for his neighbour falls into it first” (Ecclus. 26:29). You ought not, therefore, to have compared to a pit that most holy Church which, by gratuitous compassion, received me—unworthy, sinful, and, to confess the truth, “the reproach of men and the despised of the people.” Rather, you ought to have compared it to Him whose imitator it thereby became in deed: He who makes His sun rise upon good and evil and rains upon just and unjust; who, because of the exceeding love He bore toward sinners, descended from heaven to earth; who, dwelling among us, received sinners and ate with them; and who also descended for sinners as far as those places of hell where sinners were tormented, in order to release them from their torments.

[Col. 0359C] But it is no wonder that you rage shamefully in speech against the Church, since by the character of your life you so vigorously oppose the life of the holy Church. Yet we have resolved to forgive your presumption, because you do this not from reflection but from the immensity of your grief; and as the bodily loss for which you grieve so deeply is irrecoverable, so the grief which you have inflicted upon me is inconsolable. But you must greatly fear divine justice, lest, just as the tail with which you formerly stung indiscriminately while you could do so was deservedly taken from you on account of your uncleanness, so also the tongue with which you now sting may be taken away. For formerly, by stinging with your tail, you bore the likeness of a bee; now, by stinging with your tongue, you bear the image of a serpent.

[Col. 0359D] Of such persons it is said in the Psalm: “They sharpened their tongues like a serpent; the poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. 139:4). But lest we seem to grieve excessively over the insult done to us and now to wish to avenge ourselves by speaking against you, let us turn to your letter and show what in it must be conceded and what refuted. The beginning of your letter concerns my uncleanness and an insult to the church of Saint Martin. I grieve for the Church, but I rejoice concerning myself, because I recognize in truth that I am such as you portray me in writing. For you said that I am marked by every foulness of life. Since this is so, I embrace this assertion of yours as truth with, as it were, certain arms of charity, and in your words I behold my entire self as in a mirror. But God is able to raise up children of Abraham from these stones.

[Col. 0360A] I do not wish to justify myself, because if I seek my own glory, my glory is nothing. Far be it from my heart to turn aside into words of malice, “to make excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4). But as for the three further charges—that I have been convicted of the gravest heresy, made infamous, and now expelled from the whole world—I refute them in every way and declare them false on the testimony of the Churches of Soissons and Reims. For if at any time I slipped in speech or departed from the truth, I did not obstinately defend either an error of expression or an assertion of falsehood; rather, always readier to learn than to teach, I prepared my mind for correction. For he is not a heretic who, though he errs, nevertheless does not defend his error.

[Col. 0360B] Hence blessed Augustine says: “Men are heretics for no other reason than because, not rightly understanding the holy Scriptures, they obstinately defend their own opinions against their truth.” And to Vincent Victor: “Far be it from you to suppose that you have departed from the Catholic faith, since that very disposition of readiness and expectation for correction was Catholic.” Therefore, since I have never defended either my own error or another’s, it is beyond doubt that I have never been a heretic.

But because, as though with a vomit of speech from an unclean spirit, you spew me forth as infamous and condemned in a council, I shall prove both assertions utterly false by the testimony of the aforesaid Churches, among and under which I was born, raised, and taught, when I come shortly to deal with you at Saint-Denis, of whose monks you appear to be one—though you flee. Do not fear, however, that our arrival will be concealed from you: I shall announce it to you through your abbot in truth, and there I shall wait for you as long as you wish.

[Col. 0360C] But if you prove disobedient to your abbot—which you do not hesitate to do—I shall find you wherever in the world you hide, having sought you out. How, moreover, can what you said—that I have been expelled from the whole world—stand, when Rome, which is the head of the world, gladly receives me, eagerly welcomes hearing me, and, having heard me, most willingly complies? Nor are the Church of Tours, or that of Loches—where you, the least of your master’s disciples, sat so long at my feet—or the Church of Besançon, in which places I am a canon, outside the world. All of them honour and cherish me, and gladly receive with eagerness to learn what I say. From the manifest falsehood of this statement, therefore, the remaining inventions of your letter must fairly be judged false as well.

[Col. 0360D] Yet I grieve not a little that you called me a persecutor of good men. Although I am not good, I have always honoured every good person with the honour due to them. Those whom you bring forward as examples—namely Lord Anselm of Canterbury and Robert, men of good life and good repute—I have never persecuted, although certain things they said and did appear blameworthy. Nor is this surprising, “for now we see through a glass, in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12). For these two wise and religious men are not of greater merit or wisdom than Peter, prince of the apostles and glorious martyr, and blessed Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, most gracious teacher and most glorious martyr.
