[Col. 0361A] Rejoicing in Cyprian’s praises, blessed Jerome says: “Blessed Cyprian, like a most pure spring, proceeds sweetly and calmly; and, though wholly engaged in exhorting to the virtues, amid the straits of persecution he did not abandon the divine Scriptures. Hence, most fittingly, concerning the martyrs: ‘Everyone who loves Christ will read your writings, Doctor Cyprian.’” Yet this man, raised so high by the proclamation of saints, thought differently about the baptism of heretics—and left this view in his own writings—than truth later disclosed.

[Col. 0361B] Hence blessed Augustine says in his book *On Baptism*: “It seemed to certain distinguished men, among whom blessed Cyprian especially stood out, that the baptism of Christ did not exist among heretics or schismatics. Therefore, rendering such reverence and honour as I can to Cyprian, the peaceable bishop and glorious martyr, I nevertheless dare to say that he thought differently concerning the baptism of schismatics and heretics from what I have afterwards set forth—not on my own judgment, but on that of the universal Church, confirmed by the authority of a plenary council.”

But Peter, prince of the apostles, because he compelled Gentiles coming to baptism to be circumcised, was deservedly rebuked first by the apostle Paul and afterwards by the holy Fathers. For the Apostle says: “When Cephas was at Antioch, and was not walking rightly in the truth of the Gospel, I openly resisted him to his face, because he was blameworthy” (Gal. 2:11). Hence blessed Augustine says: “Reverencing Peter, for his merit, as the first of the apostles and an outstanding martyr, I nevertheless dare to say that he acted wrongly in compelling Gentiles to Judaize.”

[Col. 0361C] Hence blessed Augustine says: “Those who call themselves Nazarene Christians are born heretics from that error in which Peter, having gone astray, was recalled by Paul.” Again: “When Peter faltered on the sea; when he carnally recalled the Lord from His Passion; when he denied the Lord three times during the Passion; when he fell into superstitious dissimulation—we see that he obtained pardon and reached the glory of martyrdom.” What wonder, then, if those whom you assert that I have unjustly persecuted sometimes acted less prudently in certain words or deeds, since they were in no way superior to the two holy doctors and martyrs mentioned above?

[Col. 0361D] For I saw Lord Robert receive women fleeing from their husbands, while the husbands themselves protested; and, when the bishop of Angers commanded him to return them, I saw him obstinately and disobediently keep them until death. Consider how irrational this deed is. If a wife denies her husband the marital due, and he is thereby compelled to commit adultery, the guilt of the one compelling is greater than that of the one acting. Therefore the woman who leaves her husband is guilty of adultery when he subsequently sins of necessity. How, then, will the man who keeps and protects her be innocent and not a participant in the same crime? For she would by no means do this unless she found someone to retain her.

[Col. 0362A] Hear blessed Augustine speaking more harshly: “If a woman who has been left is compelled through incontinence to unite herself with another, that is, to commit adultery—although she does not do so, he nevertheless, so far as lies in him, has compelled her to do it; and therefore God will impute this sin to him, even if she remains chaste.” If, therefore, the husband who leaves his wife is guilty of a crime even when she does not subsequently sin, how much more so if she sins?

Hear also blessed Gregory speaking to a certain abbot concerning a married man, whom he judged ought to be received only if his wife likewise wished to convert. For since, by the union of marriage, the body of both has become one, it is unfitting for one part to be converted and the other to remain in the world. Therefore either both must depart or both remain.

But what shall I say about Lord Anselm the archbishop, whom both holiness of life honours and singularity of learning elevates above the ordinary measure of humanity? In the book entitled *Why God Became Man*, he says that God could not save human beings otherwise than as He did—that is, unless He became man and suffered all those things which He suffered. The sayings of the holy doctors, by whose teaching the Church shines, vigorously oppose his opinion.

[Col. 0362B] Saint Leo says: “Though many other means were available to Him for redeeming the human race, He chose especially this way: to employ not the power of might but the reason of justice.” Hear blessed Augustine, *On the Trinity*: “Why, after setting aside innumerable ways by which the Almighty might have used means to redeem us, was His death especially chosen?” Again: “Those who say, ‘Did God lack another means by which He could free human beings from the misery of this mortality, so that He wished His only-begotten Son to become man and suffer death?’—it is too little to refute them merely by saying that this method, by which He deigned to free us through the Mediator, is good. Rather, we must also show that no other method was lacking to God, to whose power all things are subject; but that no other method was, or ought to have been, more fitting for healing our misery.”

[Col. 0362C] Again: “God could certainly have taken a human being from elsewhere to be Mediator between God and human beings, not from the race of that Adam—just as He created the first man himself not from the race of anyone. He could, either in that manner or by whatever other manner He wished, have created another man by whom the victor over the first man might be conquered. But He judged it better to assume humanity from the very one who had been conquered.” The same author, in *On the Christian Conflict*: “Foolish are those who say: ‘Why could not the wisdom of God otherwise free human beings, unless [Col. 0362D] He assumed humanity and was born of a woman?’ To them we reply: He certainly could; but if He had acted otherwise, your foolishness would likewise have been displeased.”

If, then, among those whom you declaimed that I was shamelessly persecuting we find anything contrary to Holy Scripture, why are you surprised that something in your own statements could be reproved, when it is plain that you have made no effort whatever in the study of Holy Scripture? The writings of the holy Fathers Ambrose, Augustine, and Isidore by no means agree with that singularity which you attributed to the divine substance. I have therefore taken care to set down these collected passages, so that what I must maintain may be supported not by my own authority but by divine authority.

Thus blessed Ambrose, in his work *On the Faith*, addressed to the Emperor Gratian, speaks as follows:

> “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He says this lest a distinction of power be understood.

Likewise:

> “They are one with the Father—one in eternity, one in divinity. For the Father is not himself the Son; what is one is not confused, nor is what is undifferentiated multiple. For if the heart and soul of all believers were one; if everyone who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit; if husband and wife are one flesh; if all human beings, so far as nature is concerned, are of one substance—much more are Father and Son one in divinity, where there is no difference either of substance or of will.”

Likewise:

> “Equality is neither diverse nor singular, because no one is equal to himself alone.”

Likewise:

> “God is a name common to Father and Son.”  
> “[Col. 0363B] Likewise: They strive, in Sabellian impiety, to maintain that the Father was incarnate.”  
> “What is of one substance cannot be separated, although it is not a matter of singularity but of unity. Singularity detracts either from the Father, or from the Son, or from the Holy Spirit.”  
> “The Father and Son are not one person, but one thing.”  
> “One dignity, one glory: whatever diminution you suppose in one is a diminution common to both.”

Augustine, in *On the Trinity*:

> “Whoever thinks it belongs to God’s power that he should beget himself errs all the more grievously, because not only is God himself not such, but no spiritual or bodily creature is such. For no soul is a thing which begets itself.”

Likewise:

> “Occupied with the creature and with the assumed condition, you do not understand the equality which I have with the Father.”

Likewise:

> “[Col. 0363C] We appropriately say that he who appeared in the flesh was sent, while he who did not appear sent him.”

Likewise:

> “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son—as though he had said: no one will see the Father in the judgment, but all will see the Son, so that he may also be seen by the ungodly.”

Likewise:

> “Three were seen, and none of them appeared greater than the others in form, age, or power.”

Likewise:

> “When the question is asked, ‘What are the three?’ human intellect suffers a very great poverty indeed. Yet ‘three persons’ has been said, lest we be altogether silent.”

Likewise:

> “The Son can in no way be called the Trinity.”

Likewise:

> “It may universally be said that the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, and that the Father is holy and the Son is holy. Therefore, if Father and Son are Holy Spirit, the Trinity may be called Holy Spirit. Yet that Holy Spirit who is understood not as the Trinity but as in the Trinity, when he is properly called Holy Spirit, is spoken of relatively and referred to Father and Son, because the Holy Spirit is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son; but this relation is not apparent in the name itself.”

Likewise:

> “[Col. 0363D] Our Greek writers have said: one essence, three substances; the Latins: one substance or essence, three persons.”

Likewise:

> “The necessity of speaking and disputing permitted the use of ‘three persons,’ not because Scripture says so, but because it does not contradict it.”

Likewise:

> “When human poverty endeavoured by speech to express what it holds concerning the Lord God, it feared to say ‘three essences,’ lest some diversity be understood in that supreme equality.”

Likewise:

> “Why do we not call these three one person, as we call them one essence and one God, but say three persons? Yet we do not say three essences and three gods, except when we wish that even one word should serve to signify that which is understood as Trinity, lest we be altogether silent to one asking, ‘What are the three?’”

Likewise:

> “Let him say one essence in such a way that he does not suppose one greater or better than another or in any respect different; yet not in such a way that the Father himself is the Son and the Holy Spirit.”

Likewise:

> “[Col. 0364A] There is no interval of unlikeness, such that one is understood to be greater or a little less than another; nor is there such a distinction as contains anything unequal.”

Likewise:

> “We say three persons or three substances, not in order that any diversity of essence be understood, but so that it may be possible to answer even with one word when it is asked, ‘What are the three?’ or ‘What are the three things?’ And the equality of essence in that Trinity is so great that not only is the Father not greater than the Son, but neither are Father and Son together greater than the Father alone.”

Likewise:

> “One God, one faith, one baptism. Although faith is one, it is not the same faith in different persons, but similar; it is not absolutely one, but one in kind. Yet on account of similarity and the absence of all difference, it is called one rather than many; for we say that two very similar men have one face.”

Likewise:

> “The Word is therefore in every respect like and equal to the Father.”

Likewise:

> “Because the Holy Spirit is common to both, he is himself properly called that which both are commonly: namely, Holy Spirit.”

Augustine, addressed to the Arian Count Pascentius:

> “[Col. 0364C] Since one Spirit and one body are spoken of for diverse things joined together, and one man is spoken of for soul and body joined together, why should one God not especially be spoken of concerning Father and Son, when they cleave to one another inseparably?”

Likewise:

> “By these names it is signified that they are referred to one another.”

Likewise Augustine, in a homily:

> “‘Let not your heart be troubled’ (John 14:1): to those who knew the Son it was said concerning the Father, ‘and you have seen him.’ For this was said because of the complete likeness which he has with the Father, so that they were said to know the Father because they knew the like Son. To this applies what was said to Philip: ‘He who sees me sees the Father also’ (ibid., v. 9), not because he himself is both Father and Son, but because Father and Son are so alike that whoever knows one knows both. For we commonly say of two very similar persons to those who have seen one of them: ‘You have seen this one; therefore you have also seen that one.’ Thus it was said, ‘He who sees me sees the Father also,’ not because he himself is Father and Son, but because the Son differs from the Father in absolutely no respect in likeness.”

Boethius, in *On the Trinity*:

> “[Col. 0364D] The cause of this unity is indistinguishability.”

Augustine, in *On the Trinity*, says:

> “God is love,” so that it is uncertain and must therefore be asked whether God the Father is love, or God the Son, or God the Holy Spirit, or God the whole Trinity.

Thus Augustine—and, so that I may speak not only of what blessed Ambrose but also of what Saint Jerome says:

> “The eyes of flesh cannot behold not only the divinity of the Father, but neither the nature of the Son nor that of the Holy Spirit.”

The same writer, in *On Christian Doctrine*:

> “[Col. 0365A] The things which we enjoy are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; and this Trinity is in a certain manner one thing.”

Likewise:

> “Among all things, those alone are to be enjoyed which we have called eternal and unchangeable.”

The same writer, in *On the Christian Conflict*:

> “Let us believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit: these are eternal and unchangeable.”

Whence John says: “There are three in heaven who bear witness: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit” (1 John 5:7).

It must indeed be understood that, in the substance of the Holy Trinity, whatever names are used do not signify one thing and another, whether as to parts or qualities; rather, they signify the substance itself alone, not divided into parts nor changed by qualities. Therefore by “person” we do not signify something other than what we signify by “substance,” although by a customary manner of speech we are accustomed to make “person” threefold and not substance, just as the Greeks are accustomed to make substance threefold. Nor should it be said that they err in the faith of the Trinity by making substance threefold, because although they speak otherwise than we do, they nevertheless believe what we believe; for, as we have said, person, substance, and essence signify precisely the same thing in God. There is diversity only in expression, unity in faith; otherwise there would no longer be a Church among the Greeks. But if they, in speaking thus, affirm one thing, I do not see why we should be lying in affirming the same.

On the diversity of the divine substance, whether through qualities or through parts, blessed Ambrose in *On the Faith* and blessed Augustine in *On the Trinity* speak thus. Ambrose:

> “[Col. 0365C] God is the name of a simple, not a conjoined or composite, substance, to which nothing accidental attaches, but which has in its own nature only what is divine.”

Augustine:

> “Whatever appears to be said of the Father according to qualities must be understood according to substance and essence.”  
> “There are four names, but one thing.”

Therefore, when we vary these names, whether speaking them in the singular or plural, we do not do this because one signifies something other than another, but solely according to the will of speakers, to whom such usage of speech has seemed fitting. For if there were different parts there, so that one were called person and another substance, perhaps there would be some reason why we should utter one in the singular and the other in the plural; as, in the case of a human being, because one part is the body and another the soul, we say one soul but many bodies, on account of the various parts of the body. But neither would one quality be signified by person and another by substance or essence, because, as we have already said, there is absolutely no quality in God.

From this abundance of Holy Scriptures, therefore, the diligent reader understands that the saints who wrote them by no means understood such a singularity in God that one sole thing, one singular substance, should be designated by those three names—lest, in thinking this of God, they fall into the Sabellian heresy. For many incongruities seem to follow from this Sabellian singularity.

Nor have I said these things in order to teach anyone, but rather so that, if I do not understand the Holy Scriptures rightly, I may learn; for in all things I am readier to learn than to teach, and prefer to hear a master rather than to be heard as a master. With Augustine speaking thus to blessed Jerome:

> “[Col. 0366A] Although it is more becoming to teach an old man than to learn, nevertheless no age is too late for me to learn.”

But what you say—that I have recognized one singular substance of the Holy Trinity—is indeed true, yet not that Sabellian singularity in which one sole thing, and not several things, is designated by those three names. Rather, it is one in which a threefold and triple substance has such unity that nowhere do any three have such unity; for no three things are so singular and so equal as those of which it is written: “In this Trinity there is nothing before or after, nothing greater or less, but the whole three persons are co-eternal with one another and coequal.”

But although the Law says that “every word shall stand in the mouth of two or three witnesses” (Deut. 19:15), let us, now that a fourth has been added to the three, add a fifth and a sixth, whose testimonies strengthen the unity of likeness and equality. Thus, lest we seem merely to shelter behind the number of witnesses and the occasion provided by distinguished men, rather than daring to join battle for the refutation of singular unity, let us [reading uncertain: *compr…emus*] it.

Speak, then, blessed Athanasius, defender of the divine substance against the Arians: speak what you think of that substance; and, as you conquered the Arians who made it diverse by grades, so also convict the Sabellians, who confuse the persons. Say:

> “[Col. 0366B] Neither confusing the persons nor separating the substance.”

He confuses the persons who calls the Father the Son and the Son the Father. This he must say who wishes those three names to signify one sole singular thing. For all the names of one and singular thing are predicated reciprocally of one another. Thus the Father was incarnate and suffered, because he himself is the Son who suffered all this; consider how much this conflicts with sound faith.

It follows: “Nor separating the substance.” It must carefully be considered whether he forbids the substance of the Holy Trinity to be separated in every respect, or only in a certain manner. For how is it not separated, if it is one in such a way that there are also several, as the Greek Church proclaims? For all several things are separated by the law of plurality, because it is written that every difference consists in the plurality of things that differ. Let us therefore investigate what difference exists in this plurality of persons according to us, but of substances according to the Greeks.

For the substance of the Father is nothing other than the Father, and the substance of the Son nothing other than the Son, just as the city of Rome is Rome, and the creature water is water. Therefore, because the Father begot the Son, the substance of the Father begot the substance of the Son. Since, then, one substance is that of the begetter and another that of the begotten, one is other than the other; for begetter and begotten are always several, not one thing, according to the aforesaid statement of blessed Augustine, in which he says that there is absolutely no thing which begets itself. That which begets is unbegotten; what is begotten is only-begotten. But unbegotten and only-begotten are several, as Augustine says in *On the Trinity*:

> “[Col. 0367A] The Son owes the very substance to the Father; that is, he has his being as substance from the Father and from his substance.”

Therefore we cannot altogether avoid making a separation in the substance of the Holy Trinity. It remains, then, that he forbids separation in a certain manner; and what manner that is he shows when he adds: “In this Trinity [there is] nothing before or after, nothing greater or less.”

For he was acting against Arius, who posited a diversity of inequality in the substance of the Holy Trinity, distinguishing Father, Son, and Holy Spirit by degrees of dignity. Therefore he says: “The whole three persons are co-eternal with one another and coequal”; for if co-eternal, there is nothing before or after; if coequal, nothing greater or less. Athanasius therefore forbids that Arian separation, against which he was writing, namely separation by a distinction of degrees; but he does not remove separation altogether when he calls them co-eternal and coequal. For if they are coequal, they are also equal; and equality is always between several things, since nothing is equal to itself, as blessed Ambrose says: “No one is equal to himself alone.” Therefore, when he places equality and co-eternity in the substance of the Holy Trinity, he surely leaves within it the separation of plurality. But by calling them co-eternal he abolishes degrees of priority and posteriority, and by calling them coequal, degrees of lesser and greater.

That he calls the substance one not singularly but by likeness and equality he clearly demonstrates when he says:

> “[Col. 0367B] One divinity, equal glory, co-eternal majesty.”

For unless, after first saying “one,” he had added “equal glory, co-eternal majesty,” we should have understood “one” in the customary sense—that is, as singular. But he wholly removes this when he says “equal glory,” and declares that he has understood “one” according to equality.

And just as we have shown that, when he spoke of the separation of substance, he did not mean every separation but only the Arian separation by distinction of degrees, so we must investigate most carefully whether, when he says, “not three eternal beings, but one eternal being,” he removes multiplicity of eternity in every respect or in a certain manner. For if he denies that they can at all be called eternal beings, he contradicts himself, since he called the three persons eternal by saying they are co-eternal. If they are co-eternal, they are eternal; how, then, are they not three eternal beings, if those three persons are eternal?

Blessed Augustine also, in *On Christian Doctrine* and *On the Christian Conflict*, calls them eternal in the plural:

> “[Col. 0367D] Among all things, therefore, those are the things to be enjoyed which we have called eternal and unchangeable.”

For he had said before:

> “The things which we enjoy are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

The same writer, in *On the Christian Conflict*:

> “We believe in the Father and Son and Holy Spirit. These are eternal and unchangeable.”

If, therefore, this writer absolutely denies that they are eternal beings, he truly conflicts both with himself and with Augustine. It must therefore be said both that they are eternal beings in the plural and, in a certain manner, that they are not. For when the Saviour called John a prophet, John denied that he was a prophet. Yet, so that neither the herald nor the preacher of truth should lie, the former denied in one way and the latter affirmed in another.

For John did not deny that he was a prophet altogether, but that he was a mere prophet, because he was more than a prophet, since he showed forth what he had foretold. Thus here too it must be said that he did not wholly deny the three eternal beings, but only in the sense in which Arius affirmed them, varying the measure of eternity among the persons. They were eternal beings in the plural, as several eternal things; and they were not eternal beings in such a way that eternity might appear varied among them. Let one who can speak better do so. I cannot do better. But neither do I obstinately defend what I say.

Speak also, holy Isidore, teacher of all the churches of Spain, and declare what you have determined should be thought concerning the substance of the Holy Trinity:

> “[Col. 0368A] The Trinity is so called because one whole is made from a certain three.”  
> “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are Trinity and unity: unity because of the communion of majesty, Trinity because of the property of the persons; alike simple, alike immutable good, and co-eternal. The Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called unbegotten. The Son alone is born from the Father. Divinity is not tripled, because, if it were tripled, we should introduce a plurality of gods. But the name ‘gods’ is used in the plural of angels and holy men because they are not equal in merit. Of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of one and equal divinity, the name is shown to be not ‘gods’ but ‘God.’ Among the Greeks the faith is stated in this manner: one *ousia*—that is, one nature or one essence—three *hypostases*, which in Latin corresponds either to ‘three persons’ or to ‘three essences.’”

You have heard that the Trinity is one because of the communion of majesty, not because of the singularity of majesty; for what is singular is in no way common, and what is common cannot be singular. Therefore, since the majesty of the Trinity is common, how can it be singular?

You have also heard that the name is applied to the Trinity in the singular because of equal divinity, lest, if it were said in the plural, inequality of divinity should be understood. But the divinity of the Trinity finds no equal divinity outside itself. Therefore within the Trinity divinity finds divinity equal to itself; yet how several equal things can be one single and unique thing, I do not see.

Therefore, so that the ship of Christian faith, running unharmed between the two rocks, may pass safely through, it must most carefully beware lest it strike upon the rock of Sabellian singularity—in which it is necessary to confess that the Father was incarnate and suffered—or incur the danger of Arian plurality, varying the substance by before and after, by greater and lesser, and introduce a plurality of gods through the enormity of diversity.

For the singular number “God” has been reserved for the Trinity alone in order that it may signify in it and within it complete equality. But it is given to human beings in the plural in order that they may be shown not to have the same merit or dignity, as: “I said, You are gods” (Ps. 81:6); and: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). Thus, although we seem to disagree about the unity of the divine substance—you, indeed, presumptuously ascribing to it the solitude of singularity through the slender effort of your little intellect, whereas I, armed with the judgments of Holy Scripture, defend a unity of likeness and equality—

nevertheless, we must agree in this: that we unanimously pray to God, who is one and three—however this should be understood—that he may illuminate in us the darkness of ignorance, wash away the stain of unbelief, pour into our minds knowledge of his truth, and, having quieted the desire for contention, grant that we may think the same thing toward one another: Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

But because you have lingered long over the fables of our alleged detraction—which you yourself shamelessly invented—as over the delights of a banquet, like one made drunken by wine, and because you have been filled, in swinish fashion, with the filth of our “detraction,” let us also in turn, not biting with the tooth of hatred nor striking with the rod of vengeance, but laughing at the barking of your letters, discuss the unheard-of novelty of your life and show to what disgrace you have deservedly sunk by your uncleanness.

Nor is there any need for us, after your fashion, to invent anything for your insult; rather, let us repeat what is known from Dan to Beersheba. For your misery is now manifest, and although the tongue may keep silent about it, the fact itself cries it aloud. I myself saw at Paris that a certain clerk named Fulbert received you as a guest in his house, honourably fed you at his table as an intimate friend and member of his household, and entrusted to you for instruction his niece, a young woman of exceptional prudence and noble disposition.

But you, not forgetful but contemptuous of that noble man and clerk, a canon also of the Church of Paris, moreover your host and lord, who provided for you freely and honourably—you spared not the virgin entrusted to you. You ought to have kept her safe as one entrusted to you and taught her as a pupil; instead, driven by the unbridled spirit of lust, you taught her not to reason but to fornicate. In this one act you became guilty of many crimes: namely, treachery and fornication, and a most vile violator of virginal modesty.

But God of vengeance—the Lord God of vengeance—acted openly, depriving you of that very part by which you had sinned so greatly. For the rich man buried in hell burned more intensely in the part in which he had sinned more greatly, when he begged that his tongue might be cooled by a drop of water.

[Col. 0369D] Therefore, tormented by pain from so shameful a wound and compelled by fear of impending death because of the foulness of your former life, you changed your habit and became as it were a monk. But hear blessed Gregory speaking of those who flee to religion from fear:

> “He who does good from fear has not wholly departed from evil, because he sins precisely in this: that he would have wished to sin, if he could have sinned with impunity.”

Hear also blessed Augustine:

> “He vainly thinks himself the conqueror of sin who does not sin from fear of death, because, though the business of desire is not outwardly carried out, that desire itself is nevertheless an enemy within. And how will he appear innocent before God who would do what is forbidden, if you remove what is feared? Therefore he is already guilty by his very will who would do what is unlawful but does not do it because he cannot do so with impunity. For, so far as he is concerned, he would prefer that justice did not exist. And if he preferred that justice did not exist, he would, if he could, bring it about that justice did not exist. How, then, is such an enemy of justice righteous? But he would be a friend of justice if he did not sin from love of justice. He who fears hell does not fear to sin, but to burn. Yet he fears to sin who hates sin as he hates hell.”

Hear the same writer:

> “[Col. 0370A] Not without reason among sinners have been established the power of the king, the right of the sword, the claws of the executioner, and the arms of the soldier. For these things are feared, and good people live more peacefully among the wicked. Yet those who do not sin through fear of such things should not be called good, because no one is good through fear of punishment but through love of justice. But let it be so: may conversion through fear avail, provided that good conduct follows.”

Let us see, then, how you have conducted yourself since your conversion. In the monastery of Saint Denis, where all things are tempered not so much by the severity of the rule as by the dispensation, according to the means of each individual, of a most wise abbot’s mercy, you could not endure to remain. You received from the brethren, under the name of obedience, a church in which to serve your own will and pleasure. When you perceived that it could not suffice for your extravagances and desires, you chose another, suited to every wish of yours, and received it from the lord abbot with the general consent of the brethren.

There, to pass over other things, having gathered from every direction a crowd of barbarians, you do not cease to teach what ought not to be taught, turning the truth of learning into trifles partly through ignorance and partly through pride—although you ought not even to have been teaching what should be taught. And the payment collected from the falsehood which you teach you do not send to your prostitute as the reward of fornication; you carry it there yourself. What, while you were able, you gave as the price of anticipated pleasure, you now give as a reward—sinning more, indeed, by rewarding past fornication than by purchasing future fornication. What you formerly enjoyed with pleasure, you still abuse by your will; but through God’s grace you cannot prevail by necessity.

Hear, therefore, the judgment of blessed Augustine:

> “[Col. 0370C] You wished something but could not do it: God records this as though you had done what you wished.”

Before God and his chosen angels I speak as witness: I have heard your fellow monks testify that, when you return late to the monastery, you shamelessly trample modesty underfoot and fly off to a prostitute, carrying to her money collected from every quarter as the price of the falsehood which you teach, and shamelessly rewarding past fornication.

Since, then, after assuming the habit, you have usurped the office of teacher by teaching lies, you have surely ceased to be a monk. For blessed Jerome, himself a monk, defining a monk, says:

> “The monk has not the office of a teacher but of a mourner: that is, one who laments the world and awaits in fear the coming of the Lord.”

Nor does the abandonment of clerical dress prove you to be a cleric; but still less are you a layman, as the display of your tonsure sufficiently proves. Therefore, if you are neither cleric nor layman nor monk, I cannot discover by what name I should classify you.

But perhaps you will falsely claim that custom permits you to be called Peter. Yet I am certain that a masculine name, if it falls away from its own sex, will refuse to signify its customary thing. Proper names, indeed, commonly lose their signification when what they signify has happened to fall away from its perfection. A house whose roof or wall has been taken away is not called a house, but an imperfect house. Therefore, with the part that makes a man removed, you should be called not Peter but an imperfect Peter.

[Col. 0372A] To the full measure of this imperfect man’s disgrace belongs the fact that on the seal with which you sealed those foul letters you yourself fashioned an image having two heads, one of a man and the other of a woman. Who, then, can doubt how passionately you still burn with love for her, when you did not blush to honour her by such a conjunction of heads?

I had intended to compose many more true and manifest things to your disgrace; but because I am proceeding against an imperfect man, I leave the work I began imperfect.

## LETTER XVI. Of Fulk, Prior of Deuil, to Peter Abelard.

[Col. 0371]

[Col. 0371B] Brother FULK, to PETER, thanks be to God, wearer of the cowl: consolation in the present and future life.

The person who thinks that he will pass through the dangers of secular life without danger seems to me no less foolish than someone who, being foolish, considers himself wise. How deeply he is entangled in the error of folly, I need not show, since it is clearer than light to the wise. Those who promise themselves that they will remain long in this changeable prosperity are ruled by Fortune. How contrary to reason such a belief is, fickle prosperity shows by its own changes. It is not human to endure in stability. And although human affairs daily decline for the worse, and the pleasant vanity of prosperity is often struck by reverses, wretched human beings—intimate friends and familiars of this age—neglect to consider the end of things; and, beguiled by however slight a prosperity, they measure with the eye of foresight how many dangers they lie under. But when adversity strikes, it either hurls them into despair or raises them to the fruit of reflection; and only then do they recognize that they are human. For those who despair and do not repent, no pardon of remission remains, either in this world or in the world to come; but “mercy shall surround those who hope in the Lord” (Ps. 37:16).

A little while ago, the glory of this world flattered you most abundantly and did not allow you to notice that you were subject to the uncertain turns of Fortune. Rome sent you her pupils to be taught; and she who once used to pour the knowledge of every art into her hearers showed you, wise as you were, to be wiser than herself by the pupils she sent. No stretches of land, no mountain summits, no hollow valleys, no road, however beset with difficult danger and robbers, held them back from hastening to you. The sea lying between, and the terrible storm of the waves, did not frighten the crowd of young Englishmen; but, despising every danger when they had heard your name, they flocked to you. Distant Britain sent its living creatures to be trained. The men of Anjou, their fierceness subdued, served you among their own people. Poitevins, Gascons, and Iberians; Normandy, Flanders, Germans, and Swabians all zealously strove without ceasing to kindle, praise, and proclaim your genius. I pass over all who inhabited the city of Paris, and those in the nearest and remotest regions of Gaul, who thirsted to be taught by you as though no learning could be found except with you. Moved by the brilliance of your intellect, the sweetness of your speech, the ease of your highly accomplished language, and likewise the subtlety of your knowledge, they hastened as though toward the clearest fountain of philosophy.

But that matter which, as they say, so cast you headlong—namely, the love of individual women and the snares of their lust, by which they capture their fornicators—I think it better to pass over than to say anything not in harmony with our order and the rule of our religious life, since speech about such things often tends to harm the good more than to help them.

Perhaps, lifted up in yourself and over yourself by this gathering of good things (although a wise man, unless he extinguishes in himself the meaning of that name, ought not to be moved by such goods of the mind), you had boiled over most vainly into pride—the beginning and pest of all evils—and, borne along by the wind of boastful display, you considered almost everyone else, even the saints who had devoted themselves to wisdom before you, inferior to yourself, as those who heard you more frequently report. [Note: [Col. 0371D] Cf. *Historia calamitatum*, middle section.]

But the condescension and goodness of almighty God, who makes the wind of pride vanish and multiplies the grace of humility, who by just judgment does not overlook anyone sick with the disease of pride and afflicted with other disorders of the soul, pitifully subdued the swelling of your mind and the haughtiness of your eyes by this kind of adversity: so that you might neither think proudly of yourself nor continue to disregard all other good persons by criticizing them, but henceforth might excel in the holiness of chastity and in praiseworthy devotion to continence.

How much this small part of your body, which by the judgment and benefit of almighty God you lost, had harmed you and did not cease to harm you as long as it remained, the diminution of your possessions teaches better than my speech can show. Whatever you could acquire by declaiming and selling your knowledge, beyond your daily food and necessary use, as I have learned by report, you did not cease to plunge into the abyss of spending on a prostitute. The greedy rapacity of prostitutes had stripped you of everything. No age has heard of a prostitute wishing to spare another, or sparing the property of her pursuers which she could take in any way whatever. Your profound poverty seems to prove this: when you first fell under these turns of Fortune, you had, it is said, nothing from so great a profit except rags.

You have indeed suffered a loss in your body in this life, and according to the vanity of the world perhaps you consider yourself—or think yourself considered—less valuable: a wholly unhappy estimate, and an appraisal utterly devoid of true reason. If you wished, alone and with diligent, frequent meditation, to seek with yourself more truly what is just and good, putting vanity aside, you would find how much benefit this mutilation of your members brings you.

First, you have escaped many sufferings by which those who have lost no such thing are frequently shaken, and to which those are by no means liable who, as physicians assert, most foolishly believe that, through deprivation of this bodily part, they have fallen away from every happiness. Next, you will now suffer no disturbance from the heat of lust and the torches of luxury—a malady which sometimes touches even saints—except through thought alone. Since the deadly flame of that conflagration has been extinguished, you must return to yourself and gather together firmly the mind which wandered through the manifold and sweet madness of luxury.

Now, free and with no lust drawing you back, you will be able to know the paths and causes of every kind of reasoning—matters which those who are carried away by various incitements of lust understand little or not at all. Add that your money, if you are permitted to possess any (for monks may not possess anything of their own without permission), will not be exposed to the vexation of those who draw it away. Henceforth you will begin to possess what shortly before was being scattered through many drainings-away.

You should also value highly the fact that, suspected by no one, you will be received most safely as a guest by every host. A husband will not fear violation of his wife or disturbance of his bed from you. You will pass through bands of elegantly adorned matrons without violating them. The choirs of virgins, shining with the flower of youth—who are accustomed by their movements to inflame even old men, now deprived of bodily heat, into the fervor of lust—you will behold securely and without sin, not fearing their approaches and snares. It is true that henceforth you will avoid without interruption the secret retreats of Sodomites, whom the truth of divine justice detests above all most shameful persons, and their foul and wicked associations—which indeed you have always hated.

And, altogether, after the emissions of this most frail frailty, I judge it a great gift of God’s grace in this order that you will not experience the nocturnal deceptions of dreams; as certain as it is that, if desire should perhaps be present, no effect will follow it. The blandishments [variant: caresses] of a wife, bodily contact—without which one cannot have a wife—and the particular care of children will not hinder you at all from pleasing God. How great a good do you think it is to be withdrawn from the dangers of sin and placed in the security of not sinning? You will therefore be able, with confidence, to avoid the leonine ferocity which prostitutes display to those first entering upon relations with them, the cunning of their serpent-like deceit, and the unrestrainedness of their enslaving luxury. What I say, you will henceforth come to know better by experience than I can explain in words.

That Origen whose lofty wisdom is everywhere proclaimed and honored, although he did not correct certain errors—yet, as blessed Jerome says, he placed the blame upon his disciple Ambrose, who had secretly published writings and brought them into the light before their time—that Origen, I say, in order to avoid every suspicion of lust, voluntarily deprived himself of this part of his body. [Note: [Col. 0373D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 7.] John and Paul, Protus and Hyacinthus, and many other glorious martyrs, crowned with glory and honor in the supercelestial realms in the presence of God, rejoice during this brief span of time that they lacked genital organs. And blessed are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven. I might perhaps offer many such examples, but let those already given suffice.

Therefore, brother, do not grieve, be distressed, or be shaken by the disturbance of this misfortune, especially since, as has been said, it brings so many fruits of usefulness, and since what has happened in this way remains forever irreparable and torn out. Let this be your continual consolation: what nature does not permit to be restored can be borne more lightly:

> “Bear also these consolations with you,” as he says  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, VI, v. 802),

because at the time of this mutilation you were not caught either violating another’s marriage-bed or in any poison of fornication. You had given your limbs to rest and sleep, and were preparing harm for no one, when, behold, the hand of impiety and a deadly weapon did not hesitate gratuitously to shed your innocent blood.

Therefore the compassionate kindness of the venerable bishop laments this wound and loss of yours—he who, as far as he could, strove to devote himself to justice. A multitude of generous canons and noble clerics laments. The citizens lament, considering this a disgrace to the city and grieving that their city was violated by the shedding of your blood. Why should I recount the lamentation of individual women, who, when they heard this, moistened their faces with tears in womanly fashion for you, their knight whom they had lost, as though each had found her husband or lover slain by the chance of war? So great, therefore, was the grief of everyone that it seems to me you ought rather to wish that you had perished than that you had preserved what has perished. A happy man does not know himself to be loved. Almost the whole city wasted away in your grief. You possess in yourself the pledge of true affection, which, had you recognized it earlier, you would, in my judgment, have considered comparable to no riches.

But perhaps you will try to answer me with that prophetic saying: “My soul refused to be comforted” (Ps. 76:3). “I cannot but grieve, touched by so disgraceful a misfortune, since this condition generally overtakes men in their old age. Soon the cheeks are stripped of the adornment of hair, the glory of the skin upon the face is drawn into wrinkles, an unseemly pallor disfigures the countenance; and those who once knew me, as soon as they see my face, will immediately know that I am mutilated in this bodily part. I shall therefore exact vengeance for my disgrace, and I shall endeavor to make known the whole weight of my injury to Roman ears; and I shall disturb, as far as I can, both the bishop and the canons, because they have contrived to reverse the first judgment against the man who had wronged me; and then at last they will understand how contrary to honor it is to depart from the rigor of justice.”

[Note: [Col. 0375D] Fulco proceeds to dissuade Abelard from going to Rome by arguments which Catholic ears could not receive without the greatest scandal, since he assails the Roman curia with such insults as heretics—indeed, the most impious persons of our age—have been accustomed to employ. We have therefore not hesitated to expunge this passage, exceedingly troublesome both to the holy Church and to our readers. (Patrologia edition.)]

[lacuna]

If you complain of vengeance, how greatly your soul thirsts for and desires it, do not immediately be bitten by grief and waste away because it has already been seen to be fulfilled in very great measure. For some of those who harmed you have been mutilated by the loss of their eyes and the cutting-off of their genitals. But he who denies that the deed was done by himself has already been driven from every possession through the removal of all his goods. Therefore do not call the canons or the bishop shedders or destroyers of your blood, for they have attended to justice as far as they could, both for your sake and for their own; rather, hear the good counsel and consolation of a true friend.

You are a monk, and you have assumed the habit of holy religion, not unwillingly but voluntarily. You are therefore no longer permitted to exact vengeance, if you wish truly to maintain and love what is shown to be contained in the meaning of this name. But if you should hate even the enemy who did this deed and do not cease hating him, let anyone bring forward whatever else he wishes: I confidently assert that you may wear Christ’s garment, but it will bring you no benefit at all. “Pursue peace with all people,” says the Apostle, “and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12:14). “Vengeance is mine,” says the Lord, “and I will repay” (Rom. 12:19). If you wish to be perfect, begin to love Christ perfectly, and you will attain even to love. Abandon threats and pouring out pompous words in vain. For you cannot accomplish what you desire.

An injury unjustly inflicted is a disgrace not to the person upon whom it is inflicted, but to the one who inflicts it. Henceforth do not grieve for the happiness you have lost, which the inconveniences of adversity always attend. If, therefore, you remain in your holy purpose to the end and do not fail, Christ will restore, in manifold and wondrous fashion, everything you have lost in the future glorification of the bodies of the blessed; and then at last the rule of the dialecticians will appear false, which says that a privation can never return to a state of possession. Farewell in the Lord.

## LETTER XVII. Peter Abelard’s Confession of Faith, to Heloise

(We possess this letter, though not entire, in Berengar of Poitiers, Abelard’s disciple, in his *Apology for His Master against St Bernard*, which appears in the Appendix.)

My sister Heloise, once dear to me in the world, now dearest in Christ: logic has made me hateful to the world. For malicious persons, who perversely pervert and whose wisdom is unto destruction, say that I am most eminent in logic but stumble not a little in Paul. While they praise the sharpness of my intellect, they take away the purity of my Christian faith. For, as it seems to me, they are brought to judgment more by prejudice than by the authority of experience.

I do not wish to be such a philosopher as to kick against Paul. I do not wish to be such an Aristotle as to be separated from Christ. For “there is no other name under heaven in which I must be saved” (Acts 4:12). I adore Christ reigning at the right hand of the Father. I embrace with the arms of faith him who, in virgin flesh assumed from the Paraclete, works gloriously by divine power.

And so that trembling anxiety and every perplexity may be expelled from the heart of your breast, hold this concerning me: I have founded my conscience upon that rock upon which Christ built his Church. I shall briefly set forth for you the meaning of that rock.

I believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: one true God by nature, who so approves the Trinity in persons that he always preserves unity in substance. I believe the Son to be equal to the Father in all things: namely, in eternity, power, will, and work. Nor do I listen to Arius, who, driven by a perverse intellect—indeed, seduced by a demonic spirit—establishes degrees in the Trinity, teaching that the Father is greater and the Son lesser, forgetful of the command of the Law: “You shall not go up by steps to my altar,” says the Law (Exod. 20:26). For he goes up by steps to God’s altar who places before and after within the Trinity.

I also testify that the Holy Spirit is consubstantial and equal in all things with the Father and the Son, since my writings frequently declare him to be designated by the name of Goodness. I condemn Sabellius, who, asserting that the Father and Son are the same person, declared that the Father suffered; whence they are called Patripassians. I also believe that the Son of God became the Son of Man, and that one person is constituted from two natures and subsists in two natures. After completing the dispensation of the humanity he had assumed, he suffered, died, rose again, ascended into heaven, and will come to judge the living and the dead.

I also affirm that in baptism all sins are remitted, and that we need grace by which both to begin and to complete the good; and that those who have fallen are restored through repentance. And what need is there to speak of the resurrection of the flesh, when I boast in vain of being a Christian if I do not believe that I shall rise again? This, therefore, is the faith in which I stand and from which I draw the firmness of hope. Safely established in it, I do not fear Scylla’s barking, I laugh at Charybdis’s whirlpool, and I do not dread the deadly songs of the Sirens. If a storm rushes upon me, I am not shaken; if winds blow through me, I am not moved. For I am founded upon the firm rock.

# PART TWO OF THE WORKS OF PETER ABELARD: SERMONS AND ASCETICAL TREATISES

## SERMONS TO THE VIRGINS OF THE PARACLETE ESTABLISHED IN ITS ORATORY

(*Works of Peter Abelard*. Paris, 1616, p. 729.—The sermon for the Nativity of the Holy Innocents [Sermon 34] was supplied to us by a manuscript preserved in the monastery of St Mary of the Hermits at Einsiedeln, which the most reverend Abbot HENRY very graciously shared with us. The manuscript is parchment, small folio, apparently written in the twelfth century. It contains Abelard’s *Sic et Non* and five sermons: On the Nativity of the Lord; On St Stephen; On St John; On the Holy Innocents; On the Epiphany. Mr Victor COUSIN had already made public the sermon for the Nativity of the Innocents from this same manuscript in his *Works of Abelard*, p. 592.—The sermon in praise of St Stephen the protomartyr [Sermon 32], which is found among Abelard’s letters in the 1616 edition but in a less complete form [p. 263], occupies a more suitable place among the sermons and appears in an expanded text from the manuscript mentioned above. The rest are given in their preferable order. Patrologia edition.)

## LETTER TO HELOISE

Having recently completed at your request a certain little book of hymns or sequences, venerable and beloved sister Heloise in Christ, I have also, according to your petition, made haste—somewhat contrary to my custom—to write for you and for your spiritual daughters gathered in our oratory several small works of sermons. For I am more given to reading than to preaching; I pursue the plainness of exposition, not a composition of eloquence; the meaning of the text, not the ornament of rhetoric. And perhaps speech that is less pure than polished will be all the more suited to the understanding of the simple in proportion as it is plainer. According to the character of the hearers, the very rusticity of uncultivated discourse will be a kind of elegant ornament, and the ease with which little ones understand will be a kind of seasoning of flavor.

In writing or arranging these works, keeping the order of the feasts, I began with the very beginning of our redemption. Farewell in the Lord, his handmaid: once dear to me in the world, now dearest in Christ; then my wife in the flesh, now my sister in the spirit and companion in the profession of the sacred purpose.

## FIRST SERMON: ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

The beginning of our redemption is the conception today of the Lord’s mother. A woman conceived the Lord, so that the creature might bear the Creator. This is indeed the common salvation of humankind, but the special glory of women. The first Adam, formed from earth, was not born from a woman; rather, woman was made from his rib. The second Adam, maker and redeemer of the first and of all, decreed to assume the form of our sex from a woman, so that grace might exist in both sexes, just as guilt had preceded in both, and so that the same natures through which the wound had been inflicted might bring the remedy of healing, and from the very source whence the wound was dealt the poultice might wondrously be prepared. The devil was the author of the wound; the angel, the minister of healing.

Concerning him it is now said: “The angel Gabriel was sent from God,” etc. (Luke 1:26). The serpent was sent by the devil; this one is said to have been sent by God, so that, from the very opening face of the reading, those wounded may be raised by hope of divine grace at the announcement of salvation. The angel is fittingly identified by name when he is called Gabriel, so that, since the same one is reported to have been sent to Mary whom the Evangelist had said above was sent to Zachariah, this promise too may be believed destined for fulfillment, just as the earlier one is already known to have been fulfilled. Hence the Angel himself later adduces Zachariah’s wife as evidence for Mary: “And behold,” he says, “Elizabeth your kinswoman...” etc. (ibid., 36).

The Evangelist carefully describes the place to which he is sent when he says: “To a city of Galilee, whose name was Nazareth” (ibid., 26). A city belongs not to a few but to many. And this healing is to be not of one sick person but of the whole human race. Since it concerns not individual human beings, but only those who will not remain in their own sluggishness but will migrate from the valley of vices to the mountain of virtues, this city is rightly said to be in Galilee. It is also fittingly named Nazareth, that is, “flower,” where today that flower was conceived from the rod, of whom Isaiah foretold: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1). He also says of himself: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1).

Therefore, in order that this rod might bring forth this flower, the angel is sent to the Virgin herself, to prepare her for this and, as it were, to cultivate her for fruitfulness with the hoe of his announcement. Hence, after the place to which he is sent, the Evangelist adds the person to whom he discharges this embassy: “To a virgin,” he says, “betrothed” (Luke 1:26). He puts “virgin” before “betrothed,” not so much in temporal as in dignitary order.

But what, I ask, is the dignity of being a virgin in the flesh if she had already been corrupted in mind through consent? For neither a betrothal nor a marriage can be contracted except by the equal consent of two persons; nor otherwise would she herself be called Joseph’s spouse or wife by the Evangelist. What then was this consent? Was it consent to carnal union, so that the Virgin had already consented to that by which she would lose the flower of her dignity? Far be this from pious minds: that she who is believed to have first offered the gift of virginity to God should be thought led into that consent into which so many virgins chose loss of life rather than enter, and thus follow the Lamb wherever he goes—not only by remaining virgins, but even after becoming wives.

What consent is to be understood here in both bridegroom and virgin, the following words, unless I am mistaken, indicate. With respect to the bridegroom, his very name is not omitted: “To a man whose name was Joseph” (ibid.). Joseph, interpreted as “increase,” suggests to us nothing other than great perfection of virtues in him. As blessed Jerome records, he clearly remained a virgin, like his betrothed. [Note: [Col. 0381] *On the Perpetual Virginity of St Mary against Helvidius*, *Patrologia*, vol. XXIII, col. 185. Editor.] If he had been diminished from that perfection of virginity through consent to carnal desire, it would in no way have been fitting for the Evangelist to mention that he was called Joseph.

When he later discovered the Virgin’s conception, it is not surprising that he bore it all the more grievously in proportion as he grieved that he had been more deceived—he whom his betrothed had drawn into an agreement of continence. The Virgin herself, when she later says of herself, “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” (Luke 1:34), plainly indicates that she had in no way consented to carnal use or joined herself to a man in desire. For why would she say, “How shall this be, because I do not know a man?” if she intended in her mind to unite herself with a man? Even if she had not yet united herself with him, she could certainly unite herself afterward; thus it would not have been surprising if she too, like Elizabeth, conceived from a husband by the gift of divine grace.

She also knew that the integrity of her virginity was not concealed even from people. Why then would she ask in apparent astonishment how this could happen, when she did not know a man? If, I say, she referred this “knowing of a man” to sexual union, as it is said of Adam and certain others that they knew their wives, what else does she mean by “I have not known a man” except: “I have never consented to unite myself carnally with anyone”? In what, then, had Joseph consented when she was betrothed to him, except that they should preserve the virtue of chastity by equal consent?

For she saw that she was being compelled by her parents toward marriage, especially on account of the Law’s ordinance, which placed under a curse all who did not leave offspring in Israel. The virgin knew Joseph to be a virgin; she had him as an intimate friend because of his love of chastity and closeness of kinship. Therefore she chose as bridegroom the man whom she trusted to draw into her agreement, so that, if she were compelled to receive another, she might not be able to preserve what she had vowed to God.

When it is likewise said of her, “The angel entered to her” (Luke 1:28), her holy purpose is carefully described: she is found not out in the streets with worldly women, but with the door of her chamber shut, devoutly beseeching and praying to God, so that she might keep inviolate, both for herself and for her bridegroom, the vow of continence she had made. Thus, in her very prayers, she immediately deserved to receive consolation concerning her petition and to obtain reassurance.

Concerning this secret place of her chamber, as though it were a divine oracle, and concerning the holy occupation in which she was engaged there, blessed Ambrose writes in Book II of *On Virginity*:

> “At the angel’s very entrance she was found at home, in the inner room, without a companion, lest anyone interrupt her concentration or make noise. For she did not desire female companions, since she possessed good thoughts. Indeed, she seemed less alone to herself when she was alone. For how was she alone, who had so many books with her, so many archangels, so many prophets? Finally, Gabriel found the Virgin where he was accustomed to visit her; and Mary was alarmed at the angel as at a man whose appearance had changed, though, when she heard his name, she recognized him as not unknown. Thus she was a stranger to a man, who was not a stranger to an angel; so that you may recognize religious ears and modest eyes. Finally, when greeted, she was silent; when addressed, she answered. But she who had at first faltered in feeling afterward promised obedience.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0383] Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book II, chapter 2, no. 10, *Patrologia*, vol. XVI.]

Behold the occupation not so much of one betrothed as of a virgin: not one preparing herself for marriage, but one wholly devoted to God; not absorbed in the cares of the world, but entirely attentive to sacred reading; not seeking the consolation of a bridegroom, but deserving converse with an angel.

Attend, virgins, who have chosen not a husband but God as bridegroom, and have taken from Mary the pattern of your sacred profession. Though betrothed to a man, she sought not a man in public but God in secret. She did not turn her eyes toward the world but lifted them to heaven. She did not lend her ears to wedding songs but refreshed her mind with the nourishment of sacred reading. From this it is clear how true is what we have said: that her mind never inclined to marriage, because she certainly undertook no care for it.

Therefore, when greeted by the angel, she whose life was not carnal but angelic deserved to hear: “Hail, full of grace” (Luke 1:28). By grace we mean a freely given gift, that is, a divine benefit bestowed above merits. Hence the Apostle: “But if it is by works, it is no longer by grace; otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (Rom. 11:6). It is clear that every one of the faithful has received some grace beyond his or her merits. But to Mary is ascribed not a share in grace but fullness, so that she may be shown to have received as much as is promised to the weakness of human nature. How this could be so if she had already been drawn into consent to carnal desire admits of no explanation.

The source from which she obtained this abundance of grace is added when it is said: “The Lord is with you.” “With you,” he says, rather than “in you.” For he who was already everywhere through the presence of his divinity was preparing to unite himself to the Virgin’s flesh through assumption of humanity, so that he might be with you—that is, might become one person with your flesh.

“Blessed are you among women.” Does not Mary’s blessing also overflow to men? Was she not herself from the seed of Abraham, and did Christ not descend through her, in which seed the blessing of all nations had been promised? What, I ask, does “among women” mean, rather than among all men and women alike?

Again I say, attend to this, virgins, and rejoice that this blessing of Mary overflows especially to you. For we find few men who imitate Christ in the virtue of virginity. This grace of Mary has many followers in you, whose virtue is more pleasing in proportion as the sex is weaker. For virtue is perfected in weakness. And what is blessing except the multiplication of divine grace? Therefore Mary is said to be blessed among women rather than among men because the grace of her virginal purpose was to be multiplied chiefly among women by her imitation, as the Psalmist also foretold: “The queen stood at your right hand,” etc. (Ps. 45:10). And again: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; they shall be brought into the temple of the king” (ibid., 15). “After her,” he says, “they shall be brought into the temple of the king,” because by imitation of this supreme queen countless virgins are to be consecrated in the true temple of God.

“When she heard this, she was troubled” (Luke 1:29). It is said that she was troubled by the words of the speaker, who greeted her with great praise, not that she looked upon the one who spoke. For, with her eyes fixed upon reading, or fixed on the ground in prayer, she was wholly intent upon that toward which her mind reached and remained unmoved; nor did she care for a human sight, she who directed herself only to the divine.

Why then was she troubled? For different reasons on every side: because she shunned the company of a man, and because she gave all her effort to reading or prayer, whose uninterrupted practice she found it grievous to have hindered. “And she considered,” it says, “what sort of greeting this might be” (ibid.). That is, she considered from what intention it proceeded: whether these were words of flattery or truth; with what boldness or by what entrance he dared to disturb the secrecy of her chamber.

The angel, unable to bear her being so troubled, said: “Do not fear, Mary” (ibid.). He did not say, “Do not be troubled,” but, “Do not be afflicted by excessive anxiety”: do not either despair of obtaining what you have vowed, or incur the Law’s curse as though guilty. When he says here “Mary,” he first calls her by name, so that, as one familiar with her, he may raise her up by greater consolation.

Why she need not fear—that is, need not be anxious concerning her petition—he adds when he says: “You have found grace with God.” That is, above all merits you have become pleasing and acceptable to him.

How, then, she may both avoid the curse of the law by remaining a virgin and preserve uncorrupted the vow of her purpose, he plainly explains by saying that she is alike to give birth and to remain a virgin. She is to give birth, I say, not merely to a man, but also to the Savior of humankind—that is, Jesus. He carefully describes the greatness of the excellence of this virginal birth, saying: “He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Most High.” As though he openly said: Consider in this very thing your incomparable grace, your singular glory; see that he who is called the Son of God is also called yours. “And the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of David his father”: that is, he will accomplish in him what was promised to David in his type, as David himself declares, saying: “I have sworn unto David my servant: I will prepare thy holy one for ever; and I will build thy throne from generation to generation” (Ps. 88:4).

The house of Jacob, in which he is promised to reign for ever, is the Church of the Gentiles, which, in the time of the former things and through former grace, displaced the Synagogue and took its blessing away. This kingdom receives no end, because it does not fail even with the present life; and this is so much truer in heaven as it is happier.

But Mary said: “How shall this be?” As though she said: Great indeed is the promise, and it surpasses incomparably not only the virtue of a woman, but every human dignity. In what manner, then, and in what order shall so great a thing be fulfilled? “For I know not a man,” she says. As though she said: It seems far removed from my purpose that I should have a child, I who have resolved to remain a virgin. And this is, as we have already recalled above, for her not to know a man: never to have consented to anyone in carnal intercourse.

She had indeed read the promise made to Abraham concerning Christ, as she herself afterward declares: “He hath received Israel his servant, remembering his mercy, as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed” (Luke 1:54). Therefore she did not doubt this promise at all, but asked about the manner in which it was to be fulfilled: whether through union with a man, without the love of sin—as would have occurred in paradise had humanity not sinned—or with integrity alike of body and mind preserved, as her purpose had been.

The angel, moreover, rightly kept silent about the manner of conception when he promised her a son, until she herself, having disclosed the purpose of her vow, asked him about it—lest, since we had heard that she was betrothed, she should be thought to have entered this union through concupiscence.

“The Holy Spirit shall come upon thee”: that is, you shall be enriched by a higher gift of God, so that you may be at once virgin and mother [Col. 0385C]. The Spirit comes into many souls of the faithful through some gift of divine grace; but he came upon Mary when he bestowed upon her grace higher and more excellent than that granted to all others. What, indeed, is the Spirit of God except the love or gift of divine goodness, when something is bestowed upon us beyond our merits?

Therefore, since this mystery of the Incarnation was accomplished wholly through the working of divine goodness rather than through the customary order of nature, it is rightly ascribed to the Holy Spirit: “And the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee.” The power of God is understood to be the Son—that is, his coeternal wisdom—according to the Apostle’s saying: “But we preach Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23). For as God made all things in his wisdom, so also through it he restored what had been lost, beginning this restoration from the beginning of our redemption, as we have recalled above.

Thus the Son is called the power of God, being his arm or strength, sufficient to accomplish all that he has ordained. This power overshadowed the Virgin when, in her, it covered the radiance of his divinity with the veil of flesh; and thus divinity came forth to us, as it were, shod, so that God might appear visible in our nature while remaining invisible in his own.

This overshadowing of divine majesty was prefigured in the electrum whose appearance the prophet Ezekiel saw from the midst of fire. Electrum is a metal compounded of gold and silver. In this mixture the silver gains in brightness, while the gold is moderated from its own splendor [Col. 0386A]. This electrum, then, is understood to be Christ himself, in whose one person the two natures of divinity and humanity are so united to one another that the lower nature, represented by silver, makes itself visible, while the splendor of divine majesty, figured by gold and overshadowed by the veil of flesh, remains invisible. This electrum in fire is God-man in the Passion.

> “Therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.”

As though he openly said: Through this union of the Word of God with the living human being, not only will the Word itself be called the Son of God, but the very man assumed by the Word will also be called the Son of God. Observe that he says “shall be called,” concerning the man rather than the Word, to whom being belongs properly.

The Evangelist carefully considered this when he said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). For he did not say, “The Word was called,” but “was.” For being belongs properly to divine immutability, as God himself says to Moses: “Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: He who is hath sent me unto you” (Exod. 3:14). “He who is,” he says—that is, he who abides immutably; for nothing possesses true being except what is immutable. Wherever change occurs, being and non-being occur together. Therefore being belongs properly to him who wholly knows no non-being. Hence it was rightly said, “The Word was,” rather than “was called.”

For designation belongs not to eternity but to time; the imposition of names pertains not to nature but to human choice [Col. 0386C]. Therefore, when he spoke of the man assumed by the Word, whose nature is not eternal and who is Son of God not by nature but by grace and union with the Word, it was said “shall be called” rather than “shall be.”

Yet if we say that the whole person, existing in two natures, was born of the Virgin according to the body derived from her, and that this entire person—not humanity alone—is called Son of God, this is not incongruous. For a shoot of one nature grafted into a trunk gives its own name to the whole tree: if an oak is grafted onto a quince-tree, the whole tree will be called oak, not quince, being named from the nobler part that bears fruit, just as it is known from its fruit.

A certain grafting of divinity into humanity was accomplished today, and, from two natures agreeing in one person, there was made, as it were, one tree [Col. 0386D]. For it is written of Wisdom, which is understood to be the Word of God, that “she is a tree of life to them that lay hold on her” (Prov. 3:18). What, moreover, was humanity except a cursed tree, and formerly a kind of tree of death? Understand, then, the tree of life as grafted into the tree of death, when this grafting was made in the Virgin as in good soil.

The Spirit himself, coming upon her, was the agent of this grafting, as though foreseeing that day which seems most suitable for grafting, according to the common opinion of those skilled in the art, who have learned this through long experience. Hence they confidently maintain that scarcely, or never, is any grafting performed on this day unsuccessful [Col. 0387A].

“And behold Elisabeth.” Lest any doubt arise concerning the possibility of the Virgin’s childbirth, as though impossible because it did not follow the usual course of nature, the conception of Elizabeth is recalled. Though she was barren through both old age and sterility, she obtained by grace what she could not have by nature. Therefore the angel appropriately mentions both her old age and her barrenness: “For no word shall be impossible with God.”

The word of God here is divine utterance itself, described by blessed Augustine as a divine disposition having no noisy and passing sound, but power abiding perpetually. Therefore no word of God is impossible to him, since whatever he ordains to do cannot be hindered by any circumstance [Col. 0387B].

But Mary said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord.” What is this that you say, Lady? What is this answer from one who is to become queen not only of humankind but also of angels? You do not say: “Behold the Mother of the Lord,” or even, “the beloved of God,” or “one chosen by him,” although you have been uniquely chosen beforehand. The more the angelic promise raises you to higher things, the more the supreme virtue of humility lowers you to the least.

Where, I ask, is that honorable name which your only-begotten Son bestowed upon his faithful when he said: “I will not now call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15)? He deigned to provide for the honor of his own even in their very name; you, on the contrary, are not ashamed to ascribe to yourself the condition of a servant. Thus, Lady, the examples of humility are to be drawn especially from you, to which Scripture exhorts us when it says: “The greater thou art, humble thyself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20).

By this virtue of humility above all you deserved to ascend to the height of this promise. In accordance with this rule of your discipline, that virgin Agatha, your imitator and one of the number of the prudent, said: “I am the handmaid of Christ; therefore I show myself to be a servant person.” And again: “This is the highest nobility, in which the servitude of Christ is proved.”

Yet, if I am not mistaken, your own ancestor had introduced you to this rule and pattern of humility, saying: “Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline thine ear,” etc. (4 Kings 19:16). For when he had first announced that you would become his daughter because of the height of this promise, saying: “The queen stood at thy right hand,” etc. (Ps. 44:10), he immediately admonished you to preserve humility, adding: “Hearken, O daughter,” etc.

As though he openly said: Great, daughter, is the incomparable good that you should become the spiritual bride of the heavenly King, so that, like queen of heaven, you may stand beside him at his united side and surpass all others in garments of gold—that is, in a sound and incorrupt body, inwardly adorned with every diversity of virtues. But because such praises are great for female nature and such glory exceeds human frailty, hear what is said and see by understanding: so that, when these things are announced to you, you may not despair of their fulfillment; and receive with a humble ear the height of so great a promise, as though forgetting your people and your father’s house [Col. 0388A]—that is, neither taking pride in your Jewish lineage and royal stock nor attending to what you possess by nature, but to what is bestowed upon you by grace. And thus that heavenly King will desire your beauty, he who always resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.
