Lady, not forgetful of this exhortation, you said: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord”; and again: “Because he hath regarded the lowliness of his handmaid.” From this humility you indeed deserved to obtain what follows: “Be it done unto me according to thy word.” That is: may I, remaining whole, conceive the very Word of God according to the word of your promise, and give birth incorrupt. Amen.

## SERMON II. ON THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD.

*(We have emended the text with the aid of the Einsiedeln manuscript.)*

[Col. 0388B] Let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult, because today the King of heaven has marked every land with the glory of his birth, that from it he might gather heavenly citizens through whom he might restore the losses of heaven. Therefore the angels, rejoicing over the repair of their own fall and our advancement, immediately on the very day of this nativity announced both their own and our common joy, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (Luke 2:14).

As though they openly confess: Today he is born whom the heavenly spirits must praise spiritually, and through whom, when the strong man armed has been bound—indeed, cast down—those who believe and hope in him obtain true peace. Today God is born on earth, so that human beings may be born in heaven. Today he is born of the Virgin Mother, he who before the ages was begotten of God the Father.

For the Father himself speaks to him: “From the womb before Lucifer I begot thee” (Ps. 109:3); that is, from my own substance you were begotten before Lucifer was created. Both his births are wonderful; both his generations ineffable. Thus Isaiah’s saying may fittingly be referred alike to both—to his temporal generation from his mother and his eternal generation from his Father: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

In the type of this birth Melchizedek, king and priest, went before him, whom the Apostle records as having been without father and without mother, that is, without genealogy. Not that he lacked a father or mother, but because Scripture does not teach his genealogy, nor can it be recalled by us [Col. 0388D]. So Christ, king of all through the power of his divinity and made priest of humankind through the sacrifice of his assumed humanity, is said to be without father or mother—not because he does not have both, but because no one can discover how he has either. Thus, as there the testimony of Scripture fails, so here the capacity of human reason fails; and both his births are more wonderful in proportion as they are more ineffable: the one from the Father without a mother, the other from the mother without a father.

Concerning the wonderful birth which he has from his mother, Jeremiah prophesied: “The Lord hath created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). As though he openly said: He who, as Scripture says, made the things that are to come has already, by the most high counsel of his dispensation, predestined the future creation of a certain man to be new and unlike all others.

When he adds not “in the earth” but “upon the earth,” he shows that this creation is not only above human merits but also higher and more excellent than all other earthly creations [Col. 0389A]. What is new in this creation he subsequently explains, saying: “A woman shall encompass a man.” That is: a woman alone, from her own substance and without admixture of male seed, will provide the body with which divinity may clothe itself, taking on within her the form of a man.

Thus the womb of the Virgin, like a circle whole on every side, is said to encompass within itself the man conceived there, not introduced from without through intercourse. That entire bodily garment is woven from the Virgin’s substance; and that man was within her as in an unbroken circle, because neither conception nor birth dissolved her integrity.

How new and unlike all others this birth of creation is may be seen if we review the other creations of human beings from the beginning. The first man was formed from the earth and derived his fleshly origin neither from father nor mother. Eve, formed from his rib, was from a father alone, not from a mother. All other people are begotten from father and mother together, except this one, who, as stated, is born of the mother alone. Hence he alone is properly called Son of Man, not Son of Men [Col. 0389C], because according to the flesh the Virgin alone bore him, and he was her only and unique son, just as he was also his Father’s; so that the singularity of his excellence might be commended in every respect.

The Virgin’s flesh, with which the true Lamb clothed himself, is that snowy fleece of the most innocent sheep, concerning which the Psalmist sang long before: “He shall come down like rain upon the fleece,” etc. (Ps. 71:6). We read in the Book of Judges that, at Gideon’s request, to strengthen him for battle by a visible sign, a fleece placed on the threshing floor was so soaked with dew that the surrounding ground remained dry; and afterward, at his request, the reverse occurred (Judg. 6:39).

By this sign it is said to have been prefigured that the grace of God, signified by dew, was first bestowed upon the Jewish people, dwelling formerly in the midst of the lands, as upon a fleece laid on the threshing floor, while the Gentile people was rejected; and afterward, when this fleece was dried—that is, Judaea was deprived of grace—it flowed out upon the nations throughout the lands [Col. 0389D].

But because dew is thin compared with rain and irrigates less sufficiently, the Psalmist compared the descent of divine grace into the Virgin to rain or raindrops rather than dew. For the grace bestowed upon the Mother of the Lord surpassed, as we have said, all the grace of both Jewish and Gentile peoples; and her gifts, which received the raindrops as earth receives them, are far more eminent than other gifts.

Although fleece comes from a body, it does not feel in pain the weakness of flesh from injury, and is wholly alien to every bodily sensation. Likewise the Virgin of virgins, though she was conceived, like other human beings, amid the weakness of fleshly concupiscence, never endured this weakness in her mind through consent, nor experienced any touch of fleshly allure in her flesh [Col. 0390A]. Hence it came about that, though born from flesh, she was ignorant of the vices of flesh; and though she was of flesh, she was as if she were not flesh—like one dead to the flesh and wholly alive in the spirit, ignorant of the pleasure of carnal sensations, which are most active in the concupiscence of the flesh.

Therefore the Son of the heavenly King rightly rejoiced to obtain her before all others as a palace suitable for his dwelling, one he had not previously found; and into her he descended from above with a gentle influx, as rain upon fleece. For rain falling upon fleece floods and washes it, yet inflicts no sensation of suffering upon it; and, since it is not felt by it, it is in it as though it were not. So too heavenly wisdom, whose draught is compared with water, according to the saying, “The Lord gave them to drink the water of wisdom” (Ecclus. 15:3), because “of his fullness we have all received”: in order to take flesh from the Virgin, it watered her by its very descent with the gifts of grace, cleansed her from every contagion of human weakness, and brought her no suffering of the flesh either in conception or in childbirth. Since it consecrated her as a virgin both before and after birth, it was in her as though it had not been; and she became pregnant as though not pregnant, since she incurred from it no burden of suffering.

The drops of rain, however, when they soak the earth, turn it from its dryness to fruitfulness [Col. 0390C]. And the Son of God filled her with the gifts of his Spirit so that she not only bore God and brought forth fruit herself, but also bestowed him upon all the faithful—she who bore for the world the salvation of all.

She is that common land of all the faithful and that special field, of which the Holy Spirit was the cultivator and the Word of God the seed. The prophet mentioned above, foreseeing this through the Spirit, calls all alike to rejoice with him and to confess divine praise, saying: “Let the peoples give praise to thee, O God; let all the peoples give praise to thee: the earth hath yielded her fruit” (Ps. 66:6–7).

If anyone takes this to refer to the fruit of an earthly harvest, what relevance would David’s exhortation to praise have—as though in his days the earth had begun to bear fruit or to produce a more abundant crop? Scripture recalls that Isaac sowed and gathered a hundredfold as an object of wonder at divine beneficence, but does not record that he rendered any thanksgiving to the Lord for such an abundance of fruit [Col. 0390D].

Let us understand, then, that David, in prophecy of this fruit—which he elsewhere recalls as promised to him by the Lord, saying, “Of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne” (Ps. 131:11)—exhorts all to rejoice with him, because he perceives their common salvation in it. This is that sublime fruit of the earth which Isaiah also foresaw: “The branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth sublime, and the hope of those who shall have been saved from Israel” (Isa. 4:2).

For what else must be understood by the branch of the Lord, the sublime fruit of the earth, and the common rejoicing of all the faithful, except Christ? He was begotten of the Father before the ages, and today came forth as if from earth, born of the Virgin. The Apostle defines his exaltation and magnificence, saying: “Wherefore God also hath exalted him, and hath given him a name which is above every name” (Phil. 2:9).

The same prophet, proclaiming elsewhere this fruit of the earth, speaks also of that name—that is, Jesus, interpreted “Savior”: “Drop down dew, ye heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the Just One; let the earth be opened, and let it bud forth the Savior, and let justice spring up together. I, the Lord, have created him” (Isa. 45:6 ff.) [Col. 0391A].

What else should be understood by the names of heavens and clouds except angels or holy Fathers, surpassing others in dignity and, as it were, dwelling in the heights in mind? When they foretold the coming of the Mediator, either figuratively or openly, the faithful received their words like dew or rain. Dew, being finer than rain and consisting of exceedingly tiny drops, is scarcely visible: it signifies allegorical words difficult to understand. Open words are compared to rain.

These words watered the holy earth—that is, the immaculate Virgin—that she might bear this fruit for us. Having been taught by promises made concerning Christ through angels and prophets alike, she believed what she heard; thus she conceived, as it were, by the ear, and through faith in the word heard deserved to conceive that Word of God of whom it is written: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). This is shown immediately afterward when it is said: “And the Word was made flesh.”

Therefore the earth opened itself to receive this dew or rain of divine promises when, through understanding and faith, it held open the ears not only of the body but also of the heart, so that she understood and believed at once the things said to her [Col. 0391C]. Thus these words are rightly said to rain “the Just One” into her rather than a sinner, because this one, alone conceived without fleshly concupiscence, was wholly free from every sin.

“Let them rain the Just One,” therefore, means as though it were said: Let them convey to the Virgin the words of their teaching concerning one conceived wholly immune from sin; and let the earth—that is, the woman—open herself to receive them in faith, not doubting the possibility of such a conception, when the angelic promise has been cast into her as into earth: “Behold, thou shalt conceive,” etc. (Luke 1:31).

With him justice rises at the same time, because he is not only just in himself but also, through faith in himself rather than through works of the law, makes us just; as the Apostle says, he “is made unto us wisdom from God, and justice” (1 Cor. 1:30). “I, the Lord, have created him”: that is, from eternity I have already ordained to accomplish this creation of him not through male intercourse, but through the power of my might. What is there foretold as future—“Let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior”—is here shown as already fulfilled: “The earth hath yielded her fruit” (Ps. 66:7) [Col. 0391D].

[Col. 0392A] What follows, “May God bless” (ibid.), is the prayer of one seeking the efficacy of this fruit in the blessing thereby promised to the world, first made to Abraham when the Lord said to him: “In thy seed shall all nations be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). In the first Adam the earth was cursed; in the second it received blessing. For the former drew all with him into condemnation, from which the latter alone freed us, and thereby obtained to be rightly called Jesus—that is, Savior.

Before his coming, even the righteous were punished in the lower world because of the sin of the first human being; to free them from there, he himself deigned also to descend into the lower world, fulfilling Hosea’s prophecy: “O death, I will be thy death; I will be thy bite, O hell” (Hos. 13:14).

Therefore, once the gate of paradise had been opened to us through him, so that none of the elect should henceforth be delayed from the kingdom, he silenced that complaint of the faithful: “Our fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the children are set on edge” (Jer. 31:29). Immediately answering this complaint and promising the time of grace through his coming, he says: “As I live, this parable shall no longer be a proverb in Israel” (Ezek. 18:3). And later: “The soul that sinneth, the same shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father,” etc. (ibid., 20).

What is the eating of the sour grape, committed by the fathers and redounding as punishment even upon their children, as though they too had eaten that one grape, except the transgression of the first parents? Before the Lord’s coming it oppressed all posterity, so that no one, however righteous, could pass to blessedness; rather, all posterity was punished for the eating of the tree of one prohibition [Col. 0392C].

Many Jews maintain that the tree which the Lord calls the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was a vine, whose fruit here is called a grape. They reasonably wish it to be called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because, just as wine taken moderately sharpens the intellect, so, when it exceeds the proper measure, it dulls it. Thus, as conferring both good and perverse understanding, they judge it to be called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

This opinion also seems to receive considerable support from the fact that, immediately after eating, they felt in themselves the stirring of lust; confounded by shame, they covered their private parts. For wine is a lustful thing, as it is written (Prov. 20:1). And the Apostle says: “Wine, wherein is luxury” (Eph. 5:18).

In the midst of paradise both the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil are reported to have stood, as though joined to one another so that one adhered to the other, as a vine is customarily supported by an elm; and as though death and life were placed together in one, the tree of life administering life from its own fruit and inflicting death from the adjacent vine. For the Lord Jesus is set for the ruin and resurrection of many: from himself he grants life to believers, while the reprobate whom he bears for a long time in patience he condemns by justice [Col. 0392D].

At his coming, as has been said, that previously mentioned proverb is promised to cease, because in the elect, signified by Israel, the penalty of original sin has now come to an end. Henceforth none of the faithful is delayed from the kingdom except through personal fault. Rather, the soul that sins in Israel—that is, among those who see God and possess reason—is punished only for its own sin, not for another’s; nor does the son now bear the father’s sin, where no original sin now separates any of the faithful from blessedness.

Thus this time of grace, in which we obtain full remission, is fittingly called the time of grace, just as that former time was called the time of wrath. Of this fullness of time and abundance of divine grace, by which God had decreed to fulfill what he had begun and complete what he had promised, the Apostle says: “But when the fullness of time was come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law,” etc. (Gal. 4:4) [Col. 0393B].

This woman, therefore, woman in sex but ignorant of feminine weakness, a perpetual virgin consecrated by divine childbirth, is that eastern gate always shut, which Ezekiel describes as revealed to him through the Spirit: “This gate shall be shut; it shall not be opened, and man shall not pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel hath entered in by it” (Ezek. 44:2).

For through this Virgin, as through a gate, the Lord enters to us as into his temple when he joins himself in her to our nature. Yet this same gate remains forever shut, and no man shall pass through it, because there was no male intercourse. This gate is rightly said to face the east, since she herself is suitably compared with the east.

For as the physical sun rises there and thence is spread to the other parts of the world, so in her the true sun of justice, Christ, was born—as it is written: “That which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20)—and extended the rays of his brightness to illuminate the darkness of the whole world. Hence the Evangelist John says: “He was the true light, which enlighteneth every man that cometh into this world,” etc. (John 1:9) [Col. 0393C].

This light, that is, the Word of the Father and his coeternal wisdom, enters to us through the Virgin as the brightness of the sun passes through a pane of the most solid glass. Glass is more solid and more brilliant than all metals, yet more fragile, nor can it after fracture be restored as other materials can.

Likewise the integrity of the holy virgin, which the Apostle defines when he says, “That she may be holy both in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 7:34), possesses the greatest firmness and shines more acceptably before God in proportion as this virtue is higher. Yet, because it can easily be lost, if the mind is corrupted even once it can no longer be recovered or made whole. Thus it is clear how fragile this good nevertheless is and how careful a guarding it requires.

Therefore the power and wisdom of God himself, for whom willing is being able, fashioned for himself in the Virgin a kind of pane from this fragile glass [Col. 0393D]. Through it the highest splendor of divine brightness poured itself forth upon us, yet neither entering through conception nor departing through childbirth shattered it.

It should be noted that a pane receives the full brightness of light, but does not return it with equal fullness and cannot render as much as it receives. So too, when that divine radiance enters to us through the virginal pane, it illuminates the Virgin herself by far ampler grace than it illuminates us through the Virgin. Therefore she is rightly greeted by the angel as “full of grace” (Luke 1), and the Holy Spirit is announced as coming upon her.

For she, insofar as human nature can receive it, was filled with every gift of divine grace; she received all together what is distributed in portions to others. Thus the Holy Spirit often comes to other believers through some gift of grace, but came upon this woman because here his coming was far higher, where he wrought the salvation of all the faithful [Col. 0394A].

According to this operation, the Savior himself is said not only to have been born of the Virgin but also to have been born, or conceived, of the Spirit himself—yet in one manner from her and in another from him. From her, namely, as from a mother, from whose substance he took flesh; from him, not as from a father but as the agent of this birth. For in this conception or birth, not the custom of nature but the operation of divine grace is considered; attention is given not to what nature can do but to what the Omnipotent willed.

And because what pertains more to God’s grace than to human merits is especially attributed to the Holy Spirit, he is properly called the love or goodness of God.

By the operation of this one, as of some craftsman, that stone was cut from the mountain without hands—the stone which in Daniel is said to have shattered the statue, and afterward [Col. 0394C] to have grown into a great mountain and filled the whole earth. Promising us this stone also through Isaiah, the Lord says: “Behold, I shall lay in the foundations of Zion a tested stone, a precious cornerstone,” etc. (Isa. 28:16). Of it the Psalmist had earlier sung: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord,” etc. (Ps. 117:22).

The cutting of this stone from the mountain without hands is the divine incarnation itself, in which that grace of the Holy Spirit alone which filled the Virgin was at work. By his operation he separated from the Virgin’s flesh that flesh with which the Son of God was to be clothed, and formed it into limbs. What do hands signify but [Col. 0394D] human operation? It was therefore done without hands, where no operation of human intercourse occurred. The mountain from which this stone was cut is the lofty eminence of virginal dignity, which led a heavenly life upon earth. From its substance, according to the flesh, that man was assumed who is united in one person to the Word of God; and this whole is Jesus Christ.

By shattering the great and lofty statue, he destroyed idolatry, spread abroad among the nations, just as he himself had formerly promised through Isaiah, saying: “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a light cloud and enter Egypt; and the idols of Egypt shall be moved at his presence” (Isa. 19:1). Egypt, which is interpreted “darkness,” is the world, struck by the utter blindness of idolatry. Into it [Col. 0395A] the Lord came manifestly in the flesh, resting upon that very flesh as upon a light cloud; for that man assumed by the Word—of whom it is written, “The Word was made flesh”—drew no burden of sin from the corruptible body which weighs down the soul.

The sun, generating exhalations from the earth by its heat, draws up a cloud, from which rain afterward flows and drenches the earth so that it may bear fruit. Therefore the sun’s vapor or heat is the Spirit himself proceeding from God, who is also called his love. Breathing where he wills and setting earthly hearts aflame toward God, he produces, as it were, certain exhalations of earth, while he arouses their groans and sighs toward God. Hence the Apostle says: “The Spirit himself,” he says, “intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered” (Rom. 8:26), since he makes us petition [Col. 0395B] and pray for what he suggests.

Thus the supreme prayer and expectation of the ancient Fathers toward God was that he should send them the promised Savior, as is also recorded of the blessed Simeon (Luke 2:25). Recalling this, blessed Augustine says:

> “Understand, brethren,” he says, “how great was the desire of the saints of old to see Christ! They knew that he would come, and all who longed for him said: ‘Oh, may that birth find me! Oh, may I see with my own eyes what I believe in the Scriptures of God!’”

[Note: [Col. 0395D] *Patrologia* XXXIX, col. 1658.]

The same writer, after some remarks about that blessed old man just mentioned, depicts him as longing and sighing, and daily saying in his prayers: “When will he come? When will he be born? When shall I see him? Do you think I shall live? Do you think he will find me here? Do you think these [Col. 0395C] eyes will see him, by whom the eyes of the heart will be opened?” He said these things in his prayers; and for his longing he received the answer that he should not taste death until he saw the Christ of the Lord. [Note: [Col. 0396D] *Ibid.*]

Of these desires of the saints and of their most vehement cry of heart Isaiah also speaks: “They will cry to God because of the oppressor, and he will send them a Savior,” etc. (Isa. 19:20). Such cries and groans of the faithful were, as it were, exhalations from the earth. In answer to their petition and expectation, the true Sun drew up the cloud by his vapor: by the operation of the Holy Spirit, the Word of God took flesh from the Virgin. From that flesh too, as from a cloud, he gave rain when preaching announced the mystery of his incarnation to all lands [Col. 0395D] and brought forth from it the fruit of faith.

When, therefore, he came into Egypt with that flesh, as has been said, the idols of Egypt were moved (ibid.), because idolatry was removed from there when the nations were converted to him. Then indeed, in accordance with Daniel, the statue having been shattered, that stone grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth, because his body—that is, the Church—expanded over this land of the dying, where the faith of the lands prevailed after unbelief had been driven out (Dan. 2:35). Finally, that body will fill not only this land of the dying, but rather that land of the living.

This is that mountain of the Lord prepared on the summit of the mountains, which by the eminence of divinity transcends all [Col. 0396A] the heights of the saints. Today it is born for us as though from a valley, because from the lower sex and from a most humble virgin that supreme splendor of divine majesty comes forth today before human sight, overshadowed by the veil of flesh, so that he who remains invisible in his own substance may at least be seen in our substance.

This is that appearance of electrum which we read was revealed to the prophet Ezekiel. Electrum is a certain mixture of gold and silver, in which silver is advanced in brightness by the admixture of the better metal, while gold is tempered from its splendor when joined to the inferior metal (Ezek. 1:4). Thus we understand Christ as one person from two natures, in whom divinity is compared to gold and humanity to the inferior metal. In this person, therefore, who is Christ [Col. 0396B]—that is, God and man—the divine and human natures are so joined that the incomprehensible splendor of divine brightness, overshadowed by the veil of flesh, moderated itself to human eyes; and the humanity assumed advanced into brightness. That man, like an earthen vessel, was kindled by the incomparable light of the heavenly wisdom to which he was united; illuminating our darkness both by words and examples, he displayed to us the fullness of every virtue and restored our nature, purer and more richly endowed with understanding than it had been when created in Paradise.

But in order that the Word of God, taking flesh from the Virgin, might overshadow himself with this veil, he is also said first to have overshadowed [Col. 0396C] the Virgin herself, so that afterward he might be born from her thus overshadowed. For when Gabriel the archangel, that great heavenly bridegroom’s friend, had foretold to the Virgin, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you” (Luke 1:35), he immediately expressed wherein this higher coming of the Holy Spirit would consist, adding: “And the power of the Most High shall overshadow you. And that holy thing which shall be born of you shall be called the Son of God” (ibid.).

For the Son is called the power of the Father, whom the Apostle calls “the power of God and the wisdom of God,” because whatever God orders through his wisdom, he accomplishes powerfully through that same wisdom (1 Cor. 1:24). This coeternal wisdom of the Father, then, is said to have overshadowed the Virgin: that is, as it were, to have hidden her, specially chosen and drawn her to itself out of the whole mass of humankind, [Col. 0396D] in order to work in her the mystery of our restoration and accomplish the deepest secret of its dispensation.

What Gabriel now says—“The power of the Most High shall overshadow you, and that holy thing which shall be born of you,” etc.—had already been carefully expressed in Isaiah (7:14), according to the proper character of the Hebrew language. For where we say, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son,” the Hebrew has *alma* for “virgin,” a word which means “hidden one.” Therefore she whom the Prophet there calls hidden, we call, in accordance with the angel’s declaration, overshadowed.

How divine wisdom overshadowed the Virgin—that is, how wisely God, as has been said, [Col. 0397A] hid her for himself—is also shown by those considerations because of which he wished to be born of one who was betrothed, and did not permit her, though pregnant, to be separated from her husband. She too, meeting the reproach of human beings, determined to call him the father of her only-begotten Son, lest the truth of her conception or childbirth, heard but not believed, should bring her punishment or disgrace among unbelievers rather than glory.

Thus she is said to have been overshadowed by God in two ways: because he both concealed the truth of her childbirth from the world and hid her by protecting her. This accords with the way in which the prophet says that protection is “a shade and a hiding place,” and with the Psalmist’s words: “He protected me under the shadow of his wings” (Ps. 16:8). For what we protect against injury, we conceal.

The things which preceded and followed in her also fittingly indicate this hiddenness [Col. 0397B] of the Virgin. The angel sent to her is recorded to have entered in to her, teaching us, surely, that he found her not playing publicly among worldly women, but privately occupied with God, as though praying in a closed chamber. Her body too remains utterly hidden and withdrawn from human sight even now. She is rightly called hidden, since in this conception or childbirth she was neither known by a man nor experienced the law of her nature or sex. The explanation of this mystery is reserved for him alone who was born hidden from the hidden one and proceeded overshadowed from the overshadowed one, so that by the true brightness of his light he might illuminate the world sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, show us the way by which we might return [Col. 0397C] to our homeland, provide the means, and open the hearing.

Finally, the evangelists who undertook to recount Christ’s genealogy did not trace it down to his mother, but rather carried it to Joseph, her betrothed. They imply, though they do not state explicitly, that Mary too was of David’s line, since they relate that by law she had been betrothed to one of her own tribe. In this narrative also they seem to heed that prophetic saying already cited: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). For they narrate both, yet do not fully declare; they touch upon the matter but do not reach it, because they do not name Mary’s immediate parents. They carry the line of descent rather to the bridegroom, as stated, than to the bride, so that his may be disclosed while hers remains hidden.

Hence the Apostle aptly compared Christ here also to Melchizedek, saying that he is without genealogy (Heb. 7:3). For just as Scripture does not set forth Melchizedek’s descent, so it does not define Christ’s human genealogy either, as has been said. Thus, when Matthew, having reckoned Joseph’s genealogy, added, “Now the generation of Christ was thus” (Matt. 1:18), this seems to refer not so much to what precedes as to what immediately follows: “When his mother was betrothed,” etc. (ibid.). It is as though he plainly said: Such is Joseph’s genealogy, traced from the fathers mentioned above down to himself; but Christ’s human generation, knowing no father, [Col. 0398A] was effected from the Virgin alone by the operation of the Holy Spirit.

The unbelieving Jews themselves, professing the promised prophecy, speak of this hiddenness when they say: “But we know where this man is from; when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from” (John 7:27). We read that people of old were accustomed to celebrate the anniversary of their births, as the Evangelist also records of Herod. But after the Creator of all bestowed so great a grace upon us as, by being born of a Virgin, to raise our nature above the angels, we immediately abandon all this vanity of celebrating our own births and turn to celebrating his Nativity. We no longer consider when we are born here, but how through him we may be born again for heaven (Mark 6:21).

To him, with the Father and the Holy [Col. 0398B] Spirit, belong one essence, the same majesty, and inseparable glory through the endless ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. ON THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE LORD

For those who inquire into the rationale of the Lord’s circumcision or baptism, the first question that occurs is: Why did circumcision come first among the ancient people? Next, why, after it had ceased, did baptism succeed it? Finally, why, after John’s coming—up to whom were the Law and the Prophets—the Lord underwent both, especially since he could in no way have possessed that which they are said to have been instituted to remove?

If, with the Lord’s assent, we can resolve these three questions, we shall complete the task proposed. Let us now [Col. 0398C] consider the first. It is certain that before Abraham, from whom circumcision began, there were some righteous persons, such as Abel, Enoch, and Noah; and that Abraham himself was righteous through the true circumcision of the heart before he was circumcised in the flesh. The testimony of Genesis plainly establishes this, as the Apostle writes among other things to the Romans:

> “What then shall we say that Abraham our father according to the flesh found? For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God. For what does Scripture say? ‘Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness’” (Rom. 4:1–3).

And a little later: “We say that faith was reckoned to Abraham as righteousness. How then was it reckoned? In circumcision, [Col. 0398D] or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision. And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of faith which he had in uncircumcision,” etc. (ibid., vv. 9–11).

From this the Apostle clearly establishes that he who was the first to be circumcised in the flesh by the Lord’s command was justified by faith before that circumcision, while he was still uncircumcised, and did not obtain righteousness from circumcision. He received circumcision as a sign of righteousness already possessed, so that the outward circumcision of the flesh might display rather than effect the inward circumcision of the mind from vices—that is, the righteousness of faith.

Meanwhile, the righteousness of the earlier Fathers was acceptable to God. One of them, Enoch, was removed from the miseries of this present life and translated alive by the Lord into Paradise, as Ecclesiasticus also recounts (44:16), and as Isidore asserts in *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*:

> “Enoch deserved to be transferred alive to that place from which the first-formed man had been expelled; at the consummation of the world, together with Elijah, he will resume the condition of mortal life.”

[Note: [Col. 0399D] Ch. 3. See *Patrologia*, vol. LXXXIII, col. 132.]

Another, Noah, with his entire household, was delivered from the flood and alone deserved to be preserved as the seedbed of the human race. The holiness of Job, a Gentile who plainly lived much later than Abraham, is so commended by the Lord’s testimony that “there is no man like him on earth” (Job 1:8)—at a time, surely, when many circumcised descendants of Abraham were already living. The natural law justified him, as it did very many other Gentiles, more truly than the written law justified the Jews.

Concerning this, the Apostle says in the same epistle, as mentioned above: “For not the hearers of the law are righteous before God, but the doers of the law shall be justified. For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law unto themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them” (Rom. 2:13–15). And a little later:

> “If, therefore, uncircumcision keeps the requirements of the law, shall not its uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision? And shall not uncircumcision, which is by nature and fulfills the law, judge you who through the letter and circumcision of the flesh are a transgressor of the law? For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from human beings but from God” (ibid., vv. 26–29).

And again: “For we hold that a human being is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not also of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also, since one God justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith” (Rom. 3:28–29).

Blessed Jerome carefully observes this and does not hesitate to commend the life of such persons as acceptable to God. Explaining Matthew in one place, he says:

> “From the fact that the wicked servant dared to say, ‘You reap where you did not sow, and gather where you did not scatter’ (Matt. 25:24), let us understand that God also receives the good life of Gentiles and philosophers; that he regards differently those who act justly and those who act unjustly; and that, in comparison with one who serves the natural law, he condemns those who neglect the written law.”

[Note: [Col. 0400D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXVI, col. 187.]

It is therefore certain that in the ancient people both uncircumcised and circumcised persons alike were justified by faith; nor did those who were circumcised attain righteousness in order to become righteous through circumcision, but rather by faith working through love, as the Apostle says. [Note: [Col. 0400D] Gal. 5:6.]

What reason, then, was there that Abraham alone, together with his seed and those whom he possessed, whether from his own kin or from foreign peoples, should receive this sign of circumcision by the Lord’s command? This is rightly [Col. 0400A] asked. For the righteousness itself of which the Apostle says this was a sign existed equally, as has been said, in others as in Abraham (Rom. 4:3); yet the command did not bind them to this sign, but Abraham alone, as we have said, with his seed and those belonging to his possession.

For this is written when the Lord says to Abraham: “I will establish my covenant between me … and your seed after you throughout their generations as an everlasting covenant, to be your God and the God of your seed after you. And I will give to you and your seed the land of your sojourning” (Gen. 17:7). And again:

> “You therefore shall keep my covenant, you and your seed after you throughout their generations. This is what you shall observe between me and you and your seed after you: every male among you shall be circumcised [Col. 0400B]; you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you. Every male among you throughout your generations shall be circumcised when eight days old. Both the home-born slave and the slave purchased with money shall be circumcised, including whoever is not of your stock. And my covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant. The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised—that person shall be cut off from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (ibid., vv. 9–14).

And a little later: “Sarah your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name Isaac. I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him. Concerning Ishmael also I have heard you: behold, I will bless him and multiply him exceedingly. But I will establish my covenant with Isaac” (ibid., vv. 19–21).

The Lord afterward plainly indicated that Isaac alone belonged to Abraham’s seed, saying: “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Gen. 21:12). Accordingly, he also calls Isaac Abraham’s only-begotten, saying: “Because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son,” etc. (Gen. 22:12).

It is therefore certain that no one is bound by the commandment of circumcision except Abraham with his seed and those belonging to their household or possession. The Lord also gives the reason for this circumcision when he says: “That it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you” (Gen. 17:11). It is as though he plainly said: not that it may make you covenant-bound and joined to me, but that it may show that you are covenant-bound.

Rufinus too, expounding Paul’s Epistle to the Romans after Origen, carefully identifies the occasion of this commandment concerning circumcision, both here and elsewhere, from the words of the Law itself: which commandments belong to the Jews alone and which to all people generally. “Let us investigate,” he says, “whether this commandment also binds those who had believed from among the Gentiles. It never makes mention of a proselyte—that is, a sojourner—but commands that a home-born slave or one purchased for money be circumcised, not a free person. Let us examine, therefore, the law of Leviticus: ‘Speak,’ it says, ‘to the children of Israel, and say to them: If a woman has borne a male, he shall be circumcised on the eighth day,’ etc. [Col. 0401A] (Lev. 12:2–3).

“Observe here also how Moses is commanded to speak concerning the law of circumcision only to the children of Israel, and how no mention is made of foreigners. Yet in certain commandments he speaks not only to the children of Israel but also to proselytes, that is, sojourners. The distinction must therefore necessarily be observed. For just as in one place it is said, ‘Speak to Aaron’ (Exod. 8:16), elsewhere ‘To the sons of Aaron’ (Num. 6:23), and elsewhere ‘To the Levites’ (Num. 18:26), it is certain that the rest are not subject even to laws commanded to the children [of Israel], where no mention at all is made of foreigners. A command is not to be considered common where there is a limitation in its designation.”

[Note: [Col. 0401D] The passage is corrupt.]

Thus no one else is bound by the law of circumcision except one tracing descent from Abraham, or one home-born among [Col. 0401B] them, or one purchased with money. But do you wish to see that where God wills even foreigners to be bound by the Law, this is expressly shown? Hear what is written: “Any person from the children of Israel or from the sojourners, whoever eats any blood, I shall destroy that person; for the life of all flesh is its blood. And I have given it to you, that through it atonement may be made upon the altar for your souls; for blood shall make expiation for the soul” (Lev. 17:10–11).

You see, then, that this law given to sojourners is also observed by us who believe from among the Gentiles. Therefore the Church has received in common with the children of Israel and the Gentiles the law concerning abstention from blood. Understanding the written Law in this way, that blessed council of the Apostles then decreed, writing ordinances to the Gentiles that they should abstain from blood and from what is strangled.

But perhaps you will ask whether the law concerning what is strangled was likewise given in common to the children of Israel and the sojourners. Hear: “Any person,” it says, “from the children of Israel and from the sojourners among you, who hunts an animal or bird which may be eaten, shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth, for the life of all flesh is its blood” (ibid., v. 13).

But because among the passages from Leviticus cited above this also occurs: “Any person from the children of Israel or the sojourners among them, who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice and does not bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle in order to offer it to the Lord, shall be cut off from his people” (ibid., v. 8), it will seem that the Church from among the Gentiles is also obliged to burnt offerings. Yet the Law does not command such a person to offer; rather, if he should perhaps offer, it teaches how he ought to do so.

For it is certain that, while the Temple stood at Jerusalem and the religion handed down to the Fathers remained in force, many Gentiles also came to the Temple to worship and offer sacrifice. Yet because this was commanded to be done in one place—and here too it commands that the animal to be slaughtered be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle—it could lawfully be done only so long as the condition of that place remained unharmed. Thus the Savior said to the ten lepers whom he had cleansed: “Go, show yourselves to the priests, and offer sacrifices for yourselves, as Moses commanded” (Luke 17:14). But now what is demanded of sojourners which even its own worshippers [Col. 0402A] are not permitted to offer? If we examine this reason for the Lord’s command more carefully, it is easy to answer every objection.

Abraham was the first to be led by divine command from the land of the Chaldeans and from his kindred, and he received from the Lord the promise of a land for himself and his seed. In that land the people of God were to live separated from the Gentiles and serve God unhindered; previously, the faithful had been accustomed to live and dwell scattered among the Gentiles. Therefore, as in a certain city, the Lord was to gather his people in that land and separate them from the Gentiles both in place and in life. He determined to establish for them a law, beginning with circumcision.

Hence, as we mentioned above, when the promise of the land was made—by which the people of God would be separated from unbelievers and more firmly joined and bound in covenant to the Lord—the commandment of circumcision was immediately introduced, so that it might be a sign of this covenant. Human propagation comes from the generative member. Thus the circumcision of this member showed that Abraham and his people were separated from the rite and customs of their origin, that is, from the unbelieving Chaldeans; and that by this stripping of flesh they had already put off the old and carnal human being and put on the new and spiritual human being, who is created according to God (Eph. 4) and renewed day by day. They were especially to be reminded of this by contemplating the sign.

Moreover, the Lord foresaw no small benefit from this sign, like a certain divine seal upon a person, for more securely protecting the salvation of the faithful and, above all, separating them from unbelievers. For the enticements of fleshly pleasure are so great that this desire easily inclines people even toward idolatry, as happened to the greatest of the wise (1 Kgs. 11). Therefore, lest faithful men joined to unbelieving women should pass over into their rites and depart from the Lord, he especially cut off the familiarity of such unions by this sign, setting it between them like a wall: so that, if the sons of God should again desire the daughters of men (Gen. 6), the women might nevertheless reject union with them, abhorring the mutilation of this member as utterly shameful; while the men, on the other hand, might keep their members, consecrated by the sign of God’s covenant, untouched by the shamefulness of unbelievers [Col. 0402D].

Hence the people of Israel, during the time when they were separated from the Gentiles in the wilderness, were not compelled to be circumcised at all. But it was especially necessary for this wall to be set between them when the pilgrimage of the faithful began in Abraham among unbelievers and in the land whose promise he had already received. For travelers readily seek familiarity with inhabitants on whatever occasion they can, and such familiarity is known to be contracted especially through marriages. If by such contact the people of God had been bound to the people of the Canaanites, they would have found it difficult to destroy them or drive them from the land, as was afterward accomplished by divine counsel.

Sharing a table also tends to be a very great bond of familiarity. Hence the Law afterward, forbidding luxurious foods, removed this occasion of familiarity as well; and the more difficult the observances in which it entangled the Jews, the more it removed the Gentiles from them and produced greater hostilities by this intervening wall. This needed to be done at that time, when God had not yet determined to call the Gentile people, but only the Jewish people.

But in the fullness of the time of grace, when God deemed the Gentile people also worthy of his call, so as to expand the Church into two peoples, join them in one body to himself as their head, and bind them together in great mutual harmony, he removed that wall of legal observances which had produced hostilities, so as to bind them to one another by the bond of love.

[Col. 0403B] The chief teacher of the Church and special master of the Gentiles discloses this providence of divine counsel in writing to the Ephesians:

> “Therefore remember that once you Gentiles in the flesh, who are called ‘uncircumcision’ by that which is called ‘circumcision in the flesh made by hands,’ were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants, without hope of the promise and without God in this world. But now in Christ Jesus, you who were once far off have been made near in the blood of Christ. For he himself is our peace, who made both one, breaking down the middle wall of division—the hostilities—in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself into [Col. 0403C] one new human being, making peace, and reconcile both to God in one body,” etc. (Eph. 2:11 ff.).

For the Jews, as God’s peculiar people, priding themselves on their legal privileges, so long as the Law retained its standing, continually despised the Gentiles and would not permit themselves to be considered their equals. Even after the Gospel they were so puffed up by the Law’s former status that they claimed for themselves, by this privilege, a unique prerogative in the Church. To restrain this pride especially, the Apostle was often compelled in his Epistles to humble or diminish the works of the Law and the boasting based on it; indeed, he determined to remove them altogether, lest the Jews insult the Gentiles on their account, or the Gentiles utterly disdain to submit themselves to a law in which the Jews especially gloried against them.

The holy Fathers afterward emulated this apostolic discrimination to such a degree that, when they arranged ecclesiastical ranks among the Gentiles according to the former grades of cities, they did not raise Jerusalem, once the eminent city of God, to that honor; indeed, they humbled it so far as to subject it to a metropolis, lest that proud people perhaps boast in the privilege of its city or Temple, just as it could not boast in its ceremonies. Hence, even in the solemn prayers of Good Friday, when we bend the knee also for Gentiles, heretics, and schismatics, we pass over only the Jews, who, bending the knee in mockery, said to the Lord: “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. 27).

[Col. 0404A] But just as, when the Law ceased, the more perfect teaching of the Gospel succeeded it, so after circumcision came the sacrament of baptism. It sanctifies men and women equally and demonstrates that he has now come who wholly washes us from sin and, by opening heaven, abolishes even sin’s punishment. Thus this sacrament is rightly performed over the whole person, rather than upon any one part; for after the Savior’s sacrifice sin is so utterly destroyed that even the punishment of sin is wholly remitted.

This sacrament commends the grace of the Lord’s coming all the more because it is more perfect for salvation and easier to endure: the new Law is so much more welcome as the preceding one was burdensome. Thus Gentiles, accustomed to bear the yoke of the Law, might not be driven away in alarm by any difficulty or multitude of sacraments. Inviting them from that weighty burden to evangelical freedom, the Lord said: “Come to me, you who labor and are burdened. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11:28).

To pass over the severity of the legal retaliations, where it says, “Tooth for tooth,” etc. (Lev. 24:20), who would not shrink from having the tender part of the body circumcised with sharp stones? For the Law shows that it is performed with no other instrument: Zipporah, the wife of Moses, is written to have circumcised her son in this way (Exod. 4:25), and Joshua, by the Lord’s command, circumcised the people with stone knives [Col. 0404C] (Josh. 5:2), although the Jews by no means observe this now because of the procedure’s difficulty.

The Prince of the Apostles, carefully considering this, openly confesses that neither he nor his fathers had been able to bear the yoke of the Law (Acts 15). Nor is baptism commended only by its perfection or gentleness; it is also adorned by a certain beauty in itself. For when any soul is to be joined to God, the washing of this sacrament fittingly indicates that no one is united to him unless cleansed from the filth of sin.

In baptism we enter into a certain marriage of special betrothal with God. At the first scrutiny of the catechumens we are bound to him by our promise and, as it were, betrothed; afterward, in baptism, we are joined [reading *counimur*] to his body, which is the Church, as though a bride, after bathing, were received into the embraces of her bridegroom.

Some have said that circumcision was necessary for the remission of original sin or even actual sins, and was instituted for that reason. But the cause given above seems to us more probable and rational, since it is clear that the earlier righteous persons had no need of this sacrament, and that women—bound by the same sins and those from whom sin began in us—were not sanctified by this sacrament. Who, moreover, can doubt that the ancient sacraments would greatly detract from the excellence of the new ones and lead us into the greatest error if they too remained alongside the new, as though these could not suffice without them?

Let what has now been said concerning the first two proposed questions—namely, the institution of circumcision or of the Law, and its subsequent cessation—be sufficient.

It remains, then, that, in answering the third question, we should complete the present undertaking: namely, why the Lord, while bringing the Law to an end and inaugurating the Gospel, also accepted those legal observances which he was ending—thus, as it were, exhorting us by his example to begin from the Law and be brought to completion in the Gospel, and not to pass over to the new sacraments in such a way as to abandon the old. For indeed, as Solomon says: “The eyes of the wise man are in his head” (Eccl. 2:14). Explaining this, as it were, the Apostle says: “Whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). Therefore, just as the Lord, who said, “I came not to abolish the Law, but to fulfil it” [Col. 0405B] (Matt. 5:17), received baptism after circumcision, and celebrated the new sacrifice after the sacrifice of the old Passover, so we too, following in his footsteps, ought not, you may say, to turn aside at all from these things.

But this would certainly be rightly said if our condition were now the same as that which then existed in him. For he received the ancient sacraments in order to avoid scandal and to furnish us, as far as we could, an example of avoiding it. Otherwise he would plainly have been thought guilty under the Law and altogether alien from the seed of Abraham and from the whole people of the Jews, from whom he was expected as the promised one. For, according to the Lord’s ordinance, whoever among them had not been circumcised was cut off from his people (Gen. 17), since without this sacrament no one could then be counted among the Jews, [Col. 0405C] just as now no one can be counted among Christians without baptism.

Thus, in order to avoid giving offence to the Jews at the beginning of the nascent Church, before evangelical truth had yet been established, the apostles for a time prudently consented even to the now-superfluous works of the Law. Paul himself, the most zealous adherent of the Law, circumcised his disciple Timothy (Acts 16:3); and afterwards, at the counsel of James and of the believers who were at Jerusalem, he took certain other men and showed himself to be observing the Law according to the Nazarite rite (Gal. 9:22). Yet afterwards he openly rebuked Peter for this very dissimulation concerning the Law (Gal. 2), once he understood that evangelical truth had been confirmed. Thus God accepted both the ancient and the new sacraments for different but in both cases rational reasons: the former, as has been said, to avoid scandal; the latter, as an example for our imitation.

For just as, having become the mediator between God and humankind, he possessed in himself two natures, divine and human, which he came to reconcile, so, joining two peoples to himself and uniting, as the cornerstone, two walls, he accepted the sacraments both of the earlier and of the later faithful, so that, according to the Apostle’s saying, “Having become all things to all, he might gain all” [Col. 0405D] (ibid. 15:13). For if, by withdrawing himself from the sacraments of the Jews, he had given them offence, he would have repelled them from himself rather than drawn them to himself. Whoever chooses a manner of life unlike that of those among whom he lives deprives himself all the more of their fellowship [Col. 0406A].

Thus angels of old, when they appeared to human beings, although they needed neither lodging nor food, nevertheless asked for or accepted these things as necessity required; and they made themselves so much the more familiar to us insofar as they more fully condescended to our weakness and did not reject the customs of those to whom they came.

Maintaining this same prudence, the Lord decreed that neither he nor his disciples should avoid anything in food or human social life except sin. If he had not also accepted the burdens of the Law, he would by no means afterwards have appeared to remove it—both because of its deficiency and because of its burden. He now certainly seems to deserve greater love from us, because he both accepted its burdens for our sake [Col. 0406B] and afterwards freed us from them.

There are also several other things which we remember that the Lord did, yet which we altogether and beneficially avoid, or suitably observe at another time and in another way. We read that the Lord, invited to a wedding with his mother and disciples, attended that banquet (John 2); yet now, by prudent ecclesiastical regulation, this has been wholly forbidden by the holy Fathers to priests holding Christ’s special offices. For the rationale was different in his case and in ours. Our weakness, prone to temptation, especially at banquets exceeds the bounds not only of religion but even of ordinary decency. Nor did he deign [the text reads *dedignatus*, “disdained”] to come to the wedding so much for the banquet as for the benefit of the miracle [Col. 0406C] by which he might reveal himself and confirm his disciples in faith. The Evangelist, carefully considering this, says: “And his disciples believed in him” (ibid., v. 11).

We know also that immediately after baptism he went down into the wilderness and then began and completed a fast of forty days; nor did the apostles receive from him the sacrament of his body and blood while fasting. These things indeed had then to be done in that way, but now, for another reason, different practices have entered into the custom of the Church. Likewise the Lord accepted circumcision so as not to scandalize the Jews, while we afterwards, as has been said, reject it.

> [Note: Col. 0405D: Something is missing.]

For many things, according to the appropriateness of time, are to be approved at one time and disapproved at another, even though they are done before and afterwards by the same persons. In all things places and times have their own reasons, according to which the same acts should at one time be done and at another avoided. It is plainly the case that, to avoid scandals or the alienation of Gentiles, certain practices once lawful are now to be avoided by us: circumcision, the observance of the Sabbath or festivals, the rite of sacrifices, and abstinence from certain foods. Yet the apostles or holy Fathers did not shrink from retaining those things in which they perceived no scandal, but rather some usefulness or dignity.

Thus we still observe the fasts of the Four Seasons, and we preserve and confirm by ancient authority the ranks of ecclesiastical offices—from doorkeeper, and even from the tonsure of clerical status, up to bishop—as well as the ornaments of priestly or ecclesiastical worship: for example, candlesticks, crowns, and veils. We have likewise received from antiquity the dedication of churches and the consecration of altars, so fully that in performing these rites almost nothing is sung or recited except from the Old Testament; and, following the example of ancient sprinkling, we employ hyssop and ashes. Who, moreover, understanding the words, “You are a priest for ever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109:4), can fail to know that the form of our sacrifice preceded even the Law, and that the Law received its origin or testimony from it? In this sacrifice, while we Latins eat unleavened bread, [Col. 0407B] we retain some figure also from the old Passover, according to the Apostle’s words: “Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity” (1 Cor. 5:8). Finally, following Elisha’s example, we prepare the very mixture of salt and water for the daily sprinkling of the faithful, as the words of the blessing themselves attest.

Since, therefore, we retain some things from antiquity and reject others, the reasons and occasions must be weighed in each case. Some, paying too little attention to this, judge that all such things must now be rejected because they were figures of the truth which followed and has now been fulfilled through Christ. They therefore rightly judge those things wholly superfluous where the truth which they prefigured has been fulfilled, lest, if the figures which signified it beforehand were still retained together with the truth itself, that which has already been accomplished should still seem to be awaited as future.

But according to this reasoning, no sacrament or mystical figure of a future reality ought to remain after its reality has been fulfilled. Thus marriage, which contains the sacrament of Christ and the Church, as well as the anointing of kings and priests, must now cease along with those things which we said are retained by us. We must no longer follow the sacrifice of Melchizedek in figures, consecrate altars with chrism, dedicate churches, set up candlesticks in churches, or retain any of the other things mentioned. Since no faithful or discerning person approves this, it is clear that there are reasons [Col. 0407D] why we retain certain things from the Old Testament in material signs, just as we retain all things in words.

For although uttered words demonstrate what they signify more plainly than sacramental figures, we reject none of the words of the Old Testament, even when they appear to speak otherwise than the truth of the matter has now turned out—for example, when it says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” (Isa. 7:14). Why, then, is it surprising that, since the Old Testament foretells in both things and words what has now been fulfilled, we should receive some of its sacraments even after the fulfilment of those realities, when we presume to reject none of its words? The harmony of the Old and New Testaments is so much greater, and the latter is confirmed by the former so much more, insofar as they appear connected not only in words but in the things themselves [Col. 0408A].

It should be noted, however, that a fixed, appointed time—the eighth day—was set only for circumcising infants, because it is certain that only those who live innocently, like rational newborn infants without deceit (1 Pet. 2:2), attain the joys of that true eighth day. There we obtain true and perfect circumcision both of souls and bodies, wholly putting off the old person both in guilt and in punishment; there the mind is entirely free, and the flesh is alike free from corruption and susceptibility to suffering.

For the whole duration of the present life is comprehended in seven days. Hence that everlasting brightness of the saints which follows the sevenfold course of this life is rightly called the eighth day; accordingly, psalms that seem especially to concern the resurrection are said to be entitled “for the eighth.” We read that Joshua circumcised the children of Israel a second time with stone knives (Josh. 5), when, after crossing the Jordan, they had been brought into the land of promise. For the people who came out of Egypt and died in the wilderness had left uncircumcised the children born in the wilderness. When Joshua afterwards circumcised them, he is said to have circumcised the children of Israel a second time—not, indeed, as we can more fittingly understand it according to the historical sense, in the same persons.

For many others among the Jewish people circumcised many persons, yet no one besides Joshua is said to have carried out a second circumcision. We read that Abraham was first circumcised or circumcised others: first Ishmael and his household servants, and afterwards Isaac [Col. 0408C] (Gen. 17:26; 21:4). Likewise, the Lord compelled Zipporah, Moses’ wife, to circumcise her son with a very sharp stone (Exod. 4:25).

Yet none of these circumcisions was called second or first, nor distinguished by order, except that said to have been performed by Joshua. Why, then, is he alone said to have circumcised a second time, or in comparison with what first circumcision is this called a second? I think this cannot easily be resolved unless the pen turns toward allegory. The Apostle invites us to it when he says: “All these things happened to them in a figure” (1 Cor. 10:11).

It is called the second circumcision when we become heirs of the land of promise—that is, when we attain the land [Col. 0408D] of the living in that blessed eighth day of which we have spoken. The first circumcision is that by which here we cut away from mind and flesh, as far as is granted us, vices and fleshly enticements, in order that there we may receive the true and complete circumcision previously mentioned, from the true Joshua—that is, our Jesus, indeed the Savior of all.

For that Joshua who succeeded Moses and brought the people into the land of promise seems particularly to prefigure him, both in the very name by which he is called Joshua, that is, Jesus, and in the excellence of his deeds. Succeeding Moses, and bringing into the land of promise the people who had departed from Egypt, he completed what Moses began, because the Law, both signified and given through Moses, “brought nothing,” as the Apostle says, “to perfection” [Col. 0409A] (Heb. 7:19). “For it is impossible,” he says, “for the blood of goats or bulls to take away sins” (Heb. 10:4). Therefore Joshua had to succeed Moses, because the lawgiver would have advanced in vain unless the Savior followed.

He indeed circumcised with the stone those brought into the land of promise after crossing the Jordan, insofar as he grants us, regenerated in baptism and led to the inheritance of the heavenly calling, true circumcision through himself, prefigured in the stone. To him, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong equal glory and coeternal majesty, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ON THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD.

*(We have emended the text with the aid of the Einsiedeln manuscript.)*

[Col. 0409B]

The present solemnity of the Epiphany displayed to the world the proper meaning of its name through many and various events. For what is called in Greek *Theophania* or *Epiphania* is termed in Latin “the manifestation of God,” or “a further manifestation.” Therefore, after the manifestation of his temporal birth, when, coming forth from the Virgin’s womb, the Savior of the world made himself visible to the world in flesh and became known to shepherds in a manger, he afterwards resolved, on one and the same day in the yearly recurrence of time, to reveal himself more fully through miraculous signs, so that [Col. 0409C] those who did not know him from Scripture might at least be drawn to faith through wonder at events.

A new star revealed more clearly on earth the new birth of the heavenly King; and when the heavens were opened above the baptized Lord, the dove descended upon him, and the Father’s voice bore testimony concerning the Son, it made fully known not only to the people standing around but also to John the Baptist himself how great he was. John himself confesses this, saying: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him. And I did not know him. But he who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw and bore testimony that this is the Son of God” (John [Col. 0409D] 1:32).

Finally, by the miracle of water turned into wine, the power of his divinity is declared, as the Evangelist records: “Jesus performed this first of his signs in Cana of Galilee and manifested his glory” (ibid. 2:11). “And his disciples believed in him.” Let us now pursue in order these individual revelations of the Lord, and complete the undertaking we have begun to the glory of this present day.

It was fitting that the Magi, the firstfruits of the Gentiles, should first be drawn to faith, so that those who had held the chief mastery of error might later, by the example of their conversion, provide instruction in faith; and the conversion of teachers might become the greatest edification of their disciples. So it was afterwards with Gamaliel, Nicodemus, Paul, Dionysius the Areopagite, and many others preeminent both in the Law and in philosophy.

For who does not know that magicians or diviners are to be so greatly detested that the Law commands not only them but also anyone who turns aside to them to be put to death? (Lev. 20:6). Jerome also declares in his commentary on Isaiah that their wicked and execrable teaching was devised and adopted from demons, in these words:

> [Note: Col. 0409D; *Patrologia*, vol. 24, col. 250.]  
> “The Magi, taught by demons in the East, or understanding from Balaam’s prophecy (Num. 24:17) that the Son of God had been born, who would destroy the whole power of their art, came to Bethlehem and, guided by the star, worshipped the child” [Col. 0410B] (Matt. 2:11).

Isidore likewise, in Book IX of the *Etymologies*, distinguishing the character of magicians, says:

> [Note: Col. 0409D; *Patrologia*, vol. 82, col. 311.]  
> “Magi are those commonly called sorcerers because of the greatness of their crimes. They change the elements, disturb people’s minds, and, without any draught of poison, kill by the force of incantation alone.”

Whence Lucan also says:

> [Note: Col. 0410D: Ibid.]  
> “A mind polluted by no corruption of swallowed poison perishes under enchantment.”  
> (*Pharsalia*, Book IV, verse 457.)

For, having summoned demons, they dare to employ them so that each may destroy his enemies by evil arts. They also use blood and victims, and often touch dead bodies.

What Jerome says—that magicians taught by demons came seeking the Savior, through whom they feared their art would be destroyed—need not be understood to mean that a diabolical suggestion or exhortation sent them with the intention of converting them to the Lord Christ. Rather, it was so that, by seeking him, they might betray him, so that the wickedness of Herod or of the Jews might find him to destroy him. The demons perhaps feared him, or thought him the chief magician or sorcerer, to whom they saw the Magi flock so swiftly.

Thus they craftily directed them first to Herod and to Jerusalem, the chief city of the Jews, so that by consulting them they might betray the one whom they sought. For one who does not fail to know when human intercourse has occurred could not unreasonably have known that he was born of a Virgin, whose intercourse with no man he knew; and, whether through the angel first sent to Mary or through the angels afterwards appearing to the shepherds, he could either have known with certainty or suspected how excellent this person was and how opposed to his own malice.

Other preceding signs contained in ecclesiastical histories could also have sufficiently indicated to him how great an excellence of things was soon to be born. Such are those which Paulus Orosius recounts in Book VII of the *Antiquities from the Founding of the City*.

> [Note: Col. 0410D; *Patrologia*, vol. 31, col. 1052.]

There he teaches that, when Caesar Augustus was bringing triumphs from the East, such peace was bestowed by the Lord upon the world that Augustus himself, with all wars stilled and ended, completely shut the gates of peace, in whose temple arms were kept. Thus the prophecy of Isaiah, promising the greatest peace to the world at the Lord’s coming, was fulfilled even in the literal sense: “They shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles; nation shall not lift sword against nation, nor shall they train for war any more” (Isa. 2:4).

> “On this day,” says the aforesaid Paul [Note: Col. 0411D; *Patrologia*, vol. 31, col. 1052], “that Augustus was first hailed, and on that day the supreme control of affairs and powers began and remained in the hands of one man, which the Greeks call *monarchy*.”

Moreover, he says that this was the same day [Note: Col. 0411D: Ibid., col. 1053], the eighth day before the Ides of January, on which we today celebrate the praises of Epiphany for the supreme King. On this day the Magi, the faithful firstfruits of the Gentiles, came as if to hail [Col. 0411B] and worship him, judging him another Augustus—or rather more than Augustus—whom heaven and earth alike proclaimed through such great signs, both at Rome, the head of the Gentiles, and at Jerusalem, as has been said, the chief city of the Jews.

For the same Paul relates in the same treatise [Note: Col. 0412D: Ibid.] that, in the time of the aforesaid emperor, about the third hour, on a suddenly clear and cloudless day, a circle in the appearance of a heavenly rainbow surrounded the orb of the sun; and that at Rome, under the same Caesar, a most abundant flow of oil issued from the *taberna meritoria* for an entire day. What else, indeed, did these things foreshadow except that at that same time one would be born who would hold the monarchy both of heaven and earth? For what did the aforementioned crown of the sun, or the anointing flowing from the earth, promise except a king of heaven and earth alike?

The Savior himself is called both the sun of righteousness and Christ, from *chrisma*, that is, “anointed,” from anointing. The latter is the abundant anointing granted to him according to his human nature; the former is the full and perfect bestowal upon him of spiritual gifts and sevenfold grace, of which it is said to him: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:2). From the fullness of this anointing, as it is written, we have all received (John 1:16); oil flows abundantly from the tavern, according to the words said to him: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2).

For his assumed humanity was, as it were, a tavern or tabernacle, in which, as the Apostle recalls, “the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” [Col. 0411D] (Col. 2:9). Therefore, from this humanity of his, anointed, as we have said, with gifts of divine grace, grace flows down into us; and oil, as it were, flows abundantly from the tavern throughout the whole day. By “the whole day” he means this time of grace, which the Lord illuminated by the presence of his coming, concerning which the Apostle says: “The night has passed; the day has drawn near” (Rom. 13:12). Throughout this whole day oil flows without failing from that our head to the members, because this time is especially called the time of grace from his fullness [Col. 0412A].

Hence his very name, Christ, is rightly said to denote also the abundance of this grace, as ointment poured out and spread abroad in us, because, marked by his name, we are called Christians from Christ. The *taberna meritoria* is thought [reading: “is considered”] to have been a house in which retired soldiers were supported. It could provide more abundantly for their daily needs in proportion as its portico was more richly stocked with goods for sale.

At this site the Basilica of St. Mary, still shown at Rome and named from the oil that poured forth, is renowned. That house, which was a place of favour to those who had served well, is fittingly compared to the humanity assumed by the Lord, through which God was propitiated toward all the faithful.

For who does not see that it was done at the prompting of the Holy Spirit that Augustus, preeminent in such exalted glory, altogether forbade himself to be called “lord,” and did not permit himself to be so addressed even in jest, but allowed only the title Augustus? It was as though by a divine disposition he reserved the honor of this title for the coming Christ, who said to his disciples: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (John 13:13). Therefore, the Lord himself, regarding Augustus’ humility when he said, “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt. 22:12), decreed to exalt the proper name of Augustus so greatly that thereafter Roman emperors gloried in being generally called Augustuses; and what had formerly been a proper and personal name became a general and imperial title [Col. 0412C].

We see him plainly opposed in humility to his uncle Julius Caesar. For the latter, as Lucan also recalls, retaining in himself the ranks of every dignity, permitted himself to be referred to no longer in the singular but in the plural, regarding himself no longer as one person but as many according to the multitude of dignities. Our pride still emulates this as much as it can, embracing the glory not only of possessions but also of names so eagerly that we glory in being called not only abbots but even lords; and, although we ought to be more humble, we consider it a grave injury if another person omits the subordinate title in addressing us.

Nor is this alien to the time of grace and true freedom: Augustus entirely removed every class of slaves from his own dominion and would not permit anyone to be oppressed by slavery under himself. He delighted in the freedom of all, choosing rather to benefit them as friends than to rule them as slaves, and seeking to be loved rather than feared.
