Indeed, he strove so greatly to extirpate slavery from his realm that, as the aforesaid historian recalls, he restored all slaves whose masters he found to those masters, but caused all the remaining slaves to be killed, lest their posterity remain in the kingdom.

What else did this prefigure [Col. 0413A] than the Christian freedom to come and the removal through Christ of the slavery both of the Law and of sin? For he said: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15). And elsewhere: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36). Thus the Apostle, distinguishing the time of fear under the Law from the time of grace, writes to Jews converted among the Romans: “For you are not again subject in fear,” etc. (Rom. 8:15). And to the Galatians he says: “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not make freedom an occasion for the flesh, but serve one another through love” (Gal. 5:13).

Some maintain that the aforementioned Magi were not so called because they were sorcerers, but because they were skilled in the stars—astronomers, as it were—or because they were so named for some other reason. It is not inappropriate here to set down what Chrysostom reports had been written of them in ancient times. For the aforesaid teacher says, while expounding Matthew:

> “I read in someone that these Magi received from the books of Balaam the diviner their knowledge of the appearing of that star, whose prophecy is also set down in the Old Testament: ‘A star shall arise from Jacob,’ etc. (Num. 24:17). And I heard some people report concerning a certain writing—though not certain, yet not destructive of faith, but rather pleasing—that there was a certain people dwelling at the very beginning of the East near the Ocean, among whom a certain writing was said to be preserved under the name of Seth, concerning the appearance of this star and the offerings of such gifts. This was handed down through generations of studious people, fathers relating it to their sons.
>
> “Accordingly, they chose among themselves twelve men more studious than the rest and lovers of heavenly mysteries, and set themselves to await that star. If one of them died, his son, or someone from his relatives found to be of the same disposition, was appointed in the dead man’s place. In their language they were called *magici*, because in silence and with a quiet voice they glorified God.
>
> “Each year after the threshing harvest, they climbed a mountain situated there, called in their language the Mountain of Victory. It had in it a cave in the rock and was most delightful with springs and choice trees. Ascending it, washing themselves, praying and praising God in silence for three days, they did this in every generation, always expecting that perhaps in their own generation that star of blessedness might arise. At last it appeared to them, descending over that Mountain of Victory, bearing in itself, as it were, the form of a small child and, above itself, the likeness of a cross. It spoke to them, instructed them, and commanded them to set out for Judaea.
>
> “As they travelled, the star went before them for two years, and neither food nor drink failed in their bags. The remaining things reported to have been done by them are briefly set down in the Gospel. Finally, when they had returned, they remained worshipping and glorifying God more diligently than before; they preached to everyone among their own people and instructed many.” [Col. 0414A]

We read that the deaths of earthly kings or changes of kingdoms are customarily signified by certain stars called comets; not new stars, however, but ones newly putting forth from themselves something like a lock of hair. Hence comets, as though from *coma*, “hair,” are called “hairy.” But the new manner of birth of the supreme King, as also his conception, ought to have been prefigured by a new star of incomparable brightness. His death too, as if in terror or grieving at the enormity of the crime, the darkened sun announced to the whole world, so that heavenly signs might testify to the glory of both the rising and the setting of the true Sun and heavenly King.

Some are greatly puzzled how the Magi could have travelled from the East all the way to Bethlehem in so few days, that is, from the Lord’s Nativity to the Theophany. They would rightly wonder at this only if it were established both that this star had not appeared before the Lord’s birth and that the Magi had not then begun their journey. But since Chrysostom, from the writing mentioned above, recalls that they had the guidance of the appearing star while travelling for two years, and at last reached Jerusalem after the Lord had already been born, the question disappears.

Perhaps this causes even greater puzzlement: how did so great a radiance of the star, as is said, move the Magi alone and remain undiscovered by Herod and the others, especially since many judge it to have been nearer than the other stars, so that by coming above the child it might more precisely indicate the place? But since nothing is believed impossible to God, there is no doubt that he concealed the star from whom he wished and revealed it only to those worthy of it. These Magi may also have possessed such knowledge of the stars beyond others that they alone noticed the new star and did not go astray in its movement or station.

For, since it is written that they “saw it in the east” (Matt. 2:9), and again that “the star went before them until, coming, it stood over where the child was” (ibid.), it is clearly evident that they had the guidance of the preceding star from their own land to Jerusalem and again from Jerusalem to Bethlehem. Therefore, when it is written that, as they departed from Herod, “behold, the star which they had seen in the east went before them” [Col. 0414D] (Matt. 2:9), and again, “When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy” (ibid., v. 10), it is sufficiently indicated that, through their association with Herod or the impious city to which they turned aside, they lost sight of the star for as long as they were there. We believe this happened chiefly so that the Lord might signify to them that he did not at all wish to be known by Herod and those wicked men.

Some think that these Magi were kings, according to the Psalmist’s prophecy: “The kings of Arabia and Saba shall bring gifts” (Ps. 71:10). Hence Isidore, *Against the Jews*, chapter 13, says:

> “Because the Magi offered him gifts, Isaiah says: ‘At that time a gift shall be brought to the Lord from a terrible people’” [Col. 0415A] (Isa. 18:7).

This refers to the Persian people, terrible and such that no nation could be compared with its power. David also speaks of these gifts: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands,” etc. (Ps. 71:10). For the East had kings who were Magi.

As to how many these Magi were, many suppose from the number of the threefold offering that there were three, although this is defined by no authority of Scripture. Yet according to what Chrysostom reported above, twelve Magi are recalled, as though even in these firstfruits of the Gentiles the first apostles among Christ’s disciples were prefigured. Since the present solemnity, as we have said, is distinguished not only by the miraculous appearance of the star, but also by the Lord’s baptism and the miracle at the wedding, it is pleasant to recall a few things about these also in praise of this greatest day.

The Evangelist says: “When all the people were being baptized, and Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in bodily form like a dove. And a voice came from heaven, saying: ‘You are my beloved Son; in you I am well pleased’” (Luke 3:21).

That the Lord came with the people to baptism and deigned to be baptized amid the crowds is a great sign of humility and a fitting sign of mystery. For he was baptized with the others, but we nowhere read that he was circumcised with others. From this it is not unreasonable to infer that circumcision is no longer necessary to God’s people in the way that the sacrament of baptism is, which is evidently instituted by him for all universally [Col. 0415C].

That, once baptized, he turned to prayer plainly indicates that those who have been baptized always need to ask for divine aid, so that they may be able to remain in the sanctification which they have received, and thus have opened to them the gate of heavenly life. This is immediately shown when, at his baptism and prayer, the heavens are said to open and the Spirit is reported to descend. Baptism opens heaven, and prayer obtains for us the grace of perseverance.

Although many were baptized with Jesus, no one other than he is remembered as having heaven opened over him or the Spirit descend upon him, because whoever is not contained within his body, which is the Church, is excluded both from the gate of heaven and from the grace of God. For he alone is the one who opens [Col. 0415D], and no one shuts; through him it is necessary for everyone who is to be saved to enter into life.

Regarding the dove, in which the Holy Spirit is shown figuratively, as also regarding the star, it should be understood that both were newly created from the elements; having fulfilled the function for which they were created, they ceased to exist and were dissolved back into those same elements. But the Spirit, who through the presence of divinity is everywhere and in his incorporeal, invisible substance cannot descend locally anywhere, is nevertheless said to have descended upon the Lord in bodily form like a dove: namely, because, to demonstrate the fullness of the Holy Spirit which he always possessed, that real dove—although newly created—alighted upon him, according to the prophetic saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim to the gentle” (Isa. 61:1). Thus fittingly it was in such a bird, believed above all others to be so mild and gentle that it is said to lack the gall of anger. How greatly this Lamb of God excelled in gentleness and innocence, as the Baptist himself testifies concerning him, all his works and commands declare; they breathe such sweetness of love that one may not even be angry with enemies.

Nor should it be thought that the Holy Spirit was seen in the form of a dove in such a way as to be incorporated into it in any respect, or united to it in person; rather, he used it merely as a sign, just as he did those fiery tongues [Col. 0416B] in which he was manifested above the apostles. Hence blessed Augustine also observes [Note: [Col. 0412D] Ibid.] [Note: [Col. 0415D] Sermon 264, *Patrologia*, vol. V, col. 1079.] that we never read that the Holy Spirit is called less than the Father according to any union of nature, whereas the Son, according to his assumption of humanity, testifies that the Father is greater than he.

When the dove rested upon the Lord, distinguishing him from the rest, and when the Father pointed him out, as it were, by his finger—which is understood to be the Spirit—the Father’s voice was heard from above. That voice, spoken in the person of the Father, was produced in the air, whether through an angel or formed in whatever other way. For the Father does not possess a body, nor does he ever assume one, so that he himself might form a voice by bodily instruments. It was carefully said [Col. 0416C], not “in whom he was pleased,” but “in whom he was well pleased,” so that he might indicate not merely that the Head himself pleased him, but also proclaim acceptable to himself, with and through him, his members as well.

It remains, finally, briefly to consider the third appearance of the Lord’s manifestation: namely, in the miracle at the wedding. John relates concerning this (John 1:43) that, on the third day after Philip’s calling—that is, three days after this calling—the wedding took place, to which Jesus and his disciples were invited. That the Lord deigned to come to a wedding and to honour it both by his presence and by the benefit of a miracle plainly condemns the heresy of those who condemn marriage.

There are certain clerics who, taking this very deed of the Lord as an example [Col. 0416D], bear with resentment and take it hard that the authority of the holy Fathers has decreed to abstain from, and has forbidden, attendance at wedding banquets. They fail to consider why the Lord did this, and why it was also fittingly forbidden later. The Lord came to the wedding not in order to fill himself with fleshly food—for he could not be moved by any temptation—but rather in order to sanctify it by his presence, to draw to himself by the greatness of the miracle the bridegroom himself, as they say, and, being himself a virgin, to prove that the union of marriage is not to be condemned.

If, then, any cleric trusts that he has an occasion of such great appropriateness, let him attend without fear: [Col. 0417A] let him do what Christ did, and we grant him leave. But since human life is temptation, and especially amid feasting sobriety is lost, decency endangered, and sensual excess strengthened, such banquets must be avoided all the more because their life ought to excel in virtues. Moreover, when the Lord refreshed the guests by turning water into wine, he plainly showed that he had not come to the wedding from need of food, but, like those who contribute a customary gift, had put in more than he took out. For he is the one who receives nothing gratis, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:35).

Therefore let the whole Church consider, from what has been said, how much it owes to this present solemnity. Today the new star, as by a kind of preaching, converted the Magi, the first fruits of the Gentiles, to faith [Col. 0417B] and brought them to Christ. Therefore we, who have come by a calling from the Gentiles, should especially celebrate this feast as the beginning of our conversion. In Christ’s baptism, too, let us reverence the very beginning of all Christianity, commended to us. Finally, the honour shown to marriage by him is great consolation for the weakness of married persons. He did all things well; and blessed be he for ever. Amen.

## SERMON V. ON THE PURIFICATION OF SAINT MARY

“When we were children,” says the Apostle, “we were enslaved under the elements of the world. But when the fullness [Col. 0417C] of time had come, God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law, that we might receive adoption as sons. And because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying: ‘Abba, Father.’ Therefore he is no longer a servant but a son; and if a son, then an heir through God” (Gal. 4:3).

This present passage of Scripture plainly indicates the degree of perfection in both doctrine and life by which Christians ought to excel, distinguishing the fullness of the time of grace from the imperfection of earlier times, and the perfection of the Gospel from the law’s beginning. “When we were children,” he says, and so forth. This whole Epistle written to the Galatians is directed particularly against those who, after conversion from Judaism, wished to restore the former burden of the law, judging the perfection of evangelical teaching insufficient for salvation. Including himself among them as one likewise converted, the Apostle says: “When we were children,” and so forth.

It is evident that when little children are first applied to the discipline of letters, they learn the shapes and pronunciations of individual letters before they can form whole sentences. Thus “the elements of the world” here mean the imperfect teachings of the law, first given through Moses to a carnal people and lovers of the world—children in both doctrine and life. For, as the same Apostle writes to the Hebrews, “the law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:19); but what its imperfection lacked for the completion of righteousness, the abundance of the Gospel supplied. Hence, when the Lord gave the New Testament to his disciples, he said: “Unless your righteousness exceeds …” (Matt. 5:20).

It is also fitting that the teachings of the law, given to an unformed people, should be compared to letters rather than words or sentences. Letters lack meaning. And the understanding of the law, like the killing letter, veiled beneath mystical words, was not disclosed to that unformed people. Thus the Jews had the words of the law as letters, because they did not understand in them the spiritual and mystical senses, in which the chief usefulness of understanding consists. This spiritual understanding is “the spirit of life in the wheels” (Ezek. 1:20), without which the law itself is comparable to the killing letter. Those who are content with the letter’s meaning alone and establish in that their limit of righteousness turn that very letter into death for themselves.

For, as blessed Jerome observes: “It is the part of servants to fear; of sons, to love.” Those serve under these elements who are compelled to obedience as servants by fear of the penalties established in the law, when it says, “Tooth for tooth,” and so forth (Exod. 21:24), rather than led as sons by love. Hence later the Apostle himself, distinguishing the two Testaments through Hagar the slave-woman and Sarah the free woman, declares that the one bears, or as it were creates, a people for God in slavery and the other in freedom, for obedience to him. Therefore the one is called the Testament of slavery, the other the Testament of freedom; the one of fear, the other of love; the one of beginning, the other of perfection.

Of this perfection he now adds: “But when the fullness of time had come” (Gal. 4:24). By “the fullness of time” he means the perfect age of the world, after that period of children which he mentioned first. For Christians are no longer to be called children in life or teaching, as those people were. The fullness of time is also called the completion of what had been promised concerning Christ’s coming. Such are the words of the patriarch Jacob: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah,” and so forth (Gen. 49:10); and the passage in Daniel (Dan. 9:24) concerning the number of weeks of years and the cessation of institution or sacrifice, when the Holy of Holies will be anointed.

This fullness is therefore a kind of ending of the law: when its rite failed and Moses died, the Gospel succeeded the law and the true Joshua succeeded Moses, so that things begun in the former might be completed in the latter. “When it came,” he says [Col. 0418D]. For even if God delays what he promises, he is never late. Rather, he so orders individual times that in them he accomplishes what he promises. Thus Habakkuk says: “Though he delay, wait for him; for he will surely come and will not be late” (Hab. 2:3). This had been promised concerning Christ long before his advent.

To delay and to be late are different. To delay is to defer for some interval of time what is to be done. But something is properly called late when it is deferred beyond the time when it seems it ought to be done. Therefore, even though God postpones the fulfillment of what he promises, he can never be late, because he does not act more slowly than he ought. This is plainly shown also by the repetition: “For he will surely come”; that is, when it is fitting, he will do it without delay and without hindrance. Concerned for our salvation, the Lord does not delay to fulfill his promise insofar as he judges it necessary for us. Would that we likewise, being concerned for that salvation, were ready to obey without delay!

“God sent his Son,” namely, the Father. For because the Father is from no one, he cannot be sent by anyone. But the Son and the Holy Spirit are said to be sent to us by him when they do something for us or in us, because, just as they have their being from him, so from him they have what they do and do it. The Son plainly professes this concerning both himself and the Spirit, saying: “I do not speak from myself,” and, “I do nothing from myself” (John 14:10); and again concerning the Spirit: “He does not speak from himself” (ibid. 16:13).

“His,” he says—that is, his own and consubstantial Son, not an adopted one [Col. 0419B]. “Made of a woman,” because he was made temporal according to the humanity which he assumed from the mother from whom he was born; he was not made according to the eternity which he has from the Father. Some here say “born of a woman” rather than “made of a woman.” But the Apostle more carefully says here “made” rather than “born,” in order plainly to distinguish this birth from the birth which is from the Father, showing it to be temporal by these words.

Bede, on Luke: “Blessed is the womb that bore you,” and so forth (Luke 11:27). “For those are not to be heard who think that one should read, ‘born of a woman, made under the law,’ rather than ‘made of a woman.’ In the womb of the Virgin he drew flesh neither from nothing nor from elsewhere, but from maternal flesh. Otherwise he would not be called the Son of Man, if he did not have his origin from a human being.”

Lest what was done for us as an example of humility should seem too small—namely, that the Lord was incarnate from the lower sex—it is added that he was also made under the law; that is, he fulfilled obedience to the law, not from necessity but by dispensation. For there were no sins in him for which the sacraments of the law were necessary. Yet he was circumcised according to the custom of others, presented in the Temple with offerings, and his mother observed the legal purification according to the custom of women, although there was nothing in her requiring purification. For she who conceived and bore from the Holy Spirit owed nothing to the law in the rite of purification.

Therefore, when the Evangelist says, “the days of her purification” (Luke 2:22), although, as has been said, in her case there was no guilt to be purified under the law, he called the rite of purification “purification,” not its effect [Col. 0419D]. Since that rite, established in the law, was imposed only upon women who had borne after receiving a man’s seed, it is plainly shown that she who conceived and bore as a virgin was in no way subject to this law. Furthermore, the words “opening the womb” (ibid., 23) are judged not to apply to her whose integrity was not broken by any opening. For he was born while his mother’s womb remained closed, who later entered among the disciples while the doors were shut.

Thus the mother, like the Son, observed the law in its sacraments, not from any necessity, as has been said, but by a great dispensation of humility. Nor were they made subject only by obeying divine law, but also human law. For we read of the mother [Col. 0420A] that she travelled with her husband to Bethlehem in order to submit to the requirement of Caesar’s census; and during that journey, while they remained there, she gave birth to her only-begotten Son. Later he too, as has been said, obeyed not only God’s law but also the law of the world: he paid Caesar’s census-tax and instructed others to pay it, saying, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21).

It is written in Matthew: “When they had come to Capernaum, those who collected the didrachma came to Peter and said: ‘Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?’ He said: ‘Yes.’ When he had entered the house, Jesus anticipated him and said: ‘What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth receive tribute or tax—from their sons or from strangers?’ He said: ‘From strangers.’ Jesus said to him: ‘Then the sons are free. But lest we offend them, go to the sea and cast a hook. Take the first fish that comes up; and when you open its mouth, you will find a stater. Take it and give it to them for me and for yourself’” (Matt. 17:23 ff.).

He is therefore rightly said to have been made under the law: although he owed absolutely nothing to the law, he humbled himself under both the law of God and that of the world. Being both Son of God and Son of Man, he subjected himself through the law to both God and human beings, lest anyone perhaps, through the fear of pride, should despise the superior authority of any power.

Behold, brothers: he who claimed freedom for himself did not exempt even those free from the census or tax owed to secular authorities. We are sons of men, and have ourselves made ourselves slaves to God out of a servile condition or the lowliest common people; and in this respect we have had earthly masters favourable to us, who, at a loss to their own lordship, emancipated us and dedicated us to God, preferring his lordship to their own. When these masters themselves come before us, they bow their heads, reverence our habit, and worship God in us. We now securely receive the petitions of those at whose sight we formerly trembled. They acknowledge us as their masters, whose grievous lordship we fled, perhaps choosing this freedom more from necessity than choice.

Freed from the law of the world and its intolerable yoke, we have received his sweet yoke and light burden, whom to serve is to reign. This is a great dignity and an excellent freedom, if it is not so much bodily as spiritual, and if we flee not so much the slavery of men as that of vices. For it is neither shameful nor harmful to serve human beings, but to serve vices; and the Lord came to remove not this slavery but that one. The Apostle says that he was made under the law in order to redeem those who were under the law.

What is this, brothers: that he assumed the law and so freed us from its burden, and spared not himself so that he might spare us? What, I ask, was this plan: that he did not first overthrow it in himself and then afterward free us from it by his own example? Attend, then, to the highest counsel of the supreme counsellor, and to the great depth of the providence of heavenly wisdom. Certainly, if he had refused to assume the burden of the law—of which he himself said, “The law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16)—he would seem to condemn it as though not given by God, and to set it aside not so much because it was useless as because its commands were difficult.

Hence this passage occurs in the homily of Bishop John on the betrayal of Judas: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” (Mark 14:12). “Not that which is ours, but that of the Jews. The disciples indeed prepared that one; but he himself established that which is ours. Yet he himself became the Passover. And why did he eat that Passover? Because he fulfilled all things belonging to the law. For when he was baptized, he said: ‘Thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness’” (Matt. 3:15). Likewise: “God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, in order to redeem those who were under the law,” and to give rest to the law itself. And lest anyone say that he annulled it because, being burdensome and arduous, he was unable to fulfill it, he first fulfilled it and thus caused it to rest.

He was therefore made under the law so that he might more fittingly free us from the law, transfer us from slavery to the law into the freedom of the Gospel, and lead us from the fear of servants into the love of sons. For free is the person whom fear does not compel to serve, but whom love makes voluntarily obedient. Carefully considering these two things—the freedom of sons, whose perfect love casts out fear, and the condition of servants—the same Apostle writes at one point to the Romans: “For you have not received the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry: ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15).

And in this same Epistle: “You have been called to freedom, brothers; only do not give freedom [Col. 0421C] as an occasion for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one saying: ‘You shall love your neighbour as yourself’” (Gal. 5:13). Observe, brothers, that after saying, “God called us to freedom,” he immediately added, “Only do not give freedom as an occasion for the flesh.” It is as if he said: Take care of this one thing in the obedience of freedom: lest perhaps, because we do not fear the law’s penalty, taking occasion from impunity, we serve the flesh more securely and bodily freedom destroy spiritual freedom.

Anticipating this occasion elsewhere, he said to the Romans: “Sin shall not have dominion over you. For you are not under the law but under grace. What then? Shall we sin because we are not [Col. 0421D] under the law but under grace? By no means! Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are servants of the one whom you obey—whether of sin unto death or of obedience unto righteousness?” (Rom. 6:14). By these plain words he forbids the dishonourable and harmful slavery of sin, though he often commands service to human beings. Such is the saying: “Let every soul be subject to higher authorities. For there is no authority except from God” (Rom. 13:1). And again: “Were you called as a servant? Do not let it concern you; but if you can become free, make use of it rather. For the one called in the Lord is a servant; you were bought at Christ’s price; do not become servants of men” (1 Cor. 7:21).

For in order that we may serve God more freely, we ought to seek human servitude less. Yet, if we have already incurred it, it is unjust to withhold from them the service owed, since by this service the servitude of Christ is preserved more humbly. Thus he says again: “Servants, obey your carnal masters with fear and trembling, in simplicity of heart, as to Christ; not serving to the eye, as pleasing men, but as servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the soul, serving with good will as to the Lord and not to men” (Eph. 6:5). For when a human being is served for God’s sake, service is rendered more to God than to the human being. Hence it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6:13).

In order that this service might be free, the Lord himself, made under the law, redeemed us from the slavery of the law, that we might receive adoption as sons. The Son of God came, brothers, to make us sons and to raise us from servants into sons. Hence the Evangelist says: “He came unto his own, and his own did not receive him. But to as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:11–12). For this reason, as this same Apostle writes to the Hebrews, he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying to the Father: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers” (Heb. 2:12). And in the Gospel he says to Mary: “Go to my brothers and tell them: ‘I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God’” (John 20:17).

Removing altogether the name of servants from sons, in accordance with Isaiah’s saying, “He will call his servants by another name” (Isa. 65:15), he says to them: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15:15). For Christ’s friends are the same as God’s sons: subject to God through love [Col. 0422C] of righteousness rather than fear of punishment. This is the true freedom of which he himself says: “If the Son sets you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8:36). Moses, though faithful in God’s house, as the Apostle himself writes to the Hebrews, was nevertheless his servant, not a son; nor could he liberate, who brought the bondage of the law.

But Christ, made a curse for us, just as he was made under the law, freed us from the law’s curse and from the intolerable yoke which he assumed. He was made a curse for us according to the law when he endured the shameful gibbet of the cross, which the law had established as a curse—that is, a punishment—for the guilty, especially blasphemers. Therefore, by undergoing this curse of the law, that is, its punishment, he freed us from the law’s entire curse, so that now none of us, whatever offence he commits, ought to be punished on account of a precept of the law. Rather, the laws of the world are retained for the punishment of evildoers, more than divine law; Caesar’s enactments rather than God’s, lest that proud Jewish people have anything of which they may boast.

Yet we understand these laws of the world to be permitted, not commanded, for Christians, so that a place may be reserved for mercy. This was by no means allowed under the law, which compelled every act of vengeance by command. For the New Testament contains no command of vengeance, but only of mercy; it restrains wickedness not by fear of punishment, but by love of righteousness. No one, indeed, is to be called so innocent who ceases from evil through fear rather than will; wickedness must be said to belong more to the mind than the body, just as virtues and vices pertain only to the mind, not the body.

Therefore, in order to make true innocents, Christ transformed necessity into will and fear into love. He especially enlarged and brought that love to perfection by wishing to assume the burden of the law from which he had come to free us—thus making himself more favourable to us than to himself. Hence he is now rightly said to have been made under the law, though he was not subject to it, in order to redeem from slavery to the law those whom he would adopt as God’s sons. For he, the only-begotten of God, is alone his natural and consubstantial Son. Since his supreme goodness could not have brothers who were his own by nature, it sought adopted brothers; nor did he who made them his coheirs wish alone to possess the Father’s inheritance.

How God would accomplish this adoption of sons, the Apostle explains after the sending of the Son by adding the sending of the Holy Spirit: so that the Father possessed nothing consubstantial [Col. 0423B] which he did not bestow upon us by grace, sending to us both his own Son and the Holy Spirit. Concerning the Son, the Apostle himself had said to the Romans: “If God is for us, who is against us? He who did not spare even his own Son but handed him over for us all, how will he not also, with him, give us all things?” (Rom. 8:31). It is as though he said: He who, after such a gift, was unwilling to withhold a gift.

But now, when it is said that not only the Son but also the Spirit was sent to us, the greatest concern of divine goodness toward us is shown: he had nothing his own by nature which he did not share with us by grace. First he sent his Son, that is, his wisdom coeternal with himself, whose teaching might instruct us in what the highest good of salvation consists. Of him it is written elsewhere: “He was the true light, which enlightens …” (John 1:9). He also sent the Holy Spirit: that is, he poured into us his pure love, by which we might love him sincerely for his own sake, seeking in him not so much our own advantages as his glory and honour.

The Son himself also gave this Spirit as his own. Hence, breathing upon the disciples, he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). He also says—he who sent him: “When I have been taken up, I will send him to you” (John 7:16). This love, when it causes us voluntarily to do what the Son taught, adopts us as sons; it does not bind us as servants through fear of punishment. Hence it is now said: “Because you are now [sons],” that is, in order to make you what you already are, “the Spirit has been sent”: that is, God’s love has been poured into our hearts. “The Spirit,” he says, “of his Son,” so that, just as that natural Son obeys through love of the Father, becoming obedient unto death, so we too, as adopted sons, may do so according to our measure.

“Crying, ‘Abba’”—that is, causing us firmly to recognize that we hold him more as Father than as Lord, obeying with filial reverence rather than servile fear. *Abba* is a Hebrew or Syriac name, meaning what is called “father” in Greek or Latin. Therefore, lest this adoption of sons appear to belong only to those of whom he had spoken above as converts from Judaism—“When we were children,” and so forth—he gives words from different languages, by which God is now invoked in different lands, though formerly he was known only in Judaea.

Therefore, because he has given us the Spirit of his Son, none of us is now a servant through God, because he no longer compels anyone to obey through fear of penalties but leads them willingly by love. “And if a son,” he says, “then an heir.” For a servant does not remain forever in the house, nor does he deserve permanent possession of an inheritance, although he is not altogether deprived of recompense. We know, too, that the Jews received no heavenly reward of promise for their obedience, but that only an abundance of earthly goods was appointed to them as reward; fear made them servants, not love sons.

But in order to make us human beings sons of God and his coheirs in the kingdom of the Father—that is, God’s sons—the Son of God deigned to become the Son of Man, sharing in our weakness so that he might share with us the strength of his eternity; and, descending to the depths, raise us to the heights. A blessed exchange for us, Lord, not for you: sharing what is ours, communicating what is yours, made weak so that we might be made strong.

As a figure of this great grace, by which the Church was to be formed from the second Adam, woman was so created from the rib of the first Adam that the Lord did not in truth restore a rib in exchange for the rib, but supplied flesh in exchange for the rib. For what does a rib, which is of bony nature, signify except strength? And what does soft flesh signify except weakness? Therefore, when woman is created from the man’s rib and flesh is supplied in place of the rib, that from which the man was weakened made the woman strong; because Christ’s assumption of our weakness became our strength, and through what weakened him we have, as was said, become strong.

Moreover, this rib was transformed into woman while Adam slept, because the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion makes us strong to endure all things for his sake; and from the very fact that he slept in death for us, he makes us watchful in his commandments, as though we continually said with the Prophet: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation [Col. 0424D] and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:12). The one who shares Christ’s Passion takes the cup of salvation. From this Passion Jesus himself—that is, the Saving One or Saviour—was named, because through it, which he endured, he saved us. We repay Christ, who died for us, chiefly by fighting for him even unto death, fulfilling all that lies within our power. Hence he himself says: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

But because this virtue is not from us, he must be invoked to confer it on us—he who invites us to it by the example of his Passion. He is called the name of God because he brought the world full knowledge of God. For a thing is declared and in some fashion recognized by its name. God gives us certain things and repays us certain things. Yet we can give him nothing, though we can repay something. For he is the one who works in us both willing and accomplishing according to good will. He precedes us so that we may will; he follows us so that we may be able. He helps the very will which he inspires, lest it fail; he freely gives the will by which we merit, and rewards with the recompense of payment the merits which he effects in us. For he rewards in us nothing except his own gifts, so that both merit and reward may be not from us but from himself, bestowed upon us by himself.

May he give us that by which we may merit, to whom it belongs to repay when we have merited. May he offer us to his Father—he who on this day was presented in the Temple with the substance of our flesh. May he fulfill in us what he promised to the faithful, so that each of us who awaits him may be able to say with blessed Simeon: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace” (Luke 2:29). Amen.

## SERMON VI. ON SEPTUAGESIMA

Ecclesiastes, exhorting us to despise the vanity and instability of this life, says: “All things have their time, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted periods” (Eccl. 3:1). And after some intervening words, he adds what we ought to do or expect amid this mutability and uncertainty of life: “A time for weeping, and a time for laughing; a time for mourning, and a time for dancing” (ibid., 2).

“All things under heaven,” he says, “have a time”: that is, they change temporally and, in the manner of time, continually flow away. “Under heaven,” he says, not “above heaven”: for here is vanity, there truth; here decay, there permanence; here uncertain prosperity and joy always mingled with misery; there happiness as unfailing as it is beyond estimation. “All things pass through their allotted spans” (ibid., 1), because the longer a span of life anyone has had, the shorter that person will have left; and the longer each person’s life has been, the shorter it will be. By its own increases, it always hastens toward decline.

Even that which is called life is so entangled with miseries that it ought rather to be called death than life, decline rather than progress, night rather than day, sorrow rather than joy. The philosophers of the world, who especially despised the world, judged this so strongly that, when they saw they had lived many years, they counted as belonging to their life only those days which they remembered having passed without distress. In scarcely a hundred years they found two days which, when dying, they might inscribe on the epitaph of their burial by recording the number of the days of their life.

Jacob the patriarch, a truer philosopher of God than of the world, when Pharaoh asked him how many days of life he had—because the king saw him as long-lived—replied: “The days of the pilgrimage of my life are one hundred and thirty years” (Gen. 47:9). In this question and answer we must carefully observe that, when the Gentile man, as though ignorant of true life, asked about the days of life, the holy man did not at all regard this life as his life, but judged that it should be called the pilgrimage of life rather than life [Col. 0426A]. For, as the Apostle says, “While we are in the body, we are away from God” (2 Cor. 5:6); through exile we hasten toward our homeland, and as it were through death we hurry toward life.

To such people the Apostle says elsewhere: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things above, not on those upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:1). The life of the faithful, he says, is hidden, just as the life of the reprobate is manifest. They regard this exile as their homeland and, like fellow citizens of beasts, bent toward the earth both in body and mind, seek none of the things above and make no effort to be fellow citizens of angels.

For this earth is the homeland of brute animals, and their present life is their own proper life; they were created only for it, both in body and in soul, which here comes to an end. Therefore those are rightly called their fellow citizens who are governed more by senses than reason and, forgetful of the heavenly things for which they were created, desire earthly things alone: they ought to be called beasts rather than human beings. They pursue the bitterness of this life with all the more ardour because they give less heed to the sweetness of the future life. That sweetness was vehemently desired amid royal banquets by the one who said: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” (Ps. 30:20)—those who fear God rather than the world, and harm to the soul rather than harm to the body. This sweetness is called hidden, as though laid up and reserved for them alone in the future, not to be shared with the reprobate.

This is that hidden manna which in the Apocalypse we read that the Lord promised to the faithful: “To the one who conquers,” he says, “I will give hidden manna” (Rev. 2:17), that is, the refreshment of heavenly bread. As its type, the bodily manna refreshed the people in the wilderness; and, as we have said, he too confidently awaited its satisfaction when he said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15). Certainly here he shows himself always hungry, so that he may deserve to be satisfied there, according to that saying of Truth: “Blessed are you who hunger now, for you shall be satisfied” (Luke 6:21). “When your glory appears,” he says, “I shall be satisfied,” because when you refresh me by that vision itself, which is now hidden, nothing remains for me to seek until I arrive there; however much I may meanwhile abound in delights, I shall always recognize myself as a beggar. And elsewhere, panting with all his desire for the blessedness of his homeland and lamenting the exile of the present life, he groans, saying: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged: I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul has been greatly a sojourner” (Ps. 119:5). As though he said: “Woe is me, wandering in the exile of this life and coming so slowly to my homeland!” For what is sojourning except wandering outside one’s native soil? Hence we remember that it is called exile. He therefore laments that his sojourning is prolonged, because the present life—in which, while we are in the body, we are away from God, and as exiles desire our homeland; because, as the Apostle says, “we have here no lasting city, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13:14), just as he himself said, “I desire [Vulgate: having a desire] to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23)—we endure more grievously, and find longer than we would wish, since we seek how soon we may arrive at that homeland which has no end.

Nor does he compare this life merely to a pilgrimage, but also to darkness, in order to show it to be more burdensome: “I have dwelt,” he says, “with the inhabitants of Cedar” (Ps. 119:5), that is, with those who dwell in darkness. For *Cedar* is interpreted “darkness.” In comparison with the brightness above, the condition of the present life should be called darkness, and should be called night rather than day. Hence, repeating the burden of his long pilgrimage, he still groans, saying: “My soul has been greatly a sojourner” (ibid., v. 6) [Col. 0427B]. As though he openly said: “I grieve that I wander here greatly and long, for elsewhere I recognize my homeland.”

Indeed, in the figure of this pilgrimage and homeland, he himself, describing the lamentation of the Israelite people long afterwards taken captive by the Babylonians, says: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion. Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments,” etc. (Ps. 136:1 ff.). For there are two cities, those of the elect and of the reprobate, which are described here under the figures of Jerusalem and Babylon. One, which belongs to the reprobate, prospers here and is called Babylon. The other is continually afflicted here by the former; and the heavier the pressures it endures here, the more intensely it longs for the vision of peace above [Col. 0427C]. Thus the faithful, raising from this life the eyes of their minds to things above, sighing as from exile toward their homeland, and liberated from Babylonian captivity, continually long for the freedom of their city Jerusalem. The present psalm, composed in their person, introduces them lamenting after the manner of exiles when it says: “By the rivers of Babylon,” etc.

The rivers of Babylon are vices. Whoever enters them by consenting to them flows down into Babylon—that is, confusion—because he incurs condemnation. The city of the elect also has its own rivers, of which it is written: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:5). And again: “Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (John 7:38) [Col. 0427D]. Therefore, in contrast to these good rivers, the harmful rivers are called those of Babylon: gluttony, lust, avarice, and things like them. The faithful, observing these as rivers of Babylon, do not enter them through consent; rather, as though sitting above them, they press them down, when they restrain within themselves their movements, like swelling waves, striving with contrary virtues as with the oars of a ship, lest those movements prevail. Thus, sitting upon the deadly rivers, which they perceive as the greatest obstacle and impediment to passage into their homeland, they are remembered to weep, like captives, in recollection of that homeland from which they grieve that they are still delayed, when it is said: “And we wept when we remembered you, Zion” [Col. 0428A].

Zion is the mountain upon which the city of Jerusalem is situated. Through this mountain, therefore, is expressed the height of the heavenly homeland, in which is Jerusalem—that is, the unceasing vision of true peace. Inflamed by desire for it, the faithful continually sigh toward it as though weeping; and from this valley of tears, as from Babylonian captivity, they groan the more heavily that they are held back from it, the more they desire to ascend. The order is fitting: first sitting upon the rivers, and then the laments of weeping are reported, because no one, while subject to vices and enslaved by pleasures, is able through desire to raise himself to the heavenly city; nor, unless we first turn away from evil, do we devote ourselves to good works.

The following words show how greatly the elect flee worldly pleasures, lest a mind weighed down by lust be less able to raise itself to things above: “Upon the willows,” they say, “in its midst we hung up our instruments” (Ps. 136:2) [Col. 0428B]. Willows are unfruitful trees, and they abound in moist places, where the devil, like an unclean swine, wallows and rests; he who wanders through waterless places finds no rest. Hence it is aptly said in the description of Behemoth: “He sleeps under the shadow in the shelter of the reed, in moist places” (Job 40:16). Thus the unfruitful minds of the reprobate, rooted in the flux of carnal pleasures, are willows planted in the midst of Babylon, entangled in the vices of carnal desire, and already submerged in the depth of vices, which is understood as Babylon’s midst.

Among such persons the elect live, while the present life, like a threshing-floor, contains grain and chaff together. They hang up their instruments, since, occupied more with tears and lamentation, they refrain from songs of exultation, lamenting both their own hardships and the delay of their homeland, as well as the death of others [Col. 0428C]. Then, to explain why they hang their instruments among such people—that is, cease from joyful voices, lest they utter in the land of the curse what they judge ought rather to be reserved for heaven—they add: “For there,” etc. That is, those who had taken us captive, mocking us and ridiculing the celebration of our solemnities, as though the God whom we worship could not free us from their hands, “asked us for words of songs.” That is, they taunted us, demanding that we should now also sing as formerly. As though they openly said that the reason for this was evident: we had plainly abandoned him whose help we most often professed, for vain songs. Hence they judge that these divine praises should be called not so much songs as ditties and certain fabrications [Col. 0428D].

These Babylonian henchmen and robbers, through whom we are taken captive and cast down from the delight of paradise—where scarcely one of us had been at rest, as from the earthly Jerusalem, into these miseries—are understood to be demons. Of them it is further added: “And those who led us away”—that is, shook us loose from that delight—“said,” supply: “Sing us a hymn from the songs of Zion” [Col. 0429A]. This is to say: “Turn toward us that praise of God which you uttered in Jerusalem in those songs of yours,” as though, abandoning divine worship, they might serve demons, who promise their subjects what they cannot give. One of them burst into such madness as to dare to say to the very head of the faithful: “All these things I will give you, if, falling down, you worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

To their mockery the elect fittingly reply, and refute their demand in a plain prayer, saying: “How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136:4). This is that teaching of Truth by which he commands the faithful: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7:6). For divine utterances are not to be entrusted to the unclean and to mockers of divine words, who bark against them after the manner of dogs, lest they seem cheapened by derision [Col. 0429B]. He calls the life of unbelievers a foreign land, excluded from the portion of the faithful and subject to demons rather than God. In this manifest possession of demons, the praises of God must be wholly silent, and lamentations rather than songs must be taken up. With these lamentations, as has been said, we should bewail not only the delay of our homeland amid the miseries of this pilgrimage, but still more the devilish deceptions through which so many wretches are deluded.

Here a time for weeping is allotted to us; elsewhere a time for laughter is promised. Concerning this, Ecclesiastes, after the words which we set forth at the beginning of this discourse, adds later: “A time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance” (Eccl. 3:4) [Col. 0429C]. He says first a time for weeping or mourning, and afterwards for laughing or dancing, because present miseries must be lamented, so that, once we are freed from them, the true joys of gladness may follow. Hence also the Psalmist says: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy [Vulgate: exultation]” (Ps. 125:4). Truth himself declares the same: “Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh. Blessed shall you be when men hate you and reproach you on account of the Son of Man: rejoice on that day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven. Yet woe to you rich, for you have your consolation. Woe to you who are filled, for you shall hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep. Woe to you when all men bless you” (Luke 6:21) [Col. 0429D].

And elsewhere, distinguishing this lot of the reprobate and the elect: “The world,” he says, “will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful; yet your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16:20). Immediately comparing that sorrow and the joy which follows it to a woman in childbirth, he says: “When a woman gives birth, she has sorrow; but when she has borne a child, she no longer remembers the distress because of her joy” (ibid., v. 21). What, then, is the childbearing of a woman with the pain of her travail, except the strong works of the faithful soul, which are signified by a son rather than by a daughter? These are those seeds of the faithful mentioned above: “Those who sow in tears,” that is, amid the pressures of this life, as those who gather in summer what they sow in winter. Let us also sow, beloved, weeping, so that we may reap laughing [Col. 0430A].

To this we are especially admonished by the very observance of the present season, which precedes the joy of the Lord’s resurrection with the lamentations of penitence. In it the special cries of joy, “Alleluia,” etc., and “Glory to God in the highest,” are omitted, indicating that this is a time of grief rather than joy, and of mourning rather than song. In it, after the manner of the captives mentioned above, hanging up our instruments and ceasing from songs, we ought to devote ourselves more to sorrow than exultation, always reflecting upon the exile we endure and sighing for the homeland for which we were created. The happiness of that homeland has indeed been displayed in the resurrection of the head to the members, but has not yet been fulfilled in the members themselves. Therefore we ought to long for it all the more ardently as we know more certainly that it has been fulfilled in the head; so that, even after the mourning of penitence, tears over delay may not be absent from those perfect persons who desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.

Thus the whole time of the present life, to be spent in tears either of penitence or of delay, as has been said, is figured for us by this interval of time—from the present day until the octave of Easter—from which it is itself called Septuagesima. For what does the eighth day following the Lord’s resurrection express except the common resurrection of the faithful? This is awaited by the members all the more confidently because it has more certainly gone before in the head [Col. 0430B]. May he himself continually increase in us the desire for it, so that he may draw us from this pilgrimage to our homeland, from this valley of tears to the joy of heavenly blessedness [Col. 0430C]. Amen.

## SERMON VII. ON PALM SUNDAY

Today’s solemnity and, as it were, the joyful triumphal pomp of an imperial procession—by which the Son of God was received by the crowds in royal fashion, recognized and greeted as the son of David—had long before been prophesied by David himself, who exhorts us to it by prophetic revelation: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This has been done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes. This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it. O Lord, save me; O Lord, make us prosper: blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. We have blessed you from the house of the Lord; God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us. Appoint a solemn day amid the dense throngs, even to the horn of the altar” (Ps. 117:22 ff.) [Col. 0430D].

For whom does he call “builders” here except the priests of the Jewish people, who ought to build those subject to them through faith in Christ into the temple of God? They were striving to destroy this very foundation upon which the building was to be raised. For, as the Apostle says, “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid” (1 Cor. 3:10), namely Christ Jesus. This is the rock upon the faith of which the Church endures, as he himself said to Peter (Matt. 16:18), to whom he entrusted it. This is the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which is here said to have been rejected by the builders, but today recognized and received by the crowds: so that, when the builders rejected it, those who were to be built might receive it; the masters be blinded, the disciples illumined, and children resound with the praise of God to the condemnation of their elders [Col. 0431A].

From John’s account we know that there was already a great crowd in Jerusalem today, not only of Jews but also of Gentiles, who had gathered for the approaching feast of Passover. For he himself added concerning the Gentiles: “Now there were certain Gentiles among those who had come up to worship on the feast-day. These approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying, ‘Sir, we wish to see Jesus.’ Philip came and spoke to Andrew. Andrew again and Philip told Jesus. But Jesus answered them, saying, ‘The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified’” (John 12:20) [Col. 0431B].

Therefore, received today both by these Gentiles and by the Jewish populace, the Lord, as the stone rejected by the builders, was made by the Lord the head of the corner, just as it was said of that stone cut without hands that it would grow into a great mountain and fill the whole earth. At the corner of a house, two walls meet, and no corner can be formed except by the meeting of two. We know that in the Church, which is the house of God, two walls, as it were, are raised to meet one another from Jews and Gentiles, as we read was begun today. Hence the Lord himself says: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (ibid., v. 23). As though he said: “The multiplication of believers from both peoples has now begun, through which the Son of Man will afterwards especially be glorified: while he is rejected by the rulers of the Jews, he will be received by the whole world” [Col. 0431C].

He was therefore made the head of the corner, that is, established by the Lord so that, in this joining of the two walls which meet as it were in a corner, he might preside over all the faithful, as the head over the other members of the body; and so that the Church might be made as one person from him, in which he is the head and she the body. The Lord himself declared this today by his action, when, coming to Jerusalem, he first sat upon the she-ass and afterwards upon the colt. The she-ass, the mother of the colt, is the faithful people first converted to Christ from the Jews, such as the apostles and the other believers in the primitive Church; afterwards, by their preaching converting the Gentile people to faith, they begot that people for God as a mother gives birth. One of them said: “My little children, with whom I am again in labor until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). And again: “For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15) [Col. 0431D].

Christ’s sitting upon each people means that he presides over them as rider and ruler, and indwells by grace those whom he justifies. Hence in Proverbs (Prov. 14:33) the soul of the righteous is called the seat of wisdom—that is, the dwelling-place of Christ—because wisdom is called God’s. He comes to Jerusalem with those upon whom he sits, because he leads to the heavenly Jerusalem, the vision of eternal peace, only those over whom he presides here by ruling. Jacob the patriarch likewise signified these two peoples through the she-ass and the colt when, in the type of Christ, blessing his son Judah, from whom Christ himself descended, he said: “And he himself shall be the expectation of the Gentiles, binding his colt to the vine and, O my son, his she-ass to the vine-stock” (Gen. 49:10) [Col. 0432A]. For the Lord himself says to his disciples: “I am the vine and you are the branches” (John 15:5). Therefore the she-ass is bound to the vine—that is, to you yourself, Lord Jesus—and the colt to the vineyard, that is, to the branches of that vine; because you, Lord, by your own preaching joined to yourself the first believers from the Jews, through whom you afterwards converted and joined to them the Gentiles, who never saw your presence in the flesh.

Thus the very act by which the Lord showed himself sitting both upon the she-ass and the colt was long before foretold by this present verse of the Psalm: “He has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117:22), that is, established by God as head, as we have said, of the two walls united in the one house of God [Col. 0432B]. By whom so great a thing was done is added in the words: “This has been done by the Lord” (ibid., v. 23). By this he plainly shows that they labored in vain who strove to overthrow what God had ordained. Thus, conspiring for his death, they said: “You see that we accomplish nothing. Behold, the whole world has gone after him” (John 12:19). “And it is wonderful in our eyes.”

For what is more wonderful in human eyes than the depth of the divine dispensation, concerning which he himself said: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39) [Col. 0432C]? Behold, the teachers of the Law rejected as unknown the one whom they awaited as promised in the Law. The masters erred where the disciples did not err. “Blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter.” The natural branches of the olive tree were broken off, that the wild olive might be grafted in. That people once specially belonging to God deserved, in large part, to be rejected by God through rejecting God; and, as a son estranged, strangers succeeded to their place. This most profound counsel of God came into such admiration among the minds of the faithful that the Apostle himself, crying out over it, says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11:33) [Col. 0432D].

We are exhorted to exult and rejoice in the fullness of grace of this time when it is said: “This is the day” (Ps. 117:24 ff.). As though he said: “This is that time desired by the faithful, which the Lord himself has filled with an abundance of every good.” “Let us exult,” he says, “and rejoice” (ibid.). He repeats the joy, foreseeing the growth of the Church among two peoples. Therefore the psalmist himself, longing with all desire for this grace of time—in which he expected the salvation both of himself and of all the faithful to come—prays, saying: “O Lord, save me” (ibid., v. 25) [Col. 0433A]: “Me, I say, who recognize you, who place my entire hope in you alone as the Jesus—that is, the Savior—of all, however great the blindness with which my people is to be struck. And, in saving, make us prosper” (Ps. 107). That is, deal prosperously in everything you ordain, for those who obey your will unto eternal salvation.

How greatly he ought to prosper in the things he does is shown when the Psalmist adds: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Luke 13:35). “Blessed,” he says—that is, sanctified by God and endowed from his mother’s womb with all gifts of the Holy Spirit. He comes “in the name of the Lord,” just as he himself says: “I came in the name of my Father, and another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 5:43) [Col. 0433B]. He comes in the Father’s name who seeks not his own glory but the Father’s, and who wishes not so much to be known that he may be honored as to make the Father known that he may be glorified. “Who comes,” he says, because at the time of prophecy this was future, whereas in our own time we know it has been fulfilled.

This Psalm pertains so directly to the present day that the people themselves today cried these very words of the Psalm in praise of the Lord. Thus Matthew records: “But the crowds that went before and that followed cried out, saying: ‘Hosanna to the son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’” (Matt. 21:11). Hence Jerome writes to Damasus, *On Hosanna*, in these words:

> “The Hebrew words themselves should be set down. In Psalm 117, where we read, ‘O Lord, save me,’ etc., in Hebrew one reads: *Anna Adonai, Osianna*, etc. And because *Osianna*, which we incorrectly say *Osanna* through ignorance, means ‘save’ or ‘save me,’ this is attested by every interpretation.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0433D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXII, cols. 377–378.]

And after some intervening material:

> “The Hebrews have an interjection, so that when they wish to entreat the Lord they say: *Anna, Domine* [‘I beseech, Lord’], which the Septuagint translated, ‘O Lord.’ But *osi* they interpret ‘save’; *anna* is the interjection of one who entreats. If you wish to make it a compound word from the two, you will say *Osianna*, or, as we say, *Osanna*, with the medial vowel elided.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0433D] Ibid.]

Likewise:

> “Where we read in Latin, ‘O Lord, save me; O Lord, make us prosper’ (Ps. 117:25), according to the Hebrew we may read: ‘I beseech you, Lord, save me; I beseech you, Lord, prosper.’ Matthew, who wrote in the Hebrew language, put it thus: *Osanna barrama*, that is, ‘Hosanna in the highest.’”  
> [Note: [Col. 0434D] Ibid., col. 379.]

Thus, according to Jerome, “Hosanna in the highest” means, as though one said: “We beseech you, Lord, grant us true salvation in heaven” [Col. 0433D].

“We have blessed you.” After the blessing concerning the salvation of the Lord, who was made the head of the corner, the Psalmist turns his words also toward the blessing of the members, as of two walls joined to him, and says: “You who are from the house of the Lord, and who stand in it as two raised walls, you, I say, we have blessed,” etc. That is: “For your sanctification and the future multiplication of the Church, we prophets of the Lord often prayed, and, certain as of an event already completed, praised him” [Col. 0434A]. As a type of this future blessing upon both peoples, Jacob the patriarch is read to have blessed Joseph’s sons Ephraim and Manasseh with crossed hands, that is, hands joined in the form of a cross (Gen. 48). There it is plainly suggested that the salvation of both peoples would consist in Christ’s Passion, and that this blessing had been promised to Jacob himself, as also to Isaac and Abraham, in their seed.

And lest anyone ask how a prophet living so long before Christ’s advent had known from afar that so great a blindness would occur in Israel nearby, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, he answers as though in reply: “The same Lord who now, appearing in person, has illumined these people, shone upon us also concerning this long before. Appoint a solemn day” (Ps. 117:27) [Col. 0434B].

Having said these things, he adds a kind of conclusion, exhorting us to the solemnity of the present day, as though reasoning thus: “Since the Lord so multiplied the Church in two peoples, prefigured by those who went before and those who followed, who are reported today to have received and blessed the Lord, therefore all you faithful who are to give thanks in memory of so great a benefit: ‘Appoint a solemn day amid the dense throngs’” (ibid.), that is, in a great multitude of people, and as in a certain density of spiritual trees, signified by those incomparable branches of palms or olives which the people received today [Col. 0434C].

For what did those branches or fronds torn from trees signify except the gathering of both peoples, taken from the mass of sinners? In representation of them, the people of the faithful on this day fill the whole Church up to the altar with the density of thickets, by means of the branches or fronds of trees which they carry, so that even in the literal sense what is said may appear fulfilled: “Amid the dense throngs, even to the horn of the altar” (ibid.). Mystically, however, the horn of the altar signifies Christ’s sacrifice. For by the altar is understood sacrifice; by the horn of the altar, its extremity. Therefore the sacrifice of Christ, which succeeded the old sacrifice of the Law, is figured by the horn of the altar, because this is the final sacrifice and the supreme offering completing all the others [Col. 0434D].

At the horn of the altar, as in a kind of corner, the two sides of the altar are joined together. Thus, just as above we said that Christ was made the head of the corner, to whom the two peoples are joined, so we may also say that two sacrificial rites meet in Christ’s sacrifice: the holy sacrifice of Melchizedek in bread and wine, and the sacrifice of the Law in animal victims. For both sacrifices went before as figures of ours and met in the signification of it. It is also clear that horned animals, when they come into the clash of battle, possess their greatest force and strength for fighting in the rigidity and power of their horns [Col. 0435A]. Therefore, when Christ, sacrificed for us, overthrew the devil by the power of this sacrifice, he wounded him with his horn, as it were, and cast down the wounded foe.

Christ’s sacrifice, then, is rightly figured by the horn of the altar as by the horn of our calf; because, being efficacious and strong in battle, as has been said, it should be called horned rather than fleshy: rigid, not soft; robust, not weak. The celebration of our solemnity extends even to this horn of the altar, because Christian festivals are adorned by the dignity of so great a victim. Today’s solemnity reaches this horn of the altar in particular because, in its Mass, Christ’s Passion, by which he was sacrificed for us, is read first.

On this day the Lord, coming to Jerusalem, offered himself to the Passion: namely, on the tenth day of the month, as is evident from the Gospel of John (John 11–12) [Col. 0435B]. There we have that, after Lazarus’s resurrection and when the Jews had already entirely conspired to put the Lord to death, the Lord no longer walked openly among them, but went away into the country near the wilderness, to a city called Ephrem, and stayed there with his disciples. Then, when Passover was near, he came to Bethany six days before Passover, the true lamb approaching the sacrifice, to be seized at Passover and sacrificed. From there, coming to Jerusalem the following day, he was received today by the crowds and recognized and greeted as king of Israel and royal heir of David.

Therefore, on the fifth day before that Jewish Passover—that is, today, which was the tenth day of this month—the king came into Jerusalem [Col. 0435C]. For Passover is celebrated on the fourteenth day. He chose to enter on the tenth because this had been prefigured in the Law, where it is commanded: “On the tenth day of this month each shall take a lamb for their families and households” (Exod. 12:3). And shortly afterward: “You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; and the whole multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it in the evening” (ibid., v. 6). On the tenth day of the first month, the lamb to be sacrificed at Passover was commanded to be brought into the house, because the Lord was to enter, on the tenth day of that same month—that is, five days before Passover—the city in which he would suffer.

He therefore fittingly chose this day according to the mystery of the Law, on which, as has been said, he offered himself to the Passion. Before this he had sometimes avoided it, hiding himself; or, when held by the Jews, freely passing through their midst; or frequently withdrawing from them, because his hour had not yet come [Col. 0435D]. On this day, indeed, when he wished to be received all the more honorably by the crowds, he entered the temple and freely drove out all who were buying and selling there; overturned the tables of money-changers and the seats of those selling doves; and, after they had been driven out, healed the blind and lame who came to him in the temple itself. By this he stirred up still more the envy of the wicked against himself, so that they might hasten to carry out what they had long wished to accomplish, and that opportunity might be given by him in those whose will had preceded it. For he himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down” (John 10:18).

No one, certainly, could use force against him so as to kill him, or even seize him, as one unwilling and compelled [Col. 0436A]. But so that those already plotting the Lord’s death might be stirred to greater envy, and be more enraged with God as they saw him honored more highly, he permitted such honor to be paid to himself today as we read was paid to no king. For, passing over the divine praises and the branches or fronds which they spread in the way, how remarkable was that unique honor by which a very great crowd spread garments under the feet of lowly beasts of burden, and would not permit those feet—which bore the Lord himself—to touch them!

Nor should the mystery in this be regarded as slight. Those over whom the heavenly God presides do not touch the earth with their feet, because the affections of those whose desire dwells in heaven do not cling to earthly things; nor do those who seek Christ above and long only for eternal things cast down their minds amid transient things [Col. 0436B]. That we may be able to imitate them, we beseech you, Lord Jesus, make us too your beasts of burden, over whom you may deign to preside in faith and in rule, Savior of the world, of whom it is said in another Psalm: “You will save men and beasts, O Lord, according as you have multiplied your mercy, O God” (Ps. 35:7). Amen.

## SERMON VIII. ON THE SAME DAY

“Now there was a cave, and a stone had been laid upon it; and Jesus said: ‘Take away the stone,’” etc. (John 11:38). The Psalmist, setting the Lord’s mercies above all his works, says: “And his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9) [Col. 0436C]. Remembering the Lord’s mercies, therefore, we ought to glorify him all the more on this account, because we recognize these works of his as surpassing the others and as more necessary for us. Hence he deserved to be honored by the crowds today especially because, taking pity on Lazarus’s grieving sisters, he restored to them their brother, raised after he had already lain four days in the tomb. For John writes that the crowd came out today to meet him because they had heard that this had happened.

Returning with the eyes of our minds to this event as the origin of today’s feast, we ought to contemplate its mystery all the more carefully because this great mercy of the Lord gives greater consolation to sinners [Col. 0436D]. For we read that three dead persons were raised by the Lord, and our teachers have said that all kinds of sinners are represented by them. He raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue while she still lay in the house, before she was carried out; he raised the widow’s son when he had already been carried outside the gate of the city of Nain; and he raised this Lazarus, of whom we now speak, after he had already lain four days in the tomb. Hence he is called dead for four days. These three dead persons, then, signify three kinds of sinners, who are said to revive through the presence of God by the inspiration of grace; and they are more happily raised by the Lord from the death of the soul than those persons from the death of the body.

The dead girl, who was still kept shut up in the house when she was raised, signifies those sinners whose sins, conceived only in the mind, have not yet advanced outwardly through action [Col. 0437A]. The young man carried outside the gate signifies those whose sins have already burst forth into effect, so that they can now be seen by all. Lazarus, however, not merely buried but already dead for four days, signifies those who are weighed down by a great mass of sins through a long habit of sinning, and who, by the example of their sinful practice, corrupt others as well; hence they are said to stink.

These three dead persons, therefore, signify, as we have said, three deaths of the soul: the sin of thought, that is, contempt for God still hidden in the mind and not yet proceeding into action; the sin of action, that is, now made visible through action; and the sin of habit, already long established in action [Col. 0437B]. These three kinds of sins, as three deaths of the soul, are said to be removed from the blessed man in the first Psalm, where he is described as one “who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of mockers.” But since, as we have said, Lazarus’s resurrection is especially known to belong to the present solemnity, let our discourse continue, as we began, with its mystery. That it may do so more carefully, let the narrative be reviewed somewhat more fully.

John therefore relates that, when the Feast of Dedication had taken place at Jerusalem, and the Lord Jesus was there, and the Jews were seeking to seize him, he escaped [Col. 0437C] from their hands and went again beyond the Jordan, where John had been baptizing, and remained there.
