Then, when Lazarus was already ill, his sisters Mary and Martha sent to him, saying: “Lord, he whom you love is ill” (John 11:3). On hearing this, the Lord remained two days in the same place. Then, after telling his disciples that Lazarus had meanwhile died, he came with them to Bethany and found Lazarus already four days in the tomb. And, intending to raise the dead man, he came to the grave. Now, as we have said, it was a cave, with a stone laid over it. And Jesus said: “Take away the stone.” When they had therefore taken away the stone, Jesus cried out in a loud voice: “Lazarus, come forth.” And immediately he who had been dead came out, his hands and feet bound with grave-cloths, [Col. 0437D] and his face bound about with a napkin. Jesus said to them: “Untie him and let him go.” Many therefore of the Jews who had come to Mary and had seen what he did believed in him. But some of them went away to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done. The chief priests and Pharisees therefore gathered a council and said: “What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him,” etc. (ibid., 38–48).

From this it is certainly clear that the Jews were especially stirred against the Lord by this miracle, and that from this time in particular they conspired to kill him: as though by killing him they could destroy the one through whom they knew the dead had been raised; as though one who had raised Lazarus after four days dead could not himself rise [Col. 0438A] after three days. The Evangelist has described this resurrection all the more carefully because it contains more fully the mysteries of our salvation—those whom, as we have said, divine mercy daily and more blessedly raises from the death of the soul than it then raised Lazarus once from bodily death.

For Lazarus, as we have said, already buried and four days dead, signifies that sinner who, through a long habit of sin, has meanwhile been cast down into the deep, so that in that depth, as in a grave, he decays in his fourth day—destroying not only himself, but also corrupting others by his example, as by a kind of stench from his own decay. Therefore he is aptly described as stinking, as one dead four days. For the four days which he spent in the tomb [Col. 0438B] express the totality of sins in which each most wretched person is entangled, as though buried in that depth of vices, concerning which it is written: “When a sinner has come into the depth of vices, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). For when he has persisted in a long habit of sinning, which has now become to him like a second nature, it crushes him beneath a heavy yoke; rejecting and despising the saving exhortations of the faithful or divine warnings. Hence it is necessary for the devotion of the faithful to intercede for him, because of his obstinacy, so that through their intervention he may obtain the regard of divine grace, by which the groaning of repentance may be inspired in him, and, converted, he may be saved.

Thus the sisters rightly intervened for their brother Lazarus to be healed, reporting his sickness to the Lord. Inviting him to help, [Col. 0438C] they judged it enough to tell the Lord of his friend’s death and of their own desolation over their brother’s illness. For their message was: “Lord, behold, he whom you love is ill.” They did not add, “Come and heal him”; they requested what they wanted not so much by praying as by reporting it. They believed it enough to make known to the Lord the distress of his friend and their own, as though observing the proverb: “A friend and a physician are proved in need.” They thought their friendship sufficiently established when they said: “Behold, he whom you love.” Their great confidence in this petition strongly encourages us to ask the Lord steadily for necessary things without hesitation. They intercede for one who is sick but not yet dead, because the supplication of the faithful benefits those still living, not the departed, [Col. 0438D] so that they may have health-giving repentance.

In Mary and Martha all the faithful are comprehended: those of the contemplative as well as of the active life. When their prayers are joined together, they easily obtain even for others what those others do not deserve. It should be noted that, when the Lord came to Bethany, Martha met him, while Mary remained sitting at home. From this the life of the active and contemplative is carefully described. The active are those who, chiefly occupied with their neighbor’s need, procure temporal goods so as to have something to give to one suffering need; and, laboring in outward actions, fulfill those works of mercy [Col. 0439A] concerning which the Lord will say to them: “I was hungry, and you gave me food,” etc. (Matt. 25:35). The contemplative life, however, is that which, ardently kindled by the love of God, attends to him with all the greater purity, raises the eyes of its merits more perfectly toward his contemplation and the condition of the heavenly life, and delights all the more while suspended in this contemplation, the more it rests apart from the cares of the world.

Martha therefore, as one occupied in outward administration, at once met the Lord as he came; but Mary rests, seated at home, attending not at all to these visible goods, but longing for those heavenly joys which eye has not seen nor ear heard. The Evangelist describes her as loving her repose so deeply that she did not leave the house until first called by the Lord, [Col. 0439B] namely when Martha said to her: “The Master is here and is calling you” (John 11:28). Sometimes contemplative persons, by God’s inspiration, are compelled to leave the secret place of inward repose and, when that people calls for them, become entangled in ecclesiastical cares, as happened in the case of blessed Martin. But the more ardently the greater devotion of contemplatives clings to God, the more the Evangelist commends Mary’s devotion, saying: “When Mary came where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet. And she said to him: ‘Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.’ When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her weeping,” etc. (ibid., 32–33). Martha, who had first met the Lord, is nowhere said either to have prostrated herself at his feet in adoration [Col. 0439C] or to have wept over her brother. Martha came first to the Lord because the active life, although later in merits, is nevertheless naturally prior in temporal order. For, as blessed Gregory observes, each person begins with lesser things in order to reach greater ones. The less perfect active life is a kind of beginning for the faithful, in which they first exercise themselves before ascending to the perfection of contemplation.

That the Lord, when about to raise Lazarus, is said to have groaned in spirit and troubled himself, shows in himself what he mercifully works in us. For the greater the sins a penitent has committed, the more he is compelled to groan and be troubled by the horror of Gehenna because of the magnitude of his sins. This man, who is said to have been dead four days, is indicated by those four days already spent in death to have been defiled by every kind of sin. For in him sin first of thought and then of action had passed into habit; and finally, by corrupting others through his example, it had been consummated in death alike—his own and that of others: first, as stated, in thought; second, practiced in deed; third, established in habit; fourth, in the corruption of others.

That the Lord asks, “Where have you laid him?” as though ignorant of the place of the tomb, intimates to us that such persons are especially unknown to God, whose works he more strongly disapproves, according to what he says to the reprobate: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). First he orders the stone removed [Col. 0440A] which weighs upon the dead man, so that the dead may be able to rise; because to such people, lest they despair because of the magnitude of their sins, the forgiveness of the Gospel ought rather to be preached—as it was said to the adulteress, “Go, and sin no more” (John 8:11)—than the harshness of the law written on stone should be brought in for their condemnation.

Thus to one held fast by a long habit of sinning, heavily oppressed under the yoke of wicked custom, and so weakened in free choice that he could not only not rise to seek God, but could not even strive to pray for himself, the merciful Lord comes when he inspires in him the groaning of repentance and raises the sick man wholly bereft of strength. Crying to him in a loud voice, “Lazarus, come forth,” he signifies by the very cry how far this man stands removed from him. “Come forth,” he says: that is, by open confession reveal the fault that is in your mind, and show the wound to the spiritual physician, from whom you may receive the poultice of healing. The Lord calls Lazarus when he inspires in the sinner the groaning of health-giving repentance. In this groaning the dead person comes to life, because the death of the soul—that is, sin—departs through it. For at whatever hour the sinner groans over his sin, he shall be saved. And because after repentance the confession of sin remains, Lazarus, when called, comes forth when the penitent reveals himself through confession of sins and rises from the depth of vices as from a grave.

But because such a person deserved to be excommunicated, and was still bound by the bonds of anathema after expulsion [Col. 0440C] from the Church on account of his manifest crimes, he is said to come forth with feet and hands bound and his face wrapped in a napkin. Anyone excommunicated by ecclesiastical prelates, though already reconciled to God through repentance and confession, must nevertheless be absolved from the bonds of anathema by the same ministers of the Church, so that, once satisfaction has been performed, fellowship with the faithful may be restored to him by those through whom he had been excluded.

He has hands and feet bound when entry into the Church has not yet been granted to him, so that works of satisfaction are imposed upon him according to the quality or quantity of his sins by the prelates: as he is not free to walk where he will, so neither is he free to do what he himself has determined. For one who has long abused his own power by living wickedly ought now to correct his wrongdoing not by his own will but by another’s; in such matters he is no longer subject to his own authority, but to another’s. He also has his face wrapped, because before the completion of satisfaction the devotion of the penitent and his true groaning of repentance cannot be known. For the face, by which each person is recognized, signifies recognition. Thus those who uncover the penitent’s wrapped face, once his prescribed satisfaction has been completed, make his devotion known, as stated, and, by restoring him to the Church, acknowledge him as faithful whom they formerly regarded as unknown, like a heathen or a publican.

The disciples therefore loose the one raised by the Lord and let him go free—the one who had formerly been banished from the Church—when [Col. 0441A] they restore to him entrance into the Church and fellowship with the faithful, and leave to his choice whatever path of life he wishes to follow toward God and whatever works he may choose for this purpose. This is what the Lord says to them: “Untie him and let him go.” Behold: by raising the physically dead man, the Lord, and by loosing the man he has raised, the disciples, set before us a resurrection and a release of righteousness far better than the former, as we have explained.

The Lord performed that miracle once in a body; what he works daily, and far more blessedly, in the souls of penitents. He restored to Lazarus a temporal life, though Lazarus would die again. He grants penitents a life that will endure without end. That miracle was wonderful in human eyes; this is greatest in the judgment of the faithful. And the greater it is, the more it should be desired. This was written about Lazarus, not by Lazarus, nor for him, but for us and on our behalf. “Whatever things,” says the Apostle, “were written, were written for our instruction” (Rom. 15:4). The Lord called Lazarus once, and he was raised from bodily death. He calls us repeatedly, that we may rise more worthily from the death of the soul. He said to Lazarus once, “Come forth,” and Lazarus immediately came out at a single command of the Lord. Every day the Lord invites us through Scripture to confession, exhorts us to amendment, and promises the life which he is ready to give us—he who does not will the death of the sinner. We neglect him when he calls, scorn him when he invites, and despise him when he promises. Set between God and the devil as between father and enemy, we prefer the enemy’s counsels leading to death to the father’s counsels [Col. 0441C] leading to life.

“We are not ignorant,” says the Apostle, “of Satan’s devices” (2 Cor. 2:11): those greatest devices by which he leads us into sin and draws us back from amendment. In suggesting sin, he strips us of the two things by which he can most readily be resisted: fear and shame. For what we avoid, we abandon either through fear of some loss or through the reverence of shame. Honorable persons guard against loss of reputation [Note: [Col. 0441] Supply: “of reputation,” as below, or: “you will incur injury to your reputation.”] more than loss of possessions, just as dishonorable persons do the opposite. Therefore, when Satan drives anyone toward sin, he accomplishes this easily if he has first deprived that person, as we have said, of fear and shame. But once he has accomplished it, he restores to him the same things he had first taken away, so as thereby to draw him back from confession and cause him to die in his sin.

[Col. 0441D] Then he secretly whispers in his mind: “Priests are indiscreet, and it is exceedingly difficult to restrain the tongue. If you confess this or that to such men, it cannot remain secret; and when it becomes known, danger will threaten, or you will incur loss of reputation, or you must suffer harm, or be put to shame by humiliation.” Thus the devil mocks the wretched person: having first taken away from him those things by which he should have avoided sin, he afterward restores the same things by which he may keep him in sin. The captive fears temporal loss, not loss to the soul. He is ashamed before people and despises God. He is ashamed that what did not shame him to commit in the sight of God and of the entire heavenly court should come to human knowledge. He dreads human judgment, though he does not fear divine judgment, of which the Apostle says: “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). And Truth itself says: “Do not fear those who kill the body but have nothing they can do to the soul; rather fear him who can cast body and soul into Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28).

There are illnesses of the soul as there are of the body. Therefore divine mercy has provided physicians for the healing of both. The Lord Jesus himself, calling himself a spiritual physician, says: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Matt. 9:12). Priests hold his place in the Church; to them, as physicians of souls, we must confess our sins, that we may receive from them the poultice of satisfaction. One who fears bodily death does not delay to reveal and expose to the physician for healing whatever part of the body suffers, however secret or however shameful it may be. He endures whatever is hard, whatever is harsh, in order to defer death, though not to escape it. He does not hesitate to give whatever he has that is precious, in order to drive away for a little while this bodily death. What then must be done for the death of the soul, however grievous it may be, when it can be healed forever without great labor or great expense? The Lord seeks us ourselves, not what is ours; nor does he who provides all things need our possessions. For he is the one to whom it is said: “You have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2). Before him each person is greater insofar as he is smaller in his own eyes through humility. He is more righteous insofar as he regards himself more guilty in his own judgment. We conceal our sins there all the more when here we disclose them more readily through confession.

Let us therefore, brethren, who hold ourselves back from confession, consider what is written: “There is a shame that brings glory, and there is a shame that brings sin” (Ecclus. 4:25). And again: “When you come to Babylon, there you shall be delivered” (Jer. 20:6). Shame has a twofold character. One kind is salutary: when we are ashamed that we have committed shameful things in the sight of God. The other is deadly: when, fearing people more than God, we are ashamed to come to confession; or whenever we refuse to do humble things for God lest we seem more contemptible in the eyes of fools. This indeed is the shame that brings [Col. 0442D] sin, because, lest we become contemptible to human beings, we endure becoming contemptible to God. But that shame secures for us true glory by which we do not shrink from becoming contemptible to human beings, in order that we may become glorious to God and be great according to divine rather than human judgment.

When we have come to this Babylon—that is, commendable shame—so that we are ashamed of sin, we shall immediately be set free from it, being then ready for confession and worthy satisfaction. Hence the Psalmist says: “I made my offense known to you, and I did not hide my injustice. I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself,’” etc. (Ps. 31:5). He makes [Col. 0443A] his offense known to God who is not ashamed to confess his sin to God’s vicar holding his place in the Church. For just as Christ testifies that he endures persecution or receives a benefit in his members, saying: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4), and, “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40), so he says that sin is made known to him in his vicars, the priests. The Psalmist immediately explains this when he adds: “And I did not hide my injustice” (Ps. 31:5): that is, accusing in confession not merely his deeds but also wickedness in respect of his merits.

“I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord.’” That is: I resolved within myself and decided to confess my injustice to the priest. “I will confess,” he says, “against myself,” accusing no one else in myself on this account. There are some who, in their confession, in order to diminish their own fault, more readily draw others into blame, saying that they were led—and, as it were, compelled—by others to commit what they committed, whether by the devil or by human beings. Such was the confession when he shifted the blame onto his wife and she onto the serpent, seeming more to excuse themselves than to accuse themselves. Hence they at once deserved to receive the sentence of punishment due to them.

But the righteous person, who, as it is written, is his own accuser at the beginning, excuses himself all the more before the highest and most merciful Judge the more fully he accuses himself; and by accusing himself he obtains pardon, whereas by excusing himself he would incur punishment. For, as Cicero teaches in the *Rhetoric*, a confession of wrongdoing which has received the penalty prescribed by judges may obtain pardon from the higher authority of the senate. Judges, appointed by higher authority and sworn to the laws, do not have the power to remit but to impose the sentence of punishment. But the higher authority, whose prerogative it is both to promulgate the law and to appoint judges, has it within its discretion to temper the rigor of the law and mercifully remit prescribed penalties. For it has no authority above it to fear, which might prevent it from freely extending mercy to whom it has determined.

How much more so that highest heavenly power, which, instructing us concerning that heavenly mercy, says: “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the justice of God more than burnt offerings’” (Matt. 9:13). [Col. 0443D] He calls the justice of God, as it were, his own justice, which he renders to himself as what is especially his and uniquely fitting to him; then indeed he grants mercy, because he is to be glorified by us above all. Hence the same Prophet says: “And his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 149:9).

After first saying, “I said: ‘I will confess against myself,’” etc., the Psalmist immediately turns his speech to God, as though God had appeared and drawn near to him, and says in thanksgiving: “And you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31:5). Whoever is already ready for confession and for undertaking the satisfaction for sin that follows from it is from that very resolve so reconciled to God that, should some unforeseen occurrence prevent him from carrying it out, there is no cause to despair of his salvation, since there remains in him nothing that he does not seek with all the desires of his heart.

For the remission of this impiety every holy person also prays, presuming less upon himself the humbler he is and being more solicitous about himself, always considering what is written: “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Prov. 28:14). He prays, it says, at an opportune and prayer-suitable time—that is, in the present life, full of temptations and ignorance. Hence also the apostolic exhortation: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12). Even one who excelled in the greatest virtues and whose conscience found nothing with which to accuse him nevertheless did not reckon himself righteous on that account, since he could err in judging himself. “But I do not judge even myself,” he says—that is, my own conscience accuses me in nothing; [Col. 0444B] “yet I am not thereby justified” (1 Cor. 4:3–4)—that is, I am not therefore to be called righteous.

For as Solomon says: “The number of fools is infinite, and there is a way that seems right to a person, but its latter end leads to death” (Eccl. 1:15). And again: “Who can say, ‘My heart is clean; I am pure from sin’?” (Prov. 20:9). “For we all stumble in many things” (Jas. 3:2). Indeed, whatever persons remain in unbelief, this happens to them through error. “But the one who judges me,” he says, “is the Lord” (1 Cor. 4:4). As if he said: He does not err in judging me and truly weighs what I am, for all things are naked and open to his eyes.

If holy people presume upon themselves less as they become humbler, and do not cease to pray even for themselves, though righteous, what must we wretches do, for whom prayer must be frequented all the more because we recognize ourselves as more guilty? The more diligently must God’s wrath be appeased, the more his indignation is kindled against us. So that no one may perhaps despair of pardon, the resurrection of Lazarus described above has been set forth as a mystical example. Called by the Lord, he was immediately given life; once given life, he was told to come forth, and no delay held him back. Having come forth but still bound, he was at once loosed by the disciples.

Let us therefore pray, brethren, that the Lord may more blessedly accomplish in our souls dead through sin what was then done in the dead body. May he implant through inward inspiration the true groaning of repentance, [Col. 0444D] by which the penitent, restored to life, may rise from the death of the soul. May he make us ready for confession, all shame laid aside—for we ought to be ashamed of this one thing only: that we should commit anything shameful in his sight. May he deign so to absolve us through the ministers of the Church that we may deserve henceforth to be bound by no chains of sin. May he grant us so to make satisfaction here for our sins that he himself, the strict Judge, may find nothing to punish in the future—our hope and our salvation, whose honor and dominion know neither end nor beginning. Amen.

## SERMON IX. FOR THE SAME DAY

“King Solomon made himself a litter of the wood of Lebanon. He made its pillars of silver, its reclining-place of gold, [Col. 0445A] its ascent of purple. He paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 3:9 ff.).

A *ferculum* is here called, from *ferre*, “to carry,” a vehicle: like the litter of powerful persons or invalids, in which they are borne comfortably. The wood of Lebanon is the two beams of the cross. For *Libanus* is interpreted “whitening.” Therefore the timbers of the cross are timbers of our whitening and cleansing, because upon them was sacrificed the true Lamb, by whose blood we have been cleansed from sins. Thus the Apocalypse says: “These are they who have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7:14). These woods of Lebanon, from which the Lord’s cross was composed, were cedar; and for this reason they are said to be imperishable. Hence Jerome, on the Song of Songs: “According to the historical sense, the litter of the cross was made of cedar woods from Lebanon.”

What is expressed by these imperishable woods except the perpetual remembrance of the Lord’s passion in the hearts of the faithful? The Lord especially commended this remembrance to us when he said: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). And the Apostle: “As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (1 Cor. 11:24 ff.). While the Lord’s passion is proclaimed by preachers, the true Solomon is carried through the world, as it were, upon a litter and vehicle of the cross.

The cross, therefore, composed of two beams, is Solomon’s vehicle. When Christ crucified is preached, he is everywhere borne about in the cross itself as in a vehicle, as has been said. Solomon himself made this vehicle: by stirring the Jews to envy through good works, he moved them to crucify him. Yet this was not done through their compulsion, but solely through his own foreordination and his excellent dispensation. For he himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down” (John 10:18). And again: “I have power to lay down my life,” etc. (ibid.).

He himself made the pillars of the litter silver: these are the utterances of apostolic preaching and the teachings received from his own mouth. Of these utterances the Psalmist had foretold: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire” (Ps. 11:7). Their preaching is called pure because, as one of them says, they did not adulterate the word of God: they bestowed their preaching freely, not intending to sell it in hope of any earthly profit or to set a price upon themselves after the manner of adulteresses or prostitutes. The words of apostolic preaching are called silver because they possess the brightness of understanding, not the obscurity of a veil, as do the Law and the prophecies, which employ words more mystical than open. These, as pillars, support the litter and strengthen the Lord’s cross as they proclaim the power of the passion of the Lord’s cross. And they demonstrate what they say. Hence they are fittingly called *eloquia*, “utterances,” by preeminence, as though set above other expressions of sacred teaching because they are far more advantageous in usefulness. Every utterance is suited to understanding, indeed is discovered and instituted for the single purpose of producing understanding in the hearer. Thus words are to be preferred to others insofar as they are more intelligible and thereby more effectively accomplish what they ought.

Just as we have called the words of apostolic preaching the pillars of the litter, so also we know that the apostles themselves are called pillars because of the power of their words or the grace of miracles given them, by which they confirm what they say. Thus one of them, whose name we mentioned above, writes to the Galatians: “James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars” (Gal. 2:9). A *reclinatorium* is called not a bed in which we lie down to die, but a kind of seat in which those who sit may lean back, restore themselves by a little rest, [Col. 0446B] and refresh their weariness for a time.

The reclining-place prepared by Solomon in the litter is the sleep of the Lord’s death upon the cross, of which it is written: “And, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit” (John 19:30). This sleep came swiftly and likewise passed swiftly. We know that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour, expired about the ninth, and that Pilate wondered that he had died so quickly, before the thieves were compelled to die by the breaking of their legs. This sleep was also swift in passing, because the Lord rose quickly. Therefore the Lord slept, as it were, upon a reclining-place because he experienced a death-sleep that was swift and transitory.

The death of the faithful is compared with sleep, which especially refreshes the weary, because the more they have labored here for God, the greater the rest which they deserve to enter by dying. Of this sleep and its prompt resurrection the Psalmist had foretold in Christ’s person: “I lay down and slept, and I rose again” (Ps. 3:6). The faithful person sleeps and is separated, because by dying he passes to that repose in which he is most delighted, and, now enjoying the vision of God, his highest desire is fulfilled. Therefore Jerome says of Christ’s aforesaid sleep: “God’s sleeping is when the Only-Begotten of the Father deigned to die for us in assumed flesh.” To such persons death has rightly been called a sweet sleep, as he himself says through Jeremiah: “Therefore I awoke as from sleep and saw, and my sleep was sweet to me” (Jer. 21:26).

Solomon’s reclining-place is called golden because, while “the death of the saints is precious in the sight of the Lord,” Christ’s death must be called most precious, since he is known to be not merely holy, but the Holy of Holies. How great a price must that death be said to possess, when, given as the price of our redemption, it bought life for all and opened the gate of paradise? Hence this unique price is appropriately compared with the more excellent metal, where the reclining-place is described as golden.

Finally, Solomon is said to have fitted to this reclining-place a purple ascent; and to have paved the midst of these—that is, both the reclining-place and the purple ascent—with interposed love, joining them together by its interposition. This purple ascent to that reclining-place already fulfilled in Christ has also been made for us by him, when through his example and exhortation we resist evils even to the shedding of blood, and thus reach, as by a purple ascent, the reclining-place of heavenly rest to which he has already gone before. But because it belongs to human weakness to flee death rather than to undergo it, this ascent and that reclining-place are joined together by love in the middle; for no human being would persevere in so great a struggle as to reach there unless love intervened—love which “bears all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:7).

When he adds that this ascent to the reclining-place is made “for the daughters of Jerusalem,” or that their midst is paved with love, he plainly intimates that through the intervention of this love our weakness ascends there by so arduous an ascent. That he says “daughters” rather than “sons” expresses human frailty through the weaker sex. As daughters of Babylon signify reprobate souls, so daughters of Jerusalem signify the elect. For these are the two cities: God’s and the devil’s; the latter generates in evil, as the former does in good.

The phrase “with love in the midst” may also be understood intransitively: the substantive and adjective are joined in the same case, namely the ablative. It is then to be read as saying that he paved that purple ascent with love in the midst, by inserting love, as it were, between its steps. For there are three steps by which one ascends to the reclining-place of heavenly rest: faith, love, and [Col. 0447C] hope. Faith is the first step, love the second, hope the third. That happiness cannot rightly be hoped for or confidently expected unless we have merited it through love; and love cannot be possessed unless faith goes before it, as the foundation of all good things. Love is therefore inserted in the middle, as it were, between these two extreme steps, because, as we have said, one must proceed from faith to love and from love to hope. This is what it means for that purple ascent to be paved with love in the midst.

Having thus spoken beforehand of Solomon’s holy litter, golden reclining-place, and purple ascent prepared by Christ for the daughters of Jerusalem, the daughters themselves are next invited to go out and behold Solomon himself in his diadem. For the text continues: “Go forth, daughters of Zion,” etc. (Song 3:11). To persevere courageously for Christ in the contest of sufferings, we must always keep him before our eyes, and his passion must always be an example to us, lest we fail. In remembrance of that passion, he ordered the sacraments of his body and blood to be frequently celebrated in the Church. Thus the Apostle says: “The Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and, having given thanks, broke it and said: ‘This is my body, which shall be delivered for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup: ‘As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord [Col. 0448A] until he comes’” (1 Cor. 11:23 ff.).

But what benefit is it to recall this to our memory or that of others unless we suffer with him in such a way, as the same Apostle says, that we may also deserve to be glorified with him by rising again? (Rom. 8:17). Otherwise we shall incur the terrible judgment which he immediately adds: “Therefore whoever eats or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27). By the purple ascent, as has been said, we must descend to the golden reclining-place; for unless we share in Christ’s passion, we shall not be participants in his resurrection. That we may be able to do this as he draws us, may he who invites us to ascend stretch out his hand. Amen.

## SERMON X. FOR THE SAME DAY
“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal, and on the day of his heart’s joy” (Song of Songs 3:11). The text of the Song of Songs itself plainly indicates, from what precedes, the sense in which the daughters of Zion are urged to go forth. For after it had said, “King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon” (ibid., 3:9), and had carefully described how wonderful that marvel was, it immediately urges the daughters of Zion to go forth in order to behold the king himself in this litter of his. These are the same women whom it had just called the daughters of Jerusalem, when it said: “He paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem” (ibid., 3:10). As though urging them to climb into that litter itself, it commands them to go forth, so that, seeing the king in the litter, they may strive through love for him to ascend into his bier—that is, by taking up his cross through imitation of him—as he himself exhorts, saying: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. 16:21): that is, let him imitate me by enduring sufferings.

The daughters of Zion—that is, of Jerusalem, not Babylon—are faithful souls who belong as citizens to the city of God, not to the devil. True Jerusalem, that is, the mother Church, bears or begets them for God when she instructs them by preaching or regenerates them by baptism. Hence the Apostle, likening himself both to mother and father, says: “My little children, for whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). And again: “For though you have many instructors, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15). Of this our mother, whose manner of life is in heaven and who always dwells above through desire, the same Apostle says: “But that Jerusalem which is above is free, and she is our mother” (Gal. 4:26).

Solomon therefore exhorts the aforesaid daughters of Zion to go forth, so that, having gone forth, they may deserve to see our true Solomon—that is, Christ. They must go forth, I say, especially from earthly modes of life, so that during these most holy days of the Lord’s Passion, mortifying the flesh through abstinence, they may take up his cross; attentive to what is written: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.” “For whoever says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (2 Tim. 2:12). By putting to death the vices within us, let us prepare ourselves as a living sacrifice pleasing to God. For no one can worthily approach his sacrifice—which is now set before all Christians in common as Easter approaches—unless he has first prepared himself, as we have said, to be such a sacrifice. Otherwise, from the table of life we shall receive death, and, as though it were food, we shall swallow poison.

Hence the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord. But let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27).

The same Apostle says to the Hebrews: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought by the high priest into the holy places for sin are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we have here no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come” (Heb. 13:10 ff.).

[Col. 0449C] Our altar is the altar of Christ, upon which we celebrate his sacrifice—indeed, in the sacrament of his own body and blood, we offer him himself to the Father. Those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat from that holy altar, because those who live carnally are not worthy to receive from so great and spiritual a sacrifice. By “tabernacle” he means this mortal body, which we now have as a dwelling-place: dissoluble and weak, like the tabernacles—that is, the shelters—of shepherds or travellers, which are not firm and permanent houses but movable dwellings, fit to be inhabited only briefly. Therefore, one serves the tabernacle who obeys the desires of mortal flesh. The body must be governed, and the flesh must be subjected to the spirit: it is worthy to serve rather than rule.

“For the bodies of those animals,” and so forth. It is as though he were plainly saying: I rightly said that those who serve the tabernacle—that is, who indulge fleshly desires—are in no way worthy of Christ’s sacrifice. The Lord also decreed to foreshadow this in the ancient sacrifice, which was an image of ours: when the bodies of animals were burned outside the camp in the wilderness, their pure blood was offered by the high priest in the Holy of Holies. For the blood, in which the life of the flesh especially consists, according to Moses’ saying, “For the life of all flesh is in the blood” (Lev. 17:11), signifies the good life or soul of the faithful. This is offered, as a sacrifice, through Christ the high priest who intercedes for us, in the Holy of Holies—that is, in the second tabernacle—when it is mercifully brought into the heavenly dwelling, where holiness is pure and perfect, as signified by the Holy of Holies.

[Col. 0450A] But for this to happen, the bodies of these animals must first be burned outside the camp in this life: that is, the flesh must be afflicted and mortified by zeal for divine love, while we are thus placed outside the camp—that is, outside fleshly pleasures. These pleasures are, as it were, camps or prisons of the soul: they bind and confine it, preventing it from lifting itself altogether toward things above and rising freely, with all its affection, to heavenly things. To signify this also, our high priest himself suffered outside the gate—that is, outside the enclosure of Jerusalem and not within it—so that he might indicate that none would be sanctified and redeemed by his blood unless, as has been said, they were placed outside the camp, that is, outside fleshly pleasures, and imitated him.

Accordingly the Apostle exhorts us: “Let us therefore go out”—that is, let us follow him by imitating him—“outside the camp,” having been placed outside it as prescribed, so that we may attain him in heavenly things. To bear his reproach means to endure for him whatever is disgraceful or shameful, as he himself refused no suffering for us. “For we have here no lasting city,” and so forth. Let us go out to him, I say, leaving the camp; that is, let us hasten to reach him through every adversity, putting aside the pleasures of the flesh, because we do not have a stable dwelling in this life, nor were we created for this life, but strive to attain the future life, which does not fail.

[Col. 0450C] Therefore, what the Apostle here calls our “going out,” Solomon above foreshadowed by calling it our “going forth,” when he said: “Go forth, daughters of Zion,” and so forth. It is as though he said: Go forth in mind, always to behold him who was crucified outside the gate for you and became your sacrifice. We go forth from ourselves to him when, renouncing our own pleasures, we surrender ourselves to his will and follow him by imitation—the one who, obedient to the Father unto death, said: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:30).

In this way, indeed, we carry the cross after Jesus, as Luke relates of Simon of Cyrene, when we are prepared to persevere in obedience to him unto death, crucifying our bodies with their vices and desires, as the Apostle commands (Luke 23:26). For Simon is interpreted “obedient”; carrying Christ’s cross after him, he signifies those who follow Christ in imitation even to the point that they are prepared to render him perfect obedience unto death. Concerning this perfection of obedience, Christ himself also says to Simon Peter: “Follow me” (Luke 1:16; 2:14), so that what Simon of Cyrene performed in service, Simon Peter, bearing the type of the Church, might fulfil in deed.

The aforementioned Evangelist relates that, while Simon was carrying Christ’s cross after Jesus, “a great multitude of people and of women followed him, who were weeping and lamenting him.” Simon alone does not imitate Christ through suffering; rather, an innumerable multitude of faithful people, both men and women, follow Christ through martyrdom and in this way go forth to God, who suffered outside the gate.

[Col. 0451A] We also represent him today as having gone forth, when clergy and people alike, with the sanctuary, proceed from cities, towns, or villages into the open field to adore the cross, on the very day when the Lord’s Passion is first read in the year. By this general procession of the faithful, going forth as it were to the Lord who suffered outside the gate, we profess that we remember his Passion, as though beholding him crucified for us before our eyes. We are admonished to this sight when we are told, after our going forth, to see King Solomon “in the diadem with which his mother crowned him” (Song 3): his mother, I say, that is, Judaea, from whom he was born according to the flesh.

She crowned him with a diadem—that is, she exalted him in the manner of a victor, since in death itself he triumphed especially over the devil. Concerning this exaltation in his suspension upon the cross, he himself said to Nicodemus: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14). We also read that the Jews physically crowned the Lord himself with a crown of thorns. Although they intended this as mockery and punishment, in ignorance they performed the mystery of an event to be turned into glory. The Psalmist had long foretold this: “You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands. You subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. 8:6). Following this testimony, the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: “But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death” (Heb. 2:9). It is also written in John that “Jesus came forth wearing the crown of thorns” (John 19:5), so that even according to the letter we are to go out to see him, as foretold, in his diadem.

Whether Christ is said to go forth crowned or to go forth to be crucified, this signifies that, with the Jews who committed these things against him rejected, his grace would pass into the breadth of the Gentiles, where the salvation of his crucifixion and his exaltation in the gaining of many peoples spread abroad once the Jew had been rejected. Hence we rightly proceed today into the open field to adore his cross, mystically showing by this that both glory and salvation have gone forth from the Jews and spread among the Gentiles.

[Col. 0451D] But our returning afterward to the places from which we had gone forth signifies that, at the end of the world, the grace of God will return to the Jews, when, as is established, they will be converted through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah. Hence the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved” (1 Cor. 10:1), as it is written: “There shall come from Zion one who delivers and turns away ungodliness from Jacob” (Rom. 11:26). Thus we know that the very place of Calvary where the Lord was crucified is now enclosed within the city, though it was formerly outside.

“He crowned him,” it says, “with a diadem on the day of his betrothal.” For kings customarily receive great rejoicing when, having become betrothed to wives, they celebrate the solemnities of marriage. The day of the Lord’s crucifixion was, as it were, the day of his betrothal, because then he truly joined the Church to himself as a bride: descending to the underworld on that same day, he fulfilled in the faithful souls whom he took from there what he had promised to the thief, saying, “Truly I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Therefore this day of betrothal was a day of joy to him, when he fulfilled in the salvation of believers that for which he had come and which was especially the object of his desire.

“It was the day of his heart’s joy,” because he was, as it were, sorrowful in the body in which he endured the pains of suffering; yet although the flesh brought the sorrow of pain through what was outwardly inflicted, the heart—that is, the soul—had the highest joy inwardly, namely over our salvation, which he was thus accomplishing. Therefore, when he was going forth to be crucified, he rightly restrained the women who lamented for him, saying: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children” (Luke 23:28). It is as though he said: There is no need to grieve for me in these sufferings, as though I incurred some loss from them; rather, a most severe vengeance threatens you yourselves and your children, who will be punished for the things committed against me.

[Col. 0452C] So also, brothers, we should weep rather for ourselves than for him, because we committed by our guilt the things that he bore so grievously in punishment. Let us rejoice in him with him, while grieving for our own offences: [the text is uncertain: “the guilt of this one or of servants”] committed that for which the innocent Lord endured so great a punishment. He taught us to weep for ourselves, though he is never read to have wept for himself. Yet he did not weep when he was about to raise Lazarus, for whose raising the honour offered him today by the crowds was given. He wept today also, when he was welcomed by rejoicing crowds, as Luke records: “And when he was now approaching the descent of the Mount of Olives, the whole multitude of those going down began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen, saying, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven and glory in the highest.’ And when he approached, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying, ‘If you too had known,’” and so forth (Luke 19:38).

He wept for Lazarus, whom he was about to call back from refreshment and Abraham’s bosom to the miseries of the present life. He wept over the ruin of the city—that is, our losses—not his own. Would that we could lament our evils as he did, and be as concerned for ourselves as he was! We who rejoice in him as our Saviour, by whose death we have been redeemed, should weep over ourselves, since we committed what he was punished for so grievously.

Therefore, going forth always in mind to him, as we have said, and keeping before our memory the sight of him so crowned for us, let us follow him by taking up his cross. If we are not now in a time when we are compelled to die for him, still, as often as we suffer affliction for his sake, we take up his cross. For *crux* (“cross”) is so called from *cruciare* (“to torment”). We take up his cross when we endure any adversities for him or, through the virtue of abstinence mortifying our flesh, subject it to the rule of the spirit.

[Col. 0453A] We must provide for this especially in these days, in which it is fitting that we prepare ourselves spiritually to receive the Lord himself in the sacrifice of his own body and blood. Certainly, if some powerful person or friend were expected to be received by us as a guest, we would prepare our house with every care, lest anything unclean or unbecoming offend the eyes of the one entering. How much care and effort, then, must be taken lest the Creator and Redeemer himself, whom, as we have said, we are to receive, find in us an unclean dwelling! For he avenges a wrong done to himself all the more severely because he is more able and more entitled to do so. And since it is also by his grace that a dwelling is prepared for him in us, may he prepare it for himself: he who instituted this sacrifice for our salvation, not for judgment. Amen.

## SERMON XI. ON THE EVENTS THAT TOOK PLACE IN THE DAYS OF THE PASSION

As the time of our redemption and the solemnity of the Lord’s resurrection draw nearer, we should more frequently be built up by holy exhortations, so that we may be found worthy of such great benefits, sharing in redemption and participating in the resurrection. And because the narrative of the events themselves often stirs the devotion of simple people more than mystical interpretation, it is helpful to recount and connect, according to the letter, the events which the Lord performed on these days—full of every sweetness and all piety—and to bring them to mind for our exhortation.

John accordingly relates that, after Lazarus had been raised, many of the Jews who had seen this believed in Jesus. But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done. “Therefore the chief priests and Pharisees assembled a council, and said, ‘What are we doing?’” and so forth. “From that day therefore they planned to kill him” (John 11:45 ff.).

[Col. 0453D] To kill, I say, the one who raised the dead, and to inflict death in return for restored life! O blind and perverse men alike! Can he who restores life to the dead not protect himself from death and, if he wills, undo your schemes? You do not even doubt his power, since you have repeatedly experienced it in these and other things. Otherwise, you would not plan to ensnare him by deceit for killing as though he were ignorant, but would seize him by force. Yet the Evangelist clearly shows how foolishly you suppose that your plan and perverse intention could escape his knowledge. For after saying, “From that day therefore they planned to kill him,” he immediately indicates plainly that Jesus was by no means ignorant of it: “Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and stayed there with his disciples” (John 11:54).

Therefore, his deliberate avoidance of persecution for a time plainly took place not through ignorance but through dispensation. The time had not yet come in which these things were to be fulfilled in him. By avoiding the Passion through dispensation, as has been said, rather than through fear, he calls us back by his example from presumption, lest perhaps, by tempting God, we recklessly expose ourselves to danger at a time when we ought not.

The following statements show that fear did not induce him to withdraw to the aforesaid place and remain there with his disciples: “Now the Passover of the Jews was near” (John 11:55). And again: “The chief priests and Pharisees had given an order that, if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, so that they might seize him” (John 11:56). “Jesus therefore, six days before Passover, came to Bethany” (John 12:1).

[Col. 0454B] Consider, brothers, what that conclusion means—“Jesus therefore,” and so forth—and on what this inference depends; and you will see that, as has been said, it reveals the Lord’s dispensation, not fear. For after it has first been stated that the Passover was near, at which he knew that he was afterward to be handed over, saying: “You know that after two days the Passover comes, and the Son of Man will be handed over to be crucified” (Matt. 26:2); and after this has additionally been stated, that the chief priests and Pharisees had commanded anyone knowing where he was to report it so that they might seize him, it is immediately added: “Jesus therefore, six days before Passover,” and so forth.

It is as though it were plainly said: Because the time of the Passion was near, and the Jews had now wholly conspired to accomplish it, therefore the Lord himself, undaunted, now prepared himself for it and went to Jerusalem, where he knew that he would suffer. He offered himself to the Jews for the fulfilment of their perverse desire, so that, to their own condemnation, they might work our salvation.

[Col. 0454C] He came from the aforesaid region near the wilderness, or from the Gentile city called Ephraim, as though thereby fulfilling even literally that prophetic prayer: “Send forth, Lord, the lamb, ruler of the earth, from the rock of the wilderness to the mount of the daughter of Zion” (Isa. 16:1). For what is the rock of the wilderness except the Gentile world, abandoned by God, whose hearts the Lord had softened through the grace of the world into love for himself? The Lord also dwelt in this place as in a rock, in which he had provided himself a safe and firm dwelling. From there, therefore, the Lord sends his lamb to the mount of his daughter Zion, when Christ first came from the aforementioned Gentile city situated near the wilderness to Bethany. Then, about to suffer, he reached Jerusalem, which lies on Mount Zion. God had indeed held that city as a daughter of oil, when he elevated it above the rest by grace, so that it should be specially called the holy city, adorned both with God’s temple and sanctuary and established at the head of the kingdom.

“Six days before Passover he came to Bethany,” and on the next day—that is, on the fifth day before Passover—he was to proceed to Jerusalem, so that he might perform the mysteries of the mystical Lamb at the proper time, as we have already recalled above in another sermon.

[Col. 0455A] When the Lord had come to Bethany, they made him a supper there, and Martha served. Lazarus was one of those reclining at table with him. “Then Mary took a pound of precious ointment of pure nard, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped them with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.” The Evangelist does not state who prepared this supper, where Lazarus dines, Martha serves food, and Mary provides the ointment, because he considers it sufficiently indicated by the persons whom he names. To say nothing of Lazarus, it would scarcely have been fitting for holy women to serve in another person’s house or at another’s expense.

Lazarus dines with the Lord so that his twofold resurrection may be proved. Hence Jerome, in Book II against Jovinianus, says of the Lord himself:

> [Note: [Col. 0455D] Patrology, vol. XXIII, col. 311.] “He ate indeed after the resurrection, in order to prove the reality of his body. For whenever he raised a dead person, he ordered food to be given to that person, lest the resurrection be thought a phantom. And Lazarus, after his resurrection, is written to have entered into a meal with the Lord for this reason.”

The women rightly receive the Lord while men persecute him; and, moreover, while refreshing him, they do not fear the general decree of their elders who persecuted Christ. As we have said, while they minister to Christ and their brother Lazarus reclines at table, they are shown to have been raised in soul all the more happily as they are shown to attend Christ with greater devotion.

[Col. 0455C] We read that the Lord ministered at the tables of his disciples, as he himself declares: “Which is greater, the one reclining at table or the one who serves? Is it not the one reclining? But I am in your midst as one who serves” (Luke 22:27). Yet Scripture commemorates only women as having ministered to the Lord. We also know that he himself washed the disciples’ feet; but no man rendered him this service. Rather, only that sinful woman did so, who washed his feet with tears of repentance, wiped them with her hair, and refreshed them with ointment. By anointing not only his feet but also his head, the woman made him Christ bodily and performed in him the mysteries of both king and priest.

Consider, men, the humility of the Lord ministering as we have said; consider, women, your dignity, since you deserved to minister to him in all these ways. That a woman is repeatedly said to have anointed Christ’s feet clearly indicates that he walked shod, since his feet were thus found ready for anointing, although he had granted his disciples the footwear of sandals. Hence it is plainly evident according to the letter that he trod hard paths, concerning which he speaks to the Father: “Because of the words of your lips,” and so forth (Ps. 16:4).

That on the next day he came first from Bethany to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives and then reached Jerusalem is by no means without mystery. Bethphage is a village of priests and is interpreted “house of the mouth,” just as Bethany means “house of obedience.”

[Col. 0456A] One comes from Bethany to Bethphage because only the person who has first learned to obey is worthy to preach: he must be a disciple in obedience before he becomes a teacher in command. This village of priests—that is, preachers—is rightly described as being at the Mount of Olives, because persons such as those described are held higher in the Church both in the dignity of their order and in merits. Hence the Lord says: “Whoever does and teaches these things shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19).

The olive grove, too, which supplies oil, rightly suits holy preachers. Oil scatters light from the fire which it nourishes; and holy preachers, kindled by the fire of charity, are like a lamp burning and shining: burning in themselves, shining for others, who are enlightened by their preaching.

Luke relates that as the Lord was already approaching the descent of the Mount of Olives, all the crowds of those descending began joyfully to praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works they had seen, saying: “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord; peace in heaven and glory in the highest” (Luke 19:37). The Lord is rightly glorified by the crowds as he descends from the mountain, because unless someone humbles himself, he does not deserve to be exalted. Thus it is written concerning the Lord himself: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name,” and so forth (Phil. 2:8).

Then, while the crowds, as has been said, were acclaiming praise to him, “when he drew near, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying, ‘If you too had known … for days will come,’” and so forth; “and they shall not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luke 19:42).

[Col. 0456C] O supreme compassion toward the impious, incomparable kindness toward the cruel! Amid the praises given to him and the joyful crowds who came to meet him and showed him such devoted attention, he does not exult in the praises or rejoice with those rejoicing. Instead, grieving for those who were perishing and unable to call them back from death, he weeps for them as though already dead. He laments their death so that they may repent; he terrifies them so that they may not perish. He foretells the evils to come, by which they could have provided against punishment for themselves. He grieves because he is not heard; he weeps for their fall, not for the contempt shown him—for he came to save, not to destroy. Hence he was called Jesus, by his very name.

He laments the final and irreparable destruction of that people, to be brought about by the Roman commanders Titus and Vespasian. They are the two bears which came out of the forest and destroyed the forty-two boys who mocked Elisha as he was ascending from Jericho, where he had healed the waters, to Bethel, saying: “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (4 Kings 2:23). For the wild bears are Gentile rulers, strangers to the discipline of the law, far removed from the city of God, and untamed like beasts. When the Gentile world sends them, they come forth as though from an uncultivated forest, because they proceed from a people which knew no cultivation by divine teaching.

[Col. 0457A] While they sought in the rebellion of the Jewish people to avenge their own wrong, it was accomplished by divine dispensation that they unknowingly punished Christ’s wrong more than their own. Thus the Lord says of Assyria: “Assyria is the rod of my fury; but he did not so intend” (Isa. 10:5). When the Lord carries out vengeance upon his people by means of the Assyrian people, Assyria is like the rod of God’s wrath—that is, the instrument of his vengeance. Yet Assyria does not know that this is done by divine dispensation, because it attributes all the power it possesses not to divine ordering but to its own strength.

Foreseeing something similar concerning these Roman rulers, the Psalmist lamented the destruction of his people, thus complaining to God (Ps. 73:3 ff.): “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly in the holy place!” It is as though he said: O how many wicked deeds and abominations that people of the Romans committed in the very temple and divine sanctuary! “And those who hated you,” the true God, “boasted,” as worshippers of idolatry, because they worship demons. They boasted, I say, “in the midst of your solemnity,” that is, during the Paschal days which you yourself had instituted as solemn in your honour.

For it was just that the Jews who had killed Christ during the Paschal solemnity—fearing that through him they would lose their place and nation—should be captured in that same solemnity and by these men exterminated forever, or wholly destroyed: by Vespasian the father and Titus his son, I say, should those be punished who had sinned so grievously against God the Father and his Son. They boasted of the victory which they gained, not knowing that God had permitted these things because of that people’s sins. Hence it follows: “They set up their signs,” that is, they raised standards as signs of victory, “as at the exit”: that is, after the manner of triumphant conquerors, who raise their trophies at the gates of captured cities on the summit—that is, in the city’s higher place—where they may be more plainly seen by those entering or leaving.

[Col. 0457C] And although they did such great things by God’s permission, they did not know what they were doing: they thought they were merely avenging their own injury, not a divine one, and that they had achieved this by their own strength rather than by the divine decree through which God delivered the ungodly.

Therefore the little children destroyed by the aforesaid bears because they mocked Elisha are the Jews themselves, as people lacking understanding: they recognized Christ neither through the law nor through so many signs; and thus, alienated from true wisdom, which he himself is, they were handed over to a reprobate mind. For otherwise they would not have mocked Christ in such a way before his crucifixion, nor cried out to Pilate, “Crucify him, crucify him!” (Luke 23:21)—which is as though they said to Christ, “Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead!” (4 Kings 2:23).

For Christ’s crucifixion is his ascent upon the cross. They call bald the one whom they see deprived of earthly help or riches. Thus, “Go up, baldhead!” means: You wretch, deprived of all good things, who foretold that you would be exalted by us—come here and, ascending the cross, be exalted. They said this in mocking irony, but the Lord was in truth ordaining the exaltation of the crucified one and the election of the Gentiles.

The boys are rightly remembered as forty-two in number, corresponding to the number of years which the Lord had granted them for repentance. For in the forty-second year after the Lord’s Passion this calamity befell them. Nor is it without mystery that Elisha, after healing the waters of Jericho, was ascending to Bethel—that is, the house of God—when the Lord also, coming to Jerusalem on Palm Sunday, healed two blind men as he passed through and went out from Jericho. Before they were enlightened by Christ in both body and soul, and consequently followed him, they were like barren waters: still tossed about by every wind of doctrine, they had no settled certainty concerning what they ought to believe, and therefore lacked spiritual fruit.

[Col. 0458B] But to join the thread of our narrative to the preceding matters which had been interrupted: when, as we have said, the Lord came to Jerusalem and had lamented and foretold the city’s coming ruin, he entered the city amid a great procession of rejoicing crowds and came to the temple as to his own house. There, exercising both justice and mercy, he powerfully expelled the merchants and healed the blind and lame; thereby he reconciled the Lord’s house itself.

He had already expelled such persons from the temple on another occasion, which John alone records (Mark 2:15). But the other Evangelists write of this final expulsion, when he made a scourge of cords and drove them all out. Mark, however, relates (ch. 11:15) that this expulsion happened not on Palm Sunday, but on the following day when the Lord returned to Jerusalem. Still, Mark too records that on Palm Sunday the Lord entered the temple, but did nothing there except look around at everything present; when evening had come, he returned to Bethany with the Twelve.

Therefore the other Evangelists—Matthew (Matt. 21:12) and Luke (Luke 19:45)—seem, omitting this point, to have mentioned that expulsion briefly by anticipation and connected it appropriately to what they had previously stated. For after Matthew had said that the Lord told the disciples, “Go into the village opposite you,” and so forth (Matt. 21:2), and Luke had related that the Lord wept over the city’s ruin (Luke 19:41), they took care next to state whose fault especially brought about that opposition or that ruin: namely, that of the priests and the other ministers of the temple. Hence he decreed to enact this vengeance upon them in the very temple, thereby plainly indicating that their wickedness and negligence toward God were the cause of the matters we have described.

First, therefore, having entered the temple amid a great company of crowds shouting praises, and having looked around at everything, he left it and returned to Bethany; and, as we have said, he postponed the exercise of this power until the following day. In this he both morally instructs us and displays the greatness of his power. For before we punish evils, we ought diligently to investigate and recognize beforehand [Col. 0459A] the evils which we must correct, and patiently endure them for a time, lest we rashly pronounce a sentence of vengeance. Thus the Lord rightly wished first to observe the evils of his house before exercising in it the severity of justice. For Genesis also relates concerning him (Gen. XI) that, when he wished to repress the pride of those building the tower by the confusion of languages, and thus scatter them throughout the regions, the Lord first came down to see that folly of the proud before passing sentence upon it. So also, when he was about to punish the sins of Sodom and Gomorrah: “I will go down,” he says, “and see whether they have fulfilled in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know” (Gen. XVIII.21). So here too, having first looked around at those acting wickedly in the temple, he showed that he knew [Col. 0459B] what he ought to punish. By delaying punishment he displayed patience. He did not wish to inflict punishment as though relying upon the assistance of the crowds mentioned above, so that his power might appear greater when he accomplished this without crowds. For Matthew records that only children were then present and crying in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” (Matt. XXI.51), so that by their praises there might be recompense for what had been committed in the mockery of Elisha by children.

When evening came, as has been said, the Lord left the temple and returned with the apostles to Bethany, as though passing from the house of disobedience to the house of obedience. For no one deserves to have God as an inhabitant unless he is ready to obey his commands. He proceeds from the city to a small village because, as he himself says, “Many are called, but few [Col. 0459C] are chosen” (Matt. XX.16). Leaving Jerusalem and the temple as his own city and house, since there he had nowhere to lay his head (Matt. VIII), he fulfilled what is written concerning himself: “He came unto his own, and his own received him not” (John I.11); leaving Jerusalem—or rather, now no longer Jerusalem, which means “vision of peace,” but a refuge made into a place of tyranny. For the chief men of the city had now so openly conspired against him that he could find no lodging there. Yet this must be attributed not to his powerlessness but to his patience. Had he wished, he could have lodged there safely; for certainly no one can inflict violence upon him whose power it is to incline human hearts wherever he wills.

For when he wished, he freely did there whatever he had decreed. Sending the disciples [Col. 0459D] there to untie the ass and colt and bring them to him, he fulfilled what he had said without anyone opposing them, although he was not ignorant of the conspiracy formed against him. Concerning it he says to the disciples whom he sends: “Go into the village that is opposite you” (Matt. XXI.2), that is, into a place hostile alike to God and to you; it should no longer be called a city—that is, an assembly of people living according to law—but a fortified place of tyranny. “Go,” he says, “confidently into such a place, however hostile to you it may be, and safely accomplish what I command.” Therefore he adds: “And if anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them, and immediately he will send them” (ibid., 3). O wondrous confidence of power! As Lord, he commands this by authority to men whom he knew had already wholly conspired for his death. Thus he commands, [Col. 0460A] thus he gives orders, and thus he compels obedience. Nor do those who are sent hesitate to accomplish what is enjoined upon them, trusting in the power of him who sends them.

Those, indeed, who had most actively formed this conspiracy had experienced that power: more than once they were driven out of the temple, since many were unable to resist one. Even after this expulsion and their conspiracy, as has been said, when he taught daily in the temple, he plainly showed how fearless he was, he to whose hands the Father had given all things. Finally, when he wished to celebrate the Passover according to the law, on the very night in which he had arranged to be delivered up, he again sent disciples and prepared for himself, wherever he wished, a house in the city in which to do this. Therefore he who had so often acted powerfully in such matters could also now, if he wished, prepare lodging for himself wherever he wished, and would not have returned to Bethany under compulsion. Thus he acted providently in two respects: namely, to show that those whose dwelling he avoided were unworthy of his presence, and to grant his beloved hosts the abundance of himself in his last days, so that they might already have this itself, as it were, as the reward of their hospitality.

But when morning came, he returned with the disciples from Bethany to Jerusalem and was hungry, as Mark says (Mark XI.12 ff.): “And seeing from afar a fig tree having leaves, he came, seeking whether perhaps he might find anything on it; and he found nothing except leaves. For it was not the season for figs. And he said to it: ‘May fruit never grow from you for ever.’ And his disciples heard it; and the fig tree immediately withered. And they came to Jerusalem. And when they entered the temple, he began to drive out those selling and buying in the temple, and overturned the tables of the money-changers [Col. 0460C] and the seats of those selling doves. And he did not allow anyone to carry a vessel through the temple. And when evening came, he went out of the city.” And, as Matthew relates, he went again to Bethany and remained there. These things occurred on the second day after Palm Sunday—that is, on Monday—as Mark writes.

But what is this, Lord Jesus: hungry in the morning, you seek food in a tree, though it is known above all that you were accustomed to fast? We read that none of the disciples was then hungry, but you alone. You provided for others what you now permitted yourself. Fasting, you ministered to others; hungry, you refreshed your disciples—you who came to minister, not to be ministered to. Perhaps you had poor hosts, though voluntary ones. [Col. 0460D] You considered it too much that their abundant poverty should have refreshed the disciples. By abstaining alone, you spared the expense, although all expenditure is known to exist for your sake. You seek food in a tree, food which nature freely supplies, not food prepared by human care or increasing more lavish expense. You seek food where you know with certainty that it is not to be found. Therefore you do this not for bodily refreshment, but rather for a mystery. For you do not fail to know that it was not then the season for figs. As though angry, you curse the tree because it has no fruit, yet at a time when by nature it could not have borne fruit. Immediately the cursed tree withered; it felt the invisible power of the one cursing it, and was, as it were, condemned though it had not deserved it. Why so, Lord? We know that this was done not in cruelty but rather in mercy. What was done to the tree was to be done to human beings, for the terror of people [Col. 0461A] and the correction of the wicked. The power of might was displayed in an insensible thing, whose offense a rational being ought to avoid. By deeds he terrifies, by words he teaches the unbelieving people, lest they perish in their wickedness; he also invites them to repentance through frequent benefits of miracles. He himself, the Angel of Counsel, advises those who are perishing by every means he can, lest they perish: so that, if they repent, they may be saved; or, if not, they may deserve to be condemned without excuse. And these things occurred on the second weekday.

But on the third day, as Mark and Matthew relate, when he was returning from Bethany to Jerusalem, the disciples saw the fig tree withered. And Peter, remembering, said to Jesus: “Rabbi, behold, the fig tree which you cursed has withered” (Mark XI.21). And when he came into the temple, [Col. 0461B] the chief priests and elders of the people approached him as he taught. Having spoken many things to them in parables and reproached them with many sins, he gravely stirred them against himself, so that they might more promptly carry out what they had planned concerning his death. Thereafter, when he left the temple and went to the Mount of Olives—as Matthew and Mark plainly indicate by adding that, while seated there, he taught the disciples—one of the disciples said to him: “Teacher, look what stones and what buildings!” (Mark XIII.1). Jesus answered: “Do you see all these great buildings? There shall not be left one stone upon another that shall not be thrown down” (Matt. XXIV.2).

Then, having gone to the Mount of Olives, when he was seated there, as Matthew writes, his disciples came to him privately, [Col. 0461C] saying: “Tell us when these things will be”—that is, the destruction of Jerusalem—“and what will be the sign of your coming” (Matt. XXIV.5), namely at the end of the world and the consummation of the age itself. After the Lord had foretold many things concerning this and had delivered a lengthy discourse to them, Matthew adds: “And it came to pass, when Jesus had finished all these sayings, that he said to his disciples: ‘You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified’” (Matt. XXVI.1–2). “After two days,” that is, at the end of the fifth weekday, when the old Passover then had to be celebrated by the slaughter of a lamb or kid in the evening. For this is the Passover meant here, known to all according to the law. Thus on the third weekday, that is, Tuesday, he delivered that discourse on [Col. 0461D] the Mount of Olives; and when it was finished, he told the disciples that after two days the Passover would take place. For in that year it happened that after those two days, on Thursday, as we have said, the fourteenth day of the moon fell, so that on that day, in the evening, the sacrifice of the old Passover was performed according to the law. When that sacrifice of the old Passover—in the flesh of a kid or lamb with unleavened bread and wild lettuce—had been completed, the Lord immediately performed the new Passover in the sacrament of his body and blood, and so brought the old Passover to an end.

When the sacraments of both Passovers had been completed, he was delivered up that same night to his passion. Concerning this delivery Matthew accordingly adds, as was said: “And the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified.” “Then,” Matthew says (Matt.
