XXVI.3–5), [Col. 0462A] “the chief priests and elders of the people assembled and took counsel that they might seize Jesus by deceit and kill him. But they said: ‘Not on the feast day’”—understand, “this must be done”—“lest perhaps there should be an uproar among the people”; that is, lest the crowds who had received him with rejoicing or regarded him as a prophet should rise against them and rescue him. O blind and most wicked men! You wish to seize him by deceit, as though he were unaware of your plot; and you do not wish to accomplish this on the feast day, not indeed out of reverence for the day, but out of fear of the people, as we have said.

By “feast day” he means the first day of unleavened bread after Passover. For Passover is properly called the fourteenth day of the moon, when the slaughter took place in the evening. From the following fifteenth day until the twenty-first day were the days of unleavened bread, because after the day of Passover they ate unleavened bread for seven days. Among these days of unleavened bread, the first and the seventh were more distinguished and solemn than the others, whereas the day of Passover itself possessed no rank of solemnity by authority of the law. Hence it is written in Exodus (Exod. XII.16) concerning these seven days of unleavened bread: “The first day shall be holy and solemn, and the seventh day venerable with the same festivity. You shall do no work on them, except what pertains to eating.” Therefore they mean that first day of unleavened bread when they say, “Not on the feast day.” For then all alike, resting from work according to the law and assembled in the city, were thought more easily able to stir up an uproar. But when Matthew says, “Then [Col. 0462C] they assembled,” etc., that “then” must be referred to the aforesaid third weekday, when the Lord said: “You know that after two days…”

But what the Lord himself did afterward on that third day, or on the following fourth day, Scripture does not clearly state. We believe, however, that he did so in order to avoid this settled counsel of the Jews and not give them an opportunity to carry out their wickedness before the fitting day of his delivery or passion. But when the evangelist adds, “Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper,” and, as Mark says, reclining there (Mark XIV.3), “a woman came to him having an alabaster vessel,” etc. (Matt. XXVI.6–7), it is uncertain whether this occurred on the aforesaid third day or on the following fourth day.

Some, however, think that this reclining in Simon’s house was the supper of which John says: “Six days before Passover Jesus came to Bethany; and they made him a supper there, and Martha ministered,” etc. (John XII.1 ff.). Those who wish the supper mentioned by Matthew and Mark to be the same supper that John asserts was held six days before Passover say that it is not now narrated by the evangelists in the chronological order of the events, but recalled as something done earlier, in order to indicate that Judas received from it the occasion for selling the Lord, as though he might repair by this price the loss he had suffered. But if we carefully compare this supper with that one, we shall see [Col. 0463A] that it was by no means fitting to minister to the Lord in another’s house or at another’s expense. Moreover, John does not say there that Mary anointed anything but Jesus’ feet and wiped them with her hair; nor do these evangelists say here that she placed the ointment anywhere but upon the head of Jesus as he reclined. This she could suitably have done in another’s house, since perhaps the person who furnished the food did not supply the ointment. The woman rightly first anointed the feet of the Lord, wearied by a long journey, in order thereby to refresh him after the exertion of travel. But now she judged it sufficient that the head of one resting should be anointed, as though applying this ointment as a remedy against the heat of that very hot land.

Finally, at the former supper, where Martha ministered, John reports that no one murmured about the ointment except Judas the betrayer. But at this second supper the evangelists do not identify Judas as objecting; rather, they report indefinitely that the disciples were indignant about it. From all these points, as from certain indications, it follows that these two suppers were not the same, and that the woman’s devotion toward the Lord was greater in proportion as she rendered him this service more often. But after this second supper, as Matthew plainly shows, Judas went to the chief priests and made an agreement with them to deliver Jesus to them for thirty pieces of silver (Matt. XXVI.14). For after Matthew had related that the Lord approved the woman’s pouring of ointment upon his head, he immediately added: “Then one of the [Col. 0463C] twelve, who was called Judas, went,” etc. Mark likewise agrees. Therefore, since both report that Judas then went to do what has been said, they indicate clearly enough that he was moved and angered by this event, because on this occasion too, having been put to shame, he was unable to obtain the price of the ointment.

What the Lord did on the fifth weekday, that is, the day of the supper, on which, as we have said, the Jewish Passover then fell, is also certain from the Gospels, where it is written: “On the first day of unleavened bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying: ‘Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’ And he sent Peter and John, saying: ‘Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.’ But they said: ‘Where do you wish us to prepare it?’ And he said to them: ‘Behold, as you enter the city, [Col. 0463D] a man carrying a jar of water will meet you. Follow him into the house into which he enters, and say to the master of the house: “The Teacher says to you, Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?” And he will show you a large furnished upper room; prepare it there.’ And they went and found it as he had told them, and prepared the Passover. And when the hour had come, he reclined at table, and the twelve apostles with him” (Luke XXII.9–14).

He reclined first to celebrate the old Passover. But since both Matthew and Mark say that this occurred on the first day of unleavened bread—which day, as we recalled above, was properly called Passover, just as the seven following days were called days of unleavened bread—the reader should know that the day of Passover itself can also be included under the name of unleavened bread, since on it they too ate unleavened bread with wild lettuce. Conversely, the days of unleavened bread are sometimes included under the name Passover, as in John: “Before the feast day of Passover” (John XIII.1). Passover, too, often signifies the Passover victim rather than the day, as in: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” And elsewhere: “The day of unleavened bread came, on which the Passover had to be slain” (Luke XXII.7). And the Apostle says: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. V.7), that is, he himself is our Paschal victim.

But John says: “And supper having taken place, when the devil had already put it into Judas’s heart to betray him, he rose from supper” (John XIII.2–3), namely in order to wash the disciples’ feet. Afterward, when the washing had been done, John adds: “When he had reclined again, he said [Col. 0464B] to them: ‘Do you know what I have done to you?’” etc. (ibid.). This seems to suggest that the Lord washed feet between the supper of the old Passover and the Lord’s Supper, clearly indicating thereby that no one approaches worthily to the sacrifice of Christ unless his feet have first been washed—that is, unless the affections of his mind have been cleansed; otherwise he eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

The statement, “When he had reclined again,” indicates that, after the sacrifice of the old Passover, they came to a supper consisting of food. For the eating of one lamb or kid would not suffice as the day’s refreshment for so large a household of men. Moreover, after Luke has reported that the Lord said to the disciples concerning the old Passover, “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you” (Luke XXII.15), he afterward mentions that the Lord gave the disciples two cups: one immediately after the old Passover, the other in the celebration of the new Passover. Concerning the first cup the Lord says to the disciples: “Take this and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes” (ibid., 17–18). But concerning the other cup it is written that he gave it to them, saying: “This is my blood of the new covenant. But I tell you, I will not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Mark XXIV.28–29). Therefore the first cup, received after the old Passover and before the new, and the second reclining after the washing of the feet, seem to pertain not to sacrifice but to bodily refreshment. For the law prescribes nothing concerning drink in the old Passover, but only concerning the flesh of the lamb or kid with unleavened bread and wild lettuce.

Thus, while the disciples were eating at this meal, the Lord seems to have taken bread from the table, not from the unleavened bread of the Passover, and to have consecrated the new Passover. For on that day of Passover it was not forbidden that even leavened loaves—which are properly called “wine-bread” because wine is added—should be found in houses; the prohibition applied only to the following seven days, which for this reason were specially called days of unleavened bread. Therefore the Greeks say that the Lord made the new Passover not from unleavened bread but from leavened bread, as though he wished to retain nothing of the old Passover in the new. Moreover, wherever we have it said of the Lord in the new Passover that he took bread and blessed it, [Col. 0465A] the Greek has ἀρτόν (*arton*) for “bread,” signifying leavened bread.

But when, while the disciples were eating, the Lord said that one of them would betray him, and afterward designated him, saying, “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, or bowl, shall betray me” (Matt. XXVI.23), this must be referred to the eating of the old Passover; that is, he said this to them while they were eating it. The sign of the dish by which the betrayer is designated seems to be understood in this way: when the betrayer heard the Lord say that one of the disciples would betray him, lest it be thought that this was said of him—though his own conscience was already accusing him in this matter—he rashly chose to demonstrate that he was not to be suspected, since he trusted the Lord so fully [Col. 0465B] that he did not fear to share common food in the same vessel. Therefore then the wicked man put into his own dish that hand by which, that very night, he was to betray him to death. The sign of the dish can also be understood in this way: that the Lord, who served at the disciples’ table, customarily refreshed himself with Judas after attending to the table, since Judas, as a kind of common steward, carried the money-bag for expenses.

For a third time the Lord took care to designate the betrayer, in order to restrain him further from his wickedness. For when he had first said, “He who dips his hand with me in the dish shall betray me,” and afterward the betrayer, conscious of himself and as though already designated by the dish, asked, “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” Jesus answered him: “You have said it” (Matt. XXVI.25). [Col. 0465C] As if to say: You, having already made an agreement with the Jews and promised that you would do this, have now foretold to them what I say. John also relates that, when the Lord himself said, “He who eats my bread will lift up his heel against me” (John XIII.18), and John himself, reclining upon Jesus’ breast, asked him who it was, he replied: “It is he to whom I shall give the dipped morsel.” And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas; and after the morsel, Satan then entered into him. Jesus said to him: “What you are doing, do quickly.” But when he had received the morsel, he went out immediately. And it was night (ibid., 27 ff.).

Behold, thus for the third time the betrayer was plainly designated; immediately after the morsel he went out to perform the crime he had conceived, as though now entirely despairing of the Lord’s grace, since the devil had so completely possessed his mind that he could in no way return to pardon. Yet it is remarkable how he consented to receive the dipped morsel if he had previously heard the Lord say that it was to be given as a sign of the coming betrayal. We therefore believe that the Lord replied privately to John reclining upon his breast, so that the betrayer did not understand it. For Peter too secretly asked that this be shown, signaling to John rather than speaking, that he should ask the Lord who it was of whom he spoke.

Concerning that morsel of bread which he dipped and offered to Judas in order to designate the betrayer, [Col. 0466A] many think that he took it from the consecrated bread itself and thereby communicated it to Judas with the others. Since Judas received this communion unworthily, he received there judgment rather than salvation, as the Apostle also declares concerning those who communicate unworthily; and thus it is recorded that after the morsel Satan entered Judas and possessed him more fully. Luke also seems plainly to indicate that the betrayer was present at this communion. For while the Lord was celebrating the new Passover, Luke reports that he said: “Nevertheless, behold, the hand of him who betrays me is with me at the table” (Luke XXII.21).

Nevertheless, after receiving the morsel, the betrayer did not wait for the communion to end or for the hymn after the meal to be rendered to the Lord; he immediately left the sacred company, in order to hasten further his wicked desire, as the Lord had foretold when he said: “What you are doing, do quickly.” He gave dipped bread to the betrayer alone in order to signify that his mind was already infected and stained by the conception of sin. But to the others, whose conscience was pure, he distributed separately the sacraments of his body and blood, as though ministering bread by itself and wine by itself. Hence it has rightly been established in the Church that, when believers communicate, they receive these separately. There are, however, some who understand that the dipped bread was not from Christ’s sacrifice, but that the morsel was taken from whatever bread was at hand solely to identify the betrayer. Some of these also hold that Judas participated in the sacrament of the Lord’s body.

Augustine on John [Note: [Col. 0465D] *Patrologia*, vol. III, col. 1802]:

> “And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas. But Judas did not then receive Christ’s body, as some suppose. It must be understood that the Lord had already distributed to all of them the sacrament of his body and blood, among whom Judas himself was present, as Luke narrates most plainly. Then, by the dipped and offered morsel, he identifies his betrayer.”

Hilary on Matthew [Note: [Col. 0466D] *Patrologia*, vol. IX, col. 1065]:

> “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover? After this Judas the betrayer is judged; without him the Passover is accomplished, the cup having been received and the bread broken. For he had not been worthy of communion in the eternal sacraments. For it is understood that he departed immediately, since he is shown returning with the crowds. Nor indeed could he drink with the Lord, he who was not to drink in the kingdom, when the Lord then promised that all who drank of this fruit of the vine would afterward drink it with him.”

It should nevertheless be noted that the Lord’s words do not contain “all,” although blessed Hilary understands them so; rather, the Lord says indefinitely: “When I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.” For we know that the Lord speaks to the apostles in this way many times, in statements which must be taken as general admonitions, so that they can apply to Judas also. Such are: “Blessed are the eyes which see what you see” (Luke X.23); “You shall sit upon twelve thrones,” [Col. 0467A] etc. (Matt. XIX.28); “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X.20); and again: “And I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke XXII.29). Even when something is said generally, it is not always to be understood universally.

Thus Jerome, writing to Damasus on the Lord’s parable of the frugal and the prodigal son [Note: [Col. 0467D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, cols. 391–392], says concerning “All that is mine is yours” (Luke XV.31):

> “But how are all God’s things the Jews’? Are the angels, the thrones, theirs? Therefore understand ‘all things’ as prophecies and divine utterances, according to what we have often explained: not everything is always to be referred to the whole, but to the greater part; as: ‘All have turned aside’ (Ps. XIII.3); ‘All who came before me were thieves and robbers’ (John X.8); ‘I have become all things to all people’ (1 Cor. IX.22); and ‘All seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ’ (Phil. II.21).”

Finally, even if we suppose that Judas too was present at the communion, after it was completed the Lord said: “I will not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father.” We are not therefore compelled to admit that Judas was present when the Lord said this, or that he waited for the end of the Lord’s supper; for, as stated above, immediately after receiving the morsel he went out to summon those to whom he would deliver the Lord. After Judas’s departure, however, the Lord, as John relates, delivered a lengthy discourse [Col. 0467C] to the disciples. He spoke its first part while still reclining, up to the passage where he says: “But that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father commanded me, so I do. Arise, let us go hence” (John XIV.31).

Expounding this passage, blessed Augustine says [Note: [Col. 0468D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXVIII, col. 824]:

> “It is as though it were said: Why then do you delay, if you have no sin to which the punishment of death is owed? He immediately added: ‘But that the world may know,’ etc. ‘Let us go,’ he said. Where, if not to that place at which he was to be delivered to death? He had a command from the Father to die.”

After he had said to his disciples, “Rise, let us go from here,” and they had risen from reclining at table and sung the hymn of thanksgiving of which Matthew and Mark write [Col. 0467D], he continued the rest of his discourse until he left that house and went, according to his custom, to the Mount of Olives. Thus Luke also mentions the Lord, saying: “By day he was teaching in the temple, but at night he went out and spent the night on the mountain called Olivet” (Luke 21:37). And again: “Going out, he went according to his custom to the Mount of Olives” (Luke 22:39). His disciples followed him.

For the Lord, solicitous for our salvation, devoted the day to preaching and spent the night in prayer. For this he sought a secluded place, remote from the tumult of the world, where he and his disciples might pray more purely. When he had arrived there [Col. 0468A] and had prayed, he also invites them to prayer, saying: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41). As though he were saying: “It is easy for you to profess yourselves ready to confess me, and, with Peter, to say that you are prepared to go with me both to prison and to death; but in the flesh you are still weak for resisting temptations.”

That Christ’s humanity, with the moment of the Passion imminent, turned itself to prayer, and exhorted to prayer the disciples who were to be scandalized by this, plainly teaches us never to presume upon our own strength when placed in any danger; for human constancy cannot overcome death unless the Lord supplies us with that power. Daniel, when he was in distress, is read to have prayed to the Lord three times a day [Col. 0468B] (Dan. 6:10), as though understanding him to be one in three persons. The Lord now likewise undertakes a threefold prayer, proving himself to be truly human, like us in all things except sin, by showing that he possessed the genuine weakness of the flesh, so that both his true Passion and his assumption of flesh may be believed.

Thus praying he says: “Father, if it is possible,” etc. (Matt. 26:39). And again: “Father, if this cup cannot pass,” etc. (ibid., 42). “If it is possible,” he says—that is, if it is fitting that the human race can be saved by some other means of redemption than through my death. He calls his death a cup, one that passes, since he was soon to rise again. By this death, plainly, as though by a certain draught, he was about to refresh his desire for our redemption, as it were his thirst [Col. 0468C].

But did he fear the death which he exhorts us not at all to fear, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10:28)? Certainly, I do not recall that any martyrs, when they came to their contest, prayed that the suffering they were to undergo might pass from them; rather, they received it with joyful spirit and great desire, fulfilling the Apostle’s saying: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23). Did he, who offered himself to death, fear it more than the rest? Or did he come sadly to that death which others are said to meet joyfully?

For Mark reports of him that “he began to be alarmed and distressed” (Mark 14:33); and both Mark and Matthew write that he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. [Col. 0468D] 26:38; Mark 14:34). They also record him as declaring that he did not wish the bitterness of the Passion, and as setting his own will at variance with the Father’s will, when he says: “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26:39), or: “Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36). In Luke we read: “Father, if you will, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, let not my will but yours be done” (Luke 22:42). There it is further added: “An angel appeared to him from heaven, strengthening him; and being in agony, he prayed more earnestly. And his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground” (ibid., 43–44).

We do not read that anyone else sweated blood through fear of death; this is evidently beyond human nature [Col. 0469A]. Or perhaps he feared more than the rest—he whom fear of the Passion compelled to this? Or did he shed this sweat willingly rather than from the anxiety of fear? What strong athlete, finally, do we read to have been so troubled by the danger of death and disturbed as though in despair, as Scripture seems to say the Lord was? “Now,” he says, “my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour” (John 12:27). And later: “When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit” (John 13:31).

Now, even if in these words he seems, in some respects, to have transformed his members into himself, so that these things were said or done in the person of his members [Note: The passage is corrupt, as are several below], nevertheless this sweat certainly must never be understood literally as occurring in their person. Blessed [Col. 0469B] Ambrose, however, does not hesitate to affirm that he shrank from the suffering of death more than others. Thus he says, writing *On the Faith* to Gratian, Book II [Note: [Col. 0470D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVI, col. 568]:

> “Peter says: ‘I lay down my life for you.’ Christ says: ‘My soul is troubled.’ Both are true, and both are full of meaning: the inferior does not fear, while the superior bears the emotion of one who fears. For Peter, as a human being, does not know the force of death; Christ, as God established in a body, displays the frailty of the flesh, so that the impiety of those who abhor the mystery of the Incarnation might be excluded.”

From these words it is plainly shown that his soul, which through union with the all-knowing Word knew the supreme torment of death as though it had experienced it . . ., truly recoiled from it more than other souls could. Yet [Col. 0469C] the more he feared death and remained steadfast in the Passion, the more brightly the virtue of obedience shone in him, and the greater was the love he displayed toward us for whom he suffered. In this also he wished to offer consolation to weaker members, lest, when they trembled at the contest of suffering, they should despair of pardon because of their weakness.

How steadfastly the Lord met the Passion and persevered in it, anyone who carefully considers the magnitude of his fear may judge: his fortitude was incomparable in him. [Lacuna.] For, to omit the rest, who would not marvel that, when Pilate questioned him and he refused to answer, he heard from him: “Do you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have power to release you,” etc. [Col. 0469D] (John 19:10)?

He was also sent by Pilate to Herod, as being under Herod’s jurisdiction because he was a Galilean, so that he might thus easily be released through him; yet, though questioned at length, he deigned to answer him nothing, much less to show him some sign—which Herod especially desired. Therefore, his apparent alarm, distress, and agitation, so great that he seems almost despairing when he says, “And what shall I say?” are all signs, not of cowardice or mistrust, but of the extreme fear he assumed in order to demonstrate weakness, so that what precedes death itself might appear more grievous than death. The angel appearing in the person of the Father [Col. 0470A] strengthens him, just as had happened earlier, when the Father said to him: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John 12:28).

This consolation is to be understood as the answer to the prayer he was making for his own; it was an answer which, when heard, would console the disciples. What believer, Lord, could hear even this anxiety of your Passion without compassion? Who could endure this disturbance of yours for our sake? The Apostle says: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it,” etc. (1 Cor. 12:26), being concerned for one another. What, then, ought we to do for the head who bears our sorrows and sins? Who can understand this with dry eyes? Whose stony heart would not be split by this grief? The veil of the temple was torn at your Passion, Lord [Col. 0470B], and at the earthquake even the hardness of rocks was split. The sun was darkened, as though it could not bear to behold the enormity of the crime. Even insensible things, as though they felt your Passion, displayed the affection of compassion. But that this compassion too may penetrate and rend our hearts, let charity, sighing over what has been interrupted but not abandoned, return the pen to its work.

The Lord therefore went out to the Mount of Olives and, as Matthew relates (Matt. 26), came thence with his disciples to an estate called Gethsemane. Mark calls this place a farm; John says: “Across the Cedron [read: torrent] there was a garden, into which Jesus often went with his disciples” (John 18:1), as though it were an especially secluded place [Col. 0470C] suitable for teaching the disciples or for prayer. The estate of Gethsemane is thus understood to be that place beyond the torrent Cedron, situated at the foot of the Mount of Olives.

When it is called “the torrent Cedron,” *Cedron* is a Greek genitive, meaning “of cedars.” It is called a torrent because that water runs intermittently, not continually, in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, where cedars also grow. This place was Abraham’s garden; he had several gardens and dwellings around Salem. Jesus frequented the place with his disciples, and it was therefore well known to Judas. Thus he seeks him there in order to betray him, and finds him there as he sought him, as John immediately continues: “Judas therefore, having received a cohort [Col. 0470D] and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, came there with lanterns, torches, and weapons” (John 18:3).

The cohort of Gentiles came from Pilate the governor, so that Gentiles too might not be absent from his betrayal—those also whom he had come to redeem by his death; that is, he was delivered to death by both Jews and Gentiles, since he suffered death for the salvation of all.

Luke indeed relates that the chief priests themselves—that is, the high priests, the temple officers, and the elders—also came. This seems to be understood as being done through their servants, not in their own persons. For from the accounts of the other evangelists [Col. 0471A] we know that the Lord was seized by the cohort and officers and led to Annas or Caiaphas, the high priests. They come bearing lanterns, so that those who are in the darkness of blindness may seize the very light of the world. They come armed with clubs and weapons, either to use force against one who resisted or to drive him away from themselves.

Jesus therefore went forward, knowing all things that were to come upon him. While men prepare to use force against God, the Lord freely, not dragged there, meets the Passion, as he himself said: “No one takes my life from me; I lay it down myself.” “Knowing all things,” he says (John 10:18): that is, not ignorant of their schemes, and knowing that through the dreadful punishment of death he would accomplish your salvation and thereafter be glorified by the Resurrection, the Ascension, and the coming of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0471B].

He who had previously withdrawn from the Passion because his hour had not yet come, and had commanded his disciples: “When they persecute you from one city to another, flee to another” (Matt. 10:23), knowing that the time fitting for the Passion had now arrived, offers himself at Passover as the Passover, or lamb, for sacrifice. He went forward and said: “Whom do you seek?” (John 18:4). Truly, I say, as one ignorant of their utterly wicked search; for it is yours to be ignorant of evils which you reject and to know the good which you approve. So too, Adam, whom you knew before sin, after sin you seek as one unknown, saying: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3:9). Likewise, questioning as unknown the deed of the woman which you reject, you say: “Why have you done this?” (ibid., 13). And replying to the foolish virgins, you say: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Conversely, you say to Moses: “I know you by name” (Exod. 33:12), and it is written: “The Lord knows those who are his” (Num. 16:5).

They answered him: “Jesus of Nazareth” (John 18:5). O blind men, truly coming in darkness against the light, and at night against the day, when you answer him that you seek the very one whom you have come to destroy! He advances into battle like a standard-bearer before his followers. You do not recognize as Lord the one whom you see coming to meet you alone. For if you recognized him, you would by no means reveal to him, in your answer, the deceit of your scheme. Coming against Wisdom, because you do not know it, you remain foolish; nor can you perceive him when present unless he makes himself known to you. You answer “Jesus,” and, lest he himself be mistaken concerning himself in your reply, you add the qualifying designation, as though instructing him about himself: “of Nazareth.” Would that you sought Jesus—whom you call Jesus, that is, Savior—as Savior, so that you might hold in your hearts what you have upon your lips; lest, while seeking to destroy the Savior, you destroy yourselves instead!

Jesus said to them: “I am he” (ibid.). For they could not know him unless he himself made himself known, just as they could not seize him unless he surrendered himself. “Judas, who betrayed him, was also standing with them” (ibid.). Luke relates that Judas went before them; and Mark (Mark 14) says that when he arrived, he immediately approached him and said, “Rabbi,” and kissed him. Then they laid hands on him and held him.

It seems to me, therefore, that when they began to set out, Judas went ahead of them as their guide. But when they began to draw near, confounded and troubled by his own conscience, or hesitating, he held himself back and checked his pace so that they went ahead of him. Thus John now says that, when they reached Jesus, Judas stood with them rather than going before them. He stood with them, indeed, but not as the others stood with the Lord. He stood as one stupefied and troubled by the enormity of his conceived crime, and especially confounded at the sight [Col. 0472B] of the Lord; or perhaps struck with such blindness that he could not recognize him unless he declared himself.

Nevertheless, in order to fulfill what he had said—“Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one; seize him” (Matt. 26:48)—setting aside all shame and fearing not God but men, he came forward to kiss him, as though identifying the one who had already identified himself, so that the Lord might show that nothing was done to him except by his own disposal. Hence it follows: “When therefore he said to them, ‘I am he,’ they drew back and fell to the ground” (John 18:6). What are you doing, you who were sent? Behold, he whom you seek is present; offering himself, he says, “I am he,” and you cannot endure even that voice of his, against whom you trusted that you could use force. Going backward, unable to approach the one whom [Col. 0472C] you came to seize, you fell supine to the ground.

For this fall properly belongs to the reprobate, just as falling upon one’s face belongs to the elect. Hence blessed Gregory says in his homily on Ezekiel [Note: [Col. 0471D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, col. 872]:

> “The elect fall upon their face, and the reprobate backward; for one who falls behind himself falls where he does not see. The wicked, who fall amid visible things, are said to fall backward because they collapse where they are now unable to see what will subsequently follow them. But the righteous voluntarily cast themselves down amid these visible things in order to be raised to invisible things; they fall, as it were, upon their faces because, pierced by fear, they are humbled while seeing.”

Again, therefore, he asked them: “Whom do you seek?” And they said: “Jesus of Nazareth.” Jesus answered: “I told you that I am he” [Col. 0472D]. They had drawn back—not merely falling bodily, but also falling into such an ecstasy of fear and disturbance that they could recognize the Lord neither at his own declaration nor by the betrayer’s kiss. A second time he asks whom they seek, and a second time teaches them that he is the one whom they say they seek. In this is plainly shown both his perseverance in the Passion and their persistence in the obstinacy of their wickedness.

“If, therefore, you seek me, let these go. That the saying might be fulfilled,” etc. (ibid., 8). “If,” he says, “you seek me and no other—as is already plain from your two answers—it ought to suffice you to complete your wickedness against me” [Col. 0473A]. By this, he says, he meant the disciples who were present, so that he alone might enter the winepress of the Passion, as Isaiah had foretold in his person: “I have trodden the winepress alone,” etc. (Isa. 63:3).

“The saying,” says the evangelist, was what the Lord himself had previously said while speaking to the Father: “Of those whom you gave me I have kept them, and none of them perished except the son of perdition” (John 17:12).

Augustine, in his commentary on John, on this passage [Note: [Col. 0473D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, col. 1931]:

> “Why would he lose them if they died then, except because they did not yet believe in him as all who are not to perish believe?”

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0474D] Ibid., col. 1933]:

> “If Peter, after denying Christ, had departed from here, what else would he have done but perish?”

“Let these go,” he says; but he did not add, “And seize me,” lest, by commanding mercy, he should seem also to command the impiety which he permitted to happen [Col. 0473B].

The betrayer, approaching the Lord, said: “Hail, Rabbi,” and kissed him. But Jesus said to him: “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26:50). Or, as Luke says: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). This kiss is not a sign of peace but of betrayal—the sign Matthew mentions: “His betrayer had given them a sign, saying: ‘Whomever I shall kiss, he is the one; seize him, and lead him away carefully’” (Matt. 26:48).

Behold, leader of the blind and of the most wretchedly miserable: what is this caution to which your madness exhorts them? As though human caution could prevail against the wisdom of God! Most shameless betrayer, justifying every abomination of crimes by your own crimes. You had received from the Lord the care of stewardship among the others, keeping the money-box and stealing what you could from it, wishing to enlarge your own purse, not the Lord’s; yet you presumed to sell the Lord himself and to set the very price of the world at a money-price.

To crown your wickedness, consider the very steps of your conceived betrayal, that you may recognize that no abomination of shamelessness is lacking in your betrayal. On the very night when you were planning to betray him, daring to come to supper, you did not fear to put your criminal hand—already, as it were, stained with his blood—into his dish, so that by this act, as though it testified to your good conscience, you might remove every suspicion from yourself. A sharer in both the old and the new Passover, and afterward, in the very act [Col. 0473D] of betrayal, greeting him as teacher and kissing the lamb as a wolf, son of perdition, you hear from the gentle Father: “Friend, for what have you come?”

“Friend,” indeed—not loving, but loved; not one who loves, but one loved, so far as the display of familiarity and friendship is concerned. “For what,” he says, “have you come?” As though saying: “Consider, wretch, what a causeless abomination you dare to commit, when by the steps already described you arrive at the betrayal you have conceived.” In this also the Lord, detesting the sign of betrayal, says: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” That is: “Why, unhappy man, have you chosen a kiss as the sign of betrayal, when even among enemies it is customarily the supreme pledge of peace?”

Most unhappy of all men, it would have been better for you had you not been born; for, dying in the womb like an abortive birth, you would not have deserved so grievous a punishment!

Those who were around him, seeing what was about to happen, said to him: “Lord, shall we strike with the sword?” (Luke 20:49). Simon Peter, therefore, more ardent than the rest, having a sword, drew it, struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his right ear. But Jesus answered and said: “Allow this much.” And when he had touched his ear, he healed him (ibid., 51).

The others ask the Lord whether they ought to avenge him by striking. Peter does not wait for an answer in order to hear instruction; vehement love has no measure, nor does boundless charity consider [Col. 0474B] what it exceeds. He knew the patience of the Lord’s gentleness: when he had once reproved him privately as the Lord predicted his Passion, saying, “Be gracious to yourself, Lord; may this never happen to you” (Matt. 16:22), he heard from him: “Get behind me, Satan; you do not understand the things of God” (ibid., 23). He knew also that the Lord had commanded the disciples generally: “You have heard that it was said: ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, do not resist evil. If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5:38–39).

Instructed by these and similar lessons in patience, Peter knew that the Lord would by no means grant him this vengeance. Therefore, lest, by striking, he should become guilty of disobedience if he waited for the answer [Col. 0474C], he forestalled him, offering the others an example of what they should do, as their leader or chief: so that, just as Judas on the opposing side was a leader toward wickedness, Peter might be a leader in the Lord’s battle line toward vengeance. Thus, while the others ask whether they should strike, he, not delaying to strike, arrogates to himself the vengeance of the material sword, though it had by no means been entrusted to him. Therefore, he is immediately corrected by the Lord.

Yet what was not rightly done at that time in deed is not empty of significance in mystery. For Luke’s account tells us that there were two swords at the Lord’s supper. Thus it is written of the Lord and his disciples: “And he said to them: ‘When I sent you without purse, bag, and sandals, did you lack anything?’ They said: ‘Nothing.’ Then he said to them: ‘But now, let the one who has a purse take it, and likewise a bag; and let the one who has none sell his tunic and buy a sword. For I tell you that this which is written must still be fulfilled in me: “And he was reckoned among the lawless.” For the things concerning me have an end.’ They said: ‘Lord, behold, here are two swords.’ And he said to them: ‘It is enough.’ And going out he went according to his custom to the Mount of Olives, and his disciples followed him” (Luke 22:35).

A purse is larger than a bag, and therefore is necessary for carrying provisions for many persons on a journey; a bag, however, seems sufficient for individuals. Thus the Lord, while present here, wholly provided for their needs, so that they need not carry anything necessary on the way; in order that after his departure from the earth his presence might be loved and desired all the more, the more necessary they had experienced it to be. But now, whoever has one must henceforth provide by taking such things in bag or purse both for yourselves and for others. And whoever does not have—supply “a purse or bag from which he may obtain a sword”—let him sell the tunic that appears more necessary, in order to buy one.

Taken literally, as the following words indicate, this seems to have been said so that, when they came armed to the place of betrayal, the Lord’s patience might be proved the greater, the more powerful he came in his own defense. “They have an end” means “they have their completion,” so that all things written concerning me may be fulfilled in me [Col. 0475B].

The two swords, whether found by chance at the Lord’s supper or brought there by some of the disciples for protection as the Passion approached, signify the two swords in the Church: the material sword, which the king employs in bodily punishment, and the spiritual sword, by which the priest strikes the soul through a sentence of excommunication. Peter, taking up this spiritual sword, cut off the right ear of the one who came against Christ, because whoever is opposed to Christ’s commands must be struck by a sentence of anathema. Thus his right ear is cut off when he is removed from the preaching of the divine word and forbidden entrance to the Church.

The left ear is that by which we attend to earthly things when we are instructed about them. The right ear is that which gives hearing [Col. 0475C] to what is preached concerning heavenly things or the salvation of the soul. Therefore what Peter did, though blameworthy in deed, is nevertheless fitting in mystery. For an office is called an act appropriate to a particular person.

Moreover, the right ear here is called not so much *auris* (“ear”) as *auricula* (“little ear”). Few indeed are the elect who give their hearing to what is said concerning the salvation of the soul; what is preached concerning heavenly things can scarcely be grasped, and, because understanding is subtle, it reaches the mind’s intellect through, as it were, the narrow opening of the ear. What the Lord said concerning the two aforesaid swords—“It is enough”—and what he said after the cutting off of the ear—“Allow this much”—refer to the mystery of the thing signified [Col. 0475D].

For the two swords distinguished above are sufficient for the Church in administering justice: as a human being consists of soul and flesh, so the two swords are exercised in these two things—the king’s in the body, the priest’s in the soul. “Allow this much,” he says to the disciples: that is, be content with your authority, and do not presume to carry vengeance any further than, as has been said, cutting off the right ear. The Lord restores the ear cut off by Peter and heals the man who was struck, because it belongs to him to inspire the repentance by which the sinner returns and, reconciled by the word of salvation, gives heed.

O mercy of the Savior! O impiety of the persecutor! The Lord heals the man who was struck, yet the man healed does not cease to persecute him. He receives a benefit, yet ungratefully persists in his obstinacy [Col. 0476A]. The persecutors see the miracle, yet do not change their purpose of persecution. The persecutor is corrected so that the persecution may cease.

“Put your sword back into its sheath,” he says to Peter. “For everyone who takes the sword shall perish by the sword” (John 18:11). “Who takes,” he says, “in order to kill”—not one to whom it has been handed by lawful authority—“is himself worthy to perish by the sword.” “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will immediately provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26:53). As though he plainly said: “I do not need the protection of you twelve men, since, if I wished, so great a multitude of angels would be present to assist me.”

At that hour Jesus said to the crowds: “Have you come out with swords and clubs to seize me as though I were a robber? Daily I sat among you [Col. 0476B] in the temple, and you did not seize me” (ibid., 56). “When I was with you daily in the temple, you did not lay hands on me. But this is your hour and the power of darkness” (Luke 22:53). “All this happened that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” “Then all the disciples left him and fled” (Matt. 26:56). “A certain young man followed him, clothed in a linen cloth over his naked body; and they seized him. But he left the linen cloth behind and fled from them naked” (Mark 14:51).

Robbers lay ambushes on roads; thieves operate in houses. What he says, “as though I were a robber,” means: as though I were one who blocks the road, lies in wait for travelers, and permits them no safe or free passage—whereas you, Lord, are rather the very way, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). “Daily,” that is, frequently, in the temple where all assemble, sitting as one secure, not concealed and lurking like a robber; for a *latro* (“robber”) is so named from lying hidden. And although I sat and taught publicly in this way, you did not dare to lay hands on me—not even then when I drove them, scourged, from the temple. For his [hour], that is, the time fitting for the Passion, had not yet come; it had been appointed by his own ordering. Thus he plainly shows that they could do nothing to him unless he permitted and arranged it.

“Your hour,” as also mine: yours for destroying, mine for saving. “The power of darkness”: that is, power permitted by me over me to you who are blind. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory [Col. 0476D]. “All this,” namely the Lord’s seizure and Judas’s betrayal. These words too seem to be those of the Lord rather than the evangelist. Hence it follows: “Then all the disciples.” As though it were said: when they heard him declare that his Passion had been ordained in the prophets and that he permitted them no vengeance whatsoever, they fled, leaving the innocent one to the impious and the lamb to the wolves. For he himself had foretold this by the prophetic testimony: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered” (Zech. 13:7).

Some understand this young man to be John, especially beloved by the Lord and regarded as younger than the others; others, James the Lord’s brother.

Bede, on Mark, on this passage [Note: [Col. 0475D] *Patrologia*, vol. XCII, col. 278]:

> “The evangelist does not say who this young man was.”

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0477D] Ibid., col. 279]:

> “Nothing prevents us from understanding him to be John.”

Jeremiah, in the shorter Breviary, Psalm 36: “The Jews used violence either against Peter when they said, ‘You too are one of them’; or against James, who, when he was betrayed, leaving the linen cloth behind, fled away naked.”

“Over his naked body”: that is, directly upon it, because underneath the linen cloth he had no garment. Perhaps, in response to the Lord’s saying, he had given or pawned his tunic or another garment in order to buy a sword. The statement, “They seized him,” when they found him following alone after the others had already scattered, plainly suggests that they had by no means dared to attack the apostles while they stood armed together with the Lord.

The cohort, therefore, the tribune, and the Jewish officers, having seized Jesus, bound him and led him first to Annas [Col. 0477B] (John 18:12). The tribune was in command of the Gentile cohort. He is called *tribunus* either from “three” or from *tribus*, that is, peoples and commoners. For the Roman people are said first to have appointed three such officials over themselves, so that, just as military commanders presided over soldiers, these men might preside over the common people.

They bound him in accordance with the counsel of the one who had said, “Lead him away carefully,” so that he might not escape. O blind men! Could not he who so quickly restored the ear loosen bonds if he wished? But he endures the bonds of the wicked so that, proved in every patience, he might loose the bonds of sinners. The Lord is bound by servants for a time—he who would bind Satan, the strong man armed, forever [Col. 0477C]. Bound like a robber, he is led away, deprived of human help, though a multitude of angels stood by him.

He is first brought to Annas, the high priest, Caiaphas’s father-in-law; Caiaphas, indeed, was high priest in that year (ibid., 13). For different high priests, already appointed, performed their offices in successive years. He is first brought to Annas to be mocked there, then to Caiaphas, and finally to Pilate, so that, mocked repeatedly, he might be overwhelmed with shame and, afflicted repeatedly, be forced to fail. He is first presented to the high priests as experts in the Law, so that he might be judged according to the Law by those who professed to know the Law, and that wickedness might begin with those through whom it ought rather to have been restrained.

Although Caiaphas administered the high priesthood in that year, he nevertheless does not disdain that Jesus should first be led [Col. 0477D] to another high priest, so that he might condemn the accused with greater freedom and security, since he saw him already condemned by another, so that “the word might stand in the mouth of two witnesses.”

Simon Peter and another disciple followed Jesus. That disciple was known to the high priest, and he entered with Jesus into the high priest’s court. But Peter stood outside at the door. Therefore the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out, spoke to the doorkeeper, and brought Peter in (ibid., 15 ff.). The other evangelists report only concerning Peter that he followed Jesus at a distance. He who had stood nearer to him at the arrest and had been more ardent in vengeance, cutting off the ear of the high priest’s servant [Col. 0478A], now, when the others had scattered in flight and, as Mark reports, the young man who had been seized had left the linen cloth behind and fled naked, Peter himself, now frightened, followed the Lord from afar.

Yet the force of love did not permit him wholly to desire separation from the Lord; for however greatly the Church, signified by Peter, may tremble in adversities, even if fear compels it in some members temporarily to deny him, the foundation of charity does not allow it to perish or to be utterly separated from Christ. John’s statement that another disciple was joined to Peter in following Christ, though he does not specify who he was, seems humbly to indicate himself. As blessed Augustine notes, he commonly identifies himself in such expressions, saying, “the other disciple” [Col. 0478B]. For he alone, when the rest had already scattered, stood with the Lord’s mother beside him at the Cross, as John himself writes.

For when Peter is said to love Christ more, and John to be loved more by Christ, it is said that at that time each ought to have shown him a greater love.

The high priest then questioned Jesus concerning his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him: “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogue and temple, where all the Jews assemble; and I have said nothing in secret. Why do you question me? Question those who heard what I said to them. Behold, they know what I have said.” When he had said this, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus on the face, saying: “Is this how you answer the high priest?” [Col. 0478C] Jesus answered him: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness concerning the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” (ibid., 19 ff.)

The Lord rebukes the high priest’s questioning as superfluous and inappropriate. Superfluous indeed, because what had been said openly and was known to all needs no proof. Inappropriate, because no one ought to be commended by his own testimony. Thus the Lord rightly judges that those who heard him, rather than he himself, should be questioned about these matters. “And when he had said this, one of the attendants,” etc. As though he were a despiser of the high priest’s command because, at his bidding, he did not give testimony about himself, he is struck with a slap. “Bear witness concerning the evil,” because witnesses must be produced before punishment for a crime. But the chief priests [Col. 0478D] and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus, in order to deliver him to death. And they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two false witnesses came and said: “This man said: I am able to destroy the temple of God, and after three days to rebuild it” (Matt. XXVI, 59 ff.).

As though taking their occasion from his saying, “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness concerning the evil,” they seek false witnesses regarding his evil words—he whose true witnesses they cannot produce, nor whose deeds they can accuse. The two false witnesses, as though truth could stand in the mouth of two false men, are convicted of falsehood in the charges they bring against the Lord. For he who had said, [Col. 0479A] “Destroy this temple,” had by no means foretold either that he would do it or that he could do it; rather, he indicated that it was to be done by them—not indeed concerning the temple made by hands, as they lied, but concerning the temple of his body, to be destroyed by them through death.

“And the high priest rose and said to him: Do you answer nothing to what these men testify against you? But Jesus kept silent; and the high priest said to him: I adjure you by the living God, that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XXVI, 62 ff.). Rising up, the high priest, impatient because he could find no ground for slander, displays by the movement of his body the madness of his mind, and provokes him to answer so that he may find any occasion whatever for accusation. The Lord is silent in response to the testimony alleged against him, judging it so manifestly false as to deserve no [Col. 0479B] occasion or answer. Understanding this, the high priest attempts by adjuration to wring from him a blasphemy by which, while professing the supreme truth, he may seem manifestly convicted and guilty of the utmost falsehood. Adjured by the living God, lest he should become guilty of injury to so great a Majesty, the Lord confesses the truth—he who is truth itself, to be condemned for truth’s sake. Jesus therefore says to them . . . . . (The remainder is lacking.)

## SERMON XII. ON THE CROSS

With what devotion we ought to pursue the veneration of the Lord’s cross, the blessed Apostle carefully declares in writing to the Galatians: “But far be it from me to glory, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. [Col. 0479C] VI, 14). For the more fully the Lord’s cross, by which we have been redeemed, is to be glorified by us, the more truly a human being redeemed by this kind of redemption can glory. But what is it to glory, except to regard oneself as something great and precious? Now the worth of any thing can be known in nothing so well as in its price. So too, the price itself given for humanity’s redemption openly shows how precious humanity was in God’s sight, how great a care divine mercy always exercised for humanity, and with what bowels of compassion it embraced humanity.

Carefully considering this, and glorying uniquely in it, the Apostle says, as we have mentioned above: “But far be it from me to glory,” etc. It is as if he openly said: Let others glory in whatever they wish; let them consider themselves precious through any riches [Col. 0479D] or honor whatever. But far be it from me to glory except in this manner of my redemption, which is judged more disgraceful and worthless among unbelievers. For the more unworthy things the Lord endured for humanity, the more he showed humanity to be held worthy and dear in his sight.

No instrument of execution was in ancient times considered more accursed than the cross; no death was judged so shameful and detestable. Therefore they resolved to choose this kind of execution not only for Christ’s punishment but also for the disgrace of the impious, as had previously been prophesied of them through Wisdom when they said: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wis. II, 20). And the Apostle, after saying, “Having become obedient unto death” (Phil. II, 8), [Col. 0480A] as though this were too little unless he also specified the very kind of death as abominable, immediately added: “even death on a cross” (ibid.). That is, not only unto death, but unto so shameful a death—a death by which blasphemers especially, that is, those who presumed to commit some blasphemy against God, were punished. Thus, reproaching the Lord because he called himself the Son of God, they said: “He has blasphemed. What further need have we of witnesses?” (Matt. XXVI, 65). And, as though he had deserved this kind of death by blasphemy, they cried out: “Let him be crucified!” (Matt. XXVII, 23).

Concerning this very kind of death, how detestable and full of divine curse it seemed, the book of Deuteronomy declares in these words: “When a man has committed a sin deserving death, and, having been condemned [Col. 0480B] to death, has been hanged on a gallows, his corpse shall not remain on the wood, but you shall bury it on the same day, because he who hangs on wood is accursed by God; and you shall not defile your land, which the Lord has given you as a possession” (Deut. XX, 22 ff.). Mindful of this passage, the Apostle, writing to the Galatians, says: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on wood’” (Gal. III, 13).

From these words, then, it is clearly shown how disgraceful the punishment of the cross was held to be especially among the Jews, who seek only the surface of the letter and not the mystical senses in the Law. But what could be more absurd than to believe that all those who are punished by this kind of death rather than another deserve condemnation under the curse [Col. 0480C] of God? For it is not the manner of punishment but the fall into guilt that makes a person guilty. Thus it is written: “The righteous man, by whatever death he is overtaken, shall be at rest” (Wis. IV, 7).

But if, removing the veil of Moses, we contemplate the Law inwardly with unveiled face, we may fittingly apply this curse both to individual human beings through guilt and to Christ himself through punishment. For because of the sin of the first parents, committed on the forbidden tree, we all thereby incur condemnation and, as it were, die upon the tree, since we are born with original sin. Accordingly, the Lord rebuking Adam and, as it were, pronouncing a sentence of curse, says: [Col. 0480D] “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. III, 17). Therefore, all of us, contracting this sentence of condemnation from Adam, are born and remain like corpses without life, until, reborn from water and Spirit, we are made alive from this death of the soul.

Now it is commanded that a corpse dead by hanging on wood be buried on the same day, because in this present life itself, in which we are born, we must be buried together with Christ through baptism, lest our earth be defiled—that is, lest we remain in the contagion of earthly generation if we are not specially regenerated. Thus it is rightly said: “Accursed by God is he who hangs on wood,” because, even if we have not yet incurred sins of our own, nevertheless that one sin called original sin, committed, as has been said, upon the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, suffices for our condemnation, [Col. 0481A] to which we have been assigned by divine judgment and on account of which we have been struck by God with a certain curse.

This curse is also directed back upon Christ through punishment, whom the Prophet long before foretold as “stricken by God and afflicted” because of our crimes. And just as the others, as has been said, incurred the death of the soul upon the tree, so he incurred death of the body, so that, freeing us from the former by the latter, he might turn our curse into blessing. Hence the Apostle, after first saying, “Having become a curse for us, as it is written” (Gal. III, 13), immediately adds, “so that blessing might come among the Gentiles.” Therefore, just as Christ died bodily upon the tree—that is, for the transgression of the forbidden tree—so also he was bodily cursed by God through punishment; that is, by God’s sentence he was assigned to this punishment. [Col. 0481B] For this reason he is said to have taken up or borne our sins, that is, to have endured the punishment for our sins and thus in some manner shared in our curse.

If we review in detail his punishment or passion, by which he was brought to death, we shall find that the things preceding death were far more grievous and unbearable than death itself. For as the moment of his passion approached, we read that his soul was so distressed that his sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground. Since he knew how great the pain of the passion would be in that dissolution of body and soul, it is not surprising if, according to the weakness of his assumed humanity, he greatly shrank from this supreme passion.

Afterward, seized and held, and moreover, as John relates, bound, he was first brought before the priests. There, as Mark recalls, some began [Col. 0481C] to spit upon him and to cover his face (Mark XIV, 53); and, as Matthew writes, to spit in his face, to strike him both with fists and slaps, and to mock him, saying: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck you?” (Matt. XXVI, 67). There, among other things, when he was questioned by the high priest about his disciples and his teaching, and he answered, “I have spoken openly,” etc., one of the attendants struck him with a slap, saying: “Do you answer the high priest in this way?” (John XVIII, 20, 32). It is clear that these things were done to him during the night of his arrest.

When morning came, they brought him, still or again bound, from the council of the priests to Pilate the governor. When he had been brought there, as Matthew says (Matt. XXVII, 11), he stood before the governor. He stood, I say, as stated, bound rather than seated, so that they might afflict him in both ways—both by standing and by being bound. How steadfastly he remained there is openly shown when, questioned by Pilate, he gave him no answer. Marveling at this confidence of his, and as though at contempt for himself, Pilate said: [Col. 0481D] “Do you not know that I have power to crucify you and power to release you?” (John XIX, 10). Sent also by Pilate to Herod, when he was questioned by him too with many words, he answered him nothing. Therefore he was despised and mocked both by Herod and by his soldiers, clothed in a white garment, [Col. 0482A] and thus sent back to Pilate (John XVIII, 25).

Questioned, then, by rulers who could do very much to set him free, he did not judge them worthy of an answer; yet, as we have mentioned above, when struck by the high priest’s attendant, he did not refuse him a mild reply, saying: “If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” (John XVIII, 25). Finally, we do not fail to know how much he suffered before Pilate. Although Pilate had confessed him innocent for the third time, as Luke recalls (Luke XXIII, 14), and had demonstrated the same by washing his hands, he finally scourged him, as though carrying out what he had earlier said: “I shall punish him and release him” (Luke XXIII, 22), hoping thereby at least to bend the Jews’ cruelty to mercy. [Col. 0482B] When he could not accomplish this, he gave the man, beaten with scourges, over to their will.

Then the soldiers, as Matthew relates, receiving him, gathered the whole cohort around him (Matt. XXVII, 27). Once they had assembled, charging and reproaching him with making himself king, they mocked him as though in royal fashion: stripping him of his garments, they clothed him in cheap purple; instead of a diadem they crowned him with thorns; instead of a sceptre they furnished him with a reed; and, bending the knee and greeting him as king, saying, “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. II, 29), they also spat again in his face and struck his head with the reed.

Again, as John relates, Pilate went out to them and brought him with him, so cruelly handled, testing whether in this way he might somehow [Col. 0482C] soften their hardness and incline them to compassion. Going out to them, he said: “Behold, I bring him out to you, that you may know that I find no case against him” (John XIX, 4). Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment, and he said to them: “Behold the man” (ibid., 5). It is as if he said: Behold, what belongs to human weakness appears in me to you, not what belongs to divine power.

But after, as has been said, they had mocked him, they stripped him of the purple and put his own garments upon him. They again stripped these from him when he was to be crucified, and afterward divided them among themselves, as John records. Finally, when he was taken away to be crucified, he was compelled to carry the very instrument of the cross [Col. 0482D] as well, so that they might not spare him even then: he was first afflicted by the weight of the cross before being crucified upon it. Since, because of his bonds or the afflictions already described, he was unable to carry it easily or swiftly, the impious, unable to endure the delay of his death, compelled another man named Simon to carry the cross.

Finally, crucified, he is placed among thieves, to the height of his disgrace, so that through the similarity of punishment he might also be believed guilty of crime. No one can fail to know how great is the punishment of this instrument of execution. It is all the more prolonged, and does not immediately kill the person hanging upon it, because its more grievous suffering afflicts him for longer. And what is more painful than this execution, where the whole body is stretched out nailed in such a way that the suspended person is tortured no less by his own weight than by the very fastening of the nails? Therefore this one instrument of death is rightly called *crux* (“cross”) from *cruciare* (“to torture”). [Col. 0483A]

Behold: we have gathered from the Gospel writings the sequence of the Lord’s passion, insofar as it comes to mind. If we consider each event, as has been said, those things which preceded death were certainly more grievous than death itself, indeed unbearable. Hence it was not necessary that his legs be broken, as were those of the thieves, or that he be wounded with a lance in order to die; for through so many and such great things as he had endured before the cross, he had been brought to a swift death.

Let martyrs compare what they have suffered, and see that in comparison with the Lord’s passion the things they have endured are nothing or slight. Thus the lamentation of Jeremiah, sighing in his person, fittingly cries out: “Attend and see whether there is any pain like my pain” [Col. 0483B] (Lam. I, 12). Let women attend to this; and, as Ezekiel recalls, when a voice comes from above the firmament, let the living creatures stand still and lower their wings (Ezek. I, 25).

What else should the firmament be understood to be but the blessed angels, made steadfast while the others fell? Although they are in a certain dignity higher than us, who are still mortal, nevertheless God made man far surpasses them. A voice from the firmament sometimes comes to us when something is preached, or inwardly conceived in the mind through an interior word, concerning that blessedness of the angels which is promised to us. Another voice comes from above the firmament when what God has done for us in human nature is received by the ears of body or mind. When this occurs, the holy living creatures stand, as it were, in amazement or fear, and [Col. 0483C] lower their wings, because in considering so great a matter their own powers seem base to them.

But when they hear something from the firmament, as has been said, they still have their wings raised, because they do not regard it as great or wonderful that through so many struggles they reach that blessedness of angels which the angels received through God’s grace, preserving humility.

Behold: the martyrs, having suffered much for God and been proved in great virtues, might seem to have gained very great occasion for glorying, unless they remembered that the Lord had suffered things equally great or greater for them. When this comes to mind, they immediately lower their wings, as has been said, counting for nothing what servants have suffered when the Lord’s passion is considered. [Col. 0483D] This passion is shown to be all the more grievous and pitiable because it was more disgraceful.

For, to omit other things, who was mocked as shamefully or for as long as he was? First, after his arrest, he was brought to the Jews; after so many blows with fists and slaps, received with his face veiled while the impious taunted him to prophesy, he was so spat upon and deformed by spittle that, according to Isaiah, he had neither form nor beauty, and because of such vileness appeared the last of all men (Isa. LIII, 2). Then, presented to Pilate, he endured this injury too along with the rest.

What martyr is ever recorded as having been so covered and disfigured with spittle in insult? Who was mocked so many times—now among the Jews, now before Pilate or Herod; now stripped, now clothed [Col. 0484A] in his own or another’s garments; and so impiously dragged through so many places, in order that he might be mocked more by everyone? Finally, which saint was compelled to carry the very instrument by which he was to be killed?

What, brothers, can we reflect upon or say in response to this, except continually to groan within ourselves that prophetic saying: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. CXV, 12), and to prepare ourselves, according to our strength, to return in turn such great love as his, as it is added: “I shall receive the cup of salvation,” etc. (ibid.)? Since it is not within our strength to receive the cup of salvation—that is, to share by suffering in Jesus’ passion and, carrying our own cross, to follow him—may he by his grace grant this to us, to whose honor we venerate today the very cross [Col. 0484B] by which we have been redeemed. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. ON EASTER DAY

Both the Old and New Testament testify how greatly the Easter celebration of exultation concerns the devotion and honor of women. For when Easter was first celebrated by the people of God in Egypt, and the faithful were delivered that night through the submersion of the Egyptians, not men alone but women also, as Exodus narrates, offer to the Lord a song of thanksgiving. For it is written there: “Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the Lord, and said: Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously,” etc. (Exod. XV, 1). Concerning the song of the women, it is separately added: “Then Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a timbrel in her hand. And all the women went out after her with timbrels and dances; and she led them in song, saying: Let us sing to the Lord, for gloriously,” etc. (ibid., 20).

Consider carefully how full of mystery this song of the women is described to be. This Miriam, who led that choir of women in song, is understood to have been a virgin, since she is not recorded to have had a husband. Thus she preceded the others not only by the voice of her song but also by the privilege of her rank. She is recalled not merely as having sung, like Moses or the people, but is described also as a prophetess and as holding a timbrel in her hand. For what does *prophetes* mean except “one who sees”? [Col. 0484D] She sings a vision—that is, a revelation—to her the Lord also reveals the mysteries of the words; for in that deliverance of the people and submersion of their enemies, she discerned not so much the salvation of bodies as the salvation of souls figured there, which divine grace works daily in the sacrament of baptism.

The timbrel that she held in her hand signifies the mortification of the flesh, which she possessed in deed, so that her song might be more acceptable to God. Hence the Psalmist, exhorting us to praise God with the timbrel, says: “Praise him with the timbrel,” etc. (Ps. CL, 4). But we often have the timbrel more in our mouth than in our hand, when we preach the mortification of the flesh practiced by the saints but do not imitate it in deed. The more carefully Miriam’s song is described, [Col. 0485A] the more devout and pleasing to God it is understood to have been.

If we also review the sequence of the New Testament and understand in this Miriam and the other women with her another Mary, together with the devout women with her—to whom the Lord first showed the joy of his resurrection—we find every feature fittingly applicable to them. That woman is called a prophetess; this woman is called the apostle of the apostles. That woman took up a bodily timbrel; this one possessed a spiritual timbrel. For because this Mary had loved the living Lord more deeply, she was more afflicted at his death and, as it were, mortified. Therefore she deserved first to receive consolation from the resurrection, because she was more anxious and sorrowful over his death.

She is called the apostle [Col. 0485B] of the apostles—that is, the envoy of envoys—because the Lord first sent her to the apostles, that she might announce to them the joy of the resurrection. That Miriam led the others in the song; this Mary was the first among the others to obtain the joy of the resurrection, and, by announcing what she had first seen, she led the song. After her, this joy of the resurrection reached the other women before it reached the apostles or any men whatever. Sending them also to the apostles, the Lord said: “Go, announce to my brothers that they are to go into Galilee” (Matt. XXVIII, 10).

Here a reversed order is to be regarded as more blessed and honorable. At the old Easter, the men mentioned above are recalled as having sung first and the women afterward. But at our Easter—that is, on the day of the Lord’s resurrection—women obtained the spiritual song of exultation from the manifestation of the resurrection before men did. Easter is called *Pascha* in Hebrew, *phase* in Greek, and “passage” in Latin. At the old Easter, the Lord, passing through Egypt, killing the firstborn, and freeing his people through the passage of the Red Sea, distinguished this festival by the name of passage (Exod. XII). The present day of the Lord’s resurrection is also not inappropriately called Easter. For this very change of human nature from mortality to immortality, from corruption to incorruption, was a kind of passage and movement in Christ. For one passes immediately into another state and is, as it were, moved, because one is changed into something other than one had been before—as when what was mortal becomes immortal and what was corruptible, passible, or changeable is turned into its opposite. [Col. 0485D]

Considering this passage, the Evangelist says: “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come for him to pass from this world to the Father,” etc. (John XIII, 1). What is expressed by the name of Father except the power of divine majesty? In this world—that is, in this present troubled and miserable life—he had existed as though powerless and weak according to the frailty of his assumed humanity; and, humbling himself, he had descended and, as it were, withdrawn from the Father—that is, from the power of divinity—having been made in this respect lower even than the angels.

But now, in the resurrection, laying aside all this weakness, he is said to ascend or pass to the Father, since he retains in himself nothing now of weakness or impotence, but everything that he has belongs to power and strength. Thus he passes, as it were, wholly into God, since he is no longer properly to be called a human being like other human beings—that is, a mortal rational animal. [Col. 0486A] The blessed Apostle also carefully considered this when distinguishing his own election from that of the other apostles. Writing to the Galatians, he begins thus: “Paul, an apostle not from men nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead,” etc. (Gal. I, 1).

For the other apostles, as blessed Augustine recalls [Note: [Col. 0485D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, cols. 2107, 2108], were chosen by Christ as man—that is, while he was still mortal. But Paul afterward received a singular election from Christ now made, as it were, wholly God—that is, now living eternally more in a divine than in a human manner. The Apostle immediately explains this, as one might say, deification and glory of immortality when he says: “who raised him from the dead.”

Observe also that, in accordance with this glory of immutability and stability which Christ’s humanity obtained from the day of the resurrection, it is not inappropriate that both the day of the resurrection itself and that of the Lord’s ascension, which are now celebrated not in relation to one mortal and changeable but to one immortal and unchangeable, do not vary by weekday, but are always observed on the same weekday. The other solemnities of Christ, from the day of his conception [Col. 0486C] to Easter, and all feasts of saints, vary by weekdays, so that they are celebrated now on the first weekday, now on the second, or on another.
