Some are accustomed to be troubled as to why the day of the Lord’s passion, which most of all wrought our salvation, has no exultant festal celebration, but is observed in sorrow rather than joy, especially since the Church pays festive rejoicing to the passions of individual saints. I think the answer is that, for the glory of the Lord’s resurrection which follows the passion on the third day, the Church has carefully established this: the greater the compassion in us which has preceded from the Lord’s passion, the more welcome follows the exultation from the glory of the resurrection. Thus not only the sorrowful two days nearest to the Easter solemnity are set before its joy, but the abstinence of the whole forty days is also placed beforehand.

During that forty days, the expressions of joy—“Alleluia,” “Glory to God in the highest,” and among the clergy also “We praise you, O God”—are kept silent and reserved for the Easter joys, so that then, as though new, they may be more welcome because they had previously been less customary. It is clear that the Lord’s forty-day abstinence, after whose example or imitation ours was instituted, did not occur at the time when ours is now observed. Rather, it began on the day of Theophany, [Col. 0487A] and immediately after baptism the Lord went into the wilderness, as Mark recalls, and there underwent abstinence for forty days and nights (Mark I, 13)—not in the days near Easter, as our forty days now are observed. This was by the fitting dispensation we have mentioned, namely, that the exultation of the Lord’s resurrection might be more welcome in proportion as greater mortification through abstinence or suffering through penitence had preceded it.

What wonder, then, if we especially spend those two days of the Lord’s passion and burial in the sorrow of compassion, so that laughter may be more welcome after weeping, and, when the glory of the resurrection has come, we no longer remember the Lord’s oppression? Thus the Apostle says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus” (II Cor. V, 16). It is as though he plainly said: Even if we do not doubt that Christ’s body was once fleshly—that is, weak, passible, or mortal—we now know it as made spiritual; nor do we now attend so much to that weakness which preceded as to the glory of the resurrection which followed.

If that glory were already complete in Christ’s members themselves, as it is in the Head, their passions and deaths would by no means have solemn celebration. For, the Apostle says, “When that which is perfect has come, that which is partial will be done away” (I Cor. XIII, 10). The complete glorification of the saints will occur in the resurrection, when each will then have two robes, whereas one robe has now been given to each. [Col. 0487B]

Indeed, because of the excellence of the resurrection to come, the day immediately preceding it—the day of crucifixion—has no solemnity; yet when the Easter solemnity is imminent, we celebrate the veneration of the cross with festive joy. There can be no doubt that this all pertains to the honor of the Lord’s passion, for whose sake alone this entire reverence is offered to the cross. Hence hymns and other things concerning the passion are sung there.

I also judge that this should not be passed over: Christ is called by the Apostle “the firstfruits of those who sleep” (I Cor. XV, 20), because he was the first to rise into this glory of immortality. For although many before him were raised either by him or by the prophets, there is no doubt that they died again. Those also whom the Gospel recounts as raised in testimony to his resurrection, when it says: “And the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had slept arose; and, coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they came into the holy city and appeared to many” (Matt. XVII, 51–52), are by no means to be understood from these words to have arisen on the day of the Lord’s crucifixion itself. Rather, their graves were then opened only in the splitting of the rocks; afterward, on the day of the resurrection itself, after his resurrection, they were raised and immediately came into the city and appeared to the faithful. For the statement, “coming out of the tombs after his resurrection,” plainly indicates that they did not rise before then. [Col. 0487D]

Thus, because the Evangelist briefly and concisely mentions both the opening of their tombs and their resurrection as though they happened at the same time, he abbreviated his narrative by anticipation of a future event. It should also be noted, for the glory of the Lord’s burial, of which Isaiah prophesies, “And his tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. XI, 10), that it has contributed not a little that the tombs both of these faithful persons and of the other saints who had been in Jerusalem are now so hidden that it is unknown where they were, and no relics of saints buried there appear there. Rather, all have either been carried away from there, or God has hidden them, so that the entire celebration of honor may be reserved for the Lord’s tomb.

Since many unbelievers doubt human resurrection so greatly that they consider it utterly impossible for our bodies, reduced to dust and dissolved, to be raised again, divine mercy resolved to show us this not only in words but also by examples of things. Thus we may not doubt that divine power can sometimes do in greater matters what nature more often accomplishes in lesser ones. For no one who has learned the nature of the phoenix and the glory which divine grace has repeatedly granted it in dying and rising again should ever distrust our future resurrection. [Col. 0488B]

If we refer mystically to Christ the nature and manner of resurrection of this bird, we shall see every feature fittingly applicable to him. This bird, it is said, is unique; it is known to be neither male nor female; and because it does not produce offspring, it does not build a nest. When, after many years, it senses that death is imminent, it prepares for itself a certain pile and little sepulchral house of aromatic twigs or spices themselves, as though it sought to counteract the stench of its corpse by fragrance. It is said to enter this structure of spices and die there; and, as the sun burns from above and heats the spices themselves, it is consumed and dissolved into ashes. After some days it is raised in the form of a bee and, gradually putting on wings and feathers, returns to its former state.

All these features seem to fit no one so aptly as Christ. That it is a unique bird, knowing no equal either in dignity or mating, is most beautifully suited both to Christ’s excellence and to his virginity. For who is unique and singular in dignity as Christ is? Of him also the Apostle says that there is neither male nor female (Gal. III), because in Christ’s body, which is the Church, difference of sex produces no rank; Christ attends not to the condition of the sexes but to merits. [Col. 0488D] This bird does not seek a nest as other birds do, and the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Luke II, 58); nor was he born in his own place but in another’s.

The phoenix prepares a tomb for itself, in which it also gathers spices. The Lord likewise prepared for himself both a tomb and spices through Joseph or Nicodemus (Matt. XXVII, 57), to whom he inspired this devotion. The burning of the phoenix also is not remote from Christ’s mystery, in whose type the flesh of the paschal lamb came before us not boiled but roasted. When the phoenix rises it takes the form of a bee, which knows no corruption of flesh, because in that glory of resurrection they “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. XXII, 30).

And you, virgins of Christ, who have already obtained this glory on earth and live not so much humanly as angelically, celebrate the day of this solemnity all the more devoutly because, as we have said before, it plainly pertains more fully to the excellence of your honor. [Col. 0489A]

## SERMON XIV. EXPOSITION OF THE LORD’S PRAYER, ON THE DAYS OF ROGATION, WHICH ARE CALLED LITANIES

The present days of Rogation—that is, of prayer—invite us especially now to prayer by their very name. Among all prayers, it is clear that the one given to the disciples by the Lord himself, and therefore called the Lord’s Prayer, excels both in dignity and usefulness. For this reason it should especially be used by the faithful, so that James may seem to have spoken chiefly concerning it when he says: “For the persistent prayer of a righteous person is very powerful” (James V, 16).

How powerful and effective the prayer of a righteous person can be is clearly declared by Jerome on Jeremiah, where the Lord says to the prophet: “But do not pray for this people, and do not resist me, because I shall not hear you” (Jer. VII, 16).

> Jerome [Note: [Col. 0489D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIV, col. 732.]: “When he says, ‘And do not resist me,’ he shows that the prayer of the saints can withstand God’s wrath. Hence he says to Moses: ‘Let me alone, that I may strike this people and make you into a great nation’ (Exod. XXXII, 10).”

If, then, [Col. 0489C] the prayer of saints such as Moses or Jeremiah has such power, what should be hoped from the Lord’s own prayer—a prayer which he himself dictated and mercifully instituted, so that by it we may turn his wrath into mercy? But since prayer has either no fruit or little fruit when devotion of understanding does not accompany it—for God examines the heart rather than the mouth—it is helpful especially to unfold the meaning of this prayer, so that it may be the more fruitful for those praying it the more devoutly it is understood and spoken. The Apostle, carefully observing this, says to the Corinthians: “For if I pray with the tongue, my spirit prays, but my mind—my soul—is without fruit. What then? I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind. I will sing psalms with the spirit; I will sing psalms also with the mind” (1 Cor. [Col. 0489D] XIV). One prays or sings psalms only with the tongue, without the spirit, when by the breath of his utterance he merely forms words that he does not understand. He does this also with the mind when he applies understanding to what he says. Hence that saying of blessed Benedict [Note: [Col. 0490D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXVI, col. 476.]: “Let us so stand to sing psalms that our mind may accord with our voice.”

Indeed, the Apostle so strongly commends understanding of words that he permits nothing to be said in the Church without understanding accompanying it. Otherwise he judges those to be regarded as mad who are unable to do what they profess to do by prophesying—that is, to interpret by expounding—or who append “Amen” to blessings which they do not understand. For he accordingly adds [Col. 0490A]: “If therefore the whole Church should assemble together, and all should speak with tongues, and unlearned persons or unbelievers should enter, will they not say that you are mad?” (1 Cor. XIV, 23). Earlier he says: “Moreover, if you bless with the spirit, how shall one who occupies the place of the unlearned say ‘Amen’ to your blessing? For he does not know what you are saying. You indeed give thanks well, but the other is not edified” (ibid., 16). And, after some remarks, summing up all that is said in the Church, he says: “What then? When you assemble, let all things be done for edification” (ibid., 26). And to the Ephesians: “Be filled,” he says, “with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord” (Eph. IV, 25). A person is properly said to speak to one by whom his words [Col. 0490B] are understood, since the sole function of words is to generate understanding in the hearer. Thus we speak to ourselves when, from what we say and understand, we arouse devotion of mind; and we sing psalms alike with heart and mouth when what is uttered outwardly is grasped inwardly through understanding. What could be more ridiculous than to ask in prayer for something while not knowing what we pray, or being unable to determine whether it is beneficial or harmful?

Finally, it is evident from the Lord’s own words that we ought to pray for two reasons: namely, for his honour and for our benefit. It is for his honour when, in asking something from him, we confess that what we seek comes from him rather than from ourselves, and attribute it to his grace rather than to our own strength [Col. 0490C]. Words are also commended for our benefit when, once understood, they kindle devotion and produce compunction, so that they may be heard by the Lord more readily as they are uttered by us more devoutly. It is, indeed, natural—or almost characteristic—of those in pain that, when they express in words what grieves them, the very words kindle their pain, and the mind, pierced by its own complaints, readily bursts into tears from the very miseries it recounts. So too, when penitents recount in their prayers what they have committed, their very words wound the grieving minds like certain pricks, producing tears, so that they may offer a rich or fat sacrifice.

[Col. 0490D] It is evident that the Lord’s Prayer was written down both by Matthew and by Luke, but more fully by the former, who was not merely an evangelist but also an apostle and heard it from the Lord’s own mouth when the Lord delivered it on the mountain to him and the other apostles together. Therefore our exposition follows it especially now, since it possesses the greatest authority as well as perfection: it is distinguished into seven petitions, whereas Luke’s contains five and is said to have been delivered not to the apostles but to a certain disciple. For we recall that Luke wrote of the Lord as follows: “And it came to pass, while he was praying in a certain place, [Col. 0491A] that when he ceased, one of his disciples said to him: ‘Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.’ And he said to them: ‘When you pray, say: Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our sins, since we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation’” (Luke XI, 1).

Matthew, however, inserts the Lord’s Prayer, delivered more perfectly to the apostles as teachers and more perfect persons, into the sermon given to them on the mountain—a sermon clearly more perfect than that which Luke reports as having been delivered to the crowds on the plain. Thus Matthew writes, with the Lord saying to the apostles: “When you pray, [Col. 0491B] you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in synagogues and at the street-corners, so that they may be seen by men. Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you pray [Vulg. *oraveris*, ‘you have prayed’], enter into your chamber, and, having shut your door, pray to your Father in secret. And your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you. But when praying, do not use many words, as the heathen do. For they think that they will be heard because of their many words. Therefore do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him [Vulg. *eum*, ‘him’]. Thus, however [Vulg. *ergo vos*, ‘therefore you’], shall you pray: Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Give us this day our supersubstantial bread. And forgive us our debts [Col. 0491C], as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. VI, 9). By carefully instructing us about prayer, the Lord hands down not merely an utterance of words but also teaches us concerning intention, so that prayer may be fruitful for us.

“Like the hypocrites,” he says: that is, do not pray with the intention by which they are known to pray. Explaining their intention, he says: “that they may be seen by men,” rather than by God, because they desire to please those from whom they seek praises or earthly advantages. So that they may be seen by more people, “they love,” he says, “to do this in synagogues and at the corners of streets”—that is, in public gatherings of people. He does not simply say that they pray there because there they can be seen by more people. Nor does he say “in the streets,” but “at the corners of streets,” as though they seemed to avoid human notice by hiding themselves in corners—the very notice they most earnestly desire. They pray standing rather than sitting or prostrate, so that they may be thought more religious insofar as they are believed to afflict themselves more in prayer. “They have received,” he says, their reward for prayer from human beings in the present, and will not receive it later from God. The reward or recompense of prayer is rendered to them when they obtain the human praise or earthly advantages that they seek from it.

But you, whoever you are, when you pray, and so forth. Our chamber, in which we rest, is our mind, removed from worldly disturbances, so that, being free for God, we may have purer prayer, with our entire [Col. 0492A] intention directed toward him. Having entered the chamber, we shut its door so that we may be seen not by others but by God alone, when we provide by every means that we may not so please human beings through our prayer as to deserve to displease God. God is said to see more in secret than openly because, as examiner of heart and reins, he considers not so much what is done as the intention with which it is done, and rewards not so much works as intention.

“But when praying, do not,” and so forth: that is, do not seek prolixity of words in prayer with the intention with which unbelievers do so. For they think that the more prolonged their prayer is in words, the more they can be heard by God, whom they suppose not to be everywhere present and whom they think needs words by which we may communicate to him what we want. Therefore do not become like them in this intention [Col. 0492B].

“Our Father.” According to Matthew, this prayer is divided into eight parts [Col. 0492C]. The first is the invocation: “Our Father, who are in heaven.” Then follow seven petitions. The first three concern God; the remaining four concern us. Intending, then, to expound this order, let us first pray to the Lord himself that he may grant us understanding of his prayer, which may make it fruitful for us. When he says “Father” rather than “Lord,” he admonishes us to serve him more through love than through fear. For fear belongs to servants; love, to children. Hence the Apostle, distinguishing Christian service from Jewish service, said to Jews who had now been converted: “For you have not again been subjected to fear, but have received the spirit of adoption, in which we cry: Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII, 15).

It should be noted here that when “Father” is said, not one person of the Trinity alone is understood; rather, the prayer is addressed without distinction to God, whom the faithful commonly serve through love. It seems no small winning of goodwill when we call him whom we pray to “Father,” as though he might be moved by such a sweet name to an affection of fatherly love and remember what he owes not so much to servants as to children. When each person says “our” rather than “my,” he professes himself to be God’s son by adoption, which is common to many, rather than by substance, which belongs to Christ alone. This prayer is properly made by each person not in the singular but in the plural, when one says “our,” “ours,” “us,” or “we,” rather than “my,” “mine,” “to me,” or “me,” because we obtain what we ask more readily insofar as, through the affection of brotherly love, we join others with ourselves in prayer. “Who are in heaven”: that is, you dwell by grace in those who are, as it were, heavenly, inhabiting heaven rather than earth and established in things above, not below. Of such people the Lord says: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. LXVI, 1): that is, the soul exalted in virtues and ardent in spiritual desires [Col. 0492D].

“Hallowed be your name.” After the invocation he adds the petitions [Col. 0493A]; and because it is fitting that we seek God’s glory more than our own benefit—for this should be the end in all that we do, that God may be glorified—the first three petitions, as we have said, ask for his glorification. The Lord, complaining through Ezekiel about the rejected Jews and reproving them, says: “My holy name, which you have defiled among the nations” (Ezek. XXXVI, 22). The Apostle, introducing this same sentence, says: “For the name of God is blasphemed among the nations through you, as it is written” (Rom. II, 24), namely, in this very passage spoken through the prophet. Therefore, just as God’s name seems to be defiled or blasphemed—that is, mocked or despised—by unbelievers when they see acting perversely those who call themselves God’s people, so conversely it is hallowed and blessed, or praised and glorified, when his people live holily and religiously [Col. 0493B] and fulfil in their life what he himself commands, saying: “Let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 22).

Concerning this glorification of God, or hallowing of the divine name, the Lord further adds through the same prophet: “And I will hallow my name, which has been defiled among the nations, which you have defiled in their midst” (Ezek. XXXVI, 23). He subsequently explains how this is done, saying: “And I will make you walk in my commandments,” and so forth (ibid., 27). For as far as lies in us, we dishonour God when we despise his commandments; so conversely our obedience honours him. Therefore his name, which is holy in itself, is also hallowed in us [Col. 0493C] when we live under his name in such a way that he, whose children we are called, is glorified from our life. In order that his name may thus be hallowed in us, we must pray that, once the kingdom of the devil or of sin has been expelled from us—concerning which the Apostle says, “Let not sin reign in your mortal breast, so that you obey its desires” (Rom. VI, 12)—God’s kingdom may come in us. This is what we ask second when we say: “Your kingdom come”: that is, may your dominion be so in us that we render you willing obedience in all things. And that this may be done by us: “Your will be done in us,” which is the third petition. Your will, I say, which cannot err or be evil. We do God’s will when we fulfil what he approves and directs for our good. “Be done,” I say, [Col. 0493D] “as in heaven, so on earth,” so that earth itself may also be converted into heaven: that is, so that it may be fulfilled by those who are carnal and seek earthly things just as it is by those who are spiritual and desire heavenly things.

“Give us this day our supersubstantial bread.” Having set forth, as was said, the three petitions pertaining to God’s honour, he turns his pen to the four remaining petitions, in which four virtues are sought, wherein the perfection of the faithful soul consists: prudence, justice, temperance, and fortitude. As prudence is first both in time and in nature, so its petition is placed first when it says, “Our bread,” and so forth, which is the fourth petition. Connect it thus: May your will be fulfilled by all. [Col. 0494A] Grant us these virtues, which establish the soul’s perfection. The food of the soul and its spiritual bread is understanding of the divine word, concerning which it is said through Moses: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. IV, 4).

The Law judges the person who does not chew this bread—that is, the understanding of sacred Scripture—and who has not a cloven hoof in it, to be an unclean animal, because there is no purity of mind where ignorance remains of those things God commands. A person chews the word of God who turns it over frequently so that he may understand it more carefully, as it is written: “He shall meditate on his law day and night” (Ps. I, 2). The cleaving of the hoof by which we walk is the discernment we exercise in divine words, when we carefully consider what must be received according to the letter and what must be applied to a mystical or moral sense [Col. 0494B]. From this threefold understanding, while the soul is refreshed as if by various dishes, true prudence is illumined; nor can this variety of dishes produce weariness.

This bread is called “supersubstantial” here as understanding, because this food of the soul is far more excellent than any substantial—that is, bodily—food, which we share with animals. He therefore properly calls this bread “ours,” that is, proper to rational souls. When he says “this day,” it is as if he said: “In this present life supply us with this provision for the journey, lest we fail on the way.” It seems not without astonishment that among us it has become the Church’s custom [Col. 0494C] that, when we commonly recite the Lord’s Prayer in Matthew’s words—he who, as said, wrote it more perfectly—we change one of its words while retaining all the rest: namely, instead of *supersubstantial*, which he set down, we say *daily*, as Luke says. This is especially remarkable since the dignity of this bread seems no less expressed when it is called “supersubstantial” than when it is called “daily.” Finally, if we suppose Matthew ought better to have said “daily” than “supersubstantial,” who would not charge this to presumption: that we should wish to correct not only the Apostle but the Lord himself? For he wrote it as he had heard it delivered to the apostles; and we believe that they commonly recited it as it was delivered to them, and that it was first written by the apostle in that same language [Col. 0494D].

The fifth petition, which says, “And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors,” asks for the equity of justice. For it is fair, and justice requires it, that we find God to be such toward us as we show ourselves through mercy toward our neighbour. By “debts” he means penalties due for sins. When it says, “As we forgive others their debts,” it binds us so strictly to mercy that this prayer is spoken by us more for condemnation than salvation if we are not merciful. Here he calls our debtors, as the following words of the Gospel plainly indicate, those who, for what they have committed against us, are bound by a certain debt of punishment, so that they deserve to be punished for these things [Col. 0495A]. We forgive them this punishment, insofar as lies in us, when they are ready to make satisfaction and we do not wish any vengeance to be exercised on that account. This is to forgive penalties for offences after God’s likeness: when those who inflicted injuries repent and are prepared to make satisfaction, we remit all vengeance to them, so that we no longer wish them to be punished at all for these matters.

Otherwise, they are not worthy of pardon so long as, unrepentant, they persist in their wickedness; nor do we wish them, while they remain such, to be wholly absolved from punishment. Nor ought we to will what we know cannot or ought not to happen. But you may ask: on what grounds are penalties for sin due to those who truly repent [Col. 0495B] and no longer persist in sin—especially the great penalties of eternal damnation? Or, if these are no longer due, how can they be remitted? Yet surely, since no sin is believed to go unpunished, even penitents are by no means entirely absolved from the debt of punishment, so that, if not punishments of damnation, they are at least subject to purgatorial punishments in this life or the life to come. Blessed Augustine affirms that these punishments of the future life are more severe than any punishment whatever of the present life [Note: [Col. 0495D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXVIII, col. 879.].

Therefore we ask that these penalties still owed by penitents may be forgiven us, lest through impatience at their severity we relapse into sins, as those do who, tested beyond what they can bear, yield in defeat. From that failure of patience, when we are tested in adversities, we pray to be delivered when it is added: “And lead us not into temptation.” It asks for such a virtue of temperance that it may not give assent to the suggestions of pleasures. Thus, “Lead us not into temptation” means: do not permit us to be so tempted that we fail amid adversities or yield in defeat to depraved desires [Col. 0495C]. “But deliver us from evil”: that is, grant strength and unconquerable firmness of mind to endure every adversity, lest through any disturbance or faintheartedness we turn aside from rectitude.

It should be noted, as blessed Augustine recalls in the *Enchiridion* [Note: [Col. 0496D] *Patrologia*, vol. XL, cols. 285–286.], that Luke briefly comprehends in the five petitions which he sets forth the seven petitions distinguished by Matthew. [Col. 0495D] In the first two petitions which Luke himself gives—namely, “Hallowed be your name” and “Your kingdom come”—he includes the third, which Matthew distinguishes, namely, “Your will be done,” as though we judge that those first two are not done unless this too is fulfilled. The last petition which Matthew adds and Luke omits—“But deliver us from evil”—Luke judges to depend upon the preceding petition, so that it should be joined with it as one petition. The conjunction “but,” inserted between them, itself indicates this. Amen: that is, “May it be so.”

## SERMON XV. ON THE DAY OF THE ASCENSION

The festive joy of the Lord’s Ascension is a kind of victorious triumphal procession rendered by angels to Christ in triumph [Col. 0496A]. For he, king alike of human beings and angels, received, as was fitting, one such act of veneration from human beings and another from angels. When he came into Jerusalem amid palm branches, he was received with praises by the crowds in the manner of an emperor; they hailed and blessed him as the king of Israel and heir of David’s line. As the people’s devotion spread not only tree branches but even their own garments beneath the humble beast on which he rode, this veneration of him possessed something beyond the custom of earthly kings.

Then, led amid the people’s cries of praise to the temple as to his own palace, he powerfully expelled the sacrilege of the merchants from it; exercising royal [Col. 0496B] authority, he cleansed it, and, by divinely illuminating the blind there, consecrated his house through the benefits of miracles. Just as he was then honoured there by human beings in the manner of a triumphal procession, as we have said, so on this day, ascending into heaven, he was received by angels coming to meet him. Two of them, standing by in solemn white garments, comfort the disciples in a pious address, saying: “Men of Galilee,” and so forth (Acts I, 11).

As they sang in mutual praise the wondrous glory of this ascent, while others repeatedly asked in amazement, “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. XXIII, 8), others replied: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (ibid.). And again: “The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory” (ibid., 10). This twofold response corresponds to the twofold command that had preceded, spoken twice in this way: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be raised up, eternal gates” (ibid., 9). Hearing this, others, moved as if by amazement, attach a twofold question to the repeated command, saying, namely: “Who is this King of glory?”

We read that, after the first human beings were expelled from the earthly paradise, the Lord established there a diligent and vigilant guard of angels, one that could not be deceived (Gen. III). Hence the prophet fittingly calls them *cherubim*, that is, “fullness of knowledge.” By a flaming and turning sword they barred and prevented those expelled from entering paradise; and by that very sword they had, as it were, closed and obstructed the entrance to paradise with certain gates [Col. 0496D]. To these princes—that is, to the angels presiding there over that guard, as a figure of the heavenly paradise now opened to us in Christ’s Ascension—there is now said: “O princes,” that is, guardians set over paradise, “now lift up your gates”: remove that obstructing barrier of yours which we have mentioned, and turn aside that turning sword. It was called “turning,” that is, movable rather than fixed, because at some time it was to be turned aside and removed. And, “O eternal gates, be lifted up”: that is, be permanently raised and removed; and the King of glory shall enter—not an earthly king, indeed, but one who in this present triumph introduces with himself into the height of heavenly [Col. 0497A] glory those whom he has rescued from the devil’s power.

Concerning so glorious and wonderful a triumph, while some ask with great amazement, “Who is this,” as you say, “so great a king, whom we see in human form, formerly despised by us, ascending above every nature—that is, above the angelic height? Or how did an inferior nature deserve to attain this dignity?” others answer in song: “This Lord is strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle.” He is strong, namely, to endure every adversity and is not weak in anything, although he appears in the form of human weakness. He is mighty, as he immediately specifies by adding, “mighty in battle”; he was not conquered by the tempting devil as the old Adam was [Col. 0497B], but, having triumphed by his death over death’s very author, he now gloriously displays, as trophies of spoils, those captives whom he rescued, just as the Psalmist had long before sung of him: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII, 19). For “captive captivity” means the human race twice made captive by the devil: first, by his persuasion exiled from paradise and exposed to present miseries; afterward cast down from this light into the darkness of hell.

Therefore, bringing his own, twice made captive, with himself now into heavenly things, he triumphs today as victor over the ancient enemy whom he has overcome. He himself is the Lord of hosts [Col. 0496C]—not only of the human beings whom he thus frees, but also of the heavenly powers through whom he works mighty deeds wherever he wills [Col. 0497C]. Let us compare with the glory of this triumph the veneration which we said was first offered him amid palm branches, and see point by point by what resemblance they are joined; yet let us recognize that this triumph surpasses that one by far.

As John relates, that earlier reception was given to him because of Lazarus’s resurrection (John XII, 1), and Lazarus himself, coming with him to Jerusalem, must be believed not to have been absent. Thus, as Lazarus’s resurrection deserved that proclamation of praise from human beings, so the liberation of the captivity just described received triumphal praises from angels today. There he came to Jerusalem and, as stated, was blessed by the crowds; here, ascending into heaven, he blessed the disciples, so that this day may be accounted more excellent insofar as it is made happier by a divine blessing. Nor only those going before, but also those following, there sang praises beforehand. So also today, both the choirs of preceding angels and the captives following their liberator acclaim praises to the victor with supreme and ineffable jubilation, as it is written: “God has ascended in jubilation, and the Lord with the sound of a trumpet” (Ps. XLVI, 6), that is, with the sign of victory.

Finally, when he entered the city there amid such exultation of the surrounding crowd, others asked in amazement: “Who is this?” (Matt. XXI, 10). Others answered those asking: “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth of Galilee” (ibid., 11) [Col. 0498A]. So too, in today’s triumph, while some angels, as we have said, asked, “Who is this King of glory?” others answered: “The Lord strong,” and so forth. With the crowds accompanying him as far as the temple, that is, the palace of his own house, the Lord was brought there. And as we read in Daniel (ch. VII, 13), amid that company of angels the Son of Man, as if presented to the Father’s majesty, was led by angels as far as the Ancient of Days.

There he is described as riding upon a slow beast; here, as presiding upon a light cloud. For then he still bore a corruptible body, which weighs down the soul (Wis. IX), that is, a mortal body. But now, having laid aside every weight of mortality, he chose to preside upon a cloud and thus ascend, so that he might first show in himself how light these bodies which we now [Col. 0498B] bear, though heavy, will become. For as, by being born from us and suffering for us, he showed us supreme honour and love, so afterward, by rising again, appearing to the disciples, and now finally ascending, he displayed the future glory of bodies, so that the members might endure the struggles of bodily sufferings more willingly, insofar as in their own head they have proof of the future glory of bodies.

In the resurrection he displayed to us the immortality of bodies. When he entered through closed doors to appear to the disciples, he showed their subtlety, by which they can penetrate any solid things. Now, ascending above the height of the heavens, he demonstrates how great their lightness will be, so that wherever the soul wills, the body may immediately be conveyed there without difficulty [Col. 0498C]. Therefore, as the Apostle says, let us now seek him above in mind, where he sits at God’s right hand (Col. III, 1), so that afterward we may deserve to come to him also in body—now in mind—not so much by ascending as by being drawn by him, to whom are honour and glory through endless ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. ON THE OCTAVE OF THE ASCENSION

The Lord begins with the least things in order to arrive at greater ones, establishing faith in the highest things from the lowest, as though leading an argument from lesser to greater; so that, when we see great things in these, we may cease to marvel at such things in those. Therefore, against the errors of unbelievers concerning the things he wonderfully accomplished in himself, he first set forth certain examples in creatures by which any schisms of heresy might be cut apart and scattered [Col. 0498D].

For example, some heretics so abhorred the Virgin’s childbirth that they said: “If a Virgin gave birth, it was a phantom.” The Lord, applying a remedy to the wound of this error, sometimes causes mares, as blessed Augustine maintains in the *City of God* [Note: [Col. 0497D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI.], to conceive from the spirit of the winds, so that we may cease to marvel if a Virgin conceived from the Holy Spirit. We know that it is not unknown to many people that ravens conceive by kissing and never mate. Bees too are not deprived of the fruit of offspring without injury to their integrity. Moreover, every day we see innumerable worms and different kinds of living creatures [Col. 0499A] generated from insensible and most lowly things. Hence the Lord does not disdain to be compared with a worm, he to whom it is said: “Do not fear, worm Jacob” (Isa. XLI, 14), and who is not ashamed to say of himself: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI, 7). The frequent revivification of the dead phoenix also removes despair of resurrection.

Finally, Elijah’s rapture preceded the Lord’s Ascension: though he still bore a mortal and corruptible body, he was carried in a fiery chariot into paradise (4 Kings II, 11). It is evident that the nature of the element of fire is far more subtle and lighter than the others. Therefore, if that lightness of fire could support Elijah’s body, still heavy with earthly weight, without burning it, what wonder if Christ’s body—or our bodies, once made immortal and to be called not so much animal as spiritual—can also remain unharmed in that fiery and highest heaven, which is known to be covered with waters [Col. 0499B]?

Since we have adduced Elijah’s translation as support for faith in the Lord’s Ascension, it is fitting, finally, to derive the mystery of this Ascension from Elijah. Whom, then, does Elijah more fittingly figure, both through the interpretation and affinity of his name, than Christ, the true sun of souls? Concerning him, as blessed Gregory recalls, the following is contained in the song of the prophet Habakkuk [Note: [Col. 0499D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXIX, col. 1011.]: “The sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order” (Hab. III, 11). For after the Lord’s Ascension [Col. 0499C], the Holy Spirit, sent by him as he himself promised, saying: “Unless I go away,” and so forth (John XVI, 7), endeavoured so greatly to set the Church—signified by the moon—in order that he would not tolerate the perverse within it, but would immediately cleanse the grain from the chaff, as he did through Peter in the case of Ananias and Sapphira. Peter himself confesses this when rebuking Ananias: “Why,” he says, “has Satan tempted your heart, for you to lie to the Holy Spirit?” (Acts V, 3). And after some words: “You have not lied to men, but to God” (ibid., 4).

For when Truth says to the apostles: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. X, 20), whenever the Spirit reveals to believers some hidden matter about which they ask, it is said that he rather than they does this, because they do it by his inspiration or prompting [Col. 0499D]. Once Elijah had been taken up to heaven and his spirit doubled in Elisha, the sons of the prophets gathered to Elisha and led a life so much more ordered as they undertook a greater virtue of abstinence or continence, beginning in solitude the perfection of monastic life. After the Lord’s Ascension, the apostles likewise endeavoured no less to observe this through the sending of the Holy Spirit.

Elijah, taken up to heaven, left his cloak on earth (3 Kings XIX). Christ’s cloak, however, is understood as the body with which the Word clothed himself; of it Jacob had foretold: “He shall wash his garment in wine, and his cloak in the blood of the grape” (Gen. [Col. 0500A] XLIX, 11). Christ, ascending to the Father’s right hand, left this cloak behind in the sacrament; cleansed by participation in it and thus, in a sense, clothed with Christ, we cover the foulness of our preceding sins. Elisha, taking up Elijah’s cloak and invoking the name of God himself, struck the waters of the Jordan with it and divided them. We too, through the power of the divine sacrifice and invocation of heavenly help, divide the waters so that we are not drowned in them, when we restrain or dry up within ourselves carnal desires as though they were harmful humours, so that, as if with dry feet, we may reach the true land of permission, to which we know that our head has ascended. Since we know this is not within our own power, may he himself draw us there after him by his grace—he whose kingdom and dominion [Col. 0500B] remain for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. ON THE FRIDAY AFTER THE OCTAVE OF THE LORD’S NATIVITY

[Note: [Col. 0499] “Ascension” seems to be the proper reading, as is evident from the content of the sermon itself.]

We know three holy festivals in the Law: Passover, or Pentecost, and Tabernacles. Of these it is written in Exodus: “Three times each year you shall celebrate feasts for me: the feast of unleavened bread, at the time of the month of new things; and also the feast at the end of the year, when you have gathered all your fruits from the field. Three times in the year all your males shall appear before the Lord God” (Exod. 23:14). Hence we also read in Deuteronomy: “Observe the month of new fruits and the first season of spring, that you may keep the Passover for the Lord; and you shall celebrate the festival day of weeks for the Lord; you shall also celebrate the feast of Tabernacles for seven days, when you have gathered your fruits from the threshing-floor and winepress” (Deut. 16:10).

We understand these three festivals to be the days of which it is said concerning Elkanah in First Samuel: “That man went up from his city on the appointed days, to worship and sacrifice to the Lord at Shiloh” (1 Sam. 1:3). Of these three festivals, under their former names, though with a different meaning, two also remain among us. The Jews celebrated Passover in the sacrifice of the figurative lamb; we celebrate Passover in the resurrection of the true Lamb. From the day on which Passover was celebrated in Egypt, they had, on the first day after receiving the Law, the second festival, Pentecost, in reverence for the Law received. But we commemorate Pentecost in the coming of the Holy Spirit, by whom, as by the finger of God, the Law was written, and by whom both understanding of the Law and Christ’s words were supplied to the apostles.

But the Church of the Gentiles has not received the feast of Tabernacles, which the Law commanded only for those descended from Israel. For when the Lord instituted it and commended its observance to the Israelite people, he says in Leviticus: “Everyone of the stock of Israel shall remain in tabernacles, that your descendants may learn that I caused the children of Israel to dwell in tabernacles” (Lev. 23:42). Nor does any occasion present itself on which the Church of the Gentiles should retain the feast of Tabernacles, especially since tabernacles belong to travellers, not to those dwelling in their own homes. And what is our home or country except that heavenly one of which the Apostle says: “If this earthly house be dissolved, we have in heaven a house not made with hands” (2 Cor. 5:1)?

That earlier people, preceding the Lord’s coming, for whom heaven’s gate was not yet open, was, as it were, in pilgrimage, not in its homeland. But the succeeding Church of the Gentiles, which after the Lord’s passion is no longer delayed from the kingdom and daily migrates to heaven, celebrates festivals of homeland rather than pilgrimage, when it observes the joys of the future life in the feast-days of the saints. Our devotion now attends not so much to their birth upon earth as to their birth into heaven. It is therefore fitting for us to celebrate the dwelling-place of a home rather than the pilgrimage of exile, since heavenly blessedness is already open to us as an appointed reward; whereas to the ancient people the Lord promised only earthly prosperity as the recompense of the Law.

Leaving aside, then, the feast of Tabernacles, let us return to the two festivals mentioned above, namely Passover and Pentecost. Let us carefully compare them, to show that the latter is not inferior to the former either in the Old or in the New Testament—indeed, that it holds a certain pre-eminence over the rest.

We read (Exod. 19) that the Lord commanded Moses to sanctify the people and prepare them to receive the Law on the third day: they were to wash their garments and abstain from their wives. No other festival does the Law commend in such a way as to prescribe so great a preparation of sanctification for it. This is especially so because, as the Apostle testifies, among all God’s gifts formerly bestowed on the Jews, this is first—that is, greatest—namely, that “the utterances of God were entrusted to them” (Rom. 3:2): the teaching of the Old Testament was given to them, not to the peoples of the other nations.

Nor did that day properly called Passover, on which a lamb or kid was sacrificed at evening, have by the Lord’s command any festive observance throughout the seven following days called the days of unleavened bread; rather, on it alone was the sacrifice of the lamb at evening commanded. Many indications make clear what advantage and dignity our festival of Pentecost has acquired over the others. Today the Law was given on Mount Sinai to one people and in one language, veiled in the darkness of obscurity and filled more with smoke than light, as was openly prefigured when it was given. But today the Spirit descended upon the apostles, bringing understanding both of the Law and of the other divine words, granting the disciples every kind of language by which these might be preached everywhere, making known to the whole world the God formerly known in Judaea, and gaining the world for him.

On Passover day we know that the Lord rose in the body. On this day, by the coming of the Holy Spirit, there was accomplished that by which the whole world might be more happily raised in soul. On the day of resurrection or ascension, the disciples’ faith and hope were confirmed. But on this day charity, through the Spirit who is called the love of God, was poured in and brought the disciples to perfection, according to the Apostle’s words: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). He says “poured out” rather than “poured in”: that is, expanded in the fullness of gifts, not dripped in.

We also read that on the day of resurrection the Lord gave the Spirit to the apostles by breathing upon them and saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive,” and so forth (John 20:23). Then indeed the Spirit was poured into the apostles, not poured out upon them—that is, bestowed on them for a single gift of authority, not expanded into all charisms. That gift was to overflow chiefly upon those subject to them, rather than bear fruit in themselves. But on this day, when they were enlightened with understanding and inflamed by the fire of charity, they were brought to perfection in every good.

The Lord’s resurrection and ascension prepared them for this perfection, just as the people of God, about to receive the Law, were prepared for two days for that reception, when the Lord said through Moses: “Be ready for the third day,” and so forth (Exod. 19:15). Hence it is written concerning both resurrection and ascension: “For the Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified” (John 8:39). And again: “It is expedient for you that I go away; for unless I go, the Paraclete will not come” (John 16:7). Therefore, in order that the Holy Spirit might come, Christ had to be exalted by the glory both of resurrection and ascension, so that the disciples, strengthened in faith and hope of future blessedness, might deserve to receive the promised Spirit and, through him who is called love, be brought to perfection in charity. For this day bestowed upon the apostles charity, which after faith and hope makes one perfect and alone distinguishes the children of God from the children of the devil, as it is written: “The charity of God has been poured out,” and so forth.

This festival of charity therefore appears to surpass the others by as much as charity is known to surpass the other virtues and gifts of God. And since it is insufficient for human perfection to love God unless our preaching also knows how to kindle others in love for him—so that we may teach others what we ourselves do, according to that proclamation of Truth: “Whoever does and teaches these things shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19)—teaching was added to the disciples’ charity, so that the present day might perfect them in both respects.

Accordingly, the coming of the Holy Spirit was rightly revealed in fiery tongues appearing above them: through the fire and the form of tongues there was a manifest sign of love and teaching, so that through love they might advance themselves, and through teaching benefit others. The Law given on Mount Sinai, inspiring fear, produced people in slavery. But the Spirit given in the upper room—of whom the Apostle says, “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17)—turned slaves into sons. As the same Apostle writes to the Romans: “You have not received again a spirit of slavery in fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry: Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15). And to the Galatians: “Because you are sons,” he says, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying: Abba, Father. Therefore he is no longer a slave, but a son; and if a son, then an heir through God” (Gal. 4:6).

This is the Spirit by whom, regenerated in baptism and confirmed by the bishop, we strive, having been made Christians in Christ. This is the Spirit through whose gifts the elect are perfected in every virtue. His present festival is the consummation of all the others and the fulfilment of the divine promises. Hence Truth says to the apostles: “I send the promise of my Father upon you; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). Of this spiritual gift of power the Psalmist prophesies: “By the spirit of his mouth is all their strength” (Ps. 32:6). And again: “The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim good news with great power” (Ps. 67:12).

For true charity bears all things, endures all things, and its flame cannot be extinguished by any waves of persecution, according to the Song of Songs: “Love is strong as death; jealousy is harsh as hell. Many waters cannot quench it, nor can rivers overwhelm it” (Song 8:6). All the disciples’ strength came to be theirs when the Holy Spirit filled them with such love and knowledge that he made them not only prudent but also just, and likewise strong and temperate—perfect in the four virtues. Blessed Augustine declares that all these virtues are comprehended in charity: charity itself is to be called true wisdom; it is likewise justice; it is fortitude amid adversities and temperance amid prosperities, according to the different things it works in us. [Note: Patrologia, vol. 34, col. 1236; vol. 35, col. 2057.] Thus it is rightly said that charity was poured out in them through him, because “by the spirit of his mouth is all their strength” (Ps. 32:6).

This festival therefore surpasses the others by as much as a fullness of greater grace, through gifts of every virtue, brought the disciples to perfection. It clothed them, as it were, in arms, so that fortified with these they might suffice to conquer the whole world and gain it for God. Promising them this clothing, Christ said: “Until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). It is as if he said: “Until you who are unarmed receive armour, and you who are weak receive strength.”

Thus, when those baptized are confirmed by bishops after baptism at the hands of priests, and through the laying on of hands the Holy Spirit is bestowed upon them, this confirmation is a kind of spiritual armour of virtues, enabling them to resist vices and persevere in the purity they received in baptism, where they received full remission of sins. We also read of charity, called that wedding garment because it covers a multitude of sins; and because the Lord said to the disciples: “You shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1:5). From this it is plainly understood that the Spirit, coming upon them, both cleansed the disciples from sins and clothed them, as formerly naked, with the ornaments of virtues—as though they were at once baptized and confirmed, receiving then the fullness of every good, so that no grace pertaining either to their salvation or to the benefit of others was lacking to them.

For they were endowed not only with wisdom and strength, but also acquired every kind of language: altogether, everything necessary either for themselves or for others. Of this adornment alone it is written in the book of Job concerning the Lord: “His Spirit adorned the heavens” (Job 26:13); that is, he changed into spiritual heavens those who had been earthly and, by their merits, very low, but had now been raised aloft through so many gifts. Adorned by these graces and armed with virtues, the disciples were sent confidently throughout the world like fearless warriors; they were even allowed to be tested by many adversities, though previously the Lord had by no means allowed them to be tempted beyond what they could bear.

Thus, when he himself was seized for the passion, he did not wish any of them to be taken with him, saying: “If you seek me, let these go,” that the saying he had spoken might be fulfilled: “Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none” (John 18:8). As blessed Augustine observes, they did not yet believe in him in the manner in which all those not destined to perish believe. [Note: Patrologia, vol. 35, col. 1917.] If Peter, having denied Christ, had departed then, what else would he have done but perish? Therefore, while before the coming of the Holy Spirit the apostles were weak and unarmed, the Lord did not assign them to hard battles, lest they should fail when defeated in adversities—for at his arrest they immediately took to flight, and even their leader, stronger both in name and in faith, so lightly denied him not once but three times.

But on the day of Pentecost, having been perfected, as has been said, in every good, they were afterwards to be tested in every virtue, so that they might not merely instruct the Church committed to them by words, but also strengthen it by examples, lest it fail amid adversities.

Since the apostles were brought to perfection on Pentecost with such fullness of good things, this festival does not, among us any more than among the Jews, have seven subsequent days of observance extending it to the eighth day. For what can be added to perfection? Each person may prepare himself for perfection; but when he has arrived there, there remains nothing further for him to seek.

From Passover until Pentecost a certain festive joy continues for fifty days, in reverence, namely, and honor of the coming Pentecost. During these days the austerity of penance is relaxed, and we do not bend the knee in prayer, so that the season may more fully stir us to love of God and prepare us more devoutly for the coming festival of the Spirit—who is especially called the love of God—by which it is less burdensome, because of the grace of the aforesaid festival, to be perfected in every spiritual grace.

It was fitting that, after the people of Israel departed Egypt at the twelfth stopping-place, they should receive the Law on the fiftieth day, so that the number of stopping-places might signify the number of apostles, to whom on the fiftieth day he had promised to give the Holy Spirit and impress upon their hearts a law of love rather than fear, saying: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever” (John 14:16). And again: “He will remain with you,” he says, “and will be in you” (ibid., 17). That twelfth stopping-place of the Jews, where the Law was given, prefigured the Spirit who would entrust the true Law to the apostles and make in them not a passage but a dwelling.

That people prepared itself for two days to receive the imperfect Law on the third day. Let us also prepare ourselves at least during these two days for the supreme coming of the Holy Spirit, who brought the perfection of the Law to the apostles, that we may deserve to be participants in so great a grace. After the ascension, the apostles returned from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem; when they had gone up into the upper room, they deserved the promised coming of the Holy Spirit through prayers and fasts. Concerning those future fasts after his ascension, the Lord himself had foretold: “Days will come when the bridegroom shall be taken from them, and then they shall fast” (Matt. 9:15).

Therefore we fittingly understand the days following the octave of the Ascension and preceding Pentecost as the days of those fasts. For since the feast of the Ascension has an octave, that whole period of eight days must be called the Ascension: the bridegroom ascending to heaven is said to have been withdrawn or taken away from the apostles’ sight in the presence of his flesh. Therefore the two present days seem, according to the Lord’s saying, to be assigned to fasting. These fasts are certainly not for penance, as though we might be cleansed of sins, but so that, inflamed with desire to follow the bridegroom, we may deserve the descent of the Holy Spirit all the more as we pant more ardently to ascend to him by following Christ. Hence he himself says: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come” (John 16:7). That is: “Unless I withdraw from you by ascending on high, you will by no means rise with those desires through which you deserve the grace of the Spirit’s coming.” May the Spirit himself so cause us to anticipate this grace that we may deserve to receive it from him. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII. ON THE DAY OF PENTECOST

[Col. 0505D]

There are two festivals of the Lord, pre-eminent both in authority and in particular benefit: Passover and Pentecost, established alike in the Old and New Testaments. For although the earlier people of Abraham possessed more the shadow of realities than their truth, it is nevertheless certain that neither Passover nor Pentecost was absent from its mystical figures. In order to be freed from Egyptian slavery, they first celebrated Passover in Egypt, sacrificing flesh roasted by fire with wild lettuces. Then, on the fortieth day, after receiving the Law on Mount Sinai, they thereafter observed every year by the Lord’s command the rite of Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day.

For they were commanded to count seven weeks of days, that is, fifty days, from Passover, and thereafter celebrate the feast of Pentecost, when, in receiving the Law written by God’s finger, they received from the Lord the gift of a greater grace. Considering that the prerogative of this grace had then been granted to no other people, the Psalmist especially exhorts that people to thanksgiving; after first saying, “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion” (Ps. 147:12), he adds why it should do so especially, and thus concludes: “He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not done so for every nation, nor has he made his judgments known to them” (ibid., 19).

Paul too, preferring this grace far above other gifts, says: “What advantage then has the Jew, or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First indeed, because the utterances of God were entrusted to them” (Rom. 3:1). It is as though he plainly said: “This is the greater and first—that is, greatest—gift which the Jewish people received from the Lord above others: that the divine writings were entrusted, that is, committed, to it.”

Having attained a fuller knowledge of these writings, the same Apostle greatly longed for this feast of Pentecost and hastened to celebrate it at Jerusalem even at grave risk to his life. Thus it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Sailing, the next day we came opposite Chios; on another day we landed at Samos; and on the following day we came to Miletus” (Acts 20:15). “For Paul had resolved to sail past Ephesus, lest he should be delayed in Asia; for he was hastening, if possible, to keep the day of Pentecost at Jerusalem. But from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the Church. When they came to him and were together, he said to them: ‘You know from the first day when I entered Asia how I have been with you at all times, serving the Lord with all humility, tears, and trials that befell me through the plots of the Jews; how I withheld nothing useful from declaring and teaching it to you publicly and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and Gentiles repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. And now, behold, bound in spirit, I go to Jerusalem, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit in every city bears witness to me, saying that bonds and tribulations await me. But I fear none of these things, nor do I count my life more precious than myself, provided that I may complete my course and the ministry which I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the Gospel of God’” (ibid., 18).

We read of many festivals instituted among both the ancient and the new people; yet after they had gone to the Gentiles, we know neither this apostle nor the others to have returned to Jerusalem to celebrate any of them except this one. Paul therefore came to Jerusalem, as was said, at the gravest risk to his life, knowing beforehand what he would suffer there. He came, I say, to celebrate Pentecost: not so much the old Pentecost with the Jews in the Temple as the new Pentecost with Christians in the upper room. For there he knew that, when a more abundant grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured into the disciples, the angelic guardianship had migrated from the Temple and taken its place, and that the ancient glory of the Synagogue had been transferred to the newness of the Church.

Recalling this, blessed Augustine says in the second homily on the Epistle of John: “Where does the Church begin, except where the Holy Spirit came from heaven, filled the whole place, a sound arose as though a violent blast were being borne along, and tongues were divided as of fire?”

It is therefore clear how much the Church owes to this festival. For, as has been said, when it received the more abundant grace which the Lord had promised to the disciples—“You shall be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days hence” (Acts 1:5)—it took the beginning of spiritual life, enriched with every gift, and thereby was distinguished from the carnal Synagogue by as much as it had become more spiritual.

In the type of this upper room, dearest sisters and Paracletean virgins, your oratory has been built and gloriously marked with the name of that supreme Paraclete himself. Consider, therefore, with what devotion it should be venerated by you and by the entire people of God; consider how spiritual you must always be, since by your profession you are dedicated to the Holy Spirit as his own temple and spiritually consecrated to him. Therefore live in this man-made and bodily temple so that you may deserve to become his spiritual temple.

Truth itself testifies how great an offense against him is, and how dangerous a transgression committed against him: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man shall be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32). But if the offense of a spoken word against the Spirit bears so great a punishment, what vengeance awaits a transgression committed in deed? Nor is it enough for you merely to avoid transgression, unless you strive with all your affection to please him, from whom every gift of divine grace is to be hoped.

Though he apportions these gifts to each person as he wills (1 Cor. 12), he distributes as he wills—to such a degree that he is not only their giver but is himself called the gift of God. How earnestly, then, ought we strive to have such a great steward favorable to us? Whoever wishes to live in the household of any powerful person is little or not at all helped by possessing the favor of the master if he lacks the favor of the steward—especially when this same one is at once master of the house and steward. For the Apostle openly proclaims of the Holy Spirit: “There are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are diversities of ministries, but the same God who works all things in all” (ibid., 4).

Then he enumerates the gifts of divine grace which the Spirit himself distributes, saying: “To one is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge,” and so forth (ibid., 8); and he concludes this distribution of gifts thus: “But one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each individually as he wills” (ibid., 11). From this he plainly indicates that the same distributor and steward of divine gifts is both Lord and God, and that, as Lord himself—not as a steward appointed under a lord—he freely bestows these gifts on whomever he wills.

His generosity today enriched this present day, as his own festival, with a more abundant grace, in which he fulfilled the promises of divine benefits. For after the Son’s coming into the world and his return to the Father in the ascension, the Holy Spirit’s coming today remained, through which all that had been begun through the Son for our salvation might be completed. Hence the Son himself says: “I send the promise of my Father upon you; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). And again: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26). And again: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:12).

From these testimonies of Truth it is clear how great a grace endows the present festival, on which Christ’s disciples were brought to perfection both in the strength of steadfastness and in the fullness of knowledge. For what is it to be clothed with power from on high except to be armed with strength of soul against the terrors of the world and every adversity? What were the apostles before the coming of the Holy Spirit but, so to speak, earthen vessels of a potter, not yet hardened in the firing of the flame so as to be fit for use?

Christ the potter had formerly fashioned these vessels from earth when he had taken them from the earthly way of life of the carnal people and instructed them in faith. But when the Spirit came, he inflamed them with zeal for divine love and hardened and fired these clay vessels, still raw, with this fire, so that thereafter they might confidently preach the word of God everywhere. Thus it came about that the Prince of the Apostles himself, who had earlier been frightened by the voice of a single maidservant and denied Christ—not once, but three times (Matt. 16)—stood fearless before Nero’s swords and the cross raised as an instrument of execution for him, in confession and preaching of Christ.

Long ago the Son himself had spoken of this fire of love and flame of charity: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it should burn?” (Luke 12:49). It is as though he plainly said: “Everything that I did when I came into the world—by being born and preaching, by dying and rising, and also by ascending—looked toward this one goal and supreme end: namely, that I might burn the earth with this fire; that is, that I might set ablaze the earthly and cold hearts of human beings with the Holy Spirit, who is called the fire of divine love.”

The Son ascended so that the Holy Spirit might descend, as he himself testifies: “It is expedient for you that I go away. Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come,” and so forth (John 15:7). O how glorious, how worthy, is this descent of the Holy Spirit! It could not occur except through the Son’s ascent; nor could the Spirit be sent in this way unless the Son ascended in order to send him. Christ’s ascension is therefore, as it were, the preparation-day of the present festival and a kind of preparation.

The Apostle carefully explains how Christ’s passion also pertains to this gift of divine love. For after he has said, “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5), he adds: “For why did Christ, when we were still weak, die at the appointed time for the ungodly?” (ibid., 6). It is as though he said: “For what other reason except to bring about this outpouring of charity in our hearts did he die for a time—that is, endure a passing and, as it were, momentary death—when we were still weak, that is, feeble in faith or in enduring persecution?”

Charity was poured out: it was made broad and spacious in hearts and extended even to enemies. Of it also Christ is told through the Psalmist: “Grace has been poured out upon your lips” (Ps. 44:3); that is, all your preaching resounds with nothing other than the perfection of charity. Of it too the Apostle says: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart and an unfeigned conscience” (1 Tim. 1:5).

Therefore, just as the commandments of God, so also the commandments of Christ, all aim at this one end: the building up of charity in us. The perfection of this purpose, accomplished today through the Holy Spirit, and the distribution of the grace of every good, made the present festival more pleasing by as much as it made it richer in more excellent gifts—more illustrious, as has been said, both in strength and in knowledge.

For the Spirit, coming today, at once strengthens the disciples’ hearts, as has been said, and enlightens them, as was promised: bringing to their minds understanding of what the Son had said and teaching them all truth. Today we heard his coming carefully described when the passage from Acts of the Apostles was read: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as though of a mighty Spirit coming, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And there appeared to them diverse tongues as of fire,” and so forth. “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit,” and so forth (Acts 2:2).

The coming of the Holy Spirit is declared in the sound of wind, which here is called a violent spirit. The blast of wind, though invisible, is nevertheless audible. Likewise, the inspiration of the Spirit within the disciples’ hearts could not be seen inwardly; but through outward hearing, in the diversity of languages, the gift of spiritual grace was discerned. This sound was sudden because the grace of this inspiration exceeded human expectation. This blast of wind is called violent, in order to show that the power of the word granted today is strong against every obstacle or reasoning of human wisdom. Speaking of this power of the word, the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, overthrowing counsels and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every understanding into captivity” (2 Cor. 10:4).

Truth himself, strengthening the apostles’ hearts lest they despair or tremble because of their lack of learning before the wise of the world, says: “Lay it up therefore in your hearts not to meditate beforehand how you shall answer; for I shall give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:14). Elsewhere: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 13:11).

This prompting through the Spirit, by which an unpremeditated answer is to be made, is therefore rightly prefigured today by the sudden blast of wind. The sound is said to occur from heaven because a sound was heard from the movement of the air called wind, signifying the supreme Spirit who would speak through the apostles in every language, as it is written: “There are no speeches nor words whose voices are not heard. Their sound has gone out into all the earth,” and so forth (Ps. 18:4).

Observe that it does not say “the sound of the Spirit coming,” but “as though of the Spirit coming.” Thus, while there was in truth a bodily sound of wind, it nevertheless represented by a certain likeness the mighty sound of the preaching to come, or a kind of inner voice of speech made in their hearts: the Spirit inwardly suggesting what they should speak outwardly. That sound is rightly called violent, as though the strongest blast, in order to signify that apostolic preaching was not to be confined within the bounds of Judaea alone, as that of the prophets had been, but was to blow and spread, as it were, throughout the whole world.

That violent blast fills the house; it does not shake, drive against, or overthrow it—as though the Holy Spirit’s work were to supply what is imperfect, not to destroy good things already begun. Hence Truth says: “I have not come to destroy the Law, but to fulfil it” (Matt. 5:17). And concerning this very coming of the Spirit and the perfection of teaching, he had promised: “He will teach you all truth and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26).

We read that a wind sent by Satan, when it shook down the house that it struck, destroyed Job’s sons and daughters (Job 1:19), because it is Satan’s work to destroy, not to save, and to tear down rather than build. But this blast of wind does not shake the house at all; rather, it enters while the house remains unharmed and, by the agitation of its mighty movement, kindling fire in the air, illuminates [Col. 0510D] the very house which it enters. This fire, which both shines and warms, produced in the air by this blast of wind over the apostles, is illumination of the mind and the flame of charity inspired today into the apostles’ hearts and wrought by the Spirit in the higher part of the human being, that is, in the soul.

This fire appeared outwardly in the form of tongues, because through the words of preaching the hearers are made aware of what knowledge and what charity are possessed within. The tongues are called fiery—that is, made of fire—because the apostles, compelled to preach by the very charity in which they burned and by the knowledge they had received for this purpose, were also to enlighten and kindle their hearers’ hearts by these two things. The tongues are divided among themselves, not only because of their diversity, but also according to the discernment of the preachers. For just as, [Col. 0511A] because of the diversity of nations, different languages must be used, so preaching must also be adapted to the character of the hearers, so that we may nourish little ones with milk and refresh adults with bread.

That fire, appearing above those seated in the house, is said to have rested upon them because the Lord testifies that he rests upon a humble and quiet spirit; and those who are proud do not deserve to receive the fire of divine love. It is also rightly said that this fire settled upon them because the grace they received was to remain with them, just as the Lord had earlier promised concerning the Spirit, saying: “That he may remain with you for ever” (John 14:16).

They received the Spirit while gathered in one house because all who are not of the Church are strangers to grace. Hence the paschal lamb is commanded to be eaten in one house [Col. 0511B] (Exod. 12:4), because outside the Church there is no place for the true sacrifice; and all who were not in the ark perished, drowned by the flood.

They had already received the Holy Spirit with respect to certain gifts, when Truth breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive,” etc. (John 20:23). But they had not been filled with the Holy Spirit, as is shown to have happened today when it is said: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:4). Thus, having first been initiated by certain gifts, today they were filled to overflowing and brought to completion.

Immediately, as it were, pouring forth from this filling of the Spirit, they began to speak in other languages, as the Greek has it, which they had not spoken before. For they did not then begin to speak their own proper language, that is, Hebrew, but other languages which they had not known, [Col. 0511C] according to the diversity of the people from every nation under heaven gathered at Jerusalem for the feast day.

Concerning this diversity of languages, certain persons have thought, in order to make the miracle seem greater, that while all used the utterance of one language, they appeared to each individual hearer to speak that hearer’s own language.
