But this certainly would not be to speak in other languages, but merely to appear to speak to others; it would not be the reality of languages, but the opinion of deceived people; and nothing concerning languages would have been granted to the apostles, but understanding would have been inspired into the hearers.

Finally, that also would be false which the hearers said: “We have heard them speaking in our languages” (ibid., 11). For if there was no speech in languages, but merely an appearance of it, [Col. 0511D] it is false that they heard in those languages a word which was not in the apostles.

Therefore, today they were instructed not only in understanding the inward word, but also in the utterance of sound, so that no grace might be lacking in any respect. Hence, the more manifold the grace with which this present feast is endowed, the greater the devotion with which it ought to be celebrated and the more it ought to be honoured with the praises of every language, since every kind of language was bestowed upon the apostles for preaching to all nations.

And would that you, glorious brides of Christ, upon whom, as we have recalled above, the special duty of celebrating this feast rests, could make the divine praises resound in it in every kind of language! Since you are unable to do this, at least accomplish this: apply yourselves to the learning of the three principal languages, [Col. 0512A] in which the two Testaments were written and in whose characters the titles of the Lord’s cross were inscribed, and add something beyond other faithful Christians to these festal praises.

May the Spirit himself deign to suggest this to you in honour of himself: he who, breathing where he wills, either teaches inwardly through sound or writes with a pen in minds, and suffers no delay in teaching and no postponement in writing. May he strengthen your weakness in a holy resolve—he who today clothed the apostles with power from on high. May he make firm your earthen vessels and the clay shell which is still raw, baking it with the fire of divine love with which he filled the disciples’ hearts today.

May your Bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, continually breathe that same Spirit into your minds and preserve him for you as the earnest of your betrothal and the spiritual pledge of your dowry, so that, [Col. 0512B] as he promised the apostles, he may remain with you for ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIX. ON THE MONDAY OF PENTECOST

The greater the zeal with which you endeavour to celebrate the great feast of Pentecost, the more you desire to be stirred to this end by many exhortatory sermons. Thus, as you celebrate it for eight days, you request one sermon for each of those days. Obtain this for me by your prayers from the Spirit himself, so that I may be able to accomplish it.

And since, according to the Lord’s declaration, “a scribe instructed in the kingdom of God is like a man who brings forth from his treasure things new and old,” my inexperience, wishing to imitate this teaching as far as it can, takes care to turn its pen from the New Testament to testimonies of the Old, [Col. 0512C] so that this feast may be the more welcome as its dignity is more fully commended.

Foreseeing through the same Spirit this most glorious feast of the Holy Spirit, joining it fittingly to the Lord’s Ascension, and strongly exhorting us to celebrate its joy, the Psalmist says in one place:

> Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God;  
> sing psalms to the Lord.  
> Sing psalms to God, who ascends above the heaven of heaven toward the east.  
> Behold, he will give to his voice a voice of power.  
> Give glory to God over Israel:  
> his magnificence and his power are in the clouds.  
> God is wonderful in his saints, the God of Israel;  
> he himself will give power and strength to his people.  
> Blessed be God.  
> (Ps. 67:33 ff.; Vulgate numbering)

[Col. 0512D] Illuminated by the divine Spirit, the Psalmist therefore perceived even after the Lord’s Ascension the wonderful descent of that same Spirit and grace poured out upon all nations. No longer understanding God as formerly confined to Judaea, he invites all kingdoms, now won for God by this grace, to glorify him, saying: “Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing psalms to the Lord.” That is: All nations, who, now liberated from the slavery of the devil, have begun to reign, glorify God for this by singing with your voices and at the same time making psalmody through your deeds.

And lest we should deny the God whom, according to the humanity he assumed, we hear to be local or movable, he says: “Sing psalms to him who ascends,” etc. Above, he had said: “Make a way for him who ascends over the west.” But now he says: “Who ascends above the heaven of heaven [Col. 0513A] toward the east.” Thus he said the former concerning the Resurrection, since that occurred first; now he adds this concerning the Ascension.

He calls the bodily death of the true Sun his “west,” concerning which he himself said: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies,” etc. (John 12:24). Therefore he ascended above this west when he rose from death, in the manner of the sun, which after setting rises to the east. The disciples make a way for him who prepare themselves worthily by confidently awaiting him, so that, as he promised, he may return to them raised from the dead.

Now the words said here, “who ascends toward the east,” may fittingly be spoken by the Psalmist according to the position of the place. For the Mount of Olives itself, from which the Lord ascended into heaven, is said to stand eastward of the city of Jerusalem. [Col. 0513B] They may also be understood to mean that, wherever that mountain was situated, the Lord ascended eastward, if he performed this act with his face turned in that direction. For whoever has the west at his back directs his face toward the east.

But the west was now wholly behind him, because, raised from the dead, he dies no more and will not return again to the setting which he endured. He ascended above the heaven of heaven because he transcended the height of the ethereal heaven, which stands above the airy heaven.

What he was to do for the disciples after his Ascension, once he had sent the Holy Spirit, is then added: “Behold, he will give to his voice a voice of power.” By “his voice,” that is, God’s own inward speech, he means his inward inspiration, which was made fuller today through the Spirit, when without [Col. 0513C] sound he taught them inwardly all truth.

But because through the same Spirit various kinds of outward speech were added to this inward speech, a human voice was, as it were, joined to the divine voice that takes place inwardly: so that the word conceived inwardly in the mind might be uttered or made manifest outwardly through an audible word. Thus a human voice is given to the divine voice, so that what God speaks inwardly to us through his inspiration, we may teach to human beings through our utterance.

It is therefore fittingly said that, as the Lord ascends, he will give to his voice—made in the apostles through the Spirit, as stated—a voice of human utterance as well, so that they may suitably express and expound to anyone whatever they have rightly understood.

He further calls it a “voice of power,” [Col. 0513D] which today was prefigured over the apostles by the mighty wind, as we recalled in yesterday’s sermon. Preaching has power and is strong when someone can adequately reason about what he says, so that it cannot be refuted; or when he preaches with an outstanding spirit and does not deny the truth out of any fear; or when he does not attack in his conduct the things he preaches, nor fear the shame brought upon preaching by the consciousness of a reprobate life.

All these excellences clearly flourished in the apostles, so that their preaching deservedly may be called a voice of power. Indeed, the Lord had promised them: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries will be unable to resist or contradict” (Luke 21:15): a mouth for speaking, wisdom for understanding, and for discerning what ought to be said to whom, when, and how.

[Col. 0514A] It is also written of them that they preached the word of God with confidence. One of them testifies how religiously they lived and how carefully they provided against adulterating or discrediting the word of God through the shamefulness of their lives, saying: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become reprobate” (1 Cor. 9:27).

Observe that when he says that in those whom the Holy Spirit fills an outward word is joined to the inward word, he openly distinguishes them from demoniacs. For demons fill people and, by tormenting them, turn them to madness; they supply such people with words only, not understanding, and send into their minds the darkness of smoke rather than the brightness of fire.

But when the Holy Spirit speaks in the elect, he first illumines them inwardly, before he illumines others by their outward words. Hence, as stated, a human voice is rightly said here to be added to the divine voice, so that what is announced to others may be announced through inspiration.

Yet we should not for that reason believe that whenever the Holy Spirit spoke through prophets, he inspired into those through whom he spoke everything which he himself understood in those words. Rather, he revealed to them only one meaning at a time, or perhaps several meanings which he foresaw would be found there.

Therefore, when we see a prophecy expounded in various ways by teachers, we need not believe that the prophet possessed all those meanings; rather, the Spirit foreknew whatever could fittingly be understood there. Just as some wealthy person gives his own gold through his steward to different craftsmen, that they may make different ornaments from it, [Col. 0514C] so the Spirit gives us through the prophets his sayings, full of diverse meanings. When we expound them in different ways, however many meanings we draw from them, we make, as it were, so many works from one material.

“Give glory to God.” The kingdoms of the earth, which above he had invited to sing and make psalmody to God, he again exhorts to glorify him, so that for the great grace granted to them in these days they may give God a fuller glory of praise. For this grace must be proclaimed all the more throughout the world because it must itself be put into practice more fully everywhere, and through it all kingdoms have been won for God and transferred from the devil’s kingdom into Christ’s kingdom.

He then adds by whom this was accomplished, saying: “His magnificence [Col. 0514D] and his power are in the clouds.” As though he said: Give glory to God for this reason, because he gave magnificence and power to his clouds—that is, the apostles—through whom he converted you to his kingdom.

Clouds rise from below to on high and send rain down from on high, by which the irrigated earth becomes fruitful; and the seated apostles received the Spirit, because God gives grace to the humble and always resists the proud. Raised up today in powers through this grace and magnified by more abundant gifts, they pour rain upon the earth as from on high when, speaking in every kind of language, they instruct the hearts of earthly people by the words of divine speech.

Therefore God is rightly said to have bestowed magnificence and power upon those whom he so magnified and advanced into such powers by so many gifts, causing them to shine with miracles [Col. 0515A] and to excel in the strength both of word and spirit.

Of them he further says: “God is wonderful in his saints” (Ps. 67:36), through whom he deigned to work greater things than through himself, both by the performance of miracles and by the work of preaching—as though Elijah’s spirit had been doubled in Elisha. Hence he promised them: “He who believes in me will also do the works that I do, and he will do greater than these” (John 14:12).

We also know that the firstborn brother—that is, Christ—died, as it were, childless; and that his brothers—that is, the apostles—received his bride, the Church, and begot in her an innumerable offspring of children, and from those days onward gathered the whole world.

[Col. 0515B] Therefore let the world always consider how much it owes to the grace of this feast, for the gathering of which from every quarter every kind of language has now been bestowed. Consider all Christ’s feasts, from his Nativity itself to his Ascension, compare what the world then received with this grace, and you will see this feast greatly surpass all the others.

For in this feast the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the one hundred and twenty disciples gathered in the upper room, and through them gained about three thousand people on that very day. For this purpose, Jews who had formerly been scattered throughout all nations under Antiochus’s persecution had been gathered at Jerusalem for the present feast; we never read that this occurred at any other feast. From this it is also clear how much peoples from every place ought to come together for the present feast of grace, if they desire the gifts of spiritual grace.

[Col. 0515C] This one feast extended the Church throughout the whole world and, together with itself, established the celebration of divine feasts throughout the world. It spread the praises of God in every kind of language, so that from this it may appear how much all other feasts are indebted to this one, since through it they have been disseminated everywhere in the world.

Therefore, after the words of praise for this day, “God is wonderful in his saints,” and after its having been said that he is in some sense more wonderful in them than in himself, he immediately adds the respect in which he now appeared most wonderful: “He himself,” he says, “will give power and strength to his people.” [Col. 0515D] By “his people” he means the disciples: unlettered, rustic men taken from the lowly populace, through whom it is wonderful that he should work such great things.

Writing to the Corinthians, one of them reflects upon the rejection of the wise and powerful of this age and the choice of such uneducated and powerless persons, and says:

> Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel—not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. For the word of the cross is indeed foolishness to those who perish, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God. For it is written: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent.” Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the inquirer of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since, in God’s wisdom, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God to save believers through the foolishness [Col. 0516A] of preaching. Since Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified: a stumbling-block indeed to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God. For God’s foolishness is wiser than human beings, and God’s weakness is stronger than human beings. Consider your calling, brothers: not many were wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, and God chose the ignoble and contemptible things of the world, and the things that are not, to destroy the things that are, so that no flesh may glory in his presence.  
> (1 Cor. 1:17 ff.)

For it would not be wonderful if he performed great things through the powerful or [Col. 0516B] wise of this age, since this would be ascribed to human rather than divine power. Therefore, as is well said here, he is the God of Israel—that is, the one who chose the ancient people; he himself, I say, not another or a new God.

To these common and poor men, taken from that same people and now clothed with power from on high, he will give power of speech against the wise of the age and strength of heart against the attacks of the powerful. “Blessed be God”: understand, “let him be glorified and praised by all,” who in these days has wrought such things through such persons. Amen.

## SERMON XX. ON THE TUESDAY OF PENTECOST

We drew yesterday’s sermon from testimonies of the sixty-[Col. 0516C] seventh psalm. Now, turning our pen to the seventieth psalm, it is pleasing to add from it also a commendation of this feast. There it is written:

> You have made known among the peoples your power;  
> you have redeemed your people by your arm,  
> the children of Jacob and Joseph.  
> The waters saw you, O God;  
> the waters saw you and were afraid,  
> and the depths were troubled.  
> The multitude of the sound of the waters gave forth its voice;  
> the clouds gave voice, etc.  
> (Ps. 76:15; Vulgate numbering)

The Psalmist speaks to God, foreseeing in the Spirit the wonders which the apostles were to perform in these days through the same Spirit. “You have made known,” he says, “your power among many peoples”: namely, that power which he had promised to the apostles when he said, “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from [Col. 0516D] on high” (Luke 24:49).

And thus “by your arm”—that is, by that power or strength—you redeemed your people from the slavery of sin; you freed them through the Spirit who was given, of whom the Apostle says: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Cor. 3:17). For whoever serves God out of the charity infused through the Holy Spirit rather than out of fear ought to be called a friend rather than a servant, and renders a free, not compelled, service.

“The children of Jacob and Joseph.” When above he had said “peoples,” according to the multitude of persons or diversity of lands and regions, and now had added “people,” according to unity of faith or the bond of love—just as we have called the Churches both many and one—lest he seem by the name “people” to mean only the Jewish people or only the Gentile people, he adds: “the children of Jacob and Joseph”: that is, the descendants of both the Jewish and the Gentile people, so that in the Church the two walls might be joined to the one cornerstone, Christ.

Jacob, the supplanter of Esau, who deprived him of his inheritance, is the Jewish people, which, having expelled the Gentile people, obtained the land of promise. Joseph, however, whose name is interpreted “increase,” is the Gentile people: as it surpasses the Jewish people in the multitude of persons, so it has given the Church a great increase in the number of believers converted. For in comparison with the Gentiles, the Church contains few Jews, or none at all.

He immediately continues concerning this increase of the Church from Gentiles who have been converted, saying: “The waters saw you, O God”: that is, the peoples of the nations [Col. 0517B] understood you by believing, peoples who formerly, like water, were carried about by every wind of doctrine and had learned from the law nothing certain concerning what they ought to follow.

Of them it is written in the Apocalypse: “The waters are many peoples.” He further adds concerning them that, having seen God, they were afraid—not so much with servile fear as, in the fellowship of punishments, guarding against offending with a chaste or filial fear him whom they love. “And the depths were troubled”: that is, the depths of secular philosophy, which had formerly seemed like clearest waters and had a most delightful draught, became, as it were, troubled and muddy, and were held cheap in comparison with evangelical simplicity.

“The multitude of the sound of the waters,” understand, “gave a voice.” And why? [Col. 0517C] Because “the clouds gave voice.” For a great sound of divine praise resounds among converted peoples who have been taught by the voice of the clouds—that is, by the preaching of the apostles.

Indeed, your arrows (Ps. 66:18), O God, are transferred through these clouds from Judaea to the Gentiles. The arrows are the words of evangelical preaching, which wound the hearts of hearers like certain darts of divine love, as the bride says in the Song: “I am wounded by love” (Song 4:9).

These arrows were first kept shut up in Judaea as though in a quiver, until, when the Jews rejected the Gospel, the apostles passed over to the Gentiles, as one of them said to the Jews: “It was necessary for the word of God to be preached first to you; but since you have rejected it, behold, we turn [Col. 0517D] to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

The voice of thunder—that is, the voice made in the apostles from on high through the Spirit—was extended throughout the whole world. And because it is written of them that “they went forth and preached everywhere, the Lord working with them and confirming the word by accompanying signs” (Mark 16:30), flashes of miracles were added to that thunder of words.

Of these it is now said: “His lightnings shone upon the world” (Ps. 96:4). Since unbelievers are moved to faith more by the greatness of signs than by the authority of the Scriptures, “the earth was moved when the flashes were seen,” because, by admiration for miracles, the earthly hearts of human beings were changed from their former unbelief.

Thus God seeks to have paths in the sea and tracks in the waters: when, namely, departing from Judaea as though from his own land and imparting his grace to the Gentiles, he gained many peoples after rejecting one. The sea is greater than waters and full of bitterness; and the life of married persons, which includes many and is entangled in worldly cares, has as many bitternesses as it endures troubles. A path is broader than a track, and the life of married persons is less restricted than that of the continent. God is said to come to us or draw near to us, in order to draw us to himself, when he inspires in us an affection for good works.

Therefore, he walks in paths in the sea because he has broader works among the unmarried, just as he has narrower works among the continent, who travel by tracks. Yet these footprints of the Lord among the Gentiles “will not be known”: namely, that he would transfer his grace from his special Jewish people to the Gentiles and, abandoning the former, pass over to the Gentiles. [Col. 0518B] For no one could have foreknown this at that time.

Thus even the chief of the apostles, while he was still uncertain that the Gentiles would be called through his preaching, was admonished and taught concerning this very matter by the vision of a vessel full of every kind of creeping thing (Acts 11).

Why these footprints of God among the Gentiles would be unknown—so that blindness having occurred in Israel, the Gentiles might be enlightened—is stated in the conclusion of the psalm. It is as though he said: This could not be foreknown by human beings—that, with the Jews rejected, the Gentiles would be enlightened—because you had always possessed that former people as your own flock, for which you had appointed Moses and Aaron as such great shepherds and had exercised such great power in destroying the nations.

This is what he says: “You led,” etc.—leading that people from [Col. 0518C] Egypt and bringing it into the land of promise under the rule and leadership of Moses the leader and Aaron the priest.

## SERMON XXI. ON THE WEDNESDAY OF PENTECOST

Let us hear what the prophet Amos—or rather, the Spirit himself through him—said in praise of this feast of his:

> The Lord God of hosts, who touches the earth, and it will melt;  
> and all its inhabitants will mourn.  
> And it will rise like a river-stream  
> and will flow down like the river of Egypt.  
> He who builds his ascent in heaven  
> and founds his bundle upon the earth.  
> He who calls the waters of the sea  
> and pours them out upon the face of the earth:  
> the Lord is his name.  
> (Amos 9:5)

[Col. 0518D] The hosts of God, over whom he presides as their prince and with which he defeats the aerial powers, are those camps of angels or faithful human beings which Scripture frequently mentions. Genesis relates that, as Jacob was returning from Mesopotamia to his father in the land of Canaan, angels of God met him, as soldiers sent for his protection (Gen. 32:1). When he saw them, he said: “These are God’s camps” (ibid., 2). And he called that place Manahim, that is, “camps.”

The Song of Songs also describes the Church as an army arrayed in battle order, going forth as if girded for war. “The life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7:1). Those continually serve as soldiers in camp who, having no peace here, endure the unceasing conflict of battle against the devil’s temptations, the assaults [Col. 0519A] of the flesh, or the attacks of wicked people; they stand in that contest or combat concerning which the Apostle says: “Everyone who strives in the contest abstains from all things” (1 Cor. 9:25). And again: “Thus I fight, not as though beating the air” (ibid., 26). And again, in another of his Epistles: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

But in order that the God of these hosts might teach us by his own example to fight and grant us victory, just as he himself said in promise, “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John 16:33), he touched the earth, as the prophetic reading now says, when, first conceived of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin and afterwards born from her, he united to himself in one person the nature of our earthly substance. [Col. 0519B]

Therefore, to commend the grace of the Holy Spirit, through whom that conception too was effected at the beginning of our redemption, we see that the prophet fittingly begins here and thereafter carries his account through the divine benefits as far as the sending of that same Spirit in the present time. From the beginning of the Lord’s conception, when, as explained, he touched the earth, the prophet has taken such care to set forth what he did with this earth that, omitting neither his death nor his resurrection nor his ascension, he reaches the commendation of the excellence of today’s feast.

In fitting sequence, as from head to members, he proceeds through the wonderful operation of the Holy Spirit, since the same Spirit by whose operation the Lord was conceived brought the power of the apostolic host to perfection.

Thus the earth touched by the Lord in some way melts, since the humanity assumed by him was brought to the dissolution of death. Hence he himself said to the Father concerning this dissolution of death: “You have brought me down into the dust of death” (Ps. 21:16).

Since the apostles were especially saddened by his death, the prophet called this great sorrow of theirs “mourning” when he added: “And all its inhabitants will mourn” (Amos 9:5). The Psalmist had likewise foretold this mourning, as it were, of evening, before the morning joy of his resurrection: “Weeping will remain in the evening, and joy in the morning” (Ps. 29:6).

The faithful dwell in the earth, as it were, melting, when they place the hope of their redemption in the death of the humanity assumed. Yet they would by no means retain that hope unless he rose from the fall of death. Hence it is added: “And it will rise like a river-stream and will flow down like the river of Egypt” (Amos 9:5).

So long as a stream is held enclosed within its channel and does not rise and overflow the channel, it cannot irrigate the surrounding lands. Thus the living river rose, as it were, from its channel when the incarnate Wisdom of God rose from the very place of death into which he had been laid—that is, from the tomb.

[Col. 0520A] Then he irrigates the surrounding earth so that it can bear fruit, when he strengthened the disciples’ hearts, formerly despairing, with faith, so that through the hope of future blessedness which he displayed to them in rising, they might bring forth the fruits of good works.

Having first called him a river-stream, he then calls him the river of Egypt, carefully portraying a fitting comparison by likening the Lord to the Egyptian river called the Nile. [Col. 0520B] Bede, in his book *On the Nature of Things*, records the following concerning this river and a particular feature of its nature [Note: [Col. 0519D] *Patrologia*, vol. XC, col. 262.]:

> “Egypt uses the Nile in place of rains, rejecting showers and clouds because of the heat of the sun. For in the month of May, while the mouths through which it flows into the sea are blocked by heaps of sand as the west wind blows and casts up the waves, it gradually swells and, driven back, irrigates the plains of Egypt. But when the wind ceases and the heaps of sand are broken through, it is restored to its channel.”

The Nile, flowing from paradise, is the very Wisdom of God descending from above, to give us drink from the true fountain and to illumine the Egypt of this world—that is, its darkness—by the presence of the flesh he assumed. Of this it is written: “He was the true light, which enlightens,” etc. (John 1:9).

This river is said to flow into the sea through seven mouths. When these mouths are blocked with sand as the wind blows, it flows back into the land and has no free outlet to the sea. So, after the Lord’s resurrection and before the sevenfold grace of the Spirit was poured out upon the great sea of nations, this river was blocked, as it were, by certain sands while the wind blew: the apostles, restrained by fear of the Jews, were not allowed to depart from Judaea, [Col. 0520C] in which blindness had occurred, as though from Egypt, in order through their preaching to refresh the nations from this river.

For what is the wind except diabolical suggestion? What are the sands except those who, through desire for earthly things, flow hither and thither in the current of the world?

Therefore, as the wind blows, accumulated sand blocks the river when the covetousness of the Jews, fearing the loss of its place or nation, restrains apostolic preaching. But afterwards, when fear had been expelled from their hearts by the Holy Spirit and the sands had been broken through, the river flowed freely into the sea: apostolic preaching went forth steadfastly from Judaea to the Gentiles, every obstacle of fear having been repelled.

Thus one of them fearlessly [Col. 0520D] said: “It was necessary for the word of God to be preached first to you; but since you have judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

Yet, while they were held confined in Judaea, they were by no means wholly without fruit, since there too they gained for God a certain multitude of people. The aforesaid river—that is, Christ—bore fruit there by a kind of reflux before, flowing out into the boundless sea of the Gentiles, it gathered the Church from every side.

Accordingly, he says that the ascent of the river of Egypt signifies its reflux into Judea, and then, in fitting order, he adds its flowing down over the whole world to water the hearts of the Gentiles. Since this is known to have occurred only after [Col. 0521A] the Lord’s ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit, it is rightly said of both: “He builds his ascent in heaven, and will establish his bundle upon the earth” (Amos 9:6). He does not say merely, “He who ascended into heaven,” but “He who builds his ascent in heaven,” so that this ascent may not be understood as temporary, as though he himself would return again to earthly life; rather, without any such return, he would thereafter have a permanent dwelling there.

Already abiding in heaven, he established his bundle upon the earth when, by the Holy Spirit himself, he bound together the hearts of the disciples—still scattered, wavering through fear of death, and not yet made firm by any strength of mind—like a bundle, both to himself and to one another, by the bond of highest charity [Col. 0521B]. Thus he also established them upon the earth; that is, he confirmed them in every good thing, so that they themselves might become in the Church certain foundations for others, according to what the Psalmist had foretold of the Church itself: “Her foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. 86:1).

Now the waters of the sea are known to be salty. And he rightly says further: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5:13), by which earthly hearts are to be seasoned and, by your preaching, ordered in good conduct as by a certain salt of wisdom. Therefore, the waters of this salt are the words of apostolic preaching. These waters are called by God and poured out over the face of the earth when Christ’s apostles, called by him himself to the office of preaching, are admitted to it; they do not come of themselves in the manner of pseudo-apostles [Col. 0521C], such as those whom Truth reproves when he says: “All who came were thieves and robbers” (John 10:8). It is as though he said: They came on their own, not sent by me.

Therefore, the Lord calls the waters of the sea when he directs the words of apostolic preaching in every kind of language and throughout the entire world. And he poured them out not merely upon the earth but even upon the face of the earth, when they not only sound outwardly but, once understood, inwardly enlighten the mind. For by the face, through which each person is recognized, knowledge is not inappropriately signified. Thus the words are upon the earth but have not reached the face when the riddles of the Law or the prophets retain a veil in the letter and not an unveiling in evangelical understanding or apostolic doctrine [Col. 0521D]. For it is not thus filled with mystical words that it is poured out over the face of the earth; rather, it is poured out when the things spoken are known by being understood.

And who is this who accomplishes such great things? He fittingly adds: “The Lord is his name” (Amos 9:6). When he calls him simply “Lord” without specifying whose Lord he is, he indicates his universal lordship and all-embracing sovereignty, by which he governs and most excellently orders all things for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXII. ON THE THURSDAY OF PENTECOST

We read that both the very day of Passover and Pentecost were marked by the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that we may know that not only this feast but also that one—which are reckoned the chief solemnities—must be referred to the honor of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0522A]. For, as John relates:

“When it was evening on that day, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in their midst and said to them, ‘Peace be with you.’ And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side. Therefore the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. Jesus then said to them again, ‘Peace be with you; as the Father sent me, I also send you.’ When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained’” (John 20:19 ff.).

And it is clear that this took place in the last of the five appearances which he is read to have made on that day: appearing for the fifth time, he then gave the Spirit on earth whom he was afterwards to send from heaven, once the fifth appearance had been completed [Col. 0522B]. He had indeed earlier promised this sending and supreme advent of the Holy Spirit which we now celebrate. “I,” says Truth, “tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I will send him to you” (John 16:7).

What necessity, I ask, is this for the coming of the Holy Spirit, that Christ must first depart? While remaining on earth, could he not give him, whose fullness he always possessed? What reason was there for him to ascend into heaven, as though he were to send the Spirit from afar, whom he could give from nearby? For the Spirit is not local—not only the divine Spirit, but not even the human spirit—and spiritual nature is not moved from place to place in the manner of bodies [Col. 0522C]. “I fill heaven and earth,” God says (Jer. 23:24). And, as Truth says: “God is Spirit, who breathes where he wills, distributing to each as he wills” (John 3:8).

Beholding the Spirit’s immensity and the power of his divinity presiding over all places, the Psalmist says to the Lord: “Where shall I go from your spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 136:7). It is as if he openly said: If your supreme goodness—of which it is said, “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (Ps. 44:8)—has been made angry with me by my sins, what place of escape from your presence will lie open to me? Or where can I hide, concealed from your …? [materially uncertain: lacuna in the source] Immediately, beholding him present everywhere through the majesty of his unbounded Spirit [Col. 0522D], he adds: “If I ascend into heaven,” etc. It is as though he said: No place of refuge is safe for me, whether in the heights or in the depths, when you have resolved to pursue me, since all places are present to you for doing whatever you will.

Finally, on the very day of the resurrection, as we have already recalled above, we know that the Holy Spirit was given by him to the apostles.

Therefore, since he had already given the Spirit on earth, why was it necessary for him to ascend into heaven in order to give him again—as though he could find him there whom he did not have on earth, or send him from there whom he could no longer give on earth, as before, by breathing from himself? So necessary, I say, was it for him to say: “Unless I go away,” etc. Or perhaps this sending of the Spirit was higher [Col. 0523A] and greater, so that it was to be given from heaven, than that earlier gift bestowed upon the apostles on earth through breathing, for the remission of sins.

Indeed it was far higher and more eminent in dignity, if we can carefully distinguish that gift as well. There, certainly, was bestowed upon the apostles that power which is believed to be common to all their vicars, that is, bishops: namely, the power of forgiving or retaining the sins of others. But this grace of the Holy Spirit, infused into the apostles on the day of Pentecost, is more precious in proportion as it is more rare. For what do those fiery tongues appearing over the apostles signify except the highest perfection of a human being, consisting in three things? In these three, I say, by which a human being is made complete in every good.

These are as follows: illumination [Col. 0523B] of the mind, so that their simplicity might thereafter not go astray amid any darkness of unbelief, as the Lord himself, promising them this, says: “But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth” (John 16:7). But since, as blessed Peter observes, it is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back (2 Pet. 2:21), after the light of faith there must be poured in the ardor of charity, so that we may strive through love of God to fulfill what we now know must be done for God—this charity being understood as the Holy Spirit. Hence the Apostle says: “The charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Thus the fire in which the divided tongues appeared, because by its own nature it has both light and heat, carefully expresses the two graces already mentioned: illumination of faith, or most salutary teaching, and the kindling of charity [Col. 0523C]. But the form of tongues, said to have been divided, signifies the preaching that was to take place—not in one kind of language and not in one region through the apostles—so that they might live not only for themselves but for all people.

For the first two graces perfect a person inwardly in conduct and make him worthy of blessedness. But this still does not suffice for preaching, since one who thus advances, as it were, only for himself does not live for others. Even if he already keeps God’s commandments in his life, yet because he does not sufficiently preach them to others, he is not yet great in the kingdom of heaven, according to the Lord’s statement: “Whoever does and teaches these things to men shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19). For no one in [Col. 0523D] the Church is greater than the person who keeps God’s commandments by living them and draws others to imitate him by preaching.

What, then, should be thought of the apostles, through whose preaching not one region of the world but the entire world was converted to God? What gifts of divine generosity can be compared to this threefold grace of theirs which we have described? In order that the apostles might deserve to receive it, the Lord first had to ascend into heaven and thus in some manner prepare there for them a place of dwelling, as he himself had promised. Hence Paul says: “Our commonwealth is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Therefore Christ ascended there in deed so that the apostles might follow him in mind, and might desire all the more ardently to be where they knew their Lord had gone before them.

Thus the aforementioned Apostle, exhorting us, says: “Seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your mind on things above, not on things upon the earth” (Col. 3:1) [Col. 0524A]. For, as blessed Jerome observes, nothing greater can be prepared for a servant than to be with his Lord. And indeed, whoever greatly loves another’s presence burns with greater desires for that person in his absence. Therefore he had to depart into heaven in order to send the Spirit, because by withdrawing from them he kindled their desire to follow him all the more, and thereby made them worthy of receiving a greater grace.

He rightly first gave them on earth the Spirit by whom sins are forgiven, because remission must be effected where the sin is committed, and whoever does not obtain pardon in this life awaits it in vain in the life to come. Therefore, Lord, obtain this for us here through your Spirit, who intercedes for the saints; and may we deserve there to apprehend you, to follow whom your members might be able, you have now sent the Spirit to them from on high—the Spirit, I say, of whom the Prophet confidently says: “Your good Spirit shall lead me into a right land” (Ps. 142:10) [Col. 0524B]. For what is that right land except the land of the living, wholly free from iniquity? Through this Spirit grant us remission of sins in this land which is not right, so that under his guidance we may come to that land which is right: Savior of the world, who with the Father and the same Spirit are one God for ever and beyond [Col. 0524C]. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII. ON SAINT PETER

The feast of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, is to be venerated by the Church with greater solemnity in proportion as a greater primacy in the Church was granted to him by the Lord himself. For the Lord established him as a kind of foundation of the Church when, upon the confession of his faith in which it was said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16), he foretold that his Church was to be built as upon a most firm rock; and he entrusted to him especially the power of binding and loosing.

Blessed Cyprian, considering the foundation of this rock, recalls it in a certain letter to Jubaianus as follows: “It is manifest [Col. 0524D] through whom and by whom the remission of sins can be given. For the Lord first gave Peter, upon whom he built the Church, that what he loosed on earth should be loosed.”

[Note: [Col. 0523D] *Patrologiae*, vol. III, col. 1114, where the passage reads thus: “It is manifest where and through whom the remission of sins can be given; namely, that which is given in baptism. For the Lord first gave Peter, upon whom he built the Church, that what he loosed on earth should be loosed in heaven.”]

The same writer, concerning the same matter, to Quintus:

[Note: *Ibid.*, col. 1103.]

“Peter, whom the Lord first chose and upon whom he built his Church.”

Ambrose also, understanding Peter himself in the phrase “upon whom,” etc., says in one place: “This washes away guilt, while the very rock of the Church sings.” And Jerome, writing to Marcella concerning our faith and the teaching of the heretic Montanus, says of this same matter:

[Note: *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 475.]

“If, therefore, the apostle Peter, upon whom the Lord founded the Church, etc.”

How great Peter’s firmness and constancy in faith were, so that he was rightly called a rock on this account, the Lord himself testifies elsewhere, saying: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:33) [Col. 0525A]. It is as though he said: However much the others may waver, however much they may despair because of my death, your faith will remain unshaken. On account of this firmness of faith, Peter himself is commanded to strengthen his brethren when the Lord immediately says to him: “And when you have once turned, strengthen your brethren.”

For it should not be believed that Peter’s faith failed when, by divine dispensation, he was permitted to deny the Lord, namely through weakness of the flesh and fear of death. This is Peter, as has been said: the unique support and strengthening of the rest. After his threefold confession of love, the Lord entrusted his sheep and lambs to him, establishing him as the supreme shepherd of the whole Church. Therefore his see, which he adorned by the martyrdom of his passion, rightly received primacy among all Churches, so that, as he stood before all the apostles, so his episcopate might stand before the rest.

We know that in ancient times the Church possessed only three patriarchates—that is, three principal episcopal sees: Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch. Their dignity especially looks to the honor of blessed Peter, since both the Antiochene and Roman sees were his own, while the third, namely Alexandria, fell to Mark his disciple.

This is Peter after Christ, as another Elisha after Elijah. We read that, after Elijah’s taking up, the sons of the prophets gathered to Elisha [Col. 0525C] (4 Kings 2:3), and that, dwelling with him in huts near the streams of the Jordan, they led something like a monastic and communal life. Blessed Jerome recalls their manner of life in one place, saying:

[Note: *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 1076.]

“The sons of the prophets, whom we read to have been monks in the Old Testament, etc.”

But just as they were then gathered to Elisha, as we have said, living monastically and communally with him, so after the Lord’s ascension the faithful, united to Peter, embraced this perfection of life, or an even greater one. Luke carefully describes this in the Acts of the Apostles: “The multitude of believers,” he says, “were of one heart and one soul, and no one said that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts 4:32) [Col. 0525D].

It is also established that Elisha, because he saw Elijah when he was taken away from him, received a doubled spirit of Elijah, that is, a fuller grace in miracles. He not only raised the dead while living, like Elijah, but even after his death restored a dead man to life at the touch of his bones (4 Kings 13:21). What is it to behold Elijah when he is taken up—that is, into the aerial heaven—except to behold Christ ascending to the Father, that is, to believe that he is not inferior to the Father but, by the nature of divinity, encounters him as equal to him? Hence the Psalmist says: “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his encounter reaches unto its height” (Ps. 18:7) [Col. 0526A]. By “the highest heaven” he means the excellence of God the Father, who, because he is not from another, is called highest by existence rather than by dignity.

From this heaven the Son proceeds in being born, because Plato says that Mind is born from the highest God; that is, wisdom exists from the Father’s own substance as begotten. Of this going forth—the generation of the Son from the Father—is the prophetic saying: “His going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5:2). And the Son himself says: “I went forth from the Father” (John 16:28). Lest he seem inferior or unworthy in relation to the Father, it is added that “his encounter reaches unto its height,” because through the fullness of divinity he rises as coequal with the Father.

Rebuking doubt concerning this equality, he himself says to Mary: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17) [Col. 0526B]. It is as though he said: You are not worthy to touch me with your hands on earth, since you do not yet touch me by faith in heaven as equal to the Father; that is what it means that I have not yet ascended to the Father for you: you do not yet believe that I encounter him as equal through the fullness of divinity.

Because Peter believed this more fully, being stronger in faith than the others, he saw Elijah taken up, as another Elisha. Hence he deserved to receive the spirit of Elijah as doubled or multiplied, since he received from Christ himself a greater grace of miracles than Christ himself displayed through his own person, as he had earlier promised: “He who believes in me will also do the works that I do, and greater than these, because I go to the Father” (John 14:12); that is, I ascend in his heart through faith to equality with the Father. Therefore, the firmer Peter was in this faith, the greater grace of miracles he deserved above the others.

He not only healed the sick by the shadow of his body but is even said to have raised the dead by the same power of his shadow. Hence Augustine, on Psalm 130:

[Note: *Patrologia*, vol. XXXVII, col. 1707.]

“The apostles,” he says, “seem in Christ to have done greater things than the Lord Jesus himself. At the Lord’s voice the dead arose; at the shadow of Peter as he passed, a dead man arose.”

Isidore, *On the Life and Death of the Holy Fathers*: “Simon Peter, passing by, raised the dead by his shadow.” Thus what the Lord said—“He who believes in me will do greater than these”—though he spoke generally of whoever believes, he seems to have referred in particular to the singular constancy [Col. 0526D] of Peter’s faith.

But the miracle of Peter’s shadow was more wonderful than Christ’s fringe. For the fringe possesses something of reality, whereas the shadow bears a likeness; the former remains, the latter passes away.

If, after this grace of miracles, we also consider the dignity of honor which Peter obtained from the Lord, we shall see that Peter’s see even surpasses God’s own proper see, which he had from the beginning at Jerusalem; so that Christ himself may in some way be seen to prefer it also on earth. For who does not know that the Jerusalem Church itself, like the others, is subject to Rome [Col. 0527A]? Yet it is established that James, the Lord’s brother, was its first bishop. Nevertheless neither his first chair nor the feast of the other apostles deserved such distinction in the Church, so that this privilege should be reserved for Peter alone.

He also acquired by his own merits for his successors, in Pope Sylvester, that henceforth the Roman pontiff should be established by Constantine himself as his vicar in the imperial city, from whom he also received the insignia which adorn that dignity; so that, as one perfected according to the order of Melchizedek, he should preeminent in both priestly and royal dignity, Peter being recognized in the Church and Caesar in the city. For, having obtained a twofold grace, both in constancy of faith and in ardor of love, he deserved to claim for himself both ecclesiastical and royal monarchy.

While the others expressed more the opinions of people than their own assertion concerning Christ, and while the Lord himself asked them, “But who do you say that I am?” (Matt. 16:15), as though they still hesitated and kept silence, Peter did not delay to answer, in order to strengthen those who were wavering: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (ibid., 16) [Col. 0527B]. Therefore he alone is immediately and specially proclaimed blessed by the Lord and deserves to receive the singular privilege of ecclesiastical power, when Christ promises to entrust to him not a part but the entire kingdom of heaven: “I will give you,” he says, “the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 19).

For although it was said generally to all the apostles, “Whatever you bind on earth,” etc. (ibid.), yet to Peter alone were in addition given the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Just as there are many cities in one kingdom, so there are many parts within the Christian people. Therefore Christ’s kingdom is the universal Church, handed over to Peter’s power in such a way that nothing may be done in it except by the ordering or permission of the Roman pontiff; no one else has a general excommunication or absolution over all. When some disciples were departing and all were deeply uncertain, and the Lord asked them, “Do you also wish to go away?” (John 6:68), as though he stood at a critical moment of anxiety, Peter could not endure to remain silent but answered: “Lord [Col. 0527D], to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (ibid., 69).

Finally, from that fearless constancy which he then bore in his mind, and because he always burned with the greatest love, he did not fear to profess: “Though all should be scandalized in you, I shall never be scandalized” (Matt. 27:33). And again: “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you.” And again: “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death” (Luke 22:33). For he was no less inflamed with charity than he was firm in faith.

What was that flame of love in him, when he could not bear that the Lord should suffer even for his redemption, replying to him when he foretold his passion: “Be merciful to yourself, Lord; let this not happen to you” (Matt. 16:22)? Finally, what zeal of love he displayed at the Lord’s arrest, when all the others fled: in so great a crisis of alarm he cut off the ear of the high priest’s servant [Col. 0528A]. He would not have spared even those others who seized the Lord in that retaliation unless he had quickly been corrected by the Lord himself.

Therefore, mindful of that saying of the Lord, “No one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13), he exposed himself to the death from which he wished to save the Lord. How greatly he was armed with zeal against vices and against covetousness itself, the root of all evils, is plainly shown by that punishment inflicted upon Ananias and his wife (Acts 5:9). He did not strike them with a sword, as he had struck the servant mentioned above, but more wonderfully killed them by the power of his Lord. The Lord long endured Judas’s avarice; Peter did not endure for even a moment the sacrilege of committed covetousness.

The more ardently he burned with the strength of greater zeal, the less he tolerated anything contrary to virtue; and the more he knew himself to have been exalted by the Lord, the more he always strove to humble himself for the Lord. Thus, when he finally came to suffer crucifixion—the kind of death by which he followed the Lord most closely—as the Lord had earlier foretold to him, he was anxious not so much about his own passion as about the Lord’s honor. He did not permit himself to be crucified as the Lord was, but with his head turned downward and his feet raised upward, he chose through the very position of his body an increase of punishment [Col. 0528B].

How greatly, through this humiliation, he deserved to be exalted by the Lord cannot be doubted. Nor, I think, is it foreign to his honor that the Roman see, which stood out as the head of the world as swiftly as possible, became his, so that by this right also it might obtain primacy throughout the world. Through it, namely, the chief city of all kingdoms, which he consecrated to the Lord with his own blood, he founded it as the foundation of the others, as it were, with a kind of indissoluble cement.

Moreover, for the glory of this city the Lord granted that, although the other sees of the apostles are deprived of their relics, he did not take this distinction from Rome, lest the others be able to boast in comparison with it. Indeed, he willed it to be adorned also by the body of Paul, Peter’s fellow apostle, so that this city too might receive from these two gifts of grace a doubled spirit, as we have said concerning this our Elisha [Col. 0528D]. Thus it came about that this city, first built by the two brothers Remus and Romulus, was afterward founded much more happily in Christ by the greater brothers Peter and Paul.

To these two was apportioned all the grace sufficient for the confession of the whole world: Peter excelling in miracles, Paul in words. Paul himself distinguishes these two when he says: “The Jews seek signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Cor. 1:22).

Lest anyone perhaps be troubled that, by the privilege of divine love, John seemed to be preferred to Peter in merits, because John was more loved by the Lord while Peter is believed to have loved the Lord more, let him recognize, according to blessed Augustine, that this must by no means be understood of the persons themselves but of the two lives signified through them [Col. 0529A]. For Augustine does not doubt that the one who loves Christ more is better, nor that the one more loved by Christ is more blessed.

But if anyone perhaps dislikes our turning here to mystery and prefers not to depart from the truth of history in the persons themselves, let John, as we suppose, be said to be more loved by Christ because Christ displayed greater charity or intimacy toward him in deed: both because of purity of flesh, in which John excelled as a virgin, and because, on account of his youthful age, Christ exercised greater provident care toward him. Therefore Christ is said to love John more by the effect of his action, not by the affection of love. Let John, then, have this effect of love from the Lord as a virgin, yet without envying Peter, the martyr and superior in the affection of love [Col. 0529B]. May each of them assist us before the Lord by his great merits, so that we may be able to attain their fellowship.

## SERMON XXIV. ON THE CONVERSION OF SAINT PAUL

The conversion of the chief teacher of the Gentiles is to be celebrated with greater devotion by the Gentiles converted through him, in proportion as they are known to be more deeply indebted to him. His conversion alone, by which the entire world was converted or more carefully instructed and more perfectly taught in the faith, deserved to obtain a solemn feast in the Church. Alone among the apostles, he was formerly promised to the world by prophetic proclamations, designated by particular prophecies, and thus set apart and distinguished from the others [Col. 0529C].

This is that rhinoceros or monoceros, today bound by divine reins, who laid aside his former wildness and, subjected to the Lord’s yoke and drawing the divine plough, began to break up the clods of the valleys. Speaking to blessed Job about his marvelous conversion and magnifying his own power by which he could accomplish it, the Lord says: “Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?” (Job 39:9), as if to say, “As it does me?” Or, “Will it remain at your manger? Will you bind the rhinoceros with your cord for ploughing, or will it break the clods of the valleys after you? Will you have confidence in its great strength and leave your labors to it? Will you trust it to render seed to you and gather your threshing floor?” [Col. 0529D] (ibid., 10 ff.).

Blessed Gregory, in Book 31 of the *Moralia*, carefully expounds this passage concerning blessed Paul:

[Note: *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, cols. 589–590.]

“The rhinoceros,” he says, “is of an altogether untamable nature, so that, if it is ever captured, it cannot be kept in any way. For, being impatient, it dies immediately, as is reported. Its name, translated into Latin, means: ‘a horn in the nose.’”

—“The rhinoceros, which in Greek copies is also called *monoceros* [one-horned], is said to be of such strength that it cannot be captured by any skill of hunters. But, as those assert who have labored in painstaking investigation to describe the forms of animals, a virgin girl is set before it. She opens her bosom to the animal when it comes; in it, laying aside all ferocity, it rests its head. Thus it is suddenly found, as though enfeebled, by those who seek to capture it [Col. 0530A]. It is also described as being boxwood-colored. When it enters into combat with elephants, it is said to strike the bellies of its opponents with the single horn which it bears in its nose; so that, by wounding their softer parts, it easily lays low those attacking it.

“Therefore, by this rhinoceros—or rather monoceros, unicorn—may be understood that people which, because from the Law it received not works but only an exalted opinion of itself above all people, fought among the other beasts, as it were, with a singular horn. Hence the Lord, foretelling his passion as the Prophet sings, says: ‘Deliver me from the mouth of the lion, and my lowliness from the horns of unicorns’ (Ps. 21:22). For as many unicorns or rhinoceroses arose in that people as there were persons who gloried in works of the Law against the preaching of truth and trusted in foolish exaltation.

“Therefore blessed Job, who bears the type of the Church, is told: ‘Will the rhinoceros be willing to serve you?’ It is as though it were said: Will you bend beneath the rule of your preaching that people which you see exalting itself, through its foolish pride, in the slaughter of the faithful? The implied answer is: as I do, who see it raise itself with a singular horn even against me, and yet, when I will, immediately subject it to myself.

“But we show this better if we pass from the genus to the species. Let that man from this people, first in pride and afterward an outstanding witness in humility, be brought forward before us: [Paul], who, while he unknowingly exalted himself against God as though by observance of the Law, bore a horn in his nose [Col. 0530C]. Hence, later bowing down this very horn of the nose through humility, he says: ‘I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and insolent; but I obtained mercy because I acted ignorantly’ (1 Tim. 1:13). He bore a horn in his nose when he trusted that he pleased God by cruelty, as he himself later reproves himself, saying: ‘I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries in my race, being more abundantly zealous for the traditions of my fathers’ (Gal. 1:14).

“Every hunter feared the strength of this rhinoceros, because every preacher dreaded Saul’s savagery. For it is written: ‘But Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord,’ etc. (Acts [Col. 0530D] 9:1). When breath is drawn to be released through the nose, it is called breathing; and we often perceive by smell through the nose what we do not see with the eyes.

“Thus this rhinoceros bore in its nose a horn by which it might strike, because, breathing threats and slaughter, after killing those who were present it sought those who were absent. But behold, every hunter hides before it; every human being, that is, every rational and wise person, flees at the prospect of death from it. Therefore, in order to capture this rhinoceros, the Virgin—that is, the Wisdom of God itself, clothed in flesh through itself—opened her bosom, that is, her secret. For it is written that, while he was going to Damascus, suddenly at midday a light from heaven shone around him, and a voice came, saying: ‘Saul, Saul, why do you persecute [Col. 0531A] me?’ (Acts 9:4). He, cast down upon the earth, answered: ‘Who are you, Lord?’ To him it was immediately said: ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you persecute’ (ibid., 5).

“Surely the Virgin opened her bosom to the rhinoceros when the incorrupt Wisdom of God, speaking from heaven to Saul, disclosed the mystery of its incarnation. And the rhinoceros lost its strength because, cast down to the ground, it lost everything that swelled in pride. When, deprived of heavenly light, he is led by the hand to Ananias, it is now clear by what reins of God this rhinoceros is bound: namely, because at one and the same time he is fettered by blindness, preaching, and baptism.

“He also remained bound at God’s manger because he did not disdain to chew over the words of the Gospel. For he says: ‘I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also. I went up according to revelation and laid before them the Gospel’ (Gal. 2:1) [Col. 0531B]. And he who had formerly heard while fasting, ‘It is hard for you to kick against the goad’ (Acts 9:5), afterward, pressed by the wondrous power of preaching, obtained strength from the fodder of the word and lost the heel of pride.

“Moreover, he is not only restrained from wildness by God’s reins; what is more marvelous, he is bound for ploughing: so that he may not merely cease to attack people with the horn of cruelty, but, serving also their refreshment, may draw the plough of preaching. For he himself says of evangelists as of ploughmen: ‘He who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and he who threshes, in hope of receiving fruit’ (1 Cor. 9:10).

“Therefore he who had formerly inflicted torments upon the faithful and afterward gladly bears scourges for the faith; who, even in his written letters, preaches as humble and despised, though he once attacked terribly—such a one indeed labors well, bound beneath the plough for the harvest, who had lived wickedly free from fear in the field. Hence it is rightly said of him: ‘Or will it break,’ etc. The Lord had already entered the minds of certain persons who truly believed him to be the Redeemer of humankind. Yet because they did not at all depart from their former observance and kept the hard prescriptions of the letter, the outstanding preacher says to them: ‘If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing’” (Gal. 5:2).

> “He, therefore, who by reproving the harshness of the Law in the humble minds of the faithful broke up the clods in the valley after the Lord [Col. 0531D], did nothing other than prevent the grains of seed which the furrow of the heart, ploughed by faith, received from perishing when crushed beneath the observance of the letter. Of him it is fittingly added further: *Will he have confidence in him*, etc.? God had confidence in the strength of this rhinoceros, because the more cruelly He endured him while he inflicted harsh treatment upon Him, the more steadfastly He foresaw that he would endure adversities for Him. He also left to him the labours which He Himself endured in the flesh, because He drew him, once converted, even to imitation of His own Passion. Hence through this same rhinoceros it is said: ‘I fill up in my flesh what is lacking of the sufferings of Christ’ (Col. 1:24). Of him it is further added [Col. 0532A]: *Will you trust him, that he will repay those who sow, and gather in your threshing-floor?* Let us consider what Paul was when, from his very youth, he was an accomplice of those who stoned; when he ravaged some regions of the Church and, having received letters, sought out other regions to ravage; when no death of the faithful sufficed him, but, after some had been slain, he continually thirsted for the destruction of others. We shall surely recognize that at that time no believer would have thought that God would bend the fierceness of his pride beneath the yoke of His strength. Thus Ananias, even after he heard this man converted by the Lord’s voice, was afraid, saying: ‘Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to Your saints in Jerusalem’ (Acts 9:13). Yet he was suddenly changed: from an enemy he became a preacher, and throughout every region of the world he makes known the name of his Redeemer [Col. 0532B]; he endures punishments for the truth and rejoices to suffer what he had once inflicted. Some he calls by gentleness; others he calls back to faith by terrors. To some he promises the kingdom of the heavenly homeland; to others he threatens the fires of Gehenna. These he corrects by authority; those he draws to the way of uprightness by humility; and on every side he bends himself to the hand of his ruler. With as much skill as he had formerly tossed the threshing-floor in pride, so skillfully does he now gather it in for God.

> “Nor is it foreign to Paul that the rhinoceros is said to be boxwood-coloured and reported to strike the bellies of elephants with its horn. For since he had been accustomed to live beneath the strictness of the Law, the observance of each virtue more rigorously tamed him than it did others. For what is expressed by the boxwood colour except the pallor of abstinence? [Col. 0532C] He testifies that he clung firmly to this, saying: ‘I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should become disqualified’ (1 Cor. 9:27). Furnished with instruction in the divine Law, while rebuking the gluttony of others, he strikes elephants in the belly with his horn. He had struck elephants in the belly when he said: ‘Many walk, of whom I often told you; but now I tell you even weeping: enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction; their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame’ (Phil. 3:18). And again: ‘Such persons do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly’ (Rom. 16:18). [Note: [Col. 0531D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, col. 593.] Therefore this rhinoceros now strikes with his horn not human beings but beasts: when Paul, in the strength of his teaching, attacks not humble persons who are by no means to be destroyed [Col. 0532D], but slays proud worshippers of the belly.”

If it is pleasing to pass from the prophecy of the aforementioned pagan king Job to the predictions of the patriarchs or prophets, the first thing that occurs to us is what the patriarch Jacob foretold, in the blessing of his last and most beloved son Benjamin, as a type of this Apostle, who, as he himself declares, was from the tribe of Benjamin. “Benjamin,” he says, “is a ravenous wolf: in the morning he shall eat the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoils” (Gen. 49:27), or, according to another translation, “he shall divide food.” Let us, however, reconsider more deeply those things which concerned Benjamin [Col. 0533A], so that it may clearly appear how appropriately every detail can be applied to Paul.

Benjamin, the youngest among his brothers and most dear to his father, killed his mother Rachel by being born. As she was dying, she named him Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow.” But his father later changed the name and called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.” Therefore Benjamin, brothers—the youngest of the brothers and most beloved by his father—is Paul himself. Called by God last, after the Apostles, he was so much more beloved by God as he was more excellent in merits. Jerome says of him in his letter to Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0533D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXII, col. 580.]:

> “Paul is last in rank, first in merits, because he laboured more than all.”

It is further established that he was not only a martyr but also a virgin [Col. 0533B], so that the palms of merit which seem divided between the Apostle Peter and John are found united in him. Concerning his pre-eminent virginal crown, Ambrose says in his commentary on First Corinthians [Note: [Col. 0533D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 217.], at “But I say to the unmarried,” etc.:

> “He would not say, ‘It is good for the unmarried to remain as I am,’ unless he were sound in body; nor would he say, ‘I wish all men were as I myself.’ If he had had a wife and said this, he would not have wished them to be virgins. But far be it! From childhood he burned with the Spirit, so that he had no inclination for this matter; for while still a young man he was anticipated by the grace of God. A person is helped in that which he seems eagerly to desire in his mind.”

Likewise, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians [Note: [Col. 0533D] Ibid., col. 320.]:

> “All the Apostles, except John and Paul, had wives.”

Jerome also teaches this, writing among other things to the virgin Eustochium [Note: [Col. 0534D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 407.]:

> “Concerning virgins, the Apostle says, ‘I have no commandment of the Lord,’ because his own being a virgin was not a matter of command but of his own will. Nor should those people be heard,” he says, “who invent that he had a wife, when, in urging perpetual chastity, he added: ‘But I wish all to be as I myself’ (1 Cor. 7:8).”

In his book *On Hebrew Names*, commending Paul’s excellence even through the interpretation of his name, Jerome also says [Note: [Col. 0534D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIII, col. 852.]:

> “‘Paul’ is interpreted ‘wonderful’ or ‘chosen’; the Lord Himself called him a chosen vessel, and made him wonderful among the Apostles both in life and in doctrine.”

Benjamin, as stated, killed his mother in giving birth, and she, dying from the pain of labour [Col. 0533D], called him Benoni, that is, “son of sorrow.” But his father, changing his name, called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.” Thus Paul, now reborn in Christ, is said to have killed his mother, Judaism, which had begotten and educated him in the teaching of the Law, since he especially rendered void the precepts of carnal observances in which they lived and reduced all their glory to nothing. As though coming forth from his mother’s womb and withdrawing by conversion from the school of the synagogue, he says: “He who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through His grace” [Col. 0534A] (Gal. 1:15).

Thus his mother fittingly called him Benoni, “son of her sorrow,” because the more Paul attacked her error, the more deeply he caused her grief; and the more welcome he had been because of the excellence of his wisdom, the more he grieved her when she lost him. But his father fittingly chose to change his name, so that he might call him rather son of the right hand—that is, of prosperity or strength—than son of sorrow. For, as we have said here, the destruction of the synagogue effected through Paul should be reckoned toward the prosperity of the faithful and the common rejoicing of the Church rather than toward sorrow. The innumerable persecutions directed against him show also with what strength of mind he flourished.

That he is said to seize prey in the morning and divide food in the evening signifies that he was first a persecutor of the Church and afterward administered to it the refreshment of the word by the teaching of his preaching. That, according to another translation, he is said to distribute spoils signifies that after his conversion he tore many souls away from the devil and retained them as spoils, the enemy having been put to flight; this he afterward arranged through ecclesiastical offices or through whatever ministries of the faithful. Jerome, however, asserts in his book *Hebrew Questions* [Note: [Col. 0534D] Ibid., col. 1010.] that, according to the Hebrews, the altar on which offerings were sacrificed and the blood of victims was poured out at its base lay in the territory of Benjamin’s tribe. This appropriately refers to this shedder of Christian blood, of whom it is written: “Breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord” [Col. 0534C] (Acts 9:1), where he tore Christ’s members upon the earth as a wolf tears sheep.

But to pass from the patriarchs to the prophets, let us hear what that greatest of kings and prophets, David, foretold concerning this Benjamin of ours:

> “The princes went before, joined with those who sang psalms, in the midst of maidens playing tambourines. In the churches bless God the Lord from the fountains of Israel. There is Benjamin, a youth, in ecstasy of mind” (Ps. 67:26 [Vulgate]).

At the beginning of the Church’s birth, its princes, the Apostles, went before in election, because they were first chosen by Christ, through whom the rest might be converted. Though they were not so perfect that they could beget others by the word of preaching, they are nevertheless called singers of psalms—that is, those having a psalm in good action [Col. 0534D]. For a psalm, that is, the melody of the instrument called the psaltery, signifies by the striking of the hands the actions of good works arising from the affection of the heart. We use our hands more than the other members for working; therefore works are signified by hands.

Thus the princes in the Church are joined with those who sing psalms, because those who labour in the word of preaching are united in one faith with the peoples subject to them, who are not equal to this task but nevertheless do whatever good works they can. To prelates and subject peoples he joins maidens who play tambourines [Col. 0535A], that is, the life of the continent, who bear the tambourine of great mortification and approach more fully toward the newness of Christ in proportion as they withdraw farther from the oldness of the first human being. Therefore the two preceding orders stand, as it were, in the midst of these maidens, because the life of the continent, the greater its merit, protects more fully the orders of rulers and subject peoples, as though encompassing them with its virtues and shielding them by its prayers.

But because both the continent and the subject peoples are instructed from the teaching of the aforesaid princes, as though by drinking from certain fountains, he exhorts us especially to glorify God from these fountains, who has ordained such persons to preside over His Church. Since this Benjamin of ours waters the hearts of the faithful with the water of a more perfect doctrine, he is more rightly called by the Lord a chosen vessel and a noble cup [Col. 0535B]. Of his excellence it is immediately added: “There”—that is, among those fountains—is Benjamin, as though one of them, last by election, as was said, but first by dignity. Of his excellence and the singular grace conferred upon him it is at once added: “In ecstasy of mind,” that is, made in an ecstasy of mind and raised by such contemplation to the third heaven, caught up above the human condition, that he himself did not know whether, in that sublimity of revelation, his soul was in the body or outside it. For when the Lord answered Moses, who sought to see Him: “No human being shall see Me and live” (Exod. 33:20), he certainly seems then to have been above the human condition who enjoyed so great a vision in the heavens [Col. 0535C], where he recalls hearing such things as it is not permitted a human being to speak.

The more perfectly he was instructed there, the more perfect a doctrine he left to us. How greatly that doctrine surpasses others is not unknown not only to Christians but also to philosophers. His fellow Apostle and the chief of the Apostles, Peter, highly commending Paul’s Epistles, although he knew that he himself was rebuked in them, says:
