> “As also our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given him, wrote to you, as in all his Epistles, speaking in them of these things, in which are certain matters difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do also the other Scriptures, to their own condemnation” (2 Pet. 3:15).

Hence Jerome writes to Pammachius [Note: [Col. 0535D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXII, col. 502.]:

> “Whenever I read the Apostle Paul, I seem to hear not words but thunderclaps.”

And how highly he was regarded even among philosophers by those who had either heard his preaching or seen his writings is attested by the famous Seneca, distinguished alike in eloquence and morals, in the letters he addresses to him:

> “Having read your little book, we have been thoroughly refreshed by your wonderful exhortation, in the many letters which you addressed to certain persons, to some city or people, or to a provincial capital, to despise mortal life. I do not think that these thoughts were spoken by you, but through you—certainly at times both from you and through you. For such is the majesty of these things, and they shine with such nobility [Col. 0536A], that I think human lifetimes would scarcely suffice for the purpose of being instructed and brought to perfection by them.”

Jerome also recalls this praise of Paul by Seneca in his book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 12, writing as follows [Note: [Col. 0535D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIII, col. 629.]:

> “Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Corduba, a disciple of the Stoic Sotion and uncle of the poet Lucan, was of a most continent life. I would not place him in the catalogue of saints, unless the letters which are read by many, of Paul to Seneca or of Seneca to Paul, prompted me to do so. In them, although he was Nero’s teacher and the most powerful man of that time, he says that he wished to hold among his own people the place which Paul held among Christians.”

Time, brothers, would fail me if, pursuing Paul’s praise detail by detail, I presumed to exceed the capacity of my strength. But since it is written, “If anything remains, let it be burned with fire” (Exod. 12:10), let us leave the rest to God and prepare ourselves to offer the sacrifice of praise concerning these things at the solemnities of the Mass.

## SERMON XXV. ON SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST

*(We have emended the text with the aid of the Einsiedeln manuscript.)*

Those who compose sermons for saints’ feast-days fittingly take their beginning from the prerogative—that is, the dignity—of those saints, so that their feasts may be celebrated more devoutly by the faithful in proportion as their praise has been more fully heard, we understand that they are more pleasing to God, and we have greater confidence in their merits [Col. 0536C]. It is established, moreover, that among all the Apostles, as blessed Augustine also recalls [Note: [Col. 0536D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, col. 2113.] in expounding Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, three were more honourable: Peter, James, and John. As the Apostle says, they “seemed to be pillars,” that is, the support and strength of the others.

From many places in the Gospels we gather that these three were Christ’s closest companions; He frequently entrusted His secrets to them apart and had them as inseparable companions. Taking them apart, He revealed to them on the mountain the glory of His Transfiguration; and when He came to His Passion, again taking them apart in secret, He said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death. Remain here and watch with Me” (Mark 14:34). And after praying, returning to them, He said: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” [Col. 0536D] (ibid., 38). Thus it is plainly indicated how inseparably these three always clung to Him: He had them as undivided companions in the glory of the Transfiguration, in the agony of the Passion, and both in watching and in prayer, and never allowed them, as He did the others, to be separated from Him.

Since, then, these men are beyond doubt more honourable among the Apostles, as has been said, who can doubt how much John surpasses them in honour? Even among those who were more honourable, he obtained a certain fuller honour through the privilege of the Lord’s love; and by the Lord Himself he, a virgin, was given in the Lord’s place as another son to His virgin mother [Col. 0537A]. Thus, while both stood by His cross, He spoke from the cross to her, saying: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19:26); and to the disciple: “Behold your mother” (ibid.). John himself adds there, after saying “Behold your son”: “And from that hour the disciple received her into his own” (ibid.). “In sua” (“into his own [resources]”), I say—understand his means of support and, as it were, the reward of his virginity—not “in suam” (“into his own [woman]”), as though she were a wife.

Happy is this incomparable recompense of the disciple: entrusted with the virgin Mother of the Saviour, he was appointed by the Lord as another Christ-like son at Christ’s side, so that he might continually enjoy her joys and conversation, minister to her more diligently until her departure, prepare her undefiled little body for burial with virgin and, as it were, angelic hands, and lay it, once prepared, in the tomb [Col. 0537B]; so that he might close those blessed eyes, arrange that angelic face, and, after devoutly composing both her hands and the other members, complete the devotion of his office as a great priest.

It is certain that neither the rose of martyrdom nor the lily of virginity was lacking to his most holy life and incorruptible flesh, as he followed, according to what is written, the Lamb wherever He goes (Rev. 14:4). For he was cast into a cauldron of boiling oil and banished for a long time; yet by constancy of mind he fulfilled what the Lord had foretold both to him and his brother concerning drinking the cup of the Lord’s Passion: “You shall drink My cup” (Matt. 20:23). His constancy and invincible love were proved especially at the cross, when he alone, while the Apostles were scattered in flight, stood fearlessly by the cross and suffered with the crucified Lord together with the Lord’s Mother [Col. 0537C].

It was from this perseverance in constancy that he deserved to receive from the Lord the singular reward we have mentioned: the entrusting of His Mother. O blessed exchange! O incomparable substitution! He is removed from marriage as a virgin, separated from a wife, and set apart from the bed of desire, so that, undefiled, he might receive the undefiled Mother of the Lord; become the son of a virgin and the spiritual brother of Christ rather than the husband of a wife. How great a love Christ always showed him, both in this and in other matters, is evident from many signs. To him alone it was granted to recline upon the Lord’s breast at supper, and, fearless and steadfast in faith, to rest there at the moment of the coming Passion, when all hearts were already disturbed [Col. 0537D]. Thus his constancy too was proved, as in the case of the prophet Jonah, who, while the others despaired of the approaching danger, went down securely to sleep in the hold of the ship (Jonah 2).

The Apostle would surely not have presumed this unless he trusted in their wondrous intimacy: that he might lean in Christ’s bosom as on some bed and upon His breast as upon a pillow. From that breast, in which, as Paul recalls, all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden [Col. 0538A] (Col. 2:3), he deserved to draw out the streams of the Gospel more deeply than the others. Thus, reclining in this, as it were, sleep, he received more than the others did by listening to that lengthy discourse at supper. Therefore he alone later recorded that discourse, which had been more deeply impressed upon his spiritual ears through revelation.

The length of his life, prolonged into old age, plainly shows how necessary the Lord judged him for the instruction of His Church, preserving him so long in the world. Nor did He expose him to sufferings as He did the other Apostles, or permit him to be afflicted: He kept him unharmed in boiling oil and hastened vengeance upon his persecutor Domitian, in order to bring his exile to an earlier end. When all Domitian’s decrees had been annulled by the senate [Col. 0538B], John himself was restored from exile to the faithful peoples with the greatest rejoicing, by God’s hidden dispensation. The revelation made to him in that exile, called the *Apocalypse*, plainly bears witness to the great consolation granted him by the Lord there.

We have learned from many accounts how wonderful and joyful a conclusion of life he had, and how the Lord’s supreme love shone even in his death. For we read that he alone was invited by the Lord Himself to ascend to the heavenly banquet of his brethren, so that with his arrival the joy of all might be fulfilled. And, as he wished and when he wished, commending his soul into the hands of the Lord, he was as free from the pain of death as he had been untouched by the corruption of the flesh [Col. 0538C].

His body too, not corrupted by decay or putrefaction, is said to have been transformed into the appearance of manna, so that the whiteness of that appearance might prove the purity of his undefiled flesh. Some saints, moreover, have not hesitated to maintain that he has already been endowed with the glory of resurrection. Hence this passage from an Augustinian sermon for the Nativity of Martyrs:

> “To say nothing of the fact that all things are possible with God and that He can bring forth a spiritual body from closed tombs, we have the example of the Apostle John alone, whose tomb could enclose the body committed to it but could not retain it. For it lost the body deposited in it; it did not receive it up. Indeed, with the doors of the tomb closed, he was taken away by the grace of resurrection, so that burial might be certain while the buried man could not be found [Col. 0538D]. Finally, when priests, in order to honour him, sought his body and the entrance was opened, the tomb could not return him whom it had received.”

Gregory of Tours, in Book I of the *Miracles*, recalls how greatly God endowed with grace even the place in which John kept his most chaste body while writing the Gospel or giving himself to prayer [Note: [Col. 0537D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXI, col. 730.]:

> “At Ephesus there is a place where this Apostle wrote the Gospel. On the summit of the neighbouring mountain are four roofless walls; there, while persevering in prayer, he prayed to the Lord and obtained that no rain should fall in that place until he completed the Gospel. And even to this day the Lord so grants it [Col. 0539A] that no rain falls there and no violent shower comes.”

From these things, therefore, you virgins beloved of God, observe how honourable this special beloved of the Lord was among the rest, how acceptable to God, how great his pre-eminent merits, and how great the praises by which he should be exalted. Celebrate his feast all the more devoutly in proportion as you imitate more fully his holy excellence in purity. May his intercession so strengthen us in our holy purpose that you may arrive at that heavenly banquet to which he was invited; that there you may be refreshed more happily in mind than here in body, eternally united to your heavenly Bridegroom, the vision of whose presence is itself supreme blessedness.

## SERMON XXVI. ON THE ASSUMPTION OF BLESSED MARY

[Col. 0539B]

As we have gathered from the statements of ecclesiastical teachers, when the Lord ascended into heaven, certain angels, questioning—or rather marveling—at the magnificence of so glorified a human being, repeatedly asked the other angels standing by: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23:8 [Vulgate]). So too, in the present Assumption of the Mother of the Lord, we believe that, in angelic wonder at so great an exaltation of the weaker sex, it was fittingly said: “Who is she that comes up like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed in battle order?” (Song 6:9 [Vulgate]).

The rising dawn brings the day’s first brightness. To rise belongs to the elect—that is, to raise themselves to the summit of virtues and toward apprehending God—just as, conversely, it belongs to the reprobate to fall and plunge themselves into the depths of vices. Hence the exhorting voice speaks to those numb with the sleep of negligence and lying in their sloth: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall enlighten you” [Col. 0539C] (Eph. 5:14). Some rise and, raised as it were from the death of the soul through repentance, rise again; but they have not grown to such great merits of virtue that they can be taken up as an example of perfection, nor can they display, like the dawn, the brightness of doctrine to those who strive to raise themselves to perfection of life.

But the blessed Mother of God, the more perfectly she grew in virtues, the more widely she spread the brightness of her perfection in the manner of the rising dawn. Rising first in the purpose of virginal purity, she made known by her own example that way of perfection in which virgins alone follow the Lamb wherever He goes, just as the dawn, as stated, brings the first brightness of day. Although some are believed to have preceded her as virgins—Elijah, Jeremiah, Daniel, or certain others, as some suppose—we do not believe that they possessed this virtue from the devotion of a sacred purpose so much as from a certain necessity and the pressure of persecution. Especially so because in that time those who left no seed in Israel lay under a curse by the Law, and certain legal compulsions impelled people to marriage. Indeed, this law of marriage was so powerful that even the Mother of the Lord endured being betrothed, compelled alike by her parents and by the Law [Col. 0539D].

Yet, trusting in divine revelation, she did not despair of drawing to an agreement to preserve virginity the man whom she, though a virgin, was to marry. In order especially to obtain this, it must be believed that at the very time of her betrothal she kept the private chamber of prayer into which the angel sent to her is remembered to have entered. For he did not find her outside among worldly women; rather, he found her hidden in chastity, with the door of her chamber shut, devoutly praying to the Lord and commending to Him, by the purity of sincere prayer, the concord of her purpose. Thus amid her prayers she deserved the angelic vision, by which she was strengthened so completely that the Lord both preserved for her her vow of virginity and, by being born from her, provided at the same time for her release from the curse of the Law; and through her, blessed among women [Col. 0540A], poured blessing upon the whole world, granting her that seed concerning which He had promised Abraham: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18).

Thus, rising like the dawn, she illuminated the world with its first brightness, because she first set forth as an example the radiance of chastity and the purpose of holy virginity. But because a single good of virginity is insufficient for her praise if the grace of the other virtues is absent, her beauty is compared also to the moon: all the gifts of the whole Church were bestowed in her; all that different believers received in portions was transferred in its entirety to her; and the gifts divided among others are found united in her [Col. 0540C]. And because it is of little value to possess whatever abundance of gifts if the virtue of perseverance in them is lacking—of which it is written, “Whoever perseveres, that person shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22)—there is added, “chosen as the sun.” For her brightness is not subject to diminution like that of the moon, but perseveres in its own strength.

Three things, therefore, have been set forth in praise of this virgin. First, she was compared with the dawn, because of the example of chastity made known to the world through her; then with the moon, because of the fullness of all graces; finally with the sun, because of the perseverance granted in them. Adorned with these gifts and armed, as it were, with spiritual weapons, she is at last described as “terrible as an army arrayed in battle order.” Such an army is beloved by its own side and terrible to its adversaries, provided that it is properly arranged. It is well arranged when, against every enemy rushing in . . . , defenders have been provided who can resist them, so that no place lies open through which the enemy can break in to strike [Col. 0540D].

We know that it is written: “The life of a human being upon earth is warfare” (Job 7:1); and whoever competes in that contest of which it is said, “He shall not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5), abstains from everything, lest he lose the crown of victory. The enemies of the faithful soul and hostile agents who persecute it with their temptations are demonic spirits: the spirit of fornication and those who preside over the other vices. “Our struggle,” as the Apostle says, “is against principalities and powers” (Eph. 6:12) [Col. 0541A]; we are not found fortified with every virtue. We need fear them less for victory than they need fear us. But the Mother of God is adorned with the defence [printed *munimen*, perhaps for *munimine*] of every virtue and uniquely strengthened by the possession of virtues against the assaults of every temptation or vice; she appears more terrible to them than they do to her.

We read that angels stood by when the Lord ascended, consoling His disciples and saying: “Men of Galilee,” etc. (Acts 1:11). We believe that to the other angels, who asked in wonder, “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23:8), they replied: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (ibid.); and again: “The Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory” (ibid., 10). Escorted to the Father in a kind of triumphal procession by both companies of angels, He is known to have sat down at His right hand [Col. 0541B].

But if we carefully compare that angelic reception and triumphal procession offered then to Christ with the joy of today’s feast, we shall see that something greater was rendered to Him in the Assumption of His Mother than was shown to the Son Himself in His Ascension, and that the reception of this procession was by no small degree worthier than that one. Angels alone could go forth to meet Christ as He ascended; but He Himself, together with the whole heavenly court, both of angels and of faithful souls, received her soul—the soul in which He had previously taken both soul and flesh. Nor is it believed that He took up her soul alone, but also today raised her body to heaven, in order to reward her with the glorification alike of soul and body, she in whom, as has been said, He had decreed to assume both soul and flesh [Col. 0541C].

The tomb found utterly empty, as the Lord’s had formerly been, gives especially strong testimony to this: so that she too may be believed to have received the glory of resurrection and the twofold robe. The prayer for this feast expressly says:

> “In which the holy Mother of God underwent temporal death, yet could not be held down by the bonds of death,” etc.

Since “temporal death” is stated beforehand, it is clearly shown that the following words about the bonds of death must refer to that death of the flesh, not to the death of the soul, by whose bonds all the elect alike are not held. Blessed Gregory of Tours, attending carefully to this point, did not hesitate, when writing about her passing, also to assert the glory of her prompt resurrection. Thus, in Book I, chapter 4, of the *Miracles*, he writes [Note: [Col. 0541D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXI, col. 708.]:

> “After the glory of the Lord’s Ascension, the Apostles of the Lord, gathered with blessed Mary His Mother in one house, placed everything in common; nor did anyone call anything his own, but each possessed all things in love, as the sacred narrative of apostolic acts records. After this they dispersed into different regions to preach the word of God. At length, when blessed Mary had completed the course of this life and was now called from the world, all the Apostles gathered from their several regions [Col. 0542A] at her house. When they heard that she was to be taken from the world, they kept watch there together with her. And behold, the Lord Jesus came with His angels; receiving her soul, He entrusted it to Michael the archangel and departed. At dawn the Apostles lifted her body on its bier, placed it in the tomb, and guarded it while awaiting the Lord’s coming. And behold, the Lord stood among them again and commanded that the holy body, once received, be borne in a cloud into paradise, where now, her soul having been restored, she rejoices with His elect and enjoys the goods of eternity, whose end shall never set.”

From the assertion of so great a man, it is clear how glorious was this passing of the supreme Virgin. To consecrate and celebrate it, both the Lord Himself came forth from the heights with angels, and the Apostles gathered from every region: the latter to prepare her funeral rites, the former to receive her [Col. 0542B].

We know that at the Lord’s death the apostles were scattered in fear and turned to flight. But now, by divine dispensation, it has come about that what was lacking in the Son is increased and repaid in service to the Mother; and that what they had done wrongly there while scattered, they might amend here when assembled. From this too it appears how much more concerned the Lord seems to have been for his Mother’s honour than for his own, if one weighs both her life and her departure. For he himself endured not only in his Passion but also beforehand such insults that he was called a glutton, a drinker of wine, and one possessed by a demon; yet he allowed no stain whatever of disgrace to be cast upon the excellence of his Mother [Col. 0542C]. Hence, when he was to be born from her, he provided her with a husband, through whom provision might be made not only for her bodily needs but also for repelling from her both the charge of a curse and that of dishonour.

The Lord’s body lay in the tomb for three days, and from the day of his resurrection he deferred his ascension for forty days. This delay, as has been said, he did not permit in his Mother’s case. Indeed, he secretly bore her sacred body to Paradise before he raised it, so that the assumption and resurrection of the lifeless body might be more wondrous, judging that, once raised, it was in no way worthy any longer of earthly contact. We read that Adam was created outside Paradise, Eve in Paradise; that the Lord was raised [Col. 0542D] on earth, but his Mother’s body in heaven. Let women consider with how great a glory the Lord has exalted their inferior sex, and how both the heavenly and the earthly Paradise appear naturally to belong to them. For in the latter the female sex was first created, both in body and soul; into the former today soul and body together are exalted. Eve was created from the old Adam; but the new Adam, the Redeemer of the old, is born from Mary. That woman expelled from Paradise him who was both her husband and her parent; today this woman is assumed by him who is both her bridegroom and her Son into a happier Paradise.

And just as, ascending into heaven, the Lord is described as sitting at the right hand of God [Col. 0543A], so they do not doubt that today he has placed his assumed Mother at his own right hand—to her who was once addressed through the Prophet: “The queen stood at your right hand, in garments of gold” (Ps. 44:10). That is, she stands in a body ever unstained, now also made immortal and incorruptible. For gold is brighter and more solid than other metals, and can neither be consumed by fire nor corrupted by rust.

Therefore, just as the Lord displayed in himself the glory of resurrection to men, so now in his Mother he displayed it to women, in order that he might stir the desires of both sexes more ardently toward hope of future blessedness. To her in particular is directed that voice of the Bridegroom by which she is so sweetly invited: “Arise, make haste, my friend, and come. For winter has now passed; the rain has gone and departed” (Cant. 2:10) [Col. 0543B]. He calls her both friend and beautiful, because she is so wounded by the love of God that no place in her lies open to an enemy’s dart. In praise of her singular excellence he himself also says: “My spotless one, and there is no stain in you” (Cant. 5:2). For although many are called friends of God, according to what the Bridegroom himself says to the apostles, “I have called you friends” (John 15:15), yet in comparison with the Lord’s Mother, to whom the angel says, “Hail, full of grace” (Luke 1:28), no faithful soul is free from stain.

“Arise, make haste”: that is, hasten to the resurrection; you, Mother, must be brought to me, your Son. By winter and rain—that is, frost and rainfall—he comprehends the whole harshness of the wintry season. The more heavily a person is burdened and unwillingly held in this life, the more secure he is concerning the life to come and the more eagerly he hastens toward it with greater longing [Col. 0543C]. But which of the faithful longed to reach the Lord, as his Mother longed to reach her Son? Therefore she regarded this life more as winter and endured it more heavily, in proportion as she more ardently yearned for the summer of heavenly serenity. Rightly, then, it is now said to her that winter has passed and the rain has gone, since, all troubles ended, she is to be assumed not to Abraham’s bosom and the refreshment of the faithful, to which poor Lazarus was brought, but to the summit of the ethereal throne.

We are not unaware that blessed Jerome, when he wrote his sermon on this Assumption, so doubted this resurrection, which, as we have said, was accomplished in the Lord’s Mother, that he said that nothing could be known with certainty on this matter [Note: [Col. 0543D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXX, col. 123.], “except that on this day she departed from the body.” But since it is written in Daniel, “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied” (Dan. 12:4); and blessed Benedict says in the Rule [Note: [Col. 0543D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXVI, col. 287.] that God often reveals to the younger what he does not reveal to the older: it could happen that what lay hidden and uncertain in Jerome’s time later became manifest through the Spirit’s revelation. And if we draw an argument from the lesser to the greater, who would dare accuse the aforesaid Gregory of falsehood for asserting that the Lord’s Mother has already been raised, when blessed Ambrose [Col. 0544A] does not hesitate to maintain the same even concerning the apostle John, the Lord’s Mother’s paranymph, as we recalled in the sermon on his feast day?

As he was about to ascend, the Lord promised his disciples that he was going to prepare a place for them. Therefore you also, virgins, or whatever women are devoted to Christ, disciples of this highest Virgin—from whom you received the teaching of a holy vocation and whom you followed by the vow of continence—have become the Lord’s temple, as it is written: “Virgins shall be brought to the King after her; her companions shall be brought to you. They shall be brought with gladness and rejoicing; they shall be brought into the temple of the King” (Ps. 44:15). So persevere in discipleship under her, that through her you may deserve to have eternal dwellings prepared for you; and may she who encouraged you toward the race by her own example bring you by her aid to the prize.

How great must be the rejoicing on earth today, and how great the exultation in heaven? How much joy is bestowed alike on angels and human beings, when she has been added above to their fellowship—the one through whom the way was opened to human beings, and through human beings the losses of the angels were restored? She is our mediatrix with her Son, just as the Son himself is with the Father. The Son could not fail to heed his Mother when she pleads for us, nor could he offend her by any refusal—he who especially commends honour toward parents. We read that the prayers of saints resist the Lord’s wrath so strongly that he cannot inflict the vengeance due. Carefully observing this, blessed Jerome, when expounding that passage of Jeremiah, “But do not pray for this people, nor ask that it may obtain mercy, and do not resist me, because [Col. 0544C] I will not hear you” (Jer. 7:16), says [Note: [Col. 0544D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIV, col. 732.]:

> “When he says, ‘and do not resist me,’ he shows that the prayer of the saints can resist the wrath of God. Thus he speaks to Moses: ‘Let me alone, that I may strike this people.’ If, then, the prayer of the saints has such power to appease the wrath of the heavenly Judge, what must be hoped from the prayer of his Mother? Sinners should have so much greater confidence in her, and she should be considered bound by a certain obligation in this matter, inasmuch as it is more generally acknowledged that she obtained the singular honour of being Mother of God only for the sake of sinners. How ready and willing she is to discharge this obligation, and how prepared to assist all who invoke her in their necessities [Col. 0544D], we have already learned from the experience of many saints. Bringing forward some of these, we shall begin with the least and proceed to the greatest, so that, when we remember that she cares for small matters, we may not doubt that she is concerned also with greater ones.”

We read that wine failed at the wedding to which her Son had come, invited with her and his disciples. When the wine failed there, the Mother of Jesus says to him: “They have no wine” (John 2:3). And Jesus says to her: “What is that to me and to you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (ibid., 4). His Mother says to the servants: “Whatever he tells you, do” (ibid., 5). And shortly afterward [Col. 0545A]: “Jesus says to them: ‘Fill the jars with water,’ etc.” (ibid., 7).

Behold, Christ’s Mother, concerned about a bodily benefit, intercedes and urges her Son to grant it; and, as though sternly rebuked by him, she did not desist until she obtained what she intended. Indeed, if we attend closely, we shall see that she did not so much ask for a favour as report the lack of wine. For when she said that the wine had failed, we do not read that she asked him to supply it; rather, she judged it enough, in order to obtain what she desired, to report what was lacking. Nor did she think her prayer now necessary with her Son, since she seemed to have intimated her wish. She had not even been asked by the wedding guests to obtain this benefit for them. What, then, will she accomplish by her intercession [Col. 0545B] when she intercedes with her Son for believers who have asked her, for the salvation of those for whose sake she recognizes that she was chosen by him and made bound to them by obligation? The holier and more righteous she is, the more clearly she is shown to be concerned with fulfilling this obligation.

This is made clear not only by reason but also by the light of examples. Writing to the Colossians, the Apostle says in one place concerning God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: “And when you were dead in transgressions, he made you alive with him, forgiving you all transgressions, blotting out the written bond of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to you; and he took it from the midst, fastening it to the cross, stripping the principalities and powers” (Col. 2:13). In this manner, therefore, the Lord’s Mother, restoring the accursed and detestable written bond to the most wretched and desperate Theophilus, then did in one man, for the consolation of many, what her Son is known to have done in the human race [Col. 0545C].

Finally, how swift and ready she is to bring aid to those who invoke her, not only against demons but even against the tyranny of earthly rulers, is attested by the destruction of the emperor Julian, which we read in the Life of blessed Basil. Therefore, the more confidently we trust in her protection and help, the more devoutly it is fitting that we take part in her festival; and that each of us, longing for her, should cry unceasingly: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Cant. 1:3). For she was drawn in order that she might draw; she was assumed in order that she might assume; she was created in order that she might save, and formed in order that she might reform [Col. 0545D].

For, so that the divine work in our restoration might be more wondrous, we were raised upright through the very things by which we fell, if we consider the natures rather than the things themselves. The devil, in the serpent, tempted our first parents through the forbidden tree; he captured man and woman, and through these four things we were condemned: the forbidden tree, the serpent persuading, Eve seduced, and Adam deceived. Through four corresponding things we were also restored. Mary believed the angel sent to her, as Eve consented to the devil; the new Adam redeemed us on the wood of the cross and repaired by the wood the damage caused by the wood; and he cured, as by a medicine, the deadly taste of the harmful fruit, taking fruits from the tree of the cross [Col. 0546A], of which he himself says: “I shall climb the palm tree and seize its fruits” (Cant. 7:8).

For what is signified by the palm tree, by which victory is denoted, except the Lord’s cross, through which he triumphed over the devil and, accomplishing our redemption upon it, completed what pertains to our salvation? Hence, as he expired, he said: “It is accomplished” (John 19:30): that is, the medicine of human salvation is complete. May he deign to heal by this medicine the diseases of our own souls—he who, declaring himself the true physician, says in one place: “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do” (Matt. 9:12). Since we are in no way sufficient to obtain this by our merits, may his Mother herself obtain it for us—she who bore him so that he might bring us this medicine [Col. 0546B]. Hence he alone is properly called the Saviour, the name which, as the Apostle says, is above every name, bestowed upon him by the Father (Eph. 1:21), with whom, God, he lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through the endless ages of ages. Amen.

## EXPOSITION OF THE GOSPEL READING FOR THE SAME DAY

“Jesus entered into a certain fortress” (Luke 10:38). A fortress is a fortification and a defensive refuge from an enemy’s attack. Jesus enters it when the Word of God assumed our nature in the Virgin, in whom he accomplished our redemption; and, triumphing over the devil, established in her a certain stronghold for us. Entering this place, he is received in Martha’s house because he was incarnate in the land of Judaea, which was intent on outward works [Col. 0546C], and was first received in faith by certain members of that people, such as Simeon, Anna, and the peoples gathered therefrom.

Mary, Martha’s sister, is the Gentile world converted—that is, the Church of the Gentiles—having one Father, God, with Martha; that is, with the faithful Synagogue which had already received Christ, when a few Jews had first been converted to Christ. Martha, having received Christ through faith, prepares a meal, while Judaea renders service to God through observance of bodily works, and, like Esau, having gone out to hunt in the wild, labours to refresh her father. Martha is troubled about many things when she strives to preserve both Law and Gospel, shadow and truth. Hence, when the Gentiles are converted, she is deeply disturbed and offended because the yoke of the Law cannot also be imposed upon them; for this reason, murmuring as it were, she asks the Lord to join Mary with her in all things—namely, when that primitive Jewish Church asks the apostles, Christ’s vicars, to compel the Gentiles also to become Jews.

But while Martha persists in labouring at work and goes out to external matters, Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, and, with the Law now buried, cleaving to Christ alone, like Jacob prepares from domestic animals the more inward and better refreshment, according to the Psalmist’s words: “In me, O God, are your vows, which I shall render to you—praises” (Ps. 55:12). How attentively she fixes her mind upon Christ is shown when it is said that she heard his word [Col. 0547A], and sat beside his feet, not at a distance.

For just as, in the one person of Christ, his divinity, which is the higher nature, is compared to the head, so his humanity is understood through the feet. Cleaving to these feet as though by sitting there, she hears Christ’s word rather than Moses’, following the Gospel rather than the Law; she embraces his humanity with faith so firm that she does not doubt that this one sacrifice of his is sufficient for salvation, and thinks that no sacrifice of the Law will henceforth be necessary. Hence it is added: “One thing is necessary” (Luke 10:42), because “when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13:10). That is, when truth arrives, the shadow withdraws; and when Gospel perfection comes, the beginning of the Law ceases. Mary’s best part [Col. 0547B] is understood as the truth which she chose, the shadow being rejected. It shall not be taken from her, because the Gospel commandments shall not come to an end, as those belonging to the Law were taken from Martha; for, when the Jews were converted, legal observances were forbidden, as Paul says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2).

## SERMON XXVII. ON THE DAY OF SAINT MARCELLINUS, POPE AND MARTYR, TO THE MONKS OF ROUEN WHO POSSESS HIS RELICS

Heavenly mercy, brothers, providing from its omnipotence for all its members, guards the strong from presumption just as it guards the weak from despair. Therefore, first setting himself forth as an example in both respects, Christ now avoids persecution and hides himself; now, when the moment of his Passion is at hand, he is written to have been so greatly afraid and distressed that, entering into agony, he shed drops like blood as sweat, contrary to human nature, and, repeatedly praying to the Father, asked that the cup of his Passion might pass from him, if possible. He even deigned so completely to take weak members into himself that he said: “Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour” (John 12:27). As though he said: Grant me steadfastness in the Passion, lest fear prevail over human weakness.

Why, brothers, did Christ say this, though secure in all things and able to be overcome by no fear of suffering, by no torment of pain? [Col. 0547D] He intended by these words, brothers, to comfort our weakness, not to display any feebleness that he had. In all these matters he was providing for us, not for himself, lest perhaps, if believers should tremble at the time of suffering or shrink from it, struck by despair and doubting forgiveness, they should say that they had no part in Christ. Against this wound of despair he set before the weak not only Thomas’s doubt but also Peter’s threefold denial, and from it prepared a most healing poultice.

Finally, the Lord permitted our Marcellinus, blessed Peter’s vicar, in whose time frequent persecutions terrified many and even compelled some to deny the faith, to waver for an hour and to fall for a time, yet not to be shattered, as it is written: “When the righteous man falls, he shall not be dashed down, because the Lord supports him with his hand” (Ps. 36:24) [Col. 0548A].

Peter denied him three times; nor did he simply deny him, but, as it is written: “He began to curse and to swear that he did not know the man” (Matt. 26:74). What Matthew calls “to curse,” Mark—the disciple of Peter himself, instructed by him in writing the Gospel—calls “to anathematize” (Mark 14:71), that is, to submit oneself to excommunication, though others awaited absolution from him. Nor does Matthew mention an oath only in one denial of Peter; rather, attaching graver offences to lighter ones, he first says that Peter denied him, then that he did so with an oath, and finally with both cursing and an oath.

But of Marcellinus we know neither oath nor cursing nor anathematizing, and we do not even read the words of his denial. Rather, he is described as having been beside himself through fear of death and not permitted to deliberate upon anything. We have heard only that he placed incense in sacrifice to an idol; nor did he tolerate this transgression, but immediately, having summoned bishops, pronounced upon himself a sentence of deposition. Peter, by contrast, did not make such satisfaction for his threefold denial; nor do we read that he even came to confession or received any satisfaction for it [Col. 0548B].

And if after Peter we compare Marcellinus also with Paul, Peter’s supreme fellow apostle, we shall judge Marcellinus’s fault in this transgression to be very slight. For we read that Paul, according to the rite of the Law—whose bodily observances he most strongly opposed—was compelled by the Jews to consecrate himself to God in the manner of the Nazirite; and that he also handed over his disciple Timothy to them for circumcision. Yet he judged circumcision so superfluous or dangerous that he said: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2); and generally concerning observances of the Law: “You who are justified in the Law,” he says, “have fallen away from grace” (ibid., 4) [Col. 0548C].

The Lord foretold Peter, who was to deny him, that he would deny him; but Peter, promising his own steadfastness, made still greater promises to the contrary, and, preferring himself to all others, said: “Even if all are scandalized, yet not I” (Matt. 26:33). And again: “I am ready to go with you both to death and to prison” (Luke 22:33) [Col. 0548D]. The greater the presumption of his promise had been, the more blameworthy was Peter’s fall, and the graver was his lapse, because his profession had been greater in opposition to it. No one had forewarned Marcellinus about the transgression that occurred; he had not been forestalled by anyone’s exhortation not to undertake it. Peter was found false in his promise as in his denial—not in one denial only, as has been said, but three; and not a simple denial, but one accompanied by the curse of anathematization.

Though Peter repented, he nevertheless deferred his Passion for a long time. Finally, fleeing it, as it is written, he was compelled, as though unwilling, to return by the Lord who met him, according to what the Lord foretold him: “When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish” (John 21:18) [Col. 0549A]. Your fraternity knows that it is written: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises” (Prov. 24:16), as though it plainly said: Although a faithful person, assailed by repeated temptations, should be conquered and succumb to the seven principal vices, nevertheless, not deprived of divine aid, he emerges from so deep an abyss of vices, having obtained from the Lord that petition: “Let not the flood of waters overwhelm me, nor let the deep swallow me, nor let the pit press its mouth over me” (Ps. 68:16).

Peter denied three times; the righteous man falls seven times. Marcellinus wavered once rather than fell—he who rose so swiftly and at once expiated his wavering, not so much by tears of repentance, as Peter did, as by the courage of an intrepid Passion [Col. 0549B]. Of this perfection of virtue the Lord says: “No one has greater love than this,” etc. (John 15:13).

We know, brothers, that, by the ordering of divine grace, men outstanding in virtues have sometimes endured great falls into sins, yet for the harmony of humility and the care of providence . . . while the Lord thus comforts us through the Psalmist against the madness of despair: “Will one who sleeps not add that he may rise again?” (ibid. 5:14). For who is asleep except one sluggish in action, benumbed through negligence, and failing for a time? Exhorting such people, the Apostle says: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead,” etc. (Luke 22:34).

Behold Peter, first called Simon, later named by Christ Peter, the Rock—that is, firm from steadfastness—to whom the Lord also said: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have at last turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Ps. 40:9) [Col. 0549C]. Having fallen three times only in speech, not in mind, he denies Christ. Behold Marcellinus, Peter’s successor and his vicar alike in weakness’s trembling and afterward in courage: he slips once, wavering but not failing, immediately regaining strength. They were set as examples for those over whom they presided, so that they might not despair because of any lapse whatever. The Lord told Peter, although he would deny him, that he should strengthen his brothers.

We know also that Marcellinus sent the Theban Legion, strengthened by him in the faith, ahead to heaven. His disciple Marcellus, likewise pope and martyr and his successor, confirmed his master’s holy end; and the Theban Legion confirmed his preceding life, so that both the earlier and the later testimony worthy of praise may remove every uncertainty or despair concerning the intervening event [Col. 0549D]. Just as the Lord set these men before the clergy, so he set David and Solomon before the people, that by their grievous fall they might console those who had committed sins [lacuna], lest, after crimes however great, they despair of pardon.

That greatest of kings and prophets, David—adulterer, betrayer, and murderer together—the more he had grown in virtues, fell from the summit of virtues into a greater precipice. For the higher the rank, the graver the fall. Solomon, that Jedidiah, that is, “beloved of the Lord,” of whom the Lord also foretold: “I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me” (2 Sam. 7:14), fell so far into the pit of abominations that, conquered by the lust of the flesh, he utterly abandoned divine worship and served idols for so long a time that even the idols’ high places were not removed [Col. 0550A]. And he did this not through fear of death, but through desire for a woman. Yet lest we despair of his pardon, the Lord himself also comforts us. For after saying beforehand what was quoted—“I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me”—he immediately added: “If he does anything wicked, I shall chastise him with the rod of men and with the stripes of the sons of men. Nevertheless I shall not take away my mercy from him, as I took it away from Saul, whom I removed from before my face” (2 Sam. 7:14).

For what is God’s face but knowledge of him, just as every human being is known by his or her face? What, then, does it mean for God to bestow mercy on someone in such a way that he does not remove that person from before his face, except to reserve for that person the grace that, when through sin that person has, as it were, forgotten the Creator through negligence, he or she may afterward return through repentance, recognize him, and correct sins both through fear of the strict Judge and through love for the Lord who awaits them? [Col. 0550B]

Rightly, therefore, he set before us two rulers among the clergy and two among the laity: there Peter and Marcellinus; here David and Solomon. He did so against that supreme ruin of despair, lest anyone, whether among clergy or people, despair of pardon after crimes however great, provided that one looks ahead to repentance [Col. 0550C]. Rightly, I say, he set two here and two there as witnesses of reconciliation to be hoped for and pardon to be obtained. For, as it is written, however illustrious a person may be, one witness is not enough; but according to the divine Law: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. 19:15). If this is true in speech, how much more in action?

But, brothers, to bring the end of our sermon to the divine mercy shown toward us, consider, I ask you, how greatly the Lord has provided for our salvation and how concerned our Saviour is for us—the one after whose name this place has also been named. In many ways, brothers, we offend; into many falls we descend. But lest we despair [Col. 0550D], lest we defer correction, the Lord has sent us his great martyr and our patron, setting him before us as an example. We have him as an advocate with God, and especially in him, if we wish, we have grounds for confidence. This chief man was appointed by the Lord, as has been said, to be tested and to fall grievously, so that, from the great authority he received, he might have greater power; and, from the fall he endured, he might become readier to seek pardon and forgiveness for the fallen. Like the Father, of whom this is said, he learned in himself how he ought to sympathize with and have mercy upon the weakness of others. Therefore let us celebrate his feast with such devotion that we may obtain through his merits what we cannot obtain by our own prayers, through the favour of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom is, etc.

## SERMON XXVIII. ON THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH

[Col. 0551A]

How greatly the solemnity of a dedication surpasses all others is declared not so much by the authority of Scripture as by evident reason. For from it the beginning of all other solemnities flows, since in it the place is consecrated in which the others are celebrated and the Lord’s sacraments are performed. This is the place which the Lord, specially choosing for himself and distinguishing by the title of his own house, said through Moses: “Take care not to offer your burnt offerings in every place, but where there shall be remembrance of my name” (Deut. 12:13). And again: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21:13).

The celebrations of the other feasts [Col. 0551B], which the Lord instituted for the ancient people as especially important, did not exceed seven days. But Solomon and all Israel completed the dedication of the Temple over twice seven days, with innumerable burnt offerings and manifold accompaniment from musical instruments.

From this it is clear with what dignity and authority this celebration is endowed, and with what devotion it should be performed by all. Its institution had its beginning not from the Law, not from a prophet, but from the patriarch Jacob. He is said both to have marked out the future site of the Temple and to have first displayed the sacraments of dedication, as the history of Genesis recounts. For when he had left his parents’ home and was travelling in exile to avoid the persecution of his elder brother, he arrived at a certain place in the evening and wished to rest there. He took one of the stones lying on the ground, placed it beneath his head, and fell asleep. In a dream he saw a ladder standing upon the earth, its summit touching heaven. He also saw angels ascending and descending on it, and the Lord leaning upon the ladder and saying to him: “The land on which you sleep I shall give to you and to your seed” (Gen. 28:13) [Col. 0551C].

When Jacob awoke, he said: “How terrible is this place! This is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (ibid., 17). Rising in the morning, he took the stone which he had placed under his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil over it. He also made a vow, saying: “If God shall be with me and guard me, I shall offer to you tithes of all that you give me” (ibid., 20) [Col. 0551D].

Behold, brothers, we have briefly run through the history. Let us now seek in it chiefly a moral understanding for our edification, and disclose in these actions the figure of a better dedication. For what is the dedication of the Church except that pledge of a faithful soul which, departing from the world, dedicates itself wholly to God and, as it were, joins itself to Christ as his own bride, so that it may thereafter be wholly occupied with him, and thus, binding itself to him by the vow of its profession, consecrates itself to God as his own temple?

For just as in a single town there are many houses of people and one house of God, which we call a church, so in the people of God, among those who are married [Col. 0552A], any soul consecrated to God by an appropriate vow has become his own dwelling. Describing such a soul and distinguishing its prerogative from others, the Apostle says: “One without a wife is concerned with the things of the Lord, how to please God. But one with a wife is concerned with the things of the world, how to please his wife, and is divided. An unmarried woman and a virgin think about the things of the Lord, that they may be holy both in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 7:32–33).

Jacob, therefore, fleeing, as has been said, the persecution of his elder brother, leaving his parents’ home and travelling in exile, represents the faithful soul converted from the world to the Lord. Having broken the bonds of carnal affections, after the manner of Abraham it goes forth from its own land and kindred [Col. 0552B], and leaves its parents’ home for the cloister. It not only hears but obeys the Psalmist’s words: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline,” etc. (Ps. 44:11); and it also embraces the Lord’s teaching: “Whoever does not hate father and mother is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37).

The elder brother of such a soul is the flesh, joined with the soul into one person and formed in the womb before the soul is infused into it. When, departing from the world, we flee the temptations of this flesh—of which it is written, “The flesh lusts against the spirit” (Gal. 5:17)—we avoid, as it were, the attack of the elder brother. And because this virtue of continence and this renunciation of the world began most especially from Christ’s coming, which is the world’s last age [Col. 0552C], Jacob arrived at the place where he might sleep and rest after sunset, that is, in the evening.

This place is the cloistered life of the continent, who pass from the tumultuous life of the world into monastic quiet, and prefer Mary’s tranquillity to Martha, anxious and troubled about many things. This tranquillity is denoted by the Lord by the name of a bed, and by the Bride in the Song by the name of a couch, when it is said: “That night two shall be in one bed. On my couch by night,” etc. (Cant. 3:1).

In this bed, therefore, Jacob, about to sleep, chooses one stone from among those he sees and, placing it beneath his head, sleeps. So when any soul has entered the place of a holy community, it looks around upon many faithful persons [Col. 0552D] as living stones, strong to endure all things, founded upon Christ, the chief stone, so that it may be formed toward perfection by their examples. But because it prefers the one Christ to all others—to whom the faithful soul joins and dedicates itself as a bride—and, as though in his embraces, sleeps in the bed of contemplation bodily while keeping watch in mind, according to the Bride’s words, “I sleep, but my heart keeps watch” (Song 5:2), one stone is chosen from among all. Accordingly, he himself says of his beloved: “Chosen from among thousands” (ibid., 10). It places him beneath its head in order to sleep when it fixes the whole intention of its mind upon him, so as to rest entirely from worldly cares and cleave wholly to him in longing. For the head, the governing part of the body, signifies in us the mind.

That beloved disciple of the Lord, John the virgin, especially expressed this sleep of the continent [Col. 0553A] when, reclining upon God’s breast, he fell asleep as though this stone had been placed beneath his head. Jacob, while sleeping, beholds a ladder, because each person understands sacred Scripture more fully in proportion as he rests more from the distractions of worldly cares. This ladder, placed beside the sleeper, reaches to heaven, because through its teaching we are raised from earthly things to desire heavenly ones; and in mind we climb there, where Christ sits at the right hand of God. The Lord leans upon this ladder and speaks to us from it, because through its teaching he is impressed upon our minds, and, instructing our minds through his words to turn toward himself, kindles them.

The two sides, as it were, of this ladder—that is, of sacred Scripture—are the two Testaments. [Col. 0553B] They are joined to one another as though by inserted rungs, while, through the expositions of teachers, wheel is fitted to wheel, and what was foretold in the Old Testament is shown to have been fulfilled in the New. The angels ascending and descending by this ladder are holy preachers, one of whom says concerning himself and the others: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10:15). Of such persons Malachi also says: “The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7). They ascend or descend this ladder when, in their preaching, they instruct us now concerning the nature of divinity or heavenly mysteries, now concerning the assumed humanity or the reform of our conduct; or when they exhort us now to the lofty virtue of continence, [Col. 0553C] now provide for our weakness through allowance for marriage.

The Lord promises Jacob and his seed the land in which he sleeps, because he promises, as a reward, the land of the living—whose desire causes the contemplative soul to rest from earthly cares—both to him and to his followers, those who imitate him in this purpose. That soul, awakening from the sleep of contemplation and turning the eyes of its entire contemplation from that heavenly dwelling back toward holy pursuits, says, as though at the same time admonishing others to persevere in their purpose through hope of the promised land: “Truly the Lord is in this place, and I did not know it” (Gen. 28:16). As though it said: He who is everywhere by the presence of his divinity [Col. 0553D] dwells here in a special manner by grace. And, trembling, it says: “How terrible is this place!” (ibid., 17). It recognizes it as terrible—that is, worthy of the highest reverence—in which, as has been said, God dwells as in a spiritual temple wholly dedicated to him, through the gifts of more abundant grace.

But because many recognize that such reverence is owed to this place, yet do not render it, nor fear the Apostle’s threat, “If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:17), “trembling” was rightly stated beforehand, so that one who does not doubt that it ought to be feared may not presume to offend within it. Notice that when he had first said, “the house of God,” he immediately added, “and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:17). Such a place is an entrance to the heavenly kingdom, from which one passes there without delay from the observance of this life, with no intervening purification. [Col. 0554A]

Jacob rises in the morning and sets up as a pillar the stone he had placed beneath his head; pouring oil upon it from above, he fulfills, in the manner of a high priest, the vow of dedication—as though thereby exercising the dignity of the firstborn which he had bought. For the birthright at that time is said to have been the priestly garment or dignity, which firstborn brothers received by paternal blessing, so that they alone among their brothers performed the priestly office. Jacob is also remembered as having been clothed by his mother in Esau’s very fine garments.

Observe: just as Melchizedek’s sacraments of the Church seem older than those of the Synagogue, so in the patriarch Jacob our rite of dedication seems to have come first, because [Col. 0554B] we consecrate with oil both the altar and the church itself. We do not read that this was done in either the tabernacle or the temple. Jacob rises in the morning from the place where, resting, he had seen the vision and had learned the holiness of that place, when any such soul as has been described, after the time of its testing has now passed, advances to profession under the rule, having already experienced the religious character both of this purpose and of the place. Then, dedicating itself wholly to God and binding itself to him by its own vow, it celebrates within itself the dedication of a spiritual temple.

Then it raises as a pillar the stone upon which it had slept—that is, it fixes it before its eyes as a sign, as though it ought henceforth to behold nothing else. For after profession it is not permitted to look back, lest it perish with Lot’s wife. Yet at first the stone lay low, because it had not previously clung to it with so binding a duty. [Col. 0554C] It consecrates the upright stone by pouring oil over it, while, embracing Christ with all the affection of love, it anoints him with as many ointments as it embraces him with desires. What are ointments but a certain refreshment of pains and a soothing remedy for those in pain? Christ suffers on our account when our worldly manner of life displeases him and, by thus provoking him, we stir him against us through evil deeds. But he is fully appeased, and his pain is soothed as though by certain ointments, when, withdrawing from the world, we cling to him with our whole hearts and now unite ourselves wholly to him through perfection of virtue, according to the Apostle’s words: “But he who cleaves to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

Jacob, however, prudently [Col. 0554D] and carefully makes a vow to pay tithes, trusting not in his own strength but in God’s mercy. As though adding a condition, he says: “If God shall be with me and shall keep me” (Gen. 28:20), because whatever good we do is by his grace. Hence Paul also says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10). And again, after saying, “I have labored more than all,” he immediately adds: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (ibid.). The person who observes the Decalogue and transgresses it in no respect, nor departs in any way from God’s commandments understood through that Decalogue, pays God tithes of all things.

May the supreme high priest and king, Jesus Christ, whose priesthood and kingdom endure unto ages of ages, grant us so to fulfill this in ourselves that he may deign, by invisibly working within us in the bodily temple, to make us more truly a temple [Col. 0555A] through what was outwardly performed in visible sacraments. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX. ON HOLY SUSANNA, AS AN EXHORTATION TO VIRGINS

You have heard, dearest sisters—and would that you had also heeded—the blessed concern of the Bride in the Song of Songs, carefully set forth for your exhortation. Since she could not find in her bed the Beloved whom she had long sought, she says: “I will arise and go about the city; through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:2). She seeks the Beloved in the bed and does not find him when a perfect soul, joined to foolish virgins, considers their works and desires to be instructed by their examples, believing them to possess great perfection of virtues through bodily continence. For since even this continence of the flesh and the observance of so arduous a purpose belong to few, the life of such persons, removed from the tumult of the world, is compared rather to a couch (*lectulus*) than to a bed (*lectus*), because it is a great repose to be free from the burdens of marriage and not to devote oneself to pleasures of the flesh.

But because the uninstructed do not regard this continence, which belongs to few, as anything great, and simplicity is therefore easily drawn by self-regard into pride, Christ cannot be found in such persons: he always resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5:5). Seeing this, the Bride rises, as it were, from the couch; and, going out, goes around the city, seeking there through lanes and streets the Bridegroom [Col. 0555C] whom she could not find in the couch. That is, going out in mind, she considers the good life of the faithful who live in this world as in a city that holds many people, and from them takes examples of virtues to imitate, in whom she does not despair that he dwells by the Lord’s grace.

Since, however, in every rank of the faithful some are more perfect than others, she finds some in the streets and some in the lanes. For the higher certain people’s life is in merits, the fewer are those among whom they live—like those who remain in lanes, which are narrower than streets. Such, we read, were Job and Susanna, and many others, who have been set forth as examples to both men and women because of their great perfection of virtues. Their life was so much the more praiseworthy as it was more religious amid worldly life and, like the purest gold in a furnace, did not burn. [Col. 0555D]

Because I judge it superfluous now to write to you concerning Job’s virtues, which Scripture diligently recounts, I turn my pen to Susanna, a married woman, who was of a . . . purpose lesser than yours and of greater virtue, so that, in comparison with her, any women of sacred profession who possess less than they ought may blush for their deficiency. Her first praise is described when Scripture records that she was very beautiful and feared the Lord (Dan. 13:2). It rises from bodily beauty to beauty of mind, according to Gregory’s saying: “Each person begins with the least things in order to reach greater ones.” [Col. 0556A] Beautiful in body, but more beautiful in mind, she guarded these two things together all the more praiseworthily because it was more difficult to guard them. In one she had material for battle; from the other she received the crown of victory.

Because of her beauty the priests burned with desire for her, so that she might be tested by the steadfastness of her virtue. When condemned to death, she chose the peril of life rather than incur the defilement of her body; and she offered as an immaculate sacrifice that very body which was sought for sin. Alas for grief! Alas for shame! We see so many women established in sacred profession so ugly that, as Scripture says, they have no need of a mask, yet, utterly forgetful of divine reverence and their own vow, they are so driven by the fury of lust that, when they cannot obtain men freely for the commission of shamefulness, they are compelled to purchase incestuous partners. Those who trust in their beauty prostitute themselves for payment; or, if they distrust payment, they make for themselves their wage out of the very filth of lust which they receive. [Col. 0556B]

Both secular and divine laws have judged adulteresses worthy of death. How great a punishment must be inflicted upon corrupted brides of Christ may be understood from the fact that the canons have scarcely left even a place for repentance to them. Among them there are also certain old prostitutes who, when they realize that they are now wholly despised, practice detestable pimping by selling others’ bodies when they cannot sell their own. Of such women I recall having written somewhere: “The old prostitute propagates herself in young women.”

How severe a judgment the holy Fathers established concerning female pimps is clear from their writings: they deprived them even at the end of life of communion. Hence Canon 11 of the Council of Elvira states: “If a mother, parent, or any believing woman practices pimping because she has sold another’s body or her own, it has been decided that she is not to be admitted to communion even at the end.” [Col. 0556C] If they so detested pimping in women of the world, how abhorrent must it be in brides of Christ, where God’s own temple is violated and this punishment is specially reserved for him? “If anyone,” says the Apostle, “violates God’s temple, God will destroy him” (1 Cor. 3:17).

The blessed woman just mentioned, a laywoman and woman of the world rather than of the cloister, to be called the wife of a man rather than the bride of Christ, will rise in judgment and condemn this most wicked generation. [Col. 0556D] To preserve faithfulness to a man, she chose to perish undefiled rather than live defiled. The source of her burning zeal for chastity and her fortification by so great a wall of constancy is added in the words: “Her parents, being righteous, instructed their daughter according to the law of Moses” (Dan. 13:3). A most righteous daughter is remembered as born of righteous parents, and in their shared praise their most holy studies are proclaimed.

Blessed Jerome carefully noted this, and when he came to this passage in his exposition of Daniel, he said [Note: [Col. 0555D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXV, col. 580]: “This testimony must be used to exhort parents to teach, according to the law of the Lord and the divine word, not only their sons but also [Col. 0557A] their daughters.” Even in the darkness of its blindness, the Jewish people, still burning intensely with zeal for sacred letters, strongly rebukes our negligence—that is, the negligence of Christians. They embrace the Law with such ardor that however poor any one of them may be, and however many children he has, he allows none of them to remain ignorant of divine letters.

The Apostle, deeply sympathizing with their zeal, says: “Brothers, the desire indeed of my heart and my prayer to God for them is for salvation. For I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:1)—that is, great fervor toward God and a desire to know and fulfill the commandments which they received in the Law, though they persist in great error, believing these things sufficient for salvation. For *aemulatio*, or zeal, denotes any vehement fervor of mind toward the desire for something. Thus zeal, whether good or evil, is called a vehement stirring and concern of mind for doing something.

But there are none, or few, among Christians who embrace the perfection of evangelical teaching with such zeal or for such a purpose as to ensure that their children are instructed in sacred letters out of desire for it. Rather, they do so only for temporal advantage, to provide for themselves or their children the necessities of this life, either through clerical offices or through the monastic habit. Therefore Susanna’s parents are rightly distinguished from the purpose of such fathers, when it is said both in their praise and in that of Susanna herself that her parents, “being righteous, instructed [Col. 0557C] their daughter,” and so forth. “Being righteous” was said, not “being greedy”; for what these people now do through greed, those parents did through religion, and through love of God rather than worldly ambition, as though heeding what is written: “Blessed is the man whom you instruct, O Lord, and teach him from your law” (Ps. 93 [94]:12). The sequel of this history proclaims that they were not at all disappointed in this hope, describing such great perfection in their daughter, which the preceding words indicate had resulted from instruction in the divine law; indeed, it is for this reason that those words were recalled.

Consider, virgins, the kind of battle in which that remarkable matron won so remarkable a triumph, that from her you may learn [Col. 0557D] how you yourselves ought to fight and preserve the vow of your espousal to Christ, as she preserved faithfulness to her husband. The elders seized her, therefore, and attempted to compel her consent to adultery. “Look,” they say, “the gates of the garden are closed, and no one sees us. Therefore consent to us and lie with us. But if you refuse, we shall bear witness against you that a young man was with you, and that for this reason you sent the maidservants away from you” (Dan. 13:20–21).

O blind guides of the blind, and judges ignorant of justice: if the gates of the garden are shut, is not the gate of heaven open? In vain do you flee the sight of men, since you cannot flee the sight of God. She gave special heed to this when she said: “It is better for me to fall into your hands without doing the deed than to sin in the sight of the Lord” (ibid., 23). [Col. 0558A] “No one,” you say, “sees us.” What if God does? Are you ashamed to be caught by a man and not ashamed to be seen by God? Do you fear a temporal bodily death if caught by men, but not the everlasting death of the soul, in comparison with which she declares that even the other should not be called death? For she says: “If I do this, it is death to me; but if I do not do it, I shall not escape your hands” (ibid., 22). She judged the death of the soul rather than that of the body to deserve the name of death; and because she feared that death more, she deserved to escape both together. You, on the contrary, fearing this one more than the other, were immune from neither. She feared God as judge more than man and was freed by both divine and human judgment; you yourselves, as judges, could escape neither.

[Col. 0558B] Consider, brides of Christ, what the wife of a man said and did. If any profane person, wholly forgetful of God, demands like shamefulness from you and perhaps persists so far as to presume to use force, look to your husband—not a man but God, not Joachim but Christ—and, each of you an undaunted Susanna, say: “If I do this, it is death to me.” A wife’s fornication could have remained hidden from Joachim; but who can remain hidden from your Bridegroom? He himself, his glorious Mother, and the whole court of heaven together will behold from above the injury done to him. What woman could be so shameless, so mad, as not to blush and tremble especially before this gaze?

When some Christian falsely so called seeks—or rather seeks to entrap—you concerning this matter, one answer will immediately suffice to free you: “I will consent to you in this, if it can be done without my Bridegroom’s knowledge, or if we shall be stronger than he, so that we may fear his offense less.” Finally, when the shameless elders pressed her and Susanna could not repel them by force, using her mouth in place of hands, she checked their assault by the one means remaining, saying . . . Consider, virgins, the virtue of a married woman, and reason from greater things to lesser. You do not fear danger of death if you repel incestuous men from yourselves, as she did, as we have said. Their force is not so great that you must be compelled to free yourselves from them by shouting. Or if it is necessary to cry out, your Bridegroom will hear you more readily than Susanna’s husband heard her [Col. 0558D] and, because he has greater power, will free you more swiftly.

Go out from the couch in mind, therefore, and seek Susanna in the lane, so that you may find in the world the virtues which you do not find in the cloister. See what she did when seized in private and what she did when accused in public. Since we have already spoken of one part of her contest, let us briefly touch upon what remains. She is brought, as has been said, to judgment with her parents, children, and all her relatives. “Her own people and all who knew her wept. Then the two elders arose in the midst of the people and laid their hands upon her head. Weeping, she looked toward heaven, for her heart had confidence in the Lord. And the elders said: ‘While we were walking alone in the garden’” (Dan. 13:33), and so forth. [Col. 0559A]

You too, devout virgins, follow with devout tears this innocent matron as she endures so great an injury, so that the greater your compassion, the more joyful may be the innocent woman’s deliverance. Not only her own people wept, but all who knew her—not all who had heard her praise, which could have escaped none or few, but those who had experienced the truth of the matter by many proofs. That most holy matron is dragged into the midst, and an innocent woman is made to stand as a criminal. Her husband was distressed, as were her parents, children, all who knew her; who could recount or even think, without weeping, with what shame they were confounded and with what tears they lamented her innocence?

The elders alone, forgetful alike of nature and humanity, dared rise up for her judgment—or rather for their own—and, laying their unclean hands upon her holy head, were about to give testimony of accusation against her: “While we were walking,” they say, “alone in the garden,” and so forth. You rightly say, I say, “we were walking,” and “alone”: driven by the goads of lust, you had already become estranged alike from God and from the Law. [Col. 0559B]

When it has been said, “Rising in the midst of the people, they laid their hands upon her head,” it is well that the following is immediately added: “Weeping, she looked toward heaven, for her heart had confidence in the Lord.” [Col. 0559C] Why is it that until then, though her own people were weeping for her, she is not said to have wept, but only when the shameless hands touched her most chaste head? Did she then first, or chiefly, fear for the danger to her life? Lest we suppose this, there is immediately added: “For her heart had confidence in the Lord.” Though she had earlier said, “If I do not do it, I shall not escape your hands,” and later says, “Behold, I die, though I have done none of these things” (Dan. 13:43), yet, confident and secure concerning the salvation of her soul and the glory of the palm, she was in no way saddened by temporal death, through which she knew she would pass to the joys of everlasting life. Thus she is well remembered as looking toward heaven, to which her intention was borne with her whole desire.

Why then did she weep only when those men placed their hands upon her head, rather than when she was led to death, except because she who did not fear death grieved that her head was touched by obscene hands, when she had not consented that even the lower parts of her body should be touched by them? [Col. 0559D] Hear and understand this, consecrated virgins, who have consecrated your own bodies also as God’s own temples, so that you may permit them to be defiled by no touch of wantonness and violated by no sacrilege of uncleanness. “If a man sins against a man,” Samuel says, “God can be appeased for him; but if he sins against God, who shall pray for him?” (1 Sam. 2:25). Susanna feared that she would sin against her husband if she allowed her body, dedicated to him, to be touched by any touch of wantonness. What then must a bride of Christ do when an incestuous man approaches her, prepared to inflict the greatest injury upon God if he presumes to bring any contagion of wantonness upon this temple belonging to him? To what judge is such a great injury reserved for vengeance, if not the highest; to whom, if not to him to whom it properly belongs? [Col. 0560A]

Indeed, it is he who, chiefly exhorting us to fear him, says: “Do not fear those who kill the body and have nothing more they can do to the soul; but rather fear him who has power to destroy body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28). It is as though he openly said: Their assault is not especially to be feared, which is only upon one and the lesser part of us, namely the body, and quickly passes away; but especially that assault which rages forever against both parts. Considering this, the Apostle groans and says: “It is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10:31). If divine law has judged women who defiled the marriage-bed punishable by death, what awaits those who have prostituted God’s own temple? Did it prejudice those who sinned less, if it expiated greater crimes and the stains of their own marriage-bed by a lesser punishment?
