[Col. 0560B] It is certain, as the Apostle mentioned above says, that God does not dwell in temples made with hands, but rather in those who are properly called his true spiritual temples. To certain such persons he says: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone violates God’s temple, God will destroy him. God’s temple is holy, and that temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:16–17). Who, seeing any bodily filth inside the walls of a material temple, would not hasten immediately to remove it? Who would not shrink from committing fornication therein, and tremble all the more at defiling that true temple of the soul?

[Col. 0560C] Susanna wept, as has been said, and the reason for her weeping has now in part been explained: namely, the touch of the obscene hands, which she could not endure even for an hour. She wept over the present matter; and, if we attend more carefully, she wept not only over bodily contact but also over the future injury to her reputation, since those men were about to break forth in testimony—testimony to which, she foresaw, much credence would be given. So Scripture later records: “The multitude believed them as elders of the people and judges, and they condemned her to death” (Dan. 13:41). She wept over the disgrace of her household, and lamented not so much her own disaster as the distress of her people. For what indeed? What, I say? She saw her household around her—her husband, parents, children, relatives, as has been said, and all who knew her—placed in the utmost anxiety and lamenting both her innocence [Col. 0560D] and their own dishonor. She grieved more over their suffering than her own; she wept not so much for bodily death as for the stain upon her reputation.

For the more chaste a woman is, the more modest she is known to be; and this is the chief proof of chastity. Thus, rightly, both in fact and in name, shame (*pudor*) and chastity (*pudicitia*) are so connected that chastity itself is frequently denoted by the term *pudor*, which, as has been said, is its principal sign and proof. The Apostle carefully observed this when, describing women’s honorable dress, he first chose for their praise that by which he judged them most highly praised: “Women in becoming apparel, with modesty and sobriety” (1 Tim. 2:9), and so forth. Conversely [Col. 0561A] it is written: “You have acquired the forehead of a harlot; you refused to blush” (Jer. 3:3).

Alas! What do we now know or hear among those who lie to God by their holy clothing? Not only do they incur bodily shamefulness, but they do not even shrink from the mark of infamy. They deem it glory itself that, dishonoring Christ, they are proclaimed the mistresses of men—or rather the detestable whores of demons. If they sometimes receive small gifts from them, forgetful both of Christ and of their own pitiable death, they dare display their own pitiable death to those very persons, with utter disgrace to themselves, as though they did not value themselves cheaply when they can sell themselves to certain men; though perhaps they will give more than they receive. For they find few buyers and see more loss than gain. Merchandise that is less sought after is more easily displayed to all, and, once publicly exposed, is more quickly obtained. [Col. 0561B]

But to return to the subject [the text reads *a proposito* for *ad propositum*], and to return from the utmost disgrace done to Christ to praise of a secular woman: when the people had believed the false testimony of the elders and condemned her to death, she cried out with a loud voice and said: “Eternal God, knower of hidden things, who know all things before they come to pass, you know that they have borne false witness against me; and behold, I die, though I have done none of these things” (Dan. 13:43).

When she was first placed on trial and they were testifying in accusation against her, she is said not to speak but to weep and look toward heaven, so that her patience might first be tested—the patience which the prophet foretold in Christ in these words: [Col. 0561C] “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7). There she silently awaited the sentence of her condemnation; silent before men, she spoke by tears to God alone. But now, after receiving the sentence of condemnation, she declared her innocence not to excuse herself or secure release, but choosing to provide for her reputation rather than her life, and to make her people at least less anxious over her death because they might not doubt that she was passing to a happier life.

For the final confession of those condemned is a most certain testimony either of innocence or of guilt, especially when they despair that anything they say can now benefit them among men. The more they tremble at drawing near to divine judgment, the more earnestly they are concerned to preserve truth. It is well said that she cried out with a loud voice—not one that merely touched human ears, but one that came more perfectly to the most merciful ears of God and filled heaven rather than earth. [Col. 0561D] The result immediately following shows this, when it is said: “And the Lord heard her voice” (Dan. 13:44).

What voice of hers, I ask, did he hear—or rather, as you have heard, heed? For what did she pray, so as to deserve to be heard? “You, Lord,” she says, “know all things before they come to pass; you know how falsely they have testified against me.” Did she add in prayer that she should be freed from a penalty which she had not deserved by guilt? By no means. She had resolved not to ask this, since she regarded herself as passing to life rather than dying, and cared not so much to avert death as to avert disgrace, [Col. 0562A] providing rather for her people than for herself.

But the Lord, to whom conscience speaks more than the tongue, did not delay to free her not only from disgrace but even from death. He heard her voice by proving the truth of her confession through certain indications. Thus it is added: “When she was being led to death, God stirred up the holy spirit of a younger boy whose name was Daniel” (ibid., 45). He stirred up, he says, the spirit rather than the body, when he wonderfully raised the younger boy beyond his age, so that the Holy Spirit, who was already in him through grace, might be recognized through the efficacy of prophecy; and so that, through a virgin boy as defender of chastity, the shameless elders might be tried and condemned. From this stirring of the spirit for the defense, as has been said, of the chaste matron and the condemnation of shameless elders, we reasonably believe that this boy deserved to obtain the flower of perpetual virginity. Hence we may also reasonably believe that from this so marvelous judgment his fame grew so great that Nebuchadnezzar himself, who had captured him, appointed him, above the others, as judge over his entire land. [Col. 0562B]

“But he cried out with a loud voice and said: ‘I am innocent of this woman’s blood.’ And all the people turned toward him and said: ‘What is this word that you have spoken?’ And, standing in their midst, he said: ‘Are you so foolish, men of Israel, that, without judging and without knowing what is true, you have condemned a daughter of Israel? Return to judgment, for they have spoken false testimony [Col. 0562C] against her.’ Therefore the people returned in haste” (ibid., 46–48).

What sign could be so marvelous, or so manifest a sign of divine power, as that at the sudden rebuke of one boy the whole people should so quickly halt, and after listening to him attentively should hurriedly return to judgment? What did they see in him whom age showed to be little and contemptible, and wholly inadequate to so great a matter? Certainly it must not be doubted that the Spirit with which he was filled was seen in him through some manifest sign, and that something divine appeared in his face or bearing, as is believed of the Lord when he alone drove from the temple all alike who were buying and selling.

When the people had returned to judgment, [Col. 0562D] let us hear how steadfastly and wisely the boy acts as judge of the elders—or rather, how the Holy Spirit speaks in the boy: “Separate them far from one another, and I will judge them” (ibid., 51). First, indeed, rebuking and accusing them sternly, he had said: “Are you so foolish, sons of Israel, that, without judging and without knowing what is true,” and so forth. What, I ask, is this confidence in one who is remembered as not only a boy but a younger boy: that he alone should accuse two men so sharply, publicly rebuke elders as a boy, and so swiftly bring the judgment itself to completion?

You have heard the boy’s steadfastness; but marvel at his prudence, from which the Church throughout the world has drawn authority in examining witnesses. He was a boy and a captive, yet promulgated the law of the Church not in writing but in deed. What is this, boy, that you dare presume beyond the age of a boy and do not tremble to say: “I will judge them”? [Col. 0563A] At least say: “The Lord will judge them.” But because, as the Apostle says, “He who cleaves to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17), you confidently profess that what is accomplished by the divine Spirit is accomplished through your own spirit, especially since Truth himself says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

What, meanwhile, are you doing, O Susanna? In what great astonishment do you stand suspended! You hope for help from a boy, though you are condemned by a common judgment? But because you have read what is written of your Savior and the Savior of all: “A child is born to us” (Isa. 9:6), do not despair that he will save you through this child—he whom, according to the Law, you believed became a child in order to save all. Do not attend to the child’s age, [Col. 0563B] but to the Godhead presiding in the child, whose power you remember was described in writing: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32:9).

Trusting in the Lord, and deprived of every help except the divine, you now experience fulfilled in yourself that saying of the Apostle: “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8:31). A daughter of Judah, as Daniel himself declares, illustrious by royal blood and joined through kinship to the Lord’s lineage: he whom you were to have as kinsman is now mercifully present in your ordeal. Thus, what you hope for concerning the salvation of your soul, you may already experience in the liberation of your body; so that, made more certain of the greater gift by the lesser benefit, you may always strive to serve him in return for the reception of the more abundant grace.

You have heard, virgins and brides of Christ, the virtue of a married laywoman, whom [Col. 0563C] we wished, as we said, to be seen by you after you had gone out from the bedchamber, so that by imitating her you may find your Bridegroom in the street—him whom perhaps you do not have in the cloister. You too have heard, both priests and clerics, your judgment: you who, for some reason, associate with God’s brides or attach yourselves to them in some familiarity, withdraw from God by as much as you draw shamefully nearer to them. The priests who presumed to defile a man’s bed received, as was said, a sentence of death worthy of them. Consider what awaits those who do not fear to pollute God’s own bed. When you celebrate the solemnities of the Mass among them, or are obliged to come to the sick, you often, as I hear, place the sacramental offerings in their mouths [Col. 0563D] with those hands with which you are accustomed to touch their buttocks or shameful parts. If scarcely any remedy is granted by the holy Fathers to corrupted nuns, what is to be thought of their corrupters? The stronger their sex naturally is, the more damnable is their fall. And lest we defile the conclusion of our discourse by dwelling at length upon so abominable a stain, it is enough that we have set before each group its proper judgment, and have drawn an argument from the judgments in the proposed history from the lesser to the greater.

May the Lord himself, dearest sisters, who, as you have heard, preserved a man’s marriage-bed undefiled, keep undefiled the bed that you have consecrated to him; may he banish far from you the spirit of fornication; and may he who inspired in you the will for a holy resolve grant you also the power to persevere. Amen.

## SERMON XXX. ON ALMSGIVING, FOR THE NUNS OF THE PARACLETE

Among all the Lord’s parables, brothers, that one concerning the unjust steward especially summons us to the fruit of almsgiving. When he could not render an account of his stewardship to his lord, this was his final plan: from his lord’s money and from the revenues of the estate over which he had charge—revenues which he had previously squandered wastefully upon himself—he should prepare friends for himself, who, when he had been expelled by his lord, would receive him in remembrance of his benefactions. Thus, when he collected the revenues of that estate, [Col. 0564B] he became so lavish with his lord’s goods toward others that he forgave fifty—that is, half—to the man who owed one hundred measures of oil, and remitted twenty to the man who owed one hundred measures of wheat, thus receiving eighty. And so that popular proverb was fulfilled in him: “Broad straps from another man’s hide.”

When his lord heard this, although he had decided to remove him from his stewardship—that is, from his oversight of that estate—he praised the unjust steward, who had, of course, unjustly cheated him of his own money, because he had acted prudently in making friends for himself from another’s wealth. Concluding this parable with such an ending, the Lord Jesus said: “And I say to you, make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, [Col. 0564C] so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

See: the Lord calls the steward himself unjust, because he had unjustly cheated his lord of his money; and he calls mammon itself—that is, money—the “mammon of unrighteousness,” as though it had been stolen from the Lord by fraud. Yet the prudence of the steward excuses this unrighteousness of the steward or of the mammon—

> [Note: Col. 0563. It does not excuse unrighteousness, but praises the almsgiving by which unrighteousness is redeemed. Patrologia edition.]

—that prudence which is praised in the friends he made for himself. From this one may especially infer how great is the power of almsgiving: it obtains for us the everlasting habitations of the heavenly dwelling even from goods badly acquired and unjustly stolen from their Lord.

For whoever possesses anything in this life is like the steward of the supreme King. What he has is not his own, but has been entrusted to him by the Lord as to [Col. 0564D] an administrator and servant. He ought so to manage these goods of his Lord that he may have from them what is necessary for life and return to the Lord what remains over. But he acts unjustly and fraudulently if he keeps anything beyond his own necessities and does not feed and clothe the Lord himself in the poor from what remains, as he himself says: “Amen, I say to you: what you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40).

When divine grace inspires him, the steward understands that he is being accused before his lord when he reflects that he has not been a faithful dispenser or administrator of his lord’s goods: when, through the sins of his obstinacy and greed, and through the cry of the poor—whom he refused to assist and to render to them what was theirs—he recognizes himself as grievously accused before God [Col. 0565A] and as having made enemies of those whom he ought to have made friends. He also realizes that he must be removed from his stewardship, since he cannot give a satisfactory account of it to the Lord; for this is precisely to lose one’s stewardship: not to obtain from God the fruit of administering earthly goods. Each person ought to fear this all the more, and to be more anxious about rendering an account, in proportion as he recognizes that more has been entrusted to him by God. For when gifts increase, the accounts owed for those gifts also increase.

Considering this, the provident and prudent steward, whom his lord had put over much, prepares friends who will receive him when excluded by his lord. He judges that he is to be excluded from the Lord when he finds in himself no basis for pleasing God, considering how terrible is the Lord’s saying elsewhere about [Col. 0565B] the rich man: “It is easier for a camel to enter through a needle’s eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:24). Therefore, in order to enter there through others, he makes friends of those whose kingdom it is, as Truth itself attests: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). He shares his earthly things with them, so that they may share their heavenly things with him.

Hear Solomon—and heed one greater than Solomon—because “a man’s own riches are the redemption of his soul” (Prov. 13:8). And the Lord Jesus Christ himself says: “Give, and it shall be given to you. Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41), because “as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclus. 3:33).

[Col. 0565C] Fire and water, brothers, with which the Lord compares almsgiving and sin, are very contrary things. Fire is the hottest among the elements; water is the coldest. And you know, brothers, that charity, which, according to the Apostle, makes us fervent in spirit, is rightly compared to fire. Of this fire Truth says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I desire but that it burn?” (Luke 12:49). It is as though he said plainly: “What else did I come to seek in the world except to set it aflame with the flame of love?”

But sin, which entered the world through the envy of him who inhabits men’s cold minds—as it is written, “I shall set my seat in the north” (Isa. 14:4), that is, “I shall prepare my kingdom in the hearts of men [Col. 0565D] devoid of the fire of charity”—is rightly designated by water, the coldest element. Since charity is always fervent toward God, it is especially known to be fervent when it is displayed through brotherly compassion in almsgiving. Hence, by a certain preeminence, generosity in almsgiving itself has come to be called charity as if by its own or special name. Conversely, hardness of heart toward the poor most of all proves a cold mind, deprived of every fire of charity, as it is written: “For one who does not love the neighbor whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20).

Thus he rightly compared this obstinacy of spirit to the coldest [Col. 0566A] element, and that kindness to the hottest. When we display the effect of this kindness to the poor, we depart from the devil’s kingdom and are transferred into Christ’s kingdom. “From the north evil shall be opened,” just as “God shall come from the south.” For everyone comes from the place where he dwells. The devil, the author of evils, dwells in cold minds, which are understood through the north wind, the coldest wind; and God dwells in those set ablaze by the fire of charity, fittingly designated by the south wind, which is the hottest.

To prepare such minds for himself, the Bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; blow through my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4:16). The Lord’s garden is the holy Church, which he cultivates [Col. 0566B] and waters with holy teachings and exhortations. This garden has two spices, that is, precious ointments of the Holy Spirit. With one he is said, as it were, to anoint God, and with the other his neighbor: namely, love of God and love of neighbor. By the former, a person properly touches God in himself and hangs upon him with all his desire; by the latter, he bends and lowers himself to provide for his neighbor’s needs.

The north wind rises and withdraws from this garden, and the south wind comes, when men’s formerly cold hearts are kindled with charity’s flame. The south wind is felt as it blows; charity is displayed through almsgiving. It is the south wind, but it does not yet blow, when charity has been conceived in the mind but has not yet been displayed in action. But it is brought forth and felt by its breath when it is shown in deeds toward the needs of neighbors. Then the spices that formerly lay hidden, as though stored away in the mind, flow when love both of God and of neighbor is displayed in the visible effect of deeds. Then, as the flowing spices spread their fragrance together, the sweet odor of charity’s expenditure, coming to the knowledge of many, draws many others by its example to imitate good works.

See, brothers assembled here: we ought to be God’s garden. Let us pray to the Lord of the garden that, at his command, the north wind may rise, as we have explained, and that the south wind may come and blow through it so that its spices may flow; that is, so that your charity expended on the poor may gain not only you for the Lord, but through your example may acquire others for him. Do, according to his own exhortation, [Col. 0566D] make friends from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail they may receive you.

For there is a mammon of unrighteousness and also money of equity—that is, of justice. It is mammon of unrighteousness when goods unjustly withheld from the Lord, which ought to be distributed to the poor, have killed—like a murderer—so many poor persons whom their holder could have sustained. The printed text has *peremit* (“killed”); *peregit* is suggested as the reading. Hence Jerome, in his Epistle to the Romans:

> [Note: Col. 0565D. Patrologia, vol. XXX, col. 705.]

> “For if he sees someone endangered by hunger, does he not himself kill him, if, when he has the means, he does not give him food? Whoever can bring aid to those dying in need and does not do so, kills them.”

Augustine, Against Faustus:

> “Thus, if you come upon a hungry person who may die unless you help by offering food, [Col. 0567A] you will already be held a murderer under God’s law if you do not give.”

Pope Leo, in his sermon for the Second Sunday of Lent:

> “Whoever could save a person by feeding him, if you have not fed him, you have killed him.”

Likewise the noble pagan Seneca, endowed with the law of nature, had long before established this in his proverbs, saying:

> “Whoever can help one who is perishing, when he does not help, kills.”

How great a danger, brothers, is indicated here for us, if in this way our greed kills the poor, Christ’s members—or rather, kills Christ himself anew in his members! For concerning all that is done to these poor people, he speaks through himself: “What you did to one of my least ones, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). Even while remaining in heaven, he cries to his persecutor: “Saul, Saul, why [Col. 0567B] do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). He was once put to death for his poor, but we still kill him daily in those poor. That former killing of him, through which we were redeemed, was fruitful for us; this one is only ruinous. Judas received the mammon of unrighteousness in order to betray Christ. By retaining the mammon of unrighteousness, we do not cease to kill him. We accuse Judas because he betrayed him once for money. Do we not accuse ourselves because, through desire for money, we kill him daily, as though crucifying him anew?

Let us transfer, brothers, this mammon of unrighteousness into the mammon of equity and justice, of which it is written: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his justice [Col. 0567C] remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 111:9). That is the mammon of equity, that is, money of justice, which the virtue of justice faithfully distributes, just as that is the mammon of unrighteousness which the injustice of greed fraudulently withholds.

Do not suppose, brothers, when you spend these things on the poor, that you give them what is yours; rather, you render to them what is theirs. Whatever you retain beyond life’s necessities belongs to them; by robbery you have violently seized their goods, and by taking those goods from them you kill them. Hence Gregory, in the *Pastoral Rule*:

> [Note: Col. 0567D. Patrologia, vol. LXXVII, col. 87.]

> “The earth from which all are taken is common to all human beings; and therefore it likewise brings forth food for all in common.”

They vainly consider themselves innocent who claim God’s common gift privately for themselves. When they do not distribute what they have received, they engage in the killing of their neighbors. [Col. 0567D] For when we minister whatever necessities are needed to people in distress, we render to them what is theirs; we do not bestow what is ours. We pay a debt of justice rather than perform works of mercy. Hence Truth, when speaking of mercy that must be exercised carefully, said: “Take care not to do your justice before men” (Matt. 6:1). And the Psalmist: “He scattered; he gave to the poor; his justice remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 111:9). For justice is that which renders to each person what is his own.

But when we restore to the poor what is theirs, the greatest discernment must be exercised, lest we give to one person what belongs to another, or give less to one to whom we owe more. For discernment is the mother of all virtues. Even if you offer rightly, but do not distribute rightly, you have sinned. The Law declares unclean all animals that neither chew the cud nor divide the hoof. Mercy is not to be denied to unbelievers; yet, if the alms to be given are so abundant, it is to be bestowed especially upon believers, according to what is written: “Especially [Col. 0568A] to those of the household of faith” (Gal. 6:10). The Apostle teaches that almsgiving is indeed to be done to all, but especially to those of the household of faith. Of them too the Savior spoke: “That they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9).

Yet even among poor believers there is much difference: some are poor in the world through necessity, while others are God’s poor by their own will; of these it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). The aforesaid teacher, carefully noting this, accordingly added:

> “Can even those poor people, among whose rags and bodily gluttony burning lust rules, possess eternal dwellings—those who possess neither present nor future goods? For it is not the merely poor, but the poor in spirit, who are called blessed: that is, let one give to him who is ashamed to receive, and who, having received, grieves that he reaps carnal things while sowing spiritual things.”

But among those themselves who are poor for God rather than for the world there is again some difference, since some are more needy and others less so. Those who, utterly renouncing the world, imitate the apostolic life are the truer poor and nearer to God. But this profession includes not only men but women also; and because they are of the frailer sex and weaker nature, their virtue is so much more acceptable and perfect to God as their nature is weaker, according to the Apostle’s saying: “For power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

[Col. 0568C] These women, despising earthly marriages and the allurements of carnal pleasures, join themselves to the immortal Bridegroom. Having become brides of the supreme King, they become the ladies of all his servants. Carefully observing this, blessed Jerome, when writing to one of these brides, Eustochium, said: “For this reason, my lady Eustochium—for I ought indeed to call the bride of my Lord ‘lady.’” If so great a doctor of the Church did not blush to profess this truthfully, you also, recognizing them as your ladies more by deeds than by words, should not delay to help them in their need. Recognize that you owe far more to the brides of your Lord than to servants, and that they have greater power with their own Bridegroom than servants have.

Among the nuns themselves, moreover, this discernment must be exercised in almsgiving: those who are oppressed by greater poverty should be supported by greater assistance. For monasteries of women, just as of monks, were in ancient times founded by the powerful of this world or enriched with abundant possessions. But this monastery, newly built, was neither founded by a rich person nor enriched with possessions. Yet [Col. 0569A] we know by God’s grace that it perseveres no less earnestly than the others in divine offices and regular discipline. But its plantation, still new and tender, must be cultivated with your alms if it is to grow.

You must choose the poor for yourselves; and the alms by which you seek to purchase the kingdom of heaven must not be handed indiscriminately to just anyone. Rather, as it is written, “Let almsgiving sweat in your hand until you find one worthy,” until an occasion meets you in which you can place it well—the alms which you wish to invest at the price of so great a thing. The poor must be considered who can introduce you there by their merits and prayers; for it is foolish to hope for eternal dwellings from those who labor little or not at all to attain them, who are poor more by compulsion than by will, in goods rather than in spirit, unwillingly rather than voluntarily.

“I was in prison,” the Lord says, “and you came to me” (Matt. 25:36). It is some mercy to assist those involuntarily held in human prisons; but it is far greater to assist those women who have voluntarily bound themselves in the Lord’s prisons forever, until, meeting the Bridegroom, they enter with him into the wedding, as the Bridegroom himself declares: “And those who were ready entered with him into the wedding” (ibid., 10). There, that is, they become as wives through continual cohabitation, they who here existed as brides. May these brides themselves, through their merits and intercessions, introduce you with them into that fellowship of heavenly wedding-feasts and into the eternal dwellings, so that there through them you may receive eternal things, who here receive from you [Col. 0569C] temporal things: through the favor of their Bridegroom himself, the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory through ages without end. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI. ON THE FEAST OF SAINT STEPHEN, OR OF THE OTHER DEACONS WHO WERE APPOINTED BY THE APOSTLES FOR THE SERVICE OF HOLY WIDOWS

“Behold, sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s little bed, of the mightiest of Israel, all holding swords and most skilled for wars. Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night” (Song 3:7–8). How glorious and precious, brothers, this little bed of Solomon is, to which so vigilant a guard of so many and such great men—so prepared and so armed—is assigned, we can wonder at more readily than express. What did so great a king fear in the nights, he who even by his own name indicates how great a peace he had obtained? Why, I ask, did he fear in the nights rather than in the days, that he fortified his little bed round about with such careful provision for its guard? Finally, why is this resting place of his compared with a little bed rather than a bed?

In the Gospel we read of a bed containing two people, of whom Truth testifies that one will be taken and the other left. But nothing of this kind is said of the little bed, which is mentioned more than once in this Song of Songs; nor is anyone said to be left who rests upon it. The bed, therefore, which is larger [Col. 0570A] and holds many, signifies the life of all who practice continence. For in proportion as they are farther removed from the disturbance of worldly cares and are not entangled in marital troubles, they enjoy more abundant repose. But because even among virgins there are some foolish ones who are shut out from the Bridegroom by the closed door, and because many apostatize after taking a sacred vow and consequently do not deserve to be taken by the Bridegroom, they are said to be left.

The little bed, however, which is narrower and holds few, expresses the repose of holy continence, whose perfection of life binds itself more closely to God and becomes, as it were, one spirit with him. The life of such persons, wholly free for God and devoted to him alone, is rightly called a bride; but this title applies more properly and specially when such virtue prevails in women, who, despising union with a man [Col. 0570B] and rejecting pleasures, have chosen Christ as their husband. These are not only virgins, like Mary, but widows also, like Anna, and those who renounced the world and adhered to the apostolic fellowship.

The apostles embraced these women with such loving concern that, when the number of believers increased and they themselves could no longer minister to their tables as before, they appointed seven deacons—that is, servants—to this office. By their diligent provision for the women’s needs, the women might enjoy a more ample repose in the little bed of the spirit. From this number, moreover, just as one was sifted and winnowed from the apostolic body by diabolical temptation, only six deacons remained as guards of this little bed of Solomon and as, so to speak, night watches of the man. Of these it is now said: [Col. 0570C] “Behold, Solomon’s little bed,” and so forth. It is as though it were plainly said: “Now, in this manifest union of the incarnate Word, sixty mighty men carefully surrounding and watching over the little bed of the true Solomon protect it, lest it be violated by any adultery of diabolical temptation, stained by any contagion of carnal pleasure, or disturbed by the tumults of worldly care.”

The number sixty consists of six and ten, because six times ten make sixty. Those six deacons had the number six in their own number, and they possessed the number ten in the perfection and observance of God’s commandments, signified by the Decalogue of the Law. Thus, because six and ten were joined together in them, they are rightly said to have been sixty. Above all, those appointed as guardians over the chastity of holy women needed to be strong and not lax in carnal pleasures. From their college, only the man deserved to be expelled who was excessively inflamed with jealousy for his beautiful wife and, though rebuked, did not cease from this weakness of carnal desire; rather, stirred by the madness of violent grief, he held both his own wife, for whom he was reproved, and the other women to be publicly available. The apostles judged him so detestable that they considered no one should be substituted in his place, whereas they restored Judas’s place in Matthias (Acts 1:26). For in every religious community greed seems more tolerable and less disgraceful than the shamefulness of lust, especially [Col. 0571A] among devout women. This stain must be detested and wholly removed from them.

When, therefore, that wretched Nicholas, of such weak spirit, was expelled from the aforesaid strong company of deacons, the mystical number sixty of which we have spoken was rightly preserved. These deacons were chosen from the mightiest of Israel because they were selected from Christ’s disciples, endowed with remarkable virtue in continence and abstinence. Hence they are described as armed with swords and highly trained for battles. Instructed in the teachings of God’s word, which is called the sword of the Spirit, they cut down every temptation of the ancient enemy with this sword; and, fortified with the shields of continence and abstinence, they repelled the fiery darts of that most wicked one as by a strong buckler.

It is also wisely specified on what part of themselves they chiefly bore their swords when it is added: “Each man’s sword is upon his thigh” (Song 3:8). Those set over the holiness of women, and who had expelled from their fellowship the aforesaid wretch condemned for carnal desire, were especially on guard against this vice and most especially cut away the incentives of lust from themselves with the sword of continence. Hence they are properly described as bearing swords over that part of the body in which the seat of lust is known to reside, as it were, in lust’s proper members.

Carefully considering this, Origen, that greatest philosopher among Christians, even used a bodily sword upon himself and endured to inflict violence upon himself, so that he might have free access, without suspicion of infamy, to instruct women also. From the first book of the Dialogues of blessed Gregory we have likewise learned that the venerable abbot Equitius, in order that he might also preside over monasteries of women, was so spiritually made a eunuch by an angel in a vision that the stirrings of the flesh, by which he had first been grievously troubled, were wholly extinguished in him, as though thereafter he lived entirely without sex.

> [Note: Col. 0571D. Patrologia, vol. LXXVII, col. 165.]

There are some who have the sword upon another’s thigh rather than their own: those who live not so much well as preach well, correcting others’ unchaste life more than their own. The terrors of the night are the concerns of the saints about avoiding any snares of the devil. For everyone lying in wait hides, as it were, in darkness; and every perfected person, having already conquered manifest temptations, must still consider those that are more hidden and harder to detect. Hence, according to the old translation of Ezekiel, as blessed Gregory recalls, the four holy living creatures are said to have eyes on their backs. Explaining this carefully, he says:

> [Note: Col. 0571D. Patrologia, vol. LXXVI, col. 841.]

> “Those vices that are close to virtues must indeed be considered with greater vigilance, lest they deceive by their appearance.”

And after some intervening material:

> [Note: Col. 0572D. Ibid., col. 843.]

> “Even sinners often keep guard over what is before their faces. But because the righteous guard themselves also in things not seen readily and openly before their faces, [Col. 0572A] they have eyes on their backs: for they examine even what is before their eyes, and guard themselves against things that lie hidden.”

Consider, therefore, dearest sisters, what return of service you ought to render to these outstanding ministers, and celebrate their feast with so much the greater devotion as you are more indebted to these faithful men, your stewards. Consider also how greatly divine grace has exalted you: it first had you as its own deaconesses and afterward as the deaconesses of the apostles, since both the former and the latter holy widows are known to have ministered from their own resources. Hence holy teachers have customarily called them both female deacons (*diaconas*) and deaconesses (*diaconissas*). The order of the diaconate, begun among the tables of these women in the aforesaid men, was afterward transferred to the Lord’s altar-table, so that [Col. 0572B] those who had been deacons of deaconesses might now become Christ’s Levites.

Holy teachers declare in many places that the Apostle likewise joined women with men in this order of diaconate. Writing in his Epistle to the Romans, he says: “I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is in the ministry of the Church which is at Cenchreae” (Rom. 16:1). Cassiodorus, explaining this passage in his commentaries on that Epistle, says: “He signifies that she was a deaconess of mother Church, something which is carried on even to this day in Greek regions, where the use of baptizing is not denied to them.” Claudius likewise remarks: “This passage teaches by apostolic authority that women also are appointed to ministry in the Church; and the Apostle follows Phoebe, established in this office in the Church at Cenchreae, with great praise and commendation.” Jerome too, explaining the Apostle’s passage in writing to Timothy, says:

> [Note: Col. 0572D. Patrologia, vol. XXX, col. 883.]

> “But avoid putting younger widows in charge in the ministry of the diaconate, lest an evil example be given for evil.”

The same Apostle, when earlier in that same Epistle he had ordered the life of deacons after that of bishops, also joined to them the establishment of female deacons, saying: “Deacons likewise must be modest, not double-tongued, not given to much wine, not pursuing base gain, holding the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience. And let these also first be tested, and then let them minister, having no charge against them. Women likewise must be modest, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things. Let deacons be husbands of one wife, governing their children and their own households well” (1 Tim. 3:10–12), and so forth.

Here it should also be noted that, just as in this place he approves deacons, like bishops, as husbands of one wife, so afterward, in establishing the order of deaconesses, he especially commends those who have been wives of one husband: “Let a widow,” he says, “be chosen not less than sixty years old, who has been the wife of one husband” (1 Tim. 5:9). Thus she is more fit to administer her order in proportion as the heat of the body has cooled and she feels less the ardor of lust; and she is more able diligently to oversee ecclesiastical ministries in proportion as she is known to have been well exercised in household management. So that she may not be especially marked by intemperance in lust, if she has passed through several husbands, the wife of one husband is judged suitable to be chosen.

Finally I address you, virgins, that you may reflect, from your own privilege, upon the distinction also among ministers. See: the apostles, whose place bishops hold, appointed men of a lower order—that is, deacons—for the service of holy widows. From Christ himself, in his mother the Virgin, you have learned what bishops owe you. For he gave her not a deacon but an apostle as minister, thereby plainly indicating that you deserve ministers so much worthier as you draw nearer to the excellence of the Lord’s mother. She, who obtained not a deacon but an apostle as a minister serving her, indicates what bishops owe you, since they hold the rank of the apostles in the Church.

Therefore I do not want you to be ignorant with what zeal all devout women, both virgins and others, should celebrate the feasts both of the apostles and of the aforesaid deacons chosen by them. May he who assigned such ministers to you keep you in your sacred resolve, greatly aided by their intercessions; and may your Bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, have these same men as your advocates with him—he who with the Father, etc.

## SERMON XXXII. IN PRAISE OF SAINT STEPHEN THE PROTOMARTYR  
*(We have emended the text in accordance with the Einsiedeln manuscript.)*

[Col. 0573C]

To the handmaids of Christ, the servant of Christ: may he worthily serve with you so great a Lord.

Celebrating the most devout obsequies—or rather the triumphal contest—of the protomartyr and standard-bearer of heaven, perform it with devotion all the greater because you know yourselves to be more deeply indebted to this deacon both of Christ and of yourselves. For what does “deacon” mean but “minister”? And who, on reading through the Acts of the Apostles, does not know that blessed Stephen, together with six others full of the Holy Spirit—according to the number of the sevenfold gifts of that same Spirit—was chosen by the apostles as a deacon for the ministry of holy women, and, through the laying on of hands, carefully bound to the care of this service, as it were under oath? [Col. 0573D] Although all alike are said to have been chosen by the apostles as full of the Holy Spirit, Stephen alone is nevertheless remembered in what follows as having received this grace in a spiritual manner, when it is said: “And they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip” (Acts VI, 5), etc. And again: “Stephen, full of grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people” (ibid., 8).

Rejoice therefore, and rejoice spiritually in the victory of so great a combatant: you deserved to have him as your minister, and from the service rendered to you, as the reward of that ministry, you sent him to heaven bearing the first palm of martyrdom. Render in return for this a service of divine praise; and, as he faithfully ministered for God at your tables, so may you persist more devotedly in the service of God and the veneration of the martyr. In this consider both your honour and take no small confidence from his merits. Your honour, indeed, because, as we have said, you deserved to have such a minister, whom all righteous souls follow as the standard-bearer of the heavenly host; your confidence, because you should especially hope to have him there as your helper, whom here you had as a most faithful steward—so that he who showed himself faithful as a minister in a small matter may willingly prepare himself as your advocate in a greater one. This he will obtain from the Lord by his merits all the more easily because, having received a greater grace, he deserved, as the first deacon, to be joined to the supreme priest.

His Passion too attained such authority of privilege that, alone among such accounts, having been inserted into the canonical Scriptures, it has the same writer as the Lord’s own Passion. The apocryphal passions of the apostles are rejected, and the death of the Lord’s Mother has no securely attested title from an author. The Passion of the protomartyr alone is distinguished by the style of an evangelical writer, and is described with such care that it abounds both in his praise and in yours. For immediately after the election of him and the others to the diaconate for your service, we read: “But Stephen, full of grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people.” What dignity, I ask, does this confer upon you—that Luke does not relate Stephen’s being magnified by these wonders and signs before he undertook the office of deacon, but immediately after he assumed this charge—unless to suggest that this merit proceeded from you: that, the more he humbled himself in serving beneath the weaker sex, [Col. 0574A] the more the Lord exalted him thereby, and caused him in what follows to appear more eminent than the other saints?

It is further related of him that, since his adversaries could not endure the greatness of his wonders and signs, gathering against him from different synagogues and places, they found him marvellous both in word and deed. For after the evangelist had said, “But Stephen, full of grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people,” he added: “Then some of those from the synagogue called that of the Libertines, and of the Cyrenians, and of the Alexandrians, and of those from Cilicia and Asia, rose up, disputing with Stephen; and they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke” (ibid., 9–10). [Col. 0574D] Therefore, immediately more thoroughly refuted both by his words and by his miracles, and more violently stirred against him, they brought forward false witnesses against him and stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes, so that they might rush together, seize him, and drag him into the council, in order that he might at least be judged guilty of blasphemy against God and Moses, as charged by false witnesses.

The history plainly teaches that this happened not so much through their malice as through divine providence, so that God might glorify His soldier in all things. Thus, although it is written that, rushing together, they seized him and brought him into the council (ibid., 12), we understand that he was brought there not so much by force as by his own will. For, desiring “to be dissolved and to be with Christ,” he—the first deacon—was then borne after Christ the supreme priest by the same longing with which Christ, who says to the Father, “Father, I will that where I am, my minister also may be there” (John XII, 26), and with which Lawrence later clung to Sixtus, saying: “Where are you going without your son, father? Whither do you hasten, holy priest, without your minister?” He also remembered that proverb of the Wise Man by which he saw himself bound and which he wished to fulfil: “You have sat at a great table: know that you too must prepare such things” (Prov. XXII).

For just as there is a table of bodily food, which is called small, so that is rightly called a great table from which the food of the soul is received in the sacrament of the Lord. The Lord set up this table when He offered Himself for us upon the cross. We approach it when we receive from the altar the sacraments of His body and blood. In receiving these, we ought to heed what Christ says to those who receive them: “Do this,” He says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII, 19); as though He openly said: Celebrate this sacrament in memory of my Passion in such a way that the remembrance itself may make you ready to suffer with me. For, as the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II, 12).

But when, by suffering with Christ, we render Him a return, we repay, as it were, dishes taken from the table of the mighty, so that we too may refresh Him from what is ours, just as He has satisfied us from what is His; and He Himself may dine with us, He with whom we first dined. But who is understood as the minister at Christ’s table except the deacon, who prepares both the very table of the altar and the sacraments of the offering to be consecrated upon it? Therefore it is fitting that he should remember this sacrifice, whose ministry especially handles it, so that this first deacon might deservedly follow that supreme priest in rendering this return.

When, as we have said, he had been summoned to the council and was to be accused, the evangelist continues his praise: “And all who sat in the council, looking intently at him, saw his face as the face of an angel” (Acts VI, 15). Already the glory of the life to come shone forth in him, the glory which He promises to His faithful when He says: “For there they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. XXII, 30). And the Apocalypse says: “The measure of a man, which is also that of an angel” [Col. 0575D] (Rev. XXI, 17). We read that in His Transfiguration the Lord shone in face like the sun; but we hear that this man’s face was made like that of an angel—something which sacred history does not record of any of the apostles or saints.

When he stood and was questioned in the council, he showed by his own replies how full he was of strength of soul and constancy, ending with these words: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you. Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold him of whom you have now been betrayers and murderers—you who received the law and did not keep it” (Acts VII, 51). And it is added: “But when they heard these things, they were cut to the heart, and gnashed their teeth at him” (ibid., 54). Already assured of receiving the first fruits of the crown, and strengthened for the completion of his contests, the more eagerly he hastened toward the prize, the less he feared his adversaries and the more he rejoiced that they were stirred against him.

Indeed, the Lord displayed that constancy to him not so much through his words as through His own presence, as is immediately added: “But Stephen, being full of the Spirit, looked intently into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts VII, 54).

We read that the Lord Jesus, when He ascended into heaven, sat down at the right hand of the Father; but now, for Stephen’s sake, he saw Him appear standing rather than sitting, as though He had risen from there. What honour, I ask, or what hope for the martyr, that Christ appears to rise to meet him, or to stand to help him, as though fighting alongside him? Fittingly it was first said that his face was made like the face of an angel, when it is then added that he saw the glory of God, so that his life or knowledge may now be called angelic rather than human. For it is written that the Lord said to Moses: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. XXXII, 20). And the Psalmist, secure concerning that vision of the Godhead, speaks to God: “I shall be satisfied when thy glory appears” (Ps. XVI, 15).

But Stephen here declares that he sees not only the humanity of Christ standing at the Father’s right hand, but also the glory of God, as though he had now wholly acquired an angelic face. Of this angelic vision Truth Himself says: “Amen I say to you, that their angels always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 10). Paul was caught up to the third heaven and heard secret words which it is not permitted for a human being to utter (II Cor. XII, 4); yet he is not recorded to have seen the glory of God or the Father’s right hand, at which Christ stood. Therefore we perceive Stephen, as one already placed at the very departure from life, to live not so much humanly as angelically. Nor do we believe that he lacked the prerogative of virginity, the virtue which especially imitates angels: namely, that one may live in the flesh without the corruption of the flesh—a gift not granted to Moses, who was bound by the union of human frailty. [Col. 0576D]

Accordingly, a certain discourse written in praise of this great martyr concludes thus: “In being set over women, he earned testimony to most unblemished chastity. Blessed therefore will be the one who has imitated him. For he will obtain both the palm of purity and the crown of martyrdom.” It is as though it were openly said: Whoever, following the Lamb wherever He goes after Stephen’s example, is clothed alike in fine linen and purple, will receive a diadem interwoven at once with roses and lilies.

Thus, by a certain divine foretokening of so great a merit, it came to pass that he was called Stephen; as Bede records, [Note: [Col. 0575D] On the Acts of the Apostles, *Patrologia* XCII, col. 956.] in Hebrew it means “your rule,” and in Greek, “crown.” How greatly either interpretation of this name expresses the excellence of this soldier is easy to show. For the expression “your rule,” O faithful ones, indicates that he was adorned with such virtues that he himself is for all a rule of discipline leading to perfection of life. Since love is the fulfilment of the law, who has seemed as much as Stephen to display it both toward God and toward neighbour? Toward God, indeed, by dying for Him and after Him before all others, and fulfilling what He Himself said of this: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13). Toward his neighbour, when, praying aloud for those stoning him, he pleaded: “Lord, do not lay this sin against them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Acts VII, 59). [Col. 0577B] And immediately it is added concerning him, raised to such perfection: “And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord” (ibid.).

Scripture certainly does not fail to say that he prayed for himself, declaring: “And they stoned Stephen as he called upon God and said, ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit’” (ibid., 58). Yet assuredly, while praying for himself, he is not read to have bent his knees or cried aloud, so that he might show correspondingly greater devotion toward his enemies, because he saw that they had greater need of the protection of his prayer, since he placed no confidence in their merits. Therefore, perfected in this charity toward his enemies, once his prayer for them was completed he deserved immediately to fall asleep in the Lord; so that, from the full measure of perfect virtue, the first martyr both in dignity and in time might receive the first prize.

For it was fitting that such an athlete should be chosen first in the Lord’s battle line and preferred to the rest—one who, the more perfect in virtue, would more greatly encourage and equip others for battle by his own examples, as though through him the Lord taught all hands for war and all fingers for battle. And so that he might exhort later generations more steadfastly to the contest, looking into heaven he saw the glory of God and Jesus already standing by him; and immediately, as though to strengthen his followers in the struggle, he cried out: “Behold, I see the heavens opened, and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God” (ibid., 55). It is as though he said: Fight bravely yourselves too; contend manfully, because after the contest of battle there is now no delay in receiving the palm. Stand fearless in the battle line; fight in confidence, because Christ stands beside us in the contest: He fights for us so that we may conquer. “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. VIII, 31).

What too is the remarkable presage that Stephen is interpreted not merely as “crowned,” but as “the crown itself”? For all who are to be crowned are, as it were, crowned from him: beginning with him, they are instructed through him. Thus he is at once a rule of virtues and, in some manner, the crown of victors and their leadership toward the reward. He was also, as has been said, adorned with such great virtues that the crown of the rest might be called, as it were, the highest ornament; and in the body of Christ he should be counted not so much among the other saints in the Lord’s garment as placed in its upper part, like a crown. [Col. 0578A] Hence he deserved to be set before the other martyrs by the offering of his undefiled flesh, and, in the catalogue of the seven deacons, to be placed first as their archdeacon, both by the fact and by the title of his rank.

For it was fitting that the others assigned to you with him, as we have said, should especially be governed by the judgment of him who excelled in the virtue of chastity. Thus it was well ordered by divine providence that he should be offered first as an example to the martyrs, since, preceding them in the grace of virtues, he strengthened them more and called them onward to the crown. Looking upward at Jesus, standing alike to meet and to help him, he did not delay to proclaim that this revelation had been made to him—both to strengthen his followers more greatly to suffer with Christ and to stir his adversaries more violently against himself.

He remembered, I think, Isaiah, killed by the Jews because he had written that he saw God’s majesty. Therefore Stephen himself judged that these words would stir them more strongly, as is immediately added: “But crying out with a loud voice, they stopped their ears and rushed upon him with one accord. And casting him out of the city, they stoned him” (Acts VII, 56). I think this was the same gate by which Christ too went out to be crucified, so that king and soldier might share the same place of suffering. There was fulfilled in him, according to the history itself, what the Apostle writing to the Hebrews says: “The bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest are burned outside the camp. Therefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate. Let us therefore go forth to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we do not have here an abiding city, but seek the city to come” (Heb. XIII). If, therefore, those who seek the city to come must hasten with such longing, how much more Stephen, who already beheld it present in heaven, who saw Christ rise for him, or stand ready and prepared to meet him?

But the very impatience of his persecutors testifies how violently they raged against him, when it says: “Casting him out of the city, they stoned him” (Acts VII, 57). [Note: [Col. 0577] What follows we supply from the Einsiedeln manuscript. It is lacking in the Amboise edition. *Patrologia* edition.] For it does not say that he was stoned once he had been cast out, but that the stoning began while he was still being cast out. When he had been cast out, the laying aside of their garments indicates with what haste they gathered for his destruction, as though some hindrance were thereby removed.

But how great was his charity—charity which “bears all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (I Cor. XIII, 7)—his end makes manifest. For, kneeling, he cried aloud, saying: “Lord, do not lay this sin against them”; and when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord (Acts VII, 59). The preceding words show that Stephen also prayed for himself when it says: “And they stoned Stephen as he called upon God and said, ‘Lord Jesus, receive my spirit’” (Acts VII, 58). Here I see that one must carefully consider how great was the charity with which, amid the very blows of stones, he embraced his enemies—those for whom he not only prayed but also pleaded with bended knees, something we nowhere read that he did for himself, but rather for those whom he had first not feared severely to rebuke and to reproach for both their own crimes and those of their fathers.

He showed at the end from what a fountain of charity this proceeded, in which he especially appears to imitate the Lord Jesus, who, led to His Passion, prayed for those crucifying Him, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34). Consider, I beseech you, dearest sisters and daughters of Christ, how great was the providence of divine mercy toward you in assigning to your service this charity which could not grow angry even with its enemies while it was being put to death. From this especially gather what you ought to hope from him, who showed himself so gracious toward his enemies. [Col. 0579B]

We read that other followers of his fought bravely, but that none, or few, showed this grace toward their killers after the example of their Lord. Thus he deservedly merited to follow the Lord first in the contest, because by so great an imitation of virtue he stood nearer to Him: the more advanced he was in virtue, the earlier he was taken up as an example in the battle.

But lest we think that such an affection of charity did not obtain its effect in his prayer, consider what arose and followed from that prayer. It had been said that those witnesses, to whom he had been handed over for stoning, laid their garments at the feet of the young man Saul to be kept. Afterwards, when the martyr is said, his prayer for his enemies completed, immediately to have fallen asleep in the Lord, the same young Saul is at once introduced: “But Saul was consenting to his death” (Acts VII, 59), etc. In these words his prayer is found fruitful especially in the case of this young man, so that he is believed later to have been converted through Stephen’s merit—the one through whom almost the whole world would be converted to God—so that we may ascribe to Stephen’s merits this very conversion of all the nations which we believe.

Nor was the anger of the persecutors calmed when Stephen had been stoned; rather, it was kindled all the more on his account, as he was evidently more acceptable to God and more hateful to God’s enemies. Hence it follows: “There arose on that day a great persecution against the Church which was in Jerusalem, and all were scattered through the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles” (Acts VIII, 1). The following words indicate into how great a salvation for the Church the Lord turned this scattering caused by the persecution, so that, from the death of Stephen, He received for the desolate mother material for consolations. For this scattering of the faithful gathered many peoples into faith in Christ, as the following account says: “Therefore those who had been scattered went about preaching the word of God. But Philip, going down to the city of Samaria, preached Christ to them. And the crowds gave heed with one accord to what Philip said, hearing and seeing the signs which he performed. For many of those who had unclean spirits came out, crying with a loud voice; and many paralytics and lame persons were healed. Therefore there was great joy in that city” (Acts VIII, 4 ff.). [Col. 0580A]

Nor is the joy this brought the apostles left unmentioned, when it says: “But when the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them” (ibid., 14), etc. It is certain that this Philip is the one whom the evangelist had above counted, among the seven deacons assigned to your service, second after Stephen, saying: “And they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip” (Acts VI, 5), etc. From this too it is clear that through this deacon of yours, as though proceeding from your own household, Christ’s first preaching was extended and the first fruits of the nations came into Christ’s barns.

How great a grace the prerogative of virginity bestowed also upon his daughters, the evangelist does not fail to relate much later, saying: “On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea; and entering the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, we stayed with him. Now he had four virgin daughters who prophesied” (Acts XXI, 8–9).

To return now to what was said above, it is pleasing also to consider how great a care the Lord took to bury the body of His most holy martyr, when the Psalmist, grieving over the rest, complains to Him: “They have given the corpses of thy servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of thy saints to the beasts of the earth. They have poured out the blood of the saints around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them” (Ps. LXXVIII, 2–3). For amid that great persecution and scattering of the faithful which then occurred in Jerusalem, faithful persons were not lacking who, in the midst of such distress of their own, buried the martyr with great lamentation, as it is written: “God-fearing men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him” (Acts VIII, 2).

This is that great weeping and wailing of your Rachel; these are the devout tears of the Church in compassion, prefigured through Jeremiah when he said: “A voice was heard on high, of lamentation and mourning—Rachel weeping for her children” (Jer. XXXI, 15), etc. Therefore you too, dearest sisters in Christ, lament with devout mourning one who died in your service, so great and such a man; celebrate his venerable obsequies with the devout devotion of compassion; and, as though accompanying this one especially yours to his tomb, complete with tears the ointments of his burial and prepare, as it were, spices in return for his faithful service toward you. [Col. 0580D]

We read that even among those wicked crowds leading the Lord to be crucified, women’s compassion in mourning was not absent from Him. As the same evangelist records: “And there followed him a great multitude of people and of women, who mourned and lamented him” (Luke XXIII, 27). But Jesus, turning to them, said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me” (ibid., 28), etc. If then a natural affection of compassion, which especially belongs to your sex, moved unbelieving women—even the wives of the persecutors themselves—to tears of sympathy, you do not fail to know what you owe to your Stephen.

How many and how great were the miracles by which the Lord exalted him even after death, the teachers of the Church especially transmitted to the memory of later generations by diligent writing. Thus, among the other mighty works performed through his merits, Augustine, the greatest teacher of the Church, in the last book of *The City of God*, [Note: [Col. 0581D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, col. 766 ff.] records six dead persons restored to life in Africa—something which we do not read that the Lord granted either to Himself, or to Peter pre-eminent in miracles, or to any other saint. First a certain priest, then a boy; afterward a certain consecrated woman, then a young girl; afterward a young man, then an infant.

For the priest Eucharius suffered in his feet from an old disease and was healed on earth through Stephen’s memorial shrine. Later, however, when another illness grew worse, he died; but after the tunic of that same priest had been taken to the shrine of the holy martyr and brought back, and laid upon the body of the dead man as he lay there, he was raised through the merits of the blessed martyr. We read of the boy that, while he was playing in a threshing floor, oxen drawing a wagon swerved and crushed him with their wheels; immediately he gasped and died. His mother seized him, placed him at the same shrine, and he not only revived but appeared unharmed.

When the consecrated woman was suffering from illness, his tunic was brought to the same shrine; but before the tunic could be brought back, she died. Finally they covered her corpse with that tunic, and, her spirit restored, she was made well.

One day, when a Syrian named Basus was praying at the memorial shrine of the same martyr for his sick daughter and had brought there the girl’s garment, two servants from his household came running to tell him that she had died. But friends who were in the house prevented them from telling him, lest he should lament in public. When he returned home, overwhelmed by excessive grief, he placed upon his dead daughter the garment which he had brought, and she was restored to life. Likewise, the son of a certain man had died. Friends of the martyr anointed his body with oil, and he immediately revived. The sixth remaining person was raised in this manner: Eleustus, a man of tribunitial rank, having an infant who had died during illness, laid him upon the martyr’s memorial shrine; and after much prayer poured forth with tears, he raised the child alive.

All these events, as we have said, occurred in Africa. Blessed Augustine, who knew them by living there, recounts them, thereby indicating from those deeds which came to his knowledge in a single province how many and how much greater works of this kind the Lord must be believed to perform to the glory of His soldier in the other parts of the world.

Thus Stephen attained also this prerogative: we see basilicas of episcopal sees especially consecrated in his memory. He, Christ’s first martyr, like another Abel, became, so to speak, a founder of the Church by the shedding of his own blood, laying himself beneath its foundation like a living stone, blunted and squared by the blows of many stones. All the rest lean upon him as though in some way founded and established upon him; and he gave men an example of constancy and women likewise an example of continence. [Col. 0582A]

But since all these things which are preached concerning your first minister pertain especially to your glory, dearest sisters, his triumph ought to be remembered by you all the more because his memorial affords you greater honour and greater security. Therefore we counsel you with devout exhortation always to celebrate his memorial devotedly, in the morning and evening praises, with his proper antiphon and collect; so that you may experience before God as a more salutary advocate the one whom you had among men as a faithful minister. May the Lord Himself grant this to you, to whom be honour and glory through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII. ON SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

[Col. 0582B]

The Lord, speaking to blessed Job in parables, after describing the order of rulers through the ibexes and hinds giving birth, then turns His discourse, beloved brothers and fellow monks, to the instruction of your vocation; and, preferring its freedom to that of others, says: “Who has sent out the wild ass free, and who has loosed his bonds? To whom I have given a home in solitude, and his dwelling places in the land of salt? He despises the multitude of the city and does not hear the cry of the taskmaster. He surveys the mountains as his pasture and seeks every green thing” (Job XXXIX, 5).

Both Job’s own history and God’s testimonies had shown, brothers, that Job was great in many virtues. Yet lest the magnitude of such virtues perhaps draw him into pride, the dignity of the married life of both rulers and continent persons is placed before his eyes, so that through comparison with them he may restrain himself from pride. And because the virtue both of continence and of abstinence is pre-eminent among monks, the prerogative of this life is described under the figure of the wild ass.

For an onager is called not a domestic but a wild ass. It lives in solitude with greater freedom, the farther it is removed from human association; it is neither burdened with a load nor restrained by bonds, unlike the domestic ass. Hence the life of married people is rightly compared to the latter, and that of continent persons to the former. [Col. 0582D] What bond is greater than the marital union? What slavery is heavier than that by which a person does not have power over his or her own body? What life, finally, is more burdensome than to be tormented by the troubles of daily concern both for wife and for children? Or what life is more sluggish in God’s service than that of one bound to the world by the chains of so many affections? Thus the slowness of a sluggish beast is not out of keeping with this life’s comparison.

Monks, however, become all the more unencumbered and ready for divine service as they are freed more fully from the bonds of worldly affections, renounce everything, stand farther from the slavery of which we have spoken, and become freer.

It is of this freedom that the Lord now speaks to Job: “Who has sent out the wild ass free?” It is as though He said: Who but I gave this freedom to the quiet of monastic life, which far surpasses your married servitude? This is surely a great gift of so great a grace: that by divine inspiration and power, people born amid carnal desires and reared amid worldly enticements may live in the flesh contrary to—or beyond—the weakness of human nature, so as not to know the vices of the flesh and, forgetting human frailty, become angelic in virtue. “And who has loosed his bonds?” That is: who has broken the affections of the flesh, by which he was naturally bound to the world as by certain chains?

How fittingly the wild ass signifies the life of continent persons, which, as has been said, is pre-eminent among monks, is shown by a characteristic of that animal reported by Isidore and by those who have written on animal natures. The male wild asses, they say, castrate their sons. To prevent this, the mothers strive as much as possible to hide them. But the male wild asses signify monks strong in their vocation, who preserve in continence, by spiritually castrating them, those whom they govern as sons or receive into their community. Isaiah and Truth Himself greatly commend such eunuchs, namely those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven (Isa. LVI, 4; Matt. XIX, 12).

That these words concerning the wild ass are to be understood of monks—that is, solitaries—He plainly indicates when He says: “To whom I have given a home in solitude” (Job XXXIX, 6); that is, I have drawn him from the tumult of the world into the secrecy of the wilderness, so that, the more quietly he dwells there, the more perfectly he may devote himself to me. “And his dwelling places in the land of salt” (ibid.).

Tents are movable dwellings, fixed with no permanence, such as the shelters of shepherds or travellers. Our bodies are compared to these: still dissoluble in death and not yet possessing the permanence of immortality. Of such bodies the Apostle says: “If our earthly house is dissolved, we have a house in heaven, not made with hands, prepared by God” (II Cor. V, 1). Therefore, while we are in these muddy and mortal bodies, we dwell in tents rather than houses. Thus, though here we still have, as pilgrims, a tent, when we reach the homeland of the heavenly Jerusalem we shall dwell instead in a house.

As a figure of this, the people of God first had a tabernacle in the wilderness, and afterward a temple in Jerusalem, once they had gained the promised land and enjoyed the greatest delight of peace under Solomon—whose name, like that of Jerusalem, where he built the temple, signifies peace, which can be truly found nowhere except in that heavenly Jerusalem. Writing also to the Hebrews, the Apostle compares every mortal body to a tent, saying: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no right to eat” (Heb. XIII, 10): that is, those who obey the desires of the flesh more than the Spirit and serve the belly more than God.

Saline land consists of arid and dry places, through which the devil wanders and finds no rest; he sleeps in moist places, as the Lord says to Job himself. Therefore the tents of the wild ass are in dry land, because the virtue of abstinence flourishes in those whose bodies are by no means dampened by the flow of carnal desires.

He despises the multitude of the city (Job 39:7). To the two things he mentioned last he adds two more, as though assigning each answer to each point. To the statement, “To whom I gave a home in the wilderness,” he refers what is now said: “He despises the multitude of the city,” that is, the crowd of worldly people, which ensnares and delights many. For many are called, but few chosen, and many travel the broad and spacious road of death. There are some who, moved by fear or some necessity, withdraw into the hidden places of solitude; and they do this more under compulsion than willingly, as we read happened first in Elijah, the anchorite of the ancient people, and later in Paul, the first hermit. But withdrawal from the world is noble and acceptable to God when someone leaves the world for God’s sake, and the world does not so much drive him out as he himself rejects the world.

“And he does not hear the cry of the taskmaster” (ibid.). It is as though he said: It is evident from this that he has his dwelling in a salt land, because by the measured fasts of daily abstinence he subdues the flesh, so that he may both restrain its desires and not incur the failure of nature. The importunate and daily taskmaster within us is the belly, which, by demanding food from us, seems daily to murmur and cry, “Bring, bring!” In necessary things it indeed has a moderate voice, but in superfluities an intemperate cry. Therefore this wild ass, because he does not withhold from the belly necessary nourishment but removes what is superfluous, does not hear the cry of the taskmaster, as was said, because he does not obey it in superfluities.

Concerning him it is further added: “He surveys the mountains of his pasture, and seeks out every green thing” (ibid., 8). The mountains of pasture are the volumes of loftier teaching—that is, Sacred Scripture. Therefore, the more this spiritual wild ass abstains from bodily food, the more he needs the consolation of better food, namely the pasture of the divine word; and the less he attends to the former, the more he satisfies his soul with this refreshment. He is rightly said to survey the mountains of his pasture—that is, to inquire carefully and discern in which mountains, namely in which sacred volumes, he can find for himself more suitable refreshment from their understanding. For the reading of every book is not suitable for everyone; not all can understand all books; nor are all equally delighted by every dish.
