And because in the divine books certain things are rebuked and others commended, and not only the life of the good which we should follow, but also that of the wicked which we should flee, is described: these mountains contain not only green but also dry grass. Things belonging to worldly life are comparable to hay, which, cut off from its ground, has lost the vigor of its greenness. The life of the reprobate, alien from the land of the living, craving these transient things which stand in decline, is compared to hay; whereas, on the contrary, the life of the elect, having daily progress and tending toward the unfading delight of the heavenly homeland, as though toward ever-green meadows, bears the appearance of verdant fields. With such things, therefore, our wild ass must be refreshed in those mountains. He does not seek dry fodder but green things, because he strives after those things through which eternal life is attained, and takes care to refresh his soul here only with those things by which it may reach that heavenly refreshment.

This, then, has been our exposition of the wild ass in the general, so to speak, person of monks. Now, transferring him from genus to species, it is pleasing to consider all this more carefully in that supreme prince of monks whose feast is celebrated today, where we may find these things in a more perfect form: he who, living without the profession of a rule, surpassed every perfection of a rule. For he, as was said, coming in the spirit and power of Elijah, completed the life of this calling which Elijah began. From these two, as leaders of our calling, or princes of this Christian philosophy, its pursuits arose among both the old and the new people.

Jerome, to Paulinus, Letter II [Note: [Col. 0585D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 583]:

> “Every calling has its own leaders; and, to come to our own case, let bishops and presbyters have as their examples the apostles and apostolic men, and, possessing their honor, strive also to possess their merit. But let us have as leaders of our calling Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and Macarius. And, to return to the authority of the Scriptures, our leader is Elijah; Elisha is ours; ours are the sons of the prophets, who lived in the fields and wilderness and made themselves tents near the streams of the Jordan. Of these too were those sons of Rechab who drank neither wine nor strong drink, who dwelt in tents, and whom God praises through Jeremiah, because there shall not fail from their stock a man standing before the Lord.”

The same writer, to the virgin Eustochium, on the different kinds of monks [Note: [Col. 0586D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 421]:

> “I come to the third kind, those whom they call anchorites, who, leaving the cenobia, carry nothing more into the deserts except bread and salt. Paul was the founder of this life, Antony its illuminator, and, to ascend to higher things, John the Baptist was its prince. Jeremiah also describes such a man, saying: ‘It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth; he shall sit alone and keep silence, because he has taken up the yoke upon himself,’ etc. (Lam. 3:27).”

Chrysostom, Homily 23, which begins thus:

> “Of John it is said: ‘There was a man sent from God, whose name was John’ (John 1:6). Grace is contained in his name. For John is interpreted ‘the grace of the Lord,’ because he received greater grace. Therefore he practices philosophy in the wilderness and reserves himself for Christ’s coming, because he was to announce Christ. At once he is nourished in the wilderness; at once he grows there. He does not wish to associate with men: in the wilderness he practices philosophy with angels.”

Consider, monks, your dignity: John is the prince of your doctrine. This monk, as soon as he is born, lives in the wilderness; he is nourished in the wilderness; in solitude he awaits Christ. At the time when John was born and was in the wilderness, this Temple which we see destroyed possessed what riches—what gold, what silver; Josephus describes how many gems, how much silk, how numerous were the priests, scribes, and every kind of office. See how Christ always loves humility. Christ, the Son of God, is unknown in the Temple and preached in the wilderness. For the humble one loves the humble. Why do I say all this? To teach that John the Baptist is the prince of our doctrine.

This other Elijah in spirit—indeed, regarded as greater by a certain privilege of life—received so much greater grace from the Lord as he deserved to be distinguished by the angelic announcement of his birth and by such a name as expressed this grace’s excellence. He was truly a free wild ass, who from infancy, breaking the bonds of carnal attachments and despising his parents’ home, withdrew to the harsh desert of the wilderness—not, indeed, like Elijah, compelled by fear of persecution, but voluntarily through the virtue of abstinence. The Gospels teach how, in that solitude, he made his body a dwelling-place of salt land and dry ground. There he was content with natural foods and what the earth freely offered. We do not read that he ate bread, vegetables, or any cooked food, but that he was sustained only by wild honey, locusts, and water.

Elijah had not only monastic food but even flesh-meat, supplied by ravens. They brought it to him, not once a day, but both morning and evening, together with bread. Having also drink from the brook Cherith, he did not feel any great burden of abstinence in these three things—bread, meat, and water. The sons of Rechab likewise won no praise for fasting, but are commended by the Lord only for abstinence from wine, not from meat or any other delicacies (Jer. 35:1 ff.). But John and his disciples are said to have surpassed in daily bodily abstinence not only the earlier fathers but even Christ himself and his disciples, as we learn from Matthew’s account: “The disciples of John came to Jesus and said, ‘Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast?’ And Jesus said to them, ‘Can the sons mourn while the bridegroom is with them?’” (Matt. 9:14).

Nor do the same Gospels, nor the Lord himself, remain silent in praise of how rough his clothing was, so that he might feel no softness even in these things. For it is written: “John himself had a garment of camel’s hair, and a leather belt around his loins” (Matt. 3:4). Instead of woolen cowls, he had rough garments of camel’s hair. Instead of linen drawers, he wore a leather belt about his loins, so that by the coldness and hardness of the skin he might repress the heat and softness of lust. The son of the high priest himself—who at that time succeeded his father by hereditary right—scorned to rule over the people in the city, in order to devote himself more perfectly to God in solitude.

The pastoral mountains of this wild ass were the aforesaid men, eminent in the old people for loftiness of life. Raising the eyes of his purpose toward them, according to the saying, “I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains” (Ps. 120:1), he took from them as many examples of virtues as he possessed pastures of green grass. For he did not find in each one all gifts of divine grace; but, gathering different things from different persons, he strove, as it were, to form one perfect man out of many. Therefore, when the Lord preferred his life, both in continence and abstinence, above all others, and judged it not so much human as angelic, after introducing his praise with the words, “But what did you go out to see? A prophet? I tell you, more than a prophet,” he immediately added: “This is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel,’” etc. (Matt. 11:9).

But, brothers, what good is it to commend the life of so great a prince of ours if we disdain to imitate it? As the Apostle says: “Whatever things were written were written for our instruction, that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (Rom. 15:4). How great is the danger threatening us if we do not fulfill those instructions written especially for our edification, if we are instructed by examples that describe the practices of our calling more perfectly? For the more carefully we see these things set forth for us, the greater judgment we incur by despising them. Hence Truth says: “The servant who knows and does not do the will of his master will be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 22:47).

Behold, in the foregoing description of the wild ass what we ought to follow has been plainly expressed; but it is no less clear how contrary a path we pursue. For now that religious fervor has grown cold—indeed, is extinguished—we ought henceforth to live from our own labor, which blessed Benedict declares alone truly makes monks [Note: [Col. 0587] Rule, ch. 48. See *Patrologia*, vol. LXVI, col. 704]. Yet, pursuing idleness, the enemy of the soul, we seek sustenance from another’s labor; and using the perverse freedom of this harmful repose, devoting ourselves both to luxury in possessions and to much speaking, we have lost the true freedom of the aforesaid wild ass.

Thus entangling ourselves in secular affairs, while the desire for earthly things rules us and we strive to become richer in the monastery than we were in the world, we have subjected ourselves to earthly masters rather than to God. Receiving estates, people, male slaves, and female slaves from worldly powers as though in alms, we submit ourselves to their heavy yoke; and sometimes we pay much for the little we receive. Since they judge these things to accrue to them from what is theirs rather than ours, they show no gratitude for them, considering them not so much given as returned to themselves. Often, compelled to protect these possessions, we are dragged into external courts; and, conducting a public lawsuit before secular judges, we contend with such shamelessness that we compel our dependents not only to take oaths but even to fight duels on our behalf at the gravest risk to their lives.

The Apostle condemns this even among secular Christians: “It is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits among yourselves. Why do you not rather suffer wrong? Why do you not rather endure fraud? But you yourselves do wrong and defraud, and this to brothers. Do you not know that the unrighteous shall not possess the kingdom of God?” (1 Cor. 6:7). Who, moreover, does not know that we impose harsher exactions upon those subject to us, and rage with greater tyranny, than secular powers do? Indeed, if we can, we break out into such madness that we procure our livelihood from tributes, taxes, and tolls, although among the Lord’s great miracles is reckoned the fact that he could draw Matthew away from the toll-booth by his call (Matt. 9).

But to pass from secular to ecclesiastical powers: our ambition seems to sustain no smaller burdens from this quarter. When we usurp what belongs to clerics and obtain from bishops, by whatever means, parish revenues in tithes and offerings, we are often compelled to pay out what we have not seized. Hence we are frequently drawn to synods and councils, daily setting out for public lawsuits, and hiring advocates at no small cost—either judges or speakers to cloak our wrongs. Certainly, the frequent complaint shows how great is the rapacity of our greed even in councils themselves. There we rarely see bishops contending with bishops, or clerics with clerics. Almost every dispute either belongs to monks or has arisen concerning monks.

And, to omit the slavery and bonds of these anxieties, by which they bind themselves tightly to the world: what shall I say of the carnal affections of blood-relations or relations by marriage, for whom they commit countless sacrileges from monastic property? For example, when they have sons, nephews, or persons joined to them by any kinship or affinity in the world, they spend on them what they steal from the brothers—secretly, if they cannot do so openly. If perchance they draw such persons into monastic life or keep them as servants in their houses, they raise them to offices of authority, and everything is administered according to their will. If anyone speaks against them, he immediately experiences offended majesty.

These are the domestic enemies of the monastery, these its daily thieves—more harmful in proportion as they are more constant. Through their patronage the monks themselves break out more easily into every shameful and unlawful act, in proportion as they place greater confidence in their kinship or affinity with them. The dwelling-places of the aforesaid wild ass were said to be prepared by the Lord in solitude. But these, on the contrary, at the devil’s prompting, fleeing the peace of solitude and shamelessly throwing themselves into the tumults of the world, delight in living in cities and towns; they should be called not so much monks—that is, solitary persons—as citizens.

Jerome, that greatest of monks and ecclesiastical teachers, rebuking their shamelessness and carefully distinguishing our life from that of clerics, says [Note: [Col. 0589D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, cols. 582–583]:

> “If the work or burden of the episcopate perhaps delights you, live in cities and towns, and make the salvation of others the gain of your own soul. If you desire to be what you are called, a monk—that is, alone—what are you doing in cities, which are surely not dwellings for solitary persons but for many?”

The same writer elsewhere says:

> “Interpret the word *monk*, that is, your name. What are you doing in a crowd, you who are alone?”

We dwell all the more dangerously amid secular crowds and the multitude of people because their number is greater than ours, and we see more secular than religious persons. We incur this danger especially when two or three of us, and sometimes one alone, live among them. Even these places of ours, which we cannot call abbeys, we commend under the name of obediences; we lie all the more openly in this because we have departed further from obedience to the rule and from the order of our profession. For where the order prescribed by the rule is not kept, who would hesitate to call the house disorderly? Authority recognizes only two kinds of monks: cenobites and anchorites. But those who live in the world two or three together, or singly, and do not possess enough brothers to fulfill the observance of the rule, are certainly neither cenobites nor anchorites: not cenobites, because they do not live under a rule; nor anchorites, because they do not live in solitude.

But if neither the admonitions nor the examples of the holy Fathers call us back from the world full of temptations, and if we desire bodily gain more than we fear the loss of souls, then at least the disadvantages of our own affairs, which we frequently suffer through common intercourse with people, should restrain us from this presumption. For when enemies invade and devastate the cities themselves or what belongs to their citizens, our possessions, joined with theirs, cannot be separated from the common disaster. Even when enemies are absent, unforeseen fires in houses frequently occur in cities, by which both the oratories and workshops of monks are utterly consumed. At least let the losses which we incur by fleeing teach us to flee back to solitude, so that, as though our goods had been lost in a storm, we may hasten—even naked—from the storms of the world to the harbor of peace and solitude.

There are some who establish their dwellings in solitude but by no means persevere. This happens for many reasons. Some, exceeding the measure of their poverty and undertaking things beyond their strength, are compelled to supply from another’s resources what they do not possess of their own; and, because of their needs, they again insert themselves into the world which they had intended to flee. There are also those who, through long residence in the wilderness and abstinence, have acquired such a reputation for religion that they are often invited by worldly powers or secular men under some pretext of piety; and thus, shaken like chaff in the devil’s sieve, they are renewed from the wilderness into the world. Hunting for gifts from the rich through many flattering courtesies, they slaughter both their own souls and those of the rich, as it is written: “Woe to you who sew cushions under every elbow of the hand, and pillows under the head of every age, to catch souls” (Ezek. 13:18). And again: “My people, those who call you blessed are themselves deceiving you and destroying the paths of your steps” (Isa. 3:12).

What is it to place cushions under elbows or pillows under heads, except to caress the life of secular people with flattering words—when we ought rather to correct it with harsh rebukes and draw them to repentance by the terror of the divine judgment and the punishments of Gehenna? Once we have received their gifts, we leave them more secure in their iniquities, as they trust in the assistance of our prayers. They do not believe that they have wrongly acquired or possess those things from which they see religious men request alms. When we accept such gifts, we frequently become partners in the mammon of iniquity.

Concerning this “mammon of iniquity,” so called by the Lord, blessed Jerome, writing to Edibia on various questions—“Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9) [Note: [Col. 0589D] *Ibid.*, col. 985]—well said “of iniquity”:

> “For all riches descend from iniquity; and unless one person loses, another cannot find. Hence that common saying seems to me most true: ‘The rich man is either wicked or the heir of a wicked man.’”

Seneca, in the *Proverbs*, says:

> “Profit cannot be made without another’s loss.”

Likewise the aforesaid doctor, on Isaiah [Note: [Col. 0590D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIV, col. 39], concerning “Your princes are companions of thieves” (Isa. 1:23):

> “He calls the scribes and Pharisees princes, who, departing from the Lord, were companions of Judas the traitor and thief. We too must beware lest, receiving gifts from men who gather riches through robbery and the tears of the poor, we be called companions of thieves, and it be said to us: ‘You saw a thief, and ran with him,’ etc. (Ps. 49:18). All love gifts. He did not say those who receive them, for that often occurs through necessity; but there are those who do not consider anyone a friend except those from whom they have received gifts. They do not look at their friends’ faces but at their hands, and judge those holy whose purses they empty. Ecclesiastes also speaks of them: ‘He who loves money shall not be satisfied with money’ (Eccl. 5:9). They expect repayment, so that they may praise those from whom they have received something, or certainly give nothing to anyone unless they expect to receive something from him.”

But if anyone carefully considers what the Lord says, “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity”—that is, wealth wrongly acquired by yourselves or others, received to our profit from another’s loss—and wishes to apply more fittingly the Lord’s counsel in the preceding parable about the steward, he will see that it should be understood thus: we must restore their losses to those from whom we have taken what was theirs, and so reconcile them to friendship with us, whom we had stirred up to hatred of us. For we do not make the true poor of Christ our friends by our gifts, since they love even their enemies; rather, we make friends of those whom we have mentioned, and in the way mentioned. The parable which the Lord had set forth concerning the steward carefully expresses this: he restored their losses to those to whom he had caused them; he did not distribute to others what he had received from them. He is also said to be received by them into eternal dwellings when he has done for them that by which he deserves to be received, not so much into his own as into God’s heavenly dwellings.

Who, moreover, does not know how much our religion is despised even by those whom we do not refuse to visit when invited, and from whom we not only accept gifts but also mingle with their disorderly tables and households? If not for reverence toward God, we ought at least to avoid this for fear of harm to our reputation. For it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Withdraw from one more powerful who summons you, for this reason he will summon you all the more” (Ecclus. 13:12). And Jerome, to Nepotian [Note: [Col. 0591D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 539], says:

> “A cleric who does not refuse to go to dinner whenever invited is easily despised. Let us never ask, and rarely accept when asked. For I do not know how it is that even the person who begs to give, after you have received, judges you cheaper.”

If this is blameworthy in clerics, how much more detestable is it in monks?

But to omit for the moment the teachings of the saints: let even the examples of pagan philosophers restrain the shamelessness of our greed. Without any profession of a rule, they so despised the world that they not only rejected the gifts of the powerful but even renounced very extensive possessions. Some of them are reported to have been content with such frugality that they judged it superfluous to retain even a single cup, seeing that their own hands sufficed to draw a drink of water.

The aforesaid teacher, in the second book *Against Jovinianus*, presents that most famous Diogenes, well known for contempt of the world; among his other praises he adds this also [Note: [Col. 0592D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXII, col. 305]:

> “Once, when he had a wooden cup for drinking, he saw a boy drink from his cupped hand; he is said to have dashed it to the ground, saying: ‘I did not know that nature too had a cup.’”

When the most powerful Alexander offered him many gifts and stood beside his tub like an importunate giver, Diogenes is said to have received from him only this reply: “Young man, do not stand between me and the sun.” Socrates likewise, rejecting the gifts of King Archelaus, offered as his sole excuse that he did not wish to receive such great things when he could not return their equal.

Seneca, *On Benefits*, Book V:

> “Alexander of Macedon used to boast that he had been overcome in benefits by no one. Again, King Archelaus asked Socrates to come to him. Socrates is reported to have said that he did not wish to come to one from whom he would receive benefits when he could not return equal ones. First, it was in that man’s power not to receive; then he himself began to give an equal benefit. For he would come when asked and would give what Archelaus certainly was not going to return to Socrates. Nor was Archelaus going to give gold and silver and receive contempt for gold and silver. Could Socrates not return Archelaus’ favor? What if he had admitted the king, wandering in broad daylight, to the nature of things? What if he had prevented him from denying it? Why, then, did Socrates say this—he, a witty man, whose speech was accustomed to proceed by figures, and who mocked above all the powerful? He preferred to refuse him shrewdly rather than stubbornly or proudly. Perhaps he feared that he would be compelled to accept what he did not wish; he feared that he might receive something unworthy of Socrates. Someone will say: ‘He would have refused if he had not wished it, but he would have provoked against himself an arrogant king, who wanted everything belonging to him to be greatly valued.’ Do you wish to know what he truly wanted? He did not wish to go into voluntary slavery—he whose freedom a free city could not endure.”

But if we wish to ascend from philosophers to apostles—indeed, to Christ himself, Wisdom—as from lesser things to greater, so that, more fully instructed by their examples and authority, we may reject gifts more willingly, let us set before us Paul, the Church’s greatest teacher. He did not consent to receive not only gifts but even what was owed him, lest, as he himself says, he diminish his glory or leave others an occasion for shameful gain by his example. Although, by the authority of the Law and the Lord’s institution, he deserved to receive his sustenance from the labor of preaching, as the other apostles did, he nevertheless feared to use this right, as he himself says, for the causes mentioned above; and he was most careful not to give any stumbling-block to Christ’s Gospel (1 Cor. 9:12).

For this man of most discerning judgment and generous spirit foresaw that, if he reaped material things by sowing spiritual things, he might seem to eat in order to evangelize rather than evangelize in order to eat; to do this from ambition rather than charity; and to seek not so much what belongs to Christ as what belongs to himself. If, then, he blushed to receive even what was due to him from so great a harvest of souls, lest he incur a shameful suspicion, how great is our shamelessness! We receive sustenance not through entreaty or the conversion of people, but extort it, if we can, by any art from the flattery of the powerful.

Sometimes we burst into such disgrace that, enlarging our phylacteries (Matt. 23:5), and sometimes carrying about shrines containing relics of saints, we roam through the world with preaching for sale; and sometimes, having hired false preachers, we gain through lies what we cannot gain through truth. If at times we distribute something under the pretext of alms, we certainly do so in order to receive greater things; and, as it were, place a little bait on a hook in order to draw out a large fish. We bestow benefits not so much upon others as upon ourselves, and show charity not so much to others as to ourselves—if in such matters either benefit or charity can be called such.

For Seneca, the greatest builder of moral character, asserts that a benefit exists only toward another, and blessed Gregory says the same of charity. The former, in the aforementioned *On Benefits*, says [Note: [Col. 0593D] Seneca, *De beneficiis*, vol. IV, Book V, 9, p. 306, Panckoucke edition, 1837]:

> “No one gives a benefit to himself, but obeys his own nature, by which he is disposed to self-love; nor is someone liberal who gives to himself. A benefit is something given not for one’s own sake but for the sake of the person to whom it is given. But he who gives himself a benefit gives for his own sake; therefore it is not a benefit.”

Jerome says:

> “He sends his disciples out two by two to preach. For there are two commandments of charity, namely love of God and of neighbor; and charity cannot exist among fewer than two. No one is properly said to have charity toward himself; rather, he extends himself in love toward another, so that charity may exist. The Lord sends his disciples two by two to preach, silently indicating to us that one who does not have charity toward another ought by no means to undertake the office of preaching.”

Therefore, when this is done not for gain of souls but of coins, in accordance with the Lord’s complaint through Jeremiah, “My priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’” (Jer. 2:8)—as though he said, “but, ‘Where is the coin?’”—it ought to be called not benefit but gain, not charity but greed. The aforesaid Apostle strongly dissuades us from this shameful gain, both by his own and by the Lord’s example; repressing our shamelessness, he says, as Luke relates in the Acts of the Apostles: “I have coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing. You yourselves know that these hands supplied what was needed for me and for those who were with me. I showed you all things, because by laboring thus we ought to support the weak, and remember the word of the Lord Jesus, because he himself said: ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive’” (Acts 20:33).

Christ himself plainly indicates how much more his hand was extended to give than to receive when he answered the rich man consulting him about the perfection of righteousness: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). He did not say, “Come and bring what you have to us,” but, “First distribute what is yours to others, and then afterward receive what is ours.” But we, on the contrary, when anyone comes to conversion, seek not so much the gain of his soul as of his money; we urge him to bring what he possesses, and we do not so much give him what is ours as sell it to him. In this we certainly give him no small occasion of temptation. For he easily becomes puffed up over what he brought; when anything is lacking to him, he is indignant and murmurs; and he calls himself wretched and betrayed when he sees himself made equal with those who brought less, or nothing at all.

Christ, therefore, cutting off all these occasions, decreed that a man should be received rather stripped than laden with baggage. For he who had commanded his disciples, “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10:8), wished first to display this in himself, desiring to urge us toward it not so much by his word as by his example. He who leaves his own possessions for God’s sake shamelessly demands those of others. And it would be far better and more honorable for him to have retained his own property, so that he might have the means for the fruit of almsgiving from what was his, [Col. 0594B] than, while begging for what belongs to others, to incur injury to his reputation and grievously harm the dignity of the religious profession he has undertaken.

For while they draw upon others’ purses, they undoubtedly gather things that are most contrary to religion and, according to the Lord’s parable, plant thorns that will choke the Lord’s harvest. For what is more fitting for religion than frugality and voluntary poverty? What is more harmful than an abundance of possessions? Hence even the philosophers of the Gentiles did not think that virtues could be retained together with riches. One of them—to pass over the rest—was that man whom Jerome, setting before us an example of contempt for the world in the aforementioned book *Against Jovinian*, describes thus: “That Crates of Thebes, having cast no small weight of gold into the sea, said: ‘Sink to the bottom, evil desires! I shall drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.’” Likewise, in his letter to the presbyter Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0594D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 580]:

> “Crates of Thebes, once a very wealthy man, when he was going to Athens for philosophy, threw away a great weight of gold; nor did he think that he could possess both virtue and riches at the same time. We, loaded down with gold, follow poor Christ; and, under the pretext of almsgiving, clinging to our former wealth, how can we faithfully distribute others’ goods when we timidly keep back our own?”

The same Jerome, to Pammachius on the death of Paulina [Note: [Col. 0594D] *Ibid.*, col. 644], says:

> “It is surely no great thing for a perfected man to despise wealth, scatter money, and throw away what can in a moment both be lost and found. Crates of Thebes did this; Antisthenes did it; [Col. 0594D] many did it—men whom we read to have been most vicious. Christ’s disciple ought to do more than the philosopher of the world. Christ is sanctification; Christ is redemption; he is both redeemer and price. Christ is all things, so that he who has forsaken all things for Christ may find the One in place of all, and may freely proclaim: ‘The Lord is my portion’ (Ps. 72:26).”

There are also those who, coming forth from monasteries into the world, so claim for themselves the name of religion and desire to seem extraordinary that they pretend to possess even the grace of miracles, and glory in having such things proclaimed about them. We have seen several such men in our own times. They ought especially to have fled the crowds of men, [Col. 0595A] yet by this very art they summoned them. Indeed, by this pretence they hunt so zealously for the favor of the powerful or of ecclesiastical authorities that, abandoning the monastic profession, they are set as bishops over secular clergy.

Since they bring no religion with them, they readily decline into the secular manner of life; and, because of the wretched conduct of such men and their separation from their religious brethren, they either fail to consider or despise that well-known saying of the Psalmist: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will become perverse” (Ps. 17:27). Concerning their exaltation—into which they have been thrust not so much by others as by themselves—the words addressed to God are not inappropriately understood: “You cast them down while they were being lifted up” (Ps. 72:18). For it is certain that [Col. 0595B] spiritual men compelled from the quiet of a monastery into episcopal administration are diminished, amid the occupations of so many concerns, in that grace of virtues which they had possessed—as Martin confesses concerning himself, and blessed Gregory laments.

If, then, men so great could not pass from Mary to Martha without loss of their former virtues, what judgment remains to be made about those of whom we have spoken? “Monks,” they say, “are barren, whereas the fruitfulness of spiritual children is more blessed.” But are marriages to be preferred to continence, or married women with children to virgins? Did the fruitful but bleary-eyed Leah prove more pleasing to the patriarch than the beauty of barren Rachel? Finally, Rachel, envying her sister’s fruitfulness, when she had in this matter also fulfilled her supreme desire, was extinguished by her very childbirth; and she who had lived unharmed while barren incurred death through her fruitfulness. Such indeed are these men, who pant after the episcopate. When they are recalled from monasteries to the world and glory that, as it is said, they become fruitful from being barren, they incur peril to their religious profession through this very glory of rank.

The bride in the Song of Songs carefully observes this when the bridegroom knocks at her door and asks that it be opened to him. Lest she consent to this very thing, she excuses herself with such words: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5:3). For what is meant by the bride resting upon her bed, if not the faithful soul which, having left behind the tumultuous life of the world, loves the tranquillity [Col. 0595D] of solitude all the more because there she serves God more freely? When the faithful people require her for their governance, so that she may become entangled in ecclesiastical affairs, Christ knocks, as it were, at the door of her cell in his members and asks that it be opened to him. That is, he asks her to admit the faithful rather than exclude them, to bear with presiding over them, and to set the salvation of many before her own perfection.

But she, guarding against the temptations of the world and unwilling to endure diminution of her merits, offers this response as an excuse to the devotion of those knocking: “I have put off my tunic” (*ibid.*); that is, I have voluntarily abandoned the outward care of the world. For the tunic, which is worn over the shirt or skin garment, signifies the external administration of secular affairs. [Col. 0596A] “I have washed my feet”; that is, I have cleansed my affections from the defilements of secular temptations and purged them from the enticements of worldly cares. For we are borne along by our feet, and by our affections we are drawn to the accomplishment of an act; therefore affections are expressed through feet.

She fears to set her feet down from the bed upon the ground lest they be defiled, because she never considers true cleanliness to exist outside the seclusion of her repose. Hence, when the Lord washed even the apostles’ feet, he clearly indicated that not even perfected men can walk through the world without some contagion of dust. That is, no one can long live amid the temptations and enticements of the world without [Col. 0596B] the effects of some stain from our weakness being sprinkled upon him, even if temptation does not draw him all the way into action.

Brothers, perhaps I seem to have extended our discourse by a lengthy—indeed superfluous—digression and to have departed too far from the beginning of our purpose. I had begun to praise John, as the dignity of today’s feast required, but have now turned my pen from that subject toward our rebuke—seemingly incurring the fault of those who deserve Cicero’s criticism: they cannot praise some persons unless they censure others, nor exalt any unless they bring others low.

But because our discourse today aims not so much at John’s praise as at our own edification—for what is written is done not for the benefit of earlier persons but for the edification of those who come after—so we began to commend [Col. 0596C] John’s life as that of our leader chiefly in order to provoke ourselves to imitate him. We decided that this could not be done carefully unless, after setting forth his perfection, we noted by comparison what our own imperfection lacked, placed our defect before our eyes alongside his advance, and reproved in ourselves the opposite of those things which we praised in him.

For behold: monks are so called from solitude, that is, they are solitary persons. Although *monos* (μόνος) is translated “one,” a monk is not called “one” merely as an individual person, as any member of the populace may be, but because of his manner of living a solitary life. Hence Augustine, commenting on Psalm 132, says:

> “From the utterance of this psalm monks also received their name. Why, then, are we called monks, when the Psalmist says: ‘Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one’ (Ps. 132:1)? For *monos* means ‘one,’ and not one in just any manner. A person may be one in a crowd, yet he cannot be called *monos*—that is, alone—while he is one with many. Therefore those who so live together as one that they make one human being, so that there is for them, truly, as it is written, one soul and one heart (Acts 4:32), are rightly called *monos*, that is, one alone.”

Likewise Jerome, writing to the monk Heliodorus [Note: [Col. 0595D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 350], says: “Interpret the word *monk*: that is your name. What are you doing in a crowd, you who are alone?” And later [Note: [Col. 0596D] *Ibid.*, col. 354]:

> “O [Col. 0597A] desert, more familiar in rejoicing with God! What are you doing, brother, in the world—you who are greater than the world? How long will the shadows of roofs oppress you? How long will the prison of famous cities confine you?”

And to the presbyter Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0597D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, cols. 582–583]:

> “Since, therefore, brother, you ask me what path you ought to take, I shall speak to you with unveiled face. If you wish to perform the office of the presbyterate, if perhaps either the work or burden of the episcopate delights you, live in cities and towns, and make the salvation of others the gain of your own soul. But if you desire to be what you are called, a monk—that is, one alone—what are you doing in cities, which are surely dwellings not of solitary persons but of many?”

And to the monk Rusticus [Note: [Col. 0598D] *Ibid.*, col. 1076]:

> “The sons of Jonadab, who drank neither wine nor strong drink in tents and had their dwellings wherever night compelled them, are written of in [Col. 0597B] the psalm as having first undergone captivity, because they were compelled to enter cities when the army of the Chaldeans was devastating Judaea. Let others see what they think; for each person is led by his own judgment. To me a town is a prison, and solitude a paradise. Why do we desire the crowding of cities, we who take our designation from singleness? Moses, in order to preside over the people of the Jews, was trained for forty years in the desert. A shepherd of sheep became a shepherd of men.”

And observe that this letter of Jerome, written to a monk, is entitled not so much from the title “monk” as from that of “presbyter.” For that most discerning teacher judged that one who had not yet passed into solitude ought to be called a presbyter rather than a monk.

[Col. 0597C] But what is to be said of monks who not only do not flee cities or the dwellings of secular persons, but even seek them out? John, indeed, embraced solitude with all the greater desire because he saw that in it he could serve God more perfectly. Hence we rightly recalled, in his praise, the words spoken beforehand by the Lord: “To whom I gave a home in the wilderness” (Job 39:6). Once he withdrew from the world into the desert; thereafter he was never recalled to the world by any occasion of piety or necessity of want, until Herod had him carried off to prison, where he joined the rose of martyrdom to the lily of virginity.

Though he seemed so great that he might have been believed to be Christ, and though everyone sought him in the wilderness with the keenest longing, he might easily have corrected many things in the cities and persuaded secular people, if he had judged it fitting for any reason [Col. 0597D] to return to the world. Who also does not know that, at the time when he was to succeed his father in the high priesthood, blindness had already come upon Israel, and that his religious character would have carried great weight in this office? How much more fitting it would have been for him than for Annas and Caiaphas to serve as high priest, if we consider human judgment rather than divine ordering. Nevertheless, at the very time when he seems to have had the greatest reputation for becoming high priest, he preferred monastic life to the pontificate and chose the merit of a better life for himself rather than the advantage of others.

Having once withdrawn from the world, therefore, he remained immovable in the desert. Although everyone from Jerusalem, [Col. 0598A] Judaea, and the region around the Jordan went out to him for baptism or edification, he himself went in to no one; and having once broken his bonds, he utterly refused afterward to bind them again. The more he fled men and appeared less often to them, the dearer he was to all, and the more keenly they sought him.

Even the Lord himself did not disdain to go out to him with the people and was baptized by him along with them, as Luke also records: “It came to pass, when all the people were baptized, and when Jesus also had been baptized,” and so forth (Luke 3:21). The Lord came to his servant; the supreme high priest came to the monk, to receive baptism from him and to receive testimony from him, as another Evangelist also recalls: “John saw Jesus coming to him and said, ‘Behold, the Lamb of God,’” and so forth [Col. 0598B] (John 1:29).

Nor did the Lord come to him only once, but often, whereas we never read that John came to the Lord. The Lord could have sent for him, that he might come to him to baptize him or that he might lay upon him the office of apostleship as upon the others, had he judged this fitting. But he to whom nothing was hidden surely knew that it did not suit the purpose of so great a life for John to be recalled to the world, and that he would thereby readily become cheapened and his testimony would no longer carry such authority.

For he who had preferred Mary’s part to Martha’s part (Luke 10:41) did not judge it suitable to John’s excellence to compel him to come from Mary’s rest to Martha’s labor. He also knew what he himself, long ago under the person of the bridegroom, had commanded concerning the bride: “Do not rouse or awaken my beloved until she herself wishes” (Song 2:7). He who, as we recalled above, had abandoned the high priesthood due to him would certainly not willingly take up the apostleship. And he who could not bear to live in a city would much less consent to travel throughout the world.

Brothers, “monk” or “hermit” is a name of religious profession. “Bishop” or “cleric,” however, is a term of office and work rather than devotion. Hence the Apostle says: “He who desires the episcopate desires a good work” (1 Tim. 3:1). Elsewhere the same Apostle says of himself and those like him: “Let a person so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards,” and so forth (1 Cor. 4:1).

In the Lord’s household, the bride who remains in the seclusion of the bridal chamber and the servant [Col. 0598D] who attends to outward matters are not of the same rank, although the servant also exercises some care and concern for the bride herself. Thus, in the Church of God, the laborious occupation of clerics and bishops is not to be equated with the peaceful contemplation of monastic life—so far, that is, as the measure of merit is concerned, not ecclesiastical dignity.

Hence we often see not only clerics but even bishops descend to the humility of monks for the correction of their lives, changing their habit along with their life. But the Church does not usually presume to call monks to the offices of clerics except only to the highest rank of priesthood; and this, as we have said, is not without some loss to their religious profession. [Col. 0599A] When this happens, the man who has become a bishop, though he diminishes his religious practice, nevertheless does not change the habit of religion.

Even the sons of priests pass into this religious profession. Though they bear such a stain of disgrace from the adultery of their parents that they are not permitted even to receive ecclesiastical tonsure, once they have become monks, the whole stain is wiped away by the washing of holiness, so that afterward they may ascend through every rank of ecclesiastical orders to the height of the episcopate. Finally, how greatly monks surpass clerics in merits is attested by ecclesiastical custom itself, when in the supplication of the litany all say: “All holy monks and hermits, pray for us.” But no one presumes to say: “All holy clerics, bishops, or canons, pray for us.” For their names or manner of life do not excel in holiness as those of monks and hermits do.

If, therefore, this is so—indeed, because it is so—namely, that monastic life surpasses episcopal administration in holiness, just as conversely the latter surpasses the former in the dignity of precedence, surely no one who desires holiness more than dignity would be willing to abandon or diminish the former for the sake of the latter.

“But perhaps,” you will say, “monks take up this burden unwillingly, constrained by obedience to their superiors; and, especially for the advantage of others, they endure loss to their religious profession, choosing rather to possess a moderate merit in common with many than a great merit alone.” Would that this were so: that they were indeed dragged unwillingly and, at least with the intention we have described, were made bishops from monks for the salvation of others. Conversely, as has been said, bishops are sometimes made monks because they seek their own salvation.

But surely, just as it is credible that those who voluntarily pass from riches to poverty do so for the sake of religion, so, if the opposite happens, it is judged most likely to occur from ambition. The subsequent life indicates the intention with which they began: namely, when bishops live more laxly and softly than they did as monks and conduct themselves more luxuriously both in food and clothing. We see no one who does not do this. If anyone did not do it—that is, if he abounded in luxuries without feeling their force—we should judge him to be above human nature. Yet they declare themselves strong-minded because they trust that they can possess, along with religion, the very things most hostile to religion, which others renounce for religion’s sake.

Nor do any such persons seem to withdraw from tempting God. For what else is it to tempt God than voluntarily to expose oneself to a danger which one can avoid? For example, if someone throws himself into flames, trusting that divine power will deliver him from them, though he can guard against that danger without harm to his soul, that is surely to tempt God. What, moreover, are riches or the enticements of the world but certain flames or incitements of vices, which compel the soul to burn with carnal desires?

But if perhaps you answer that you are compelled to this burden [Col. 0600A] by obedience, or that you cannot refuse it at all without harm to your soul, I do not think that anyone should readily believe you. When you plead obedience as your reason, know that everyone whispers this proverb about you: “A sufficiently shrewd man knows whose beard he licks.” Certainly, when a bishop or abbot, under the name of obedience, invites a monk to become a bishop, he does not doubt that his command will be obtained, even when he sees the monk resist in words as he imposes it, accuse himself as unworthy, and sometimes shed whatever tears he can produce.

For ambition after honor is so naturally implanted in everyone that, once a person has attained the rank for which he formerly judged himself unworthy, he strives by every means to claim and defend it for himself. When accused so as to seem worthy of deposition, he labors as much as he can to excuse himself so that he may retain the honor he has received—though before receiving it he deemed himself unworthy of it. From this it is clear that that excuse was more pretended than true, and that he presides in this position more through desire than compulsion. For the proverb is well known to all: “What is possessed without love is lost without pain.”

“But,” you say, “blessed Augustine opposes to me this saying” [Note: [Col. 0599D] *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 448]: “He who neglects his reputation is cruel.” You will add also that it causes great harm if evil persons cast down the good by fabricated accusations and wickedness prevails over holiness. But a man who has been dragged by force to the episcopate can readily guard against this danger and loss of reputation, [Col. 0600C] relinquishing with honor what he does not possess with love, rather than waiting for it to be taken from him.

For if he is unwilling to render the proper reverence to his superiors or care to his subjects arising from the office he has accepted, and thus shows that he truly bears the burden unwillingly, he can provide at once for both his reputation and his soul. But if, trusting in his own holiness, he judges that he can suffice for this administration better than others, that is surely most proud, and he falls into Elijah’s presumption, when he said: “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I alone am left, and they seek my life.” But what, says the Apostle, was God’s answer to him? “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee before Baal” (Rom. [Col. 0600D] 11:3, 5). “So then at this present time also a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace,” and so forth.

If, then, so great a prophet, in preferring himself to others, was corrected by the Lord for this rash judgment of his presumption, which of us, having attained no grace of prophecy, dares judge himself better than others—especially since this is, according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, utterly remote from the profession of monastic religion? Hence in the aforementioned Rule, chapter 7, where Benedict instructs the monk concerning the degrees of humility, he says [Note: [Col. 0600D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXVI, col. 396]:

> “The seventh degree of humility is this: that a monk should not only pronounce himself inferior and more worthless than all with his tongue, but should also believe it in the inmost disposition of his heart,”

[Col. 0601A] humbling himself and saying with the Prophet: “But I am a worm,” and so forth (Ps. 21:7).

But how can anyone chosen from a congregation judge himself inferior to the others and consent to be placed in a rank for which a better person than he is worthy? Or else it is indeed pernicious to judge others inferior to oneself and not heed the Apostle’s words: “Who are you, who judge another’s servant?” (Rom. 14:4), especially since, according to Bede, we ought to interpret doubtful matters in the better sense. The Apostle too, observing this, after he had said: “Who are you, who judge another’s servant? Before his own Lord he stands or falls,” added: “But he shall stand”—turning what was doubtful to the better interpretation.

For what is more dangerous, or more inclined to pride, than to consider others inferior to oneself, even if they seem inferior and unequal in merits? Thus the Pharisee, looking at the publican, immediately swelled with pride and, judging himself great by comparison with one lower than himself, lost the merits he had possessed. Conversely, the publican, by comparison with the other as with one greater than himself, increased in merits through humility (Luke 10:18 and following). Nothing draws us toward pride as much as looking upon our inferiors and observing in them the goods they lack. Nothing is so conducive to acquiring or preserving humility as looking upon those who precede us in merits, so that we may know what we ourselves lack, not what others lack.

The Apostle carefully considers this when he writes to the Philippians: “Brothers, I do not yet judge myself to have attained. [Col. 0601C] But one thing: forgetting those things which are behind and stretching myself toward those which are before, I press on toward the appointed prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (Phil. 3:13–15). “Therefore, all of us who are perfect should think this.”

What the Lord had offered as counsel for restraining pride, by setting before us the parable of the Pharisee and the publican, the Apostle afterward urged by his own example, saying that he did not yet judge himself to have attained that toward which he strove—that is, that he had not yet acquired the degree of merit which he desired. He carefully explains how he can attain it, saying that he occupied himself with this one thing: that he should forget what lies behind and stretch himself toward what lies before. That is, in the works or merits of persons he should adopt this principle: he should look to those who are before him in dignity as examples for imitation, not look back toward those who are behind him.

For no one, as the Lord himself says, who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). Whoever hastens toward good works, if he looks upon persons worse than himself rather than considering those better than himself, closes to himself the entrance to the heavenly kingdom, because, through comparison with inferiors, he has greater confidence in his own merits. So did that Pharisee who, when he should have looked to Abraham and the Fathers superior in merits, looked instead at the publican, whom he judged inferior in merits.

Thus, brothers, when a man chosen from the company of monks for the episcopate compares himself with the others as inferiors, judging himself worthier than them for this administration, it would be astonishing—indeed, very astonishing—if he did not fall into self-exaltation because he was chosen while the others were rejected. To employ the argumentative form of rhetoric which Jerome calls the “horned syllogism”: surely he either judges himself better than the others and worthier of this office, or he does not judge so.

If he judges himself better, then the further he departs from the humility of a monk, the more grievously he falls into pride; and by the very fact that he believes himself better, he makes himself worse. If he does not judge himself better than the others for this office, but judges himself either equal to them or inferior, a considerable danger also arises. If he judges himself equal, he falls away from the canon stated above in the Rule, which commands, for the preservation of humility, that he should judge himself inferior to the others not only in speech but also in heart. But if, as he ought, he judges himself worse, let him see how great is the presumption of occupying the place of one better than himself and, through ambition, committing the sacrilege of robbery.

Finally, when the Apostle carefully describes a bishop, saying: “A bishop, therefore, must be irreproachable, the husband of one wife, a teacher, not covetous, ruling his own household well, having children in subjection with all chastity. But if anyone does not know how to rule his own household, how shall he take care of the Church of God? He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside, lest he fall into reproach” (1 Tim. 3:2), and so forth.

He has carefully collected many points in his description of the man worthy of election to episcopal dignity. We have brought forward only a few of them in this place, but those which we believe sufficient for people who claim that they are unwillingly dragged to the episcopate to put forward as an excuse for themselves. For if they tell those who are drawing them that they want to hear the apostolic judgment on this matter and to learn from the Apostle himself what sort of bishop should be chosen, then, when the description set forth by the Apostle has been read in full, no one, unless I am mistaken, will find grounds on which he can reasonably excuse himself from following the Apostle—or rather, the Spirit of God speaking in him—rather than human compulsion.

For why did he place “irreproachable” immediately at the head of the description? Who, anxious for his salvation, upon hearing this would not immediately draw back and consider rather that saying of another Apostle: “For we all offend in many things” (James 3:2)? How much more carefully must we consider what he added in second place: “the husband of one wife”; and afterward supplied the reason, saying: “having children in subjection with all chastity. But if anyone does not know how to rule his own household,” and so forth.

For, advising that persons proven in the world be transferred from lesser matters to greater, according to the Lord’s saying, “He who is faithful in a little thing is faithful also in a greater” (Luke 16:10), he especially offers this counsel: that those who had been married and had proved themselves to have behaved well in household care should take, as it were, a spiritual wife and undertake care of the Lord’s house. The Lord himself demonstrated this by his own example when, gathering the twelve apostles, who occupy the place of bishops, he chose none or few except married men.

And although he loved John, a virgin, more than Peter, who had experienced the union of marriage and long ruled his household, he nevertheless did not appoint John, as he did Peter, prince of the apostles. Therefore the less a person chosen from the monastic community has been tested in caring for a wife and household, the more he should hesitate to approach the episcopate. And the less he has experienced the office of teacher, according to Jerome’s saying [Note: [Col. 0603D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIII, col. 351], “A monk has not the office of teacher but of one who mourns: he mourns for himself and the world, and in fear awaits the Lord’s coming,” the less he knows what to teach the people, since he has lived all his time separated from the people.

Finally, consider what the Apostle says: that he must have a good testimony even from those who are outside. Consider how difficult it is for someone selected from subjection for authority, transferred from poverty to abundance, to retain a good reputation where an opinion of ambition creeps in more strongly than one of religion. Yet let no one object to me that in ancient times many men were drawn from monastic religion to the episcopate, and through them the Church increased into a great harvest of faithful people and an abundance of virtues. We too know these things and do not deny what is known.

But, instructed by recent experience, we distinguish the times; and, comparing the present with the past, we find that the office of bishop ought now to be refused all the more laudably and beneficially because it was once accepted all the more laudably and beneficially. Then the name of bishop was honorable and the office wholesome, when bishops took upon themselves not so much an honor as a burden; when the Church had not yet been enriched with any wealth but was afflicted by continual tribulations; when, during raging persecution, unbelievers first or most fiercely persecuted in it those whom they knew to be placed at its head.

But now that the Church has obtained bodily peace, as blessed Augustine recalls in the first book of *The City of God* [Note: [Col. 0604D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, cols. 21–22], we endure inward oppressions from vices far more grievous than those once inflicted by enemies from without. For now, in a most evil freedom, giving ourselves over to gluttony, drunkenness, and every luxury, we become murderers of our own souls, just as those earlier men were murderers of bodies; and the Church perishes through civil and internal wars, as Rome formerly was destroyed.

For, as though it belonged to episcopal rank to abound in riches just as it belongs to authority to perish, they do not judge themselves to exercise the episcopate worthily unless they live more splendidly and more luxuriously. Forgetting the bread that formerly served them for food, and returning in heart from the wilderness to Egypt, they shamelessly cling to pots of meat. Though they glory in apostolic dignity, they utterly flee the blessed poverty and frugality of the apostles, which the Lord laid down for them as a foundation when he said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). By these words he clearly showed that heaven is earned not through the honor of authority [Col. 0604A] but through the burden of voluntary poverty.

How great, moreover, is the shamelessness of such bishops who have been made from monks: they retain the monastic habit yet do not live monastically—indeed, they act altogether contrary to their profession. Who does not see how shameless this is? Who does not know of such men, to use the Apostle’s words, that “they have made void their first faith” (1 Tim. 5:12), and how contrary they are found to the holy Fathers who were similarly promoted? Blessed Martin did not exchange the austerity of haircloth or food for episcopal preeminence. Therefore, in this office he sought not what was his own, but what was Jesus Christ’s. Finally, who does not marvel at what they have grown accustomed to presume in this age: namely, that when necessity requires them to go to Rome to the supreme pontiff, they also lay aside the habit of monastic religion, so that under lay dress they may more freely dare to live secularly on the road, and by a most wicked pretence falsely deny, both in fact and word, that they are what they are? Retaining not even the signs of clerical status, they let both hair and beard grow, so that they may more easily deceive those who see them and, more safely beneath the dress of buffoons, behave buffoonishly; thus apostatizing alike from the purpose of monk and bishop, they possess neither a monk’s merit nor preserve a bishop’s reverence.

Our aforesaid wild ass condemns them all the more strongly because, without professing monastic religion, he displayed the monk more perfectly and preferred the austerity of this life to episcopal dignity. Nor was the grace of miracles bestowed on him by the Lord, so that he might more readily avoid crowds of people; for he himself, as is written of John, “performed no sign” (John 10:41). How harmful this grace is to monks’ quiet and humility was carefully considered by the man whom Postumianus, writing of his journey, introduced as an example of a grace not to be sought—indeed, one that we must flee with the utmost care.

Although this man’s holiness had, among other things, obtained a singular grace in casting out demons, and although he saw that he was troubled on this account both by crowds of people and by empty glory, he asked the Lord to give those very demons whom he expelled power over himself, and that he might likewise suffer for the same number of months during which he had cured others of this oppression. Having obtained this from the Lord, he was seized by a demon, held in chains, and endured all the things which the possessed are accustomed to suffer. At last, in the fifth month, he was cleansed—not, however, of the demon, but, what was more useful and desirable to him, of vanity.

“But,” says Postumianus, “as I recount these things, our own unhappiness, our own weakness, comes before me.” For which of us is there whom, if one humble or foolish little man greets him and a single woman praises him with flattering words, is not immediately lifted up with pride and at once puffed up with vanity? Or even if he has no consciousness of holiness, nevertheless, because through the flattery or perhaps the error of fools he is called holy, will he not think himself most holy? And if frequent gifts are sent to him, he declares that he is honoured by God’s magnificence, since necessities are supplied to him while he sleeps and lives at ease. If even a few signs of virtue should attend him, he would think himself an angel.

Yet when he is distinguished neither by deed nor by virtue, if he has become a cleric, he immediately lengthens his fringes, delights in greetings, and swells at being met. He himself runs about everywhere. He who formerly used to go on foot or by little ass rides proudly upon a foaming horse. Once content to live in a small and cheap cell, he raises lofty ceilings, constructs many chambers, carves doors, paints cupboards, rejects rough clothing, desires soft garments, and assigns these expenses to dear widows and intimate virgins: one is to weave him a stiff cloak, the other a flowing mantle. But let us leave these matters to be described more bitingingly by the blessed man Jerome.

What will those say to this whom we have seen in our time presume so far as, emerging from solitude into crowds, to desire to be thought remarkable—just as they were puffed up by a counterfeit name of religion, so too by a pretence of the grace of miracles? I pass over touchings and blessings of waters which they sent to the sick to drink for healing; the handling or signing of limbs, to drive away sufferers’ pains; and blessed portions broken from loaves and sent to the sick. I come to greater things: to those highest miracles, vainly attempted even in the raising of the dead [Col. 0605C].

We were astonished—and laughed—that Norbert recently presumed this, along with his fellow-apostle Farsitus. Long prostrate together in prayer before the people, and frustrated in their presumption, when they withdrew in confusion from their undertaking, they began shamelessly to rebuke the people, claiming that the people’s unbelief obstructed their devotion and steadfast faith. O cunning of the incautious! O frivolous excuse of the inexcusable! They may sometimes deceive some persons in such matters; but, according to Truth’s declaration, “nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed” (Luke 8:17), and, according to Jerome’s saying, a false report is soon crushed.

We are not ignorant of the devices of such persons. When they presume to cure feverish people of mild illnesses, they give remedies to several persons, whether in food or drink, or pronounce blessings or prayers over them. Their object is that, if healing follows in any fashion, it may be attributed to their holiness; but if not, it may be ascribed to the recipients’ unbelief or despair.

A certain shrewd layman is said to have given such advice to a poor woman known to him. When, as the story goes, she had fallen into extreme poverty and asked the aforesaid man for alms, he marvelled to see her begging when he had formerly known her prosperous. At length he advised her to pretend that she knew medicine: she should gather whatever herbs she could, prepare cures from them for sick people, and seek her livelihood by this art. He added [Col. 0606A] that if she gave anyone something as medicine and health followed for any reason in a person so treated, that healed person would attribute the cure to her medicine and would invite many others, following his example, to use her remedies. Thus in a short time she would gain herself a great reputation in medicine. But if her remedies had no effect in some cases, this would be attributed to the disease as incurable, and to the inability of any remedy’s power to prevail against death.

Why say more? She assented to the deceitful man in order to deceive many, and in the end acquired a great reputation among people for the effectiveness of her remedies. So these men, presuming upon miracles as she did upon medicines, clothe themselves in a certain mantle of pretence and presume to cure many slight fevers, so that when health follows in some cases, by whatever chance, it may be attributed to them. But when they fail in other cases, it is ascribed to the weak faith of those people, who were unworthy to receive or even to see these benefits.

Some also, glorying in the name of religion, when they cannot attain the grace of miracles—though this would most of all prove their religion—are accustomed to offer this in consolation to themselves: that miracles are no longer as necessary in this time, when faith has been strengthened, as they once were in the primitive Church. Supporting this also with the Apostle’s testimony, they say: “Tongues are for a sign, not to believers, but to unbelievers; prophecies, however, are not for unbelievers but for believers” (1 Cor. 14:22). Just as the various kinds of tongues suddenly bestowed upon anyone are regarded as a sign among unbelievers and received by them with great astonishment as something great, so that they may be moved to faith by such miracles, so also they say that all miracles are more necessary for unbelievers than believers. Therefore, in this age the grace of signs is not necessary for those who live among believers, in order that those who are already believers may become believers.

But assuredly, since “faith without works is dead” (James 2:20), and the servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it “shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:47), miracles seem necessary even in this time, no less for works to be supplied than for faith. Nor do we yet lack an abundance of unbelievers—heretics, Jews, and Gentiles alike [Col. 0606D]. For their conversion or for repressing their attack, miracles seem no less necessary now than formerly. But because there are none who have merited this grace, and because each person desires it not so much for others’ salvation as for display of himself, and because that faith has now wholly perished of which the Saviour said, “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move,’ and it will move” (Luke 17:6), those benefits of miracles have entirely ceased—benefits which the aforesaid wild ass, though not unworthy of them, refused, while those unworthy of them seek and shamelessly counterfeit them.

And so, not hearing the driver’s cry and seeking every green thing in the mountains [Col. 0607A], the more fully he did these things for his own glory, the more he turned them into our disgrace. For what tax-collector is as insatiable or importunate as the belly of monks—or rather of Epicurean pigs—of whom indeed Horace’s line says:

> “You will see me fat and sleek, with skin well cared for,
>
> whenever you wish to laugh at a pig from Epicurus’ herd.”
>
> (Horace, *Epistles*, Book I, epistle 4, verses 15–16.) [Note: Col. 0607D]

“You will now see me too, sleek, with skin well cared for, whenever you wish to laugh at a pig from Epicurus’ herd.” Any persons lean in the world, when they arrive at the feeding-grounds of monastic cloisters, become so enlarged and fattened in a short time that, if you visit them again after a little while, you can scarcely recognize them. Among a thousand laymen, if you add a few monks, you will more often find among the latter more fat men, more sleek men, more men intoxicated by excessive heat, and more bald heads.

## SERMON XXXIV

[Note: From the manuscript codex of the monastery of St Mary of the Hermits at Einsiedeln. Patristic edition.]

### On the Feast of the Innocents

[Col. 0607B]

If we look to bodily peace, today’s passion of the Innocents first declared how true was what Truth himself later said: “Do not think that I came to bring peace upon the earth; I came not to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10:34). For although his coming gave the world the greatest peace, after the earlier wars had ended under Augustus, he did not grant this peace to himself which he bestowed upon all others. We believe that this happened by no small providential ordering: namely, so that, when persecution of him began so swiftly, each of the faithful might take greatest comfort in his own experience, as the Lord himself, offering consolation beforehand to his disciples, said: “Remember my word which I spoke to you: a servant is not greater than his master; if they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:20).

Christ’s persecution was therefore begun from his very infancy and raged against infants, so that it might be shown all the more irrational: it cruelly pursues manifest innocence, so that punishment is ordered before age has the capacity to commit an act. Lest anyone perhaps accuse the Lord of cruelty because, himself avoiding persecution, he hid in Egypt and did not decree to free the innocence of the infants from it, let him know that this must rather be credited to the Lord’s mercy. For who does not know that those killed then would at some time have died? Or who can be certain that, if they had not been killed, they would have been saved—though no believer now doubts their salvation? Since this was bestowed on them by God’s grace alone, without any merits of their own, who would not praise God’s mercy rather than accuse him of cruelty?

Moreover, the suffering of death itself was lighter in them insofar as it was more momentary and unforeseen. “Herod,” says the Evangelist, “seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi, was exceedingly angry; and sending, he killed all the boys who were in Bethlehem,” and so forth (Matt. 2:16). Mocked by the Magi, he killed innocents who could neither mock nor sin [Col. 0608A]. Do you, impious man, think yourself mocked because you cannot accomplish the plot you conceived, because you are not permitted to forestall God’s ordinance by your crime, and because you seek to mock before being mocked, to deceive before being deceived, to inflict fraud before suffering error? Have you become so insensible that justice does not restrain you, humanity does not move you, and cruelty cannot spare those whom you do not doubt are innocent?

Made mad against others, you have been found more cruel against yourself: while persecuting the Son of God, you kill your own sons. Nor did even your own son remain immune from the cruelty of such wickedness. When he was killed with the others, the incomparable cruelty of your mockery was turned into a proverbial jest and left you the title you had earned—not one composed by Pilate in the Lord’s honour, but one proclaimed by Augustus in perpetual mockery of you.

Accordingly Macrobius, in Book II of the *Saturnalia*, recalling among other things Augustus and his jokes, says:

> “When he heard that among the boys whom Herod, king of the Jews, had ordered to be killed in Syria during his governorship, Herod’s own son had also been killed, he said: ‘It is better to be Herod’s pig than his son.’”

Augustus believed, to be sure, that Herod himself, as king of the Jews, abstained from pork according to his people’s custom, and therefore would not wish to kill pigs, from whose use he had determined to abstain [Col. 0608B].

Whether this was done knowingly, or through ignorance under the general edict of the royal power, is not sufficiently clear from the aforesaid words. It could indeed have happened that, disturbed by one infant, he feared all of them, suspected even his own son—through whom he might lose the kingdom—or believed that his grief for others might be eased in him. Therefore unrestrained madness ordered even him to be killed, so that the immensity of the crime might move all persons to astonishment at itself. But if, without his knowledge, by divine judgment and on whatever occasion it was done, blessed be God, who turned the impious man’s joy back upon himself and turned the death he had averted from his own Son into a curse upon that most wicked offspring [necem, “slaughter,” supplied editorially or uncertainly].

Divine vengeance finally cast him down into such madness that, because he could not bear the sufferings of a miserable death, he laid hands upon himself; he who had taken the lives of so many innocents deserved that he himself, and no other, should take away his own [Col. 0608D]. Mocked by the Magi, made sport of by Augustus, killed by himself, he plainly taught by both the perversity of his life and the end of his perversity what punishments he deserved. He had no herald of his wickedness more certain than himself.

Prophecy had foretold that Christ would be born in his time; his wickedness planned that Christ would perish through his deceit. What prophecy said was fulfilled, not what deceit devised. For he was not permitted to rage until the child Christ had first been sent into Egypt. While Christ lay hidden in Egypt [Col. 0609A], Herod’s son remained in the kingdom. Had he indeed crossed over with Christ, he would have escaped his father’s wickedness along with him. But in what kingdom? In Christ’s kingdom rather than that of the foreigner Herod. For it is written of Christ: “He came into his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:11). It is too little to say, “They did not receive him”; indeed, they expelled him. Transferred from Judaea into Egypt, as though migrating from his own kingdom to a foreign one, he remained safe in the foreign kingdom.

While Herod’s son was slain in his father’s realm, the son encountered his father as an enemy, because the servant did not recognize the Lord. Son was surrendered for Son: Herod’s son for God’s Son. He was delivered to death not by an enemy but by his father, so that the father’s cruelty might be made especially known through his son’s death. The Son of God, in whom the life of all was established, was preserved for life [Col. 0609B], as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). God’s death was not in human hands, nor could an earthly king prevail against the heavenly one. It belongs to the heavenly to order earthly things, not to the earthly to order heavenly things. The latter remained at rest for as long as the former willed; but when he was permitted to rage, he attacked.

Carefully setting this out, the Evangelist says that after the child had been transferred from Judaea to Egypt at the angel’s command: “Then Herod, seeing that he had been mocked by the Magi,” and so forth (Matt. 2:16). It was then indeed, not before the mockery, that he was permitted to take notice. The statement that he killed boys “from two years old and under, according to the time which he had inquired of the Magi” (ibid., 17), and not only in Bethlehem, where he had heard the prophecy, but in all its borders [Col. 0609C], magnifies the enormity of the crime: cruelty was added through the wickedness of killing both with respect to the place of birth and to the age fixed by time.
