Yet the phrase “from two years old,” that is, from two years and below, according to the time he had inquired of the Magi, raises a certain question. For if, as Chrysostom reports on Matthew from a certain writing, they spent two years on their journey, Herod appears to have reduced rather than added to the time. Certainly the Magi saw the star before those two years, and began their journey at its appearance. If, therefore, Herod reckoned two years from what he learned from the Magi about the star’s appearance, he reduced the period by more than a full year, since it is certain that this slaughter did not take place until after the revolution of the year whose anniversary of this killing we commemorate today. Therefore, in order that cruelty might be added with respect to time as well as place, we must understand the phrase as it stands: from two years *above* the appearance of the star and thenceforward until the day of the slaughter [Col. 0609D].

The Evangelist’s statement that prophecy was fulfilled then should be referred more to mystery than to history. For historically it is clear that Jeremiah prophesied this concerning Nebuchadnezzar’s persecution. But because that persecution prefigured in mystery the persecution of the Church, which began today, what had been foretold in history was fulfilled [Col. 0610A]. Rachel, whom Jacob took after Leah, is the Church, which succeeded the Synagogue from the time of John. Afflicted by frequent sufferings from Christ’s advent onward, she first suffered today in the infants.

Yet because, through the Lord’s Passion and the offering of the true sacrifice, the kingdom of heaven had not yet been opened to us, the Church’s compassion did not receive consolation concerning these first martyrs, whom she knew to be delayed from God’s kingdom. Therefore she “will not be comforted,” because these whom she laments with motherly compassionate affection do not yet exist [in their true state]; she understands that they do not yet possess true being, so long as they are excluded from blessedness and are not yet in the state for which they were created and predestined.

Hence the holy Fathers also prudently ordained that this feast of the Innocents should not have, as the festivals of other martyrs do, those cries of exultation—*Te Deum laudamus*, *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, and *Alleluia* at Mass [Col. 0610B]. For saints’ “birthdays” are not properly so called except when those born on earth have deserved to be born again in heaven. Here, therefore, are human birthdays; there are saints’ birthdays. Here, by the condition of human nature, we are born to miseries; there, by the grace of holiness, we are reborn to everlasting joys. This birth should be reckoned not so much as a birth as a death, in which, expelled from paradise, we fall through fault, so that by grace we may rise, though lower, toward paradise.

Rachel then had her time of grief, but now she has received a time of consolation. She who then wept for those descending to the underworld should now rejoice over those reigning with Christ. Let her observe the Lord’s consolation now fulfilled in them too: “Amen, amen, I say to you that you will weep and lament; but the world will rejoice. You indeed will be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:20). For what is “the world” but Herod and the other lovers of the world? Herod rejoiced that his wickedness was accomplished in the aforesaid death of the Innocents, as though he now held the world secure because he had killed the heavenly King; but he laughed deceived rather than safe. Rachel wept, afflicted by compassion for her children. But now, when all things have been reversed, she rejoices eternally over her own [Col. 0610D], as he mourns without end with his own.

Blessed in all things be God, who delivered over the wicked and saved the innocent; who, as the blessed Jerome recalls in a certain place, is so merciful and kind that those whom justice cannot save, mercy saves, and who grants benefits even to the unwilling and grace to the ungrateful, as this particular severity testifies. Hence the greatest hope is promised to the merits of the saints, if those whose merits had not preceded received so much by grace. Above all things, blessed be God. Amen.

[Col. 0611]

## PETER ABAELARD’S EXPOSITION OF THE LORD’S PRAYER

*(Edition of the Works, 1616.)*

[Col. 0611A]

Among all that human frailty can do whereby it may please its Creator or make him propitious, prayer is most beneficial, if it is made with a pure conscience and humility of heart. I say “with a pure conscience and humility of heart,” because if conscience is stained by the filth of evil will or the blemish of deed, or if our heart is filled with empty pride, our prayer is not received by God, nor is our soul heard. “He who turns away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be an abomination” (Prov. 28:9).

Therefore Christ Jesus, the Man who is mediator of God and human beings, providing for human salvation and mercifully making provision for it, established among the other words of his most holy teaching a form of prayer, and taught how we ought to pray to the Father, saying: “When you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in synagogues and on street corners; and when praying do not use many words like the Gentiles. For they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking. Thus, therefore, shall you pray: Our Father, who art in heaven,” and so forth (Matt. 6:5) [Col. 0611B].

This Lord’s Prayer is understood to contain seven petitions. The first petition is: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.” The second: “Thy kingdom come.” The third: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” The fourth: “Give us this day our daily bread.” The fifth: “And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.” The sixth: “And lead us not into temptation.” The seventh: “But deliver us from evil. Amen.”

## FIRST PETITION

[Col. 0611C]

“Our Father, who art in heaven,” and so forth. Behold, beloved: on almost every day clergy and people, men and women—but especially on solemn days—flock in groups to the basilicas. Each adorns himself as far as he can in finer garments before human eyes. They enter God’s holy house together as though children of God; they bend their knees, beat their breasts, spread their hands, open their mouths, pour forth prayers, saying, “Our Father.” Yet, what must be said with grievous sorrow: how many enter God’s house to beseech the Lord, and how few are heard! How many call the Lord in this prayer, “Our Father,” who are not his children but children of that father of whom it is written: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44)!

Those who long ago lost grace are not God’s children. They are the devil’s children, because he begot them through pride and nourishes them through sin. All unclean persons, concubinaries, finally the avaricious, the abusive, usurers, and those corrupted by any other damnable sins are children of the devil: those who say to their brother, “Fool”; those who look at a woman to lust after her. And whoever, even if not by perverse deed, is nevertheless separated from God by a perverse will—and, what is much more grievous and more to be lamented, not only common and unlearned laypeople, but also countless priests of our time, anointed with sacred oil, daily adorned with sacred vestments, standing at sacred altars, who ought with most clean hands to handle the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood and by devout prayers make the Lord propitious for themselves and those entrusted to them—these very men, I say, are involved in the filth of vices and defiled by the stains of sins [Col. 0612B].

And, what is more criminal, they are defiled not merely by crimes such as disgrace many laypeople, but by much graver ones; and, appointed not for edification but for the scandal and ruin of peoples, they have become a proverb, a laughing-stock, and an object of contempt to everyone. Let such priests also know that daily, when they sing the first hour to God, they either curse themselves or pronounce against themselves the witness of a divine curse when they utter: “Cursed are those who turn aside from thy commandments” (Ps. 118:21).

Therefore, brothers, whoever calls God Father in the Lord’s Prayer, whoever desires to be heard by him, should live in such a manner that God recognizes him as his son by grace—he who is Father of all by nature. Otherwise, when he is judged, he will go forth condemned, and “his prayer shall become sin” (Ps. 108:7).

“Our Father, who art in heaven.” He who says “Father” seeks favour; he who says “our” excludes pride. He who says “who art in heaven” shows reverence. He who says “Father” seeks favour, because he invokes one who is loving. He who says “our” excludes pride, because he declares him not arrogantly as his own or exclusive to himself, but common also to others. He who says “who art in heaven” shows reverence, because he proclaims that God presides not only over those below but also over those above [Col. 0612C].

“Hallowed be thy name.” Divine names are many. Which name, then, do we ask to be hallowed when we say, “Hallowed be thy name”? God’s name is faith in God, by which he becomes known to believers. “Hallowed be thy name”: hallowed be thy faith, which is knowledge of thee. But is not the Lord’s name already hallowed and holy? All the Scriptures cry out, all resound: “Holy is thy name.” The Lord’s name, brothers, is indeed holy, but it can still be further hallowed in certain hearts.

It can be hallowed in the hearts of pagans, in whom it has not yet been hallowed through faith; in the hearts of Jews, in whom it has not yet been hallowed through the perfection of faith; and in the hearts of false Christians, in whom it has not been hallowed through love. It can also be further hallowed in the hearts of the elect through greater confirmation of faith and greater love of God and neighbour. For the more perfectly each person believes and loves God, the more he hallows and demonstrates as hallowed the Father’s name within himself [Col. 0613B].

“Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.” May thy name be hallowed in the hearts of pagans; may it be hallowed in the hearts of Jews, so that the former may believe in thee and the latter believe more perfectly, and both may love. May it be hallowed in the hearts of false Christians, so that, as they have knowledge of thee through faith, they may likewise have it through affection and love. May it still be hallowed in the hearts of the elect through greater clarity of knowledge and greater sweetness of love: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.”

## SECOND PETITION

“Thy kingdom come.” What do we ask when we say, “Thy kingdom come”? Does God not have a kingdom? Is God not king? If God is not king or does not have a kingdom, what does the Psalmist mean when he says, “For God is king of all the earth; sing wisely” (Ps. 44:8)? Therefore God is king, and God has a kingdom. Why then do we ask that his kingdom come?

When we ask that his kingdom come, we do not ask that it come in what already exists, but in what does not yet exist; or rather, that it be manifested in what is not yet manifest. Moreover, many people yet to be born are predestined for his kingdom; and it makes manifest to all that those not yet predestined are of his kingdom. Therefore, may thy kingdom come, O heavenly Father, so that those predestined for thy kingdom may be generated through the nature of flesh, regenerated through the grace of baptism, made righteous, and through the splendour of righteousness be manifested to all as children of thy kingdom [Col. 0613D].

Therefore may thy kingdom come, so that at the end of the age, on the day of judgment, in the general resurrection, grain may be separated from chaff, lambs from goats, wheat from tares, and thy Church, which is thy kingdom, may pass at thy call from the oppression of the present age into the glory of the heavenly homeland. Again: may thy kingdom come, so that, as thou reignest in those already justified, thou mayest swiftly reign in those to be justified; and as thou reignest in those who are already good, so, once the power of demons is expelled, mayest thou reign also in those who are still evil: “Thy kingdom come.”

## THIRD PETITION

[Col. 0614A]

“Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” We know that in heaven no saint or angel departs from God’s will; none resists him. When, then, can it happen that God’s will is done on earth as in heaven—namely, so that no one on earth sins either through ignorance or through human frailty—when “an infant of one day is not without sin upon the earth” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint), and “we all offend in many things” (James 3:2)?

But it must be understood that “as” indicates not quantity but quality, and resemblance rather than equality. If someone built a small house according to the shape and arrangement of a larger house, we would not say of the small house, “This is as large as that larger one”; rather we would say, “This is such as that is”—alike in resemblance, not equal in size. Therefore, O Father, may thy will be done in heaven through angels and through saints already glorified in the first robe, and on earth through human beings who are to be justified and glorified, so that, as those in heaven do thy will, these also may do it on earth: if not according to equality, yet according to likeness; if not according to their perfection, yet according to imitation of their perfection.

May thy will be done not only in the elect through the performance of good works, but also in the reprobate through the ordering of evil things. Although thou orderest evil things, and although many evils are under thy power, nevertheless thou leavest none of them unordered; and thus thy will is done in all things [Col. 0614C].

## FOURTH PETITION
“Give us this day our daily bread.” God made man from a twofold substance, namely bodily and spiritual. Since, therefore, man is composed of two substances, he needs a twofold bread, bodily and spiritual. Bodily bread refreshes the body; spiritual bread satisfies the soul. We ask for bodily bread, because unless God makes the earth bring forth, it cannot provide its fruits. We ask God for spiritual bread, because we do not receive it unless he himself gives it. Priests have it to distribute to us. “Here now it is required among stewards that one be found faithful” (1 Cor. 4:2). But who in our times is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household, faithfully and prudently to give them food at the proper time? [Col. 0614D] (Luke 12:42).

Faithfully with respect to God: that is, that he dispense the word of God with as much faith, fear, conformity, earnestness, and diligence as the Lord commands. Prudently with respect to human beings: that he instruct each person according to that person’s capacity. But—and this cannot be said without grievous sorrow—the world is full of priests, yet, if there is anyone who might hear what is good, there is no one to speak it, according to the saying: “Little children asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4).

What will certain modern priests say on the day of judgment, who have received the priestly order but are not ashamed to live disorderly lives? Some spend the entire day seated at banquets and drinking-parties with a thoroughly unlearned populace, corrupted by depraved morals; they chatter and disgracefully do things that ought not to be mentioned. They arrogantly clothe themselves in the wool of the Lord’s flock, feed on its milk, while the sheep die of hunger and want of the word of God. Feasts pass, a whole year passes, and not a single word proceeds from their mouths by which the people entrusted to them may be instructed, corrected from evil, recalled to good, and confirmed in good. Yet, imagining that they render service to God every day, they shout—indeed, hiss—the words of divine praise; and, by the sound of their voices and the motions of their bodies, they scandalize rather than edify those who hear and attend.

Such priests ought to reflect that the prophetic denunciations were uttered against [Col. 0615B] them: “As is the people, so is the priest” (Hos. 4:9). And again: “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’ and those who held the law did not know me” (Jer. 3:8). And: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56:18). And: “Most shameless dogs, they knew no satiety” (ibid., v. 11). Therefore let no one expect to receive from these priests the bread of sacred teaching, for they either do not know how to teach or despise doing so. Let them instead seek learned and worthy priests in those places, men of good life and reputation; let them approach and hear them, and humbly ask to be taught by them.

There are, moreover, certain preachers who, like tares in the Lord’s field, have been sown by the devil. They travel throughout the whole world with their phylacteries, and with lying words pronounce blessed the unlearned populace burdened with sins, saying, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace (Jer. 8:11). Hence Isaiah says: “My people, those who call you blessed lead you astray and destroy the way of your paths” (Isa. 3:12). And again: “There will be those who call blessed, and those who are called blessed will be cast down” (Isa. 9:16).

“Our daily bread, Father, give us today. Feed, Lord, feed your own sheep; let your anointing teach them concerning all things, so that your Spirit may impart through inward inspiration or teaching what the mute mouth of such priests does not dispense. Therefore give us today our daily bread: bodily bread and spiritual bread—bodily bread, that you may make the earth bring forth and yield its fruits in their seasons; spiritual bread, [Col. 0615D] that you may inspire the prelates and teachers of your Church to strive successfully and wisely to dispense to us the teaching entrusted to them. And if they do not care to break this bread for us, feed us yourself through the hidden inspiration of your Spirit, so that inwardly through you we may receive the bread of which outwardly we are deprived by their silence. Give us this day our daily bread.”

## FIFTH PETITION

“And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.” How fearful, brethren, how destructive for many is this prayer! For to many it brings more loss than increase, more harm than profit. There are some who, hardened by great or long-standing malice or hatred [variant: *militia*, “service/warfare,” for *malitia*, “malice”], desire with their own hands to wound or kill those who, through some injury, have become their debtors; and they are unwilling, not for fear of God but except through the entreaties of others, to accept satisfaction or make peace. Of such persons it is written: “Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is most bitter. Their vine is the gall of dragons, and the incurable poison of asps” (Deut. 32:32).

Although they are such, they nevertheless secretly flock to church and, praying before God and his altar, say: “Our Father, forgive us our debts,” and so forth. But, miserable folly! unhappy presumption—to provoke God’s wrath against oneself by prayers! Does a human being reserve wrath against another human being and seek mercy from God?

There are also some who are imperfect. To their imperfection, as blessed Augustine says, divine mercy condescends, granting that they at least forgive their debtors their debts when those debtors ask that pardon be granted to them. Thus the Lord is recorded to have done to his wicked servant, as it is written: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all your debt because you asked me” (Matt. 18:32). Whoever, when asked by his debtor, disdains to remit the debt of any injury, asks the Lord in vain to remit the debt of his own sin. Indeed, this rather increases than lightens the judge’s wrath.

Although the imperfect are allowed to seek what is theirs, receive satisfaction for an injury done to them, and be asked by their debtors for forgiveness, nevertheless, if none of these things happens, [Col. 0616C] they ought altogether to restrain the anger of their own hearts and drive the darkness of hatred away from themselves, mindful of the saying of the apostle James: “The anger of a man does not work the righteousness of God” (Jas. 1:20). And: “He who hates his brother—that is, every murderer—has no share in the kingdom of God” (1 John 3:15).

It belongs to the perfect to forgive all things to all persons, with a pure heart and cheerful countenance, without restitution of goods, satisfaction for injuries, or entreaties from their debtors; indeed, to give what is theirs besides, and to render the services of charity. Let each person, therefore, take heed in this prayer: “Forgive us, Father, our debts, as we forgive our debtors”; and, if through some frailty or even ruinous disposition you see that we do not forgive as we ought, grant us the grace to forgive according to your will, and thus to obtain your pardon. Grant that we may love human beings in such a way as not to love their errors; that we may love in them their nature without loving their fault; that we may love what they are without loving what they do wrongly. Forgive us our debts.

## SIXTH PETITION

“And lead us not into temptation.” Since it is written, “God is not a tempter of evils; he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (Jas. 1:13–14), what do we ask when we say, “And lead us not into temptation”? The meaning, therefore, is: “Do not lead us into [Col. 0617A] temptation,” not that you may never permit us to be tempted, but that you may never permit us to be overcome by temptation; and grant that we may be proved by temptations, not rejected.

For temptations benefit the elect greatly, because through victory over temptations they attain the crown. Hence the apostle James: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation,” etc. (Jas. 1:12). Likewise: “Count it all joy, brethren, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith”—understand, the testing effected through temptations—“produces patience” (ibid., v. 3). Hence: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19).

There are four kinds of temptations: one is light and hidden; another light and manifest; another grave and hidden; another grave and manifest. There are three things that tempt us: the flesh, the world, and the devil. [Col. 0617B] The flesh tempts us through gluttony and lust; the world through prosperity and adversity—through prosperity in order to deceive, through adversity in order to crush. The devil attacks us in every way and attempts to bring us to every wickedness.

“Father, lead us not into temptation; do not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, but with the temptation also provide an escape, so that we may endure” (cf. 1 Cor. 10:13). Lead us not into temptation.

## SEVENTH PETITION

“But deliver us from evil.” There are many evils to which the human condition is subject and from whose pressure it is utterly unable by itself to escape. Considered generally, we may distinguish them in six ways. One evil [Col. 0617C] is of the body, another of the soul. Again, one evil is fault, another punishment. [Col. 0618A] Again, one belongs to this present age and another to the age to come. We ask to be delivered from all these, and from the other evils comprehended under them. They are contained under this when we pray, saying: “Deliver us from every evil,” because unless you deliver us, we cannot be delivered without you. Deliver us, therefore, Father, from evil.

## CONCLUSION OF THESE PETITIONS

“Amen.” It means “truly,” and concludes all the petitions of the preceding prayer. “Amen,” as though we said: “O our Father, who art in heaven, truly may your name be hallowed; truly may your kingdom come; truly may your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth; truly give us this day our daily bread; truly forgive us our debts, as we forgive [Col. 0618B] our debtors; truly lead us not into temptation; truly deliver us from evil.”

This, brethren, is the prayer to be meditated upon continually and said continually, since the Savior himself taught it and commanded us to pray to the Father by it. No prayer is loftier; none is more useful. There are some who, like the Gentiles, glory in pouring forth many words, reading many psalters, chanting various hours, and continuing lengthy prayers; yet, while speaking to the Lord with their mouths, they sometimes wander to the ends of the earth. Let such persons remember the Scripture which says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15:8).

In saying this, we do not blame the diligence of holy prayer or persevering devotion, which we greatly praise when the length of prayer [Col. 0618C] is accompanied by the greatest fervor of devotion.

[Col. 0617]

# PETER ABAELARD’S EXPOSITION OF THE CREED CALLED THE APOSTLES’ CREED

[Col. 0617D] We have received, brethren, from the holy Fathers the institution that both the Creed of Faith, called the Apostles’ Creed, and the Lord’s Prayer should be known and retained by memory by all Christians in common, so that they may be more readily used frequently. For in the former the confession of faith is briefly expressed; in the latter we are taught by the Lord to ask for necessary things.

From the Council of Rheims, chapter 8:

> “Let every priest either himself teach, or command to be taught, the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer to all his parishioners, so that when they come to confession during Lent, he may require each of them to recite these from memory before him. Nor may he admit anyone to holy communion before that person knows how to pronounce these from the heart. For no one can be saved without knowledge of these. In one, Christian faith and belief [Col. 0618D] are contained; in the other is expressed what we ought to pray for and ask from God.”

That no one can be saved without faith, the Lord shows when he says: “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Mark 16:16). But no one can believe what he does not know and has not heard. For Paul says: “How shall they believe in him whom they have not heard?” (Rom. 10:14). Nor is faith in the heart alone sufficient unless it is also uttered in speech, as the same Apostle bears witness: “For with the heart one believes unto righteousness; with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (ibid., v. 10).

Let no one plead dullness of mind or weakness of intellect, because these matters are so small that no one is so slow-witted or uncultivated as to be unable to say them and pronounce all their words, yet so great that anyone who can fully grasp knowledge of them may be believed to have what is sufficient for eternal salvation.

[Col. 0619A] This too must be observed: no one should receive an infant from the sacred font in baptism before reciting this same Creed and the Lord’s Prayer before the priest.

From the Council of Chalon, chapter 3:

> It must be commanded that the Lord’s Prayer, in which all things necessary for human life are comprehended, and the Apostles’ Creed, in which the Catholic faith is comprehended in its entirety, be learned by everyone both in Latin and in the vernacular, so that what they confess with their mouths they may believe in their hearts.

From the Council of Paris, chapter 2:

> “Let no one receive anyone from the sacred font unless he knows the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed according to his own language and understanding, and recites them before the priest, so that all may understand the covenant which they have made with God.”

From the Council of Garinaz, chapter 1:

> “Let priests take care that neither men nor women receive sons or daughters from the sacred font unless they have retained the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by memory.”

From the Council of Agde, chapter 12:

> “It was also resolved that, in all churches, the Creed be publicly delivered in church to the candidates on the eighth day before the Lord’s resurrection.”

Therefore, instructed by this authority of the Fathers, on this present day, the eighth before the resurrection, we have resolved not to teach the words of the aforementioned Creed—which you have already learned—but to disclose the meaning of what you profess. For faith is of the heart rather than of the mouth, and it must be possessed before its confession is made. The Apostle likewise sets out this order: “With the heart,” he says, “one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” [Col. 0619C] For Scripture says: “Everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Rom. 10:10). And a little later: “How shall they believe if they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?” and so forth (ibid., v. 14).

Accordingly, brethren, the Church, providing this most salutary counsel from its beginning, composed a very brief symbol of faith, which both contained the summary of faith and did not burden the confessor with a multitude of words. This, moreover, is that Creed believed to belong not to councils but to the apostles themselves, and said to be comprised of as many statements as their number.

A *symbolum* is called a contribution, when people intending to dine together contribute their shares into one common fund from which a feast may be made. Hence the saying in Proverbs: “Do not be among the drinking-parties of drinkers, nor among the feasts of those who contribute flesh for eating; for those devoted to drink and giving contributions are consumed” (Prov. 23:20). By this analogy, the collected statements of different persons, containing the summary of faith, are called a *symbolum*.

Hence also Eusebius of Emesa, in his homily *On the Creed of Faith*:

> “As some are permitted to know, among the ancients *symbola* were so called because companions gathered together contributed from their substance into a common fund for solemn feasts, for the expenses of common suppers. So too the Fathers of the Churches, solicitous for the salvation of peoples, collected from the various books of Scripture testimonies pregnant with divine mysteries, brief words for the health-giving banquet of the soul’s covenant, [Col. 0620A] and called this the Creed.”

For it is, as it were, a spiritual banquet—the refreshment of the divine word—and, as it were, a table of Scripture set before us, upon which there are as many dishes as there are opinions of teachers. Of this table it is written: “Let their table before them become a snare” (Ps. 68:23). Likewise concerning the bread of the divine Word: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Luke 4:4).

But even among the philosophers, Plato’s *Timaeus* arranges a comparison of various opinions under the figure of a certain banquet, saying:

> “One, two, three; but I seek your fourth, Timaeus: you who were guests at yesterday’s feast, sit down today, by agreement, as providers and reciprocators.”

We also read of Cyprian’s supper, in which the holy Fathers are introduced as offering, like certain dishes, the virtues in which they excelled. Thus too the apostles, as though contributing to one another, are believed to have established by common deliberation the present Creed of Faith. In it, as has been said, both the summary of the Catholic faith is taught and its salutary confession is set forth in few words, so that the doctrine of faith may at once be complete and no burdensome prolixity of words remain. This was afterward confirmed by the holy Fathers with such diligence that no believer may be permitted to be ignorant of its words for confession, even if not yet sufficient to understand them.

But since sound without understanding can merely please the ears and cannot refresh the mind, and should be called bleating rather than feeding; and since things heard do not stir the mind if they are not understood at all, it is now fitting that we, who seem to be little scholars, strive to take from the meaning of words food for the soul, and receive not so much sound with the mouth of the body as meaning with the mouth of the heart. The Lord, requiring precisely such ears, says: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.”

Since faith is the foundation of all good things, without which it is impossible to please God (Heb. 11:6), and belongs to the heart rather than the mouth—for, as has been said, “with the heart one believes”—the ears of the heart rather than those of the body should be applied to it, so that we may grasp by understanding what we affirm in words. For one who professes what he does not know is not far from lying, and one who swears to what he does not know is guilty of perjury. Let us be restrained from presuming this by that rebuke of the Apostle, in which he reproaches certain persons, saying: “Not knowing what they say, nor whereof they affirm” (1 Tim. 1:7).

No lie or error is more dangerous than one in matters pertaining to faith; and an utterance of words not followed by understanding is hollow, although words were instituted solely in order to convey understanding through what is heard. The more salutary the understanding of divine words is, the more it ought to be required of us. The Apostle mentioned above exhorts us to it, so that when blessings of divine praise or any prayers are offered in church, or something is said to confirm a matter or conclude a petition, “Amen,” or “So be it,” should be answered; and he does not permit anyone to answer it [Col. 0621A] who does not understand what preceded. Thus, writing to the Corinthians concerning an unlearned person ignorant of letters, and as it were standing by to answer someone in church: “How shall he say ‘Amen’ to your blessing, when he does not know what you are saying?” (1 Cor. 14:16).

Blessed Jerome, retaining this in memory while instructing Marcella about various Hebrew names, says:

> “In Hebrew, ‘Amen’ is read, meaning that the things said above, which are thereby confirmed, are true.”

[Note: [Col. 0621D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 431.]

Hence Paul also asserts that no one can answer “Amen”—that is, confirm what has been said above—unless he understands the preaching. And, strongly urging us toward understanding everything said in church, he says: “Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph. 5:19). For one does not speak to oneself or with oneself if one does not understand what one says, since, as stated, the whole office of speech is ordered toward understanding; nor should speech uttered without understanding be considered speech so much as sound.

Therefore, that we may, according to the Apostle, be children in malice but perfect in understanding, and may hold firm the foundation of faith, let us complete, insofar as the Lord grants, what we have proposed: its exposition in the light of understanding.

“I believe in God.” But in order to preserve the truth of one’s confession, lest “the mouth that lies slay the soul,” one must first consider what it is to believe in God. For it is one thing to believe that God exists (*credere Deum*), another to believe God (*credere Deo*), another to believe in God (*credere in Deum*). To believe that God exists is to judge that he is. To believe God is to assent to his words, judging them true and entirely free from falsehood. But to believe in God is, by believing, to love him, and thus to become or be his member.

This is the fruitful faith which, as the Apostle says, works through love; and of which, as we have said, it is written: “Everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Rom. 10:11). He says “in him” rather than “him” or “to him.” For the first two modes of faith—believing that God exists or believing God—are common to us with the reprobate, and even with the demons themselves. Blessed James also speaks of them, saying that “the demons believe and tremble” (Jas. 2:19), and: “Faith without works is dead” (ibid., v. 20). [Col. 0621D] But this third manner of believing, namely believing in God, alone distinguishes the elect from the reprobate.

Therefore, in order that our confession of faith may be true, when each day we say individually, “I believe in God,” let us strive to live so that we may truly say it. Otherwise we shall not be members of truth, and the falsehood of our confession harms us more than its utterance helps us. Since every point that follows in this confession of faith coheres with and depends on this beginning, so that if its truth is violated it cannot be preserved in the rest, when we say, “I believe in Jesus Christ and in the Holy Spirit,” and so forth, we confess the remainder in vain if the beginning of the confession rests on falsehood.

“Father almighty.” Having first stated “God”—one, not many—he established the unity of the Godhead. Now he adds the distinction of persons when he mentions Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. As blessed Augustine observes, he is called almighty not because he can do everything—that is, perform any actions whatsoever in himself—but because no power able to resist his will or ordering, nor the force of any nature, can impede it.

It is fitting, moreover, that when we confess belief in God, we recall his omnipotence, so that we may declare how right it is to believe in him or place our hope in him whose power is so great. [Col. 0622B] Hence also the Apostle: “If God is for us, who is against us?” (Rom. 8:31).

“Creator of heaven and earth.” When about to call him the creator of all things, he first stated that he is almighty, in order to show that he who can do all things, and whose will nothing can resist, is able to do this. By “Creator of heaven” he means that he made from nothing, not from pre-existing matter, all things of which the world consists. For by “heaven,” both aerial and ethereal, he here denotes the upper parts of the world; by “earth,” the lower parts which remain below by their own weight, namely both watery and earthy substance.

We may also comprehend the whole creation through heaven and earth in this way: calling heaven the higher dignity, that is, every spiritual nature; and earth every bodily nature. When, therefore, he calls God the creator of all things in this manner, he clearly indicates how much all things owe him.

“And in Jesus Christ.” In commending to us the person of the Son of God, the present Creed recalls both his divinity and his humanity, and signifies the dignity of both his kingship and his priesthood, from which he is called Christ. Through these two he becomes Jesus—that is, Savior—to us. For since both royal and priestly dignity are established through anointing, this highest King and supreme Priest, and true Savior, is rightly called Christ. Hence he has deserved to acquire these names as if proper names, so that when we now hear “Christ” or “Jesus,” we understand him alone in the highest sense.

He is our king as our supreme Lord, presiding over us and steering his Church, his own ship, through the storms and tempests of this age to the harbor of eternal tranquility; and by words as well as examples handing down to us the rule of discipline. He became a priest—indeed, a high priest—for us when, hanging upon the cross as upon an altar, he was sacrificed for us. He carefully reveals why he is truly both Christ, as has been said, and Jesus for us, when he then adds that he is the Son both of God and of man, saying:

[Col. 0623A] “His only Son,” that is, the only Son of God the Father, lest he be considered adoptive rather than consubstantial. And again, “who was conceived,” and so forth. Yet some think that “only” should be joined rather to “Lord” than to “Son,” or to both together, so that as he is the Father’s only Son, so also he may be our only Lord. For as, in commending the person of the Father, he called him both almighty and creator of heaven and earth, so now, to honor the Son, we confess him not only as Christ and Jesus, but also as our Lord and only one—that is, as our sole Lord—because we were purchased by his precious blood alone.

Or, if anyone is troubled because the Father and the Holy Spirit too are no less called our Lord, let that person know that the Son alone is called our Lord in such a way that apart from him there is no other Lord of all. For although each of the other two persons must equally be called our Lord, just as each is God, because one person is not another Lord, just as neither is one another God, nevertheless God or Lord alone must be called so, that no other thing whatsoever may be judged Lord, nor another [Note: [Col. 0623] “Another” was supplied from Victorine manuscript 397 by D. Cousin, *Works of Abaelard*, p. 608.] be believed Lord besides him, since the same Lord, just as the same God, is one person with another.

“Who was conceived.” He, I say—Christ, or the Son of God—was conceived according to assumed humanity, and so forth. It is as though one said: “Whose humanity was conceived and born from the very substance of the Virgin through the operation of divine grace.” For although individual human beings consist of soul and body, they are said to be conceived by mothers or born only according to the nature of the body, which is transmitted.

Appropriately, moreover, when about to say that he was born of the Virgin, he first said that he was conceived by the Holy Spirit, lest anyone inquire how this happened; just as the angel said to his mother when she asked, “How shall this be?”: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you,” and so forth (Luke 1:34–35). By this he also commends to us, not insignificantly, the person of the Spirit itself, saying that through his operation that body was conceived in whose sacrifice the redemption of all was completed. The Apostle says that it was offered for us through that same Spirit, no less than it was conceived. Hence the passage to the Hebrews, where, recalling the operation of the whole Trinity in this completion of our salvation, he says: [Col. 0623D] “For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctify unto the cleansing of the flesh, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself immaculate to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works?” (Heb. 9:13).

When we hear that he was conceived or born of the Holy Spirit, we must understand differently his conception by the Virgin and his conception of the Spirit; or differently his birth of the Spirit and his birth of the Virgin. He was conceived by, or of, the Virgin insofar as he received flesh from her substance as from a mother; but of the Spirit insofar as this occurred through the new and wondrous operation of divine grace, as has been said—an operation for which no natural process could suffice.

Therefore, in this birth or incarnation of the Lord, we must not understand the Holy Spirit as his father in the way that we profess the Virgin as his mother. For as his eternal generation is from the substance of the Father without a mother, so this temporal generation is from a mother without a father.

Understand, therefore, the Holy Spirit here as an agent rather than a father, just as in all things God does he is called an agent or creator rather than, properly, a father. Observe that when the Creed says that the Son of God was born of the Virgin, and thus asserts that the same one is Son both of God and of man, it confirms the unity of person in two natures, divine and human.

Although according to divinity he is begotten from the Father alone, and according to humanity he is born from the mother alone; although the nature of God differs from that of man, and divinity from humanity: nevertheless in Christ there is one person, subsisting in two natures, and the Son of God is not one person while the son of man is another. Although in nature the Word which assumed the human being is other than the human being assumed, there are not two Christs, the one assuming and the one assumed, but one Christ. Likewise, the human soul and its flesh are not two human beings or two persons, although soul differs in nature from flesh: the former is an incorporeal substance, [Col. 0624C] the latter bodily—that is, the former is body, the latter spirit.

Therefore, if in individual human beings there are two natures, bodily and incorporeal, yet only one person, so also in Christ there are two natures, divine and human, yet only one person. A person is so called as being one through itself—that is, any rational substance so distinct in itself from other things that it does not constitute one substance with any other thing. So long as the human soul is in the body, it cannot be called a person, because, joined to flesh, it constitutes with it one human person and one rational substance. Thus the Word united to the human being in Christ makes one person of Christ, not two.

According to this unity of person, we confess the same Christ as Son both of God and of man; and we say that the same Christ, the Son both of God and of man, was crucified, died, and was buried, although these things must be understood only according to humanity. Hence Paul does not hesitate to say that the Lord of glory was crucified (1 Cor. 2:8), and that he who descended from heaven and he who ascended are the same. The Lord Christ himself, speaking of himself, says: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). And again: “If, then, you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before,” and so forth (John 6:63).

Since, therefore, Christ is properly called God and man together—that is, those three things distinct in their proper natures: the Word, the human soul, and flesh—yet in order to show the unity of person of such diverse natures in Christ, we often mingle the terms, so that we speak now of the Word, now of the soul, now even of the flesh; and sometimes attribute what properly belongs to God to the human being, or conversely.

For when the Apostle calls Christ “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:25), and again says: “Who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and so forth (Phil. 2:6), who would not refer this to his divinity? Yet when Christ himself, speaking of himself and the Father, says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and again, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), who does not see that this and that are said of him according to one nature and another?

When we say that he descended into hell or was in the tomb, who does not understand the former of the soul alone and the latter of the body alone? In this way we confess both that Peter is in a tomb at Rome and that the same Peter rejoices in heaven with Christ, although we say the one of one substance and the other of another—not, however, of a different Peter. Although after the dissolution of body and soul there is no longer one person in Peter composed jointly of soul and body, nevertheless, looking to that unity of person which once existed rather than that which now exists, we say that Peter himself is both in the tomb and in heaven with Christ.

And, looking at someone’s tomb, we do not hesitate to say: “This man who lies here possessed great learning and beauty,” although that corpse is now neither a human being nor possessed learning, which belonged only to the absent soul; nor could the soul itself, which possessed that learning, possess that bodily beauty. Rather, that learning and beauty existed entirely in different natures: the former in the soul, the latter in the body.

Thus, when we say that this man who lies here was wise, on account, of course, of the unity of the person—which now is not, but was—why should we not say of Christ that he who is God is man, or that he who descended from heaven ascended; that is, that there is one person of God and man, or of the descending Word and man? [Col. 0625D] Otherwise, how shall we say, on seeing a man, “He who is beautiful is wise,” unless indeed according to the unity of the person, in whose diverse, as stated, parts beauty and wisdom are so distinguished that one has beauty—namely, the body—and another wisdom—namely, the soul? Therefore, just as we say that he who is beautiful, or who is animate, is wise, although beauty or animation belongs to the body alone, just as wisdom belongs to the soul alone, so too we call one and the same Christ both God and man; that is, we say that one person subsists from, or in, these natures. And when Christ, while still abiding on earth, says that the Son of Man is in heaven, or had formerly been in heaven [Col. 0626A], what else does this mean but that human nature is united to him, which, through the presence of divinity existing everywhere, is not removed from heavenly loftiness? What, then, is so remarkable if, after “Son of God” has been stated above, it is immediately added, “who was conceived by the Spirit” or “born of the Virgin”; that is, the humanity assumed was thus conceived or born? For so too we understand that the Lord of glory was crucified: that is, the man, or the body assumed by him, was fastened to such a cross. Accordingly Mary Magdalene says that her Lord has been removed from the tomb—that is, the body of her Lord—just as we say that Peter is buried here, meaning his body alone; and again, as has been said, that he himself is in heaven, meaning this of his soul alone. For transfers of names from the whole to the parts, or from the parts to the whole, are often made: thus at one time we call the soul, at another the flesh, “the whole man”; and sometimes we designate a soul entangled in carnal desires by the name of flesh.

“He suffered,” namely according to the same nature of humanity which is said to have been conceived by the Spirit or born of the Virgin. “Under Pontius Pilate,” that is, while he was governing there where Christ suffered. That Pontius is either a surname or a gentile name is evident from some passage. He fittingly recalls a Gentile governor, thereby also indicating that the time had now come when, according to the prophecy of Jacob or Daniel, royal anointing had failed among the Jewish people.

[Col. 0626C] “Crucified.” He also specifies the kind of execution, which was more shameful, as had been foretold: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wisdom 2:20). And thus he died and, moreover, was buried, so that the reality of his humanity might be proved in every respect, and that he might be loved by us all the more because he endured graver and more unworthy things for us.

“He descended into hell.” He who is said to have died and been buried is also declared to have descended into hell, although the former is understood only with respect to the body, and the latter with respect to the soul. The soul itself, which had suffered in the flesh, is said to have descended into hell because the ancient righteous experienced the efficacy of that suffering, being freed through it from punishments. For no soul or spirit, as blessed Augustine observes, [Col. 0626D] moves from place to place; only a body does so. Therefore, just as God, who is everywhere, is also said to descend in accordance with some effect of his operation, so that soul is said to have descended by freeing people according to the efficacy of its own suffering, which it exercised among the elect.

For sensation and suffering belong to the soul alone, although they come to it through the flesh, as through a kind of instrument for such things. By “hell,” therefore, he means those penal darknesses which even the righteous endured, being still placed outside the sight of divine glory, for which they panted with all their desires. The vision of that glory is the highest happiness, entirely immune from every punishment, which the Lord himself promises to the thief when he says: [Col. 0627A] “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

“On the third day he rose from the dead.” That is, from among the dead, having truly died in body, he was raised by his own will, not another’s. As he himself says: “I have power to lay down my life, and power to take it up again” (John 10:18). Note the order: before he rose, descending into hell, he wrought the saving work of our liberation before the glory of his resurrection, because in all these things he sought not so much his own interest as ours. Therefore, on the very day of his passion, before he rose or ascended into heaven, he brought both the aforementioned thief and the ancient righteous into paradise; for, displaying to them the vision of his divinity, he satisfied their souls with that true blessedness [Col. 0627B] which they call paradise. Of this satisfaction the prophet had said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Psalm 16:15). Apart from that vision of glory, whatever exists must, in comparison with it, be called darkness; nor is it wholly free from punishment, however great its consolations of repose may be.

“He ascended into heaven.” Just as he rose bodily from the tomb, so he also ascended bodily into heaven; and he did both by his own power, so that he is not said to have been drawn up, but rather to have ascended. For, as he himself says: “No one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John 3:13). Others should rather be said to be drawn than to ascend. But far be it from us to suppose that Christ, already glorified by the resurrection, received any increase of blessedness through his bodily ascent into heaven. For what is our blessedness in the life to come but that vision of divinity of which the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Psalm 16:15)? Promising through Isaiah the light of this vision to the city, the Lord says: [Col. 0627C] “The sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illuminate you; but the Lord shall be for you an everlasting light, and your God your glory. Your sun shall set no more, and your moon shall not diminish; for the Lord shall be for you an everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be completed. And your people, all righteous, shall inherit the land forever,” etc. (Isaiah 60:19 ff.). Who, moreover, does not know that before God, who is everywhere, we become present or absent not by places but by deeds? Thus the angels, who always see the face of God, are not deprived of the blessedness of that vision when they are sent to us. How much more could the soul of Christ, which always enjoys this vision more perfectly, never have been deprived of it? What, then, does it mean that his humanity ascended into heaven—or, as the Apostle states more carefully, that he ascended above all the heavens in order to fill all things (Ephesians 4:10)—except that by a bodily ascent in place he showed that it surpasses the height of all the blessed? Of this excellence of dignity, by which it surpasses all things, it was said through the prophet: “Your hand has been lifted up like a cedar” (Ezekiel 10:4). And through the Apostle: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). And again: [Col. 0628A] “He sits at the right hand of Majesty on high, having become so much superior to the angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs” (Hebrews 1:3).

He is therefore said to have ascended into heaven, not in order that his blessedness or glory might be increased by his bodily ascent, but in order that it might be made manifest through it. For, as has been said, far be it from us to believe that, after the resurrection, anything was added to his blessedness or glory, whether in soul or body. Rather, he already possessed what he displayed when he showed his body glorified with such lightness that it could ride upon a cloud, penetrate the heavens, and had already become far different from this corruptible body which weighs down the soul and burdens the vigor of our senses. Therefore, so that the faithful might await this glorification in their own bodies [Col. 0628B]—so that wherever the Spirit wished, there the body might immediately be, without any difficulty—the head first displayed this in himself, so that his members might hope for it on the basis of his example. Thus, just as the Son of God is said to have descended from heaven in humiliation and, according to the humanity assumed, to have been made in some sense lower than the angels, so the Son of Man is said to have ascended in exaltation, although he did not lack a bodily ascent attesting that he was exalted. For what is added immediately—“he sits at the right hand of the Father”—must not be understood of his bodily sitting, or of a bodily right hand of the Father. For what is it for the man Christ to sit at the right hand of God, except to hold the worthier rank in the glory of God the Father, that is, in that heavenly blessedness, as one appointed by God judge of all? [Col. 0628C] Hence it follows: “From there,” that is, accordingly, “he will come to judge the living and the dead.” As though, while the other elect stand at God’s left, he alone stands at the right, because, just as the right hand prevails over the left, so he surpasses all in blessedness. Since sitting belongs to judges, just as standing belongs to those judged, his sitting fittingly expresses judicial power. He will judge the living and the dead because he will render either punishment or reward according to merits to both elect and reprobate. Since “the righteous live by faith,” and wickedness is a kind of death of the soul, according to the words, “The dead shall not praise you, O Lord, but we who live shall bless the Lord” (Psalm 113:17), he calls the elect “living” and the reprobate “dead.” Or he calls “living” those whom that still-hidden coming [Col. 0628D] of the Judge will find alive in the body; the rest he calls “dead.”

“I believe in the Holy Spirit.” This confession of faith plainly asserts him to be God equally with the Father and the Son. Otherwise it would not say “in the Holy Spirit,” but merely “the Spirit,” just as it subsequently says “the Church,” not “in the Church,” and so forth. Therefore, just as we say, “I believe [the] holy Church,” that is, that it is holy, so we may say, “I believe [that] Peter is holy,” or “I believe holy Peter,” and “I believe [the] holy Church.” Or we are [members] of Peter, as of a head, just as we are reckoned members of God. Yet they are called members of the Church as of a body, but of God alone as of a head. This is indicated by the preposition when “in God” is said, as our exposition set forth above has already explained. The Greeks, however, do not hesitate to say “also in the Church,” as is contained in that Creed which Leo III established as a safeguard of orthodox faith and had inscribed on a silver tablet and fastened at Rome to the altar of St Paul. “Catholic,” that is, universal and not confined to one part of the world, as are the gatherings of heretics, but spread everywhere, just as was promised to Jacob as a figure of Christ, when it is said: “You shall spread abroad to the East and the West” (Genesis 28:14).

“The communion of saints.” That is, either that by which saints are made or confirmed in holiness—namely, participation in the divine sacrament—or the Church’s common faith or union of charity. [Col. 0630A] We may also take *sanctorum* in the neuter: that is, of the bread and wine sanctified for the sacrament of the altar. “The forgiveness of sins,” both through repentance and through the power of ecclesiastical sacraments. “The resurrection of the flesh,” namely in both elect and reprobate, and thereafter in the bodies of both without any dissolution intervening. “Life everlasting,” whether unto glory or unto punishment. “Amen,” that is, “it is true.” Yet, according to the Apostle, as we have mentioned above, we ought not say this unless we understand what has preceded. Hence, for the instruction of children, we have judged this small exposition necessary.

[Col. 0629]

# PETER ABAELARD’S EXPOSITION OF FAITH ON THE ATHANASIAN CREED

[Col. 0629B] “Whoever wishes to be saved . . .” For we are saved by our own will, not by another’s compulsion. “Before all things it is necessary . . .” Understand: this is necessary for him. “Before all things,” that is, before hope and charity, or the other goods by which eternal life is attained. “That he hold . . .” Not merely that he possess it, but that he preserve what he possesses, as the foundation and source of all goods; for, as the Apostle says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6). “Catholic,” that is, universal and common to all believers, and thus necessary for all, so that even the righteous of old, both before the Law and under the Law, could not be saved without it. “In Trinity,” that is, existing in three persons; and we should not merely believe, but also venerate, the three persons in one God. [Col. 0629C] How this Trinity is to be believed according to the properties of the persons, and this unity according to the nature of the divine substance, he immediately determines when he says: “Neither confusing the persons.” That is, intermingling the persons with one another, so that we say the person of the Father is the same as that of the Son or the Holy Spirit—as that heresy asserted which said of the Father that, when he wills, he is Father, and when he wills, Son. “Neither dividing the substance,” that is, believing different substances in God, but only one. For just as we must believe diversity of persons in God, so must we believe unity of the divine substance. Explaining this at once, he says: “For the person of the Father is one,” etc. And again: “But the Godhead of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one.” “Equal glory,” that is, reverence to be rendered. “Majesty,” that is, dignity. Why? Because “such as the Father is,” that is, as great in dignity. He immediately continues with this dignity, saying: “The Father uncreated,” etc. “The Father immense,” not in bulk, but in power encompassing all things; or “immense,” that is, incomprehensible. “Eternal,” lacking both beginning and end. “And yet not three almighties.” According to Augustine’s testimony, there is no name of God which is said in the singular separately of individual persons while its plural applies to them together, except this name, “person.” For the Father is a person, and the Son a person, and these two are persons. But while the Father is God and the Son is God—or Lord, Creator, Principle, Light, or Almighty—the Father and Son are nevertheless not several gods, creators, principles, lights, or almighties. For when “persons” is said in the plural, diversity of properties is indicated, not a numerical plurality of things or things essentially different. Conversely, if we said “gods” or “creators,” etc., we would indicate a plurality of things essentially different, each of which would be God, etc. “Prior,” in time or existence. “Greater,” in the conferring of dignity. “Unity,” namely of substance in three persons. “Trinity,” conversely, of persons in unity of substance. “Let him believe,” that is, let him believe; understand: that salvation is to be obtained. “That we believe,” etc., in accordance with: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10). There are not two Christs, but one Christ in person. [Note: [Col. 0629C] From the Victorine codex Dr Victor Cousin restored this passage as follows, *Works of Abaelard*, p. 616: “Let him believe,” that is, let him believe that salvation is to be obtained, “that we believe,” [Col. 0630C] etc. “Not two”—understand, Christs—“but one,” etc.]

[Col. 0631A] Therefore, although in Christ there are diverse natures, namely divine and human, there are not on that account diverse persons. This he immediately confirms by a fitting comparison, saying: “For ‘just as the soul’”: that is, just as in one human being there are diverse natures, spiritual and bodily, yet not therefore two human beings or two persons, so in Christ there are, as stated, two natures, yet not two Christs, indeed not two persons. For a person is said to be, as it were, one existing through itself, not a thing joined with another thing into one rational substance. Therefore, the divinity joined to the humanity in Christ is not to be called one person existing there through itself, and the humanity another; rather, the two together are one person, properly called Christ. All human beings will rise again, even those found alive at that time. For while they are caught up [Col. 0631B] to meet Christ in the air, in that very rapture by which they meet the Judge, they will die and immediately come to life again; and for them this coming to life again will itself be rising again. If, however, objection is raised concerning some whose resurrection is believed already to have been completed, such as those who were witnesses of the Lord’s resurrection through their own resurrection, this must be understood to mean that all will rise then in such a way that the resurrection of all will then be completed, so that thereafter no one will happen to rise again, just as no one will be dissolved by death. “With their bodies.” That is, having taken up again the same bodies they had before they fell into death. For nothing will rise unless it has fallen. But whether those who die as children, or those who lived long, will possess there only that amount of bodily size [Col. 0631C] which they possessed here is a question of some difficulty. Whatever we think about this, however, it is beyond doubt that resurrection cannot be spoken of without that bodily substance which underwent the fall in death.

“And we shall render an account.” If this too is understood generally of all, it seems necessary to ask how it applies to those dying as children, or to the perfected righteous, [Col. 0632A] who will be judges there rather than persons judged. For what examination must then be conducted, what accounting of their deeds demanded from those who will appear in so perfect a blessedness that they will sit with the Lord himself in judgment? They will render an account not so much for themselves as exact it from others. Finally, what account of their own deeds are children, to whom no works are imputed, to give there? But assuredly, just as we said that all human beings will rise there—not such that we are compelled to understand this of every individual then to rise, but that the resurrection of all will then be completed, so that none occurs thereafter—so too here all are said to render an account then, in the sense that judgment concerning all will then be so consummated that no examination remains thereafter, and no further doubt exists concerning anyone as to whether he is worthy of reward or punishment. And this is for them to render an account there of their own works: that it be made manifest to all what they have deserved. He immediately specifies these two, namely both reward and punishment, saying: “And those who have done good,” that is, who have completed their lives with the intention of good works, whatever deeds may have preceded. “Eternal life,” that is, unfailing blessedness. “Eternal fire,” that is, supreme and unfailing torment, whether that fire is merely bodily and material, or whatever inward torment of the soul is expressed by the term “fire,” as the element which torments us most and consumes more powerfully, since it is sharper and more penetrating than the others and cannot be resisted. And note that nothing here appears to be said concerning children, [Col. 0632C] who have no merits, although it is certain that they too are no less than adults saved or condemned. For just as this Scripture and the others are composed for the instruction only of adults and of those capable of reason, so it has been thought sufficient here to instruct them only concerning matters that pertain to them.

# [ETHICS]

[Col. 0631]

# NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING TREATISE

(R. Fr Bernard Pez, “Introductory Dissertation to Part II of Volume III of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*,” p. XIX.)

[Col. 0631] Should there be any who reproach us because we have brought from darkness into light Peter Abaelard’s book *Know Yourself*—or, as he himself calls it elsewhere, *Ethics*, or more truly a theology of morals—which was so odious to St Bernard and condemned as notorious for errors by great men of the twelfth century, let them remember that in this matter we have followed the authority and example of men of the greatest learning and erudition. Most distinguished among them was André Duchesne, who brought to light from every quarter most of Abaelard’s works of every kind and published them at Paris in 1616, in quarto, together with an apologetic preface for Abaelard written by Fr. Ambroise, knight and privy councillor to the king of France. Since, moreover, Abaelard’s *Christian Theology* was especially lacking in that edition, the exceedingly devout and learned Fr Edmund Martène published it, in five books, in volume V of his *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, together with Peter Abaelard’s *Exposition on the Hexaemeron*, although it had been committed to the flames at the Synod of Soissons in 1120. These most prudent men were not ignorant of the use such writings, which once caused so great a stir in the Church, might have in our age if soberly read and weighed by sober persons—especially since in recent years there have not been lacking those who, in striving to clear Abaelard, as Martène notes in the preface to volume V, have not feared to accuse Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, a most holy and gentle man, of rash judgment. In order that one may render a sound judgment in this matter, nothing is more necessary or more fitting than that the charges on which St Bernard attacked Abaelard should be compared with Abaelard’s genuine writings. That Peter’s book *Know Yourself* occupies no small place among these is sufficiently clear from St Bernard’s letters 188 and 192, in the edition prepared by Mabillon in 1690. In the former letter, to the cardinals of the Roman Church, he says: “Read, if you please, Peter Abaelard’s book which he calls *Theology*; it is at hand, since, as he boasts, it is read by many in the curia. And see what things are said there about the Holy Trinity, the generation of the Son, the procession of the Holy Spirit, and countless other matters wholly alien to Catholic ears and minds. Read also another book which they call his *Sentences*, and likewise the one entitled *Know Yourself*; and observe how greatly these too run wild with a crop of sacrileges and errors: what he thinks concerning Christ’s soul, Christ’s person, Christ’s descent into hell, the sacrament of the altar, the power of binding and loosing, original sin, concupiscence, the sin of delight, the sin of weakness, the sin of ignorance, the deed of sin, the will to sin,” etc. Here you see what Bernard reproved, especially in this book of Abaelard’s, *Know Yourself*.

Bernard states his opinion more plainly and fully in the *Chapters on the Heresies of Peter Abaelard*, the eleventh minor work in volume II of the *Works of St Bernard*. In the preliminary admonition to these, however, Mabillon notes that some of the chapters of errors attributed to Abaelard are lacking from his published works. “Hence,” he says, “some take occasion to accuse Bernard, as though he had falsely attributed errors to Abaelard and fought against masks and shadows. Yet it is clear that most of the errors are found even in the published writings, as we shall show in their places; and, if some further ones no longer exist, William of St Thierry, Geoffrey, and that anonymous abbot, once Abaelard’s disciple, read them formerly in Abaelard himself. The latter both knew his teacher’s doctrine and quotes his very words, as does William, drawn both from Abaelard’s *Apology* and from his *Theology*, which do not appear in the printed editions. And certainly Abaelard himself, in Book II of his commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, p. 554, reserves for treatment in his *Theology* certain matters of which there is no mention in what has been printed; the printed work ends as follows: ‘the rest is missing,’ so that it appears that the published *Theology* is mutilated. Therefore, those who, in order to absolve Abaelard, charge Bernard with having been impelled by blind zeal, as they say, serve Christianity—and indeed Bernard himself—very badly.” Thus Mabillon wrote, before Abaelard’s book *Know Yourself* had been brought into the light. But now that we have published it from the parchment codex of Emmeram at Regensburg, about six hundred years old, there is no such need to strain oneself in defence of Bernard’s good faith. For the chapters of errors imputed to Abaelard which are absent from his other works and concern morals are contained almost verbatim, especially in the book *Know Yourself*, as will be clear to anyone who examines the summaries of the chapters. As for whether Abaelard taught so badly about the sin of ignorance, suggestion, delight, and consent, etc., as St Bernard thought in Chapters XI and XIII of the errors attributed to him, we leave that judgment to others. Certainly modern schools commonly teach that inadvertence in military service and invincible ignorance excuse from formal sin; Abaelard perhaps intended no more than this. But whatever Abaelard may ultimately have written or thought, it is altogether clear that he was never a heretic, since these are his words in the *Apology*: “Perhaps I wrote some things in error which ought not to have been written; but I call God as witness and judge over my soul that in the matters of which I am accused I presumed nothing through malice or pride.” At these words of Abaelard we are surprised that Mabillon, otherwise a most fair-minded man, observed: “Grant, then, that it is permissible to remove from him malice and even heresy; yet it is not permissible to conceal that he had at least certain errors, an eagerness for novel expressions, frivolity, perhaps even pride, and an itch for disputation.” Surely, if we do not give credence to Abaelard when he calls God as witness and judge over his soul that, in the matters of which he was accused, he presumed nothing through malice or pride, to whom, pray, shall we ever give credence? The most learned Martène recently made the same observation in volume V of the *New Treasury of Anecdotes*, in the preliminary observations on the *Christian Theology*. There he judges that, if anything can excuse Abaelard, it is especially that he seems to have subjected his writings to the judgment of those more learned and consequently of the Church itself. For he testifies that Peter argues thus in Book III: “Whatever we shall discuss concerning this most exalted philosophy, we profess to be a shadow, not truth, and as it were a certain likeness, not the thing itself. The Lord knows what is true; but I shall set forth what I judge probable and most consonant with the philosophical arguments by which it is attacked. In this matter, if through faults requiring correction I should depart—God forbid!—from Catholic understanding or expression, may he forgive me who judges works by intention, I being always ready to make every satisfaction concerning statements to be corrected or regretted whenever any one of the faithful corrects me either by the force of reason or by the authority of Scripture.” Certainly these words of Abaelard signify anything but a mind obstinately fixed in error and the pertinacity which alone makes a heretic. Yet no one should therefore suppose that we have wished here to undertake a defence or exculpation of all Peter’s errors and faults. Abaelard’s faults are more certain from his own *Apology* than that they can be excused or concealed. But neither should it be passed over that, having become a Cluniac monk of the Order of St Benedict, he finally washed away the errors of a more impetuous age and a more vigorous intellect through serious repentance.

[Col. 0633]

# PETER ABAELARD’S *ETHICS*, OR THE BOOK CALLED *KNOW YOURSELF*

(Extracted from the manuscript codex of the imperial monastery of St Emmeram at Regensburg, Order of St Benedict, by the Reverend Lord Father Benedict Bonetus, Benedictine of Melk; edited by Bernard Pez, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, III, II, 626.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0633A]

By morals we mean the vices or virtues of the soul which make us inclined to evil or good deeds. There are, however, [Col. 0634A] vices or goods not only of the soul but also of the body: for example, bodily weakness or strength, which we call physical powers; slowness or swiftness, lameness [Col. 0635A] or straightness, blindness or sight. Hence, to distinguish these kinds, when we say “vices,” we prefaced it with “of the soul.” These vices of the soul are opposed to virtues: injustice to justice, cowardice to constancy, intemperance to temperance.

## CHAPTER I. On the vice of the soul that pertains to morals

There are also certain vices or goods of the soul that are separate from morals and do not make human life deserving of blame or praise: dullness of mind or quickness of intellect; being forgetful or having a good memory; ignorance or knowledge. Since all these happen equally to the wicked and the good, they have nothing to do with the ordering of morals and do not make life base or honorable. Therefore, having above prefaced “vices of the soul,” to exclude [Col. 0635B] such things we added, “which make us inclined to evil deeds”; that is, which incline the will toward something which it is by no means fitting either to do or to leave undone.

## CHAPTER II. What is the difference between sin and a vice inclining one to evil?

Such a vice of the soul is not the same as sin, nor is sin the same as an evil action. For example, to be irascible—that is, prone or readily subject to the disturbance of anger—is a vice, and it inclines the mind toward doing something rashly and irrationally which it is by no means fitting to do. But this vice is in the soul, so that it is disposed to anger even when it is not moved to anger; just as lameness, from which a person is called lame, is in that person even when [Col. 0635C] he is not walking with a limp, because the vice is present even when the action is absent. Thus nature itself, or bodily constitution, makes many people prone to lust just as to anger; yet they do not sin merely because they are such, but have thereby material for struggle, so that, triumphing over themselves through the virtue of temperance, they may receive a crown in accordance with Solomon’s words: “The patient person is better than a strong man, and one who rules his own spirit than a conqueror of cities” (Proverbs 16:32). For religion judges it shameful not to be conquered by a human being, but to be conquered by vice. The former happens even to good people; the latter is what we must avoid. Commending this victory to us, the Apostle says: “No one is crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Timothy 2:5). He contends, I say, not so much by resisting people as by resisting vices, lest [Col. 0635D] they draw us into wrongful consent. Even if people cease attacking us, vices do not cease; their conflict is therefore more dangerous the more frequent it is, and victory the more glorious the more difficult it is.
