However greatly people prevail, they introduce no baseness into our lives unless, after the manner of vices and as though we had been turned into vices, they subject us by shameful consent. While they rule the body, so long as the mind remains free, nothing of true liberty is endangered and we incur no disgraceful slavery. For it is shameful not to serve a human being but to serve vice; not bodily servitude but subjection to vices deforms the soul. Whatever is common alike to good and evil persons has no bearing on virtue or vice.

## CHAPTER III. What is a vice of the soul, and what is properly called sin?

[Col. 0636A]

A vice, therefore, is that by which we are made prone to sin; that is, we are inclined to consent to what is unfitting, namely, to do or to leave it undone. This consent, however, we properly call sin: that is, the soul’s guilt by which it deserves condemnation or is constituted guilty before God. For what is this consent except contempt of God and an offence against him? God cannot be offended by injury, but by contempt. For he is that supreme power which is not diminished by any injury, but avenges contempt of itself. Therefore our sin is contempt of the Creator, and to sin is to despise the Creator: that is, not to do for [Col. 0636B] his sake what we believe ought to be done by us for his sake, or not to leave undone for his sake what we believe ought to be left undone. When, therefore, we define sin negatively, saying, namely, “not to do” or “not to leave undone” what is fitting, we plainly show that sin has no substance, since it subsists in non-being rather than being, just as, when defining darkness, we say: “the absence of light where light ought to be.”

But perhaps you will say that the will for an evil action is also sin, which makes us guilty before God, just as the will for a good action makes us righteous; so that, just as virtue consists in good will, sin consists in evil will, and not merely in non-being but also in being, just as virtue does. For just as, by willing to do what we believe pleases God, we please him, so by willing to do what we believe displeases God, we displease him and seem to offend or despise him.

But I say that, if we consider more carefully, we must think very differently about this than appears at first sight. Since we sometimes sin without any evil will, and since evil will itself, restrained but not extinguished, produces for those who resist it the palm of victory, material for struggle, and the crown of glory, it should be called not so much sin as a certain now-necessary weakness. Consider a man innocent of wrongdoing whose cruel master, moved by rage to such a degree, pursues him with drawn sword in order to kill him. After fleeing him for a long time and avoiding his own death as much as possible, the man is finally compelled, unwillingly, to kill his master so as not to be killed by him. Tell me, whoever you are, what evil will did he have in this deed? In wishing to escape death, he wished to preserve his own life. But was this will evil? “No,” you will say, “I do not think this was evil; rather, the will he had to kill his pursuing master was evil.” I reply: You speak well and shrewdly, if you can identify the will which you assert was in him.

But, as has already been said, he did this unwillingly and under compulsion; as far as he could, he postponed the loss of his life, and he also knew that this killing exposed his own life to danger. How, then, did he voluntarily [Col. 0637A] do what he undertook even at the peril of his own life?

If you reply that this too was done from will—namely, since it is agreed that he was led to it by the will to escape death, not by a will to kill his master—we do not deny it. But, as has already been said, this will is by no means to be condemned as evil, by which he wished, as you say, to escape death rather than to kill his master. Yet he sinned by consenting—although compelled by fear of an unjust death—to a killing which he ought rather to have endured than inflicted. For he took up the sword on his own initiative; it had not been entrusted to him by authority. Hence Truth says: “All who take up the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52); that is, by this rash act he incurred damnation and the destruction of his own soul [Col. 0637B]. Thus, as has been said, he wished to escape death, not to kill his master; but because he consented to a killing to which he ought not to have consented, this unjust consent of his, which preceded the killing, was sin.

But perhaps someone will say: because he wished to kill his master in order to escape death, it cannot simply be inferred that he wished to kill him. For example, if I say to someone, “I wish you to have my cloak on condition that you give me five shillings,” or, “I willingly wish it to become yours for this price,” I do not thereby grant that I wish it to be yours. Or if someone imprisoned wishes to put his son in prison in his place, in order to obtain his own ransom [Col. 0637C], do we therefore simply grant that he wishes to send his son to prison—something he is compelled to endure with great tears and many groans? Certainly such a “will,” if one may call it so, which consists in great distress of mind, is not to be called a will, but rather a suffering.

And “he wills this for the sake of that” means, as though it were said, that he endures what he does not will for the sake of what he desires. Thus a sick person is said to wish to be burned or cut, in order to be healed; martyrs to suffer, in order to attain Christ; Christ himself, that we may be saved by his passion. Yet we are not thereby compelled simply to grant that they will these things. For suffering can exist only where something occurs against the will; nor does anyone suffer in that wherein he fulfils his own will and what delights him to be done [Col. 0637D].

And certainly the Apostle, who says, “I desire [Note: [Col. 0637D] Vulgate: ‘having a desire,’ etc.] to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23)—that is, to die in order to come to him—elsewhere says: “We do not wish to be unclothed, but to be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. 5:4). Blessed Augustine also recalls this saying as uttered by the Lord, when he said to Peter: “You will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18). He too, according to the weakness of the assumed human nature, said to the Father: “If it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26:39). For his soul naturally feared the great suffering of death [Col. 0638A], and what he knew to be painful could not be voluntary for him.

And where Scripture elsewhere says, “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53:7), this must either be understood according to the divine nature, in whose will it was that the assumed man should suffer; or “he willed” is said in the sense of “he ordained,” according to the Psalmist’s saying: “Whatever he willed, he did” (Ps. 113:3). It is therefore clear that sin is sometimes committed wholly without an evil will; from this it is plainly evident that sin is not identical with will.

“But,” you say, “it is so where we sin under compulsion, but not where we act willingly—for example, if we wish to commit something which we know ought not to be committed by us. For there that evil will and sin appear to be the same. For instance, someone sees a woman, falls into desire for her, and his mind is touched by carnal pleasure so that it is inflamed toward the shamefulness of intercourse. What else,” you ask, “is this will and shameful desire than sin?”

I answer: what if this will is restrained by the virtue of temperance, yet not extinguished; it remains for battle, persists for conflict, and, though conquered, does not fail? For where is battle if the material for fighting is lacking? Or whence comes a great reward if there is nothing grievous for us to endure? When the contest has ceased, there remains no longer fighting but receiving the reward. But here we contend by fighting, so that elsewhere, as victors in the contest, we may receive the crown. For there to be battle [Col. 0638C], there must be an enemy who resists, not one who wholly fails. This, indeed, is our evil will: we triumph over it when we subdue it to the divine will, yet do not wholly extinguish it, so that we may always have something against which to contend.

For what great thing do we do for God if we endure nothing contrary to our own will, but rather fulfil what we will? Who would thank us if, in what we say we do for him, we fulfil our own will? “And what,” you ask, “do we merit before God by what we do willingly or unwillingly?” Certainly nothing, I reply, since in rewarding he weighs the disposition rather than the action, and action adds nothing to merit, whether it proceeds from a good will [Col. 0638D] or an evil one, as we shall show below. But when we set his will before our own, so as to follow his rather than ours, we obtain great merit before him, according to that perfection of Truth: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

Exhorting us to this, he also says: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother . . . yes, even his own life, he is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:26); that is, unless he renounces their promptings or his own will, and wholly subjects himself to my commands. Therefore, just as we are commanded to hate our father, not to kill him, so too we are commanded not to follow our own will [Col. 0639A], not to destroy it utterly. For he who says, “Do not follow your desires” (Ecclus. 18:30), and, “Turn away from your own will” (ibid.), commands us not to fulfil our desires, not to be wholly without them. The former is vicious; the latter impossible to our weakness. Therefore it is not desiring a woman that is sin, but consenting to desire; and it is not the will for intercourse, but the consent of the will, that is damnable.

Let us apply to gluttony what we have said of lust. Someone passes through another’s garden and, seeing delightful fruits, falls into desire for them; yet he does not consent to his desire so as to take anything from there by theft or robbery, though the pleasure of food has inflamed his mind with great longing [Col. 0639B]. But where there is desire, there undoubtedly is will. He therefore desires to eat those fruits, in which he does not doubt there is pleasure. For the very nature of his weakness compels him to desire what he may not take without the owner’s knowledge or permission. He restrains the desire; he does not extinguish it. But because he is not drawn into consent, he incurs no sin.

What is the purpose of these points? It is, finally, to make clear that in such cases even the will or desire to do what is not permitted is by no means to be called sin, but rather the consent itself, as we have said. We consent to what is not permitted when we do not at all hold ourselves back from its commission: when we are altogether ready, if the opportunity were given, to carry it out. Whoever is found in this disposition adds nothing to the guilt for an increase of sin; but he is already equally guilty before God—he who strives, so far as he can, to perform it and does it so far as lies in him—as though, as blessed Augustine recalls, he had also been caught in the very deed [Col. 0639C].

But although will is not sin, and although we sometimes commit sins unwillingly, as we have said, some nevertheless say that every sin is voluntary. In this they find a certain difference between sin and will, since *will* and *voluntary* are said to be different: that is, will is one thing, and that which is committed through will another.

Yet if by sin we mean what we previously said is properly called sin—that is, contempt of God [Col. 0639D], or consent to what we believe ought to be abandoned for God’s sake—how can we say that sin is voluntary? That is, how can we say that we wish to despise God, which is to sin, to become worse, or to become deserving of damnation? For although we may wish to do what we know deserves punishment, or for which we are worthy to be punished, we nevertheless do not wish to be punished. In this very point we are plainly unjust: we wish to do what is unjust, yet do not wish to undergo the justice of the punishment that is just. The punishment, which is just, displeases us; the action, which is unjust, pleases us.

It also often happens that, though we wish to have intercourse with a woman whom we know to be married, attracted by her appearance, we would nevertheless not wish to commit adultery with her, since we would prefer her not to be married [Col. 0640A]. Conversely, many desire the wives of powerful men for their own glory all the more because they are such men’s wives than if they were unmarried; they desire adultery rather than fornication—that is, to transgress more rather than less. There are some who are altogether reluctant to be drawn into consent to desire or into an evil will, and who are compelled by the weakness of the flesh to will what they would by no means wish to will. How then will this consent, which we do not wish to have, be called voluntary? Thus I do not see how, according to some, as has been said, every sin can be called voluntary, unless “voluntary” is understood in contrast to “necessary,” since no sin is unavoidable. Or let “voluntary” mean what proceeds from some will. For even the man who, under compulsion, killed his master had no will in the killing, yet committed it from some will—namely, because he wished to escape or defer death [Col. 0640B].

Some are greatly disturbed when they hear us say that the performance of sin adds nothing to guilt or damnation before God. They object that a certain pleasure follows in the action of sin, which increases sin—as in intercourse or the eating of which we have spoken. They would not speak unreasonably if they proved that carnal pleasure of this kind is sin, and that nothing of this sort can be committed without sinning. But if they accept this, then surely no one may have this pleasure of the flesh. Thus married persons are not free from sin when they unite with one another with this permitted carnal pleasure [Col. 0640C]; nor is the person who enjoys eating the delightful fruit of his own tree. Any sick people would likewise be at fault who, to be restored from illness, are nourished with more agreeable foods, which they do not take without pleasure—or, if they took them without pleasure, would derive no benefit.

Finally, even the Lord, creator of foods as also of bodies, would not be without fault if he had put such tastes into them as would necessarily compel the ignorant, by their pleasure, to sin. For how could he prepare such things for our food, or permit us to eat them, if it were impossible for us to eat them without sin? How, moreover, can sin be said to be committed in what is permitted? For even things which were once unlawful and forbidden, if afterwards they are permitted and thereby become lawful, are then done entirely without sin—for example, the eating of pork and many other things formerly forbidden to the Jews but now permitted to us [Col. 0640D].

When, therefore, we see even Jews converted to Christ freely eating such foods as the Law had forbidden, how do we defend them as blameless unless we maintain that this has now been permitted them by God? If, therefore, in eating such food—once forbidden to them but now permitted—the permission itself excuses sin and removes contempt of God, who would say that anyone sins in that which divine permission has made lawful for him? Therefore, if intercourse with one’s wife or the eating even of delightful food was granted to us from the first day of our creation—when in paradise life seemed to be lived without sin [“*vivebatur*” is likely the intended reading] [Col. 0641A]—who will charge us with sin in this, provided we do not exceed the limits of the permission?

But again they say that marital intercourse and the eating of delightful food are indeed permitted, but that pleasure itself is not permitted, and that these acts must be done wholly without pleasure. But surely, if this is so, they are permitted to be done in a manner in which they cannot possibly be done. Nor was a permission rational which allowed them to be done in a way in which it is certain they cannot be done. Moreover, for what reason did the Law formerly compel marriage, so that everyone might leave seed in Israel? Or why does the Apostle compel spouses to render one another the marital due, if these acts cannot at all be done without sin? How can he call it a due where sin is already necessary? Or how can anyone be compelled to do that by doing which he will offend God [Col. 0641B]?

From these considerations, I think, it is clear that no natural pleasure of the flesh is to be charged as sin, and that they are not guilty in taking pleasure in that which, once attained, necessarily produces pleasure. For example, if someone compels a religious man bound in chains to lie among women, and he is drawn by the softness of the bed and the contact of the women around him into pleasure but not into consent, who would dare call this pleasure—which nature makes necessary—a fault?

But if you object that, as some think, pleasure of the flesh is imputed as sin even in lawful intercourse, because David says, “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities” (Ps. 50:7) [Col. 0641C], and because the Apostle, after saying, “Return again to the same,” etc. (1 Cor. 7:5), finally adds, “But I say this by way of concession, not command” (ibid., 6), they appear to constrain us by authority rather than reason to admit that carnal pleasure itself is sin. For David was plainly conceived not in fornication but in marriage; nor, as they maintain, does indulgence—that is, pardon—intervene where fault is wholly absent.

Yet, as it seems to me, when David says that he was conceived in iniquities or sins, without adding whose, he introduces the general curse of original sin, by which every person is subjected to damnation because of the fault of his own parents [Col. 0641D], according to what is written elsewhere: “No one is clean from defilement—not even an infant whose life has been one day upon the earth.” For, as blessed Jerome observes and clear reasoning holds, so long as the soul remains in infancy, it is free from sin. If, then, it is clean from sin, how is it unclean from the defilements of sin, unless the former statement is understood of guilt and the latter of punishment? For one who does not yet understand by reason what he ought to do has no guilt from contempt of God. Yet he is not free from the defilement of his first parents’ sin, from which he already contracts punishment, though not guilt; and he suffers as punishment what they committed as guilt.

Thus, when David says that he was conceived in iniquities or sins, he saw himself subject to the general sentence of condemnation resulting from the fault of his own parents [Col. 0642A]; and he referred these sins not so much to his immediate parents as to earlier ones.

When the Apostle calls it “indulgence,” this is not to be understood, as they wish, as though he called the pardon of sin an indulgence of permission. For his words, “by way of indulgence, not by way of command,” mean as though he said, “by permission, not by compulsion.” For if spouses wish and have mutually resolved it, they can abstain entirely from the use of the flesh, and they are not to be compelled by command to it. But if they have not resolved this, they have indulgence—that is, permission to descend from a more perfect life to the practice of a less strict life. Thus the Apostle here understood indulgence not as pardon for sin [Col. 0642B], but as permission for a less strict life in order to avoid fornication: so that the lower life might prevent a greater magnitude of sin, and might be less in merit lest it become greater in sins.

We have introduced these points lest anyone perhaps, wishing to assert that every pleasure of the flesh is sin, should say that sin itself is increased by action when someone puts the consent of the mind into operative exercise, so that he is contaminated not only by consenting to shamefulness but also by the stains of the action—as though what is externally done in the body could contaminate the soul. Therefore no execution of works, of whatever kind, contributes to an increase of sin; and nothing defiles the soul except what belongs to the soul itself, namely consent. This alone, we have said, is sin, whether will precedes it [Col. 0642C] or performance of the deed follows it.

For even if we will or do what is unfitting, we do not therefore sin, since these things often occur without sin. Conversely, consent can occur without these things, as we have already shown in part: will without consent, in one who falls into desire for a woman he has seen or for another’s fruit but is not drawn into consent; and evil consent without evil desire, in one who unwillingly killed his master.

I think no one is unaware how often things that ought not to be done are done without sin—when they are committed through force or ignorance [Col. 0642D]. For example, if a woman subjected to force has intercourse with another man’s husband; or someone, in whatever way deceived, sleeps with a woman whom he believed to be his wife; or kills by mistake someone whom he believed was to be killed by him as a judge. Therefore sin is not desiring another man’s wife or having intercourse with her, but rather consenting to this desire or action. Indeed, this consent to desire is what the Law calls “desire” when it says, “You shall not covet” (Deut. 5:21). For it should not forbid us to covet what we cannot avoid, or in which, as has been said, we do not sin; rather, it forbids assenting to it.

So too must be understood what the Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her” (Matt. 5:28)—that is, whoever looks in such a manner that he falls into consent to desire [Col. 0643A]—“has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28), even though he has not committed adultery in deed. That is, he already bears the guilt of sin, even though he still lacks its effect.

And if we consider carefully, wherever deeds appear to be contained under command or prohibition, these are to be referred more to the will or consent concerning deeds than to the deeds themselves. Otherwise, nothing belonging to merit would be set under a command; and they are the less worthy of being commanded the less they lie within our power. For we are forbidden to perform many things, but will and consent are always in our free choice. Behold, the Lord says: “You shall not kill. You shall not bear false witness” (Deut. 5:17, 20). If we understand these only of outward action, as the words sound [Col. 0643B], guilt is by no means forbidden, nor is fault thus prohibited, but only the action arising from fault.

For killing a human being is not sin, nor is intercourse with another’s wife, since these can sometimes be done without sin. Nor, if such a prohibition is understood of deed as the words sound, does one who wishes to give false testimony, or even consents to giving it, become guilty under the Law provided that, for whatever reason, he remains silent and does not give it. For it was not said that we should not wish to give false testimony or consent to giving it, but only that we should not give it. Or when the Law forbids us to take our sisters as wives or have intercourse with them, no one can observe this command if it concerns act rather than consent, since no one can recognize his sisters [Col. 0643C]. I say, no one.

Therefore, when it happens that someone unknowingly marries his sister, is he a transgressor of the command because he does what the Law forbade? “He is not,” you say, “a transgressor, because he did not consent to transgression in what he did ignorantly.” Therefore, just as he is not to be called a transgressor who does what is forbidden, but one who consents to what is known to be forbidden, so prohibition is to be understood not of the act but of consent. Thus, when it is said, “Do not do this or that,” the meaning is: “Do not consent to doing this or that”; as though it were said: “Do not knowingly undertake this.”

Blessed Augustine, carefully considering this, reduces every sin or prohibition not to deeds but rather to charity, or, more precisely, to cupidity. He says: “The Law commands nothing but charity and forbids nothing but cupidity” [Col. 0643D]. Hence also the Apostle says: “The whole Law is fulfilled in one saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Rom. 13:8, 10). And again: “Love is the fulfilment of the Law” (ibid.).

For it makes no difference to merit whether you give alms to a needy person, provided charity makes you ready to give and the will is at hand, even when means are lacking; and provided that, whatever circumstance impedes you, you do not fail to do what you can. It is clear that deeds which ought, or ought not, to be done are performed alike by good and evil people, whom intention alone distinguishes. For in the same act, as the aforesaid teacher observes, in which we see God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, we also see Judas the betrayer [Col. 0644A]. The handing over of the Son was done by God the Father, and by the Son, and by that betrayer: for the Father handed over the Son, and the Son handed over himself (Rom. 8:32; Gal. 2:21), as the Apostle recalls, and Judas handed over the Master.

Thus the betrayer did what God also did; but did he do well? Even if the thing was good, he certainly did not do it well, nor in a way that ought to benefit him. For God weighs not the things done, but the disposition in which they are done; merit or praise for the agent lies not in the deed but in the intention. The same thing is often done by different people: through one person’s justice and another’s wickedness. Thus if two men hang one criminal, one from zeal for justice and the other from hatred born of an old enmity, the act of hanging is the same [Col. 0644B]; and indeed both bring about what is good and what justice requires. Yet through the diversity of intention, the same thing is done by different persons—badly by one, well by the other.

Who does not know that the devil himself does nothing except what God permits him to do—whether he punishes the wicked according to their deserts, or is permitted to afflict some just person for purification or as an example of patience? But because he does, at the prompting of his own wickedness, what God permits him to do, his power is called good, or even just, while his will is always unjust. He receives the former from God; he has the latter from himself. Who among the elect can equal hypocrites in things that concern works? Who endures or does as much from love of God as they do from desire for human praise [Col. 0644C]?

Who, finally, does not know that things God forbids to be done are sometimes rightly done or ought to be done, just as, conversely, he sometimes commands things which nevertheless ought by no means to be done? For we know some of his miracles in which, after he had healed infirmities, he forbade their disclosure, namely as an example of humility, lest anyone perhaps seek similar glory from grace bestowed upon him. Yet those who had received these benefits nonetheless did not cease to publish them, in honor of him who had both performed them and forbidden their disclosure. Of such persons it is written: “The more he commanded them not to speak, the more they proclaimed it,” etc. Will you judge such persons guilty of transgression because they acted knowingly against the command they had received [Col. 0644D]? Who will excuse them from transgression except that they did nothing from contempt of him who gave the command, since they resolved to do it in his honor?

Tell me, I beg you: did Christ command what ought not to have been commanded, or did they omit what ought to have been observed? It was good to command what was not good to do. Indeed, you will also accuse the Lord in the case of Abraham, whom he first commanded to sacrifice his son and afterwards himself forbade it. Did God not rightly command that which it was not good to do? If it was good, how was it afterwards forbidden? But if it was both good to command and good to forbid the same thing—for God permits nothing without reasonable cause, much less consents that it be done—you see that the intention of the command alone [Col. 0645A], not the performance of the act, excuses God when he rightly commands what is not good to do.

For God did not intend, nor command with this end, that Abraham should sacrifice his son. Rather, he intended especially that Abraham’s obedience, steadfastness of faith, and love toward him should thereby be proved and left to us as an example. The Lord himself openly declares this afterwards when he says: “Now I know that you fear God” (Gen. 22:12); as though he plainly said: “I commanded this to you for the end for which you showed yourself ready: that I might make others know what I myself had known about you before the ages.” Thus God’s intention was right in an act which was not right; and so also his prohibition was right in the cases we mentioned, which he prohibited not in order that the prohibition should be observed, but in order to give us who are weak examples for avoiding vain glory [Col. 0645B].

God therefore commanded what was not good to do; just as conversely he forbade what was good to do. And as intention excuses him there, so here it excuses those who did not fulfil the command in act. For they knew that he had not commanded it in order that it should be observed, but in order that the aforesaid example should be set forth. Thus, preserving the will of the commander, they did not despise him, since they understood themselves not to be opposed to his will.

If, therefore, we weigh works rather than intention, we shall see that something is sometimes not merely willed contrary to God’s command, but even done knowingly, without any guilt of sin. Nor is a will or action to be called evil merely because it does not observe God’s command in deed [Col. 0645C], when the intention of the person to whom the command is given does not depart from the will of the one who commands. For just as the intention of the commander excuses the one who commands to be done what nevertheless ought not to be done, so the intention of charity excuses the person to whom the command is given.

To sum up the foregoing briefly, there are four things which we have set forth, in order carefully to distinguish them from one another: first, the defect of the soul which makes us prone to sin; then sin itself, which we have located in consent to evil or contempt of God; next, evil will; and evil action. But just as willing is not the same as fulfilling one’s will, so sinning is not the same as completing sin. The former must be understood of the consent of the mind [Col. 0645D] by which we sin; the latter, of the result of action, when we fulfil in deed that to which we previously consented.

Therefore, when we say that sin or temptation is carried out in three ways—suggestion, pleasure, and consent—it must be understood that through these three we are often led to the performance of sin, as happened to our first parents. The devil’s persuasion came first, when he promised immortality from tasting the forbidden tree. Pleasure followed when the woman, seeing that the tree was beautiful and understanding it to be pleasant for eating, was inflamed with desire for it, seized by the pleasure of food which she expected. Although she ought to have restrained desire in order to keep the command, she was drawn into sin by consenting. And although she ought to have corrected that sin by repentance, in order to deserve pardon, she finally completed it in deed [Col. 0646A]. Thus she advanced by three stages to the commission of sin.

Likewise, we often arrive not at sinning but at the perpetration of sin through the same passions: suggestion, that is, the urging of someone who incites us outwardly to do something unfitting. If we know that it is pleasant to do this, our mind is seized, even before the act itself, by pleasure in the act; and in the thought itself we are tempted through pleasure. When we assent to this pleasure by consent, we sin. Finally, through these three stages we arrive at the performance of sin.

Some wish the suggestion of the flesh, even when there is no person making the suggestion [Col. 0646B], to be included under the name “suggestion”—for example, when someone sees a woman and falls into desire for her. But this suggestion seems truly to be nothing other than what should be called pleasure. The Apostle calls this pleasure, made as if necessary, and other similar things which we have above recalled are not sin, “human temptation,” when he says: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human. But God is faithful, and he will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able; but with the temptation he will also provide the way out, that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13).

Temptation, generally speaking, is any inclination of the mind toward doing something unfitting, whether it is will or consent. But human temptation [Col. 0646C] is that without which human weakness can scarcely, or never, subsist: such as carnal desire or desire for delightful food. He who said, “Deliver me, Lord, from my necessities” (Ps. 24:17), asked to be freed from these—namely, from the temptations of desires which have become as if natural and necessary—lest they draw him into consent, or so that, once this life full of temptations has ended, he may be wholly free of them.

Therefore, when the Apostle says, “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human,” he means something similar to this: if the mind is inclined by pleasure, which, as we have said, is human temptation, it should not be drawn as far as consent, in which sin consists. Someone might ask, as it were, by what strength of ours we can resist these desires. “God is faithful,” he says, “who will not permit you to be tempted.” It is as though he said: confidence should rather be placed in him than presumption in ourselves. He who promises us help is true in all his promises—that is what it means for him to be faithful—so that faith must be placed in him in all things [Col. 0646D].

He does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear when, through his mercy, he so moderates this human temptation that it does not press us toward sin beyond what we can endure by resisting it. Moreover, he turns this very temptation to our advantage when he exercises us through it in such a manner that, when it next confronts us, it can burden us less. We then fear less the assault of the enemy over whom we have already triumphed [Col. 0647A] and whom we know we can endure. For every battle which we have not yet experienced we bear more grievously [Note: [Col. 0647D] Thus the manuscript in both places.] and fear more greatly [Note: [Col. 0647D] See above.]. But once victors have become accustomed to it, both its force and its terror vanish together.

## Chapter IV. On the Suggestions of Demons

There are suggestions not only from human beings but also from demons, because they too sometimes incite us to sin, not so much by words as by deeds. Skilled in the nature of things through both subtle intelligence and long experience—whence they are called *daemones*, that is, “knowers”—they know the natural powers of things by which human weakness can easily be moved toward lust or other impulses. Thus, with God’s permission, they sometimes inflict illness on certain persons and afterwards offer remedies to those who entreat them; and when they cease to harm, they are often believed to cure [Col. 0647B].

Finally, in Egypt they were permitted to perform many marvelous works through magicians against Moses; and indeed, by the natural power of things which they knew, they should be called not so much creators of the things they did as arrangers of them. It is as if someone, following Virgil’s instruction, were by labor to cause bees to arise from the beaten flesh of a bull [Note: [Col. 0648D] *Georgics*, book IV, line 310.]: he would be called not the creator of bees but a preparer of nature.

By this knowledge of the natures of things which demons possess, they move us toward lust or other passions of the mind, applying those things to us by whatever art while we are unaware [Col. 0647C]—whether placing them in taste or in bedding, or positioning them in any manner inwardly or outwardly. For there are many powers in herbs, seeds, and the natures both of trees and stones suited to stirring or calming our minds; and whoever knew them carefully could easily do this.

## Chapter V. Why Are the Works of Sin Punished More Than Sin Itself?

There are also those who are greatly troubled when they hear us say that the act of sin is not properly called sin, nor does it add anything to the increase of sin: why, then, is a heavier satisfaction imposed upon penitents for the effect of the act than for the guilt of the fault? To such persons I first reply: why do they not especially marvel [Col. 0647D] that sometimes a great penalty of satisfaction is established where no fault has intervened, and that we sometimes ought to punish those whom we know to be innocent?

For behold, a poor woman has a nursing infant and does not possess enough clothing to suffice both for herself and for the little one in the cradle. Moved by pity for the child, she lays it beside herself, so as additionally to warm it with her own garments; and at last, overcome by weakness through the force of nature, she is compelled to crush the one whom she embraces with the greatest love. “Have charity,” says Augustine, “and do whatever you wish.” Yet when she comes to the bishop to make satisfaction, a severe penalty is imposed on her—not for a fault she has committed, but so that she herself thereafter, and other women as well, may be made more cautious in providing against such things.

Sometimes, too, someone is accused before a judge by his enemies, and some charge is brought against him from which the judge knows him to be innocent. Yet because his accusers persist and demand a hearing in court, they enter upon the case on the appointed day and produce witnesses, although false ones, to convict the person whom they accuse. Since the judge cannot refute these witnesses on manifest grounds, he is compelled by law to admit them; and, once their proof has been admitted, he must punish the innocent man, who ought not to be punished. Thus he must punish him although he has not deserved it, while the judge nevertheless acts justly in doing so because the law commands it. From these examples it is clear that punishment is sometimes reasonably imposed upon one in whom no fault has preceded.

What wonder, then, if, where fault has preceded, the ensuing act increases punishment among human beings in this life, though not before God in the life to come? For human beings judge not hidden things but manifest ones, and weigh not so much the guilt of the fault as the outcome of the act. God alone, however, who attends not so much to what is done as to the disposition in which it is done, truly weighs guilt in our intention and examines fault by true judgment. Hence He is called the “tester of heart and kidneys” (Jer. 20:12), and is said to “see in secret” (Matt. 6:4). For He sees most especially where no one sees: in punishing sin He attends not to the act but to the mind, just as we, conversely, attend not to the mind, which we do not see, but to the act, which we know. Hence, through error or through the compulsion of law, as we have said, we often punish innocent persons or acquit the guilty. God is called the tester and knower of heart and kidneys—that is, of whatever intentions arise from the disposition of the soul, or from weakness, or from the pleasure of the flesh.

## CHAPTER VI. On spiritual and carnal sins

Although all sins belong only to the soul and not to the flesh—for guilt and contempt of God can exist only where knowledge and reason concerning Him can subsist—nevertheless some sins are called spiritual and others carnal; that is, some arise from vices of the soul, others from the weakness of the flesh. And although desire belongs to the soul alone, just as does [Col. 0648D] will—for we cannot desire or crave anything except by willing it—nevertheless there is said to be the desire of the flesh, just as there is the desire of the spirit. For, says the Apostle, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:7); that is, from the pleasure which it has in the flesh, it seeks certain things which the judgment of reason nevertheless rejects, or judges ought to be sought.

## CHAPTER VII. Why God is called the inspector of heart and kidneys

Accordingly, in relation to these two things which we have set forth—the desire of the flesh and the desire of the soul—God is called the tester [Col. 0649A] of heart and kidneys; that is, the inspector of the intentions or consents arising from them. But we, who cannot examine and judge this, direct our judgment chiefly toward acts; we punish not so much faults as acts. Nor do we strive so much to punish what harms a person’s own soul as what may harm others, so that we may prevent public injuries rather than correct individual ones. Thus the Lord also said to Peter: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. 18:15).

What does “sins against you” mean—as though not against another, so that we ought rather to correct or avenge injuries inflicted upon ourselves than those inflicted upon others? Far from it. He said “sins against you” when he openly does something by which he can corrupt you through his example. For if he sins only in himself, when his hidden fault makes himself alone guilty, he does not, so far as lies in him, draw others into guilt through example. Even if there are none who imitate or even know his bad action, nevertheless the action itself, rather than the fault of the mind, ought to be punished among human beings, because it could have incurred greater offence and become more harmful through example than the hidden fault of the mind.

For everything that can result in common destruction or public harm ought to be punished with a greater correction; and what incurs greater offence deserves among us a heavier penalty. The greater the scandal of human beings, the greater is the punishment incurred among human beings, even if a lighter fault preceded it. Suppose, for example, that someone by intercourse has violated a woman in a church. When this reaches the ears of the people, they are stirred not so much by the violation of the woman, the true temple of God, as by the breach of the material temple; although it is more serious to presume against a woman than against walls, and to inflict an injury upon a human being than upon a place. We also punish the burning of houses more severely than accomplished fornication, although before God the latter is far more serious than the former.

Such matters are administered not so much by the requirement of justice as by the moderation of prudent governance, so that, as we have said, by forestalling public harms we may provide for the common good. Therefore we often punish the smallest sins by greater penalties, attending not so much to the equity of justice—what fault has preceded—as, by the discernment of prudence, considering how great an evil may result if it is punished lightly. Thus, reserving the faults of the mind for divine judgment, we pursue by our own judgment their outward effects, concerning which we are able to judge; in such cases attending more to prudential administration—that is, the principle of prudence which we have mentioned—than to the purity of equity.

God, however, assigns each person’s punishment according to the measure of the fault; and whoever equally despise Him are afterward punished with equal penalty, whatever their condition or profession. For if a monk and a layman alike consent to fornication, and the layman’s mind is so inflamed that he too, were he a monk, would not refrain from that shamefulness out of reverence for God, he deserves the same punishment as the monk.

The same must be held concerning two persons, one of whom sins openly, scandalizes many, and corrupts them by example, while the other sins secretly and harms himself alone. For if the person who sins secretly has the same purpose and equal contempt of God as the other—so that his not corrupting others happens rather by chance than because he refrains for God’s sake, since he does not even restrain himself for God’s sake—he is certainly bound by equal guilt before God. For God attends solely to the mind in rewarding good or evil, not to the effects of acts; nor does He weigh what proceeds from our fault or good will, but judges the mind itself according to the purpose of its intention, not according to the outcome of the outward act.

For acts, as we have said before, are alike common to reprobate and elect, and are all indifferent in themselves. They are to be called good or bad only according to the intention of the agent—not, indeed, because performing them is good or bad, but because they are performed well or badly, that is, with the intention with which they ought, or ought not, to be performed. For, as blessed Augustine observes, even the existence of evil is good, since God also uses it well and does not otherwise permit it to exist, although it is by no means itself good.

Therefore, when we say that a human being’s intention is good and that his act is good, we distinguish two things—namely, intention and act—but only one goodness, the goodness of the intention. It is as if we were to say “a good man” and “the son of a good man”: we indicate two men, but not two goodnesses. Just as a man is called good from his own goodness, whereas, when he is called the son of a good man, this shows that he has no goodness in himself on that account, so each person’s intention is called good in itself, while an act is not called good from itself, but because it proceeds from a good intention. Thus there is one goodness from which both intention and action are called good, just as there is one goodness by which a good man and the son of a good man are so called; or one goodness by which a good man and a human being’s good will are so called.

Those, therefore, who are accustomed to object that the act too deserves a reward together with the intention, or contributes to some increase of reward, should observe that their objection is frivolous. “There are two goods,” they say: “a good intention and the effect of a good intention; and a good joined to a good ought to be worth something more than each separately.”

I answer them: even if we grant that the whole is worth more than each separately, are we thereby compelled to concede that it deserves a greater reward? Certainly not. There are many animate and inanimate things whose multitude is more useful than any individual thing included in that multitude, yet no reward whatsoever is due to all of them. For example, an ox joined to an ox, or to a horse, or a piece of wood to wood, or iron: these are good things, and their multitude is worth more than each separately, yet it has no additional reward at all.

[Col. 0651A] “Indeed,” you will say, “that is so because they are not things capable of merit, since they lack reason.” But does our act possess reason, so that it can merit? “Certainly not,” you say; “yet the act is said to merit because it makes us merit—that is, makes us worthy of reward, or at least of greater reward.” But this we have certainly denied above. To see why it must be denied, beyond what we have already said, consider this. Two persons have the same purpose of building houses for the poor. One fulfills the devotion of his desire; the other, through no fault of his own, is prevented from completing what he had proposed because the money he had prepared is violently taken from him, violence alone hindering him. Can what was outwardly done diminish the latter’s merit before God, or can the wickedness of another make less acceptable to God one who did, so far as he was able, what he did for God?

Otherwise, the amount of money could make each person better and more worthy. If it could contribute to merit or to an increase of merit, the richer people were, the better they could become, since through an abundance of wealth they could add more works to their devotion. To think that riches can contribute anything to true blessedness or to the worthiness of the soul, or can take anything away from the merits of the poor, is utter madness. But if possession of things cannot make the soul better, surely neither can it make it dearer to God, nor obtain anything in the blessedness of merit.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the recompense of outward acts

Nevertheless, we do not deny that in this life something is assigned to these good or bad acts, so that through present recompense—reward or punishment—we may be more strongly urged toward good or withdrawn from evil, and so that some may take examples from others in doing what is fitting or avoiding what is unfitting.

## CHAPTER IX. That God and man united in Christ are not something better than God alone

Finally, to return to what was said above, namely, that a good added to a good makes something better than either separately: take care not to be led so far as to call Christ—that is, God and man mutually united in one person—something better than Christ’s divinity or humanity itself; that is, than God Himself united to man or man himself assumed by God.

For it is certain that in Christ both the assumed man and the assuming God are good, and that neither substance can be understood except as good; just as in individual human beings both corporeal and incorporeal substance are good, although the goodness of the body contributes nothing to the dignity or merit of the soul. But who would dare prefer the whole called Christ—that is, God and man together—or any multitude of things whatsoever, to God, as though it could be something better than He, who is the highest good and from whom all things receive whatever good they possess?

Although certain things seem so necessary for doing something that God could not do it without them, as though they were aids or primary causes, nevertheless no magnitude of things, however great, can be called better than God. For although there is a number of good things, so that goodness exists in more things, it does not follow that there is greater goodness. For instance, if knowledge abounds in more persons or the number of fields of knowledge increases, it does not follow that each person’s knowledge must increase, so as to become greater than before.

Likewise, since God is good in Himself and creates innumerable things which have neither existence nor goodness except through Him, goodness exists through Him in more things, so that there is a greater number of good things; yet no goodness can be preferred or equated to His goodness. There is goodness in a human being and goodness in God; and though the substances or natures in which goodness inheres are different, the goodness of no thing can be preferred or equated to divine goodness. Therefore nothing better—that is, no greater good—than God, or equally good with God, should be asserted.

## CHAPTER X. That a multitude of goods is not better than one good

But in act and intention there does not appear to be a number either of goodnesses or of good things. When we say “good intention” and “good act,” meaning an act proceeding from a good intention, only the goodness of the intention is designated; nor is the name “good” retained in the same sense, so that we may call them several goods. For when we say that a human being is simple and that an expression is simple, we do not thereby concede that these are several simple things, since the word *simple* is understood differently here and there.

No one, therefore, should compel us to concede, when a good act is added to a good intention, that good is added to good as though there were several goods for which reward should increase; for, as has been said, we cannot properly call them several goods, because the term *good* does not apply to them in one and the same sense.

## CHAPTER XI. That an act is good by a good intention

We call a good intention good—that is, right—in itself; but we call an act good not because it receives anything good in itself, but because it proceeds from a good intention. Hence, even when the same thing is done by the same person at different times, his act is called now good and now bad according to the diversity of his intention, and so seems to vary with respect to good and evil.

[Col. 0652D] This is like the proposition “Socrates is sitting,” or our understanding of it, which varies with respect to truth and falsehood—now while Socrates is seated, now while he is standing. Aristotle says that this alteration of variation in respect to truth and falsehood occurs in such propositions not because the things that vary with respect to truth or falsehood receive anything through their own change, but because the underlying thing, namely Socrates, is moved in himself—from sitting to standing, or conversely.

## CHAPTER XII. From what is an intention to be called good?

There are some who think an intention good or right whenever a person believes that he is acting well and that what he does pleases God. Such were also those who persecuted the martyrs, concerning whom Truth says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2). The Apostle, pitying the ignorance of such people, says: “I bear them witness that they have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom. 10:2). That is, they have great fervor and desire in doing those things which they believe please God; but because they are deceived in this zeal or pursuit of their mind, their intention is erroneous, and the eye of the heart is not single, so that it can see clearly—that is, guard itself against error.

Therefore, when the Lord distinguished acts according to right or wrong intention, He carefully called the eye of the mind—that is, intention—single and, as it were, pure from dirt, so that it can see clearly; or conversely dark, when He said: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” [Col. 0653B]. That is, if the intention is right, the entire mass of acts proceeding from it, which can be seen after the manner of bodily things, will be worthy of light—that is, good; and conversely.

An intention, therefore, is not to be called good because it seems good, but also because it is such as it is believed to be: namely, when the thing toward which it tends, if it believes it pleases God, does not in fact deceive it in that belief. Otherwise unbelievers too would have good acts just as we do, since they believe no less than we that through their acts they are saved or please God.

## CHAPTER XIII. That sin exists only against conscience

Yet if someone asks whether those persecutors of the martyrs or of Christ sinned in believing that they pleased God, or whether they could without sin omit what they judged must by no means be omitted, then certainly, according to the definition of sin given above as contempt of God, or consenting to that to which one believes one ought not consent, we cannot say that they sinned in this, nor that anyone’s ignorance—or even unbelief itself, with which no one can be saved—is sin.

For those who do not know Christ, and therefore reject the Christian faith because they believe it contrary to God—for what contempt of God have they in doing this for God’s sake, and therefore believing that they act well? This is especially so since the Apostle says: “If our heart does not reproach us, we have confidence before God” (1 John 3:2), as if he were saying: where we do not presume against our conscience, why should we vainly fear that we are held guilty of fault before God?

Or, if the ignorance of such persons is not at all to be ascribed to sin, how does the Lord Himself pray for those crucifying Him, saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)? Or how does Stephen, instructed by this example, pray for those stoning him: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59)? For forgiveness does not seem appropriate where no fault has preceded, and nothing else is ordinarily said to be forgiven except the punishment which fault has deserved. Moreover, Stephen plainly calls sin that which arose from ignorance.

## CHAPTER XIV. In how many ways is “sin” said?

[Col. 0654A]

But, to answer the objections more fully, one must know that the term *sin* is used in different ways. Properly, however, sin is called contempt of God itself, or consent to evil, as we mentioned above. Infants and those naturally devoid of reason are free from this; since they have no merits, being without reason, nothing is imputed to them as sin, and they are saved only through the sacraments.

A sacrifice for sin is also called “sin,” in accordance with the Apostle’s statement that the Lord Jesus Christ was made sin. The punishment of sin is likewise called sin or curse, in accordance with our saying that sin is forgiven—that is, its punishment remitted—and that the Lord Jesus Christ bore our sins—that is, endured the punishment of our sins or the punishments arising from them.

But when we say that infants have original sin, or that all of us, according to the Apostle, sinned in Adam, it is as though we said that our punishment has its origin in his sin, or that the sentence of our condemnation was incurred from it. The acts of sin themselves, too, or whatever we knowingly do or will wrongly, are sometimes called sins. For what is it to have committed a sin except to have fulfilled the effect of sin?

Nor is this surprising, since conversely we call sins themselves “deeds,” according to Athanasius: “They shall render an account,” he says, “of their own deeds; and those who have done good shall go into eternal life, but those who have done evil into eternal fire.” What does “of their own deeds” mean? Does judgment have to be made only concerning what they have fulfilled in action, so that he who has more in outward act receives more in reward? Or is he free from condemnation who lacked the outcome in that which he intended, like the devil himself, who did not obtain in effect what he had presumed in desire? Far from it.

Thus he says “of their own deeds” concerning consent to the things they resolved to accomplish—that is, concerning sins, which before the Lord are reckoned as the completed deed itself; since He punishes them just as we punish acts. But when Stephen calls sin that which the Jews committed against him through ignorance, he calls it either the punishment which he endured on account of the sin of the first parents, like other punishments arising from it, or their unjust act in stoning him. He prayed that this should not be held against them—that is, that on account of it they should not be punished even bodily.

For God often punishes some persons bodily in this life although no fault of theirs requires it, yet not without cause. Thus He brings afflictions even upon the righteous for their purification or testing; or He permits some to be afflicted so that afterward they may be delivered and, through the benefit bestowed, He may be glorified. This occurred in the case of the blind man of whom He Himself said: “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, that he should be born blind, but that the works of God might be manifested in him” (John 9:2).

Who, moreover, denies that innocent children sometimes suffer danger or affliction together with wicked parents because of their parents’ fault, as occurred in Sodom and often happens among many peoples, so that, as punishment is extended more widely, the wicked may be more greatly terrified? Blessed Stephen carefully considering this, prayed that the sin—that is, the punishment—which he endured from the Jews, or what they were doing wrongly, might not be held against them; that is, that they should not on this account be punished even bodily.

The Lord was of the same mind when He said: “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), that is, do not avenge what they do to me by bodily punishment. This could reasonably occur even if no fault of theirs had preceded, so that others who saw it—or they themselves—might recognize from the punishment that they had not acted rightly in this matter.

But it especially befitted the Lord, by the example of His prayer, to exhort us to the virtue of patience and to the exercise of the highest love, so that what He had taught us in words—namely, to pray even for enemies—He might present to us in deed by His own example. Therefore, when He said “forgive,” He did not look to a preceding fault or contempt of God which they had here, but to the ground for a punishment to be inflicted, which, as we have said, might ensue not without cause although no fault had preceded.

This is like what happened to the prophet sent against Samaria, who, by eating, did what the Lord had forbidden. Yet, since he presumed nothing through contempt of God, but had been deceived by another prophet, he incurred death not so much because of the guilt of fault as because of the performance of the act. For God, as blessed Gregory observes, sometimes changes His sentence but never His counsel; that is, He often decides not to fulfill what He had decreed to command or threaten for some cause. But His counsel remains fixed: what He ordains in His foreknowledge that He will do never lacks efficacy.

Thus He did not maintain the command concerning Abraham’s sacrifice of his son, nor the threat made to the Ninevites, and so, as we have said, changed His sentence. Likewise the aforesaid prophet, to whom He had forbidden eating on the way, believed that His sentence had been changed; and he thought himself especially at fault if he did not obey the other prophet, who declared that he had been sent by the Lord to refresh his weariness with food.

He therefore did this without fault, intending to avoid fault in doing so. Nor did sudden death harm him, since it freed him from the hardships of the present life and benefited many by making them more provident when they saw a righteous man punished without fault, and saw fulfilled in him what is elsewhere said to the Lord: “You, God, though just, order all things justly, even when you condemn one who ought not to be punished.” [Note: [Col. 0655D] The passage is cited incorrectly by Abelard. Wisdom 12:15 reads: “Since you are just, you order all things justly; you consider it alien to your power to condemn even one who ought not to be punished.”] “You condemn,” he says, to death—not eternal death, but bodily death.

For just as some are saved without merits, such as infants, and attain eternal life by grace alone, so it is not absurd that some should endure bodily punishments which they have not deserved. This is clear also in the case of infants who die without the grace of baptism, who are condemned both to bodily and eternal death; and many innocent persons likewise suffer affliction. What wonder, then, if those crucifying the Lord, by that unjust act, though ignorance excuses them from fault, could nevertheless reasonably incur temporal punishment, as we have said, and therefore it was said: “Forgive them,” that is, do not inflict the punishment which they could reasonably incur from this?

Just as what these persons did through ignorance, and even ignorance itself, is not properly called sin—that is, contempt of God—so neither is unbelief, although it necessarily bars adults already possessing the use of reason from entrance into eternal life. For disbelief in the Gospel, ignorance of Christ, and failure to receive the sacraments of the Church suffice for condemnation, although this occurs not so much through malice as through ignorance. Of such persons Truth says: “He who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). And the Apostle: “If anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38).

But when we say that we sin unknowingly—that is, by doing something which ought not to be done—we take “sin” not in the sense of contempt, but in that of action. Philosophers too call it sin to do or say something improperly, although this seems to have nothing to do with offence against God. Thus Aristotle, when speaking in the category *relation* about a defective assignment of relatives, says: “But sometimes conversion will not seem to occur unless that in relation to which something is said is assigned appropriately. For if the person assigning errs—for example, if wing is assigned to bird—it does not convert, so that bird belongs to wing.”

If, then, we call sin in this manner, we shall call sins everything that we do defectively or that stands contrary to our salvation. Thus we shall call sins both unbelief and ignorance of those things which must be believed for salvation, although no contempt of God appears there. Properly speaking, however, I think that only that is called sin which can nowhere occur without fault. Ignorance of God, disbelief in Him, or the acts themselves that are wrongly done can occur in many people without fault.

For if someone does not believe the Gospel or Christ because preaching has not reached him, as the Apostle says: “How will they believe in Him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?” (Rom. 10:14), what fault can be assigned to him for not believing? Cornelius did not believe in Christ until Peter was sent to instruct him concerning this. Although before that time he acknowledged and loved God according to the law of nature—thereby deserving that his prayer be heard and that his alms be accepted by God—yet if it had happened that he departed from this life before faith in Christ, we would by no means dare promise him life, however good his works might appear. We would count him not among the faithful but rather among unbelievers, however zealously he had pursued salvation.

For the judgments of God are a great abyss. He sometimes draws those who resist, or who are less concerned for their salvation, and by the most profound counsel of His governance rejects those who offer themselves or are more ready to believe. Thus He rejected the one offering himself: “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go” (Matt. 4:19). And He did not tolerate even for an hour another man who excused himself because of his concern for his father, in this excuse of filial devotion.

Finally, rebuking the obstinacy of certain cities, He said: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11:21). Behold, He offered those cities not only His preaching but also the display of miracles, although He knew beforehand that they would not believe. But He did not then judge worthy of His visitation other cities of Gentiles, which He did not fail to know were ready to receive faith. In some of these, persons prepared to receive Him nevertheless perished because the word of preaching was withheld from them. Who would impute this to their fault, when we see that it happened through no negligence?

Yet we say that this unbelief in which they died suffices for condemnation, although the reason why the Lord left them in this blindness appears less clearly to us. Perhaps one may, if it seems absurd to him that such persons are condemned without sin, ascribe this to their sin without fault.

Nevertheless, as we have often said, we think that in the proper sense only that is called sin which consists in the fault of negligence and cannot exist in any person, of whatever age, without deserving condemnation on that account. But how failure to believe in Christ, which belongs to unbelief, ought to be imputed as fault to infants or to those to whom He has not been proclaimed, I do not see; nor do I see this in anything done through invincible ignorance, which we were unable to foresee.

For example, someone may unknowingly kill with an arrow a man whom he does not see in the forest while aiming at wild beasts or birds. When we say that he sins through ignorance, just as we sometimes confess that we sin not only in consent but also in thought, we do not here use the word in the proper sense of fault, but broadly: for what it is not fitting that we should do, whether it occurs through error, negligence, or in whatever unfitting manner.

Thus to sin through ignorance means not to have fault in it, but to do what is unfitting for us. To sin in thought means, in the same way, to will what it is not fitting for us to will; and to sin in speech or action means to speak or act in a manner in which we ought not, even though this should happen to us against our will through ignorance. Thus, if they persecuted Christ or His followers whom they believed ought to be persecuted, we say that they sinned in action; yet they would have sinned more gravely in fault if, against their consciences, they had spared them.

## CHAPTER XV. Whether every sin is forbidden

The question is raised whether God forbids us every sin. If we accept this, He seems to act unreasonably, since this life cannot be lived without sins, at least venial ones. For if He commanded us to avoid all sins, while we cannot avoid all of them, then He imposes upon us not the sweet yoke or light burden which He promised, but something far exceeding our strength, which we are wholly unable to bear—as the Apostle Peter also declares concerning the yoke of the Law.

For who can always guard against even an idle word, so as never to transgress in it and to maintain that perfection of which James says: “If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (Jas. 3:2)? He had first said: “We all offend in many things.” And another apostle of great perfection says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). I think it is evident to everyone how difficult—indeed impossible—it seems to our weakness to remain wholly free from sin.

This is so, I say, if we take the word *sin* broadly, as we have said, and call sins also whatever things we do improperly. But if, understanding sin properly, we call only contempt of God sin, then this life can indeed be lived without it, although with the greatest difficulty. Nor, as we have noted above, is anything forbidden to us by God except consent to evil, by which we despise God, even when a command seems to concern an outward act, as we explained above and showed also that His commands could not otherwise be kept by us.

[Col. 0658C] Of sins, some are called venial and, as it were, slight; others damnable or grave. Again, among damnable sins some are called criminal, since, if they come to public notice, they make the person involved infamous or criminal; others do not. Venial sins, or sins of this kind, occur when we consent to something to which we know we ought not consent, yet at that moment what we know does not come to mind; for we know many things even while asleep, or when we do not remember them. We do not lose our knowledge by sleeping, become foolish, or become wise when we wake. Thus we sometimes consent to idle talk or to excessive eating or drinking, [Col. 0658D] although we certainly know that this ought not be done; yet at that moment we did not remember that it ought not be done. Such acts of consent, which we incur through forgetfulness, are called venial or slight sins: that is, they are not to be corrected by a punishment requiring great satisfaction, so that we should be punished for them either by exclusion from the church or by severe abstinence. For these negligences, to be forgiven upon repentance, we regularly use the words of daily confession, in which there should by no means be a recital of graver offenses, but only of lighter ones. For there we ought not to say, “I have sinned by perjury, by homicide, by adultery,” and the like, which are called damnable and graver sins. For we incur these not through forgetfulness, as we do the former, [Col. 0659A] but commit them as if deliberately and intentionally, becoming abominable even to God, according to the Psalmist’s words: “They have become abominable in their designs” (Ps. 13:2): that is, execrable and exceedingly hateful because of the things in which they knowingly presumed.

Some of these are called criminal sins: those which, when known through their outward result, bring a great stain of guilt upon a person, such as consent to perjury, homicide, or adultery—sins that greatly scandalize the Church. But when we indulge excessively in food, beyond what is necessary, or adorn ourselves with immoderate finery from vainglory, although we knowingly presume to do this, such acts are not reckoned as crimes, and among many receive more praise than blame.

## Chapter XVI. Whether it is better to abstain from lighter faults than from graver ones

[Col. 0659B]

There are those who say that it is more perfect, and therefore better, to guard against venial than against criminal sins, because this seems more difficult and to require a more painstaking diligence. To them I first reply with Cicero: “If something is laborious, it is not therefore glorious.” Otherwise those who bore the heavy yoke of the Law would have greater merit before the Lord than those who serve under evangelical freedom, because fear has punishment, which perfect charity casts out; and all who are governed by fear labor more in deed than those whom charity makes willing. Therefore the Lord exhorts those who labor and are burdened to take up the sweet yoke and light burden, so that they may pass from the slavery of the Law, under which they were oppressed, to the freedom of the Gospel, [Col. 0659C] and that those who began from fear may be perfected by charity, which without difficulty bears all things and endures all things. Nothing, indeed, is difficult for one who loves—especially when the love is not carnal but the spiritual love of God, which is so much stronger as it is truer.

Who also does not know that it is harder for us to guard against a flea than against an enemy, or against the obstacle of a small stone than a large one? But do we therefore judge that avoiding what is more difficult is better or more beneficial? Certainly not. Why? Because what is harder to avoid can do less harm. Therefore, even if we grant that guarding against venial sins is harder than guarding against criminal sins, it is nevertheless fitting to avoid the more dangerous sins rather than these, those which deserve a greater punishment, by which we believe God to be more offended, [Col. 0659D] and which displease him more. For the more closely we cling to him in love, the more carefully we should avoid those things by which he is more offended and which he more strongly disapproves.

For one who truly loves someone strives to avoid not so much his own loss as the offense or contempt of his friend, according to the Apostle: “Charity does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5); and again: “Let no one seek what is his own, but what is another’s” (1 Cor. 10:24). If, then, we ought to avoid sins not so much because of our own loss as because of offense to God, surely those sins are to be avoided more carefully in which he is more offended. And if we attend to that poetic maxim concerning moral uprightness:

> The good hate to sin from love of virtue.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* XVI.57

[Col. 0660A] then sins of every kind ought to be hated the more intensely the more shameful they are judged in themselves, the further they depart from virtuous uprightness, and the more naturally they offend everyone.

Finally, that we may judge individual sins more carefully by comparing them with each other, let us compare venial with criminal sins—for example, excessive eating with perjury and adultery—and ask in whose transgression sin is greater, or God more greatly despised and offended. Perhaps, I do not know, you will answer as some philosophers did, who held all sins equal. But if you choose to follow this philosophy—or rather, manifest folly—it is equally good to abstain from criminal and venial sins, because committing these and those is equally evil. Why then would anyone dare to prefer abstinence from [Col. 0660B] venial sins to abstinence from criminal ones?

If someone perhaps asks how we can infer that the transgression of adultery displeases God more than excess in food, the divine Law, I think, can teach us. It established no penal satisfaction for punishing the latter, but decreed that the former should be condemned not by just any penalty but by the affliction of the supreme punishment, death. For the more the love of neighbor—which the Apostle calls the fulfillment of the Law—is injured, the more one acts against it and the greater the sin.

And if, in this manner, we wish to compare each venial sin with each criminal sin, and likewise compare all these together with all those, in order to give complete satisfaction, [Col. 0660C] I do not shrink from doing so. Let us suppose, then, that someone very diligently avoids every venial sin but takes no care to avoid any criminal sin; and while avoiding all the former, he commits the latter. Who would judge that he sins less in this, or is better, because he avoids these while incurring those? Therefore, once comparison has been made both among individual sins, as we have said, and among all sins together, I think it plain that avoiding venial sins is not better, nor a mark of greater perfection, than avoiding criminal sins.

Yet if someone, having first avoided the latter, should afterward be able, as he ought, to avoid the former, I admit that in this his virtue has reached perfection. Still, the later acts, in which the completion of virtue consists, are not for that reason to be preferred to the earlier ones, nor are they worthy of so great a reward. For often, in constructing a building, those who complete it do less than those who worked before them; and those who finish it by setting the final beam in place, so that the house becomes complete, do less than the earlier workers, since while it was incomplete, the house was not a house but a work.

I think that we have labored enough thus far, insofar as memory has supplied material, toward knowledge of sin, so that it may be avoided the better the more carefully it has been known. For knowledge of evil cannot be lacking to the righteous person, nor can anyone avoid a vice unless it is known.

## Chapter XVII. On the reconciliation of sinners

And since we have shown the wound of the soul, let us endeavor to show the remedy for its healing. Hence Jerome’s saying: “O physician, if you are skilled, just as you have set forth the cause of the disease, so point out the means of health!” Since, therefore, we offend God by sinning, it remains to consider in what ways we may be reconciled to him. There are, then, three elements in the reconciliation of the sinner to God: namely repentance, confession, and satisfaction.
