## Chapter XVIII. What is properly called repentance?

Repentance is properly called grief of mind over that in which one has sinned: namely, when someone regrets having transgressed in some matter (Wis. 5:2–3). This repentance sometimes arises from love of God and is fruitful; sometimes from some loss by which we would not wish to be burdened, such as the repentance of the damned, of whom it is written: “Seeing, they shall be troubled with terrible fear, and shall marvel at the suddenness of unexpected salvation, [Col. 0661B] saying within themselves, repenting, and groaning for anguish of spirit: ‘These are they whom we once held in derision’” (Wis. 5:2–3), etc.

We also read of Judas’s repentance over having betrayed the Lord. We believe that this happened not so much because of guilt for the sin as because of his own vileness, since he felt himself condemned in everyone’s judgment. For when someone has drawn another to destruction by corrupting him with money or in some other way, no one considers the traitor more contemptible than that other person, and no one trusts him less than the one who has more fully experienced his unfaithfulness.

Every day, indeed, we see many people about to depart this life repent of crimes they have committed and groan in grievous remorse—not so much from love of God, whom they offended, or hatred of the sin they committed, as from fear of the punishment [Col. 0661C] into which they fear they are about to be hurled. They remain wicked even in this: they dislike not the iniquity of their fault so much as the severity of the punishment, which is just. They hate not so much what they committed because it was evil as God’s just judgment, which they fear in its punishment; hating justice rather than iniquity.

Those who have long been blinded, and have been called to turn from their wickedness, divine justice at last gives over to a reprobate mind and, having struck them with blindness, utterly casts them away from its face, so that they possess neither knowledge of salutary repentance nor the ability to discern how satisfaction should be made.

For we daily see a great many dying persons groaning grievously, accusing themselves much [Col. 0661D] for usury, robbery, oppression of the poor, or whatever other wrongs they have committed, and consulting a priest about making amends for these things. If they are first given this counsel, as they ought to be—namely, to sell everything they possess and restore to others what they have taken, according to Augustine’s saying, “If another’s property, when it can be restored, is not restored, repentance is not practiced but feigned”—they immediately reveal by their answer how empty their repentance is. “Then,” they say, “how would my household live? What would I leave to my children and my wife? By what means could they support themselves?”

To such persons the Lord’s rebuke first applies: “Fool, this night they demand your soul of you; and the things which you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20). O wretch, whoever you are—indeed, most wretched of all wretches [Col. 0662A] and most foolish of all fools—you make no provision for what you may preserve for yourself, but for what you may store up for others. With what presumption do you offend God, to whose dreadful judgment you are being dragged, so that you may have those favorable to you whom you enrich from the plunder of the poor? Who would not laugh at you if he heard you hope that others would be more favorable to you than you yourself? You place confidence in the alms of those whom, because you believe you will have them as heirs, you likewise make heirs of your iniquity, leaving them others’ possessions to hold by robbery.

You take life from the poor by taking from them the means by which they are sustained; and you plot in them to kill Christ again, according to his own words: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). What, then, do you—mistakenly compassionate toward your own people, and cruel alike toward yourself [Col. 0662B] and toward God—expect from the just Judge, before whom you hasten to be judged whether you wish it or not, who requires an account not only of robberies but even of an idle word?

How strict he is in vengeance, he at once showed by the punishment of the first humans. Adam sinned only once, and, as blessed Jerome observes by comparison with our sins, his sin was very slight. He oppressed no one by violence and took nothing from anyone; once he tasted fruit that could be replaced. By such a slight transgression, whose punishment also overflowed to all posterity, the Lord determined to foreshadow what he would do with greater sins. The rich man whom the Lord says descended into hell had not seized another’s goods, but had failed to share his own goods, which he enjoyed as though lawfully, with needy Lazarus. He plainly teaches what punishment is to strike those who seize others’ goods, if that man was condemned and buried in hell because he did not give his own goods.

Your memory will be buried with you, and soon, when the tears of those who attended your funeral have dried, according to the rhetorician Apollonius, “Nothing dries more quickly than a tear.” Your wife will shortly prepare herself for a new marriage, to serve the pleasures of a new husband from the robberies that you left her; and while your body is still present, she will warm the bed for another, while you, miserable man, will pay for those pleasures in the flames of Gehenna. The same is to be expected from your children.

If someone perhaps asks why, remembering you, they will not make you propitious through their alms, they seem able to excuse themselves on many grounds. For if they answer: “Since he was unwilling to be favorable to himself, what folly it was to hope that others would be favorable to him and to entrust to others the salvation of his soul, for which he himself ought to have made the greatest provision! Whom did he believe more favorable to himself than himself? He who was cruel to himself—whose mercy did he trust?” They can also, in excuse of their own greed, allege and say: “Moreover, we know that what he left us is not the sort of property from which we ought to make alms.” All who hear these things will laugh, and ought to laugh. But that wretched man who compelled the despoiled poor to weep for a time will weep there forever.

[Col. 0663A] There are people who, wishing to hide their negligence from human beings but not from God, utter excuses to excuse sins, saying that those whom they despoiled are so numerous that they cannot possibly know or find them. Since they make no effort in the matter, they incur the judgment of the Apostle’s saying: “Whoever does not know will not be known” (1 Cor. 14:38). They do not find them because they do not seek them; the right hand of God, whom they despised, will find them. Of it too it is written: “Your right hand will find all who hate you” (Ps. 20:9). The same Prophet who said this, deeply terrified and seeing no place of escape, says elsewhere: “Where shall I go from your spirit, or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend to heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138:5).

And because often the greed of the priest is no less [Col. 0663B] than that of the people, according to the prophet’s words, “As with priest, so with people” (Hos. 4:9), the greed of priests will deceive many dying persons by promising them vain security if they offer what they possess for sacrifices and purchase Masses which they would by no means receive free of charge. In this trade there is, among them, an established price: one denarius for one Mass, and forty for one annual Mass. They do not advise the dying to restore their robberies, but to offer the robberies themselves in sacrifice; although, on the contrary, it is written: “Whoever offers sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the sight of his father” (Ecclus. 34:24). For the killing of a son before his eyes weighs more heavily upon a father than if he did not see it; and a son is, as it were, killed by sacrifice when the property of the poor, in which his life consisted, is placed in sacrifice.

And Truth, preferring mercy to sacrifice, says: “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice’” (Matt. 9:13). Yet it is worse to retain robberies than not to show mercy: that is, worse to take from the poor what is theirs than not to give them what is ours, as we have noted above in the condemnation of the rich man.

## Chapter XIX. On fruitful repentance

Since we have spoken of unfruitful repentance, let us consider fruitful repentance with all the greater care because it is more salutary. Inviting every obstinate person who does not consider God’s dreadful judgment to this repentance, the Apostle says: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness and patience and long-suffering? Do you not know that the goodness of God leads you [Col. 0663D] to repentance?” (Rom. 2:4). By these words he plainly declares what repentance is salutary and proceeds from love of God rather than fear: namely, that we should grieve because we have offended or despised God because he is good, more than because he is just.

For the longer we despise him because we do not believe that he immediately judges the contempt shown to him—as earthly rulers do, who, when offended, do not know how to spare or defer vengeance for their injuries—the more justly he inflicts a graver punishment for contempt of himself; and he is so much stricter in vengeance as he was more patient in waiting. The Apostle just mentioned shows this in what follows: “By your hardness [Col. 0664A] and unrepentant heart, you store up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath” (ibid., 5): then a day of wrath, now a time of gentleness; then of vengeance, now of patience. There, justice demanding it, he will avenge contempt of himself all the more severely because he ought to have been less despised and endured it longer.

We fear to offend people, and when we cannot avoid their displeasure through fear, we avoid it through shame. When we fornicate, we seek hiding places so that people may not see us, and we cannot then endure even the gaze of one human being. We know that God is present, whom nothing can escape; yet we do not blush to be seen by him and by the whole court of heaven in this shameful act, though we would be ashamed under the gaze of one little human being. Before an earthly judge we are exceedingly afraid to presume anything, knowing that we are to be judged by him only with temporal, [Col. 0664B] not eternal, punishment. Carnal affection compels us to do or suffer many things; spiritual affection, few. Would that we did or suffered as much for God, to whom we owe everything, as we do or suffer for a wife, children, or any prostitute whatsoever!

By what punishment, I beg you, is this injury to be judged—that we even place a prostitute above him? Through the prophet he complains that neither love is shown to him as Father nor fear as Lord: “A son honors his father, and a servant fears his master. If I am Father, where is my honor? And if I am Lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. 1:6). He complains that a father or master is preferred to him. Consider, then, how greatly he is indignant that even a prostitute is preferred to him, and that the supreme patience of his goodness—by which [Col. 0664C] he should have been loved more—is instead more despised.

Those who repent salutarily consider this goodness and the long-suffering of his patience, and are moved to compunction not so much by fear of punishments as by love of him, in accordance with the Apostle’s aforementioned exhortation, where he carefully described salutary repentance. Conversely, he said: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness?”—that is, rich and abundant goodness, or the overflowing kindness of long-suffering patience, by which he bears with you for so long—because he does not swiftly punish you. “Not knowing,” that is, not considering, that such great kindness, so far as it lies in itself, leads you to repentance—that is, makes you see, by considering it, why you ought to turn to repentance: because you have despised one so kind.

And this truly is fruitful repentance for sin: when this grief and contrition of mind proceed from love of God, whom we recognize as so kind, rather than from fear of punishments.

With this groaning and contrition of heart, which we call true repentance, sin does not remain—that is, contempt of God or consent to evil—because the charity of God which inspires this groaning does not permit guilt. By this groaning we are immediately reconciled to God and obtain forgiveness of the preceding sin, according to the prophet’s words: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 33:14); that is, he will be made worthy of salvation of his soul. He did not say, “In what year,” or “month,” or “week,” or “day,” but “at what hour,” so as to show that without delay the person becomes worthy of pardon [Col. 0665A] and owes no eternal punishment, in which the condemnation of sin consists.

Even if, prevented by the moment of necessity, he has no opportunity to come to confession or to complete satisfaction, one who departs this life in this groaning does not thereby enter Gehenna. For God’s forgiving sin means making that person such that his soul is no longer worthy to be eternally punished by God for the preceding sin. When God forgives sin to the penitent, he does not forgive them every punishment, but only the eternal punishment. For many penitents who, overtaken by death, have not completed penitential satisfaction in this life are reserved in the future for purgatorial, not damnatory, punishments. Therefore it is uncertain over how great a span of time the final day of judgment, on which many believers are suddenly to be punished, will extend, although the resurrection takes place in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye (1 Cor. 15:52), so that there they may make satisfaction, as much as God decrees, for the faults for which they delayed making satisfaction or were not permitted to do so.

## Chapter XX. Whether someone can repent of one sin without another

There are those who ask whether someone can repent of one sin and not another—for example, of homicide but not of fornication, which he does not yet cease to commit. But if we understand that fruitful repentance which the love of God imparts, and which Gregory describes when he says, “Repentance is to weep over sins committed and not to commit the sins that ought to be wept over,” then no repentance can be called repentance, to which the love of God impels us, so long as one contempt of God is retained.

For if the love of God, as it ought, leads and draws me to grieve over this act of consent solely because in it I offended God, I do not see how the same love would not compel me to repent for the same reason of that contempt also. That is, it establishes my mind in the resolve that, whenever any transgression of mine comes to memory, I should similarly grieve over it and be ready to make satisfaction. Wherever, therefore, repentance is true, proceeding solely from love of God, no contempt of God remains—especially since Truth says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John [Col. 0665D] 14:23).

Therefore, all who persist in the love of God must be saved; and that salvation could by no means occur if even one sin—that is, one contempt of God—were retained. But when God finds no sin remaining in the penitent, he finds in that person no cause of condemnation. Therefore it follows that, sin having ceased, condemnation does not remain—that is, the affliction of everlasting punishment. This is what it means for the preceding sin to be forgiven by God from the eternal punishment which, as we said, it had deserved to have imposed by God.

For although God no longer finds in the penitent anything that he ought to punish forever, he is nevertheless said to forgive the punishment of the preceding sin when, by inspiring in the person the groaning of repentance, he has made that person worthy of pardon; that is, such a person that no eternal punishment is then owed, [Col. 0666A] and one who, departing this life in that state, must be saved. But if the person perhaps falls back into the same contempt, then just as he returns to sin, so he also relapses into the liability to punishment, and must again be punished—he who formerly, by repenting, had merited not to be punished.

If someone should say that God’s forgiving sin means as though one said, “God will by no means condemn a person because of what was committed,” or, “God has determined within himself not to condemn that person because of it,” then surely it seems necessary to grant that, even before the penitent sinned, God had forgiven that sin—that is, had determined within himself that he would not condemn the person because of it. For God determines or arranges nothing newly within himself; rather, from eternity, whatever he will do stands in his predestination and is fixed in his providence, both the forgiveness of every sin and all other things that occur.

Therefore it seems better to us to understand God’s forgiveness of sin as making anyone, as we said, worthy of pardon through the groaning of repentance inspired in him; that is, making him such that condemnation is not then owed to him, nor will ever afterward be owed if he perseveres in such a resolution. Thus God forgives sin when he, who ought to have inflicted punishment, by inspiring repentance brings it about that the punishment should no longer be imposed.

## Chapter XXI. That it is not unjust not to give a reward to one worthy of it

[Col. 0666C] But perhaps you ask whether one who repents is already worthy of eternal life, since he is not worthy of condemnation. If we grant this, the objection is made that one who fell after repentance and perished was, while repenting, worthy of eternal life; and that God appears chargeable with injustice because he did not at least then give him the reward of which he was then worthy, and thus prevent his condemnation. For just as, if he had died then, he would have been saved as worthy of eternal life on account of the resolution in which he then stood, so, if he later fell, he had been worthy of salvation on account of the same disposition which he had before.

But I say that, just as many are often worthy of condemnation and yet do not die in their wickedness so that the condemnation they deserved is imposed upon them by God—and God is not therefore chargeable with injustice because he did not impose the punishment they deserved—so also in granting rewards, which are promised only to those who persevere, as Truth attests: “Whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). Therefore we are not compelled to concede that, because someone has at some time been worthy of punishment or reward, it is therefore fitting or just that God grant it, when he has foreseen that the person can be put to better use in another way; for he makes good use even of the wicked and orders even the worst things in the best manner.

But if someone should say that one who truly repented for a time by loving God, yet did not persevere in that repentance or love, was not therefore worthy of the reward of life, then surely, since it is also granted that he was not then worthy of condemnation, he will seem at that time to have been neither righteous nor sinful.

## Chapter XXII. On the unforgivable sin

Since, as we have said, every sin immediately receives remission through repentance, the question arises why Truth called a certain sin unforgivable, or said that it would never have remission—that is, forgiveness—namely the sin of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Matthew reports that he spoke of it thus: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to human beings, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven” (Luke 12:31); and: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” [Col. 0667B] (ibid., 32; 12:10).

Mark explains why he said this: “Because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit’” (Mark 3:30). Some call this sin despair of pardon: namely, when someone, because of the greatness of his sins, utterly distrusts the goodness of God, which is understood through the Holy Spirit, so that he cannot obtain forgiveness by repentance or any satisfaction. But if we call this sinning or blaspheming against the Spirit, what shall we call sinning against the Son of Man?

So far as it seems to me, sinning or blaspheming against the Son of Man in this passage means detracting from the excellence of Christ’s humanity, as though we denied that it was conceived without sin or assumed by God, because of the visible weakness of the flesh. This could indeed be discovered by no human reasoning, but only believed through God’s revelation. Thus his saying, “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to human beings, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven,” means as though he said: “Concerning no other blasphemy has God determined that it will be forgiven to no human beings, except this one.” And, “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven,” means that no one who detracts, as we have said, from the dignity of the assumed man will be condemned for this reason, unless other causes of condemnation intervene. For no contempt of God can be charged against someone who contradicts the truth through error and does not act against conscience—especially when the matter is such that it cannot be investigated by human reasoning and indeed seems contrary to reason.

But to blaspheme against the Spirit is to slander works of God’s manifest grace in such a way that things which they believed were mercifully done through the Holy Spirit—that is, through divine goodness—they nevertheless asserted were done through the devil. It is as if they said that the one whom they believed to be the Spirit of God was an evil spirit, and thus that God was the devil.

Therefore, all who sinned against Christ in this way—namely, by saying against conscience that he cast out demons through Beelzebub, prince of demons—were so utterly proscribed from the kingdom of God and excluded entirely from his grace that none of them would thereafter merit pardon through repentance. We do not deny, indeed, that they could be saved if they repented; we say only [Col. 0668A] that they will not attain even the act of repentance.

## Chapter XXIII. Whether the penitent carry with them the groaning of their sorrow from this life

Someone perhaps asks whether those who depart this life repentant, in this groaning of heart and contrition of sorrow—where a true sacrifice is offered to God according to the words, “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50)—whether, I say, such persons departing this light carry this groaning and sorrow with them, so that in that heavenly life too they grieve that they committed these things, although, as it is written, “sorrow and groaning” and sadness flee away there (Isa. 35:10).

But surely, just as our sins displease God and the angels without any painful suffering—because they do not approve what they recognize as evil—so those things in which we sinned will then displease us as well. But whether we will wish that we had done those things which we know were rightly ordered by God and which also worked together for our good, according to the Apostle’s words, “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. 8:28), is another question, which we have resolved to the best of our ability in the third book of our *Theology*.

## Chapter XXIV. On confession

We must now discuss confession of sins. Exhorting us to it, the apostle James says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another that you may be saved; for the persistent prayer of a righteous person avails much” (Jas. 5:16). There are those who think confession should be made to God alone, a view that some attribute to the Greeks. [Col. 0668C] But what value confession has before God, who knows all things, or what pardon the tongue obtains for us, I do not see, although the Prophet says: “I made my offense known to you, and did not conceal my injustice” (Ps. 31:5).

For many reasons the faithful confess sins to one another, according to the Apostle’s statement just cited: first, because of the reason supplied there, that we may be aided more by the prayers of those to whom we confess; and also because a great part of satisfaction is accomplished in the humility of confession, and in the remission of penance we obtain a greater pardon. Thus it is written of David: when, accused by the prophet Nathan, he replied, “I have sinned” (2 Sam. 12:13), he immediately heard this answer from the same prophet: “The Lord also has taken away your sin” (ibid.). The greater the king’s eminence, the more acceptable to God was his confident humility.

Finally, priests, to whom the souls of those making confession are entrusted, ought to impose upon them the satisfactions of penance. Those who have wickedly and proudly used their own judgment in despising God should be corrected by the judgment of another’s authority; and they perform this all the more safely the better they obey their superiors, following not so much their own will as theirs. If priests perhaps prescribe wrongly, then, provided the penitent is prepared to obey, it is to be imputed more to the priests than to the penitents.

“We are not ignorant,” says the Apostle, “of Satan’s devices” (2 Cor. 2:11). Nor should his malice here be passed over, by which he impels us toward sin [Col. 0669A] and withdraws us from confession. For in inciting us to sin, he strips us alike of fear and shame, so that nothing remains to recall us from sin. We do not dare to commit many things through fear of punishment; we are ashamed to undertake many things because of injury to our reputation, even if we could do so with impunity. Thus, once any person has been wickedly released from these two restraints, he becomes headlong in committing any sin whatever.

By this device Satan afterward gives back the very things which he first removed so that the person might complete the sin, in order to hold him back from confession. The person then fears or is ashamed to confess what, when he first ought to have done so, he neither feared nor was ashamed to do. He fears perhaps that through confession he will be known and punished by human beings, though he did not fear punishment by God; he is ashamed for people to know what he was not ashamed to commit before God. But one seeking medicine for a wound must reveal it to the physician, however foul it may be, however offensive its smell, so that fitting treatment may be applied. The priest occupies the physician’s place, and he, as we have said, must prescribe the satisfaction.

## Chapter XXV. That confession can sometimes be omitted
Yet it should be known that confession can sometimes be avoided by a salutary dispensation, as we believe in the case of Peter: we know of his tears after his denial, but we do not read of any other satisfaction or confession. Hence Ambrose, commenting on Luke concerning Peter’s very denial and weeping, says: “I do not find what he said; I find that he wept. I read of his tears [Col. 0669C]; I do not read of his satisfaction. Tears lift the sin which shame is reluctant to confess aloud; weeping serves both pardon and modesty. Tears speak of guilt without horror; they confess without offending modesty. Tears do not ask pardon, but deserve it. I find why Peter kept silence: namely, lest a request for pardon made so soon should give greater offence.”

[Col. 0669D] But what this modesty or reverence concerning confession was, such that Peter made satisfaction more by weeping than by confessing, must be considered. For if he was ashamed to confess solely lest, once his sin was known, he should be held in lower esteem, he was certainly proud, caring more for the glory of his own honour than for the salvation of his soul. But if he was restrained by shame not so much for his own sake as for that of the Church, this is not to be disapproved. Perhaps he foresaw that the Lord was to appoint him ruler over the Lord’s people, and he feared that, if his threefold denial were quickly made public through his confession, the Church would be gravely scandalized thereby; and it would be intensely ashamed that the Lord had set over it one so ready to deny and so faint-hearted. If, therefore, he delayed confession both to preserve his honour and because of this inward shame on behalf of the Church, he acted prudently, not proudly. Fear also had a reasonable place here: fear of harm to the Church rather than loss of his own reputation. For he knew that the Church had been specially entrusted to him by the Lord when He said: “And when you have once turned back, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32) [Col. 0670A].

If, therefore, once he had been convicted by his own confession, this utterly abhorrent fall of his had reached the ears of the Church beforehand, who would not readily have said: “We do not want this man to reign over us” (Luke 19:14)? And who would not readily have condemned the Lord’s decision in choosing, to strengthen the brethren, one who had first failed? By this same prudence many might defer confession, or even entirely omit it, without sin—if they believed that it would do more harm than good. For we incur no offence against God in a matter in which we do not in any way despise Him. Peter delayed confessing his sin while the Church was still tender in faith and weak, until Peter’s strength had been proved through his preaching or miracles. Afterwards, when this was already established, Peter himself could confess it, without any scandal to the Church, against the despair of the fallen, so that it might even be recorded by the Evangelists.

[Col. 0670B] Perhaps there are some who think that Peter, who was set over all the others and had no superior to whom his soul was entrusted, had no need to confess his sin to a human being, as though satisfaction were to be imposed upon him by that person and he were to obey that person’s command as a superior. But even if he did not have to confess to someone for the imposition of satisfaction, he could fittingly have done so for the aid of prayer. For when it is said, “Confess your sins to one another,” it is added: “and pray for one another, that you may be saved” (James 5:16). Nor is there anything to prevent prelates from choosing subjects to make confession to, or to undertake satisfaction under, so that what is done may be more acceptable to God insofar as it is done more humbly [Col. 0670C].

Who also forbids anyone, in such matters, to choose a more religious or more discerning person, to whose judgment he may entrust his satisfaction and by whose prayers he may be greatly assisted? Thus, immediately after the words, “and pray for one another, that you may be saved,” it is added: “for the persistent prayer of a righteous man is very powerful.” For just as many physicians are unskilled, to whom it is dangerous or useless to entrust the sick, so among the prelates of the Church many are found who are neither religious nor discerning and who, moreover, are careless in disclosing the sins of those who confess. Thus confession to them seems not merely useless but even harmful. Such persons neither devote themselves to prayer nor deserve to be heard in their prayers. Since they are ignorant of the ordinances of the canons and do not know how to exercise moderation in prescribing satisfactions, they frequently promise vain security in such cases and deceive those confessing with empty hope, according to the saying of Truth: “They are blind guides of the blind”; and again: “If a blind man guides a blind man, both fall into a pit” (Matthew 15:14). And since, as we have said, they carelessly reveal the confessions they receive, they stir penitents to indignation; those who ought to heal sins inflict new wounds of sin and deter their hearers from confession.

Sometimes, too, by revealing sins either in anger or through carelessness, they grievously scandalize the Church [Col. 0671A] and expose those who have confessed to serious dangers. Therefore those who have resolved to avoid their prelates because of such disadvantages, and to choose others in these matters whom they believe more suitable, are not to be blamed; rather, they are to be approved because they turn aside to a more diligent physician. Yet if, in doing so, they can obtain their prelates’ consent to be directed by them to others, they act all the more fittingly insofar as they do this more humbly in obedience.

But if proud prelates forbid them this, deeming themselves held in lower esteem if better physicians are sought, nevertheless the sick person, concerned for his salvation, should seek with greater care the remedy he believes better, and should yield chiefly to better counsel. For no one ought to follow into a pit a guide entrusted to him by another if he discovers that guide to be blind; and it is better to choose one who sees, in order to arrive where one is heading, than to follow badly, toward a precipice, one who was badly entrusted to him [Col. 0671B]. For did the one who entrusted such a guide to him as one who would show the way do so knowingly through malice, or innocently through ignorance? If through malice, care had to be taken that his malice should not be fulfilled; if through ignorance, one does not act against his will if one does not follow into danger the person whom he gave us as a guide.

It is nevertheless useful first to consult those to whom we know that our souls have been entrusted and, having heard their advice, more safely not to abandon the remedy we hope for [Col. 0671C]—especially when we believe that they are ignorant of the law, do not care what they do, and do not know what they ought to grieve over. They are to be considered worse than those of whom Truth says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat; therefore observe and do whatever they tell you, but do not do according to their works” (Matthew 23:2). It is as though He said: Such persons hold the teaching office of the law. Although their works are evil and therefore to be rejected, the words of God which they utter from Moses’ seat—that is, from the teaching office of the law—are to be received, so that we may at once reject what belongs to their works and retain what belongs to God’s words.

The teaching, then, of those who preach well but live badly is not to be despised; nor that of those who instruct by word though they do not build up by example; they point out a way which they refuse to follow, being judged not so much guilty of the blindness of ignorance as of negligent fault [Col. 0671D]. But those who cannot even show the way to their subjects—how can they be entrusted with their guidance, or how can instruction be sought from those who do not know how to teach?

Nevertheless, subjects must not despair of God’s mercy when they are wholly ready for satisfaction and entrust themselves to the judgment of their prelates, even though blind; and when those prelates prescribe too little through error, the subjects diligently follow them through obedience. The error of prelates does not condemn subjects, nor does the former’s vice accuse the latter. Nor does a fault by which they may die remain in subjects whom repentance had already reconciled to God, as we have said, before they came to confession or undertook the prescribed satisfaction [Col. 0672A].

If, however, less is prescribed of the penalty of satisfaction than ought to be, God, who leaves no sin unpunished and punishes each according to its due, will preserve the equity of satisfaction in proportion to the quantity of the sin—namely, by afflicting those penitents, not with eternal punishments, but with purgatorial penalties in this life or the next. This is so if we have been negligent in our satisfaction. Hence the Apostle says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:31); that is: if we ourselves punished or corrected our sins, they would by no means need to be punished more severely by Him. Great indeed is God’s mercy [Col. 0672B], when He leaves us to our own judgment so that He need not punish us more severely.

These present-life penalties by which we make satisfaction for sins—fasting, praying, keeping vigil, mortifying the flesh in whatever ways, or giving to the needy what we withhold from ourselves—we call “satisfaction.” In the Gospel they are known by another name as “fruits worthy of repentance,” where He says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3:8). It is as though He said openly: by making worthy satisfaction for what you have sinned, amend it so that you are reconciled to God here, and He may thereafter find nothing to punish; and forestall heavier penalties by lighter ones. For, as blessed Augustine declares: “The penalties of the future life, even if purgatorial [Col. 0672C], are more severe than all those of the present life.” Great caution and great effort must therefore be applied, so that, according to the ordinances of the holy Fathers, such satisfaction may be undertaken that nothing remains to be purged there.

When priests are undiscerning and ignorant of these canonical ordinances, so that they impose less satisfaction than they ought, penitents thereby suffer great harm: placing wrongful confidence in them, they are afterwards punished with heavier penalties for that for which they could have made satisfaction here by lighter ones.

Some priests deceive their subjects not so much through error as through greed, remitting or relaxing the penalties of imposed satisfaction in return for an offering of money. They attend not so much to what the Lord wills [Col. 0672D] as to what money can do. Of them the Lord Himself complains through the prophet: “My priests did not say: ‘Where is the Lord?’” (Jeremiah 2:6)—as though He said: “But where is the money?” We know that not only priests but even chief priests—that is, bishops—have been so shamelessly inflamed by this greed that, when they have public assemblies at church dedications, altar consecrations, cemetery blessings, or certain solemnities, from which they expect abundant offerings, they are lavish in relaxing penances: now commonly granting to all a third, now a fourth, of their penance, under a certain appearance of charity, but in truth [Col. 0673A] from the highest greed.

Boasting of their authority, which, as they say, they received in Peter or the apostles when the Lord said to them, “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them,” or, “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (John 20:23), they especially glory in doing what belongs to them when they bestow this kindness on their subjects. Would that they did so at least for the subjects’ sake and not for money, so that whatever it might be, it would seem kindness rather than greed. But assuredly, if it is to be reckoned praiseworthy kindness that they relax a third or fourth of a penance, their mercy would deserve far greater proclamation if they remitted half or the whole penance entirely, as they profess that they are permitted to do and that it has been granted them by the Lord; and as though heaven had been placed in their hands according to the aforesaid testimonies about forgiving or absolving sins [Col. 0673B].

Conversely, they seem liable to the charge of great impiety for not absolving all their subjects from all sins, thereby permitting none of them to be damned—if, that is, it lies in their power to remit or retain whatever sins they will, or to open or close heaven to whomever they decide. They would surely deserve to be proclaimed most blessed if they could open heaven to them whenever they wished. But if they cannot, or do not know how to do so, they certainly incur, so far as I judge, the poet’s saying:

> Arts which benefit everyone do not benefit their master.

[Col. 0673C] Let anyone else seek—not I—that power by which he may benefit others rather than himself, as though he had in his power to save other people’s souls more than his own; whereas every discerning person feels the contrary.

## Chapter XXVI. Whether the power to loose and bind belongs generally to all prelates

When, therefore, the question is asked what that power, or the keys of the kingdom of heaven, is which the Lord delivered to the apostles and is likewise said to have granted to their vicars, namely bishops, no small question arises. For since many bishops possess neither religious devotion nor discernment, although they possess episcopal authority, how shall we say that the words apply to them equally as to the apostles [Col. 0673D]: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained”?

If a bishop wishes indiscreetly or excessively to increase or relax the penalty of sin, is this in his power—so that God should apportion penalties according to his judgment, punishing more severely what ought to be punished less severely, or conversely, when God ought to consider the equity of the matter rather than human will? If, through anger or hatred toward someone, a bishop decides that he should do as much penance for lighter sins as for graver ones; or decrees that his punishment be extended forever or never relaxed, however much he repents [Col. 0674A]—will the Lord confirm his sentence?

Therefore, what the Lord said to the apostles, “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them,” and so forth, seems to refer to their persons and not generally to all bishops, just as elsewhere He said to them: “You are the light of the world,” and “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:18); and many other things must be understood as applying especially to their persons.

> [Note: [Col. 0673D] Abelard’s error.]

For the Lord did not grant their successors equally the discernment or holiness which He gave to the apostles. Nor did He say equally to all: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see” (Luke 10:23); and again: “I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John 15:15); and again: “When that Spirit of truth comes, He will teach you all truth” (John 16:13) [Col. 0674B].

But if someone perhaps objects concerning Judas, who was also one of the apostles when these things were said, let him know that the Lord was not ignorant of those toward whom what He said was to be directed. Likewise, when He said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34), this prayer of His is not held to apply to all who persecuted Him. When “these” or “you”—demonstrative pronouns—are used, the speech is directed according to the speaker’s intention either to all those present together or to some among them whom He has chosen. Thus the preceding words also are not to be applied generally to all the apostles, but only to the elect.

Perhaps we should understand in the same way what He said: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven” (Matthew 16:19) [Col. 0674C], in which the sense is thought to be similar. Blessed Jerome carefully observed this when he came to expound these words in Matthew, where the Lord says to Peter, “Whatever you bind on earth”:

> “Bishops and presbyters, not understanding this passage, assume something of the Pharisees’ arrogance for themselves, so that they either condemn the innocent or think themselves able to absolve the guilty. Yet before God it is not the sentence of priests but the life of the accused that is examined. We read in Leviticus about lepers, where they are commanded to show themselves to the priests; and if they have leprosy, then they are declared unclean by the priest—not because priests make persons clean or unclean, but because they have knowledge of lepers and non-lepers and can [Col. 0674D] discern who is unclean and who is clean. Therefore, just as there the priest declares the leper unclean, so here the bishop or presbyter binds or looses, not those who are guilty or innocent, but, in accordance with his office, when he has heard the different kinds of sins, he knows who ought to be bound and who ought to be loosed.”

From these words of Jerome, unless I am mistaken, it is clear that what was said to Peter and likewise to the other apostles about binding or loosing the bonds of sins must be understood as applying rather to their persons than generally to all bishops—unless perhaps, according to what Jerome himself says, we understand this binding or absolution as the aforesaid judgment granted generally to all: namely, that they are to judge who ought to be bound or absolved by God and to distinguish between clean and unclean [Col. 0675A].

Hence also Origen, commenting on the same passage in Matthew, distinguishes elected bishops, who have deserved the grace granted to Peter, from the rest:

> “Since those who claim the office of bishop use this text as Peter did, and teach that they have received from Christ the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that those whom they bind are bound in heaven and those whom they loose—that is, to whom they grant remission—are loosed also in heaven, it must be said that they speak rightly if they possess the works for which that word was spoken to Peter, ‘You are Peter’; and if they are such that Christ’s Church is built upon them, and the gates of hell do not prevail against them [Col. 0675B]. Otherwise, it is ridiculous to say that one who is bound with the chains of his own sins, who draws his sins like a long rope and his iniquities like the perpetual strap of a heifer, has, merely because he is called a bishop, such power that those loosed by him on earth are loosed in heaven, and those bound by him on earth are bound in heaven. Let, then, the bishop who binds or looses another be blameless, worthy to bind or loose in heaven: the husband of one wife, sober, chaste, orderly, hospitable, apt to teach, not given to wine, not violent, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not greedy for money; ruling his own household well, having children submissive with all chastity. If he is such, he will not bind unjustly on earth, nor loose without judgment. Therefore, whatever such a person [Col. 0675C] looses will be loosed in heaven, and whatever he binds on earth will be bound in heaven. For if anyone is, so to speak, Peter, but does not possess the qualities stated in this passage as addressed to Peter, and thinks that he can bind so that persons are bound in heaven, and loose so that they are loosed in heaven, he deceives himself. Not understanding the will of Scripture and puffed up, he falls into the judgment of the devil.”

Origen thus plainly shows, as obvious reason also maintains, that in the matters we have mentioned what was granted to Peter was by no means bestowed by the Lord upon all bishops, but only upon those who imitate Peter not in the exaltation of his chair but in the dignity of his merits [Col. 0675D]. For those who follow their own will and turn away from the will of God can do nothing contrary to the justice of divine rectitude; nor, when they act unjustly, can they bend God toward injustice and make Him, as it were, like themselves.

He sharply rebukes and gravely threatens such people, saying: “You wickedly thought that I would be like you; I will rebuke you and set it before your face. Understand this, you who forget God,” and so forth (Psalm 49:21). For who can be said more to forget God and to be given over to a reprobate mind than one who arrogates to himself such authority that he says God’s judgment is subject to his own will in binding and loosing his subjects, so that whatever he unjustly presumes, he can overturn God’s supreme justice—as if he could make guilty or innocent whomever he wishes [Col. 0676A]?

To prevent them from ever presuming this, that great doctor of the Church, Augustine, distinguished among bishops themselves, states in the sixteenth sermon on the Lord’s words: “You have begun to treat your brother as a publican; you bind him on earth. But see that you bind him justly, for justice breaks unjust bonds.”

Blessed Gregory likewise openly asserts, and proves by the Lord’s examples, that ecclesiastical authority can accomplish nothing in binding or loosing if it departs from the equity of justice and does not accord with the divine judgment. Thus he says in the twenty-fifth homily on the Gospels:

> “It often happens that someone holds the place of judge whose life is in no way suited to that office; and it often occurs that he either condemns the undeserving or, though himself bound, looses others. Often, in loosing [Col. 0676B] or binding his subjects, he follows the impulse of his own will rather than the merits of their cases. Thus one who exercises the power of binding and loosing according to his own wishes and not according to the conduct of his subjects deprives himself of that very power. It often happens that a pastor is moved toward some neighbour by hatred or favour. But those who follow either their own hatred or favour in the cases of their subjects cannot judge them worthily. Hence, through the prophet: ‘They put to death souls that ought not to die, and make alive souls that ought not to live.’ He puts to death one who ought not die when he condemns the righteous; and he tries to make alive one who will not live when he seeks to absolve the guilty from punishment. Therefore cases must be weighed, and then the power of binding and loosing exercised. It must be considered what fault there was, or what repentance followed the fault, so that those whom the Almighty visits through the grace of compunction may be absolved by the sentence of the pastor [Col. 0676C]. For then the absolution of the presiding minister is true, when it follows the judgment of the Judge alone.

> “This is aptly signified by the resurrection of the man dead four days, which shows that the Lord first called the dead man and made him alive, saying: ‘Lazarus, come forth’; and afterwards the man who had come forth alive was loosed by the disciples. Again: behold, the disciples now loose him whom the Master had raised from death; for if the disciples had loosed Lazarus while he was dead, they would have displayed a stench rather than power. From this consideration we must understand that we ought by pastoral authority to loose those whom we know our Creator has made alive through the grace of resurrection [Col. 0676D]. This quickening we already recognize before the work of rectitude in the very confession of sins. Thus the dead man is not told, ‘Come to life,’ but ‘Come forth’; as though it were openly said to anyone dead in sin: ‘Come forth now by confession, you who hide inwardly within yourself through negligence.’ Let the sinner therefore come forth—that is, confess his fault—and let the disciples loose one who has come forth, so that the pastors of the Church may relax the penalty of one who was not ashamed to confess what he had done.

> “Again: But whether the pastor binds justly, the flock must nevertheless fear the pastor’s sentence, lest the person subject to him, even though perhaps bound unjustly, may deserve the sentence of binding because of another fault. Again: whoever is under the pastor’s hand should fear to be bound, whether justly or unjustly, and should not rashly condemn his pastor’s judgment [Col. 0677A], lest, even if he has been bound unjustly, through the fault of pride in his haughty condemnation there arise a guilt which was not there.”

From these sayings of Gregory and the examples of divine authority, it is clear that the judgment of bishops has no force if it departs from divine equity, since they seek to put to death or make alive those whom they cannot do so. Bishops, too, are deprived of communion by the judgment of bishops when they presume unjustly to deprive their subjects of communion. Hence the African Council, canon 210: “Let no bishop rashly deprive anyone of communion; and so long as his own bishop does not communicate with the excommunicated person, that bishop shall not be communicated with by other bishops, so that a bishop may be more careful not to say against anyone what he cannot prove by other evidence” [Col. 0678A].

[Col. 0677]

# Problems of Heloise, Deaconess of the Paraclete, with the Solutions of Peter Abelard

## Letter of Heloise to Peter Abelard

[Col. 0677B] Your wisdom knows better than my simplicity with what lofty praises blessed Jerome extolled and vehemently approved Saint Marcella’s zeal, with which she was wholly aflame for questions concerning the sacred Scriptures. While writing his Commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, he recalls her in the first book as follows:

> “I know her ardour; I know her faith; I know what flame she bears in her breast: she transcends her sex, forgets human beings, resounds with the timbrel of the divine books, and crosses this Red Sea of the age. Certainly, while I was at Rome, she never found me so hurried that she would not ask some question about the Scriptures. Nor, in Pythagorean fashion, did she judge whatever I answered to be correct; nor did authority prevail with her without rational examination and prior judgment [Col. 0677C]. Rather, she tested all things and weighed everything with a discerning mind, so that I felt that I had not so much a pupil as a judge.”

> [Note: [Col. 0677D] Patrologia, vol. XXVI, col. 307.]

From this zeal he plainly knew that she had progressed so far that he set her above others who were equally ardent in the pursuit of learning. Hence, writing to the virgin Principia, he recalls among other instructions:

> “There you have, in devotion to Scripture and in sanctity of mind and body, Marcella and Asella. One of them may lead you through green meadows and the varied flowers of the divine books to Him who says in the Song: ‘I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys’ (Song of Songs 2:1). The other, herself a flower of the Lord, may deserve with you to hear: ‘As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters’ (ibid., 2).”

> [Note: [Col. 0678D] Patrologia, vol. XXXI, col. 624.]

But why these things, beloved by many, yet most beloved by us? They are not examples but reminders, that from them you may remember what you ought to do and may not be reluctant to discharge your obligation [Col. 0678B]. You gathered together Christ’s handmaids and your spiritual daughters in their own oratory and bound us to divine service. You have always been accustomed earnestly to exhort us to attend to divine words and devote ourselves to sacred reading. You so often commended to us the teaching of sacred Scripture that, calling it the mirror of the soul by which its beauty or deformity is known, you allowed no bride of Christ to lack this mirror if she desired to please Him to whom she had devoted herself.

You further added, for our exhortation, that reading Scripture without understanding it is like setting a mirror before the eyes of one who cannot see. Greatly stirred by these admonitions, both I and our sisters, carrying out as far as we can your obedience in this also, while we apply ourselves to this study—seized, that is, by the love of letters of which the aforesaid doctor says somewhere, “Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh”—are made more sluggish in reading by many questions. And we are compelled to love less what we more greatly fail to understand in sacred words, while we feel the work to which we devote ourselves to be fruitless.

Accordingly, sending certain small questions from pupils to teacher, from daughters to father, we beg in supplication and supplicate in begging that you may not disdain to attend to their resolution. It was at your urging—indeed, at your command—that we especially undertook this study. In these questions, certainly, we do not keep the order of Scripture; rather, we set them forth and send them to be solved as they occur to us day by day [Col. 0678D].

## Heloise’s First Problem

Why is it that the Lord, in the Gospel of John, promises concerning the Spirit whom He was to send, saying: “And when He comes, He will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment: concerning sin, because they did not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father and you will see me no more; and concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has now been judged” (John 16:8–11) [Col. 0679A]?

## Abelard’s Solution

He will convict, through the apostles whom He will fill, not one part of the world but the whole of it, concerning sin—namely, sin persisting in or retained by human beings, because they did not believe in me. He will convict concerning righteousness—namely, righteousness offered through me personally while I was present but not received at that time, when I was present and when they can no longer recover me now that I am going to the Father and am no longer to be seen here. He will convict concerning their judgment concerning the foregoing matters [Col. 0679B], namely sin or righteousness: they place the matters which make persons guilty or righteous more in actions than in intention and judge merits not so much according to the mind as according to deeds, as the Jews especially do, thinking that no one is damned, whatever he wills, provided he does not complete it in action.

Thus the Apostle says to the Romans: “Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness. Why? Because it was not from faith, but as though from works” (Romans 9:31). Although the law also forbids concupiscence, they nevertheless do not consider it so great a sin that it suffices for condemnation. The Lord now says that this error must be exposed by the fact that the ruler of this world has been judged. The devil himself, who rules over carnal persons and lovers of the world and is the author and origin of all sin, fell at once into condemnation so grievous not because of what he did, but because of what he presumptuously willed [Col. 0679C].

## Heloise’s Second Problem

What is meant by the statement in the Epistle of James: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all. For He who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ also said, ‘You shall not kill.’ But if you do not commit adultery, yet kill, you have become a transgressor of the law” (James 2:10–11)?

## Abelard’s Solution

All the commandments of the law together, not each commandment separately, are the law itself. Therefore, whoever has observed the entire law except for one commandment becomes guilty of all; that is, he is to be condemned because he does not keep all the commandments which, taken together, as has been said, constitute the law itself. It is as though he said openly: Although no one can be a fulfiller of the law by observing one of its commandments, he nevertheless becomes a transgressor of the law if he transgresses even one commandment.

Therefore, immediately explaining what he had said, “guilty of all,” the apostle added: “You have become a transgressor of the law,” namely because he omitted one commandment, which had been enjoined equally with the others [Col. 0679D]. Otherwise, the following words, “For He who said, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’” and so forth, would by no means prove the preceding statement, “he has become guilty of all.”

Accordingly, when he says, “For He who said,” and so forth, it is as though he said: I rightly said that by transgressing one commandment he has become guilty of all—that is, he is to be condemned for this, that in failing to observe all he has despised God. For the Lord Himself, who gave the law, commanded both this commandment and that to be observed—that is, all of them, not any one alone among them. And therefore, just as a person becomes a transgressor of the law by transgressing even one commandment, so he becomes guilty of all, as has been explained: he is thereby also to be condemned because he has not fulfilled all of them [Col. 0680A].

## Heloise’s Third Problem

Why is it that the Lord, often questioned by individuals, answers them separately by saying, “You said it,” or “You say it,” and sometimes replies to several people questioning Him together, “You say it,” as though He were asserting that they had said what they were asking about in doubt? Thus, when Judas asked, “Surely it is not I, Rabbi?” (Matthew 26:25)—that is, I who am to betray you—He replied: “You said it.” And when questioned by the chief priest whether He was the Son of God, He answered similarly (ibid., 64). To the people also asking, “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John 10:24), or, “Then are you the Son of God?” (John 18:37), He answered: “You say that I am.” Finally, when examined by the governor, that is, Pilate, whether He was the King of the Jews, He replied: “You say it: for I am king” (Matthew 27:11) [Col. 0680B].

These answers rightly seem to raise a difficulty. For someone who asks whether this or that is so does not state affirmatively that it is this or that, but asks in doubt whether it is so [Col. 0680C].

## Abelard’s Solution
Indeed, these answers of the Lord would raise a difficult, or altogether insoluble, question if what the Lord says—“You have said it,” or “You say [it],” or “You say [so]”—were referred to the words of the preceding questions, as though he asserted that those things had been said in them; for this is wholly unsuitable. Therefore, when he replied to Judas, who asked whether he himself was the one who would betray him, “You have said it,” rather than “You say [it],” he referred to that agreement which Judas had already made with the Jews, promising, for the desire of the promised money, to hand him over to them. But when he answered the chief priest, who asked whether he was Christ, the Son of God, “You have said it,” this must be understood as meaning that the man who at that time denied that the Christ whom he saw was the Son of God had long before confessed this repeatedly by reciting the Law and the Prophets. But when he answered the Jews asking whether he was Christ or whether he was the Son of God, “You say [it],” using, that is, the verb in the present tense both to them and to Pilate, he indicates that the present day has now arrived on which they confess it.

For where, mocking him, they said, “Prophesy, Christ: who is it that struck you?” (Luke 22:64), or, “Hail, King of the Jews!” (Matt. 27:29), they certainly detested that he was Christ—that is, Anointed—whatever their intention in doing so. Perhaps in this they imitated the prophecy of Caiaphas, who said: “It is expedient for you that one man should die and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 18:14). Yet by the testimony of the crowd receiving him with palm branches, he is himself both the Son of David, according to Matthew (Matt. 21:9), and in him comes the kingdom of David, according to Mark (Mark 11:10); and he is “the blessed king who comes,” according to Luke (Luke 19:38); and finally, according to John, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel” (John 12:13). These things they said not in mockery, like those mentioned above, but in faith. Thus what he says to the Jews, “You say [it],” is as if he said: “There are still many among you who not only utter this with their lips but also hold it in their hearts.” For although those asking the question neither said nor believed it, nevertheless, when he said, “You say [it],” he looked not to the persons then present but to the people itself.

Likewise, elsewhere, when he says to the Jews concerning Zechariah, “Whom you killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. 23:35), this is to be understood not of the Jews then alive, but of the people from whom they sprang. So too, when Joshua is said to have circumcised the children of Israel a second time (Josh. 2:1 ff.), it is clear that he did this not to the same persons but to the same people.

We also read that on the day of the Passion the centurion and those with him who were guarding the crucified Lord, when he had expired and they saw the veil of the temple torn, the earthquake, and the tombs opened, said: “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54). And all the crowd of those who had gathered together for this spectacle and saw what was happening returned, beating their breasts (Luke 23:48). [Col. 0681C] Therefore, as we have said, this is the sense in which he answered the Jews asking whether he was the Son of God: “You say [it]”; that is, the present day or time has now come in which you will confess this concerning me.

Similarly, he answered Pilate, asking whether he was king of the Jews, “You say [it],” rather than “You have said it.” For the Gentile knew nothing of the prophecies; he had not read the words in which Christ had been promised and his kingdom foretold, as in: “And of his kingdom there shall be no end” (Luke 1:33), or: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes” (Matt. 21:5). Yet Pilate repeatedly affirmed this verbally on that very day and mentioned it in the inscription written upon the cross. He said to the Jews:

> **[Note: [Col. 0681D] The distinguished Victor Cousin, following the Victorine manuscript, restored this passage thus (*Works of Abelard*, p. 242): “and confirmed it in [Col. 0682D] the inscription written upon the cross.” For, as Matthew relates, he said to the Jews:]**

“Do you wish me to release to you the king of the Jews?” (John 18:39), and again, “Shall I crucify your king?” (John 19:15). And when he had previously asked the Lord, “Are you the king of the Jews?” (John 18:33), and he had replied, “Do you say this of yourself, or have others told you about me?” (ibid., 34), Pilate again said: “Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests have handed you over to me” (ibid., 35). See how often and how plainly Pilate professes him to be king of the Jews, and calls the Jewish people his nation. When the Lord says to him, “Do you say this of yourself?” and so forth, it is as if he said: “Do you ask this for yourself, that you may know the truth, or through the deceit of the Jews, as though you were one of them, in order to seize from this an occasion to kill me?”

[Col. 0682A] Finally, by writing the title, Pilate confirmed in writing what he had stated verbally, in three languages, so that it could be read by all coming to Jerusalem and understood that he was truly king of the Jews. For it was written: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19:19). In adding “of Nazareth,” he carefully distinguished this Jesus from the others in the ancient people who had borne this name, not so much properly as by appellation: namely Joshua, Jesus the priest, and Jesus son of Sirach.

The Jewish chief priests were fiercely indignant at this honour of the title, as though it had been written for their condemnation because they had crucified their own king. They said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but, ‘He said: I am king of the Jews’” (ibid., 21). But since it had been prophesied, “Do not destroy David in the inscription of the title” (Ps. 56:1), Pilate, as though he understood this to be spoken to himself, replied: “What I have written, I have written” (John 19:22). It is as though he said: “What I judged should be written, I have established without any reconsideration of correction,” as though what he exhibited in letters for the second time had first been written in his mind. Thus this repetition of the phrase, “What I have written, I have written,” signifies the persistence or immutability of the act, like the phrase, “Going, they went” (Ps. 125:6).

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM IV

How can it stand that, when the Jews asked the Lord for signs, he answered concerning the time of his burial: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale for three days and three nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Matt. 12:40)? For it is established that the Lord, having been taken down from the cross on Friday, was buried; that he rested in the tomb on the Sabbath; and that on the following night, the Lord’s Day, he rose in the fourth watch. Thus it is certain that he was in the tomb only for the one whole night preceding the Sabbath and for the whole day of the Sabbath itself—the one whom Jerome, in his Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, says rose in the fourth watch of the night.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

What the Lord says, “for three days and three nights,” is not to be understood as meaning that he was there for three whole days and nights, but that he rested buried during a period containing three days with their nights. Thus, when it says “for three days and three nights,” it appropriately adds, “as Jonah”; Jonah, whom the fish vomited onto dry land on the third day and who therefore was in the whale’s belly for only one whole night and one whole day.

Understand the period containing three days with their nights as extending from the beginning of the night following the Preparation until the end of the Lord’s Day; and you will find that, within that span of time, although not throughout the whole period, the Lord lay in the tomb for three days and three nights. For something which happens within a particular time need not happen throughout that entire time.

Perhaps also the phrase “in the heart of the earth” seems to refer not so much to the Lord’s burial as to the hearts of human beings, who at that time so despaired of Christ that even the disciples, and indeed his mother, gravely wavered in faith. Hence Augustine, in a chapter of his *Questions on the Old and New Law*, says:

> **[Note: Patrologia, vol. XXXV, col. 2401.]**
>
> “Even Mary, through whom the mystery of the Savior’s incarnation was accomplished, doubted at the Lord’s death, so that she might be strengthened at the Lord’s resurrection. For all doubted at his death; and because every uncertainty was to depart at the Lord’s resurrection, he said that the sword would pass through.”

Therefore, by the heart of the earth—as it were, an earthly and still carnal heart, not yet made spiritual through firmness of faith or ardour of love—he means the human heart, so long as people in that critical time regarded Christ more as flesh, that is, as a human being, than as God, and as earthly rather than heavenly. Therefore, when the Jews asked for a sign of power by which they might recognize him as God, his answer that he would rather give them the sign of Jonah means that they deserved rather to recognize weakness in him: just as Jonah, cast into the sea, was judged to have more injustice than piety and to have suffered this through his own fault, so that he even deserved condemnation.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM V

The evangelists have left us a very great difficulty concerning the appearances of the risen Lord that were made to the women. Mark and John indicate that he first appeared to Mary Magdalene, who came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb and saw the stone removed from the tomb. After she reported this to Peter and John, and they ran to the tomb and returned from it, she saw two angels and then Jesus, whom she supposed to be the gardener (Mark 16:1 ff.; John 20:1 ff.). This first appearance is said to have been made to her alone.

Matthew, however, reports that she came to the tomb with the other Mary; that an earthquake then occurred, an angel descended and rolled back the stone, and announced that the Lord had risen; and that Jesus met the two women, who held his feet (Matt. 28:1 ff.). Mark, however, relates that Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome came very early to the tomb, the sun having already risen, asking one another who would roll away the stone from the entrance of the tomb for them. Looking, they saw it rolled away; and, having learned through the angel speaking to them and through the empty tomb that the Lord had risen, they fled from the tomb trembling, saying nothing of this to anyone because of fear (Mark 16:1 ff.). Immediately afterward it is added: “But Jesus, rising early on the first day of the Sabbath, appeared first to Mary Magdalene. She went and reported it to those who had been with him, and they did not believe” (ibid., 9–11).

Luke relates that Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary of James, and the other women with them came very early to the tomb, found the stone rolled away from the tomb, entered and did not find the body of Jesus, and, having been instructed by angels concerning the Lord’s resurrection, reported this to the disciples, who did not believe them (Luke 24:1 ff.).

Having set out the words of the evangelists, we first ask how, according to John, Mary Magdalene, coming to the tomb early while it was still dark, saw the stone removed, and afterward, as Mark says, she herself, Mary of James, and Salome came very early to the tomb after the sun had risen, saying to one another: “Who will roll away the stone for us?” (Mark 16:3). For if Mary Magdalene had already seen the stone rolled away while it was still dark—that is, when it was night—how does she now, after the sun has risen, complain with the others about rolling away a stone which she had already seen removed?

Second, it also seems necessary to ask how, in Mark, the women are said through fear to have reported the Lord’s resurrection to no one, when the other evangelists assert the contrary. Finally, John reports that Mary Magdalene, and no one with her, announced to Peter and John, before she saw Jesus, that he had been taken from the tomb, and that they immediately ran there. Luke, however, reports that the same Mary and several other women with her, after they had learned that the Lord had risen, reported this to the disciples, and that Peter then ran to the tomb.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

John alone mentions Mary Magdalene, and not the other women, in connection with the Lord’s resurrection, not because she alone was present at what then happened, but because he especially wished to commend her devotion as much greater than that of the others; at her urging and by her example the other women were chiefly stimulated. Therefore, since she was more fervent than the others in love and more anxious concerning the joy of the resurrection, she came first and fearlessly to the tomb while it was still night; and she returned again to her companions, diligently asking whether anyone had yet been assured of the Lord’s resurrection.

When she found that this was not at all so, she returned to the tomb after the sun had risen with the others; and then the rolling away of the stone took place, although John, by anticipation, says that Mary saw this rolling away as though it had happened earlier. Thus Mary, more concerned than the others, first learned that the stone had been rolled away; believing that the Lord had been taken away, she hurried back and reported this to Peter and John. Then, having returned with them to the tomb, after they had departed from it she stood weeping outside the tomb itself, while the others present did not dare to come so near. Then she deserved to see the angels, and afterward the Lord, before anyone else.

Thereafter the other Mary, who, according to Matthew, had earlier come with her, approached. Both were comforted, though still afraid of the guards who were present; for at the earthquake and at the appearance of the angel sitting upon the stone which he had rolled away, the guards were terrified and became like dead men. As these two went to report to the disciples what the angel had commanded, Jesus met them, appearing to them both a second time. But the other women, who were more timid and weaker in faith, did not then deserve to see the Lord; from the angels’ announcement alone they had heard that he had risen.

Therefore, since not all were equally certain of this at first, all were initially silent and delayed reporting it to the disciples, still fearful and astonished by the angelic vision and afraid that they would not immediately be believed, until, joined by more women, they could speak with greater confidence. Hence later, as Luke relates, Magdalene herself, Joanna, Mary of James, and the other women with them told these things to the apostles. Peter, stronger in faith than the others, who did not believe, ran again to the tomb; and, because he saw neither angels nor the Lord, he returned in great amazement.

Since he was greatly astonished that appearances of angels or of the Lord had been made to women rather than to himself or the disciples, lest he should remain long in doubt and grief, we may believe that the Lord then appeared to him, as Luke reports the apostles saying: “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon” (Luke 24:34).

But when Matthew and Luke say, “At the evening of the Sabbath” (Matt. 28:1; Luke 24:1), they mean its end—that is, the following night up to the dawn of the Lord’s Day. This evening grows light on the first day of the Sabbath when it reaches the daylight of the next day. By saying “which grows light,” using the feminine gender, he had regard to the meaning; for, as we have said, by “evening” he understood the night, so that “which grows light” is as if one said: “the night which comes to brightness.” Thus *vesperum* or *vespera* of a day means its final hour, while *vesper* means the whole period of the following night.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM VI

Why is it that, when the Lord handed down and commended to his disciples the sacraments of his body and blood, he did not say of his body, “This is my body of the New Testament” (Matt. 26:26), while he said of the blood, “This is my blood of the New Testament” (ibid., 28), as though he commended the blood more than the flesh? And what also is the meaning of this: “I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (ibid., 29)?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

The body of Christ received in the sacrament is the humanity which he assumed when he was born of the Virgin, when, as it is written, “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14). His blood given as drink is his Passion, in which all of us who are his members ought to share. Hence it is written: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

For when Gregory says, “For to have been born would have profited nothing unless to have been redeemed had profited; and in his Passion our redemption is consummated”—which Christ himself, dying, confesses when he says, “It is finished” (John 19:30)—the blood poured out, that is, his Passion, is not unsuitably preferred to the flesh conceived, that is, to his birth. His blood also should more properly than his flesh be called that of the New Testament, that is, the confirmation of evangelical preaching, because, as the Apostle says, “a testament is confirmed in the dead” (Heb. 9:17).

What is the Gospel but a testament of love, just as the Law had been one of fear? Hence the Apostle says to converted Jews: “You are not again subject to fear” (Rom. 8:15). And again: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart” (1 Tim. 1:5). And Truth himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it burn?” (Luke 12:49).
