Therefore the Lord’s Passion above all confirmed this testament of love, because, dying for us, he displayed to us the love than which none can be greater. Hence he himself says: “No one has greater love than this, that a person lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

He also confirmed this testament in that he remained steadfast in the doctrine of evangelical preaching even unto death and showed by dying what he could not show by being born. Likewise, one who makes some testament for his heirs confirms it when he dies while remaining in his former will: without deleting or altering it in anything, he then fully ratifies it. Hence, as we have said, the Lord’s blood rather than his body was rightly to be called that of the New Testament.

But I understand his saying, “I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in the kingdom of my Father” (Matt. 26:29), as though he said: “I shall no longer celebrate, in a sacrament, the Passion of my flesh until I do this with you as something new in the kingdom of my Father.” For Christ’s sacrament is then received as new when, received with full faith, it renews those who approach it and transforms them from the old person, whom they imitate through transgression, into a new one, while they are prepared to follow him through obedience even unto death.

Such, however, were by no means the disciples then present, still especially weak in faith and especially frail because of that critical time. Nor had they yet been brought into the kingdom of God, so that God might reign in them; they did not yet cling to him with firmness of faith, wholly subject to his dominion. Thus they then received the sacrament as old and not new, and as persons still remaining outside the kingdom of God, because steadfastness of faith had not yet so confirmed them in God that, already made new by receiving it, they deserved to be confirmed in that newness as they were after the resurrection.

Then Christ will drink this fruit of the vine with them—that is, his blood, who is their vine as they are branches—when they worthily share the sacraments of his Passion; thus he will satisfy in them his thirst from it. For one who thirsts or hungers for human salvation is satisfied by that salvation when he rejoices to see it fulfilled. Perhaps also for this reason the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion was, as it were, old before the resurrection and afterward new: while he still bore a passible, corruptible, or mortal body, he was thereby like the old person, before by rising he passed from this penal life into the newness of the life to come.

Therefore, while he was mortal and gave himself in the sacrament as he then was, it was in a certain way old and not new in comparison with the new reality which we now receive in a humanity already immortal and incorruptible. But Luke says: “This cup is the new testament in my blood” (Luke 22:20), that is, the covenant or promise made to you by God concerning your redemption in my Passion. For where we have “testament,” the Hebrew has “covenant.” Those who receive the law of the Lord enter into a certain covenant with him—or he with them—when they promise obedience to the Law and he promises reward.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM VII

Why also do we read in Luke that the Lord gave two cups, or gave the same cup twice, to the disciples? For it is written:

> “When the hour had come, he reclined, and the twelve apostles with him. And he said to them: ‘With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you that from this time I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled in the kingdom of God.’ And having received the cup, he gave thanks and said: ‘Take and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.’ And having received bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: ‘This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the new testament in my blood’” (Luke 22:14 ff.).

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

The Passover which he had sent the disciples to prepare according to the Law is the old Passover: namely, the eating of lamb or kid with wild lettuces. He says that he desired to eat this Passover with the disciples before he suffered because, before the Passion and not afterward, he wished the old things to be celebrated in figures, since they were to be cast aside when the new things came.

The Lord himself clearly indicates this when, concerning the new sacrament alone, he says: “Do this in remembrance of me,” as though now ending the old and thereafter establishing the new alone. For after saying, “This is my body, which will be handed over for you,” he immediately added, “Do this in remembrance of me.” Hence the Apostle says: “As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 11:24).

Therefore the celebration of Mass is the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion, and every believer ought to approach it with as great a devotion of compassion as he ought to behold him crucified for his own sake. Therefore, that this memory of the Lord’s Passion may cling to our minds and always kindle us in love for him, this sacrifice of his ought daily to be offered upon his altar. “Do this,” he says: that is, make this very body of mine—not now handed over for you, but to be handed over—in remembrance of so great a love of mine, so that you too may be kindled by the flame of so great a love and may be able to share in the Passion.

He wished to give the same cup twice in order to express by this that we must receive his cup not only in receiving the sacrament but also in imitating his Passion. Hence the Psalmist says: “I will take the cup of salvation,” that is, of the true Jesus (Ps. 115:13), namely, by imitating him also through the power of suffering. And because enduring death is not a capacity of human weakness but a power granted us by God, he is to be invoked from whom this power is to be hoped for; and in that power we ought to seek not so much our own advantage as his glory, which is signified by his name. For just as things are called dishonourable when they do not seem worthy of a name, so conversely all glorious things are worthy of a name and of renown.

Therefore we invoke the name of God when we direct what we do to his glory, so that he rather than we ourselves may be glorified and praised in us. From him we receive the strength for those things for which we are weak in ourselves. Hence the Apostle says: “Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:34); that is, whoever recognizes any strength or worth in himself should seek that God, not himself, be honoured for it. He should attribute it not to his own capacity but to divine grace, recognizing that it is from God and not from himself.

Concerning this cup, which we receive by imitating Christ’s Passion, he says to the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup which I am about to drink?” (Matt. 20:22). That is: “Do you trust that you can imitate me through suffering?” It is fitting that, concerning this first cup and not the second, he says to the disciples: “Take and divide it among yourselves.” For we receive Christ’s cup from him and divide it among ourselves when we imitate him through different kinds of sufferings. But in receiving the sacrament there is no division, because there is one offering there: that of the head himself, not of the members; it is effected by the power of the divine words equally through wicked and through good priests.

“Take,” he says, “this cup from me, which afterward you may divide among yourselves, because henceforth I shall not drink of the fruit of the vine”; that is, “I shall not celebrate this offering of my Passion until the kingdom of God comes,” that is, until heavenly life is opened to believers through my Passion, the life in which the Lord alone, and not sin, reigns. He fittingly set the cup of imitation before the cup of the sacrament, because only those are worthy to share at the Lord’s table who imitate his Passion and are prepared to take up his cross. Hence it is written: “When you sit down at a great table, know that you must prepare such things” (Ecclus. 31:12, according to the Septuagint).

While handing down the New Testament rather than the Old, he gives thanks over both bread and cup, indicating that what had been prefigured there is fulfilled here, and that God is to be glorified for the reality rather than the shadow.

Yet above he said that he desired also to celebrate the old Passover with the disciples, lest they receive the new sacraments from him in such a way that they should not esteem the old ones handed down by God. These old things were also then especially suited to them while they were still old, so that the Lord ought especially to celebrate with them what he saw was most appropriate to them; as though, in this desire of his, he meant to indicate that this was particularly fitting for their oldness, which needed rebuke.

To indicate or remind them that they must be transferred from this oldness to newness, he immediately joined the New Testament to the Old, so that in a certain way the old itself might pass into the new: namely, while they laid aside oldness and passed from the kingdom of sin into the kingdom of God, and in the old Passover followed not the letter but spiritual understanding; and thus were carried from the oldness of the letter to the newness of the Spirit. This is what it means for Christ even now to eat the old Passover with them and transform it into the new: when we perceive that what we believe is fulfilled in the New was prefigured there.

Hence, immediately after the resurrection, beginning from Moses and interpreting in all the Scriptures, he transformed the old sacrament into the new, applying the former to the latter through understanding; he enclosed, as it were, a wheel within a wheel, and changed the water of the Law into the wine of the Gospel. Even now he eats the old Passover with us as transformed into the new, because we refresh and delight him when we receive it in the way in which we have been mystically taught that it ought to be received there: namely, in the eating of lamb and kid, wild lettuces, and the other things prescribed for it.

Christ eats the old Passover, not the new, with the disciples; for he himself is the new Passover, according to the Apostle: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7), when he himself became our offering and we receive him daily in the sacrament. He also rightly celebrated the old Passover with the disciples because he himself was still in the old person by reason of the mortality of his body, as they were through resemblance in conduct.

Conversely, he now drinks the new fruit of the vine as new with the new: he through immortality and they through changed conduct, having put off the old person. They delight in the newness of the true sacrifice; and he is, as it were, drinking with them while the head acts in the members. The old Passover had no cup, because “the Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:19); therefore perfect refreshment ought not to have been present in its sacrifice.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM VIII

The Lord’s answer to the Jews for the freeing of the adulteress—“Let him among you who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7)—and his consequent rescue of her raise some difficulty. For when he does not permit her to be stoned except by one who is free from sin, he appears to forbid every human being to exercise vengeance, since no one is clean from defilement—not even an infant whose life upon earth is but one day (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

The Lord Jesus alone among the Jews was without sin. He stones the adulteress and preserves the woman, when he mercifully spares her and thus converts her, repentant, from her crimes. Therefore, when he says, “Let him among you who is without sin be the first to cast a stone at her,” it is as though he plainly says: “Leave her to be stoned by that one among you who alone is free from sin.” He first casts a stone at her to stone her when he first inspires her to repentance; afterward she mortifies herself through satisfaction and subdues the flesh so that it may no longer resist the spirit, so that, now dead to the world, she may thereafter live to God, and the vices may be slaughtered while nature is preserved.

Finally, the Lord says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Rom. 12:19). We reserve vengeance for God when he himself works it in us rather than we ourselves. Hence “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13) was said to man, not to God. It is forbidden to us by him who, being bound under no command, openly professes that this is due to himself: “I will kill,” he says, “and I will make alive” (Deut. 32:39).

He kills and spares in us when, using us as a kind of instrument, he causes us by his commands to kill the guilty or spare the innocent, so that these actions should be attributed to him rather than to us. For when some powerful person does something through his workmen, the deed is said to be not so much theirs as his—that is, not of those who perform it by working, but rather of the one who caused it to be done through them.

Thus a human being is forbidden to kill, but God is not forbidden to kill in a human being. Yet a human being kills, and God does not kill in him, when he acts from his own malice, not at God’s command; that is, when he acts from himself and not from the Law, obeying his own wickedness rather than divine justice. Then he takes up the sword not to exercise justice, that he may punish iniquity, but to fulfill his own impiety. Of such a person Truth says: “Whoever takes up the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). “Whoever takes up,” he says, on his own initiative, not one to whom it has been entrusted by authority: that person is rightly to perish by the sword, who has presumptuously used the sword unjustly.

But when a soldier wields for vengeance a sword entrusted to him by his king, the king acts in him, since the soldier has become his agent in this matter. Hence Augustine, in Book I of *The City of God*, says:

> **[Note: Patrologia, vol. XLI, col. 35.]**
>
> “‘You shall not kill,’ he says, except those whom God commands to be killed, whether by a law given or by an express command addressed, for the time being, to a particular person. The person who owes service to the commander does not himself kill, just as a sword is an instrument of the one using it.”

The same author, in the *Questions on Exodus*, says:

> **[Note: Patrologia, vol. XXXIV, col. 608.]**
>
> “The Israelites did not commit theft in despoiling the Egyptians, but rendered service to God who commanded it, just as the officer of a judge kills the one whom the law commands to be killed. Certainly, if he did it voluntarily, he would be a murderer, even if he knows that the person whom he killed ought to have been put to death by the judge.”

Likewise, in the *Questions on Leviticus*:

> **[Note: Patrologia, vol. XXXIV, col. 707.]**
>
> “When this man is killed, the law kills him, not you.”

From these words we are plainly taught that neither homicide nor theft is properly called that which we do out of obedience, when we rightly carry out that in which we fulfill God’s command. Whatever appears to belong to the Lord’s possession ought to be said to be God’s rather than a human being’s. No one is its owner, but only its steward, so long as he possesses it by the Lord’s permission; and no one unjustly steals it from him who receives it at the Lord’s command. These things belong only to him by whom they have been entrusted to us for as long as he wills, and they will pass to different stewards as he wills. Those are less worthy to administer and possess them in proportion as they less acknowledge him from whom these things have been entrusted to them. Such, indeed, were the unbelieving Egyptians, more worthy to lose these things than to have them.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM IX

As Matthew relates, the Lord cleansed a leper by his touch, sent him to the judgment of the priest, and commanded him to offer what the Law prescribes as the offering for such persons (Matt. 8:2). This raises the question why, in this act, the Lord seems at once to oppose and to obey the Law. For he touched the leper, which the Law forbids; yet he sent the cleansed man to the priest and to offer a sacrifice, as the Law commands.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION
[Col. 0691C] As the Lord himself says: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke 16:16); that is, until the time of grace, the commandments both of the Law and of the Prophets were to be fulfilled even according to the letter. Therefore the Lord now contradicts the Law in no respect, since no one is any longer bound to obey it by God’s command—especially since the Law itself, as the Apostle says, was “ordained through a mediator” (Gal. 3:19), that is, placed in his power, so that he who had established it for a time might cause it to cease at his will, when it was fitting that, in the time of grace, perfect charity should cast fear out.

Now it belongs especially to the time of grace to show mercy toward all persons, to invite to piety, by examples, those whom we can, and to abhor nothing unclean in human beings except sin. [Col. 0691D] Thus in the case of the leper the Lord acts mercifully in every respect: he did not disdain to touch him because of his bodily infirmity, and he commanded him to do that without which he could by no means have been received back into human society. For this reason he was to be seen by the priest, and, by the priest’s judgment and by the sacrifice prescribed by the Law, be formally certified.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM X

What is meant by what Abraham says in Luke’s Gospel to the condemned rich man: “And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot do so, nor can anyone cross from there to us” (Luke 16:26)?

For how could any be so blinded as to wish to pass from the refreshment of so great a repose to the punishments [Col. 0692A] of the condemned, or vainly desire to bestow any benefit upon those whom they see entirely excluded from God’s mercy?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

Abraham, into whose bosom Lazarus is received, is God, who receives his faithful people from the miseries of this life into the refreshment of the life to come, still hidden from us, as into a certain secret place of rest. The condemned soul speaks to him as though in supplication, when it desires him to have mercy on it. Abraham answers it concerning the judgment already established, when he makes it understand that it desires in vain what can in no way happen to it.

This is what he makes it understand when he adds: “And in all these things a great chasm has been fixed between us and you,” etc. “Besides all this,” that is, in both of the things just mentioned—namely, the consolation of the righteous and the torment of the wicked—a great chasm has been fixed. This is an obstacle so permanently established by divine judgment that those who wish to pass from here to you cannot do so.

By passing here from the refreshment of the righteous to the punishments of the wicked, we understand wishing also to aid those who are condemned and, as it were, to bring them this benefit of the righteous; or to lead them thence hither, as the faithful do daily in this life when, by their prayers or alms, they endeavor to aid also those whom they think to be in purgatorial punishments, though they are in fact utterly condemned. Therefore we do not understand this of those who are in that refreshment, as though [Col. 0692C] they had such compassion upon the condemned, but, as has been said, of the faithful still living.

For Abraham did not say, “so that those of these who are here wish to pass from here to you”; rather, he simply said, “those who wish,” whether they are still alive or have already died. But we, as we have said, understand this statement as referring to the living, who are figuratively said to pass from the refreshment of the righteous to the places of punishment of the condemned, or to cross from there to here. These expressions appear to have the same meaning. For to pass from the refreshment of the righteous to the punishments of the condemned, or to go hence, is to have such compassion also on those who are condemned that they wish to impart and in some manner convey to them that refreshment through their good works, or lead them from there to here—so that one meaning seems to be expressed in different words.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XI

[Col. 0692D]

What is meant by the Lord’s saying, which we read in the same Evangelist: “I tell you that there will be such joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance as over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of penance” (Luke 15:7)?

For it is far better and more perfect to avoid sin than to correct sin once committed, and for many rather than one to act well. Hence the former plainly pleases God more than the latter. Why, then, does God approve the repentance of one sinner more than the perseverance of many righteous persons?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

The more anyone grieves over someone’s sin, the more he rejoices at that person’s correction. The greater the grief caused by the loss, the less hope there seemed to be of recovering the benefit, and the more difficult its occurrence appeared, the greater the joy with which it is received when it occurs. Greater joy in the recovery of a benefit succeeds greater concern over its loss.

But concerning the righteous whom we trust will persevere in goodness—and therefore attend to less anxiously, since we are more secure about them—we are stirred to less joy than by the conversion of a sinner, which seemed most difficult. Yet this does not mean that this person’s conversion is worth more than their perseverance; rather, we rejoice more when that occurs about which we had been especially anxious that it should occur.

Thus, when it is said, “There will be joy in heaven,” it means the exultation of the present Church of the faithful, which the Lord sometimes also calls the kingdom of heaven.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XII

[Col. 0693B]

The passage which we read in Matthew concerning laborers sent into the vineyard likewise presents some difficulty. The earlier laborers seem to have envied the last alone and murmured against the householder, so as to deserve this reply: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. 20:15).

For in the life to come the reward received will so suffice for each of the blessed that no one there will desire to have more than he receives. There will be such charity among all that each will love another’s good as his own; no one can disagree with the Lord’s will; nor can anyone, through the evil of envy, have an evil eye toward another—especially since envy so afflicts and torments those in whom it exists that the poet said of it:

> The Sicilian tyrants devised  
> No greater torture than envy.  
> —Horace, *Epistles*, epistle I.V, vv. 58–59

And elsewhere:

> The envious person wastes away at another’s abundant prosperity.  
> —Ibid., v. 57

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

It must be understood that in every parable not so much the truth of an event is expressed as a likeness to the matter is introduced in some respect; and often a likeness is attached to historical truth as though it were an event that had occurred.

For, although in the story of the rich man and Lazarus we believe that what is narrated of two persons—or more often of many—has happened, namely that one soul is saved and another condemned, nevertheless the rich man’s words to Abraham cannot be taken according to the letter: “Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue” (Luke 16:24). Souls do not have fingers or tongues within themselves; bodies alone do. Therefore what is said of them does not concern the truth of the event according to the literal propriety, but a likeness introduced in some respect.

So also here, when some are said to murmur and, as it were, resent others being made equal to themselves, this murmuring must be understood not as indignation but as amazement. Those who murmur are astonished that something occurs which they did not believe would occur. Thus this murmuring is now called the astonishment of many faithful persons when they see made equal to themselves in reward those whom they knew to have labored for a shorter time.

Likewise, the “evil eye” is said figuratively of envious people, who are stirred against others because they are astonished at something that they had not believed would occur and that seems, as it were, contrary to reason. Therefore, “Is your eye evil because I am good?” is as though he said: “Are you moved, after the manner of the world, to indignation through injustice because you see something brought about through my goodness?” As if he said: “It is by no means fitting that this should be so.”

For the Lord to say this to anyone is for him to make that person understand that he ought not to be indignant at this, but rather to praise God.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XIII

The question concerning the unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit troubles us also, as it troubles many. For how can someone sin against the Son of God and not against the Holy [Col. 0694B] Spirit, when one cannot be offended without the other, and an offense against one must necessarily redound to both, since neither can be reconciled to anyone by whom the other was offended?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

Before setting forth a solution, so far as we can, the words of this saying must first be stated and gathered from the different Evangelists; and the context on which it depends must be set forth beforehand, so that the solution may be reached more easily.

Thus, as Matthew relates, when the Lord had cured a demoniac and the envious Pharisees said that he did this through an evil spirit, not through the Holy Spirit, the Lord said: “If I cast out demons by Beelzebub, by whom do your sons cast them out? But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matt. 12:27). And after some further words: “Therefore I tell you: every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings; but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (ibid., 31).

Mark puts it thus: “Amen, I tell you: all sins and blasphemies which the children of men have uttered will be forgiven them; but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not have forgiveness forever, but is guilty of an eternal sin,” because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit” (Mark 3:28–29).

Luke writes that the Lord spoke thus: “Everyone who confesses me before men, the Son of Man also will confess him before the angels of God. But whoever denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God. And everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but he who has blasphemed against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven” (Luke 12:8).

Having set these passages before us, we must first distinguish what the sin of blasphemy against the Son of Man is and what it is against the Holy Spirit. As I judge, one sins by blaspheming against the Son of Man when one disparages Christ by denying that he is God, not so much through malice as through error arising from the assumed nature of our weakness which one sees in him. This is what he indicates when he says “the Son of Man” rather than “the Son of God”: because of the human weakness which he assumed by being born from a mother, God’s power is not believed to be in him.

This sin appears highly excusable because it arises from an ignorance that is, as it were, invincible, since it could in no way be grasped by human reason but only by God’s inspiration: namely, that God became man. Hence Christ himself declares: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” (John 6:44), because it does not belong to human reason to grasp this concerning Christ; it happens only through God’s inspiration.

But to blaspheme against the Holy Spirit is knowingly, out of envy, to disparage the manifest goodness of God—understood as the Holy Spirit—so that they attribute to an evil spirit, through envy, benefits which they do not doubt are accomplished through the Holy Spirit, that is, through the grace of divine goodness. This is what the Pharisees did when, seeing the crowd believe in the miracles, they sought through envy to turn it away from Christ. If we consider their sin more carefully, it seems graver than that through which the devil fell.

For although the Pharisees did not believe Christ to be God, they could not fail to recognize from his life and works that he was a righteous man, nor that the things he did were done through the Holy Spirit. Since, then, contrary to their conscience, they said that these things were done through an evil spirit, though they did not doubt that they were done through the Holy Spirit, they knowingly lied and asserted that the Holy Spirit himself was an evil spirit.

In this they seem to have committed a far greater presumption by lying than the devil did by pride. Although the devil desired to be like God and to possess a kingdom independently, he should not be thought to have exceeded so far as to dare burst forth into such blasphemy as to maintain that God is a liar and evil. Hence their blasphemy appears not less but even more detestable than his pride, so that it is altogether worthy to be excluded from pardon.

Nevertheless, we do not say that the repentance of such persons, if it existed, would not obtain forgiveness. Rather, on the basis of the Lord’s saying, we believe that all such persons have so provoked the Spirit of God that, obstinate in their wickedness, they have been altogether excluded from grace.

Luke designates this manifest grace of God, which reveals itself in Christ through the effect of miracles, above by the “finger of God,” when the Lord himself says: “But if I cast out demons by the finger of God” [Col. 0695D] (Luke 11:20). The hand, right hand, or arm of God is called his Son; in this hand, the finger is any manifest operation of the Holy Spirit. We use the finger especially in pointing out bodily things; hence he calls the Spirit of God his finger when he openly displays his grace through some effective benefit, so that the deed is believed to be God’s work alone, even though some, in envy and after the manner of the Pharisees, slander it.

And this is why that sin of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, through whom forgiveness of sins is effected, remains unforgivable. The statement, “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven,” should be understood thus: no one who, as has been said, disparages Christ’s honor not through malice but through error will be condemned on that account, since this invincible ignorance makes such a person like those for whom the Lord in his Passion, or Stephen, prayed.

For it accords with piety and reason that those who, recognizing by the natural law the Creator and Rewarder of all as God, cling to him with such zeal that they endeavor not to offend him through consent—which is properly called sin—should be judged not to be condemned. Whatever they must learn for salvation, God will reveal to them before life’s end, whether by inspiration or through someone sent to instruct them in these matters, as we read occurred in Cornelius concerning faith in Christ and the reception of baptism (Acts 2).

This also seems plainly established by the saying: “If our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence toward God” (1 John 3:21). And since the Lord says that “no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13), we must by no means despair of those who, through zeal for the Law, though they do not know Christ, endure death for God. For it is easy for God immediately to inspire such people, before the soul departs the body, with what ought to be believed concerning Christ, lest they leave this life as unbelievers.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XIV

Why is it that, while the Lord instructs the minds of the faithful and enumerates the goods through which they can merit blessedness, he calls them blessed severally in the qualities they possess, as though each one by itself sufficed to make one blessed, as seems clear from the reward appended to each? Thus it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:2). A reward is likewise added to each of the others, from which every grace seems sufficient for salvation. We ask that these be carefully distinguished, so that it may appear more clearly whether each individually suffices if they do not occur together in the same person.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

There are seven goods, distinguished as seven beatitudes, through which we merit to attain the joys of the heavenly life. For the saying added as though it were an eighth is rather a test of the preceding beatitudes than something different to be counted together with them: namely, “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:10).

Since persecutions plainly threaten the blessed faithful especially, lest anyone suppose them less blessed on this account, he added this to the beatitudes already mentioned, as though saying: “Such persons are no less blessed when they endure persecutions; rather, they are proved more fully by this when they do not fail in them.”

There are plainly three orders among the faithful: that of the continent, that of rulers, and that of married persons. In the first three beatitudes, I think the continent are carefully described; after these, I judge that the next two should especially be referred to rulers, just as the last two should be referred to married persons. This is a fitting order according to degrees of merit.

For the order of the continent comes before the others in perfection of life. The second is that of rulers, who, although they are more worthy in authority even than the continent, are nevertheless inferior to them: fair Rachel, though barren, was more pleasing to the patriarch than bleary-eyed and fruitful Leah (Gen. 29); and Mary’s better part, as one free in leisure, was preferable to Martha’s serving food (Luke 10:39 ff.). The final order is that of married persons. They are far removed from the continent and do not deserve to be made equal to rulers, although both are occupied in active life. For, as Truth himself later says: “Whoever teaches and does the Law”—which applies to teachers and prelates of the Church—“shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:19), as the continent person is greatest and the married person least.

Beginning, therefore, with those who are greatest in virtue and first before God in the dignity of religious life, he comprehends their holiness in three qualities, describing them as poor in spirit, meek, and mourning. One is called blessed, as if *well-actuated*, that is, rightly disposed in good moral habits.

Those are called poor in spirit who endure poverty not by necessity, but who, instructed by God’s reason and fervently embracing it, desire poverty, despising riches and fleeing them as harmful, considering what the Lord says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:24). Here, therefore, he calls reason “spirit,” as the Apostle also does when he says: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17).

For who does not know that desire belongs to the soul rather than the body? But then the flesh desires against the spirit when, in the same soul, sensuality—that is, pleasure arising from bodily weakness—opposes reason, so that, as the Apostle says, often overcome, we do what we do not will: that is, what we do not approve as things to be done. Therefore, when the spirit, that is reason, prompts us to do what we ought and carnality draws us back from it, because some difficulty attends its accomplishment, the spirit is defeated by the flesh’s dominion and subjected to it, so that a person must now be called carnal or animal, given over like cattle to the desires of the flesh.

“For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” He proves the poor in spirit to be blessed from the fact that those who reasonably despise earthly things merit heavenly things.

The poor in spirit, therefore, are those who, for God’s sake, set aside ambition for possessions and honors and seek nothing for pleasure. Content with necessities, they abstain even from what is lawful, lest they be captivated by earthly pleasures; and they strive to devote themselves to God rather than to the world. Such are those who pass from the tumultuous life of the world to monastic quiet, so that they may give themselves more purely to God and themselves the farther they are removed from worldly cares, and may fly to heaven more easily the more they are unburdened by earthly loads.

Jerome, observing this prefigured in that prince of monks, says in one place: “Elijah, hastening to the kingdoms of heaven, left his sheepskin cloak on earth.” When such persons have become poor in spirit, they must necessarily become meek and gentle. For those who seek nothing in earthly things are not stirred to anger by loss of possessions or injuries inflicted upon them.

To such persons, who rightly possess themselves and by governing restrain the impulses of the flesh, the land of the living—that is, the true stability of the blessed—is set forth as a reward, when he says: “For they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4). Jeremiah, describing this virtue of meekness and patience in such people, says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke from his youth. He shall sit alone and be silent, because he has lifted himself above himself. He shall put his mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope. He shall give his cheek to him who strikes him; he shall be filled with reproaches, because the Lord does not cast off forever” (Lam. 3:27 ff.).

A person bears the monastic yoke from youth when he does not delay undertaking it until, exhausted in old age, he presumes to take up what he cannot carry—seeking bodily ease rather than peace of soul, and seeking in the monastery the worldly pleasures which he falsely claims to flee. Unable now to work, he becomes like a drone among bees and shamelessly devours what they gather. When his bodily strength is already spent—strength which, while he could, he expended in the devil’s service—he gives himself, under pretext of the infirmity of old age, to luxurious idleness, when he ought to live all the more strictly and combat vices all the more because he knows that he has less time to live and will more swiftly reach the palm of the prize, if he merits it.

Such a wretched person, unaccustomed from youth to bear the yoke, is compelled to collapse beneath the very burden which he cannot bear. The professed adherent of monastic discipline “sits alone and is silent” when he claims for himself both the name of monk and perfection of life. For “monk” means “solitary.” Rebuking such a person, blessed Jerome says: “What are you doing in a crowd, you who are alone?” Blessed Benedict asserts that he ought at all times to study silence [Note: [Col. 0697D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXVI, col. 669], confirming from Isaiah’s testimony that silence is the cultivation of righteousness (Isa. 32:17). The Apostle, especially commending this virtue, says: “If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is a perfect man” (James 3:2).

He “lifts himself above himself” when, governing and subduing himself, he subjects the flesh to the spirit and, subjecting his own will to the will of God, triumphs gloriously over himself, considering what is written: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his spirit than one who captures cities” (Prov. 16:32). But he ought especially to be silent when others proclaim his virtue, lest, becoming his own herald, he vanish into a light breath and, the higher he seems in virtues, incur a heavier guilt through pride.

Let him therefore be silent because he has lifted himself above himself, lest, if he has done these things, he take notice of it, and let him pray fearfully lest he fall; for in this life victory is secure for no one. But if perhaps he presumes to speak of himself, let him proclaim not his virtue but his weakness. Hence it follows: “He shall put his mouth in the dust, if perhaps there may be hope” (Lam. 3:29). That is to say: let him confess himself to be like dust stirred by demonic temptations—not steadfast in works but unstable. If any elevation of mind should tickle him, let him immediately rebuke himself and say: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Sirach 10:11). “What do you presume, most weightless dust, which the wind casts from the face of the earth?”

Saying these things and fearing for himself, let him consider with terror whether perhaps there may be hope for him, lest at last he be conquered by pride, which triumphs only over virtues. And lest he be exalted by virtues, he must be humbled by persecutions, so that his virtue, tested through patience, may be crowned—the virtue which makes the poor in spirit truly meek.

“He shall give his cheek to him who strikes him, and he shall be filled with reproaches,” because, whether he is wronged by deeds or words, he will be delighted and refreshed by them as by a certain sweetness of taste. The person who rejoices to suffer insult for God gives his cheek to the one who strikes him. Conversely, the person who avoids injuries or endures them unwillingly withdraws his cheek.

Why, then, should the righteous person willingly endure these things and rejoice in suffering, in accordance with what is said of the Apostles: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5:41)? The reason is also added, when the prophet says: “For the Lord will not cast off forever” (Lam. 3:31).

The righteous person seems rejected from the Lord’s grace and exposed to miseries in this life. Thus it is written even of the head of the righteous: “We desired him, despised and the last of men, and we considered him as a leper, struck by God and humbled” (Isa. 53:2). Of this contempt or rejection by God, when he does not protect us amid adversities, it is written: “O God, you have rejected us” (Ps. 49:3).

But because, as has been said, he rejects us here in order that we may be tested, and receives us after victory in order that we may be crowned, the hope through which the afflicted triumph is set forth in the words: “For the Lord will not cast off forever.” That is, he will end the punishments of those afflicted, while he will not end the punishments of those who afflict them.

It should be noted that, when the Lord delivers the New Testament to the Apostles and immediately at the outset exhorts them to poverty, so that we may exchange the fruitfulness of earthly things for heavenly blessedness, he plainly distinguishes the Gospel’s reward from the Law’s reward. There he sets heavenly promises; here, only earthly promises, as the recompense of obedience.

For the carnal people of Israel, desiring earthly more than heavenly things, received in recompense what they most desired. They had to be drawn more toward obedience by the things they coveted, so that at least by this promise they might be recalled from perverse action, if their mind could not yet be cleansed of wickedness. For, as the Apostle says, “The Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:19); nor did it have perfection in its promises, and thus neither in its commandments.

“Blessed are those who mourn” (Matt. 5:5). Saving grief properly belongs to monks, whether it is the grief of repentance for sin or grief over delay from the kingdom. These two kinds of tears were prefigured in Achsah, daughter of Caleb [Col. 0700A], who complained to her father that he had given her dry land and asked for watered land; and her father gave her both the upper spring and the lower (Josh. 15:19).

How fitting it is for a monk to mourn both his own sins and those of others is declared by Jerome, the foremost representative of this profession, when he says: “The monk’s office is not that of a teacher but of one who weeps—who mourns himself and the world, and fearfully awaits the Lord’s coming.” For what is monastic life except a stricter form of penance?

Therefore let monks mourn in either of these ways, as has been said, so that they may deserve the laughter of consolation, of which it is truly said: “For they shall be comforted” (ibid.). Let them attend to what the Lord promised the Apostles: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:20). Hence, conversely, he says to the reprobate: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall weep” (Luke 6:25).

For contrary ways of life have contrary conditions and outcomes: the righteous, weeping now, will later laugh; and the wicked, laughing now, will conversely weep. The righteous receive consolation, whether for having committed sin or for delay from the kingdom, when they arrive at that life wholly free from pain.

“Blessed are those who hunger” (Matt. 5:6). After the life of the continent, he passes to the order of rulers, instructing the latter in two things as he had instructed the former in three. Rulers among God’s people are not only ecclesiastical authorities among priests, but also secular authorities among kings.

It should be noted that the number two, which suits married people, is unclean according to Jerome’s testimony. Therefore the works of the second day did not deserve praise, and unclean animals were commanded to enter the ark two by two. Hence it seems fitting that the continent should be described by the number three, which is odd, rather than by two. For the rest, in whom the virtue of continence does not at all predominate, the number two seems more appropriate.

Hunger or thirst for justice is in rulers a great desire for due punishment: namely, that they wish to punish evils committed as much as they recognize they ought to do, though not as much as those who have sinned deserve. Otherwise mercy would have no place in them, if they remitted nothing of the penalty which the guilty had deserved.

For the heavenly Judge himself, whom earthly judges ought to imitate, so tempers justice through mercy that he punishes the guilty not as much as they deserve but as much as is fitting for him, whose mercies are over all his works. Thus it is written of him: “Will God forget to show mercy, or in his anger restrain his mercies?” (Ps. 76:10). And again: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. 3:2). For mercy exalts itself above judgment and commends the judge more than vengeance.

These two, therefore, ought always to be joined in a judge: that he punish the guilty through justice, and through clemency remit something of what they deserve—which he here calls mercy. Mercy, so called from the miserable, is human compassion arising from the miseries of others, through which, from weakness of mind rather than virtue, we abhor punishments because they afflict those who suffer them—whether those punishments are just or unjust. Such natural compassion of mind, whether rational or not, is properly called *misericordia*, according to Seneca.

But clemency—which here is called mercy—is called only rational compassion, by which we desire to help those whom we ought to help. Whoever has justice without mercy, wishing to punish and remit no penalty, is cruel. But conversely, one who lacks justice is lax. Therefore the Lord, here instructing the character of rulers, never approves the exercise of justice without mercy; and for that reason he joins them here as inseparable companions.

There may be some mitigation of punishment even for those who are put to death, if we endeavor to shorten their sufferings or choose a milder kind of death. Otherwise we incur the sentence: “Judgment without mercy to the one who has not shown mercy” (James 2:13). For contraries suit contraries: just as the merciful are worthy of mercy, so the unmerciful deserve to be deprived of it.

Finally, coming after the continent and rulers to married persons, he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. 5:8). By saying “in heart” and not “in body,” he indicates the life of married persons, which indulges considerably in the pleasure of the flesh and yields to the lust of concupiscence.

Although marital intercourse is permitted when spouses seek in it a remedy for their lack of continence and do not seek it for pleasure and bodily delight after the manner of cattle, nevertheless the flesh contracts some contagion, impurity, or foulness of stain from the taint of lust. Yet those are pure in heart, though not in body, who seek this not for pleasure, as we have said, but only from necessity, lest they offend God by fornicating. These too are to be saved and will not lack the vision of God, in which the summit of true blessedness consists.

They too are called peacemakers because, avoiding the great conflict of the flesh through the concession of marriage, they use it so rationally and moderately that they also have peace with God, whom they do not offend through intemperance. Hence they are to be numbered among the children of God, although they are now compelled by the bond of marriage to serve one another’s flesh.

Jerome understands the Apostle to speak of this servitude when he says: “Were you called as a slave? Do not let it trouble you” (1 Cor. 7:21). For what greater servitude can be named than that a husband or wife does not have authority over his or her own body, nor can they abstain from sexual intercourse even to devote themselves to prayer, except by mutual consent?

Yet such persons will be called children of God when they have come from this servitude into the liberty of the heavenly life, where “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven” (Matt. 22:30).

[Col. 0702A] Let these brief remarks, such as they are, suffice for distinguishing the aforesaid beatitudes—that is, the virtues or gifts of divine grace by which we are made blessed. It remains to ask how those who possess one gift without the others are to be called blessed, since observing a single commandment of God is by no means sufficient; indeed, one who fulfils everything except one commandment incurs condemnation even for omitting that one. But, as it seems to me, he who first said, “Blessed are the poor,” and added, “in spirit,” intended the same addition to be understood in the others—as though it were said, “the meek in spirit,” or “those who mourn in spirit”—so that the faithful may not only possess these things, or the other things which follow, through the Spirit of God, understood as his charity, but may [Col. 0702B] also surpass and abound beyond others in one another’s works.

For just as things known to consist of the four elements receive their names from the prevailing one—that is, they are said to be chiefly that element which abounds in them—so here too the graces of the faithful are distinguished according to that which is proved to abound in them. For the charity of God is said to make poor those whom it makes more zealous and perfect in contempt for riches. Likewise it makes meek those whom it sets above others in the virtue of patience; and we should think similarly concerning the rest. Yet it is the charity of God that makes all blessed, or worthy of blessedness; with it no one can perish, although in God’s gifts it makes some more perfect than others.

[Col. 0702C] The different expressions attached to the reward, when it is said, “For theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3), or, “For they shall possess the earth,” etc. (ibid., 4), do not seem different in the meaning of receiving the reward. Rather, avoiding the weariness of repetition, the Lord varied them with a certain appropriateness which they possess in relation to what precedes, according to the proper sense of the words and the likeness of the matter. This is easy to see in each case. For the kingdom of heaven is suitably promised to the poor, so that those who despise earthly riches for God’s sake may deserve heavenly ones. To the meek, who possess themselves by right conduct, belongs possession of the land of the living; to those who mourn, consolation. To those hungering and thirsting for righteousness, satiety—that is, the fulfilment of their desire to attain God, [Col. 0702D] for love of whom they devote themselves most earnestly to practising righteousness in punishing evildoers. Thus in the remaining expressions of reward too, a certain harmony can be assigned with the preceding beatitudes.

Therefore, the Lord does not so much command that the beatitudes themselves be possessed as urge those who desire to be more perfect in each rank to abound in them. For the abundance of perfection is what he subsequently professes here to hand down as the New Testament from God, saying: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20).

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XV

Why is it that the Lord afterward says, “Do not think that I came to abolish the law” (Matt. 5:17), [Col. 0703A] when John says: “Therefore the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God” (John 5:18)?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

When he said, “I did not come to abolish,” and afterward added, “but to fulfil,” namely in moral precepts rather than figurative ones—as the following matters, which he adduces as fulfilment, show—he indicated what abolition of the commandments of the law he had first meant: namely, abolition in moral precepts.

Moral precepts concern the life to be lived, just as figurative precepts concern what is to be figured. The moral precepts, which were naturally always to be fulfilled by everyone, even before the written law was given, so necessarily order human conduct that unless what they command is fulfilled, no one has ever deserved to be saved. Such are: to love God and one’s neighbour; not to kill; not to commit adultery; not to lie; and the like, without fulfilment of which no one can ever be justified. Figurative precepts, however, are commandments of the law which, taken according to the letter, confer no righteousness through their performance; rather, they were instituted for a time in order to signify something pertaining to righteousness: such as Sabbath observance, circumcision, abstinence from certain foods, and the like.

Therefore, the Lord’s statement that he came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it must be referred only to the moral precepts of the law. That is, he did not come to cause what the law contains in moral precepts to cease, but through the Gospel to supply in them what the law lacks. For [Col. 0703C] the law of Moses does not command that an enemy be loved, but a friend; nor does it teach that sin is consummated in the mind, but forbids deeds more than intention. Even if the law also prohibits coveting, it nevertheless does not establish that a person should be considered guilty on account of it; nor does it forbid coveting another’s property, except that of one whom it defines, according to the letter, as a neighbour—that is, one who is never a foreigner from his own people. For according to the letter the law does not call every human being a neighbour, but plainly distinguishes a foreigner from a neighbour when it says that a Jew must not lend at interest to a neighbour, but may do so to a foreigner.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XVI

How, furthermore, does he set the abundance of the Gospel above [Col. 0703D] the imperfection of the law, saying: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes or Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20)? Or how, as the Apostle says, is the preceding commandment set aside because of its weakness and uselessness? “For the law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:18–19). For when the Lord answered the rich man who asked how he might possess eternal life by speaking of the two commandments of love that are in the law, “Do this, and you shall live” (Luke 10:28), and when the Apostle says, “He who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law. For: You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill” (Rom. 13:8), etc.; and again, “Love of one’s neighbour works no evil. Therefore love is the fulfilment of the law” (ibid., 10)—how does the law lack anything for perfection of the commandments, when even those two precepts of love for God and neighbour seem altogether sufficient, and to lack nothing of perfection?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

When the Lord says, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees,” understand “righteousness,” not “the righteousness of the law.” Hence he also says later: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (Matt. 5:43). This cannot be found in the law at all, but rather in the traditions added to the law by the Scribes and Pharisees, concerning whom the Lord says, “You have made void the commandment of God for the sake of your traditions” (Matt. 15:6).

Especially since the law itself commands love of an enemy, or even benefits bestowed upon him, saying: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or ass straying, bring it back to him. If you see the ass of one who hates you lying beneath its burden, you shall not pass by, but shall lift it up with him” (Exod. 23:4). And in the Psalmist: “If I have repaid evil to those repaying me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” (Ps. 7:5). And Solomon in Proverbs: “Do not say, ‘I will repay evil for evil’; wait for the Lord, and he will deliver you” (Prov. 20:22). “When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and let not your heart exult at his ruin, lest perhaps the Lord see and be displeased, and turn away his wrath from him” (Prov. 24:17). “Do not say: ‘As he did to me, so I will do to him; I will render to each according to his work’” (ibid., 18). Again: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him water to drink. For you will heap coals upon [Col. 0704C] his head, and the Lord will repay you” (Prov. 25:22). And blessed Job says: “If I rejoiced at the ruin of him who hated me, and exulted when evil overtook him—for I did not give over my throat to sin, to seek his life with a curse” (Job 31:29–30). Therefore this was neither commanded nor permitted to the ancients in the law, namely, that they should hate their enemy; rather, as has been said, it was found in human traditions more than in God’s commandments.

Therefore, when the Lord says, “more than that of the Scribes and Pharisees” (Matt. 5:20), not “more than that of the law,” we are by no means compelled to confess on this account that the Lord prefers this abundance of the Gospel to an imperfection of the law. Yet we do not for that reason deny that the law was so imperfect in its commandments that it was necessary for the Gospel to succeed it, as the Apostle, as we recalled above, plainly professes.

But neither could the commandment concerning love of one’s neighbour be perfect before Christ’s coming. He, coming and becoming our neighbour, made it perfect both by assuming flesh and by displaying love, so that anyone now loving him as his neighbour becomes perfect through this love. Hence, when the rich man asked him who his neighbour was, he answered in a parable, signifying that he himself was that neighbour whom the Samaritan represented, who had compassion upon the wounded man; and the rich man himself acknowledged that this man, by his compassionate feeling, had truly been a neighbour.

Whether, then, the law contains, “You shall love your friend,” [Col. 0705A] or “your neighbour” (Matt. 5:43)—so that we understand there a neighbour as one joined to us either by kinship or love—no one can more rightly be called our neighbour than Christ. Thus love of neighbour is now made perfect in him, whereas formerly it was imperfect, so long as the law retained its own status and preserved its force until John. It was therefore imperfect beforehand, as long as it was properly called law, to which obedience was due in all things; because of this very imperfection it was set aside when the perfection of evangelical teaching arrived, in which whatever is necessary is expressed more plainly than in parables.

For even if we attend carefully to the letter of the law, which was given to the Jewish people alone, no one but one of them is to be understood as a neighbour. Hence that commandment concerning love of neighbour does not seem, even through Christ, to extend to others, since they alone were contained under the law. Therefore the Gospel, imposed universally upon all, necessarily had to succeed the law, so that all might be saved through it.

Accordingly, the Apostle looked to the aforesaid neighbour—that is, Christ—when, after first saying, “He who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law” (Rom. 13:8), he immediately added this as proof: “For, You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill” (ibid., 9), etc. For if a Jew loves this one, included among his neighbours, as he himself says, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my commandments” (John 14:23), he will sin in no adultery or murder, avoid all similar things contained in the law, and fulfil its righteous requirements.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XVII

[Col. 0705C]

What, furthermore, is meant by the Lord’s later saying: “Neither shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black” (Matt. 5:36), as though, if one could do this, it would be lawful to swear by one’s head?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

We must repeat what was set forth immediately before, so that from it we may judge this matter more easily. “I say to you,” he says, “not to swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by earth, because it is his footstool; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great king; nor by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black” [Col. 0705D] (Matt. 5:34–35).

There are, therefore, four things—heaven, earth, Jerusalem, and our head—by which we are forbidden to swear, because in swearing we most often invoke those things which we consider more venerable, so that we may be believed the more on their account. These, however, seem worthy of greater reverence because they are known especially to belong to God: heaven, which is called God’s throne, that is, the soul of Christ, in which the Godhead especially sits and dwells more fully through grace; earth, called God’s footstool, is Christ’s humanity, as an earthly and lower creature in Christ; Jerusalem, the city of God, is the holy Church, whose head is Christ himself. The hairs adhering to the head and adorning or protecting it are the divine utterances by which Christ is commended and preserved in us through faith. Some of these are called white, others black: the meaning of some is clear and manifest, while that of others is obscure, especially those which have been spoken allegorically. None of these, whether white, as has been said, or black, is ours to make, because God’s utterances are not of human invention; they are not our teachings, but divine.

Therefore, when he says, “You shall not swear by your head, because you cannot,” etc., it means: You ought not to invoke Christ in an oath, because to devise these things, some of which, as we have said, are white and others black, belongs solely to the supreme wisdom of God. Similarly, when he commands us not to swear by heaven, which is God’s throne, understand it thus: we ought not choose to swear by it because it is of such dignity that it surpasses other creatures.

In these words, therefore, a negative adverb placed before the statement excludes the cause itself; when inserted within it, it leaves and establishes the cause itself. For a negative particle has one force when placed before the whole statement, namely to deny it altogether, and another when inserted, namely when attached only to one part of that statement. For it is one thing to say, “You did not sin because you did this,” and another to say, “You sinned because you did not do this.” In the former, the cause of sinning is removed—namely, one did not sin on account of this—and it is certain from this that one did not sin where that cause intervened. In the latter, it is not shown that one did not sin, but only that one did not sin on account of this; thus the cause of sin is removed rather than [Col. 0706C] the sin itself.

This, then, is what the Lord commands or urges concerning an oath: because swearing is dangerous, lest we commit perjury we should avoid it altogether as far as we can; we should not desire to swear by something on account of whatever dignity that thing may possess, whether it be God himself, namely Christ, or any creature which has received some dignity above others from God.

To swear by something is to grant the person to whom we swear that we may thereafter have no benefit in that thing by which we swear unless what we affirm by oath is true. But since, as the Apostle says, an oath is the end of every dispute in ecclesiastical matters (Heb. 6:16), the Lord does not here command us not to swear, but rather exhorts us.

For some things are commanded, some forbidden, some advised, and some permitted. All evils are forbidden, and all goods are commanded—but only those goods that appear necessary for salvation, such as believing in God and loving not so much him as one’s neighbour, not committing adultery, and the like. Those goods, however, which are not so necessary, whether because they belong to a stricter or a more relaxed way of life, and are as it were too exalted or too lowly, are not confined under a commandment; rather, they have either the persuasive counsel of advice, as virginity does, or the permission of indulgence, as marriage does. For if a commandment compelled virginity, marriage would be condemned; or if it compelled marriage, [Col. 0707A] virginity would be condemned.

Therefore counsel or persuasion concerns the higher goods; permission concerns the lesser goods, that is, those of lesser merit, when the counsel concerning better things is not undertaken through some hesitation or dispensation. Thus things which it is lawful both to do and to leave undone have not a commandment but an admonition, as not swearing at all; or a permission, as when it is done from necessity—for example, when witnesses are needed in order to discover the truth. Permission is expressed when it is said, “Let each man have his own wife because of fornication” (1 Cor. 7:2); command when it is said, “Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek release” (ibid., 27); and persuasive counsel when it immediately adds, “Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife” (ibid.).

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XVIII

[Col. 0707B]

What is meant in the same Evangelist: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’” (Matt. 6:31), and again: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow. For tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (ibid., 34)? Does he forbid provision for the future? Does not the Lord himself advise one who wishes to build a tower to consider the costs? And the Apostle says: “He who presides, [let him do so] with diligence” (Rom. 12:8); as he himself did, saying of himself: “My daily pressure, the concern for all the churches” (2 Cor. 11:28).

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

By “anxiety” the Lord properly means a superfluous concern about the future: namely, when more necessary things are neglected to prepare certain others. For instance, if in preparing tomorrow’s food we neglect by prayer to seek from God his kingdom—that is, to make us such that he, not sin, may reign in us.

“For tomorrow” means, as though he said: Do not afflict yourselves with superfluous cares for the future time before it arrives, because, when it has arrived, it will bring enough anxiety from itself to those who trust too little in the Lord concerning necessities and fail to heed the Prophet’s words: “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he will nourish you” (Ps. 54:23). “Sufficient for the day,” etc., means: for each period of this wretched life, the punishment of its own anxiety should suffice—the anxiety brought upon us by superfluous cares for temporal matters, when on their account we forget eternal things.

But the Apostle calls anxiety in a good sense, or anxiety concerning things belonging to eternal life, “providence”: that is, a reasonable concern for future or profitable matters, provided that we make provision for temporal things for the sake of eternal ones, so that those hastening to the latter may be sustained by the former as by necessary travelling provisions.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XIX

What is meant by the subsequent words: “Do not judge, that you may not be judged. For with whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged” (Matt. 7:1)? For if we render an unjust judgment, shall we receive a similar one?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

“Do not judge,” that is, do not presume, on uncertain grounds, [Col. 0708A] to burden anyone with a definite sentence. For when an angry person is evident, the matter itself judges him, not you. Hence also the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of hearts” (1 Cor. 5:4). The Lord comes by revealing hidden things when, by his ordering, things that were concealed appear; or when we investigate something to be examined according to his law, or impose a punishment upon those who have been proven guilty. Then it is he rather than we who judges or punishes.

“For with whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged.” As though he said: Therefore you ought not presume in judgment so as to desire to burden others, because you will incur a like burdensome judgment before God. Finally, he did not say, “Do not judge” in the subjunctive, but, “Do not judge”; that is, so that we may not willingly seek what we are nevertheless sometimes compelled to do when the office of judge has been entrusted to us.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XX

We also ask concerning what he adds later: “Therefore all things whatsoever you wish that people should do to you, do also to them. For this is the law and the prophets” (Matt. 7:2). For if someone wishes another to consent with him in evil, must he offer that person consent in a similar matter?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

There are two precepts of natural law concerning love of neighbour: one, namely, which is given in this place; the other which we read in Tobit, where he says to his son: “What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you never do to another” (Tob. 4:16). Therefore, just as the latter is to be understood concerning evils, so the former is to be understood concerning goods: namely, just as we do not wish evils to be inflicted upon us, so we should not inflict them on others; and conversely, we should be ready to bestow upon others the goods we wish to receive from them.

When, therefore, it is said, “What you wish people to do to you,” this means: what you approve in your conscience as something others ought to do to you. For no one approves in conscience that another should consent with him in evil, but only in things which he considers good and worthy to be done. So too when the Apostle says, “What I will, this I do not do” (Rom. 7:15), he uses “I will” to mean “I approve as fit to be done.”

But what does he mean by “all things whatsoever you wish”? Many people, on account of the rank or difference of persons, judge that many things ought to be done for them which they in no way acknowledge ought to be done for others—as we see in superiors and subjects, when the former demand that many things be done for them by the latter, though they ought by no means to do those things for the latter. But it must certainly be understood thus: whatever we believe people ought to do for us, we should be ready to do for them—not indeed for anyone whatsoever, but for those like ourselves, that is, those worthy to receive these things from us as we are from them.

Tobit’s statement too—“What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you never do to another”—raises some question, since one who kills another for the sake of justice could never wish to suffer this from another. But when someone exercises justice for God’s sake, God rather than that person does it, as we said above long ago. Therefore it is commanded that what a person himself hates to have done to him, he should not do to another; for when he rightly punishes someone, it is God, or the law, rather than the human being who does this.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XXI

What is meant by the Apostle’s saying (1 Thess. 5:17), “Pray without ceasing”?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

To omit no time in which we ought to pray.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XXII

What is meant by the account in Matthew concerning the faith of the centurion who pleaded for his servant: “But when Jesus heard it, he marvelled, and said to those following him: Amen, I say to you, I have not found such great faith in Israel” (Matt. 8:10)? For persons are said to marvel only when they see something unexpected happen, which they had not previously known or believed would happen at all.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

He is said to have marvelled because he made himself like one marvelling, since he caused others to marvel at the centurion’s faith, whom he so greatly praised.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XXIII

What is meant by the passage in Luke: “Give to everyone who asks you, and do not demand back from one who takes what is yours” (Luke 6:30)?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

When he says “give,” he does not add “what he asks for.” By this he indicates that we should send no petitioner away empty of a gift, so that at least, in our answer, by suitably excusing ourselves, we may not embitter him but strive in charity to build him up. Thus a gentle or suitable reply may be some gift of grace.

“Do not demand back what is yours”—that is, do not demand it back because it is yours, so as to make yourself rather than God the end of reclaiming it. For a religious person does not transgress if, for God’s sake, he reclaims things offered to him which he possessed for God’s sake, spends them in good uses, and frees one oppressed by violence from plunder.

For when he adds shortly afterward: “And if you love those who love you, and if you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you?” (Luke 6:32), when he says “those who love you,” it is like saying, “Do not demand back what is yours”—that is, because they love you, just as because the things are yours. Otherwise it would be unjust for us not to love those by whom we are loved, since we are commanded to love everyone; indeed, [Col. 0709D] not even God himself, who loves us, as he himself says, “I love those who love me” (Prov. 7:17). We ought to love him with the highest love rather for his own sake, because he is supremely good, than because he is useful to us.

This is ordered charity: that we love each person more for the reason that he is better and worthier—that is, that we desire a greater good for him, as is just.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XXIV

How does the Lord say: “Not what enters the mouth defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth” (Matt. 15:11)? Does one who eats from plunder, or eats what he believes unlawful even if it is lawful, or receives a sacrament unworthily, not incur a stain of sin from these things? The Apostle says of certain Jews converted to the faith, who still, because of the law, distinguished some foods from others as unclean: “But he who makes distinctions, if he eats, is condemned, because it is not from faith. But whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). He also says of those who ate things sacrificed to idols out of reverence for the idol: “Some even now, with the consciousness of the idol, eat it as a thing sacrificed to an idol; and their conscience, being weak, is defiled” (1 Cor. 8:7). How, then, does the Lord now say that what enters the mouth does not defile a person, but rather what proceeds from the mouth?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

In this passage the Lord especially distinguished carefully where sin is to be understood to reside; by reproving the Jews on this point, he instructed us. For they, looking more to deeds than to the mind, judge both good and evil more from things done outwardly than from what is held in the mind. But the Lord, reducing everything to intention, judges that a person is condemned more by what is in the heart than by what appears in deed; and he judges that the soul is not defiled except by things which are in it and touch it. Thus the stains of souls are spiritual, just as bodily filth is corporeal.

Hence, explaining what he had said—“But what proceeds from the mouth, this defiles a person”—he continues: “But those things which proceed from the mouth come out of the heart, and they defile a person. For evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies come out of the heart. These are what defile a person. To eat with unwashed hands does not defile a person” (Matt. 15:18–20). As though he openly said: Bodily dirt on the hands does not reach the soul so that it can defile it with sin.

The defiling thoughts proceed from the heart when we consent to carry out what we have thought. But where there is no understanding, there can be no consent, as in infants or the insane. When such persons do what they ought not, no sin is imputed to them for it. And the Lord calls neither murder nor adultery nor any other thing sin unless it proceeds from the heart—that is, unless we recognize those unlawful things to which consent inclines us.

Therefore, just as thoughts proceed from the heart when by consent they tend toward deeds, so he teaches that murder, adultery, and other sins proceed from the heart, and that they are not sins in any other way than when they have first been present in the heart through consent before being displayed in deed. For after someone consents to do things which he knows he is not permitted to do, that consent is properly called sin; and on account of that alone he is held before God to be a murderer or adulterer.

Hence Truth itself says: “Whoever looks upon a woman to desire her”—that is, whoever looks at her and comes to consent to desire—“has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). That is, he has sin perfected in his mind, even if it has not yet been consummated in deed. When we take something to eat wrongly because we believe it unlawful for us, the food which enters the mouth does not at all defile the soul; rather, our preceding conscience had already done this. What we now take with the mouth contributes nothing to the sin; what matters is that we consented to take it.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XXV
