What is meant by the statement in Matthew in which the Lord rebukes certain cities: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida; for if the miracles which were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes” (Luke 10:13)? For the Lord had come to save humankind; hence he was himself called Jesus, that is, Saviour, by his own name. Why then did he withhold from the Gentile cities of Tyre and Sidon those miraculous benefits through which they would be saved, and bestow them upon those whom he knew they would harm rather than benefit? But, you will say, because, as he himself professes, he was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel (Matt. 15:24). But I say: Why to them, except that they might be saved? And if that was so, what good was it to them that those things were done for them by which they would be more grievously condemned, since they did not turn to repentance but remained in their obstinacy? Hence the Lord himself adds: “Nevertheless I say to you, it shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you” (Luke 10:14).

Further, John reports that many Samaritans believed on account of his word (John 4:36), and that he bestowed certain miraculous benefits upon Gentiles, both men and women, through which they might believe or be strengthened in faith—such as that concerning the centurion’s servant [Col. 0711C] (Matt. 3:5; Luke 7:2), and that concerning the daughter of the Syrophoenician woman, who came from the region of Tyre itself (Mark 7:26).

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

Indeed, the Lord Jesus was sent in his own person to the Jews alone. Therefore, what he did mercifully among the Gentiles, he did not do by the office of his mission but by grace; he added what was not owed to what was owed, bearing in mind what he himself says: “When you have done all that is commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were bound to do’” (Luke 17:10). As though he openly said: Do not consider it a great thing if you fulfil the obligation of obedience, unless you further add some grace beyond what is owed, as those do who cultivate virginity or continence, a virtue by no means included under a commandment.

Moreover, he came to confer those benefits upon the Gentiles not so much as one sent to do so as one invited and, as it were, drawn by prayers to do them. But from his withholding preaching from those whom he testifies would have been so converted to repentance, we are by no means compelled to confess that they would have persevered in this repentance so as to be saved. For many people are fickle: they are easily moved to the compunction of repentance and, with the same ease, like those returning to vomit, relapse into the evils they had mourned. Though they eagerly receive the word they have heard preached, they lack firmness of root to persevere in what they have begun.

But even if we suppose that those from whom he nevertheless withheld the grace of preaching would have been converted and saved by the Lord’s preaching, it belongs to him to know why he did not decree to do this, he who does nothing without reason; just as the Apostle raised a question about Esau, from whom grace was withheld, and left it unresolved.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XXVI

It also seems necessary to ask with what mystery, or for what reason, the Lord, seeking fruit on the fig tree and finding none when, as Mark says, it was not the season for figs (Mark 11:13), nevertheless struck it with his curse and immediately made it wither, so that it remained thereafter dried up—as though he had inflicted this curse upon it because of some fault of the tree.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

[Col. 0712B] The fruitless tree is Judaea, then rejected by the Lord because of its wickedness, so that it deserved to be deprived of the fruit of good work, since it did not recognize the time of its visitation. Its fault, however, was that the time for its fruits was not present when it rejected the grace of the Lord’s preaching offered to it.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XXVII

What is meant by: “Let his prayer become sin” (Ps. 108:7)?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

May he be handed over to a reprobate mind, so that he chooses rather to pray for harmful things than profitable ones, and to obtain by prayer things which draw him more toward sin than lead him to salvation.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XXVIII

From Paul’s First Epistle to the Thessalonians: “May the God of peace himself sanctify you wholly, so that your whole spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23). What are “spirit” and “soul,” as though the soul were not spirit, or as though there were two spirits in one person?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

The Apostle here uses “spirit” for reason—that is, for the discernment of the mind—as also in the phrase, “the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17). Thus, “May your spirit be whole” means: may your reason be so perfect and uncorrupted that it deviates from truth in no respect through error.

By “soul,” however, he means the will, in accordance with the saying: “He who loves his soul will lose it” (Matt. 10:39). That is: whoever follows his own will here will afterward be deprived of his will, so that whoever fulfils his own will here may not have what he wishes in the future. Therefore our soul, that is, our will, is whole when it does not disagree with the divine will.

The body too is kept whole when the exercise of bodily senses is not corrupted by carnal allurements, and our eye does not plunder our soul, nor death enter through our windows (Jer. 9:21). We are wholly sanctified in these three when we exceed neither in the discernment of reason, nor in the agitation of our own will, nor in sensual pleasure, so that the flesh rules the spirit. Thus we are indeed preserved blameless—that is, without reproach—until the coming of the Lord, if we persevere in this state until the final judgment, or deserve to be found such at that time.

## HELOISE’S PROBLEM XXIX

What is meant by the passage to the Ephesians: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth; and also to know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God” (Eph. 3:19)?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION
“To comprehend” means to experience in yourselves how great is the breadth of those persons, namely the saints, in charity, by which they extend themselves even to their enemies. The length is the long-suffering perseverance of charity, or patience amid adversities, through that same charity which bears all things and endures all things; [Col. 0713B] their height and depth signify how great they are before God through the magnitude of their merits, and how small or weak they are in their own estimation through humility. For “depth” denotes what is lowest or humble. How great and exalted they are before God they will experience in their reward, where they deserve to be raised so much the more as they have been humbler here; and to receive so much the more from God as they acknowledge themselves here to possess the less of themselves.

These four things—the breadth of the saints, or of the Church, which is Christ’s body—are understood to have been prefigured in Christ’s very cross, to which his body was fastened. In the breadth [Col. 0713C] of the cross, to right and left, where he was stretched out with his hands nailed fast, is signified the breadth of charity which embraces even enemies, who are to us, as it were, on the left—that is, in adversity—just as friends are on the right. The hands fastened to the right and left sides of the cross are works of charity extended in benefits alike toward enemies and friends. The Lord indeed displayed this breadth of charity to us from the cross itself, when, both taking care for his mother, he entrusted her to the disciple, and prayed for those crucifying him.

But as breadth extends rightward and leftward, so length looks upward and downward; in it the Lord himself stood erect upon the cross from head to feet. By this length is figured his perseverance in patience, even to the [Col. 0713D] completion of his life, or of our redemption. Of this he himself said: “It is finished” (John 19:30). And the Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:8). The height of the cross is that addition upon which the inscription was written above the Lord’s head. In that inscription his written name, Jesus, is that most excellent name of which the same Apostle added: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name” (ibid., 9).

In the elect also, that added upper portion signifies what, in the reward of the saints, is bestowed upon them by grace beyond their merits, according to the saying of the same [Col. 0714A] Apostle: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory which shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18). The depth—that is, the lower part of the cross by which it stands fixed in the earth—is the lowly and despised instrument of the cross, or the shameful kind of death, by which Christ’s supreme humility is commended and by which he deserved to be more highly exalted, as we recalled above: “Therefore God also exalted him,” etc. Of this kind of death it had been foretold in the person of the ungodly: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death” (Wisdom 2:20).

In the elect likewise, that lower part of the cross, by which it is held fast in the earth, expresses the virtue of humility. In comparing themselves to dust and earth, the more they humble themselves here and consider themselves lesser, the more they deserve afterward to be exalted. [Col. 0714B] This humility of theirs keeps them firm and upright on the summit of the virtues, just as that part fixed in the earth keeps the cross firm and erect.

After the charity of the saints, he passes to Christ’s supreme charity, which Christ displayed to us; and he admonishes us to know and continually consider it, so that by comparison with it we may be kept more humble and more fervent in love for him. He calls Christ’s charity surpassing our knowledge because it is far greater than we can comprehend by intellect or experience. When, then, in considering this charity of Christ, we compare it with our own as incomparably superior, we shall, as has been said, be made humbler and more fervent, and be filled [Col. 0714C] with every perfection of virtues bestowed upon us by God.

## HELOISE’S THIRTIETH PROBLEM

What is meant by the statement in the First Book of Kings concerning Elkanah: “That man went up on the appointed days in order to worship” (1 Sam. 1:3)? Who appointed these days, and by whom were they appointed?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

Rabanus Maurus, in his books on Kings [Note: [Col. 0713D] *Patrologia*, vol. 109, col. 12], follows the opinion of a certain Hebrew scholar, whom he follows literally in many places:

> “When it says, ‘on the appointed days,’ this means at the three festivals: Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles.”

Accordingly, the Lord commanded in Exodus: “Three times in every year you shall celebrate feasts for me” [Col. 0714D] (Exod. 23:14). And again: “Three times in the year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God, in the place which the Lord your God shall choose” (ibid., 17). Therefore, since the ark of the Lord was then at Shiloh, Elkanah, being himself a Levite, ate there with his wives, sons, and daughters after the victims had been offered.

## HELOISE’S THIRTY-FIRST PROBLEM

What is the meaning of Anna’s subsequent reply to Eli the priest: “No, my lord. I am a woman exceedingly unhappy; I have drunk neither wine nor anything that can intoxicate, but have poured out my soul in the presence of the Lord. Do not regard [Col. 0715A] your handmaid as one of the daughters of Belial” (1 Sam. 1:15)?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

She calls herself unhappy, as though disgraced, because a barren woman—one who has left no seed in Israel—was cursed. Hence Elizabeth’s words: “Thus has the Lord dealt with me in the days when he looked upon me, to take away my reproach among men” (Luke 1:25). Hence also the passage in Deuteronomy, where the Lord promises the people, among other things, for keeping his commandments: “There shall not be among you one barren of either sex, neither among human beings nor among your flocks” (Deut. 7:14).

Her statement, “I have drunk neither wine nor anything that can intoxicate,” expresses the great perfection of a laywoman or married woman. If she then practiced this abstinence [Col. 0715B] so that the Lord might more readily hear her prayer concerning the child she sought, how much more does such abstinence befit virgins of Christ, who strive after a spiritual and far better fruit? She calls those women especially daughters of Belial whom the devil begets for himself as his own offspring. Drunkenness overturns the state of the mind and extinguishes whatever we possess of God’s image through reason, so that, compared with irrational beasts, we become like horse and mule, which have no understanding.

The ancient enemy is called *diabolus*, that is, “flowing downward”; and *Zabulus* or Satan, which in Latin means “adversary” or “transgressor”; and Belial, that is, “without a yoke.” This name is rightly used here because of drunkards, since drunkards, like madmen, are subject to no yoke of God [Col. 0715C] or of discipline. Thus she calls them daughters of Belial, such as the frenzied priestesses of Bacchus are described to be.

## HELOISE’S THIRTY-SECOND PROBLEM

What is also meant by this statement concerning Anna: “Her face was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Sam. 1:18)?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

Thereafter she displayed only a cheerful countenance, not one sorrowful or tearful.

## HELOISE’S THIRTY-THIRD PROBLEM

What is meant by this: “Anna prayed and said: ‘My heart exulted in the Lord,’” etc. (1 Sam. 2:1)? For this song contains words of thanksgiving or rather of prophecy, not of prayer.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

[Col. 0715D] As I judge, she offered a prayer before the song, so that her song, or act of thanksgiving, might become more acceptable to God. Thus “She prayed” is said of the preceding prayer; and “she said: ‘My heart exulted,’” etc., is added concerning the song. It is also the Church’s custom at each of the Hours to precede with prayer those things that are to be sung in the praises of God.

We read several songs by holy women: those of Deborah (Judg. 5:1 ff.), Judith (Judith 16:2 ff.), and this one of Anna, Samuel’s mother; likewise that of Mary, the Lord’s mother, concerning the birth entrusted to her by the Lord (Luke 1:46 ff.): to the one, barren though she was, that she might become the mother of so great a prophet; to the other, a Virgin, that she might become the Savior’s mother. The Church has especially been accustomed to use Anna’s song, as also that [Col. 0716A] of the supreme Virgin, not only because of the mother’s holiness or the dignity of the birth granted to her in Samuel—namely, he from whom prophets are said especially to have begun, and who was the first to be offered to the Lord by his mother—but also because no one before the time of the prophets appears to have prophesied Christ and his reign in songs as openly as Anna does here. For she says of Christ’s Father and of Christ himself: “The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth, and shall give dominion to his king, and shall exalt the horn of his Christ” (1 Sam. 2:10).

For no king had yet been established in Israel to whom this prophetic woman’s rejoicing could apply. She was the first to deserve openly to express Christ—that is, the true Messiah. She clearly foretells as future what Mary sings as accomplished, as though the barren woman’s prophecy and childbirth were to instruct [Col. 0716B] the Virgin’s faith.

## HELOISE’S THIRTY-FOURTH PROBLEM

This also causes difficulty: “Until the barren woman bore very many” (ibid., 5). Although Scripture subsequently relates that Anna bore three more sons and two daughters after Samuel, nevertheless when she sang this song she is reported to have had only Samuel. How, too, does she say “very many” of her own children and “many” of the children of her rival Phenenna, as though she herself had more than Phenenna? Although Scripture does not state how many children Phenenna had, some nevertheless maintain that she had more than Anna, namely seven.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

[Col. 0716C] It is unnecessary here to understand “very many” comparatively, as meaning “more” in comparison with fewer; rather, she says “very many” absolutely, just as she says “many,” varying expressions with the same meaning. Nor is there any obstacle if Anna had already had many children when she rendered this song to the Lord, even though Scripture has not yet reported her as having had any but Samuel. Scripture’s sequence often does not preserve historical order, but tells certain matters out of order.

Anna could also have said this through the spirit of prophecy while she still had Samuel alone. Finally, she could fittingly have said it of Samuel alone, namely because he was of greater value than Phenenna’s children, though one in number. In this way we sometimes say that one person has more than another when he possesses fewer things in number but more precious things. [Col. 0716D]

## HELOISE’S THIRTY-FIFTH PROBLEM

We also ask what this means: “But Samuel ministered before the face of the Lord, a boy girded with a linen ephod; and his mother made him a little tunic, which she brought on the appointed days when she went up with her husband to offer the solemn sacrifice” (ibid., 18). Whether Samuel was a Levite, as is more probable, or a priest, the age of childhood could in no way, according to the Law, have been suitable for his ministry: that is, for him as a boy, girded with an ephod as either Levite or priest, to perform ministry. We also ask what tunic, and at what appointed times, his mother brought to the boy.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

[Col. 0717A]

As a boy he could minister in certain lesser offices and wear a linen ephod. Thus Rabanus, following Augustine, says [Note: [Col. 0717D] *Patrologia*, vol. 109, col. 20]:

> “Samuel was girded with an *ephod bad*, that is, with a linen shoulder-garment, distinct from the ephod worn by the high priest. For this one was only linen and was permitted for persons of lower ranks to use. But that which clothed the high priest was woven from four colors—hyacinth, fine linen, scarlet, and purple—and from gold.”

It is evident that the appointed days were the aforementioned three festivals under the Law, so that at each of those principal annual solemnities the mother carefully brought her son a new tunic, in which he might minister to the Lord more cleanly or honorably, wearing a linen shoulder-garment [Col. 0717B] over it; girded with this and not burdened by it, he could minister more freely. Unless I am mistaken, monks now imitate this dress when they customarily perform manual work in a tunic with a scapular girded over it. For what are shoulders but *scapulae*? And what is a scapular but a shoulder-garment?

Finally, who would censure Samuel, though a boy, for ministering in the office of the Levites out of necessity, with Eli’s command, when no one in Eli’s house was then found worthy of that office? For the proverb is well known: necessity has no law.

## HELOISE’S THIRTY-SIXTH PROBLEM

We ask and seek who that man of God was whom the Lord sent to Eli, to rebuke him and foretell the evils that would come upon his house. What is also meant by this, which is said among other things concerning the priest better than Eli who would succeed him: “I shall raise up for myself a faithful priest, who shall do according to my heart and my soul; I shall build for him a faithful house, and he shall walk before my anointed one all his days. And it shall come to pass that whoever remains in the house shall come so that prayer may be made for him, and shall offer a silver coin and a cake of bread, and shall say: ‘Assign me, I beg you, to one priestly portion, that I may eat a morsel of bread’” (1 Sam. 2:35–36). We know indeed that Samuel, who survived Eli, was most faithful to the Lord. But it is commonly held that he was a Levite rather than a priest, and that his house was not faithful, since his sons were rejected. We ask whether the statement, “He shall walk [Col. 0717D] before my anointed one,” is to be understood of the priest himself or of his house, and who that anointed one is. Finally, we request an explanation of what follows concerning the offering of a silver coin and a cake of bread, as though it were a new offering not prescribed by the Law, and of the other matters added.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

The man of God is believed to have been an angel appearing in human form. The priest who would succeed Eli is to be understood not so much as Samuel—who was a Levite and had not a faithful but a rejected house—as any other holy man who succeeded Eli in the priestly order, perhaps such a man as Abinadab, [Col. 0718A] into whose house the ark of the Lord was brought back to Kiriath-jearim from the Philistines (1 Sam. 7:1); or Eleazar, his son, consecrated there to guard the ark (ibid.); or finally Ahimelech himself, whom Saul killed with the other priests in Nob, the city of priests (1 Sam. 22:9 ff.).

But understand the words, “He shall walk before my anointed one,” not of the priest but of his house while he ministers over it. Finally, concerning the added words, “And it shall come to pass,” etc., I heard a certain Hebrew explain as follows. The silver coin is the silver shekel by which each person redeemed himself from the priest. The cake of bread is *quicar*, that is, a quarter-part of a loaf, which was an offering of the poor. The priestly portion consisted of the right shoulder and the breast—that is, the upper part of the chest—the cheeks, [Col. 0718B] the stomach, and the tail, though it was not always the same; for according to the various rites of sacrifices, as is read in Leviticus, a portion was given to the priest (Lev. 10:12).

Eli is therefore told that his house will come to such poverty that those who are now receivers of redemptions and offerings, and to whom a priestly portion was given because of Eli himself, will ask others to redeem them as priests and will beg for sustenance, praying that some tiny portion of the priesthood and a morsel of bread—the cake called above—may be granted to them.

## HELOISE’S THIRTY-SEVENTH PROBLEM

What is meant by the statement at the beginning of Mark the Evangelist, where he says: “As it is written in Isaiah: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare [Col. 0718C] your way before you. The voice of one crying in the wilderness,’” etc. (Mark 1:2)? Why does he say “in Isaiah,” when the first testimony which he immediately adds is from Malachi and the second from Isaiah? If he had done the reverse, the truth could stand: namely, the preliminary words, “As it is written in Isaiah,” could apply only to the first testimony.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

But because the same meaning is contained in the words of both prophets, the concise Evangelist attributed to Isaiah what Malachi said, since Isaiah was of greater authority and perhaps Malachi had learned this from him. The sending of the angel to prepare the Lord’s way, or that preparation itself, and the voice crying in [Col. 0718D] the wilderness, are John’s preaching. Isaiah also describes him more carefully, for he does not call him an angel but foretells him as one crying in the wilderness. Thus the Evangelist rightly adds at once, after the testimony from Isaiah, which he placed second: “John was in the wilderness baptizing and preaching” (ibid., 4). In saying “in the wilderness” and “preaching,” he more openly accords with Isaiah’s words: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness.”

Mark also providently, having prefaced the words, “It is written in Isaiah,” added “the prophet,” as though Isaiah, even on the testimony of Malachi (Mal. 3:1), were more properly a prophet than Malachi, who, I think, received this testimony from the prophecy of Isaiah that he had read, rather than through inspiration of the Spirit alone. I think the testimony which Matthew introduces from two prophets, Zechariah and Jeremiah, can be resolved in the same manner. He attributes all of it to Jeremiah, saying: “Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet: ‘And they received thirty silver pieces, the price of the one valued, whom they valued from the sons of Israel, and gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me’” (Matt. 27:9; Zech. 11:12). Since the first testimony is from Zechariah and the second from Jeremiah, and both are joined in the same meaning concerning the Lord, Matthew nevertheless attributes the entire passage to Jeremiah, who was of greater authority and from whom Zechariah may have received what he said.

## HELOISE’S THIRTY-EIGHTH PROBLEM

[Col. 0719B]

The testimony of the prophet Zechariah which the Lord introduces in Matthew concerning himself—“For it is written: ‘I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock shall be scattered’” (Matt. 26:31)—also creates some question. For Zechariah seems to speak this rather of a false prophet than of the Lord. For this is written there:

> “And it shall come to pass, when anyone prophesies any longer, that his father and mother who begot him shall say to him: ‘You shall not live, because you have spoken a lie in the name of the Lord.’ And his father and mother, his parents, shall pierce him when he prophesies. And it shall come to pass on that day that the prophets shall each be confounded because of his vision, when he prophesies; nor shall they cover themselves with a sackcloth mantle in order to deceive. But he shall say: ‘I am not a prophet; I am a husbandman, because Adam has been my example from my youth.’ And it shall be said to him: ‘What are these wounds in the midst of your hands?’ And he shall say: ‘I was wounded by these in the house of those who loved me.’ Sword, arise against my shepherd and against the man joined to me, says the Lord of hosts. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered” (Zech. 13:3–7). [Col. 0719C]

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

Although Zechariah said this concerning a false prophet, while the Lord applied it to himself, the Lord’s testimony taken from Zechariah is such as fits both a good and a bad shepherd. Whether a shepherd is good or bad, if he is struck by some adversity and prevented from the pastoral care entrusted to him, the flock he had gathered is scattered from his governance; dispersed, it wanders in different directions, deprived of shepherd and guide. Therefore, because persecution by adversaries causes this scattering of the flock in both good and bad shepherds, the Lord fittingly applied to his own passion what is said generally of shepherds—as though he said: “What is true generally of shepherds must also be fulfilled in me, and so it will be in me as it had been foretold concerning the false shepherd,” so that in this also he might be reckoned among the wicked, because in this respect too he was made like them. [Col. 0719D]

## HELOISE’S THIRTY-NINTH PROBLEM

[Col. 0720A]

We also ask how the words by which the Lord foretold Peter’s denial at the crowing of the cock are written so variously by the Evangelists. Matthew writes: “Jesus said to him: ‘Amen I say to you that in this night, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times’” (Matt. 26:34). But Mark, who is said to have written his Gospel at Peter’s dictation, says: “Amen I say to you that today, in this night, before the cock has given its voice twice, you will deny me three times” (Mark 14:30). Luke says: “I tell you, Peter, the cock shall not crow today until you have denied knowing me three times” (Luke 22:34). John says: “Amen, amen I say to you, the cock shall not crow until you deny me three times” (John 13:38). What, then, does such diversity of words mean, if the Lord said only one of these things to Peter once? What does Mark mean by “today, in this night,” since night is by no means within the day? And why did he add “twice” to the cock’s crowing, which the others omit?

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

It is Scripture’s custom to comprehend both day and night under the name “day,” as when we say that someone lived or sat for so many years and so many days, or was there for so many days. Thus, when Mark says “today,” he includes the night with its day. By adding “in this night,” he means not the time of night but the adversity of the impending night.

To resolve both statements about the cock’s crowing, let us suppose that the Lord first spoke to Peter with the qualification reported by Mark: before the cock should give its voice twice; and then, when Peter promised his constancy, added that he would do it even before the cock crowed. For Mark recalls Peter as overly confident and repeatedly resisting the Lord’s words almost impudently:

> “But Peter said: ‘Even if all are scandalized, yet not I.’ And Jesus said to him: ‘Amen I say to you that today, in this night, before the cock has given its voice twice, you will deny me three times.’ But he spoke all the more: ‘And if I must die with you, I will not deny you’” (Mark 14:29–31).

He who had first said that he would not be scandalized now adds something further: he says that he is even prepared to die with Christ before denying him. In answer to this greater presumption of his constancy, it is not unfitting to believe that the Lord also added something further: namely, that Peter would deny him three times even before the cock crowed, as we have said. [Col. 0720D]

But this gives rise to considerable difficulty: Mark orders Peter’s denials and the cock’s crowing in such a way that after the first denial the cock crows once, and after the other two, a second time. From this it seems impossible to maintain the statement of the other Evangelists that Peter denied him three times before the cock crowed—unless perhaps “twice,” which Mark expressly gives and thereby indicates is to be supplied, is also to be understood in their words, and unless this alone is what the Lord said. For when something is stated more precisely in one place than in another, the qualification must often be understood where it is not expressed; or what is excepted elsewhere must be carefully noted, lest falsehood confound the meaning.

Even unbelievers recognize this. Thus, when we sometimes object to Jews, “You shall not lend at interest” (Ezek. 18:8), as though they ought not lend at interest to us either, they say that “to your neighbor” must be understood, since elsewhere it is expressly stated. Likewise, although the Gospel truth says, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:3), one must understand, “or sanctified by his own passion,” since elsewhere we have a general declaration concerning martyrs, the Lord saying: “Whoever loses his life for my sake shall find it” (Matt. 10:39).

Augustine, however, in Book III of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* [Note: [Col. 0721D] *Patrologia*, vol. 34, col. 1172], resolves this difference concerning Peter’s denial [Col. 0721B] by referring Mark’s words to the utterance of the voice of the one denying, whereas what the others say refers to the purpose of his mind, already so struck and disturbed by fear that he was ready to deny a third time before the cock had crowed at all.

If someone should ask why the Lord said “three times,” rather than four or more, though Peter was similarly prepared by the greatness of his fear to do so, it seems to me that there is some reason in this number three for denial, by which every denial may be understood. Everyone who denies Christ does so either through error, or under compulsion of some fear or desire. Thus when the Lord foretells that Peter will deny him three times, he indicates that Peter is prepared for every kind of denial.

For it must not be doubted, from what Peter had already seen happen to the Lord before his first denial, that he had fallen with the others into the scandal of despair. Subsequently freed from this when the Lord looked upon him, he erased by a bitter weeping of repentance what he had committed. Nor perhaps is it absurd to say that the first cockcrow after Peter’s first denial was not natural; rather, stirred by some noise—either Peter’s leaving the courtyard or the movement of any persons walking there—a nearby cock, awakened before its hour, crowed first. Thus that first crowing did not happen naturally but was forced out by some cause. Yet the Lord did not order this without reason: immediately at Peter’s first denial, a cock immediately crowed as though rebuking Peter, and Peter nevertheless did not cease denying, so that the truth itself might appear. Therefore, when the Lord foretold that Peter would deny him three times before the cock crowed, he seems to have meant the hour of the cock’s natural crowing. Mark alone, in adding “twice,” took the cock’s natural and accidental crowing without distinction. [Col. 0721D]

## HELOISE’S FORTIETH PROBLEM

Why are only beasts and birds said to have been brought into Paradise to Adam, that he might see what he would call them, and not also reptiles of the earth, such as serpents, or water creatures, such as fish? (Gen. 2:20)

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

We rightly believe that this was done in view of a mystery. In the present Church, the continent—those who raise themselves especially to heavenly things by desire and fly upward as birds—are compared to birds. Good married persons are compared to beasts, which touch the earth in part, namely with their feet, and in part are separated from it, since they do not wallow upon it with their bodies. For one joined in marriage is divided, partly serving God and partly attending to the world because of the pressing necessities of marriage. Thus he touches the earth with his feet, that is, with the lower part of himself, because he has given himself to earthly cares through the occupation of marriage, which belongs to a more fallen life. [Col. 0722B]

Reptiles, however, which lie wholly upon the ground and can in no way raise themselves up, are the reprobate, entirely occupied with earthly desires and dwelling in the depths of vices. Of such persons it is written: “When a sinner has come into the depth of vices, he despises” (Prov. 18:13). Thus fish were never permitted to be offered in God’s sacrifice. Therefore, since only birds and walking animals, and not reptiles, were brought into Paradise, Adam is rightly said to have given them names: because from the entire people of the present Church, in which chaff is still mixed with grain, only the continent and good married persons will attain the true Paradise of the heavenly country and prove worthy of God’s calling; their names are already written in the book of life. Concerning this calling of God, the Apostle says: “Those whom he predestined, them he also called; and those whom he called, them he also justified” (Rom. 8:30). [Col. 0722C]

## HELOISE’S FORTY-FIRST PROBLEM

We ask who added, at the end of Deuteronomy (Deut. 33 and 34), the last of Moses’ five books, the account that tells of Moses’ death and what follows: whether Moses himself also said this by a prophetic spirit, so that it may be counted among his books, or whether it was afterward added by someone else.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

As Bede recalls in his commentary on Ezra, Ezra himself, who not only rewrote the Law but also, as the common tradition of the Fathers has it, rewrote the entire sequence of sacred Scripture that had likewise been consumed by fire, insofar as he thought sufficient for readers, added both this and many other things to the writings of the Old Testament. Thus we see certain things added by translators even to Gospel writings, such as this in Matthew: “Eli, Eli, lamma sabacthani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). Likewise, in the other Evangelists, who wrote not in Hebrew but in Greek, the explanation of these Hebrew words is found added with them. In Jerome’s book *On Illustrious Men* [Note: [Col. 0722D] *Patrologia*, vol. 23, cols. 716–720], where he placed himself at the end of the work, the length and end of his life were added by someone else. [Col. 0723A]

## HELOISE’S FORTY-SECOND PROBLEM

We ask whether someone can sin in doing what has been granted or even commanded to him by the Lord.

## ABAELARD’S SOLUTION

If, as is proper, this is granted to be true, we are pressed by a serious question: how married persons, whether among the old people or the new, can be said to sin in exercising carnal desire, through which they transmit original sin to their descendants. For the earlier people were constrained to beget children by the Lord’s command and by the curse of the Law pronounced upon those who left no seed in Israel. Hence he said not only to the first parents before sin: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28), but imposed this very command also upon Noah and his sons after the flood (Gen. 9:1).

Concerning the aforesaid curse of the Law, by which people were compelled to the propagation of children, Jerome says in *Against Helvidius: On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary* [Note: [Col. 0723D] *Patrologia*, vol. 23, col. 203]:

> “As long as that law remained: ‘Increase and multiply and fill the earth’; and: ‘Cursed is the barren woman who does not produce seed in Israel’ [Exod. 23:26], all men married and were married.”

Hence also Blessed Augustine says in *On the Good of Marriage* [Note: [Col. 0723D] *Patrologia*, vol. 40, col. 392]:

> “John possessed continence in deed, but Abraham in disposition alone. For at that time, when the Law following the days [Col. 0723C] of the patriarchs pronounced cursed the person who did not raise up seed in Israel, the one who could do so did not bring it forth, but nonetheless possessed it.”

The same author says to Julian in *On the Preservation of Widowhood* [Note: [Col. 0724D] Ibid., col. 436]:

> “Because I called Ruth blessed and Anna more blessed—though the former married twice, while the latter, a woman of one husband, was widowed early and lived long—do not therefore suppose yourself better than Ruth. For in prophetic times there was a different dispensation for holy women, whom obedience, not desire, compelled to marry, so that the people of God might be propagated, from whom Christ’s flesh also would be born.”

Therefore, in order that that people might be propagated, one who did not raise up seed in Israel was held accursed by the judgment of the Law. Hence holy women were inflamed not by a desire for intercourse but by the devotion to bear children, so that they are most rightly believed not to have sought intercourse if offspring could have arisen otherwise. Men were also allowed the use of several living wives. Accordingly, holy Ruth, when she lacked in her deceased husband the seed then necessary in Israel, sought another man from whom she might have it (Ruth 4:13). [Col. 0723D]

In view of this curse of the Law, which the aforesaid teacher recalls and treats as the greatest reproach of the faithful, the Law made such provision for that people that later brothers, even if they had offspring of their own by their wives, were compelled to take the wives of their earlier brothers in order to raise up seed also for those brothers, and to beget children for the dead rather than for themselves, so that it might thus absolve from the Law’s curse those who were not without offspring. [Col. 0724A]

The Lord himself also established this as a reward for observers of the Law: that none among them should remain barren, whether among human beings or livestock. For thus it is written in Deuteronomy: “If, after you have heard these judgments, you keep them, the Lord will keep you, love you, and multiply you; he will bless the fruit of your womb and of your land, your herds, and your flocks of sheep. You shall be blessed among all peoples. There shall not be among you one barren of either sex, whether among human beings or among your flocks” (Deut. 7:13). Hence we read of none of the holy Fathers as deprived of offspring, although they had barren wives, whom they took not in order to indulge the pleasure of carnal desire but to propagate the people of God, so that they might beget children not so much for themselves as for God. Such also is the saying of Tobit: “And now, Lord, you know that I take my sister not for the sake of lust, but solely for the sake of posterity, in which your name shall be blessed for ages of ages” (Tob. 8:9). With this intention Abraham, united in marriage, deserved to receive offspring from a barren wife (Gen. 16:1 ff.). So too Isaac (Gen. 25), Manoah, Samson’s father (Judg. 13), Elkanah by Hannah (1 Sam. 1:19), and Zachariah by Elizabeth (Luke 1:5 ff.) obtained the offspring they desired, lest they incur the Law’s curse or the reproach of marriage. Marriage [*matrimonium*] is so called because it is entered into for making a woman a mother of a household [*materfamilias*]. Considering this curse of the Law, Jephthah’s daughter bewailed her virginity, because, dying a virgin, she would leave no offspring in Israel (Judg. 11:38). Elizabeth rejoiced that she had been freed from this reproach, saying: “For thus has the Lord dealt with me in the days when he looked upon me, to take away my reproach among human beings” (Luke 1:25).

The doctor mentioned above, carefully considering all these matters, commends marital intercourse undertaken for children—not so much to be begotten as to be reborn in Christ—so highly that he calls it more free from sin than intercourse undertaken to avoid fornication. Yet the Apostle establishes this latter as the sole reason, strongly exhorting us to continence: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: it is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” (1 Cor. 7:2). Thus it is better that marital intercourse be rendered to God rather than ourselves: that we should aim to beget children for him rather than to provide for our own advantage. The aforesaid doctor so prefers that intention to the other that he does not at all assign to indulgence the intercourse which he entirely removes from fault, so that it should be avoided not as blameworthy but sought as praiseworthy. He also commends the good of marriage, so that, if marriages are entered for the proper reason—namely, the begetting of children—they may excuse even those acts of intercourse that do not occur with that proper intention; and he establishes that marriages are good in themselves, rather than merely as an instrument for avoiding fornication.

Accordingly, in the aforementioned work, *On the Good of Marriage*, he says:

> [Note: Col. 0725D. *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 375.] “The good of marriage, therefore, which the Lord himself confirmed in the Gospel, not only because he forbade dismissing a wife except on account of fornication, but also because he came when invited to a wedding—the reason why it is good is rightly sought. It seems to me that it is good not merely for the procreation of children, but also for that natural companionship itself which exists between the sexes.”

Likewise:

> [Note: Col. 0725D. *Ibid.*, col. 378.] “So great is that social bond of spouses that, although it is joined together for the purpose of procreation, it is not dissolved even when the very purpose of procreation fails. A man could indeed dismiss a barren wife and take another by whom he might have children; nevertheless, he is not permitted to do so: so powerful is the social bond of spouses that, although formed for the purpose of procreation, it is not dissolved even when that purpose of procreation itself is absent.”

Likewise:

> [Note: Col. 0725D. *Ibid.*, col. 380.] “We must certainly observe that God gives us certain goods which are to be sought for their own sake, such as wisdom, health, and friendship; and others which are necessary for the sake of something else, such as instruction, food and drink, sleep, marriage, and intercourse. Some of these are necessary for wisdom, as instruction; some for health, as food, drink, and sleep; some for friendship, as marriage or intercourse. For from these proceeds the propagation of the human race, in which friendly fellowship is a great good. Therefore, whoever uses these goods which are necessary for another end, but not for the purpose for which they were instituted, sins—sometimes venially, sometimes damnably. But whoever uses them for the purpose for which they were given does well.”

Likewise:

> [Note: Col. 0726D. *Ibid.*, cols. 381–382.] “It seems to me that at this time only those who do not contain themselves ought to marry, according to the statement of the same Apostle: ‘But if they do not contain themselves, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn’ (1 Cor. 7:9). Yet marriage is not sin even for them; if it were chosen as an instrument of fornication, it would be a lesser sin than fornication, but would nevertheless be sin. But what then shall we say against the most manifest declaration of the Apostle: ‘Let him do what he will; he does not sin if she marries’ (ibid., 36); and: ‘If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin’ (ibid., 28)?

> [Col. 0725D] “From this it is certainly no longer permissible to doubt that marriage is not sin. The Apostle therefore does not permit marriage by way of indulgence. For who would not see that it is utterly absurd to say that those to whom pardon is granted have not sinned? Rather, he permits by way of indulgence that intercourse which takes place through incontinence, not solely for the sake of procreation, and sometimes for no purpose of procreation at all. Marriage does not compel this act to occur, but obtains forgiveness for it, provided that it is not so excessive as to hinder the times which ought to be set apart for prayer, nor altered into that use which is contrary to nature. The Apostle could not be silent about this latter when he spoke of the excessive corruptions of unclean and impious human beings.

> “For intercourse necessary for begetting is blameless, and it alone is properly marital intercourse. But intercourse which goes beyond this necessity obeys not reason but lust. Yet for one spouse to render this to the other, though not to demand it, lest the other commit damnable sin by fornication, pertains to the married condition. If, however, both are subject to such desire, they do something not wholly belonging to marriage. Nevertheless, if in their union they love more what is honorable than what is dishonorable—that is, what belongs to marriage more than what does not belong to marriage—then, on the Apostle’s authority, this is granted them by way of indulgence.”

Likewise:

> [Note: Col. 0726D. *Ibid.*, col. 382.] “That natural use, when it exceeds the marriage compact—that is, the necessity of propagation—becomes venial with one’s wife, damnable with a prostitute. The use contrary to nature is done execrably with a prostitute, but more execrably with a wife. So great is the force of the Creator’s ordering and the order of creation that, among things permitted for use, even when measure is exceeded, one or even a rare excess is far more tolerable than among things not permitted. Therefore, in a permitted matter, a spouse’s immoderation must be tolerated lest lust break out into a matter not permitted.

> “Hence even the most frequent intercourse with one’s wife sins far less than even the rarest intercourse in fornication. But when a man wishes to use a woman’s sexual organ for a purpose not granted to it, the wife is more shameful if she permits this to be done to herself than if she permits it to be done to another woman. Therefore, marital honor consists in chastity directed toward procreation and faithfulness in rendering the carnal debt. This is the work of marriage; this the Apostle defends from every charge, saying: ‘If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she does not sin’; and, ‘Let him do what he will: he does not sin if she marries’ (1 Cor. 7:28). But an immoderate advance in demanding the debt from either sex is granted to spouses by way of indulgence, for the reasons stated above.

> “When, therefore, he says, ‘She who is unmarried thinks of the things of the Lord, that she may be holy both in body and spirit’ (ibid., 34), this is not to be understood as though we should think that a chaste Christian wife is not holy in body. For to all the faithful it was said: ‘Do you not know that your bodies are the temple within you of the Holy Spirit whom you have from God?’ (1 Cor. 6:19). The bodies of married persons also are holy when they preserve faithfulness to one another and to the Lord. The same Apostle bears witness that not even an unbelieving spouse hinders the holiness of either one, but rather that the holiness of a wife benefits an unbelieving husband, or the holiness of a husband benefits an unbelieving wife, saying: ‘For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified in the faithful wife, and the unbelieving woman has been sanctified through the faithful husband’ (1 Cor. 7:14). Therefore that was said with reference to the greater holiness of unmarried women than of married women.”

Likewise:

> [Note: Col. 0726D. *Ibid.*, col. 385.] “The bond of marriage remains even if offspring, for the sake of which it was begun, does not follow because of manifest barrenness; so that, even when spouses know they will not have children, they are nevertheless not permitted to separate, even for the sake of children, and unite themselves to others. If they do this, they commit adultery with those to whom they unite themselves; yet they remain spouses. Certainly, among the ancient Fathers it was lawful, with the wife’s consent, to bring in another woman, so that common children might be born through the intercourse of one man, yet be another’s by legal right and authority. Whether this is also lawful now, I would not rashly say. For there is not now the necessity of propagation which then existed, when even childbearing spouses were permitted to take additional wives for the sake of more abundant posterity; this certainly is not lawful now.”

Likewise:

> [Note: Col. 0727D. *Patrologia*, vol. XL, cols. 385–386.] “What food is to the preservation of human life, intercourse is to the preservation of the race; and neither is without carnal pleasure. Yet that pleasure, moderated and restrained by temperance within natural use, cannot be lust. What unlawful food is in sustaining life, fornication or adulterous intercourse is in seeking offspring. What unlawful food is in the luxury of belly and throat, unlawful intercourse is in lust that seeks no offspring. And what a certain more immoderate appetite is in lawful food, that venial intercourse is among spouses.

> “Therefore, just as it is preferable to die of hunger rather than eat food sacrificed to idols, so it is preferable to die childless than to seek offspring by unlawful intercourse. Yet wherever human beings are born, if they do not follow their parents’ vices and rightly worship God, they will be upright and saved. For human seed, from whatever person it comes, is God’s creature; it will be bad for those who use it badly, but it will never itself be evil. And just as good children of adulterers furnish no defense of adultery, so bad children of married persons furnish no charge against marriage.”

The same author says above:

> [Note: Col. 0727D. *Ibid.*, col. 377.] “There are men so incontinent that they do not spare even pregnant wives. Whatever married persons do between themselves that is immodest, shameless, or filthy is a vice of human beings, not a fault of marriage. Even in the more immoderate demand for the carnal debt—which the Apostle does not prescribe to them by command but permits by indulgence, so that they may unite even apart from the purpose of procreation—if depraved habits urge them to such intercourse, marriage nevertheless protects them from adultery or fornication. For this is not allowed on account of marriage, but forgiven on account of marriage.

> “Married persons therefore owe each other not only the fidelity of sexual union for the sake of begetting children, which is the first fellowship of the human race in this mortal condition, but also a certain mutual servitude in bearing one another’s weakness so as to avoid unlawful intercourse. Thus, even if perpetual continence pleases one spouse, it cannot be undertaken without the other’s consent. For this reason also a wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise, a husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Consequently, what he seeks from the marriage, or she from her husband, not for the begetting of children but because of weakness and incontinence, they must not deny to one another, lest through this they fall into damnable corruptions, Satan tempting them through the incontinence of both or of either of them. For marital intercourse for the sake of begetting is without fault.”

Likewise:

> [Note: Col. 0727D. *Ibid.*, col. 382.] “To render the marital debt is no crime; but to demand it beyond the necessity of begetting is a venial fault.”

The same author, in the first book of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, addressed to Count Valerian:

> [Note: Col. 0727D. *Patrologia*, vol. XLIV, col. 415.] “But who would dare to say that God’s gift is sin? Soul and body, and whatever goods of soul and body are naturally implanted even in sinners, are gifts of God, because God, not they themselves, made these things. Of the things they do, it has been said that ‘everything which is not from faith is sin’ (Rom. 14:23). Far be it, therefore, that one be called truly chaste who does not preserve marital fidelity to his wife for the sake of the true God. The union of male and female for the purpose of begetting, then, is the natural good of marriage. But one uses this good badly when one’s intention lies in the pleasure of lust, not in the will to propagate.”

> [Note: Col. 0728D. *Ibid.*, col. 419.] “With this intention of heart, one who possesses one’s own vessel—that is, one’s spouse—does not, without doubt, possess it in the disease of desire, as does a nation that does not know God, but in sanctification and honor, as do believers who hope in God. For a human being uses, rather than is conquered by, that evil of concupiscence when he curbs and restrains it as it rages in disordered or unseemly motions; nor does he relax and employ it except with concern for offspring, so that he may carnally beget those who are to be spiritually reborn, not so that he may subject spirit to flesh in shameful servitude.”

Likewise, concerning the marriage of Joseph and Mary:

> [Note: Col. 0728D. *Ibid.*, cols. 421–422.] “Every good of marriage was fulfilled in those parents of Christ: offspring, fidelity, sacrament. We recognize the offspring as the Lord Jesus himself; the fidelity, because there was no adultery; the sacrament, because there was no divorce. Only marital intercourse was absent, because it could not occur in flesh of sin without that concupiscence of the flesh which follows from sin. He who was to be without sin willed to be conceived without it, not in flesh of sin but in the likeness of flesh of sin, in order thereby to teach that all flesh born from intercourse is flesh of sin, since the only flesh not born from it was not flesh of sin. Although marital intercourse undertaken with the intention of begetting is not itself sin, because the good will of the mind leads the bodily pleasure which follows, rather than following it; nor is human choice drawn under sin’s dominion, when the wound of sin is rightly directed toward the use of begetting.”

Likewise, concerning the Apostle’s words, “But this I say by way of indulgence, not by command” (1 Cor. 7:6):

> [Note: Col. 0728D. *Ibid.*, col. 423.] “Wherever pardon is to be granted, it cannot reasonably be denied that there is some fault. Therefore, since intercourse undertaken with the intention of begetting is not blameworthy, and properly belongs to marriage, what does the Apostle grant by way of indulgence except that spouses, because they do not contain themselves, demand the carnal debt of one another not from the will to propagate but for the pleasure of lust? Yet this pleasure becomes blameworthy not on account of marriage but receives pardon on account of marriage. Thus marriage is praiseworthy here also, because it causes even what does not belong to it to be forgiven on its account.

> “Nor is intercourse, in which concupiscence is served, so performed that the offspring demanded by marriage is prevented. Yet it is one thing to have intercourse only from the will to beget—which involves no fault—and another to seek carnal pleasure in intercourse, but not on account of one’s spouse—which involves venial fault.”

Likewise, in the second book:

> [Note: Col. 0729B. *Patrologia*, vol. XLIV, col. 457.] “We do not condemn bread and wine on account of the luxurious and the drunken, any more than we condemn gold on account of the covetous and the avaricious. Accordingly, neither do we condemn the honorable union of spouses on account of the shameful lust of their bodies. The former could have existed without any preceding commission of sin, and married persons would not have been ashamed of it. The latter was forced forth after sin, and they were compelled, in their confusion, to cover it.

> “Hence, even for later married persons who use this evil well and lawfully, there remains in such activity the avoidance of human sight, and thus the acknowledgment that what is shameful is shameful, although no one ought to be ashamed of what is good. Thus these two things are indicated: the good of the praiseworthy union from which children are begotten, and the evil of shameful lust through which those who are begotten must be reborn lest they be condemned. Therefore, one who has intercourse lawfully with shameful lust uses an evil well; but one who does so unlawfully uses an evil badly. It more rightly receives the name of evil than of good, because both good and evil persons are ashamed of it.

> “And we believe more rightly the one who says, ‘I know that no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh’ (Rom. 7:18), than the person who calls that good which, if he is ashamed of it, he confesses to be evil, and, if he is not ashamed, adds the worse evil of shamelessness. We therefore rightly said that the good of marriage cannot be accused on account of the original evil derived from it, just as the evil of adulterers cannot be excused on account of the natural good born from it. For human nature, which is born whether from marriage or adultery, is God’s work; if it were evil, it ought not to be begotten; if it had no evil, it would not need to be reborn.”

# PART THREE OF THE WORKS OF PETER ABAELARD: THEOLOGICAL AND PHILOSOPHICAL WRITINGS

[Col. 0729]

# EXPOSITION OF THE HEXAEMERON

(Edited by D. Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. V, col. 1362, from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Michael-at-the-Peril-of-the-Sea.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATION

Among the passages of Sacred Scripture more difficult to understand, the ancient Fathers of the Church especially enumerate three, the reading of which the Jews permitted only to those skilled in the Law: namely, the beginning of Genesis, the Song of Songs, and Ezekiel’s prophecy. Hence arose in the first centuries the remarkable zeal to explain and elucidate these by commentaries. Jerome testifies in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapters 37, 48, and 61, that Rhodon, Tatian’s disciple, Candidus, and Hippolytus in particular devoted their labor to this task—to say nothing for the moment of Basil, bishop of Caesarea, and Ambrose, bishop of Milan, all of whom undertook to explain the beginning of Genesis in some distinctive work.

Following their example, Peter Abaelard composed the following *Exposition of the Hexaemeron* according to a threefold sense: literal, moral, and allegorical. It is not sufficiently clear at what time he undertook this work, written at the request of Heloise, to whom he could refuse nothing. We judge, however, that he undertook it after his reconciliation with Saint Bernard, when he had already become a monk of Cluny. For in recounting the philosophers’ opinion concerning the soul of the world, the stars, and the planets, he no longer interprets it as concerning the Holy Spirit, as he had done in his *Theology*. But at whatever time this *Exposition* was written, one delights to admire in it Abaelard’s remarkable genius and learning.

Moreover, among the works hitherto published under his name, and those published here by us, we found in an old manuscript codex of the monastery of Blessed Mary of Fontaines in the diocese of Tours Abaelard’s *Elucidarium*. In the Clairvaux codex this work bears the name of Angeldus of Mont-le-Lion, and it was published among the spurious works of Saint Anselm.

# ABAELARD’S PREFACE

[Col. 0731]

[Col. 0731A] Those learned in Sacred Scripture have judged three places in the Old Testament to be more difficult to understand: the beginning of Genesis, according to the history itself of the divine operation; the Song of Songs; and Ezekiel’s prophecy, especially its first vision concerning the living creatures and wheels, and its final vision concerning the building established on the mountain. Hence, they say, the Hebrews instituted that the exposition of these writings, because of their excessive difficulty, should be entrusted only to mature minds among the elders. Origen likewise recalls this in the first homily on the Song of Songs, saying:

> “They say that the Hebrews also observe that, unless a person has reached a perfect and mature age, he is not permitted to hold this book in his hands. But we have received this further observance from them: among them all the Scriptures are delivered by teachers to children, while four books are reserved until the end—namely, the beginning of Genesis, in which the creation of the world is described; the beginning of the prophet Ezekiel, in which the cherubim are discussed; its conclusion also, in which the building of the Temple is contained; and this book of the Song of Songs.”

Hence also Jerome writes in the prologue to his *Exposition on Ezekiel*:

> “I shall undertake the prophet Ezekiel, whose difficulty is proved by the tradition of the Hebrews. For unless a person among them has completed the age for priestly ministry, that is, thirty years, he is not permitted to read either the beginning of Genesis, the Song of Songs, or the beginning and end of this volume, so that the full span of human nature may attain perfect knowledge and mystical understandings.”

[Col. 0731C] By entreating you ask, and by asking you entreat, sister Heloise, once dear in the world, now dearest in Christ, that I apply myself all the more eagerly to expounding these matters because their meaning is acknowledged to be more difficult, and that I render this spiritual service to you and your spiritual daughters. Therefore, as you ask me, I ask you: because you compel me to this task by your request, obtain for me effectiveness by praying to God. And because, as the saying goes, one must begin from the head, may your prayers assist me more abundantly at the beginning of Genesis, in proportion as its difficulty is acknowledged to exceed that of the others, as the very scarcity of expositions bears witness.

For although many have composed many mystical or moral explanations of Genesis, among us the penetrating genius of blessed Augustine alone has undertaken here to explain the history. He judged it so difficult that what he said there he advanced rather as opinion than as an asserted judgment, investigating matters as doubtful rather than determining them as certain—attending, as it were, to Aristotle’s advice: “Perhaps it is difficult to make confident declarations about such matters unless they have often been examined; but it will not be useless to doubt concerning each particular.”

Accordingly, the aforesaid doctor, intending to revise his twelve books *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, says in the second book of his *Retractions*:

> [Note: Col. 0731C. *Patrologia*, vol. XXXII, col. 640.] “In this work more things have been asked than found; and of those things which have been found, fewer have been established; the rest are set forth as matters still requiring investigation.”

But since the statements of this work also appear so obscure to you that even the exposition itself is judged to need exposition, you demand my own opinion as well in explaining the aforesaid beginning of Genesis. Know that I now undertake this exposition at the urgent insistence of your prayers in such a way that, wherever you see me fail, you should expect from me that apostolic excuse: “I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Cor. 12:11).

# THE EXPOSITION OF THE HEXAEMERON BEGINS

[Col. 0731]

[Col. 0731D] Therefore, as we investigate the immeasurable abyss of Genesis’ depth by a threefold exposition—historical, moral, and mystical—let us invoke that Spirit at whose dictation these things were written, so that he who granted the prophet the words may himself open their meaning to us.

First, then, insofar as he himself assents—or rather, grants—let us establish the truth of the event as a kind of historical root. Desiring to draw a carnal people to divine worship, the prophet, who was about to give it the institutions of the former Testament as still crude and undisciplined, first admonishes them to obey God as creator and disposer of all things, through consideration of his bodily works [read: “works”] [lacuna] in the excellent creation and ordering of the world itself. He sets forth these things in careful narration from the world’s very beginning down to his own time.

Accordingly, we rightly assign as the subject matter of this work that creation and ordering of the world which we have mentioned—that is, the grace itself which acted in the world’s creation and divine ordering. Concerning this operation, which leads us to knowledge of the Maker, the Apostle says: “His invisible things are understood and seen from the creation of the world through the things which have been made,” etc. (Rom. 1:20). For whoever wishes to understand whether an artisan is good or skillful in his work ought to consider not the artisan himself but his works. Thus God, who is invisible and incomprehensible in himself, provides us with our first knowledge of himself from the greatness of his works, since all human knowledge arises from the senses.

Moses carefully considering this, and addressing that carnal people devoted to bodily senses and not endowed with spiritual understanding, resolved to write this Old Testament in five books according to the number of the five senses, beginning with the beginning of divine creation. In doing so he followed the natural order; hence we rightly assign this very divine operation as the subject matter of this prophet.

[Col. 0733B] The intention is that which we set forth above: by this narration and teaching to draw the still carnal people to divine worship at least through visible works, so that human beings may thereby understand how great an obedience they owe God, who created them in his own image, placed them in Paradise, and set them over the other creatures, as over all things made for their sake, as it is written: “You have subjected all things under his feet,” etc. (Ps. 8:8). Even after their sin, when expelled from Paradise, he did not abandon them to deprivation of his benefits. Rather, now correcting them through hardships, now drawing them through kindnesses, now instructing them by the Law, now confirming them by miracles, now frightening them by threats, now attracting them by promises, he does not cease with the greatest concern to invite them to pardon. Moses thus began his careful narrative of all these things, as we have said, from the world’s beginning down to his own time.

## ON THE WORK OF THE FIRST DAY

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” By the names “heaven” and “earth,” I think that the four elements are here understood, from which all other bodies are composed as from a material first principle. By “heaven” he means the two light elements, namely fire and air. But he generally calls “earth” the other two, which are heavy. For we call heaven both aerial—as in the words, “the birds of heaven”—and ethereal, which is fiery. Hence he does not incongruously name both air and fire “heaven” here. The ethereal heaven also exists, in which the purer fire is customarily called heaven in the proper sense. Therefore the name “heaven,” because the purer the fire, the lighter its nature, is rightly understood here to stand for the two light elements, fire and air, as stated. Conversely, by “earth,” whose nature is most heavy and weighty, he denotes both earth itself and the water adjoining it. Thus he declares that God made these four elements, as the first principles of all other bodies, in the beginning.

The phrase “in the beginning” is as if he said: before all those things which he subsequently enumerates, and whose completion he afterward also mentions: “Thus the heavens were completed,” etc. (Gen. 2:1). “In the beginning” means at the beginning of the works that follow, as if he said: at the beginning of the world—that is, before he made anything of the things belonging to the world. For angels, since they are incorporeal natures, are not included among worldly creatures, as are human beings, of whom the Philosopher speaks in the third book of the *Topics*: “The world,” he says, “is governed by Providence; but human beings are part of the world; therefore human affairs are governed by Providence.”

It can also be understood thus: “In the beginning he created these things,” as if to say that the elements named were the original cause from which the other bodies were to be made. Hence the elements are aptly called, as it were, “nourishments” [*alimenta*], because all other things derive their being from them, just as all living things have life and subsistence through the nourishment of food.

It was fittingly said of the elements, however, “he created” rather than “he formed,” because “to create” properly means to bring something from non-being to being in such a way that it has no pre-existing matter and did not first subsist in any state of nature. But when something is made from matter already prepared by the addition of form, it is rightly said to be formed, as in what follows: “Thus he formed man from the slime of the earth” (Gen. 2:7); and again: “Therefore, when all the living creatures of the earth had been formed from the ground” (ibid., 19). For when pre-existing matter is indicated—as when “from the ground” is prefaced, because something was being formed into a particular shape—it is most correctly said to be formed.

“Now the earth was empty and void.” Since this discussion especially concerns the creation of man, who was to be formed from earth and to live upon earth, and since the prophet, as we have said, intends to draw humanity to God’s worship, he turns his pen toward earthly works, passing over the creation of the heavenly and higher nature—that is, the angels—lest, perhaps, if he investigated it and displayed its excellence to the praise of its Creator, he might draw humanity less toward the love of God, when it saw another nature set above itself.

Having therefore stated in advance that the earth was empty and void at its creation, he explains through the works of the later days how divine operation supplied for its emptiness and void. He calls the earth empty of fruit, which it had not yet produced; void of an inhabitant, not only of humanity but of every kind whatsoever of living creature, since no dwelling, whether terrestrial or aquatic, yet contained any living creatures. Both dwellings, as we have said, he includes under the designation “earth.” Thus “earth,” in the sense explained, means the lower region of the world composed of the heavy elements.

It should be noted that, when he says, “But the earth was empty and void,” he implies through the adversative conjunction added that heaven is not to be understood in the same manner, since angels are understood to have been created either before heaven itself or together with heaven. They are called, as it were, heavenly inhabitants. Thus, although the prophet does not relate their creation, he nevertheless touches upon it in passing, lest anything belonging to his narrative of divine works appear to be lacking.

“And darkness was upon the face of the abyss.” By “abyss,” that is, “depth,” he means the whole confused, not-yet-distinguished mass of the elements, such as it was later to become. Some philosophers or poets called this confusion *chaos*, since what is deep is less visible and open to sight. Thus he calls “abyss” that mass of elements not yet separated into ordered parts, so as to be open to our knowledge or vision even if humanity had already been created; and he uses “face,” by which each thing is recognized, to mean knowledge. Therefore the face of the abyss was covered by darkness: that is, knowledge of that mass was impeded by its original confusion, so that it did not at all present itself as visible, nor did any usefulness of it yet appear to the Creator’s praise.

“And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.” The Hebrew has: “was fluttering over the face of the waters.” One translation, however, has “was warming the waters”; another, “was borne over the waters,” as does the present version before us, which first calls for explanation. So far as it appears to us, by the name “waters” too he includes that fluid and unstable mass, not yet stabilized by a definite arrangement of its parts. Over it the Spirit of the Lord was borne, because divine grace was disposing it, as subject to his command, in order to order it, so that it might no longer be empty or void, dark or fluid.

For what is the Spirit of God except his goodness, by participation in which all things are good? Because this goodness of God did not yet appear in that confusion of the elements, it was said rather to be borne over it than to be within it, because it had not yet acted in it so that the mass might show forth some usefulness. Hence it is not said in its commendation, “God saw that it was good,” as it is in the commendation of the remaining works. He also carefully says, “was borne over the waters,” rather than “was,” as though showing that it was moving through these things, in order to bring them from darkness into light, not abiding in them, since he did not intend to leave them in this confusion.

Another translation, as we have said, reads: “And the Spirit of the Lord brooded over the waters,” in the manner of a bird which sits upon an egg in order to warm and bring it to life; hence we rightly call the Holy Spirit the giver of life. This confused mass is aptly compared to an egg not yet quickened or formed, in which, as in an egg containing four things within itself, the four elements are contained. For an egg has an outer shell; then, inside, a membrane—that is, a sort of cartilage adhering to the shell; then the white; and finally that central portion of the egg, as it were its marrow. This central part, which we call the yolk, is like earth in the world; the white, like water adhering to earth; [Col. 0736A] the membrane, like air; and the shell, like fire. Now the chick is formed and born in the egg from its yolk and white; and this book recounts that all living creatures are produced and formed from earth or water.

Therefore, just as a bird sitting upon an egg and applying itself to it with intense affection warms it by its own heat and, as has been said, forms and gives life to the chick, so divine goodness—which is understood to be the Holy Spirit, and is properly called the love of God, which, poured into the hearts of the faithful, makes them burn toward God and thus renders them warm by a certain warming of its own—is said to preside over that still fluid and unstable mass, as it were over waters, in order later to bring living creatures forth from it. For it held that mass, as it were, beneath itself—that is, in its own power—so that later it might form from it man and the other living creatures [Col. 0736B] as a chick from an egg, and give them life once formed.

It should be noted, however, that where we say, “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” the Hebrew has *ruauh* for “spirit,” a word which denotes both “spirit” and “wind.” And where we say, “was borne over the waters,” the Hebrew reads, “was fluttering over the face of the waters,” as we also mentioned above. The same verb for fluttering is found elsewhere in the same prophet, where it is said: “Like an eagle provoking her young to fly and fluttering over them” (Deut. XXXII.11). Thus, the statement that the wind of God was already fluttering over the face of the waters—that is, stirring them—may perhaps, in its literal sense, mean that a wind sent by God into the waters [Col. 0736C] was agitating upward their upper portion, which in every mass of waters is admittedly always lighter, so that they might later be held suspended and made firm.

For when he later says, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters,” and again, “He divided the waters which were under the firmament from those which were above” (ibid., 7), he suggests that they had already been divided, but had not yet been made firm. Nor should you be surprised that Moses here calls a wind sent by the Lord into the waters “the Spirit of the Lord,” since this same prophet, as though accustomed to this usage, says elsewhere: “By the spirit of thy wrath the waters were gathered together” (Exod. XV.8); and again: “Thy spirit blew, and the sea covered them” (ibid., 10). Nor is it strange that a wind sent by the Lord should be called his spirit, since even an evil spirit, when permitted by him to rage, is sometimes called an evil spirit of the Lord, as we read in Saul.

The wind sent into the waters and raising them up so that they covered the whole world aptly prefigured our regeneration from water and Spirit. For the Holy Spirit set this element above and before the others in dignity, by granting it this benefit of his grace: that all the sins of whatever persons are washed by the water of baptism should be so covered or blotted out that no satisfaction by bodily punishment would remain.

If someone should also refer this to the natural order of the elements, saying that air is surrounded by water, just as water then wholly surrounded the earth, or as heaven surrounds the air, and that the spirit then fluttered over the waters in the sense that, by its mobile lightness, it surrounded them, [Col. 0737A] this interpretation too seems consonant with the natural order of things—unless perhaps the difficulty is that, when “spirit” is said of air, “of the Lord” is added, whereas this is said of neither earth nor the other elements.
