But perhaps the prophet wrote it all the more carefully because he grasped the event as both historical and mystical more perfectly. “The Spirit of the Lord was fluttering over the waters,” then, is as though he said: “A wind was blowing among them, bearing a type of the Holy Spirit, who would by his grace make the waters fruitful for baptism and, as it were, breathe this benefit into them.”

When, therefore, the prophet had first made manifest mention of heaven and earth, saying, “He created heaven and earth,” and had thereby plainly included two elements—namely fire and earth—especially since by the names “heaven” and “earth” one ordinarily understands only the earthly element and the fiery element from which are formed the outermost regions of the world, that is, the ethereal regions properly called heaven, he next took care to express the other two, namely water and air. Though he had not then explicitly said that these were created as he had said of the former—although, as we have said, they too are included in those names—he now took care to distinguish them openly, in order carefully to declare that the entire constitution of the world consists in these four.

God also said: “Let there be light.” The saying of God himself is the Word of the Father, understood as his coeternal Wisdom, in which all things are first ordered before they are completed in act, as it is written: [Col. 0737C] “who made the things that are to be”: he made them, I say, by ordering them before he made them by bringing the work to completion. As there is a word of the mouth, so too there is said to be a word of the heart, according to the text: “They spoke with heart and heart” (Ps. XI.3).

Therefore, when the prophet, in the making of the various created things, prefixes “God said,” and immediately joins the result to the saying, declaring, “And it was done,” he shows that God created all things in the Word—that is, in his Wisdom—meaning that he did nothing suddenly or rashly, but all things rationally and providently. Thus the Psalmist also says: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. XXXII.9), that is, with reason and providence going before, he created or ordered all things. Elsewhere, making clearer that this Word is not audible and passing [Col. 0737D] but intelligible and abiding, he says: “Who made the heavens in understanding” (Ps. CXXXV.5)—first establishing them within himself by reason, then completing them in act. It is as though there were a twofold creation of all things: one first in the ordering of divine providence itself, the other in the work.

In accordance with these two creations, philosophers also maintained that there are two worlds, one intelligible and the other sensible. This does not conflict with evangelical teaching, if we attend more to the truth of the thought than to the strict propriety of the terms. For it is written in the Gospel concerning this very Word of God: “What was made in him was life” (John I.3). Yet the philosophers’ calling this conception of divine providence itself “the intelligible world” seems greatly to depart from ecclesiastical usage. Hence Augustine, in the first book of the *Retractations* [Note: [Col. 0737D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXII, col. 388.], says:

> “I am displeased,” he says, “that I declared philosophers not endowed with true piety to have shone with the light of virtue; and that I so commended two worlds, one sensible and the other intelligible, as though the Lord himself had intended to signify this also, because he did not say, ‘My kingdom is not of the world,’ but, ‘My kingdom is not of this world’ (John XVIII.36).”

Likewise, Plato himself did not err in saying that there is an intelligible world, provided that we attend not to a term quite unused in ecclesiastical custom for that matter, but to the thing itself. For he called “the intelligible world” [Col. 0738B] the very reason by which God made the world. Whoever denies that such reason exists is consequently compelled to say that God made what he made irrationally. The same Augustine, in Book XVI of *The City of God*, carefully describes this inward speech of God and the intellectual, not audible, Word [Note: [Col. 0738D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, col. 484.]:

> “God’s speech before his work is the unchangeable reason of his work: it has no sounding, clamorous, passing noise, but abides there eternally and acts in time.”

Therefore, “God said: Let there be light; and light was made” means that, just as he had first ordered in the word of his mind, or decreed by his own reason that it ought to be done, so he afterwards completed it in act. We understand this light, which removed the aforesaid darkness, as the distinction of the works that follow. By this distinction that confused mass, which had not yet made itself visible, which could not be known as fit for any use, nor reveal from itself what it had been created for, was brought into such an ordering that it now made itself wholly fit for them. “And light was made,” that is, God completed in act what he had ordered in the word of his mind, removing by the light of the ensuing distinction those darknesses of confusion of which we have spoken. [Col. 0738C]

Nor must it be passed over that, above, in the creation of heaven and earth, it is not written, “God said, and it was so,” as we see written in the subsequent works one by one; rather, God was silent at first and began to speak with the light. This is fitting. For the Lord seems to speak by commanding, “Let it be,” and the creature subject to him serves, however irrational or brute it may be, as though it had heard and understood his command. Jeremiah likewise recalls this, saying: “He perfected the earth and filled it with cattle; he called it, and it heard in trembling. The stars gave light in their watches and rejoiced; they were called and said, ‘Here we are,’ and shone with gladness” (Baruch III.32).

How, then, when matter had not yet been created and did not yet exist—so that there was nothing to which a command could be addressed—could words of command fittingly be uttered? Moreover, that saying of God, that is, his Word, [Col. 0739A] is the one of whom it is written: “He was the true light that enlightens every human being,” etc. (John I.9). The prophet rightly first displayed it then, when he came to the light of God’s works, through which light of works God in some way first began to speak to humanity and reveal himself, as the Apostle plainly teaches: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that were made,” etc. (Rom. I.20).

Thus, while that confused mass neither presented itself to human sight or knowledge nor appeared suitable for any use, whether to an angel or to a human being, had one already been created, God is shown as though silent, because he had not yet done in it anything through which he could speak—that is, instruct human reason and impart some knowledge of his excellence.

It should also be noted that, in this very beginning of Genesis, the prophet carefully expressed the foundation of our faith concerning the unity of God and the Trinity. When he said “the Spirit of the Lord,” he plainly distinguished both the person of the Holy Spirit and that of the Father, from whom, as blessed Augustine states, the Spirit proceeds principally. When he added, “God said,” he plainly expressed, together with the Father himself, God’s saying—that is, his Word, who is the Son. No one of sound mind can be so foolish as to suppose this saying bodily, since divinity is not bodily, cannot speak bodily, and there was not yet anyone present to whom it would be necessary for him to speak bodily. Where we say, “God created,” [Col. 0739C] the Hebrew has *Eloim* for “God,” indicating a plurality of divine persons. For *El* is singular and is interpreted “God,” whereas *Eloim* is plural, by which we understand the diversity of persons, each of whom is God.

Why then is it said, “Eloim created,” rather than “they created”—that is, why is a singular verb joined to a plural noun? So that it might be suggested that in those three persons we are to understand not three creators but only one. Thus, in saying “Eloim created,” by which he taught that the divine persons cooperate together, he established that the works of the Trinity are undivided. And when, as we have said, he later distinguished the persons of the Father, the Spirit, and the Word, he defined wherein that Trinity consists.

[Col. 0739D] It should be noted that, for what we say, “Let there be light, and light was made,” the Hebrew reads, “Let light be, and light was”; and similarly throughout what follows, wherever we have, “God said, Let this be, and it was so,” the Hebrew reads, “Let this be, and it was so.” Perhaps these words express the greatest swiftness of the divine operation. When something is made that does not yet exist, some delay in making may occur; but when it is said, “Let it be, and it was,” the thing is shown to be completed with no delay intervening.

“And God saw the light, that it was good.” Whenever it is said after the completion of God’s various works that God saw that it was good, it is as though it were said: “He understood that nothing had been made there by error which needed correction.” It also suggests that something had become perfect in comparison with the preceding imperfection. God fittingly approves the light—that is, the distinction of the works—because through it he manifests to us the praise of his excellence; for praise of a work reflects upon its maker. Thus also, concerning what he does for humanity, when he is said to see that these things are good, I think this can be understood most correctly only in the sense that he orders them so that he makes us too see that they are good, just as Abraham says: “Now I know that you fear the Lord” (Gen. XXII.12), that is, “I have caused it to be known.” Hence it is that the works of the second day—namely, the suspension of the upper waters—are said not to be approved, since he does not make us praise that whose rationale or usefulness [Col. 0740B] we do not perceive.

“And he divided the light from the darkness.” That is, by his operation he distinguished the perfect from the imperfect, and the ordered from the confused. Above, when he said, “And God said: Let there be light, and light was made,” he showed that light was made at God’s command. But here, when he says, “And he divided the light from the darkness,” he also shows that this distinction of the works, which he calls light, was made by God himself, so that he may be understood as both Creator and Former of matter, and so that all praise may be ascribed to him alike for the creation of matter and the formation of the works.

“And he called the light day, and the darkness night.” That is, he made it worthy of this designation: namely, that the accomplished distinction of the works should be called “day” by analogy, and that preceding confusion should be called “night,” which above was also called “darkness.”

“And evening and morning were one day.” Here he calls “one day” the entire completion of those works of God—first held in the mind and then completed in act on the sixth day. He calls the evening of this whole period, which he here calls one day, the entire operation of God insofar as it previously lay hidden in his mind before it emerged into light through its effect. Conversely, he calls this same operation morning insofar as, afterwards completed in act, it made itself visible. Thus he calls the conception of the divine mind in the disposition of the future work “evening,” but “morning” [Col. 0740D] the operation of that conception itself and the effect of the divine disposition, completed in six days.

Therefore, when it is said, “And evening and morning were one day,” it is as though it were said: “The operation which was first hidden in the mind of God, as in evening, and that which afterwards broke forth into light through the effect of the works are the same.” That is to say: as he first conceived it in mind, so he afterwards completed it in act, according to what is written: “What was made in him was life” (John I.3). For God brings forth individual things from a kind of bosom of his secret when he displays in act what he had first conceived in mind; and the work does not differ from its conception, because what is disposed in the mind is completed in act.

Since both evening and morning, as stated, comprehend the whole sum of divine works—those conceived in mind as well as those displayed in act—it is rightly said “one day” rather than “the first day.” For since it comprehends all the works, there is no day of works in relation to which this could be called first. This unity denotes the great harmony and correspondence of the divine works, namely, in this one day the entire sum of the different works. The prophet himself explains this one great day—that is, the whole period of those divine works—when he says later: “These are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, in the day in which the Lord made heaven and earth and every shrub of the field,” etc. (Gen. II.4).

But when he subsequently speaks of the second and third day, etc., he understands by “the first day” that on which heaven and earth were created, as was said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” on which day also light was created or divided from darkness. For to the works of the first day belongs only the creation of heaven and earth, which must be assigned to the first day; and it is in reference to that first day that the second or third day is so called. Thus “in the beginning he created” is as though he said: “On the first day,” that is, before the other works which follow. For matter had to be created before it was formed. If, however, someone wishes to refer the statement “And evening and morning were one day” only to the work of the first day, just as it is referred to the works of the other days, nothing prevents this. For God also had matter itself, just like things made from matter, first in his mind, as in evening, [Col. 0741C] before producing it in morning by creation.

## ON THE SECOND DAY

God also said. It should be noted that in these divine sayings our translation sometimes has “God also said,” sometimes “But God said,” or “God said moreover,” or “God said also”—all of which mean the same thing—and sometimes, as above, “And God said”; whereas the Hebrew truth everywhere has “And God said.” This Hebrew wording accords particularly well with our foregoing exposition of this passage: namely, that “And God said” should be written rather than “God also said.” Since, as we have said, the distinction of all the works that follow is understood in the light that was made, this conjunction “also,” properly signifying some addition to the saying, ought not to have been used here; for the operation of this day, like that of the others, was already comprehended in the light that was made.

Therefore, when the Hebrew says “And God said,” so that the manner in which this light was made may be distinguished, it should be connected with what precedes, as though it said: “Light was made,” that is, the distinction of the preceding confusion, as God said; and it was so made at the command of his saying, as is distinguished both now and later. Now the first work of that distinction is discussed: “And God said,” etc. “God said,” that is, in the Word coeternal with himself, as has already been determined; that is, in the providence of his own Wisdom he first disposed it before completing it in act.

“Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters, and let it divide waters from waters.” By “firmament” he means the aerial and likewise the ethereal heaven, of which it has been said: “and the waters that are above the heavens” (Ps. CXLVIII.4). Both of these now lie between these lower waters or the earth and those upper waters. It is called a firmament because, by its interposition, it makes firm the fluid nature of the upper waters, lest they flow downward and fall back below. Hence Jerome says that *samaim* in Hebrew, that is, “heavens”—the ethereal and aerial heavens which Moses here calls the firmament—derives its name from waters: it is so called because it holds the waters firm above, lest they flow downward.

But it is asked how fire and air can support the substance of water, which is heavier. Yet surely those waters may be so rarefied and subtle, and the mass of fire and air beneath them so great, that they can be supported by these; just as wood and certain stones are supported by water, though they are of an earthly and heavier nature. [Col. 0742B] Who does not know that the adjacent air, though lighter than water, nevertheless suspends and supports waters drawn up as vapor by the exhalation of the earth, before they gather into drops? If, therefore, the upper waters are more rarefied and less corporeal than these vaporized waters, why should they not be perpetually supported by the fire and air beneath them, just as the more corporeal waters are suspended for a time by air alone? It is evident also that dense clouds and the enormous bodies of dragons or birds are sustained by air.

Nor does any believer doubt that human bodies, though earthly in nature, will after the resurrection be of such subtlety and lightness that they can not only remain above the heavens, but also be carried without delay wherever the Spirit wills. Moreover, who does not know that air enclosed in a bladder, surrounding its skin, suspends and supports the skin of the bladder on every side, although it is wholly lighter than that skin? Indeed, it could support any mass of bodies whatsoever as long as it could remain enclosed and confined. So too, that mass and globe of air and fire enclosed in the body of those waters is not prevented by its own lightness from suspending or supporting them.

Nor could the surrounding water in any way slip, since it confines fire and air on every side, until the fire or air gave way in some direction; for one body cannot occupy the place of another unless the latter first withdraws. The air and fire themselves, lest perhaps they should fly away, are compressed by the surrounding waters and have waters laid over them on every side, just as in every sphere the exterior parts are the upper parts. But in order that they may confine and compress them, the waters must possess some weight, and that moderately, so that they can be supported by them. Now it is agreed, as has been said, that only two elements are heavy, namely earth and water, and that earth is heavier than water. Therefore, in order that the weight might be more moderate, water rather than earth had to be placed above them, since it could also be supported more easily by the light elements.

Finally, in bodies composed of the four elements, animate and inanimate alike, who can reasonably deny that these four elements are so joined together that some particles of the lighter elements lie beneath certain particles of the heavier? For the lower parts of any large body do not entirely lack an admixture of fiery or aerial element, just as the upper parts are not wholly free from water and earth. Rather, both the upper and lower parts of such a body consist of the four elements, joined together in a fitting natural balance, according to the saying addressed to God: “You bind the elements by number.” What wonder, then, if in the composition of the world water, heavier than fire or air, could be placed above them and be supported by them?

[Col. 0743B] Some have maintained that those upper waters were solidified by icy congelation and hardened into crystal. If this is so, the more solid they are, the more forcefully they confine the enclosed fire and air lest they depart in any direction, and the more firmly they are supported by them. Indeed, perhaps they no longer need to be supported by them, since they are no longer fluid but solidified into crystal. Thus Josephus, in Book I of the *Antiquities*, says:

> “On the second day he placed heaven above all things; distinguishing it from the others, he established it in itself; and, surrounding it with crystal, he suitably fashioned it moist and rainy for the earth’s benefit derived from showers.”

Jerome, in his letter to Oceanus, *On the Husband of One Wife* [Note: [Col. 0743D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 659.], says:

> “Between heaven and earth the firmament is constructed; and, according to the etymology of the Hebrew language, heaven—that is, *samaim*—derives its name from waters, so that the waters above the heavens may be set apart for the praises of the Lord. Hence in Ezekiel crystal is seen spread out above the cherubim, that is, waters made compact and denser. Bede, *On the Natures of Things*: Heaven contains the angelic powers of the higher sphere; when they come forth to us they assume ethereal bodies, so that they may resemble human beings even in eating, and when they return there they lay them aside. God tempered this with icy waters, lest it set the lower elements ablaze; then he called the lower heaven the firmament because it supports the upper waters; likewise, he called the waters placed above the firmament heavens, indeed lower than spiritual beings but higher than every corporeal creature.”

Some claim that these waters were reserved for the flood; others, more rightly, that they were suspended to moderate the fire of the stars. But blessed Augustine, passing over these opinions concerning the upper waters—whether they are icy or not, and what uses they contain—says: “Certainly, what kind of waters they are there, or for what uses they are reserved, their Creator himself knows; but that they are there, Scripture testifying, no one doubts.” What so great a teacher left uncertain for himself seems most arrogant for us to affirm.

The opinion of some that they were established and reserved there for the inundation of the flood, so that, flowing down from there in their abundance, they might cover the earth, is found wholly frivolous. For since the Psalmist, living long after the flood, says, “And the waters that are above the heavens, let them praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. CXLVIII.4), it is evident that they still exist there now as before. For he does not say “which were,” but “which are.” If some part of them had flowed down, the firmament was not interposed beneath that part; it did not so make them firm that they could not afterwards fall.

It is also plain, as Genesis relates, that the flood came from an abundance of rains, when the fountains of the great deep were also broken open; after these were shut and the rains restrained, the flood itself ceased. It is certain, moreover, that rains arise only from the exhalation of the earth, when the sun, heating them, draws up by its warmth the thin waters ascending like smoke from the heated earth. Therefore that abundance of water in the rains arose not from the upper but from the lower waters. When, as the flood was ending, it is added not only that the rains were restrained but also that the fountains were shut, it is plainly suggested that the entire abundance of waters in the flood came solely from the lower waters, which were gathered together on the third day so that dry land might appear.

But when it is said that the cataracts of heaven were opened during the flood and rain fell, “heaven” means the aerial heaven from which rain flows, not the ethereal heaven; and by “cataracts” he does not mean narrow openings but indicates an abundance of rain, as though at that time the air retained no vaporized water anywhere. Therefore, as water fell from above as rain and the openings of the earth were blocked, the earth necessarily had to be covered with waters on every side, just as it was on the third day before those same lower waters were gathered into one place so that dry land might appear.

What usefulness that suspension of the waters has, since no definite judgment about it has been given even by the saints, I judge very difficult to discuss. Yet this opinion seems more probable to us: that they were established chiefly in order to temper the heat of the upper fire, lest that higher heat entirely draw up either the clouds themselves or the lower waters, since fire naturally has the power of attracting moisture. Thus, when phlebotomists wish to draw blood with cups applied to vessels, they put fire into enclosed tow so that the heat of the fire may draw the moisture of the blood.

It should also be noted that where we say, “Let there be a firmament in the midst of the waters,” the Hebrews have: “Let there be an expanse beneath the waters”—that is, an interval by which they may be permanently separated from one another, lest they touch again—as it is written: “Stretching out the heaven like a skin; who coverest its upper parts with waters” (Ps. CIII.2); and elsewhere: “Gathering the waters of the sea as in a bottle” (Ps. XXXII.7). Therefore, that expanse by which upper and lower waters are separated, like an intervening skin, encloses the lower waters as in a bottle [Col. 0745A] and suspends and supports the upper waters as a firmament.

But when he says, “He divided the waters which were under the firmament,” etc., it seems as though he said, “He divided things that were already divided.” For he does not say, “which are now under the firmament and which are above,” but “which already then were.” From this it is clear that from the first day waters had already stood above the ether, whether, as we have said, thrown up there by a blast of wind, or made there in their creation itself and carried around the whole world—not lifted there from the lower waters by some blast of wind. Thus, when on the second day the waters above are said to have been divided from those below, this division is understood as having made them firm by the interposition of the firmament on the second day, so that they could no longer fall. Although they had already been there on the first day, they had not yet been made firm there so as to be unable to fall; that was done on the second day, when the firmament is said to have been made.

The Hebrew, however, where we have, “He divided the waters which were under the firmament,” etc., does not have “were,” because it uses the substantive verb either rarely or never, and customarily makes statements without it—as when it says, “Blessed man,” for “Blessed is the man.” Thus the text there is as though it said: “He divided the waters under the firmament from those above the firmament.” If “are” is understood, being a present-tense verb, as in “Blessed man” for “Blessed is the man,” then what the prophet says means: “He then divided that which is now under the firmament, etc.,” because in the time of the prophet who speaks, the firmament had long since been made, and the division of the waters was by its interposition, just as it is now.

If someone asks how long they remained there before being made firm, wishing to know what that first day before the second was, he should know that these six days in which the world was completed must by no means be measured according to the days we now have from the sun’s illumination, especially since the sun had not yet been made during those first three days. Therefore, when we reckon days in these works of God and say, “And evening and morning were one day,” we do not understand day, evening, or morning according to our present days, [Col. 0745D] but understand one day and another according to the distinction of the works. Thus the first day is called the first operation of God, by which he first acted so that he might enlighten us concerning knowledge of himself, according to the Apostle’s saying: “For his invisible things,” etc.

Although that formless matter created on the first day was less sufficient for knowledge or praise of the Creator so long as it remained in that confusion or formlessness, yet that confusion of the first creation, which was later to be formed and distinguished into this adornment of the world that we now use—and which, understanding it to be necessary for us, we praise God on its account—was not improperly called the first day, because from it the beginning of human knowledge concerning God arose. For heaven and earth first had to be created—that is, the matter of future things had to be prepared in the elements—before it was formed into the subsequent works. Therefore, as we recalled above, he calls the first creation of matter in the elements the first day. We have long since taught concerning the evening and morning of this day as of the others.

But now, to return to matters interrupted but not abandoned, let the reader know that we inserted these remarks so that, when he hears one day or another named by the prophet, he may not understand the stretches of time that we now understand by our days, but may refer the diversity of days to the diversity of works, however long a duration they may have in their succession or execution. Therefore let no one be surprised on hearing that, on the second day, waters already existing above the heavens were made firm, as though some interval had occurred between their being there and their establishment; for they were made firm there immediately after they had arrived there.

Thus, the statement now made—“Let there be a firmament,” or “He divided the waters which were,” etc.—must be understood as their making firm or division in this sense: without delay, after they had been there, they were hardened into indissoluble ice like crystal, and were so stabilized and made firm through the interposition of ether and air that they could not fall down to the lower regions, although by the nature of the watery element they possessed some heaviness; and, according to the philosophers, all weights are borne to the earth by their own inclination.

Perhaps someone may also ask this: if, as is said, those upper waters, placed above the fire, hardened into ice, by what force of nature this occurred. To this I reply first [Col. 0746C] that when, in certain effects of things, we now inquire into or assign the force of nature or natural causes, we do not do so with reference to that first operation of God in the establishment of the world, in which God’s will alone possessed the efficacy of nature in creating or arranging those things then; but only after that operation of God had been completed in the six days. Thereafter we are accustomed to weigh the force of nature, when things themselves had already been so prepared that their constitution or preparation sufficed for bringing about, without miracles, whatever might be done. Hence we confess that things done through miracles are done rather against or above nature than according to nature, since that prior preparation [Col. 0746D] of things could by no means suffice for accomplishing the deed, unless God conferred upon the things themselves some new power, as he did in those six days, when his will alone held the force of nature in bringing each thing about. If indeed he did these things now as then, we should surely say that they were done contrary to nature: for example, if the earth of itself, without any sowing, produced plants, or formed beasts from itself or birds from water.

We therefore call nature the force bestowed upon things by that first preparation, sufficient for something to arise from them—that is, to be brought about. Let no one, then, ask by what natural force he hardened those upper waters, set above the fire, into ice, or even lifted them upward, since at that time his will alone, as has been said, held the force of nature. Plato too declares that this will, in bringing things about [Col. 0747A] or preserving them, is stronger than all their nature, where . . . in his *Timaeus* he introduces God speaking to the stellar gods, when he says:

> “You are indeed not immortal, nor wholly indissoluble; yet you shall never be dissolved, nor undergo the necessity of death, because my will is a greater and more vigorous bond for the preservation of eternity than those vital bonds from which your eternity has been compounded and augmented.”

Perhaps it may also be plausibly said that the very wind which threw them upward bound them into ice by the coldness of its blast, so that on the second day the firmament came to be; namely, when those waters, which had been there before they were thus solidified, were made solid there. That they were already there before being so solidified is plainly indicated, as we noted above [Col. 0747B], when the text says “which were” rather than “which are.” The Hebrew, however, as has likewise already been said, does not have *were*, so that the question has less force.

**And it was so.** That is, this division of the waters was established permanently, so that those upper waters would never afterward fall back upon these lower ones. I think this is said lest anyone suppose that rain drips from those upper waters and that they are still suspended above, as Josephus also supposed, as we mentioned above.

**And he called.** That is, through this he brought it about that the firmament itself would afterward be called by us “heaven,” since we now call both the aerial and ethereal heaven the upper parts of the world in comparison with [Col. 0747C] our dwelling-place. But since the Hebrew has *Samaim* for heaven—a word derived, as was said, from waters—it rightly seems to be called *Samaim* from the division of the waters, or from the suspension and securing of those above.

**And there was evening.** As above we understood evening and morning as the conception of the divine mind and the accomplishment of the work, so this must be understood both here and elsewhere. Thus, when it is said in this work or in the others, “There was evening and morning, one day,” it is as though one said: the accomplishment of this work, designated by this day, was brought to morning as it was in evening; that is, it was completed in visible work just as it had first been arranged in the divine mind [Col. 0747D]. Thus the concluding words of each work convey the same sense as the earlier words, as though the end were brought back to the beginning. For in sense it is the same when, in each work, “God said, Let this be,” and “it was so” are placed first, as when at the end it is added that “there was evening and morning, one day”: that is, the completion of this operation corresponded to its preceding arrangement in God.

It should be noted, as we have also mentioned above, that on this day it is not said, “And God saw that it was good,” as in the others. That is, God did not approve the work of this day as he did those of the rest, for the reason already given: God does not yet make us see what good or usefulness [Col. 0748A] the suspension of the upper waters possesses. Nor did this division of the waters yet appear worthy of praise, since the divided waters had not yet been arranged and fixed in the manner in which they were to remain, and in which they were necessary for the creation of things to come. For the lower waters still had to be gathered into one place, so that the dry land might appear. Finally, the prophet did not wish to commend that bodily suspension of the upper waters, by which they covered the whole world, foreseeing that baptism in waters, by which every multitude of sins is covered, would be prefigured in these superimposed waters.

## ON THE THIRD DAY

**And God said: Let the waters be gathered together.** God prepares the lower region of the earth, in which he was to create [Col. 0748B] and place humankind, as was necessary: namely, by removing the flooding waters from the surface of the earth and adorning the earth itself with grasses and trees.

**Which are under heaven.** This is said in contrast with those which are suspended above heaven—that is, above the firmament.

**Into one place.** That is, so that they may no longer cover the whole earth, but, withdrawing into one part of the earth, may leave another habitable.

**And it was so.** That is, as the waters withdrew into one part of the earth, the other was uncovered, as it is written: “He founded the earth upon the waters.” For just as a globe may be placed in water so that one part rises above it, so that globe of earth settled in [Col. 0748C] the waters, so that on one side the sea touched it and poured itself through its channels, whence springs or rivers might arise for us. The water of this sea, now gathered into one place, became deeper than when it had been dispersed, unless perhaps what entered through the channels of the earth diminished its depth.

**And he called.** That is, he made that earth uncovered by the waters worthy to be called dry land, that is, dry. It was earth even when the waters poured over it made it muddy; but now, as the waters withdrew, it became dry.

**And the gatherings of the waters.** That is, their continuities, although divided among different places. For among the Hebrews all collections of waters, whether salt or fresh, are called seas. Note that, in the work of the second day, after first stating, “And God made the firmament and divided the waters,” etc., the text later adds, “And it was so.” I do not find this observed in the present gathering of waters [Col. 0748D]. It does not first say, “And the waters were gathered,” and then add, “And it was so”; it says only that “it was so.” For if here, as there, it had added “it was so,” it would seem to imply that this gathering of the waters was permanent just as that suspension of the waters is. This is by no means true, since the same waters which were then brought together into one place so that dry land might appear were brought back in the Flood so as to cover it.

**And he saw.** That is, he so made this gathering [Col. 0749A] that it would later appear to be good and necessary for the things he was to make.

**Let the earth bring forth vegetation.** That is, let it first conceive within itself what it will then bring forth, just as a child is brought into the light from conception. He immediately adds concerning this birth: “And it brought forth.” But the inserted words, “And it was so,” pertain only to the conception of germination. What he immediately adds, “And it brought forth,” is as though he said, “And it immediately brought forth what had germinated.” Note that when some things are said to be produced or born from earth or water, this should not be understood as meaning that they consist of one element only; rather, they receive their names from the predominant element, as do the things from which they are said to be produced.

**Green vegetation.** Since plants adhere by their roots to the earth [Col. 0749B] and have their life and growth from the moisture of water, they are rightly included under one day in the aforesaid ordering of earth and water. Some think it is especially suggested by this that the world was adorned in spring, because we see that spring’s mildness is necessary for these things to be born from the earth or preserved. Yet I do not see on what grounds the world could then have had the spring mildness we now experience, since the sun had not yet been created, and its approach is what now produces this mildness. Indeed, on the day when the earth brought forth these things, the weather seems to have been colder than on winter days, which the sun now warms, however little. Therefore, how the earth could then naturally germinate these things [Col. 0749C] or preserve some of them is a question.

But, as we have already mentioned above, in the works of the first six days God’s will alone held the force of nature, when nature itself was being created—that is, when a certain power was being conferred upon the things then made. Thereafter this power would suffice for their multiplication and for whatever effects were to proceed from them or, as it were, to be born from them. For, as has been said, we now call nature nothing other than the force and capacity bestowed upon those works at that time, by which they sufficed to bring about the things which afterward came to pass from them.

Perhaps some natural explanation may also be given for how the earth could then produce these things: namely, that the newness of the earth had greater powers for producing or preserving [Col. 0749D] plants than afterward, and especially that it had received this from its excessive moisture, imparted by the abundance of waters before they were gathered together; and that it was assisted in preserving them by the heat of the sun, created on the next day. Perhaps when it was created, the sun immediately produced by its heat the whole appropriate temperature in some region of the earth—though not, I think, everywhere. For all regions are never equally heated and cooled at the same time; nor do the things in them arise or revive at the same time; fruits do not everywhere reach maturity simultaneously; nor do the same herbs or trees grow in all lands.

If, therefore, the earth brought forth every species of herb or tree on this day, so that God might complete his works in six days, and if a spring mildness could not be present in all lands at once [Col. 0750A], why must this have happened in spring, unless perhaps in that part of the earth where it was spring? From that region they could afterward have been moved and transplanted to other lands. Spring mildness, moreover, is believed to be perpetual in paradise; and perhaps there the earth could then produce and preserve everything at once, where both the soil was suitable for all things and the temperature of heaven itself was fitting.

We know that many things grow from the earth: some require warm soil, some cold, some temperate. Thus it could have happened that, at whatever season the earth germinated, it produced different things in different places. Nor does mildness seem as necessary for producing plants as for preserving fruits. Scripture makes no mention here of fruits. [Col. 0750B] But we believe that in paradise, where humankind was to be placed, the fruit-bearing plants produced fruits together with their trees at once, insofar as was necessary for humankind. Scripture records that the humans transgressed by means of the fruit of the forbidden tree, and that the fruits of the other trees were granted to them for food as necessary.

Nothing, however, prevents different plants from preserving their fruits at the same time in different lands according to the quality of their soils and the differing temperature of heaven; or the same plants from existing with fruit in one land and without fruit in another until the suitable temperature arrived, as happens every day, since we see that not all lands yield the same fruits equally soon.

**Bearing seed.** Either so that, once born, it immediately had its seed as though it had reached maturity; [Col. 0750C] or so that it was created capable of having seed.

**And a fruit-bearing tree.** That is, fruitful trees, either bearing their apples—that is, their fruits—as soon as they arose, or not immediately. For *pomum* is commonly understood in the general sense of every fruit of a tree.

**According to its kind.** That is, according to the nature of its material, so that the herbs or trees, rather than the lands, may bear different fruits according to their diversity, not the same ones. Its seed—that is, while it remains rooted in the earth—should possess in itself the power of its propagation, whether from seed, from grafting branches, or from planting.

Note that when it says “a fruit-bearing tree,” it seems to speak only of fruitful trees, not fruitless ones, as having then been created. Thus not all trees were created at that time, but some afterward, as is believed of thorns and thistles, produced from the earth after sin as a punishment for humankind. Yet if someone says that those trees too which are now fruitless were first created fruitful but afterward became fruitless because of human sin, or understands “the fruit” or *pomum* of a tree as any usefulness of wood whatsoever, this is not absurd. For even fruitless woods have certain uses, though they yield no fruit for food. Since, however, ordinary speech does not use *pomum*, as it does *fruit*, for every kind of usefulness, after first saying [Col. 0751A] “fruit-bearing” the text adds, by way of explanation, “bearing fruit,” that is, having any usefulness whatever. On account of this explanatory specification, after first saying “it was so,” it immediately joins, “And the earth brought forth vegetation,” etc.

## ON THE FOURTH DAY

**Let there be lights.** Between the creation of plants, now completed, and the creation of animals, which was to follow, lights were made so that plants might be warmed and thrive by their heat, and animals might have comfort from their light, lest they wander about as though blind in darkness, and so that they might be able to choose their food.

**In the firmament of heaven.** This is used intransitively: in that which was last called heaven—the firmament interposed between the waters and distinct from those waters which it secures above, as has been said.

**And let them divide.** He explains the purposes for which they were made. First, by their illumination, to distinguish daytime from nighttime. Daytime is that which is illuminated by the sun, just as nighttime is that which is lit by the moon and stars or lacks the sun’s illumination.

**And as signs.** Not signs whose observance is vain, as in auspices and auguries, but signs of certain natural indications of future or present events. Sailors are accustomed, by observing the stars, to know toward what regions of the world they are being carried; and many indications of changing seasons are drawn from the sun, moon, or stars, since at one time they seem to us of one color or heat and at another [Col. 0751C] of another, or vary in whatever way before our eyes.

**And for seasons.** That is, for the reckoning of times, such as days and years, which he immediately supplies as examples. We calculate and number days according to the motions and courses of the sun from east to west; and we are accustomed to calculate years according to its revolutions and sometimes those of the other planets, so that however many revolutions they make to the same point, we call that many years of the sun, Saturn, or other planets.

**And let them shine.** So that they may be in one place and illuminate the earth in another, scattering their brightness from there where it is needed.

[Col. 0751D] **And he made.** He explains how what he had previously said about dividing day and night was accomplished: he appointed the sun to illuminate the daytime, and the moon and stars to illuminate the night.

**The greater light.** Namely, the sun: greater not so much by the size of its sphere as by the power of its illumination with respect to our perception, since we receive from it a greater illumination.

**To rule the day.** That is, as producing the daytime itself by its illumination or carrying light around, just as the moon and stars do the night.

**The lesser light.** He means the moon, as second to [Col. 0752A] the sun in the effect of illumination, because it is nearer to the earth than the stars and therefore has a greater power of shining upon us than they, even though some of them, more distant from us, are believed to possess more brilliance or magnitude.

**And the stars.** Supply: “He similarly made [them] to rule the night.” He set those also—namely, the stars—in the firmament, as he did the sun and moon.

**That they might shine.** This must be referred jointly to the stars, sun, and moon. Otherwise it is not clear how he could say that they were to rule day and night, since the stars are to rule the night only, not the day.

There is no small question concerning the planets, which are said to move contrary to the firmament: whether they are animate, as the philosophers thought, and whether certain spirits preside over those bodies and impart this motion to them; or whether, by God’s will and ordering alone, they maintain this course immovably. The philosophers maintain that both they and the entire world itself are animate, and do not hesitate to assert that they are certain rational, immortal, and impassible living beings, saying that every motion in bodies begins from the soul and that a body cannot afterward be moved except through it. They further maintain that the world is everywhere so filled with living beings that each part of the world has its own: this lower and denser air up to the moon has demons; while the upper part of the world, which we are accustomed to call the ethereal heaven, has the planets and the other stars. Blessed Augustine, recalling this view in Book Eight of *The City of God* [Col. 0752C; Note: [Col. 0751D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, col. 238], says this of the Platonists:

> “They say that there is a threefold division of all living beings in which there is a rational soul: into gods, humans, and demons. The dwelling of gods is in heaven, of humans on earth, and of demons in the air.”

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0751D] *Ibid.*]:

> “Demons have immortality of body in common with the gods, but passions of soul in common with human beings.”

And, after adding a description of demons from the sayings of the Platonist Apuleius, he says [Note: [Col. 0752D] *Ibid.*, col. 241]:

> “Apuleius, briefly defining demons, says that they are living beings by genus, passive in soul, rational in mind, aerial in body, eternal in time.”

From these statements of the philosophers, especially the Platonists, it is clear that heaven and air too are furnished with their own living beings [Col. 0752D]: the latter they call demons—that is, rational, immortal, passible living beings; the former they call gods, that is, rational, immortal, impassible living beings, such as all the stars, not only the planets but every star whatsoever. They hold that Plato calls the planets not merely gods but gods of gods, as superior to the other stars and possessing greater efficacy; there, as they say, he especially invites them to the creation of humankind, so that the human body may be fashioned from earth by a certain power of theirs, and God may infuse a soul into it.

Although they admit that no god is anything but good, they distinguish among demons, as among humans, some as good [Col. 0753A] and some as evil; hence they call the former in Greek *kalodaemones* (“good demons”), the latter *kakodaemones* (“evil demons”). They know nothing of the devil’s fall, but believe that demons, like humans and other animals, were created bodily. They thus distinguish the bodies of all rational living beings according to the region or part of the world which they inhabit: some are earthly, like those of humans; others aerial or ethereal, like those of demons or gods.

It is therefore clear, according to Plato’s or the Platonists’ opinion, that the stars themselves are certain living beings and that souls reside in the visible stellar bodies by which they can be moved or driven. Blessed Augustine, indeed, not presuming to refute this opinion [Col. 0753B], says in the *Enchiridion* that it is still uncertain to him whether the sun and moon belong to the society of angels, or whether certain angelic spirits are assigned to those stellar bodies, drawing and carrying them around so as to supply such great benefits to human needs. But whether the world is a living being which contains both these living beings and all others within itself, he indicates in the first book of the *Retractations* to be less consonant with reason.

We have thought it not inappropriate to set down his words, now collected from both works. Thus he says in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 58 [Note: [Col. 0753D] *Patrologia*, vol. XL, cols. 259–260]:

> “Whether the archangels are called ‘powers,’ and what difference there is among thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers—let those say who can, provided that they can prove what they say [Col. 0753C]; I confess that I do not know these things. Nor do I have it certain whether the sun, moon, and stars belong to the same society, although they appear to be luminous bodies, not bodies possessing sensation or intelligence.”

The same author, in the first book of the *Retractations* [Note: [Col. 0754D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXII, col. 602], says:

> “Whether this world is a living being, as Plato and many other philosophers thought, I was unable either to discover by certain reasoning or to find capable of persuasion by the authority of the divine Scriptures. Therefore I noted as rashly said something stated by me which may be understood in this sense, even in the book *On the Immortality of the Soul*—not because I affirm this to be false, but because I do not comprehend that it is true that the world is a living being.”

The Apostle too seems to distinguish both the celestial living beings whom [Col. 0753D] philosophers call gods and the aerial beings whom they call demons. If, then, as the philosophers thought—and as the saints do not altogether presume to refute—certain spirits preside over the heavenly bodies of the stars and can move or drive them, the proposed question concerning the movement of the planets is easily solved. But if they possess an ordered and stable movement from another source, it is enough to attribute this to the divine will, which, as has been said, held the force of nature in the primordial causes and, according to Plato, is more powerful in bringing all things about than the natural capacity of created things themselves.

There are some who so exalt and extol the teaching of astronomy and the power of the stars that they hold even contingent future events can be foretold from them, and confess that by this art they can judge even matters which philosophers declare unknown to nature. They thus falsely claim that the stars are signs not only of natural future events, as we have said, but also of contingent ones. Natural future events are those which have some natural cause of their occurrence: they happen from preceding things as from certain natural causes, and are so connected with them that it can scarcely, or never, be prevented that these things result from those preceding; for example, death is soon to follow after poison has been swallowed, rain after thunder, or barrenness of the earth after excessive heat [Col. 0754B] or immoderate rains.

Contingent future events, however, are those which stand equally open to occurring and not occurring, so that no cause preceding in the nature of things compels them to occur or not occur, nor can it be known beforehand from anything whether they will occur or not: for example, that I shall read today, and whatever it is within the power of our choice either to do or to leave undone.

There are, then, certain natural and, as it were, determinate future events, since they can be known in advance from a natural connection with their preceding causes; and for this reason they are said already to be known to nature, just as all things present or past are. For when it is already presently the case that the stars are equal or unequal, though we do not know which is now the case, Boethius asserts that it is nevertheless known to nature, since there is already in the stars themselves such a number as can provide knowledge of itself; and that is for it to be known or determined by nature. For a voice or audible sound is called natural in itself, even if no one is present who can hear it; and a field was fit for cultivation before there was a human being who could cultivate it.

Contingent future events, however, are likewise called unknown to nature, since they cannot be known in advance through any operation or institution of nature. I therefore wonder that some profess themselves able through astronomy to know and judge even these things, and to be, as it were, diviners of such matters. Since astronomy is a branch [Col. 0754D] of physics—that is, natural philosophy—how can they investigate by it what philosophers of nature themselves declare unknown, that is, incapable of being foreknown from any nature of things?

We do not deny that certain natural future events can be known through astronomy, any more than through medicine. Physicians, according to the temperaments of bodies, can foresee many things about the sick: whether they may recover or not. Likewise, those skilled in the stars, who know their natures—whether they are hot or cold, dry or moist, or temperate—and who have learned through astronomy those regions of heaven which they call their domiciles, where they exercise their powers most strongly, can foresee many natural future events [Col. 0755A]: whether drought or rain, heat or cold, will prevail in the following season. This is of great value not only for the prudent cultivation of the earth but also for regulating medicines. Thus philosophers dared to call the planets themselves gods and to profess them as, in some sense, rulers of the world, because our region is greatly varied according to their natures and qualities: at one time sterility results, at another abundance; at one time one must sow in wet places, at another in dry; at one time hot or moist medicines, or other remedies, must be provided.

But whoever promises any certainty by the teaching [Col. 0755B] of astronomy concerning contingent future events, which, as we have said, are unknown even to nature, must be considered not so much an astronomer as diabolical. That they know nothing about such things we can readily prove. If we ask them about something to be done which is equally within our power to do or leave undone, they do not dare make any judgment from any teaching of their art, knowing that, if they were to say something, we would turn ourselves to the opposite course.

But if another person asks them this same question about us, and does so, they say, not to test them but with a sincere intention of truth, then they promise to tell the truth. Who does not see how this ought to be received with derision? For if through their art they possess certainty concerning the outcome about which they are consulted, what difference does it make who asks them about it, or even with what intention? [Col. 0755C] Or why are they unable to judge even the intention, which, because it is present, already has a determinate outcome, yet promise certainty about a future event that is wholly uncertain?

From this, I think, it is clear that if it happens that they tell the truth about anyone in such matters, they utter it not instructed by the said art but by diabolical suggestion. Just as, when we see the preparation of certain things, we predict what will result more by conjecture than certainty, so the devil whom they consult leads them into this divination, so that, though uncertain, they may pronounce many things truthfully. When they have foretold truths concerning some matters, they believe that they foreknow all the rest. Often too, by diabolical prompting, they report present facts about absent persons or past facts [Col. 0755D], and do not lie. The unlearned regard this as something great, not noticing that the devil announces what he already knows by seeing it, so that he may be believed also concerning the future.

Let no one, therefore, attribute the divinations of such persons to the aforementioned art, but rather to diabolical contrivance. Accordingly, what is said of the stars, “and let them be for signs,” must be understood not of contingent future events—that is, chance or fortuitous events, which Aristotle says are open either way [Col. 0756A]—but, as stated, of natural future events. It is as though the study of astronomical science chiefly took its beginning from this, or as though its usefulness were here especially indicated by the authority of this passage. Moses himself is believed to have excelled in the learning of the Egyptians.

## ON THE FIFTH DAY

**A creeping thing of living soul.** Ambrose, in the *Hexaemeron*, on the fifth day [Note: [Col. 0755D] *Patrologia*, vol. XIV, col. 207], says:

> “We know that kinds of serpents are called creeping things because they creep upon the earth; but much more does everything that swims possess either the appearance or the nature of creeping. For when they swim upon the water, they creep with the whole body by which they are carried over certain backs of the waters. Hence David also says: ‘This sea, great and wide; there are creeping things without number’ [Psalm 103:25]. Indeed, although very many have feet and the use of walking because they are amphibious and live either in water or on land, such as seals, crocodiles, river-horses [perhaps *river-horse*; Latin *fluviales*], which they call hippopotamuses because they are produced in the river Nile, nevertheless, when they are in deep water, they neither walk nor swim nor use the track of a foot for going, but use it like an oar for creeping.”

From Ambrose’s words it is clear that all fish are also included among creeping things, since they move themselves without the motion of feet.

**Of living soul.** This is said in contrast to the life of plants. Even if plants are said to have some soul—that is, life—they do not possess life from themselves, as do things which live by inhaling and exhaling; rather, being attached only to the earth, they have as their life the moisture of the earth rising into them [Col. 0756C]. Thus “of living soul” means life enduring from itself, as has been said, not from the infusion of earthly moisture.

**And a flying creature.** From this it is clear that both fish and birds have bodies produced from waters and of the same nature; and that their flesh does not provide human bodies with as great a power for indulgence as the flesh of terrestrial animals, which are of the same nature as our bodies. Hence the Rule of blessed Benedict does not prohibit those meats to monks as it does these [Note: [Col. 0755D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXVI, col. 616], since it commands abstinence only from the flesh of quadrupeds, not from other kinds [Note: [Col. 0755D] Rule of St Benedict, ch. 39.—The same view is held by Theodemar, abbot of Monte Cassino, in his letter to Charlemagne; by Rabanus Maurus, Book II of *On the Instruction of Clerics*, ch. 27; and by St Hildegard in her *Exposition of the Rule of St Benedict* [Col. 0756D]. The common opinion, however, is that St Benedict prohibited monks not only quadrupeds but birds as well. On this matter see the commentary on chapter 39 of the Rule of St Benedict].

**Over the earth, beneath the firmament of heaven.** The phrase [Col. 0756D] “over the earth, beneath the firmament of heaven” seems to refer not only to the flying creature but also to the creeping thing, if the stars themselves are thought animate. For since the stars move without feet, they would have to be included among creeping things like fish; but since they are in no way beneath the firmament of heaven, it is clear that they are excluded by the words “beneath the firmament of heaven.” Thus “a creeping thing and a flying creature” means, as it were, an animal fitted to creep or fly over [Col. 0757A] the earth, that is, so as not to touch the earth. For afterward, when it says “creeping things of the earth” rather than “over the earth,” it clearly distinguishes this kind of creeping thing from the other.

Certain aquatic birds are said to have feet attached so far back that they cannot walk with them, but only swim, like fish with their little fins. These ought, I believe, to be called creeping rather than walking creatures. Since they are never seen to come out upon land, there is a question how they brood over their eggs—or whether the waters themselves, receiving the eggs of such creatures as they do those of fish, suffice to give them life through some warmth of their own.

When it says “beneath the firmament of heaven,” this seems to be used intransitively, as though “beneath the firmament which is heaven,” just as one says “the city of Rome,” “the river Tiber,” “a creature of salt,” or “the body or substance of a stone.” This firmament, as was said above, is so called because, being interposed between the waters, it secures the upper waters in such a way that they cannot fall back upon the lower or ever touch them. Therefore, that which is mixed with the waters of clouds is not properly called the firmament; rather, it is that upper region wholly empty of waters. Birds cannot fly through the firmament, because their bodies could not be supported by air without the density of waters [Col. 0757B].

**And he created:** namely, from the waters themselves.

He uses “soul” for the entire living creature, consisting of body and soul together, comprehending the whole by the name of one part [Col. 0757C]. So elsewhere he says, “Give me the souls; take the rest for yourself.” And again: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls.”

**Living.** Supply: living from itself, not from the earth, as plants are attached by their roots to the earth.

And movable. That is, in distinction from the other animals which the earth afterwards produced, since earth is a heavier element than water. Hence these animals, produced from water, are by nature more mobile and agile, since they consist of a lighter element. Notice too what he said above concerning plants: that the earth caused them to germinate and brought them forth. But of animals it is said only that water or earth produced them [Col. 0757D], not that it caused them to germinate; thereby indicating that they do not receive their growth from being rooted in the earth, as plants do.

Which the waters had produced according to their kinds. Read it thus: “He created every living soul,” that is, every such animate being, according to kinds; as if he said: every one, that is, according to kind, not according to number. For not all the individual members of these kinds, but the several kinds both of birds and fishes, were then created. Hence, when the following passage says that God rested from all His work, this is not to be understood of the multiplication of the individual members of the kinds, but of the natures of the kinds, already prepared for whatever might afterwards be generated from them. Which the waters had produced: that is, for producing which the waters had already been prepared [Col. 0758A], whether fresh, as rivers, or salt, as seas.

And God saw. Observe that in the works of this day, when their creation is repeated, it is by no means said, “And it was so,” as it was above on the second day. Or, when He had first said, “And God made the firmament,” and so forth, He afterwards added, “and it was so,” thereby indicating, as it were, that this division of the waters would remain permanently. Likewise, in the creation of man, after He said, “God created man,” and so forth, He added, “and it was so.” Therefore, wherever “and it was so” is said, a certain permanence of the works is signified—that they should remain as they were made. Thus it does not seem rightly applicable to the kinds of birds, since some kinds among them are at some time [Col. 0758B] to perish altogether, as is written concerning the phoenix, and perhaps this happens with certain other kinds both of birds and fishes, which belong to the works of this day.

And He blessed. God is recorded to have blessed only these living creatures produced from water, as also human beings afterwards created, as though these living creatures approached humanity in a certain dignity, because they were generated from that element from which human beings were also to be regenerated. Therefore birds seem not without reason to have held the second place in the ark, after humankind, because they were made from that element which would be more necessary to our salvation in the sacrament of baptism. Rightly, then, did God’s blessing begin with aquatic creatures, since from this element, as was said, the blessing of our salvation, perfected in the remission of sins, was to have its beginning [Col. 0758C]. Thus, “He blessed them” means, as though he said, that even then He provided a type of the sanctification of those to be regenerated from water, or of their multiplication, in comparison with the circumcised. For although circumcision is said to have effected in the remission of sins what baptism effects, it could not have had this efficacy in as many persons as the grace of baptism continues to have; for only males were circumcised, and only Jews or proselytes.

Saying. That is, determining within Himself what He would later manifest to us.

Increase and multiply: that is, receive increase in the number of individuals [Col. 0758D], not in diversity of kinds. This must not be understood as though they first grew in themselves until they reached the mature age at which they could generate, since the creation of such creatures must be believed to have been perfect from the outset; otherwise they would have had to be reared for a long time before reaching perfection. And if we understand this also of birds, it is not readily apparent from where they would receive nourishment.

Fill. That is, be fruitful to the extent sufficient for this purpose.

The waters of the sea. Yet fresh waters also contain both fishes and birds. But it is agreed that every gathering of waters, salt as well as fresh, is called “sea,” and all waters come from the sea. Here too, where it says, “a living and movable soul” [Col. 0759A], concerning the living creatures produced from water, this seems highly fitting to the sacrament of baptism: there, freed from sin and as though raised from death through the life-giving Spirit, we begin to be born and to live in God; we are advanced from the old Adam into the new and transformed into the members of Christ. Notice that God is recorded to bless, among these works, only the living creatures created from water, then human beings, and finally the seventh day; the blessing of humanity is placed between the other two, as though corresponding to both. For the blessing of humanity begins with baptism, where full remission of sins is received, and is afterwards brought forward and consummated in the Sabbath of heavenly blessedness. Thus it is also fitting that above [Col. 0759B] a living and movable soul should be said to be brought forth from the waters. In baptism we begin to live, so that afterwards, advanced into the aforesaid Sabbath, we may rest together.

## ON THE SIXTH DAY

A living soul. That is, an animate being living from itself, not deriving life from the earth, although it is from the earth, as plants do contrariwise. “Living,” he says, “according to its kind,” because even if those living creatures first created have now failed in themselves, and the same individuals which were first made do not remain in number, nevertheless they always in some manner live in their kind, because, though individuals perish, the genus or species does not perish. Therefore they live in their kind—that is, in [Col. 0759C] their species—although they no longer live in themselves, just as one may say of a tyrant now dead that he lives in his children. Observe that when he says “a living soul” of those which the earth produced, he did not add “movable,” as he did before of those which the waters produced; because, since water is a lighter element than earth, animals produced from water certainly have easier movement, and their bodies can more readily be moved and agitated by the soul, as we noted above.

Cattle. That is, domestic quadrupeds, as though placed beneath our yoke and dominion.

Creeping things of the earth. For it must be joined thus, namely in distinction from the aforesaid creeping things of the water.

Beasts. Namely wild beasts, or whatever creatures are remote from human society [Col. 0759D].

And He made. First He said, “and it was so,” namely, that the earth produced the animals according to their bodily substance; but afterwards the Lord made them in completing them—made them, as it were, perfect—by giving them a life-giving spirit from water, as some suppose, or from the other elements, which are not so corporeal or heavy but lighter and more mobile. God is not said to have blessed the beasts as He blessed the fishes and birds, because the serpent, whom He was to curse, was then among the beasts. But He blessed man, although man was to sin; and He says that He cursed not man but the earth on account of him.

Let Us make man. When all other things had been created or ordered for humanity [Col. 0760A], He made man last and placed him, as it were, at the end of His works. All other things tended toward him as toward the end and purpose of their creation, since all things were made for his sake. Therefore man ought not to have been created until the things over which he was to preside—those necessary to him for food, or at least fitting for the glorification of God—had first been created and prepared for him, lest perhaps he might plead some want as an excuse for his sin. And he might be recalled all the more from offending God insofar as he had a greater reason to love Him, who had set him over all things; or even after the Fall he might be moved more quickly to repentance, grieving that he had offended Him to whom he owed so much. The excellence of this creation is plainly indicated [Col. 0760B] when, speaking as though after a certain deliberation, He says, “Let Us make.” But why is it said in the plural, “Let Us make man in Our image,” if there is absolutely no plurality in God, who alone is afterwards recorded to have created man in His image in these words: “And God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him”?

Let the Jews answer, if they can, or let them confess with us that in the one essence of the Godhead there is plurality of persons rather than of things. Carefully considering this, the prophet, in order to distinguish the persons, says in the plural, “Let Us make”; but to establish the unity of God, he adds in the singular, “and God created man,” and so forth. Thus someone speaking with himself may treat himself and his own reason as though they were two when he consults it, as Boethius does in *The Consolation of Philosophy*, or Augustine in the *Soliloquies*. So God the Father, inviting both Wisdom and Goodness—that is, the Son and the Holy Spirit—to the creation of man, says: “Let Us make him such and so great that he may be Our image or likeness.” How excellent this creation is, and how far superior to the other creations placed above it, is expressed by the very words, as though they were exchanged in a counsel for accomplishing some great thing: “Let Us make.” But in the other creations this was not said; it was merely said, “Let this or that be,” or “let earth or water produce this or that.” Since “man” is a common name for both male and female, since each is a rational, mortal animal, it follows that [Col. 0760D] when it is said below that God created man, it is immediately added, “male and female He created them.” We understand that the man was created in God’s image, but the woman according to His likeness. For the Apostle says concerning man: “A man indeed ought not to cover his head, because he is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11:7). That is, his likeness is more glorious and more precious. There is this difference between image and likeness: a likeness of a thing may be said of that which has some agreement with it and can therefore be called like it. But an image is called an expressed likeness only, as human figures which represent persons more perfectly in every limb.

Therefore, since man is worthier than woman and thereby [Col. 0761A] more like God, he is called His image; but woman, His likeness, although she too, like man, imitates God through reason and the immortality of the soul. Man, moreover, has this further point by which he is made more like God: just as all things have being from God, so from one man, through bodily descent, both woman herself and the whole human race have their beginning. But if anyone wishes to consider more carefully and fully this image or likeness of God in which man is said to have been made, according to the distinction of the divine persons themselves, he will see that human beings, by their constitution, have received a very great likeness both to the Father and to the Son and the Holy Spirit. For it is agreed that to God the Father, who has being from Himself and not from another, that which belongs to divine power is [Col. 0761B] specially ascribed according to this property; likewise to the Son, who is called His Wisdom, that which belongs to wisdom; and to the Holy Spirit, who is called the love of both and is properly called charity, that which concerns the goodness of divine grace is attributed as proper.

Humanity, therefore, as has been said, was made according to the dignity of the soul in a likeness of the individual persons, since through power, wisdom, and love it was made more like God and set above other living creatures. For by the power of its own nature the human soul is stronger than all other things, because it alone was created immortal and incapable of failing. It alone is capable of reason and wisdom and shares in divine love. For those who cannot recognize God by reason cannot [Col. 0761C] love Him. These three things are common to man and woman alike; hence both are recorded to have been made in the likeness of God when it says below: “In the day when God created man, He made him in the likeness of God; male and female He created them.” Although both, according to what has been said, have likeness to the divine persons, the man, because he bears a greater likeness to them, is said to be created not only according to likeness but also according to image. For as the other persons have being from the Father, so in human creation the woman had being from having been created from the man, not the man from the woman. We have also taught above that man surpassed woman in wisdom or reason, and that he was wiser in this respect: he could not be deceived by the serpent. Nor should it be doubted that [Col. 0761D] he is loved more by God, since he could not believe that God envied him, spoke anything deceitfully, or broke out into falsehood, as the deceived woman did. From these points it is clear that the man first created received, through the cooperation of the divine persons in his creation, not only a likeness but also an image of the divine persons, because in these respects he was created more like them. Therefore it is rightly said of man: “in Our image,” that is, in an expressed likeness; and of woman it is added only: “according to likeness.”

And let him have dominion over the fishes. God does not set one human being over another, but only over insensible or irrational creatures [Col. 0762A], so that man may receive them into his power and rule those which lack reason and sense, as He says later: “Have dominion over the fishes of the sea,” and so forth. Power or dominion is said to have been granted to man over these because all these things would be ordered according to his judgment and he would make full use of them according to his will, so long as he himself remained subject to the will of his Creator. Yet it is not easy to explain in detail for what uses he would then have had all these things if he had always remained in Paradise, having all necessities, as it were, at hand, and being granted sufficient food from the fruits of trees or herbs—especially since all living creatures could not reach him.
