To pass over beasts and birds: who would suppose that great whales or [Col. 0762B] sea-fish could arrive there, or even live there? What sort of dominion could he exercise over things he would never see, whose location he would not even know, and perhaps whose existence he would not know? Moreover, how could he rule or preside, as it is said, over the whole earth, if he were always confined in one place in Paradise, ignorant of all the other regions of the world because he had not yet seen them? Or how could what is afterwards said, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” ever occur if, confined in so small a part of the world, they had not yet gone forth into the various regions of the world? There is therefore no reason to suppose that the whole future multitude of humankind would always live in that one place of Paradise if they had not sinned; rather, they would afterwards have been dispersed through the world from there, as from the ark [Col. 0762C], finding nowhere anything penal, since the earth would not have been struck by God with any curse for sin. Yet we believe that the first human beings were placed first in Paradise because the climate of that place, which the Lord had planted from the beginning, was especially abundant in fruits, before these had been so propagated there or elsewhere throughout the world. Nor should it be denied that before the curse of the earth the tree of life could have been multiplied in lands by planting. Then indeed humanity could preside and rule over the whole earth, and perhaps the other animals would afterwards have served many uses and even been granted as food, as the Lord granted them to Noah after the flood. They could also bring some delight to man according to the diversity of the senses: soothing hearing by song, delighting sight by beauty of form, refreshing smell by sweetness of scent, or, when the diverse natures of animals were carefully known by whatever means, stirring us more greatly to love and praise the Creator, as the Psalmist says to Him: “You have delighted me, Lord, in Your workmanship, and in the works of Your hands I shall rejoice” (Ps. 91:5).

Perhaps some think questions of this sort frivolous and not reasonably raised, when someone asks about something which never happened and says what would occur if it were so. “What reason,” they ask, “is there to inquire whether it would be so, when it is neither going to happen nor can that state itself exist?” They therefore say that God, foreknowing future things [Col. 0763A], granted this to man, that by reason he might rule the other living creatures and be able to bind and subdue them, although stronger in body, so that by the reason granted to him man might love God all the more as he recognized that he had received more in this respect from Him.

When he says, “the birds of heaven,” that is, birds, “of heaven” is not added to distinguish one kind of bird from another, but to show through what part of the world they are to fly. So too it was said, “fishes of the sea,” or we say “the stars of heaven,” not to identify certain ones but rather to express their proper place. “Heaven,” then, here includes both the aerial and the ethereal regions, calling by this term whatever lies from the lower waters up to the upper waters [Col. 0763B].

And the beasts. What above he distinguished as beasts and cattle, here he comprehends generally under the name “beasts.”

And over all the earth. Observe that, while man is here granted rule both over the beasts which are on earth and over the earth itself, it was not likewise granted above that he should rule both over the fishes of the sea and the sea itself, or over the birds of heaven and heaven itself. For the sea or heaven is not in our power as the earth is, on which we dwell, establish our buildings, and cultivate what we prepare for our uses.

Every creeping thing that moves upon the earth. That is, in this lower part of the world, perhaps in distinction from the [Col. 0763C] heavenly animals—that is, the stars—which, as philosophers thought, are animate; and these should be called creeping rather than walking in their movement, since they lack feet.

Man in His own image. Namely, He first made the man such that he was His image, as we have explained. Rightly, after it was said, “Let Us make man in Our image,” it is here added, “God created man in His own image,” that is, God’s image, not the image of another thing; as is immediately stated as well, “in the image of God He created him.” This prevents “Our” from being understood to mean that man was made not only in God’s image but also in the image of certain others to whom He might seem to be speaking when He said, “Let Us make man” [Col. 0763D]. Observe also that when he says here, “In the image of God He created him,” and later adds, “Male and female He created them,” he does not repeat “in the image of God” when he speaks of “them” in the plural, as he did when speaking of “him.” He plainly indicates that the statement that man was created in God’s image is to be understood of the male alone. It may also seem that the addition, “In the image of God He created him,” should be understood differently from “in His own image.” For the Son of God is called the image, being from the Father alone, whereas the Holy Spirit is said to be from the Father and the Son. Man, therefore, was created in the image of God because in this he bears his chief likeness to the Son of God: as the Son is from the Father alone, as begotten, so man has being from God alone, as created, and was not taken from any animal [Col. 0764A], as woman was taken from man and formed from his rib.

Male and female. That is, such as were sufficient for the propagation of the human race. Concerning this propagation He afterwards says, “Increase and multiply.” When He calls them by the masculine gender, including man and woman together, this is done because of the dignity of the male sex. We preserve this practice even to the present day: when one man is joined with many women, if we speak of them together and use a plural adjective, we are content with the masculine gender, as when we say that they are good or white.

And He blessed. That is, He was already determining for them the better state of a future life, immortal and incorruptible [Col. 0764B]. The Prophet said this in anticipation of their future Fall, lest anyone, upon later hearing that they were expelled from the earthly Paradise, might despair of the heavenly one.

Increase and multiply. As He is recorded above to have said to the aquatic creatures, “Increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea,” so here He is narrated to say to the human beings created, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth.” Thus this utterance also, like the former, should be understood not as spoken speech but as the ordering of a divine operation, especially since no institution of any language had yet taken place, and Adam had not yet assigned names, as he is later related to have done. Therefore this speech of God, like the sayings mentioned above, seems to be understood not so much as a vocal utterance [Col. 0764C] as a divine determination: God ordered within Himself to act toward them in such a way that they should increase and multiply—that is, receive the increase of multiplication through the union of male and female, whom He had already distinguished above as created male and female for this purpose. From this it is plainly indicated how far the abominable intercourse of the Sodomites departs from God’s creation and nature’s institution: by it they merely defile themselves, gaining no fruit of offspring. From this passage, moreover, those who condemn marriage are especially condemned, since marriage was immediately sanctioned by the Lord’s authority when the first human beings had been created.

[Col. 0764D] Living creatures that move upon the earth. The addition, “that move upon the earth,” may seem intended to exclude both the heavenly animals, according to that opinion of philosophers by which they call the stars gods—that is, rational, immortal, impassible animals—and aerial beings, that is, demons.

Behold, I have given. As if He said, “In the present time or place,” since after the flood the Lord also permitted human beings to eat flesh. But since we now see some beasts or birds for which the eating of flesh is necessary, how is it that only herbs and trees are now granted to these as food, as to human beings? It is as though these were originally sufficient for them, and they would not have needed flesh unless after humanity’s sin [Col. 0765A], so that the punishment resulting from human sin might overflow also upon those over which man was to preside and rule: namely, that some animals might be handed over to others for prey and food. Perhaps there are no animals among those which today require fleshly food among us for which sufficient nourishment cannot be found in herbs or trees in some parts of the world. Observe how entirely God wishes man to obey Him: He wills that man should not even eat in order to live except through obedience, nor touch anything necessary without His permission, not even for sustaining life. From this He plainly indicates that the whole life of man consists only in obedience to God, and that man ought to live for this alone.

[Col. 0765B] For you and for all living creatures of the earth. Some foods are for you, others for them, or some jointly for you and them. For not all fodder seems suitable either for man or for animals, although before sin no kind of food was harmful or perhaps unsuitable to man. But if we suppose that all things were suitable for human beings, it is by no means credible that we should grant this also of animals: that the tree of life and all other things were granted to them as well—unless someone wishes to maintain that they too, like human beings, had in it a remedy against death and old age. We never read that the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was forbidden to them, as it is later said to have been forbidden to human beings. For it is not apparent how this grant could have been made concerning all trees to human beings and the other animals [Col. 0765C], if that forbidden tree had never been granted either to human beings or to them. Observe too that trees called unfruitful can provide some nourishment to certain animals, at least in leaves, flowers, or bark. And observe that, since He provides food for man as well as food for animals, and grants earthly nourishment to all alike, He plainly indicates that human beings too were created mortal and made in animal rather than spiritual bodies, and that food was then necessary for man, as now, lest he be dissolved by death. Hence this state of soul or life in which man was created did not deserve praise in comparison with that spiritual life into which he was to be transferred. For of man [Col. 0765D] too, when created, it was not said, as of the other living creatures, that God saw that he was good, because that life to which he was not created in order to attain ought not to be commended in man; rather, he was to pass from it to one far better. Yet he could be praised jointly with the others, because in comparison with other things even this mortal state of man was to be commended as excellent and best. Nonetheless, compared with that which he was to become, it was not considered worthy of such praise that, by itself, it should be called best—that is, very good.

And it was so. This seems to refer not only to the creation of man or to the work of the sixth day, but to the whole sum of the preceding works [Col. 0766A]. He immediately comprehends them all when, breaking forth in their praise, He says: “All things which He had made”—that is, both the creation of heaven and earth and the additional works of light, completed in the creation of man. All things looked to man as to their end—that is, their final cause—because they were created or ordered for man’s sake. But man was created not for their sake, but only to glorify God. Therefore, when those things have reached humanity through their respective uses, they complete their course, as it were, at a goal and at the boundary of a course set before them. But man must come to God and rest in His vision as in the true Sabbath.

Observe that He did not say, “Seeing that all things [Col. 0766B] were very good,” as above it was said of the different works, “He saw that it was good.” Rather, He distinguished it thus: “God saw all things which He had made,” and afterwards, without repeating “He saw,” added: “and they were very good.” For, according to what we explained concerning each instance of “God saw that it was good”—that is, He caused us to see and understand this from their evident usefulness—it could be said of all that He saw all things good, at least on account of the work of the second day concerning the suspension of the waters, whose usefulness, as we said, we are not yet able to prove. Therefore, “He saw all things, and they were very good” means that, having perfectly known them, He judged nothing in them to require correction, but created all things good to precisely the degree to which they ought to be created good, so that nothing ought fittingly to have received more good in its [Col. 0766C] condition. This accords also with Plato’s opinion, by which he proves that the world, made by an omnipotent and non-envious God, could not have been made better. Moses too, considering this, declares that all things were created very good, although we believe that not even he was granted the ability to give an account of everything. Yet he does not call each thing by itself, but all things together, very good; for, as blessed Augustine also observes, individual things are good in themselves, but all things together are very good, because things which, considered in themselves, seem to have little or no value are very necessary in the whole totality of all things. Hence it is said: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all His wills” (Ps. 110:2).

The phrase “very good” perhaps raises for some the question what we are to say of certain poisonous animals or plants, or of certain others judged altogether superfluous, or finally of the apostate angels themselves, who by their pride became evil from the very beginning of their creation [Col. 0766D]. But because they afterwards acquired this malice from themselves and did not receive it in their creation, they were not made evil by God but corrupted themselves through pride. Therefore, because those spirits too were made good and without sin, though they did not remain such, one must not on this account deny that God’s works were good, since He created even those spirits good in the nature of their spiritual substance itself, which they stained but did not destroy by the blemish of pride. Thus [Col. 0767A] all God’s works are good, and every creature is to be called good, because they receive no sin or evil in the origin of their creation; rather, God grants to each only what is fitting, so that individual creatures are made by Him not merely good but best—that is, very good. And this is true not only when they were first created, but also daily when they are born, generated, or multiplied from those primordial causes. For even if an infant when born is not yet called a good human being in respect of morals, it is nevertheless a good creature. So too, when a foal is born, although it is not yet a good horse and fit for ordinary use, it is nevertheless a good creature and has received from God, in its creation, whatever is fitting for it. God does nothing, nor permits anything to occur, without reason, even [Col. 0767B] when miscarried fetuses are produced or creatures are born deformed. As for the shoots of plants which seem superfluous and which it is often proper for us to cut back, like our hair or nails, and as for the poisonous things mentioned: perhaps this suffices as an answer, that “they were very good” then, before human sin, not now, when, after sin, they have been turned into punishments for us. For it is certain that if man had not sinned, he would face danger from no poison nor torment from anything; rather, all animals, however savage or cruel, would be tame as domestic creatures and wholly subject to his dominion, so long as he himself remained subject in obedience to his Creator, who had subjected them to him. But after he neglected this, many [Col. 0767C] things among them became dangerous to him and were permitted to prevail against him even unto death, so that from them the wretched man might learn how greatly he had sinned by disobeying God. He had deserved to hold these things in his power only so long as he was subject to the supreme Power, from which he had received his own dominion over them. Thus irrational or even insensible creatures, made dangerous to him, now plainly teach how greatly he has sinned—acting as though by a certain divine force they perceive that they owe humanity no subjection once humanity has neglected to be subject to God, since they owed man nothing except for God’s sake. From this it is plainly shown that even things lacking reason or sense instruct us in our foolishness, lest we [Col. 0767D] obey anything that presumes to act against God, since we owe anything to anyone only for God’s sake and the end of all our actions must be placed in God.

Therefore no one is to be accused of disobedience, nor is anyone to be accused wherever the offense against God is avoided; that offense alone makes anyone guilty. Let anyone swear to another whatever that person requires of him, and let him keep the oath so long as he has not recognized that, in fulfilling what he swore, he would offend God. We have learned this, as was said, even from things devoid of reason, which now disregard our dominion, as though they understood that we had rejected the divine dominion. When they kill or torment us [Col. 0768A], exercising in this God’s judgment and inflicting due punishment, we falsely censure God’s works as though they were evil, because they turn to our pain according to our deserts. Otherwise we could find fault with punishment itself, though it is just, and with God or any just judge when he punishes the guilty and does what he ought. Therefore no works of God are to be called evil, although some are, as is just, dangerous and harmful, whether sometimes by killing the righteous they free them from the straits of this life, or cleanse them through afflictions. Nor should any things in creation be called superfluous, although they sometimes burden us greatly, because things of no use for one purpose are useful for another. Thus cut vine shoots, which would harm the vine’s fruit if they remained on it [Col. 0768B], are not useless for making fire or for other needs. Finally, the more this life is considered dangerous or penal, the more ardently that life is desired which is free from all these things. But what is properly called good in itself—that is, without qualification—or evil or indifferent, has, I think, been sufficiently defined in our second *Collation*.

But concerning creatures there is a question: whether, as some think, whatever exists and is not the Creator is called a creature; or whether only substances, and not their accidents, are to be called creatures; or whether certain things such as sitting are also things. For when it happens that someone sits, do we then say that some thing exists [Col. 0768C] which did not exist before, or that some thing has perished which existed when he was standing?

And there was evening. As on the other days he thus concludes their works with such an ending that nothing further is to be understood as belonging to the work of each day, so it seems that the same must be understood of this day also: namely, that nothing beyond what has been said is to be counted as belonging to the operation of this day, but that, as soon as the first parents were created, the whole work of this sixth day was completed. Hence, what is added in the following passages about the prohibition concerning the tree, the transgression of the command, the expulsion from Paradise, the naming imposed by Adam, or anything else, does not require us to maintain that all these things were done on the sixth day. Especially since it is uncertain [Col. 0768D] how long those parents remained in Paradise, so that all the things later reported as done there might have taken place before their expulsion. For both authority and reason seem to indicate that they were in Paradise for many years or days before the transgression, as we have decided to set forth later in its proper place.

Sixth day. That the prophet related that God completed his works in six days is not devoid of mystery: the perfection of the number itself bears witness to the perfection of the works. For this number called six is the first among those numbers called perfect. Three kinds of number are distinguished according to the calculation of their parts [Col. 0769A]: some are called perfect, others abundant, others deficient. Perfect numbers are those for which the calculation of their parts equals the sum of the whole. For example, six has three as its half, two as its third, and one as its sixth; these, joined together—one, two, three—make precisely six. Abundant numbers are those whose calculated parts, exceeding the number itself, produce a greater number, as with twelve. Six is its half, four its third, three its fourth, two its sixth, and one its twelfth; all these joined together make sixteen, which is plainly greater than twelve. Deficient numbers are those for which the total [Col. 0769B] cannot be produced by calculating and joining their parts, as with eight. This number has four as its half, two as its fourth, and one as its eighth; joined together they make seven, which is clearly less than eight.

Therefore, they are perfect. Since, as has been said, the elements were created and arranged and adorned with stars, plants, and living creatures, they were not merely made in creation but also made perfect in their ordering. By “their adornment” he means not only the things that are in them, but also those which come from them: not spiritual but bodily substances, which especially contribute to the world's excellence because they have their origin from it—“all their adornment,” namely that of heaven, such as the stars, and that of earth [Col. 0769C] or water, such as plants and animals.

Which he had made. That is, during the six preceding days. But how did he complete his work then and not on the sixth day, if he did nothing then? Thus we understand the seventh day as the entire future age of the world, during which he does not cease to multiply created species into some number of things from their already prepared natures, according to that saying of Truth: “My Father is working still, and I am working” [John 5:17]—as though he said: Just as he has not yet ceased to work, namely by daily multiplying what was made at first, so neither do I cease likewise to cooperate, as his coeternal Wisdom, through whom he makes all things.

And he rested. That is, by ceasing, as he immediately explains, [Col. 0769D] from the species which he had created—not from the number of things to be multiplied within them. For none of those species was afterwards to perish in such a way that its already prepared nature would not suffice of itself to restore it, just as it suffices to multiply the individual members of species. Even if we suppose that the phoenix is a species, or that some kinds of herbs or flowers at times perish, nature has nevertheless already been prepared from primordial causes so as to suffice for their restoration. He rightly says, therefore, “which he had completed,” namely in species, not what he was to multiply in the number of individuals. Although the mule was not created among the species of animals, and although many worms were later born from some putrefaction or corruption, they nevertheless had within those previously mentioned species a seedbed and some power of their future creation. [Col. 0770A] Although souls are not propagated from souls by transmission, because the species of soul had already been created, their daily multiplication does not prevent its being said that God rested from the whole, and so forth.

And he blessed and sanctified. That is, he preferred it to the other days and appointed it for celebration.

Had ceased. His saying “had ceased” explains what he had said, “he rested,” lest we perhaps suppose that he rested from labor.

Created. In the Word, in order that he might make in the work, according to the saying: “He spoke, and they were made.” Notice that it is not said of the seventh day, as it is of the others, “and there was evening and morning, the seventh day.” For God is not recorded as having made anything on it [Col. 0770B] as on the other days, but only as having rested; and the works of multiplication which occur in this seventh day will be carried on daily until the consummation of the age.

Since we have pursued, to the extent of our ability, the foregoing matters according to the root of the history and the truth of the event, it is fitting that we now investigate the same things by moral and then mystical exposition. An exposition is called moral whenever what is said is applied to the building up of conduct, in the manner in which the good things necessary for salvation ought to occur in us or be done by us; as when our exposition instructs the reader concerning faith, hope, charity, or good works. An exposition is called mystical when we teach that things were prefigured which were to be accomplished through Christ in the time of grace [Col. 0770C], or when we show that any future history is signified in advance.

## MORAL INTERPRETATION

That confused mass of heaven and earth, first created in matter and not yet brought into a created distinction of parts, is the human being, composed of a higher and lower substance—that is, soul and body—but still, as it were, unformed and disordered in morals. The flesh is not yet subjected to the spirit as it ought to be; rather, it dominates the spirit, and thus confuses and disturbs the natural order, until divine grace transforms and forms this animal human being into a spiritual one, just as it afterwards ordered that brutish and confused heap of elements. [Col. 0770D] Over this confusion, which is again figured through the fluid element of water, the Spirit broods, while divine goodness intends to make a spiritual person out of one still animal; and so, in a sense, it warms that confusion as a brooding bird does, in order to bring forth from it, as it were, a chick, while it prepares to reform the old human being into the new. This it accomplishes first by inspiring the light of faith, then hope, then charity, and finally by perfecting the person in works of charity, so that he may live not only for himself but also for others, and may be good not only in himself but may make others good as well, both by the example of his works and bestowed benefits and by the teaching of preaching.

The creation of light, therefore, is the illumination of faith. By inspiring this in whom [Col. 0771A] he wills, the Holy Spirit begins from this foundation the spiritual building of the soul, without which, as the Apostle says, it is impossible to please God. Thus the prophet rightly recalls immediately after the creation of heaven and earth that light was made. Hope follows faith. It raises the human being, formerly falling down through desire toward earthly things and drawn by diverse longings, as it were from earthly to heavenly things; it steadies and establishes a mind previously wandering in many directions; like an anchor it preserves a ship against every storm of adversity; and it strengthens the person, through desire for heavenly things, to endure or undertake whatever may be required. This is well figured by the suspension of the upper waters made on the second day, firmly established above through the interposition of heaven. [Col. 0771B]

On the third day, when the waters withdraw or are lowered through certain channels of the earth, the earth is dried and becomes dry land. So the soul, kindled with the fire of charity, subjects the flesh to the spirit; dried by this heat from the flow and desires of carnal concupiscence, it becomes in some manner dry land. Thus it becomes one of those waterless places through which the devil passes with his suggestions and finds no rest, because he cannot draw such a soul by its desires to consent. But in order that such a soul may also be perfected by works, the earth first produces plants, and afterward the luminaries set in the firmament provide light. The earth thus dried, as stated, produces plants when any soul displays in outward bodily works the charity with which it inwardly burns. If it grows to such perfection that it can also build up and enlighten others by the word of preaching, it will be a luminary in heaven: that is, the words of the preacher in the Church will be illumination for lesser persons, who are as yet, so to speak, earthly. This is what it means for them to “illuminate the earth.” [Col. 0771C]

And not only in day but also in night: for preaching is necessary to weak minds alike in prosperity and adversity, lest they be lifted up by the former or broken by the latter. Of such luminaries, building up others not only by example but also by word, the Apostle says: “Among whom you shine as luminaries” [Phil. 2:15]. And Truth himself says: “You are the light of the world” [Matt. 5:14]. Therefore, when the perfected person builds up others both through the light of works and through the instruction [Col. 0771D] of preaching, the world brings forth living creatures everywhere—flying creatures, walking creatures, and creeping creatures—that is, faithful persons of three orders: the continent, rulers, and married persons. Finally, that human being, created outside Paradise, is transferred into Paradise when one who has flourished in this life by so many good things through God's grace is transferred from this exile to the heavenly homeland, attaining, according to merits, first the Sabbath and then the eighth day.

## ALLEGORY

The six ages of the world are expressed by this number six of days in which the world was perfected and adorned. The first age of the world, from Adam to Noah, is as its infancy. The second, from then to Abraham, is as childhood. The third, extending to David, is as [Col. 0772A] adolescence. The fourth, to the Babylonian deportation, is as youth—that is, mature adulthood. The fifth, from there to Christ, is as old age. Finally, the sixth, extending to the end of the world, is as senility or decrepit old age.

Thus that confused and not-yet-distinguished heap of elements fittingly figures the first age of the world, uncultivated and rough, without law and discipline, which is called the world's infancy. It is rightly called infancy, because it was not yet able to form the words of God through the instruction of the Law, just as infants are not yet capable of speech. This age was destroyed by the Flood, just as the memory of things done in infancy is obliterated by forgetfulness.

The second age is not destroyed by the Flood, since each person can remember what he has done in childhood. [Col. 0772B] In this age the ark preserved the faithful amid the Flood, and, like a firmament set between waters, kept them unharmed from the waters raining down above and the waters flooding below.

In the third age the Law was given, to restrain by fear of punishments the flow of carnal desire in the ancient people. So on the third day the earth was freed from the lower waters, and immediately, germinating, produced its earthly offspring in herbs and trees. For the ancient people, desiring earthly rather than heavenly things, received an earthly promise; clinging chiefly to earthly desires, it was, as it were, an earthly generation, wholly leaning upon the earth and fixing its life in earthly things.

The luminaries made on the fourth day signify the light of the prophets [Col. 0772C] who, after the Law, spoke of Christ much more openly than the ancient Law had done. Thus Daniel says: “Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied,” both among men, as in Samuel and Nathan, and among women, as in Anna. Properly speaking, the age of prophets began from the time of Samuel, as is carefully expressed in the Acts of the Apostles, where it is written: “And all the prophets from Samuel and those after him,” and so forth [Acts 3:24]. Bede also bears witness while explaining that passage:

> “Although the patriarchs and holy persons of earlier times prophesied many things about Christ by words and deeds, nevertheless the age properly called that of the prophets—I mean those who wrote openly concerning the mystery of Christ and the Church—took its beginning from Samuel [Col. 0772D] and continued until the ending of the Babylonian captivity.”

The fifth age, like the old age of the world, signifies the failure of former good things, since the patriarchs and prophets had already passed away, the anointing was transferred to a foreigner, and sacrifice was no longer celebrated according to its former rite—something which the Babylonian captivity had also removed. In this old age, when the world was already languishing, the Savior was sent to renew the old human being and to preach baptism. In this baptism, human beings put off the old person and put on the new, as it is written: “All of you who have been baptized have put on Christ” [Rom. 6:3]; and thus, as it were, living creatures were brought forth from the waters.

In the sixth age the renewed human being is placed in Paradise [Col. 0773A], because after the Lord's Passion the heavenly entrance was opened to humanity to such an extent that it first celebrates the Sabbath in the soul and afterwards the eighth day in body and soul together. Hence the thief was told: “Today you will be with me in Paradise” [Luke 23:43], showing that heaven was opened to human beings only in this age.

These are the generations. As if he said: I rightly said, “he had ceased,” because these are the generations; no others will afterwards arise from some new preparation of nature: “the generations of heaven and earth.” That is, the species of things materially made from the elements, first signified, as we have said, through heaven and earth.

When they were created. That is, when these generations were first made, before this seventh day in which they are multiplied daily. [Col. 0773B]

In the day. That is, during the time of those six preceding days.

When the Lord made heaven and earth. In the Hebrew the order is changed thus: “when the Lord made earth and heaven,” whereas in the beginning it was said in the reverse order, “he created heaven and earth.” This change of order indicates a certain diversity of signification, in order to include the previously mentioned generations. For by earth and heaven he includes animals, and by shrub and herbs he includes plants. Animals, because they receive life not from moisture as plants do but from spirit—according to Gregory's distinction of three vital spirits—are here indicated by earth and heaven [Col. 0773C], since they consist, in respect of body, of a bodily and heavy substance, and, in respect of soul, of a spiritual and light substance. Because bodies were formed before spirits were infused, he rightly named earth before heaven here. He seems also to suggest concerning the stars, if he includes all things made from the elements, that certain spirits are present in them, by which they may be animals and numbered among animals, as philosophers assert. Blessed Augustine professes himself so uncertain of this that he says he does not know whether the sun and moon belong to the society of angels, as we mentioned above.

[Col. 0773D] Shrub of the field. That is, still wild and not yet cultivated, grafted, or tended by human care as now.

Would spring up in the earth. That is, it would bear fruit, scattered through all lands as it now prospers through the irrigation of rains.

Of the region. In the Hebrew, “of the field,” as above; as if he said: still uncultivated, and not multiplied, as it is now, through propagation and the aid of rains. Hence he adds:

For not yet. That is, rain had not yet fallen, by which this multiplication then, as now, might occur throughout the world, while a human being cultivated the earth, as now happens—since the human being who would cultivate the earth did not yet [Col. 0774A] exist. This he immediately adds, saying:

And there was no human being. He does not simply say “there was not,” since the human being too was included above among the generations of heaven and earth and shown to have been made; rather, there was no human being to work the earth, because laborious cultivation was not yet necessary for him—a cultivation which he afterwards received as punishment for sin and which he now practices everywhere on earth.

But a spring. Lest someone perhaps ask from where plants had the moisture by which they were nourished or preserved when there was no rain, he answers that thin water, rising from below like a spring, watered those parts of the world in which plants were scattered. Notice that above, throughout the seven [Col. 0774B] days, God is called only God and not also Lord; here, however, where he recalls the completed generations of heaven and earth, he calls him not only God but also Lord, and thereafter frequently designates him by the title Lord. For the name Lord belongs only in relation to creatures over which he has dominion and rule—and not merely to some creatures but to all together. Hence it seemed fitting that this title be used only after the completion of all things.

Therefore he formed. This also refers to what was stated concerning the creation of the human being on the sixth day, when it says: “And God created the human being,” and so forth. There it was stated that the human being, both male and female, was created, but the manner of creation was not expressed. Here he carefully reveals it, teaching that the man's body was first formed [Col. 0774C] from the mud of the earth and then a soul was infused; but that the woman was not created independently, but taken from the man, as the following passages teach. I said continuously that the human being was created, but did not state the manner of creation; now, therefore, I shall do so. This is what he now does in saying: “he formed the human being,” that is, he fashioned the human body into the form which we now have.

From the mud of the earth. That is, from moist earth, as it were compacted and not loose; and thus he infused a soul into the already-created body. From this he clearly indicates that the human soul is unlike other souls by the very manner of its creation. In the creation of other living creatures [Col. 0774D], indeed, earth or water is said to have brought them forth with body and soul together. This suggests that their souls too arise from the elements themselves, as a kind of rarity or subtlety of them. On account of that subtlety those souls are also called spirits, just as wind is sometimes called spirit in comparison with earth and water, which are of a grosser and more bodily substance. He also uses a careful term when he says that the human being was formed from *humus*, “earth,” rather than created. For where something is made from matter with form added to it, it is properly said to be formed.

Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XI, chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 0773D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXXII, col. 397, and passim]:

> “The human being (*homo*) is so called because he was made from earth (*humus*), as Genesis also says: ‘And God created the human being from the mud of the earth.’ [Col. 0775A] Yet, by an improper usage, the whole composed of both substances—that is, the union of soul and body—is called human being; for properly speaking, the human being is so called from earth. Again: The human being is twofold, inward and outward: the inward human being is the soul; the outward human being is the body. Again: The human soul is not the human being; only the body, made from earth, is the human being.”

Bede, *On Genesis*, book II:

> “And he called their names Adam on the day when they were created.” Adam means “human being,” so that it may be applied to both sexes. Hence it is rightly said: “He called their names Adam,” that is, “human being.” As the Latin *homo* is named from *humus*, so among the Hebrews Adam is named from earth. Thus it can also be interpreted as “earthly” or “red earth.” Among the Greeks, however [Col. 0775B], “human being” has another etymology. For he is called ἄνθρωπος (*anthrōpos*) because he ought to look upon things above and raise the eyes of the mind to contemplate heavenly things.

He breathed the breath of life. That is, as it were directly and not from some material beginning, he gave a soul to the already formed body, so that this soul might have its being from God alone as its principle and not from another primordial cause. He says “breath of life” to distinguish it from the blowing of wind, which is also called breath but does not give life; similarly, the soul is sometimes called a breath, according to Isaiah: “I have made every breath” [Isa. 57:16]. The soul is also rightly compared to blowing or breath because it is most evident whether it remains in the body through exhaling or breathing, since life cannot be preserved in animals without these. [Col. 0775C]

Into his face. I say, the breath into his face—that is, into the face of the human being—so that this soul alone, unlike those of other living creatures, might possess knowledge or understanding through reason. For the face, by which each person is recognized, signifies knowledge.

And he became. That is, the human being was completed.

A living soul. That is, through such a soul as always lives, since it has no failing.

A paradise of delight. That is, a delightful garden, so that the human being might attend not only to how much he owed God because of the dignity of his creation, but also because of the charm and pleasantness of the place, chosen from the whole world, in which he was placed. [Col. 0775D] Some maintain, concerning this place, that Paradise is located in the eastern part of the globe, though separated by an immense intervening distance of ocean or lands from all the regions now inhabited by humankind. Hence the waters of the Flood, which covered the surface of our world to a great height, could not reach it. This seems especially apparent from the fact that Enoch, transferred into Paradise before the Flood, could not have been submerged.

Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*:

> “Paradise from the beginning,” etc. From this it is most clearly proved that before God made heaven and earth, he had previously established Paradise. And in Hebrew one reads: “But the Lord God had planted a paradise [Col. 0776A] in Eden from the beginning.”

Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XIV, chapter 3, on Asia, in which Paradise is located:

> “Paradise is a place situated in the regions of the East; its name is translated from Greek into Latin as ‘garden.’ In Hebrew, however, it is called *eden*, which in our language is interpreted ‘delights.’ The two together make ‘garden of delights.’ It is planted with every kind of tree and fruit-bearing tree and also contains the tree of life. There is neither cold nor heat there, but a perpetual mildness of air. From its midst a spring bursts forth and waters the entire grove; it divides into four rivers which arise from it. After sin, access to this place was barred to humankind. For it is enclosed on every side by a flaming *romphaea*, that is, girded by a wall of fire, so that its blaze almost joins heaven. A guard of cherubim—that is, angels—has also been stationed above the flame of the *romphaea* to repel evil spirits, so that the flame may drive back human beings and angels may drive back evil angels, lest access to Paradise be open to any flesh or spirit guilty of transgression.”

When it says “from the beginning,” “of the planting” is understood. It indicates that Paradise existed before the other plants, so that it might possess some delight beyond other places when the human being was brought into it—prepared beforehand with greater care in proportion as more time was expended upon its preparation. [Col. 0776B]

He placed the human being whom he had formed. That is, the man whose formation has already been described. The man was made outside Paradise from the mud of the earth and transferred into Paradise; but the woman was created in Paradise from the man. [Col. 0776C] Yet she expelled both the man and herself from Paradise, as what follows plainly relates. From this it is clearly indicated that salvation concerns dispositions rather than places, since the woman, made in the better place, became worse through seduction.

And he brought forth. He explains why he said “of delight”: beautiful to behold and pleasant for eating, so that it might delight by its appearance and refresh by the pleasantness of its taste.

The tree of life also. Since he has said “every tree,” why does he also mention these two trees, as though they had not been among all the trees delightful to see and taste—especially when it is written in the following passages concerning the tree in which the transgression occurred that the woman saw that the tree was good and delightful? But “also” was surely said not because of a difference in the kinds of trees, but because of a difference in the place where he set and joined these two trees: in the middle of Paradise, not around its perimeter as the others were. [Col. 0776D] For when he had said that the earth brought forth in Paradise the other trees as well as these, he did not distinguish how they were placed or by what arrangement they were disposed in relation to one another. He does this now, describing these as in the middle and the others as arranged around them.

He calls the tree of life that tree which was created and granted them as a medicine to preserve life and bodily soundness without the failing of old age. Thus it is written in the following passages concerning those who were expelled from Paradise after sin: “Lest perhaps he take from the tree of life and live forever.” And again: “He placed cherubim before Paradise to guard the way of the tree of life.” [Col. 0777A] The other trees they possessed for daily food, to sustain life and refresh the body, not for medicinal health. The tree of knowledge of good and evil is so called not from what it received in its creation, but from what resulted in those first parents through the transgression they committed in it. For by this they learned from experience itself the difference between the good of the delightful life which they formerly possessed and the evil of the punishment which they incurred—as, it were, between rest and labor.

And the tree of knowledge. It was in the middle of Paradise together with the tree of life, so that when the human being saw that this tree, the better and more necessary one, had been granted to him, he might be especially recalled from transgressing the other, if not by love of God, at least by the desire [Col. 0777B] to retain so great a benefit established in the tree of life. Scripture gives no authoritative definition of what kind of tree it was in which they transgressed. Some, however, have thought it was a fig tree, chiefly because those parents are later said to have sewn coverings for themselves from fig leaves. They also wish to understand in this way the Lord's reply to Nathanael, when he asked how he knew him: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you” [John 1:48]—as though the Lord said: You have not only now first become known to me; from the beginning I knew you by foreknowledge as existing in the first parents in the seed. For the Apostle likewise says that Levi was in Abraham's loins.

[Col. 0777C] But the Hebrews maintain that this tree of knowledge of good and evil was a vine, placed beside the tree of life in the middle of Paradise, just as we often now see a vine supported by an elm and joined to it, as it were, in one body. They also explain that the vine is called the tree of knowledge of good and evil because wine produced from its fruit, taken moderately or immoderately, makes a person knowing in a good or evil manner; that is, it gives him good or bad judgment, sharpening or corrupting his intelligence. Hence they understand that the fruit in which the first parents transgressed was a grape, according to the prophet's saying: “Our fathers ate a sour grape” [Jer. 31:29], that is, the fruit through which we incurred the bitterness of punishment. Immediately explaining this, he says: “And the teeth of the children were numbed” [ibid.], that is, the punishment transmitted to their descendants [Col. 0777D] continues.

Perhaps this opinion also receives fitting support from the fact that immediately after eating this tree they felt incitements of lust. This fruit, or the wine pressed from it, is plainly of a hot nature and most strongly stirs toward sexual excess, according to the Apostle: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” [Eph. 5:18]. In view of this movement of lust, which then occurred in those first human beings and because of which, ashamed, they covered their genitals, that tree seems fittingly to have been called the tree of knowledge of good and evil. Finally, Adam's descendants later so abhorred or resolved to avoid tasting this tree, by which Adam's transgression consigned both himself and his descendants to punishment, that before the Flood no one is believed to have touched wine, [Col. 0778A] as though remembering the punishment incurred through contact with the forbidden fruit. After the Flood Noah planted a vineyard and, as though forgetful of the aforesaid transgression, is recorded to have become drunk with wine; immediately, with his genitals uncovered, his shamefulness appeared. So it had happened in the first parents, who after committing the eating of the forbidden tree are said to have been made naked, immediately ashamed of their nakedness, and hastening at once to cover their shameful parts—as Noah's two sons also did, while the third mocked his father.

And a river. This also belongs to the description of the place's pleasantness, so that the delight of a river, together with the trees, might please its inhabitants.

From the place of delight. That is, from Paradise itself—not [Col. 0778B] flowing in from outside, but rising within Paradise itself—so that it might be shown to contain within itself all things necessary and not receive them from elsewhere.

To water it. And to confer perpetual greenery upon it, so that no rain would be needed there.

From there. Namely, from where it rose out of the earth, or from Paradise itself when it went outside, although in Paradise it was, as it were, a single river.

Into four heads. That is, the division is made into the sources of four rivers. Where this division begins, there the rivers begin to be distinguished, since before this division all that water, running in one channel, must be called one river, or one spring and source of those four rivers.

[Col. 0778C] The name of one. Namely, of one head among these four. For just as each of these four rivers is distinguished by its head, so it is named by its head, because all the water of that river bears this or that name from the beginning of the division until it enters the sea.

It is. This relative pronoun *ipse*, although masculine by grammatical construction [Col. 0778D], must be referred to the name Phison, not to the preceding phrase, “one head.”

The whole land. He says this for the greater part, since no river can flow around an entire land, as it cannot possibly flow out through the part into which it flows.

Evilat. That is, India, which derives this name from the fact that it was occupied after the Flood by Evilat, son of Jectan, son of Heber, from whom the Hebrews derive. Pliny says that the regions of India abound in veins of gold more than other lands.

Bdellium is an aromatic tree, black in color; its resin is bright, bitter in taste, and of good scent, but more fragrant when soaked in wine.

Onyx is a precious stone so called because it contains a mixed color or resembles a human fingernail. For the Greeks call a fingernail ὄνυχον (*onychon*). The ancient translation has, in place of these, “carbuncle and green stone.” A carbuncle is a stone of fiery color, which illuminates the darkness of night. A green stone has a green appearance. [Col. 0779A] It takes its name from the leek, which the Greeks call πράσον (*prason*). When he describes the excellence of any river issuing from Paradise, this appears to redound to the praise of that place, as though the river drew its abundance in these goods from the place of its birth. Notice that, to make these rivers better known, he distinguishes them not only by their names but also by the lands to which they reach, so that, being chiefly known there from their usefulness, they may be more highly commended. When he calls these rivers first, second, third, or fourth, this seems not to be understood according to the order of their placement but rather the order of the narrative—unless someone perhaps says that this order also obtains in their aforesaid division, so that one after another is divided first into its own channel from the very source of its origin.

It is Euphrates. He does not describe this one by the places through which it runs [Col. 0779B] as he does the others, because, as they say, it was nearer and better known to the Jewish people. These rivers are very well known to the peoples through whom they flow. Antiquity changed the names of two of them. Geon is the one now called the Nile; Phison was the river now called the Ganges. The other two, Tigris and Euphrates, retained their ancient names. But it may cause difficulty that the sources of some of these rivers are said to be known and those of others wholly unknown. Thus it cannot be taken literally that they divide from one spring [perhaps: “derive from one spring”], when it ought rather to be believed that the place of Paradise, remote [Col. 0779C] from human knowledge, divides into four waters, as the most trustworthy Scripture testifies. But rivers whose sources are said to be known are thought to run somewhere beneath the earth and, after passing through long stretches of regions, burst forth elsewhere, where they are said to be known as though at their own sources. Who does not know that some waters are accustomed to do this? They judge that this also resolves the following passage of Boethius, who said in book V of *The Consolation* concerning the Tigris and Euphrates:

> Where, among the crags of the Achaemenian rock,  
> the swift-fleeting battle, its darts turned back,  
> fixes them in the breasts of its pursuers.  
>
> Tigris and Euphrates issue forth from one spring.
>
> (*Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy*, V, metrum 1, vv. 1–3.)

Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XIII [Note: [Col. 0779D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXXII, col. 490]: “It is called Geon because, by the increase of its overflow, it irrigates the land of Egypt.” Γῆ in Greek means “earth” in Latin. Among the Egyptians this river is called the Nile because of the mud which it carries and which makes the land fertile; hence it too is called Nile, as if *Niahomon* [read: νέαν ἰλύν, “new mud”]. For formerly the Nile was called *Melo* in Latin. The Ganges, which Scripture surnames Phison, proceeds toward the regions of India. It is called Phison, that is, “a multitude,” because, with ten great rivers joined to it, it is filled and made into one. It is called the Ganges after Gangarus, a king of India. It is said to rise like the Nile and to burst forth over the lands of the East. The river Tigris, passing through Mesopotamia toward the Assyrians, after many windings flows into the Dead Sea. It is called by this name because of its speed, like the beast called the tiger, which runs with excessive swiftness. The Euphrates, the most abundant river of Mesopotamia, flowing through the midst of Babylon, is rich in gems. It received its name from crops or fertility; for in Hebrew *Euphrata* means “fertility.” For it irrigates Mesopotamia in certain places as the Nile irrigates Alexandria. Sallust, a most reliable author, moreover affirms that the Tigris and Euphrates spring from one source in Armenia, but, proceeding by different routes, are divided at a great distance, with many miles lying between them. Yet the land encircled by them is called Mesopotamia. From this Jerome observed that the rivers of Paradise must be understood otherwise. Bede, *On the Nature of Things* [Note: [Col. 0780D] *Patrologia*, vol. XC, col. 262]: “Egypt uses the Nile as rain, rejecting showers and clouds because of the heat of the sun. For in the month of May, while the mouths through which it flows into the sea are blocked by banks of sand thrown up by the waves as the west wind blows, it gradually swells and, driven back, irrigates the plains of Egypt; but when the wind ceases and the banks of sand are broken through, it returns to its channel.”

Therefore he took. For that place of Paradise was indeed so delightful and pleasant. Fittingly, the man was made outside Paradise and transferred thence into Paradise, so that he might desire and strive to retain its pleasantness all the more, insofar as it appeared to surpass that outer land in which he had been created.

[Col. 0780C] To cultivate it. That is, to cultivate Paradise itself and, by preserved obedience, to keep it for himself, lest he should lose it by being expelled through transgression. But he at once indicates the command in which he was to obey there, when he says:

And he commanded him. He does not say “them” in the plural, but “him” in the singular, referring only to the man whom he said had been transferred into Paradise—although the woman later acknowledges that God had given this command jointly to her and the man, saying: “Of the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of Paradise God commanded us not to eat.” Hence it must be understood that, when in this place the Lord forbids that tree to the man, he speaks in him generally to humankind, not directing his speech specifically to that individual person, but generally to human nature: that is, absolutely forbidding anyone of human nature to presume upon it. Thus also when a priest, sanctifying some water which is present, says, “He who walked upon you with his feet, who changed you into wine,” the speech is directed to the element water, not to that particular water before him.

But how is it true that God placed the man in Paradise in order that he might cultivate and keep it for himself, when it never came to pass that the man kept it for himself? For we say that something is done so that something else may result or occur in two ways: namely, according to intention [Col. 0781A] and according to the effect of the outcome. Thus, if I say of someone that he went out to battle in order to kill, or that he went out in order to be killed: the former is understood as done with his intention of killing another; the latter as done in such a way that he happened thereby to be killed. But when we say that God placed man in Paradise so that he might keep it for himself, he did not do this with the intention of bringing about what he knew would never be; nor did he do it in such a way that this would thereby happen. Therefore, “to cultivate it,” and so forth, must be understood as though it were said that, by placing him there, God established him as the cultivator and keeper of that place, commanding him to cultivate and preserve it for himself: to cultivate it, indeed, by delightfully performing some work there—such as tending the trees or herbs [Col. 0781B]—rather than with laborious toil.

It may also be asked, if this command was audible, in what language it was uttered which Adam could understand, since he himself is later reported to have invented language when the animals were brought to him and he assigned them names. But we know that many things in the Scriptures are sometimes recounted out of the order in which they occurred, either by interruption or anticipation. For behold, above, on the sixth day, after both man and woman were created but the manner of their creation had not yet been explained, that creation is afterwards repeated and carefully and fully narrated, as though it were then occurring for the first time and had not occurred earlier. Therefore, just as the thing previously done is later repeated because its manner had been interrupted, so it is not to be disapproved if certain matters are here related by anticipation out of their order: namely, that Adam first established utterances for speech, before he heard the Lord’s command in those utterances which he himself had established, so that he could understand them; utterances in which he himself later said, “This now is bone of my bones,” and so forth; in which the serpent spoke with the woman, or the woman with the serpent; and in which the Lord himself again spoke with Adam and Eve in rebuking their sin, or they with the Lord.

For this reason, those who think that the first parents lived in Paradise for some years before sin seem to have no little reason on their side, even though they begot no child there. For, leaving other matters aside, no short interval of time could have sufficed for the invention of a language; nor is the mere invention [Col. 0781D] of names, mentioned here alone, contained in the utterances reported to have been spoken in Paradise. On the contrary, none of the names of land animals or birds which Adam is said to have assigned is contained in these utterances.

That they lived innocently in Paradise for several years seems to be established, in addition to the reason stated, by the authority of the prophet Malachi, with whom blessed Augustine strongly agrees on this point. Accordingly, introducing the prophet’s words in book XX, chapter 26, of *The City of God*, the same doctor says:

“We must explain how the words ‘as in the former days and as in former years’ (Mal. III, 4) are to be understood. Perhaps he recalls that time when the first human beings were in Paradise. [Col. 0782A] For then, pure and whole from every stain and blemish of sin, they offered themselves to God as utterly spotless sacrifices. But after they were expelled thence because of the transgression they had committed, and human nature was condemned in them—excepting the one Mediator and infants still in their infancy after the washing of regeneration—no one is clean from defilement, as it is written: ‘Not even an infant whose life upon earth is one day’ (Job XIV, 4, according to the Septuagint). If it is answered that those also may rightly be said to offer sacrifices in righteousness who offer in faith—for ‘the righteous shall live by faith’ (Rom. I, 17)—although he deceives himself if he says that he has no sin (I John I, 8), and therefore says now that he lives by faith: will anyone say that this time of faith is to be made equal to that end, when those who are to offer in righteousness will be cleansed by the fire of the last judgment? And therefore, since after such cleansing the righteous must be believed to have no sin, certainly that time, insofar as it concerns having no sin, is comparable to no time except when the first human beings lived in Paradise, before transgression, in a most innocent blessedness. Thus it is rightly understood that this was signified when it was said, ‘as in the former days and as in former years.’

“For, through Isaiah also, after a new heaven and a new earth have been promised, among other things which he sets forth there concerning the blessedness of the saints through allegories and riddles—whose fitting exposition concern for avoiding prolixity has forbidden us to give—he says: ‘The days of my people [Col. 0782C] shall be according to the days of the tree of life’ (Isa. LXV, 22). Who has touched the sacred writings and does not know where God planted the tree of life? When those human beings were separated from its food, after their own wickedness expelled them from Paradise, a fiery and dreadful guard was placed around that tree. But if anyone maintains that the days of the tree of life mentioned by the prophet Isaiah are these present days of the Church, and that Christ himself is prophetically called the tree of life because he is the Wisdom of God, of whom Solomon says, ‘She is a tree of life to all who embrace her’ (Prov. III, 18); and further maintains that those first human beings spent no years in Paradise, from which they were expelled so swiftly that they begot no child there, and therefore that that time cannot be understood in the phrase, ‘as in the former days and as in former years’—I pass over this question, lest I be compelled to examine everything at length in order that the truth when made manifest may establish one of these positions. For I see another sense, lest we should think that the former days and former years were foretold to us through the prophet as a great gift consisting in carnal sacrifices. For those sacrifices of the old Law, in the various animals which seemed to be offered spotless and wholly without defect, signified holy persons—such as Christ alone was found to be, entirely without sin.”

Yet, in order to make an effort to satisfy also those who wish the first parents to have spent not even the interval of one day in Paradise, perhaps the Lord there used certain signs instead of speech, whose meaning it was easy for him to inspire in the man. For the serpent too is believed to have spoken to the woman not in words but in hissing; and those first parents were of such keen intelligence that they recognized the serpent’s dispositions from its hissing, or those of birds from their calls. If we posit this, we are by no means compelled to maintain that Adam established language in Paradise; rather, the prophet related by anticipation what occurred outside Paradise.

From every. Only what follows—“but of the tree of knowledge,” and so forth—seems to belong to the command. What precedes, “from every tree,” seems rather a permission [Col. 0784A] than a command. For they would not be guilty if they did not eat from all the other trees while they were in Paradise. Hence the woman too, replying to the serpent, says only that she received a command concerning the tree which is in the midst of Paradise.

On whatever day. By a threat of punishment he exhorts him to obedience, saying that on whatever day he should touch that forbidden tree, because of the death of the soul—that is, the sin then committed—he would afterwards incur the death of the body: as it were, a double death.

The remainder is lacking.

[Col. 0783]

# FIVE BOOKS OF PETER ABAELARD’S COMMENTARY ON ST PAUL’S EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

(Edition of the Works, 1616, p. 489, from the manuscript codex of the monastery of St Michael in Peril of the Sea.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0783B] All divine Scripture, in the manner of rhetorical discourse, aims either to teach or to move. It teaches when it indicates what ought to be done or avoided. It moves when, by its sacred admonitions, it either draws our will back from evils by dissuasion or directs it toward goods by persuasion, so that we may now wish to fulfil what we have learned must be fulfilled, or to avoid the contrary things. Accordingly, on this principle the teaching both of the Old and of the New Testament is threefold.

In the Old Testament, the Law, contained in the five books of Moses, first teaches the Lord’s commands. Then the prophets or histories, together with the other Scriptures, exhort people to accomplish in deed what has already been commanded, and stir human affections to obey the commands. For when the prophets or holy [Col. 0783C] Fathers perceived that the people were insufficiently obedient to the divine commands, they added admonitions, in order to draw them to obedience by promises or threats. It was also necessary to add examples from the histories, in which both the reward of the obedient and the punishment of transgressors were placed before their eyes. These are those old rags which, bound round ropes, were used to draw Jeremiah from the pit (Jer. XXXVIII, 11): namely, examples of the ancient Fathers, which are joined to sacred admonitions in order to draw the sinner from the depths of vices.

Likewise, the discipline of the New Testament is threefold. In it the Gospel takes the place of the Law, teaching the pattern of true and perfect righteousness. Then the Epistles, together with the Apocalypse, are placed in the position of the prophets, exhorting people to obey the Gospel. The Acts of the Apostles and the greater number of Gospel narratives contain sacred histories. From this it is clear that, since the Gospel’s purpose is to teach, the Epistles and the Acts of the Apostles serve that purpose by moving us to obey the Gospel or by confirming us in what the Gospel teaches. Therefore, after the Gospel, which is perfect teaching, no one should disparage the Epistles as superfluous, since we should remember that they were written more for admonition than for teaching, although they contain certain wholesome instructions or counsels which the Gospel does not contain. Hence, writing to the Corinthians, he says: “But to the rest I speak, not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife” (I Cor. [Col. 0784C] VII, 12), and so forth. He also teaches that circumcision and the other carnal observances of the Law ought now to cease, which had not yet been revealed in the Gospel. Writing to Timothy, he likewise teaches much concerning episcopal, priestly, and levitical rank which the Gospel had not expressed.

Nevertheless, we say that the Gospel’s teaching was handed down as perfect insofar as it sufficed for the pattern of true righteousness and for the salvation of souls, though not insofar as it concerned the adornment of the Church or the enlargement of salvation itself. For among the goods of a city, some pertain to its preservation and some to its enlargement, as Julius also mentions at the end of the second book of the *Rhetoric*. Things pertaining to preservation are those without which a city cannot stand secure and safe, such as farmland, forests, and other things of this kind that are very necessary to a city. Other things are not so necessary but rather more distinguished: when it possesses, beyond what is necessary, certain things which make it worthier than other cities or render it more secure—such as fine buildings, an abundance of treasures, extensive dominion, and the like.

Perhaps those things which the Gospel had handed down concerning faith, hope, charity, and the sacraments could suffice for salvation, even if apostolic institutions were not added, nor any disciplines or dispensations of the holy Fathers, such as canons, decrees, monastic rules, and the many writings of saints full of sacred admonitions. For no transgression would be chargeable for omitting these things if no command concerning them had been issued. Yet the Lord willed that certain additional commands or dispensations should be supplied by the apostles and holy Fathers, through which the Church, as his city, might be adorned or enlarged, or the safety of its citizens be more securely fortified—as is easy to show in each case. Thus the Lord reserved for his disciples or their successors certain matters to be commanded or arranged, so that, having granted them also to perform works in miracles greater than his own, he might reserve for them a certain authority to issue commands; thereby exalting them further and making them so much more beloved by his Church as the Church recognized them to be more necessary to itself.

Since, then, as stated, the intention of the Gospels is to teach us the things necessary for salvation, the Epistles pursue this purpose by moving us to obey evangelical teaching, or by handing down certain matters for enlarging and more securely safeguarding salvation. This, indeed, is the general purpose of all the Epistles. But in each one it is appropriate to seek its particular purpose, subject matter, or manner of treatment. Thus in this Epistle itself the purpose is to recall the Romans converted from Jews and Gentiles—who, in proud contention, preferred themselves to one another—to true humility and fraternal concord. It accomplishes this in two ways: by magnifying the gifts of divine grace and by diminishing the merits of our works, so that no one may now presume to glory in works, but may attribute wholly to divine grace whatever strength he possesses, recognizing that he has received from it whatever good he has. In these two matters, then—our works and divine grace—the entire sum of the subject matter consists. The manner of treatment is the depreciation of our works, as stated, and the magnification of grace, so that no one may presume to glory in works, but “he who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31).

The Gentiles gloried because they had so quickly submitted to the Gospel, as it is written: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII, 45); and because they had not previously sinned in the things they had done, since they had as yet known the Lord through no law. But the Jews were especially puffed up by the bodily observances of the Law. Therefore, in order to crush the pride of both, he attacks now these, now those, and sometimes both together in alternating invectives: showing that the Gentiles were inexcusable in their sins, since, although they had not received the written Law, they possessed a natural law through which they could know God and distinguish evil from good; and showing that the Jews cannot be justified, as they suppose, by works of the Law, but that both peoples have obtained through the grace of God alone, who calls them, the mercy by which they are justified.

The question is raised concerning these Romans to whom this Epistle is addressed: by whose preaching had they previously been converted? Ecclesiastical History, Jerome, and Gregory of Tours report that they had already been converted through the apostle Peter. Haymo, however, takes the opposite view, saying that they were not first instructed in the faith by Peter or by any of the twelve apostles, but by certain other believing Jews who came from Jerusalem to Rome. Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 14, says: “In the times of Claudius, the mercy of divine providence brought Peter to the city of Rome. On arriving, he first opened in the city of Rome, by the keys of his Gospel, the gate of the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, when the bright light of the Word of God had arisen for the city of Rome, the darkness of Simon, together with its author, was extinguished.”

Jerome too, on this Epistle, where it is written, “That I may impart to you some spiritual grace,” says thus [Note: [Col. 0785D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXX, col. 648]: “Paul says that he wishes to confirm the Romans, who hold the faith through Peter’s preaching: not because they had not received it from Peter, but so that, with two apostles and teachers bearing witness, their faith might be strengthened.” Gregory of Tours likewise, *Histories*, book I, chapter 25, records [Note: [Col. 0785D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXI, col. 173]: “The apostle Peter comes to Rome under the emperor Claudius; and there, preaching and with very many miracles, he most clearly proved that Christ is the Son of God. For from those days Christians began to exist in the city of Rome.” But Haymo, in the prologue to his exposition of this Epistle, speaks thus [Note: [Col. 0786D] *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, col. 361]:

“The Apostle wrote this Epistle to the Romans from Corinth. They were not first instructed by Peter himself, nor by any one of the twelve disciples, but by certain believing Jews [Col. 0786D] who came from Jerusalem to Rome, where the ruler of the world resided and to whom they themselves were subject; they preached to the Romans the faith which they had learned at Jerusalem.”

It should be noted, however, that if we carefully consider what has been said, there will be no disagreement between the earlier doctors and Haymo. For if we read through the aforementioned chapter of Ecclesiastical History in full, we shall find that it says Peter was the first of all the apostles, not of all teachers, to preach to the Romans. Jerome likewise, when he says that the Romans received or held the faith through Peter’s preaching, offers no obstacle, since this could have been done not through Peter himself but through Peter’s disciples coming from Jerusalem. Haymo, however, denies that it was done through Peter’s own person. Hence, when Peter is named by him, *ipse* (“himself”) is added. Moreover, Haymo does not say that Peter did not instruct them, but that he did not do so first. And when the aforesaid Gregory says that Peter preached at Rome under Claudius, he does not add that Peter preached first, but that he openly proved, by many miraculous powers, that Christ is the Son of God. What he further adds—that Christians then began to exist at Rome—can be understood to mean that they were made known through Peter at that time, although they may earlier have been hidden.

Although this Epistle is not believed to have been written first, it was nevertheless placed first by the holy Fathers because it is directed against the first vice and root of the others, namely pride, as it is written: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X, 15). Or it was placed first because it is addressed to the Church of the first see. Haymo says of this [Note: [Col. 0787B] *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, col. 365]:

“This Epistle does not hold in the collection of Epistles the order in which it was written, [Col. 0788A] but it obtained primacy because of the dignity of the Romans, who at that time ruled all nations. This was done not by the apostle, but rather by the person who took care to gather all his Epistles into one body.”

The same author says [Note: [Col. 0787B] *Ibid.*, col. 366]: “Romans are interpreted ‘lofty’ or ‘thundering,’ because at the time when the Apostle sent them this Epistle, they ruled all nations and thundered forth commands.”

The Apostle is believed to have sent this Epistle to Rome from Corinth through Phoebe, a minister of the Church at Cenchreae, a place near Corinth—indeed, Corinth’s harbor—as Origen mentions in his commentary on this Epistle. At the end of the Epistle the Apostle himself says of Phoebe: “I commend to you Phoebe our sister,” and so forth [Col. 0788B] (Rom. XVI, 1). Explaining this passage, Jerome says [Note: [Col. 0788B] *Patrologia*, vol. XXX, col. 714]: “Here the Apostle shows that no distinction is to be made between the person of a man and a woman, when, as is reported, he sends a letter to the Romans through a woman,” and so forth.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0787]

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0787B]

Paul. Following the custom of those who write letters, he prefaces a greeting, since he exhorts them to true salvation. [Col. 0787C] He sets down this greeting, together with certain matters attached to it, as a kind of prologue, in which he briefly makes them attentive, receptive, and well disposed.
