He makes them attentive both by his own person and by that of Christ who sends him, and also by the thing itself—that is, the evangelical teaching to whose observance he exhorts them. By his own person, indeed, he commends himself as one set apart for the apostleship and called by God to preach the Gospel. He also commends the person of the Lord Jesus Christ, whom he calls the Son of God and declares to be the one promised to the Fathers as the Redeemer of humankind, conceived of the Holy Spirit, and a magnificent raiser of the dead. Nor does he omit to commend the Gospel, when he recalls that it was promised through the holy Scriptures of God’s prophets. Their receptiveness, moreover, is indicated in this very point: by saying that the office of evangelical preaching has been entrusted to him, he indicates that he will write concerning matters that belong to the teaching of the Gospel.

And, since he calls himself Christ’s servant and their servant, he makes them well disposed toward himself both through his humility and through the love which they had for Christ; also through what he adds concerning his love for them—namely, that he especially gives thanks to God for their conversion and desires to come to them to instruct or [Col. 0788B] strengthen them further. Let us now proceed to the text.

It should be noted that, according to Rufinus’s exposition of this Epistle—which exposition is believed to be a translation of Origen’s exposition—this Apostle had two names even before his conversion: namely, he was formerly called both Paul and Saul, as, he says, it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Saul, who is also Paul.” According to Jerome, Augustine, and others, the Apostle changed his own name after the proconsul Paul whom he first converted by a miracle. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles that he took this name, so that he who had formerly been called Saul was now called Paul; so that, after his conversion, just as he assumed a new life and a new office of preaching, he might also receive a new name. Thus the Lord did with the apostle Peter, who after his conversion was called Peter, whereas he had previously been called Simon.

Thus the Roman Church has now adopted the custom of changing the names of those whom it raises to the chair of blessed Peter. Saul had formerly been called, as it were, after Saul, who belonged to the same tribe, namely Benjamin, and whom he imitated in persecuting the faithful: Saul persecuted David and his followers, as this Saul persecuted Christ and his members. To him Christ himself said: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts IX, 4). Jerome testifies that, just as *Jacob* translated into our language is called *Jacobus*, and *Joseph* *Josephus*, so *Saul* is now called *Saulus*, as though it were a trisyllabic [Col. 0789A] name, though we commonly pronounce it as a disyllable by means of a diphthong. It also seems to be a diminutive from *Saul*, *Saulus*, as *Julius* from *Julus*.

But just as Saul was at first humble and afterwards became proud, so this man, conversely, was first proud and the Church’s greatest persecutor, but is now called Paul—that is, “small” or “quiet”—through humility. For according to Augustine, *Paulus* in Latin means “small” [Note: [Col. 0789D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, col. 2037]. Thus we say, “Wait a little” (*paululum exspecta*), that is, “wait briefly.” Hear from himself how humble he was: “For I,” he says, “am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle” (I Cor. XV, 9). According to Ambrose, however [Note: [Col. 0789D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 47], he calls himself Paul from Saul—that is, changed—because *Saul* is interpreted “restlessness” or “temptation,” whereas, when this man came to faith in Christ, he calls himself Paul, that is, as though now quiet, since formerly, through zeal for God’s Law, he inflicted temptations upon God’s servants. How quiet and patient he had now become, and how he always strove not to give scandal to anyone, he himself also teaches: he worked with his hands lest he burden anyone, not living from the Gospel like the other apostles.

Jerome, in the book *On Hebrew Names*, says that Paul is interpreted “wonderful” or “chosen” [Note: [Col. 0789D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIII, col. 852]. The Lord himself called him a vessel of election, and made him wonderful among the apostles both in life and in teaching. It is certain that he was both a virgin and a martyr, so that the merits divided between the great apostles Peter and John are found united in him; and that he received beyond the others graces both of preaching and of power; through him almost the whole world was converted; and even the prince of the apostles himself was necessarily corrected for his pernicious dissimulation, so that in him too that saying of Truth was wonderfully fulfilled: “The last shall be first, and the first last” (Matt. XX, 16). We do not doubt that Benjamin, the last among his brothers and greatly loved by his father, was a type of him.

Concerning this illustrious standard-bearer of Christ and mighty trumpet of the Lord, Peter himself—who had been corrected by Paul—humbly bursts forth in praise of his excellence: “So also our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you, as also in all his Epistles, speaking of these things, in which are certain things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as also the other Scriptures, to their own condemnation” (II Pet. III, 15).

Holy teachers both acknowledged and feared this difficulty, arising from the excessive subtlety of his reasoning. Hence Ambrose, in a certain letter beginning: “Although I know that nothing is more difficult than to discuss the apostle’s reading, since Origen himself is far inferior in the New than in the Old Testament,” and so forth. Augustine, *Retractations*, book I [Note: [Col. 0789D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXII, cols. 623–624]: “I had begun an exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, but, if this work had been completed, it would have consisted of several books. I completed only one of them, entirely occupied with discussion of the greeting; but then I ceased, deterred by its magnitude and labor.” And blessed Jerome, to Pammachius [Note: [Col. 0789D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 502], says: “Whenever I read the apostle Paul, I seem to hear not words but thunderclaps.” The same, to Paulinus [Note: [Col. 0790D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 580]: “Paul is last in order, first in merits, because he labored more than all.” The same, to Eustochium [Note: [Col. 0790D] *Ibid.*, col. 407]: “The Apostle says, ‘Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord’ (I Cor. VII, 25). His own being a virgin was not a matter of command but of his own will. Nor,” he says, “should those be heard who fabricate that he had a wife. For, commending perpetual chastity, he added: ‘But I wish all to be as I myself’ (ibid., 8).”

How highly he was regarded even among philosophers who heard his preaching or saw his writings is attested by Seneca, renowned both for eloquence and character, in the letters which he addresses to him [Note: [Col. 0790D] *Letters of Seneca and Paul*, in *Seneca the Philosopher*, vol. VII, col. 555, Panckoucke edition]:

“Having read your little book, consisting of many letters addressed to certain persons and sent to some city or capital of a province, we have been everywhere greatly refreshed by its wonderful exhortation to despise mortal life. I do not think that these thoughts were spoken by you, but certainly at some time they came from you and through you. For the majesty of these matters is so great, and they shine with such nobility, that I think scarcely any human lifetimes would suffice for them to be illuminated and brought to completion.”

Jerome also recalls this praise of Paul by Seneca in book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 12, writing thus [Note: [Col. 0790D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIII, col. 629]:

“Lucius Annaeus Seneca of Corduba, disciple of the Stoic Photinus and uncle of the poet Lucan, was a man of most restrained life. I would not place him in the catalogue of saints, had not those letters moved me which are read as from the apostle Paul to Seneca, or from Seneca to Paul. In them, though he was Nero’s teacher and the most powerful man of that time, he says that he wished to hold among his own people the position which Paul held among Christians.”

If to the philosophical panegyric you add the praise drawn from the authority of prophecy, you will find that this Apostle’s excellence received some special and distinguished praise above the rest, both among the patriarchs [Col. 0790D] and among the prophets. For this man, as he himself says, taking his origin from the tribe of Benjamin, is he in whose type both the patriarch Jacob and David, greatest of prophets and kings, sang beforehand in exultation.

Jacob indeed says: “Benjamin is a ravening wolf; in the morning he shall seize the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the food” (Gen. XLIX, 27). Or, according to another translation: “In the evening he shall distribute the spoils.” But David, foreseeing in the Spirit the leader of the future Church, and as though setting him before the others, says: “There is [Col. 0791A] Benjamin, a youth, in an ecstasy of mind” (Ps. LXVII, 20).

That Benjamin, Jacob’s son, who bore the type of this man yet to come from his seed, though last among his brothers in rank, was first with his father through grace; and his father, who had received him in old age, loved him especially. So too Paul, last among the apostles in the order of calling and conversion, was first before God in merits, as has been said.

Benjamin also, at his birth, killed his mother in giving birth; she, dying from the pain of childbirth, called him Benoni, that is, “son of my sorrow.” But his father changed his name and called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand.” Paul likewise, now reborn in Christ, is said, as it were, to have killed his mother, Judaism, which had begotten and reared him in the teaching of the Law, since he especially [Col. 0791B] rendered void the commandments of carnal observances in which they lived and reduced all their glory to nothing. He thus came forth, as it were, from his mother’s womb and withdrew through conversion from the schools of the synagogue, according to his own words: “He who set me apart from my mother’s womb and gave me life through his grace” (Gal. I, 5).

Thus his mother fittingly called him Benoni, “son of her sorrow,” because the more Paul attacked her error, the more he made her grieve; and the more pleasing he had been to her because of the excellence of his wisdom, the more he distressed her when she lost him. His Father, however, fittingly wished to change his name, so that he should rather be called son of the right hand—that is, of prosperity or strength—than son of sorrow. For this destruction [Col. 0791C] of the synagogue, brought about through Paul, is to be counted as prosperity for the faithful and as the Church’s common rejoicing rather than as sorrow. The innumerable persecutions directed against him also show how great was his strength of spirit.

The statement that he seized prey in the morning and divided food in the evening signifies that he was at first a persecutor of the Church and afterwards administered the nourishment of the spiritual word through the teaching of his preaching. The alternative rendering, “he shall distribute the spoils,” signifies that, after his conversion, he snatched many souls from the devil; and, after the enemy had been put to flight, kept them as spoils, whom he afterwards arranged through ecclesiastical offices and every ministry of the faithful.

Jerome, in the prologue to his book *Hebrew Questions on Genesis* [Col. 0791D] [Note: [Col. 0791D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIII, col. 98.], asserts, following the Hebrews, that the altar on which offerings were sacrificed and the blood of victims poured out at its base was in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. This is suitably applied to the one who shed Christian blood, of whom it is written: “Breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord,” etc. (Acts IX, 1), so that he might tear Christ’s members upon earth as a wolf tears sheep.

This is Benjamin, the youth: though last among the apostles, he excelled the others in mind and reason. For he was caught up to the third heaven and heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter. By him even the chief of the apostles was corrected from harmful dissimulation, [Col. 0792A] and the whole Church was spiritually instructed; hence, among all the writings of the saints, his Epistles have acquired a privilege both for usefulness and for subtlety. We have now undertaken to expound this Epistle addressed to the Romans, which in the judgment of all the most learned is intricate both in the difficulty of its wording and in the subtlety of its arguments.

**“A servant.”** Since the Lord says to the apostles, “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John XV, 15), why does the Apostle now call himself a servant? Leaving aside the distinction between two kinds of servants—that is, subjects—some of whom are held in subjection by fear of punishment, of whom it is said: “The servant does not remain in the house for ever” (John VIII, 35); and again: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: We are useless servants” (Luke XVII, 10). Others are made obedient by love, to whom it is said: “Well done, good and faithful servant,” etc. (Matt. XXV, 21).

The foregoing question may readily be answered also in this way: “servant” is said in one sense simply, and in another sense “servant of Christ,” or “good servant.” In the former case a certain compulsion arising from servile fear, a submission not voluntary, is indicated; here obedience through filial love is signified. Nor perhaps is it necessary that the bare use of the term “servant” always signify compelled and non-voluntary submission, unless some accompanying expression removes the friendly kind of submission—as when it is said: “I shall no longer call you servants, [Col. 0792C] but friends.” For when “but friends” is added, in opposition, as it were, to “servants,” the servants meant are understood to be those who are only servants and not also friends.

In another and general sense all those are called servants, whether good or evil, to whom the Lord entrusted his talents. Thus those are generally called servants whether they love those set over them or not, provided that they are so subject to them that both their possessions and themselves remain wholly under their power, and that those called servants possess neither themselves nor anything as their own. In this sense the Apostle here calls himself Christ’s servant: he had subjected himself utterly to Christ, leaving nothing to his own judgment, but submitting his whole self to Christ’s will, saying to him in all things: “Your will be done” (Matt. VI, 10).

Who, moreover, would blame the apostles if, though the Lord in grace no longer wished to call them servants, they nevertheless professed themselves servants in humility? For he did not say, “You shall no longer call yourselves servants, but friends”; rather, “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends.” The Apostle aptly professes himself obedient first when he invites others to obedience, so that he may move his hearers not only by word but even more by example. He follows the one of whom it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I, 1)—that is, first to do and then to teach.

Having first put the name Christ, which is common to all who have been anointed, whether as king or priest, according to the text, [Col. 0793A] “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Ps. CIV, 15), he added his proper name, Jesus, in order to distinguish this Christ from the rest both by the singularity of his person and by his dignity. For he alone is properly called Jesus, who alone can truly and eternally save. Therefore, when he is called Christ, that is, “anointed,” because both kings and priests were anointed, it shows that he has been appointed for us by the Lord both king and priest, through these two offices saving us—which is the meaning of the name Jesus. He became our priest by offering himself for us upon the altar of the cross; he is called king because of the strength and power by which he can subject all things to himself and, as the stronger one, bind the strong devil, since the Father has given all things into his hand.

[Col. 0793B] **“A called apostle.”** That is, called by God and chosen for the apostolate; he did not come to preach of his own accord, for otherwise he would be a thief and a robber, according to the saying of Truth: “All who came are thieves and robbers” (John VIII, 10). “They came,” Jerome says, “not those who were sent.” Hence *apostle* is rightly interpreted as “one sent” or “ambassador.”

Observe also the commendation of his humility: he said “called” rather than “chosen.” A calling is the cry of a voice to those at a distance, that they may approach or hear. And he was as far from God as he had been savage in persecuting the Church. He therefore carefully says not “chosen” or “taken up,” but “called,” as though drawn by the Lord from afar to preach his Gospel.

[Col. 0793C] **“Set apart for the Gospel of God.”** That is, chosen separately and by himself, not with the other apostles; not by Christ still dwelling on earth as a mortal, but by Christ already established in heaven at the Father’s right hand and glorified through both resurrection and ascension. Thus, writing to the Galatians to commend his own election against those who slandered him as not to be counted among the other apostles because he had not been chosen with them by the Lord Jesus Christ upon earth, he says: “Paul, an apostle, not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (Gal. I, 1). It is as though he said: Paul, an apostle not through a human being—that is, a mortal—but through Christ [Col. 0793D] already glorified by the resurrection and now possessing nothing of mortal or corruptible nature.

He is also said to have been set apart in the preaching of the Gospel because, while the other apostles were still engaged in preaching to the Jews, he was specially sent to the Gentiles as their own apostle. Hence he alone was especially called the Teacher of the Gentiles. This is the statement in the Acts of the Apostles, where the Holy Spirit says: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul for the work of the ministry to which I have taken them” (Acts XIII, 2). *Gospel* means “good announcement,” because evangelical preaching announces that what had previously been promised has been fulfilled.

**“Which he had promised beforehand.”** This commends the Gospel, which he says was long ago promised us by God. **“Through his prophets”** [Col. 0794A]. No one, as Ambrose says, announces a cheap thing through great heralds. Through Jeremiah the Lord says: “Behold, days are coming, and I shall establish the new covenant,” etc. (Jer. XXXI, 31). He calls them *his* prophets to distinguish them from false or reprobate prophets, such as Balaam, or those who sometimes foretell the future through an evil spirit. For a prophet is one who reveals by foretelling future things. Thus *prophet* is named, as it were, from *prophesying*, that is, foretelling.

**“In the holy Scriptures.”** So that the prophets should announce this not only by words but also confirm it by writings. **“Holy.”** That is, writings composed for instruction in holiness and as a pattern of religion, and composed at the dictation of the Holy Spirit.

**“Concerning his Son.”** That is, his own and substantial Son, not an adopted son. **“Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh”** [Col. 0794B]: that is, according to human nature, while according to the divine nature he is begotten only. “For him,” namely for God the Father—that is, for his Father’s honor, who is always glorified and honored in the Son, since the Son of God himself says that he does not seek his own glory but that of the one who sent him (John VIII, 50).

“From the seed of David,” that is, from Mary, who was of David’s line. For a promise concerning Christ was made to both Abraham and David: that he should be born from their seed through his mother. Yet he mentions only David, who sometimes sinned grievously, and not Abraham, who appeared especially righteous, so that the whole mystery of this incarnation may be ascribed to divine grace rather than to human merits. It is also sufficient to name David without Abraham, since through David, who is of Abraham’s family, he teaches that Christ is of Abraham’s family.

[Col. 0794C] **“Who was predestined according to the flesh.”** That is, divinely prepared, on account of which it was said also to his mother: “Hail, full of grace” (Luke I, 28). For predestination is called the preparation of divine grace. The Son of God, I say, was predestined **“in power”**—that is, to be the strength and power of all those united to him through faith.

**“According to the Spirit of sanctification.”** To the two previous statements he adds two others, as though supplying one corresponding statement to each. To the first statement, “who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh,” he joins this: “according to the Spirit of sanctification”—that is, through the operation of divine grace, called the Holy Spirit, which first cleansed and sanctified his mother from sin, so that he might assume most holy flesh from the seed of sinful David. To the second statement, “who was predestined Son of God in power,” he attaches: **“by the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ”** [Col. 0794D]. It is as though he said: From the time when his resurrection was accomplished, he became the strength or power of all who are united to him by faith; this was attested by the resurrection of the dead which occurred on that same day, of whom it is written that “they came into the holy city and appeared to many” (Matt. XXVII, 53).

Then every doubt of unbelief departed, including that which had arisen in the disciples on account of the Passion; some of them, already despairing, said: “But we hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV, 21). He calls them “the dead of Jesus Christ,” that is, dead for his honor, since they had died in order to glorify him by the testimony of their resurrection.

We may also understand a spiritual resurrection of the soul from vices, of which Simeon says: “This one is set for the fall and resurrection of many” (Luke II, 34). For Christ alone can free from the death of the soul: namely, the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John I, 29).

It should be noted, however, that, as blessed Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* [Note: [Col. 0795D] *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 252.], although Christ is said to have been born of the Holy Spirit and Mary, he is not therefore called the Son of the Holy Spirit as he is the son of Mary. For he was not born or conceived from the substance of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0795B] as from the substance of Mary; rather, his exceptional conception or birth came about through the operation of the Spirit—that is, of divine grace—and for that reason he is also said to have been born of him, that is, conceived through him.

Not everything born from something is called its son: hair grows from the head, or lice are born from us. Likewise, though we are born again from water and Spirit, we are by no means called children of water. People may also be called the children of those from whom they are not born: adoptive children, children of the devil, children of Gehenna, or children through teaching. Yet if anyone calls Christ, according to his humanity, Son of God or of the Holy Spirit in the manner in which the other faithful, subject to him through filial love, are called sons, I do not think this absurd.

Nevertheless, they do not thereby have several fathers because of God—namely, the Father [Col. 0795C] and the Holy Spirit—especially since the other elect do not have several fathers in God because of diversity of persons. There should no more be said to be several fathers there than several gods or lords, since there is no diversity of things or difference of names there.

But if it is asked whether that human being in Christ, assumed by the Word, was an adopted Son of God like the other elect, since he too has this good through grace, I do not think it should be conceded. For those who are adopted and thus become sons were certainly previously not sons in the way in which they became so. But that human being assumed by the Word, wholly without sin both in birth and conception, was Son of God through grace from the very moment he came to be. We others, however, who are born with sin and are called children of wrath, begin through adoption at our rebirth in baptism to be what we were not before. Therefore, although he is called Son according to his humanity through grace, he did not receive this by adoption, for he had it from the moment he was. Hence Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book XII [Note: [Col. 0796D] *Patrologia*, vol. X, cols. 440–441]:

> “And we are children of God, but children through creation. For we were once children of wrath, but have been made children of God through adoption; and we deserve rather to be called this than to be born it. Since everything that is made was not before it was made, we, who were not children, are made into what we are. For we were not children before, but after we merited it we became so. Yet we are not born but made; not begotten, [Col. 0796A] but acquired. For God acquired a people for himself and through this begot it. But we never know the Lord to have begotten children with the proper signification of that term.”

**“Through whom we received grace and apostleship.”** Having commended Christ’s person, he adds a commendation of his own person or office, declaring that he has been sent to preach by so great an author, so that at least on the authority of the sender his preaching ought to be received. “Grace and apostleship” means the office of preaching bestowed freely upon him, not for his merits. Or it may mean, first, grace in his conversion and remission of sins, or in the bestowal of virtues, miracles, or any gifts whatever; and afterwards apostleship, when he was sent to preach.

The Romans might say to the Apostle: “Even if you were called to the apostleship, you were not called over the Gentiles; or, if over certain Gentiles, still not over us.” He therefore adds: **“Among all nations”** [Col. 0796B]—that is, so that he might preach wherever he went to all nations of the Gentiles. *Gentes*, “nations,” are so called as though they were merely begotten or born, that is, living like cattle without the discipline of the Law. But *pagani*, “pagans,” are named from *pagus*, a village—that is, any habitation outside a city—and are, as it were, rustic rather than urban people, not yet instructed by the laws of the city in living rightly and honorably. A city is indeed an assembly of people living under equal law. Therefore those wholly alien from the city of God, not yet instructed by any divine laws, were deservedly called pagans. They now prefer to call themselves Saracens rather than Hagarenes, glorying in being named rather after Sarah, the free woman, than after Hagar, the slave woman.

**“For obedience to the faith.”** That is, for performing those works which they have first believed ought to be performed. For it is necessary first to know what must be done before it is fulfilled in deed. **“For his name,”** that is, for the name of God or Christ, so that he himself may be known and thus loved, according to Christ’s words concerning himself and the Father: “That they may know you alone and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” Every thing is signified and known by its name; thus “name” here stands for knowledge. So great a good cannot truly be known without immediately being loved.

**“Among whom you also are”**—that is, you Romans too already belong among those nations called. [Col. 0796D] **“Called of Jesus Christ.”** That is, called Christians from his glorious name.

**“To all who are at Rome.”** Up to this point the entire preceding wording of this greeting is suspended, as though it said, after all the foregoing has been repeated: “Paul, servant,” etc., sends—understand this—to all who are at Rome, beloved of God, called saints; he sends, I say: “Grace be to you and peace,” etc.

**“Beloved of God.”** It is as though he said: I do not speak simply to all who are at Rome, both faithful and unfaithful, both elect and reprobate; but only to those who, through their conversion, have already entered into friendship with God, now subject to him in the manner of Christians—that is, from love rather than fear. To them the saying applies: “I shall no longer call you servants” (John XV, 15), and again: “But I have called you friends” (ibid.). Or “beloved of God” means beloved by God, who first loved them, so that through his prevenient grace, rather than their merits, he chose them.

**“Called saints”** [Col. 0797A]: that is, called by inward inspiration or by the grace of preaching in order that they may be saints. In saying that they were called by God rather than that they called upon the Lord, he magnifies God’s grace, which sometimes bestows benefits upon the unwilling or upon those who do not ask.

But since this greeting concerns all those to whom the Epistle is addressed, how does he say “beloved of God” or “called saints,” when the Epistle was directed especially to correct, or because of, those who wished, as has been said, to set themselves above one another through proud contention? For how can those who act proudly be called beloved of God? Must the Apostle lie or write something false in order to win their goodwill?

But certainly this greeting does concern them all, although not all are yet beloved of God. For when he greets only those who are beloved of God, he judges only them worthy of his greeting and invites the others to imitate them, so that they too may strive to become beloved of God. It was also fitting that, even if some there were beloved by God, he could call them beloved of God according to the opinion of those who professed this of themselves, just as some people sometimes speak ironically [Col. 0797C]. For, as blessed Augustine testifies [Note: [Col. 0797D] *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 489.], a lie is not spoken except where there is false signification with an intention to deceive. The Apostle here, however, intends not to deceive but to admonish.

**“Grace to you and peace.”** By grace he means a gratuitous gift, that is, bestowed not on account of preceding merits. “Grace and peace” means the gift of peace, by which those who contend proudly may be reconciled both with one another and with God himself. For “the one who does not love the neighbor whom he sees, how can he love the Lord whom he does not see?” (1 John IV, 20).

**“From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”** God’s gift, which he calls grace, is called the Holy Spirit. Thus, when we speak of the sevenfold Spirit or name the seven Spirits of God, we indicate the seven gifts of divine grace. He therefore rightly asks that the gift of God called the Holy Spirit be given jointly by the Father and the Son, from whom that Spirit himself proceeds jointly.

Thus construe it: “From God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ”—I say, from God our Father, namely the Father both of the Lord Jesus Christ and of us. Hence the Son himself calls God the Father both his own and ours, saying: “I ascend to my Father and your Father” (John XX, 17): his by nature, ours by adoption. By this he especially commends God’s grace toward us, through which we become brothers and co-heirs of the Lord Jesus Christ. We are indeed called sons through love and are subject more from love than fear. He calls him “the Lord Jesus” because constant and [Col. 0798A] perpetual obedience is owed to him, as by servants to a master, as he above also called himself a servant.

**“First indeed.”** Lest the greeting prefixed to the Epistle seem to have been uttered more from the occasion and custom of letter-writing than from an affection of charity, he adds how greatly he embraces them in love. He says that first—that is, chiefly—he gives thanks to God for the conversion and faith of the Romans, although this ought to be done for all converts. It was also necessary that the Apostle first show the grace which he had toward them, so that when he afterwards rebuked them severely, they might understand that it was done from love and more willingly receive his correction or admonition. Thus, by flattering them first in the manner of a careful orator, he draws them to himself, making them more attentive and kindly disposed to listen.

**“I give thanks.”** To give thanks to someone is to praise, bless, and glorify that person for a benefit freely bestowed by him. **“To my God through Jesus Christ,”** that is, through him who has been gracious to me, as to other sinners, through his Son, our redeemer and mediator. Or, “I give thanks through Jesus Christ,” because I recognize that the conversion of the Romans was accomplished through Christ, not through our power or that of other human beings. I also recognize that I am not fit of myself to praise God, but through the grace of his Son, whom I serve. I give thanks, I say, for this: **“Because your faith is proclaimed”**—that is, spread abroad for the praise of God and as an example of conversion to others throughout the whole world, that is, everywhere on earth or throughout its greater part.

The more widely known the Roman people were, as the head, as it were, of the whole world, the more widely what was done among the Romans became known; and the more eminent they were, the more they invited the rest to conversion by their example. Hence Quintilian says concerning a blind man: “The higher each person reaches in rank of honor, the more he lies open as an example to those who look on.” Likewise: “This is the condition of those in high position: whatever they do, they seem to prescribe.”

From these and similar words of the Apostle, by which he says that he gives thanks to God through Jesus Christ, the Church, unless I am mistaken, adopted the custom that when thanks are rendered to God the Father in the celebration of Masses, or in the petitions of prayers themselves, the words “Through our Lord Jesus [Col. 0798D] Christ,” or something similar, should always be added. It is as though we acknowledged that nothing we do can please God the Father except through that mediator who reconciled us to him, and that we have obtained no good from him except through the same one who made him peaceful toward us.

**“For God is my witness.”** He shows, as though from the cause, that he gives thanks to God especially for the grace bestowed on them because he embraces them with such affection that he remembers them in all his prayers. That is, whenever he prays for himself, he also prays that he may be able to come to them, so that among them too he may have some fruit. “God,” he says, “is my witness”—he to whom I make this prayer, who cannot be deceived and who alone can examine intention.

He does not say simply “without ceasing,” but “without ceasing in his prayers,” so that no prayer of his may be made without remembrance of them. **“Whom I serve in my spirit,”** that is, in the inner person, from the whole affection of the heart, as a friend, not merely for appearance’s sake like a servant afraid of being flogged. **“In the Gospel of his Son,”** that is, in preaching the Gospel which the Lord Jesus himself delivered and taught us.

**“Entreating, if somehow”**—whether through tranquility or tribulation, by land or sea—I may reach you also bodily. He calls a journey prosperous when it accords with God’s will, not his own; for God makes even the perils of the saints work together for their good and provides for them better than they can provide for themselves. Thus every devout person sings in all things: “Your will be done,” not mine.

[Col. 0799B] **“For I desire.”** This is the reason why he prays to come to them: that he may confer upon them some spiritual gift by strengthening them through his exhortations in the doctrine which they had received. When he says that strengthening them would be his own mutual consolation among them, just as they would be consoled in him, he means that this consolation would be common both to himself, who would instruct, and to them, who would be instructed. They would be consoled because, if they doubted or faltered in anything, they would be strengthened by his arguments; he would be consoled because, once they were strengthened, he would be more secure concerning their perseverance.

This is that mutual consolation which Boethius mentions at the very beginning of his *Hypothetical Syllogisms*, speaking of teachers and learners [Col. 0799C] [Note: [Col. 0799D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXIV, col. 831.]: “Since in learning and treating all the disciplines of philosophy I consider the highest consolation of life to be placed,” etc.

**“A spiritual gift.”** That is, some spiritual, not bodily, gift freely bestowed by the Apostle, not in hope of temporal gain. **“Through that faith”** which you already have in common with me: that is, to strengthen you in that faith already preached to you, not in some new faith.

**“Which is mutual”** means that which we have in common with one another, or that which is common to all the faithful. Therefore it is called Catholic, that is, universal, not private or particular like that of heretics, which may exist in some corner of the earth but is not spread everywhere. When he adds, “yours and mine,” he shows that his faith, which belongs to all believers, belongs both to the Romans themselves and to the Apostle. Faith may also be called mutual when it binds the faithful themselves to one another by reciprocal charity. For this is the true faith which, as he himself says, works through love.

**“But I do not want.”** Lest the Apostle’s desire to come to them seem slight because he had not yet undertaken it, he says that he had often already set about it in preparation, but had not yet been permitted to complete it, because God’s hidden dispensation so arranged matters. I wish to come to you, [Col. 0800A] he says, in order that I may bring some fruit—that is, some benefit—to you. The fruit of a tree is useful not to the planter but to the recipient; and for the Apostle the desire of good will suffices if the result is lacking, nor is anything taken away from his merit if the result is prevented.

**“To Greeks and barbarians.”** It is as though he said: I ought indeed to desire this because, according to the office of preaching entrusted to me, I have been made a debtor by God to all nations. Apart from Greeks, he calls all other nations barbarians, as wholly alien both from the worship of one God and from the law of God. Among the Greeks, however, faith in one God had already become known through philosophers, and the Law translated by the seventy interpreters was known.

**“To wise and unwise.”** That is, both to those already enlightened through Christ and God’s wisdom, as you are, and to unbelievers: to the former, that I may strengthen them; to the latter, that I may convert them. **“Thus, so far as I am concerned.”** I am a debtor, he says, and willing to pay what I owe. This is the meaning: I am such a debtor that it is ready in me to preach the Gospel to you—that is, so far as I am concerned, I am already inclined and willing to discharge what I owe through the office entrusted to me, namely to preach to you, as I preached to other nations.

For although they had already been converted to faith, they still needed preaching or exhortation in many matters. This may also be understood of the other Romans who had not yet been converted. Hence he says generally, “to you who are at Rome,” not “to you who have been converted.”

**“For I am not ashamed.”** Thus it is ready in me, because [Col. 0800C] I am not ashamed to preach the Gospel, although certain things which are preached concerning the Lord Jesus according to the weakness of assumed humanity seem worthy of shame. Alternatively, “I am not ashamed of the Gospel,” that is, of Gospel preaching: I cannot be refuted as those are who fail when required to give reasons.

**“For it is the power.”** It is as though he said: Therefore it is ready in me to preach the Gospel, or I am not ashamed of the Gospel because of the weakness of assumed humanity, because the Gospel is, for every person who believes and receives it, the power of God—that is, power bestowed on us by God for salvation, not power by which a person merely makes progress.

The Gospel—that is, good news—is called the New Testament par excellence, not only, as we have indicated above, because it teaches that what was promised in the Old Testament has been fulfilled, but also because its teaching is wholly perfect and truly sufficient for righteousness. For the old Law, as the Apostle himself says, brought nothing to perfection, correcting deeds rather than intention.

**“To the Jew first.”** First in time, and afterwards to the Greek. For the apostles were first converted from the Jews, and through them Gospel preaching then passed down to the Greeks and finally to the Latins. Hence the expression “first” may also be referred, in relation to the Romans or other nations, to Jews and Greeks together. Or “first” may mean especially, since in Paul’s time people from other nations had already been converted.

[Col. 0801A] **“For the righteousness of God.”** It is truly unto salvation because it contains the doctrine of the whole of salvation, in which God’s righteousness—that is, his just recompense, whether toward the elect in glory or toward the impious in punishment—is clearly and perfectly contained and set forth. This is the meaning: in it, namely in the Gospel, the righteousness of God is revealed—that is, it is taught in its preaching—namely his just recompense in every case, both to the elect, as stated, and to the reprobate.

**“Revealed from faith to faith.”** That is, from faith in punishments, leading us toward faith in rewards. For it follows, as it were, by contraries that, when we know that people deserve punishment from God, we understand also that they obtain reward, because he who hates evil must love good, as it is written: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (Ps. XLIV, 8).

I think these things are especially revealed and distinguished in the Gospel, where the Lord examines everything done according to the root of intention, saying: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light. If your eye is dark, your whole body will be dark” (Matt. VI, 23). This is indeed the test of true righteousness, where everything done is weighed according to intention more than according to the quality of the actions. The Jews attended more to actions than intention; Christians, now having natural righteousness restored, attend not so much to what is done as to the spirit in which it is done.

We also have both recompenses clearly in the Gospel, where the Lord says: “Go, you cursed” (Matt. XXV, 41), and: “Come, you blessed” (ibid., 34). As he says elsewhere: “For with the same measure,” etc. (Matt. VII, 2). When it is said, “from faith in those to be punished to faith in those to be glorified,” we keep the order of the day of judgment, when, the impious having been punished, the elect will be crowned.

Just as it is written in the prophet Habakkuk: “The righteous lives by faith” (Hab. II, 4), that is, according to the revelation made concerning what must be believed—both the punishments of the wicked and the rewards of the righteous—each elect person, persevering [the text reads *perseveratus*; read *perseverans*] in his righteousness, avoids what he believes must be punished and pursues the opposite, which he believes will please [Col. 0801D] God. In order to strike terror into the proud Romans, he here pursues that part of divine justice by which God punishes them, saying: “Wrath is revealed.”

Having said that the righteousness of God is revealed there from faith—that is, as we said, concerning the unrighteous who are to be punished—he now defines this plainly, saying that there, that is, in the Gospel, the wrath of God is made manifest: namely, his just vengeance upon the wicked. “Of God from heaven.” He says this to distinguish it from false gods, or from God’s vicars in the Church, to whom it is said: “I said: You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI, 6). Or: it is revealed from heaven, that is, from the fall from heaven of the angels who grew proud and were irrecoverably separated from eternal blessedness. For if he endured to condemn creatures so precious by an irrecoverable punishment so swiftly, what is to be hoped for men who offend him by so many sins?

Alternatively, the reason why he is angry so as to condemn is plainly shown by that vengeance for the angelic transgression: namely, because of a perverse will before any deed. For the devil did not accomplish in deed what he willed in pride, saying within himself: “I will set my throne,” etc. (Matt. XIV, 14 [apparently an erroneous citation]). Hence it was not the effect of the deed, which followed, but the will that condemned him. Thus Simon Magus, desiring the gift of miracles which he did not obtain, was condemned not for a deed but for unbelief—because he believed the Holy Spirit to be purchasable—as Peter likewise said to him: “Because you thought,” etc. (Acts VIII, 20).

“Ungodliness”: with respect to the greater transgression of the Jews, who had also been instructed by the written law. [Col. 0802B] “And unrighteousness”: with respect to the transgression of the Gentiles, who used the natural law alone. “Upon all ungodliness,” that is, in order to punish every kind, etc. And it is aptly said to be “upon,” as though prevailing over those who cannot in any way defend themselves against him as their superior.

“Who hold down the truth of God in unrighteousness.” They do not allow what they know of the true God to bear fruit, because they pursue their unrighteous desires and set their own will before the divine will.

“Because what is known of God.” Note that in this Epistle, as we recalled above, the Apostle, in order to repress the proud self-exaltation of both Jews and Gentiles, attacks them alternately—now the Gentiles, now both together. He has already directed a certain attack against both alike [Col. 0802C] when he said, “Upon all ungodliness and unrighteousness,” showing the Lord ready for vengeance. Now he attacks especially and particularly the Gentiles, who appeared less blameworthy by their own arguments and almost entirely excusable because they had not served the true God, whom, as they said, they could not know without a written law.

He plainly refutes this excuse: even without writing, the Lord had previously been known to the Gentiles through the natural law, since he himself gave them knowledge of himself through the reason he had given them—that is, natural law—and through his visible works. This is what he means by “what is known.” It is as though he said: I said that they hold down what they know of the true God, and I rightly said that they know it. [Col. 0802D] For what is known of God—that is, what has now been revealed to the world concerning the nature of the Godhead through the written law—had formerly been evident even without writing through natural reason. “In them,” that is, not only in them, but also through them to others. Thus many explicit testimonies concerning the Trinity are found in the books of the philosophers, who were teachers of the Gentiles; and the holy Fathers carefully collected these against the attacks of the Gentiles in commendation of our faith. We too have included many of them in our little theological work. “For God revealed it to them,” at least through the effects of his works. And this is what he adds.

“For his invisible things,” etc. Here he distinguishes the entire mystery of the Trinity, so that they could discern from the works themselves not only the unity of God but also the Trinity, just as from the quality of any work we infer the kind and skill of its maker. [Col. 0803A] Carefully observe the statement that what is known of God had been revealed to them: that is, they believed what we now believe concerning matters pertaining to the Godhead rather than the mystery of the divine Incarnation. For the mystery of the Incarnation could in no way be conceived by human reason from God’s visible works; but God’s power, wisdom, and goodness were clearly perceived from what they saw.

I believe that the whole distinction of the Trinity consists in these three. For “God the Father,” it seems to me, signifies divine power begetting divine wisdom, that is, the Son; “God the Son” signifies precisely divine wisdom begotten from God the Father; and “God the Holy Spirit” signifies the love or goodness of God proceeding from God the Father and the Son. [Col. 0803B]

The connection is this: “God revealed it to them,” because, through the reason God bestowed on them, his divine Trinity became known from his visible works; and through his effects the maker himself imparted knowledge of himself to them. This is what he means by “For his invisible things”: that is, the manifold, or sevenfold, Spirit of God—who is sometimes also called the seven spirits, like the gifts of sevenfold grace—this sevenfold Spirit of God, I say, is “seen by understanding”; that is, he is apprehended [Col. 0803C] not by bodily eyes but by the intelligence of reason.

“Understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made”: that is, understood through the effects of worldly works, which he willed to be made and ordered so excellently. “His eternal power.” Here we understand his wisdom—that is, God’s wisdom—which, as we said, is the Son of God, of whom the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 24). The Evangelist calls this wisdom “the Word,” that is, the conception of the mind; the philosopher calls it “mind,” and affirms that it is born from God. God’s wisdom is called his power insofar as he makes and orders all things excellently in wisdom. For a work not made skilfully is weak and defective.

But “Godhead” [Col. 0803D] is here taken for the majesty of divine power, which, I think, is especially indicated by the name of Father. For, according to Isidore, Θεός, *Theos*, that is, “fear,” is its interpretation; and every power is a fear to those subject to it. Hence divine power is fittingly expressed especially by the name God or divinity—that is, deity. The greatest bishop carefully indicates this in his exposition of the Creed called Apostolic, read on the Fifth Sunday in Lent, in these words:

> “Do you believe in God the Father Almighty? In ‘God’ the unbegotten nature is shown; in ‘Father,’ the truth of the unbegotten one; in ‘Almighty,’ the fullness of power. For through unbegotten divinity he is almighty, and through almightiness he is Father.”

We have discussed these matters as carefully as we could in the first book of our Theology. It is therefore especially evident from the whole fabric of the world, so wonderfully made and so fittingly adorned, how great is the power, wisdom, and goodness of its maker, who was able and willing to make so great and such a work from nothing, and who ordered all things so skilfully and rationally that in each particular nothing was done more or less than was fitting. [Col. 0804A] Hence Plato himself, when speaking of the generation of the world, extolled the goodness of divine power and wisdom so highly as to maintain that God could in no way have made the world better than he did.

Nor did Gentile philosophers perceive the wonderful maker merely from the world’s composition or marvelous adornment; from its excellent ordering they also supplied coherent arguments for the most excellent providence of divine governance. One of them, Tully, in the first book of his *Rhetoric*, demonstrated by a strong argument that the world is governed by providence, not chance. He proposed that things governed by counsel and providence proceed and are administered better than other things; then immediately took up the fact that nothing is administered or ordered better than the world itself, and at once established this by a manifest argument, showing how usefully and rationally the things in the world persist in their order. [Col. 0804B]

[Col. 0804C] We may also explain the Apostle’s words, “For his invisible things from the creation of the world,” etc., not only in this way—that the power, wisdom, and goodness of the maker himself can be apprehended by human reason from the composition and adornment of the world, according to which, as we said, three persons are distinguished in God—but also by saying that human reason ascended so far through likenesses of bodily things as to be able, by fitting examples of similarity, to set forth both the unity of God and the Trinity of persons in him, and how those persons stand in relation to one another.

It might, for example, set before its eyes some creature of the world, such as a bronze substance [Note: St Bernard, Epistle 190, refutes this analogy; Col. 0803], and consider something made in that bronze substance: for instance, a bronze image made by our operation from the bronze itself. The bronze and the bronze statue [Col. 0804D] made in the bronze itself or from the bronze are essentially, or numerically, the same thing, yet they differ in their respective properties: for one thing is proper to the bronze, another to the bronze statue. Although bronze and a bronze statue are essentially the same, the bronze statue is from the bronze, not the bronze from the statue.

So too in the divine Trinity: although the substance of the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is the same, the persons differ in their properties, since one property belongs to the Father, another to the Son, another to the Holy Spirit. And although each person is essentially the same as the others, the Son is from the Father as the bronze image is from the bronze, not the Father from the Son, [Col. 0805A] just as the bronze itself is not from the bronze image; and the Holy Spirit has personal being from the other two persons, not they from him. We believe that we have treated these matters sufficiently, so far as was necessary, in the second book of our Theology. Let us now return to the literal sense.

“Understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made”: that is, through some creature of the world, such as the bronze itself, and through things made in the bronze, such as a bronze image or something similar. The rest of the exposition remains unchanged.

“So that they are without excuse”: that is, the Gentiles can no longer excuse themselves through ignorance with respect to knowledge of the one God, even though they did not possess the written law. He explains why they are without excuse: “Because, although they knew the Lord,” namely through human reason, which is called the natural law, [Col. 0805B] “they did not glorify him as God”: that is, they did not render him the worshipful reverence owed through humility. “Nor gave thanks,” recognizing that this knowledge of him, which they had above others, was a gift of his grace, and praising him for it.

“But they became vain in their thoughts,” like smoke, which diminishes and is reduced to nothing the higher it rises. So too, the more they swelled with arrogance on account of the knowledge they had acquired—attributing it to their own effort or talent rather than divine grace—the more they deserved to be blinded and cast further into error. This is what he adds by way of explanation: “And their foolish heart was darkened.” They were foolish because they attributed his own gift to themselves rather than to God, and believed that they possessed it from themselves rather than from him. Hence their heart was deservedly darkened, and natural reason itself was obscured in them.

[Col. 0805C] It was truly darkened, because they became fools and were deprived of that noble knowledge, “professing themselves to be wise”: that is, boasting that they were wise from themselves rather than made wise by the Lord. He then adds how great a folly—indeed, madness—they rushed into, both through the error of unbelief and through ignorance in life:

“And they changed the glory,” that is, the honor and sacrifices which they ought to have offered to the true God, who cannot be corrupted or changed in any respect; these they offered to a false human being, that is, to an imaginary likeness of corruptible and mortal man, [Col. 0805D] becoming idolaters, and not only to the likeness of man but also to those of irrational animals of every kind—birds, quadrupeds, and reptiles. Perhaps they believed that certain spirits, whom they called gods, presided over human beings, and others over the remaining animals; and for this reason they worshipped them in the forms of those over which they seemed to preside.

Haymo [Note: *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, col. 375]:

> “The Assyrians worshipped as God the image of Bel, father of King Ninus; the Babylonians worshipped him whom they call Bel; the Sidonians, Baal; the Indians, Beelzebub; and the Philistines likewise. The Romans worshipped the goose, and the Egyptians the hawk. Likewise the Egyptians worshipped Apis, that is, a white cow; the Babylonians, the dragon; and the Egyptians, the crocodile, [Col. 0806A] which is an aquatic serpent, swimming in water like a fish and feeding on land like an ox.”

“Therefore,” namely because they became foolish by departing from the Lord, so as to worship false animals—that is, images of animals—as God, “God gave them up”: that is, he permitted them to follow their unclean desires, so that what they had shamefully conceived in mind they might fulfill still more shamefully in deed. “To dishonor”: that is, to afflict, force into a kind of contrary nature, and disgrace their bodies with the shameful uncleannesses of Sodomitic sin committed among themselves, so that they mutually defiled one another.

“Who exchanged”: a resumption or repetition of the reason why God permitted this concerning them, namely because, he says, they sinned most grievously against him. “Exchanging the truth of God for a lie”: that is, worshipping false gods under the name and honor [Col. 0806B] of the true God. “And they served the creature”: that is, demonic spirits, whom they believed to inhabit the images. “Who is blessed”: that is, glorified—he who appears praiseworthy from all his creatures through every succession of times. The ages are called *saecula*, as it were, from following: they are the very successions of times. “Amen,” that is, “it is true.” This word is sometimes an adverb of confirmation, sometimes of wishing.

“Therefore God gave them up”: because, namely, they had meanwhile detracted from the excellence of divinity. It is not enough to say this once, so that he may deter the hearer more strongly from such things. By “dishonorable passions” he means the defilements of unnatural lust. Every substance is rightly said to suffer, and as it were to sustain a certain violence, whenever something is done in it contrary to nature. He immediately adds what such shameful acts are, assigning them to both women and men, in order to demonstrate more fully God’s vengeance.

[Col. 0806C] “The women” are called theirs because the men, by the teaching of their most evil example, had made them as it were their own in this matter. “What is contrary to nature,” and therefore should be called abuse rather than use. Contrary to nature—that is, contrary to nature’s institution, which prepared women’s genitals for the use of men, and conversely, not so that women might cohabit with women. “They burned”: that is, they were inflamed in their desires, or in natural pleasures, contrary to the law of nature. “And the recompense”: that is, the repayment due for their error, namely their blindness and idolatry. “Receiving in themselves,” namely mutually defiling one another in body, [Col. 0806D] just as their minds had been corrupted by unbelief.

“And since they did not approve,” that is, praise and choose, “to have the Lord whom they knew in knowledge”: that is, to retain him in memory by cleaving to him, “God gave them over to a reprobate mind”: that is, he permitted them to be so thoroughly blinded that they had altogether written [*conscripserant*, a materially uncertain reading], “so that they do”—that is, fulfill in deed—“things not fitting”: not only things evil before God, but things conforming to no human discipline and incapable of rational excuse even among the ungodly.

I mean those “filled with all unrighteousness”: not that all were filled with every sin together, but that each was filled with particular sins, so that every form of iniquity [Col. 0807A] was found in them full and complete. He therefore immediately divides the parts of wickedness by enumerating them, showing the ways in which they were filled.

“Malice,” through which they seek to inflict harm on others; “fornication,” which is every unlawful sexual union, namely outside marriage; “avarice,” that is, an immoderate desire for earthly things; “wickedness,” by which they delight in corrupting others, not content to perish alone; “envy,” grieving over another’s good; “murders,” both in deed, if possible, and in will; “strife,” openly contradicting truth; “deceit,” that is, pretense, when one thing is done secretly and another is feigned; “malignity,” against themselves and their benefactors; “whisperers,” that is, those who slander secretly when they cannot do so openly, and openly when they dare; [Col. 0807B] “slanderers,” and thereby hateful not only to the people whom they slander or wish to harm, but also to God; “insolent,” uttering insults; “proud,” desiring to be above their equals; “haughty,” desiring to be equal to their superiors; “inventors of evils,” that is, devising some new kind of sin in which they might delight; “disobedient to parents,” and in this inhuman and more untamed than the wild beasts themselves; “foolish,” having through long habit of evil no discernment of good; “disorderly,” with respect to outward bearing, which announces a mind badly ordered; “without affection,” namely without natural kindness toward neighbors of their own kind; “without mercy,” that is, without compassion for others’ miseries; “without covenant,” that is, without a mutual bond of charity with anyone, or observance of any agreement.

[Col. 0807C] They have also fallen into such blindness that they do not know how to return through repentance, “not understanding” any longer—that is, neither attending to nor caring that “those who do such things are worthy of death,” namely eternal death—although they had first known the righteousness of God, that is, his due vengeance for individual sins.

“And those who consent.” Here to consent means not to resist another’s sin when one can and ought to do so. For perhaps God could resist the sins of many by disrupting them so that they might not occur; yet, because our sins deserve it, or because he uses the sins themselves for good, he ought not to do so. Therefore he must in no way be called one who consents to sins.

[Col. 0807D] It should be noted, however, that this previously described blindness or wickedness is not to be understood of all philosophers or all who use the natural law, since many of them have been acceptable to God both in faith and morals—for example Job the Gentile, and perhaps some pagan philosophers who lived lives of the greatest continence before the Lord’s own coming. Of such persons blessed Jerome, commenting on Matthew, says [Note: *Patrologia*, vol. XXVI, col. 188]:

> “From the fact that the evil servant dared to say, ‘You reap where you have not sown, and gather where you have not scattered,’ we understand that the Lord receives even the good life of pagan philosophers, and that those who act justly and those who act unjustly are treated differently: compared with one who obeys the natural law, [Col. 0808A] those who neglect the written law are condemned” (Matt. XXV, 24).

Thus, according to Jerome, we understand the Lord to reap where he has not sown in the sense that he gathers to life even those who act well through the natural law, among whom no word of preaching was sown. But because perhaps few such persons existed among the philosophers, this was said above concerning them as though generally and without exception, so that the wise may place less confidence in their wisdom, which tends more to puff up than to build up; as the Apostle himself testifies elsewhere: “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (I Cor. VIII, 1).

For even here it was sufficient for the Apostle, in order to repress the proud contention of the Roman Gentiles and preserve humility, to show [Col. 0808B] that knowledge or faith in God became known to the Gentiles through some philosophers, yet that these very teachers of faith sinned grievously, so that their blindness led even to idolatry, and together with the supreme error of idolatry they fell into the utmost shamefulness of life, as he mentioned above. He teaches that all these things are punishment for the sin of pride, so that, in accordance with the purpose of this Epistle—which was also written throughout against the plague of pride—he may immediately discourage pride at the very opening of the Epistle.

A subsequent sin is called the punishment of a preceding sin, its just recompense unto punishment, when someone who neglects to correct a preceding sin merits to fall into another sin, according to that saying of the Apocalypse: “Let him who is filthy be filthy still” (Apoc. XXII, 11).

[Col. 0808C] Three questions arise in this passage. The first is: What makes idolatry, since we Christians too possess certain sculptures or paintings in the worship of God, angels, or holy persons? The second question is: Why is God said to give someone over to other sins because of previous sins, and to do this justly, since the person handed over deserved it? Is God also the author or cause of sin, since, by withdrawing his grace, he seems to compel to sin one who, once it is withdrawn, cannot at all guard himself against sin? It is like someone who, for whatever reason, takes away a ship from a person amid waves [Col. 0808D] and leaves him there: he certainly does not compel him.

The third question is: How can it be just for the Lord to withdraw his grace from the ungodly, when, once it has been withdrawn, that person becomes worse and sins further, unless it is also just for him to become worse and sin further—that is, to offend and despise his Creator more? But who would call just what is most unjust, when a sinner ought rather to come to his senses than increase his sins? For if it were just for him to sin further, how could he be held guilty, or even be said to sin, by doing what it would surely be just for him to do? We reserve the solutions of these three questions proposed [Col. 0809A] for examination in our Theology.

## CHAPTER II

“Therefore.” He passes from a particular attack upon the Gentiles to a general one, as though saying: Since these persons who were not given the written law cannot excuse themselves from sin—that is, contempt of the Creator—through ignorance of God, therefore no one can. This is what he means: “Therefore you are inexcusable, every man who judges.” “Every man,” I say, “who judges”: that is, who possesses the judgment of reason and discernment of good and evil. Infants who have not yet acquired discernment are free from this contempt. In what respect, then, are such persons truly inexcusable? Because you are condemned even by your own judgment, when you condemn in others the same things you do, or similar things.

This bears especially upon the proud contention of the Romans, by which they wished to set themselves above one another and, defending themselves individually, judged others criminal. “For in that wherein you judge”: that is, concerning the same sin for which you judge—that is, rebuke—and deem another worthy of condemnation, you condemn yourself; that is, by doing those things you make or declare yourself condemnable, and pronounce sentence against yourself by your own judgment. He adds why and how, saying: “Yet you do the same things which you judge”: that is, the evil works which you rebuke in others and commit against your own conscience. [Col. 0809B]

And I said, “which you judge” by rebuking; but you rightly judge in condemning those things which God himself judges in punishing. This is what he means: “For we know,” etc. Or thus: I said, “you condemn yourself,” that is, you make yourself condemnable by doing them. And this is true: “For we know,” namely, we who are enlightened by divine grace, “that the judgment of God,” which is according to the truth of the matter itself, cannot be deceived, “is upon them,” that is, against those who do such things, in order to punish and condemn them.

[Col. 0809C] And since it is so—that is, since God condemns such persons—do you, who judge, that is, accuse or charge, those who do such things and yet do them yourself, think that you will escape the judgment of God, that is, his just vengeance for such things? Or do you not even know that you are so much the more condemnable as God waits for you with greater patience, and that by waiting long his kindness invites you to repentance, while you turn this kindness of his patience into contempt and fear him less [Col. 0809D] the more he bears your offenses and does not immediately punish? This is what he means by “Or do you not know?”

“Do you despise the riches of his goodness,” that is, of God—his rich and abundant sweetness of disposition—“of goodness,” I say, “and patience and long-suffering,” that is, his long patience? Do you not know that “the kindness of God,” that is, this display of his goodness by which he waits for you, “leads,” so far as it lies in itself—that is, invites and exhorts—to repentance for your sins rather than to contempt of the one who waits?

“But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you store up for yourself”—that is, diligently accumulate for yourself, as though precious riches—“wrath,” that is, vengeance to be exercised upon you, “in the day,” that is, at the time, “of wrath and revelation,” that is, of God’s vengeance to be revealed against you. And lest that wrath be understood as cruelty rather than justice, or as rashness rather than deliberation, he adds: “of the just judge,” that is, wrath—namely vengeance—proceeding from the judgment of the just deliberation of God, who cannot act unjustly. He then adds how just the divine judgment is:

“Who will render to each one” what he has deserved, “according to his works,” that is, according to the quality of works, which consists more in intention than in action. [Col. 0810A] The quality of recompense corresponds to the quality of works: as works are, so is recompense—good for good and evil for evil—since before God the will itself is reckoned as the deed performed. Hence he who tests hearts and reins is said to see in secret.

[Col. 0810B] Here he uses “work” for the disposition underlying the work, the term being transferred from effect to cause. Otherwise God’s judgment would not be shown to be just, since works are in themselves indifferent—that is, neither good nor evil, nor apparently worthy of recompense—unless they are judged according to the root of intention, the tree that bears good or evil fruit. Thus “according to his works” means, as though he said, according to the will with which they desire things to be done or not done. Otherwise the pride of the devil and Simon’s desire, which did not attain their intended effect, would not seem to belong to this judgment.

Infants who die before the years of discernment do not seem to have a judgment; they do not belong to this revelation of judgment, of which it is said: “He will render to each one according to his works,” that is, grant each what [Col. 0810C] he has deserved.

The Apostle therefore carefully stated what is to be understood by the judgment of God when he said “the revelation of judgment.” For each person will be judged there not by words but by the showing of the deed: that is, it will be made manifest whether he was worthy of reward or punishment. While he lived, even the saints had no certain knowledge of his end—whether, that is, he was predestined to life or not.

This judgment—that is, this revelation or examination of the divine inquiry—takes place individually each day at the death of those who die, and will take place generally at the end of the age. There all will be revealed to all, namely what they had previously been like, whether worthy of reward or punishment. In that general examination two orders are said to exist among the elect and the reprobate. Some of the elect—that is, the predestined—will there judge only and not be judged. Likewise there will be two orders among the reprobate: some of them will be judged only, while others will not be judged at all. [Col. 0810D]

For all elect persons who are not found purified before the day of judgment will be judged there—that is, revealed; of such persons he says elsewhere: “But he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire.” But those found to have lived a perfect life, or purified before judgment itself, will not be judged there—that is, revealed—but instead will judge together with Christ himself. They will share in such majesty and glory and shine so brightly that it will at once be apparent from them, as from Christ himself, how well those who adhered to them acted and how wickedly those who despised them acted. Thus they too will sit as judges with Christ, entirely secure concerning themselves and judging others—that is, as was said, revealing whether others acted well with them or wickedly against them, and whether they are therefore worthy of reward or punishment.

But the reprobate who die in their unbelief have already been judged at their very death—that is, revealed—and need not be revealed further in the general judgment, according to the saying of Truth: “He who does not believe has already been judged” (John III, 18). But those who possessed faith while leading an uncertain life in secret, and whose end is therefore uncertain, are to be judged there—that is, revealed. [Col. 0811A]

“To those indeed who according to.” He shows how the quality of recompense corresponds to the quality of work, so that good is rendered for good and, conversely, evil for evil. [Col. 0811B] This is what is meant here by “those who according to the patience of good work”—supply “are,” so as to show that tribulations are not lacking to those who act well, by which they are purified or advance.

“Glory and honor,” that is, glorious honor, when our humanity reaches the height of angels and we shall reign with him as heirs of God and fellow heirs of Christ. And lest this glory be referred only to the soul, he adds concerning glorified bodies, which will be incorruptible: “and incorruption,” namely of bodies, for those, I say, who seek life—not transitory, as we have seen, but eternal, as Christians do—so that he may show that they rightly obtain what they longed for with their whole desire and are not defrauded of their hope, as is written of every righteous person: “He asked life of you, and you gave it to him” (Ps. XX, 5); and again: “You have granted him the desire of his soul” (ibid., 3). [Col. 0811C]

“But to those who are contentious”—supply “there are,” that is, those who knowingly resist the divine will. He immediately explains this by saying: those “who do not obey the truth” which they know, so as to act according to what they truly believe ought to be done, “but rather believe”—that is, obey or assent to—“unrighteousness,” so that they fulfill in deed, or endeavor to fulfill, the evil they conceive in mind. There shall be rendered—supply—“wrath and indignation,” which they have deserved: that is, God’s vengeance without their patience.

But if the elect are ever punished in any way so that they may be purified, they bear it patiently; they do not become angry because of it, but rather rejoice and give thanks, recalling what is written: “The Lord has chastened me severely, and has not delivered me to death” (Ps. CXVII, 18); and again: “Those whom God loves he corrects, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. XII, 6). [Col. 0811D] Hence Jerome, writing to Castrutius [Note: *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 652], says: “It is great wrath when God is not angry with sinners.”

“Tribulation and distress.” He shows from what the aforesaid wrath and indignation arise. Tribulation is distress in which the person tortured is deprived of every hope of escape, so that no hope of remedy remains, and he is tortured also by despair itself. Since he had said “to those” indefinitely, he adds that this comes generally “upon every soul of man who does evil,” [Col. 0812A] both Jew and Gentile—that is, both those instructed by the written law and those by the natural law. He says “doing,” not “having done”: that is, persevering in wickedness and not ceasing. Even amid their torments they will not lay aside their evil will, being confirmed with the devil; if they could, they would still wish to do the same things. Therefore the punishment will deservedly be eternal, because guilt will persist eternally in the mind.

Thus, as blessed Jerome testifies, the Lord will rightly say on the day of judgment: “Depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matt. VII, 23), that is, you who not only committed it, but still work it in your hearts. There, as we said above, before God the will is counted as the work performed.

[Col. 0812B] He properly says that vengeance is inflicted “upon the soul,” not upon the human body, because it belongs to the soul alone, not the body, to suffer or feel, to be grieved or delighted, angered or joyful. And if we consider carefully, it is the soul alone, which can will, that merits from God, the rewarder of wills, either reward or punishment from good or evil will; it alone is properly said to sin, just as it alone possesses virtues, and it alone is made blessed through the vision of the divine majesty, which is beheld only by the eyes of the mind, not of the body.

That the five bodily senses are called senses of the soul, although the soul alone feels; or that some sins are called carnal and others spiritual, although the soul alone sins—the soul alone having reason and the capacity to will—must not be understood as though the body itself feels or sins. Rather, bodily means are used either to exercise the senses or fulfill the wills: for example, gluttony through the throat, lust through the genitals.

Accordingly, the soul alone, by a good or evil will, deserves and receives reward or punishment before God, and it alone can share in blessedness or misery, although its punishment or glory is increased through the body when it is resumed. Hence we speak of the twofold contrition of the wicked and the double robe of the saints, namely according to soul as well as body.
