The good soul will rejoice more abundantly and glorify the Creator more when it sees that very body which it bore here, so weak and liable to suffering, fitted there in such a way that it can no longer be dissolved, nor can the soul itself suffer any injury through union with it. This restoration of the human body itself is called the glorification or blessedness of the body [Col. 0812D]. Likewise, the punishment of the body may be spoken of—a punishment which the soul itself will endure through bodily members.

Yet, although the glory or punishment of souls is doubled through bodies, we do not therefore prefer this double glory or punishment to the single glory or punishment of angels or demons, who are not of bodily nature. That the soul alone, as has been said, suffers or perceives is also affirmed by the saints themselves. Thus Augustine, *The City of God*, book XX, chapter 11:

> “If we consider more carefully, the pain called bodily pain belongs rather to the soul. For it is the soul’s office to suffer pain, not the body’s, even when the cause of its pain arises from the body, when it feels pain in the place where the body is injured.”

The same author, *On Genesis*:

> “Perception is not the body's, but the soul’s through the body.” [Col. 0813A]

Again:

> “For the body does not perceive; rather, the soul perceives through the body.”

The same, in the letter to Dioscorus, in the epistle beginning, “You ask me innumerable questions, etc.”:

> “The mind therefore receives from the body neither the highest good nor any part of the highest good. Those who do not see this are blinded by the sweetness of carnal pleasures, which they do not perceive to arise from a deficiency of health. But the perfect health of the body will be that final immortality of the whole human being. For God made the soul of such power that, from its most complete blessedness—which is promised to the saints at the end of time—there overflows even into the lower nature, which is the body, not the blessedness proper to one who enjoys and understands, but the fullness of health and the strength of incorruption.”

[Col. 0813B] **To the Jew first, and also to the Greek.** By “Jew” he means every person instructed by the written law; by “Greek,” every rational person among the Gentiles after the manner of the philosophers, who were Greeks—that is, one most fully instructed by the natural law. The greater their discernment, the greater their transgression. Therefore he says, “to the Jew and to the Greek first,” that is, chiefly: “upon one who does evil,” that is, who sins, in comparison with other people who are as it were brute animals.

**But glory and honour.** He repeats the reward of the righteous which he had previously set forth, so that, by more frequent remembrance of it, he may kindle us more strongly toward it. By “peace” he means not only rest from the assault of external enemies, but also that harmony of spirit and flesh in which the flesh no longer resists the spirit in any respect, all the troubles of carnal promptings having entirely ceased [Col. 0813C]. “To the Jew first, and to the Greek,” namely, who does good. For insofar as these persons had known the supreme good, the Lord, more fully, either through writing or through reason, so they adhered more fully to His will by sober living. Thus here too he uses “first” in the sense of “chiefly.”

**For there is no…** I have spoken generally to everyone, yet with distinction, making no difference in recompense according to the rank of persons. And rightly so, because “there is no respect of persons with God”; that is, the divine judgment never punishes anyone there less, or glorifies anyone more, because of some dignity or eminence which that person seemed to possess here. Rather, it renders equally to all according to their merits: both to those who have the law and to those who do not; both to those who glory in descent from Israel [Col. 0813D] and to the rest.

He shows that God renders according to merits alone because the measure of punishments corresponds to the measure of transgressions. Hence it is clear that the same must be understood concerning rewards. Therefore, just as the transgression of one who has also received the written law is greater than that of one instructed by the natural law alone, so he shows the former’s punishment to be greater and the latter’s less, saying: “All who have sinned without the law”—namely, the written law, as the Gentiles, that is, those who do not possess it for their instruction—“will indeed perish,” that is, be condemned; but they “will perish without the law,” that is, they will incur no punishment for transgressing the written law, but only for transgressing the natural law. “And all who have sinned in the law,” that is, by transgression also of the written law, as the Jews, “will be judged by the law” [Col. 0814A], that is, they can openly be convicted as guilty by their profession of the law which they have undertaken but have not kept.

But since the transgression of those who are also transgressors of the written law is greater than that of the natural law, why did he say there, “they will perish,” and here, “they will be judged”? For sins reserved for judgment seem not to be as great as those which do not await judgment, but immediately condemn and compel the guilty person to perish, without any examination of judgment. But surely, as we have said, he used “be judged” to mean “be openly convicted,” so that the sin may appear all the greater insofar as it can be convicted more openly—namely, through transgression of the written law, which was openly delivered by God before all and confirmed by miracles. For those condemned by public judgment are openly accused, and after the judgment’s sentence has been approved they find no defender [Col. 0814B].

**For not the hearers…** He begins an invective against the Jews… I said, “they will be judged by the law,” as guilty persons, because, though they hear the law, they are not therefore righteous unless they do the works which the law commands. And this is the meaning of: “For not the hearers…” That is, people are not righteous before God merely because they are hearers of the law—that is, in divine judgment, however it may be in human judgment—but because they are doers, that is, because they do what the law commands.

But since elsewhere he says that no one is justified by works of the law, how does he now say that the doers of the law will be justified? Unless here he calls “doers” those who are spontaneously moved to action by love of God, in accordance with what we have said: a good will is counted as the completed work. For we please God not by external work [Col. 0814C], but rather by the will; there he speaks of external work.

We may here also understand the natural law, which the Gentiles alone employ. But concerning those of whom he speaks in what follows, understand the statement about the written law’s works, so that it may be understood thus: not only those who hear the words of the natural law are righteous, but those who fulfil them in deed. The words of the natural law are those which commend love of God and neighbour, such as: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4:16); and: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. 7:12).

**For when the Gentiles…** And indeed, as has been said, the force of justification consists not in hearing the written law but in doing it [Col. 0814D]. This is apparent from the Gentiles, who, though they do not possess a written law which they can hear, are nevertheless saved equally with the Jews when they do the works commanded by the law. And this is what is meant by “for when the Gentiles”: namely, Gentiles who do not possess the written law, “by nature do” what it commands—that is, instructed by the natural law, by knowledge of God and rational discernment, which they possess naturally, that is, from their creation, not from someone’s written teaching.

These people, I say, who do not possess such a law—that is, a law written outwardly, as the Jews do—“are a law to themselves”; that is, through themselves without a written law they attain the same reward which the Jews attain through obedience to the written law. For they outwardly display in action the good will which they have in the mind: this is “the work of the law written in their hearts” [Col. 0815A]. When he says “written,” he indicates the permanence of good will. For, as blessed Gregory says, what we speak passes away; what we write remains. Those who are hearers of the law, then, as it were speak the law which they keep written on parchments but do not hold fixed in their hearts. These persons, by contrast, act rightly, “their conscience bearing them good witness”; that is, their good conscience and right intention, known to them and not to others, makes them secure concerning the righteousness of their works. God weighs works according to that intention.

**And among themselves.** A different textual form is commonly read here. Sometimes the plural genitives are given as follows: *cogitationum et accusantium, aut etiam defendentium*—“of thoughts accusing or even defending”; sometimes the ablatives: *cogitationibus accusantibus*—“with thoughts accusing” [Col. 0815B], etc. Hence Augustine, *The City of God*, book XX [Note: [Col. 0815D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, col. 702]:

> “For ‘in thoughts,’ as it is written, ‘there shall be an examination of the ungodly’ (Wis. 1:9). And the Apostle says: ‘With thoughts accusing, or even excusing, on the day when God shall judge the secrets of men,’ etc.”

The same author, on Psalm 108 [Note: [Col. 0815D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXVII, col. 1571]:

> “All works, whether good or evil, proceed from thought. In thought each person is innocent; in thought each person is guilty. Therefore it is written: ‘A holy thought shall keep you’ (Prov. 2:11).”

And elsewhere: “There shall be an examination in the thoughts of the ungodly” (Wis. 1:9). And the Apostle says: “With thoughts accusing or even excusing,” etc.

The same author, on Psalm 5 [Note: [Col. 0816D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXVI, col. 88]:

> “‘Let them fall from their thoughts’ means: let them fall by their own thoughts accusing them, by their own conscience, as the Apostle says [Col. 0815C]: ‘of thoughts accusing or defending,’ etc. (ibid.).”

I think that this variation in the wording arose chiefly from the usage of the Greek language. Since the Greeks lack the ablative, they use the genitive in place of the ablative. Thus, in different translations from Greek into Latin, the genitive has sometimes been retained in Latin as it was in Greek, and sometimes, as the sense required, has been changed among us into the ablative. Although this Epistle directed to the Romans is understood to have been written first in Latin, even if it was written at Corinth in Greece, we nevertheless believe that there were later different translators or expositors who imitated the Greeks, as stated above, perhaps because they did not have the Latin writing at hand and therefore resorted to Greek copies [Col. 0815D]. Let us therefore expound both textual forms.

Since it has been said above, “their conscience bearing them witness,” he adds, “and the conscience of their thoughts,” etc. It is as though he said: And this is such a conscience as does not err in discerning works, because it examines them according to the thoughts of the mind itself—that is, intentions. These thoughts have the power to accuse or defend before God more than external works do. And this is the meaning of “the conscience, I say, of thoughts”: that is, a conscience which gives greater attention to thoughts themselves than to works.

He adds why it weighs them especially: because they accuse or excuse before God [Col. 0816A]. “Of thoughts,” I say, “among themselves,” namely, thoughts held by them, so that they judge concerning themselves as concerning others, according to the above-mentioned rule of natural law: “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another”; and: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them.”

“On the day,” that is, at the time when God will judge through His Son, that is, Jesus Christ, as it is written: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). “The secrets of people,” that is, intentions rather than external works. “According to my Gospel,” that is, as I preach: namely, that God assigns recompense according to intention rather than according to works.

But if it is an absolute ablative in this form, “and among themselves, with thoughts accusing,” etc., it will be joined to the preceding ablative as follows: I said, “their conscience bearing them witness, and their thoughts, which they have among themselves”—that is, by which they weigh themselves as they do others, as stated—“their own thoughts,” I say, that is, their own intentions, supplying: “bearing them witness” [Col. 0816B]. It is as though an explanation of what was said before, namely “their conscience”: that is, their thoughts, etc. He then adds why their thoughts bear witness to them—that is, make them secure before God—because, as has been said, thoughts alone have power before God to accuse or defend. And this is what he adds: “accusing or even defending,” etc.

[Col. 0816C] But the question is raised how, after the commandment concerning circumcision had been given—“Every soul whose foreskin of flesh has not been circumcised,” etc. (Gen. 17:11)—uncircumcised Gentiles, such as Job and perhaps many others of the sort mentioned in “For when the Gentiles,” etc., were saved.

But if we carefully consider the very words of Scripture and the beginning of circumcision itself, which was first enjoined upon Abraham, we shall see that the command of circumcision was not universal, but belonged only to Abraham and his seed—that is, Isaac; for the Lord said to Abraham: “In Isaac shall seed be called for you” (Gen. 21:12), not in Ishmael. Thus, when the Lord commanded Abraham concerning circumcision, He said: “This shall be the covenant between me and you and your seed after you” (Gen. 17:10).

Origen also, in his exposition of this Epistle later on, plainly demonstrates from other words of Scripture itself that the sign of circumcision was commanded only for the people of Israel and for those born in their household or bought with their money. For, after expounding the verse, “If the uncircumcised person keeps the righteous requirements of the law,” etc., he carefully examines the command and rationale of circumcision and says:

> “It does not seem inappropriate to examine the general rationale of circumcision. The Lord said to Abraham: ‘But you shall keep my covenant, and all your seed after you throughout their generations. And this is the covenant between me and you, and between me and the midst of your seed [Col. 0817A] after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised, and the child on the eighth day. Every male among you throughout your generations shall be circumcised, one born in the household and one bought with money’ (Gen. 17:10–14). Let us examine whether the command also binds those who believed from among the Gentiles. He never mentions a proselyte, that is, an immigrant; rather, He commands that a household slave or one bought for a price be circumcised, not a free person. Let us therefore investigate the law of Leviticus.

> “‘Speak,’ he says, ‘to the children of Israel, and say to them: If a woman has borne a male child, on the eighth day she shall circumcise,’ etc. (Lev. 12:3). Observe here also how Moses is commanded to speak concerning the law of circumcision only to the children of Israel, and how no mention is made of foreigners, whereas in some commandments he speaks not only to the children of Israel, but also to proselytes and immigrants [Col. 0817B]. The distinction must certainly be observed. For, just as where it says, ‘Speak to Aaron,’ and elsewhere, ‘to the sons of Aaron,’ and elsewhere, ‘to the Levites,’ it is certain that the rest are not subject to those laws; so, where commandments are given to the children and no mention at all is made of foreigners, one must not suppose the command common where the designation itself makes an exception.

> “If, therefore, no one else is bound by the law of circumcision except one descended from Abraham, or one born in their household, or one bought with money, do you wish to see how, wherever it is intended that foreigners too be bound by a law, this is expressly indicated? Hear what is written: ‘Any person from the children of Israel and from the immigrants, whoever eats any blood, I will destroy that person; for the life of all flesh is its blood, and I have given it to you, that by it atonement may be made upon the altar for your souls, because blood shall make expiation for the soul’ (Lev. 7:1 ff.) [Col. 0817C]. You see, therefore, that we who have believed from among the Gentiles observe this law which was also given to immigrants. Thus the Church, understanding the written law in this way, received the law concerning observance of blood as common to the children of Israel and the Gentiles. Accordingly, that blessed council of the apostles then issued its decrees, writing to the Gentiles that they should abstain from blood and from what has been strangled (Acts 15:20).

> “But perhaps you will ask whether a law concerning what has been strangled was likewise given in common to the children of Israel and immigrants. Hear: ‘Any person from the children of Israel and from the immigrants among you who has hunted a beast or bird which may be eaten shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth, because the life of all flesh is its blood’ (Lev. 7:13).

> “But because among the passages from Leviticus which we have cited above, this too occurs: ‘Any person from the children of Israel or from the immigrants among them who offers a burnt offering or sacrifice and does not bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle to offer it to the Lord shall be cut off from his people’ (ibid., 9) [Col. 0817D], the Church from the Gentiles also appears by this to be made liable for burnt offerings. Yet He does not command it to offer; rather, if it should happen to offer, He teaches how it must do so. For it is certain that, while the temple stood in Jerusalem and the religion handed down to the fathers remained in force, many people from the Gentiles also came to the temple to worship and offer sacrifices. But because this was commanded to be done in one place only—and here too He commands that the victim to be slaughtered be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle—it could lawfully be done only so long as that place remained intact.

> “Thus the Savior also said to the ten lepers whom He had cleansed: ‘Go, show yourselves to the priests, and offer sacrifices for yourselves as Moses commanded’ (Luke 17:14) [Col. 0818A]. But now, how can that be demanded from immigrants which even their own worshippers are not permitted to offer? We have said these things in order to show especially concerning the command of circumcision that it was enjoined upon none but those who trace their descent from Abraham, those born in their households, and those bought with money. Those Gentiles who believe in God through Christ are free from laws of this kind. Likewise, let them first recover the established temple, etc.”

**But if you are called a Jew.** O Jew, the Gentiles, who are removed from the inheritance of the holy Fathers’ lineage and who are not instructed by the written law, seem to you to be such as are excluded when the Lord says to Abraham, “In Isaac shall seed be called for you” (Gen. 21:12); yet they act well. But with you the opposite is true. He heightens this point by presenting it in a certain composition and with indignant reproach, saying: “If you are called a Jew,” that is, if you are not truly a Jew through imitation of the faithful Fathers, but are called a Jew in name alone—called so from the patriarch Judah or from Judas Maccabaeus, etc.

Origen teaches in what follows: “You are not said to be a Jew, but are merely called one,” because the true Jew is the one circumcised in secret. “But one who is outwardly such as to be seen by people is not truly a Jew, but is merely called one” [Col. 0818C]. And in the Apocalypse: “Those who say that they are Jews and are not” (Rev. 3:9).

The person who is truly a Jew derives the name from that Judah concerning whom it is written: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you,” etc. (Gen. 49:8), words prophesied concerning the Savior. Augustine, on Psalm 71:

> “The Jews were called chiefly from the patriarch Judah, because Saul, who was first given from another tribe, was rejected as evil. David was the first king from the tribe of Judah, and from him they always had kings from the tribe of Judah. Hence they were called Jews; and foreign kings began with Herod. Therefore, at the Lord’s coming, the kingdom of the Jews was overthrown and taken from the Jews because they would not acknowledge the true King. Now consider whether they ought to be called Jews [Col. 0818D]. By their own voice they renounced this name, so that they should not be considered worthy to be called Jews except merely according to the flesh. They raged against Christ—that is, against the lineage of Judah, David’s seed—and said: ‘We have no king but Caesar’ (John 19:15). O Jews, if you have no king but Caesar, then the ruler has already failed from Judah; the one to whom it was promised has come. Those Jews who became Christians are therefore more truly called Jews. The true Judaea is Christ’s Church. We believe in Him who came from the tribe of Judah through Mary.”

Haymo: “But if you are called a Jew,” understand, “from the patriarch Judah,” etc.

Ambrose:

> “‘To the Jew first, and also to the Greek.’ The Jews began to be called so from the time of Judas Maccabaeus, who, at a time of calamity, resisted the sacrilegious and, trusting in God [Col. 0819A], gathered the people and defended his race.”

It should be noted, however, that here Ambrose does not say that the Jews are called after Judas Maccabaeus, but that they began to be called so from his time—especially since they are not found called thus in the other books of the Old Testament as they are in the books of the Maccabees. Even if they had been called thus after Judas Maccabaeus, they still appear to be named after the patriarch Judah, since Judas Maccabaeus himself was so called after that Judah.

**And you rest in the law.** That is, so that you need not weary yourself through error in seeking what you ought to do; all your study is occupied with it, so that you do not seek other writings, namely those of poets and philosophers. “And you glory in God,” that is, you boast that you are glorious because of your knowledge of God and the law given to you by Him; through this law you know His will, namely, what pleases Him to be done. “And you approve,” that is, you discern not only useful things from useful things, but also more useful things from useful ones.

“You are confident,” namely, that you can show others the way of righteousness in God’s commandments. By “the blind,” “those in darkness,” “the foolish,” and “children,” he means the same thing; and similarly he takes “guide,” “light,” “instructor,” and “teacher” in the same sense. This is a certain repetition of words intended to shame them, not a diversity of meaning. He next gives the ground on which the Jew is confident of being a guide of the blind, that is, competent to teach others: I mean you, “having in the law the form of knowledge and truth,” that is, true knowledge which can instruct others and shape them for right action [Col. 0819C].

You, therefore, so great and such a person in your own judgment, who teach—that is, correct—others, etc.: he adds what you ought to correct in yourself, saying: “You who preach,” namely from the words of the law, etc.; “you who abhor idols,” that is, images of idols because of what they signify, while you do not avoid sacrilege for its own sake, because it is evil in itself.

Sacrilege is the violation of a sacred thing, especially things pertaining to God’s worship, such as the temple and what belongs to it. The Jews violated God’s temple, whether material and figurative or spiritual and true: the handmade temple, by conducting business in it, for which the Lord expelled them; or the Lord Himself, by crucifying Him. Speaking of the temple of His body, He said: “Destroy this temple,” etc. (John 2:19) [Col. 0819D]. “You dishonour the Lord,” that is, you make Him contemptible to others, as far as lies in you.

He employs here a rhetorical figure called repetition, which has the same beginning repeated in different clauses of the sentence, as “you who,” “what,” and “as far as” are repeated.

**For the name…** Although above he had said in the singular, “But if you,” he now says in the plural, “through you.” He plainly indicates that he has introduced the person of the Jew in general, as if reproving generally the rebellious people from whom those converted Jews who were at Rome gloried in being descended. In that people he says that some had been, or still were, guilty of theft; others, of adultery; and so forth.

The connection is: I rightly say that you dishonour, you people of the Jews, because “through you the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles,” that is, among unbelievers, as is also the knowledge of Him in which you glory [Col. 0820A]. For, as Cicero observes, knowledge is often blamed because of a person’s vice, as though that knowledge taught one to act badly. As it is written in the prophet Ezekiel in these words: “My holy name, which you have polluted among the Gentiles” (Ezek. 20:39), that is, you caused it to be held in contempt or ridicule; and although it was in itself most precious, you made it contemptible.

**For circumcision indeed…** Above he took away their boasting in the law given to them, because they do not do what the law commands and thus are more accused than justified by the law. Now, through this same fact—that they do not obey the law—he takes away the glory of circumcision. For just as the giving of the law benefits those who receive it in no way unless they keep it, so circumcision is of no benefit unless they obey the law, that is, fulfil the other commandments as they fulfil the commandment of circumcision.

For, as another apostle says, “whoever stumbles in one point is guilty of all” (Jas. 2:10), that is, a transgressor or despiser of the entire law which contains all God’s commandments. Since the law commands everything together, not one thing only, whoever transgresses one commandment does not keep the law. Thus, by transgression of any individual commandment, one becomes guilty of a violated law. Carnal circumcision therefore contributes nothing to salvation if the law is violated in other matters. Similarly baptism, in whose place circumcision stood, as blessed Gregory attests, does not save if we remain transgressors in other respects [Col. 0820C].

But since circumcision now has no force at all, according to the Apostle himself writing to the Galatians: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5:2), that is, that sign will now confer no benefit upon you, it is clear that here the Apostle looks back to the earlier state of the law, in which circumcision was beneficial. The converted Jews were even then glorying in that state of the law, though it had already passed away and died with respect to its carnal observances.

But if the Apostle, looking to his own present time, says, “Circumcision indeed profits, if you keep the law,” it is as though he said: Circumcision now profits if it is spiritual rather than carnal, a circumcision common to Gentile and Jew alike [Col. 0820D]. Keeping the law therefore brings about spiritual circumcision, that is, separation from vices, which is figured by carnal circumcision. Thus “if you keep the law” means as if he had said: if circumcision is spiritual—of the heart rather than of the body—because the sign is superfluous where that which is signified is absent through negligence.

**But if you are a transgressor…** A *praeputium* (“foreskin”) is the piece of the genital member which those performing circumcision cut away from its extremity. It is called *praeputium* as though from *amputando*, “cutting away,” that is, *praescindendo*, “cutting off,” although *putare* is not now used for “to cut,” as *amputare* is. Nevertheless it is said in the Song of Songs: “The time of pruning has come” (Song 2:12), that is, of cutting away.

Just as circumcision of the flesh signifies circumcision of the heart—that is, separation from carnal vices—so retained foreskin represents the impurity of carnal desires. Hence Jews and Gentiles, who had a foreskin, called not the uncircumcised persons *praeputiati*, that is, “unclean,” but the foreskin itself *praeputium*, that is, impurity itself [Col. 0821A].

**Your circumcision…** That is, the circumcision in your flesh alone, which you approve and perform, not God. “Has become a foreskin to you,” that is, in a certain sense an impurity, because after receiving the sacrament of circumcision and professing that the law should be kept, you are convicted as more guilty if you do not keep it than if you had not done this.

**If therefore…** He argues as from opposites: Since your circumcision—that is, carnal circumcision—becomes a foreskin to you, that is, defiles and condemns you more if you do not keep the law, then the Gentile’s foreskin, if that Gentile fulfils by the natural law what is written, “will be reckoned to him as circumcision”; that is, those possessing bodily foreskin will be reckoned by divine judgment to possess the same merit as those spiritually circumcised.

For he does not here repeat “your circumcision” in order that we might understand carnal circumcision, as he had used the term above; he says simply “circumcision,” thus indicating spiritual circumcision performed by God. Likewise, when he says “his foreskin,” as above “your circumcision,” he understands the foreskin carnally: the bodily part, not the impurity of the heart. Otherwise he would not say that the foreskin is reckoned as circumcision [Col. 0821B].

“If the foreskin,” that is, the Gentile people possessing foreskin itself, which you Jews call “foreskin,” as it were in reproach, “keeps the righteous requirements of the law” rather than its figures—that is, fulfils the moral commandments of love, which justify each person—will not that person’s foreskin, that is, that Gentile people possessing its own bodily foreskin with which it is born, be reckoned by God as worthy of reward? Truly, and spiritually, the foreskin itself, fulfilling the law—that is, completing it—will be reckoned among the circumcised, as stated. For, as is said later, “the fullness of the law is love.”

That it fulfils the law comes to it from nature, that is, from the instruction of the natural law which contains those two commandments of love of which we have spoken: “What you do not wish,” etc. “Will judge you,” that is, will openly convict you as guilty—you, I mean, a Jew who, though instructed by the written law in which you glory, neglect to act rightly [Col. 0821C]. You are “a transgressor of the law through the letter which kills,” that is, through the literal sense: clinging to the carnal signs in which you trust, especially to what signifies rather than to what is signified, that is, to figures rather than the things themselves, and to likeness rather than truth.

**For not the one who…** I rightly say that foreskin is reckoned as circumcision through the performance of good works, and that circumcision passes into foreskin through evil works. For those circumcised carnally, even though they are called Jews openly, are not truly Jews—that is, Jews in heart—but rather those Gentiles mentioned above are Jews, although they were in no way reckoned Jews or circumcised.

Open Jews are those called Jews merely by the name and nation of Judah, confessing the Lord outwardly with their voice while departing from Him in mind. Of them it is said: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15:8) [Col. 0822A].

“But the one who is a Jew in secret” consists in those who confess God in the heart, where God sees, and who strive to serve God rather than seek human notice. “Neither is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh”: that is, circumcision made by human hands, in the cutting away of flesh, is not circumcision—that is, it is not the true condemnation of vices and destruction of concupiscence. Rather, true circumcision is that of the heart, by which vices and concupiscences are cut away from the mind.

This circumcision, I say, is “in the spirit, not the letter,” that is, performed according to the spiritual and mystical, not the literal, sense. Its—namely, the spiritual Jew’s or spiritual circumcision’s—praise is from God, because God approves it, not people: that is, carnal people, who understand the law only carnally and not spiritually, and weigh works more than the mind, seeing the face and not the heart [Col. 0822B].

## CHAPTER III

**What then is the advantage…?** The Apostle raises against himself the objection which the Jews could make against the foregoing argument, so that he may answer it. For the Jews could say: You have said that circumcision passes into foreskin and foreskin passes into circumcision. What, then, does the Jew have more than the Gentile? What greater benefits did God confer upon the Jews than upon the Gentiles, who were called dogs and unclean? Or what is the benefit of circumcision, that is, of those circumcised?

This is added as though an explanation of what precedes. For when he said “to the Jew alone,” it could have been understood of those belonging to the tribe of Judah, from whom Jews are named. And “what advantage” could have reference either to good or to evil, and perhaps more to evil, since he had most strongly criticized the Jews just before. Yet it is the Apostle’s custom, just as he uses “foreskin” for Gentiles, so to use “circumcision” for Jews.

Indeed, in former times the Lord conferred much greater benefit upon the Jew than upon the Gentile, “in every way,” that is, by every means: instructing them by the law, confirming them by innumerable miracles and benefits, and drawing them toward His love. But this was first, that is, the greatest among God’s gifts: that He gave them the law, so that they might be instructed not only by the natural law, as Gentiles are, but in addition by a written law. This is what he says: “first,” that is, the greatest benefit, was that “the oracles of God” in the law and prophets “were entrusted” to them [Col. 0822D].

This gift could both instruct them and preserve them for ever. Note, however, that he does not say “committed,” but “entrusted,” as if this teaching had been lent to them for a time, and would pass on to us through its spiritual and correct interpretation while ceasing in its carnal observances, in which the Jews especially trusted. God is called, as it were, the creditor of His oracles, because from those to whom He entrusts them He requires obedience as their price. He calls the words of God “oracles,” as if by excellence beyond other kinds of utterance [Col. 0823A], because of their fruit of obedience and life-giving teaching.

For what reason, someone might ask, although divine utterances were given to that people, did God nevertheless not fulfil for them the goods promised—whether concerning the restoration of humankind through his Son or concerning any promises whatever? The Apostle refutes this in two ways: by showing that not all among the people were unbelieving, so that the promises could be wholly denied to that people; and that, because God is truthful, his promises cannot fail. Read it thus: I rightly said that the greatest benefit lay in the divine utterances, by which he might draw his people to himself. For what hinders the divine purpose? If some of them did not believe those utterances—that is, the things promised or foretold there [Col. 0823B]—has their unbelief, namely the unbelief of those who did not believe, nullified faith in God, by which they believed God, so that what Moses, Joshua, and the other faithful believed did not occur? Far be it that their faith should be nullified—that is, frustrated—in those promises foretold there which they believed. But God is—I said, “Far be it,” not thoughtlessly but advisedly—truthful, that is, steadfast or unchangeable, in what he promises or foretells.

But every human being is false, that is, changeable in purpose, so that one’s counsel or will can easily be altered. Perhaps one asks whether the human being in Christ, united to divinity, could lie or sin. [Col. 0823C] Although in the preceding statement, “But God is truthful,” it is immediately added, “but every human being is false,” the God-man seems excluded, so that “every human being is false” should be understood only of the mere human being, not of the human being who is God. Yet no one should doubt that that human being united to God, after being united to him, or while united to him, could in no way sin—just as one who is predestined, after being predestined or while predestined, cannot be damned.

But if it is stated simply that that human being who is united can in no way sin, anyone may doubt it. For if he cannot sin or do evil at all, what merit has he in avoiding a sin which he can in no way commit, or what sense is there in saying that he avoids what he cannot possibly incur? Hence Boethius, in *Against Eutyches and Nestorius*, says concerning the man whom God assumed: “How, I ask, could it be that he assumed such a man as Adam was before sin, when in Adam there could be a will and inclination to sin?” Moreover, it is written in praise of the righteous: “Who was able to transgress and did not transgress, to do evil and did not do it? He shall dwell in the heights,” etc. (Ecclus. 31:10). This pertains to human free choice: that it lies within one’s power to act well or badly. But if Christ did not have this, he seems deprived of free choice, avoiding sin by necessity rather than by will, and possessing this by nature rather than by grace. For what is bestowed on anyone through grace comes to him from a gift rather than from the property of his own nature; what we have from another’s gift rather than from ourselves should be called not so much natural as gratuitous.

[Col. 0824A] Who, moreover, would deny that the human being united to God, consisting of soul and flesh in one person, could subsist in his own nature, as other human beings do, even without that union? Otherwise he would seem of weaker constitution, if he could not subsist by himself as other human beings do, and to possess more the nature of an accident than of a substance. But if he could exist by himself, why could he not likewise sin as other people can?

Therefore, it seems to us that in this matter too, as in others, we must carefully attend to the force of propositions: namely, when they assert “possible” or “necessary” with a qualification [Col. 0824B] and when they are stated simply, that is, without an added qualification. It is true if it is simply stated that one who is predestined and will be saved can be damned, since it was altogether possible for him not to have been predestined and not to be saved. Yet it is not true, with the qualification added, to say that he can be damned while he is predestined or while he will be saved. Likewise, one who is maimed can have two feet, since every human being is two-footed; and one who is blind can see. Yet it is not possible after he has been maimed, or after he has become blind. Otherwise a return from privation to possession would be possible, [Col. 0824C] which is wholly false. Thus perhaps it is not absurd to grant simply that the human being united to God can sin, but not after he is united or while he is united. But for Christ—that is, God and human being together—it is in every way impossible to sin, since the very name “Christ” expresses the union of God and human being. Thus the statement “every human being is false” appears in every way true.

“As it is written: that you may be justified.” He proves by the authority of the Psalm how truthful God is in fulfilling his promises and how steadfast in his purpose. For the Lord had promised David that Christ would be born from his seed. After David’s adultery this promise seemed altogether liable to be annulled, and it seemed altogether unfitting that the Son of God should thereafter assume flesh from the seed of so sinful a man; consequently, God, who had promised this to him, would have to become false. But realizing that this could in no way happen, he who had sinned so gravely said: “Against you alone have I sinned” (Ps. 50:6), that is, against your honour alone—you who order even iniquity well and turn all things to your glory—“and I have done evil before you” (*ibid.*), that is, with you knowing, from whom nothing is hidden. Thus it may appear how just you are: although you know that I have deserved that you not keep the promises made to me, nevertheless, because you are just and truthful, you cannot frustrate your promise. For if this sin were hidden from God, no reason would appear why he should not fulfil the promise. But now, although he knows [Col. 0825A] that the sin has been committed and that the sinner has deserved the contrary, he nonetheless preserves the immovable constancy of his truth by fulfilling the promises.

“That you may be justified in your words”: that is, by carrying out your words concerning the promises you made to me, you may be justified—that is, shown to be just and truthful. “And may prevail”—namely, over human judgment—“when you are judged by human beings,” that is, accused of falsehood, as though you could no longer fulfil your promise because of my sins.

“But if.” The Apostle himself introduces an objection to what has preceded, as if saying: God has been said to be justified, that is, to appear especially just and truthful by means of sins, since they cannot hinder his promise and indeed he turns them to his own glory. But if my sins, as was said in the preceding example of David, commend God’s righteousness—that is, advance the praise and glory of his truth—what shall we say? That is, what can we answer to the following objection: “Is God unjust when he brings wrath,” that is, vengeance, “because of sins which, as stated, commend his righteousness,” that is, show him especially praiseworthy because of the unchangeable purpose of his truth?

And because the Apostle does not raise this objection in his own person, as though it seemed to him that God acted unjustly in this, he adds: “I speak according to man,” that is, according to the merely natural person, who does not perceive the things of God—not according to the spiritual person, who judges all things, maintains the equitable judgment of reason in divine [Col. 0825C] as well as human matters, and therefore says: “Far be it”—that is, far be it that we should accept that God acts unjustly in punishing sins which also advance his glory, so that, although sins are not good, it is nevertheless good that there be sins.

Hence Augustine says in the *Enchiridion* [Note: [Col. 0825D] *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 276.]: “Nothing happens unless the Almighty wills it to happen, either by permitting it or by doing it himself. There must be no doubt that God acts well, even in permitting whatever things happen wickedly. For he permits this only by a just judgment. And assuredly everything that is just is good.” Likewise [Note: [Col. 0825D] *Ibid.*]: “For unless it were good that evils should exist, they would in no way be permitted by the omnipotent Good.” Otherwise—that is, if matters were otherwise than we say, namely, if God acted unjustly in inflicting vengeance for sins—how could he judge [Col. 0825D] the world, that is, all people, both good and bad, repaying them according to their merits with either glory or punishment?

“For if the truth.” He returns again to the objection set out above, as though reinforcing it: God certainly appears unjust in punishing sins if they commend his very righteousness, because they ought no longer to be reckoned as sins but as goods that commend his truth. This is the meaning: “For if the truth of God has abounded unto his glory through my falsehood”—that is, the immovability of his truth is made more praiseworthy by the mutability and inconsistency of my profession, since although I lie to him, he cannot lie [Col. 0826A] to me—why am I still judged, although what I do advances his glory, as a sinner? That is, on what grounds are the things I do to be reckoned as sins? “And why do we not rather do evil that good may come?” That is, why should we not sin, so that God may be glorified through our sins? “As we are slanderously reported by some people, and as they say that we”—that is, I and the other spiritual persons—“teach,” since we say that even evils are so well ordered that they advance God’s glory.

Thus the previously mentioned teacher himself says in Book XI of *The City of God*, when speaking of the goodness and wickedness of the devil: “As God is the best creator of good natures, so he is the most just arranger of evil wills.” Likewise, in the same place, concerning the devil: “When God created him, he was not ignorant of his future malice, and foresaw what goods he himself would make from his evils.” And later: “For God would not have created any—not to say angels or human beings—whom he foreknew would be evil, unless he knew at the same time to what good uses he would assign them.” The same author says in the *Enchiridion* [Note: [Col. 0826D] *Ibid.*, col. 236.]: “For God, being almighty and supremely good, would in no way permit anything evil to exist in his works unless he were so almighty and good as to make good even from evil.”

“Whose”—namely, those who slander us—that is, people saying this not so much because of their own judgment as in order to slander us. For it has been granted that even evils are well ordered by God, so plainly that the pagan philosopher Plato himself professed it, saying: “Nothing occurs whose origin is not preceded by a lawful cause and reason.” [Col. 0826C]

“What then?” I said that the condemnation of those who slander us is just, by which we seem especially to have commended ourselves, as though we were such by our own merits, with nothing in us to be slandered. What then? Can it be said that we excel those who are justly condemned—that is, that by our own merits and virtue we are more worthy than they? By no means. Rather, if we have anything good, it comes from God rather than ourselves, as he says in what follows: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” because his mercy is sufficient for salvation more than our own strength. For of ourselves we are all alike guilty, as we showed above [Col. 0826D] concerning both Jews and Gentiles: all are without excuse. This returns to the general indictment, gathering testimonies from Scripture by which he may convict all alike as guilty and without excuse.

“As it is written,” namely in Psalm 12: “For there is no one righteous,” etc. This Psalm, in which these testimonies are found in our text, makes a kind of general indictment against all who, failing to recognize the time of their visitation, regarded it as an abomination that the Lord should be incarnate and suffer for human redemption. Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “But we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling-block to Jews and folly to Gentiles” (1 Cor. 1:23).

The Psalm therefore says: “The fool”—that is, the merely natural person, who does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14)—said, concerning that hidden mystery of our restoration, when he saw the weakness of the assumed human being: “There is no God.” He said this not merely by denying with words, as Peter denied him, but also in his heart. For even if he believed—this means that very few, almost none, are righteous, that is, rendering to each what is his. Far be it that we should believe that the Church, from the first elect person [Col. 0827B] to the last, would fail to persevere even in some faithful persons; the Church gathers many both before the Law and, still more, after the Law, as also the very author of this Psalm, and many under grace. Hence, at the Lord’s coming itself, although blindness had already come upon Israel in very great measure, we read that some remained: Simeon, Anna, the Lord’s own mother with her spouse Joseph, and the father and mother of John the Baptist together with John himself.

Often, moreover, when “all” or “none” is said, it is not said universally but of the greater part. Thus, if one says of a city in which there are few good people, “All who live in it are evil,” or, “There are no good people in it.” Hence Jerome’s statement to Pope Damasus concerning the prodigal son: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:[Col. 0827C]31). “Are angels thrones?” Therefore, understand “all” as the prophets and divine utterances, according to what we have often explained: not everything is to be referred to the whole, but to the greater part—as in: “All have turned aside” (Ps. 13:3); “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John 10:8); “I have become all things to all people, that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9:22); and, “All seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21).

He then gives the reason why there is no one righteous: “For there is no one who understands the Lord or seeks him.” “There is no one who understands the Lord,” that is, no one takes care to heed his promises or threats, because the natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. [Col. 0827D] 2:14), but is like horse and mule, which have no understanding (Ps. 31:9). And because there is no one who understands the Lord, no one knows how to seek through repentance him whom he lost through negligence. He adds this negligence, saying: “All have turned aside,” that is, leaving God, they have turned their concern toward the world, so that for temporal things they despise eternal things; and thus all alike, both Jews and Gentiles, “have together become useless.”

For no one is so wicked as to become wholly useless, since, as has been said, God makes the best use even of evil persons, such as Judas’s wickedness and the devil’s. In one and the same deed the Father, the Son, and Judas cooperated: the Father handed over the Son, the Son handed over himself, and Judas handed over the Lord. That betrayal, which Judas too performed, effected the redemption common to all. Through the preaching of the apostle Peter, some were converted and saved. The Lord turned Judas’s wickedness into the salvation of all. Divine grace employed that man’s evil for greater benefit to us than another’s good. Who can doubt that the devil’s wickedness too is always well ordered by God, since the devil does nothing except with God’s permission—whether punishing the guilty, testing the righteous, or doing anything else? Hence his power can only be just, as his will can only be unjust: he has power from the Lord, but will from himself. For, as the Apostle himself later declares, “There is no power except from God” (Rom. 13:1). Thus Truth says to the unjust governor: “You would have no power over me [Col. 0828B] unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11).

Those who act wickedly, therefore, should be understood to be useless rather to themselves than wholly useless, since, as we have shown, divine providence permits nothing in the order of things to be done uselessly or superfluously. But how have all turned aside, or from what have they turned aside? He adds: from good work—“There is no one who does good,” who works well and fulfils what ought to be done. For although the handing over of the Lord performed by Judas, and at the same time, as said, by the Father and Son, appears good, Judas did not do well in doing it, because he committed it with a perverse intention, namely from greed for money. The Lord taught that all works must be weighed according to intention, saying: “If your eye is single,” etc. (Matt. 6:22). Otherwise Judas’s work also, in which Father and Son acted mercifully, would have to be called good.

“There is none, even unto one.” This repeats the preceding statement, “There is no one who does good,” in order to add a qualification, lest it be thought universally stated. It is as if he said: There is no one who does good, that is, until he comes by faith and by joining himself through love to him who is truly one, unchangeable by nature and singular in eminence—namely, God or Christ, who is the one mediator of God and human beings. Through faith in him the Apostle will subsequently maintain that we are saved without works of the Law. It can also be understood thus: “There is no one who does good, even unto one,” as if he said: Hardly anyone does good; that is, almost no one does. For almost no one exists; not even one remains.

“An open grave.” These three following verses, which occur in our Psalter, are not read in such continuous sequence in the Hebrew, according to Origen or Jerome. Hence Origen, on this Epistle, says: “In some Latin copies, the words that follow are found consecutively in Psalm 13; but in almost all Greek copies Psalm 13 is written as far as: ‘There is no one who does good, not even one.’ But the Apostle said: ‘As it is written: There is no one righteous, no one who understands, no one [Col. 0829A] who seeks God.’ And the statement, ‘There is no one righteous,’ I think he took from: ‘There is no one who does good, not even one.’ But the phrase, ‘Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they acted deceitfully,’ you will find in Psalm 5. ‘The poison of asps is under their lips’ I think was taken from some Psalm with the wording altered. ‘Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness’ appears to have been taken from Psalm 9. ‘Their feet are swift to shed blood’ you will find either in Isaiah or in Proverbs. But ‘destruction and misery are in their ways, and they have not known the way of peace’—I do not remember exactly where it is written, but I suspect it can be found in one of the prophets. In the Psalms, however, it is written: ‘There is no fear of God before [Col. 0829B] their eyes.’”

These testimonies seem to have been collected to show that when he charges Jews and Greeks alike with being under sin, he declares not so much his own as Scripture’s judgment: all are under sin whom it is established were taught, whether by natural or written law, not to sin. Jerome, in the Preface to Book XVI on Isaiah, to Eustochium [Note: [Col. 0829D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIV, cols. 547–548.], says: “You raised the small question why the Apostle should use eight verses, read in the churches but not found in the Hebrew, of the thirteenth Psalm: ‘Their throat is an open grave,’ etc. I observed that this testimony is woven together from the Psalms and Isaiah. For the first two verses, ‘Their throat is an open grave,’ etc., are from Psalm 5. The following phrase, ‘The poison [Col. 0829C] of asps is under their lips,’ is from Psalm 139. Again, ‘Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness’ is written in Psalm 9. But the three verses which follow—‘Their feet are swift to shed blood,’ ‘destruction and misery are in their ways,’ and ‘the way of peace’—are not found in Isaiah. The final verse, the eighth, ‘There is no fear of God before their eyes,’ is at the beginning of Psalm 35. Finally, all the Greek commentators who have left us commentaries on the Psalms recording their learning note and pass over these verses [lacuna], openly confessing that they occur neither in the Hebrew nor among the Seventy Translators, but in the Vulgate edition called in Greek *koinē* [κοινή, “common”], which differs throughout the world.” Now let us follow the text.

[Col. 0829D] It was said: “All have turned aside, and there is no one who does good.” And not only have they turned aside: they also strive to make others turn aside and to do them great harm. As though it did not suffice for them to be damned alone, they seek a crowd as a companion, as though for their own defence. Since the throat is the instrument for forming or uttering a voice, it signifies speech emitted through the throat. Their speech, therefore, persuading people to evil, is like an open grave: from the wickedness conceived in the mind, it corrupts others like the stench of an enclosed corpse and offends the nostrils of those standing by—that is, it disorders and corrupts their natural discernment.

“With their tongues.” This is, as it were, an explanation of the preceding metaphorical statement, when it says that they speak deceitfully: they commend, against their conscience, the things to which they persuade others, or condemn those from which they dissuade them.

“The poison of asps.” Moses himself calls it incurable, and thereby attests that it is deadly beyond other punishments. It signifies criminal sins, which they inflict on others like poison through their persuasions. These sins, namely those to which they persuade, are said to be under their lips: that is, so hidden by their crafty speeches that their hearers cannot notice them. By the incurable poison of asps we may also understand the unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit, when someone, through envy or some greed, attributes to the devil works [Col. 0830B] which he does not doubt are done by God. Thus some Jews acted: in order to turn the people away from Christ, they denounced his works as devilish, although they did not doubt that they were performed by the Spirit of God, that is, by divine grace. They were therefore said to sin against the Spirit of God, that is, against the gift of divine grace, since knowingly they attributed to the devil what they ought to have used to glorify God, lying against their own conscience.

Although this sin could be wiped away through repentance, it has nevertheless been established by divine judgment that no one who falls into it returns by coming to repentance; therefore it is called unforgivable. This sin lay hidden under their lips and did not appear upon their lips, because, while thus sinning against their own conscience, they had one thing in their heart and uttered another with their mouth.

“Their mouth,” that is, brings upon both themselves and those who assent to them a curse from the Lord, and that bitterness of which the prophet says: “The voice of that day is bitter; the mighty man shall be distressed there” (Zeph. 1:14). “Full of cursing and bitterness” means that bitter curse which will be spoken to the reprobate in their condemnation: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). There is, however, another cursing which is, as it were, sweet and paternal, when we impose an anathema’s curse on some for correction rather than condemnation.

“Their feet are swift,” that is, they have inclinations ready for murders, even if they are not allowed to carry them out in deed. For the foot by which we walk signifies the inclination, that is, the will by which we are brought to action. [Col. 0830D] “Destruction and misery”—that is, unhappy destruction—are in their ways, namely their works, through which they are prepared for eternal death. They also destroy others with themselves and corrupt them through their examples, so that they are like scattered dust “which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Ps. 1:4): that is, diabolical temptation, which drives them here and there and casts them down from the stability of the land of the living.

“And they have not known the way of peace”: that is, they are altogether destroyed in their paths by condemnation because they have not known the way of God, namely Christ, through whom, as mediator of God and human beings, we have been made peaceful and reconciled to God. He is “our peace,” as the same Apostle says, “and has made both one” (Eph. 2:14). He also says of himself: “I am the way” (John 14:6); “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved” (John 10:9). They did not know this way, namely Christ, because they despised him on account of the weakness of his flesh or believed him a mere human being; and thus they did not revere him as Lord, nor did they believe John [Col. 0832A] when he threatened concerning him and said: “Now indeed the axe is laid to the root of the tree. Therefore every tree that does not bear fruit,” etc. (Matt. 3:10). This is what follows: “There is no fear of God.” With their carnal eyes, by which they perceived his weakness, they came to the point of not fearing him as God, since only the weakness of his humanity, not the majesty of his divinity, appeared.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0831]

[Col. 0831B] “But we know.” The Apostle returns to his indictment of the Jews, so that, just as he removed their boasting in circumcision, he may remove their boasting in the Law or in any carnal observances. Otherwise he might seem especially to have commended the Law when he said: “First, because the divine utterances were entrusted to them.” Thus he first removes boasting in the Law by proving that through the Law they are more accused than justified.

The connection is this: he brought forward testimonies from the Law, that is, the Old Testament, by which he established that all, Jews and Gentiles alike, are guilty. But we know that the Jews are especially accused by those texts to which alone—not concerning them alone—the Law speaks, since it was given and imposed upon them alone. This is what he says: “But we know,” etc. It is as if he said: Although we have collected the preceding testimonies from the Law against Gentiles too, we know that the Law did not speak to those to whom it was not given, even though it spoke concerning them, but only to those who are “in the Law,” that is, bound under the obligation of the Law they have undertaken.

It should be noted that “Law” sometimes properly comprises only the five books of Moses, but sometimes also the whole Old Testament, as here. Thus Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book XV: by the name “Law” all the utterances of the Old Testament are sometimes meant; at other times it properly means the Law given through Moses. “So that every mouth may be stopped,” that is, restrained and silenced in its boasting, and opened only for God’s glory, when we understand that even the greatest glory of that particular people of God—the glory they had from the Law, imagining themselves justified by its works—must be reckoned as nothing. “And so that all may be subject”—that is, may humble themselves before God, presuming nothing from their own boasting, which was taken away even from those who seemed great before God.

“For by works of the Law”—that is, its bodily observances, to which that people especially attended, such as circumcision, sacrifices, Sabbath observance, and the other such figurative commandments—“no flesh shall be justified before him,” that is, before God: no one who fulfils them only carnally and not spiritually, although before human beings—that is, in human judgment, which judges external and visible things—such people may be considered righteous.

“For through the Law.” He relates two following statements to the two preceding. To “so that every mouth may be stopped, and all may be subject,” etc., [Col. 0832B] he adds “for through the Law.” To the other statement, “by works,” etc., he adds “but now,” or “yet.” The sequence is: why people ought to be restrained from their boasting by the Law, since it renders them especially without excuse for their sins, which they came to know through it rather than lost through it—indeed, they even increased them. And later he will say: “That sin might become exceeding sinful through . . . .”

“But now.” I said that no one is justified before God by the works proper to the written Law—that is, by those figurative commandments unknown to natural law. But now, in the time of grace, “the righteousness of God”—that which God approves and by which we are justified before God, namely love—has been made manifest through evangelical teaching, “apart from the Law,” that is, apart from those carnal observances peculiar to the Law. Yet this righteousness, I say, is “attested by the Law and the Prophets,” who also command it.

He immediately adds from what this righteousness depends: “But the righteousness of God.” He calls it faith in Christ, which we have concerning him, by believing him, believing in him, or believing upon him. Therefore, when he added “who believe,” he added none of these qualifiers, so that it might apply equally to them all. From the faith we have concerning Christ, love has been spread abroad within us: because by holding that God united our nature to himself in Christ, and in suffering in that nature displayed toward us that greatest love of which he said, “No one has greater love than this” (John 15:13), etc., we cling both to him and to our neighbour for his sake by an indissoluble bond of love. Hence it is written later: [Col. 0832D] “Who then shall separate us from the love of God? Shall tribulation?” (Rom. 8:35), etc.; and again: “For I am certain that neither death,” etc. (*ibid.*, 8:38).

I mean righteousness possessed “upon all believers,” that is, in their higher part, namely the soul, where love alone can exist, not in the performance of external works.

“For there is no distinction.” I have rightly said “upon all alike,” both Gentiles and Jews, because there is no distinction between them in this righteousness of God through faith in Christ, as there formerly was through the works of the Law. For just as all sinned, so all alike are justified through this highest grace shown to us by God. This is what he says: “For all have sinned and need the glory of God,” that is, they need, as though by a debt, to glorify the Lord, “being justified freely”—that is, because they are justified not by merits preceding them but through the grace of him, namely God, who first loved us.

[Col. 0833A] He adds what this grace is, namely his free and spiritual gift: “through our redemption accomplished by Christ, whom God the Father set forth for us as a propitiation,” that is, a reconciler, “in his blood,” that is, through his death. And because this propitiation is set forth, that is, appointed, by God not for all but only for believers, he adds “through faith,” since this reconciliation comes only to those who have believed and awaited it. “For the showing of his righteousness,” that is, his love which, as stated, justifies us before him: to display his love toward us, or to make known to us how greatly we ought to love him, who did not spare his own Son for us. “Because of the remission”—that is, so that through this righteousness, namely love, we may obtain remission of sins; just as Truth himself said concerning the blessed sinful woman: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47).

I mean remission of preceding offences, “in the forbearance of God,” that is, because of God’s patience: he does not immediately punish the guilty and destroy sinners, but waits long for them to return through repentance, cease from sin, and thus receive pardon.

“For the showing.” At first he said simply, “for the showing of his righteousness”; now he adds, “at this time of grace,” that is, of love rather than fear. Therefore, when he says “his righteousness,” namely his righteousness at this time of grace, he plainly indicates what righteousness he first meant: love, which properly belongs to human beings of our time, that is, the time of grace. The phrase “in the forbearance of God” may also be referred to what follows, namely “for the showing of his righteousness at this time,” so that the sense is that the Lord endured or delayed during the preceding time in order to reveal in this time his righteousness, which we have described as love: so that he may be just in will and the justifier in action—that is, that he both wills to fulfil through Christ what he promised, namely our redemption or justification, and fulfils by deed what he wills—of the one who is of the faith of Jesus Christ, that is, who believes that he is Jesus, namely Saviour, inasmuch as he is Christ, namely God and human being.

### QUESTION

A very great question presents itself at this point: what precisely is this redemption of ours through Christ, or when the Apostle says that we are justified in his blood, since we seem worthy of a greater punishment because we, as wicked servants, committed the deed for which the innocent Lord was killed.

First, therefore, it seems necessary to ask why God assumed humanity in order to redeem us by dying according to the flesh; or from whom he redeemed us, since someone held us captive either by right or by power; and by what justice he liberated us from that person’s power—what commands that person had given which he wished God to accept in order to release us.

It is said that he redeemed us from the devil’s power, since, through the transgression of the first man, who had voluntarily subjected himself to the devil by obeying him, the devil possessed all his power by a certain right and would always possess it unless the Liberator came. But since he liberated only the elect, when did the devil possess them—whether in this age or in the future—more than he does now? Did the devil torment that poor man who rested in Abraham’s bosom as he tormented the condemned rich man, although he tormented him less severely? Or did he exercise dominion even over Abraham himself and the other elect? When could that wicked torturer have had dominion over one who is said to have been carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom, concerning whom Abraham himself testifies, saying: “But now he is comforted, while you are tormented”? (Luke 16:25.) Moreover, Abraham asserts that a great chasm has been fixed between the elect and the reprobate, so that these cannot cross over to those, lest the devil, while holding dominion there over all the wicked, should hold dominion where no wicked person has either place or passage.

What right, moreover, could the devil have had in possessing a human being, unless perhaps because, with the Lord’s permission—or even by his delivery—the devil had received him for torment? For if some servant wished to desert his master and submit himself to another’s authority, and were permitted to do so, would not his master rightly reclaim and bring him back if he wished? Who can doubt, further, that if a servant of one master, by his persuasions, seduced his fellow servant and made him turn aside from obedience to his own master, the seducer would be held much more guilty before his master than the one seduced? How unjust it would be if the one who had seduced another deserved thereby to obtain any privilege or power over the person whom he seduced! Even if he had previously possessed some right over him, he would deserve to lose that right through the very wickedness of his seduction. For it is written: “He deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the authority entrusted to him.”

It would by no means be fitting for one of these fellow servants to be placed over the other and to receive power over him, so that the more wicked should preside, since he has absolutely no basis for privilege. Rather, it would be more consonant with reason that the one who was seduced should exercise the severity of vengeance against the one who harmed him by seducing him. Moreover, the devil could not give the immortality which he promised humanity through transgression, and therefore could not retain humanity by any right on that account.

[Col. 0834D] By these arguments, therefore, it seems proved that the devil acquired no right over the human being whom he seduced by seducing him, except perhaps, as we said, insofar as this belonged to the Lord’s permission, since God had handed him over to the devil as though to his jailer or torturer for punishment. For he had sinned only against his own Lord, whose obedience he had abandoned.

If, therefore, his Lord wished to forgive him his sin—as was done for the Virgin Mary, and as Christ did for many even before his Passion, as was said of Mary Magdalene, and as is written concerning the paralytic, when the Lord said: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9:2)—if, I say, the Lord wished to forgive the transgressing human being without the Passion and to say to his torturer, “I do not wish you to punish him any longer,” how could the torturer justly inflict torment, when, as has been shown, he had received no right to torture except from the Lord’s own permission? If, then, the Lord ceased to permit this, no right would remain to the torturer. To him, should he complain or murmur against the Lord, the Lord ought immediately to reply: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matthew 20:15).

The Lord did the devil no injury when, from the sinful mass, he assumed pure flesh and a human being free from every sin. This man did not obtain by his merits that he should be conceived, born, and remain without sin, but by the grace of the Lord who assumed him. Could not that same grace, if God wished to forgive other human beings their sins, free them from punishments? Once the sins for which they were suffering punishment had been forgiven, no reason seems to remain why they should further be punished on their account. He, therefore, who bestowed such great grace upon a human being as to unite him to himself in one person, could not bestow the lesser grace of forgiving sins?

What necessity, then, what reason, what need was there—when divine mercy could have freed humanity from the devil by its mere sight—for the Son of God, after assuming flesh, to endure for our redemption so many and such great fasts, reproaches, scourges, spittings, and finally the most bitter and disgraceful death of the cross, even suffering execution with the wicked? How, too, does the Apostle say that we are justified or reconciled to God through the death of his Son, when God ought to have been so much more angered against humanity as human beings sinned more grievously in crucifying his Son than in transgressing his first command in paradise by tasting one fruit? For the more sins were multiplied by human beings, the more justly God ought to have been born for human beings.

If Adam’s sin was so great that it could not be expiated except by Christ’s death, what expiation will there be for the murder committed against Christ himself, or for the many and great crimes committed against him or his followers? Did the death of the innocent Son please God the Father so greatly that through it he was reconciled to us, though by sinning we committed the deed for which the innocent Lord was killed? Could he not forgive that much lighter sin unless this greatest sin were committed, nor bring about so great a good unless evils were multiplied? In what way, also, have we become more just through the death of the Son of God than we were before, so that we ought now to be freed from punishments?

To whom was the price of blood given for redemption, except to the one in whose power we were—namely, as has been said, God himself, who had entrusted us to his torturer? For torturers do not settle or receive the ransom of captives; their masters do. How, moreover, did he release these captives by a price, if he himself first demanded or instituted that price in order to release them? How cruel and unjust it appears that anyone should demand the blood of an innocent person as a price, or in any way take pleasure in the killing of an innocent person—much less that God should have regarded his Son’s death as so acceptable that through it he was reconciled to the whole world! These matters and others like them seem to raise no slight question for us concerning our redemption or justification through the death of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### SOLUTION

It seems to us, however, that we are justified in Christ’s blood and reconciled to God in this: through this singular grace shown to us—namely, that his Son assumed our nature and, by instructing us both in word and example, persevered even unto death—he bound us more closely to himself through love. Thus, kindled by the benefit of so great a divine grace, true love no longer fears to endure anything for him.

We do not doubt that this benefit also kindled the ancient Fathers, who awaited it in faith, into the highest love of God, as persons belonging to the time of grace, since it is written: “Those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying, ‘Hosanna to the Son of David,’” etc. (Mark 11:9). Each person also becomes more just—that is, loves the Lord more—after Christ’s Passion than before, because a benefit accomplished kindles love more than one merely hoped for.

Our redemption, therefore, is that supreme love produced in us through Christ’s Passion. It not only frees us from slavery to sin, but also gains for us the true liberty of the children of God, so that we fulfill everything through love of him rather than through fear—him who has shown us so great a grace that, as he himself testifies, no greater can be found. “No one,” he says, “has greater love than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

Concerning this love the Lord says elsewhere: “I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire but that it be kindled?” (Luke 12:24). He testifies that he came in order to spread this true liberty of love among human beings. Carefully observing this, the Apostle says in what follows: “Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). “For why [then did] Christ,” etc. Again: “But God commends his love in us. For while we were yet,” etc. We shall explain these passages more fully in their proper place.

For the present, briefly, as the brevity of exposition requires, let this suffice concerning what seems to us to be the manner of our redemption. If anything is lacking for completeness, we reserve it for the treatment in our *Theology*, where it says: “I said that righteousness without the law is now made manifest through faith in Christ, unto all alike who believe.”

Therefore, O Jew, where now is your boasting—namely, that distinctive boasting which you had in the law and its bodily observances? For it has been excluded, that is, taken away from you and annulled.

“By what law?” Is it excluded by the law of works—that is, of certain external acts? No, but by the law of faith, as has been said, in Jesus Christ; that is, by the love arising from faith in our salvation through Christ. For even before someone is baptized, if he already believes and loves—as Abraham, of whom it is written, “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness”; perhaps also Cornelius, not yet baptized, whose alms were accepted by God (Acts 10:4); and, concerning past sins, if he is truly repentant, like the publican who went down from the temple justified (Luke 18:14)—I do not hesitate to call him just, or to say that he possesses righteousness, since he renders to each what is his due.

Thus we say that Jeremiah and John were sanctified from the womb, where they were specially enlightened and already knew and loved the Lord, although it was still necessary for them to receive circumcision, which then held the place of baptism.
