Why then, you will ask, did persons such as these later have to be circumcised or baptized, though already beforehand, by the faith and love they possessed, they were such that, if they had then died, they necessarily would have been saved? For no one who dies justly, or while possessing love, can be damned.

Again, no one can be saved without baptism or martyrdom after the decree concerning baptism has been given. Yet someone could die while possessing love before baptism or martyrdom, at that time when, you say, if he died, it would be necessary both that he be saved and that he be damned.

But when we say that everyone who already loves the Lord sincerely and purely for his own sake is predestined to life, we also say that such a person will never be overtaken by death until the Lord reveals to him, either through preaching or through the Holy Spirit, whatever is necessary for him concerning the sacraments, and additionally gives him the means of receiving it.

The objection that one who was already just before baptism, through believing and loving, could be at a time when, if he died, it would be necessary both that he be saved and that he be damned, may be raised concerning anyone who sins mortally and is predestined to life—for example, David while committing adultery. For just as it would be necessary that the person who was just be saved, so it would be necessary that the just person who was predestined, but unbaptized, be damned; likewise with that adulterer.

David, therefore, was at a time when, if he died, it would be necessary both that he be damned and that he be saved. But again, even if he was at a time when he could not die well, and at no time when he could not die badly, as long as he possessed freedom of will, he was nevertheless not at any time when it was necessary for him both to die well and to die badly. Indeed, at no time [Note: *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, col. 395.] was it necessary for anyone to die well, nor at any time was it necessary for anyone to die badly. Rather, at every time at which someone can die well, he can also die badly. Yet it is never jointly true to say that he can die simultaneously both well and badly.

Likewise, concerning the person who has love before baptism and is thereby just, we grant that he was at no time when, if he died, it was necessary that he simultaneously be both saved and damned. For one who possesses love before baptism could at that time be without love, and thus die and be damned only. He could also die baptized at the time when he has not yet been baptized, and thus be saved. But if you say jointly that he can simultaneously possess love and be unbaptized, I accept this no more than if you said that someone could die an adulterer and predestined.

The person predestined must act well in order to be saved, just as one who is already just through believing and loving must be baptized, because of the Lord’s fixed decree concerning baptism or because of the very perseverance of righteousness. For if one who possesses love before baptism ended his life before being baptized, he would by no means persevere in that love, lest he entirely lose hope of eternal blessedness and perceive that he was immediately, at the moment of death, to be damned eternally.

Just as we already call someone just before baptism through faith—that is, love—although his sins have not yet been forgiven in baptism, that is, although their punishment has not yet been wholly remitted, so after baptism we do not yet call infants, and those without any capacity for discernment, just, although they have received remission of sins. Though clean before God, they cannot yet be capable of love or righteousness or possess any merits.

If, nevertheless, they die in this weakness, when they begin to leave the body and see that glory has been prepared for them through God’s mercy, the love of God is born in them together with discernment. Therefore, lest any of the Jews be able to object to us—or rather, to the Apostle—that we too are justified through the law of works, that is, external acts such as baptism, let what we have said suffice concerning our justification, indeed all justification that consists in love, even before sacraments, whether ours or theirs, are received. The prophet, considering this, says: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezekiel 33:12).

“We judge.” That is, we whom the Lord has placed in authority judge, or testify. “Hence,” as Haymo says [Note: *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, col. 395], “we call judges or witnesses *arbitri*.” We judge that every human being, both Jew and gentile, is justified through faith, as something necessary to him, because “without faith it is impossible to please God.” Through faith, I say, apart from works of the law—that is, those external and bodily observances.

“Is he the God of the Jews?” They judge rightly that the gentiles also attain God’s grace through faith, although they do not observe the works of the law, as Job, formerly a gentile, and gentiles now converted. This is what he shows when he says: “Is God only the God of the Jews through grace?” “Since indeed.” As if he said: He is God of both through grace, because he justifies both through faith, which, as we said, leads to love. “Circumcision,” that is, Jews; “uncircumcision,” that is, gentiles.

His saying “by faith” and “through faith” is a difference of expression, not of meaning. Hence Augustine says in *On the Spirit and the Letter* [Note: *Patrologia*, vol. XLIV, col. 231]: “It was not said to indicate a difference, as though ‘from faith’ meant something other than ‘through faith,’ but for variety of expression.”

“Do we then destroy the law?” Since indeed we say that people can be saved through faith apart from works of the law, do we destroy the law through faith—that is, by commending faith, do we show the law to be invalid? Far from it. Rather, we establish the law; that is, we desire the law to be fulfilled in every respect. For one truly fulfills even the figurative commandments now who does or believes what those commandments now only signify, rather than effect, attending not so much to the sound of the speaker’s voice as to the sense and intention of the one commanding. Finally, as the Apostle himself says, “love is the fulfillment of the law” (Romans 13:10); and after recalling its commands, the Lord says to the rich man: “Do this and you shall live” (Luke 10:28).

### CHAPTER IV

“What then?” Since those external works of the law do not confer righteousness, what righteousness or benefit, then, shall we say Abraham, our father according to the flesh, found through those carnal observances, such as circumcision or sacrifices? As though he said: none.

When he says “our father,” that is, the one whom we ought to imitate as his children through his teaching, he proposes his question as though we too ought to follow him in these matters. “For if.” And truly Abraham did not attain righteousness by those external things, in God’s judgment, because through them he has no merit before the Lord. This is what is meant by: “If he was justified by works”—that is, if he performed external deeds which seemed to people to be righteous—“he has glory,” indeed, but not before God. That is, he is considered great before people, who judge by visible things, but not before the Lord, who searches hearts and tests inward parts, and sees what is hidden.

“For what?” And I rightly say that Abraham was justified before God not by works but by faith, because this is what we have from the testimony of Scripture. This is the meaning: “For what does Scripture say?” We attend to what is written in Genesis, namely what follows: “Abraham believed God,” that is, the divine promises—whether when he left his own land so that he might multiply in a foreign land, or concerning the promise of his son, or whatever God promised him, however incredible or great it seemed.

This is that true faith which works through love. Thus when it says, “he believed God,” its meaning is that in believing he willingly carried out the Lord’s commands. “And this was reckoned to him by the Lord as righteousness,” that is, it established him as righteous before the Lord through the obedience of faith; not circumcision or the other bodily observances later written in the law.

“But to him.” As though he said: I do not say without cause that, if Abraham were justified by works, he would have glory—that is, the greatest praise among human beings—but not before God. I say this because, to the one who works, the reward is reckoned by people as a debt; that is, it is said to belong to his own acquisition and virtue rather than to be conferred by another’s grace. Yet before the Lord faith alone—that of a person who loves—suffices for righteousness.

This is what follows: “But to the one who does not work”—namely, legal works—“but truly clings by faith to him who justifies the ungodly,” that is, “to the one believing in him who justifies the ungodly,” his faith is reckoned by him who justifies the ungodly, namely God, as righteousness—that is, God rewards him for this faith as though he were righteous.

Here the Apostle plainly determines, when he says “believing in him,” what kind of faith he understands. For it is one thing to believe God, namely, that he exists; another to believe God—that is, to believe that his promises or words are true; another to believe *in* God. To believe in God, as Augustine says in his commentary on John [Note: *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, col. 1631], is “to love, to love through believing, and through believing to tend toward becoming his member.”

Thus demons and reprobates also believe that God exists and believe God, but they do not believe in God, because they do not love him and do not unite themselves to him by loving, that is, do not join themselves by devotion to the Church, which is his body. He then adds how faith is reckoned: according to the purpose of God’s grace. This rests in the purpose of divine goodness, which rewards disposition more than deeds. Otherwise many who lack the ability to act, although they possess the will, would be rejected.

“Just as David also says,” that is, he explains to us the blessedness of the person to whom God brings righteousness when, received by God through his mercy, he could not rise to God by himself. God brings righteousness because the one to whom it is brought could not obtain it himself. He brings it, I say, apart from works of the law, namely legal works.

For when he says, “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven,” etc., this is said generally: whoever they may be, Jews or gentiles. Iniquity is forgiven when its punishment, which might have been exacted by justice, is remitted through grace. Thus Scripture establishes grace itself as, so to speak, the foundation, so that whatever is subsequently built upon it may be reckoned to the grace which goes before.

After iniquities have been forgiven, David continues by showing how divine grace brings the human being to perfection: then he adds that sins are covered, and finally that they are not imputed. Sins are forgiven through the groaning of repentance, concerning which it is said: “At whatever hour the sinner groans” (Ezekiel 33:12). For before iniquity truly displeases him and all evil will departs from him, the sinner is already so reconciled to God that he is freed from the punishments of Gehenna and will never incur Gehenna if he dies in this groaning, prepared for every satisfaction he can make.

But sins are covered when satisfaction follows in this life. Such satisfaction also extinguishes the purgatorial punishments of the age to come, when repentance has first removed the condemnatory punishments of Gehenna. Sins, therefore, are then covered before the judge’s eyes when he sees nothing remaining to punish for them.

“Blessed is the man.” He first pronounces blessedness in the plural, then names “the man,” saying: “Blessed is the man,” etc. Is this not because he shows the benefits of divine grace extending even to that singular human being who was united to God in the one person of Christ? His blessedness is likewise described by the same prophet at the very beginning of the book: “Blessed is the man who has not walked” (Psalm 1:1).

For *vir* (“man”) is derived from *vires* (“strengths”), because he drew no weakness from the corruption of sin; because he, stronger than the strong man, bound him and plundered his weapons, he is uniquely called *vir*, “man,” by excellence. All others, by contrast, are as though effeminate and weak in comparison with him, being subject to earthly pleasures.

Since he was entirely free from sin, the Lord imputed no sin to him, because he judged him deserving of no punishment for any sin, whether original or personal. He had neither been conceived in sin nor committed any sin.

We may also understand, under the name of blessedness, the classes of people saved or to be saved. One class consists of children sanctified by baptism or martyrdom, and all who are truly repentant but are not permitted in this life to complete penitential satisfaction. Another class consists of those who correct their sins, as it were, by worthy satisfaction. The third class remains in the singularity of the one Savior, as explained above.

When, therefore, he says, “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven,” he understands forgiveness alone—namely, that which no satisfaction in this life follows. Infants, according to the Psalmist, are conceived in iniquities; in them, when they are conceived and born, iniquities are forgiven, since they do not incur the condemnation of original sin, as we said. Others, as we noted above, correct past sins through the satisfaction of good works.

The very character of the construction seems to require that, when it says “whose” and again “whose,” we understand not the same people but different ones. For there is one sense if *quorum* (“whose”) occurs only once: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and sins are covered.” There is another if it is repeated twice, as the present text has it. Used once, it indicates the same persons; repeated, it suggests different persons.

At this point a question arises concerning God’s grace and human merits: what precisely our merits are before God, since all good things ought to be ascribed solely to his grace, who, as the Apostle himself testifies, works in us both willing and accomplishing for good will (Philippians 2:13). Hence he says elsewhere: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

It must be asked whether our merits consist only in will or also in action; that is, what God rewards in us with glory without punishment; whether virtue suffices for blessedness if it does not issue into action; whether an outward deed following a good or evil will increases merit; whether, since every virtue belongs to the mind and exists founded in it, every sin likewise belongs to the mind; what difference there is between a vice of the mind and sin; and in how many senses “sin” is spoken of.

But because this belongs especially to ethical inquiry, and because one would have to linger longer in resolving these questions than the brevity of this exposition allows, let us reserve it for our ethical discussion.

“Blessedness, therefore.” Since it has been shown in how many ways blessedness is spoken of or possessed, let us also see by whom it is possessed: by the circumcised only, or also by the uncircumcised. This is what he asks: Does this blessedness, which we attain in God by believing and not even by works of the law, remain only in circumcision, that is, among the circumcised, or also among the uncircumcised?

He defines what this blessedness is, namely, the blessedness attained by Abraham when he was justified by faith. This is what follows: “For we say,” that is, we prove from the testimony set forth, “that Abraham’s faith,” by which, as explained, he believed in God, “was reckoned to him before God as righteousness”; that is, God reckoned him righteous and judged him worthy of the reward of the righteous.

I said, “was reckoned”; therefore let us inquire in Abraham himself how, that is, when, his faith was reckoned to him as righteousness: before he was circumcised or afterward. Thus we may judge through him concerning other human beings, whether only the circumcised attain this blessedness of righteousness or not. This is what he says, asking “how,” and immediately answering: “In circumcision,” that is, before he was circumcised; “in uncircumcision,” that is, before he was circumcised, while he still retained his foreskin.

“And he received a sign.” Someone might perhaps ask why Abraham received circumcision superfluously, since he had been justified beforehand and received no justification in it. Anticipating this question, he says that Abraham received this outward sign not for any justification, but for the sanctification and manifestation of the righteousness he already possessed in his mind while still uncircumcised. This is the meaning: “He received a sign,” etc. He received circumcision as a sign; and he immediately adds of what it was a sign.

“A seal,” that is, as a seal or sign, “of the righteousness of faith which is also in uncircumcision,” that is, among the uncircumcised no less than among the circumcised, so that by such a sign he might designate righteousness rather than acquire it. It is called “the righteousness of faith,” which is in the mind, to distinguish it from what people usually call righteousness: namely, that which they exercise outwardly in punishing evils or exacting certain benefits. Hence it is written: “Take heed that you do not perform your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them.”

We may also distinguish “sign” and “seal” thus: circumcision itself is the sign of one thing and the seal of another. It is a sign of Abraham’s carnal children and a seal of his spiritual children, since he was made father both of Jews according to the flesh and of gentiles through faith. For, according to Haymo, a *seal* is like an impress placed upon something so that it may remain hidden; therefore it seems fittingly referred to Abraham’s future spiritual children from the gentiles, who had not yet appeared.

Circumcision, then, which began in Abraham and was preserved in his carnal descendants, was both sign and seal. Through it Abraham’s carnal children were distinguished from other peoples, and his future spiritual children from the gentiles were prefigured, namely those who would imitate him through faith. Thus Ishmael, whom Abraham fathered according to the flesh and not by the power of the miracle, is read to have been circumcised, signifying the outward circumcision of Abraham’s carnal children, by which, as stated, carnal Israel would be recognized.

Isaac, however, who was born afterward, expresses the spiritual circumcision from vices of the gentile people later called, which was also foreshadowed by proselytes.

[Col. 0843B] Therefore the Apostle rightly distinguishes sign and seal with regard to the carnal Jewish children of Abraham and his likewise spiritual gentile children. First he says “the sign of circumcision,” that is, the sign of carnal Israel, by which that people was distinguished from others; afterward, “the seal of the righteousness of faith which is in uncircumcision,” that is, the sacrament of spiritual circumcision, possessed only by believers gathered from the gentiles.

A seal may also be understood as an impressed sign, as is said in praise of the apostate angel: “You are the seal of likeness,” etc. (Ezekiel 28:12). For through this sign of circumcision the just and spiritual person is especially represented: the person who renounces bodily pleasures for God’s sake and cuts them away from himself—pleasures which chiefly rule in the loins and are exercised through the genitals.

A seal may also be taken as a diminutive derived from “sign”: that is, the first, small sign of Abraham’s righteousness. For it was no great thing to cut away that little piece of skin at God’s command, in comparison with the things which afterward Abraham’s spiritual children, both martyrs and other saints, endured for Christ.

“Sign” and “seal” may also be distinguished thus: what is a great sign in the flesh, common to both good and evil persons, is a small sign of righteousness, since few are joined to Abraham through righteousness as they are through flesh. It is therefore a sign according to the flesh, but a seal—that is, a small sign—according to righteousness, because it is extended among many of Abraham’s descendants according to the flesh but restricted to few according to righteousness. Thus he rightly says “the sign of circumcision,” namely, the outward circumcision common equally to all, and “the seal of righteousness,” which belongs to few.

Now, however, a few points must be examined concerning the efficacy and sacrament of circumcision: namely, what it itself conferred or prefigured; why it was instituted in the genital and male member rather than the female; and why infants were commanded to undergo it on the eighth day. For adults, indeed, no fixed time for circumcision was prescribed, except when they converted to Judaism. It is clear that among the ancients circumcision had the same efficacy that baptism now has among us. Hence Augustine says in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I [Note: [Col. 0843D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLIV, col. 450.]:

> “From the time circumcision was instituted among the people of God, when it was then a seal of the righteousness of faith, it had the force, even in little children, of signifying the cleansing of ancient original sin; just as baptism began, from the time of its institution, to have force for the renewal of the human being.”

Gregory, in *Morals*, book IV [Note: [Col. 0844D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXV, col. 633.], says:

> “What the water of baptism accomplishes among us, this among the ancients was accomplished, for little children, by faith alone; for older persons, by the efficacy of sacrifice; and for those descended from Abraham’s stock, by the mystery of circumcision.”

From these statements it is therefore evident that among the ancients circumcision possessed the same power for the remission of sins that baptism now possesses. Yet those who are now baptized and immediately die immediately enter the kingdom of heaven; this did not then occur, because the sacrifice had not yet been paid—namely, in the shedding of Christ’s blood. Likewise, perhaps even those baptized with Christ’s baptism who died before his Passion could not yet have access to the gate of heaven. For the Israelites had no passage to the promised land except through the Red Sea. That is, baptism, which is signified by the sea, cannot convey anyone to the true promised land—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem—without redness, namely the shedding of Christ’s blood. But just as, when the sacrifice was afterward joined to Christ’s baptism, it conferred the kingdom of heaven, so the same sacrifice, following upon the circumcision of those before Christ, granted the same thing to them.

Circumcision of the flesh is a sign of the inward circumcision of the soul, just as the outward washing of baptism is a sign of the inward cleansing of the soul through remission of sins. Above all, this sacrament had to be performed on the genital member, through which, by carnal concupiscence, the sin of original fault is propagated together with offspring, so that the member through which sin is transmitted to descendants might deservedly itself be punished. But the woman, to whom it was said, “In pain you shall bear children” (Gen. III, 16), was not to be subjected to such a punishment. In her genital member, through which sin is likewise transmitted, the exceedingly severe pain of childbirth which she endures ought, for punishment, to have been sufficient; and for that sex, I think, the sacrifice offered for her suffices for pardon and for a remedy against original sin [Col. 0844D].

Moreover, it seems to us that the male genital rather than the female ought especially to have been circumcised for this reason: that it might signify to all in that people who were begotten through that member that the remedy of this sacrament was necessary, by which they might be cleansed from the contagion of the old man. This is not so with the woman, since the Lord Jesus was born from a woman without any sin. The circumcision of the male may also spiritually signify that blessed Man himself, who alone, conceived without concupiscence, assumed pure flesh wholly without the foreskin of impurity. In his type Abraham’s thigh [Col. 0845A], which was first circumcised, was taken by his servant in an oath, as though he were swearing by him who was first promised to Abraham as to be born from that seed—namely, Christ.

A fixed day, namely the eighth, was rightly assigned for the circumcision of infants, so that it might prefigure the brightness and blessedness of that eighth day promised to the saints, and show that these are owed only to those who lived innocently in the manner of little children; nor is the sacrament of purification sufficient for this unless innocence of life is preserved. Exhorting us to this, the Lord set a little child in the midst and said: “Unless you are converted and become like this little child,” etc. (Matt. XVIII, 3). The eighth day on which the child is circumcised signifies the future brightness of the saints on the day of resurrection, when the reality of the reassumed flesh will remain, with the added corruption of sin removed. This will be true circumcision: the stripping off of the old man with his deeds. Then, although the impulses of carnal concupiscence remain, we shall have to live in an angelic manner, where, Truth says, “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God” (Matt. XXII, 30). Since the whole time of this present life is passed through seven days, that perpetual brightness of the future life is rightly understood through the eighth. Hence it is certain that the psalms entitled “For the Eighth” refer to the day of resurrection.

A question is raised concerning infants who die before the eighth day: are they condemned, since they may not yet lawfully be circumcised according to the Lord’s command [Col. 0845C], and since we do not read that sacrifices are to be offered for them before the day of the mother’s purification—that is, the fortieth day from the birth of a boy? Yet it is written: “Every soul whose foreskin has not been circumcised shall perish from his people” (Gen. XVII, 14). And again, if little ones are forbidden by the Lord’s command to be circumcised before the eighth day, the divine judgment appears cruel in condemning such persons: he instituted circumcision as necessary even for them, yet does not permit them to be circumcised when they are able.

Nor ought anything to have been commanded or instituted by the Savior that would obstruct salvation; nor should a remedy capable of benefiting more persons have been weakened—such as the faith of parents or the rite of sacrifices, by which, as is evident, little children and adults were formerly cleansed, according to the statement of Gregory [Col. 0845D] most recently added. But this objection appears also to bear upon the institution of our sacrament, baptism: because baptism, which the Lord instituted only in water, sometimes fails some persons merely through such absence, and yet, even if they themselves strive for it or others strive on their behalf, we do not determine that they are saved without baptism unless martyrdom intervenes.

Therefore, entrusting every arrangement of this matter to divine providence, which alone knows why it has chosen this person and rejected that one, let us hold immovably to the authority of Scripture which he himself gave: namely, that in the time of circumcision we should not rashly assert that any descendants of Abraham who died without it were saved [Col. 0846A], unless perhaps they were killed for the Lord, as is believed of the Innocents.

Observe, however, that it was said, “descendants of Abraham.” For certain faithful persons, even after the institution of circumcision and before Christ’s coming, died uncircumcised and were nevertheless saved by the law of nature, as Job and perhaps certain other Gentiles, content with the natural law and with the rite of sacrifices—which Job too is read to have offered for his children—were cleansed from original or personal sin, as Abel or Noah were before the law or the institution of circumcision. The Apostle refers above to persons of this kind, saying: “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law,” etc.

Hence Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, book I, chapter 15, says:

> “The holy men who foretold Christ’s coming did not await it only among the Jewish people [Col. 0846B]; there were also among the nations many holy men possessing the gift of prophecy, to whom Christ was revealed through the Holy Spirit and by whom he was awaited, as Job and Balaam, who certainly proclaimed Christ’s coming.”

Although Job is believed to have descended from Abraham and Isaac through Esau, nevertheless no one is to be counted among the seed of Abraham or Isaac who was begotten from sons of the patriarchs who did not remain in God’s worship. Thus the Lord, easing Abraham’s distress about the expulsion of his servant Hagar and his son Ishmael at Sarah’s command, said: “Do not let it seem harsh to you concerning the boy and your servant. In all that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice; for in Isaac your seed shall be called. But I will also make the son of the servant woman into a great nation, because he is your seed” (Gen. XXI, 12–13).

The Apostle also pursues this matter later in the present Epistle and, as it were, explains it spiritually:

> “For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor are all who are Abraham’s seed children, but ‘In Isaac your seed shall be called’” (Rom. IX, 6–7);

that is, not those who are children of the flesh are children of God, but those who are children of promise are counted as the seed. Therefore, according to historical truth, neither Job nor many others, although they belong to Abraham’s race, ought to be called Abraham’s seed, because, as was said, they were born from unbelievers. Yet the fathers of such persons, although unbelievers—for example Ishmael or Esau—are Abraham’s seed, because they were not begotten from unbelievers, according to what the Lord said above to Abraham concerning Ishmael: “Because he is your seed.” And yet no seed of Abraham was to be called such in the manner in which Isaac was.

It is therefore one thing for Isaac or Ishmael to be called Abraham’s seed. “In Isaac your seed shall be called” means: in Isaac’s descendants, namely those joined to him both in flesh and faith, not those descendants of Isaac in whom intervening fathers, departing from God’s worship both in flesh and faith, stand between them. This, I believe, is signified when the Lord, making the covenant of circumcision with Abraham and his seed, first said: “I will establish my covenant between me and you, and your seed after you in their generations” (Gen. XVII, 7), and immediately added: “An everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed after you” [Col. 0847A] (Gen. XVII, 7). “In their generations, by an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God,” etc., means: in your descendants who are continuously bound to me by obedience to the covenant, and who are not separated from my worship by the intervention of unbelieving fathers.

In this way neither Job nor the other Gentiles descended from Ishmael or Esau are to be reckoned among Abraham’s seed; nor does circumcision or any other figurative command of the law concern them, since these were imposed only upon Abraham and his seed, as we have determined above. For it is written concerning circumcision, when the Lord first commanded it to Abraham:

> “I will establish my covenant between me and you, and your seed after you in their generations, as an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed after you. And I will give to you and to your seed [Col. 0847B] the land of your sojourning, all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession; and I will be their God. You therefore shall keep my covenant, you and your seed after you in their generations. This is my covenant which you shall keep between me and you and your seed after you: every male among you shall be circumcised. You shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you. An infant of eight days shall be circumcised among you. Every male in your generations, whether born in the household or bought with money, shall be circumcised; and whoever is not of your stock. And my covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant. The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised, that soul shall perish from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (ibid., 7–14).

And shortly afterward:

> “Concerning Ishmael also I have heard you, and I will multiply him exceedingly. But I will establish my covenant with Isaac, whom Sarah shall bear to you” (ibid., 20–21).

Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I, on those to be circumcised [Note: [Col. 0847D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLIV, cols. 449–450.], says:

> “God thus declared concerning infants: ‘The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised in the flesh on the eighth day, his soul shall perish from his race, because he has broken my covenant’ (ibid., 14). Let this man say, if he can, how that eight-day-old child broke the covenant. So far as concerns the child himself, he is an innocent infant. Therefore he broke God’s covenant—not the covenant concerning commanded circumcision, but that concerning the prohibition of the tree—when ‘through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into [Col. 0847D] all human beings, in whom all sinned’ (Rom. V, 12).”

Behold how blessed Augustine explains that each person transgressed in the first parents the Lord’s testament or covenant—that is, his first law given by the Lord in Paradise—so that even an infant is bound by the bond of original sin. Thus, even if born from Abraham and other faithful parents, he is to be excluded from his people—that is, from the lot and blessedness of his faithful parents—unless, as stated, the remedy of circumcision is supplied to him.

But what is added in the command of circumcision—“whether born in the household or bought with money shall be circumcised, and whoever is not of your stock” [Col. 0848A]—must be understood as a command concerning their household-born slaves or purchased slaves, whether they are Hebrews, that is, of Abraham’s stock, or not; it is not a command concerning other nations. Thus “whether born in the household or bought with money shall be circumcised, and whoever is not,” etc., means: among household-born and purchased slaves, even all those who are not of your stock. Circumcision, therefore, is not a universal command, as baptism and the Gospel are; it was handed down only to the people of Israel, not to the Gentiles.

Origen carefully demonstrates this later, distinguishing from the very testimonies of Scripture which commands of the law are universal—namely, which concern Jews and Gentiles alike—and which are not. Hence it is also evident that the giving of the law was not universal. Moses himself carefully distinguishes this, saying in Deuteronomy: “And now, Israel, hear the commandments and judgments which I teach you, that by doing them you may live and, entering in, possess the land which the Lord will give you” (Deut. IV, 1). Again: “For what other nation is so renowned as to have ceremonies and righteous judgments and the whole law which I set before your eyes today?” (ibid., 8). And again: “You shall teach it to your children and grandchildren” (ibid., 9). And shortly afterward: “The Lord your God has chosen you, that you may be his special people from among all the peoples upon the earth” (Deut. VII, 6). And the Psalmist says: “He declares his word to Jacob, his statutes and judgments to Israel. He has not done so to every nation, nor has he made his judgments known to them” (Ps. CXLVII, 19–20). The Apostle also expressly stated above that the law does not speak to, nor was it given to, all, saying: “We know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law” (Rom. III, 19).

Having offered these preliminary remarks on circumcision, we should not pass over, though briefly, the statements of the ancients that pertain to it. Origen, commenting on this Epistle of Paul upon the words cited above, “If therefore the uncircumcision,” etc., says:

> “God said to Abraham: ‘But you shall keep my covenant, and all your seed after you in their generations. And this is the covenant between you and me, and between me and your seed after you: every one of your males shall be circumcised, and the boy on the eighth day. Every male among you shall be circumcised [Col. 0848D] in your generations, whether household-born or bought with money.’ Let us examine whether the command also binds those who have believed from among the Gentiles. He never mentions the proselyte, that is, the stranger; rather, he commands that a household slave or one purchased for a price be circumcised, not a free person. Let us also investigate the law of Leviticus. ‘Speak,’ he says, ‘to the children of Israel, and say to them: If a woman bears a male, he shall be circumcised on the eighth day’ (Lev. XII, 2–3). Observe here also how Moses is commanded to speak about the law of circumcision only to the children of Israel, and no mention is made of foreigners, whereas in certain commands he speaks not only to the children of Israel but also to proselytes, that is, strangers. The distinction must certainly be maintained. For where it is said, ‘Speak to Aaron,’ and elsewhere, ‘to the sons of Aaron,’ and elsewhere, ‘to the Levites,’ it is certain that the rest are not subject to those laws which are commanded to the children of Israel and in which no mention at all is made of the foreigner. Therefore the command must not be thought common where there is an exception in the form of address. Thus no one else is bound by the law of circumcision except one deriving his origin from Abraham, or one of their household-born slaves, or one purchased for a price.”

Again:

> “We have said these things in order to show especially concerning the command of circumcision that it was imposed for circumcision upon no others than those who derive their race from Abraham, and their household-born slaves or slaves bought for a price. But those who are brought into covenant with God through Christ from among the Gentiles [Col. 0849B] are free from laws of this kind.”

Again:

> “Let us also see what the allegorical laws teach concerning circumcision. In circumcision, a part is cut off from the genital member through which carnal offspring is produced. By this I think it is figuratively indicated that, if any impurity of the flesh clings to the soul as an excuse, it must be cut away. For this reason this cutting is inflicted upon the genitals: such vices of the soul arise not from its own substance but from the incitement of the flesh. The present age is assigned to the week; but the eighth day contains the mystery of the future age. Therefore spiritual circumcision belongs to those who serve the future age, in which they neither marry nor are given in marriage; to those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of God; and to those whose manner of life, while they walk on earth, is in heaven. But in Ezekiel the Lord says: ‘No foreigner uncircumcised in heart and flesh shall enter into my holy things’ (Ezek. XLIV, 9). Yet let us see whether this perhaps may be referred to two general commandments: the one uncircumcised in heart is the person who lacks faith; the one uncircumcised in flesh is the person who lacks works. For one without the other is rejected, since faith without works is called dead, and no one is made alive without faith.”

Again:

> “A person is said to be circumcised in the ears when, in accordance with Solomon’s admonitions, he does not admit vain hearing; and he is called uncircumcised in the lips when he does not cut off blasphemy, buffoonery, and foul speech from his mouth, and has not set a guard upon his mouth. Why, in like manner, should the person who pours himself out excessively in response to the natural impulse to intercourse not be called uncircumcised in the foreskin of his flesh, whereas one who uses this function within lawful offices and only to the extent sufficient for posterity should be regarded as circumcised? Therefore, since we have discussed the rationale of circumcision, it will not seem inappropriate to add that Joshua son of Nun is recorded, at the Lord’s command, to have circumcised the children of Israel a second time with stone knives. Taken literally, this certainly seems impossible. Once the foreskins have been circumcised in the flesh, what can the second circumcision find? But it is evident how our Jesus, who truly led the children of Israel into the holy land after Moses, circumcises believing peoples a second time. The first circumcision cut away from them either the worship of idols or the inventions of philosophical persuasion [Col. 0850A]; but the second cuts away the habit of the old man and the vices of the flesh. Then is fulfilled what is written concerning Joshua son of Nun: ‘Today I have taken away from you the reproaches of Egypt’ (Josh. V, 9), that is, the manner of the Egyptians and the barbarous motions of the mind.

> “The Stoics say: ‘Circumcision must signify something mystical and bear the form of allegory. Was it necessary, then, that images of figures and the riddles of the law should be believed at the cost and peril of little children, with the torments of tender and innocent infancy? Did the lawgiver have nowhere to establish firm laws of justice except in the mutilation of the private parts, and no seal of God except on obscene members? Does God, creator both of soul and body, indicate that he created superfluously that part of the body which he afterward commands to be cut off, correcting his own error through the sufferings of the wretched? Or does he wrongly command the removal of what he made usefully? Accordingly, if God is concerned to bring very many persons to the worship of sound religion, circumcision creates the greatest obstacle. For each person avoids both its punishment and the shame of ridicule.’

> “I think it necessary to answer them. No wise person reproaches others for things which he judges honorable and great among his own people. For circumcision is held among us Gentiles in such public esteem that it is entrusted not indiscriminately to the common, low-born populace, but only to priests, and to those among them who have devoted themselves to more distinguished studies. For among the Egyptians, who are regarded by you as most ancient and most learned in superstitions, and from whom nearly all the others borrowed the rites of sacred worship and ceremonies—among them, I say, no one studied geometry or astronomy, which among them is held foremost; indeed, no one investigated the secrets of astrology and *genesis* (natal astrology), which they regard as nothing less than divine, unless he had undergone circumcision. Every priest among them, or diviner, or minister of whatever sacred rite, or—as they call him—every prophet, is circumcised. No one learned the priestly writings of ancient Egypt unless circumcised. No seer, no *simsustes* [sic; perhaps *symmystes*], that is, initiate of the heavenly or, as they think, infernal mysteries, nor any confidant, is believed among them to be such unless he has been circumcised. Therefore you judge shameful among us what is held among you so honorable and great [Col. 0850D] that you believe the secrets of heaven and hell cannot be disclosed to us except through tokens of this kind. Therefore, if you review your histories, you will find that not only Egyptian priests used circumcision, but Arabs, Ethiopians, Phoenicians, and others whose devotion to superstitions of this kind flourished more notably.

> “These things have been said against the Gentiles. Now let the discourse be directed toward those who indeed believe in Christ but do not accept the law and the prophets. It is written in Peter’s Epistle that we were redeemed by the precious blood of the Only-Begotten: undoubtedly bought from someone whose slaves we were, who set the price that he wished in order to release what he held. But the devil held us, for we had been sold to him by our sins. He demanded [Col. 0851A] the blood of Christ as our price. Therefore, until Jesus was given, it was necessary for those being instructed in the law, each on his own behalf, to give his own blood as a kind of imitation of the future redemption. And therefore we, for whom the price of Christ’s blood has been paid in full, have no need to offer the blood of circumcision as a price for ourselves. If, then, it seems blameworthy that God commands this to be inflicted upon infants, you will also condemn what was done in Christ, who was circumcised and shed blood under the punishment of the cross.

> “If the horror of circumcision seems to make entrance into religion difficult, entrance into the Gospel will appear much more difficult, since a person is commanded to give up not a small part of the body but his very soul. The examples of our martyrs too will deter people from approaching the faith. Or is religion believed the firmer precisely because it promises nothing relaxed, nothing delicate or soft? But even if circumcision contained no sacrament, what would be absurd if the people instructed under God’s law bore some distinctive mark to distinguish them from the other nations? And if the removal of some part was thought necessary, what could be more fitting than to diminish that which seemed indecent and remove that whose diminution would hinder no bodily function?

> “But they say that if this part of the member was not necessary, it ought not to have been made by the Creator; and if it was made necessary, it ought not to have been removed. Let us ask them in turn whether they call the procreation of children necessary. Without doubt they will answer that it is necessary. Then those who, for the sake of continence and virginity, do not perform the necessary functions of nature will be blameworthy. In sum, it must be said that, just as many sacrifices were necessary before the one sacrifice—the spotless Lamb, Christ—offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father, so many circumcisions were necessary until the one circumcision in Christ was handed down to all; and the shedding of many persons’ blood preceded the redemption of all through the blood of one.”

Ambrose, in his Epistle to Constantius, agreeing especially with Origen in the foregoing matters about circumcision, says:

> “Many are troubled by the question why circumcision is commanded as though useful by the authority of the Old Testament, and rejected as though useless by the teaching of the New Testament. What, then, shall we say? That Father Abraham first taught what his inheritance would not follow?”

Again:

> “We find in the history of the ancients that not only Egyptians, but also Ethiopians, Arabs, and some Phoenicians used circumcision among their own people; and they think that they still preserve this as a means of proving reason, because, having first been initiated by their own body and blood, they suppose that the snares of demons which those demons devise against their race are destroyed by the cutting away of a small part. But I think there is already a non-idle reason for considering this small part of the member in which the boy is circumcised on the eighth day, when the mother begins to be in pure blood; before the eighth day she is said to sit in impure blood” [Col. 0852A].

Jerome, in his Epistle to the Romans, says:

> “It is asked why circumcision was given if it is not beneficial in itself. First, so that God’s people might be recognized among the nations; when they were alone in the wilderness, they were not circumcised. Or so that their bodies might be recognized in war. The reason why it is marked on such a member is this: first, lest another member become weak or shameful, since it is publicly seen.”

Again:

> “Because of the promise of grace, in which one was to please God by chastity; or so that Christ, who was to be born from his seed, might be signified, until whom this carnal circumcision was to remain, since he was to bring the spiritual one. Joshua son of Nun bore its type, when he was commanded to circumcise the people a second time.”

There is, I recall, a question sometimes raised as to why [Col. 0852B; perhaps *why*] Joshua circumcised the children of Israel a second time with stone knives at the Lord’s command, as though those who had previously been circumcised could be circumcised again. But blessed Augustine, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*, removes every error from this doubt, teaching that this second circumcision was performed not upon the same persons but within the same people. The very words of the narrative in the book of Joshua clearly contain this:

> “At that time the Lord said to Joshua: ‘Make yourself stone knives, and circumcise the children of Israel a second time.’ He did what the Lord commanded, and circumcised the children of Israel. This, however, is the reason for the second circumcision. All the male people who came out of Egypt, all the men of war, died in the wilderness during the exceedingly long circuits of the journey [Col. 0852C]; all of them had been circumcised. But the people born in the wilderness during the forty years’ journey through the broad desert were uncircumcised, until those who had not obeyed the Lord’s voice had been consumed. Their sons succeeded their fathers in their place and were circumcised by Joshua, because they had been born in foreskin and no one had circumcised them on the journey. After all had been circumcised, they remained in the same place of the camp until they were healed. And the Lord said to Joshua: ‘Today I have taken away the reproach of Egypt from you’” (Josh. V, 2–8).

I am therefore surprised that Origen, so learned a man, erred so greatly regarding this second circumcision performed by Joshua that he asserted above that it could in no way have occurred according to the letter. Yet the narrative itself immediately adds that it was performed by Joshua, saying: “And he did what the Lord commanded, and circumcised the children of Israel.” Now let us return to the exposition of the Epistle.

“That he might be the father of all.” He had said two things: namely, that Abraham’s faith was reckoned to him as righteousness while he was in uncircumcision—that is, while he had a foreskin—as though he had already been spiritually circumcised; and that he afterward was circumcised also in flesh. By these two facts he is set before the rest as father and author, in example and teaching, both for spiritual and for carnal circumcision. This is what “that uncircumcision” means: that the faith through which he was justified before he was circumcised might be reckoned also to those who believe as righteousness, although the outward sign is lacking [Col. 0853A]. And he may be “the father of circumcision,” namely the outward circumcision: that is, the first set before all in example and authority in both spiritual and carnal circumcision. Not only the father, that is, of those who are of the circumcision—those to whom circumcision of the flesh is commanded—but also of those who follow, etc., that is, of those who have faith while uncircumcised.

Construe it thus: “the steps of the faith of our father Abraham, which faith is in uncircumcision”—that is, in the uncircumcised as much as in the circumcised.

“For not through the law.” When above he showed that a human being is justified by faith without works of the law, thereby removing from the Jews their boasting in the law, he introduced the manifest example of Abraham, their father. Hence he now returns to overturning their boasting in the law and, as though repeating the statements above in order to prove them, says: Above I said that I hold a human being to be justified by faith without works of the law. This is clear also in Abraham himself, who undertook a great work—the circumcision prescribed by law—but was justified rather by the righteousness of faith than by that work of the law itself, and rightly so.

For he did not merit the promise of inheritance through the law—that is, through any [work] of the law, or through obedience to a law not yet given—but through the righteousness of faith, that is, through faith that justifies, or through righteousness proceeding from faith. The same applies to his seed, that is, those instructed by his example: “that he should be heir of the world,” namely the perpetual possessor of all goods signified by the fertility of the promised land. For the one who has all that is necessary possesses every good, and one who lacks nothing is said to need nothing. Therefore the Apostle says of those who, following Abraham’s example, are pilgrims and seek heavenly things by despising earthly things: “As having nothing, and yet possessing all things” (II Cor. VI, 10). Or, “heir of the world” means that they alone would be chosen out of the whole world in order to become heirs.

“For if those who are of the law.” I rightly say that believers do not attain the promised inheritance through works of the law. Otherwise faith would be emptied, that is, the merit of faith would be nullified, since unbelievers as well as believers can have those works of the law and thereby become heirs; and the promise would be abolished, that is, rendered ineffective and void. Through that promise, indeed, the nations are to be blessed in Abraham’s seed, though they do not have the works of the law. And this is what “if those who are of the law” means: supply “are heirs,” that is, if those who possess works of the law merit the inheritance on that account, etc. [Col. 0853D]

The Law indeed. He again proves that the inheritance is not acquired through the law—that is, through those outward works of the law which the law commands—but rather that through the law people are made guilty, so that they lose the inheritance. For many works of the law are so burdensome that they afflict those by whom, or upon whom, they are performed to such a degree that its commands can scarcely, or never, please them or be fulfilled willingly: for example, taking tooth for tooth and eye for eye, and inflicting death upon some persons. For who would willingly exercise such things upon those whom he loves, or willingly submit to them in his own case? Hence Peter, in the Acts of the Apostles, refuting those who wished to impose the works of the law upon Christians, so that they too [Col. 0854A] might observe them, said: “Men, brothers, why do you test the Lord by putting upon the neck of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that through the grace of the Lord Jesus we shall be saved, just as they also” (Acts 15:10).

Thus the law made a carnal, stiff-necked people more guilty by the works of the law than it cleansed them. Yet it contributed nothing of righteousness to spiritual people through those outward works peculiar to itself. And this is what he says: for that law—that is, its legal works—produces God’s wrath upon them rather than pardon or any justification. And why wrath? Because it makes them its transgressors, not others; and this is: “For where there is no law,” etc. Those to whom those legal commands have not been given do not incur through it the guilt of prevarication and transgression [Col. 0854B] when they do not voluntarily obey it. Therefore they are heirs by faith, since they are not heirs by the law.

Or the connection may be made thus: I said that the promise of inheritance was made not through the law but through the righteousness of faith. Therefore they are heirs by faith. And this is: “So that the promise,” namely, of the inheritance, “may be sure,” that is, brought to fulfillment, “to all the seed” of Abraham—that is, to those who imitate his faith, both Gentile and Jew. And this is what follows: not only to one who is of the law—that is, to a Jew subject to the law—but also to one who is of Abraham’s faith—that is, to a Gentile who imitates Abraham by faith alone. According to the grace of God, that promise is made sure, not according to the merits of legal works. He—namely Abraham—is father of us all, both Jews and Gentiles; that is, he has been set before human beings as an example to imitate [Col. 0854C].

As it is written, namely in Genesis—as though he were saying: in precisely that way he is father and founder, set before all as an example to imitate, in which the Lord promises that he will be father of many nations, that is, of diverse lands, through believing rather than practicing the works of the law. This he plainly indicates when he adds: “Before God whom you believed.” These are the words of the Lord speaking to Abraham: “Because [I have made] you father,” etc. For it is written thus: “Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but you shall be called Abraham, because I have made you father of many nations” (Gen. 18:5).

From these words, therefore, the interpretation of Abraham’s name is suggested: it means “father of many.” But the added phrase “of nations” is rather an explanation of what sorts of “many things” are meant [Col. 0854D], than an interpretation [of the name]. Moreover, the phrase of the Apostle, “Before God whom you believed,” has either been omitted from our translation or added in part by the Apostle, so that he might determine that Abraham was set forth as father to all by faith rather than by circumcision.

He is made father before God—that is, in God’s good pleasure—who seeks to beget children not for himself but for God; who seeks not to satisfy his own pleasure by intercourse, but rather to prepare children of God by the example of faith than by propagation of the flesh. This he plainly indicates when he adds: “Whom you believed,” namely concerning all His promises; as though he said: “I have set you as father before God, whom you believed, so that through this—that you [Col. 0855A] believed Him—you might beget for Him ministers like yourself by the example of your faith.” God, speaking to Abraham, says it thus: “I have made you father of many nations before the Lord.” He does not say “before me,” but speaks of Himself as though of another.

This is a custom of the Hebrew manner of speech. Thus the lawgiver himself, who wrote this, habitually speaks of himself as though of another, as when he says: “The Lord said to Moses,” and again: “Now Moses was a most meek man,” etc. (Num. 12:3). This seems not to have been done without reason: namely, that one should speak of another as though he were someone else. For it is certain that in saints, and especially in prophets, the Lord speaks rather than they themselves. Hence, when prophets are about to say something, they frequently declare: “Thus says the Lord.” And Truth Himself says to the disciples in the Gospel: “For it is not you who speak” [Col. 0855B] (Matt. 10:20). Likewise, when the Lord formerly appeared and spoke to Abraham or to others, because He did this through an angel, He carefully distinguished from Himself the true identity of the angel who appeared or spoke, so that even by this manner of speech another might be understood to confirm the words than the one of whom the words were spoken—that is, the angel [was distinguished] from the Lord.

“Who gives life.” And deservedly you believed Him concerning His promises, because He is such a one as gives life to the dead—that is, He converts unbelievers to faith as He wills. Unbelievers, the wounded, and sinners are called dead. For faith is called the life of the righteous, according to the saying: “The righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17). Whoever is an unbeliever has absolutely no good by which he can please God, because, as the Apostle himself says, “without faith it is impossible to please God” [Col. 0855C] (Heb. 11:6). And He calls—that is, by His words He makes things that do not exist obey, for “He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32:9)—as though they existed.

“He, contrary to hope.” Having commended the Lord’s power, so that there may be no doubt at all concerning His promises, he also commends the steadfastness of Abraham’s faith, urging its imitation. When Abraham had first despaired concerning Sarah, he hoped to receive an heir through Hagar. But afterward, on the contrary, through the Lord’s promise, he believed and hoped. And this is: “He believed in hope against hope”; that is, believing the divine promises, he was led to hope for receiving an heir—a hope contrary to his former hope.

Otherwise: when he married Sarah, he believed that she was fertile and would bear him children in her youth according to nature [Col. 0855D]. But afterward, disappointed of this hope, he on the contrary wholly believed and hoped, because of the Lord’s promise, that she, barren in old age, would bear contrary to nature. It was wonderful that he could believe this, according to that rule of dialectic: “For if what seems more likely to be present is not present, neither will what seems less likely to be present be present.” “That he might become father”—that is, that by such great steadfastness of faith concerning God’s promises he might deserve to be put before even the nations as an example. According to what was said to him by the Lord in Genesis itself: “So shall your seed be”—that is, the people to beget for Me by the example of your faith—namely, so innumerable. “As the stars,” etc.

We may also distinguish by the stars and the sand the Jewish and Gentile peoples, from which [Col. 0856A] Abraham’s spiritual children have alike been gathered, so that not only the multitude of the children but also the diversity of the peoples may be expressed. Jews are compared to stars because, being already enlightened by faith under the law and restrained through the law from the flow of worldly desires, they were made, as it were, heavenly in their hope; whereas Gentiles, constrained by no law, flowed freely after every desire, intent only upon earthly longings. But because the words of promise concern the Gentiles alone, among whom Abraham’s faith was especially to bear fruit, perhaps it is more fitting to distinguish in the stars and the sand of the sea three orders of the Church: by the stars, which are both fiery and bright, the two higher orders—those of the continent, that is, contemplatives, who burn more ardently with the fire of divine love [Col. 0856B]; and preachers, who enlighten others by their teaching; by the sand of the sea, however, the married, who dwell as it were in the sea and its moistness, indulging luxury, tossed by the anxieties of worldly concerns, and heavily enduring their bitterness.

He believed, I say, “and was not weakened in faith”; that is, his faith was not relaxed in any respect or made weak, however much the promise was delayed or seemed impossible. Rather, he believed just as firmly what he knew to be wholly contrary to nature as what he had earlier expected to occur by nature.

“He did not consider his own body as dead”; that is, he did not attend to the impossibility arising from his own nature or that of his wife, but to the power of the One making the promise. He calls the body dead—that is, now altogether incapable by nature of the promised begetting [Col. 0856C]. “When,” that is, although Abraham himself was now almost a hundred years old—namely ninety-nine—and Sarah’s womb was dead, likewise for the work of generation, both on account of old age and barrenness.

Observe that, when he says that Abraham was nearly a hundred years old, he suggests that Abraham was unable to beget only because of age, not because of barrenness. Yet Abraham should not be believed wholly incapable of begetting, since after Sarah’s death he took Keturah and had sons by her. For the nature of an old man could accomplish in a young woman what it could not in an old and barren woman. The Apostle’s own words sufficiently determine this. For he does not simply say Abraham’s body was dead, but immediately adds: “and Sarah’s dead womb,” in order to show Abraham’s impossibility in conjunction with Sarah—namely, with Sarah, not with another woman. He does not repeat the negative conjunction [Col. 0856D], but inserts a copulative one. For he does not say: “He did not consider his own body as dead, nor Sarah’s dead womb.” Rather, he adds: “and Sarah’s dead womb.” From this he suggests that neither was wholly incapable of begetting separately, but [that they were incapable] joined together.

It should be noted that this promise, “So shall your seed be as the stars of heaven and as the sand of the sea,” is not found to have been made to Abraham when Isaac was promised to him, but after he had been willing, according to the Lord’s command, to sacrifice him to the Lord. For it is written: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only son for My sake, I will bless you, and multiply your seed as the stars of heaven and as the sand which is on the shore of the sea” [Col. 0857A] (Gen. 22:16–17). We know, indeed, that before Ishmael was even born, God promised Abraham that his seed would be innumerable as the dust of the earth; and at another time afterward, as the stars of heaven. But He then added nothing about the sand of the sea.

We have noted this because the Apostle seems to arrange the final promise and the conception—that is, Isaac’s conception—so that the promise appears to have been made before Isaac was conceived. For above he says: “Who against hope believed in hope, that he might become father of many nations, according to what was said: ‘Your seed shall be as the stars of heaven and as the sand of the sea’;” and immediately there is added, “and he was not weak in faith,” etc. But only to the phrase inserted, “that he might become father,” etc., pertains what follows, “according to what was then said: ‘So shall [it be],’” etc.

I think we should ask when Abraham was not weak in faith concerning the promise of Isaac, since he too, like Sarah, is reported to have spoken as though distrustfully concerning this promise and to have laughed. For it is written thus in Genesis: “Abraham fell upon his face and laughed, saying in his heart: ‘Shall a son be born to a man of a hundred years, and shall Sarah, ninety years old, bear?’” (Gen. 17:17). He said to the Lord: “Would that Ishmael might live before You.” But surely, when it is prefaced: “Abraham fell upon his face”—that is, returning thanks for the promise by worship and supplication—it is at the same time suggested that he did not despair of it [Col. 0857C]. We nowhere read that Sarah did this when she laughed. Sarah is said to have laughed secretly behind the door; Abraham, however, is said to have laughed in his heart rather than with his mouth: namely, laughter of the heart is understood as joy of mind, not mockery of the promise. The words which follow—“Shall a son be born to a man of a hundred years,” etc.—are words of wonder rather than despair. And his addition, “Would that Ishmael might live before You,” shows Abraham’s humility: he did not so much presume upon divine grace as [to expect] what God Himself offered without being asked; rather, it was enough for Abraham if Ishmael might live to him as seed.

“In the promise,” etc. Two promises were made to Abraham: concerning seed to be given or multiplied for him, and concerning the land of Canaan to be given to him or his seed [Col. 0857D]. We read that both promises were made to him repeatedly while their fulfillment was delayed. But the promise concerning possession of the land received the greatest delay, being promised for fulfillment long after his death. The Apostle therefore calls this second promise a re-promise, as though he said: Not only in the first promise, namely concerning seed, did he not doubt, but neither in the second, concerning the possession of the land, though it was to occur long afterward—in the fourth or fifth generation of Jacob’s children who went down into Egypt.

“He did not hesitate through unbelief”; that is, he had no doubt in his heart, although in speech he seems to have uttered words of doubt and not immediately believed. He did not first receive a sign in a vision, as he immediately believed the earlier promise concerning seed. For it is written concerning the Lord and Abraham: “He who shall come forth from your womb, him you shall have as heir.” And He brought him outside and said: “Look up at heaven and count the stars, if you can.” And He said to him: “So shall your seed be.” Abraham believed, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. And He said to him: “I am the Lord who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans, to give you this land, that you may possess it.” But he said: “Lord, how can I know that I shall possess it?” And the Lord answered: “Take for Me a three-year-old heifer,” etc. [Col. 0858A] (Gen. 15:4–9).

We believe that Abraham took up these words of doubt, seeking a confirming sign, more for the sake of his descendants than for himself [Col. 0858B]. Just so John the Baptist inquired of the Lord not for himself but for his disciples, saying: “Are you He who is to come?” etc. (Matt. 11:3). “But strengthened in faith”—that is, in expectation, not in the event itself, which was to occur long after his death—“giving glory to God,” that is, returning thanks to Him for these things, attributing nothing to his own merits. “Fully knowing,” that is, firmly believing, that whatever [God has promised, He is able to perform]. He shows the re-promise to be provident and reasonable: namely, that the One promising promises nothing except what He can, or indeed ought, to fulfill. For it is certain that He cannot do anything except what He ought—that is, what is fitting for Him. Therefore it was reckoned [to Abraham], because he was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, fully knowing, etc. That is, even this firmness of faith, if outward works are absent, is reckoned to him by the Lord as righteousness, so as to suffice for his justification [Col. 0858C].

“But not [for him alone],” as if someone should say: What has so great a rehearsal of Abraham’s praise to do with us? He answers that this praise was written not only for him—that is, to commend him—but also for us, who, instructed by his example, are to have it reckoned as righteousness. “For those who believe in Him,” etc.; that is, if, by believing in God, we imitate Abraham. He says “in Him,” not “Him” or “to Him,” as we explained above. “Who raised,” that is, who has already fulfilled in Abraham’s seed through Christ what Abraham expected to come, and what he understood as prefigured for himself in the promise of land or in the blessing of that seed. For Abraham’s whole rejoicing is understood to have been in the prefigured Isaac—that is, Christ—rather than in Isaac as prefiguring [Christ]. Hence Truth Himself says: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see My day; he saw it and was glad” [Col. 0858D] (John 8:16).

In this passage, moreover, the Apostle comprehends in a few words the whole sum of human restoration and salvation, in head and members alike, saying that Christ rose from the dead, “who was handed over,” etc. Note, however, that when the Apostle says that God the Father raised Christ and assigns this work of power especially to God the Father, he suggests that divine power belongs chiefly to the person of the Father, just as divine wisdom belongs to the Son and the goodness of divine grace to the Holy Spirit. The text of our Theology explains this more fully.

[Col. 0859A] “From the dead,” that is, bodily from among the dead, of whom He Himself was one. “Who died.” He brings the cause of Christ’s death back to us as the cause of resurrection. He is said to have died for our sins in two ways: first, because we sinned, on account of which He died, and committed the sin whose penalty He bore; secondly, so that by dying He might take away our sins—that is, by assuming the penalty of sins He might remove it, bringing us into paradise by the price of His death; and that, by displaying such great grace—because, as He Himself says, “No one has greater love” (John 13:13)—He might draw our minds away from the will to sin and turn them toward His highest love. “And He rose for our justification.” By justification he means the perseverance of righteousness that makes one righteous. For a person is not called righteous because he acts justly at some time, but because he has made it a habit [Col. 0859B]. Therefore the statement, “He rose for our justification,” means that, by the hope of the glory of resurrection which He displayed to us in Himself, He may make us persevere in righteous works.

## Chapter V

“Therefore, justified by faith.” Since it was written also for our sake concerning Abraham’s justification by faith, so that we too may similarly be justified by his example, therefore, justified by faith rather than by works of the law, “let us have peace with God”; that is, let us thus be reconciled to Him. And however righteous we may be, we need Christ as mediator. He adds: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ,” from whom every good flows to us from head to members, both through the example of His life and through the preaching of His teaching. And this is: “Through whom we have access to this grace in which we stand.” He adds what glory belongs to it, saying: “In hope of the glory of the children of God”; that is, from the hope we have of attaining that highest blessedness which is due to children, not slaves. And this is through antecedent faith. For hope is born from faith, since the elect rise from the faith they have to the hope mentioned above, and no one can hope for anything unless he first believes it.

He calls grace a gift given freely, not bestowed for merits, because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come” (Rom. 8:18). “And not only,” namely, do we glory in the hope of the glory of God’s children, “but [we glory] also in tribulations”; that is, we count it a great honor to be afflicted for God, according to what is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “They went away rejoicing from the presence of the council,” etc. [Col. 0859D] (Acts 5:41). “Knowing also,” that is, considering the greatest fruit, we glory in these things only because tribulation “produces patience”; that is, it displays patience in the exercise of virtues, and the very practice of tribulation makes us stronger in enduring them.

“But patience,” according to what is written, “The Lord tested the elect like gold in a furnace” (Wis. 3:6), displays their constancy—that is, their tested character—both to yourself and to others [Col. 0860A]; “and testing, hope,” so that we ourselves as well as others may now be confident concerning our merits through God’s grace. And lest this hope seem vain, as it is said of the ungodly, “The hope of the ungodly shall perish” (Prov. 10:28), he adds: “But hope,” namely this hope, “does not put to shame”; that is, it does not bring us shame in the future, because we shall obtain what we hope for. And, as if someone should ask how we can know this, he adds: “Because we have charity, through which we merit what we hope for.” And this is: “Because the charity of God,” etc. It is called God’s charity—that is, charity held purely for the Lord’s sake—in distinction from carnal love. By charity he means a love poured abroad, which embraces even an enemy. Of it it is written: “I have seen an end of all perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” [Col. 0860B] (Ps. 118:96); that is, I have considered and understood that Your broad command concerning charity is the end of all perfection, namely that to which the intention of all Your commandments is directed. This is through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us—that is, through the operation of divine grace bestowed on us.

Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV [Note: [Col. 0859D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV, cols. 93–94]: “Tribulation produces patience,” etc. “There is recognized here the figure which some Latin writers have called *gradatio* [climax], when words or meanings are linked one from another, as here we see patience connected from tribulation, testing from patience, and hope from testing.”

“For why indeed?” With good reason I said that charity has been poured abroad in our hearts. For for what other purpose was Christ dead, except that God’s charity might be expanded within us? Christ died “according to the time,” that is, as if for an hour and detained only in the passing of death, for He rose quickly. He died for the ungodly, in order to free them from condemnation. “When we were still weak.” It should be noted that in this passage the Apostle plainly expresses the manner of our redemption through Christ’s death: namely, he says that Christ died for us for no other reason than to propagate within us that true freedom of charity, through which He displayed to us the highest love, as He Himself says: “No one has greater love than this,” etc. [Col. 0860C] (John 13:13). I think that above we have sufficiently discussed this manner of redemption.

“For scarcely.” I said that Christ died for the ungodly, so that charity might be poured abroad in our hearts—as though what He did were something great. And truly it was great and salutary that God should die for the ungodly, because this man scarcely endures to die for a human being. I said “scarcely”; I did not deny it utterly, because perhaps, though very rarely, persons may be found who die for love of a good man—that is, a righteous one. And this is: “For perhaps someone,” that is, some person, “would dare to die for a good man,” knowing that he will be rewarded by the Lord. By saying “perhaps” and “would dare,” he suggests the difficulty.

But Christ not only dared to die but died for sinners; and by displaying such great glory God “commends”—that is, builds up or confirms—His charity in us, because Christ, God’s Son, died for us while we were still sinners [Col. 0861A]. If He so regarded us when we were sinners, namely by handing over His only Son to death for us, then much more—namely, much more readily, willingly, or plausibly—will He now regard us for salvation, justified in His blood; that is, already through the love which we have for Him as a result of this highest grace He showed us by dying for us while we were still sinners. And this is: “We shall be saved from wrath,” namely future wrath—that is, from the vengeance for sins—“through Him,” namely Christ, who died once for us, prays more often, and constantly instructs us.

[Col. 0861B] “For if, when.” I said that, justified in Christ’s blood, we shall be saved from God’s wrath through Him. And rightly so, because we have now been reconciled to God through His death, whereas previously God held us as enemies to be punished.
