And if His death had such power as to justify or reconcile us, much more will His life be able to protect us and save us from His wrath. For it is certain that every person can do more alive than dead. “In His life,” that is, through Him now raised and living. “And not only,” namely, shall we be saved—that is, shall obtain salvation through Him. And this is: we have attained the greatest glory and count it the highest honor that the Lord has given us such reconciliation. And this is: “We glory in God, not in ourselves”; that is, [we glory] in so great a benefit bestowed upon us through Christ by His grace, not by our merits [Col. 0861C].

“Therefore, just as.” The text appears defective here unless we endeavor to connect it somehow with either what precedes or what follows. It may perhaps be connected with what precedes as follows: We receive reconciliation through Christ, therefore—that is, on account of what has been said above, because He died for us—just as, conversely, we incur condemnation through Adam. And this is what he adds: “Just as through one man,” namely Adam, “sin entered,” because the first sinner gave sin an entrance, “into this world,” that is, into this earthly part of the world in which people dwell—not true human beings who had sinned earlier. “And through sin, death,” namely bodily death. And thus, beginning from Adam, both death and sin, at least original sin, passed into all human beings—into the one man, I say, Adam, “in whom all the rest sinned,” that is, incurred the penalty of sin.

Perhaps the verse may instead begin with “therefore,” and its construction be directed much further on to what follows: namely, “and through one man’s righteousness [comes] to all people,” etc. Thus one might say: Because we have received reconciliation through Christ, so through one man’s righteousness—supply, “justification of life”—[it comes] to all human beings, just as through one man sin entered this world, etc. The intervening words, however, constitute a suspended construction.

[Col. 0862A] “For until the law.” I rightly say that sin passed into all, since there were no persons before the law who proved immune from sin. Of these this seems especially true. Since, throughout all that time before the law was given through Moses, they were not yet made guilty of any written transgression, sin was in the world until the law, although it was not imputed—that is, reproved by human beings or punished through any law—because the law had not yet been written. There was only the natural law, through which they possessed some discernment of good and evil, whereby they could know sin.

It may also be said that sin before the law was not imputed by human beings—that is, no one or few knew what sin was—before the law forbade concupiscence as sin and taught that sin consists rather in the heart than in outward action. The Apostle plainly teaches this in what follows, saying: “Is the law sin? By no means! But I did not know sin except through the law. For I did not know concupiscence,” etc. [Col. 0862B] (Rom. 7:7). Therefore sin, whether original or personal, was not imputed—that is, it was unknown to people—until the law declared it.

For even the sin of the first parents itself consisted in concupiscence, as it is written: “The woman saw, therefore, that the tree was good for food, beautiful to the eyes, and pleasing to behold; and she took from its fruit and ate” (Gen. 3:6). And although sin before the law, as stated, was not imputed by human beings, it was nevertheless imputed even then by God, because on account of it He inflicted the punishment of bodily death upon all. By this He suggests to us that we must chiefly beware of our own sins, since we endure this for another’s [sin]. And this is: “But death reigned,” namely bodily death—that is, it held undisputed dominion—“also before the law,” that is, from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin by knowingly transgressing as Adam did: that is, infants or any innocent persons. Adam is the type of the one to come—that is, the likeness of the new Adam, namely Christ, who was to come after him.

Adam, like “human being,” is a common name for both man and woman. Therefore, when the new Adam is spoken of, it is as though one said “the new human being,” entirely contrary in obedience to the old human being [Col. 0862D]. The Apostle himself explains the likeness of Adam and Christ: namely, he shows that Christ is father of all spiritual people just as Adam is father of carnal people—that is, that Christ presides over all in begetting for God just as Adam does in begetting for the world; and that Christ is author of life and rest just as Adam is author of death and punishment. The saying which the same Apostle elsewhere understands, “This is a great sacrament; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:32), may also be referred to this likeness of Adam and Christ. But for the present text the likeness already mentioned, which the Apostle pursues, namely that of carnal and spiritual generation, is sufficient.

[Col. 0863A] “But the gift of Christ is not like Adam’s offense”; that is, these things which they transmit to their descendants are not equal. Through Christ more is transmitted to descendants for salvation than through Adam for condemnation. And rightly so, because it was more fitting to divine justice or mercy that Christ should benefit more than Adam harmed—that is, that through Christ He should give more advantages than Adam brought disadvantages. For God is far more inclined to confer good than to inflict evil. And this is: “If through the offense of one,” namely Adam—one, that is, not several—“many died,” that is, were condemned, as unbaptized infants are, who are lost for no other reason, “much more” [does] the grace of God “abound unto many”: that is, unto many likewise, not merely one person, so that “many” is understood absolutely, not comparatively [Col. 0863B]. And the gift in Christ’s grace [abounded] through the gifts bestowed by God upon that man, from whose fullness we have all received, and who obtained for us by His merits whatever good we have.

And not as sin passed through one man, namely Adam—supply, as we said above, one sin into all, namely original sin—so also the gift, one gift, passed through one man, namely Christ; rather, many gifts [passed] to many. This is what the Apostle had already summed up in the preceding verse, but he repeats it in order to prove it, saying:

“For the judgment indeed,” etc.; that is, from the one sin, namely Adam’s, comes God’s judgment unto the condemnation of his descendants—that is, He appoints them to be handed over to eternal punishment. But the grace of God, that is, the free gift of remission from many offenses, both original and personal sins forgiven through Christ, is for us unto justification—that is, release from punishments [Col. 0863C]. Thus it is clear that more has been bestowed upon us by Christ for salvation than by Adam for condemnation: Adam brought into the world one sin—that is, the penalty of one sin, namely original sin—whereas Christ brought remission of that sin as well as of the others. And rightly, because so many and such great goods of Christ ought to help more than that one offense of Adam harmed, nor could it harm greatly in comparison with the others.

Hence Jerome, writing to the daughter of Mauritius, also diminishing the gravity of this sin, says: “Adam deserved greater indulgence, because he was still inexperienced and was not drawn back by the example of anyone who had sinned before him and died because of sin. But if you should wish to sin after so many warnings, after the law, after the prophets, after the Gospels, and after the apostles, I do not know how forgiveness could be granted you” [Col. 0863D].

Explain it thus. Since through the offense of one, namely Adam, and through one offense, death—even death of the soul—reigned, that is, held his descendants in undisputed possession, much more fittingly and justly, through the one Jesus Christ, perfect in the fullness of every good, His spiritual descendants, receiving an abundance of divine grace—that is, more goods bestowed on them beyond their merits, goods, I say, of gift and of righteousness—will reign in eternal life; that is, they will possess life as a kingdom, not as an unstable consulship. Only those gifts to which no merit is attached, as in infants, are called gifts of donation; gifts of righteousness are those in which something is bestowed according to merits. For righteousness is called that which renders to each person what is his own [Col. 0864A].

Do not wonder that the Apostle mentions this statement repeatedly, since he especially intends in this matter to commend Christ and by strong reasoning to establish that all should trust more in Christ than fear Adam. In order to commend this firmly to memory, he repeats it often:

“Therefore, as through one.” Since through Adam we incur condemnation and through Christ attain justification—that is, remission—therefore it is bestowed through one, namely through that one. And this is: “As through the offense of one,” supply, “it is brought about,” “unto condemnation,” so that people are liable even on account of that offense to eternal death, “unto all people”: namely, both those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, as he mentioned above, and others; or both those who lived before the law and others, as he likewise mentioned above. So also, through the righteousness of one, it is brought about unto “justification of life”—that is, remission of sins which confers eternal life—unto all people likewise; not indeed unto every individual person, but unto the two specified classes of human beings [Col. 0864B].

For the Apostle does not speak of every individual is suggested immediately by what follows [Col. 0864C], where he says only “many.” “Many” does not mean all. And the Apostle plainly explains how above he called the first Adam the type—that is, the likeness—of the second, namely Christ: namely, in this, that just as Adam transfers to his descendants what is his, namely sin, so Christ transfers to His own what is His, namely the grace of justification.

Just as. Truly this came about through transgression and righteousness, because it came about through disobedience and obedience. And this is what “just as,” etc., means. By Adam’s sin he says that many, not all, were made sinners—that is, handed over to eternal punishment. For, leaving aside the man Christ, always free from every sin, there are many whose original sin has already been forgiven through the sacraments of the Church and who are afterwards condemned for their own sins. Adam did not make these sinners [Col. 0864D] in the way stated above; rather, they themselves do so, since Adam’s sin no longer appears to be punished in them—indeed, it has already been forgiven them—but only their own sins. Although some, following the Lord’s parable concerning the two fellow-servants, wish even sins already forgiven to return upon the condemned and ungrateful, and to be joined to their punishment, so that what has already received forgiveness may be punished again. But the Apostle plainly contradicts this in what follows, saying that the gifts and calling of God are without repentance. We shall discuss this more carefully in its proper place. Perhaps we may also say that none of those to be saved are made sinners by Adam, as stated—that is, subjected to eternal death—but only those condemned without the sacrament.

[Col. 0865A] Through the obedience of one. He, namely, having become obedient unto death, they shall be made righteous—that is, wholly free from every sin, even from its punishment. Note that concerning Adam he says, “were made,” but concerning Christ, “shall be made.” Adam’s very sin, transmitted into us, is as it were present and fixed in us through its punishment. But that justification through Christ is still as it were future, since it is hidden, and especially because Christians are subject to afflictions in this world. Hence the Apostle John: “We are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that, when he appears, we shall be like him,” etc. (1 John 3:2.) And Paul himself: “Our life,” he says, “is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3).

[Col. 0865B] Nor should it be passed over carelessly that in this place the Apostle repeatedly speaks of sin and grace transmitted through Adam and Christ, and maintains—as though required by necessary reason and evident justice—that more good things ought to be conferred through Christ, although not upon more persons, than evil things through Adam: as though the former could do more in helping than the latter in harming. This is evident. But from considering this, unless I am mistaken, the Apostle has left us the conclusion that in the incarnation of his Son God also devised this: that sinners might be aided through him not only by mercy but also by justice, and that what our sins impeded might be supplied by his righteousness.

For when God made his Son man, he surely placed him under the law which he had already given as common to all [Col. 0865C] human beings. Therefore that man was bound by the divine command to love his neighbour as himself, and to exercise among us the grace of his charity, both by instructing us and by praying for us. Accordingly, by divine command he was bound to pray for us—and especially for those adhering to him in love—as in the Gospel he very often intercedes with the Father for his own. But the perfection of his righteousness required that his prayer should in no respect meet with refusal, since the divinity united to him permitted him to will or do nothing except what was fitting.

The Apostle himself carefully indicated this in two other places. Writing to the Galatians concerning him: “Made of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4:5). And to the Hebrews: “Who, in the days of his life, offering prayers and supplications with a loud cry and tears to him [Col. 0865D] who could save him from death, was heard because of his reverence,” etc. (Heb. 5:7.) Therefore, having been made man, he is bound by the law itself of love for one’s neighbour, so that he might redeem those who were under the law and could not be saved through the law, and might supply from his own merits what was lacking in ours. And, just as he was singular in holiness, so he might become singular in usefulness also for the salvation of others. Otherwise, what great thing would his holiness have merited, if it sufficed only for his own salvation and not for that of another? Would Adam, by obeying, have saved only himself—something which each of the saints also obtains by God’s grace? Divine grace ought to have worked something far greater in that singular righteous man. Nor are the riches of the powerful abundant if they are insufficient to enrich others.

### Questions or Objections concerning Original Sin

We must now address that ancient complaint of the human race and inexhaustible question—original sin, namely, which in the present passage the Apostle declares to flow from the first parent to his descendants—and labour, as we can, at its solution. First, then, the question is what we call original sin, with which each human being is begotten. Next, by what justice an innocent son is made guilty before God, the most merciful judge, because of his father’s sin—something which would not be approved among secular judges—and why what we believe has already been forgiven to the one who committed it, or has been removed in others through baptism, [Col. 0866B] is punished in children, who have not yet been able to consent to sin; why a sin not their own damns them; and why the iniquity of a more remote father draws them into condemnation more than the sins of nearer forebears, however much graver those may be. Again, how cruel and inconsistent with God’s supreme goodness it is—he who desires rather to save than to destroy souls—that he should damn a son for his parent’s sin, though he would not save him for that parent’s righteousness.

Sacred Scripture uses the name “sin” in several ways. In one manner, properly, it means the soul’s guilt itself and contempt of God: that is, our perverse will, by which we are made guilty before God. In another manner, sin means the punishment of sin itself, which we incur by sin or to which we are held liable because of it. [Col. 0866C] In this sense sins are said to be forgiven—that is, the penalties of sins are remitted—and the Lord is said to have borne our sins—that is, to have endured the penalties of our sins. And when someone is said to have sin, or still to be in sin, though he does not sin through a wicked will, as an unrighteous person asleep, this is as though we acknowledged that he is still liable to the punishment of his own sin. In a third manner Christ himself is called “sin” by the Apostle—that is, a sacrifice for sin.

Therefore, when we say that human beings are begotten and born with original sin, and contract this original sin itself from their first parent, this seems to refer more to the punishment of sin, to which punishment they are liable, than to guilt of soul and contempt of God. [Col. 0866D] For one who cannot yet use free choice and has as yet no exercise at all of reason—so that he might acknowledge God as his author or deserve a command of obedience—has no transgression or negligence to be imputed to him, and no merit whatsoever by which he might be worthy of reward or punishment any more than the beasts themselves, when they appear in some way to harm or help.

Hence Augustine, in the book *On Faith to Peter*, discussing the souls of irrational animals, says: “For this reason eternity has not been given to irrational spirits, nor is any judgment prepared for them in which blessedness for good works or condemnation for evil works may be rendered to them. Therefore no distinction of works shall be required in them, because they have received no [Col. 0867A] faculty of understanding from God. Therefore their bodies will not rise again, because neither righteousness nor unrighteousness belonged to the animals themselves, for which eternal blessedness or punishment might be repaid to them.” The same writer, in book XXX of the *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter 16: “God is just in governing all things: he permits no punishment to be inflicted on anyone undeservedly, and no reward to be given undeservedly. The merit of punishment is sin, and the merit of reward is right action. But neither sin nor right action can rightly be imputed to anyone who has done nothing by his own will. Therefore both sin and right action are in the free choice of the will.”

[Col. 0867B] Boethius, moreover, in book III of the second edition of his commentary *On Interpretation*, carefully explaining what free choice is, says: “We understand free choice as occurring when, with nothing external compelling us, we judge and consider whether something ought or ought not to be done by us. We come to accomplish and carry out this matter only after knowledge has first been assumed, so that what originates from us may take its beginning from our judgment, with nothing external compelling or hindering us either forcibly or violently.” Again: “We do not call free choice of the will whatever a person may wish, but what each has established through judgment and examination. Otherwise many animals too would possess free choice of the will. For we see them spontaneously avoid some things and spontaneously run toward others. But if willing or not willing something were properly comprised under the name of free choice, this would belong not only to human beings but also to other [Col. 0867C] animals—although who does not know that this power of free choice is absent from them? Free choice, however, as the words themselves show, is free judgment concerning our will. Whenever images occur to the mind and stimulate the will, reason weighs them, judges concerning them, and does what, after weighing it by choice and determining it by judgment, seems better to it. Thus we reject certain sweet things that display an appearance of advantage, and endure certain bitter things bravely, though unwillingly. Hence free choice clearly lies not in willing but in judging the will, and not in the image but in the inclination toward the image itself. Therefore we ourselves are the principles, not the followers, of certain actions. This is what it is to use reason, to use judgment.”

[Col. 0867D] From these words of Boethius it is clear that free choice is nothing other than the mind’s own capacity for deliberating and judging what it wishes to do—whether, namely, what it chooses to follow ought or ought not to be done. Thus one who actually deliberates about nothing, because he is nevertheless capable of deliberating, is not without free choice. No sound-minded person would deny this capacity to infants, or to the insane and deranged, who do not possess discriminating judgment; nor would anyone grant that persons acting merely by will, or driven by an impulse of mind and not moved by some deliberation of soul, earn anything deserving either punishment or reward. Nor would they be subject even to human laws, so as to be judged [Col. 0868A] liable by a human tribunal for anything.

Hence Augustine himself, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*, says: “How is one made guilty who does not know what he has done?” And Jerome, on Ezekiel: “So long as the soul is established in infancy, it is free from sin.” And again: “You will object to me the previously cited saying of blessed Augustine: that God permits no punishment to be inflicted on anyone undeservedly and no reward to be given undeservedly—that is, permits neither punishment nor reward to be conferred upon one who has not merited it. This seems open to objection not only in infants condemned because of original sin and saved through the grace of baptism alone, but also in many other cases: as in Job when he was struck, and in the man whom the Lord healed, who had been born blind, not—as the Lord says—because he or his parents had sinned, but that the works of God might be manifested in him” (John 9:3).

[Col. 0868B] Blessed Gregory, carefully attending to this, distinguishes different kinds of divine dispensations in book I of the *Moralia*. Who, moreover, does not know that God not only promises but also commands us to return good for evil to our enemies, not according to their merits; and that we obtain many things from God by grace, which precedes or follows us, not through merits? Hence the Apostle: “But if it is from works, it is no longer from grace; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:6). What Augustine means by the statement first quoted and afterwards raised as an objection—that the Lord permits punishment to be inflicted on no one undeservedly, nor reward to be conferred on anyone undeservedly—I do not see can easily be resolved unless we observe a certain force in the fact that, having said “God,” he added “just”: namely, to indicate that the Lord does not permit by justice what nevertheless he permits by some dispensation, or [Col. 0868C] commands rather from abundance of charity than from the equity of justice.

For justice renders to each person what is his own: no more than is his own, and no less—that is, only what the person receiving it has merited. But if someone bestows more good upon another than that person has merited, or inflicts less evil, this belongs rather to grace than to justice. Conversely, it seems to belong to injustice if someone grants another less good or renders more evil than that person has merited.

[Col. 0868D] To return, then, to the point at issue: how great must that cruelty be considered which God seems to exercise in infants, when, finding no merit at all, he nevertheless brings upon them the most grievous punishment of hellfire? Hence Augustine says in the book *On Faith to Peter*: “Hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that not only persons already using reason, but even infants who either begin to live in their mothers’ wombs and die there, or who, once born, depart from this world without the sacrament of baptism given in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, are to be punished eternally with the everlasting torment of eternal fire. For although they have had no sin of their own action, nevertheless through carnal conception and birth they have contracted the condemnation of original sin.”

Would it not even among human beings be judged most unjust if [Col. 0869A] someone handed over an innocent son to these transient flames for his father’s sin, much less to everlasting ones? Certainly, I say, this would be unjust among human beings, who are even forbidden to avenge their own injuries. But it is not so with God, who says: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Rom. 12:19). And elsewhere: “I kill, and I make alive” (Deut. 32:39). For God does no injury to his creature, however he may deal with it, whether he assigns it to punishment or to rest. Otherwise animals, created for the labour of human service, could justly complain and murmur against their Creator. To such murmurers the Gospel would answer concerning them: “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will?” (Matt. 20:15); or the Apostle: “O man, who are you to answer back [Col. 0869B] to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or has not the potter authority over the clay, from the same mass to make one vessel for honour and another for dishonour?” (Rom. 9:20–21.) Certainly no one could contend with him on any grounds.

On this reasoning I maintain that, however God may wish to deal with his creature, he cannot be accused of any injury. Nor can what is done according to his will in any way be called evil. For we can distinguish good from evil only by whether something accords with his will and stands within what pleases him. Thus, things which in themselves appear most evil and therefore blameworthy, when done by the Lord’s command, no one ventures to blame. Otherwise the Hebrews who despoiled the Egyptians would have to be gravely charged with theft, and those who killed their neighbours committing fornication with the Midianites would be judged not avengers but murderers.

[Col. 0869C] Indeed, the distinction between good and evil lies in the ordering of the divine will. Attending to this, we daily cry, “Your will be done,” as though we said: “May all things be ordered in the best way.” Thus, by his command or prohibition, the same act is good at one time and evil at another, since, owing to differences of times, certain observances of the old and new covenants appear wholly contrary. Who does not know that the ancient people were formerly commanded for each person to take a wife from his own tribe, while this is now wholly forbidden; that they were then especially to be bound by marriage, while now they are to enjoy the freedom of continence; and that circumcision and the other sacraments of the law, which [Col. 0869D] were then held in the highest veneration by divine command, are now abominable?

It is therefore clear, as we have said, that the entire distinction of good and evil lies in what pleases the divine dispensation, which orders all things best, though we are ignorant; and that nothing ought to be called well or badly done except what accords with, or opposes, his most excellent will. Accordingly, as we proposed, however God may wish to deal with infants or with his other creatures, we should not doubt that it is done best; and if he assigns them all to punishment as he wills, he cannot be accused of injury, however he orders them, whether for glory or punishment.

[Col. 0870A] But because, for commending the divine dispensation in this condemnation of infants, it is too little merely to absolve God from injury unless we can also establish some benefit of his goodness, it seems to us that this too is done by a dispensation of his manifold grace, overflowing both upon the infants themselves and upon others. We know, indeed, that this is the mildest punishment, as blessed Augustine testifies in the *Enchiridion* [Note: [Col. 0869D] *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 275.]: “Certainly the mildest punishment of all will be that of those who, beyond the sin which they contracted originally, have added no other.”

I think this punishment is nothing other than suffering darkness—that is, lacking the vision of the divine majesty without any hope of recovery. This, unless I am mistaken, is the torment of conscience which blessed Augustine above called everlasting fire. [Col. 0870B] We also believe that no one overtaken by death in infancy is assigned to this mildest punishment unless God foresaw that he would become exceedingly wicked if he lived, and would therefore have to suffer greater punishments. Hence infants do not undeservedly seem to receive some benefit of divine goodness in this remission or mitigation of punishment.

God also fittingly uses this mildest punishment of infants for our correction, so that we may become more cautious in avoiding our own sins, when we believe daily that persons so innocent, to whom neither burial nor the prayers of the faithful are granted, are damned for another’s sins; and so that we may return greater thanks to God, when he keeps us free, by his grace, from that everlasting fire after we have committed many crimes—a fire from which he does not save them. He also wished at once to show, in the first and perhaps slight transgression of the first parents, which he thus punishes in descendants who as yet deserve nothing, how greatly he abhors all iniquity [Col. 0870C] and how great a punishment he reserves for graver and repeated sins, if he does not defer so to punish in descendants this one act, committed in the reparable eating of a single apple.

Hence Jerome, in his letter to the daughter of Mauricius, or to a virgin consecrated to God, says: “Adam deserved more indulgence, because he was still new, and no example of anyone previously sinning and dying because of sin drew him back. But if, after so many teachings, after the law, prophets, Gospels, and apostles, you wish to sin, I do not know how he can spare you.” There are also, in the condemnation of individual infants, certain proper and particular causes, though hidden from us, which are known to him who orders all things in the best way. We too can infer some such causes from things which we frequently observe.

[Col. 0870D] For it often happens that divine grace transforms the death of such infants into life for their parents, when the parents—especially as they inquire into the infants’ damnation and consider how much they have brought upon those begotten by their own concupiscence—attribute it entirely to their own fault and charge it upon themselves; and both they and others seeing this become more fearful toward God and [Col. 0871A] more contrite over, or repentant of, their own sins, when they see so severe a sentence upon infants arising from the concupiscence in which all have begotten them. From this also we are invited rather to the good of continence, because we indulge a concupiscence so dangerous, through which so many souls are continually sent down to hell.” By these or similar arguments I think it is apparent that, on account of that mildest condemnation of infants, the Lord is not only not to be accused of injury, but is even to be glorified for the bestowal of some grace, as stated, both upon the infants and upon others.

Original sin, then, with which we are born, is the debt of condemnation itself by which we are bound, when we are made liable to eternal punishment because of the fault [Col. 0871B] of our origin—that is, of the first parents, from whom our origin began. For in him, as the Apostle mentioned above, we sinned: that is, because of his sin we are so assigned to eternal condemnation that, unless the remedies of the divine sacraments assist us, we are damned eternally. And it must be noted that, though we say infants sinned in Adam, as has been explained, we do not therefore simply grant that they sinned, just as, when we say that some tyrant still lives in his children, we do not therefore simply concede that he is living.

“They are damned, then,” you will say, “who have not sinned, which is most unjust; those are punished who have not merited it, which is most atrocious.” But perhaps this ought to be admitted with respect to human beings, not with respect to God. Otherwise, how is God not accused when he afflicts infants [Col. 0871C] also with the punishment of the flood or the fire of the Sodomites? Or how did he permit blessed Job and holy martyrs to be afflicted or killed? Indeed, he handed over even his only Son to death. “He did this,” you say, “by a most advantageous dispensation of his grace, wisely and cleverly.” So too, I say, human beings may, under some dispensation of most salutary counsel, afflict innocent persons along with guilty ones without sinning: for example, when, because of the wickedness of some tyrant, good rulers are compelled to ravage and plunder his lands and thereby harm faithful good persons subject to him, and united with him in possession but not in mind, so that the loss of a few chosen persons may provide for the benefit of many.

[Col. 0871D] It may also happen that certain false witnesses, whom nevertheless we cannot refute, lay some charge against a person whom we know to be innocent. After they have provided the testimony required of them, we are compelled even against our conscience to burden the innocent person, so that—marvellous to say—while obeying the laws, we justly punish one who is not justly punished, and justly do what is not just, after due deliberation on the matter, lest by sparing one we harm many. So also in the condemnation of infants, when those who have not merited it are punished, there may be many causes of a most salutary divine dispensation, besides those we have assigned, so that it is not unjust for them to be punished thus although they have not merited it. For God, who makes [Col. 0872A] not unprofitable use of such punishment both for them and for others, as we have above set forth according to certain not implausible opinions. Thus this mildest punishment of infants seems to be referred rather to God’s grace than to justice; and where God’s greatest cruelty seems apparent, a dispensation of great grace ought to be proclaimed.

Nor is it contrary to reason if what has been forgiven in the parents is punished in the children, although the children do not contract it through the fault of their parents. For some satisfaction is made for the parents, and it suffices for them alone, not for their children. For example, after Adam and Eve were expelled from paradise, they performed penance for their transgression in the sweat of their faces, the pain of childbirth, and other afflictions; and God was propitiated by their own satisfaction. Finally, since they themselves were punished for that transgression by temporal death, they are by no means to be reserved for eternal death because of it, according to the prophetic statement: “The Lord will not judge twice in the same matter, and a double affliction shall not rise up” (Nah. 1:9)—that is, no one is to be punished for one and the same personal sin by both bodily and eternal death.

[Col. 0872B] But their children—the children, namely, of the first parents—against all of whom God was likewise angry because of their fathers’ fault, as though conceived in the sin of carnal concupiscence which the fathers incurred through the first transgression, require each an individual absolution. This has been instituted for us in the very light rite of baptism, where [Col. 0872C] for the alien sin by which they are bound, the faith and confession of sponsors intervene. For one born bound by sin cannot yet make satisfaction for the sin by which he is held, nor act for himself; but he is cleansed by the sacrament of divine grace.

It should not seem strange if what is pardoned to the parents is exacted from the children, since the very defective generation of carnal concupiscence transmits sin and deserves wrath. Hence the Apostle: “Children of wrath by nature”; from which wrath the first parents were freed by their own satisfaction. It can happen in ordinary life that a poor person places himself and his little children under someone’s lordship, but later acquires freedom for himself, not for his children, by some deed of his own merit or by payment. [Col. 0872D] The Lord has also impressed upon the natures of things themselves a not unsuitable likeness of this matter, which seems in some way to answer such an objection: from both the seed of the olive and that of the wild olive, only a wild olive is born; just as from the flesh of a righteous person and from the flesh of a sinner only a sinner is born; and from wheat cleansed of chaff there is produced not cleansed wheat but wheat together with the chaff itself. So, from parents cleansed of sin through the sacrament, no one is born except with sin.

Whether we have also contracted sins from our nearer parents, as from the first parents, and whether, original sins being multiplied, each person is born so much worse the later he is born, is asked before [lacuna]. [Col. 0873A] Blessed Augustine, however, in chapter 16 of the *Enchiridion*, allows that it may probably be said that children are bound also by the sins of their nearer parents. For he says that infants are bound by the sins of their parents—not only of the first human beings, but also of those from whom they themselves were born—which is not implausibly said. For the divine sentence, “I will repay the sin of the fathers upon the children” (Exod. 20:5), holds them, certainly, before through regeneration they begin to belong to the New Testament. That testament was prophesied when Ezekiel says that children will not receive their fathers’ sins, and that this proverb will no longer be in Israel: “The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge” (Jer. 29:31).

[Col. 0873B] Regeneration has indeed been instituted because generation is defective, so much so that one begotten even in lawful marriage says: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50:7). For he did not say here “in iniquity” or “in sin,” because in the one word which passed into all human beings there is such greatness that human nature was changed or converted into the necessity of death. As I discussed above, several sins besides those of the parents are found which bind children in guilt unless divine grace intervenes. But concerning the sins of the other ancestors from Adam himself down to one’s own father, it may be disputed whether the person born is entangled in all their evil deeds and in multiplied original sins, so that each is born worse the later he is born.

These statements of blessed Augustine seem, however, to be referred more to the plausible opinion of others, as he himself [Col. 0873C] indicates, than to his own assertion. For who would suppose that Jeremiah and John the Baptist, sanctified in the womb, were born worse than Cain merely because they came much later? Finally, the Lord Jesus, tracing his origin in the flesh through many sinful fathers, was born of the Virgin long after Cain. And though he had more sinful ancestors than Cain, the number of such fathers, from whose flesh he received flesh in the Virgin, did him no harm.

But this should indeed provoke wonder: when original sin is forgiven, the state of immortality lost through it is not restored. It should be sufficient evidence of the abundance of divine grace toward us if we escape even the most grievous and eternal death, since by that sin [Col. 0873D] we incur both deaths. For God’s forgiving sin is nothing other than relaxing its eternal punishment. For this purpose, as I think, the punishment of bodily and transient death is retained: that we may desire temporal life less, the more readily we see it ending and subject to miseries, and may love more deeply that life which is truly blessed and has no end. Let it suffice that we have said these things concerning original sin for the present, not as an assertion so much as as an opinion. Let us now return to the exposition of the text.

The law, however, entered in. As though someone asked: “What then did the law accomplish before Christ’s coming, if Christ afterwards came and took away sins?” He answers [Col. 0874A] that the law not only did not take sins away, but increased them, so that Christ necessarily descended also to remove the burden of sins. And this is what it means: the written law entered in after the natural law, so that transgression might abound. This is said as when one says of someone, “He went out to die”: that is, he went out, and consequently death followed, not that he went out with this intention. So too, because the law was given to a rebellious people, sin abounded greatly through transgression.

But where—that is, among the same people in whom sin abounded even through transgression of the written law—grace also superabounded: the grace of Christ, that is, good things granted by him freely and not according to merits. This was so both because he worked our salvation there in a special manner, by suffering and preaching, and because he said, “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24); or by forgiving sins, performing miracles, suffering, rising again, ascending, sending the Holy Spirit, and gathering from there the Apostles and the first chosen ones, through whom the whole world was afterwards won for God.

[Col. 0874B] He says that sin abounded and grace superabounded: grace which not only removed sin but also conferred and multiplied virtues, both visibly in miracles and spiritually in the inner goods of the soul. Thus, just as—that is, for this purpose—this grace, the gifts freely bestowed by Christ, abounded: that it might reign through righteousness, that is, establish in us a kingdom of righteousness ruling over every passion and restraining unlawful impulses, thereby preparing us for eternal life. And this is through Christ, offering himself as a sacrifice for us. Just as sin formerly reigned—that is, held its kingdom and dominion in us—thus leading us to death, namely the death of eternal condemnation.

## Chapter VI
What then shall we say? etc. Since where the offence abounded—someone might, as it were, say: “What shall we say except that we should continue in sin, so that grace may abound in us as it did in them?”—“Far be it!” says the Apostle, for our part, that we should grant this: namely, that we ought ever, on any pretext, to persevere in sin. For we have died to sin. [Col. 0874D] As though he said: We must not remain in sin, since in no way ought we to remain in that to which we have already died, through the grace bestowed upon us even for the remission of sins. Or do you not know? As though he said: Even by the sacrament and likeness of Christ’s death, which you received in baptism, you are warned, once you have become dead to sin, that you must not live in it. For just as he, having died once in the body, rose once from death, never thereafter to die, so you too, freed from the death of the soul—that is, from sin—by the grace of Christ’s baptism, not John’s, ought not return to sin.

And this is the meaning: Do you who raise this objection not know the sacrament—that is, the sanctification—of Christ’s baptism? Do you not know that all of us who [Col. 0875A] were baptized into Christ Jesus—that is, in his baptism rather than John’s—were baptized into his death? That is, into the likeness and signification of his bodily death. As has been said: so that, just as he died once bodily and rose again, we too should strive to die once to sin and no longer wish to sin, even though we may be able to rise again through penance.

For we were buried together. After the likeness of death and burial, he also adds that of resurrection, saying that we were buried with Christ in baptism for the death of sin—that is, we received the likeness of his three-day burial, through which we die to sin—for this purpose, namely: that, just as Christ rose once, never to fall again into death, through the glory of God the Father—that is, [Col. 0875B] through the power of divinity, which is especially expressed by the name of Father—so we may walk through the degrees of virtues that make the new human being, not returning to the vices that are the death of the soul.

For if. I said that in baptism we received the likeness of Christ’s death and burial, so that we may hold to the likeness of his resurrection by newness of life. And rightly so: because if we have been planted together in the likeness of Christ’s death—that is, if we have been firmly rooted in the grace of baptism, which is the likeness of Christ’s death, just as he stood immovable in obedience to the death imposed on him by the Father—then we shall also share his resurrection. His death, indeed, was like the planting of a grain that bears fruit and multiplies, as he himself says: “Unless a grain of wheat,” etc. (John 12:24). Thus we shall also share his resurrection, that is, [Col. 0875C] through the degrees of virtue we shall attain the glory of his resurrection, or that very newness of life which, even on earth, is a kind of likeness of the future life announced first by Christ in rising again.

Newness of life is, as Origen says, when we put off the old human being with his deeds and put on the new one, who is renewed in the knowledge of God. In this way, newness itself may be said to require renewal daily. For he says: “Even though our outer human being is decaying, our inner one is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16). Those who advance in faith always add better works to good ones.

Knowing this—that is, attending to and considering that in the very manner of Christ’s death there is signified that our [Col. 0875D] old human being is crucified together with Christ, that is, the transgressor Adam within us—so that, just as Christ died bodily on the cross, we may believe that the old human being in us dies and is crucified spiritually through baptism: that is, that every transgression through which we imitate the old and first Adam is forgiven. Explaining this, he adds: so that the entire body of sin may be destroyed in us—not one member, that is, all sins, both original and personal, so that not merely this or that sin may be forgiven. Anyone crucified has the whole body so stretched out that he cannot move his limbs, as though all were deadened. By this it is signified that all sins have been erased in the baptized.

That henceforth—that is, for this purpose—[Col. 0876A] grace of remission has been bestowed upon us: that, cleaving to it as much as we can and remaining in this purity, we may no longer serve sin. That is, may not the long habit of sin rule us, which holds even the unwilling like slaves forever, rather than having them subject as servants for an hour.

For he who. I rightly said that the old human being is crucified and dead in us, so that he may no longer serve sin in us, because every dead person, as Jerome says, has been justified from sin—that is, is now estranged from the work of sin—although he is not entirely without the will to sin, just as he lacks free power to act. But if—that is, if by death to sin we imitate Christ’s death—we believe, that is, firmly hold in mind, that we shall also live with Christ, [Col. 0876B] glorified forever both in body and soul.

He then adds the perpetuity of this life, saying that we know now by experience what we now believe: namely, that Christ, rising from the dead—that is, from among the dead, of whom he was one—now, that is, in the present age, does not die, nor will he die in the future. And this is: “Death shall no longer have dominion over him.” But why does he say “shall not have dominion,” as though it had formerly ruled over him and oppressed him like an enemy? Perhaps he who seemed so greatly to fear death that he said, “Father, if it is possible,” etc., and again, “Yet not as I will,” etc., did not wish to die at all, but permitted it? Yet according to his divinity, just as he is one with the Father, so he is of one will with him, according to what he says of [Col. 0876C] himself: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down” (John 10:18). And again: “I have power to lay down my life and power to take it up again” (ibid.). And Isaiah says: “He was offered because he willed it” (Isa. 53:7).

The soul of that man indeed desired our salvation, which it knew depended upon his death; and for the sake of the salvation it desired, it endured that death—just as some sick or wounded person, for the health he desires, endures many harsh things under compulsion rather than voluntarily, because he believes that through them he will obtain health. Whatever someone endures under compulsion, he should not properly be said to will but rather to tolerate. For nothing burdens someone by afflicting him unless it occurs [Col. 0876D] contrary to his will. Nor does anyone suffer anything except what opposes his will. Therefore the soul of Christ should be said not so much to have willed the afflictions of the Passion as to have endured them.

But Christ himself also declares elsewhere that he came not to do his own will but the will of the Father. Hence it is to be counted great merit and virtue when someone, through love of God, wholly renounces his own will; indeed, as Christ himself says elsewhere, when he even hates his own soul. Thus, in a certain manner, death itself had dominion over Christ’s humanity when, because of its distress, he dreaded it and preferred that it pass away rather than come; he endured it, as though unwillingly, because of the obedience imposed on him by the Father. He was also made under the law, though he owed nothing at all to the law. [Col. 0877A] Therefore what the Apostle says—“Death shall no longer have dominion over him”—means: It will not oppress one unwilling, nor violently afflict one innocent. For death seemed to exercise violence upon him when it overcame one innocent and wholly subject to no sin, although death was imposed upon humankind only because of sin.

It may, however, be more suitably distinguished that “he now dies no more” refers to bodily death, while “death shall no longer have dominion over him” refers to death of the soul. “He now dies no more” is as though one said: He will not incur the present death of life, that is, bodily death. But “death shall no longer have dominion over him” is as though one said: The later death which follows bodily death among the reprobate, and which [Col. 0877B] rules even over the ungodly after the resurrection, will by no means overcome him. This is the death that rules over all whom it seizes and can retain no one except against his will. The following text appears to require this distinction: “For in that he died,” etc. For from this he proves that that death which is last—that is, which follows this transitory death—will not have eternal dominion over him, because he died once only in the body.

For in that he died wholly to sin—that is, he was never at all in sin, either actual or original, for which sin the death of damnation is due—therefore he could die only once, as was said: that is, in body only, not in soul. But in that he lives. He died, I say, but now lives, having been raised. And in that he lives, he lives to God, just as he had died to sin; indeed, because in the present age he is dead to sin, it is necessary that in the future he live to God. He lives to sin who sins while living; he lives to God who does not dissent from God’s will. This is truly ascribed to Christ alone, whether in the head himself or in his glorified members.

So also you. What he set forth concerning the head, he applies by a certain likeness to the members: namely, that they should die to sin and live to God. [Col. 0877C] Since they might say that they did not know when they lived to sin and when to God, he forestalls and removes this excuse, saying that they should at least strive to accomplish this according to their own judgment and the capacity of their understanding. And this is what he says: “Reckon,” etc.—that is, live at least in such a way [Col. 0877D] that your conscience does not reprove you, but that you may know fully how one ought to live in purity; because, even if you think otherwise, as the Apostle himself says elsewhere, God has also revealed this to you, correcting the insufficiently instructed judgment of your simplicity. In Christ Jesus, that is, through the grace bestowed upon you in Christ, with whom all things have been bestowed upon you, not through your merits.

Therefore not. He returns to the earlier words: “What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin, that grace,” etc.? And, after inserting many reasons, he concludes that one must not continue in sin: that is, sin ought not, for any reason, reign in us. The connection is: Since [Col. 0878A] you must live in such a way as to reckon yourselves dead to sin, therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body—that is, let it not persist in the frailty of your flesh. He does not say, “Let it not be,” but “Let it not reign,” that is, let it not persist by ruling. That he does not say “Let it not be” is suggested when he says, “in your mortal body,” that is, in the frail substance of human nature, prone to sin. It is difficult—indeed, in a certain sense impossible—that this mortality of ours should never incline toward sin; but though sinning is human, persisting in sin is diabolical.

How sin reigns in us and gains dominion he defines when he adds: “so that you obey its desires.” Sin has, as it were, passage rather than dominion in us [Col. 0878B] when reason restrains what desire suggests. But it makes a stable dwelling in us, as though reigning and ruling, when we fulfill in deed the evil that we conceive in mind—or, what is worse, bring it into habit—and are unwilling to correct it through penance. To obey desire, then, is to bring sin to the point of willing it, as the perverse desire that belongs to sin urges.

But neither. Not only should you not obey evil desire; you should also strive to forestall it by your foresight, so that when it wishes to rule it cannot do so. You will do this if you do not present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin: that is, if you do not prepare them as instruments for [Col. 0878C] completing in deed the iniquity conceived in the mind, that is, evil desire. We prepare our members for evil desire brought into action when we indulge excessively in food or drink, so that the flesh can easily become wanton; or when we arrange and adorn ourselves in order to please women; or when we practice boxing or gladiatorial combat, so that by these means we may overcome whomever we wish; or when we exercise the tongue in lawsuits so as to acquire money from them; or whenever we make some part of our body ready or suited to do some evil.

But present—that is, prepare—yourselves to God: that is, dedicate yourselves to the divine will, as persons spiritually raised by him through faith from the death of the soul. And this is the meaning of “present your members.” Since faith without [Col. 0878D] works is dead, he adds: present your members as weapons of righteousness to God—that is, instruments which anyone may use for every righteous work. For example, one may restrain the appetite by abstinence, in order to give to another what one denies oneself; or exercise the hands in labor, in order to have something to give to one who suffers need; or apply the ears to preaching and the eyes to sacred reading, in order also to be able to instruct others; and so forth.

For sin. I said that you should present your members to God, and you ought especially to do so because the grace of the Gospel has been added and the very severe penalty of the law removed. And this is: sin—that is, the law of sin, that is, of punishment rather than grace—shall not have dominion over you who have now been converted to Christ: that is, it shall not oppress and afflict you [Col. 0879A] with those avenging penalties that are unbearable. He then attaches the reason, saying:

For you are not under—that is, you are no longer subject to the legal ordinances, as though pressed under that exceedingly grievous yoke of the law: “tooth for tooth, eye for eye,” etc.—but under the grace of the Gospel. This Gospel should be called a testament of love and mercy, just as the former was one of fear and vengeance. Hence the Psalmist sings in praise of Christ: “Grace is poured out upon your lips,” that is, charity extended even to enemies, as he says elsewhere: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad”; and all your preaching resounds with this. It commands, or urges, that all things be forgiven in such a way that we vainly hope for forgiveness of sins from God unless all of us forgive all injuries to all persons.

[Col. 0879B] What then—shall we sin? On the occasion of the preceding words, he introduces and resolves a question, saying: What then is to be said or maintained? That is, do we plausibly raise this question: shall we sin because we are not under the law? Shall we turn this freedom of grace which we have received into an opportunity for sin, because we do not fear this bodily vengeance? Far be it! For then this would not be freedom but slavery. And this is what he adds: “Do you not know?” That is, are you so foolish [Col. 0880A] that you do not know that you are servants of the one to whom you offer yourselves as servants for obedience—that is, to whom you voluntarily hand yourselves over, not under compulsion, in order to carry out what he commands—without considering whether it ought not to be done, but only that it has been commanded by him: whether of sin, that is, of the perverse will leading to death, that is, damnation, which as an urging commander enjoins wicked deeds; or of obedience, that is, of a servant—namely, of good will, or of a command to which one must obey unto righteousness, that is, some righteous action.

But thanks. I said “whether of sin or of obedience,” as though I doubted whose servants you are; but I give thanks to God that, though you were formerly servants of sin, you have now become servants of obedience. And this is: you obey from the heart—that is, from love rather than [Col. 0880B] fear—the form, that is, the manner of teaching in which you were instructed by preachers; and thus you have been freed from the slavery of sin, to which you formerly obeyed. You have become servants of righteousness: that is, of a just or right will, or of the divine command, which is not merely just but is itself called righteousness.

I speak in human terms. As though he said: And since you have now been freed from the yoke of sin and brought over to obedience to righteousness—

## Book Three

[Col. 0879]

[Col. 0879C] I speak in human terms. I exhort you to persevere in it; and because I see that you are still weak and carnal—that is, prone to fall back into sins—I speak to you in human terms, more leniently than justice requires: namely, that if you do no more, you should at least strive to fulfill works of righteousness as much as you strove to serve iniquity. This is what is said in human terms, because of the weakness of their flesh—that is, the weakness which they derive from fleshly desires—which he immediately adds, saying: “For just as.” As though he said: I truly speak to you in human terms, because I say this: just as formerly you presented—that is, openly and shamelessly prepared—your members to serve uncleanness, that is, fleshly shamefulness, lust or gluttony, and iniquity, that is, spiritual vices such as anger or hatred toward another, [Col. 0879D] or desire for another’s property; just as, I say, you presented them to serve those things for the perpetration of iniquity, so that you might bring the perverse desire of the mind into effect, so now prepare them to serve righteousness, that is, just desires, in sanctification, that is, in the accomplishment of holy work.

Those who sin not so much from weakness as deliberately prepare their members for iniquity, as some use warm baths (*calidis*) for lust, or *falsis* [the term is uncertain], so that they may devote themselves longer to drinking; and they often force the very members of their body, against their nature, into shameful acts. A person also prepares his hand for committing iniquity [Col. 0880C] if he provides it with a sword to use against one whom he hates. Conversely, one prepares one’s members for righteousness if one strives to regulate and restrain them so that they do not break out into unlawful acts but advance toward the crown; if, when one had the ability to sin by means of them, one did not transgress, but courageously extinguished in them every onset of perverse suggestion and showed what they could do for good: for example, sacred writings for the eyes, readings for the ears, gifts of alms or instruments of religious labor for the hands.

For when. I rightly said that, now freed from sin, you have become servants of righteousness, because, conversely, when you were formerly servants of sin, you were free from righteousness—that is, estranged from the service of righteousness. This is an argument from opposites. Just as a servant of righteousness is said to be one who serves it, so conversely one is called free from it who is removed from its service: that is, who does not care to fulfill it. What fruit, then—that is, since you formerly so served sin, wholly estranged from righteousness—what fruit, that is, what benefit, did you then have from the things set forth above, namely uncleanness and iniquity, deeds whose commission now makes you ashamed? And their end—that is, the goal to which they lead, or the result formerly due to them—is death, namely death of the soul, that is, the punishment of everlasting torments.

But now, freed from sin—that is, from the grievous yoke of evil habit—you have your fruit here in sanctification: that is, you have as recompense the very remission of sins by which you have been sanctified. And you have already prepared for yourselves the end—that is, the outcome to which this sanctification leads: eternal life. He rightly calls both the life and death of the soul eternal ends, because, when this bodily life and temporal death are ended, these ultimate states follow.

For the wages. To those two foregoing statements—“the end of those things,” and “but now freed,” etc.—he attaches these two, “for the wages,” and “but the grace of God,” etc., showing how one reaches the two ends he distinguished, namely death and life: death indeed from justice, but life from grace previously bestowed through Jesus. “For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed in us” [Col. 0881B] (Rom. 8:18). Hence he aptly calls the recompense of sin in death wages, but calls the recompense of obedience to God in eternal life not wages but grace.

For *stipendium* (“wage”) is said from *stips* (“payment”) and *penso* (“I weigh”). A *stipes* or *stips* is the pay given to soldiers, after their labor has been weighed or the advantage of their masters considered. But Haymo says as follows: “*Stipendia*, that is, recompense, is called *stipendium* from *stips pendenda*, that is, substance to be weighed. For in ancient times money was more often weighed than counted.”

The connection is thus: I said that the end of those things—that is, of uncleanness and iniquity—is death, and rightly so, because the wages of every sin are death: that is, death is the just and due recompense for those who persevere in it. [Col. 0881C] But eternal life ought rather to be called the grace of God than our wages: that is, it is bestowed upon us freely rather than owed to our merits. And this is through Christ Jesus, through whom we have been reconciled to God.

## Chapter VII

Do you not know? The Apostle had said above: “For you are not under the law but under grace”; and here, most recently, he added that through Jesus Christ our Lord, rather than through the law, we have now attained the grace of eternal life. Someone might therefore ask: after the law was given, when can anyone be saved without its observances, though grace be added? By a fitting comparison the Apostle anticipates and resolves this question, showing [Col. 0881D] that just as a woman, once her former husband has died, may without blame pass to another, so the people of God, formerly bound under the yoke of the law like a woman to a husband whom she must obey, may now, once the law has died, pass without fault to the freedom of the Gospel.

“For the law and the prophets were until John,” who is interpreted “grace of God”: that is, until the time of the singular grace of Christ’s coming. As the Apostle himself recalls in the Epistle to the Hebrews, this time of the change of the testament—that is, the passing away of the old and birth of the new—the Lord had promised through Jeremiah, saying: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord,” etc.

The connection is: I said that we are no longer under the law and indicated that after Christ it is no longer necessary for us. Nor should this seem strange, [Col. 0882A] because, brothers, do you not know—I do not believe that you are ignorant—that the law has dominion over a person, that is, must be obeyed by a person, as long as it lives: that is, for the period appointed and granted to it by the Lord, so that obedience to it may be maintained fully, even in its figurative precepts. When he inserts, “for I speak to those who know the law,” that is, to you who learned the law long ago, he shows that this address is especially directed to those who had believed from among the Jews. He here introduces, as it were, the reason why they should not be ignorant of what he says: because they learned the law, which teaches that it has a prescribed or God-determined time, so that it does not live forever, as has been said. This is confirmed by the testimony of Jeremiah cited below, or by other passages of the Old Testament.

[Col. 0882B] For the woman who. He proves by a fitting comparison that the law has dominion over the people subject to it only during the time it lives. For likewise no husband has dominion over the wife bound to him except while he lives. And this is: “For the woman who is under a husband”—that is, joined to him as to a superior—is bound while he lives by his law, that is, by the marital law, so that she cannot marry another. Therefore, while he lives, because she is thus bound by the law of marriage.

Therefore, brothers. He now adapts the preceding comparison, saying: And thus, just as you who formerly lived to the law, subject to it through obedience, have now become dead to it through the body of Christ—that is, through the very presence of the truth displayed to you in Christ. The shadow of this truth had preceded in the law. [Col. 0882C] For once the reality itself arrived, which is sufficient in itself, there was no longer need for those figures that had preceded as signs of a future reality and were held venerable only in hope of it. Otherwise, if those figures still continued, what is now past would still be expected as future; Jews, glorying in their oldness, would mock our newness; and some would attend more to the works themselves than to faith in Christ, which they would believe could by no means suffice without works.

It should be noted, however, that although, according to the comparison introduced, it would seem more fitting to say that the law had died to us rather than that we had died to the law, nevertheless the meaning is the same, and it makes no difference whether it is said in this manner or that. That you may belong to another, [Col. 0882D] namely Christ, bound only by obedience to him and to the precepts of Gospel teaching. Lest anyone object that Christ himself had also died and that his own were therefore now released from his yoke, he prudently added: “who rose from the dead,” that is, who by his own power raised himself from among the dead to everlasting life, so that, kindled by hope and desire for his glory, we may bear fruit not for the world but for God: that is, abound in spiritual goods which delight God rather than in worldly and earthly ones, which Jews always eagerly sought. According to the letter to which they adhere, no promise but an earthly one is found among them; thus they would be said to bear fruit for the world rather than for God from the law’s promise.

[Col. 0883A] For God promised that hard-necked people what he knew they especially desired, so that he might thereby draw those who were carnal—that is, intent on carnal rather than spiritual goods—to obedience. Observe that, when he added to what he had promised, “that you may belong to another, who rose from the dead,” the words “that we may bear fruit to God,” he did not say “that you may bear fruit,” but that you and we together—that is, all of us—may bear fruit, whether by preaching or obeying.

For when we were. I said that you should be disciples and imitators of another, namely Christ, rather than what you had hitherto been, so that you may bear fruit to God: that is, that you may be spiritual in desire rather than carnal, as formerly you were when following the temporal promise of the law. He rightly gives this warning, because then, through that promise of the law, you who loved carnal desires could by no means [Col. 0883B] render spiritual fruit to God; rather, through ever more closely cleaving to earthly things in desire, you bore fruit for death—that is, a mortal and damnable fruit—as it is written:

> Growing wealth is followed by care.  
> (Horace, *Odes*, III.16.18.)

And elsewhere:

> The love of money grows as money itself grows.  
> (Juvenal, *Satires* 14.139.)

Read it thus: “When we were in the flesh,” that is, intent upon carnal rather than spiritual desires, “the passions of sins”—that is, the various desires causing us to sin, so that “passions of sins” is said, as it were, intransitively, meaning passions which were sins, just as one says “a creature of salt,” or “the substance or body of a stone”: that is, a creature which is salt, or a substance or body which is stone. These passions were through the law, which praised and promised an abundance of the things they greatly desired: namely, a most excellent land flowing with milk and honey, greatest peace and prosperity in it, long life, and whatever belongs to earthly happiness, which they especially desired. By the praise, promise, and hope of these things, their desire for them was kindled more greatly than it would have been if they had not hoped for them or learned that they were so great. For what we despair of obtaining does not hold us long [Col. 0883D] or strongly in desire.

They worked in our members so that we might bear fruit to death: that is, they acquired for us the mortal outcome of damnation. Desires work in the members when we fulfill in deed through some member a desire conceived in the mind—for example, lust through the genitals, theft or robbery through the hands. But now we have been released from that obedience to the law, which, as was said, was rendered for the recompense of temporal things, so that we may now serve God spiritually, fulfilling those figures of the law more in mind than in outward deed, as it is said elsewhere: “For the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). We serve in newness of spirit—that is, in spiritual desires and understanding, which did not exist before—and not in the oldness [Col. 0884A] of the letter, that is, in the old works done according to the letter alone, such as carnal circumcision, Sabbath observance, sacrifices, and countless other things.

Someone may perhaps ask why the law did not also contain the promise of eternal life, so that the people might be drawn more strongly to obedience not only by desires for earthly but also for heavenly gifts. But it had imperfect commandments, as the same Apostle recalls elsewhere, saying that the law “brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7:19). And Truth himself says: “You have heard that it was said to those of old,” etc. (Matt. 5:21); and, “Unless your righteousness exceeds,” etc. (ibid., 20). Its recompense could not be perfect, and heavenly things did not suit earthly desires; nor can anyone who serves God as much for earthly things as for heavenly things be fittingly disposed toward God. Hence Truth himself warns, saying: “Let not your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. 6:3): that is, do not mingle an earthly intention with a heavenly one in any work of yours, so as to obey God at once for transitory and eternal goods.

[Col. 0884B] But perhaps, while we seek to untie the knots of the question proposed, we incur greater ones from the solution itself. For the law contains the command of love both for God and neighbor, and these two commandments suffice for life. Thus the Lord answered the rich man who asked what he must do to possess eternal life: he should keep these two commandments, and they would suffice. Paul himself declares that love is the fulfillment of the law. It therefore seems remarkable that the law brought nothing to perfection and did not suffice for life, so that evangelical righteousness ought rightly to abound beyond it.

[Col. 0884C] In truth, the commandments of the law, whether concerning love or other matters, did not bring one to perfection—that is, they could not suffice for salvation. Rather, Christ had to come, he who is the end and completion of the law, because without him, who was promised in the law, the law could in no way be fulfilled. Further, if we carefully examine the words of the law, it nowhere extends the name “neighbor” beyond persons of that people, namely the Jewish people; nor is it written anywhere for us in the whole law of Moses, “You shall love your neighbor,” but rather, “You shall love your friend” (Lev. 19:18).

[Col. 0884D] The Lord himself carefully observed this. When, questioned by the rich man, he recited the commandments of the law and said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 19:19), he clearly indicated from the parable that “neighbor” is used for “friend” or “benefactor,” showing, by the rich man’s own judgment, that only the one who had bestowed mercy upon the man who fell among robbers was his neighbor. Therefore it is evident that, since love of neighbor is confined according to the letter of the law to a friend alone, the commandment of love found in the law is by no means perfect as is that of the Gospel, in which we are commanded also to love enemies and do good to them, so that we may be perfect like the heavenly Father, who makes his sun rise upon good and evil alike (Matt. 5:44–45). The Apostle himself observed this: he did not say, “Whoever loves his neighbor fulfills righteousness” or “the Gospel,” but “fulfills the law” [Col. 0885A] (Rom. 13:8).

Yet we again encounter a serious knot in the question: when the rich man asked what he must do to possess eternal life, and after the two commandments concerning love of God and neighbor had been recited by him, Christ answered, “Do this, and you shall live” (Luke 10:28), especially since he elsewhere says: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have?” (Matt. 5:46). But surely no one could be understood more properly as neighbor or friend than the one signified by that Samaritan who bestowed mercy upon the wounded man: namely Christ, who was indeed neighbor to the Jews both by kinship and by the affection of true charity, and by innumerable benefits, whether by preaching [Col. 0885B] or by performing miracles. Therefore, if that rich man then loved every neighbor or friend, he would certainly love through Christ. And thus, by cleaving to him and to his commandments, he would certainly merit eternal life.

Nevertheless, the commandment concerning the love of neighbor, friend, or benefactor given by the law was not thereby perfect, since it did not encompass every human being, friend and enemy alike. Even though at Christ’s time this neighbor or friend seemed—indeed, through Christ, who had already come, had become, as was said—to possess perfection, the commandment or law would have had perfection only if it were sufficient in itself, so that nothing at all were lacking for the fullness of righteousness to those obeying it and nothing else needed to be added. This is by no means true, since before Christ’s coming the love of those then regarded as neighbors and friends was imperfect and did not extend to enemies, as it was subsequently extended through Christ. What we said above—that “neighbor” in the law, according to the letter, is not understood of every human being—can be supported not only from the law itself but also from the testimonies of certain ecclesiastical teachers.

Thus Ambrose, in his commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, where it is said, “Owe no one anything,” etc. (Rom. 13:8), says:

> “[Col. 0885D; *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 164.] He wishes us to have peace, if possible, with all; but love with the brethren. And this will be to owe no one anything: to render to each person the duty appropriate to his station.”

Again below:

> “[Col. 0885D; Ibid., col. 165.] ‘Love of one’s neighbour does not work evil’ [Col. 0885D] (ibid., 10). It works no evil, because love is good and no sin can be committed through that which is the fulfilment of the law. But because in Christ’s time something had to be added, it was commanded that not only neighbours but enemies also should be loved. Hence: ‘Love is the fullness of the law’ (ibid.); so that to love one’s neighbour is righteousness, while the abundant and perfect righteousness is to love even one’s enemies.”

This is heavenly righteousness; this makes persons like God the Father, who bestows yearly gifts even on those who do not worship him. Nor are we unaware that very many of the holy Fathers understand every human being to be one’s neighbour in the commandment itself concerning love of neighbour, and confirm this by plausible [Col. 0886A] arguments.

Thus Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book I:

> “[Col. 0885D; *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV, col. 31.] It may be asked whether the love of angels also belongs to those two commandments. For that he who commanded us to love our neighbour excluded no human being is shown both by the Lord and by the Apostle Paul.”

Again, he had set forth the two commandments and had said that the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon them. Again, the Lord says, “Go and do likewise,” so that we may understand him to be our neighbour to whom an office of mercy ought to be rendered if he is in need, or would have to be rendered if he were in need. From this it follows that he also, from whom an office of mercy must in turn be rendered to us, is our neighbour. For the term “neighbour” is relative: no one can be a neighbour except to a neighbour.

Again:

> “[Col. 0886D; Ibid.] Paul [Col. 0886B] says: ‘For, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not kill, You shall not steal, You shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: You shall love your neighbour as yourself’ (Rom. 13:9–10).”

Again:
