> “Whoever therefore supposes that the Apostle commanded this not concerning every human being is compelled to admit what is most wicked: that the Apostle thought it was not a sin if anyone should commit adultery with the wife of a non-Christian or of an enemy,” etc.

Again:

> “[Col. 0886D; Ibid.] Further, if he to whom an office of mercy is to be rendered, or he from whom it is to be rendered to us, is rightly called a neighbour, it is manifest that holy angels too are included in this commandment by which we are ordered to love our neighbour, since offices of mercy are rendered by them.”

[Col. 0886C] These words indeed of our most diligent teacher Augustine seem wholly to prove that, in the Law, every human being must be understood as a neighbour. Otherwise the Law would by no means seem fulfilled through love of neighbour, since it also commands many things concerning foreigners, whose offence must be avoided just as that of neighbours must be avoided.

But since there are two branches of love—namely, love of God, which Truth himself calls the first and greatest commandment, and love of neighbour—when the Law is fulfilled through love of neighbour, must not that love include the former also? For no one is more rightly to be understood as our neighbour or friend than our Creator and Redeemer himself, from whom we have both ourselves and all good things, as the Apostle himself recalls when he says: “What have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). Of his ineffable love toward us he says elsewhere: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. 5:8). Again: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.” And the Son himself says: “No one has greater love than to lay down his life,” etc. (John 15:13).

Accordingly Origen, understanding Christ spiritually as the neighbour meant in this commandment of love, says in the continuation of this Epistle:

> “If you inquire more carefully [Col. 0887A] who our neighbour is, you will learn in the Gospel that he is the one who carried us, as we lay fallen, to the inn of the Church, and gave to the innkeeper Paul, or to him who presides over the Church, two denarii of the Old and New Testaments for the expenses of our care. If we love this neighbour, we fulfil the Law. For Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. 10:4).

Therefore, since the name “neighbour” includes God also—and especially God himself, for otherwise love of neighbour would not fulfil the Law—it is certainly evident that the Law is fulfilled through this love as through the love of God. For one who truly cleaves to God through love despises none of his commandments, as it is written: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14:23).

How, moreover, can love—which is called *caritas*—be true unless it is referred to the Lord? Augustine himself, *On Christian Doctrine*, book IV, says:

> “[Col. 0887D; *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV, cols. 105–106.] By charity I mean the movement of the mind toward enjoying God for God’s own sake.”

The same writer, in *On the Morals of the Church against the Manichaeans*, says:

> “[Col. 0888D; *Patrologia*, vol. XXXII, col. 1317.] It is written: ‘For your sake we are afflicted all day long’ (Ps. 43:22). Charity could not have been marked more expressly than by the words ‘for your sake.’”

Whoever, then, cleaves to God in charity—by which alone the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil—and consequently strives to obey his commandments, endeavours to fulfil both those commandments which concern strangers and those which concern neighbours, and strives equally in both to follow the divine will.

Therefore it makes no difference, if we may speak with due reverence for the Fathers and brethren and confess that the Law stands far from Gospel perfection, [Col. 0887C] while preserving in addition all apostolic and evangelical authority. It makes no difference, I say, whether in the Law we understand every human being as neighbour or not, provided that, as has been said, God is included in the neighbour and love of neighbour includes love of God also. For when it is said, “You shall love your neighbour” (Matt. 22:39), and is added, “as yourself,” how could we fulfil this unless we loved ourselves also? Yet how can we love even ourselves if, despising God’s commandments, we act unjustly? For “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6).

## “What then shall we say? Is the Law sin?”

Continuation: [Col. 0887D] I said that formerly the passions of sins worked through the Law, so that it was useful even for us to be released from the Law as though from sin. What then shall we say? That is, what is to be thought about the Law which we considered good? Does it not now seem that it ought rather to be called evil than good?

This is what he says, as though raising an objection against himself: “Is the Law sin?” That is, does it lead us rather to condemnation than to salvation, so that it earns for us condemnation rather than salvation, can only harm and not help, and contains in itself no more good than sin does? “By no means!”—that is, let us not believe this. Rather, it is opposed to sin [Col. 0888A]: it thoroughly teaches and forbids sin so that it may be avoided, restraining not only deeds but even desires, as does the Gospel, though far less fully. For it restricts them only to things belonging to one’s neighbour, saying: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s property, nor desire what belongs to him” (Exod. 20:17).

Why it was necessary for sin to be taught by the Law he passes over, saying that before the instruction of the Law that in which sin was chiefly committed was unknown—namely, sin in the heart rather than in deed. This is what he says about himself in the general person of human beings, whose minds had by then been darkened through the transgression of the first parents, so that they blamed deeds rather than desires: “I did not know sin”—that is, I did not possess discernment sufficient for a true knowledge of sin—[Col. 0888B] “except through the instruction of the Law,” because I was ignorant that that in which one sins only, or especially, namely concupiscence, was sin.

This is what he adds: “For I did not know that concupiscence”—that is, the perverse desire of the mind in the pursuit of earthly things or carnal pleasures—“was sin, unless the Law, by teaching it, said: ‘You shall not covet.’” That is, unless it prohibited concupiscence, although not universally but, as stated, in regard to a neighbour’s possessions. Observe that when it says, “You shall not covet,” it both teaches sin and forbids it in order that it may be avoided.

Hence he proves that the Law is entirely good, because whatever belongs properly to it is good, whether in teaching or forbidding. If [Col. 0888C] sin increased after the Law, and after instruction in the commandments and neglect of them we became worse and more inexcusable than before, this is to be attributed not to a fault in the Law but to human beings. As it is written: “The servant who knows his lord’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes.” Again: “It is better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back.”

Therefore it was rightly said, “By no means is the Law sin,” that is, useless and evil in itself. Yet through it we received an occasion for a sin which had not previously existed, just as we often incur concupiscence from certain good things which God gives, if we lack them, or pride if we possess them. Yet these things should not on that account be called evil, if we desire them wrongly or use them wrongly.

Thus “sin”—that is, the punishment and affliction of this temporal life which we endure because of the fault of our first parents—worked in us through the Law every concupiscence for whatsoever earthly goods, so that by their abundance we might avoid every anxiety of present miseries. How it worked this he shows when he says:

“Having received an occasion through the commandment,” that is, through obedience to the Law which promises these earthly goods. For since the Law promised this reward for obedience to itself, we did not seem to be sinning, however much we coveted such goods, provided that we fulfilled the obedience required. But by “sin” here he indicates [Col. 0889A] the very fuel and nourishment of sin, concerning which, in the preceding little book, when we treated of original sin, we did not remain silent.

“For without the Law”—that is, before the Law brought its commandments and promises—“that sin,” namely that fuel of sin, as stated, though it existed even then, was weaker in its power to awaken concupiscence than afterwards. For the more certainly we await what we desire, the more we are kindled into longing for it, as we mentioned above.

“But I was alive once,” that is, in a certain manner, if not wholly: I lacked the death brought about by that fuel, and was as it were without concupiscence in comparison with the concupiscence which followed after the Law. “But when the commandment came,” when the Law was given, “sin revived” [Col. 0889B]—that is, after the commandment concupiscence grew strong. Or it revived in the offspring what had preceded in the parent: concupiscence was stirred in us after the commandment just as it first began in the first parents after the commandment, especially since that which is forbidden is often desired more ardently, according to the poet’s saying:

> We always strive toward what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.  
> (Ovid, *Amores*, book III, elegy 4, verse 17.)

“But I died.” Previously I had been as though infirm rather than dead, as though needing correction rather than condemnation, needing to be chastised rather than killed, being stirred by concupiscence, if there was any, with a lesser degree of guilt. “And it was found to be unto me”—that is, through the occasion of the Law, as stated—that from which I ought to have become better I became far worse, [Col. 0889C] and from that through which I ought to have avoided sin I incurred it more abundantly.

This is what he adds: “For sin, having received an occasion”—that is, having found a cause for inciting us to concupiscence through the commandment, namely the Law, in obedience to which we placed excessive confidence—“deceived me.” It deceived me by making me suppose that I was singularly dear to God because of the obedience to the Law which I rendered him, so that I scarcely, or never, feared my condemnation whatever I did; and especially because I did not judge the concupiscence of promised goods, however great it might be, condemnable, since we obeyed the commandments, for obedience to which those goods were promised. “And through it it killed me,” that is, condemned me.

“Therefore the Law indeed”—since the Law was given for knowledge [Col. 0889D] of sin and for life rather than death—“is holy”: that is, it is in no respect defective or blameworthy. Its commandment is holy, commanding and forbidding nothing except what ought to be commanded or forbidden; and therefore it is in itself just and good, that is, useful and health-giving to those who obey.

## “Then has that which is good become death to me?”

He said two things: that the commandment was good, and yet that, through it, he was killed after sin had received an occasion. Therefore, as though reasonably objecting, he asks whether that which is good in itself, namely the commandment, became death—that is, condemnation—to him. “By no means!” For no commandment should be called condemnable unless obedience to it is harmful, as was the devil’s commandment to Eve.

“But sin.” I said that the commandment is good and must not be called death, that is, condemnable, either for me or for anyone else; yet it became in some manner a cause of my condemnation, because, as stated, concupiscence took occasion from it. This accords with the historian’s statement: “For all evils arose from good beginnings.”

Thus read it: “But sin,” namely the fuel of sin of which we spoke, “through the good”—understand, through the commandment of the Law, or through the Law itself, as we showed above—“worked death of the soul,” that is, every concupiscence, [Col. 0890A] so that sin might appear: namely, that fault of concupiscence might become manifest and inexcusable, and might be exceedingly great. He immediately shows that it is exceedingly great, saying: “that sin,” namely the aforesaid fuel of sin, “might become exceedingly sinful”—that is, might incline us most strongly to sin—“through the commandment,” namely through the occasion, as stated, taken from the Law.

Perhaps someone may ask how the commandment of the Law, or the Law itself, is called good, or said to have been given for life; or why it was given even by God, if it could not save those who obeyed it. We answer that the Law was given for life in this respect: that it might initiate the people of God into the merit of eternal life, though not bring it to completion. It is good, moreover, because, as stated, all its commandments are just, even according to the letter, though not perfect; and all that the Lord commanded has reasonable grounds, even if we do not know them.

It was, moreover, an act of great providential ordering to give a people still wholly untaught, undisciplined, stiff-necked, and ever rebellious, commandments of a beginning rather than of perfection, so that those who had hitherto experienced no obedience, or almost none, might at least learn to obey in some measure. As the poet observes:

> It is something to have advanced thus far, if one is not permitted to go further.  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, book I, epistle 1, verse 32.)

Nor, when we tame beasts of burden, do we first lay great loads upon them; rather, having first subdued their unruliness in small matters, we gradually lead them to bear greater burdens.

Nevertheless, we believe that to all those who obeyed the imperfect commandments from love of God rather than fear, there was revealed before the day of their death—either through some spiritual teacher or through inward inspiration of divine grace—what they lacked through ignorance concerning perfection, what the Law had left unsaid. For the former people taught very many spiritual persons, already instructed through the inspiration of evangelical preaching, and possessing love even of enemies, not only by writings but especially by deeds.

Thus the Psalmist says: “If I repaid evil to those who repaid me,” etc. (Ps. 7:5). Again: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful” (Ps. 119:7). And though his enemy Saul had been delivered into his hands by the Lord, he not only did not kill him but deeply mourned him when he was slain, and immediately punished with death the man who declared himself Saul’s killer. Solomon also, commending kindness toward enemies, says: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him,” etc. (Prov. 25:21).

Yet the sayings of both the Law and the Prophets are far removed from evangelical perfection. Exhorting his disciples to that perfection, Truth said: “I give you a new commandment: love your enemies, as I have loved you” (John 13:34). This is the true and sincere love which the Apostle describes when he says: “It does not seek its own; it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. 13:5, 7), so that it is even ready to lay down its life for the brethren and to spend not merely its possessions upon them, but itself.

And if we carefully consider what Truth says, “as I have loved you,” and what the Apostle says, “Love does not seek its own,” we shall truly find the evangelical commandment concerning love of neighbour singular and new. For Christ’s love toward us was so sincere that he not only died for us, but also, in [Col. 0891B] all that he did for us, sought no advantage of his own, whether temporal or eternal, but ours. He acted not with any intention of his own reward, but entirely from the desire for our salvation.

This is indeed true and sincere love. Attending carefully to it, the Apostle commends it to us both by writing and by example, saying: “Thus I too please all persons in all things, seeking not what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:33). Yet one who acts thus ought to be certain of the fullest reward for so great a love; nevertheless, if he loves perfectly, he does not act with this intention. Otherwise he would seek his own interest and would be like a hireling, though in spiritual matters.

Nor can it now be called charity if we love him for ourselves—that is, for our own advantage and for the happiness of his kingdom which we hope to receive from him—rather than for his own sake, setting the end of our intention in ourselves rather than in Christ. Such people should surely be called friends of fortune rather than friends of persons, and subjects through avarice rather than through grace.

Blessed Augustine carefully observes this in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 35:

> “[Col. 0891D; *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 23.] To love is nothing other than to desire a thing for its own sake.”

Again, explaining the words written, “I will sacrifice willingly to you, and I will confess your name, because it is good” (Ps. 53:8), he says:

> “[Col. 0891D; Ibid., vol. XXXVI, col. 626.] What shall I offer except what he says: ‘The sacrifice of praise will glorify me’ (Ps. 49:23)? Why willingly? Because I love freely what I praise; what is loved and praised becomes gratuitous. What is gratuitous? It is himself for his own sake, not for something else. For if you praise God because he gives you something, you no longer love God freely. Be ashamed if your wife loved you for your wealth and, should poverty perhaps befall you, thought of adultery. Therefore, while you desire to be loved freely by your wife, will you love the Lord for something else? What reward, O greedy person, will you receive? He who made heaven and earth keeps for you not the earth, but himself. ‘I will sacrifice willingly to you.’ Do not act from necessity. For if you praise for some other reason, you praise from necessity. If that which you love were present to you, you would not praise. Again: despise all things; attend to him himself. And these things which he has given are good because of the giver.”

Again:

> “[Col. 0892D; *Patrologia*, vol. XXXVI, col. 627.] Love him freely, because you find nothing better for him to give than himself. Or, if you find something better, ask freely for that which is free. For ‘because it is good’ means nothing other than that which is good.”

From these words of blessed Augustine it is therefore plainly declared what true and sincere love for someone is: namely, that the person himself be loved for his own sake. Finally, if I love God because he loves me, rather than because, whatever he may do to me, he is such that he must be loved above all things, that saying of Truth is spoken of me: “If you love those who love you, what reward shall you have?” (Matt. 5:46). Certainly no reward of righteousness, because I attend not to the worthiness of the thing loved but to my own advantage. I would love another equally, or more, if that person benefited me equally or more; indeed, I would no longer love God if I did not hope for my own advantage in him.

Hence very many people, indeed almost all, have fallen into such a reprobate mind that they openly admit they would in no way honour or love God if they believed he would not benefit them. Yet he would deserve no less love if he punished them, since he could do so only justly and in accordance with merits that had gone before, or for some reasonable cause which, precisely because it was just, ought to please all.

Finally, who would judge anyone worthy of gratitude who was known to serve another not freely, but from desire for recompense? If gratitude must be returned to anything for such service, it should rather be returned to our possessions, on whose account services are rendered to us, than to those who perform the service. For example, when a hired labourer whom I have engaged serves me diligently and profitably for great wages, or when someone serves me from love of another and not of myself. Gratitude is to be returned to those for whose sake this is done, not to those who do it.

But perhaps you say that God is going to reward us with himself and with no other thing; that he will give us himself, than whom, as blessed Augustine also recalls, there is nothing greater. Therefore, when you serve him because of what you expect from him—that is, the eternal blessedness promised to you—you act purely and sincerely for his own sake, and for that reward which you ought to seek, as he himself advises when he calls blessed those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0892D] (Matt. 19:12). And the Psalmist says: “I inclined my heart to perform your statutes for the sake of recompense” (Ps. 118:112).

But then we would love God purely and sincerely for his own sake if we did this only for him and not for our own advantage; if we attended not to what kinds of gifts he gives us, but to what he himself is in himself. If we made him alone the cause of our love, then, whatever he did either to us or to others, we would love him equally, since he does nothing except what is best. For, as stated, we would always find in him the full cause of our love: he always remains wholly and in the same manner good in himself and worthy of love.

Such is the true affection of a father’s love for his son, or of a chaste wife for her husband, when they love them, though useless to themselves, more than they could love any others who might be more useful. Nor can love be diminished if they suffer disadvantages because of those they love, since the full cause of their love remains in those whom they love: they possess them not in the advantages which they obtain through them, but in themselves.

Pompey, defeated and in flight, aptly recalled this in his consolation of Cornelia, his wife: “What you weep for is what you loved.” Often persons of generous spirit follow honour more than advantage. If they happen to see persons like themselves, from whom they expect no gain, they embrace them with a greater affection of love than their own servants, from whom they receive daily benefits.

Would that we had so sincere an affection for the Lord that we loved him more according to the good that he is in himself than according to his usefulness to us, and rendered to him with entire righteousness that which is his own, so that, because he is supremely good, he might be supremely loved by all.

But when the faithful soul said above in the Psalm that it had inclined itself to good works for the sake of recompense, it showed the beginning, not the perfection, of good action. Every imperfect person is first drawn to good action—that is, to fulfilling God’s commandments—by hope of reward, and by fear rather than love, as it is written: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). Charity is its consummation or end, that is, its perfection, as it is said elsewhere: “I have seen an end of all perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96).

Thus he appropriately said, “I inclined”: that is, at the beginning of his action, he undertook it in hope and desire of recompense. But when Truth calls blessed those who made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven—that is, who lived continently for eternal blessedness—I think this should be understood to mean that they attained it through that continence. It is like saying that someone went out in order to die: he went out and consequently met death, but not with the intention that it should happen to him.

## “For we know”

He proves what he had said: namely, that the Law of Moses is good, though he received from it an occasion for sin, because it is a spiritual Law, not a secular one, as though written by God’s finger—that is, composed and given at the prompting of the Holy Spirit, not devised by human beings.

“But I am carnal,” that is, I pursue carnal wills and earthly desires. Indeed, I am so carnal that I am “sold under sin”: I willingly subject myself to sin and its servitude for the price of earthly goods, exercising every concupiscence in order to acquire and possess them. Or I was sold under sin in the first parents along with them, because of the love and taste of the fruit which Eve coveted. Behold how we became captives: we were able to sell ourselves; we cannot redeem ourselves. Innocent blood was given for us, and we cannot be freed from the dominion [Col. 0894A] of sin by our own strength, but only by the grace of the Redeemer.

## “For what I do”

He shows how carnal and infirm he has become, and how heavily he is oppressed by the yoke of evil habit, saying that he knowingly commits the very evil which he does not will, as if someone performed, at another’s compulsion, what he does not will. This is what “I do not understand what I do” means: I do not consider it something that should be done; indeed, I know without doubt that it is evil and therefore ought not to be done.

“For not what”—he proves that he acts badly against his own conscience, because he abandons even the good which he recognizes as good, and does what he does not doubt is evil. This is what he says: “If I do”—that is, do not do—“the good which I will,” that is, which I approve as needing to be done and to which I consent by reason.

“But the evil which I hate,” that is, which, as stated, I do not will, but reject and condemn by the judgment of reason. “But if”—he returns to praise of the Law in order to prove that it is good also by our own judgment, because it forbids precisely what we discover by reason to be evil, such as concupiscence, when it says: “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17).

This is what the phrase means: “If I do what I do not will,” that is, what I do not approve, “I consent to and agree with the Law that it is good,” because I see that it forbids what I myself judge to be evil, such as concupiscence, of which he spoke above, or anger, hatred, and envy. We have these even unwillingly, because certainly we would not wish to experience concupiscence, although we willingly pursue with love the things we covet.

[Col. 0894C] Therefore, when it is said, “Every sin is voluntary,” and, “No one sins unwillingly,” this must be understood of the act of sin, not of concupiscence. Every act of sin … is called voluntary rather than necessary because it proceeds in time from some preceding will, even if it takes place under compulsion.

For example, someone throws a stone carelessly and by chance, not knowingly, and kills a human being. This clearly proceeds from the will to throw the stone, not from the will to kill the person. Another person, compelled by an enemy rushing upon him, kills that enemy in order not to be killed by him; and he is said to sin unwillingly, because he does this also from the will to escape death rather than from a prior desire to kill a human being.

Every act of sinning, then, is called voluntary and not necessary in the sense that it proceeds from some will, as stated. Yet if someone calls that occasion of the person’s death through the throwing of a stone voluntary, I do not concede it, just as I call the throwing of the stone voluntary. For terms often vary in meaning through their adjuncts. Thus, although we grant every substance, we do not thereby grant every human being. So also, although we call every sin voluntary and every act of sin as proceeding from some will, as stated, we do not therefore concede that occasion to be voluntary—that is, committed from a will which someone had to kill that person.

In this way, when compelled, we commit sins and at once do what we will and what we do not will. In the example above, when compelled to kill a human being, we avoid death, which we will, and commit homicide, which we do not will. So in intercourse with another’s wife, the intercourse itself pleases us, not the offence or guilt of adultery which we incur. Therefore we delight only in intercourse, not adultery, because the guilt of adultery contributes nothing to pleasure but rather to the torment of conscience. And, insofar as we would not sin and would avoid adultery, we would wish the woman with whom we fornicate not to be married.

Therefore, when it is said, “Not what I do, but what I do not will,” there is no difficulty if we take “to will” and “not to will” in their proper and ordinary sense of “to please” and “to displease.” For, as stated, we often find in the same act both that which pleases and that which displeases, as in sexual intercourse the pleasure of the flesh and the guilt of adultery.

We may also, following the preceding explanation, understand willing and unwilling as approving and disapproving, when God too is said to will and not to will certain things. There can be no movement of mind in him, such as is called will or pleasure—that is, delight—in us; but when we say that he wills something, we signify either his approval or his disposition of it.

Otherwise, when Truth says, “How often I wished to gather your children together, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23:37), or the Apostle says, “He wills all to be saved and none to perish” (1 Tim. 2:4), and again the Psalmist, “Whatever he willed, he did” (Ps. 113:3), or the same Apostle, “For who resists his will?” (Rom. 9:19), we would encounter the greatest difficulty.

In the first two passages above, God’s willing means approving: that is, what he approves or counsels to be done, and what, if done, he rewards as pleasing to himself, is said to be willed by him. But in the latter two passages, his willing means disposing and establishing within himself what he will do. This will never lacks its effect, nor is it resisted by anyone.

## “But now”

Since I thus consent to the Law by reason, while disagreeing with myself through that same reason and through carnal concupiscence—since the spirit desires against the flesh and the flesh against the spirit (Gal. 5:17)—“it is no longer I who do that evil, but sin,” that is, evil concupiscence.

He does not say simply, “It is not I who do it,” but says, “Not I, but sin.” This means: I am drawn to it not by nature, but by a defect of nature now ruling over me. Indeed, by that nature through which I was created rational by God, I resist concupiscence and condemn it rather than consent to it.

When he says, “Sin dwells in me,” and not “sin is in me,” he presents it as a newcomer and resident, not a natural citizen; as something that has acquired a dwelling in him through long habit, not merely a passing presence.

“For I know.” In me, now made carnal as stated, sin dwells—that is, it remains continually, so that it has become for me almost a settled disposition. “The good,” that is, virtue, which is the best disposition of the mind, no longer remains in me now made carnal, [Col. 0896A] as he indicates when he says, “That is, in my flesh.”

“For to will.” He proves that he is deprived of virtue because he cannot, through the weakness of carnal concupiscence, fulfil the good which he wills—that is, which he approves by reason as needing to be done. To accomplish good is to join an act to good will; and this, he says, “I do not find in myself,” if I examine and investigate myself carefully.

Thus willing is naturally present to me, because from myself and my own creation I have reason, by which I approve that good ought to be done. But I do not have from myself the power to accomplish it, except through grace added to me. “For not what”—as though he said: I do not find that I accomplish the good which I will, because, contrariwise, I abandon it and do evil, just as he mentioned above. “But what I do not will, that I do.”

“It is not I who do it,” etc. “I find therefore.”

Since, as stated above, the Law brought me knowledge of sin, through which knowledge I will to do the good that it teaches and consent to it through reason, although sin received an occasion from it, I therefore find—that is, discover by my own judgment of reason—that the Law is good, useful to me, or a minister of great good. For by its teaching I have acquired discernment of good and evil: useful, I say, to me who will “to do it,” that is, to fulfil the good which it commands.

For in this very fact—that I will to do what it commands and desire it through reason—I truly recognize that it is good, namely in its commandments. Why he said “to one willing” rather than “to one doing,” he adds in saying: “Because evil lies close at hand to me,” that is, I am weighed down by the heavy yoke of habit, which impedes a good will.

For I delight in. Because he said that he wills to do the good which the law commands, and yet does not do it, he explains whence both things arise, saying that he delights in the law according to the inward man: that is, that what the law commands pleases him, and that he desires it by reason. This he here calls the inward man, that is, the spiritual and invisible image of God, in which man was made with respect to the soul, inasmuch as he was created rational and thereby set above the other creatures. And again, in saying that he sees another law in his members, etc., he means that he recognizes [Col. 0896D] the very tinder of sin in the flesh, or the impulses of concupiscence, to which, as to a law, he obeys through the weakness of the flesh; that these reign and hold dominion in the members of his body, as gluttony in the throat, lust in the sexual organs, and the other vices in the other bodily parts through which they are exercised. I call that law of concupiscence warring against, that is, contrary to, the natural law of my mind, that is, reason, which ought to govern me as a law. For by reason I seek good, but by concupiscence I seek evil. And making me captive: that is, drawing me, as it were, captive and unwilling, into the law, that is, into obedience to sin conceived in the mind, so that I may fulfill it in deed. This law, making me captive in this way and turning me away from God, my own Lord, is, as has already been said, in my members. Hence [Col. 0897A] it is also called the concupiscence of the eyes, through which we desire things seen; and similarly it can be called the concupiscence of the other members, according to their respective exercises in fleshly pleasures. That he repeats, “which is in my members,” serves to emphasize and impress still more deeply upon our memory our weakness: for, since we have almost as many enemies continually enduring in us as we have members, we bear them inseparably with us. Therefore, greatly terrified, he cries out in inquiry.

Wretched man that I am—understand, truly I am—who am now surrounded in my very body by so many enemies, by whom, as I said above, I have sold myself and been handed over as a captive; nor can I now free or redeem myself from this slavery. And since this is so, who will [Col. 0897B] deliver me—that is, who will be so powerful and so gracious toward me as to free me from this body of death, that is, one so prone and prepared to destroy the soul—lest fleshly suggestions prevail over me and the spirit yield to the flesh; that is, lest reason, overcome, succumb and consent to pleasure? The grace of God: that is, neither the law, nor one’s own powers, nor any merits whatever, but divine benefits freely bestowed upon us through Jesus, that is, the Savior of the world. When, however, he adds “Christ and our Lord,” he shows us the power and justice by which he is able to save us. For Christ, that is, “the Anointed One,” expresses the royal power which he possesses. But when he says “our Lord,” he shows the right which he has over us as his servants, so that he can justly [Col. 0897C] rescue us from the dominion of sin or the devil, and bring us back from the aforesaid captivity as his own. Therefore I. Since, as was said, by reason I will the good which the law commands, but through the sin dwelling in my flesh I work evil: therefore with my mind, that is, with reason, I serve the law of God . . . namely, the Lord, by obeying him through reason. But I myself with the flesh—that is, when fleshly desire for pleasure spurs me on—serve the law of sin; that is, I obey the wicked suggestions of concupiscence as though they were a law.

## Chapter VIII

Therefore there is no. Since, namely, as has been said, the grace of God through Christ frees his own, there is therefore no condemnation [Col. 0897D] for those who, etc.; that is, for those who have been built upon this foundation. He defines how we may recognize them: namely, those who do not walk according to the flesh. That is, if at some time they fall through weakness of the flesh, as Peter did when he feared bodily death, they do not persist in following their desires, proceeding from vice to vice. For he said that the grace of God would free a person through Christ, and he now explains how this happens: because the law of the Spirit of life—that is, the law of charity and divine love, rather than of fear, as the old law was—in Christ Jesus, that is, given and bestowed upon us through him, will free me from the law of sin and consequently of death; that is, from the commands or suggestions of fleshly concupiscence, so that I may not obey them by consenting to them. The Spirit of life is the Holy Spirit [Col. 0898A], who is the life of souls because he is love; therefore the law of this Spirit is called the law of love, begetting children rather than binding slaves—that is, the Gospel, which is wholly filled with charity. Hence it is also said to Christ, “Grace has been poured out upon your lips,” because all his preaching is full of charity. Thus too the Spirit, filling the apostles with knowledge, did as the Son had promised when he said, “He will teach you all things.” This doctrine too is signified when it is said, “There came suddenly a sound from heaven”: that is, through inspiration, a word of understanding arose for them in the mind. It was fittingly manifested in tongues of fire, since their tongues were to preach nothing but the fervor of charity.

For what. He explains how he has been freed in Christ [Col. 0898B] from the law of sin. For God the Father—that is, the majesty of divine power—sent his Son: that is, he caused Wisdom, coeternal with himself, to be humbled even to the assumption of a passible and mortal human being, in the likeness of sinful flesh. Thus, by the penalty of sin to which he was subject, he too seemed to possess sinful flesh, that is, flesh conceived in sin. And concerning sin—that is, concerning the penalty of sin which he endured for us in the flesh, that is, in the humanity assumed, not according to divinity—he condemned sin; that is, he removed from us the penalty of sin by which even the righteous had formerly been held, and opened heaven. That the righteousness of the law. He does not say “the works of the law,” which by no means justify, but what the law commands concerning those things that pertain to justification, without which we cannot be justified, [Col. 0898C] such as love of God and neighbor. The law renders this love imperfect, as we noted above, but through Christ it is perfected in us. This is what he says: that love of God and neighbor, which the law commands, might, when perfected in us, justify us. Indeed, the supreme benefit which Christ himself has shown us compels us truly to love Christ himself, as God and as our neighbor. This benefit is to condemn sin in us, that is, to destroy every liability and fault through the charity arising from this supreme benefit. “More truly,” he says, “the Greeks have: ‘For sin he condemned sin,’ he himself having been made a sacrifice for sin.” Through this sacrifice of flesh, which is called “for sin,” he condemned—that is, destroyed—sin, because he also accomplished for us remission [Col. 0898D] of sins in his blood and reconciliation. Or, concerning the sin committed against him by the devil or the Jews, he condemned sin in us, as has been said, making the best use even of those evils and turning them to good.

The two preceding statements must be referred and joined to the two following statements. To the words, “For sin he condemned sin,” is appended the statement that it was impossible for the law, namely, to condemn or remove sin. But to the words that follow, “that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled,” must be joined the statement in which the law itself is said to be weakened, namely, through the flesh. That is: the law was weak for attaining full and perfect justification because of the fleshly people to whom it was given, as we showed above when discussing the imperfection of its commandments [Col. 0899A]. Therefore it was impossible for the law, through obedience to itself, to remove sin, since it did not, as has been said, possess perfect commandments. It was especially weakened and hindered with regard to that perfection by the carnality of an unruly people.

For those who are according to. I say that it might be fulfilled in us through Christ, because by his teaching, example, and that supreme manifestation of charity, we who had been fleshly in desire have become spiritual. This is what it means: we do not walk according to the flesh; that is, we are no longer led by fleshly desires, but are governed by the grace of God, that is, by the Holy Spirit, and advance from virtue to virtue. For those who. I said that those who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit are justified. And rightly so, because those who are according to the flesh [Col. 0899B]—that is, entangled in fleshly desires—mind those things which are of the flesh: that is, they experience those things which belong to fleshly pleasures. But those who are according to the Spirit—that is, kindled by spiritual desires—experience the gifts of the Holy Spirit itself. For the wisdom. Truly those who are according to the flesh mind the things of the flesh, because through the experience of those fleshly desires which allure us we acquire death of the soul, that is, condemnation. Conversely, the wisdom of the Spirit—that is, experience of virtues and of God’s goods—becomes life and peace for us, that is, it grants a life quieted from every disturbance. Because the wisdom. The wisdom of the flesh acquires death because it is opposed to God and wholly displeasing to him. [Col. 0899C] He immediately adds why it displeases him: because it is not subject to the law of God, that is, it does not allow obedience to the divine commands. Nor indeed can it preserve obedience to God. But those who. He explains what he calls the wisdom of the flesh hostile to God: namely, to be in the flesh, that is, to delight in fleshly pleasures, and thereby to displease God. The connection is this: I said that the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, and not without cause, but because those who are in the flesh, etc. But you. Lest the Romans to whom he wrote should despair on hearing that those who are in the flesh cannot please God—as though this too had been said about themselves—he consoles them, saying: But you, by the grace of God, are now not in the flesh but in the Spirit; that is, not in fleshly but in spiritual desires. Yet lest, because he testifies to this as though he were too certain, they should again be excessively emboldened and incited to pride—those to whom he writes especially in order to check their self-exaltation—he indicates that he states this, as it were, doubtfully: “If indeed the Spirit,” that is, if you have the Spirit of God dwelling as an inhabitant rather than as a guest, remaining in you through his indwelling grace, not departing from you or merely passing through you [Col. 0899D]. He adds how great is the danger of lacking the Spirit of God: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his,” namely, a member of his body, because his Spirit is love itself and the bond by which his members adhere to this head. Of this Spirit it is specifically said, “God is charity” (1 John 4:8). But when he first said “the Spirit of God,” and then “of Christ,” he plainly shows that Christ himself is called the Spirit of God, and that the divine Spirit is also called Christ’s Spirit. But if—as though he said: Yet we have the Spirit of Christ, God—which is to say, if Christ is in us through his Spirit, that is, through the grace of his gifts, such as remission of sins and the bestowal of virtues: our body indeed is dead, that is, liable to bodily death, because of the sin [Col. 0900A] of the first parents, or the stain of fleshly concupiscence in which it was conceived. But our spirit lives because of justification: that is, through the virtues which justify it, it escapes the death of condemnation. As though he said plainly: Although in Christ we receive remission even of original fleshly sin, of which the death of the flesh is also the penalty of sin, nevertheless he who removed the cause did not remove this penalty.

Hence no small question is commonly raised: why is this penalty retained where the sin which causes it is forgiven, so that those who receive full remission of sins in baptism do not immediately recover at least that immortality which they possessed in Paradise before sin? Isidore, answering this question in *On the Highest Good*, book I, chapter 23, says:

> “If people were delivered from their present penalty through baptism, they would regard this as the value of baptism, rather than that eternal reward. Therefore, though the guilt of sin is removed, a certain temporal penalty nevertheless remains, so that the life which will be free from every penalty may be sought more ardently. For who does not know [Col. 0900C] that almost all people desire temporal life more than eternal life, since they labor far more for the life which they cannot retain than for eternal life; that they fear the death of the body more than that of the soul, and are more troubled by the miseries of the present life than by those to come? If, then, they thought that they could retain the happiness of this mortal life, they would prepare themselves for the sacraments of the Church more for its sake than for that of eternal life; and, satisfied with whatever relief it afforded, they would either wholly despise or less eagerly seek the advancement to that glory. In this they would be unjust, because they would set what is lower before the highest good.”

But if the Spirit. I said that our body is dead, that is, it remains subject to temporal death [Col. 0900D], even after the remission of all sins. Yet in the resurrection it too will be freed from this mortality, so that divine grace may glorify not only the soul but also the body. This is what he says: if his Spirit, that is, the Spirit of the Father—by whom divine power is especially designated—the Spirit, I say, of him who by his own power has already raised our head from the dead, namely Jesus, dwells in us as has been said, then he himself who raised Jesus, not from weakness but from death, etc. He repeats Christ’s resurrection in order that, being more often reminded of it, we may be made more secure. He will also give life to our mortal bodies, so that head and members may share the same glory of resurrection. He will give life not as he will to the bodies of the reprobate, which will be passible and fitted for torment, but because of the indwelling Spirit: that is, in accordance with the reverence due to the Spirit of Christ, who now dwells and rests in those bodies as in a temple, their fleshly deaths having already been repressed through his grace [Col. 0901A].

It is no small question: since the divine substance has united human nature to itself in the one person of Christ, and since the substance of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is wholly one and indivisible, why is the Son rather than the Father or the Holy Spirit said to have been incarnate? Or, since the works of the Trinity are undivided—so that whatever one of the persons does, the others also do—how is the Son said to have assumed flesh, and not the Father or the Spirit? But let this be sought from our *Anthropology* [printed: *Atropologia*].

Therefore, brethren. Since those who are in [Col. 0901B] the flesh cannot please God, we are therefore not debtors to the flesh; that is, we ought not to obey fleshly desires, because we owe nothing to anyone against God, for whose sake we are also rightly commanded to lay down our soul. Let secular powers take note of this: that no obedience is owed to them by their subjects when they command anything forbidden by God, even if they have bound their subjects to themselves in this respect by faith or oath. That you may live according to the flesh. He explains what he promised, namely how we are to understand that we are not debtors to the flesh, lest anyone perhaps take this as said of the substance of the flesh. We are indeed debtors to it insofar as its necessary care is concerned, namely, that we supply it with food and clothing. Therefore it is as though he said: We are not, I say [Col. 0901C], debtors to the flesh so as to live according to the flesh, although we are in the flesh—that is, so as to pursue fleshly desires. For if: that is, you are not subject to the flesh, because obedience to it would condemn you. This is what “you shall die” means: by consenting to it, you will incur the death of the soul, which is sin, if, when it spurs you on, you do not resist as far as you can. But if by the Spirit—that is, by some gift of divine grace rather than by your own strength—you mortify the deeds of the flesh, if you cannot yet entirely uproot its suggestions, you shall live. Conversely, the true life of the soul—whether here in virtues or in eternal blessedness—comes through mortifying deeds, as though a little child conceived in the womb were extinguished before birth: when we prevent the evils that we conceive in the mind from proceeding to deeds [Col. 0901D], removing from them, as far as we can, every occasion. As it is written: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Ps. 136:9); that is, he will mortify and kill sins conceived in the mind through some suggestion while they are still, as it were, little ones, dashing them against the rock—that is, breaking and scattering them against that stable foundation of all good things, which is Christ—while reason, strengthened by love of Christ, strives to prevent the accomplishment of that which the human mind desires through the weakness of the flesh. As the same Apostle says elsewhere: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17); that is, reason represses the suggestions of the flesh, lest they proceed to deeds [Col. 0902A]. And Solomon says: “The patient man is better than a strong man, and he who rules his own soul than a conqueror of cities” (Ps. 16:32).

For whoever. You will rightly, I say, live if you mortify the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, because all who are led rather than compelled—that is, drawn by love rather than forced by fear—by the Spirit of God are sons of God rather than servants; that is, they are subject to him more through love than through fear. For not. As though someone should ask: Does God have many sons, when Christ is called his Only-begotten? He answers: he indeed has many, but by adoption, not by nature. For you yourselves have received the Spirit of adoption [Col. 0902B], by whom they are made sons of God. Hence he himself says elsewhere: “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Therefore the Spirit of adoption is called the gift of charity, through which we are adopted by God as sons. In this Spirit—that is, in professing and recognizing this gift—we cry earnestly to the Lord and exultantly say, “Abba, Father”; that is, we profess him to be Father rather than Lord, and thereby recognize ourselves as sons rather than servants. Thus the Truth himself frequently taught us in the Gospel to call God Father rather than Lord, that he might thereby exhort us also to filial submission. Therefore, when he gave the disciples that spiritual prayer, he said: “When praying, say, Our Father, who art in heaven,” etc. (Matt. 6:9). Thus we rightly call abbots of monasteries Fathers, so that the name itself may plainly remind them that they ought to be loved as fathers rather than feared as masters.

“We Hebrews cry ‘Abba’; we from the Gentiles, ‘Father,’ since the former name is Hebrew or Syriac, while the latter is Greek or Latin.” Augustine, in his *Epistle to the Galatians* [Note: [Col. 0901D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, col. 2127]:

> “‘Abba, Father’ are two words which he used, so that the latter might explain the former. For *Abba* means ‘father,’ on account of the whole people called from Jews and Gentiles: the Hebrew word belongs to the Jews and the Greek word to the Gentiles.”

The same, book III of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* [Note: [Col. 0901D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV, col. 1166]:

> “*Abba* in Hebrew is what *Pater* is in Latin.”

Haymo, on this passage [Col. 0902D] [Note: [Col. 0902D] *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, col. 430]:

> “*Abba* is Hebrew and Syriac; *Pater* is Greek and Latin. Therefore, foreseeing that both peoples would be gathered to the faith, the Apostle placed two names under one meaning, so that those who believe from among Hebrews and Syrians may say, ‘Abba, have mercy,’ while those from among Greeks and others may say, ‘Father.’ Something of this kind occurs in the Gospel of Mark, when the Lord says: ‘Abba, Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me’ (Mark 14:36).”

The spirit of slavery in fear. He means that gift of servile fear by which we are restrained not from an evil will but from evil action, through fear of punishment; as formerly the Jews were restrained through the bodily penalties of the law. You have not received [Col. 0903A] the spirit. Through the Gospel, as the Jews formerly did through the law. For the Spirit himself. The Spirit of adoption, of which we have spoken and which we have, makes our spirit—that is, our reason—recognize that we are sons of God; that is, subject to him through love. For no one recognizes anything better than his own conscience, and whether he ought rather to be called servant or son. It should be noted, however, that in addressing the Romans, some of whom deserved severe rebuke, the Apostle here presents himself as the universal father of the faithful, and explains not so much what they were as what they ought to be. But if sons, namely sons by adoption, then also heirs, because they are adopted—that is, freely chosen—in order that they may obtain an inheritance: heirs indeed of God, that is, of the Father, and co-heirs [Col. 0903B] with Christ, that is, his natural Son, in that eternal possession of blessedness. He shows how great it is to attain that inheritance of God, by which we are made like his Son Christ: “If indeed.” I said that we are heirs, but with this proviso: if we suffer with Christ himself; for no one will be crowned unless he has competed lawfully (2 Tim. 2:5), namely against the assault of enemies or vices. And because, as Cyprian says [Note: [Col. 0903D] *Patrologia*, vol. IV, col. 311], punishment does not make a martyr, but the cause does, he adds “that we may be glorified together”; that is, if we suffer in such a way as to be worthy of being glorified with Christ. This occurs when charity prepares one to suffer, rather than necessity dragging one along, and when one suffers for Christ as he suffered for us, so that we may render him a reciprocal return.

[Col. 0903C] Therefore all, insofar as lies within them, suffer with him, whoever, as we have said, are ready to suffer for him, if they themselves do not fail the persecutor, even though a persecutor fails them. For I reckon. As though someone asked: Is that inheritance so great that, in order to merit it, one must suffer even unto death, as Christ suffered? He answers: Indeed, I judge it so great that it far exceeds all human merits, however much people may merit through suffering. This is what he says: “The sufferings of this time”—that is, those temporal and passing tribulations, however great they may be—are not of such merit that that ineffable and eternal glory of the future life, which shall be revealed in us, is owed to them. For we are already sons of God, as it is written, but it does not yet appear what we shall be (1 John 3:2) [Col. 0903D]. No perpetual good is rendered as a due reward for anything transitory, however good; rather, through the grace of God added to our merits, we obtain that for which our merits alone were wholly insufficient. And, if we attend carefully, nothing transitory is worthy even of a good reward. Charity alone, which never fails, merits eternal life; and all who are equal in charity have equal rewards before God, even if one is deprived of some effect of charity through an intervening circumstance. Hence blessed Augustine rightly maintains that John, who did not suffer martyrdom, has a crown equal to that of Peter, who did suffer, so that God regards not so much the effect of suffering as the disposition.

[Col. 0904A] For the expectation. I rightly spoke of the future glory which will be revealed in us, namely the sons of God, because the expectation of all the faithful awaits this revelation of the glory owed to the sons of God. As though he said: Each person waiting waits, just as one says, “Going, they went”; that is, they hope perseveringly and confidently, meriting it by good works. The revelation of the sons of God means that recompense in which it will be revealed who are sons of God and predestined to life, something still hidden. He calls them “creation” because they strive to preserve uncorrupted in themselves God’s creation and to reform it [Col. 0904B] according to the image of God in which they were created, resisting as far as they can the sins which erase or stain it. And the faithful truly await this revelation, because for its sake they despise the vanity of the present life and unwillingly endure it, already desiring rather to be dissolved and to be with Christ. This is what he says: “The creation itself was subjected unwillingly”; that is, insofar as it lies within it, it unwillingly bears this vain life, both transitory and full of miseries. But it bears it for the sake of him who subjected it in hope of that future revelation: that is, he humbles it by afflicting it here, so that he may exalt it in the revelation hoped for. He adds what that hope of creation is—that is, what the afflicted faithful hope here—when he says: “Because it also,” etc.; that is, those here hope that there they will be freed [Col. 0904C] from the yoke of passible and corruptible flesh, under which they are unwillingly oppressed. He calls freedom the glory of that life in which there will be no oppression, since no one will undergo anything contrary to his will.

For we know. He shows in parts that creation, afflicted here, yearns with all desire for that freedom of glory which it hopes for there: namely, both those who are lesser among the faithful and those who are greater. He distinguishes the lesser by saying “all creation.” He distinguishes the greater by adding “having the firstfruits of the Spirit.” Thus, when he says “all creation,” it is as though he said: those who are entirely creation, or wholly creatures, not creators; namely, those not seeking through preaching to create or beget anyone for God. But the apostles and their vicars are in some manner creators of others, as we said, according to the Apostle’s words elsewhere: “For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15); and again: “My little children, whom I am again in labor to bring forth, until . . . is formed” (Gal. 4:19). It groans and labors in childbirth: that is, it labors in childbirth through groaning. The groans of the faithful arise either from earthly affliction, according to the words, “Going, they went and wept, casting their seeds” (Ps. 125:6), or from longing for the heavenly homeland, as in: “Alas for me, because my sojourning has been prolonged” (Ps. [Col. 0905A] 119:5); and again: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, until we remembered you, Zion” (Ps. 136:1). They labor in childbirth, that is, they strive through the greatest toil to produce the fruit of good works. And they strive “until now,” that is, not merely for an hour, but as long as one lives. For *parturio*, “I am in labor,” is a verb of an ongoing, not completed, form; and it is therefore aptly applied to the lesser and imperfect, who are, as it were, at the beginning of thought, not at the perfection of action. These words of the Apostle, “it groans and labors in childbirth,” agree with those words of the Lord: “A woman, when she is in labor, has sorrow,” etc. (John 16:21). “Having the firstfruits of the Spirit” means possessing the greater gifts of the Holy Spirit, as do holy preachers, who acquire for God both themselves and others. To this office [Col. 0905B] of preaching, as to the greatest gift of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle himself exhorts us in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, saying: “For be zealous for the better gifts, and I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31). And shortly afterward: “Pursue charity; be zealous for spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy” (1 Cor. 14:1), that is, that you may undertake the office of prophets by preaching.

“And we ourselves groan”: we groan, namely, burdened by the passibility and corruption of the flesh, while, like the others, possessing consolation from hope. This hope is as an anchor for our ship amid the waves of this world, because he immediately added this consolation, saying: “Awaiting”—that is, hoping confidently—the adoption [Col. 0905C] of the sons of God from among the Gentiles; that is, that they themselves may be adopted by God and established as heirs in the heavenly kingdom. I call this adoption “the redemption of our flesh,” that is, of the Church, whose members we are. For there is nothing else in our being thus adopted by God than our being redeemed through his Only-begotten Son from the devil’s power or from the yoke of sin, so that this whole adoption may be ascribed to divine grace, not to our merits. For by hope. Above he said that we await, in hope, the revelation of the sons of God, and that in this hope we are subjected to the vanity of the present life, lest we lose courage because of our labors. Lest anyone object that this hope is not certainty and therefore ought not to be trusted, he says that all of us who are saved are saved [Col. 0905D] through hope. He immediately adds that hope is spoken only of things not seen: “But hope,” that is, knowledge of things seen, cannot in any way be called hope. “For what a man sees,” that is, why does he hope for something which he sees? As though he said: There is nothing that one hopes for by seeing it; for example, if someone sees that he has become rich, though he may formerly have hoped for it, he now has not hope or estimation concerning it, but certainty. But if what. He shows how we are made saved through hope: namely, because the hope described, that of the future life, makes us patient, lest we fail amid the tribulation of the present life. This is what he says: “For if”—because, namely, we hope for what we do not see—“we await it patiently,” not failing in the contest of the present struggle. Likewise [Col. 0906A], as hope helps us by giving patience, so too the Holy Spirit helps our weakness in this contest by suggesting the prayers necessary for us. This is what he says: for we often do not know what, precisely as we ought and as is necessary for us, we should pray for, especially when we are placed amid tribulations, doubting in many matters which may be useful to us. So too the Apostle himself, when three times he asked the Lord that Satan’s thorn be removed from him. But the Spirit himself intercedes for us: that is, he makes us pray for what we did not know, by teaching us and inspiring the greatest desire. But he who. I said that he makes us pray with inexpressible groanings, that is, with desires so great that they can be felt rather than explained. But [Col. 0906B], although they are inexpressible, they are known to him who searches hearts and is the inspector of the heart, attending rather to what takes place in the heart than to what is uttered by the mouth. He knows what the Spirit desires—that is, what he makes us desire—because he intercedes for the saints, that is, makes the saints intercede, according to God: that is, according to what this Spirit of God has received from God, from whom he has his being by proceeding from him, and according to what he knows to be ordained in God’s own disposition. Hence it is certain that God cannot be unaware of what the Spirit does while he himself orders it.

For we know. As though someone objected, “How does the Spirit help those whom we see suffering under so many afflictions?” he says that he turns even afflictions [Col. 0906C], and whatever happens to the saints, both prosperity and adversity, to their good and brings them to their advantage. He adds who are those who love God: “those who are called saints,” that is, sanctified through the inspiration of an inward calling, according to God’s purpose rather than according to their preceding merits; that is, according rather to what pleased divine grace than to what they themselves deserved. For those whom he foreknew. He carefully explains how they are sanctified according to God’s purpose, that is, according to the good pleasure of divine grace, saying that he afterwards made those whom he foreknew conformable to Christ by predestining them. God is said to know those things which he approves and which are worthy of his knowledge, according to the words: “The Lord knows the way of the righteous”; conversely, he is said to ignore or not know evils. Thus the Son himself says to the reprobate: “I do not know you.” Therefore he is said to have foreknown those whose future election he approved before they existed. Whomever he thus foreknew, he afterward predestined [Col. 0906D]; that is, he prepared them by the gifts of his grace. Divine predestination is called the preparation of grace, and it exists only in the elect. He predestined them, I say, to become conformed—that is, to become like the image of his Son, namely Christ, who is the image of God, that is, the express likeness of the Father, equal to him in every good thing according to divinity. This accords with his words: “Philip, he who sees me sees the Father” (John 14:9), as though he said: “Because from me it can be fully known what the Father is like, or how good he is.” We are conformed to Christ when, putting off the old man with his deeds, we put on Christ himself, as it is written: “He who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). Thus, I say, they are made conformable, so that he himself, namely Christ, may be firstborn among many brethren [Col. 0907A]: that is, among many who are sons of the same Father through adoption. He who is Son by nature excels, in the manner of firstborn sons, in dignity, and is not made equal to them by likeness, just as he is equal to the Father, whose image he is. But those elect who are predestined—that is, prepared for eternal life—are first enlightened through faith, which they receive as the foundation of all good things; [Col. 0907B] afterward they are called, drawn by hope, when, having recognized God’s mercy and the power of the sacraments, they are enticed to work well for the sake of eternal recompense; then they are justified by the disposition of sincere charity, no longer adhering to God so much for his gifts as for his own sake; and finally they are glorified, exalted in the heavenly homeland.

A question arises here concerning divine providence, or predestination, which seems to take free choice away from us: for since everything is foreseen by God as it is, it must necessarily come to pass, and no one who has been predestined can possibly perish. For it is certain that, before they occur, all things are foreseen by God in the manner in which they will occur, whether good or evil; nor can his providence fail in any respect. [Col. 0907C] Therefore, when he has foreseen that this man, who perhaps is going to commit adultery, will commit adultery, it is necessary that he will commit adultery. But if he must commit adultery, this is unavoidable; it is no longer within his free choice or power to avoid this sin. Therefore he ought not to be held guilty on account of this sin, which he could in no way avoid. And thus all evils seem to be referred back to God’s providence as their necessary cause, and so everything seems to occur necessarily in the way it occurs, since it was thus foreseen by God and could in no way happen otherwise.

We, however, grant that one who is going to commit adultery will necessarily commit adultery, since God foresaw it; but it is not therefore proper simply to say that he is necessarily going to commit adultery. For this modal proposition with its qualification does not entail the unqualified proposition. We reserve a more careful discussion of this point for our *Theology*, together with the question of what difference there is between providence and predestination, or fate.

What then? Since God is so concerned for our salvation that he foreknew, predestined, calls those predestined, justifies those called, and glorifies those justified—what shall we say to these things, that is, what obstacle can we find against them? Certainly none. For although we are weak in ourselves, who can prevail against us if God is for us—that is, if we have God as our protector? To assure us that we may be secure concerning this protection or defense, [Col. 0908A] he adds a reminder of the singular love which he showed us, saying: “He who did not spare even his own Son,” consubstantial, not adopted, “but delivered him up,” namely, to death, “for us all”—that is, for those whom he foreknew or, as has been said, predestined—so that in his blood he might wash away the stains of our sins.

But when he says, “even his own Son,” he indicates that God had not previously spared, for our sake, other adopted sons as well—such as Isaiah, Jeremiah, or certain other prophets—who, sent to God’s people, were killed as martyrs for human salvation. For how, that is, on what ground, can it be said that in so great a gift—the handing over of his Son—he did not give us all things necessary for our salvation? Who shall accuse? [Col. 0908B] Since God is so concerned, as has been said, for our salvation, whose accusation can prevail in anything against us? Could it be the accusation of God himself, who not only does not accuse, but even, as has been said, justifies? As though he said: No. Or if there were any accuser, could he persist in our condemnation? Could it be Christ himself, who showed us so great a love, as he himself said, “Greater love than this,” etc., so that he might die for our salvation? As though he said: No. Indeed, he who—

As though correcting what he had said, “who died,” which pertains to weakness, he adds the glory of the resurrection displayed and promised to us in him, which most especially consoles us in every tribulation. And because some have returned from death only to die again, as Lazarus did, and the reprobate too will rise in order to be placed at the left, he adds: “Who is at the right hand of God”—that is, according to the very humanity which was raised, he remains in eternal blessedness. There also he is not forgetful of our salvation, where, as advocate, he intercedes with the Father for us, always presenting to the Father’s eyes that humanity in which he suffered so greatly for us, and thus reconciling us to him as mediator. [Col. 0908C] He intercedes, therefore, as has been said, in order to mediate between us and God through the substance of our nature itself.

We say also that the saints themselves intercede and pray for us more by the disposition of charity, or by the assistance of their merits, than by utterance of voice. Hence when we say, “Saint Peter, pray for us,” it is as though we said, “God, have mercy on us because of the merits of blessed Peter.” [Col. 0908D]

Who, then, shall separate us? Since God has shown us such grace by such great benefits, and has confirmed it in himself, what thing can henceforth tear us away from his love? As though he said: Nothing. And he immediately proves this by those things which seem most able to turn people away from God. First, concerning adversities, he says: “Tribulation”—as though to say: No. Tribulation means any bodily affliction or beating; distress, anxiety of mind, such as fear; persecution, being driven from place to place; danger, preparation for death; the sword, death itself. As it is written in Psalm 43, as though he said: Certainly it is true that none of these can separate us, because, as the prophet says, “for your sake”—that is, because we cling to you inseparably—we are subjected to life-threatening dangers. “All day long,” that is, throughout the whole time of our life, which in comparison with the life of unbelievers who walk in darkness ought to be called day, namely because it is illuminated by faith. [Col. 0909A] “We were accounted,” as it is written concerning the ungodly speaking of the righteous: “We considered their life madness,” etc. (Wisdom 5:4). “Sheep for slaughter,” that is, sheep worthy of slaughter and possessing no other usefulness, yielding no profit even from their death for food, and in no way resisting their killers, both because of the weakness of their nature and because of their gentleness.

“But in these things.” I said that all these oppressions cannot overcome our constancy so as to separate us from God; rather, on the contrary, by persevering we conquer all these things through God’s grace rather than through our own strength. This is what he says: “through him who was given to us,” that is, through his assisting grace. “I am certain.” I speak so confidently concerning divine grace assisting the faithful, so that they cannot be separated from God by any causes whatever, because through experience I have now attained concerning these matters not merely faith but also the certainty of an image: namely, that neither death threatened nor life promised in this world, nor angels—that is, angelic dignity promised to us by anyone tempting us, just as the devil promised Eve that they would be like gods—nor principalities nor powers, [Col. 0909B] that is, the excellence of these orders, which is greater in dignity than the angelic order. Blessed Gregory, carefully distinguishing these orders, says:

> “In the Greek language, *angels* are called messengers, and *archangels*, supreme messengers. Those who announce lesser matters are called angels; those who announce the greatest matters, archangels. Hence it is not just any angel but the archangel Gabriel who is sent to Mary.”

[Note: [Col. 0909D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, cols. 1250–1251.]

Likewise:

> “Powers (*virtutes*) are those through whom signs and miracles are more frequently performed. Authorities (*potestates*) are those who have received this more powerfully than others in their order, so that adverse powers are subject to their dominion; by their power these are restrained, lest they prevail to tempt human hearts as much as they wish. Principalities (*principatus*) are those who preside even over the good spirits of angels; while they arrange what is to be done for those subject to them, they rule them in carrying out the mysteries.”

[Note: [Col. 0910D] *Ibid.*]

Nor “things present,” that is, present goods or evils; nor “strength,” that is, the violence of any power; nor “height” nor “depth,” that is, the exaltation of some human glory or a casting down and humiliation toward any advantage. As though he said: neither any human prosperity nor adversity, nor any creature whatever, such as the foregoing—angels, authorities, and so on—can separate us from the charity of God, because we sincerely love him for his own sake. This charity “is in Christ Jesus,” that is, inspired in us through Christ our Savior, [Col. 0910A] or built, rooted, and founded in him.

## Chapter IX

“I speak the truth.” What he said—that he and faithful people like him cannot be torn away from the charity of God—he wishes to prove by his own experience. For he says that, while he was the Church’s greatest persecutor, he labored to turn away from the faith of Christ servants who had been converted to it. This is what “in Christ Jesus” means: “I swear through Christ Jesus that I speak truthfully,” with respect to the event itself; and it is as I say. “And I do not lie,” my conscience bearing testimony to me; that is, I am not guilty of lying, since I believe as I speak. For someone may, through ignorance, have truth in his words with respect to the event of the matter, [Col. 0910B] and yet speak against his conscience and thereby incur the guilt of lying. For no one lies before God—that is, is not regarded by God as guilty of lying—unless he speaks with duplicity. One’s conscience bears testimony to one speaking when the mind does not dissent from the words—that is, when the speaker believes what he says.

“To me,” he says, “who know it, though not to you, I say: my conscience exists in the Holy Spirit,” that is, it is founded and rooted in the charity of God, from which a lie cannot spring. Hence the Holy Spirit is rightly called the Spirit of truth. “I speak this truth: that I have great sorrow,” great in amount, “and continual” in duration, “in my heart,” that is, not feigned in outward bearing but genuine in the very disposition of my mind. He adds the reason for his sorrow: namely, because formerly—not now—“I myself,” who now seem to be of some importance and more hostile than others to Judaism, and contrary to my former life, “wished,” he says, “to be anathema from Christ for my brothers”: that is, I strove in every way to bring about the separation of my own people—the Jews—from Christ, so that not only might I myself be separated from Christ, but might be the cause of others’ separation, and might turn away from him in both word and deed those also who already clung to him through faith, as it is written: “Saul, still breathing threats,” etc. (Acts 9:1). Or thus: in wishing to turn my brothers away from Christ, I wished to turn all people away generally, as it is written, [Col. 0910C] “if he found any men of this Way,” not Jews only, etc.

That by “brothers” he means generally all who were of his race, that is, whatever Jews, he makes clear by adding:

“Who are my kinsmen according to the flesh,” that is, of my fleshly kinship, and therefore at that time more closely bound to my heart, so that I acted greatly on their behalf. And lest we understand only those who belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, from which the Apostle came, he adds, “who are Israelites,” that is, of the race of the patriarch Jacob, who was first called Jacob by his parents and afterward Israel by the Lord—that is, “a man seeing God.” Hence the whole posterity especially gloried in being distinguished by his name, as though it had been granted to them alone to see—that is, to know—God; as though they now had no further need of Christ’s teaching or anyone else’s.
