Thus Paul also suggests for some reason that he had preferred Christ’s teaching; and likewise from what follows, concerning the condemnation of that people once peculiarly God’s own, when he says: “Whose is the adoption as sons,” that is, they were first adopted by grace as sons of God, and are shown to have been specially loved by him through the bestowal of innumerable benefits. [Col. 0911A] “And the glory,” that is, the glorification in the present arising from this adoption, by which they wished even now to set themselves above the Gentiles converted in the Church.

He carefully sets forth the chief sources from which their adoption or glorification proceeded, saying that “the testament” was theirs and was first brought to them, not to the Gentiles, as it is written: “He has not dealt thus with every nation, and he has not made his judgments known to them” (Psalm 147:20). This relates to what he had said above: “What advantage then has the Jew?” etc.—“Much in every way” (Romans 3:1). “First indeed, because the oracles of God were entrusted to them” (*ibid.*, 3:2). [Col. 0911B]

“And the service,” that is, the public office of divine worship in the tabernacle or the temple; and the promises already made, both concerning possession of the land of Canaan and earthly benefits, and concerning spiritual goods through Christ, who was to be born from them, as he immediately adds, saying: “Whose are the fathers,” according to the flesh rather than through imitation of faith—those, namely, from whom Christ himself is according to the flesh: namely, the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whom promises about Christ were made, that in their seed all nations would be blessed. But lest, by saying “Christ’s fathers,” Christ might seem to have begun from those fathers, he adds: “Who is over all, blessed”—that is, to be praised [Col. 0912A] and glorified “for ever,” through all successions of times, most excellently ordered by him as divine wisdom. “Amen,” that is, it is true. The doubling of an affirmation signifies a profession both of mouth and heart, as also in “Amen, amen, I say to you” (Matthew 6:2), and “Let your speech be, Yes, yes; no, no” (Matthew 5:37).

## Book Four

[Col. 0911]

[Col. 0911C] “But it is not as though the word had failed.” Someone might perhaps say: How then have the divine promises been made to the Israelites, which that people, always rebellious against God, cannot obtain because of its wickedness and has now been wholly rejected by him? To this the Apostle replies: No, he says, the promises made to them are not such that the very word of promise has failed—that is, the promise is not void and wholly unfulfilled. For a promise which is fulfilled is said to stand or remain; conversely, it is said to fail.

Observe the same thing above. For when the question had been asked what advantage circumcision had, and the answer given, “Much in every way; first indeed,” etc., it was added: “For what if some of them did not believe? Shall their unbelief make void the faithfulness of God?” [Col. 0911D] Thus here too it is said that the promise made, as has been said, to the Israelites has not been rendered void if it has not been fulfilled in certain persons who are of Israel’s race according to the flesh. For not all are Israelites. Only those among the children of Israel are to be counted who, remaining in the worship of the one God, imitate the faith of their father Israel—that is, Jacob. He immediately demonstrates this by the analogous case of Abraham, saying: “Nor are all who are Abraham’s seed,” namely according to the flesh, counted among Abraham’s children. This he at once confirms by the very testimony taken from Genesis, where the Lord said to Abraham, after Sarah had ordered the slave-girl Hagar to be expelled with her son: “All that Sarah says to you, listen to her voice; because in Isaac shall your seed be called” (Genesis 21:12).

[Col. 0912C] The Apostle explains what was said above: “In Isaac shall your seed be called.” He calls “children of the flesh” those who derive from father Abraham only an origin of flesh and do not take the example of faith. Yet where one might expect him to say, “These are the children of Abraham,” the Apostle instead says, “These are the children of God,” showing that no others ought to be called Abraham’s children than those who are children of God—that is, believers. Abraham indeed signifies faith. Therefore only those are rightly called Abraham’s children whom the Lord adopts to himself through faith, both from Jews and from Gentiles, as the Apostle himself has mentioned above when speaking of Abraham: “That he might be the father of all believers, not only those who are of the circumcision, but also those who follow the footsteps of the faith which is in uncircumcision.”

“But the children of promise”: he calls children of promise those who belong to faithful Isaac, namely by imitating him in faith, because Abraham begot him from an aged and barren mother through God’s promise alone, not through the nature of flesh. “They are counted as seed,” namely Abraham’s—that is, they are to be reckoned among Abraham’s children. By what words the promise concerning the future son Isaac was made to Abraham, he adds, saying:

“For this is the word of promise,” etc. These are the words of the angel speaking to Abraham: “At this time,” that is, at such a time as the present season next year, when the year has turned, “I shall come, and Sarah shall have”—that is, through my coming and operation rather than through nature, Sarah will then conceive. This statement is expressed in Genesis in these words: “Returning, I will come to you at this time, life accompanying, [Col. 0913A] and Sarah your wife shall have a son” (Genesis 18:10). Again below: “The Lord visited Sarah as he had promised and fulfilled what he had spoken; and she conceived and bore a son in her old age, at the time which the Lord had foretold to them” (Genesis 21:1).

From these words it is not sufficiently clear, when it is said, “Sarah shall have a son,” whether this should be understood of her conception or of her giving birth. But when it says, “in her old age,” it clearly indicates that this son was not so much of flesh as of promise—that is, not of nature but of grace. And although it was said, “In Isaac shall your seed be called,” this was nevertheless not true of all who would be born from Isaac according to the flesh, since Esau himself was immediately rejected and Jacob alone chosen by God. This he now pursues, saying: “And not only she,” that is, Sarah, understood, “had the promise concerning offspring from God; but Rebekah also,” already having in her womb, before she had that promise—having, I say, in her womb from one intercourse, Isaac our father, not so much according to the flesh as according to faith.

And truly, how did she have this promise? Because she had that promise concerning the election of the younger son, namely that the elder should serve the younger. This is what follows: “For when they were not yet born,” namely those whom she had by Isaac, “nor had done anything,” that is, had no merit yet from good or evil work. For it could happen that, after the manner of Jeremiah or John the Baptist, they might be enlightened in the womb and know God, and by loving or not loving him might already merit something, [Col. 0913B] so that . . . [lacuna] namely, those who had not yet merited anything—“the purpose of God according to election might remain,” his purpose in one of them, that is, in Jacob and not Esau: according to what God had proposed with himself and had from eternity disposed in one of them by his providence, Jacob’s election would remain—that is, his predestination would endure immovably. “Not from works,” that is, not because of any merit of works in the one who was chosen, but solely from God who called him—that is, solely from his grace, by which he afterward drew him to himself through inward inspiration.

“It was said to her,” that is, to Rebekah, that “the elder”—that is, Esau, who was to be firstborn—“shall serve the younger brother,” that is, Jacob. This servitude is to be understood not so much in the persons of the two brothers as in their posterities—that is, in the peoples who were promised to be born from them. The Lord said to Rebekah: “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; one people shall overcome the other, and the elder shall serve the younger” (Genesis 25:23). [Col. 0913C] For if you look to the persons of the brothers, you will never find Esau to have served Jacob or been subject to him in anything; indeed, Jacob always greatly feared Esau and humbled himself very much before him. But it is clear that this is to be understood of the peoples, since even by the command of the Law the Israelites were forbidden to have slaves from their own people, but only from the nations. Hence it is written in Leviticus:

> “If your brother, compelled by poverty, sells himself to you, you shall not oppress him with the service of slaves; but he shall work with you as a hired laborer and resident alien until the year of jubilee. Afterwards he shall go out with his children and return to his kinship and to the possession of his fathers. For they are my servants. He shall not come under the condition of slaves; you shall not afflict him by force. Your slave and maidservant shall be from the nations; these you shall have as servants, and shall transmit them by hereditary right to your descendants, and possess them forever” (Leviticus 25:39–46).

“I say, from God who calls,” as it is written in the prophet Malachi in these words: “Was not Esau Jacob’s brother? says the Lord. Yet I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated” (Malachi 1:2)—that is, I called the one by choosing him, but rejected the other. Concerning this sort of election the same Apostle says above: “Those whom he called, them he also justified” (Romans 8:30). [Col. 0913D]

[Col. 0914B] “What then?” The Apostle draws from the immediately preceding words a suitable objection, as though to accuse and charge God with injustice: before Esau could merit anything, God judged him worthy of his hatred by not predestining him. And because he gave grace to the other brother, who had likewise previously merited nothing, he withheld it from Esau; and once it was withheld, Esau plainly could not act well. Thus it seems to be due not so much to Esau’s fault that he was unrighteous as to God’s, who did not wish to give him the grace by which he could act well.

The Apostle himself later provides the solution to this objection where he says, “O man, who are you?” But everything inserted up to that point belongs to the objection. The connection is this: Since Jacob obtained his election [Col. 0914C] and calling no more than Esau from his own merits, but only from the choice of the one who called, and Esau did not lose it because of his prior merits, what should we say? What can we say in answer to the objection that follows immediately: “Is there injustice with God?” That is, by what reasoning can we defend God from blame and establish that he is not guilty of injustice, when by withholding his grace he made reprobate one who had not yet deserved it? For it was said: “When they were not yet born, nor had done any good,” etc.

“By no means,” the Apostle at once says on his own behalf: there must in no way ever be believed to be injustice in God. But before he shows that God should not be called unjust because of the objection, he further strengthens the objection itself, as a good disputant does, so that the stronger the objection, the more difficult and remarkable its eventual solution will appear. “For Moses”—as though he said: The question has rightly been raised, so that we may be able to defend God from blame; and from the very testimonies of Scripture itself God seems blameworthy and inexcusable in such matters, since he has power to bestow on whomever he wishes the mercy by which they are saved, while no one can be saved without his mercy. [Col. 0914D]

He first states that God has this power, saying: “I will have mercy,” etc. Then he immediately adds that no one can be saved except through mercy that goes before: “Therefore it is not of him who wills or runs.” “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy”: by predestining, before there is any human merit; afterward by calling him through inward inspiration; and finally, in him on whom I have mercy by calling, I shall bestow mercy in the prize of the heavenly calling itself. Therefore, says the Apostle in the person of the objector, this bestowal of divine mercy is not a matter of a person’s own power, however much he may will it or run—that is, however eagerly and strenuously he may seek to obtain it—but of God who has mercy. That is, it is not within our power to receive it, but in his hand to give it. Thus it seems to follow that no one is at fault if he is without this mercy, but rather the one who had it in his power to bestow it and did not wish to do so. [Col. 0915A]

“For Scripture says.” From opposites he shows that people’s salvation is God’s work of having mercy, and their damnation the work of hardening—as the testimony of God himself makes clear in Pharaoh. Yet he does not say “hardening,” but as though impelling Pharaoh toward evil, he says: “I raised you up.” To increase God’s alleged fault, he adds: “That I might show in you,” etc., as though God condemned others in order to glorify himself and sought his own glory in their death, which seems most unjust. “For this very purpose,” that is, to afflict the people, persecute them, or even not to heed me, as it is written: “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart.” “I raised you up,” that is, by resisting you I made your malice against me burn more fiercely, just as it is written: “Let the one who is righteous be made more righteous still” (Revelation 22:11)—whereby, as it were, gold is purified in the furnace of tribulation—“and let the one who is filthy be made filthier still” (*ibid.*). [Col. 0915B] “My power,” that is, power shown both in the plagues of Egypt and in the drowning of the Egyptians. “That my name may be proclaimed,” that is, that knowledge of my power may be spread throughout all the earth.

The phrase “that by this” seems to be more effective than causal. As one is accustomed to say of someone, “He went out in order to merit,” that is, he went out and did not obtain the effect of death; so here it is said, “I raised you up,” and by this I afterward showed my power in you—that is, in the things which I did concerning you and yours. [Col. 0915C]

“Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills.” Thus, the Apostle says in the person still of the opponent, it appears that he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills—that is, people are saved by his mercy or damned through his hardening in their sins in accordance with his will and choice rather than their own merits. This hardening he accomplishes by not having mercy, so that salvation or damnation seems to be wholly attributable to God’s choice.

“You will say to me then,” says the Apostle in his own person, or in that of whatever faithful people praise God in all things: You, whoever you are, seem to speak and object reasonably, on the basis of the foregoing testimonies and arguments, what follows: “Why then does he still find fault?”—that is, complain. From what source can God justly make any complaint against us, namely concerning our offenses, when all fault seems to arise solely, or principally, from him? For, as has been said, he hardens whom he wills; and, as is now said, no one can resist his will. [Col. 0915D] “Still,” that is, after such manifest testimonies or arguments tending to accuse him. “His will,” that is, his disposition, of which it is written: “Whatever he willed, he did.”

God is also said to will in another way: not by disposing things, but by counseling us to do the things through which we are saved, according to: “How often I wished to gather,” etc. (Matthew 23:37). And he wills all to be saved—that is, he counsels them to act accordingly. [Col. 0916A]

“O man, you.” At this point the Apostle responds on his own behalf to the preceding objections, which seem wholly to draw God into blame; and he sufficiently resolves them by a fitting comparison drawn from the potter. Thus, resolving a question by a question and giving satisfaction, he says: “O man”—that is, carnal and animal rather than spiritual—who until now have railed against God as though charging him with injustice, as the objection began, “Is there injustice with God?” and was afterward intensified by examples or arguments: “Who are you,” I say, “to answer back to God?” That is, you who defend yourself while accusing God in the ways stated above, answer him so as to defend yourself from an absurdity, if he himself asks you this question: “Does the thing formed say”—that is, can it justly complain against the potter because he made it such a formed thing, namely a vessel fashioned from clay, that is, composed? For “to form” means “to compose.” [Col. 0916B]

“Or does the potter not have authority?” That is, may the potter, without doing any injustice to the vessel, make one vessel for honor—that is, for some honorable office—and another for dishonor—that is, for some low and contemptible service? This is the meaning of: “from the same lump of earth,” that is, even if there is no cause for this dishonor in the quality of the material, which is the same. The potter of clay is the shaper of moist and soft earth, not the creator of the material itself.

From this it is clear that he has less right over his work than God has over his, since God is not merely its shaper but also the creator of its material. Whatever answer this man gives to the objections, he is, as it were, wounded by a two-pronged argument. For if he answers that the potter does not have this power, he utterly condemns the potters’ craft and shamelessly accuses its public usefulness, common benefit, and necessity. But if he chooses what is obvious—namely, that the potter may make such vessels without any injustice to the vessel of dishonor—then it is likewise clear, indeed much more so, that God may treat and dispose his creature in whatever way he wills, since he is bound by no obligation to it before it has merited anything. [Col. 0916C]

Otherwise all animals created for labor could rightly murmur and complain against him: why he created them merely for toil and human service, though they did not deserve this affliction which endures until death. But if it is rightly granted that they were created for toil for his glorification or for some human benefit, then by the same reasoning it must certainly be granted that God has deservedly withheld his grace from certain people and has not freed them from unrighteousness. For there is no unrighteousness of which God does not make the best use, and he permits nothing to happen without a reason, even in the judgment of secular wisdom. Hence Plato says in his *Timaeus*: “Nothing happens whose coming into being is not preceded by a lawful cause and reason.” [Col. 0917A]

For what believer does not know how excellently God made use of that supreme impiety of Judas, by whose detestable betrayal he accomplished the redemption of the entire human race? Certainly he worked more profitably through Judas’s wickedness than through Peter’s righteousness, and made far better use of the former’s evil work than of the latter’s good one—not, I say, insofar as Judas himself is concerned, but for the common benefit of all, which must always be preferred to private benefit. By Peter’s preaching and example of life, some were converted and saved; but Judas’s betrayal was turned to the salvation of all. It was accomplished alike by the Father and the Son, but with a different intention.

Thus also whatever acts of malice occur are most excellently ordered by divine disposition; and in all that he does or permits to be done, he himself knows the reasons, although they are hidden and unsearchable to us, why it is fitting for him to do or permit them. Otherwise he would do or permit certain things irrationally. [Col. 0917B]

Yet I think it right to ask: although God cannot be accused of injustice because he does not wish to give his grace to some, how nevertheless can it be charged to unrighteous people, to whom he did not wish to give the grace by which they would be saved, that they are damned, so that they are said to be damned by their own fault? Or if they bear no fault, by what desert can they be said to be damned by God, who renders to each according to his works? But again, what fault is it of a person if he is not saved when God never willed to give him the grace through which he would be saved, and he could not be saved without it? [Col. 0917C]

Perhaps someone will say that his fault is that God did not wish to give him that grace which he offered to him equally, just as to the righteous, but which he himself did not wish to accept when offered. To this I reply that even accepting it cannot occur without God’s grace. Since God did not wish to give him the grace for accepting the offered gift, and he cannot accept it without that grace, it is falsely ascribed to his fault that he did not accept the grace offered to him. It is as if a physician coming to a sick person offered a potion by which he could be cured, but the sick person could not raise himself to receive the medicine unless the physician himself also lifted him up. What is the sick person’s fault if he does not receive the offered cure? Or what credit belongs to the physician for offering it, if, by not lifting him up, he removes the efficacy of the remedy? [Col. 0917D]

Accordingly, we say that it is not necessary for God to bestow on us a new grace in each individual good work, so that, that is, we could in no way do or will good without a new, prior gift of divine grace. Rather, although God often distributes an equal gift of his grace to certain persons, they nevertheless do not happen to act equally; indeed, often the person who has received more grace for acting does less.

> **Note:** [Col. 0917D] On this point Abelard seems to have been censured. For he was charged with saying that free choice suffices of itself for some good. But [Col. 0918D] he says something quite different: namely, “without new grace,” yet not “without grace.”

For as happens with love or desire for temporal things, so it occurs with true and eternal goods. A very powerful man comes and sets forth and offers his wealth equally to certain needy persons as a reward, if they fulfil what he commands them. One of them, then, inflamed by desire for the reward displayed and promised to him, undertakes and completes the labor of the work. Another, however, being lazy and unable to endure great labor, is inflamed by that desire all the less in proportion as he is more frightened by the magnitude of the labor; and it often happens that one stronger in body is more sluggish in mind, and that one poorer is found more idle.

What, then, is the reason that, although the wealth of both has been equally displayed and offered as a reward, one, inflamed by desire for it, endures labor in order to become rich, while the other neglects to work and chooses prolonged poverty rather than endure labor for an hour? What is this, I ask, except the virtue of the one and the idleness of the other? What more did that rich man do for one than for the other, when he presented and promised the same reward equally to both?

“But,” you will say, “he kindled desire in this one, so as to make him patient in labor and bringer of it to completion.” Yet this, I say, followed from that action of the rich man; [Col. 0918C] it is not something belonging to the action itself—that is, it is not any part of it. What obstacle, then, did he encounter in the other, such that he did not likewise move him? You can certainly point to none except the laziness of the man who rejects labor.

So too, while God daily offers us the kingdom of heaven, one person, inflamed with desire for that kingdom, perseveres in good works; another grows torpid in his own idleness. Yet God offers it equally to both and does what is his own part, working equally toward each by setting forth and promising the blessedness of that kingdom—enough to kindle the desire of each—without the addition of another new grace. For the greater a reward is known to be, the more naturally each person is drawn toward it by his own desire, especially when that alone suffices to obtain it, and all can attain it with far less expense, toil, or danger than is required for acquiring earthly kingdoms.

What grace, then, must go beforehand in order to kindle our desire for God and make us long for the heavenly kingdom, except that the blessedness to which he invites us, and the way by which we can reach it, be expounded and imparted? This grace he bestows equally upon the reprobate as upon the elect: that is, he instructs both equally concerning this matter, so that from the same grace of faith which they have received [Col. 0919A] one may be stirred to good works, while another may, through the negligence of his own torpor, be rendered inexcusable.

This faith, therefore, which works through love in one person, remains inactive, sluggish, and idle in another, is the grace of God which precedes each elect person so that he begins to will rightly, and which in turn follows the beginning of good will so that that will itself may persevere. Nor is it necessary that, for each of the new works which arise daily, God should set forth another grace beyond that faith by which we believe that for what we do we shall obtain so great a reward. For worldly merchants too, although they endure so many and such great labors, bear all things through the one hope of earthly reward which they conceived at the outset; and, though they perform diverse things, they are not moved toward them by diverse hopes, but are drawn [Col. 0919B] by one and the same hope.

### “But if willing…”

The Apostle showed, by the fitting comparison introduced concerning the potter, that God cannot at all be charged with injustice if he is unwilling to give certain persons the grace through which they might be saved, as with Pharaoh or Esau, concerning whom the objection came before. But now he turns this very thing which was done in their case to the commendation of God, showing that God bore Pharaoh’s wickedness with great patience in order that he might repent; and, when Pharaoh’s wickedness had shown him to be wholly incorrigible, God made excellent use of vengeance for the common benefit of others: namely, that the people set free—that is, the Jewish people, or the whole world hearing this—might at least be restrained from evil by fear of punishments and invited to good.

Connection: As has been shown, God is not to be accused of injustice if he does not bestow his grace, by which they may be saved, upon whomever he wills. Nor have you, O man, who formerly accused God, anything to answer him when pressed by the present comparison; rather, you have much more reason to praise him, since even in those things in which he seems to you most cruel, his mercy must be proclaimed.

And this is what is meant by “what,” that is, “but what can you answer or say,” when he, in what he did concerning Pharaoh, willing to deter other wicked persons, made known his wrath—that is, the punishment which he exercises upon the wicked—and his power in the miracles which he performed both in the plagues of Egypt and in the drowning of the Egyptians. He “endured with much patience,” that is, through [Col. 0919D] his great patience, “vessels of wrath”: he long tolerated those wicked persons, though they deserved to be utterly destroyed by him. He calls them vessels of wrath because they are full of every vice, persons upon whom wrath ought immediately to be inflicted. This is what he adds by way of specification: “fitted for destruction,” that is, worthy to be utterly destroyed.

He endured them, I say, not without reason, but so that, in proportion as the wickedness of oppression abounded, the power of divine mercy might abound in those oppressed, by which he might rescue his own people for the glorification of himself. “The riches of glory,” that is, the excellence of his power, by which he is glorified “in vessels of mercy,” that is, toward his elect, whom he mercifully preserves lest they be broken by adversities.

He fittingly calls them vessels of wrath and vessels of mercy in accordance with the proposed comparison of the potter’s vessels: namely, those vessels [Col. 0920A] of mercy “which he prepared for glory,” that is, predestined to the blessedness of eternal life, or for his own glory, so that they too, by praising him for mercy received, may glorify him.

### “Whom he also called…”

In accordance with the meaning of the matter, rather than the grammatical property of the preceding noun, he supplies the relative pronoun, saying *whom* in the masculine rather than *which* in the neuter, although the preceding noun, “vessels,” to which the relative refers, is neuter. A similar change of gender according to meaning occurs in Virgil: *Praeneste sub ipsa*—“Praeneste beneath her very [walls].”

Those, namely, whom he also called—that is, whom he drew to himself by inward inspiration; they did not come to him of themselves. This was especially so through the miracles concerning Pharaoh, which he displayed to all, as was said above: “that my name may be proclaimed in all the earth.”

“Not only from the Jews,” I say, did he call them, but also from the Gentiles, when the Gentiles heard how greatly he had exercised his hand against Pharaoh, as Rahab too confesses after receiving the spies. As he says in Hosea—that is, through the prophet Hosea—the Lord himself first introduces testimony concerning the calling of the Gentiles, and afterwards, in the passage “But Isaiah,” concerning that of the Jews.

“I shall call,” that is, I shall subjugate by fear of terrible things the Gentiles who were formerly in no way subject to me; for “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom,” but love is its completion, when servants become friends. Thus he immediately adds: “And her who was not beloved, beloved”; that is, afterwards I shall transfer them from servants to friends, [Col. 0920C] as it is written: “I shall no longer call you servants,” etc. (Matt. XV, 15).

“I shall call,” that is, I shall truly cause them to be called; and “her who had not obtained mercy,” “one who has obtained mercy.” It is much greater to become a son than to obtain mercy. The former belongs to a beginning; the latter is perfection. We obtain mercy when, God calling us and threatening us unless we turn back, we turn to him lest we be punished by him. But we become sons when perfect love has already cast out this fear (1 John IV, 18).

Therefore, to the two preceding statements these two are referred individually, as a confirmation and exposition of what preceded. “In the place,” that is, in the land of the Gentiles, where they were not formerly my people—that is, were not even subject to me through fear—“sons,” that is, serving with filial reverence, “of the living God.” He says “living God” in contrast to the gods which Gentile error, deceived in various ways, had previously established either from senseless things or from dead human beings.

### “But Isaiah…”

Isaiah openly prophesies, just as Hosea had prophesied the aforementioned calling of the Gentiles, concerning the future conversion of the Jews: “Though they shall be”—though the Jews may be innumerable while persevering in their barrenness, that is, unbelief—“as the sand of the sea,” which is innumerable and barren, “yet their remnant shall be saved”: namely, those whom the Lord left for himself, while repelling the others from his grace and rejecting them from himself.

Or by “remnant” he means the simple and unlearned members of the people, who were despised among them, such as the Apostles were, and [Col. 0921A] many of the crowd who adhered to Christ, as the impious themselves acknowledge when they say: “Has any one of the rulers believed in him? But this crowd, which does not know the law, is accursed,” etc. (John VIII, 48).

But because someone might ask by whose preaching this calling of both peoples takes place, he answers: by the preaching proper to the incarnate Lord himself. This is what is meant by: “The Lord will accomplish through himself a shortened word upon the earth,” that is, a concise preaching—namely, as the saying goes, “a wise man makes himself known in few words.” “Upon the earth,” that is, above every teaching of earthly and human wisdom, as that great man of the Lord, John, declares: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth,” etc. (John III, 31).

How this teaching excels all others he first indicates by saying that he will make “a word accomplishing and abbreviating.” To accomplish is to bring to perfection, when that which has been begun is led to completion. Thus the evangelical preaching which the Lord brought through himself completed—that is, perfected—the necessary edification begun in the old law, adding what was lacking to the fullness of righteousness, as he himself declares: “Unless your righteousness exceeds…” etc. (Matt. V, 20).

“Accomplishing in equity,” that is, supplying what had been deficient in equity, namely what had been lacking in the perfection of righteousness and virtues. And, leaving aside innumerable carnal observances, he “abbreviates” this equity in the two commandments of love; to the rich man who sought counsel from him concerning the salvation of his soul, [Col. 0921C] he answered: “Do this and you shall live” (Luke X, 28). “On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII, 40).

We may also say, with regard to the number of words, that what the Old Testament commanded was abbreviated in the New. For the things which the Lord said on the mountain when delivering the New Testament to the Apostles are few in comparison with those which he commanded through Moses; and the volumes of the four Gospels are small in comparison with the five books of Moses. Great, therefore, is the excellence of the Gospel: it is more perfect in meaning and briefer in words.

And as the same Isaiah foretold: “Unless the Lord of Sabaoth,” that is, of armies, who daily directs his warriors against the kingdom [Col. 0921D] of the devil—as it is written, “like an army arrayed in battle order” (Song VI, 3)—“had left us a seed”: that is, when on account of its fault he blinded our people, the Jewish people, removed it from his grace, and, as it were, cast spoiled grain out from his storehouse, he retained certain persons for himself as seed, such as the Apostles and the other faithful of the primitive Church—“we should have been like Sodom and like Gomorrah,” where parents together with their offspring were exterminated, so that they left no seed.

In seed the usefulness of the former grain is preserved: old things live and are renewed, and many are produced from few. So in the Apostles and the other members of the primitive Church the usefulness of the preceding Fathers was restored, religion revived, and a great benefit from the divine harvest sprang up throughout the whole world.

### “What then?”

Since he made her who was not beloved beloved, and now conversely we see her who was beloved made not beloved—that is, while the Gentile people has been chosen, almost all Israel has been rejected—what cause shall we assign for this, namely, for the rejection of his people?

And this is what is meant by “What shall we say concerning this?” Namely, the Gentiles, who did not formerly know righteousness—that is, the faith which leads to righteousness—now attain that righteousness: the true righteousness of the mind which comes from faith, not that which consists in external works. But Israel, that is, the Jewish people, pursuing “a law of righteousness,” that is, exercising the authority of bodily retribution, did not attain the law—that is, did not receive the perfect doctrine of the Gospel, which alone justifies.

“Why,” he asks, “was this so?” Because it did not attain—supply, “righteousness”—which is from faith, but a supposed righteousness, not true righteousness, which is from works. That is, following the killing letter of the law in external and carnal observances, it was not justified by the spiritual and mystical understanding which builds up from faith in Christ; and it was not justified, as it is written: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Rom. I, 17).

And this happened because they stumbled over the stone of stumbling: that is, they were scandalized by Christ, whom, because of the weakness of his human nature, they refused to believe to be God. Feet ordinarily strike against and stumble over small stones, which because of their smallness can scarcely be noticed. So Christ, because of the lowliness of his humility [Col. 0922C] which he displayed to the world, was despised by the Jews and became for them a stone of stumbling, so that, not believing in him, they took offense at the things which he said.

As is written in Isaiah himself: “Behold, I place”—these are the Father’s words and the promise concerning the sending of his Son—“Behold, I place,” that is, I have already resolved with myself to lay in the Church a humble but strong foundation, namely, the incarnate Word. For he is strong because he is a stone; humble because he is a stone of stumbling, to be trampled underfoot by those who stumble over him.

“Everyone,” whether Jew or Gentile, “in him”—not, however, “to him,” nor “him”—“shall not be confounded,” that is, shall not be ashamed through disappointment in his hope. He therefore says “a stone of stumbling” and “a rock of scandal”; and this frequently occurs in the prophets, that words are varied within the same sense. Zion, that is, “watchtower,” is called the Church, which, raising itself on high through desire, carefully surveys every action it performs, lest it impede its heavenly desire.

## Chapter X

### “Brethren…”

Lest the Apostle, who had departed from the Jews, might seem to have censured them from some hatred rather than from a desire to correct them, he shows in effect how great an affection of love and compassion he has toward them, saying that he earnestly prays to God for their salvation. When he says, “The desire of my heart and prayer,” he shows that prayer proceeds from devotion of heart and consists more in devotion than in words.

[Col. 0923A] As if he said: Although I censure them in this way, nevertheless, O brethren, I do not cease to pray that they may be saved. Hence the Church also has each year a special prayer for the Jews: that God may remove the veil from their hearts and, once the truth—which is Christ—has been recognized, that they may turn to him.

> **Note:** [Col. 0923D] *Offices of the Church*, at Mass, in the Admonition on the day of Holy Parasceve [Good Friday].

He calls those to whom the Apostle writes “brethren,” in accordance with what Truth says: “For one is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. XXIII, 9), so that they might more willingly accept his correction as coming from a brother and equal, not a superior. Hence this custom has also become established in the Church: at the beginning of readings taken from the apostolic Epistles, the word “Brethren” is announced beforehand.

But that one ought to pray for the Jews, or especially to have compassion upon their error, he adds in saying: “For I bear them witness,” from my own case, since I once acted similarly. “They have zeal, but not according to knowledge”: that is, zeal for God which is neither rational nor good, because it is erroneous—thinking, namely, what is contrary to that saying of Truth: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God; and they will do these things because they have not known either the Father or me” (John XVI, 2–3).

Zeal, whether good or evil, means any fervor and stirring of an inflamed mind toward doing something. How it is not according to knowledge he immediately adds: “For, being ignorant of what God approves”—namely, the righteousness which comes from faith in Christ—“and seeking to establish their own,” that is, the righteousness which they themselves regard and approve as righteousness, namely in carnal observances, seeking to preserve it immovably, “they are not subject to the righteousness of God”: that is, they are not obedient to those commands of God [Col. 0923C] which justify those who obey, such as this: “Do you believe in God? Believe also in me” (John XIV, 1).

“For Christ is the end…” They truly ignore the righteousness of God because they do not have the faith of Christ, by which every believer is justified. That each person is justified through faith in Christ, rather than through his own righteousness consisting in legal works, he states thus: “For to everyone who believes”—that is, to every faithful person—“Christ,” that is, faith in Christ, is “for righteousness,” that is, so that through it he may be justified; or else Christ is the end of the law—that is, legal works. For those who place their hope of salvation in the delight of those works, Christ will not benefit them. Hence he says also to the Galatians: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V, 2). And Christ himself says: “The law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. XI, 13).

### “For Moses…”

By the testimonies of Moses himself, the lawgiver, he shows that no one obtains eternal life from the righteousness of the law when fulfilled—that is, from those carnal works—nor was eternal life promised by it; but rather by faith in Christ. “The man who does the righteousness which is from the law,” that is, fulfils legal works, “shall live upon the earth,” namely, he shall enjoy the goods of this life because of his observance of the law, not those of eternal life.

But the righteousness which is from faith, since faith concerns things not seen, promises rather that eternal life which is hidden in Christ than the present life, and invisible rather than visible goods. This is [Col. 0924A] the righteousness which is from faith in Christ—that is, faith itself placed in Christ, which justifies us. In the same place, namely in Deuteronomy, that righteousness speaks through Moses himself, who was truly righteous by it, strengthening us so that we may not fail or despair in any adversities.

That is, he speaks from that righteousness which he already possessed, as he says: “Do not say in your heart,” that is, do not think, whoever you are, O man, or you, people of Israel: “Who shall ascend into heaven?” That is, do not despair of that heavenly life in which faith in Christ consists and by whose promise Christ chiefly draws us, as though human nature could in no way ascend to that life. For this would be, the Apostle says, on one’s own part to bring Christ himself down from that life: that is, to believe that he himself had not ascended there in the human nature which [Col. 0924B] he assumed.

“Or who shall descend into the abyss?” that is, even into hell itself, so that he may lead to heavenly things with himself those whom he did not free? For this would be to bring Christ back into the abyss, that is, by believing, to draw Christ back from that descent by which he freed his faithful dead from hell and transferred them with himself to heaven.

“But what does it say?” That is, the Apostle says: attend to what Moses himself adds there, namely: “The word is near you,” etc. That is, it is easy for you to profess or believe that this has been fulfilled in Christ: namely, the ascent of a human being to heavenly things and the descent of a human being to the lower regions. It is easy because it is not contrary to reason, but most fitting to divine mercy. “This,” the Apostle says, “is the word of faith”: that is, a word concerning that which faith holds and concerning that which, when believed, makes persons faithful; this is the word which we Apostles have been sent to preach. And rightly so, because our salvation consists in confession and faith in this word.

And this is what is meant by: “For if you,” whoever you may be, etc. A person confesses with his mouth when he understands what he declares. He believes with his heart when he applies his heart and will to the things he believes, so that this faith may draw him to works: for example, when someone, believing that Christ rose from the dead to eternal life, strives insofar as he can, by following in Christ’s footsteps, to reach the blessedness of that same life.

It should be noted that when testimonies from the Old Testament are introduced in the New, it is often easy, if considered in themselves, to apply the cited testimonies to the point for which they have been introduced. But if we at the same time attend to the circumstances of the passage from which they are drawn, and to how the preceding and following parts of Scripture may cohere with what is taken from it, our understanding is greatly constrained. This occurs also in the testimony now expounded. To consider it more carefully, let us set out the words of Scripture itself more fully.

For it is written in Deuteronomy, chapter XXX, when, after giving the law, Moses exhorted the people to keep it in these words: “This commandment which I command you today is not above you, nor is it set far away; nor is it situated in heaven, so that you can say: ‘Who among us can ascend, in order to bring it down to us, that we may hear it and fulfil it in deed?’ Nor is it situated across the sea, so that you should make excuse and say: ‘Who among us can cross the sea and bring it even to us, that we may be able to hear and do what is commanded?’” (Deut. XXX, 11–13). Again, in the same chapter: “But the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do it” (ibid., 14).

Behold, from these words, if we follow them according to the letter, the whole passage appears to admonish the Jews not to complain about the difficulty of understanding the law, as though something had been spoken obscurely in a riddle; rather, everything is commanded so plainly that they can understand it of themselves. Nor do they have any excuse if they delay obedience to the commandments, on the ground that they cannot understand them.

But because it is especially fitting that we follow the Apostle, most skilled in the law, we must, in accordance with his sense, apply what is said to faith in Christ. Moses therefore knew that the law itself which he had given was full of mystical and obscure meanings, which could be opened only through Christ’s coming and ascension, as it is written: “Beginning from Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted the Scriptures to them” (Luke XXIV, 27); and as he himself says: “Unless I go away,” etc. (John XVI, 7), and again: “But the Paraclete,” etc. (John XIV, 26).

He admonishes the people not to despair of that spiritual understanding of the law which was to be disclosed, as though the world would not have one coming from heaven to reveal the meaning of God which he had placed in the law. For truly the Son of God was to come from heaven, and to ascend again, in order to impart this understanding to the world, both by himself and through the Holy Spirit, whom he was to send after his ascension for this very purpose.

It should be noted, however, that the words the Apostle adds—“Or who shall descend into the abyss?”—are not contained in the foregoing words of Moses; instead, Moses says there, “nor is it situated across the sea,” etc. These words, therefore, the Apostle either added in pursuing the sense himself, or perhaps, according to another translation than the one we now use, selected only those words which he saw to suit the point he proposed. For “it is not situated across the sea” can be understood to mean that it is not located in the abyss, that is, in hell, so that someone would have to descend there on its account [Col. 0925D] and penetrate the sea of this world in order to reach that depth of hell. Thus “beyond the sea” means, as it were, “down below after the sea”: in that further bitterness of hell beyond the misery of the present life.

### “For with the heart…”

I rightly said, “you shall confess and believe,” because both are necessary: with the heart one believes so that the person who believes may be justified, since “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI, 6). Afterwards confession is made of the very thing believed, so that one may be added to the faithful Church and participate in its sacraments.

For he says—as was set forth above in Isaiah—not all, whether Jews or Gentiles, and rightly so, because for attaining this salvation diversity of peoples matters nothing, provided that faith is one: that we believe “in him” rather than “to him” or “him,” as we noted above. “Rich toward all,” that is, sufficient to enrich all with true riches, “who invoke,” not merely “who call.” Calling is the outward sound of words, concerning which it is said: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. VII, 21). But invocation is an inward cry—that is, the devotion of a mind sighing toward God—concerning which Moses is told: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. XIV, 15).

“For everyone,” on the authority of Isaiah, “who asks for the name of the Lord,” that is, seeks in devotion his knowledge and manifestation—of which it is said: “And I shall manifest myself to him” (John XIV, 21)—shall be saved. And the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. XVI, 15).

### “How then?”

He commends the office of himself and the other Apostles, showing how necessary their preaching is if people are to believe and be saved.

Connection: Since whoever invokes shall be saved, he must be invoked by people if they are to be saved. But how shall they invoke one in whom they have not yet believed? As if he were plainly saying: In no way shall they invoke him—indeed, not only “in him,” but not even “to him,” that is, to his commands or admonitions—whom they have not heard, either through his own preaching or through another who preaches him. Nor can anyone preach, without a preacher—whether himself or another—unless they are sent, as the Son himself was sent by the Father and the Apostles by the Son, when he said to them: “As the Father sent me, I also send you” (John XX, 21).

Here the author touches upon false Apostles who, not sent by God, come of their own accord to preach; concerning them Truth himself says: “All who came were thieves and robbers,” as it is written (John X, 18).

Origen: “This example appears to have been taken from Isaiah.”

Ambrose: “The prophet Nahum says this. The feet of the Apostles were beautiful because their affections were free from the contagion of worldly, earthly desire; pure in God, they did not seek in preaching what was their own, but what belonged to Jesus Christ, serving not their belly but God. Hence their feet were fittingly washed by the Lord. Because of this mystical beauty of theirs, he also forbade them to be hidden by shoes: for what is hidden is ugly, and where evil is done light is concealed.”

“Of those who proclaim peace,” that is, who preach and teach reconciliation with God. In the same mystery they are commanded to say to every house which they enter: “Peace to this house.” “Good things,” namely, true goods, “which eye has not seen,” etc. (1 Cor. II, 9). In this life we already attain this peace and reconciliation with God through repentance, as it is written: “Turn to me, and I shall turn to you” (Zech. I, 3); but those goods come afterward in the future life. Hence he fittingly placed peace first and goods afterwards. “The Gospel,” that is, divine preaching.

“Who has believed?” That is, who has received faith through what he heard from us? As if he said: no one, or few. “Therefore,” that is, it appears from this testimony that faith comes by hearing, through the word of Christ rather than ours, because we do not speak from ourselves but from what he himself taught us, so that whatever results from our preaching should particularly redound either to his glory or to his reproach.

“But have they not heard?” That is, can any part of the world excuse its unbelief on the ground of ignorance, as though evangelical preaching had not come, or would not come, to all? As if he said: not at all. He immediately proves this by the testimony of the Psalmist: “And what if not all obey? Their sound,” that is, the fame of the Apostles or preachers of the Gospel, etc., “has gone forth… and their words to the ends of the earth,” through which they preached. “To the ends,” I say—that is, even to the outer regions of the world, which are certainly inhabited by Gentiles.

“But did Israel not know?” Namely, did the Jews not know that this preaching had passed so far to the Gentiles? That is, can they excuse themselves as though preaching had not been offered to them, and charge this to the fault of the preachers? He does not merely say, “Did Israel not hear?” but also, “Did Israel not know?” that is, did it not perceive the truth of this preaching? As if he said: it truly did, although it resisted out of malice, envy, or zeal for earthly desire. Hence its unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit persists.

He establishes this too by the testimony of Moses himself, who, as he was the first of the prophets to write, likewise first prophesied in writing their wickedness: “I”—these are God’s words—“will provoke you to jealousy”: that is, by preaching through myself, says the Son of God, I shall bring you into envy and hatred both of myself and of my own people. Since envy is hatred of another’s good, this plainly shows that they sinned against Christ knowingly.

“I shall send you into a non-nation by means of a foolish nation”: that is, through your dispersion, to be brought about by the unbelieving Romans, I shall make you not to be a people. For a people or nation is not properly so called except as an assembly of human beings. “I shall send you into the anger of other human beings,” even though dispersed, so that they may continually oppress and afflict you with harsh exactions.

“But Isaiah…” Not Moses alone, but Isaiah also openly dared to speak thus concerning their rejection and the election of the Gentiles, although he foresaw that he would be killed by them. “I was found by those who did not seek me,” says the Lord, that is, by the Gentiles. Clearly the Church has been far more instructed concerning God than the Synagogue. “They did not ask,” that is, they did not know even how to seek anything from me, whom they entirely did not know.

“But to Israel,” that is, to the Jews, “all day,” that is, throughout the whole time of my preaching—which ought truly to be called the day and illumination of the world—“I stretched out my hands,” that is, I freely offered myself in order to gather them, through the hands, that is, the works daily displayed to them, turning altogether aside from the way of the Gentiles so that I might give myself wholly to them. “To a people that contradicts”—what is worse in every respect—“and maligns me.”

## Chapter XI
Therefore I say. Since by so many authorities he had refuted the Jews, and had most recently shown that the election of the Gentiles and the rejection of the Jews had been plainly prophesied, lest the Gentiles, especially on this account, should in their dispute presume an occasion for boasting against the Jews—as though they understood that that people had been wholly rejected—[Col. 0928A] he begins also to take this boasting away from the Gentiles and this despair from the Jews; and he returns now to an attack upon the Gentiles, in order to crush their pride as well. The connection is this: Since the rejection of the Jews has been confirmed by such manifest testimonies, I say—that is, I judge that the following question must be raised and resolved. “Has he wholly rejected his people?”—that is, the Jews, so as never again to receive any from among them? “For I also am an Israelite,” that is, one who sees, not a proselyte; and I am of Abraham’s race, not descended from Ishmael or Esau, but through Benjamin, and from the stock of the accursed Saul, whose posterity was rejected from the kingdom. “His people whom he foreknew,” that is, those whom he formerly predestined from among that people, then his own peculiar people.

“In Elijah,” that is, where he speaks of Elijah in the Book of Kings: how [Col. 0928B] Elijah himself “intercedes with God against Israel,” that is, by prayer or complaint calls God to vengeance against the wickedness of the Jews who persecuted him. “They have killed”—supply, Jezebel—“they have dug down,” that is, they have utterly overthrown from the foundation, so that idols alone might be worshipped. “But what does the divine answer say?” That is, he thought himself to have been left alone; but by God’s own testimony he is shown to have been mistaken. “I have reserved for myself,” that is, I have not cast Baal—that is, the idol Baal and Jezebel—away from my grace.

“So then.” Since we have introduced the example of Elijah, let us explain why it was introduced. This is what he says: “So at the present time also there is a remnant,” that is, those whom the Lord has not cast away, “according to the election of the grace of God,” not according to their own merits. “But if by grace,” that is, through [Col. 0928C] grace—supply, they have been saved—“then it is no longer by works,” that is, by their merits. He does not say “through merits,” but “from merits,” because God’s grace does not exclude the merits of Paul and others. But it would be from merits, not from grace, if [lacuna] proceeded from our merits and God’s grace did not go beforehand, so as at least to inspire faith or direct the preachers. “Otherwise,” that is, if it had happened otherwise—namely, in the contrary manner from what I say—what is now grace, that is, bestowed freely, our merits not preceding God’s grace, would not be grace, but merit alone.

Suitably the Apostle introduced the comparison from Elijah to our own time, and by an appropriate example begins to refute the rash judgment of the Gentiles, since they saw that even so great a man was rebuked by the Lord for a like presumption. [Col. 0928D] We know that John the Baptist, as another Elijah, preceded the Lord’s first advent; and, as though he despaired of the salvation of the Jewish people, he severely rebuked them in these words: “Offspring of vipers,” etc. Thus, even in this time of grace, of which it is written, “The Law and the Prophets were until John,” the things now said about Elijah seem to correspond.

“What then?” Since only the remnant of Israel has been or has become saved by the election of God’s grace rather than by its own merits, it is consequently evident what must be said—namely, what follows: “Israel did not obtain what it was seeking,” that is, what it demanded from God as its own and as due to itself through works: eternal life, namely, or the eternal inheritance. [Col. 0929A] “But the election,” that is, Paul and those who were chosen by God’s grace from that people, “obtained” what it sought, that is, eternal life. “But the rest were blinded”: not only did they fail to obtain what they sought, but they were utterly rejected so that they might no longer believe.

“As it is written, God gave them a spirit of compunction.” Origen: “I have not yet been able to discover where it is written, ‘God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear, unto this day.’ But I think that the Apostle spoke in this manner: ‘But the rest were blinded; and, as it is written of them’ (Isa. 6:9), ‘he gave them a spirit of compunction.’ Yet the things said through Isaiah concerning blindness of eyes and hearing of ears are: ‘By hearing you shall hear and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see and shall not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown gross,’ etc. (Isa. 29:10).” [Col. 0929B] Thus the Apostle now seems to have expressed Isaiah’s sense in his own words. Likewise, the same must be done with what Scripture declares concerning David: “Let their table become,” etc. (Ps. 68:23).

“A spirit of compunction,” etc., that is, of envy and hatred, by which their minds might be pricked—that is, goaded—against Christ and his followers. “Eyes,” that is, reason unable to see by itself; and “ears,” that is, those not understanding unless another teaches them. “Let their table become.” What seems to be taken from Isaiah or David has in both places, in some manner, one meaning.

Again, what he says, “into a snare,” is not found written in the Psalm, neither in the Septuagint nor in the Hebrew. And again, the Psalm has “before them,” but the Apostle did not [Col. 0929C] include “before them.” “Their table before them,” that is, the Scripture of the Old Testament delivered to them and constantly used by them, from which those who understand draw food for the soul, becomes “a snare and a trap”: a snare by which they do not catch others but are themselves caught and held back from walking in the way of truth, who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” This happens when they receive nothing there mystically, but expound everything according to the letter that kills. Or it becomes “a trap” when, in frequent disputes with the Lord or holy teachers, they are so caught and bound by the testimonies from Scripture brought against them that they cannot extricate themselves from the objections. Such is the question which the Lord set before them: “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord?” etc. (Ps. 22:43 [sic]).

“Into a stumbling-block and a recompense,” that is, into recompense for the stumbling of their soul—namely, condemnation, not salvation. But this is the Lord’s saying: “Moses is the one who accuses you” (John 5:45); and according to what the Apostle says: “Those who have sinned under the Law shall be judged through the Law.” The Law also became a stumbling-block to them, a cause of offence and indignation, when they saw Christ and his followers say or do many things which they believed contrary to the Law. Hence their saying: “We have heard from the Law that Christ remains forever” (John 12:34).

“Let them be darkened.” He indicates that this stumbling or ensnaring proceeds from their blindness and their desire for earthly things, which always [Col. 0930A] reigns most strongly among the Jews. “Bend” is an imperative verb, as though it said: “You, God, bend their back, so that through the desire of seeking earthly things they may not rise to heavenly things.” It should be noted that words of this kind, which appear to be imprecations when spoken by saints, belong more to prophetic utterance than to a desire for vengeance; so that, when “let it be” is said, it is as though a prediction were being made.

For just as Scripture sometimes uses a future indicative verb imperatively—for example, “You shall love the Lord” (Matt. 23:37), for “Love”; “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13), for “Do not kill”—so it sometimes does the reverse. Moreover, what harm is there if a saint, enlightened by the Spirit and assenting to the divine judgment, wishes that even the vengeance upon the wicked should take place which he understands ought rightly to be done and sees to have been decreed in the divine sentence? For what injustice is there in willing what is just to be done? Otherwise, some justice would displease us, and we should regard as hateful even the Lord’s own known sentence. But we reserve a more careful treatment of this matter for our Theology.

Therefore I say. Since rejection of them was thus prophesied, did they “stumble” against God so that they merely faltered in faith? Or did they fall utterly—that is, were they condemned by God without any compensating benefit? God makes good use of all evils. But through their offence, namely, when they repelled Christ’s preaching from themselves and the apostles passed over to the Gentiles, the apostles were received by the Gentiles all the more easily because the Gentiles saw them rejected [Col. 0930B] and afflicted by the Jews, their greatest enemies. Further, in being scattered throughout the world into perpetual captivity for the sin committed against Christ, they bear powerful witness to our faith and furnish great proclamations of Christ’s power.

“That they may emulate them,” that is, so that henceforth, conversely, the Gentiles may do to the Jews what Jews formerly did to Gentiles in the case of proselytes: namely, through zeal for God, turn or provoke them to imitate themselves. To emulate someone is to have zeal—that is, an intense desire—toward him, so as to imitate him, or conversely that he may imitate oneself; as he will immediately say: “If by any means I may provoke to emulation,” etc. But if they emulate them, it is deservedly so. For if God has made such good use of their offence—that is, if so great [Col. 0930C] a benefit has followed from it that the whole world has advanced among the Gentiles—how great will the benefit be from their conversion together with the Gentiles? This is what he says: “If their offence is the riches of the world,” that is, if through their offence and the rejection of that people the world has been spiritually enriched in the rest of the nations, “and their diminution,” that is, what the world now has less in them, is compensated in the Gentiles by spiritual goods, “how much more their fullness” will be, supply, riches for the world. That is, if they too together with the Gentiles fill the world with good works, it will be enriched much more abundantly.

“And this indeed”: the word “indeed” is adversative in relation to what he first said concerning their sin; he now speaks concerning their conversion, so that the sequence may be joined to what preceded according to the letter: “Thus the world among the Gentiles has been enriched by their offence. But if their offence,” etc.

“For to you.” And as though someone despaired concerning this future fullness, he now shows, by an example proposed, that the Jews have not been utterly rejected by God beyond hope. For he himself, though apostle to the Gentiles, labours daily to convert even some Jews. This is indeed to honour his office—that is, to commend it most highly—when, beyond what is required, he says that he gains even these, of whom he is not appointed apostle—that is, preacher—although he is apostle to the Gentiles and by no means to the Jews.

“If by any means”: by words as well as examples, by authority as well as reason, by open truth as well as useful simulation or dissimulation, of which elsewhere he says: “I became a Jew to the Jews, and became all things to all, that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9:23). “My flesh,” that is, Jews who are of my own race, he seeks to provoke to emulation—that is, to imitate him in conversion—at least some, if not many.

“For if.” And deservedly I persist in this, to convert them too; because, since their rejection is the reconciliation of the world among the Gentiles, and is therefore beneficial, their reception will be much more wonderful and beneficial: it will be as the resurrection of the dead. For it is more wonderful to raise the dead than to animate one who has not lived—that is, to restore life rather than to give it. Every day we know that flesh is naturally animated in mothers’ wombs, and do not marvel; but for the dead to live again would belong rather to miracle than to nature. [Col. 0931C] Thus we may more properly say that Gentiles converted to God, whose people had not previously lived by faith, are animated—that is, vivified—than raised again. But the Jews, if they return to God and the hearts of fathers are turned to children, are raised as though dead, since that people had formerly lived by faith.

Certainly it is more difficult to raise a just person after he has fallen than to draw to righteousness one who has remained wicked. We experience this daily in religious communities: those who turn from the wickedness of the world to monastic life are easily seen to persevere in their good purpose, while secular monks scarcely, or never, return. The Jews’ rejection is rightly so called because God lost them through unbelief, [Col. 0931D] whereas he had formerly held them subject to himself through faith. By “world” he denotes the Gentiles, who, while worshipping idols, were to be counted more among the irrational parts of the world, lacking sense and reason, than among rational human creatures.

“What will it be?” That is, what sort of thing will be the reception of the rejected Jews, if not “life from the dead”—that is, the resurrection of those dead in sins?

Now “firstfruits” is the tasting of some part taken from the whole, by which it may be discovered what the whole is like—that is, of what flavour. Yet there was always among the Jewish people some body of faithful persons awaiting the incarnation of God and his passion for their redemption: such as Zechariah and Elizabeth, Simeon and Anna, Nathanael and Nicodemus, and some others who were found even in Christ’s time. To these, indeed, the very person was divinely revealed and distinctly shown, in whom they should believe the fulfilment of the promise which they awaited. [Col. 0932A] Perhaps all the apostles had previously been such persons; hence they so readily followed Christ when he called, whether previously inspired by God or instructed by John’s testimony. One of them, Andrew, John’s disciple, said to his brother Simon: “We have found the Messiah” (John 1:41). And Philip said to Nathanael: “We have found Jesus, of whom Moses wrote in the Law and the Prophets” (ibid., 45).

These words show that they had been instructed from the Law and the Prophets to await Christ, but did not yet know the appointed time or the definite person. To know this, or even to make it known to others, divine grace received them; and when they had been taken from the mass of preceding believers and all followed Christ so readily at the word of a single command, they became, as it were, a firstfruits offering, in which it might be shown what faith that mass had possessed. Hence they were received as a remnant in order visibly, or in actual fact, to display what they had held by faith.

The connection is this: “And how,” says the Apostle, “can any be received from a people so wicked and always so rebellious?” “Well,” says the Apostle, “and more easily in accordance with the nature of their origin than from the Gentiles; for the mass from which the firstfruits was taken must there have been holy.” For as are the firstfruits, so is the mass; and conversely, as he immediately adds: “If the root is holy, so are the branches.” By the root he means that mass of preceding faithful persons; by the branches he now means those who believe and have been received from it. [Col. 0932C]

“But if some of the branches,” that is, some from that mass of faithful persons who had previously believed rightly while awaiting what was still to come, “were broken off,” that is, lost the former standing in faith which they possessed—“and you,” namely, a Gentile, “although you were a wild olive,” that is, naturally barren and uncultivated, “were grafted among them,” that is, by another’s action were put in their place, and through faith made a sharer in the root of the fruitful olive and in its richness through charity. For richness is of a warm nature and therefore signifies the fire of charity; and faith is the root and foundation of charity. “Do not boast against the branches,” that is, do not insult them over the loss caused by their breaking-off, nor pride yourself on your own standing, attributing it, namely, to your merits or virtue. [Col. 0932D] “But if you boast, know that you do not support the root”: that is, what you possess has passed to you from their root, not from you to the root. For the faithful Jewish people is the ass, the mother of the colt—that is, it gives birth in faith to the Gentile people.

“You will say then”: since you cannot boast against the root, you wish at least to prefer yourself to those branches, because “they were broken off that you might be grafted in”—that is, they were broken off and [lacuna] again grafted in their place. The Apostle says this well—that is, what he says is true—but you cannot boast on that account. For they were not broken off because of some good which you previously possessed, on account of which God chose you to be grafted in; rather, they were broken off because of their own evil, namely, unbelief. “Do not think high things,” proudly, namely, against them; “but fear,” namely, lest you commit something such that you too may be broken off.

And indeed you ought to fear. What you should fear he adds: “For if he did not spare”—from breaking off, namely—“the natural branches,” those belonging to their own root from which they sprang, fear—supply, lest perhaps, etc. And in order that you may fear this, whether corrected by the example of others or kindled by love of the grace you have received, remember attentively the goodness of grace and the severity of justice: if you remain in that received goodness—that is, if through your own fault you lose the grace received. “Otherwise,” that is, if matters are otherwise than I warn, you too will be cut off from the holy root into which you have been grafted accidentally, not born from it. [Col. 0933A]

“But they too,” even after their breaking-off, will be grafted in in place of you when you have been cut off, just as you were formerly, conversely, put in the place of the broken branches. And as though one asked how this could happen, when God broke them off because of their fault, he says that God himself can do this through his mercy—he who broke them off because of their own fault. This is what he says: “For God is able to graft them in again,” that is, after your grafting in and their breaking off.

I have said that God is able to graft them in too; nor is this surprising, because according to the foregoing comparison of the olive it seems much easier and more natural for native branches to be grafted in than foreign ones. This he proves from the lesser case: “For if you, a Gentile, were cut from an olive tree naturally wild to you”—that is, taken from the unfruitful tree of the Gentile people—“and were grafted contrary to nature,” that is, contrary to the usual practice of grafting. For unfruitful trees are not normally grafted into fruitful ones, nor wild trees into cultivated ones; nor does a scion ordinarily bear the fruit of its root. [Col. 0933B] “How much more” naturally—that is, how much more easily in accordance with the nature of their origin—will they be grafted into their own origin, from which they were born.

“For I do not wish”—as though he said: Therefore, O Gentiles, I recall so often the grace of your election, the justice of their rejection, and their future conversion.

“For I do not wish you to be ignorant of this mystery,” that is, the hidden judgment of the divine dispensation: namely, that blindness has happened “in part” to Israel, that is, some Jews, who did not recognize Christ’s advent, through which they might have been enlightened in faith, have been blinded; until “the fullness of the Gentiles has entered,” that is, many from the totality of all nations will be converted and enter the spiritual city of God, the Church. And then, after their entry, “all Israel” will at last be saved according to the individual tribes, from which many will be converted at the end through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah—yet not all. For Truth says to them concerning Antichrist: “Another will come in his own name; him you will receive” (John 5:43). Thus neither at the end of the world nor at Christ’s advent will all Jews be converted, but only the Lord’s remnant.

Hence Jerome, writing to Hedibia on the ninth question, says [Note: [Col. 0933D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 1000]: “Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: ‘Though the number of the children of Israel be,’ etc.; that is, even if the multitude does not believe, yet [Col. 0934A] a few will believe.”

On the end of the world Isidore speaks thus in Book II *Against the Jews*, chapter 6: “Malachi likewise says that Elijah is to be sent before the end of the world for the conversion of the Jews: ‘Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and he will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers’ (Mal. 4:5).” Again: “This is the people to be converted in the last times, which the patriarch Jacob foretells under the figure of Benjamin, the wolf eating in the morning and dividing spoil in the evening: because at the beginning it received the Law, but at the evening of the world, when it shall believe, it will divide between the New Testament and the Old.”

The same author, chapter 12, on the prophet Amos: “‘The house of Israel has fallen; it shall not rise again’ (Amos 5:1). Therefore Israel has been cast down in its own land; there is none to raise her. The same prophet continues: ‘The end has come upon my people Israel’ (Amos 8:2).”

All these things pertain to its carnal kingdom or observance, because beyond this they will be objects of rejection. For those promises of restoration which their language contains are promised to that part which will believe from among the Jews. For neither are all Jews to be redeemed nor will all be saved; but those who have been chosen by faith will be saved. As for what some saints say, that at the end Jews will be converted through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch—with whom the Apostle himself seems to agree when he says, “And so all Israel shall be saved”—either this must be understood, as we have said, of the entirety of the tribes, not of every individual; or [Col. 0934C] perhaps those who first receive Antichrist when he restores Jewish rites, afterwards corrected through the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, or converted by seeing his destruction—of whom Truth says, “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matt. 24:22)—will be saved by turning to Christ.

Gregory, in the *Moralia*, Book [lacuna]: “But at the end all Israelites, having recognized Elijah’s preaching, will come to the faith; and then that extraordinary banquet will be celebrated by the manifold gathering of peoples.”

Remigius on Psalm 12, “When the Lord has turned back the captivity,” etc.: “While Jewish unbelief remained impenitent in its cruelty, it entangled itself in a harsher snare of captivity. Yet this captivity will be loosed at the preaching of Elijah and Enoch, when, through their preaching, all Jews [Col. 0934D] shall believe in Christ.”

Haimo: “He will fully turn away impieties from Jacob, as it is written: ‘And he himself will redeem Israel from all his iniquities’ (Ps. 12:8).” And when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.

“That you may not be wise in yourselves”: that is, I do not wish you to be ignorant of this hidden thing, lest, seeing their blindness, you should proudly insult them on account of the enlightenment of wisdom which you possess and boast of God’s gift as though it were your own. That would be to be wise for oneself rather than for God—that is, to direct his wisdom toward one’s own glory rather than to the glory of him who gives it.
