Haimo: [Col. 0935A] “A mystery is a hidden thing, containing some secret within itself: namely, why he rejected the Jews, once his peculiar people, and joined Gentile sinners to himself by faith.”

“As it is written.” Origen: “In Isaiah, from which Paul took this testimony, it is written: ‘He will come because of Zion’ (Isa. 59:20); and what he says here, ‘when I shall take away their sins,’ is not written there at all. Yet by apostolic authority this is assumed. He puts Zion, that is, Jerusalem, for Judaea: the part which is the head of the kingdom, for the whole itself.”

And this is what he says: “He will come from Judaea,” namely, by being born in it, he who saves the Jews; or, in Origen’s words, “He will come because of Zion,” that is, in order to save it, as he defines it in saying: “who may rescue it” and free it from the captivity of the devil or the yoke of sin, which takes the soul captive away from God. And immediately explaining this he says: “And he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob,” that is, from the Jewish people. We may also distinguish it thus: “He will rescue,” namely, from the sin with which we are born, original sin, or from that which he himself found in them; “and he will turn away” the remaining sins which they would have committed unless he had turned them away.

Observe that when he says that he will be born in Judaea or will come because of Zion, he ascribes a certain glory to the Jews, in order to restrain the proud insult of the Gentiles. “And this is from me to them”: where we say “testament,” the Hebrew says *pactum*, “covenant,” that is, a firm promise. The Lord says this. For the things confirmed by a testament are especially stable: a promise, I say, to be fulfilled then, “when I shall take away,” that is, forgive, [Col. 0935B] “their sins.”

According to the Gospel. These two plural nominatives, “enemies” and “beloved,” do not clearly depend, in the sequence of the construction, on anything unless they are referred far above to what preceded—where it was said: “How much more shall these be grafted according to nature into their own olive tree.” They themselves, I say, are now also enemies according to the Gospel, on your account, etc. Perhaps the Apostle has used nominatives absolutely without a verb according to the custom of the Hebrew language, as where it is said: “When the Lord turned back” (Ps. 125:1), and: “The Lord—his seat is in heaven” (Ps. 10:5).

In the Epistle to the Galatians Paul himself, rebuking Peter for harmful dissimulation, says: “If you, being a Jew, live as a Gentile and not as a Jew, how do you compel Gentiles to Judaize?” (Gal. 2:14). Again: “But I, brethren, if I preach circumcision, why do I still suffer persecution?” (Gal. 3:11 [sic]). From this it is clear that Paul especially, and the other preachers of evangelical freedom, endured the greatest enmities from the Jews and Jewish converts because they refused to impose upon the Gentiles the burdens of the Law, knowing that those legal observances were now wholly useless and that Gentiles could scarcely or never be brought into them.

This is what Paul now recalls when he says: I call them “enemies,” that is, opponents of me and those like me according to the Gospel—that is, as is evident from our preaching, which is most hostile to their boasting because it wholly forbids the burdens of the Law—and this “on your account,” O Gentiles, upon whom we do not wish to impose these burdens. [Col. 0936A] Yet they are “beloved” by us, that is, above others they cling to our desire that, when converted, they may be saved, on account of their fathers, the most righteous and of great authority—namely, the patriarchs and prophets. Yet this is according to God’s election more than according to their own merits: he chose them through his grace when the Gentiles were rejected, and wonderfully exalted them.

For it is well known that God himself has shown his grace to children because of their fathers. We know that he spared Solomon the idolater because of his righteous father; and that Moses implored and obtained pardon for a sinful people because of the fathers’ merits.

“For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” As though someone said: What concern is there for the election of the ancient fathers, or for the promises and benefits once bestowed on them by God, when it now plainly appears, in the wickedness of their children, that what the Lord did in response to their prayers displeases him? The Apostle replies: No; “the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” That is, it never displeases him that he has given something to someone, or called anyone to faith, because his will is altogether unchangeable; nor does he ever disapprove having done what he once judged ought to be done. That would indeed be to repent of his act.

In another sense, however, God is sometimes said to repent, namely, by changing or grieving over what he had done—not by disapproving his act, that is, not by judging that it had been evil; for this alone would properly be called repentance, according to the saying of the philosophers: “Repentance accompanies an evil deed.” [Col. 0936B] In God’s elect, his gifts precede their calling, when he prospers their will so that they assent to his call and obey his command.

“For just as.” I have said that by the fullness of Gentiles converted, the Jews too are to be converted to faith. Nor is it surprising that it should happen to them, O Gentiles, just as it happened to you. This is what the phrase means: “For just as,” etc. “Through their”—that is, when they repelled the preaching from themselves, the apostles were quickly compelled to pass over to the Gentiles. “So these,” that is, the Jews, “now have not believed in your mercy”: that is, they have not received the preaching through which you obtained mercy from God, so that after you they too may subsequently come to the faith, and may be made humbler because they follow you into the faith, being taught in this respect, as it were, by the instruction of your example.

“But he has shut up all,” that is, he has allowed all to be bound in the blindness of unbelief, both Jews and Gentiles, in order that in the subsequent conversion of all he might show his great mercy: for it is clear that before faith no merit is present in them, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

“O the depth.” This is an exclamation of wonder at this vast abyss of divine judgment: namely, at the first election of the Jewish people and rejection of the Gentiles; and at the new election of the Gentiles now, in the conversion of many, and the rejection of the Jews—only so few having now been converted, though they are to be converted more fully later—so that those who once preceded the Gentiles in faith may afterwards follow and become “the last first” (Matt. 19:30). [Col. 0937A]

“Depth,” that is, the hidden profundity of the rich and abundant wisdom of God, as regards his foreknowledge; and of knowledge, as regards the effect of his own work, from which those things foreseen may now be known. “How incomprehensible”: that is, how incapable we are of knowing those causes of his dispensations or arrangements—why it was fitting that things should be done thus before they were done; and, after the works have been effected, “how unsearchable are his ways.” For the ways of God, by which knowledge of him is attained, are his works, as the same Apostle mentioned above when he said: “For his invisible things from the creation,” etc. God’s works, then, which we daily experience by sense, are unsearchable to us because we have not yet undertaken by reason to investigate their hidden natures.

Nor is this surprising: “For who has known the mind of God?” That is, who has been able of himself to comprehend the reasoning he had in his foreknowledge concerning what he would do? Or whom did he consult concerning what he would do, so as to be instructed by that person’s counsel what or how he ought to act? “Or who”—after displaying the supreme incomprehensible wisdom of God, he shows his supreme goodness—has first given to him? For he bestows everything on us before he receives anything from us.

Then, bringing his admiration to an end in an act of thanksgiving, the Apostle says: “For from him are all things”: that is, every nature of substance, as created by him; “through him,” namely, preserved by him, that it may remain; “and in him,” as brought to perfection in the best end, when their most excellent maker and disposer is glorified and praised in them. For this purpose he creates and preserves them, as it is written in Proverbs: “God created all things for himself, even the wicked for the evil day” (Prov. 16:4).

As blessed Augustine observes in Book V on Genesis [Note: [Col. 0937D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV, col. 235], each creature is “evening” insofar as it is considered in itself, but “morning” insofar as it is referred to the praise of the Creator: considered in itself it has, as it were, a deficiency, but in the Creator’s praise an advancement.

Perhaps someone will ask how every nature of substance is preserved so as to remain, when the spirits of irrational animals are believed to be governed by the flesh and to perish utterly with the flesh. But indeed, if those spirits too, like ours, are substances—namely, as some think, a certain rarefaction of the elements—then when they cease to be spirits, that is, cease to animate those bodies, they nevertheless do not cease to be substances. Similarly, when flesh, with which they are said to perish, ceases to be, it does not lose the nature of bodily substance. [Col. 0937D]

It may also be asked: since God himself is to be praised for his own sake rather than for his works, how does the Apostle say that he is to be glorified for his works—that is, worthy of the highest praise? For he is good or worthy of praise from himself rather than from his works; and his works ought rather to be praised or called good because of him than he because of his works. But although he himself is good and worthy of praise more from himself than from his effects, the very action of thanksgiving, or the effect of our praise which we render to him, follows from the works which we know through him. Thus the praise of any craftsman is known in his works: although he is already worthy of praise because of the skill he possesses, his praise follows upon knowledge of his works.

Nor does the Apostle here say that God is worthy of praise because of the works he has made; rather, he exhorts us to praise him because of the works which we know. “To him be glory,” he says—that is, the best, highest, and far-reaching renown—“unto the ages,” that is, through every succession of times. “Amen,” that is, “let it be,” which is an adverb of wishing, though sometimes also of confirmation, when it is used to mean “so it is” or “it is true.” [Col. 0938B]

## CHAPTER XII.

Therefore I beseech you, since he is indeed such and so great, “from whom are all things, through whom,” etc., to prepare yourselves as a sacrifice rather than slaughtering your cattle for him. He constrains them as if by adjuration when he says, “By the mercy of God”; as though he said: “As you trust in his mercy, so prepare yourselves, as far as you can, to obtain it.” When the bodies of animals were offered in sacrifice, they were killed; but when our bodies are offered to God, they die to vices in such a way that they are not deprived of life. This is what he means by “a living sacrifice.” And then indeed the service of our immolation is rational [Col. 0938C], if we thus sacrifice ourselves rather than slaughter our cattle for him, or kill ourselves for his sake.

“To be conformed to this age,” that is, to imitate worldly people who love the present life; “but be reformed,” that is, strive to restore and renew the faculty of human reason, long darkened by sins. “So that you may prove,” that is, may be able to know, or also to show others and demonstrate by reason, what the will of God is: what God wishes us to do, so that we may be good in ourselves—indeed, also good to others, or pleasing to God himself—and finally perfected, consummated in virtues, ever growing toward what is better, or toward the perfect blessedness of heavenly life.

“For I say.” I have said, “Do not be conformed to this age, but be reformed,” etc.; and I rightly admonish you of this [Col. 0938D], because I say it through the grace given to me—that is, I am compelled to say it by the teaching-office imposed upon me over you—to all who are among you, that is, scattered among the Gentiles, for whose sake I was specially sent as an apostle: “Not to think more highly than one ought, but to think unto sobriety.”

He thinks more highly than he ought who not only distinguishes evils from goods by rational knowledge, according to the philosopher’s saying, “For knowledge of evil cannot be lacking to the righteous,” but also learns them by experience—according to which the tree was called “the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” This is indeed the disposition of the age, that is, of worldly and carnal persons: enticed by the experience of pleasures, as by a certain sweetness of taste, they come to know evils themselves [Col. 0939A]. In this experience they exceed the bounds of sober and honorable living, while shamefully serving their pleasures.

“And to each one,” namely, of us, I say this very thing: namely, not to think more highly, etc. “As God has divided the measure of faith,” that is, let each fulfill this according as he believes it ought to be done. “For as”—as though someone asked, “Is there a different judgment among unbelievers in distinguishing good and evil?” The Apostle answers that there is; but the gifts of divine grace among them are also different. This he shows by an apt comparison, saying: “So indeed [the members] do not have the same action,” that is, the same office; so we, many as we are according to the diversity of persons, are united in one body, Christ, and in the same sacraments [Col. 0939B].

“Members one of another,” that is, supplying one another’s office and administering to the other what that person cannot fulfill. For the eye becomes, as it were, a member of the hand when it supplies sight so that the hand can work. Likewise, every believer ought to minister the gift of grace which he has to another, so that the faithful may be bound together most closely in mutual charity when they help one another reciprocally and each recognizes the other as himself.

I have said, “each [is] a member of the other”; and rightly so, because they possess diverse gifts of God’s grace bestowed on them. He immediately subdivides these gifts, saying: “Whether prophecy,” namely, having it—that is, the grace of interpreting, that is, expounding, divine words. Hence he says also to the Corinthians: “He who prophesies speaks to men for edification” (I Cor. XIV, 3), “according to the proportion of faith.”

He has prophecy who, in his preaching, regulates his words according to what he believes his hearers need, and discerns what ought to be preached to this group or that according to their capacity: now administering milk to little ones, now solid food to the more mature, just as Paul himself teaches by his own example in writing to those same Corinthians. The Psalmist foresaw this discernment of the apostles when he said: “Day pours forth speech to day, and night reveals knowledge to night” (Ps. XVIII, 3). Thus “according to the proportion of his faith” means, as though one said, according to the discernment which he believes himself to possess; where, if perhaps he errs, his charity excuses that ignorance.

“Or ministry [Col. 0939D] in ministering.” Throughout all these expressions, “according to the proportion of faith” must be understood: that is, we should do all things discerningly, according to what we believe ought to be done. By ministry he means the office of bodily work, such as sewing or building. He has ministry in serving others who seeks in it the greater benefit of others rather than his own, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another” (I Cor. X, 24).

“Or he who teaches, let him be in teaching,” that is, let him teach what he believes ought to be taught. Likewise, “he who exhorts,” that is, let him be engaged in persuasion. He speaks “according to the proportion of faith” who does not distinguish the prophecy understood above from teaching and exhortation. For whoever speaks for edification speaks either by teaching something or by exhorting to something.

Explain it thus: “Or he who teaches,” namely, the proportion of faith, “let him be discerning in exhorting,” namely, as far as he is able, what things are to be commended to which people, just as what things are to be taught; according to that saying of Truth: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine” (Matt. VII, 6).

“He who distributes,” that is, gives his goods generously to the needy, “in simplicity”: let him do this, it must be understood, that is, let him not have a double intention there—namely, one for temporal and one for eternal recompense. The Lord forbids this elsewhere when he says: “When you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matt. VI, 2).

Alternatively, “in simplicity” means: let there not be a double end in his intention, so that he establishes the end of his almsgiving both in himself [Col. 0940B] and in God, but only in God; or let him not do it deceitfully, as hypocrites do, who feign one thing while intending another. They pretend to do for God’s sake what they do more for human glory; or like those who give something to another, hoping to receive more from it, and pretend that they act from charity when they act rather from greed.

“He who is over others,” that is, holds the place of a prelate, “in diligence”: let him preside, it is understood, seeking their advantage rather than his own. Solomon warns concerning this diligence of prelates toward subjects, saying: “My son, if you have become surety for your friend, you have fastened your hand with a stranger; you are ensnared by the words of your mouth and caught by your own sayings. Therefore, my son, do what I say and free yourself, because you have fallen into your neighbor’s hand. Run, hasten, awaken your friend. Give not sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” [Col. 0940C] (Prov. VI, 1–4).

“He who shows mercy,” that is, forgives those who sin against him, should do so cheerfully and without any resentment of mind. Let him not shame the penitent, nor disgracefully reproach him with his sin, as though showing himself more saddened by his own injury than glad at the sinner’s conversion.

“Let love,” it is understood, “be unchanging, true, not feigned,” as it is written elsewhere: “Little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (I John III, 18). “Hating vices, clinging to virtues”; or departing in conduct and morals from a perverse person and imitating [Col. 0940D] the good, observing what is written: “With the holy man you will be holy,” etc. (II Kings XXII, 26).

“[Exercise] brotherly charity,” that is, mutually performing the effects of fraternal charity, so that each may help others as a brother and obey God as a Father. He admonishes us to provide not only for our neighbors’ benefit but also for their honor, saying, “in honor,” namely, “preferring one another”: that is, provide among yourselves for this, that when another wishes to honor you, you honor him first, and your benefit may precede his, so that it is rendered to you as though a debt rather than bestowed.

There are people who do not need our benefits and who are drawn more to love by honor than by usefulness; therefore, after the benefit of assistance, the Apostle provides for the honor by which they love [Col. 0941A]. “Not slothful in diligence”: that is, not delaying to fulfill the effects of our care for those subject to us, as it is written: “Whatever your hand can do, do earnestly,” etc. (Eccl. IX, 10). “Fervent in spirit”: as though he said, “Even if you cannot wholly fulfill the aforesaid things, at least burn with zeal of charity to fulfill them, and the will of good desire will suffice before God.”

“Serving the Lord.” After brotherly charity toward one’s neighbor, he ascends to the charity of God by which service is rendered. And when he was about to say, “serving the Lord,” the Apostle appropriately first said, “fervent in spirit,” so that this service may be understood as the submission of filial reverence arising from love rather than as servile submission arising from fear; as Christian rather than Jewish [Col. 0941B].

We serve the Lord alone, whatever service we render to anyone, if we establish in God the whole end of our submission: namely, if we render to prelates only for God’s sake the reverence that we show them, since they are his vicars and have received the authority of preeminence from him. For he who renders service to the envoy or vicar of some superior solely for the sake of that superior who sent him is said in this to serve that superior alone, and to render service or honor to him alone for whose sake it is done.

“Rejoicing in hope,” so that you may be “patient in tribulation.” Hence the Apostle James says: “Count it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into temptations, knowing that the testing,” etc. (Jas. I, 2). Being about to say, “patient in tribulation,” he fittingly first says, “rejoicing in hope,” so that the hope of recompense, going before, may make them strong against sufferings, while they attend to what is written: “Having been afflicted in few things, they shall be well ordered in many,” etc. (Wis. III, 5).

“Rejoicing in hope,” that is, in expectation of future blessedness, since hope is only of a good and of what is future. And because we cannot possess such constancy in suffering by our own strength, he admonishes us to persist in prayer for this, saying: “Continuing instant in prayer,” that is, standing in prayer rather than lying down. For those who do not raise themselves to God through devotion are, as it were, lying down, so that prayer may obtain its effect; they prepare words alone [Col. 0941D], not hearts. Of these the Lord complains through Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. XV, 8).

“Sharing in the necessities of the saints,” that is, sympathizing so with believers enduring poverty or adversity that we become participants in their poverty or tribulation: namely, when we bestow on them what we withhold from ourselves, or even incur danger or loss to rescue or defend them. Hence he says elsewhere: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. VI, 2). “Pursuing hospitality”: not merely offering it, but pursuing those who depart from us, so that we may draw even unwilling persons into lodging, as Lot did in receiving the angels.

“Bless those who persecute you”: that is, pray that it may go well even with them, so that you may thus build charity in them, as it is written: “For then you will heap coals of fire upon his head” [Col. 0942A] (Prov. XXVI, 21); or do this so that your prayer may more readily attain its effect, insofar as it will be more pleasing to God, who says: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have?” (Matt. V, 46). Both the Lord himself and his protomartyr Stephen displayed to us this perfection of love in their sufferings by praying for their enemies.

“Bless, and do not curse.” He says “bless” twice, so that we may have blessing both in mouth and in heart. Nor did he say, “Do not pronounce curses,” but, “Do not wish to curse.” For when we excommunicate someone because of obstinacy in his fault, we surely direct against him a sentence of cursing. Paul himself is read in the Acts of the Apostles to have cursed the man to whom he said: “May the Lord destroy you, whitewashed wall” (Acts XXIII, 3). But because saints do such things when compelled by zeal for justice, they have the act of cursing, not the will to curse.

This is the one place where it is not said that they should not curse at all, but that they should not wish to curse: namely, that the will to curse, not the act, is forbidden, just as the Lord says: “Do not swear” (Matt. V, 34). He forbids the will to swear rather than the act. So too, when a judge constrained by his law kills someone without willing it, he is excused from homicide, because it is not done by his will. He entirely dislikes the fact that the person punished has committed that for which the law commands him to be put to death; thus it is the law itself rather than the man that punishes him [Col. 0942C]—indeed, God himself, who established the law, who says: “I will kill and I will make alive” (Deut. XXXII, 39); and, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Deut. XXXII, 35; Heb. X, 30)—because he is God’s minister.

It seems not without reason to ask why, although God looks rather to hearts than to words, we nevertheless entreat him also with words. I think this is done for two reasons: one suited to God’s honor, the other to our benefit. When we ask something from God in prayer, by our very words we show that we can have from no one but him what we ask. The words we utter stir and move our affection and devotion toward God by their meaning, so that prayer itself is more effective [Col. 0942D] insofar as devotion is greater in the one praying.

“Rejoice with those who rejoice.” He uses infinitives in place of imperatives, saying “to rejoice” and “to weep” for “rejoice” and “weep”: that is, rejoice with the faithful over their progress, or grieve compassionately over their distress. For there is a false joy of the wicked with which one ought not rejoice, and a false sorrow of theirs with which one ought by no means grieve. Hence the Lord says: “The world will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful” (John XVI, 20). And Solomon says in Proverbs concerning the perverse: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. II, 14).

But since the same Solomon says elsewhere, “Nothing that happens to him will make the righteous sorrowful” (Prov. XII, 21), and the Apostle himself above says, “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God,” etc. [Col. 0943A] (Rom. VIII, 28), what can happen to the elect that should cause weeping? Or how are Rachel’s tears over the killing of her sons—who thus pass from misery to blessedness—reasonable?

Hence it is written concerning the weeping of the faithful at the passing of blessed Martin: “When he perceived that there was rather cause for rejoicing, if the force of grief did not rob him of reason.” Jerome, to Tyrasius, on the death of his daughter:

> “She has escaped such great and such severe storms of life, so many assaults of the devil, so many wars of the body, so many disasters of the world; and do we shed tears, as though we ourselves did not know what we suffer every day? For this reason the Lord also thus admonishes the disciples: ‘If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I go to the Father’ (John XIV, 28). Certainly, he wept for dead Lazarus; he grieved not for one dying, but rather for one about to rise again, and he wept for one whom, for the salvation of others, he was compelled to call back to the world. The Lord groaned in giving that life which you grieve has been taken away. Your tears contend against his. He did not wish to restore to labors one whom he loved, while you believe that you love one for whom you wished the torments of labors still to remain. He migrated from the hostile homeland to heaven. The Apostle recalls: ‘As long as we are in this world, we are pilgrims from God’” [Col. 0943B] (II Cor. V, 6).

Whence, then, are Rachel’s tears? Whence the compassion of the faithful over the killing of the righteous, which ends their misery and confers glory upon them? Or, since all things that happen to the elect work together for their good, as was said (Rom. VIII, 28), why is it that they are not saddened by whatever happens to them? (Prov. II, 14.) Why is it fitting for us to grieve over them, or for them to repent of anything, when in the other life, though they remember their sins, it is nevertheless certain that they are affected in no way by the sorrow of repentance, considering, namely, that even their sins worked together for their good?

Finally, since we do not doubt that all things are [ordered] best by God, to such an extent that it is good even for evils to exist; and since, according to the saying of Truth, “it is necessary that scandals come,” what can happen for which they may reasonably grieve? For if, as blessed Augustine recalls, it is good that evil should exist, whoever grieves over evil surely grieves over what it is good to exist; and whoever wishes it not to exist surely wishes not to exist what it is good to exist. Thus he seems contrary both to the divine dispensation and to reason [Col. 0943D], and it is said to God in vain, “Your will be done,” when, so far as lies in him, he opposes that will or disposition. But because the examination of these matters belongs to a higher philosophy, we reserve it for the perfection of our Theology.

“Thinking the same thing toward one another”: namely, through the affection of charity, regarding others as oneself, according to that saying of Truth: “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do also the same to them” (Matt. VII, 12); and: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. IV, 16). Or, thinking the same thing with others, as though regarding their goods as our own losses; or holding the same thing concerning faith, so that there may be no schisms in the catholic faith.

This seems especially to be the point of what follows: “Not thinking high things,” that is, not presumptuously advancing something through heresy, while seeking glory from some novelty. “But agreeing with the humble”—those, namely, to whom God gives grace, while resisting the proud (I Pet. V, 5)—joining ourselves to them in the unity of faith.

He teaches how we should do this when he adds: “Do not be wise in your own eyes,” that is, if you have any wisdom, do not turn it to your own glory or boast of it within yourselves. “I say also to you: repaying evil to no one for evil,” that is, punishing no one because he injured us, but rather because it is just.

We may also understand what was said, “Do not be wise,” etc., in a way that more fittingly joins it to this. For he is called wise in his own eyes who relies wholly on his own judgment, so that whatever he has decreed to be the case, he wishes to carry out. Since to no one who is angry does his anger seem hateful, whatever offense he suffers he considers must be avenged. He meets this danger when he says: “Repaying evil to no one for evil.” Above he had said: “Do not curse those who persecute you”; here he forbids evil deeds as well as evil words [Col. 0944B].

“Providing things good,” etc.: that is, striving as far as we can that our works may appear good not only to God but also to men, so that they may wish to imitate them or glorify God because of them, as Truth also says: “Let your light shine before men,” etc. (Matt. VII, 16). “If possible, having peace with all men.” Therefore, as we have said, repaying evil to no one for evil and providing good things also before men.

“That,” namely, having peace with all, “is from you”: that is, you have it from your own nature, namely, that you should be most harmonious with those whom you see to be more closely related to you by nature. Hence another Apostle says: “For if he does not love the neighbor whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (I John IV, 20). For the more closely related we are by nature, the more nature itself invites us to love.

Have peace, I say, with all to such a degree that, if you have gone too far by offending someone, you do not defend yourselves, that is, excuse your own faults; but “give place to wrath,” that is, yield patiently to an angry and offended brother, bearing his anger and not stirring him again by your excuse. For then we would resist [Col. 0944D] his anger so that it would burn more fiercely or remain in him; we would not yield so that it might pass from him.

“For it is written,” namely, in Proverbs [Deuteronomy]: “Vengeance is mine” (Deut. XXXII, 35). As though he said: “Therefore, when you offend others, you ought patiently to bear those who have been offended and, as far as you can, to soothe their anger, because even if you had been offended by them, the Lord exhorts you not to avenge yourselves for it, but to reserve vengeance for him who says, ‘Vengeance is mine’—understand, ‘reserve it’—‘and I will repay’ (ibid.), namely, so that I may avenge you.”

It should be noted that if this is understood as an exhortation to perfection rather than a command, as also is what Truth says, “Do not demand back what is yours” (Luke VI, 30), then the statement above, “Not ourselves,” etc., may likewise be understood as an exhortation to perfection: that when we are able to defend ourselves against persecutors, he nevertheless says it is more perfect not to defend ourselves at all, but rather to endure the violence inflicted on us than, in defending the body, to wound our soul by killing through anger the person against whom perhaps we cannot otherwise defend ourselves [Col. 0945A].

But just as we explained the earlier statement as a command, perhaps this too, “Vengeance is mine,” etc., can be understood as a command. For just as a judge constrained by law or by love of God, who instituted the law, kills the guilty person, he is said not so much to do this himself as the law or God himself, who commands it and uses him as an instrument for doing it; so too vengeance is to be attributed to zeal for justice or to love. Therefore, God’s command that vengeance be reserved for him, so that he may do it, means that no one should presume to avenge himself, nor, as has been said, should God do this through that person who says: “I will kill, and I will make alive” (Deut. XXXII, 39).

Hence Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus*, ch. 68 [Note: [Col. 0945D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV, col. 707]:

> “When a man is justly killed, the law kills him, not you.”

The same, *City of God*, book II [Note: [Col. 0946D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, col. 35]:

> “‘You shall not kill,’ excepting those whom God commands to be killed.”

But he does not himself kill who owes service to the one commanding, namely, assistance to one using the sword. A person, therefore, kills when he acts from himself and not from God. But when he acts by divine institution or command, God does it through him as an instrument rather than the person himself. For we say that any powerful person builds or does something when it is carried out at his command. Thus killing is forbidden to man, not to God [Col. 0945C].

Perhaps we similarly prohibit suddenly reclaiming “our own things,” because they are ours, just as [we prohibit] loving those who love us, that is, because they love us. For what we ought not to possess for our own sake, establishing in ourselves the end of that possession, we should much less reclaim when taken from us for our own sake. Perhaps God wishes to dispose of it better through others than through us, or foresaw that it would harm us.

Therefore, we may lawfully reclaim those things that are God’s rather than those that are ours: that is, for God’s sake rather than for our own, so that we may dispose of things according to his will rather than ours. Then God, rather than we, reclaims his own things in us, since we act so as to make them God’s rather than ours [Col. 0945D].

“But if.” I have said, “Do not avenge yourselves, but rather let God [avenge],” as has been said; but on the contrary, do good to those who do evil. This is what “but if,” etc., means. For the phrase gives the reason why this should be done to enemies: because by this means we may readily draw them to salvation.

The head is the chief part of the body, as though adorned with all the bodily senses; it signifies our mind or soul. Coals of fire are the burnings of charity, or the laments of repentance by which the soul is deeply tormented and kindled against itself with flames of indignation. Therefore let us heap these coals upon the mind of our enemy [Col. 0946A] by doing him good, when thereby we kindle him to love toward us or to repentance for the evils which he inflicted on us.

“Do not be conquered,” that is, overcome, by your vice: namely, if anger so rules you that you render evil for evil. Rather conquer and restrain that anger itself through good returned for evil. For it is not evil to serve a human being, but to serve vice. Hence he immediately adds:

## CHAPTER XIII

“Let every soul,” that is, every rational creature, “be subject,” that is, obey willingly. He says this against the opinion of certain faithful persons, to whom it seemed wholly unjust and unfitting that anyone already converted to the faith of Christ should thereafter serve or obey earthly power, as though such authorities had not altogether been established by God. Hence the Lord himself, paying Caesar’s tax for himself and Peter, exhorted us to this by his own example.

“To higher powers,” that is, those set over them by God, as he immediately adds: “For there is no power,” whether it appears good or evil, “except from God,” that is, established by his dispensation. When rulers are good, this is a divine gift. But when they are evil, they are established by God either for the punishment of perverse persons or for the purification or testing of the good; for he orders even every impiety well. Hence the power of the devil or of any impious person is called good, although their will is most evil and their action perverse. For they receive power from God [Col. 0946C], but have an evil will from themselves.

Thus Truth says to the wicked Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above.” And the devil could not attack Job in any respect until permission for this power was granted him by God. “But those things which are from God,” namely, are instituted, though not merely permitted. For God permits sins, but does not institute them. “Are ordered,” that is, rationally instituted.

“Therefore, he who”—since every power has been instituted by God—“acquires condemnation”: that is, those who do this deserve to be condemned, because they resist God rather than man. But it is one thing to resist the tyranny of an evil prelate, another to resist his just power which he has received from God. When he acts violently in something which does not belong to his authority and institution, then surely, by resisting him in this, we oppose tyranny rather than power, the man rather than God, because he presumes this from himself and does not act from God. But when we resist him in matters for which he has been lawfully established, then we oppose the power [Col. 0946D].

“For rulers,” that is, their power, “are not to be feared by those who do good, but by those who do evil.” He immediately shows this by saying: “Do you wish,” you, anyone, “not to fear authority rather than man? Do good, and by sparing you it will approve your works and testify that you act well.” “He bears the sword,” that is, he is not irrationally equipped even to kill, because in this he serves God, who established him for this purpose, to avenge evils. This is the meaning of “for he is God’s minister, an avenger unto wrath”: an avenger, being angry at the evildoing rather than at the human being, that is, at his malice rather than his substance [Col. 0947A].

Therefore, because he is God’s minister, obey him as God, and do this “of necessity,” that is, because of the evident benefit you receive from the ministry of rulers, “not only because of wrath”—namely, theirs—“but also because of your conscience”: that is, not only because of the force of their vengeance, by which they would immediately punish our disobedience to them, but also because you yourselves know that they are necessary to restrain wickedness. Therefore, because they are necessary to you in avenging those who do evil, as has been said, you pay them taxes. In this they serve God, namely, when they avenge evils, so that from the very fact that they receive taxes they may be able to fulfill their office, which they could not exercise without such expenses; and therefore [you pay] because you know this, or because in this matter they serve under God.

[Col. 0948A] “Render to all what you owe them for this. To whom tribute,” namely, you owe tribute, “render tribute.” Origen: “Tributes are for land; taxes are for commerce.” Haymo: “Render to him to whom you ought to render tribute, just as the Creator himself paid the didrachm for himself and Peter.”

*Tributum* (“tribute”) is said to derive from *tribuni* (“tribunes”), and tribunes from *tribus* (“tribes”), since Romulus divided the people subject to him into three parts: senators, who were also called consuls; soldiers; and farmers. Over each part he set one leader, who was also called a tribune because he presided over one of the parts. The assessment exacted from subjects was called tribute.

“To whom tax”: a tax is a fiscal tribute and is called *vectigal*, from *vehere* (“to carry”), because it is collected from goods carried, that is, transported merchandise. “To whom fear”: fear is especially to be shown to irascible prelates [Col. 0948B], lest, stirred by anger, they exact more vengeance than is fitting. But the gentle should be honored all the more, because patience makes them worthier and kinder.

## BOOK V

[Col. 0947]

[Col. 0947C] “Owe no one anything,” that is, free yourselves from all debts in such a manner that you recognize yourselves to owe nothing except charity. Charity is always to be paid in such a way that it is always owed, and always to be given in such a way that it is then most retained when it is given. But when money is paid, it comes to the person to whom it is returned and departs from the payer.

To love another is to wish him good for his own sake. “One another,” that is, among yourselves, so that love may be mutual. Understand “neighbor” as every human being joined to us by the nature of humanity and declaring a common origin with us from the same father, Adam. For if the Apostle understood “neighbor” to mean only a Jew, according to what the law says, “You shall not lend at interest to your neighbor, but to a foreigner” (Deut. XXIII, 19–20), his statement that one who loves his neighbor does not commit adultery [Col. 0947D], etc., could not stand, since these acts can also be committed among unbelievers.

He means the Law of Moses, in which the commandments that follow are contained. “For you shall not commit adultery.” The law seems to use adultery or fornication for every unlawful sexual union; otherwise it would nowhere exclude that fornication committed by persons who are not married. Thus, when it says, “You shall not commit adultery,” it uses the species for the genus, just as conversely it adds, “You shall not kill” (Exod. XX, 13): the genus for the species. For it does not forbid a person to kill an animal, but a human being.

A human being kills another human being, and not God through him, as we have also indicated above, when he acts by his own will and is not constrained by the sanction of divine law. Concerning this unjust killing, the Lord, instructing Peter, said: “He who takes up the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. XXVI, 52). He says, “He who takes it up on his own,” not one to whom it is given by authority for the exercise of justice; such a person is worthy to perish by the sword [Col. 0948C]. A person likewise acts entirely without God when, acting to fulfill his own will rather than to administer justice, he is a murderer.

Hence Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, ch. 20 [Note: [Col. 0947D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV, col. 622]:

> “When an officer of a judge kills one whom the law has commanded to be killed, certainly, if he does so voluntarily, he is a murderer, even if he kills one whom he knows ought to have been killed by a judge.”

“You shall not steal” (Exod. XX, 13–14), that is, you shall not fraudulently take what belongs to another. The Hebrews did not commit theft when, by divine command, they despoiled the Egyptians of possessions that belonged more to God than to the Egyptians themselves. “You shall not speak false testimony,” that is, by speaking against your conscience. “You shall not covet,” namely, what belongs to another, not merely refrain from taking it.

“And if [there is] any commandment,” understand, the commandment of love is fulfilled in this precept: “You shall love,” etc. It is one thing to say “as yourself,” another “as much as yourself.” In the former, likeness is shown; in the latter, equality. Thus when Truth says, “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father [is merciful],” he expresses likeness in mercy rather than equality.

But if I ought to love each person as much as I love myself, all would have to be loved equally by me. Yet since no one seems to be loved except for God’s sake, each person is worthy to be loved more insofar as he is held dearer to God and is better. For if God, because he is better, is to be loved above all, then whoever is better after him is to be loved more than others. Otherwise charity is not ordered. We love more the person for whom we wish greater blessedness, though we take less care concerning his bodily goods than concerning our own or those of persons specially attached to us [Col. 0949A].

We love any person as ourselves when we wish him to attain blessedness as we wish ourselves to attain it, holding the same intention toward him as toward ourselves: namely, because we judge this good for him as for ourselves. For perhaps when someone hates another, he may wish him already to be in paradise, than which he can wish him nothing better; yet he does not thereby love him, since he does this not so much for that person’s sake as for his own, to be rid of him.

“Love of neighbor”: truly, whoever loves his neighbor will not commit adultery, will not kill, etc., because he works absolutely no evil. Hence it is evident that David, when he fornicated with Bathsheba or delivered Uriah to death, did not love his neighbor. And since another Apostle says, “For he who does not love the neighbor whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (I John IV, 21), he clearly seems then not to have loved God either. How can anyone be said to love another as himself when he does not truly love even himself, since by sparing himself he does not spare himself from the death of the soul? For it is written: “He who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. X, 6).

Therefore, fulfilment. Since, that is, love even of one’s neighbour fulfils the law, as has been said, it is certainly much more true that love, its genus, receives this designation. Since the whole sum of our merits consists in the love of God and of neighbour, each must, if possible, be carefully described by us; and it must further be shown how, omitting the love of God, which is the greater, the Apostle dared to say that love of neighbour fulfils the law. Love of God with all one’s heart is that best disposition of will toward God by which we strive to please him all the more insofar as we recognize that he ought to be pleased all the more. We do this with all our heart, or with all our soul, when we direct the intention of our love wholly toward him, attending not so much to what is useful to ourselves as to what is pleasing to him. Otherwise, we should establish ourselves rather than him as the end of our love—that is, as its final and supreme cause. God’s love toward us, however, is the very disposition of divine grace concerning our salvation. One loves one’s neighbour as oneself who, for God’s sake, has such a good will toward him [Col. 0949D] that he strives so to conduct himself toward him that the other cannot justly complain of him, just as he himself does not wish that the other should do anything to him of which he could justly complain.

The two precepts of the natural law belong to this love of neighbour: “What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16); and: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. 7:12). Perhaps the proper understanding of these precepts is not evident to everyone. For we often bestow honour or a benefit upon others out of charity which we refuse to receive from others; or we often punish others for justice’s sake, even kill them, though we would in no way wish to suffer this at the hands of others. Who, moreover, does not know that we sometimes wish things done to ourselves which it is not fitting to wish? Yet we ought not on that account [Col. 0950A] to do them to others. For instance, if I wish someone to agree with me in wrongdoing, ought I likewise to agree with others in sinning? Often too superiors demand from subordinates services which it is altogether unfitting for them to render to their subordinates; and the poor wish the rich to do many things for them which they themselves cannot possibly do for others. How, then, can they fulfil, “Whatever you wish them to do to you,” etc., unless perhaps it is said that this is not a general commandment, but is prescribed only for those able to return benefits—as when it is said, “Give alms” (Luke 11:41), or “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isa. 58:7): it is imposed only on those who can do this.

To respond briefly to these objections: when it is said, “What you do not wish,” etc., and, “Whatever you wish,” etc., [Col. 0950B] these must be understood so that the former concerns avoiding injuries and the latter bestowing benefits, as if it said: “As you do not wish to be injured, so abstain from wronging others; and as you wish merciful aid in your needs, so aid others in theirs, if you can.” But no good person admits that he can do what he believes not to be in his power, or what he believes does not suit him. Since God alone is to be loved for his own sake, while one’s neighbour is to be loved for God’s sake, it is evident that love of God is included in love of neighbour, since the latter cannot exist without the former. Thus, when we described it, we prudently added “for God’s sake.” Yet, although love of God is naturally prior to love of neighbour, just as God is naturally prior to one’s neighbour, it does not conversely include love of neighbour as necessarily as God can be loved and can exist without a neighbour. Thus the Apostle appropriately seems to have said that love of neighbour fulfils the law, rather than that love of God does so.

It may reasonably be asked whether we ought also to love those who are in hell, or those not predestined to life; or whether the saints, even in the other life, love every neighbour as themselves—both those whom they already see damned or, through divine revelation, foresee as to be damned, and the elect. But since, as we have said, every human being must be understood as a neighbour, how will they retain love of neighbour if they do not love some persons? Or how are they held more perfect there than here if love of neighbour in them is contracted or diminished? For [Col. 0950D] when we love holy angels, we ought not to love perverse ones. How then is either their love or ours rational if it embraces even the members of the devil? Is it because in this life we do not know who is predestined and who is not that we reasonably love all and pray even for all? Or, if doing this is not rational, how are we commanded to do it for them rather than for ourselves, when it benefits us more than them? How can an intention be right when it is mistaken? For we do this because we believe it will benefit them. Or, if ignorance still excuses us, what answer do we give to the fact that, although we know that not all, or only very few, will be saved, according to the saying of Truth, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:15), and: [Col. 0951A] “Narrow is the way that leads to life,” etc. (Matt. 7:14), nevertheless we wish all to be saved and pray for all, knowing that neither our will nor our prayer will attain its effect?

But you cite Augustine: “Have charity, and do whatever you wish.” And you recall Jerome: “Charity has no measure.” Hence charity often compels us to exceed due measure, so that we wish something to happen which is in no way good or just, and conversely do not wish something to happen which is good—for example, that saints should be killed or afflicted, though these things also work together for their good. But we reserve discussion of this for our *Ethics*.

And knowing this. Construe it thus: “And knowing this time, because it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep. [Col. 0951B] Let us cast off the works of darkness,” etc.—that is, from sleep and from negligence or torpor in good work. When he says “hour,” which is a brief time, rather than a week, month, or year, he urges us to do this without delay. The shorter the time in which something must be done, the sooner it must be done.

“For now.” We must rise quickly from sleep because now, with good works added to our faith, we are nearer to receiving the prize of eternal life than when we first believed—that is, at the very beginning of our conversion. He continues the metaphor drawn from sleep in fitting words, saying that the night, the time for sleeping, has already passed and the day has arrived. Night is ignorance of salvation; day is knowledge or illumination. It is no wonder that, while we were oppressed by this night, we were sluggish in working. The blindness of unbelief was expelled from our hearts with the coming of the teaching of Christ, who said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). Yet it was not so much we who withdrew from this night as it withdrew from us; nor was it so much we who approached it as it approached us, because divine grace worked thus when we had in no way sought it, as is written of the Lord himself: “I was found by those seeking me,” etc.

“Let us therefore cast off.” Since, that is, this night has already passed and day has drawn near. He does not say, “Let them be cast off now,” but “Let us cast them off,” because, now enlightened through faith, we are able to act. “Works of darkness” means evil works, according to the saying of Truth: “Everyone who does evil hates the light” [Col. 0951D] (John 3:20); or the works of unbelievers and persons in darkness, upon whose hearts that Sun of righteousness has not yet risen to illuminate them. “Armour of light” means the virtues of believers, by which they fight against vices or demonic temptations. Let us, I say, put on the armour of light, so that, thus clothed, we may walk honourably as in the day, when each person puts on more precious clothing.

He first teaches what works are to be cast off. “Not in revelries”—supply, “let us walk”; that is, let us not place our feet, understood as the affections of the mind, in these things. A *commessatio* is called a banquet assembled from different households, where each contributes something different from his own supplies; and thus each eats more freely, as though feeding from his own, and more greedily, lest, by consuming less food and spending equally, he seem to do an injury. [Col. 0952A] He indulges his gluttony all the more freely because he is stirred by the examples of very many people. Thus *commessatio* is called, as stated, a corporate eating, from *comedere*, “to eat together.” Jerome: “A *commessatio* is a pooling of the table.” Such revelries Solomon also forbids in Proverbs, saying: “Do not be among drinking feasts, nor among the revelries of those who contribute flesh for eating; for those given to drink and those who pay shares will be consumed” (Prov. 23:20–21). Haymo: “A *commessatio* is an alternation of tables.” For there are banquets held in turn, prepared by companions on successive days and occasions. There are others held in common, when one brings bread, another meat, another wine, and so forth. [Col. 0952B] *Tria*—the printed, grammatically anomalous term—is said in the masculine gender to mean a cup fit for drinking; from it *ebrietas* (“drunkenness”) is named, and this is excessive drinking. What the Apostle says here, “not in revelries and drunkennesses,” refers to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “See that your hearts are not weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 23:34), that is, by excessive food and drink.

“Not in beds,” which follow revelries and drunkenness. He adds this consequently, so that they may be avoided all the more because worse things arise from them. *Cubilia*, “beds,” properly belong to beasts or irrational animals, to which the beds of drunkards are compared: there, the image of God—that is, reason—having been extinguished by drunkenness, “[they] became like horse and mule, which [Col. 0952C] have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9). Drunkenness is also followed by unchastity. Hence the Apostle elsewhere exhorts: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is licentiousness” (Eph. 5:18). The drunkenness of blessed Lot furnished us a most evil example of this. Thus “in beds and unchastities” means, as though he said, “in unchaste beds,” where drunkards lust like cattle without any reverence.

Ovid, preacher of impurity, urges fornicators to go especially to such revelries and drunkennesses, so that from them they may readily take an occasion for their fornications. “Not in strife.” Drunkenness is tumultuous and readily bursts forth into quarrelling. By “jealousy” he means evil zeal, that is, a stirring of hatred against another; for strife most often follows insults or injuries. Nearly all people, and especially free-born persons, are more readily inflamed to hatred by the shamefulness of words than by the infliction of losses.

[Col. 0952D] After the works of darkness which he says are to be cast off, he adds the armour of light—that is, the virtues of Christ which we are to put on—saying: “But put on.” Whoever assumes the disposition of one meek or cruel is said to put on a lamb or a lion. Likewise, whoever follows Christ’s footsteps and strives, to the extent of his ability, to adorn himself with all virtues is said to put on Christ, who is the fullness of every virtue. The same Apostle elsewhere says of Christ: “He became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30). It is as if he openly said: He became all virtues for us, so that, when we are adorned with virtues, we may rightly be said to put on Christ [Col. 0953A]. And so that you may be able especially to put on Christ, do not live carnally, since the flesh desires against the spirit—that is, against Christ. “Make no provision for the desires”: “for desires,” he says, that is, not for the superfluity of pleasures but for the necessity of nourishment. For necessities must be provided even for our body, just as superfluities must be withheld, so that the substance of nature may be preserved and the incentives to vice denied. He therefore does not say simply, “Have no care for the flesh,” but “for its desires,” that is, for pleasures rather than necessities. We ought to be enemies not of nature but of vices.

## Chapter XIV

“But receive the weak.” [Col. 0953B] When he had said above, “not in strife,” here he immediately strives, by exposition, to put an end especially to a perverse contention in the primitive Church. Some Jews newly converted to the faith and not yet sufficiently instructed in the liberty of Christian faith thought that the carnal observances of the law still had to be kept, and especially that we ought to abstain from pork and other foods forbidden by the law—perhaps chiefly because whatever appears to be abstinence is reckoned as a virtue. Therefore, just as above he forbade superfluous revelries, so here he counsels against superfluous abstinences, lest through the dissension of this contention the still weak—that is, imperfect—faith of converted Jews should be scandalized away from God, so that they might return to Judaism if they were forbidden these abstinences which the law had previously sanctioned, indeed which the Lord himself had sanctioned through the law. Hence the Apostle counsels those among the Romans who were already perfect in faith or teaching [Col. 0953C] that, if any of the newly converted Jews is still weak—that is, imperfect—in faith, not yet believing that Christ or evangelical doctrine suffices for salvation without the carnal observances of the law, they should not reject him on that account, but receive him as he comes to conversion, not disputing about his scruples—that is, not contending over his belief in such matters. For it can readily happen that one whose faith is imperfect at the beginning of conversion, after being instructed little by little, later attains perfection.

[Col. 0953D] Another explains the source of these disputes, saying that one person—other, that is, than the previously mentioned one whose faith is imperfect—believes that he may eat all things, that is, that he may eat any foods without thereby incurring guilt under the law. “But he who”—as though he said: “But he who does not believe this should abstain from those foods [lacuna], lest, by acting against his own conscience, he sin.” And this is: “He who is weak,” namely in this faith of the foregoing words, fearing that he will be defiled by certain foods, “let him eat vegetables”; that is, I advise him to use foods which he can easily obtain, which occasion less scandal to others, and from which he may also gain some commendation for his religious devotion. For if he ate some meats but not others, he would easily be convicted of Judaizing. But when he abstains from all alike [Col. 0954A] and is content with poorer foods, it is imputed to religious devotion rather than to error of faith.

“He who.” After saying that there should be no disputing in such matters, he also says that one person should not inwardly judge and, as it were, consider condemnable another who does not eat all things—that is, who abstains from some things. And one who does not eat all things should not therefore judge—that is, consider condemnable—the one who eats, as if he were a transgressor of the law. For God receives and does not reject him, both the one who eats and the one who abstains. Many, indeed, were converted to the faith while still erring in many matters, and were later gradually corrected and taught.

Note that he says that the person coming is “received” by God rather than coming by his own power, according to the saying of Truth: “No one comes to me unless my Father draws him” [Col. 0954B] (John 6:44). “Who are you?” As though he said: “Who do you think you are, that you presume to judge another’s servant—that is, to prescribe according to your own judgment what he ought to do?” This means: Leave the ordering of the servant’s life to his Lord, who, whether by himself or through his vicars, may instruct him in these matters when he wills—not to you, who are a fellow servant and have come not to command but to obey, like him. His state in faith, whether sound or fallen into error, is left to his Lord—that is, to the judgment of his Lord alone; and to him alone it belongs to determine either matter, from whom he himself will receive what he has deserved.

[Col. 0954C] “But he will stand.” As though he said: “I said, ‘he stands or falls.’ But because the things said must be interpreted or expounded in the better sense, I say rather, ‘he will stand’; that is, he will not be condemned on this account, because he abstains from zeal for the law lest he sin against conscience.” “For God is able.” As though he said: “For this, I think—or charitably affirm—is indeed better, since no obstacle appears why this ought not to be hoped for.” And this is: “God is able,” etc. God is said to be able because no rationale appears by which his doing something may be prevented—that is, no authority contradicts it. Thus, “God is able” means as though it said: “No reason seems opposed to his doing this.”

“For one.” The Apostle adds the reason why some judge or rebuke others: from their own consciences. One person judges that a day among days should be observed in abstinence from the things mentioned above [Col. 0954D]—that is, one day with another day intervening, as now Wednesday and Friday, on which it is customary for all especially to abstain even from every fleshly food for the taming of the flesh, not because of any commandment of the law. Another judges every day to be observed, namely by abstaining from those meats forbidden by the law.

“Let each be fully convinced” in judging or deliberating about such matters, concerning which no examination has yet been made through reason or authority, “in his own mind”; that is, let him follow his own opinion rather than another’s. For the Romans had not yet been given by the Apostle or other teachers a clear reason why this abstinence need not be observed because of the commandment of the law. “He who regards a day.” As though he said: “Therefore each of you should still be left entirely [Col. 0955A] to his own judgment in these matters, because otherwise he would sin by acting against conscience,” as it is subsequently said: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). And this is: “He who regards a day”—that is, believes that some day must be observed—does so for the honour of the Lord, whom he believes he pleases by this moderate abstinence. “And he who eats”—that is, believes that he never needs to abstain from any foods, because he feels no rebellion of the flesh needing to be tamed, or suffers no infirmity contrary to abstinence. For we do not believe that abstinence in Lent or on Friday had in the time of the Apostles been so instituted or confirmed. He eats “for the Lord,” that is, likewise for his honour, for the reason immediately added: because [Col. 0955B] he gives him thanks—that is, returns praise to him—for the refreshment granted to him by God. From this one should infer how great a fault it is not to return these thanks to the Lord after food.

“And he who does not eat”—that is, entirely abstains, because of the law, from the things which it forbids—does not eat for the honour of the Lord; that is, he abstains. For he does not render this reverence of obedience to the law except for God’s sake, who gave it. And though he abstains, he also gives thanks for receiving another food permitted and granted by God. “For none.” Both the one who eats and the one who abstains thus act for God’s honour, because the elect always honour and glorify the Lord, both in living and in dying. In living they glorify him, according to the saying of Truth: “Let your good works shine, so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). The death of the righteous also glorifies the Lord, as is said of Peter: “Signifying by what death he would glorify God” (John 21:19), since even at his departure the righteous person does not cease from good works, prayer, and praise of his Creator. Each prepares himself more carefully insofar as he draws nearer to receiving his crown. A person is said to live or die for himself who intends to order things toward his own advantage or glory rather than toward the honour of God. Many, indeed, displaying greatness of soul even in their deaths, desired to acquire glory for themselves; or, laying hands upon themselves, believed that their sufferings could be ended by death.

[Col. 0955D] “Whether therefore.” Since we, the elect, live or die for God, not for ourselves, as has been said, “therefore we die.” Consequently, whether we live—that is, both our life and our death should be attributed to God, for whose honour they are undertaken, rather than to ourselves; they should be called his rather than ours. “For in this”—as though he said: In that he died, namely for us and for our justification, as the same Apostle said above, Christ earned lordship over both our death and our life, so that, just as he did both for us, so in both dying and living we should seek only to obey him and fulfil his will. Otherwise he is not Lord of the dead, but rather their enemy in punishing them, unless we persist in obedience to him even unto death, prepared to lay down our lives not only for confession of him but also for our brothers.

[Col. 0956A] “But you who.” After saying, “Who are you who judge another’s servant?” he now adds, “your brother,” so that if he does not refrain from judging him out of regard for the injury done to his Lord, he may at least cease from judging him in this manner out of brotherly love, lest he scandalize his brother. Or if you do not judge, why do you despise him in matters where intention rather than action should be examined, when no certain definitive judgment has yet been given concerning them? For the determination of these and similar matters over which the Romans disputed was why the Apostle said at the beginning of his Epistle that he desired to come to them, that he might have some fruit among them as among the other nations.

[Col. 0956B] “For who?” As though he said: “Do not presume to judge doubtful matters, since you, with all other human beings, are to be judged by God in other matters; rather reserve this judgment to him who must judge all.” And this is: “For all.” Hence Truth rightly says: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged”—that is, do not desire to judge, lest you also be judged and condemned for this. The Apostle likewise says elsewhere: “Do not judge before the time, until,” etc. (1 Cor. 4:5). If we consider more carefully, as it belongs more to God than to us to kill, so also to judge. And finally, just as we must do everything for his glory, so he ought rather to work all these things through us than we ourselves to do so.

God performs judgment rather than a human being when he instructs us, either through some law or through inward [Col. 0956C] inspiration, as to what must be said, so that afterward his judgment is recited by us, not made by us. Thus a matter previously doubtful seems to be judged in three ways: by the Lord himself, as we have explained; by some manifestation of the fact; or by a human being presuming upon his own opinion. When the matter that was doubtful is disclosed by some event, the fact itself, not the human being, is said to judge. A human being is therefore said to judge only in doubtful matters—which is altogether forbidden—when, following merely his own estimation, he presumes to decide, though he has not yet become certain either through God or through experience of the matter itself.

“We shall stand,” he says, as persons standing upright, so that all may recognize us, before the tribunal—that is, the judicial seat—of God [Col. 0956D] rather than of a human being, for God cannot be deceived and is just. Understand this seat of God to be the human being assumed by the Word. For the Father gave all judgment to the Son, because he is his Son (John 5:22, 27). In this assumed human being the Son of God both died and rose again, as we have just said; and from this there especially threatens a judgment of condemnation if our death and our life do not inseparably adhere to him who died and rose again for us, as stated, and remain ready to obey.

“For it is written.” By Isaiah’s testimony he proves that all are to be judged by God. “As I live.” As though he said: “I swear by myself, who live unfailingly.” The knee is bent to a judge when his sentence is carried out and awaited—a sentence which cannot be resisted. [Col. 0957A] In that judgment every tongue will make a confession of praise to God, because no conscience will be able to murmur against the rectitude of that judge. Hence even the wicked, doing penance within themselves and groaning, will by this very act testify that you receive a just sentence of condemnation. In that judgment, then, those judging, those being judged, and even those already judged will bend the knee, because all will humble themselves beneath so great a judge, whether through fear of punishments or through the benefit of grace received.

“Therefore,” because all shall thus stand before the tribunal of so great a judgment, each “will render an account”—that is, will receive from the Lord, in punishment or reward, as much as reason demands. “Let us therefore not,” because he must judge all, and especially those whose [Col. 0957B] intention is doubtful, “any longer”—that is, after this our admonition or command—judge one another, reckoning the other condemnable for such matters. “But rather judge this”—that is, determine rather to observe that you do not place a stumbling-block before a brother: do not do anything by whose example he is corrupted and falls, or, scandalized by your harsh rebuke, withdraws from the faith.

Since this whole contention arose from foods forbidden by the law, he says that no one is defiled by the nature of foods, but only through a consciousness of transgression, if he eats them against conscience. And this is: “I know”—that is, I say this confidently, not from myself but from the teaching of the Lord, who says that a person is defiled only by things coming out of the heart, not by things entering the mouth [Col. 0957C] (Matt. 15:11). And when sending his disciples to preach, he said: “Eating and drinking whatever they have” (Luke 10:7), because no food is common and unclean of itself, but rather becomes so through the eater’s conscience. And this is: “Except to him”—as though he said: “But to the one who considers some food to be unclean—that is, thinks that his soul is defiled by it—it is unclean, because in eating it against his conscience he sins.” Things that are shared or made public are more unclean the less they are guarded; therefore *common* is used for *unclean*. Hence, Origen says, in the Acts of the Apostles the Lord says to Peter: “What God has cleansed, do not call common” [Col. 0957D] (Acts 10:15). Mark the Evangelist likewise uses *to make common* for *to defile*, saying: “Do you not understand that everything entering a human being from outside cannot defile him, because it does not enter his heart but goes into the stomach? The things coming out of a human being defile the human being” (Mark 7:18–20).

“For if.” I said, “Do not place a stumbling-block before a brother,” because whoever you are, if because of your food, etc.—that is, if you allow him to be offended in this way. “Do not.” After forbidding a stumbling-block, he also forbids scandal, because the offended person might readily depart from the faith—he for whose salvation Christ also … [the source sentence is incomplete]. As though he said: “Do not regard as insignificant his salvation, for which so great a price was given.”

[Col. 0958A] “Therefore let not.” In general he warns us to avoid every blasphemy by which we repel others from our faith, as though he said: Since people ought rather to be gained for us than lost, after the example of Christ, let us take care, as far as possible, not to act in a way by which our good faith may be blasphemed. “For the kingdom of God is not”—that is, by no sort of food or drink do we merit that God should reign or dwell within us.

For whatever things appear outwardly to be done well, especially those pertaining to abstinence, are common alike to reprobate and elect, and to hypocrites as to true believers. But righteousness—that equity by which you do not do to another what you do not wish done to yourself—and peace arising from concord with the brethren, and then the spiritual joy springing from this: in this, namely what I said, that he avoids scandal to a brother and pursues righteousness [Col. 0958B] and keeps peace, as stated, he serves Christ—that is, obeys Christ who commands this—and is approved, that is, also approved, praised, and commended by human judgment. Therefore—that is, thus—as I have said, avoiding beforehand the scandals that concern peace, let us pursue what pertains to peace; that is, let us make it our chief effort to keep concord with the brethren, including, as stated, those weak in faith. And then let us mutually preserve what belongs to edification: let the person whose faith is more perfect instruct the other’s faith, still imperfect, and strive to bring it to perfection.

“Do not”—you, namely, who, having the more perfect faith, eat all things—destroy the work of God, that is, the faith which the newly converted and still weak brother already has in him, by scandalizing him. “All things indeed.” [Col. 0958C] As though he said: “Truly we agree with you that no kinds of food defile the soul by being eaten. Yet it is harmful to eat this knowingly where a brother is offended.” “It is good for a human being.” As though he said: “Yes, as I said, eating is evil in this case; but conversely, complete abstinence for the avoidance of a brother’s stumbling-block is salutary,” after the example of Daniel, who abstained even from the wine of an unbelieving king. Converted Jews also judged that all wine of unbelievers ought to be avoided. A person is “offended” by wholly withdrawing from the faith, or at least is “scandalized,” that is, inwardly disturbed, judging the faith to which he has converted to be contrary to the law and perverse; or “made weak” in the faith of his profession, doubting it, if not wholly condemning it.

[Col. 0958D] “Do you have faith?” As though he said: “You indeed, who believe that all things may be eaten,” have faith before yourself,” that is, so that it may please him and be approved by his judgment. For we can see and know things that are before us, and God is said to know those things which he approves, and not to know those which he disapproves.

“Blessed is”—supply, “the person who does not judge himself,” that is, who does not incur condemnation for himself from things which he himself rather than God judges—that is, approves, or does not disapprove—as to be done. As though he said: The blessed person has such discretion that even in things he believes may lawfully be done, he so discerns that by doing them indiscreetly he does not incur condemnation or God’s wrath. For Solomon says: “There are ways of a person which seem right, but their end leads to death” (Prov. [Col. 0959A] 14:12). And the Lord said to Cain: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned?” (Gen. 4:7, according to the LXX).

“But he who.” As though he said: “Just as that person is blessed who abstains even from lawful things lest by using them indiscreetly, to the scandal of a brother, he incur condemnation, so conversely the person who uses unlawful things against his conscience sins.” And this is: “But he who distinguishes”—that is, distinguishes certain foods as he eats, considering them not to be eaten because of the law’s prohibition—yet eats them against conscience, while believing that he ought not to eat them, is thereby made guilty, because what he does is not from faith; indeed, he acts against his faith, that is, against what he believes. For he believes that it must not be eaten, and yet eats, and thereby sins. “For everything”—as though he said: Whatever is done against what is believed, whether in eating or in other matters, is sin. For God, inspector of the heart, attends not so much to what is done as to the disposition in which it is done.
