[Col. 0959B] It may reasonably be asked concerning those who killed believers whom they thought deceivers, according to the saying of Truth: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will suppose that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2), whether they sinned in this. For if they believed these people to be deceivers of souls and therefore deserving of death, how were they obliged to spare them against their consciences? Indeed, if they spared them, they would act against conscience and thus sin. But again, when they kill the innocent—indeed, God’s elect—which is unjust, shall we say that they do not sin, or that they have a good intention in this—an intention that is gravely mistaken and is therefore judged good rather than actually being good? How, moreover, does ignorance excuse them from sin, when it is established that some sins are called sins of ignorance? Otherwise, how could the Psalmist say to God: [Col. 0959C] “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you” (Ps. 78:6)? And Truth says of his persecutors: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Where no fault preceded, what need is there of forgiveness? If ignorance or even error of faith entirely excuses from fault, why are Jews, Gentiles, or any unbelievers to be condemned for their unbelief, when each thinks his own faith right? For who would willingly persist in a faith which he believed erroneous, choosing for himself [Col. 0959D] the worse part? Yet Truth says of such persons: “He who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). But we reserve discussion of this matter for our *Ethics*.

I think it should also be asked why the Apostle here counsels abstinence from provisions and foods because of the scandal to weak brethren, whereas in the Epistle to the Galatians he says that he opposed Peter in this matter because he was blameworthy. But we reserve the decision of this question for that passage. It should also be asked whether, according to the Apostle himself, all things are clean to the clean, and whether nothing in foods is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. Why, then, did the apostles or holy Fathers prohibit us from certain foods, just as the Law also prohibited them? Thus it is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles: “Some of the sect of the Pharisees who had believed rose up, saying that it was necessary to command them to be circumcised and to keep the law of Moses” (Acts XI, 5). Peter rose and said to them: “Why do you test the Lord by placing a yoke upon the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we shall be saved, just as they also” (ibid., 10–11). Likewise James answered and said: “The Lord’s work is known to him from eternity. Therefore I judge that those who turn to God from among the Gentiles should not be troubled; but that we should write to them that they abstain from the pollutions of idols, from fornication, from things strangled, and from blood. For Moses from ancient times has in every city those who preach him, and he is read in the synagogues every Sabbath” (ibid., 18–20).

Origen, on this Epistle above, where it is written, “If therefore uncircumcision [keeps] the law,” etc.: “But do you wish to see how far it is his very blood? You will find it above, in the eleventh quaternion.”

Ambrose, in the Epistle to the Galatians, concerning the apostles [Note: Col. 0959D, *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 346]:

> Moreover, when they had given the law that those who believed from among the Gentiles should not be troubled, but should observe only these things—that is, abstain from blood, fornication, and idolatry—they were certainly not forbidden murder when they were commanded to abstain from blood. Rather, they received what Noah had learned from God: that they should abstain from eating blood with flesh. The Greek sophists, not understanding this, though knowing that one must abstain from blood, corrupted it by adding a fourth commandment to the text—namely, that one must abstain from what is strangled—because this had already been stated, which they added.

Jerome, on Ezekiel [Note: Col. 0960D, *Patrologia*, vol. XXV, col. 444]:

> Priests do not eat anything found dead or taken by a beast, whether of birds or cattle. And according to the letter, these commandments suit every chosen order—that is, the royal and priestly order—which properly applies to Christians, who have been anointed with spiritual oil, of which it is written: “God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Heb. I, 9). They are commanded not to eat a carcass, whether of birds or cattle, whose blood has by no means been poured out. This is called “what is strangled” in the Acts of the Apostles; and because the apostolic Epistle instructs that it must necessarily be observed, it includes what is taken by a beast, since that too has likewise been strangled.

[Col. 0960D] From the Penitential of Theodore:

> Animals torn by wolves or dogs are not to be eaten; nor is a bird or goat, if found dead, unless it is first killed by a human being while still alive. Rather, they are to be given to pigs and dogs. Birds and other animals, if strangled in nets, are not to be eaten; nor if a hawk has crushed them, if they are found dead in this way, because the Acts of the Apostles commands abstinence from fornication, blood, what is strangled, and idolatry.

Likewise:

> If pigs or hens have eaten human blood, let them immediately be killed; let their entrails be thrown away, and let the rest of the flesh be eaten. But if their killing is delayed, they are not to be eaten. If they have torn the corpses of the dead, let them be fattened, and after the passing of a year let them be eaten. But if pigs have killed a human being, let them immediately be killed and buried.

Likewise:

> Whoever eats unclean flesh, carrion, or flesh torn by beasts shall do penance for forty days. But if it happens through the necessity of hunger, the penance is much lighter.

Likewise:

> Whoever is defiled by blood or by any unclean thing, if he does not know what he is eating, commits a slight offence.

Likewise:

> Whoever drinks blood or semen for any purpose shall do penance for four years.

Likewise:

> A fish found dead in a river is not to be eaten. But if it has been caught while fishing and is found that same day, let the person who does not hesitate eat it; but the person who doubts should not eat it.

From the Council of Gangra, after the Council of Nicaea, chapter II [Col. 0961B]:

> If anyone who eats flesh in faith and with reverence eats it apart from blood, things sacrificed to idols, and things strangled, he is to be condemned as one who has no hope in the foods he eats; let him be anathema.

Augustine, *On Faith to Peter* [Note: Col. 0961D, *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 777]:

> Hold most firmly, and do not doubt at all, that every creature of God is good and that nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving (I Tim. IV, 4); and that the servants of God who abstain from meats or wine do not reject as unclean things made by God, but abstain from the stronger food and drink solely for the chastening of the body.

But if we examine at the root of the intention the things found in the apostles and apostolic men which seem contrary, we shall discover that both these and those things are, according to time and place, sometimes to be prohibited and sometimes permitted; and that in prohibiting certain things, provision has sometimes been made more for decency of life than for the religion of faith. Thus, in Saint Ambrose’s *Hexaemeron*, he permits one thing to be taken as a medicine but forbids it to be taken as food, namely because honorable men may easily be scandalized by its stench. We believe the same is done with certain other lowly foods, to preserve decency. Nor is it surprising if, by the same discernment whereby the Apostle here teaches abstinence from certain foods because of the scandal of weak brethren, James in the primitive Church—still weak in faith—forbade the eating of those things in which he saw believers were then especially offended.

[Col. 0961D] For even the Apostle himself, though he utterly forbids circumcision, nevertheless yielded to it for a time, allowing Timothy to be circumcised, and even consecrating himself in the Jewish rite together with certain converted Jews. Therefore what some holy Fathers reasonably prohibited in certain places or times because of the scandal of those with whom they lived was afterwards commendably permitted by others, now that our faith has been most fully strengthened. Otherwise the Apostle would be found opposed to Moses, if what was prohibited or permitted at one time were always to be maintained.

There may also be some question concerning Jews or proselytes who, before Christ’s coming, made their profession or vow by observances of the Law: whether, after their conversion to the faith, they may transgress that vow, whether in foods or in other matters. For since the Law still retained its standing at that time, such a vow seems to have been lawfully made. Hence it seems by no means to be violated; nor does one who then made it, and later became a Christian, seem released from that abstinence from foods—especially since living by abstaining from no foods at all is more lax than abstaining from some, and no one rightly abandons a lawful and good vow unless he ascends to greater things that prevent its observance.

To this, I think, one must answer that if he observes this not so much on the authority of the Law as in accordance with the arrangement of his vow, he is in no way to be blamed, nor is he to be released from that vow—unless perhaps because of the scandal of some who would still think that he was Judaizing in this, as though he believed that the Law still lawfully retained its standing and abstained for that reason. Indeed, such a vow seems not even then to have been made lawfully or reasonably, but to have been promised in profession through his error, since he believed that the Law would continue in its former force.

## CHAPTER XV

**“We ought.”** Above I said that nothing is common—that is, unclean—but that all things are clean to believers. Yet we ought to bear the weakness of those who believe otherwise and are weaker in faith, and not to please ourselves—that is, not to carry out our own will concerning them, by rejecting them—but to seek their salvation, namely by bearing with them. “Let each please”: that is, let him strive to please his neighbor in what is not blameworthy, namely for that person’s edification. For he cannot otherwise be edified by us unless he receives our teaching; and let us do this after Christ’s example.

And this is what “for even” means. That man assumed by the Word, who according to his anointing is specially called Christ, strove to fulfill not so much human as divine good pleasure. Hence he himself says: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John VI, 38). For the human will is properly called that will which arises from the weakness or passibility of the flesh and naturally seeks to set it at rest: it desires that the flesh suffer no troubles and be altogether free from every penalty, as was granted to our first parents before sin and will be granted to us more fully in the life to come. For just as misery is a penalty, so rest plainly is; and as each person desires what belongs to blessedness or rest, so he flees what belongs to misery or toil. Such an appetite is called the human will in us, and each person follows that will by obeying it.

But, you will say, how did Christ not please himself if he pleased God the Father? Can something please one person while displeasing another? Do all the righteous please Christ as they please the Father? Or is the Father’s will different from Christ’s will? What, then, does it mean that Christ did not please himself, or did not come to do his own will, except that the man assumed never desired to do anything because he hoped it would be pleasant to himself, but because he believed it would please God? All others, however holy they may be, since they are not altogether without sin, desire certain things from the weakness or passibility of the flesh for no reason other than to satisfy that weakness and avoid present suffering or affliction. This is to please oneself, and to do one’s own will: that is, to act only, or chiefly, because one believes that the act is pleasant to oneself, placing in oneself the end of one’s own action. This was wholly absent from Christ.

Thus, “Christ did not please himself, but God the Father,” means that the man assumed desired nothing because it was pleasant to him, but because he knew that God approved it or had commanded it. He himself says: “For the words of your lips I have kept hard ways” (Ps. XVI, 4). The Apostle immediately adds the penalty of suffering or toil undertaken through obedience, in order to show that Christ pleased the Father more than himself: “as it is written in Psalm LXXVIII: ‘The reproaches,’” etc.

For whoever reproaches the messenger of someone else, or dishonors or honors him in any respect, does so not so much to the one sent as to the one who sent him. Thus Saul is told: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts IX, 4)—me, I say, rather than mine, because it is on my account rather than theirs. What is it, however, to reproach [Latin: *improbare*; perhaps *improperare*] God the Father except to mock the fact that there is generation in the Godhead, which their carnal understanding could not grasp? This mockery therefore fell upon Christ because, when he preached that generation or called himself the Son of God, seeking in this the Father’s glory and not his own, he was not only mocked for it but also handed over to death, as it is written: “He boasts that God is his Father; let us see whether his words are true,” etc. (Wisdom II, 16). And in the Gospel: “He trusted in God; let him now deliver him if he will. For he said, ‘I am the Son of God’” (Matt. XXVII, 43).

**“Whatever things were written.”** It is as though he said: What concern is the testimony of the Old Testament to us, professors of the New Law, especially when we reject its works? He answers that whatever things were written—namely, both in the Old and in the New Testament—were written for our instruction, that is, the instruction of Christians, etc. For those who follow there the killing letter are not taught but blinded; rather, those are chiefly taught who break the outer crust and are nourished by the inner crumb. Moreover, God permitted even secular writings to be written only for some instruction, whether of morals or letters, or in order that they might in some respect help sacred Scripture, although their writers did not know this.

**“That through.”** We are, I say, instructed and taught for this purpose: that through patience in adversities, and through the consolation given in the Scriptures concerning the prize of eternal blessedness, we may in every way be strengthened in hope in God, knowing that “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II, 12), and “in your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke XXI, 19). This hope is that of which it was said above: “Hope does not disappoint.” And fittingly, after mentioning adversities, saying, “The reproaches of those who reproached,” etc., he added patience, which is necessary against them, and the consolation of the Scriptures.

But since at the beginning of this Epistle he had said beforehand that all divine Scripture aims either to teach or to move, how does he now say that whatever things were written were written for our instruction? Certainly even those things which exhort were written for instruction—not indeed in order to teach what is to be done, but in order that teaching may have efficacy, that is, that we may wish to fulfill what we have learned.

“But the God”: that is, just as Christ did not please himself but God, and sought not his own glory but the Father’s, so may God himself, whose gift it is both to give patience and consolation, grant you to think the same thing toward one another: that is, among yourselves to seek that each may please the other for good, according to Jesus Christ—that is, by his example, as has been said—so that with one mind, namely both those weak and those strong in faith together, you may with one harmonious mouth praise God for the mercy of our redemption shown us through his Son.

Accordingly, when he has said “God,” he adds, “the same, and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” who glories in having such a Son not only for his own glory but also for our salvation, so that through him he may also be our Father, since the Son came down to seek brothers. Therefore, so that God may thus be honored jointly by all, “receive one another”: that is, let not one reject or exasperate another, but let the person stronger and more perfect in faith bear with the weak. Do this after Christ’s example: seeing us stiff-necked and not merely weak in faith but dead in unbelief, he did not reject us but received us; indeed, he also drew us to glorify and praise God, both for our own conversion and that of others through us.

He was “a minister of circumcision,” that is, of the Jews, to whom alone he ministered the word of life by personally preaching, as he himself says: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV, 24). This was “for the truth of God,” that is, in order that God’s promise might stand, for he had specially and repeatedly promised them that he would send himself as Savior. This is what he adds: “to confirm”—that is, so that those promises made to the ancient fathers concerning the sending of Christ to them might remain firm and unshaken. For by promising he wished to be held as a debtor, so that by showing mercy he might become the payer.

**“But the Gentiles.”** It is as though he said: I say that Christ was a minister, etc.; but I also say that the Gentiles—understand, on account of the mercy bestowed upon them by God—are now especially to honor God. For the more they had formerly been removed from God through idolatry, the more abundantly they have now drawn near to God’s worship, so that where sin abounded, grace might superabound. Notice that above, in regard to the promise made to the Jews, he understood not so much mercy as debt. But concerning the Gentiles he more rightly called it mercy alone, since less was owed to them because of the guilt of their manifold error.

Thus it is written in the Psalm, speaking to the Father in the person of Christ, who says to the Father: “I will confess you among the Gentiles” (Ps. XVII, 50): that is, I shall cause you to be praised also by Gentiles who have been converted and gained for you through me. Their firstfruits were the Magi, or also those Samaritans to whom he became known through that Samaritan woman; perhaps also those Gentiles who, around the time of the Passion, came to him through Philip and Andrew, wishing to see him, concerning whom he said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” (John XIII, 31). “And to your name”: for your honor, namely, to spread abroad your knowledge, I shall cause them to devote themselves to spiritual songs.

The “therefore” said above continues in the Psalm, where it was first said: “And deliver me from those who rise up against me,” etc. (Ps. XVII, 49). For he was exalted by those who, in crucifying him, believed that they would destroy his name. He himself also foretold this exaltation: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32)—that is, by converting not only Jews but also Gentiles.

Again, foreseeing through Isaiah the Church to be gathered both from Jews and Gentiles, he exhorts both together to exult and praise God for their conversion. He calls the Jews “the people of God” and once his peculiar people. “And again,” through David himself, “magnify,” that is, glorify by good works, “all peoples,” that is, every multitude of the faithful, not only that gathered from the Gentiles.

**“There shall be a root.”** This is another testimony concerning the conversion of the Gentiles after the Lord’s incarnation: they are to be ruled by him and to hope in him. Just as a root is what remains of a tree that has been cut down and, though hidden in the ground, puts forth many shoots of little branches, so Jesse, David’s father, having long ago died and been cut off from this present life as from a tree, had Christ, who was to be born much later from his seed, as his root and surviving remnant.

This root was hidden in the earth when Christ was buried in his own flesh, which is of earthly substance, according to what he says of himself: “As Jonah was in the belly of the whale,” etc. (Matt. XII, 40). By rising again, it sprouted into a great offspring of believers, according to his parable: “Unless a grain of wheat,” etc. (John XII, 24). We also know that a root is then especially generated and, as it were, enriched so as to multiply, if dung and manure are applied to it, according to that parable of the Lord: “Leave it also this year, until I put in manure” (Luke XIII, 8). What, then, is the dung or manure applied to this root except the filth of our sins, which he took upon himself [lacuna] and bore in his body, so that from him as the root and origin of all, the fruits of an innumerable offspring might arise in the Church? For it would have profited nothing to be born unless it also profited to be redeemed.

Therefore, promising this through Isaiah, the Spirit says: “There shall be a root of Jesse”—that is, after Jesse has died, there will remain to him descendants from his seed through whom what was lost in the tree may be restored more abundantly in offspring, since more believers will arise than had previously existed from Jesse. “And he who”: as though he said, “And that root will be he who rises up by mounting mightily, until his body, which is the Church, is spread everywhere; and he will always preside over its governance as its head,” as he promises: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII, 20). Of this governance the same prophet says elsewhere: “And a little child shall lead them” (Isa. XI, 6). “In him”—that is, in his grace, not in the Law or in their own powers—will they trust.

This is the root of which the Prophet also says elsewhere: “The root of Jesse, which stands as a sign to the peoples—the Gentiles shall seek him, and his tomb shall be glorious” (ibid., 10). From that tomb the root arose and grew into a great thicket of fruitful branches.

**“But the God.”** I said: “Rejoice, Gentiles,” and: “The Gentiles shall hope in him.” May this very thing be fulfilled in you Romans. And this is “the God of hope,” by whose grace all must hope: the elect alone can possess all joy, both in this life in hope and in that life in reality, and peace—namely, by removing from you that proud contention for the quieting of which this Epistle was written.

“In believing”: as though he said, “So that through faith, by which one believes and which is the foundation of all good things, you may advance in hope and charity, which naturally follow from it.” By “the power of the Holy Spirit” he means in us the love of God, which is strong against all things, as it is written: “Love is strong as death” (Song VIII, 6); and again: “It bears all things, endures all things” (I Cor. XIII, 7).

**“I am certain.”** Those whom he had long frightened by rebuking, he softens at the end by praising them, lest they despair. He says that among them there are persons full both of love and knowledge, so that they are willing and able to instruct others. This is “I am certain”: as though he said, “Although I correct or admonish you in this way, you yourselves—as in certain persons you are full of proud contention or ignorance—are likewise in certain respects full,” etc., “of all knowledge,” that is, you have knowledge sufficient for the purpose that you may be able to exhort one another to do good.

“But more boldly in part”: that is, I have written to you with somewhat greater confidence, because you are in the place entrusted to me, since I am specially teacher both of Gentiles and Jews. This he explains when he says that he does so as one concerned for them, because of the grace—that is, the office of apostleship for preaching to the Gentiles—laid upon him. Of this grace he himself says: “Freely you have received, freely give” (Matt. X, 8).

A preacher is a minister of Christ when he seeks not his own gain but Christ’s. And because some preach well while living badly, he adds “sanctifying”: that is, also by my life commending the preaching I make concerning God, so that the offering—that is, even my prayer which I make for them—may become acceptable to God, that is, sanctified in the Holy Spirit, through the Holy Spirit, who, as was said above, teaches us what we ought to pray for and intercedes for us with groanings. [Col. 0967A] [lacuna], that it may attain a holy effect, making us all holy.

**“Therefore I have.”** Because I thus act by seeking the things of Christ, I have grace from this for Christ, whom I serve in this, by which I gain God—that is, a reward according to divine judgment, if not according to human judgment. By saying this, he exhorts them by his example to care for brotherly love.

For he does not show how he sanctifies or commends his preaching by saying that he does not presume to speak anything—that is, arrogantly attribute to himself anything—of those things whose efficacy he does not possess, as the pseudo-apostles did. “In the obedience of the Gentiles”: that is, in order that I might draw obedience among the Gentiles, he accomplishes these things, I say, “in word,” that is, through his word, “and deeds,” that is, through miracles.

He immediately subdivides these deeds, saying: “in the power,” that is, through power granted to me, “of signs and wonders,” that is, wonderful signs. For there are certain natural signs at which we do not marvel, such as those of the planets, of which it is written: “Let them be for signs and seasons” (Gen. I, 14). But those which occur contrary to nature—that is, contrary to the customary course of nature—such as cleansing lepers or raising the dead, are called *prodigia*, “wonders,” because they are worthy of amazement. Thus a *prodigium* is, as it were, something to be pointed out with the finger.

“By the power of the Holy Spirit”: that is, from the power granted to me through God’s grace, in distinction from the miracles of Antichrist or magicians.

Origen:

> Signs are called those events in which, along with something marvelous, something future is also indicated; but wonders are those in which only something marvelous is shown. Scripture sometimes uses the terms improperly, putting “wonders” for “signs,” and “signs” for “wonders.”

Here “signs and wonders” are taken as one expression, so that, I say, I have glory before God through the greatness of my labor: I have filled all that land from Jerusalem to Illyricum with the preaching of the Gospel, in order to show that he deserves to be heard by the Romans, since he has been heard by so many and such great peoples.

Haymo:

> Illyricum is a province at the end of Asia and the beginning of Europe.

Thus, by word, deeds, and the power of signs, in places where nothing at all had previously been heard of Christ, I acted so that it is not remarkable if my preaching should now find place among you, who already confess Christ. “Lest upon”: as though he said, “This was granted to me, so that I should not lay the building of faith upon another’s preceding preaching, which would be, as it were, the foundation of my preaching.” In this he shows that what he did there was more difficult than what he wishes to do among the Romans. “It is written in Isaiah”: that is, so that through me what was prophesied by him concerning Christ might come to pass—namely, that they should see by understanding. He immediately explains this when he says: “And they who,” etc.

**“For which reason.”** Because I was intent upon converting so many who were entirely ignorant, I was hindered—either to exclude the fabrications of pseudo-apostles, who said that he did not dare approach such people or such great ones, especially when they were present, or to excuse himself on reasonable grounds. He says “very much,” that is, chiefly, because there may also have been certain other causes of this hindrance: namely, the need to establish thoroughly all people in a place of preaching or a reason for remaining there.

Origen:

> He seems to say this to those in Achaia, at Corinth. In Spain he promises to see them in passing, as though indicating that he ought not to remain long among those who had already been converted. So too, at the beginning of the Epistle, he said that they needed to be strengthened in certain matters rather than converted. It also befits a good man to promise less than he does, and the stay of a good teacher becomes more welcome and more desired the shorter it is expected to be. Thus he prepares them beforehand, so that at his coming they may prepare themselves and foresee the matters about which they wish to be instructed.

“I hope,” namely, presuming nothing about himself from himself, but committing everything to God; “and by you.” For he wishes them to be companions on his journey, both so that the remaining Gentiles may more easily be converted by the authority of the Romans, and so that they may be able to testify against pseudo-apostles and any others who malign him concerning the preaching they themselves have heard. Thus, when they accompany him for a long time in preaching, he may at least repay them in this way: that he has seen them in passing.

He aptly says that he is to be “sent forward” by them, showing himself safe under the escort of those who command the others. In this he also consoles them concerning the duration of his stay among them, as though placing it at their discretion.

“If first I have enjoyed you.” Haymo:

> To enjoy is to possess, embrace, and behold something with delight. Note that although, as the blessed Augustine observes, it properly belongs to us to enjoy God, he does not here say simply “to enjoy,” but “to enjoy in part,” just as when he said to Philemon, “May I enjoy you,” he immediately added, “in the Lord.” For we enjoy God wholly when we desire to possess him solely for his own sake; but we enjoy our neighbor in part when we embrace him in love for his own benefit, while nevertheless placing the end—that is, the final and highest cause—of this enjoyment in God. Our neighbor is indeed partly a cause, but God is the highest cause. Therefore we enjoy our neighbor in part, but enjoy God wholly, because God himself is the whole cause of his enjoyment, whereas our neighbor, as we have said, is not the whole cause of his own enjoyment, since God is higher: that is, since we think even of our neighbor for God’s sake.

Notice that he says, “when I begin my journey,” because, although he comes to the Romans for their sake, he does not regard himself as beginning his journey to Spain until he has departed from them, when he will be acting wholly for the Spaniards’ sake. Notice too that, when he says “if first [I have enjoyed] you,” he again wins their goodwill, as though he judges their visit necessary to himself and cannot otherwise proceed concerning Spain unless he first visits them.

**“But now.”** Because I have no further place here, now—that is, before I come to you—since I received the apostleship especially among the Gentiles (whence he alone is called the Teacher of the Gentiles), he shows also how great a care he has for converted Jews when he says elsewhere: “the care of all the churches” (II Cor. XI, 28). Perhaps he also offers this as some excuse if he delays coming to them.

“To minister to the saints”: that is, to carry to the faithful converted from Judaism who are there food collected by me for their need. For the Apostle, as he often testifies concerning that Jerusalem Church converted long ago through Christ himself, then through Peter, James, and the other apostles, was accustomed to show the greatest concern for its bodily necessities, so that he might at least minister bodily food to those to whom another’s preaching ministered spiritual food. He considered that they especially ought to be helped for many reasons.

That converted people bestowed very great authority upon our faith: that place, having received the Law from God, had been called his peculiar people; and, because it had first believed and had thus been set as the foundation and example of our faith to the rest, it needed especially to be supported lest it fail.

Thus, as is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, they were converted with such devotion that, leaving all personal property altogether, they laid everything they had at the apostles’ feet. As he recalls in the Epistle to the Hebrews, they had endured greater violence from the Jews in the loss of their possessions. The Apostle accordingly proposes this as a pattern and example to the churches in his Epistles: when they see poor churches or monasteries, their preaching should gather provisions for them.

**“They have approved.”** Observe how carefully he invites the Romans by the example of others likewise to give this alms to the people of Jerusalem. He says that those who give it have themselves approved it—that is, rather, commended it—without any compulsion or exhortation from the Apostle. Thus he says, “They have approved”: that is, approving it as though by their own judgment, they compelled me to do this.

Haymo [Note: Col. 0969D, *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, cols. 501–502]:

> These people, who did not possess the knowledge of preaching by which they might go out to preach to the Gentiles, were in Jerusalem, devoting themselves to prayers and fasts. The apostles, from the several provinces and places in which they preached, strove to send them whatever money, silver, gold, grain, and clothing they received—especially Paul, who preached to more nations. Therefore teachers say that he sometimes sent them more than three or five measures of silver.

Likewise [Note: Col. 0969D, ibid., col. 502]:

> Macedonia and Achaea—called Achaea, from which its peoples are also called Achaeans—are most noble and neighboring provinces of the Greeks, which the Apostle filled with churches.

When Macedonia and Achaea are named, the container stands for the contained: that is, the names of the lands stand for the names of their inhabitants, just as we call a drink “a cup.” “A collection,” which in Greek we call *symbolum*, is where different contributions are brought together from different people, as often happens at communal banquets. These people, however, collected their resources for the poor rather than for banquets from their own means.

“For it pleased them”: as though he said, “I rightly said, ‘they approved,’ so that they may do this voluntarily rather than under compulsion. Since it is done more by their will than through our urging, it rightly pleased them, because they are debtors.” He immediately proves this from the lesser to the greater, saying: “For if the Gentiles have become partakers of their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in carnal things”—that is, since they have become partakers of the spiritual goods which the Jews possessed, such as the Law, the prophets, and also the prayers and divine services which they celebrate there daily for the salvation of the Gentiles. Therefore, because it pleased them, as is just, to do this for them.

When I have completed—that is, carried out—this commission, and upon arriving there have delivered to them this fruit, namely the alms; that is, have distinguished those who send them gifts well, so that they may pray for them as for their benefactors [Col. 0970B], I shall proceed, etc. Although the Apostle says that he will go on to Spain, it is still uncertain whether he did so, because of differing opinions.

Jerome, *On Isaiah*, book IV [Note: [Col. 0970D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIV, col. 151]: “They shall fly in ships of foreigners and shall plunder the sea together” (Isa. X, 14, according to the Septuagint). “We may understand this from the example of the one Apostle Paul, who travelled through Pamphylia, Asia, Macedonia, Achaia, and various islands and provinces, even to Italy (Acts XXVIII, 14), and, as he himself writes, was carried in the vessels of foreigners to the Spains” (Rom. XV, 28).

Cassiodorus on this same Epistle of Paul, “I shall proceed through you into Spain”: “He says this frequently, but we never read that it was fulfilled. Thus what is said is desired, but is not fulfilled with prophetic truth [Col. 0970C]. Yet let no one accuse the Apostle of lying if he did not fulfil what he believed. For he did not speak deceitfully, saying one thing while intending another—that is, with his mouth rather than his heart.”

“But I know that, when I come to you,” that is, I have learned by the Spirit’s revelation—although, to be sure, I had said that I would pass through you. Here it should indeed be noted that, when he says that this was revealed to him so that he knows it, he implies that what he had previously said about Spain was put forward from expectation rather than assertion. “I shall come in the abundance of Christ’s blessing,” so that, just as is read concerning Joseph, at my arrival the Lord may pour out upon you an abundant blessing of heavenly grace; that is, may multiply you in spiritual things.

[Col. 0970D] “Therefore I beseech you, brothers,” so that what I wish may be possible through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Holy Spirit: that you may assist me, if indeed you wish to make further progress in him and have the love of God, by prayers to God, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judaea, and that my ministry may be accepted. For the leader of many believers, though imperfect, is believed to obtain much from God. “From the unbelievers,” while I labour thus for the believers who are there; “and that my ministry,” that is, that it may not be hostile to me from those who send this through me, or even from the Lord, who has appointed me minister or steward of the Church. May the offering brought by me for them, as a sacrifice to God’s altar, [Col. 0971A] be acceptable to the saints in Jerusalem, so that I may come to you with joy through the will of God—that is, pleasing and glad. For if some grievous event should happen to me there on this account, they will be especially distressed. “And that I may be refreshed with you,” both by resting after a long labour and by fulfilling my desire.

“But may God,” whether indeed I come or do not come, “be with you all—the God of peace. Amen.” That is, may he reconcile you to one another from proud contention. By reserving this for the end of the Epistle, he indicates the point toward which the Epistle itself chiefly tends, and what its final cause or purpose is.

## CHAPTER XVI

“But I commend to you Phoebe,” namely, to my prayers. Phoebe, through whom this Epistle is believed to have been sent from Corinth to the Romans [Col. 0971B], is said to have been a certain wealthy and noble woman, who supplied from her own resources, or from those of others, the necessities of the faithful who were at Cenchreae—following the example, to be sure, of the holy women remembered as having done this for the Lord or the Apostles. She had some business for which it was necessary for her to come to Rome. Therefore the Apostle exhorts and asks the Romans to receive her honourably and to assist her in her business as far as they can.

“Our sister … and assist her in whatever business she may need of you”: by faith, not by flesh. “In ministry,” that is, in service to those faithful who are at Cenchreae, that is, in the place so called, which is said to be the port of Corinth. “Receive her in hospitality [Col. 0971C] in the Lord,” that is, in the love of God; and receive her so honourably and kindly as is worthy and fitting for saints to receive a holy woman. “And assist her,” that is, help her. “For she herself also has assisted many, and myself.” What is due to her because of her many preceding merits is not so much bestowed upon her as repaid.

Origen teaches, on apostolic authority, that women also are appointed to the ministry of the Church. He commends Phoebe, established in this office in the Church which is at Chone [perhaps Cenchreae], with great praise and recommendation, because she stood by in needs and apostolic labours. This passage teaches two things: that women ministers are found in the Church, and that such women ought to be admitted to ministry as have assisted many and, through good services, deserved to attain apostolic praise [Col. 0971D].

Jerome: “In the ministry of the Church, even now in eastern regions women deacons appear to minister within their sex in baptism or in the ministry of the word; for we find that women taught privately, as Priscilla did, whose husband was named Aquila.”

The same author, on the Epistle to Timothy: “Avoid younger widows” (I Tim. V, 11), that is, appoint them to the ministry of the diaconate.

Saint Epiphanius, to John of Jerusalem: “I have never ordained deaconesses and sent them to other provinces, nor have I done anything to divide the Church.” “Those, therefore, whom in ancient times we called deaconesses—that is, female ministers—we now call abbesses, that is, mothers.”

[Col. 0972A] Cassiodorus, on this same passage, understands Phoebe to have been a deaconess of Mother Church; this is still performed in Greek regions, as it were on military service, and the practice of baptizing is not denied them in the Church.

Likewise Claudius, in his exposition of this Epistle: “This passage teaches that women also are appointed to the ministry of the Church. The Apostle follows Phoebe, appointed to this office in the Church at Cenchreae, with great praise and recommendation.”

“Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow-workers.” At the end of the Epistle, by greeting certain persons by name, he greatly commends them, so that the Romans may especially comply with the counsel and authority of those who were more perfect than the rest [Note: [Col. 0971D] *Patrologia*, vol. CXVIII, col. 504]. Here the Apostle calls her Prisca, whereas in the Acts of the Apostles she is called Priscilla; perhaps by a pleasing allusion to her name, in order to suggest that she was a mother in … disposition and character [lacuna]. Priscilla was the wife of Aquila, and both had been converted from Judaism to Christ.

“In Christ Jesus,” who were fellow-workers—that is, for Christ they assisted in many things. The Apostle, when he came to Corinth, found them there after they had formerly been expelled from Rome along with the other Jews under Claudius; and because he was altogether of the same trade, namely tent-making, he joined them so that they might work together.

Hence Bede, *On the Acts of the Apostles* [Note: [Col. 0972D] *Patrologia*, vol. XCII, col. 981]: “Being, as it were, exiles and strangers engaged in the craft of tent-making, they made for themselves tents to use on the road. For in Greek tents are called *skenai* [σκῆναι], deriving their name from shade; among them shade is called *skia* [σκία]. Thus *skenai*, or *skenōmata* [σκηνώματα], signify, as it were, shelters. The ancients described these as made from linen, wool, goat-hair cloth, branches of trees, or brushwood. Mystically, however, as Peter drew us from the waves of the world by fishing, so Paul, by erecting shelters of protection, defends us by word and deed from the rain of sins, the tree of temptations, and the winds of snares.”

Chrysostom, *Homily 1 on the Epistle to the Hebrews*: “‘Who is the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his substance’: this is an apostolic utterance—or rather, the wonderful grace of the Holy Spirit. For they did not say these things from their own understanding. How could that man have known this? Did such an operation of majesty arise from knives, hides, or …? [lacuna] They did not procure these understandings by their own mind, [Col. 0972D] which at that time was so weak and lowly that it had nothing more than common people and the populace. For how could one whose whole life and study were occupied with the prices of selling and with making hides conceive anything divine?”

Ambrose, on Priscilla and Aquila: “Having become believers, these became partners in the Apostle’s labour, so that they too might exhort others to faith. Indeed Apollos, although trained in the Scriptures, was more carefully instructed by them in the way of the Lord. Therefore he calls them his fellow-workers in Christ Jesus. For they were his co-workers in the Gospel. Hence he especially teaches how greatly [Col. 0973A] the Romans ought to obey them.”

Origen: “It may be that, because at that time the Jews had come to Corinth after being driven from the city by Caesar’s decree, they were later greeted by Paul after the severity of the edict had ceased and they had returned.”

It nevertheless appears that, when Paul was endangered by Jewish plots, they exposed themselves so that he might depart unharmed: “who laid down their own necks for my life,” that is, they opposed themselves to death in order to preserve his life. “To whom not I alone give thanks, but also all the churches”—of which, to be sure, the Apostle is specially called preacher or teacher—“and greet the church in their house.”

“Greet Epaenetus, beloved to me, who is,” that is, their entire household likewise converted to the faith, “the firstfruits of Asia in Christ. Greet Mary.”

Haymo [Note: [Col. 0973D] *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, cols. 504–505]: “Either because she first of all believed [Col. 0973B], or because she was of great rank and nobility, so that he might show that nobles too come to faith and thereby invite the leading Romans to faith. ‘Who laboured much.’”

Origen: “He teaches also that women ought to labour for the churches. They labour when they teach younger women all those things recorded as written concerning the duties of women.” “She laboured among us.”

“Greet Andronicus and Junia.” Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0973D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 179]: “At their exhortation.”

Haymo [Note: [Col. 0973D] *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, col. 505]: “‘She laboured,’ namely by rendering the office of preaching to women of her own sex from house to house. For women did not teach in church.”

“My kinsfolk.” Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0973D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 179]: “Both according to the flesh and according to the Holy Spirit.”

“My fellow-prisoners, who are notable.” Haymo [Note: [Col. 0973D] *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, col. 505]: “These became exiles from their own country for the grace of God, as Paul also did.” “Among the apostles, and before me,” that is, among preachers. This passage seems also to call a woman an apostle, unless perhaps we forcibly refer this only to Andronicus and the men mentioned above. “In Christ.”

“Greet Ampliatus, beloved to me in the Lord. Greet Urbanus, our fellow-worker in Christ, and Stachys,” that is, ours in the faith of Christ—mine, namely, and others’. “Greet my beloved Apelles,” even though he was not as much a fellow-worker.

Origen: “I think that this Apelles passed wisely through many tribulations, and therefore he pronounced him approved, in accordance with what he himself says elsewhere: ‘suffering produces approval’” (Rom. V, 4). It should be considered whether he is the same one called an Alexandrian, learned in the Scriptures, [Col. 0973D] in the Acts of the Apostles.

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0973D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 179]: “He greets this Apelles not as a friend or a leading worker, but because, tested by temptations, he was found faithful in Christ.”

Haymo [Note: [Col. 0973D] *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, col. 505]: “Although some make two proper names from this, saying: ‘Greet Apelles and Probus,’ that is, one approved in faith and worthy of praise.”

“Those of the household of Aristobulus. Greet Herodion.” Perhaps [Col. 0974A] Aristobulus was already dead; the Apostle sufficiently praises him by greeting his household and commending his faith in it.

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0974D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 179]: “This man is understood to have been a gatherer of brothers in Christ. ‘My kinsman. Greet those who are of …’”

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0974D] Ibid., col. 179]: “The one whom he calls merely a kinsman is shown to be devoted in love, yet he does not indicate his vigilance.”

“Of the household of Narcissus, who are in the Lord. Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who …”

Origen: “He calls them neither beloved nor approved nor helpers; perhaps they had nothing useful in the way of merits, and therefore he honoured them with the title of greeting alone. ‘Of the household of Narcissus’: several appear to have belonged to Narcissus’s household or family, but not all to have been in the house.”

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0974D] Ibid., col. 179]: “Narcissus is said to have been a presbyter at that time, as is read in other manuscripts; and because he was not present, the Apostle greets the saints who belonged to him. Thus this presbyter Narcissus performed the office of a pilgrim, strengthening believers by exhortations.”

“Who labour in the Lord. Greet Rufus.” Origen: “Many labour, but not in the Lord.”

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0974D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 180]: “With one utterance he declares these women worthy in Christ: they labour, namely, by ministering to the saints.”

“Who laboured much.” Origen: “She seems here to be praised especially in exhortation, in ministry to the saints, in affliction, and in poverty for Christ’s sake, because she abandoned her house to those driven out and suffered reproach from the unbelieving.”

“Chosen in the Lord, and his mother.” Haymo [Note: [Col. 0974D] *Patrologia*, vol. CXVII, col. 505]: “That is, promoted to the priesthood—his [mother].” “And mine.” Thus I formerly read, “his mother and my mother,” so that there are two mothers, or so that she is the same woman: his mother according to the flesh, the Apostle’s according to the benefit that perhaps she had once bestowed upon him elsewhere, nourishing him from her own resources as a mother would; or he calls her his mother out of reverence for her holiness, to whom, that is, honour ought to be rendered as to a mother.

“Asyncritus and Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, and the brothers who are with them. Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympias, and all the saints who are with them. Greet …”

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0974D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 180]: “He greets these together because he knew that they were harmonious in Christ, that is, united in Christian friendship, and not merely believers in friendships.”

“Hermas.” Origen: “I think that this Hermas is the writer of that little book called *The Shepherd*, a writing which seems to me very useful and, I think, divinely inspired. That he wrote nothing in praise [of himself] has, I suppose, this reason: as that writing itself declares, he appears to have been converted to repentance after many sins. It should be understood that those whose greeting is joined lived together.”

*Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 1: “The little book of Hermas called *The Shepherd*, of whom Paul makes mention in his Epistles, has not been received by many; by others, however, it has been judged necessary for the instruction of those first brought to faith [Col. 0975A]. Therefore it is read in certain churches, and many ancient writers have used its testimony.”

Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 10 [Note: [Col. 0975D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIII, col. 625]: “They assert that Hermas, whom the Apostle Paul mentions when writing to the Romans—‘Greet Phlegon, Hermas’—is the author of the book called *The Shepherd*, which is publicly read in some churches of Greece.” It is truly a useful book, and many ancient writers have employed its testimonies. But among the Latins it is almost unknown.

“Philologus and Julia.” Origen: “It may be that they were husband and wife, and that the others were members of their household.”

Jerome teaches us by his own example what sort of persons we should greet in our letters: not the rich, honoured by worldly resources [Col. 0975B], but those enriched by God’s grace and faith. Therefore, a little earlier, we understand all those whom he greets to be firstfruits of the Asian Church, or persons from every region who had become strangers, by whose example and teaching he thinks it not absurd that the Romans had believed.

“Greet one another with a kiss,” namely yourselves. Since he could not greet all individually, he commands them to greet one another mutually on his behalf and in his place, as he would do if present; and thus, reconciled to one another with a kiss, to end their proud contention. They greet you with a kiss—not a lustful or deceitful kiss such as that of Judas the betrayer, but one which reconciles us in brotherly love. “All the churches of Christ,” that is, congregations of Christians, in distinction from the church of evildoers which the Psalmist denounces, desire or pray for your welfare with the same affection of love as I do [Col. 0975C]. For one who says to another in greeting, “Be well,” undoubtedly prays that the other may be well.

“But I beseech you, brothers, to watch those who …” He refers to false apostles, so that they may beware of them lest their faith be corrupted by them. “Watch,” that is, discern; “dissensions,” that is, dangers of error in faith. I mean those who cause them contrary to the teaching which you have learned; “and turn away from them.” “For such persons do not serve Christ our Lord, but their own belly,” and through—namely, being devoted to carnal indulgences—“smooth words,” that is, flatteries.

Jerome, *On Amos*, book XI: “Among philosophers a flatterer is well defined as a pleasing enemy who turns bitter things [into sweet].” Hence the Apostle: “Have I become your enemy by speaking the truth to you?” (Gal. IV, 16), etc.: “Compliance makes friends; truth produces hatred.” Therefore let us eat the Passover with bitter herbs, etc. The vessel of election teaches that the Passover must be celebrated with truth and holiness.

“Blessings deceive the hearts” of the innocent, that is, simple or unlearned people who cannot detect them, as though conferring gifts of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands or confirmation. “For your obedience has been made known everywhere.” Therefore I ask this of you, because your deception would be so much more dangerous as the obedience of your faith has been more widely published—since you are situated, as it were, at the head [Col. 0976A] of the world. “Therefore I rejoice over you; but I want you to be wise in what is good,” because your obedience is indeed known for good, namely for discernment, “and innocent in what is evil,” that is, as though not knowing how to devise evil against anyone, in accordance with that saying of Truth: “Be prudent as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matt. X, 16).

“But may the God of peace crush …” As though he said: I indeed ask that it may happen thus, but may the God of peace rather than dissension bring about what I request. May he crush Satan—that is, every adversary of your soul—under your feet swiftly; that is, may he subject him to you as powerless, so that you may prevail against him in all things and trample down all his schemes, as things pressed underfoot. “Swiftly,” namely at my coming. Again, I ask you to watch those persons. “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.”

“Timothy greets you.” Although he has said, “All the churches greet you,” nevertheless he determined especially and by name to greet them on behalf of those whom he held most eminent, so that the written Epistle might be strengthened by the testimony of such great men. “My fellow-worker, and Lucius and Jason”—in preaching, namely, as a co-bishop, as Ambrose says. This is that disciple of Paul, the son of a certain faithful Jewish woman and a Gentile father, whom Paul himself was compelled to circumcise, as is contained in the Acts of the Apostles.

Origen: “Some maintain that Lucius is Luke, who wrote the Gospel, because names are sometimes rendered to Romans according to the first Greek declension [Col. 0976C]. Jason is the one of whom it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles that, when crowds stirred up a disturbance at Thessalonica against Paul and Silas, he gave himself up so as to secure freedom for the apostles to depart.”

“Sosipater, my kinsman. I, Tertius, greet you …” I suspect that he is the same person who is called Sosipater of Berea in the Acts of the Apostles. It may cause surprise that Paul, a Hebrew, is said to be Timothy’s kinsman, or Jason’s, or Sosipater’s. But because he does not grant this designation to the others, it is certain that he uses some term of relationship which he undoubtedly knows as kinship or consanguinity.

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0976D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 181]: “He calls them kinsmen partly by reason of race and partly by reason of faith.”

“Tertius, who wrote the Epistle in the Lord, greets [Col. 0976D] you.” Gaius is the first name of the man who wrote this Epistle at Paul’s dictation, as the Apostle’s secretary, as there is now an apostolic chancellor. Perhaps it happened by a certain divine forewarning that he should be called Tertius by name, who was third in the process: for the Holy Spirit inspired what the Apostle dictated or uttered, and this man called Tertius wrote it down with his own hand.

Ambrose: “This is the scribe of the Epistle to whom the Apostle allowed the greeting of the Roman people in his own name. Nor was it done without reason that he should use his own words, which were approved only by human judgment.”

“My host.” Origen [Col. 0977A]: “He seems to indicate that this man was hospitable, receiving not Paul only, but also providing in his house a meeting-place for the whole Church. It is handed down by the tradition of the elders that this Gaius was the first bishop of Thessalonica.”

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0977D] *Patrologia*, vol. XVII, col. 182]: “This is Gaius, I think, to whom John the Apostle writes, rejoicing in his love which he showed to the brothers by supplying their necessary expenses.”

Haymo: “This is also Gaius the captive, who was baptized by the Apostle, as he says in the Epistle to the Corinthians: ‘I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius’” (I Cor. I, 14). “And of the whole Church. Erastus greets you.”

Ambrose [Note: [Col. 0978D] Ibid., col. 182]: “He understands this as a plural nominative, as though it said, ‘All the churches greet you.’ But according to Origen it is better understood as a singular genitive, as has been said: ‘my host, and the host of the whole Church.’ For since the Apostle had already said above, ‘All the churches of Christ greet you,’ what need was there to repeat, ‘All the churches greet you’?”

“Erastus, treasurer of the city.” Origen: “I think this is the Erastus of whom he says that he remained at Corinth, and that he is treasurer—that is, steward—of that city whose builder is God.” According to Jerome: “He is called treasurer of the city according to what he once was, not what he was then.”

Haymo: “Treasurer, that is, the chief officer or steward who was over the chest in which the king’s taxes and revenues were placed.” “And Quartus the brother.” This is a proper name, like Tertius.

“The grace of our Lord …” Jerome [Col. 0977C]: “This is the writing of his hand in all his Epistles, that it may also mention the benefits of Christ.”

Haymo: “Grace is called that which is given freely; and by the name of grace we ought to understand every good thing which the elect receive freely from God, namely hope, love, and forgiveness of sins.”

“But to him who is able to establish you …” Marcion, by whom the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures were interpolated, entirely removed this chapter from the Epistle. Moreover, from the place where it is written, “Whatever is not from faith is sin,” to the end, he cut out everything. But in other copies not corrupted by Marcion, this chapter itself is found placed differently. In some manuscripts [Col. 0977D], immediately after the passage, “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (I Cor. XIV, 23), there follows at once, “But to him who is able to establish you.” Other manuscripts contain it at the end, where it is now placed.

Having completed the greetings, he ends his Epistle in thanksgiving, as though returning thanks for his completed work to him who inspired it. It is as though he continued thus: “Grace be with you,” I say; but to him who is able, etc., may glory be everlasting. It should be noted that, when it has been said, “to him who is able,” the “to whom” placed at the end appears superfluous for either sense or construction, since he had said “to him” at the beginning—unless one says that this is done because of the long interruption. For many things [Col. 0978A] intervene between that “to him” which is introduced first and the “honour and glory” joined at the end. Therefore, lest an unskilled reader, as though forgetful, should not know to whom “honour and glory” are joined, “to whom” has been supplied.

Therefore, that the construction of the sentence may in some manner be woven together, join the beginning of this verse to its end: “But to him who is able to establish you,” etc., “be honour and glory”; understand again “to whom” and understand “is,” as though it said: “To him be honour and glory, whose it is”—as though saying, “since it truly is”—“let it be, I say, through Jesus Christ,” through whom the Father is to be glorified.

From this ending of the Epistle, I think, ecclesiastical teachers conclude their expositions and sermons with a similar ending, namely in thanksgiving to God. “To establish,” namely in faith, which is the foundation of all [Col. 0978B] good things, “according to my Gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ”: according to the doctrine of my preaching, which is also that of Jesus Christ. It is not another preaching, because I preach the same thing as he; I call my Gospel, or the preaching of Jesus Christ, something made “according to the revelation of the mystery,” or “to be established according to my revelation.”

A mystery is called something secret and hidden. Hence mystical speech is called significant speech which is not open. The mystery now made manifest is the manner of our redemption, which formerly lay hidden in prophetic writings not yet expounded, but is now revealed, once they have been expounded both by Christ and by us. For it is written of Christ that, “beginning with Moses and all the prophets” (Luke XXIV, 27)—that is, kept silent through eternal ages [Col. 0978C]—it “has now been made manifest through the writings of the prophets according to the command of the eternal God for the obedience of faith”; that is, it had always been hidden until now and had never been revealed by exposition before.

Indeed, since even the seventy translators are believed in their translations especially to have kept silent about, or veiled, those things which are said concerning the Son of God, he says “of the prophets” rather than “of the law,” because this mystery is contained most especially in the prophets, where Christ had been predicted more openly or fully. “Made manifest,” I say, “among all nations according to the command of the eternal God,” that is, of Christ, who says, “Go into all the world,” etc. (Mark XVI, 15). I say “God, eternal,” although according to his humanity he had a beginning.

[Col. 0978D] For this purpose, he says, it has been made manifest: not merely that all nations may believe, but rather that they may obey him—that is, work according to faith. To him, I say, now known through Jesus Christ, “to God alone wise”: that is, who now appears uniquely wise from what he has accomplished through Christ in this mystery of our redemption, concerning which John says: “By his wisdom he struck down the proud one.” He is called alone wise in comparison with whom no one is to be called wise, just as he is called good according to that saying of Truth: “None is good except God alone” (Mark X, 18). He is also called alone wise because he possesses that sole and unique wisdom from which nothing can be hidden. “Honour and glory,” that is, glorious and singular honour. Amen.

[Col. 0979]

# PETER ABAELARD’S *INTRODUCTION TO THEOLOGY*, DIVIDED INTO THREE BOOKS

(Edition of Abaelard’s Works of 1616, edited by Amboesius, pp. 973–1136.)

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0979A] In response, so far as we can, to the request of our students, we have composed some summary of sacred learning, as an introduction, so to speak, to divine Scripture. For since they had eagerly read with us many works of philosophical study and writings of secular literature, and had been greatly pleased by what they read, it seemed to them that our mind would penetrate the understanding of the divine page, or the arguments for the sacred faith, much more easily than it had exhausted, as they say, the wells of the philosophical abyss.

They added that I could neither complete philosophy’s course nor reach its goal, nor gather any fruit from it, unless I brought its study to its end in God, to whom all things ought to be referred. For this reason believers are permitted to read the writings on secular arts and the books of the Gentiles [Col. 0979B]: so that, through their kinds of expression and eloquence, their modes of argument, and prior knowledge of the natures of things, we may attain whatever pertains to the understanding or adornment of sacred Scripture, or to defending or establishing its truth.

For the more difficult questions in which our faith—that is, the Christian faith—appears to be entangled, and the farther it seems to stand from human reason, the more surely it must be fortified by the protection of arguments, especially against the attacks of those who profess themselves philosophers. The subtler their inquiry appears, the more difficult it is to refute, and the more easily it is found to disturb the simplicity of our faith.

[Col. 0979C] Since they judged me equal to resolving these controversies—me whom they know to have been occupied from almost my cradle in philosophical studies, and especially in dialectic, which appears to be the mistress of all arguments, and whom they have learned by experience, as they say—they unanimously ask that I not delay to multiply the talent entrusted to me by the Lord, since it is unknown when that strict and terrible Judge will demand it with interest.

They add also that it befits my present age and profession that, as I have changed my conduct and habit, so I should change my study also, preferring divine books to human ones, since I have resolved, leaving the world behind, now to transfer my whole self to God. And because formerly I undertook study in order to gain money, now I should turn it toward gaining [Col. 0980A] souls, so that at least about the eleventh hour I may enter, as far as I can, to cultivate the Lord’s vineyard.

As our students frequently pressed these and similar arguments upon us, we at last agreed—so that, if they could not obtain our assent by reason or because of their importunity—that we would attempt, according to our strength, or rather by the assistance of divine grace, to undertake what they requested; not promising so much to state the truth as to set forth the sense of our opinion which they demand.

In this work, if, through faults deserving blame, I should depart—God forbid!—from Catholic understanding or expression, may He forgive me who weighs deeds by their intention; for I am always prepared to make satisfaction for statements wrongly made, whether by correcting or deleting them, whenever any one of the faithful corrects me either by the force of reason or by the authority of Scripture. For I know what is written: “The righteous man shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but the oil of the sinner shall not make my head fat” (Ps. 140:5). And in Proverbs: “The way of life is the rebuke of discipline; but he who hates rebukes is foolish” (Prov. 12:1). And again: “He who keeps rebukes shall become wiser; and he who hates rebukes shall die” (Prov. 15:5). And again: “The pestilent man does not love one who corrects him; but if he correct a wise man, he will understand discipline” (ibid., 12). Likewise: “Upon a man who despises correction with a stiff neck, sudden destruction shall come” (Prov. 29:1).

We are also prompted to this by the example of the most blessed Augustine, who, though he had received from God such great eloquence and wisdom, nevertheless acknowledged that he had set down many things erroneously in his writings, retracting and correcting them. He says: “No one, unless he is imprudent, will dare to reproach me because I reproach my errors. Let each take what I do as he wishes; yet it was fitting for me to consider in this matter too that apostolic saying where he says: ‘If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord’” (1 Cor. 11:31). Also that which is written: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. 10:19). Likewise: “Whom among his sons [variant: faithful] did Christ not terrify when he said: ‘For every odious word which a man speaks, he shall render account for it on the day of judgment’” (Matt. 12:36)?

Hence the apostle James also says: “Let every person be swift to hear, but slow to speak” (Jas. 1:19). And elsewhere: “If anyone does not stumble in word, he is a perfect man” (Jas. 3:2). I do not claim this perfection for myself even now, when I am old; how much less when I began writing as a young man! Therefore, instructed by the example of so great a man, if I should perhaps utter anything through error, I shall not defend it through contempt or presume upon it through pride, so that, even if I am not yet free from the fault of ignorance, I may nevertheless not incur the charge of heresy.

For ignorance does not make a heretic; rather, it is the obstinacy of pride—when someone, desiring to acquire a name for himself through some novelty, boasts of producing something unusual and improperly strives to defend it against all, so that he may be regarded either as superior to others or inferior to none. Hence Gennadius, bishop of Marseilles, in *On the Orthodox Faith and Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: “In whatever way a person may acquiesce, he is not a heretic unless, in contention, he becomes a heretic.” Augustine, in his Letter to Optatus: “If a false assertion concerning the soul is put forward, falsehood makes one a liar, and an unsuitable defense of falsehood makes one a heretic.” Again, the same author, on Genesis: “Heretics are such for no other reason than that, not rightly understanding the canonical Scriptures, they stubbornly maintain their own false opinions against their truth.”

The same author, carefully defining a heretic in *On the Usefulness of Believing*, says: “A heretic, in my opinion, is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage, and especially of glory, either devises or follows false and novel opinions.” Likewise, the same author in Book XVIII of *The City of God*: “Those who hold some perverse opinion in the Church, if, when corrected, they stubbornly resist and refuse to amend their pestilential doctrines, but persist in defending them, become heretics.” Again, the same author, *On the One Baptism*, Book IV: “I do not yet call this man a heretic unless, when the doctrine of the Catholic faith has been made known to him, he prefers to resist it and chooses to retain what he held.” But enough of this. Let us now proceed to the matter at hand.

## ARGUMENT OF THE WORK

This first book of *Theology* briefly comprises the substance of the entire foregoing treatise: namely, faith, charity, and sacraments—what faith is, what hope is, what charity is, what a sacrament is; in what sense “faith” is properly or improperly used; and what Catholic faith is. It sets forth the doctrine concerning faith in the Holy Trinity, or Unity: why the Father alone is called unbegotten; what is meant by the distinction of three persons in one essence of divinity; that divine power is especially denoted by the term “Father”; why the works of the three persons are called undivided; that divine wisdom is expressed by the name Son or Word; that the goodness of divine charity is called the Holy Spirit; testimonies of the prophets concerning the Trinity; and testimonies of philosophers.

The second book of *Theology* discusses the matters concerning the Trinity proposed by the first book, and commends the reasoning of understanding to the authority of testimonies.

The third book, returning more carefully to what has been set forth, investigates and discusses more fully the power, wisdom, and goodness of God, in which the Trinity consists.

## BOOK I

### I

[Col. 0981C]

There are, I think, three things in which the sum of human salvation consists: faith, charity, and sacrament. But I consider hope to be included in faith, as a species in its genus. For faith is an estimation of things not apparent—that is, not subject to the bodily senses; whereas hope is the expectation of obtaining some good, when someone believes that he will attain some good.

Faith, therefore, concerns both good and evil things, and things present or past as well as future, as blessed Augustine discusses at the beginning of the *Enchiridion*. [Note: [Col. 0981D] *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 234.] Hope, however, concerns good things only, and future things. For expectation of some misfortune should be called not so much hope as despair—that is, distrust of good. Charity, moreover, is honorable love, directed to the end to which it ought to be directed; whereas, conversely, cupidity is called dishonorable and shameful love.

Love is a good will toward another person: namely, the will by which we desire that he be in such a state as we believe it good for him to be, and desire this for his sake rather than for our own. For it often happens that, hating someone and wishing in any way to be delivered from him, we desire him now to be transferred to heavenly things and to enjoy that supernal glory—than which nothing better can happen to him. Yet we do not do this from love of him, because we act more for ourselves than for him, attending in this not so much to his advantage as to our own. Perhaps we wish something better for him in this very matter than for ourselves, still desiring for ourselves more the misery of the present life than the glory to come.

Tully too, when defining friendship in the second book of the *Rhetoric*, carefully guarded this point, saying: “Friendship is a will toward someone for good things, for the sake of that very person whom one loves.” When he added “for the sake of that very person whom he loves,” he clearly distinguished true friendship from false. For there are those who are said to love others because, under whatever intention, they desire another to fare well. But since they do this for their own sake rather than for the others’, they do not so much love the person as pursue his fortune; they hunt in him not so much his benefits as their own. Nor should such desire be called charity—that is, honorable love, as stated above—but cupidity, that is, dishonorable and shameful love.

The former is called love of God, the latter love of the world: through the former we are joined to God; through the latter we are occupied with worldly cares and serve earthly desires. By the former we care for the things that are God’s; by the latter we provide for what is our own. In the former, God is the end—that is, the final and highest cause to which our intention is directed—when we love both him and our neighbor for his sake, following not so much our own will as his. In the latter, however, we make ourselves our own end; it is enough for us if we fulfill our desires and obey our own will.

Foreseeing such persons, the Apostle says: “People will be lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 3:2)—that is, they establish the end of their self-love in themselves rather than in God. For, although we are commanded to love our neighbor as ourselves, we do not sin by loving ourselves; rather, we sin by placing, as stated, the end of love in ourselves. And although we ought to take care of our own needs as well as those of our neighbor, and therefore must do some things for our own sake, so that we too may be in some sense a cause of what we do, we are not thereby the end—that is, the superior and supreme cause—which is God.

For the very things we do for ourselves, if we act rightly, we do for God, whom we believe to be pleased by them; and love of him is our reason for doing this, so that we too may love ourselves for his sake, not him for ours. Otherwise, by acting perversely, we would establish the end of our love in ourselves rather than in him. We love both ourselves and our neighbor for his sake when we love ourselves because we believe that this pleases him, not because it will be useful to us—although it cannot in fact be useless to us.

Therefore nothing is to be loved, and nothing at all is to be done, except for God’s sake, so that we establish in God the end of all things. Hence he is also called Alpha and Omega, that is, beginning and end: the supreme beginning, from whom all things are; and the end, that is, the final and supreme cause, for whom all things are. For we ought neither to eat nor sleep, nor take a wife, nor do anything else whatever, except for his sake. Otherwise we would live like beasts, given over merely to our own pleasures.

We ought, however, to eat for his sake, at least in this respect: that we provide the body—which belongs to him and has been entrusted to us—with what is necessary, so that it may be sustained in his service. Likewise, by sleeping we ought to restore it, so that we may be able, when necessary, to keep vigil in his service. A man who is incontinent should also take a wife, not merely in order to beget children for God, but also lest he offend God by fornication. Even when we pray to him for ourselves, or do something beneficial for us before him, his charity itself impels us to these acts, by which we desire to attain him whom we love above all things. Thus all other things likewise must be done for his sake; otherwise we would vainly expect recompense from him if we did not do what we do for his sake.

The Apostle carefully observes this when he says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “Therefore, whether you eat or do anything else, do all things for the glory of God” (1 Cor. 10:31).

### II

A sacrament is a visible sign of the invisible grace of God. Thus, when someone is baptized, the outward washing of the body that we see is a sign of the inward washing of the soul, when the inner person is cleansed from sins just as the outer person is cleansed from bodily filth.

Having thus briefly set forth and defined the three things mentioned above—faith, charity, and sacrament—we must discuss each more carefully, insofar as they pertain to the proposed account of human salvation, and especially those matters that seem entangled in the greater questions.
