First, then, faith, which by nature precedes the others, as the foundation of all goods. For what can be hoped for, or loved as hoped for, unless it is first believed? Yet can something be believed if it is not hoped for or loved?

Hope therefore arises from faith, when we trust through God’s mercy that we shall attain the good we believe. Hence the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing” (Heb. 11:1). “The substance of things hoped for,” that is, the foundation and source from which we are led to hope for something—namely, by first believing that such things exist, so that afterward we may hope. “The evidence of things not appearing,” that is, proof that there are things which do not appear. For since no one doubts that faith exists, he must consequently grant that there are things not appearing, since faith, as stated, is properly spoken only of things which do not yet appear.

Hence, according to the Apostle, although three things are now said to remain—faith, hope, and charity (1 Cor. 13:13)—charity alone “never fails” (ibid., 8), enduring both in this age and in the future one. It is therefore rightly called greater, both because of the dignity of its continuance and because of its claim to reward; for it alone, I think, is worthy of reward. But if anyone says that faith is also held concerning things apparent, he uses the term “faith” improperly.

Nevertheless, faith is found to be spoken of concerning things apparent as well as things not apparent. We have examples of both before us. Gregory, Homily VI, Book II on the Gospels: [Note: [Col. 0983D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVI, col. 1202.] “Since the Apostle says, ‘Faith is the substance of things hoped for,’ etc. (Heb. 11:1), it is clearly evident that faith is the evidence of those things which cannot appear. For things that are apparent do not have faith, but knowledge.” The same, *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 8: [Note: [Col. 0985D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXVII, col. 329.] “Since Paul says, ‘Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not appearing,’ what cannot be seen ought truly to be believed. For what can be seen can no longer be believed.”

Augustine on John: [Note: [Col. 0985D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, col. 1837.] “‘And now I have told you before it happens, that when it has happened you may believe’ (John 14:29). What does this mean, when these things should rather be believed before that which is to be believed happens? For this is the praise of faith: if what is believed is not seen. For what great thing is it if that is believed which is seen, according to that saying of the Lord in which he rebukes the disciple, saying: ‘Because you have seen, have you believed? Blessed are,’ etc. (John 20:29). But he saw one thing and believed another. Divinity could not be seen by a mortal man. He therefore saw the man, and so confessed, saying: ‘My Lord and my God’ (ibid., 28). For faith itself is thus defined: ‘Faith is the substance of things hoped for’ (Heb. 11:1), things which are not seen. What, then, is meant by ‘that when it has happened you may believe’? For even the one to whom it was said, ‘Because you have seen, you have believed,’ did not believe what he saw. He beheld flesh, and believed God hidden in the flesh. Yet if we say that visible things are believed—as each person says that he has believed his own eyes—this is not the faith built up in us; rather, through the things we see, it is brought about in us that we believe things which are not seen.”

Likewise: [Note: [Col. 0985D] *Ibid.*, col. 1838.] “They would believe not with a new faith but with an increased faith; or certainly, when he had died, faith had failed, and when he had risen it was restored.” Likewise, in Sermon Thirty-Nine: [Note: [Col. 0986D] From Tractate XL, chapter 8, *Patrologia*, vol. XXXV, col. 1690.] “What does he promise believers? ‘You shall know the truth’ (John 8:32): they believed not because they knew, but in order that they might know. We believe in order that we may know; we do not know in order that we may believe. For what is faith except believing what you do not see? Faith, therefore, is believing what you do not see; truth is seeing what you have believed. It is truth, but it is still believed, not seen.”

The same author, in *On the Word of the Lord and Certain Sayings of the Apostle Paul*, Sermon Eighty: “‘The righteous lives by faith’ (Rom. 1:17), because he believes that which he does not see: we are children of God; and, ‘It has not yet appeared what we shall be’ (1 John 3:2). For as long as we are in the body, we are away from God. ‘For we walk by faith, not by sight’ (2 Cor. 5:6). When we arrive, we shall possess; and vision will then exist, not faith; reality, not hope. We shall love by seeing and possessing. Charity, therefore, will be perfect, as the Apostle says: ‘Faith, hope, charity: these three; but the greatest of these is charity’ (1 Cor. 13:13). Securely persevering in him with his help, let us say: ‘Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress,’ etc. (Rom. 8:35).” The same author, Book II of *Questions on the Gospels*: “‘The righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith’ (Rom. 1:17): this is understood as faith by which things not seen are believed.”

### III

[Col. 0986A]

Yet there is also a faith concerning things, when what is to come is believed not through words but through the things themselves being present, when the very wisdom of God will present itself to the saints for contemplation through manifest sight. Perhaps Paul speaks of this faith of things and of the presence of light itself when he says: “For the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith.” For elsewhere he says: “We all, beholding the glory of God with unveiled face, shall be transformed into the same image from glory to glory” (2 Cor. 3:18). As he says here “from glory to glory,” so there “from faith to faith”: from the glory of the Gospel, by which believers are now enlightened, to the glory of manifest truth.

Among philosophers too, faith seems to be spoken of even concerning things apparent: namely, when any thing is held in the mind in such a way that there is no doubt concerning it, whether through opinion or through the experience of the senses. Hence Boethius, in the first book of his commentary on Cicero’s *Topics*: [Note: [Col. 0986D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXIV, col. 1098.] “An argument is a reasoning which produces belief concerning a doubtful matter. For there are many things that produce belief, but because they are not reasonings, they cannot be arguments; for example, sight produces belief in the things seen. But because sight is not a reasoning, it cannot be an argument.”

These testimonies show, then, that the name “faith” is used sometimes properly and sometimes improperly, since faith is spoken not only of hidden things but also of manifest ones. Yet there are many things relating to God which it does not matter to us whether we believe or do not believe, because, whether they are believed or not believed, we incur no danger—for example, whether we believe that God will or will not cause rain tomorrow, or will or will not show mercy to this utterly wicked man. But it is enough for you who speak about faith for edification to treat and teach only those things which, if not believed, bring condemnation. These are the things that belong to Catholic faith.

### IV

Catholic faith is universal faith: it is so necessary for all that no person possessed of reason can be saved without it. Athanasius, after stating, “This is the Catholic faith,” at once explains why it is called Catholic, as if interpreting the phrase: “Unless each person believes it faithfully and firmly, he cannot be saved.”

There are also those who wish “Catholic faith” to be distinguished from the faith of Catholics—not as faith spread everywhere with the Church, but as faith lurking, as it were, in some corner or confined to some region of the earth. Catholic faith consists partly in matters concerning the very nature of divinity, and partly in divine benefits and whatever necessary dispensations or ordinances of God are carefully expressed for us in the creeds of the apostles or holy Fathers.

First, then, let us consider matters concerning the nature of divinity: namely, how in one and the same substance of divinity three persons are believed—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and what reason or benefit this distinction of persons has in the one God. Let us therefore first state this chief article of faith concerning divine unity and Trinity; then, having stated it, let us discuss it as the Lord grants.

### V

The religion of the Christian faith, then, holds that there is only one God and in no way several gods: one Lord of all, one Creator, one principle, one light, one good, one infinite being, one almighty being, one eternal being, one substance or essence wholly immutable and simple, in which neither any parts nor anything that is not itself can exist. It proclaims and believes one unity in every respect, except insofar as a plurality of persons is concerned.

It truly confesses that this substance—so simple, indivisible, and pure—contains three persons equal and coeternal with one another in every respect, different not by a numerical plurality of things but by a plurality of properties: God the Father, as stated; God his Son; and God his Spirit, proceeding from both. One person is not another, although each is the very same thing as another. For he who is Father is not Son or Holy Spirit, nor is he who is Son Holy Spirit. Yet what the Father is, the Son is, and the Holy Spirit is also; and conversely. For the same God is Father as he is Son or Holy Spirit. They are absolutely one in nature, one both in number and substance; but according to their properties they are personally distinguished from one another, so that this is another than that, not another thing.

A human being is personally, not substantially, different from another human being, since this person is not that person, although this one is altogether what that one is—that is, he is precisely the same substance as that one, though not the same person. Hence Sedulius: “Not because the Son is that person whom the supreme Father is, but because what the supreme Father is, that the Son is.”

### VI

The proper characteristic of God the Father is to be unbegotten (*ingenitus*), that is, to exist from himself and not from another; just as the proper characteristic of the Son is to be begotten from the Father, not created or made; and that of the Holy Spirit is to proceed from both and to be neither created nor made. For what subsists eternally and lacks a beginning cannot fittingly be called created or made.

Therefore we call the Father alone unbegotten—that is, existing from himself and not from another. Hence Augustine, against Felician the Arian: “I call the Father unbegotten because he did not proceed from another.” Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VI: [Note: [Col. 0987D] *Patrologia*, vol. LXXXII, col. 271.] “The Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called unbegotten.”

It is one thing, then, to say that the Father is unbegotten, another to say that he is not begotten. Just as it is one thing to say “unjust,” another “not just.” For whatever is unjust must necessarily be not just; but not conversely: a stone is not just, yet it is not unjust. Thus, since God the Father is unbegotten, he is clearly not begotten—that is, he is not the Son. The Holy Spirit too is not begotten, since he also is not begotten—that is, he is not the Son—yet he is not therefore unbegotten, because he is from another, proceeding both from the Father and from the Son.

The Father alone, then, is called unbegotten, just as the Son alone is begotten. But the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but, as stated, proceeds from both. Hence Augustine, *To Orosius*, chapter 2: “Certain faith declares the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten; for, if we say unbegotten, we seem to affirm two Fathers, but if begotten, we are blamed for affirming [variant: believing] two Sons. But what certain faith holds is that he is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeds from both—that is, from the Father and the Son.”

Gennadius also affirms this in chapter 1 of *On the Orthodox Faith and Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: “The Father, therefore, is the principle of divinity, from whom the Son is born, from whom the Holy Spirit is not born, because he is not the Son; nor is he unbegotten, because he is not the Father.” Hence blessed Pope Gregory also recalls in the creed prefixed to his letters: “We believe that the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but coeternal, proceeding from the Father and the Son.”

Although each of these persons is God or Lord or Creator, and one person is not another, there are not therefore several gods, lords, or creators, as there are several persons. For when we say “gods,” “lords,” or “creators,” we indicate a number of things, each of which is God, Lord, or Creator; but in an individual reality there can be no plurality of things. Hence we call the Trinity indivisible. But when we confess many persons in God, we show a plurality of properties, not of things, as we have recalled above.

Some predicates, therefore, are said only of individual persons: “unbegotten” of the Father alone; “begotten” or “incarnate” of the Son alone; “proceeding from both” of the Holy Spirit alone. Some are said only jointly and not severally: “Trinity,” of the three persons alone. Some are said equally of them both separately and jointly: God, Lord, Creator, almighty, wisdom, power, justice, and so forth.

But we use only this name, “person,” in the plural, when we speak of several persons; we do not speak of several gods or lords, nor admit any plurality in the other predicates. Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book VII, chapter 7: “Father is said to be a person with reference to himself, not to the Son or Spirit.” Likewise: “This alone is not so, that when it is said of each severally with reference to itself, it is understood plurally, not singularly, in the whole.” We say, therefore, “The Father is a person, the Son is a person, the Holy Spirit is a person”; yet Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not one person but several.

Nevertheless, as these persons have precisely the same substance, so they have undifferentiated glory and undivided operation and will. Having set forth this summary of faith concerning unity and Trinity, it remains for us to defend and establish it against the inquiries of doubters by suitable examples of likenesses. For what benefit is there in speaking for instruction if what we wish to teach cannot be expounded so as to be understood?

Blessed Augustine carefully considered this when he wished to explain the very difficult passage on the Trinity with which the Evangelist John begins: [Note: [Col. 0989D] *Patrologia*, vol. XL, col. 276.] “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). “The natural man,” he says, “does not receive this. What then, brothers? Shall we be silent about it? Why then is it written, if it is to be kept silent? Or why is it heard, if it is not expounded? But why is it expounded, if it is not understood? Therefore, since again I do not doubt that among you there are some by whom it can not only be received when explained but understood before it is explained, I shall not defraud those who can receive it while fearing that I may be superfluous to the ears of those who cannot receive it.”

### VII

First, then, we must discuss what this distinction of persons means within the one nature of divinity: namely, why the same divinity is called Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Then we must consider how, while the substance remains wholly one and indivisible, a Trinity of persons can be assigned; and how what we have previously set forth concerning divine unity and Trinity may be defended against vehement philosophical attacks.

It seems to us that the perfection of the supreme good is carefully described by the names of the three persons given above. For when God is proclaimed Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we understand through this distinction of Trinity that he is the supreme good and perfect in all things.

### VIII

By the name Father, indeed, the power of divine majesty is designated: namely, that by which he can accomplish whatever he wills. Hence Augustine in the *Enchiridion*: [Note: [Col. 0990D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLIV, col. 235.] “He is not truly called almighty except because he can do whatever he wills, and the effect of the will of the Almighty is not hindered by the will of any creature.” The same author, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “He cannot do unjust things, because he himself is supreme justice and goodness. But he is almighty not because he can do all things, but because he can accomplish whatever he wills.”

As divine majesty of power is especially expressed by the title God the Father, so divine wisdom is denoted by the appellation Son or Word, because he can discern all things and thus cannot in any respect be deceived.

### IX

But by the title Holy Spirit, his very charity or benevolence is expressed: namely, that by which he wills all things to be done or ordered in the best way, and each thing to come about in the way in which it can best come about; by which he uses other things well, orders all things most excellently, and brings them also to their best end.

No one is perfect in all things who is found powerless in any respect; no one is perfectly blessed who can be deceived in any respect; and no one is wholly benevolent who does not will and order all things to be done in the best way. But where these three meet—where one is perfect in power, wisdom, and good will—there is no good lacking from his fullness. Thus, to confess God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is to proclaim, as stated, that he is the supreme good: one from whose fullness of every good nothing is absent, and through participation in whom all other things are good.

This distinction of the Trinity is suitable not only for describing the perfection of the supreme good, as stated, but also greatly helps persuade people to religious worship of God. For this reason, divine Wisdom itself, incarnate in its preaching, most rightly decreed to adopt it. Two things make us wholly subject to God: fear and love. Power and wisdom especially inspire fear, since we know him to be judge, know that he can punish whatever he wills, and know that nothing is hidden from him. Benevolence, however, especially pertains to love, so that we may love most of all him whom we hold to be most benevolent. From this it is also certain that he wills to punish impiety, because the more justice pleases him, the more iniquity displeases him, as it is written: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (Ps. 44:8).

This distinction of the Trinity is necessary not only for inspiring fear or love of God in people, but is also of great value in commending all his works, so that whatever he does may be believed to be done excellently: since he can accomplish all that he wills, knows how to preserve all things in every way, and wills all things to be done or proceed in the best manner.

Hence, when we implore divine grace to work something else through us, we first make mention of the Trinity, saying: “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” or “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity,” so that, by mentioning divine power, wisdom, and benevolence, we show that whatever God accomplishes is done excellently.

Thus Moses too, when treating of the creation of the whole world, immediately at the beginning of Genesis makes mention of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that whatever he relates as made by God may be believed to have been made excellently. For when he says, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), and afterward adds, “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (ibid., 2), he carefully expresses the divine Trinity.

In God the Creator he suggests the Father—that is, he mentions divine power, by which all things could be created from nothing. Yet the name “God” may also, not inappropriately, according to its proper interpretation, suggest this: that it is interpreted as though *theos* (θεός), “fear,” because the reverence of fear is especially rendered to power. By the name “beginning,” however, he designates the Son—that is, divine reason or wisdom—in which all things first somehow had their existence through providence, and began there before being brought into the effect of works. Hence the Evangelist, speaking of the Father’s Word, says: “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3–4).

Likewise Macrobius, following Plato, states that the mind of God, which the Greeks call *nous* (νοῦς, “intellect”), contains the original forms of things, which are called ideas. “Before they came forth into bodies,” says Priscian—that is, before they emerged into the completed effects of works. “The Spirit of the Lord,” however, plainly suggests the Holy Spirit—that is, the benevolent goodness of divine grace.

In accordance with this careful consideration of the prophet, when he came to the excellent creation of humankind, assigning this work precedence over the others and commending it, as it were, above the others, he prudently made a forceful distinction of the Trinity. For the Lord said rather, “Let us make man,” than “I shall make [man],” “in our image,” he says, “and likeness” (Gen. 1:26): man indeed in the image, woman in the likeness. For according to the Apostle, man is the image of God, not woman (1 Cor. 11:7). But as man is the image of God, so woman is called the image of man. An image is called an expressed likeness of something; yet a likeness may be called such even if it does not greatly express that of which it is a likeness.

Man, therefore, was made in the image of the Trinity because, being created more perfect than woman, he is more like the perfection of the supreme good described above. He was also set over both woman and the other earthly creatures through power, was worthier through wisdom, and was more inclined through love toward those things in which perfection consists.

The Apostle rightly testifies that he was not deceived by the serpent when the woman was deceived (1 Tim. 2:14). Yet, out of love for the woman offering him the fruit she had tasted, and unwilling to make her sad, he burst into transgression, presuming more upon God’s mercy than he should have: he thought God ready to forgive such a slight offense as it seemed to him, provided that he did not in any manner cause the woman entrusted to him by the Lord to stumble—especially as this seemed to have been done more piously than maliciously. And who would not agree that God was loved more by him than by the woman? For how could she then have truly loved God when she believed that he had spoken deceitfully to her, since she yielded to the serpent’s counsel?

### X
For although the divine power is specially expressed by the name Father, the divine wisdom by the name Son or Word, and the very kindness or charity of God by the name [Col. 0991D] Holy Spirit, neither authority nor reason leaves us in doubt. That power is specially expressed by the name Father may be gathered from many testimonies. Hence Bishop Maximus, in his exposition of the creed called that of the Apostles, read on the fifth Sunday of Lent, states it in these words [Note: [Col. 0991D] *Patrologia*, vol. LVII, col. 433.]:

> “Do you believe in God, the almighty Father?” In “God” the unbegotten nature is shown; in “Father,” the reality of the Only-Begotten; in “almighty,” the fullness of power. For through unbegotten deity he is almighty, and through omnipotence Father.

Here he calls “unbegotten” uncreated: by the Father’s “unbegotten deity” he declares that he alone of the three persons is unbegotten—that is, as we have already recalled above, he alone is not from another. The other persons, however, are from him. But when it is said that the Father himself is almighty through unbegotten deity—that is, because, while he is God, he is also, as stated, alone unbegotten—and again, Father through omnipotence, it is plainly suggested that, just as being unbegotten is proper to God the Father, so divine power belongs specially to his property; although each of the other persons, being of the same substance as the Father, is altogether of the same power.

For according to the properties of the three persons, certain things are customarily said or understood specially and, as it were, properly of one of them, though according to their nature and unity we do not doubt that they belong to each individually. Thus wisdom is specially attributed to the [Col. 0992B] Son, and charity to the Holy Spirit, though the Father, the Holy Spirit, and indeed the whole Trinity are wisdom; and likewise both the Father himself and the Son can be called charity. So also, according to the properties of the persons, certain works are specially attributed to one person, although the works of the whole Trinity are proclaimed indivisible, and whatever is done by one of them is known to be done by each.

The assumption of flesh is assigned to the Son alone; and people are said to be regenerated from water and the Spirit only—not also from water and the Father or the Son—although in these matters the operation of the whole Trinity was present. Thus, in accordance with the very property of the Father, matters pertaining to power are customarily assigned specially and chiefly to him, since, as stated, divine power is specially signified by his name; and because he alone is called unbegotten, that is, existing from himself and not from another, a certain power proper to him remains according to the mode of substance. That is: although the Father can do all that the Son and Holy Spirit can do, he has, in addition, this: he alone can exist from himself and does not need to be from another.

Yet we proclaim neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit less almighty than the Father. For, as blessed Augustine observes, God is called almighty for no other reason than that he can accomplish whatever he wills—namely, that no obstacle may oppose his will in accomplishing anything. The works of the three persons are called indivisible—that is, common—because whatever is carried out by power is directed by wisdom and brought into being by goodness. Hence, rightly, in the things for which we pray to God, we make mention of the Trinity, saying: “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity,” or, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”; so that, just as the operation of the three persons is indivisible, their invocation also may be inseparable. Thus, while the faith of the benefit sought is established, the efficacy of the divine work itself is commended. For one readily believes that he will do the good requested who both can do it as he wills and is known to be most kindly disposed.

By the name Father, as stated, [Col. 0993A] God’s omnipotence is recalled; by the name Spirit, his supreme kindness. When the remembrance of divine wisdom is added—that wisdom which is expressed by the name Son, through which he knows how to preserve measure in all that he accomplishes—then the excellent result is shown that proceeds from him who can do all that he wills, who knows how to observe measure in all things he does, and who wills that all things be done in the best way.

But although each of the three persons is called almighty because each can accomplish whatever any one of them wills to accomplish, it does not follow that one is in every respect the same as another, since they differ in their properties. The Father alone can be Father or unbegotten; the Son alone begotten; and the Holy Spirit alone proceeding. Therefore whatever one person can do another also can do, and hence each is called almighty; but whatever one can be, or can be in the mode in which one is, need not be what the other is.

Jerome testifies that the Father is found to have this more than the Son: he alone is from himself, whereas the Son is not from himself, but is begotten from the Father. For, in expounding the faith of the Council of Nicaea, he says in the creed:

> “Far be it that anything greater or lesser be found in the Son of God—whether in place, time, power, knowledge, equality, or subjection—when this is said of his divinity, not of his flesh. For if any greater or lesser thing is found, except that the Father begot the Son, and except that the Son was not born from himself but was born from the Father, then the Father is thereby acknowledged to be either envious or impotent, and moreover temporal.”

From these words of Jerome, when he professes that nothing greater is found in the Father than in the Son, nor less in the Son than in the Father, except that the Son is not from himself—as the Father certainly is—it seems that he ascribes to the Father, according to nature or mode of existence rather than operation, this power as, so to speak, proper to him: that he alone can subsist through himself, or have existence from himself—that is, not from another—whereas the other two persons in the Trinity must be from him and do not have subsistence through themselves.

This also accords with blessed Ambrose in his commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians, where it is written: “One God and Father [Col. 0993D] of all, who is above all,” etc. (Eph. 4:6). If, therefore, we refer power both to the nature of subsisting and to the efficacy of operation, we shall find that omnipotence belongs properly or specially to the property of the Father’s person. For he not only can accomplish all things with the other two persons, but he alone has existence from himself and not from another; and as he has existence from himself, so he has power from himself. The other persons, however, as they have being from him, so also have from him the power to accomplish what they will. Hence the Son says of himself: “I can do nothing of myself” (John 5:30); and elsewhere: “Of myself I do nothing” (John 8:28), or, “I do not speak of myself” (John 14:10).

Therefore, when Maximus says of the Father that he is almighty through unbegotten deity—that is, because, while he is God, he is also unbegotten—the power proper to the Father, by which he alone subsists from himself and not from another, and is therefore alone called unbegotten, is included in omnipotence. Thus Maximus understood him as almighty in such a way that he attributed to him as proper everything pertaining to power, not only as regards the effect of operation, but also as regards the mode of subsisting. Thus “almighty through unbegotten deity” means, as though he had plainly said: “Because he is God and unbegotten, he is properly almighty in both ways, as we have said.” And when he immediately adds, “and Father through omnipotence,” it is as though we acknowledged that he properly possesses this omnipotence as he understood it.

Perhaps “Father through omnipotence” may also be understood more carefully in this sense: that through the omnipotence specially attributed to him, as stated, he generates his Wisdom from himself as a Son, since divine Wisdom itself is something of divine omnipotence, being itself a certain power. For we call wisdom the power of discerning, or of foreseeing deception and fraud, so that he cannot be deceived in anything or anything else can be hidden from him.

Divine wisdom, therefore, is a certain divine power through which God has the ability perfectly to discern and know all things, so that he cannot err in anything through ignorance. Accordingly, the very Word of God is said to be from the Father’s own substance—which is to say that the Son is begotten from the Father—as [Col. 0994C] we shall discuss more fully later, God permitting, when we come to expound the mode of this generation. For the present, our task is to introduce authorities by which we may establish that divine power is principally expressed by the designation Father.

If we examine both Gospel and apostolic sayings, we understand that, according to the propriety of the expression itself, matters pertaining to power are specially ascribed to the Father. From this also it may plainly be inferred that omnipotence itself is specially designated by the name Father. For the Son says: “Which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7), not “which the Son himself or the Holy Spirit has placed,” though the power of the three persons is the same. And elsewhere he says: “As my Father has appointed for me” (Luke 22:29).

Moreover, whenever the Son’s humanity implores the help of the divinity united to it or offers any prayers to it, he employs the name Father alone, thereby recalling the power able to accomplish what is requested. Thus he says: “Holy Father, keep them” (John 17:11); “Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46); and similar expressions belonging to prayer. Ecclesiastical practice still especially observes this: in those particular prayers made at the altar during the celebration of Mass, the prayers direct their address to the Father alone.

And when the Apostle says that Christ rose from the dead through the glory of God the Father (Rom. 6:4), that is, through the strength of divine power; or that the Father raised him from the dead and will give life to our bodies; or that the Son or Holy Spirit was sent by him; or that the Son obeyed him—he attributes, as if properly or specially to the Father, things which appear to pertain to power. From these also it is suggested that matters of power should chiefly be ascribed to the person of the Father, in accordance with his property, as stated; just as matters pertaining to the reason of the mind or wisdom are ascribed to the Son, such as judging, which belongs to discernment.

Hence it is written: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son,” because power yields to wisdom in the examination of judgment, where equity must be assessed more than the force of power exercised. The added words, “because he is the Son of Man,” show why divine judgment especially depends on this, as the Son himself declared: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22). That is, the ungodly justly incur the greatest condemnation because they proved ungrateful and without excuse for so great a divine benefit, even rejecting the Son sent by the Father.

To this also belongs the inscription of the ninth Psalm: “For the hidden things of the Son,” namely, judgments, concerning which it is added in the same Psalm: “The Lord shall be known in executing judgments” (Ps. 9:17); and elsewhere: “Thy judgments are a great deep” (Ps. 35:7). For, as stated, it belongs to wisdom to judge—that is, to know what is due to each person according to justice.

The Apostle calls Christ the wisdom of God and the power of God [Col. 0995C] (1 Cor. 1:24): wisdom, indeed, through which he knows all things completely; power, through which he brings to completion the efficacy of every good thing. Thus it is written: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3); and elsewhere: “Thou hast made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24). Hence he is called the Father’s right hand or hand, through which the Father made all things. He is also fittingly called the Father’s mind, reason, or Angel of Counsel, because in this wisdom the Father rationally orders all things, whether in creating the world or restoring it after its fall. And in this the Father gave true counsel to our ignorance, when, through the Word’s incarnation, he visited us.

Moreover, whenever God is said to have appeared to human beings for the purpose of teaching something, this is attributed to the Son rather than another person, because teaching necessarily belongs to wisdom. Whether in ancient times God appeared in an angel or in some bodily form in order to teach something else, or in the time of grace made himself visible to the world through the assumed human being, this is ascribed properly or specially to the Son for the reason given above. For when God teaches us through him, he instructs us as through his Word whenever he imparts to us something from the fullness of his wisdom, as it is written: “And from his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16).

XI.

Therefore, when the Son of God is called *Logos*, that is, Word, the term is taken in the sense in which λόγος among the Greeks also signifies the conception of the mind itself, or the mind’s reason, not the utterance of the voice. Hence Boethius, in the second book of his *Categories of Aristotle*, says:

> Since in Greek speech λόγος means both thought of the mind and inward reasoning, and λόγος also means speech, Aristotle, lest anyone suppose, when he said that the *logon*—that is, reason—is a quantity, that he meant that *logos* which anyone arranges in thought, added: “which is produced with the voice.”

Hence also blessed Augustine, in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 44, observes: “‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1:1), which is called λόγος in Greek, but in Latin signifies both discourse and Word. Yet here it is better translated *Word*, so that reference may be made not only to the Father but also to those things made through the Word. *Reason*, however, is called reason even though nothing is made through it.”

The same author, in *Against Five Heresies*, says: “‘In the beginning was the Word’; the Greeks say λόγος more fittingly. For λόγος signifies both word and reason.”

Blessed Gregory also speaks in the seventh homily on the Gospels concerning this intelligible Word of God—that is, wisdom as understood above—distinguishing the intelligible Word itself from the audible word, which is voice:

> “You know that the Only-Begotten is called the Word of the Father, as John testifies when he says, ‘In the beginning was the Word.’ From our own speech you know that the voice first sounds, so that the word may afterward be heard. John, therefore, declares that he is a voice because the Word precedes.”

The same author, in Homily 23 on John the Baptist, says: “‘I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.’ He was called a voice by the prophet because the Word went before.”

This means: just as, in the hearer, the audible word precedes the intelligible, because the voice first sounds so that understanding may afterward be conceived from it, so John’s preaching went before, announcing the Lord’s coming. Thus “Word” means the conception of the mind and a certain discourse of understanding formed in the mind. In its likeness, the Only-Begotten is the Word of God, and, as it were, God’s intellectual and eternal discourse, in whose providence the eternally predetermined ordering and operation of all things subsists.

Hence when Moses, in describing the making of the various creations, first says, “God said” (Gen. 1:3), and immediately joins the effect to the saying: “And it was so” (ibid., v. 7), he shows that God created all things in the Word, that is, in his wisdom—in other words, rationally. The Psalmist also says: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32:9), that is, he created or ordered all things by reason.

Elsewhere the Psalmist shows this Word more plainly, declaring it not to be an audible and passing word but intelligible and enduring: “Who made the heavens in understanding” (Ps. 135:5). That is, he made them according to the manner in which he first ordered them in the word of his mind—that is, in the presence of his eternal intelligence, which foresees all things. Augustine, in *The City of God*, book XVI, chapter 6, describes this intellectual discourse of God—that is, the eternal ordering of his wisdom—as follows:

> “God’s speech prior to his work is the unchangeable rationale of the work itself; it has no resounding and passing sound, but a power eternally abiding and operating in time.”

XII.

Just as matters pertaining to power are specially attributed to the Father, and matters pertaining to wisdom to the Son, so matters pertaining to the operation of divine grace and the goodness of divine charity are ascribed to the Holy Spirit. Such are the forgiveness of sins and the distribution of whatever gifts proceed from his goodness alone, not from our merits: for example, regeneration in baptism for the remission of sins; confirmation through the bishop’s laying on of hands, [Col. 0997B] for the giving of the armor of virtues, by which, after receiving forgiveness of sins, we may resist the enemy who then rises more violently against us.

So also the other sacraments performed in the Church should be attributed to God’s goodness and to the Spirit, so that it may plainly be suggested from this that the affection of divine goodness and the sweetness of divine grace are expressed by the term Holy Spirit. For by the breath of our mouth—that is, by our breathing—the emotions of the mind are chiefly revealed: when we sigh from love or groan under the pressure of labor or pain. Hence in this place Holy Spirit is appropriately understood as affection, according to the saying of Wisdom: “The spirit of wisdom is kind,” etc. (Wis. 1:6); and the Psalmist’s words: “Thy good Spirit shall lead me into a right land,” etc. (Ps. 142:10).

Hence also the Apostle says, “God is charity,” because, as Gregory testifies, the Spirit himself is love. Augustine likewise, in the first book on Genesis, at the place where it is written, “The Spirit was borne over the waters,” says:

> “Needy and indigent love loves in such a way that it is subjected to the things it loves. Therefore, when the Spirit of the Lord was mentioned—by which his holy good will and love are understood—it was said to be borne above, lest God should be thought to love in making his works through the necessity of affection rather than through the abundance of beneficence.”

The same author, in book XIV of *On the Trinity*, says:

> “Finally, if in us nothing of God is greater than charity, and there is no greater gift of God than the Holy Spirit, what follows more fittingly than that he himself is the charity called God and from God? And if the charity by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father ineffably displays the communion of both, what is more fitting than that he who is the common Spirit of both be called charity in a proper sense?”

The same author, above, in book V:

> “The Holy Spirit, according to what has been said, because God is spirit, can indeed be called universally so: for the Father is spirit, and the Son is spirit; the Father is holy, and the Son is holy.” 

And shortly afterward:

> “The Holy Spirit is a certain communion of the Father and the Son, and perhaps is therefore so called because the same designation can belong to the Father and the Son. Therefore, so that from the human being that which belongs to both may signify communion of both, the Holy Spirit is called the gift of both.”

The same author, in book XV:

> “By many examples it may be said that the names of many things are used both universally and applied properly to particular things. I say this so that no one may think us improper for calling the Holy Spirit charity, because both God the Father and God the Son can be called charity.”

It is therefore clear, I think, from the testimonies set forth above, that divine power, as we have said, is expressed by the name Father; that the Son is understood as divine wisdom; and that the goodness of divine grace is called the Holy Spirit. Thus to speak of the power of the Lord is as though we said the divine power from which divine wisdom is begotten. To call the Son God is as though we called him divine wisdom begotten from divine [Col. 0998B] power. And when we speak of the Holy Spirit, it is as though we recalled the charity of divine goodness proceeding equally from Father and Son.

The mode of this generation or procession, as the Lord grants, we shall explain in what follows. But now, in support of our faith against all mockers of the Christian faith, Jews as well as Gentiles, I wish to bring forward testimonies from their writings, so that they may understand that this distinction of the Trinity was proclaimed to all. Divine inspiration deigned to reveal it through prophets to the Jews and through philosophers to the Gentiles, so that the acknowledged perfection of the highest good might invite both peoples to the worship of one God—from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things—and so that this faith of the Trinity might more readily be received by both peoples in the time of grace, when they saw that it had also been handed down by ancient teachers.

XIII.

First let us consider the very opening of the Law, where Moses the lawgiver puts forward the Catholic faith concerning unity together with Trinity as the foundation of all goods. For when it is said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” where we say “God,” the Hebrew text has *Elohim*, the plural of the singular *El*. Why, then, is it not said *El*, meaning “God,” but *Elohim*, which among the Hebrews is interpreted “gods” or “judges,” unless this be fitted to a plurality of persons, so that plurality in God may thereby be indicated in the same way as Trinity? God is, in a sense, called multiple as he is threefold—not according to some diversity of substance, but according to the properties of persons.

Thus *Elohim* means, as it were, not many things but many persons, each of whom is God; otherwise they would call them several gods, whereas there is only one. For in the same passage careful provision is made for showing the unity of substance, when it says “created,” not “created [plural],” preserving the singular number in the verb according to the unity of substance understood through the subject noun, although that noun, in its vocal form and declensional ending, is plural. Conversely, when it is said, “A crowd rushes,” a plural verb is applied to a singular noun according to the plurality of things understood through the subject noun.

Thus “*Elohim* created” means, as it were, “the Trinity of divine persons created,” that is, worked together. Immediately afterward Moses also joins a distinction of persons, as though to specify why he had used *Elohim* in the plural, namely, to denote this distinction. The eternity of the Holy Spirit is plainly shown when it says: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2). The Word, that is, the Son, is likewise plainly suggested when it says: “God said, ‘Let there be’” (ibid., v. 3): that is, in his utterance or Word, in his coeternal Wisdom, the Father ordered the things to be made. This cannot be understood of bodily speech.

Likewise, in what is written, “God saw that it was good” (ibid., v. 10), the goodness of God, which we call the Holy Spirit, is suggested, just as in “God said” the Word and the Father are understood. “God saw that it was good” means, as it were, that, understanding that the work he had made was good, he loved it precisely because it was good. From this it is also clearly shown that he himself is good.

What could be clearer as a demonstration of the Trinity than what is later added in the creation of humankind, when the Lord says: “Let us make man,” etc.? Why is “Let us make” said in the plural, except to express the cooperation of the whole Trinity? For whom would God be exhorting to create humankind, or whom would he ask to help him in anything, when he alone was to create? For it is written: “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? With whom has he taken counsel?” etc. (Isa. 40:13).

Humanity is fittingly said to be made in the image and likeness of the Trinity—that is, in a certain express likeness of the three persons—since it imitates the Father through the power received over other creatures; the Son through reason; and the Spirit through the kindness of innocence, which it afterward lost through sin. The serpent’s words in the following passage also seem to concern this plurality of divine persons: “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3:5), which, as stated above, sounds in Hebrew as *elohim*, that is, divine persons rather than different gods. So too does the Lord’s rebuke: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Gen. 3:22); and again what the Lord says: “Let us go down and confuse their language” (Gen. 11:7), although God alone accomplished this. Hence it is added: “And thus he scattered them” (ibid., v. 8).

But now, after the Law, let us turn to the prophets.

David, the greatest of prophets and kings, who says, setting his own understanding above that of others, “I have understood more than all my teachers” (Ps. 118:99), and “I have understood more than the elders” (ibid., v. 100), plainly suggests the distinction of the Trinity when he says: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth [Col. 1000A] all their power” (Ps. 32:6).

Elsewhere he suggests unity together with Trinity, saying: “May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. 66:8). The threefold confession of God expresses the Trinity of persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. In designating the Son of God he fittingly added “our,” as though showing him to share our nature and to have been given to us by the Father, when divine Wisdom illumined us through the incarnation of the Word. Of this Word the Apostle also says: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

The Psalmist reveals the unity of divine substance in the same passage. After uttering the divine name three times, understanding one God only in three persons, he did not join them with a plural verb but with a singular one. This agrees also with Isaiah’s statement that he saw the Seraphim and heard them crying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts” (Isa. 6:3). The prophet rightly used the title Lord to signify power, because it belongs to lords to rule. This power is also often designated by the name God, since, according to Isidore, Greek Θεός (*Theos*), that is, “God,” is interpreted “fear,” and any power is a source of fear to subjects.

That the Word of God is to be understood as his very Wisdom is plainly shown in Ecclesiasticus:

> “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and was always with him and is before the age. Who has investigated the wisdom of God, which precedes all things? Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from eternity; the fountain of wisdom is the Word of God on high,” etc. (Ecclus. 1:1 ff.)

David also plainly suggests the Son’s eternal generation from God the Father when he introduces the person of the Son speaking thus: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2:7–8). “Today I have begotten you” means, as it were: “You are eternal light from my own substance.” For in eternity there is nothing past or future, but only the present; therefore he used an adverb of present time, saying “today,” for “eternally.”

He fittingly added “I have begotten,” a present perfect, to “today,” in order to show that the generation is always present through “today” and completed through “I have begotten”: namely, that it has never ceased or begun. What is past is already completed and perfected; therefore he used the past tense, as it were, for perfection, showing that the Son is always begotten from the Father and always begotten.

Elsewhere he declares the Son’s eternity more plainly: “He shall remain with the sun and before the moon, through generation and generation” (Ps. 7:5); and again: “With thee is the beginning” (Ps. 109:3). Isaiah, marveling at this ineffable and eternal generation, and also at the temporal generation—both of which are wonderful—says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). That is, plainly: it is not for human ability to expound this, but for God alone—though his Spirit speaks of these matters in those faithful persons whom he wills, as he himself testifies: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

Jerome also, commenting on Ecclesiastes at the passage, “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of men goes upward, and the spirit of the beast goes downward into the earth?” (Eccl. 3:21), interprets the words, “Who shall declare his generation?” as an example of something difficult rather than impossible:

> “By adding ‘who,’ he wished to demonstrate the difficulty of the matter. For in the Holy Scriptures the pronoun ‘who’ is always understood not as indicating impossibility but difficulty, as there: ‘Who shall declare his generation?’ (Isa. 53:3), that is, Christ’s,” etc.

This coeternity of Wisdom with the Father is likewise plainly shown in Proverbs:

> “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel. The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning. From eternity I was established, before the earth was made. The deeps did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; not yet the fountains, not yet the mountains. Before the hills I was brought forth. He had not yet made the earth or the poles of the world. When he prepared the heavens I was present; when he set the foundations of the earth in balance, I was with him, arranging all things; and I delighted day by day, playing before him at all times” (Prov. 8:12 ff.).

What could more plainly attest the eternal generation of the Word than Wisdom’s own testimony that before the world’s establishment she was conceived and brought forth, and that, abiding eternally with the Father, she always plays before him? For what is conceived and brought forth is surely in the one from whom it is generated; and wisdom is in the very substance or essence of power, since it is itself a certain power, as we shall show later.

Thus that Wisdom is conceived and brought forth by God means, as it were, that wisdom is generated from the Father’s own substance, from which it exists. That Wisdom plays before the Father and arranges all things with him means that divine power orders all things in wisdom according to the will of his goodness, so that in that play we understand the very effect of goodness, of which it is written: “By the spirit of his mouth, all their power” (Ps. 32:6). And when Wisdom is said always to stand before God the Father, it means that omnipotence itself accomplishes nothing except with reason preceding and Wisdom’s guidance.

Again, in the same Proverbs he wrote most plainly of the Son of God and of the ineffable name of the Son, as though introducing the person of some wonderful prophet, prophesying and marveling at this unutterable generation. For he says:

> “The vision which the man spoke, with whom God is, and which he, strengthened by God dwelling with him, said: Who has raised up all the ends of the earth? What is his name, or what is the name of his Son?” (Prov. 30:1 ff.)

A firm and very clear testimony to our faith also appears in Ecclesiasticus, where the Wisdom of God says that she is firstborn before all things according to the nature of divinity, and afterward created according to the assumption of our nature, when, at the Father’s command, she visited Israel in the garment of the Incarnation. For it is written there:

> “Wisdom shall have praise in the multitude of the elect, and among the blessed she shall be blessed, saying: I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature. I made unfailing light arise in the heavens, and like a mist I covered all the earth. I dwell in the highest places, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud. I alone compassed the circuit of heaven,” etc. (Ecclus. 24:4 ff.).

And shortly afterward:

> “Then the Creator of all commanded and said to me, and he who created me rested in my tabernacle; and he said to me: Dwell in Jacob, take your inheritance in Israel, and strike your roots among my elect” (ibid., vv. 12–13).

[Col. 1002B] In the same book he also prophesies most plainly that the remission of sins consists in the incarnation of the divine Wisdom which is Christ, saying that David’s sins were cleansed through Christ. For there, when much was said concerning David’s praise, the whole sum of that praise is gathered into this one statement which follows: “Christ cleansed his sins, and exalted his horn for ever, and gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Israel.” Micah likewise says concerning this eternal generation of the Word from the Father, and also the temporal generation from the mother: “And thou, Bethlehem Ephrata, art little among the thousands of Judah: out of thee shall come forth one who shall be ruler in Israel, and his goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5:2). Let rebellious and unbelieving Jews say of whom, to be born at Bethlehem, this was spoken—namely, that [Col. 1002C] his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity. For that is eternal which lacks an origin. But if they refer this to that Messiah—that is, as they say, the greatest prophet—whom they await, and who nevertheless according to them will be a mere man and not also God, let them show whose going forth is eternal, or whence he proceeds eternally. But if they say that he proceeds eternally from Bethlehem because his birth in that place was from eternity foreseen and predestined by God, then in this manner the birth of any human being, or of any thing whatever, is eternal, since it was foreseen from eternity.

[Col. 1002D] Let them therefore learn that the generation which they read in Scripture and profess in their reading, yet do not believe when professing it, is eternal. Let them also answer me, when they hear the Prophet say, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6), what they understand by the word of the Lord, by his mouth, and by the spirit. For it is agreed that God is the one principle of all other things. And everything which exists either is God, and therefore eternal, or remains created by that eternal principle. Moreover it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), whence they maintain that nothing was created before this. Therefore that Word by which the heavens were established—and which is consequently prior to those which it established—is not created; indeed, it is the Creator himself, who is God, by whom the heavens were established. But if they call this Word some passing utterance of God, as is a human word—[Col. 1003A] on the ground, that is, of what is written, “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32:9)—and thus suppose that God too, like a human being, sometimes speaks, when he says, “Let there be light” (Gen. 1:3), and at other times is silent, then the eternity of divinity is plainly changeable, since it does not always say, “Let there be light,” and so forth, regarding things already created. Why, moreover, was an audible word needed before the constitution of the world, when there was not yet one who might speak or one who might hear? Did he not utter an empty word if there was no need for speech, especially since will alone sufficed and there was no one to be instructed by hearing the word? Into what place, moreover, could he send forth a word, when no place had yet been created and no air yet formed from which words are shaped? By what instruments could he form words, [Col. 1003B] when neither a mouth nor any part can belong to one who is altogether simple and indivisible? For everything composed of parts is naturally later than those things of which it is composed and by whose union it is perfected, since it derives its being from those elements out of which it is constituted. “Everything that is joined together,” Plato says, “is by nature dissoluble.”

But if they understand the Spirit of the Lord to mean wind, as they wish to take it in the passage, “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2), because, as they say, wind is especially apparent in waters which it stirs, how can the spirit—that is, the breath—of the Lord be called the breath of his mouth, when, as has been said, he possesses neither a mouth nor any part? How also does the power of heaven and earth consist through wind?

[Col. 1003C] Let them therefore understand that this is that Spirit of the Lord whose sevenfold grace Isaiah describes, saying: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength,” and so forth (Isa. 11:2). And elsewhere: “And now the Lord has sent me and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:16). Again: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to announce to the meek” (Isa. 61:1). Of him too it is said in Wisdom: “The Holy Spirit will flee deceitful discipline; for the spirit of wisdom is kindly,” and so forth (Wis. 1:5). Again, when it is added of him, “And that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (ibid., 7), the Spirit himself is plainly declared to be God, since he is said to contain all things. And again [Col. 1003D] Wisdom, speaking to God, says: “But who has known thy mind, unless thou gavest wisdom and sentest thy Holy Spirit from the heights?” (Wis. 9:17). Again: “O how good and gentle, Lord, is thy Spirit within us!” (Wis. 12:17).

XIV.

Hence, when the Spirit of wisdom himself is described, he is plainly proclaimed true God, since among other things it is written of him in Wisdom: “Possessing all power, overseeing all things, and comprehending every spirit” (Wis. 7:23). Elihu too confesses him to be Creator in the book of Job, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life” (Job 33:4). The Son of God himself likewise, ascribing equal dignity to himself and the Father, [Col. 1004A] says in the Gospel: “Go, teach all nations,” and so forth (Matt. 28:19). The Apostle too, as Augustine testifies, when he called believers the temple of the Holy Spirit, plainly pronounces him to be God, since a temple is said to belong to God alone. For it is written in the Apostle: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). Here he plainly indicates that God, whose temple it is, and the Spirit of God, whom he says dwells there, are the same. Thus blessed Peter in the Acts of the Apostles professes that the Holy Spirit is God, saying: “Why have you lied to the Holy Spirit, Ananias? You have lied not to men but to God” (Acts 5:4). Again, concerning this Spirit, the same Acts contain: “The Spirit says, commanding: Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul,” and so forth [Col. 1004B] (Acts 13:2); and again: “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28). The Psalmist professes that the Spirit of God is everywhere, as uncircumscribed, saying: “Whither shall I go from thy Spirit?” (Ps. 136:7). And immediately, to indicate that the Spirit of God whom he professes to be everywhere is the same as the God to whom he speaks, he plainly shows this by assigning that the Spirit himself is everywhere through God himself, whom he asserts to be everywhere, saying: “If I ascend into heaven, thou art there,” and so forth (Ps. 138:8). But when Truth itself declares that sin against the Spirit is not remissible, while saying that sin against the Father or the Son is remissible (Matt. 12:32), whom does he not plainly indicate thereby to be no less than the Father or the Son, and therefore [Col. 1004C] himself fully God, just as the Father himself or the Son is?

It is therefore clear from what has been set forth above that both the Word of God and his Spirit are God, just as he himself whose Word or Spirit they are. Let them understand, therefore, as was said, that this Word, God—that is, the Son of God—is not a passing or audible word, but an intellectual one: namely, reason itself or wisdom coeternal with God. It is fitting to call this all-wisdom, just as we speak of omnipotence; whence it is written: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and was always with him, and is before the age” (Ecclus. 1:1). In the book of Wisdom he is also shown to be the true and consubstantial Son of God, in distinction from adopted sons, of whom it is written, as acquired for God through his preaching: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name” [Col. 1004D] (John 1:12). Thus, when his Passion was plainly prophesied in Wisdom, the ungodly said among other things: “For if he is the true Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hand of his adversaries” (Wis. 2:18). The holy soul delivered by God also openly professes this generation when it says in Ecclesiasticus: “I called upon the Lord, the Father of my Lord, that he might not forsake me in the day of my tribulation” (Ecclus. 51:14).

XV.

Now, after the testimonies of the prophets concerning faith in the Holy Trinity, it is pleasing also to add the testimonies of philosophers. [Col. 1005A] The reasoning of philosophy itself brought them to an understanding of the one God, by which, according to the Apostle: “His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through those things which are made” (Rom. 1:20). Their exceptional sobriety of life also obtained for them, by a certain merit, this same understanding. For it was fitting that God should then foreshadow in them, through some gift of more abundant grace, how much more acceptable to him is one who lives soberly and withdraws himself from this world’s enticements by despising it, than one who, given over to its pleasures, plunges himself into every impurity.

How great the philosophers’ self-restraint and abstinence were, holy teachers too relate. They invoke the philosophers’ lives to rebuke us, and employ many things from their moral teachings or [Col. 1005B] testimonies of faith for our edification. Whoever does not know this should at least read Jerome against Jovinian and see how much he recounts concerning their virtues and those of other pagans, in order to crush the shamelessness of that heretic. Above all, it is fitting that we too should rely in this work on the testimonies or arguments of philosophers, since we are acting chiefly against those who strive to assail our faith with philosophical doctrines—especially because no one should be refuted or convicted except through those things which he accepts. He is crushed by the greatest confusion who is defeated through the very means by which he was striving to conquer.

One of the philosophers themselves, Cicero, attests in the first book of his *Rhetorics* that philosophers know only one God, saying: “Those who devote themselves to philosophy do not suppose [Col. 1005C] that there are gods”—as though he said plainly: rather, they suppose there is one God, not many gods. The Apostle Paul likewise plainly indicates how, through God’s revelation, they rose to the knowledge of the divine Trinity itself, saying: “What is known of God is manifest in them, for God has revealed it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made; likewise his everlasting power and divinity, so that they are without excuse, because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God nor give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts,” and so forth (Rom. 1:19 ff.).

Hence Claudianus, writing to the patrician Praefectorius on the state of souls, recalls in these words: [Col. 1005D] “And because it has been granted to the human race by nature that it seeks hidden things more ardently, doubts more over what is denied [perhaps *ambiat*, ‘pursues’], and loves more deeply what it has attained slowly, truth is perceived with greater ardour the longer it is desired, the more laboriously it is sought, or the more slowly it is found. Hence it came about that philosophers also, endowed with outstanding abilities, have always existed throughout the long course of ages, beginning with the Italian Pythagoras or the Ionian Thales, who, although others disagreed, perceived something worthy of so great an investigation, whether in the whole work or in a part of it. Hence also the Teacher of the Gentiles accuses philosophers not so much of ignorance of the truth as of contempt for knowledge, saying: ‘The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, understood through the things that are made,’” [Col. 1006A] and so forth. [Note: [Col. 1005D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, col. 234.]

Hence too comes that passage of Augustine’s *City of God*, book VIII: “A Christian man trained only in ecclesiastical writings is wary of those who philosophize according to the elements of this world. For he is warned by the apostolic command: ‘Beware lest anyone deceive you through philosophy and empty seduction according to the elements of the world’ (Col. 2:8). Then, lest he suppose that all such people are alike, he hears from the same Apostle concerning some of them: ‘Because what is known of God is manifest in them,’ and so forth. And when, speaking to the Athenians, he had said something great concerning God and something intelligible to few—‘In him we live and move and are’ (Acts 17:28)—he added: ‘As some also of your own have said.’” The same author, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “The wise Life which made the world is understood by contemplating the world. [Col. 1006B] Question the world and the adornment of heaven, the earth fruitful with herbs and trees and full of animals, the sea full of such great multitudes of swimmers, the air full of such great multitudes of birds; question all things and see whether they do not all answer you, as it were with their own appearance: ‘God made us.’ Distinguished philosophers investigated these things and recognized the craftsman from his art.” Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, book I, chapter 4: “Just as praise for a work reflects praise upon its maker, so the Creator of things is praised through his creature, and how much more excellent he is is shown by the condition of the work itself.” Likewise: “Even insensible things praise God through us, when, contemplating them, we praise God.”

The ancients said that nothing comes to be which does not have an apprehension of God. Therefore let no one wonder if we introduce testimonies also from those [Col. 1006C] philosophers who, by the assertions of so many saints, rose to a knowledge of divinity, with the Lord himself also revealing it. Although very many of them are severely rebuked even by the Apostle, because, in accordance with his own saying, “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1), they became reprobate through pride in the very privilege of divine knowledge: for we do not here take them as examples for living, but for teaching or believing, just as we frequently do Solomon. Although the excellence of his wisdom, which by the testimony of the Lord himself was to be preferred to all others, was overcome by lust and carnal pleasures, he consented to idolatry, abandoning the worship of God which in his writings he both taught and preached. Yet he himself built, at God’s command, a temple to magnify that worship of God—a work from which his righteous father had been forbidden.

[Col. 1006D] God, however, sometimes distributes very great gifts to reprobate and unbelieving persons, when he sees that these will be necessary for the instruction or benefit of others. He also works many miracles through reprobate persons, of whom Truth says in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name, cast out demons in thy name, and performed many mighty works in thy name?’ And then I shall confess to them that I never knew you: depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Matt. 7:22–23). But when God displays miracles through reprobate persons, or speaks prophecies, [Col. 1007A] or performs any great deeds, he does this not for the benefit of those whom he uses as ministers, but rather for that of others whom he intends to instruct through them. Nor does he withhold the gifts of his grace because of unworthy ministers; daily, at the invocation of his name, he spiritually accomplishes the sacraments of the Church through them for the salvation of believers. God rightly works great things through unworthy or unbelieving people, he who taught the prophet through the words of an ass (Num. 22:28), lest, if he worked great things only through great people, these things should be ascribed more to human virtues and merits than to divine grace.

Nevertheless, lest anyone despair of the salvation of all philosophers, or judge the lives of all who preceded the Lord’s incarnation to have been reprobate, let him hear blessed Jerome expounding the Gospel [Col. 1007B] of Matthew. For among other things he says: [Note: [Col. 1007D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXVI, col. 188.] “From the fact that the evil servant dared to say, ‘You reap where you have not sown, and gather where you have not scattered’ (Matt. 25:24), let us understand that God also receives the good life of Gentile philosophers: he regards differently those who act justly and those who act unjustly.” For if we examine the reason given above by the Apostle—that he mentions some of them as having been delivered over to a reprobate mind after attaining divine knowledge, because they became vain in their thoughts, “professing themselves to be wise” (Rom. 1:19 ff.), that is, attributing their wisdom to their own study or natural ability rather than crediting it to the gift of divine grace—we shall find that those regarded as foremost, especially Socrates and Plato, attribute all philosophy principally to divine [Col. 1007C] grace.

Blessed Augustine extols Socrates in such praises in book VIII of the *City of God*: [Note: [Col. 1007D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, cols. 226–227.] “Socrates, Plato’s teacher, is remembered as having directed the whole of philosophy toward correcting and ordering morals. He fixed his attention upon what was necessary for the blessed life, which alone seems to have been the object of the zeal and labour of all philosophers. He did not wish minds defiled by earthly desires to attempt divine things, since he saw that they investigated the causes of things, which first and supreme causes he believed could exist only in the power and will of the one supreme God. Therefore he thought they could be comprehended only by a purified mind, and so he judged that effort must be applied to cleansing life by good morals, so that a mind unburdened from the passions which weigh it down might rise by its natural vigour to eternal things and, through the purity of understanding, behold the incorporeal and unchangeable nature of light, in which the causes of all created natures are stably united.”

It is likewise written in the first book of Plato’s *Republic*, where he introduces the persons of Socrates and Timaeus:

SOCRATES. “Come then, Timaeus, begin the undertaking, after calling, as is customary, upon the divinity for aid.”

TIMAEUS. “Certainly, my Socrates. For since it is customary among all people, and almost a kind of religious observance, for those who are about to undertake anything, whether great or small, to pray for the aid of divinity, how much more fitting is it for us, who are about to set forth an account of the nature and substance of the universe, to [Col. 1008A] invoke divine assistance—unless indeed we are carried away by some savage frenzy and implacable madness?”

Behold, from these words of Plato it is plainly maintained that philosophers have this custom: to invoke divine aid in matters both great and small which they are about to undertake; and that among them it is considered the height of frenzy and implacable madness to omit it.

Therefore, when the Apostle says that some philosophers and Gentile sages attributed to themselves rather than to God what they understood concerning God or other matters, and hence deserved to be blinded, this seems to be charged against a few rather than many—just as the punishment of sexual disgrace which he subsequently adds, saying, “Therefore God gave them up to passions of dishonour” (Rom. 1:26), and again, “Males,” he says, “working shamefulness with males,” [Col. 1008B] and so forth (ibid., 27). For it is agreed that philosophers lived with the greatest self-restraint and left us many exhortations to chastity, both in their writings and by their examples.

But if someone denies that they could be saved without faith in the one who was to come, how will he prove that they did not believe in him, whom they saw prophesied through a Gentile woman, namely the Sibyl, almost much more openly than through all the prophets? Nor should it therefore be maintained that they did not expect or believe that the Lord’s incarnation would take place because this is nowhere found in their writings. For perhaps it is not expressed sufficiently even in all the writings of the prophets, divine counsel so ordaining that the mystery might not be revealed to just anyone, or merely through just anyone. Indeed, we know that by a providential dispensation the Seventy Translators, in many places of the Scriptures which they were translating, are said to have found written “the Son of God,” yet wholly passed it over and [Col. 1008C] kept silent about it, lest they provoke scandal among unbelieving hearers rather than establish faith.

For we know that philosophers, while they held views about the gods worshipped by the people different from those of others, and consequently differed from the people in faith, nevertheless, compelled by fear, maintained common temples with them, attended their ceremonies, and pretended together with them to be idolaters.

Hence Augustine, *On True Religion*: [Note: [Col. 1008D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV, col. 123.] “The wise men called philosophers had dissenting schools and common temples. For neither the people nor the priests were unaware how differently they thought concerning the nature of the gods. Yet all of them, together with their followers who held diverse and opposing views, came without hindrance to the common rites. But certainly, as far as I can see, it must be that they accepted one thing in religion together with the people and defended another thing privately, while the people themselves listened. Socrates, however, is reported to have been bolder than the rest, swearing by any dog or stone, and by whatever happened to come to hand when he was about to swear. I believe he understood that whatever works of nature are generated under the governance of divine providence are much better than human works and therefore more worthy of divine honours than those things [Col. 1009A] worshipped in temples. Not that a dog or a stone really ought to be worshipped by wise men, but so that men might understand in this way that they had been overthrown by such great superstition that there was so shameful a degree to which, if they would be ashamed to descend, they might see how much more they ought to be ashamed to remain at a still more shameful level. Likewise he reminded those who suppose this visible world to be the supreme God of their shamefulness, teaching that it follows that every stone, as a particle of the supreme God, ought rightly to be worshipped.” Likewise: [Note: [Col. 1009D] *Patrologia*, vol.
