XXXIV, col. 123.] “Socrates worshipped images together with the people; but after his condemnation and death no one dared to swear by a dog or call anyone Jupiter, but only to commit this to memory and writings. Whether they did this out of fear or some knowledge is not for me to judge.”

[Col. 1009B] From these words, therefore, we are plainly taught that the schools—that is, the doctrines—of philosophers differed greatly in faith from the common people, with whom nevertheless they shared temples, although both people and priests knew that they all differed from them in faith. Indeed, they existed not merely as different from that faith, but as opposed to it. While they openly performed external religious observances with the people in temples, they nevertheless feared the multitude of fools, “whose number is infinite” (Eccl. 1:15); yet privately, and as though “speaking wisdom among the perfect,” sometimes even while the people themselves listened, they professed and defended a contrary religious doctrine. Socrates, the greatest mocker of idolatry among them, brought the many gods—that is, idols—into such contempt that he dared to prefer a dog to them, using it in the oath by which he pursued this mockery; thus [Col. 1009C] he stripped the idols themselves of the glory of ancient names. It remains now for us to put forward the proposed testimonies of philosophers concerning faith, so that from their own teachers we may refute each unbelieving people: the Jews from the prophets, and the Gentiles from the philosophers.

XVI.

Let Mercurius now appear first, that most ancient and illustrious philosopher, whom because of his excellence they even called a god. Augustine, disputing *Against Five Heresies*, introduces his testimony concerning the generation of the Word, saying: [Note: [Col. 1009D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLII, col. 1103.] “Hermes, who in Latin is called Mercurius, wrote a book entitled *Logos Teleios* [Λόγος τέλειος], that is, ‘The Perfect Word.’ Let us hear what he says concerning the Perfect Word. ‘The Lord and maker of all gods made a second Lord. He made him first, and only, and true. He seemed good to him, and full to the utmost of all good things; he rejoiced in him and loved him greatly as his only-begotten.’” Likewise, in another passage: [Note: [Col. 1009D] *Ibid.*] “The Son of the blessed God and of good will, whose name cannot be uttered by a human mouth.” Augustine: [Note: [Col. 1010D] *Ibid.*] “Whom he first said was made, he afterwards called only-begotten. How full he is, John the Evangelist says: ‘From his fullness we have all received.’”

[Col. 1010A] Philosophers were accustomed to call gods—that is, immortal rational living beings—the planets, and even the world itself. Hence the prophet too calls the sun, moon, and other heavenly bodies “the host of heaven,” following the custom of the Gentiles, who sacrificed to them as their rulers and protectors. The supreme God, according to Plato, addresses the more excellent of these gods when the creation of man is to be undertaken, as though all things which take place below on earth were administered from above through the hidden natures of the planets and stars. Thus he says: “Gods, whose maker and father I am: my works are by nature dissoluble, but by my will they are indissoluble,” and so forth. This also relates to what is said concerning the Platonists in book VIII of the *City of God*: [Note: [Col. 1010D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, col. 238.] “They say that among all living beings possessing a rational soul [Col. 1010B] there is a threefold division: into gods, humans, and demons. The dwelling of gods is in heaven, of humans upon earth, and of demons in the air.” And Boethius, commenting on Porphyry: “Whenever,” he says, “we place God under the genus ‘living being,’ we do so according to the opinion which maintains that heaven, the stars, and this whole world are animated, and which also called them by the name of gods.”

Blessed Augustine, however, does not dare at all to refute what is said concerning the sun and other heavenly lights, but professes himself uncertain whether certain governing spirits are present in them, through whom they are even given life. And—what seems marvellous to say—he declares that he does not know whether these too [Col. 1010C] belong to the fellowship of those whom we Christians call angels or heavenly spirits. Thus he says in the *Enchiridion*: [Note: [Col. 1010D] *Patrologia*, vol. XL, cols. 259–260.] “Whether the archangels are called virtues, and how thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers differ among themselves, let those say who can—if indeed they can prove what they say. I confess that I do not know these things. Nor do I know for certain whether the sun, moon, and other stars belong to the same fellowship, although to some they seem to be luminous bodies without feeling or intelligence.”

Lest anyone trained in sacred letters should recoil from the words of the philosopher Hermes, by which he says concerning God the Father that he made a second Lord—that is, begot the Son—although God the Son was neither made nor created by God the Father, but only begotten: let him know also that Catholic and holy teachers have made many similarly improper statements concerning that same generation. For they sometimes improperly declare the Father to be the author of the Son, or say that he begot him, or that the Son was formed by the Father and is an effect of the Father himself. Thus Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book III: “According to the Apostle, because in Christ dwells bodily all the fullness of divinity” (Col. 2:9), “yet incomprehensibly and ineffably, before all time and ages, he begot the only-begotten from those things which were unbegotten in himself, imparting to his birth, through love and power, all that God is. Thus, corresponding to the unbegotten, perfect, and eternal Father, the Son is only-begotten, perfect, and eternal. But those things which belong to him according to the body which he assumed are willed by his goodness for our salvation.” [Col. 1011A] The same author, in book XI: “‘The words which I speak to you I do not speak from myself’” (John 12:49). “For, since he does not speak from himself, he must owe what he says to his author.” Likewise: “With regard to what he does according to his birth, the Father is his author.” Again, the same author in book XII, speaking of God the Father as unbegotten [Col. 1011B] and of the Son as begotten from him, says: “Neither is the unbegotten himself to be confused with being born, because the latter is from another, while the former is from no one; and it is one thing always to be eternal without an author, another to be eternal in relation to the Father, that is, to an author. For where the Father is author, there also is birth; but where the author is eternal, there also is eternity of birth. For as birth is from an author, so eternal birth is from an eternal author.” Likewise: “That which is born from the eternal, if it is not eternal, will no longer be born; and the Father will not be an eternal author. If, therefore, anything should be lacking from eternity to him who is born from the eternal Father, then what is infinite to the begetter—who is unquestionably the Father as author—would be lacking to the one born; but what is infinite to the begetter is also infinite to the one born.” Likewise: “From the eternal comes nothing other than the eternal; if it is not eternal, then the Father, who is the author of generation, is no longer eternal.” Likewise: “He is shown to be born from thee, so that he may signify no other author for himself than thee.”

[Col. 1011C] The same author, on Psalm 137: “Thou hast formed me and laid thy hand upon me”; each expression signifies something: what he formed is ancient, while what he laid upon is most recent. For the Apostle teaches that he was formed according to the nature of divinity, saying: “Who, being in the form of God” (Phil. 2:6). “For what is in a form is formed. In the form, the Father is to him Father of nature and divinity, so that it may be referred to the Father and he may be said to have been formed by him.” Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chapter 57: “God the Father begot God the Son, in whom he appears, so that nothing differed from him and an affection answering suitably to his greatness might be present.” Likewise: “Therefore, creating his most similar Son, he added, from himself, as it were another himself.” The same author in the same work: “He therefore possessed before the world the primacy of his created offspring, so that, destined to be Father of things, he had first to be the proper Father—that is, Father of his own proper offspring.”

[Col. 1011D] In Ecclesiasticus too, the Wisdom of God itself, which is called his Son, is described as both created and begotten by him: “Who shall investigate the Wisdom of God, which precedes all things? Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from eternity. The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God on high” (Ecclus. 1:3–5). Again: “One is the Most High, Creator, Almighty, and Lord God; he created her in the Holy Spirit and poured her out over all his works” (ibid., 8–11). Likewise below: “Wisdom shall be blessed among the blessed, saying: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature. Alone I went around the circuit of heaven,’” and so forth (Ecclus. 24:4 ff.). Again: “From the beginning and before the ages I was created, and unto the age to come I shall not cease,” and so forth (ibid., 14 ff.).

[Col. 1012A] What wonder, then, if even in the words of ecclesiastical and holy teachers certain expressions are used so improperly in order to demonstrate the generation of the Word: that God the Father is the author of his Son and procreated him; or that the Son was procreated by him or is called his effect? This is said in accordance with the fact that he is begotten from him rather than created or made, and that the Father is only begetter rather than creator or author. What wonder, I say, if the philosopher Hermes mentioned above, being trained in those ecclesiastical disciplines, did not concern himself with this improper use of words, saying “made” for “begotten”? What wonder also if, when he called the Son second from the Father, he did not depart from the language of the saints? Thus Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book XII: “The Son, true God from thee, God the Father, and begotten by thee, is to be confessed after thee as with thee, [Col. 1012B] because thou art an eternal origin, or eternal author. For since he is from thee, he is second from thee.” Second, I say, in manner of existence, not in difference of dignity. For he subsists from God the Father, as it were in the first place, while the Spirit is from both, as it were in the third place.

Hence Jerome, in his work *On the Three Virtues*, calls the Father the principal Spirit in relation to the Son. David, speaking thus in the Psalm, asks for three spirits: “Confirm me with a principal Spirit” (Ps. 50:14); “renew a right spirit within my bowels” (ibid., 12); “do not take thy Holy Spirit from me” (ibid., 13). Who are these three spirits? The principal Spirit is the Father; the right Spirit is Christ; the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1012C] Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chapter 58: “The Holy Spirit is third from the Father, but second from Christ, according to numerical order”—as though he said: according to the ordered and fitting arrangement of enumeration, namely according to the very sequence of existence in the persons, not according to any degrees of their dignity. For the Father is from no one; the Son is from the Father alone; and the Holy Spirit derives his being from both together.

XVII.

Let that greatest of philosophers, Plato, and his followers also be recalled—those who, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers, came nearer than the other philosophers of the Gentiles to the Christian faith, and after the prophets openly set forth the substance of the whole Trinity. They assert that the mind [Col. 1012D], which they call νοῦς (*nous*, “intellect”), is begotten of God and coeternal with Him—that is, the Son, whom we call the Wisdom of God, eternally begotten from God the Father. Nor do they seem to have omitted the person of the Holy Spirit when they maintained that the soul of the world is a third person after God and the *nous*.

That Plato not only taught the faith of the Holy Trinity but also proved that it is so, Claudianus, writing to the patrician Praefectorius on the state of souls, affirms in these words:

> “Let Plato,” he says, “come forward, who indeed so many ages before the Virgin’s childbirth, before God’s incarnation, before the truth concerning the supreme Trinity was foretold among the Gentiles, with marvellous intellect and unchangeable eloquence sought out, discovered, and declared the ineffable fact that there is one Godhead and three persons: God the Father, the paternal mind—activity or counsel—and the mutual love of these two; one supreme, equally threefold, undivided Godhead. He taught not only that this ought to be believed, but proves that it is so.” [Col. 1013A]

Moreover, since Claudianus called this the mutual love of Father and Son, Plato not inappropriately named it the soul of the world—that is, the life and salvation of all believers. Outside that love of God every soul lies dead. Let us carefully consider what Plato said about this soul of the world, for other philosophers too are believed to have derived from him what they said concerning that soul.

Thus, distinguishing this soul of the world as, so to speak, a third person after God and the *nous*, he develops a longer and more careful account and describes it with complete precision, both in itself and in its effects. In the same manner we too are accustomed to speak of the Holy Spirit now according to the effects of His works, now according to the natural disposition of His goodness, which He has had in Himself from eternity, as we shall distinguish more carefully later.

But now let us examine carefully Plato’s words on the soul of the world, so that we may recognize that the Holy Spirit is most fully designated in them.

Plato therefore says that it was made or begotten by God before the constitution of the world. In this, unless I am mistaken, he indicates to us the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit, by which He is from God the Father. For philosophers commonly call “made from God” or “begotten” everything that has being from God. Hence Hermes above called the Son of God made by God, inasmuch as He has being from Him as eternally begotten—not as made or created by Him in time. Plato likewise calls everything that has being from God begotten from Him, though not therefore everything that is from God is His Son, as is the world itself and His other works.

He speaks as follows, when, after speaking earlier of the world, he came to the soul of the world:

> “Nevertheless, in the matter of which we are at present speaking, God did not allow the origin of the soul to be in that order, making it inferior to and later than bodies. For He would not have taught that what was older was ruled by what was produced later.”

And again:

> “God commanded the soul to precede the nature of body both in antiquity and in power, and willed it to be mistress, with sovereign right, over that which it would protect.” [Col. 1013C–D]

Here it should also be noted that, when he says that it presides over the government of the world as mistress, he surely places it above every creature and declares it to be God—the being whom he afterwards called the soul of the world. He says:

> “And finally, the remnants of the former mixture from which He had compounded the soul of the world,” etc.

He fittingly posited the Holy Spirit as the soul of the world, as the life of the universe, since in the goodness of God all things in some manner have life; all things are, as it were, living before God, and none are dead—that is, none are useless—not even evils themselves, which are most excellently ordered by His goodness. In accordance with this, we remember that it is written both among the Evangelists and among the Platonists: “What was made in Him was life” [Col. 1014A] (John 1:3–4). It is as though he said: All things made in time through Him—that is, established through the very goodness of God—lived in some manner eternally in that goodness of God, since in divine providence all things had been ordered from eternity, through His goodness, in the best way, so that He willed each to proceed as well as was fitting.

Hence the Apostle’s statement seems not inappropriately to agree with this, when he reports that certain philosophers said, “In God we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28), as though they understood this soul of the world to be God Himself. And when he says that God conceived a third kind of soul, which we call the soul of the world, this is as though he asserted the Holy Spirit to be a third person after God and the *nous* in that spiritual divine substance. God is said to “conceive,” that is, to apprehend completely the distinction of one person—a distinction which we are not able worthily to conceive or fully distinguish from the Father and the Son. For the divine Trinity is truly known only to itself. Likewise, for something else to be conceived from God in some way amounts to the same as its existing in that way—that is, its truly being so.

Then he immediately provides a careful description of this third person, whom he places as the soul of the world, when he says that the soul itself consists of an indivisible and immutable substance, and again of a divisible one, insofar, that is, as the soul is thought to divide itself through bodies. For to say that the soul consists of this and that is as though to say that it has both in itself, so that the substance of the soul is both indivisible and in some fashion divisible.

For the Holy Spirit is both an altogether simple substance in Himself and, by the nature of divinity, remains wholly unchanging and immutable in Himself. Yet this same Spirit is in some manner called manifold through His effects, and is sometimes called the seven spirits, according to the efficacy of His sevenfold grace. Thus, in praise of divine Wisdom, the spirit is described as both one and manifold, penetrating and steadfast.

The philosopher therefore says that the soul consists of an indivisible substance that always remains in its own condition, and also of another substance which, as an inseparable companion of bodies, is thought to divide itself through those bodies [Col. 1014D]. For the Holy Spirit is such that, in respect of His own state—which He has in Himself, not in His effects—He is altogether simple and immutable; yet He is thought to be in some manner manifold according to His effects. This is what it means for Him to divide Himself through bodies, namely, that the soul itself is an inseparable companion of bodies.

This division of multiplicity, however, cannot in any way belong to Him in respect of Himself, but, as stated, in respect of the effects arising from the distribution of His gifts: He grants one grace to one person and another to another, and does not communicate Himself to every individual equally or in the same way. Hence one person is said to have one spirit and another another spirit. It is excellently said that this is “thought,” and not that it is so; for, if we speak truly and properly, this is not a multiplicity of the Spirit but of His effects. We call Him manifold in this one respect, because He produces many things; that is, His effects are diverse rather than He Himself.

Since therefore in this soul of the world an indivisible and a divisible substance—or, as has been said, sameness and difference—concur, he adds that a certain mixture is produced from the indivisible and divisible, that is, from the same and different: from the immutable and mutable. In this mixture, so to speak, the property of the Holy Spirit is distinguished and appears fully expressed both in Himself and in His effects, as has been said.

He therefore says that God placed this third kind of substance, mixed as described, midway between the two substances—namely, the indivisible and divisible—because, since the Spirit Himself is from God, as proceeding from Him, He has both of these wrought in Him by Him from whom He has being. This is what it means to say that God placed this kind of soul between the two things mentioned above as their middle: namely, mixed from them. It is as though he said that from God Himself, from whom the soul is, it has both characteristics: it is indivisible in its substance and divisible according to its effects. The word “placed” is fittingly used according to the metaphor whereby a middle is said to be positioned among surrounding things.

After setting forth the soul’s mixture from the indivisible and divisible, he turns to its mixture from sameness and difference, saying that the soul likewise consists of the same and different, just as it consists of indivisible and divisible substance. “One part of it,” he says, “is called the same through the different,” since that Spirit is the same in substance with God and the *nous*—that is, with the Father and Son—yet different in the property of His person.

We may also call Him the same, that is, immutable in Himself, and in some manner different through His effects. For He not only makes things that are different, in the sense already mentioned when He was said to consist of divisible substance; He also changes and orders them through the succession of times, as He judges expedient, according to Boethius’ saying:

> “Remaining steadfast, He causes all things to move.”

Above he had already declared Him immutable when he said, “a substance always remaining in its own state.” But he had not yet added that He was variable through His effects and their changes; this he does now.

He fittingly therefore says that the soul is a certain middle—that is, a mixture of indivisible substance in itself and divisible substance through bodily conjunction, that is, through its conjunction with bodies, whenever it applies itself to creating, ruling, or ordering anything. It is like the soul of an animal, imparting its benefits to its body. The philosopher also ascribes to this soul the whole power and proportional harmony of numbers, so that he may teach that the concord of all things subsists by the goodness of divine grace.

For every order of nature and harmonious arrangement is traced and explained by numerical proportions [Col. 1016A], and number appears as the most perfect model, suitable to all things. This does not escape those who investigate the secrets of philosophy. Hence arithmetic, which is wholly concerned with numerical proportions, is called the mother and mistress of the other arts, because the inquiry and teaching of other things depend upon the division of numbers.

Moreover, to express the ineffable sweetness of its beneficence, they ascribe to it the whole harmony of musical consonances, by which the firmament itself is said to resound continually and the higher regions of the world to be filled. For nothing delights so greatly or draws minds by excessive sweetness as melody; nothing is so apt to compose, stir, or calm them. Thus philosophers knew, according to the first chapter of Boethius’ *On Music*, that the whole frame of our soul and body is united by musical proportion.

Indeed, they observed and brought about the calming by melody of anger and madness, and the healing of the pains of very grave illnesses. Whoever does not know this or has not learned it by experience should read that chapter on music, and will find how Pythagoras restored to sobriety and self-command a drunken young man who had been inflamed by the sound of the Phrygian mode, while a spondaic melody was played.

For, he says, when a harlot had shut herself in the house of the young man’s rival and he, in fury, wished to burn down the house, Pythagoras was observing the courses of the stars by night, as was his custom. When he learned that the youth, inflamed by the sound of the Phrygian mode, had refused to desist from his crime despite many admonitions from friends, he ordered the mode changed; and thus he tempered the raging young man’s mind into the state of the most peaceful composure. [Col. 1016C]

One will also find there that, when drunken young men, stirred up, as happens, by the sound of pipes, were wantonly breaking down the doors of a modest woman, Pythagoras is said to have instructed the piper to play a spondaic melody. When she did so, the slowness of the modes and gravity of the performance calmed their insolence.

He will see also how Terpander and Arion rescued Lesbians and Ionians from very grave diseases through the aid of song; and likewise how Ismenias of Thebes, they say, wiped away every suffering by musical modes from many Boeotians afflicted by the torments of painful illness. [Col. 1016D] There too Empedocles, when a certain man was furiously attacking his host with a sword in his ancestral vineyards [the printed reading is corrupt], altered the musical mode and thus moderated the youth’s anger.

“So greatly,” says Boethius, “was the power of the art of music recognized in the studies of ancient philosophy that, when the Pythagoreans put aside the cares of the day in sleep, they used certain songs so that gentle and quiet slumber might receive them; and when they awoke, they cleansed away the stupor and confusion of sleep by other modes. For they knew that the whole fabric of our soul and body is joined by musical adjustment; for as the condition of bodily affections stands, so also the pulses of the heart are stimulated by its movements.”

Democritus is said to have communicated this to the physician Hippocrates when he visited Democritus in custody for treatment, since all the fellow citizens of Democritus considered him mad. [Col. 1017A] But why say these things? Because there can be no doubt that the condition of our soul and body seems in some manner composed by the same proportions by which the following discussion will show harmonic modulations to be joined and connected.

If what we have said from the philosophers about the power of harmony seems slight to believers unless it is also confirmed by the testimony of Sacred Scripture, let them recall how, when an evil spirit rushed upon Saul, the counsel of prudent men—who were not ignorant of the force of harmonic sweetness—provided that David’s melodies might heal the impulses of such great madness. Therefore later, when the man full of God intended to build the Temple in order to enlarge the worship of God, he composed the psalms that were to be sung and assembled every kind of musical instrument, so that he might attract an untutored people by harmonies of voices and sounds—by means of which he had earlier mitigated the devilish torment in the reprobate king. [Col. 1017B]

From this is especially shown how natural harmonic modulation is: by its sweetness it can so order and restore nature that even the torments of malignant spirits cannot disturb it. We also read that the souls of certain saints, lest they suffer any pain at their departure, voluntarily went forth from here to the sweetness of melody.

Thus we remember it is written in the *Lives of the Fathers* that, when a certain brother wished to see how the soul of a sinner and of a righteous person is taken away from the body, and God did not wish to grieve him by denying his desire, he found a traveller lying ill in the street, with no one to care for him. When the hour of his falling asleep came, that brother saw Michael and Gabriel descending for his soul. One sat at his right side and the other at his left, and they asked his soul to come forth; but it did not come forth, as though unwilling to leave its body.

Gabriel said to Michael: “Take this soul now, that we may depart.”

Michael replied: “We have been commanded by the Lord that it be drawn out without pain; therefore we cannot tear it away by force.”

Then Michael cried aloud: “Lord, what do You will concerning this soul, since it does not consent to come forth with us?” [Col. 1017D]

A voice came to him: “Behold, I send David with the cithara and all those singing psalms in Jerusalem, so that, hearing the psalm at their voice, it may come forth.”

When they had all descended around that soul, singing hymns, the soul leaped forth, sat in Michael’s hands, and was taken up with joy.

Philosophers, therefore—or rather the Lord through them, though perhaps they did not know it—rightly ascribe an immense and supreme sweetness of modulation both to the soul of the world and to the higher regions of the firmament, in order to express as fully as possible the peace and harmony they enjoy, and how harmoniously the divine goodness orders all things in the world. They call this goodness the soul of the world; Truth, as has been said, calls it the Holy Spirit.

Who, moreover, if he attends carefully, will not perceive what they said concerning the heavenly harmony which resounds without ceasing in the higher regions of the firmament? For heavenly spirits are bound together by the continual vision of the divine majesty and by the highest mutual concord; and with perpetual, ineffable exultation in praise of Him whom they behold, they sing what, according to Isaiah, the seraphim never cease to cry by day and night: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts,” etc. [Col. 1018A] (Isa. 6:3).

Accordingly, by the higher regions of heaven or of the firmament we understand these blessed spirits or their dwelling-place. They also seem fittingly designated by the name of the seven planets, on account of the excellence of their brightness, since divine grace—which is called sevenfold—spiritually illumines them. They are also aptly called in Isaiah *seraphim*, that is, “burning,” because through this spiritual illumination of grace they are especially kindled into love of God.

Their dwelling is to be called higher both in dignity and in position. Those who grew proud are said to have been cast down from it into this dark and dense air, which, being lower in location and worse in habitation, may not unfittingly be understood by the name of hell. The blessed spirits or their heavenly dwelling are also well compared with the firmament, since, as a reward for their fidelity and humility in contrast with those who fell through pride, they received such confirmation in the contemplation of the divine majesty that they can never again fall.

Thus Gregory says in Book XXVI on Job:

> “Heaven is first said to have been made, and afterwards this same thing is called the firmament, because angelic nature was first created subtle in the heights and afterwards more wonderfully confirmed so that it could never fall.” [Col. 1018C]

And the same writer says in a homily on Ezekiel:

> “‘God created heaven’ (Gen. 1:1), which He afterwards called ‘the firmament’ (ibid., 8). Thus those who were first well created were heaven; but they were afterwards called firmament because they received the power of immutability, so that they might no longer fall at all.”

Plato’s further statement that the soul was placed by God in the middle of the world and extended equally through the whole sphere of the rounded universe beautifully signifies God’s grace, offered commonly to all, benevolently ordering all things in this great house or temple of His as is wholesome and just. The Book of Wisdom plainly agrees: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,” etc. (Wis. 1:7). And so does the Psalmist: “By the Spirit of His mouth, all their power” (Ps. 32:6).

When Plato calls the entire world one living creature, he demonstrates the greatest harmony of all God’s works, like the different members in the one body of an animal. One soul presides over them all, wholly present to each individual member, one and the same in different members and accomplishing different things. Thus the Apostle, demonstrating the concord and unity of the whole Church, calls it one body of Christ: joined together from different believers through certain bonds and a framework of faith and charity, serving and ministering to one another as different members in one body, each needing the service of the other, while one Spirit presides over all and works different things in different persons, as the soul does in the different members of the whole body.

“For,” he says, “one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing to each one as He wills” (1 Cor. 12:11). [Col. 1019A]

Blessed Ambrose most plainly applied this comparison, in the First Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians, also to the constitution of the world’s body:

> “Although the many members need one another, they do not differ in the unity of nature, though they are diverse; for diversity converges into unity, so that the unity of the body may be complete. So too the things of which the world consists, though different not only in functions but also in natures, nevertheless contribute to the perfection of one world; and from all these there arises a certain harmony.” [Col. 1019B]

The divine actions themselves, understood through the service of allegory, manifestly accord with this covering—that is, with the position of the soul placed in the middle of the world, meaning divine grace commonly offered to all. For when the Lord intended to spread His teaching and the worship of true religion through the world, He chose Jerusalem, which is in the middle of the earth. He established it as, so to speak, the head of His kingdom; there He first willed to build for Himself a Temple, like a royal palace, for the magnifying of His worship; and there He poured out upon the Apostles an abundant grace of the Holy Spirit, through which, and through them, the whole world might be spiritually quickened.

Hence it is written: “But God, our King, has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73:12). And again: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3). [Col. 1019C]

Jerome, commenting on the passage in Ezekiel where it is written, “Thus says the Lord: This is Jerusalem, set in the midst of the nations, with lands round about her” (Ezek. 5:5), declares in these words that Jerusalem is situated in the middle of the world:

> “This same prophet testifies, showing that it is the navel of the earth. And the Psalmist, setting forth the Lord’s passion, says: ‘He has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth.’ From here was planted the vine which extended its branches even to the sea” (Ps. 79:12).

For Christ here is the true vine, who, sending His Apostles like branches throughout the whole world, drenched the whole world with the abundance of spiritual teaching.

On this quickening and enlivening activity of the Holy Spirit, Saint Salvian, bishop, in Book I of *On the Governance of God*, addressed to Saint Salonius, bishop, introduces the testimony of Pythagoras, saying:

XVIII.

> “Pythagoras the philosopher, whom philosophy itself received almost as its master, speaking of the nature and benefits of God, spoke thus: ‘A mind passing through and diffused through all parts of the world, from which all living creatures that are born receive life.’”

How then can God be said to neglect the world, when He sufficiently loves it in this very fact that He continually attends to the whole body of the world?

Gennadius, a presbyter of Marseilles, writing *On Illustrious Men*, mentions among illustrious men and their works Salvian himself, bishop of the church of Marseilles, his book addressed to Bishop Salonius [Col. 1020A], and his other works. After Pythagoras’ testimony, Salvian also introduces Cicero, observing that the same God whom Pythagoras calls *animus* (“spirit” or “mind”) is called *mens* (“mind”) by Cicero, saying:

XIX.

> “Cicero also says: ‘Nor indeed can God Himself, as understood by us, be understood otherwise than as a certain mind, free, unbound, and separated from every mortal association, perceiving and moving all things.’”

And elsewhere:

> “Nothing is more excellent than God; therefore the world must be ruled by Him. He obeys or is subject to no nature; therefore He Himself rules all nature.” [Col. 1020B]

Augustine also, in Book XII, chapter 32, of *The City of God*, speaking of Varro, says:

> “This same most acute and learned author also says that only those seem to have perceived what God is who believed Him to be a soul governing the world by motion and reason.”

Thus they called God mind—that is, *animus* or soul—because He presides over the government of the whole world as the soul presides over the body. Hence a certain wise man, exhorting one not to worship God worthily unless one’s mind is cleansed of vices and adorned with virtues, aptly says at the very beginning of his exhortation and teaching:

> If God is mind for us, as songs declare,  
> Let Him especially be worshipped by you with a pure mind. [Col. 1020C]

It is as though he openly instructed his son: Since God is mind, that is, true and spiritual life for us, as the poets’ writing itself declares—as, for example, those words of Virgil which Macrobius adduces on this very point, as we shall show later—glorify Him, namely God, especially by living well.

Likewise, when Plato called the world a living creature, he also declared it to be intelligent—that is, a rational living creature—inasmuch as its soul is superior to all others and consequently acts and orders everything in it more rationally. When it is further said that this soul of the world foresees the causes of all things that come to pass, the providence of God over all natures and the fullness of divine knowledge are indicated; and through this the soul itself is suggested to be God.

It is said to measure and deliberate future things from present things because, according to what already exists, things must be prepared so that they can cohere and be fitted together in a suitable ordering. What is added—that our souls, that is, worldly souls, were formed from the remnants of the mixture of the soul of the world—means that they imitate the soul of the world in powers and virtues, yet are far removed from its dignity in this very respect. For just as that soul presides over the administration of the whole world, so individual souls preside over individual bodies, providing them with animal, not spiritual, life. [Col. 1020D]

These souls are fittingly called remnants of the soul of the world because they belong to animal life, for this is what that soul leaves to lower souls—things which it is not worthy for it to accomplish directly. Thus the heresy of those is refuted who profess that the Lord Jesus had no soul other than the Holy Spirit.

He also not inappropriately calls “remnants of the soul of the world” those things which belong to its operation in us, inasmuch as it is said to degenerate in bodies, as we shall explain in its place. For just as remnants appear inferior and less worthy than the things that remain over them, so these things which concern not the eternity of the Spirit but His temporal operations are judged later in dignity.

He also fittingly says “the soul of the world,” not the soul of some particular thing in the world, just as we say “the soul of a man,” not the soul of some particular human member. For “soul” is so called from giving life; and, properly speaking, only that is said to be animated in which the entire power of life is so brought to completion that nothing external need adhere to that living body in order to preserve in it the life it has.

Since the world, according to the philosophers, contains all things, so that nothing remains outside it to be divinely ordered, it is rightly called the soul of the world, just as it is called the soul of a human being, because the whole force of soul is completed in it. Thus the world itself need not have eyes or other instruments of sense, as Plato himself asserts, because nothing remains outside it to which these could be of use. [Col. 1021B]

Having briefly collected these things from Plato and, as I think, explained them sufficiently carefully as testimony to our faith, I judge it consequent to proceed to his followers, in order to show that what they too have said concerning the soul of the world cannot reasonably be understood in a fitting way unless the Holy Spirit is designated through the most beautiful figure of a covering.

For this manner of speaking is especially familiar to philosophers as to prophets: when they come to the secrets of philosophy, they express nothing in common words but draw the reader on more by likenesses and comparisons. Things which previously seemed almost fabulous and remote from all usefulness are more pleasing according to the surface of the letter, yet when afterwards found to be full of great mysteries, they contain within themselves great edification of doctrine. [Col. 1021C–D]

For this reason, as Augustine testifies, they are veiled so that they may not become cheap. In the second book of *On Christian Doctrine*, while explaining the causes of Scripture’s difficulty and accessibility, he says:

> “Some things said obscurely cast a very dense darkness over us. I do not doubt that all this has been provided by God in order to tame pride by labor and to recall the intellect from disgust, since things easily discovered commonly become cheap.”

And again:

> “Those who do not find at all what they seek suffer hunger; but those who do not seek because what they desire is ready at hand often waste away from disgust. Therefore the Holy Spirit beneficially ordered the Scriptures so that in clearer places He might meet hunger, and in more obscure places wipe away disgust.”

Thus the Lord delights to rest as though in hiding, so that, the more He conceals Himself, the more pleasing He may be to those to whom He manifests Himself. The more labor is expended because of Scripture’s difficulty, the greater is the merit of readers. Thus the Psalmist says: “He made darkness His hiding-place” (Ps. 17:12); and again: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (ibid.), because, Gregory says, “the meaning in the prophets has been obscured.” It is written in the Law: “Moses approached the darkness wherein God was” (Exod. 20:21). [Col. 1022A]

Solomon also says in Chronicles: “The Lord promised that He would dwell in darkness” (2 Chron. 6:1). Likewise in Proverbs: “It is the glory of God to conceal a word, and the glory of kings to search out a saying” (Prov. 25:2).

He also invites us in Proverbs to investigate the obscurity of Scriptures as though hidden places in which God is announced, saying: “The wise person will understand parable and interpretation, the words of the wise and their riddles” (Prov. 1:6). These become more precious in proportion as greater labor has been spent in understanding them.

Hence Jerome, writing to the great orator concerning Solomon’s warning at the beginning of Proverbs that we should understand sayings of prudence, subtleties of words, parables and obscure speech, sayings of the wise and riddles, says that these are properly the concern of dialecticians and philosophers.

How consistently philosophy has disdained to disclose its secrets in bare public words, and how it especially customarily spoke through fabulous coverings concerning the soul and the gods, is taught most carefully by that no insignificant philosopher and interpreter of the great Cicero, Macrobius. After excluding kinds of invention or fable unbecoming to philosophers, he sets forth the kind which they most honorably employ. [Col. 1022C]

XX.

For he says:

> “When they utter knowledge of sacred matters beneath a pious covering of inventions, hidden beneath worthy subjects and clothed in names, this is the kind of invention which the caution of one philosophizing about divine matters admits.”

And a little later:

> “It must be known that philosophers admit the fabulous into every discussion, but they are accustomed to employ it when they speak either of the soul or of ethereal powers. But when discourse dares to rise to the highest God and ruler of all, whom the Greeks call τὸ ἀγαθόν (*to agathon*, ‘the Good’) and also πρωτοπάντων (*prōtopantōn*, ‘first of all things’), or to the mind which the Greeks call νοῦς (*nous*), containing the original forms of things called Ideas, born from the highest and perfect God—when, I say, they speak of the highest God and mind, they touch nothing at all fabulous. But if they attempt to set forth anything concerning those realities which surpass not merely human speech but human thought as well, they flee to likenesses and examples.

> “Thus, when Plato undertook to speak of τὸ ἀγαθόν (*to agathon*, ‘the Good’), he did not dare to say what it is, holding only that men cannot know what it is like. But among visible things he found the sun alone most like it, and through the sun’s likeness he opened for his discourse a path of ascent to the incomprehensible. Therefore antiquity devised no image of it when it established images of the other gods. [Col. 1023A] For the highest God and the mind born from Him are as far above the soul as they are above nature; nothing fabulous may fittingly reach them.

> “But concerning the other gods, as I have said, and concerning the soul, philosophers do not turn to fables without purpose or merely to entertain. They know that open and naked exposition of itself is hostile to nature, which, just as it has withdrawn the understanding of itself from common human senses beneath the varied veil and covering of things, so has willed its secrets to be treated by the wise through fabulous forms. Thus the mysteries themselves are covered by the tunnels of figures, lest the nature of such realities offer itself nakedly even to those who have attained them; rather, only the most eminent persons, with Wisdom as interpreter and conscious of its secret, should be satisfied, while the rest are brought to reverence by figures that preserve the secret from cheapness.”

In accordance with this, Truth itself speaks to the Apostles concerning the covering of His parables, saying: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand” (Matt. 13:11). [Col. 1023B]

From this Macrobian tradition, then, it is clear that what philosophers say about the soul of the world must be understood figuratively. Otherwise we should find Plato, the greatest of philosophers, to be the greatest of fools. For what could be more ridiculous than to suppose the whole world to be one rational living creature, unless this is put forward under such a covering? For it cannot be a living creature unless it is sentient, since the well-known definition of a living creature is “an animate, sentient substance.” Which of the five senses, moreover, could belong to the world—unless perhaps touch, which is common to all [Col. 1023C] animals? For it lacks the instruments of the other senses, as Plato himself testifies, where he explains why eyes, nostrils, and the other parts of the human body were not necessary for it. And what part of the body of the world is there by which it could perceive if touched, any more than trees or plants, which, rooted in the earth, are said to be animated by the same soul? Would the world feel the digging up of the earth more than trees feel the stripping away of their leaves or the cutting off of their whole body? Yet it is agreed that trees and all plants are insentient; and therefore, to exclude them, “sentient” is placed after “animate” in the definition of a living creature.

Moreover, when they say that the soul of the world is infused into individual [Col. 1023D] bodies and animates those which it finds suited to animation, what need was there for the creation of our souls, which Plato says were made afterwards? Or what need is there for the soul of the world to be present in these bodies of ours, which it does not animate? For what is clearer than that our bodies possess animal life through their own human souls rather than through the soul of the world? For when these souls are present, they are immediately animate; when the same souls are absent, they are inanimate—although, as they say, the soul of the world continues in them even after death, being wholly in all bodies, including those in which it is idle. Why too, when human souls are absent, is the soul of the world unable to animate our bodies, although it is present in them, when Plato testifies that it was made by the most excellent Creator more excellent than all invisible things [Col. 1024A]? Is it less effective in us than other souls? Or, when our bodies are dead, are they no longer fit to be animated as they were before while human souls were present? Can it give life to countless worms out of one body, when it cannot animate the body itself? What fitness is absent from a dead body, either for its own animation or for being animated, except solely the presence of the human soul, which gives life to the body when present and causes its death when departing?

But if we turn into a figurative sense these things said by philosophers about the soul of the world, everything may readily be understood reasonably, without departing from the rule of sacred faith. Human souls confer animal life upon our bodies; the Soul confers it upon the world.

[Col. 1024B] Unless I am mistaken, philosophers understood the Holy Spirit to give spiritual life to our souls through the distribution of his gifts: just as individual souls are the life of bodies, so the Holy Spirit is the life of souls, advancing them, by quickening them, toward the increase of good works. Thus our souls, which must now be called bodies of the Holy Spirit, are those which he himself inhabits as a temple through some gift of his grace and gives life by virtues. Hence also Augustine says in Sermon 6, *On the Words of the Lord*: “As the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. As the body expires when it sends forth the soul, so the soul expires when it loses God. God lost is the death of the soul; the soul lost is the death of the body. The death of the body is necessary; the death of the soul voluntary.”

And what they say—that the soul, wholly infused into individual bodies, gives life to all things, and that no hardness or diversity of those which it finds fit to be animated hinders the soul, by reason of nature—is a beautiful covering: namely, that the love of God, which we call the Holy Spirit, first infused into human hearts through the gift of faith or reason, gives life to some by advancing us toward the fruit of good works, so that we may attain eternal life; while in some the Spirit himself is said to be inactive, because the hardness of their wickedness resists him.

[Col. 1024C] This teaching concerning the worldly soul was especially set down by Macrobius, the most diligent of philosophers, in his *Commentary*. If we examine his words carefully, we find almost the whole of our faith concerning the Holy Spirit expressed in them [Col. 1024D], since he calls this very soul “Creator,” and maintains that it is from God the Father and from νοῦς (*nous*), that is, God the Son. When at times he calls it *mind*, he uses *mind* generally for soul or spiritual nature. Thus he calls the Son νοῦς, that is, Mind, in one sense; and the soul itself “mind” in another. For the Son is called the Father’s Mind insofar as he is called his Wisdom or Reason. But when he calls the soul “mind,” he indicates that it is of a spiritual, not bodily, nature.

Explaining this himself while expounding certain words of Virgil, he says: “To testify to its purity, he called it mind.” Again: “To assert the dignity of that soul of the world, he testified that it is mind.” It is as if he openly taught that it is called mind in order that the purity and dignity of its spiritual nature might be displayed in it. So too, when we say that the Lord Jesus possessed a human mind, by the term *mind* we mean his very soul.

These, moreover, are the words of Macrobius which we proposed:

> “The Soul, therefore,” he says, “creating and forming bodies for itself. For nature begins from soul, which the wise call Mind and say is from God and νοῦς [Mind]. From that utterly pure fountain, which in being born it had drawn in abundance from its own origin, it first animated the bodies of heaven and of the stars which it created.”

And after some intervening remarks, distinguishing the powers of the soul itself which it exercises in bodies, according to which the nature of all animate things is ordered, so that some, namely, rule over others, he added:

> “Virgil too expressed this order of things. For he gave a soul to the world, and, to testify to its purity, called it mind. For he says:
>
> > ‘Heaven, lands, sea, and stars …  
> > an inward Spirit sustains’  
> > (*Virgil, Aeneid* VI.726),
>
> that is, the soul. And, to assert the dignity of that soul of the world, he testified that it is mind:
>
> > ‘Mind moves the mass’  
> > (*Virgil, ibid.* 727).
>
> Moreover, to show that all living animals subsist through that same soul, he added:
>
> > ‘Hence comes the race of men and beasts,’ etc.  
> > (*Virgil, ibid.* 728).
>
> And to affirm that the same vigor is always in the soul, but that its use is dulled in souls by the density of the body, he added:
>
> > ‘So far as harmful bodies do not impede them.’  
> > (*Virgil, ibid.* 731).”

[Col. 1025C] All these words, both Virgil’s and Macrobius’s, may easily be accommodated, in accordance with our purpose, to the rule of our faith; nor should they be expounded otherwise. Thus, when he says that the use of the soul is dulled in animals through the density of the body, this means that the grace of the Holy Spirit has less efficacy in its benefits among the carnal—those given over to pleasures—so that by “density of body” we understand the magnitude of carnal allurements.

When he also says that the soul creates and forms bodies for itself, he asserts that it is the Creator of things, and hence God [Col. 1025D]; and that it orders created things and prepares them for good works through the distribution of its gifts, so as to make them a worthy dwelling for itself. He says that nature begins from soul because through the grace of the Holy Spirit we are spiritually born and are sons of God rather than servants. For as we should die in vices if this grace were withdrawn, so by its bestowal we are born into the true life of virtues. This indeed we possess by nature, and vices are contrary to nature, since vice is corruption of nature.

The soul is named from God and Mind because the Spirit is equally the Spirit of Father and Son, proceeding from both. Hence, as Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, Book XV, chapter 19, because that Spirit is common to both, he is properly called that which both are commonly called—since both Father and Son are Spirit and holy.

But when philosophers sometimes say that the soul is born, created, or made from God or νοῦς, this is an improper use of words rather than of meaning. For “created” or “made” is properly said only of things which began, that is, which are not eternal. “Born,” however—that is, existing from the very substance of the Father—is proper to the Son, as we shall discuss later in its place. Yet philosophers sometimes use “to be created,” “to be born,” or “to be made” merely for “to be,” as we have noted above. Thus Macrobius says that νοῦς itself is from God, and that the soul is created from νοῦς—that is, that it is from him. We use “to be born” in the same sense here.

Hermes also, when above he said that God made the Son of God second, showed that he himself is from God the Father. He calls νοῦς, that is, the Wisdom of the Father, the utterly pure fountain of wisdom, from which nothing, however obscure it may be, can be hidden.

[Col. 1026B] From the abundance of this fountain, the goodness of God first animated the bodies of heaven and of the stars: that is, the angels or heavenly spirits themselves, who were created before humankind, as it is written: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). “Heaven and stars” are said according to differences of dignity, since we believe that some spirits are set over and superior to others; hence we speak of angels and archangels, and of dominions. Angels too may be called the bodies of the highest Spirit, animated spiritually by him, as has been said; or he calls them bodies in the sense in which we call every creature bodily—that is, circumscribed.

Hence Gennadius, in *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 10:

> “Nothing incorporeal and invisible in nature is to be believed except God alone. He is believed incorporeal because he is everywhere and fills all things, and therefore invisible to all creatures because he is incorporeal. Every creature is bodily; angels and all heavenly beings are bodily, though they do not subsist in flesh. We believe intellectual natures to be bodily because they are locally circumscribed, as also is the human soul, which is enclosed by flesh, and demons, who are bodily by the substance of angelic nature.”

It was well said that they are animated from Wisdom itself, because this is eternal life: that we may know as we are known, beholding God face to face [Col. 1026D]. The Spirit draws from that fountain when he fills us with understanding of divine wisdom, according to the saying: “He shall receive of mine and shall declare it to you” (John 16:17). Hence he is called the Spirit of wisdom, understanding, or knowledge.

But the statement, “Mind moves the mass”—that is, the bulk of the whole fabric of the world, as though it gives life to or moves everything in the world—continues Plato’s teaching, expounded above, concerning the Spirit of God: that he disposes all things most excellently,

> “And, remaining unmoved, gives all things motion.”

Solomon too carefully expressed this activity of the Soul in Ecclesiastes: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place, illuminating all things. The spirit goes round in its circuit and returns in its circle” (Eccles. 1:5, 7). What is that circle except the circumference of the round and spherical world, concerning which it is written that “the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world” (Wisdom 1:7)? For the grace of divine goodness so fills everything that nothing whatever is exempt from the governance of its activity. As it causes the sun to rise and set before our sight, so it orders every other thing most excellently.

[Col. 1027A] Indeed, Virgil’s foregoing words about the soul of the world appear so full of truth that holy teachers did not shrink from adopting them almost as authoritative. Thus Jerome, explaining the passage of Ezekiel where it is written, “He brought me into the inner court by way of the east” (Ezek. 11:1), says:

> “If we understand the court as outer and inner, it must be understood thus: that God both surrounds and is infused within, saying through the prophet: ‘He holds heaven in his palm and earth in his fist,’ so that all things appear to be enclosed by him. And again: ‘Heaven is my throne, and earth my footstool,’ so that he must be believed to be within all things, according to that Virgilian passage:
>
> > ‘First, heaven and lands and the flowing plains,  
> > the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars,  
> > an inward Spirit sustains; and Mind, infused through all the limbs,  
> > moves the whole mass and mingles with the mighty body.’  
> > (*Virgil, Aeneid* VI.724 ff.)”

The same writer, in Book II on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians, says:

> “The diversity of the prepositions in the statement, ‘one God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in all,’ conveys a different meaning. God the Father, the author of all, is above all [Col. 1027C]. The Son is through all, running and moving through all things. The Holy Spirit is in all, because nothing exists without him. Zeno too, with the Stoics, supposes something of this kind concerning creatures and God; Virgil follows him. For he says that God
>
> > ‘… goes through all lands and empty …’
>
> and the rest. And:
>
> > ‘First, heaven and earth and the flowing plains,  
> > the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars,  
> > an inward Spirit sustains,’ etc.”

For all things are said to live in God, as we have noted above, because in him nothing is dead—that is, useless—but everything is made or ordered usefully and fittingly. Hence it is written: “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3–4): that is, in the providence of divine Wisdom, before they were made, things were most fittingly ordered. Hence it is again said: “God, to whom all things live.” And the Apostle says: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). He gives life both to human beings and beasts. Some gifts of his belonging to life are possessed both by the wisest and by the simple and unlearned. Hence Ecclesiastes says: “Who knows the spirit of the children of Adam, whether it ascends upward, and whether the spirit of beasts descends downward?” (Eccles. 3:21 [printed “2”]). That is: who among the wise and the unlearned are predestined for life, and who assigned to death?

[Col. 1028A] Let these remarks on Macrobius suffice.

But if anyone accuses me of being an intrusive and violent interpreter, because I wrench philosophers’ words too far from their proper exposition toward our faith and impose upon them what they themselves did not at all think, let him consider the prophecy of Caiaphas, which the Holy Spirit uttered through him, applying it to a meaning far other than that intended by its utterer. For even when the Holy Spirit speaks something through holy prophets, they do not understand all the meanings to which their words extend, but often grasp only one meaning in them, while the Spirit himself, who speaks through them, provides many meanings there, so that later he may inspire some persons with one exposition and others with another.

Hence Gregory, writing in the *Register* to Januarius, bishop of Calagurris, says:

> “In the understanding of sacred Scripture, nothing which does not resist the sacred faith should be rejected. For as from one gold some make little chains, others rings, others bracelets for adornment, so from a single meaning of sacred Scripture expositions are composed through innumerable understandings, as varied ornaments; yet all contribute to the adornment of the heavenly Bride.”

Macrobius himself recalls that the things philosophers have said about the soul of the world are to be interpreted mystically. Since, as we have noted above, they can in no way be truly or fittingly expounded according to the letter, the letter itself compels us to mystical exposition. We have also learned from many testimonies of the saints that the Platonic school agrees very greatly with Catholic faith [Col. 1028C]. Thus the greatest philosopher, Plato, is for good reason commended above the rest by all—not only by those skilled in secular arts, but also by the saints.

Concerning him, Father Augustine says in Book IX of *The City of God* [Note: [Col. 1027D] *Patrologia*, vol. XLI, col. 235.]:

> “Some joined with us in Christ’s grace wonder when they hear or read that Plato entertained concerning God views recognized as greatly consonant with the truth of our religion. Hence some have thought that, when he travelled to Egypt, he heard Jeremiah or read prophetic Scriptures during that journey. But if the chronology contained in historical chronicles is carefully reckoned, it indicates that Plato was born nearly a hundred years after the time when Jeremiah prophesied [Col. 1028D]. And since Plato lived eighty-one years, nearly nine years are found from the year of his death until the time when Ptolemy, king of Egypt, arranged for the prophetic Scriptures to be translated and kept through seventy Hebrews who knew Greek. Therefore Plato could neither have seen Jeremiah on that journey, since he had died so long before, nor have read the same Scriptures in Greek, since they had not yet been translated into Greek—unless, being of the keenest zeal for learning, he studied these also through an interpreter, as he did Egyptian materials.”

Indeed, Plato’s sayings seem so consonant with the Lord’s words and preaching that, as the same doctor declares in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine* [Col. 1029A], certain readers and lovers of Plato dared to break forth into such madness as to say that our Lord Jesus Christ learned from Plato’s books the sayings which they are compelled to admire and proclaim.

Hence, I suppose, Ptolemy the king is said to have perceived the same thing in Plato’s doctrine, because he had learned from Platonic writings about God and Mind—that is, the Father and the Word. Therefore, when the Seventy Interpreters translated the Law for him, they entirely kept silent, by a prudent counsel as they say, about the mystery of divine generation, lest, if he heard that it too was proclaimed among the Hebrews, he should discover there to be a twofold divinity. Formerly he had worshipped only one God; they feared that, because of Platonic doctrine, he might depart from the unity of deity, although he had heard several persons distinguished within it, while the singularity of one deity remained intact. Hence Jerome recalls in the Prologue to the Pentateuch that the aforesaid Seventy suppressed many such things, such as: “Out of Egypt I called my Son,” etc. (Matt. 2:15).

From this it is evident that the Platonic school has always agreed greatly with faith in the holy Trinity, and that Plato and his followers distinguished and described it more carefully than all other philosophers. Thus Valerius Maximus deservedly bursts into these words in Plato’s praise:

> “While Plato, still an infant, slept in his cradle, bees placed honey upon his lips. When this prodigy was heard of, its interpreters declared that a singular sweetness of eloquence would flow from his mouth.”

But I do not doubt that it is more excellent and fitting to refer this miracle to the glory of the divine Godhead: God bestowed upon him this sign of prophecy because he would reveal more carefully through him the mysteries of his divinity [Col. 1029C]. For it was fitting that the supreme philosopher and his followers should bear very great witness to the supreme Wisdom, which is Christ—the Word, namely, and Wisdom of God the Father.

Therefore, according to Augustine, as we have noted above, when the Apostle spoke to the Athenians and had stated a great matter, intelligible to few—namely, that “in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28)—he added, “as certain also of your own have said” (ibid.). For Plato was certainly an Athenian.

But the point on which Plato appears, and is said, to have erred considerably is this: that he says the soul of the world was made [Col. 1029D], that is, that it had a beginning; and that, as Macrobius asserted above when speaking of the soul of the world, God and νοῦς are beyond the soul, as though superior in dignity. Yet Catholics agree that the three persons in the Godhead are in every respect equal and coeternal with one another. If these matters are examined more carefully, Plato does not depart from the truth, as we shall later show concerning his disagreement about the procession of the Holy Spirit. For not without reason is this philosopher commended above the rest by all, both believers, as noted above, and unbelievers.

Since the Platonic school has excelled in every branch of philosophical teaching, it is useful also to adduce certain testimonies of Platonists which Father Augustine recalls in Book VII of the *Confessions* that he found in their writings. In these, almost the whole summary of our faith concerning the divinity of the Word is contained very clearly [Col. 1030A], as it was later handed down by the principal writers of the New Testament, namely John and Paul the Apostles. Augustine, addressing God in the same discourse, says there:

## XXI

“You procured for me, through a man swollen with monstrous pride, certain books of the Platonists translated from Greek into Latin. There I read, not indeed in these words, but urged by many varied arguments to precisely the same effect, that:

> ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men; and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it’ (John 1:1–5).

And that every soul, though it bears witness to the light, is not itself the light; but God the Word is the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world. And that he was in this world, ‘and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him’ (ibid. 10).

But that ‘he came unto his own, and his own did not receive him; but to as many as received him he gave power to become children of God, to those believing in his name’ (ibid. 11–12), I did not read there.

Again, I read there that ‘they were born not of flesh, not of blood, not of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God’ (ibid. 13). But that ‘the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us’ (ibid. 14), I did not read there.

I discovered in those writings, expressed in many ways, that the Son, being in the form of the Father, did not regard equality with God as a thing to be seized, because he is by nature the same. But that ‘he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted him from the dead and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at his name every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father’ (Phil. 2:7–11)—those books do not contain that [Col. 1030D].

For that your only-begotten Son, coeternal with you, remains unchangeably before all times and above all times; and that souls receive from his fullness in order to be blessed; and that by participation in Wisdom abiding in itself they are renewed in order to be wise—this is there. But that he died for the ungodly is not there.”

But lest any sex among human beings eminent above the rest in the reputation of wisdom should be absent from testimonies to our faith, let the celebrated Sibyl also be introduced. In writing she omitted neither the divinity of the Word, nor his humanity, nor both his comings, nor both his judgments: the first judgment, in which Christ was unjustly judged in his Passion, and the second, in which he shall justly judge the world in majesty.

Augustine, in *Against Five Heresies*, says:

> “Let us hear what the Sibyl, their prophetess, says concerning him: ‘The Lord gave another to faithful people to worship.’ Again: ‘Know that he is your Lord, the Son of God.’ Elsewhere she calls the Son of God Σύμβολον (*Symbolon*), that is, ‘Counsellor’ or ‘counsel.’ And the prophet says: ‘His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor.’”

Again, the same Father Augustine in Book VIII of *The City of God* says:

> “At that time, some report that the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied; others think her rather the Cumaean. There are twenty-eight verses of hers which, as someone translated them into Latin verse, contain this:
>
> > ‘A sign of judgment: the earth shall be wet with sweat;  
> > and from heaven shall come a king, to reign through ages to come,  
> > present indeed in flesh, that he may conquer the world,’ etc.”

[Col. 1031B] The initial Greek letters of these verses, taken together, say: “JESUS CHRIST, SON OF GOD, SAVIOUR.”

Lactantius also adduces certain prophecies of the Sibyl concerning Christ:

> “Afterwards he shall come into the hands of unbelievers;  
> they shall strike God with unclean hands,  
> and with polluted mouths shall spit poisonous spittle.  
> But he shall give his holy back to blows;  
> humbly he shall receive buffetings, that none may recognize  
> what Word he is or whence he came, that he may speak to those below,  
> and be crowned with a crown of thorns.  
> For food they gave gall, and for thirst vinegar;  
> they shall display this table of inhospitality.  
> For you, foolish people, did not understand your God,  
> who played with the minds of mortals; but you crowned him  
> with thorns and mixed gall.  
> The veil of the temple shall be torn, and in the middle of day  
> there shall be night for three days, sleep having been undergone.  
> Then, returning from below to the light,  
> he shall come first, displaying the beginning of resurrection.”

This prophecy of the Sibyl, unless I am mistaken, that greatest of our poets, Virgil, had heard and understood when, in the Fourth Eclogue, he foretold that shortly, under Caesar Augustus during Pollio’s consulship, there would be born a wonderful boy sent down from heaven to earth, who would take away even the sins of the world and marvellously establish, as it were, a second new age in the world. He was prompted, as he himself says, by the oracle of the Cumaean song—that is, the Sibyl called Cumaean or Cumana. He speaks thus, as if urging all persons to rejoice with him and to sing or compose concerning this great boy who was to be born, in comparison with whom he judges all other subjects comparatively low and worthless:

> “Sicilian Muses, let us sing a somewhat loftier song.  
> Not all delight in groves and lowly tamarisks.  
> Now comes the last age of the Cumaean song;  
> the great order of the ages is born anew.  
> Now the Virgin returns; Saturnian kingdoms return;  
> now a new offspring is sent down from lofty heaven.”  
> (*Virgil, Eclogue* 4.1 ff.)

And shortly after:

> “You, Pollio, with you as consul, shall enter upon this glory;  
> if any traces of our sin remain,  
> they shall be made void and free the lands from perpetual fear.”  
> (*Virgil, ibid.* 11)

[Col. 1032A] Again, concerning the boy:

> “And he shall rule the peaceful world by his father’s virtues.”  
> (*Virgil, ibid.* 17)

These verses contain a most explicit prophecy of the Incarnation of the Son of God, perhaps without the poet himself knowing that the Holy Spirit spoke in the Sibyl or in him, as happened with Caiaphas, who said: “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the people and that not the whole nation should perish” (John 11); and it is added there: “He did not say this of himself” (ibid. 51).

It can very readily be proved from what follows that this Eclogue cannot truly or fittingly be understood of anyone except the incarnate only-begotten Son of God, if the words are typologically spoken in the prophetic manner. For they are found to be plainly false and impossible if expounded literally, and are not even fitly advanced as flattery, as some suppose, since they are immediately rejected by everyone as unbelievable. Thus they would provoke indignation against the poet rather than win goodwill. But elsewhere we shall have occasion to demonstrate and expound these matters more carefully, when we bring forward testimonies concerning the Incarnation of the Word rather than his divinity.

Later, in another Eclogue, Virgil not obscurely hints at the divine Trinity. Speaking in the person of one person to another, he says:

> “First I bind around you these three threads, differing in threefold colour;  
> and three times I lead this image around these altars.  
> God delights in an odd number.”  
> (*Virgil, Eclogue* 8.73)

Here, to be sure, describing magical rites which have great force to bind a recalcitrant person, he threatens, saying: “I bind three threads of the same substance—that is, wool—but differing by threefold colour, around you in your image, in order to bind and capture you,” as though attending to Solomon’s saying: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccles. 4:12). Then, he says, “I lead your image, thus bound, three times around the altars.”

Finally, why he mentioned three threads, a threefold colour, and a threefold circuit of the altar—as though he perceived in every instance a great force in the number three for the celebration of sacred rites—he added: “God delights in an odd number.” It is as if he said: “Because God wills his perfection to be described in this number according to the Trinity of persons [Col. 1032D].” These persons are of the same substance but different in properties; hence they appear to be represented by three woollen threads of different colours.

## XXII

Let us now return to the proposed testimonies concerning the divinity of the Word. Along with David and Solomon, kings of Israel, let us bring in a third king of the nations to prophesy concerning the supreme King. For what is clearer than Nebuchadnezzar’s testimony concerning the Son of God? “Behold,” he says, “I see four men unbound, walking in the midst of the fire, and the appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God.”

It is useful also to adduce the testimony of Didymus, king of the Brahmans, so that our assertion of faith may stand preeminent in the authority of four kings: two Jews, David and Solomon, and two Gentiles, Nebuchadnezzar and Didymus. Let these four kings be like the four wheels of the noble chariot of the supreme King, through which the faith of the four Evangelists concerning the Holy Trinity is carried throughout the world. The authority of kings is all the firmer insofar as their power is more alike; and those who issue edicts and laws to peoples also hand down testimonies to the sacred faith.

## XXIII

Thus Didymus says—indeed, says thus—in his first letter to Alexander:

> “Among the other distinguishing marks of the religion or faith of his people, God does not accept bloody sacrifices; he loves bloodless worship and despises deadly libations. He is propitiated by the word of those who pray, which alone he has in common with humanity, and he delights in his likeness in the divine nature. For the Word is God: he created the world; he governs and sustains all things; him we venerate, him we love; from him we draw spirit. For God himself is Spirit and Mind, and therefore is pleased not by earthly riches or lavish generosity, but by religious works and thanksgiving.”

From these clear words it is handed down that both God’s Word itself and the Spirit infused by him into believers are God. That king not only believed this, but proclaimed it in writing to another great king.

What great piety and abstinence the people of the Brahmans possessed, such that God should inspire them above all nations with an understanding of the sacred faith, is contained in Didymus’s letters to Alexander. If those letters deserve credence, no life of human beings, however religious, seems comparable to the innocence and abstinence of the Brahmans. Thus blessed Jerome too set them before us as an example of abstinence. Among other remarks in Book II *Against Jovinianus*, he says [Note: [Col. 1033D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXIII, col. 304.]:

> “Bardesanes, a Babylonian man, divides the Indian Gymnosophists into two schools, calling one Brahmans and the other Samanaeans.
