They are of such continence that they live either on the fruits of trees near the river Ganges or on a common diet of rice and flour; and when the king comes to them, he is accustomed to worship them and judges the peace of his province to depend upon their prayers.”

The very same letter to the orator Magnus testifies that divine grace also directed the preaching of the Gospel to them, in these words [Note: [Col. 1034D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 667.]:

> “Pantaenus, a philosopher of the Stoic school, was sent to India by Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, because of the renown of his exceptional learning, to preach Christ among the Brahmans and the philosophers of that nation.”

## XXIV

Seneca too, who among all philosophers attained distinction both in moral teaching and in manner of life, openly professes that the Holy Spirit is the distributor of all good things. Writing about him to the Apostle Paul in the fourth letter, he says:

> “I profess that I have gladly received the reading of your letters which you sent to the Galatians, Corinthians, and Achaeans. For the Holy Spirit within you, higher than the exalted, expresses thoughts sufficiently worthy of reverence.”

## XXV
Finally, it remains to come down to that greatest of Latin philosophers, namely Boethius. He transmitted in Latin almost all the disciplines of the liberal arts, whether by writing, translating, or even expounding them; and, carefully explaining the faith of the Holy Trinity in writing to his father-in-law and patrician Symmachus, he also argued excellently, in writing to John the deacon (who later became pope), against Eutyches and Nestorius, concerning both the unity of Christ’s person and the diversity of the natures in Christ, namely the divine and the human. [Col. 1034B] By his treatment of both the Godhead and the incarnation of the Godhead, he established our faith—and his own—impregnably, so that it might not waver in any respect.

It is established that this distinguished Roman senator, consul, and patrician flourished in the time of the aforesaid Pope John, the twentieth pope after Sylvester, and that in the persecution of Christians in which Theoderic raged against Pope John and the other Christians, he perished together with the aforesaid Symmachus. In the Acts of the Pontiffs, and likewise in the book of the miracles of blessed Benedict, it is written how King Theoderic of the Goths killed them both. In the Acts, indeed, you will find it written thus:

> The heretical king Theoderic put to the sword two senators, consuls, and patricians, Boethius and Symmachus, and caused their bodies also to be hidden and ordered it so.

But in the book of the miracles of the aforesaid saint it is stated thus:

> After Odoacer, Theoderic assumed the rule of the Goths with the royal title. A pestilent man of the Arian sect, among his other crimes he finally killed Pope John by wasting him with bodily hunger; and he pierced with the sword in prison two men of senatorial rank and former consuls, namely Symmachus and Boethius.

Since, therefore, the Lord has announced the tenor of the catholic faith both to the Jews through the prophets and to the Gentiles through eminent philosophers or seers, both Jews and Gentiles are rendered without excuse if, while having these as teachers in other matters, they do not listen to them concerning the salvation of the soul, whose foundation is faith. [Col. 1034D] Indeed, many from among the Gentiles and some from among the Jews, instructed also in this matter by the teachers of their own people, recognized the faith of the Holy Trinity in the one body of the Church, like two walls joined together. From among the Gentiles, first came the Greeks, among whom were the aforesaid philosophers; after the Greeks came the Latins, who, just as they imitated the Greeks in the disciplines of secular arts, so also took examples from them in the true doctrine of faith—when, that is, they heard that those whom they had known to be endowed with subtle intellects and armed with every philosophical argument had embraced the Christian faith.

## BOOK II

[Col. 1035]

[Col. 1035A] In the preceding part of this work we assembled certain testimonies, both of prophets and of philosophers, by which we might establish the faith of the Holy Trinity. In doing so, when we introduced the assertions of unbelieving philosophers, as also those of the holy Fathers, as though into the place of authority, we foresaw that we would be gnawed at by the detractions of many, and that some would reproach us with what, long ago, we read had been objected by many against blessed Jerome: namely, that he inserted into his writings testimonies not only of pagans but even of heretics.

Accordingly, writing an epistle against the calumnies of Magnus, orator of the city of Rome, he began as follows:

> Why do you ask why we sometimes put examples from secular literature into our little works and defile the brightness of the Church with pagan filth? You would never ask this if you read the sacred Scriptures, if you reviewed their interpreters. For who does not know that in Moses and in the volumes of the prophets some things are taken from the books of the Gentiles; and that Solomon both philosophizes, proposes certain things, and gives certain answers? Hence, at the beginning of Proverbs he advises us to understand sayings of prudence, subtleties of words, parables, obscure speech, sayings of the wise, and riddles—things which properly belong to dialecticians and philosophers.

> But the Apostle Paul too made use of a verse of the poet Epimenides when writing to Titus: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies” [Titus 1:12; printed citation: 1:22]. In another epistle he quotes a senarius of Menander [1 Cor. 15:33]:

> “Evil conversations corrupt good morals.”

> And, disputing among the Athenians in the court of Mars, he calls Aratus as a witness: “For we too are his offspring” [Acts 17:28]. The father—that is, the teacher—of the Christian army, and the unconquered orator pleading Christ’s cause, even skillfully twists a chance inscription into an argument for faith [ibid., 23 ff.]. For he had learned from the true David to wrench the sword from the hands of enemies and to sever the head of the most arrogant Goliath with his own blade. Let them read in Deuteronomy that the captive woman’s head is to be shaved, her eyebrows, every hair, and the nails of her body cut off, and that thus she is to be taken in marriage [Deut. 21:12 ff.]. What wonder, then, if I too desire, because of the beauty of her expression and the loveliness of her limbs, to make secular wisdom, once a handmaid and captive, into an Israelite? If there is anything dead in her—of idolatry, pleasure, error, or lust—I either cut it off or shave it away; and, united with the most pure body, I beget from her household servants for the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1035D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, cols. 665–666, book II.]

Likewise:

> Cyprian, a man powerful in eloquence and martyrdom, is criticized, as Formanus relates, because, writing against Demetrianus, he made use of testimonies from prophets and apostles—which Demetrianus regarded as fictitious and fabricated—instead of philosophers and poets, whose authority, as a pagan, he could not oppose.

[Note: [Col. 1035D] *Patrologia*, same place, col. 666.]

Likewise:

> Josephus wrote two books against Apion of Alexandria and adduces so many secular testimonies that I am struck with wonder how a Hebrew, instructed in sacred letters from infancy, could have gone through the entire library of the Greeks.

Likewise:

> There are extant books of Julius Africanus and Theodoric, a man renowned for apostolic signs and powers; and of Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, as well as Anatolius, Pamphilus, Pierius, Lucian, Malchion, Eusebius bishop of Caesarea, and others, who all so filled up their books with philosophers’ doctrines and opinions that one does not know what should first be admired in them: their secular learning or their knowledge of letters.

[Note: [Col. 1036D] *Patrologia*, same place, cols. 667–668. The printed reading “referserunt” is corrected contextually to *resarciunt*, “fill up, patch together.”]

The same writer, to the presbyter Vigilantius:

> I state in your absence what I said also in your presence: that I have read, or read, Origen, Apollinaris, and other expositors, whose books the Church does not receive in certain cases. For it is my work and study to read many authors, that I may gather many flowers from many sources, testing everything and choosing what is good. I take many books in hand so that I may learn many things from many sources, according to what is written: “Reading all things, hold fast what is good” [1 Thess. 5:21]. Hence I am quite astonished that you wished to throw Origen’s doctrines in my face. What is Origen the heretic to me, who do not deny that he is a heretic in very many respects? He erred concerning the resurrection of the body, the condition of souls, the devil’s repentance, and—what is greater than these—he declared in his Commentary on Isaiah that the Son and the Holy Spirit are the seraphim.

[Note: [Col. 1036D] *Patrologia*, same place, cols. 662–663.]

Likewise:

> We ought not to receive his good things in such a way as to be compelled also to receive his evil things. Therefore, if I have translated what is good and cut off, passed over in silence, or corrected what is evil, am I to be blamed because through me the Latins possess his good things and do not know his evil things? If this is a crime, let Hilary the confessor be accused, for he translated from Origen’s books the interpretation of the Psalms and homilies on Job. Let Eusebius of Vercelli be guilty, for he translated into our language the commentaries on all the Psalms by that heretical man, though passing over the heretical material.

[Note: [Col. 1036D] *Patrologia*, same place, col. 663.]

Jerome gave this answer against the calumnies of those who think catholic expositors should be censured because they dare to insert into their writings testimonies or sayings of unbelievers, as though they thereby grant authority to persons worthy of no authority, or as though truth uttered through unbelievers could defile sacred statements. He knew, certainly, as one most discriminating, how to distinguish grain from chaff, and how, like a wise goldsmith, to set a pearl sometimes more precious than others, found in a dung heap, into royal ornament. [Col. 1037A]

He most certainly held that God’s gifts cannot be contaminated by any evil person, nor divine sacraments defiled by contact with the wicked: whether unbelievers baptize in the name of the Trinity, utterly evil people preach divine words, or utter prophecies and sometimes perform miracles. For whatever things are good must come from God, and the malice of any persons cannot contaminate them.

Thus sacred authority did not reject the prophecy of Balaam the Gentile or that of the diviner Ariolus, by which the Magi, the firstfruits of the Gentiles, are afterward believed to have been prompted, upon the appearance of a new star, immediately to seek the new king. Nor did the spiritual teacher Augustine fear to insert the prophecies of the Sibyl or of Virgil among those of the holy prophets, attending to the Apostle’s saying: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” [1 Cor. 12:3]. Nor did the Evangelist fear to commend Caiaphas’s prophecy when he said: “He did not say this of himself; but, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied” [John 11:51].

Nor did the Gospel pass over in silence the testimonies of demons themselves, when, at the Lord’s coming to expel them, they cried out and confessed him to be Jesus Christ or the Son of God. Indeed, blessed Gregory bears witness that even insensible things in some manner perceived his power—whether in his birth, death, resurrection, ascension, or miracle-working—in order to render testimony to him in their own way: angels and a star appearing immediately at his birth; at his death, the sun darkened, rocks and the veil of the Temple rent, and the tombs of risen saints opened, with many appearing; at the resurrection, an earthquake occurring together with a vision of angels; and at the ascension, a cloud receiving him. [Col. 1037C]

The whole adornment of the world likewise does not cease to announce, proclaim, praise in its own way, and commend his power and wisdom by its own wondrous composition and ordering. Hence the Apostle says: “His invisible things, understood through the things that are made, are clearly seen from the creation of the world—his eternal power also and divinity,” and so forth [Rom. 1:20]. Therefore the Psalmist too, applauding the praises of even insensible creatures, calls all creation together to praise God, as though God rightly required praise from us from all things excellently made, since he made all things in the world for us. Thus, beginning from the height of heaven and the solemn assembly of angels, he extends divine praises down to dragons, serpents, and all deeps, saying: “Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all deeps” [Ps. 148:7]. And again: “Serpents and winged birds” [ibid., 10]. Nor did he omit any creeping things, saying: “The heavens and earth shall praise him, the sea and all creeping things in them” [Ps. 68:35].

[Col. 1038A] We also read in the Life of Paul the Hermit, written by blessed Jerome, that a satyr appeared to blessed Antony. Protesting the Savior’s coming, it said to the holy man:

> I act as ambassador for my herd. We ask that you pray to the common God for us, whom we have learned came long ago for the salvation of the world, and whose sound has gone forth into all the earth.

The aged traveler, marveling and rejoicing at this confession and testimony of the satyr concerning Christ, because even monsters preached Christ, and being violently angered at the hardness and blindness of Alexandria, immediately struck the ground with his staff and said:

> Woe to you, Alexandria, which venerates prodigies as God. What will you say now? Beasts speak of Christ.

It is as though he openly cried out: “At least the confession of monsters will crush your shamelessness.” This confession perhaps proclaims God’s glory and power all the more wonderfully because it is to be accounted a greater miracle; and its assertion seems all the truer because it is farther removed from human instruction and must be wholly attributed to the prompting of the Holy Spirit.

Thus too the words of Balaam’s ass, and the voices made in the air—as we read concerning the baptized or transfigured Lord—when they announced something to those standing by, moved their hearers to faith all the more readily because they appeared more wondrous to all. The same is manifestly taught by reason concerning philosophers also and certain Gentiles, however unbelieving or hostile to our faith they may have been. For the more hostile they were to our faith, the less they could be suspected in its praise; and the testimony of an enemy in praise of anyone is more credible than that of a friend, just as the reverse is true in accusation. [Col. 1038C]

Therefore, when we read the testimony of Josephus the Jew concerning Christ or his saints, we are greatly moved toward faith by it; and when we hear that Philo the Jew approved and commended the life of Egyptian monks, it satisfies us more than if one of our own number commended it. Consequently, both deserved to be numbered and enrolled among illustrious men by blessed Jerome.

What is more necessary for the defense of our faith than that, against the importunity of all unbelievers, we should possess from those very persons the means by which to refute them? Thus, if philosophers attack us, let their own teachers and philosophers be convicted through themselves; and if heretics attack us, let them be refuted by the testimonies of sacred Scripture. And so, according to the Apostle, “let every mouth be stopped, and let the whole world become subject to God” [Rom. 3:19]. Who does not know that heretics are far worse than Gentiles and certain philosophers? For, according to the Apostle Peter’s declaration, “it would have been better for them not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back” [2 Pet. 2:21; printed citation: 2:2].

If, then, because of the unbelief of Gentiles, those who use certain of their testimonies or sayings are to be blamed, much more should those be blamed who have so zealously translated and introduced for our edification Origen’s expositions and opinions, entangled as they are in so many and such great heresies; since, as has been said, heretics are demonstrably more damnable than all others on account of their unbelief. [Col. 1039A] Yet they did not endure that his innumerable and utterly abominable heresies should perish in silence, as though they foresaw some usefulness even in reviewing them: namely, that once these errors had been identified and condemned, others might more easily guard against them, or might learn the arguments by which to dissolve them should anyone entangle them in those errors.

Accordingly blessed Jerome addressed an epistle to the presbyter Auctum, in order to disclose in part those heretical opinions which Origen had set forth in the books *Periarchon* (“On First Principles”). Who, moreover, can reasonably accuse me for introducing philosophers’ testimonies without drawing into blame with me the holy teachers on this very point? For the testimonies which I collected above from philosophers I collected not from their own writings—which I know only slightly—but from the books of the holy Fathers.

Would such a person presume also to accuse the Apostle, who, as blessed Augustine says in book VIII of *The City of God*, when speaking to the Athenians had stated something great concerning God, something that only a few could understand—namely, that “in him we live and move and are” [Acts 17:26; cf. 17:28]—added, “as some have also well said” [ibid.], introducing for persuasion the testimony of those very philosophers through whose studies that celebrated city had flourished? Of them Augustine himself had previously said in the same work, writing to the Romans: “What is known of God is manifest among them, for God revealed it to them,” and so forth [Rom. 1:19]. From this the Apostle openly teaches that the mystery of the Trinity was revealed also to them.

But here certain words of the Apostle occur which we must expound in what follows. For the present, having collected and expounded many testimonies concerning the faith of the Holy Trinity against the objections of both heretics and philosophers, it remains to disclose by what arguments that which has been confirmed by testimonies may be defended. Every controversy, as Tully states in his *Rhetorics*, concerns either writing or reason; and, as blessed Augustine attests, in all matters it is fitting to put authority before human reason. Above all in matters concerning God, we rely more safely on authority than on human judgment. [Col. 1039C]

Hence is the saying which he makes in book I, chapter 1, of *On the Morals of the Church against the Manichees*:

> The order of nature is such that, when we learn something, authority precedes reason. For reason may appear weak if, after it has been supplied, it does not thereafter assume the authority through which it is formed.

It remains, then, for us now, after laying the foundation of authorities, to bring in the supports of arguments—especially so that the verbosity of Christ’s enemies may not mock our simplicity. Whenever they have entangled certain unlearned or less educated Christians in the snares of their inferences, they claim this for themselves as the height of glory. It is not enough for them to perish alone, unless they force others into their errors, after the manner of those Jews of whom Truth says that they travel sea and land to make one proselyte [Matt. 23:15].

## II

[Col. 1040A]

We set the faith of the Holy Trinity as the foundation, as it were, of all goods, so that the beginning of every good may be drawn from the knowledge of the divine nature itself. Whoever can shake this foundation leaves us nothing profitable among the things that are to be built upon it. Hence we have taken care first to oppose to so great a danger the shield both of authorities and of arguments, trusting in him who strengthens his own people and says: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not be anxious,” and so forth [Matt. 10:19].

Relying upon his help, the little David slew the immense and swollen Goliath with Goliath’s own sword. Let us likewise turn against philosophers and heretics the sword of human arguments by which they attack us, and in the Lord scatter their strength and the edge of their arguments. Then they may be less ready to assail the simplicity of believers, once they have been refuted in the matters in which it seems to them especially impossible to answer: the distinction of persons in the one, wholly indivisible and simple divine substance, and the generation of the Word or procession of the Spirit.

We do not promise to teach the truth concerning this, a truth to which we believe neither we nor any mortal is adequate. But we are willing at least to offer something plausible and near to human reason, and not contrary to sacred faith, against those who boast that they attack faith with human arguments, attend only to the human arguments they know, and readily find many supporters, since nearly all human beings are fleshly and very few spiritual. It is enough for us in some manner to scatter the force of these supreme enemies, particularly since we cannot do so otherwise than by adducing from their own arts the arguments they recognize. Far be it from us to believe that God—who makes good use even of evil persons—does not also rightly order all arts, which are his gifts, so that they too may serve his majesty, however badly the perverse misuse them.

Thus blessed Augustine and the other ecclesiastical teachers declare that the secular arts, and especially dialectic itself, are exceedingly necessary for sacred Scripture. So greatly did the aforesaid doctor venture to commend dialectic in book II of *On Order* that he seems to profess it to be the sole science, since he says that it alone can make people knowing:

> The discipline of disciplines, which they call dialectic, teaches how to teach and teaches how to learn. In it reason displays and reveals itself: what it is and what it wills. It knows that it knows; it not only wishes to make people knowing, but can do so alone.

[Note: [Col. 1039D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXII, col. 1013.]

The same writer, in book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, declares that among all arts dialectic and arithmetic are especially necessary to sacred Scripture: dialectic for resolving questions, arithmetic for examining the mysteries of allegories, which we frequently investigate in the properties of numbers. He exalts dialectic all the more because he declares it necessary for settling every kind of doubtful question, saying:

> There remain those things which pertain not to bodily senses but to reason, where the discipline of disputation and numbers hold sway. But the discipline of disputation is of very great use for all kinds of questions contained in the holy books. Yet there one must beware the desire for quarreling and a certain childish display of deceiving an opponent. For there are many things called sophisms, such as conclusions of arguments, often imitating truths so closely that they deceive not only the slow-minded but even intelligent persons who are less attentive. Scripture, I think, detests this kind of captious conclusion in the passage where it is said: “He who speaks sophistically is hateful” [Ecclus. 37:23].

[Note: [Col. 1041D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXIV, cols. 57–58.]

Again, in the same work, observing much moral edification in philosophers’ sayings but no doctrine concerning faith in and worship of the one God, he added:

> Those who are called philosophers, if they have by chance said things suited to our faith, especially the Platonists, should not merely not be feared; rather, they should be claimed for our use from them as from unjust possessors. For Egypt possessed not only idols, which the people of Israel detested, but also vessels and ornaments of gold and silver, and clothing, which that people, departing from Egypt, secretly claimed for itself, as it were for a better use, by God’s command—while the Egyptians unknowingly lent them things which they used badly [Exod. 3:22; 12:35]. So all the teachings of the Gentiles and liberal disciplines more suited to the use of truth contain certain moral precepts, and among them some true things are found concerning worship of God himself.

[Note: [Col. 1041D] *Patrologia*, same place, col. 63.]

Likewise, in the same work, concerning philosophers:

> They gave their gold, silver, and clothing to the people of God departing from Egypt, not knowing how the things they gave would be rendered into Christ’s service.

[Note: [Col. 1041D] *Patrologia*, same place.]

This greatest doctor among ecclesiastical writers, then, knew—having turned from formerly pagan philosophy to true wisdom, which is Christ—what he had read concerning God in philosophical writings; and he knew how unworthy it would be for philosophical disciplines also, which have always flourished on earth among God’s greatest gifts, not to acknowledge their own author and the author of all things, or not to serve him to whom all things obey. Nor was he unaware of what is written in Ecclesiasticus:

> A wise man will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients, and will give himself to the prophets. He will preserve the narratives of famous men and enter at once into the subtleties of parables. He will seek out the hidden things of proverbs and converse amid the secrets of parables. [Ecclus. 39:1–3]

Likewise Solomon himself, as we recalled above on Jerome’s testimony, warns us immediately at the beginning of Proverbs to understand sayings of prudence, subtleties of parables, obscure speech, sayings of the wise, and riddles. These, as Jerome says, properly belong to dialecticians and philosophers. Hence later the holy Fathers very greatly commend the study of the liberal arts as highly necessary to sacred Scripture, while utterly forbidding Christians poetic fictions, not only because they are full of falsehood—and “a lying mouth kills the soul” [Wis. 1:11]—but also because, through thoughts of empty tales, they entice the soul toward desires for the shameful things they invent and draw us away from the study of sacred reading.

The testimonies of the saints concerning both matters are readily available to us:

The synod in the time of Pope Eugenius and Louis says:

> It is reported to us that in certain places no masters or concern are found for the study of letters. Therefore let every care and diligence be applied by all bishops, the peoples subject to them, and other places where necessity arises, so that masters and teachers may be appointed who possess studies in letters and liberal arts and teach doctrine, because in these divine commandments are especially manifested and explained.

But concerning poetic fictions, books which some have customarily called “Grammar” because children are accustomed to read them for instruction in grammatical reading, the authority of the saints decreed as follows. Jerome, writing to Pope Damasus concerning the prodigal son:

> The food of demons is the poems of secular poets, the knowledge of rhetoricians, and pompous language.

[Note: [Col. 1042D] *Patrologia*, vol. XXXI, col. 385.]

And, after some intervening material, as though the statement of Exodus came to his mind, “You shall not swear by the name of foreign gods, nor shall it be heard from your mouth” [Exod. 23:13], he says:

> Far be it that “Jupiter Almighty,” “by Hercules,” “by Castor,” and other things more monstrous than divine should sound from a Christian’s mouth. Yet now we see even priests of God, laying aside the Gospels and prophets, read comedies, sing the amorous words of the verses of the *Bucolics*, and keep Virgil; and what is necessity in boys they make for themselves a voluntary crime.

[Note: [Col. 1042D] *Patrologia*, same place, col. 386.]

The same writer, on the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> “Bring up,” says the Apostle, “your children in the discipline and correction of God” [Eph. 6:4]. Let bishops and presbyters who educate their children in secular letters, have them read comedies, and sing shameful writings of love, take heed. They educate them at the Church’s expense, and whatever a poor person, pouring out his whole substance, offered into the treasury for sin, they divert into a gift-basket for the Saturnalia and Minerva, or into household expenses, or filthy prostitutes.

Likewise the same author, in his epistle to the virgin Eustochium:

> What communion has light with darkness? What concord has Christ with Belial? [2 Cor. 6:15] What has Horace to do with the Psalter, Maro with the Gospel, Cicero with the Apostle?

That these remarks are made concerning poetic fictions, not philosophical teachings or studies of the liberal arts, Isidore clearly indicates in *On the Highest Good*, book [lacuna], chapter 13, saying:

> Christians are therefore forbidden to read the fictions of poets because, through the delights of empty tales, they excite the mind toward incentives to lust. For sacrifice is offered to demons not only by offering incense, but also by receiving their sayings too willingly.

Likewise:

> Books of the Gentiles are to be avoided and shunned for love of the sacred Scriptures. The flavor of grammatical art is not to be preferred to simpler letters. For common and simpler writings, pertaining solely to usefulness, are better; the others are worse, because they introduce elegance of expression into the mind. Grammarians are better than heretics. The teaching of grammarians can even contribute to life when taken up for better uses.

From the fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 9:

> A bishop shall not read books of the Gentiles; books of heretics only as necessity and occasion require.

Gregory, to Bishop Desiderius:

> It has reached us that your Fraternity expounds grammar to certain persons. At the time we received this so painfully and rejected it so vehemently that what had previously been said turned into groaning and sorrow, because the praises of Christ cannot be contained in one mouth together with Jupiter’s praises. Consider for yourself how grave and impious it is for a bishop to sing things which do not suitably befit even a religious layman.

Thus Plato himself, when he set forth an institution for organizing the new state, decreed that poets must be expelled from the city. Blessed Augustine recalls this in book II of *The City of God*:

> Or should the palm rather be given to Plato, who, when by reason he formed the conception of what a city ought to be, judged that poets, as enemies of the state, should be driven from the city?

And, after some intervening material:

> Plato himself, of course, was unwilling that poets, whether lying at their own discretion or setting before miserable human beings the worst deeds of the gods as models for imitation, should live at all in a well-ordered city.

It is as though he already openly preached to the saints: “A lying mouth kills the soul” [Wis. 1:11]; and that saying of the Apostle: “Fornication and every impurity must not even be named among you, as befits saints; nor shamefulness, foolish talk, or buffoonery, which is not fitting,” and so forth [Eph. 5:3–4].

What Philosophy thinks of philosophical or poetic Muses, and how much she resents any pupil of hers ever turning aside to those harlots, is carefully expressed at the very entrance of Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*. There, when Philosophy herself comes to console the philosopher and, while the philosopher himself is present, sees the poetic Muses attending him, Philosophy says:

> When she saw the poetic Muses standing by my bed and dictating words to my tears, she was disturbed for a while; then, with eyes aflame with a triple light: “Who,” she said, “permitted these stage-harlots to approach this sick man? They not only offer no remedies to relieve his pains, but actually nourish them with sweet poisons. For these are they who destroy reason’s fruitful harvest with the barren thorns of passions and accustom human minds to sickness rather than set them free. If your blandishments had led away from us some ordinary uninitiated person, as commonly happens, I should bear it less painfully, since I should think that nothing in our work had been harmed in him. But you have led away this man, nourished upon Eleatic and Academic studies. Depart rather into exile, O Sirens, sweet as you are, and leave him to be tended and healed by my Muses.”

Rebuked thus, that chorus cast down its face to the ground more sorrowfully; acknowledging shame by its blush, it sadly left the threshold.

But perhaps you will say that Christians should be forbidden to read not only poets but also liberal arts, since blessed Jerome in his epistle to Eustochium declares that he was severely rebuked and beaten by the Lord for reading philosophers’ books. But then, certainly, grammar too ought not to be read by a Christian, though without its instruction neither sacred Scripture nor any writing can be understood. So too rhetoric, which conveys all the ornaments of eloquence, with which sacred Scripture is especially filled; nor can Scripture’s beauty shine forth unless these are carefully explained.

Why then, you will ask, was the aforesaid doctor so severely scourged and corrected on account of Cicero’s books that, under the solemn attestation of an oath, he was compelled wholly to renounce the reading of secular books? Surely because he applied himself to them not for any usefulness but for the delight of their eloquence, neglecting the study of sacred Scripture, whose uncultivated style, as he himself says, disgusted him.

But I judge that the reading of no art should be forbidden to any religious person, unless perhaps some greater benefit is hindered by it. We know that this should be done in the case of other writings also: that lesser things should be interrupted or entirely omitted for greater things. For when there is no falsehood in a discipline, no obscenity in its words, and some usefulness in its knowledge, who deserves blame for speaking or teaching it, unless the cause mentioned above arises—namely, a better good has been neglected or abandoned?

No one would say that any knowledge is evil, even knowledge concerning evil; it cannot be absent from a just person. This knowledge is not possessed so that he may do evil, but so that he may guard himself against evil foreseen—evil which, unless it were known, he could not avoid, according to Boethius’s testimony. For it is not evil to know how to deceive or commit adultery, but to do these things, because the knowledge of a thing whose action is utterly evil may itself be good; and no one sins by knowing sin, but by committing it.

If any knowledge were evil, then surely it would be evil to know certain things. But then God could not be free from evil, because he knows all things. For in him alone is the fullness of all kinds of knowledge; every kind of knowledge is his gift. Knowledge is the comprehension of all things that exist, and by it he truly distinguishes all things; even things which do not exist stand before him as though present. Therefore, when the gifts of his Spirit are enumerated, he himself is called “the Spirit of knowledge” [Isa. 11:2].

And just as knowledge even of evil is good, being necessary for avoiding evil, so too the power even of evil is clearly good, being necessary for merit. For if we could not sin, we would merit nothing by not sinning; and no reward is due for actions performed under compulsion by one who does not possess free choice. On the contrary, as the prophet says: “He who was able to transgress and did not transgress, to do evil and did not do it—for this reason his good things are established in the Lord” [Ecclus. 31:10–11].

It is therefore clear from these considerations that neither knowledge nor power is evil, however evil their exercises may be, since God both bestows all knowledge and orders all power. He himself says, even of the power of the most unjust Pilate exercised against him: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above.” We therefore approve forms of knowledge, but resist the deceptions of those who misuse them. For, as Tully testifies, those err no moderately who blame knowledge for a human being’s fault. Thus, when teaching in the *Rhetoric* about the criticism of arguments, he says among other things:

> No part of an argument will be suited to the purpose for which it is constructed if a matter is blamed because of a human being’s vice—for example, if someone censures learning because of the vices of some learned person.

I think that none who have been instructed by sacred writings are unaware that, in sacred doctrine, spiritual men have advanced more through the study of knowledge itself than through religious merit; and that the holier anyone was before his conversion, the more powerful he became afterward in his sacred learning. For although the Apostle Paul may not appear greater in merit than Peter, nor the confessor Augustine than Martin, yet each after conversion had a greater grace in doctrine than the other, in proportion as he had formerly possessed greater learning in letters. From this I think especially that even the study of secular letters is commended by divine dispensation, not only because of the usefulness they contain, but because they would appear alien to his gifts if he made no use of them for any benefit.

Yet we know that the Apostle also said, “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1), that is, it produces pride. But precisely from this it is proved to be good: it draws one who is conscious of it toward the evil of pride. For just as there are certain goods which arise only from evil, so there are certain evils which derive their origin from good. Repentance, or satisfaction by amendment, although good things, so accompany an evil deed that they can be born only from it. Conversely, envy and pride, although utterly evil, take their beginning from goods. For no one is diminished by envy of another except because of that other’s goods; and no one is raised up into pride except from goods which he knows himself to possess.

Hence that Lucifer who rose in the morning was so much the more prone to pride as he surpassed the other angelic spirits in the brilliance of wisdom or knowledge. Yet it does not follow that his wisdom or his knowledge of the natures of things, which he had received from God, ought to be called evil; rather, by being proud, he used them badly. So too, whenever anyone is proud of his philosophy or learning, we must not blame knowledge itself because of the vice attached to it. Each thing should be weighed in itself, lest perhaps, acting without discrimination, we incur that prophetic curse: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good, who make light darkness and darkness light” (Isa. 5:20).

Let these statements against those suffice: those who seek consolation for their own ignorance and, when they see us introduce examples or comparisons from philosophical teachings in order to make our meaning clearer, immediately raise an outcry, as though the very natures of things created by God were hostile to sacred faith and divine reasonings. Yet philosophers themselves have received from God the greatest expertise in precisely those natures. Thus, when holy teachers investigate the mysteries of allegory in the very natures of animals or of any other things, they assign these meanings according to the sayings of the philosophers, declaring that this or that is the nature of a particular thing, as writers on natural philosophy have handed down.

God so delights in the created order itself that he often wishes to be signified by the very natures of things which he created rather than expressed by our words, which we have fashioned or devised. He delights more in the likeness of things themselves than in the propriety of our words; and, for the beauty of expression, Scripture prefers to employ the natures of things themselves according to some resemblance in place of words, rather than follow the strict completeness of ordinary speech. Therefore let no one presume to blame me if, for setting forth our proposition, I introduce certain comparisons either from ourselves or from philosophers, by which I may more easily disclose what I wish.

For it is written: “It is right to be taught even by an enemy.” And when we serve understanding, we must take every possible care to do this as far as we can. Hence that counsel of blessed Augustine in Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, where he treats and teaches the methods of Christian teaching:

> The teacher should be concerned not with how eloquently he teaches, but with how plainly. Careful attention sometimes neglects more polished words; hence one author, speaking of this kind of style, said that it possesses a certain careful negligence.

And again:

> What profit is there in correctness of speech if the hearer’s understanding does not follow it? There is no reason whatever for speaking if those for whose understanding we speak do not understand what we say. Therefore the teacher will avoid all words which do not teach.

Again: “It is the mark of an outstanding disposition to love truth in words, not the words themselves.”

### III

What use is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish? Or what harm is a wooden one if it can, when we seek nothing but that what is closed may be opened?

“But,” you say, “we labor in vain if we seek to open either what others have already opened, so that our further labor is unnecessary, or what cannot be opened at all—namely, the ineffable mystery of the Trinity.” Certainly nothing is truer than this. But if it cannot be opened by a human being, what were the holy Fathers doing, who left us so many treatises on the Trinity? If, however, those who treated it were able to teach what they intended and to open what was closed, why was it necessary for one person after another to write, and for a later writer to unlock what the former had already opened?

Whatever position anyone may adopt on these alternatives, I wonder with what face anyone can accuse me, while praising the foresight of others who wrote on these subjects—unless perhaps he says that our present treatise is wholly superfluous because their teachings suffice, because no heresies now spring up that must be opposed, and because no doubts about our faith remain that seem to require arguments for its instruction or defense. Would that this were so.

But, to pass over the innumerable multitude of unbelievers outside the Church—Jews and pagans alike—who would dare profess that all heresies have been suppressed, that there are now no schisms of faith among us, and that there will be no further dissensions? How long will the present Church contain chaff indiscriminately with grain? How long will the enemy, the human being, not cease to sow tares over the Lord’s harvest? Until, of course, at the end of the age, the angels of God, the reapers, gather the tares into bundles and cast them into the fire to burn.

Schismatics cannot fail to exist; heretics cannot be absent; nor will a safe path lie open among scorpions and serpents. Rather, Mother Church, under Christ’s name, will always have many whom she may nurture as Antichrists, for the testing or stirring up of the faithful. Groaning for them, she daily says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:19); and with maternal affection she yearly offers public sacrifices of prayer for them, that they may return. For, the Apostle says, “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 11:19).

We especially expect this to happen in the last times, when the kingdom of Antichrist approaches. According to the sentence of the Lord and of the Apostle, dangers are then evidently ever more threatening and increasing, and, as love grows cold, all evils grow more abundantly. Hence the same Apostle writes to Timothy: “But know this: in the last days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, haughty, proud, blasphemers, without peace, having indeed an appearance of godliness but denying its power” (2 Tim. 1:5). Elsewhere he says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11). And Peter says in the second Epistle: “Knowing this first, that in the last days mockers will come with deception,” and so forth (2 Pet. 3:3). And John says: “Little children, it is the last hour; and as you heard that Antichrist is coming, now many Antichrists have arisen. From this we know that it is the last hour. For they went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:18–19).

Hence it is written also in the Epistle of Jude: “But you, beloved, remember the words foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, who told you that in the last times mockers will come. These are those who separate themselves; and rebuke those who have been judged,” and what follows (Jude 17 ff.). It is as though he openly exhorted us, saying: Take care that you may be able to judge such persons and refute them by arguments, “always ready,” as blessed Peter reminds us, “to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason for the hope and faith that are in you, so that in the matter in which they speak against you, those who slander your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame” (1 Pet. 3:15–16). The Apostle Paul, his fellow apostle, also admonishes: “Let your speech be seasoned with salt in grace, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. 4:6).

Blessed Augustine, carefully considering these apostolic sayings, writes to Count Valerius in *On Marriage and Concupiscence*:

> Although you may have mocked it with a most robust faith, it is nevertheless good that you should also know how to assist by defending what we believe. And the Apostle Peter commanded us to be ready “to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason concerning our faith and hope.” And the Apostle Paul says: “Let your speech be seasoned with salt in grace, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.”

Likewise, in the treatise *On Mercy*, he exhorts us toward matters which we are not yet able sufficiently to grasp by understanding: “Ask by praying, seek by disputing, knock by entreating.” For heretics ought to be restrained more by reason than by force, since, according to the authority of the holy Fathers, even believers, for whom “all things work together for good” (Rom. 8:28), are made more watchful and cautious through their disputes.

Hence Jerome, on Jeremiah, Book XI, says: “Heresy is useful for a time, so that the elect may be made manifest and proved.” Augustine, *Against the Letter of Parmenian*: “If heretics were in the Church, they would nevertheless be in error; but when they are outside, they are of great benefit—not by speaking the truth, which they do not know, but by stirring up carnal Catholics to seek the truth and spiritual Catholics to receive it.”

Let us therefore make use of heretics, not in order to approve their errors, but so that, in defending Catholic teaching against their snares, we may become more vigilant and cautious, even if we cannot call them back to salvation. Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, Book I, chapter 16:

> The holy Church exercises wisdom when it is tested by words; it exercises patience when it is tested by swords. When the teaching of heretical perversity was spread abroad, the Church was exercised; formerly it had flourished only by simple faith. Thus teachers in the faith were multiplied through the occasion of heretics, and through the sharpness of heresies masters have grown up to this day.

Therefore, since holy teachers saw that the disputes or inquiries of heretics were so necessary for the exercise of believers, as has been said, they decreed that heretics should be restrained by reason rather than power, and they especially exhorted us—almost from desire for so great a victory—to the study of sacred learning.

Such is Jerome’s saying to Nepotian: “Learn what you may teach, so that you may exhort in sacred doctrine and refute opponents, always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks a reason concerning the hope within you.” Gregory, to Boniface: “If, as I had heard, your greatness had reflected with anxious purpose upon the life of its soul, it would by no means have asked me by letters to answer concerning its faith, but would have asked in person, so that you might rejoice in our reasoning and we in your belief. For although in all causes, especially in those concerning God, we hasten to bind people more by reason than by authority.”

The same Gregory, to Bishop Dominic: “Although we desire all heretics always to be restrained by Catholic priests with vigor and reason.” The same, in the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 30: “The wise of this world must be admonished differently, and the dull differently. The arguments of reason usually convert the former; examples sometimes convert the latter better. It benefits the former, certainly, to remain connected in their reasonings; for the latter, it is sometimes enough to know the praiseworthy deeds of others.”

Pope Nicholas, in his responses to the Bulgarians, chapter 41:

> Concerning those who refuse to receive the good of Christianity, we can write nothing else to you except that you should convince them toward the faith by necessary admonitions, exhortations, and reason rather than force.

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, Book II:

> Faith is by no means extorted by force, but persuaded by reason and examples. Those from whom it is violently demanded cannot persevere in it—like, as someone says, the young tree whose top, if anyone forcibly bends it down, immediately returns to what it was when released.

Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book XII:

> Those who preach Christ to the world must oppose the irreligious world and its imperfect doctrines by knowledge of omnipotence, according to the Apostle’s saying: “For our weapons are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds of reasoning, destroying every height raised up against the knowledge of God” (2 Cor. 10:4–5). He did not leave the apostles a faith bare and destitute of reason. Although it is most powerful for salvation, nevertheless, unless it is instructed through teaching, it will indeed have a safe retreat for fleeing amid adversities, but it will not retain the steadfast security of standing firm. It will be like a camp for weaker persons after flight, not the fearless strength present in those who hold the camp. Therefore insolent disputations against God must be set in order, the strongholds of deceitful arguments destroyed, and minds raised up to impiety crushed—not by carnal weapons, but spiritual; not by earthly teaching, but heavenly wisdom—so that, by as much as divine and human matters differ, heavenly reason may surpass earthly studies by that much.

How then are those to be heard who deny that faith should be established or defended by arguments? Especially since the saints themselves, reasoning concerning matters of faith, commonly use many arguments from examples or comparisons to refute or restrain opponents. For if, when belief in something is urged, nothing is to be examined by reason—whether it ought to be believed or not—what remains except that we should assent equally to those who preach falsehood and those who preach truth, and put forward the defense of the heretic Faustus? By that defense he attempted to protect himself from the attack of believers and to refute them through the prophet and their own principle.

For, as blessed Augustine recalls in Book I *Against Faustus*, he said:

> This is the feeble confession of faith in Christ: to believe without witness and argument. Surely you yourselves are accustomed to say that nothing should be sought too curiously, because Christian belief is simple and absolute. How then do you now destroy the simplicity of faith by supporting it with judgments and witnesses?

We read that a similar objection was raised by Jews against blessed Sylvester when he pressed them by arguments concerning faith in Christ. Thus it is written: “Rabbi Joasi said: Faith must not be entrusted to human reason, which would persuade us to believe this God, whom you confess as the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

One similar saying of blessed Gregory is cited by those who seek consolation for their ignorance. When they are asked concerning matters of faith to which they cannot adequately respond, they immediately object—namely, what Gregory said in Homily XX on the Gospels while speaking of the resurrection of bodies: “We must know that if a divine operation is comprehended by reason, it is not wonderful; nor does that faith have merit to which human reason supplies proof.”

From this sentence they plainly assert that, lest faith be useless and without merit, nothing pertaining to the mysteries of Catholic faith ought to be investigated by reason; rather, in every matter authority must immediately be believed, however remote it may appear from human reason. But if this is accepted, we shall find Gregory himself contrary to himself in those passages previously collected from his sayings. Indeed, he will be contrary not only to himself but also to almost all holy teachers, who, together with him, exhort us to investigate or render reasons for our faith.

Otherwise, as we have also noted above, the faith of any people, however great a falsehood it may assert, could not be refuted, even if it had fallen into such blindness as to confess that some idol is God and creator of heaven and earth. Whoever adopted this position could immediately reply, when we began to assail him on this point—as the martyrs once did when they reproached pagans for the worship of idolatry—that, according to our own principle, faith ought not to be reasoned about, and that we ought not to attack others concerning that for which we judge that we ourselves ought not to be attacked by others.

For we know that blessed Gregory himself frequently establishes the resurrection against those who doubt it by reasoning from suitable examples and comparisons of things—although above he said of it that faith has no merit where human reason supplies proof. Yet no one could, on the basis of Gregory’s own principle, refute the arguments by which he sought to build people up in faith in the resurrection: on that principle he is said to maintain that faith must by no means be discussed by human arguments, a proposition he himself disproved by his deeds.

Nor did he say that faith ought not to be reasoned about, nor that it has merit before God through human reason. For he introduces not so much the testimony of divine authority as he compels assent by the argument of human reason. It is received not because God said it, but because it is proved to be so. Such faith is therefore distinguished from Abraham’s faith, who “against hope believed in hope,” and attended not to the possibility of nature but to the truthfulness of the promiser.

Yet if the beginnings of our faith do not immediately have merit, it must not for that reason be judged entirely useless: charity, following afterward, obtains for it what it lacked. Many people, when they did not believe what was preached, were compelled to believe by the manifestation of the things themselves and by the greatness of miracles. We know that this occurred also with the Apostle Thomas when he doubted the Lord’s resurrection. So too we see it in Paul’s conversion: when he could not be overcome by argument, he was constrained by the deeds themselves and compelled to faith. And the more vehement he had been before conversion, the stronger his faith afterward proved to be. For one who believes lightly scarcely remains firm in faith; nor will what is done lightly be strengthened by stability.

Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “Whoever believes quickly is light of heart and will suffer loss” (Ecclus. 19:4). A person believes quickly or easily when, indiscriminately and imprudently, he assents to what is said before he examines, by such reasoning as is available to him, what force the thing urged upon him has—whether faith ought to be given to it.

> **[Note: Col. 1051.]** Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, criticizes this, because the passage is not speaking there about faith in God, but about mutual trust.

Jerome carefully considered this point when he commended the zeal and discernment of holy Marcella. In Book I of his *Commentary on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians*, he says:

> I know her ardor, I know her faith, what flame she bears in her breast: she overcomes her sex, forgets humankind, and, with the drumbeat of the divine volumes sounding, crosses the Red Sea of this age. Certainly, while I was at Rome, she never saw me in such haste that she did not ask me something from the Scriptures. For, after the Pythagorean manner, she did not think whatever I answered was necessarily right; nor did authority prevail with her merely because it was prejudged, without reason. Instead, she examined everything and weighed all matters with a keen mind, so that I felt that I had not so much a pupil as a judge.

But now, by contrast, very many seek consolation for their ignorance. When they attempt to teach matters of faith which they cannot sufficiently discuss even so that they may be understood, they especially commend that fervor of faith which believes what is said before understanding it, assents to and receives things before seeing what they are or knowing whether they should be received, or examining them according to one’s capacity.

They especially profess this when matters are preached which pertain to the nature of divinity and to the distinction of the holy Trinity. They assert that these cannot at all be understood in this life, but say that to understand them is eternal life itself, according to that saying of Truth: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). And again: “I will manifest myself to them” (John 14:21).

But certainly understanding or believing is one thing; knowing or manifesting is another. Faith is called an estimation of things not apparent, whereas knowledge is experience of the things themselves through their presence. Blessed Gregory distinguishes these two in Homily 6, Book II on the Gospels:

> It is clear that faith is the proof of those things which cannot appear. For things which are apparent do not have faith, but recognition.

Understanding, properly speaking, is also said of invisible things, according to the distinction between intellectual and visible natures.

Whoever thinks that what is said about the Trinity cannot be understood in this life surely falls into the error of the heretic Montanus. Condemning him, Jerome says in the prologue to his *Commentary on Isaiah*:

> The prophets did not, as Montanus dreams, speak in ecstasy so that they did not know what they were saying, and so that they themselves were ignorant of what they said while instructing others. Rather, in accordance with Solomon speaking in Proverbs, “The wise person understands what he speaks from his heart, and on his lips he will bear knowledge” (Prov. 15:14), they themselves knew what they said.

Again:

> How could the prophets, wisely, after the manner of brute animals, have been ignorant of what they said?

Origen likewise says, while expounding Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: “‘According to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal times,’” and so forth (Rom. 16:23). But one must ask whether I say that it was kept in silence in such a way that no one at all knew it, not even the prophets themselves who announced it. It seems very absurd to me to say that the prophets wrote about divine sacraments in such a way that they did not understand what they were saying, when Scripture says: “The wise person understands what proceeds from his mouth, and bears understanding on his lips” (2 Cor. 12:4). But if they did not understand what they uttered from their own mouth, they were not wise. Therefore, if it is foolish to deny that the prophets were wise, it remains that they understood what they uttered.

Paul says that he heard words which a human being is not permitted to speak—not because he himself was ignorant of what he had heard, but because he was not permitted to disclose to others what had been revealed to him. Thus this sacrament may also seem here to have been said to be kept in silence: the prophets knew it, certainly, but did not reveal it to people, that is, to the multitude; rather, according to God’s command, they concealed it until the time should come and the Word should become flesh.

Indeed, the Apostle commands that whatever is preached should be spoken in such a way that it can be understood. He even orders that preaching should altogether cease if, in matters that must be preached, there is no one able to prophesy—that is, to expound what is said and open its meaning. Hence, exhorting us in the First Epistle to the Corinthians to desire spiritual gifts, he says: “Desire spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy” (1 Cor. 14:1). That is, above the other gifts of the Holy Spirit, desire this especially: that you may enable what is uttered by the tongue—that is, what sounds forth in words—to be seen through understanding and that you may be able to expound it.

Because prophets were formerly called “Seers,” the Apostle here calls prophesying the supplying of the sight of understanding. Continuing at once, he describes how great is the usefulness of prophesying, and how much more excellent it is to prophesy than to speak merely in a tongue—that is, to expound words rather than merely produce them:

> “For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to human beings but to God” (1 Cor. 14:2).

For no one hears—that is, understands. It is this hearing which the Lord demands when he says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 13:9).

Again the Apostle adds concerning the usefulness of prophesying: “But one who prophesies speaks to human beings for edification” (1 Cor. 14:3). And again: “One who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but one who prophesies builds up the Church. Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. For one who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless perhaps he interprets, so that the Church may receive edification. But now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, what benefit will I bring you?” (ibid. 4–6).

He immediately introduces an apt comparison:

> Even lifeless things which give sound, whether flute or harp, unless they make a distinction in their notes, how will it be known what is being played on the flute or harp? For if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare for battle? So also you: unless through the tongue you give intelligible speech, how will what is said be known? For you will be speaking into the air (ibid. 7–9).

That is, you will be uselessly striking only the air outwardly with the tongue, without touching the heart inwardly through understanding. Again: “If I do not know the force of the sound, I shall be a barbarian to the one to whom I speak, and the speaker a barbarian to me. So also you—and everyone who speaks in a tongue—should pray that he may interpret” (ibid. 11–12).

What, I ask, does he mean by “the force of the sound” except its meaning, for the sake of which it was devised? Blessed Augustine also perceived this, as we noted above: “What profit is there in correctness of speech if the hearer’s understanding does not follow it, since there is no reason at all for speaking if those for whose understanding we speak do not understand what we say?”

He also says that understanding of words is so necessary in the Church that, when blessings are pronounced there, “Amen” should not be answered except by those who understand—those, that is, who can discern whether the words are a blessing or a curse: “How,” he says, “will he say ‘Amen’ to your blessing when he does not know what you are saying?” (ibid. 14). And again: “I thank my God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. But in the Church I wish to speak five words with my understanding, that I may instruct others also, rather than ten thousand words in a tongue” (ibid. 18–19).

Immediately exhorting us to the full understanding of sacred words, he says: “Brothers, do not become children in understanding; but be little children in malice, and mature in understanding” (ibid. 20). He does not conceal how much ridicule is deserved by those unable to explain what they preach: “If therefore the whole Church comes together and all speak in tongues, and unlearned persons or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are mad?” (ibid. 23). Therefore, after some remarks about the person who preaches, he adds: “But if there is no interpreter, let him be silent in the Church, and let him speak to himself and to God” (ibid. 28).

It is as though he openly said: Let one who is unable to expound what he says not presume to speak to people; instead, let him turn words into a confession of his faith to God, who does not need exposition, rather than uselessly utter words not understood for the instruction of people.

If it is fitting for those who preach to cease from preaching when they cannot expound what is said, how much more when they do not even understand what they utter, and their whole faith consists more in the mouth than in the heart—although the Apostle says, conversely: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). Whoever does not understand what he says surely does not know what he himself says. He rashly presumes to teach matters which he himself still does not know, and he deserves to be numbered among those to whom Truth reproachfully says: “They are blind guides of the blind” (Matt. 15:14). And the Apostle says: “They do not understand what they are saying or what they affirm” (1 Tim. 1:7).

Even after the revelation of the Gospel, after so many revelations of the holy Fathers, [lacuna] they still have the veil of Moses over their heart and do not yet, with the Apostle, contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face (2 Cor. 3:18). Let those hear this who sit as teachers of sacred Scripture and teach children rather to utter words than to understand them. Nor does the proverb of that wise person which the children have learned check their shamelessness unto salvation: “To read and not understand is to neglect.”

Since they are blind in matters said about God, their error is all the more dangerous because teaching in this matter is more necessary: it is laid down as the foundation of all goods. Unless it is carefully examined, nothing built upon it will bring security. Finally, what could be more ridiculous than if someone wishing to teach another, when asked whether he understands what he says, should deny that he understands what he says or admit that he does not know what he is speaking about?

How much laughter would the apostles have provoked among philosophers and Greeks seeking wisdom when preaching the Son of God, if at the very beginning of their preaching they could have been refuted thus—if those who first had to preach and teach them had themselves confessed that they did not know? Yet let us not suppose this even of the apostles, to whom Truth, promising the Holy Spirit, says: “He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance everything that I have said to you” (John 14:26). Let us hear also how much confidence Truth itself left them in so great a teacher: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). Of him it is elsewhere written: “They could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke” (Acts 6:10).

Therefore, if we have previously discussed any mysteries concerning God, he acts in us here rather than we ourselves; and what is impossible for us is easy for him. Everything which we confess for salvation so depends upon him that no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12:3). Taught by him, therefore, we understand; prompted by him, we discuss what we ourselves could not—the very mysteries of God and of the Trinity.

Blessed Jerome carefully distinguishes this point, professing both that the generation of the Word cannot be discussed by us and that it can be discussed through us. Hence, in his commentary on Ecclesiastes, as we have already recalled, where it is written, “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of men ascends upward, and whether the spirit of the beast descends downward into the earth?” he says that, by adding “who,” Scripture intended to indicate difficulty. For the pronoun “who” in sacred Scripture is used not for what is impossible but for what is difficult, as in: “‘Who shall declare his generation?’—that is, Christ’s” (Isa. 13:8).

The same Jerome, expounding “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ” (Matt. 1:1), says:

> In Isaiah we read: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 13:8). Therefore let us not suppose that the Gospel contradicts the prophet, as though what the latter says is impossible to utter the former begins to narrate. There the generation of divinity is meant; here, that of the incarnation.

Blessed Augustine likewise, professing this very generation of the Word, asserts that, although it is vainly read or expounded by many, it can be understood by many even before it is expounded. When he approached its exposition and had first quoted John’s words, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), he immediately began, as we have already recalled:

> The natural person does not receive this. What then, brothers? Shall we be silent about it? Why then is it read, if it is not to be spoken? Or why is it heard, if it is not to be expounded? But why is it expounded if it is not understood? Therefore, since I do not doubt that there are again among us some who can grasp not only what has been expounded, but understand it even before it is expounded, I shall not defraud those who can grasp it because I fear that it may be superfluous for the ears of those who cannot grasp it.

What wonder is there that faithful Christians, after so many teachings, can understand matters which Paul plainly testifies were understood and known, through God’s revelation, even by reprobate pagans? For he says: “What may be known of God is manifest in them, because God has revealed it to them,” and so forth (Rom. 1:19). And again: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God,” and so forth (ibid. 21).

“But perhaps,” you say, “what then was the benefit of so many treatises on faith by the holy Fathers, if doubts still remain to which no answer has yet been given?” Hear the saying of the Poet:

There is a certain point to which one may advance, if one is not granted to go farther. (Horace, *Epistles* I, epistle 1, verse 32.)

It was enough for them to resolve the questions they heard, settle the doubts of their own time, and leave to posterity an example of applying themselves when similar cases should perhaps arise. You may well say, “if they arise”; weapons are to be taken up when the enemy threatens. I grant that they must then indeed be taken up, but they must beforehand be forged and made ready. What if the enemy were always present? Should we consider it enough to maintain our own peace and not extend it by gaining others? Would that we could at least do that, if we cannot attain this greatest good! But consider also, I beg you, that poetic line:

> …Your enemy has not yet failed you.

I pass over Jews and pagans.

## IV.

I come to heretics, who, the more domestic they are, are the worse, and who do not cease to disturb the Church with civil wars. And, to come to our own times, in which, people say, they have now been so suppressed that there is no longer any need of a foundation of faith: no one, surely, has heard that heretics of old burst forth into so great a madness as that in which certain of our contemporaries have raged. Tanquelmus, a layman, recently in Flanders; Peter, a priest, recently in Provence—to bring forward a few from among many. One of these, namely Tanquelmus, raised himself to such madness that he caused himself to be called and celebrated as the Son of God, and, as is said, caused a temple to be built for himself by the people whom he had deceived. The other had so weakened almost the entire institution of divine, sacred, and ecclesiastical teaching that he compelled many to be rebaptized, judged that the venerable sign of the Lord’s cross ought utterly to be removed, and maintained that the sacrament of the altar ought henceforth in no way to be celebrated. [Col. 1056A–B]

## V.

Nor do we think that the teachers of the divine books, who now especially occupy pestilential chairs around us, ought to be passed over. One of them in France, another in Burgundy, a third in the district of Anjou, a fourth in that of Bourges, hold—and even teach—many things contrary to the catholic faith or to holy teaching. [Col. 1056C]

## VI.

The first of those whom we mentioned asserts that many who lived before Christ’s incarnation will be saved without faith in the one who was to come; that our Lord Jesus Christ was born through the Virgin’s open womb, like other human beings, except that he alone was conceived without male seed. In the very nature of divinity and the distinction of the divine persons, he is found to be so presumptuous an assertor that, because God the Father begot the Son, he professes that God begot himself. Blessed Augustine openly refutes this error—indeed, this heresy—in the first book *On the Trinity*, saying:

> Whoever thinks God to be of such power that he himself begot himself errs all the more, because not only is God not so constituted, but neither is any spiritual or bodily creature; for there is absolutely no thing that begets itself. [Col. 1056D]

## VII.

The second, likewise entangled in just as many errors, establishes in God three properties according to which three persons are distinguished, and three essences distinct both from the persons themselves and from the nature of divinity itself; so that, namely, God’s fatherhood, filiation, or procession are certain things distinct both from the persons themselves and from God himself. He also denies that the Lord Jesus grew in body according to the manner of other human beings, and denies that his body in his mother’s womb or in the cradle had the stature which it afterward had upon the cross. He maintains, moreover, that monks and nuns, even after the public vow of their profession and the bond of blessing or consecration, can contract marriage; and that, although this is a violation of the vow, the union once contracted is nevertheless not to be dissolved, but that they should remain in the marriage and do penance for the transgression. [Col. 1057A]

## VIII.

The third of those mentioned establishes not only the properties of the aforementioned persons as things distinct from God, but also God’s power, justice, mercy, wrath, and the like—things which are predicated of God in accordance with ordinary human speech—as certain things and qualities distinct from him, just as they are in us; so that he establishes in God almost as many distinct things as words are spoken of God. [Col. 1057B]

## IX.

The fourth has burst into such madness that, because things can happen otherwise than God had foreseen, he grants that God can be deceived. Let those attend to this who maintain that nothing further ought to be written concerning faith, when, as they say, a thousand heresies are springing up at this time—as if they had known the consciences and faith of all persons. [Col. 1057C]

## X.

Now let us return to our subject: namely, how, amid so great a unity of the divine substance, three persons can be understood and discussed, so that the understanding may not recoil from the words pronounced. For we profess such unity, simplicity, and identity of the divine substance that, just as it remains wholly free from parts, so too it remains wholly free from accidents; it can in no respect whatever be changed, and nothing can be in it which it itself is not. Therefore the same substance—wholly simple and indivisible—which is the Father is also the Son and the Holy Spirit; and the same whole substance is the Trinity, that is, these three persons together. It must be called indivisible; nor is the essence of the whole Trinity, that is, of the three persons together, greater than that of the individual persons—that is, of all together than of any one of them separately. [Col. 1057D]

Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book VII, chapter 7:

> It is not because God is Trinity that he must be thought threefold; otherwise he would be less in each one than in the three together.

Likewise:

> When we say three persons, one essence, we predicate neither as a genus of species nor as a species of individuals. It may seem possible to say, “three men, one nature”; but three men are more than one man. Yet the essence of Father and Son is not greater than the Father alone or the Son alone.

Likewise:

> One man is not as much as three men together, and two men are something more than one man; but it is not so in God. For the essence of Father and Son is not greater than that of the Father alone or the Son alone; rather, the three persons together are equal to each one.

From the examples of the holy men Augustine and Alypius, addressed to Maximus, physician of Thenita:

> The Trinity, of one and the same nature and substance, is not less in each person than in all, nor greater in all than in each; but in the Father alone, or in the Son alone, it is as great as it is in the Father and Son together, and in the Holy Spirit it is as great as in the Father and Son. [Col. 1058A]

Since, therefore, the essence of the whole Trinity is not greater than that of the individual persons, it is also evident that the Trinity itself, like the individual persons, is indivisible—that is, that it has absolutely no parts in the quantity of its essence. For everything composed of parts is naturally said to be posterior to those parts from which it derives its being. But how can that supreme Trinity, which is the highest principle of all things, be said in any respect to be posterior to anything? [Col. 1058B]

Further, Plato says: “Everything that is joined together by nature is dissoluble.” And blessed Hilary, on Psalm 129:

> Whoever can believe that God is bodily, because man was made in his image, will establish that God is composite. But whatever is composite necessarily was not eternal, because composition has a beginning by which the composite thing remains.

Concerning the sincerity and purity of the divine substance—namely, that it has no accidents whatsoever and no forms, just as it has no parts—Boethius, *On the Trinity*, book I, while affirming its supreme unity, says:
