> Therefore this is truly one, in which there is no number, nothing in it other than what it is; nor can it become a subject, for it is form, and forms cannot be subjects.

Here Boethius calls the divine substance “form,” insofar as it is the foundation of no forms. [Col. 1058C]

Holy Augustine also, establishing the purity of the divine nature, says in book XI of *The City of God*:

> We do not call that nature of the good simple because the Father alone is in it, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone—that is, because this Trinity is merely a name without the substance of persons, as the Sabellians thought. Rather, it is called simple because it is what it has, except that a person is also relatively spoken of in relation to another. For the Father has the Son, yet he himself is not the Son; and the Son has the Father, yet he is not the Father. But in that in which it is spoken of in relation to itself, not to another, it is what it has; thus it is said of itself to have life, and that same life is Christ. Therefore this nature is called simple, because it is not one thing having and another thing which it has, as in other things. For a vessel is not the liquid which it contains; a body is not color; air is not light or heat; nor is a soul wisdom. Hence they can also be deprived of the things which they have and be turned and changed into other states. [Col. 1058D]

The same author, in book VII of the *Confessions*, speaking to God, says:

> You are not compelled unwillingly toward anything, because your will is not greater than your power. Yet it would be greater if you yourself were greater than yourself.

Likewise: “God’s will and power are God.”

Concerning the unchangeability and invariability of the divine substance, of which he himself speaks through the prophet—“He Who Is sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14)—and elsewhere, “I am God and I do not change” (Mal. 3:6), let one who is not content with the teaching of Holy Scripture consult the philosophers themselves. Thus Macrobius, assigning four virtues to God in accordance with Plotinus, says: “His fortitude is that he is always the same and is never changed.” This is what the aforementioned doctor and greatest of Latin philosophers, Boethius, maintains in book III of *The Consolation of Philosophy* in these words: [Col. 1059A]

> O you who govern the world by eternal reason,  
> Creator of earth and heaven, who command time  
> To move from age to age, while yourself remaining stable, you give all things motion!

For everything that is altered, whether through alteration or any change whatsoever, is evidently moved. We call this unchangeability of God his immortality. Hence Augustine, *On the Nature of the Supreme Good*:

> True immortality is that supreme unchangeability which God alone possesses, who cannot be changed at all. [Col. 1059B]

The same author, above:

> Corruptible natures are no longer unchangeable, because there is nothing from which they were made. For every change causes a thing not to be what it was; therefore he alone truly is who is unchangeable.

Since, therefore, there is such unity, simplicity, purity, and identity of the divine substance—that is, no diversity in it of parts, accidents, or forms of any kind, and no change whatever—how can three persons be assigned or understood in it? For where there is only one wholly indivisible substance, there is no multitude of things, no number of things by which we can say “three” or “many.” Rather, the same substance, wholly simple and indivisible, is each person individually and all together—that is, each of the three persons, or, as has been said, the Trinity itself. [Col. 1059C]

Indeed, where there is no multiplicity of things—rather, no multiplicity at all—no plurality and no diversity, how will there be a multitude of persons or any diversity among them? On what ground is one person distinct from another, or even from the Trinity itself, since, as has been said, the substance of the three persons is altogether the same and they are not separated from one another by any diversity of essence, accident, or property of form?

Perhaps it is difficult—indeed impossible—for a human being to explain this, especially for one who strives to satisfy every assertion by human reasons and, when discussing something particular with regard to a property belonging to it, endeavors to confirm it from a multitude of other things. For each thing has something proper through which it differs from all others, and it is not easy to identify its dissimilarity in other things. But the farther the excellence of the divine nature stands removed from the natures which it created, the less do we find fitting likenesses among them by which we may adequately account for it. [Col. 1059D]

The philosophers themselves, professing this nature to be an unknown God, feared to approach an excellence surpassing the thought of all mortals so greatly that they did not dare even define what it is. Plato, that greatest philosopher, as we have mentioned above, scarcely dared to say what it is, knowing only this concerning him: that human beings cannot know what he is like. Hermes likewise says concerning the Son of God: “His name cannot be uttered by the human mouth.” Behold: the one denies that he can be known by humanity; the other denies that he can be explained. [Col. 1060A]

Therefore, when philosophers distinguished the natures of all things, they passed him over altogether—him whom they profess can neither be explained by speech nor conceived by mind—and thus excluded him from the number of things, as though they maintained that he was nothing. For since they place every thing either under substance or under one of the other highest genera, surely, if they had included God among things, they would have counted him either among substances, quantities, or the other categories; yet he is shown to be none of these.

For all things other than substances cannot subsist through themselves unless they are sustained by underlying substances: whiteness, for example, cannot exist except in an underlying body; piety cannot exist except in a soul; nor can any thing belonging to the nine categories exist unless it inheres in underlying substances. Substances, however, can exist or continue in their own nature through themselves, even if all other things are destroyed. Hence substances are called, as it were, “subsistences,” and they are naturally prior to other things which stand by them and do not subsist through themselves. [Col. 1060B]

From this it is clear that God, who is the beginning and unique principle of all things, cannot in any way be included in the number of things which are not substances. Yet according to them God is not placed under substance either, although he preeminently exists through himself and alone has from himself true and unchangeable being, while all things are from him. [Col. 1060C]

Concerning the truth, simplicity, and unchangeability of his substance, Augustine says in *On the Trinity*:

> Let us understand God, if we can, as far as we can: good without quality; great without quantity; creator without need; present without position; containing all things without having a condition; wholly everywhere without place; eternal without time; making changeable things without any change in himself; and suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God in this way, even if he cannot yet discover altogether what God is, nevertheless let him devoutly take care, as far as he can, not to think of him as something which he is not. Yet without doubt he is substance—or, if this is a better word, essence—which the Greeks call οὐσία (*ousia*, “essence”). [Col. 1060D]

That God ought not, even according to the philosophers, be called substance can easily be shown from the writings of those who treated dialectic—namely, the Latin tradition of Porphyry, Aristotle, and Boethius. Porphyry says in the *Isagoge*, which he wrote as an introduction to Aristotle’s *Categories*: “Every substance participates in one species, but in many accidents, both separable and inseparable.” Aristotle also, assigning the distinctive property of substance in the *Categories*, says: “The most distinctive property of substance seems to be that, while it is one and the same in number, it is capable of receiving contraries.” Again, speaking of the same matter: “Therefore it will be distinctive of substance that, being one and the same in number, it is capable of receiving contraries.” [Col. 1061A]

Since all these cannot be fitted to God, whose substance can neither be altered by accidents nor lie under any forms whatsoever, it is clear that the philosophers did not receive him among substances. This is precisely the reason why Plato placed matter (*hylē*, ὕλη), which he conceived as still altogether unformed, between no substance and some substance.

For God is not not-substance, if we attend to the fact that in him there is a nature truly subsisting and unchangeable. Yet again he is not substance, if we follow the customary use of the name “substance,” since he cannot be subject to accidents. Hence God is plainly shown not to be substance in the argument in which Boethius, though a Christian, follows the opinion of philosophers. When treating philosophy and pursuing Themistius and Cicero in his *Topics*, he proves in the fifth book of the *Topics* that whiteness is not a substance, in these words: [Col. 1061B]

> Substance is that which can be subject to all accidents; but whiteness is subject to no accidents. Therefore whiteness is not substance.

Augustine himself openly professes this customary and proper signification of “substance” in book VII of *On the Trinity*, chapters 4 and 5, speaking of God as follows:

> Just as essence is called from “being,” from him who is, so we call substance from subsisting. But it is absurd for substance to be spoken of relatively. For every thing subsists in relation to itself; how much more does God?—if indeed it is fitting to say that he subsists. For this is understood in the case of those things which are subjects for things said to exist in a subject, such as color in a body. [Col. 1061C]

Likewise:

> Changeable things, therefore, are not properly called simple substances.

Likewise:

> It is impious to say that God subsists and subsists to his goodness, while that goodness is not substance—or rather essence—and while God himself is not his goodness, but goodness is in him as in a subject. Hence it is evident that God is called substance improperly, so that by a more customary name essence may be understood, which is truly and properly so called; perhaps God alone ought to be called essence. For he alone truly is because he is unchangeable. And he declared this name to Moses when he said: “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14), and, “Say to them: He Who Is sent me to you” (ibid.). [Col. 1061D]

But whether it is called essence, which is the proper term, or substance, which is improper, each is said of God in relation to himself, not relatively. Hence for God to be is the same as to subsist; and therefore, if the Trinity is one essence, it is also one substance.

Job likewise speaks of this: “For he alone is, and no one can turn aside his thoughts” (Job 23:13).

From these points, then, it is clear that God is properly called substance neither according to the saints nor in any way according to the philosophers. It is therefore evident that the supreme majesty is altogether excluded from the treatment of philosophers who distribute the natures of all things into ten categories; their rules and traditions cannot at all ascend to that supreme and ineffable height. Rather, they are content to investigate the natures of creatures, according to what is written: “He who is from the earth speaks of the earth” (John 3:31). Yet they are not sufficient even to comprehend and examine these by reason. [Col. 1062A]

Solomon, that greatest of the wise, considering this, says: “All things are difficult; a human being cannot explain them in speech. And the deep abyss—who shall discover it?” (Eccles. 1:8). And Wisdom herself says:

> The thoughts of mortals are timid, and our providences uncertain. For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things. We scarcely estimate the things on earth, and we discover with labor the things before our eyes. Who, then, shall investigate the things in heaven? (Wisdom 9:14–16) [Col. 1062B]

That all this speech is especially suited to the condition of creatures appears particularly from that part of speech without which no complete utterance is said to exist: namely, that which is called the verb. For this word signifies time, and began with the world. Thus, if we attend to the meaning of this part of speech, the sense of every construction is enclosed and limited by the boundary of time; that is, it pertains only temporally to those things which we wish to indicate as happening in time, not as subsisting eternally.

Accordingly, when we say that God is prior to the world or exists before times, what true sense can these words have concerning God’s procession and the succession of these things, if, in accordance with their temporal signification, we take them as human expressions? Is he prior to the world in time, or did he exist in past time before time existed? [Col. 1062C]

Therefore, when we transfer any words to the unique nature of divinity, we must confine them to a certain unique signification or usage. And because God exceeds all things, he necessarily exceeds their customary usage.

For according to Boethius and Plato, words must be akin to the things of which they speak. Gregory rightly observes this in the prologue to the *Morals*:

> I consider it extremely unworthy to confine the words of the heavenly oracle beneath the rules of Donatus. [Col. 1062D]

Nor did the great philosophers know how to apply even the proper and customary name “God” to that unique majesty of divinity which cannot be conceived, still less explained. When they call Mars a god and place him under the genus “rational animal,” they understand that name, as we mentioned above, as referring to the world and the heavenly bodies.

What wonder, then, if God, who transcends all things ineffably, also exceeds every utterance of human convention? And since his excellence far surpasses every understanding, while voices were established for the sake of understanding, what wonder if he transcends understanding, who transcends its causes? For a thing can much more easily be conceived than explained. [Col. 1063A]

And what wonder if God himself overturns the rules or examples of philosophers, when he frequently sets them aside in his works? For he does some new things contrary to nature or above nature—that is, beyond what the original constitution of things can accomplish. Does not the healing of blindness overturn that well-known rule of the philosophers stated by Aristotle: “Change does indeed occur from possession to privation, but from privation back to possession it is impossible. For one who has become blind does not see again,” and so forth? Does the Virgin’s childbirth not wholly prejudice that proposition which philosophers frequently introduce as an example of a necessary consequence or argument: “If she gave birth, she had intercourse with a man”? Thus it may also appear what the Apostle says: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1 Cor. 1:20). [Col. 1063B]

But if, in order to preserve the philosophers, you exempt from their disciplines or rules the things done by miracles, or say that in these cases words do not retain their proper signification—so that sight or childbirth occurring by miracle is properly so called—how much more ought this to be granted in the very author of miracles: that the singularity of his excellence possesses something proper which, just as it transcends human thoughts, so also transcends the traditions of human disciplines. The Apostle rightly warns concerning these:

> See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ. (Col. 2:8) [Col. 1063C]

For according to the Lord’s own teaching, as we recalled above, we are compelled to profess from Job’s testimony that he alone properly is—he whom, according to that discipline of secular teachers which distributes the natures of all things into ten categories, is evidently nothing at all. Attend, brothers and verbose friends, to how greatly divine and human traditions, spiritual and animal philosophies, and the disciplines of sacred and secular letters differ from one another. Do not act as rash judges and accuse us when faith has uttered such words, whose meaning is unknown to your disciplines.

For it is certain that every science and the treatment of every art employs its own words, and every teaching delights in its own expressions. Often those who treat the same art take pleasure in varying their words, because, as Cicero testifies, sameness is always in all things the mother of satiety—that is, it produces weariness. Indeed, they vary them so greatly that they often transfer the same word from one signification to another in such a way that, if we follow sameness of word rather than diversity of meanings, we find them contradicting themselves. [Col. 1063D]

How much more, then, ought those who treat the unique and supreme good to have certain unique words, or to bend words toward some special meaning, by which that which is unique is expressed uniquely and that ineffable, incomprehensible reality is not confined within common and vulgar expressions? If we transfer words to the Creator from some likeness among creatures, those are words which human beings established to designate creatures which they were able to understand, when they wished by them to disclose their own understandings. [Col. 1064A]

Since, therefore, human beings devised speech to disclose their own understandings, while they are not sufficient to understand God, they rightly did not dare to utter that ineffable good by a name. Hence no word of human invention seems to retain its proper meaning in God. Rather, everything said of God is wrapped in figurative and parabolic enigmas, and is sought through a likeness introduced from some part, so that we may taste something of the ineffable majesty through belief rather than understanding. Since we find less complete likenesses to introduce for that which is unique, we can give less adequate account of it through likenesses. [Col. 1064B]

Blessed Augustine, carefully observing this, wrote in his book *Against Felicianus the Arian*, when the latter inquired about this very matter:

> **FELICIANUS:** I do not know how one substance is believed when one person is not said to be one. I ask that you clarify what has been said by an easier example.
>
> **AUGUSTINE:** In incomprehensible matters, examples for disputation are not available. Nevertheless, so far as it can be done, I shall not fail you in this respect either. Behold, a man who is a father has a son who is a man. That they are human is common to both; yet it seems proper to one that he is a son, and proper to the other that he is a father.
>
> Again: I call the Father unbegotten and the Son begotten, teaching only that the Father is unbegotten because he did not proceed from another, and the Son begotten because he also exists from himself. [Col. 1064C]

Let us nevertheless approach these matters as best we can, especially in order to refute the importunity of pseudo-dialecticians. We too have touched somewhat upon their disciplines and have advanced so far in their studies that, with the Lord’s help, we are confident that we can satisfy them in this matter by human reasons—the only reasons they desire. For the creator of reason himself also has human reasons by which he can shut the mouths of animal human beings; through Wisdom he admonishes us, saying: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself” (Prov. 26:8). Of Wisdom itself, moreover, the Book of Wisdom says among its other praises: “It knows the subtleties of words and the dispositions of arguments” (Wisdom 8:9). We shall then offer them more probable likenesses if we can draw them from the very arts in which they are occupied and apply them to each objection which they raise. [Col. 1064D]

## XI.

They ask how, while one substance or essence remains altogether in God, there can be a diversity of properties there, according to which the Trinity of persons consists. Or how it can be that, although each person there is God, one person is nevertheless not another, and yet several gods are not to be spoken of, just as several persons are. Finally, they ask what is the generation of the Son from the Father or the procession of the Spirit from both. In order to do this more carefully, we must first set forth in how many ways “the same” and “different” are understood. [Col. 1065A]

## XII.

Each is commonly spoken of in three ways, and perhaps in more. For we speak of something as the same by likeness, the same essentially without number, and the same by property.

It is the same by likeness when Aristotle asserts that the same things, like understandings, exist among all persons; and we say that the same wares are found in this city and that.

Things are the same both in number and essentially when the same essence is both this and that, so that they contain no number of things in themselves and cannot be called several things in number—as in Socrates, “human being” and “animal,” or “human being” and “capable of laughter.” [Col. 1065B]

Things are the same by property or definition when they are not only the same in number, but do not differ by any properties or proper likenesses—for example, “sword” and “blade,” or “white” and “bright.”

Boethius, observing in the first book of the *Topics* that this is the greatest identity according to the proper and explicit being of a thing, says:

> Again, a dispute may arise concerning what is the same—for example, whether the useful is the same as the honorable. But how is this to be joined to definition? For things whose definition is the same are themselves the same; but things whose account of substance is different are themselves different. [Col. 1065C]

“Different” is likewise commonly understood in three ways: essentially, namely in number; by property; or by definition.

We call things essentially different if the same essence which is this is not that, and if the essence of a human being is not contained as a part in that of something else, as a hand and a human being.

They are different also in number when they are so distinct in the whole quantity of their essence that they can be added together in counting, when we say “one,” “two,” “three,” and so forth. This can occur when not only is this not that, but neither it itself nor anything of it belongs to the substance of the other—for example, this human being and that human being, and likewise in the same hand, this finger and that finger.

Things are different by property or definition when, although they can be predicated of one another because they are essentially the same, nevertheless, according to their proper states, the property of one is different from that of the other, and each must be delimited by its own definition, distinct in meaning.

We call those their proper definitions which express their whole being—for example, “bodily substance” for body, “capable of laughter” for what is laughable, or “having whiteness” for what is white. [Col. 1065D]

Boethius, carefully considering the difference of property or definition in the book *On Divisions*, asserts that “rational” and “two-footed,” although they can be the same in number, nevertheless differ, in these words:

> Since there are certain things which differ but ought not to be placed opposite one another in divisions, such as rational and two-footed in animal—for no one says of animals, “some are rational and others have two feet”—therefore, although rational and two-footed differ, they are nevertheless distinguished from one another by no opposition, etc.

The same author, in the first book of the *Topics*, after defining proposition, question, and conclusion, and distinguishing each by its own properties [Col. 1066A], showed that these three are numerically the same, by showing what each required from its own force and nature; nevertheless, he says that they differ according to the properties he had assigned, saying: “A proposition, therefore, is the same as a conclusion in a certain respect, but they differ in the aforesaid manner.” Blessed Gregory also, carefully considering this difference, says in Book XXI of the *Moralia*: “The difference between sin and crime is this: every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime.”

Again Boethius, in the aforementioned book of the *Topics*, as we have already recalled above, teaches, concerning the question “Whether the useful is the same as the honorable,” that it is a matter of definition, saying in what way it is to be classed with definition. For he plainly shows that things having the same definition are themselves the same, while things whose account of substance is different are themselves different; thus whatever differ by their proper definitions, even if they happen to be numerically the same—for example, if one and the same thing is this and that—are nevertheless called different. Porphyry had taught this earlier in his *Isagoge*, saying: “Things whose terms are different are themselves also different.” And when he says: “Of differences, some are those by which we divide genera into species; others are those by which things that are different are specifically determined”—that is, some are divisive of genera, others constitutive of species—how did he call these different from those, when every divisive difference is constitutive, and conversely, except according to the differing property [Col. 1066C] of dividing and constituting? For one thing is required by its being divisive, and another by its being constitutive, although in every respect the divisive and constitutive difference is numerically the same.

Thus, to say that one difference is divisive and another constitutive is as though we said that the divisive is of one property and the constitutive of another, although that which is divisive is altogether the same as that which is constitutive, and conversely. In this way it can readily be assigned in individual things both that one thing remains numerically and essentially one, and that several properties belong to it, according to which things are different in definition, though not in number, and that the same things receive different terms in sense. For example: this man [Col. 1066D] is substance, body, animate, and sentient; he is also rational and mortal—that is, man. Perhaps he is white and curly, and subject to the other accidents which he receives. Although substance is numerically or essentially the same as body, animate being, and so forth, these are nevertheless distinct from one another by their properties, according to which they must be bounded by different definitions. For the property of substance is one thing, that of body another; the status of the remaining predicates is one thing, that of substance another; that of body another, that of the rest another.

Accordingly, since in individual things, while one substance remains, innumerable things can be assigned which are distinct from one another according to their properties [Col. 1067A], what wonder is it if, while one divine essence remains, there are diverse properties in it according to which three persons can be distinguished? For just as, in one man, who is at once substance and body, and each of the other things mentioned above, and perhaps, in different respects, father and son, the property of substance is one, that of body another, that of the others another, and that of father and son another; so too in God, although the same essence is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the property of the Father is one, insofar as he begets; that of the Son another, insofar as he is begotten; that of the Holy Spirit another, insofar as he proceeds. We shall explain these properties more fully.

If anyone perhaps says that what we show concerning the identity of things or the diversity of properties does not sufficiently bear upon the matter we have proposed [Col. 1067B], unless we also show that, in certain things, while one essence remains, several persons are in some way present, let him recognize that no likeness is wholly exact, but that some likeness is introduced in part. Otherwise it would be called identity rather than likeness. Yet, that we may satisfy him even in this, divine grace has provided for us from their own disciplines.

For grammarians too, when they distinguish three persons—namely, the first, which speaks; the second, to which it speaks; and the third, concerning which, as distinct from both, they speak—understand their diversity according to the diversity of their properties. Thus they admit that these three persons belong to the same thing: the same man is first person insofar as he speaks, second insofar as someone speaks to him [Col. 1067C], and third insofar as conversation takes place among some persons concerning him. The first person is, as it were, a beginning, origin, or cause of the others; and again the first and second are causes of the third. For unless there is a first person, namely the one who speaks, how will there be a second, to whom the speaker’s discourse is directed? Or how will there be a third, concerning whom they speak to one another, unless they speak to one another? Therefore, with regard to the very rank or modes of existence, that is rightly called first from which the others have their being; and that second, after the first, from which, together with the first, the third has its being.

XIII.

If anyone wishes to apply this likeness also to the persons of the divine [Col. 1067D] Trinity, he may perhaps fit it appropriately: namely, since both the Son and the Holy Spirit have being from God the Father, and the Holy Spirit has being from the Father and the Son together. According to these modes of existence, blessed Augustine also—as we recalled above long ago—calls the Son second from the Father and names the Holy Spirit third.

Moreover, just as, according to grammarians, person is more easily described disjunctively in this way: “A person is one who speaks, or one to whom one speaks, or one concerning whom one speaks as distinct from oneself”; so the divine persons seem to be more clearly described disjunctively in this way: “A person in [Col. 1068A] that supreme Trinity is God the Father, or his Son, or the Holy Spirit of both.” And just as no grammarian says that the first person is the second or third, since their properties are different, although, as we said, the same thing which is first person is second or third; so in God, although the same essence which is Father is Son and Holy Spirit, no orthodox person says that one person is another.

But if, after grammar, a discipline almost childish, it is pleasing to ascend to philosophical perfection, so that we may take from it some likeness suitable to our purpose, the aid of divine grace will not fail us there either—especially since the Apostle, speaking of the philosophers themselves, declares that “from the creation of the world, his invisible things are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made; his everlasting power also and divinity” (Rom. 1:20). When he says “his invisible things,” that is, God’s invisible things—since even by the very name *spirit* an invisible nature is declared—and uses the plural, I think, as has been said, that the sevenfold Spirit is to be understood, that is, the Holy Spirit, who is sometimes called “the seven spirits” because of the diversity of gifts. By “everlasting power” the Son of God is understood, according to the same Apostle elsewhere: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). But when he says “his invisible things” or “his power,” by saying “his” he indicates the Father himself, whose Spirit and Son are said to be. When he adds “and divinity,” one must likewise supply “are clearly seen by understanding” [Col. 1068C], so that the unity of divinity is assigned in those three persons. But if it is understood as “his divinity,” just as “God’s invisible things” or “his power,” then rightly, when “his divinity” is said—that is, God himself, whose are those invisible things and that power—God the Father is understood.

How philosophers could trace out and discover this distinction of persons in one essence of divinity through a likeness drawn from some worldly creature and from the things in that creature may, I think, readily be shown in those things which they say consist of matter and form, or by analogy with matter and form. For example, bronze [Col. 1068D] is among created things. When an artisan works it and impresses the form of a royal image, he makes a royal seal, which, when occasion requires, is pressed into wax for sealing letters.

> [Note: [Col. 1067] St Bernard wrote against this comparison in Epistle 190.]

In that seal, therefore, the bronze itself from which it is made is its matter; the figure itself of the royal image is its form; and the seal itself is called materialized and formed from these two, by whose fitting together it is composed and perfected. For a seal is nothing but bronze formed in this way. Therefore the bronze which is the matter of the bronze seal, and the seal itself of which it is the matter, are essentially the same; yet they are distinguished in their properties, so that the property of bronze is one thing and that of the bronze seal another. Although they are essentially the same, the seal is bronze from bronze, not bronze from the bronze seal; bronze is the matter of the bronze seal, not the seal the matter of bronze. Nor can bronze in any way be the matter of itself, although it is the matter of the seal which is itself bronze. For bronze is not made from bronze, as the seal is constituted from bronze; and although the matter itself is the same as what is materialized, nevertheless in that seal what is materialized is not matter, nor is matter materialized.

Once a seal has been made from bronze, it is sealable—that is, fit for sealing—even if it is not yet actually sealing. But when it happens that wax is sealed by it, there are already, in the one substance of bronze, three things distinct in property: bronze itself, the sealable, and the sealing. These stand to one another in such a relation that the sealable—that is, the seal—is made from bronze, and the sealing comes to be from bronze together with the sealable. For from the bronze which existed first, the bronze itself was brought forth so as to be sealable; then, so that the bronze which was already sealable might become sealing. Thus, although the essence of bronze, of the sealable, and of the sealing is the same, these three are distinct in property and are joined to one another in such a manner that the sealable has its being from bronze, and the sealing from bronze and the sealable together [Col. 1069B].

If all these things are brought, in fitting proportions, to the doctrine of the divine Trinity, we can readily refute from the teachings of the philosophers the false philosophers who assail us. For as the bronze seal is bronze and is in some manner generated from it, so the Son has being from the substance of God the Father himself and is accordingly said to be begotten from him. For, as we have already shown above, divine power is specially designated by the name Father, just as divine wisdom is signified by the name Son. Divine wisdom is a certain power of God himself, so to speak: namely, that by which he can guard himself against every deception or error, and thus judge truthfully and penetrate by searching, so that he can be deceived or err in nothing.

Divine wisdom, therefore, is that power and faculty of reasoning through which all things are naked and open to his eyes (Heb. 4:13), and no ignorance can belong to him. For just as Aristotle maintains that “healing” or “hard” are said from certain powers, because things themselves are able to resist their adversities, so wisdom is called a power in a certain respect, because deception or ignorance is resisted, and the mind, blinded by error, does not fall in any matter. Thus we call sight a certain power, and conversely blindness an incapacity. The same may properly be said of any knowledge, which is a kind of sight of the mind, and of ignorance.

Since, therefore, wisdom is a power, as has been said, and since a bronze seal is a certain bronze, it is certainly clear that divine wisdom has its being from divine power, by the likeness in which a bronze seal is said to be from bronze [Col. 1070A], which is its matter; or in which species is from genus, the genus being called, as it were, the matter of the species—as animal is of man. For just as the fact that something is a bronze seal necessarily requires that it be bronze, and that it is a man requires that it be an animal, but not conversely; so divine wisdom, which is the power of discerning, requires that it be divine power, but not conversely. For as bronze relates both to a bronze seal and to other things, animal to man and to other things, and divine power to discerning and to acting; and as a bronze seal is said to be of the substance or essence of bronze itself, because to be a bronze seal is to be a certain bronze, and to be man, that is, a rational animal [lacuna], is to be a certain animal; so divine wisdom is said to be of the substance of divine power, because to be wisdom, that is, the power of discerning, is to be a certain power. This is for the Son to be of the substance of the Father, or to be begotten from him.

> [Note: [Col. 1069D] Blessed Bernard, Epistle 190, refutes this passage.]

For philosophers also say that species are, as it were, generated or created from a genus, because, as has been said, they derive their being from it. Boethius, in the *Book of Divisions*, asserts that a genus is divided into species as into certain productions, as it were, proceeding from itself.

Yet when species are said to be created or begotten from a genus, it does not follow that the genus must precede its species in time or in existence, so as to have existed before them. For a genus never exists except through some species of its own; nor was animal ever in any way before it was rational or irrational. Thus certain species exist naturally together with their genera, so that the genus could in no way exist without them, nor they without the genus: for example, quantity and unity, or number and two. Thus divine wisdom, although, as has been said, it has all that it is from divine power—which is for the Son to be begotten from the Father—was nevertheless not preceded by that power, since God could in no way exist without wisdom.

Likewise innumerable things seem to be generated or to have being from others which do not at all precede them in time, as radiance or heat from the sun. Some are accustomed to adduce these as a likeness of the Trinity: namely, that the Son is from the Father as radiance from the sun, and again the Spirit from him as heat from the sun. Radiance rightly seems to pertain to wisdom, which is nevertheless of the soul; and of the wisdom of God, understood as his Son, the Evangelist wrote: “He was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into this world” (John 1:9). The Son himself said: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). And the Apostle says: “The radiance of his glory” (Heb. 1:3). The Holy Spirit, however, who is called God’s love, seems rightly to be understood through heat, since in all such cases love, by which hearts are said to grow warm, is frequently called heat or fire. Of this the Son himself says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it should burn?” (Luke 12:49)—that is, to fill earthly hearts with love rather than fear. And the Psalmist, seeing no one without some gift of divine grace, says: “There is none who hides himself from his heat” (Ps. 18:7).

And I think this comparison from the sun is the one which Plato is recorded, as we recalled above, to have used in expounding the divine Trinity. But because, even according to philosophers, the substance of the sun itself is not its radiance or heat, as the essence of Father and Son is the same; nor does heat come from sun and radiance together, as the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son together; and because heat, which is substantial to fire, seems more to be of its substance and therefore to pertain more to the Son, who is from the very substance of the Father, than to the Spirit—this comparison from the sun perhaps serves less than we might wish for demonstrating our proposition.

Some of our own, perceiving this, and seeking to assign the same essence to the three persons, and to show that as the Son is from the Father, so the Spirit is from both, seem to have devised a more familiar comparison from a spring, a stream, and a pool. For the same water is first a spring and then a stream, and afterward a pool; and as the stream derives being from the spring, so the pool derives being from stream and spring together. They compare the Father to the spring, the Son to the stream, and the Holy Spirit to the pool. To illustrate the incarnation of the Word, they consider the stream in a pipe as the Son in human flesh, as though, when we say “the stream in the pipe,” we said “the Word incarnate” [Col. 1071C].

The foundation of this comparison, unless I am mistaken, Anselm of Canterbury drew from blessed Augustine, writing to Pope Laurence on this very subject, where he introduces a spring and its stream, which have the same substance, as an example of divine generation. There the same substance of begetter and begotten is introduced. But this comparison too seems insufficient for the identity of substance of the three persons, because the same water is not at the same time spring, stream, and pool, but only in succession through time; whereas the essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is the same simultaneously. Indeed, at one time the water of the spring is essentially other than that of the stream or pool. Hence perhaps this comparison rather supports that heresy which confuses the properties of the persons temporally, so as to say that the same person is Father when it wishes, Son or Holy Spirit when it wishes. Foreseeing this, we have introduced above other comparisons, both according to grammarians and according to philosophers, which we believe better suit our purpose—especially that taken from philosophers endowed with greater reason and therefore less remote from the teaching of true philosophy, which is Christ.

XIV, XV.

It remains now, after the generation of the Son, to discuss the procession of the Holy Spirit [Col. 1072A]. In this especially, trusting in him of whom the Lord said, in promising him to the apostles: “He will teach you all things and will bring to your remembrance all things whatsoever I have said to you” (John 14:26), we hope for a grace from him proportionately greater because the subject we desire to discuss pertains more particularly to him.

Spirit is called *spirit* as if from breathing; hence Truth says: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8). And the Prophet, distinguishing the Spirit of the Lord by an appropriate metaphor, calls him “the Spirit of his mouth” (Ps. 32:6). Therefore, by his very name, he is shown to proceed from God the Father or the Son rather than to be begotten. For the benignity itself which is signified by this name is not some power or wisdom in God, since being benign does not consist in being wise or powerful in any respect; rather, his goodness must be understood according to the effect—or, perhaps, the affection—of charity.

> [Note: [Col. 1071] Passage cited by Blessed Bernard, Epistle 190, after the middle.]

But charity, according to Gregory’s testimony, cannot exist with fewer than two. “No one,” he says, “is said to have charity toward himself; rather, he extends love toward another, so that charity may exist.” Therefore, for God to proceed is, as it were, to extend himself toward some thing by an affection of charity, so that he may love it and unite himself to it through love. Accordingly, although both the Son and the Holy Spirit are from the Father—the former begotten, the latter proceeding—generation differs from procession in that he who is begotten is from the very substance of the Father, since wisdom itself, as has been said, has this very being, that it is a certain power; whereas the affection of charity pertains more to the benignity of the mind than to power. Hence the Son is rightly said to be begotten from the Father—that is, to be properly said to be from the very substance of the Father.

Therefore the Nicene Synod, as though explaining this generation of the Son from the Father, says: “We believe also in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father, only-begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light.” I do not deny that some ecclesiastical doctors maintain that the Holy Spirit too is from the substance of the Father—that is, that he is from him in such a way that he too is of one substance with the Father. Yet, properly speaking, we do not say that he is from the substance of the Father; this should be said of the Son alone. The Spirit, although of the same substance as Father and Son—whence the Trinity is proclaimed *homoousios*, that is, “of one substance”—must nevertheless not, if we speak properly, be said to be from the substance of Father or Son, since that would require him to be begotten from Father or Son. Rather, he proceeds from them, which is for God to extend himself by charity toward another. For everyone, in a manner of speaking, proceeds from himself to another through love, since, as has been said, no one is properly said to have charity toward himself or to be benign toward himself, but toward another. Above all, because God has need of no one, an affection of benignity cannot be stirred in him toward himself, so that he might bestow something upon himself from benignity, but only toward creatures, which need the benefits of divine grace not only in order to exist, but in order to exist well.

In what way, therefore, is God said to go out from himself toward creatures through an affection or effect of benignity, when his being benign, or acting kindly from charity, is said according to the affection or effect which he has in creatures? He would remain in himself through benignity if he could be benign to himself, exercising some beneficence in himself and bestowing some benefit upon himself. But the Spirit has procession from Father and Son together because the good affection or effect of willing, doing, or disposing something proceeds from his power and wisdom. For God wills something else and does it because he can fulfill it and can accomplish it skillfully. If he could not, he would will it in vain, because it would lack efficacy; and if he did not know how to accomplish it skillfully, it would not have an excellent effect. Some persons happen to will what they are unable to fulfill, or what, even if they can do it, they do not know how to accomplish as they ought; their will is made irrational both by their incapacity and by their ignorance. Therefore, so that the good will of God regarding whatever is to be done or ordered may be shown wholly rational according to the foregoing account, the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from Father and Son, as stated above.

Thus, as a bronze seal has being from bronze, and again the sealing has being from bronze together with the seal—that is, the sealable—so the Son has being from the Father alone, and the Holy Spirit from Father and Son, as we have explained. And as the seal consists in the form of the image impressed upon it, so the Son alone is said to be in the form of God and is called “the figure of his substance,” or the very image of the Father—that is, his expressed likeness—because the Son is united to the Father by so great a kinship, so to speak, that he is not merely of one substance with the Father, but also, as stated, from the very substance of the Father. Hilary perhaps had regard to this likeness of bronze and the bronze seal, as of the unformed and formed, when, as we recalled above, he said that the Son was formed from the Father: that is, that he has his being from the Father in the way in which a formed thing is said to be from the very substance of its matter [Col. 1073D]. Yet we do not admit that there is matter or something materialized in God in any manner, but only in creatures or mutable things capable of receiving accidents.

Therefore, just as the sealing, precisely in being sealing, proceeds into another softer thing into which it is impressed, so as to impart to it the form of that image which was already in its own substance; so the Holy Spirit, poured into us through the distribution of his gifts, reforms in us the image of God that has been effaced, so that, according to the Apostle, we may become “conformed to the image of the Son of God” (Rom. 8:29), that is, to Christ, and may follow the footsteps of him “who did no sin” (1 Pet. 2:21–22), passing from the old man into the new.

But as bronze, seal, and sealing are distinct in their properties according to the modes of existence which they have in relation to one another, so that none of them shares the property of another, so too are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For example, the bronze seal is materialized from bronze as from matter; bronze is the matter of the bronze seal; and the bronze seal is materialized from bronze. These properties of bronze and the bronze seal are so interwoven that neither is bronze materialized from bronze, nor is their seal matter of bronze, although the same thing is that which is the matter of the bronze seal and that which is materialized from bronze—that is, bronze itself and the bronze seal. So it is with the divine persons: insofar as divine wisdom, as we have said, has being from divine power, that power is called Father of this wisdom, and this wisdom Son of that power; and in God, to say “Father” is equivalent to saying “wisdom begotten from the Father.”

If, therefore, we say that the Son is Father, it is as though we said that the wisdom of God the Father is the begetter of the Father’s wisdom—that is, of itself—so that divine wisdom itself is begotten from itself and has being from itself. Similarly, if we say that the Father is Son—namely, of himself—it is as though we said that divine power begot itself. For although bronze and bronze seal are essentially the same, it does not follow that, because the bronze seal is from bronze, bronze is said to be from itself; nor that, because the seal is subsequent from bronze, it is said to be subsequent to itself. For the pronoun “of itself” can properly establish a relation only where a thing is the same not merely in essence but also in property. Bronze and bronze seal are different in property; hence it does not follow that, if the bronze seal is from bronze, something else is therefore from itself.

Likewise, although Father and Son are the same, because they differ from one another in their properties, as has been said, it in no way follows that, if the Son is begotten from the Father or has being from the Father, the Son should be granted to be begotten from himself or to have being from himself. Blessed Augustine, carefully considering this, confirms it in Book I of *On the Trinity* in these words: “Whoever thinks that God is of such power that he has begotten himself errs all the more, because not only is God not so, but neither is a spiritual creature nor a bodily one. For there is no thing at all which begets itself.”

Thus, in bronze and the bronze seal, their absolute names are joined to one another predicatively when we show that they have the same substance, as when we say, “Bronze is a bronze seal,” or conversely, and the like. Yet their relative names, which predicate their properties according to which this has being from that, cannot be joined to one another: for example, “matter of the bronze seal” and “materialized from bronze.” No one says, “The matter of the bronze seal is matter from bronze,” or “What is materialized from bronze is the matter of the bronze seal.” The same applies in the divine persons. For the Almighty himself is wise or benign, and conversely; but the Father himself is not the Son, namely, of himself, nor is he the Holy Spirit, since the Father does not proceed from the Father—that is, from himself—or from the Son, as the Spirit proceeds from Father or Son. For just as the good affection of God proceeds, as stated, from his power and wisdom, so power itself or wisdom cannot proceed from themselves; for that would make Father or Son the Holy Spirit.

The Greeks, however, profess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, not also from the Son, because Truth, speaking in the Gospel which contains the doctrine of the Spirit’s procession in full, mentions the Father alone, saying: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26). They do not argue vehemently against our saying that he proceeds also from the Son, but assert that we are liable to anathema, because in the principal councils held among them their creeds were established with appended anathemas in such a manner that no one may say or preach anything else concerning faith in the Trinity than what is contained there. In those creeds, since only the Father is mentioned in speaking of the procession of the Spirit, they say: “Whoever adds the Son incurs anathema.”

To heighten the charge of our impudence, they also add as testimony to the condemnation of our faith that, according to the tradition of the aforesaid councils, Leo III left a transcription at Rome on a silver tablet for posterity, “for the love,” as he himself says, “and safeguarding of the orthodox faith.” In that creed he too mentions only the Father in speaking of the procession of the Spirit, in these words: “And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son,” etc.

Blessed Gregory carefully makes clear how greatly those principal councils ought to be revered. He professes that he receives and venerates them as the four Gospels, and therefore permits nothing to be added to or subtracted from their words any more than from the Gospel words. Thus, writing to Constantine, bishop of Milan, concerning one of them, he says: “We confess, with Truth as author and conscience as witness, that we preserve the faith of the Chalcedonian creed wholly inviolate, and dare neither add anything to nor subtract anything from its definition. But if anyone desires to presume against it—against the faith, that is, of the same kind—to hold a view more or less, we anathematize him without any delay and decree that he is alien from the bosom of mother Church.”

But surely, when it is forbidden that anyone teach or preach the Catholic faith otherwise than as it is contained in the aforesaid councils, I think that “otherwise” means not according to a diversity of words but according to a diversity of faith: as if it said “otherwise,” that is, in a contrary way, not with a different sound of words. For we say in Latin what they say in Greek. Thus, as “different” is said in the sense of “opposite,” so “in a different way,” that is, “otherwise,” is not inappropriately understood as an opposite way. Otherwise, since each of those councils composed and established its own creed, and the creeds differ from one another in words [Col. 1076A], and perhaps in certain propositions, since one sometimes contains what another does not have, surely a person who, having received one creed, recited or accepted the others in confessing them would be liable to anathema.

For the same reason we should be bound by the addition made in the supplement to the Gospel, since Moses says in Deuteronomy: “What I command you, that alone you shall do for the Lord; add nothing to it and take nothing away” (Deut. 12:32). Thus he prohibited the addition of anything contrary, not the supplying of what was lacking to perfection. Yet it may also be understood as an absolute prohibition against a person’s supplying anything from himself in words. A person would then add something else from himself if he presumed it from his own judgment rather than from the inspiration of the Spirit, concerning whom it is written: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you” (Matt. 10:20).

[Col. 1076B] We also proclaim many things concerning the miracles of the saints and concerning what the holy Fathers wrote after the apostles. Yet the Apostle, writing to the Galatians, says: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel other than that which we have preached to you, let him be anathema. As I foretold, so now I say again: if anyone should preach to you a gospel other than that which you have received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:8–9).

But when the Greeks object that Gospel tradition is sufficient for the whole teaching of faith and that nothing further ought to be added beyond what is contained in the Gospel’s words, they pronounce judgment even upon themselves. For when they say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone—for the Gospel, when it says that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, does not add “alone,” [Col. 1076C] as they themselves add it, but says only “from the Father”—we ask and inquire of them, since they believe that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, whether they believe that he proceeds from the Father alone, or not.

If they do, and if this faith is true, then it is certainly the case that he proceeds from the Father alone; and it is not inappropriate that what they think on this matter should be taught or confessed as salutary, and that it is dangerous not to believe—especially since the Apostle says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10). But if they do not believe that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, while not doubting that he proceeds from the Father, they must grant that he proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, or from another source. [Col. 1076D] And what must necessarily be believed ought salutarily to be confessed, just as do all the other things pertaining to the catholic faith.

Nor is a right confession impeded if certain words of confession are not found in the canonical Scriptures. For this is chiefly why the creeds of the councils were added to those Scriptures: to teach or expound matters not openly contained there. Who, indeed, recalls that the Trinity, or three persons in it coeternal and coequal—each of whom is God—are spoken of in those Scriptures? Or that he is called Pontius Pilate; or that Christ’s soul descended to the underworld; or certain other things not contained in canonical language? Indeed, many things necessary to faith were added after the Gospel by apostles or apostolic men, which are not at all demonstrated from the words of the Gospel—such as the perpetual preservation of the Lord’s Mother’s virginity even after giving birth, [Col. 1077A] and perhaps many other things.

Having answered the Greeks’ objection concerning the Spirit, I am also pleased to bring forward testimony from their own teachers, by which they teach that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well.

Athanasius, in the Creed of Faith, says: “The Holy Spirit, from the Father and the Son, not made, not created, nor begotten, but proceeding.” Since he first stated that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, and then added “proceeding,” he plainly taught that he proceeds from both, just as he reported that he is from both—especially since the Spirit has no other manner of being from the Father except by proceeding.

Didymus also, their greatest teacher, plainly professes in his book *On the Holy Spirit* that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well, saying: “The Savior, who is also Truth, says: ‘For he will not speak from himself’ (John 16:13). ‘He will speak,’ that is, not without me, not without the will of me and the Father; because he is inseparable from my will and the Father’s; because he is not from himself, but is from the Father and from me. For this very fact that he subsists and speaks is from the Father and from me. ‘I speak the truth’ [Col. 1077B] (ibid., 7), that is, I inspire what I speak. For to say ‘Spirit of truth,’ and ‘to speak’ in the Trinity, is not to be understood according to our customary usage, but in accordance with the manner of incorporeal natures, and especially of the Trinity, by which it impresses its will upon the hearts of believers.”

Likewise: “The Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom, cannot hear from the Son speaking things which he does not know, since he is himself what proceeds from the Son: that is, God proceeding from God, the Spirit of truth proceeding from Truth, the Comforter remaining from the Comforter.”

The Creed of the Council of Ephesus—which is also known to have belonged to the Greeks—plainly determines what that Truth is from whom he proceeds in these words: “Although in his substance he is the Spirit of the Son, and in person is understood as a property, insofar as he is Spirit and not Son, yet he is not alien from him; for he is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is the Truth.”

Likewise Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, in his eighth letter addressed to Nestorius, which begins, “To the most reverend and most beloved lord,” etc., says: “Although the Spirit is distinct in substance, or at any rate exists … through himself insofar as he is Spirit and not Son, [Col. 1077D] nevertheless he is not alien from him. For he is called the Spirit of truth and flows forth from him, just as he does from God the Father.”

John Chrysostom, Homily 27, *On the Exposition of the Creed*, which begins, “The universal Church rejoices”: “This is the Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, who distributes his own gifts as he wills.”

Likewise, Homily 28, in another exposition of that creed, which begins, “Upon the structure of the whole Church”: “Therefore it must be believed that the Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and to the Son.” Likewise: “We say that this Holy Spirit is coequal with the Father and the Son, and proceeds from the Father and the Son. Believe this, lest evil conversations corrupt your good morals.” Likewise: “See everywhere the mystery of the Trinity: behold, we also believe in the Holy Spirit, the Spirit who proceeds from the Father and the Son and is joined by love.”

[Col. 1078A] Augustine, in *Questions Addressed to Orosius*, book 11: “Our Lord Christ, after his resurrection, in order to show that the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself as from the Father, breathed upon his disciples and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20:22).

The same, book IV of *On the Trinity*: “Nor can we say that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Son. For it is not without reason that the same Spirit is called the Spirit of both Father and Son; nor do I see what else he intended to signify when, breathing upon them, he said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’ That bodily breath was not the substance of the Holy Spirit, but a demonstration that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well.”

Likewise in *On the Trinity*: “Just as we properly call the only Word of God by the name ‘Wisdom,’ although both the Holy Spirit and the Father are universally Wisdom itself, so the Spirit is properly called by the name ‘Love,’ although both Father and Son are universally Love. That he proceeds from both is taught in this way: for the Son himself says, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ and he breathed upon his disciples and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit,’ in order to show that he proceeds from himself as well. And he is the power which went out from him and healed all, as is read in the Gospel” (Luke 6:19).

For since the Spirit is called, as it were, a breath because of breathing, and since he is equally called the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son, who can rightly deny that he proceeds from both, from whom he has being as the Spirit of both, and breathes? Yet we do not deny that he proceeds properly, or principally, from the Father.

Thus Jerome, explaining the definition of catholic faith and the Nicene Creed, says: “We also believe in [Col. 1078C] the Holy Spirit, who properly proceeds from the Father.” Likewise: “We find in Scripture that the Holy Spirit is true God and is properly from the Father.” And again: “The Spirit also properly and truly proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

First, therefore, understand that the Holy Spirit is properly from the Father, as Scripture says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32:6), “and by his Spirit all their power” (John 15:26). And the Savior says: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father.”

And blessed Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XV, chapter 18: “It is not without reason that in this Trinity only the Son is called the Word of God, and only the Holy Spirit the gift of God. Nor is anyone except God the Father the one from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds principally.”

The same, *Sermons on the Words of the Lord*, sermon 9: “The Holy Spirit proceeds principally from him from whom the Son was born. I added ‘principally’ because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son. But the Father gave this to him not when he already existed, though did not yet possess it; rather, whatever he gave to the only-begotten Word, he gave by begetting. Thus he begot him so that the common good might proceed from him also.”

It is as though Augustine plainly determined by these words that the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father and not principally from the Son, because he proceeds from the Father as from the first source: the Father does not possess him from another, but from himself, just as he is from himself—that is, not from another. But since the Son is not from himself, but from the Father, he also has the Spirit from the Father, from whom he has his own being through generation.

[Col. 1079A] But what does it mean when it is said that the Spirit proceeds properly from the Father? Is “properly” said there in the same sense as “principally” here? Perhaps it could seem to be said in the same way, were it not added there that the Son too was properly born from the Father, just as the Spirit is said properly to be from the Father. For it is said in the same passage: “The Son was not born from himself, but was properly born from the Father: not in time, but always; not from elsewhere, but from one substance; not from another’s substance, but from his own proper substance.”

But if “properly” is taken in the same way of both Son and Holy Spirit—so that the Son is said properly to be born from the Father and the Spirit properly to proceed from the Father—and if “properly” means the same as “principally,” how shall we say that the Son is principally born from the Father, when he was born from him alone? Unless perhaps, because it was immediately added there, “not in time,” this was said with reference to the Son’s temporal generation from his mother: namely, that the eternal generation is principal and first, and by it he does not depart from equality with the Father; whereas the other is, as it were, later and temporal, according to which the Son himself is called less than the Father.

[Col. 1079B] We may also say that the Son is properly born or begotten from the Father because he is his natural, not adoptive, Son—as is immediately specified when it is added, “not from elsewhere, but from his own substance.” Moreover, in the philosophical sense in which all things are called born or generated that have being from another, the Son alone is properly born from the Father, because he alone is from the Father’s very substance by being born.

But the Holy Spirit is properly said to proceed from the Father alone because he proceeds from him as from the highest principle, which is not itself from another. For something is properly said to proceed from the place whence it first began to come and move—just as a lake is said to proceed from a spring, not from a stream, though it proceeds through the stream, into which the water of that lake, emerging from the spring, passes and through which it arrives at the pool.

So too the Holy Spirit is said properly to proceed from the Father, as from the supreme origin which is not from elsewhere; and from the Father into the Son, as into a stream, because the Son has from the Father whatever he has, from whom he also has the very fact that he is; and through the Son he comes at last to us, as to the pool of this [Col. 1079D] age. For he who does and orders all things in wisdom grants, in that same wisdom, the Spirit as the distributor of his gifts—not without foresight or consideration.

Hence blessed Hilary declares that the Spirit proceeds or is from the Father through the Son, rather than from the Father and the Son, just as he declares that the Spirit is sent through the Son. Thus, speaking to God the Father concerning the Holy Spirit and the Son in book XII of *On the Trinity*, he says: “In your Holy Spirit, who proceeds from you and is sent through him.” Likewise: “Your Holy Spirit is from you through him.” Likewise: “May I merit to worship your Son together with you, and your Holy Spirit, who is from you through your only-begotten Son.”

And perhaps if the Greeks understand that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone in this way—namely, that he is from him as from the highest source, which is not itself from another—there is no disagreement in doctrine, but only a diversity of words. For it is certain that only the person of the Father ought to be proclaimed supreme in this manner, and that the Spirit is from him as he is from the Son, since he is called the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son.

But some are troubled because we say that the Son is from the Father through generation, while the Spirit is from the Father and the Son through procession. Yet that the Father is not therefore prior in existence to the Son, nor the Father and Son prior to the Holy Spirit, can be refuted from the analogy of many examples. For the substance of the sun is both radiant and illuminating—that is, capable of illuminating something; and although radiance is from the sun and the capacity for illumination is from the sun together with radiance, nevertheless none of these three has preceded another in existence.

## XVI

But if anyone examines more deeply that philosophical consideration of Platonic reasoning which treats God the maker by a certain analogy with a careful craftsman or artisan—one who first considers and deliberates what he is to make, lest he compose anything unsuitably, and forms each thing first by reason and then by workmanship—then Plato accordingly considers in the divine mind the universal and exemplary forms, which he calls *ideas*, and which divine providence afterwards worked out as though according to the model of the supreme craftsman. Thus the Holy Spirit rightly proceeds from the Son as well, or through the Son, since all God’s works are administered through the reason of Wisdom, [Col. 1080C] and the conception of the divine mind thus in some manner comes forth into effect through operation.

But effects belong to the Spirit, since they arise from the goodness of the Creator, because the Spirit himself is goodness. Let us therefore say that the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well, when the plan of divine providence is brought to the effect of beneficence, and when that which God foresaw from eternity as to be done, he does in time when he wills.

Priscian carefully explains this conception—by which the mind’s conception emerges into effect through operation—in the first book of his *Constructiones*, saying that the general and particular forms of things existed intellectually in the divine mind before they emerged into bodies, that is, into effects through operation. This means: God foresaw what and how he would act before he completed it in work. As though he said: “He did nothing without prior thought or without discrimination.”

## XVII

Macrobius also plainly declares that the soul of the world itself, which we take to signify the Holy Spirit, exists especially from *Nous* (Νοῦς), that is, the Son. For he openly professes that it was created or born from *Nous*, just as *Nous* itself is from God the Father. Thus, beginning generally from the origin of the soul, he says:

> “God, who is and is called the first cause, is the ruler and origin of all things that are and that seem to be. By the fruitfulness of his overflowing majesty, he created Mind from himself. This Mind, which is called *Nous* (Νοῦς), looks upon the Father and preserves the full likeness of its author. But it creates the soul from itself, looking toward lower things.”

Again: “The soul looks upon the Father, and gradually, turning its gaze back toward the construction of bodies, though itself incorporeal, it degenerates.”

[Col. 1081A] Here Macrobius uses “created” or “born” improperly, as we established in the first book, since he calls both Mind itself and the soul itself created. He calls Mind created from God—that is, the Son from the Father—and the soul created from Mind—that is, the Spirit from the Son. He also indicates that both are born, since he assigns each a father: God to Mind, and again Mind itself to the soul.

Thus “to be created” or “to be born” means to be from something, so that his statement that one thing is born or created from another is as though he simply said that one thing is from another. For it is sufficient for the philosopher, in order to show that the soul is from both Father and Son, to mention the Son alone here. Since the Son is from the Father himself and the Spirit—that is, the soul itself—is said to be from the Son, it is clearly evident that the soul is also from the Father. For the philosopher, cited above, also asserts that the soul itself is called by the wise both “God” and *Nous*.

When he says that Mind is from the fruitfulness of majesty, this is as though he said that Wisdom is born from omnipotence itself; for majesty and reverence are properly attributed to power. When he says that Mind, looking upon the Father, preserves the likeness of its author, I think he means expressly that the Son, in every respect in which he is like the Father, is wholly equal to him. For he is powerful as the Father is powerful, and as good as the Father is good. Thus in all other respects in which he has likeness to the Father, he also has equality; but he does not have likeness to the Father in all respects, since he alone is begotten and the Father is begetter. This concerns the distinction of persons according to their properties.

According to us, too, who believe that the Son alone was incarnate, we shall say that in this one respect the Son is less than the Father, not equal to him. *Nous*, looking toward lower things, creates the soul because the Holy Spirit, who is from the Son—or every soul deriving its origin from its Creator—is what it is as a soul, that is, the life of created things, by the regard which it has toward its Creator: that is, through the benefit of divine Wisdom disposing all things, so that the divine benefit is understood in that regard toward God.

[Col. 1081D] For “soul” (*anima*) is named from giving life (*animare*), that is, enlivening. As we distinguished in the first book, the Holy Spirit is, as it were, a soul—that is, the soul of our souls; and our souls are, as it were, certain bodies of his, enlivened by the gifts of his grace.

And it is certain that he imparts animal life to us. Macrobius says that the soul is clothed in its Father—that is, in *Nous*—by that faculty through which it looks, namely reason; because through the reason which they possess, souls hold the greatest likeness to divine Wisdom, since reason is especially attributable to wisdom. The soul gradually looks toward bodies because, in comparison with the fullness of that supreme good, whatever we possess is slight, however great the gifts of virtues which we have received from him.

We may also understand “gradually” to mean that, through stages and at intervals of time, the mind advances its faithful spirits to the greatest things, and does not confer its gifts all at once. The soul is said to degenerate in the very effect of its operation, from which it is called soul, because what it does is not eternal but temporal. By this, if I am not mistaken, it is easy to resolve the question why Plato wished the world-soul to have begun and not to be coeternal with God and Mind.

For since he calls the Holy Spirit “soul” rather than “spirit,” as though from enlivening us by the gifts of grace through the growth of virtues, that Spirit was not always soul—that is, life-giving. Since created things did not yet exist, to which he might distribute his gifts, he did not exercise the distribution of his goods upon them.

[Col. 1082B] Therefore, just as we call the Holy Spirit—who is utterly simple in himself—yet manifold, and call him the seven spirits according to the diversity of his gifts, so the philosopher held that the same Spirit, who subsists eternally in his proper essence, began with respect to his effects, because of which he called him soul rather than spirit. For “spirit” is the name of a nature; “soul,” however, is the name of an office, namely that of giving life.

Likewise we profess that the heavenly spirits are always spirits but not always angels, because “angel” is the name of an office, not of a nature; and we proclaim that our Lord Jesus Christ began according to his humanity but is eternal according to his divinity. So too we should say that the Holy Spirit is eternal according to the substance of his essence, but began according to his effects—that is, rather, that the effects began, not he himself.

And I judge this to be the philosopher’s meaning under the figure of the soul: that he describes it as a creature, that is, as having begun, and as temporal rather than eternal. Accordingly Macrobius would not have shrunk from presenting both God and *Nous* as belonging to the soul. Let Plato, then, call the Holy Spirit soul according to the effect of works. But let us call him Spirit according to the natural disposition of his goodness, which he possessed from eternity in such a way that he fulfilled it in action when he foresaw that it was to be fulfilled.

Let him say that the soul began according to effects; but let us say that the Spirit abides eternally in the disposition of his goodness. Let him say that the soul began; let us say that the Spirit is altogether eternal. Let the procession of the Spirit be eternal according to disposition, because he so willed from eternity. Let the procession of the soul be temporal according to effect. We have learned that the holy Fathers distinguish both processions of the Spirit: that according to efficacy and that according to effect.
