Bede, in his homily for the first Sunday after the Ascension, speaks of the procession of efficacy in this way: “When the grace of the Spirit is given to human beings, the Spirit is indeed sent by the Father and sent also by the Son; he proceeds from the Father and proceeds also from the Son, because his very sending is procession, since he proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

[Col. 1083A] Augustine himself carefully distinguishes both modes of procession when he says that the Spirit proceeds both insofar as he is given and insofar as he is able to be given. Thus in book V of *On the Trinity*, when he came to the procession of the Spirit, he says: “He proceeds not as begotten, but as given. But what has been given is referred both to him who gave and to those to whom he gave. But if he does not proceed except when he is given, then he certainly would not proceed before there was someone to whom he might be given. For a gift may exist before it is given, but it cannot in any way be called bestowed unless it has been given.”

What wonder, then, if we say that the Spirit proceeds in two ways, if in one mode of procession he is called “Spirit” by us and in the other is called “soul” by philosophers? The former belongs to the Spirit eternally, the latter temporally. Hence immediately in the same work he adds:

“Nor should it disturb us that the Spirit is coeternal with the Father and the Son. Nevertheless, something is said of him in time, as, for example, that he is bestowed; for the Spirit is eternally a gift, but temporally bestowed. For even the Lord is not called Lord except when he begins to have a servant; and this designation too is relative and belongs to God in time. For the creature to whom he is Lord is not eternal.”

Likewise: “Behold, he has ‘Lord’ not eternally, lest we be compelled also to say that the creature is eternal; for he would not rule eternally unless that creature also served eternally.”

[Col. 1083B] In the preceding chapter of the same work, Augustine also plainly calls the Spirit “Spirit” according to effects, when he assigns him a beginning. He says: “What has been given is referred both to him who gave and to those to whom he gave. Thus the Holy Spirit is called both the Spirit of God, who gave, and our Spirit, who receive. Hence it is written of John that ‘he will come in the spirit of Elijah’” (Luke 1:17).

This must also be understood of Moses, when the Lord says to him: “I shall take from your spirit and give to them” (Num. 11:17), that is, “from the Holy Spirit whom I gave you.” “Therefore, if what is given has as its principle the one from whom it is given, because he did not receive from elsewhere what proceeds from him, we must confess that the Father and the Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit—yet not two principles, but one principle.”

It is clear, therefore, that Augustine here understands “Spirit” according to effects when he says “given,” rather than according to the natural disposition of his goodness [Col. 1083D] or beneficence. Hence according to effects the Father and Son are rightly said to be prior to the Spirit and, as it were, his principle, because the effect of grace descends from power moderated by wisdom. The Spirit is called so here on this account; and power and wisdom must first exist, so that something else may afterwards be brought into effect.

Thus for the Father and Son to be the principle of the Holy Spirit means, as though we said, that the Spirit proceeds from both through effect: that is, that he is brought to accomplishment by God’s power moderating his reason. And if anyone takes the name “Spirit” in this way, namely according to the effects of his grace, the Spirit is not rightly called eternal—just as neither “Lord” nor “Creator” is eternal—because, as we said, he did not always exist as Spirit according to effects.

Hence the evangelist John, beginning from God’s eternity, seems, when he showed the Word to have been eternally with God by saying, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), and “All things were made through him” (ibid., 3), to have made no mention of the Spirit by which he might establish that the Spirit is eternal. Speaking of God and his Word, he ascribes eternity only to the Father and the Word, saying: “He was in the beginning with God” (ibid., 2).

[Col. 1084A] Yet perhaps, in what he subsequently added concerning the effect of works—“All things were made through him”—he seems to have indicated the Spirit according to the effects which God created in his goodness. According to these effects, as we have said, the Spirit is not eternal—that is, as given—just as the world-soul of which Plato speaks is not eternal. Nor is it remarkable that the evangelist’s passage agrees especially with Plato, since Augustine, as we recalled above, found the whole sense of these words in the books of the Platonists.

There are some, however, who hold that God’s love extends not only toward creatures but also from one person to another: namely, that the Father’s love for the Son, or the Son’s love for the Father, is the Spirit himself. Augustine expressly affirms this in book XV of *On the Trinity*:

“Finally, if among God’s gifts there is nothing greater than love, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit, what follows more fittingly than that he is the love called both God and from God? And if the love by which the Father ineffably loves the Son and the Son loves the Father demonstrates the communion of both, what is more fitting than that he who is the Spirit common to both should properly be called Love?”

Hence Jerome’s comment on Psalm 7: “The Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but the love which the Father has in the Son and the Son in the Father.”

[Col. 1084C] This perhaps ought especially to be said and maintained—that the Father’s love for the Son and the Son’s love for the Father should be called the Holy Spirit, and not merely love toward creatures—lest it otherwise seem possible for the Holy Spirit not to exist, and thus for the Trinity itself not to exist necessarily. For it could be that no creature ever existed, since no creature exists by necessity; and it would consequently seem that the effect which God has toward creatures would not exist by necessity, and thus that the Spirit himself, whom we call God’s own disposition or love, would not exist by necessity.

But if we understand God’s love not only toward creatures but also from one person toward another, we plainly avoid this incongruity. And perhaps, although creatures themselves do not exist by necessity—since with respect to their own nature they can fail to exist—God’s love toward them nevertheless exists so necessarily that God cannot exist at all without it. For by his own nature he possesses this love and every good in such a way that he cannot lack it at all; and it is evident that he cannot possibly be either less good or more good than he is.

But we reserve fuller treatment of this point for later, when the principal business of discussing divine power presents itself.

Yet I do not think that the Spirit should be called the Father’s gift with respect to the Son, or the Son’s gift with respect to the Father, because he cannot be given to one from whom he cannot be absent—that is, to one in whom he necessarily inheres, since he is necessarily the Spirit of both.

## XVIII

Nor do I think that this question is irrelevant to the present inquiry: namely, how only Christians hold this faith of the Trinity, and not Jews or Gentiles also. For when saying that God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit means, as we have said, that God is generating power, begotten wisdom, and proceeding beneficence, no rational person—Jew or [Col. 1085B] Gentile—doubts this. Therefore this faith seems to be lacking to no one, which we too concede, following the Apostle who says: “What is known of God is manifest in them” (Rom. 1:19). It is as though he said: “They perceived by reason what pertains to divinity, because natural reason teaches this about God to every person.”

Thus, when Augustine above set forth the teachings of the Platonists concerning the Word of God, he confirmed that he had found in them only what pertains to the Word’s divinity, and nothing concerning the mystery of the incarnation, in which the whole sum of human salvation certainly consists, and without which the other things are believed in vain.

It will be easy to convince even those who reject the language of our faith, when, upon hearing “God the Father” and “God the Son,” they recognize that they agree with us in the sense of the words. Let us ask them whether they believe in the wisdom of God, concerning which it is written: “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24); they will immediately answer that they believe. Then let us properly infer that they believe, in this very thing, in the Son of God as we do, since by the Word or Son of God we understand the same thing that they understand by the wisdom of God.

Moreover, whoever accepts that there is a Son undoubtedly does not doubt that the one whose Son he is exists—that is, the Father. We shall likewise prove that they believe in the Spirit if we explain what we mean by this name: namely, the goodness of divine grace. From this, I think, an easy opportunity may be taken to convert to our faith any who are strangers to it, if by such arguments we prove that they already share with us the common meaning of faith. Although they do not confess it with the mouth as we do, because they do not know the meaning of our words, they nevertheless already hold it in the heart, as it is written: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Rom. 10:10).

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1085]

[Col. 1085C] Having dealt with those matters that appear to pertain to the distinctive profession of the Christian faith—namely, the distinction of three persons in one and the same wholly simple substance of divinity—it is pleasing to direct the mind’s gaze more deeply toward contemplating the perfection of this highest good. Let us also, by examining each point more carefully, determine with most plausible and honorable reasons whatever seems to contain a question, so that the more fully the perfection of this highest good becomes known, the more strongly it may draw every person toward itself by desire.

First, then, we must recapitulate the unity of the divine substance, and afterwards the Trinity of persons. In the preceding little books labor was devoted to defending the profession of our faith; here, however, labor must be devoted to its enlargement.

## I

[Col. 1085D]

First, then, let there be an inquiry into the rational grounds for believing in one God, and into why it is more fitting to believe in one than in many. Here the first question presents itself: whether the divine majesty could be investigated even by human reason, and the Creator recognized from His creature through it; or whether God Himself first gave man some sensible sign by which to make Himself known—appearing, for example, first in an angel or in whatever spirit He chose—as is reported of the first parents, to whom He is said to have spoken in paradise. And perhaps this was indeed done at first: that the invisible Creator Himself revealed Himself to man in some visible form. Yet if we consider more carefully the very power of reason, whose proper function is to transcend every sense and investigate what sense cannot reach, then surely the subtler a thing’s nature is, and the farther removed from sense, the more properly it ought to submit itself to reason’s judgment and call forth reason’s inquiry into itself.

Accordingly, since man is especially compared with God through the noble image of reason, he ought to have directed it toward nothing more readily than toward Him whose image—that is, whose more expressive likeness—he possessed through it. Nor should reason be thought more disposed to perceive anything than that whose likeness it has attained more fully. For it is easy to infer like things from like things; and the more similar one thing is to another, the more easily it can arrive, from itself, at knowledge of that to which it is naturally closer. But if the very experiences of the senses also seem necessary for this purpose—namely, that man may be led from sensible things to intelligible things—then it was likewise easy for God, the best maker and governor of all, to indicate through the things He so wonderfully makes and orders how great He is in His works themselves; for from the quality of visible works we judge the skill of an absent craftsman.

In this way, indeed, the Apostle himself declares that God bestowed knowledge of Himself even upon the reprobate. Writing to the Romans, he proves every human being inexcusable and liable to accusation for contempt of his Creator, since the natural law itself, which consists in reason, brought knowledge of Him to all, even without written teaching, through the manifestation of His works. For he says:

> “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and injustice of men who hold down the truth of God in injustice. For what is known of God is manifest among them, because God has manifested it to them. For His invisible things are clearly seen, being understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made—His eternal power also and divinity—so that they are without excuse; because, when they knew God, they did not glorify Him as God or give thanks” (Rom. 1:18–21).

And a little later: “Therefore you are inexcusable, O every man who judges” [Col. 1087B] (Rom. 2:1)—that is, who employs the judgment of reason in distinguishing good and evil, and in examining the natures of the Creator and creatures themselves.

Thus Solomon indicates that he greatly marvels at certain wise men of the world: namely, how they investigated the world by reason and attempted to discuss its nature through its individual parts, while not yet perceiving its Creator, whom they could more easily have apprehended by reason. “For if,” he says, “they were able by reason to know so much that they could judge the world, how did they not more easily find the God and Creator of that world?”

This too Tully, the greatest of Latin philosophers, carefully observed. Seeing that the world was not only excellently made but also excellently ordered, he maintained that this was accomplished by providence rather than chance, and set forth both his own reasoning and that of the other philosophers. Hence the passage in the first book of the *Rhetoric*:

> “Things conducted by deliberation are managed better than things administered without deliberation. A house administered by reason is supplied with every resource and better furnished than one managed rashly and without any plan. An army commanded by a wise and shrewd general is governed more advantageously in every respect than one administered through someone’s rashness or folly. The same reasoning applies to a ship.”

Having appropriately established this proposition by comparison of similarities, he immediately adds the minor premise of the syllogism: “But nothing,” he says, [Col. 1087D] “is administered better than the whole world. For the risings and settings of the stars preserve a certain fixed order; changes in living beings not only always occur in the same way by a kind of necessity, but are also adapted to the benefit of all things; and the alternations of day and night, never altered in any respect, have never caused harm. All this is a sign that the nature of the world is administered by no slight deliberation.” Therefore, if things managed by deliberation are managed better than those managed without deliberation, and nothing is managed better than the whole world, the world is administered by deliberation.

Plato, greatest of all philosophers, carefully considering how all things in the world come to be and are ordered by reason, says: “Nothing comes to be whose origin is not preceded by a lawful cause and reason; for those things which, so far as we are concerned, are called accidental and happen unexpectedly are fixed in God by definite laws of reason and are done with the best deliberation.”

This principle—that all things are most excellently made and ordered—some have customarily called deliberation, others God, others the nature of things itself, others the mind or soul of the world. Yet all understood it to be the highest good. Socrates professed this. But Anaxagoras is reported to have been the first of all philosophers to recognize the divine mind as the maker of all natures, as blessed Augustine recalls in Book VIII of *The City of God*. Hence also the statement in Augustine’s letters to Macedonius: “Truth ought not to be dear because it did not escape Anaxagoras, [Col. 1088B] but because it is truth, even if none of them had known it.”

Moreover, it could easily be established by reason that the world itself, and the things in it, do not exist from themselves or subsist through themselves, but are both made and governed in the best way by some other being far surpassing all things. For what exists from itself is evidently more worthy by nature than what exists from another. And everything capable of reason and understanding is found to excel all other things. For we must not concede that a rational substance exists from another if we suppose that something lacking reason exists from itself. None of us is ignorant that he does not exist from himself but is begotten by another. How, then, shall we deny that things lacking reason exist from another?

Therefore the parts of the world which are naturally prior must have been made; and consequently the world has its origin from another and has been made. Indeed, since it is manifest that the world was made also for man, whom it serves in each of its parts, it must be far less worthy than man. Consequently we ought by no means to concede that it was not made when man was made; still less is it fitting that rational things should depend upon their own governance rather than non-rational things.

But it is plain that man, although rational, is by no means sufficient for his own governance, since he cannot govern himself as he wishes in the sea of this life. Much less, therefore, is it fitting to entrust to their own government things which certainly lack the reason by which they might govern themselves. Such are the world and its individual parts. By these, or similar, arguments, I think it manifest that everything in the world has a maker or governor, whom we call God.

## II

It remains now to discuss His unity: namely, why it is more fitting that one creator rather than many should preside over the world, and why one God and Lord of all, rather than many, ought to be believed in. For it is certain that all things are governed with so much the greater harmony as the care of their government is entrusted to fewer persons. But nothing is known to be better or governed with greater harmony than the whole universe, as Tully’s reasoning above has shown. Therefore it is subject to one governance.

For, as has been said, nothing is governed with greater harmony than the world; nor indeed is any thing governed with such harmony as that over which a single ruler presides. Thus the world is in no way subject to many rulers, but to one alone. For the greater the unity maintained in all things, the greater the harmony preserved; and the farther one departs from unity, the farther one departs from harmony. Therefore, for harmony to be supreme, identity must be supreme and unity pre-eminently maintained. But nothing can be identical or one with another as it is with itself, nor can anything agree with another as it agrees with itself, since nothing is unlike itself.

Accordingly, all things should look and be referred to one, so that what is accomplished through the diversity of things may be administered harmoniously by one reason, with the proper order observed in all things. Nor should many be believed necessary for the creation of things any more than for their general governance. Rather, all natures ought to be made by one, as they are appropriately believed to be governed by one, so that they may be governed with greater harmony in proportion as they are joined in greater harmony.

Their harmony is greater in proportion as they flow more completely from one and the same single principle, and as their craftsman recedes from multiplicity and diversity. They were first made in order that they might afterwards be governed in the best way; and the things made in order to be governed were, in being made, certainly prepared for governance. Therefore, that they might be governed in the best way, they had to be made in the best way and prepared, while being made, for governance. But how could they be prepared in the best way while being made, so that afterwards, once made, they might be governed in the best way, unless they were bound together by the highest mutual harmony even in their very creation? Thus they are governed more harmoniously and better in proportion as their natures are more harmoniously joined to one another in their creation.

For this harmony of creation, no less than for that of governance, the supreme unity and identity of the Creator is beneficial. Hence it is also clear that the one and utterly identical Creator, as likewise Governor, of all things is He whom we call God and rightly profess to be the highest good. How could He be called highest unless He excelled all other goods? But what excels all other things must certainly be one and unique. And what is granted to be perfect in itself, sufficient through itself and by its own will for everything that is to be done—whence it is called omnipotent—cannot have any good as a part. For that which is superfluous cannot be good. But another creator or governor would be superfluous if one were equally sufficient for all things as many would be. Yet He is sufficient, since, as was said, He is the highest, perfect, and all-sufficient good. Therefore there can in no way be, or be believed to be, many gods.

But perhaps you will say: because the better any good is, the better its multiplication would be, therefore the highest good called God would be better if multiplied than if unique; and, if we desire to exalt and magnify Him, we ought to proclaim Him multiple rather than simple. But I think the first answer to this is that, on this reasoning, the more gods we proclaim, the more we magnify the glory of divine excellence. Therefore infinitely many gods ought to be proclaimed, that we may magnify His glory infinitely—especially since there is no reason by which their number could be reduced to any fixed limit. According to this reasoning, we magnify it all the more as we extend their number further.

Thus there would have to be more highest goods than inferior goods—indeed, infinitely many altogether—so that there could be no knowledge of things for which no limit occurs in nature, nor could God Himself comprehend them by knowledge, since they would not be comprehended by any limit of nature. Further, if there are many gods, how shall we call any one of them the highest good, since something else is greater than he: namely, the multitude of gods itself, greater than any single one from that multitude? Nor would what is superfluous be called good, as we have already shown.

Finally, every multitude is a whole, and every whole is naturally posterior to its own parts. And everything simpler must necessarily be firmer, since every composite thing is by nature capable of dissolution, and is weaker in proportion as it is more liable to dissolution. Who would deny that any good is more precious in proportion as it is rarer, and more glorious in proportion as it is more unique? Thus things often less necessary than others are nevertheless preferred to them altogether because of their rarity: gold to iron, pepper to grain.

Therefore even God’s uniqueness commends the glory of divine excellence; it is also the greatest commendation of His works, both in making them and in ordering and governing them. Nothing can properly be made or governed with as great harmony as that which one alone both creates and governs. I think these arguments sufficient for establishing the singularity of divine excellence; and I judge that any good person will readily assent to them—a person who envies no one and greatly rejoices in the excellence of all things.

Yet we use arguments of fitness more than arguments of necessity, because among good people that is always judged pre-eminent which is more highly commended by its fitness; and the argument which tends more toward fitness than necessity is always stronger, especially since fitting things please in themselves and immediately attract us by a certain power of their own. For how fitting and salutary it is that all things should look to one best ruler and maker, and that all things should rather be made and governed by reason than by chance—there is no one whose own reason does not suggest this to his conscience.

What concern for good works would exist in us if we wholly failed to know the God whom we now venerate through love or fear? What hope would restrain the wickedness of the powerful or draw them toward good works, if the most just and powerful ruler of all were believed in vain? Let us therefore suppose that, while we seek to benefit and please the good, we cannot compel the obstinate because we do not stop their mouths with arguments of necessity. Let us suppose this, if they wish; but let us set before them what they do not wish, reproving their utter shamelessness if they calumniate what they cannot in any way refute and what is so highly commended by both fitness and utility.

Let us ask why they prefer to choose that God does not exist rather than that He does. Though they cannot be compelled necessarily to either position, one is commended by many arguments and the other by none. Let us confound the most unjust shamelessness of those who refuse to follow what they do not doubt to be best and consistent with all reason and authority, and instead embrace the contrary. If, concerning hidden natures of things and the condition even of heavenly bodies—matters which they cannot investigate by experience so as to be certain of them—they believe human authorities, why do they not likewise rest content with those authorities concerning God, the author of all? But enough of this against this first and greatest obstinacy of unbelievers.

## III

[Col. 1091B]

Now, from the unity of the divine substance, which we have laid down as a kind of foundation, we must proceed in order to the distinction of the three persons contained in that same substance. It remains to discuss, with careful examination, divine power, wisdom, and goodness, according to which, as has been said, the three persons are distinguished for the complete and perfect commendation of the highest good. Thus, in proportion as the perfection of this good is more fully known—as we recalled above—it may draw each person more strongly to love of itself. This is especially necessary because questions concerning these matters can trouble even the minds of the faithful; and, in proportion as they seem more difficult to resolve, they can more easily draw the less learned into the greatest scandals and aid unbelievers. Let our first consideration, then, concern God’s omnipotence.

## IV

It seems first necessary to ask how God is truly called omnipotent if He cannot accomplish everything; or how He can do everything if we can do certain things which He cannot do. For we can do certain things—walk, speak, perceive—which are altogether alien to the nature of divinity, since an incorporeal substance cannot possibly possess the bodily instruments necessary for such actions.

To these objections, I think we must first say that, even according to the philosophers themselves and common usage of speech, the power of any thing is never understood except in those matters which concern that thing’s advantage or dignity. No one counts it as a power of man that he can easily be overcome; rather, he counts it as man’s powerlessness and weakness that he cannot resist what harms him. Whatever tends toward human vice and discredits rather than commends the person must be ascribed to powerlessness rather than power.

Thus Aristotle, in the second genus of quality, where he treats of natural power and weakness, classifies the curative and the hard under power, and the liable-to-sickness and the soft under weakness. Yet we call a thing liable-to-sickness when it can easily become sick—that is, when it cannot readily resist this affection—and soft when it can easily be cut or broken apart. By contrast, he classifies the curative and hard under power, although “curative” means what cannot easily become infirm, and “hard” what cannot easily be cut. Therefore, just as in the cases mentioned above—what is liable-to-sickness and soft—the ability to undergo what concerns a thing’s harm or weakness belongs rather to weakness than power, so conversely the inability to undergo these things must be attributed to power. Otherwise, on the contrary, we should call weakness power and power weakness.

Therefore let no one presume to call God powerless in any respect because He cannot sin as we can; for even in ourselves this must not be attributed to power but to weakness. Hence Augustine says in Book XV of *On the Trinity*: “It is a great power of His not to be able to lie.”

There are also certain things which must be reckoned powers in some beings but not at all in others, and which are praiseworthy in some but blameworthy in others, although the same qualities often commend the dignity of certain things while not commending that of others. For example, if a man could surpass another man in the use of physical strength, this should be ascribed to great human power. By it he would excel other men and be more commendable. Yet no one would regard this as a great thing in a lion or elephant. For we call a man powerful by comparison with other men, but not so a lion or elephant.

Likewise, in a man the ability to walk must be attributed to power, since it suits his need and in no respect diminishes his dignity. But in God, who accomplishes all things by will alone, what is necessary in us would be altogether superfluous and should therefore be attributed not to power but rather to defect—especially since the ability to walk would detract in many respects from His excellence. It would entail that He could move locally, possess a composite arrangement of feet, and have a corporeal and compounded substance which was mobile and dissoluble.

Nevertheless, with respect to all the things we can accomplish, we rightly proclaim God powerful and ascribe all that we do to His power: “in Him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28), and He “works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:6). For He employs us as instruments to accomplish what He wills, and is in some manner said Himself to do what He causes us to do—just as a rich man is said to construct a tower through the workmen he employs. He is said to be able to accomplish all things who works all that He wills, and in whatever way He wills, whether through Himself or through subject creation.

For although He cannot walk, He can cause walking to occur—that is, He can cause another to walk—since by creating each person He prepares that person for this, preserves and sustains him even in the act itself, and thereby the person performs the action. Thus God is said to be able to do all things not because He can undertake every action, but because in all things which He wills to be done nothing can resist His will.

Hence blessed Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*: “He is truly called omnipotent for no other reason than that He can do whatever He wills; and the effect of the omnipotent will is not hindered by the will of any creature.” The same author says in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “He cannot do unjust things, because He is supreme justice and goodness. But He is omnipotent not because He can do everything, but because He can bring about whatever He wills, so that nothing can resist His will so as to prevent its fulfillment or impede it in any way.”

John Chrysostom, in Homily 28 on the exposition of the Creed, beginning, “Upon the fabric of the whole Church,” says:

> “I believe in God the Father almighty.” He is called almighty because no inability can be found in His power, as the Prophet says: “He has done whatever He willed” (Ps. 113:3). He is therefore omnipotence itself, so that He can do all that He wills. Hence also the Apostle: “Who shall resist His will?” (Rom. 9:19); and the Psalmist: “He has done whatever He willed.”

But elsewhere the Apostle says: “God wills all to be saved and none to perish” (1 Tim. 2:4), in accordance with the prophet’s words: “I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn and live” (Ezek. 18:32). And Truth Himself says to the obstinate city destined for condemnation: “How often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks,” etc. (Luke 13:34). It is therefore clear that the term “divine will” must be understood in two ways. Otherwise, since God does whatever He wills and wills all to be saved, we shall certainly be forced to profess that all will at some time be saved.

God is thus said to will in two ways: either according to the ordinance of His providence, when He arranges, deliberates, and establishes within His providence that something shall later be accomplished; or according to the exhortation or approval of counsel, by which He admonishes each person toward that for which He would be prepared to reward him by His grace.

In the former manner—in which God is said to will something, that is, to ordain it by His grace and determine within Himself that certain things shall occur—we and the apostles say that nothing can resist His will in the things He wills to happen, nor can it be impeded by any event, since everything must obey it. In the latter manner, however, He is said to will many things to occur which do not occur: that is, He exhorts people to many things which He would certainly reward by His grace if they were done, but which are not done. Thus He counsels every human being concerning salvation and exhorts him toward it, though few obey.

God therefore wills the sinner to turn because He counsels this, which He would graciously reward. In the same way, something is called pleasing to Him in which we would experience His favor; conversely, He is said not to will those things which He dissuades, or whatever He ought rather to punish than reward with some gift, and in which we would experience His wrath rather than His favor—that is, vengeance rather than reward.

## V

I think it must be asked whether God can make more things, or better things, than He makes; or whether He could in any way refrain from those things which He does make, and never make them. Whether we grant or deny this, we may perhaps encounter many perplexities of inconsistency.

For if we suppose that He can make more or fewer things, or can refrain from those which He makes, we surely greatly detract from His supreme goodness. For it is clear that He can make only good things. But if, being able, He does not make good things and withholds Himself from some things which ought to be made, who would not accuse Him as envious or unjust? Especially since no labor in making anything burdens Him, since all things are equally subject to His will, according to what is written: “He spoke, and they were made; He commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32:9).

Hence Plato’s most true argument, by which he proves that God could in no way have made the world better than He made it. For in his *Timaeus* he says:

> “We must state why the founder and maker of this creation judged that this whole universe should be established. He was best. But envy is far removed from the best; therefore He wished all things to be made like Himself, insofar as the nature of each could be capable of blessedness. If anyone should posit this will of God as the most certain origin of things, I should agree that he judged rightly. For God, wishing all good things to arise and no progeny of any evil, insofar as the nature of things born permits, left no propagation of evil.”

These words of Plato plainly seem to affirm that God makes all things as good as they can be made, or as good as He Himself can make them. The saints also appear to have followed this reasoning when they proved that God the Father begot the Son as good as He could, so that He might be equal to Him. Hence Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter 63: “The God whom He begot, since He could not beget one better than Himself. For nothing better than God ought to be equal to Him. If He willed it and could not, He is weak; if He could and would not, He is envious.”

This also concerns the statement of the Nicene Council which, as we mentioned in the first book, blessed Jerome records:

> “Far be it that there be in the Son of God any more or less—whether in place, time, power, knowledge, equality, or subjection—when these things are said so as to be attributed to His divinity, not His flesh. For if any more or less is found, apart from this—that the Father begot the Son, and that the Son was not born from Himself but from the Father—then the Father is recognized as envious, or powerless, and even temporal.”

Therefore, by the reasoning which proves that God the Father begot the Son as good as He could—since otherwise He would be guilty of envy—it is clear that God makes everything He makes as excellent as He can, and is unwilling to withhold any benefit that He can confer. For He makes or omits nothing except for the best and rational cause, though that cause is hidden from us.

Hence also Plato’s statement: “Everything that is generated is necessarily generated from some cause; for nothing comes to be whose origin is not preceded by a lawful cause and reason.” And hence Augustine’s statement when proving that all things in the world are made or ordered by divine providence, that nothing happens by chance or fortuitously, but that everything proceeds from divine counsel. He says in the aforesaid book of *Questions*, chapter 26:

> “Whatever happens by chance happens rashly. Whatever happens rashly does not happen by providence. Therefore, if some things happen in the world by chance, the whole world is not governed by providence.”

Again:

> “That good by participation in which other things are good is good not through another, but through itself. This is what we also call divine providence. Therefore nothing happens in the world by chance.”

Moreover, in everything God does, He attends so closely to what is good that He is said to be inclined to do each thing by the value of goodness itself rather than by the mere pleasure of His own will. Hence Jerome, on Daniel, in explaining the third vision, where Nebuchadnezzar speaks of God as follows: “He has done according to His will, both in heaven and on earth; and there is none who can resist His hand or say, ‘Why have You done this?’” (Dan. 4:32), says:

> “This,” Jerome says, “he speaks as a worldly man; for God does not do what He wills, but wills what is good. Nebuchadnezzar spoke in such a way that, while he proclaims God’s power, he seems to accuse His justice, because he suffered punishments deservedly.”

Jerome’s meaning, then, in saying, “God does not do what He wills, but wills what is good,” is as though he said: God does not act as Nebuchadnezzar supposes—that is, in the manner of those who, in what they do, attend not so much to what is good as to satisfying their own will, whatever its character. Of such people it is written:

> “This I will; thus I command; let my will stand in place of reason.”  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* 6.223

Rather, God should be said to will each thing to come to pass because He saw that it was good for it to come to pass. In this sense each person is forbidden to follow his own will. Christ Himself too is said not to have pleased Himself, because we should do nothing with the end or intention that we will it, or that we please ourselves in it—that is, that we delight in it—but rather because we judge it good that it should be done by us.

It is therefore clear that whatever God makes or omits has an underlying just and rational cause: He makes or omits only those things which ought to be made or omitted and which befit Him. But if He ought to make whatever He makes, it is always just that He makes whatever He makes, and without doubt He must make whatever He makes. For whatever it is just to do, it is unjust to omit; and whoever does not do what reason requires sins just as much as if he did what does not accord with reason.

But perhaps you will say: what is just or good or reasonable for Him to do now would equally be good and just if He did something else and omitted this. But if what He omitted was equally good to do when He chose this, there was certainly no reason why He should omit that and choose this. “There was,” you say, “because, though both ought not to occur and it was equally good for this or that to occur, whichever occurred would have been done reasonably.”

But it is scarcely possible, I maintain, to offer a reason why what was not done ought equally to have been done as what was done, and why it was equally good that that should occur as that this should occur. For whenever something is good to do, and this is the rational reason why it should be done, one plainly acts irrationally who omits what he knows ought to be done by him. Thus we shall fall back into the inconsistency already stated.

But if you say concerning the other thing which was not done that it was not good for it to be done except on condition that the other ceased, then by the same reasoning it must not simply be conceded concerning the thing which was done that it was good for that to be done, since it has equally been conceded that both this and that were good to do. Did God then do what He knew to be good to do? Far be it! But if only what He does is good to be done by Him, then He can do only what He does, since He can do nothing whose being done by Him is not good.

By this reasoning, therefore, God appears able only to do what He does, or able only to omit what He omits. For in every act or omission He has a rational cause why it is done or omitted by Him; and He, who is supreme reason, can neither will nor do anything contrary to what reason requires. No one can rationally will or do what departs from reason.

Blessed Jerome seems to have carefully observed this when exhorting the virgin Eustochium to keep her purpose of holy virginity. He says: “‘The virgin Israel has fallen, and there is none to raise her’” (Amos 5:2). “I shall speak boldly: although God can do all things, He cannot raise up a virgin after her fall.”

One defender of Jerome against detractors, among other things he wrote concerning Jerome’s life, says:

> “Saint Jerome sought, by exhorting Eustochium, to command her to strive for better things: ‘Although God can do all things, He cannot raise up a virgin after her fall.’ The inability of God could in no way be expressed otherwise than as God’s unwillingness.”

For a certain Wise Man says to God: “But You, Lord of power, judge with gentleness, and govern us with great reverence; for when You will, power is at Your command” (Wis. 12:18). Therefore, where God’s will is absent, power is absent. For God, immutable in nature, is likewise immutable in will.

From these considerations, therefore, drawn both from reason and from Scripture, it is established that God can do only what he at some time does. But if we suppose that God can do only what he does, we seem, on the contrary, to incur many consequences contrary both to reason and to authority [Col. 1096D]. For who does not know that this man, who is to be condemned, can be saved? Or that this man, who is good, can become better than he will ever in fact be? Yet neither can occur except through God. For if this man who is to be condemned could in no way be saved, neither could he do those things through which he would be saved by God; surely he ought not then to be blamed or held guilty for not doing what he could not do. Nor would it be right for the Lord to command him to do those things by which he might be saved, since he could by no means do them. But if he could be saved by God through works that he might perform, who can doubt that God can save him, though he is never to be saved?

For how can he be saved by God unless God can save him? What else is it for him to be saved by God than for God to save him? Therefore, if it is possible that he be saved by God, how can it not be possible for God to save him? For when the antecedent is possible, the consequent is possible also, since an impossibility does not follow from a possibility—whereas, if the consequent is known to be impossible, an impossibility follows from it. Who, moreover, would deny that “this man is saved by God” is antecedent to “God saves him,” since, as we have said, it is altogether the same thing for one who is to be condemned to be saved by God and for God to save him? Therefore, since it is possible that this man who is to be condemned can be saved by God, who would deny that it is also possible for God to save him? God, then, can do what he will by no means do.

And it is plainly altogether false what we previously maintained: namely, that God can do only those things which he does at some time [Col. 1097B]. Otherwise, no thanks ought to be rendered to him for the things he does, since he performs things which he cannot refrain from doing, compelled more by a kind of necessity of his own nature than led to perform them by free will.

Many testimonies also concur which plainly assert that God can do more than he ever brings to completion in act. Thus Truth itself says according to Matthew: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will at once furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26:53). From these words of the Lord Jesus it is plainly implied that he could then ask when he was not asking, and when it was not fitting to ask; or that the Father could then furnish him with those legions through whom he might be delivered from his enemies—which was by no means fitting at that time, since then he was appropriately coming to suffer, as had previously been foretold or ordained by God [Col. 1097C]. Hence he immediately adds: “How then will the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen thus?” (ibid., 54).

If, therefore, it had to happen thus at that time, how could the Son then ask that it not happen, or the Father intervene that it not happen, when it was by no means good for it to be prevented then? Indeed, it had to happen then, as it had been ordained and foretold. Yet, if the truth of the sense of the Lord’s words is to be preserved, and nothing contrary to reason is to appear in them [Col. 1097D], the statement, “Do you think,” and so forth, means this: “Do you not know that, if I asked my Father for my deliverance, I would immediately obtain it through as many legions of angels as there are men adhering to me as disciples and ready, if they could, for my defense?” The sum of the sense is: “Do you think that my prayer lacks efficacy even in this matter, if I ought to ask this of the Father?”

According to this interpretation, then, it must by no means be granted either that the Lord could then pray for what ought not to be prayed for, or that the Father could aid him in what ought not to be aided [Col. 1098A]. The Lord’s saying, as we have explained, must be understood conditionally rather than absolutely: not that he could ask or obtain it, but that he would obtain it if he asked, since his prayer could in no way be ineffective. We cannot, therefore, be compelled by this saying of the Lord to hold that he can do something which he never does. Rather, it seems that we should think that he can do only what ought to be done by him. Nothing ought to be done by him which will never be done by him. Otherwise he would not be supremely good, if he omitted doing something which he foreknew ought fittingly to be done by himself.

Likewise, if he could prevent the evils which occur only when it was fitting to do so, and could act only in an unfitting way [Col. 1098B], I truly do not see how he would not be said to consent to sins. For who is to be called consenting to evil except one through whom it can fittingly be prevented? But, as blessed Augustine also observes, it is good even that evils occur, which God himself orders most excellently. Therefore it is not fitting that he prevent them, lest things occur which—by his own testimony—must occur, when he says: “For offenses must come; but woe,” and so forth (Matt. 18:7). Therefore, since he cannot fittingly prevent offenses which it is good should occur—or indeed cannot prevent them at all, since he can do nothing contrary to reason—he is by no means to be said to consent to sins.

First, then, and fittingly, it was said of God that power is subject to him when he wills: namely, that in every act to be done his power and will accompany one another in such a way that he cannot do what he does not will, nor can he do it at the time when he does not will it to be done [Col. 1098C]. For example, he does not now will to make rain; and he does not will this now because he judges that it is not fitting for it to happen now, and that this is not a suitable time for rain, certainly for some rational reason, though hidden from us. If, therefore, he can or wills to make rain now, he can or wills to do it at a time when it is not proper for him to do it—something which conflicts with all reason.

Therefore, insofar as I judge, since God can do only what it is fitting for him to do, and nothing is fitting for him to do which he omits to do, I hold that he can do only what he does at some time [Col. 1098D], although this opinion of ours has few or no supporters and seems greatly to disagree with the sayings of the saints, and to some extent with reason.

> [Note: [Col. 1097] Against this opinion St Bernard writes, Epistle 190; and Abelard himself retracts it in his *Confession of Faith*, printed above at the end of his letters.]

For, they say, this belief greatly derogates from the divine excellence: that he can do only what he does at some time, and omit only what he omits, whereas we ourselves, though far more powerless, can do and omit many things which we neither do nor omit.

To these persons I reply that we ought not for that reason to consider ourselves more powerful or better because we can do certain things which he cannot do—such as eat, walk, or finally sin [Col. 1099A]. Such things are wholly remote from the power of the Godhead and entirely alien to its dignity. Nor does it follow that God can do things which he never does, or things which it is by no means fitting for him to do. For the fact that we can do certain things which we ought not to do is to be ascribed to our weakness rather than our dignity. We should be altogether better if we could do only those things which we ought to do, and if nothing shameful could be done by us.

Yet God did not without reason grant us the power of doing evil or sinning: namely, that, in comparison with our weakness, he who cannot sin at all might appear more glorious; and that, when we refrain from sin [Col. 1099B], we might attribute this not to our own nature but to his assisting grace—he who orders for his own glory not only good things but evil things also.

There are, however, some who judge that God can also do things which he does not do, because it is certain that nothing could resist him if he willed to do even those things which he does not do, according to the saying: “For who has resisted his will?” (Rom. 9:19). Thus blessed Augustine also observes that God is called omnipotent not because he can do everything, but because he can do whatever he wills, and the effect of his will can by no means be hindered. Hence whatever he willed would necessarily occur when he willed it, because his will could in no way lack its effect.

But by this argument of theirs, and as it were under a condition of his will, we could say that he can also sin or act dishonorably [Col. 1099C], since it is certain that nothing could resist him in this either, if he willed to do what ought not to be done. Moreover, when they say that he is called omnipotent because he can do whatever he wills, they plainly join his power and will so that, where his willing is absent, his power is absent as well.

The foregoing objection—that no one can be saved by God unless God can save him, especially since it is the same thing for someone to be saved by God and for God to save him—does not sufficiently bind us. For it is also the same thing for a speaker to be silent and for the one who speaks to be silent; yet perhaps it is not as possible for the speaker to be silent as it is possible for the one who speaks to be silent. Or, although it is the same thing for that which is white to be black and for whiteness and blackness to inhere simultaneously in the same thing [Col. 1099D], nevertheless it is not as possible for what is white to be black as it is possible for whiteness and blackness to inhere simultaneously in the same thing.

What wonder, then, if we maintain that it is the same thing for someone who is not to be saved to be saved by God and for God to save him, yet do not therefore admit that God can save him in the same way as we grant that he can be saved by God? For when we say that he can be saved by God, we refer possibility to the capacity of human nature; as though we were saying that it is not repugnant to human nature that he be saved, since in himself he is so mutable that he can consent either to his salvation or to his condemnation, and can make himself tractable to God in either way. But when we say that God can save one who is by no means to be saved [Col. 1100A], we refer possibility to the very nature of the Godhead, as though it were not repugnant to God’s nature to save him. This is utterly false. It is wholly repugnant to the divine nature that he do what derogates from his dignity and what is by no means fitting for him to do.

In this manner, too, when we call a sound audible—that is, capable of being heard by someone—and say that someone can hear a sound; or when we say that a field can be cultivated by someone and that someone can cultivate a field, we refer possibility to different things. In the first cases, to the nature of the sound or field; in the second, to the nature or aptitude of the thing capable of hearing the sound or cultivating the field. Hence it does not follow that, because a sound is audible—that is, fit in itself to be heard by someone—there is already someone fit to hear it [Col. 1100B]. Even if all human beings were deaf, or even if they did not exist at all, any sound would still be of such a nature as to present itself as audible to a human being; and nothing would need to be prepared in it for it to be fit to be heard, although no human being yet existed who could hear it or was fit to hear it.

Finally, the objection drawn from the tradition of the philosophers—that, when the antecedent is possible and the consequent impossible, an impossibility follows—does no harm, as we said in the preceding book, if we understand the teaching of their rules to be confined to the natures of creatures. Thus, when they call something possible or impossible [Col. 1100C], they understand this with respect to the natures of creatures, so that they call possible only what is contrary to the nature of no creature. But when we say that it is possible for God to do this or that, we take possibility with reference to the nature of the Godhead rather than to creatures.

Again, although it is the same thing for a judge to punish this man and for this man to be punished by a judge, it must not be granted that, if it is just for a judge to punish this man, it is also just for this man to be punished by a judge. For the term “just,” like “possible,” has different significations in such cases. When it is said that it is just for the judge to punish this man, we show that he ought to do so by the ordinance of the law. But if we say that this man ought to be punished by the judge, we say that he has deserved to be punished [Col. 1100D].

It often happens, therefore, that under the sanction of the law a judge ought to punish someone who nevertheless ought by no means to be punished by him on account of his deserts. For example, false witnesses, whom the judge nevertheless cannot refute, may rise against an innocent person and convict as guilty under the laws one who is not guilty, causing a nonexistent crime to be believed. It then happens, as stated, that the judge ought to punish one who nevertheless ought not to be punished by the judge; and it is just for the judge to do this, though it is not just—that is, not deserved—for the other to suffer it.

Therefore, just as here, although it is the same thing for the judge to punish this man and for this man to be punished by the judge, it does not follow that, as it is just for the judge to punish this man, whom he justly punishes according to the law as stated, so it is also just for the man to be punished by the judge for the same reason [Col. 1101A]; so, although it is the same thing for someone to be saved by God and for God to save him, it is not surprising if, while the former is possible, the latter is conceded to be by no means possible.

I think that from what has been said it can readily be refuted what might seem capable of being objected concerning God’s providence or his will in relation to creatures: namely, that God could not have existed without those things which he has eternally in himself, because it was not fitting otherwise; but that we ought not therefore to suppose that things foreseen, or things which he willed to exist, could not have failed to exist—that is, that they occurred by necessity.

For although he could not have existed without providence because this was not fitting, and although it is necessary that his providence be followed by the event of things, we ought not therefore to grant that things foreseen could not have failed to exist [Col. 1101B]. Although we maintain that he could not have existed without the will to create the world or the will to show mercy, we are not thereby compelled to say that the world, or the things created, could not have been absent. In the former case, as has already been determined, possibility is referred to the nature of God; in the latter, to the nature of creatures. Hence it does not follow that, although God by his own nature must have providence for things or a good will toward them—because this is supremely fitting for him—their nature requires that they exist, since they can altogether not exist.

The final objection—that no thanks should be rendered to God for what he does, because he cannot refrain from doing it and acts from a kind of necessity rather than will—is wholly frivolous. For here a certain necessity of his nature or goodness is not separate from his will; nor should it be called compulsion, by which he is compelled to do something unwillingly [Col. 1101C]. For when it is necessary that he be immortal, or when he is called immortal, the necessity of the divine nature is by no means thereby separated from his will, since he wills to be what it is necessary for him to be—that is, what he cannot fail to be.

But if he acted necessarily in such a way that, whether willing or unwilling, he were compelled to do it, then surely no thanks would be owed him for it. Yet since his goodness and most excellent will are so great that they incline him to act not unwillingly but spontaneously, he is to be loved from his own nature and glorified for this all the more, because this goodness is not present in him accidentally but substantially and immutably [Col. 1101D]. For he is better in this respect insofar as he persists in it more firmly.

Would we not give thanks to someone who aided us, if he were of such great compassion that, seeing us violently afflicted, he could not refrain from helping, his compassion itself impelling him to do so? For what is it to owe thanks to someone for benefits received, except to acknowledge that he has deserved well of us, or that he is to be praised for what his kindness has freely bestowed upon us?

By the foregoing arguments and solutions of objections, I think it clear to all that God can do or omit only those things which he does or omits at some time, and only in the manner or at the time in which he does so, not otherwise [Col. 1102A]. Yet some think that he can do certain things in another manner than he does, but that he always chooses the more fitting manner of doing them. This too entirely conflicts with reason: that he could act in a less fitting manner than he does, or could choose the less fitting manner and omit the more fitting. For he is not perfectly good unless in accomplishing all things he has the best will, so that he wills each thing to be done in the manner in which it would be done more fittingly.

But perhaps you will say: if, at the time when he does one thing, he can do another thing, and not, that is, at another time, it is established that he can do at one time what he cannot do at another; and that he is not always equally able to do all things, nor always equally omnipotent [Col. 1102B], but now possesses a certain power and now does not possess it.

But if we consider carefully, he is always equally omnipotent and at no time possesses a power which he does not always possess. Yet you say: “He could formerly become incarnate, which he cannot now, since it is in no way fitting for this to occur now; and so he formerly had a power which he does not now have.” I answer: when we say, “He can do at one time what he cannot do at another,” this can be understood in two ways: rightly, if the temporal determination is applied to “do,” and wrongly, if it is joined to “can.”

For it is one thing to say, “I can do this now,” that is, “I now have the power of doing this whenever”; another to say, “I can do this now,” that is, “I can do it in this present time” [Col. 1102C]. Likewise, a local determination, referred to different things, produces different meanings. For when a person, wherever he may be, is capable of walking there—that is, has the power of walking—even when swimming in water; nevertheless, when it is said, “He is able to walk on the waters,” if this determination is referred rather to the act of walking than to the power, so that we understand him to have the power of performing this act upon the waves, it is false. But if it is referred to the power of walking possessed even amid waters, it is on the contrary true.

If, therefore, it is true that he does not lack this power even amid waters, although he cannot exercise that power there, so neither is it necessary that God or anyone be deprived, at some time, of the power of doing something, although at that time he cannot exercise that power [Col. 1102D]. Thus a little child, still altogether too weak to walk, is nevertheless already capable of walking and already has the power of walking at some time, although not yet at so tender an age.

On this reasoning God is not deprived of the power of becoming incarnate which he formerly exercised, although he cannot exercise it now because it is by no means fitting for it to be exercised now. Nor is anyone ever said to be deprived of any power when it is certain that, if he willed, he could exercise it and that no one could resist his will. Since, as we have recalled above, he is called omnipotent because he can always do whatever he wills, he is always equally omnipotent, since it is certain that he can always accomplish whatever he wills [Col. 1103A], and that his will can never be thwarted by any impediment.

Just as he always knows all things which he knows at any time, or always wills what he wills at any time, and never loses any knowledge or changes any will that he has ever had, so he can always do all things which he can do at any time and is never deprived of any of his powers. For although he formerly knew that I would be born, and does not now know that I will be born, it does not follow that he formerly knew something which he does not now know. Rather, he now knows of my birth what he knew before it occurred, though this knowledge must then and now be expressed in different words.

For what was then future is now completed, and therefore the words are changed in order to designate the same thing; just as speakers at different times designate the same day now by the adverb “tomorrow,” while it is still future; now by “today,” while it is present; and now by “yesterday,” when it is past [Col. 1103B]. Therefore, before I was born, when God knew that I would be born, he likewise now knows that I was born at the very time at which I was to be born. Likewise, concerning my same birth, he now wills what he then willed: namely, that it should occur then, when from eternity he willed and knew that it would occur.

Observe that just as, when we say “God now knows that this has been done,” or “he now wills that this has been done,” the word “now,” joined to different elements, changes the force of the statement, so also, as we recalled above, when I say “he can now do this,” the same adverb joined differently varies the meaning [Col. 1103C]. For in the statement, “God now knows that this has been done,” “now” may be referred either to “knows” or to “has been done.” Thus one may say either, “He now has this knowledge, that this has been done,” or “He knows that it has now been done”—which are very different.

Likewise, if it is said that he knows this to occur now, which he does not know to occur later, it is false if both “now” and “later” are referred to “knows.” For from this one would have to concede that he sometimes knows it and sometimes does not know it. But if both are joined to “occur,” the statement is true; and we need not therefore admit that he knows one thing at one time which he does not know at another [Col. 1103D].

That is, when such adverbs are joined with the verbs “wills” and “can,” they likewise vary the meaning. If it is said, “God can do this now,” and the adverb is referred to the verb “can,” the statement is utterly false, because he would then have at one time a certain power which he would not have at another. But if the adverb is joined to “do,” it is entirely true. And just as different items of knowledge are not indicated when it is said of him that he formerly knew he was to be incarnate, so too, when it is said that he could formerly become incarnate and can now be incarnate, possibility is indicated.

For when we say successively in time, “God becomes incarnate” and “God has become incarnate,” we do not indicate different things which he has done; rather, these are said concerning the same thing which he did once. Likewise [Col. 1104A], when it is first said that it is possible for God to become incarnate, and afterward that it is possible for him to have become incarnate, neither a different deed nor a different possibility is shown. Both are truly said of the same thing which was formerly future and is now past.

It is clear, therefore, that God is changed neither in knowledge nor in will, nor in possibility. **[Lacuna: “O . . . . .”]** Therefore, what he knows once he always knows, and what he wills once he always wills; so also, a power which he has once he never lays aside. Finally, if in human fashion we say that he can do one thing at one time which he cannot do at another, solely because it is fitting for him to do it at one time and not fitting at another, no impotence or diminution of his power is to be understood in this [Col. 1104B]. For what is in no way fitting for anyone does not belong to that person’s power, such that one could be commended for it; indeed, on the contrary, it would derogate from his dignity.

## VI.

Since his very immutability belongs to the power or firmness of the divine nature, we must now discuss it, especially because from certain things which he performs he seems, like ourselves, to undergo variation: namely, because he does some things at one time and, when they have been completed, rests from them at another. Thus it is written of him that, after completing his works which he performed in six days, he rested on the seventh day (Gen. 2:2), that is, he ceased working. Therefore, just as physical reasoning shows that we undergo alteration by doing one thing and afterward resting, so he also seems to undergo this change of alteration [Col. 1104C].

He also seems subject to local movement, since he is said at one time to descend somewhere, pass through certain places, or go forth somewhere and return from there. Thus we profitably hand down and truly proclaim that both the Word of the Father and the Holy Spirit descended into the Virgin. In that Virgin, moreover, God made man seems to be changed so greatly that he is said to have become something other than he had been; this seems to belong to that principal movement of substance which philosophers call generation.

God, therefore, does not seem altogether immutable, since, as has been said, he appears to undergo the movement of alteration, of place, and even of generation. But if we consider carefully, he undergoes no variation of change either in these matters or in others [Col. 1104D]. For when we say that he does something, we do not understand that any movement belongs to him in acting, or any suffering in laboring, as commonly happens to us. Rather, we signify some new effect of his eternal will.

Therefore, when we say that he does something, this is to say that something occurs according to his will, so that nothing new occurs in him, but something new comes to pass while his will remains fixed. Hence the philosophical verse is well said:

> “Remaining stable, he gives all things to be moved.”

When he is said to rest from working, we signify the completion of his work, not that he ceases from any movement of action. But we are said to be changed by working at one time and ceasing at another, because in this we have a certain motion of limbs or affection of mind differently than before, and are varied in ourselves [Col. 1105A].

We understand God’s doing something in no other way than that he is a certain cause of the things that come to pass, although he makes them without any agitation of his own—so that it can properly be called action, since every action consists in movement. For his very disposition, which he held in mind from eternity, is called his action when it is brought to effect. Nothing new occurs in that disposition when some new work comes to pass through it, nor is God changed by it, since he always holds it equally in his mind. Thus, after the completion of the thing, he remains in the same purpose of disposition as before, willing it to be completed just as he had formerly willed it to be completed.

Just as, therefore, when something is warmed by the sun’s heat, no change occurs thereby either in the sun or in its heat, although the thing warmed is changed; so God is not to be said to be changed when he orders some new thing, although he is the cause or author of a new work or of a change in things [Col. 1105B].

That he cannot move locally, since he is spirit, is taught both by the assertions of philosophers and of saints, as we showed when discussing quantity while writing the *Grammar* [read: *Dialectic*]. Only that which is spatial can be moved locally or be contained somewhere locally, as a body is. Nothing is spatial or can be locally contained unless, by its interposition, it can produce a spatial interval between surrounding things. Thus, if a stylus or some small body is inserted into a continuous body, its interposition immediately makes some interval between surrounding parts that had formerly been continuous with one another. But if whiteness or something incorporeal were present in those parts, none of their continuity would thereby be lost.

Therefore nothing incorporeal can be moved locally, since it cannot be anywhere locally [Col. 1105C]. Above all, God, who is granted to be everywhere in substance, has nowhere to which he can move locally, since he is essentially everywhere. For he cannot move locally—that is, pass from place to place—unless, leaving one place, he migrates to another. But one who is always present in all places by the presence of his substance leaves no place by local movement.

Therefore, when God is said to come into the Virgin or to descend somewhere, this must be understood according to the equal efficacy of his operation, not according to local approach. For what else is it for him to have descended into the Virgin in order to be incarnate, except that he humbled himself to assume our weakness, so that this humiliation of his is understood as his descent? Likewise, whenever God is said to descend or come somewhere, no local approach of his is indicated, but some effect of a new operation [Col. 1105D].

When he is said to come to some persons or to depart from others, this too is understood according to the bestowal or withdrawal of his gifts, not according to a local arrival or departure. For, as has been said, since he always exists everywhere through the presence of his substance, he has nowhere to which he can move locally. Yet I think that his being said to be everywhere “in substance” is said in reference to his power or operation; as though it were said that all things are so present to him in place that he never ceases to work something in them, nor is his power idle anywhere.

For places themselves, and whatever is in them, cannot remain unless they are preserved by him. He is said to be in them in substance where he never ceases to work something by the power of his own substance—either preserving them, as stated, or himself effecting something in them [Col. 1106A]. Even if kings are said to have long hands because they exercise their power in distant places, they cannot accomplish by their own substance what they do through deputies.

Thus the soul is said to be in the body through its substance rather than through local position, because by the strength of its own substance it gives the body life and motion and preserves it from dissolution into decay. By its operation of nourishing and sensing it is wholly present in each member, so as to animate each and sense in each. In the same manner God must be said always to be not only in all places but also in each individual thing through some efficacy of his power. And when he moves all the things in which he is, he himself is not moved in them [Col. 1106B], just as the soul is not moved in the body when it moves each of the members and, as stated, is wholly and simultaneously present in each.

Finally, the objection that God was changed when he became man, so as to become something other than he had been and thereby undergo the greatest movement of substance, called generation, is easily refuted if we weigh the sense of the words rather than the words themselves. For what is it to say that God becomes man except that the divine substance, which is spiritual, unites to itself in one person human nature, which is bodily? That which is spiritual cannot become bodily. Rather, in that union of Christ’s person, in which the divinity of the Word, soul, and flesh are together, these three natures meet in such a way that each of the three substances retains its own nature [Col. 1106C], and none is changed into another.

Thus the divinity joined to humanity does not become either soul or flesh, just as the soul can never become flesh, although in individual human beings soul and flesh are one person. For the soul is a certain spiritual and simple essence, whereas flesh is a human thing, bodily and composed of members. Therefore the one cannot be the other, since the soul can receive no parts whatsoever in its quantity. The Lord himself plainly explains this when he says: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

Just as soul and flesh, joined together in one person, remain distinct in their own natures, so that neither is changed into the other—otherwise they would by no means be called two things—so too the divinity joined to humanity, that is, joined in one person to the human soul and flesh, is by no means converted into its nature [Col. 1107A]. That is, the spiritual substance of God which assumed humanity is not changed into that bodily substance, since it remains altogether what it was before. Thus he assumed what was ours without laying aside what was his.

A change into something else cannot occur unless what existed before ceases to be. But the spiritual substance which was joined to bodily nature was previously spiritual, and it still remains spiritual now; it has not become bodily. Therefore, since God is now, as before, spirit according to the assertion of Truth itself, and what is spirit never becomes bodily or receives parts, how can the Word properly be said to become flesh, or God to become man, when the Word is even now spirit because he is God, as he was before the incarnation?

For man is a bodily thing, composed of members and capable of dissolution. But God is neither a bodily thing nor composed of parts so as to be capable of dissolution [Col. 1107B]. Therefore God is not properly to be called either flesh or man. Otherwise, conversely, man would properly be called God. It would then be necessary to grant that God is something created, or something that has not always existed, since man is certainly a creature and has a beginning.

But far be it from us to maintain that God is any thing which has not always existed, or has not always been God! For this is to confess a new or recent God. Warning us against this perversity, God says: “Israel, if you will listen to me, there shall be no new god in you” (Ps. 80:10 [Vulgate]).

Accordingly, as has been set forth, when God is said to become flesh, or God to be man, this must be understood to mean that the divine substance is joined to the human in one person, not that it becomes that with which it is joined; just as the human soul does not become the flesh to which it is united, nor is converted into its nature. Carefully explaining this, blessed Athanasius, when defending the unity of Christ’s person subsisting in two natures, says of him: “Although he is God and man, yet he is not two, but one Christ. One, however, not by conversion of the Godhead into flesh, but by the assumption of humanity into God. One altogether [Col. 1107D], not by confusion of substance, but by unity of person. For as rational soul and flesh are one man, so God and man are one Christ.”

What he says is this: God and man are one Christ, not two Christs, just as soul and flesh are one man, not two men. For although there is diversity of natures in Christ—namely, divine and human—just as in one man there are corporeal and incorporeal natures, soul and flesh, it does not therefore follow that there must be two Christs, any more than there are two men; nor that there is a diversity of persons, as there is of natures joined together in one person.
