These natures are so distinct in their respective properties that neither substance is in any way converted into the other on account of this union of person.

He explains this consequently when he says: “One, however [Col. 1108A], not by conversion of the Godhead into flesh,” that is, into humanity, “but by the assumption of humanity by God.” For the substance or nature assumed is other than that which assumes it, though the person is not other. Explaining this again, he says: “One altogether by unity of person, not by confusion of substance”; that is, not by a mingling of substances into one nature, or by conversion of one substance into another.

For just as in the one God there are three persons and one substance, so conversely in Christ there are two substances, namely human and divine, but one person in the two substances or natures. Hence the same doctor, earlier in the same Creed of Faith, when showing the diversity of persons in the one substance of God, says: “Now the Catholic faith [Col. 1108B] is this: that we worship one God in Trinity,” etc., “neither confounding the persons,” etc. We should then confound the persons—that is, mingle them with one another—if we maintained that this person was that person; just as, conversely, we should separate God’s substance if we held that there were diverse substances in him. Immediately explaining this carefully, he adds: “For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another,” etc.

Therefore, as in God there is one substance but diverse persons, so conversely in Christ there is one person but diverse substances, divine, as stated, and human. Neither of these has been changed into the other; rather, each retains its own nature in that union of person, and both remain unmixed in their natures. For even in individual wholes [Col. 1108C], different parts come together to compose them, while nevertheless remaining distinct in their own natures, though joined by a certain aggregation; as bones and flesh in a human body, or timber and stones in the construction of a single house.

Thus bones adhering to flesh in one man do not pass into the nature of flesh; nor do stones joined to timbers in one house change their own substance so as to become something other than what they formerly were; nor does flesh joined to soul become other than flesh, nor the nature of its former substance [lacuna]. So neither does divinity, joined to humanity in one person, become other than it was before, although it joins something other to itself in unity of person.

According to this union of person, then, when God is said to have become man, or is granted to be something other than he was originally [Col. 1108D], this must not be understood as a change of substance but as unity of person: namely, that God has joined man to himself in one person and associated with himself in this union a thing of another nature. God, therefore, has not been changed into something other than he was, though, as stated, he has joined something other to himself in this union.

For neither will our souls, when they are joined to their resumed bodies in one person, thereby be made something other than they were, although the body itself is again made alive by being animated, and is advanced from inanimation to animation. Hence the body itself should rather be said to be changed through the soul than the soul because of the body. For the body advances from the soul, and not the soul from the body, into a certain state, receiving from it heat and motion [Col. 1109A], while the soul itself remains immovably in itself. Much less should God, united to man, be said for this reason to become something other, since a creature can contribute nothing to him. Hence we profess God to be wholly exempt from every mutability. For the present, I judge that these remarks concerning the divine power, or matters pertaining to it, are sufficient.

VII.

Let us now proceed to his wisdom. Some have called this the Word; others, reason or mind: that is, as it were, a power of discernment for knowing all things fully, so that its ordering can err in nothing and nothing at all can escape it. Hence also the Son of God is the power of God and the wisdom of God; that is, that power of divine might by which he knows all things, that is, truly [Col. 1109B] discerns them, so that, as has been said, he can err in nothing, nor can anything resist his knowledge.

This knowledge or science of his comprehends future things just as fully as present or past things; and he is always equally certain concerning the former as concerning the latter. Things still said to be unknown to nature or contingent are already wholly certain and determined for him. For nothing can happen except by the ordinance of the divine disposition. Therefore, just as God cannot be ignorant of what he foreordains concerning the future, so he cannot fail to foreknow its occurrence.

Things, therefore, which are said to occur by chance with respect to our certainty, and not to proceed from free choice, occur with respect to him neither by chance nor without free choice. For when philosophers, defining chance, say: “Chance [Col. 1109C] is an unforeseen occurrence of a thing, arising from converging causes begun for another purpose,” they mean unforeseen with respect to us or the nature of creatures, not with respect to the ordering of divine providence.

It is as though one said: What happens by chance happens in such a way that from no established arrangement of nature could we know beforehand that it would occur. For although eclipses of the sun or moon often happen contrary to our expectation, they occur naturally, not fortuitously; and it has been fixed in the constitution of things how we might know them. But when someone digging a field for agriculture finds a treasure, this discovery is called fortuitous. For it plainly occurs from diverse causes begun for another end [Col. 1109D], and, as we said, unexpectedly. The treasure is found because it had been hidden there and because that man was digging the field. These two causes came together for the discovery, though they had been begun for another purpose. For the man who hid the treasure there did not intend that the other should find it; nor did the latter dig with the intention of seeking a treasure, but of cultivating the field.

Both causes, then, from which that discovery occurs, were directed to another end; and for that reason the discovery proceeds rather by chance than from free choice. For in free choice, the intention of the thing which results from it comes first. Thus, if I deliberate about going to church and then carry this out by the freedom of my choice, I accomplish what I intended. Hence this should be said to occur not so much by chance [Col. 1110A] as by reason. Yet neither of these occurs naturally; rather, both alike proceed from some will of ours, not from any establishment of nature compelling us to this, so that it is called voluntary rather than necessary.

Defining free choice, the philosophers said: “Free judgment concerning the will.” For choice is the very deliberation or judgment of the mind by which anyone proposes to do or omit something. This judgment is free when it is compelled by no force of nature to carry out what it has proposed, but has equally within its power both to do and to omit it. Therefore, where there is no reasoning of the mind by which it can be deliberated and judged whether something should be done or omitted, so that both alternatives are equally within our power, there is no free choice at all.

For although brute animals can do or omit some things according to their will, nevertheless, because they lack rational judgment, they do not possess free choice. If anyone also wills and purposes to do something that is not within his power, or that would occur equally without his own purpose, he has no free choice in this matter. For example, we often propose to do things which, deceived, we trust that we can accomplish; and sometimes we strive or desire that things happen which would happen no less without our purpose. Thus, if persons are compelled to die by prolonged punishments, and desire and strive for death itself to end their torments, when this happens they do not in any way attain through their free choice that which [Col. 1110B] would have happened to them no less even if they had given it no prior thought.

This definition of free choice does not at all apply to God, but only to those who can change their will and turn it to contraries; that is, those in whose power it is both to omit and to do what is chosen. Indeed, some have restricted free choice so as to grant it only to those who can do both good and evil. Blessed Jerome too, following their opinion, says among other things in that homily on the prodigal son: “God alone is he in whom sin has no place; all other beings, since they possess free choice, can turn their will in either direction.”

But anyone who examines free choice more carefully will say that it is absent from no one who does good [Col. 1110C], and most especially not from God and all those who are strengthened by such great blessedness that they can no longer fall into sin. For the farther anyone is from sin and the more inclined toward good, the freer is his judgment in choosing good, in proportion as he stands farther from that ultimate slavery of sin concerning which it is written: “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34).

Therefore, free choice is generally and most truly said to exist when anyone can voluntarily and without compulsion carry out what he has determined by reason. This freedom of choice belongs equally and unquestionably to God and to human beings, whoever are not then deprived of the capacity of willing, and especially, as we said [Col. 1111A], to those who can no longer sin at all. For although they cannot sin or withdraw themselves from the good they do, because they ought not to do so, they do not therefore act through the necessity of any compulsion; for if they did not will it, they would by no means be compelled to do it.

Blessed Augustine, carefully observing this, establishes it in these words in Book XXII of *The City of God*: “As the first immortality was that which Adam lost by sinning—not being able to die—so the first free choice was being able not to sin, and the last is not being able to sin.” Again: “Surely God himself—because he cannot sin, is he therefore to be denied free choice?” etc.

Whatever we do, whether by chance or after deliberation, because we do it by God’s most excellent ordering and providence, for the reason why it ought to occur, proceeds from his free choice, if not from our own. And although we do things by chance, nothing nevertheless happens by chance with respect to him, whose providence precedes all things and by whose ordering whatever we do occurs. Hence the aforementioned doctor, in *Eighty-Three Questions*, question 26, says: “Whatever happens by chance happens rashly. Therefore, if some things happen in the world by chance, the whole world is not administered by Providence.” Again: “That good by participation in which other things are good is good not for another reason, but through itself. This we also call divine providence. Therefore nothing happens in the world by chance.”

It is as though he plainly said: Nothing happens which does not proceed from some providence, at least divine providence. Yet we do not therefore say that those wholly err who profess that very many things happen by chance with respect to our uncertainty, as stated. When, according to the philosophers, they call things unknown to nature those that happen by chance—that is, when no nature of a thing is sufficient to know this beforehand, so as to be certain about it—they attend not at all to the divine majesty here, but only to the nature of creatures.

Likewise, when they call impossible things that happen through miracles, or profess that they occur contrary to nature—as when a virgin gives birth or a blind person afterwards sees—they undoubtedly look to the customary course of nature or to the primordial causes of things, not to the excellence of divine power. It is clear that this power can by its own nature accomplish whatever it has decreed and can alter the natures of things beyond their customary course in whatever way it wills [Col. 1111D]. If even now it formed a man from the clay of the earth or produced a woman from a man’s rib, as was done with the first parents, surely no one would judge that this did not occur contrary to, or beyond, nature; because, as stated, the establishment of primordial causes could in no way suffice for this unless God, beyond the customary course, imparted to things by his own will a certain power enabling this to happen from them—the same will by which he could create all things from nothing.

From this it is clear, as we have already mentioned more than once, that philosophical discussions, by which especially the natures of things are investigated, are so content with the natures of creatures and their daily operation that they scarcely, if ever, dare to touch that supreme nature of divine power, which commands all natures [Col. 1112A], and to whose will nature itself ought properly to be said to obey. Rather, they hold all their rules to stand wholly below or outside it. Thus, when they call something possible or impossible—that is, consonant or repugnant to nature—they measure these matters by the capacity of creatures alone, not by the power of divine might.

From this it appears how true is what we mentioned above concerning that rule of the philosophers, “of which the antecedent and consequent are possible”: they apply this only to the name of creatures. Perhaps this needed to be noted beforehand for what follows, where, according to that ancient complaint, as philosophy calls it, all things seem to happen necessarily in accordance with the immutability of divine providence [Col. 1112B].

It remains for us now to discuss this, since it plainly pertains especially to divine wisdom. For this wisdom, in foreseeing future things, is called providence or foreknowledge. God’s foreseeing is his providing; or foreknowing future things means knowing before they occur all things that are to occur, and being already as certain about them as about present or past things, as we confirmed above by reasoning.

But if we examine carefully the philosophers themselves, and especially Aristotle, so discriminating in his argumentative reasoning that he deserved to be called the chief of the Peripatetics, that is, of the dialecticians, we shall find in them how we may refute pseudo-philosophers [Col. 1112C] and dismantle not their arguments but their sophisms. By these they are accustomed so to disturb the faith of the simple concerning God’s providence that they assert that not only good things but even evil things occur necessarily, and that sins cannot in any way be avoided by us, but that each person necessarily commits whatever sin he commits—since, namely, this too has been foreseen by God, whose providence plainly cannot in any way be deceived.

Breaking this snare of theirs, let us consider that very strong web which Aristotle weaves in the first book of *On Interpretation* (*Peri Hermeneias*, περὶ ἑρμηνείας), in order to establish even for propositions about the future that property of contradiction which he had stated generally of all propositions: namely, that of every affirmation [Col. 1112D] and negation one must be true, just as the other must be false. For example: “There will be a naval battle tomorrow,” and “There will not be a naval battle tomorrow,” are a divided affirmation and negation. Hence one of them must be true and the other false, since neither can both be true at once nor both false at once; nor is there any proposition which is not necessarily either true or false.

Hence this or that must be true: that is, a battle of this kind must occur tomorrow. Aristotle carefully teaches us how to determine these words, which have different consequences, so that we may preserve and defend everywhere the aforementioned property of contradiction. At last he carefully instructs us concerning the predication of “necessary,” both simple and absolute and qualified.

He says, therefore, that it is necessary that there will or will not be a naval battle tomorrow. Yet it does not follow that it is necessary that a naval battle will occur tomorrow or that it is necessary that it will not occur tomorrow [Col. 1113A]. For this proposition, “It is necessary that there will be, or will not be, a naval battle tomorrow,” has two senses. One is a false disjunctive hypothetical, as if, repeating the term “necessary,” we said: “It is necessary that there will be a naval battle tomorrow, or it is necessary that there will not be one tomorrow.” The other is a true categorical proposition, having a disjunctive subject, as though the disjunction were placed in the subject and the term “necessary” placed once in the predicate. It is as though we said: “That there will be, or will not be, a naval battle tomorrow—this whole thing is necessary”; that is, it is necessary that it occur or not occur tomorrow.

In this latter manner, the term “necessary,” used once and predicated absolutely, makes the statement true; and its predication is truly applied generally to any affirmations and their negations, so that we say of each: “It is necessary that this or that be true.” This is what Aristotle meant in assigning the property of contradiction. Yet we cannot therefore apply absolutely the predication of “necessary” to either one of them, so as truly to say that it is necessary that this be true or that it be false [Col. 1114A].

We add “absolutely” because he teaches there that a qualified predication of necessity can be applied to all true propositions of this kind, saying: “Therefore, what is, when it is, necessarily is; and what is not, when it is not, necessarily is not. But not therefore is it to be said simply that it is necessary.” For such a qualified predication of necessity does not entail a simple one: because it is necessary that a thing be while it is, it must not therefore be granted that it be said simply to be necessary—that is, wholly inevitable that it be.

By this weighty and rational teaching of so great a philosopher, the objection previously mentioned concerning divine providence can readily be refuted. “Divine providence,” they say, “cannot be deceived.”

The rest is lacking.

[Col. 1113]

# PETER ABAELARD’S *CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY*

(Edited by D. Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. V, col. 1139, from a manuscript codex of Marmoutier at Tours.)

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

It is not my intention to discuss at length here Peter Abaelard’s changing fortunes, since many before me have undertaken this subject and have pursued it not unsuccessfully. He himself also vividly described nearly the whole course of his life in the *History of His Calamities*. Born at Le Pallet, a town in the diocese of Nantes, to parents as devout as they were noble, Berengar and Lucia, and possessing a ready and facile intellect for letters, he wholly renounced the court of Mars in order to be reared in Minerva’s bosom. In dialectic he obtained Roscelin as his teacher; in philosophy, William of Champeaux, archdeacon of the Church of Paris and a most celebrated professor of Peripatetic philosophy.

From a disciple he soon became a master. Since he possessed a remarkable facility for teaching, easily surpassed everyone in disputation, and had so many students flocking to him from every quarter that other teachers seemed deserted in comparison with him, this restless man acquired, as commonly happens, quite a number of rivals. Abaelard attributed this to his opponents’ envy; we attribute it to his own arrogance.

He then went to Laon and heard Anselm, the most celebrated professor of theology. But after attending only a few of his lectures, he despised his teacher and himself undertook the office of teaching. This won him new rivals. Forced to depart and returning to Paris, he completed the lectures he had begun at Laon and quickly spread his reputation.

“But because,” he says, “prosperity always inflates fools, worldly tranquility weakens the vigor of the mind, and easily dissolves it through carnal enticements, when I thought that I alone remained a philosopher in the world and feared no further disturbance, I began to loosen the reins of lust.” And while, as he himself says again, he was wholly absorbed in pride and luxury, it happened that Fulbert, a distinguished canon of the Church of Paris, entrusted to him for instruction the exceedingly beautiful girl Héloïse, whom he had taken care to train in every kind of learning, ostensibly in order that she might acquire more advanced scholarship. In other words, to use Abaelard’s own words, he entrusted a tender lamb to a hungry wolf.

And indeed, not long afterwards he seduced the young woman. When she conceived, he secretly carried her away to Brittany, where she bore a son in the house of one of his sisters, naming him Astrolabe. When Fulbert learned of this, he blazed with such anger that he could not be placated unless Abaelard married his violated niece, though she resisted. But the force of his rage did not stop there. For when Abaelard sent Héloïse to the convent of nuns at Argenteuil, where she had formerly been educated, and clothed her in monastic dress, Fulbert became so enraged that he had Abaelard, sleeping at night and thinking of no such thing, made a eunuch.

To swallow so great a humiliation, Abaelard fled into the hiding places of monastic cloisters, becoming a monk at the monastery of Saint-Denis neither voluntarily nor from devotion to conversion. Those who undertook to defend his cause thereafter extolled him, no less than Héloïse, with extraordinary praises and almost equated both with the saints themselves. Yet what the sanctity of each was may readily be inferred from their letters.

Certainly, as concerns Héloïse, who would not abominate these words from a letter to Abaelard written at least ten years after her conversion? “Although the name of wife seems holier and more binding, the title of mistress has always been sweeter to me; or, if you are not offended, that of concubine or whore . . . I call God as witness: if Augustus, ruling the whole world, should deem me worthy of the honor of marriage and should secure the whole world for my possession, I should regard it as dearer and more worthy to be called your prostitute than his empress.” And in another letter to him: “In every condition of my life, God knows, I still fear offending you more than God; I seek to please you more than him. It was not divine love that drew me to the religious habit, but yours.”

Nor, after she was placed over the monastery of the Paraclete, does she appear to have followed a stricter discipline of the rule, even in food; rather, that she lived an altogether soft life is sufficiently indicated in another letter to Abaelard, where she writes: “It should be considered quite enough for our weakness, and accounted a great thing, if, living continently and without private property and occupied in divine offices, we equal the leaders of the Church or religious laypeople in food.” From this it is evident that she was content with the manner of life of religious laypeople in food and rejected every austerity which nevertheless befits repentant sinners.

We report these things not because we wish Héloïse’s reputation—she whom some rather foolishly compare with martyrs—to be diminished, but lest we seem to approve vice.

Abaelard changed his clothing but not his heart: in the cloister he was the same man he had been in the world, everywhere restless and acquiring new rivals. If we believe him, the abbey to which he withdrew was “of a very worldly and most shameful life; its abbot, the greater than the others in rank, was so much the worse in life and the more notorious in infamy. Frequently and vehemently rebuking their intolerable filthiness, now privately, now publicly,” he made himself burdensome and hateful to all.

If this were true, Abaelard would be far more blameworthy for choosing to live among so many and such dissolute monks. But although perhaps no very strict discipline flourished at the monastery of Saint-Denis, the stain branded upon it by Abaelard was long ago wiped away by André Duchesne in his notes to the *History of His Calamities*. There he demonstrates from the charters of the same monastery that not long before Adam, abbot of Saint-Denis, that monastery had been restored to a purer discipline of the Rule through the ministry of Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny; and he proves Adam’s outstanding charity toward the poor, his piety, and his concern for the honor and enlargement of divine worship.

About this time Abaelard composed for his pupils the theological treatise *On Unity and Trinity*, full of errors. Denounced by Alberic and Rudolf, masters of the schools of Rheims, at the Council of Soissons, it was soon condemned to the fire, and he himself was ordered to throw it into the flames with his own hands.

Returning to the monastery, he stirred up new disturbances among the brethren over Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, whom Bede identifies with Dionysius the Areopagite. This gave the man, impatient of any yoke, an occasion to flee secretly from the monastery by night; and, though recalled by the abbot, he could not be persuaded to return.

A few days later Adam died and Suger succeeded him. When Suger pressed Abaelard to return to the monastery, Abaelard secured, through the intervention both of friends and secular powers, that the abbot at last granted him leave to live as a monk—not wherever he might find a suitable place, as he had requested, but to withdraw to whatever solitude he wished, provided that he subjected himself to no abbey.

Delighted at attaining his desire, he laid the foundations of the monastery of the Paraclete in the diocese of Troyes. Students flocked to him from every quarter and turned the solitude, as it were, into a city. Later made abbot of the monastery of Saint-Gildas-de-Rhuys, in the diocese of Vannes in Armorican Brittany, he found himself there among “Christians and monks far fiercer and worse than pagans.” He abandoned the office and returned to the wilderness of Troyes.

Abaelard paints the monks of Rhuys in the blackest colors; he deserves no more belief in this than when he slandered Abbot Adam and the brethren of Saint-Denis as living most shamefully. It is far more likely that, grieving to be separated by so great a distance of land from his beloved Héloïse and his friends, he abandoned the monastery of Rhuys.

Certainly, at the time when Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, expelled the nuns from Argenteuil for unchastities in order to establish monks of his own monastery there, Abaelard judged it advantageous to provide for the needs of Héloïse—who at that time held the office of prioress in the monastery of Argenteuil—and her sisters. He did this when, abandoning the monastery of Rhuys, he received them into his cell at the Paraclete, which, together with its attached oratory, he granted them. The donation was confirmed by the bishop of Troyes, indeed also by Pope Innocent II.

Up to this point Abaelard had restrained his pen; or, if perhaps he had written anything, he had abstained from the errors condemned at the Council of Soissons. But when he observed that the opponents he had then suffered had departed this life, he could no longer contain himself. “For when nearly all the masters of ecclesiastical doctrine had died,” says William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, “the domestic enemy of the Church, rushing as it were into an empty commonwealth, seized for himself a singular mastery in it: doing in Holy Scripture what he was accustomed to do in dialectic—his own inventions, yearly novelties; a censor of faith, not a disciple; a corrector, not an imitator.”

By chance, William came upon a reading of a certain little book by this man, entitled *Theology of Peter Abaelard*. Its title made him curious to read it; he found certain things which troubled him considerably, noted them, and appended why they troubled him. “There were then two little books containing nearly the same material,” says William, “except that sometimes more was found in one and less in the other.” He sent these, together with his observations—that is, with his refutation of the errors he had found—to the venerable Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, so that from reading them they might judge more readily whether he had been rightly troubled.

Upon reading the chapters containing the errors, Bernard was horrified and wrote back to William: “I judge your concern both just and necessary. And that it is not idle is shown by the little book striking and stopping the mouths of those who speak iniquity.” Yet, lest he seem rashly to judge the author himself, he appointed William a day after Easter on which they might meet together, read, and examine Abaelard’s *Theology* more attentively.

When, by diligent reading of his books, they had detected the poison contained in them, Bernard, “in his customary goodness and kindness, desiring that the error be corrected and the man not confounded, approached him in private admonition. He dealt with him so modestly and so reasonably that Abaelard himself, moved to compunction, promised to correct everything according to Bernard’s judgment [Note: [Col. 1115] Geoffrey, Book III, *On the Life of St Bernard*, chap. 5, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXV.].”

It was worthwhile to note these things, so that it may appear how undeservedly—indeed, how unjustly—Otto of Freising wrote that the most holy abbot was “so jealous through zeal for Christian religion as, through habitual gentleness, in some measure credulous” in Abaelard’s case. But this man, “arrogant and trusting only in his own genius, so that he scarcely humbled himself enough to descend from the height [Col. 1117] of his mind to listen to teachers,” as Otto of Freising himself, Abaelard’s defender, admits, after the man of God had departed from him, was goaded by wicked counsels and recoiled from his sounder resolution.

Indeed, having sought out the metropolitan of Sens because a great council was soon to be held in his church, he accused the abbot of Clairvaux of secretly disparaging his books, and added that he was prepared publicly to defend his writings, asking that the aforesaid abbot be summoned to the council if he had anything to say. These facts come from Geoffrey, the accurate as well as devout author of the *Life of Saint Bernard*.

Otto of Freising, on the contrary, writes that Abaelard had been summoned by the bishops and Abbot Bernard to a hearing at Sens. But, apart from the fact that the authority of Geoffrey, a domestic author free from every suspicion of falsehood, ought to prevail over Otto, a foreign author, the fathers of the Council of Sens expressly affirm that Abaelard was not summoned to the council by Saint Bernard, but Bernard by Abaelard.

For in their letter to Pope Innocent, which in the new edition of Bernard’s letters is no. 337, after saying that Abaelard had endured with insufficient patience and excessive distress Bernard’s admonition first privately and then publicly, before witnesses, to correct his errors, they say:

“Master Peter began repeatedly to press us, and would not desist until, writing on this subject to the lord abbot of Clairvaux, we summoned him to appear before us at Sens on an appointed day, namely the octave of Pentecost. For Master Peter called him and offered himself ready to prove and defend the positions for which the lord abbot of Clairvaux had rebuked him in the manner stated above. But the lord abbot replied to us that he would not come on the appointed day, nor would he dispute against Peter.”

From Bernard’s modesty Abelard was made more arrogant. He began on every side to summon and entreat his disciples to come to the forthcoming disputation between himself and the abbot of Clairvaux, in order that, together with him, they might defend both his position and his learning. Bernard, however, moved by the counsels of eminent men—lest his absence give scandal to the people and add horns to his adversary—at last agreed to come to the council, and did so sorrowfully, not without shedding tears. Present at the council were Louis VII, king of the Franks; William, the religious count of Nevers; the archbishop of Rheims with certain of his suffragan bishops; many abbots; and very learned clerics.

Saint Bernard produced Abelard’s book of *Theology* before the assembly and set forth the propositions he had marked in it as absurd—indeed, plainly heretical—so that Abelard might either deny having written them, or, if he acknowledged them as his own, prove or correct them. Abelard was unwilling to do either; rather, in order to gain time from the most equitable judges, whom he himself had selected, he appealed, contrary to the canons, to the Apostolic See. If we believe Otto of Freising, Abelard refused to answer because he “feared a popular uprising.” But with King Louis, Count William, and other noblemen present, what was there for him to fear from the people? Hence it appears that Otto learned what he writes about Abelard and the Council of Sens not so much from truthful witnesses as from uncertain popular rumors.

It is fairer to credit Geoffrey, author of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, who was Abelard’s disciple when these events occurred, writing as follows:

> “But when he had been warned by that eminent advocate of the Catholic faith”—namely Bernard—“that, since he now knew that nothing was to be done against his person, he should answer, being heard as freely as securely, and endured with every patience, not struck by any sentence—he refused this altogether as well. For he afterwards confessed to his own people, as they say, that at that hour his memory had in some measure been disturbed, his reason clouded, and his inward understanding had fled.”

Thus Abelard was not deprived of liberty to defend himself; nor did he refuse because of fear of a popular disturbance, but because he was utterly unable to sustain an unjust cause. Nevertheless, out of reverence for the Apostolic See, to which he had appealed, the council, having condemned his perverse doctrines, spared his person.

After leaving the council, Abelard wrote an *Apology* for his errors, in which he attacked Saint Bernard in a rather sharper style. We learn this certainly from the disputation of the anonymous abbot against Abelard. In its second book we read:

> “In his *Apologetic*, in his reply upon this chapter, Peter, driven by furies, raves; and he attacks the man of God with such excessive intemperance that he would assert not that Bernard speaks the things he says, but that Satan, who transforms himself into an angel of light, speaks through him.”

And in the third book:

> “But in his *Apology* he is carried away much more violently by a spirit of dizziness and suffers more unhappily; for, with more careful treatment and as though his powers had been gathered into one, he pursues this chapter”—namely, *On the Power of God*—“more fully than the others.”

Afterwards he resolved to go to Rome to defend his cause before the pope, relying on the assistance of friends and disciples, of whom he had no few there. But when he arrived at Cluny, he heard that the articles of his errors had been duly condemned by Innocent II. He was therefore compelled to halt there. Admonished by Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, to be reconciled to Bernard and to remove from his utterances, and erase from his books, anything that he had either written or said which offended Catholic ears, he went with the Cistercian abbot to Clairvaux, retracted all his false doctrines, and, his earlier complaints having been silenced, returned into favor with the most holy abbot.

We possess this retraction prefixed to the published works of Abelard; the editor chose to entitle it an *Apology*. Yet it must be entirely distinguished from his *Apology* and should more properly be called a *Retraction*. Returning to Cluny, he lived there religiously for two years; and at last, in the priory of Saint Marcellus at Chalon, he rested in the bosom of the Church.

Against Abelard wrote William, abbot of Saint-Thierry; Saint Bernard; and the anonymous abbot, whom some consider identical with Geoffrey. Geoffrey, formerly Abelard’s disciple, became a monk of Clairvaux in 1140, Bernard’s secretary, and after Robert and Fastred became his successor. We have the works of the first and the last in the Cistercian library; in them they reproduce Abelard’s very words which they attack.

Yet Abelard had certain defenders, above all Otto of Freising, who was little fair to Saint Bernard—an outsider and, as we think, not very well informed. His authority certainly ought not to prevail over that of Abbot William, Saint Bernard, or Geoffrey, who knew the man, had attentively read his writings, and were free from every suspicion of improper bias. Still less should the authority of Peter Berengar of Poitiers, Abelard’s disciple, prevail. He undertook Abelard’s defense expressly and wrote an *Apologetic*, bearing with it its own condemnation. It may more properly be called an insulting pamphlet against Saint Bernard, a work born in darkness and worthy of eternal oblivion. Indeed, he offered not even a single word in defense of his master, to demonstrate his Catholic faith, or to attack his adversaries, although he had boldly promised to do so. Rather, having himself become sounder in judgment, he retracted his insulting writings in a letter to the bishop of Mende and wished them to be regarded as unwritten:

> “For,” he says, “as time went on, my judgment increased, and I went over, as the saying is, at the feet into the opinion of the abbot. I did not wish to be the defender of the articles brought against Abelard, because, although they might have a sound meaning, they did not sound sound.”

Perhaps these matters ought to suffice for those who in our age have undertaken to defend Abelard’s cause and do not shrink from accusing Saint Bernard of precipitate judgment against him. They could doubtless be adequately answered if we possessed Abelard’s *Introduction to Theology* entire. For it is mutilated in the printed editions, and we have not found it complete in manuscripts. Some light may be supplied for its deficiency by the treatise *On the Trinity*, which we here publish from a very ancient handwritten manuscript of Marmoutier. It seems certain to me that this is the same work as the treatise *On the Trinity* condemned to the flames at the Council of Soissons, or one of those two booklets which fell into the hands of Abbot William and which contained nearly the same things, except that sometimes more was found in one and less in the other.

Abelard asserts in the *History of His Calamities* that two matters in particular from his book were condemned at the Council of Soissons. One, on p. 21, was that “although God begot God, and there is only one God, he nevertheless denied that God begot himself.” Abelard says he proved this by the authority of Saint Augustine, book I of *On the Trinity*, where we read:

> “He who thinks God to be of such power that he himself begot himself is all the more mistaken, because not only is God not so constituted, but neither is any spiritual or bodily creature. For there is absolutely no thing that generates itself.”

These statements are indeed found in our treatise together with the same authority of Saint Augustine. The other, on p. 24, was his assertion that “God the Father alone is omnipotent,” a proposition readily inferred from what is read in this treatise, as will appear from passages cited below.

What Abbot William of Saint-Thierry says in writing to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and to Saint Bernard—that two booklets under the title *Theology* by Abelard had come into his hands, “containing nearly the same things, except that sometimes more was found in one and less in the other”—perfectly agrees with our treatise if it is compared with Abelard’s *Introduction to Theology*. Indeed, the first and fifth treatises of our book are found nearly complete in the *Introduction to Theology*, almost word for word; and in that work we also read several things occurring in the other books of our treatise. Thus no room remains for doubt that it is one of those two booklets which fell into Abbot William’s hands, and perhaps the very one condemned at Soissons about twenty years earlier, to which Abelard may have added some things.

Whether it was justly committed to the flames by the fathers of the Council of Soissons, and attacked by Abbot William, Saint Bernard, and the other anonymous abbot as containing perverse doctrines, fair-minded and learned readers will not find it difficult to judge from the following propositions found in the ensuing treatise.

1. First, in the chapter-headings of the books of his *Theology*, he says “that all human beings naturally possess faith in the Trinity,” excluding not even Jews and Gentiles from this benefit. For thus he writes near the end of book IV:

> “For since God’s being Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is, as we have said, God’s being power that generates, as stated, wisdom that is begotten, and goodness that proceeds; since no person of discernment, whether Jew or Gentile, doubts this, this faith seems lacking to no one. We too concede this, following the Apostle, who says: ‘What is known of God is manifest to them’; as though he said: ‘They perceive by reason what pertains to divinity, because natural reason teaches every person these things about God.’”

2. In the chapter-headings he so commends pagan philosophers “that they seem worthy even for God to deign to reveal to them the secrets of his faith.” And in book I he attributes this revelation not to divine grace but to their continence, in these words:

> “Then the sobriety itself of their most continent life acquired this for them by a certain merit,”

namely, the knowledge of God.

3. Yet he grants this privilege pre-eminently to the Platonists:

> “Let that greatest of philosophers, Plato, also be considered, and his followers, who, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers, above the other pagan philosophers, in attending to the Christian faith, plainly set forth after the prophets the sum of the whole Trinity. They declare that the mind, which they call *nous* [νοῦν], was born from God and is coeternal with him—that is, the Son, whom we call the Wisdom of God, eternally begotten from God the Father. Nor do they appear to have omitted the person of the Holy Spirit, when they asserted that the soul of the world was the third person after God and *nous* [νοῦς].”

His adversaries could not tolerate Abelard’s assertion that the Holy Spirit is the soul of the world. I do not, however, deny that Abelard tried to bend the words of the Platonists into a Catholic sense. But he did so altogether contrary to the mind of Plato and his followers, who made *nous*, or mind, inferior to the highest God, and the soul of the world inferior to God and to *nous*, or mind. Saint Augustine indeed teaches in *The City of God* that Plato admitted many gods. Saint Bernard therefore rightly rebukes Abelard because “while he labors greatly to make Plato a Christian, he proves himself a pagan.”

Abelard tried to make not Plato alone but all his disciples Christians. For not long after the words already cited from his first book, he adds:

> “We have also learned from many testimonies of the saints that the Platonic school agrees with the Catholic faith.”

And shortly afterward:

> “From this,” he says, “it is clear that the Platonic school has always greatly assented to faith in the holy Trinity, and that Plato and his followers distinguish and describe it more carefully than the other philosophers.”

Then, recounting what Valerius Maximus writes—that a swarm of bees settled on Plato’s mouth while he was asleep as a little child—he attributes this wonder not to the sweetness of Plato’s eloquence, as poets do, but says:

> “I do not doubt that it should be interpreted more excellently and suitably by referring this miracle to the glory of divine dignity: that God might grant him this token of prophecy, since through him he was to disclose more carefully the secrets of his divinity. For it was fitting that the supreme philosopher and his followers should bear especially abundant witness to the Word—that is, the Word and Wisdom of God the Father—of the supreme Wisdom, which is Christ.”

4. He gives the gift of faith not only to Platonists but to all philosophers. Thus in book II:

> “Perhaps all philosophers were Gentiles by nation, but not by faith.”

5. He expressly asserts that the mystery not only of the Holy Trinity but also of the Incarnation of the Word was revealed to them:

> “Who would also assert that the faith of the Incarnation was revealed to none of those philosophers, as it was to the Sibyl, though it does not appear expressly in their writings?”

6. From principles of this kind he concludes that heavenly blessedness ought by no means be denied to philosophers:

> “We seem compelled by no reason to despair concerning the salvation of such Gentiles, who before the coming of the Redeemer, instructed by no written law, were by nature doing, according to the Apostle, the things of the law, and were a law unto themselves” (Rom. I).

And not long afterward:

> “We have introduced these matters lest anyone, even after the law had been given and until the coming of Christ, despair of the salvation of believing Gentiles, if they lived soberly and justly without receiving the sacraments, among whom certain philosophers are known to have shone both in life and doctrine.”

And again:

> “Why should we be compelled to doubt concerning philosophers, most illustrious before Christ’s coming both in faith and in life, that they obtained forgiveness?”

7. Abelard was far more certain of the salvation of philosophers than of that of catechumens dying without baptism. Hence, shortly before the end of book II, he rejects Ambrose’s statement that one ought by no means despair of the salvation of the emperor Valentinian, who died a catechumen [Col. 1121], “since this,” he says, “appears wholly opposed not only to the Gospel but also to the holy doctors.”

8. He not obscurely prefers his philosophers even to the Jews themselves, whom God had chosen as his own people. Thus in book II:

> “For it is established that they”—the philosophers—“had this end set before them: namely, the attainment of eternal life. This is the end which the Lord himself assigned to us, and which Israel paid less attention to, being more subject to hope and ambition for earthly happiness than to desire for eternal things. Hence for those worshippers of the letter no reward for observing the law according to the letter is promised or to be expected in the law except earthly prosperity, which they pursue with their whole desire.”

9. Among philosophers he does not hesitate to compare Socrates with holy martyrs. For according to him, both sacred and secular writings record that Socrates “died as though a martyr, certain of his reward.”

10. In order to make Socrates a saint, he was not ashamed to excuse what that philosopher had prescribed to his followers concerning community of wives, twisting his words into figurative senses contrary to Socrates’ manifest intention. For Socrates, as Abelard himself admits, “established that wives also should be common, so that no one might seek his own children,” since their true fathers would be unknown.

11. These words of Abelard in book II certainly do not seem tolerable:

> “Moses also said that all things were made very good by God; but Plato seems to assign somewhat more praise to divine goodness.”

12. He does not hesitate even to attribute true miracles to the pagan emperor Vespasian, as may be seen shortly before the end of book II.

13. In book IV he attributes omnipotence to the Father alone, a certain power to the Son, and no power to the Holy Spirit. Thus he writes:

> “Let us therefore posit God the Father, as we have indicated above, as the divine power, and God the Son as the divine Wisdom; and let us consider that Wisdom itself is a certain power, since it is namely the power of truly discerning, foreseeing, and deliberating all things, so that nothing capable of deceiving it or lying hidden from it may exist.”

And shortly afterward:

> “But the Son’s being begotten from the Father is the divine Wisdom’s being, in the way defined, from the divine power; since Wisdom itself, as stated, is a certain power, and Wisdom itself is as it were a certain portion of God’s power, which is omnipotence, just as any son is in some manner called a certain portion of his parents,”

etc. And somewhat later:

> “The Spirit is called from breathing; whence Truth says: ‘The Spirit breathes where it wills’ (John III.8). Therefore by his very name he is said rather to proceed from the Father and the Son than to be begotten. For Goodness itself, which is denoted by that name, is not any power or wisdom, since to be good is not to be wise or powerful,”

etc.

Saint Bernard, Abbot William of Saint-Thierry, and the anonymous abbot rose vehemently against this doctrine concerning the persons of the Trinity. And rightly so. Yet there are some who, defending Abelard’s cause, boast that Bernard and the others who wrote against him entirely failed to grasp his meaning, because he expressly asserts that the Son and Holy Spirit are omnipotent just as the Father is. He teaches this in more than one place.

But this was not unknown either to Bernard, Abbot William, or the other anonymous abbot, who had read Abelard’s books attentively, not carelessly. They observed, however, that what he rightly asserted in one place he also destroyed in another—not merely by words, but by comparisons confirming his words and leaving no room for doubt: the comparison of bronze and a bronze seal, wax and a waxen image, matter and what is made of matter, genus and species, animal and human being, one of which extends much more widely than the other. Thus in book IV:

> “Therefore divine Wisdom is from divine Power, as a waxen image is from wax, or as, according to philosophers, species itself is said to be from genus—although species and genus are the same thing, as a human being is the same as an animal, and a waxen image the same as wax. For the waxen image is from wax, and the human being from animal, in such a way that from the fact that something is a waxen image it follows that it is wax, and from the fact that something is a human being it follows that it is an animal; but not conversely. For power extends both to discerning and to doing other things, just as wax extends both to a waxen image and to what is not a waxen image, and animal both to human being and to non-human being.”

Certainly Abelard never alleged, either in private or public discussions with Bernard, that Bernard had taken his words in a hostile interpretation. Rather, when Bernard pressed him at the Council of Sens either to correct the error or to state anything he had to answer to the charges, he refused to do both. At the end of book III of this treatise, when the objection is raised against him why he distinguishes Father and Son through power and wisdom rather than through eternity or another attribute, he gives no reason but answers thus:

> “To this it must be answered that we have not undertaken the task of showing why the divine persons are distinguished in this mode rather than another, but of showing that they may fittingly be understood in the mode in which they are distinguished, and of defending our faith,”

etc.

Finally, in his *Retraction*, or confession of faith, he gives no benign interpretation to his words, but boldly denies and emphatically denies that he ever said them:

> “But as to the malicious accusation against me that I wrote that the Father is full power, the Son a certain power, and the Holy Spirit no power: I abhor, detest, and, as is most just, condemn those words together with their author, not merely as heretical but as diabolical. If anyone finds them in my writings, I declare myself not only a heretic but even a heresiarch.”

Here the anonymous abbot, who had once been Abelard’s disciple and thus could know his teaching extremely well, rightly rebukes Abelard’s impudence in denying that he had said in the clearest words what he explicitly asserted. For if his words admit of a favorable interpretation, why did he not offer it here? Certainly one who asserts that “all human beings naturally” possess faith in the Holy Trinity cannot be said to think rightly concerning the Trinity.

14. Abelard is also reproved by his adversaries because he asserted that the Word was made flesh not in order to redeem humankind from sin, but solely to instruct people by words and inflame them by examples to the love of God. In this treatise, although he does not altogether deny that the Son of God redeemed humankind from sins, he nevertheless asserts that instruction was the principal end of his Incarnation. Thus in book IV:

> “He performed all things in the flesh in order that true Wisdom might instruct us in what would suffice for salvation.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For this alone and especially God was incarnate: that he might enlighten his predestined people through the visible clothing of flesh truly assumed by him.”

And not much earlier he had said:

> “Through this Incarnation the light of divine Wisdom shone forth upon carnal people; and this alone, or especially this, was the benefit God intended to impart to us in this clothing of flesh, for which reason he was called the Angel of Counsel, or Counselor,”

etc.

15. He imposes such necessity upon God that, according to him, God cannot act otherwise than he acts. In book V he says:

> “Whatever he does, as he necessarily wills it, so he necessarily does it,”

etc. And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore God necessarily willed and made the world to exist, and he was not idle, since before making it he could not make it, because before he made it, it ought not to be made.”

The anonymous abbot rightly attacks this doctrine in book III against Abelard [Col. 1123]. I pass over the fact that Abelard often truncates the sayings of the holy Fathers, indeed of Scripture, which he cites.

From all these things, unless my judgment deceives me, it sufficiently appears how rightly his book *On the Trinity* was committed to the flames at the Council of Soissons, and how rightly his teaching was later censured by the Church at Sens and by Innocent II. For whatever interpretation may be given to these matters, no one can certainly deny that all of them sound bad and readily furnish the unwary a path into error; nor is the understanding of learned men sufficient in these matters. “Catholic words are also required,” as Abelard himself says.

If anything can excuse him, we think it chiefly this: that he appears to have submitted his writings to the judgment of the more learned and therefore of the Church itself. For in book III he argues thus:

> “Whatever we shall discuss concerning this most exalted philosophy, we profess to be a shadow, not truth; as it were a certain likeness, not the reality. The Lord knows what is true; but what is probable and most consonant with the philosophical arguments by which it is attacked, I think that I shall state. In this matter, if—God forbid!—through faults which I deserve I depart from Catholic understanding or speech, may he forgive me who judges works by intention; for I am always ready to give every satisfaction concerning things wrongly said, whether they must be corrected or deleted, when any one of the faithful corrects me by the force of reason or the authority of Scripture.”

Would that Abelard had done this voluntarily; he certainly would not have incurred the deserved censure for his errors.

## CHAPTER-HEADINGS OF THE BOOKS

[Col. 1123]

The first book contains the meaning of the distinction of the three persons in God, or what the personal names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit signify in him; testimonies both of prophets and philosophers concerning the Holy Trinity; and also why the Wisdom of God is called the Word, or his Goodness is called the Holy Spirit. It also shows that what philosophers have said concerning the soul of the world is rightly understood concerning the Holy Spirit.

The second book is written wholly against the reproaches of believers concerning the admixture of philosophical testimonies. In it great praise is bestowed on the lives, virtues, and doctrines of philosophers, and upon persons of the natural law, so that they seem worthy even for God to deign to reveal to them the mysteries of his faith.

The third contains attacks upon dialecticians and all who wish God also to be comprehended by human reasoning, and who judge that those matters ought not to be accepted by faith which cannot be established or defended by human arguments. It also sets forth the summary of faith concerning unity and Trinity; objections against the propositions; the various senses in which “same” and “different” are understood; and the various senses in which “person” is used.

The fourth contains solutions to objections; the generation of the Word from the Father—that is, of divine wisdom from divine power—and the analogy by which divine Power is called Father and divine Wisdom Son. It further contains the procession of the Spirit; how Plato intended the soul of the world, which he understood as the Holy Spirit, to be created, that is, to have a beginning; and that all human beings naturally possess faith in the Trinity.

The fifth concerns the reason for believing in one God rather than many, and the perfection and immutability of this highest good, which cannot increase, diminish, or change in any respect.

# FIRST BOOK OF CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY

[Col. 1123]

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1123]

[Col. 1123A] In describing the perfection of the highest good, which is God, Christ the Lord—the incarnate Wisdom of God himself—carefully distinguished it by three names, when he called the one, singular, individual, wholly simple divine substance Father, Son, and Holy Spirit for three reasons.

Ambrose, *On Faith*, addressed to Emperor Gratian:

> “What is of one substance cannot be separated, although it is not a matter of singularity but of unity. Singularity pertains to person; unity, to nature.”

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1124]

[Col. 1124A] He called the Father the same divine substance according to that unique power of his majesty which is omnipotence, by which he can accomplish whatever he wills, since nothing can resist him. He called the Son the same divine substance according to the discernment of his own wisdom, by which he can truly judge and distinguish all things, so that nothing capable of deceiving it may be hidden from it. He also called the Holy Spirit that same substance according to the grace of his goodness, by which with supreme goodness he orders all that supreme wisdom has created and directs everything to its best end, always making good use even of evil [Col. 1125A] and wonderfully ordering most excellently things done however perversely—as though he used either hand as his right hand and knew no hand but the right.

Hence Blessed Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*:

> “For God Almighty, being supremely good, would in no way permit any evil to exist in his works unless he were so omnipotent and good that he could bring good even out of evil.”

The same author, in book XI of *The City of God* [Note: [Col. 1125D] Augustine, *The City of God*, book XI, ch. 17.], speaking of God’s goodness and the devil’s malice, says:

> “As God is the best creator of good natures, so he is the most just disposer of evil wills; so that, while the devil makes evil use of good natures, God makes good use even of evil wills.”

Likewise, in the same work, concerning the devil:

> “When God created him, he was not unaware [Col. 1125B] of his future malice and foresaw what good things he himself would bring about from that evil.”

Again, after some intervening matter [Note: [Col. 1126D] Ibid., ch. 18.]:

> “For God would not have created anyone—not, I say, among angels or human beings—whom he foresaw would become evil, unless he had also known for what good uses he would employ them.”

Hence also comes that Platonic saying:

> “Everything,” he says, “which [perhaps: that which] comes to be comes to be through some necessary cause. For nothing comes to be whose origin is not preceded by a legitimate cause and reason.”

Therefore, from that highest goodness by which, according to Moses, God created all things very good, and according also to Plato’s assertion that he is the best Creator of all, from whom envy has been banished far away, God willed to make all things like himself, insofar as the nature of each could be capable of blessedness: for God wills all good things indeed to come to be, but leaves no propagation of any evil, so far as the nature of things that arise permits; nor is it fitting for surpassing goodness to make anything except what is most beautiful. From this, I say, from his so great goodness, by which he makes each thing good as far as he can and ought, and by his highest counsel, incomprehensible to us, orders even evils well, the Holy Spirit himself, as we have recalled above, receives his name.

To confess three persons in the Godhead—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is therefore as though we named divine Power that generates, divine Wisdom that is begotten, and divine Goodness that proceeds. By naming these three, the perfection of the highest Good is proclaimed: God is shown to be supremely powerful, that is, omnipotent; supremely wise; and supremely good. Concerning such generation or procession, in what follows, insofar as we can and the Lord himself grants—or rather, insofar as his grace gives us—we shall attempt to offer some explanation through whatever analogies may be available.

In these three—Power, Wisdom, and Goodness—consists the whole perfection of the Good; and any one of them apart from the other two is of little account. For if someone has power but does not know how to use what he can do in accordance with the rule of reason, his power is deadly and destructive. If he is wise and discerning in action but cannot act, he lacks efficacy. And even if he is powerful and wise but by no means good, he becomes all the more inclined to injure, the more secure he is, through his power and cunning, in accomplishing what he wills; nor does one who is not moved by affection of goodness offer others hope of his benefits.

But where these three meet—where someone can fulfill what he wills, wills what is good because he is good, and does not exceed through wisdom the measure of reason—it is clear that he is truly good and perfect in every respect, and that under his governance all things which he has created most excellently are preserved most excellently: since he can, knows, and wills. Thus this distinction of the Trinity is suited not only to describing the perfection of the highest Good, [Col. 1126B] but also greatly assists in persuading human beings to the religious worship of God. For this reason the incarnate Wisdom of God himself most rightly determined to employ it especially in his preaching.

For two things render us wholly subject to God: fear and love. Power and Wisdom chiefly instill fear, since we know that he can punish faults and that nothing is hidden from him. Goodness, however, pertains to love, so that we may especially love him whom we regard as most good. From this goodness it is also certain that he wills to punish impiety, because the more justice pleases him, the more iniquity displeases him, as it is written: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity” (Ps. XLIV.8).

By the name Father, as we have said, Power is signified; by the name Son, Wisdom; and by the name Holy Spirit, the good disposition toward creatures. The reasons for these names will be given below: that is, why these names have been transferred from their customary meanings to distinguish these things in God. But first let us show that this distinction of the divine Trinity was not begun by Christ, but was handed down more openly and carefully by him—a distinction which divine inspiration deigned to reveal both through the prophets to the Jews and through philosophers to the Gentiles. Thus the acknowledged perfection of the highest Good might invite both peoples to worship the one God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things; and thus the faith of the Trinity might be more readily received in the time of grace by both peoples when they saw it taught also by ancient teachers.

## CHAPTER III
First let the very beginnings of the Law come before us, where the lawgiver Moses sets forth the Catholic faith concerning unity together with Trinity, as the foundation of all good things. For when it is said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), where we say *God*, the Hebrew text has *Eloim*, the plural of the singular *El*. Why, then, is not *El* said, meaning God, but *Eloim*, which among the Hebrews is interpreted “gods” or “judges,” unless this is fitted to the plurality of divine persons, so that plurality in God may thereby be suggested in the same way as Trinity; and so that God may in some sense be called manifold, just as he is threefold—not, indeed, according to any diversity of substance, but according to the properties of the persons?

> [Note: Col. 1127D] In the *Introduction to Theology*, book I, col. 996, the following is added after these words: “That is, *ELOIM* is such as though one said: not many things, but many persons, each of whom is God; otherwise they would also say ‘gods,’ although there is only one.”

For there too provision is cautiously made to demonstrate unity of substance, when it says “created,” not “created [plural].” Immediately thereafter it also adds the distinction of persons, as though to determine that *Eloim* was spoken in the plural in order to denote this distinction. For the eternity of the Holy Spirit is plainly shown when it says, “The Spirit of the Lord was moving over the waters” (Gen. 1:2). The Word—that is, the Son—and the Father are likewise suggested when it says, “God said, ‘Let there be’” (ibid., 3): that is, in his coeternal Wisdom the Father ordained that things should be made. This cannot be understood as bodily speech, as we shall prove later.

Moreover, in what is written, “And God saw that it was good” (ibid., 4), the goodness of God, which we call the Holy Spirit, is suggested, just as Word and Father are understood in the words “God said.” For “God saw that it was good” means as much as: understanding that the work he had made was good, he loved it precisely because it was good. From this it is also clearly shown that he himself is good.

Appropriately, for establishing faith in the works and commending them, the divine persons are mentioned—namely, God’s omnipotence, his wisdom, and his goodness—so that, because he is able to do this and is good, he may be believed to have made the things which he both could and willed to make. Again, the beauty of the works is shown through the wisdom and goodness of the maker, so that, because the maker is supremely good and perfectly skillful, he produces a most excellent work.

What could be clearer evidence for the Trinity than what is subsequently added in the creation of man, when the Lord says, “Let us make man,” etc. (ibid., 26)? Why is “Let us make” said in the plural, unless to express the cooperation of the whole Trinity? For whom would God be exhorting to create man, or to swear something by himself, if he alone were to create him? For it is written: “Who has assisted the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor, with whom he entered into counsel?” etc. (Isa. 40:13).

And rightly is man said to be made in the image and likeness of the Trinity—that is, in a certain express likeness of the three persons—since he imitates the Father through the power which he received over the other creatures, the Son through reason, and the Holy Spirit through the benevolence of innocence, which he later lost through sin.

The plurality of divine persons also seems relevant to what the serpent said later: “You shall be as gods” (Gen. 3:5), which, as stated above, in Hebrew is *Eloim*; and likewise to that rebuke of the Lord: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (ibid., 22). So too the Lord says: “Let us go down and confuse their tongues,”

> [Note: Col. 1128D] In our Vulgate and in chapter 13, middle, of the *Introduction to Theology*, “their tongue” is read in the singular.

although God alone accomplished this. Hence it is added: “And so he divided them” (Gen. 11:7–8).

But now, after the Law, let us pass to the testimonies of the prophets.

Thus says that greatest of prophets and kings, David, who, preferring his own understanding to that of others, says: “I have understood beyond all who teach me; I have understood beyond the elders” (Ps. 118:99). He says, I repeat, plainly suggesting the distinction of the Trinity: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of their mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6). Elsewhere he likewise suggests unity together with Trinity, saying: “May God bless us; may our God bless us; may God bless us; and may all the ends of the earth fear him” (Ps. 66:7).

Cassiodorus:

> [Note: Col. 1128D] *Exposition on the Psalter*.

> “*Deus* is a Greek word, which in Latin is interpreted ‘fear.’ For this reason, I suppose, our forefathers wished God to be named from fear. Hence one of the pagan poets says:
>
> ‘Fear first made gods in the world.’  
> (Statius, *Thebaid* III, 661.)
>
> For this threefold confession of God expresses the Trinity of persons: namely, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And in aptly designating the Son he added ‘our,’ as though showing that he has been given to us by the Father, since through the Incarnation of the divine Word, Wisdom has enlightened us. Of this Word the Apostle also says: ‘He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all’” (Rom. 8:32).

Augustine, *Seventy-Four Questions*, chapter 44:

> “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), which in Greek is called *Logos* [Λόγος], and in Latin signifies both “reason” and “word”; but in this place it is better translated “Word.” It signifies not only a relation to the Father, but also a relation to those things which were made through the Word. But “reason,” even if nothing is made through it, is rightly called reason.

Chapter 45:

> “Christ, the Wisdom of God, was both in Mary’s womb and in heaven, just as a human word, although many hear it, is heard whole by each individual.”

The Psalmist also reveals the unity of the divine substance in the same passage. After the threefold utterance of the divine name, understanding one God in three persons, he did not add “them” in the plural, but “him” in the singular. This also accords with Isaiah, who says that he saw seraphim and heard them crying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isa. 6:3).

The prophet rightly used the title “Lord” to designate power, because it belongs to lords to rule. This power is indeed often denoted by the name God as well, because *Theos* [Θεός], Greek for “God,” according to Isidore, is interpreted “fear,” and every power is a fear to those subject to it.

## CHAPTER IV

The Word is called Wisdom because the term is transferred from effect to cause: for it is especially from each person’s words that his understanding, and the nature of his knowledge, are made manifest. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: “For wisdom is recognized in speech, and understanding and teaching in the word of the wise” (Ecclus. 4:29). Thus Truth itself also says: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12:34).

Just as we speak of the sight of both the mind and the eyes, so in some manner we speak of the utterance or word of the heart as well as of the mouth, according to that saying of the Psalmist: “They spoke with heart and heart” (Ps. 11:3); and that of the Book of Wisdom: “The ungodly said within themselves, reasoning wrongly” (Wis. 2:1); as also that in the Gospel: “They said within themselves: ‘This man blasphemes’” (Matt. 9:3), that is, they thought it. And Truth says: “It is not what enters the mouth that defiles a person, but what proceeds from the mouth” (ibid., 15:11). And a little later: “What proceeds from the mouth comes forth from the heart, and this defiles a person. For evil thoughts come forth from the heart,” etc. (ibid., 18:19).

Accordingly, following this usage of Scripture, we here call the utterance of the heart—that is, the very thought or understanding of the mind—the word of the mind. But in God, his very thought or understanding is called the same thing as his reason or Wisdom, which is the Word of the Father, that is, the Son of God.

Thus Moses, as we recalled above, when he prefaces the making of different created things with “God said” (Gen. 1:7), and immediately joins the effect to the saying—“and so it was” (ibid., 7)—shows that God created all things in the Word, that is, in his Wisdom: namely, nothing rashly or suddenly, but all things rationally and providently. Of this the Psalmist says elsewhere: “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32:9): that is, with reason and providence going before, he created or ordered all things.

And, showing more plainly elsewhere that this Word is not audible and passing, but intelligible and enduring, he says: “Who made the heavens in understanding” (Ps. 135:5). That is, he made them according to the manner in which he first ordered them in the word of his mind—that is, in the conception of his eternal understanding, which foresees all things.

Concerning this Word—that is, the intelligible Word—blessed Gregory, in Homily 7 on the Gospels, speaks thus, distinguishing the intelligible Word itself from the audible word, which is voice:

> [Note: Col. 1129D] St. Gregory, Homily 7, no. 2.
>
> “You know,” he says, “that the Only-Begotten is called the Word of the Father, as John testifies when he says: ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1:1). From your own speech you know that a voice sounds first, so that the word may afterward be heard. But John declares himself to be the voice, because the Word goes before.”

The same author, in Homily 23, *On John the Baptist: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness”*:

> “The prophet was called the voice,” he says, “because the Word went before.”

That is to say: just as, for a hearer, the audible word precedes the intelligible word—for a voice first sounds, so that understanding may afterward be conceived from it—so John’s preaching went before the Lord’s advent by announcing it.

The Word, then, denotes a conception of the mind and a kind of utterance of understanding which is formed in the mind. In likeness to this, the Only-Begotten of God is called the Word, and, as it were, a certain intellectual and eternal utterance of God, in whose providence the operation and ordering of all things are fixed from eternity.

Augustine, in describing this intellectual utterance of God—that is, the eternal ordering of Wisdom—in *The City of God*, book XXVI, chapter 6, says:

> “God’s utterance before his act is the unchangeable reason of that very act; it has no resounding and passing sound, but a power remaining forever and working in time.”

The same author, in the book *Against Five Heresies*:

> [Note: Col. 1129D] Chapter 6.—This book, although by a very ancient writer, is nevertheless not by St. Augustine; it has been relegated to the appendix of volume VIII of the new edition.

> “‘In the beginning was the Word.’ The Greeks say *logos* [λόγος] better; for *logos* signifies both word and reason.”

Of this Word he also says in book VIII of *On the Trinity*:

> “He called the Word the Son in order to show that he came forth from himself.”

That the Word of God is to be understood as his very Wisdom is plainly shown in Ecclesiasticus in these words: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him, and is before the age. Who has investigated wisdom, which goes before all things? Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of wisdom from eternity. The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God on high,” etc. (Ecclus. 1:1).

Do not wonder if, as I have said, the conception of the mind itself is called a word, with the name transferred from effect to cause, since conversely we employ many transfers from cause to effect. Thus we sometimes call the very benefit of almsgiving—by which the charity of the giver is especially made known—“charity”; and we designate the penitent’s satisfaction by the name “penance.” Properly speaking, charity is nothing but love, and penance nothing but sorrow of mind.

Yet we may also regard the conception of our mind as both an effect and a cause of speech: in the speaker it is a cause, and in the hearer an effect, because the speaker’s very utterance, proceeding from his understanding, is generated from it in order to generate that same understanding again in the hearer. Therefore, because of this great kinship between utterances and understandings, it is not unfitting that their names be transferred reciprocally. This also frequently occurs among things and names because of an association of meaning. What has now been said concerning the transfer of this name *Word* in this passage, and its meaning, is enough.

But the Son of God the Father is called this very Word—that is, his coeternal Wisdom—according to that mode of generation by which divine Wisdom is from divine Power, as we shall endeavor to explain later, insofar as the Lord grants.

That divine power is expressed especially by the name Father is also suggested by that greatest bishop in his exposition of the Creed called the Apostles’ Creed, read on the fifth Sunday of Lent:

> “Do you believe in God the Father Almighty? In God, unbegotten nature is shown; in Father, the truth of the Only-Begotten; in Almighty, the fullness of power. For by unbegotten deity he is almighty, and by omnipotence Father.”

This is as though he plainly said: In that he is unbegotten God, God the Father has this as his proper and special attribute: that he is almighty—just as the Son, in that he is Son, is wise or Wisdom; and the Spirit, that he is benevolent, indeed Benevolence itself.

This does not mean that God alone is almighty and neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit is; or that the Son alone is wise, or the Holy Spirit alone benevolent. Rather, according to the distinction of each person, some things belong especially to one person and are principally attributed to that person, and some to another. Thus, as the Father is named from omnipotence, as we recalled above, the Son from wisdom, and the Holy Spirit from benevolence, “almighty by unbegotten deity, and Father by omnipotence” means that omnipotence belongs especially to the property or distinction of the person of God the Father, since omnipotence itself, begetting Wisdom, is the expressed property of the Father—or is altogether identical with the Father himself.
