And the name Father, in this person, expresses divine power itself, which is omnipotence, simply, in such a way that it does not distinguish wisdom or benevolence within it, but is content merely to designate the omnipotence from which Wisdom is begotten.

It should be noted that, according to the authority of the holy Fathers, we call only the person of the Father unbegotten. Here “unbegotten” seems to mean the same as being from oneself, not from another, since each of the other persons is from the Father, while the person of the Father alone is not from any of the others.

Therefore, just as philosophers call generated everything which is from another—and we accordingly read of the generation of the world, insofar as the world itself is called God’s work, though not his Son; and Plato calls God the generator of the universe, from whom all other things have being—so, conversely, in this place we call the Father alone unbegotten, because he alone does not have being from another.

For this reason blessed Augustine denies that the Spirit himself is either unbegotten or begotten. Thus he says in *Questions Proposed by Orosius and Explained by Augustine*, chapter 2:

> “Certain faith declares the Holy Spirit to be neither begotten nor unbegotten. For if we call him unbegotten, we seem to affirm two Fathers; but if begotten, we are charged with believing in two Sons. Yet what certain faith holds is that he is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeds from both—that is, from the Father and the Son.”

Gennadius, *On the Orthodox Faith of Ecclesiastical Doctrines*:

> [Note: Cols. 1131D–1132D] This book, commonly entitled *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, is attributed to St. Augustine in certain manuscripts. Trithemius and Balaeus make Alcuin its author; Gratian makes Paterius; others, more rightly, Gennadius—not Gennadius bishop of Constantinople, as Ratramnus held, but Gennadius the priest of Marseilles, and not a bishop, as some have wrongly supposed.

> “The Father, therefore, is the source of deity: from him the Son is born; from him the Holy Spirit is not born, because he is not the Son; nor is he unbegotten, because he is not the Father.”

Blessed Pope Gregory, following him, mentions this in the creed prefixed to his letters:

> “The Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but coeternal, proceeding from the Father and the Son.”

Isidore too, in book VI of the *Etymologies*, explaining why only the Father is called unbegotten, says:

> “The Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called unbegotten.”

It should also be noted that, insofar as we call the Father alone unbegotten—that is, not from another—“unbegotten” seems most appropriately to bear upon power, as though he were shown to be supreme, not by any rank of dignity, but by the capacity for subsisting. For he alone, as has been said, has being from himself; the other two persons could not exist at all except from him. He alone needs no other from whom to derive being, as though he alone were sufficient for his own existence, since he has being from himself, not from another.

Thus philosophers too say that existent nature—that is, the Son—is from the supreme God, the Father, whom they call *Tagathon*; and they call him supreme because he is not from another. And when they call the Father himself *protopanton*, that is, “first principle of all things,” they ascribe omnipotence to him as his proper and special attribute, because from him not only creatures but also, as stated, the other two persons have being—not by creation, as other things do, but by generation or procession.

Thus the Father himself seems to have power in all things in a special and natural manner, because all things are from him and are, as it were, naturally his by right—just as any son is said by natural right to belong to his own father as his proper being. Hence Sacred Scripture is especially accustomed to join the name Almighty to that of Father, although each of the other two persons is equally almighty.

Therefore, when Maximus said above that God is almighty by unbegotten deity, it is as though he said that almighty power ought to be attributed most especially and, as it were, distinctly to unbegotten God—that is, God the Father—precisely because he is unbegotten: existing from himself, not from another. For, just as he himself is from himself and not from another, while all other things are from him, so he has from himself and not from another the power to do all things. He is dependent upon no one for being, power, or action; he is supreme among all existent natures and seems, as stated, to possess by right authority over all other things as naturally his, since those which have being from him necessarily receive from him also what they are able to do.

He alone, just as he is supreme in existence—that is, not from another—so is said to possess supreme power, because he has power from himself and not from another, just as he has being. The other persons, however, just as they are from him, so have from him what they can do or do. Hence the Son himself testifies that he does nothing from himself, just as he does not speak from himself. For he who is not his own Word but the Father’s Word must necessarily have from the Father also what he does, since he has from him what he is.

Thus the Father seems in a certain way supreme through power, but not greater: he can do all things from himself, as stated, and subsists from himself, not from another. This is why omnipotence is attributed to him, as it were, properly or specially: he so can do all things that he has this from himself and does not receive it from another. And when he says that in the name “God” unbegotten nature is shown, he means a substance not made or created, but eternal.

## CHAPTER V

By the name Holy Spirit is expressed the affection of benevolence and charity, because especially through the breath and exhalation of our mouth the emotions of the mind are disclosed: either we sigh from love, or groan under the constriction of toil or pain. Thus Holy Spirit is used for good affection, according to the saying in the Book of Wisdom: “The spirit of wisdom is benevolent, and will not acquit the evil-speaker of his lips” (Wis. 1:6); and that of the Psalmist: “Your good Spirit will lead me into the straight land,” etc. (Ps. 142:10).

Concerning this, St. Augustine in the first book *On Genesis*, at the passage where it is written, “The Spirit of the Lord was moving over the waters,” says:

> “Needy and wanting love loves in such a way that it is subject to the things it loves. Therefore, when the Spirit of God was mentioned, in whom his holy good will and love are understood, he was said to move above, lest God be thought to love the works he was to make from the necessity of need rather than from the abundance of beneficence.”

This also plainly agrees with the Apostle’s saying: “God is charity” (John 4:16), because, as Gregory testifies, the Spirit himself is love.

Hence, in the salutations which Paul customarily prefixes to his Epistles, when he says, “Grace to you from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ,” he fittingly designates the Spirit himself by the name grace; we also call him the gift of God. This grace—that is, this Spirit—is rightly said to be given by those from whom he proceeds, namely the Father and the Son.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, rightly chose to reveal himself both in a dove and in fire, since, as has been said, divine benevolence or charity is expressed by the name Spirit. For the dove is believed to be the gentlest and most benevolent of all birds; it is said to lack gall and to be especially remote from the impulses of anger; and it is thought to possess a kind of fiery and very warm nature, since fire itself is called love. Of this Truth says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49), that is, to preach and plant charity rather than fear, which is compared to coldness. Thus doves are able to breed and bear young more frequently than other birds, since they are of a warmer nature.

Nor is it without significance that they bear in pairs, are sociable, and dwell together. For there are two branches of charity: one toward God, the other toward one’s neighbor; and whoever possesses charity preserves the unity of concord.

In this place Holy Spirit is the proper name of one person, although in another sense it is common to all three persons: namely, insofar as the divine substance is spiritual rather than bodily, and holy. Augustine also mentions this in book V of *On the Trinity*:

> [Note: Col. 1133D] Augustine has similar material in book XV, chapter 19.
>
> “The Holy Spirit, according to what is written, ‘God is spirit,’ can indeed be called universally so, because the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit; the Father is holy and the Son is holy.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The Holy Spirit is a certain communion of Father and Son, and perhaps is so called because the same designation can apply to Father and Son. Therefore, so that the communion of both may be signified by a name that belongs to both, the gift of both is called Holy Spirit.”

The same author, in book XV:

> [Note: Col. 1134D] Chapters 17 and 30.
>
> “By many examples it can be shown that names of many things are used both universally and properly for particular things. I have said this so that no one may think us improper for calling the Holy Spirit charity because God the Father and God the Son can also be called charity. Thus, just as we properly call the only Word by the name Wisdom, although the Holy Spirit and the Father himself are Wisdom, so the Holy Spirit is properly called by the name charity, although both Father and Son are charity.”

For it frequently happens that a name common to many things is transferred, as though proper, to one of them: when the other things have proper names by which they differ from one another, whereas this one has none, the name formerly common to all becomes proper to this distinction. Thus we call clergy in distinction from monks, although monks too are clergy; and we call confessors in distinction from martyrs, although martyrs especially—that is, witnesses—should be called confessors, since they persevere even unto death in confessing the divine name.

There are also many other passages of prophecy from which the distinction of the Trinity is plainly taught.

David himself clearly taught the Son’s eternal generation from the Father, where he introduces the person of the Son speaking thus: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance,” etc. (Ps. 2:7 ff.).

“I have begotten you today” means as much as: “You are eternally from my very substance.” For since in eternity there is neither past nor future, but only present, he used an adverb of present time for eternity, saying “today” for “eternally.” He aptly added “I have begotten” to “today,” joining a past tense to the ever-present “today,” so as to indicate that the generation is always present through “today,” and perfect through “I have begotten”: namely, that it neither ceases nor has begun. For things which are past have already been completed and perfected. He therefore used the past tense as though for perfection, showing that the Son is always begotten from the Father and always has been begotten.

Elsewhere David more plainly declares the Son’s eternity, saying: “He shall endure with the sun, and before the moon, from generation to generation” (Ps. 71:5). And again: “With you is the beginning in the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints; from the womb, before the day-star, I have begotten you” (Ps. 109:3).

Isaiah, marveling at this ineffable and eternal generation, and also at the temporal generation—both of which are wonderful—says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). This is as though he plainly said: This is not a matter for human ingenuity to expound, but for God alone—whose Spirit nevertheless speaks in those faithful persons whom he wills, as he himself testifies: “It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

Jerome also, commenting on Ecclesiastes at the passage: “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of men ascends upward, and whether the spirit of cattle descends downward into the earth?” (Eccl. 3:21), applies “Who shall declare his generation?” as an example of what is difficult, not impossible:

> [Note: Col. 1135D] The Vulgate reads: “the spirit of the children of Adam . . . and the spirit of beasts.”
>
> “By adding ‘who,’ he wished to show the difficulty of the matter. For the pronoun ‘who’ in Holy Scripture is always taken not for what is impossible but for what is difficult, as in: ‘Who shall declare his generation?’—that is, Christ’s generation,” etc.

The coeternity of this Wisdom with the Father is also plainly shown in Proverbs in these words:

> “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel . . . The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning. I was ordained from eternity, before the earth was made. The depths did not yet exist, and I was already conceived; the fountains of waters had not yet burst forth. The mountains had not yet stood in their heavy mass; before the hills I was brought forth. He had not yet made the earth and the foundations of the world. When he prepared the heavens, I was present . . . When he established the foundations of the earth, I was with him, ordering all things; and I delighted day by day, playing before him at all times” (Prov. 8:12, 22 ff.).

What could state the eternal generation of the Word more plainly than Wisdom’s own testimony that she was conceived and brought forth before the world’s establishment, and that, abiding eternally with the Father, she always plays before him? For what is conceived is brought forth from the very one by whom it is generated. Wisdom, in substance or essence, is power, since it is itself a certain power, as we shall show later. Thus for Wisdom to be conceived and brought forth by God means that Wisdom itself is generated from the very substance of the Father in which it exists.

And for Wisdom to play before the Father and order all things with him means that divine Power disposes all things in Wisdom according to the will of its goodness, so that in this play we understand the affection of goodness. Of this it is written: “By the Spirit of his mouth is all their power” (Ps. 32:6). And when he says that Wisdom always stands before God the Father, this means that Omnipotence accomplishes nothing except with reason going before and Wisdom guiding.

Again, in the same Proverbs he writes most plainly concerning the Son of God and the ineffable name of the Son himself, as though assuming the person of some wondrous prophet declaring and marveling at this inexpressible generation. For he says:

> “The vision . . . which the man with whom God is spoke, and who, strengthened by God dwelling with him, said: ‘Who has raised up all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is the name of his Son?’” (Prov. 30:1, 4).

A very firm and clear testimony to our faith also occurs in Ecclesiasticus, where the Wisdom of God declares herself first-born before all things according to the nature of divinity, and afterward created according to the assumption of our nature, since at the Father’s command she visited Israel in the garment of the Incarnation. For it is written there:

> “Wisdom shall have praise in the multitude of the elect, and among the blessed she shall be blessed, saying: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, first-born before every creature. I caused unfailing light to rise in the heavens, and like a mist I covered all the earth. I dwelt in the heights, and my throne was in a pillar of cloud. I alone traversed the circuit of heaven,’” etc. (Ecclus. 24:4–8).

And shortly afterward:

> “Then the Creator of all things commanded and said to me; and he who created me rested in my tabernacle, and said to me: ‘Dwell in Jacob, and take your inheritance in Israel, and put down roots among my elect’” (ibid., 12–13).

In the same book he also prophesies most plainly that the remission of sins consists in the Incarnation of divine Wisdom, which is Christ, saying that David’s sins were purged through Christ. For when much had been said there in praise of David, the sum of all his praise is gathered into this single statement which follows:

> “Christ purged his sins, exalted his horn forever, and gave him a covenant of kings and a throne of glory in Israel” (Ecclus. 47:13).

Micah too speaks of this eternal generation of the Word from the Father, as well as of his temporal generation from his mother: “And thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, art little among the thousands of Judah; from thee shall come forth unto me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and whose goings forth are from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5:2). Let the rebellious and unbelieving Jews say of whom, to be born in Bethlehem, this was said—namely, that his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity. For that is eternal which lacks an origin. But if they refer this to the Messiah, that greatest prophet, as they say, whom they await, and who according to them was merely a man and not also God, let them show what going forth of his is eternal, or whence he proceeds eternally. If, however, they say that he proceeds eternally from Bethlehem because his birth in that place was eternally foreseen and predestined by God, then in that manner the birth of any man or of any thing [Col. 1137B] is eternal, since it was foreseen from eternity. Let them therefore learn that there is an eternal generation, which they both read as written and profess in reading, yet do not believe when professing it.

Let them also answer me, when they hear the Prophet say, “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6), what they understand by the Word of the Lord, by his mouth, or by his Spirit. For it is agreed that God is the one principle of all other things; and everything which exists either is God, and is therefore eternal, or remains created by that eternal principle. Moreover, it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1); whence they hold that nothing had been created before these. Therefore that Word by which the heavens were established—and which is consequently prior to those which it established—is not created; indeed, it is the Creator himself, who is God, by whom the heavens were established.

But if they call this Word some transient utterance of God, like a human word, because it is written, “He spoke, and they were made” (Ps. 32:9), and thus God, like a man, now speaks when he says, “Let there be light” (Gen. 1:3), and now falls silent, then the eternity of the Godhead is surely changeable, since he does not always say, “Let there be light,” and the other things which have now been created. What need, moreover, was there of an audible word before the constitution of the world, when there was as yet no one to whom he might speak or who might hear? Would he not have uttered an empty word, if no work were to be effected by the word—especially when will alone sufficed, [Col. 1137D] and no one yet existed to be instructed by hearing it? Into what place, moreover, would he emit the spoken word, when no place had yet been created, nor had air yet been made from which words are formed? By what instruments, too, would he form words, when neither a mouth nor any part can belong to him who is altogether simple and indivisible? For everything consisting of parts is naturally later than those things of which it consists and by whose union it is produced, since it derives its being from those of which it is constituted. “Everything,” Plato says, “which is compounded is by nature dissoluble.”

But if they understand the Spirit of the Lord as wind, as they wish to take it in the passage, “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2), because, they say, wind is especially manifest in the waters which it stirs, [Col. 1138A] how is it called spirit, that is, the breath of the Lord’s mouth, when he has neither mouth nor any part, as has been said? How also does the power of heaven and earth subsist through wind?

Let them therefore understand that this is that Spirit of the Lord whose sevenfold grace Isaiah describes: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might,” etc. (Isa. 11:2). And elsewhere: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:16). Again: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim to the meek” (Isa. 61:1). Of this Spirit Wisdom also says: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit. For the Spirit of Wisdom is gracious,” etc. (Wis. 1:5). Again, [Col. 1138B] when it is added, “And that which contains all things has knowledge of speech” (ibid., 6), the Spirit himself is plainly declared to be God, since he is said to contain all things. And again Wisdom, speaking to God, says: “But who has known thy mind, unless thou hast given wisdom and sent thy Holy Spirit from on high?” (Wis. 9:17). And again: “O how good and sweet, Lord, is thy Spirit within us!” (Wis. 12:1).

Here too, when that very Spirit of Wisdom is described, he is plainly proclaimed true God, since among other things it is written of him in Wisdom: “Possessing all power, overseeing all things, and a Spirit comprehending all things” (Wis. 7:23). Elihu also confesses him to be Creator in the book of Job, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life” (Job 33:4). To him the Son of God himself, assigning equal dignity with himself and the Father, says in the Gospel: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19). The Apostle also, Augustine testifying, when he calls believers the temple of the Holy Spirit, openly declares him to be God, since only God is said to have a temple. For it is written in the Apostle: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16). Here he plainly indicates that God, whose temple it is, and the Spirit of God, whom he says dwells therein, are the same.

So too blessed Peter, in the Acts of the Apostles, confesses that the Holy Spirit is God: “Why have you lied to the Holy [Col. 1138D] Spirit, Ananias? You have lied not to men, but to God” (Acts 5:3–4). Of this Spirit it is likewise recorded in the same Acts: “The Spirit commands, saying: Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul,” etc. (Acts 13:2). And again: “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28). The Psalmist confesses that the Spirit of God is everywhere, as uncircumscribed: “Whither shall I go from thy Spirit?” (Ps. 138:7). And, immediately indicating that the Spirit of God whom he confesses to be everywhere is the same as God himself, to whom he speaks, he plainly shows this by at once ascribing the Spirit’s universal presence to God himself, whom he affirms to be everywhere: “If I ascend into heaven, thou art there,” etc. (ibid., 8). But when Truth himself declares that sin against the Spirit is not remissible, while saying that sin against the Father and the Son is remissible (Matt. 12:32), to whom does he not plainly indicate that the Spirit himself is not less than the Father and the Son, and therefore is fully God, just as the Father himself and the Son are?

It is therefore clear from the foregoing that both the Word of God and his Spirit are God, just as he himself is God whose Word and Spirit they are. Let them understand, then, as has been said, that this Word of the Lord—that is, the Son of God—is not a transient or audible word, but an intelligible one: namely, Reason itself, or Wisdom coeternal with God. It is fitting to call this all-wisdom, just as we speak of omnipotence. Hence it is written: “All Wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him, and is before the age” (Ecclus. 1:1).

In the book of Wisdom he is also shown to be the true and consubstantial Son of God, in distinction from adoptive sons, of whom it is written that through his preaching they were won for God: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1:12). For when his Passion was openly prophesied in Wisdom, the ungodly say among other things: “For if he is the true Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hand of his adversaries” (Wis. 2:18). The holy soul delivered by God also openly confesses this generation when it says in Ecclesiasticus: “I called upon the Lord, the Father of my Lord, that he should not forsake me in the day of my affliction” (Ecclus. 51:14).

Now, after the testimonies of the prophets concerning faith in the Trinity, it is pleasing to add the testimonies of the philosophers, whom both the very reasoning of philosophy led to an understanding of the one God—for, according to the Apostle, “the invisible things of God, understood through those things which have been made, are seen from the creation of the world” (Rom. 1:20)—and the sobriety of their exceptionally restrained life acquired for them this knowledge by a certain merit. For it was fitting that even then God should foreshadow in them, through some more abundant gift of grace, how much more acceptable to him is one who lives soberly and withdraws himself from the enticements of this world by despising it, than one who, given over to its pleasures, plunges himself into every impurity.

Holy teachers also relate how great was the philosophers’ abstinence and self-control [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*, “incontinence,” altogether wrongly and contrary to the author’s meaning.]; [Col. 1139D] they bring forward their lives to rebuke us [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*: “bring [them] forward.”], and draw many things from their moral teachings or testimonies of faith for our edification. Whoever does not know this should at least read Jerome *Against Jovinianus*, and will see how much he reports concerning their virtues, and those of other pagans, in order to crush the shamelessness of that heretic. Above all, it is fitting for us too in this work to rely upon the testimonies or arguments of philosophers, since we are acting especially against [Col. 1140A] those who endeavor to assail our faith with philosophical doctrines—particularly since no one ought to be argued against or refuted except through what he accepts, and he is crushed in the greatest confusion who is defeated by the very means through which he sought to conquer.

One of the philosophers themselves, Tully, declares in the first book of the *Rhetorics* that philosophers acknowledge only one God: “Those who devote themselves to philosophy do not suppose that there are gods”—as though he were plainly saying: rather, one God, not many gods. Concerning such persons the Apostle too, Augustine testifying, when speaking to the Athenians had uttered the great and difficult saying, namely, that “in him we live and move and are,” added, “as certain also of your own have said” (Acts 17:28). Again, writing to the Romans concerning such persons, the same Apostle says:

> What is known of God is manifest to them, for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made—even his eternal power and divinity—so that they are without excuse; because, when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts.  
> (Rom. 1:19–21)

Nor is this surprising, since even Solomon’s wisdom, conquered by concupiscence and fleshly pleasures, consented to idolatry, abandoning the divine worship which he taught and preached among his own people. Yet it was to magnify that worship of God that he himself built the temple at God’s command—a work from which his righteous father had been forbidden.

God also sometimes distributes the greatest gifts even to the reprobate and unbelieving, when he sees that they will be necessary for the instruction or use of others; and he works many miracles through the reprobate. Of them Truth says in the Gospel: “Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name, and cast out demons in thy name, and done many mighty works in thy name? And then I will confess to them: I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity” (Matt. 7:22–23). But when God displays miracles, utters prophecies, or performs any great works through the reprobate, this is not done [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*, *agere* is read for *agitur*, which yields no sense.] for the benefit of those whom he uses as instruments, but rather for that of others whom he intends to instruct through them. He does not abandon the gifts of his grace even through unworthy ministers, but daily performs the sacraments of the Church, specially [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*: “spiritually”; our manuscript’s “specially” is better.] at the invocation of his name, for the salvation of believers. God rightly works great things even through the unworthy or unbelieving, since he instructed a prophet through the words of an ass [Note: Scripture calls him a diviner, not a prophet.], lest, if he worked great things only through great men, these works should be attributed more to human virtues and merits than to divine grace.

[Col. 1141A] Let Mercury now come first, that most ancient and renowned philosopher, whom they called a god on account of his excellence. Augustine, disputing *Against Five Heresies*, adduces his testimony concerning the generation of the Word:

> “Hermes, who in Latin is called Mercury, wrote a book called *Logostilcos*, that is, ‘the Perfect Word’ [Note: *Against Five Heresies*, ch. 3. In the *Introduction to Theology*, λόγος τέλετος is read; λόγος τέλειος is better, as in *Against Five Heresies*.]. Let us hear what he says of the Perfect Word. ‘The Lord, maker of all gods, made a second Lord. This one he made first and sole and true [Note: In *Against Five Heresies* one reads “sole and one”; but the brethren in the most recent edition of St Augustine’s works note that certain manuscripts read “sole and true.”]. He seemed good to him and full of all good things. He rejoiced in him and loved him greatly as his only-begotten.’”

Elsewhere he says: “The Son of the blessed God and of good will, whose name cannot be spoken by a human [Col. 1141B] mouth.”

Augustine calls him whom he had first said was made “only-begotten.” John the Evangelist says how full he is: “Of his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). By “gods”—that is, immortal rational living beings—the philosophers were accustomed to mean the planets or even the world itself. Hence the Prophet calls the sun, moon, and other heavenly bodies “the host of heaven,” following the usage of the Gentiles, who sacrificed to them as their rulers and protectors. According to Plato, the supreme God addresses the more excellent of these gods concerning the creation of man, as though all things occurring below upon earth were administered from above through the hidden natures of planets and stars. For Plato says:

> “Gods of gods, whose maker and father I myself am [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*: “While the maker and father of gods is sought, I myself …”], you are indeed my works, dissoluble by nature, yet, so long as I do not will it, indissoluble,” etc.

This is also relevant to what is said in book VIII of *The City of God* concerning the Platonists: “They say that there is a threefold division of all living beings possessing a rational soul: into gods, human beings, and demons. The dwelling-place of gods is heaven, of human beings earth, and of demons the air.” And Boethius, commenting on Porphyry, says: “Whenever we place god under ‘living being,’ we do so in accordance with the opinion which maintains that the sun, stars, and this whole world are animate; these too they called by the name of gods.”

Blessed Augustine does not dare wholly to refute what is said about the sun and other heavenly lights, but declares himself uncertain whether ruling spirits may dwell in them, by whom they might also be animated; and, astonishingly, he says that he does not know whether these too belong to the fellowship of those whom we Christians call angels or heavenly spirits. Thus in the *Enchiridion* he says:

> “Whether the archangels are called Powers, and what distinction there is among Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers, let those say who can—if indeed they can prove what they say. I confess that I do not know these matters. Nor do I hold it certain whether the sun, moon, and stars belong to the same fellowship, although some seem to be luminous bodies without sensation [Note: In the cited work: “without consensus.”] or intelligence.”

Lest anyone schooled in sacred letters should be disturbed by the words of the philosopher Hermes, when he says that God the Father made a second Lord—that is, generated the Son—although God the Son is neither made nor created by God the Father, but only begotten, let him know that Catholic and holy teachers too have similarly used improper expressions concerning this same generation. For they sometimes call the Father the author of the Son, or say that he begot him, that the Son was formed by the Father, or that he is an effect of the Father. They say this improperly. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book III, writes:

> “According to the Apostle, because in Christ ‘all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily’ (Col. 2:9), yet incomprehensibly and ineffably, before all time and ages he procreated the Only-begotten from those things which were unbegotten in himself, imparting through love and power all that God is to his birth. And thus, to the unbegotten, perfect, and eternal Father corresponds the only-begotten, perfect, and eternal Son. But the things which belong to him according to the body which he assumed are the will of his goodness for our salvation.”

The same author, in book XI:

> “The words which I speak to you I do not speak from myself” (John 14:10). For, in not speaking from himself, he necessarily owes to the author that which he speaks.

Again: “For that which he does according to birth, the Father is author to him.”

Again, in book XII, speaking of God the Father as unborn and the Son as born from him, he says:

> “Being unborn and being born are not the same, because the one is from another, while the other is from no one; and it is one thing always to be eternal without an author, another to be eternal to the Father—that is, to the author [Note: In Hilary, not simply “eternal,” but “coeternal,” is read.]. Where there is an author, there also is birth. But where the author is eternal, there too is the eternity of the birth; for as birth is from an author, so from an eternal author comes an eternal birth.”

Again:

> “That which is born from the eternal, if it is not eternally born, then neither will the Father be an eternal author. If anything should be lacking in eternity to him who is born from the eternal Father, then it is beyond doubt that the very same thing is lacking to the author, who is the Father [Note: The words “who is the Father” are lacking in Hilary, though they occur in two manuscripts. In the *Introduction to Theology*, however, “indeed Father is” is wholly wrong.]; for what is infinite to the begetter is infinite also to the one begotten. Again, from the eternal comes nothing other than the eternal; if it is not eternal, then neither is the Father, author of the generation, eternal.”

Again: “He is shown to be born from thee, so that he signifies thee alone as his author.”

The same author, on Psalm 138: “Thou hast formed me and laid thy hand upon me” (Ps. 138:5): “Both expressions signify that what he formed is ancient, while what he laid his hand upon is most recent. For the Apostle teaches that he was formed according to the nature of divinity, saying: ‘Who, being in the form of God’ (Phil. 2:6); for that which is in a form is formed in a form, and the Father is to him the Father of nature and divinity [Note: In Hilary: “is formed into a form, indeed the form of the paternal nature and divinity.” In the most recent edition of St Hilary’s works, Abelard’s reading, found in a single manuscript, is rejected as corrupt.], so that it may be referred to the Father, and he may be said to have been formed by him.”

Augustine [Note: This book is not by St Augustine. Most learned men of the present age hold that its author was Hilary the deacon, who lived in the time of Pope Damasus.], *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chapter 57:

> “God the Father generated the Son from himself, in whom he himself is seen, since nothing differed from him, so that an effect corresponding to his greatness might answer to him.”

Again:

> “Creating his most like Son, he brought him forth from himself as though another self.”

The same author, in the same work:

> “Before the world, therefore, he possessed the preeminence of created offspring, since, in order to be Father of future things, he must first have been the proper Father—that is, Father of his own offspring.”

What wonder, then, if even in the words of ecclesiastical and holy teachers some expressions are employed so improperly to demonstrate the generation of the Word—such as that God the Father is the author of his Son and begot him, or that the Son was created by him or is said to be his effect—when this means that the Son is begotten from him rather than created or made, and that he is only begetter rather than creator or author? What wonder, I say, if the aforesaid philosopher Hermes, [Col. 1143C] trained in no [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*, “in those” is read for “in no,” producing an altogether contrary sense.] ecclesiastical disciplines, did not avoid [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*: “did not take care.”] the improper use of terms, saying “made” for “begotten”?

Moreover, when he called the Son second after the Father, he was not remote from the words of the saints. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book XII, says:

> “The Son is true God from thee, God the Father, and begotten by thee after thee; he is to be confessed as after thee in such a way that he is with thee, for thou art the eternal author of his eternal origin. For since he is from thee, he is second from thee—second, I say, in the mode of subsistence, not in difference of dignity. For he subsists from God the Father as though in the first place, while the Spirit is, as it were, in the third place from both.”

Hence Jerome calls the Father the principal Spirit in relation to the Son, speaking thus in his work *On the Three Virtues* [Note: No work *On the Three Virtues* survives among the works of St Jerome.]:

> “David in the Psalm asks for three Spirits, saying: ‘Strengthen me with a principal Spirit . . . renew a right Spirit within my inward parts . . . take not thy Holy Spirit from me.’ Who are these three Spirits? The Principal Spirit is the Father; the Right Spirit is Christ; the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit.”

Augustine, *Old and New Law*, chapter 58, says that the Holy Spirit is third from the Father, but second from Christ, according to numerical order.

Let Plato too be considered, that greatest of philosophers, together with his followers. According to the testimony of the holy Fathers, they, above all the philosophers of the Gentiles, attentively set forth [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*: “approaching.” In my judgment, our manuscript’s “attentively” is better.] after the prophets the full doctrine of the Trinity. They assert that Mind, which they call *Nous* (νοῦς), is born from God and coeternal with him—that is, the Son, whom we call the Wisdom of God, eternally begotten from God the Father. Nor do they seem to have omitted the person of the Holy Spirit, since they maintained that the soul of the world is the third person after God and *Nous* [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*, “from God *nous*,” wholly corrupt unless restored to “from God and *nous*.”].

Let us first carefully consider what Plato said [Col. 1144B] about this soul, from whom the other philosophers who spoke of the soul itself are believed to have derived their views. Distinguishing this soul of the world as, so to speak, the third person after God and *Nous*, and pursuing its description at greater length and with greater care, he defines it most fully both in itself and in its effects. In a similar way, we are accustomed sometimes to speak of the Holy Spirit according to the effects of his works, and sometimes according to the natural affection of his goodness which he had eternally in himself, as we shall distinguish more carefully below.

But now let us examine Plato’s words about the soul of the world attentively, so that we may recognize that the Holy Spirit is most fully signified in them. He says that before the constitution of the world it was made or begotten by God; in this, unless I am mistaken, he indicates to us the eternal procession of the Holy Spirit, by which he is from God the Father. For philosophers are accustomed to call “made from God” or “begotten” everything which has its being from God. Thus Hermes above called the Son of God made by God, because he has being from him as eternally begotten, not because he was temporally made or created by him. Plato too calls everything which has its being from God begotten from him, though he does not therefore call everything which is from God his Son—for example, the world itself and his other works.

When, having previously spoken of the world, Plato came to the soul of the world, he said:

> “Yet God did not approve the origin of the soul in the order in which we are now speaking; rather, he made it younger and subsequent [Col. 1144D] to bodies. For it was not fitting that the more ancient thing should be subject to the later-born thing [perhaps *rei regi*, ‘be ruled by the thing’].”

Again:

> “God commanded the soul, by both antiquity and powers, to take precedence over the nature of the body; and he willed it to be mistress and to possess principal authority over that which it would govern.”

Here it should also be noted that, in calling it mistress over the governance of the world, he surely places it above every creature and asserts it to be God. Later he called it the soul of the world in these words: “He said this and then [Col. 1145A] the remnants of the former mixture from which he had blended the soul of the world,” etc.

He fittingly called the Holy Spirit the soul of the world, as the life of the universe; for in the goodness of God all things in a certain manner have life, and all things are, as it were, living before God, and none are dead—that is, none useless—not even evils, which are also most excellently ordered through his goodness. Thus we recall that it is written both in the Evangelist and among the Platonists: “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3). This is as though it were plainly said: all things temporally made through him—that is, established through the very goodness of God—were in a certain way living eternally in the goodness of God, since under divine providence all things had from eternity been most excellently ordered through his goodness, so that he willed each to proceed as well as was fitting.

The saying of the Apostle, that some philosophers said, “In God we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28), appears not incongruous with this, as though they understood this soul of the world to be God himself. But to say that God conceived the third kind of soul, which we call the soul of the world, is as if he asserted that the Holy Spirit is the third person after God and *Nous* in that spiritual divine substance. God is said to conceive—that is, to apprehend wholly—the distinction of this person, which we cannot worthily conceive or fully distinguish from the Father and Son. It amounts to the same thing for something in some way to be conceived by God as for it to possess itself in that way, that is, truly to be so.

Then he immediately applies a careful description to this third person, whom he places as the soul of the world, saying that the soul itself consists of indivisible and immutable substance, and again of divisible substance, insofar as the soul is thought to divide itself among bodies. For the Holy Spirit is both an altogether simple substance in himself and, by the nature of divinity, remains wholly unvarying and immutable in himself; yet through his effects that same Spirit is in a certain way called manifold, and is sometimes called the seven Spirits, according to the efficacy of his sevenfold grace. Thus in praise of divine Wisdom his Spirit is described as one and manifold, active and stable.

The philosopher therefore says that the soul itself is composed of indivisible substance, always remaining in its own state. Yet because it is the inseparable companion of bodies, it is thought to divide itself among those bodies. This also applies to the Holy Spirit: according to his state in himself—not in his effects—he is altogether simple and unchangeable; yet he is thought to be in some way manifold according to his effects. This is what it is for him to divide himself among bodies, insofar as that soul is the inseparable companion of bodies. For he can in no way possess this division of multiplicity in relation to himself, but only in relation to his effects. It was excellently said that this is “thought,” and not that it is so; for, if we speak truly and properly, this multiplicity belongs not to the Spirit but to his effects. We call him manifold in this one respect, namely that he produces manifold things; that is, his effects are more properly diverse than he himself is.

Therefore, when in the soul of the world an indivisible and divisible substance—or, as was said, sameness and difference—meet together, Plato adds that a certain mixture is made from the indivisible and divisible, or from sameness and difference: that is, from the immutable and mutable. In this mixture, if I may so speak, the property of the Holy Spirit seems carefully and fully expressed, both in himself and, as has been said, in his effects. He says that God placed this third, mixed kind of substance midway between the two substances—the indivisible and divisible—because the Spirit too is from God, proceeding as it were from him, and has both these qualities from him from whom he has being. To say that God placed this kind of soul between the two aforesaid substances, as their middle, means that it is mixed from them; as if he said that from God himself, from whom the soul has its being, it has both this and that: that it is indivisible in its substance and divisible in its effects. The word “placed,” moreover, is aptly employed according to the metaphor by which something is called “middle,” as though set among surrounding things.

After he has designated the mixture of the soul from the indivisible and divisible, he proceeds to the mixture from sameness and difference, saying that the same soul consists in the same way of sameness and difference as it does of the indivisible and divisible. “One part of it,” he says, “is called same, another different.” The Spirit himself is the same in substance as God and *Nous*—that is, the Father and Son—and different in the property of person. We may also call him the same, that is, immutable in himself, and in a certain way different through his effects: for not only has he made things which are diverse, as was said above in relation to the indivisible substance, but he also changes and varies them through the succession of times, as he judges fitting, according to Boethius’s words:

> “… And, remaining stable, gives all things motion.”

Above he had indeed already shown him to be immutable, when he said, “substance always remaining in its own state”; but he had not yet added that he is variable through the change of his effects [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*: “through effect and of their change.”], which he now does.

He therefore rightly says that the soul is a kind of middle—that is, a mixture—of substance indivisible in itself and divisible through bodily conjunction, [Col. 1147A] that is, through its conjunction with bodies, when it applies itself to creating, governing, and ordering any things whatsoever, just as any soul [Note: In the *Introduction to Theology*: “an animal soul.”] confers its benefits upon its body. The philosopher also attributes to this soul the whole power and proportional harmony of numbers, in order to teach that the harmony of all things consists in the goodness of divine grace. For every order of nature and harmonious disposition is traced and defined by numerical proportions; and the most perfect pattern of numbers, fitting all things universally, presents itself—something not unknown to those who explore the mysteries of philosophy.

Hence arithmetic too, which consists wholly in the proportions of numbers, is called the mother and teacher [Col. 1147B] of the other arts, because the investigation and study of other things depend upon the discrimination [Note: [Col. 1147D] *Ibid.*, “from the dissection.”] of numbers. And, in order to express its ineffable sweetness of beneficence, they ascribe to it the whole harmony of musical consonances, by which they report both that the firmament itself continually resounds and that the higher regions of the world are filled.

For nothing delights and draws minds to itself by its excessive sweetness as melody does. Nothing is so apt to compose, move, or calm them, since, as philosophers knew according to the first chapter of Boethius’s *On Music*, the whole fabric of our soul and body is joined by a musical fitting-together: so much so that they observed and brought about the calming by melody of anger and madness, and the curing of the pains of very severe [Col. 1147C] illnesses. Whoever does not know this and has not yet learned it by experience should read the aforesaid chapter on music; there he will find how Pythagoras made milder and restored to self-possession a drunken [Note: [Col. 1147D] In the *Introduction to Theology*, “Ebrum” as though a proper name; our manuscript more correctly has *ebrium*, “drunken,” as what follows shows.] young man, who had been excited by the sound of the Phrygian mode, by accompanying it with a spondaic rhythm.

“For,” he says, “when a prostitute was shut up in the house of a rival, and he, raging, wished to burn the house down, and Pythagoras, according to his nightly custom, was observing the courses of the stars: when he learned that the young man had been incited by the sound of the Phrygian mode and that, despite many admonitions from his friends, he had refused to desist from the crime, he ordered the mode to be changed, and thus brought the raging young man’s mind into the state of the most peaceful temper.” There too he will find that, [Col. 1147D] when drunken young men, as often happens, urged on by the playing of pipes, were breaking down the doors of a chaste woman [Note: [Col. 1147D] *Ibid.*, “Instructed in letters, they were chastely breaking down doors”; better in our manuscript: “urged on, they were breaking down the doors of a chaste woman.”], Pythagoras is said to have instructed the flute-player to play a spondaic rhythm. When she did so, the slowness of the modes and the gravity of the music subdued their raging insolence.

There he will also see how Terpander and Arion rescued Lesbians and Ionians from very serious diseases by the aid of song; and likewise how Ismenias of Thebes is said to have wiped away every affliction, by means of musical modes, from many Boeotians [Col. 1148A] whom the torments of sciatic [Note: [Col. 1148D] *Ibid.*, “infected.”] pain afflicted. There also, when a certain madman was attacking Empedocles’ host [Note: [Col. 1148D] *Ibid.* adds: “in the *Lives of the Fathers*.”] with a sword, Empedocles is said to have altered his mode of singing and calmed the young man’s anger.

“So great,” says Boethius, “was the recognition of the power of the musical art in the studies of ancient philosophy that, when the Pythagoreans dismissed the day’s cares in sleep, they used certain songs so that gentle and quiet slumber might steal over them. And when they awoke [Note: [Col. 1148D] *Ibid.*, “when they had awakened.”], they cleansed away the numbness and confusion of sleep by certain other modes. They knew, doubtless, that the entire fabric of our soul and body is joined by musical fitting-together [Note: [Col. 1148D] *Ibid.*, “is joined.”]. For as the condition of the body is, so too the pulses [Col. 1148B] of the heart are excited by its motions.”

Democritus is said to have communicated this to Hippocrates the physician when he visited him, as though insane, under guard for the purpose of treatment, all the citizens [Note: [Col. 1148D] *Ibid.*, “Democritus’ citizens”; but *Democriti* is redundant.] holding that opinion. But why dwell on this? Because there can be no doubt that the condition of our soul and body seems in some way composed according to the same proportions which the following discussion will show to be combined and united in harmonic modulations.

And if what we have said concerning the power of harmony according to the philosophers seems insufficiently credible unless we confirm it also by the testimony of Sacred Scripture, let us recall how, when an evil spirit rushed upon Saul, men of wisdom—who did not fail to understand the force of harmonious sweetness—gave counsel that David’s melodies should remedy the goads of such great [Col. 1148C] madness. Hence afterward, when the man full of God was planning to build a temple in order to enlarge the religious worship of God, he composed psalms to be sung and assembled every kind of musical instrument, so that by harmonies both of voices and sounds he might attract the unformed people—by those same means through which he had earlier mitigated the diabolical torment in the rejected king.

From this it is especially taught how natural harmonious modulation is to the soul: by its sweetness it can so order and restore the soul’s nature that even the torments of malignant spirits cannot disturb it. Philosophers therefore rightly—or rather, perhaps the Lord through philosophers themselves unaware of it—assign the abundant and supreme sweetness of harmonious [Col. 1148D] modulation both to the soul of the world and to the higher regions of the firmament, in order to express, as fully as they could, the peace and concord they enjoy, and how harmoniously the divine goodness orders everything in the world. That goodness they call the soul of the world; Truth, as has been said, calls it the Holy Spirit.

And who, if he attends carefully, will not recognize what they said about heavenly harmony, which continually resounds in the higher regions of the world? For the heavenly spirits are bound both by the continual [Col. 1149A] vision of the divine Majesty and by the highest mutual concord; and in unceasing and ineffable exultation they sing the praises of him whom they behold, namely what, according to Isaiah, the seraphim do not cease to cry day and night: “Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord God of Hosts,” etc. (Isa. 6:3).

By the higher heavens, therefore—that is, the regions of the firmament—we understand these blessed spirits or their dwelling-place. They seem also not inappropriately to have designated them by the name of the seven planets, because of the excellence of their brightness, which divine grace, said to be sevenfold, spiritually illuminates. They are also aptly called in Isaiah *seraphim*, that is, “burning,” from the special illumination of grace [Note: [Col. 1149D] In the *Introduction to Theology*: “called so because, through the spiritual illumination of grace, they are especially inflamed with love for God.”].

Their higher dwelling should be understood as such both in dignity and [Col. 1149B] position; whereas [Note: [Col. 1150D] *Ibid.*, “from which,” perhaps better than “whereas.”] those who became proud are said to have been cast down into this dark and dense air. This place, lower in position and worse in habitation, may not inappropriately be understood by the name hell. Those blessed spirits also, or their heavenly dwelling-place, are fittingly compared with the firmament. When the others fell through pride [Note: [Col. 1150D] *Ibid.*, “singing,” entirely wrong.], these received, as the reward of their faithfulness and humaneness, that they should be so confirmed in contemplation of the divine majesty that they can never thereafter fall.

Hence Gregory says in Book XXVI of his *Moralia on Job*: “First heaven is said to have been made, and afterward this same thing is called the firmament, because the angelic nature was first created subtle in the heights, and afterward, lest it could ever fall, it was more wonderfully [Col. 1149C] confirmed.” The same author says in a homily on Ezekiel: “God created heaven, which he afterward called the firmament.” Thus these were heaven, who were first created good; but afterward they were called the firmament, because they received the power of immutability so that they might never fall at all.

Plato’s further statement that the soul was placed by God in the middle of the world and extended equally through the whole globe of the earthly orb beautifully signifies the grace of God offered universally to all, benevolently ordering everything in this great house or temple of his, as is wholesome or just. The words of the Book of Wisdom openly agree with this: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world,” etc. (Wis. 1:7). So too do the words of the Psalmist: “By the spirit of his mouth, all their host” (Ps. 32:6).

[Col. 1149D] Jerome, in Book II on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians:

> “The diversity of all things, in which one God and Father of all is spoken of, who is above all and in all, suggests a diverse understanding. For God the Father is above all, as the author of all things; the Son is through all, passing through and going through all things; the Holy Spirit is in all, and nothing exists apart from him.”

Zeno too, with the Stoics, held some such view about creatures and God; Virgil, following him, says that God goes through all lands and tracts of sea, and the rest; and:

> In the beginning, heaven and earth and the flowing plains,  
> The shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars,  
> An inward Spirit nourishes; and Mind, infused through all the limbs,  
> Stirs the whole mass and mingles itself with the mighty body.  
> —Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.724–27

Plato’s statement that the whole world is one living creature demonstrates the greatest concord of all God’s works, like that of diverse members in the one body of an animal. One soul presides over all, wholly present in each individual member and, though one and the same in diverse things, performing diverse works. Thus the Apostle too, when he demonstrates the concord and unity of the whole Church, calls it the one body of Christ, joined together from diverse believers by certain bonds and joints of faith and charity, serving [Col. 1150B] or ministering to one another as diverse members in one body, each of which needs the service of another.

The divine acts themselves also plainly agree with this allegorical covering concerning the soul’s position in the middle of the world—that is, concerning divine grace offered universally to all. For when the Lord was going to spread his teaching and the worship of true religion in the world, he chose Jerusalem, which is in the middle of the earth, appointed it as the head of his kingdom, and there first wished a temple, as it were a royal palace, to be built for the magnification of his worship. There too he poured out upon the apostles the most abundant grace of the Holy Spirit, by which the whole world might be spiritually quickened through them. Hence it is written: “But God, our king, has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. [Col. 1150C] 73:12). And again: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3).

On the passage of the prophet Ezekiel which says, “Thus says the Lord: This is Jerusalem; I have placed it in the midst of the nations, with lands around it” (Ezek. 5:5), Jerome wrote the following concerning the middle of the world and, as it were, the navel of the earth:

> “This same prophet here testifies that Jerusalem is situated in the middle of the world, showing it to be the navel of the earth.”

And the Psalmist, expressing the Lord’s passion, says: “He has wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73:12). Here the vine was planted which extended its branches as far as the sea. For Christ, the true vine, sent his apostles like branches throughout the whole world and made the whole world drunk with the abundance of spiritual teaching.

Concerning this quickening and enlivening of the Holy Spirit, the holy bishop Salvian, in Book I of *The Government of God*, addressed to Bishop Salonius, adduces Pythagorean testimony, saying:

> “Pythagoras the philosopher, whom philosophy itself received as almost its teacher, discussing the nature and benefits of God, speaks thus: ‘Mind, passing through and diffused throughout all parts of the world, from which all living creatures that come into being receive life—how then is God said to neglect the world, when he sufficiently loves it in this very fact that [Col. 1151A] he always directs his attention to the whole body of the world?’”

Concerning this Salvian, bishop of the Church of Marseille, his book to Salonius, and his other works, Gennadius, priest of Marseille, writing *On Illustrious Men*, makes mention among illustrious men of him and his works. After Pythagoras’s testimony Salvian also adduces Cicero, observing that the God whom Pythagoras calls *animus* (“mind” or “spirit”) is called *mens* (“mind”) by Cicero:

> “Indeed God himself, whom we understand, cannot be understood otherwise than as a certain mind, unbound, free, and separated from every mortal conglomeration [Note: [Col. 1151D] In the *Introduction to Theology*, “assembly.”], perceiving and moving all things.”

Elsewhere:

> “Nothing,” he says, “is more excellent than God. Therefore the world must be governed by him. God is subject or obedient to no [Col. 1151B] nature; therefore he himself governs all nature.”

Augustine, Book IV, chapter 34, of *The City of God*, speaking of Varro, says:

> “This same most acute and learned author says that only those seem to him to have understood what God is who believed him to be the soul governing the world by motion and reason. And therefore, although he did not yet hold what Truth holds—for the true God is not a soul but also the creator of the soul—nevertheless he confesses and urges that one God should be worshipped.”

Likewise, in Book XXII:

> “Cicero, a great authority among them, wishing, as he could, to define God, says: ‘He is a certain mind, unbound and free, separated from every [Col. 1151C] mortal conglomeration, perceiving and moving all things, and itself endowed with everlasting motion.’ This he found in the teaching of the great philosophers.”

Thus they called God *mens*, that is, *animus* or soul, because he presides over the governance of the whole world as a soul over a body. Accordingly, a certain wise man, exhorting us to worship God with a worthy mind—that is, one cleansed of vices and adorned with virtues—aptly said at the very beginning of his exhortation and instruction:

> If God is mind, as the poems tell us,  
> He must especially be worshipped by you with a pure mind.

It is as though, openly instructing his son, he said: Since God is *animus*, that is [Note: [Col. 1151D] *Introduction to Theology*: “to us, that is.”], true and spiritual life, as the writings [Note: [Col. 1151D] *Introduction*: “Scripture.”] of poets themselves declare—for example, those words of Virgil which Macrobius adduces on this very matter, as we shall show below—glorify him, namely God, especially by living well.

Plato also rightly called the world an animal and declared it to be an intelligent—that is, rational—animal, because its soul, insofar as it is more excellent than all others, acts and orders everything within it more rationally. When it is further said that this soul of the world provides the causes of all things [Col. 1152A] that come to pass, this ascribes the providence of the divine and of all [Note: [Col. 1151D] *Introduction*: “the divine and of all,” not so correctly.] natures, and the fullness of divine knowledge, from which it is further implied that it is God. It is said to measure and deliberate future things from present ones because future things must be prepared in accordance with those that already are, so that they may adhere and be fitted together by a congruous ordering.

The further statement that our souls—that is, human souls—are fashioned from the remnants of the world-soul’s composition is as though he said that they imitate the soul [Note: [Col. 1151D] *Introduction*: “that soul”; our manuscript better has “those souls,” namely human souls.] of the world in powers and virtues, but in this very respect fall far short of its dignity. He also fittingly calls it the soul of the world, and not the soul of some thing in the world, just as we call it the soul of a human being, not of some human limb. For soul is so called from giving life; nor is anything properly said to be animated except that in which the entire force of vital activity is so complete that nothing external need adhere to that living body in order to preserve the life it has in itself.

Since, according to the philosophers, the world contains all things, so that nothing remains outside it to be divinely ordered, it is rightly called the soul of the world, just as it is called the soul of a human being when the whole power of the soul is complete in that person. Thus, indeed, the world itself had no need to possess eyes or the other instruments of sense [Note: [Col. 1152D] *Introduction*: “had need.”], as Plato himself maintains, since nothing remains outside it for which these could have any use.

Having briefly gathered these points from Plato and, as I think, sufficiently carefully explained them as a testimony to our faith, [Col. 1152C] I think it follows that we should proceed to his followers, in order to show that what they too have said about the soul of the world cannot reasonably be understood except as assigned, by the most beautiful figure of an allegorical covering, to the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 1152D] *Introduction to Theology*: “the Holy Spirit,” quite plainly wrong, as is evident to an attentive reader.].

This manner of speech is especially familiar to philosophers no less than prophets: when they arrive at the secrets of prophecy, they do not express anything in common words, but rather draw the reader on by comparisons of likenesses. Things that formerly seemed fabulous and remote from all usefulness are more pleasing on the surface of the letter, but when afterward found full of great mysteries, they contain in themselves the edification of great [Note: [Col. 1152D] *Introduction*: “great.”] instruction.

For this reason, Augustine testifies, they are covered over, lest they become cheap. In Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, explaining the causes of the difficulty and accessibility of Sacred Scripture, he says:

> “Certain obscure sayings cast over it a very dense darkness. I do not doubt that all this was divinely provided in order to tame pride by labor and to recall the understanding from disgust, since things easily discovered commonly become cheap.”

Likewise:

> “Those who do not find at all what they seek suffer hunger; but those who do not seek because they have it ready to hand often languish from disgust. Therefore the Holy Spirit wisely arranged the Scriptures so that in clearer places it might meet hunger, but in more obscure places wipe away disgust.”

Thus the Lord seems to delight in resting in hiding, so that the more he conceals himself, the more pleasing he may be to those to whom he reveals himself; and the more [Note: [Col. 1153D] *Introduction*: “from which.”] labor is expended because of the difficulty of Scripture, the greater may be the readers’ merit. Of this the Psalmist says: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Ps. 17:12). And again: “Dark water in the clouds of the air” (*ibid.*), because, says Gregory, “knowledge is obscure in the prophets.” Of this it is also written in the Law: “Moses approached the darkness in which God was” (Exod. 20:21). Solomon says in Chronicles: “The Lord promised that he would dwell in darkness” (2 Chron. 6:1). The same author says in Proverbs: [Col. 1153B] “It is the glory of God to conceal a word, and the glory of kings to investigate a matter” (Prov. 25:2).

He also invites us in Proverbs to search out the obscurities of Scripture as hiding places in which God may be found: “The wise person will understand [Note: [Col. 1153D] *Introduction*: “when he understands.”] a parable and an interpretation, the words of the wise and their riddles” (Prov. 1:6). These things are understood as much more dearly as greater effort has been spent in understanding them.

Jerome too, writing to Magnus the orator on this very saying of Solomon at the beginning of Proverbs, says:

> “At the beginning of Proverbs he warns us to understand sayings of prudence, subtleties of words, parables and obscure speech, sayings of the wise, and riddles, which belong properly [Col. 1153C] to dialecticians and philosophers.”

How consistently philosophy has disdained to publish its secrets in bare words, and has especially been accustomed to speak by certain fabulous coverings concerning the soul and the gods, Macrobius—no mediocre philosopher and the interpreter of the great philosopher Cicero—teaches with the greatest care. Having set aside types of invention or fable unworthy of philosophers, he puts forward the one kind that they most honorably employ. For he says:

> “When knowledge of sacred matters is set forth beneath the pious covering of fictions, concealed by honorable things and clothed in names, this alone is the kind of fiction that the caution of one philosophizing about divine things admits.”

A little later he says:

> “It must be known,” he says, “that philosophers do not admit fabulous matter into every [Col. 1153D] discussion [Note: [Col. 1153D] *Introduction to Theology*: “into every,” omitting *not*, contrary to the author’s manifest meaning.], but usually employ it when they speak either of the soul or of the ethereal powers.”

But when their inquiry ventures to rise to the supreme God and ruler of all, whom the Greeks call *Tagathon* (τὸ ἀγαθόν, “the Good”), who is also called *Protopanton* (“before all things”), and to the Mind which the Greeks call *Nous* (νοῦς), containing the original forms of things, called Ideas, born and proceeding from the supreme God—when, I say, they speak of the supreme God and Mind, they touch nothing whatever fabulous. But if they try to set forth anything concerning [Col. 1154A] those things which transcend not only human speech but human thought as well, they have recourse to likenesses and examples.

Cassiodorus, on Psalm 50:

> “At ‘Restore to me joy,’ etc.: Some Fathers offer the following likeness of corporeal things existing together. We find three properties in the sun. First is the bodily substance itself, which is the sun; next, its brightness, which remains in it; third, the heat which reaches us from its brightness. If any likeness can be found for so great a reality, I think it should be understood in this way: what is bodily substance in the sun may in some manner be understood in the Trinity as the person of the Father; what is brightness, as the person of the Son, as the Apostle says, ‘The brightness of his glory’ [Col. 1154B] (Heb. 1:3); and what is heat, as the person of the Holy Spirit, as we read, ‘Who can hide himself from his heat?’ (Ps. 18:7).
>
> “Another example is given from incorporeal things. The soul is an incorporeal substance in which are intellect and life. Therefore what is substance in the soul may, if it is lawful to say it, be understood in the Trinity as the person of the Father; what is power and knowledge in the soul is understood as the Son, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God; and what is the property of giving life in the soul is understood as the Holy Spirit, through whom the work of giving life is proclaimed in many places to be accomplished. Thus Peter the Apostle says in his Epistle: ‘Put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit’ (1 Pet. 3:18). Likewise the Apostle: ‘The letter kills, but the spirit gives life’ (2 Cor. 5:6). And in the Gospel [Col. 1154C] the Lord says: ‘It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing’ (John 6:63).”

Thus, when Plato undertook to speak of *Tagathon* [Note: [Col. 1154D] *Introduction*: τῷ ἀγαθῷ, “the Good.”], he did not dare to say what it is, knowing [Note: [Col. 1154D] *Introduction*: “thinking.”] only this of it: that human beings cannot know what it is like. Among visible things he found only the sun most like it; through that likeness he opened a path by which his speech might rise to what cannot be comprehended. For this reason antiquity decreed [Note: [Col. 1154D] *Introduction*: “invented.”] that no image of it should be set up with the gods, because the supreme God and the Mind born from him are, as they are beyond the soul, so above nature; to them nothing from the realm of fables may reach.

But concerning the other gods, as I have said, and the soul, philosophers turn to fables not aimlessly or for entertainment, but because they know that open and naked exposition of itself is hostile to nature. Just as nature withdrew knowledge of itself from common human senses under the covering and veil of diverse things, so it wished its secrets to be treated by the wise through fables. Thus the mysteries themselves are covered in the tunnels of figures, lest even for those who attain this . . . . . nature should make itself available in such matters; rather, let the rest be content with reverence, while the figures preserve the secret from cheapness for eminent men alone, who, with Wisdom as interpreter, are conscious of its hidden mystery.

In accordance with this, Truth itself speaks to the apostles about the covering [Col. 1155A] of his parables: “To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the rest in parables, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand” (Mark 4:11–12).

From this teaching of Macrobius it is therefore clear that what philosophers say concerning the soul of the world must be understood through an allegorical covering. Otherwise we shall discover that Plato, the greatest of philosophers, is the greatest of fools. For what could be more ridiculous than to think the whole world one rational animal, unless this has been set forth through a covering [Note: [Col. 1155D] *Introduction*: “unless through this covering”; where there is an obvious transposition of words, to be restored thus: “unless this has been set forth through a covering.”]? For it cannot be an animal unless it is sentient, since the well-known definition of animal is “an animate, sentient substance.” Which of the five senses could belong to the world, except perhaps touch, which all animals share? It lacks the instruments of the other senses, as Plato himself attests where he explains why it had no need for eyes, ears, or the other parts of the human body. Or what part of the world’s body is there by which, if touched, it could feel more than trees or plants, which they say are given life by the same soul while rooted in the earth? For [Note: [Col. 1155D] *Introduction*: “surely?”] what would the world feel more from the digging up of earth than trees from the tearing off of their leaves or the cutting away of their entire bodies? Yet trees and any plants are certainly insentient; and therefore, to exclude them, “sentient” is placed after “animate” in the definition of animal.

Furthermore, when they say that the soul of the world is infused into individual [Col. 1155C] bodies and animates those which it finds suited to animation, what need was there for the creation of our souls, which Plato says were made afterward? Or what need is there for the world-soul to be in bodies which it does not animate? For what is more evident than that our bodies have animal life from their own human souls rather than from the soul of the world? When these souls are present, the bodies are immediately animate; when they are absent, they are inanimate—even though, as they say, the soul of the world remains in them even after death, being wholly in all bodies, including those in which it is idle.

Why, moreover, when human souls are absent, is the soul of the world not sufficient to animate our bodies although it is present in them, seeing that, according to Plato’s testimony, it was made by the most excellent Creator more excellent than all invisible things? Is it less efficacious in us than the other soul, so that our bodies, now dead, are no longer fit to be animated as they once were when human souls were present? It can give life to countless worms from one body when the body itself can no longer animate. What fitness—perhaps *igitur*, “therefore”—is lacking to the dead body so that it is not now animated [Col. 1156A] [Note: [Col. 1155D] *Introduction*: “nor likewise by which it may be animated.”], except only the presence of the human soul, which gives life to the body when present and makes it dead on departing?

But if we turn these things too, which philosophers said about the soul of the world, toward an allegorical covering, all can easily be understood rationally and without departing from the tenor of sacred faith.

Let human souls give animal life to our bodies. Let the soul of the world—which, unless I am mistaken, the philosophers understood to be the Holy Spirit—give our very souls spiritual life through the distribution of its gifts, so that individual souls may be the life of bodies [Note: [Col. 1156D] *Introduction*: “so that, just as souls are…”], while the Holy Spirit is the life of souls. By quickening them he advances them toward the progress of good works. Thus, in a certain manner [Note: [Col. 1156D] *Introduction*: “thus in what manner.”], our souls should be called certain bodies [Note: [Col. 1156D] *Introduction* omits “certain.”] [Col. 1156B] of the Holy Spirit: he inhabits them, as a temple, by some gift of his grace and gives them life through virtues.

Their assertion, too, that the soul, wholly infused into individual bodies, gives life to and animates everything that it finds suited to animation [Note: [Col. 1156D] *Introduction*: “and the soul which it finds suited to quickening.”], with no hardness or density [Note: [Col. 1156D] *Introduction*: “or diversity.”] of their nature impeding it, is a beautiful allegorical covering. For the charity of God, which we call the Holy Spirit, is first infused into human hearts through the gift of faith or reason. It has given life to some, advancing us toward the fruit of good works so that we may attain eternal life; and in some persons the Spirit himself is said to be inactive, because the hardness of their wickedness resists.
