This teaching concerning the soul of the world was especially left to posterity by Macrobius, the most diligent of philosophers, in his exposition. If we examine his words closely, we shall find our whole faith concerning the Holy Spirit truly expressed in them. For he calls this very soul both creator and says that it is from God the Father and *Nous* (νοῦς), that is, God the Son. He even dared sometimes to call it *nous* (νοῦς), in order to signify the unity of substance which it has with the Son from whom it is. Thus, explaining Virgil and speaking of the world-soul, he says: “For he gave a soul to the world, and, to attest its purity, called it mind.” Again: “In order to affirm the dignity of that world-soul, he declared it to be mind”—as though to say that it is of the same substance as the Word himself, from [Col. 1156D] whom it is.

The purity of mind means the subtlety of reason, which penetrates all natures in examining them. These are the words of Macrobius which we proposed:

> “The soul, therefore,” he says, “creating and fashioning bodies for itself—for nature begins from the soul, which the wise call from God and from Mind, *nous* (νοῦς)—from that most pure fountain, from which it had drawn, by being born, the abundance of its origin, gave life to the bodies of heaven and stars which it first created.”

And later, when he distinguished the powers of that soul itself which it exercises in bodies, according to which the nature of all animated things is ordered, so that some, namely, preside over others, he added:

> “Virgil too expressed this order of things (*Aeneid* VI.727 ff.). For he gave a soul to the world and, to attest its purity, called it mind. ‘Heaven,’ he says, ‘and lands and seas and stars an inward spirit nourishes’—that is, the soul. And, in order to affirm the dignity of that soul, he declared it to be mind: ‘Mind stirs the mass.’ Further, to show that all living things consist of and are animated by that soul, he added: ‘Hence the race of men and cattle,’ etc. And, to affirm that the same vigor always exists in the soul, but that its use grows dull in living creatures through the density of the body, he added: [Col. 1157B] ‘As much as harmful bodies retard.’”

All these words of both Virgil and Macrobius can easily be accommodated to the tenor of our faith according to our purpose; nor ought they be interpreted otherwise. Thus, where he says that the use of the soul grows dull in animals through the density of the body, it means that the grace of the Holy Spirit has less efficacy in its benefits among carnal and bestial people, who are governed more by the senses than by reason and are devoted to carnal pleasures. By the density of the body we understand the greatness of carnal enticements.

Where he also says that the soul creates and fashions bodies for itself, he asserts that it is the creator of things and therefore God, as well as the organizer and disposer of created things for good works through the distribution [Col. 1157C] of its gifts, so that it may make them a worthy dwelling-place for itself. He says that nature begins from the soul because we are born spiritually through the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that we may be children of God rather than servants. For just as, if this grace were withdrawn, we would die in vices, so when it is bestowed we are born into the true life of virtues, which we possess according to nature; whereas vices are contrary to nature, since vice is the corruption of nature.

The soul is said to be named from God and Mind because it is the same Spirit of both Father and Son, since it proceeds from each. Hence, as Augustine says in Book XV, chapter 19, of *On the Trinity*: “Because that Spirit is common to both, it is properly called what both are in common; namely, both the Father himself and [Col. 1157D] the Son are Spirit and holy.”

But when philosophers say that the soul is born, created, or made from God and *nous* (νῷ), this is an impropriety of words rather than an error of meaning. For “created” or “made” is not correctly [Note: [Col. 1157D] *Introduction*: “necessarily.”] said except of things which began—that is, which are not eternal. But “to be born,” that is, to exist from the very substance of the Father, belongs properly to the Son, of whom we shall speak later in the appropriate place. Yet philosophers sometimes use “created,” “born,” and “made” to mean “to be from something” [Col. 1158A] [Note: [Col. 1157D] *Introduction*: “to be something.”].

Thus Macrobius says that both *Nous* (νοῦς) [Note: [Col. 1157D] *Introduction*: “it, *nous*.”] itself is created from God and the soul from *Nous* (νῷ), that is, that each exists from it. In the same sense he improperly uses “to be born” here [Note: [Col. 1157D] *Introduction*: “we use improperly.”]. Hermes, however, having said above that God made a second Lord, shows him—that is, the Son [Note: [Col. 1157D] *Introduction*: “the Son of God.”]—to be from God the Father. He calls *Nous* (νοῦς) itself the most pure fountain of Wisdom, that is, the Father’s wisdom, from which nothing, however obscure, can remain hidden.

From the abundance of this fountain, the goodness of God itself gave life to the bodies of heaven and the stars—that is, to the angels themselves or the heavenly spirits, who were created before humankind—according to what is written: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). “Heaven and stars” [Col. 1158B] is said according to the difference of ranks, since we believe that some spirits are set over and superior to others. Hence we speak of angels and archangels, or dominions. Angels, spiritually quickened by the supreme Spirit himself, as has been said, may also be called bodies. Or he calls them bodies in accordance with Augustine’s statement that every creature is corporeal, that is, circumscribed.

Thus he says in chapter 10 of *On the Orthodox Faith* [Note: Chapters 11 and 12 in the Introduction: “Hence Gennadius [Col. 1158D], in the book *On the Orthodox Faith*—and certainly more correctly, for Augustine is not the author of the book *On the Orthodox Faith*, although it is found among his works, but Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles, as we observed above.”]:

> “Nothing incorporeal and invisible ought to be believed to exist in nature except God alone, who is believed to be incorporeal because he is everywhere and fills all things, and therefore invisible to all creatures because he is incorporeal. Every creature is corporeal; angels and all heavenly powers are corporeal [Note: The Introduction omits “powers,” incorrectly.], although they do not subsist in flesh. But [Col. 1158C] we believe intellectual natures to be corporeal because they are spatially circumscribed, just as the human soul, which is enclosed by flesh, and demons, who by the substance of angelic nature are corporeal [Note: In the printed editions of Gennadius among Augustine’s works, the word *corporei* (“corporeal”) is lacking.].”

It was well said that they are animated from Wisdom itself, because this is eternal life: that we may know as we are known, seeing God face to face. The Spirit draws from that fountain when he imbues us with understanding of divine Wisdom, according to what was said: “He shall receive from what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:14). Hence he is called the Spirit of wisdom, or understanding, or knowledge.

But the statement, “Mind moves the mass,” that is, the magnitude of the whole fabric of the world, as though it quickened or moved everything in the world [Col. 1158D], should be understood in this sense: that it disposes all things excellently and, remaining stable, causes all things to be moved. All things are also said to live in God, inasmuch as in him nothing is dead—that is, useless—but all things are made or ordered usefully and fittingly. Hence it is written: “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3), that is, before they came to be, they were most suitably ordered in the providence of divine Wisdom itself. Thus it is further said: “God, to whom all things live” [Col. 1159A]; and the Apostle says: “In whom we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). He gives life both to human beings and to beasts; gifts of his for life are possessed by both the wisest and the simple and unlearned. Hence Ecclesiastes also says: “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of Adam ascends upward, and whether the spirit of beasts descends downward?” (Eccles. 3:21)—that is, which among the wisest and the unlearned are predestined to life, and which appointed to death.

Let these things collected from Macrobius suffice. But if anyone accuses me as an intrusive and violent interpreter, because by too bold an exposition I twist the philosophers’ words toward our faith and impose upon them what they never [Col. 1159B] understood, let him consider that prophecy of Caiaphas, which the Holy Spirit uttered through him, adapting it to a sense far different from that intended by the speaker himself. For even when the Holy Spirit speaks some things through the holy prophets, they do not understand all the meanings to which their words extend; rather, they often have only one meaning in them, while the Spirit himself, who speaks through them, provides many there, so that [Note: Introduction: “to the end that.”] afterward he inspires different meanings to different interpreters.

Hence Gregory, writing in the *Register* to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari [Note: Introduction: “of Calahorra.”], says:

> “In the interpretation of Holy Scripture, nothing that does not oppose sound faith ought to be rejected. For just as from one piece of gold some make chains, others rings, others bracelets for adornment, so from one statement of Holy Scripture interpreters [Col. 1159C] each compose, through innumerable [Note: Introduction: “interpretations also through innumerable.”] senses, as it were varied ornaments; all of which nevertheless contribute to the adornment of the heavenly bride.”

Moreover, Macrobius himself has previously observed that the things philosophers have said concerning the world-soul are to be interpreted mystically. Since these cannot in any way be explained truly or suitably [Note: Introduction: “which can also be expounded according to the letter.”], as we have mentioned above, the letter itself compels us toward a mystical interpretation. We have likewise learned from many testimonies of the saints that the Platonic school agrees with Catholic faith. Therefore, not without reason, Plato—the greatest of philosophers—is commended above the rest by all, not only by those skilled in secular disciplines but also by saints.

Concerning him Augustine says in Book VIII [Note: Introduction incorrectly reads Book IX.] of *The City of God* [Col. 1159D]:

> “Some joined to us in Christ’s grace wonder, when they hear or read Plato, that he held such views concerning God as are recognized to agree greatly with the truth of our religion. Hence some have thought that, when he travelled to Egypt, he heard Jeremiah or read the prophetic Scriptures on that journey. But if the chronological sequence contained in historical chronicles is carefully calculated [Note: Introduction: “if it is carefully calculated”; our reading conforms to Augustine’s text.], it shows that Plato was born nearly a hundred years after Jeremiah prophesied. Having lived eighty-one years, nearly sixty [Note: Introduction: “nine”; our reading is as in Augustine.] years are found from the year of Plato’s death until King Ptolemy of Egypt arranged for the prophetic Scriptures to be translated and possessed through the seventy Hebrews, who also knew Greek. Therefore Plato could neither have seen Jeremiah on that journey, since he had died so long before, nor read those Scriptures in Greek, since they had not been translated into Greek—unless perhaps, because he was of most acute diligence, he learned these too through an interpreter, just as he learned Egyptian matters.”

Indeed, Plato’s sayings seem to agree so closely with the words and preaching of the Lord that, as blessed Augustine declares in the second book of *On Christian Doctrine*, certain readers and lovers of Plato dared to burst into such madness as to say that our Lord Jesus Christ had learned from Plato’s books all the sayings of his which they are compelled to admire and proclaim. Hence King Ptolemy too is said, if I am not mistaken, to have perceived these same things in Plato’s doctrine, because from Platonic writings he had learned of God and Mind—that is, the Father and the Word. Therefore, when the Seventy Interpreters translated the Law for him, they completely kept silent about the mystery of divine generation, by prudent counsel, as the Jews say [Note: Introduction: “as they say appears,” words which produce no sense.], lest, if he heard that this too was preached among the Hebrews, he should discover that there was a twofold divinity—he who had previously [Note: Introduction: “because previously.” More correctly our manuscript has “he who previously.”] been a worshipper of one God only—and lest, because of Platonic doctrine, he should stray from the unity of the Godhead [Col. 1160C], although there he had heard several persons distinguished, while the singularity of one Godhead was preserved.

Hence Jerome recalls in the prologue to the Pentateuch:

> “By the aforesaid Seventy many things of this kind were omitted, such as: ‘Out of Egypt I called my Son’ (Hosea 2:1), and similar passages.”

From this it is clear that the Platonic school has always agreed very greatly with faith in the holy Trinity, and that this doctrine is distinguished and described more carefully than by all other philosophers by Plato and his followers. Thus Valerius Maximus not undeservedly burst forth in Plato’s praise with these words:

> “While Plato was a little child sleeping in his cradle, bees placed honey upon his lips. When this was heard, interpreters of portents declared that a singular sweetness of eloquence would flow from his mouth.”

But I do not doubt that this is interpreted more excellently and suitably if the miracle is referred to the glory of divine dignity [Note: Introduction: “deity,” less correctly.]: namely, that God bestowed on him this mark of prophecy because through him he was to disclose [Note: Introduction: “reveal.”] more diligently the mysteries of his divinity. For it was fitting that the supreme philosopher [Col. 1161A] and his followers should bear very great witness to the supreme wisdom, which is Christ—namely, the Word and Wisdom of God the Father.

Thus too, according to blessed Augustine, when the Apostle spoke to the Athenians, as we mentioned above, and had stated a great matter, one that could be understood by few—that in him we live, move, and are—he added, “as certain of yours have said” (Acts 17:28). [Note: Acts reads “your poets,” but Abelard suppressed the word “poets,” so that the Apostle’s saying could be attributed to Plato, whom he presents as an Athenian and a philosopher, not a poet.] For Plato was certainly an Athenian.

But the point in which Plato appears, and is said, to have erred not a little—namely, his assertion that the world-soul was made, that is, had a beginning, and Macrobius’s earlier assertion, while speaking of the world-soul, that God and *nous* (νοῦς, “Mind”) are above the soul, as though superior in dignity—does not depart from truth if it is considered more carefully, although all true Catholics agree that the three persons in the Godhead are in every respect equal and coeternal with one another [Col. 1161B], as we shall later show when discussing the procession of the Spirit. [Note: Introduction reads “disagreeing,” contrary to the author’s meaning.] For not without reason is this philosopher commended above the others by all, both believers, as we have noted, and unbelievers.

Since, then, the Platonic school has shone forth in every branch of philosophical teaching, it is useful also to introduce testimonies from certain Platonists. Father Augustine recalls in Book VII of the *Confessions* that he found these in their writings; in them almost the entire substance of our faith concerning the divinity of the Word is set out most openly, just as it was afterward delivered by the greatest writers of the New Testament, John and Paul. For Augustine there directs his discourse to God:

> “You procured for me, through a certain man swollen with monstrous pride, certain books of the Platonists translated from Greek into Latin. And there I read—not indeed in these words, but with this very thing urged by many and varied arguments—that: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of human beings, and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it’ (John 1:1). And that the human soul, although it bears witness concerning the light, is not itself the light; but the Word, God, is the true light, because he enlightens every human being coming [Col. 1161D] into this world; and because he was in this world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. But that he came into his own, and his own did not receive him; while to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those believing in his name—I did not read that there.
>
> “Likewise, I read there that the Word, God, was born not of flesh, nor of blood, nor of the will of a man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God. But that the Word was made flesh and dwelt [Col. 1162A] among us, I did not read there. I searched out in those writings that it is said in many ways that the Son, being in the form of the Father, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, because he is naturally that very thing. But that he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being, humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross; for which reason God also raised him from the dead and gave him the name above every name, so that at his name every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and all should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:7–11)—those books do not contain this.
>
> “That your Son, coeval with you [Note: Introduction: “your only-begotten Son, coeternal with you.”], remains unchangeably before all times and above all times [Col. 1162B], and that souls receive from his fullness in order to be blessed, and are renewed by participation in Wisdom abiding in itself in order to be wise—this is there. But that he died for the ungodly is not there.”

But lest any sex among human beings distinguished above the rest by a reputation for wisdom should be absent from the testimonies to our faith, let that famous Sibyl also be introduced. In describing the divinity of the Word, she omitted neither his humanity, nor either advent, nor either judgment of the Word: first, the judgment by which Christ was unjustly judged in his passion; and second, that by which he will justly judge the world in majesty [Note: Introduction omits “in majesty,” which fits better.].

Augustine says in *Against Five Heresies*:

> “Let us hear what the Sibyl, their prophetess, also says concerning him: ‘The Lord has given another to human beings to be worshipped.’” [Col. 1162C]

Again:

> “Know that he himself is your Lord, the Son of God.”

Elsewhere she calls the Son the *Symbol* of God, that is, his counsellor or counsel. And the prophet says: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor” (Isa. 9:6).

Again, the same Father Augustine says in Book XVIII [Note: The Introduction incorrectly reads Book VIII.] of *The City of God*:

> “At that time some report that the Erythraean Sibyl prophesied; others more readily believe her to have been the Cumaean. There are twenty-seven verses of hers which, as a certain person translated them into Latin verse, contain the following:
>
> > The sign of judgment: the earth will drip with sweat;  
> > From heaven the King will come, who shall be forever,  
> > Present in the flesh, indeed, to judge the world, etc.”

[Col. 1162D] The first letters of these verses, joined together in Greek, signify: “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” Lactantius also adduces [Note: LACTANTIUS, *Divine Institutes*, book IV, chapter 18.] prophecies of the Sibyl concerning Christ:

> “Thereafter he shall come into the hands of unbelievers;  
> They will strike God with unclean hands,  
> And with defiled mouths spit out poisonous spittle.
>
> Yet he will yield his holy back humbly to blows,  
> And, receiving blows with the fist, will remain silent [Note: Introduction: “will receive,” omitting “will remain silent.”], lest anyone recognize
>
> [Col. 1163A] What the Word is, or whence it came, so that it may speak further below [Note: Introduction: “from hell.”],
>
> And he shall be crowned with a thorny crown.
>
> But for food they gave him gall, and for thirst vinegar.
>
> They will display this table in hospitality.
>
> For you, foolish people, did not understand your God.
>
> Playing with the minds of mortals, you crowned him
>
> With thorns; you mixed gall.
>
> The veil of the temple shall be torn, and in mid-day
>
> There will be darkness for three hours, and he will die [Note: In the Introduction the words “for three hours, and he will die” are missing.]
>
> Having received sleep for three days;
>
> And then, returning from below to the light, he will come.
>
> First displayed as the beginning of resurrection.”

This prophecy of the Sibyl, if I am not mistaken, had been heard and considered by that greatest of our poets, Virgil, when, in the Fourth Eclogue, he foretold that in the near future, under Caesar Augustus during Pollio’s consulship, there would be born a wondrous child sent down from heaven to earth [Col. 1163B], who would also take away the sins of the world and wonderfully establish, as it were, a new age in the world. He was prompted, as he himself says, by the prophecy of the Cumaean song—that is, of the Sibyl called Cumaean. For he speaks as though exhorting all to rejoice with him and sing together, or write, concerning this great child to be born; compared with him, he considers all other subjects low and worthless:

> Sicilian Muses, let us sing things a little greater;  
> Not all delight in groves and lowly tamarisks:
>
> [lacuna]
>
> Now comes the final age of the Cumaean song;  
> The great order of the ages is born anew;  
> Now too the Virgin returns, the reign of Saturn returns;  
> Now a new offspring is sent down from high heaven.  
> (VIRGIL, *Eclogue* IV, vv. 1 ff.)

[Col. 1163C] And shortly afterward:

> Under your consulship, Pollio, this glory of the age  
> Shall begin for you. [lacuna]
>
> If any traces of our sin remain,  
> They shall become void and free the earth from perpetual fear.  
> (Ibid., vv. 11–44.)

Likewise, concerning the child:

> “And he shall rule a pacified world by his father’s virtues,” etc.  
> (Ibid., v. 17 ff.)

These lines contain a most open prophecy of the incarnation of the Son of God, perhaps with the poet himself unaware of what the Holy Spirit was saying in the Sibyl or in him—just as happened with Caiaphas when he said: “It is expedient that one should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John 11:50). There it is also added: “He did not say this of himself” (ibid., 51).

It can likewise very easily be proved from what follows [Col. 1163D] that this Eclogue cannot truly or fittingly be understood of anyone except the incarnate only-begotten Son of God, if it is spoken typologically in the prophetic manner. For if expounded literally, its claims are found to be openly false and wholly impossible; nor can they even suitably be adduced as flattery, as some suppose, since they are at once rejected by everyone as unbelievable, and thus move the hearer more toward indignation against us [Note: Introduction: “so that they move [Col. 1164D] more against the poet toward unworthiness.”] than draw him toward goodwill. But elsewhere it will fall to us to demonstrate or expound these matters more carefully, when we present testimonies concerning the incarnation of the Word rather than his divinity.

Now therefore let us return to the proposed testimonies concerning the divinity of the Word; and, together with David and Solomon, kings of Israel, let us bring forward a third king of the Gentiles for the prophecy of the supreme King. For what is clearer than Nebuchadnezzar’s testimony concerning the Son of God? “Behold,” he says, “I see four men, unbound [Note: Introduction: “the heavens unbound.”], walking in the midst of the fire; and the appearance of the fourth is like the Son of God” (Dan. 3:92).

It is useful also to introduce the testimony of Dindimus, king of the Brahmans, so that our assertion of faith may stand out through the authority of four kings: two Jews and two Gentiles—David and Solomon, Nebuchadnezzar and Dindimus. Let these four kings be like the four wheels of the noble chariot of the supreme King, by which the faith of the four evangelists concerning the holy Trinity may be carried throughout the whole world [Col. 1164B]; and let the authority of kings be all the firmer in proportion as their power is higher, so that those who issue edicts and laws to peoples may also hand down the doctrines of sacred faith.

Dindimus says, therefore, in his first letter to Alexander—he says, I repeat, as follows:

> “Among the other distinguishing features of the religion or faith of his people, God does not accept bloody rites; he loves bloodless worship; he rejects death-bearing libations; he is propitiated by those praying with the word, which alone he shares with humankind; and he takes the greatest delight in his own [Note: Introduction: “divine.”] likeness. For the Word is God; it created this world, governs and sustains [Col. 1164C] all things; we worship it, we love it, and from it we draw our spirit.”

From Seneca’s fourth letter to Paul:

> “I declare that I have been well received by reading your letters which you sent to the Galatians, Corinthians, and Achaeans. The Holy Spirit also expresses through you senses lofty above the exalted, and sufficiently venerable.”

For God himself is spirit and mind, and therefore is pleased not by earthly riches or lavish generosity, but by religious deeds and thanksgiving. What great religious devotion or abstinence the people of the Brahmans possessed—so that God ought to inspire them above all nations with understanding of the sacred faith—is contained in Dindimus’s letter to Alexander. If credit is to be given to those letters, no human life, however religious, seems comparable with the innocence and abstinence of the Brahmans.

Blessed Jerome likewise sets them before us as an example of abstinence. Among other things, he recalls them in Book II *Against Jovinian*:

> “Bardesanes, a Babylonian, divides the Indian Gymnosophists into two schools, one of which he calls Brahmans and the other Samaneans. They are of such continence that they live either on the fruits of trees beside the river Ganges, or on the public provision of rice [Col. 1165A] [Note: Introduction: “ozizae.”] and flour. And when the king comes to them, he is accustomed to worship them and to regard the peace of his province as dependent upon their prayers.”

The same Jerome’s *Letter to Magnus the Orator* also attests that the preaching of the Gospel was directed to them by divine grace:

> “Pantaenus, a philosopher of the Stoic school, was sent to India by Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, because of the renown of his exceptional learning, in order to preach Christ among the Brahmans and the philosophers of that people.”

It remains, finally, to descend to that greatest of Latin philosophers, Boethius, who conveyed to the Latin-speaking world nearly all the disciplines of the liberal arts by writing, translating, and expounding them [Note: Introduction: “in Latin.”]. In writing to his father-in-law and fellow-countryman Symmachus, he carefully explained the faith of the holy Trinity; and in writing to John the Deacon, who afterward became pope, he argued most effectively against Eutyches and Nestorius concerning the unity of Christ’s person and the diversity of the natures in him, divine and human. By treating both the divinity and the incarnation of the Godhead, he established our faith—and his own—unassailably, lest it waver in any respect.

It is established that this eminent Roman senator, consul, and patrician flourished in the time of the aforesaid Pope John, twentieth from Pope Sylvester, and that he died with the aforementioned Symmachus [Col. 1165C] in that persecution of Christians in which Theoderic raged against Pope John and the other Christians. The *Acts of the Popes*, as well as the *Book of the Miracles of Blessed Benedict*, record how King Theoderic of the Goths killed both of them. In the *Acts* you will find this written:

> “The heretical King Theoderic put to the sword two senators, consuls, and patricians, Boethius and Symmachus, and commanded that their bodies also be hidden.”

But the *Book of Miracles* of the aforesaid saint contains this:

> “After Odoacer, Theoderic took up the rule of the Goths with the royal title. A pestilent man of the Arian sect, among his other crimes he killed Pope John by bodily starvation, and pierced with the sword in prison two men of senatorial rank and former consuls, namely Symmachus and Boethius.”

Since, therefore, the Lord has proclaimed the tenor of Catholic faith both through prophets to the Jews and through outstanding philosophers or seers to the Gentiles [Col. 1166B], both Jews and Gentiles are rendered without excuse if, while they have teachers in other matters, they do not listen to them in the matter of salvation of the soul, whose foundation is faith. Indeed, many from the Gentiles and some from the Jews, instructed in this matter also by the teachers of their own people, have recognized the faith of the holy Trinity in the one body of the Church, as two walls joined together. From the Gentiles, first came the Greeks, among whom were the philosophers named above. After the Greeks came the Latins, who, just as they imitated the Greeks in the disciplines of secular learning, so also took examples from them in the true doctrine of faith when they learned that those whom they knew to be endowed with subtle intelligence and armed with every philosophical argument had received the Christian faith.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1165]

[Col. 1165C] In the earlier part of this work we collected certain testimonies from prophets as well as philosophers, by which to establish faith in the holy Trinity. Since there we employed the assertions of unbelieving philosophers, like those of the holy Fathers, as though with authority, we foresaw that we would be exposed to the corrosive criticisms of many, and that they would reproach us with the very charge which, long ago, we read was made against blessed Jerome by many, because he inserted into his writings testimonies not only from pagans but also from heretics.

Thus, writing an epistle against the slanders of Magnus, the orator of the city of Rome [Note: Jerome, Epistle LXX in the *Patrologia*.], he begins as follows:

> “You ask why in our little works we sometimes introduce examples from secular literature and pollute the brightness of the Church with pagan filth. You would never ask this if you read the sacred Scriptures, if you examined their interpreters. For who does not know that in Moses and in the books of the prophets certain things are taken from books of the Gentiles, and that Solomon both proposed some things to the philosophers of Tyre and answered certain things? Thus, at the beginning of Proverbs he admonishes us to understand sayings of prudence, subtleties of words, parables, and obscure speech, sayings of the wise and riddles—matters properly belonging to dialecticians and philosophers.
>
> “Likewise, the Apostle Paul used a line of the poet Epimenides when writing to Titus: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies’ (Titus 1:12). In another epistle he gives a senarius of Menander: ‘Bad conversations corrupt good morals’ (1 Cor. 15:33). And disputing among the Athenians in the court of Mars, he calls Aratus as a witness: ‘For we are also his offspring’ (Acts 17:21). Nor is this a small thing: the leader [Note: Introduction wrongly reads “teacher,” for an army needs a leader, not a teacher.] of the Christian army and unconquered orator pleading Christ’s cause turns even a chance inscription, by skill, into an argument for the faith. For he had learned from the true David to wrench the sword from the hands of enemies [Col. 1167A] and to cut off the head of most proud Goliath with his own blade (1 Sam. 17:51).
>
> “He had read in Deuteronomy that a captive woman’s head, eyebrows, all the hair, and the nails of her body must be shaved or cut away, and that then she might be taken in marriage (Deut. 21:12–13). What wonder [Note: The Introduction adds “as in Jerome.”], then, if I too wish to make secular wisdom into an Israelite woman from a handmaid and captive, because of the loveliness of her speech and beauty of her limbs? If I cut away or shave off whatever in her is dead—idolatry, pleasure, error, lusts—and, joined [Note: Jerome has “joined,” *mixtus*.] to the most pure body, beget from her native-born servants for the Lord.”
>
> Again: “Cyprian, a man eminent in eloquence and martyrdom, is criticized by Firmianus [Note: Introduction: “Formanus”; Jerome has “Firmianus.”], who complains that, when writing against Demetrianus, he used testimonies from prophets [Col. 1167B] and apostles, which that man [Note: Introduction: “those,” but Jerome and our manuscript read “that man,” namely Demetrianus.] considered fabricated and invented, rather than from philosophers and poets, whose authority, as a pagan, he could not oppose.”
>
> Again: “Josephus wrote two books against Apion the Alexandrian [Note: Read, as in Jerome, “Apion the Alexandrian.”], and he adduces so many secular testimonies that I marvel how a Hebrew, trained from childhood in sacred literature, could have examined the entire Greek library.”
>
> Again: “There are also the books of Julius Africanus and Theodore, men of apostolic signs and powers; and of Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria; also of Anatolius, Pamphilus, Pierius, Lucian, Malchion, Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, and others. All these so filled their books with doctrines and sayings of philosophers that one does not know what one should admire first in them [Col. 1167C]: their learning or their knowledge of Scripture.”

The same writer, addressing the presbyter Vigilantius:

> “I say in your absence what I also said in your presence: I have read and read Origen in the same way as Apollinaris and the other [Note: Introduction: “or Apollinaris, or the others.”] interpreters, whose books the Church does not accept in certain respects. For it is my work and study to read many writers, so that from the many I may gather diverse flowers: not [Note: The Introduction omits “not,” although it appears in Jerome.] so as to approve everything, but so as to choose what is good. I take many in hand so that, having learned many things from many, I may know [Note: In Jerome and the Introduction, *cognita* (“things learned”) is absent and certainly does not seem necessary.] much, according to what is written: ‘Reading all things, hold fast what is good’ (1 Thess. 5:21). Hence I greatly wonder that you wished to cast Origen’s doctrines in my teeth. Origen is a heretic—what is that to me, who do not deny that he is a heretic in very many respects? He erred concerning the resurrection of the body, the state of souls, and the punishment of the devil; and, what is worse than these, in his commentaries on Isaiah he declared the Son and the Holy Spirit to be seraphim.”
>
> Again: “We must not receive his good things in such a way that we are compelled to accept his evil things as well. If, therefore, I have translated what is good and have either cut away, passed over in silence, or corrected the evil, am I to be blamed because—not [Note: The word “not” seems to be deleted here, since it does not occur in Jerome’s text.] through me—the Latins possess his good things [Col. 1168A] and are ignorant of his evil things? If this is a crime, let the confessor Hilary be accused, who translated from his books an interpretation of the Psalms and homilies on Job. Let Eusebius of Vercelli be held guilty, who rendered into our language commentaries of a heretical man on all the Psalms, though omitting the heretical material.”

These are Jerome’s answers to the slanders of those who think Catholic interpreters should be reproved because they dare to insert into their writings the testimonies or sayings of unbelievers—as though they thereby grant authority to those worthy of no authority, or as though truth uttered by unbelievers could defile sacred statements. For that most discerning man knew how to discover grain amid chaff, and a pearl sometimes more precious than the rest amid dung [Col. 1168B], and, like a wise goldsmith, to set it in royal ornament. He held with complete certainty that gifts of God cannot be contaminated through any evil person, nor divine sacraments polluted by contact with the wicked, whether unbelievers baptize in the name of the Trinity, or utterly wicked persons preach divine words, speak prophecies, and sometimes work miracles. For whatever gifts [read perhaps: “good things”] exist must be from God, and cannot be contaminated by anyone’s wickedness.

Thus sacred authority did not reject the prophecy of Balaam, a Gentile and diviner; by it the Magi, the firstfruits of the Gentiles, are believed afterward to have been prompted, when a new star appeared, immediately to seek the new king. Nor did Augustine, a spiritual teacher, fear to insert the prophecies of the Sibyl or Virgil among the prophecies of the saints, considering the Apostle’s words: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3). Nor did the Evangelist fear to commend Caiaphas’s prophecy when he said: “This he did not say of himself; but being high priest that year, he prophesied” (John 11:51).

Nor does the Gospel suppress the testimonies of demons themselves, when, at the Lord’s coming for their expulsion, they cried out and confessed him to be Jesus Christ or the Son of God. Blessed Gregory indeed testifies that even insensible things in some manner perceived his power, whether at his birth, death, resurrection, ascension, or in his working of miracles, so as to bear witness to him in their own way [Col. 1168D]: angels and a star appearing immediately at his birth; at his death, the sun darkened, rocks and the veil of the temple torn, tombs opened, and saints rising and appearing to many; at the resurrection, an earthquake occurring together with the vision of angels; and at the ascension, a cloud receiving him; and so forth.

The entire adornment of the world also does not cease to announce and proclaim, praise and commend in its own way, his power and wisdom [Col. 1169A], through the wondrous composition and ordering of itself. Hence the Apostle says: “His invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made; even his eternal power and divinity,” etc. (Rom. 1:20). Thus too the Psalmist, applauding the praises of even insensible creatures, invites every creature together to praise God, as though God, who made all things in the world for us, rightly demands from us praise drawn from all things excellently made.

Accordingly, beginning from the height of heaven and the exaltation [Note: Introduction: “solemnity.”] of angels, he extends divine utterances down to dragons, serpents, and all abysses, when he says: “Praise the Lord from the earth, you dragons and all abysses” (Ps. 148:7). And again: “Serpents and winged birds” (ibid., 10). Nor did he omit any creeping things, saying elsewhere: “Let the heavens and earth praise him, the sea and every creeping thing in them” (Ps. 68:35).

We read also in the *Life of Paul the Hermit*, written by blessed Jerome, that a satyr appeared to blessed Antony. Declaring the coming of the Saviour, it said to the holy man: “I come as ambassador from my herd. We beg you to pray our common God on our behalf—the one whom we have learned came long ago for the salvation of the world, and whose sound has gone out into all the earth.”

The aged traveller, marvelling at this satyr’s confession and testimony concerning Christ, and more greatly rejoicing [Note: [Col. 1169D] *Introduction*: “rejoicing”] that even monsters proclaimed Christ, and being vehemently angered at the hardness and blindness of Alexandria, immediately struck the ground with his staff and said: “Woe to you, Alexandria, who worship marvels as God! What will you say now? Beasts speak of Christ!”—as though he openly cried out: “May even the confession of monsters break [Note: [Col. 1169D] *Introduction*: “will break”] your shamelessness.”

This confession perhaps proclaims the glory and power of God all the more wonderfully because it must be regarded as a greater miracle; and its assertion appears all the truer because it is further removed from human teaching and must be wholly attributed to the prompting of the Holy Spirit. Thus the words of Balaam’s ass, and voices made in the air—as we read concerning the Lord at his baptism or transfiguration—when they announced something to those standing by, moved their hearers more readily to faith the more marvellous they appeared to everyone.

The same is manifestly taught by reason concerning philosophers also, or any Gentiles whatsoever, however unbelieving or hostile to our faith. For the more opposed they were to our faith, the less liable they would be to suspicion in praising it; and the testimony of an enemy in praise of anyone is more credible than that of a friend, just as the reverse is true in accusation. Hence, when we read the testimony of Josephus the Jew concerning Christ or his saints, we are greatly moved thereby toward faith; and when we hear that Philo the Jew approved and commended the life of the monasteries of Egypt [Col. 1170A], perhaps he gives us greater satisfaction [Note: [Col. 1169D] *Introduction*: “gives satisfaction”] than if one of our own people commended it. For this reason both deserved to be numbered and recorded among illustrious men by blessed Jerome.

What is more necessary for the defence of our faith than that, against the importunity of all unbelievers, we should possess from their own writings the means by which to refute them? Thus, if philosophers attack us, let them be convicted through their own teachers and philosophers; and if heretics attack us, let them be refuted by certain testimonies [Note: [Col. 1169D] *Introduction*: “by whom”] of Holy Scripture; and so, according to the Apostle, “every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may be made subject to God” (Rom. 3:19).

Who does not know that heretics are far worse than philosophers and any Gentiles whatsoever [Note: [Col. 1169D] *Introduction*: “Gentiles and certain philosophers”]? For, according to the assertion of the apostle Peter, it would have been better for them not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back. Therefore, if, because of the unbelief of the Gentiles, those who rely on certain of their testimonies or sayings must be reproved [Note: [Col. 1170D] *Introduction*: “make use of them”], much more must those be reproved who, ensnared by Origen’s many and great heresies, so studiously transferred and introduced his expositions and opinions for our edification. For, as has been said, heretics are plainly more condemnable than all others because of their unbelief.

Yet they would not allow his innumerable and utterly abominable heresies to perish in silence, as though they foresaw some benefit even in reconsidering them: namely, so that, once these errors had been set forth and condemned, others might more easily guard themselves against them, or might learn by what arguments to dissolve them if anyone should be caught in their snares. Hence blessed Jerome addressed an epistle to the presbyter Avitus [Note: [Col. 1170D] *Introduction*: “augmented”], in which he reveals in part those heretical propositions which Origen had set down, innumerable [Note: [Col. 1170D] *Introduction*: “very small”], in the books *Periarchon*.

Who, moreover, can rightly reproach me for introducing the testimonies of philosophers unless he also draws the holy doctors into blame with me in this very matter? For the testimonies which I collected above from the philosophers I collected not from their writings—which perhaps I have never seen—but indeed from the books of blessed Augustine [Note: [Col. 1170D] *Introduction*: “of which I know little; indeed, I collected them from the books of the holy Fathers”].

Will they dare to accuse the Apostle also? As Augustine himself says in Book VIII of *The City of God*, when Paul was speaking to the Athenians and had made that great statement about God, intelligible to few—“In him we live and move and are”—he added, “as certain of your own people have said” (Acts 17:28), introducing for persuasion the testimony of those very philosophers through whose studies that glorious city had flourished. Of them, as Augustine himself previously states in that same work, the Apostle wrote to the Romans: “What may be known of God is manifest to them; for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that have been made; even his everlasting power and divinity,” and so forth (Rom. 1:19–20).

[Col. 1171A] From these words the Apostle plainly teaches that the mystery of the Trinity also was revealed to them. But these words of the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1171D] *Introduction*: “but certain words of the Apostle here”] will present themselves for exposition later. For the present, after gathering and expounding many testimonies concerning faith in the holy Trinity against the objections both of heretics and philosophers, it remains to show by what arguments that which has been confirmed by testimonies may be defended.

For every controversy, as Tully observes in his *Rhetorics*, turns either upon a written text or upon reason. And, as blessed Augustine testifies, in all matters it is fitting to set authority before human reason; but especially in matters pertaining to God, it is safer to rely upon authority than upon human ingenuity. This is the point of what he says in the first chapter of the book *On the Morals of the Catholic Church against the Manichaeans* [Col. 1171B] [Note: [Col. 1171D] Our manuscript does not give Augustine’s text here, but only its first and last word. Readers may consult Augustine, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church against the Manichaeans*, ch. 2 [Col. 1172D]. Nor do the words enclosed in parentheses cohere sufficiently with what follows, though they follow rightly from what precedes; we therefore believe they have been inserted here secondarily.]: “They ascribe [these matters] to nature.” How can three persons be distinguished within one substance that remains wholly undivided, when none of them is in any way the other? Next, how can this person be called begotten and that one proceeding?

It must first be discussed in how many senses the term “person” is customarily taken, so that this designation may carefully be distinguished from the rest. We understand “person” differently in rhetoric, differently in grammar, and differently in theology.

The statement that God’s invisible things were revealed to them is not unsuitably applied to the person of the Spirit, who is invisibly suggested by the very name “Spirit.” And because he is called the gift of God, and is manifold according to sevenfold grace, and is sometimes called the seven Spirits as though seven gifts [Col. 1171C], it was not inappropriately said in the plural, “the invisible things of God”—that is, his Spirit, the distributor of the gifts of sevenfold grace.

But the Apostle declares the Word of the Father, Christ the Lord, to be “the power of God and the wisdom of God.” Hence, when in this passage “the everlasting power of God” is mentioned, the person of the Son is expressed; and when “divinity” is then added, the person of the Father is also expressed, because, as we recalled above, the majesty of power is especially expressed by the name God or Lord.

But if neither the authority of the Apostle himself nor that of the holy Fathers seems to me sufficiently supportive, nor even the argument we adduced above—namely, that in this work we are especially dealing with disciples of philosophers [Col. 1171D], who attack us with philosophical arguments and themselves rely entirely on their authority—it remains for us to blunt the darts of hostile malice with more numerous arguments, and, by answering each of their objections, to restrain their barking. Thus what we have written with sincere intention in defence of our faith may not become cheap in the eyes of believers through their envious or erroneous accusations, precisely where it appears more hostile to unbelievers; and because they accuse philosophers, as Gentiles, of unbelief, and thereby remove the authority of faith from them as though they were wholly condemned [Col. 1172A], our defence should concentrate especially upon the very point on which their entire attack rests.

Perhaps all philosophers were Gentiles by nationality, but not by faith, as is said of Job and his friends. For how could we consign all of them to unbelief and condemnation when, as the Apostle himself testifies, God revealed to them the secrets of his faith and the profound mysteries of the Trinity, and when their virtues and deeds are wonderfully praised even by holy doctors? The same Apostle nevertheless reports that some of them were blinded through pride and lapsed into idolatry and a shameful life—as we read also concerning Solomon himself, and as has happened to many believers.

Who, moreover, would assert that the faith of the Incarnation was revealed to none of them, as it was to the Sibyl, even though this does not appear expressly in their writings? Nor is it openly preached by Job and certain prophets; and even the Seventy Interpreters, translating the Law for Gentiles, passed over nearly all the mysteries of faith—perhaps because, if revealed to an uncultivated people, they would have caused more scandal and offence than edification.

If it were permissible also to take the sayings of philosophers allegorically, who would not observe that Plato’s assertion concerning the mystery of the redemption of the world should fittingly be understood in this way: that, in the very composition of the world, God applied two lengths to one another in the shape of the Greek letter chi, χ, and bent them into a circle so as to complete the globe of the world? It is as though he mystically declares [Col. 1172C] that the salvation of all human beings—which we understand as the true constitution of the world itself—was accomplished in the passion of the Lord’s cross.

But if those who lived before the Saviour’s advent did not receive the sacraments, we need not believe this even of Job the Gentile. Nor does the Law appear to have been given to all people as the Gospel was, but only to Israel, which alone, among all peoples, was first called and received the Law. Thus the institution of the Law is not to be understood as universal in the same way as the Gospel, nor the first calling as the second.

Hence Moses says to Israel in Deuteronomy, chapter XV: “Ask concerning the ancient days, from the day when God created man . . . whether any such thing has ever happened . . . whether a people has heard the voice of God speaking from the midst of fire, as you heard and saw; [Col. 1172D] whether God has acted so as to enter in and take for himself a nation from the midst of nations, by signs and wonders . . . before your eyes, so that you might know that he is God and there is no other; from heaven he made you hear his voice, that he might teach you . . . because he loved your fathers and chose their seed after them” (Deut. 4:32–37).

Likewise, in chapter XXIII [Note: [Col. 1172D] He errs concerning the number: below, V.]: “You are a holy people to the Lord your God. The Lord your God chose you to be his own special people from all the peoples that are upon the earth,” and so forth (Deut. 7:6). Hence also the Psalmist says: “He has not dealt thus with every nation, nor has he made his judgments known to them” (Ps. 147:20).

We therefore seem by no argument compelled to despair of the salvation of such Gentiles who, before the Redeemer’s advent, were instructed by no written Law, yet, according to the Apostle, naturally did the things of the Law. They were a law to themselves, showing the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them.

For it is written in the Epistle to the Romans: “For it is not the hearers of the Law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law shall be justified. For when the Gentiles, who do not have the Law, naturally do the things of the Law, these persons, though they do not have the Law, are a law to themselves. They show the work of the Law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them” [Col. 1173B] (Rom. 2:13 ff.). And a little later: “We reckon that a human being is justified by faith without the works of the Law. Is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not also the God of the Gentiles? Yes, of the Gentiles also, since there is one God who justifies circumcision by faith and uncircumcision through faith” (Rom. 3:28).

Likewise: “What then does Scripture say? Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. 4:3). And again: “We learn [read: ‘We say’] that Abraham’s faith was reckoned as righteousness. How was it reckoned? In circumcision or in uncircumcision? Not in circumcision, but in uncircumcision; and he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which is in uncircumcision, that he might be the father of all who believe through uncircumcision” (ibid. [Col. 1173C], 9).

And again: “For if those who are of the Law are heirs, faith has been made empty and the promise abolished. For the Law works wrath; for where there is no Law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:14–15). And later: “I did not know sin except through the Law. For I did not know desire unless the Law had said: ‘You shall not desire.’ But sin, taking occasion through the commandment, produced in me every kind of desire. For without the Law sin was dead. And I once lived without the Law; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. And the commandment which was for life was found to be death to me . . . so that sin might become beyond measure sinful through the commandment” (Rom. 7:7–13).

From these words of the Apostle it is fittingly shown [Col. 1173D] that righteousness began from the natural law, and that human beings were justified by faith altogether without a written Law. It is further added that, after the prohibitions of the written Law, people would easily incline toward the gravest sins, according to that poetic saying:

> We ever strive for what is forbidden, and desire what is denied.  
> (Ovid, *Amores* 3.4.17)

“But perhaps,” you will say, “that decree concerning circumcision could not be annulled after it was first given to Abraham: ‘The male whose flesh of the foreskin has not been circumcised—that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has made void my covenant’” (Gen. 17:14).

But if we consider what precedes carefully, we shall find that this was imposed only upon Abraham and his seed—that is, those who were to descend from Isaac, not Ishmael [Col. 1174A]. Hence Abraham was told: “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Gen. 21:12). We read also that Jeremiah and John were sanctified in the womb before receiving bodily sacraments.

Far be it, then, from us to profess that the sacrament of circumcision is as universal as baptism. Rather, with Ambrose, let us always call the sacraments of the Church more excellent and more perfect than those of the Synagogue, since the former have been given to all, the latter, as stated, to some; and since without the former no remission or sanctification can now be hoped for.

We have introduced these points lest anyone should despair, even after the Law had been given and until Christ’s advent, of the salvation of believing Gentiles, if they lived soberly and justly without receiving the sacraments. Among such persons philosophers are known to have been eminent in both life and teaching [Col. 1174B].

How great was the abstinence, how great the continence, and how many the virtues to which natural law and the love of honour itself once raised not philosophers alone, but secular and unlearned people also—we have learned this from many testimonies. The holy doctors have sometimes taken care to introduce such people, like blessed Job, in rebuke of our negligence, and to propose persons of both sexes to our shamelessness as examples of religious conduct to be imitated. We, instructed by the pages of both Testaments and the innumerable writings of the saints, are worse than they in every respect; for we refuse even so to obey. Along with blessed Job, according to Gregory, they reproach us with that prophetic saying: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” [Col. 1174C] (Isa. 23:4).

It was therefore right that, before the giving of the written Law or the display of his miracles, the Lord should set before us certain persons of each sex whose virtues we might imitate: both so that our negligence might appear inexcusable through them, and so that the humility of the obedient might be more securely preserved if, after so many lessons of miracles and writings and after so many examples of saints, we perform any good works. For they, without the written Law, without the admonition of preaching, shone with such great virtues and such discipline of character, and showed such constancy in rebuking vices, that some underwent death in defence of truth. Let us now establish these points one by one by the testimonies and examples set below.

Philosophers, then, as we have said, proclaim faith [Col. 1174D], teach the immortality of the soul, and affirm a future recompense of souls according to merits, either for punishment or for glory. Thus they especially exhort us to good works, through hope of heavenly blessedness and the threat of infernal punishment. Macrobius speaks at length about these matters.

Hence Jerome, writing to Bishop Heliodorus in the epitaph for Nepotianus, says: “I pass over Greeks, Hebrews, and Latins, nations which the Lord dedicated by the title of his cross. The immortal soul, subsisting after the dissolution of the body—a doctrine Pythagoras dreamed, Democritus believed for the consolation of his condemnation, and Socrates discussed in prison.”

Their own lives and teaching also show with what great virtues they shone. For, in my judgment, they would by no means have described the virtues so carefully when setting forth moral precepts unless they knew them in themselves by certain experiences. Holy people and doctors did not disdain to adopt these descriptions of the virtues from them when they express justice, fortitude, or the other virtues to us in their words, as though they did not doubt that the same Spirit had spoken through them.

One of them, when giving the pattern of honourable conduct, excellently said:

> The good hate to sin through love of virtue.  
> (Horace, *Epistles* 1.16.57)

It is as though he openly teaches that one ought to abstain from the shamefulness of vices more through love of virtue itself—which is called moral excellence—than through fear of punishment, by which ungrateful slaves are restrained [Col. 1175B].

But if “love of virtue” seems insufficient for the merit of salvation, and “love of God” rather is required—as though we could possess virtue or any good work that was not in accordance with God himself and for his sake—it is easy to find this also among philosophers: namely, that they establish the highest good, which is God, as both the beginning of all things—that is, their origin and efficient cause—and their end—that is, their final cause. Thus all good things are done through love of him, from whose gift they proceed.

Hence we rightly call him Alpha and Omega, that is, beginning and end: all things are from him and for him. Plato declares him to be the best and ineffable Creator of all natures. Since he can do all things and all envy is far removed from him [Col. 1175C], he made all things as good as the nature of each permitted, or as the order and harmony of things required. Moses also said that all things were made very good by God (Gen. 1); but Plato seems to assign somewhat greater praise to divine goodness, when he says that every individual thing was made as good as its nature allowed, or as was fitting.

There he also added that the will of God itself should rightly be judged the cause of all created things. It is as though he understands that all things were made, and made most excellently, because the best craftsman decreed that they should be so made; his will is sufficient for all things and can in no way be fruitless. After first saying this concerning God—that he therefore wished all things in consequence to be made like himself, insofar as the nature of each could be capable of blessedness [Col. 1175D]—he immediately added: “If anyone holds this will of God to be the most certain origin of things, I agree that he judges rightly.”

Blessed Augustine, following him, says in the *Enchiridion*, chapter XI [read: IX]: “It is sufficient for a Christian to believe that the cause of created things is nothing other than the goodness of the Creator, who is the one God; and that there is no nature which either is himself or is not from him.”

Socrates, Plato’s teacher, had also left this cause assigned: namely, that the causes of all natures that have been made may remain unchangeably with the unchangeable will of the Creator and live steadfastly there, as is said: “What was made in him was life” (John 1:3).

In this connection Socratic authority also established, concerning the investigation of the causes and origins of things in natural philosophy, that we can attain no certainty unless we ascend by mental contemplation to that place where, as has been said, the causes of all things remain immovably fixed—namely, in the will of the Creator. He also declares that this ascent cannot be made unless the mind is purified from vices, according to that saying of Truth: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Thus, even for the acquisition of natural philosophy or of any philosophy whatsoever—which consists only in investigating hidden causes [Col. 1176B] [read: “consists”]—he judged that one must first labour to purify one’s life by good morals. It is as though he assigned ethics the first step in every branch of philosophy, so that those whom he could not draw to an honourable life through love of God might at least in some measure initiate themselves into it through desire for philosophy.

Augustine worthily extols him in Book VIII of *The City of God* in these praises:

> Socrates, Plato’s teacher, is remembered as having directed the whole of philosophy toward correcting and ordering morals. He fixed his mind upon what was necessary for the blessed life, for the sake of which alone the industry of all philosophers seems to have watched and laboured. He did not wish minds polluted by earthly desires to attempt to rise to divine things, since he saw that they sought there the causes of things—causes which he believed to be first and highest only in the goodness of the one true and highest God. He therefore thought that these could be comprehended only by a purified mind, and for that reason believed that one must labour to purify one’s life by good morals, so that the mind, relieved of its crushing passions, might rise in its natural strength to eternal things and, through purity of understanding, behold the incorporeal nature [Note: [Col. 1175D] In Augustine: “of incorporeal [light].”] and unchangeable light, where the causes of all created natures live steadfastly.

And shortly afterward:

> Socrates, he says, left many followers of his philosophy, whose rival endeavour was to engage in the discussion of moral questions, where the highest good is considered, without which no one can become blessed [Note: [Col. 1175D] In Augustine: “by which a human being can become blessed.”].

[Col. 1176D] It now seems fitting to add from that same Book VIII of *The City of God* how carefully, in Platonic teaching, he investigated God; how he determined him to be the highest good in which the entire sum of blessedness consists; and how correctly he defined philosophizing as loving God, making the love of God the end of all good things:

> Perhaps those who are praised as having understood Plato more keenly and subtly than other Gentile philosophers, and as having rightly placed him far above them [Note: [Col. 1176D] In Augustine: “and are praised as having attained this with more celebrated fame”], think something such as this about him: that in him are found the cause of existing, the principle of understanding, and the order of living [Col. 1177A]—of which three, one belongs to natural philosophy, another to rational philosophy, and the third to moral philosophy [Note: [Col. 1177D] In Augustine: “is understood to belong”]. For if the human being is so created that by that which excels in him he may attain that which excels all things—that is, the one, true, best God—without whom no nature subsists, no creature is instructed, and no use is desired: let him be sought, where all things are secure for us; let him be seen, where all things are certain for us; let him be loved, where all things are right for us. If, then, Plato said that the wise person is an imitator, knower, and lover of this God, by participation in whom one becomes blessed, what need is there to examine the rest?

Likewise:

> These philosophers, therefore, whom we see deservedly exalted above the rest by reputation and favour [Note: [Col. 1177D] In Augustine: “glory”], saw that no body is God; and therefore they transcended all bodies in seeking God. They saw that whatever is changeable is not the highest God; and therefore they transcended every soul and every changeable spirit in seeking the highest God. [Col. 1177B]

Again, concerning the philosophers:

> Those whom we deservedly set before the rest distinguished the things perceived by the mind from those grasped by the senses, neither taking from the senses what they can do nor granting them more than they can do. They said that God, from whom all things were made, is the light of minds for discerning [Note: [Col. 1178D] In Augustine: “learning”] all things. The remaining part is moral philosophy, which they call by the Greek word *ethics*, in which the highest good is sought. Referring all that we do to this good, desiring it not for the sake of something else but for its own sake, and attaining it, we seek nothing further by which we may be blessed [Col. 1177C]. It is therefore called the end, because we desire other things for its sake, but desire it only for its own sake.

Likewise:

> It is now enough to recall that Plato determined the end of the good to be living for the sake of virtue, and that this can happen only to the person who has knowledge and imitation of God; nor is anyone blessed for any other reason. Therefore he does not hesitate to say that philosophizing is loving God. Hence they conclude that the student of wisdom—that is, the philosopher—will then be blessed when he begins to enjoy God. Whoever enjoys what he loves loves the true and highest good. Who but one utterly miserable would deny that such a person is blessed?

We have learned, moreover, from Plato’s own teachings and from philosophical studies that true philosophers strive, through the investigation of rational arguments, to please God. Before undertaking any arguments, they offered a prayer to him, asking in humble supplication that they might be able to perceive and expound the truth, and that by this means they themselves might please him. Indeed, they considered all those mad and incapable of expiation who did not invoke divine aid in all that they undertook rightly.

From this both their intention is most clearly manifested and their humility commended: they wish all things to be done rightly for God’s sake, that he may be pleased thereby; and they attribute every good thing to him, from whom they ask all things. Thus Plato says, in the passage where Socrates and Timaeus are introduced:

> **SOCRATES:** “Come then, Timaeus, begin the undertaking, invoking the Divinity to aid you, as is customary.”  
>
> **TIMAEUS:** “Truly, my Socrates. Since it is customary among all people, and something like a religious duty, that when they are about to undertake something concerning matters great or small, they should call upon the Divinity for aid, how much more proper is it for us, who are about to set forth an account of the nature and substance of the universe, to invoke divine help—unless indeed we are carried away by some savage frenzy and implacable madness? Let this then be included in my prayers: first and chiefly, that we may say what is pleasing to God; then, that we may also set forth our matter suitably, consistently, and appropriately to our proposed work.” [Col. 1178A]

Who also could fail sufficiently to admire Pythagoras’s humility? In the manner of the ancients, he would not permit himself to be called a *sophos*, that is, “wise,” but rather a *philosophos*, that is, “lover of wisdom.” It is as though he proclaimed that true wisdom belongs not to a human being but to God alone, and professed himself, by comparison with participation in it, more indolent than capable.

Hence Augustine says in Book VIII of *The City of God*:

> Two kinds of philosophers are handed down: one Italian, from that part of Italy which was once called Greater Greece; the other Ionian, in those lands where Greece is still so named. The Italian school had as its founder Pythagoras of Samos, from whom the name “philosophy” itself is said to have arisen. For whereas those who seemed to excel others in some manner by a praiseworthy life were formerly called “wise,” when this man was asked what he professed, he answered that he was a philosopher—that is, a student or lover of wisdom. For to profess oneself wise [Col. 1178C] seemed excessively arrogant.

The admonition of Truth was certainly quite unnecessary for him: “Do not be called masters, for one is your master, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23:10) [Note: [Col. 1178D] Vulgate: “for your Master is one, Christ.”]. For it would have been less presumptuous for him to arrogate to himself the title “wise” than that of “master.”

Augustine’s very words deserve notice: he says that a *sophos* or philosopher is customarily named from the praise of life rather than of knowledge—“those who seemed to excel others in some manner by a praiseworthy life.” Hence Boethius, in his eleventh exposition on Porphyry, defining philosophy, says: “Philosophy is the knowledge of human and divine things joined with the pursuit of living well.” And Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VIII, chapter 6, says: “A philosopher is one who has knowledge of divine and human things and follows every path of living well” [Col. 1178D].

Therefore no one was called either *sophos*, that is, wise, or philosopher, merely on account of however great a knowledge, if purity of life were lacking. For cunning or shrewdness in mere knowledge is one thing; wisdom in uprightness of life also is another.

Tully says in his *Rhetoric* that this wisdom ought to be joined with eloquence, because he wishes eloquence to benefit states, in accordance with the definition of the orator given by Victorinus: “a good man, skilled in speaking,” and so forth. He is good through the uprightness of wisdom, so that he wills rightly; skilled in rhetorical knowledge [Col. 1179A], so that he can act effectively.

Blessed Jerome too, following him as his instructor in rhetoric, says in the letter he writes to Oceanus [Note: [Col. 1179D] In Jerome, “orators” is absent]: “Rhetoricians define an orator as a good man skilled in speaking. Before [eloquence], an irreproachable life is sought, then an irreproachable tongue, so that he may deservedly be accepted as learned. The person whose speech is destroyed by his deeds loses the authority to speak.”

Concerning this wisdom of kindness or goodness—by which that which we rightly apprehend through understanding tastes sweet to us through desire—Augustine speaks in chapter 1 [read: chapter 2] of the *Enchiridion*: “In the book of holy Job we read that Wisdom itself said to humankind: ‘Behold, piety is wisdom’” (Job 28:28) [Note: [Col. 1179D] Vulgate: “Behold, the fear [of the Lord].”].

But if, after the faith and moral teaching of philosophers, and the end or intention of right living which they assigned, we inspect their own lives also—how diligently they established the order of the commonwealth and regulated the life of citizens and fellow inhabitants—we shall find that both their life and their teaching express in the highest degree evangelical or apostolic perfection, and that they differ little or not at all from the Christian religion.

For we find that we are joined to them both in moral reasoning and in the very name. In name, certainly, because we are called Christians from true *sophia*, that is, the wisdom of God the Father, who is Christ; and we may truly be called philosophers in this respect if we truly love Christ [Col. 1179B]. In faith too, in hope, and in principles of morality and moral excellence, according to the freedom of charity in which we have been called by grace—not according to Jewish servitude, through fear of punishments and ambition for earthly things, rather than desire for eternal things—it is certain that philosophers agree with us to a very great extent.

For, as we have said, the faith of the Trinity was revealed to them and preached by them; they awaited the hope of the immortal soul and eternal recompense; and in pursuit of it they did not hesitate entirely to despise the world, renounce all earthly things, and afflict themselves with severe fasting. With us they placed the love of God as the end and cause of all things, as we have sufficiently recalled above.

Thus the preaching of the Gospel was more readily received by philosophers than by Jews, because they found it especially suited to their own end, and perhaps discordant with them in nothing, except possibly in matters pertaining to the mysteries of the Incarnation, the sacraments, or the resurrection [Col. 1179D].

For if we carefully consider the moral precepts of the Gospel, we shall find them to be nothing other than a restoration of the natural law, which philosophers plainly followed. The Law rests more upon figurative than moral commands and abounds more in external than internal justice. The Gospel, however, carefully examines virtues and vices and weighs all things according to the intention of the mind, just as philosophers do.

Since, therefore, so great an agreement between evangelical and philosophical teaching is evident, some Platonists, as we recalled above long ago [Col. 1180A], burst forth into such blasphemy as to say that the Lord Jesus had received all his opinions from Plato—as though the philosopher had taught Wisdom itself.

Now, moreover, beyond the careful description of the virtues given by the philosophers, it is useful to examine their teaching on the uprightness of the active life, since they ordered the life of cities and of their rulers according to right principles of living; and then to see how far they themselves also obeyed their own pronouncements concerning upright living, or did more than they imposed upon others—according to what is written of true Wisdom, that “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1), as though it said: first to do, then to teach.

In accordance with evangelical preaching, they laid down a way of life alike for married persons, [Col. 1180B] for rulers, and for the continent; for they assigned a rule of life to cities, as assemblies of married persons, defined what the rulers of the commonwealth ought to be, and in themselves displayed the life of the continent and abstinent which clerics or monks now profess. They bound civic assemblies together by such love of neighbour that, all things having been made common, a city seemed to be nothing but a brotherhood, and the city’s rulers were called nothing other than stewards of the commonwealth. Thus they already foreshadowed that apostolic life of the primitive Church of which it is said in the Acts of the Apostles: “They had all things in common, and no one called anything his own; but distribution was made to each according as anyone had need” (Acts 4:32). This is the life [Col. 1180C] now claimed by monks as its professed adherents, although philosophers rightly assigned it to all who live rightly together, in accordance with that rule of charitable equity: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 19:19).

What, moreover, prohibited all private ownership and reduced everything to common possession more fully than that saying of Socrates introduced in Plato’s *Timaeus*, by which he ordained that wives too should be common, so that no one should recognize children as his own? Surely, brothers, this ought not to be interpreted as inclining toward any obscenity—so that so great a philosopher, from whom the whole pursuit of moral discipline and investigation of the supreme Good [Col. 1180D] took its beginning, should have instituted so great, so obvious, and so abominable a filthiness. For adultery is condemned not only by philosophers but also by poets and by all persons under the natural law; indeed, some count even ardent desire for one’s own wife as adultery.

Thus Jerome, in Book I *Against Jovinian*, says: “Sextus says in his maxims: ‘He is an adulterer who is an excessively ardent lover of his own wife.’ For all love directed toward another man’s wife is shameful, and excessive love toward one’s own is likewise so. A wise man ought to love his wife with judgment, not with passion. He will govern the impulses of pleasure, lest he be carried headlong [Note: In Jerome: “lest he be carried headlong.”] in intercourse. Nothing is fouler than to love one’s wife as though she were an adulteress. Certainly, those [Col. 1181A] who say that they marry wives and beget children for the sake of the commonwealth and the human race should at least imitate cattle: after their wife’s womb has swelled, they should not destroy their children; nor should they present themselves to their wives as lovers, but as husbands.”

[Note: At [Col. 1180D], Henry has “Xystus,” but the manuscripts read “Sextus.”]
