Therefore, since Socrates ordained that wives too should be made public—although, in their case, nothing at all seemed capable of being held in common—he plainly left nothing whatsoever private which he did not reduce to common ownership. He wishes wives, then, to be common in their fruit, not in their use: that is, for the benefit to be received from them, not for pleasure to be gratified in them. Thus charity is to be so widely extended among all that each person should wish to possess everything he has—children as well as whatever else [Col. 1181B] he possesses—only for the common benefit of all.

This was carefully observed by the man of whom Valerius Maximus, among other things, writes:

> “Aulus Fulvius punished with death his son, who had followed Catiline’s friendship in a wicked design and was rushing with rash zeal into his camp. Seizing him in the middle of the journey, he declared that he had begotten him not for Catiline against his country, but for his country against Catiline.”

[Note: Valerius Maximus, Book V, chapter 8.]

Perhaps he understood all such men to be true rulers of the commonwealth: those, namely, who reckon the things they appear to possess not to themselves but to the common good. And this truly ought to be called a commonwealth whose administration is conducted for common benefit; and these truly ought to be called fellow citizens who dwell together in such unity both of body and devotion [Col. 1181C] that there seems fulfilled in them what the Psalmist says concerning the perfection of the primitive Church, now imitated by monastic communities: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1).

Accordingly, their unanimous common life is rightly called a city: there an equal rule of equity preserves for each what is his; equal distribution is maintained among all; all things are distributed according to each one’s need and as resources permit; and all that is done is directed toward one end, namely, the common welfare of the city, so that sincere charity may be preserved among all without murmuring.

Thus Clement, writing to James, urges communal life:

> “Finally, a certain very wise Greek, knowing these things to be so, says: ‘Just as the air cannot be divided, nor the brightness of the sun, so neither should the other things which in this world have been given to all for common possession be divided; rather, they should be held in common. [Col. 1182A] Otherwise love of neighbour is not perfect when it seeks what is its own, but [not] the advantage of its friend.’”

[Note: In Migne, the sections “Clement to James … love of neighbour” and “Jerome to Heliodorus … entered the city” are printed in parallel.]

Jerome, to Bishop Heliodorus, in the *Epitaph of Nepotian*:

> “Why should I recall Roman commanders, by whose virtues Latin histories shine as though by certain stars? When Pulvillius was dedicating the Capitol, news was brought that his son had died; he immediately ordered him buried in his absence. Lucius Paulus entered the City in triumph seven days between the funerals of his two sons.” [Col. 1181D–1182A]

This standard of equity is surely the concern of that definition of cities which Macrobius, explaining the words of Cicero, gives:

> “What definition could be more exact, what more cautious, concerning the name of cities, than this: ‘assemblies and gatherings of men joined together by law, which are called cities’?”

According to this definition, every assembly of the Christian religion ought properly to be called a city, and fellow citizens properly brothers, reborn in it through grace. Hence Truth itself says of the fellowship of the Church: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” [Col. 1182B] (Matt. 5:14). In harmony with this is what Ezekiel says about the structure of a city shown upon a mountain, and the Psalmist’s words: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city” (Ps. 121:3).

When philosophers exhorted us, I believe, to this communal life of the commonwealth, they excellently commended through natural justice positive justice—that is, the justice which they themselves began to establish and enact in civic assemblies. Suitably, in order to promote the concord and common life of people on earth, they introduced the harmony of higher and heavenly things, which have been assigned in common for our use. Since we all receive in common the benefit of the sun and of other things, we are thereby admonished that we too should aid one another in common. And since the greater world, by divine ordering, [Col. 1182C] supplies our needs in each of its parts—being made not for itself but for us—the lesser world, that is, individual human beings, should especially be admonished by this to aid one another with mutual benefits and to order everything we have for the common good. This is especially so because God, the rewarder of all, plainly shows that this is his will by subjecting heavenly things and everything in the world, even insensible things, to the use of us all, for whose use they were made. Thus it is said to God concerning man in the Psalmist’s words: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet,” and so forth (Ps. 8:8).

How greatly too must it be extolled and proclaimed that, while Plato established the uprightness of civic honour, he also guarded against indecent and fabulous words just as against shameful deeds, so that he would permit the ordering of the city to be weakened in no respect. Thus, when he set forth a plan for rightly ordering a city, he decreed that poets should be expelled from cities, as blessed Augustine records in Book II of *The City of God*:

> “Or should the palm perhaps be awarded rather to Plato, who, when he formed by reason what a city ought to be, judged that poets, as enemies of the city, [Col. 1182D] ought to be expelled from the city?”

[Note: Book II, chapter 14. In manuscripts of Augustine, the reading is commonly “enemies of truth.”]

Again, after some intervening words:

> “If Plato did not wish poets themselves at all to live in a well-ordered city, whether because they lied at will or because they set before miserable human beings the worst deeds of the gods as examples to imitate.”

Thus he was already proclaiming openly by deeds themselves: “Everyone who lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11); and the Apostle’s words: “Fornication and every impurity must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or coarse jesting, which are not fitting,” and so forth (Eph. 5:3).

What philosophy thinks of the poetic Muses, and how indignant it is that one of its own pupils should ever turn aside toward those harlots, is carefully expressed at the very opening of Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*. There, when Philosophy herself comes to console the philosopher and sees the Muses standing by him, the philosopher himself says:

> “When she saw the poetic Muses standing beside my bed and dictating words to my tears, she was for a little while moved; then, with fierce eyes ablaze, she said: ‘Who permitted these theatrical harlots to approach this sick man? They not only foster his pains with no remedies, but nourish them besides with sweet poisons. For these are they who kill the fruitful harvest of reason with the barren thorns of passions, and accustom human minds to sickness rather than free them from it. If your blandishments had taken away someone uninitiated and commonly given to such things, I should think it less grievous. Nothing of our own work would then be harmed in him. But this man has been nourished by Eleatic and Academic studies! Go away instead, Sirens, sweet unto destruction, and leave him to be cared for and healed by my Muses.’ Rebuked thus, that chorus cast its face downcast toward the ground, confessed its shame by blushing, and departed sadly.” [Col. 1183A–C]

[Note: Commenting on this passage of Boethius, St Thomas says: “Elis [Elis/Elys] is a city of Greece in which Aristotle studied; hence his studies are called Eleatic. The Academy, however, was a city or estate in which Plato studied; hence his studies are called Academic.”]

Philosophers also laid down a firm principle concerning the affection which rulers of cities ought to show toward the people subject to them: they should recognize that they are set over them in order to assist them by love rather than to harm them by domination, and that they are ministers rather than masters. They described rulers such as those of whom Cicero says that, for the liberty of their country, they do not fear not only to fight but even to lay down their lives, confident of that abode of heavenly blessedness promised in the revelation to Scipio.

Among the Gentiles themselves we have ready examples of persons who preferred the safety of their own people to their personal safety, and showed that they loved their own people more than themselves. We are especially compelled to marvel at this in the two Decii, in Plato, and in many others. The former are reported to have devoted themselves to death for the salvation of their people and to have endured it courageously. Plato, when endangered by thirst, refused water offered to him and chose to perish with his companions in their common danger rather than preserve himself alone by being refreshed with a draught. David, beloved of the Lord, had previously left an example of this disposition.

Let the abbots of our own day, to whom the highest care of monastic religion is entrusted, blush at this; let them blush, I say, and at least come to their senses, moved by the example of the Gentiles. Before the eyes of brothers chewing their poor food, they thoughtlessly devour choice and manifold dishes. Let Christian rulers also consider with what zeal of courage the ancients embraced the justice of their nation, and let them hold always before their eyes, as an example among others, this account of Valerius Maximus:

> “Zaleucus’s son [the text reads “with his sons”; read “his son”], condemned on a charge of adultery, ought according to the law established by his father to lose both eyes. Though the whole city, in honour of the father, wished to remit the young man’s penalty, he resisted for a time. At last, overcome by the people’s prayers, he first had one of his own eyes and then one of his son’s removed, leaving each of them the use of sight in one eye. Thus he rendered to the law its due measure of punishment. Great was his love for his son in this, but greater justice was displayed. He indulged nature as far as he could; yet virtue overcame nature. He wished to declare himself more a ruler than a father.” [Col. 1184A–B]

[Note: Valerius Maximus, Book VI, chapter 15.]

How much they endured in preserving truth and fidelity, and with what zeal of courage they claimed freedom of spirit for themselves, is shown by the example of the man who, lest a tyrant force him to disclose the conspiracy for the tyrant’s punishment which he and his accomplices had made, and compel him to betray his companions, bit off his own tongue with great force and spat it into the mouth of the raging tyrant—as Book II of Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy* relates.

If we raise the standard of our reason to examine the perfection of the philosophers’ life, we shall marvel at the supreme abstinence of anchorites or monks among them and at the loftiness of the contemplative life. [Col. 1184C] Many have taken care to write for posterity about their conversion from the world to the quiet of solitary life, both to flee the enticements of the world and to attain the desire of divine contemplation and the pursuit of philosophy.

Thus blessed Jerome, in Book II *Against Jovinian*, to crush the insolence of that Epicurean heretic, introduces the philosophers’ conversion from worldly enticements:

> “We, whose citizenship is in heaven, owe allegiance not to him by whom we are born but to him by whom we are reborn. Eating meat and drinking wine are a fullness of the belly [Note: In Jerome: “and a fullness of the belly”], the seedbed of lust. Hence the comic poet says: ‘Without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold.’ Through the five senses, as through certain windows, vices gain entrance into the soul. The citadel and stronghold of the mind cannot be taken unless the hostile army has burst in through the gates. If anyone delights in circuses, athletic contests, the movements of actors, women’s beauty, the splendour of gems, garments, and so forth, the soul’s freedom is captured through the windows of the eyes; and that prophetic saying is fulfilled: ‘Death has entered through our windows’ (Jer. 9:21). Therefore, when through these gates certain wedges of disturbances have entered the citadel of our mind, where will its freedom be? Where its strength? Where its thought of God? Especially since touch paints for itself even past pleasures and, by the recollection of vices, compels the soul to suffer with them and in some manner to enact what it does not do.

> “For these reasons many philosophers left crowded cities and suburban gardens, where there are irrigated ground, leafy trees, the whispering of birds, a mirror-like spring, a murmuring stream, and many delights for eyes and ears, lest through luxury and abundance of resources the strength of the soul should grow soft and its chastity be violated. It is useless to see repeatedly what has once captured you, and to expose yourself by experience to things from which you can scarcely abstain. The Pythagoreans too, disdaining such crowds, were accustomed to live in solitude and desert places. The Platonists and Stoics likewise frequented temple groves [Col. 1185B; Note: Jerome reads “places.”] and porticoes, so that, reminded by the holiness of a more august dwelling, they might think of nothing but virtues.

> “Plato himself, though rich and though Diogenes trampled his couch with muddy feet, chose, in order to devote himself to philosophy, the Academy [Note: Jerome reads “the Academic estate”], an estate far from the city, not merely deserted but unhealthy, so that the impulses of lust might be broken by care and continual bodily ailments [Note: Jerome reads “diseases”], and his disciples might feel no pleasure except in the things they learned.” [Col. 1184C–1185B]

Jerome, writing to Eustochium, after describing the austere life of Egyptian monks living separately in cells, says:

> “Such persons, he says, imitate the philosophy of Platonic discourse; Josephus, in the history of the Jewish captivity, reports that the Essenes ought to be such.” [Col. 1185B–C]

[Note: Abelard does not quote Jerome’s text quite faithfully here. Jerome reads: “Such people Philo, an imitator of Platonic discourse, [reports]; such people Josephus, the Greek Livy, reports to be Essenes in the second history of the Jewish captivity.”]

He calls it “the philosophy of Platonic discourse” which Plato himself, or the Platonists, proclaimed in their discourse. According to Macrobius, these persons seem to have reached such a height of life that some believed them alone to possess virtues and through these alone to become blessed. Plotinus, indeed, foremost among the professors of philosophy after Plato, as Macrobius says, divided the four virtues into four classes: the Platonic virtues, the purificatory virtues, those of the purified and cleansed soul, and the exemplary virtues. [Note: In Macrobius they are called “political,” not “Platonic,” virtues.] He assigns the purificatory virtues as especially proper to those practicing philosophy. These, he says, belong to the human being capable of the divine; they set free only that person’s soul who has resolved to cleanse himself from bodily contamination and, through a kind of flight from human things, to join himself to divine things alone.

Their prudence, he says, consists in despising this world and everything contained in it through contemplation of divine things, and directing every thought of the soul to divine things alone. Their temperance consists in abandoning, so far as nature permits, everything required by bodily use—as though they too, together with Truth itself, urged all [the text has *omnibus*, perhaps read *omnes*] both by deed and word: “Enter through the narrow gate” [Col. 1186A] (Matt. 7:13), and “Blessed are those who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19:12).

For it is plain that they too set before themselves this end, namely, the attainment of eternal life, which the Lord himself also assigned to us. Israel paid less attention to it, being more subject to hope and ambition for earthly happiness than to desire for eternal things. Therefore, to those who revere the letter, no reward is promised or to be expected in the Law for keeping the Law according to the letter except earthly prosperity, toward which they stretch with their whole desire. This promise is set forth plainly in Deuteronomy, chapters 24 and 28. But those who despise transitory things here must necessarily hope for something better—eternal things—as do philosophers and Christians.

[Col. 1186B] Thus Jerome above introduced Socrates’ consolation concerning his undeserved condemnation to death. We should understand that philosophers were joined with us both in faith in the Holy Trinity and in hope of future blessedness, and that the same end and prize were set before both: namely, the supreme Good, which is God. Therefore, when blessed Augustine above discussed Socrates himself, it was said of him among other things:

> “He directed his mind to what was necessary for the blessed life, for the sake of which alone the whole industry of all philosophers seems to have kept watch and laboured.” [Col. 1186B–C]

[Note: Augustine, *The City of God*, Book VIII, chapter 3.]

Augustine also added concerning Socrates’ disciples:

> “Their rival aim was to engage in the discussion of moral questions, where the supreme good is treated—a good without which no one can become blessed.”

This also bears upon the exhortation which Cicero writes to rulers of the commonwealth, introducing Scipio’s grandfather as speaking thus to him in a dream:

> “But in order that you, Africanus, may be more eager in defending the commonwealth, hold this firmly: for all who have preserved their country there is appointed and fixed a place in heaven where they may enjoy blessedness through everlasting time. Nothing is more pleasing to that sovereign God [lacuna], who rules the whole world, than the assemblies and gatherings of men joined together by law which are called cities, among the things that occur on earth.” [Col. 1186D–1187A]

[Note: In Migne, the following paragraph is printed in parallel with the section beginning “Thus, when …” and ending “who rules the whole universe” in the preceding paragraph.]

Jerome, writing to the priest Paulinus concerning all the books of sacred history:

> “We read in ancient histories that some people travelled through provinces, visited unfamiliar peoples, and crossed seas in order that they might also see face to face those whom they had known from books. Thus Pythagoras most laboriously travelled through the priests of Memphis; thus Plato travelled through Egypt, Archytas of Tarentum, and that coast of Italy which was once called Greater Greece. Though he was a master and eminent man at Athens, and the schools of the Academy resounded with his teaching, he became a traveller and disciple, preferring modestly to learn the things of others rather than rashly to force forward his own teachings. Finally, while he pursued learning as it fled, as it were, through the whole world, he was captured by pirates and sold; [Col. 1187A] bound and a slave, he even submitted to a most cruel tyrant. Yet, because he was a philosopher, he was greater than the one who purchased him.” [Col. 1186C–1187A]

Cicero rightly added, among things done on earth—that is, in the common dwelling of human beings—what should be referred to the active life. This life labours in earthly matters for the needs of one’s neighbour, with whom one dwells, and out of love for that neighbour, so that one may have something to give to the needy and may join the fruit of one’s own labour to that neighbour’s need.

But the solitary life of contemplation is of greater merit, [Col. 1187B] in which an excessive fervour of divine love lifts us up to the contemplation of the divine vision, all concern for worldly needs having now been set aside, and holds our citizenship as it were in heaven. Nor did Macrobius’s exposition fail to observe this, distinguishing by it the active life of rulers from the contemplation of philosophers.

Thus philosophers included two ranks of continent persons. Some, they say, are still being purified through the continual practice of abstinence and study; perhaps they should more properly be called students of philosophy than philosophers. By their communal dwelling for study they present the model of cenobitic monks, such as Josephus describes in Book XVIII of the *Antiquities* as the life of the Essenes. For Josephus distinguishes three kinds and sects of philosophers among the Hebrews, calling some Pharisees, others Sadducees, and others Essenes. He extols the last of these with remarkable praises.

Others are already of a purified and cleansed soul: in their flesh, mortified by prolonged abstinence, no movement of desire can now creep in or rule. Since they now live in solitary dwelling, they are sufficient to themselves by their own protection. We call this the perfect life of anchorites. According to Jerome writing to the monk Rusticus, such persons ought to leave the monastic community as though leaving the school of those practicing philosophy, so that there they may be trained under the rule of discipline and instructed toward perfection both by the example of others and by word; and, having been drawn away from their recent habit of pleasures, may be purified. [Col. 1187C–D] Once purified, instructed in all things, and having repelled every movement of temptation, they are like victors over themselves: securely they take up their own governance and with wholly purified minds pant to see God, so that no crowd or sight of human beings may draw them back from that height of contemplation.

We have also learned from many testimonies of the holy Fathers how great was the philosophers’ contempt for the world, how austere a life they established for themselves when they withdrew from the world, and how greatly they exhorted others to the same thing by deeds as well as words. Jerome testifies that Socrates and many others left everything, as did the apostles: first, because they judged that there was no glory in possessions which might be owned by both the worst and the best persons, and saw it to be most unjust that the excellence [Col. 1188B] of the human spirit and the splendour of the divine image should be subjected to the lowest and perishable things; second, because they recognized such things as an obstacle to study and to the attainment of true blessedness. It is as though Truth’s preaching were already saying in these philosophers: “Unless someone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33); and again: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. 6:24).

One of them carefully considering the difference between having money and serving money, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying, “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11), recalled among other things:

> “I strive that things may be mine, not that I may be subject to things: that is, that I may rule them, not they me, having captured me through some desire for themselves and dragged me even to unlawful acts.”

Hence Jerome’s exhortation to Julian:

> “Do you despise gold? The philosophers of the world despised it too. One of them—to say nothing of the rest—threw the price of many possessions into the sea, saying: ‘Go to the depths, evil desires! I shall drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.’” [Col. 1188C–D]

Jerome seems to name him in Book II *Against Jovinian*, where he speaks of the philosophers’ love of study:

> “We read that some dug out their own eyes, lest by their sight they should be diverted from the contemplation of philosophy. Thus Crates of Thebes, throwing no small weight of gold into the sea, said: ‘Go to destruction, evil desires! I shall drown you, lest I myself be drowned by you.’”

Again, in the same work:

> “I would recount the frugality of Pythagoras, Socrates, Antisthenes, and the rest to our shame, were it not both lengthy [Col. 1189A] and requiring a work of its own. Antisthenes certainly was the man who, after teaching rhetoric with distinction and having heard Socrates, is said to have told his disciples: ‘Go and seek a master; for I have found one.’ Immediately selling what he possessed and distributing it publicly, he kept for himself nothing beyond a little cloak. Xenophon in the *Symposium* bears witness to his poverty and labour, as do his innumerable books, some written in the style of a philosopher, others in that of an orator.

> “That famous Diogenes was his follower, more powerful than King Alexander and conqueror of human nature. Since Antisthenes admitted none of his disciples and could not drive away the persevering Diogenes, at last he threatened him with a club unless he went away. Diogenes is said to have offered his head and said: ‘No staff will be so hard as to be able to separate me from obedience to you.’ [Col. 1189C] Satyrus, who writes histories of distinguished men, relates that Diogenes wore a double cloak against the cold; kept a wallet as a pantry; and carried with him a club because of the frailty of his little body, using it in old age to support his limbs. He was commonly called *hēmerobios* [‘living from day to day’], because he asked and received food for the present day from anyone.

> “He lived in the entranceways of gates and in city porticoes; when he lay curled in a jar, he jested that he had a movable house and changed himself with the seasons. In winter he turned the mouth of his jar toward the south, [Col. 1189D] in summer toward the north; and wherever the sun inclined, Diogenes’s dwelling was turned likewise. Once, having a hollow wooden vessel for drinking, he saw a boy drink from his cupped hand; he is said to have dashed it on the ground, saying: ‘I did not know that nature too has a cup.’”

What will the monks of our own time say to this, and those who profess to despise the world with Christ? What, I say, will those say who, in order to drink wine sweetly, carefully prepare spiced drinks, seek costly and shining cups, and are not content with the common food or equipment of humankind?

Add also this account in praise of the philosopher which Valerius Maximus [Col. 1190A] records concerning his unconquered constancy:

> “Alexander could not overcome the self-control of Diogenes. When he came to him as he sat in the sun and urged him to say if there were anything he wished bestowed upon him, Diogenes said: ‘Leave all else aside; only do not stand between me and the sun.’ Therefore Alexander is said to have moved Darius from his position with his arms sooner than he moved Diogenes with his wealth.”

[Note: Valerius Maximus, Book IV, chapter 3. The text reads *primus*; probably *prius*, “sooner.”]

[Note: In Migne, the following two paragraphs are printed in parallel with the sections “crowd or sight … in accordance with,” and “had taught rhetoric … No staff will be so hard,” respectively.]

Ambrose, in a letter to Irenaeus:

> “In the writings of some we find proclaimed a Pythagorean precept: that he forbade his disciples to walk on the common and well-used road of the people. But the source from which he took this is not unknown. For, as many suppose, since he drew his origin from the Jewish people, he derived from their discipline even the precepts of his teaching; and deservedly he was held great among philosophers, scarcely finding an equal, as they say. He had read, then, in the Exodus of Moses that Moses was commanded to ascend the mountain with the priests, while the people should stand below. Therefore he separated the priests from the people, and afterward ordered Moses himself to enter into the cloud.

> “Do you see the distinctions? Nothing vulgar is required in priests: nothing popular, nothing shared with the pursuits, practices, and customs of the uncultivated multitude. Let us therefore rise above common opinions; let us leave the beaten tracks of herd-like association and of worn-out life; let us turn aside from the path of the common road. Let us seek for ourselves alone a path inaccessible to the words of arrogant people, untrodden by the works of the unskilled, and worn down by no stained person.” [Col. 1187D–1188C]

Jerome, to Avigus [Abigaus] the Spaniard:

> “Do not grieve if you lack what ants, flies, and serpents possess—that is, the eyes of the flesh. Rather rejoice that you possess that eye of which it is said in the Song of Songs: ‘You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride, with one of your eyes’ (Song 4:9); that eye by which God is seen; that eye concerning which it is said to Moses: ‘I will pass over and see this great vision’ (Exod. 3:3); that eye concerning which we read that some philosophers of the world even plucked out their own eyes, so that they might direct their whole thought toward purity of mind. And the Prophet says: ‘Death entered through your windows’; and the Apostles hear: ‘Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart’ (Matt. 5:28).” [Col. 1189A–C]

[Note: Jerome reads “Abigaus,” not “Avigius.” At [Col. 1189B], Jerome reads “finally, we read that some.” At [Col. 1190D], read *cogerent* (“might constrain”), as in Jerome.]

[Col. 1190A] Very many philosophers, moreover, wholly renouncing their many possessions, embraced so strict and laborious a life that by the work of their hands they provided for themselves all necessities—as though even then, through abstinence and manual labour, they were setting before us the pattern of the perfection of anchorites; and as though they had already heard that divinely inspired saying of the Apostle: “He who does not work shall not eat” (2 Thess. 3:10); and that of the Psalmist: “Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127:2). Hence Jerome, writing to Heliodorus, says: “Among the Greeks, that philosopher was praised who took pride in everything he used, down to his cloak and ring, having been made by his own hand.”

Nor have the holy doctors kept silent concerning the strength of their souls and their great love of chastity. Thus both sacred and secular writings relate that Socrates persisted even unto death in correcting fools and the vicious, and that for the defence of truth he died, as it were, a martyr, certain of recompense. Hence that saying of Valerius Maximus: “They condemned Socrates, who seemed to be introducing a new religion” [Col. 1190C]. What, indeed, was this new religion? It was plainly the commending of virtues and rebuking of vices, since in his ethical teaching he shaped human conduct toward uprightness. Blessed Augustine explains this in Book VIII of *The City of God*, saying:

> It is established that he treated, with marvellous charm and most penetrating wit, the folly of the unlearned, who imagined that they knew something, even in moral questions themselves. Hence, when enmities had been stirred up, he was condemned on a slanderous accusation and punished with death. But afterward the very city of Athens which had publicly condemned him publicly mourned him; and popular indignation turned so strongly against his two accusers that one of them perished, crushed by the violence of the multitude, while the other escaped a like punishment by voluntary and perpetual exile. Thus Socrates left behind him so illustrious a reputation in life and death, and so many followers of his philosophy, whose eager study was to engage in the discussion of moral questions, where the supreme good is treated of, without which no one can be happy.

The aforesaid saint also reports in the same work that Aulus Gellius [*Agellius*] said he had read that the Stoics held the following concerning sudden disturbances of the mind arising from fear: when they arise from terrifying events, they necessarily move even the mind of the wise person, so that for a brief while he trembles or is saddened. Yet they judge that this is the difference between the mind of the wise person and that of the fool: the fool’s mind yields to such passions and gives them assent, whereas the wise person, although necessarily suffering them, nevertheless retains with unshaken mind a true and stable judgment about what he ought reasonably to seek or avoid.

> [Note: In Migne, the following paragraph is printed in parallel with the section “whose eager study was … arising from fear” in the preceding paragraph.]

[Col. 1190D] Jerome to Heliodorus, in the epitaph of Nepotian:

> That most mighty Xerxes, who overthrew mountains and bridged the seas, is said, when from a lofty place he saw his innumerable army, to have wept because after one hundred [Col. 1191A] years none of those whom he then beheld would remain alive.

Who would not receive with the greatest admiration that constancy and unconquered strength of soul of Diogenes [Col. 1191B], who chose rather to banish fevers by death than allow them to rule over him, and to preserve himself more as conqueror of infirmity than as conquered by it? Accordingly Jerome, in the second book *Against Jovinian*, added this also concerning his greatness of spirit, speaking either in his own person or in that of Satyrus, who wrote histories of illustrious men:

> His virtue and self-control are shown also by his death. For when, already an old man, he was making his way to the Olympic contest, celebrated by a great gathering of Greece, and was seized by a fever on the journey, he is said to have died on the roadside. When his friends wished to lift him onto a beast of burden or into a carriage, he would not consent; but going beneath the shade of a tree, he said: “Go, I beg you, and continue on to see the spectacle. This night will prove me either victor [Col. 1191C] or vanquished. If I conquer the fever, I shall come to the contest; if the fever conquers me, I shall descend to the underworld.” And there, during the night, having cut his throat, he said that he was not so much dying as banishing the fever by death.

What would this man have done in a persecution of the faithful, when he would have faced the need to fight for the faith, to spend temporal life for eternal life, and would have believed that by doing so perpetual death was to be avoided—he who, lest he be overwhelmed by fevers, applied death as a remedy, openly declaring how little he valued this life entangled in miseries?

Add to this also that remarkable endurance of philosophers which we mentioned above: some of them submitted to having their eyes gouged out, lest through them they be called away from philosophical contemplation [Col. 1191D], as though interpreting literally that saying of Truth: “If your eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it from you” (Matt. 18:9). In this they plainly taught how much they preferred the eyes of the mind to bodily light, and how greatly they subjected the flesh itself to the spirit, since they endured to close, with such painful suffering, the windows of the body, concerning which the prophet says in lament: “My eye has plundered my soul” (Lam. 3:51).

Perhaps someone will say that this appears not to be fortitude or virtue at all, but rather should be regarded as madness: that Diogenes laid hands upon himself. We do not presume to excuse either him or Samson [Col. 1192A], or anyone else, unless they did this under some special command divinely inspired in them—as is believed to have happened in Samson’s case, namely to take vengeance upon the Philistines whom he crushed with himself; and in the case of certain Christian virgins who threw themselves into flames or waters so that they might not be violated by pagans. Hence Augustine, in Book I of *The City of God*:

> “Certain holy women,” they say, “in the time of persecution, in order to escape the pursuers of their chastity, threw themselves into a river that would carry them away and kill them; and having thus died, their martyrdoms are celebrated with most famous veneration in the Catholic Church.” I dare not make any rash judgment concerning them. For I do not know whether divine authority, by some trustworthy testimonies given to the Church, persuaded her to honour their memory in this way; and it may indeed be so. For what if they did this not through human deception but by divine command—not in error, but in obedience?

This seems especially to be the point of what Jerome says on the prophet Jonah, at the place where Jonah says, “Take me up and cast me into the sea, and the sea will cease from troubling you” (Jon. 1:12). Jerome says:

> “For it is not ours to seize death, but willingly to accept it when it is brought upon us. Hence in persecutions it is not permitted to perish by one’s own hand, except where chastity is endangered.”

Likewise, in the same book of *The City of God*:

> “Samson is excused in no other way for crushing himself with his enemies beneath the ruin of the house, except that the Spirit secretly commanded this—He who worked miracles through him.”

Likewise in the same work:

> “We may believe nothing else concerning Samson. But when God commands, and makes known without any ambiguity that He commands, who calls obedience a crime? Who accuses dutiful compliance? For even a soldier [Note: Here *miles* is used in the sense of an executioner or torturer, a usage not wholly unfamiliar to Augustine; he also uses it in Sermon 302, §13.] who, obeying the authority under which he has been lawfully placed, kills a man is guilty of no homicide under the law of his state; indeed, if he does not do it, he is guilty of abandoning and despising authority. If this is so when an emperor commands, how much more when the Creator commands?”

In those cases, therefore, such greatness and constancy of soul could be the virtue of fortitude; but we find nothing of the kind in Diogenes. For where endurance of sufferings is not deliberate—that is, prudent and rational—there is no ground for endurance; and it is certain that fortitude is absent, since this belongs to the definition of fortitude [Col. 1192D]. Nor indeed can we sufficiently commend Diogenes’ virtue in this matter, since we do not recognize his act as rationally done. Rather, we agree with the judgment of blessed Augustine, who adds in the same chapter of Book I of *The City of God*, concerning those who kill themselves:

> Whoever has perpetrated this upon himself is to be wondered at for greatness of spirit, but not praised for soundness of wisdom. And indeed, if you consult reason more carefully, not even greatness of spirit can rightly be named where someone, unable to endure either harsh circumstances or the sins of others [Col. 1193A], kills himself. Rather, a weak mind is disclosed, unable to bear either the harsh severity [servitude] of its own body or the foolish opinion of the crowd—as we read of Cato and Lucretia. Cato, esteemed for such great name and sternness, killed himself at Utica lest he lose his liberty under Caesar; and Lucretia, excessively eager for praise, feared that people might think that what she suffered by force while alive she had suffered willingly had she continued to live.

Likewise:

> If it is to be thought an act of great spirit when a person brings death upon himself, Theobrotus [Note: Thus almost all manuscripts of Augustine read; the common reading is *Cleombrotus*. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, calls him Cleombrotus of Ambracia.] is found to surpass him in this greatness of spirit. They say that, after reading Plato’s book in which the immortality of the soul was discussed, he threw himself headlong from a wall and thus departed this life for that [Col. 1193B] which he believed to be better … Yet Plato himself, whom he had read, could testify that this was done greatly rather than well. For Plato surely would himself have done this above all, or even commanded it, unless with that very mind by which he perceived the soul’s immortality he had judged it by no means to be done, but even to be forbidden.

Likewise, after some intervening material:

> One ground remains, of which I had begun to speak, on which it is thought useful for someone to kill himself: namely, lest he fall into sin, whether through alluring pleasure or raging pain. If we admit this ground, it will proceed so far that people ought to be urged to kill themselves immediately after they have been washed in the laver of holy regeneration and have received forgiveness for all their sins. For then is the time to guard against all [Col. 1193C] future sins, when all past sins have been erased.

Likewise: “O maddened minds! What is this great thing, if not error, then madness?”

It is established even by the judgment of the philosophers themselves that it is detestable for anyone for any reason to lay hands upon himself. They condemned it without any exception at all, as we have already learned from Plato’s own judgment. Macrobius, carefully following both Plato and Cicero, explains this in his commentary on the passage where Cicero, describing the Dream of Scipio, represents Scipio as speaking with his father Paulus, who appears to him; Scipio desires somehow to hasten to the blessedness of eternal life, which he had understood from his grandfather [Col. 1193D] to be revealed to him and prepared by God in heaven for good governors of the commonwealth:

> “I beg you, most holy and excellent father, since this is life, as I hear Africanus say, why do I remain on earth rather than hasten to come here to you?” “It is not so,” he replied. “For unless God has released you from these bodily guards, an entrance here cannot lie open to you. Therefore, Publius, you and all the devout must keep the soul in the guard of the body; nor may you depart from human life without the command of Him by whom it was given to you, lest you appear to have fled the duty assigned by God himself.”

Macrobius, on this passage [Note: Macrobius, Book I, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, ch. 13.]:

> This is Plato’s doctrine and precept: in the *Phaedo* he lays down that a human being ought not to die by his own will. Yet in the same dialogue he says that death should be desired by those who philosophize, and that philosophy itself is a meditation upon death. But Plato recognizes two deaths of human beings; and I do not now repeat what was said above, that there are two deaths, one of the soul and the other of the living being. He also asserts that the living being itself—that is, the human being—has two deaths, one bestowed by nature, the other by virtue. For a human being dies when the soul leaves the body, released by the law of nature. But he is also said to die when, while the soul still remains in the body, he despises bodily enticements under philosophy’s instruction [Col. 1194B], strips off the sweet snares of desires and all other passions. Plato therefore says that the wise should desire this death. But he forbids the other, which nature has appointed for all, to be forced, inflicted, or summoned; teaching that nature must be awaited. He adds also that we are under the dominion of God [Note: Macrobius reads “the gods,” not “God.” But Abelard, so as to show that his philosophers surpass even Christians, and to remove plurality of gods from them, does not hesitate to alter Macrobius’ text.], by whose guardianship and providence we are governed. Nothing belonging to another should be removed, against the owner’s will, from the place in which he had placed it. And just as one who violently takes life from another’s slave will not be free from guilt, so one who seeks an end for himself before the Lord has commanded does not obtain acquittal but guilt.

Plotinus develops these seeds of the Platonic school more deeply:

> Since it is established that there a recompense must be given to souls according to the degree of perfection to which each has attained in this life [Col. 1194C], the end of life is not to be hastened, since further progress may still be possible. You will say, then: “One who has already been perfectly purified ought to lay hands on himself, since he has no reason to remain, because one who has reached the heights requires no further progress.” But by that very fact—by summoning a swift end for himself in hope of enjoying blessedness—he is entangled in the snares of passion; for hope, like fear, is a passion. And this is what Paulus forbids and repels when his son hastens to come to him in hope of a truer life: “For unless God has released you from these bodily guards, an entrance here cannot lie open to you.” Nor does he say, “Unless natural death [Col. 1194D] comes, you cannot die,” but rather, “You cannot come here.” With equal constancy, death is neither to be feared when it comes by nature nor compelled contrary to nature’s order.

Therefore, although no one should presume to defend Diogenes or Theobrotus for the death they inflicted upon themselves, I nevertheless judge that the holy Fathers have beneficially set this before us as an example of endurance, contempt for this life, and longing for eternal life: that at least this may be praised in the former, that he despised this [Col. 1195A] life so greatly—not that he laid hands upon himself; and in the latter, that he embraced the immortal blessedness of the soul with such longing.

And if, after considering the abstinence and greatness of spirit of the philosophers, we also consider their continence, we shall find much written about them and by them to our confusion; and we shall find that in them the beauty of Christian chastity, which the Jews did not understand, began. Of this Wisdom says: “O how beautiful is the chaste generation with glory!” (Wis. 4:1), that is, continence of life with the illumination of wisdom—for there are also foolish virgins. and it immediately continues its praise:

> “For its memory is immortal, because it is known with God and with men.” When it is present, they imitate [Col. 1195B] it; and they desire it when it has withdrawn; and crowned, it triumphs forever, winning the prize of undefiled contests.”

This is what Truth also enjoins upon the apostles: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35); and the Apostle especially commends it, saying: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Cor. 7:1). Again: “I wish all people to be as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that. But I say to the unmarried and to widows, it is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry” (ibid., vv. 7–9). And again: “Concerning virgins I have no command from the Lord, but I give counsel. Therefore I judge this to be good because of the present necessity: that it is good [Col. 1195C] for a person to remain thus” (ibid., vv. 25–26). And after some intervening words:

> I want you to be free from anxiety. He who is without a wife is anxious about the things of the Lord, how he may please God; but he who is with a wife is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife, and is divided. The unmarried woman and the virgin think about the things of the Lord, that they may be holy in body and spirit. But she who is married thinks about the things of the world, how she may please her husband. Now I say this for your benefit, not to cast a snare upon you, but for what is honourable and what affords opportunity to entreat the Lord without hindrance. (1 Cor. 7:32–35)

Likewise: “Thus he who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her in marriage does better. A woman is bound for as long [Col. 1195D] as her husband lives; but if her husband sleeps, she is free: let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she will be happier if she remains thus, according to my counsel” (ibid., vv. 38, 40).

How many hindrances, troubles, and dangers marriages contain we have learned from many earlier testimonies and from the experience of falls: in paradise, woman immediately captivated man; and the desire for a woman drew Samson, the Nazarite of the Lord, whose birth had been announced by an angel, all the way to destruction. One glance at Bathsheba so ensnared that greatest of prophets and kings, David—of whom the Lord had given so great a testimony, saying, “I have found a man according to my heart” (Acts 13:22)—that after the death of the most valiant and faithful Uriah, he was made guilty at once of adultery, homicide, and the highest treachery [Col. 1196A]. And pleasure so cast down Solomon, that greatest of the wise, even to idolatry, as though in that idol—so that I may express what is most shameful in a shameful way—he worshipped the cunt of a pagan woman through lust more than he worshipped the idol itself through ignorance; becoming worse by as much as he was more inexcusable in his own conscience.

He himself, who experienced this so grievously, explains to us in Proverbs how easy and dangerous this temptation of lust is:

> “A woman takes the precious soul of a man. Can a man hide fire in his bosom and his garments not burn? Or walk upon coals and his feet not be scorched?” (Prov. 6:26–28).

Likewise:

> “Say to Wisdom, ‘You are my sister,’ and call prudence your kinswoman, that she may guard you from the strange woman who makes her words sweet. For from the window of my house … I looked out … a young man … and behold, a woman met him, dressed in the attire of a harlot, prepared to catch souls” (Prov. 7:4 ff.).  
> “At once he follows her, like an ox led to slaughter … not knowing that the fool is drawn to bonds, until an arrow pierces his heart; like a bird hurrying to a snare, and he does not know that his soul is in danger. Therefore now, my son, listen to me: let not your mind be drawn away into her paths, nor be deceived by her ways; for she has cast down many wounded men, and all the strongest have been slain by her. The ways of hell are her house, penetrating to the depths [Col. 1196C] below” (ibid., v. 22).

The same author in Ecclesiastes: “I examined all things with my mind, that I might seek wisdom and reason; and I found woman more bitter than death: she is the snare of hunters, and her heart a net; her hands are chains. He who pleases God will escape her, but the sinner will be caught by her” (Eccl. 7:26–27). Likewise: “One man out of a thousand I have found; but a woman among them all I have not found” (ibid., v. 29).

These are in harmony with the sayings in Ecclesiasticus concerning the troubles and dangerous company of women, both one’s own and strangers:

> “Do not be jealous of the wife of your bosom, lest she teach wickedness by an evil lesson. Do not give a woman authority over your soul, lest she enter through your strength and you be put to shame. Do not look upon a woman who is eager for many men, lest perhaps you fall into her snares” (Ecclus. 19:1–2).

Likewise: “A drunken workman shall not become rich, and he who despises small things shall fall little by little. Wine and women make wise men apostatize and rebuke the prudent” (Ecclus. 19:1–2; citation printed as “XIO”). Likewise: “Every wound is grief of heart, and every wickedness is the wickedness of a woman” (Ecclus. 25:17). “There is no head more wicked than the head of a serpent, and no anger above the anger of a woman. It will be more agreeable to dwell with a lion and a dragon than to live with a wicked woman” (ibid., v. 23). “All wickedness is brief compared with the wickedness of a woman; let the lot of sinners fall upon her” (ibid., v. 26). “If a woman has preeminence, she is opposed to her husband; and a wicked woman is a plague of death” (ibid., vv. 30–31). “From woman sin had its beginning, and through her we all die. Do not give your water [Col. 1197A] an outlet, nor a wicked woman permission to go out. Cut her off from your flesh, lest she continually abuse you” (ibid., vv. 33, 34, 36). And again: “I do not wish to dwell in the midst of women, for moth comes from garments and wickedness from woman. Better is the wickedness of a man than a woman who does good, and a woman who brings shame unto reproach” (Ecclus. 42:13–14).

Thus Wisdom itself bursts forth in praise of virgins or continent persons, saying:

> “Blessed is the barren woman who is undefiled, who has not known the bed in sin: she shall have fruit in the visitation of holy souls; and the eunuch who has not worked iniquity with his hands, nor conceived most wicked things against God. For there shall be given to him the chosen gift of faith and a most acceptable portion in the temple of God” (Wis. 3:13–14).

And again what we have already quoted above: “O how beautiful is the chaste generation with glory! For its memory is immortal, because it is known with God and with men” (Wis. 4:1).

It rightly says that this virtue is known not only with God, as specially approved by Him—for in the Gospel He assigns it a hundredfold fruit, and He who was born of a Virgin wished to preach it both in word and example; those who are without stain, that is, virgins, are said to follow Him, the true and spotless Lamb, wherever He goes. Indeed, the virginity of eight Sibyls obtained the spirit of prophecy, according to the testimony of blessed Jerome. It is also known among human beings, since virgins to be consecrated to God alone are veiled by the hand of the high priest [Col. 1197C], and hold precedence among deaconesses.

Blessed Jerome also explained in Book I *Against Jovinian* how great an honour even unbelieving virginity always had among pagans:

> Certainly, how greatly the Roman people always honoured virgins is shown by this: consuls and emperors, even while riding in triumphal chariots and bearing trophies from conquered nations, and every rank of dignity, were accustomed to yield them the way.

For no one doubts that they placed a virgin among the twelve signs of heaven by which they think the world revolves. Hence there is great wrong done to marriage: they did not place wife and husband even among scorpions, centaurs, crabs, fishes, and rhinoceroses.

[Col. 1197D] Moved by these and similar reasons, philosophers set before themselves a life of continence: partly so that they might devote themselves entirely to philosophy; partly lest their fortitude, weakened and made effeminate by the soft allurements of women, should succumb; or lest affection for children force them into certain unlawful or shameful acts; or lest they contract some stain of infamy from the vices of their wives which they did not have from their own life. Socrates experienced their shameless audacity sufficiently to serve as an example to others of how a philosopher ought to preserve purity of life and not add to philosophy, to which he has joined himself, the union of another as though with an adulteress.

For, as blessed Jerome recalls in Book I *Against Jovinian*:

> Socrates had two wives, Xanthippe and Myro, granddaughter of Aristides. Since they often quarrelled with one another and he was accustomed to ridicule them because they disputed over him—a most ugly man, with snub nose, a balding forehead, hairy shoulders, and bowed legs—they at last turned their attack against him [Col. 1198A], punished him severely, and pursued him for a long time as he fled. On one occasion, when he had endured Xanthippe’s endless abuse poured down upon him from above, she drenched him with filthy water. He gave no further answer than, after wiping his head: “I knew,” he said, “that this thunder would be followed by rain.”

Theophrastus knew that such troubles, shameful incidents, and continual disturbances belong to marriage. Having carefully set out nearly all of them, he maintains by many arguments that a wise man ought not to take a wife—as though he understands that true wisdom of which the apostle James says: “The wisdom which is from above is first indeed chaste, then peaceable” (Jas. 3:17). It is as though he plainly says: “He is not fit for contemplation and the study of divine things who does not embrace a life of continence, so that, free from the most burdensome yoke of a wife and undisturbed by so many and such great troubles of marriage, he may live in peace.” Indeed, one who binds himself in the bonds of marriage makes himself a slave and, according to the Apostle, loses power even over his own body; so that, if he should ever wish to turn from the world to religious life, he cannot do so if his wife forbids it.

Hence, as Jerome says in Book I *Against Jovinian*, the Apostle’s saying is this: “Were you called as a slave? Let it not concern you; but even if you can become free, use it rather” (1 Cor. 7:21). This means:

> Even if you have a wife, he says, and are bound to her, pay your due, and do not have power over your own body—and, to speak more plainly, are your wife’s slave—do not for this reason be sad, nor sigh over lost virginity. But even if you can find some grounds for separation, so that you may enjoy the freedom of chastity, do not seek your own salvation through another’s death, etc.

That Theophrastus also understood the wisdom which is from above—through which we begin, by the taste of contemplation, to savour something of God—he makes clear in the same chapter, where he declares that the wise man is never alone, since he is always either conversing with wise persons or speaking with God. Jerome says of this in the same first book *Against Jovinian* [Col. 1198D]:

> A book of Theophrastus entitled *On Marriage* is current, in which he asks whether a wise man ought to take a wife. Having determined that, if she is beautiful, well behaved, of honourable parents, and he himself healthy and rich, a wise man sometimes ought to enter marriage, he immediately adds: “Yet all these conditions rarely agree together in marriages. Therefore a wise man ought not to take a wife. First, the studies of philosophers are hindered, and it is impossible to serve books and a wife at the same time. There are many things necessary for the needs of married women: costly clothing, gold, jewels, expenditures, maidservants, furniture, various litters, and gilded carriages. Then, throughout the whole night, there are chattering complaints: ‘That woman goes out in public more splendidly dressed; this one is honoured [Col. 1199A] by everyone; I, poor wretch, am despised. Why were you looking at the neighbour? Why were you speaking with the maidservant? What did you bring home from the forum?’ We cannot have a friend or companion; she suspects another woman’s love to be hatred toward herself. If there is a most learned teacher in any city, we can neither leave our wife nor travel with baggage [or *potest*, “he can”]. It is difficult to support a poor wife; to endure a rich one is torture.
>
> “Add that no choice of wife is available: whatever sort falls to one’s lot must be kept. Whether she is bad-tempered, foolish, ugly, proud, or foul-smelling—whatever fault there is, we discover it after marriage. A horse, an ass, an ox, a dog, and the cheapest slaves are inspected first and then bought; only a wife is not shown, lest she displease before she is taken. Her face must always be attended to and her beauty praised, lest if you look at another woman she think herself displeasing. She must be called mistress; her birthday celebrated; one must swear by her health and pray that she may outlive one; her nurse, bearer, paternal slave, foster-child, handsome attendant, curled procurator, and eunuch cut for long and secure lust must be honoured—under which names adulterers [or: adulteries] hide. Whomever she loves must be loved without charge.
>
> “If you entrust the whole household to her management, you must be her servant. If you reserve anything to your own discretion, she will think herself not trusted; she will turn to hatred and quarrels, and, unless you quickly take counsel, she will prepare [Col. 1199C] poisons. If you admit old women, goldsmiths [perhaps *aruspices*, ‘soothsayers’], diviners, and sellers of jewels and silk garments, chastity is endangered; if you exclude them, there is the injury of suspicion. But what use is even careful guarding, when an unchaste wife cannot be guarded and a chaste wife ought not to be? The necessity of a guard is an untrustworthy guardian of chastity, and she alone should truly be called chaste who was free to sin if she wished. A beautiful woman is quickly loved; an ugly one desires to be loved. What many desire is difficult to guard; it is troublesome to possess what no one deigns to have. Yet an ugly wife is kept with less misery than a beautiful one is guarded. Nothing is secure when the desires of the whole populace sigh after it: some are enticed by beauty, others by intelligence, others by charm, others by generosity. What is assailed from every side is conquered somehow.
>
> “If wives are taken for the management of the household, comfort in illness, and escape from loneliness, a faithful servant manages much better, obedient to the master’s authority and complying with his direction, than a wife, who thinks herself mistress precisely if she acts against her husband’s will—that is, does what she pleases rather than what she is commanded. Friends and household women bound by benefits can sit with the sick person more readily than she who charges us with her tears, sells her foulness for hope of inheritance, and, while boasting of her anxiety, disturbs the sick man’s mind with despair. If she becomes ill, one must be ill with her and never leave her bed. Or, if she is a good and agreeable [Col. 1200A] wife—yet this is a rare bird [Note: In Jerome: “a rare bird”]—we groan with her when she gives birth and are tortured with her when she is in danger.
>
> “But the wise man can never be alone: he has with him all good persons who are and who have ever been, and he carries his free mind wherever he wishes. What he cannot embrace in body, he embraces in thought; and if there is a lack of human beings, he speaks with God. He will never be less alone than when he is alone. Moreover, to take a wife for the sake of children—so that our name may not perish, or that we may have supports for old age and use assured heirs—is most foolish. For what does it matter to us when we depart from the world that another is not called by our name, when a son does not immediately bear his father’s name and innumerable persons [Col. 1200B] bear the same name? Or what support for old age is it to rear at home one who may perhaps die before you, or be of depraved character, or certainly, when he has reached maturity, think you slow to die? Better and more reliable heirs are friends and relatives whom you choose by judgment than those whom you are compelled to have whether you wish it or not. Indeed, it is a more certain inheritance, while you live, to make good use of your own property than to leave what you acquired by your labour for uncertain uses.”

Thus far Theophrastus.

Then Jerome: “When Theophrastus discusses these and similar matters, who among Christians—whose citizenship is in heaven, who daily say, ‘I desire to depart and be with Christ’ (Phil. 1:23)—would not blush? Such a person will surely desire an heir . . . and delight in a succession of children and grandchildren, whom perhaps Antichrist will seize; when we read that Moses and Samuel preferred others to their own sons and did not consider as children those whom they saw displeasing to the Lord.” The same author, in the same work: “When Cicero was asked by Hirtius, after divorcing Terentia, to marry her sister, he entirely declined, saying that he could not devote attention equally to a wife and to philosophy.” Again: “Herodotus writes that a woman puts off modesty with her clothing; and our comic poet considers fortunate the man who has never taken a wife. Epicurus, the defender of pleasure, says that a wise man should rarely enter marriage, because many inconveniences are mixed with wedlock.”

[Col. 1200D] How scrupulously the honor of the Gentiles avoided not merely shameful deeds but even the suspicion of shameful deeds, Valerius Maximus teaches in writing thus concerning a certain young man [Note: Valerius Maximus, book IV, chapter 5]:

> “Spurinna, a youth of outstanding beauty, because his remarkable appearance attracted the eyes of distinguished women, and because he perceived that he was therefore suspected by their husbands and parents, disfigured the beauty of his face with wounds.”

By deeds themselves he especially exhorted us toward that saying of the Wise Man: “A good name is better than great riches” (Prov. 22:1). And cruel is the person who neglects his own reputation. How zealously they likewise embraced chastity and forestalled, in every possible way, obscene shamefulness is contained in the same book:

> “Vergilius,” he says, “killed his daughter when she was brought into the forum, because Claudius, relying on the force of his official power, sought to violate her; the father preferred that she should be chaste rather than corrupted.”

[Note: In Valerius Maximus the name is not *Vergilius* but *Virginius*, a man of plebeian birth but patrician spirit.]

Again:

> “Metellus struck his wife to death with a staff because she had drunk wine; for whatever woman immoderately desires the use of wine closes the door to virtues and opens it to offences.”

The same author:

> “Sulpicius divorced his wife because he learned that she went about outdoors with her head uncovered. Antistius repudiated his wife because he had seen her publicly conversing in private with a certain common freedwoman. Sempronius divorced his wife because, without his knowledge, she attended the games.”

Shame! Yet we know many Christians who act as procurers through their wives. But this virtue of continence, or love of chastity, was not lacking even among women themselves distinguished by an abundance of philosophy and letters. Thus we may recognize that this supreme emblem of virtues especially accords with philosophical excellence, and how greatly the dignity of philosophy has always withdrawn itself from the obscene pleasures of desire. Hence Jerome, in the same book *Against Jovinianus*:

> “Why should I mention the Erythraean and Cumaean Sibyl, and the other eight? For Varro thinks that there were ten, whose distinction is virginity, and the reward of virginity, prophecy.”

Again in the same work:

> “Diodorus the Socratic is said to have had five daughters, dialecticians of remarkable chastity, concerning whom Philo, Carneades’ teacher, wrote a most extensive history.”

If, after philosophers or learned women, one also takes pleasure in turning to secular persons or laypeople, examples inviting us to chastity will not be lacking among such people, whether unmarried or married. Thus Jerome, in the first book *Against Jovinianus*, pursuing the praise of such women, says:

> “The virgin daughter of Demotion, leader of the Areopagites, on hearing of the death of her betrothed Leosthenes, killed herself, declaring that although her body was untouched, yet, if compelled to take another husband, she would be taking a second, since in mind she had married the first.”

Again:

> “Who,” he says, “could pass over in silence the seven Milesian virgins, who, when the onslaught of the Gauls was laying everything waste, took death upon themselves lest they suffer anything dishonorable, leaving to all virgins an example of themselves: that to honorable minds chastity is greater than life.”

[Note: In Jerome: “that chastity was of greater concern than life.”]

> “Nicanor, after Thebes had been conquered and overthrown, was overcome by love for one captive virgin. Seeking marriage with her—a thing that a captive ought to have desired—he learned that to chaste minds virginity is worth more than a kingdom. Weeping and mourning, her lover held her after she had been killed by her own hand. Greek writers also relate that another Theban virgin, violated by a Macedonian enemy, concealed her grief for a little while, then cut the throat of the sleeping violator of her virginity, and joyfully killed herself, wishing neither to live after her chastity had been lost nor to die before she had become her own avenger.”

How greatly God approves the virtue of chastity, he did not disdain to show by manifest miracles in such virgins also. Hence, among other things, the same book of Jerome contains this:

> “When the Vestal virgin Claudia fell under suspicion of unchastity, she is said to have drawn by her girdle a ship which thousands of men had been unable to pull.”

To this also belongs Sidonius’ statement in the *Propempticon* to his little book:

> “Such as neither Tanaquil was, nor she whom you begot for Teipitina; such as she dedicated in Phrygian dress, who drew the ship, swollen against a sufficiently white [uncertain reading], by her virgin hair.”

But if it pleases us to pass from virginal chastity to marital chastity, there will likewise be no lack of examples showing with how great reverence and with what undivided love even the nations strove to preserve inviolate the faith of marriage. Lucretia stands first as an example: almost all Roman poets and historians endeavored to extol her in worthy praises for her love of chastity. Thus Valerius Maximus says [Note: Valerius Maximus, book VI, chapter 1]:

> “Lucretia, compelled by Tarquin to suffer violation by force, after lamenting her wrong before her friends, killed herself with a sword that she had brought concealed beneath her clothing.”

Again [Note: Ibid., book IV, chapter 6]:

> “Plautius, on hearing of the death of his wife Horestilla,” fell upon a drawn sword and killed himself for love of her.”

Again [Note: Ibid.]:

> “Portia, Cato’s daughter, when she heard that her husband Brutus had been killed at Philippi, because no sword was available, did not hesitate to swallow burning coals, adopting a novel kind of death.”

Again [Note: Ibid.]:

> “Hypsicratia truly loved her husband Mithridates,” for whose sake she changed the beauty of her appearance into male attire: having cut off her hair, she accustomed herself to horse and weapons, in order more easily to share in his labors.”

Who, then, would fail to observe how acceptable to God bodily integrity and continence of life have always been among every people, when, as blessed Jerome also attests, the above-mentioned eight Sibyls earned the spirit of prophecy through the beauty of their virginity? He also did not pass over Claudia, the Vestal virgin, whom God protected from the stain of suspicion by the miracle of a wondrous sign. And why should it be surprising if continence of life obtained this for her, when so great was the merit before God of the abstinence and continence of the philosophers? These things appear all the more praiseworthy in them and are to be reckoned of greater merit because they were less stirred toward them by the preaching or examples of others, but were moved by their own reason and the instruction of natural law.

For just as it is evident that we, instructed both by natural law and by the written law of both Testaments, and by so many examples of the Lord himself and of the holy Fathers, are the more grievously at fault [the text reads *relinquere*, “to abandon”; read *delinquere*, “to sin”], the more inexcusable we are; so, conversely, their evils were more pardonable and their goods appeared more praiseworthy. Hence the Lord not without reason preferred the Gentile Job to the other faithful of his time, saying: “There is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil” (Job 1:8), although many descendants of Abraham still survived at that time; for Job is said by blessed Gregory to have lived after the Law had been given, in the time of the Israelite Judges.

From this comes Jerome’s commendation, in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, of the emperor Titus, to our confusion:

> “Titus, son of Vespasian, who, in vengeance for the blood of the Lord, entered Rome in triumph after Jerusalem had been overthrown, is said to have been of such goodness that, when late one night at supper he remembered that he had done no good deed that day, he said: ‘Friends, today I have lost a day.’ We think that no hour, day, moment, time, or lifetime is lost to us when we speak an idle word, for which we shall render an account on the day of judgment.”

If he, without law, without Gospel, and without the teaching of the apostles, naturally both spoke and acted thus, what ought we to do, in whose condemnation there stand even Juno’s women married only once, Vesta’s virgins (*univirgines*), and other continent idols?

[Col. 1203C] The aforesaid saint had read, unless I am mistaken, Suetonius’ statement—or something similar—on the excellence of the above-named emperor:

> “Titus, the love and delight of the human race, most obstinately maintained this rule: never to dismiss without hope anyone who came to him with a request. Indeed, when his household officers warned him that he promised more than he could perform, he said that no one ought to depart sadly from an emperor’s conversation. Remembering at supper that he had granted nothing to anyone throughout the day, he said: ‘Friends, I have lost a day.’ When he contracted the fever of which he died, he is said, while being carried in a litter, to have looked up to heaven and bitterly complained that his life was being taken from him though undeserving of it. For, he said, there was no deed of his that he needed to regret, except only one; what it was, he did not then disclose, nor was it known to anyone.”

How remarkable also is what Suetonius [Note: *Suetonius*, book VIII] prefaces concerning his father Vespasian, and how clearly the very gifts of miracles testify that his deeds were acceptable to God! For it is written thus:

> “While Vespasian was not yet emperor, a certain man of the common people who was blind, and another lame in one leg, approached him together as he sat on the tribunal, begging for help with their health. Serapis had shown them in a dream that he would restore the man’s eyes if he spat upon them, and strengthen the other’s leg if he would deign to touch it with his heel. At the urging of his friends, although unwilling, he attempted both acts, and the result was not lacking.”

If we consider also how much the deeds of their former life benefited persons such as these, who died even in their unbelief or without sacramental grace, testimonies will not be lacking here either. Let anyone read chapter 43 of book II of the *Life of Blessed Gregory* [Note: John the Deacon, *Life of St Gregory*, book II, chapter 45], and he will discover how acceptable to God himself and to the aforesaid saint was the justice of the Gentile emperor Trajan. For the aforesaid saint is said, by the persistence of his prayers and abundance of tears, to have rescued Trajan’s soul—though he had died after the Gospel had been handed down, without faith and without the grace of baptism—from penal places and the torments of hell. Gregory had been intensely moved by recalling the justice which that emperor, in a difficult circumstance, had done to a widow who confronted him. It is there written as follows:

> When Trajan was once hastening urgently to make preparations for an impending war, and answered a widow crying out for vengeance for her murdered son that, if he returned safe from battle, he would in every respect exact vengeance, the widow said: “If you die in battle, who will provide it for me?” Trajan answered: “He who shall rule after me.” The widow said: “And what will it profit you if another does justice for me?” Trajan replied: “Certainly nothing.” And the widow said: “Is it not better for you to do justice for me yourself and receive your reward for it, than to pass this on to another?” Then Trajan, moved by reason and compassion, dismounted from his horse and rendered judgment.

[Note: In Migne, the following paragraph is printed parallel to the section “If he . . . at supper that” in the preceding paragraph.]

Augustine, *City of God*, book XVII:

> “Now if we turn to those miracles which they set forth as done by their gods in opposition to our martyrs, will they not be found to work even for us and to benefit us altogether? For among the great miracles of their gods, surely this is a great one which Varro relates: that a Vestal virgin, when she was endangered by a false suspicion of unchastity, filled a sieve with water from the Tiber and carried it to her judges without a single drop escaping. Who held the weight of water amid so many open holes? Then will almighty God be unable to remove heavy weight from an earthly body, so that a vivified body may dwell in the same element in which the life-giving Spirit has willed to dwell?”

[Col. 1204D] The most merciful pope, therefore, remembering the justice of this most merciful and just emperor, and giving particular attention to the fact that the emperor had performed this deed for eternal recompense, is said to have dared to go to the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle and there to have wept so long over the error of that most merciful ruler until, on the following night, he received the answer that he had been heard for Trajan, whose soul had indeed been rescued from penal places. Yet, as is said in the same place, we need not therefore believe that Trajan was admitted into the kingdom of heaven, lest perhaps we prejudice the words of Truth: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5).

But perhaps what blessed Ambrose is understood to have written in the *Consolation on the Death of the Emperor Valentinian*, addressed to Valentinian’s sisters, is received with even greater astonishment. In it the aforesaid saint seems wholly to affirm that Valentinian—already catechized by Ambrose but not yet baptized—obtained pardon after death through the good works of his former life and received the lot of the elect without the grace of baptism, although this appears wholly contrary not only to the Gospel but also to the holy doctors. Hence Augustine [Note: Gennadius of Marseille, *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*, chapter 41; as already observed, this book is not Augustine’s but Gennadius’s, though Abaelard cites it more than once under Augustine’s name], *On the Orthodox Faith*:

> “We believe that only the baptized share in salvation; that no catechumen, even though he has died in good works, possesses eternal life, except in martyrdom, where the whole sacraments of baptism are fulfilled.”

These, however, are Ambrose’s words in the aforesaid letter *On the Death of Valentinian*, addressed to his sisters:

> “I hear that you grieve because he did not receive the sacraments of baptism. Tell me: who had long before desired this, so that when he came into Italy he might be initiated, and who recently made known to me that he wished to be baptized by me? For this reason, setting other matters aside, he considered that I should be summoned. Does he not, then, possess the grace he desired? Does he not possess what he asked for? And because he asked, he received. And where is that saying: ‘The righteous person, whatever death overtakes him, his soul shall be at rest’? Therefore release, holy Father, your gift to your servant.”

Again:
