> “He did not fear to displease men, so that he might please you alone in Christ. He who had your Spirit—how did he not receive your grace? Or if this troubles you, because the mysteries were not solemnly celebrated: then neither are martyrs crowned if they are catechumens. But if they are washed in their own blood, your mercy and their will have washed this man also.”

Again:

> “I learn still to add intercession for one for whom I presume a reward; let us ask for his rest with devout affection.”

Again:

> “I grieve for you, my son Gratian; I grieve for you also, my son Valentinian. You thought that through me you would be rescued from dangers; you loved me not only as a parent, but hoped in me as your redeemer and deliverer. You said: ‘Do you think that I shall see my Father?’ Beautiful was your desire concerning me, but ineffective your confidence. Alas for me! Vain hope in a human being! Alas for me! Why did I not know your desire earlier? Lord, because no one has anything he can offer more than what he desires for you, do not separate me after death from those whom I found most dear in this life. Lord, I ask that where I shall be, they also may be with me. I beseech you, highest God, that you raise up and restore these most dear young men by a timely resurrection, and compensate this prematurely ended course of life by a timely restoration.”

If these persons, after the Gospel had been handed down, obtained so much before God from the merits of their former lives without faith in Jesus Christ or the grace of baptism, what are we compelled to despair of concerning philosophers before Christ’s coming, most illustrious both in faith and in life? Why should we doubt that they obtained forgiveness, or that their life and worship of the one God—which they especially possessed and proclaimed in writing in their own time—won for them great gifts from God both in this life and in the future, and showed them what was necessary for salvation? For it is written: “Good understanding belongs to all who do it” (Ps. 110:10), and the mercy of divine grace is so great that it grants its benefits even to the unwilling.

If, after the lives of philosophers proposed by the holy Fathers for the confusion of our shamelessness, we wish to examine their learning, we shall understand, both from the testimonies of the saints and from evident reason, how necessary it is also for sacred letters—not only in matters pertaining to moral instruction or testimonies of the sacred faith, but for every kind of question to be settled by arguments, and for investigating the mysteries of allegories, which we frequently examine through the natures of numbers.

Therefore blessed Augustine especially commends to us both dialectic and arithmetic. In book II of *On Order*, he dared to commend dialectic in such a way that he seems to profess it alone to be knowledge, since he says that it alone can make people knowing:

> “The discipline of disciplines, which they call dialectic, teaches this: to teach; it teaches this: to learn. In it reason itself demonstrates and makes itself plain, knowing what it wills.” It knows how to know; it not only wishes, but is able, alone, to make people knowing.”

In book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, when he professed that among all arts dialectic and arithmetic are especially necessary for sacred Scripture—the former for resolving questions, the latter for investigating the mysteries of allegories which we frequently examine through the natures of numbers—he exalted dialectic by so much the more as he assigned it a broader necessity for settling every uncertainty of questions. He says:

> “There remain those matters that belong not to bodily senses but to reason, where the disciplines of disputation and number hold sway. But the discipline of disputation is of very great value for penetrating every kind of question found in the holy Scriptures. Only the desire for wrangling and a certain childish display of deceiving an opponent must be guarded against. For there are many things called sophisms, false conclusions of arguments, and for the most part such close imitations of true conclusions that they deceive not only the slow-minded but even intelligent persons who are insufficiently attentive. Scripture, I think, condemns this kind of deceptive conclusion in the place where it says: ‘He who speaks sophistically is hateful’ (Ecclus. 37:23).”

In the same work, reflecting in the sayings of philosophers both great moral edification and some teaching concerning faith and the worship of the one God, he added:

> “Those who are called philosophers, especially the Platonists, if they have perhaps said anything true and suited to our faith, need not be feared; rather, it should be claimed for our use from them as from unjust possessors. For Egypt possessed not only idols which the people of Israel were to detest, but also vessels and ornaments of gold and silver, and clothing, which that people, when leaving Egypt, secretly claimed for itself by God’s command, as if for a better use, while the Egyptians unknowingly lent them things which they used badly. Thus all the teachings of the Gentiles and liberal disciplines better suited to the use of truth contain certain precepts of morals, and among them are found some truths concerning the worship of God himself.”

Again, concerning philosophers:

> “They gave their gold, silver, and clothing to the people of God departing from Egypt, not knowing how what they gave would be returned in Christ’s service.”

That greatest doctor of the Church therefore knew, having once been converted from Gentile philosophy to the true wisdom, which is Christ, what he had read concerning God in philosophical writings; and he knew how unworthy it would be not to acknowledge their Author and the Author of all things in the philosophical disciplines too, which have always flourished on earth among God’s greatest gifts, nor to serve him whom all things obey.

He also considered what is written in Ecclesiasticus: “A wise man will seek out the wisdom of all the ancients and will be occupied with the prophets. He will preserve the discourse of famous men and will enter together into the subtleties of parables. He will seek out the hidden meaning of proverbs and will dwell among the secrets of parables” (Ecclus. 39:1–3). Accordingly Solomon too, as we have noted above on Jerome’s blessed testimony, immediately at the opening of Proverbs warns us to understand words of prudence, subtleties of expressions, parables and obscure discourse, sayings of the wise, and riddles; for, Jerome says, these belong to dialecticians and philosophers.

Hence studies of the liberal arts are later commended most strongly, and not inappropriately, by the holy Fathers as very necessary for sacred Scripture, while poetic fictions are wholly forbidden to Christians: not only because they are full of falsehood, and “a lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11), but also because, through thoughts of empty tales, they entice the mind toward desires for the shameful things they invent and draw us away from meditation on sacred reading. Testimonies of the saints concerning both are readily available.

[Col. 1207D] A synod in the time of Pope Eugenius and King Louis says:

> “It is reported to us that in certain places neither teachers nor concern for the study of letters are to be found. Therefore all bishops and the peoples subject to them, and other places in which necessity arises, must take every care and diligence that masters and teachers be appointed, who, possessing the studies of letters and liberal arts, may teach doctrines; for in these above all the divine commandments are made manifest and explained.”

But concerning poetic fictions, which some have customarily called books of grammar because children were accustomed to read them for instruction in grammatical expression, the authority of the saints has decreed as follows. Jerome, to Pope Damasus, *On the Prodigal Son*:

> “The food of demons is the poems of poets, the rhetorical pomp of words belonging to secular wisdom.”

And later:

> “Far be it that ‘almighty Jupiter,’ ‘by Hercules,’ ‘by Castor,’ and the other things more monstrous than divine should sound from a Christian mouth! Yet even now we see priests of God, setting aside the Gospels and prophets, reading comedies and chanting the words of the amorous verses of the *Eclogues*; they hold Virgil and make into a voluntary crime what was a necessity in childhood.”

The same author, on the Epistle to the Ephesians, concerning the Apostle’s words, “Bring up your children in the discipline and correction of the Lord” (Eph. 6:4):

> “Let bishops and presbyters who educate their children in secular letters, make them read comedies and sing shameful writings of loves—perhaps educated at the Church’s expense—read [this]: what some poor person, pouring out his entire substance, offered into the treasury for sin, they turn into a handout for the Saturnalia and Minerva, or into household expenses or filthy prostitutes.”

[Note: In Jerome: “writings of mimes.”]

The same author, in his letter to the virgin Eustochium:

> “What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? (2 Cor. 6:15). What has Horace to do with the Psalter, Maro with the Gospel, Cicero with the Apostle?”

In that same letter he immediately asserts that, because he was reading Plato and other philosophers to whom he was devoted, while the unpolished language of prophetic speech repelled him, he was caught up in the spirit before the tribunal of the severe Judge. When asked his condition, he answered that he was a Christian. But the one presiding said: “You lie: you are a Ciceronian, not a Christian; for where your treasure is, there also is your heart” (Matt. 6:21). At length, after many words, through the prayer of the saints standing by and as if under the solemn affirmation of an oath that he would never again read secular books, he scarcely obtained pardon by which he might escape.

Hence Rabanus, *On Ecclesiastical Oppressions*, part II:

> “We read of blessed Jerome that, when he read Cicero’s book, he was rebuked by an angel because a Christian man devoted himself to the fictions of pagans.”

Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 13:

> “A Christian is therefore forbidden to read the fictions of poets, because through the pleasure of empty tales he arouses his mind to incentives of lust. For sacrifice is offered to demons not only by offering incense, but also by willingly accepting their sayings.”

Again:

> “The books of the Gentiles must be guarded against and avoided out of love for the holy Scriptures. The savor of grammatical art is not to be preferred to simpler letters; for grammarians are better than heretics. The teaching of grammarians can also profit life when it has been adopted for better uses.”

From the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 9:

> “A bishop shall not read Gentile books, but heretical books only as necessity and time require.”

[Col. 1209A] Gregory, to Bishop Desiderius:

> “It has come to us that your Fraternity expounds grammar to certain persons. We received this matter with such displeasure and have so vehemently condemned it that what had previously been said turned into groaning and sorrow. For the praises of Christ and the praises of Jupiter do not fit in one mouth; and consider yourself how grave and unspeakably wicked it is for a bishop to sing things unsuitable even for a religious layman.”

Hence Plato himself, when setting forth the constitution of a rightly ordered state, decreed that poets must be expelled from cities, as blessed Augustine records in book II of *The City of God*:

> “Or should the palm rather be given to Plato, who, when he reasoned out what a city ought to be like, judged that poets, as enemies of the city, should be expelled from it?”

Again, later:

> “That Plato, of course, did not wish poets themselves to live at all in a well-ordered city, whether because they lied at will or because they set before wretched human beings the worst deeds of gods as examples to imitate.”

As though by these deeds themselves he already openly proclaimed: “A lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11).

But perhaps you will say that readings not only of poets but even of the liberal arts must be forbidden to Christians, since blessed Jerome asserts in his letter to Eustochium that he was severely corrected and beaten by the Lord for reading philosophical writers. In that case, certainly, grammar too ought not to be read by a Christian, although without its instruction neither the divine page nor any writing can be understood. So too rhetoric, which teaches the ornaments of every kind of eloquence—ornaments with which sacred Scripture is especially filled—and whose elegance cannot shine forth unless they have been carefully identified.

Why then, you ask, was the aforesaid doctor so severely corrected and scourged on account of Cicero’s books that he was compelled, under the solemn affirmation of an oath, wholly to renounce reading secular books? Certainly because he devoted himself to them not for some usefulness but for the pleasure of eloquence, neglecting the study of sacred Scripture, whose unpolished language, as he himself says, repelled him.

But I judge that the reading of no art ought to be forbidden to any religious person, unless perhaps through it some greater good is hindered—as we know must be done in other good things as well, namely, that lesser goods should sometimes be set aside or wholly omitted for greater ones. For where there is no falsehood in the teaching, no shamefulness in the words, and some usefulness in the knowledge, who could deserve blame for learning or teaching these things, unless the aforementioned cause intervenes: that is, neglect or abandonment of a superior good? For no one can rightly call any knowledge evil. How greatly this serves our condemnation and confusion, every discerning person will perceive, since not only is it said to us that “a lying mouth kills the soul” [the citation given is Matt. 12:36], but a strict account is required of every idle word.

If a Christian wishes to read for instruction in forms of expression or in thought, can this not be fully achieved without studying poetic fictions and empty tales? What kinds of expression or ornaments of language does sacred Scripture lack, especially filled as it is with riddles of parables and allegories and almost everywhere overflowing with mystical veils? What refinements of speech has Hebrew, the mother of languages, failed to teach? This is especially so since it is well known that even the common people of Palestine were accustomed to parables, so that the Lord Jesus himself needed to speak to them in parables when he preached the Gospel. What dishes can be lacking from the Lord’s spiritual table—that is, sacred Scripture—in which, according to Gregory, both the elephant swims and the lamb walks?

Its understanding so abounds in every wealth of nourishment and delight that it alone, in its threefold exposition, possesses the perfection of teaching. In it anyone will learn, far more and more easily than from poets, sweetness of composition, and at the same time fully receive uprightness of morals and edification of soul. For who, I do not say among poets but even among philosophers, equals blessed Jerome in mature composition; who equals blessed Gregory in sweetness; who equals blessed Augustine in subtlety? In Jerome indeed you will find Cicero’s eloquence; in the latter two, Boethius’ sweetness and Aristotle’s subtlety—and, unless I am mistaken, much more if you compare their individual writings.

What should be said of the eloquence of Cyprian, Origen, and countless other ecclesiastical doctors, Greek and Latin alike, most learned in every study of the liberal arts? Blessed Augustine declares that Cyprian surpassed all Gentiles in composition, even in the judgment of the Gentiles themselves. Certain words from a letter of Cyprian were produced by Christians during the contest held between Christians and Gentiles concerning which of their teachers prevailed in literary composition. These are Cyprian’s words in one place:

> “Let us seek this seat. Nearby retreats offer seclusion, where the wandering tendrils of vines, creeping by hanging bonds over reed supports, have made a leafy covering, a green-roofed portico.”

Concerning the ornament of these words blessed Augustine recalls, in book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, saying: “Small and fragile goods are adorned with the foaming circuit of words. There is something of this kind in Cyprian’s letter. For he says in one place: ‘Let us seek this seat,’ and so forth.”

If Christian readers desire quickly to acquire both the kinds of construction and the ornaments of language, they will fully learn these from the arts themselves, which teach them completely and plainly: grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric. There is no need to linger long among the fabulous poets in order to gather these matters, which there are either rarely, obscurely, or imperfectly marked. Hence Cicero himself, when fully instructing readers concerning expression in rhetoric, did not wish to use poetic examples but examples of his own, in which, as he himself says, the art stood out more fully.

Why, then, do bishops and teachers of the Christian religion not keep poets away from the city of God, whom Plato excluded from the city of the world? Indeed, why, on the solemn days of great feasts—which ought to be spent entirely in God’s praise—do they summon to their tables jesters, dancers, enchanters, and singers of shameful songs; feast and keep festival with them all day and night; and afterward reward them with great gifts, which they seize from ecclesiastical benefices and from the offerings of the poor, in order surely to sacrifice to demons? For what are such performers except heralds—and, so to speak, apostles—of demons, through whose mouths and gestures they do not cease to plunder miserable souls?

What is spoken in God’s Church indeed weighs upon and wearies hearers. It is burdensome to those who make offerings at Christ’s altars; even during the solemnities of the Mass they cannot restrain their tongues from idle chatter for the space of one hour. Their whole mind burns and pants to be outside, at the court of demons and gatherings of performers, where they are lavish in offerings and, with utter silence and entire desire, attentive—as has been said—to that diabolical preaching.

Perhaps the devil considers even this too little—that they perform such things outside the sacred places of basilicas—unless he brings stage obscenities into the Church of God itself. Alas for the pain! He dares it; and, shame upon us, accomplishes it. With every kind of shamefulness now introduced everywhere, temples are dedicated to demons before Christ’s very altars through the gatherings of festivals; and under a pretext of religion and prayer, when men and women come together from every side to indulge lust freely, the vigils of Venus are celebrated.

## Book Three

[Col. 1211]

[Col. 1211B] Since the examination of every controversy consists either in written authority or in reasoning, so that it may be resolved by these means—if it is of a kind that admits of resolution—we have thought it necessary first to bring forward, from the writings of eminent sages, authorities supporting our faith; then it remains to buttress those authorities themselves with reasoning, for the completion of our argument. This is especially necessary in matters in which they seem, not without some show of reason, to be attacked, lest the saying of the comic poet perhaps be thrown at us: “This man needs an advocate, whom I am preparing as my defender.”

Blessed Augustine likewise, in chapter 1 [Book I, chapter 2] of *On the Morals of the Church against the Manichaeans*, holds that authority ought to precede reason, saying: “The order of nature is indeed such that, when we say something, authority precedes reason. For a reason cannot appear weak when, after it has been given, it subsequently takes up the authority by which it is strengthened.” It remains, therefore, that after the foundation of authorities we should add the supports of reasoning, especially so that the wordiness of Christ’s enemies may not insult our simplicity. When they have entangled certain unlearned or less educated Christians in the snares of their arguments, they claim this as their highest glory. It is not enough for them to perish alone unless they also bury others with their errors—following, that is, the custom of the Jews, of whom Truth says that they “travel sea and land to make one proselyte” (Matt. 23:15).

But as the foundation, as it were, of all good things, [Col. 1211D] we set down faith in the Holy Trinity, so that the beginning of all good may be drawn from contemplation of the divine nature itself. Whoever can undermine this foundation leaves nothing fruitful even among those things [which] are to be built upon it. Hence we have taken care first to oppose to so great a danger both authority and the shield of reasoning, trusting in him who strengthens his own, saying: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not consider how or what you shall speak; for in that hour what you shall speak will be given to you” (Matt. 10:19). Trusting in his help, the little David slew the huge and swelling Goliath with Goliath’s own sword.

And so we too, with the very sword of human reasonings by which both philosophers and heretics attack us—[Note: [Col. 1211] A word seems to be missing here, such as “we may gird ourselves” or “we may use [it].”]—turn their force back against them. For many great heralds of Antichrist are already crying out, through whom the enemy of the human race attempts to undermine faith, the foundation of all good things. The mouths of such persons were once stopped by miracles, when they fought with words but the holy Fathers with deeds. Miracles have passed away; [Col. 1212C] malice has increased; deceit, unbridled, now arms its members against truth. One course remains: since we cannot fight by deeds, let us fight by words, trusting in Truth itself, which strengthens us, saying: “Lay it up in your hearts not to prepare beforehand how you shall answer; for I will give you a mouth and wisdom which all your adversaries will not be able to resist or gainsay” (Luke 21:14).

Above all Christ’s enemies—heretics, Jews, and Gentiles alike—those who profess dialectic, or the importunate tribe of sophists, investigate the faith of the Holy Trinity more subtly and strive to assail it more sharply. Plato mockingly judges such men happy because of their host of words and flood of discourse. [Col. 1212D] Relying on the practice of argument, we know what they murmur when they are not given an opportunity openly to chatter [read: “is given to them”]. These, I say, are not users of an art but abusers of it. For we condemn not the knowledge of dialectic, nor of any liberal art, but the deceitfulness of sophistry—especially since, as we have recalled above, this art is highly commended and preferred to the others by the judgment of the holy Fathers as well.

This philosophy is like a very sharp sword: a tyrant uses it recklessly for destruction, but for defence and according to the intention of those using it, it can both help greatly and harm greatly. We know that by sound arguments the Peripatetics, whom we now call dialecticians, suppressed some great heresies both of the Stoics and of the Epicureans. Such is the doctrine against which they argue with the Stoics and establish with very powerful arguments: although God has foreseen everything from eternity, and his providence cannot at all be deceived, nevertheless not everything therefore happens by necessity, lest human freedom of choice perish. Otherwise, says Aristotle, prince of the Peripatetics, in Book I of *On Interpretation*, “there will be no need to deliberate or to transact business.” We reserve a more suitable discussion of free choice for another place.

Nor do we grant that any knowledge is evil, even knowledge concerning evil. Such knowledge cannot be lacking to a just person—not so that he may do evil, but so that he may guard against an evil known beforehand; for, as Boethius testifies, he could not avoid it if he did not know it. It is not evil to know how to deceive or commit adultery, but to commit these acts; for knowledge of a thing whose action is most wicked is good. No one sins by knowing sin, but by committing it. If any knowledge were evil, then it would also be evil to know certain things; and God, who knows all things, could no longer be acquitted of evil. For in him alone is the fullness of all knowledge, and every kind of knowledge is his gift. Knowledge is the comprehension of the truth of things that exist; and that person truly discerns all things for whom even those things which do not exist stand, as it were, present before him. Hence, when the gifts of his Spirit are enumerated, that Spirit himself is called the Spirit of knowledge.

But just as knowledge even of evil is good, being necessary in order to avoid evil, so it is evident that even the power to do evil is good and necessary for earning merit. For if we could not sin, we would earn no merit by not sinning; and no reward is owed for acts done under compulsion to one who does not possess free choice. On the contrary, as the prophet says: “He who was able to transgress and did not transgress, to do evil and did not do it—therefore his good things are established in the Lord” (Ecclus. 31:10).

From these considerations it is clear that no knowledge or power is evil, however evil their exercises may be, since God grants every kind of knowledge and orders every power. Concerning the power of the most wicked Pilate against himself he also said: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given you from above” (John 19:11). Therefore we approve branches of knowledge, but resist the deceptions of those who abuse them. For, as Tully testifies, those err very seriously who blame a branch of knowledge because of a human vice. Thus, when teaching in his *Rhetoric* about criticizing arguments, he says among other things: “No part of argumentation will be suited to its purpose if a subject is criticized because of a man’s vice—for example, if someone should criticize learning because of the faults of a learned man.”

I think that none educated in sacred literature is unaware that, in sacred doctrine, spiritual men have advanced more through the pursuit of knowledge itself than through religious merit; and that the greater a saint’s knowledge of secular literature before conversion, the more powerful he was after conversion in sacred learning. The apostle Paul, although he may not seem greater in merit than Peter; Augustine the confessor, than Martin—yet after conversion each had a greater grace in teaching than the other, in proportion as he had formerly possessed greater literary learning. For this reason especially I judge that the study of secular literature also is commended by divine dispensation: not only because of the usefulness it contains, but lest it appear alien to God’s gifts if it were directed to no beneficial purpose.

Yet we know that the Apostle said: “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1), that is, it produces pride. But by this very fact it is proved good, since it gives self-awareness that may turn to the evil of pride. For just as there are certain good things that arise only from evil, so there are certain evils that draw their origin from good. Repentance, or satisfaction by amendment, though good, so accompanies an evil deed that it can arise only from it. Conversely, pride and envy, though most evil, take their beginning only from good things. No one is puffed up with pride except from goods which he knows he possesses, and no one envies another except on account of that person’s goods.

Thus that Lucifer who rose in the morning was all the more inclined to pride because he surpassed the other angelic spirits in the brightness of wisdom or knowledge. Yet wisdom or knowledge of the natures of things, which he had received from God, ought not therefore to be called evil, though in his pride he used it badly. So too, when anyone is proud of his philosophy or learning, we ought not blame knowledge itself because of the accompanying vice. Each thing should be weighed in itself, lest by acting without discrimination we incur that prophetic curse: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good, who put light for darkness and darkness for light!” (Isa. 5:20).

[Col. 1214D] Let these remarks suffice against those who seek comfort for their own ignorance. When they see us introduce examples or comparisons from philosophical teachings, in order to make what we intend clearer, they immediately protest as though the natures of things created by God were hostile to sacred faith and divine reasoning. Yet philosophers themselves have received from God the greatest knowledge of these natures. Thus, when holy teachers investigate allegorical mysteries in the natures of animals or other things, they identify these natures in accordance with the statements of the philosophers themselves, saying that this or that is the nature of a particular thing, as writers on natural philosophy have handed down.

God delights so greatly in his own creation that he frequently wishes rather to be represented by the natures of things which he created than expressed in words which we have fabricated or devised; and he delights more in the likeness of things themselves than in the precise propriety of our words. Thus, for the beauty of eloquence, Scripture prefers to use the natures of things in accordance with some likeness in place of words, rather than to preserve the strict completeness of literal expression.

Therefore let no one presume to blame me if, in order to demonstrate our proposition, I introduce comparisons drawn either from ourselves or from philosophers, by which I may more easily explain what I desire. For it is written: “It is right to be taught even by an enemy.” And when we serve understanding, every possible care must be taken to make our study as easy as we can. Hence comes the counsel of blessed Augustine in Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*, where he sets forth and teaches the methods of Christian teaching: “The teacher,” he says, “does not concern himself with how eloquently he teaches, but with how clearly. Careful desire sometimes neglects more polished words; hence someone, discussing this kind of speech, said that it contains a certain careful negligence.”

Likewise: “What use is correctness of expression if it is not followed by the hearer’s understanding, since there is no reason at all for speaking if those whom we speak to, in order that they may understand, do not understand what we say? Therefore the teacher will avoid every word that does not teach.” Likewise: “It is a mark of distinguished character to love truth in words, not the words themselves. For what benefit is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish? Or what harm is a wooden one if it can, when we seek nothing but that what is shut should be opened?”

But just as we have no doubt that such criticism is utterly erroneous and irrational, so we declare the very great impiety of those who, by their own wickedness, cause God’s greatest gift—which they have received through the acquisition of knowledge—to be blamed and despised. They draw an undeserving and innocent art into partnership with their own guilt. Tully recalls that this had once happened to rhetoric at the very beginning of his *Rhetoric*; and we know that it occurs daily now with dialectic. For just as the skill of malicious orators had made rhetoric hateful to nearly all good men, because of the injuries frequently inflicted through it upon states, so the life and chatter of shameless students of dialectic have now rendered it contemptible to nearly all religious persons, while they greatly disturb God’s holy city, which is the Church.

While they strive by intolerable verbosity to acquire glory for themselves, their singular pride does not allow these wretches to perceive into what disgrace they bring the very art in which they glory. Against their shamelessness Tully likewise inveighs in the second book of *Rhetoric for Herennius*, when discussing the case of an ambiguous document:

> There are those who think that, for handling this case, the knowledge of ambiguities put forward by dialecticians is highly relevant. We, however, think that it is not only of no assistance but rather a very great hindrance. For they occupy themselves with all those ambiguities which cannot yield any interpretation on either side. Thus they are troublesome interrupters of another’s speech, and interpreters of written text who are both hateful and obscure. While they wish to speak cautiously and promptly, they are found to be utterly childish. So, while they fear that they may say anything ambiguous, they cannot pronounce even their own names. When you wish, we shall refute their childish opinions by the soundest arguments. For the present, it was not irrelevant to give this warning, that we may despise this chattering discipline of childishness.

Nor did Aristotle himself, their greatest teacher, pass over the importunate antics of sophists. In the first book of *On Interpretation* he says: “And whatever other matters of this kind we determine against the sophistical importunities of arguments.”

The most salutary exhortation both of the apostle Paul and of blessed Ambrose, contained in Book II of *On Faith* addressed to Emperor Gratian, agrees with these points: “It is written: ‘See that no one plunders you through philosophy and empty deception, according to human tradition and according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ’” (Col. 2:8). “For they place the whole force of their poisons in dialectical disputations, which by the judgment of philosophers are defined as having not the force of establishing, but the endeavor of destroying. [Col. 1216C] But God was not pleased to save his people through dialectic. For the kingdom of God is in the simplicity of faith, not in contention of speech.”

The replies of Pope Adrian to certain objections addressed to Charles, chapter 49, recall this judgment of blessed Ambrose in the same exhortation: “Heretics place the whole force of their poisons in dialectical disputation, which by the judgment of philosophers is defined as having not the force of establishing, but the endeavor of destroying,” etc. Likewise: “Take arguments away from here, where faith is sought.” [Note: [Col. 1215D] Read, as in Ambrose: “where faith is sought.”] “Even in its own schools let dialectic now be silent. I do not ask what philosophers say; I ask what they do. They alone have remained in their schools. See how faith outweighs arguments. Those who argue copiously are daily abandoned by their companions; those who believe simply increase daily. Philosophers are not believed; fishermen are believed. Dialecticians are not believed; tax collectors are believed. Those men bound the world with pleasures and delights; these stripped the world bare by fasts and sufferings. Thus injury has now begun to attract more people there than pleasure.”

Likewise, concerning the Arians: “Did they not derive the whole coloration of their impiety from philosophy?” And the Apostle says to the Corinthians: “If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God” (1 Cor. 11:16). Writing his first Epistle to Timothy, he carefully warns him at the end to avoid, with all diligence, unusual words as profane things and the snares of falsely named knowledge, through which, he says, some have already fallen away from faith: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of language and oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some professing have fallen away from concerning the faith” (1 Tim. 6:20).

To the same man, in the second epistle: “Remind them of these things [variant: *commone*, ‘warn’], testifying before God: do not contend about words; it is useful for nothing except the ruin of the hearers. But avoid profane and empty talk, for it advances greatly toward impiety, and their speech spreads like cancer” (2 Tim. 2:14). Likewise: “Flee youthful desires, but pursue justice, faith, love, and peace with those who call upon God from a pure heart. Avoid foolish and undisciplined questions, knowing that they generate quarrels. But the servant of God ought not to quarrel, but to be gentle toward all, teachable, patient, correcting with meekness those who resist” (ibid., 22–25). Hence Truth also warns us to avoid those whom we see to be obstinate and importunate wanderers, saying: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest perhaps they trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart” (Matt. 7:6).

But concerning those whom we see devoted to the inquiry by which truth is to be perceived, so that we should endeavor to satisfy them by reasons, the apostle Peter exhorts us, saying: “Sanctify the Lord Christ, being always prepared to give satisfaction to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the faith and hope that are in you” (1 Pet. 3:15). And his fellow apostle Paul says: “Let your speech be seasoned with salt in grace, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. 4:6).

For it is one thing to seek truth by conferring together, another to contend in disputation for display. The former is a devoted pursuit directed to edification; the latter an impulse of pride directed to self-glorification. There we strive to acquire knowledge that we do not possess; here we display knowledge which we trust that we possess. The more excellent a good knowledge is, the more readily it draws one toward pride, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Knowledge puffs up; love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1).

Thus that great apostate angel, whom the prophet set above the others because of his greater penetration in understanding the natures of things, and compared to Lucifer because of the excessive illumination of his knowledge—“You, Lucifer, who rose in the morning,” says the prophet, etc. (Isa. 14:12)—the greater the wisdom with which he saw himself endowed, the more readily and deeply he swelled with pride; and, cast down, he fell more disastrously. The dialecticians of our time, if I am not mistaken, claim his image for themselves among all philosophers, as though they had acquired the more eminent philosophy because it is the more wordy.

These men, I say, are as hostile to God as they are ungrateful to men, as it is written: “A talkative man shall not be directed upon the earth,” etc. (Ps. 139:12). And Boethius says: “If a man is arrogant, he is hateful.” For everyone becomes hateful through arrogance. This beginning of every sin immediately expelled the first angel, as we have said, from the sight of his Creator—that is, from true blessedness. As it made him an apostate, so it still wins many others for him through heresy.

For ignorance does not make a heretic, but pride: namely, when someone, desiring to make a name for himself by some novelty, glories in putting forward something unusual and strives importunately to defend it against everyone, so that he may appear superior to all, or so that, if his opinion is refuted, he may not be thought inferior to others. Hence Augustine, carefully defining a heretic in *On the Usefulness of Believing*, says: “A heretic, in my opinion, is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage—especially glory and his own preeminence—either produces or follows false and novel opinions.”

The same author says in Book VIII of *The City of God*: “Those who hold something wrong in the Church, if, after correction, they resist obstinately and are unwilling to amend their deadly doctrines but persist in defending them, become heretics.” Likewise, in his letter to Optatus: “If an assertion of falsehood concerning the soul is put forward, the falsehood makes one a liar, and the importunate defence of falsehood makes one a heretic.” Again, commenting on Genesis: “Heretics exist for no other reason than that, not rightly understanding the canonical Scriptures, they stubbornly assert their own false opinions against the truth of those Scriptures.”

Professors of dialectic are especially prone to be drawn into this, in proportion as they think themselves more fully armed with arguments; and the more confidently they presume freely either to defend or to attack whatever they please. Their arrogance is so great that they think nothing exists which cannot be comprehended or expounded by their petty reasonings. Despising all authorities, they glory in trusting only themselves. For since they admit only what their own reason persuades them, they assuredly rest content with themselves alone, as though they possessed eyes which had never known dimness.

Against such persons Augustine says in his exposition of Psalm 39: “Are you not found proud when you say, ‘First let me see, and then I will believe’?” What is astonishing is that ignorance arises for them from knowledge, so that virtue produces its opposite. Pride accompanies knowledge, and blindness accompanies pride: when a man attributes to himself the greatest gift which he has received from God, he loses the gift by failing to acknowledge its giver. Later he becomes worse in proportion as, having previously been made better, he disdained to give thanks to his maker. For it is just that more should be required from the person to whom more has been entrusted.

Seeing the just blinding of such persons, and the shame of their corrupt understanding and life, the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened . . . For, claiming to be wise, they became fools . . . Therefore God gave them up to disgraceful passions,” etc. (Rom. 1:21–26). And the Psalmist says of contentious and proud people of this kind, who regard themselves as teachers and leaders of others: “Contempt was poured out upon princes, and he caused them to wander in a trackless place and not in a way” (Ps. 106:40).

A heretic, as they say, is interpreted as “chosen,” because no one becomes a heretic unless the estimation born of his own pride places him above others, so that he is now ashamed to appear in communion with them. Hence Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book IV, chapter 3: “Heresy is called in Greek from choice, because each person chooses for himself what seems better to him.” As if he were saying: they follow not God’s Spirit but their own. Moreover, every proud person must be contentious just as he is impatient, once anyone begins in any way to oppose him. And this is precisely the contention which, as we have recalled above, makes heretics.

Hence Gennadius, *On the Orthodox Faith and Ecclesiastical Doctrines*, chapter 7, says: “However a person may hold an opinion, he is not a heretic unless he becomes a heretic through contentiousness.” The same author, Book IV of *On the One Baptism*: “I call him just, not heretical, unless he prefers to resist a doctrine plainly set before him of the Catholic faith and chooses [read: ‘has chosen’] what he had held.” The Psalmist refers to such chosen persons when he says: “I will not share with their chosen ones” (Ps. 140:4). The Apostle also follows this judgment when he writes to Titus: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction, knowing that such a one is subverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3:10). For he prepares himself more for contention than for instruction, desires his own glory more than salvation, and recognizes in himself a fitting occasion for contention; his own conscience accuses him by its own judgment.

Let those unbridled and untamed wanderers consider these things. Raising the horn of singular pride, they rush even against their Creator and “set their mouth against heaven.” The one who says, “Save me from the lion’s mouth, and my humility from the horns of unicorns” (Ps. 21:22), prays that the simplicity of believers may be protected from their deceptions. The Apostle also warns us most earnestly to beware of them—that is, to guard against their deceits—saying: “See that no one deceives you through empty philosophy according to the elements of the world” (Col. 2:8). It is as though he said: Guard yourselves against the arguments of those who presume to reason from bodies composed of elements to the singular and incorporeal nature of Divinity—not so much to perceive truth as to display their philosophy. Therefore they rise not at all to knowledge of it, for God always resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.

Of such persons it is written in Proverbs: “Every scoffer is an abomination to the Lord, but his conversation is with the simple” (Prov. 3:32). “He himself will mock scoffers, and gives his grace to the meek.” Hence Truth itself says: “I confess to you, Father of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25). And the Apostle says: “It is written: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the prudence of the prudent’” (1 Cor. 1:19). Likewise: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For since the world did not know God through wisdom in God’s wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save believers” (ibid., 20).

And after some words: “Consider your calling, brethren: not many wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and he chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and the ignoble and despised things of the world he chose, and those things which are not, to destroy those which are, so that no flesh may glory in his presence; that, as it is written, ‘Let him who glories glory in the Lord’” (ibid., 26). Therefore, in the same Epistle, he adds counsel concerning the way of instruction, which must be undertaken through humility: “Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you seems to be wise in this age, let him become foolish so that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written: ‘I will catch the wise in their craftiness’” (1 Cor. 3:18). And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain. Therefore let no one glory in men” (ibid., 20). And shortly thereafter, attributing every good thing to divine grace: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (ibid., 4:7). Elsewhere: “Do not think proudly, but fear” (Rom. 11:20).

The Apostle also proves by a powerful analogy that even those things which concern the knowledge of God can be perceived only when he reveals them, and only by the pure in heart: “Who among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him?” (1 Cor. 2:11). So likewise, “no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.” Above all, no one can be taught even the smallest thing unless he inwardly enlightens us; unless he inwardly instructs the mind, the one who teaches outwardly strikes the air in vain. For when a teacher’s words are brought equally to the ears of different persons, why are they not equally understood by them, except because the inward teacher is at hand for some, but not at all for others—the teacher who teaches whom he wills even without sound?

Concerning the wisdom of this teacher, the Book of Wisdom itself says: “Think of the Lord with goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart; for he is found by those who do not test him, and appears to those who have faith in him. For perverse thoughts separate from God, because wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins” (Wis. 1:1–4). And the Apostle says: “The natural man does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). But, according to the Psalmist, “Good understanding belongs to all who do it” (Ps. 110:10), that is, to those who strive to fulfill in action what they rightly understand. Thus we are plainly taught that before God we advance more in understanding through the religious conduct of life than through subtlety of intellect. Otherwise the Lord would show that human talent pleased him more than holiness of life.

For the more we understand of God, the more we love him; and as understanding grows, the flame of love is kindled. Yet those who seem to us simple and unlearned, and therefore are intensely fervent, may be unable to express or expound as much as divine inspiration gives them in understanding. Would that those persons also considered this—those who rashly claim for themselves the title of teacher in the divine Page, while they do not amend their lives, and while they live carnally and foully. They falsely claim that a special understanding of divine enigmas has been revealed to them and heavenly secrets entrusted to them, as though they openly boasted that they were the temple of the Holy Spirit.

May pagan philosophers at least crush the shamelessness of these false Christians: they judged that the rule for knowing God must be acquired not by reasoning but rather by living well, and that one must strive for it by conduct rather than words. Thus Socrates, as we have already said, did not wish souls made impure by earthly desires to attempt divine matters. He saw them investigating the causes of things, which he believed existed only in God’s will; therefore he judged that one must strive to purify one’s life by good morals.

Augustine himself, mindful of this judgment, explained it in other words in Book I of his work on Genesis against the calumnies of the Manichaeans:

> To one who says, “Why did God make heaven and earth?” the answer must be: “Because he willed it.” For God’s will is the cause of heaven and earth, and is therefore greater than heaven and earth. But one who says, “Why did he will it?” seeks something greater than God’s will. Yet nothing greater can be found. If anyone desires to know God’s will, let him become God’s friend; for if he wished to know the will of a man whose friend he was not, everyone would mock his imprudence or folly. But one does not become God’s friend except through thoroughly purified morals and through that end of the commandment of which the Apostle says: “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:5)—“and if these men had it, they would not be heretics.”

How great Socrates’ reverence toward God was—so that he ascribed and attributed to Him all our goods, especially those belonging to the discernment by which truth is apprehended—he himself declares. Introduced as a speaker in Plato’s *Timaeus*, as we have also recalled above, he holds that all understanding and reasoning in investigating every truth must be sought from God by simple prayer; [Col. 1221D] so much so that he regards as mad and beyond expiation all who do not invoke divine aid in every right action. In this he openly declares that he can do nothing of himself, but only through the benefit of divine grace.

Let those who profess themselves philosophers at least listen to the counsel of philosophers. Let those who despise the saints listen to their teachers, so that, if they desire to understand God, they may be willing to prepare themselves for understanding by living well and to take up the way of humanity [read: humility], by which alone one approaches that loftiness of understanding—though one never reaches it while living in this mortal flesh. “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). Thus the Lord answered Moses, when he asked to see His face: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). For the vision of the Godhead itself will be the future blessedness, of which the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12). And elsewhere: “Into which angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12).

And when it is said, “Let the wicked person be taken away, lest he see the glory of God,” it means: lest he enjoy it by seeing; for to see is to enjoy. So great is the blessedness of that glory that no one can see it without at the same time experiencing it. Hence the Psalmist says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15). Then indeed will be fulfilled what the Wisdom of God itself promises, saying: “If anyone loves me, he will be loved by my Father, [Col. 1222B] and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14:21).

Unless God Himself reveals Himself, even then our nature will not suffice to see Him; nor should mortals, now filled with every filthiness of sins, attempt to comprehend the incomprehensible by their little reasonings—mortals who cannot by reason sufficiently discern even themselves, or the nature, however slight, of any creature. This too that greatest of sages, considering it in Ecclesiastes, declares when he says: “All things are difficult, and a human being cannot explain them all in speech” (Eccl. 1:8). Again, in the same work: “I, Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem, and I set my mind to seek and investigate wisely concerning all things done under the sun” (ibid., 12). Again: “And I applied my heart to know wisdom and to understand the travail [Col. 1222C] that goes on upon the earth, and I understood that a human being cannot discover the explanation of all God’s works that are done under the sun; and the more he labours in seeking, the less he will find; even if a wise person says that he knows, he will not be able to discover it. I tested all these things [Note: At Col. 1221D, the book of Ecclesiastes reads: ‘I treated/examined.’] in my heart, that I might understand carefully” (Eccl. 8:16–17; 9:1). And again: “I tested all things by wisdom. I said, ‘I shall become wise’; but it withdrew farther from me—far more than it was, and the deep profundity: who will find it?” (Eccl. 7:24–25).

As though that great sage openly confessed himself to be inadequate and weak in investigating the natures of all things and examining them by reason—he who had formerly thought himself sufficient for this and appeared endowed with the highest wisdom. [Col. 1222D]

Consult also Wisdom itself, and consider what it advises concerning this matter: that Wisdom, I mean, which is proclaimed by a certain supreme sage to be unique and greatest, so that it seems more divine than human. For in the Book of Wisdom it is written, with that supreme sage speaking thus: “God gave me to speak according to right judgment and to conceive worthy thoughts concerning the things given me . . . . . For He gave me true knowledge of the things that are, so that I might know the constitution of the world, the powers of the elements, the beginning, end, and middle of times, the changes of their alternations, and their ends [Note: At Col. 1222D, the Book of Wisdom reads: ‘the changes of times.’], the courses of the year and arrangements of the stars, the natures of animals, the rages [lit. ‘wraths’] of beasts, the force of winds [Col. 1223A], the thoughts of human beings, the varieties of shrubs, and the powers of roots. And whatever is hidden and unforeseen I learned” (Wis. 7:15–21).

See how great this wisdom is, and how far it surpasses every human understanding. Yet observe what it itself says in what follows: “The thoughts of mortals are timid, and our forethoughts uncertain. For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things; and we scarcely conjecture the things on earth, and discover with labour what lies before our eyes. But who will investigate the things in heaven?” (Wis. 9:14–16).

This was that greatest and most diligent investigator of nature, upon whom He who bestowed wisdom likewise bestowed incomparable riches, [Col. 1223B] peace, and uninterrupted security, lest any anxiety of necessity or pressure of dangers hinder his study. The third Book of Kings records this concerning his wisdom and learning:

> Solomon’s wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the Eastern peoples and of the Egyptians; and he was wiser than all human beings, and was renowned among all the nations round about. He also spoke three thousand parables, and his songs were five thousand. He discoursed concerning trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon even to the hyssop that grows out of the wall; and he treated of beasts, birds, creeping things, and fish. And people came from all nations to hear Solomon’s wisdom, and from every region of the earth. (3 Kings 4:30 [Col. 1223C])

And concerning his incomparable abundance of riches, among other things the same book records:

> All King Solomon’s drinking vessels were of silver, and all the furnishings of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold. There was no silver, nor was it accounted of any value in Solomon’s days. (3 Kings 10:21)

Again, shortly afterward:

> He caused silver to be as plentiful in Jerusalem as stones, and made cedars as numerous as the sycamores that grow in the plains. (3 Kings 10:27)

Wonderful indeed were Solomon’s riches, wonderful the works that he built; but more wonderful was the wisdom by which, while ruling a small kingdom, he amassed such things. Through the exorcisms which he discovered, or through certain hidden powers of natural things which he came to know, he is also said certainly to have exercised dominion even over demons. Thus Josephus relates in the eighth book of the *Jewish Antiquities*, declaring that he himself proved it by sight: namely, when a demon was drawn out through the nostrils of a man whom it was tormenting, after Solomon’s ring, under which was a root of Solomon, had been inserted into the man’s nostrils. [Col. 1223D]

Therefore, since one of such outstanding wisdom understands all things to be so difficult that they cannot in any way be explained in speech, as though he too cried out the philosophical saying, “All truth lies hidden,” consider, whoever you are, how great a presumption it is to examine by reason that which transcends all human things, and to refuse assent unless the things said [Col. 1224A] are manifest either to human sense or human reason. This is utterly to abolish faith and hope, since both are admittedly concerned with things not apparent. Hence Ambrose says: “If I am convinced by reason, I renounce faith.” And the Apostle says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Heb. 9:1). Elsewhere: “Hope that is seen is not hope. For what a person sees, why does he hope for it?” (Rom. 8:24).

From this it is clear that those people are the most wretched of all human beings: deprived both of faith and hope, they neither believe with the philosophers in the immortality of the soul nor await God as the rewarder of good deeds. They devote themselves wholly to sensory experience like cattle, assigning themselves the lot of cattle, which perish completely with the flesh and altogether die here. [Col. 1224B] They cannot be compelled to receive and believe these things either by sensory experiences or by human reasonings, but must be brought to them by authority alone. But if they assent on authority to matters which nevertheless cannot be satisfied by reason, why do they reject such things concerning God as have been confirmed by so many testimonies of such great sages?

We all know that in matters which can be examined by reason, the judgment of authority is unnecessary. This too ought sufficiently to serve as a reason: that He who far transcends all things in every respect exceeds the powers of human examination and understanding; and that what cannot be contained in a place cannot be comprehended by the human mind. What greater indignation should believers feel than to profess that they have a God whom human little reasonings [Col. 1224C] can comprehend or mortal speech can expound?

This did not escape the philosophers themselves. The greatest among them says in his *Timaeus*: “To find the maker and father of the universe is difficult; and, once found, to declare him worthily is impossible.” When he asserted that *nous* (νοῦς, intellect) was born from God, he did not presume to explain what he knew and professed to be beyond explanation; but concerning that ineffable generation he said only as much as the divine will permitted. Macrobius also testifies that he did not dare to say what God is, knowing only this concerning Him: that human beings cannot know what He is like. Nor is He fully known even by those heavenly spirits endowed with greater wisdom. Hence Augustine says in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*: “The cherubim and seraphim do not wholly comprehend what God is, because no one knows the Father except the Son.”

Hermes too, after speaking above concerning the Son of God, added: “Whose name cannot be narrated by a human mouth.” Hence he rightly called God “Unknown,” as though He were understood or believed by few—even the greatest sages—and did not enter into the common opinion of the multitude. According to Macrobius, they did not dare to erect even an image of Him. According to the philosophers, He can be contemplated only by the pure in heart and by purified minds. Lucan likewise says, “Judaea of the uncertain God,” that is, the hidden and unknown God. The great philosopher Dionysius the Areopagite is read to have pointed out to the Apostle Paul at Athens, that city outstanding in learning, [Col. 1225A] an altar of this unknown God.

This altar, unless I am mistaken, is that altar of mercy on which suppliants offered no sacrifice except the sacrifice of the Brahmans—that is, prayers and tears. Statius too mentions this altar in Book XII, saying:

> In the midst of the city stood an altar, yielded to no mighty power;  
> Kindly Clemency had established there an altar, the seat of the gentle gods, etc.

What will professors of dialectic answer to these things, if they attempt to examine by reason what their foremost teachers declare impossible to explain? Will they ridicule their teachers because they did not keep silent about the truth inspired in them by God, though they themselves profess that it cannot be expounded? Their teachers held it all the more venerable because it more fully surpasses every capacity of human [Col. 1225B] understanding. They were not ashamed to confess that they heard, or even spoke, many things which they professed true but could not adequately explain.

Indeed, as we have recalled above, they so delighted in the obscurity of riddles that even in matters which they could readily explain they drew a veil of letters over them, lest naked and open truth should be despised because it was easily understood. Hence Macrobius, in support of the philosophers’ mystical modes of speech, adduces this story [Note: Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, I.2]: how divine powers appeared angry in a dream to the philosopher Numenius; and how the Eleusinian goddesses themselves appeared to him dressed as prostitutes, standing before a brothel and complaining that he had violently dragged them from the sanctuary of chastity, because [Col. 1225C] he had interpreted them in a plain exposition rather than, like others, speaking of them mystically and obscurely.

Would that these people too, who profess themselves philosophers, might at least be checked in their presumption by a dream, so that they would not deny the incomprehensible majesty of the true and highest Godhead unless they heard it openly analyzed! But perhaps they say: “What point is there in someone’s calling something true if he himself cannot explain it so that it may be understood?” I answer: very much. For when something is heard concerning God that is not understood, it arouses the hearer to inquiry; and this would not happen unless it were heard. Inquiry, moreover, readily produces understanding if devotion is present, for God may deign to reveal Himself to such a person. And often what is said by divine inspiration or accomplished by divine action is not done for the benefit of those through whom it is done, but is intended for the benefit of others, as we recalled above concerning miracles. Thus the grace of speaking is given to some, while understanding is reserved for others, until [Col. 1226A] this is needed according to the counsel of divine providence and the sincere devotion of certain people has merited it through prayer and good works.

Meanwhile, while reason remains hidden, authority will suffice; and let that most familiar and weighty proposition concerning the force of authority, handed down by philosophers in the very body of the art, be maintained: “One ought not to contradict what appears true to all people, or to most people, or to the learned.”

[Note: At Col. 1226, Migne prints the following paragraph in parallel with the passage “he himself cannot … done through whom” in the preceding paragraph.]

Gregory, in the *Pastoral Rule*:

> There are some who, unwilling to be thought dull, often exert themselves beyond necessity in certain inquiries and are deceived by excessive subtlety. Hence it is here also added: “with a large or crooked nose.” For a large and crooked nose is an immoderate subtlety of discernment; when it has grown beyond what is fitting, it itself confounds the rectitude of its action.

Therefore one should beneficially believe what cannot be explained, especially since what human weakness can expound should not be regarded as something great, nor should what we accept concerning manifest things under compulsion of human reason be counted as faith. Before God there is no merit in a matter where one believes not God speaking in the saints, [Col. 1226B] but human little reasonings, which frequently deceive and can scarcely be recognized as reasonings when they are such.

Hence Gregory says in Homily 26 on the Gospels: “We must know that if a divine operation is comprehended by reason, it is not wonderful; and faith has no merit when human reason furnishes proof.” To this belongs Ambrose’s counsel in *On Faith to the Emperor Gratian*, written in these words:

> It is impossible for me to know the secret of the generation; it is above powers, above angels, above cherubim, above seraphim, above every understanding. It is not permitted to search the heavenly mysteries; it is permitted to know that He was born, but not permitted to investigate how.

Again he says: “We are commanded to believe, not permitted to investigate.” And again he adds: “Not even angels could comprehend the mystery of the Father.”

Hence also blessed Augustine, writing *On Faith in the Creed* to Pope Laurence, says among other things: “The prophet says: ‘Unless you believe, you will not understand’” (Isa. 7:9). Again in the same work: “Do not wish to investigate how God the Father begot the Son, lest you intrude too curiously into the secret of this depth, lest perhaps, while obstinately searching out the splendour of inaccessible light, you lose even the slight sight itself which has been granted to mortals by divine gift.” Hence too comes the sage’s warning—or counsel—“The investigator of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25:27).

And Jerome, in Book VI on Jeremiah: “What the Vulgate edition intended [Col. 1226D] in this place I could say, and find some meaning, if it were not sacrilege to argue concerning God’s words by human understanding.” Again Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*: “When a matter of the greatest obscurity is disputed without the assistance of certain and clear evidences from the divine Scriptures, human presumption ought to restrain itself, doing nothing by inclining to one side or the other.”

Finally, I think this should be put to them: perhaps such people wish to say that they reject our faith not because it cannot be proved or expounded, but rather because it cannot be defended, since plainly manifest arguments do not permit it to stand. I think they should be asked [Col. 1227A] what they think of their own teachers, who taught this and did not discover it to be false. We know that from Boethius alone has been handed down to us the instruction in all the arguments we now employ, and that we have learned from him the force of every argument. We know also that he carefully and philosophically discussed the faith of the Trinity according to the distinction of the ten categories. They will accuse the very teacher of arguments and say that he erred in the arguments which they nevertheless boast that they learned from him. Did the teacher fail to notice what the disciples notice: namely, by what arguments what he maintained could be attacked?

I pardon the manifest shamelessness of such people, however much those who do not know how to spare their own may now disparage us, provided that they do not disturb the simplicity of believers or draw others into their own pit by the same snares of sophisms by which they themselves have already been caught. To prevent this, one remedy remains to be sought from the Lord against this pestilence: that He Himself may scatter the devices of those who frequently attempt to demolish His true temple with the battering-ram of their arguments.

[Note: At Col. 1227, Migne prints the following paragraph in parallel with the passage “we have learned from him … disciples, namely” in the preceding paragraph.]

Augustine, Book II *Against Maximinus*:

> I do not know, cannot, and am not sufficient to distinguish between that generation and this procession; for both that and this are ineffable. As the prophet says concerning the Son: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8). Thus it may most truly be said concerning the Holy Spirit: “Who shall declare his procession?”

[Col. 1227C] Therefore, since the troublesome importunity of such fault-finders can be restrained neither by the authority of saints nor by that of philosophers unless human reasonings are brought against those who attack with human reasonings, we have decided to answer fools according to their folly and to shatter their attacks from the very arts by which they attack us. For David, though small and relying on divine aid, slew the enormous and swollen Goliath with his own sword. And let us likewise turn back upon them that same sword of dialectic by which, emboldened, they strive to attack our simplicity; let us in the Lord scatter their strength and the battering-ram of their arguments, so that they may no longer dare to attack the simplicity of believers [Col. 1227D] after they have been refuted in those matters in which it seems especially impossible to them to give an answer: namely, the distinction of persons within the one, utterly indivisible and simple divine substance, and the generation of the Word or procession of the Spirit.

We do not promise to teach the truth concerning this, for we believe that no one, including ourselves, is adequate for that. But we wish at least to propose something plausible, close to human reason, and not contrary to sacred faith, against those who boast that they attack faith with human reasonings and care for no reasonings except the human ones which they know. They easily find many supporters, since almost all people are animal and very few spiritual. It is enough for us in whatever way to scatter the strength of our greatest enemies, especially since we cannot do so otherwise than by bringing forward from their own arts the reasonings that they know.

Far be it from us to believe that God—who makes good use even of evils—does not also rightly order all the arts, which are His gifts, [Col. 1228B] so that these too may serve His majesty, however wickedly perverse people misuse them! Hence blessed Augustine . . . . . . . . Church teachers declare that even secular arts, especially dialectic itself, are exceedingly necessary for sacred Scripture.

Having made these preliminary remarks against our adversaries, let us hasten to the subject, first recalling and establishing this point: lest, if reason should grow dim in so great an obscurity—a matter perceived more by religion than by intellect—or if our small capacity should not suffice for so many and such exceedingly subtle inquiries, or should even be overcome and yield, they should on that account, I say, presume to blame or criticize our faith, which is not thereby any less valid in itself if someone fails in expounding it. Nor should anyone charge me with presumption if I do not complete what I have undertaken; rather, let him pardon the devout will, which suffices before God if ability is lacking.

Whatever, therefore, we shall discuss concerning this most lofty philosophy, [Col. 1228D] we profess to be a shadow, not the truth; and, as it were, a certain likeness, not the thing itself. The Lord knows what is true; but I think that I shall state what is plausible and most consonant with the philosophical reasonings by which the faith is attacked. If, indeed, because my faults deserve it, I should depart—may it never be!—from Catholic understanding or expression, may He forgive me who judges works by their intention; for I am always prepared to make every satisfaction concerning statements that must be corrected or deleted whenever one of the faithful corrects me either by the force of reason or by the authority of Scripture.

For I know what is written: “The righteous person shall correct me in mercy and rebuke me, but the oil of the sinner shall not anoint [Col. 1229A] my head” (Ps. 140:5). And in Proverbs: “The reproof of discipline is the way of life; but whoever hates reproofs is foolish” (Prov. 6:23; 12:1). Again: “Whoever keeps reproofs will become wiser, and whoever hates reproofs will die” (Prov. 15:5–9). Again: “A pestilent person does not love one who reproves him; but if you reprove a wise person, he will understand instruction” (Prov. 15:12; 19:25). Again: “Sudden destruction shall come upon the person who despises one who reproves him with a stiff neck” (Prov. 29:1).

[Note: At Col. 1228, Migne prints the following paragraph in parallel with the passage “almost all people are animal … perceived more by religion” in the preceding paragraph.]

[Note: At Col. 1227: Thus in the manuscript; but these words seem to be to be placed after Augustine’s words cited above.] He also instructs us by his own example that sometimes, when divine matters are under discussion, one must have recourse to arguments when we are debating with people who do not admit sacred authorities. Hence in chapter 11 of *On the Morals of the Church against the Manichaeans*, he says:

> From what, then, shall I begin: authority or reason? The order of nature is such that, when we learn something, authority precedes reason. For reason may seem weak, and once it has been supplied, it then receives authority by which it may be strengthened. But since we have to deal with people who think, speak, and act in every respect contrary to order, and whose chief assertion is simply that reason must first be supplied, I shall accommodate myself to them. I shall undertake what I confess is faulty in disputation. Let us therefore seek the reason by which human beings ought to live, etc.

First, then, we must set forth the theme of our whole discussion and briefly state the sum of the faith: namely, the unity of the divine substance and the Trinity of persons who are in God—or rather, are the one God. Then we shall set forth objections to what has been proposed, [Col. 1229B] and finally replies to the objections.

The religion of the Christian faith holds, holds unchangeably, believes beneficially, asserts firmly, and professes truly that the one God is three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. He is one God only, I say, and in no way several gods; one Creator of all visible and invisible things [read: “of all things, visible and invisible”], one principle and one good, one disposer and Lord of all, one eternal being, one omnipotent being, one immeasurable being. In every respect it proclaims and believes the singularity of unity alone, except for the distinction of the three persons—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Only in these persons [Col. 1229C] does it profess plurality, multiplicity, or diversity; in all other respects, as has been said, it preserves unity. For we call three persons distinct from one another by their properties: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; but not three gods or lords. Thus we profess unity in every respect, except for the multiplicity of persons. Yet none of these persons is any of the others, and each is in itself fully God and Lord. Thus, according to the assertion of blessed Jerome, writing *On Faith* to Pope Damasus, apart from terms indicating the property of the persons, whatever is said of one person may most fittingly be understood of all three.

For the Father is not the Son [Col. 1229D] or the Holy Spirit, nor is He Himself the Holy Spirit. But the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Spirit is God. Nevertheless, they are not therefore three gods or several gods; rather, one God alone exists eternally and unchangeably in three persons. Likewise, He is one Creator and one Lord, and so in all other matters. It makes no difference to the statement of truth whether we call the one God the individual three persons or the three together; for each of the three is equally the one and same God with the other two, and the three together—that is, the Trinity itself—is one God, one Lord, and so forth.

Therefore these three persons are one and the same substance altogether, an utterly indivisible and simple essence: one power without qualification, one glory, one majesty, one reason, one will, the same undivided operation. In every respect they are one and the same, except as concerns the difference of their properties, by which they remain perpetually distinct from one another, so that the property of one person is never transferred into another person or shared by another person; otherwise it would not be a property but a common possession.

It is proper to the Father to exist from Himself alone and not from another, and eternally to beget, or to have begotten, a Son coeternal with Himself. It is proper to the Son eternally to be begotten, or to have been begotten, from the Father alone. [Note: At Col. 1229, the words enclosed in brackets are absent from the manuscript but must necessarily be restored: “It is proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed from Father and Son.”] The Holy Spirit is neither created, made, nor begotten, but proceeds only. [Col. 1230B] This, then, is the distinction of the three persons from one another according to the properties of each.

Some things are thus said of God that they can be said of only one of the three persons and not of more than one; again, some can be said of several persons, both separately and jointly—that is, of each of them individually and of them together; while some are said only jointly. For example, “Father,” “begetting,” and “unbegotten” are said of the Father alone. Although the Holy Spirit too, since He is not begotten, is likewise unbegotten, we nevertheless do not customarily call Him “unbegotten,” but the Father alone. Thus in this place “unbegotten” means that He does not exist from another, as we have stated in the preceding little book. [Col. 1230C]
