There is therefore here a difference between saying “unbegotten” and saying “not begotten,” just as there is some difference between saying “unjust” and “not just.” For whatever is unjust must be not just, but not conversely. A stone, for example, is not just, just as it is not rational; yet it is not called unjust or irrational. For the latter terms are infinite or negative names; the former are privative.

Augustine, however, in Book V of *On the Trinity*, uses the term “unbegotten” negatively, for “not begotten,” where, in chapter 7, he discusses the divine persons in these words:

> Therefore, when “unbegotten” is said, this is shown: that He is not the Son. “Begotten” and “unbegotten” are suitably said; but “Son” is said in Latin, whereas customary speech does not permit one to say “non-son.” Yet nothing is taken away from the understanding if one says “not Son”; just as, if “not begotten” is said in place of “unbegotten,” nothing else is said.

Again:

> Therefore we shall no longer say “unbegotten,” although it can be said in Latin; but in its place let us say “not begotten,” which has the same force. We say nothing else than “not Son.”

Again:

> What indeed is “unbegotten” but “not begotten”? For just as “begotten” is not said with reference to itself, but because it is from the Father, so, when “unbegotten” is said, it is not said with reference to itself, but shows that it is not from a begetter.

From these passages it is clear that Augustine here uses “unbegotten” broadly for “not begotten,” unless perhaps a careful reader should turn this toward a hypothesis based on concession rather than an assertion of truth: so that, as we have already maintained above, “Father,” “begetting,” and “unbegotten” may be said only of the Father; but not “not begotten” of the Son alone [Note: At Col. 1231, something seems to be missing here; the sense requires: “likewise ‘Son’ and ‘begotten’ of the Son alone,” or something similar.]; and “Holy Spirit,” or “proceeding from Father and Son,” only of the Holy Spirit.

But “God,” “Lord,” “Creator,” “omnipotent,” “immeasurable,” “eternal,” “principle,” “life,” “light,” and whatever pertains to the dignity of the divine nature rather than to the signification of the persons, must be said both of the individual persons and of them together. “Trinity,” however, is said only of the three persons together and jointly, not separately of one of them, or of two by themselves, but only of all three. [Col. 1231B] For the Father is not the Trinity—that is, the three persons together—though the Trinity itself is one God and the Father Himself is God; yet the Father is not therefore the Trinity. Likewise neither the Son nor the Holy Spirit can be called the Trinity, but each is only one person in the Trinity.

“Father,” therefore, “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” are the proper names of the individual persons; “Trinity” is the proper name of the three together; while “God,” “Lord,” and the other terms set above are common alike to the individual persons and to the whole Trinity. Yet there is one name common to the individual persons and not to them together: namely, the name “person,” which you will not find in the other cases. It is therefore no wonder if this name alone possesses this solitary feature: that it alone among the common names of the persons is expressed in the plural. [Col. 1231C]

For we say “several persons,” because we proclaim three persons, but not “several gods” or “several lords,” though each of the three persons is in itself God and Lord, and no one person is another. Thus several persons are spoken of because of the diversity of properties, which we assigned above to the individual persons. But if we were to say several gods or lords—or likewise express in the plural the other names which are said of God more substantially than relatively, that is, with reference to Himself and not to another, such as “great” and “good”—we would imply a multiplicity of different things and a number of essentially different substances, and would thereby declare each to be God and Lord, great or good.

Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book V, chapter 8:

> Therefore let us especially hold this: whatever is said of the divine sublimity in reference to itself is said substantially; but what is said in relation to something is said not substantially but relatively. And the same substance has such force in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that whatever is said of the individual persons in reference to themselves is understood not in the plural in the highest reality, but in the singular.

Again:

> Therefore whatever is said of God in reference to Himself is said personally of each individual person and together of the Trinity itself, not in the plural but in the singular. For in God, being is not one thing and being great another; rather, for Him, to be is the same as to be great. Therefore, [Col. 1232A] just as we do not say three essences, so we do not say three magnitudes.

For in the individual persons there is only one and the same thing: one utterly indivisible substance and altogether simple essence, in which are the three properties according to which the diversity of persons exists. There is no multiplicity in the number of things, since there is only one single thing, utterly indivisible. Hence we call the Trinity holy and indivisible, since in it there is no multiplicity of things but only diversity of properties. It is therefore clear that the three persons are wholly equal to one another, just as they are coeternal with one another, because there can be no difference of dignity among those whose essence is altogether the same, singular, and indivisible.

It is clear from this also that none of the three persons is substantially distinct from another [Col. 1232B], or even numerically separate as to things, but that one differs from another solely by its property, not by being unlike in substance or number, as Arius supposes. Hence Ambrose’s statement in Book II of *On the Faith addressed to Gratian*: “The Apostle says that Christ is the image of the Father; Arius says that he is unlike, and wishes the Father to have begotten one unlike himself, as though he were powerless, unable to beget one like himself.” Likewise: “The image teaches that he is not unlike.”

Therefore the Father is not something other than the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor the Son something other than the Holy Spirit; nor are they divided in number. They are not, I say, other in nature, since each of the three persons is altogether the same divine substance; but they are other in person, one from [Col. 1232C] another—that is, each differs from another in its own property—since this one is not that one who is the other, although he is that very thing which the other is; nor does one share another’s property, as we recalled above. Otherwise, by mingling the persons together, we should confuse them.

Yet Socrates, although numerically distinct from Plato—that is, other than him by the distinctness of his own essence—is not thereby called something other than him, that is, substantially different from him, since both are of one nature through their agreement in the same species, namely in that each is a human being. Thus they are not separated by any substantial difference, such that this one is something other than that one by a substance of a different species; but they are other, as stated, in person, namely through the distinctness of their individual substance. Much less, then, should any one of the three [Col. 1232D] persons that are in God be called something other than another, since their substance is altogether one, singular, admitting no diversity of parts or forms.

For whatever consists of parts is naturally posterior to the parts of which it is constituted, through which it is brought into being and receives its being. Hilary, on the psalm *Out of the Depths*: “I think it beyond doubt for any of the faithful that the divine substance is free both from composition of parts and from every formation by properties, so that there can be nothing in it which is not itself.”

Hence Augustine, disputing in Book XII of *The City of God* concerning the simplicity [Col. 1233A] and purity of the divine substance, says:

> “We do not call this nature of the good simple because the Father alone is in it, or the Son alone, or the Holy Spirit alone, or because this Trinity is merely a name or a subsistence of persons, as the Sabellians supposed. Rather, it is called simple because it is what it has, except insofar as each person is relatively spoken of in relation to another. For certainly the Father has the Son, yet he himself is not the Son; and the Son has the Father, yet he is not the Father. But insofar as it is spoken of in relation to itself, not to another, it is what it has: thus it is said to be living in relation to itself, certainly having life, and that very life is itself. This nature is therefore called simple because it is not one thing having and another thing which it has, as in other things. For [Col. 1233B] a vessel having liquid is not liquid; nor is a body color, nor air light or heat, nor is a soul wisdom. Hence they can also be deprived of the things which they have, and be changed and transformed into other conditions.”

The same author, speaking to God in Book VII of the *Confessions*, says: “You are not compelled unwillingly toward anything, because your will is not greater than your power. But it would be greater if you yourself were greater than yourself.” Likewise: “God’s will and power are God himself.”

Boethius also, in his book *On the Trinity*, when speaking of that highest unity of divinity in which there can be no diversity either of parts or forms, says: “Therefore this is truly one, in which there is no number, nothing in it other than that which it is. For it cannot become a subject, since it is form; but forms cannot be subjects” [Col. 1233C]. Here Boethius calls the divine substance “form,” inasmuch as it is not the support of any forms.

The authority of all theologians has rightly maintained that the divine substance is altogether simple—that is, free from every accident and from every participation in form—so that there is nothing in God which is not God. For everything which exists by nature is either eternal, as God is, or has its origin from that highest principle which is God; for nothing exists from itself, except that from which all things are. Hence Gennadius [Note: This passage is not found in Gennadius, but in Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 9], in chapter 9 of *On the Orthodox Faith*: “For a Christian, it is enough to believe that the cause of created things is only the goodness of the Creator [Col. 1233D], and that there is no nature which is not either himself or from him.”

By “nature,” I think, he means a natural thing which does not belong to the efficacy of human action. For sin and an idol should be called our works rather than natures. Hence the Apostle says: “We know that an idol is nothing in the world” (1 Cor. 8:4); that is, an idol is not among the whole of God’s creatures, nor does it belong to natural things or to the works of nature themselves, which are said to be in the world, but to our own fashioning. Thus what is called an idol is itself shown to be of less worth than what is called wood, since the former is manufactured and the latter natural.

If, therefore, power or wisdom, or [Col. 1234A] even some part, or anything else, is in God which is not God, then it began from him from whom all things are. But if his power or wisdom began, then he who is eternal existed without these, so that he was not always either powerful or wise, until, that is, he himself [lacuna: “being powerless in himself, had created power, or, still unwise, had produced wisdom for himself”]. Since he did these things without the discrimination of wisdom, which indeed he did not yet possess, some of his works are necessarily irrational.

But if someone says that qualities are in God in such a way that they are neither God nor made by God, but remain eternally in God and are coeternal with the divine substance itself in which they are [Col. 1234B], it remains to ask whether they are in him substantially or accidentally. If substantially, so as to constitute the divine substance, they plainly seem naturally prior to God himself, to whom they confer being; just as rationality is said to be prior to a human being, because it is his constitutive form and a certain formal part in his very constitution, by whose conjunction with the substance of animal, as with matter, the human being himself is completed.

Nor does it matter, for a constitution arising from matter and form, whether the wisdom present in God is substantial or accidental to him, provided that it is some form in God and a thing distinct from the divine substance itself. For in like manner a white human being or a white body consists of a human being or body and whiteness [Col. 1234C], in the analogy of matter and form, just as a bronze statue consists of bronze and composition. By the same reasoning one must grant that a wise God would be constituted from the substance of divinity itself and wisdom, if wisdom in God were a thing other than God: by its conjunction with that substance, God would be wise through the coming together of two things. Thus wise God would be some composite whole of matter and form, and the matter and form from which he is made would be its principles.

Who, moreover, would dare to say that something can be in God accidentally, and that he himself is subject to accidents—a claim anathematized by the authority of philosophers and Catholics alike? Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book V, chapter 8:

> “Nothing is usually called an accident except what can be lost through some change in the thing to which it happens. Therefore there is nothing accidental in God, because there is nothing mutable or liable to loss. Accordingly, nothing in him is said according to accident, because nothing happens to him; yet not everything said of him is said according to substance. For something is said relatively, as Father in relation to Son and Son in relation to Father; and this is not an accident, because the one is always Father and the other always Son. If the Son had at some time begun to be, or at some time ceased to be, he would be said according to accident. But if what is called Father were said in relation to himself rather than to the Son, it would be said according to substance” [Col. 1235A].

Furthermore, philosophers determine accidents to be of a posterior genus and an adventitious nature. Hence Porphyry confirms that even the proprium itself, which appears implanted in the nature of a species, is naturally posterior to the species, because it does not constitute the substance of the species, as substantial—that is, specific—differences do. For he says: “The species subsists before the proprium; the proprium comes about afterward in the species. For a human being must exist in order for him to be capable of laughter.”

When he also defined accident generally, saying, “An accident is what is present and absent without the destruction of the subject,” he plainly taught that every accident can both be present in and absent from its subject without destruction of that subject. But how shall we call the wisdom of God in him [Col. 1235B] either of a posterior genus or of an adventitious nature, or say that it can be absent from him without destruction, when it can in absolutely no way be absent from him? For God must altogether be wise; nor can he in any way either not exist, or exist without wisdom, or undergo any corruption so that anything can happen to him.

For when accident is defined as that which is present and absent without destruction of the subject, it is plainly implied that an accident is not present in a corruptible thing—that is, in a thing which can fail to exist or be corrupted. The meaning is as though one said: Accident is the form of a corruptible thing, without which that thing can both exist and not exist without destruction, that is, without the departure from substance which it would incur through that form. For to say “without destruction of the subject” [Col. 1235C] is as though he said more plainly that the subject incurs none of the destructions which it can suffer through the arrival or departure of such a form. We have had occasion to discuss this more fully elsewhere.

Therefore wisdom in God is neither a substantial nor an accidental form for him; rather, his Wisdom is God himself. The same must be thought concerning his power, and concerning the remaining things which, through an affinity of names, appear to be forms in God as they are in creatures.

These arguments therefore show that the divine substance remains altogether indivisible and altogether formless, and is therefore rightly called the perfect good: needing no other thing, but having from itself, and receiving from no other source, what it has. Creatures, however good they may be [Col. 1235D], require the addition of another thing; and by this need they confess their imperfection. For the virtues which make the soul good require a subject to support them, because piety cannot exist unless it has a foundation in which it is present. The soul itself, in order to be good, needs the adornments of virtues.

Concerning this formlessness, purity, or simplicity of the divine substance, Boethius says in the book which he is said to have composed *On the Trinity*: “What is not this and that, but only this, truly is that which is, and is most strong, relying on nothing. Therefore this is truly one, in which there is no number, nothing in it other than that which it is.” In the same place he immediately calls the divine substance itself “form” rather than “substance,” insofar as it is subject to no accidents and is not a support, as other substances are [Col. 1236A], as we recalled above. Again, in what follows he declares it to be a substance beyond substance, and denies that it is properly called substance according to the customary sense of that word:

> “Substance in him is not truly substance, but is beyond substance. When we say ‘God,’ we seem indeed to signify substance, but a substance beyond substance. When we say ‘Just,’ we seem indeed to signify quality, but not accidental quality: rather, that which is substance and beyond substance. Likewise, when we say ‘Great’ or ‘Greatest,’ we seem indeed to signify quantity, but that which is substance itself, such as we say is beyond substance” [Col. 1236B].

Thus Boethius denies that God is properly called substance, namely substance as a support of accidents. So too it is not fitting to call the properties present in the divine substance itself accidents or forms of substance. Rather, the term “accident,” as well as “form” and the names of the nine predicaments contained under those two, is properly understood only of created things. Thus, when Boethius says in the same work, “Substance in him is not truly substance, but is beyond substance,” he immediately adds: “Likewise quality and the rest of the things that can occur—that is, can happen, so as to be called accidents—are not truly in him.”

Since, then, the divine substance is altogether singular and unique, and the three persons subsist in it in such a way that [Col. 1236C] each person is altogether the same substance as the other, and there is no diversity of parts or forms in that simple good, this person can much less be called something other than that one than Socrates can be called something other than Plato. For the three persons have one singular essence, whereas Socrates and Plato do not have essentially the same substance, but their substances are distinct, such that this essence of Socrates is not that of Plato.

Yet the very same essence which is the Father’s is altogether the Son’s; it is also altogether the Holy Spirit’s. Nevertheless, the Father is other—that is, distinct in person—from the Son or the Holy Spirit, and likewise the Son from the Holy Spirit, since this one is not that one, although he is that which [Col. 1236D] the other is.

A great and most subtle distinction must be employed here: neither may the identity of singular substance and the individual unity of essence obstruct the diversity of persons, so that, wandering with Sabellius, we profess only one person as we profess one God; nor may the diversity of persons obstruct the singularity of substance, so that, falling into the pit of Arius, we assert three gods as we assert three persons. Rather, God must be at once altogether one in the singularity of substance and wholly himself in the distinction of the three persons.

At this point there arise the gravest and most difficult questions of the dialecticians. For from the unity of essence they attack the Trinity of persons; and again, from the diversity of persons they labor to overthrow the identity of essence. Let us first set out their objections [Col. 1237A], and afterward resolve them.

For, they say, this diversity of persons consists either in words alone and not in reality—so that only the words differ and there is no diversity of thing in God—or in reality alone and not in words, or both in reality and in words. But if either of these is removed, both will not remain. If we look to the words, the Trinity of persons is no longer eternal, since the imposition of the names was made by human beings.

Further, if this distinction of persons is to be understood according to the number of names, we must confess far more than three persons, because there are many other names of the divine substance [Col. 1237B], such as “God,” “Lord,” “eternal,” “immeasurable,” “creator,” and infinitely many others.

But if this diversity of persons is to be understood more in the thing itself than in names, while in God there is nothing in reality except the singular, individual, and formless substance, who can doubt that the Trinity is understood according to the unity of substance, so that God must be said to be threefold in substance?

Or, if in God substance and persons are altogether the same, so that substance is nothing other than persons and persons nothing other than substance, is he not one in persons if he is one God in substance? Or, if he is threefold in persons, is he not threefold in substance?

[Col. 1237C] How also are there three persons where there are in no way three things? Or how are there three things if there are not many? Or how can there be many if there is no multiplicity of things? Yet a multiplicity of things cannot arise from one thing alone unless it consists of several parts. But no parts can be in him, as we confirmed above. How then is there a Trinity where there is no multiplicity? For everything similar is dissimilar in some respect. Or how are there three if they are not many?

Further, how do you say, “The Father is such as the Son” or “the Holy Spirit,” if there is no likeness of persons, since there is no multiplicity? For everything similar is dissimilar in some respect, and there is no likeness except among distinct things [Col. 1237D]. Hence, when speaking of the same human being, no one calls this human being and this white thing similar, since they are not essentially distinct from one another.

Moreover, since everything which exists is either a substance or a form subsisting in a substance, such as whiteness, piety, or any thing belonging to the nine predicaments, how can there be many things unless they are either substances, forms, or composites of both?

Or, since God is a substance, and the name “God” belongs to substance rather than person—that is, it was devised on account of the nature of the substance, not to distinguish a person, as “Father” and “Son” were—how is “threefold God” said more fittingly than “threefold substance,” or than “threefold Father” [Col. 1238A]? For just as there is only one substance and one Father, so there is only one God, not several.

Moreover, what does “threefold God” or “threefold substance” mean other than three gods or three substances? For what is a threefold discourse but three discourses? Or a twofold blow but two blows? Perhaps also the following statement is adduced in objection: Augustine, in chapter 11 of the *Enchiridion*, calls God tripartite in these words: “For a Christian, it is enough to believe that the cause of created things is only the goodness of the Creator, who is the one God; and that there is no nature [Col. 1238B] which is not either himself or from him; and that he is tripartite [Note: In Augustine I do not read “tripartite,” but “and that he is the Trinity”], namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit” [Note: Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 9]. “For how,” they will say, “is God tripartite if he is not divided or does not have parts? Or how is he divided unless he was first whole or afterwards divided?” But who is so faithless as not to anathematize this?

How also can it be that three persons are so distinct from one another that this is not that, and each of them is substance and God, yet they are not therefore several substances or gods? For what is it to say “several substances” except to say “several things,” each of which is a substance? The plural word itself is nothing other than a doubling or multiplication of its singular, so that [Col. 1238C] the plural names many things together to each of which the singular applies separately.

By the same reasoning, why are three persons, because each is a person, said more fittingly than three gods or three substances, when each is God or substance?

But if we deny that they are called several substances or several gods because, although each person is substance or God, one person differs from another in no respect in which it is substance or God, then by the same reasoning we must never say “several human beings,” nor even “several persons,” since this human being does not differ from that one in being human, nor this person from that one in being a person [Col. 1238D].

How also do we truly say, “There are three persons,” if there are not many beings—that is, many essences? For the participle everywhere follows its verb in number: thus, of one of whom we say “walks,” we say “is walking”; and of several of whom we say “walk,” we say “are walking.” Hence Aristotle, in Book II of the *Physics*: “It makes no difference,” he says, “to say that a human being walks and that a human being is walking.” From this it appears that of all those of whom we say, “They are,” we must say, “They are beings,” that is, essences.

[Col. 1239A] How also is the name “God” singular rather than universal, if there are several things personally distinct—that is, different in number—of each of which it is predicated, since the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and this one is not that one?

What difference of things can exist where the same essence is altogether singular and individual? Every difference is understood either among distinct things, where this essence is not that one, or in the same thing according to its variation or some change through succession of time, as when someone now stands and now sits. But there is no distinctness of things where the essence is unique and individual. Nor can there be any variation in God, since it is written: “With whom there is no change, nor shadow of turning” [Col. 1239B] (James 1:17). Of him too that philosopher says:

> Who commands time to proceed from eternity,  
> and, remaining stable, gives all things motion.  
> (*Boethius, Consolation of Philosophy*, Book III)

The Lord himself also reveals his true and immutable being to Moses, saying: “I am who I am. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent me to you” (Exod. 3:14).

Further, since the Father is God—that is, this divine essence—and the Son is God, is the Father also the Son? For how is “the Father is eternal” better demonstrated from “the Father is God” and “God is eternal” than it is demonstrated from “the Father is God” and “God is Son,” or incarnate, that the Father is also [Col. 1239C] Son or incarnate? This is especially so since the name “God” is evidently singular, like the name “Socrates,” or indeed appears even more singular—that is, individual—since it signifies an individual, wholly indivisible, altogether simple and unique substance.

But when this seated person is Socrates and Socrates is white, it is clear that this seated person too is white, since the essence of this seated person and of this white person is altogether the same. This seated person and this white person are not called numerically many, since the essence of this one and that one is the same; although it is occupied by different forms, Socrates is not said to be either many persons or numerically many. Otherwise the name “Socrates” would be universal [Col. 1239D] rather than singular, since it would be said of things different in number.

Much less, then, are things numerically many in God, where there is not even any multiplicity of forms. It should be granted much more readily concerning God that he who is Father is Son than it is concerning creatures, in which there is at least diversity of forms, instability of substance itself, and continual change.

How, then, if we grant concerning creatures, because of identity of essence, that this seated person is this white person, or that he who is Father is Son, should we not receive this more readily in God—namely, that he who is Father is Son—when the substance of both is one, altogether individual and pure? Or that he who is Father is incarnate as the Son is, since the same substance [Col. 1240A] which is Father assumed flesh, as did that which is Son, given that the substance of the two persons is altogether the same?

Finally, since there is nothing in God except the one essence of a wholly simple and individual substance, and God begets God—that is, the Father the Son—does substance beget substance? And since the substance which is begotten is altogether the same as that which begets, does the same thing beget itself? But that a thing should beget itself is rejected not only by all reason but by the writings of the holy Fathers, especially in this divine generation itself. Augustine says in Book I of *On the Trinity*: “Whoever thinks God of such power that he himself begot himself errs all the more, because not only is God not thus [Col. 1240B], but neither is any spiritual or bodily creature.” For there is absolutely no thing which begets itself.

It is clear that everything said of God must be said of the persons themselves either singly or jointly—that is, of one of them or of several together. If, therefore, God begot himself, either one of the three persons begot itself, or several of them begot themselves. If one of the three persons begot itself, then either the Father begets himself, or the Son himself, or the Holy Spirit. If the Father begets himself, he is plainly his own Son, and thus the persons are confused, since he who is Father is Son. The same confusion—that is, mingling of the persons—follows if either of the others begets itself, that is, is its own father.

[Col. 1240C] Further, if God begets God, then he begets either himself or another God. But one God cannot be another from another; there is only one God, and, according to Augustine and the reasoning set out above, God cannot beget himself. For if God begot himself, then God himself is his own Father. But if God himself is his own father, then either God the Father is his own father, or God the Father is not his own father. Yet God the Father is Father of the Son alone, and not father of himself. Therefore God the Father is not his own father. Again, if it is false that God the Father is his own father, then it is certainly false that God the Father is father of his own father. Yet who would assert that something is its own father and dare deny that its own father is father of itself?

By what reasoning also, since there is but one substance [Col. 1240D] of the three persons—so that the substance of the Father is altogether the same as that of the Son and the Holy Spirit—is the Son alone said to be from the substance of the Father, which is the Son’s and the Holy Spirit’s, and not from the substance of the Holy Spirit or his own?

Or, since the wisdom of the three persons is likewise one and the same, and each is equally wise with the others, and the charity of each is the same, why is the Son not equally called the Wisdom of the Holy Spirit, or of himself, as he is called the Wisdom of the Father? Or why is the Holy Spirit not called the love of himself, as he is the love of the Father or of the Son? For is either the Son or the Holy Spirit wise, but not through wisdom of his own? Or is he wisdom, but not his own wisdom, rather another’s? Or [Col. 1241A] is he loving, but not his own love? He himself is his own power, greatness, justice, piety, and will.

How can it be, moreover, that the Son was begotten from the Father, or that both the Son and the Holy Spirit have their being from the Father, while the Father is not from them, and yet the Father is not prior to them?

Let us not delay to answer these and similar objections, trusting in him of whom we speak, secure in him for whom we contend.

The sum, as I think, of all the questions is this: how we may discern a diversity of persons within so great a unity of an individual and altogether pure substance, when no mode of difference distinguished by philosophers seems capable of being assigned here [Col. 1241B], by which diversity of persons can be shown.

To this I think the first answer must be that it ought not to seem remarkable if the nature of Divinity, as it is singular, has also a singular mode of speech. It is fitting, indeed, that what is far removed from all creatures should be expressed in a kind of speech far different from theirs; that the unique majesty should not be confined by common and public usage of speech; and that what is wholly incomprehensible and ineffable should not be subject to rules to which all things are subject, since it cannot be understood even by the human being who established words to make his thoughts known.

Nor was this reverence hidden from the philosophers, who always hesitated so greatly to touch in words [Col. 1241C] that highest good which they professed to be wholly incomprehensible and ineffable. This is clear from what has been set out above: the greatest of philosophers did not dare even to say what it is, knowing only this about it, that it cannot be known by a human being. For it was fitting that the teaching of this should be reserved for incarnate true Wisdom: God himself was to bring knowledge of himself through himself, since no creature could rise to knowledge of him.

He alone therefore plainly revealed what he himself is when he said to that Gentile and Samaritan woman: “God is spirit” (John 4:24)—that is, Divinity is a spiritual, not a bodily, substance. But as among bodies some are more subtle than others—for example, water than earth, air than water, and fire [Col. 1241D] than air—so Divinity surpasses the nature of all spirits by the subtlety of its own purity in a manner far beyond expression, so that in comparison with it all other spirits must be called, as it were, bodily or certain bodies.

Hence Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* [Note: Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, ch. 11]:

> “Nothing incorporeal and invisible in nature is to be believed except God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. He is believed incorporeal because he is everywhere, fills and binds all things; and therefore he is invisible to all creatures, because he is incorporeal. Every creature is bodily: angels and all heavenly powers are bodily, although they do not subsist in flesh. But we believe intellectual natures incorporeal [Note: Read “bodily,” as in Gennadius], because they are circumscribed locally, as is the human soul enclosed by flesh, and demons, who are bodily through the substance of angelic nature” [Col. 1242A].

From this it is evident how subtle the divine substance is, and how utterly set apart it is from the soul and from bodily nature, and remote from the power of our senses. If philosophers dared to say anything about it, they resorted to likenesses and examples, as though veiling their presumption in speaking of the ineffable. They sought and indicated its glory, not in itself, but somehow in creatures—as we recalled above concerning Plato, who returned to the analogy of the sun when he ventured to speak of God [Col. 1242B].

It is also clear from the writings of our teachers who give the greatest attention to logic that they did not at all dare to approach that highest majesty, which they profess to be an unknown God, or to comprehend it within the number of things. For, since they subject every thing either to substance or to one of the other highest genera, if they included God among things, they would count him either among substances, quantities, or things of the other predicaments. Yet it is evident that he is none of these.

For all things other than substances cannot exist by themselves, unless they are supported by substances; just as whiteness cannot in any way exist except in a bodily subject [Col. 1242C], piety except in a soul, or any thing belonging to the nine predicaments except as present in subject substances. Substances, however, can subsist and endure in their own nature by themselves, with all other things destroyed. Hence substances are called, as it were, subsistences, and are naturally prior to the other things which stand by them and do not subsist by themselves [emended from “not” to “nor”].

Thus it is evident that God, who is the unique and singular principle of all things, is in no way included in that number of things which are not substances. Yet, according to them, God is not placed under substance either, although he is preeminently a thing existing through himself and alone has true and immutable being from himself, he from whom all things are. Therefore he says to Moses: “Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: He Who Is has sent [Col. 1242D] me to you” (Exod. 3:14).

Concerning the truth, simplicity, and immutability of his substance, Augustine says in Book V of *On the Trinity* [Note: Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book V, ch. 1]:

> “Let us understand God, if we can, as far as we can: good without quality, great without quantity, Creator without need, present without position [Note: Thus the printed editions of Augustine; but many manuscripts read “presiding”], containing all things without condition, wholly everywhere without place, eternal without time, making mutable things without any change in himself, and suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God in this way, although he cannot yet altogether discover what he is, nevertheless piously takes care, as far as he can, not to think of him as something which he is not [Col. 1243A]. Yet without doubt he is substance—or, if this is a better term, essence—which the Greeks call οὐσία (*ousia*).”

That God himself must not be called substance according to the philosophers can readily be shown from the writings of all who treat dialectic, which Latin scholarship [lacuna], namely Porphyry, Aristotle, and Boethius. For Porphyry says in the *Isagoge*, which he wrote as an introduction to Aristotle’s *Categories*, that each substance participates in one species but in several accidents, both separable and inseparable. Aristotle too, in the *Categories*, assigning what is especially proper to substance, says: “It seems most especially proper to substance that, while it is one and the same in number, it is capable of receiving contraries.” Again, he says of the same matter: “Therefore it will be proper to substance that, while it is one and the same in number, it is capable of receiving contraries” [Col. 1243B].

Since, therefore, these predicates cannot at all be fitted to God—whose substance can neither be altered by accidents nor be subject to any forms whatsoever—it is clear that the philosophers did not admit him among substances either. For the same reason Plato placed matter (*hylē*) between no substance and some substance, since he conceived it as altogether still without form. For God is not not a substance, if we attend to the nature of true subsistence and immutable being in him. [Note: [Col. 1243D] In *Introduction to Theology*, book II: “if we attend to the nature of true subsistence and immutable being in him.”] Nor, again, is he a substance, if we follow the customary use of the name “substance,” since he cannot be subject to accidents. Hence God is plainly shown not to be a substance by that argument [Col. 1243C] through which Boethius—though a Christian, following the opinion of the philosophers when treating philosophy, namely Themistius and Cicero in his *Topics*—proves in the second [Note: [Col. 1244D] *Introduction*, fifth.] book of their *Topics* that whiteness is not a substance, in these words: “A substance is that which can be subject to all accidents. But whiteness is subject to no accidents. Therefore whiteness is not a substance.”

Augustine himself likewise openly professes this customary and proper meaning of “substance” in book VII of *On the Trinity*, chapters 4 and 5, when discussing God, in these words: “If for God to be is to subsist, then it will not be proper to say [Note: [Col. 1244D] Read *dicenda*, as in Augustine.] three [Col. 1243D] substances, just as three essences are not said; just as, because for God to be is to be wise, we say neither three essences nor three wisdoms. For because for him to be God is to be, it is not permissible to speak either of three essences or of three Gods. But if for God to be is one thing and to subsist another, just as for God to be is one thing and to be Father or Lord another: what he is is said in relation to himself. But Father subsists in relation to Son, and Lord in relation to a serving creature, just as he begets relatively and rules relatively. Then substance will no longer be substance, because it will be relative. For just as essence is named from being [Col. 1244A], so we call substance from subsisting. But it is absurd for substance to be said relatively. For every thing subsists in relation to itself—how much more God?—if indeed it is fitting that God be said to subsist. For this is understood of those things in which are subjects those things said to be in a subject, as colour is in a body.”

Likewise: “Mutable things, therefore, are not properly called simple substances.”

Likewise: “But it is impious to say that God subsists and is subject to his own goodness, and that goodness is not substance—or rather essence—and that God himself is not his own goodness, but that goodness is in him as in a subject. Hence it is evident that God is called substance improperly [Col. 1244B], so that essence may be understood by a more customary name; essence is what is truly and properly said. Thus perhaps God alone ought to be called essence. For he alone truly is, because he is immutable; and he made this his name known to Moses [Note: [Col. 1244D] In Augustine: “declared.”], when he said: ‘I am who I am,’ and ‘You shall say to them: He Who Is has sent me to you’ (Exod. 3:14). Yet whether he is called essence [Col. 1244C], which is proper, or substance, which is improper, each is said in relation to himself, not relatively. Hence for God to be is to subsist; and therefore, if the Trinity is one essence, it is also one substance.”

[Note: [Col. 1244] In Migne, the following paragraph is printed parallel to the passage “God is called substance improperly . . . not relatively. Hence” in the preceding paragraph.]

On the passage in Job, “For he alone is, and no one can turn aside his thoughts” (Job 23:13). Gregory: “To be is one thing; to be pre-eminently is another. To be mutably is one thing; to be immutably is another. For all these things exist, but they do not exist pre-eminently, because they do not subsist at all in themselves and cannot exist unless they are held by the hand of their governor. Hence it is also said to Moses: ‘I am who I am.’ Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He Who Is has sent me to you’ (ibid.).”

From these passages it is therefore clear that, even according to Augustine, God is not properly called a substance; nor, according to the philosophers, is he a substance in any way, since there is nothing in him as in a subject—that is, as an accident—as we have sufficiently explained above. Therefore, since God is neither properly called a substance according to Augustine nor a substance in any way according to the philosophers—who nevertheless assign every thing either to substance or to one of the other categories [Col. 1244D]—it is surely evident that that supreme majesty is altogether excluded from the treatment of the Peripatetics, and that their rules or teachings cannot in any way rise to that supreme and ineffable height. Rather, they must be content to investigate the natures of creatures, according to what is written: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth” (John 3:31); and they are still unable fully to comprehend or rationally examine even these.

That all human speech is especially fitted to the condition of creatures appears from that principal part of speech [Col. 1245A] without which, as Priscian testifies, no complete utterance exists: namely, what is called the verb. For this word signifies time, which began with the world. Hence, if we consider the signification of this part, the sense of every construction must be confined within the bounds of time; that is, it must be directed only to things which we intend to show happen temporally, not subsist eternally. Thus, when we say that God is prior to the world, or existed before times, what true sense can these words have concerning God’s precedence and their succession, if, for the purposes of human instruction, we take the words according to their very temporal signification? That is, if we say that God was prior to the world in time, or [Col. 1245B] existed—that is, was in past time—before any time existed.

Accordingly, whenever we transfer whatever words we please to the singular nature of the Divinity, we must restrict them to some singular signification or construction; and, through that which surpasses all things, they must necessarily transcend their ordinary institution. For, according to Boethius and Plato, it is evident that speech must be akin to the things of which it speaks. Gregory rightly says in the prologue to the *Moralia*: “I consider it utterly unworthy to confine the words of the heavenly oracle within the rules of Donatus.” Nor did even the great philosophers know how to apply the proper and customary name of God to that unique majesty of the Divinity which cannot be conceived, much less discoursed upon. [Col. 1245C] For when they name God in the highest place, which they subordinate to a rational animal, they understand it, as we recalled above, of the world and the heavenly bodies.

What wonder, then, if God, since he ineffably transcends all things, also surpasses every discourse of human institution? And since his excellence far surpasses every understanding, while words were instituted for the sake of understanding, what wonder if the effect transcends that which transcends its causes? For a thing can far more easily be conceived than explained. What wonder, too, if God in his own person breaks the rules of the philosophers, or examples which are frequently nullified even in his own deeds [the printed addition reads: “have been nullified”], when he performs something new contrary to nature [Col. 1245D], or above nature—that is, above what the first institution of things allows?

Does not the restoration of sight to a blind person overthrow that well-known rule of the philosophers stated by Aristotle: “Change indeed occurs from possession to privation, but from privation to possession it is impossible. For one who has become blind does not see again,” and so forth? Does not the Virgin’s childbirth altogether prejudice that proposition which philosophers frequently offer as an example of necessary consequence or argument: “If she has given birth, she has had intercourse with a man”? Thus it may also appear what the Apostle says: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?” (1 Cor. 1:20). But if, in order to save the philosophers, you except what occurs through miracles, or say that in these cases words do not retain their proper signification [Col. 1246A]—so that sight or childbirth are not properly so called when they occur miraculously—how much more must this be granted in the very author of miracles?

Answer, you subtle dialectician of mine, or crafty sophist, who strive to accuse me on the authority of the Peripatetics, concerning the distinction of the persons and their properties which are in God: how do you acquit your own teachers, according to whose traditions, as we have now shown, you are compelled to confess both that God is not a substance and that he is not anything else? Yet both he himself, as has been said, when speaking to Moses, and the true philosophers instructed by him, made known that he alone truly and properly is—namely, by his perpetual and immutable permanence. Hence blessed Job too says among other things concerning him: “For he alone is, and no one can turn aside his thoughts” (Job 23:13).

Consider, brothers and verbose friends, how greatly divine and human traditions differ from one another; spiritual and animal philosophers; the disciplines of sacred and secular writings. For, as we taught above, it follows from the disciplines of your arts, which distribute the natures of all things among ten categories, that God is absolutely nothing—yet by the testimony of God himself and of his disciples we are compelled to profess that he alone is. But if, in order to defend your disciplines, you acknowledge that, as we said, they are content with distinguishing the natures of creatures and have not presumed to address the height of Divinity, [Col. 1246C] then you too, relying on them, should be less presumptuous in attacking us when faith has uttered such words as are unknown in meaning to your disciplines.

For it is certain that every proposition and treatment of any art employs its own words, and every discipline delights in its own expressions; and often the expositors of the same art delight in varying their words, because, as Cicero testifies, sameness is always the mother of satiety—that is, it produces weariness. How much more, therefore, ought the expositors of that singular and highest good to possess singular words, by which what is singular might be expressed singularly, and that ineffable, incomprehensible reality not be confined within common and vulgar expressions? Whenever anything is said of it, we transfer words from creatures to the Creator by some likeness. Men instituted these words to designate creatures which they were able to understand, when they wished by those words to make their understandings known. Therefore, since man devised sounds to disclose his own understandings, but is insufficient to understand God at all, he rightly did not dare to utter that ineffable good by a name of his own invention.

Hence no word of human invention seems to retain its proper meaning in God; rather, all things said of him are wrapped in metaphors and parabolic enigmas and are traced through some likeness introduced from some respect, so that we may taste something of that ineffable majesty by conjecture rather than understanding. [Col. 1247A] And because we find less adequate likenesses to apply to that which is singular, we can give less satisfactory account of him through likenesses. Yet we shall undertake such likenesses as we can, especially in order to refute the importunity of the pseudo-dialecticians. We too touch somewhat upon their disciplines, and have so advanced in their studies that, with the Lord’s help, we are confident that we can satisfy them in this matter by human reasons—the only kind they desire.

For the Creator of reason himself also possesses human reasons by which he can stop the mouths of animal men; he admonishes us through that Wise Man, saying: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself” (Prov. 26:5). And concerning his wisdom, the Book of Wisdom says among its other praises: “He knows the subtleties of speeches and the arrangements [Note: [Col. 1247D] In the Vulgate edition: “solutions.”] of arguments” (Wis. 8:8). But let us first remove the obstacle which they raise concerning the distinction of persons of one and altogether the same essence, since this mode of distinction appears unknown both to philosophers and to everyone else.

Nor does it impede us that they oppose Porphyry, who, in treating differences, distinguished modes of differences under which this mode of the difference of the persons who are in God does not fall. For there he treats only differences consisting in forms: namely, where distinct things differ from one another by different forms, or where the same thing is changed through forms successively replacing one another. [Col. 1247C] But in God there are no forms; nevertheless, we say that he differs no less from creatures, although Porphyry did not include this difference in his treatment of Difference.

We are also compelled to acknowledge many other modes of difference besides those which Porphyry distinguishes. In order to set all these forth more fully and carefully, we must distinguish in how many and in what ways “same” is understood, and likewise “different,” especially since the whole point of the controversy depends upon the identity of the divine substance and the diversity of the persons. Nor can the controversy itself be resolved otherwise than by showing that this identity is not contrary to that diversity. To do this more carefully, we must first set forth, as we said, in how many ways “same” and “different” are spoken. [Col. 1247D]

Each, considered in itself, seems to be spoken of in five ways, and perhaps more. For one thing is said to be the same as, or one with, another according to essence or according to number; the same in property; the same in definition; the same in likeness; and the same in the sense of being unchanged. Conversely, we call things different in as many ways, and perhaps more.

We say that one thing is essentially the same as another when they have one and the same essence numerically: namely, when this and that are the same essence in number, as sword and blade are the same essence in number; or substance [Col. 1248A] and body, or animal or human being, or even Socrates; and white is numerically the same as hard. For it is true that substance is this body or this animal, though not every substance is so. All these things which are essentially the same are called numerically the same, because, when each has the same essence, the number of things cannot be multiplied in them, nor can counting proceed from the distinction of the things themselves—so that one, two, and so on may be said of them. For number exists only in distinct essences: that is, in things so altogether different that not only is this not that, but neither is one predicated of the other, nor is anything of this of that; that is, neither is one a part, in quantity, of the other, nor do they share the same part.

But one thing is said to be the same as another in property when it shares that other’s property, as white does with hard, or hard with white. For white shares hardness, which is a property of what is hard; that is to say, “the white is hard”; and conversely hard shares the property of white. Yet some things are essentially the same which are nevertheless distinguished by their properties, where their properties remain so altogether unmixed that the property of one is not shared at all by the other, even though the substance of each is altogether numerically the same.

For example, in this wax image, this wax—that is, the matter itself—and the thing made from the matter are numerically the same; yet the matter itself and the thing made from it do not there share their properties. For the matter of the wax image is not itself made of matter—that is, the wax itself is not made from wax—nor is the thing made from matter itself matter there—that is, the wax image is not matter for the wax image—since nothing is in any way a constitutive part of itself or naturally prior to itself. Therefore the matter of the wax image and the thing made from wax, although they are numerically the same essence, are nevertheless unmixed in their properties. For the matter itself of the wax image and the thing made from it—namely, the wax itself and the wax image itself—are the same wax, this wax; yet the thing made from matter is by no means matter there, nor is the matter itself made from matter, although it is the thing which has been made from matter.

It belongs to the property of matter to precede the thing made from it; [Col. 1248D] it belongs to the property of what is made from matter, conversely, to follow and be later. Thus the property of matter is priority itself, in accordance with which something can be made materially from it. Conversely, the property of what is made from matter is posteriority itself. The properties themselves are therefore unmixed in predication, although the things characterized by them, if one may put it so, are promiscuously predicated of the same thing.

For it is one thing to predicate a form and another to predicate the thing formed itself—that is, the thing itself subject to the form. If I say, “The wax image is prior to wax,” that is, “it has priority with respect to wax,” then I couple and predicate the form itself; and what is said is false. But if I say, “The wax image is [Col. 1249A] something prior to wax,” that is, “some thing is prior to wax,” then I couple and predicate the formed thing itself, and the proposition is true, since the image itself is a body which is prior to wax. Likewise, Socrates does not have perpetuity—that is, he is not perpetual—although he is a perpetual thing, just as this body is. Having thus shown which things are different in property, it is clear conversely which things are the same by agreement of properties.

Of those things which are said to be the same essentially or in property, some are also the same in definition, such as sword and blade, or Maro and Tullius, and any things whose definition is altogether the same. For not only is sword blade and blade sword, but also, because it is a sword, it is a blade, and conversely; so that they must be delimited by the same definition, since the expressed and proper being of the one is the same as that of the other.

Boethius understands “same” in this way in the first book of the *Topics*, where he says that a question concerning definition is a question concerning the same thing—for example, when it is asked whether the useful is the same as the honourable—“because,” he says, “the things whose definition is the same are themselves the same, and the things whose definition is different are themselves different.” Here we understand by definition that which completely expresses the force and property of what is defined, and neither exceeds nor is exceeded by the meaning of the name. Thus, if one defining body says that it is corporeal substance, not coloured substance: although the definition “coloured substance” applies only to bodies, just as the former does, nevertheless it does not disclose the force and meaning of the name “body” as the former does. For the name “body” does not determine colour, which is an accident of body, as it determines corporeity, which is substantial to it. Nor does that definition show what the property requires from its being body as the other does.

Therefore, to say that sword and blade are the same in definition is as though one said that the same essence is so sword and blade that, from its being a sword, nothing is required except that it be a blade, and conversely. Thus not only is sword and blade the same essence, but being a sword is altogether the same as being a blade. Accordingly, things are said to be the same in definition when they are so conjoined [Col. 1249D] that it is not merely the case that this is that, but from its being this it requires only that it be that, and conversely. In this way substance and body, or white and hard, cannot be called the same, although they are essentially the same.

Therefore all things the same in definition are essentially the same, but the converse does not hold. And only according to these two above-mentioned meanings is this pronoun “same” customarily used with relative reference: that is, either according to identity in number or according to identity in definition. For when we say, “A woman condemned the world and the same woman saved it,” there are two senses. One is false if the reference is made to identity of number—namely, if the same woman personally and numerically is understood both to have condemned and to have saved. The other sense [Col. 1250A] is true if “same” is understood according to identity of definition: that is, if it signifies no more than the simple repetition of the noun “woman,” “a woman condemned and a woman saved,” which is true through Eve and Mary.

Things essentially distinct are said to be the same by likeness when they are mutually alike in something: for example, species are the same in genus, or individuals are the same in species; or one thing, or any things agreeing in something, are called the same—that is, alike. Hence Porphyry says: “By participation in the species, many human beings are one; but one common thing is many in relation to particulars.”

We also say “same” in the sense of being unchanged, as when God is always the same: that is, he is never altered [Col. 1250B] or changed in anything, because the nature of Divinity never has in itself anything of which it may at some time be deprived, nor lacks anything which has the power of efficacy—just as “the same” is said of things which have the same force. Thus “same” or “one” is said in the five above-mentioned ways, although often the same thing falls under more than one of these modes, so that it may be called the same as something in both this and that way.

We likewise say “different” or “differing” in as many ways: things are said to differ sometimes essentially, that is, numerically; sometimes in property; in definition; in likeness; or by change.

We call things essentially different from one another when they differ so that this is not that: as Socrates is not Plato, nor is Socrates’ hand Socrates. Thus we also call any disparate things essentially different, since the essence of one is not the essence of the other, although it is of the essence of the other—for example, a hand is of a human being, or a wall of a house. Therefore, just as Socrates is essentially other than Plato, so Socrates’ hand is essentially other than Socrates, and every part other than its whole. In this sense we call one thing simple and another composite, since what is simple is not the composite thing itself, although it belongs to the composite. Therefore we call all things essentially different which are so removed from one another that this is not that.

Porphyry himself also plainly suggests this difference in his discussions of commonalities [Col. 1250D], where he shows that the most general and the most specific differ in that the most general is not the most specific, nor the most specific the most general. Of things essentially different, however, some are also numerically different and some are not.

For we call things numerically different when they are so distinct from one another in the whole quantity of their essence that not only is this not that, but neither is one part of the other nor do they share the same part. Thus those things alone, and all those things, are different in number which are distinct in the whole quantity of their essence: whether they differ from each other in number alone, as Socrates and Plato; or also in species, as this human being and that horse; or even in genus, as this human being and [Col. 1251A] this whiteness; or by whatever form they differ from each other—whether that form is a common difference, that is, a separable accident, such as curvature of the nose, or a more proper difference, that is, a substantial one, such as rationality. A substantial difference makes not only another thing, that is, something different in some way, but also an other thing, that is, something substantially and specifically different.

These alone are properly called several or many, because “several” and “many” properly pertain to number and are understood according to number. Some things, then, are essentially different which are not different in number—for example, a house and a wall, and any integral whole together with its proper part. In both of the aforesaid modes of diversity God too is said to differ from creatures: namely, both essentially and numerically.

We understand “different” in this way too when we deny that there are distinct pairs in one group of three. For although the third unit together with each of the other two units constitutes a pair, and this pair is not that pair, we nevertheless deny that the pairs are distinct, because they are not distinct in the entire capacity or comprehensiveness of their essence, since they share the same unit. And when we say that someone possesses only a house—that is, a house and nothing else different from the house—we understand “different” according to number rather than according to essence. For whoever possesses a house also possesses a wall, which is not a house. But though the wall is essentially different from the house, it is not numerically different from it, since [Col. 1251C] it is included within the very quantity of the house.

And it should be noted that, although everything essentially the same as something is numerically the same as it, and conversely, not everything essentially different from something is numerically different from it, as we taught above. Every part is essentially different from its whole, but is not numerically different, nor perhaps numerically the same, unless one happens to call it numerically the same negatively—that is, not numerically different. For if a part were called numerically different from its whole, Socrates would surely be conceded to be predicated of things different in number, since this whole composed of a hand and the remaining body is Socrates, and the remaining body apart from the hand must likewise be called Socrates—that is, vivified by this soul. We had to deal with this more fully elsewhere in the category of substance. [Col. 1251D]

Things differ in definition when they cannot be delimited by the same definition in meaning: that is, when they are such that they do not mutually require one another, although each is the same thing, as substance and body, or white and hard. For it does not follow from something’s being substance that it is body, nor from its being white that it is hard, since one can exist without the other and does not require it of itself. Boethius teaches us this difference in the first book of the *Topics*, where, although he says that proposition, question, and conclusion are the same, he nevertheless says that they differ, since a proposition can exist when there is no question or conclusion, and a question [Col. 1252A] when there is no conclusion, because the one does not require the other and each must be delimited by its own definition.

In his *Divisions* he also says that rational and biped differ in this way: “Although,” he says, “they are separated from one another by no opposition.” Porphyry too, in his *Isagoge*, did not omit this kind of difference, namely according to definition, when he says: “Those whose terms—that is, definitions—are differences are themselves also different.” For it is certain that all things which can in any way be separated by affirmation and negation differ from one another.

For example, if we can show of certain things that this one is an animal and that one is not an animal, it is clear that they differ. Hence we must concede that any things differing in definition, even if they are connected by predication, differ in some way from one another—as animal and human being, or white and hard—since they too are in some way separated from each other by affirmation and negation. For an animal can be such that it is not a human being; but a human being cannot be such that it is not an animal [the text prints “human being”]. And animal requires only this: that it be animate and sentient; but human being requires not only this, but also that it be rational and mortal.

In the same way phoenix and this phoenix; this body and this soul; this human being and this white body, can be shown to be different, although they are altogether of the same essence. The statement of Porphyry that some differences divide genera while others constitute species also seems to pertain to this diversity. For although the divisive and constitutive differences are altogether the same, they are constitutive from one consideration—namely, from the fact that they constitute—and divisive from another—from the fact that they divide from one another, that is, diversify species. Therefore the property or definition of the constitutive is one thing and that of the divisive another, just as when we say that “infinite” is one thing according to time, another according to measure, another according to multitude, and so forth, we understand it as different in definition.

Likewise, according as things are the same or different in definition, we are accustomed to call a state the same state or different states; nor do we say that this state is that state unless this thing is altogether the same in definition as that, or that this state is not that unless this thing is not altogether the same as that in its expressed being—that is, in altogether the same definition. [Col. 1252D]

What things are different in property, I think, has been carefully discussed above, where we were taught conversely what things are the same in property.

Likewise, from the definition of what things are the same in likeness—that is, alike—it is clear conversely what things are different in likeness, that is, unlike in some respect.

It is likewise evident from the foregoing, by contrariety, that whatever is changed in some respect—that is, made different from what it was before, as if Socrates now stands and now sits—is different by change.

These points have been stated in order to show in how many ways “same” and “different” are understood by their proper force even when said absolutely [Col. 1253A], although when joined with other words they often acquire other meanings or lay aside these. For when we say “different places,” we mean different according to containment, not according to number or essence. Otherwise the wine which is in a cask and in a house would be in different places, although no body is conceded to be in different places. Therefore, since the name “place” applies by containment or capacity, when “different” is added to it, difference of containment is signified: as though one said, places are different which do not contain and enclose the same thing.

Likewise, when we call the Holy Spirit manifold, or speak of seven Spirits, because “Spirit” is customarily said according to the working of his goodness and the distribution of his grace, we refer this multiplicity and diversity of the Spirit wholly to his effects. Thus too is understood what Truth says: “I will give you another Paraclete” (John 14:16), that is, one to effect something else in you.

And when we say, “one craftsman, another painter, another smith,” and so forth, because the name “craftsman” applies from an operation or office, we say “one” and “another” according to effects or offices, not according to persons, since perhaps the same person is sometimes of both offices.

But when your Aristotle says in the first *Perihermeneias* that utterances, like letters, are not the same for all people, but differ among different persons according to the office of signifying, he says this of utterances and letters, not according to the actual utterance of sounds. For while the production of sounds is natural to all, the office of signifying is not maintained among all, but only among those who do not lack knowledge of their imposition. He likewise says later in the second *Perihermeneias* that the voice is one and the affections many. Or when Priscian says that many nouns fall upon one voice, “many” or “different” is understood according to the office of signifying, for producing diverse understandings; hence they are called affirmations or nouns. But he calls the voice one from the form of its utterance and sound, not from its office, since the name “voice” is given from the quality of the sound, not from the office of signifying.

Thus, through the addition of subjects, “same” and “different” frequently alter their meanings, just as other words often do: for example, when I say [Col. 1253D] “a good cithara-player” and “a good man,” or “a simple voice” and “a simple proposition,” or “a true definition” and “a true statement.”

I think I have carefully distinguished, so far as the present inquiry requires, the ways in which “same” and “different” are understood, so that it may afterwards readily be examined wherein consists the diversity of the persons who are in God, whose substance is altogether the same. The same, I say, essentially and numerically, just as the substance of a sword and a blade is the same, or that of this man and this animal. Yet the persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are different from one another, after the likeness of things which differ in definition or property: namely, although God the Father is altogether the same essence as God the Son or God the Holy Spirit, yet the proper characteristic [Col. 1254A] of God the Father, namely that He is Father, is one thing; that of the Son another; and that of the Holy Spirit another.

The Father’s proper characteristic, as we have also mentioned above, is to be from Himself and not from another, and eternally to beget a Son coeternal with Himself. The Son’s is to be begotten by the Father alone; the Holy Spirit’s, to proceed from both. Hence the holy Fathers rightly said that these persons differ from one another by certain, as it were, properties, in accordance with Gregory’s saying: “In the persons there is property, and in the essence unity”; and with Jerome’s statement in the letter on the exposition of the faith addressed to Pope Damasus, where it is said: “Confounding Arius, we declare one and the same substance of the Trinity. Again, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons expressly under their respective properties.” And shortly afterwards: “He also calls the properties themselves persons, saying: ‘For we confess not only the names, but also the properties of the names—that is, the persons, or, as the Greeks express it, hypostases, that is, subsistences.’” There he further adds: “Thus they are one in substance, but distinguished in persons and names.”

When, however, we hear them called properties, we must not understand this to mean that we imagine certain forms in God. Rather, we call them properties as things proper, in the way Aristotle says that it is common to every substance not to be in a subject, not to admit more and less, and to have nothing contrary to it. Yet by these common features which he assigns, he understands no forms; for he assigns such common features by removing something rather than by positing something. So too [Col. 1254C] we say that it is proper to substance to subsist through itself, because this alone follows from its being substance; and we say that it is proper to a formless thing, such as God Himself, not to have forms, or to a simple thing, to lack parts. By this we seem to posit no forms whatsoever, but wholly to remove both forms and parts. Or, if someone understands forms in this case too, it is certain that they are in no way things distinct from the substances in which they are present. Thus we say that this belongs properly to the Father, that to the Son, and the other to the Holy Spirit.

I do not wish, however, to pass over in silence why I have persisted so long in assigning the properties of the divine persons, in order to establish that those properties [Col. 1254D] are not something other than God Himself or the persons themselves. I judged this especially necessary because in our own times certain men counted among the truly Catholic, and even raised through diligent study of the divine books to the chair of a teacher, have dared to break forth into such madness as to profess that the properties of the persons are things other than God Himself or the persons themselves: namely, paternity, filiation, and the procession of the Spirit, which the authority of the holy Fathers itself calls relations.

They have been led into this heresy chiefly because, unless they posit those properties—by which the persons differ—as things distinct from the divine substance itself, they cannot at all explain wherein the diversity of persons consists, though their essence is altogether the same. But they seek this evasion in vain in order to acquit themselves, and they establish this falsehood in vain in order to defend the truth—men who are ashamed, when questioned, to profess that they do not know. For, since they do not dare to deny that the divine essence is one alone and indivisible, and say that those three properties are in it, what greater diversity is there between God the Father and God the Son than between this man, the father of this person, and the same man, the son of that person, since the same man is both this one’s father and that one’s son? Or, if the diversity there is no greater than here, on what grounds do they grant that this man is a father and this man a son, but not that God the Father is God the Son? [Col. 1255B]

What does it avail to establish something which does not remove the chief point of controversy? How can a Christian presume what even a pagan and any unbeliever shrinks from: namely, to invent in God something which is not Himself? For if paternity, which is in God, is an essence other than God Himself, is it true that God the Father consists of two things, namely God and paternity, and that He Himself is a whole composed of those two constituents? Or, because we call these properties relations, must they be understood as things distinct from the substance itself, which is called relative to something according to them? Certainly not. Otherwise, when God is relatively called Lord, His lordship would be an essence other than Himself; and by acquiring it God would undergo change when He began to be Lord.

Against this detestable heresy blessed Augustine openly inveighs in Book V of *On the Trinity*, chapter 16, defending God’s immutability in those things which belong to Him in time:

> “Certainly,” he says, “it happened to God in time that He should be Lord of man, and that He should be your Lord or mine, since we have only now begun to exist.
