How then shall we persist in saying that nothing is predicated of God accidentally, unless it be because nothing happens to His nature whereby He is changed, or unless these be [Note: [Col. 1255D] In Augustine: ‘or unless these be.’] relative accidents, which happen with some change in the things of which they are said? Thus one is called a friend relatively, and there is some change of will in order that he may be called a friend. But when a coin is called a price, it is called relatively; yet it has not been changed, nor when it is called a pledge. If, then, a coin can without any change in itself be so often called relatively, so that neither when it begins nor when it ceases to be so called does any change take place in its nature or form by which it is a coin, how much more readily ought we to understand concerning the immutable substance of God that something is said relatively of a creature, so that, although it begins to be said temporally, it is nevertheless not understood to have happened to God’s own substance, but to that creature of which it is said: ‘Lord, Thou hast become a refuge for us’ [Ps. 89:1]. A change therefore occurs in us, and by fleeing to Him we become better; but in Him there is none. But He also begins to be [Col. 1256A] our Father [Note: [Col. 1256D] In Augustine: ‘But He also begins to be our Father.’] when we are regenerated through His grace. Thus our substance is changed for the better. Therefore, when God begins to be called something temporally, it is plainly said relatively—not according to an accident in God, but altogether according to an accident in the one of whom something begins to be said relatively of God. And when a righteous person begins to be called God’s friend, he himself changes; but far be it from us to suppose that God loves anyone temporally, as if with a new love! Accordingly, He loved all the saints before the foundation of the world, just as He predestined them; but when they are converted and find Him, they are then said to begin to be loved by Him, so that what is said may be grasped in a way suitable to human feeling. Likewise, when He is said to be angry with the wicked and gracious to the good, they change, not He—just as light is harsh to weak eyes and gentle to strong ones, through their change, not its own.”

No one, therefore, because he knows that God is called Father or Son relatively, should presume to confess that these relational properties are things other than God, since, by Augustine’s own testimony cited much earlier, the divine substance is called simple precisely because there is nothing in it. Augustine also openly professes that every nature either is God or is made by Him, as we have likewise recalled above. Jerome too, as we have mentioned above, calls the properties themselves persons: “For,” he says, “we confess not only the names, but also the properties of the names, that is, the persons.”

For many things are understood relatively even in ourselves, though no sensible person grants that the relations themselves are something other than us. Indeed, each thing is said to be like any other in respect of what it has in being, or opposed or unlike in respect of what it is not. If likeness or opposition is essentially distinct from the thing of which it is called a relation—since likeness itself is again like, and opposition itself opposed—who can reasonably avoid the greatest absurdity of infinity, when no limit occurs in the nature of things? Thus even the number of things would not be fixed for God, since it is not fixed in the nature of things, where no limit occurs. For what could be more ridiculous than that, when someone is now born to whom I become similar, some new thing should come to exist in me because of him, and should necessarily perish when he dies?

[Col. 1256D] Therefore, in this place we call one person different from another because it is separated from it by definition—that is, by the singularity of its property—so that what is proper to this one is not proper to that one. These properties have been distinguished above. Thus the Father is different from the Son in property or definition—that is, He is other—and likewise each of them is other than the Holy Spirit. Unless blessed Augustine had attended to this diversity of properties or definitions, how, I ask, could he have said in Book VII of *On the Trinity*, as we have also recalled above, that for God to be is one thing and for Him to be Father another, although in God the being itself and the Father are numerically the same?

If we wish to explain more expressly what “person” signifies in God, it amounts to saying that He is either Father—that is, divine power begetting; or Son—that is, divine Wisdom assumed; or Holy Spirit—that is, the procession of divine goodness. And to say that God is three persons amounts to saying that He is at once Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Likewise, to say that Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons distinct from one another is as though we said that the three persons are so separated from one another in predication by the diversity of their properties that none is another: that is, the Father is not the Son or the Holy Spirit, nor is the Son the Holy Spirit. We shall have to discuss fully in what follows this mode of predicative statement [Col. 1257B].

And perhaps when we say that there are different persons in God—namely, not only different in definition, but also separated from one another in predication, so that this one is not that one—it is not necessary for the word “different” by itself to bear this meaning; rather, it acquires it from the adjunct “person.” When the noun “person” is uttered in reference to the Godhead, it means as much as if one said disjunctively: God the Father, or God the Son, or God the Holy Spirit. In a certain manner it is said not substantially but relatively, since it denotes those things said relatively—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—under disjunction, although its grammatical construction has no term to which it is said relatively.

Otherwise, when we use “persons” in the plural, it would not seem to prove what we have recalled blessed Augustine said above in Book V of *On the Trinity*, chapter 8: namely, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of such powerfully identical substance that whatever is said of each severally in relation to itself is understood not plurally in the sum total, but singularly. Augustine had also stated at the end of the preceding chapter that, just as the Son is related to the Father, and not-son to not-father, so begotten must be related to begetter, and not-begotten to not-begetter. He called “not-son” and “not-father,” and “not-begotten” and “not-begetter,” relatives in a sense very different from our customary usage; for in these negative names relations are removed rather than conferred, nor do they naturally exist together, as is evident of relatives. For it is not necessary that, if some thing is non-begetting, there should be something non-begotten, or conversely. Thus he called these relatives too in a certain improper sense, according to that sense of relations which they retain by negation, just as “not-man” is said to signify man by destroying him, and every infinite term its finite counterpart.

Do not wonder that three persons are distinguished in the same divine substance in the manner explained, when even according to grammatical teaching we grant that the same man is three persons: the first, inasmuch as he speaks; the second, inasmuch as speech is directed to him; and the third, when one person speaks of him to another. Since these persons have the same substance, they can be distinguished only according to the properties expressed by their definitions. For the property of the speaker, namely of the one who speaks, is one thing; that of the hearer, or of the one concerning whom one speaks to another, another thing. So too the diversity of the divine persons consists in their proper definitions as applied to their significations.

If you do not shrink in this case from calling the persons different because of the diversity of their properties, though they are not separated from one another in predication—so that it is not permissible to call the first person the second, and the second the third—then Socrates himself is granted by grammarians to be every person. Much more must it be granted that there are different persons in God, whom we know to be separated from one another even in predication. Furthermore, just as in grammar, when we say “three persons,” we understand determinately the speaker, the one to whom he speaks, and the one of whom he speaks, as we mentioned above; so, when we say that there are three persons in the Godhead, we must understand determinately the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as we have likewise established above. Otherwise, perhaps we should be compelled to confess more than three persons.

Rhetoricians also understand “person” differently from theologians or grammarians: namely, as a rational substance, when they treat of person and matter, and distinguish rhetorical topics into attributes of the person and attributes of the matter. Boethius follows this meaning in Book IV of the *Topics*:

> “You clear persons of blame for an act when it is attributed to those whom it was impossible to resist or avert; yet they are not persons. For that falls under another constitution.”

And, disputing against Eutyches and Nestorius concerning the unity of the person of God and man in Christ, he pursued this meaning of person with the following definition: “A person is an individual substance of a rational nature.” This definition cannot at all be said of the three persons in the Godhead distinguished by us above, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Otherwise, since there are three persons, there would be three individual rational substances.

We also call the human beings themselves the persons of comedies, namely those who represent to us certain deeds or words through their gestures. Boethius himself distinguished these in the same place, saying: “The name ‘person’ seems to be derived from elsewhere, namely from those *personae* which in comedies and tragedies represented the human beings concerned.”” Therefore the word “person” is used in three or four ways, and perhaps more: differently by theologians, differently by grammarians, differently by rhetoricians, and in comedies, as defined above.

Now, as we stated at the beginning of this work, all perfection of goodness consists in the three divine persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and everything pertaining to the perfection of goodness is comprehended in these three. These three persons alone are therefore rightly distinguished, because these three names, by the force of their signification, contain in themselves all other things suited to commending goodness. For God’s eternity pertains to power, inasmuch as He needed no beginning through which to subsist; whereas His justice or mercy pertains to goodness. Justice is that which renders to each person what is his, repaying either punishment or glory according to merits. This proceeds from the affection of goodness, because just as it is impious not to judge evils, so, conversely, it is pious to avenge injuries inflicted. Therefore vengeance too is to be ascribed to goodness; and this goodness is signified by the name of the Spirit, as it is written: “By the Spirit of His mouth He shall slay the wicked” [Isa. 11:4]. Similarly, the other names of God which serve to define the perfection of that highest good are referred back to these three.

But a serious objection may perhaps arise here. Since Father and Son are especially so called from power and wisdom, as I established at the very beginning of the work, why is one person better distinguished by God’s wisdom than [source: *quae*; perhaps *quam*, “than”] by eternity, when according to eternity too there is some diversity of definition? For just as, according to Augustine, for God to be is one thing and for Him to be Father another, so for God to be eternal is one thing and for Him to be Father another. Must we then, on this reasoning, confess many and innumerable persons in God? For God Himself is powerful, wise, just, eternal, merciful, and many and innumerable things can be said of Him according to the diversity of definitions and properties; yet it is not permitted to assign persons in God according to these, since there are only the three persons we have distinguished: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The answer is that we have not undertaken to determine why the divine persons are distinguished in this mode rather than another, but to show that they can suitably be understood in the mode in which they are distinguished, and that our faith can be defended if someone argues that it cannot stand as we believe. To investigate this belongs to God Himself, from whom this faith has been handed down, and in whose will the causes of all things unchangeably subsist—causes of which no human reason can comprehend even the least.

We do not at all concede that there are more than three persons in God, or fewer, since “person” in God has the determinate force, as we have already defined above, of Father, Son, or Holy Spirit. Philosophers teach many things which are accepted solely because they are confirmed by the authority of philosophers, and not by any evident reason. How much more should we accept what God hands down, especially when a reason is at hand why this distinction of three persons is made: namely, for the commendation or description of the highest good, or, as we have mentioned above, for a stronger persuasion toward divine worship. Yet we may lack even the reason why the perfection of the highest good was described in this mode rather than another, though it could perhaps equally be described or taught in many other ways.

It is also clear that the diversity of persons consists not only in diversity of definitions and properties, but also in the removal of their mutual predication, since no one of the persons is another. The other things mentioned above do not have this mutual exclusion: God the Father Himself is eternal, just, and merciful, and likewise the Son and the Holy Spirit are the same. Having set forth these points concerning identity and diversity of things, and having further assigned wherein the unity of God and the Trinity of persons are to be understood, let us return to the questions and objections set forth above and answer them, in order, as the Lord grants—resolving the first question first.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1259]

[Col. 1259D] The first question is whether the Trinity of persons which are in God is to be understood in words or rather in reality.

We proclaim that it must be understood in reality itself: that from eternity the one, wholly simple and indivisible reality which is God is three persons, as determined above—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Three, as we have said, according to definitions or properties, not according to number. For this soul, and every thing whatsoever, is many and infinite according to the properties of its definitions, not according to numerical distinction: that is, it is such a thing as falls under different definitions, or to which different definitions can be applied—different, I say, in meaning, not in the plurality of things.

For this soul is wise and just, yet the meaning or understanding of the definition “just” is not the same as that of “wise.” Thus, as we say that this soul is diverse in definitions, inasmuch as it is wise and just, so we concede that God is persons diverse in definition, inasmuch as He is God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And although essence and persons are numerically the same in God, it does not follow that, if God is triune in persons, He is triune in essence; or that, if He is one in essence, He is one in persons. That is, it does not follow that if there are three persons, there are three essences, or that if there is only one essence, there is one person.

For when we say “triune in persons,” that is, “three persons,” we understand three according to definitions or properties, as we have sufficiently taught above. But when we say “triune in essence,” that is, “three essences,” we understand three essentially or numerically. We may also understand God to be triune in persons and one in essence as though we said that He is of three definitions or properties, as determined above from the persons themselves, which He Himself is: He is of three definitions inasmuch as He is those persons; and again, He is of one definition in respect of the essence which He Himself is, inasmuch as He is that essence.

If essence and persons were the same in definition—so that “essence” meant precisely the same as “persons”—then perhaps it would be necessary that God be triune in essence as He is in persons, or one in persons as He is in essence: in the sense that He would be of three definitions or properties from persons and likewise from essence, or one from essence and one from persons. But since essence and persons are not the same in definition, this is not necessary.

For though man is numerically the same as “capable of laughter” and “capable of navigation,” and Socrates the same as speaker, hearer, and the person of whom one speaks to another, it does not follow that, if man is many in definition—because he is capable of laughter and navigation—he is for that reason many in respect of being man; nor, if he is one in definition in respect of being man, is he therefore one in respect of being capable of laughter and navigation [the printed text has *si*; perhaps *sic*, “thus,” and is syntactically corrupt]. Likewise Socrates, though he is three persons according to grammarians—namely speaker, hearer, and one of whom another speaks to another—is not therefore three in respect of being Socrates or substance. Indeed, he is one in substance and triune in persons according to the grammatical sense.

Thus God is wholly one in essence and triune in persons: in essence He is one alone numerically, while in persons there are three, diverse in definitions or properties. This Trinity therefore belongs to the diversity of definitions or properties, as stated; unity belongs to essence. Hence they are in no way opposed to one another, since Trinity and unity are understood in different respects: the former according to diversity of definitions or properties, the latter according to number.

Perhaps someone is troubled by our saying that the Trinity of divine persons is to be understood in reality, as though we said that God is triune in persons inasmuch as He is a reality; whereas, inasmuch as He is a reality, He is only one reality numerically and has in Himself neither multiplicity nor diversity even of properties. Whoever says this rightly understands what he says, but not what I have said and determined above. For we do not say that the Trinity is understood in reality in such a way as to call God triune inasmuch as He is a reality. Rather, we determine that His Trinity is in reality and does not consist in words, in that the reality which is God is itself the Trinity—not insofar as it is a reality, but rather insofar as from eternity it is those three persons distinguished by names.

The Trinity does not exist because a distinction of names has been made; rather, because it is eternally Trinity, the temporal distinction of names was made in order to make known to us, who began in time, what it eternally is. Hence when Augustine says that God is one in substance and triune in words, “triune in words” means triune in those things distinguished by words—that is, in persons. The same occurs in Isidore, who says in Book VII, chapter 4, of the *Etymologies*: “Accordingly, the Trinity is in the relative names of the persons, according to that which is expressed and signified in them.”

Thus we understand the Trinity in the reality which is God, not in the force of words; if words were wholly absent, that Trinity would remain no less in reality itself. We understand it in reality in this sense: the reality which is God is that Trinity, not merely insofar as it is a reality, but insofar as it is the persons distinguished above. But for the reality itself to be Trinity is far different from its being Trinity insofar as it is a reality, just as it is one thing for a man to be white and another for him to be white insofar as he is a man; or for Socrates to be three persons according to grammarians and for him to be those three persons insofar as he is Socrates.

Therefore God is not to be said to be Trinity either insofar as He is one reality, or insofar as He is many realities—which is wholly false—but only insofar as He is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: that is, as possessing the three properties determined above, namely that God begets, is begotten, and proceeds.

[Col. 1262C] It should also be noted that although we concede no multiplicity of things in the Godhead, but only a multiplicity of persons, Augustine nevertheless dared, somewhat improperly, to use “things” in the plural when looking to the diversity of persons. In Book I of *On Christian Doctrine* he says:

> “Some things are to be enjoyed, others used. Those which are to be enjoyed make us blessed; by those which are to be used we are helped as we strive toward blessedness. For to enjoy is to cling in love to a thing for its own sake; but to use is to refer what comes into use to obtaining what one loves, if it ought to be loved. For illicit use should rather be called misuse or abuse. If we wish to return to the homeland where we can be blessed, we must use the world, not enjoy it, so that the invisible things of God may be discerned, understood through the things that have been made [Rom. 1:20]. The things to be enjoyed, then, are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and the same Trinity is one supreme thing, shared by all who enjoy it—if indeed it is a thing and not the cause of all things; and if it is also a cause, for a name suited to so great an excellence cannot easily be found.”

In these words, by saying “if” and “if,” he suggests, more doubtfully than affirmatively, that none of the names of creatures is worthy of the divine excellence. Jerome likewise, according to the properties of the divine persons, improperly spoke of three Spirits—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—when, writing of the three virtues, he says:

> “David asks for three Spirits in the Psalm, saying: ‘Strengthen me with a sovereign Spirit; renew a right Spirit within me; and do not take Thy Holy Spirit from me’ [Ps. 50:12–14]. Who are these three Spirits? The sovereign Spirit is the Father; the right Spirit is Christ; the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit.”

Their objection that God is not three persons unless He is also three things, and that consequently there is in God a multiplicity joined from parts, is frivolous. We grant that He is called three persons, and many persons; but it does not therefore follow that He should be called “three” by itself, or simply “many.” For when we say “three persons,” we add “three” to persons accidentally; and hence we need not say “three things” by itself.

Things conjoined in accidental predication need not be said separately, though they are said jointly, as we learned long ago from the second book of *On Interpretation*. For it does not follow that, if something is twenty-first, it is twentieth or first; or that, if these are twenty-one, they are twenty or one; or that, if something is a half-house or an imperfect house, it is a house; or that, if this body is laughing only slightly, it is laughing; or that, if a place is large, it is large; or that, if someone is a good lyre-player according to reputation, he is good; or that, if the Word was made flesh—that is, incarnate—it was made; or that, if God was made a helper, He was made; or that, if this expression “Is” is a simple proposition—that is, one having no propositions among its terms—it is simple, that is, not composed at all of words successively uttered.

Nor does it follow that, if this soul is many persons or many topics according to dialecticians, it is many—that is, many realities distinct from one another. This soul is many persons according to grammarians when someone speaks to it, another speaks about it, and diverse arguments can be made concerning the same soul; or inasmuch as it is opposed to something, similar to something, or has other relations by which it belongs to different topics. Yet because the soul is many topics according to dialecticians—that is, because it has diverse powers of proof—it need not be conceded that it is simply many.

Likewise, although God is many persons—that is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—it must not therefore be granted that He is many, that is, many realities or many essences, since the very same essence which is Father is Son and is Holy Spirit. For “many,” “three,” and all numerical names properly pertain to number; hence they are rightly understood by themselves only of things numerically diverse.

This also agrees with Boethius’s *On the Trinity*, where he says of God: “It has been shown above concerning His form that He is form and truly one, with no plurality; whence we also call the Trinity holy and indivisible.” Yet perhaps God may in some sense be called both three and many, if “three” and “many” are understood according to definition or property rather than number, and if we attend more to the truth of the meaning than to the strict propriety of the words. For He is eternal, immeasurable, creator, omnipotent, and many other things diverse in definition; and He is God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Thus in some sense a multiplicity may be considered in Him according to diversity of definitions or properties, not number.

According to this diversity the Apostle says: “And there are three who bear testimony in heaven, and the three are one” [1 John 3:8, as printed], adding nothing to “three,” neither “persons” nor anything else. Augustine too confirms this in Book VII of *On the Trinity*, chapter 4:

> “Provided that what is said is understood, at least in a riddle, it pleased them to speak in this way, so that something might be said when it was asked what the three are which the true faith declares to be three, since it does not say that the Father is the Son, nor that the Holy Spirit, who is the gift of God, is either the Father or the Son.”

And shortly afterwards in the same chapter:

> “When human poverty strove by speech to bring forth what it holds concerning the Lord God, it feared to say three essences, lest some diversity be understood in that supreme equality. Yet it could not say that there were not three certain things, which Sabellius, because he fell into heresy, did say.”

Thus Augustine plainly affirms that “three” ought to be said according to the diversity of the persons themselves, as stated.

But again, how will three be spoken of unless there is also some plurality? If anyone grants that a plurality of persons may itself be called a plurality, since every plurality is assembled from many parts, will not the plurality of persons that are in God also have parts? But a part, according to Boethius’s testimony, is prior to that of which it is a part, and a thing is constituted by its division into prior elements, as a genus is into subsequent ones. Therefore each of the three persons must be prior to the Trinity which they constitute, and the Trinity itself subsequent to each of them, if not in time, at least in nature. Again, Boethius himself testifies that a part is not the same as the whole, because the essence of the whole and of the part cannot be one and the same, since the part is included, together with others, within the quantity of the whole itself and is therefore smaller. But both the whole Trinity and each individual person are altogether one and the same divine substance. Let us therefore state firmly, as we began: [Col. 1264D] absolutely no plurality subsists in the Godhead, although there is there a plurality of persons; and let us confess the Trinity itself to be wholly indivisible. For although, as was said, there are distinct persons in it, there is nevertheless for that reason no plurality of parts, nor any plurality whatever where there is no diversity of things and essences. Thus we by no means concede that that plurality of persons is absolutely called a plurality, nor that, because the persons are many, they are simply called “many.” For however much anyone may wish to misuse words, neither the term “many” nor the term “plurality” can properly be understood except according to number—that is, except according to some plurality and diversity of things distinguished in their essences: so diverse, namely, that this essence [Col. 1265A] is not that one. Such plurality can in no way exist in the simplicity of the divine substance; and thus there can be no whole composed of some plurality of parts, since there are in no way many things there, although there are many persons, and in no way a diversity of things, although there is a diversity of persons.

Hence Pope Leo, in a sermon on Pentecost, says: “In the divine Trinity there is nothing dissimilar, nothing unequal.” For his saying “nothing” is as though he said “no thing”; and his saying that nothing there is dissimilar is as though he said: “No thing there is different from another,” although the persons are distinct from one another according to their properties, distinguished above, not according to number. Hence Augustine also, *On the Trinity*, book VII, chapter 6: “One man is not as great as three men [Col. 1265B] taken together; and two men are something more than one man. But it is not so in God. For the Father and Son together are not a greater essence than the Father alone or the Son alone; but the three persons together are equal to each one.”

That is, they do not exceed one another in any number of things—lest anyone perhaps be troubled because Isidore, in *Etymologies*, book VI [book VII], chapter 4, while tracing the etymology of the name of the divine Trinity, called the Trinity one whole in relation to the individual persons.

“By these words, indeed, it is called Trinity because one whole is made from three things”—as though *Trinity* were improperly understood to mean a whole from any plurality, whether of things or of properties. In the same chapter, moreover, when he distinguished proper and appellative names of God, he departed so far from all human reasoning and usage that he called proper those which appear more appellative, and conversely called proper names appellatively:

> “In this Trinity some names are appellative, others proper. Proper are the essential names, such as God, Lord, Almighty, Immutable, Immortal; and they are proper because they signify the substance itself by which they are one. But Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; Unbegotten, Begotten, and Proceeding, are appellative; these may also be called relative.”

Since Isidore supplied the etymology of this name “Trinity,” he expressed for us the force of the name generally, not uniquely in [Col. 1265D] the divine Trinity alone. And it is indeed true that, according to its proper and customary meaning, if “Trinity” or “three” is said, it indicates a plurality of things and number; this is least of all appropriate in God, where there is no plurality of things but a diversity of persons.

But when it is said, “Such is the Father as the Son and the Holy Spirit,” a certain likeness is suggested—namely, that the Father is like the Son or the Holy Spirit. This is as though one said: “He is not different from him in any good of majesty”; so that it is to be understood more by negation than affirmation. Similarly, when he is said to be equal, this is as though one said: in [Col. 1266A] that glory of the Godhead, one person cannot be lesser [addition: *non potest*], since they are altogether of the same essence.

And when Athanasius, after saying, “Such is the Father, such the Son, and such the Holy Spirit” [Note: [Col. 1265D] These words are taken from the Creed which the Church sings at Prime every Sunday, [Col. 1266D] and which, as here, is commonly attributed to Athanasius, but is not his.], immediately added—as though to specify in what they are alike, that is, not different—“The Father is immeasurable, the Son immeasurable, the Holy Spirit immeasurable,” etc., he plainly declared how his preceding words should be understood: namely, that what belongs to one person also belongs to the other, with respect to those matters which he immediately adds.

Nor perhaps is it inappropriate if we call alike not only things that are essentially or numerically distinct, but also things distinguished by properties. Thus we say that a proposition and a conclusion agree in their terms and in many other respects, [Col. 1266B] although proposition and conclusion are not thereby distinct from one another numerically or essentially. Hence it is not inappropriate for the divine persons to be called like one another in this way. “Like” is also sometimes used for “the same,” as in the third book of the *Topics*, where Boethius says that the topic from contraries and from incompatibles appears to be similar—that is, the same.

For just as we say that something becomes different from itself, or differing, or unlike, and does not remain the same when it changes, why should we not in some sense call something like itself when it remains and does not vary? For what is like something except to be such as that thing is? And similarly, to be like itself is to be such as it was at first. Augustine follows this reasoning in book I of *On True Religion*, when discussing the identity and immutability of divine beauty:

> “Therefore the mind must be healed for the contemplation of the unchangeable form of things, and of beauty that always remains in the same manner and is on every side like itself, neither extended through places nor varied by time, but preserving one and the same thing in every respect,” etc.

Thus he used “like” for “the same”; and in this sense too the Father may be said to be like the Son or the Spirit: that is, altogether the same with him in substance, or in those things which Athanasius immediately specified—since that same thing which is immeasurable in the Father is also in the Son, and so forth.

But the objection that everything [Col. 1266D] which exists is either substance or form, and so how things can be called many if there are not many substances, many forms, or many compounds of both, has already been cut off by what we have altogether denied: that God is many. For although there are many persons, he is perhaps not therefore simply “many,” since plurality, as said, is properly taken only of distinct essences and numerically diverse things. But if someone accepts that God is many with respect to diversity of properties, as explained, or of definitions, the conclusion does not follow that, if God is in this way many, he is therefore either many substances—which [Col. 1267A] means numerically distinct—or many forms, and so forth. For the same soul, or any substance whatever, is many in definitions, and yet is not therefore many substances or the like. If it were many in number, then the foregoing conclusion would undoubtedly follow.

The question asked—why God is called triune rather than the substance triune—is reasonable; and, I think [Note: [Col. 1267D] This was also the opinion of Hincmar, Archbishop of Rheims, who wrote against Gottschalk a collection from Holy Scripture and the sayings of orthodox writers concerning one Godhead and not a triune Godhead. But the universal Church approved Gottschalk’s view, and daily resounds in churches: “You, O triune and one Godhead, we beseech.”], it ought rather to be said that God is Trinity than that God is triune. Although this can have a sound and proper meaning if we call God triune with respect to the properties of the persons, there seems nevertheless no reason why we should call him triune rather than call the substance triune. Still less do we approve calling God tripartite, although that holy man who said it did not err in intention, understanding the Trinity of persons.

But the assertion is refuted in many ways that, although each of the three persons is God or substance, and one person is not another, there are nevertheless not for that reason several gods or substances. For it is not necessary that, when a singular noun is said separately of several things, a plural noun should be said of them together. For when Plato is the brother of one man and Socrates the brother of another, and it is thereby granted both that Plato is a brother and that Socrates is a brother, it perhaps does not follow that Plato and Socrates are brothers. That is not usually said unless to show [Col. 1267C] that they are brothers to one another.

Again, although both this whiteness and that color are color, we do not therefore call them different colors, since they are not colors differing in species. Likewise, when two men stand before me and I utter the word “man,” by which each is understood as a rational mortal animal, the essence of this understanding and of that understanding is indeed different. Therefore each is an understanding; yet we do not for that reason speak of many understandings, since they conceive different things, though not in a different way.

And when many names or many relationships attach to one utterance, although every relationship and every name is an utterance or an essence, we do not therefore say that there are many utterances or many essences. Again, although the cask in a house is a place and the house itself is also a place, and the one place is not the other, we nevertheless do not call the cask and the house different places; otherwise the wine in the cask would be in different places, although, as we recalled above, no body can be in different places. And although each thing has only its own duration—that is, however long its existence lasts—we do not therefore recognize different times except through succession.

Further, in one man there are many parts so distinct from one another that this is not that; likewise in one [Col. 1268A] piece of wood or one pearl. When the other parts have been cut off or removed, these are still called men, woods, or pearls; and each of those parts, before its severance, was a man, or wood, or pearl. For our act of separation adds nothing in substance to what remains or to what is removed which it did not possess before. When a hand is cut off, what then remains a man was also a man before the cutting. If some hidden part in a man who was whole is likewise afterward cut off, the remainder is a man—which was not a man before the severance—although it then possessed the definition of man, since it was then an animal, being animate and sentient, and rational and mortal in the same manner as it is now.

Since therefore before every severance there were many parts in one man, each of which was a man, there were not for that reason many men in one man; for we call men many only when they are animated by many souls. But if, when there are essentially distinct things, each of which is an understanding or a man, we do not therefore call them many understandings or many men, how much less ought we to call many gods or many substances things of which each person is God or substance, and whose essence is altogether the same?

For, according to grammarians, each of the three persons present in Socrates is Socrates or man—namely, he who speaks is a man or Socrates, as also he to whom someone speaks or [Col. 1268C] of whom someone speaks. Yet we do not for that reason call them three Socrateses or three men, since the essence of the three persons is the same: that is, the essence of the one who speaks, of the one to whom someone speaks, and of the one about whom someone speaks. For the same reason, regarding the three persons in God, whose essence is one, although each is God or substance, we ought not therefore call them three gods or three substances; since, as we have often recalled above, words alter their signification through what is joined to them—such as the expression “three” and many others.

We call the same man three craftsmen by reason of his knowledge of three crafts, yet not therefore three men. The Greeks, however, Augustine testifies, do not hesitate to say three substances rather than three persons. Hence in *On the Trinity*, book VII, chapter 4, he says:

> “For the sake of speaking about ineffable things, so that we might in some way say what we are in no way able to utter, our Greeks have said one essence, three substances; the Latins, one essence or substance, three persons, because, as we have already said, in Latin usage essence is not ordinarily understood otherwise than substance.”

Likewise:

> “What we call persons according to our usage, they call substances according to Greek usage. For they say three substances, one essence, just as we [Col. 1269A] say three persons, one essence or substance.”

But we are not now disputing against the Greeks; nor perhaps do they differ from us in meaning, but only in words, misusing the name “substance” for “person.” They do not refuse, even in the substance of the soul itself, as also in all other substances to which this name is common throughout the category of substance, sometimes to call *ousia*, that is, substance, the nature of the essence itself rather than the property of the person. Indeed, to express the identity of substance to be understood in the three persons, they instituted the new name *Homoousion*, meaning “of one substance.”

Jerome too follows this usage in writing to Damasus, confessing the Trinity itself to be *homoousion*: that is, of one substance, not of one person. Hence Gennadius, *On Orthodox Faith* [Note: [Col. 1269D] Gennadius, *On the Dogmas of the Church*, ch. 5.], says: “Therefore the Son is *homoousios*, that is, coessential in divinity, with the Father; the Holy Spirit is *homoousion* [Note: [Col. 1269D] Read *Homousios*, as in Gennadius.] with the Father and the Son.”

It is therefore clear that, when some of them say “three substances,” they misuse “substances” for “persons.” Jerome openly and rightly rebukes this misuse, writing to the same Pope Damasus [Note: [Col. 1270D] Jerome, Epistle 14.] concerning the new expression “three hypostases”:

> “We ask what they suppose *hypostasis* can be understood to mean. They say: three subsisting persons. We answer that we believe this. The meaning does not suffice; they demand the very word, because I know not what venom lurks in its syllables. But whoever, understanding *hypostasis* as *ousia*, does not say one hypostasis in three persons, is alien from Christ.”

Likewise, the same writer says:

> “The whole school of secular letters knows *hypostasis* as nothing other than *ousia*; and who, I ask, with sacrilegious mouth will proclaim three substances? God’s nature alone is one. Whoever says that there are three, that is, three hypostases, strives to assert three natures. And if this is so, why are we separated by walls from Arius, joined to him in faithlessness? It is enough for us to say one substance, three perfect persons, equal and coeternal. It is not a good sign when words differ while the meaning is the same. Or if you think it right that we should say three hypostases with their interpretations, we do not deny it. But believe me: venom lies beneath honey. Satan transforms himself into an angel of light.”

The objection why we say three persons rather than three gods or three essences is, I think, now clear from the foregoing: the diversity of persons belongs to a distinction of properties, not to a distinction of essences. Thus there are three persons because distinct proper characteristics inhere in the same essence: from being Father he has one proper characteristic or entails one thing; from being Son or Holy Spirit, another. Therefore for God to be three persons is as though we said that he is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. [Col. 1270A] But if we say that there are several gods, as several men, we indicate a distinction of essentially diverse things, each of which is God. Thus, according to grammarians, we call Socrates several persons, but not several men. By the same reasoning it is not fitting to say several Lords or several mighty ones, nor is any plurality at all to be assigned to God except in persons.

It has also been objected: how do we say “Persons are,” unless we say “essence”—that is, “essences are”? But this is said in the way in which we say “Athens is,” just as “this white thing” and “a sitting man” are the same. For plurality or singularity of grammatical form does not always concern signification; sometimes it concerns the ending or construction of the word. Thus we say [Col. 1270B] “number is,” that is, “units are”; and “Athens is,” that is, “this city is.” Sometimes too we utter a plural verb with plural signification because of a plurality of words, or even a plural noun, although the understanding conveyed by the terms is altogether the same, but not the same essence; as when we say that “sword” (*ensis*) and “sword” (*gladius*) are multivocal. Hence Boethius in the first book of the *Topics* says: “Things whose definition is the same are themselves also the same things.” But when we use “are” figuratively wherever only one thing exists, it is not necessary to say “beings” or “essences,” because often, although words taken separately have the same signification, one may by figure have one construction in one sense which the other does not have.

I think the point has likewise been settled that the name “God” should be called more universal than singular when it is said of the divine persons. For that diversity of persons does not consist in a distinction of essence but rather in diversity of properties or definitions, as we have said—just as the diversity of the grammatical persons that are in Socrates does not make the name “Socrates” any less singular.

But here the greatest obstacle arises: the persons in God seem also to be essentially distinct from one another, inasmuch as this one is not that one—a feature not present in grammatical [Col. 1270D] persons. The answer is that these persons are no more essentially distinct than those, since these too, like those, possess one and altogether the same essence in comparison with the unity of which—that is, the divine essence—no bodily or spiritual creature can be called one. For this essence can admit absolutely no diversity either of parts or forms, nor can it be changed in any respect. “Therefore,” says Boethius in *On the Trinity*, “that is truly one in which there is no number, nothing in it other than what it is.” Hence philosophers rightly chose to call it *monad*, that is, unity, rather than “one.”

But although there is no distinction of essence among the persons, it must not therefore be said, “The Father is the Son or the Holy Spirit,” or “The Son is the Holy Spirit.” Even if someone could perhaps attach a sound sense to these words—namely, that the same essence which is Father is also Son and Holy Spirit—the sense according to the usage of the holy Fathers is altogether false. It is as though we said that the person begetting [reading uncertain: *...ntem*, perhaps *generantem*] is the begotten person, or the person proceeding from both: which is to say that the property of each person is the same, so that both persons are to be delimited and expressed by the same definition. This is altogether false.

For although the state of being capable of laughter and the state of being capable of sailing are numerically the same, and moreover whatever is called laughable is also called navigable, we do not say that this state is that state—that is, that “laughable” is the same in definition as “navigable.” For the name “laughable” means one thing and “navigable” another, although the very same thing is subject to both names by appellation: namely, the man to whom both “laughable” and “navigable” are assigned as properties.

Since therefore we do not call a state the same or different except according to its expressed and complete definition or property, when this state is called that state, one thing is thereby shown to be altogether the same as another, without an expressed property. So likewise in the divine persons: since their entire diversity concerns their properties, not the number of things, this person cannot truly be called that person while there is some diversity of property, even [Col. 1271C] if the persons are expressed by names differing in sense—as happens in the persons themselves. For “God the Father” means one thing, “God the Son” another, and “God the Holy Spirit” another. God the Father has one proper characteristic, namely that he begets God the Son; God the Son another, namely that he is begotten by him; God the Holy Spirit another, namely that he proceeds.

Therefore whoever says of God, “The Father is the Son [reading: *Filii*, evidently *Filius*],” does not make a simple assertion merely to demonstrate identity of essence, as though saying, “That which is Father is Son”; but further asserts an identity of properties, as though saying that the same proper characteristic belongs to each, as explained. This is altogether false, even though each person has the same essence.

For we also customarily say that what is useful is not the same as what is honorable, even though what is useful is honorable; and that the grammarian is not the same as the orator, since one proper characteristic belongs to the former, another to the latter. For though grammarian and orator have the same essence, being a grammarian is one thing and being an orator another; being this grammarian is one thing and being this orator another; and being laughable is one thing and being navigable another, although the substance of both is altogether one. Likewise, although the Father and Son have the same substance, being Father is nevertheless different from being Son. Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book V: “Although being Father and being Son are different, the substance is not different.” And in book VII: “Being God is one thing; being Father is another.”

Again, although the same utterance is at times a noun and a verb, or both a word and a sentence, we nevertheless grant that a noun is not a verb, since the former is without time and the latter with time; and that a word is not a sentence, since a word does not have significant parts as a sentence does. Nor perhaps is it fitting to join grammatical persons by predication, such that one person is another, although one is the same as the other, as we recalled above. For though there are three distinct grammatical persons—first, second, and third—perhaps one person is not another person, since each person is distinct from the other.

For when the diversity of certain things consists only in their properties or in a difference of states, not in number or essence, their identity with one another is correctly shown by predicating them of one another: so that when this person is said to be that person—persons separated only by property or definition, that is, diversity of states—it is understood that this is the same as that precisely in property or definition. This is altogether false both in these persons and in the divine persons.

Further, as we recalled above, many things are numerically the same whose names nevertheless are separated in predication. This is especially caused by a force of relation contained in those names, since every relation exists between opposites. For Socrates’ matter and Socrates are numerically the same; likewise Socrates’ prior and Socrates; likewise Socrates’ perpetual and Socrates—since this body or this animal is the same as Socrates. Yet it is not fitting to say that Socrates is Socrates’ matter, although he is the same as Socrates’ matter; or that he is prior to Socrates, that is, to himself; or that he is perpetual, though he is that which is perpetual, namely this body.

Likewise it is not fitting to call the Father his own Son, or the Son his own Father: that is, for one to be from himself, by begetting himself, just as [Col. 1272D] Socrates is not said to be from himself, so as to be his own matter or to be made from himself, although Socrates is the same as his matter—namely, this body—or as that which is made from his matter, namely white Socrates. In the same way, the Father is the same as the Son according to identity of substance, not according to the property of person.

But someone will say to me: “I shall say ‘Father and Son,’ and understand soundly, namely that the same essence which is Father is also Son. For Augustine himself testifies in *On Two Souls*: ‘When the thing is agreed upon, no dispute should be made about words.’ Likewise, in book IV *On Genesis*: ‘Provided that what ought to be understood is understood, one need not be greatly concerned what it is called.’ And shortly afterward: ‘This is what I said: when the matter is granted, there is no need to labor over terms.’”

I reply that I approve a sound understanding alone; but I require words that are Catholic. The Apostle does not without reason warn us to avoid novelties of words: first, lest we appear to despise the saints and the Holy Spirit speaking in them; and, still more, lest, although you may have a sound meaning in your words, another who does not understand your meaning should be offended by them and derive from them a scandal of error.

Therefore, along with the meaning, use words suitable for edification rather than scandal. To express this sense, say not “The Father is the Son,” but “That which is Father is Son”: that is, the essence or substance of both is the same. Nor say that this person is that person, which is to say that the proper characteristic of both is the same; rather say that this person is the same as that person is—that is, that they are of the same substance.

How great a reverence must be accorded even to divine words is shown by their power: God daily brings about wondrous works through the Church’s sacraments at the invocation of his name, even through the most unclean ministers. Hence Christian religion, rightly displaying reverence even toward divine words, does not customarily appropriate the word “God” alone to itself, but preserves it unchanged—although both pagans and Jews have at times diverted it to creatures, when both call things “gods.”

Priscian himself, teacher and writer on speech, warns that usage is especially to be imitated in expressions. And rightly so, since an expression does not have its signification merely from human convention. But Augustine’s saying, “When the thing is agreed upon, no dispute should be made about words,” must be understood where a dispute has arisen about things: that is, about investigating and examining the truth of things rather than the propriety of words. For when we already possess what we sought—the certainty about things which we were investigating—we need not care by what kind of words it is signified or established for us, since we already hold that it is so. But if a question is raised about words—whether the expression spoken says this or that, as here the question is whether “The Father is the Son” is truly said—then the entire controversy must be referred to the force of the words.

[Col. 1273D] Someone may perhaps say that, according to the proposed explanation in which it is said “The Father is not the Son”—that is, the proper characteristic of the one is not the same as that of the other—it would also be permissible to say “The Father is not God,” or “Man is not animal,” since the proper characteristic of these is not the same either. The answer is that our words, when transferred to God, as we recalled above, acquire, from the very singularity of the divine substance, not only a singular signification but sometimes also a singular sense in construction.

Further, figurative and improper expressions should not be extended beyond what authority or usage has established, if we intend to speak for instruction and intelligibility. Thus, when it is said figuratively of God that he does not know the wicked, we should not, by extending the figure, say that he does not know all human beings or does not know everything. Or if I say that I adore the cross, I should not therefore concede that I adore an insensible thing or wood. Or if I say that I believe in Christ or adore him, who is also figuratively called a stone or a serpent, I should not therefore concede that I believe in a stone or serpent, or adore a stone or serpent.

Again, since Christ is one composite person formed from divinity and humanity, and is called God in one respect and man in another, and in him the man is said to be God because he is united to God in one person, and since the divine substance is eternal while the human [Col. 1274B] is not eternal, we are nevertheless not compelled to concede that what is not eternal is eternal, nor that Scripture’s figurative expressions must be extended beyond what is written.

Nor is it lawful for anyone to alter an expression from its accustomed signification, except one whose authority appears most weighty, or unless some grace of ornament recommends it. And what wonder if words, when transferred from creatures to God, change their signification—such as the names “Father” and “Son”—and also change their force in construction, when even words that appear not to change their signification at all do the same? No one rightly understanding unity or most other forms separates them from the substances in which they inhere so as to suppose them numerically or essentially distinct from those substances.

Nor does anyone, when speaking of God’s unity or of one God, or God’s simplicity or a simple God, take these names in God in a sense other than when speaking of the soul’s unity or one soul, or the soul’s simplicity or a simple soul. Yet we do not say that unity or simplicity is soul in the same way as we say that it is God. For any names of forms, when joined to God, show only identity of essence—as though we said that unity is the same as God—which does not occur at all in other substances, as we showed elsewhere when discussing the distinction of the categories.

What wonder, then, if the names “Father” and “Son,” transferred from creatures to God, when joined to each other in creatures show only identity of essence, but in God do not do this alone and additionally show identity of property; whereas, conversely, names of forms joined to God show only identity of essence, though they do not do so when joined to creatures?

Athanasius’s statement, “The Father is almighty, the Son almighty, the Holy Spirit almighty,” perhaps seems especially to confirm that we should concede that the Son or the Holy Spirit is also the Father. For, as we said above, Father is named from power, as Son from wisdom and Spirit from goodness. Who could deny that each person is powerful, wise, and good? Since then the Son is almighty God, [Col. 1275A] and saying “almighty God” has as much force as saying “Father,” is the Son also Father?

To this I think it sufficient first to answer that, as we have said, words considered by themselves often have altogether the same force and equivalence according to their proper signification, yet do not retain the same force in construction. For, according to Priscian’s testimony, “loving” and “one who loves” have the same force; yet, although it is true to say of someone who does not now love that he will be loving, it is not true to say that he will be one who loves. Likewise, “unity” and “one,” “sitting” and “seated,” are perhaps altogether the same in signification, but not in construction, as we taught elsewhere when treating the distinction of categories.

What wonder, then, if we posit that in God the names “Father” and “almighty God” are altogether the same in signification, but concede that they are not of the same construction and do not retain altogether the same sense in the context of a sentence? Thus it may be said that the proposition “The Father is powerful, wise, or good” is suited only to identity of essence—as though one said that he who is Father is powerful, wise, or good. But the proposition “The Father is Son or Holy Spirit” concerns, as said, only identity of property: namely, that the proper characteristic of each is the same, as explained. Therefore that proposition alone is false.

Moreover, who could not be taught from the foregoing that these names do not have exactly the same force in God: Father and Powerful; Son and Wise; Holy Spirit and Gracious? Otherwise Father and Son would not be spoken of relatively to one another more than Powerful and Wise; nor the Holy Spirit in relation to the Father and Son more than Gracious. Therefore the name Father does not signify divine power alone, but determines it also as begetting; as though one said: “Divine power begetting divine Wisdom.” Nor does Son simply indicate divine Wisdom, but signifies it as begotten from the Father. The Holy Spirit likewise determines divine Goodness as proceeding from the Father and the Son. Hence the names Father, [Col. 1275D] Son, and Holy Spirit rightly distinguish the persons—that is, they show their difference from one another—since these names distinguish this person as begetting, that one as begotten from this one, and again another as proceeding from these two.

For some difference between things mutually separated in predication is implied by relative names; hence Aristotle himself calls them opposites. And a certain separation of predication is indicated in the one who begets and the one begotten by him, and in the one who proceeds and those from whom he proceeds. It is therefore not surprising that, because of such distinction among the persons, these names are mutually separated in predication—names which both signify and join relations—whereas the foregoing names [Col. 1276A] are by no means relative. This can also easily be assigned in the generations or creations of other things, even where the essence of the generating thing and of the thing generated is the same.

For philosophers teach that what is made of matter is in a certain manner generated and created from matter itself. Thus Plato posits *hyle*, that is, corporeal nature, as the mother of bodies; and Boethius, in the book *On Divisions*, says that a genus is divided into species as into certain creations, as it were, from itself, because species are born and constituted from the substance of the genus itself when form supervenes: as a human being comes from an animal when rationality and mortality supervene upon the animal, just as a statue comes from bronze when a shape supervenes.

And although the matter is the same as the thing made of matter, just as animal is the same as human being, or this bronze [Col. 1276B] as this statue, nevertheless the thing made of matter is not its own matter, nor is the matter made of matter from itself, although it is the very thing that is its matter. Or it is the very thing that is made of its matter: for example, this statue is this bronze, and this bronze is this statue. And although, taken by themselves, the terms “matter” and “that from which something consists materially,” or “thing made of matter” and “that which is made materially from something,” have the same force, nevertheless they need not be predicated of the same thing in construction, since this term completes the substance by that property—a property which consists in the relation of matter or of the thing made of matter. I think that above we have sufficiently discussed this difference of predication.

Great discrimination must therefore be used in these propositions [Col. 1276C] made concerning God: namely, to determine which are fitted only to identity of essence and which also to identity of property. The following concern identity of essence only, not of property: “The Father is God,” “The Son is God,” “The Holy Spirit is God,” or eternal, or Lord, or creator, or almighty, or immense, or just, or merciful, and many others; and these are therefore true. But such propositions as “The Father is the Son or the Holy Spirit,” or “The Father is Begotten or Proceeding,” concern identity of property and are therefore altogether false.

For in the former cases it was shown only that the thing of the predicate term and that of the subject term are the same—for example, that God is the same as Father, and so forth. But here it is asserted that the thing of the subject term has also the property of the predicate term [Col. 1276D]: that what is proper to one person is proper to the other, or that the property present in one person is also present in the other. That is, it would belong to the Father to be begotten from the Father—that is, from himself—as it belongs to the Son to be begotten from the Father himself. This is wholly false, as we shall show more carefully when we discuss generation later.

Therefore, if, in accordance with Athanasius, we are neither to confuse the persons—that is, mingle them, one in the property of another—nor separate the unity of substance, we must carefully distinguish the force of the individual propositions: which are fitted to identity of substance and which to identity of property.

It should also be noted that, when in describing [Col. 1277A] the Highest Good his power, wisdom, and graciousness are mentioned, as we have often taught above, these are assigned relatively rather than simply. For God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are described as mutually related and eternally connected, so that the unity and concord of the Trinity of persons may be more greatly commended: we confess that one person is begotten from another and another proceeds from these two—that is, one is from another, or from those persons.

From what has been said concerning the distinction of propositions, it is clear that the objection advanced above is refuted. It was objected that, just as it is shown from “The Father is God” and “God is eternal” that the Father is eternal, so likewise [Col. 1277B] from “The Father is God” and “God is the Son” it could be shown that the Father is the Son. For there the proposition resulting from the two premises, namely “The Father is eternal,” concerns identity of essence alone, just as the premises do, as we have already established above; and therefore it is rightly inferred from them.

But “The Father is the Son” shows not only identity of essence, but also identity of property; and so it does not follow from the premises, which concern simply identity of essence. Indeed, it is plainly false; and hence it is plainly false that from “The Father is God” and “God is the Son” one must concede that the Father is the Son. This would mean, as we have already explained, that the Father’s and the Son’s proper characteristic is the same: namely, that the Father, insofar as he is Father [Col. 1277C] and Son, begets himself—that is, himself.

If, to prove this inference also, someone invokes the dialecticians’ rule which says: “Whenever something is predicated of something, whatever is predicated of the predicate is also predicated of the subject”—that is, whenever some thing is something and that same thing in turn is something else, the first is the last—one may readily see that the rule has nothing to do with this inference and cannot establish it. For the rule pertains only to propositions concerning identity of essence alone, not also identity of property, as does this proposition, “The Father is the Son.”

Indeed, if we attend carefully to the force of the words, the following rule would rather have to be invoked, if it were true: “Whenever something is predicated of something, and something is predicated of the predicate, the proper characteristic of the first subject and of the final predicate is the same.” Since this is plainly false, it is not to be regarded as a rule. We may also say, if we attend more carefully to the force and meaning of the words than to their sound, that when “The Father is the Son” was inferred from the premises, what was first predicated was not the same as what was now predicated. For the statement was “God is the Son,” just as when one says, “This wax is this image, and this image is from this wax”: as though, “The Son who is from the Father; therefore this wax is from this wax.” But we shall have to speak carefully of this later, when we discuss the generation of the Word.

There are other arguments of a similar arrangement, in which the foregoing rule seems applicable because of the arrangement of the terms, though it is far from the meaning of the words. Such are these inferences: “This man is this body; but this body always exists; therefore this man always exists.” Again: “This man is this body, and this body is the matter of this man,” or “this man has been made,” or “this is prior to the man”; therefore “this man is the matter of this man,” or “this man has been made,” or “this is prior to the man.” Again: “This cithara-player and this good or praiseworthy cithara-player; therefore this soldier.” We have treated these kinds of argument more fully in our *Dialectic*.

That the Son alone, and not also the Father or the Holy Spirit, is said to have been incarnate, although the same essence which is Father, Son, or Holy Spirit [Col. 1278B] was incarnate, has been handed down for a weighty reason. For by the words “the Son of God was incarnate” it is shown that the light of divine Wisdom shone upon those who are fleshly through this incarnation, and that God intended by assuming flesh to impart to us this benefit alone, or particularly this benefit. For this reason he was called the Angel of Counsel, or Counsellor.

John the Evangelist also indicates this: “Life,” he says, “was the light of men; and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:4). Of this illumination it is also written: “Arise, be enlightened, Jerusalem, because your light has come” (Isa. 60:1); and again: “The nations shall walk in the light” (ibid., v. 3). And the Psalmist says: “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10). And Simeon: “A light for the revelation of the Gentiles” (Luke 2:32). And the Platonists: “The Word, God, is the true light,” and so forth.

When asked by the Jews who he was, so that they might hear what he intended, he answered: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25), as though saying: “I am the Word before time, who have come in time to instruct you by words and to preach the kingdom of God.” Therefore, to say that the Wisdom of God was incarnate is as though one said that God was incarnate for this purpose: truly to instruct us in the doctrine of righteousness, both by preaching and by the example of his bodily life.

Hence Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, book I, chapter 14:

> “God came in a human being because he could not be known by human beings through himself, whose reason, namely, was already so oppressed and darkened by the multitude of sins that it was unable to rise to invisible things [the correction reads: ‘was by no means able’], unless it were led by certain visible judgments.”

Thus, for the Wisdom of God to be in flesh is for fleshly persons—that is, human beings—to have received through this incarnation the light of true wisdom, and for it to have kindled the shell of our mortality with its light. As it is written: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). This is as though he said openly: “Wisdom itself was incarnate for this purpose: that by illumination the true knowledge of Wisdom might dwell in us.” In the flesh which he assumed, by the manner of his life, as I have said, and also by his deathly passion, and by the glory of his resurrection and ascension, he perfectly instructed and taught us.

By dying, indeed, he taught [Col. 1279A] us how greatly he loved us, in accordance with what he himself says: “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). In this very act he set before us an example of striving for him even unto death. Hence the apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you may follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21). By rising again, he proclaimed the life of immortality by displaying it. By ascending, he taught us that we, his soldiers, are to be drawn there where our substance already reigns in the King, and that we are always to dwell there in mind, where our head has already gone before us. Hence the Apostle says: “Seek the things that are above, where Christ is, at the right hand of God the Father” (Col. 3:1).

[Col. 1279B] Since, then, in everything the Lord did in the flesh the purpose is our instruction, Wisdom alone is rightly said to have been incarnate and to have displayed this to us in the flesh which it received. For he did all things in the flesh in order that true Wisdom might teach us what was sufficient for salvation. And although in certain miracles or other deeds he displayed his power, all belong to the purpose of teaching, so that by his deeds also he might teach us, from his own power, to receive faith.

Thus a human being first had to be taught what to believe or do, and then drawn to love the things known. The things which the Lord did in the flesh, as we have said, pertain to teaching. But for the fervour of love, which would endure [the correction reads: “tolerate”] every adversity, so that the word of God might be preached throughout the earth with free voice, there was that infusion of the Spirit which was revealed over the disciples in fire on the day of Pentecost.

But someone may tell me that, since this incarnation was accomplished by the grace of divine mercy alone and not from our merits, it ought above all to be attributed to the Spirit, so that the Spirit rather than the Son should be said to have been incarnate. For it is written: “Conceived by the Holy Spirit”; that is, he was incarnate from the graciousness of his mercy alone. To this one must answer that it is one thing to be conceived from the Spirit and another for the Spirit to be conceived—that is, to be incarnate—just as it is one thing to be reborn from water and Spirit and another for water and Spirit to be reborn.

If, then, anyone attends to the force of the proposition, “The Son was incarnate,” which the authority [Col. 1279D] of the saints established, the Son alone was incarnate, not also the Father or the Spirit. For its meaning is as though we said that God was incarnate solely, or chiefly, in order that by the visible assumption of flesh he might illuminate those predestined to be his own with the light of true Wisdom.

Although the operation of the three persons is not different, since their essence is in no way different, nevertheless, because the persons and works differ, some works are specially attributed as proper to one person and others to another. To the Father are properly attributed things pertaining to power: creating all things from nothing, though through his Word and not the Word through the Father; disposing all things according to his will; commanding; granting powers; sending his Son into the world; and receiving obedience. Thus it is written: “obedient to the Father” (Phil. 2:8). Finally, all things pertaining to power and to reverence for majesty are specially attributed to the Father.

Christ’s words themselves plainly suggest this. When his humanity was placed in distress and sought help of strength from the divinity united with it in one person, or whenever it poured out prayers to him, it used the name “Father” alone, thus recalling the power by which he is able to accomplish what is asked. [Col. 1280C] This is especially preserved even now in the ecclesiastical custom of its special prayers made at the altar during the celebration of Mass: these prayers are directed to the Father alone. But when the Son himself says, “the things which the Father has placed in his own power,” rather than “which the Son has placed in his own power,” or “which the Holy Spirit has placed in his own power,” he suggests that divine power is properly and specially to be ascribed to the Father.

To the Son, moreover, are especially ascribed those things which pertain to Wisdom, such as judging, which belongs to discernment. Hence it is written: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), because in the examination of judgment the power of wisdom has precedence, where equity is to be examined more than power exercised. The title of Psalm 9 also pertains to this: “For the hidden things of the Son,” namely judgments. He is also rightly called the mind of the Father, or reason, or Angel of Counsel, because the Father rationally orders all things in this Wisdom, whether creating the world or restoring it after the Fall. And in this the Father gave true counsel to our ignorance, when he visited us in the incarnation of the Son.

[Col. 1281B] Therefore, when the Son of God is called *Logos*, that is, Word, it is understood according to the sense in which *logos* among the Greeks signifies the mind’s very concept or reason, not the utterance of the voice. Hence Boethius, in book II of his commentary *On Aristotle’s Categories*:

> “Since in Greek speech *logos* means both thought of the mind and inward reasoning, and *logos* also means discourse, lest anyone should suppose that Aristotle, when he said *logon*, that is, discourse, is a quantity, meant the *logos* which each person arranges in thought, he added: ‘which comes about with the voice.’”

Hence also blessed Augustine recalls in book 83 of the *Questions*, chapter 44:

> “In the beginning was the Word, which in Greek is called *logos*; in Latin it signifies both reason and word. For *logos* is called reason.”

The same author, in book V *Against Heresies* (on John 1), says:

> “In the beginning was the Word. The Greeks say *logos* more aptly. For *logos* signifies both word and reason.”

Concerning this Word of God, namely the intelligible Word, which, as has been said, is understood as his Wisdom, blessed Pope Gregory in a homily … “working.”

> [Note: [Col. 1281D] Thus the manuscript leaves a blank space, which should have been occupied by a passage from St Gregory; it gives only its final word, namely “working.”]

To the Spirit, however, are ascribed as proper those things which pertain to the bestowal of divine grace: such as remission of sins and the distribution of every gift [Col. 1281D] proceeding from his goodness alone rather than from our merits. Such is regeneration in baptism for the remission of sins; confirmation through the laying on of a bishop’s hand, for giving the armour of virtues by which, after receiving remission of sins, we may resist the enemy when he then rises more violently against us. Thus the other sacraments conferred in the Church are likewise to be attributed to the Spirit from God’s goodness. For although the dialectician and the orator are the same person, one thing is nevertheless to be attributed to the orator according to the character of his office and another to the dialectician.

> [Note: [Col. 1279] In Migne the following paragraph is printed in parallel with the section “some works are specially … Boethius on the *Categories*.”]

[Col. 1279D] Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord and Certain Sayings of the Apostle Paul*, Sermon 74:

> “This question is commonly proposed by the studious: Does the Father do something which the Son does not do, or the Son something which the Father does not do?
