I shall speak of the Father and the Son. But when our effort here has been completed—for we say, ‘Be my helper; do not forsake me’ (Ps. 26:9)—it is understood that the Holy Spirit does not at all depart from the operation of Father and Son.
>
> “Brothers, listen: Does the Father do anything without the Son? We answer: No. For what does he do without him through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made? We understand, certainly, that the immense creation was made through the Son. Therefore the Father does nothing without the Son, and the Son does nothing without the Father.
>
> “A question arises: if the Father does nothing without the Son and the Son does nothing without the Father, will it not consequently follow that we should also say that the Father was born of the Virgin, suffered, rose again, [Col. 1280C] and ascended into heaven? The question proposed pleases us; may God grant that its solution also please us. The Son indeed, I say, not the Father, was born of the Virgin. But both the Father and the Son effected that birth. The Father did not suffer, but the Son did. Yet both the Father and the Son effected the Passion. The Father did not rise again, but the Son did; both the Father and the Son effected the Son’s resurrection.
>
> “The Apostle says: ‘God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, that he might redeem those who were under the law’ (Gal. 4:4–5). Behold: the Father caused the Son to be born of the Virgin. We have proved that the Son’s birth was effected by the Father; let us prove that it was also effected by the Son. What is the Son’s birth from the Virgin? Surely, the assumption of the form of a servant in the womb of the Virgin. Therefore, because the Son [Col. 1281A] ‘emptied himself, taking the form of a servant’ (Phil. 2:7), we see that the Son’s birth was also effected by himself.
>
> “The Father effects the Son’s Passion, ‘who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all’ (Rom. 8:32). The Son too effects his own Passion. ‘He loved me,’ says the Apostle, ‘and gave himself up for me’ (Gal. 2:20). This Passion happened to one person, but was effected by both. The Father effects the Son’s resurrection. The Father raised the Son, and the Son raises himself. Referring to the temple as a figure of his body, he said: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up’” (John 2:19).

Perhaps some may be troubled by our saying that the operation of the Trinity is undivided: that each of the three persons performs the very same thing which one of them performs, so that whatever the Father does, the Son or the Spirit does also, and conversely. For the Son alone is said to have assumed flesh and suffered; the Spirit alone is said to regenerate us in baptism; and the Father alone begets the Son.

To this I think one must answer that, although we cannot say that either the Father or the Spirit assumed flesh—that is, was incarnate or suffered—nevertheless we truly profess that in this very incarnation both the Father and the Spirit worked. From it we cannot exclude either divine power or graciousness. For when someone clothes or arms himself, many cooperate in the same act, though they are not themselves clothed or armed. Therefore, although not every verb of operation which suits one person suits another, the operation of one person must nonetheless be said to belong no less to the others, because all necessarily cooperate together in the same thing.

Likewise, all our actions are not improperly attributed to the soul itself, which moves and animates the body; yet not every action-word in predication is referred to the soul. For no one says that the soul walks or eats, but that the animal itself does so; yet it is certain that the action by which the soul thus moves and animates the body in walking or eating belongs to the soul alone, which walks and eats through its actions. These verbs are signified in the soul itself when the animal is said to walk and eat. That is to say [Col. 1282C] that the animal is so moved and animated by its soul that the soul alone is understood to act in this, while the body itself is acted upon.

Since, therefore, these verbs indicating the soul’s actions cannot in any way be predicated of the soul, although those actions belong to it alone, it is not surprising that among the three divine persons, although their action is common, the Word himself is nevertheless said specially of one of them, according to a certain expression, as we have said, of the property of that person. What we put forward, however, to establish the conclusion of the work—that the Father alone begets—appears irrelevant, since this generation, which is eternal, is not any work or creation of God.

There remains the final objection: namely, that the same thing is born from itself or proceeds from itself. This cannot properly be examined unless we determine what such generation or procession is.

And first let us discuss generation, asserting nothing as the teaching of truth, as we have sufficiently recalled above, but defending under a kind of devout veil of likeness what Truth has taught us. For in this little work we intend not to teach truth but to defend it, especially against pseudo-philosophers, who attack us chiefly by philosophical arguments. Therefore we have resolved to satisfy them principally through the same philosophical arguments which alone they accept and by which they assail us, defending truth rather than teaching it.

If any believer should object to me that, after so many and such great teachings of the saints, neither my teaching nor my defence is now necessary, he may perhaps be right with respect to teaching, but not with respect to defence. For since each person abounds in his own opinion and, with differences of persons and times, new questions and attacks arise every day, I think that they must be resisted every day by new arguments and that new remedies must be sought for diseases as they arise. It may be that in ancient times the holy Fathers refuted with sound arguments the objections which they then heard advanced against the Catholic faith, and treated the diseases which they then encountered, but not those which perhaps they had not yet detected as multiplying each day.

For as long as the present Church indiscriminately contains chaff with grain, and the enemy does not cease to sow weeds over the Lord’s harvest until, at the end of the age, the reapers—the angels of God—gather the weeds and bind them into bundles to be burned in fire, schismatics cannot be absent, heretics cannot be lacking, nor will a safe road lie open among scorpions and serpents. Rather, for the testing or exercise of believers, Mother Church will always have under Christ’s name many antichrists to endure. Groaning over them, she may say every day: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (John 11:19), and with motherly affection, every year, offers public sacrifices of prayer that they may return.

“For there must,” says the Apostle, [Col. 1283C] “be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 2:19). We expect this especially in the last times, as the kingdom of Antichrist approaches, when, according to the sentence of the Lord and the Apostles, graver dangers are always known to threaten and increase, and, as charity grows cold, every evil to spring up more abundantly. Hence the same Apostle says to Timothy: “Know this: in the last days perilous times will come, and people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, puffed up, proud, blasphemers, without peace, having indeed an appearance of godliness but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3:1 ff.). Elsewhere he says: “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10:11).

And Peter, in his second Epistle: “Knowing this first, that in the last days mockers will come in deception,” and so forth (2 Pet. 3:3). And John: “Little children, it is the last hour; and as you have heard that Antichrist is coming, now many antichrists have arisen. From this we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2:18–19). Hence it is also written in the Epistle of Jude: “But you, beloved, remember the words foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said to you that in the last times mockers will come … These are those who separate themselves … [Col. 1284A] and rebuke these as judged” (Jude 18, 19, 22).

It is as though he openly exhorted us, saying: “Take care that you may be able to judge such persons and convict them by arguments, always prepared, as blessed Peter says, to give satisfaction to everyone asking you a reason for the hope and faith that are in you, so that those who speak ill of you may be put to shame when they slander your good conduct in Christ” (1 Pet. 3:15). The same Paul, his fellow apostle, likewise admonishes: “Let your speech,” he says, “be seasoned with grace and salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. 4:6).

Heretics are to be restrained more by argument than by force, since, according to the authority of the holy Fathers, believers, for whom all things work together for good, are made more watchful and cautious through their disputations. Hence Jerome, in book II on Jeremiah: “Heresy is useful for a time, so that the elect may be made manifest and approved.” Augustine, *Against the Letter of Parmenian*:

> “If heretics were within the Church, they would nonetheless err. But when they are outside, they are of very great benefit—not by speaking the truth, which they do not know, but by stirring up carnal Catholics to seek the truth and spiritual Catholics to receive it. Let us therefore make use of heretics, not so as to approve their errors, but so that, by defending Catholic teaching against their snares, we may be more watchful and cautious, even if we cannot call them back to salvation.”

Isidore, *Sentences*, book I, chapter 19:

> “Holy Church exercises wisdom when it is tried by words; it exercises patience when it is tried by swords. The Church’s teaching has been propagated because of the perversity of heretical doctrine. For previously the Church flourished by simple faith alone. Therefore, through the occasion of heretics, teachers in the faith have multiplied, and through the acuteness of heresies the masters of the Church have increased.”

Thus the holy teachers, observing that the disputations and inquiries of heretics were so necessary for the exercise of believers, as has been said, ordained that they be restrained by reason rather than force; and, as though desiring so great a victory, they especially urged them to the study of sacred learning. Hence Jerome, to Nepotianus: “Learn,” he says, “what you teach, so that you may be able, by sound teaching [Col. 1284D] [Note: [Col. 1283D] In Jerome, ‘sound’; so too in the Apostle.], to refute those who contradict, always prepared to give satisfaction to everyone asking you a reason for the hope that is in you.”

Gregory, to Boniface: “… convince them rather than by force.”

> [Note: [Col. 1283D] Here too a blank space is left for the text of St Gregory, of which the writer has supplied only the final words, namely “convince them rather than by force.”]

But by what reasoning can we convince those who refuse to accept the good of Christianity? By what admonitions or exhortations can we draw them to faith, if we put forward something doubtful in the very profession of our faith which we cannot defend, much less establish? No one can be argued with by the authority of Scripture if he does not accept it.

If anyone still persists in censuring me and, since those dangerous [Col. 1285A] times have not yet arrived, wholly rejects or disregards our writings, let him at last hear Jerome: “Foreign merchandise sails only for those willing to voyage.” We write these things only for those who wish them—indeed, for those who press and assail us insistently because we have not dared to defend the faith we preach—especially since faith is plainly the foundation of all goods, and whoever can shake it will leave nothing of what is built upon it firm.

But if it is permissible to profess the truth [understood: then it is especially permissible], whenever we judge that no [read: some] heresies or schisms even of this time are to be censured or corrected—heresies or schisms which we ourselves have not heard from those who profess them or learned from those who have heard them. For, as we have recalled above, there are people who, in assigning a distinction among the three persons, understand three properties in God as though they were three things essentially distinct from God himself.

One of these, a teacher of great reputation flourishing in the district of Anjou, has dared to rush into such madness that he wishes all names of creatures transferred to God to suit God himself through forms essentially distinct from God, as they are in creatures. Thus, when God is called just, just as a human being is just, he understands justice as essentially distinct from God, just as it is distinct from a human being; and similarly when God is called wise or strong. He also wishes even God’s own proper names to posit in God qualities or forms just as in creatures: for example, the name “eternal,” and likewise “God” or “Creator.” He especially strives to establish this from Priscian’s assertion that it belongs to a noun to signify substance and quality, and from the definition of a noun itself, by which Priscian asserts that every noun assigns proper or common qualities to subject bodies or things.

Concerning such people, the saying of Gregory which we recalled above may fittingly be thought applicable: “I judge it utterly unworthy to restrict the words of the heavenly oracle under the rules of Donatus.” There is another in France who sets himself above all as the singular teacher of the divine Page. Although he himself vehemently maintains the point made in the case of the others—namely, that we concede that absolutely nothing exists in God which is not God—he nevertheless seems to have fallen into no lesser error because of the supreme unity of divinity which he maintains, when he professes with us that nothing exists in God besides substance itself.

For from this he has been compelled, as I myself heard from him, to confess that God begets himself, because the Son is begotten from the Father. And, most arrogant of all, he plainly calls heretics all who do not hold this view. Those who have studied under him also assert that he has now so separated himself from the Church in faith that he maintains that many who lived before God’s Incarnation are saved and redeemed through his Passion, although they never believed either his Incarnation or his Passion.

And, what is astonishing to all Catholics, as was recently reported [the text reads *ablated*, apparently for *allatum*, “reported”] to us, he was not afraid publicly to assert in his schools that the incarnate Lord was born with the Virgin’s womb opened, as other human beings are, except that he alone was conceived without intercourse with a man.

I also know of a certain man of no small name among the masters of our time who has been brought, by certain lines of argument which he maintains, to profess that God can even be deceived, namely because things can turn out otherwise than he foresaw them. I do not believe that this was ever permitted to be said even among pagans, or however great unbelievers. We know also two brothers who count themselves among the highest masters. One of them attributes such force to the divine words in the making of the sacraments that, by whomever they are uttered, they have equally their own efficacy, so that even a woman, or anyone whatever of whatever rank or condition, can by the words of the Lord consecrate the sacrament of the altar. The other relies so greatly on philosophical schools that he professes that God is in no way prior to the world in existence. There is also a compatriot of theirs, most celebrated among theological masters, who has broken out into such madness as to maintain that the Lord’s body in the Virgin’s womb was of the same length and thickness as it was when he had reached mature age. Nor is it certain that that greatest controversy concerning the sacrament of the altar has yet received a conclusion: whether the bread which is seen is merely a figure of the Lord’s body, or is also the true substance of the Lord’s own flesh. And there are countless other matters, at the daily reports of which we are often astonished, and which cannot be checked even by the burnings of those caught by the people. Let those who judge that nothing further ought to be written about the faith attend to these things, when, as they say, a thousand heresies are springing up in this age—as though they themselves knew the consciences and faith of all.

Let us now return to our purpose: to discuss, insofar as we can, the generation [of the Son], in order, as we have said, to defend our faith, not to teach it. I have decided that this must especially be done because the analogies which we learned from the holy Fathers for defending this generation of the Son or the procession of the Spirit, or for assigning the distinction of persons, seem insufficiently satisfying to some. For in the things introduced by analogy, identity of one essence cannot be preserved. Hence I have often heard certain of the faithful murmuring, almost mockingly, when an analogy is drawn to these matters from things that are not of the same essence. For example, in that sermon on the Nativity of the Lord, blessed Augustine, in defending the claim that the Son alone was incarnate, took an analogy from a lyre and from the sun. By it he showed that it is not surprising that, although three persons coincide in one substance of divinity, something may belong fittingly to one of them that does not belong to another—namely, incarnation to the Son alone.

“As,” he says, “in one act of playing the lyre three things cooperate—art, hand, and strings—yet different things are done by each: art dictates, the hand touches, the strings resound. So too in the sun heat and radiance do different things: heat dries, radiance illuminates.”

But I know what some people mutter in response: they say that these examples do not touch the force of the question, which arose from the identity of one substance in three persons. “No one,” they say, “doubts that different things perform different actions in the same work, or that different qualities have different powers in the same substance. But this is what we find astonishing: since the substance or essence of the three persons is altogether one, why is this one said to be incarnate and not that one, when the substance of divinity itself, which is one and the same and belongs equally to each person, assumed flesh?”

There was also in our own recent times a certain Anselm, metropolitan of Canterbury, who, while preserving the unity of substance, seems to have introduced a stronger analogy for the matters we have mentioned. The foundation of this analogy, unless I am mistaken, he took from blessed Augustine, writing to Pope Laurence on this very subject and adducing a spring and its stream, which have the same substance, as an example of divine generation, in which the substance of generator and generated is the same.

Accordingly, the aforesaid archbishop posits, as it were, three things of the same substance: a spring, a stream, and a pool. The spring, from which the stream comes, represents the Father, from whom the Son comes; the pool, which proceeds from spring and stream, represents the Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and the Son. He also placed the stream in a pipe, as the Son in human flesh; so that, if we call the stream “piped,” we mean the incarnate Word.

Yet this analogy too can be no more satisfactory [read: *maius*, “more”], because the substance of spring, stream, and pool is not simultaneously the same. Rather, by succession in time, the same water was first a spring, then a stream, and finally became a pool. Hence it is not surprising if, through temporal succession, the same substance of water exists in different modes, since the same numerically identical substance is never simultaneously that of spring and stream or pool. Thus one can never truly say, “The water of the spring is now the water of the stream or pool,” as we always say that the substance of the Father is the substance of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

Indeed, this analogy perhaps chiefly supports that heresy which so confuses the properties of the persons through time that it says the same person is Father when it wishes, Son when it wishes, or Holy Spirit when it wishes. Therefore, if by analogy we are to give a satisfactory account of this generation or procession, an analogy of generation or procession must be devised in which the substance of generator and generated, or of the proceeding one and that from which it proceeds, is simultaneously the same, while their properties remain unmixed: so that the generated is not the generator, nor the proceeding one that from which it proceeds.

I think that we can find this more easily if, according to the Apostle’s testimony, we carefully observe how, “from the creation of the world, through the things that have been made,” even the philosophers themselves—whose arguments are used to attack us—were able, through fitting proportions of analogies, by the Lord’s revelation, to trace and assign three persons in one and the same divine substance, distinct from one another in their properties. For it is written: “What is known of God is manifest to them” (Rom. 1:19), that is, not only manifest to them, but also in them—that is, through them and their writings, to others. “For God revealed it to them” (ibid.), illuminating their reason so that from the likeness of bodily or visible things they might rise to contemplate the incorporeal and invisible nature of divinity.

“From the creation of the world, through the things that have been made” (ibid. 20): both from ourselves and from nature, according to that philosophical account whereby some things are said to consist of matter and form, others by an analogy to matter and form. In these constitutions, although the substance of constituent and constituted is wholly one—for example, matter and the thing made of matter—the matter itself and the thing made of matter are nevertheless distinct from one another in property: for instance, wax itself and the wax image made from it. Let us first proceed concerning generation.

Let us therefore place before our eyes a wax image and consider in it the nature of wax itself—that is, the wax substance from which, according to philosophers, the wax image exists as a thing made of matter from matter. Yet wax itself and the wax image are the same essence, so that wax itself and the image itself may even be joined in predication, and one may say that the wax image is the wax itself. Nevertheless, we do not on that account cease to say that the wax image is from wax, not wax from the wax image; and that wax itself is the matter of the wax image, not that the wax image is the matter either of the wax itself or of the wax image.

Again, we say that the wax image is made of matter from wax itself, but we do not say either that wax itself or the image itself is made of matter from the wax image. In this matter one must observe that, if we take names of wax itself and of the wax image which are said absolutely and not relatively, they may truly be joined to one another in predication because of the identity of the substance of wax itself and wax image. Thus, if the wax itself is yellow and the image is upright, the yellow thing and the upright thing are one and the same, or conversely.

But if we take names which are said relatively to one another according to the generation or constitution of the wax image from wax—such as matter and that which is made of matter, constituent and constituted, cause and effect, generator and generated—it is not permissible to join them to one another in predication according to their properties. Thus we may not say that the matter itself is the thing made of matter, or that the thing made of matter is matter, and so forth.

If we apply the reasoning of this analogy to divine generation, it is easy to assign and defend there all that we hear. Let us therefore posit, as we recalled above, God the Father as divine Power and God the Son as divine Wisdom, and let us consider that Wisdom itself is a certain power—for it is the very power of truly discerning, foreseeing, or deliberating all things, so that nothing can deceive God or escape his notice.

> **Note:** Peter Abelard uses another analogy in his *Introduction to Theology*, namely that of bronze and a bronze seal; but this serves his purpose equally well. His adversaries rightly attacked it: St Bernard, William, abbot of St Thierry, and an anonymous abbot who had been Abelard’s disciple.

Divine Wisdom, then, is from divine Power as a wax image is from wax; or as, according to philosophers, a species itself is said to be from a genus, although species and genus are the same thing—as man is the same as animal, and a wax image the same as wax. The wax image is from wax, and man from animal, in such a way that it belongs to being a wax image that it be wax, and to being a man that it be animal; but not conversely. Power extends both to discerning and to other actions, just as wax extends both to a wax image and to what is not a wax image, and animal to man as well as to what is not man.

For the Son to be begotten by the Father, then, is for divine Wisdom, in the sense now defined, to be from divine Power. Wisdom itself, as was said, is a certain power and, as it were, a certain portion of God’s Power, which is omnipotence—just as any son is in some manner called a portion of his parents. We call Wisdom, however, as it were a portion of omnipotence, and not properly a portion, because in the altogether simple nature of divinity there is no plurality of things whose combination composes the quantity of any whole, as we have already often recalled above.

Yet we call Wisdom, as it were, a portion of Omnipotence in this respect: God, by his omnipotence, extends to performing infinitely many things; by Wisdom, he extends only to discerning. And when we call God’s omnipotence, as it were, all his power, we in some manner speak of several powers of his, with reference to effects—that is, to the diversity of things which he can do—when we say that he does different things, though he remains one and utterly the same.

Hence we call the one and same Holy Spirit manifold, even “seven spirits,” according to the operation of sevenfold grace, not according to substance. Observe also that, as in the generations mentioned above—of image and species—those names of the generating thing and the generated thing which were said absolutely could be joined in predication, but those names which are said relatively to one another according to such generation could not; so too in this divine generation itself.

For the wax image is wax, and man is animal, and not conversely. But the thing made of matter is not there the matter, nor is matter made of matter from itself. For “matter” and “that which is made of matter” are said relatively to one another, just as “Father” and “Son” are. The terms mentioned above, however, are predicated according to substance rather than relation. We call something matter because something is from it; we call something made of matter because it is from something. So too Father and Son are said relatively to one another, because the one generates the other and the other exists through generation from the former, just as the latter exists from the former through material constitution.

For the same reason, therefore, that one may not say that matter is made of matter from itself, or that what is made of matter is matter of itself, or that a constituent is constituted from itself, or later than itself, or generates itself—although in such cases matter and what is made of matter are generally the same thing, as this bronze is the same as this statue, constituent the same as constituted, prior the same as posterior, and generator the same as generated—for the same proportional reason, I say, among the divine persons neither is the Father the Son, that is, God the Father begotten from himself, nor is the Son the Father, that is, God the Son the generator of himself. To say this would be to say that divine Power is from itself, or that divine Wisdom is from itself.

Rather, Wisdom alone is from Power itself, as has been defined: just as an image is from wax, not an image from itself, nor wax—understood as image—from itself or from the image, although wax itself and that image are the same thing. Thus Father and Son are the same according to substance, but not according to property or definition; and God himself, who is omnipotent, is wise or good, and conversely.

And as there, that which is from matter is what is made of matter from it—wax itself is a wax image, or conversely—yet the matter is not thereby made of matter from itself, nor is the thing made of matter its own matter; so here, what the Father is, that indeed the Son is, and conversely, yet the Father is not the Son, nor conversely. There a predication of substance occurs when it is said, “It is that which is made of matter,” or “It is that which is the Son”; but here a predication of property occurs when one says, “It is made of matter,” or “It is the Son.” The substance is the same, but the properties are unmixed.

According to the proposed reasoning, it is therefore clear why divine Power is called Father and divine Wisdom Son: namely, because the latter is from the former, as we distinguished above. It is also clear why the names of relative properties may by no means be joined to one another in predication.

But if someone asks whether, according to this mode of generation assigned in divine Power, it may be said to be the matter of divine Wisdom—that is, Father of the Son—or cause, principle, or in some way at least prior by nature, if not in time, we reply that none of these appears to us capable of being said properly. We grant that it can in no way be called matter here, since Boethius defines matter as that which receives a form placed upon it, and it is certain that there is no form whatever in God. Nor do we rightly call anything matter unless it precedes in time too that which is made of matter, like wax itself, which existed before the image existed. Hence philosophers distinguished things which consist of matter and form from things which subsist by analogy to matter and form, as we taught elsewhere when treating matter and form.

For the present, however, let it suffice that we have introduced the analogy of matter and what is made of matter for this purpose: that, just as we say that the latter is generated from the former because it is from it, so we say that the Son is from the Father—that is, Wisdom itself from Power itself—as has been defined.

Nor do we properly call anything a cause except in relation to an effect, where something has been made. For an effect, as Boethius testifies, is that which a cause brings about [the text has: “that which brings about a cause”]; and according to Tully, every cause except the final cause is called efficient and is prior to its effect by nature. Hence, when Boethius discusses the topical argument from cause according to Tully in the third book of the *Topics*, defining cause, he says that it is that which, preceding any thing, produces it—not in time but by the property of nature—as the sun does the day.

Augustine himself, following this reasoning, calls every cause efficient in chapter 30 of the book *Thirty-Three Questions*, in these words:

> “He who asks why God willed to make the world seeks a cause of God’s will. But every cause is efficient, and everything efficient is greater than that which it effects. Nothing, however, is greater than God’s will. Therefore its cause is not to be sought.”

By this reasoning it is manifestly proved that God the Father is not the cause of the Son, since he does not effect him, whom he in no way makes, but only begets; nor is he greater than the Son, except perhaps according to the assumption of flesh. How, moreover, shall we say that what is eternal has a principle or origin? It is certain that the three persons are eternal and coeternal with one another. Therefore none is the principle of another; rather, each is without principle, because each is eternal and is the principle of all other things. For what is eternal, as Boethius defines it in the third book of the *Topics*, lacks origin—that is, principle.

Nor does it hinder this that we call God the Father “principle without principle” and the Son “principle from principle,” that is, from the Father who is the principle of all creatures. For when we say “from principle,” we do not add “his own”; thus the Father is not understood to be the Son’s principle, but the principle of all creatures, just as the Son himself says of himself: “The Principle, who also speak to you” (John 8:25).

But perhaps you say that there is no reason for saying that this person is from that one, and not conversely, unless the latter is in some way the cause, origin, or principle of the former—especially when we say that the one is born from the other, which is to arise, from which “origin” takes its name. The Catholic doctors themselves seem strongly to support this reasoning when they sometimes call the Father himself the cause of the Son or the principle of the other two persons; likewise, they call both the Father himself and the Son the principle of the Holy Spirit, who is from them not by generation but by procession; and they call both the Father the head of the Son and the Son the head of the Holy Spirit.

Thus Augustine, in book 83 of the *Questions*, chapter 17, discussing the Son of God, says:

> “God is the cause of all things that are. But that which is the cause of all things is also the cause of its own Wisdom; and God is never without Wisdom. Therefore he is the eternal cause of his own eternal Wisdom, and is not earlier in time than his Wisdom.”

In *On the Orthodox Faith*, chapter 1:

> **Note:** Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 1.

> “We believe that there is one God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Father, because he has a Son; Son, because he has a Father; Holy Spirit, because he is from Father and Son. The Father, therefore, is the principle of Deity, from whom the Son is born; from whom the Holy Spirit is not born, because he is not Son; nor unbegotten, because he is not Father; nor made, because he is not from nothing, but is God proceeding from God the Father and God the Son.”

From these testimonies it is therefore clear that the Father himself is in some sense called the cause or principle of the other persons, because the other two persons have their being from him: the one by being born, of whom we have spoken; the other by proceeding, of whom we must speak.

We, indeed, while reverencing the meaning of the holy men, judge that their words are less to be approved here: namely, that we should say that what is eternal has a principle, and therefore is without principle; or that what cannot properly be called an effect has a cause, since what can in no way not exist cannot in any way be effected or made, but exists altogether necessarily. For if something is, as Aristotle himself also says, it is not [the text is apparently defective or corrupt].

Augustine himself also sufficiently indicates that he does not approve these expressions, when above he called every cause efficient and greater than its effect, and consequently removes every cause from God’s will, so that nothing might be the cause of the divine will. In the very book *On the Trinity*, where he especially undertakes to define the Trinity itself, he left uncertain what he did not dare to assert, but expressed it doubtfully and left it as a question: namely, whether the Father ought to be called the principle of the other persons. For he says in book V, chapter 13:

> “Father is said relatively, and principle likewise relatively. But Father is said with reference to the Son; principle, however, with reference to all things which are from him. The Son too is called principle. For when it was said to him, ‘Who are you?’ he answered: ‘The Principle, who also speak to you’ (John 8:25). For when he called himself principle, he wished to show himself to be Creator, just as the Father is the principle of creation, because all things are from him.”

And again:

> “God is therefore called one principle with reference to creation, not two or three principles. But in relation to one another in the Trinity, if the begetter is a principle in relation to that which is begotten, the Father is a principle in relation to the Son because he begets him. Whether the Father is also a principle in relation to the Spirit, because it has been said, ‘He proceeds from the Father’ (John 15:26), is no small question.”

And a little later, in the following chapter:

> “If that which is given has as its principle the one by whom it is given, it must be confessed that the Father and the Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit.”

Nor do we concede that the Father is prior to the Son by nature. Rather, they are simultaneous by nature, since Father and Son are mutually said relatively to one another. According even to the philosophers, all mutual relatives are simultaneous by nature, because each relates to the other in such a way that neither can exist at all without the other.

Conversely, as Aristotle says, one thing is naturally prior to another if it must necessarily be followed by the latter but does not follow it—for example, one is prior to two. One can exist without two existing, but not conversely. Yet none of the persons can exist in such a way that another does not exist; none of them can in any way fail to exist, since all equally must exist. That is, it is altogether impossible that the Trinity of persons should not exist.

> **Note:** In Migne, the following two paragraphs are printed in parallel with the sections “God the Father … must be spoken of. And” and “by necessity … Father is said relatively,” respectively.

John Chrysostom, in Homily 11 on Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews:

> “Sadech is called ‘righteousness,’ while Melcha is ‘king.’ Melchizedek, therefore, is ‘king of righteousness.’ In what way did he have neither beginning of days nor end of life? In that his genealogy is not related. So also in Christ, the very nature of the thing is without beginning and without end. For as we know neither his beginning of days nor his end of life because it is not written, so we know neither the beginning nor the end of the Son.”

Again:

> “You behold the Son as without beginning, not because he lacks a cause from which he is—for this is impossible: he has the Father, otherwise how could he be Son?—but because he had no beginning of life nor end.”

From the book of Orosius’s *Questions to Augustine*:

> **OROSIUS:** Did the Father beget the Son by will or by necessity?  
> **AUGUSTINE:** Neither by will nor by necessity, because there is no necessity in God. Will cannot precede Wisdom. Therefore, to be wise rationally is prior to willing rationally. For when a heretic asked one of our number whether the Father begot the Son willingly or unwillingly, he is reported to have answered commendably: “You too, heretic, tell me: Is God the Father God by necessity or by will?” If he had said “by necessity,” a great absurdity followed; if “by will,” the answer given him was: “Therefore God is God by will, not by nature.”

Nor do they have any priority of dignity over one another, so that the Father might be called worthier than the Son or the Holy Spirit because they are from him and he is not from them; or, by the same reasoning, the Son worthier than the Holy Spirit. Otherwise animal too would by the same proportion be worthier than man, when the nature of man seems rather to surpass the nature of animal: man is rational by his own nature, whereas animal does not possess this by its nature.

So also “man” could be called worthier than some man who was most worthy or best of all, because the best man would be from man, not man from the best man. But if someone prefers the Father to the other persons also because the Father is not from another while both Son and Spirit are from another, namely from the Father himself, then by the same reasoning he should prefer an evil angel to a good angel: the former has what he is from himself and not from another, while the latter has it from God.

What dignity could be discerned in not being from another, when the greatest dignity consists in being from God? For it is great to be God from God and the Highest Good from the Highest Good. A kind of doubling of dignity is expressed in this. Yet the supposed dignity in the expression “not from another” is shown to be empty, since it could be applied even to things which do not exist and which have no dignity whatever.

But if it could happen that one man existed from himself and another from God, would the one who was from himself thereby be better or worthier than the one who was from God, because the former was from himself and the latter from another? Certainly not, since the latter could be made far better by God than the former could be through himself.

Let us posit also that one man has begotten another equally wise, equally powerful, equally good in every respect, and equal to his father. Let us posit this, I say, as perhaps sometimes happens or can happen, since sons are often even to be preferred to their parents. Then I ask: is one who is in every respect equal to his father, or perhaps better, in any respect less worthy than his father? Certainly not, since he is equal to him in every respect, or perhaps better. But if such a person is in no respect whatsoever less worthy than his father, how shall he be called less worthy in being from him? Or how could being from another detract from anyone’s dignity, rather than being from oneself, if the one who is from another is in every respect equally good as the one from whom he is?

For nothing precedes another in dignity which does not surpass it in some good. But God the Father surpasses God the Son in no good, since the Son is equally powerful, wise, and good; and the same perfection of every good belongs to each person, just as the same entirely individual substance belongs to them.

What Mercury reports—namely, that the Son is a “second Lord from the Father”—means, then, as though he said both that the Son is Lord and that he is second from the Father: that is, personally distinct from God the Father, from whom alone he is, though he is not alone, since the Spirit too is from both. The Son is therefore, as it were, in the first place from the Father, with no intermediary; the Spirit, as it were, in the third place, because he is from the Father in such a way that he is also from the Son. “Second,” therefore, means, as it were, one who is in the first place from the Father, from the Father’s very substance and with no other person intervening.

And when philosophers say that mind is born from the highest God—that is, that the Word is from God the Father—they call the Father “highest,” as was said, not because of any dignity, but because he is from no one, while the other two persons are from him.

The objection that, because the Son is essentially the same as the Father and the Father generates the Son, the same thing generates itself—that is, because the Son, as we said, is from the Father, the same thing is from itself—can easily be shaken by the analogy introduced above of wax and wax image. Wax itself and the wax image are essentially the same. And though the image itself is from wax itself, it is not thereby from itself—that is, the wax image is not thereby from the wax image itself—because it is from wax itself, although that wax and that image are altogether the same essentially, though not in definition or property.

For when relative expressions are applied to an identity of the same thing under preceding names, they are fitted not only to identity of essence but also to identity of definition and of wholly the same condition. Thus, if I say that some thing is from itself, the thing which exists and that from which it exists must be altogether the same according to their expressed being; for example, if this wax and this wax image were the same in definition, as sword and blade are the same. Then, if we granted that the image was from wax, we would have to grant that the same thing was from itself.

But when it cannot be shown that what is said to be from something is the same as it in definition, it is not therefore true that the same thing is from itself, even if it is essentially and numerically the same as that thing. Much less, since Father and Son are different from one another both in definition and in property, although they are essentially the same, is it necessary that, because the Son is from the Father or is generated from the Father, the same thing is from itself or generated from itself.

But you tell me: “God is from God,” since the Son is from the Father; and hence we confess that we believe in the Son of God, “God from God, light from light.”

You will therefore say: “Since God is from God, and ‘God’ is the proper name of one individual and singular substance, and God from God cannot in any way differ in definition but is altogether the same, it must be granted that the same thing is from itself.”

To this I reply: just as we say that man is different from man in definition or property, if this is understood according to the diversity of persons existing among human beings—so that one human person is different from another, as Socrates from Plato—yet the same thing is not thereby different from itself, since this person is not that person; so we say that God is different from God in definition or property according to the diversity of persons, each of whom is God. The one who is God, namely the Father, differs in property from the one who is God, namely the Son; yet the same thing is not thereby different from itself, since this person is not that person.

It is therefore false to say that God cannot in any way differ from God in definition or property, since the one who is God differs in property from the one who is God—that is, one person from another, the Father from the Son. And the further claim, that the name “God” is proper to one individual substance and therefore, if God is from God, the same thing is from itself, proves nothing. For we say “God from God” with reference to the persons themselves: while each is God, one is nevertheless from another and is in no way the other.

Thus it is not necessary that, because one person who is God is from one person who is God—which is for God to be from God—the same thing is from itself. For the person who is from the other is in no way the one from whom it is. Likewise, the persons that are in God may be kept distinct from one another in predication, just as those which are under “man” and species.

The objection that, if God generates God, he generates either God himself or another God, is readily refuted according to the analogy of generation introduced above, namely that of wax and wax image. Wax is the matter of any wax, however formed, and in some manner generates every thing made of matter from itself, as we said. Therefore, when wax constitutes and generates, as matter, this wax so formed, wax certainly generates a certain wax. According to the reasoning given above, it would then be necessary that it generate either itself or another wax.

Yet the same wax is not generated from itself or from itself, though wax so formed is essentially the same as the wax itself from which it is and is not the same in definition. Hence we recalled above that relative expressions are properly applied only where there is identity of definition also. Wax is therefore the matter of a certain wax, and its mother, according to Plato, who makes matter, as it were, the mother of that which is made of matter; yet it is not thereby either matter or mother of itself, or of another wax. So likewise, when God generates God—that is, is Father of God—he generates neither himself nor another God.

[Col. 1296C] Concerning the eternity of the generation, the question has been raised whether the Son is always being begotten, or is always begotten. At virtually the beginning of our preceding discussion we set forth what we think: namely, that he is both always being begotten and begotten; that is, that he is always from the Father, and that his generation is always full and perfect in this very respect. It never began or ends; and this is what it is for him always to be begotten and always to have been begotten, since for him being begotten is the same as having been begotten. For when we say either that the Son is begotten from God the Father or that he has been begotten, we do not understand this according to a distinction of times, since that eternal generation does not yield in any respect to time, but stood complete before the times just as it does now [Col. 1296D]. Accordingly, we understand that it makes no difference whether we maintain that the Son is being begotten or has been begotten.

Furthermore, how can it be said that the Father begot the Son unless he was begetting the Son? For “he begot” conveys nothing other than “he was begetting,” just as “he will beget” conveys nothing other than “he will be begetting,” or “he begets” than “he is begetting.” But if the Father was begetting and is no longer begetting—since the Son is now said rather to have been begotten by him than to be begotten—then surely the generation of the Word must be said first to have been begun and afterwards completed: he who had formerly been begetting would subsequently have ceased from begetting once the Son had been begotten by him. Yet in eternity no imperfection, cessation, or alternation of change [Col. 1297A] can occur [perhaps: “is evident”]. It is therefore clear from this also that the Son of God’s being begotten and his having been begotten are the same thing; for we cannot in any way understand something to have been begotten if it in no respect happened that it was begotten, nor that anyone begot if it never at all happened that he was begetting. Here, however, we take “never” in the sense of “eternally,” not temporally, since, as has been said, that generation is eternal, not temporal.

Nevertheless, certain authorities seem wholly to reject the statement that the Son of God is born or begotten from the Father, maintaining only that he has been born or begotten.

> [Note: [Col. 1297D] An anonymous abbot also argues this point sharply against Abelard in Book III of the treatise he composed against him. He proves the contrary by the authority both of St Augustine and of St Hilary, and also of St Leo, against Arian subtleties. The Arians alleged some imperfection in the Son of God [Col. 1298D], because he was always being begotten from the Father; whereas the holy Fathers maintained not that he is always being begotten, but that he is always begotten.]

Hence Augustine, discussing this very generation in the *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter 39, says:

> “It is better to be always born [Col. 1297B] than always being born; for one who is always being born is not yet born, and has never been born, nor will be born if he is always being born. For being born is one thing, having been born another. Accordingly, the Son is never [the Son], if he is never born. And if he is always the Son, therefore he is always born.”

Likewise Gregory says in *Morals*, Book XXIX:

> “The Lord God Jesus Christ, insofar as he is the power and wisdom of God, was born from the Father before the ages; or rather, since he neither began to be born nor ceased, let us say more truly that he is always born. Yet we cannot say, ‘he is always being born,’ lest he seem imperfect. But in order that he may be designated both eternal and perfect, let us say both ‘always’ and ‘born’: so that ‘born’ may pertain to perfection and ‘always’ to eternity. Yet even in saying that he is perfect [Col. 1297C], we depart far from an expression of that truth; for what has not been made cannot be called perfect. Nevertheless, the Lord, condescending to the words of our weakness, says: ‘Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect’ (Matt. 5:48).”

What blessed Augustine said in that book of the *Eighty-Three Questions* about “always being born” and “always born,” I think was said according to the customary meanings of the words. Perhaps someone raising that question had understood *nasci* (“to be born”) and *natum* (“born”) in the manner in which we speak about our own generations. We say “being born” when birth is not yet completed but has begun; but “born” when it is already complete. Therefore, when [Col. 1297D] someone who understood the words in this way raised such a question, the holy man fittingly answered him in the same terms, preferring the complete and perfect generation which he attributes to the Son of God to one that has begun and is not yet complete. His meaning is that a birth which, never having begun, is always complete is better than one which, having begun, would always remain imperfect.

The statement [Col. 1298A] that the Son is from the substance of the Father means here precisely as much as that he is begotten from the Father. The expression is transferred from our generations, in which one who is begotten is said to be from the father’s substance, because in the generation of the human body something from the substance of the father’s body is transmitted and transformed into the son’s body. Therefore, since the Son’s being from the Father’s substance is such as saying that he is begotten from the Father, just as he is begotten from the Father alone, so he is said to be from the Father’s substance alone—not also from the substance [perhaps add: “of the Son”] or of the Holy Spirit. For that would mean that he was begotten from himself or from the Holy Spirit.

Gregory, in Book XXXIV on Job:

> “My tongue is the pen of a scribe” (Ps. 44[45]:2). “What we speak passes away; what we write remains. The tongue of the Father is called the pen of a scribe because from it his coeternal Word is begotten without passing away.”

Ambrose, *On Faith to the Emperor Gratian*:

> “These things must not be assessed in God according to bodily realities. The Son is begotten incomprehensibly. The Father begets impassibly; yet he begets from himself, and begets before every act of understanding, so that true God may beget true God.”

Jerome, in his definition of the Catholic faith and the Nicene Creed:

> “That he was always born from the substance of the Father, the Savior himself says in the Gospel: ‘What [Note: [Col. 1298D] In the Gospel of John it is written, “what is born from flesh,” and immediately afterwards, “what is born from spirit.”] is born from flesh is flesh, and what is born from spirit is spirit,’ because God is spirit” (John 3:6).

Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book V, chapter 13:

> “If one who begets is a principle in relation to that which he begets, the Father is a principle in relation to the Son because he begets him.”

The same author, in a sermon on the Creed:

> “Learned and spiritual men have discussed in many books that he is the begetter and he the begotten. The former is the principle of the latter, whence he is also called the head of Christ; although Christ too is a principle, but not of the Father. The latter, however, is the image of the former. Although in no respect unlike him and in every way equally equal, the Son owes to the Father what he is; and he likewise owes to the Father the fact that he is equal to the Father. But the Father owes to no one whatever he is.”

It should also be noted that “the Wisdom of the Father” and “the Love of the Father and the Son,” when uttered to distinguish the persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit—as “Holy Spirit” is also uttered to distinguish the third person [Col. 1298D]—are used relatively, as though they were proper names of those persons. Thus, “the Wisdom of the Father” means as much as “begotten from the Father,” namely the Word itself, that is, the Son. And “the love of the Father or of the Son” means as much as “proceeding from them,” namely that third person, the Holy Spirit. When these phrases are thus used relatively, they have the force of the proper names of the individual persons, as “Holy Spirit” also does when [Col. 1299A] it is spoken of in terms of procession.

But if “Holy Spirit” is used commonly rather than properly—that is, insofar as every good spirit is a holy spirit, rather than according to the distinctive property of procession belonging to the third person in the Trinity—then, according to blessed Augustine, both the Father himself and the Son may be called Holy Spirit. Perhaps similarly, when “Wisdom of the Father” or “Love of the Father” is said not relatively among the persons, so that we are not determining either the generation of the Son or the procession of the Spirit, but simply, as though we said, “the Wisdom which is the Father’s” or “the Love which is the Father’s,” indeed “which is the Father himself,” nothing prevents us from saying that the Father himself is the wisdom of himself: that is, that very [Col. 1299B] Wisdom by which he is wise—indeed, which he himself is. For according to Augustine, for him to be wise is also to be. Thus, just as he has wisdom in himself, not in relation to another, so likewise the Son or the Holy Spirit may be said to be his own Wisdom; and each person, in this manner, the Wisdom that belongs to that person, or likewise the love belonging to each person, since each person has wisdom and love and there are not different wisdoms or loves.

If anyone should altogether refuse to say this because the phrase is more readily and commonly understood in another sense and might cause offense, although he does not reject the doctrine itself—as, for example, if he altogether refuses to say “the Father” or “the Son is the Holy Spirit”—I do not think he should be compelled. [Col. 1299C] Let us conclude what has been said about the generation of the Word, and now, with his inspiration, speak of the procession of the Holy Spirit.

> [Note: [Col. 1299] William, abbot of St Thierry, quotes this passage in full and refutes it in his disputation against Peter Abelard, chapter 4.]

“Spirit” (*spiritus*) is so called, as it were, from breathing (*spirare*), whence Truth says: “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8). Therefore, by his very name he is said rather to proceed from the Father and the Son than to be begotten. For the very goodness (*benignitas*) denoted by this name is not a power or wisdom, since being good is not the same as being wise or powerful. No one is wise or powerful in virtue of being good; rather, it is more fittingly called the affection or effect of love. Love, moreover, as Gregory testifies, cannot exist between fewer than two persons. [Col. 1299D] “No one,” he says, “is said to have love for himself; rather, by affection he reaches out from himself toward another, so that love may be love.” Therefore, God’s proceeding is, in a certain manner, his extending himself toward some thing through the affection of love: namely, loving it and joining himself to it through love.

Since both the Son and the Holy Spirit are from the Father—the former begotten, the latter proceeding—the difference between generation and procession [Col. 1300A] lies in this: the one who is generated is from the Father’s very substance, since Wisdom itself, as has been said, has this nature, that it is a kind of power. But the affection of love pertains more to goodness of disposition than to power. Accordingly, the Son is rightly said to be begotten from the Father—that is, to be from the Father’s own substance. The Spirit, however, is by no means said to be begotten, but rather to proceed [Col. 1300B], that is, to extend himself through love toward another. For in a certain sense, through love each person proceeds from himself toward another; since, properly speaking, as was said, no one is said to have love for himself or to be good to himself, but to another.

Most of all, God, who lacks nothing, cannot be moved by an affection of goodness toward himself so as to bestow something upon himself out of goodness, but only toward creatures, which always need the gifts of his grace. In a certain manner, therefore, God is said to go forth from himself to creatures through the affection or effect of goodness, since the fact that he is good, or that he acts benevolently out of love, is said with reference to the affection or effect that he has in creatures. He would remain in himself through goodness if he could be good to himself by exercising some beneficence toward himself.

The Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son because the good affection or effect of doing something proceeds from God’s power and wisdom. God wills and acts because he can accomplish it and knows how to bring it about skillfully [perhaps: “and acts skillfully”] [Col. 1300D]. For unless he could do something, he would will it in vain, since it would lack efficacy; and unless he knew skillfully how to accomplish it, he would not have an excellent effect. It is also evident that he can will nothing except what is best, nor would he rationally will what he did not know. Therefore, in order rationally and excellently to will to do something, he must both be able to do it and know beforehand what he does, and know how to do it best. Thus God’s good affection descends, as it were, from his power and wisdom. This is for the Spirit himself to proceed simultaneously from the Father and the Son, because, as has been said, God wills to accomplish all things most excellently because he both can and knows how.

> [Note: [Col. 1299] In Migne, the following paragraph is printed in parallel with the passage, “namely, loving it … moved by an affection of goodness,” in the preceding paragraph.]

[Col. 1299D] Ambrose, *On Faith to Gratian*, Book I:

> “Believe that the Son went forth from God, as he himself testifies, saying: ‘I proceeded from God and came’ (John 8:42). And elsewhere: ‘I went forth from God’ (John 16:27). [Col. 1300A] He who proceeded from God and went forth from God can possess nothing other than what belongs to God.”

Likewise:

> “He came forth by being born from the Father, as he himself who was born said: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High’ (Ecclus. 24:5).”

The same author, Book IV:

> “The Wisdom of God says: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High’; that is, not compelled but free, not subject to power but born by the mystery of generation.”

From the book of Orosius’s *Questions to Augustine*, Augustine’s reply:

> “No son is the son of fewer than two, father and mother. Far be it from us to suppose anything of that sort between God the Father and the Son; for not even a human son proceeds at once from father and mother, since when he proceeds from his father, he does not then proceed from his mother!”

Yet the Greeks confess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, and not also from the Son [Col. 1301A], because Truth, speaking in the Gospel that fully contains the faith concerning the procession of the Spirit, mentions the Father alone, saying: “the Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26). They also sharply rebuke us because we believe that he proceeds from the Son as well, and assert that we are liable to anathema. For in the principal councils held among them, their creeds were established with appended anathemas in such a way that no one may teach or preach anything concerning the faith of the Trinity other than, or differently from, what is contained there. Since in those creeds only the Father is mentioned in connection with the procession of the Spirit, whoever, they say, adds the Son incurs an anathema.

They further adduce, to heighten the charge of our audacity [Col. 1301B], the testimony of a creed of faith which Leo III, following the tradition of the aforementioned councils, left inscribed at Rome on a silver tablet for posterity, “for the love,” as he himself says, “and safeguarding of the orthodox faith.” In that creed he too mentions only the Father in connection with the procession of the Spirit, in these words: “And [we believe] in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son,” etc.

Blessed Gregory carefully explains how greatly those principal councils must be held in reverence, professing that he receives and venerates them as the four Gospels. Accordingly, he permits us to add [Col. 1301C] or subtract no more from their words than from the evangelical words. Thus he writes to Constantius, bishop of Milan, concerning one of them:

> “We confess, Truth being our author and conscience our witness, that we preserve wholly inviolate the faith of the Chalcedonian Creed, and that we dare neither add anything to nor subtract anything from its definition. But if anyone, against it and the faith of that synod, desires to presume to think either more or less, we anathematize him without any delay and decree him alien from the bosom of mother Church.”

But certainly, when it is forbidden that anyone teach or preach the Catholic faith otherwise than as it is contained in the aforesaid councils, I take “otherwise” not according to a difference of words but according to opposition to the faith: as though it said “otherwise,” that is, in a contrary manner, not with a different sound of words. For we say in Latin what they say in Greek. Just as *diversum* (“different”) may be used in the sense of “opposed,” so *diverso modo*, that is, *aliter* (“otherwise”), is not inappropriately taken in the sense of an opposite manner, not merely a different [Col. 1301D] expression.

Otherwise, since each of those councils composed and established its own creed, and their creeds differ from one another in words, and perhaps in some formulations, since one sometimes contains what another does not, surely anyone who received one creed and recited the others would be liable to anathema. By the same reasoning we would be liable because of the additions supplied by the Gospel, when Moses says in Deuteronomy: “What I command you, that alone shall you do for the Lord; add nothing and take nothing away” (Deut. 12:32). Thus he prohibited the addition of something contrary, not the supplying of what was lacking to perfection [Col. 1302A]. Though it may also be understood in this way: that a human being is altogether forbidden to add anything of himself to the words of the Lord. A human being would add something of himself if he presumed it from his own understanding, rather than from the inspiration of the Spirit. Of that Spirit it is written: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

We also preach many things concerning miracles of saints and matters which the holy Fathers wrote after the apostles, although the Apostle says in writing to the Galatians: “Even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you beyond what we preach to you, let him be anathema. As I have said before, so now I say again: if anyone should preach to you beyond what you received, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1:8).

But when [Col. 1302B] the Greeks object that the evangelical tradition is sufficient for the complete rule of faith and that nothing further should be added beyond what is contained in the Gospel’s words, they pronounce judgment upon themselves when they say that the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone. For when the Gospel says that the Spirit proceeds from the Father, it does not add “alone,” as they do, but says only “from the Father.” Moreover, many things necessary to faith were added after the Gospels by the apostles or apostolic men which are by no means demonstrated from Gospel words—for example, the perpetual preservation of the Lord’s Mother’s virginity even after childbirth, and perhaps many other things.

Having answered the Greek objection concerning [Col. 1302C] the procession of the Spirit, it is pleasing also to bring forward testimony from their own teachers, by which they are shown to teach that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well.

Athanasius, in the Creed of Faith, says:

> “The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, not made, not created, not begotten, but proceeding.”

Since he first stated that the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son and then added “proceeding,” he clearly taught that he proceeds from both [Col. 1302D], since he referred “proceeding” to each, just as he did “is”; especially because the Spirit has no other manner of being from the Father than by proceeding.”

Didymus also, their greatest teacher, says in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, translated by blessed Jerome. Introducing and explaining Christ’s words concerning that same Spirit, he says:

> “The Savior, who is also Truth, says: ‘For he shall not speak from himself’ [Col. 1303A] (John 16:13); that is, not without me and without the will of me and the Father, because he is inseparable from my and the Father’s will. For he is not from himself but from the Father and me. For the very fact that he subsists and speaks is from the Father and me for him. I speak truth; that is, I inspire what he speaks. For he is the Spirit of truth. In the Trinity, ‘to speak’ and ‘to say’ must not be understood according to our customary usage, but according to the manner of incorporeal natures, and especially of the Trinity, which instills its will into the hearts of believers.”

Likewise:

> “The Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of truth and the Spirit of wisdom, cannot hear, while the Son speaks, things he does not know, since he himself is what is brought forth by the Son: that is, God proceeding from God, the Spirit of truth proceeding from Truth, the Comforter abiding from the Comforter.”

Likewise Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, in Epistle 8, addressed to Nestorius, which begins, “To the most reverend and God-loving …”:

> “If [Col. 1303C] the Spirit is spiritual in subsistence, or indeed is understood as existing in himself insofar as he is Spirit and not Son, yet he is not alien from him. For he is called the Spirit of Truth and flows forth from him, just as indeed he does from God the Father.”

St John Chrysostom, Homily 26, *On the Exposition of the Creed*, beginning “The universal Church rejoices,” says:

> “This is the Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, who distributes his own gifts to each as he wills.”

The same author, Homily 28, in another exposition of the same Creed, beginning “Upon the structure of the whole Church,” says:

> “Therefore it must be believed that the Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son.”

Likewise:

> “Do not say that the Son begotten from the Father is lesser, but [say this] of him who was born from the Holy Spirit [Col. 1303D] and the Virgin Mary.”

Likewise:

> “We say that this Holy Spirit is coequal with the Father and the Son and proceeds from the Father and the Son. Believe this, lest evil conversations corrupt your good morals.”

Likewise:

> “There are heretics who say that the Holy Spirit is numbered among creatures.”

Likewise:

> “See everywhere the mystery of the Trinity. Behold, you also believe in the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from the Father and the Son, is joined by love.”

Augustine, *Questions to Orosius*, Book I, chapter 2:

> “Our Lord Jesus Christ himself, after the resurrection, to show that the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself as from the Father, breathed upon them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20:22).

The same author, Book IV of *On the Trinity*:

> “Nor can we say that the Holy Spirit does not [Col. 1304A] proceed from the Son. For it is not without reason that the same Spirit is called the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son. Nor do I see what else he intended to signify when, breathing upon them, he said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’ For that bodily breath was not the substance of the Holy Spirit, but a demonstration that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son also.”

We think it sufficient that Truth mentions the Father alone concerning the procession of the Spirit. For Wisdom itself, as has been said, is a certain power, and wisdom is contained in that very power; hence the Spirit’s procession from Power makes his procession from Wisdom sufficiently probable. Jerome too, writing *On the Faith*, mentions the Father alone, as is also contained in the creeds of the principal councils. Thus he writes to Damasus:

> [Col. 1304B] “We also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God, proceeding from the Father.”

Augustine too, in chapter 1 of the *Enchiridion*, mentions the Father alone in connection with the procession of the Spirit, although he calls the Spirit the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son:

> “For a Christian it is enough to believe that the causes of created things are nothing other than the goodness of the Creator, and that there is no nature which is not either himself or from himself; and that he is Trinity: namely, Father, Son begotten from the Father, and Holy Spirit proceeding from that same Father, yet one and the same Spirit of the Father and the Son.”

Yet in many other places, both Augustine himself and almost all Latin theologians profess and establish that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well. Hence, in Book XV of *On the Trinity*, [Col. 1304C] chapter 26, discussing the procession of the Spirit, Augustine says:

> “Holy Scripture calls him the Spirit of both, of whom the Apostle says: ‘God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts’ (Gal. 4:6); and of whom the Son himself says: ‘The Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matt. 10); and of whom he also says: ‘Whom I shall send to you from the Father’ (John 15:26). And elsewhere: ‘Whom the Father will send in my name’ (John 14:26). And when he had risen from the dead, he breathed upon his disciples and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John 20:22), in order to show that he proceeds from himself as well.”

For how could he teach more openly than by breathing upon them that the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself also? Especially since *spiritus*, “spirit,” is clearly called, as it were, *spiramen*, “breath,” from *spirare*, “to breathe,” [Col. 1304D] and since Holy Spirit, according to its proper meaning, as has been said, here signifies one who proceeds. Hence it must be conceded that the Spirit is from whomever he is said to belong to, to be sent by, or to proceed from.

Yet the Spirit is said properly, or principally, to proceed from the Father. Thus Jerome, discussing the definition of the Catholic faith in the Nicene Creed, says:

> “We also believe in the Holy Spirit, who proceeds properly from the Father.”

Likewise:

> “We find in Scripture that the Holy Spirit is true God and is properly from the Father.”

And again:

> “The Son and the Spirit are from the Father; and the Spirit truly proceeds properly from the Father. Therefore first receive this: that the Holy Spirit is properly from the Father, Scripture saying: ‘By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their host’ [Col. 1305A] (Ps. 32[33]:6). And the Savior says: ‘The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father’” (John 15:26).

Blessed Augustine also, in Book XV of *On the Trinity*, chapter 18, says:

> “Not without reason in this Trinity is only the Son called the Word of God, only the Holy Spirit called the Gift of God, and only God the Father called that from whom the Word is begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds principally. I added ‘principally’ because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son. But the Father gave this too to him—not as already existing and lacking it, but whatever he gave to the only-begotten Word, he gave by begetting.”

Thus he begot him so that the common good [Note: [Col. 1305D] In Augustine: “common gift.”] might proceed also from him. Augustine seems openly to determine by these words that the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father and [Col. 1305B] not principally from the Son, because he proceeds from the Father as from the first source, since the Father does not have his being from another but from himself, just as he is from himself—that is, not from another. But the Son, because he is not from himself but from the Father, has this same Spirit from the Father, from whom he has his being through generation.

But what does it mean that the Spirit is said to proceed properly from the Father? Is “properly” there said in the same sense as “principally” here, and perhaps appearing to be used in the same way? For it is also stated there that the Son is properly born from the Father, just as the Spirit is properly said to be from the Father. For it was there said: “The Son was not born from himself, but [Col. 1305C] was properly born from the Father—not in time but always; not from elsewhere but from his substance; not from another’s substance but from his own.” But if “properly” is taken in the same way regarding both the Son and the Holy Spirit, when the former is said properly to be born from the Father and the latter properly to proceed from the Father, and if saying “properly” is equivalent to saying “principally,” how shall we say that the Son is born principally from the Father [Col. 1305D], when he is born from him alone?

Perhaps, since it is immediately added there, “not temporally, but always,” this was said in comparison with the temporal generation of the same Son: namely, that this eternal generation is the principal and first one, by which he does not depart from equality with the Father; whereas the other is, as it were, later and temporal, according to which the Son himself is said to be less than the Father. We may also say that the Son is properly born or begotten from the Father because he is his natural Son, not [Col. 1306A] adopted, as is immediately specified by the words, “not from another, but from his own substance.”

Moreover, according to the philosophers, all things which have being from something are called born or begotten. In that sense the Son alone is properly born from the Father, because he alone, by being born, is from the Father’s own substance. But the Holy Spirit is said properly to proceed from the Father alone because he proceeds from him as from the highest principle, which is not from another. For something is properly said to proceed from the source from which it first began to come and move: as a lake is supplied from a spring, not from a stream, but through a stream sent out from the spring, through which water passes and reaches the lake. So too the Holy Spirit is said properly to proceed from the Father, as from the highest origin [Col. 1306B], which is not from elsewhere; and from him into the Son, as into a stream, because the Son has from him everything that he has, including the very fact that he is; and finally through the Son to us, as into the lake of this age. For God does and orders all things in Wisdom, and in this very Wisdom gives his Spirit, the distributor of his gifts, not without foresight or consideration.
