Hence blessed Hilary declares that the Spirit proceeds, exists, and is sent from the Father through the Son rather than from the Father and the Son. Thus, speaking to God the Father of the Spirit and the Son in Book XII of *On the Trinity*, he says:

> “In your Holy Spirit, who has proceeded from you and is sent through him.”

Likewise:

> “Your Holy Spirit is from you through him.”

Likewise:

> “May I merit to adore your Son together with you, [Col. 1306C] and your Holy Spirit, who is from you through your only-begotten Son.”

Perhaps, if the Greeks understand the Spirit to proceed from the Father alone in this sense—that he is from him as from the highest source, which does not itself exist from another—there is no controversy of doctrine, but only a difference of words. For it is certain that only the person of the Father ought in this sense to be called supreme, and that the Spirit is from him as well as from the Son, since he is called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son alike.

> [Note: [Col. 1302] In Migne, the following two paragraphs are printed in parallel with the passages “they are shown to teach that he proceeds. Athanasius … incorporeal natures, and” and “the Son was not … not temporally, but,” respectively.]

[Col. 1302C] Ivo of Chartres, in a sermon for Pentecost:

> “The Lord says in the Gospel: ‘When the Spirit of truth comes, who proceeds from the Father, he will teach you all truth; he will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will declare it to you’ (John 16:13). Didymus interprets these words thus: ‘The Spirit is inseparable [Col. 1302D] from my will and that of the Father. Moreover, he is not from himself but from the Father and me. For the very fact that he subsists and speaks is from the Father and from me for him.’”

Likewise:

> “It is an indication of agreement. The Holy Spirit is indeed the Spirit of Truth and the Spirit of Wisdom. He cannot hear, while the Son speaks, things he does not know, since he himself is what is brought forth [Col. 1303A] by the Son: that is, God proceeding from God, the Spirit of Truth proceeding from Truth, the Comforter abiding from the Comforter.”

Likewise:

> “The same is plainly affirmed in the creed of the Council of Ephesus, which is known to have been Greek, in these words: ‘Although in his substance the Spirit is the Spirit of the Son, and in person his property is understood according to his being Spirit and not Son, yet he is not [Col. 1303B] alien from him. For he is called the Spirit of Truth, and Christ is Truth.’”

[Col. 1305B] The love of God, by which he extends himself through creatures to an effect [Col. 1305C]—that is, his good will toward them, both in creating and ordering them, by which God wills not merely what is good but wills it well, so that he may be shown rational—is said to proceed from the Father and the Son. That is, it has in them, as it were, the origin and cause of its existence, since God rationally wills whatever he determines concerning the creation or [Col. 1305D] ordering of creatures because he possesses full power and skill in creating and ordering them.

But some are troubled because we say that the Son is from the Father through generation, and the Spirit from the Father and the Son through procession, while we nevertheless do not for that reason hold the Father to be prior in existence to the Son, or the Father or Son prior to the Holy Spirit. This can [Col. 1306D] be refuted by the analogy of many examples. The substance of the sun is both radiant and illuminative—that is, capable of illuminating something. And although radiance is from the sun, and illuminative power is from both sun and radiance, none of these three has ever preceded any of the others in existence.

But if anyone examines more deeply that philosophical consideration of Platonic reasoning which treats of God the maker after the analogy of a skilled craftsman—one who forethinks and deliberates about the things he is to make, lest he compose anything unsuitably, and who forms each thing first by reason and then by work [Col. 1307A]—he will see that the Holy Spirit rightly proceeds also from the Son, or through the Son. For all God’s works are ordered through the reason of Wisdom, and thus the conception of the divine mind in some manner comes forth into effect through operation. Effects, however, belong to the Spirit, since they arise from the goodness of the Creator, because the Spirit himself is goodness. Let us therefore say that the Spirit proceeds also from the Son when the plan of divine providence is brought to the effect of benevolence, and when that which God foresaw from eternity was to be done, he does in time when he wills.

Priscian carefully explains this procession—namely, that by which the conception of the mind comes forth into effect through operation—in the first book of the *Constructiones*. He says that the general and particular forms of things existed intelligibly in the divine mind before they came forth into bodies, that is, into things effected by operation. This is to say: God foresaw what and how he would act before he fulfilled it in deed; as though he said that God did nothing without forethought or without discrimination. Macrobius also [Note: [Col. 1307D] Macrobius, book I, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, ch. 14.] declares that even the soul of the world itself, which we understand to mean the Holy Spirit, is especially from the *nous* (νοῦς, “intellect”), that is, from the Son. He openly professes that it was created or born from the *nous*, just as the *nous* itself was from God the Father. Thus he begins generally concerning the soul’s origin:

[Col. 1307C] “God, who both is and is called the first cause, is the sole ruler and source of all things which are and which appear to be. Through the overflowing fecundity of his majesty he created from himself intellect. This intellect, which is called *noüs* (νοῦς), preserves the full likeness of its author insofar as it beholds the Father. But it creates soul from itself, looking toward lower things. Again, the soul is clothed with the Father whom it beholds; and, as its gaze gradually turns back [Note: [Col. 1307D] In Macrobius: ‘as its gaze recedes.’] toward the fashioning of bodies, it degenerates into bodily things themselves.”

Here Macrobius uses “created” or “born” improperly, as we established at the outset, since he calls both intellect and soul created: intellect from God—that is, the Son from the Father—and soul from intellect—that is, the Spirit from the Son. There too he indicates that both are born [Col. 1307D], since he assigns a father to each: God to intellect, and intellect itself in turn to soul.

He understands “to be created” or “to be born” as “to be from another,” so that his saying that this is born or created from that means simply that this is from that. For the philosopher’s purpose of showing that the soul itself is from both Father and Son, it suffices that he mentions the Son alone here. Since the Son is from the Father himself, and the Spirit—that is, the soul itself—is assigned as being from the Son, it is plainly evident that it too is from the Father, just as the philosopher himself, quoted above, asserted that the soul is named by the wise from God and from the *nous* (νοῦς) [Col. 1308A].

When he says that intellect is from the fecundity of majesty, this is as though he said that Wisdom is by nature from omnipotence itself. For majesty and reverence are properly attributed to power. When he says that the intellect by which it beholds the Father preserves likeness, I take this as though he said openly that the Son is altogether equal to the Father in every respect in which he is like him. For he is powerful as the Father is powerful, and equally powerful; he is good as the Father is good, and equally good. So too in all other respects in which he has likeness to the Father, he also has equality. Yet he does not have likeness to the Father in every respect, since he alone is begotten and the Father alone begets; and this pertains to the distinction of the persons according to their properties.

According to us also, [Col. 1308B] who believe that the Son alone was incarnate, we say that in this one respect the Son is less than the Father, not equal to him. The *noüs* (νοῦς), looking toward lower things, creates soul, because the Holy Spirit, who is from the Son—or any soul whatever which derives its beginning from its Creator—has precisely this, that it is soul, that is, the life of created things, from a certain regard of the Creator himself; that is, from the beneficence of divine Wisdom ordering all things, so that God’s beneficence is understood in that regard. For *anima* (“soul”) is named from *animare*, that is, “to give life.”

As we distinguished in the first book, the Holy Spirit is, as it were, a soul—that is, the life of our souls; and our souls are, as it were, certain bodies of his, made alive by him through the gifts of his grace [Col. 1308C] [Note: [Col. 1308D] Thus in the manuscript; a small blank space has been left.] . . . , and which it is certain in turn impart animate life to us. He says that the soul is clothed with its Father, that is, the *nous* (νοῦς), in that power by which it beholds, that is, by which it uses reason; for through the reason it possesses, it maintains the greatest likeness to divine Wisdom, since reason is especially to be attributed to Wisdom.

The soul gradually looks toward bodies because, in comparison with the fullness of that highest Good, whatever we have is slight, however great the gifts of virtues we may have received from him. We may also understand “gradually” to mean that, by certain stages and at intervals of time, he advances his faithful spirits from the least things to the greatest, and does not bestow all his gifts at once. The soul is said to degenerate in the very effect of its operation, from which it is called soul [Col. 1308D], since what it does is not eternal but temporal.

Here, unless I am mistaken, it is easy to resolve the point that Plato held the soul of the world to have begun and not to be coeternal with God and intellect. For since he called the Holy Spirit “soul” rather than “spirit,” as though from giving life to us through the gifts of his grace by increases of virtues, the Spirit was not always soul—that is, life-giving. For [something seems omitted: “when”] creatures did not yet exist to whom he might distribute his gifts, he did not exercise upon them that distribution of his gifts. Therefore, just as we say that the Holy Spirit, who is altogether simple in himself, is nevertheless multiple, and call him the seven Spirits [Col. 1309A] according to the diversity of his gifts, so too the philosopher held that the same one who subsists essentially in his own essence began with respect to his effects, on account of which he called him soul rather than Spirit.

For “Spirit” is a name of nature, whereas “soul” is a name of office, namely from giving life. Thus we profess that the heavenly spirits are indeed always spirits, but not always angels, since “angel” is a name of office, not of nature; and we preach that the Lord Jesus Christ began according to his humanity, but is eternal according to his divinity. So too let us say that the Holy Spirit is eternal according to the subsistence of his essence, but began according to his effects. That is to say, it was his effects rather than he himself that began. And I judge this to be the philosopher’s meaning under that figure of the soul by which he declares it to have been created—that is, to have begun—and, as it were, to be temporal rather than eternal. In accordance with this, Macrobius does not hesitate to place both God and the *nous* (νοῦς) before the soul itself [Col. 1309B].

Let Plato, then, call the Holy Spirit soul according to the effect of works; but let us call him Spirit according to the natural activity of his goodness, which he had from eternity in such a manner that he fulfills it in work when he foresees that it should be fulfilled. Let Plato say that the soul began according to its effects; but let us say that the Spirit endures eternally in the activity of his goodness. Let him say that the soul began; let us say that the Spirit is altogether eternal. Let the procession of Spirit be eternal according to disposition, because from eternity he so willed; let the procession of soul be temporal according to effect.

We have learned that the holy Fathers distinguish both processions of the Spirit, namely according to effects and according to disposition. Concerning the procession of efficacy, Bede speaks thus in his homily for the first Sunday after the Ascension:

“When the grace of the Spirit is given to human beings, the Spirit is certainly sent by the Father and is sent also by the Son. He proceeds from the Father and proceeds also from the Son, and his very sending is the procession by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

Augustine likewise declares that he proceeds in both ways: both insofar as he is given and insofar as he is able to be given. Hence, in book V of *On the Trinity*, when he came to the Spirit’s procession, he says:

“He proceeds not in the manner of one born, but in the manner of one given. But what is given is referred both to him who gave and to those to whom he gave.”

Again:

“But if he does not proceed except when he is given, then surely he would not proceed before there was someone to whom he might be given. For a gift can exist even before it is given; but what has been bestowed cannot in any way be called bestowed unless it has been given.”

What wonder, then, if we say that the Spirit proceeds in two ways, if according to one mode of procession he is called Spirit by us, and according to the other he is called soul by philosophers? The former he has eternally, the latter temporally. Hence Augustine immediately adds in the same place:

“Nor should it trouble us that the Holy Spirit, although coeternal with the Father and the Son, is nevertheless said to be something in time, as when we say that he has been bestowed. For the Spirit is eternally a gift, but bestowed in time. For even if one is not called lord except when he begins to have a servant, and this designation is relative and applies to God in time—since the creature of whom he is Lord is not eternal—”

Again:

“Behold, he does not have being Lord eternally, lest we be compelled to say that the creature too is eternal, because he would not eternally be ruling unless it too were eternally serving.”

In the preceding chapter of the same book he also plainly calls the Spirit according to effects, when he assigns him a principle. He says:

“What is given is referred both to him who gave [Col. 1310B] and to those to whom he gave.” Thus the Holy Spirit is called both the Spirit of God, who gave, and ours, who received. Hence it is written of John that he would come in the spirit of Elijah. The same must be understood concerning Moses when the Lord says to him: “I will take from your spirit and give to them” (Num. 11:17), that is, from the Holy Spirit whom I gave you. Therefore, if that which is given has as its principle him by whom it is given, because he did not receive from elsewhere what proceeds from him, we must confess that the Father and Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit—not two principles, but one principle.

It is clear, then, that Augustine here understands Spirit according to effects, when he says “given,” rather than according to the natural disposition of his benevolence. Thus, according to effects, Father and Son are rightly said to be prior to Spirit and, as it were, his principle, because the effect of grace descends from power guided by wisdom. For this reason he is here also called Spirit; and power and wisdom must first exist, in order that something may afterwards be brought into effect. Therefore, for Father and Son to be the principle of the Holy Spirit is as though we said that the Spirit proceeds from both through effect—that is, that God’s power, guided by his reason, is brought into act [Note: [Col. 1309D] Incorrectly expanded in the *Introduction to Theology*.].

And if anyone understands the name “Spirit” in this way, namely according to the effects of his grace, the Spirit is not rightly called eternal, just as neither Lord nor Creator is; for, as we have said, he has not always existed as Spirit according to effects. Hence the Evangelist John, beginning from God’s eternity, when he showed that the Word was eternally with God by saying, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him,” etc. (John 1:1), seems to have made no mention of Spirit by which he might establish that he is eternal. Speaking of God and his Word, he attributes eternity only to the Father and the Word, saying, “This was in the beginning with God” [Col. 1310D].

Perhaps, however, in what I added concerning the effect of works—“All things were made through him”—he seems to have indicated the Spirit according to the effects which God created by his goodness. According to these effects, as we have said, Spirit is not eternal—that is, not given—just as Plato’s soul of the world is not. Nor is it strange that the Evangelist’s passage should agree especially with Plato, since Augustine, as we recalled above, found the entire meaning of these words in the books of the Platonists.

There are, moreover, some who wish the love of God to extend not merely to creatures but also from one person to another, so that the Spirit himself is the Father’s love for the Son and the Son’s love for the Father. Augustine expressly maintains this in book XV of *On the Trinity*:

“Finally, if among God’s gifts nothing is greater than love, and no gift of God is greater than the Holy Spirit, what follows more fittingly than that he himself is the love which is called God and is from God? And if the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father ineffably manifests the communion of both, what is more fitting than that he should properly be called love who is the Spirit common to both?”

Hence also Jerome’s statement on Psalm 17: “The Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but the love which the Father has in the Son and the Son in the Father” [Col. 1311B].

This perhaps seems especially necessary to say and maintain: that the love of the Father for the Son, and of the Son for the Father, should also be called the Holy Spirit, and not merely love directed toward creatures. Otherwise it might seem that the Holy Spirit could fail to exist and consequently that the Trinity itself would not exist necessarily. For it could be that no creature ever existed, since no creature exists of necessity; and it consequently seems to follow that God’s disposition toward creatures—that is, the affection he has toward them—would not exist of necessity, and therefore that the Spirit himself, whom we call God’s own disposition or love, would not exist of necessity [Col. 1311C].

But if we understand God’s love as directed not only toward creatures but also from one person toward another, we plainly avoid this difficulty. And perhaps, although creatures themselves do not exist of necessity—that is, they can wholly fail to exist—God himself nevertheless necessarily remains in his own will and, being wholly immutable, cannot lack any good of his own. But we reserve fuller treatment of this for later, when the subject presents itself and we carefully distinguish the mode of procession chiefly in connection with divine power.

Yet I judge that the Spirit ought by no means to be called the Father’s gift with respect to the Son, or the Son’s gift with respect to the Father, because he cannot be given to one from whom he cannot be absent—that is, to one in whom he exists necessarily, since he is necessarily the Spirit of both [Col. 1311D].

I do not judge it foreign to the question to ask whether these names of personal properties which are in God—namely fatherhood, sonship, and procession—may be predicated of God as the others are. That is, just as one says, “God is omnipotence,” or wisdom, or love, goodness, justice, mercy, piety, so may one also say, “God is fatherhood,” or sonship, or procession. For, as we stated long before, it is established that nothing is in God which he himself is not, since everything that is good—that is, every nature—must be either Creator or creature [Col. 1312A].

Either, therefore, we must say that these properties are not certain good things or natures, or we must profess that God is them, since it is established that they were never created: they could in no way have begun, but are wholly eternal. And perhaps nothing prevents us from maintaining that, just as we take God’s omnipotence to be God omnipotent, because we understand God’s Wisdom as nothing other than God wise, and his goodness as God good, so we may admit God’s fatherhood to be God the Father, sonship to be the Son, and procession to be the one proceeding, that is, the Holy Spirit.

Yet we do not recall any authority of the Fathers using these propositions, as they use the foregoing ones. Wherever they treat the properties themselves, they call them properties [perhaps “or properties”] or relations; and no one has ever called God by these names. It is therefore not unfitting that, just as in other things we do not take relations to be things distinct from their subjects, and yet do not therefore join their names to those subjects by predication, so we should observe the same here. That is, if we entirely separate divine substance, or the individual persons, by predication from the relative properties which they have, just as we separate a human being or Socrates from the fatherhood he possesses, then we should in no way grant that God’s fatherhood, or any relation to the Son, is God the Father or even God [Col. 1312B].

Yet fatherhood itself is not another thing from those persons, nor perhaps the same thing, since that which does not possess true entity [perhaps “essence”] in itself cannot properly be called a thing—so as to be in itself one thing numerically, essentially distinct from all other things which are not it. But my *Grammar* contains, as I judge, a careful treatment of this in its reconsideration of the categories. Therefore we do not call the three properties three things—that is, three essences—but three diversities of relations in one essence, through which, as stated, the three persons subsist.

Since, then, we maintain that these properties are not things, and it has been said, “Whatever is in God is God”—that is, there is no thing in him which is not himself—we plainly cannot be compelled on this account to grant that these properties are God, since, as stated, they are not some existences among things, but properties subsisting in one thing [Col. 1312D].

If someone perhaps objects that, if they are not things, they are not all things or are nothing, since everything which exists is some thing, he is plainly mistaken, not knowing how to distinguish the force of propositions. Aristotle, on the authority of Por… [text defective], asserts that the verb “is” is used equivocally: in one way of substances, in another of their properties. For when we say that a human being is, it is as though we posit that the human being remains in his substance—that is, that someone is himself or is some human being. But if we say that fatherhood is, it is as though we posit that something is a father, not that fatherhood itself is its essence.

Hence it is wholly false that fatherhood is nothing—that is, does not exist—so long as something is a father, that is, has it. The statement, “Whatever is, is a thing; therefore fatherhood does not exist if it is not a thing,” likewise has no bearing upon the form of the syllogism, if we attend to the force and meaning of the propositions rather than their sound. For “Whatever is, is a thing” is as though one said, “Whatever thing exists is itself a thing.” But when it is added, “Fatherhood is not a thing,” and it is inferred from these that fatherhood does not exist, the sense of the conclusion, as we have said, is as though we said that nothing is a father.

Once the propositions have thus been resolved by explanation, the argument will be as though it said: Every thing which exists is a thing; but fatherhood is not a thing; therefore nothing has fatherhood—which plainly does not follow [Col. 1313B].

If anyone takes it badly that we have here invited the reader to the reconsideration of the categories, and says that this treatise cannot suffice him and therefore charges it with being incomplete, he may briefly be instructed concerning the predication of father and fatherhood: why, although we do not wish fatherhood to be a different thing from father, we nevertheless do not join them to one another by predication, so as to say that father is fatherhood, and conversely.

For if father were fatherhood, father would certainly have to be assigned through participation in father, so that it would be altogether the same for someone to be the one who is father and for him to have fatherhood in himself—that is, for him to be father—which is wholly false. For just as it is one thing for something to be that which is prior, or that which is perpetual, and another thing for it itself to be prior or perpetual—for there formed things are predicated, but here the forms themselves—so it is one thing for something to be the one who is father and another for it itself to be father. That is, it is one thing for it to be the one who has fatherhood and another for it itself to have fatherhood, although the former cannot exist without the latter [Col. 1313C].

Therefore, whoever says of something that it is father predicates fatherhood, not father. But if he said that it is the one who is father—that is, the one who has fatherhood—then he would indeed predicate father himself. Father, therefore, is not fatherhood, since father is not assigned through participation in father, but, as stated, through participation in fatherhood. Nor conversely is fatherhood father—that is, one having fatherhood in relation to his son—since fatherhood is not a substance at all and cannot beget a son from itself. Rather, it is a relational property of substance than a substance. But enough of this for the present [Col. 1313D].

The final question remaining is how only Christians hold this faith of the Trinity, and not Jews or Gentiles also. For, as we have said, for God to be Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is for God to be generating Power, begotten Wisdom, and proceeding Goodness. Since no intelligent person, whether Jew or Gentile, doubts this, this faith seems lacking to no one. We too grant this, following the Apostle, who says: “What is known of God is manifest to them” (Rom. 1:19). That is, they perceive by reason what pertains to divinity, because natural reason teaches every person these things concerning God.

Hence, when Augustine above presented the opinions of the Platonists concerning God’s Word, he affirmed that he found in them only what pertains to the divinity of the Word, and nothing concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, in which it is certain that the entire sum of human salvation consists and without which the other things are believed in vain. Those too who recoil from our language about the faith can readily be convinced that, when they hear “God the Father” and “God the Son,” they agree with us in the meaning of the words [Col. 1314B].

Let us ask them whether they believe in God’s Wisdom, concerning which it is written, “You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103:24); they will immediately reply that they do. Then let us duly infer that in this very matter they believe in the Son of God as we do, since by the Word or Son of God we understand the same thing which they understand by God’s Wisdom. Whoever accepts that there is a Son undoubtedly also does not doubt that he whose Son he is exists—that is, the Father. We shall likewise prove that they believe in Spirit if we explain to them what we understand by this name, namely the Goodness of divine grace itself.

I think an easy opportunity may be taken from this to convert any persons alien to our faith, if by such arguments we convince them that they already share with us the meaning of the faith. Although they do not profess it with their lips as we do, because they do not know the meanings of our words, nevertheless they already hold it in their hearts, as it is written: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness” (Rom. 10:10) [Col. 1314C].

We have dared to write these things concerning the most lofty and incomprehensible philosophy of divinity, compelled often and provoked by the importunity of unbelievers. We assert nothing concerning what we say, nor do we intend to teach truth, which we profess ourselves unable to know. But neither do those who glory in attacking our faith seek truth; they seek conflict. If, when provoked, we can resist them, it should suffice that we defend ourselves. Those who attack, however, fail and fall away from their purpose unless they conquer.

And since they especially assail us with philosophical arguments, we too have chiefly pursued such arguments—arguments which, I believe, no one can fully understand unless he has laboured in philosophical studies, and especially dialectical ones. It was necessary, moreover, that we resist our adversaries also by means of what they accept, since no one can be argued against or refuted except from premises he has granted, so that the judgment of Truth may be fulfilled: “From your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant” (Luke 19:22) [Col. 1314D].

# BOOK V

[Col. 1315]

[Col. 1315A] Having dealt with those matters which seem to concern the distinctive profession of the Christian faith—namely, the distinction of the three persons in one and the same wholly simple substance of divinity—it is pleasing to direct the mind’s gaze more deeply toward the contemplation of the perfection of this highest Good, and, by reconsidering each point more carefully [Note: [Col. 1315D] The *Introduction* has “repeating.”], to determine with highly plausible and honourable arguments whatever seems to involve some question. Thus, the more fully the perfection of this highest Good becomes known, the more strongly it may draw each person to itself by desire.

First we must recapitulate the unity of the divine substance, and afterwards the Trinity of persons. In the preceding books labour was expended in defense of our profession; here labour must be expended in its amplification.

[Col. 1315B] The first inquiry, then, concerns the basis for believing in one God, and why it is fitting to believe in one rather than many. Here the first question presents itself: whether the divine height could be investigated even by human reason, and whether through reason the Creator could be recognized by his creature; or whether God himself first supplied human beings with some sensible sign of his knowledge, appearing first, as it were, in an angel or in some visible form, as is related of the first parents, to whom he is said to have spoken in paradise.

And perhaps this happened first: the invisible Creator revealed himself to human beings in some visible form. Yet if we consider more carefully the power of reason itself, whose proper function is to transcend every sense and investigate what sense cannot reach [Col. 1315C], then surely the subtler in nature and more remote from sense a thing is, the more rightly it submits itself to the judgment of reason and the more it ought to provoke the application of reason to itself.

Moreover, since by the distinguished image of reason [Note: [Col. 1315D] The *Introduction*: “image.”] the human being is particularly compared to God, a human being ought first to have directed reason toward nothing other than him whose image—that is, whose more express likeness—he possessed through it. And perhaps reason should be considered more readily disposed to perceive no thing than that whose likeness it has more fully acquired. For it is easy to infer like from like; and the more like one thing is to another, the more easily it can attain from itself a knowledge of that to which it is nearer by nature [Col. 1315D].

But if experiences of the senses themselves also seem necessary for this purpose, namely that we might be led from sensible things to intelligible things [Col. 1316A] [Note: [Col. 1315D] The *Introduction* has “might be led,” singular], this too was easy: God, the best creator and disposer of all, could show by the things he both makes and orders so wonderfully how great he is through his own works. For by the quality of visible works we judge the skill of an absent craftsman.

In this way the Apostle himself declares that God granted even the reprobate knowledge of himself. Writing to the Romans, he proves every human being inexcusable and liable to be charged with contempt of the Creator, since natural law itself, which consists in reason, offered them knowledge of him even without writing, in the manifestation of his works. For he says:

“The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the impiety and injustice of those human beings who hold the truth of God in injustice, because what is known of God is manifest [in] them. For God has made it manifest to them. For his invisible things are understood and perceived through the things which have been made, from the creation of the world—his eternal power also and divinity—so that they are without excuse. For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. 1:18) [Col. 1316B].

And after some words: “Therefore you are inexcusable, every human being who judges” (Rom. 2:1); that is, every person who uses the judgment of reason in discerning good and evil, and in discerning the very natures of Creator and creatures.

Solomon also indicates that he greatly marvels at certain wise persons of the world: they investigated the world by reason and attempted to discuss its nature in each of its parts, while not yet discerning its Creator, whom they could more easily perceive by reason. “For if,” he says, “they were able to know so much that they could estimate the age, how did they not more easily find the Lord and Creator of that world?” (Wis. 13:9) [Note: [Col. 1315D] The *Introduction* adds “by reason,” but it is absent from Scripture.]

This was also carefully perceived by Tully, the greatest of Latin philosophers. Seeing that the world was not only made excellently but also excellently ordered, he maintained that this was accomplished by providence rather than chance [Note: [Col. 1316D] The *Introduction*: “maintaining.”], and set forth for us both his own reasoning and that of the other philosophers. Hence, in the first book of the *Rhetoric*, he says:

“Things carried out by counsel are managed better than things administered without counsel [Note: [Col. 1316D] The edition adds: ‘A household governed by reason is furnished and equipped in every respect better than one administered rashly and without any plan.’]. An army commanded by a wise and shrewd general is governed more advantageously in all its parts than one administered through the rashness or folly of someone. The same is true of a ship.”

Having set forth this proposition and suitably established it by comparison of analogies, he immediately adds the minor premise of the syllogism: “But nothing of all things,” he says, “is administered better than the entire world. For the risings of the constellations preserve a definite order, and the yearly [Note: [Col. 1317D] The *Introduction*: ‘souls.’] changes not only occur always in the same way through a certain necessity, but are also suited to the uses of all things; and the long alternations of night and day, never changed in any respect, have never harmed anything. These are all signs that the nature of the world is administered by no mediocre counsel.”

“And if,” he says, “things are managed better by counsel than without counsel, and nothing of all things is administered better than the whole world, therefore the world is administered by counsel” [Col. 1317B].

Plato, the greatest of all philosophers, carefully considering how rationally all things happen and are ordered in the world, says:

“Nothing occurs whose origin is not produced by a lawful cause and reason. For things called accidental or unforeseen with respect to us are fixed in God by certain laws of reason, and each thing comes to pass by the best counsel. This counsel by which all things are done and ordered most excellently some customarily call God, others the nature of things itself, others the mind or soul of the world; but all understood it to be the highest good proclaimed by Socrates.”

Anaxagoras is said to have been the first among all philosophers to have perceived a divine mind as the maker of all natures, as blessed Augustine recounts in book VIII, chapter 2, of *The City of God* [Col. 1317C]. Hence also Augustine’s statement in the letter [or letters] to Macedonius: truth should not be dear because it did not escape Anaxagoras, but because it is truth, even if none of them had known it.

It could also readily be inferred by reason that the world itself and the things within it do not exist from themselves or subsist through themselves, but that all things are both made excellently and governed by some other being far surpassing all things. For what is from itself is evidently nobler in nature than what is from another. And there is no doubt that whatever is capable of reason and intelligence surpasses all other things [Note: [Col. 1318D] The *Introduction*: “is found.”]. Therefore one ought not to concede that a rational substance is from another if one posits that what lacks reason is from itself.

None of us is unaware that he himself is by no means from himself, but is begotten by another. How, then, shall we deny that things lacking reason are from another? Therefore it is fitting that the parts of the world, which naturally are prior, were made; and consequently that the world derives its beginning from another and was made. For the world was made for the sake of humankind, to whom it ministers in all its parts; and it is fitting that it is far inferior to humankind. Hence one ought by no means to grant that it was not made when the human being was made [Col. 1317D].

Still less is it fitting that irrational things should rely upon their own governance rather than rational things [Note: [Col. 1318D] The *Introduction*: “rational rather than irrational.”]. Yet it is clear that, though rational, a human being is by no means sufficient for his own governance, since he cannot govern himself in the sea of this life as he wishes. Much less, therefore, should things be entrusted to their own governance when it is certain that they lack reason by which they could govern themselves. Such is the world and each of its individual parts. By these and similar arguments, then, I judge it manifest that everything in the world has a creator or governor, whom we call God.

### On whose unity it now remains to dispute

It remains now to discuss his unity: namely, why it is more fitting that one creator and ruler should preside over the world than many, and why one God and Lord of all rather than many ought to be believed. [Col. 1318B] For it is certain that all things are governed with so much the greater harmony the fewer persons are entrusted with their governance. But nothing is known to be governed better or with greater harmony than the whole universe, as the Ciceronian argument set forth above has explained. Its governance is therefore subject to one. [Note: [Col. 1318D] *Introduction*: “Its governance is therefore subject to one governance.”] For, as has been said, nothing is governed with greater harmony than the world—nor indeed any thing whatever over which one ruler alone presides. Therefore the world is in no way subject to several rulers, but to one alone. For harmony is preserved in all things in proportion as greater identity is maintained; and one withdraws from harmony in proportion as one departs further from unity. Therefore, if harmony is to be supreme, identity must be supreme and unity pre-eminently preserved.

Nothing can be so identical or one with anything else as it is with itself; nor can anything agree with another as it agrees with itself, since nothing is unlike itself. Thus it is fitting that all things look to and be referred to one, so that what is carried on amid the diversity of things may be administered harmoniously by one rational principle, with due order observed in all things. Nor should it be believed that several are more suitable for the creation of things than for their universal governance; rather, it is rightly believed that all natures are made by one, just as they are governed by one, so that they may be governed more harmoniously in proportion as they are joined by greater harmony. Their harmony is greater in proportion as they flow more fully from one [Note: [Col. 1318D] *Introduction*: “from one more fully.”] and the same principle, wholly and always, and as their maker departs from multiplicity and diversity.

But things were first made in order that they might afterward be governed in the best manner; [Col. 1318D] and the things that were made in order to be governed were, while being made, of course prepared for governance. Therefore, if the things made were to be governed in the best manner, they had to be prepared in the best manner for governance while they were being made. But how are they best prepared, while being made, so that afterward, once made, they may be governed best, unless from their very creation they are bound together by the highest mutual harmony, so that they may be governed more harmoniously and better in proportion as their natures have been more harmoniously joined to one another in their very constitution? To this harmony of constitution, as also [Col. 1319A] to the unity of governance, the very unity and highest identity of the creator brings about the result. Hence it is also evident that there is wholly one and the same creator as well as ruler of all things: him whom we call God and rightly confess to be the Supreme Good.

For how could he be called the Supreme Good unless he surpassed all other goods? But whatever surpasses all other things must surely be one and unique. And that which is acknowledged to be perfect in itself and, by its own will, sufficient through itself for all things that must be done—whence it is also called omnipotent—cannot have any equal [Note: [Col. 1319D] *Introduction*: “any good as a part.”] good. For that which is superfluous cannot be good. Yet another creator or ruler would be superfluous if one is equally sufficient for all things as several are. But he is sufficient, since, as has been said, he is the supreme [Col. 1319B] and perfect good, sufficient for all things. Therefore, in no way is it fitting that there should be, or that one should believe there to be, several gods.

“But perhaps,” you will say, “the better any good is, the better its multiplication would be; and thus that Supreme Good called God would be better multiplied than unique. And if we desire to exalt and magnify it, we ought to proclaim it multiple rather than simple.” But I think that the first answer to this is that, on this reasoning, the more gods we proclaim, the more we amplify the glory of divine excellence. We should therefore proclaim infinitely many gods, so that we may magnify its glory infinitely—especially since there is no reason by which it could be reduced to some fixed [Col. 1319C] number, when, according to the argument just given, we magnify it all the more as we extend its number further.

Thus there would have to be more supreme goods than inferior goods—indeed, infinitely many altogether—so that there could be no knowledge of them, since no limit would be found in nature; nor could even God comprehend by knowledge things not circumscribed by any natural limit. Further, if there are several gods, how shall we call any one god the Supreme Good, when something is greater than him—namely, the multitude of gods itself, greater than any single one from that multitude? Nor could that be called good which, as we have already shown, would be superfluous.

Finally, every multitude is a certain whole [Note: [Col. 1319D] *Introduction*: “indeed.”], and every whole is naturally posterior to its own parts. And everything simpler must necessarily be firmer, since every composite is by nature capable of dissolution, and is weaker in proportion as it is more liable to dissolution. Who, moreover, would deny that any good is more precious in proportion as it is rarer, and more glorious in proportion as it is more unique? Hence even things that are less necessary than others are often nevertheless altogether preferred to them because of their rarity: gold to iron, pepper to grain. Therefore its very singularity commends the glory of divine excellence; and that singularity is also the greatest commendation of [Col. 1320A] his works, both in making them and in ordering and governing them. For nothing [Note: [Col. 1320D] *Introduction*: “properly.”] can be made or governed with as great harmony as those things which one alone both creates and governs.

I think these considerations sufficient to establish the singular excellence of God; and I suppose that every good person will readily assent to them—one who envies no one and greatly rejoices in the excellence of all things. Yet we rely more on arguments from nobility than from necessity [Note: [Col. 1320D] *Introduction*: “we employ.”], since among good persons that is always judged foremost which is more highly commended by its nobility; and that argument is always weightier which inclines more toward nobility than necessity, especially since [Col. 1320B] noble things please through themselves and immediately draw us to themselves by their own power.

How noble and salutary it is that all things should look to one best ruler and creator, and that all things should be made or governed by reason rather than chance, no one’s reason fails to suggest to his own conscience. For what concern for good works would be in us if we revered no one through love or fear, if we were wholly ignorant of God? What hope would restrain the malice of the powerful or attract them to good works if the most just and most powerful being were believed in vain?

Let us grant, then, that while we seek to benefit and please the good, we cannot compel the obstinate, even though we stop their mouths with arguments that are not necessary. Let us grant this, I say, if they wish; but let us oppose what they do not wish, accusing their supreme shamelessness if they attack by calumny what they can in no way refute, and what is commended by the greatest nobility and usefulness. Let us ask them on what ground they prefer to choose that God does not exist rather than that he exists. Since they can be compelled necessarily toward neither alternative, while one is commended by many arguments and the other by none, let us confound their most unjust shamelessness: they refuse to follow what they do not doubt is best and what accords with all arguments and authorities, and embrace the contrary.

But if, concerning the hidden natures of things and even the state of heavenly things—which they cannot investigate by experience and therefore cannot know with certainty—they yield to human authorities [Note: [Col. 1320D] *Introduction*: “believe.”], why do they not likewise acquiesce in those same authorities concerning God, the author of all things? But enough of this against this first and greatest obstinacy of unbelievers.

Now, from the unity of the divine substance, which we have laid down as a foundation, the order of discussion is to proceed to the distinction of the three persons that are in the same substance. It remains to discuss, with careful examination, divine power, wisdom, and goodness—according to which, as was said, the three persons are distinguished—in order to commend perfectly and completely that Supreme Good. Thus, in proportion as, [Col. 1321A] as we have mentioned above, the perfection of this good is more fully known, it may draw each person more strongly to love of itself; especially because difficult questions about these matters can disturb even the minds of believers, and can more easily draw the less educated into grave scandals and assist unbelievers, in proportion as they appear more difficult to resolve. Let our first consideration therefore concern God’s omnipotence.

It seems necessary first to ask how he is truly called Omnipotent if he cannot accomplish everything; or how he can do everything if we can do certain things that he cannot. For we can do certain things—walk, speak, perceive—which are wholly alien to the nature of divinity, since an incorporeal [Col. 1321B] substance can in no way possess the necessary instruments for such acts.

In response to these objections, I think it should first be stated that, according even to the philosophers and to ordinary usage, the power of any thing is never understood except with respect to what pertains to that thing’s advantage or dignity. No one counts it as a human power that a person may easily be overcome; rather, it belongs to his impotence and weakness that he cannot resist what harms him. Whatever tends toward a human defect and discredits rather than commends the person must be ascribed to impotence rather than power.

Thus Aristotle, in the second genus of quality—where he treats natural power and impotence—refers the curative and the hard to power, and the liable-to-illness [Col. 1321C] and the soft to impotence. Yet we call something liable to illness when it can easily become ill, that is, when it cannot readily resist such an affection; and soft when it may easily be cut or broken apart. Conversely, he refers the curative and the hard to power, though “curative” is said of what cannot easily be cut. Thus, in the preceding cases—namely, liability to illness and softness—the ability to undergo what pertains to a thing’s disadvantage or weakness belongs to impotence rather than power; and conversely the inability to undergo such things must be ascribed to power. Otherwise, we would call impotence power and power impotence.

Therefore let no one presume to call God impotent in any respect because he cannot sin as we can; for even in ourselves this must not be attributed to power, but to weakness. Hence Augustine, in book XV of *On the Trinity*: “His great power is that he cannot lie.”

There are also things which ought to be counted as powers in certain beings but not in others, and which are praiseworthy in some but blameworthy in others, since the same things often commend the dignity of some beings but not that of others. For example, if a man can overcome a bear by strength, this should be attributed to the man’s great power. Thus he would surpass other [Note: [Col. 1321D] *Introduction*: “other men.”] men and be more highly commended; [Col. 1322A] but no one would regard the same ability as remarkable in a lion or elephant. We would call the man powerful in comparison with other men, but not the lion or elephant in the same way.

Likewise, in a human being the ability to walk should be attributed to power, because it suits human need and diminishes human dignity in no respect. But in God, who accomplishes all things by will alone, what is necessary in us would be altogether superfluous, and therefore should be attributed in him not to power but wholly to defect—especially since the ability to walk would detract in many ways from his excellence. For then he could be moved locally and would admit a composition of feet, so that his bodily and compounded substance would be both mobile and dissoluble.

Nevertheless, we rightly proclaim God powerful in respect of all those things that we can accomplish, and attribute to his power all that we do: “in him we live and move and are.” And he “works all things in all,” for he uses us as instruments to accomplish what he wills. He is also said to do what he causes us to do, just as a rich man is said to build a tower through the workmen he employs. He is said to be able to accomplish everything who, either by himself or through subject creation, does everything that he wills and in the manner he wills; and he himself also causes it to be done in that way. [Note: [Col. 1321D] The *Introduction* omits: “and he himself also causes it to be done in that way.”] For though he cannot walk, he can cause walking to occur—that is, can cause someone to walk—since by his creation [Note: [Col. 1321D] *Introduction*: “by his creation for this purpose.”] he prepares each person [Col. 1322C] fit for this, and even in the act itself preserves and sustains that person so that he may perform this [Note: [Col. 1322D] *Introduction*: “and so that he may perform this.”] act.

God, therefore, is said to be able to do all things not because he can undertake every action, but because in all things that he wills to be done nothing can resist his will. [Note: [Col. 1322D] In the *Introduction*, the material appearing in the other part of this column follows here, beginning “Hence this is so.”] Hence the Apostle says: “Who shall resist his will?” (Rom. IX.29). And the Psalmist: “Whatever he willed, he did” (Ps. CIII.13).

But when the same Apostle elsewhere says, “God wills all to be saved and no one to perish” (I Tim. II.4), in accordance with the prophet’s words, “I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather that he be converted and live” (Ezek. XXXIII.11); and when Truth himself says to the obstinate and condemned city: “How often I wished to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!” (Matt. XXIII.37)—it is clear that the term “divine will” must be understood in two ways. Otherwise, since God does all whatever he wills and wills all to be saved, we would be compelled to profess [Note: [Col. 1323D] The *Introduction* adds “that all are at some time to be saved,” omitting what follows through “God is therefore said to will.”] that, according to Origen’s detestable error, salvation extends even to demons, that all [Col. 1323B] will at some time be saved, and that Truth itself contradicts Truth when it says concerning the wicked and the righteous: “These shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV.46). Again, he says to the wicked: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (ibid., 41).

God is therefore said to will in two ways: either according to the ordinance of his providence—that is, when he disposes and determines something within himself, establishing by his providence that he will afterward accomplish it in this way—or according to the exhortation or approval of his counsel, by which he warns each person toward that for which he would be prepared to reward him by grace. According to the former way in which God is said to will something [Note: [Col. 1324D] *Introduction*: “something else.”]—that is, to ordain by his grace [Col. 1323C] and establish within himself that certain things should occur—we and the Apostle say that, in the things he wills to occur, nothing can resist his will, nor can it be impeded by any event, since all things must obey it.

According to the latter way, however, he is said to will many things that do not occur: that is, he exhorts toward many things which, if they occurred, he would certainly reward by his grace, but which do not occur. Thus he counsels every person concerning salvation and exhorts him to it, though few obey. God therefore wills the sinner’s conversion because he counsels him toward what he would graciously reward. In a certain sense, something is said to be pleasing to him in which we would experience his grace. Conversely, he is said not to will those things which he dissuades, [Col. 1324A] or whatever things he ought rather to punish than reward with any gift, and in which we would experience his wrath rather than his grace—that is, punishment rather than reward.

I think we must ask whether God can do more things or better things than he does, or whether he could in any way desist from what he does, so as never to do it. [Col. 1324B] Whether we grant or deny this, we shall perhaps incur many troubling difficulties. For if we suppose that he can do more or fewer things, or can refrain from what he does, we greatly derogate from his supreme goodness. For it is certain that he can do nothing but good things. But if, though able, he does not do good things, and withdraws himself from some things which [Col. 1324C] ought to be done, who would not accuse him as envious or unjust? Especially because no labor in doing anything burdens him, whose will subjects all things equally to itself, as it is written: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. CXLVIII.5).

Hence Plato’s most true argument, by which he proves that God could in no way have made the world better than he made it. Thus in the *Timaeus* he says: “It must be said why the Maker, etc.” Who would deny, moreover, that everyone wishes to act well as much as he can, or that everyone ought to act well as much as he can? If we maintain this judgment concerning ourselves, [Col. 1325A] how much more must we maintain it concerning him who is supremely good and whom no labor of operation can burden? How does God will and have power if he does not accomplish? Or how is he just if he does not do what he ought and also can do? And if he did less good than he could, he would not be perfectly good.

God therefore does all that he can and does as much good as he can. Nor can he refrain from what he does—namely, fail to do it when it ought to be done. For if he refrained from good things that he could do when they ought to occur, he would thereby be proved not perfectly good. Further, he cannot lack whatever belongs to him naturally. But good will belongs naturally and substantially—not accidentally, as in us—to him who must necessarily be supremely good and benevolent and who cannot be diminished in his goodness. Hence he cannot lay aside the good will that he has, and which must be acknowledged to be God. He cannot lack any good will that he has; therefore it is necessary that he will everything that he wills. Nor can [Col. 1325C] his will be ineffective. Therefore he must accomplish whatever he wills, provided that we understand “will” as the will pertaining to his ordinance.

These arguments, then, seem to establish that God can in no way do more than he does, or do better, or desist from what he does, but must do all things as he does. Yet against each of these propositions most difficult objections arise, so that this dilemma attacks our faith severely from either horn. For who would dare deny that God can save one who is to be damned, or make one who is to be saved better than he will be by the bestowal of God’s gifts, or entirely refrain from ever creating him?

For if God [Col. 1325D] cannot save this man, then neither can he himself be saved by God. This consequence of reciprocity is necessary. If this man is saved by God, God saves this man. Hence, if it is possible for this man to be saved by God, it is possible for God to save this man. For the antecedent cannot be possible unless the consequent is possible; otherwise an impossibility would follow from a possibility, which is altogether false. Thus Boethius, in the first book of the *Hypotheticals*, defining the impossible, says: “Impossible is that upon the positing of which something false and impossible follows.” That is, impossible is what has a necessary inferential connection with something impossible. [Col. 1326A] He introduced this definition because of the structures of syllogisms, in which he intended to prove premises impossible through the derivation of impossible conclusions.

But who would dare deny the necessary force of this inference: “This man is saved by God; therefore God saves this man”? Since the inference is possible, the conclusion is possible. Thus, if it is possible for this man to be saved by God, it is possible for God to save him; and if it is not possible for God to save him, it is not possible for him to be saved by God. That is, as we stated above, if God cannot save this man, then he himself cannot be saved by God, and consequently cannot be saved at all, since it is certain that he can be saved only through God.

But if this man cannot be saved, free choice already perishes; and commands concerning salvation are imposed in vain upon the person [Col. 1326B] who cannot at all be saved and cannot do the things by which he may be saved. Similarly, if God cannot make him better, neither can he be made better by God, and thus cannot become better in any way, since, if that occurred, it would necessarily be done by God. Far be it from us to concede that any one of us is so good and perfect that he cannot grow further—although Plato appears strongly to incline to the contrary view, when he says that all things are made by God as good as the nature of each permits, and that God, from his own supreme good will by which he established the cause of all things to be made, was compelled to make each thing, and to make it as good as its nature [Col. 1326C] bears.

For thus it is written in the *Timaeus*:

> “It must be said,” he says, “for what reason the creator and artificer judged that this whole generation should be established. He was best; and envy is far removed from the best. Therefore, consistently with himself, he willed all things to become like himself, insofar as the nature of each could be capable of blessedness. If anyone holds this will of God to be the most certain origin of things, I should agree that he thinks rightly. For God, willing all things indeed to come forth good and no evil at all, left no propagation of evil, insofar as the nature of things that come into being permits.”

These words of Plato appear plainly to declare that all things are made by God as good as they can be made, or as good as he can make them. The saints too appear to have followed this reasoning when they proved that God the Father begot the Son as good as he could, so that he might be equal to him. Hence Augustine, in book 64 of the *Eighty-Three Questions*:

> “God,” he says, “whom he begot, because he could not beget one better than himself—for nothing is better than God—ought to beget as his equal. For if he willed it and could not, he is weak; if he could and did not will it, he is envious.”

This also bears upon the statement of the Council of Nicaea which, as we said in the first book, blessed Jerome recites:

> “Far be it, then, that there should be anything more or less in the Son of God, whether in place, time, power, knowledge, equality, or subjection—when this is said, let it be attributed to his flesh, not to his divinity. For if anything more or less is found, except that the Father begot the Son and except that the Son was not born from himself but from the Father, then the Father is found to be either envious or powerless, and indeed temporal.” [Note: [Col. 1327D] *Introduction*: “is recognized.”]

[Note: [Col. 1322] In Migne, the following two paragraphs are printed in parallel with the passages “he prepares each person fit . . . the term ‘divine will’ must be understood in two ways,” and “in the latter way he is said to will many things . . . God can do.” respectively.]

[Col. 1322C] Hence comes the statement which blessed Augustine records in the *Enchiridion*:

> “For he is truthfully called omnipotent for no other reason than that he can do whatever he wills, and the effect of the will of the Omnipotent is not hindered by the will of any creature.”

The same writer, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*:

> “He cannot do unjust things, because he himself is supreme justice and goodness. But he is omnipotent not because he can do everything, but because he can accomplish whatever he wills, so that nothing can resist his will so as to prevent its fulfilment or hinder it in any way.”

John Chrysostom, Homily XXVIII, *On the Exposition of the Creed*, which begins, “Upon the fabric of the whole Church”:

> “He is called omnipotent because his power cannot discover an inability, as the prophet says: ‘Whatever he willed, he did’” (Ps. CIII.13).

He himself, therefore, is omnipotence, so that he can do all that he wills.

[Col. 1323C] God does not act as Nebuchadnezzar thinks: that is, in the manner of those who, in what they do, attend not so much to what is good as to satisfying their own will, whatever it may be—those of whom it is written: “Thus I will, thus I command; let my will stand in place of reason.” Rather, he ought to be said to will individual things to occur because he saw that it was good for them to exist. It is therefore clear that, whatever God does or omits, a just and rational cause underlies it: he does or omits only those things which ought to be done or omitted [Col. 1324A] and which befit him.

But if it is necessary for him to do what he does, then it is certainly just that he does whatever he does, and without doubt whatever he ought to do. But if he ought to do it, he surely cannot justly omit to do it. For everything whose occurrence is just is unjust to omit; and whoever does not do what reason requires sins just as much as one who does what is not at all consonant with reason.

“But perhaps,” you will say, “just as what he now does is just, good, or rational, it would be good—and equally good—if he did something else and omitted this.” But if the thing he omitted to do were equally good when he chose this, there was surely no reason why he should omit that and choose this. “But there was,” you say, “because, although it was not necessary for both to occur [Col. 1324C] and it was equally good for this or that to occur, whichever of them occurred would have been rationally done.”

But by this reasoning, what was not done ought equally to have been done as what was done, and it was equally good for that to occur as for this. Yet when something is good to do and has a rational cause why it should be done, the person who omits [Col. 1324D] what he knows ought to be done by him plainly acts irrationally; and so we fall back into the difficulty stated above. But if you say of the alternative that was not done that it was not good for him to do it except on the condition that the other ceased, then by the same reasoning it must not simply be conceded that it was good for the other—the one that was done—to occur, since it has equally been granted that it was good for both this and that to occur. Did God, then, do what was not [Note: [Col. 1325D] *Introduction*: “what he knew was not.”] good to do? Far be it. But if only what he does is good for him to do, then he can do only what he does, since he can do nothing except what it is good for him to do.

By this reasoning, then—by which it is proved that God the Father begot the Son as good as he could, since otherwise he would be guilty of envy—it is clear also that God makes everything he does as excellent as he can, and does not will to withhold any benefit that he can bestow. For there is nothing that he does or omits except for the best and rational cause, although that cause is not hidden. Hence also the Platonic saying:

> “Everything that is generated is necessarily generated from some cause. For nothing comes to be whose origin is not preceded by a lawful cause and reason.” [Col. 1327B]

Likewise Augustine, when proving that all things in the world are done or ordered by divine providence, and that nothing occurs by chance or accident but all things proceed from divine counsel, says in question 26 of the *Eighty-Three Questions*:

> “Whatever happens by chance happens rashly; whatever happens rashly does not happen by providence. Therefore, if some things happen by chance in the world, the whole world is not administered by providence.”

Again:

> “That good by participation in which the other things are good is good not through another but through itself. This too we call divine providence.”

Therefore nothing happens by chance in the world. Moreover, in all that God does, he attends so greatly to what is good that he is said to be inclined to do each thing more by the value of goodness itself than by the mere pleasure of his own will. Hence Jerome’s statement in his exposition of the version of Daniel 3, where Nebuchadnezzar says of God: “For he does according to his will [Note: [Col. 1327D] In Daniel: “among the powers of heaven as well as among the inhabitants of heaven.”] both in heaven and on earth, and there is none who can resist his hand or say, ‘Why have you done this?’” (Dan. IV.32).

Jerome says:

> “And he speaks this as a worldly man. For God does not do what he wills; rather, he wills what is good. Nebuchadnezzar spoke thus so that, while he proclaims God’s power, he seems to accuse his justice, because he has suffered punishments undeservedly.”

Thus Jerome’s saying, “For God does not do what he wills; rather, he wills what is good,” means: In all things, therefore, [Col. 1327D] which God does or omits, he has a rational cause why they should be done or omitted by him.

If, therefore, there is a reason why he ought to do or omit something, then it surely ought to be done or omitted by him. But how can he omit what ought to be done by him, or how can he do what he ought to omit? For one who does what is in no way fitting for him to do does not act rightly. But whenever God altogether omits something, so as not to do it, he surely sees why it is never to be done by him. [Note: [Col. 1328D] I fear that something is missing at this point, perhaps omitted through the copyist’s carelessness.] This is as remote both from the truth and from our own opinion as possible; yet later, if we can, we shall smooth it over by some explanation. [Col. 1328A] Let us now return to what we began. How, I ask, could we also say that he cannot omit doing at some time the things he does, unless he necessarily does them at some time? Yet he makes this man good; therefore it is necessary that this man become good, and that he in no way be capable of being damned—which is wholly false. For it is written in praise of the righteous man concerning him who “was able to transgress and did not transgress, to do evil and did not do it” (Ecclus. 31:10).

It is also written that God could have redeemed the human race in another way than the way in which he did. Hence blessed Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, book XIII, chapter 10:

> “To those who say, ‘Did God lack another means by which to free human beings, so that he willed his only-begotten Son to become man and, having become mortal, to suffer death?’ it is too little merely to answer that this means by which he deigns to free us is good. We must also show that no other possible means was lacking to God, to whose power all things are equally subject. Yet no other means was more fitting for healing our misery. Why should Christ’s death not occur—or rather, why, passing over countless means by which the Almighty could have freed us, should this one in particular be chosen?”

Likewise [Note: [Col. 1328D] *Ibid.*, ch. 18.]:

> “God could certainly have assumed a human being from another source, in whom there would be a mediator between God and human beings, not from the race of that Adam—just as he created the first man not from anyone’s race. He could have created, either in this way or in whatever other way he wished, another man by whom the conqueror of the first man would be conquered. But he judged it better [Col. 1328C] to assume a man from the very race which had been conquered.”

Likewise, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*:

> “God could have made all things at once, but reason forbade it.”

Likewise:

> “He could have mingled the soul with the clay of the earth and thus formed the body; but this was rendered unsuitable by reason, because the house had first to be put together and then its inhabitant introduced.”

The same author, in the *Enchiridion*:

> “The will of the Almighty can never be evil. Moreover, he can do many things which he neither does nor wills. For he could have brought it about that twelve legions of angels fought against those who seized him.”

The Evangelist Matthew says: “Do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will at once provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26:53). [Col. 1328D]

Likewise:

> “Then, in the brightest light of Wisdom, what faith now holds will be seen: how certainly the will of God is unchangeable and most efficacious; how many things he can do and does not will; but that he wills nothing which he cannot do.”

The same author, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*:

> “Does it seem absurd to you to say that something can be done for which an example is lacking, when, as I believe, you do not doubt that it has never happened for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle? Yet he said that even this was possible to God.”

Likewise:

> “To these may be added what is read in the book of Wisdom: that God could inflict many new torments upon the ungodly, with creation serving him at his command, [Col. 1329A] though he did not inflict them. He can also do what concerns that mountain which faith would remove into the sea, though we have nowhere read or heard that this has happened. Whoever says that any of these things are impossible to God, you see how foolishly he speaks and how contrary to faith in his Scripture. Many other such things may occur to one reading or thinking, which we cannot deny are possible to God, although there is no example of them.”

The same author, in *On Nature and Grace*:

> “The Lord raised Lazarus: without doubt he could do so. But because he did not raise Judas, should one say, ‘He could not’? He could, therefore, but he did not will it. For if he had willed it, he would have done this also by the same power, because ‘the Son gives life to whom he wills.’”

Entangled, then, by arguments as well as authorities of such weight on both [Col. 1329B] sides of the dilemma, I do not easily find a way by which we may disentangle ourselves. For the more forceful the assaults of the questions, the more difficult, surely, must their solutions be. But since we intend in all things to preserve intact and, as far as we can, magnify the divine honor, let us confidently implore his aid in this matter: that he who frees his own from sins may free us from words also, and may deign by his grace to untie these snares, as he unties those, to the praise of his name; lest we be accused before him himself of falsehood or presumption against him—he who, as the tester of hearts and reins, attends in all things more to intention than to action, and not to what is done but to the spirit in which it is done.

Therefore, relying upon the method by which we began to discuss God, [Col. 1329C] let us set forth what seems to us on this matter, without any obstinate assertion. It seems to us, then, that God, who is supremely good and cannot increase or diminish in his goodness—which he possesses naturally and substantially from himself, not, as we do, through acts—is from his own ineffable goodness always so inflamed, if I may speak in human fashion, that he necessarily wills what he wills and [Col. 1330A] necessarily does what he does. For he cannot lack the good will which he has, since it is natural and coeternal to him, not acquired, as ours is to us. And everything that belongs to the nature of divinity necessarily and in every way inevitably belongs to him—such as justice, loving-kindness, mercy, and every good will toward creatures.

Therefore, he who is necessarily as good as he is good, and cannot be diminished in goodness, must will concerning each individual thing as well as he wills, and must deal with each individual thing as well as he can. Otherwise, even according to Plato, he would be envious and not perfectly beneficent. But if he necessarily has the will which he has to do something, and if that will can never lack efficacy, it follows that he necessarily does the things which necessarily accompany his will. Whatever, therefore, he does, he does necessarily just as he wills necessarily. For so great is his goodness that, since it necessarily impels him to do the good things which he can do, he cannot at all refrain from effecting the good things which he can effect, and doing so as well as or as swiftly as he can.

Hence, even concerning things which he delayed for a long time, it is said in his praise that “he will not delay.” For no one ought to be called slow in something which he defers precisely so that it may be done more fittingly; only one who fails to do what he ought to do may be called slow. For to defer, like to take away, a good which you can provide is not perfect goodness; that is, it is not perfect goodness to postpone until the future what you judge ought already to be done, when you can do it already just as well as in the future. Therefore God necessarily willed and made the world to exist, and he was not idle [Col. 1330C] in not being able to make it before he made it, because before he made it, it was not fitting that it should be made. For if he had made it earlier, it would certainly have been fitting for it to be made earlier, since he cannot do anything except what is opportune—indeed, except what is best, that is, as good as is fitting in any given case—which is reserved to his lofty counsel.

[Col. 1329]

# PETER ABAELARD’S *SIC ET NON*

First published complete by Ernst Ludwig Theodor Henke, Doctor and Ordinary Professor of Theology, Inspector of the Philippian Theological Seminary, Director of the Academic Library, and Georg Stephan Lindenkohl, Minister of the Divine Word, senior member of the Philippian Theological Seminary.

(Marburg in Hesse, at the expense and press of the Elwert Academic Bookshop, 1851, octavo.)

# PREFACE

The “collection of opinions called by him *Sic et Non*” [Note: [Col. 1329] These are either Abaelard’s own words or those of the copyist who transcribed and prepared the Munich manuscript. Compare below, col. 1349.], which all earlier editors of Peter Abaelard’s works had regarded as a matter of conscience not to have printed, seemed fifteen years ago to have been brought to light by the most distinguished Victor Cousin—Peter’s successor in the chair of philosophy, and at this time the supporter and defender of philosophical study as it languished in France—in the volume of Abaelard’s writings which he published at Paris in 1836 and adorned with a most learned introduction. [Note: [Col. 1331] *Ouvrages inédits d'Abélard pour servir à l'histoire de la philosophie scolastique en France*, published by M. Victor Cousin. Paris, 1836, quarto.] He seemed at last to have fulfilled the hopes of all who expected that no small fruits would be gathered from this book for a correct understanding of the character and method of medieval schools.
