But when the new edition was more carefully examined by those most concerned with illuminating the studies of the scholastic period through it, it at once became evident that so many portions of the book *Sic et Non* had deliberately been omitted and cut out—whether to provide brevity or to comply even then with the scruple by which the book’s publication had until then been prohibited—that not even half the entire work had been copied out. There was indeed an index recording the questions on which Abaelard had collected the sayings of the ancients; but only sixty-eight collections of opinions, and those the shorter ones, had been appended to the proposed questions, while the others, longer ones, had once again been cut away and prohibited. Thus the hope of those who wished to know the complete work, and through it the whole historical-theological apparatus upon which Peter’s doubts or positions had been built, was again frustrated.

Moreover, the distinguished editor, being occupied, as was proper, with more serious tasks in editing Abaelard—namely, discerning his doctrine and method and tracing them to their sources—had not bestowed upon the text of the ancient pronouncements, even those which he had arranged to be copied, such care, whether his own or perhaps that of others working rather cursorily, that he could seem to have fully restored it in every respect. Nor, when in the preceding year that eminent man began a new edition of Abaelard’s works, [Note: [Col. 1331] *Petri Abaelardi Opera*, ed. Victor Cousin, with the assistance of C. Jourdain and E. Despois. Paris, 1849, quarto, vol. I.] did he promise therein to supplement anything perhaps left unfinished here; rather, by the list of works to be published which he inserted in the preface, he indicated that he would not return to books which he appeared already to have completed in the collection published in 1836.

Since this was so, we judged that not every task to be undertaken in these studies ought to be entrusted to the care and labor of learned men in Abaelard’s native country—men who, even so, have deserved far more than our own countrymen in illustrating the scholastic age—but that we ourselves ought to make provision for that literary diligence of which Germans sometimes boast excessively in comparison with other nations. It had become generally known that the oldest manuscript of the book *Sic et Non* also existed in Germany: namely, the manuscript formerly kept in the monastery of Tegernsee, which the Munich Library added to its less inaccessible treasures. This was known from the time when Friedrich Heinrich Rheinwald published from it Abaelard’s *Epitome of Christian Theology* and briefly described the manuscript in the preface to that edition. [Note: [Col. 1331] *Petri Abaelardi epitome theologiae Christianae*, first published by Fr. W. Rheinwald. Berlin, 1835, octavo.]

Ten years ago I was able, through the kindness of the distinguished men who preside over the incomparable library of this city, and through the intervention of the eminent Friedrich Thiersch, to see it at Munich, so that I might examine it more carefully at home over a sufficiently long period and compare it with the text of Cousin’s edition and with the writings from which Abaelard himself had excerpted his opinions. In that work I soon discovered both how much value the manuscript retained, even after Cousin’s labors, for restoring and correcting Abaelard’s text in what he had already published, and how worthwhile it was to draw forth and supply from it those materials omitted in his edition.

But it likewise soon appeared that this task was obstructed by so many difficulties—especially if the sayings collected by Abaelard from other writers had to be sought in their own works and restored, so far as possible—that, given the limitations of my strength and leisure, it would have been hopeless unless the excellent young man most closely associated with me, Georg Stephan Lindenkohl, Minister of the Divine Word, who had been assigned as my colleague both in administering the academic library and the Philippian Seminary, had been willing to lend me his labor and strength and had bravely undertaken much work in elucidating the text from the manuscript and comparing it with editions of the Fathers. Accordingly, joining our forces, we judged that we could—and perhaps ought to—undertake a new edition, indeed the first edition, of the entire book *Sic et Non*. We must now briefly state the procedure and method we followed in preparing it.

The Munich manuscript, written on 105 parchment leaves in the manner and in the script of which we append a specimen below, presents an image of the entire work as completed by its author. For it also contains what Abaelard judged should be prefixed to the book’s prologue after being copied from elsewhere. “It pleased us,” he says, [Note: [Col. 1331] Below, col. 1349.] “to prefix to this work of ours, which we have compiled into one volume from sayings of the saints gathered together, that decree of Pope Gelasius, so that it may be known that we have introduced nothing from apocryphal writings.”

Thus that so-called decree of Pope Gelasius—really, if not Pseudo-Isidorian, at least somewhat earlier—occupies the first place also in the Munich manuscript, in the same form in which it was inserted first into the collections of Pseudo-Isidore, Burchard, and Ivo, and then also into Gratian’s *Decree*, distinction 15, chapter 3: namely, from the words “the holy Roman Church” to the words “we confess to be condemned forever.” Only a few matters are omitted. At the beginning of the list of received writers, after the mention of Athanasius and Basil, five names of Fathers are lacking: John of Constantinople, Theophilus and Cyril of Alexandria, Ambrose, and Augustine himself. Yet the names themselves seem to show that these were omitted not deliberately by Abaelard or by an earlier editor of the decree, but through the negligence of a later copyist. For a similar reason, the names of Hesychius and Lucian seem to be missing from the list of prohibited writers; and, in the catalogue of heretics, the evidently corrupt names Calixtus, Subianus, and Euticius seem to have been substituted for the sounder readings which at these points give Caelestius, Jovinian, and Eutyches.

Immediately afterward four passages are added, placed below in the margin, [Note: [Col. 1331] Augustine, *On John* (Maurist ed. III, 2, p. 805): “Nicodemus came, who had first come to Jesus by night.” Here, therefore, it must be understood that Nicodemus came to Jesus not only then, but that he first came then; and that afterward he came in order to become, through hearing, a disciple—something now certainly made known to almost everyone in the *Revelation of the Body of the Most Blessed Stephen*. Gennadius the presbyter, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 46: “Lucian the presbyter, a holy man, to whom God revealed in the times of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius the place of the tomb and relics of St Stephen, the first martyr, wrote this revelation in Greek for the whole Church.” Likewise, ch. 47: “Avitus the presbyter, Spanish by race, translated into Latin the writing of Lucian mentioned above.” Bede, in the chronicles (*On the Six Ages of the World*): “Lucian the presbyter, to whom God revealed in the seventh year of the emperor Honorius the place of the tomb and relics of blessed Stephen, the first martyr, and of Gamaliel and Nicodemus, who are mentioned in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles, wrote that revelation itself in Greek for all the Churches. Avitus the presbyter, a man Spanish by race, translated this revelation into Latin and, adding his own letter, sent it to the Western peoples through Orosius the presbyter. Orosius too, having arrived at the holy places, where Augustine had sent him to Jerome to learn the nature of the soul, received relics of blessed Stephen and, returning to his country, was the first to bring them into the West.”] whose purpose in following is difficult to conjecture, unless perhaps they were added in order that, at the very threshold of the work, other men no less distinguished for orthodox faith might immediately contradict the writer who asserted—namely Gelasius, who fixed a definite number of writers to be received and prohibited the use of many others as apocryphal—and might acknowledge revelations other than those sanctioned by Gelasius and the witnesses of those revelations. By this very fact their sayings, if they did not openly state, at least suggested and compelled the reader to anticipate the disagreement and discord among authorities which the nature of the whole work entailed.

“We have also added,” Abaelard continues in the prologue, “excerpts from the *Retractations* of blessed Augustine, so that it may appear that nothing is set down here from what he himself corrected in retracting it.” Therefore in the Munich manuscript also, the decree of Gelasius and the four passages added to it are followed by an epitome of the entire book of *Retractations*. First, indeed, the titles of all the works there described are listed in the same order in which Augustine himself enumerates them, after these words of Abaelard:

> “As is gathered from Augustine’s book of *Retractations*, before writing these retractions [Col. 1333] he had already composed ninety-three works in 232 books. What these works are and in what order they were written is indicated by the same *Retractations* and by their chapters; these chapters are as follows.”

Then three passages from Augustine’s *On the Trinity* are inserted. [Note: [Col. 1333] Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book I, ch. 3: “Therefore, whoever reads these things: where he is equally certain, let him proceed with me; where he equally hesitates, let him inquire with me; where he recognizes his own error, let him return to me; where he recognizes mine, let him call me back. Thus let us enter together upon the way of charity, and I urge this pious agreement upon all who read what I write, and in all my writings, especially in those where the unity of the Trinity is investigated; for nowhere is error more dangerous, nothing more laborious to seek, and nothing more fruitful to discover. Whoever therefore says as he reads, ‘This is not well said, because I do not understand it,’ criticizes my manner of speaking, not my faith. Perhaps it could indeed have been said more plainly; nevertheless, no human being has ever spoken in such a way as to be understood in every respect by everyone, nor do all writings composed by everyone come into everyone’s hands. It may happen that those able to understand our writings do not find other books clearer and at least happen upon these. Therefore it is useful for many works to be made by many persons in a different style but not with a different faith, even on the same questions, so that the matter itself may reach a greater number—one group in this way, another in that.” Likewise: “I think that some slower readers, in certain places in my books, will suppose that I held what I did not hold. Who does not know that their error ought not to be attributed to me, if, as though following me but not grasping me, they wandered into some falsehood?” Likewise, book III, ch. 1: “Certainly, although in all my writings I desire not only a devout reader but also a free corrector [Maurist edition: ‘corrector’], this is especially true in those where the greatness of the question itself is at stake. Would that I could have as many discoverers as I have opponents! Yet, as I do not want my reader to be devoted to me, so I do not want my corrector to be devoted to himself. Let the former not love me more than the Catholic faith; let the latter not love himself more than Catholic truth. As I say to the former, ‘Do not be subject to my writings as though to canonical Scriptures, but in them, when you discover what you did not believe, believe it without hesitation; in the Scriptures, however, do not firmly maintain what you do not hold as certain unless you have understood it as certain’; so I say to the latter, ‘Do not correct my writings on the basis of your own opinion or contempt [Maurist edition: ‘contention’], but on the basis of divine reading or unshakable reason.’”]

This was doubtless done so that, in the Church’s greatest teacher, they might show a mind free from excessive self-admiration and always ready to be taught better things by others, and thereby express at the very opening of the work not only the nature and excellence of the books of *Retractations* but also Abaelard’s own mind. Then follows, over ten leaves, a fuller epitome of Augustine’s *Retractations*, prepared in the same manner as the book *Sic et Non* itself: the author did not attempt to summarize and reproduce Augustine’s sense in his own words, but extracted the finest sayings of Augustine from his text and combined them, in the manner of a tessellated work, into a new arrangement. Thus he both adequately expounds the book’s subject and selects and joins what he especially commends from these works and wishes at the same time to be held as his own above the rest.

Finally, before the prologue, he brought this introduction to an end by adding several sayings of the Fathers on Augustine’s praises. [Note: [Col. 1333] Jerome to Augustine (Martianay IV, 644): “I have not been able at present to reply to your two most learned little books, dedicated to my name and shining with every splendor of eloquence, not because I think that anything in them deserves criticism. For whatever could be said and drawn by subtle intellect from the fountains of the holy Scriptures has been set forth and discussed by you. But I have resolved to love, receive, and admire you, and to make your sayings my defense.” The same, to Desiderius, *On Twelve Writers* (Martianay V, 416): “Augustine the bishop, flying over mountain summits like an eagle and not considering what takes place at the foot of the mountains, clearly proclaims the vast spaces of heaven, the situations of lands, and the circuit of waters. For one who wishes to climb a fruitful tree hastens gradually upward to gather the higher and greater fruits, leaving the branches close to the little ones. But we, who are little, weak, and inferior: if we wish to gather the lower things, all goes well with us.” Gregory in the *Register* (Maurist ed. II, 1067): “If you desire to be nourished with delicious food, read the little works of blessed Augustine, your fellow-countryman, and do not seek our bran in comparison with his fine flour.” From the Decrees of the Popes: “Augustine, whom no report of sinister suspicion has stained.” After this passage, the beginning of the work itself is indicated in the manuscript by these words: “The excerpts from Augustine’s *Retractations* are finished. The prologue of Abaelard begins,” etc.]

In these sayings too, after he had portrayed Augustine as like himself in nobility of mind and desire for learning, there was something of an apology, by which his own character and method were defended and commended.

I do not know whether all these materials ought also to have been repeated verbatim and printed here, in order that the altered image of the book *Sic et Non* might be restored. But since the Gelasian catalogue, together with Gratian’s decree in which it is inserted, is read in every edition of the *Decree* and of the body of canon law, and since the *Retractations* normally occupy the first place in every edition of Augustine’s works, there was no need for them to be repeated here. It was enough to indicate in what order and with what purpose they had been placed in the vestibule of the whole work, and to append in the margin—as has been done above—the remaining sayings added to them by Abaelard from other sources.

In editing Abaelard’s text itself, our chief concern was, so far as possible, to use the Munich manuscript as the foundation of the work; nevertheless, we did not neglect materials which might serve our purpose, whether from Cousin’s edition, which followed the Avranches and Tours manuscripts, or, where it was lacking, from the works and editions of those writers whose sayings Abaelard himself had excerpted. First, whenever the Munich manuscript contradicted Cousin’s text, we adopted the former not only where it appeared to contain the better reading but also where it appeared tolerable, and we noted Cousin’s reading in the annotations. But where we found the manuscript corrupted by manifest copyists’ errors, we placed its reading in the margin, [lacuna] [Col. 1335] and followed Cousin in the text. We furthermore added from Cousin four questions, from 139 through 143, which were entirely absent from the manuscript.

Yet we hesitated more doubtfully about how to write whenever the best editions of the Fathers—especially those owed to the notable industry of the Maurist monks—seemed to indicate a sounder reading than either the Munich text alone or even that text together with Cousin’s. Errors could indeed have crept into those editions also and require remedy; but they could also have been introduced by copyists living either before or after Abaelard. Since, however, it was Abaelard’s text, not that of the ancient Fathers, which had to be restored, there could scarcely be doubt about the rule by which we ought to proceed: namely, that the latter kind of error should, if possible, be corrected, but the former deliberately retained. Yet when a decision had to be made in individual instances, it could scarcely ever be determined whether a suspicious reading was due to older copyists or only to the few through whom Abaelard’s text had been transmitted and transcribed from his autograph to the copyist of the Munich manuscript.

What then was to be done? Since, for Abaelard’s purpose in appending a saying of a writer to a particular question, disagreement between a faulty transcription of that saying and one which seems sounder is usually of no consequence, one can scarcely ever doubt that Abaelard himself, if he had known the sounder reading, would not have disapproved it but would gladly have admitted it into his text. Thus, just as it is the office of a good interpreter not merely to attend separately to an author’s words and explain them through other words, but also by whatever other aids to discern his meaning—a meaning which, if the author himself has sometimes expressed it less satisfactorily in words, he will not resent being understood and distinguished by the interpreter of his words—so it is the office of one who wishes to grasp the mind of a writer collecting the sayings of others to wipe away perhaps the stains scattered upon those sayings, even if it is uncertain whether the writer himself had already detected them.

We certainly could not always bring ourselves to refrain from receiving into the text readings which we judged sounder, although we found them neither in the manuscript nor in Cousin, but only in editions of the Fathers. Yet, well remembering that we were not permitted to mix ancient with modern materials and thus to seek to correct Abaelard’s book, we never admitted into the text from editions of the Fathers, against the authority of both the Munich and French manuscripts, anything which we did not mark with brackets—indeed, usually with an indication of the edition from which it had been received—and to which we did not append at least the reading of the Munich manuscript in the margin.

We shall be more readily excused, we hope, for not judging it worthwhile to reproduce letter for letter the manuscript’s orthography, variable here and there and conformed to no fixed rule, but preferring to follow common spelling for readers’ convenience. Nor do we expect to be blamed for transcribing more fully, from the Vulgate translation, the citations of sacred Scripture which in the manuscript we found indicated only by the first letter of each word, and for generally adding the references to chapter and verse. We certainly have not left the text of the Munich manuscript altogether unchanged by all this, nor have we persuaded ourselves that in doing so we have come nearer to what Abaelard himself wrote in his own hand. Yet we judged that the book would thereby be more convenient and welcome to the greatest number, and we preferred to assist the use of as many readers as possible rather than to earn praise for preserving or restoring even the smallest traces of ancient times.

We fully grant that the mind and purpose by which Abaelard appears to have been moved to write this book are not in every respect to be praised. We grant that in this desire to discover and explain disagreements there is perhaps some partisan spirit and pleasure in another’s embarrassment. We do not deny that weighty grounds existed for those to whom the Catholic Church and its unshaken authority were dear, for judging the book “worthy rather of eternal darkness than of light,” [Note: [Col. 1335] Thus in the preface of Martène and Durand, *Thesaurus novus Anecdotorum*, vol. V.] since it makes the agreement of those whom the Church regards as witnesses of the truth entrusted to herself alone disappear not only in minor questions but also in certain highest articles of faith; and since it often indeed exaggerates and simulates the disagreement of these witnesses through a fictitious appearance of it, but not seldom also actually demonstrates it in such a way that no ground for doubting it remains, so that by all this the very foundation of the Church seems shaken and overthrown.

Finally, we do not deny that our age is far different from the twelfth century, and that our contemporaries have less need of that salutary remedy—or poison—by which the theologians of that age especially had to be healed: awakened from their torpor and from a lifeless repetition of ancient opinions, they had to turn to the use of their own powers and to their first exercises in theological and critical studies. Not a few of our contemporaries have already fallen into the opposite vice: they regard as a drug, only sparingly beneficial to the sick, even the living water that would satisfy thirsty souls, and the critics’ razor, “the sword of the Spirit” (*μάχαιραν τοῦ πνεύματος*), which would overcome the world.

Yet we know also that at every time the same diseases, though clothed in varying forms, break out again and must always be opposed. At every time the crowd of human beings is prone to stupor and sloth, to languor in loving and seeking truth, to cowardice and dullness in devoutly hearing the testimony of the soul, to self-admiration and contempt for those who think more rightly; and it is afflicted and corrupted all the more seriously if persons arise who persuade the deceived populace that these vices are virtues and ought not to be corrected but cherished.

Nor do we see these evils to have ceased even now in the schools of theologians; indeed, they have returned from the commonwealth into the Church. And now, in a manner like that sixth century when the emperor, having closed the schools of philosophers and left monasteries alone, thought that he had made excellent provision for the training of future ministers of the Church, a new barbarism threatens us also. Day by day those increase who offer receptive ears to the seductive speech of persons professing that one becomes better equipped for the sacred office not through labor, sweat, and honorable diligence devoted to theological and philosophical studies, but through the passion for shouting and the audacity of calumniating; that one must refrain from the ancient exertion of all one’s powers in investigating truth, which has so often fostered pride, and from the desire to learn and to hear as many persons as possible, by which, they say, everyone is excessively disturbed; that one must yield to idleness, by which no one can be proud or deprived of tranquility of mind—that is, one must consider it necessary to hold many things by a single obedience to the formula received from those who wield power, combined with contempt for those who investigate it, that is, with the extinction of love for truth; and that by this single sacrifice one makes satisfaction for every other virtue and expiates their absence.

These evils have indeed spread more widely and still grow more vigorously than can be suddenly uprooted. Yet it may happen, no less in our own age than in the twelfth century, that this book will bring them some remedy, even if it is like a drug. For although it displays, in a time almost deprived of all the literary resources in which we abound, the beginnings—however unpolished—of theological disciplines hitherto almost unknown, namely sacred criticism, the history of dogmas, biblical theology, and the dogmatic theology to be built upon them, it not only urgently commends to our contemporaries these historical studies and the more careful use of the resources now available for them, and offers them an anthology ingeniously selected from the Fathers, but was composed by its author principally in order “to summon readers to the greatest exercise of investigating truth and to make them keener through inquiry.”

May God turn it to good.

Written at Marburg, in the academic library, 15 April 1851.

E. H.

[Col. 1337]

# HERE BEGINS PETER ABAELARD’S PROLOGUE [Note: [Col. 1339D] Munich manuscript: “of Abaelard the philosopher,” with the word “Peter” omitted.] TO *SIC ET NON*

[Col. 1339]

[Col. 1339A] Since, amid so great a multitude of words, certain sayings even of the saints seem not only to differ from one another but actually to conflict with one another, we must not rashly judge those by whom the world itself is to be judged, as it is written: “The saints shall judge the nations” (Wisdom III); and again: “You too shall sit in judgment” (Luke XXII). Nor should we presume to accuse as liars or despise as mistaken those to whom the Lord said: “Whoever hears you hears me; whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke X). Returning, therefore, to the consideration of our own weakness, let us believe rather that grace is lacking to us in understanding than that it was lacking to them in writing, to whom Truth itself said: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking in you” (Matt. X).

[Col. 1339B] What wonder, then, if, in the absence from us of that very Spirit through whom these things were written and spoken [Note: [Col. 1339D] Cousin: “dictated.”] and also inwardly communicated to their writers, we lack an understanding of them—an understanding to which we are especially hindered from attaining by an unfamiliar manner of expression and, often, by the differing sense of the very same words, since the same word is used now in this sense, now in that? For just as each person abounds in his own thought, so too in his own words. And since, according to Tully, sameness in all things is the mother of satiety—that is, it produces weariness—words themselves must be varied even for the same matter [Note: [Col. 1339D] Munich MS: “narrate”], and not everything laid bare in popular and common words. As blessed Augustine says, such things are veiled lest they become cheap, and are more pleasing [Col. 1339C] [Note: [Col. 1339D] Munich MS: “weightier”] in proportion as they have been investigated with greater effort and sought with greater difficulty.

Often, too, words must be altered according to the differing character of those to whom we speak, since it frequently happens that the proper meaning of words is unknown or less familiar to some people. If we wish to speak to them for instruction, as we ought, we must imitate their usage of speech rather than its strict propriety, as Priscian himself, the foremost authority on grammar and instructor in modes of expression, teaches. Blessed Augustine, the most diligent doctor of the Church, attended to this also. When in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine* he instructed the ecclesiastical teacher, he admonished him to pass over everything that hinders the understanding of those to whom he speaks, and to disregard both elegance and propriety of expression if, without them, understanding may more readily be achieved:

[Col. 1339D] “[Col. 1340A] The one who teaches,” he says, “should be concerned not with how eloquently he teaches [Note: [Col. 1340D] Munich MS: “is fitting”], but with how clearly.” A careful desire sometimes neglects more polished words. Hence someone, discussing this manner of speaking, said that it contains a certain “careful negligence.” Again: “In good teachers there should be such concern for teaching that a word which, unless obscure or ambiguous, cannot be Latin, should, in the manner of the common people—as people say it—be spoken so as to avoid ambiguity and obscurity; it should not be spoken as the learned speak, but rather as the unlearned customarily speak. For if our translators did not hesitate to say *de sanguinibus* [‘concerning bloods’], because they perceived that the matter required this noun to be stated in the plural in that place, although in Latin it is used only in the singular [Note: [Col. 1340D] Psalm XV, 4: “I shall not gather their assemblies concerning bloods.”], why should a teacher of piety, when speaking to the unlearned, hesitate to say *ossum* [‘bone’] rather than *os*, lest this syllable be understood not from *ossa* [‘bones’] but from *ora* [‘mouths’]? For what good is correctness of expression if the hearer’s understanding does not follow it, when there is no reason at all for speaking if those for whose understanding we speak do not understand what we say? Therefore, the one who teaches will avoid every word that does not teach.”

Again: “It is the mark of an outstanding disposition to love the truth in words, not the words themselves. For what good is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish? Or what harm is a wooden one if it can, when we seek nothing but that what is shut should be opened?”

How rash it is for one person to judge another’s meaning and understanding, who does not see? For hearts and thoughts are open to God alone. Recalling us even from this presumption, he says: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged” (Luke VI). And the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time, until he comes who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV). It is as though he openly said: Entrust judgment in such matters to him alone, who knows all things and is also the discerner of thoughts themselves. Thus, concerning the hidden mysteries of God, it is written figuratively [Note: [Col. 1340D] Cousin: “tropically.”] regarding the Passover lamb: “If anything remains, let it be burned with fire” (Exod. X); that is, if there is anything in the divine mysteries that we cannot understand, we should reserve it to be taught by the Spirit through whom it was written, rather than rashly define it.

[Col. 1340D] We must also carefully take heed lest, while certain sayings of the saints are set before us as though [Col. 1341A] opposed or alien to truth, we be deceived either by a falsely ascribed title or by corruption in the text itself. For many apocryphal works were entitled with the names of saints in order to gain authority; and some passages, even in the writings of the divine Testaments themselves, have been corrupted through scribal error. Hence Jerome, the most faithful writer and most truthful translator, writing to Laeta on the education of her daughter, warned us beforehand [Note: [Col. 1341D] Cousin: “fortified beforehand”], saying (Maur. IV, 569): “Let her beware of all apocryphal writings; and if she should ever wish to read them, not for the truth of doctrines but for reverence for their signs, let her know that they are not by those whose names stand at their head, and that it is great prudence to seek gold in mud.”

The same Jerome, on Psalm LXXVII, concerning its title, which is of this sort, “An understanding [Col. 1341B] of Asaph,” says [Note: [Col. 1341D] Cousin: “which is of this sort: ‘An understanding of Asaph,’ he says: Thus, etc.”]:

“It is written according to Matthew: when the Lord had spoken in parables and they did not understand, and so forth, ‘these things happened,’ he says, ‘that what was written through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: I shall open my mouth in parables.’ The Gospels have it thus even to this day. Isaiah does not say this, but Asaph. Again, then, let us simply say, as it is written in Matthew and John, that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour, but in Mark at the third hour. It was a scribal error, and in Mark the sixth hour was written; but many thought that gamma stood for the Greek *episēmon* [ἐπισήμῳ, “the marked sign”] [Note: [Col. 1342D] Thus Cousin (ἐπισήμω). Munich MS: *episomo*.], just as there was a scribal error there, when they wrote Isaiah instead of Asaph. For we know that the Church was made up in great part of unlearned Gentiles. Therefore, when they read in the Gospel, ‘that what was written by Asaph the prophet might be fulfilled,’ the first person who copied the Gospel began to say: ‘Who is this prophet Asaph?’ He was not known among the people. And what did he do? To correct the error, he made an error. Let us say something similar in another passage of Matthew (XXVII, 9): ‘He returned,’ he says, ‘the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him who was valued, as it was written in Jeremiah the prophet.’ We cannot find this at all in Jeremiah, but in Zechariah. You see, therefore, that there was an error here just as there.”

What wonder, then, if some things in the Gospels themselves were corrupted through the ignorance of scribes, and if the same sometimes happens in the writings of later Fathers, whose authority is far less? If, therefore, something discordant with truth should perhaps seem to occur in the writings of the saints, it is pious, fitting to humility, and required by charity—which “believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things,” and does not readily suspect faults in those whom it embraces—to believe either that the passage of Scripture was not faithfully interpreted, or that it has been corrupted, or to confess that we do not understand it.

Nor, I think, should we pay less attention to whether those things that are brought forward from the writings of saints are such as they themselves elsewhere retracted and, after recognizing the truth, corrected—as blessed Augustine did in many instances; or whether they stated them more according to the opinion of others than according to their own [Col. 1342A] judgment—as Ecclesiastes in many places introduces the conflicting opinions of different people and indeed is interpreted as “the disturber,” as blessed Gregory attests in the fourth book of his *Dialogues*; or whether, rather, they left them as matters to be investigated under a question, instead of determining them by a fixed definition. Thus the aforesaid venerable doctor Augustine reports that he did in his work *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, as he recalls concerning that work in the first book of his *Retractions* (Maur. I, 28): “In this work more things were sought than found; and of those found, fewer were established, while the rest were set forth as still requiring investigation.”

As blessed Jerome also attests, we know that it was the custom of Catholic doctors to insert even certain very bad opinions of heretics among their own [Col. 1342B] views in their commentaries, since, striving for completeness, they delighted in having passed over none of the ancients. Thus, replying to blessed Augustine, who had challenged him concerning his exposition of a passage of Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, he says (IV, 618):

“You ask why I said in my commentaries on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians that Paul could not rebuke in Peter what he himself had done. You maintain that the apostolic dissimulation was not a matter of economy but genuine, and that I ought not to teach falsehood. I answer that your prudence ought to remember the preface to my commentaries: conscious of the weakness of my powers, I followed Origen’s commentaries. That man wrote volumes on Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians; I pass over my teacher Didymus the Seer, Apollinaris of Laodicea, recently departed from the Church, and the old heretic Alexander, who likewise left several commentaries on this subject. I read all these things and, gathering much into my mind, summoned a secretary and dictated both my own views and those of others.”

Again: “It was for your learning to inquire whether the things we wrote were found among the Greeks; so that, if they had not said them, you might then condemn my own judgment in particular—especially since I freely confessed in the preface that I had followed Origen’s commentaries and had dictated both my own opinions and those of others, so that I might leave it to the reader’s judgment whether they ought to be approved or disapproved.”

Likewise, we do not doubt that blessed Hilary and certain other saints inserted many things from the writings of Origen himself, or of others who erred, among their [Col. 1342D] views, presenting to us the opinion of others rather than setting forth their own judgment. Yet this became known to us afterward not so much through them as through others. Thus the aforesaid doctor Jerome, writing to the presbyter Vigilantius and excusing himself for sometimes quoting or translating Origen’s sayings, says: “If this is a crime, let the confessor Hilary be accused, for he translated his interpretation of the Psalms and homilies on Job from Origen’s books” (IV, 276).

Accordingly, when we find certain things there discordant with truth or contrary to the writings of other saints, they should be attributed to Origen rather than Hilary, although Hilary himself does not distinguish this. Such is the statement immediately following, in which he endeavors to establish that the first Psalm is not to be understood of the Head, Christ, but generally of any other righteous person. Jerome too, in an exposition of certain Psalms, following Origen in the same way, included this statement. It must also not be doubted that Origen himself, as he testifies, set forth certain things entangled in serious errors according to the opinions of others. Thus Jerome, writing to the presbyter Avitus and collecting the manifold errors which Origen set down in his books *Peri Archon* [*On First Principles*], spoke thus of Origen:

“After so impious a discussion, by which he wounded the reader’s mind, these things,” he says, “are, according to our judgment, not doctrines but merely questions raised and proposed, lest they appear to have been left wholly untouched” (IV, 763).

Thus Jerome himself said above that he often dictated either his own opinions or those of others, in order to leave it to the reader’s judgment whether they should be approved or disapproved. Blessed Augustine too, when retracting and correcting many parts of his works, confesses that he set down many things there more according to the opinion of others than according to his own judgment.

Some things even in the Gospel seem to be said according to human opinion rather than according to the truth of things: for example, when Joseph is called the father of Christ even by Christ’s mother herself, in accordance with common opinion and custom, as she says: “Behold, your father and I have sought you sorrowing” (Luke II). So too, according to what is perceived by sight, we say now that the sky is starry, now that it is not; now that the sun is hot, now that it is not; now that the moon shines more or less, now that it does not shine at all—although these things always remain equally so in reality, even though they do not always appear equally so to us.

The Apostle too, following in several cases the language of those who disparaged him, does not hesitate to declare himself to be otherwise than he thinks himself to be: for example, “We are fools for Christ’s sake, but you are wise in Christ” (I Cor. IV, 10). The same Apostle also says that Melchizedek was without father, without mother, and without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end, because this is hidden from our knowledge and Scripture does not teach it—not because the truth of the matter is actually so. Samuel also is said to have appeared to the Witch of Endor in a phantom, not so much according to truth [Col. 1343D] as according to the appearance of the thing, which produced a false opinion in those who saw it. For, as blessed Augustine observes, that phantom was called Samuel because it displayed Samuel’s likeness, just as someone says in a dream that he saw Rome because he conceived its likeness in his mind.

Poetic and philosophical writings likewise often speak according to opinion as though it rested upon truth, though they plainly differ wholly from truth. Thus Ovid says (*Art of Love* I, 350):

> The harvest is always more fruitful in another’s fields,  
> And the neighboring herd has larger udders.

[Col. 1344A] Boethius too, when in the fourth book of the *Topics* he calls accident and substance the two primary kinds of things, has regard to opinion rather than truth. That philosophers also often set forth matters more according to the opinion of others than according to their own judgment, Tully openly declares in these words in Book II of *On Duties*:

“Although justice has sufficient authority without prudence, prudence without justice has no power to establish trust. For the more crafty and cunning a person is, the more odious and suspect he is when the reputation for uprightness has been removed. Therefore understanding joined to justice will have as much strength as it wishes for creating trust. Justice without prudence can achieve much; prudence without justice has no power at all. But lest anyone wonder why, although it is agreed among all philosophers and I myself have often argued that whoever possesses one virtue possesses all virtues, I now separate them as though someone who is not prudent could be just: one thing is the discussion in which truth itself is refined; another is speech adapted to everyone. Therefore, like the common people, we speak in such a way that we call some brave, others good men, and others prudent; for when we speak we must use popular and customary words.”

Finally, common speech ordinarily says many things according to the judgment of bodily senses otherwise than they are in fact. Though no place in the whole world is entirely empty, since every place is filled either with air or with some body, we nevertheless say that a chest is completely empty when we perceive that it contains nothing visible. A person who judges things according to [Note: [Col. 1343D] Munich MS: “also according to.”] the appearance of the eyes [Col. 1344C] says now that the sky is starry, now that it is not; now that the sun is hot, now that it is not; now that the moon shines more or less, now that it does not shine at all—although these things always remain alike in reality, though they do not always appear alike to us.

What wonder, then, if even holy Fathers sometimes stated or wrote certain things more according to opinion than truth? We must also carefully examine, when different things are said about the same subject, what is intended as a restriction of a precept [Note: [Col. 1343D] Cousin: “a removal of restriction”], what as the leniency of an indulgence, and what as an exhortation to perfection; so that, according to the diversity of intentions, we may seek a remedy for the apparent contradiction. And if it is a precept, we must ask whether it is general or particular—that is, directed to all in common or especially to certain persons. Times and the reasons for dispensations must likewise be distinguished, because what is permitted at one time is often found forbidden at another; and what is frequently commanded with rigor is sometimes moderated by dispensation. These distinctions are especially necessary in the enactments of ecclesiastical decrees or canons. Often a ready solution to controversies will be found if we can show that the same words have been used in different senses by different authors.

By all the methods stated above, the diligent reader will endeavor to resolve controversies [Col. 1345A] in the writings of the saints. But if a controversy should perhaps be so manifest that it cannot be resolved by any reasoning, authorities must be compared, and the one which possesses the weightier testimony and stronger confirmation must above all be retained. Hence Isidore’s statement to Bishop Massio: “At the end of the letter I thought this should be added: whenever a discordant opinion is found in the acts of councils, the opinion should be held rather whose authority is older or weightier.”

It is also certain that the prophets themselves sometimes lacked the grace of prophecy, and that from the habit of prophesying, when they believed themselves to possess the spirit of prophecy, they uttered false things by their own spirit. This was permitted them for the preservation of humility, so that they might more truly know [Col. 1345B] what they were through God’s Spirit and what through their own, and might know that when they possessed the gift of him who can neither lie nor be deceived, they possessed it as a gift. And he, when he is possessed [Note: [Col. 1345D] Cousin: “when they possessed it”], just as he does not confer every gift upon one person, so he does not illuminate the mind of the one whom he fills concerning every matter; rather, he reveals now this, now that, and when he discloses one thing, he conceals another.

Blessed Gregory, in the first homily on Ezekiel, demonstrates this with clear examples. Even the chief of the apostles, who shone with so many gifts and miracles of divine grace, after that special outpouring of the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord, who teaches [Note: [Col. 1346D] Cousin: “would teach”] his disciples all truth, fell into error concerning the continued observance of circumcision and certain ancient rites. When he had been severely and salutarily rebuked in public by Paul, his fellow apostle, he was not ashamed to cease from his destructive dissimulation. What wonder, then, when it is evident that even prophets and apostles were not wholly free from error, if some things in the manifold writings of the holy Fathers appear to have been stated and written erroneously for the reason set forth above?

But saints ought not to be accused as guilty of lying if, on occasion, believing things to be otherwise than the truth of the matter is, they speak not through duplicity but through ignorance. Nor ought anything said from charity for some edification to be charged to presumption or sin, since it is established that before the Lord all things are judged according to intention, as it is written: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. VI).

Hence blessed Augustine, treating of ecclesiastical discipline, says: “Have charity, and do what you will.” Again, on the Epistle of John: “Whoever does not have charity is not from God. Have whatever else you wish; unless you have this alone, nothing profits you. If you lack other things, have this, and you have fulfilled the law.” Again: “Therefore one brief precept is given you once for all: love, and do what you will.”

Again, in the first book of *On Christian Doctrine* (Maur. III, pt. I, p. 17):

“Whoever thinks that he has understood the divine Scriptures, or any part of them, in such a way that by that understanding he does not build up this twofold charity [Col. 1346A] of God and neighbor, has not yet understood them. But whoever derives from them an interpretation useful for building up this charity, though he has not said what the author whom he reads is proved to have intended in that place, is not deceived perniciously, nor does he lie at all. For in one who lies there is a will to speak falsely.”

Again, *Against Lying* (IV, 464): “A lie is a false signification by speech with the will to deceive.” Again, in the *Enchiridion* (VI, 202), chapter 23: “Certainly, no one who says what is false but believes it true is to be judged a liar, because, so far as he is concerned, he does not himself deceive but is deceived. Therefore he is to be charged not with lying but sometimes with rashness, because he too incautiously holds false things, believed, as true. On the contrary, the one who says what is true but believes it false is the liar; for, so far as his mind is concerned, because he does not say what he thinks, he does not speak truth, although what he says is found to be true. Nor is the one who unknowingly speaks truth with his mouth in any way free from lying if he knowingly lies in his will.” Again: “Everyone who lies speaks, with the will to deceive, against what he thinks in his mind.”

Again, on the Gospels, Book I (VI, 461): “What Jacob did at his mother’s prompting, so that he seemed to deceive his father, if carefully considered, is not a lie but a mystery. For a true signification can in no way rightly be called a lie.” For in this place the spiritual doctor understands a lie only as sin, weighing it more according to the speaker’s intention than according to the character of the utterance. The Lord, who tests heart and reins, considers not so much what is done as the spirit in which it is done [Col. 1346C]. Whoever speaks sincerely, without fraud or duplicity, according to what he believes, is free from this; as it also follows and is written: “He who walks simply walks confidently” (Prov. X).

Otherwise the Apostle Paul too would have to be accused of lying; for, following his expectation rather than the truth of the matter, he wrote to the Romans (XV, 28): “Therefore, when I have completed this and assigned to them this fruit, I shall depart through you into Spain.” Thus it is one thing to lie, another for a speaker to err and, through error rather than malice, to depart from truth in words. If God permits this to happen even to the saints themselves, as we have said, it occurs in matters that involve no harm to faith; nor does it happen fruitlessly to those for whom all things work together for good.

Ecclesiastical doctors themselves carefully observed this, and, believing that certain things in their works required correction, granted their successors permission to amend or not follow those things which they themselves had been unable to retract and correct. Thus the above-named doctor Augustine says in the book of *Retractions*: “It is written: ‘In much speaking you will not escape sin’ (Prov. X, 19).” Again, the apostle James (I, 19): “Let every person be swift to hear, slow to speak.” Again: “For we all offend in many things. If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (James [Col. 1347A] III, 2). “I do not claim this perfection for myself even now, when I am old; how much less when, as a young man, I began to write?”

Again, in the prologue to Book III of *On the Trinity*: “Do not submit to my writings as though they were canonical Scriptures. But in those Scriptures, when you find something you did not believe, believe it firmly. In my writings, however, do not hold firmly what you did not regard as certain unless you have understood it to be certain.”

Again, to Vincent Victor, Book II (Maur. I, 2): “I cannot and should not deny that, just as in conduct itself, so in so many of my works there are many things that can be censured by a just judgment without any rashness.” Again, in a letter to Vincent Victor: “Brother, do not seek to gather objections against such clear divine testimonies from the writings of bishops, whether ours, Hilary’s, Cyprian’s, or Agrippinus’s; for this kind of literature must be distinguished from the authority of the canon. It is not read in such a way that testimony is drawn from it as though it were not permissible to think differently if, in some place, they happened to judge otherwise than truth requires.”

Again, to Fortunatianus: “We ought not to treat the disputations of any persons, however Catholic and praiseworthy, as canonical Scriptures, so that it may not be permissible for us, while preserving the honor due to those persons, to disapprove and reject something in their writings if we happen to find that they held otherwise than truth does. Such am I in the writings of others as I wish my readers to be in mine.”

Again, *Against Faustus*, Book I, chapter 11 (VIII, 222): “Far be it from us to say that Paul ever erred and, through progress, changed his judgment! It may be said of those books that they contain something not consonant with truth, books written by us not with the authority of command but for the exercise of progress.” Again: “We are among those to whom the Apostle says: ‘And if you think otherwise about anything, God will reveal even this to you’ [Note: [Col. 1347D] Cousin: ‘to us’ (Phil. III, 15).]. Such writings are to be read not with a necessity of belief but with freedom of judgment.”

Nevertheless, so that no place might be closed off to such writings, and so that the most salutary labor of language and style might not be taken away from later generations for handling and examining difficult questions, the excellence of the canonical authority of the Old and New Testament was distinguished from later books. If anything there should disturb one as though absurd, it is not permissible to say, “The author of this book did not hold the truth”; rather, either the manuscript is faulty, or the translator erred, or you do not understand [Note: [Col. 1347D] The Munich MS inserts here: “Jerome, on Psalm LXXXVI.”].

But in the works of later writers, which are contained in innumerable books, if anything is thought perhaps to differ from truth because it is not understood as it was said, the reader or hearer nevertheless has free judgment there either to approve what pleases or disapprove what offends. Therefore, in all matters of this kind, unless they are defended either by certain reason or by that canonical authority, so as to show that what was discussed or narrated there either is wholly so or could have happened, anyone who dislikes it or refuses to believe it is not blamed.

Thus he calls the canonical Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments instruments in which it is heretical to profess that anything differs from truth. Concerning these Scriptures, he says likewise in his fourth letter to Jerome:

[Col. 1348A] “In the exposition too of the Apostle Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians, we find something that greatly troubles us. For if even useful lies are admitted into the holy Scriptures, what authority will remain in them? What judgment will then be pronounced from those Scriptures? By what weight will the contentious wickedness of falsehood be crushed?”

Again, to the same person concerning the same Scriptures: “It seems to me most ruinous to believe that there is any lie in the sacred books; that is, that those persons through whom that Scripture was administered and written down for us lied in anything in their books. For once any useful lie has been admitted into a summit of authority so lofty [Col. 1348B], no part of those books will remain which, wherever it seems difficult in morals or incredible in faith, may not be referred, by the same most destructive principle, to the design and purpose of the author’s lie.”

Blessed Jerome also, when he ranked certain ecclesiastical doctors above the rest, advised that they be read so as to be judged rather than followed. Thus is his counsel to Laeta concerning the education of her daughter: “Let her always keep Cyprian’s little works in her hands; let her run through the little works of Athanasius and the book of Hilary with an unimpeded step; let her delight in the treatises and talents of those in whose books the piety [Note: [Col. 1348D] Cousin: “whose piety,” omitting “in” and “books”] of faith does not waver. Let her read the rest in such a way as to judge them rather than follow them.”

Again, on Psalm LXXXI, as though entirely removing authority from all such writers, he says: “The Lord will recount in the writing of peoples and of these princes who were in her. He did not say, ‘who are in her,’ but ‘who were.’ ‘Of peoples’ is not enough; he also says ‘of princes.’ And of which princes? ‘Who were.’ See, therefore, how Holy Scripture is full of mysteries. We read the Apostle saying: ‘Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?’ (II Cor. XIII). What Paul speaks, Christ speaks—for ‘whoever receives you receives me’ (Luke IX)—in the writings of princes, in the writing of peoples, which is written for all peoples. See what he says: ‘who were,’ not ‘who are,’ so that, with the apostles excepted, whatever else is said afterward may be cut off and have no authority thereafter [Col. 1348D]. Therefore, though someone be holy after the apostles, though eloquent, he has no authority.”

Jerome to Vigilantius: “Whoever reads the little works of many writers ought to be like an approved money-changer: if any coin is counterfeit and does not bear Caesar’s image or is not stamped by the public mint, it should be rejected; but whatever displays Christ’s face with clear brightness should be stored in the purse of the heart. For it is not the preconceived opinion of a teacher but the reason of the doctrine that is to be weighed, as it is written: ‘Test all things; hold fast what is good’ (I Thess. V).”

This, however, was said about commentators, not about the canonical Scriptures, to which undoubting faith must be given. Again, Jerome, to Paulinus concerning holy doctors, on the phrase, “A good man from the good treasure of the heart” (Matt. XII): “I pass over the rest, whether dead or still living, concerning whom others after us will judge on either side.”

Having thus set these matters forth beforehand, it pleases us, as we have proposed, to collect sayings of the holy Fathers that occur to our memory and that, through some [Note: [Col. 1349D] Cousin: “some particular.”] apparent disagreement, raise a question, so that they may summon tender readers to the fullest exercise of seeking truth and render them keener through inquiry. For this is defined as the first key of wisdom: namely, persistent or frequent questioning. Aristotle, that most discerning of all philosophers, exhorts students in his discussion of the category “relative” to seize upon it with their whole desire, saying:

[Col. 1349B] “Perhaps it is difficult to make confident declarations about matters of this sort unless they have often been examined. But it will not be useless to doubt each point. For by doubting we come to inquiry; by inquiring we apprehend truth.”

In accordance with this, Truth itself says: “Seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. VII). Teaching us morally by his own example, he chose to be found, about the twelfth year of his age, sitting and asking questions among the teachers, presenting to us the pattern of a disciple through questioning rather than that of a teacher through preaching, though in himself he is the full and perfect wisdom of God.

When sayings of Scripture are brought forward, they stimulate the reader more greatly and attract him to seek truth in proportion as the authority of Scripture itself is more highly commended. Therefore, we have thought fit to prefix to this our work, which we have compiled into one volume from sayings of the saints collected together, that decree of Pope Gelasius concerning authentic books, so that it may be known that we have introduced nothing here from apocryphal works. We have also added extracts from blessed Augustine’s *Retractions*, so that it may appear that nothing has been placed here from those matters which he himself corrected in retracting them.

The prologue ends.

Here begin the sayings collected by the same author which seem contradictory. On account of this contradiction he himself called this collection of sayings *Sic et Non*—“Yes and No” [Col. 1349D] [Note: [Col. 1349D] Cousin: “Here begin sayings collected from the divine Scriptures which seem contradictory. On account of this contradiction this compilation of sayings is called *Sic et Non*.”].

I [Note: [Col. 1349D] We have assigned numerical signs to the questions; they are absent from the manuscript.]. That faith is to be established by human reason, and the contrary.

Gregory, in Homily XXVI: We must know that a divine operation, if it is comprehended by reason, is not wonderful; nor does that faith have merit to which human reason supplies verification. The same, to Theuderic and Theudebert, kings of the Franks [Note: This passage is entirely absent in Cous.]: In priests faith is to be chosen together with life; if life is lacking, faith [is to be chosen]. The same, in Homily V: At the word of a single command, Peter and Andrew, leaving their nets, followed the Redeemer. They had seen him perform no miracles; they had heard nothing from him concerning the reward of eternal recompense; and yet [Note: Cous.: but] at one command of the Lord they forgot what they seemed to possess. The same, in the *Moralia*, book XX: “Have you found honey? Eat what is sufficient for you, lest perhaps, sated, you vomit it up.” For one who desires to consume the sweetness [Note: Cous.: “sweetnesses”] of spiritual understanding beyond what he can contain vomits up even what he had consumed; because, while he seeks to understand the highest things beyond his strength, he loses even what he had understood well. [Col. 1350B] Hence he says again: “As one who eats much honey, it is not good for him; so one who searches into majesty will be overwhelmed by glory.” The glory of the invisible Creator [Note: Cous.: “indeed the majesty of the invisible Creator, because,” etc.], which raises us when moderately investigated, crushes us when explored beyond our strength.

From the first book of Augustine against Faustus (VIII, 225): Faustus: “Yet this too is a feeble confession of faith in Christ: not to believe without witness and proof. Surely you yourselves are accustomed to say that nothing further should be sought out inquisitively, because Christian belief is simple and absolute. How then do you now destroy faith’s simplicity by supporting it with judgments and witnesses?”

From the *Life of Saint Sylvester*, where, while he was disputing with the Jews, Rabbi Roasi [Note: Mon.: Joasi] said to him: Faith is not to be entrusted to human reason, which would persuade us to believe in this God [Col. 1350C] whom you confess as one God [Note: Cous.: “the living Lord”], Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Augustine, *On Faith and the Creed*, to Pope Laurence: The prophet says: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. VII); likewise, do not wish to investigate how God the Father begot the Son, nor thrust yourself too curiously into the secret of this abyss [Note: Cous.: “this depth of waters”], lest perhaps, while you persistently scrutinize the brilliance of inaccessible light, you lose even that slight sight which has been granted to mortals by divine gift [Note: Cous.: “by divine power”].

The same, *On the Baptism of Infants*: Where a most obscure matter is disputed, without the assistance of sure and clear proofs from the divine Scriptures, human presumption ought to restrain itself, doing nothing by inclining to either side.

The same, in *On the Morals of the Church against the Manichaeans*, chapter 2: The order of nature is indeed such that, when we say something, authority precedes reason; for reason may appear weak if, after it has been given, it then takes up the authority by which it may be confirmed. The same: There are innumerable questions in sacred Scripture [Note: Mon.: “Scripture of the sacred”] which are not to be brought to an end before the end, lest life end without faith; but, once faith has certainly been retained, questions are diligently to be pursued for the exercise and delight of believing minds; what shines forth in them is to be communicated without pride, and what remains hidden is to be endured without loss of salvation. [Col. 1351A]

The same, on Psalm XXXIX: Are you not found proud when you say, “First let me see, and then I shall believe”? Likewise: In matters of faith, it is easier to believe on testimonies than to investigate by reason [Note: This passage is absent in Cous.].

The same, on John, Homily XXVII: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John VII) [Note: “My … sent me” is absent in Cous.]. Let the person who says, “I do not yet understand,” hear the counsel. Christ therefore saw that not all would understand this depth, and immediately gave counsel. Do you wish to understand? Believe; for God says through the prophet: “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. VII). To this belongs what he added next: “If anyone is willing to do his will, he shall know concerning the teaching whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself” (John VII). If you have not understood, I say, believe; for understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order that you may believe, but believe in order that you may understand; for unless you believe, you shall not understand. What is, “He shall know concerning the teaching”? That is, he shall understand. What is, “If anyone is willing to do his will”? That is, to believe. Who does not know that doing the will of God is performing his work? Yet he himself says elsewhere: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent.”

The same, Homily XXXVII: Therefore, with faith going before, which heals the eye of the heart, let us grasp without obscurity what we understand; what we have not understood, let us believe without doubt.

The same, book VIII of *On the Trinity* [Note: Cous.: “the City”; cf. Maur. VIII, 870]: Before we understand, we must believe, and we must be watchful [Note: Cous.: “watchful that”] lest our faith be false. But if we believe falsely concerning it, hope will be empty and love impure.

Ambrose: If I am refuted by reason, I renounce faith [Note: Cous.: “the faith”].

Jerome on Jeremiah, book IV: What the Vulgate edition intended in this passage I could state and find some sense for, were it not sacrilege to argue concerning the words of God by human understanding.

Gregory, to Bishop Dominic: Although this is so, and although we desire all heretics always to be restrained by Catholic priests through vigor and reason.

The same, in the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 30: The wise of this world must be admonished differently from the dull; arguments of reason commonly convert the former, examples sometimes more effectively convert the latter. It benefits the former, certainly, to remain defeated in their own arguments; for the latter it sometimes suffices that they know the praiseworthy deeds of others [Note: Cous.: “their deeds”].

The same, *Moralia*, book XIX: Turning away from truth, they turn bare judgment [Note: Cous.: “judgment”] toward fables. God’s writings are set before their eyes everywhere, but people disdain to know them; almost no one seeks to know what he has believed.

The same, to Boniface: If, as I had heard, your greatness were thinking with earnest concern concerning the life of its soul, you would by no means ask me by letters to answer concerning your faith, but in person; so that both you might rejoice in our reasoning and we in your belief. For although in all cases, yet especially in those which concern God, we hasten to bind people by reason rather than by power. [Col. 1352A]

Pope Nicholas, in response to the inquiries [Note: Cous.: councils] of the Bulgarians, chapter 12: Concerning those who refuse to receive the good of Christianity, we can write nothing else except that you should overcome them toward the right faith by warnings, exhortations, and reason rather than by force.

Isidore, *Sentences*, book II, chapter 2: Faith is by no means extorted by force, but is persuaded by reason and examples. Those upon whom these are violently imposed cannot persevere in them; as, according to someone’s illustration, if a person forcibly bends down the top of a young tree [Note: Mon.: “presses it down”], when released it immediately returns to what it was.

Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book XII: Those who preach Christ to the world must oppose the irreligious and imperfect doctrines of the world by the knowledge of wise omnipotence, according to the Apostle’s saying: “For our weapons are not carnal, but powerful through God for the destruction of strongholds, destroying arguments and every height raised up against the knowledge of God” (2 Cor. X, 4). He did not leave to the apostles a faith bare [Note: Cous.: “the apostle”] and destitute of reason. Although it is most powerful for salvation, yet unless it is instructed through teaching, it will indeed have, amid adversities, a safe refuge for flight, but it will not retain the firm confidence to resist; it will be like a camp for the weaker after flight, but not like a camp whose occupants possess fearless courage. Therefore insolent disputations against God must be crushed, the fortifications of deceitful arguments destroyed, and intellects exalted unto impiety broken down—not with carnal weapons but spiritual ones, not with earthly doctrine but heavenly wisdom—so that, as great as is the distinction between divine and human things, so greatly may heavenly reason surpass earthly pursuits. [Col. 1352C]

Jerome, in the Epistle to the Galatians, book I, praising Saint Marcella: I know indeed her ardor; I know what faith, what flame she bears in her breast: she transcends her sex, forgets humankind, and, with the tambourine of divine books sounding, crosses the Red Sea of this world [Col. 1352D]. Certainly, while I was at Rome, she never saw me so hurried that she did not ask some question concerning the Scriptures. Nor, in Pythagorean fashion, did she think whatever I answered was correct; authority had no force with her without reason already weighed, but she examined everything and assessed all things with a discerning mind, so that I felt I had not so much a pupil as a judge.

Augustine, to Count Valerius, judging concerning marriage and concupiscence: Although you have ridiculed this with most robust faith, it is nevertheless good [Col. 1353A] for you to know how to assist in defending what we believe. For the Apostle Peter commands us to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks us for a reason concerning our faith and hope. And the Apostle Paul says: “Let your speech be always in grace, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. IV, 6).

The same, in the treatise *On Mercy*: Ask by praying, seek by disputing, knock by requesting.

The same, in the second book of *On Christian Doctrine* (III, part I, p. 38): There remain matters which pertain not to bodily sense but to reason, where the disciplines of disputation and number reign. But the discipline of disputation is especially useful for penetrating every kind of question found in the holy books [Note: Mon.: “letters”]. Only there one must beware the desire for wrangling and a certain childish display of deceiving an opponent. For there are many things called sophisms—false conclusions of arguments—which often imitate true ones so closely that they deceive not merely the slow-minded but even intelligent persons who are insufficiently attentive. Scripture, so far as I judge, condemns this kind of deceptive conclusion in the place where it is said (Ecclus. XXXVII, 23): “He who speaks sophistically is hateful.”

Bede, on the First Epistle of the Apostle Peter [Note: Cous.: Paul (1 Pet. III, 15)]: “But sanctify the Lord Christ in your hearts, always ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the hope that is in you, so that those who slander your good conduct in Christ may be put to shame in what they speak against you” [Note: These words through “conduct” are absent in Cous.]. We ought to give an answer in two ways to those asking concerning our hope and faith: [Col. 1353C] both to make known to all the just grounds of our hope and faith, whether they inquire faithfully or faithlessly, and always to keep unviolated the profession itself of our faith and hope even amid the pressures of opponents.

## II. That faith concerns only things not apparent [Note: Cous.: “nevertheless”], and the contrary.

Gregory, Homily VII, book II on the Gospel: “Because you have seen me, you have believed.” Since the Apostle says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not apparent” (Heb. XI, 1), it is plainly clear that faith is proof of those things which cannot appear. For things which are apparent [Col. 1353D] do not have faith, but recognition; but he saw one thing and believed another. Divinity could not be seen by a mortal human being; therefore he saw a human being and confessed the Lord, saying: “My Lord and my God.”

The same, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 8: Since Paul says, “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not apparent,” what cannot be seen is truly said to be believed; for what can be seen can no longer be believed.

Haimo, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: Faith, therefore, is that by which [Col. 1354A] we truly believe what we are utterly unable to see. But if we now see what we believe, it must not be called faith, but knowledge.

Augustine, *On the Words of the Lord and Certain Sayings of the Apostle Paul*, Sermon LXXX: “The righteous lives by faith,” because he believes what he has not seen. We are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared; because it has not yet appeared, there is therefore faith. Thus faith exists now, before what we shall be appears. We know indeed that, when he appears, we shall be like him. Why? Because we shall see him as he is. The Apostle says that we have [Note: Cous.: “says that Christ dwells”] Christ in our hearts through faith: now through faith, then through sight; now through faith, as long as we are on the way [Note: Cous.: “in life”], as long as we are in pilgrimage. For as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; “for we walk by faith, [Col. 1354B] not by sight” (2 Cor. V, 7). What will sight be? Hear: “That God may be all in all.” Whatever you sought here, whatever you held great here, he himself will be that to you. When we arrive, we shall possess; and there will now be vision, not faith; reality, not hope [Note: Cous.: “appearance”]. We shall love by seeing and possessing. Therefore love will be perfect, as the Apostle says: “Faith, hope, love—these three; but the greater of these is love” (1 Cor. XIII, 13). Secure, persevering in him through his help, let us say: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or the sword?” etc. (Rom. VIII, 35).

The same, book II, *On the Baptism of Infants* [X, 63]: For what great thing was it for those who believed not to die while living, to believe that they would not die? How much greater is it to believe in such a way as to hope that, though one will die, one will live without end? Finally, to some at the end he will grant this: that they will not experience this death through a sudden change, but will be caught up together with those rising again to meet Christ, and thus will live forever with the Lord. And rightly so for them, because there will no longer be descendants who believe for this reason—not hoping for what they do not see, but loving what they see. Nor should this at all be called faith, since faith is defined thus: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not apparent.” [Col. 1354C]

The same, on John, Homily: “And now I tell you before it happens, so that, when it has happened, you may believe” (John XIV, 29). What does this mean, when a person ought rather to believe [Note: Cous.: “I ought to believe”] before what is to be believed happens? For this is the praise of faith: that what is believed is not seen. What great thing is it, indeed, if what is seen is believed? According to that saying of the Lord, when he reproved the disciple, saying: “Because you have seen, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John XX, 29). For faith itself is defined thus: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for which are not seen.” Why then does he mean, “so that, when it has happened, you may believe”? For even the man to whom it was said, “Because you have seen, you have believed,” did not believe what he saw: [Col. 1355A] he saw flesh and believed God hidden in flesh. Yet even if things that are seen are said to be believed, as each person says that he has believed his own eyes, this is nevertheless not the faith built up in us; rather, things which are seen work in us so that things not seen may be believed.

The same: Those who were to believe—not with new faith but with faith increased; or certainly, when he was dead, faith diminished, and when he rose again, renewed.

The same, Homily XXXIX: What does he promise those who believe? “You shall know the truth.” They did not believe because they knew; rather, they believed in order that they might know. We believe in order that we may know; we do not know in order that we may believe. For what is faith except believing what you do not see? Faith, therefore, is believing what you have not seen; truth is seeing what you have believed. It is truth, but it is still believed, not [Col. 1355B] seen.

The same, book II, *Questions on the Gospels*: “In it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith unto faith” (Rom. I, 17). Faith is indeed understood as that by which things not seen are believed; yet there is also a faith of realities, when what is to come is believed not on words but through realities themselves being present, when Wisdom will already offer herself to the saints of God for contemplation by manifest sight. Perhaps Paul speaks of this faith of realities and of light itself presented, when he says: “For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith unto faith.” For he says elsewhere too: “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of God, are transformed into the same image from glory unto glory” (2 Cor. III, 18). For just as here he says “from glory unto glory,” so there “from faith unto faith”: namely, from the glory of the Gospel, by which believers are now enlightened, to the glory [Col. 1355C] of manifest truth.

Haimo, on the Epistle to the Ephesians (IV, 11): “And he gave some apostles,” etc.; until we all meet Christ at the resurrection in the truth of faith and in the knowledge of the Son of God—that is, until after the resurrection we have one faith and all know God equally. In the present age, indeed, as there is diversity of knowledge, so there is diverse faith, because one understands more and another less concerning God, and according [Note: Cous.: “together”] to what one understands and knows, one has faith. But after the resurrection there will no longer be diversity of faith, because, as all will see the Lord equally, so all will have faith equally.

Boethius, on Cicero’s *Topics*, book I: An argument is [Col. 1355D] a reason which produces belief concerning a doubtful matter [Note: “Argument … produces belief” is absent in Cous.]. For many things produce belief; but because they are not reasons, neither can they be arguments. Thus sight produces belief concerning things seen; but because sight is not reason, it cannot be an argument.

## III. That recognition does not concern things not apparent, but faith alone [Note: Cous.: “nevertheless”], and the contrary.
