Gregory, Homily VI, book II on the Gospel: It is plainly clear that faith is proof of those things which cannot appear; for things which are apparent do not have faith but recognition.

Haimo [Col. 1356A], on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: Faith, therefore, is that by which we truly believe what we are utterly unable to see. But if we now see what we believe, it must not be called faith but knowledge.

Paul, in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians: “And we believe; therefore we also speak, knowing that he who raised Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and establish us with you” (2 Cor. IV, 13–14). Likewise: “For we know that, if our earthly house is dissolved, we have in general an eternal house in heaven” (2 Cor. V, 1).

Augustine, book I of the *Retractations*: What I said, that there is a great difference between whether something is held by a certain rational judgment of the mind, which we call knowing, or is usefully commended to posterity to be believed on hearsay or in writings. And shortly after: What we know, therefore, we owe to reason; what we believe, to authority. This should not be understood so as to make us fear, in more customary speech, to say that we know what we believe on the testimony of credible witnesses; for when we speak strictly, we say that we know only that which we comprehend by the firm reasoning of the mind. But when we speak in words better suited to ordinary usage, we need not hesitate to say that we know both what we perceive by the senses of our body and what we believe from trustworthy witnesses. [Col. 1356B]

The same, to Paulinus: It is enough to say that the difference between seeing and believing is this: present things are seen, absent things are believed. Likewise: Our knowledge, therefore, consists of things seen and things believed. Likewise: And not without reason do we say that we know not only those things which we saw [Note: Cous.: “are seen”] or see, but also those which we believe when moved by trustworthy testimonies.

## IV. That one must believe in God alone, and the contrary.

[Col. 1356C]

Augustine, to the newly baptized, Homily III: When we asked, “Do you believe the holy Church?” we did not ask in the manner in which one believes in God, as though one also believed in the holy Church. Therefore we did not say that you should believe in the Church as in God.

The same, on John, Homily XXIX: The Lord says, “That you may believe in him whom he sent”: “in him,” not “him.” The demons believed him, but did not believe in him. We believe Paul, but not in Paul; Peter, but not in Peter. “To one believing in him who justifies the ungodly, [his faith is reckoned for righteousness].” What is believing in him? It is, by believing, to love; by believing, to cherish; by believing, to go into him and be incorporated into his [Col. 1356D] members. This is the faith which the Apostle defines most fully when he says: “Faith which works through love” (Gal. V, 6).

Jerome on Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians, or Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*, book I: “To one believing in him who justifies the ungodly” (Prov. XVII). Whoever, therefore, has dared to say, “I justify you,” must consequently also say, “Believe in me”; and no saint could rightly say this except the Holy of holies: “Believe in God, and believe also in me.”

The same, on the Epistle of John, Sermon X: What more could the demons believe than to say, “We know that you are the Son of God” (Mark I, 24)? What [Col. 1357A] the demons said, Peter also said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”; and he hears from the Lord: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona,” etc. (John VI). The demons said this in order that Christ might depart from them; for they said: “Why have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. VIII, 29). Likewise: The Christian’s faith is with love; the demon’s faith is without love. But those who do not believe are worse and slower than demons. Whoever [Note: Monac.: “I know not who”] does not wish to believe in Christ does not yet even imitate a demon; he already believes in Christ, but hates Christ. He has confession of faith from fear of punishment, not from love of the crown; for they too feared punishment.

The Nicene Creed established by 318 Fathers, as it is preserved at Rome [Note: Cous.: “from the creed of faith preserved at Rome,” etc.] behind the altar of Saint Paul, on a silver tablet placed upon wood, which Leo III had prepared as a safeguard of the Catholic faith, as is appended there on the same tablet:

> “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, who was born from the Father before all ages; light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made; who, for us human beings and for our salvation, descended from heaven, was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and was made human; and was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, suffered and was buried, rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand [Col. 1357C] of the Father; and shall come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom shall have no end; and [I believe] in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who is to be adored and glorified together with the Father and the Son, who spoke through the prophets; [and] in one holy, Catholic, and apostolic Church. I confess one baptism for the remission of sins. I hope for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the age to come. Amen.”

Leo, the unworthy third bishop, had this made out of love for and as a safeguard of the orthodox faith.

Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, Sermon I: The catechumen also believes in the cross of the Lord Jesus, by which he too is signed.

The same, Sermon II: You were asked, “Do you believe in God the Father [Col. 1357D] almighty?” You said, “I believe,” and you were immersed [Note: Cous.: “you deserved”]. Again you were asked, “Do you believe in our Lord Jesus Christ and in his cross?” You said, “I believe.”

The same, in *On the Mysteries*: You are bound to believe in the Son as also in the Father, and likewise in the Holy Spirit; with this one exception, that in the cross of the Lord Jesus alone you confess that you must believe.

Jerome, to Paula and Eustochium, in the exposition of Paul’s Epistle to Philemon: “The people believed the Lord and Moses his servant.” One and the same belief is attributed to Moses and to God, when the people who believed in the Lord are written equally to have believed in the servant. This is so not only in the case of Moses but in all saints: whoever believes God cannot receive his faith otherwise than by believing also in his saints. What I say is this: unless one has first believed that what has been written concerning his saints is true, [Col. 1358A] he cannot be led to faith in the Old Testament; unless he has approved whatever the history relates concerning the patriarchs, prophets, and other distinguished persons, so that from faith in the law he may come to faith in the Gospel, and the righteousness of God may be revealed in him from faith unto faith.

The same, in the *Disputation between a Luciferian and an Orthodox*: The Luciferian said: “But a layman ought to be pardoned for this, because, thinking simply that it was the Church of God, he approached it and, believing according to his faith, was baptized.” The Orthodox said: “You assert a new thing: that someone should become a Christian through one who is not a Christian. Approaching the Arians, in what faith was he baptized? Surely in that which the Arians held. Or, if he himself already believed rightly and knowingly was baptized by heretics, he does not deserve pardon for error.” Likewise: “Moreover, since it is customary in the laver, after confession of the Trinity, to ask: ‘Do you believe in the holy Church? Do you believe forgiveness of sins?’ In what Church do you say he believed? In that of the Arians? But they do not have [belief] in ours? [Note: Cous. omits “in.”] Yet, baptized outside this Church, he could not believe in that Church which he did not know.” [Col. 1358B]

## V. That God is not singular, and the contrary.

[Col. 1358C]

Athanasius, in the Creed of Faith: And yet there are not three gods, but one God.

Augustine, *Questions of the Old and New Law*, chapter LIX: He is one indeed, but not solitary; from eternity he has in mystery another, who is with the other. The same: God the Father has in himself another with the other, as I have said.

Ambrose, *On Faith*, to Emperor Gratian: What is of one substance cannot be separated, even if [Note: Cous.: “unless”] it is not of singularity but of unity. Singularity pertains to person; unity, to nature.

Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book IV: And God said: “Let us make humankind in our image and likeness” (Gen. I). By the profession of companionship he removed the understanding of singularity; but no one can be a companion to a solitary person himself [Note: Mon.: “something”], nor again can the expression “let us make” admit the likeness of one who is solitary. Likewise: “I shall make” and “my” [Note: Cous.: “my [neuter]”] suit one who is solitary; “let us make” and “our” do not suit one who is solitary. Likewise [Hilary, *Works*, p. 847]: In the bush the angel of God appeared as God; he is not God because he is the angel of God, nor, again, is he not the angel of God because he is God. But, with the distinction of the persons signified and the dispensation of the heavenly mysteries made manifest, God ought not to be considered solitary. [Col. 1358D]

Pope Hormisdas, to Emperor Justin: Let us preserve what is proper to each person, so that singularity may neither be denied to the persons of the Godhead nor what belongs properly to names be transferred to the essence.

Gregory, to Bishop Leander: It cannot in any way be reprehensible to immerse an infant in baptism either three times or once, since in three immersions the Trinity of persons may be signified and in one the singularity of the Godhead.

Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, chapter IV: Trinity is in the relative names of the persons; but deity is not tripled, but exists in singularity; because, if it is tripled, we introduce a plurality of gods. The name “gods,” however, is said in the plural concerning angels and holy human beings because they are not equal in merit; concerning them the Psalm says: “I have said: You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI). But concerning Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, because of the one and equal divinity, the name is shown to be not “gods” but “God.” [Col. 1359B]

## VI. That God is tripartite, and the contrary.

Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter IX: It is enough for a Christian concerning the cause of created things only to believe in the goodness [Note: Cous.: “goodness”] of the Creator, who is the one God; and that there is no nature which is not either himself or from himself; and that he is tripartite, namely Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The same, *On the Trinity*, book VII, chapter VII: It is not because God is Trinity that he must be considered threefold; otherwise he would be less in each than in all three together.

## VII. That in the Trinity several eternal beings should not be spoken of, and the contrary.

[Col. 1359C]

Athanasius, in the Creed of Faith: And yet there are not three gods [Note: Cous.: “eternal beings”], but one God. Likewise: But all three persons are coeternal with one another and coequal.

Augustine, in book V *Against Heresies*: The Father is Father; the Son is Son. The former was never not Father, and the latter was never not Son; both are eternal, neither beginning to be nor ceasing to be. Fire and brightness are temporal, but Father and Son are eternal. Duality is in offspring [Note: Cous.: “quality is in the Father”]; unity is in the Godhead.

The same, in *On the Christian Contest*: Therefore we believe in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. These are eternal and immutable—that is, one God of one [Col. 1359D] substance, eternal Trinity: God, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things.

## VIII. That there is not a multiplicity of things in the Trinity, or that the Trinity is not some whole [Note: In Mon. “Trinity” is absent], and the contrary.

From Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*, ch. 228: In the divine Trinity there is such unity of substance that it retains equality and admits no plurality. Likewise, when in this Trinity we speak of the person of the Father, we say nothing other than the substance of the Father, because the person of the Father is nothing other than the Father himself [Col. 1360A]. For “person” is said with reference to itself, not to the Son or to the Holy Spirit, as are “God” and similar terms. This alone is a name [Note: Col. 1360D, Cous.: “ut.”] which, although said of each individually, is understood in the supreme reality plurally, not singly; for we say: the Father is a person, the Son is a person, and the Holy Spirit is a person. Yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not one person but three persons. Therefore, when we say “three persons, one essence,” we do not predicate this as a genus of species or as a species of individuals. It may appear possible to say “three men, one nature,” but two men are more than one. Yet the essence of Father and Son is not greater than that of the Father alone or the Son alone. Likewise, one man is not as much as three men together, and two men are something more than one man [Col. 1360B]. But it is not so in God. For the Father and Son together are not greater in essence than the Father alone or the Son alone; rather, the three persons together are equal to each one individually. [Note: Col. 1360D, Cous.: “each one.”]

From the letter of Saints Augustine and Alypius to Maximus, physician of Thena: This Trinity, of one and the same nature and substance, is neither less in each person than in all nor greater in all than in each; rather, in the Father alone or in the Son alone it is as great as in Father and Son together, and in the Holy Spirit it is as great as in Father and Son together.

Augustine, on John, Homily 37: Three persons, but not three gods. There is there something ineffable which cannot be explained in words: number both is and is not present, yet there are three. Three what? Here number fails. Thus God neither departs from number nor is contained by number: because there are three, number seems to be present. If you ask, “Three what?” there is no number; hence it was said, “Great is our God, and great is his power,” etc. [Col. 1360C]. When you begin to think, you begin to count; when you have counted, you cannot answer what you have counted. What are these three? Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—not three gods, not three almighty beings, not three creators. This alone suggests number: that they are relative to one another, not what they are in themselves. The Father, in himself, is God; in himself, he is almighty. He is not Father in himself, but in relation to the Son. We cannot say “three” except of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

The same, in the *Book of Questions to Orosius*: [Col. 1360D] Just as we do not say three gods or three essences, so neither do we say three wisdoms or three spirits. If the Father is wisdom, the Son wisdom, and the Holy Spirit wisdom, there are nevertheless not three wisdoms but one; not three spirits but one; not three essences but one, because for him to be is the same as to be wisdom or to be spirit. [Note: Col. 1360D, Mon.: “spirit.” In Cous., this passage is entirely absent.]

Boethius, *On the Trinity*, speaking of the simplicity of the divine substance: “That which is not this and that, but nevertheless is this, truly is what it is; and this is strongest, because it depends on nothing.” Therefore this is truly one, in which there is no number and nothing other in it besides what it is [Col. 1361A]. For it cannot become a subject, since it is form; and forms cannot be subjects. Likewise: Therefore there is in it no diversity, no plurality arising from diversity, no multiplicity arising from accidents, and consequently no number. Likewise: Where there is no difference, there is absolutely no plurality; therefore no number, but unity alone. Likewise: Number is twofold: one by which we count, the other consisting of countable things. Likewise: Therefore, in the number by which we count, repetition of units produces plurality; but in the number of things repetition of units does not produce plurality—for example, if we call the same thing “one sword,” “one blade,” “one weapon,” this is a certain repetition of the same thing, not a counting of different things [Col. 1361B], as if we were to say “sun, sun, sun.” Therefore, if “God” is predicated thirdly of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, this threefold predication does not produce a number. [Note: Col. 1361D, Cous. omits *if*; Cous.: “counting.”]

Likewise: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not spoken of as though the term were a kind of equivocal (*multivocum*) term; for “blade” and “sword” are both the same thing and the very same thing. But Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are indeed the same, yet not the very same person. Here one must pause briefly for consideration: when asked whether the Father is the one who is the Son, they say, “Certainly not”; again, one is denied to be identical with the other. Thus there is not complete indistinction between them in every respect; therefore number enters in, which, as explained above, is produced by the diversity of subjects.

Likewise: It was demonstrated above concerning his form that he is form and truly one, and that there is no plurality [Col. 1361C]. [Note: Col. 1361D, Cous.: “because”; Cous.: “beyond.”]

Likewise: Therefore, according to the property of a thing insofar as it is what it is, they do not make predication; they can alter or change nothing, and can vary no essence at all. Accordingly, if Father and Son are said relatively, and, as was said, differ in nothing except relation alone, relation is not predicated of that of which it is predicated as though it were the thing itself; rather, it is said according to the thing of which it is spoken, and does not make another thing of that of which it is said. But, if it may be said so, this was interpreted by “persons,” in the manner in which what can scarcely be understood was interpreted.

Likewise: The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. But God has no differences by which he differs from God; he differs from none of them. Where differences are absent [Col. 1361D], plurality is absent; where plurality is absent, unity is present. Likewise: Thus unity is suitably established. [Note: Col. 1362D: “Thus—unity” is absent in Cous.]

But because no relation can be referred to itself, a numerical plurality of Trinity arises in the predication of relation, while unity is preserved in the indistinction of substance, operation, and absolutely every predication made in itself. Thus substance contains unity; relation multiplies Trinity. For the Father is not the same person as the Son, nor indeed [Note: Col. 1362D, Cous.: “both.”] the same person as the Holy Spirit; nevertheless Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same God [Col. 1362A], the same just, the same good, the same great, the same everything that can be predicated in itself. It should certainly be known that a predicative relation is not always such that it is predicated of what is different: an equal is equal to an equal, a like is like to a like, and that which is the same is the same as that which is the same. Such is the relation in the Trinity of Father to Son and of both to the Holy Spirit, namely, of that which is the same to that which is the same. If this cannot be found in all other things, it is produced by the difference proper to perishable things.

Athanasius, *On the Trinity*, book 6, ch. 2: “Accursed, accursed be whoever confesses diverse substances in these three persons.” Likewise: “Accursed, accursed be whoever, because of the three names of the persons, confesses three gods, three substances [Col. 1362B], or three spirits.”

Jerome, in his letter to Pope Damasus on the explanation of the faith: In confuting Arius, we declare one and the same substance of the Trinity. Likewise, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons explicitly by their proper characteristics. Likewise: For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names—that is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, *hypostaseis*, that is, subsistences. Thus they are one in substance and distinguished in persons and names.

Gennadius, *On the Orthodox Faith*: Therefore the Son is *homoousios*, that is, coessential in divinity with the Father; the Holy Spirit is *homoousios* with the Father and the Son. [Note: Col. 1362D: This passage is absent in Cous.]

Jerome, against the Arians, to Damasus, on the new term “three hypostases”: Let us ask what they think can be understood by *hypostasis* [Col. 1362C]. They say, “Three subsisting persons”; we answer that this is what we believe. The meaning does not suffice them; they demand the word itself, because I know not what poison lies hidden in its syllables. But whoever, understanding *hypostasis* as *ousia*—that is, substance—does not say that in the three persons there is one hypostasis, is alien from Christ. Likewise: The entire school of secular literature knows *hypostasis* as nothing other than *ousia*. And who, I ask, would ever with sacrilegious mouth proclaim three substances? God’s nature is one alone. Whoever says that there are three—that is, three hypostases—endeavors to assert three natures. And if this is so, why are we separated from Arius by walls while joined to him in faithlessness? It is enough for us to say one substance, three perfect, coequal, coeternal persons [Col. 1362D]. It is not a good sign when words disagree while the meaning is the same. Or, if you think it right that we should say three hypostases with their interpretations, we do not deny it. But believe me: poison lies beneath honey; Satan’s angel transforms himself into an angel of light.

Hilary, on Psalm 129, “Out of the depths”: Whoever wishes to believe that God is bodily because man was made in his image will judge God to be composite. But whatever is composite necessarily was not eternal, because composition has a beginning by which it is embodied so as to endure. [Note: Col. 1362D, Cous.: “eternal.”]

Gennadius, *On the Orthodox Faith*: Therefore the Son is *homoousios*, that is, coessential in divinity with the Father; the Holy Spirit is *homoousios* with the Father and the Son.

Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 6, ch. 4: Trinity is so called because a whole is made one out of three things, as it were a tri-unity. Likewise: In this Trinity some names are appellative and others proper. The proper names are essential, such as God, Lord, almighty, immutable, immortal; and they are therefore proper because they signify the substance itself, which is one. [Note: Col. 1363D, Cous.: “the same” for “which is one.”] The appellative names are Father, Son, Holy Spirit, and proceeding; these are also relative.

Origen, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans (10:15), book 8: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim good things.” Let us inquire what the good things are, to which he added “good” [Col. 1363B]. He called them “good things” because the one true good is in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. [Note: Col. 1363D: In Cous., this passage appears at the end of this question.]

Augustine, book 1, *On Christian Teaching*: Some things are to be enjoyed, others used. Those which are to be enjoyed make us blessed; by those which are to be used we are helped, as we tend toward blessedness. [Note: Col. 1363D, Cous.: “we may live.”] To enjoy is to cling in love to something for its own sake; to use is to refer what comes into use to obtaining what you love, provided that it ought to be loved. For unlawful use should rather be called abuse or misuse. If we wish to return to the homeland where we can be blessed, we must use the world, not enjoy it, so that God’s invisible things may be discerned through the things that have been made. Therefore the things to be enjoyed are Father, Son, and Holy Spirit [Col. 1363C]; and this same Trinity is one supreme thing, common to all who enjoy it, if indeed it is a thing and not the cause of all things—if indeed it is also the cause. [Note: Col. 1364D, Cous.: “a certain thing.”]

The same, book 7, *On the Trinity*, ch. 4: Since what is said is understood at least in a riddle, it was thought fitting to speak in this way, so that something might be said when the question was asked, “What are the three?”—those three which true faith declares to be three, since it does not say that the Father is the Son, and says that the Holy Spirit, who is God’s gift, is neither Father nor Son. Likewise: When human poverty attempted to bring forth in speech for human understanding what it holds concerning the Lord God, it feared to say “three essences,” lest some diversity be understood in that supreme equality. Yet it could not say that they were not three certain things, as Sabellius, having fallen into heresy [Col. 1363D], said. Likewise: For the sake of speaking about ineffable things—so that we might somehow say what we can in no way fully express—our Greek writers said “one essence, three substances”; the Latins, “one essence or substance, three persons,” because, as we have already said, in Latin usage *essence* is ordinarily understood no differently from *substance*. [Note: Col. 1364D, Cous.: “substances.”] Likewise: What we call persons, according to our usage, the Greeks call substances. Thus they say three substances, one essence, just as [Col. 1364A] we say three persons, one essence or substance.

The same, book 5, *On the Trinity*, ch. 8: Therefore let us especially maintain this: whatever the divine sublimity is said to be in itself is said substantially; but whatever is said in relation to something is said not substantially but relatively. And there is such power of the same substance in Father, Son, and Holy Spirit that whatever is said of each individually in himself is understood in the supreme reality not plurally but singly. Likewise: Whatever God is said to be in himself is said personally of each one and at the same time of the Trinity itself, not plurally but singly.

The same, book 7, ch. 7: “Person” is said of the Father in himself, not in relation to the Son or the Holy Spirit.

The same, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*: The statement that the Son is the Father’s teaching refutes Sabellius’s heresy, for he dared to say that Father and Son are two names but one reality. For the Son’s teaching belongs to someone, if it is not his own [Col. 1364B].

The same, in an exposition to Pope Laurence: Just as heavenly fire generates from itself the brightness of light and emits vapour, and though there are three things they are one in substance, so the Trinity is one majesty. [Note: Col. 1364D, Cous. omits “one.”]

Jerome, on Psalm 86: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains,” whether of God or indeed of the Church. But what are the foundations except Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? Paul says: “Like a wise architect, I laid a foundation” (1 Cor. 3), that is, faith in the Trinity. And elsewhere: “They awaited the city having foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (Heb. 11). Whom can we call [Col. 1364C] mountains? The apostles; in them were the foundations, where the Church’s faith was first laid.

The same: Concerning David’s three powers, in the psalm he asks for three spirits, saying (Ps. 50:12): “Strengthen me with a ruling spirit; renew a right spirit in my inmost parts; do not take your holy spirit from me.” Who are these three spirits? The ruling spirit is the Father; the right spirit is Christ; the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit.

The same, on Psalm 50: “A right spirit”: for living and discerning, as it formerly was right within me. Likewise: You who read Holy Scripture, understand here the supreme Trinity: the Holy Spirit, that is, the spirit of prophecy; the ruling spirit, the Father; the right spirit, the Son; the holy spirit, the Holy Spirit himself [Col. 1364D].

## IX. That God is not substance, and the contrary

[Note: Col. 1364D, Cous. omits “God.”]

Boethius, *On the Trinity*: Ten categories altogether are handed down, which are predicated universally of all things: namely substance, quality, quantity, and so forth. Likewise, concerning God: in him substance is not substance but beyond substance; likewise quality, and so forth … such things as can occur. For when we say “God,” we seem indeed to signify substance, but [Col. 1365A] substance which is beyond substance. When we say “just,” we seem indeed to signify quality, but not an accidental quality, rather one which is substance beyond substance. For what he is is not one thing and what he is as just another; rather, for God to be is the same as to be just. Likewise, when he is called great or greatest, we seem indeed to signify quantity, but a quantity which is that very substance of the kind we have described as beyond substance.

The same, in the second book of the *Topics*: Substance is that which can be subject to all accidents; but whiteness cannot be subject to any accidents; therefore whiteness is not substance.

Augustine, book 7, *On the Trinity*, ch. 4: For if for God to be is the same as to subsist, then three substances must not be spoken of without also speaking of three essences; just as [Col. 1365B], because for God to be is the same as to be wise, we say neither three essences nor three wisdoms. Thus, since for him to be God is the same as to be, it is not lawful to speak either of three essences or of three gods. But if for God to be is one thing and to subsist another, just as for God to be is one thing and to be Father or Lord another—for what he is is said in relation to himself, but “Father” in relation to the Son and “Lord” in relation to a serving creature—then he subsists relatively, just as he begets relatively and rules relatively. Thus substance will no longer be substance, because it will be relative; for as essence is named from being, so we call substance from subsisting. But it is absurd for substance to be said relatively; for every thing subsists in relation to itself—how much more God? Yet, if it is fitting [Col. 1365C] to say that God subsists, this is rightly understood of those things which have in them as subjects things said to exist in some subject, as colour in a body. [Note: Col. 1365D, Cous.: “subject.”]

Likewise: Mutable things are not properly called simple substances. But it is impious to say that God subsists and is subject to his own goodness, and that this goodness is not substance—or rather essence—and that God himself is not his goodness, but that goodness is in him as in a subject. Hence it is clear that God is called substance improperly, so that by a more familiar name essence may be understood. For he alone truly is, because he is immutable; and he announced this as his name to Moses when he said (Exod. 3:14): “I am who I am”; and “You shall say to them: ‘He Who Is has sent me to you.’” Yet, whether it is called essence, which is the proper term, or substance, which is improper [Col. 1365D], both are said absolutely, not relatively. Therefore for God to be is the same as to subsist; and thus the supreme essence, the Trinity, is also one substance.

Likewise, in the same chapter of the same book: For the sake of speaking about ineffable things, so that we might somehow say what we cannot fully express at all, our Greek writers said “one essence, three substances”; the Latins, “one essence or substance, three persons,” because, as we have already said, in Latin usage essence is ordinarily understood no differently from substance. [Note: Col. 1365D, Cous.: “substances.”] What we call persons according to our usage, the Greeks call substances according to theirs [Col. 1366A]. Thus they say “three substances, one essence,” just as we say “three persons, one essence or substance.”

Likewise, book 5: Let us understand God, as far as we can, as good without quality, great without quantity, creator without need, present without position, containing all things without possession, wholly everywhere without place, everlasting without time, making mutable things without any change in himself, and suffering nothing. Whoever thinks of God in this way, even if he cannot yet wholly discover what God is, nevertheless piously takes care, so far as he can, not to think of him as something he is not. Yet he is without doubt substance—or, if this is a better term, essence—which the Greeks call *ousia*. [Note: Col. 1365D: “Which—the Greeks call” is absent in Cous.]

Jerome to Damasus [Col. 1366B], *On the New Term “Three Hypostases”*: Let us ask what they think can be understood by *hypostasis*. They say, “Three subsisting persons”; we answer that this is what we believe. The meaning does not suffice them; they insist upon the word itself because I know not what poison lies hidden in its syllables. But whoever, understanding *hypostasis* as *ousia*, does not say that in the three persons there is one hypostasis, is alien from Christ. Likewise: The entire school of secular literature knows *hypostasis* as nothing other than *ousia*. And who, I ask, would ever with sacrilegious mouth proclaim three substances? God’s nature is one alone. Whoever says three—that is, hypostases—endeavours to assert three natures. And if that is so, why are we separated from Arius by walls while joined with him in faithlessness? It is enough for us to say one substance [Note: Col. 1366D, Mon.: “essence.”], three perfect, equal [Col. 1366C], coeternal persons. It is not a good sign when words disagree in the same sense. Or if you think it right that we should say three hypostases with their interpretations, we do not deny it. But believe me: poison lies beneath honey; Satan’s angel transforms himself into an angel of light.

The same, to the same: In confuting Arius, we declare one and the same substance of the Trinity. Likewise, avoiding the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish three persons explicitly by their proper characteristics. And after some intervening material: For we confess not merely names, but also the properties of the names—that is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, hypostases, that is, subsistences. Likewise: Thus they are one in substance, distinguished in persons [Note: Col. 1366D, Cous.: “in persons.”] and names.

## X. That God is to be counted among all things—that is, that he is one thing among all things—and the contrary

[Col. 1366D]

Paul, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (15:27): “For he has subjected all things under his feet. But when he says, ‘All things are subjected to him,’ it is beyond doubt that he is excepted who subjected all things to him.”

Ambrose, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*: Let us beware lest what was said to Cain be said also to one of us: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; be still.” That is, lest we fail to distinguish what belongs properly to divinity and to incarnation; lest we compare the Creator [Col. 1367A] with his works; lest we say that the author of times himself began after times. For it cannot be that he through whom all things exist is one among all things. [Note: Col. 1367D, Mon.: “himself”; Cous.: “in.”] I do not wish that we should be believed; [Note: Col. 1367D, Cous.: “believe.”] let Scripture be cited. I do not say of myself that “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1); I hear it. I do not invent it; I read what all read, though not all understand. When it is read, we all hear: “In the beginning was the Word”; that is, let heaven remain. For “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”: “made” is one thing, “was” another. What is made begins; what was did not receive a beginning, but preceded it. Let times also remain, because times are after heaven. Let angels also remain: although I do not find their beginning, nevertheless there was a time when they were not. [Note: Col. 1367D, Cous.: “when.”] Therefore, if [Col. 1367B] I cannot find the beginning of angels, though it is certain that they have a beginning, how can we find the beginning of the Word, from whom comes every beginning—not only of creatures but even of our thoughts?

The same, *On Faith*, to Gratian: The Holy Spirit is not among all things but above all things. Likewise: But if the Spirit does not serve, while all things serve, the Spirit is above all things because he does not serve as all things do. That all things serve is clear, as the mouth of the Spirit said through the Prophet: “All things serve you” (Ps. 118). Therefore, since all things serve, if the Spirit does not serve, the Holy Spirit is certainly not among all things. Likewise, Scripture says that all things which were made exist through the Son. But since the Holy Spirit is not taught to be made [Col. 1367C], he certainly cannot be proved to be among all things. [Note: Col. 1367D, Cous.: “raised up”; Cous.: “nor among.”] Likewise it is written (1 Cor. 8:6): “For us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we through him; and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things and we through him.” When it says, “Jesus, through whom are all things,” it certainly excepted the Son of God from all things, as it also excepted the Father. Therefore those who think that the Spirit ought to be counted among all things because they read that all things were made through him should also think that the Son is to be counted among all things, because they read that all things are from God.

## XI. That the divine persons differ from one another, and the contrary

Athanasius, in the creed of faith: The person of the Father is one, that of the Son another [Col. 1367D], and that of the Holy Spirit another. Likewise: The Father is made, created, or begotten by none; the Son is from the Father alone—not made or created, but begotten; the Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son—not made, begotten, or created, but proceeding.

Pope Leo, in a sermon for Pentecost: In the divine Trinity there is nothing unlike, nothing unequal.

Ambrose, *On Faith*, to Gratian, book 2: The Apostle says that Christ is the image of the Father. Arius says that he is unlike, and wishes [Col. 1368A] the Father to have begotten one unlike himself, as though powerless to beget one like himself. Likewise: The image teaches that he is not unlike.

Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Law*, ch. 148: “Whoever sees me sees the Father,” because Father and Son are one in nature; that is, neither differs from the other in anything. Likewise, ch. 58: Whoever sees one sees three, since one differs from another in nothing.

Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book 1: God from God, the only-begotten from the unbegotten, one differing from the other in nothing, because the life of the living is in the living. Book 4: When therefore we read, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1), because each term signifies neither one who is merely solitary nor one who is different, we too must confess him as neither merely solitary nor diverse; this is known [Col. 1368B], because he says “our image,” not “our images,” by the property of one nature in both. [Note: Col. 1368D: “Known—nature” is absent in Cous.; Mon.: “of both.”]

## XII. That in the Trinity one is with another, and the contrary

[Note: Col. 1368D, Cous. omits “one.”]

The Ambrosian hymn for the third hour: “Now, Holy Spirit, be with us, one with the Father and the Son.”

Jerome, in the Epistle to the Galatians, book 2: Although he is one with the Father according to Godhead, according to the office of mediator he is understood as other than him. [Note: Col. 1368D, Mon.: “understand.”]

Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book 1, speaking of Father and Son: Let both be one in our faith, not one person. [Note: Col. 1368D, Mon.: “faith.”]

## XIII. That God the Father is the cause of the Son, and the contrary

[Col. 1368C]

Augustine, book 1, on Genesis, *Against the Manichaeans’ Calumnies*: Whoever asks, “Why did God make heaven and earth?” should be answered, “Because he willed it.” For God’s will is the cause of heaven and earth, and is therefore greater than heaven and earth. But whoever asks, “Why did he will it?” seeks something greater than God’s will; but nothing greater can be found.

The same, in the *Eighty-Three Questions*, ch. 30: Whoever asks why God willed to make the world seeks a cause of God’s will. But every cause is efficient, and everything efficient is greater than what is effected; yet nothing is greater than God’s will. Therefore its cause must not be sought.

The same, book 7 of the *Confessions*, speaking to God: You are not unwillingly compelled to anything, because your will is not greater than your power; but it would be greater if you yourself were greater than yourself. Likewise: God’s will and power are God himself.

In the *Eighty-Three Questions*, ch. 7, speaking of the Son of God, he says: God is the cause of all things that are. But whatever is the cause of all things is also the cause of its own wisdom, and God was never without his wisdom. Therefore the cause of the everlasting is everlasting [Col. 1369A], and is not prior in time to his wisdom.

## XIV. That the Son is without beginning, and the contrary

Jerome, on Psalm 119: “With you is the beginning.” The Father is beginning, but the Son also is beginning. For beginning has no beginning; if it had another beginning, it would cease itself to be beginning. Whatever, therefore, we grant to the Father, let us grant also to the Son. For if the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and all that is the Father’s is the Son’s and all that is the Son’s is the Father’s, then the Father’s beginning is the Son’s beginning. Therefore what he says means this: at the time when you were suffering, you said (Luke 23:46), “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”; and you spoke, as it were, from human feeling [Col. 1369B], not asking as one who was weak. Beginning was with you; divinity was with you. Yet you prayed for help in order that, having received help, you might give it to your saints and that they might shine. [Note: Col. 1369D, Cous.: “that they may shine.”] Likewise: He speaks according to his humanity; for if he assumed a human body, it was necessary that he should also take up human words. [Note: Col. 1369D, Cous.: “Again, through.”]

Fulgentius, in *On the Immensity of the Son of God*: “In the beginning was the Word.” Or perhaps, because there was something in the beginning, shall we dare to assign a beginning of existence to the Son and therefore refuse to believe that he was born without a beginning? Far be it! He himself said (Rev. 1:8), “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end,” because he began the things to be completed and himself completed what had been begun. Therefore we believe that the Son of God was begotten from the Father’s substance without any beginning of his birth. [Note: Col. 1369D, Cous.: “divinity.”]

John Chrysostom, on Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews, Homily 12: Just as Melchizedek has neither beginning of days nor end, because his genealogy is not narrated, so Christ, by the very nature of the matter, is both without beginning and without end. For just as we know neither the beginning nor the end of that man’s life because it is not written, so likewise we know neither the beginning nor the end of the Son. [Note: Col. 1369D, Cous.: “nor—nor.”] Likewise: You see the Son as without beginning, not because he has no cause from which he is—for that is impossible, since he has the Father; otherwise how would he be Son?—but because he had no beginning or end of life. [Note: Col. 1369D, Cous.: “Seeing.”]

The same, in the exposition of the creed which begins, “The universal Church rejoices”: We confess that this only Son of God was born and begotten from the Father’s substance [Col. 1369D], and we say that he has his beginning from the Father.

Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book 5, ch. 12: “Father” is said relatively, and “principle” is likewise said relatively; but Father is said in relation to the Son, and principle in relation to all things that are from him. Likewise: The Son too is called principle; for when it was said to him, “Who are you?” he answered, “The principle, who also speak to you” (1 John 8:25). For in calling himself principle he wished to show himself as Creator, just as the Father is principle of creation, because all things are from him [Col. 1370A]. Likewise: Therefore God is called one principle in relation to creation, not two or three principles. Yet, in their mutual relations within the Trinity, if the begetter is principle in relation to what he begets, the Father is principle in relation to the Son because he begets him. But whether the Father is also principle in relation to the Spirit, since it is said, “he proceeds from the Father,” is no small question. [Note: Col. 1370D, Cous.: “When it is said: ‘Is he principle? The Father proceeds from the Father,’ etc.”]

Likewise, after some intervening matter, in the following chapter: If what is given has as its principle the one by whom it is given, it must be confessed that Father and Son are the principle of the Holy Spirit. Likewise: What proceeds from him who nevertheless proceeds from the Son is to be known. But the Father is the principle of the whole divinity—or, more properly said, deity.

The same, in the *Questions on the Old and New Law*, ch. 58: The Son is the head of the Holy Spirit, because the Spirit received from him; and just as the Father sent the Son, so the Son sent the Holy Spirit. Likewise, ch. 33: This is what it means for man to have been made in the image of God: as all things are from one God, so the whole human race is from one man. Woman was made from man [Col. 1370B], so that birth might arise through her; but the Son of God was born so that creation might come to be through him. [Note: Col. 1370D, Cous.: “him.”] Likewise, ch. 94: No believer doubts that the Son of God was born perfect from God. For in being born from God the Father, he received all the Father’s divinity. Therefore he then received the name above every name—that is, that he should be called what the Father is called, God. For nothing is said to be future for him; all things are before him. Therefore he was born for the creation and restoration of all these things. For order and reason certainly require that every knee should bow at the paternal name [Col. 1370C]. The Father gave this to the Son because of the things he was to do; and he gave it when he begot him. For he begot him in such a way that he might be in the same honour in which the Father himself is.

Gennadius, *On the Orthodox Faith of Ecclesiastical Doctrines*, ch. 1: We believe that one God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the Son, because he has the Father; the Holy Spirit, because he is from the Father and the Son. Therefore the Father is the principle of deity, from whom the Son was born, while God proceeds from God the Father and God the Son.

## XV. That God did not beget himself; or that, even according to divinity, the Son is said to have been made or created; or that the Father precedes by a certain primacy or authority—and the contrary

[Note: Col. 1370D, Cous.: “or that the Father proceeds by a certain primacy without authority—and the contrary” (?)]

Augustine, *On the Trinity*, I: “He who thinks that God is of such power that he himself begot himself is so much the more mistaken, because not only is God not so, but neither is any spiritual or bodily creature. For there is absolutely no thing that begets itself.”

The same, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*, ch. VII: “God is perfection and needs nothing. Why, then, was it necessary for Christ to be born? When God the Father wished things which were not to exist, and knew this to be a work worthy of his majesty, [Col. 1371A] he first begot from himself the Son, in whom he himself might be seen, since the Son differed from him in nothing, so that an effect corresponding to his greatness might answer it. For what more could he do than beget from himself another who is perfect? This, therefore, is the perfect work, than which no other more excellent can be seen. God, from whom are all things, wishing first to bring forth the Son from himself before the creation—him whom he had in mystery within himself or with himself—begot him, through whom he might make the things which were made, in order to reveal to creation the mystery which had lain hidden in him from eternal ages, as the Apostle says.”

Likewise, ch. CLXVIII: “Since almighty God surpasses all in greatness and goodness, he ought to have produced and displayed from himself something great and supremely [Note: [Col. 1371D] Cous.: ‘greatest.’] good. But if he had produced something beneath the measure [Col. 1371B] of his excellence, this would seem either to mean that he could not do more—which cannot be attributed to the Almighty—or that he would not, which would appear most unkind. Certainly, it would not have been great in the highest God to make something placed within himself which did not possess the force of complete supremacy. Yet there was nothing above him; for nothing overcomes God. Below him would have been too little, because what is less does not suit the greatest. Therefore, creating his Son most like himself, he brought forth from himself, as it were, another self.”

Likewise: “He therefore who had a Son corresponding to himself in every respect of likeness—that is, the only one to the only one, the blessed to the blessed, the greatest to the greatest, the everlasting to the everlasting—had before the world the primacy of created offspring, from whom he imparted an example to things arising, so that the shoots of those that generate might be compelled to correspond to their [Col. 1371C] seeds. Nor indeed did the lawful order allow otherwise than that he who was to be Father of things should first be a proper Father, that is, Father of his own proper offspring.”

Likewise: “From himself he brought forth and produced that which he had always had in himself and with himself. Thus, if I say that light is born from the sun and proceeds from it, I certainly do not mean that the sun either cannot be or ever was without light [Note: [Col. 1371D] Cous.: ‘certainly not because some …’].”

The same, in Book V *Against Heresies*: “Hermes, who in Latin is called Mercury, wrote a book called *Logos Teleos*, that is, ‘The Perfect Word.’ The book’s title is great, because he of whom it was written is great. Let us hear what he says concerning the perfect Word. ‘The Lord,’ he says, ‘made him lord also, second after all the gods that had been made; he made him first, sole, and true.’ He appeared good to him and most full [Col. 1371D] of all goods. Let the Evangelist say how full he is: ‘From his fullness we all receive’ (John 1). ‘He rejoiced greatly and loved him as his only-begotten,’ whom he first called made, and afterward called his only-begotten.”

Likewise, elsewhere he said: “The Son of the blessed God and of good will.” You were seeking, pagan, God’s consort? Hear Mercury: “Do you seek God’s consort? God’s consort is good will.”

The same, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*, ch. LVIII: “[The Holy Spirit], who is third from the Father [Note: [Col. 1371D] Mon.: ‘is from the Father’], but second from Christ according to [Col. 1372A] the arrangement of number [Note: [Col. 1372D] Mon.: ‘our’], is not, in respect to substance, something other than, nor different from, the one or the other.”

From the book of Orosius’s *Questions*: Orosius to Augustine: “Did the Father beget the Son by will or by necessity?” Augustine: “Neither by will nor by necessity. For necessity is not in God, and will cannot precede wisdom. Therefore, rationally speaking, to be wise was prior to willing rationally. For when a heretic asked one of our number whether the Father begot the Son willingly or unwillingly, he is reported to have replied commendably: ‘Tell me, heretic, whether God the Father is God by necessity or by will.’ If he had said, ‘By necessity,’ a great absurdity followed; if ‘By will,’ the response would have been: ‘Therefore he is God by will, not by nature.’”

The same, *On the Words of the Lord*, sermon IX: “There is indicated in us [Col. 1372B] authority in the Father, nativity in the Son, and the communion of Father and Son in the Holy Spirit.”

Ecclesiasticus (1:1): “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has been with him always and is for every age. Who has investigated the wisdom of God, preceding all things? Wisdom was created before all things, and prudent understanding from eternity; the fountain of God’s wisdom is on high.”

Hilary on Psalm 137: “You formed me and laid your hand upon me. Both are signified: what he formed is ancient; what he laid his hand upon is latest. For that he was formed according to the nature of divinity, the Apostle teaches when he says, ‘Who, being in the form of God’ (Phil. 2). For what is in a form is formed; and the Father is also in form, so that he may be referred to the Father in respect of nature and divinity, [Col. 1372C] and may be said to have been formed by him.”

The same, *On the Trinity*, III: “According to the Apostle, because in Christ ‘all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily’ (Col. 2:9), incomprehensibly and ineffably, before all time and ages, he begot the Only-Begotten from those things which were unbegotten in himself, imparting to his nativity, through love and power, all that God is. Thus from the unbegotten, perfect, and eternal Father, the Only-Begotten Son is himself only-begotten, perfect, and eternal. But those things which belong to him according to the body which he assumed are the will of his goodness for our salvation.”

The same, XI: “‘The words which I speak to you, I do not speak from myself.’ For, while he does not speak from himself, he must owe what he speaks to his author. Likewise, with respect to that which he does according to nativity, [Col. 1372D] the Father is his author.”

Again, in XII, speaking of God the Father as unbegotten and of the Son as begotten from him, he says: “To be unbegotten and to be born are not the same thing: the latter is from another, while the former is from no one. And it is one thing always to be eternal without an author, another to be eternal from the Father—that is, from an author. Where the Father is author, there also is nativity. But where the author is eternal, there the nativity too is eternity; for as nativity is from an author, so from an eternal author comes eternal nativity.”

Likewise: “That which is born from eternity, if it is not born eternal [Note: [Col. 1372D] Cous.: ‘eternal.’ Cf. *Works of Hilary*, p. 1123], then the Father will no longer be an eternal author. If, therefore, anything is lacking in eternity to him who is born from the eternal Father, it is unquestionably lacking also to the author who is Father, because what is infinite to the begetter is infinite also to the one begotten.” [Col. 1373A]

Likewise: “From the eternal nothing is other than eternal; but if it is not eternal, then neither is the Father, who is the author of generation, eternal.”

Likewise: “He is shown to have been born from you, so that he signifies you alone as his author.”

Likewise, in XII: “The Son, true God from you, God the Father, and begotten from you, is to be confessed after you in such a way as to be confessed with you, because you are the eternal author of his eternal origin. For, being from you, he is second from you.”

Ambrose, on the First Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians: “‘The head of Christ is God.’ It is fitting that the Father be called the head of the Son, because he is his begetter.”

The same, on the Second Epistle: “‘But all things are from God.’ Although Christ redeemed us, nevertheless all things are from God, because all fatherhood is from him; therefore the person of the Father must be set before [Col. 1373B] the others.”

The same, on the Epistle to the Ephesians: “‘One God and Father of all, who is above all,’ etc. He called God the Father above all because he owes to no one what he is, etc.”

Jerome, explaining the faith of the Council of Nicaea: “Far be it that there should be anything greater or lesser in the Son of God, whether in place, time, power, knowledge, equality, or subjection, when this is said: that such things be ascribed to his divinity, not to his flesh. For if any greater or lesser thing is found—except that the Father begot the Son, and except that the Son was not born from himself but properly born from the Father—the Father is shown to be either envious or powerless, and moreover temporal.”

Augustine, *On the Incarnate Divinity*, to Januarius, says thus concerning the Son of God: “Let us consider also how we should understand what we read in the Wisdom of Solomon, where he says of wisdom that it is a certain vapor of God’s power, etc.”

Likewise: “From this it is shown that this vapor of God’s power has always existed, having no beginning except God himself; for it was not fitting that there should be another beginning besides him from whom it both is and is born—God.”

Likewise, after some intervening material: “‘The image of his goodness.’ For the principal goodness is undoubtedly the Father, from whom [Note: [Col. 1373D] Cous.: ‘which.’] the Son is born; and since he is in every respect the image of the Father, he is without doubt fittingly called the image of his goodness. For no goodness exists in the Son other than that which is in the Father.”

Likewise: “The principal [Col. 1373D] goodness must be understood to be in God the Father. From him the Son is born and the Holy Spirit proceeds, and without doubt bears in himself the nature of goodness which is in that fountain from which the Son is born and the Holy Spirit proceeds.” [Note: [Col. 1373D] Cous.: “The principal goodness is to be known in God the Father, from whom [are] the Son and the proceeding Spirit.” See the Maurists’ *Works of Augustine*, VIII, Appendix, p. 56.]

Chrysostom on Matthew: “‘Jesus was led into the wilderness by the Spirit’: he was led by the Holy Spirit, but not as one lesser by the command of one greater; rather, as one greater by the exhortation of one lesser. For not only is one said to be led or brought who is led by another’s power, but also one who is persuaded by another’s reasonable [Col. 1374A] exhortation [Note: [Col. 1374D] Cous.: ‘otherwise: reasonably by exhortation’].”

Likewise: “‘The master of the household said to his steward.’ Without doubt the Son speaks to the Holy Spirit; and, if you wish, grant that the Father speaks to the Son. I do not ask whether the Son is the Father’s steward or the Holy Spirit the Son’s; but I say this: a steward of a house and the master of the household can neither be of the same substance, nor one person, nor of equal dignity. If, then, one is master of the household and the other the steward of the master, how can your Trinity stand? But if he is of the same substance and is lesser, you do an injury to the substance. If their dignity is not equal, where is the one substance?”

Likewise: “‘And he saw the Holy Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him’ (Matt. 3:16). He did not say, ‘This is our beloved Son,’ lest Christ should appear to have been Father in respect to the Holy Spirit as well as God. For if they are equal in all things, then just as he is more honored in fatherhood [Note: [Col. 1374D] Mon.: ‘honored’], so too is the Holy Spirit. But if God is indeed Father because he has a Son, whereas the Holy Spirit is not Father because he has no Son, he is not equal in all things. Nor was it said, ‘These are my beloved sons’; nor is he a Son together with Christ in the way that Christ is. But if he is not a Son as Christ is, but Christ’s faithful minister, he is not equal to Christ.”

Paul the Apostle, to the Philippians: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. 2:5–6).

Athanasius, in the Creed: “The Son is from the Father alone: not made, nor created, but begotten.”

Likewise: [Col. 1374C] “But in this Trinity nothing is earlier or later, nothing greater or lesser; rather, all three persons are coeternal with one another and coequal.”

## XVI. That the Son is said to be begotten by the Father, yet not begotten; and the contrary.

Gregory on Job, XXXIII: “‘My tongue is the pen of a scribe.’ What we speak passes away; what we write remains. The tongue of the Father is called the pen of a scribe because his coeternal and untransitory Word is begotten from him.”

Ambrose, *On the Faith*, to Emperor Gratian: “These matters in God are not to be understood bodily. The Son is begotten incomprehensibly; the Father begets impassibly; yet he begets from himself [Col. 1374D] and before every understanding, as [Note: [Col. 1374D] Cous.: ‘begets’ instead of ‘as.’] true God true God.”

Jerome, in the definition of the Catholic faith and creed of the Council of Nicaea: “That he was born from the Father’s substance, the Savior himself always declares in the Gospels: ‘What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of Spirit is spirit’” (John 3:6).

Augustine, *On the Trinity*, V, ch. XIII: “If the begetter is a principle in relation to that which he begets, the Father is a principle in relation to the Son, because he begets him.”

The same, discussing the generation of the Son from God the Father in *Eighty-Three Questions*, ch. XXXVIII: “It is better,” he says, “to say ‘always born’ than ‘always being born’ [Col. 1375A], because one who is always being born is not yet born, and has never been born or will be born, if he is always being born [Note: [Col. 1375D] The words ‘because one … being born’ are absent in Cous.]. For being born and having been born are different things. Consequently, if the Son is never born, he is never Son; and if he is always Son, therefore he is always born.”

The same, to Pascentius, an Arian count: “What then do we say? If the Son was born of the Father, the Father has now ceased begetting; and if he has ceased, he began. But if he began to beget, there was once a time when he was without the Son. Yet he was never without the Son, because his Son is his Wisdom; therefore the Father always begets and the Son is always being born. Here again we must fear lest the generation be thought imperfect if we say not ‘born’ but ‘being born.’ Bear with me, I beg you, [Col. 1375B] in these straits of human thought and speech; and let us flee together to the Spirit of God saying through the prophet: ‘Who shall declare his generation?’” (Isa. 53:8).

Gregory on Job, XXIX [I, 917]: “The Lord God Jesus Christ, insofar as he is the power and wisdom of God, was born of the Father before times; or rather, because he neither began to be born nor ceased, let us say more truly: always born. Yet we cannot say, ‘He is always being born,’ lest he seem imperfect. But so that he may be designated both eternal and perfect, let us say ‘always’ and ‘born’: ‘born,’ in order that perfection may be signified; ‘always,’ eternity. Though by saying ‘perfect’ we depart far from expressing that truth itself, because what was not made cannot be called [Col. 1375C] perfect. Nevertheless, the Lord, accommodating himself to the words of our weakness, says: ‘Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect’” (Matt. 5:48).

## XVII. That the Father alone is called unbegotten; and not.

Isidore, *Etymologies*, VI: “The Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called unbegotten.”

Athanasius, *On the Trinity*, VIII: “The nativity of the Son of God is before the beginning with the Father. I confess one unbegotten and one begotten. I confess the almighty Father, without beginning and without end, who holds all things and is held by none, governs all things and is governed by none. The begotten is not diminished by him who is unbegotten. The Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten; [Col. 1375D] if I should call him begotten, I establish two Sons.”

Augustine, *On the Orthodox Faith*: “The Father,” he says, “is the principle of divinity, from whom the Son is born; from whom the Holy Spirit is not born, because he is not the Son; nor is he unbegotten, because he is not the Father.”

Gregory, in the *Register*, ch. I: “The Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but coeternal, proceeding from the Father and the Son.”

Augustine, in the questions proposed by Orosius and answered by himself, ch. II: “The certain faith declares that the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten. For if we call him unbegotten, we seem to affirm that he is Father; but if begotten, we are charged with believing in two Sons. But, as certain faith holds, he is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeds from both, namely from the Father and the Son.” [Col. 1376A]

The same, *On the Trinity*, V, ch. VII: “What is called unbegotten therefore indicates that it is not Son. ‘Begotten’ and ‘unbegotten’ may suitably be said; ‘Son,’ however, is said in Latin, but common speech does not allow *in-filius* [‘un-son’] to be said. Yet nothing is removed from the understanding if ‘not Son’ is said; just as, when ‘not begotten’ is said and ‘unbegotten’ is used for it, nothing else is said.”

Likewise: “Therefore we shall no longer say ‘unbegotten,’ though it may be said in Latin; but in its place let us say ‘not begotten,’ which has the same force. Thus we say nothing other than ‘not Son.’”

Likewise: “What, moreover, is ‘unbegotten’ except ‘not begotten’? For just as ‘begotten’ is not said with reference to itself, but signifies that it is from the Father, so, when ‘unbegotten’ is said, it is not said with reference to itself, but indicates that it is not from a begetter.” [Col. 1376B]

Ambrose, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*: “When certain persons had long heard us say that the Son of God, who was begotten, cannot be unequal to the Father who begot him—although the one was begotten and the other begot, because generation belongs not to power but to nature—they think that their voice is closed against that question. But they change their course, altering the terminology and saying: ‘How can unbegotten and begotten be of one nature and substance?’ To answer: first of all, I nowhere find ‘unbegotten’ in the divine Scriptures; I have neither read nor heard it. Of what changeability [Note: [Col. 1375D] Cous.: ‘wonderfulness.’] are persons of this kind, that [Col. 1376C] [Note: [Col. 1376D] Cous.: ‘where.’] they say that we employ what is unwritten when we speak what is written, while they themselves object what is not written? Let them likewise assert where they have read that the Father is unbegotten; let them show where they have read the word ‘unbegotten.’”

“They say: ‘It has been read; for Arius called the Father unbegotten and the Son begotten and created.’ By what authority do they contend [Note: [Col. 1376D] Cous.: ‘contend.’] against apostolic writings—if indeed they confess themselves disciples of Arius? But if they say what Arius says is more just, I ought to say what the Apostle said: he did not call the Father unbegotten, but called the Son begotten. What I have read, I do not deny; indeed, I gladly employ it. What I have not read, I ought not to employ. Yet let them employ it, lest perhaps they say that, because we do not read that the Father is begotten, [Col. 1376D] we ought therefore to consider him unbegotten. This, then, is understood, not read; but neither have I read that the Holy Spirit is begotten. Therefore, according to our position, the Holy Spirit too must be called unbegotten.”

## XVIII. That the eternal generation of the Son can be narrated, known, or understood; and not.

Jerome on Ecclesiastes, at the place where it is said: “Who knows whether the spirit of the children of men goes upward, and whether the spirit of the beast goes down into the earth?” (Eccl. 12), adding: “Who wished to indicate difficulty? For the word ‘who’ in the holy Scriptures is always taken not for impossibility but for difficulty, as there: ‘Who shall declare his generation?’—namely Christ’s generation” (Isa. 53:8). [Col. 1377A]

The same, in the prologue to Isaiah: “Nor, as Montanus dreams, did the prophets speak in ecstasy, so as not to know what they said, and so that while teaching others they themselves were ignorant of what they uttered. Rather, according to Solomon, who says in Proverbs: ‘The wise man understands what he brings forth from his mouth, and on his lips he bears judgment,’ they themselves knew what they said.”

Likewise: “How could wise prophets, like brute animals, have been ignorant of what they said? We also read in another place of the Apostle: ‘The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets’ (1 Cor. 14:32), so that they have within their own power [Col. 1377B] when to be silent and when to speak.”

The same, on Isaiah, Book I: “‘By hearing I heard from the Lord.’ For this reason those who could say, ‘Our eyes are always toward the Lord’ (Ps. 24), were properly called seers. The bride too had these eyes of the heart in the Song of Songs, to whom the bridegroom says: ‘You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride, with one of your eyes’ (Song 4:9). And in the Gospel it is read: ‘The lamp of your body is your eye’ (Matt. 6:22). In the Old Instrument [Note: [Col. 1377D] Cous.: ‘Testament.’] also it is said that the people heard the voice of God. Therefore let the ravings of Montanus be silent, he who thinks that the prophets spoke of future things in ecstasy and mental derangement; for they could not see what they did not know.”

Origen, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans [16:25]: “‘According to the revelation of the mystery kept silent in eternal times,’ etc. But it must be asked whether he says that it was kept in silence in such a way that absolutely no one knew it, not even the prophets who proclaimed it. It seems very absurd to me that we should say that the prophets wrote about divine mysteries in such a way that they did not understand what they said, when Scripture says: ‘The wise person shall understand what proceeds from his mouth and bears understanding on his lips.’ But if they did not understand what they uttered from their own mouth, they were not wise. Hence, if it is foolish to deny that the prophets were wise, it follows that they understood what they uttered.” [Col. 1377C]

“Paul says that he heard words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12:4), not because he himself did not know what he had heard, but because he was not permitted to disclose to others what had been revealed to him. Thus this too may seem to have been said here: that the mystery was kept in silence, because the prophets indeed knew it but did not reveal it to people—that is, to the multitude—if they concealed it in silence according to the [Note: [Col. 1377D] Cous.: ‘holy.’] command of God, until the time should come and the Word should become flesh.”

Augustine on John: “‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.’ The natural man does not receive this. What then, brothers? Shall we be silent about it? Why then is it read, if it is to be kept silent? Or why is it heard, if it is not [Col. 1378A] explained? Or what is explained, if it is not understood? Since, therefore, I do not doubt that among you there are some who can receive not only an explanation, but can understand even before it is explained, I shall not defraud those who are able to receive it while fearing to be superfluous to the ears of those who are unable to receive it.”

The same, *On the Trinity*, II: “For him, being from the Father—that is [Note: [Col. 1377D] Cous.: ‘or.’] being born from the Father—is not other than seeing the Father; nor is seeing the Father at work other than working equally with him.”

Jerome on Matthew, on “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ”: “In Isaiah we read: ‘Who shall declare his generation?’ (Isa. 53:8). We should not therefore suppose the Gospel to contradict the prophet, as though this one began here to narrate in words what the other declared impossible; for there it is said of the generation of divinity, [Col. 1378B] here of the incarnation.”

Augustine, Book II *Against Maximinus*: “I do not know, cannot, and am unable to distinguish between that [Note: [Col. 1377D] Cous.: ‘this.’] generation and this procession, because both the one and the other are ineffable. As the Prophet says of the Son, ‘Who shall declare his generation?’ so it may most truly be said of the Holy Spirit, ‘Who shall declare his procession?’” [Note: [Col. 1378D] Cous. omits the words “Thus … declare?”]

Athanasius, *On the Trinity*, V, ch. II: “Accursed be he who does not confess that the Son is truly begotten ineffably from the Father’s substance; let it be, let it be.”

The same, VIII: “O human being, do you inquire into divinity? I rebuke you. If you believe, you do well; you are commanded to believe, not permitted to investigate. But if you investigate and say, ‘How is he Father?’ you have fallen from the light; and if you say, ‘How is he Son?’ there will meet you: ‘Who shall declare his generation?’ [Col. 1378C] Take care [Note: [Col. 1378D] Cous.: ‘therefore.’] lest you likewise fall from the light. For no one knows the Father except the Son, nor the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11:27).

Ambrose, *On the Faith*, to Emperor Gratian: “It is impossible for me to know the secret of the generation; it is above powers, above angels, above cherubim, above seraphim, above every understanding. It is not permitted to search the heavenly mysteries; it is permitted to know that he was born, but not to inquire how.”

Likewise: “You are commanded to believe, and not permitted to investigate.”

Likewise: “Not even the angels could comprehend the mystery of the Father.”

Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Law*: “Cherubim and seraphim have not fully comprehended what [Note: [Col. 1378D] Cous.: ‘who.’] God is, because no one knows the Father except the Son.”

## XIX. That “I have begotten you today” is to be understood of the eternal generation of the Son; and the contrary. [Note: [Col. 1378D] “And the contrary” is absent in Cous.]

[Col. 1378D]

Augustine on the second Psalm: “‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’ (Ps. 2:7). Although that day in prophecy may also seem to be the day on which the Lord was born according to his humanity, nevertheless ‘today,’ because it signifies presence, and because in eternity nothing is past as though it had ceased to be, nor future as though it were not yet, but only the present is understood [Col. 1379A] according to [Note: [Col. 1379D] Cous. omits this word.] what is said, ‘Today I have begotten you,’ is that whereby sincere and Catholic faith proclaims the everlasting generation of God’s Wisdom, which [Note: [Col. 1379D] Mon.: ‘who.’] is the Only-Begotten Son.”

The same, in Book V *Against Heresies*: “Listen still, you who deny that God begot a Son; listen [Note: [Col. 1379D] Mon.: ‘I heard.’] to what the Father says through Isaiah: ‘Shall I, who cause others to give birth, not myself give birth?’ says the Lord. ‘Shall I who grant generation to all others be barren?’ says the Lord” (Isa. 66:9). “To him it was said: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’ You mock when you hear ‘today’; with God there is never a tomorrow, never a yesterday, but always today.”

The same, in the *Enchiridion*, ch. XLIX: “Those baptized with John’s baptism were not regenerated, but were prepared by a kind of forerunning ministry of him who said: ‘Prepare [Col. 1379B] the way of the Lord.’ They were prepared for him in whom alone they could be regenerated. For his baptism is not only in water, as John’s was, but also in the Holy Spirit, so that whoever believes in Christ may be regenerated by that Holy Spirit; Christ, begotten by that Spirit, had no need of regeneration.”

“Therefore that voice of the Father which was uttered over the baptized one, ‘Today I have begotten you,’ indicates not the one temporal day on which he was baptized, but unchangeable eternity, in order to show that that man belongs to the person of the Only-Begotten [Note: [Col. 1379D] Cous.: ‘Father.’]. For where the day neither begins with the end of yesterday nor ends with the beginning of tomorrow, it is always today. He therefore wished to be baptized in water by John, that his great humility might be commended.”

The same, in the sermon for the second day of Easter, beginning: “We ought to rejoice no less now than we rejoiced yesterday”: “Christ, who enlightened us, has become day for us; he himself has today been begotten for us, according to what David says in the person of God the Father: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’ Not that he begot the Son on that day, but that he begot the Son himself, day and light, that he might shine upon all and give light to all. It is called ‘today’ because, as a present and unfailing light from the eternity of brightness, it seemed to be one day [Note: [Col. 1380D] Cous.: ‘seems.’]; neither ancient antiquity eludes him nor future ignorance passes him by.” [Col. 1379C]

Likewise: “But we ought to know that the time when it was said to the Son, ‘Today I have begotten you,’ was neither that in which he was born from Mary according to the flesh, nor that in which he proceeded from the mouth of God the Father according to divinity, but that in which he rose from the dead. For, as the apostle Paul says: ‘Raising up the Lord Jesus, as it is written in the Psalm: You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Acts 13:33). “Therefore ‘today’ is rightly called that time when, from the gloomy night of hell, he shone forth to the heights as a brilliant light.”

The same, in the *Treatise on the Incarnation of the Lord*: “Of him, insofar as he is less than the Father and consubstantial with his mother, the Prophet sang, saying: ‘Today I have begotten you.’”

Likewise: “That prophecy shows the nativity [Col. 1380A] of the flesh to come, because he was recently born from the Virgin Mary. For concerning the equality of his divinity with the Father it does not say, ‘Today I have begotten you,’ but ‘Before the morning star I have begotten you’ (Ps. 109), namely, before days or angels were made.”

Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, III (II, 361): “What is regeneration? You have in the Acts of the Apostles that verse in the Psalm, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you,’ seems to concern the resurrection. For in the Acts of the Apostles Peter the Apostle thus interpreted it: that when the Son rose from the dead, the Father’s voice resounded: ‘You are my Son,’ etc. Hence he is also called the firstborn from the dead. Resurrection is when we pass from death to life. So too in baptism: since, when you are immersed and rise, there is a likeness of death and a likeness of resurrection. Therefore, according to the interpretation of the Apostle Peter, just as that resurrection was generation, so this resurrection is regeneration.” [Col. 1380B]

Hilary on Matthew, ch.
