II, concerning the Lord’s baptism: “When he had been baptized, the entrances of heaven were opened, the Holy Spirit was sent forth and visibly recognized in the form of a dove, and he was anointed with such a gift of fatherly love; then a voice from heaven spoke thus: ‘My Son,’ etc.”

The same, on Psalm 2: “He was born again from baptism and was then God’s Son, so that he might be born both into that same thing and into another. For it is written that, when he came up from the water: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’ But according to the generation of a human being reborn, he himself was then reborn by God [Col. 1380C] as Son. But what is now in the Psalm, ‘You are my Son,’ etc., apostolic authority applies neither to the Virgin’s childbirth nor to regeneration in the washing, but to the firstborn from the dead. For in the book of Acts it is said thus: ‘Raising our Lord Jesus, as it is written in the first Psalm: My Son,’ etc., when he raised him from the dead, no longer to return to corruption.”

The same, *On the Trinity*, XI: “It is beyond doubt how Jesus was anointed in the power and Spirit of God: when he came up from the Jordan, the Father’s voice was heard, ‘You are my Son,’ etc., so that through this testimony the anointing of the flesh sanctified in him might be recognized as an anointing of spiritual power.”

Likewise: “Finally, that prophetic utterance indicates this later anointing, which was in time, saying: ‘You loved righteousness and hated iniquity,’ etc. (Ps. 44). To have merited comes later than to be. If, therefore, we attribute to the nativity of the Only-Begotten the anointing of God, which anointing was granted because of the merit of righteousness loved and iniquity hated, the Only-Begotten God will be understood as advanced through anointing rather than as begotten; and through stages he will be made perfect [Note: [Col. 1380D] Cous.: ‘advanced.’] God, who was not born God but was anointed into God on account of merit. Then Christ will be God by a cause, [Col. 1381A] and not every cause through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

## XX. That the first Psalm is to be understood of Christ; and not.

Jerome, in the larger breviary (II, appendix, p. 122): “‘And he did not stand in the way of sinners’ (Ps. 1). It does not say, ‘He did not walk’; for that would be impossible, because no one is without sin. ‘He did not stand’ means that he did not persist in sin, but through repentance turned to better things.”

Likewise: “‘And whatever he does shall prosper’ (ibid.). The Jews think this Psalm was said of Josiah, because alone among profane kings he did not go in the counsel of the ungodly, but followed the law of God. Hence, ‘Whatever he does shall prosper’ [Col. 1381B] cannot be understood of any of the saints, except perhaps in the age to come. It is better, therefore, to understand it of that man whom the Savior assumed—not in such a way that we testify that one person assumed and another was assumed, but so that one and the same is both Son of God and Son of Man.”

The same, in the smaller breviary, beginning, “The Psalter is like a great house”: “‘Blessed is the man who did not go’ (ibid.). Some think that this blessed man is Christ according to his humanity. The intention is good [Note: [Col. 1381D] The words “The intention is good” are absent in the Munich manuscript.], but it is ignorant. For if this blessed man is Christ, and Christ gave the law, how is it said of Christ: ‘His delight is in the law of the Lord’ (ibid.)? Finally, how is he compared to another tree and said to be ‘like a tree planted by streams of water’ (ibid.)? Everything that we compare is less than that to which [Note: [Col. 1381D] Cous.: ‘which.’] it is compared. You see, therefore, that the Psalm cannot be interpreted concerning the person of the Lord, but generally concerning anyone.”

## XXI. That “My heart has uttered a good word” (Ps. 44) is to be understood of the generation of the Son; and not.

Jerome on Psalm 44: “‘My heart has uttered a good word.’ This Psalm is introduced [Note: [Col. 1381D] Cous.: ‘announced.’] in the voice of the Father. ‘My heart has uttered a word,’ not through bodily union but from the heart: it brought forth the Word equal to itself, through whom all things were made. ‘I speak my works to the king’: I speak to the Word himself, the King-Son, and all things [Col. 1381D] are accomplished.”

The same, *On the Prodigal Son* (IV, 155): “The fatted calf, which is sacrificed for the salvation of repentance [Note: [Col. 1381D] Cous.: ‘of the homeland.’], is the Savior himself; we are daily fed on his flesh and given his blood to drink, filled with fatness, and break forth into a belch of praises [Note: [Col. 1381D] In place of ‘into a belch of praises,’ Cous. has [Col. 1382D] ‘the praise of virtues.’], saying: ‘My heart has uttered,’ etc. Yet some, more superstitiously than truly, without considering the text of the Psalm, judge this to be understood in the person of the Father.”

## XXII. That the Son alone is not from the substance of the Father; and the contrary.

[Col. 1382A]

Jerome, Book II to Pammachius and Marcella, *A Defence against an Accuser*: Many scandals and very manifest blasphemies are found in the books of Eusebius. He calls the Son the Father’s minister, and says that the Holy Spirit is not of the same substance as the Father and the Son. Ambrose, Book IV, *On the Trinity*, chapter 5: “She was found with child by the Holy Spirit.” [Note: [Col. 1382D] Mon. adds in the margin: “The Greek has: ‘from the Holy Spirit’” (Matt. 1:18).] Therefore, what is from something is either from its substance or from its power: from its substance, as the Son, who says, “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” (Ecclus. 24); as the Spirit, who proceeds from the Father; from its power, as in: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things.” The Council of Nicaea: “We believe [Col. 1382B] in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible; and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten, the only-begotten from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light,” etc.

### XXIII. That “the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” is to be understood of the Holy Spirit, and not otherwise

Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, sermon 1: You saw not waters alone; believe that the presence of divinity was there. “The Spirit was borne over the waters,” says the Prophet. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their strength” (Ps. 32). He who was borne over them was at work. Take another testimony: “My spirit,” he says, “shall not remain in human beings, [Col. 1382C] because they are flesh” [Note: [Col. 1382D] Cous.: “flesh.”] (Gen. 6). By this God shows that spiritual grace turns away carnal uncleanness. [Note: [Col. 1382D] Mon.: “is turned away.”]

The same, in the *Hexaemeron*, on the first day (Book I, chapter 8): “And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1). We understand this as the Holy Spirit, so that in the constitution of the world the works of the Trinity [Note: [Col. 1382D] Cous.: “of divinity.”] may shine forth. For after the statement, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (ibid.), that is, God made them in Christ or through the Son, because all things were made through him, there remained the fullness of operation in the Spirit, as it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established,” etc. The Spirit of God was borne over the waters; for, while adorning [Note: [Col. 1382D] Mon.: “forming”; editions: “adorning the pole.”] the vaults of heaven and the earths about to germinate, the Spirit was beautifully borne over them, because through him they had the seeds of new births [Col. 1382D] to sprout, according as the Prophet said: “Send forth your Spirit,” etc. (Ps. 103).

Finally, the Syriac, which is close to Hebrew, has it thus: “And the Spirit of the Lord brooded over the waters,” that is, gave them life, so as to gather them into new creatures and animate them to life by his warming. For we also read that the Holy Spirit is creator, as Job says: “The divine Spirit who made me” (Job 33). The same: Or, if some wish to understand it as air, let them answer why he said “the Spirit [Col. 1383A] of God,” when it would have been enough to call it simply “spirit.”

Jerome on Genesis, in the book of *Hebrew Questions*: “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” For what is written in our codices as *ferebatur*, “was borne,” the Hebrew has *merefeth*, which we may call “was brooding” or “was warming,” in the likeness of a bird giving life to eggs by its heat. From this we understand that it is said not of the spirit of the world, as some suppose, but of the Holy Spirit, who himself is called from the beginning the giver of life to all things; and if giver of life, then creator and God. “Send forth your Spirit,” he says, “and they shall be created.”

Augustine on Genesis, Book I: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.” A needy and dependent love loves in such a way as to be subject to the things it loves. Therefore, when the Spirit of God is mentioned, in whom his holy goodwill and love are understood, he is said to be borne over them, lest God be thought to love his works-to-be because of a necessity of need rather than from an abundance of beneficence.

The same, *On the Incarnate Deity*, to Januarius: Therefore the Spirit of God, who was borne over the waters in the beginning, I think is none other than the Holy Spirit—not, however, [Note: [Col. 1383D] Cous.: “not only.”] according to the historical sense, but according to spiritual understanding.

The same, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chapter 56: If he is thought to be the Holy Spirit merely because he is read to be God’s spirit, the assertion is empty. The Lord says: “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6). And in what follows: “But I will destroy,” he says, “all things from human being to beast” (ibid.). [Col. 1383C] He said this, of course, because he was going to bring a flood upon the earth. Can the Holy Spirit be understood here? For he spoke of souls. And in Ezekiel it is said: “Thus says the Lord to these bones: I will stretch skin over you, and I will put my spirit into you, and you shall live.” Likewise, the soul of a human being is called “spirit,” and so are wind, air, the soul of a beast, angels, and whatever have received, through their own substance, the capacity to live. Likewise, whenever Scripture wishes to signify the Spirit who properly is from heaven [Note: [Col. 1383D] Cous.: “from God.”], it adds the words “Holy Spirit,” so that a creature may not be understood by this expression.

But Moses, when describing material creation—that is, the confused mass of things, which is certainly senseless—declared that the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the earth [Col. 1383D] and the dark abyss, so that from that spirit, and from the place over which it was borne, the higher creature, which we call spiritual, might be recognized. For by saying that it was borne over them, he indicated it to be a creature; because every creature is borne by the power of God, from whom it has received existence. For what sense is there in saying that the Spirit of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1384D] Cous.: “Holy.”] was borne over the waters, when it is certain that he is above every creature?

### XXIV. That the Holy Spirit can also be called Father and Son, and not otherwise

Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book V: The Holy Spirit, according to what is written, since God is spirit, may universally be called the same, because the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, and the Father is holy and the Son is holy. And shortly afterward: The Holy Spirit is a certain communion of Father and Son, and perhaps is therefore so called because the same designation can apply to Father and Son. Therefore, so that the communion of both may be signified by a name fitting each alike, the Holy Spirit is called the gift of both.

The same, Book XV: By many examples it can be shown that the names of many things are used both universally and properly of particular things. I have said this lest anyone think we improperly call the Holy Spirit “love,” because God the Father and God the Son can also be called love.

Likewise: Finally, [Col. 1384B] if there is nothing greater in us than love, and no gift of God greater than the Holy Spirit, what follows more naturally than that he himself is the love which is called God and is from God? And if the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son loves the Father ineffably displays the communion of both, what is more fitting than that he should properly be called love, who is the Spirit common to both?

Ambrose, *On the Faith*: The Virgin conceived from the Spirit of God, and what she conceived she bore: namely, God united to his own human being. As he himself said: “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit,” because God is spirit and he is born of God; as the angel said to Mary (Luke 1:35): “The Spirit of God shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore [Col. 1384C] the holy thing born from you shall be called the Son of God.” You see, therefore, that the Spirit himself—that is, the Son of God—came to the Virgin, and that from her there proceeded the Son of God and of man; yet the Son of God was not changed by that clothing of flesh.

Ephraem the Deacon, Book V: God, the Holy Spirit, alone without sin, did not spare his own Son for your sake; and you, unhappy person, do not spare yourself?

Jerome on Psalm 17: The Holy Spirit is neither Father nor Son, but the love which the Father has in the Son and the Son in the Father.

Bede, Homily I after the Ascension: When the grace of the Spirit is given to human beings, the Spirit is certainly sent by the Father and also sent by the Son; he proceeds from the Father and also proceeds from the Son, because his mission itself is that procession which proceeds from [Col. 1384D] Father and Son.

Augustine, *On the Trinity*, V (VIII, 841): What is given is referred both to him who gave and to those to whom he gave; thus the Holy Spirit is called both the Spirit of God, who gave, and our Spirit, who received. Hence it is written of John that he would come in the spirit of Elijah. This is also to be understood of Moses, when the Lord says: “I will take from your spirit and give to them”—that is, from the Holy Spirit whom I gave to you.

Likewise: If he does not proceed except when he is given, he certainly would not proceed before there was someone to whom he might be given. For a gift can exist before it is bestowed; but it cannot in any way be called “bestowed” unless it has been given.

Likewise: Nor should it trouble us that the Holy Spirit, although [Col. 1385A] coeternal with the Father and Son, is nevertheless called something temporal—for example, when we call him “bestowed.” For the Spirit is eternally gift, but temporally bestowed. Thus the Lord is not called Lord except when he begins to have a servant, and this designation is temporal and relative in God: for the creature of whom he is Lord is not eternal.

Likewise: Behold, he does not have being Lord eternally, lest we be forced to say that the creature too is eternal, because he would not eternally rule unless it also eternally served.

### XXV. That philosophers also believed in the Trinity or the Word of God, and not otherwise

Paul the Apostle, to the Romans: “What is known of [Col. 1385B] God is manifest in them, for God revealed it to them; for his invisible things,” etc.

Augustine, Book VIII of *The City of God*: Let the Christian, instructed only in ecclesiastical writings, beware of those who philosophize according to the elements of this world; for he is warned by the apostolic precept: “Beware lest anyone deceive you through philosophy and empty seduction, according to the elements of the world” (Col. 2:8). Yet, lest he suppose that all such persons are alike, he hears the same Apostle say of certain people that “what is known of God is manifest in them. For God manifested it to them . . . His invisible things,” etc. (Rom. 1:19). And when, speaking at Athens, he had said the great thing concerning God which only a few can understand—“In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28)—he added: “As certain [Col. 1385C] of your own have said.” He certainly knew that they too must be avoided in the matters in which they err.

The same, on John, tractate 2: Certain philosophers of this world arose and sought the Creator through creation, as the Apostle plainly says: “For his invisible things,” etc. They had seen that all things were made through the Word of God; they could see that which is. They were unwilling to embrace Christ’s humility, and Christ’s cross was vile to them.

The same, Book XIII of *On the Trinity*: The leading philosophers of the nations, who were able to discern God’s invisible things intellectually through the things that were made, philosophized without the mediator, that is, without the man Christ. They believed neither the prophets who proclaimed that he was to come nor the apostles who declared that he had come.

The same, *On the Spirit and the Letter*: The wise Life which made [Col. 1385D] the world is understood by contemplating the world. Question the world: the adornment of heaven, the earth fruitful in herbs and trees, full of animals; the sea, full of how many living births [Note: [Col. 1385D] Cous.: “births.”]; the air, full of how many birds. Question all things, and see whether they do not answer you of themselves, as if with a voice: “God made us.” Noble philosophers investigated these things and recognized the artificer from his art.

The same, in the exposition of certain propositions in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: Solomon also says of the wise people of the world: “If they were able to know so much as to estimate the created work, how did they not more easily find its Lord and Creator?” But those whom Solomon rebukes did not know the Creator [Col. 1386A] through creation; while those whom the Apostle rebukes knew him but did not give thanks. The Apostle himself plainly shows that the wise among the nations found the Creator when speaking to the Athenians. For after saying, “In him we live and move and are,” he added, “as one among you has said.”

Jerome to the presbyter Paulinus, on all the books of sacred history: John was an unlearned countryman, a fisherman; yet whence, I ask, came that utterance: “In the beginning was the Word,” etc.? This learned Plato did not know; this eloquent Demosthenes did not know. “I will destroy,” he says, “the wisdom of the wise,” etc.

Likewise: I pass over persons like myself, who perhaps, after secular literature, come to the sacred Scriptures and, by polished speech, charm the ear of the people. Whatever [Col. 1386B] they say, people think it the law of God; nor do they deign to know what the apostles and prophets meant. Rather, they fit unsuitable testimonies to their own interpretation, as though it were a great achievement rather than a fault to draw resisting Scripture to one’s own will; as though we had not read Homeric and Virgilian centos, and could not likewise call Maro a Christian without Christ because he wrote:

> “Now the virgin returns,” etc.  
> “Now a new offspring,” etc.

And the Father speaking to the Son:

> “Son, my strength, my sole great power.”

And, after the Saviour’s words on the cross:

> “Such things he kept recalling, and remained fixed fast.”

### XXVI. That God judges according to foreknowledge, and not otherwise

[Col. 1386C]

Ambrose on the Epistle to the Romans (9:22): “But if God, willing to show wrath,” etc. By foreknowledge he judged Pharaoh worthy of condemnation, knowing that he would not correct himself; but he chose the Apostle Paul, foreknowing, indeed, that he would become faithful. To some, however, grace was given for use, as to Saul. See to whom he said: “Behold, your names are written in heaven,” and yet they afterward turned back (Luke 10:20).

Likewise: Their names were written in heaven because of the righteousness which they served [Note: [Col. 1386D] Mon.: “which they discerned.”]; but according to foreknowledge they were among the number of the wicked. For God judges according to righteousness, not according to foreknowledge. Thus he says to Moses: “If anyone sins before me, I will blot him [Col. 1386D] from the book of life” (Exod. 32:33). Thus, according to the justice of the Judge, one is seen to be blotted out when one sins; yet according to foreknowledge one was never in the book of life. Conversely, one is seen to be inscribed when one ceases to be wicked, though according to foreknowledge one never was absent from it.

### XXVII. That God’s providence is the cause of events, and not otherwise

Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, Book IV: Some say that a thing is not going to happen because providence has foreseen that it will happen; rather, on the contrary, because something is going to happen, divine providence [Col. 1387A] cannot fail to know it, and in this way necessity is thought to fall back in the opposite direction. For what is foreseen need not happen; but what will happen must be foreseen.

Likewise: How absurd it is to say that the occurrence of temporal events is the cause of eternal foreknowledge! For what else is it to suppose that God foresees future things because they are going to happen, than to suppose that things which happened long ago are the cause of that supreme providence?

Origen on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans (8:30): “And those whom he called.” How did he justify those whom he called, when it is certain that many are called but few chosen? All indeed are called, but not all are called according to purpose. For those who are called according to the good purpose and good [Col. 1387B] will which they exercise in God’s worship [Note: [Col. 1387D] Cous.: “which they conduct concerning worship.”] are those said to be called according to purpose. But if this is referred to God—that is, if they are said to be called according to God’s purpose, since he knows that a religious mind and a desire for salvation are present in them—it will not seem contrary to what we have explained.

Therefore, in this way the cause either of our salvation or of our perdition does not lie in God’s foreknowledge, nor will justification depend upon calling alone, nor is all ground for boasting in our own power removed. For even if we understand foreknowledge in the common sense, something does not exist because God knows that it will be; rather, because it will be, it is known by God before it occurs. But that you may know that the cause of each person’s [Col. 1387C] salvation is not placed in God’s foreknowledge, but in his own purpose and acts, consider Paul, who, fearing that perhaps, after preaching to others, he himself might become reprobate, disciplines his body, etc. (1 Cor. 9:27).

### XXVIII. That nothing happens by chance, and the contrary

Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter 27: Whatever happens by chance happens rashly; whatever happens rashly does not happen by Providence. Therefore, if some things happen by chance in the world, the whole world is not governed by Providence.

Likewise: That good by participation in which all other things are good is good not for some other reason, but through itself; this we also call divine providence. [Col. 1387D] Therefore nothing happens by chance in the world.

Likewise, chapter 1 of the *Retractations*: I do not approve of my having so often called it “fortune,” though by this name I did not mean some goddess, but the chance occurrence of events. From this come those words which no religion forbids one to say: “perhaps,” “possibly,” “maybe,” “by chance.” Yet all this [Note: [Col. 1387D] Cous.: “only.”] must be referred to divine providence. I regret having called it fortune there, since people have the very bad habit of saying, where they ought to say, “God willed this,” “Fortune willed this.”

Likewise, in the book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, on Matthew [Note: [Col. 1387D] “On Matthew” is absent in Cous.]: Nothing happens by chance under him who disposes all things, though no one understands the reason. Hence the Lord says: “I came into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). For this is the depth of the riches, wisdom, and knowledge of God, by which from the same mass one vessel is made for honor and another for dishonor, and by which it is said to flesh and blood: “O human being, who are you to answer God?” (Rom. 9:20).

### XXIX. That God’s predestination is to be understood only in relation to good, and not otherwise

Augustine, *On the Predestination of the Saints*: Predestination is the preparation of grace, which cannot exist without foreknowledge; but foreknowledge can exist without predestination. For by predestination God [Col. 1388B] foreknew those things which he himself would do. Hence it is said: “He made the things that were to be.” But he can also foreknow things which he himself does not do, such as all sins. Therefore, God’s predestination, which concerns good, is, as I said, the preparation of grace; grace, however, is the effect of predestination.

Likewise: By the name “predestination” no compulsory necessity of human will is expressed, but the eternal, merciful, and just [Note: [Col. 1388D] Cous. reads thus.] ordering of the divine work.

Likewise: It is possible to believe that God foreknew sinners, because nothing could be hidden from him; yet he did not predestine any human being to sin. For if he predestined a human being to sin, he would not punish the human being for sins. For by God’s predestination either a merciful remission of sins is prepared, or a just punishment of sins. [Col. 1388C]

The same, in the exposition of certain propositions in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: He predestined no one except one whom he foreknew would believe.

The same, on John: “But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep.” He said, “You are not of my sheep,” because he saw them prepared for eternal destruction.

Likewise: “No one snatches them out of my hand.” What can the thief and robber do? They destroy none except those predestined for destruction. But from those sheep of whom the Apostle says, “The Lord knows those who are his,” and whom he foreknew and predestined—“those whom he predestined,” etc. (Rom. 8:29)—neither wolf snatches, nor thief takes away, nor robber kills.

The same, *Enchiridion*, chapter 104: “Great are the works of the Lord, sought out according to all his wills” (Ps. 110 [Col. 1388D]:2), so that through the creature’s will—by which what the Creator did not will came about—he himself might fulfill what he willed, making good use even of evils, as supremely good: for the damnation of those whom he justly predestined to punishment, and for the salvation of those whom he kindly predestined to grace. [Note: [Col. 1388D] Cous.: “glory.”]

Prosper’s *Responses to Rufinus*: In foreknowledge he knows both good and evil.

Likewise: God’s predestination is always in relation to good, either pertaining to the recompense of justice or to the condemnation of grace.

Likewise: Foreknowledge may therefore exist without predestination, but predestination cannot exist without [Col. 1389A] foreknowledge.

From Ambrose’s statements on predestination: By all these testimonies the wicked are shown to be predestined to punishment, but not predestined to sin, because God is predestiner of those things which he will do; but things which he neither does nor will do, he has not predestined.

Likewise: He predestined the impious to punishment, and predestined punishment for them; but he did not predestine them to sin, because he is not the author of iniquity. For as righteousness and every good are from God, so iniquity and every wicked work are from the devil.

Likewise: Therefore God foreknew wicked persons who would end this life in sin, and predestined them to punishment. In this the predestination of vengeance is most justly to be praised, so that it may be recognized that God did not predestine a human being [Col. 1389B] to sin when he predestined him to be punished for the desert of sin. Therefore God foreknew all works [Note: [Col. 1389D] Cous.: “his works.”], whether good or evil; but he predestined good works alone. Yet he foreknew and ordered by provident goodness the future evil works of those whom he did not predestine to the kingdom but to destruction.

Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, Book II, chapter 6: Predestination is twofold: that of the elect to rest, and that of the reprobate to death.

From the statements of the same author: God was able, as he willed, to predestine some to glory and some to punishment. But those [Note: [Col. 1389D] Cous.: “some.”] whom he predestined to punishment, he did not predestine to guilt.

### XXX. That even sins please God, and not otherwise

Ambrose Autpert [Note: [Col. 1389D] Cous.: “Rutpert.” Ambrose Autpert, St Ansbertus, flourished around the year 770.] on the Apocalypse, Book IX: [Col. 1389C] “For God put it into their hearts to do what pleased him: to give their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God should be fulfilled.” The deserts of their preceding iniquities demand that the reprobate, being permitted by God to proceed into error, should act in such a manner that they are not released by the mercy of one sparing them but condemned by the justice of one punishing them. For they accomplish what pleases God because, by loving the iniquity which God hates, they prepare themselves to be condemned by the justice which above all things pleases God, as it is said: “You loved righteousness,” etc. For iniquity cannot please him; yet the righteousness which condemns one who commits [Note: [Col. 1390D] Cous.: “which condemns perpetual.”] iniquities does please him. Therefore, by that through which they displease him, they accomplish what is pleasing to him.

### XXXI. That God is also the cause or author of evils, and not otherwise

[Col. 1389D]

The Lord through Isaiah: “I am the Lord, and there is no other, forming light and creating darkness, making peace and creating evil; I am the Lord who does these things.” The prophet Amos: “Can there be evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” [Note: [Col. 1390D] Cous.: “not” (Amos 3:6).] Simeon said to Mary concerning Christ: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many.” And Christ himself: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not [Col. 1390A] have sin.” And elsewhere: “I came into this world for judgment, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind.” And the Apostle in the Epistle to the Romans: “For this reason God gave them over to the desires of their heart, to impurity,” etc. Likewise: “For this reason God gave them over to dishonorable passions,” etc. And shortly afterward: “God gave them over to a reprobate mind,” etc.

The same further on: “Israel did not attain what it was seeking; but the election attained it; the rest, however, were blinded, as it is written: ‘He gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes that they should not see, and ears that they should not hear, unto this present day.’” The same, in 2 Corinthians (4:3): “But if our Gospel is veiled, it is veiled in those who are perishing, in whom the god of this age blinded [Col. 1390B] the minds of unbelievers, so that the illumination of the Gospel of the grace of Christ might not shine upon them.”

Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chapter 85: For everything which God permits he is said to do, because if he does not permit it, it does not happen. [Note: [Col. 1390D] Cous.: “is.”] Hence the Lord says to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given from above” (John 19).

The same, *Enchiridion*: Nothing occurs unless the Almighty wills it to occur, either by permitting it to occur or by doing it himself. Nor should it be doubted that God acts rightly even in permitting whatever is done wrongly. For he permits this only by a just judgment, and certainly everything just is good.

Likewise: For unless it were good that evils should exist, they would in no way be permitted by almighty God [Note: [Col. 1390D] Cous.: “good.”] to exist.

The same, *On Grace and Free Will*: Divine Scripture, if carefully [Col. 1390C] examined, shows that human wills are so in God’s power that whenever he wills, he causes them to be inclined either toward benefits to be granted to some or toward punishments to be inflicted on others. For we find that some sins are also punishments for other sins, as are the vessels of wrath which the Apostle says are perfected for destruction; so too is Pharaoh’s hardening, the reason for which is said to be the showing forth in him of God’s power.

Likewise: David said (2 Kings 16:11): “Behold, my son seeks my life, and now also this son of Benjamin. Let him curse, because God has told him to do so.” How did the Lord tell this man to curse? He did not tell him by commanding, where obedience would be praised; rather, by a just and hidden judgment he inclined to this sin his will, already evil through its own fault.

Likewise: Through Ezekiel God said (14:9): “And if the prophet is deceived and has spoken, I the Lord have deceived that prophet, and I will destroy him from among my people Israel.” The same, in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: “For this reason God gave them over,” etc. And in the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians (2:10) he says of certain people: “Because they did not receive the love of truth so as to be saved, therefore he will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe a lie, so that all may be judged who [Col. 1391A] did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity.”

The same, *On Grace and Free Will*: It is written in Proverbs: “The heart of the king is in God’s hand; wherever he wills, he inclines it.” And in the Psalm it is read of the Egyptians: “He turned their heart so that they hated his people, and dealt deceitfully [Note: [Col. 1391D] Cous.: “of God.” Cf. Ps. 104:25.] with his servants,” etc. (Ps. 104:25). The Apostle likewise: “For this reason he gave them over to the desires of their heart, to impurity” (Rom. 1:24).

By such testimonies it will, I think, be sufficiently demonstrated that God works in human hearts so as to incline their wills wherever he wills, whether toward good according to his mercy or toward evil according to their deserts—by a judgment sometimes manifest, sometimes hidden, but always just. Accordingly, when you read that people are deceived by God, made dull, [Col. 1391B] or hardened in heart, do not doubt that their evil deserts had preceded, so that they might justly suffer these things. Nor incur that proverb of Solomon: “A man’s folly corrupts his ways, but in his heart he blames God.”

The same, *On Rebuke and Grace*: They were chosen to reign with Christ, not as Judas was chosen for the work suited to him; for he was chosen by him who knows how to use even evils well, so that through Judas’s condemnable work the venerable work for which Christ had come might be fulfilled. Therefore, when we hear, “Did I not choose you twelve? And one of you is a devil” (John 6), we ought to understand that the former were chosen through mercy, the latter through judgment. Therefore, he chose them to obtain his kingdom, but Judas to shed his blood.

The same, Book XX of [Col. 1391C] *Questions on Exodus*: The cause of Pharaoh’s hardening of heart was not only that the magicians performed similar things, but also God’s patience itself. In accordance with hearts, this patience spares: for some, usefully, unto repentance; for others, uselessly, unto resistance against God and perseverance in evil.

Jerome to Castricianus: It is great wrath when God does not [Note: [Col. 1391D] In Cous. “not” is absent.] grow angry with those who sin.

Likewise: It is also punishment when the sinner is left to his own will. Hence it is that he repays the sins of fathers unto the third and fourth generation, when he does not wish immediately to strike sinners; but, innocent himself, he condemns the latter after the former.

The same, in Book I on Hosea: It is a great offense, after [Note: [Col. 1391D] Cous.: “to descendants, when.”] you have sinned, not to fear God’s wrath.

Likewise: He is so [Note: [Col. 1391D] Cous.: “neighbors.”] angry that he does not strike [Col. 1391D] offenders at all.

Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, Book II, chapter 18: Preceding sins are the cause of subsequent crimes, so that those which follow are punishments for those which precede. The punishment itself is called hardening, coming from divine justice. Hence the prophet says: “You hardened our heart, so that we should not fear you” (Isa. 63:17). So too the Apostle says: “Because they did not receive the truth of God, God sent upon them a spirit of error.” Thus God causes some to sin, but only in those whose preceding sins have already been such that, by his just judgment, they deserve to proceed into worse things.

From the Third Book of Kings (22:19): The prophet Micaiah said: “Hear the word of the Lord: I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne [Note: [Col. 1391D] Cous.: “his.”], and all the host of heaven [Note: [Col. 1392D] Cous.: “his.”] standing by him on his right and on his left. And the Lord said: ‘Who will deceive Ahab king of Israel, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ And one spoke words of this kind, and another otherwise. But a spirit went out and stood before the Lord and said: ‘I will deceive him.’ The Lord said to him: ‘How?’ And he said: ‘I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ And the Lord said: ‘You shall deceive him and prevail; go out and do so.’ Now therefore, behold, the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouth [Col. 1392B] of all these prophets of yours, and the Lord has spoken evil against you.”

Jerome on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: “For this reason God gave them over,” not because he himself is the cause, but because, through long-suffering and patience, by not bringing vengeance he allows them to act according to the will of their heart.

Likewise: He is said to give them over when he does not restrain offenders, as he said: “And I dismissed them according to the desires of their hearts.”

Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter 22, “Whether God is the author of evil”: Whoever is the author of all things that are, and to whose goodness it belongs solely that everything which is should exist, cannot in any way [Note: [Col. 1392D] Cous.: “manner.”] be concerned with non-being. But everything which fails falls away from being and tends toward non-being. To be, and not to fail in any respect, [Col. 1392C] is good; to fail is evil. But he to whom non-being does not [Note: [Col. 1392D] In Cous. “not” is absent.] belong is not the cause of failing—that is, of tending toward non-being—because, so to speak, he is the cause of being. Therefore he is the cause only of good, and for that reason he is the supreme good. Accordingly, he is not the author of evil, because he is the author of all things that are, since they are good insofar as they are.

*On Divine Predestination*: “He hardens whom he wills” is not to be understood as though God produces in a person the very hardness of heart, which does not exist. For what is hardness other than to oppose [Note: [Col. 1392D] Mon.: “rebuke.”] God’s commands?

Likewise: He is said to harden one whom he is unwilling to soften; thus to blind one whom he is unwilling to enlighten; thus to reject one whom he is unwilling to call. [Note: [Col. 1392D] “Thus—call” is absent in Cous.]

Gregory on Ezekiel, Homily 11: We must consider with fear [Col. 1392D] how God, being angry because of preceding sins, permits the blinded mind to fall into evils. Hence Moses says: “The sins of the Amorites are not yet complete” (Gen. 15:16). David also says (Ps. 68:28): “Add iniquity to their iniquity,” etc. Paul says: “That they may fill up their sins.” And John is told through the angel (Rev. 22:11): “Let him who does harm do harm still; and let him who is filthy become filthy still.” Therefore the Lord now also says (Ezek. 3:20): “If anyone, turning from his righteousness, does iniquity, I will put a stumbling-block before him”—as though he plainly said: “Because by repenting he was unwilling to see where he had already stumbled, I will abandon him by a just judgment and place something before him so that he may stumble elsewhere.”

But what is God’s “placing” something? It is not at all to press a person into sin, but to be unwilling to free him from sin; as it is said of Pharaoh: “I will harden his heart” (Exod. 7:3). For the Lord does not harden the heart by sins, but he is said to harden when he does not free it from hardening.

Prosper’s *Responses to Rufinus*, chapter 3: What is from God is nothing but good, and what is good is not the cause of evil. Therefore, one is not right who thinks that the one who prolongs life for persons about to fall is the author of their sin. For they were not abandoned by God so that they might abandon the Lord; rather, they abandoned him and were abandoned. [Col. 1393B]

### XXXII. That God can do all things, and not otherwise
Chrysostom, Homily XXVI, in his exposition of the Creed, which begins: “The universal Church rejoices together: I believe in God the Father almighty.” You believe in God Almighty, because no inability can be found in His power; yet there are some things He cannot do—for example [Note: [Col. 1393D] *Ut puta* is used for *utpote*; cf. Du Cange, s.v. *puta*. Cous.: “yet He cannot, Father, for example, lie,” etc.] lie, be deceived, be ignorant, have a beginning or an end, fail to foresee, forget the past, attend to the present, or not know the future; finally, He cannot deny Himself. See how many things He cannot do! [Note: [Col. 1393D] “See—cannot do” is absent in Cous.] Yet He is almighty because He cannot do the things just mentioned. [Note: [Col. 1393D] Cous.: “rebuked.”] The same, Homily XXVIII, on the exposition of the Creed, which begins: “Upon the structure [Col. 1393C] of the whole Church: I believe in God the Father almighty.” He is called almighty because no inability can be found in His power, as the Prophet says: “Whatever He willed, He did” (Ps. 113:3). Therefore omnipotence is [Note: [Col. 1394D] Cous.: “therefore He is almighty.”] the ability to accomplish everything that He wills.

Jerome, in his letter to Eustochium: “I shall speak boldly: although God can do all things, He cannot restore a virgin after her fall. He is indeed able to free her from punishment, but He does not wish to crown one who has been defiled.”

Ambrose to Chromatius: “It is impossible for God to lie. This impossibility does not arise from weakness, but from strength, from majesty, because truth admits no falsehood. This impossibility belongs to His fullness; whence it follows that God’s impossibility is most powerful.” [Col. 1393D] For what is more powerful than not knowing anything that belongs to weakness? Yet there is also “the weakness of God,” which is stronger than human beings, and “the foolishness of God,” which is wiser than human beings; but the former concerns the cross, the latter divinity.

Augustine, Against the Letter of Gaudentius: “Why could this not be done, except because it could in no way be done justly? Thus we also say: ‘Would that I could kill myself!’ Thus too the Lord says to Lot: ‘I cannot do anything until you have entered there’” (Gen. 19:22). He said that He could not, because undoubtedly He could by power, but could not by justice.

Augustine [Col. 1394A], *Enchiridion*: “For He is truthfully called almighty for no other reason than that He can do whatever He wills, and the effect of the Almighty’s will is not impeded by the power of any creature.” [Note: [Col. 1394D] Cous.: “by power.”] The same, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “He cannot do unjust things, because He Himself is supreme justice and goodness. But He is almighty not because He can do everything, but because He can bring about whatever He wills, so that nothing can prevail against His will to prevent its fulfillment or hinder it in any way.”

The same, *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chap. CLIX: “God can indeed do all things, but He does not do anything except what accords with His truth and justice.”

The same, in the *Treatise on the Creed*: “God cannot die; He cannot change; He cannot be deceived.”

### XXXIII. That God cannot be resisted, and the contrary

[Col. 1394B]

The Psalmist (Ps. 76:8): “You are terrible; and who shall resist You?” Esther (13:9, Vulgate): “Lord, almighty King, all things are placed under Your dominion, and there is no one who can resist Your will.” The Apostle, to the Romans (9:19): “For who resists His will?” The Psalmist (Ps. 17:7): “Keep me from those who resist Your right hand.” [Note: [Col. 1394D] Cous.: “my.”] Stephen, in the Acts of the Apostles (7:51): “You always resist the Holy Spirit, as your fathers did also.”

Mark (6:4, 6): Jesus said to them: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country, among his own kindred, and in his own house.” Therefore He could perform no miracle there, except that He healed a few sick persons by laying His hands upon them. And [Col. 1394C] He marvelled because of their unbelief.

### XXXIV. That God does not have free choice, and the contrary

Jerome to Damasus, *On the Prodigal Son* (IV, 159): “Let no one consider it dangerous or blasphemous that we have said that the evil of envy could have crept even into the apostles, since we suppose that this was said even of angels: ‘For the stars are not pure in His sight, and against His angels He perceived something perverse’” (Job 4:19). “And in the Psalms (143:2): ‘No living being shall be justified in Your sight.’ He did not say, ‘every human being,’ but ‘every living being’; that is, neither evangelist nor apostle, and, ascending to greater things, neither angels nor thrones nor dominions nor the other powers. God alone is one into whom sin does not enter. [Col. 1394D] All other beings, since they possess free choice, can bend their will in either direction.”

The same, to Paula and Eustochium, in his exposition of Paul’s Epistle to Philemon (IV, 450): “So that your good might not be, as it were, from necessity, but voluntary.” A question commonly raised about the present passage can be resolved. For if God is good voluntarily and not from necessity, He ought to have made humankind in His image and likeness, so that the human being too might be good voluntarily and not from necessity. From this it is clear that they demand mutually contrary things. [Col. 1395A] For when they say, “A human being ought to have been made like God,” they demand that he be made of free choice, as God Himself is. But when they add, “He ought to have been made such that he could not admit evil,” by imposing upon him a necessity of goodness, they intend that the human being should not be made like God.

Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, chap. IV: “A human being who is good by will is better than one who is good by necessity. Therefore free will had to be given to humankind.”

The same, *On Genesis*: “The first human being had to be made so that he could will both good and evil; afterward, however, [Note: [Col. 1395D] Cous.: “Afterward, however, he is to be such that he can will evil and good; afterward he is to be such that he cannot will evil, and yet does not therefore lack free choice. Much more, etc. For free will is not to be said not to exist because, when blessed, [Col. 1396D] we will not only not to be miserable, but cannot be miserable.”] he is to be such that he cannot will evil, and yet does not therefore lack free choice. For the choice which can never serve sin will be much freer. Nor is free will to be said not to exist because, when blessed, we will [Col. 1395B] to be so blessed that we not only [not] will to be miserable, but cannot be miserable.”

The same, *City of God*, book XXII: “That blessed city will also see this as a great good within itself: no inferior being will envy any superior, just as angels now do not envy archangels. Nor will they lack free choice because sins will be unable to delight them; rather, it will be freer, from the delight of sinning to the delight of not sinning.” Again: “As the first immortality, which Adam lost by sinning, was the ability not to die, so the final immortality will be the inability to die; likewise, the first free choice was the ability not to sin, and the final choice will be the inability to sin.” Again: “Surely God Himself—because He cannot sin, is He therefore to be denied [Col. 1395C] free choice? Therefore in each person of that city the will shall be free: freed from every evil, filled with every good, forgetful of faults, forgetful of punishments; yet it shall not be forgetful of its own deliverance, so as to be ungrateful to its Deliverer. So far as rational knowledge is concerned, it remembers even its own past evils; but so far as the experiential sense is concerned, it is altogether forgetful.” [Note: [Col. 1396D] In Cous., *experientis* is absent.]

The same, *On Rebuke and Grace* (X, 770): “What is freer than free choice, since it will be unable to serve sin? This will be the reward of merit for humankind, as it has become for the holy angels.” Again: “The first freedom of the will was the ability not to sin; the final will be much greater: the inability to sin.” Again: “That first human being was given, when created, a free will without any sin, [Col. 1395D] and he made it serve sin. But when the will of these persons had been a slave of sin, it was freed by Him who said: ‘If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free’” (John 8:36).

### XXXV. That where God’s willing is absent, His power also is absent, and the contrary

From the *Life of Saint Jerome*, which begins, “Our Jerome”: “Saint Jerome undertook to commend to Eustochium, by exhortation, the pursuit of better things: ‘Although God can do all things, He cannot restore virginity after [Col. 1396A] its fall’; God’s inability could in no other way be expressed as His unwillingness. For a certain wise man says to God: ‘But You, ruler of strength, judge with tranquility, and dispose with great reverence. For power is subject to You whenever You will it.’ Therefore where God’s will is absent, power is absent. For as God is of an immutable nature, so He is also of immutable will.”

Augustine, in the *Treatise on the Creed*: “What the Almighty does not will, this alone He cannot do.” Again: “But because I have said that the Almighty can do only what He wills, lest anyone think I have rashly said that the Almighty cannot do something, the Apostle also says this: ‘If we do not believe, He remains faithful; He cannot deny Himself,’ because He cannot even will to do so.” [Col. 1396B] “For justice cannot will to do what is unjust.” Again: “Therefore, if that can be which He does not will, He is not almighty. But He is almighty; therefore whatever He wills He can do, and what He does not will cannot be; for this reason He is called almighty, because whatever He wills He can do.” [Note: [Col. 1396D] Cous.: “therefore.”]

The same, *On the Trinity*, book XIII, chap. X (VIII, 936): “Those indeed who say, ‘Was there no other way available to God by which He could free human beings, that He should will His only-begotten Son to become human and, having become mortal, to suffer our death?’—it is too little to refute them merely by asserting that this method, by which He deigns to free us, is good. We must also show, not that no other method was possible to God, to whose power all things are equally subject, but that no other method was more fitting for the healing [Col. 1396C] of our misery: why the death of Christ should take place, or rather why, passing over innumerable ways by which the Almighty could have freed us, this particular way should especially have been chosen.”

Again (VIII, 943): “Certainly God could have taken up a human being from another source, in whom there might be a mediator of God and human beings—not from the race of that Adam, just as He created the first man Himself not from anyone’s race. He could, therefore, in this way or in some other way He chose, create another person by whom the victor over the first man might be conquered. But He judged it better to assume a human being from that race which had been conquered.”

The same, in *Questions on the Old and New Law*: “God could have made all things at once, but reason prohibited it. He could have mingled the soul with the clay of the earth and thus formed the body, but this was opposed by reason, because the house had first to be constructed and then its inhabitant introduced.”

The same, *Enchiridion*: “The will of the Almighty can never be evil. Furthermore, He can do many things which He neither does nor wills. For He could have caused twelve legions of angels to fight against those who seized Him.” Matthew the Evangelist (26:53): “Do you think that I cannot ask the Father, and He will provide Me with more than twelve legions of angels?” Again: “Then, in the clearest light of wisdom, what faith now holds will be seen: namely, that the will of God is certainly immutable and [Col. 1397A] most effective, because He can do many things and does not will them, but wills nothing that He cannot do.” [Note: [Col. 1397D] Cous.: “Although.”]

The same, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “Does it seem absurd to you to say that something can be done for which no example exists? For, as I think, you do not doubt that it has never happened that a camel passed through the eye of a needle; and yet He said that even this is possible for God.” Again: “To these may be added also what is read in the Book of Wisdom: that God could inflict many new punishments upon the ungodly, with creation serving His will, but does not inflict them. He can also do with that mountain which faith would move into the sea something which nevertheless we have nowhere heard or read to have happened. Whoever says that any of these things is impossible for God, you see how foolishly he speaks and how [Col. 1397B] Scripture speaks against his faith. Many other things of this kind may occur to one reading or thinking, which we cannot deny to be possible to God, although no example of them exists.”

The same, in *On Nature and Grace*: “The Lord raised Lazarus; without doubt He could do so. But because He did not raise Judas, must it be said, ‘He could not’? Therefore He could, but He did not will to. For had He willed it, He would have done this also by the same power, because the Son gives life to whom He wills.”

### XXXVI. That God does whatever He wills, and does not

David, in Psalm 134: “Whatever the Lord willed, He did in heaven and on earth,” etc. And [Col. 1397C] the Apostle, to the Romans (9:19): “Who resists His will?” The same, in the First Epistle to Timothy (2:3): “For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all people to be saved.” And Truth Himself speaks to Jerusalem: “How often I willed to gather your children,” etc. (Matt. 23:37). Jerome on Daniel, in the third vision, where he speaks thus of God and Nebuchadnezzar: “For He does according to His will both in heaven and on earth, and there is none who can resist His hand and say, ‘Why have You done this?’ He speaks as a worldly man.” [Note: [Col. 1397D] Cous.: “namely.”] “For God does not do whatever He wills; rather, He wills whatever is good. But Nebuchadnezzar spoke in such a way that, while proclaiming God’s power, he appears to accuse His justice, because he suffered punishments undeservedly.” [Col. 1397D]

### XXXVII. That nothing happens against God’s will, and the contrary

From the words of the prophet Habakkuk: “Lord, I do not say that anything happens without You, and that the ungodly person has such great power against Your will. Since, then, You are Creator and Lord of all things, it must be that You do what cannot happen without You.”

Augustine, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “Unbelievers indeed act against God’s will when they do not believe His Gospel.”

The same, *City of God*, book XXII: “Many things indeed happen against God’s will, but He possesses such wisdom [Col. 1398A] and power that everything which seems opposed to His will tends toward those outcomes or ends which He Himself foreknew to be good and just.” Again: “God works in us even to will; therefore, according to that will by which we say that the Lord wills what He causes others to will, He wills many things and does not do them. For His saints, inspired by a holy will, will many things to be done by Him, yet they are not done—for example, they pray piously and holily for certain persons, and He does not do what they pray for.”

The same, *Enchiridion*: “Sometimes a human being of good will desires something that God [Note: [Col. 1398D] Cous.: “wills by will; sometimes He does not will.”] does not will; for example, a good son may wish his father to live, whom God in good will desires to die. Conversely, it can happen that a human being wills with an evil will what God wills with a good will: for example, an evil son may wish his father to die, and God wills this too.” [Col. 1398B] Again: “‘He wills all people to be saved,’ as if it were said: ‘No human being is saved except the one whom He has willed to be saved’; or certainly it is said thus: ‘all people,’ that is, people from every class of humankind, to be saved.”

### XXXVIII. That God knows all things, and does not

The Apostle to the Hebrews (4:13), concerning the Spirit of God: “All things are naked and laid open to His eyes,” etc.

From the *Book of Sentences* of Prosper, chap. CCLXXXI: “When the Savior says that not one sparrow falls to the ground without God’s will, and that He Himself fashions and clothes the grass of the field which shortly is to be cast into the furnace, does He not confirm that not only the entire part of the world assigned to mortal and corruptible things, [Col. 1398C] but even its lowest and most despised particles, are governed by divine providence, so that we may not suppose that things whose causes we cannot comprehend are disturbed by chance movements?”

Jerome on Habakkuk the prophet (1:14), explaining his words: “Lord, Your eyes are pure, so that You do not see evil, and You cannot look upon iniquity. Why do You not look upon those acting wickedly, and remain silent while the ungodly devours one more righteous than himself? And You make human beings like [Note: [Col. 1398D] Cous.: “as.”] the fish of the sea, and like [Note: [Col. 1398D] Cous.: “as.”] creeping things that have no ruler. I do not say that anything happens without You, and that the ungodly person has such great power against Your will. Since, then, You are Creator and Lord of all things, it must be that You do what cannot happen without You.” The prophet does not think this, but expresses human impatience in his own person, just as the Apostle assumes many persons in himself; whence: “But this, brothers, I have transferred in figure to myself,” etc. (1 Cor. 4:6). [Col. 1398D] Otherwise God cannot make human beings like fish of the sea and creeping things without a ruler, whose angels daily see the face of the Father who is in heaven.

“Therefore, just as God’s providence extends even to individual human beings, so also in other animals we can understand a general ordering, [Note: [Col. 1398D] Mon.: “arrangement.”] order, and course of things. For example: how the multitude of fish is born and lives in waters; how creeping things and four-footed animals [Col. 1399A] arise on earth, and on what foods they are nourished. But it is absurd to bring God’s majesty down to this level, that He should know at each individual moment how many gnats are born or die; what is the number of fleas and flies; how many fish swim in the water; and which of the smaller should fall prey to the larger. Let us not be such foolish flatterers of God as to drag all His power even down to the lowest things, and thereby wrong ourselves by saying that His providence for irrational creatures is the same as for us. Therefore that apocryphal book is to be reckoned folly, in which it is written that a certain angel named Tyri [Note: [Col. 1399D] Cous.: “Tyn.”] presides over creeping things, and likewise that particular angels are assigned as guardians to fish, trees, and every kind of beast.”

### XXXIX. That the works of human beings are nothing, and the contrary

[Col. 1399B]

Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chap. IX: “For a Christian it is enough to understand no cause of created things except the goodness of the Creator, who is God, and that there is no nature which either is Himself or is from Him.”

The same, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church* (I, 696): “Paul cries out: ‘Creation has been subjected to futility’; nor can what is subjected to futility separate itself from futility and join itself to truth. And the Holy Spirit grants this to us. Therefore it is not creation, because everything that exists is either God or creation.”

Paul, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (8:4): “We know that an idol is nothing in the world.”

Prudentius, hymn:

[Col. 1399C] Isis, Apollo, Venus are nothing;

Maximian himself is nothing;

She is nothing because she was made by a hand;

He is nothing because he worships things made by hands.

From Psalm 112: “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, works of human hands.”

### XL. That God also moves from place to place or is localized, and the contrary

[Note: [Col. 1399D] Cous.: “located.” The chapters XVII following here are omitted by Cous.]

The Prophet: “The Lord shall go forth from His holy place,” etc. (Mic. 1:3.) And Truth Himself: “Because I came down from heaven, not to do My own will,” etc. (John 6:38.) Therefore also the Apostle: “But what does ‘He ascended’ mean except that He first also descended into the lower parts of the earth?” (Eph. 4:9.)

Augustine, *City of God*, book XVI: “God, who is always wholly everywhere, does not move from place to place; rather, He is said to descend when He does something unusual on earth.”

The same, to Dardanus: “Therefore God is diffused through all things. For He Himself says through the prophet: ‘I fill heaven and earth’ (Jer. 23:24). And it is written of His Wisdom: ‘She reaches from end to end’ (Wis. 8:1). And in the Psalm: ‘Where shall I go from Your Spirit?’ etc. ‘If I ascend into heaven,’ etc. (Ps. 139:7). God is everywhere substantially.” Again: “We must confess that God is everywhere by the presence of His divinity, but not everywhere by the grace of His indwelling.” Again: “We must carefully consider what we said: that God is everywhere wholly in Himself. He is said to be everywhere [Col. 1400A] because He is absent from no part of things; wholly, because He is wholly present alike to every part. Those are said to be far from Him who, by sinning, have made themselves utterly unlike Him; and those to draw near to Him who, by pious living, receive His likeness.” Again: “What we added, ‘in Himself,’ must be explained more carefully. He is in Himself because He is not contained by the things to which He is present, as though He could not exist without them. Take spatial extension from bodies, and they will be nowhere. Take the bodies themselves from bodily qualities, and there will be nowhere for them to be; and therefore they must not exist.”

Augustine to Volusianus: “The Word of God is wholly everywhere. But He comes when He is revealed; He departs when He is hidden.”

Gregory, in the Greater Breviary of the Psalter, on Psalm 30: “Is God localized? Both localized and not localized: localized for those coming to Him; not localized, because He is everywhere.”

### XLI. That God Himself appeared to the ancient Fathers, and the contrary

Ecclesiastical History, chap. II: “He is shown previously to have stood by many people, but more evidently and intimately by Abraham and his household, as far as was permitted. God is described as having made Himself known to human beings because the Lord appeared to Abraham, sitting by the oak of Mamre, as though an ordinary man. But Abraham, rising when he saw a man, worships Him as God and reveres Him as God. Moreover, by the confession of his own voice, he testifies that he does not fail to recognize the divine presence, saying: ‘Sovereign, Lord’” (Gen. 15:8). “All of this, surely, is to be referred not to the Father but to the Son, as the more fully accomplished dispensation of the later incarnation indicates.”

Again, the Prophet: “He sent His word,” etc. (Ps. 106:20). Scripture likewise indicates that He who appeared to Jacob was God, saying: “Your name shall be Israel, and you have prevailed with God” (Gen. 35:10; 32:28). And shortly afterward it says: “I saw the Lord face to face,” etc. For it is not permissible to think these things of any angel or heavenly power. None of them, whenever they are perceived by mortals to be present on a heavenly command, is called Lord or God by the divine utterance.

“He also stood by Joshua, Moses’ successor; when Joshua asked who He was, He made Himself known by most explicit answers, saying: ‘I am the prince [Col. 1400D] of the host of the powers of the Lord.’ When the servant, having heard this, worshipped Him as was fitting, He said: ‘Loosen the strap of your sandal,’ etc. (Josh. 5:14, 16). Here one must note the similarity of the commands, since this was no other than He who had said to Moses from the bush: ‘Do not come near here; take off your sandals,’ etc. (Exod. 3:4–5). And He added: ‘I am the God of your fathers,’ etc. Therefore from all these things it became clear that the Word of God was designated God.”

Jerome, to Marcellinus and Anapsychia: “It was the eternal God who was seen by Adam in Paradise,” etc.; “He spoke with Jacob.”

The same, to Damasus: “In accordance with this, we have seen both the Lord Himself and angels change themselves into human forms, in order to remove fear from those who saw them.”

And the epistle of blessed Hilary, sent to various provinces, which begins, “To the most beloved and blessed brethren”: “If anyone says that it was not the Son, as a man, who wrestled with Jacob, but the unbegotten God or His Father, let him be anathema.”

The same, book XII of *On the Trinity*: “Here too there is often shipwreck, because the only-begotten God is maintained under prophetic authority to be a creature, because it is said in the person of Wisdom: ‘The Lord created me, the beginning of His ways’” (Prov. 8:22). Again: “Let us see, then, for what ways of God and for what works Wisdom, born from God before the ages, was created from the ages. Adam heard the voice of the Lord walking in Paradise. Do you suppose that the sound of one walking was heard otherwise than in the form of an assumed creature, so that He who was heard walking might stand in some created form?” [Col. 1401B]

Again: “The Angel speaks to Hagar, and surely He is the same God” (Gen. 16:9, 13). “Is His form, when He is seen as an angel, identical with the nature in which He is God? But why speak of an angel? A man comes to Abraham. Does Christ, in the outward appearance of this creation, stand in a human manner as He stands in the manner in which He is God? Yet a man speaks, stands present in a body, and is nourished with food; nevertheless, He is worshipped as God. Certainly He who was formerly an angel is now also a man, lest the diversity of the assumed creature permit this to be understood as God’s natural form. He is also present to Jacob, even to an embrace, in human guise; He joins hands, exerts Himself with limbs, bends at the sides, and appears in every one of our motions and movements. Yet later He is shown to Moses as fire. Run through the times and understand what manner of appearance He had to the others to whom He presented Himself in the form of human creation; He also entered into the ways of the Lord and works of God, namely for the knowledge of God and the advancement of our eternity. Even in all these cases, God, who is a consuming fire, is so present as created that He could consume the creation by the power with which He assumed it, being able again to abolish what had existed solely for the purpose of contemplation.” [Col. 1401C]

The same, book I (IV, 23): “‘And the Angel of the Lord said to Hagar: Multiplying, I will multiply your seed.’ And she called the name of God who spoke with her: ‘You are God who saw me’” (Gen. 16:13). “The Angel of God speaks; in the Angel of God there is a twofold signification: He who is, and He whose Angel He is.” Again (IV, 23): “First, the Angel of God; second, the Lord—for she called the name of the Lord who spoke with her; third, God: ‘For You are God who saw me.’ He who is called the Angel of God is the same Lord and God. But according to the prophet, the Son of God is the Angel of Great Counsel” (Isa. 9:6). “So that the distinction of the persons might be complete, He was called the Angel of God; for He who is God from God is Himself the Angel of God. But that due honor might be rendered, He is proclaimed both God and Lord.” Again (IV, 26): “The Angel began to speak to Hagar. The confession of the hearer teaches that He is both Lord and God. Thus He who is an angel by the ministry of announcing the Great Counsel is Himself God both by nature and by name.”

Again: “With fuller advance [in teaching], the divine discourse proceeds. God [Col. 1402A] speaks to Abraham. Three men stand by him as he sits; he worships one and confesses Him as God. The same one whom he worshipped and confessed promises that at that same future time He will return and that Sarah will have a son. God spoke to Abraham. The same God later appears to him as a man and addresses him concerning the very events. Although he saw a man, Abraham nevertheless worshipped the Lord, recognizing the sacrament of the future embodiment.”

Ambrose, *On the Faith* (Orthodoxa, chap. 8, p. 431, Maurists): “If angels have often been seen in the form of human beings, and yet are not other than what they know themselves to be, nor change their substance when they assume the form of a human body, how much more is this true of the Lord Himself? Thus we acknowledge that the Son of the Lord was seen by the Fathers, not so that all that He is as God was seen in Him, [Col. 1402B] but so that, through an image, they might behold in Him the dispositions of future things which had to be fulfilled. For who could see the Son of God before He assumed, when it pleased Him, visible matter, or deigned to put on human nature? Even though He was seen by Abraham, He was seen in a human bodily form, in order to show that in the final times He would come in a human being. Jacob, however, is seen in one place in an angel, in another in a human being. He showed Himself in an angel in order to indicate that He was the messenger of the Great Counsel. But in the human being with whom He is described as having wrestled, He indicated the image of the future conflict which He would have with Israel when He came according to the flesh. But so that Israel might believe that He with whom he wrestled under the figure of a human being was Lord, he receives the name Israel—that is, ‘the human being seeing God’—though he had seen the human figure which the Son of God had assumed.

“He appeared to Moses in the bush in a flame of fire, in order to show light to believers and judgment to unbelievers. He went before the people of Israel as their guide on the journey, in a pillar of cloud by day and in a pillar of fire by night, in order to show the grace of baptism through the cloud and the gift of the Holy Spirit through the fire; for Paul wrote that the fathers were baptized in the cloud, and the Acts of the Apostles declare that the Spirit is fire. Finally, when Moses prayed that he might see the Lord’s face purely, He said: ‘You cannot see My face, for no human being shall see My face,’ etc.” (Exod. 33:20.) [Col. 1402C]

Augustine, book VIII of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis* (VIII, 49, Maurists): “If we ask in what manner God spoke, we must hold most certainly that God speaks either through His own substance or through a creature subject to Him; but He does not speak through His substance except in creating natures. To spiritual and intellectual natures, however, not only when creating but also when enlightening them, once they are able to receive His speech as it is in His Word—which in the beginning was the Word, etc. But when God speaks to those who cannot receive it, He speaks only through creation: either solely spiritual creation, in dreams or ecstasy and in a likeness of bodily things, or bodily creation, when either some appearance is presented to bodily senses or voices sound.”

Again: “Some heretics think that the substance of the Son of God is visible in itself without the assumption of any body, [Col. 1403A] and therefore that He Himself was seen by the Fathers before He assumed a body from the Virgin. This impiety must be driven far from Catholic minds.”

The same, *City of God*, book X (chap. 13): “Nor should it trouble us that, although He is invisible, He is remembered as having visibly appeared to the Fathers. For just as the sound by which a thought is heard is not the thought itself, so the appearance in which God was seen, who exists in an invisible nature, was not Himself. Nor were they ignorant that they saw the invisible God in a bodily appearance which was not Himself. For Moses spoke with the One who spoke to him, yet said to Him: ‘If I have found favor before You, show Yourself to me knowingly, that I may see You’” (Exod. 33:13).

The same, on John, Homily IV (Tractate III on John 1; Maurists III, p. 310): “‘No one has ever seen God.’ Moses saw an angel, a cloud, fire. All that creation bore the type of its Lord; it did not display the presence of the Lord Himself. For you have it plainly in the Law: ‘Moses spoke with the Lord face to face, as a friend with his friend.’ If you consult Scripture itself, you will find Moses saying: ‘If I have found favor in Your sight, show me Your face clearly, that I may see You.’ He received the answer: ‘You cannot see My face’” (Exod. 33:20). “An angel bearing the type of the Lord spoke with Moses, and all the things that were done there through the angel promised this future grace and truth. All the things seen bodily were not that substance of God; for those visible things were bodily made through creation, [Col. 1403C] in which a type might be shown; they certainly did not display the substance itself.”

The same, *On the Trinity*, book III, chap. XI: “It is evident that everything seen by the Fathers when God was presented to them was made through creation. Although we do not know how He effected these things through ministering angels, still we say that they were made through angels. [But someone says], ‘Why then is it written, “the Lord said,” rather than, “the angel said”?’ Because when a herald announces the words of a judge, the official record does not state, ‘That herald said it,’ but, ‘That judge said it.’” Again: “Before the incarnation of the Savior, when God was said to appear, those voices and bodily appearances were made through angels, who themselves spoke or acted something in the person of God.”

### XLII. That the Son alone formerly appeared in angels, and the contrary

[Col. 1403D]

Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, ch. X: Wherever in the Holy Scriptures an angel is put in place of the Lord, it is understood not of the Father, nor of the Holy Spirit, but of the Son alone, through the economy of the Incarnation.

Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book IV, ch. X: Concerning the angels in whom the Lord appeared and spoke. In the angels, certainly, were the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; and at one time the Father, at another the Son, at another the Holy Spirit, and sometimes God without any distinction of person, was represented through them.

The same, book II, ch. XI: When three men were seen by Abraham, and no one among them was said to be greater than the others either in form, age, or authority, why should we not understand here that the equality and the same substance of the Trinity were visibly indicated through a visible creature? [Col. 1404A]

The same, in the same book, ch. XVII: If Christ was shown in those voices which occurred in Exodus and in all those bodily manifestations—or Christ in one instance, the Holy Spirit in another, as the things we said above suggest—this does not establish that God the Father was never seen by the fathers in such a form. For many such visions occurred in those times, without the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit being clearly designated in them; so that it would be exceedingly rash to say that God the Father never appeared to the fathers through some visible form. For those persons arrived at this opinion [the printed reading is syntactically defective], who were unable to understand, in the unity of the Trinity, what was said: [Note: [Col. 1403D] Maurist ed.: “For those persons gave birth to this opinion.”] “But to the King of the ages,” etc., and, “Whom no human being has seen or can see” (1 Tim. 6:16). The divine substance is understood there, in which the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. But those visions were made through changeable creation, showing God not properly, as he is, but figuratively.

Yet I do not know how these people understand what appeared to Daniel: the Ancient of Days, from whom the Son of Man is understood to have received the kingdom—but, of course, from him who says to him, “You are my Son,” etc.; “Ask of me,” etc. (Ps. 2:7). If therefore both the Father, giving the kingdom, and the Son, receiving it, appeared to Daniel in bodily form, how do these people say that the Father was never seen by the prophets and therefore alone ought to be understood as invisible? It is therefore not unfittingly believed that God the Father too is accustomed to appear to mortals in that manner.

Unless perhaps someone should say that the Father is not visible because he appeared before one dreaming, while the Son and the Holy Spirit are visible because Moses saw all those things while awake. As though Moses saw the Word with bodily eyes, or as though a spirit, even a human one, could be seen—much less the Spirit of God! Or would anyone dare say that the Son and the Holy Spirit are visible even to those awake, but the Father only to those dreaming? Therefore no sound-minded person ought to affirm that the person of the Father has nowhere been shown to waking eyes through any bodily appearance. [Col. 1404C]

Likewise: What do they say of Abraham, to whom, while awake, after Scripture had prefaced the account by saying, “God appeared to Abraham,” not one or two but three men appeared—of whom none was said to have stood out above the others more highly, shone more honorably, or acted more authoritatively? [Col. 1404D]

### XLIII. That no created spirit is moved from place to place—and the contrary

Augustine, *On Genesis*, book VIII: God set the spiritual creature above the bodily: the spiritual can be changed only through time, whereas the bodily can be changed through time and place. The mind is moved through time, either by remembering what it had forgotten, or by learning what it did not know, or by willing what it had not willed; but a body is moved through places. [Col. 1405A]
