Likewise: Whoever tries to understand how the immutable God, himself moved neither through time nor through place, moves his creature temporally and locally, I do not think can attain it unless he first understands how the soul—that is, a created spirit—moved not through place but through time, moves the body through time and place.

Likewise: To whom does it not readily occur that what is not moved through place is not extended through the intervals of place? But whatever is extended through the intervals of place is a body. Hence it follows that the soul is not thought to be moved if it is believed not to be a body.

The same, on the words written, “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters”: Since by the name “waters” that formless matter is indicated, which was made from nothing and from which all things were to be made, what prevents us from understanding the Spirit of the Creator, who was borne over this matter not by degrees of place and intervals of space—which can by no means rightly be said of any incorporeal thing—but by superiority and the pre-eminence of dominion over all things, so that all things might be created? [Col. 1405B]

The same, in the book of Questions of Orosius addressed to him: A created spirit, such as that of angels, is rightly believed to be moved in time, because it carries out God’s commands in lower regions in time; but it moves its body locally when it descends from heaven and ascends.

Likewise: Therefore, according to the foregoing reasoning, a created spirit can be moved through time, not through place; the Creator Spirit without time and place; but a body through both place and time. [Col. 1405C]

Likewise: Living creatures and birds obey God within their kind, as he moves all things at suitable times, though he himself is not moved temporally. Thus he moves himself without time and place; he moves a created spirit temporally without place; he moves bodily creation temporally and locally.

Likewise, Orosius: What reason has made it so that God, whom you maintain is moved, is not moved in time?

Augustine: Because God is before times, nothing in him is past or future, and there is no new thought. For if it is new, it is accidental; but if anything happens to God, he is no longer immutable. If God is immutable, nothing happens to him, etc. [Col. 1405D]

Boethius, book III of the *Topics*: The soul neither increases nor diminishes, nor passes from one place to another.

The creed called the Apostles’ Creed: “He died and was buried; he descended into hell.”

Ambrose, *On the Faith*, addressed to the Emperor Gratian: A seraph passes from place to place, for it does not fill all things.

Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, ch. IX: Whoever perceives that the soul is moved by itself perceives that there is will within himself; yet this motion is not from place to place, like that of a body. For local motion belongs properly to bodies.

### XLIV. That God alone is incorporeal—and the contrary

Gennadius, bishop of Marseilles, *On the Orthodox Faith, or Ecclesiastical Dogmas* (chs. XI–XII, Elmenhorst ed.): Nothing incorporeal and invisible in nature is to be believed to exist except God alone. He is believed incorporeal because he is everywhere and fills and encompasses all things; and therefore he is invisible to all creatures, because he is incorporeal. Every creature is bodily; angels and all heavenly powers are bodily, although they do not subsist in flesh. We believe intellectual natures to be bodily because they are locally circumscribed, as is the human soul, enclosed by flesh, and demons, who are bodily by the substance of angelic nature. [Col. 1406A]

Gregory, book II of the *Morals*: The angelic nature is now distinguished from the condition of our nature in this respect: we are circumscribed both by place and by the constriction of blind ignorance; angelic spirits, however, are indeed circumscribed, but their knowledge is incomparably more extended than ours.

Likewise: Their knowledge is therefore greatly extended in comparison with ours, but narrow in comparison with divine knowledge. So also their spirits, compared with our bodies, are spirits; but compared with the supreme and uncircumscribed Spirit, they are bodies. [Col. 1406B]

Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, ch. XXII: God is not somewhere; for whatever is somewhere is contained by a place, and whatever is contained by a place is a body. But God is not a body; therefore he is not somewhere, and rather all things are in him—yet not in such a way that he himself is a place. For a place is in space, which is occupied by the length, breadth, and height of a body. Nevertheless, God’s temple is called a place only figuratively, not because he is contained by it, but because he is present to it.

Conference VII, called that of Abbot Serenus, ch. XIII: Although we declare that there are certain spiritual natures—such as angels, archangels, the other powers, and our own soul, or even this subtle air—nevertheless they are by no means to be reckoned incorporeal. They have within themselves a body by which they subsist, though much more tenuous than our bodies, according to the Apostle’s statement: “There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies”; and: “A natural body is sown; a spiritual body shall rise” (1 Cor. 15:40, 44). From these words it is manifestly concluded that nothing is incorporeal except God alone; and therefore he alone can penetrate all spiritual and intellectual substances, because he alone is wholly everywhere and in all things, so that he looks upon and searches through every hidden thing of the mind. [Col. 1406C–D]

Hilary, *On Matthew*, ch. V (Maurist ed., p. 632): “Is not the soul more than food,” etc., “and more than clothing?” There is nothing which is not bodily in its own substance and creation; and the elements of all things, whether in heaven or on earth, visible or invisible, have been formed. For the forms of souls, whether possessing bodies or exiled from bodies, receive a bodily substance of nature, because everything created must necessarily exist in something.

The same, on Psalm 129 (Maurist ed., p. 439): The inner human being was made rational, mobile, moving, swift, incorporeal, subtle, and eternal in the image of God. So far as lies in itself, it imitates the form of the governing nature: while it runs through things, while it flies about, it is now beyond Ocean, swifter than speech; now it flies up to heaven; now it is in the depths; now it surveys the East, now the West; while it is never annihilated so as not to exist. God’s nature is indeed in all things and does not depart from one place in order to be elsewhere. But the human mind, in this mobility of its perception, was made in the image of its Maker, while the perpetual mobility of the soul imitates God’s nature; it has in itself nothing bodily, nothing earthly, nothing heavy, nothing perishable. [Col. 1407A]

Augustine, *The City of God*, book XXII: Again, against what I said above, those who consider and discuss this order of elements in which they trust find absolutely nothing to say. For earth is first upward, water second, air third, heaven fourth, so that the nature of the soul is above all. Aristotle also called it a fifth body; Plato, no body at all. [Col. 1407B]

The same, in the book *Against the Letter of the Manichaean Foundation*: Concerning every incorporeal nature, even though mutable, such as the soul.

Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, book II, ch. XII: Some wrongly believe the human soul to be bodily. It was made in God’s image so that, though not immutable as God is, it might nevertheless be incorporeal as God is, like the angels.

Gregory, book IV of the *Dialogues*: If you have believed, on the satisfactory authority of sacred utterance, that the souls of saints are in heaven, you ought consistently to believe that the souls of the wicked are in hell.

Peter: And on what reasoning should one believe that a bodily fire can hold an incorporeal thing?

Gregory: If the incorporeal spirit of a living human being is held in a body, why should a spirit after death not also be held by bodily fire?

Peter: In any living being, the spirit is held in the body because it gives life to the body. [Note: [Col. 1407D] Maurist ed. IV, 28: “In a living being.”]

Gregory: If the spirit can be held in that which it gives life to, it can also be held there in punishment, where it is put to death. We say that a spirit is held by fire so that it is in the torment of fire by living and feeling. For it suffers fire precisely by seeing it, because, seeing itself burned, it is burned. Thus a bodily thing burns an incorporeal one, while an invisible burning and invisible pain are drawn from invisible fire.

Likewise: At the end, Truth will say to the reprobate: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil,” etc. If therefore the devil and his angels are incorporeal, they are nevertheless to be tortured by bodily fire. [Col. 1407D] What wonder, then, if souls, even before they receive bodies, can feel bodily torments?

Claudius Mamertus, addressed to the patrician Prefect, *On the State of the Soul*, book I, ch. XI: You append a certain chapter from a work of Saint Jerome, which you clearly have not understood, where he says: “We consider the globes of the stars to be embodied spirits.”

The same: Under the very name of Saint Jerome he adds: “If angels, even heavenly bodies, are said to be unclean in comparison with God, what do you think a human being should be considered?”

Likewise: Can it be thought that the learned Jerome said anything else here than that the bodies of angels surpass human bodies greatly in their capability and power? When he said alike, “if angels,” and added, “even heavenly bodies,” he intended two things to be understood: “angels and heavenly bodies.” For, although angels are embodied spirits, there are in heaven certain things which are bodies only. [Col. 1408A]

Likewise, ch. XIII: For we firmly hold on divine authority that the bodies of the saints which deserve to be changed will be made equal in glory to angelic bodies, as the Lord says: “And they shall be like angels in heaven.”

Likewise: Therefore angelic substance, like human substance, is twofold: possessing a body of the greatest agility and beauty, which appears when it is seen by human beings; and possessing an incorporeal part, by which it always sees God.

Likewise, ch. XIV: We ought to understand that a human being consists of a bodily and an incorporeal part; an angel consists of body and spirit, fashioned with dignity pre-eminent among the others. Its spirit is more powerful than every created spirit. Its body is more sublime than the most excellent of all elements, according to that prophetic passage where angelic substance is without doubt declared twofold: “You make your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4). But it is manifest that fire is not spirit. For this must not be understood allegorically, as in the passage where the Lord says, “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49), when he spoke of the Holy Spirit. For it is not permissible to believe that human souls are inflamed to divine love by participation in the Spirit, because the good by which a human being is good is the same good by which an angel is good, and by the same good each is blessed. [Col. 1408B–C]

### XLV. That God is not to be represented through bodily images—and the contrary

From the book of Deuteronomy (5:8): “You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, what is on earth below, or what is in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them.”

Likewise, from the same book (4:15): “The Lord spoke to us from the midst of the fire. You heard the sound of words, but saw absolutely no form; you saw no likeness on the day when the Lord spoke to you at Horeb from the midst of the fire, lest perhaps, deceived, you make for yourselves a carved image or likeness; lest perhaps, lifting up your eyes, you see the sun and moon and stars of heaven, and, deceived by error, worship and serve those things which God created for all nations as a mystery.” [Col. 1408D]

Likewise (27:14): “And the Levites shall proclaim and say to all the men of Israel in a loud voice: ‘Cursed is the man who makes a carved or molten image, an abomination to the Lord, the work of craftsmen’s hands, and sets it up in secret.’ And all the people shall answer and say, ‘Amen.’”

Origen, *Homilies on Exodus*, homily VII (de la Rue, p. 158): “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness,” etc. If anyone makes the appearance of something, he makes a likeness. But of an idol the Apostle says that “an idol is nothing in the world” (1 Cor. 8:4). He makes an idol who makes what does not exist. What is it that does not exist? An appearance which the eye has not seen, but which the mind itself invents—for example, if someone imagines two faces in one human figure, or attaches the hind parts of a horse or fish to a human breast. Whoever makes these and similar things makes what does not exist; it has nothing like itself.

“You shall not worship them or serve them.” Someone may at times worship unwillingly; but to serve is to devote oneself to such things with one’s whole affection and zeal. [Col. 1409A]

Augustine, on Psalm 113 (Maurist ed. IV, 1259), on the passage: “Lest perhaps the nations say: ‘Where is their God?’” etc. (Ps. 113:10): Because we worship the invisible God, known to no bodily eyes but to the most pure hearts of a few, the nations might seem able to say, “Where is their God?” because they themselves could show their gods.

Likewise: It would be far more honorable for you not to have something that you could show than for the blindness of your heart to be shown in what is displayed by you to these eyes. [Col. 1409B]

Likewise (p. 1260): Do not add human hands, so that from that metal which the true God made, a person may wish to make a false god—or rather, a false human being, whom you may worship as the true God. Whoever admitted him to friendship as a true human being would be insane. For the likeness of form and the imitation of the arrangement of limbs, by a certain weak affection, leads and carries off the weak hearts of mortals. But as you display each fashioned part, so display the functions of each part, by which the image and human vanity draw you. “For they have a mouth, and shall not speak,” etc. (Ps. 113:13). The craftsman, then, is already better, since he was able to fashion them with the movement and function of limbs. You too are better, although you did not make them, because you do what they cannot do. A beast is better too; for it is said of them: “They shall not cry out with their throats” (Ps. 113:15). [Col. 1409C]

Likewise: Certain beasts, such as monkeys, handle things with their hands.

Likewise: He made the reader or hearer attentive, so that he may find himself admonished that not only human beings but even beasts ought to be preferred to the images of the nations. Thus, if it is shameful to worship a beast which God made able to see, hear, etc., they may see how shameful it is to worship an image that is mute and lacks life and sensation.

Likewise: How much better, then, do mice and serpents and other creatures of that kind, so to speak, in some way judge concerning images: because they do not perceive human life in them, they do not care about their human form. Thus they often nest in them; and unless frightened away by human movements, they seek no dwellings more secure for themselves. A person therefore moves himself in order to drive a living beast away from his god; and he worships as powerful one that does not move itself, though he has driven away from it something better. For he has driven away one that sees from one that is blind, one that hears from one that is deaf, etc.; one that lives from one that is dead—indeed, from something worse than dead. For it is evident that a dead person once lived. Therefore even a dead person is superior to a god that neither lives nor ever lived. [Col. 1409D]

Likewise: Although, as they maintain, an image of limbs has been artfully made in some sign, once it begins to be worshipped and honored by a multitude, it produces something base in each person. An image invites such human affection.

Likewise: Therefore, lest anyone say, when images have been mocked, “I do not worship this visible thing, but the divinity which invisibly dwells there,” Scripture itself condemns those divinities in another psalm: “For the gods of the nations are demons” (Ps. 95:5). The Apostle also says, not that an idol is anything, but that what the nations sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons. [Col. 1410A]

But those seem to themselves to have a purer religion who say: “I worship neither an image nor a demon; rather, I behold the bodily likeness as a sign of that thing which I ought to worship.” Thus they interpret an image so as to say that by one image the earth is signified—whence they commonly call its temple that of Tellus; by another, the sea, as by Neptune’s image; by another, the air, as by Juno’s; by another, fire, as by Vulcan’s; by another, the morning star, as by Venus’s; etc. When they are again attacked because they worship bodies, especially earth, sea, air, and fire, whose use is readily available to us, they dare reply that they do not worship the bodies themselves, but the divinities presiding over their governance. “They served the creature rather than the Creator.” For in the first part of this statement he condemned images; in the latter, the interpretations of images. By calling the figures made by a craftsman with the names of things made by God, they exchange the truth of God for a lie; and by regarding and venerating the things themselves as gods, they serve the creature. [Col. 1410B–C]

But who worships or prays while looking at an image without being affected in such a way that he thinks himself heard by it and hopes to receive from it what he desires?

Likewise: For in some manner that figure of limbs compels the living mind, immersed in the senses of the body, to think that the body which it sees as most like its own body is capable of sensation.

Likewise: But we have many implements and vessels of such material for use in celebrating the sacraments. And surely these implements are what else but works of human hands? Yet do they have mouths and not speak? Do they have eyes and not see? Do we pray to them because through them we pray to God? The chief cause of mad impiety is that, in the affections of the wretched, a form resembling a living thing—which makes them pray to it—has more force than the evident fact that it is not living and therefore ought to be despised by one who lives. Images have greater force to bend down the unhappy soul because they have eyes, ears, nostrils, hands, and feet, than they have to correct it because they do not speak, do not see, etc. [Col. 1410C–D]

Thus it follows that this too comes to pass: “Let all who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113:8). Let such people therefore see, with eyes open and sentient, and worship with minds closed and dead images which neither see nor live. “But the house of Israel trusted in the Lord” (Ps. 113:9). “For hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees?” (Rom. 8:24). [Col. 1411A]

Likewise, in book IV of *The City of God*, ch. XXXI, speaking of Varro, he says: This same most acute author also says that only those seem to him to have perceived what God was who believed him to be the soul governing the world by motion and reason. And thereby—even though he did not yet grasp what truth possesses, namely that the true God is not a soul but also the creator of the soul—he nevertheless confessed and commended the worship of one God.

Likewise: He also says that the ancient Romans worshipped gods without images for more than one hundred and seventy years. “If this had remained,” he says, “the gods would be observed more purely.” Among other things, he calls even the Jewish nation as a witness to this opinion, and does not hesitate to conclude the passage by saying that those who first set up images of gods for peoples both removed fear from their cities and added error, wisely judging that gods could easily be despised in the stupidity of images. But because he did not say that they “handed down error,” but that they “added” it, he clearly wishes it to be understood that error already existed even without images. Therefore, when he says that only those perceived what God was who believed him to be a soul governing the world, and when he judges religion to be observed more purely without images, who does not see how nearly he approached the truth? [Col. 1411B]

Saint Epiphanius, in the letter to John of Constantinople translated by Blessed Jerome (Petavius, 2:317): I heard certain people murmuring against me when we were travelling together to the holy place called Bethel. Having come to the village called Anablatha, I saw, as I passed, a lamp burning; and, having asked what place it was, I learned that it was a church. I entered to pray and found there a curtain hanging in the doors of that church, dyed and painted, bearing an image as it were of Christ or of some saint. When therefore I saw in Christ’s church an image of a human being hanging contrary to the authority of the Scriptures, I tore it down and rather advised the guardians of that place to wrap a poor dead man in it and carry him out. But they murmured against me and said: “If he wished to tear it, it was right that he should give another curtain and thus replace it.” When I heard this, I promised that I would give one and send it. Now I have sent what I was able to find, and I ask you to see that the presbyters of that place receive from the bearer the curtain sent by us, and thereafter to order that curtains of this kind, which conflict with our religion, not be hung in Christ’s church. [Col. 1411C–D]

From the second collection of Abbot Isaac: It is not surprising that a most simple man, never fully instructed concerning the nature of divinity, should through the fault of rusticity and the habit of ancient error still be held fast and persist in his former error. For, according to the custom of that error by which they worshipped demons fashioned with human form, they now also think that the incomprehensible and ineffable majesty of the true Godhead is to be worshipped by means of some depicted outline. They believe that they possess or hold nothing unless, while engaged in supplication, they have before them some image which they continually address and carry in their mind, keeping it always fixed before their eyes. [Col. 1412A]

From the Council of Elvira, ch. XXXVI: It has seemed good that pictures ought not to be made in churches, lest that which is worshipped and adored be painted on walls.

Gregory, to Secundinus, servant of God and recluse (to Serenus, XI.13; Maurist ed. II, 1100): For it is one thing to worship a picture, another to learn from the history represented in a picture what should be worshipped. For what writing provides for those who can read, a picture provides for the unlearned who look at it, because in it they see what they ought to follow; in it those who do not know letters read. [Col. 1412B]

Likewise: Therefore it ought not to have been broken, since it had been placed in churches not for worship but solely for instructing the minds of the ignorant.

(*Act* IV of the Seventh Synod of Nicaea, 787): John, apocrisiarius of the eastern sees, said: The statement of our father Sophronius signifies that it is better for one who has sworn to commit perjury than to keep an oath concerning the destruction of sacred images. We say this because some excuse themselves by appealing to an oath.

Leo IX, to Michael the Patriarch (Mansi XIX, 649): Remember that abominable synod which our heresiarchs wished to call the Seventh, by whose conspiracy the venerable images of our Lord Jesus Christ himself and of the saints were either handed over to flames or submerged in waters, while paintings were erased from the walls of basilicas. Although the authority of the Roman pontiffs resisted them, above all that of the most holy Pope Nicholas, who through his legates closed the church of Saint Sophia, both on account of the sacred images and on account of the deposition of Ignatius and the installation of Photius, until it submitted to the decrees of the Apostolic See. [Col. 1412C]

### XLVI. That angels were made before heaven and earth, or before all other creatures; or that all angels were created equal and blessed—and the contrary
Ambrose, in the *Hexaemeron*, on the first day: “In the beginning,” he says, “God made,” etc. The world was made and began to be what it had not been; but the Word of God was in the beginning and always was. Yet angels also—dominions and powers—although they began at some time, nevertheless existed when this world was made. For all things, visible and invisible, were created and established.

Jerome, to Paula and Eustochium, in the letter on Titus [Martianay IV, 411]: “Before eternal ages.” Six years of our world are being completed; and how many earlier eternities, how many times, how many beginnings of ages, must we suppose to have existed, in which angels and thrones, dominions, and the other powers served God and, at God’s command, subsisted without the changes and measures of times.

Isidore, in the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*: Before every creature the angels were made, etc.

Augustine, *City of God* XI.9: It is not plainly read in what order the angels were created. But they are represented either under the name of heaven, where it is said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” or rather under that light of which I speak. Likewise: It does not seem to me an unreasonable opinion that, when the first light was made, the angels are to be understood to have been created; and that the distinction between holy angels and unclean ones was made where it is said: “And God divided between the light and the darkness.”

The same, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chapter IV (III Maur. 3, Appendix, p. 43): First heaven and earth were made, then light, which in function is day. Likewise: By the earth, which he says was made after heaven, he does not mean earth alone, but signifies matter—that is, all lower things—which developed into every form of the world. But heaven is not this fleshly heaven, but that higher, spiritual one [Col. 1413B], made in the beginning, so that, when he says heaven was made first, he may signify that all invisible things were created. For he embraces the highest and lowest of all nature, so that whatever lies between may beyond doubt be believed to have been made.

The same, on Genesis: “Let there be light, and there was light”—that is, the angelic and heavenly substance, from among which was created the one spirit called Lucifer, wiser and more eminent than all the others, as Job (40:14) says of him: “He is the beginning of the ways of God,” that is, of His actions or works.

The same, in the book of Orosius’s *Questions to Augustine*: The first day itself is the angelic nature, which was first called by the name of heaven. Likewise: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” that is, in the Son, all spiritual and bodily nature. Likewise: What He called heaven seems to me to be the dark abyss of waters: life in some sense previously drifting about, unless it turns toward its Creator. “And let there be light”: let it contemplate God. Likewise: “He divided the light from the darkness”; for He divided good and evil angels, calling the evil darkness and the good light.

Jerome, on Ezekiel (28:13): “You were in the delights of the paradise of God,” for which the Hebrew has *Eden*. *Eden* is translated “delights”; by this expression he shows that the passage concerns not a human being, of whom it is written, but an opposing power which once dwelt in God’s paradise. Likewise: “Gold was the work of your adornment”; the Septuagint: “You filled your treasuries with gold.” This indicates that his thought was open to divine mysteries and that he gathered spiritual riches for himself, concerning which the Lord commands [Col. 1413D]: “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven,” etc. This is the hidden treasure of which He speaks as “treasure hidden in a field.”

Gregory, in the *Morals*: “He is the beginning of the ways of God.” When God created created things, He made this one first, and made him more eminent than the remaining angels. The Jews understood this first in the Law and the Prophets, speaking of Beelzebub, prince of demons.

The same, in the homily on angels beginning “The summertime” (Maur. I, 1604): Without doubt there are nine orders of angels. Hence the angel himself who was created first is told through the prophet: “You, the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty, were in the delights of paradise.” Here it should be observed that he is said not to have been made in God’s likeness, but to be “the seal of likeness,” so that, because his nature is more subtle, the image of God may be indicated in him as expressed more sublimely. Immediately afterward it is added: “Every precious stone was your covering: sardius, topaz,” etc. (Ezek. 28:13). Behold, he names nine stones, because indeed there are nine orders of angels. This first angel was adorned and made perfect with those orders for this reason: because, while he was set over all the ranks of angels, he was brighter by comparison with them.

From the book of Orosius’s *Questions to Augustine* (Maur. VI, Appendix, p. 10):

Orosius: Were all angels created equal or unequal? And if equal, why did not all remain firm and stable? If unequal, by what merit did some deserve to receive foreknowledge of their own stability?

Augustine: All angels indeed were created equal; but when those fell through pride, the others adhered to the Lord in devout obedience, receiving certain knowledge of their own stability, which the fallen ones never had.

The same, *City of God* XII.11: Before they sinned, they shared in that wisdom and were equal to the good angels. How then shall we speak? For if they had been equal in it, they too would have remained equally blessed in its eternity, because they were created equally. Therefore, if truly and perfectly blessed life is not blessed except when it is perfect, theirs was not such a life, since it was at some time to cease, and therefore was not eternal—whether they knew this or did not know it. For if they knew it, fear did not allow them to be blessed; if they did not, error did not allow them to be blessed.

The same, XII.6: The cause of the angels’ blessedness is that they turned away from Him who supremely is toward themselves, who are not supreme. For pride is the beginning of every sin (Sir. 10:15). Likewise: The cause of the blessedness of the former is that they adhered to God; the cause of the misery of the latter is not adhering to God.

The same, *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 10: Certain angels, whose prince is called the devil, became deserters from God through free choice. The rest, however, stood in the truth through free choice. Likewise: Although the devil and his angels were blessed before they fell and did not know that they would fall into misery, something still remained to be added to their blessedness: namely, that, through the great abundance of the brightness of God given by the Holy Spirit, they might henceforth be wholly unable to fall, and might know this of themselves with complete certainty [Col. 1414D]. Likewise: But because they did not know their future misery, they enjoyed a lesser, yet still faultless, blessedness. For if they had known of their future fall and eternal punishment, they certainly could not have been blessed, since fear of so great an evil would already then have compelled them to be miserable. Likewise: In the same way He made man with free choice; and, though ignorant of his own fall, he was nevertheless blessed because he felt it lay in his own power neither to die nor to become miserable.

Saint Philip the priest, a hearer of Jerome, on Job (4:18): “Behold, those who serve Him are not stable, and in His angels He finds perversity.” This is indeed said concerning the devil, who was once a holy angel.

Ambrose Autpert, on the Apocalypse (12:10), book VI [Col. 1415A]: “The accuser of our brethren fell,” etc. These words are understood not to have been spoken of his first ruin. For, if, as is true, the angel was created on the first day and man on the sixth, and the apostate, as the Lord asserts, “did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44), then accordingly he fell immediately when he was created, etc.

### XLVII. That the angel fell before the creation of man, and the contrary

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, chapter X (Arev. 6, 136): The devil fell from heaven before man was created. For as soon as he was made, he burst forth into pride and was cast down from heaven. For according to the testimony of Truth, he was a liar from the beginning, because he did not stand in the truth [Col. 1415B].

Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, XI, chapter 16, concerning the devil: Some say that he was cast down from the highest heavens because he envied man, who was made in the image of God. But envy follows pride. Since, therefore, pride is love of one’s own excellence, while envy is hatred of another’s happiness, it is quite evident what arises from what. For in loving his own excellence, anyone envies either equals because they are clearly equal to him, or inferiors lest they become equal to him, or superiors because he is not equal to them. Thus one is envious through being proud; no one is proud through being envious. And rightly Scripture defines pride as the beginning of every sin. This accords with the Apostle’s statement that covetousness is the root of all evils, if we understand avarice in a general sense [Col. 1415C], by which each person desires more than he ought.

Likewise: Scripture does not say when pride cast down the devil; nevertheless reason shows that it happened before man was made, and that for this reason he envied man. For it is plain that pride does not arise from envy, but envy from pride. Nor is it without reason that the devil may be thought to have fallen at the beginning of time, and that there was no time before this in which he lived peacefully with the holy angels; but that he apostatized from the very origin of creation. Thus we may understand both statements as “from the beginning” when the Lord says: “He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44). Therefore he was a murderer from the beginning, because he killed the first man.

Likewise, XI, chapter 23: The view that he never stood in the truth, never lived a blessed life with the angels, but fell from the beginning of his creation, must not be understood as though he were not corrupted by his own will but created evil; otherwise he would not be said to have fallen from the beginning. Rather, immediately upon being made, swollen with pride and corrupted by love of his own power, he turned himself from the light of truth. Thus he did not taste the sweetness of blessed and angelic life. Accordingly, he could not have foreknown his own fall; and he fell not from what he had received, but from what he would have received had he been willing to submit to God.

The same, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*: The devil foresaw that man was made for his accusation.

The same, chapter III (Maur. III, Appendix, p. 42): And lest we seem to have omitted why the world was made, we say that the devil, by apostasy, drew many angels with him into transgression, while he wished by impious presumption to secure a kingdom for himself. Lucifer, who rose in the morning and appeared brighter than the rest, was like a prince of many, among whom he was more brilliant; with their fellowship he descended to the impious contest. For, seeing beneath himself many spiritual powers, since he was pre-eminent in the paradise of God through knowledge of the heavenly mystery, he was puffed up with arrogance and wished to be called God.

Eugippius, from Augustine’s statements in Book XI of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, concerning the devil: Some say that he fell because he envied man. But envy follows pride. Envy is not the cause of pride; pride is the cause of envy [Col. 1416B]. For whoever loves his own excellence envies either his equals because they are equal to him, or his superiors. Thus a person is envious through being proud; by being envious, a person is proud. Pride is the beginning of every sin, to which the Apostle’s saying is suited: “Avarice is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10), if we understand general avarice, by which everyone desires more than is fitting for the sake of his own excellence. But spiritual avarice is what is commonly called the love of money; by this term, the Apostle, indicating the genus through the species, intended general avarice to be understood when he said: “The root of all evils,” etc.

Cyprian, to Emistrianus [Note: [Col. 1415D] Pamel. edition: *On Jealousy and Envy*, p. 324]: The devil could not patiently endure man’s creation in God’s image; hence he was the first to perish and the first to cause loss. Let us see whence jealousy began, and when and how. Likewise: At the very beginnings of the world the devil was the first both to perish and to cause loss. Supported by angelic majesty, acceptable and dear to God, after he beheld man made in God’s image, he burst into jealousy through malicious envy. He did not first cast down another [Note: [Col. 1416D] Pamel.: “another.”] by jealousy before he himself had first been cast down by jealousy. While envy spurred him to rob man of the grace of blessed immortality, he too lost what he had formerly been. What an evil, by which an angel fell!

Jerome, on the Epistle to the Ephesians: “Our struggle is not against flesh,” etc. (Eph. 6:12). Spiritual weapons must be taken up against spiritual enemies, against whom our struggle is in heavenly things—that is, through the promise of heavenly rewards [Col. 1416D]. It was not, as some suppose, before the earth was founded and all things in it were created that they sinned; rather, after they saw man held in such honor and glory before God, they were drawn by jealousy and began to exercise hostile enmity against man. Thus it is read in the Book of Wisdom (2:24): “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world”; and the Lord says in the Gospel: “He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth.”

John, bishop, in a certain sermon on the beheading of Saint John, beginning: “Alas for me, what shall I do? Woman, the devil’s weapon!” Through a woman he cut off John’s head. And what shall I say of human beings? Through a woman he cast angels down from heaven; through a woman he prostrates and subjugates all things [Col. 1417A].

### XLVIII. That good or holy angels, enjoying the vision of God, know all things, and the contrary

From the book of Orosius’s *Questions to Augustine* (Maur. VI, Appendix, p. 12):

Orosius: You maintain that the first day is a spiritual creature; how, then, did it have evening and morning?

Augustine: Every creature, before it was made in its own time, first existed in the Word of God to be known by angels, and thus to be made in its own time. Therefore the creature’s knowledge of itself was evening; its knowledge in God was morning, because the creature itself is seen more fully in the Lord than in itself. Hence he says: “What was made, in Him was life” (John 1:4) [Col. 1417B]. In God all things are life. All the principles or ideas of creatures live in the Lord without beginning and unchangeably. Accordingly, holy angels see them more fully in the Word of God, where they are life, than in themselves, because angelic knowledge, by comparison with God, is in some sense evening. Thus, in the knowledge of the firmament, the second day; in knowledge of the division of sea and land, the third; in knowledge of sun, moon, and stars, the fourth; in knowledge of creeping things and birds, the fifth; in knowledge of beasts of burden, wild animals, and man himself, the sixth. For the knowledge was not made six times in the one day which we understand to be the nature of spiritual creatures, that is, angels. He made six days because of the perfection of the number six.

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, chapter X: Angels know all things in the Word of God before they come to exist in reality.

Gregory, *Dialogues*, IV, chapter 33 (Maur. II, 425), concerning the spirits of saints: Since there all behold God in a shared brightness, what is there that they do not know there, where they know Him who knows all things?

The same, in the homily on angels beginning “The summertime” (Maur. I, 1604): Those higher ranks are called Cherubim because they are filled with a more perfect knowledge insofar as they contemplate the brightness of God more nearly. (Maur. I, 1608): Thus in that highest city certain spiritual things belong severally to individuals, so that they are not common to all; and what each possesses partially in his own order, another order possesses wholly. Yet they are not all generally designated by one and the same title, because that order ought to be called by the particular name of the thing which it has received more fully as its gift. Thus we have said that Seraphim are “burning,” and yet all burn together in love of their Creator. Cherubim, however, signify fullness of knowledge; yet who there fails to know anything, where they all see the Lord Himself, the fountain of knowledge?

The same, in the homily on the rich man and Lazarus: Those who see the brightness of their Creator cannot fail to see anything that is done in creation.

The same, *Morals*, V (Maur. I, 39): Since angelic spirits contemplate the very fountain of knowledge, what among things that must be known do they not know, who know Him that knows all things? Likewise: Their knowledge, therefore, is very extensive in comparison with ours [Col. 1418A], but narrow in comparison with divine knowledge.

The same, IV, chapter 29: That angels are administered by the powers of higher angels is testified by the prophet Zechariah, who says: “Behold, the angel who spoke in me went out, and another angel went out to meet him and said to him: Run, speak to this young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls” (Zech. 2:3). For unless higher powers ordered the lesser ones even in the offices of holy spirits, the angel would in no way have learned from an angel what he was to say to a human being.

Jerome, on Psalm 23, concerning the words “Who is this King of glory?”: This is also understood as said in the voice of angels, as though they themselves asked: “Who is this King of glory?”—the One to whom the prophet commands the heavens to open so that His humanity may ascend. “For we,” they say, “always see the Father and Son together.” It is not absurd if some angels, who do not possess fullness of knowledge, did not know the mystery of the Incarnation. Therefore, they were astonished at Christ’s humanity seated above them at the Father’s right hand, as though asking among themselves: “Who is this King of glory?”

The same, in the Christmas sermon beginning “Today the true sun has risen for the world”: O day brighter than every sun of the age! O time more glorious than all ages! What angels awaited, what Cherubim, Seraphim, and the ministries of heaven did not know, has been revealed in our time. What they saw through a mirror and an image, we behold in truth.

Ambrose, *On the Mysteries*, chapter VII: Even angels doubted when Christ rose; the powers of heaven doubted when they saw flesh ascending into heaven. Thus they said: “Who is this King of glory?” And when some said, “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter,” others doubted, saying: “Who is this King of glory?” In Isaiah also you have the powers of heaven asking in doubt: “Who is this who comes up from Edom, the redness of His garments from Bozrah, beautiful in a white robe?” (Isa. 63:1).

The same, *On the Faith*, to Emperor Gratian, IV, chapter 1: What wonder if human beings could not comprehend the mystery of God through the wisdom of the world, when even angels could not know it except by revelation? For who could follow Jesus by opinion rather than faith: now penetrating the lower world from heaven, now rising from the lower world to heavenly things; suddenly emptied, so as to dwell in us, yet never diminished, though the Son was always in the Father and the Father in the Son? The very forerunner doubted concerning Him, albeit under the type of the synagogue. Thus, after sending disciples, he asks: “Are you He who is to come?” (Matt. 11:3). Angels too were astonished at the heavenly mystery. Hence, when the Lord rose and the stars could not bear Him rising from the lower world, the heavenly beings were uncertain in their apprehension. Seeing the Lord coming in triumph from death, angels command the princes to lift up the gates, saying in amazement: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and the King of glory shall enter” [Col. 1419A]. Yet there were still heavenly beings who were astonished and marvelled at the new pageant, the new glory, and therefore asked: “Who is this King of glory?” But because angels have stages of knowledge and capacity for progress, they certainly possess discernment of power and wisdom. God alone is without progression, because He is eternally always in every perfection. Others spoke—namely, those who had been present at the resurrection, those who had seen or already recognized Him: “The Lord strong in battle.” Again the multitude of angels sang before Him in triumphal procession: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter.” Again others, astonished, said: “Who is this King of glory? We see Him with neither form nor beauty. If He is not that one, who is this King of glory?” Those who knew answered: “The Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory.”

The same, on Luke, Book I: And why do we speak of human beings, when we read even concerning the heavenly powers and authorities themselves that no one has ever seen God? And he added: “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, is above the heavenly powers; He has declared Him” (John 1:18). Therefore no one has ever seen God, because no mind or eyes comprehend the fullness of divinity dwelling in God. Likewise: Indeed, not even all the apostles saw Christ; hence He says: “Have I been with you so long, and you still have not known me?” (John 14:9).

The same, *On the Faith*, to Gratian: It is impossible for me to know the secret of the generation. It is above powers, above angels, above Cherubim, above Seraphim, above every understanding. Likewise: Even angels could not comprehend the mystery of the Father.

Augustine, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*: Cherubim and Seraphim do not fully comprehend what God is, because no one knows the Father except the Son.

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, I, chapter III: However much human nature after the resurrection advances toward equality with angels and rises untiringly to contemplate God, it nevertheless cannot fully see His essence, which even angelic perfection itself cannot wholly attain in knowledge. This accords with the Apostle, who says: “The peace of God, which surpasses every understanding” (Phil. 4:7)—understand: even that of angels. For the Trinity alone is wholly known to itself, and the humanity assumed by Christ, which is the third person in the Trinity [Col. 1419D]. God’s essence may be known insofar as it is believed to exist. But His work and judgments are wholly known by no one. They cannot be penetrated by either angelic or human understanding. They need only be reverenced and feared, not examined or investigated, according to the Apostle, who says: “For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Rom. 11:34).

Haymo, on the Epistle to the Ephesians: “That the manifold wisdom of God may be made known through the Church to the principalities and powers in heavenly places” (Eph. 3:10). Therefore, in order that this manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in heaven—whom blessed Jerome understands to be angelic powers dwelling in heaven—the Son of God, coming into the world, revealed it to the apostles. And through the Church—that is, while the apostles preached in the Church—He made it known to angelic powers [Col. 1420A]. For blessed Jerome says that there were certain angelic ranks which did not clearly understand the mysteries mentioned above until Christ’s Passion had been accomplished and the apostles began through their preaching to draw Gentiles of every nation to faith. This may be proved by the angels’ wondering words when He ascended into heaven: “Who is this who comes from Edom?” (Isa. 63:1), that is, from the bloody and blood-stained world. Or in the Psalm: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23:8). For those of greater dignity, through whom these things were announced, knew them as counsellors and messengers; but to those of lesser power they may have been partly unknown.

Likewise (Eph. 4:10): “And He who ascended above all heavens,” that is, spirits, “that He might fill all things,” that is, the oracles of the Law and Prophets, or also heavenly and earthly things, with the knowledge and revelation of His divinity. Heavenly things were filled because certain angelic powers did not clearly know the mystery of Christ’s birth, Passion, resurrection, and ascension until these things had been accomplished. Hence it is said in astonishment in the Psalm: “Who is this King of glory?”

### XLIX. That all orders of heavenly spirits are generally called angels, and the contrary

Gregory, in Homily XXXIV on angels: The woman had ten drachmas because there are nine orders of angels [Col. 1420C]. But in order that the number of the elect might be completed, man was created as the tenth. Likewise: We have said that there are nine orders of angels because, as sacred Scripture testifies, we know that there are angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominions, thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim. Likewise: When thrones are joined with principalities, powers, virtues, and dominions, there are five orders. When angels, Cherubim, and Seraphim are added to these, there are beyond doubt nine orders of angels. Likewise: Behold, we have named nine stones because indeed there are nine orders of angels. Likewise: In the Greek language, *angeloi* means “messengers,” while archangels are called “messengers of the highest God.” Likewise: The word “angel” is a name of office, not of nature [Col. 1420D]. For those holy spirits of the heavenly homeland are indeed always spirits, but they cannot always be called angels, because they are angels only when something is announced through them. Thus the Psalmist says: “He makes His angels spirits” (Ps. 103:4). It is as though he plainly said: “He who always has them as spirits makes them angels when He wills.” Those who announce lesser things are called angels; those who announce supreme things are called archangels. Thus it was not just any angel but the archangel Gabriel who was sent to the Virgin Mary.

Likewise: The ancient and venerable Father Dionysius the Areopagite is reported to say that members of the lower ranks of angels are sent out, visibly or invisibly, to perform ministry; namely, that angels or archangels come to provide help to human beings. But the higher ranks never depart from the inner presence, because those that are pre-eminent have no role in external ministry. This seems contrary to what Isaiah says (6:6): “One of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal, which he had taken from the altar with tongs, and he touched my mouth.” But in this saying of the prophet it is meant that those spirits who are sent receive the names of those whose office they perform. For the angel who carries a coal from the altar to burn away sins of speech is called a Seraph, because *seraphim* means “burning.” This understanding is not inappropriately supported also by what Daniel says (7:10) [Col. 1421B]: “Thousands of thousands ministered to Him, and ten thousand times one hundred thousand stood before Him,” etc. For it is one thing to minister and another to stand before. Those who go out to us with messages minister to God; those who so enjoy inward contemplation that they are not sent forth to perform external works stand before Him.

But since we have learned in some places of Scripture that certain things are done through Cherubim and others through Seraphim, whether they do these things themselves or they are done through subordinate ranks—which, as is said, take the names of the greater ones when they come from them—we do not wish to affirm what we do not prove by clear testimonies. Yet we know this with complete certainty: one spirit sends another to perform heavenly ministry, as the prophet Zechariah testifies (2:3), saying: “Behold, the angel who spoke in me went out, and another angel went out to meet him,” etc. Likewise: The lesser ones are sent, but the greater send. Yet concerning even those ranks which are sent, we hold this certain: when they come to us, they so perform ministry outwardly that they nevertheless are never absent inwardly from contemplation.

Haymo, on the Epistle to the Hebrews: As Didymus the Greek says in the book *On the Holy Spirit*: From all orders of angels some are sent.

### L. That no one advances in heavenly life, and the contrary

Augustine, on John, Sermon XXIX: To the homeland above, where no one dies because no one is born, where no one now advances and no one declines.

Ambrose, *On the Faith*, to Emperor Gratian: There were still in heaven those who were astonished and marvelled at the new pageant, the new glory; and therefore they asked: “Who is this King of glory?” But because angels too have stages of knowledge, God alone being without progression, others spoke—those, namely, who had been present at the resurrection and had seen: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:8). Again a multitude of angels sang before Him in triumphal procession: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter.” Again others, astonished, said: “Who is this King of glory? We see Him without form or beauty. If He is not that one, who is this King of glory?” Those who knew answered: “The Lord of hosts, He is the King of glory” (ibid., 10). Likewise: How shall we ascend to heaven? There powers are stationed and princes appointed, who guard the gates of heaven and question the one ascending. Likewise: The everlasting gates are Peter, John, and James. Likewise: Great is the mystery of Christ, at which angels too were astonished.

Jerome, to Pammachius and Marcellinus against his accuser concerning his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians (1:20): I shall briefly set down the second passage in which Paul says: “Making Him sit at His right hand in heavenly places, above every principality and power and virtue and dominion and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the future.” After a manifold exposition, when I had come to the offices of God’s ministers and spoken of principalities, powers, and dominions, I added this also: “It is necessary that they have subjects who fear and serve them, and those who are strengthened by their power.” These distributions of offices will exist not only at present but also in the future age, so that through individual advances and honors, ascents and descents, someone may either increase or decrease and come to be under one power, virtue, principality, and dominion after another [Col. 1422C]. And after the example of an earthly king and a full description of a palace, by which I showed the diverse offices of God’s ministers, I added: “And do we suppose that God, the Lord of lords, is content with merely a simple ministry? Just as someone is not called an archangel unless he is first among angels, so principalities, powers, and dominions are not called such unless they have subjects and lower ranks.” But if he thinks that I follow Origen because I set forth advances and honors, ascents and descents, increases and diminutions in my exposition, let him know that it is very different to say that angels, Cherubim, and Seraphim become demons and human beings, as Origen affirms.

Augustine, on Psalm 85: “You have helped me and comforted me.” Blessed Cyprian was saddened in his Passion; now he is comforted in his crown. Now, though comforted, he is still sorrowful. For the Lord Jesus still intercedes for us; all the martyrs who are with Him intercede. Their intercessions will not cease until our groaning has ceased. When it has ceased, we shall be in the city of the living. Who groans there? Paul says in the Epistle to the Romans (8:22): “For we know that the whole creation groans and labors in birth together until now.”

### LI. That the first parents were created mortal, and the contrary
Augustine, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*, ch. 21: God made man so that, as long as he did not sin, he would flourish in immortality, and would himself be the author either of life or of death for himself: by keeping himself from sin, he would rejoice through his own effort that he was immortal; but, if negligent, he would himself impute to himself the fact that he had begun to be mortal. For as long as he remained in the law of the Creator [Col. 1423A], he was worthy to eat from the tree of life, so that he could not die. For the body was not of such a kind that it appeared impossible for it to be dissolved; rather, the taste of the tree of life restrained the body's corruption. Indeed, even after sin it could have remained indissoluble, had he only been permitted to eat of the tree of life. For how did he possess an immortal body when it was sustained by food? One who was immortal would not need food or drink. But the tree of life, in the manner of a medicine, prevented every corruption.

The same, *City of God*, book XIII: Nor will the body which we now bear be even such as it was in the first human beings before sin, who would not have died unless they had sinned. Yet human beings used food, while they bore bodies not yet spiritual but still other, earthly bodies [Col. 1423B], etc.

The same, *On the Baptism of Infants*, book I: Although Adam was earth according to the body, and bore the animal body in which he was created, nevertheless, had he not sinned, he would have been changed into a spiritual body and would have passed, without the risk of death, into that incorruption which is promised to the faithful and holy.

Likewise: Therefore, had Adam not sinned, he was not to be stripped of his body, but clothed over with immortality and incorruption, so that what was mortal might be swallowed up by life—that is, that he might pass from animal to spiritual. Nor was there any need to fear that, if he lived here longer in an animal body, he would be burdened by old age and, growing old, would arrive at death. For if God granted to the Israelites’ garments and shoes that they were not worn out through so many years, what wonder if [Col. 1423C] the same power were granted to the obedient man: that, while possessing an animal—that is, mortal—body, he would have in it a certain condition by which he could be aged without deterioration, until at the time God willed he should pass from mortality to immortality without death? For just as this very flesh which we now have is not therefore invulnerable because it need not be wounded, so that body was not therefore non-mortal because it need not die. I think that such a condition, while still in an animal and mortal body, had already been granted also to those who were translated hence without death. Nor have Enoch and Elijah withered in old age through so long a time. Nor do I think that they have already been changed into that spiritual quality of body [Col. 1423D] which is promised in the resurrection, and which first went before in the Lord—unless perhaps they do not need even those foods that restore by being consumed, but since their translation live so as to have a satiety like that which Elijah had during the forty days in which he lived without food from a cup of water and a cake of bread; or, if they need these supports, perhaps they are fed in paradise as Adam was before he deserved, because of sin, to be driven out from there. For he had, as I judge, refreshment from the fruits of the trees against exhaustion, and from the tree of life stability against aging.

The same, *On Genesis* (Maur. III, 210): That body before sin could be called both mortal [Col. 1424A] for one reason and immortal for another: mortal because it could die; immortal because it could avoid dying. For it is one thing not to be able to die, another to be able not to die.

Likewise: The first human being was created immortal by what was granted him from the tree of life, not from the condition of his nature. Separated from that tree, he could die; had he not sinned, he could have avoided dying. Therefore he was mortal by the condition of his animal body, immortal by God’s benefit. For it was certainly animal—and therefore mortal, since it could die—although also immortal, since it could avoid dying. For only that which cannot die at all will be immortal: namely, the spiritual body promised to us in the resurrection.

Gregory, replying to Augustine, bishop of the English: When our first parents [Col. 1424B] first sinned in paradise, by God’s just judgment they lost the immortality which they had received.

Bede, *On Luke*: “They also strip him,” that is, they take away the garments (Luke 10:30) of spiritual grace, immortality, and innocence.

Likewise: “Leaving him half-dead,” because they can strip him of immortality, but cannot destroy his faculty of reason.

## LII. That Adam was created outside paradise, and the contrary

Genesis (2:8): “Now the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning, in which he placed the man whom he had formed.”

Likewise [Note: Perhaps it intended to indicate Augustine’s book *On Genesis*, Col. 1423D]: “Therefore the Lord God took the man and placed him in the paradise of delight.” From the statement that the human being is said to have been placed in paradise, it is understood that he was not created there, but [Col. 1424C] on this mortal earth of ours, because divine foreknowledge knew that he would sin and that on this account he would be driven from another, holy land into this vale of misery.

[The same], *On the Words of the Lord*, in a sermon: “Let not your heart be troubled” (John 14:28). By that authority by which he formed Adam in paradise, he fashioned for himself flesh from the substance of Mary herself; assuming it for our salvation, he was born God and man.

## LIII. That Adam’s sin was greater [Note: Cous.: “great.”], and the contrary

Ambrose, *On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans* (5:12): “Therefore, as through one man sin,” etc. Because Adam and Eve are one, because Adam’s woman sinned.

Likewise: “In whom,” that is, in Adam, all sinned. [Col. 1424D] He therefore said “in whom,” though speaking of the woman, because he referred not to the particular individual but to the kind.

In the likeness of Adam’s transgression, Terah, Abraham’s father, and Nahor and Laban had their own gods. Adam’s sin is not far from idolatry. For he transgressed, thinking that he would become a human god; he judged that what the devil suggested would benefit him more than what God commanded, setting the devil in God’s place. Hence he was also made subject to the devil.

Augustine, *Enchiridion*, ch. 45: Although in that sin which entered into the world through one human being and passed into all human beings, for which reason even infants are baptized, [Col. 1425A] many sins can be understood, if that one sin itself is divided, as it were, into its individual members. For there is pride in it, because man preferred to be under his own power rather than God’s; sacrilege, because he did not believe God; murder, because he hurled himself into death; spiritual fornication, because the integrity of the human mind was corrupted by the serpent’s persuasion; theft, because prohibited food was appropriated; greed, because he desired more than ought to have sufficed; and whatever else may be found in this one act when carefully considered.

Likewise, ch. 46: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Ps. 50:7). He did not say here “in iniquity” or “in sin,” though this too could rightly have been said; rather, he preferred to say “iniquities” and “sins.” For in that one sin which passed into all human beings, and which was so great that human nature was changed and transformed in it, there are found, as I explained above, very many sins [Col. 1425B].

Jerome, to a virgin consecrated to God: Adam deserved greater indulgence, since he was still new and was not held back by the example of anyone who had sinned before him and was dying because of his own sin. But for you, if after so many warnings—after the Law, after the Prophets, after the Gospels, after the Apostles—you should wish to abandon them, I do not know how pardon could be granted you.

## LIV. That the first human sin did not begin from the devil’s persuasion, and the contrary

Augustine, *On Genesis*: One must not suppose that the tempter would have cast down the human being, unless there had first preceded [Col. 1425C] in the human soul a certain self-exaltation to be repressed by the humiliation of sin—an exaltation by which he falsely presumed something of himself.

The same, on Psalm 118: The Apostle understood the universal greed which is the root of all evils. For the first human beings themselves would not have been deceived and cast down through the serpent, unless they had wished to have more than they had received. For he had promised them: “You shall be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). Therefore they were overthrown by this *pleonexia*—this grasping desire for more.

Jerome, *On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*: “Therefore, as through one man.” If sin entered the world through one human being, Eve, those who say that sin was in the world before the devil deceived Eve are mad.

## LV. That Eve alone was deceived, not Adam, and the contrary

[Col. 1425D]

Augustine, *On Genesis*: The Apostle says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived” (1 Tim. 2:14). For when questioned, he did not say, “The woman deceived me,” but, “She herself gave me from the tree.” But she said: “The serpent deceived me.” Thus Solomon: should we believe that, in the worship of idols, he believed there to be any benefit in it? Rather, he could not resist his love for women, doing what he knew ought not to be done, lest he grieve his pleasures. So too Adam, after the deceived woman had eaten and given to him, did not wish to grieve her. He was overcome not by fleshly desire, which he had not yet experienced, but by a kind of friendly [Col. 1426A] goodwill, through which God is often offended lest one become an enemy to a friend. The just outcome of the divine sentence showed that he ought not to have done this. Therefore he too was deceived in another way; but I do not think that he could in any way have been deceived by that serpentine guile by which the woman was deceived. The Apostle called this specifically “deception”: when what was being urged, though false, was thought true—namely, that God had forbidden them to touch that tree because he knew that, if they touched it, they would become like gods, as though he begrudged them divinity.

Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, on the fifth day: Adam was deceived through Eve, not Eve through Adam. It is fitting that the woman who called him to guilt should take him as her ruler, lest he fall again through feminine fickleness [Col. 1426B].

Paschasius, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, ch. 12: Divine wisdom likewise brought her forth from his side, so that from the source whence the woman who deceived the first Adam was created, the Church might be formed.

From Chrysostom’s sermon 40: Finally, the consenting woman became toward her husband such as she had found the serpent’s malice toward herself: she was so persuaded, and persuaded; infected, and infected; deceived, and deceived.

Augustine, *On the Singularity of Clerics*: We wonder that Adam was deceived through Eve, though no examples of mortals had preceded him.

## LVI. That by sinning man lost free choice, and the contrary

Augustine, *Enchiridion* (VI, 207): For by using free choice badly, the human being destroyed himself. Just as one who kills himself kills himself while living, and cannot raise himself again, so, when sin was committed by free choice, free choice itself was lost once sin had conquered. For whoever has been conquered by another has become that person’s slave. What freedom can a slave have, except when he delights in sinning? For one serves freely who willingly does his master’s will. Accordingly, one who is a slave to sin is free for sinning.

The same, *On Rebuke and Grace*: We must confess that we have free choice both for doing good and for doing evil. But in doing evil, each person is free from righteousness and a slave of sin.

The same, *On Grace and Free Choice*: The will in us is always free, but it is not always good. It is either free from righteousness, when it serves sin, and then it is bad; or free from sin, when it serves righteousness, and then it is good [Col. 1426D]. But God’s grace is always good, and through it [Note: Mon.: “this.”] a person whose will was formerly bad comes to have a good will.

Likewise: A human being did not receive grace so as to lose his own will. Yet, lest the will itself be thought able to do anything good without God’s grace, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me”—that is, not I alone; and for [Note: Cous.: “because of.”] this reason neither God’s grace alone nor he alone.

## LVII. That Adam was buried at Calvary, and the contrary

Ambrose, to Horontianus (ep. V, 19): This daughter, the Church, raising herself to higher things by good counsels, Christ received at Golgotha [Col. 1427A], where Adam’s tomb was, so that upon his cross he might raise that dead man. Therefore, where in Adam was the death of all, there in Christ was resurrection again.

Jerome, to Marcella, *On Holy Places*, praising the city of Jerusalem (Martian. IV, 547): In this city—indeed, at this very spot—Adam is said both to have lived and to have died. Hence too the place where the Lord was crucified is called Calvary: namely, because the skull of the ancient man is said to have been buried there, so that the second Adam, and Christ’s blood trickling down, might wash away the sins of the first Adam and the progenitor lying there, and then the Apostle’s saying might be fulfilled: “Awake, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14).

The same, in the book *On Places and Names*: In our codices “Arboc” is written corruptly, whereas in Hebrew it is read *arbe*, that is, “four,” because there the three patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are buried, and great Adam, as is written in the book of Joshua—although some suppose that he was buried at Calvary. This Hebron was once the metropolis of the Philistines [Col. 1427B].

Isidore, *On the Life and Death of the Holy Fathers*: On Adam: Cast out from paradise, he inhabited earth bristling with thorns. Having lost immortality, he returned to dust. He was buried at Arbe, that is, Hebron, a city which was the metropolis of the Philistines [Note: Arevalo ed., V, 154: “At the place Arbee, that is, four, etc. But this place is not far from Hebron, the metropolitan city of the Philistines.”].

Likewise: In the field of Ephron, in the double cave, in the inner part of which Adam was buried, while Abraham was buried in the outer part. This place, as Josephus teaches, is seven stadia from the city of Hebron [Col. 1427C].

## LVIII. That Adam was saved, and the contrary

From the Book of Wisdom [9:19]: “By wisdom all who pleased you, Lord, from the beginning were healed. She guarded him who was first made by God, the father of the world, when he alone had been created; and she brought him out of his sin, and gave him power to govern all things.”

Augustine, in a letter to Evodius, on Peter’s words in which he asserts that Christ loosed the pains of hell: Who, then, except an unbeliever, would deny that Christ was among the dead?

Likewise: Why did he wish to come where there were pains? Because, as it is written, he was “free among the dead” (Ps. 87:6), where the prince of death found nothing that was due to punishment.

Likewise: [Col. 1427D] And indeed almost the whole Church agrees that he loosed that first man there; and it ought to be believed that she has not believed this in vain, from whatever source it has been handed down. Yet that which is written in the Book of Wisdom (10:1), “She guarded him who was first made, the father of the world, when he alone was created, and brought him out of his sin,” seems to make still more for this view.

Likewise, *On the Baptism of Infants*, book II, concerning Adam and Eve: Thus those first human beings, though afterwards living righteously, are nevertheless believed by merit to have been freed by the Lord’s blood from eternal punishment [Col. 1428A]. Adam was the first of human beings to sin; Abel the first to live righteously.

Hilary, on Psalm 14: Finally, Adam, having confessed, was preserved for pardon and glorified in Christ.

Gregory, to Eulogius bishop of Alexandria and Anastasius of Antioch: We say that the first human being died in soul on the day he sinned; yet Adam afterwards returned to life through repentance.

Augustine, *On the Singularity of Clerics*: But I tell you, it will be more tolerable for Adam on the day of judgment than for you.

## LIX. That Mary doubted the promised conception [Note: Cous.: “the promised Holy Spirit.”], and the contrary

Bede, *On Luke* (1:34): “How shall this be, since I do not know a man?” How, he says, can it happen that I should conceive and bear a son, I who have resolved to complete my life in the chastity of virginity? Yet she does not ask, as though disbelieving the angel’s words, how these things can be fulfilled; rather, certain that what she then heard from the angel—and had previously read as foretold by the prophet—must be fulfilled, she asks in what order it is to be accomplished. For the prophet who foretold that this would happen did not say how it could happen, but reserved that statement for the angel [Col. 1428B].

Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Law*, ch. 80: To Mary, who was uncertain about the possibility of conception, the angel proclaims: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1:35): do not doubt this because you know no man, since the Holy Spirit will work so that you may conceive without a man.

## LX. That the Word of God assumed soul and flesh simultaneously in the Virgin’s womb [Note: Cous.: “holy.”], and the contrary

[Col. 1428C]

Augustine, to the bishops in Ireland: Flesh was not first conceived in the Virgin’s womb and divinity came into the flesh later; rather, immediately the Word, with the power of his own nature preserved, became flesh and was made perfect man, truly possessing flesh and a rational soul. Hence he is said to be anointed above his fellows (Heb. 1:9), namely by the gift of the Holy Spirit. For this very act—of being conceived of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin’s flesh—was to be anointed by the Holy Spirit.

Likewise: There he was anointed by the same Spirit by whom he was conceived; he was not first conceived and later anointed, but this very act—of being conceived of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin’s flesh—was to be anointed by the Holy Spirit [Col. 1428D].

Augustine, *On the Secret of Christ’s Incarnation*: Forgive, Christ, and spare my mouth, because I, a rash narrator, touch upon the mystery of your incarnation.

Likewise: In the Virgin’s womb there was generative blood and seminal fluid. The Word mingled himself with this blood or fluid as if coagulated with it, and from the substance of the blood or fluid made flesh concealed within. The Holy Spirit came and, by giving life, formed what had been kneaded together by the Word’s bond; he differentiated what had been formed.

The same, in the book *Questions on the Old Testament*, ch. 23: Moses handed down (Exod. 21:22): If [Col. 1429A] anyone strikes a pregnant woman and causes an abortion, if it has been formed, he shall give life for life; but if it is unformed, he shall be fined money—so as to prove that a soul is not present before formation.

Likewise: If we look more closely, we shall see what we ought to follow. Let us consider Adam’s making. In Adam an example was given, so that it may be understood from him that the body receives the soul once formed. For God could have mixed the soul with the mud of the earth and thus formed the body. But it was formed in this order because first the house had to be put together and then its inhabitant introduced. Certainly the soul, being spirit, cannot dwell in a dry place; therefore it is borne in the blood. When the bodily features have not been joined together, where will the soul be?

Jerome, to Algasia (IV, p. 193): Seeds are gradually formed in the womb, and it is not counted homicide until the confused elements receive their proper forms and limbs [Col. 1429B].

## LXI. That Joseph suspected Mary of adultery [Note: Cous.: “did not suspect”], and the contrary

From Origen’s homily on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity. “But Joseph her husband,” he says, “being a just man and unwilling to expose her, wished to dismiss her secretly” (Matt. 1:19). He did not wish to expose her, did not wish to receive her, did not wish to defame her, but wished secretly to dismiss her. “While he thought these things,” he says (ibid., 20). We must ask what he thought. He thought of dismissing her. If he suspected her, [Col. 1429C] how was he just? If he did not suspect her or think anything of the sort, why did he wish to dismiss one who was immaculate and holy? For this would have been unjust. But hear the straightforward sense of this statement: he wished to dismiss her because he recognized in her the power of a mystery and some magnificent sacrament, and thought himself unworthy to draw near it. Therefore, humbling himself before so great and ineffable a reality, he sought to withdraw far away—as blessed Peter, humbling himself before the Lord, said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5:8); or as the centurion, sending to the same Lord, said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. 8:8); or as holy Elizabeth said to blessed Mary: “And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43). So Joseph too, humbling himself rightly in every respect, was careful and feared to bring upon himself a union with such holiness [Col. 1429D]. Therefore he wished secretly to dismiss her, saying: “Her dignity is greater; her holiness surpasses all; it does not suit my unworthiness.”
