Jerome, *On Matthew*: “But Joseph her husband, being just and unwilling to expose her,” etc. This is testimony to Mary: Joseph, knowing her chastity and wondering at what had happened, concealed in silence that whose mystery he did not know.

From a sermon on the Nativity beginning, “The most chaste womb of the Virgin Mary”: Hear, brothers, hear Mary speaking with you—absent in body, present in spirit! Joseph, my husband and betrothed, did not know that my God had loved me, and thought that my womb had been made pregnant by adultery.

Likewise: Joseph, a just man, was troubled because he found Mary—whom he had received from the temple and had not known—to be pregnant; and long inwardly agitated and debating, he said: “Shall I expose her or remain silent? If I keep silent while aware of evil, I assign myself a share with adulterers” [Col. 1430A].

Augustine, in a sermon on the words of the Gospel, “If your brother sins against you,” etc.: Observe how the just Joseph spared with such kindness so great an offence as he had suspected in his wife. Yet he knew that he had not approached her. Therefore a certain suspicion of adultery remained; and yet, because he alone had perceived it, and because he did not wish to disclose her, he wished secretly to dismiss her.

The same, *Enchiridion*, ch. 15: And Joseph, when he did not wish to dismiss her, suspected her of adultery, knowing that she was pregnant not by him, etc.

The same, in a letter to Macedonius: Thus Joseph, to whom the mother of the Lord had been betrothed, when he discovered that she was pregnant, though he knew that he had not had intercourse with her and therefore believed her to be nothing other than an adulteress, nevertheless did not wish her to be punished, nor was he an approver of the offence. For this intention of his too is reckoned as righteousness. For it is written of him: “Being just and unwilling to disclose her, he resolved to dismiss her secretly”; while he thought these things, an angel appeared to him [Col. 1430B].

Ambrose, *On Luke*, ch. 5: Holy Matthew fittingly taught what a just man ought to do when he discovers the disgrace of his wife: he ought to keep himself free from bloodshed and chaste from adultery. For one who is joined to a prostitute is one body.

## LXII. That Christ was born while the Virgin’s womb remained closed, and the contrary

The creed of the Council of Ephesus: He underwent our birth from the womb, coming forth as man from a woman, without casting off what he was.

Likewise: He undergoes bodily birth from the womb.

Bede, *On Luke*: When it says “opening the womb,” it speaks according to the customary manner of birth; not that the Lord, in departing, is to be believed to have violated the dwelling-place of the sacred womb which he had sanctified on entering it, but that, according to Catholic faith, [Col. 1430D] he came forth from the closed womb of the Virgin like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber.

Augustine, *On the Secret Incarnation of the Lord*: Christ, although you left the womb closed, you nevertheless permitted us to open your Gospel to unbelievers.

In the *Enchiridion*, ch. 34: If her integrity had been corrupted even in giving birth to him, he would no longer have been born of a Virgin.

From a homily of Pope Gregory on the octave of Easter: That body of the Lord entered to the disciples while the doors were closed, which came forth before human eyes at his birth from the closed womb of the Virgin. What wonder, then, if after his resurrection, when now to live forever, he entered through closed doors, when, coming to die, he left the Virgin’s womb without opening it [Col. 1431A]?

Jerome, to Pammachius: Christ is a virgin; the mother of our Virgin is a perpetual Virgin. This is the eastern gate in Ezekiel, always closed. Let them answer me how Christ entered while the doors were closed, and I shall answer how she is a virgin after childbirth, a mother before marriage.

The same, in his second *Dialogue against the Pelagian*: The statement, “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exod. 13:2), refers more to the Savior’s special birth than to that of all human beings. For Christ alone opened the closed doors of the virginal womb, which nevertheless remained continually closed. This is the closed eastern gate, through which the high priest alone enters and goes out; nonetheless, it always remains closed.

The same, to Eustochium: The Son of God, for your salvation, O human beings, became the son of man; he waits ten months to be born; he endures nausea; he comes forth bloody.

Pope Hormisdas, to Emperor Justin: So that he who had previously been the Son of God might become the son of man and be born in the manner of a human being, opening his mother’s womb in being born, yet not dissolving his mother’s virginity by his power [Col. 1431B].

Anastasius, to a bishop: Gabriel is sent to Mary not as a virgin only temporarily, but as a betrothed virgin.

Likewise: The fact that Scripture mentions birth and says, “She wrapped the child,” and, “Blessed are the breasts which he sucked,” and, “A sacrifice was offered because the one who was born opened the womb”—these, however, were signs belonging to a woman giving birth.

Ambrose, *On Luke* (2:23): “Because every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord.” In the words of the Law, the Virgin’s offspring was foretold [Col. 1431C]—and truly holy, because immaculate. “What shall be born of you shall be called holy, the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). For if we follow the letter, how is every male holy? Will every male be sanctified? But he is holy through whom the prescriptions of the Law marked out a figure of the mystery to come [Note: Nearly all editions: “whom in the figure of what was to come,” etc.; Maurists: “through whom [they marked] the figure,” etc.], because he alone opened the generative secret of the Virgin, the holy Church, of immaculate fruitfulness for the begetting of God’s people. Thus he alone opened the womb for himself.

Likewise: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you” (Jer. 1:5). Therefore he who sanctified another’s womb is he who opened his mother’s womb so that he might come forth immaculate.

## LXIII. That Christ according to the flesh was of the tribe of Judah [Note: Cous.: “was not of the tribe,” etc.], and the contrary

[Col. 1431D]

Paul, in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, of which tribe Moses said nothing concerning priests.”

Origen, *Homilies on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*, homily 1: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3). How does Christ appear to descend from David’s seed according to the flesh, when it is agreed that he was not born of Joseph, while the genealogy of generations descending from David is traced to Joseph? Although it is troublesome to meet these objections according to the literal account, our people answer [Col. 1432A] that Mary, who was betrothed to Joseph, was undoubtedly joined according to the Law to a man of her own tribe and kin. And although the angel says to her, “Elizabeth, your kinswoman, shall also bear a son in her old age” (Luke 1:36), while Elizabeth is said to be from Aaron’s daughters, our people maintain that the name of kinship may be applied not only to members of the same tribe but to all who are of Israel’s race, just as the same Apostle says of all together: “Who are my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Rom. 9:3). These and similar answers are given.

But these matters seem to us to be understood rather according to a spiritual or allegorical sense, in which it causes no difficulty even that Joseph is called Christ’s father. Matthew also reports (1:8) [Col. 1432B] that Joram begot Uzziah. Yet in Fourth Kings it is written that Joram begot Ahaziah; Uzziah, Joash; Joash, Amaziah; Amaziah, Azariah himself, who is sometimes called Uzziah; and Azariah, Jotham.

Likewise: The explanation of this matter is certain: it is established not according to history, but according to spiritual understanding, which we need not pursue now.

Likewise: It is sufficient for us to answer those who object that, just as Jesus is called the son of Joseph and Uzziah is said to have been begotten by Joram, though he was not begotten by him, so Christ may be understood to be from David’s seed according to the flesh. Whatever explanation they advance regarding Joram and Joseph, let us say the same concerning David.

Jerome, *On the Epistle to the Hebrews* (7:11): “What further need was there [Col. 1432C] for another priest to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not according to Aaron,” etc. Wishing to show that Melchizedek’s genealogy derived not from the line of Shem, from whom Abraham came, but from Ham, whose later posterity Scripture does not record, the Apostle says that he is without father, without mother—that is, without a recorded genealogy—and that neither the beginning nor end of his life is written down.

Likewise: The Apostle does this in order to show that he who was not from the generation of the Hebrews blessed the patriarch, and that he was a likeness of Christ, who was not from the tribe of Levi—that is, the priestly tribe—but from Judah.

Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 23, ch. 7: Lord and God according to divinity, he is himself David’s son, from David’s seed according to the flesh. If it did not benefit us to believe this, the Apostle would not so earnestly commend it to Timothy (2 Tim. 2:8), saying: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, of David’s seed, according to my Gospel.” He solemnly warned the faithful: whoever should preach another gospel contrary to this Gospel, let him be anathema (Gal. 1:9) [Col. 1432D].

Likewise: He carries the line of descent not as far as Mary, but as far as Joseph—first, because Joseph was her husband, and the male person ought more to be honoured because of the male sex. For the fact that he had not joined her sexually did not make him not her husband, since Matthew himself relates that the angel called Mary the wife of Joseph [Col. 1433A].

Likewise: We ought to consider that Joseph, Mary’s husband, could have been called her husband while having her as his wife not by sexual intercourse but by affection, which is more precious. Therefore the husband of the virgin mother of Christ ought not to have been separated from the lineage of Christ’s parents; and Mary herself must have drawn some vein of blood from David’s stock, so that the flesh begotten for Christ even from the Virgin could not be without David’s seed.

Likewise: What remains except that Mary too was not alien to David’s kinship?

Likewise: Whoever says that Mary did not belong to David’s blood-kindred plainly struggles against the exceptionally weighty authority of Scripture.

## LXIV. That God did not assume a human person, but a nature, and the contrary

[Col. 1433B]

Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*: “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14), so that, although the Word is not naturally what flesh is—because the reality of two natures remains in Christ—nevertheless, according to one person, the same Word was made flesh from the very beginning of maternal conception. For God the Word did not assume the person of a human being, but human nature.

Boethius, *Against Eutyches and Nestorius* (ch. 4): Let this at least [Note: Cous.: “again.”] stand: as we have said before, nature and person differ, because nature is the specific property of any substance, while person is an individual subsistence of a rational nature.

Ambrose, *On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans*: “A servant of Jesus Christ”: he used both terms, “Jesus Christ,” so as to signify the person of God and man, because he is Lord in both.

Likewise: Whenever Scripture says either Jesus or Christ, it sometimes signifies the person of God, sometimes the person of man [Col. 1433C].

Augustine, book II *Against the Manicheans*: He left the Father when he said, “I came forth from the Father” (John 16:28); when appearing to human beings, the Word was made flesh. This does not signify a change in God’s nature, but the assumption of an inferior person—that is, a human one.

## LXV. That the Son of God was changed in assuming flesh, and the contrary

Jerome, on Psalm 76: “This is the change of the right hand of the Most High”: unless his right hand—that is, his Son—was changed and received a human body [Note: Cous.: “his.”], we cannot receive mercy. Though he was established in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.

Augustine, *On the Nature of the Supreme Good*: Corruptible natures are not immutable because they were made from nothing.

Likewise: For every change causes a thing not to be what [Note: Cous.: “who.”] it was; therefore he truly is who is immutable.

Likewise: True immortality is that supreme immutability which God alone possesses [Col. 1434A].

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, ch. 1 (Arevalo ed., VI, p. 116): What is God’s immortality except his immutability? For angels and souls are immortal, but they are not immutable. God alone is called immortal, because he alone is immutable. For a soul dies when, God abandoning it, it changes from good to evil; so too an angel dies when, God abandoning it, he falls. Whatever has matter from which it exists is mutable, because it passes from the unformed to form; but what has no matter is immutable, as God is.

## LXVI. That God and man appear to be parts in Christ, and the contrary
Athanasius: For just as a rational soul and flesh [Col. 1434B] are one human being, so God and man are one Christ; one, however, not by a confusion of substance but by unity of person. [Note: [Col. 1434D] In Cousin, the words “one, however, … person” are absent.]

Jerome on Psalm 2: The voice of Christ: “But I have been established king by him” is spoken with reference to the flesh. The same, on Psalm 23: “Who is this King of glory?”—the voice of the angels who had always been with the Father, as though they were saying: “We always see the Father and the Son together; who is this King of glory?”

Augustine, in the book of Prosper’s Sentences: This is what we say, and what we strive by every means to establish: that the sacrifice of the Church is made up of two things and consists of two things—the visible species of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body. So too the person of Christ consists [Col. 1434C] and is made up of God and man, since Christ himself is true God and true man, and contains in himself all those things—the nature and reality of those things—of which he is made up. Therefore there is the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body.

The same, in the book *Questions of Orosius Addressed to Him*: Just as soul and flesh are one human being, so the Word and man are one Christ. We acknowledge two substances in the one Son of God, divinity and humanity, not two persons. If we were to say that there are two persons, there would no longer be a Trinity but a quaternity.

The same, *On the Trinity*, book IV: Thus it came about that there is there not only the Word of God and human flesh, but also a rational human soul; and this whole is called both God on account of God and man on account of man. If this is difficult to understand, let the mind be purified by faith. [Col. 1434D]

The same, *On the Predestination of the Saints*: This is that ineffable and singular assumption of a human being by God the Word, so that the Son of God and the son of man might at once, truly and properly, be called the son of man because of the man assumed, and the Son of God because of the God who assumes; lest a quaternity rather than a Trinity be believed.

The same, in the letter to Volusianus on Christ’s incarnation: Just as, in the unity of person, the soul makes use of the body so that there may be a human being, so, in the unity of person, God makes use of man so that there may be Christ. Therefore, in that person there is a mixture of soul and body; in this person there is a mixture of God and man. Thus the person of a human being is a mixture [Col. 1435A] of soul and body, but the person of Christ is a mixture of God and man. For when the Word of God is joined to a soul having a body, he assumed both soul and body together. The former occurs daily in the procreation of human beings; the latter occurred once for the liberation of human beings. Yet the union of two incorporeal things ought more readily to have been believed than that of one corporeal and another incorporeal thing; and consequently the union of the Word of God and the soul ought to be more credible than that of soul and body. Therefore the Word of God, in a manner altogether different from that in which he is present to [Note: [Col. 1435D] Cousin: “in that in which.”] other creatures, assumed a human being and made himself and that human being one Jesus Christ.

Remigius on Psalm 34: “And my prayer into my bosom,” etc. For we know that Christ consists in two substances and from two substances, [Col. 1435B] namely, divine and human. [Note: [Col. 1435D] This passage is absent from Mon.]

Augustine against Maximinus (VIII, p. 698): No division into parts occurs in the Trinity of the Godhead. Christ is one person of double substance; nevertheless God cannot be called a part of this person. Otherwise the Son of God, before assuming the form of a servant, was not whole, and grew when man was added to his divinity. But if this is absurdly said of one person, since Christ cannot be a part of that thing, how much more can any one among the three not be a part of the Trinity? Therefore, in the Trinity, which is God, the Father is God, the Son also is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; and these three together are one God. Nor is one a third part of this Trinity, nor are two a greater part there than one; nor are all greater than each singly, because this greatness is spiritual, [Col. 1435C] not bodily.

The same, on John, Homily 45: By resemblance Christ is many things which he is not by strict property. By resemblance he is rock, door, cornerstone, lamb, shepherd, lion, and other things too numerous to list. But if you examine the proper characteristics of the things which you are accustomed to see, he is neither rock nor door, etc.

The same (III, pt. 2, p. 610): “I lay down my soul,” he says. Who lays it down? What does he lay down? What is Christ? The Word and man; yet not man in the sense of flesh alone, but [Note: [Col. 1435D] Cousin: “as though he were flesh alone,” etc.] because a human being consists of flesh and soul, and the whole human being is in Christ. For he would not have assumed the inferior part and abandoned the better. [Note: [Col. 1435D] Cousin: “assumed and abandoned.”] The better part of a human being is the soul [Col. 1435D] rather than the body. Since, then, the whole human being is in Christ, what is Christ? The Word, I say, and man. What are Word and man? Word, soul, and flesh. Hold fast, therefore, that certain heretics held this opinion too. The Apollinarian heretics dared to teach dogmatically that Christ is [only] Word and flesh, and they maintain that he did not possess a human soul. Who lays down the soul and takes it up again? Is it Christ insofar as he is the Word, who lays down and takes up the soul? Or insofar as he is a human soul, does the soul itself lay itself down and [Col. 1436A] take itself up? Or insofar as he is flesh, does flesh [Note: [Col. 1435D] Cousin omits the word “flesh.”] lay down and take up the soul? If we say that the Word of God laid down the soul and took it up again, we must fear that it may be said: therefore that soul was at some time separated [Note: [Col. 1436D] Cousin: “restored.”] from the Word, and at some time that Word, after assuming the soul, existed without a soul.

The same: What did the passion accomplish, what did death accomplish, except to separate the body from the soul? It did not, however, separate the soul from the Word. The Lord died; beyond doubt his flesh expired. For a time the soul left the flesh; but I do not say that the soul was separated from the Word. He said to the thief’s soul: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Did he not abandon the thief’s soul, yet abandon his own? Far be it! Rather, he possessed his own inseparably. Just as Christ laid down his soul, [Col. 1436B] so we too must lay down our souls for the brethren. To lay down the soul is to die; thus Peter [Note: [Col. 1436D] Cousin: “to Peter.”] also said: “I will lay down my soul for you” (John 13:37), that is, “I will die for you.” Attribute this to the flesh: the flesh lays down the soul and takes it up again. “And, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit” (John 19:30): this is to lay down the soul. The flesh gave it up, sent it forth, expired. Hence “to expire” is to become outside the spirit, just as “to be exiled” is to become outside one’s soil, and “to go astray” is to become outside one’s course. If, therefore, the flesh laid down the soul, how did Christ lay down the soul? For flesh is not Christ. Indeed, flesh is Christ, soul is Christ, and Word is Christ; yet these three are not three Christs but one Christ. For just as one human being is soul and body, so one Christ is Word and man. See [Col. 1436C] what I have said and understand: soul and body are two things, but one human being; Word and man are two things, but one Christ. Ask concerning a human being: Where is he? Where is the apostle Paul now? If someone answers, “At rest with Christ,” he speaks truly; if someone says, “At Rome in the tomb,” he too speaks truly. For the former is understood of his soul, the latter of his flesh. Yet we do not call them two apostles, one resting in the tomb and the other resting with the Lord.

The same, *On the Trinity*, book I: Because the form of God assumed the form of a servant, both are God and both are man; but both are God because of the God who assumes, and both [Note: [Col. 1436D] Cousin consistently writes “each” rather than “both” in this passage.] are man because of the man assumed.

The same (VIII, p. 767): He was crucified from the form of a servant, and yet the Lord [Col. 1436D] of glory was crucified. For such was that assumption as made God man and man God; but a careful reader understands what is said on account of what, and in what respect.

The same, book IV: Thus it came about that there is there not only the Word of God and human flesh, but also a rational human soul; and this whole is called both God on account of God and man on account of man. If this is difficult to understand, let the mind be purified by faith.

## LXVII. That Christ, or God, ought not to be called a creature [Note: [Col. 1437D] Cousin: “a creature or servant.”], and the contrary.

[Col. 1437A]

Bede, in a homily on the Nativity: “All things were made through him.” For if no creature was made without him, it is plainly evident that he himself is not a creature, through whom every creature was made.

Jerome, on the creed of the Council of Nicaea: Understand, therefore, that the true Lord cannot be a creature, nor can a creature save creatures, since Scripture says: “They worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever” (Rom. 1:25). You see, therefore, that this belongs rather to paganism than to Christianity.

Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book XII: For we know Christ the Lord not to be a creature, because [he is the one who created [Col. 1437B] all things, nor a made thing] [Note: [Col. 1437D] Mon.: “because he is not; nor a made thing because,” etc.], because he is Lord of all things made, but to be God, the proper generation of God the Father.

The same: This alone is our religion: to confess the Son not adopted but born, not chosen but begotten.

The same: Because Paul rebukes those who serve the creature.

The same: Human understanding rejects the notion that the Creator is a creature, because the creature exists through the Creator. For if he were a creature, he would be subject to corruption, liable to expectation, and subject to servitude. For the Apostle says: “For the far-reaching expectation of the creature awaits the revelation of the sons of God. For the creature was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope; because the creature itself also will be set free,” etc. (Rom. 8:19). If, therefore, [Col. 1437C] Christ is a creature, he must be uncertain under the hope of a far-reaching expectation; and his far-reaching expectation would be awaiting ours rather than we his; and, while waiting, he would be subjected to vanity, and through subjection by necessity he would be subjected unwillingly. But if he is subjected unwillingly, he must be a servant. And if he is a servant, he remains also in the corruption of nature. For the Apostle teaches that all these things are proper to a creature. O shameless and impious confession concerning God, to assign him, through the insult of calling him a creature, even to these humiliations: that he should hope, serve, be compelled, and be set free in us, not in himself!

The same above, book XI: God the Son, confessing God as his Father.

The same: Thus the dispensation of the holy sacrament [Col. 1437D] of birth made the Father also God of the assumed condition, while he who was in the form of God was found in the form of a servant.

The same: If, whereas before he was not by nature a servant, he afterwards began by nature to be what he had not been, no cause of lordship is to be understood other than that which gave rise to servitude. Thus you have the Lord by the dispensation of nature, when through the assumption of man he presented himself as a servant.

The same: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20:17). When Christ, a human being in the form of a servant, speaks these words to all human servants, there is no doubt [Col. 1438A] that the Father is his Father, as he is ours, in that respect in which he is man; and that the Father is his God, as he is God of all, in that nature in which he is a servant.

Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 13: We confess that he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary—certainly not of the former as of a father, but of the latter as of a mother.

The same, in the First Epistle of John: God came in the flesh in order to show us the hope of resurrection. This could not otherwise have happened unless he put on mortal flesh. For God could not die.

Ambrose, *On Faith to Gratian*, book I: It remains that this sacrilege too should be refuted, and that we should prove that the Son of God is not a creature. We have heard the Lord saying, “Preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16:15). He excepts none; and therefore where are those who call Christ [Col. 1438B] a creature? For if he were a creature, would he command the Gospel to be preached to himself? Christ is not a creature but Creator. For the creature was subjected to vanity, as the Apostle says (Rom. 8:20). Was Christ, then, subjected to vanity? Again, according to the same Apostle, the creature groans together (ibid., 22). Does Christ, then, groan—he who has delivered our groanings from death? “The creature,” he says, “shall be liberated from the bondage of corruption” (ibid., 21). We see, therefore, that there is a great distance between creature and God, because the creature is in servitude, whereas God is Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. Who introduced this error, to call him who created all things a creature? Did God create himself? If all things were made through him, [Col. 1438C] did he make himself? If it has been read that God made all things in wisdom, can it seem plausible that wisdom was made in itself [Note: [Col. 1438D] Edition: “by itself.”]?

The same: The Apostle called the Lord of majesty crucified; therefore the Son is both Son and Lord of majesty. Majesty is not subject to creatures. Therefore the Son is not a creature.

The same: The Son is the image of the Father’s substance; but every creature is unlike the higher substance, whereas the Son is not unlike God the Father. Therefore the Son is not a creature. No creature is equal to God, but the Son is equal to him; therefore the Son is not a creature.

The same: Every creature admits accidents of good and evil and experiences their loss; but nothing can either be removed from or added to the divinity of the Son of God. [Col. 1438D] Therefore the Son of God is not a creature.

The same: “God will bring every work into judgment.” But the Son of God is not brought into judgment. Therefore the Son of God is not a creature.

The same: The Son said that he is one with the Father. How can a creature say this? Therefore the Son of God is not a creature.

The same: To reign and to serve are not the same. But Christ is king and son of a king. Therefore the Son of God is not a servant.

The same: Every creature serves, but the Son of God does not serve; he makes sons of God out of servants. Therefore the Son of God is not a creature.

The same, *Against the Arians*: Let them say that he was begotten from the Father and created from a mother; or let them say how the Son of God can be both begotten and created. [Col. 1439A] A single nature, especially God, does not admit diversity. Paul forbids me to serve a creature and urges me to serve Christ. Therefore Christ is not a creature. “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ,” he says. How, then, would Paul himself serve Christ if he considered Christ a creature? Therefore let them either cease worshipping him whom they call a creature, or cease calling a creature him whom they pretend to worship, lest under the designation of worshippers they commit graver sacrileges.

The same, in the same work: “My God and your Lord.” Yet the testimonies teach me that whenever he calls God “my God,” he says this from the person of man. “God, my God, look upon me,” and “from my mother’s womb you are my God” (Ps. 21:11), signify that God was his God from the time when he was cast forth from his mother’s womb. Therefore, when we read of Christ’s generation, [Col. 1439B] in what respect do they dare to say that he was created or made? They ought indeed to consider in what respect they have read “created,” and in what respect “made.” For the Son of God is taught to have been begotten from God. But let them carefully observe in what respect they have read “made.” For God was not made; rather, God the Son of God was born. Afterwards, according to the flesh, man was made. “God sent his Son, made of a woman” (Gal. 4:4). When he says “his own,” he marks the property of eternal generation. “Made of a woman” means that the making is to be ascribed not to divinity but to the assumption of a body.

The same: They are accustomed vainly to boast that it is written: “God made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). [Col. 1439C] Divinity was not crucified, but flesh. That could indeed be made which could be crucified. Therefore the Son of God is not a made thing.

The same: “The Lord created me.” He did not say, “The Father created me.” The flesh recognized the Lord; our creature confesses the Lord. Who, then, does not know that this is said on account of the incarnation? Understand also that he says he was created in that respect in which he bears witness that he is human. [Note: [Col. 1439D] Editions: “Therefore he says that he was created in that respect in which he testifies that he is human.”]

The same: “He who believes in me does not believe in me, but in him who sent me.” But see what follows: “He who sees me sees him who sent me” (John 12:44). Therefore he explains what he first set forth: that the person who believes in the Son confesses the Father. For whoever does not know the Son does not know the Father; that is the meaning of “does not believe in me”: he does not believe in what you see bodily. For he says, “I have not come of myself” (John 7:28), because, if he is man, he did not come of himself. And elsewhere: “That everyone who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:36); and elsewhere: “Believe in God, and believe also in me” (John 14:1).

The same: At one time presenting himself from the person of man, at another in the majesty of God, he signifies both that he does not seek his own teaching and that his testimony is not true, then that it is true. For he himself says: “If I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is not true” (John 5:31); and later: “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true” (John 8:14). How is your testimony not true, Lord, except according to the frailty [Col. 1440A] of human beings? For every human being is a liar. Finally, to show that he spoke this of himself according to man, he says: “The Father who sent me himself bears witness concerning me” (John 5:37). But his testimony is true according to divinity, as he himself says: “My testimony is true, because I know whence I came and where I am going” (John 8:14).

The same, book V: Therefore it is one thing for the Son to be named according to divine substance, another according to the assumption of flesh. For according to divine generation the Son is equal to God the Father, and according to the assumption of a body he received the form of a servant; nevertheless, he is one and the same Son. He is Lord of the patriarch David according to his glory; according to the line of bodily assumption he is David’s son. Nor did he assume from David’s race according to power [Col. 1440B] only in the person of man, but also from the Lord, as you have: “Behold, I will send you my servant; Branch is his name” (Zech. 3:8). And the Son himself says: “The Lord who formed me from the womb as his servant, and said to me: Behold, I have set you as a light of the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth” (Isa. 49:6). To whom did he say this except Christ? He who, though in the form of God, emptied himself (Phil. 2:6), says in the Psalm (118:135): “Make your face shine upon your servant.” He is called servant in that respect in which he was anointed. He is called servant in that respect in which he has a mother: “I am your servant and the son of your handmaid” (Ps. 116:16). And in Ezekiel (34:23): “I will raise up over them my shepherd, and my servant David shall rule them, and David shall be [Col. 1440C] prince in their midst.” [Note: [Col. 1440D] Vulgate: “in their midst.”] David had of course already died; therefore this is spoken of Christ.

Chrysostom, on Psalm 50: Astonishing miracles of events! What worthy word can I utter? O madness of the heretics who say: “How is the Creator a creature?” Tell us how he who is everywhere was within a womb.

Augustine, *On Virginity*: Consider the beauty of your lover; reflect that he is equal to the Father and subject also to his mother, ruling even in heaven and serving on earth, creating all things and created among all things.

The same, *On Faith to Peter*: He, the Lord and creator of all spirits and all bodies—that is, of all natures—created the Virgin, being about to be created from a virgin.

The same, *Enchiridion*, chapter 12: He was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. Both substances, namely divine [Col. 1440D] and human, are the Son of God.

The same, on John, tractate 5: “All things were made through him.” If all things, then Mary too was made through him, from whom he was afterwards born. Just as he created Mary and was created through Mary, so he gave baptism to John and was baptized by John.

Pope Leo, in a sermon on Pentecost: For if man, made in the image and likeness of God, had remained in the honor of his nature and, deceived by the devil’s fraud, had not departed through desire from the law laid down for him, the Creator of the world would not become a creature. But because through the devil’s envy death entered the world, human captivity could not otherwise be released unless he [Col. 1441A] assumed our flesh who, without loss to his majesty, could become true man and alone be free from the contagion of sin.

## LXVIII. That Christ was made according to the flesh, and the contrary.

Paul, in the Epistle to the Romans (1:3): “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh.”

Augustine against Faustus: Christ, insofar as he is God, is he through whom all things were made. Insofar as he is man, he too was made.

The same, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chapter 70: It is plain that the Savior had no need of baptism, because Christ was not made but born, as the angel says to the shepherds: “Behold, today a Savior has been born to you, who is Christ the Lord” [Col. 1441B] (Luke 2:10).

Bede on Luke, homily on the reading “Jesus was casting out a demon”: “God sent his Son, made of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4). For those who think that “born of a woman” should be read must not be heeded, since, conceived in the virgin’s womb, he derived flesh not from nothing or from elsewhere but from his mother’s flesh.

## LXIX. That the Son of God was predestined, and the contrary.

Augustine, tractate 105 on John: “And now glorify me, Father, with yourself.” It is rightly said that he was not predestined according to that in which he is the Word of God, God with God. For what could be predestined when he already was what he was, without beginning? But this had to be predestined: that at its own time [Col. 1441C] it should come to be as it had been predestined before all times that it should come to be. Whoever therefore denies that the Son of God was predestined denies that this same one is the son of man. But for the contentious, let us also hear the Apostle on this point: “What he had promised beforehand concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined Son of God in power,” etc. (Rom. 1:2). Therefore according to this predestination he too was glorified before the world existed, [that there might be] his glory from the resurrection of the dead.

Origen, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans (1:2): “Who was destined Son in power,” etc. Although in Latin copies *praedestinatus* (“predestined”) is usually found, nevertheless what the truth of the translation has is *destinatus* (“destined”), not *praedestinatus*. For one who is, is destined; one who is not, is predestined. Those who do not yet exist can be foreknown and predestined. But he who is and always is, is not predestined but destined. We have said this because of those who speak impiety against the only-begotten Son of God and, ignorant of the distinction between *destinatus* and *praedestinatus*, think that he must be reckoned among those who formerly did not exist.

The same: Therefore, he who always is, is destined. But he who is predestined did not yet exist when he was predestined. The Apostle thus employs a necessary distinction: he calls the one who was made from David’s seed according to the flesh [Col. 1442A] “predestined”; but the one whom he names Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, he calls “destined.” Nor does he add “in power” superfluously, indicating thereby that he is Son in substance according to the Spirit of sanctification. For Christ is called God’s power and wisdom, and is also the vapour of God’s power and the utterly pure emanation of the glory of the Almighty.

## LXX. That God can be made lesser [Note: [Col. 1441D] Cousin: “cannot.”], and the contrary.

Moses the prophet (Deut. 6:4): “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one”; he cannot be greater, he cannot be lesser.

The Psalmist (8:6): “You made him a little lower than the angels.”

## LXXI. That the Son appears lesser than the Father even according to divinity, and the contrary.

[Col. 1442B]

Jerome, on the creed of the Council of Nicaea: Far be it that in the Son of God there should be anything greater or lesser in place, time, power, knowledge, equality, or subjection, when this is said in such a way that it is ascribed to his Godhead and not to his flesh. For if anything greater or lesser is found—apart from this, that the Son was not born from himself but was properly born from the Father—then the Father is shown to be either envious or powerless, and even temporal.

Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book IX (p. 1021): In order to disclose the sacrament of birth and the mystery [Note: [Col. 1441D] Cousin: “the sacrament of birth into the ministry”] of the assumed body, he said, “because the Father is greater than I,” from whom, that is, he was to receive glory again, [Col. 1442C] with whom and in whom he was to be glorified.

The same: The Father who is to glorify the Son is greater; the Son glorified in the Father is not lesser. Or how is he lesser who is in the glory of God the Father? Or is the Father greater? Therefore the Father is greater insofar as he is Father; but the Son, insofar as he is Son, is not lesser. The Son’s birth establishes the Father as greater; but the nature of that birth does not allow the Son to be lesser. The Father is greater when he is asked to restore glory to the assumed man; the Son is not lesser when he resumes glory with the Father. Thus both the sacrament of birth and the dispensation of embodiment are fulfilled. For the Father, insofar as he is Father and glorifies the Son of man, is greater; and Father and Son [Col. 1442D] are one when the Son, born from the Father, after assuming an earthly body is glorified in the Father.

## LXXII. That Christ did not grow even according to the body, and the contrary.

Jerome on Jeremiah, book VI: “The Lord will create a new thing upon the earth,” something which you had never previously known: without a man’s seed, without intercourse, without conception, a woman shall encompass a man in the enclosure of her womb. Though he will appear to advance in wisdom and age through the stages of infancy, with cries and childhood, he will nevertheless be held in the womb for the customary months as a perfect man.

The same: [Col. 1443A]

What the Vulgate edition intended in this passage I can state and can find some meaning, unless it would be sacrilege to argue about God’s words by human reasoning.

Ambrose on Luke (1:57): “Elizabeth’s time was fulfilled.” The same: For he did not experience any stage of infancy who, above nature and above age, placed in his mother’s womb, began from the measure of Christ’s fullness at perfect age.

Chrysostom, Homily 26 on the exposition of the Creed, beginning, “The universal Church rejoices”: The Virgin’s womb grew; she was a virgin, and while pregnant preserved virginity and did not lose it. Therefore this one who was born grew and came to the Passion.

From Pope Leo’s letter to the Palestinian bishops (Ballerini I, 1240): Although, therefore, from that beginning when the Word became flesh in the Virgin’s womb, no division ever existed [Col. 1443B] between the divine and human substance, and throughout every bodily stage of growth the actions of the entire time belonged to one person of one body, nevertheless we do not confuse in any mingling those very things which were done inseparably; rather, from the character of the works we perceive what belongs to which form. For divine things do not impair human things, nor human things divine things, since both concur so fully into one that in them neither property is abolished nor person doubled.

The same, to Bishop Julian against the error of Eutychean impiety: His flesh was not of a nature other than ours.

Augustine on Psalm 54: We know whence the Lord Jesus received flesh: from the Virgin Mary. He was nursed as an infant, fed, grew, and was brought to the age of youth [Col. 1443C], etc.

The same, in the letter to Volusianus on Christ’s incarnation and Mary’s virginity: You ask whether the Lord and ruler [of the world] underwent the years of childhood, grew into adolescence, was established in youth, was nourished with food, experienced all the affections of mortals, etc. One need not fear the tiny body of infancy, lest God seem therein to have endured such constrictions. For God is great not in bulk but in power. If reason is sought here, it will not be wonderful; if an example is required, it will not be unique. Let us grant that God can do something which we admit that we cannot investigate. In such matters, the whole explanation of what is done is the power of the doer. What if he had not passed through [Note: [Col. 1443D] Maurists: “changed.”] any stages from infancy to youth, had taken no food, [Col. 1443D] no sleep? Would he not confirm the mistaken opinion and not be believed in any way to have assumed a human being, and, while doing everything wonderfully, remove what he did mercifully? What does God not make wonderful in all the movements of creation, except that such things have become cheap through daily familiarity? Therefore he who made a human being without seed is the one who, in the nature of things, makes seeds without seeds. In his own body he observed the numbers of times and the measures of ages, he who, without any change in himself, wove together by change the order of the ages. For that grew in [Note: [Col. 1444D] Munich manuscript: “from.”] time which began from time.

Bede on Luke: “And the child grew and was strengthened.” By these words those [Col. 1444A] heretics are refuted who denied that he had a true soul, because, just as growth belongs to the body, so wisdom belongs to the soul.

## LXXIII. That Christ’s humanity did not grow in wisdom, or that it knew as much as divinity, and the contrary.

Bede on Luke: He is rightly said to be “full of wisdom,” not as making progress in wisdom at intervals of time—a wisdom with which he had always been full from the moment of his assumption—because, as the Apostle says, “in Christ the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” For the grace of God was in him, because no mortal was ever given grace so great and such that, from the moment he was conceived in the Virgin’s womb, he was perfect God. This man was never, even for a [Col. 1444B] moment, anything other than God.

Ambrose, *On Faith to Gratian*: There are many who are not so timid as I am. For I prefer to fear lofty matters rather than to presume to know them. There are many, because it is written, “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace before God and men” (Luke 2:52), who say that he professed not to know through the assumption of the human condition.

Likewise: I rather think that he said he did not know through our ignorance, not because he himself was ignorant of anything.

The same, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*: Therefore God before the flesh, God in the flesh, I assumed the perfection of human nature; I assumed human awareness, but I was not puffed up by the awareness of the flesh. In human awareness I said, “My soul is troubled”; in human awareness I hungered, prayed, and advanced, as it is written: “And Jesus advanced in age and wisdom and grace before God and men” [Col. 1444C]. How did the wisdom of God advance? Let the order of the words teach you. The advance in age and the advance in wisdom are human. Therefore age is mentioned first, so that you may believe this to have been said according to his humanity. For age belongs not to divinity but to the body. Therefore, if he advanced in the age of man, he also advanced in the wisdom of man. Wisdom advances through understanding, as understanding does through wisdom. Jesus, then, advanced, namely also in age. What understanding advanced? If it was human, then human understanding was assumed; if divine, then it is changeable through advancement. For whatever advances is certainly changed for the better. But what is divine is not changed. Therefore what changes is not divine. Thus human understanding advanced [Col. 1444D]; therefore he assumed human understanding.

And because he was speaking according to humanity, he prefaced it by saying: “But the child grew and was strengthened and was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was with him” (Luke 2:40). “Child” is the name of our stage of life; the power of God could not be strengthened, God could not grow, nor could the height of God’s wisdom or the fullness of divinity be filled. Therefore the wisdom that was filled was not God’s wisdom but ours. But in what sense did Isaiah say: “The child did not know father or mother” (Isa. 8:4)? For it is written: “Before the child knows mother or father, he shall receive the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria” (ibid.). Things future and hidden do not escape the wisdom of God [Col. 1445A]. But infancy, lacking knowledge, is ignorant, through human inexperience, of what it has not yet learned.

But, I say, we must beware lest, if we attribute to Christ two principal understandings or a double wisdom, we divide Christ. Do we divide Christ when we believe both in his divinity and in his flesh? Do we divide him when we venerate in him the image of God and the cross? Certainly the Apostle, who said of the same one, “For though he was crucified from our weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4), himself said that Christ is not divided. Do we divide him also when we say that he assumed a rational soul capable of our understanding? For God the Word himself was not in his flesh in place of a rational soul capable of understanding [Col. 1445B]; rather, God the Word, assuming a rational soul capable of understanding—truly human and of the same substance as our souls—and flesh like ours and of the same substance as our flesh, was also perfect man, yet without any stain of sin.

Fulgentius: The soul of Christ together with the Word is one Christ; and because the only-begotten God is equal to the Father, and one who does not know the Father wholly cannot know the Son wholly, we must beware lest, if Christ’s soul is believed not to know the Father wholly, knowledge of not only the Father but also of himself and the Holy Spirit be denied in some respect to the one Christ himself. If it seems alien to faith to say that Christ’s soul does not possess full knowledge of the divinity with which it is believed to possess one person, the assertion of John appears to oppose this, when he says that the Spirit was not given to Christ by measure (John 3:34): in him the divinity did not receive the Spirit, but Christ’s soul did. Where no measure is said to exist, the fullness of perfection and the perfection of fullness are found. Therefore Christ received the Spirit, but not by measure. But if it was given to Christ’s soul even by measure, it must have no deficiency in wisdom or knowledge. The Apostle says of the same one: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3). If he received not by measure, he must possess all the treasures of wisdom. But if anything is removed from his fullness, it follows that he received wisdom by measure [Col. 1445D]. Therefore, where the Spirit is without measure, full knowledge of divinity must be present.

Paul says of Christ: “In him it pleased all fullness to dwell” (Col. 1:19). “In him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” Therefore one must not suppose that the soul which is one person with the Word lacks, in any respect, full knowledge of divinity. Wisdom assumed that soul in such a way that the same Wisdom itself became mistress over all things made from the beginning, so that with his own divinity he is a person in the Trinity—that is, Christ.

Likewise: That soul has full knowledge of the Trinity, though it does not possess one nature with the Trinity. I do not know how we understand the Only-begotten as “full of grace and truth” from the Father, if either that fullness of truth lacks any fullness of grace [Col. 1446A], or the whole fullness of truth is not present in that fullness of grace. For one does not possess the whole fullness of truth when one is ignorant of anything of Truth itself. Far be it that this should be thought of Christ.

The same, *On the Mystery of the Mediator*: Isaiah says: “Before he knows or brings forth evil things, he will choose the good; because before the child perceives good, he will not believe malice, so that he may choose what is good” (Isa. 7:16). If a soul or intellect belonging to human nature is believed to have been lacking in Christ, what is it that he is said to have been ignorant of—the good and evil—as an infant? Or do we subject the divine nature of the Son of God to ignorance of good and evil, in order to deny a human soul in Christ? Accordingly, the man assumed by God must not be believed to have been able in any way to know the things of God, if Wisdom itself is said to have lacked knowledge [Col. 1446B] of good and evil.

Therefore the human soul, naturally made capable of reason, is said not to have known good and evil in the infant Christ; and, according to evangelical truth, wisdom and grace are said to have advanced in the child Jesus, as Luke says: “But the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom.” And shortly afterward: “Jesus advanced in age and grace before God and men.” For just as it belongs to flesh to advance in age, so it belongs to the soul to advance in wisdom and grace; yet it would not advance at all in wisdom if it did not possess the natural intelligence granted to all.

Likewise: The effect of the merciful assumption requires that, when flesh and soul are assumed by God, both should alike be saved [Col. 1446C]. For the flesh itself was not to be assumed by the Son of God unless it was to be delivered through divine assumption.

Alcuin to Charles, Book II, chapter 11: “You subjected all things beneath his feet.” It is perverse and wholly alien to sound faith to say that Christ’s soul does not possess within itself full knowledge of divinity, with which it is believed naturally to have one person. Hence John the Baptist said that the gift of the Spirit had been given to Christ uniquely and without measure: “For God,” he says, “does not give the Spirit by measure,” because the whole fullness of divinity dwells in him.

Likewise: Where no measure is said to exist, fullness of perfection is found.

Likewise: We must not suppose that Christ’s soul lacks in any respect full knowledge of divinity, since it is one person with the Word, whom Wisdom assumed in such a way [Col. 1446D] that, together with his own divinity, he is one person in the Trinity—that is, Christ.

Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*, Book II: “I do not believe,” he says, “that the weakness which we see in infants existed in the infant Christ.”

Ambrose, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians (2:10): “The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things.” Because he knows all God’s power and foreknowledge, something altogether impossible for a creature.

Likewise: No one knows the mind of the Lord except one who is from God, the Spirit of God. Inferior beings cannot know the counsel of superior beings, nor can a creature discern the will of its Creator.

On the same Epistle and the same passage: “Even the deep things of God.” This is a distinguished argument against heretics who call the Holy Spirit a creature; for it is shown here not merely that he is not a creature [Col. 1447A], but also that he alone searches the inward depths of God, because he is of the same nature and substance.

Claudius, on the same Epistle and passage: Since this Spirit is from God, he knows all the things of God; and therefore do not doubt that he is God, who is said to know not merely human secrets but even God’s hidden things. He says “deep things” because he knows all God’s power and foreknowledge, something entirely impossible for a creature.

Jerome on Psalm 15: “I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding.” He who is the wisdom of God does not himself need wisdom. But it must be understood in accordance with the saying: “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom.”

Ambrose Autpert, in a homily on that Gospel reading: “Joseph and Mary his mother were wondering. But the child grew and was strengthened, full of wisdom” [Col. 1447B]. These things are said of him according to his humanity. For in his own nature he is neither strengthened nor filled with wisdom, but in ours, in which he emptied himself for us. Or indeed all these things can better be referred to his body, which is the Church, than to the Head himself. Daily the child Jesus grows in faith; daily he is strengthened in virtues, etc.

From the homily for the Sunday after Theophany, which begins, “Reasonably, teachers”: For unless he had had true flesh, he could by no means have advanced and grown in age; and unless he had had a true soul, he could by no means have been capable of advancing and growing in wisdom. And just as the body grows through the successive stages of life, so the soul advances as it grows in wisdom.

The same, on Revelation (5:12), Book III: “Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and divinity and wisdom,” etc. The human nature in Christ so merited to be united to the power and wisdom of God that God and man are one power, God and man are one person, and God and man are one wisdom. Moreover, although that human nature in Christ advances in wisdom on earth, it now teaches the angels in heaven [Col. 1447C].

The same, Book IV: Thus speaking of the Jews: “These say: ‘Your Christ is not that Wisdom which reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly, since as a man he advances in wisdom through the growth of time.’” That Wisdom suffered no diminution in the man assumed, although the same one, according to humanity, advanced in wisdom by succession; rather, this wisdom, assumed by that Wisdom, remained one wisdom, by which the world was made and by which the world was restored.

Remigius on Psalm 29: “But I said in my abundance.” Christ according to the flesh possessed no riches; for he was poor, so that he had nowhere to lay his head. Therefore he calls his abundance the fullness of graces, both spiritual and the treasury of all divinity, because it remained bodily in him. “I said,” he says, “in my abundance,” that is, in the fullness of divinity.

Likewise: “And I was troubled,” that is, I died through the weakness of the flesh, ignorant of the light of truth.

### LXXIV. That Christ is read to have been anointed bodily, and that he was not.

[Note: Col. 1447D, Cous.: adds “also.”]

[Col. 1448A]

Luke the Evangelist (7:37): “A woman in the city, who was a sinner, when she learned that he had reclined at table in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster vessel of ointment; and standing behind him at his feet, she began to wet them with tears and kissed his feet and anointed them with ointment.”

Matthew (26:6): “When Jesus was in Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him with an alabaster vessel of precious ointment and poured it upon the head of him as he reclined.”

John (19:38): Joseph of Arimathea came and took the body of Jesus. Nicodemus also came, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. Therefore they took [Col. 1448B] the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the Jewish custom for burial.

Cassiodorus on Psalm 132: Some of old were anointed as kings, others as prophets, others as priests. By all of these Christ was prefigured, though he is not read to have been bodily anointed. But he was anointed by the Holy Spirit descending upon him, once baptized, in the form of a dove. Hence: “God, your God, has anointed you,” etc. (Ps. 109:4.)

### LXXV. That in Christ he who is the Son of God is not he who is the son of man, or that he who is eternal is not he who is temporal—and conversely.

Jerome on Psalm 114: “The Lord has sworn.” When it says “has sworn,” he did not swear to him who was begotten before Lucifer [Col. 1448C], but to him who was born after Lucifer from the Virgin.

Likewise: For this is that Melchizedek, without father, without mother, without genealogy. All ecclesiastical writers have said: without father according to the flesh, without mother according to God.

The same, from the sermon on the Assumption of Saint Mary (Mart. V, p. 89): The Word which was in the beginning and was with God—the glorious Virgin Mary gave birth from herself to that same God, made flesh.

Likewise: “Who chose us before the foundation of the world,” because certainly whatever God made from the beginning, Christ made wholly through the union of the sacrament; and therefore Christ was already in the Son, whom [Note: Col. 1447D, Cous.: “because . . . it is not doubted.”] one must not doubt always to have been in God through the unity of the sacrament.

Likewise: One in flesh, one in sacrament [Col. 1448D], and one in spirit; nor does reason [Note: Col. 1448D, Cous.: “at all.”] allow us to understand one as the son of man and another as the Son of God, because he is separated neither by time nor by suffering. Rather, God wholly passed into Christ and Christ into God, so that whatever the Son of God is is called Christ, and whatever Christ suffered is rightly said to have been suffered by God. Nor do we worship or adore a man separately, but God incarnate, who united to himself his own animate body.

Likewise: We worship the very Son of God, who was not increased in himself by the assumed man, nor diminished or changed when the Word became flesh. Therefore the one and same Son is always worshipped with God the Father [Col. 1449A], not departing in time, not alien in nature or kind. If it seems new to you that he assumed a man, know that he was always with him and in his counsel.

Likewise: In Christ Jesus, in whom are God and man, they are so one in one person that one repeatedly reads in the divine Scriptures of man as coeternal with God because of the unity of substance; and then God is seen as suffering with man, though man is not immutable [Note: Col. 1449D: thus the Munich manuscript and the Martianay edition, *initialis* (“having a beginning”); the Cousin manuscripts, *initiabilis* (“capable of being begun”).] and God is not passible. Yet God is so united to his body that no distance between God and man may be admitted by human opinion, lest perhaps—far be it!—one Son of God and another son of man should be believed, especially because Scripture so joins and incorporates God and man that no one can distinguish man from God in time [Col. 1449B], nor God from man in the Passion.

Hence, if you consider time, you will find the son of man always with the Son of God; if you consider the Passion, you will find the same Son of God always so united and indivisible with the son of man, so far as the language of Scripture is concerned, that man cannot be separated from God in time, nor God from man in the Passion. Indeed, that you may understand this more clearly, examine Christ’s own words: “No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

Likewise: The same one is God and man in one substance or person, without division or mixture.

Likewise: The Word is God and not flesh, although he assumed animate flesh. Likewise flesh is animate and not the Word, although the Word of God was beheld and seen as flesh [Col. 1449C]. Hence John says: “What was from the beginning, what we have seen and beheld, and what our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life.” Yet no one can see God the Word or touch him with hands except through the mystery of the man united to him; indeed, the union is so wonderful that it cannot be distinguished.

Likewise: Hence the one and same remaining only-begotten Son is seen as inseparable in both natures, and performs what belongs to each substance according to the essence or natural property of each.

Likewise: Since Emmanuel is one, and in that one are both—namely God and man—he truly performed what belongs to each nature, acting in one respect as God in things divine, and in another respect as the same one, as man, in things human [Col. 1449D]. It was not one who worked miracles and another who performed human deeds and bore sufferings; but one and the same Christ, Son of God and son of man, who both performed divine deeds and human deeds. For Christ possessed common actions inseparably and indivisibly. Yet the qualities of the acts themselves must be understood, and we must always consider to what the humility of the flesh is raised and to what the height of divinity stoops.

The same, *On the Likeness of Flesh and Sin*: “The first man [was] from earth, earthly; the second [is] from heaven, heavenly.” Who is this heavenly one? Undoubtedly he who caused him whom he bore to hear at baptism: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). And how is “today” said, if “in the beginning the Word was with God”? For it was not that Word, who is believed always to have been and to be with the Father as Son, but the man whom God the Word had assumed, who heard this: that this son of man might be Son of God through the Son of God, he obtains this in the Son of God [Col. 1450A].

Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, Book VI: “I,” he says, “am the living bread which came down from heaven,” etc. (John 6:41). But flesh did not descend from heaven. How, then, did the living bread descend from heaven? Because our Lord Jesus Christ is participant both in divinity and in body; and you, who receive his flesh, share in that divine substance through the food.

Augustine, *Against Maximinus*, Book II: Christ, God and man, is one person. Therefore he says also: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” If, therefore, you attend to the distinction of substances, the Son of God descended from heaven and the son of man was crucified; if to the unity of person, both the son of man descended from heaven and the Son of God was crucified. Therefore, because of this unity of person, he not only said that the Son of Man descended from heaven, but said that he was in heaven while he spoke on earth [Col. 1450B].

The same, Book I, *On the Trinity*: He was crucified in the form of a servant, and yet the Lord of glory was crucified. For such was that assumption [Col. 1450C] as to make God man and man God—though the prudent reader understands in what sense this is said. For behold, we have said that, according to the fact that he is God, he glorifies us, namely because he is the Lord of glory; and yet the Lord of glory was crucified. For God is rightly said to have been crucified, not through the power of divinity but through the weakness of flesh.

The same, *Against Faustus*: We say that the Lord of glory himself, insofar as he became man, was predestined as Son of God. The teacher of the Gentiles proclaims: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined Son of God in power” (Rom. 1:3): so that he who was to be, according to the flesh, son of David, might nevertheless be, in power, Son of God according to the Spirit of sanctification, because he was born [Col. 1450D] of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin. This is that uniquely and ineffably accomplished assumption of man by God, so that he might truly and properly be called both Son of God and son of man: son of man because of the man assumed, and Son of God because of the God who assumed him; lest not a Trinity but a quaternity be believed.

From the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*: So that he who assumed and that which he assumed might be one person in the Trinity. For by the assumption of man a quaternity did not arise; the Trinity remained, that assumption ineffably establishing the truth of one person in God and man.

### LXXVI. That Christ’s humanity was ignorant of the day of judgment, and that it was not.

[Col. 1451A]

Gregory to Eulogius the Patriarch: It is written that neither the Son nor the angels know the day and hour. The Only-begotten indeed knows the day and hour of judgment, but not from the nature of his humanity. At the wedding, where wine failed, he answered his mother: “What is that to me and to you, woman?” (John 2:4). As though he said: “I do not have the power to work miracles from my mother; when the hour of death comes, I shall acknowledge you as mother.”

The same, *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 1: When Jesus at twelve years of age is said to have sat among the teachers, he is found not teaching but questioning. By this example it is shown that no weak person should dare to teach, since that child wished to be taught by questioning [Col. 1451B], though through the power of his divinity he supplied the word of knowledge to his very teachers.

Jerome, in the shorter breviary on Psalm 138: Here the humanity of the Son is signified, who said in the Gospel that he did not know the end of this world, and who says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38).

Cassiodorus on the same Psalm (Ps. 139:16): The human nature, which said in the Gospel that it did not know the end of the world, testifies that it saw its Father as incomplete. Its incompleteness is indeed still present: the Church is being gathered until the end of the world.

Jerome, chapter 260 on Matthew: The Apostle says of the Savior: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom” (Col. 2:3). After the resurrection, when questioned concerning that day, he answered more plainly: “It is not for you to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7) [Col. 1451C]. Here it is shown that he himself knows, but that it is not expedient for the apostles to know, so that they may always live uncertainly in fear.

The same, chapter 355: Christ does not fail to know the day on which he knows that he will be with the apostles.

Gregory of Tours, *Histories*, Book I: Concerning the end of the world, I hold what I learned from those before me. Antichrist will first introduce circumcision, asserting himself to be Christ. Then he will set up his own statue in the Temple at Jerusalem to be worshipped, as we read that the Lord said: “You will see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place” (Matt. 24:15). But the Lord himself declares that that day is hidden from all human beings, saying: “But of that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:32) [Col. 1451D].

But here we shall answer the heretics who attack us by asserting that the Son is less than the Father because he is ignorant of this day. Let them recognize that the Christian people are called “this son,” of whom God foretells: “I will be a father to them, and they shall be sons to me” (2 Sam. 7:14). But if he had foretold this concerning the only-begotten Son, he would never have placed the angels before him. For he says: “Neither the angels of heaven nor the son,” showing that he said this not about the Only-begotten but about the adopted people.

### LXXVII. That the Jews or demons knew Christ even before his Passion, and that they did not.

[Col. 1452A]

From Chrysostom’s homily, *On the Chair of Moses*: They did not kill him without knowing him to be the Son of God, but because they could not endure his being such, as Solomon prophesies concerning them: “Come, let us entrap the righteous man, because he is useless and reproaches us with the sins of the law” (Wis. 2:12).

Augustine on the First Epistle of John, Homily IX: Demons also believe. What more could demons believe than to say: “We know that you are the Son of God” (Luke 4:34)? What the demons said, Peter also said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”; and we heard from the Lord: “Blessed are you, Simon,” etc., and: “Upon this rock,” etc. [Col. 1452B] (Matt. 16:18). Great praise. The demons also say, “You are the Son of God, the Holy One of God.” This Peter said; this the demons said. The words are the same, but not the disposition, because Christian faith is with love, while the demon’s is without love. Christian faith is faith with love. But those who do not believe are worse and slower than demons. Whoever refuses to believe in Christ does not yet imitate even the demons.

The Apostle, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (2:7): “But we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predestined before the ages for our glory, which none of the rulers of this age knew; for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.”

Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chapter 64: The demons did not know him otherwise than the rulers of this age knew him. For they knew that he was the one promised in the Law through prophetic signs. Nevertheless, they did not know that he was the Son of God from eternity, nor the mystery of the Incarnation [Col. 1452C].

The same, to Simplician, Bishop of Milan: If, further, one is troubled by how true things were foretold by Saul’s evil spirit, this too may seem remarkable: how demons recognized Christ whom the Jews did not recognize.

The same, to Dulcitius, *On Eight Questions*, first response: Thus far is your proposition. To this I reply from my book entitled *On Faith and Works*, where I spoke on this matter as follows. James is so vehemently opposed to those who think faith without works avails for salvation that he even compared them with demons, saying: “You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe and tremble” (Jas. 2:19) [Col. 1452D]. What could be said more truly, briefly, or forcefully? For in the Gospel we read that the demons said this when they confessed Christ as Son of God, and were rebuked by him for what was praised in Peter’s confession.

Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXXIII: “He will take him in his eyes as with a hook” (Job 40:19). This Behemoth knew the incarnate Son; but he did not at all know that our same Redeemer would pierce him through by dying. Hence it is well said: “He will take him in his eyes as with a hook.” We say that we have before our eyes what we see set before us. The ancient enemy of the human race saw our Redeemer set before him [Col. 1453A]; knowing him, he confessed him, and confessing him, he feared him, saying: “What have we to do with you, Son of God? Have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8:29). He was taken in his own eyes as with a hook, because he both knew and bit: he knew before he feared, yet afterward did not fear, when he hungered for the death of the flesh in him as though for his own food.

Likewise: “Will you mock him as a bird?” (Job 40:24). The Lord mocked him as a bird when, in the Passion of his only-begotten Son, he showed him bait but concealed the snare. For he saw what he might take into his mouth, but did not see what would seize him by the throat. For although he had confessed him to be the Son of God, he nevertheless believed him to be a mere man who would die, and he stirred up the minds of the persecuting Jews toward his death. Yet at the very time of his betrayal he is understood at last to have realized that he himself would be punished by that death. Therefore he also terrified Pilate’s wife with dreams, so that her husband might cease from persecuting the Just One. But, since the matter had been ordered by an inward dispensation, he wished to oppose it by no contrivance [Col. 1453B].

### LXXVIII. That Christ appears to have had servile fear, and that he did not.

Augustine, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” that is, those not puffed up, when the soul, fearing after this life that it may proceed to punishments, submits itself to divine authority, even if perhaps in this life it seems happy to itself. Likewise: It seems to me, therefore, that the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, of which Isaiah also speaks [Col. 1453C], corresponds to these stages. But the order differs: there the enumeration began with the more excellent things, whereas here it begins with the lower. Likewise: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Likewise: Fear of the Lord suits the humble, of whom it is said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” that is, the non-proud; to them the Apostle says: “Do not think highly, but fear” (Rom. XI.20), that is, do not be exalted.

The same, in *On Grace and Free Will*: Let us not suppose that we have not received the spirit of the fear of the Lord, which is without doubt a great gift of God, concerning which Isaiah says (XI.2): “The spirit of wisdom shall rest upon him,” etc.—the spirit of the fear of the Lord, concerning which Christ says (Luke XII.5): “Fear him who has power to destroy body and soul in Gehenna.”

Jerome, *On the Encampments of the Children of Israel* [Col. 1453D]: “Do not think highly, but fear God” (Rom. XI.20). For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble (I Pet. V.15); and: “Let him who thinks that he stands see that he does not fall” (I Cor. X.12). “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. VI.7). Fear is the guardian of the virtues; security readily leads to a fall. Hence also in the Psalm (XXIII.4), after the Savior had said, “The Lord guides me,” etc., he joins fear, the guardian of blessedness, and adds: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me.” The sense is: while I fear torments, I have preserved the grace which I had received.

Gregory, *Morals*, book I [Col. 1454A]: “Fearing God and withdrawing from evil.” It is written of him: “And he filled him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.” For the incarnate Lord displayed in himself everything that he inspired in us, so that what he taught by precept he might persuade by example. Therefore, according to the nature of his humanity, our Redeemer feared God, because, in order to redeem proud humanity, he assumed a humble mind for its sake.

The Lord in the Gospel: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.” Likewise: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather, fear him who can cast soul and body into Gehenna.”

Chrysostom, *On Matthew* (XXII.37): “Teacher, what is the great commandment in the Law? You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.” He says, “You shall love,” not “You shall fear,” John saying (I John IV.18): “Perfect love casts fear out.” For so long as a person fears God, he does not love him. To fear belongs to slaves; to love, to sons [Col. 1454B]. Fear is under necessity; love, in freedom. Whoever serves God in fear indeed escapes punishment, but does not receive the reward of righteousness, because unwillingly he does good on account of fear. Therefore God does not wish to be feared by human beings as a Lord, but to be loved as a Father, who gives to human beings the spirit of adoption.

What is it to love God with all one’s heart? That your heart should not be inclined toward the love of anything more than toward God. How is a wife’s complete love recognized? A wife ought to think no one wiser than her husband, even if someone else is wiser; no one stronger, even if someone else is stronger; no one more handsome, even if someone else is more handsome. Perfect hatred and perfect love do not recognize a judgment of things [Col. 1454C]. For example, if you perfectly hate someone, whatever qualities he may have, all things about him displease you, whether what he says or what he does. So too, if you perfectly love someone, whatever may be in him pleases you. Therefore, if a woman, on seeing someone, says, “What a wise man! If only my husband were like him!” her love already lacks something of perfect love. So too the Christian soul, which is Christ’s bride, ought to love God in such a way that there is nothing in the world that it loves more than him.
