In whatever measure it loves something else more, in that measure it loves God less.

What is it to love God with one’s whole heart and soul? To have a most certain mind in truth and firmness in faith. The love of the heart is one thing, the love of the soul another [Col. 1454D]. The love of the heart is in some manner carnal, so that we may love God even carnally.

Likewise: “Whether it is lawful for a man to [put away] his wife,” etc. (Matt. XIX.3). To a chaste husband whatever wife he has seems good, because perfect charity does not perceive faults.

Bede, *On Proverbs*: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. I.7). There are two fears. The first is servile, which is called the beginning of knowledge or wisdom; the second is friendly, which accompanies the perfection of wisdom. Servile fear is the beginning of wisdom, but perfect love casts this fear out. Yet the holy fear of the Lord succeeds it, enduring for ever and ever; charity does not exclude it, but increases it. It is that by which a good son fears lest he offend the eyes of his most loving father even in the slightest matter. Both fears, however, will cease in the age to come; but charity [Col. 1455A] never fails, and will remain in the fullness of eternal wisdom, which is to know the true and one God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.

Augustine, *On Psalm XVIII*: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever.” It is not that fear which, under the penal law, dreads having temporal goods taken away—by love of which the soul commits fornication—but the chaste fear by which the Church, the more ardently she loves her bridegroom, the more diligently avoids offending him. Thus perfected love casts this fear out, yet it endures for ever and ever.

Likewise [Col. 1455B]: The fear of the Lord is not servile but chaste: it loves freely, not fearing to be punished by God, whom it trembles before, but fearing to be separated from him whom it loves. This is chaste fear—not that which perfected charity casts out, but that which endures for ever and ever. This is the Holy Spirit.

The same, *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter XXXV (Maurists’ question XXXIII): No one doubts that there is no other cause of fear than lest we lose what we love after acquiring it, or fail to attain what we hope for [Col. 1455C].

Likewise: If one desires, since desire is nothing other than love of transient things, one must necessarily fear either losing them when one has acquired them or failing to attain them.

Chapter XXXVI: No one who is supremely happy fears. Therefore not to fear is not a fault. But rashness is a fault. Thus not everyone who does not fear is rash, although everyone who is rash does not fear.

Likewise: Since freedom from fear is common to the supremely happy person and the rash person, the supremely happy person possesses it through tranquility of mind, the rash person through recklessness.

The same, above, chapter XXVI: The Wisdom of God assumed a human being as an example by which we might live rightly. But it belongs to right living not to fear things that are not to be feared. Death, however, is not to be feared. Therefore this very point had to be shown by the death of that human being whom the Wisdom of God assumed. There are some who, although they do not fear death itself, nevertheless dread a certain manner of death. This too had to be shown by the cross. Among all kinds of death, none was more accursed and fearful than that kind.

Chapter LXXII: Everyone who wishes to live happily, if he lives as he wishes, is happy. But every human being wishes to live happily. Therefore every human being who lives as he wishes is happy [Col. 1455D]. From this it follows that no one who lives shamefully lives as he wishes, because no one who lives shamefully is happy. He does not live as he wishes because, although he does many things according to his own will, more things follow contrary to that will.

Jerome, *On the Same Psalm*: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for ever and ever.” It is fear with charity, concerning which he said: “Perfect charity casts fear out” (John IV.18). Fear, not with fear of punishment or fear of Gehenna, but with holy fear. Fear in such a way that you do not lose through negligence what you love.

## LXXIX. That Christ deceived, and that he did not.

Ambrose, *On Luke*, book II: There is also no slight reason [Col. 1456A] why Mary’s virginity should deceive the prince of this world: when he saw her betrothed to a husband, he could not suspect the birth. That it was the purpose of the Lord himself to deceive the prince of this world is declared by his words: when the apostles are commanded to be silent about Christ; when those healed are forbidden to boast of the miracle; when demons are commanded to be silent about the Son of God. Moreover, the Apostle also declared that it was the purpose to deceive the prince of this world, saying (I Cor. II.7): “But we speak God’s wisdom in a hidden mystery, which none of the rulers of this age knew. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” Therefore he deceived in order to conquer; he deceived the devil when he was tempted, so that the devil might never acknowledge Christ’s own divinity. Yet he deceived [Col. 1456B] the prince of this world even more.

The same, in the *Apology for David*: Rightly did he come hidden, so that he might deceive the prince of this world, like that Uriah whose name is interpreted “my light,” who transforms himself into an angel of light.

Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter XV (Maurists’ question LIII): If Christ’s body was a phantom, Christ deceived; and if he deceives, he is not truth.

The same, chapter LVI: The highest and perfect virtue is to deceive no one and to exhibit what was said: “Let what is in your mouth be: yes, yes; no, no” (Matt. V.37). Therefore, just as it is the highest and almost divine virtue to deceive no one, so it is the worst fault to deceive anyone.

Likewise: He is nearer to the highest virtue who, although he wishes to deceive an enemy, does not deceive him [Col. 1456C] except by divine authority. For God knows more truly what punishment or reward each person deserves.

Likewise: God deceives no one by himself. For he is the Father of truth, the truth, and the Spirit of truth. Yet, distributing fitting things to those worthy of them, he employs souls according to their merits and ranks; thus, if anyone is worthy to be deceived, God not only does not deceive him himself, but neither does he do so through such a human being as has already undertaken to keep: “Let what is in your mouth be: yes, yes; no, no”; nor through an angel, to whom the role of deception is unfitting; but through either such a human being as has not yet stripped himself of the desires of this world [Note: Col. 1455D, Maurists: “of the present world”], or through such an angel as, because of the perversity of his own will, has been appointed for the punishment of sins. For we read that a king was deceived by the prophecy of false prophets [Col. 1456D] because he deserved to be deceived in this way.

Likewise: Since the Egyptians were worthy of deception, and the people of Israel, at that stage of the human race, still stood at such a level of morals that they could without impropriety deceive an enemy, it came about that God commanded—or rather, for the sake of their desire, allowed—that they should ask the Egyptians for vessels of silver or gold, things after which those who still desired an earthly kingdom thirsted; and that they should receive them as though intending to return them, though they would not return them. God was willing that this should be both a not unjust reward for so long a labor or work, considering the stage of such souls, and a punishment of those whom he justly caused to lose what they ought to have returned. Therefore God is not a deceiver [Col. 1457A]—who does not understand that it is impious to believe this?—but the most just distributor of merits and persons.

Likewise: It was arranged that one set of commands should be given to a carnal people, another to a spiritual people, according to what suited the times. Therefore it is not surprising that those who were still worthy to deceive an enemy were commanded to deceive an enemy worthy of deception. They were not yet fit to be told: “Love your enemies” (Matt. V.44), but rather to be told: “You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy” (ibid. 43). A certain beginning was made under a pedagogue, so that perfection might be reserved for the teacher.

## LXXX. That Christ neither suffered nor feared even according to his humanity, and the contrary.

Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book XII: Even [Col. 1457B] now every pretext of impious assertion must be overthrown, and all the proclamations of heretical blasphemy must be passed through, so that the truth of the Gospel may shine forth by the very means through which it seemed capable of being obscured. For many of them wish, from fear of his Passion and from weakness in suffering, that he was not by nature the impassible God: so that, because he feared and grieved, he was neither in that security of power which does not fear, nor in that incorruption of spirit which does not grieve; rather, being of a nature inferior to God the Father and subject to human passion, he trembled in fear and groaned at the severity of bodily punishment. For it is written: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38); and again: “If it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid., 39); and: “My God, why have you forsaken me?” [Col. 1457C] (Ps. 21:2; Matt. 27:46). Also: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46).

And first, before we demonstrate from these very sayings that no weakness either of fear or grief befell him in himself, we must ask what he could seem to have feared: whether it can reasonably stand that he feared to die, when, driving all terror of death from the apostles, he exhorted them to the glory of martyrdom: “He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me; and he who loses his life for my sake shall find it” (Matt. 10:38). For since to die for him is life, what grief in the mystery of death is he to be thought to have suffered, who repays life to those dying for him? [Col. 1457D] And when he teaches that those who kill the body are not to be feared, did death itself terrify him with fear of bodily suffering? Finally, what pain of death would he fear, when he was about to die by the freedom of his own power?

For the human race either has death hastened upon the body by an external force attacking it, or nature itself, defeated by bodily old age, yields to that death. But the Only-begotten of God, having power to lay down and take up his life, in order to accomplish in himself the mystery of death, after drinking vinegar and testifying that he had completed the whole work of human sufferings, bowed his head and gave up the spirit. If this right has been left to human nature—that, breathing out the spirit by itself, it rests in death, and that the soul does not depart as the body is dissolved and weakened, or that the spirit, as though violated in its own seat by limbs cut off, pierced, [Col. 1458A] or crushed, does not burst forth or flow away—then let fear of death befall the Lord of life, if, because he died after sending forth his spirit, he did not use the power of his freedom to die. But if he died of himself and surrendered his spirit through himself, there is no terror of death where there is power to die.

Likewise: These things are foolish and ridiculous: that he should fear to die while possessing power to lay down and take up his own life, when he was to die, by the freedom of his own will, for the mystery of human life.

Likewise: Death cannot be feared where there is both a will to die and power to live.

Likewise: For the Virgin gave birth only by the Holy Spirit. And although she contributed from herself to the birth of the flesh as much as women contribute from themselves, according to the received origins of bodies to be born, Christ nevertheless did not grow together through the nature of human conception. Rather, the whole cause of his birth, introduced through the Spirit, retained in his human birth what belongs to a mother, while nevertheless possessing in his origin what belongs to God. Hence the Lord himself showed the mystery of the man he had assumed, saying: “No one has ascended into heaven except him who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). His descent from heaven is the cause of an origin conceived from the Spirit. For Mary did not give origin to the body, although she supplied everything natural to her sex for the body’s growth and birth. [Col. 1458B]

Likewise: “And the Word was made flesh”; although he was flesh, he nevertheless did not cease also to be the Word.

Likewise: The Apostle spoke plainly of the mystery of this indescribable bodily birth, saying: “The first man was from the clay of the earth; the second man was from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:47). When he calls the second man “from heaven,” he bears witness that his origin was through the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the Virgin. [Col. 1458C]

Likewise: The Lord himself, revealing the mystery of this birth of his, spoke thus: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven. If anyone eats of my bread, he shall live for ever” (John 6:51). For he himself is the origin of his own body. And lest it should be thought that the power and nature of the Word had failed in the flesh, he again said that he was his own bread, so that because he is bread descending from heaven, the origin of his body might not be thought to derive from human conception, since the body is shown to be heavenly. [Col. 1458D] Yet since it is his own bread, this is a declaration of the body assumed by the Word; for he added: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves.” Thus, because that which is the Son of Man and the bread from heaven is himself who descended, the assumption of flesh conceived from the Virgin is to be understood through his bread descending from heaven and through the blood and flesh of the Son of Man.

Likewise: Therefore Christ Jesus, man and Only-begotten God through flesh and Word, as Son of Man and likewise Son of God, assumed a true man according to the likeness of our own humanity. Although blow or wound might fall upon him, knots be tightened, or suspension raise him up, these things indeed brought the assault of suffering, but did not bring the pain of suffering—just as a weapon piercing water, pricking fire, or wounding air. Such things inflict all these assaults upon their respective natures, in order to pierce, prick, and wound; but the inflicted assault does not retain its nature in those things, since it is not in their nature for water to be pierced, fire pricked, or air wounded, although it is the nature of the weapon to pierce, prick, and wound. [Col. 1459A]

Likewise: The Lord indeed suffered when he was struck, suspended, crucified, and died. But the suffering which rushed upon the body was not not suffering, yet it did not exercise the nature of suffering: it raged in the ministry of punishment, while the power of the body, without sensation of punishment, received in itself the force of punishment raging against it. For what are we to judge concerning flesh conceived by the Spirit through the nature of a human body? That man is from God: he possessed a body capable of suffering and did suffer, but did not possess a nature capable of feeling pain. For that body belongs to his own proper nature. And when he thirsted, hungered, or wept, he is not shown to have drunk, eaten, or suffered pain; rather, bodily habits were assumed to demonstrate the reality of the body. Even when he took drink and food, he gave himself not to bodily necessity but to custom. [Col. 1459B]

Likewise: The Apostle preserved the mystery of this birth that was to be demonstrated when he said: “Established in likeness and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7). That appearance was not merely that of a man, but “as a man,” since both the appearance of flesh was real in the truth of his birth, and the likeness of sinful flesh was free from the defects of human suffering. Thus he has human birth because he is man; yet he is not in the defective weakness of man because he is Christ. For although the form of our body was in the Lord, the form of our defective weakness was not in his body, since that which the Virgin bore from conception by the Holy Spirit was not such in its origin. [Col. 1459C]

Likewise: Does the Passion seem to you, O heretic, to have been feared by the Lord of glory? Yet because of the error of this ignorance, Peter too became Satan and a stumbling-block to him.

Likewise: What Christ will you follow in hope, if you deny that he is God and add fear of suffering to him? Did he fear who went forth to meet those armed to seize him? Was weakness in his body, at whose approach the terrified ranks of his pursuers fell down? What weakness, then, do you suppose ruled in that body whose nature possessed such great power? But perhaps he feared the pain of wounds. I ask: what horror did he feel at the nail piercing the flesh, when he restored the flesh of a severed ear by touch alone? Does the hand feel pain from the nail? Does he feel his own wound who leaves no pain from a wound in another? [Col. 1459D]

Likewise: Heretic, why do you not remember that, when Judas went out to betrayal, it was said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” (John 13:31)? If the Passion was to glorify him, how did fear of the Passion make him sorrowful? Unless perhaps one is so irrational as to suppose that he feared to suffer those things which would glorify him by his suffering.

Likewise: “The cup which the Father has given me, do you not wish me to drink it?” [Col. 1460A] (John 18:11). How, then, would he pray that the cup be taken from him through fear of suffering, when he hastened to fulfill it in zeal for the divine dispensation? For it is not consistent that one should be unwilling to suffer who willed to suffer.

Likewise: You ought not to have forgotten this saying: “Truly I say to you, from now on you shall see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power of God and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Matt. 26:64).

Likewise: Everything feared must, while it is feared, necessarily be avoided; whatever is weak draws fear from its weakness. But by what rational understanding do you suppose that the Lord Jesus feared what he hastened toward, that he who struck down the strong should tremble in weakness, and that he who did not permit wounds to cause pain should himself, when wounded, feel pain? Or do you think he feared the abyss of hell, when he said to the thief on the cross: “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” [Col. 1460B] (Luke 23:43), promising paradise to his martyr and pledging the delights of consummate blessedness?

Likewise: Therefore, from the combined force of his sayings and deeds, it is undeniably shown that there was not in the nature of his body the weakness of bodily nature. By the power of his nature he expelled every weakness of bodies; and that Passion, though inflicted upon the body, did not impart to the body the nature of feeling pain. For although the form of our body was in the Lord, the body was not subject to our defective weakness, because that which the Virgin bore from conception by the Holy Spirit was not such in its origin. Although she bore it through the office of her sex, she did not receive it through the elements of earthly conception; and that which took its beginning from spiritual conception lies outside the weakness of our body. [Col. 1460C]

Likewise: To be sorrowful because of death and to be sorrowful unto death are not of the same meaning. Where sorrow is because of death, death itself is the cause of sorrow; but where sorrow is unto death, death is the end of sorrow.

Likewise: He prayed: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39). He does not ask that it not be with him, but that it pass from him. Then he prays that his own will not be done, and does not wish that the very thing he wills should be granted to him. For he says: “Not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.), thereby indicating, through the human concern in himself expressed by praying that the cup be removed, a participation in human willing, while not separating from himself the judgment of the will united and common with the Father.

Likewise: “Pray that you may not enter into temptation,” etc. (ibid., 41). Those who promised that they would not be scandalized were going to fall into scandal through the weakness of the flesh. Therefore he is not sorrowful for himself, nor does he pray for himself, but for those whom he warns to pray vigilantly, lest the cup fall upon them—the cup which he prays may pass from himself, so that it may not remain in them. [Col. 1460D]

Likewise: By saying, “If it is possible,” he taught what he said to Peter: “Behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat” (Luke 22:31). The Lord’s sorrow is unto death because, at death, through the opening of tombs and the resurrection of the dead, the faith of the apostles was then to be confirmed.

Likewise: Because after his death, through the glory of his power, the scandal arising from apostolic weakness would be driven away.

Likewise: He added that, after the Lord had prayed at length, an angel stood by strengthening [Col. 1461A] him; and with the angel standing by, he began to pray more earnestly, so that a sweat like drops of blood flowed from his body.

Likewise: Heresy should remember that the Creator of angels did not need the assistance of his own creation.

Likewise: He is sorrowful for us; necessarily he is strengthened for us and from us. But no one will dare attribute his sweat to weakness; to sweat blood is contrary to nature, and what power has done against nature is not weakness.

Likewise: The Apostle (2 Cor. 13:4) said: “For he was crucified from our weakness, but he lives by the power of God.” And although in the same one there was weakness for suffering and, as it were, the power of God for life, he who suffered and lived was not another, separated from himself.

The same, in Psalm 53: “God, save me by your name.” The Passion itself was voluntarily undertaken. It was indeed to satisfy the penal office, but not to injure the sufferer through the sensation of punishment. This is not because it lacked the nature of causing injury, but because the nature of divinity does not feel pain. Therefore God suffered because he voluntarily subjected himself to suffering; yet he did not fall from the power of his nature so as to feel pain. [Col. 1461B]

The same, *On Matthew*, chapter 32: Some think that sorrow could have come upon God on his own account, and that fear of the coming Passion broke him, because he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38); “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid., 39); again, “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (ibid., 41); and finally, twice to him: “Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink [Col. 1461C] it, let your will be done” (ibid., 42). They wish misery from the weakness of the flesh to attach itself to the spirit, as though the assumption of flesh had infected that power of incorruptible substance with the lot of its weakness, and frailty had overtaken the nature of eternity. For if it is sorrowful from fear, weak toward pain, and trembling before death, it will already also be subject to corruption; and if eternity, changed into fear, can become what it was not, then what is in it could likewise at some time cease to be.

But God always is, without measure of times; and as he is, so he is eternal. Eternity, remaining in infinity, always extends—whole and incorruptible—both into things that have been and into those which are to follow. But all their thought is this: that they suppose fear of death to have befallen the Son of God, who maintain that he was not brought forth from eternity nor existed from the infinity of the Father’s substance. Had they been capable of the Gospels, they would have known that the Word of God was God in the beginning. Therefore nothing in God could die, nor is there from himself any fear in God. [Col. 1461D]

But because we read that the Lord was sorrowful, let us discover the causes of his sorrow. After taking Peter, James, and John with him, he began to be sorrowful. Therefore he was not sorrowful before he took them, and all his fear began after they had been taken with him. Thus the sorrow did not arise from himself but from those whom he had taken with him. Then, when he said, “My soul is sorrowful unto death,” he did not say “because of death.” For if fear were about death, it ought certainly to have been referred to that on account of which it existed.

Earlier he had said: “You will suffer scandal this night.” For he knew that they would be terrified, flee, and deny him; but because the spirit of blasphemy is forgiven neither here nor in eternity, he feared that they might deny him as God, whom they were about to behold beaten, spat upon, and crucified. This reasoning was maintained in Peter, who, though about to deny, denied in this manner: “I do not know the man,” because it was said that something against the Son of Man would be forgiven. Therefore his soul is sorrowful unto death. Thus it is not death, but the time of death, that is feared, because after it the faith of believers would be established by the power of the resurrection. [Col. 1462A]

Finally, he prays: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” He does not say: “Let this cup pass me by.” He who asks that it pass from him does not pray that he himself be passed over, but that what passes from him should proceed to another. Therefore all the fear concerns those who were to suffer. And because it is not possible that he should not suffer, he prays for those who were to suffer after him, saying: “Let the cup pass from me, and as it is drunk by me, let it be drunk by them without despair of hope, without sensation of pain, without fear of death.” And he says, “if it is possible,” because dread is grievous to flesh and blood, and it is difficult for human bodies not to be overcome by its bitterness. But when he says, “Not as I will, but as you will,” he indeed wished that they should not suffer, lest perhaps they should despair in suffering, but that they might merit the glory of their co-inheritance without the hardship of suffering. [Col. 1462B]

Likewise: He rebukes the sleeping disciples and Peter, asking why he did not keep watch with him even one hour. Peter was singled out from the three because, above the rest, he had boasted that he would not be scandalized.

Likewise: He prays that the strength of drinking the cup—which the Father wills—may pass from him into them.

Likewise: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” Certainly this is not said of himself, for the discourse here is directed to them. Or how could the spirit now be willing, if above he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death”? But he commands them to watch and pray, lest they enter into temptation and yield to bodily weakness.

Likewise: For disciples about to suffer, through the justification of faith he assumed into himself every weakness of our body, and with himself he fastened to the cross all those things by which we were weak. Therefore he bears our sins and suffers pain for us, so that, when we are burning with the heat of faith and must contend against the devil in the battle of suffering, all the pains of our weaknesses may die together with his body and Passion. [Col. 1462C] Therefore the cup cannot pass from him unless he drinks it, because we cannot suffer except through his Passion.

The same, on Psalm 141: The faith of all the apostles was fearful until the time of the resurrection; hence comes the saying: “My soul is sorrowful unto death.” It was not because of death, since, though he gave himself to the Passion, eternal power did not receive the pain of the Passion.

Ambrose, *On the Incarnation of the Lord*: Foreshadowing the weak in himself, the Lord said: “Let this cup pass from me.” For the Lord did not truly fear to suffer when he was to rise on the third day. When Paul burned with desire to be dissolved and be with Christ, does this one who rejoices to receive a crown become sorrowful as he is about to bestow the crown? But he assumed sorrow as he assumed flesh: he was sorrowful, but voluntarily assumed true sorrow just as he voluntarily assumed true flesh. [Col. 1463A]

The same, *On the Trinity to Gratian*, Book II: “It is written,” say the heretics, “Father, if it is possible, remove this cup from me; and therefore, if he is omnipotent, how does he doubt concerning possibility?” Since I have proved him omnipotent, I have surely proved that he cannot doubt concerning possibility. “They are Christ’s words,” you say. You speak truly. But observe when and in what form he speaks. He bore the arrogance of man; he assumed human feeling. Therefore he speaks not as God but as man, since it is written of God: “Nothing is impossible for you.” But concerning whom did he doubt—himself or the Father? He doubted, with human feeling, concerning him to whom he says, “Remove it.”

Does Christ fear while Peter does not fear? Peter says: “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:37); Christ says: “My soul is troubled” (John 12:27). Both are true, and both full of reason: the inferior does not fear, while the superior bears the feeling of one who fears. For the former, as man, does not know the force of death; the latter, as God existing in a body, displays the frailty of the flesh, so that the impiety of those who renounce the mystery of the Incarnation might be excluded. [Col. 1463B]

The same, in the same work: “All that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15); beyond doubt, because he excludes nothing. The Son has the same will as the Father. Therefore there is one will where there is one operation. But the will of man is one thing, the will of God another. When Peter wished to draw the Lord back from the Passion, the Lord said: “You do not savor the things of God, but those of men” (Matt. 16:23). Therefore he assumed my will and my sorrow. I confidently call it sorrow, because I preach the cross. The will which he called his own is mine, because as man he assumed my sorrow; as man he spoke, and therefore said: “Not as I will, but as you will.” The sorrow that he assumed with my feeling is mine. For no one who is about to die rejoices. He suffers for me, is sorrowful for me, feels pain for me. Therefore he suffered pain for me and in me, he who had nothing in himself for which to suffer pain. You grieve, Lord, not over your wounds but mine, not your death but our weakness, as the prophet says: “because he suffers pain for us.” And what wonder if he suffered pain for all, who wept for one? If he was distressed as he was about to die for all? [Col. 1463C]

Therefore, as man he doubts, as man he is troubled. His power is not troubled, nor is his divinity; but his soul is troubled, troubled according to the assumption of human frailty. And therefore, because he assumed a soul, he also assumed the soul’s affections. For God, in that he was God, could neither be troubled nor die.

Likewise: Therefore the flesh suffered, while divinity remained free from the suffering of death.

Athanasius, *On the Trinity*, Book VI, chapter 2: Cursed be whoever does not confess that the true man whom he assumed truly suffered: let it be, let it be.

Likewise, chapter 4: If anyone confesses that the true man whom he assumed did not truly eat, drink, weep, sweat blood, and suffer, let him be anathema.

Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter 81: We have shown in countless passages that the Evangelists relate concerning him things which prove that he possessed those affections which cannot exist without a soul. Therefore I do not adduce: “My soul is sorrowful” (Matt. 26:38); “I have power to lay down my life” (John 10:18); and “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13)—sayings which an obstinate opponent might call figurative when spoken by the Lord. Rather, we have that he was born, arrested by the Jews, scourged, crucified, killed, and buried. Just as these things testify that he had a body, so those affections, which can exist only in a soul and which we nevertheless read of, show that he had a soul: Jesus wondered, became angry, was sorrowful, and did many other things. [Col. 1464A]

Likewise: It is foolish to believe the Evangelist when he reports that Christ ate, yet not believe him when he reports that he hungered. Nor are we frightened by the foolish slander with which opponents say: “Then he was placed under necessity, because he was arrested, scourged, crucified, and died.” Let them finally understand that he assumed the soul’s affections by the will of the dispensation—real affections nevertheless, as he pleased—just as he assumed bodily sufferings by that same will of the dispensation, without any necessity. He displayed both by will, as was fitting, and nevertheless displayed both most truly.

Therefore, just as no one removes either us or them from faith in the truest Passion—through which his body is shown—by using the word “necessity,” so no one terrifies us, by that very name of necessity, away from faith in the truest affection through which we know his soul. [Col. 1464B]

The same, on Psalm 29: He did many things according to the body, from which we understand that he had a body. He walked, sat, slept, was scourged, crucified, and died. Therefore, just as from these signs we recognize that he had a true body, so also from certain other functions we recognize that he had a soul. To hunger and thirst belong to the soul. If they say these were false, then those things believed of the body will also be false.

From the Council of Carthage, chapter 1: He who is to be ordained bishop must first be examined as to whether he believes that he who was Son of God in the divinity was himself made Son of Man in manhood, and that he suffered a true Passion of the flesh and died a true death of his own body, etc.

Ambrose, *On Faith to the Emperor Gratian*, Book I: As man he doubts, as man he is troubled; because he assumed a soul, he assumed also the soul’s affections.

Likewise: “My God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). As man he speaks, bearing my fears, because when placed in dangers we think ourselves abandoned by God.

Likewise: Through the nature of man he both doubted and experienced weariness. [Col. 1464D]

Augustine, *Eighty-Three Questions*, chapter 35: No one doubts that there is no cause of fear except lest we lose what we love and possess, or fail to obtain what we hope for.

Likewise, chapter 36: No one who is supremely blessed feared. Therefore not to fear is not a defect.

Claudianus, to the prefect Patricius, *On the State of the Soul*: As the place requires, I note that Hilary of Poitiers could agree with your opinion; for, among many of his lofty discussions, holding a somewhat different view, he argued two things contrary to the truth: first, that nothing incorporeal was created; second, that Christ felt no pain in the Passion. If his Passion was not real, our redemption also could not be real. But because blessed Hilary abolished the defect of such an opinion through the power of his confession, he bears the pen of censure in such a way that he does not suffer loss to his merits. Therefore interpreters of the divine Scriptures should be trusted only insofar as they agree with the same tenor of truth. [Col. 1465A]

Bede, on Tobit: Terrified by the fish, Tobias cried out in a loud voice, saying: “Lord, it will attack me” (Tob. 6:3). And the Lord, when the moment of death was approaching, began to fear and to be distressed—not dreading the devil, but recoiling, through the frailty of fleshly nature, from death which entered the world through the devil’s envy. Hence he also prayed that, if it were possible, it might pass from him. He prays: “Abba, Father, all things are possible to you; remove this cup from me; yet not what I will, but what you will.”

### LXXXI. That in Christ’s death there was a separation of divinity and humanity, and not [Note: [Col. 1465D] Cous.: “may be …” (*sit..*)].

Athanasius, *On the Trinity*, Book III: Our mortal or passible man truly bore our weaknesses, and afterward was again assumed by God.

Likewise: Understand that this man was first assumed in birth from the Virgin Mary; in the Passion he was handed over by permission of his power; and after the Passion he was again assumed or received by him. [Col. 1465C]

Likewise, Book VI, chapter 2: Cursed be whoever does not confess that this whole man—that is, both soul and body—whom he assumed was again assumed or liberated, and rose from the dead after the third day: let it be, let it be.

Hilary, on Matthew: The cry to God is the voice of the body testifying to the rupture caused by the Word of God’s withdrawing from it. Accordingly, it cries out why it is forsaken, saying: “My God, why have you forsaken me?” But it is forsaken because the man was to undergo death.

Ambrose, on Luke: Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying: “God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27:46). Therefore I too shall not be ashamed to confess what Christ was not ashamed to proclaim with a loud voice. The man cried out, being about to die through the separation of divinity. For since divinity is free from death, there could certainly be no death unless life departed, because life is divinity. [Col. 1465D]

Augustine, on John, Homily 45: If we say that the Word of God laid down the soul and took it up again, we must fear lest it be said to us: therefore that soul was at some time separated from the Word, and at some time the Word which assumed that soul existed without a soul.

Likewise: What did the Passion do, what did death do, except separate the body from the soul? But it did not separate the soul from the Word. The Lord certainly died. His flesh breathed its last; for a time the soul left the flesh. But I do not say that the soul was separated from the Word. He said to the thief’s soul: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” [Col. 1466A] (Luke 23:43). Did he not abandon the thief’s soul, yet abandon his own? Far be it! Rather, Christ possessed the soul inseparably.

The same, *On the Trinity*, Book II, chapter 5: Therefore it is nowhere written that God the Father is greater than the Holy Spirit, because a creature was not assumed in which the Holy Spirit might appear in the same way that the Son of Man was assumed. For the Spirit did not make the dove blessed or join fire to the unity of his person forever.

Claudianus, *On the State of the Soul*, Book III: The Lord himself also cried from the cross: “My God, why have you forsaken me?” If he did not depart, he did not forsake; if he forsook, then certainly he departed. Thus, just as God is not deprived of non-spatiality because he forsook the man Christ by departing, so the soul does not lose the privilege of non-spatiality when it departs with the dying body. [Col. 1466B]

Likewise, above: The body which weighs down the soul is more in the soul than the soul, which is weighed down by the body, is in the body: that is, the burden is in its bearer, not the bearer in its burden. This being so, the following is evidence that the soul has a great likeness to its Maker: just as the world is non-spatially in God, so the body is non-spatially in the soul.

Fulgentius, *On the Immeasurability of the Divinity of the Son of God*: The unity of divinity and flesh accomplished their common Passion in Christ. Through this unity the Lord of glory is affirmed to have been crucified.

Likewise: When Christ died and the soul left the flesh, then that temple was destroyed.

Likewise: Christ’s very divinity—which deigned to be sorrowful according to the soul and to die according to the flesh—must, according to the property of its substance, be proclaimed both immortal and impassible. [Col. 1466C]

Likewise: Therefore the humanity of the Son was not wholly in the tomb, nor wholly in hell. According to the flesh Christ lay in the tomb; according to the soul he descended into hell; according to that same soul he returned from hell to the flesh which he had left in the tomb. But according to divinity—which is neither confined by place nor enclosed by limit—he was wholly in the tomb with the flesh and wholly in hell with the soul. Thus Christ was wholly everywhere, because God was not separated from the humanity which he had assumed: he was in his soul, so that, once the pains of hell had been loosed, it might return victorious from hell; and he was in his flesh, so that it could not be corrupted before the swift resurrection. [Col. 1466D]

Likewise: Whole Christ descended into hell according to the soul alone; the same and inseparable Christ rose from the tomb according to the flesh alone; the same and inseparable Christ, according to the entire man whom he assumed, left the earth locally and ascended.

### LXXXII. That in Christ there was even a suggestion of delight, and the contrary.

Jerome, on Psalm 14: “Even unto night my reins rebuked me.” The delights of the flesh rebuke me when they suggest that I should sin, when the flesh takes delight. But unless you had been at my right hand, perhaps I should have been weak. “But I kept the Lord always before my sight”: the Son before the Father, the Church before Christ. “Because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved.” [Col. 1467A] It is as if he said: If you had not been at my right hand, perhaps I would have been moved—that is, from faith to unbelief, from good to evil.

Gregory, Homily 16 on the Gospels: Jesus was led into the wilderness. Temptation occurs in three ways: suggestion, delight, and consent. When we are tempted, we commonly slip into delight or even consent, because, propagated from the sin of the flesh, we carry in ourselves that through which we endure conflicts. But God, who came without sin, endured no contradiction within himself. Therefore he could be tempted by suggestion, but the delight of sin did not bite his mind. Consequently, that entire diabolical temptation was external, not internal.

### LXXXIII. That Christ or the saints willed to die, and the contrary.

[Col. 1467B]

Isaiah the prophet (53:7): “He was offered, because he himself willed it.” The Lord himself in the Gospel (John 10:18): “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down.” Likewise: “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Likewise: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” And again: “Not my will, but yours be done.” Paul to the Philippians (1:23): “But I am constrained by the two, having a desire to depart and to be with Christ,” etc. The same, to the Laodiceans (Phil. 1:21): “For to me true life is in Christ, and death is joy.” The same in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians (5:4): “For we who are in this tabernacle [Col. 1467C] groan, burdened; because we do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.”

Jerome, *On the Love of God and the World*: “The love of the flesh torments you. Take up your cross and follow the Lord. The Lord himself and your Savior, although God in the flesh, nevertheless showed a human affection when he said: ‘Father, if it can be done, let this cup pass from me.’ He knew that this cup could not pass away without being drunk by him; he knew this by will, not by necessity. For your sake he uttered the voice of man, the voice of flesh; he deigned to transfigure you in himself. He showed the will by which he could be tempted, and immediately taught which will you ought to prefer to which will. ‘Father,’ he says, ‘if it is possible, let this cup pass from me’: this is the voice of flesh, not of spirit; [Col. 1467D] the voice of weakness, not of divinity. ‘If it is possible, let this cup pass.’ This is the will of which Peter also is told: ‘When you have grown old, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish’ (John 21:18). Whence, then, did the martyrs conquer? Because they set the will of the spirit before the will of the flesh. They loved this life, and therefore weighed it. From this they considered how greatly the eternal life ought to be loved, if this perishing life is loved so greatly. A man about to die does not wish to die, yet he will necessarily die.”

The same, on Psalm 132: “Behold how good and how pleasant.” Martyrdom is good, but it is not pleasant; for it has punishments and pains, and there is always suffering amid torments; and certainly [Col. 1468A] there is no pleasantness in pain.

Augustine, on Psalm 85: “You have helped me and comforted me.” Blessed Cyprian was saddened in his passion, but now he is comforted in his crown, etc.

The same, on John, sermon 123: “‘You will stretch out your hands,’ he says; that is, you will be crucified. But in order to arrive at this, another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish. He first said what would happen, and then said how it would happen. For he was led, not when crucified, but when about to be crucified, where he did not wish; for when crucified, he went where he wished. Once released from the body, indeed, he wished to be with Christ—but, if it could be so, without the distress of death, to which he was led unwillingly. He came to it unwillingly, but conquered it willingly; and he retained that affection of weakness, by which no one wishes to die, so natural that even old age [Col. 1468B] could not take it away from blessed Peter, to whom it was said: ‘When you have grown old, you will be led where you do not wish’ (John 21:18). For our consolation the Savior also transfigured us in himself, saying: ‘Father, if it is possible, let it pass,’ etc. He had indeed come to die; nor did he have a necessity for death, but a will—having power to lay down his life and to take it up again. Likewise: For if death involved no distress, or only slight distress, the glory of the martyrs would not be so great.”

Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, homily 3, adding an exhortation concerning Saint Felicity: “She desired to leave none behind her, lest, if she had someone surviving, she might not have a companion. Therefore let no one suppose that even carnal affection did not in the least touch her heart as her sons died. [Col. 1468C] For she could not see without pain her sons, whom she knew to be her own flesh, dying; but there was a force of inner love which overcame the pain of the flesh. Hence Peter, when about to suffer, is told: ‘Another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish.’ For Peter could not have suffered for Christ fully if he had not wished it; but he loved by the strength of the spirit the martyrdom which he did not wish by the weakness of the flesh. While through the flesh he trembles at punishments, through the spirit he exults at glory; and thus it came about that, by not willing the torment of martyrdom, he willed it. So too, when we seek the joy of salvation, we take the bitter cup of purgation. The bitterness in the cup displeases, but the salvation to be restored through bitterness pleases.”

From Prosper’s *Book of Sentences*, chapter 182: “No one loves what he endures, even if he loves to endure it; for strong patience is one thing, secure happiness another. The labor of battle and the blessedness of victory are not of the same time.”

### LXXXIV. That Christ, descending [Note: Col. 1467D: absent in Cousin’s edition, “to hell.”] to hell, freed all from it, and the contrary.

Origen, on Genesis, final homily: “The lion’s whelp of Judah,” etc. The death of Christ was the overthrow and triumph over the demons. For this lion rescued all the prey which that opposing lion had seized when man was struck down and cast down.

Ambrose, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: “For both Jews and Greeks sinned; for which reason Christ’s death benefits all [Col. 1469A] people. In this world he taught what must be believed and observed, and he rescued all from hell.” Likewise: “As he also says to the Galatians (3:13), ‘Christ redeemed us,’ offering himself for us. For he allowed himself to be taken by the devil who desired it, but who did not foresee the consequence. For, thinking that he could retain Christ, since he could not bear his power, he lost all whom he held together with the ransom.” Likewise: “It is manifest that all sinned in Adam, as it were in a mass.” Likewise: “The second death is in Gehenna, which we suffer not through Adam’s sin but, on the occasion of it, acquire through our own sins; from it the good are nevertheless immune—except that they were in hell, but in its upper region.” Likewise: “But he says that the grace of God abounded in many, both in those said to have died through Adam’s transgression while sinning in like manner, and in those [Col. 1469B] who did not sin in the likeness of this transgression [the grace of God abounded]. By reason of their ancestral sin they were in hell under God’s sentence; the grace of God abounded in the Savior’s descent, granting forgiveness to all and, in triumph, taking them up into heaven.”

The same, on the Epistle to the Colossians (1:13): “Who rescued us from the power of darkness,” etc. “In whom we have redemption,” etc. “For no one departed from hell without faith in Christ, because one bound by sins cannot go forth through the gates of Tartarus.”

Gregory, in the homily for the Saturday within the octave of Easter: “This feast may rightly be called the solemnity of solemnities. Through it the elect, who, although in the bosom of tranquility, were nevertheless held at the gates of hell, were brought back to the delights of paradise. What the Lord said before his passion, he fulfilled in his resurrection: ‘If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself’ (John 12:32). For he drew all things, because he left none of his elect in hell. He took away all things—that is, all the elect. For in rising again he did not restore to pardon every unbeliever and those consigned to eternal punishments for their crimes; but he snatched from the gates of hell those whom he recognized as his own in faith and deeds. Hence it is rightly said through Hosea (13:14): ‘I will be your death, O death; I will be your bite, O hell!’ What we kill, we bring about so that it no longer exists at all. But from what we bite, we take away one part and leave another. Therefore, because he utterly destroyed death in his elect, he became the death of death. But because [Col. 1469D] he took one part away from hell and left another, he did not utterly destroy hell, but bit it.”

Augustine, to Optatus: “Yet let that faith remain secure by which we believe that no human being is delivered from the contagion of death contracted by the first birth except through the one Mediator. By the most health-giving faith in this man, who is likewise God, even those were saved who, before he came in the flesh, believed that he would come in the flesh. For their faith and ours are the same: they believed that he would come, and we believe that he has come. Hence the Apostle says (2 Cor. 4:13): ‘Having the same spirit.’ If, therefore, they who foretold Christ’s coming [Col. 1470A] in the flesh had the same spirit of faith as those who announced that he had come, their sacraments could indeed differ according to the diversity of times, yet all return in fullest harmony to the unity of the same faith. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles (15:10), Peter speaking: ‘Why do you tempt God by imposing a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But through the grace of the Lord Jesus we believe that we shall be saved, as they also.’ If, therefore, they too believed that they would be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, it is manifest that this grace also made the ancient righteous live by faith. ‘But the righteous lives by faith.’ Accordingly, since all righteous people—that is, true worshippers of God, whether before or after Christ’s incarnation—neither lived nor live except through faith in the incarnation of Christ, in whom is the fullness of grace, certainly the statement that ‘there is no other name under heaven by which we must be saved’ (Acts 4:12) has been effective for salvation from the time when the human race was corrupted in Adam.”

The same, to the Questions of Hilary: “That we may know that whatever ancient righteous persons there could have been were delivered only through the same faith by which we are delivered, namely faith in the incarnation of Christ, which was foretold to them just as it is proclaimed to us.”

The same, to Dardanus: “The manifest Mediator willed the sacrament of our regeneration to be manifest. Yet it was in some respect hidden from the ancient righteous, although they were saved through the same faith that was to be revealed in its own time. [Col. 1470C] For we do not dare to prefer believers of our time to the friends of God through whom these things were prophesied to us, when God identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob [Note: Col. 1469D, Maurists: ‘Thus God commends himself as God’], so that he calls this his name forever.”

The same, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2: “It is not that there was no righteousness of faith before circumcision; for while still uncircumcised Abraham himself, the father of the nations that would follow his faith, was justified by faith. But in earlier times the sacrament of justification by faith was in every way hidden. Nevertheless, the same faith made the ancient righteous—small and great—saved: not the Old Testament, which gives birth into slavery; not the law, which was not so given as to be able to justify; but the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. For as [Col. 1470D] we believe that Christ came in the flesh, so they believed that he would come; as we believe that he died, so they believed that he would die; as we believe that he rose, so they believed that he would rise; and both we and they believe that he will come to judge the dead and the living.”

The same, in *On Rebuke and Grace*: “For if, as Truth says, no one is delivered from the condemnation brought about in Adam except through faith in Jesus Christ, and yet those who can say that they did not hear Christ’s Gospel will not thereby deliver themselves from this condemnation, since faith comes by hearing, how much less will those deliver themselves who will say, ‘We did not receive perseverance’? For the excuse of those who say, ‘We did not receive hearing,’ appears more just than that of those who say, ‘We did not receive [Col. 1471A] perseverance,’ because one may say to a person: ‘If you had wished, you would have persevered in what you heard and held’; but one cannot at all say: ‘If you had wished, you would have believed what you had not heard.’”

Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Colossians (1:13–14): “Who rescued us from the power of darkness,” etc. “In whom we have redemption,” etc. “For no one departed from hell without faith in Christ, because one bound by sins cannot go forth through the gates of Tartarus.”

Jerome, on the Epistle to the Galatians, book 1: “Some say that, if it is true that no one is justified by works of the law but by faith in Jesus Christ, the patriarchs and saints who lived before Christ’s coming were imperfect. They should be reminded that the saints of old were justified by faith in Christ. For Abraham saw Christ’s day; Moses considered the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, for he looked to the reward; Isaiah saw his glory, as John relates; and Jude (5), giving a general warning to all, says: ‘I wish to remind you that Jesus, having saved a people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe.’”

Gregory, on the final part of Ezekiel, homily 5: “‘Those who went before and those who followed cried out, saying: Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord’ (Matt. 21:9). For all the elect who could be in Judah, as well as those who now exist in the Church, believed and believe in the Mediator between God and human beings.”

The same, to George the priest and Theodore the deacon: “I learned from deacons reporting that your charity had said that the Lord Jesus Christ, descending to hell, saved and released from punishments all who there confess him to be God. On this matter I desire your charity to think very differently. For in descending to hell, by his grace he freed only those who believed that he would come and kept his commandments in the world.” Likewise: “But lest I delay your charity with my own discussion, let it learn what Philaster said concerning this heresy in the book he wrote on heresies. His words are these: ‘There are heretics who say that the Lord descended into hell and there also proclaimed himself to everyone after death, so that those confessing there might be saved; whereas this contradicts the prophet David, who says: [Col. 1471D] “For who shall confess you in hell?”’ (Ps. 6:6).”

Bede, on the Acts of the Apostles (4:11–12), concerning the words of the apostle Peter: “‘This is the stone rejected by you, which has become the head of the corner; and salvation is in no other.’ If salvation of the world is in no one else but Christ alone, then the fathers of the Old Testament too were saved by the incarnation and passion of the same Redeemer in which we believe that we are saved. For although the sacraments differ according to the condition of times, the faith is nevertheless one and the same in agreement: for they had learned through the prophets that the dispensation of Christ which we know through the apostles to have occurred was to come.”

### LXXXV. That it is uncertain at what hour of the night [Note: Col. 1471D: Cousin omits “of the night.”] the Lord rose, and the contrary.

[Col. 1472A]

Jerome, to Hedibia, book 12 of the *Questions*: “No one knows at what hour the Lord rose.”

The same, on the Epistle to the Galatians: “In the fourth watch of the night the Lord came to the disciples, walking upon the sea. Thus also, in the fourth watch of the night, he was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January; in the fourth watch of the night he rose on the sixth day before the Kalends of April; and in the fourth watch of the night he will come for judgment. The night is divided into four watches. One watch consists of three hours.”

Bede, chapter 352 on Matthew: “The Lord rose in the final part of the night.”

### LXXXVI. That the Lord, rising again, first appeared to Mary Magdalene, and the contrary.

[Col. 1472B]

Mark the Evangelist (16:9): “But rising early, on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons.”

Ambrose, book 3, *On Virgins*: “Consider that virgins deserved to see the Lord’s resurrection before the apostles. For when Joseph had placed the Lord’s body in his new tomb, the virgins kept watch.” Likewise: “Therefore Mary saw the Lord’s resurrection, and she saw and believed first. Mary Magdalene also saw, although she was still being reproved in this respect.” Likewise: “Finally, Mary Magdalene is forbidden to touch the Lord because she doubted the faith of the resurrection. Therefore she touches who touches by faith.”

That eminent poet Sedulius, whose Paschal work Pope Gelasius also mentions among the authoritative writings (V, 315–318):

> Meanwhile, after the mournful Sabbath, the blessed day  
> Began to shine forth—the day which draws the summit of its lofty name  
> From the Lord who rules it, and which first deserved  
> To see the world created and Christ rise again.

Likewise (V, 323–327):

> At this rising of the light,  
> The virgin Mother, and other mothers likewise, bearing the offering  
> Of fragrant harvest, came grieving to the familiar tomb;  
> And they see the place already made empty of the body,  
> Yet full of power. For an angel sent from the stars  
> Sat upon the summit of the astonished [Note: Col. 1472D, editions: “removed”] rock.

Likewise (V, 358–366):

> Christ joined the Church to himself in beautiful love—  
> That is, Mary radiant in conspicuous honor;  
> And although she is always Mother by her glorious name,  
> [Col. 1472D] she remains always Virgin. Standing before her sight,  
> The Lord first openly offered himself in light, so that the good Mother,  
> Proclaiming the great miracles, who once had been  
> The herald of his coming journey, might also be the herald of his return.  
> Soon he appeared to others, recognized as the mighty guest  
> In the breaking of bread.

### LXXXVII. That those who rose with Christ died again, and the contrary.

John Chrysostom, homily 28 on the exposition of the Creed, beginning, “Upon the fabric of the whole Church”: “He descended to the lower regions, so that there too he might not be without a miracle. For many bodies of saints rose with Christ, and afterward died, as Lazarus, as the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, and as the widow’s son. For many bodies of saints rose with Christ, concerning whom the Apostle said: ‘Of whom many remain even until now, but some have fallen asleep’ (1 Cor. 15:6).”

Augustine, on John (21:22): “‘If I will that he remain until I come.’ Just as for a time many bodies of saints rose when Christ suffered, and after his resurrection appeared to many.”

Athanasius, in the Creed of Faith: “At whose coming all human beings shall rise again with their own bodies.”

Jerome, on Matthew: “‘And many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep’: namely, just as Lazarus rose after dying, so also many bodies of saints rose, to show the Lord rising again; yet, though the tombs were opened, they did not rise before the Lord rose, so that he might be the firstborn of the resurrection from the dead.”

The same, in the sermon on the Assumption of Saint Mary: “Lest perhaps, if that apocryphal work *On the Passing of the Same Virgin* comes into your hands, you receive doubtful things as certain; and many Latins, out of love of piety, embrace another view more eagerly—especially since nothing else can be known for certain concerning her except that on this day she gloriously departed from the body.” Likewise: “I have said these things because many of our people doubt whether she was assumed together with her body, or died [Note: Col. 1473D, editions: ‘departed’] leaving her body.” Likewise: “Whether she rose is unknown, although some wish to maintain that she has already been raised and clothed with immortality.” Likewise: “Which of these things ought to be judged truer, [Col. 1473C] we are uncertain. We do better to commit everything to God, to whom nothing is impossible, than rashly to define something [Note: Col. 1473D, Munich manuscript: ‘something else’] which we cannot prove—as also concerning those whom we believe to have risen with the Lord. But whether they returned to the dust of the earth we do not know with certainty. Some teachers, indeed, have held and left in their writings that in them the perfect resurrection has already been completed. For they confess that they would not be true witnesses unless their resurrection also were true. Hence blessed Peter is recorded to have said, speaking of David in testimony: ‘And his tomb,’ he says, ‘is with us’—as though he had not dared to say that David himself, or his body, is with us. From this they say that he too rose [Col. 1473D] with the other saints, and that therefore the tomb remained empty. Since nothing is impossible to the Lord, neither do we deny that this happened to blessed Mary; nevertheless, for the sake of caution and with faith kept safe, it is more fitting to hold this as a pious desire than heedlessly to define what is not known without danger.”

Bede, on the Song of Songs (v. 1), book 3: “‘I ate my honeycomb with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk.’ In body and soul together they deserved through him to ascend to the courts of the heavenly city. The Evangelist plainly testifies of them that, when the Lord died on the cross, the tombs were opened and many bodies rose. And after his resurrection they came into the holy city [Col. 1474A] and appeared to many. Those, therefore, who rose from the dead when the Lord rose should be believed also to have ascended with him when he ascended into heaven. Nor should faith by any means be lent to the rashness of those who think that afterward they returned to ashes and were again shut up, as dead persons, in the very tombs which [Note: Col. 1474D, editions: ‘previously’] had been opened by them, and in which they had appeared alive a little earlier.”

Ambrose, on the Nativity of the Martyrs, concerning the resurrection: “If the martyrs have not yet been freed from hell, they have been freed from sins. Yet perhaps very many of these same martyrs attained bodily resurrection with the Lord, either then or afterward. For if we read that at the first festival of the Resurrection, when the Lord raised himself, many bodies of saints came to life, why should we not believe that as often as the festival of the Resurrection is celebrated, so often his saints rise? For where the solemnity of vows is greater, there too the gifts are greater. But perhaps someone will say: ‘The graves are shut, the tombs sealed; how can they come forth from them?’ Without mentioning that all things are possible to God, and that he can bring forth a spiritual body from closed tombs, even if I set all this aside, we nevertheless have the example of the apostle John: his tomb could close over the body entrusted to it, but could not keep it. For it lost the body deposited in it; it did not take it up. For by the grace of the resurrection this was removed behind the closed doors of the tomb: though the burial-place remained, the buried man was not found; finally, when priests sought the body for honor’s sake, [Col. 1474C] the tomb, with its entrance opened, could not return the one it had received.”

### LXXXVIII. That after the resurrection Christ showed scars, not wounds, to the doubting, and the contrary.

Augustine, to the priest Deogratias: “Let him who has raised these questions know that after the resurrection Christ showed scars, not wounds, to the doubting. For their sake he wished to take food and drink, not once but repeatedly, lest they should think it was not a body but a spirit, and that he appeared to them not in substantial reality but merely as an image. But those scars would have been false if no wounds had preceded them.”

Sedulius, book 5, 376–385:

> When the faithful company sat with doors closed,  
> He brought himself in, bringing greeting of peace; and stretching forth  
> His pierced [Note: Col. 1474D, Munich manuscript: “let him free”] palms, he uncovered his side. But Thomas,  
> Whose surname was Didymus, had not been with  
> His brethren; and he bore doubtful faith in his heart,  
> Until, when they were again gathered there, he came—  
> He who had never been absent. Then, though the threshold was closed,  
> He stood in their midst, not disdaining to show  
> His open side to the disciple, and to have the wound proved by touch,  
> Patiently bearing the wavering of his mind.

### LXXXIX. That a creature is to be worshipped, and the contrary.

Chrysostom, on the Epistle to the Hebrews (1:6), sermon 3: “‘And let them worship him.’ Above he had said that God did not speak to us through prophets but through the Son, because the Son is better than angels; and he argued this from the name itself. Here, however, he wishes to draw arguments from another matter, namely worship: Christ according to the flesh was commanded to be worshipped by all the angels.” Likewise, sermon 5: “‘For he did not take hold of any angel’ (Heb. 2:16). It is full of wonder that our flesh sits above and is worshipped by angels, archangels, cherubim, and seraphim.”

Jerome, on the Epistle to the Philippians: “The divinity which was in Christ bestowed this name upon the assumed man, because he suffered and died for human beings, so that every creature might offer prayer in his name, so that all might worship the assumed man together with the Word.”

Augustine, book 1 against Maximinus: “‘Because he bestowed upon him the name,’ etc. (Phil. 2:9). He bestowed these things upon the man, not upon God. For when he was in the form of God, he was not without exaltation, nor did knees fail to bow to him. In the form, therefore, in which he was crucified, he was exalted. To him was bestowed the name above every name, so that the only-begotten Son of God is named together with the form of God.”

The same, on John 122: “The Arians say: ‘Why do you worship the flesh, which you do not deny to be a creature, together with divinity?’ I worship it because it is united to divinity, so that God the Son is both God and man. Finally, if you separate the man from him, I will never serve him. Just as, if someone found a royal purple robe or diadem lying on the ground, he would never worship it. When the king is clothed in them, however, one who disdains to worship them with the king incurs danger. Therefore, whoever disdains to worship the flesh united to divinity shall suffer the punishment of eternal death.”

Ambrose Autpert, on the Apocalypse, book 3: “Unless that human nature itself in the Word of God were to be worshipped by every creature, the Psalmist would never say: ‘Worship the footstool of his feet’ (Ps. 98:5). Therefore the footstool of his feet is rightly called the incarnation itself of the Redeemer, in which eternity is shown to be present.”

Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Philippians (2:9): “‘And he bestowed upon him the name.’ Whoever denies that the perfect Son of God was born from God is an Arian. Hence it is clear that he was born perfect. For in his birth he appears to have received all things. He was born in the fullness of divinity to perform all the things he performed, so that he received the gift before he performed the things for which he was born to perform them. Therefore the Father’s gift seems to be his being the Son, and his name above every name to be God. For the name of God is above every name by nature. He explains what these heavenly things are: there are no others. Yet to some it seems that the name was given to the man, and that it is above every name; but this is in no way fitting: the name of God cannot have been given to a body, because it is neither fitting that God should be changed into flesh nor possible that flesh should become what God is. If Scripture signifies that it was bestowed upon him who emptied himself, who took the form of a servant, who was made in the likeness of a human being, [Col. 1476A] who obeyed the Father—if a human being obeyed God the Father—what great thing is it that the Apostle said? But he calls this great, because, being equal, he obeyed. And what praise is there if a human being was made in the likeness of a human being, so that a human being may be said to have been made like a human being? But this cannot be. No one is made in the likeness of another unless he is other before he is made. He was made similar by cause, not by substance. Let us now consider the words and thus observe the force of the expression. Certainly the name above every name is the name of God. But by nature a creature does not bend the knee to an adoptive god, but to the true God, who is not a fellow creature. And how can a man be the glory of God the Father? Even if the man were an adoptive god, he cannot be in the glory of God the Father. For this belongs to him who was born from God. For to be in the Father’s glory is nothing other than to be God, so that Father and Son have one glory by common substance and power. This is unity of nature. What is contrary in saying that the Son received a gift from the Father, since everything of the Son is from the Father, from whom all things are believed to have their being? We call God’s substance nature because Christ was born from it.”

Augustine, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*: “The creature, Paul cries, was subjected to vanity (Rom. 8:20); and that which is subject to vanity cannot separate us from falsehood and join us to truth. The Holy Spirit grants this to us; therefore he is not a creature, because everything that exists is either God or creature. We must therefore love God as a certain threefold unity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” Likewise: “Rightly, therefore, the Catholic Church, the truest mother of Christians, not only preaches that he whose attainment is the most blessed life is to be worshipped with utmost purity and caution [Note: Col. 1475D, editions: ‘chastely’], admitting no creature for our worship or service and excluding from that inviolable eternity, to which alone humanity must be subject, everything that has been made; [Note: Col. 1475D, Munich manuscript: ‘believing’] you also embrace love of neighbor in such a way that with you every remedy is especially powerful for the various diseases [reading uncertain: *morborum*] by which souls are sick because of their sins.”

### XC. That after the ascension the Lord did not speak on earth, and the contrary.

[Col. 1476D]

Augustine, homily 9 on the Epistle of John: “When he was about to ascend, he spoke his final words; after those words he did not speak on earth.”

Gregory, *Homilies on the Gospels*, book 2, homily 23, concerning a hospitable man who received the Lord Jesus himself in the guise of a traveler—the Lord himself declaring this and saying to him in a vision on the following night: “On other days you received me in my members; yesterday you received me in myself.” Behold, when coming for judgment he says: “What you did to one of the least of mine, you did to me” (Matt. 25:40). Behold, before the judgment, when he is received through his members, he seeks out those who receive him also through himself; yet we are sluggish in showing hospitality.

The same, in the same [Col. 1477A] book, homily 39, concerning the monk Martyrius, who lifted the Lord Jesus himself, in the form of a leper, upon his shoulders and carried him: “When he was now approaching the doors of the monastery, the spiritual father of that monastery began to cry out in a loud voice: ‘Run, run! Open the monastery gates quickly, for Brother Martyrius comes carrying the Lord.’ Immediately, when Martyrius reached the entrance of the monastery, he who was thought to be a leper leaped down from his neck and appeared in the form in which the Redeemer of humankind, Christ Jesus, God and man, is usually recognized. Returning to heaven as Martyrius watched, he said to him as he ascended: ‘Martyrius, you were not ashamed of me on earth; I will not be ashamed of you in heaven.’ As soon as that holy man entered the monastery, [Col. 1477B] the father of the monastery said to him: ‘Brother Martyrius, where is the one whom you carried?’ He answered: ‘If I had known who he was, I would have held his feet.’ Then Martyrius himself related that, when he carried him, he felt no weight at all. Nor is this surprising: how could he feel the weight of him who carried the one carrying him?”

### XCI. That Mary alone suffered in her soul, and the contrary.

From Jerome’s sermon on the Assumption of Saint Mary: “Therefore the blessed Mother of God was rightly both virgin and martyr; and that she truly suffered is also testified by the prophet Simeon, speaking to her: ‘And a sword,’ he says, ‘shall pierce [Col. 1477C] your soul’ (Luke 2:35). From this it is evident that other saints, although they suffered for Christ in the flesh, nevertheless could not suffer in the soul, which is immortal; but the blessed Mother of God, because she suffered in that part which is held to be incapable of suffering, therefore—to confess it thus—because she suffered spiritually and grievously, she suffered more than all others, so that the force of grief pierced and possessed her whole soul as testimony to her exceptional love. Because blessed Mary suffered in mind, she was more than a martyr. Indeed, her love was stronger than death in a greater degree, because she made Christ’s death her own.”

Augustine, *City of God*, book 22: “If we consider more carefully, the pain called bodily belongs more to the soul than to the body. It is the soul’s property to feel pain, not the body’s, even when the cause of pain arises from the body, when the body is injured in the place where the pain is felt.”

The same, on Genesis: “Sensation belongs not to the body but to the soul through the body. Although it is acutely argued that the senses are distributed to the body according to the diversity of bodily elements, the soul—which has the power of sensation, although it is not bodily—exercises the power of sensation through a subtler body. It therefore initiates motion in all the senses from the subtlety of fire.” Likewise: “For the body does not feel; rather, the soul feels through the body, which it uses as a messenger to form within itself what is reported from without.”

### XCII. That the apostles were taught all things before Pentecost, or at Pentecost itself, and the contrary.

[Col. 1478A]

The Lord to the apostles according to John (15:15): “But I have called you friends, because I have made known to you whatever I heard from my Father.” Likewise (16:12): “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will teach you all truth.”

Paul in the Epistle to the Galatians (2:11): “But when Cephas came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he was blameworthy.”

### XCIII. That Peter and [Note: Col. 1477D, Cousin: “or.”] Paul and the other apostles are equal, and the contrary.

[Col. 1478B]

Ambrose, On Luke, book I: In the perfect human being there is a twofold excellence: intention as well as action. Likewise: When Peter says, “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:37), the intention of suffering was present, but not yet the action. Likewise: After he had accomplished many things with apostolic courage, he later bore the cross and underwent the deed of suffering; but in Peter, Andrew, John, and the other apostles there was equality both of intention and of action. From a certain sermon on the Passion of the apostles Peter and Paul, beginning thus: Although all the blessed apostles possess an equal grace of holiness before God, yet, I do not know how, Peter and Paul seem to excel the others by a certain special strength of faith in the Savior; and this we may prove from the judgment of the Lord himself. For he gave Peter, as a good steward, the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and Paul, as a competent teacher, the office of ecclesiastical instruction. Likewise: Paul too received from Christ, in a manner, the key of knowledge. Thus both received keys from the Lord: the one of knowledge, the other of power. For the treasures of knowledge are as it is written: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. 2:3). Therefore the blessed Peter and Paul stand out among all the apostles and excel by a certain special prerogative; hence it is uncertain which of the two should be preferred to the other. For I think them equal in merits.
