From a sermon of Pope Leo on the feast of Peter and Paul: Regarding their merits and virtues, which surpass every capacity for speech, we ought to think nothing different, nothing distinct, because election made them equal, labor similar, and the end equal.

Paul, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (15:8): “Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me was not empty; rather, I labored more abundantly than they all—yet not I, but the grace of God with me.”

Gregory, Homilies on Ezekiel, homily XVIII: Certainly, when the apostle Peter still wished to observe the custom of the law concerning circumcision, Paul opposed him to his face; and, speaking to the disciples, he called this zeal of Peter’s not only a fault but, what is worse, hypocrisy—that is, pretense—saying: “The other Jews joined in his pretense” (Gal. 2:13). Yet this first of the apostles, when he learned that some were criticizing Paul’s writings, says: “As our most beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him, speaking in them of these matters, in which there are some things difficult to understand, which the unlearned distort to their own destruction” (2 Pet. 3:15). Behold, Paul writes in his Epistles that Peter was blameworthy; behold, Peter in his own writings affirms that Paul is admirable in what he wrote. Certainly, unless Peter had read Paul’s Epistles, he would not have praised them. But if he read them, he found there that he himself was said to be blameworthy. He was rebuked, and this very fact pleased him, because he had not been pleasing in those matters in which he had thought otherwise than he should. He also yielded assent to his younger brother, and in the same matter made himself his inferior, so that in this too he might take the lead; in order that he who was first in the height of the apostolate might also be first in humility. Likewise: Behold, he is rebuked by one inferior to himself and does not disdain to be rebuked. He does not call to mind that he was first called to the apostolate, that he received the keys of the heavenly kingdom, that whatever sins he loosed on earth would be loosed in heaven, etc.

Jerome, To the Priest Paulinus: The apostle Paul, the chosen vessel transformed from a persecutor, was last in order and first in merits, because, though last, he labored more than all.

Jerome, To Damasus: The Lord and Savior is not all things in each person, but a part in each: for example, wisdom in Solomon, faith in Peter, virginity in John, and other things in the others. But when the end comes, then he will be all things in all, so that each of the saints may possess all virtues and Christ may be whole in all.

Ambrose, On Luke (9:27): “There are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” He speaks not of all, [Note: [Col. 1479D] editions: “one”], but of many. For Peter has not died, against whom the gate of hell could not prevail; nor have James and John died, the sons of thunder, who, having been taken up to behold heavenly glory, are not overcome by earthly things but have them subject beneath them. [Col. 1479D] Likewise: Therefore, so that you may know that Peter, James, and John did not taste death, they deserved to see the glory of the resurrection. For after these words he took these three alone, eight days later, and led them up the mountain. Likewise: Three alone, and three chosen, are led up the mountain. Peter ascends, who received the keys of the kingdom of heaven; John, to whom the mother is entrusted; James, who first ascended the priestly throne.

Augustine, On the Epistle to the Galatians: Peter, James, and John were more honored among the apostles, because the Lord showed himself to those three on the mountain.

The Creed of the Council of Ephesus: Finally, Peter and John are equal to one another in dignity, [Col. 1480A] which is why they are shown to be apostles and holy disciples.

### XCIV. That Peter, at the devil’s prompting, urged the Lord to avoid death, and the contrary

Hilary, On Matthew: When he had begun to preach that he must go to Jerusalem, then suffer many things from the elders of the people, the elders and chief priests, be killed, and rise after the third day, Peter took hold of him and said: “May this be far from you, Lord! This shall not happen” (Matt. 16:22). But he turned and said to Peter: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a stumbling-block to me” (ibid.). Therefore, after the prediction of the Passion, the devil, having obtained an opportunity—for he had departed from him only for a time, because it would have seemed quite unbelievable to the apostles that he in whom God was could be capable of suffering—used this occasion of human unbelief and instilled in Peter the sentiment of that opinion. Accordingly, Peter so detested the Passion that he said, “May it be far from you,” an expression containing an imprecation against abhorrent things. But the Lord, knowing the prompting of the devil’s art, said to Peter: “Get behind me,” that is, follow him by the example of the Passion. Yet, turning toward him through whom this opinion was being suggested, he added: “Satan, you are a stumbling-block to me.” For it is not fitting to suppose that the name Satan and the offense of being a stumbling-block were attributed to Peter after those great declarations of granted blessedness and authority. But because every unbelief is the devil’s work, the Lord, offended by Peter’s answer, repudiated with the reproachful name of this unbelief’s author.

Jerome, On Matthew (4:9): “‘All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.’ Then Jesus said to him: ‘Get behind me, Satan.’” To Peter it is said: “Get behind me, Satan,” that is, “Follow me, you who are opposed to my will.” But here he adds, “Get behind me, Satan,” and does not say “behind me,” so that it may be understood: “Go into eternal fire.”

### XCV. That Christ alone is the foundation of the Church, and the contrary

Paul, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.”

Augustine, Retractions, against the Donatian epistle [Note: [Col. 1480D] Cousin: “Donatist”]: I said concerning the apostle Peter that the Church was founded upon him as upon a rock. This sense is also sung in verses of blessed Ambrose, where he says of the cock: “when this, the very rock of the Church, sang, he washed away his guilt.” But I know that I later explained the saying, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16:18), so that it was understood to mean the one whom Peter confessed, saying: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God”; and thus Peter, called from this rock, represented the person of the Church when the Church was built upon this rock. For it was not said to him, “You are the rock,” but “You are Peter”; and the rock [Col. 1481A] was Christ.

Cyprian, in the epistle On the Discipline and Dress of Virgins: Peter also, to whom the Lord entrusted his sheep to be fed and guarded, upon whom he placed and founded the Church, etc.

The same, To Jubaianus, On Repeating the Baptism of Heretics: It is manifest where, and through whom, forgiveness of sins can be given. For first the Lord gave to Peter, upon whom he built the Church, that what Peter loosed on earth should be loosed.

The same, on the same matter, To Quintus: Peter, whom the Lord first chose and upon whom he built his Church.

Origen, On Matthew: “Whatever you bind on earth.” Since those who claim the place of the episcopate use this text in the manner of Peter, and teach that they received from Christ the keys of the kingdom of heaven—that those bound by them are bound in heaven, and those loosed by them, that is, who receive forgiveness, are loosed in heaven also—it must be said that, when they pronounce blessing, they must possess those works for which it was said to Peter: “You are Peter”; and they must be such persons that the Church of Christ may be built upon them.

Ecclesiastical History, book VI, on what Origen says in his exposition of the first Psalm: Peter, upon whom the Church is founded, writes only two Epistles.

Ambrose, Hexaemeron, on the works of the fifth day, speaking of the cock: “Finally, when the very rock of the Church sang, he washed away his guilt, which he had contracted by denying before the cock crowed.”

Jerome, On the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “If anyone builds upon [the foundation],” any teacher builds upon faith. [Col. 1481C] Likewise: Here he signifies teachers and instructors who rightly or wrongly instruct people upon the foundation which is Christ; the teaching of such teachers will be revealed in fire on the day of judgment, where, when sinners have been consumed, those proved worthy will remain. Teachers will receive the reward of recompense on account of those who have been approved; but in the case of those whom the fire has consumed, they will suffer loss because they labored in vain.

The same, On Jeremiah (16:16), book III: “They shall hunt them from every mountain and from the caverns of the rocks.” Not only is Christ the rock, but he also granted to the apostle Peter that he should be called a rock.

The same, To Marcella, On Our Faith and the Doctrine of the Heretic Montanus: Therefore the apostle Peter, upon whom the Lord founded [Col. 1481D] the Church, etc.

The same, On Psalm 86: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” Its foundations, whether of God or certainly of the Church. But who are God’s foundations except the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? Paul says (1 Cor. 3:10): “Like a wise architect, I laid a foundation,” that is, faith in the Trinity. And elsewhere: “They were awaiting a city having foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (Heb. 11:10). Whom may we call mountains? The apostles. In them were the foundations, where the faith of the Church was first laid. “The Lord loves the gates of Zion” (Ps. 86:2). Let us read the Apocalypse and Isaiah, where the city Jerusalem is built and its twelve gates are described; it is plain that he wrote about the apostles. Otherwise, the gates of Zion seem to me to be virtues (Jerome, Works II, 347).

The same, On Matthew: “Upon this rock I will build my Church.” Just as he gave light to the apostles so that they might be called the light of the world, and they received their other names from God, so too he bestowed the name “rock” upon Simon, who believed in Christ the rock; and according to the metaphor of a rock, it is rightly said to him: “I will build my Church upon you.” Likewise: “May this be far from you, Lord! This shall not happen to you” (Matt. 16:22). Let the person who investigates this consider that the rock, the blessing, the authority, and the building of the Church upon him were promised for the future, not granted in the present. “I will build,” he says, “my Church upon you, and the gates [Col. 1482B] of hell,” etc. Had he granted these things to him immediately, an error of perverse confession would never have found a place in him.

Leo, To All the Bishops of the Province: The Lord Jesus ordained that the truth, formerly contained in the proclamation of the Law and the Prophets, should go forth through the apostolic trumpet for the salvation of the whole world, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18). But he willed this mystery of office to belong to the duty of all the apostles in such a way that he placed it principally in the most blessed Peter, in order that from him, as from a certain head, he might spread his gifts as through the whole body, so that anyone who dared to depart from Peter’s firmness might understand himself to be excluded from the divine mystery [Note: [Col. 1481D] Cousin: “from the benefit of this mystery”]. For, having taken Peter into partnership in indivisible unity, he willed to call him what he himself was, saying: [Col. 1482C] “You are Peter,” etc., so that, by the wonderful gift of grace, the construction of the eternal temple might rest upon Peter’s firmness.

First sermon of Bishop Maximus on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul: This is Peter, to whom Christ the Lord willingly granted participation in his own name. For, as the apostle Paul taught, “the rock was Christ”; so through Christ Peter was made a rock, the Lord saying: “You are Peter,” etc. For just as water flowed from the rock in the wilderness for the Lord’s thirsty people, so from Peter’s mouth there sprang forth a fountain of saving confession for the whole world, wearied by the drought of unbelief [Note: [Col. 1482D] Cousin: “torn to pieces”].

### XCVI. That Peter did not deny Christ, and the contrary

[Col. 1482D] Ambrose, On Luke, book X, chapter 22: Let us consider in what condition Peter denies. “It was cold,” he says (John 18:18). If we consider the season, it could not have been cold. But it was cold where Jesus was not recognized, where there was no one to see the light, and where the consuming fire was denied. It was coldness of mind, not of body.

Likewise: Therefore, when the maidservant betrayed Peter as being among those who were with Jesus the Galilean, Matthew records that he answered at the first utterance: “I do not know what you are saying.” Mark also says this, for he followed Peter and could know more truly from Peter himself. Thus this first utterance of Peter, who was denying, nevertheless seems not to deny the Lord but to separate himself from the woman’s betrayal. Yet consider what he denied: namely, that he was among those who were with Jesus the Galilean, or, as Mark puts it, with Jesus the Nazarene. Did he deny that he was with the Son of God? This is to say: “I do not know the Galilean; I do not know the Nazarene, whom I know as the Son of God.” Let human beings have names derived from places; a homeland cannot name the Son of God, whose majesty no place contains.

And so that you may know this is true, it is proved also by an example. Elsewhere, when the Lord asked the disciples, “Whom do people say that the Son of Man is?” some said Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets. But Peter said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Did he there also deny, because he preferred to confess Christ not as the son of man but as the Son of God? Surely, what do we consider ambiguous here, when Christ himself also approved it?

Take another point. Peter was asked: “Are you among those who were with Jesus the Galilean?” Here he avoids the word of eternity; for those who had begun to exist were not “are.” This is to say: he alone was, who was in the beginning. Accordingly he said: “I am not.” For being belongs to him who always is. Hence Moses also says: “He who is sent me” (Exod. 3:14). Again, when pressed that he was among those, according to Mark he denied it. He denied that he was among those who were with the Galilean; he did not deny that he was with the Son of God. Finally, according to Matthew, when exposed as having been with Jesus the Nazarene, he said: “I do not know the man.” The same two Evangelists mentioned above record that, in the third utterance also, he answered with an oath that he did not know the man. And he rightly denied the man whom he knew to be God. Finally, where there is an oath, the response is guarded. For even if Peter denied, he nevertheless did not commit perjury, because the Lord had not said that he would commit perjury. And if there is doubt in Peter’s case, how dangerous is an oath!

But John puts it this way: when the maidservant asked Peter whether he was among that man’s disciples, he answered at the first utterance: “I am not.” For the apostle was not an apostle of a man, but of Christ. Paul too denied that he was an apostle of a man, saying: “Paul, an apostle, not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father” (Gal. 1:1). But lest he seem to introduce some ambiguity concerning the Incarnation, he added: [Col. 1483D] “who raised him from the dead,” so that you may believe him to be man after first believing him God. He preserves the same order elsewhere as well, when he says: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:2). For he calls him mediator of God before mediator of human beings. For it is not enough to believe both, unless the order of faith is observed.

Thus the answer agrees everywhere. For he who said, “I do not know the man,” rightly said, when asked whether he was among that man’s disciples: “I am not.” Therefore he did not deny himself to be Christ’s disciple; he denied himself to be the disciple of a man. Thus Peter and Paul denied the man whom they confessed to be the Son of God. What Peter thought, Paul expressed; the one advanced in this from the other. Peter’s error is the teaching of the apostles; Peter’s wavering is everyone’s rock. At last he wavers upon the waves, but Christ extends his right hand. He falls on the mountain, but is raised by Christ. Peter did indeed waver on the sea, but he walked. Peter’s wavering is firmer than our steadiness. He falls where no one else ascends; he trembles where no one else walks. Yet, though he wavers amid the waves, he does not slip; he trembles, but does not fall; he floats, but is not thrown headlong. And if he fell, he nevertheless fell on the mountain; but he fell more happily than others stood, more happily fell he whom Christ raised.

Again, John wrote that, when asked whether he was one of his disciples [Note: [Col. 1483D] editions: “whether”], he denied it. And he rightly denied it, because he was said to be among the disciples of one whom they had above called a man. For the third time he also denied that he had been seen with him; and this too derives from the preceding question. “I was not with him whom you call a man, but I did not depart from the Son of God.”

Luke too wrote that Peter, asked whether he was one of them, replied at the first utterance: “I do not know him,” and he spoke rightly. For it would have been rash to say that he knew him whom the human mind cannot comprehend. “No one knows the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11:27). Again, in the second utterance, according to Luke, the same Peter said: “I am not.” He preferred, clearly, to deny himself rather than Christ; or, because he seemed to deny association with Christ, he denied himself. Certainly, when he denies concerning a man, he sinned against the Son [Col. 1484C] of Man, so that it might be forgiven him, not against the Holy Spirit. Questioned a third time, he said: “I do not know what you are saying,” that is, “I do not know your sacrileges.” But we excuse him; he did not excuse himself. For an evasive answer confessing Jesus is not enough; open confession is required. What advantage is there in disguising one’s words if one wishes to appear to have denied? Therefore Peter is not represented as having answered thus deliberately, because afterward he remembered and wept. For he preferred to accuse his own sin, so that he might be justified by confessing, rather than be burdened by denying. “The righteous person is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17), and therefore he wept. Why did he weep? Because fault had crept upon him. I am accustomed to weep if fault is absent from me—that is, if I do not avenge myself, if I do not obtain what I perversely desire. Peter grieved and wept because he had erred as a man.

The same, in the Hexaemeron, on the fifth day: “The cock will not crow before you deny me three times.” Peter, strong by day, is disturbed by night; before the cock crows he falls, and falls three times, so that you may know that he did not fall through an unconsidered outpouring of speech, but also through a change of mind.

Matthew (26:33): Peter answered and said: “Even if all are offended because of you, I shall never be offended.” Jesus said to him: “Amen I say to you, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Likewise: Peter sat outside in the courtyard. One maidservant came to him, saying: “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” But he denied before everyone: “I do not know what you are saying.” [Col. 1485A] As he was going out through the gate, another maidservant saw him and said to those who were there: “This man also was with Jesus the Nazarene.” Again he denied with an oath: “I do not know the man.” A little later those standing there came and said to Peter: “Truly you also are one of them, for even your speech makes you known.” Then he began to curse and swear that he did not know the man.

Mark (14:29): Peter said to him: “Even if all are offended because of you, yet not I.” Jesus said to him: “Amen I say to you, today, in this night, before the cock crows twice, you will deny me three times.”

Luke (22:31): The Lord said to Simon: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers.” He said to him: “Lord, I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death.” And he said: “I tell you, Peter, the cock will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know me.”

John (13:38): Peter says to him: “Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.” Jesus answered: “Will you lay down your life for me? Amen, amen, I say to you: the cock will not crow until you deny me three times.”

Augustine, On John, tractate LXVI: He denied and said: “I am not.” Did the apostle Peter, as those who perversely seek to excuse him try to maintain, not deny Christ because, when asked by the maidservant, he replied that he did not know the man—as though one who denies Christ as man does not deny Christ? [Col. 1485C] Whoever therefore confesses Christ as God in such a manner as to deny him as man, Christ did not die for that person, because Christ died according to his humanity. Whoever denies Christ as man is not justified, because “through the disobedience of one man,” etc. (Rom. 5:19). Whoever denies Christ as man will not rise to the resurrection of life, because “through a man came the resurrection of the dead.” Likewise: If Peter, having denied Christ, had departed from here, what else would have happened but that he would have perished?

Bede, On Luke (22:56): “But he denied him, saying: ‘Woman, I do not know him.’” Some, out of pious affection toward the apostle Peter, interpret this passage as though he had blessed himself for not knowing him whom the human mind does not know how to comprehend, because no one knows the Son except the Father. Again, when questioned, he supposedly said: [Col. 1485D] “Man, I am not,” preferring to deny himself rather than Christ. But, when asked the third time and saying, “Man, I do not know what you are saying,” he supposedly meant that he did not know their sacrileges—that is, that by rejecting and execrating them he condemned them. But how frivolous this exposition is, both the Lord, who said that Peter would deny him three times, and Peter himself show; for Peter reveals by his subsequent tears that he spoke not deliberately but through a sudden lapse.

### XCVII. That Peter and Paul suffered on precisely the same day, not after a full year had elapsed, and the contrary

From Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 25, from the statements of Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, concerning Peter and Paul: For both, arriving together, taught in the Corinthian Church; and throughout all Italy, teaching together in this city also, they were crowned together by martyrdom at one and the same time.

Anacletus, to all bishops and priests, in the same [letter]: Blessed be God! Paul, the chosen vessel, was crowned in glorious death with Peter, under Emperor Nero, on one day and at one time.

Jerome, On Illustrious Men, chapter 1: Simon Peter, son of John, from the village of Bethsaida in the province of Galilee, brother of the apostle Andrew and leader of the others, after the episcopate of the Church of Antioch and the preaching to those of the Dispersion who had believed from the circumcision—in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia—went to Rome in the second year of Claudius to oppose Simon Magus. There he held the priestly chair for twenty-five years, until the final year of Nero, that is, the fourteenth, by whom he was fastened to a cross and crowned with martyrdom, his head turned toward the ground and his feet raised on high, declaring that he was unworthy to be crucified in the same manner as his Lord.

Likewise, chapter 5, concerning Paul: He too, in the fourteenth year of Nero, on the same day on which Peter was crucified at Rome for Christ, was beheaded and buried on the Ostian Way, in the thirty-seventh year after the Passion of the Lord.

Gregory of Tours, book I of Miracles, chapter 28: The apostle Paul died after the cycle of a year had elapsed, on the very day on which the apostle Peter suffered.

Martyrology, commemoration of the holy apostle Paul: Heaven received him, slain by the sword, when blessed Peter had been hung upon the cross—not indeed on the same day, but after the cycle of a year had elapsed—as the eloquent Arator writes. [Note: [Col. 1485] Arator, a Christian poet who wrote two books on apostolic history in the sixth century.]

### XCVIII. That Paul, even before his conversion, was called both Paul and Saul, and the contrary

Rufinus, following Origen, On Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: Some have thought that the apostle took his name from the proconsul Paul, whom in Cyprus he had subjected to faith in Christ, just as kings customarily, after conquests, are named, for example, Parthicus from the Parthians and Gothicus from the Goths. We too do not think this opinion ought entirely to be dismissed. Nevertheless, [Col. 1486D] because no such custom is found in the divine Scriptures, we seek an explanation rather from examples that occur there. Thus we find in the Scriptures some who used two names, and others even three. According to this custom, then, Paul seems to us to have used a double name: while he ministered to his own nation, he was called Saul, a name appearing more native to his country; but he was called Paul when he wrote instructions to the nations. For the very statement of Scripture, “Saul, who was also Paul” (Acts 13:9), clearly indicates that the name Paul belonged to his earlier appellation.

Jerome, To Paula and Eustochium, in the exposition of Paul’s Epistle to Philemon: Nor should Saul be thought to have been formerly called “Saulus” rather than Saul, because he belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, in which this name was more familiar; indeed Saul the king, David’s persecutor, was from the tribe of Benjamin. That we call him *Saulus* is not surprising, since Hebrew names are declined in imitation of Greek and Roman forms: just as *Josephus* is used for Joseph and *Jacobus* for Jacob, so also *Saulus* is said in our language for Saul.

Likewise, concerning Paul and Barnabas: When they reached Paphos, they found a certain magician with the proconsul Sergius Paul, who, summoning Barnabas and Paul, desired to hear from them the word of God. But the magician resisted and separated Sergius from the faith. Then Saul, Scripture says, who was also Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked at him and said: “O son of the devil, do you not cease to overthrow the ways of the Lord? Behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you shall be blind for a time.” Immediately darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking someone to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed. And when they had sailed from Paphos, Paul and those with him came to Perga in Pamphylia (Acts 13:9–13).

Observe carefully when he first received the name Paul. For just as Scipio, after Africa was subdued, assumed for himself the name Africanus, so Paul, admitted to preach to the nations, bore the trophies of his victory from the first spoil of the Church—the proconsul Sergius Paul—and raised a standard of victory, so that from Saul he might be called Paul. If the interpretation of the name is also sought, *Paulus* in Hebrew signifies “wonderful.” Truly it is wonderful that after Saul, which means “requested king” [Note: [Col. 1487D] editions: “sought”], because he had been sought from the devil in order to harass the Church, a chosen vessel should be made from a persecutor.

The same, On Paul’s Epistles: Just as the names of other saints—Abraham, Peter, and the rest—were changed in their progress and growth, so that they might be new even in name, so Paul too, advancing in grace, changed his very name.

Augustine, Confessions, book VIII: He himself, the least of the apostles, when the proconsul Paul had been sent beneath the yoke of your Christ through his service, likewise loved to be called Paul instead of Saul because of so great a mark of victory.

The same, On the Spirit and the Letter: Since Paul had formerly been called Saul, he chose this name, as it seems to me, for no other reason than to show himself small, as the least of the apostles, against the proud and those who rely upon their own works, in order to commend God’s grace.

The same, On Psalm 71: First Saul, then Paul; first proud, then humble. King Saul was proud. From Saul was made Paul, from the proud man one who was small; for *Paulus* means “small.” Hear how he was Saul, and how he is Paul: “I was,” he says, “a persecutor, a blasphemer, and a violent man” (1 Tim. 1:13). You have heard Saul; hear Paul: “For I am,” he says, “the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called [Col. 1488A] an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God; but by God’s grace I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:9): least in himself, great in Christ.

### XCIX. That James the Just, the Lord’s brother, was the son of Joseph, Mary’s betrothed, and the contrary

Ambrose, On the Epistle to the Galatians: Except James, the brother of the Lord. This James was appointed bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles; he was the son of Joseph, who was called the Lord’s father, and for this reason he was called the Lord’s brother.

Ecclesiastical History, book II, chapter 1: James, who was called the Lord’s brother because he was the son of Joseph, who was regarded as Christ’s father, since the Virgin Mary had been betrothed to him.

Gregory of Tours, Histories, [Col. 1488B] book I, chapter 22: It is reported that the apostle James, when he saw the Lord now dead upon the cross, vowed and swore that he would never eat bread unless he saw the Lord risen. At last, on the third day, the Lord returned after despoiling Tartarus, and, appearing to James in triumph, said: “Rise, James; eat, for I have now risen from the dead.” This is James the Just, whom they call the Lord’s brother because he was Joseph’s son, born of another wife.

Jerome, On Illustrious Men, chapter 2: James, who is called the Lord’s brother and surnamed the Just, was, as some think, the son of Joseph by another wife; but, as seems to me, the son of Mary, sister of the Lord’s mother, whom John mentions in his book. Immediately after the Passion of the Lord, he was appointed bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles.

The same, Against Helvidius: With the possibility of this supposition we might argue that Joseph had several wives also, and that the Lord’s brothers were from those wives—a fiction that many devise with an audacity less pious than reckless. You say that Mary did not remain a virgin; I claim more for myself: that Joseph himself was a virgin through Mary, so that from a virginal marriage a virgin son might be born. For if fornication cannot be attributed to a holy man, and it is not written that he had another wife, while he was rather the guardian of Mary, whom he was thought [Note: [Col. 1488D] Munich manuscript: “desired”] to have as a wife, it follows that he remained a virgin with Mary—he who deserved to be called the Lord’s father.

The same, 130, chapter 3 (Commentary on Matthew 13): Some, following the ravings of the apocrypha, suppose that the Lord’s brothers standing outside were sons by some little woman. But here we must understand the Savior’s cousins as his brothers, namely the children of his maternal aunt, that is, of the mother of James the Less, Jude, and Joseph.

The same, On the Epistle to the Galatians: James is called the Lord’s brother because he is shown to have been born of Mary of Clopas, sister of the Lord’s mother.

### C. That James the Just, the Lord’s brother, was the first bishop of Jerusalem, and the contrary
Ecclesiastical History, Book II, Chapter I: It is established, however, that there were two Jameses [Col. 1489A]: one who was thrown down from the pinnacle of the Temple, struck with a fuller’s [Note: [Col. 1489D] Monac.: “troubled” (*sollicitus*).] club, and put to death; the other is he who was beheaded by Herod. This James, I say—the one surnamed “the Just” by the ancients because of his merit in virtue and the distinction of his life—is reported by the histories to have first received the episcopal seat of the Church at Jerusalem, as Clement asserts in the sixth book of the *Disputations*, saying:

> Peter, James, and John, after the Saviour’s ascension, although they had been set by him above almost all the others, nevertheless did not claim for themselves the glory of precedence, but appointed James, who was called the Just, bishop of the apostles.

From the preface of the Nicene Council: For the bishop of Jerusalem too is held honourable by all, especially because [Col. 1489B] there the most blessed James, who was called the Just, who was also called the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained bishop by the apostles Peter, James, and John.

Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter II: James, who is called the Lord’s brother, surnamed the Just, was ordained bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles immediately after the Lord’s Passion.

Ambrose, *On the Epistle to the Galatians* (I, 19): “Except James, the Lord’s brother.” This James had been appointed bishop of Jerusalem by the apostles.

The same, *On Luke* (IX, 27): “There are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” For Peter did not die, nor James and John, the sons of thunder; when they were taken up into the sight [Col. 1489C] of heavenly glory, earthly things did not prevail over them, but lay beneath them. For he led these three alone up the mountain.

Likewise: Three alone, and three chosen by the Lord. Peter went up the mountain [Note: [Col. 1489D] Editions: “the three chosen are led up the mountain. Peter went up,” etc.], he who received the keys of the kingdom; John, to whom the Mother was entrusted; and James, who was the first to ascend the priestly throne.

## CI. That James the Just, the Lord’s brother, wrote the first of the seven canonical epistles; and the contrary.

Ecclesiastical History, Book II, Chapter XXI: Concerning James the Just, whose is that epistle which is written first among those called Catholic Epistles.

Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter II, on James the Just: He wrote only one Epistle, which is among the [Col. 1489D] seven Canonical [Note: [Col. 1489D] Editions: “Catholic.”] Epistles.

Isidore, *On the Life and Death of the Holy Fathers*: James, son of Zebedee and brother of John, fourth in order, wrote to the twelve tribes that are scattered among the nations; he preached the Gospel to Spain and to the peoples of the western regions, and shed forth the light of preaching at the setting of the world [Note: [Col. 1490D] Editions: “poured forth” (*infudit*).]. He was slain by the sword under Herod the tetrarch. He was buried in a marble shrine [Note: [Col. 1490D] Editions: “in Marmarica.”].

## CII. That Philip the deacon, who had four virgin daughters who were prophetesses [Note: [Col. 1490D] The words “who had four virgin daughters who were prophetesses” are absent in Cous.], and Philip the apostle were not the same person; and the contrary.

[Col. 1490A]

Acts of the Apostles (VI, 2), concerning the apostles themselves choosing seven deacons: “Then the twelve, calling together the multitude of the disciples, said: ‘It is not right for us to leave the word of God and serve tables. Therefore, brothers, choose from among yourselves seven men of good repute, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this task. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.’ And the proposal pleased the whole multitude, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, and Philip, and Prochorus,” etc.

Likewise, concerning Stephen’s killing (VIII, 1): “There arose on that day a great persecution against the Church which was [Col. 1490B] at Jerusalem, and all were scattered through the regions of Judaea and Samaria except the apostles. But Saul was ravaging the Church, entering house after house; and, dragging off men and women, he handed them over to custody. Therefore those who had been scattered went about, preaching the word. And Philip, going down into the city of Samaria, preached Christ to them. The crowds gave unanimous attention to what was said by Philip, hearing and seeing the signs that he performed.”

Likewise (VIII, 14): “When the apostles who were at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they had come, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For he had not yet come upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.”

Likewise, after much intervening material, Luke, who wrote these things concerning himself and Paul, says (Acts XXI, 8): “On the next day, having departed, we came to Caesarea; and, entering the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, we stayed with him. Now this man had four daughters who prophesied.”

Bede, *On the Same Acts of the Apostles*: “And Philip, going down into the city of Samaria”: Philip was among those scattered abroad, and was the first to preach Christ to Samaria.

Likewise, after some remarks on Peter and John: “Then they laid hands on them,” etc. Philip, who was evangelizing in Samaria, was one of the seven. For if he had been an apostle, he could have laid hands on them so that they might receive the Spirit, a power permitted to bishops alone. For a presbyter, whether the bishop is present or absent, when he baptizes anoints with chrism consecrated by the bishop; yet he does not mark the forehead with oil, which the bishop alone does when he imparts the Paraclete Spirit to the baptized.

Likewise, concerning Philip: “Until he came to Caesarea.” He means Caesarea of Palestine, where the house which he is described below as having is still shown to this day, as is also the chamber of his four virgin daughters who prophesied.

Rabanus, *On the Same Acts of the Apostles*: [Col. 1491A] “But when they had believed Philip preaching the Gospel”: Some say that this Philip was the apostle and one of the twelve, but this does not appear true from the sequence of this book.

Likewise: “The Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away,” or, “The Spirit of the Lord rushed powerfully upon him,” as it also came upon the apostles. The stronger the faith, the greater the spiritual impetus. From the fact that the Spirit rushed upon the eunuch, Philip is said to have been an apostle; yet we do not read that he performed either the laying on of hands or the invocation of the Holy Spirit. Hence it is clear that at the first fruits of the Gentiles the Spirit descended spontaneously, not through laying on of hands or invocation, so that the apostles might have an excuse against Jews accusing them because they baptized Gentiles. For who can prevent the Spirit [Col. 1491B] of the Lord, or who could bar someone from water upon whom the Spirit had descended?

Likewise, concerning Philip: “Now this man had four daughters who prophesied.” Elsewhere the daughters of Philip the apostle are said to have been prophetesses; but the truth of this passage must not be contradicted, unless perhaps it is understood that both had prophetess daughters.

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter XXVIII: Since in the preceding sections we have explained the life and death of Peter and Paul, and have already mentioned in part the time when John departed this life, I think it appropriate now to give an account, on the authority of Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, of the place of his resting. For Polycrates, writing to Victor, bishop of the city of Rome, also mentions Philip the apostle and his daughters together, saying:

> As we have already stated above, great lights have fallen asleep in the regions of Asia; the Lord will raise them on the last day of his coming, when he comes in glory and seeks out all his saints. I mean Philip, who was one of the apostles, who fell asleep at Hierapolis. Two of his daughters also grew old there as virgins; and another of his daughters, filled with the Holy Spirit, remained at Ephesus. And John, he who reclined upon the Lord’s breast, who was a priest of God, wearing the pontifical *petalum*, and a martyr and most excellent teacher, fell asleep at Ephesus.

It is enough to have added these matters concerning the places where they rest in the sleep of peace. Gaius too, previously mentioned, in his *Dialogue*, which he writes in debate with Proclus, recalls in agreeing words both Philip’s daughters and his death, saying:

> After these things there were four daughters of Philip; his tomb stands at Hierapolis, a city of Asia, together with his daughters.

Luke also mentions them in the Acts of the Apostles, while they were still living at Caesarea. He says: “We came to Caesarea and, entering the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, we stayed with him. Now this man had four daughters who prophesied” (Acts XXI, 8).

Isidore, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, concerning Philip the apostle: He died, crucified and stoned, at Hierapolis, a city in the province of Phrygia; his body rests there together with those of his daughters.

Martyrology, the Kalends of May: The feast of the apostles Philip and James. Of these, Philip, after converting almost Scythia to faith in Christ, came to rest by a glorious end at Hierapolis, a city of Asia.

Likewise, the eighth day before the Ides of June: The feast of blessed Philip, who was one of the seven deacons. Distinguished by signs and wonders, he came to rest at Caesarea; beside him lie buried three of his virgin daughters, prophetesses. For his fourth daughter, full of the Holy Spirit, died at Ephesus.

## CIII. That all the apostles had wives except John [Note: [Col. 1491D] Cous.: “apart from John”], and the contrary.

Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter XXX: This Clement, indeed, whose words [Col. 1492B] we have noted, writing against those who despise marriage, says among other things:

> Or do they disapprove also of the apostles? For Peter and Philip had wives, and even gave their daughters in marriage to men. Paul too does not hesitate, in one of his Epistles, to mention—or offer a greeting to—his own consort, whom he says he does not take about with him, in order that he may be freer for the preaching of the Gospel.

Ambrose, *On the Second Epistle to the Corinthians*: All the apostles, except John and Paul, had wives.

Jerome, to the virgin Eustochium: “Concerning virgins,” says the Apostle, “I have no commandment of the Lord” (I Cor. VII, 25): this, that he himself might be a virgin, was not a matter of command but of his own choice. [Col. 1492C] For those must not be heard who invent that he had a wife, since in urging perpetual chastity he added: “I wish all people to be as I myself am” (I Cor. VII, 7). And elsewhere (I Cor. IX, 5): “Do we not have authority to take women about with us, as do the other apostles?”

The same, *On Illustrious Men*: James, the Lord’s brother, drank neither wine nor strong drink; he was holy from his mother’s womb; he ate no flesh; he was never shorn, nor anointed, nor did he use a bath; his knees were believed to have acquired the hardness of camels.

The same, *Against Jovinian*: James, the Lord’s brother, was of perpetual virginity, as Josephus too reports. He himself writes in his Epistle (I, 16): “Do not be deceived, brothers. Every good gift,” etc. A virgin teaches virginity, because every perfect gift is from above, descending where there are no marriages.

Haymo, *On the First Epistle to the Corinthians*: “But I wish all people to be as I myself am,” that is, if it were possible, I would wish all people to be virgins, as I am, and to love virginity as I love it.

## CIV. That in the figures of the four living creatures Matthew is prefigured by the man, Mark by the lion [Note: [Col. 1492D] Cous.: “designated beforehand”], and the contrary.

From Jerome’s general preface to the four Gospels: These four Gospels were foretold long before, as the book of Ezekiel also proves, [Col. 1493A] in which the first vision is set forth thus: “And in the midst, the likeness of four living creatures; and their faces were the face of a man, the face of a lion, the face of a calf, and the face of an eagle.” The first face, that of the man, signifies Matthew, who began his book as it were from a man: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” The second signifies Mark, in whom is heard the voice of a lion roaring in the wilderness: “A voice crying in the desert: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.” The third, that of the calf, prefigures the evangelist who took his beginning from Zechariah the priest. The fourth signifies John the evangelist, who, taking up the wings of an eagle and hastening toward higher things, discoursed on the Word of God. Therefore the Apocalypse also introduces the four living creatures full of eyes, saying (IV, 7): “The first living creature was like a lion, and the second living creature like a calf, [Col. 1493B] and the third like a man, and the fourth like an eagle flying.” By all this it is plainly shown that only four Gospels ought to be received.

From another preface, which begins thus: “First it must be asked what the four evangelists signify”: Matthew, the face of a man; Luke, that of a calf; Mark, that of a lion; John, that of an eagle. The Lord Jesus Christ fulfilled all: man in being born, calf in being sacrificed, lion in rising again, eagle in ascending.

Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, Book I: Hence it seems to me that those who interpreted the four living creatures in the Apocalypse as referring to the four evangelists observed something more probable when they understood the lion as Matthew, the man as Mark, the calf as Luke, [Col. 1493C] and the eagle as John, than those who assigned the man to Matthew, the eagle to Mark, the calf to Luke, and the lion to John. For they sought to draw a certain inference from the beginnings of the books, rather than from the evangelists’ entire intention, which ought rather to have been examined as a whole. For he who especially commended Christ’s royal character is much more suitably understood as the lion. That Luke is signified by the calf neither party doubted. Mark, therefore, who chose to recount neither Christ’s royal lineage nor his priestly lineage, kinship, or consecration, yet is shown to have been occupied with the things Christ did as man, seems to be signified, among those four living creatures, only by the figure of a man.

Bede, *On the Apocalypse*: “And the first living creature was like a lion,” etc. [Col. 1493D] These living creatures are interpreted in many ways. But blessed Augustine, following the order of this book, says that Matthew is understood in the lion, because he recounts Christ’s lineage of royal dignity—he who also “the Lion of the tribe of Judah conquered.” For Judah is a lion’s cub; and in Matthew Christ is feared by a king as king, adored by the Magi, the king who settles accounts with his servants, the king who makes a wedding feast for his son, and finally separates the sheep from the goats. But the face of a man signifies Mark, who says nothing about the Lord’s royal and priestly power, but simply recounts the deeds of Christ as man, etc.

The same, in the prologue to his exposition on Luke: As to your statement that some are troubled by the reason why, in the Apocalypse, they wished by a new interpretation to assign Matthew to the lion and Mark to the man: whoever those are whom this troubles should have observed [Col. 1494A] that I said this was handed down not by my novel explanation but by the ancient exposition of the Fathers. For it did not seem so to me of myself; rather, I recalled that it had been set forth in this way by blessed Augustine, and I also added briefly the grounds on which he maintained it.

## CV. That the same Mary anointed both the Lord’s head and feet; and the contrary.

From a homily of Bishop John on Judas’s betrayal: “Then one of the twelve went,” etc. Before the time of betrayal, before the hour of delivery, a prostitute came, carrying an alabaster vessel in her hands, and poured ointment over the Lord’s head. A little earlier the prostitute suddenly came forth chaste; and when the woman of the brothel left the brothel, the disciple entered Gehenna. [Col. 1494B] When she renounced the payment for her body, he demanded the price of his master and blood. When she kissed the feet in order to be received, that man kissed the Lord’s lips in order to betray him. Therefore I said that he showed himself the master of his teacher, he who made even prostitutes hasten in flight to obedience. Why, then, could he who wished to change the conduct of prostitutes not retain a disciple? He did indeed wish, I say, and unquestionably wish, to retain him; but he did not wish to bring about good by compulsion.

Jerome, *On Hosea*, in the prologue: This is the prostitute and adulteress who in the Gospel dried the Lord’s feet with her hair and honoured them with the ointment of her confession. When the disciples, and especially the betrayer, were indignant that it had not been sold and its price distributed for feeding the poor, the Lord answered: “Why do you trouble this woman? She has worked a good work upon me; for you will always have the poor with you, but me you will not always have” (John XII, 8). And, lest what she had done be thought insignificant, and lest nardus pisticus—that is, most faithful ointment—be referred to anything other than the Church, he gives us an occasion for understanding and promises her the rewards of great faith, saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: wherever this Gospel shall be preached in the whole world, what she has done shall also be spoken of in remembrance of her.”

The same, to Damasus, second treatise on the *Song of Songs*: The Gospel relates that a woman came having an alabaster vessel of costly pure nard ointment; she was then indeed a sinner, but holy—the woman concerning whom [Col. 1494D] you sent me a discourse. For I know that Luke spoke of a sinner, whereas Matthew, John, and Mark did not speak of a sinner. Therefore there came not that sinful woman but a holy one, whose name John also supplied, having an alabaster vessel of costly ointment, and she poured it upon Jesus’ head. Thus, in the figure of this woman who now speaks, “my nard gave its fragrance” (Song I, 11): she poured ointment upon God.

Bede, *On Luke* (VII, 37), Book III: “And behold, a woman in the city who was a sinner,” etc. Some say that this was not the same woman who, when the Lord’s Passion was approaching, poured ointment upon both his head and feet, because this woman washed his feet with tears, dried them with her hair, and is explicitly called a sinner; while concerning the other no such thing is written, nor could a prostitute immediately become worthy to anoint the Lord’s head. But those who investigate more carefully find that she was the same woman—Mary Magdalene, the sister of Lazarus, as John relates—and that she performed this service twice. First, indeed, in this passage, when she first came and obtained forgiveness of sins; but a second time, at Bethany, no longer a sinner but holy, she is found to have anointed not only his feet but also his head. This also accords most beautifully with the allegorical rule. For every faithful soul is first humbled at the Lord’s feet and bows down to be freed from sins. Then, as its merits increase over time, it pours upon the Lord’s, as it were, head the fragrant spices of joyful faith.

The same, in his homily for the Tuesday after Palm Sunday: Mary, Lazarus’s other sister, received a pound of costly pure nard ointment as a token of great love, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped them with her hair. But it must first be noted that, as we have learned from the accounts in Matthew and Mark, Mary not only anointed the Lord’s feet, but also poured nard upon his head. Nor is it to be doubted that she was also the woman who, as Luke relates, once a sinner, came to the Lord with an alabaster vessel of ointment and, standing behind at his feet, began to wet his feet with tears; she wiped them with her hair, kissed them, and anointed them with ointment.

## CVI. That now no one can be saved without baptism in water; and the contrary.

[Col. 1495C] According to John (III, 5), Jesus answered: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God.” Ambrose, *On the Sacraments*, sermon I: Understand that water does not cleanse without the Holy Spirit; and therefore you have read that the three witnesses in baptism are one—water, blood, and the Holy Spirit—because if you remove one of these, the sacrament of baptism does not stand. For what is water without the cross of Christ? An element without any sacramental effect. Nor likewise is there a sacramental mystery of regeneration without water. For unless someone is born again of water, etc. The catechumen also believes in the cross of the Lord; but unless he is baptized in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, he cannot receive remission of sins [Col. 1495D] nor draw the gift of spiritual grace.

Augustine, in *On Nature and Grace*: In the statement, “through the righteousness of one [came justification of life] to all people” (Rom. V, 18), no one is omitted; not because all believe in him and are washed by his baptism, but because no one is justified unless he believes in Jesus and is washed by his baptism.

The same, *On Rebuke and Grace*: I shall dwell also upon the baptism of infants, because none of them can say, when it is given to that little one but not to this one, that both are within the power of God and that without that sacrament no one enters the kingdom of God.

Prosper’s *Replies to Rufinus*, ch. IX: For the redemption of human beings it is not enough [Col. 1496A] that Christ was crucified, unless they die with him and are buried with him in baptism. [Note: [Col. 1495] Munich manuscript: “are commemorated” (*commemorantur*).] Otherwise, once the Savior had been born and crucified for us all, it would not have been necessary for us to be reborn and planted together in the likeness of his death. But since no human being attains salvation without this sacrament, the one who has not been crucified in Christ has not been saved by the Lord’s cross. And one is not crucified in Christ who is not a member of Christ’s body. Nor is one a member of Christ’s body who does not put on Christ through water and blood.

Matthew (XVI, 25): “Whoever has lost his life for my sake will find it.” Likewise (X, 32): “Therefore everyone who confesses me before men, I also will confess him before my Father.”

Augustine, *The City of God*, book XIV: For he who said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John III, 5), made these persons exceptions by another statement, where he says no less generally: “Whoever has confessed me,” etc.; and elsewhere: “Whoever has lost his life for my sake will find it.”

The same, *On Faith to Peter*: From the time when the Savior said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,” apart from the sacrament of baptism—except for those who, in the Catholic Church, shed their blood without baptism—we believe that no one can receive either the kingdom of heaven or eternal life, save through martyrdom. The candidate for baptism confesses his faith before the priest. This [Col. 1496C] is also what the martyr does before the persecutor. The one receives the Holy Spirit by the bishop’s laying on of hands; the other becomes a dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit, since it is not he himself who speaks, but the Spirit of the Father who speaks in the Spirit. The one has partaken of the Eucharist in remembrance of the Lord’s death; the other dies together with Christ himself.

Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, book IV [Note: [Col. 1495] *On Baptism against the Donatists*, IV, Maurists XI, 139.]: Blessed Cyprian adduces no slight argument from that thief to whom, though unbaptized, it was said: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43), to show that suffering for Christ’s name sometimes supplies the place of baptism. Yet, after considering this again and again, I find that not suffering for Christ’s name alone can supply what was lacking from baptism, but also faith and conversion of heart, if in the straits of time it is impossible to obtain the ministry of baptism [Col. 1496D] for its celebration. For that thief was not crucified for Christ’s name, if he suffered for the deserts of his crimes; nor did he suffer because he believed, but while suffering he believed. Thus the power, even without the visible sacrament of baptism, of the Apostle’s statement, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10), was made plain in that thief. But this is then fulfilled invisibly when not contempt for religion but an emergency of necessity prevents the ministry of baptism. And just as in that thief what was lacking from the sacrament of baptism is to be believed supplied by the same grace [Col. 1497A] of the Almighty in infants who die unbaptized, because through the incapacity of their age, not through an impious will, they can neither believe with the heart unto righteousness nor confess with the mouth unto salvation. Therefore, when prayer is made for them so that the celebration of the sacrament may be fulfilled on their behalf, it surely avails for their consecration, because they themselves cannot answer. For it is another’s act when one believes through another, just as it was another’s act when one sinned in another.

Likewise: But if bodily baptism was absent in the thief through necessity, salvation was perfect because it was spiritually present through piety. So also, when piety itself is present, if through necessity there is lacking what was present to the thief, salvation is perfected. This is the tradition held by the whole Church when infant children are baptized, who in heart [Note: [Col. 1497D] Munich manuscript: “certainly” (*certe*).] cannot yet believe unto [Col. 1497B] righteousness or confess with their mouth unto salvation, as the thief could; indeed, by crying and wailing while the mystery is celebrated in them, they interrupt the mystic words themselves, and yet no Christian would say that they are baptized in vain.

Likewise: By all these things it is shown that the sacrament of baptism is one thing and conversion of heart another, but that human salvation is completed by both. Nor, if one of these is absent, ought we therefore to think it follows that the other is absent also, because the former can exist without the latter, as in an infant, and the latter could exist without the former in the thief, God supplying in either case what would not have been lacking through the will. But when one of these is absent through the will, a person is involved in guilt. Baptism [Col. 1497C] can be present where conversion of heart is absent. Conversion of heart, however, can indeed be present when baptism has not been received, but it cannot be present when baptism has been despised. For there can in no way be said to be conversion of heart to the Lord when God’s sacrament is despised.

The same, in the second book of the *Retractions*: When I said that suffering takes the place of baptism, I did not use the example of that thief sufficiently aptly, because it is uncertain whether he was not baptized.

Likewise: What I said, that the thief had not received baptism itself, we find that other leaders of the Church before us also stated in their books; but by what evidence it can be adequately shown that he was not baptized, I do not know.

Likewise: I stated as certain that the thief had not visibly been baptized, although it is uncertain and it is rather to be believed [Col. 1497D] that he was baptized, as I later argued.

The same, *On the Origin of the Soul*, book I, to Vincentius Victor: Do not believe, do not say, if you wish to be Catholic, that an infant who is overtaken by death before being baptized can attain forgiveness of original sins. The examples which mislead you, whether that of the thief who confessed the Lord on the cross, or that of Dinocrates, Perpetua’s brother, offer you no support for this erroneous opinion. For although that thief might by divine judgment have been counted among those cleansed by the confession of martyrdom, you nevertheless do not know whether he was not baptized. For, apart from the belief that he could have been sprinkled with water [Col. 1498A] together with blood springing from the Lord’s side, while fastened nearby, and cleansed by a baptism of this most holy kind—what if he had been baptized in prison, as some later, in the time of persecution, were able secretly to obtain? What indeed if before he was arrested? For if we maintain that persons about whom it is not written whether they were baptized departed this life without baptism, we calumniate the apostles themselves, since, apart from the apostle Paul, we do not know when they were baptized. If you suppose that they were baptized, this could have become known to us through the Lord’s saying to Peter: “He who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet” (John XIII, 10). What shall we say of the others, concerning whom we do not read even such a statement—Barnabas, Timothy, Titus, the evangelists Mark and Luke themselves, and countless others—whom, far be it from us to doubt, were baptized, although we do not read it?

Moreover, Dinocrates, a boy of seven years—at which age, when children are baptized, they already recite the Creed and answer questions for themselves—why did he not seem to you to have been baptized? I do not know why you instead considered that he had been drawn back by his own father to the sacrileges of the pagans, and that this had harmed him in the punishments from which he was delivered through his sister’s prayer. For you have not read either that he was never a Christian or that he was a catechumen, although that narrative itself is not in the canon of Scriptures from which testimony must be brought forward for these questions of mine.

The same, to Seleuciana: It is written when the apostle Paul was baptized, [Col. 1498C] but it is not written when the other apostles were baptized. Yet we ought to understand even these to have been baptized, whether by John’s baptism or, more credibly, by Christ’s baptism. Concerning Peter this is understood from what he heard from the Lord: “He who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet.”

The same, *On Nature and Grace*: I say that an infant born in a place where he could not be helped by Christ’s baptism, and overtaken by death, was therefore such—that is, departed without the washing of regeneration—because it could not have been otherwise. But the Apostle does not absolve him when he says: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and death through sin, and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.” Therefore, by the condemnation which runs through the whole mass [Col. 1498D], the kingdom of heaven is rightly not lost to him, although he was not only not a Christian, but could not even have become one.

Jerome, to Heliodorus: Ecclesiastical rank does not make one a Christian. Cornelius the centurion, still a pagan, is cleansed by the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Ambrose, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians: We know also that the Holy Spirit was given by God without the laying on of hands, and that one not baptized obtained the remission of sins.

The same, in the letter *On the Consolation at the Death of the Emperor Valentinian*, to his sisters: I hear that you grieve because he did not receive the sacraments of baptism. Tell me: had he not long before desired this, so that, when he came into Italy, [Col. 1499A] he might be initiated? And most recently he made known that he wished to be baptized by me, and for this reason he thought that I should be summoned before other matters. Does he then not have the grace which he desired? Does he not have that which he asked for? Certainly, because he asked, he received. And whence comes that saying: “The righteous man, whatever death overtakes him, his soul shall be in rest” (Wisdom IV, 7)?

Loose, therefore, holy Father, the hands of your servant.

Likewise: He did not fear to displease men, so that he might please you alone in Christ. How did he who had your Spirit not receive your grace? Or if the fact that the mysteries were not solemnly celebrated causes concern: then martyrs too, if they were catechumens, are not crowned. But if they are washed in their own blood, then both their piety and their will wash them.

Likewise: Shall I still seek intercession for him for whom I presume a reward? Let us seek his rest with pious affection.

Likewise: I grieve for you, son Gratian; I grieve also for you, son Valentinian! You thought that through me you would be rescued from danger; you loved me not merely as a parent, but hoped in me as your redeemer and deliverer. You said: “Do you think that I shall see my father?” Your will toward me was beautiful, but your confidence was not effective. Alas for me, vain hope in a human being! Alas that I did not know your will sooner. Lord, since no one has anything by which he may show greater devotion to others than what he desires for himself, do not separate me after death from those whom I felt most dear in this life. Lord, I ask that where I am, they also may be with me. I beseech you, supreme God, that you raise again these beloved young men by a timely resurrection, that you may compensate by a timely resurrection for this untimely course of life [Col. 1499C] of theirs.

From the *Life of Saint Gregory* [Note: by John the Deacon], book II, ch. 45, one reads: That most blessed pope delivered by his prayers and tears the soul of Trajan, the deceased pagan emperor, from the torments of hell. It is said that he was moved to venture this prayer on behalf of Trajan because, when he had come to the basilica of Saint Peter on account of the gentleness of that judge, he wept there so long over the error of that most merciful ruler that on the following night he received an answer that he had been heard for Trajan. For, when Trajan was at one time hurrying most urgently to the preparations for an imminent war, a certain widow cried out for vengeance for her murdered son; he dismounted from his horse [Col. 1499D] and did not depart until he himself had conducted the widow’s case.

And it should be noted that one does not read that Trajan’s soul was placed in paradise, since it is written: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the divine kingdom.” Rather, it is simply said that by God’s mercy he does not feel the torments of hell; just as one fire of Gehenna can hold all sinners alike, yet does not burn them equally, so that each feels punishment and guilt in proportion to the guilt he has deserved. Therefore Trajan did not attain grace, even if he escaped the bodily punishment of Gehenna; nor does he enter the kingdom of heaven [Col. 1500A] if he avoids bodily fire and enjoys the very mild punishment of infants. Perhaps it was rightly shown to the spiritual man that Trajan’s justice and clemency had merited this, since he himself is known to have done this as a recompense for justice.

For when Trajan answered the aforementioned widow, as she cried out, that, if he returned safely from battle, he would in every respect exact vengeance, the widow said: “If you are going to die in battle, who will provide for me and my children?” [Note: [Col. 1499D] Munich manuscript: “remain” (*moraturus*).] Trajan answered: “He who will rule after me.” The widow said: “And what will it profit you if another renders justice to me?” Trajan answered: “Certainly, nothing.” And the widow said: “Is it not better for you to render justice to me yourself and receive your reward for it, than to pass this on to another?” Then Trajan, moved by reason and compassion, [Col. 1500B] dismounted from his horse and rendered judgment.

Jerome, to Rusticus: A pagan or Jew is by no means to be mourned, since they were not in the Church and died once; concerning them the Savior said: “Let the dead bury their dead.” Rather, mourn those who depart from the Church through crimes and do not willingly return to it, to the condemnation of their vices.

Augustine, book I, *On the Baptism of Infants*: As through one all are unto condemnation, so through one all are unto justification. Nor is there any middle place for anyone, where he could be neither with the devil nor with Christ.

The same, *On Faith to Peter*: Hold most firmly and do not doubt in the least that not only persons already exercising reason, but also infants, who either begin to live in their mothers’ wombs and die there, or who, once born, depart from this [world] [Col. 1500C] without the sacrament of baptism given in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, are to be punished with the everlasting penalty of eternal fire; because, although they have committed no sin by their own act, they nevertheless contracted the condemnation of original sin through fleshly conception and birth.

Likewise: Hold most firmly and do not doubt in the least that, except those baptized in their own blood for Christ’s name, no human being will receive eternal life unless in this life he has been turned from his evils through repentance and faith and freed through the sacrament of faith and repentance and through baptism. For adults it is necessary both to repent of their evils, to hold the Catholic faith according to the rule of truth, [Col. 1500D] and to receive the sacrament of baptism. For infants, however, who can neither believe by their own will nor repent for the sin which they derive originally, the sacrament of faith, which is holy baptism, suffices for salvation so long as their age cannot be capable of reason.

From the letter of Pope Siricius, ch. 13: He who baptizes in wine because of an immediate [Note: [Col. 1500D] Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, III, p. 676: “nearest”; in Hardouin: “because of the greatest.”] necessity, so that a sick person may not be endangered, incurs no blame for such an act. But if water was available and no such necessity pressed, he is to be deprived of communion and subjected to penance. The person [Note: [Col. 1500D] Mansi: “pressing”; perhaps “infant.”] who has been baptized in the holy Trinity [Col. 1501A] is to remain in that baptism.

## CVII. That baptism destroys all sins, both original and personal; and the contrary

Augustine, *Enchiridion*: There is no one who does not die to sin in baptism; infants, however, die only to original sin, while adults die also to all those sins which, by living badly, they have added to that which they contracted by being born.

The same, book I of *The City of God*, concerning those who kill themselves: If we are willing to admit this reason, it will proceed so far that people ought to be urged to kill themselves immediately after they have been washed in the laver of holy regeneration and have received remission of all [Col. 1501B] sins. For that is the time to guard against all future sins, when all past sins have been erased.

Likewise: O mad minds! What is this great thing—not error, but madness?

Gennadius, *On the Orthodox Faith*: The baptized person confesses his faith before the priest; the martyr does the same before the persecutor. All sins are remitted to the former; in the latter they are extinguished.

From the Council of Carthage, ch. 1: The person to be ordained bishop must first be examined whether he believes that in baptism all sins are remitted—that is, both the original sin contracted and those sins voluntarily committed, etc. When he has been examined in all these matters and found fully instructed, then he is to be ordained bishop.

Ambrose, book I, *On Penance*: Therefore in baptism there is remission of all [Col. 1501C] sins. What difference does it make whether priests claim this authority as granted to them through penance or through the laver? In both there is one mystery.

The same, *On the Mysteries*: “He who has bathed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John XIV, 10). Peter was clean, but he had to wash his foot; for by succession he possessed the sin of the first man, when the serpent tripped him and persuaded him into error. Therefore his foot is washed, in order that inherited sins may be taken away. For our own sins are remitted through baptism.

The same, *On the Sacraments*, book III: You came up from the font: what followed? You heard the reading; the high priest, girded for service, washed your feet. What is this mystery? “Unless I wash [Col. 1501D] your feet,” he says, “you shall have no part with me” (ibid., 8). We know that the Roman Church does not have this custom, although in all things we follow its type and form. Yet it does not have the custom of washing feet; perhaps it has declined it because of the multitude. For there are those who say, and try to excuse themselves, that this ought not to be done as a mystery, not in baptism or regeneration, but because the feet of a guest must be washed. Humility is one thing, sanctification another. Finally, hear that it is a mystery and sanctification: “Unless I wash your feet, you shall have no part with me” (ibid., 8). I say this not in order to rebuke others, but to commend my own observances [Col. 1502A]. In all things I desire to follow the Roman Church, but we too are human beings and possess understanding; therefore, where something is observed more rightly elsewhere, we too preserve it more rightly. We follow the apostle Peter himself; we adhere to his devotion. What does the Roman Church answer to this? Certainly the apostle Peter himself, who was priest of the Roman Church, is the author for us of this assertion. Peter himself said: “Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands” (ibid., 9). You see faith: what he first excused belonged to humility; what he afterward offered belonged to devotion and faith.

The Lord answers: “The one whom I have washed need not be washed again, except only the feet.” Why is this? Because in baptism every fault is washed away. Therefore guilt departs; but because Adam was tripped by the devil, and poison was poured over his feet, [Col. 1502B] therefore you wash the feet, so that in the part in which the serpent lay in wait, a greater help of sanctification may be added, by which afterward he may not be able to trip you. Therefore you wash the feet, in order to wash away the serpent’s poisons.

Likewise: After the font, it remains for perfection to take place, when by the priest’s invocation the Holy Spirit is poured in—the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, etc. These are the seven powers when you are sealed. Likewise: After this you must come to the altar.

## CVIII. That infants to be baptized have no sin; and the contrary

Jerome, on Ezekiel: So long as the soul [Col. 1502C] has been joined to an infant, it is free from sin. [Note: [Col. 1501D] Cousin edition: “Because the Lord’s soul was established in infancy [Col. 1502D], etc.”]

The same, to Heliodorus, in the epitaph for Nepotian: “Death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over them,” etc. (Rom. V, 14). If Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are in hell, who is in the kingdom of heaven? If your friends were under the punishment of Adam’s offense, and those who had not sinned were held liable for another’s sins, what is to be believed of those who said in their hearts: “There is no God”?

Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*: Therefore eternity was not given even to irrational spirits, nor is any judgment prepared for them, in which either blessedness for good deeds or condemnation for evil deeds might be rendered to them. Therefore no distinction of works will be required of them, because they have received no faculty of understanding from God. [Col. 1502D] Therefore their bodies will not rise again, because their souls likewise had neither justice nor injustice [Note: [Col. 1502D] Cousin edition: “animals” (*animalibus*)] for which either eternal blessedness or punishment should be rendered to them.

The same, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*: How is someone made guilty who does not know what he has done?

The same, in the Sermon on this reading: “When we were in the flesh,” says the Apostle, “the passions of sins,” etc.; “I did not know covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Rom. VII, 5–7). A person came to know that what he thought good was evil; he wished to restrain covetousness; he tried and was defeated; he began to be not merely a sinner, but also a transgressor. For he was already a sinner, [Col. 1503A] but before hearing the law he did not know that he was a sinner; he became a transgressor, though before he had been an ignorant sinner.

Haymo, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: For without the natural law and Moses, sin was dead—that is, hidden, unknown, not apparent. Before natural law and understanding begin to be active in infants and other persons, even if they strike father and mother and curse them, they do not sin. Likewise, before the law of Moses was given, there were certain sins which were not known to be sins; when committed, they were not of so great a gravity, or, even if they were known to be sins, it was hidden what punishment they deserved.

Augustine, in the sermon on the words of the Apostle: Behold, infants are certainly innocent in their own deeds, having with them nothing except what they derived from [Col. 1503B] the first parent. Answer me: why do they die, if all human beings die because they sin? What do you suppose can be said? “They too sinned.” Where did they sin, I ask you? When? How? They do not know what good and evil are. Do those who have not received a command receive sin? What do you say of those who die in the womb? “They too,” you say, “sinned.” The Apostle contradicts you; I listen to the Apostle rather than to you: “When they were not yet born and had done nothing good or evil,” etc. (Rom. IX, 11).

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, book I: Infants are innocent in deed, but not innocent in thought, because they cannot yet put into practice by deed the movement which they bear in their mind; and therefore in them the age is weak, not the mind.
