For the frailty of the body does not obey them at the command of the will; nor can they injure by deed as much as they are moved in thought.

Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, ch. 18, concerning the blaspheming boy: Although all baptized infants who die in infancy must be believed to enter the kingdom of heaven, not all little children who are already able to speak must be believed to enter the kingdoms of heaven, because for some little children entrance into that heavenly kingdom is closed by their parents if they are badly brought up. For a man very well known in this city had, three years ago, a son, about five years old, as I think. Loving him too carnally, he brought him up indulgently. And this little child, grievous as it is to say, as soon as anything opposed his will, used to blaspheme the majesty of God [Col. 1503D]. Struck by the mortality three years ago, he came to death. While his father held him in his lap, the child, seeing evil spirits come toward him, as those present testified, began to cry: “Keep them off, father, keep them off! Black men have come who want to take me away.” Having said this, he immediately blasphemed the name of the Majesty and gave up his soul. Thus, in order that God might show for what guilt he had been handed over to such executioners, he allowed him, while dying, to commit that very thing for which his father had refused to correct him while he was alive, so that his father might recognize his guilt: negligent of his little son’s soul, he had brought up for the fires of Gehenna a sinner who was no longer little.

## CIX. That circumcision among the ancient people was of equal efficacy to baptism now; and the contrary

[Col. 1504A]

Augustine, against Pelagius: From the time when circumcision was established among the people of God, which was then the seal of the righteousness of faith, it availed also for infants as a signification of cleansing from old and original sin, just as baptism began to avail for the renewal of the human being from the time when it was instituted.

Gregory, *Morals*, book IV: What the water of baptism accomplishes among those born, this likewise was accomplished among the ancients either by faith alone for infants, or by the power of sacrifice for adults, or, for those descended from the Hebrew stock, by the mystery of circumcision.

Ambrose, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: “Blessed are those whose iniquities [Col. 1504B] have been forgiven,” etc. (Ps. XXXI, 1). Foreseeing the happy time at the Savior’s coming, the prophet calls blessed those whose sins are remitted, cleansed away, and not imputed through the laver without labor or any work. The Apostle, however, on account of the fullness of time, and because there is more grace in the apostles than there was in the prophets, declares greater things which we obtain from the gift of baptism: he professes that we not only receive remission of sins, but are also justified and made children of God, so that this blessedness may have perfect glory and security.

Haymo, in the Gospel homilies on the Lord’s circumcision: Nor should it be thought that circumcision had little usefulness in its own time; rather, it should be known that circumcision then had as much force against original sin [Col. 1504C] as the water of baptism has now, except that he had not yet come who could absolve sins or open the gate of the kingdom of heaven.

## CX. That one baptized by anyone is not to be baptized again; and the contrary
Bede, in Homilies, Book I, Homily 38: If a heretic, a schismatic, or any criminal baptizes while confessing the Trinity, one baptized by good Catholics must not be rebaptized, lest the confession or invocation of so great a Name appear to be nullified.

Augustine on John (1:33), Sermon 5: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending.” [Col. 1504D] Let them not say, “My baptism”; for it is not theirs. Let them hear John himself. Behold, John was full of the Holy Spirit and had baptism from heaven, not from men; yet, insofar as he had it, he himself said: “Prepare the way of the Lord” (Matt. 3:3). But once the Lord himself, having become known, was the Way, John’s baptism, by which the way was prepared for the Lord, was no longer needed. Some are accustomed to say: “Behold, people were baptized after John!” They are not baptized after heretics, because heretics gave Christ’s baptism, which John did not give.

The same, in *On Faith to Peter*: If anyone in any heresy or schism has received the sacrament of baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he has received an unimpaired sacrament; but he will not have the salvation which is the power [Col. 1505A] of the sacrament if he possesses that sacrament outside the Catholic Church. Therefore he must return to the Church, not in order to receive again the sacrament of baptism—which no one ought to repeat in the case of any baptized person—but in order to receive eternal life within the Catholic communion.

The same, in *On the Words of the Lord*, Treatise 11: Whoever are baptized in schismatic or heretical congregations, although they are not reborn by the Spirit of God, when they come to the Catholic Church do not have the washing of the flesh repeated.

Gregory, to Quirinus, bishop in Ireland: By the ancient institution of the Fathers we have learned that all who are baptized among heretics in the name of the Trinity, when they return to the holy Church, should be restored to the bosom of mother Church either by anointing with chrism, by the laying on of hands, or by profession of faith alone. [Col. 1505B] But those heretics who are by no means baptized in the name of the Trinity, such as the Bonosiacs [Note: On Bonosus and his followers, see the Maurist editors, at this place (II, 1168).] and the Cataphrygians—for the former do not believe in Christ the Lord, while the latter, in a perverse sense, believe that the Holy Spirit is a certain wicked man, Montanus—and many others resemble them: when they come to the holy Church, they are baptized, because what they received while set in error was not baptism, since they had not received it in the name of the holy Trinity. Nor can this baptism itself be called repeated, since it had not been given in the name of the Trinity.

Nicholas, in reply to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, chapter 104: You assert that many in your country have been baptized by a certain Jew, though you do not know whether he was a Christian or a pagan, [Col. 1505C] and you ask what ought to be done. Certainly, if these persons were baptized in the name of the holy Trinity, or even only in the name of Christ, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles—for, as Saint Ambrose shows, the two are one and the same—it is clear that they should not be baptized again.

Augustine, in *On Baptism against the Donatists*: The person baptized possesses the sacrament of baptism. The person ordained possesses the sacrament of administering baptism. Just as a baptized person does not lose the sacrament of baptism if he departs from unity, so also an ordained person does not lose the sacrament of administering baptism if he departs from unity. For no sacrament is to be injured.

Likewise: Therefore, if Marcion consecrated baptism with the evangelical words “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” [Col. 1505D] the sacrament was unimpaired, although his faith—under those same words, while thinking something different from what Catholic unity teaches—was not unimpaired, but polluted by fabulous falsehoods.

Likewise: The laying on of hands, however, is not such that it cannot be repeated, as baptism cannot. For what else is it but prayer over a person?

From the Decrees of Pope Leo: Those who received baptism from heretics, having not previously been baptized, are to be confirmed by the invocation of the Holy Spirit alone through the laying on of hands, because they received only the form of baptism without the sanctification of its power. We prescribe that this rule be diligently observed in all cases: that the washing once administered [Col. 1506A] be not defiled by any repetition. For the Apostle says: “One God, one faith, one baptism”; its cleansing is not to be repeated, but, as we have said, the sanctification of the Holy Spirit is to be invoked, so that a person may receive from Catholic priests what no one receives from heretics.

From the Council held at Compiègne, chapter 5: If anyone has been ordained after reaching adulthood and discovers that he was not baptized, he shall be baptized and ordained again, as shall all whom he had previously baptized.

From Cyprian’s twenty-fifth letter, to Jubaianus: You wrote, brother, desiring to be informed what seems right to us regarding the baptism of heretics, who, being outside the Church, claim for themselves a thing that belongs neither to their right nor to their authority. We can neither regard it as valid nor reckon it lawful, since it is established that among them it is unlawful. [Col. 1506B] And because we set forth in our letters what we thought on this matter, I sent you a copy of those letters: what, when many of us were assembled in council, we decreed; and what we later replied to our colleague Quintus when he inquired concerning the same matter. And now also, when seventy-two bishops of the provinces of Asia and Numidia had assembled together, we again confirmed this same point by our judgment, decreeing that there is one baptism, established in the Catholic Church; and consequently that those coming from adulterous and profane water are not rebaptized by us but baptized, since they must be washed and sanctified by the truth of saving water.

Likewise: The faith among heretics is altogether different; indeed, among them there is nothing but faithlessness. How then can one baptized among them seem to have obtained remission of sins and the grace of divine mercy through his faith, when he did not possess the truth of that faith? For if, as some think, a person could receive anything outside the Church according to his faith, he surely received what he believed. But believing falsely, he could not receive what is true; rather, in accordance with what he believed, he received something adulterous and profane. [Col. 1506C] Jeremiah (15:18) sharply touches upon this matter of profane and adulterous baptism, saying: “Why do those who afflict me prevail? My wound is fixed; it has become to me like deceitful water, having no trustworthiness.” Is there then deceitful and faithless water? Certainly: it falsely claims the image of baptism and frustrates, by a shadowy pretense, the grace of faith.

But if, according to a perverse faith, someone outside the Church could be baptized and obtain remission of sins, then according to the same faith he could also obtain the Holy Spirit; and it would not be necessary to lay hands upon one who comes, so that he might receive the Holy Spirit and be sealed. For either he could obtain both outside by his faith, or one who was outside received neither. But it is clear where, and through whom, remission of sins can be given. For the Lord first gave it to Peter, upon whom he built his Church, so that what Peter loosed on earth might be loosed in heaven. Afterwards he speaks to the Apostles, saying: “As the Father sent me, I also send you” (John 20:21). Hence we understand [Col. 1507A] that only those set over the Church are permitted to baptize and give remission of sins.

The sons of Aaron, who placed strange fire upon the altar, were immediately destroyed in the sight of the indignant Lord. This punishment awaits those who falsely introduce alien water for baptism, so that the divine judgment may punish heretics for doing what belongs to the Church alone.

As to what some say concerning those baptized in Samaria, namely, that when the Apostles Peter and John arrived, hands were merely laid upon them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit, and that they were not rebaptized: we see that this does not at all apply to the present case. For those people had believed with true faith and had been baptized within the Church by Philip the deacon, whom those same Apostles had sent. But only [Col. 1507B] what was lacking was done by Peter and John, namely, that through the laying on of hands the Holy Spirit might be poured upon them; this is also now done among us.

Can one who is not within the Church water from the Church’s fountains? Heretics are not in the Church; indeed, they act against the Church. How, then, can they baptize with the Church’s baptism? For if anyone could be baptized among heretics, he could surely also obtain remission of sins. If he has obtained remission of sins, he has been sanctified and made a temple of God. I ask: of which God? If of the Creator, he could not become this who did not believe in him. If of Christ, he cannot become his temple who denies that Christ is God. If of the Holy Spirit, how can the Holy Spirit be favourable [Col. 1507C] to one who is the enemy either of the Son or of the Father?

Therefore baptism cannot be common to us and the heretics, with whom neither God the Father, nor Christ the Son, nor the Holy Spirit, nor faith, nor Church is held in common. Hence those who come from heresy to the Church ought to be baptized, when they have learned from us that those already baptized with John’s baptism were also baptized by Paul, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (19:5).

But if a heretic was able to acquire the right of baptism because he baptized first, baptism will belong not to one who possesses it but to one who occupies it; and since baptism and the Church cannot be separated or divided at all, the one who was first able to occupy baptism also occupied the Church at the same time.

We have written this in reply to you, brother, prejudging no one, [Col. 1507D] so that each bishop may do what he thinks right, possessing the free power of his own judgment.

The same, in the Letter to Quintus: By I know not what presumption some are led to think that those who have been dipped among heretics ought not to be baptized when they come to us. But we say that those who come from there are not rebaptized among us, but baptized. For they receive nothing there, where there is nothing.

The same, to Januarius, Book II: Water must first be sanctified by a priest, so that by its baptism it may be able to wash away sins. How can one who is himself unclean cleanse and sanctify water, and [Col. 1508A] one in whom the Holy Spirit is not, when the Lord says in Numbers (19:22): “Whatever an unclean person touches shall be unclean”? But who can give what he himself does not have? Or how can one perform spiritual acts who has himself lost the Holy Spirit? Therefore such a person must be baptized and renewed.

Judgments of bishops: Cyprian said: We have often determined that heretics coming to the Church ought to be baptized and sanctified with the Church’s baptism.

Caecilius of Bilta [Note: See Augustine, Maurist edition, IX, 166.] said: I recognize baptism only in the Church, and none outside it; among heretics everything is done through falsehood.

Primus Felix of Migirpa said: I judge that every person coming from heresy must be baptized; for there he vainly thinks himself baptized.

Augustine against Petilian, *On the One Baptism*: [Col. 1508B] The most glorious martyr Cyprian, who, in detesting heretics and schismatics, would not recognize Christ’s baptism as given among them, attained such great merits even to the triumph of martyrdom that the shadowing darkness was dispelled by the light of charity in which he excelled; and, if there was anything in him needing purification, the final sickle of his passion removed it, so that the sacrament might become more fruitful through its fruit. Nor are we already better than Cyprian because we recognize the truth of baptism even amid the wickedness of heretics, any more than we are better than Peter because we do not compel Gentiles to Judaize.

*Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, chapter 6: Concerning the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. It also orders that Paulianists, who are Photinians, be rebaptized.

Likewise, Book VI, chapter 2: In [Col. 1508C] the city of Rome, Cornelius then governing as bishop, and at Carthage Cyprian—both eminent in faith and strength—a question arose in the greater part of Africa whether heretics ought to be rebaptized. Although Cyprian and nearly all other clergy throughout Africa maintained that this ought to be done, Cornelius and all the clergy throughout Italy rejected such a decree, while priestly concord remained intact.

Jerome against Vigilantius: Therefore the bad vigils of some will not destroy the vigils of others; rather, those who sleep in lust should be compelled to keep watch in chastity. For what is good to do once cannot be evil if it is done frequently; or, if it must be avoided because of some fault, it is blameworthy not because it is often done, but because it is ever done.

The same, on Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians (4:4), Book II: “Diligently preserving the truth of the Spirit in the bond of peace. One body and one Spirit,” etc. This also makes against heretics, so that they may know that they do not possess baptism, but that the life-giving fountain is in the one Church of Christ.

Cassiodorus the senator, *On the Institutions of the Divine Scriptures*, Book I [19]: It is altogether impossible to express how much the most blessed Cyprian surpasses other writers—apart from the repetition of [Note: Editions: “apart from the foregoing argument.”] baptism, which the Church’s usage and reason [Note: Editions: “usage and grace.”] rejected—like oil flowing down into every healing [Note: Editions: “sweetness”]; he was an accomplished speaker, an outstanding declaimer, and a remarkable teacher.

## CXI. That sins are remitted even through baptism when one approaches deceitfully, and the contrary. [Note: Cousin: “and the contrary” is absent.]

[Col. 1509A]

Augustine, *On the One Baptism*, Book I: If someone comes to baptism deceitfully, are his sins remitted to him, or not? If they say, “They are remitted,” how will the Holy Spirit of discipline flee from one who is deceitful, if in this deceitful person he has effected remission of sins? If they say that they are not remitted, I ask whether, if he afterwards confessed his deceit with a converted heart [Note: Editions: “a stricken heart.”] and genuine sorrow, a person could be baptized again; yet his heart, persisting in wickedness, would not allow the washing away [Note: Editions: “abolition.”] of sins to occur. Thus it is to be understood that persons can be baptized in assemblies separated from the Church, where Christ’s baptism is given and received in the same sacramental celebration; [Col. 1509B] yet it benefits them for the remission of sins only when, having been reconciled, a person is stripped of the sacrilege of dissension by which his sins were held bound and prevented from being remitted.

Likewise: The grace of baptism is not hindered from remitting all sins even if hatred of a brother persists in the mind of the person to whom they are remitted. For yesterday is loosed, and everything earlier is loosed; the very hour and moment before baptism, and in baptism, are loosed. Thereafter, however, he immediately begins to be guilty, not only of subsequent days but also of former days, hours, and moments, all the things that were remitted returning.

The same, Book IV: Thus one baptized in heresy in the name of the holy Trinity nevertheless [Note: Munich manuscript: “flesh.”] does not become a temple of God if he does not depart from heresy, just as neither does idolatrous service.

Likewise: A faithless and blasphemous person, if he remains in faithlessness and blasphemy, receives no remission of sins either outside the Church or within it; or, if he receives it for a moment through the power of the sacrament, the same power operates both outside and inside, just as the power of Christ’s name operated in casting out demons even outside. [Col. 1509C]

The same, *On the Words of the Lord*, Treatise 11: A person is not to be said to be in the Church or to belong to the communion of the Spirit if, with a feigned heart, he is mingled with all Christ’s people only by bodily association. For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from one who is deceitful.

The same, *On the Remedy of Repentance*: Everyone who has already become the master of his own will, when he approaches the sacrament [Col. 1509D] of believers, cannot begin a new life unless he repents of his former life. Infants alone are exempt from this repentance when they are baptized, for they cannot yet make use of free choice.

Likewise: No other human being passes to Christ, so as to begin to be what he was not, unless he has repented of being what he was. This repentance is commanded, as Peter says: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized.”

The same, *On the Benefit of Performing Repentance concerning Former Life*: No one chooses a new life unless he repents of the old.

Jerome, to Sabinianus, a fallen deacon: Nothing so opposes God as an unrepentant heart; it is the one offense that cannot obtain forgiveness. [Col. 1510A]

The same, on Ezekiel (16:4): “And it was not washed with water for salvation.” This can indeed be understood not only of heretics but also of churchmen who receive saving baptism without full faith. Of them it must be said that they received water but not Spirit, just as Simon Magus was also baptized in water, but by no means unto salvation.

The same, on the Letter to the Galatians (3:27), Book II: “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” He shows how we are born through faith which is in Christ. Therefore, if those baptized into Christ have put on Christ, it is clear that those who have not put on Christ were not baptized into Christ. For it was said to those considered to be believers and to have obtained Christ’s baptism: “Put on Christ.” If anyone [Col. 1510B] has received only this bodily washing of water, he has not put on Christ. For that Simon also had received the washing of water; yet, because he did not have the Holy Spirit, he had not put on Christ. Heretics, hypocrites, and those who live foully seem indeed to receive baptism, but I do not know whether they possess Christ’s garment. Therefore let us consider whether perhaps someone may be found even among us who, because he does not have Christ’s garment, is proved not to have been baptized into Christ.

The same, on Matthew (28:19), Book IV: “Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them.” First they teach; then at last they immerse in water. For it cannot happen that the body receives the sacrament of baptism unless the soul has first received [Col. 1510C] the truth of faith.

## CXII. That one immersion in baptism is sufficient, and that it is not.

The Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 7: To avoid scandal to schismatics or the practice of heretics, let us retain a single immersion in baptism.

Gregory, to Bishop Leander: Concerning triple immersion in baptism, no truer answer can be given than the one you yourself judged: in one faith a diversity of Church custom does no harm. Since in three subsistences there is one substance, it is by no means blameworthy to immerse an infant in baptism either three times or once, since in three immersions the Trinity of persons, and in one immersion the singularity of the Godhead, can be signified. But because up to now an infant has been immersed a third time in baptism by heretics, [Col. 1510D] I do not judge that this should be done among you, lest, while they count the immersions, they divide the Godhead; and lest, by doing what they did, they boast that they have prevailed over our custom.

But when we immerse three times, we signify the mysteries of the three-day burial, so that when the infant is raised from the water a third time, the resurrection of the three-day period is expressed. If anyone perhaps judges this to be done also in reverence for the supreme Trinity, neither does it in any way prevent one from immersing the baptized person once in water; for, since in three subsistences there is one substance, it is by no means blameworthy to immerse infants in baptism either three times or once, since in three immersions [Col. 1511A] the Trinity of persons, and in one immersion the singularity of the Godhead, can be signified.

Haymo, on Paul’s Letter to the Romans: Cyprian abounds in his own understanding when he immersed infants once in baptism, because he diligently fulfilled with abundant good works what he understood; although in this he erred unknowingly, yet because he abounded in good works, once corrected he abounded with us in a higher understanding, immersing them three times.

## CXIII. That baptism alone, without the sacrament of the altar, is sufficient, and that it is not.

Bede, in a homily on the Circumcision of the Lord: Baptism bestows such great grace that, if the one baptized should die while coming up from the font, he immediately enters the heights of heaven without any delay of time. [Col. 1511B]

Haymo, on Paul’s Letter to the Romans (3:24): Where it is written: “Being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption by which Christ redeemed us with his blood,” and through faith and the water of baptism: anyone reborn by this water, if he dies immediately, shall be saved unto life. But if he lives, he must adorn faith with works, because faith without works is dead.

Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*: Hold most firmly and do not doubt in the least that holy baptism suffices for the salvation of infants, who can neither believe by their own will nor perform repentance for the sin which they inherit originally, so long as they are incapable of the age of reason.

The same, *On Baptism to Marcellinus*: To those asking how infants can repent of original sin, since they are not yet liable for any sins of their own, it should be answered: If they are rightly called believers because they profess faith through the words of those who carry them, why should they not also be regarded as penitents, since through those same persons they renounce the devil and this age? [Col. 1511C]

Likewise: No one except the baptized rightly approaches the Lord’s table of the body.

Likewise: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54). What further do we seek? What can be answered to this unless obstinacy stretches its combative sinews against the constancy of everlasting truth?

Augustine: Will anyone dare to say that this declaration does not apply to infants and that they can have life in themselves without participation in this body and blood because he did not say, “Whoever has not eaten,” as he said concerning baptism, “Whoever has not been reborn,” but said, “Unless you eat,” as if addressing those who could hear and understand—something infants clearly cannot do? But whoever says this does not observe that, if everyone holds this declaration, namely, that they cannot have life without the body and blood of the Lord, then the older age also needlessly concerns itself with this; for it can be so without volition, provided you attend to the speaker’s words. I see that it was said only to those to whom the Lord was then speaking. [Col. 1511D]

Likewise: “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52). Who can doubt that by the name “world” he signified human beings who come into this world by being born? Accordingly, Christ’s flesh must also be called the life of infants; and unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man, neither shall they have life.

Likewise: This grace may be hidden when it comes to one person and does not come to another, but it cannot be unjust. Nor is it said without reason: “Your judgments are like a great abyss” (Ps. 35:7); and, as though terrified by the multitude of that abyss, the Apostle exclaims: “O the depth of the riches of wisdom,” etc. (Rom. 11:33). Punic Christians call baptism itself nothing other than “salvation,” and the sacrament of the body nothing other than “life.” Whence, unless from an ancient and, I think, apostolic tradition, which they hold as implanted in the Churches of Christ [Note: Munich manuscript: “who maintain the passage of the Church of Christ.”], that apart from baptism and participation in the Lord’s table no one can attain at all—not merely to the kingdom of God, but not even to salvation [Col. 1512B] and eternal life? For Scripture also testifies to this. What else do those maintain who call baptism by the name “salvation,” except what was said: “He saved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5), and what Peter says (1 Pet. 3:21): “Thus baptism in a like figure also saves us”? What else do those maintain who call the sacrament of the Lord’s table “life,” except what was said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51); and: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (ibid., 52); and: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (ibid., 54)? Therefore, if, as so many and such great divine testimonies agree, neither salvation nor life is to be hoped for by anyone without baptism and the body and blood of the Lord, it is vainly promised to infants without these. [Col. 1512C]

## CXIV. That sins were remitted in John’s baptism, and that they were not.

Augustine, *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chapter 18 of the second part: John’s baptism, once begun, did not cease, but that which it lacked was added to it. For John only baptized; he did not give the Holy Spirit to believers, as he himself says of the Savior (John 1:26): “I indeed baptize you in water unto repentance, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.” That is: through me remission of sins is given, but the Holy Spirit is not given, so that they may be called purified children; this was reserved for the Savior, so that they might not become children of God except by receiving the Holy Spirit from the Son. Therefore John’s baptism was enlarged, not nullified.

From Chrysostom’s sermon on the beheading of Saint John: “Herod,” he says, “seized John and bound him; he who had loosed the bonds of sins is bound in the bonds of a sinner, so that bound forgiveness may leave no place for forgiveness.”

Ambrose, on the Letter to the Galatians (3:2): “This only I wish to learn from you,” etc. Those who had been, not immersed in John’s baptism, but defiled in an adulterous baptism under the name of John’s baptism, Paul commanded to be baptized in the name of the Trinity. [Col. 1513A]

Gregory, in the Twenty Homilies, Book I: “And he came into all the region of the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins” (Luke 3:5). It is clear to all readers that John not only preached a baptism of repentance but also gave it to some; yet he could not give his baptism for the remission of sins. For remission of sins is granted to us only through Christ’s baptism. It should therefore be noted that he is said to have been “preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins,” because he preached the baptism that loosed sins, though he could not give it. Thus, as he preceded the incarnate Word of the Father by the word of preaching, so the baptism of repentance, by which sins are loosed, was preceded by his baptism, by which sins cannot be loosed. And since his preaching preceded [Col. 1513B] the Redeemer’s presence, his baptism also, by preceding it, became a shadow of the truth.

## CXV. That nothing has yet been determined concerning the origin of the soul, and the contrary.

Augustine, *Retractations*, Book I: Elsewhere likewise I said concerning the soul: “More safely, as about to return to heaven.” But I should have said “as about to go” rather than “as about to return,” on account of those who think that human souls, because of the merits of their sins, have fallen or been cast down from heaven and are thrust into these bodies. Yet I said “into heaven” as though I had said “to God,” who is its Creator; just as blessed Cyprian did not hesitate to say: “For since we possess the body from earth, we possess the spirit from heaven.” And in the book of Ecclesiastes (12:7) it is written: [Col. 1513C] “Let the spirit return to God who gave it.” This must certainly be understood in such a way that we do not contradict the Apostle, who says that those not yet born have done neither good nor evil. Therefore, beyond dispute, God himself is a certain original region of the soul’s blessedness: he did not beget it from himself, but created it from no other thing. But concerning its origin—whether it derives from that one soul which was first created when man was made, or whether individual souls are made in like manner for individual persons—I neither knew then nor know even now.

Gregory, to Secundinus, a servant of God enclosed in reclusion (*Works*, II, 970): Among the holy Fathers there has been no small inquiry concerning the origin of the soul. But whether it descends from Adam, or rather is given individually to each person, has remained uncertain; and they have acknowledged that in this life the question is insoluble. For the question is difficult and cannot be comprehended by man: if the soul is born from Adam’s substance along with the flesh, why does it not also die with the flesh? But if it is not born with the flesh, why is it held bound by sins in that flesh which has proceeded from Adam? Yet although this is uncertain, this is not uncertain: unless a person has been reborn by the grace of sacred baptism, [Col. 1514A] every soul is bound by the chains of original sin. For this reason it is written: “Not even an infant of one day upon the earth is clean in his sight” (Job 14:4). Hence David says (Ps. 50:7): “In iniquities I was conceived.”

From the Book of Wisdom (8:19): “I received a good soul by lot, and, being more good, I came into an undefiled body.”

From the office for the dead, in which it is said to God: “That you may gently and tenderly receive the soul returning to you.”

From a work of Jerome addressed to Augustine [Note: [Col. 1513D] Cousin: “Jeremiah in Augustine,” rightly complaining in a note that no book of Jeremiah is found among Augustine’s editions. In fact, this passage occurs not in Jerome’s books addressed to Augustine, but in Jerome’s letter to Pammachius against the heresies of John, bishop of Jerusalem. *Works*, Martianay ed., IV, 318.], which begins, “Concerning the remaining matters that pertain to the faith” [Note: [Col. 1513D] Cousin: “the end.”] [Note: [Col. 1514D] Cf. Jerome, *Works*, IV, 314.]:

“Or is it rather the ecclesiastical teaching, according to the words of the Savior (John 5:17): ‘My Father works until now [Note: [Col. 1514D] Cousin: ‘with me.’], and I work’; and according to that saying of Isaiah: ‘He who forms [Col. 1514B] the spirit of man within him’ (Zech. 12:1; Isa. 42 and 57); and in the Psalms (32:15): ‘He who fashions [fingit] their hearts one by one’: does God daily fashion souls and not cease to be their Creator?”

Likewise: “Let those who say that souls existed before they were born, and are not made daily by God for the body after the pattern of the first man, be anathema.”

Ambrose, Book II of *On Cain and Abel* [Note: [Col. 1514D] This passage is entirely absent from the Munich manuscript.]: “At this point is introduced the doctrine concerning the incorruptibility of the soul: that it is in that true and blessed life in which each person lives well with his own people; much more purely and blessedly when our soul has laid aside the covering of this flesh and, as though released from a kind of bodily prison, flies upward to that higher place, whence, when infused into our inward parts together with the body’s suffering, it groaned.”

Gennadius, *On Christian Doctrine* [Col. 1514C] [Note: [Col. 1514D] Editions: *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapters 14 and 18.]:

“We say that human souls did not exist from the beginning among the other intellectual natures, nor were they created all at once, as Origen imagines; nor are they sown with bodies through sexual intercourse, as the Luciferians, Cyril, and certain presumptuous Latin writers assert, as though maintaining a consequence of nature [Note: [Col. 1514D] Cousin: “as though a consequence of nature being maintained.”]. Rather, we say that only the body is sown through the union of marriage, while by God’s judgment it is congealed, compacted, and formed; and that, once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that a human being may live as constituted of soul and body. But the creation of the soul is known only to the Creator.”

Likewise: “The human soul does not die with the flesh, because, as has been said, it is not sown with the flesh; rather, once the body has been formed in the mother’s womb, it is created and infused by God’s judgment.”

[Col. 1514D] Hilary, on Psalm 129: “God, making man in his own image, composed him of a lowly and a heavenly nature, namely soul and body. First, indeed, he established the soul by that one work of his power which is incomprehensible to us. For when he made man in God’s image, he did not then also make the body. Genesis teaches that, long afterward, when man had already been made in God’s image, a body was taken and formed from dust [Note: [Col. 1514D] Cousin: ‘dust’ in the accusative.]; [Col. 1515A] then again, by God’s breathing, it was made into a living soul, this nature—that is, the earthly and the heavenly—being joined together by a kind of covenant of inspiration.”

Augustine, *On Faith to Peter*: “We believe that, once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that in the womb a human being may live, constituted of soul and body.”

The same author, in the book *Questions on the Old and New Law*, chapter 23: “I think it unbecoming that souls should be generated, so that soul should be born from soul. For if the soul exists along with the seed, many souls perish daily with discharged seed.”

Likewise: “Moses makes this clearer when he says: If anyone strikes a woman with child and causes a miscarriage, if it is indeed formed, he shall render soul for soul; but if it is unformed, he shall be fined in money [Col. 1515B]—plainly declaring that there is no soul before form.”

Likewise: “Let us consider Adam’s making; for in Adam an example was given, so that it may be understood that the already formed body received a soul. God could not mix the soul with the clay of earth and so form the body; rather, the house first had to be constructed, and then the soul, its inhabitant, introduced.”

The same, *On the Greatness of the Soul*: “The soul was made like God, because God made it immortal and indissoluble; it was made from nothing.”

Likewise: “Just as the pure elements have no pre-existing things, either in actuality or in nature, from which they are naturally composed, so too the soul.”

The same, in *On the Origin of the Soul*: “The soul is not from God, but was created by him from nothing.”

Likewise: “But if it was made from no other thing, then without doubt it was made from nothing, [Col. 1515C] but by him.”

The same, to Jerome: “You certainly hold that God now makes individual souls for individual persons as they are born.”

The same, to Optatus [*Works*, II, 705]: “Blessed Jerome, following both the most holy martyr Victorinus and very many Catholics, indicated that he believed souls to be made rather than propagated; adding also that he was accustomed to hold the propagation of souls as the Western view.”

The same, to the same person: “Those who defend the propagation of souls with unreflecting rashness.”

The same, to the same person: “Who would prefer to understand these words thus: ‘all the souls of those who came out of his loins,’ so that even in this way men may be understood to have come out of their father’s loins only according to the body?”

The same again, in a letter to Jerome, speaking of the same question: “I would wish this opinion [Col. 1515D] to be true; if it is true, may it be defended by you most invincibly. For the statement, ‘The spirit returns to the Lord who gave it,’ does not confirm that opinion which we wished to be ours.”

The same, to the same person, on the statement that God rested on the seventh day from all his work: “By creating new souls, one for each individual person born, he is not said to make something which he had not made before. For he had already made this human being, and now makes him not by instituting what did not exist, but by multiplying what did exist.”

The same, *On Genesis according to the Letter*: “If it is asked whence Christ had his soul, I would rather say, ‘whence Adam had it,’ than ‘from Adam.’”

Likewise: “He who gives life to [Note: [Col. 1515D] Cousin: ‘loves.’] flesh [Col. 1516A] in mothers’ wombs, so that they may be born.”

Remigius, on Psalm 34:17, “Lord, when will you look? Restore my soul,” etc.: “Christ’s soul is called unique, because uniquely born of the Virgin, it lived uniquely, rose singularly, and ascended singularly into heaven.”

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, Book I, chapter 12: “We believe that the soul does not exist before it is joined to the body, but is created when the body also is created to which it appears to be joined.”

## CXVI. That the sins of fathers are repaid upon children, and the contrary

Origen, Homily VIII on Exodus: “When we are persuaded by the devil to sin [Note: [Col. 1516D] Munich manuscript: ‘urged.’], we receive his seed. But when we also fulfill it in deed, then he has already [Col. 1516B] begotten us. Yet because it scarcely ever happens that we sin without an assistant, all, as it were, begotten one from another according to the order of persuasion, draw a progeny of harmful birth from their father the devil.

“Let us now see, according to this descent of which we have spoken, how God repays the sins of the fathers upon the children, to the fourth and third generation, and does not repay them upon the fathers themselves. For God said nothing about the fathers. The devil will not be cleansed in this age, nor is he rebuked for sin, nor scourged. For all things are reserved for him in the future. Hence he himself, knowing that this time of punishments had been fixed for him, said to the Savior: ‘Why have you come before the time to torment us?’ (Matt. 8:30).

“But sins are repaid upon the children—that is, upon those whom he has begotten [Col. 1516C] through sin. For people placed in the flesh are rebuked by the Lord in order that they may return. Thus the kindly Lord repays the sins of the fathers upon the children, so that, because the fathers—that is, the devil and his angels—are unworthy to be rebuked in this age, their children may here receive the consequences of what they have done, in order that they may proceed more purified to the age to come and may no longer become companions of the devil in punishment. Therefore he says (Ps. 88:33): ‘I will visit their sins with scourges; but I will not take my mercy from them.’”

Ezekiel the prophet (18:1): “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: What is this proverb which you turn among yourselves into this saying: ‘Our fathers ate a sour grape, and the teeth of their children are set on edge’?”

Jerome, on this passage: “He warns that what was said in Exodus (20:5), ‘I am a jealous God, who repay the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and show mercy unto thousands to those who love me’; and likewise, ‘Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of great mercy’ (Ps. 85:15), and ‘I repay the iniquities of fathers upon children and upon children’s children to the third and fourth generation,’ must be understood as a parable and proverb, so that one thing sounds in the words and another is held in the sense.

“And until the present day we had thought this was not a parable, but a plain statement to be explained simply; nevertheless a hidden stumbling block arose, since it seemed to be God’s injustice that one should sin and another pay for the sins. But by what follows, ‘of those who hate me,’ the scandal of his threat is resolved. For they are punished not because their fathers sinned, when their fathers rather ought to have been punished, but because they proved imitators of their fathers and hated God by hereditary evil, even as a branch growing from the root [Note: [Col. 1517D] Editions: ‘branches.’].”

Likewise: “We shall answer that in this too the Creator’s mercy is shown. For he does not preserve an anger of cruelty and severity until the third and fourth generation; rather, it is a sign of mercy to defer the punishment of sin. For when he says, ‘Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of great mercy,’ and adds, ‘repaying the iniquities of fathers upon children and children’s children,’ he indicates [Col. 1517B] that he is of such great mercy that he does not punish immediately, but postpones the sentence of punishment.”

Likewise: “It is written in Proverbs (10:26): ‘As a sour grape is harmful to the teeth, and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who use it.’ From this it is clear that not other people’s teeth ache and are set on edge, but those of the persons who ate the sour grape. The meaning is this: just as it would be ridiculous and wholly incoherent if someone wished to say, ‘The fathers ate sour grapes and the children’s teeth were set on edge,’ so it is unjust and perverse for fathers to sin and children and grandchildren to be tortured.”

Likewise: “There are some who explain the words written, ‘repaying the iniquities of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation,’ by applying the statement to the human soul. They say that the father in us is the slight first impulse of the senses, the incitements of vices; the son, when the thought has conceived sins; the grandson, when you commit in deed what you have thought and conceived; and the great-grandson, that is, the fourth generation, when you have not only done what is evil but glory in your crimes, according to what is written (Prov. 18:3): ‘When the ungodly man has come into the depth of evils, he despises.’

“Therefore God does not punish the first and second stirrings of thoughts, without which no human being can exist; but he punishes if someone resolves to do what he has thought, or refuses through repentance to correct the deeds he has done.”

Likewise: “As proof that the first impulse of thought is by no means [Col. 1517D] punished by God, but only if you complete in deed what you have conceived in mind, there is that passage from Genesis (9:25): Ham sinned by mocking his father’s nakedness, yet the sentence was received not by the one who mocked but by his son Canaan: ‘Cursed,’ he says, ‘be Canaan; he shall be the servant of his brothers.’ The judgment seems to lack justice.”

Likewise: “Let this for the moment suffice concerning the proverb or parable. But if anyone can discover either a better or another meaning which removes the stumbling block posed by testimonies apparently contrary to one another, that person’s opinion should rather be accepted.”

Likewise (Ezek. 18:3): “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘this parable shall no longer be for you as a proverb in Israel.’ ‘The soul which sins, it shall [Col. 1518A] die.’ A parable is by no means spoken in Israel, but among those who have no knowledge of God and cannot discern the truth.”

Likewise: “Just as the sins of children do not harm fathers, so the sins of fathers do not pass over to children.”

From the Book of Job (21:19): “God will preserve for that man’s children the sorrow due to their father; and when he repays it, then he will know.”

Gregory, Book XV of the *Morals*: “We know that it is written: ‘You repay the sins of fathers upon children and grandchildren to the third and fourth generation’ (Exod. 20:5). And again it is written: ‘The soul that sins, it shall die.’ He therefore repays the sins of fathers upon children when, because of a parent’s fault, the soul of the offspring is defiled through original sin. And again he does not repay them, because, once we are freed from original fault by baptism, we have no longer the sins of our parents, but those which we ourselves commit [Col. 1518B].

“Whoever imitates the iniquity of a wicked parent is also bound by that parent’s offense. Thus it comes about that the wicked son of a wicked father pays not only for his own sins, which he has added, but also for his father’s sins, since, although he knows that the Lord is angered by his father’s vices, he does not fear to add his own further wickedness to them.”

Likewise: “‘The soul that sins, it shall die,’ because children are sometimes killed in the flesh even because of their father’s sin. But once original sin has been removed, they are not held in their souls by their parents’ wickedness.”

Likewise: “An unrighteous father is often struck in his children, so that he may burn more sharply, inasmuch as the wicked mind of the father is punished through the sufferings of his children.”

Likewise: “It is rightly said, ‘to the third and fourth generation,’ because children can see the life of their parents, which they imitate, as far as the third and fourth generation. Vengeance extends to those who have seen what they wickedly follow.”

## CXVII. On the sacrament of the altar: that it is essentially the very reality of Christ’s flesh and blood, and the contrary
Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book VIII:

The Father is in Christ, and Christ is in us; these make us one in them. If, therefore, Christ truly assumed the flesh of our body, and that Christ is truly man, and we truly receive, under the mystery, the flesh of his body, then through this we shall be one, because the Father is in him and he in us. How, then, is a unity of will asserted, when the natural property through the sacrament is the sacrament of perfect unity? For in matters concerning God we must not speak according to human or worldly understanding, nor must the sound meaning of heavenly sayings be forcibly and impudently distorted into an alien and impious interpretation.

For unless we have learned from him what we say concerning the natural reality of Christ in us, we shall speak foolishly and impiously. For he himself says (John 6:56): “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink. He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.” No room for doubt has been left concerning the reality of the flesh and blood; for now, both by the Lord’s own declaration and by our faith, it is truly flesh and truly blood. Received and drunk, these bring it about that we are in Christ and Christ is in us. Therefore he is in us through the flesh.

That we are in him through the sacrament of the flesh and blood shared with us, he himself testifies when he says: “And you in me, and I in you.” If he had wished only a unity of will to be understood, why did he set forth a certain degree and order for the completion of unity, unless it was that, as he is in the Father through the nature of divinity, so we, on the other hand, should be believed to be in him through his bodily birth, and he again to be in us through the mystery of the sacraments? Thus perfect unity through the Mediator would be taught: while we abide in him, he abides in the Father; and while abiding in the Father, he abides in us. So we advance to the unity of the Father, since we too naturally abide in him in whom he naturally abides according to divinity [Col. 1519B], while he himself naturally abides in us.

That this unity is natural in us, he testifies thus: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.” For no one can be in him unless he himself is in that person, having taken into himself only the flesh of him who has taken his own flesh.

Likewise: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats my flesh shall also live because of me” (John 6:58). As he lives through the Father, so we shall live through his flesh. This, indeed, is the cause of our life: that we have Christ abiding in us through the flesh, and shall live through him under the condition by which he lives through the Father. If, therefore, we naturally live through him according to the flesh [Col. 1519C], that is, having obtained the nature of his flesh, how does he not naturally have the Father in himself according to the Spirit, when he himself lives through the Father?

Likewise: These things have been recalled by us because heretics, falsely asserting that this unity between Father and Son is only a unity of will, used the example of our unity in relation to the Lord—as though we were united to the Son, and through the Son to the Father, only by religious obedience and will, with no natural communion proper to the sacrament of flesh and blood granted to us. Yet, through the honor given us by the Son, through the Son abiding carnally in us, and through our being bodily and inseparably united in him, the mystery of true and natural unity must be proclaimed.

The same: The body of Christ which is received from the altar is a figure insofar as bread and wine are outwardly seen; but it is reality insofar as the body and blood of Christ are inwardly believed and received.

From the Ephesian Creed:

We necessarily add this also. We celebrate in the churches the bloodless ministry of sacrifice, and we are sanctified as partakers of the holy body and precious blood of Christ—not receiving common flesh, nor flesh of a man sanctified and united to the Word by a unity of dignity, but flesh truly life-giving and made the very own flesh of the Word himself. For God, being life by nature, because he is united to his own flesh, declared it to be life-giving. Therefore, although he says, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man,” etc., we nevertheless must not regard it as the flesh of one man from among us [Col. 1520A]. For how could a man’s flesh be life-giving according to its own nature? Rather, it must be regarded as having truly become his own.

Likewise: If it is believed that he became flesh—indeed, rather, that he became a human being endowed with a rational soul.

Ambrose, *On Duties*:

Those things, therefore, must be sought by us in which there is perfection and truth. Here there is shadow; here there is image; there, in heaven, is truth. Formerly water was offered; now Christ is offered, as man, as receiving suffering; and he offers himself as priest, in order to forgive our sins. Here it is in an image; there, in truth. There, before the Father, he intervenes for us as advocate.

The same, *On the Sacraments*, Book I:

I promise that the sacraments of Christians are more divine and earlier than those of the Jews.

Likewise: Receive what I say: the Christian mysteries are earlier than the Jewish. Melchizedek offered bread and wine. Therefore understand that these sacraments which you receive here are earlier ministrations than the sacraments of Moses; and that the Christian people began before the Jewish people—though we in predestination, they in name.

Likewise: This bread is bread before the words of the sacraments; when consecration has been added, from bread it becomes Christ’s flesh. But by what words, and by whose utterance, does consecration take place? By the words of the Lord Jesus. For in all the rest that is said, praise is rendered to God; prayer is first offered for the people, for kings, and for the others. When the point is reached at which the sacrament is to be effected, the priest no longer uses his own words, but Christ’s.

What saying of Christ effects the sacrament here? The saying of Christ by which all things were made. God commanded, and heaven, earth, sea, and every creature came to be. If, therefore, there is such power in the saying of the Lord Jesus that things which did not exist began to exist, how much more effective is it that things which existed should be changed into something else.

Likewise: Christ’s saying changes the established order of nature when he wills. Let us first take an example from his birth. You see that, contrary to the established order of nature, a man was born of a Virgin.

Likewise: If the heavenly saying works in other things, does it not work in the heavenly sacraments? Therefore you have learned that Christ’s body is made from bread, and that when wine and water are put into the cup, it becomes blood through the consecration of the heavenly word. But perhaps you say: “I do not see the appearance of blood.” Yet it has a likeness. As you received the likeness of death, so you drink the likeness of blood, so that there may be no horror at bloodshed. Therefore you have learned that what you receive is Christ’s body.

Do you wish to know that it is consecrated by heavenly words? Receive what the words are. The priest says: “Make this offering for us approved, rational, acceptable, which is a figure of the body and blood of the Lord Jesus Christ; who, on the day before he suffered, took bread into his holy hands, looked up to heaven—to you, holy Father, almighty eternal God—gave thanks, blessed it, broke it, and, once broken, gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take,’” etc.

Likewise: Observe: all the words up to “Take” are the Evangelist’s words; from that point they are Christ’s words. Consider each point. “Who, on the day before he suffered,” he says, “took bread.” Before it is consecrated, it is bread; but when Christ’s words have been added, it is Christ’s body. Before Christ’s words, the cup is full of wine and water; when Christ’s words have done their work, blood is brought about there.

Likewise: Which is greater: manna from heaven or Christ’s body? Certainly Christ’s body, whose author is the Lord of heaven. Then, whoever ate manna died; whoever eats this body will receive forgiveness of sins and shall not die eternally. Therefore you do not say “Amen” idly, already confessing in spirit that you receive Christ’s body. The priest says to you, “The body of Christ,” and you say, “Amen”—that is, “It is true.” Let the heart hold fast what the tongue confesses.

Know how great the sacrament is. Observe that he says: “As often as you do this [Col. 1521B], you shall make remembrance of me.” And the priest says: “Therefore, remembering his most glorious passion and resurrection from the dead,” etc.

Likewise: Wine and water are put into the cup. But you say, “How, then, did Melchizedek offer bread and wine?” What is the meaning of the admixture of water? “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ.” It was not an immovable rock, since it followed the people. You too, drink, so that Christ may follow you.

Observe the mystery: Moses—that is, the prophet; the rod—that is, the word of God. The priest touches the rock with God’s words, water flows out, and God’s people drink. [Thus the priest touches the cup]; water overflows in the cup and springs up into eternal life.

Likewise: Receive another point. From his side flowed water and blood: water, in order to cleanse; blood, in order to redeem. Why from the side? Because grace came from the same place as guilt. Guilt came through a woman; grace through Christ.

Likewise: You have heard Psalm 22; see how suitable it is to the heavenly sacraments: “The Lord feeds me, and I shall lack nothing,” etc. “Upon the water of refreshment,” etc. “For even if I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, because you are with me. Your rod,” etc. The rod is authority; the staff is the Passion. Eternity is Christ’s divinity; the Passion is temporal [Note: [Col. 1521D] Editions: “bodily.”]. The former created; the latter redeemed. “You have prepared a table before me,” etc.; “and how excellent is my cup.”

Likewise: Whenever you drink, you receive forgiveness of sins and are made drunk in the Spirit. Therefore the Apostle says (Ephesians 5:18): “Do not become drunk with wine, but be filled with the Holy Spirit” [Col. 1521D].

Likewise: A splendid intoxication, which produces sobriety of mind.

Likewise: “May your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11:3). By Christ’s blood all things in heaven and on earth have been reconciled. Heaven has been sanctified; the devil has been cast down. He dwells where the human being is, whom he deceived.

I told you that before Christ’s words, what is offered is called bread; once Christ’s words have been pronounced, it is no longer called bread, but body. Why, then, does he say in the Lord’s Prayer, “our bread”? He indeed said “bread,” but *epiousion*, that is, “supersubstantial.” This is not the bread that goes into the body, but that which sustains the substance of our soul [Col. 1522A]. Therefore in Greek it is called ἐπιούσιον (*epiousion*, “supersubstantial”). But the Latin translator called this bread “daily.” If it is daily, why do you receive it after a year, as the Greeks in the East are accustomed to do? Receive daily what benefits you daily. Live so that you may deserve to receive daily, as holy Job offered for his sons.

Likewise: He who has a wound seeks medicine. If you receive daily, every day is “today” for you. If Christ is “today” for you, he rises for you every day. How? “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). Therefore it is “today” when Christ rises. “He is the same yesterday and today,” says the apostle Paul (Hebrews 13:8).

For the Lord himself says: “Forgive us our debts!” (Luke 10:4). Where is the debt? Where I sin. You received a debt from the devil, and, though you were free in Christ, you became a debtor to the devil [Col. 1522B]. The enemy held your bond, but the Lord nailed it to the cross and blotted it out with his blood. He removed your debt and restored freedom.

From Book VI:

As the Lord Jesus Christ is the true Son of God—not as human beings are sons by grace, but as Son from the substance of the Father—so Christ’s flesh is true flesh, as he himself said, which we receive; and his blood is true drink.

Likewise: “I,” he says, “am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:41). But flesh did not come down from heaven. How did the living bread come down from heaven? Because the same Lord Jesus shares both in divinity and in body; and you who receive his flesh participate, in that food, in his divine substance.

Likewise: “Give us this day our daily bread” [Col. 1522C]. This petition is the greatest among those requested. “And forgive us,” he says, “our debts.” Therefore receive daily, that daily you may seek pardon for your debt.

The same, in the book *On the Mysteries*:

Truly it is wonderful that God rained manna upon the fathers. Hence it was said: “Man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77:25). Yet all who ate that bread died in the wilderness. But this food which you receive, this living bread which came down from heaven, supplies the substance of eternal life; and whoever eats it shall not die eternally, because it is Christ’s body.

Consider whether the bread of angels or Christ’s flesh is greater. That manna was from heaven; this is above heaven. That was of heaven; this is of the Lord of heaven. That was subject to corruption if kept for another day; this is free from all corruption, and whoever tastes it reverently cannot experience corruption. For them water flowed from the rock; for you, blood flows from Christ. The Jew drank and thirsted; when you have drunk, you cannot thirst. That was in shadow; this is in truth.

Likewise: Light is greater than shadow, truth than figure, the body of the Author than manna from heaven.

Likewise: Let us prove that this is not what nature formed, but what blessing consecrated, and that the power of blessing is greater than that of nature, because by blessing nature itself is also changed. You see that by prophetic grace the nature of both serpent and rod was twice changed [Col. 1523A].

Likewise: The sacrament which you receive is effected by Christ’s saying. You have read concerning all the elements of the world that he himself spoke, and they were made (Psalm 32:9). Can Christ’s saying, which could make from nothing what did not exist, not change things which exist into what they were not?

Likewise: Beyond the order of nature, the Virgin gave birth; and this body which we effect is from the Virgin. Why do you seek here the order of nature in Christ’s body, when the Lord himself was born of a Virgin beyond nature? Certainly Christ’s flesh, which was crucified and buried, is true flesh; therefore this is truly the sacrament of that flesh. The Lord himself cries out: “This is my body.” After the consecration, body is signified and blood is named. And you say: “Amen,” that is, “It is true.” Let the inward mind confess what the mouth speaks; let the heart feel what the saying sounds.

Likewise: Christ is in that sacrament, because it is Christ’s body. Therefore it is not bodily food but spiritual food. Hence the Apostle says concerning its type that our fathers ate spiritual food (1 Corinthians 3:9). For God’s body is a spiritual body; Christ’s body is the body of the divine Spirit.

The same, in the sermon on Abel and Cain:

For if you believe that flesh was assumed by Christ and offer the transfigured body upon the altars, yet do not divide the nature of the Word and of the body, then it is said to you: “If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, you have sinned” (Genesis 4:7, according to the Septuagint).

Jerome, to Hedibia:

Moses did not give us the true bread, but the Lord Jesus himself—both guest and banquet, himself eating and also being eaten [Col. 1523C].

The same, on Matthew 26:26:

“Take and eat: this is my body.” After the typical Passover had been fulfilled and he had eaten the lamb’s flesh with the apostles, he takes bread, which strengthens the human heart, and passes over to the true sacrament of the Passover, so that, as Melchizedek, offering bread and wine, had done in prefiguration of him, he too might set forth the reality of his own body and blood.

The same, in the book *On the Members of the Lord*:

The Son of God is called priest of God the Father according to his humanity, in which he offered himself to God for us as an acceptable sacrament, so that he himself might be both priest and sacrifice.

Augustine, *On the Usefulness of Doing Penance*:

Then Peter proclaimed to them that they must worship him whom they had crucified, so that by believing they might now drink his blood, which they had shed in their fury [Col. 1523D].

The same, in the Letter to Irenaeus:

That bodily manna is now not such a great miracle, because that which is perfect has come. And the perfect thing is bread from heaven, the body from the Virgin.

The same, Homily II on Psalm 33:

The Jews approached Jesus in order to crucify him; let us approach in order to receive his body and blood.

Likewise: Truly great is the Lord and great is his mercy, who gave us his body to eat—the body in which he suffered so much—and his blood to drink.

In the homily on Psalm 28 addressed to the Jews:

Now safely drink the [blood] which you shed.

In Homily LXXV:

The very blood which they shed in madness, they drank through grace.

In the homily on Psalm 29:

From Mary’s flesh he took flesh [Col. 1524A], and he gave that very flesh [to us] to eat for salvation. No one, moreover, eats that flesh unless he has first adored it.

The same, on Psalm 33:

David was carried in his own hands. No one is carried in his own hands. We do not find how this is to be understood of David himself according to the letter, but we find it in Christ. For he was carried in his own hands when, commending his body, he said: “This is my body.” For that body was carried in his own hands.

In Homily XXXI on John:

They despaired until they drank the blood which they had shed.

The same, in Prosper’s books of *Sentences*:

This is what we say and what we strive by every means to establish: that the sacrifice of the Church is effected by two things and consists of two things—the visible appearance of the elements and the invisible flesh and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ; sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, that is, Christ’s body. Thus Christ’s person consists and is constituted of God and man, since Christ himself is true God and true man; for every thing contains in itself the nature and reality of those things of which it is constituted. Therefore there is the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament—that is, Christ’s body.

Likewise: His flesh, which we receive in the sacrament covered under the form of bread, and his blood, which we drink under the appearance and taste of wine, are flesh and blood—the sacrament of blood. By both flesh and blood, invisible, intelligible, and spiritual, Christ’s visible and tangible body is understood and signified, full of the grace of every virtue and [Col. 1524C] divine majesty.

Likewise: Therefore, just as the heavenly bread which is truly Christ’s flesh is in its own manner called Christ’s body, although it is in fact the sacrament of Christ’s body—namely, of that body which was laid upon the cross—so the very offering of the flesh performed by the priest’s hands is called Christ’s passion, death, and crucifixion, not in the reality of the thing but by the signifying mystery. So also the sacrament of faith, which is understood as baptism, is faith.

The same, on Psalm 53:

The Jews fed, as it were, upon the Lord’s punishment, and we feed upon the Lord’s cross, because we eat his body. Therefore the impious have their feasts; the pious have theirs—those blessed persons who hunger and thirst for righteousness, etc.

Pope Leo, in the sermon on the fast of the seventh month:

Since the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54), you ought to partake of the sacred table in such a way that you entertain absolutely no doubt concerning the reality of Christ’s body and blood. For what is received by the mouth is what is believed by faith; and “Amen” is vainly said by those who dispute against what they receive.

The same, in a letter sent to Bishop Anatolius:

For otherwise in the Church of the Lord, which is Christ’s body, neither are priesthoods valid nor sacrifices true, unless the true blood of the immaculate Lamb cleanses us in the property of our nature. Although he is established at the right hand of the Father, he nevertheless performs the sacrament of propitiation in the same flesh which he took from the Virgin.

The same, in the sermon *On the Lord’s Passion*:

He inflicted punishment upon the Son of God and shed righteous blood, which, for the reconciliation of the world, might be both reward and cup [Col. 1525A].

Gregory, in a Paschal homily:

What the blood of the Lamb is, you have learned no longer merely by hearing but by drinking—the blood placed upon both doorposts when it is drawn not only with the mouth of the body but also with the mouth of the heart.

The same, in Dialogue IV:

Then there will truly be an offering for us to God when we have made ourselves an offering. Indeed, even for sinners and unworthy recipients, Christ’s flesh is true flesh and Christ’s blood true blood; but it is so in essence, not in salutary effect.

Eusebius of Emesa [Note: [Col. 1525D] From a homily on the body and blood of the Lord, published among Jerome’s works; its author is said to be uncertain. Compare Jerome’s works, Martianay edition, V, 391.]:

The true, unique, and perfect sacrifice is to be judged by faith, not by appearance, nor assessed by the outward sight [of a human being], but by inward devotion. Hence heavenly authority confirms this: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Let, therefore, every ambiguity of unbelief depart [Col. 1525B], since he who is the author of the gift is himself also witness to the truth.

For the visible [Note: [Col. 1525D] Munich manuscript: “although invisible.”] priest, by his word and hidden power, changes visible creatures into the substance of his body and blood, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.” And lest it seem new [Note: [Col. 1526D] Munich manuscript: “not true.”] and impossible to you that earthly things are changed into Christ’s substance, ask yourself, etc.

From the Passion of Saint Andrew, where he says to Aegeas:

Although his flesh is eaten on earth and his blood is truly drunk, he nevertheless remains whole and living in heaven at the right hand of the Father.

Preface for the Fifth Sunday after Theophany:

Each receives Christ the Lord [Col. 1525C], and he is whole in each portion. He is not diminished by being distributed among individuals, but gives himself entire in each.

Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, *On the Life and Miracles of Saint Basil*, chapter VII:

While he was celebrating the divine mysteries, a certain Hebrew mingled among the Christian people as though he were a Christian, wishing to investigate the mystery of the rite and offering. He saw an infant prepared in Basil’s hands; and when all were communicating, he too came and was given that which had truly become flesh for him. Then he approached the cup, filled with blood as it truly was, and became a partaker of it. Preserving portions of both, he departed to his house, showed them to his wife to confirm his words, and told her what he had seen with his own eyes.

Believing, then, how terrible and wonderful the Christian mystery truly is, on the next day he came to Basil [Col. 1525D], asking without delay to receive the seal that is in Christ. Holy Basil did not delay, but baptized him, together with all his household, as believers in the Lord.

From the *Lives of the Fathers*, Treatise on Charity, chapter XXVI:

Abbot Daniel also related, saying: My father Arsenius spoke of a certain old man who was great in his way of life but simple in faith, and who erred because he was unlearned. He said that the bread which we receive is not naturally the body, but its figure.

When two elders heard this and knew that his life and conduct were great, they thought that he spoke innocently and simply. They said to him: “We have heard the saying of a certain unbelieving abbot, who says that the bread which we receive is not by nature Christ’s body, but its figure.”

But the old man said to them: “I am the one who said this.”

They entreated him, saying: “We believe that the bread itself is Christ’s body and the cup is blood according to truth and not according to figure. Just as God formed the human being in his image, and no one can say that it was not God’s image, although it was incomprehensibly made, so we believe that the bread of which he said, ‘This is my body,’ is truly Christ’s body.”

The old man said: “Unless I know the thing itself, your reasoning does not satisfy me.”

They said to him [Col. 1526B]: “Let us pray to God during this week about this mystery, and we believe that God will reveal it to us.”

The old man gladly accepted this, and prayed to God, saying: “Lord, you know that I do not disbelieve this thing through malice, but err through ignorance. Reveal it to me, Lord, for you are merciful to me.”

The two elders also departed to their cells and prayed, saying: “Lord, reveal this mystery to the old man, so that he may believe and not lose the fruit of his labor.”

The Lord heard both parties. When the week was completed, they came to church, and the eyes of their understanding were opened. When the loaves were placed on the altar, they alone saw a little child lying upon the altar. When the priest stretched out his hands to break the bread [Col. 1526C], an angel came down from heaven holding a knife in his hand and sacrificed that child. He caught the child’s blood in the cup. When the priest divided the bread into small portions, the angel likewise cut the child’s limbs into [many] portions [Note: [Col. 1526D] Munich manuscript: “ways.”].

When the old man came forward to receive communion, he alone was given flesh stained with blood. Seeing this, he was terrified and cried out: “I believe, Lord, that the bread placed upon the altar is your body, and the cup is blood.” Immediately that flesh became bread in his hand according to the mystery, and he received it with thanksgiving.

The elders said to him: “God knows human nature: it cannot eat raw flesh, and therefore he transformed his body into bread and his blood into wine for those who receive it in faith.”

From the Gospel:

Taking bread, he blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: “This is my body,” etc.

From the First Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Corinthians (10:1):

For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink—for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock [Col. 1527A] was Christ.

Likewise: I speak as to prudent persons; judge for yourselves what I say. The cup of blessing which we bless—is it not a sharing in Christ’s blood? And the bread which we break—is it not a participation in the Lord’s body? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, all of us who partake of the one bread and cup (1 Corinthians 10:15).

Likewise: What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons; you cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons (ibid., 20).

Likewise: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Therefore whoever eats this bread [Col. 1527B] or drinks the Lord’s cup unworthily will be guilty of the Lord’s body and blood. Let a person examine himself, and thus eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For whoever eats and drinks [unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself], not discerning the Lord’s body. Therefore many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep. But if we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (1 Corinthians 11:27–31).

Ambrose, on Luke 9:27:

“Some standing here will not taste death until they see the kingdom of God.” We have bread which came down from heaven. He eats that bread who keeps the things that are written.

Likewise, on Luke 17:37:

“Where the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.” The souls of the righteous are compared with eagles [Col. 1527C], which seek the heights.

Likewise: Concerning the body we can no longer doubt, especially apart from the gifts, because Joseph received the body from Pilate. Do Mary of Clopas, Mary Magdalene, the Lord’s mother, and the assembly of apostles about the Lord’s burial not seem to you like eagles about the body? Do they not seem like eagles about the body when the Son of Man comes with intelligible clouds and every eye sees him? For it is the body of which it was said: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Around this body are the true eagles, which fly about with spiritual wings. For the Church is a body.

The same, in the book *On the Sacraments*:

“Make this offering acceptable for us, which is a figure of the body and blood of the Lord.”

Likewise: The altar is a figure of the body [Col. 1527D].

The same, in the Epistle to the Corinthians:

Because we have been freed by the Lord’s death, mindful of this fact, in eating and drinking we signify the flesh and blood which were offered for us.
