Likewise: The blood is witness to the divine benefit, as a type of which we receive the mystical cup.

Origen, on Matthew 26:26:

“For this is my body,” and “taking the cup,” etc. The bread which God the Word confesses to be his body is truly food nourishing the soul: the Word proceeding from God the Word, and bread from the heavenly bread, placed upon the table of which it is written (Psalm 22:5): “You have prepared a table before me against those who afflict me.”

And this drink, which God the Word confesses to be his blood, is the Word that gives drink and gloriously intoxicates the hearts of those who drink [Col. 1528A]; it is in the cup of which it is written: “And how excellent is your cup which intoxicates.” This drink is the fruit of the true vine, which says: “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). It is the blood of that grape which, cast into the winepress of the Passion, produced this drink.

Likewise, the bread is Christ’s word, made from that wheat which, falling, yields much fruit. For God the Word did not call that visible bread which he held in his hands his body, but the Word in whose mystery that bread was to be broken. Nor did he call that visible drink his blood, but the Word in whose mystery that drink was to be poured out. For what else can the body or blood of God the Word be except the Word which nourishes and the Word [Col. 1528B] which gladdens the heart?

Jerome, to Hedibia, concerning various questions:

How should the words be understood, “I shall not henceforth drink of this fruit of the vine,” etc. (Matthew 26:29)? Let us hear that the bread which the Lord broke and gave to his disciples is the Lord’s body.

Likewise: “This is my blood of the New Testament.” Therefore, if the bread that came down from heaven is the Lord’s body, and the wine which he gave to his disciples is his blood, shed for the forgiveness of all sins, let us go up with the Lord to the upper room and receive from him the cup of the New Testament from above; and there let us be intoxicated with him by the wine of sobriety.

Likewise: Moses did not give us the true bread, but the Lord Jesus—the guest and the banquet, himself eating and also being eaten. We drink his blood; and daily, in his sacrifices [Col. 1528C], we tread the red must of the fruit of the true vine and of the vine Sorec, which is interpreted “chosen,” and drink from them new wine in the kingdom of the Father—not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit—singing the new song which no one can sing except in the kingdom of the Church, which is the Father’s kingdom.

Likewise: All who are baptized into Christ put on Christ, eat the bread of angels, and hear the Lord proclaiming: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me.” Let us therefore do his will, and Christ will drink his own blood with us in the kingdom of the Church.

The same, on Psalm 147:

“And he satisfies you with the fat of wheat.” Our Lord fell into the earth as a grain of wheat [Col. 1528D] and multiplied us. This grain of wheat is exceedingly rich. Blessed is the person who understands richness in this wheat.

I consider the body of Jesus to be the Gospel; I consider it to be the holy Scriptures. And when he says, “Whoever has not eaten my flesh and drunk my blood,” although this can also be understood in the mystery, yet more truly Christ’s body and blood are the word of the Scriptures, the divine teaching. When we go to the mystery, the faithful person understands; if he falls into a stain, he is in danger. Whenever we hear the word of God and Christ’s flesh and blood are poured into our ears, but we think of something else, into how great a danger do we run? The divine word is exceedingly rich. It contains every delight in itself.

As the Jews relate that manna, when they ate it, tasted in each person’s mouth according to that person’s wish [Col. 1529A], so in Christ’s flesh—which is the word of teaching, that is, the interpretation of the holy Scriptures—we receive what we wish.

Likewise: “He sends forth his utterance to the earth” (Psalm 147:15). “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). This Word is sent forth in flesh: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14). “He sends forth his utterance to the earth.” He speaks of evangelical preaching and the teaching of the apostles. Accordingly it follows: “His word runs swiftly” (Psalm 147:15), and apostolic teaching goes throughout the world.

The same, in a certain sermon on the paschal lamb, which begins, “Today the people of Israel”:

It is commanded that we eat in one house, that is, lest we suppose that the lamb sacrificed outside the Church is ours. From this it is clear [Col. 1529B] that Jews, heretics, and the assemblies of every perverse doctrine, who do not eat the lamb in the Church, do not eat the lamb’s flesh but that of the dragon, “given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.”

Likewise: What follows—that we are not to eat the lamb’s flesh raw or boiled—means that we must neither understand the divine Scriptures, which are truly the Lamb’s flesh, merely according to history, nor divert and weaken them by certain allegories and the cloudiness of interpretation toward perverse doctrines.

“You shall eat its head with its feet and entrails” (Exodus 11:9). The head is spiritual understanding; the feet are the simple narrative according to history; the entrails are whatever lies hidden in the letter.

Likewise: Know, brothers, that whoever renders the marital debt cannot devote himself to prayer, nor abstain from meat [Col.

[Col. 1529C] …to eat the Lamb. For if the loaves of the Presentation could not be eaten by those who had touched their wives, how much more may that bread which came down from heaven not be violated and touched by those who shortly before have clung in marital embraces?

The same [Note: [Col. 1529D] Not Jerome’s, but Origen’s.] in a certain homily [VII] on Leviticus: The Lord says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:56), because all his work is holy and all his word true. In the second place after his flesh, Peter and Paul are pure food; and so each person, according to the purity of his merits, becomes pure food for his neighbour. Whoever cannot hear this perhaps turns away his hearing, like those who said: “Who can hear him?” But if you are children of the Church, if you have been imbued with the mysteries of the Gospel, recognize that what we say belongs to the Lord, lest he who is ignorant be ignored. Recognize that the things written in the divine books are figures; therefore, as spiritual persons and not carnal ones, understand what is said. There is also a letter in the Gospels which kills. For if you follow according to the letter this very saying which is written, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood” (ibid., 54), this letter kills.

Therefore, as we have said, every human being has within himself some food; from it, whoever takes, if that person is good and brings forth good from a good treasure, brings forth pure food for his neighbour. Thus every person, when speaking to his neighbour, whether he benefits or harms that neighbour by his words, becomes for him a clean or an unclean animal. If we say, according to this understanding, that God promulgated laws for human beings, the legislation will seem worthy. But if we adhere to the letter, I blush to confess that God gave such a law. [Note: [Col. 1530D] Editions: “That God gave such laws.”]

The same in the Epistle to the Ephesians: Thus the flesh and blood of Christ are understood in two ways: either that spiritual and divine flesh of which he himself says, “My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink,” and, “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you shall not have eternal life”; or my flesh which was crucified, and the blood which was shed by the soldier’s lance. According to this distinction, a difference of flesh and blood is also recognized among his saints: one flesh is that which shall see the salvation of God; another flesh and blood are those which cannot possess the kingdom of God.

The same on Isaiah: They eat the foods of impiety when they are not holy in body and spirit, and do not eat the flesh of Jesus or drink his blood, of which he himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood shall have eternal life” (ibid., 55). “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed,” and is eaten not outside but in one house and within.

From a sermon of Augustine: Whether the sacrament of the mystical cup is under a figure or under truth. Truth says: “My flesh is truly food and my blood is truly drink.” Otherwise, how will it be great that “the bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (ibid., 52), unless the flesh is true? But because it is not permitted to devour Christ with the teeth, he willed that this bread and wine should, in the mystery, truly be created as his flesh and blood through the power of the consecration of the Holy Spirit, and mystically sacrificed daily for the life of the world; so that, just as true flesh is created from the Virgin through the Spirit without intercourse, so through that same Spirit the same body of Christ may mystically be consecrated from the substance of bread and wine.

The body of Christ is both truth and figure: truth, when the body and blood of Christ are made from the substance of bread and wine by the power of the Spirit through his own word; figure, in what is outwardly perceived. This offering is repeated daily, although Christ suffered once, because we sin daily, at least by those sins without which mortal frailty cannot live; and therefore Christ is mystically sacrificed for us daily.

Within the Catholic Church, in the mystery of Christ’s body, nothing greater is received by a good priest, nothing less by an evil one, because it is accomplished not by the merit of the consecrator but by the word of the Creator and the power of the Holy Spirit. For if it were in the priest’s merit, it would in no way belong to Christ. But now, just as he himself is the one who baptizes, so he himself is the one who by the Holy Spirit makes this his flesh and transfuses the blood.

Likewise: This offering is blessed, through which we are blessed; enrolled, through which we may all be enrolled in heaven; ratified, through which we may be reckoned to be in Christ’s bosom; rational, [Col. 1531A] through which we are stripped of bestial understanding [Note: [Col. 1531D] Monac.: “sexual intercourse”]; acceptable, so that through it we may be acceptable to his only Son. Nothing is more rational than that, having received in baptism the likeness of his death, we should also receive the likeness of his flesh and blood, so that truth may not be lacking in the sacrament and no mockery may be made by pagans—that we drink the blood of a slain human being. For if the disciples could not patiently endure what the Lord had said, “He who eats my flesh,” and so forth, but said, “This saying is hard” (John 6:61), how could unbelievers endure these things?

For it must be believed that the sacraments are made by Christ’s words. For by whose power they are first created, by that one’s word they are surely recreated for the better. Everything else which the priest says or the clergy chant is nothing [Col. 1531B] but praise and thanksgiving, or certainly entreaties, requests, and petitions of the faithful. Among the words of God are: “Take and eat of this, all of you” (Matt. 26:26). In this word, therefore, that body is created.

Likewise: The same principle applies to the Lord’s body as to the manna which preceded it in figure, concerning which it is said (Exod. 16:18): “He who had gathered more had no excess, nor did he who had obtained less have less.” In this mystery visible quantity is not to be assessed, but the power of the spiritual sacrament; just as the bodily quantity of the man Christ is not to be measured, but his power and divinity are to be considered.

Likewise: This mystery was handed down to the disciples before the Passion, because a shadow can never exist unless light is shining. Alternatively: Christ knew that this mystery would be received worthily by the good and unworthily by the evil. He wished to show all communicants what good or evil is received from it; therefore Judas, as the figure of all evildoers, was permitted to receive first. For if it had taken place after the Resurrection, Judas could no longer have communicated with the holy apostles, since he would already have been condemned. Flesh is rightly joined with blood, because flesh cannot properly be communicated without blood, nor blood without flesh. The whole human being, consisting of two substances, is redeemed; and therefore is nourished at once by Christ’s flesh and blood. Finally, not—as some wish—is the soul alone fed by this mystery; rather, through it the flesh also passes [Col. 1531D] into immortality and is restored to incorruption.

The same, *Seventy-Two Questions*, chapter XII: Every soul is better than every body. For everything which gives life is better than that which is given life.

The same, book XI of *The City of God*, on good and evil angels: The cause of their blessedness is their cleaving to God; the cause of these others’ misery is their not cleaving to him.

Likewise: Just as a sentient nature, which can also suffer with another, is better than a stone which cannot suffer at all.

Likewise: A rational creature, even when miserable, is more excellent than one devoid of reason or sensation, and misery therefore does not befall the latter.

The same, in a sermon *On the Benefit of Doing Penance*: He who was prefigured through manna had delivered them from death. In brief, then: whoever understood Christ in the manna ate the same spiritual food as we do.

The same, in the exposition of the Gospel (John 6, tractate 26; Maur. III, 498): Why do you prepare tooth and belly? To believe in him is to eat the bread and wine. One is invisibly filled, because one is invisibly reborn. This is the bread which came down from heaven. Manna signified this bread. “All,” he says, “ate the same spiritual food.” Spiritually, indeed, the same; but bodily another, because they had manna and we something else; spiritually, however, the same as we. “And all drank the same spiritual drink.” They had one thing, we another, in visible appearance; yet it is the same [Col. 1532B] in spiritual power. [Note: [Col. 1531D] Maur.: “signified.”] How the same drink? “They drank,” he says, “from the spiritual rock following them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). From there came the drink; from there, the bread. The rock was Christ in sign; the true Christ is in flesh and word. This is the bread coming down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he may not die (John 6:50). This pertains to the power of the sacrament, not to the visible sacrament: the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; who eats in the heart, not the one who presses with the tooth.

Likewise: Therefore, he who does not eat his flesh nor drink his blood does not have eternal life in himself; and he who eats and drinks has eternal life. He wishes this food and drink, then, to be understood as the fellowship of Christ’s body and his members, [Col. 1532C] which is the Church. The sacrament of this reality—that is, of the unity of Christ’s body and blood—is received from the Lord’s table in some places daily, in others at fixed intervals of days: by some unto life, by others unto destruction. But the reality itself, of which it is a sacrament, is unto life for every person and unto destruction for none who have become its participants.

The same, in a sermon *On Infants*: No one ought in any way to doubt that every one of the faithful is then a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when in baptism he is made a member of Christ; nor is he alienated from the fellowship of that bread and cup, even if, before eating that bread and drinking that cup, he departs from this world while established in the unity of Christ’s body. [Col. 1532D] For he is not deprived of participation in or benefit from that sacrament when he finds in himself that which the sacrament signifies. [Note: [Col. 1532D] Monac.: “The sacrament—he who, because of participation in it, is not deprived of the benefit, when … he finds.”]

The same, in a sermon *On the Sacraments*: Because he suffered for us, he commended to us in this sacrament his blood and body—and he also made us ourselves. For we too have been made his body, and through his mercy we are what we have received.

Likewise (Maur. V, 976, fragment): You have been brought to the Lord’s threshing floor; you were threshed by the labours of oxen—that is, of those proclaiming the Gospel—when, as catechumens, you were being held back; you were preserved in the granary; you began to be ground by fasts [Col. 1533A] and exorcisms. Afterwards you came to the water and were sprinkled, and you were made the Lord’s bread. Be one by loving one another, holding one faith, one hope, and indivisible charity.

Likewise: Wine was in many bunches, and is now wine. It is wine in its natural state, the cup after the pressures of the winepress. [Note: [Col. 1533D] Maur.: “and now it is one. It is one in the sweetness of the cup, after the pressure of the winepress.”] And after those fasts, labours, and crushings, you have now come in Christ’s name as it were to the cup; and there you are on the table and in the cup. You are with us. For together we receive this, together we drink, because together we live.

The same, on John (12:8), sermon I: “For you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me.” This can also be understood thus: he spoke of the presence of his body. For according to his majesty and [Col. 1533B] invisible grace, what he said is fulfilled: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). But according to the flesh which the Word assumed, you do not always have me with you. Why? Because he associated with the disciples in bodily presence for forty days, ascended into heaven, and is not here. He is there, seated at the right hand of the Father, and he is here. For the presence of his majesty has not departed. Alternatively: according to the presence of his majesty, we always have Christ; according to the presence of his flesh, only for a few days. Now faith holds him; sight does not see him.

The same, in the exposition of Psalm 54: Saying, “This saying is hard,” they separated themselves from him; he remained with the Twelve and instructed [Col. 1533C] those who remained. “It is the Spirit,” he says, “that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64). “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life,” that is, they are to be understood spiritually. Have you understood carnally? They are not spirit and life to you. Understand spiritually what I have said. You are not going to eat this body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me will shed. I have commended some sacrament to you; spiritually understood, it will give you life. But flesh profits nothing. For they understood flesh as it is sold in a corpse [Note: [Col. 1534D] Monac.: “truly said.”], or cut to pieces in a butcher’s shop.

But Jesus, knowing this, said: “Does this scandalize you, because I said that I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink? What then if you see the Son of Man [Col. 1533D] ascending where he was before?” (Ibid., 62.) What does this mean? By this he resolved what troubled them; by this he disclosed that over which they had been scandalized; by this, plainly, if they understood. But they thought that he would distribute his body; he said that he would ascend whole into heaven. “When you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before,” surely even then you will see that he does not distribute his body in the way you think; even then you will understand that his grace is not consumed by bites.

Likewise: Until the age is ended, the Lord is above; nevertheless, the Lord as truth is also here with us. For the body in which he rose must be in one place, but his truth is spread everywhere.

[Col. 1534A] Likewise: We cannot touch Christ, now seated in heaven, with our hands, but we can touch him by faith.

Likewise: Who would dare to eat his Lord? And yet he says: “He who eats me lives because of me” (ibid., 58). Since Christ is eaten, life is eaten; nor is he killed in order to be eaten, nor, because he is eaten, do we make parts of him. Indeed, this occurs in the sacrament; the faithful know how they eat Christ’s body. Each receives his own portion; he is eaten in portions, yet remains whole in heaven and whole in your heart.

Likewise: What you see upon the altar is bread and a cup, as our very eyes report to us. But what faith, needing instruction, requires is this: the bread is the body, the cup is the blood.

Likewise: He ascended into heaven; there [Col. 1534B] he raised his body, and there he sits at the right hand of the Father. How then is the bread his body? And how is the cup—or what the cup contains—his blood? These, brethren, are called sacraments because one thing is seen in them and another understood. What is seen has a bodily appearance; what is understood has spiritual fruit.

The same, in the letter to the priest Boniface: We often speak in such a way that, as Easter approaches, we say that the Lord’s Passion will be tomorrow or the day after tomorrow, although he suffered so many years ago. On the Lord’s Day itself we say, “Today the Lord rose,” although so many years have passed since he rose. We name these days by likeness to those on which these things were done, so that the very day may be called the day which is not that day itself, but is like it through the cycle of time. Was Christ not sacrificed once in himself? Yet in the sacrament he is sacrificed for the people every day. For if sacraments did not possess some likeness of those things of which they are sacraments, they would not be sacraments at all. Yet from this likeness sacraments also commonly receive the names of the things themselves. Thus, in a certain manner the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood; so too the sacrament of faith is faith.

The same, book X of *The City of God*: A visible sacrifice is the sacrament—that is, the sacred sign—of an invisible sacrifice.

Likewise, in book XX: “He who eats my flesh and drinks [Col. 1534D] my blood remains in me, and I in him” (ibid., 57). He shows what it is to eat Christ’s body and drink his blood, not merely sacramentally but in reality. For this is to remain in Christ: that Christ may remain in him. For he said this as though saying: whoever does not remain in me, and in whom I do not remain, should not say or suppose that he eats my body or drinks my blood. Therefore those who are not his members do not remain. And those are not Christ’s members who make themselves members of a prostitute, unless they cease to be that evil person through repentance.

Likewise, book XXI: Therefore such persons are not to be said to eat Christ’s body, because neither are they to be counted among [Col. 1535A] Christ’s members. For, to say nothing of other matters, they cannot likewise be members of Christ and of a prostitute. Finally, he himself says: “He who eats my flesh,” and so forth.

The same, in a certain letter: A sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace.

The same, book I of *On Instructing Beginners*: A sacrament is a visible seal of an invisible divine reality.

The same, in the book *On Penance*: A sacrament is the seal of a divine mystery.

The same, book II of *On Christian Doctrine*: A sign is a thing which, beyond the appearance it presents to the senses, causes something else to come into thought of itself.

The same, against Faustus: For what else are bodily sacraments but certain visible words, as it were—most holy indeed, yet nevertheless mutable and temporal?

The same, in the exposition of Psalm 98, where he says: “Understand spiritually [Col. 1535B] what I have spoken. You are not going to eat the body which you see, nor drink that blood which those who crucify me will shed. I have commended some sacrament to you; spiritually understood, it will give you life. Although it must be celebrated visibly, it must nevertheless be understood invisibly.”

The same, in the *Confessions*: “I am the food of the mature; grow, and you shall eat me. You will not change me into yourself, but you will be changed into me.”

The same, in the book *On the One Baptism*: If we turn our attention to the visible things through which the sacraments themselves are administered, who does not know that they are corruptible? But if we look to that which is effected through them, who does not see that it cannot be corrupted?

The same, book III of *On Christian Doctrine*: “‘Unless you eat,’ he says, ‘the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves’” (John 6:54). He seems to command a crime or an outrage. Therefore it is a figurative command, requiring that the Lord’s Passion be shared and stored in memory: that his flesh was crucified and wounded for us.

Likewise, in book VII of *On Baptism*, he introduces Saint Cyprian saying: When the Lord calls his body bread from heaven, compounded by the unity of many grains, he indicates our people gathered from the nations; and when he calls his blood wine, pressed from many clusters and grapes and brought together into one, he signifies our flock joined by the intermingling of a united multitude.

The same, on Psalm 20: What was done once is enacted in your memory every year. [Col. 1535D] Whenever Easter is celebrated, is Christ killed as often? But the yearly commemoration presents what was done long ago and thus moves us as if we saw the Lord present upon the cross.

The same, to Dardanus: God and man are one person, and each is the one Christ: everywhere in respect of what he is as God, but in heaven in respect of what he is as man.

Likewise: Do not doubt that Christ is everywhere present as God, and in a certain place of heaven according to the mode of his true body.

The same, in book I of the *Retractations*, against Adimantus, a disciple of Mani: From the fact that it is written that the blood of a beast is its soul, besides what I have said above, I can also interpret [Col. 1536A] that command as having been set forth in a sign. For the Lord did not hesitate to say, “This is my body,” when he gave the sign of his body.

Bede, in a homily on the Gospel reading, “On the first day of the week, very early” (Luke 24:1): We ought also to imitate the women, who were distressed in mind when they did not find the Lord’s body. For we must continually remember that we cannot find the body of our Lord on earth, and humble ourselves all the more because we know that from the depths we must cry to him who dwells in heaven; and be all the more distressed in mind because we ought to know that we are still far away, journeying from him, in whose presence alone we can live blessedly.

Likewise: We should especially believe that angelic spirits are present with us when we are spiritually devoted to divine [Col. 1536B] services.

Haymo, on the Epistle to the Romans (7:4): When he says, “Through the body of Christ you have been made dead to the law,” of which body does he speak? For Christ’s body is that which he assumed in the virginal womb; Christ’s body is that which is daily consecrated in the Church. It is clear that the Apostle spoke of that body which he assumed in the virginal womb. Therefore Christ set us free from the law through his body; that is, through the Passion of his body he gave us remission of sins, so that we may no longer be subject to the law, if we cease from sinning.

From the decrees of Pope Pius, chapter III: But if through negligence anything from the Lord’s cup drips onto the ground, it shall be licked with the tongue [Note: [Col. 1535D] Monac.: “shall be licked”] and the board scraped. If there is no board, then, lest it be trampled underfoot, [Col. 1536C] the place shall be scraped away and burned with fire, and the ashes shall be placed in the altar.

From Theodore’s Penitential: Whoever vomits the sacrifice and it is consumed by dogs shall do penance for one year.

From the Council of Tours, chapter IV: The sacred offering shall always be kept upon the altar, because of mice and wicked persons; and it shall always be changed every seventh day and consumed by the people, while another offering, consecrated on that same day, is substituted in its place, lest, if kept longer, it should—God forbid—become mouldy.

From the Council of Orléans, chapter IV: The offerings placed upon the altar shall always be renewed from Sabbath to Sabbath, because the loaves of the Presentation were changed from Sabbath to Sabbath, lest, if kept long, they become mouldy or, as some rage, be consumed by fire. But if anyone, prompted by the devil, presumes to do this, [Col. 1536D] let him be anathema.

Likewise, chapter V: Every sacrifice spoiled by filthy age is to be burned with fire, and its ashes buried beside the altar.

Likewise, chapter VI: Whoever has not guarded the sacrifice well, and a mouse or some other animal has eaten it, shall do penance for forty days. But whoever loses it in church, or if a part of it falls and is not found, shall do penance for thirty days.

Likewise: Whoever acts negligently with regard to the sacrifice, so that it has been consumed by a worm and reduced to nothing, shall do penance for three forty-day periods on bread and water. If it is found whole, the worm in it shall be burned, and the ashes placed beneath the altar; and the negligent person shall expiate his negligence by four days’ penance. If the sacrifice is discoloured through loss of flavour, twenty days shall be completed in fasting.

From the Council of Rheims, chapter III: The corporal, upon which the sacred offering is sacrificed, shall never remain upon the altar except during the time of Mass; rather, it shall either be placed in the sacristy with the book, or put away with the paten and chalice; or, when it is washed, it shall be washed in a vessel prepared for this purpose, because it has been affected by the Lord’s body and blood.

Clement, in the second Epistle to James: The remnants of the Lord’s body, of the fragments, must be kept with fear and trembling.

### CXVIII. That the Eucharist must never be given dipped, and the contrary.

From the decrees of Pope Julius sent to the bishops throughout Egypt [Col. 1537B]:

They hand to the people the Eucharist dipped, as if for the completion of communion; yet they have not received this testimony from the Gospel, where he entrusted his body and blood to the apostles. For the bread is mentioned separately, and the cup separately. We do not read that Christ gave dipped bread to others, except to the one whom the dipped morsel revealed as the betrayer of his master—not as signifying the institution of this sacrament.

Augustine on John (XIII, 26): “The one to whom I shall give the dipped bread,” etc. What he received was good, but he received it to his own harm, because an evil man received a good thing evilly. For it matters greatly not what a person receives, but who receives it; nor what the thing given is like, but [Col. 1537C] what the recipient himself is like. Therefore Satan entered the betrayer of the Lord after this bread, so that he might possess more fully one already delivered over to him—into whom he had first entered in order to deceive him. For presumption in receiving the sacrament led to the sin of betrayal: when bread entered the ungrateful man’s stomach, the enemy entered his mind.

“And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas” (ibid.). But Judas did not then, as some suppose, receive Christ’s body. For it must be understood that the Lord had already distributed to them all the sacrament of his body and blood, among whom Judas himself was present, as Luke narrates most clearly; then, by the dipped and offered morsel, he identifies his betrayer—perhaps signifying his deceit by the dipping of the bread.

The same author, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book I:

But if, when the Lord said, “Do not give what is holy to dogs,” he had meant what these people think must be avoided, he himself would not have given to his betrayer what that unworthy man received, among the worthy, to his own destruction and without fault on the giver’s part.

From the Council of Tours, chapter III:

Every priest shall have a pyx or vessel worthy of so great a sacrament, in which the body of the Lord may be stored as viaticum for those departing from this world. The sacred offering, however, ought to be dipped in Christ’s blood, so that he may truly say to the sick person: “May the body and blood of the Lord profit you,” etc.

### CXIX. That a married priest is not to be rejected by those subject to him, and the contrary.

From the Council of Gangra:

If anyone rejects a married priest [Col. 1538A] on the ground of his marriage, holding that he ought not to offer, and therefore abstains from his offering, let him be anathema.

Likewise, chapter III:

Whoever rejects a priest because he has had a wife, and does not wish to receive the offering when he ministers, let him be anathema.

Alexander II:

Moreover, we command by decree that no one shall hear the Mass of a priest whom he knows certainly to have a concubine or a woman secretly introduced into his household. Therefore the holy synod also established this from the outset under excommunication, saying:

Whoever among priests, deacons, or subdeacons, after the decree of our predecessors, the holy Popes Leo or Nicholas, concerning clerical chastity, shall openly take a concubine or shall not dismiss one already taken—from God’s part and by the authority [Col. 1538B] of the blessed chief apostles Peter and Paul, we command and altogether forbid that he sing Mass, read the Gospel or Epistle at Mass, remain in the presbytery for divine offices with those who have obeyed the aforesaid decree, or receive a share from the Church. And we decree that those of the aforesaid orders who have obeyed these same predecessors of ours and preserved chastity shall eat and sleep together by their churches, as religious clerics ought, and shall hold in common whatever is due to them from the churches. Entreating them, we urge them earnestly to strive to attain the apostolic or common life, so that, having attained [perfection], [Col. 1538C] they may deserve to be enrolled in the heavenly homeland among those enriched with the hundredfold fruit. (MANSI, XIX, 1025.)

### CXX. That the offering of heretics does not profit, and the contrary.

Cyprian:

A heretic’s offering cannot sanctify, because the Holy Spirit is not there; nor does the Lord benefit anyone through his prayers and petitions. For Christ’s body, which is eaten, is not consecrated without the faith by which it is eaten.

Jerome, in the letter to Epithalamus:

Those whom you see in ecclesiastical office to be usurers, adulterers, and concubinarians, intent upon heaping up Mammon’s money—treat them as heretics in their manner of life. If he is a priest, you should not hear him handle the body and blood of the Lord; indeed, you should not permit him to handle them [Col. 1538D] at all.

Likewise:

“You cannot,” says Truth, “serve God and Mammon” (Matt. VI, 24). Whom, then, does one serve who serves Mammon? Do you wish to hear whom? The worship of idols. Hear the Apostle (Eph. V, 5): “A covetous person, which is the service of idols, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God.” Can one who through his greed becomes an idolater [*idololatra*] be called a worshipper of Christ? He does not worship Christ, nor his holy body; nor does Christ act through him.

The same author, on the prophet Amos:

God hates the sacrifices of heretics and has cast them away from himself; and whenever they gather under the Lord’s name, he detests their stench and closes his nostrils. And if they offer burnt offerings—so that they may appear to fast, give alms, and promise chastity, which would be true burnt offerings—God does not receive them [Col. 1539A]. He judges not the magnitude of the sacrifices, but the merits and motives of those who offer. Thus the widow who put in two small coins is preferred by the Savior to all, because the Lord looks not at the things offered, but at the will of the offerers.

The same author, on Zephaniah:

Priests act wickedly in the law of the Lord, thinking that it is the words of the person praying, not his life, that make the Eucharist; and that the solemn prayer alone is necessary, not the merits of priests—of whom it is said: “The priest in whatever blemish he may be shall not approach to offer offerings to the Lord.”

Augustine, book II against the letter of Parmenian:

Through Isaiah (LXVI, 3), the Lord says: “The criminal who sacrifices a calf to me is like one who kills a dog; and one who offers fine flour is like one who offers swine’s blood; and one who offers incense for remembrance is like a blasphemer.” [Col. 1539B]

Likewise:

The sacrifices of the wicked harm those themselves who offer wickedly. For the sacrifice becomes such for each person as is the heart with which he approaches to receive it. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

Likewise:

All sacraments, although they harm those who handle them unworthily, nevertheless benefit those who receive through them worthily.

Likewise:

The Holy Spirit is present in a ruler or minister of the Church in such a way that, if he is not false, he works through him both his own reward and the regeneration or edification of those who are either consecrated or evangelized through him. But if he is false, he is indeed lacking for his own salvation.

Likewise:

How do Catholics fail to glorify God, when they treat his sacraments with such due reverence that, even if they have been handled by unworthy persons—who are condemned by their own perversity—they show that the sacraments remain in their undefiled holiness? [Col. 1539C]

The same author, in the dialogue addressed to Petilian:

Remember that human conduct does nothing to harm God’s sacraments, so that they either cease to exist altogether or become less holy.

Likewise:

I give thanks because you have finally confessed that Christ’s invoked name can avail for the salvation of others even when it is invoked by sinners. Therefore understand from this why, when Christ’s name is invoked, the sins of others do not harm another person’s salvation.

The same author, in the book *Questions on the Old Testament*:

It was said of the most wicked Caiaphas: “He did not say this from himself; but, being high priest that year, he prophesied” (John XI, 51). From this it is understood that the Holy Spirit “begets” [Note: [Col. 1539D] Maur.: *spectare*, “regards.”] not the person, whether worthy or unworthy, but the order of transmission; so that, although someone may be of good merit, he nevertheless cannot bless unless he has been ordained to perform the office of the mystery. But it belongs to God to grant the efficacy of blessing.

The same author, *On the One Baptism*, book II:

It is one thing not to possess something, and another not to possess it lawfully or to usurp it unlawfully. Therefore they are not for that reason not the sacraments of Christ and of the Church; and not only heretics, but all the unjust and ungodly use them unlawfully. Yet those persons are to be corrected or punished, while the sacraments are to be acknowledged and venerated.

Pope Nicholas, in response to the inquiries of the Bulgarians, chapter LXXI:

Whatever the character of the priest, holy things cannot be defiled; therefore communion must be received from him until he is rejected by the judgment of bishops. For evil men, by administering good things, harm only themselves. A lighted wax torch brings loss to itself but light to others; and from that from which it provides benefit to others, it suffers loss itself. Therefore receive Christ’s mysteries fearlessly from every priest, because all things are purified in faith; and because, as blessed Jerome teaches, baptism is perfect in every soul for the believer not by virtue of the giver but of the recipient. Again, in agreement with Sacred Scripture, he says: “Before hearing, do not judge anyone; and before the proof of the charge brought, suspend no one from your assembly,” because one who is accused is not at once guilty, but one who is convicted is criminal. [Col. 1540B]

### CXXI. That Mass must not be celebrated before the third hour except at the Nativity, and the contrary.

Telesphorus, seventh from Peter, in his Decretal:

On the holy night of the Lord’s Nativity they shall celebrate Masses; but at other times celebrations of Mass are by no means to be held before the third hour of the day.

The same author, in his letter, chapter VI:

Celebrations of Mass are by no means to be held before the third hour of the day, because at that same hour the Lord was crucified and the Holy Spirit is read to have descended upon the apostles—except on the night of the Nativity.

From the sayings of Augustine:

This too must be observed: particular Masses [Col. 1540C] celebrated by priests on solemn days should not be held so publicly that the people are diverted by them from the public solemn celebrations of Mass, which are canonically held at the third hour. For it is a most pernicious custom among some people on Sundays or any feast-days to celebrate Mass immediately, even if it is for the dead; after hearing it, people depart and, from early morning throughout the whole day, give themselves to drunkenness and feasting rather than to God.

### CXXII. That marriage is permitted to all, and the contrary.

Paul the Apostle, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians [VII, 1]:

Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife and each woman her own husband. [Col. 1540D]

Acts of Pope Stephen of the First See, chapter III:

The condition of the Eastern churches is one thing; the law of the holy Roman Church another. For their priests, deacons, and subdeacons enter into marriage; but in this Church and in the Western churches none, from subdeacon through bishop, have permission to enter into marriage.

Leo, against the letter of Nicetas, abbot:

Let us set out in order and plainly [Note: [Col. 1539D] Mansi XIX, 696: “sets out.”] what the holy Roman Church does in the ranks of clergy. It permits clerics who are doorkeepers, readers, exorcists, and acolytes—if they are found outside the vow [Note: [Col. 1540D] Mansi: *vomitum* (“vomiting”), with *solitum* (“customary”) in the margin.] and habit of a monk, and do not wish to profess continence—to marry a virgin with priestly blessing; but not a widow or [Note: [Col. 1541D] Mansi omits “or.”] a repudiated woman. For on this account he will thereafter not deserve to be promoted to the subdiaconate [Note: [Col. 1541D] Mansi: “who … may be promoted.”]; nor may a layman who has married a non-virgin wife, or a bigamist, be admitted to the clergy.

Bede, *On the Tabernacle* (book III, chapter 9; cf. Exod. XXVIII, 42):

The breeches commanded to be made for covering the shamefulness of the flesh properly signify that portion of chastity which restrains one from the desire of marital union [Note: [Col. 1541D] Monac.: “The breeches given to Aaron’s sons for covering the flesh’s shamefulness signify properly that portion of chastity which restrains from desire …”], without which no one can either receive the priesthood or be consecrated to the mystery of the altar, unless he has remained a virgin or dissolved the bonds of a contracted marital union [Note: [Col. 1541D] Monac.: “or the bonds of union with a wife.”].

Gregory to Venantius, bishop of Luni (Maur. II, [Col. 1541B] 729):

We decree that the deacon and abbot of Portus Veneris, whom [Note: [Col. 1542D] Monac.: “whom of Portus Veneris.”] you judge to have fallen, ought not and cannot in any way be restored to sacred order. Subdeacons likewise, whom a similar fault binds [Note: [Col. 1542D] Monac.: “The subdeacons also bind us with a similar fault, from, etc.”], having been irrevocably deposed from their office, shall receive communion among the laity.

The same author, to Anthemus, subdeacon:

If we learn that any monks have rushed into so great a crime as publicly to take wives, seek them out with every vigilance, and, once found, send them back under restraint to the monastery of which they are monks.

Likewise:

It has come to us that a certain very wicked man, by the devil’s prompting, persuaded a woman consecrated to God to leave a monastery; and that she was recalled by a certain man from whom she had gone out. Again this wicked man, by an iniquitous persuasion, removing her from the monastery, has until now retained her with himself shamefully. We wish and command that she be recalled and brought back by the authority of your bishopric.

The same author, *Morals*, book XII:

“It is better to marry than to burn” (I Cor. VII, 9). They enter marriage without fault, provided that they have not yet vowed better things. For whoever has undertaken a resolution to embrace a greater good makes the lesser good, which was permitted, unlawful. For it is written: “No one who puts his hand to the plough,” etc. (Luke IX, 62).

Pope Gelasius:

We have learned that some men associate themselves with sacred virgins and, after their dedication, unite with them in incestuous and sacrilegious bonds. Such persons must immediately be excluded from holy communion and not received except through public and approved penance; nevertheless, viaticum is not to be denied them when they depart this world, if they have repented. [Col. 1541D]

From the Council of Chalcedon:

We decree that a deaconess is not to be ordained before the age of eleven, and this only after careful examination. But if she has received ordination and has exercised ministry for any period, and afterward gives herself to marriage, doing injury to God’s grace, let her be anathema with the man whom she marries.

Likewise:

It is not lawful for a virgin who has consecrated herself to God, nor likewise for a monk, to contract matrimonial rights. If they are found to have committed this, let them be excommunicated; but in the case of those who confess, we decree that the bishop of that place has authority to grant mercy and humane consideration. [Col. 1542A]

Jerome, against Jovinian, book I:

“And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned” (I Cor. VII, 28)—but not the virgin who has once dedicated herself to God’s service. If any one of these marries, she will incur condemnation, because she has made her first pledge void. But if he added this concerning widows, how much more will it apply to virgins, when even those are forbidden to marry who were once not forbidden? For publicly consecrated virgins who marry are not so much adulteresses as incestuous women.

Augustine, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, chapter XXXIV:

Permission to marry is given to some—that is, those who have not professed virginity or virginal chastity [Note: [Col. 1542D] Maur.: “those who have not professed virginal or widowed chastity,” etc.]; but it is not given to others, namely those who have resolved to be virgins or continent persons. Fornication is granted to no one with impunity.

The same author, in the letter to Count Boniface:

We know—we are witnesses—what you discussed with us at Tubunae concerning your purpose and intention. You were alone with us, myself and brother Alypius. You wished, of course, to leave all the public affairs with which you were occupied, devote yourself to holy leisure, and live the life which God’s servant monks live. Since, then, we rejoiced that you had this purpose, you sailed away and took a wife. If you had no wife, I would say to you what we said at Tubunae [Col. 1542C]: live in the chastity of continence. But your wife is an obstacle to my urging you toward that life, since you may not live continently without her consent. For even though you ought not to have taken her after those words you spoke at Tubunae, she, knowing none of these things, married you innocently and simply. Would that you could persuade her to continence, so that without impediment you might render to God what you know you owe him. But if you cannot undertake this with her, preserve marital chastity nevertheless, and pray to God that you may one day be able to do what you cannot now.

The same author, *On Widowed Continence*:

“For some have already turned back after Satan” (I Tim. V, 15): that is, falling and perishing by looking back from the excellent purpose of virginal or widowed [Col. 1542D] chastity. Therefore, if they do not contain themselves, let them marry before they profess continence, before they vow to God; if they fail to fulfil their vow, they will justly be condemned. For elsewhere he says of such persons (I Tim. V, 11): “When they have lived luxuriously in Christ, they wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have made their first pledge void”—that is, they have turned their will toward marriage away from their purpose of continence.

Likewise:

She who has not begun, let her deliberate; she who has undertaken it, let her persevere. Let no offering be withdrawn from Christ. In the marriage bond, if chastity is preserved, condemnation is not feared; but in widowed and virginal continence the excellence of a greater gift is sought. Once that gift has been sought, chosen, and offered as the debt of a vow, it is now damnable not only to enter marriage, but even, if one does not marry, to wish to marry. For, to show this, the Apostle did not say, “When they have lived luxuriously in Christ, they marry,” but, “They wish to marry, incurring condemnation because they have made their first pledge void.” This is not because marriages—or such women—are judged condemnable, but because fraud against their purpose is condemned; the broken fidelity of the vow is condemned; not the taking up of a lower good, but the fall from a higher one. Such women are condemned not because they later entered into marital fidelity, but because they made void their first pledge of continence. [Col. 1543B]

To indicate this briefly, the Apostle did not wish to say that women who marry after the purpose of greater holiness incur condemnation—not because they are not condemned, but lest marriage itself be thought condemned in them.

Likewise:

“Incurring condemnation because they have made their first pledge void”: so that the will that has fallen away from its purpose may appear to be condemned, whether marriage follows or does not follow. Therefore those who say that such marriages are not marriages but rather adulteries do not seem to me to consider carefully enough what they say. The resemblance to truth deceives them.

Likewise:

Some reason from this, saying: “If a woman who marries another while her husband lives is an adulteress, then, while Christ lives—over whom death no longer has dominion—a woman who had chosen his marriage is an adulteress if she marries a man.” Those who say this are indeed moved by a subtle point, but they pay too little attention to the absurdity that follows from such reasoning. For when a woman may laudably vow continence to Christ, even while her husband is alive and with his consent, then according to their reasoning no woman ought to do this, lest she make Christ himself an adulterer by marrying him while her husband lives.

Further, since first marriages are of greater merit than second marriages, far be it that holy widows should think of Christ as a second husband. They had him before as well, when they faithfully served their husbands—not carnally, but spiritually—him whose spouse is the Church, of which they are members. [Col. 1543D]

But this insufficiently considered opinion—that women who have fallen from a holy purpose, if they marry, have not marriages—produces no small evil: wives are separated from their husbands as though they were adulteresses, not wives; and while people wish to restore them, once separated, to continence, they make their husbands genuine adulterers when, while their wives are living, they take other women.

Therefore I cannot say that women who have fallen from a better purpose, if they marry, have adulteries rather than marriages; but I would certainly not hesitate to say that falls and ruins from the holier chastity vowed to the Lord are worse than adulteries. For if, as cannot in any way be doubted, it pertains to Christ’s offense when one of his members rightly does not keep faith, how much more grievously is he offended when faith is not kept with him himself in what he demands as having been offered, though he had not demanded that it be offered? For when someone does not pay what he vowed—not compelled by command but admonished by counsel—the iniquity of the broken vow is increased in proportion as there was less necessity to vow. [Col. 1544A]

Likewise:

After the profession of a vow, what pleases one must be restrained and overcome, because it is no longer lawful.

Likewise, on Leviticus:

He willed that a sister should not be brought in over her sister, as Jacob seems to have done—either because it had not yet been forbidden by law, or because he was deceived by the fraud of the substituted other woman, and the one he received later came more from his approval. But it was unjust for the former to be dismissed, lest he make her commit adultery.

“Hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke I, 28).

Bede:

Truly she was full of grace: it was bestowed by divine gift that she should be the first among women to offer God the glorious gift of virginity. Therefore she deserved rightly to enjoy the angelic sight and affection alike, she who strove to imitate the angelic life. Truly the Lord was with her, whom he had previously consecrated in a new chastity.

“The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke I, 35).

Because he both cleansed her mind, insofar as human frailty permits, from every stain of vices; filled her heart; restrained it from every heat of carnal desire; cleansed it from temporal desires; and consecrated together her mind and body with heavenly gifts. [Col. 1544C]

### CXXIII. That there was marriage between Mary and Joseph, and the contrary.

According to Luke (II, 5):

Joseph also went up to register with Mary, his pregnant wife.

According to Matthew (I, 20):

Joseph, son of David, do not fear to take Mary your wife.

Ambrose, *Exhortation to a Virgin*, book II [Note: [Col. 1543D] Editions: *On the Institution of a Virgin*, chapter 6.]:

Being betrothed to a man, she received the name of wife. For when marriage is initiated, it then receives the name of marriage [Note: [Col. 1544D] Editions: “assumes.”]. In short, marriage exists when a girl is joined in betrothal, not when she is known by a man’s intercourse.

Likewise:

It is not the defloration of virginity, but the marital agreement, that makes a marriage. [Col. 1544D]

Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, I:

As for those who have resolved by agreement to abstain forever from the use of carnal concupiscence, far be it that the marital bond between them should be broken. Rather, it will be firmer, in proportion as they have made agreements with one another which must be observed more dearly and harmoniously—not by pleasurable bonds of bodies, but by voluntary affections of minds. Nor was the angel speaking falsely to Joseph when he said: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife” (Matt. I, 20). She is called wife by reason of the first pledge of betrothal; nor was the designation of wife untrue where there had been, and would be, no carnal intercourse. Therefore both deserved to be called parents of Christ through a faithful marriage—not only she his mother, but also he his father; each being the spouse of the other in mind, not flesh. [Col. 1545A]

Likewise:

Thus every good of marriage was fulfilled in those parents of Christ: offspring, fidelity, sacrament. We recognize the offspring as the Lord himself; fidelity, because there was no adultery; sacrament, because there was no divorce.

Isidore, *Etymologies*, book IX, chapter VII:

They are more truly called spouses from the first pledge of betrothal, although marital cohabitation is still unknown between them [Note: [Col. 1545D] Editions: “is unknown”; “intercourse.”].

Hilary on Matthew, chapter I:

Many people quite alien to spiritual teaching seize corruptly upon an occasion for their opinion from the statement: “Before they came together, she was found with child by the Holy Spirit,” [Col. 1545B] and: “Do not fear to take Mary your wife,” and: “He did not know her until she gave birth.” They do not remember that she had been betrothed and, because she had been betrothed, was received as a wife. Thus after childbirth she is “known,” that is, she passes into the title of wife; she is not sexually joined. For when Joseph is instructed to go into Egypt, it is said: “Take the child and his mother”; and again in Luke: “And Joseph and his mother were.” Whenever both are mentioned, she is called mother rather than Joseph’s wife, because she was called what she was, not what she was not. But the angel also observed this distinction: when he indicated that she was betrothed, he called her wife. Therefore a betrothed woman receives the title of wife; but after giving birth, once recognized as wife, she is shown only as Jesus’ mother. Thus, just as the marriage of that same Mary was reckoned to the righteous Joseph, her venerable virginity was shown in Jesus’ mother. [Col. 1545C]

But most perverse people derive authority for their opinion from the tradition that our Lord had several brothers. If these had been Mary’s sons rather than Joseph’s children from an earlier marriage, she would never, at the time of the Passion, have been assigned to the Apostle John as mother, when the Lord said to them both: “Woman, behold your son,” etc. (John XIX, 26). In the disciple, he left the affection of a son as consolation for one left desolate.

Ambrose on Luke, chapter V:

“From that hour the disciple received her into his own home” (ibid., 27). Certainly, if they had had intercourse, she would never have left her own husband, nor would a just husband have permitted her to depart from him. How, moreover, could the Lord have commanded divorce, when his own judgment is that no one should dismiss his wife except for the cause of fornication? Holy Matthew has beautifully taught what a just man who discovers disgrace in his wife ought to do: he ought to keep himself free from bloodshed and chaste from adultery. For one joined to a prostitute is one body.

Leo:

Not all marriages constitute sexual union, when intercourse of the sexes does not follow them; nor could that woman belong to a marriage with whom there was no intercourse of the sexes.

From a certain antiphon concerning Saint Mary [Col. 1546A]:

Blessed mother and unwedded Virgin, etc.

### CXXIV. That it is lawful to have a concubine, and the contrary.

Institution of the Novels, LXXIX:

No one is to be understood to have a concubine who is at any time accustomed to marry many women. For just as one who has a lawful wife cannot have another while the same marriage endures, so one who has one concubine cannot have others at the same time.

*Pandects*, book XXXIII, title II:

In the relationship with a free woman, not concubinage but marriage is to be understood, if she has not practised prostitution with her body.

First Council of Toledo, chapter XVII:

One who has no wife and has a concubine in place of a wife is not to be excluded from communion, provided only that he is content with union with one woman—either a wife or a concubine, as he prefers. [Col. 1546B]

Isidore, *On the Harmony of the New and Old Testaments*, chapter III:

For a Christian it is lawful, I do not say to have many women, but not even two at once—only one, either a wife or, certainly, if the term “wife” is unavailable, a concubine.

From the sayings of Augustine (Maur. V, 1504):

Listen, beloved members of Christ; may God hear you if you are deaf; may the angels hear if you despise yourselves. It is not lawful for you to have concubines whom you afterward dismiss and marry wives. It is not lawful for you to have a woman who has departed from her husband through repudiation. Wives who commit adultery may be dismissed only for the cause of fornication; but while she lives it is not lawful to take another. [Col. 1546C]

Likewise:

Before God and his angels I testify and declare that, especially in Christian times, it is never lawful and never will be lawful to have concubines.

From the Council of Arles, chapter XV:

It is never lawful for anyone to have a concubine.

### CXXV. That there is [Note: [Col. 1546D] Cous.: “there is not.”] marriage among unbelievers, and the contrary.

From the First Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians (VII.38): “A woman is bound for as long a time as her husband lives. But if her husband has fallen asleep, she is widowed; let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.”

Ambrose, likewise commenting on this epistle (1 Cor. VII.15): “But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; the brother is not, etc.” That is, the [Col. 1546D] reverence due to marriage is not owed to one who recoils from the author of marriage. For a marriage that lacks devotion to God is not valid. Consequently, it is not a sin for one who is dismissed on account of God to join herself to another. For contempt of the Creator dissolves the right of marriage in respect to the one who is left behind, lest one joined to another be accused. But the unbeliever who departs is known to sin both against God and against marriage, because he did not wish to retain his marriage under the love of God. Therefore marital fidelity is not to be kept toward one who withdrew for the very reason that he might not hear that the God of Christians is the author of marriage. [Note: [Col. 1546D] Munich manuscript: “authority and [of] Christians.”]

For if Ezra caused unbelieving wives or husbands to be dismissed, so that God might become propitious and not remain angry if they took others from their own people [Col. 1547A] (for they were not commanded in such a way that, after dismissing these, they were by no means to marry others), how much more, then, if the unbeliever has departed, will one have free choice, should one wish to marry a husband of her own law? For that marriage which was contracted outside God’s ordinance ought not to be reckoned against a person; but when afterward one comes to know and grieves that one has sinned, one reforms oneself so as to deserve pardon. But if both come to believe, they confirm their marriage through knowledge of God. “Let the widow marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord,” that is, a husband of her own religion.

Jerome, to Pammachius: “‘Let her marry only in the Lord,’ that is, a Christian.”

Likewise, *Against Jovinian*, book I: “If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, [Col. 1547B] let him not dismiss her” (1 Cor. VII.12). Concerning those whom faith found already married—that is, if one out of the two had become a believer—he commands that the believer not leave the unbeliever. Conversely, he commands that if the unbeliever repudiates the believer on account of faith in Christ, the believer must depart, lest one prefer a spouse to Christ, to whom even one’s soul must be subordinated. But now very many women, despising the Apostle’s command, join themselves to Gentiles and prostitute the temples of God to idols. The Apostle pardons the union of unbelievers when women already having husbands afterward came to believe in Christ, not those who, though Christians, married Gentiles; to them he speaks elsewhere: “Do not take up the yoke with unbelievers. For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ [Col. 1547C] with Belial? Or what share has the believer with the unbeliever? What consent has the temple of God with idols?” (2 Cor. VI.14).

Do you wish to learn more plainly that it is wholly unlawful for a Christian woman to marry a pagan? Hear the same Apostle: “Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord,” that is, a Christian (1 Cor. VII.39). He allows second and third marriages in the Lord; he forbids a first marriage to a pagan.

Likewise, book IV on the Epistle to the Ephesians: “Just as not every assembly of heretics can be called Christ’s Church, so not every marriage in which a wife is not joined to her husband according to Christ’s commandments can rightly be called matrimony, but is rather adultery.”

From the decrees of Pope Eutychian: “If a pagan dismisses a pagan wife before baptism, after baptism it shall be in his power to have her or not.”

Augustine [Col. 1547D], *On Adulterous Marriages*: “When her husband has died, she has the power to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (ibid.). This may be understood in two ways: either as remaining a Christian woman, or as marrying a Christian man. For I do not recall that it is declared without ambiguity in the Gospel or apostolic writings whether the Lord forbade believers to be joined to unbelievers, although the most blessed Cyprian says that to join in marriage with unbelievers is to prostitute Christ’s members to pagans. But because the question is different concerning those already joined, let the Apostle here too be heard saying: “If any brother has an unbelieving wife” (1 Cor. VII.12).

The same, *On the Good of Marriage*: “Adultery is said to occur when, either at the prompting of one’s own lust or with another’s consent, a person lies with another man or woman [Col. 1548A] contrary to the marriage covenant, and thus fidelity is broken.”

Bede, on Luke (IX.7): “Herod the tetrarch heard of Jesus’ reputation,” etc. Philip took as wife Herodias, the daughter of Aretas, king of the Arabs; afterward the same Aretas, having taken her away from him, gave her to Herod, because he was of greater power, and a public adultery resulted.

Likewise: “For Herod feared John, knowing him to be a holy man; and he protected him, and on hearing him he did many things and heard him gladly” (Mark VI.20). But love for the woman overcame him.

Likewise: Since he wished to restrain his lust, he fell into the guilt of homicide; and, by the strict judgment of God, the lesser sin became the cause of a greater sin for that sinner, so that, through desire for the adulteress whom he knew [Col. 1548B] ought to be detested, he shed the blood of the prophet whom he knew to be acceptable to God.

Likewise: “And the king was grieved” (Matt. XIV.9). He displayed grief on his face over that in which he secretly rejoiced: that what was being asked was what he had already intended to do, if he could do it with an excuse.

A sermon of Bishop John for the same day: “And this great man is handed over to an adulteress, condemned to a dancing girl.”

Likewise: “Herod, you commit adultery, and John goes to prison.”

From the Council of Meaux, chapter I: “If anyone had a virgin wife before baptism, he cannot have another. Crimes are absolved in baptism, not marriages.”

Innocent, to Rufus and Eusebius, bishops of Macedonia: “Then it is maintained that a man who, while a catechumen, had and lost a wife, and after baptism obtained another, ought not to be called a bigamist; [Col. 1548C] and that the latter should be regarded as his first wife, because the former marriage was washed away by the sacrament of baptism together with other crimes. Tell me: are only crimes remitted in baptism, or also those things which are carried out according to God’s commands and institutions? Is taking a wife a crime or not? If it is a crime, then He Himself is the author of guilt who, in paradise, while joining them together, blessed them so that crimes might be committed. But if it is not a crime, how is it believed to have been remitted among crimes? What judgment is made concerning the children of such persons? Surely they will not be excluded from sharing the inheritance and called illegitimate?”

Likewise: “The Lord Himself, when questioned by the Jews whether it was lawful to dismiss a wife, [Col. 1548D], explained that this ought not to happen, adding: ‘What God has joined together, let no human being separate’” (Matt. XIX.6). “And lest He be thought to have spoken of those who take wives after baptism, let them remember that He was questioned by Jews and gave His answer to Jews.”

Likewise: “The marital union, because it is accomplished by God’s command, cannot be called sin. It is therefore reasonable to judge that the designation of the former wife cannot be abolished, since it was not dismissed as a sin, because it was completed by God’s will.”

Ivo of Chartres, to Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans: “This, therefore, seems to me to require consideration concerning a woman who, having abandoned Judaism, hastened to baptism: whether she was related by blood to her former husband or not. If this is found to have been so, I believe that, according to the Christian law [Col. 1549A] which she has professed, she may be separated from her former husband and marry whom she wishes in the Lord. Otherwise, the man she has married will be an adulterer, and she an adulteress. For baptism, according to Pope Innocent, forgives sins; it does not dissolve marriages.”

Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, to Count Valerius: “Blessed Paul shows that marital chastity too is a gift of God, when, speaking on this matter, he says: ‘I wish all people to be as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that’” (1 Cor. VII.7).

Likewise: “What then do we say when marital chastity is found even among certain impious persons? Must they be said to sin because they use God’s gift wrongly, not referring it to the worship of Him from whom they received it? Or perhaps are these not to be regarded as gifts of God [Col. 1549B] when unbelievers do these things, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: ‘Everything that is not from faith is sin’ (Rom. XIV.23)? Who would dare say that sin is a gift of God? ‘Everything that is not from faith is sin’ was said of the things they do. But far be it from us to call one truly chaste who does not preserve the fidelity of marriage to his wife for God’s sake!

“The union, therefore, of male and female for the purpose of begetting offspring is a natural good of marriage. But one uses this good wrongly who acts beastially, so that his intention lies in the pleasure of lust rather than in the will to produce offspring. When unbelievers possess this manifest good, they turn it into evil and sin because they use it without faith. They do not beget children with this intention or for this end: to transfer them from the members of the first human being into the members of Christ. Rather, unbelieving [Col. 1549C] parents glory in unbelieving offspring. Even if they observe such restraint that, according to the marriage contract, they have intercourse only for begetting children, true marital chastity is not in them; for chastity is a virtue. How can a body rightly be claimed to be chaste when the mind itself commits fornication against the true God? The Psalm indicts this fornication when it says: ‘You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you’ (Ps. LXXII.27). The Apostle says: ‘Everything that is not from faith is sin’; and: ‘Without faith it is impossible to please God’ (Heb. XI.6).”

The same, *On the Good of Marriage* (Maur. VI, 337): “The good of marriage [Col. 1549D], then, among all nations and all people lies in the matter of begetting and in the fidelity of chastity; but among the people of God it lies also in the holiness of the sacrament. By that sacrament it is unlawful for a woman who has departed through repudiation to marry another while her husband lives; nor is the bond of marriage dissolved except by the death of a spouse, even when the sole purpose for which marriages are made, namely childbearing, does not follow.

“Just as if a cleric is ordained for gathering a people, and no gathering of people follows, the sacrament of ordination remains in those who were ordained; and if someone is removed from office for some fault, he will not lack the sacrament of the Lord once conferred, although it remains to his judgment. The Apostle is therefore witness that marriages are made for the purpose of generation: ‘I wish,’ he says, [Col. 1550A] ‘the younger women to marry’ (1 Tim. V.14). As though someone had asked him, ‘For what purpose?’ he immediately added: ‘to bear children, to be mistresses of households.’

“But the following belongs to fidelity of chastity: ‘The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife’ (1 Cor. VII.14). And the following belongs to the holiness of the sacrament: ‘Let the wife not depart from her husband; but if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband’ (ibid., 10); and: ‘Let the husband not dismiss his wife’ (ibid., 11). These are all goods for the sake of which marriage is good: offspring, fidelity, sacrament.”

The same, *Against Julian*: “Other things properly belong to marriage, by which marriages are distinguished from adulteries, such as the marital bed,” etc.

### CXXVI. That, after dismissing an adulterous wife, a husband may lawfully take another; and conversely.

[Col. 1550B]

Ambrose, on the First Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians (VII.10): “But to those joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife not depart from her husband. But if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let the husband not dismiss his wife.”

“It is not permitted to a woman to marry if she has dismissed her husband on account of fornication, because an inferior party does not employ the same law as the superior. Yet if the husband apostasizes or seeks to reverse the use of his wife, the woman can neither marry another nor return to him.”

Likewise: “And that the husband is not to dismiss his wife is understood with the exception of the cause of fornication. Therefore he did not add, as he did concerning the woman, [Col. 1550C] saying that if she departs she must remain thus, because a husband is permitted to take a wife if he has dismissed a sinful wife; for the man is not bound by the law in the same way as the woman.”

From the Council of Tribur, chapter XV: “If anyone sleeps with his brother’s wife, the adulterer and adulteress shall remain without marriage for the days of their life. But the man whose wife she was may, if he wishes, take another wife.”

Jerome, to Oceanus, on the death of Fabiola: “The Lord commanded that a wife ought not to be dismissed except on the ground of fornication, and that, if she is dismissed, she should remain unmarried. Whatever is commanded to men applies correspondingly to women. For an adulterous wife must not be dismissed while an adulterous husband is retained. ‘Whoever is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her’ (1 Cor. VI.16) [Col. 1550D]. Therefore, she who is joined to a fornicator and impure man becomes one with him.

“The laws of the Caesars are one thing, those of Christ another: Papinian commands one thing, Paul another. Among them the reins of sexual impurity are loosened; and, only seduction and adultery being condemned, lust is freely permitted through brothels and female slaves. Among us, what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to men, and the same servitude is judged under equal conditions. She therefore dismissed, as they say, a vicious man; she dismissed one guilty of this or that crime; he dismissed one whom, almost—[Note: Martianay: “I said almost, because … she alone did not betray it.”]—a good wife did not lose despite the neighborhood’s outcry.”

Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II: “Since a woman is bound [Col. 1551A] as long as her husband, whether adulterous or chaste, is alive, she commits adultery if she marries another; and a husband is bound as long as his wife, whether adulterous or chaste, is alive, and he commits adultery if he takes another. Therefore, if a husband dismisses an adulterous woman and does not wish to receive her back even after repentance, let him preserve continence—not, indeed, from the desire to choose the greater good, but at least from the necessity of avoiding a destructive evil.”

Likewise: “I think that no Christian resists the conclusion that a man is an adulterer if, while his own wife is long ill, absent, or desirous of living continently, he has intercourse with another woman. Thus a man whose adulterous wife has been dismissed is likewise an adulterer with another woman, because it is said not merely that this or that man, but that everyone who dismisses his wife and takes another commits adultery.”

The same, in the same work: “Those to whom it is displeasing [Col. 1551B] that an equal standard of chastity be observed between husband and wife, and who prefer in this matter to be subject to the laws of the world rather than those of Christ—because they see that civil laws do not seem to bind men with the same bonds of chastity as women—should read what the emperor Antoninus, himself not a Christian, decreed on this matter. A husband is not allowed to accuse his wife of adultery if he has not provided her, by his own conduct, an example of chastity. ‘Indeed,’ he says, ‘it seems very unjust to me that a husband should demand chastity from his wife which he himself does not exhibit.’”

The same, in the book *On the Ten Strings*: “‘You shall not commit adultery’ [Col. 1551C]: that is, you shall not go to another woman besides your wife. You demand this from your wife and do not wish to render it to your wife; and though you ought to precede your wife in virtue, do you wish your wife to be the victor? You lie defeated; and though you are the head of your wife, do you wish your household to hang head downward?”

The same, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II: “Husbands are indignant if they hear that adulterous men suffer punishments like those of adulterous women, although they ought to be punished much more severely, insofar as it belongs more especially to them both to conquer by virtue and to govern women by example.”

The same, *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, book I: “For nothing is more unjust than to dismiss one’s wife on account of fornication if one is oneself convicted of fornication. For this applies: ‘In passing judgment on another, you condemn yourself; for you do the very things which you judge’ (Rom. II.1). Therefore whoever wishes to cast away his wife on account of fornication ought first to have been cleansed of fornication himself; and I would say the same concerning a woman.”

The same, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book I: “Therefore that woman is commanded [Col. 1551D] to remain unmarried if she departs—the woman who departs from an adulterous husband.”

Likewise: “It remains for us to show that the statement, ‘if she departs, let her remain unmarried’ (1 Cor. VII.11), was said of her whom we have learned is permitted to depart from an adulterous husband.”

Likewise: “The Lord says: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and takes another, commits adultery’ (Matt. V.32).
