If this is to be understood in such a way that whoever dismisses her on account of fornication and takes another does not commit adultery, there does not appear to be an equal rule for husband and wife in this matter. For a woman, even if she departs from her husband on account of fornication [Col. 1552A] and marries another, commits adultery; but if a man dismisses his wife on the same ground and takes another, he does not commit adultery. But if the rule is equal for each, each commits adultery if joined to another, even when separated from an adulterous spouse.

“The Apostle shows that the husband and wife have an equal rule in this matter where he says: ‘Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does’ (1 Cor. VII.4). Why then, you ask, did the Lord introduce the ground of fornication rather than say generally, ‘Whoever dismisses his wife and takes another commits adultery,’ if he too is an adulterer who takes another after dismissing an adulterous wife? I believe it is because the Lord wished to state [Note: Editions: “recall.”] the greater matter. For who denies that it is a greater adultery to dismiss a non-adulterous wife [Col. 1552B] and take another than to dismiss an adulterous wife and take another?

“Accordingly, if I now say, ‘Whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband apart from the cause of fornication commits adultery,’ we undoubtedly speak the truth; yet we do not thereby absolve from this crime the man who marries one dismissed not on account of fornication, but we do not doubt that both are adulterers. So we pronounce an adulterer the man who dismisses his wife apart from the cause of fornication and takes another; yet we do not thereby defend from the stain of this sin the man who dismisses his wife on account of fornication and takes another. For we recognize both as adulterers, although one more seriously than the other.”

Likewise: “On account of every kind of fornication, whether of the flesh or of the spirit—in which unbelief too is understood—it is not lawful either for a woman to marry another after dismissing her husband or for a man to take another after dismissing his wife, because the Lord said without making any exception: ‘If a wife dismisses her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.’”

Likewise, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I (Maur. X, 286): “The rights of marriage once entered into remain between living persons to such an extent that those separated from one another are still spouses of one another rather than spouses of those to whom they have joined themselves. For they would not be adulterers with others unless they remained spouses of one another. Finally, when the husband with whom there was a true marriage has died, there can be a true marriage [Note: Munich manuscript: “cannot.”] with the person with whom there was previously adultery. Thus, even among the living, something marital remains [Col. 1552D] which neither separation nor union with an adulterer can remove. It remains for the guilt of sin, not for the bond of covenant, just as the soul of an apostate, departing as it were from marriage with Christ, does not lose the sacrament of faith which it received in the laver of regeneration even when faith has been lost.”

The same, to Pollentius, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book I: “It seems to you that a woman who departs from her husband ought not to marry if she has not departed under compulsion from any fornication of her husband. For then, in your view, it would be lawful for them to seek other marriages if divorce arose on account of fornication.”

Likewise: “It was said: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, except on the ground of fornication, makes her commit adultery.’ [Col. 1553A] For then, by dismissing her, he does not make her an adulteress, but dismisses an adulteress.”

Likewise: “Therefore, when we say that even the woman who has dismissed an adulterous husband is not permitted to marry another, whereas you say that it is permitted indeed but not expedient, both of us undoubtedly say that she who dismisses an adulterous husband ought not to marry. But this is the difference: when both spouses are Christians, we say that a woman who has departed from an adulterous husband is not permitted to marry another, and that she is not permitted to depart from a husband who is not [Col. 1553B] adulterous. [Note: Munich manuscript omits “not.”]”

Likewise: “The Apostle—or rather, the Lord through the Apostle—since he does not permit a woman to depart from a husband who is not adulterous, necessarily forbids her, if she departs, to marry, though he permits her to depart from an adulterous husband. For she of whom it is said, ‘if she departs from her husband, let her not marry,’ is told not to marry on that condition.”

Likewise: “What the Lord says—‘Whoever dismisses his wife except on account of fornication and takes another commits adultery,’ etc.—uses a manner of expression like that of James when he says: ‘To one who knows how to do good and does not do it, it is sin’ (IV.17).”

Likewise: “Therefore, when we say, ‘Whoever marries a woman dismissed apart from the cause of fornication commits adultery,’ we speak of one person; yet we do not thereby deny that the one who marries the woman whom her husband dismissed on account of fornication commits adultery. Thus, since both are adulterers—both he, namely, who dismisses his wife apart from the cause of fornication and takes another, and he who, after dismissing his wife on account of fornication, joins himself to another [Col. 1553C]—we surely ought not, when we read of one of them, to understand it so that the other is denied to be an adulterer.

“But if Matthew, by expressly mentioning one case and passing over the other, makes this difficult to understand, have not the others stated the same point in a way that can be understood of both? For according to Mark (X.11) it is written: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife and takes another commits adultery against her; and if a wife dismisses her husband and marries another, she commits adultery.’ According to Luke (XVI.18): ‘Everyone who dismisses his wife and takes another commits adultery; and whoever marries a woman dismissed by her husband commits adultery.’”

Likewise: “‘For what do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband,’ etc. (1 Cor. VII.16): he seems to have exhorted them to win spouses and children for Christ, even from examples which had already occurred. Why it is not expedient for unbelieving spouses to be dismissed by believers is clearly expressed. He forbids departure from unbelieving spouses not in order to preserve the marital bond with such persons, but so that they may be gained for Christ.”

Likewise: “The Apostle says: ‘All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient. Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another’” (1 Cor. VI.12).

Likewise: “Therefore they are lawful, that is, not prohibited by any command of the Lord.”

Likewise: “Some things are said not to be commanded by the Lord, although believers are advised to offer them to the Lord, so that they may be understood to be more pleasing [Col. 1554A] in proportion as they are shown to be not obligatory.”

Likewise: “For those who do not restrain themselves, marriage is certainly expedient. But for those who have vowed continence, it is neither lawful nor expedient. Moreover, to depart from an unbelieving spouse is lawful but not expedient, because if it were not lawful it could not be expedient. Consequently not everything lawful is expedient. There are, indeed, lawful things which are not expedient, as we have learned from the Apostle’s testimony.

“But it is difficult to define by some universal rule the difference between what is unlawful and therefore not expedient, and what is lawful but nevertheless not expedient. For someone might more readily say: everything not expedient to do is sin; but every sin is unlawful; therefore everything not expedient is unlawful. And where then will be those things which the Apostle said were lawful but not expedient? [Col. 1554B]

“Therefore, since we do not dare say that certain sins are lawful, it remains for us to say that something may be done which is not expedient and yet, if it is lawful, is not sin, although, because it is not expedient, it certainly ought not to be done. But if it seems absurd that something not expedient may be done and that the one who has done it may be said not to have sinned, this must be understood from ordinary usage of speech [Note: Munich manuscript: “from the condition of expressions—absurd that,” etc. [Col. 1554D]], which extends so widely that we often say even beasts of burden, though devoid of reason, ought to be whipped when they sin. Yet sinning properly belongs only to one who uses the rational freedom of the will, which has been divinely granted among all mortal living creatures to human beings alone. But one thing is when we speak properly; [Col. 1554C] another when we borrow words by transferring or misapplying them from other things.”

Likewise: “Those things seem to me to be lawful and not expedient which are indeed permitted by the justice that is before God, but are to be avoided on account of offending people, lest they be hindered from salvation on that account.”

Likewise: “If it were not lawful to dismiss an unbelieving spouse, the Lord would forbid it; nor would the Apostle, while forbidding it, say: ‘I say, not the Lord.’ For if a person is permitted to separate from a spouse on account of fornication of the flesh, how much more detestable is fornication of the mind in a spouse—that is, unbelief—concerning which it is written: ‘For behold, those who make themselves far from you shall perish; you have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you’ (Ps. LXXII.27).

“But because it is lawful in such a way as not to be expedient—lest people, offended by separations of spouses, recoil from the teaching of salvation and remain in the same unbelief unto destruction—the Apostle, by advising, forbids what is lawful in such a way as not to be expedient.”

Likewise: “At one time the Lord commanded through Ezra the prophet (1 Esdr. X.11), and it was done: the Israelites dismissed foreign wives, through whom they themselves were being led away to foreign gods; not so that those women might be gained for the true God through their husbands. Therefore the Lord had commanded through Moses that no one should take a foreign wife. Rightly, then, those whom they had taken contrary to the Lord’s prohibition they dismissed at the Lord’s command.”

Likewise: “The fornication of an unbelieving person is greater in the heart; nor can there be called true chastity with a spouse [Col. 1555A] in such a person, because ‘everything not from faith is sin’ (Rom. XIV.23), although a believer has true chastity even with an unbelieving spouse. Believers, however, ought not to have been commanded to separate from unbelievers, because both pagans had been joined together not contrary to the Lord’s command.”

Council of Toledo, chapter XVII: “Neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband shall be joined to another; but let them remain thus, or be reconciled to each other.”

### CXXVII. That a bigamist may not be promoted to the clergy; and conversely.

[Note: In Cousin’s edition, not even the title of this question is found.]

Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage* (Maur. VI, 331): The sacrament of marriage has in the present age been reduced to one husband and one wife, so that it is not lawful to ordain as a steward of the Church [Col. 1555B] any man except the husband of one wife. [Note: Col. 1555D. Editions: “to ordain only a man of one wife.”] Those understood this more acutely who judged that a man who had had a second wife while a catechumen or pagan ought not to be ordained.

Likewise: It did not seem absurd that one who had exceeded the singular number of wives had committed no particular sin, but had lost a certain norm of the sacrament, necessary not for the merit of a good life but for the [seal] of ecclesiastical ordination.

Gennadius, *On the Orthodox Faith*: A husband of two married women after baptism is not to be ordained a cleric, etc.

Jerome to Bishop Oceanus, on how one ought to be instructed in the house of God: Both the new and the old commandment judged that a priest should be chosen as the husband of one wife.

[Col. 1555C] Likewise: Very many bishops have admitted twice-married men to ministry, and argue thus: “That woman was a concubine, not a wife,” as though the same filthy intercourse were not practised with her as with the woman alleged to be a wife. Or, because he did not draw up marriage documents, was his desire not alien? By no means ought a twice-married man, or one who keeps concubines, to undertake ministry. [Note: Col. 1556D. Editions: “it is fitting for those entangled in the chains of concubines,” etc.] It is written in Leviticus (21:13): “A priest shall take a virgin; he shall not take one widowed and abandoned, or left by a living husband.”

Likewise: Therefore, if a cleric is monogamous but his wife has been twice married, do not admit him to ministry. For he has married a twice-married wife.

The same author to the same person, on what is written, “the husband of one wife” (1 Tim. 3:2) (Martianay IV, 645): A heresy rises up, and the viper [Col. 1555D] long dead lifts its crushed head. For it says that there are some things which Christ cannot cleanse by his blood, and that the deep scars of former crimes cling to [bodies and souls], so that they cannot be worn away by his remedy. What else does this do but make Christ’s death vain? Far be it from us to believe of the Almighty that he is powerless in anything. The whole of the Apostle’s epistles resounds with Christ’s grace. Lest the simple naming of grace seem too little, he says: “May grace and peace be multiplied” [Col. 1556A] (1 Pet. 1:2). Is multiplication promised, while scarcity is asserted by us?

Carterius [Note: Col. 1556D. Munich manuscript: Archemus.], a bishop of Spain, a man advanced in years and in priesthood, took one wife before he was baptized and another after the washing, when the former had died [Note: Col. 1556D. Munich manuscript: “an adulteress.”]; and do you suppose that he acted contrary to the Apostle’s judgment, who commanded that the husband of one wife be ordained? Yet I wonder that you have brought forward one man alone, when the whole world is full of such ordinations. I do not speak of presbyters or lower ranks; I come to bishops. If I wished to name them one by one, so great a number would be assembled that it would exceed the multitude of the Synod of Rimini. But it is unbecoming to defend one in such a way that you seem to accuse many; and to defend by association in sin one whom you cannot defend by argument. [Col. 1556B] [Note: Col. 1556D. Editions: “to defend by association with sinners.”]

At Rome I endured from a most eloquent man a “horned,” as they call it, syllogism, so that whichever way I turned I was held all the more tightly. “Is it a sin,” he said, “to take a wife, or not?” I, simple-minded and not knowing how to avoid traps, said that it was not a sin. He proposed again: “Are evils remitted in baptism?” I answered that sins are remitted. When I thought myself safe, horns began to grow against me from both sides. “If,” he said, “taking a wife is not a sin, but baptism remits sins, whatever is [not] remitted is retained.”

Likewise: Returning to myself, I turned the twist of the proposition against my adversary. “I ask you,” I said, “to answer. Does baptism make a person wholly new, or only partly?” [Col. 1556C] He answered, “Wholly.” Therefore nothing of the old person is retained in baptism; nothing is left that can be charged against the new person because it once belonged to the old.

Likewise: “Did the Apostle choose baptized persons or catechumens for the episcopate? If the Apostle chose not catechumens but believers for the clergy, the vices of the catechumen shall not be imputed to the believer.” Therefore the Apostle’s epistles are brought forward, one to Timothy and another to Titus. In both, bishops and presbyters alike—for among the ancients bishops and presbyters were the same, since the former is a title of rank and the latter of age—are commanded to be chosen for the clergy as monogamous men. Certainly the discussion is of baptized presbyters. Therefore, if all the things required in an episcopal ordination do not prejudice the candidate for ordination, though he did not possess them before baptism—for the question is what he is, not what he was—why should the name of wife alone impede him, when it alone was not a sin? [Col. 1556D] You say that, because it was not a sin, it was therefore not remitted in baptism. I hear a new doctrine: because it was not a sin, it will therefore be counted as sin. All prostitutes and the filth of public debauchery, parricide, and incest are cleansed by Christ’s font; shall the stains of a wife cling, and brothels be preferred to marriage chambers?

I do not charge against you hosts of prostitutes or the shedding of blood, and you drag out for me from the grave a little wife long dead [Col. 1557A], whom I took precisely so that I might not do what you did. Let pagans hear it; let catechumens hear it: let them not take wives before baptism, let them not enter honourable marriages; rather, let them have Plato’s promiscuous wives and children in common. Indeed, let them beware of any designation of spouse, lest, after they have believed in Christ, it harm them that they once had not concubines or prostitutes, but wives.

Truly, like the scribes and Pharisees, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel, we tithe mint and dill and pass over God’s judgment. What likeness is there between a wife and a prostitute? The misfortune of a dead wife is imputed, and prostitute lust is crowned? That man, if his first wife had lived, would not have had another wife; what excuse can you give for contracting dog-like unions indiscriminately? He desired children in a wife; you destroyed offspring in a prostitute. Private chambers concealed him as he obeyed nature and the Lord’s blessing, “Increase and multiply and fill the earth” (Gen. 9:1); the public face abhorred you as you mounted for intercourse. He concealed with modest shame what was lawful; you thrust before all eyes with shamelessness what was unlawful. To him it is written: “Marriage is honourable, and the bed undefiled” (Heb. 13:4); to you it is read: “God will destroy fornicators and adulterers” (ibid.).

Likewise: “How were your stains washed away in baptism, while my cleanliness was made filthy?” You say, “I do not say that yours were made filthy, but that they remained in the same state in which they were.” What evasion is this, and an edge blunter than every pestle? Because what is not sin is sin; because what is not filthy is filthy.

Likewise: What he says, “the husband of one wife,” can also be interpreted differently. The Apostle knew that the Law permitted the begetting of children by many wives. Even priests themselves had the option of this licence open to them. He therefore commanded that priests should not claim that same licence for themselves in the Church, but should have one wife at a time.

Accept another explanation as well. Some forcibly interpret wives as Churches and husbands as bishops. The decree, they say, means that a bishop is not to be transferred from one Church to another, lest, despising the fellowship of a poor virgin, he seek the embraces of a wealthier adulteress. “That interpretation,” you will say, “is forced and quite harsh.” Then give Scripture back its own plain meaning, lest we contend against you by your own laws.

[Col. 1557D] I shall ask something else: if a man had a concubine before baptism and, after her death, was baptized and took a wife, should he become a cleric? You will answer that he may, because he had a concubine, not a wife. Therefore it is marriage documents and dowry-rights, not intercourse, that the Apostle condemns.

Likewise: See whether the phrase “husband of one wife” can be understood as “a man of one woman,” so that it refers more to sexual intercourse than to dowry documents.

Likewise: “The husband of one wife”: we have spoken of this above. Now we merely warn that, if being the husband of one wife is required even before baptism, we should also require before baptism all the other things that are commanded. [Col. 1558A] For it is not appropriate to understand every requirement after baptism and this one command before baptism: “sober, prudent, hospitable, a teacher,” etc.; “not a novice, lest, lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Tim. 3:2–6). I cannot sufficiently marvel at how great is men’s blindness in disputing about wives before baptism and dragging into accusation something dead in baptism—indeed made alive with Christ—when no one observes a command so open and evident. Yesterday a catechumen, today a bishop; yesterday in the theatre, today in church; in the evening at the circus, in the morning at the altar; lately a partisan of actors, now a consecrator of virgins. Did the Apostle not know our evasions and our foolish arguments? He who said, “the husband of one wife,” himself commanded that he be irreproachable, sober, prudent, and so forth. We shut our eyes to all these things; we see wives alone.

Likewise: Son Oceanus, see how great is the testimony of this man whom husbands accuse, against whom opponents can allege nothing besides the marriage bond—and that before baptism. Therefore, when they object to us wives before baptism, let us require from them everything commanded after baptism. They pass over what is not permitted and object to what is allowed.

## CXXVIII. That an adulteress must in no way be retained, and the contrary

Ambrose on Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians: Certainly, it is lawful to have a wife; but if she has committed fornication, she must be rejected.

Jerome on Matthew: Since she has divided one flesh into another and has separated herself from her husband by fornication, she ought not to be retained, lest she also make her husband accursed; for Scripture says: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious” (Prov. 18:22). Therefore, wherever there is fornication or suspicion of fornication, a wife may freely be dismissed.

Chrysostom on Matthew, chapter 19: Just as he who dismisses a chaste woman is cruel and unjust, so he who retains a prostitute is foolish and unjust. For he who conceals his wife’s crime is the patron of her shamefulness.

Augustine, *On Adulterous Marriages*, book II: What seems harsh to you in the reconciliation of a wife to her husband after adultery? Under the old Law these crimes were cleansed by no sacrifices [Col. 1558D], and therefore it was then altogether forbidden to take back a wife defiled by another man. Yet David, as a prefiguration of the New Testament, received without defilement [Note: Col. 1557D. Edition: “without delay.”] Saul’s daughter, whom her father had separated from him and given to another (2 Kings 3:14). But now, after Christ said to the adulteress, “Neither do I condemn you; go, sin no more” (John 8:11), who does not understand that a husband ought to forgive what he sees God has forgiven, and ought no longer to call her an adulteress when he believes that the crime of the penitent has been erased by divine mercy?

Likewise: Reconciliation of spouses will be neither shameful nor difficult even after adulteries have been committed and cleansed [Col. 1559A], where remission of sins through the keys of the kingdom of heaven is not doubted; not so that an adulteress may be recalled after divorce from her husband, but so that she may not be called an adulteress after union with Christ.

Hermas, *The Shepherd*, book II, Mandate IV: The shepherd said to me: “If a husband knows that his wife has sinned and lives with her, he will be guilty of her sin and a participant in her adultery.” [And I said:] “What if the dismissed woman does penance and wishes to return to her husband?” “If her husband does not receive her, he sins and commits a great sin. But he ought to receive the sinner who has repented, though not repeatedly; for God’s servants have one repentance. The case is alike for woman and man.”

## CXXIX. That it is lawful to marry repeatedly, and not

[Col. 1559B]

Paul in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (7:39): “A woman is bound for as long as her husband lives. But if her husband falls asleep, she is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.”

The same author in the First Epistle to Timothy (5:11): “Avoid younger widows.”

Likewise: “Therefore I wish younger women to marry, bear children,” etc. (ibid., 5:14).

Augustine, *On the Profession of Holy Widowhood*, to Juliana (Maur. VI, 376): People are accustomed to raise a question about third, fourth, and still more numerous marriages. I answer briefly: I dare neither condemn any marriages [Note: Col. 1559D. Editions: “any marriage.”] nor take away from them the modesty that is due in respect of their number.

Likewise: Nor, contrary to the sense of human modesty, do I dare say that a woman may marry whenever she wishes after husbands have died; nor, apart from the authority of Scripture and from my own heart, do I dare condemn marriages of however great a number.

Jerome to Pammachius: Let my detractors see that I have allowed second and third marriages.

Likewise: I now declare in a free voice that bigamy is not condemned in the Church—indeed, neither is trigamy—and that it is as lawful to marry a fifth, sixth, or further husband as a second. Let any woman have an eighth husband and cease to be a prostitute.

The same author, *Against Jovinian*, book I: It is more tolerable to be a prostitute to one man than to many; indeed, that Samaritan woman in the Gospel, saying that she had a sixth husband, is rebuked by the Lord because he was not her husband. Where there is a number of husbands, there the husband—who properly is one—ceases to be a husband.

Likewise: Once the number one is exceeded [Col. 1559D], it makes no difference whether it is the second or third, because the person ceases to be monogamous. I do not condemn twice-married persons, indeed not even thrice-married persons, or, if the expression may be used, persons married eight times. I go further still: I even receive a repentant debauchee.

The same author to Agorochia [Note: Col. 1559D. Editions: Ageruchia]: I saw two equals paired against one another, the most lowly people from the populace: one man who had buried twenty wives, and one woman who had had twenty-two husbands; they were united in what they themselves thought would be their final marriage. Everyone waited in great expectation to see which would bury the other first. The husband prevailed, and, with the people of the whole city gathering, he went before the bier of his many-married wife wearing a crown. What shall we say to such a woman? Surely what the Lord said to the Samaritan: “You have had twenty-two husbands, and the one by whom you are now buried [Col. 1560A] is not your husband.”

The same author to Salvina: The first Lamech, accursed and bloodstained, descending from the line of Cain, divided one rib into two; and the plantation of bigamy was immediately overthrown by the punishment of the Flood. Hence that saying of the Apostle, which he is compelled by fear of fornication to permit: “I wish younger women to marry, giving no occasion to the adversary for reproach” (1 Tim. 5:14). Why he allowed it, he immediately added: “For already some have turned aside after Satan.” From this we understand that he does not give a crown to those standing, but stretches out a hand to those fallen. See what sort of second marriages these are, which are preferred to brothels because some have turned aside after Satan. Therefore the young widow who cannot, or will not, remain continent should take a husband rather than the devil. Certainly it is a fine and desirable thing that is accepted by comparison with Satan.

## CXXX. That no human sexual intercourse can be without fault, and the contrary

Ambrose on Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, book II: “But if you take [a wife], you have not sinned.” Certainly, one who does what is allowed does not sin.

Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: Although intercourse undertaken with the intention of begetting children is not undertaken for sin, because the good will of the mind leads what follows; it does not follow what leads.

The same author, *On the Good of Marriage*: Marital intercourse for the sake of procreation has no fault. But adultery or fornication has mortal fault.

Likewise (Maur. VI, 326): What then shall we say against the Apostle’s most evident declaration: “Let him do what he wishes; he does not sin if she marries”; “if you have taken a wife, you have not sinned”; and “if a virgin marries, she has not sinned” (1 Cor. 7:28)? Hence it is no longer lawful to doubt that marriage is not sin. The Apostle therefore does not permit marriage by way of indulgence; for who would not see that it is utterly absurd to say that those are not sinners to whom pardon is granted? Rather, he permits by way of indulgence that intercourse which occurs through incontinence, not for the sole purpose of procreation and sometimes for no purpose of procreation at all. Marriage does not compel this intercourse to occur, but obtains pardon for it [Note: Col. 1560D. Munich manuscript: “disapprove.”], provided that it is not so excessive as to hinder times of prayer [Note: Col. 1560D. Munich manuscript: “to facilitate times of ordination.”] and is not changed into a use contrary to nature.

[Col. 1560D] For intercourse necessary for procreation is without fault and alone is marital. But intercourse which proceeds beyond this necessity now obeys not reason but lust. Yet not demanding it, but rendering it to one’s spouse so that the spouse may not sin damnably by fornication, belongs to the marital role.

Likewise (Maur. VI, 333): Marriage, then, is good, especially if those who carnally desire children also nurture them spiritually. Nor does the Law’s command that a person be purified even after marital intercourse declare it to be sin, if it is not that intercourse permitted by indulgence, which, when excessive, also hinders prayer. But just as the Law sets forth many things in sacraments and shadows of things to come, a certain material formlessness in seed, which when formed will yield the human body, was set as a sign of life unformed and untaught. Since a human being must be cleansed of that formlessness by teaching, formation, and instruction [Note: Col. 1561D. Editions: “by the form and instruction of teaching”], that purification after emission of seed was commanded as a sign of this reality. For it does not occur by sin even in dreams, and yet purification was commanded even then.

Or, if anyone thinks this is sin, supposing that it occurs only from some such desire—which is undoubtedly false—are women’s ordinary menstrual flows [Note: Col. 1561D. Thus the Munich manuscript with many codices; Maurists: *menstrua*; Col. 1562D. Other codices: *mensium*.] sins as well? Yet the same antiquity of the Law commands that they be purified from them, solely because of that material formlessness which, once conception has occurred, is added as though to the building of a body. And so, when it flows without form, the Law intended by it to signify [Col. 1561B] a mind indecently fluid and undisciplined, lacking the form of instruction and dissolved; it signifies that this mind ought to be formed when it commands purification of such a bodily flow.

Finally, is dying a sin? Or is burial not also a good work of humanity? Yet purification was commanded for that as well, because a dead body abandoned by life is not sin, but signifies the sin of a soul abandoned by righteousness.

“Marriage,” he says, “is good and can be defended by sound reasoning against every calumny.”

Likewise: Continence is a virtue not of the body but of the mind. The virtues of the mind are sometimes manifested in the body and sometimes hidden in disposition, just as the virtue of martyrs appeared when they endured sufferings.

[Col. 1561C] Likewise: Job already possessed the patience known to God and attested by him; but it became known to human beings through the test of temptation.

Likewise: To make clearer how virtue can exist as a disposition even if it is not present in action, I speak of an example no Catholic doubts. No one who is faithful on the basis of the Gospel doubts that the Lord Jesus truly hungered, thirsted, ate, and drank. Was there not, then, in him as great a virtue of continence from food and drink as there was in John the Baptist? “For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they said, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they said, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners’” (Matt. 11:18).

Likewise: What the Lord then added after saying these things about John and himself—“Wisdom is justified by her children” (Matt. 11:19)—means that they see that the virtue of continence ought always to be present as a disposition of the mind, but must be manifested in action according to the fitness of circumstances and times, just as the virtue of patience in holy martyrs. Therefore, just as the merit of patience is not unequal in Peter, who suffered, and John, who did not suffer, so the merit of continence is not unequal in John, who experienced no marriage, and Abraham, who begot children. For both John’s celibacy and Abraham’s marriage served Christ according to the distribution of times. But John possessed continence in action, whereas Abraham possessed it in disposition alone.

[Col. 1562A] At that time, when the Law—following the age of the patriarchs—pronounced a curse upon one who did not raise up seed in Israel, the person who could act did not act, though he nevertheless possessed the virtue. But after the fullness of time came, so that it could be said, “Let him who can receive it, receive it” (Matt. 19:12), the person who has it acts; and anyone who wishes to act must not falsely claim not to have it. Accordingly, those who corrupt good morals through evil conversations say with empty cleverness to a Christian person who is continent and refuses marriage: “Are you therefore better than Abraham?” But the chastity of celibates is better than the chastity of marriage. Abraham possessed the latter in practice and both in disposition. For he lived chastely in marriage; he could have been chaste without marriage, but it was not then fitting.

Likewise: It may happen that the virtue of continence is less in the mind of one who does not make use of marriage, which Abraham did use, yet it is greater than in the mind of one who observed marital chastity because he could not attain a greater continence. Likewise, let an unmarried woman, who considers the things of the Lord so that she may be holy in body and spirit, when she hears that shameless quibbler say, “Are you therefore better than Sarah?” answer: “I am better than those who lack the virtue of this continence; I do not believe that Sarah lacked it. She therefore did, with this virtue, what suited her time; I am free from that, so that in my body also may appear what she preserved in her mind” [Note: Col. 1562D. Munich manuscript: “constructed.”]

If we compare the things themselves, there must be no doubt whatever that the chastity of continence is better than marital chastity; but when we compare people, the better person is the one who possesses more good.

Likewise: Obedience is a greater good than continence. For marriage is nowhere condemned by the authority of our Scriptures, whereas disobedience is nowhere absolved. Therefore, if a virgin who will remain so but is disobedient, and a married woman who could not remain a virgin but is obedient, are proposed, which shall we call better? Shall we call the married woman less praiseworthy than she would have been if she were a virgin, or condemnable like the virgin? Likewise, if you compare a drunken virgin with a sober married woman, who could endure the contrary judgment? Marriage and virginity are two goods, one greater than the other; but sobriety and drunkenness, like obedience and obstinacy, are respectively good and evil. It is better to have all lesser goods than a great good with a great evil; just as among bodily goods it is better to have Zacchaeus’s stature with health than Goliath’s with fever.

Likewise: What food is for the preservation of human life, intercourse is for the preservation of the race; neither occurs without carnal pleasure. Yet pleasure, moderated and restrained by temperance and reduced to natural use, cannot be lust. What unlawful food is in sustaining life, that is fornication or adulterous intercourse in seeking offspring. And what an excessively immoderate appetite is in lawful food for some people, that is the pardonable intercourse of spouses.

[Col. 1563A] Likewise: It is one thing to have intercourse only for the will to generate, which has no fault.

The same author, *Enchiridion*, chapter 46: Regeneration was instituted only because generation is defective, so much so that one born from lawful marriage says: “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Ps. 50:7).

Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, 49: For that is indicated to be a fault which is said to be forgiven.

*Morals*, book 33: He permitted lesser things so that greater evils might be avoided, saying: “Because of fornication, let every man have his own wife” (1 Cor. 7:2). And because spouses are free of fault in intercourse only when they come together not to satisfy lust but to receive offspring, he added, to show that what he had permitted was not without even the smallest fault: “But I say this by way of indulgence, not command” (1 Cor. 7:6).

## CXXXI. That no one may marry the woman with whom he has committed fornication, and the contrary

Ambrose to Felix, bishop of Sicily: No Christian may take in marriage a woman whom he has defiled by any unlawful pollution, because such intercourse is incestuous.

Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*: It is clear that lawful marriages can indeed arise from persons badly united, when an honourable resolution subsequently follows.

The same author, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: Finally, when the husband with whom there was a true marriage has died, a true marriage may be formed with the man with whom there was previously adultery.

Ivo of Chartres to Walter, bishop of Meaux: Your fraternity asks whether anyone can have as wife a woman whom he previously had as a concubine. On this matter we have differing judgments, some prohibiting and others permitting. For Gregory says: “No one,” etc. It is also read in the Council of Chalon, chapter 26, that according to canonical authority abductors cannot lawfully claim for legitimate marriages women whom they have abducted. We also have in the decree of Pope Hormisdas that marriages secretly contracted are not lawful. Pope Evaristus also calls cohabitations, not marriages, those unions of women who have not been given by their parents, endowed according to law, and solemnly blessed by priests. It is held in the Council of Aachen: “Whoever abducts, steals, or seduces a woman shall never have her as wife.”

On the other hand, we read in the decrees of Pope Eusebius, chapter 5: Virgins who have not preserved virginity, if they take as husbands the very men who violated them, because they have violated only their marriages, shall be reconciled after one year of penance. Blessed Augustine likewise says: “It is clear that lawful marriages can indeed arise,” etc.

Therefore, as it seems to me, those Fathers who forbade concubines to become wives, commending the honourableness of marriage and wishing to restrain the shameful practice of concubinage, decreed that the rigour of justice be maintained. But I understand those who wrote otherwise to have preferred, from an impulse of mercy [Note: Col. 1563D. Editions: “in view of mercy.”], to temper the rigour of the canons in response to the weakness of some. In these judgments I see no other difference than that which exists between mercy and judgment.

## CXXXII. That a barren woman ought not seem fit to be taken in marriage, and the contrary

Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book I, chapter 19: I ask why you think it contemptible to dismiss a wife whom you judge should be kept not for the fidelity of marriage but only for desire. For marriage receives its name from this: a woman ought to marry for no other reason than to become a mother, which is hateful to you.

The same author, *On the Good of Marriage*: The Apostle is thus witness that marriages are contracted for the sake of generation: “I wish younger women to marry,” etc. (1 Tim. 5:14).

The same author, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I: Many women would never lawfully be joined to one man unless many children were thereby born. Hence, if one woman lies with many men, because this produces not a multiplication of offspring but a multiplication of lust, she cannot be a wife but is a prostitute.

The same author, *On the Good of Marriage*: I wonder whether, just as it is lawful to dismiss an adulterous wife, it is lawful, after dismissing her, to take another. For Scripture creates a difficult knot here, when the Apostle says by command of the Lord that a woman should not leave her husband; but if she leaves, she should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. I do not see how a husband can be permitted to take another wife if he has left an adulteress, when a wife is not permitted to marry another if she has left an adulterer. If this is so, nevertheless the social bond of spouses remains valid, so that, when they have been joined for the sake of procreation, not even the cause of procreation itself dissolves them. For a man may dismiss a barren wife and marry one by whom he may have children; yet this is not lawful.

The same author in the same work: A marriage once entered into can in no way be dissolved except by the death of one of the parties. For the bond of marriage remains [Note: Col. 1564D. Editions: “also remains.”] even if offspring, for whose sake it was contracted, do not follow owing to evident barrenness; so that, though the spouses now know they will have no children, they may nevertheless neither separate on account of children themselves [Col. 1564D] nor join themselves to others. If they do so, they commit adultery with those to whom they join themselves.

The same author, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: This is preserved in Christ and the Church: one living with the other living is never separated by any divorce for eternity. The observance of this sacrament is so great among faithful spouses that, although women marry and men take wives for the sake of begetting children, it is not lawful to dismiss a barren spouse in order to marry a fruitful one. If a man does this, he is guilty of adultery not under the law of this world, where, after a divorce, marriage with others is allowed without crime—a concession which the Lord testifies Moses made to the Israelites because of their hardness of heart—but under the law of the Gospel.

The same author, *On the Good of Marriage*: Now no child is sought by anyone perfected in piety except spiritually; but then it was an activity [Note: Col. 1565D. Munich manuscript: “a reason.”] of piety itself to propagate children carnally, because the generation of that people was an announcement of future things and belonged to the prophetic dispensation. Therefore, just as one man was permitted to have several wives, one woman was not permitted to have several husbands—even for the sake of offspring, if perhaps she could bear but he could not beget. For by a hidden law of nature, those who rule love singleness; things subject to them, however, are subjected many to one, not without dishonour. One slave does not have several masters in the way several slaves have one master; just as many souls are rightly subject to one God, while one soul can commit fornication after many gods [Note: Col. 1565D. Editions: “through many gods.”], but cannot be made fruitful.

The same author, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: Lustful cruelty goes so far as even to procure poisons of sterility. If both spouses are such, they are not spouses; and if they were such from the beginning, they came together not through marriage but through sexual vice. But if they are not both such, I dare say that either she is in a sense her husband’s prostitute or he his wife’s adulterer.

The same author, *On Christian Doctrine*, book III: The blameless custom of one man’s having several wives at once existed for the purpose of receiving offspring [Note: Col. 1565D. Editions: “for the purpose of providing offspring.”]; and therefore it was not honourable for one woman to have many husbands, for a woman is not thereby more fruitful. In matters of this sort [Note: Col. 1566D. Editions: “customs.”], whatever holy persons of those times did not lustfully, although they did things which in this age cannot be done except through lust, Scripture does not blame.

## CXXXIII. That virginity is not commanded, and the contrary

Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, book I, chapter 21: In the Law he commands marriage; in the Gospel, virginity.

The same author, book II, chapter 60: Marriage has been permitted; virginity has been urged, not commanded, because it is too exalted.

Origen on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, book X: The Saviour says: “When you have done all that I command you, say: ‘We are useless servants; we have done what we ought to do’” (Luke 17:10). But what we do above what is owed, we do not do by command. For virginity is not rendered as a debt, nor is it demanded by command, but is offered above what is owed.

Ambrose, *Exhortation to Virginity*, book I: Virginity alone may be advised; it cannot be commanded: it is a matter of vow rather than command.

Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book I: What is commanded must be done; what must be done entails punishment. For what is left to choice is commanded in vain. If God had commanded virginity, he would seem to condemn marriage and remove the nursery of humankind from which virginity arises.

## CXXXIV. That marriages also are commanded, and the contrary

[Col. 1566A]

Paul the Apostle, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians [VII.8]: “But I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I also am. But if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn.”

John Chrysostom, on the Epistle to the Hebrews, at the end of Sermon VII: “If the Beatitudes were spoken only for monks, and it is impossible for a secular person to fulfil them, then he who commanded marriage has himself ruined everyone. For if, together with ungodly [marriages], he cannot fulfil those things which belong to monks, they have perished and been corrupted, and he has shut up within a narrow compass the things that belong to virtue. And how are marriages honorable, if they have hindered us so greatly?”

Augustine: The Apostle commands second [Col. 1566B] marriages on account of incontinence, saying that it is better to marry a husband than, in pursuit of lust, to fornicate with many persons. For permission to marry repeatedly is not religion but sin.

From Julian’s Letter to Demetrias: In the divine Scriptures some things are forbidden, some commanded, some permitted, and some advised. Evils are forbidden; good things are commanded; intermediate things are permitted, such as marriage, the eating of meat or the drinking of wine; virginity is advised.

### CXXXV. That marriages are good, and the contrary

Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*: “Marriage,” he says, “is a good, and can be defended by sound reasoning against every calumny.”

Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, Book I, chapter XI: Marriages and positions of authority are in themselves good; but become evil through the circumstances surrounding them: marriages, through that of which the Apostle says (I Cor. VII.33), “He who has a wife is concerned with the things of the world”; positions of authority, through pride, oppression, and violation of justice.

Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, Book I: I grant that marriages also are a gift of God, but there is a great distance between one gift and another.

Likewise: Remove the burning of lust, and you will not say [Note: [Col. 1566D] Editions: “will say.”] that it is better to marry. “Better” always has reference to the performance of something inferior, not to the simplicity of a good incomparable in itself. What are you doing, Apostle? You know the proper meanings of words. Where you speak of continence and virginity, you say: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (I Cor. VII.1); [Col. 1566D] where marriage is concerned, you do not say, “It is good,” but, “It is better to marry than to burn.” If marriage is good in itself, do not compare it to a fire; simply say, “It is good to marry.”

The same, Book I: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” He did not say, “not to have,” but “not to touch,” as though there were danger in the touch, as though one who touched her could not escape that which seizes [Note: [Col. 1566D] Editions: “carries off.”] precious souls. “Can a man bind fire in his bosom and not be burned? Or walk upon coals of fire and not be scorched?”

The same, to Pammachius: If I say that it is better to be a virgin than married, I have set the better above the good. There is a great difference between the “better” [Col. 1567A] which is preferred to marriage and that which is preferred to fornication. But if I take the second step, “It is better to marry than to fornicate,” I have set good above evil.

The same, *Against Jovinian*, Book I (Martian, IV.2, p. 150): “Do not deprive one another, unless perhaps by consent for a time, that you may be free for prayer” (I Cor. VII.5). What kind of good is that which prevents the receiving of Christ’s body [Note: [Col. 1567D] Monac.: “Unless for prayer one is prevented from receiving it.”], and does not permit prayer? The same Apostle commands elsewhere that we pray always. If prayer must always be made, then one must never be occupied with marriage, since whenever I render the marital due to my wife, I cannot pray. [Note: [Col. 1567D] Monac.: “If, therefore, it is required that one always pray and serve in grace, whenever I render the marital due to my wife, can I not pray?” Cf. p. 362.]

Peter the Apostle, having experience of marital bonds, see what he teaches (I Pet. III.7): “Likewise, husbands, living together according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman as to the weaker vessel, and as to co-heirs of manifold grace, so that [Col. 1567B] your prayers may not be hindered.” If we abstain from intercourse, we give honor to the wife; if we do not abstain, it is evident that an insult contrary to honor is involved.

Likewise: “If anyone considers his virgin”—that is, his flesh—to be growing wanton, and he cannot restrain himself, let him do what he wishes; he does not sin if he takes a wife (I Cor. VII.36). He says, “Let him do what he wishes,” not what he ought. He does not sin if he marries; nevertheless, he does not do well if he marries.

Likewise: “Therefore he also who joins his virgin in marriage does well.” More pointedly [Note: [Col. 1568D] Editions: “Pointedly.”] and properly he had said above: “He who takes a wife does not sin.” It is one thing not to sin, another to do well. “Turn away from evil and do good.” In the one is a beginning; in the other, perfection. Therefore [Note: [Col. 1568D] Editions: “But.”], lest anyone suppose that my observation fails in what he said, “he who joins [Col. 1567C] his virgin in marriage does well” (ibid., 38), he immediately diminishes and overshadows this very statement by comparison with the better, saying: “And he who does not join her does better” (ibid.). Likewise: There is as much difference between marriage and virginity as between not sinning and doing well.

Likewise: What is this necessity by which, casting off the bond of marriage, virginity seeks freedom? “Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing in that day” (Matt. XXIV.19). Here prostitutes or brothels are not condemned, concerning whose condemnation there is no doubt; rather, swollen wombs, infants’ cries, and the fruits and works of marriage. If it is good to be thus, it is evil not to be thus.

Likewise: “If you have taken a wife, you have not sinned.” [Col. 1567D] It is one thing not to sin, another to do well; and “if a virgin marries, she will not sin.”

The same, in his apology to Pammachius (Martian, IV, pt. 2, p. 229): Some rebuke me because in the books which I wrote against Jovinian I was excessive in praising virgins or in disparaging marriages [Note: [Col. 1568D] Editions: “married women.”], and say that it is a condemnation of marriage to preach chastity so greatly that no comparison seems to be left between a wife and a virgin. Therefore, if I remember the issue correctly, this is the dispute between Jovinian and us: he makes marriages equal to virginity; [Col. 1568A] we place them below it.

Likewise: We said: “If it is good not to touch a woman, then it is evil to touch her; for nothing is contrary to good except evil.” But if it is evil and is forgiven, it is permitted in order that something worse than evil may not occur, etc. We added this because the Apostle had said: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication,” etc. In what do my words differ from the Apostle’s meaning? Unless perhaps in this: he declares, while I doubt; he determines, while I inquire; he openly says, “It is good for a man not to touch a woman,” while I cautiously ask, “If it is good not to touch a woman, is it therefore evil to touch her?” This is the language of one doubting, not affirming. Therefore he did not say, “It is good not to have a wife,” but, “It is good not to touch a woman,” as though [Col. 1568B] there were danger in the touch, as though he who touched her could not escape. You see, therefore, that we are not expounding marriages, but are discussing intercourse simply: in comparison with virginity and angelic likeness, it is good for a man not to touch a woman.

Likewise: If anyone finds it harsh and deserving of reproach that we have made so great a distance between virginity and marriage, let him read St. Ambrose’s book *On Widows*. Among other things which he discussed concerning virginity and marriage, he will find that Ambrose said this also: “Therefore the marital union is not to be avoided as though it were a fault, but to be declined as a burden of necessity. For the Law binds a wife, so that in toil and sorrow she may bear children; her turning shall be toward her husband, so that he himself may rule over her.” And elsewhere: “You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men” (I Cor. VII.23). You see how evident is this definition of marital servitude. And shortly afterward: “Therefore, if marriage is good and servitude evil, what is it when they cannot sanctify one another but destroy one another?” All that we poured forth at length concerning virginity and marriage, he compressed into a short summary.

Likewise (p. 238): Let husbands swell [Note: [Col. 1568D] Monac.: “fear.”] against me because I said: “I ask you, what kind of good is that which prevents prayer, which does not allow the receiving of Christ’s body? The same Apostle commands elsewhere that we pray always. If prayer must always be made, then one must never be occupied with marriage; since whenever I render the marital due to my wife, I cannot pray.” Why I said this is evident: because I was interpreting [Col. 1568D] the Apostle’s statement, “Do not deprive one another, unless perhaps by consent for a time, that you may be free for prayer” (ibid., 5).

Likewise: Which is greater: to pray, or to receive Christ’s body? Certainly, to receive Christ’s body. If intercourse prevents what is lesser, much more does it prevent what is greater. In the same volume we said that David and his companions could not eat the loaves of presentation under the Law unless they answered that they had kept themselves from women for three days—not, certainly, from prostitutes, which was condemned in the Law, but from wives, to whom they were lawfully joined. Likewise, when the people were about to receive [Col. 1569A] the Law, they were commanded to abstain from their wives for three days.

I know that this is the custom at Rome: that Christ’s faithful receive Christ’s body always. I neither condemn nor approve this. “Each abounds in his own judgment” (Rom. XIV.5). But I challenge the consciences of those who communicate on that very day and, in Persius’s words, “cleanse the night with a river” [Note: [Col. 1569D] Persius, *Satires* II.16]: why do they not dare to go to the martyrs? Why do they not enter churches? Is Christ one person in public and another at home? What is not permitted in church is not permitted at home either. Nothing is hidden from God; even darkness shines before him. Let each person test himself and thus approach Christ’s body, so that, while I grieve that I have not communicated in Christ’s body, I may refrain for a little while from my wife’s embrace, in order that I may prefer love for Christ [Col. 1569B] to love for a spouse.

Likewise: I shall come also to the passage in which I am accused because I said that on the second day there was not added, as on the first, third, and remaining days, “God saw that it was good”; and I immediately added that this leaves us an interpretation: that the double number is not good, since it divides from unity and prefigures the bonds of marriage. Hence also in Noah’s ark all animals which enter two by two are unclean. An odd number is clean.

Likewise: Let them either give another, more plausible reason why it is not written, or accept what we have said. Moreover, if all animals entering two by two in Noah’s ark are unclean, and an odd number is clean, let them explain why this too is written; but if not, whether they wish it or not, let them accept my interpretation. Either provide better fare and use me as your guest, or be content with our little meal, whatever it may be.

### CXXXVI. That love of one’s neighbor embraces every human being, and not

Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book I (chapter XXVIII): All persons are to be loved equally. But since you cannot benefit all, you must give special care to those who, by the opportunities of places, times, or any circumstances whatever, are joined to you more closely, as though by some lot. [Note: [Col. 1569D] Cousin omits *pro*. Cousin: “have been joined.”]

Likewise: One who wishes to be loved does so not in order that something may be given to himself, but that eternal reward may be bestowed upon those who love him. Hence it follows that we must love even our enemies. For we do not fear them, since they cannot take from us that which we love; rather, we pity them, because they hate us all the more insofar as they are separated from him whom we love. [Note: [Col. 1570D] Cousin: “who.”]

Likewise: It may be asked whether love for angels also belongs to those two commandments. For both the Lord and the Apostle Paul showed that he who commanded us to love our neighbor excluded no one.

Likewise: He had set forth two commandments and said that the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon them.

Likewise: The Lord says, “Go and do likewise,” so that we may understand him to be our neighbor to whom an office of mercy must be rendered if [Col. 1570A] he is in need, or would have to be rendered if he were in need. From this it consequently follows that the person from whom such an office is to be rendered to us in return is also our neighbor; for “neighbor” is a relative term, and no one can be a neighbor except to a neighbor.

Likewise: Paul says: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not murder; you shall not steal; you shall not covet; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Rom. XIII.9). Therefore, anyone who thinks that the Apostle did not command this concerning every human being is compelled to confess—which is most wicked—that the Apostle considered it no sin if someone committed adultery with the wife either of a non-Christian or of an enemy.

Likewise: Further, if the person to whom an office of mercy must be rendered, or from whom it must be rendered to us, is rightly called a neighbor, it is clear that the holy angels too are included in this command by which we are ordered to love our neighbor, since they perform so many offices of mercy for us. [Col. 1570B]

Ambrose, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans: “Owe no one anything.” He wishes us, if possible, to have peace with all, and love with the brethren. For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the Law, the Law of Moses. For the commandment of the new Law is to love even enemies. “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII.39): this was written in Leviticus.

Likewise: Love of neighbor does no evil; for love is the fulfilment of the Law. It does no evil because love is good, and one cannot sin through that which is the perfection of the Law. But because something had to be added in Christ’s time, he commanded that not [Col. 1570C] only neighbors but enemies also be loved. Thus love is the fulfilment of the Law, so that to love one’s neighbor is righteousness; but surpassing and perfect righteousness is to love even enemies.

### CXXXVII. That love alone should be called virtue, and not

Augustine, to the judge Macedonius: Virtue is nothing other than loving what ought to be loved. Prudence is choosing it; fortitude is not being turned away from it by any hardships; temperance, by no allurements; justice, by no pride.

The same, *On the Morals of the Catholic Church* [Maur. I, 696]: Therefore the highest good of the human being, to which it is most blessed to cling, is nothing other than God; and surely we cannot cling to him except through love. [Col. 1570D] Indeed, what is called the fourfold virtue is named from a certain variety of affections of love itself: temperance is love presenting itself whole to that which is loved; fortitude is love readily enduring all things for the sake of that which is loved; justice is love serving the beloved alone and therefore ruling rightly; prudence is love sagaciously choosing the things by which it is aided from those by which it is hindered. But we have said that this love is not love of just anything, but love of God.

It may also be defined thus: temperance is love keeping itself whole and incorrupt for God; fortitude, love readily enduring all things for God’s sake; [Col. 1571A] justice, love serving God alone and therefore ruling well over all other things subject to a human being; prudence, love of God rightly distinguishing the things by which it may be aided toward God from those by which it may be hindered.

What more need be discussed concerning morals? For if God is the highest good—which cannot be denied—it follows, since to seek the highest good is to live well, that living well is nothing other than loving God with one’s whole heart: so that love is kept in him incorrupt and whole—which belongs to temperance; is broken by no misfortunes—which belongs to fortitude; serves no other—which belongs to justice; and watches in discerning things lest deceit or trickery gradually steal in—which belongs to prudence.

From Prosper’s book *Sentences of Augustine*, chapter VII: Love of God and neighbor is the proper and distinctive virtue of the devout and holy, whereas other virtues can be common to good and bad persons.

Gregory, on Ezekiel, Homily XVI: There are three virtues without which one who is able to act cannot be saved: namely faith, hope, and love.

The same, Homily VII on the Gospels: Knowledge is indeed a virtue; humility too is the guardian of virtue.

Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, Book II, chapter XXXVI: Faith, hope, and love are the highest virtues; for whoever possesses them possesses them truly. Other virtues are intermediate; they can be possessed either to benefit or to ruin, if anyone becomes arrogantly puffed up because of them—for example, learning, fasting, chastity, knowledge, or temporal riches—concerning which [Col. 1571C] we can act either well or badly.

Paul the Apostle, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “But I wish all people to be as I myself am; yet each has his own gift from God, one indeed in this way, another in that. But I say to the unmarried and widows: it is good for them if they remain as I also am; but if they do not exercise self-control, let them marry.”

Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, chapter IX: Although justice without prudence has sufficient authority, prudence without justice has no power to establish trust. For the more crafty and shrewd anyone is, the more hated and suspected he is once the reputation for uprightness has been removed. Therefore intelligence joined with justice will have as much power as it wishes for establishing trust. Justice can do much without prudence; prudence can do nothing without justice.

But lest anyone wonder why, when [Note: [Col. 1571D] Cousin: “not.”] it is agreed among all philosophers—and has often been argued by me myself—that whoever has [Note: [Col. 1571D] Cousin: “has.”] one virtue has all virtues, I now [Note: [Col. 1571D] Cousin: “and not.”] separate them as though anyone [Note: [Col. 1572D] Cousin: “each person.”] who is not equally prudent could be just: one thing is the case when truth itself is refined in discussion, another when speech is adapted to all. Therefore here we speak as the common people do, calling some brave, others good men, others prudent. For when we speak, we must use popular and customary words.

Jerome, to Fabiola, *On the Stages of the Children of Israel*: Passing from one province to another, one must not always devote one’s effort to a single virtue, but, as it is written, “They shall go from virtue to virtue” (Ps. LXXXIII.8); because the virtues are so interconnected that whoever lacks one lacks them all.

From the first book of his *Dialogues against Pelagius*:

**PELAGIUS:** Therefore no saint, so long as he is in this world, can possess all virtues.

**JEROME:** No one can, because now we prophesy in part and know in part. Nor can they be fully present in human beings, because the son of man is not immortal.

**PELAGIUS:** And how do we read that whoever has one virtue has all virtues?

**JEROME:** By participation, not by possession as a property. For individuals must necessarily excel in certain things; and yet I do not know where this is written.

**PELAGIUS:** Do you not know that this is a philosophical maxim?

**JEROME:** But not an apostolic one. For I care not what Aristotle teaches, but what Paul teaches.

Augustine to Jerome, concerning the saying of the Apostle James [Maur. II, 595]: When he says, “Whoever keeps the whole Law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (Jas. II.10), how is this to be understood? I beg you: is one who has committed theft—or indeed one who has said to a rich man, “Sit here,” but to a poor man, “Stand there”—guilty also of homicide, adultery, and sacrilege?

Likewise: Unless it is shown that this must be understood otherwise, it seems to follow that the person who says to the rich man, “Sit here,” and to the poor man, “Stand there,” giving the former greater honor than the latter, must be judged guilty of idolatry, blasphemy, adultery, [Col. 1572C] homicide, and, not to mention everything at length, every crime. For, by stumbling in one point, he has become guilty of all. But whoever has one virtue has all, and whoever lacks one has none. If this is true, that proposition is confirmed. But I wish it to be explained, not confirmed; for in itself it is among us more firmly established by the authorities of all philosophers.

And if this is truly said concerning virtues and vices, it does not follow that all sins are therefore equal. For that assertion concerning the inseparability of virtues—even if perhaps I am mistaken, yet, if it is true—I remember pleased all philosophers who said that those virtues were necessary for the conduct of life [Note: [Col. 1572D] Cousin: “virtues necessary for the conduct of life.”]. But only the Stoics dared to argue that sins are equal, against all human sense. You most clearly refuted their folly in that Jovinian, who was a Stoic in this opinion; and your very distinguished discussion made sufficiently evident that it did not please our authorities—or rather Truth itself, which spoke through them—that all sins are equal.

Likewise: Certainly those who maintain that whoever has one virtue has all, and that all are lacking to whoever lacks one, argue this because prudence cannot be cowardly, unjust, or intemperate. For if any of these is lacking, [Col. 1573A] there will be no prudence. But if there is prudence, and it is brave, just, and temperate, then wherever it exists, it surely has the other virtues with it. Thus fortitude cannot be imprudent, intemperate, or unjust. Thus temperance must be prudent, brave, and just; and justice does not exist unless it is prudent, brave, and temperate. Therefore wherever one of these is genuine, the others likewise exist. But where the others are absent, that one is not genuine, even if it seems in some way to coexist; for, as you know, there are certain vices [Note: [Col. 1573D] Cousin: “beginnings.”] deceptively resembling virtues.

Likewise: We are compelled to confess that vices are more numerous than virtues. Hence sometimes one vice is removed by another vice.

Likewise: But wherever a virtue has entered, since it brings the others with it, the vices that had been present surely give way. Whether this is so must be examined more carefully; for the saying that whoever has one virtue has all, and that one who lacks one has none, is not a divine pronouncement.

For my own part, I do not know how I can say that not merely a man—from whom the word *virtue* (*virtus*) is said to derive—but even a woman who keeps faith with her husband’s bed, if she does this because of God’s command and is first of all faithful, does not possess chastity, or that chastity is no virtue, or only a small virtue; and the same applies to a husband who preserves this same fidelity toward his wife. Yet there are very many such persons whom I would say are not without some sin; and certainly whatever that sin may be comes from some vice. Therefore marital chastity in religious men and women, though beyond doubt a virtue, does not nevertheless have all virtues with it; for if all were there, there would be no vice and no sin at all. Who, then, is without some vice—that is, without a certain tinder or, as it were, root of sin—when he who reclined upon the Lord’s breast cries out (I John I.8): “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves,” etc.?

Likewise: It is written (Jas. III.2): “We all stumble in many things.”

Likewise: Love from a pure heart, [Col. 1574A] a good conscience, and unfeigned faith is a great and true virtue. It is itself the end of the commandment and is deservedly called “strong as death,” because, just as death tears the soul away from the senses of the flesh, so love tears it away from fleshly desires.

Likewise: Or perhaps because love is the fulfilment of the Law—by which God and neighbor are loved, and upon whose commandments of love the whole Law and the Prophets hang—one who acts against it rightly becomes guilty of all, because all things hang upon it? No one commits sin except by acting against it. Therefore, “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not murder; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Love of neighbor does no evil. Thus one becomes guilty of all by acting against that upon which all things hang.

Origen, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, Book VIII: “For they have zeal for God, but not according to conscience.” Similarly, the Apostle can say of others that they have fear of God, but not according to conscience [Note: [Col. 1574D] Cousin: “knowledge.”]; and of still others, that they have love of God, but not according to conscience. For if anyone has affection toward God but does not know that love ought to be patient, kind, and so forth—if he does not possess these and similar things in love, but loves God in affection alone—it may fittingly also be said of him that he has love of God, but not according to conscience.

### CXXXVIII. That love, once possessed, is never lost, and the contrary
[Col. 1574C] Solomon in Proverbs, chapter XVII: “A friend loves at all times, and a brother is proved in distress.” Likewise in the Song of Songs (VIII, 7): “Many waters could not extinguish love, nor shall rivers overwhelm it.” [Note: [Col. 1574D] Cous.: “will be able,” rather than “could.”] The Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Romans (VIII, 35): “Who shall separate us from the love of God?” [Note: [Col. 1574D] Vulgate: “of Christ.”] “Tribulation, or distress?” etc. The same in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (XIII, 8): “Love never fails; whether prophecies shall be abolished, or tongues shall cease, or knowledge shall be destroyed.” Jerome on the Epistle to the Corinthians: “Love never fails”; that is, it alone remains in the future; or certainly, true love does not come to an end. The same, to Heliodorus: “Love never fails”; [Col. 1574D] it lives forever in the breast. The same, to Rufinus: A friendship which can cease was never true. In a friend, one does not seek possessions but goodwill. A friendship which can end was never true; for we are more endangered by the snares of our own people than by those of others. Hence it is said (Ps. XL, 10): “For even the man of my peace, in whom,” etc. Some persons devoted to higher ranks change their character, and, after attaining the summit of honour, disdain to retain as friends those whom they had held closely joined to themselves. True friendship is excluded by no force and abolished by no time; wherever time turns itself, it endures steadfastly, because it truly [Col. 1575A] loves its friend. However many injuries it suffers from him, it is in no way turned aside from love of him. “A friend loves at all times, and a brother is proved in distress.” [Note: [Col. 1575D] Cous. omits “and a brother is proved in distress.”]

Augustine on Psalm XXI: Love—but take care what you love. Love of God and love of neighbour are called charity; love of this world, covetousness. The same, Book IV of *On Christian Doctrine*: By charity I mean the movement of the mind toward enjoying God for his own sake, and oneself and one’s neighbour for God’s sake; by covetousness, the movement of the mind toward enjoying oneself, one’s neighbour, or any bodily thing, not for God’s sake. The same, in Book of Eighty-Three Questions, chapter XXXVII: To love is nothing other than to desire some thing for its own sake. Likewise: Love of things that ought to be loved is more properly called charity or affection. Likewise, [Col. 1575B] chapter XXXVIII: Covetousness is the desire to acquire or possess temporal things.

The same, on the verse (Ps. LIII, 8), “I will freely sacrifice to thee,” etc.: What shall I offer except what he says (Ps. XLIX, 23): “A sacrifice of praise shall glorify me”? Why “freely”? Because I love freely what I praise. Let that which is loved and praised be gratuitous. What is gratuitous? Himself for his own sake, not for something else. For if you praise God in order that he may give you something, you no longer love God freely. Be ashamed: if your wife loved you for your riches, and poverty should perhaps befall you, she would contemplate adultery. Therefore, while you wish to be loved freely by your wife, will you love God for something else—for a reward you expect to receive from God, O miser? He who made heaven and earth keeps for you not earth, but himself. “I will [Col. 1575C] freely sacrifice to thee”: do not do so under compulsion. For if you praise for some other reason, you praise under compulsion; if what you love were present to you, you would not praise. For example, you praise so that he may give you money; if you had it from elsewhere, would you praise? If, then, you praise for money, you do not freely sacrifice, but under compulsion, because apart from him you love I know not what else. Despise all things; attend to him himself; and these things which he has given are good because of the giver. For he gives these temporal things indeed—some to their good, some to their harm—according to the deep abyss of his judgments. But love him freely, because you will not find from him anything better for him to give than himself; or, if you find something better, ask for that. “I will freely sacrifice to thee,” because freely. “And I will confess to thy name, O Lord,” [Col. 1575D] etc., for no other reason than because it is good. Did he say, “because thou givest me gold”?

The same, *On the Morals of the Church against the Manichaeans*: God is the highest good for us; God is our supreme good. We must neither remain below him nor seek beyond him; the one is dangerous, and the other nonexistent. Likewise: As it is written (Rom. VIII, 36): “Because for thy sake we are afflicted all day.” Charity could not have been expressed more plainly, since it is said, “for thy sake.” The same, treating *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*: Have charity, and do whatever you wish. The same, on the Epistle of John, sermon II: Love alone distinguishes [Col. 1576A] between the children of God and the children of the devil. Likewise: The children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil only by charity. The same, sermon VI: A person may have baptism and be evil; may have prophecy and be evil; may receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood and be evil; but one cannot have charity and be evil. What does the Spirit himself intercede for the saints, if not that very charity which has been made in you through the Spirit? Therefore the same Apostle says (Rom. V, 5): “The charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit.”

Tully, in the second book of *Rhetoric*: Friendship is goodwill toward someone, for the sake of that person’s own good, whom one loves, together with an equal goodwill on his part. The same, in *On Friendship*: Friendship surpasses kinship in this respect: goodwill can be removed from kinship, but not from friendship. For when goodwill is removed, the name of friendship is removed, while kinship remains. How great the power of friendship is may be understood especially [Note: [Col. 1575D] Cous. omits *maxime*, “especially.”] from this: from the fellowship of the human race established and brought together by nature itself, the matter has been so contracted and narrowed that every affection is joined either between two persons or among a few. For friendship is nothing other than harmony concerning all things divine and human, together with goodwill and charity. I do not know whether, wisdom excepted, anything better than this has been given to humankind by the immortal gods.
