Augustine, *On the Trinity*, Book XIV, chapter IX: Whether also those virtues by which one lives well in this mortal life cease to exist when they have brought us to [Col. 1576C] eternal things is a question of some difficulty. Some have thought that they will cease, and that good minds will be blessed by knowledge alone—that is, contemplation of the nature which created all creatures. [Note: [Col. 1576D] Cous.: “the other creatures.”] To be subject to that governing nature, if this belongs to justice, then justice is altogether immortal; nor will it cease in that blessedness, but it will be such and so great that it cannot be more perfect or greater. Perhaps also the other three virtues will exist in that happiness: prudence without any longer a danger of error; fortitude without the burden of evils to be endured; temperance without the resistance of lusts—so that prudence consists in preferring or equating no good with God; fortitude, in adhering most strongly; temperance, in taking delight in no harmful falling-away. [Note: [Col. 1576D] Cous.: *de flexu*, “from a turning”; Maurists: *defectu*, “from a falling-away.”] But [Col. 1576D] what justice now does in aiding the miserable, prudence in avoiding snares, fortitude in enduring troubles, and temperance in restraining corrupt pleasures, will not exist there, where there will be no evil at all. Consequently, these works of the virtues, like the faith to which they must be referred, now make one Trinity when we hold them as present, and will then make another when we find in memory not that they are, but that they were.

Likewise: When it is said of the three virtues—prudence, fortitude, temperance—that they cease, this seems to say something. Justice, however, is immortal. Tully said that the four virtues are necessary only in this common life; [Col. 1577A] none of them, however, when we depart from this life. Likewise: To be subject to governing nature, if it belongs to justice, is immortal justice. The same, on Genesis: These virtues, indeed, which are now very necessary for passing through this pilgrimage, will not exist in that life for the attainment of which they are necessary.

The same, on Psalm XXI: “The tunic,” says the Evangelist, “was woven from above” (John XIX, 23). What is that tunic but charity, which no one can divide? What is this charity but unity? Lots are cast for it; no one divides it. Heretics have divided the sacraments among themselves, but not charity; and because they could not divide it, they departed. But it remains whole; whoever possesses it is secure. No one removes it from the Catholic Church; and if someone begins [Col. 1577B] to possess it outside, he is brought inside, as an olive branch by the dove. Likewise: The faith of Christian grace—that is, that which works through love—when laid as a foundation, permits no one to perish.

The same, on the passage in John’s Gospel, “These things I command you, that,” etc. (John XV, 7): Therefore the good teacher rightly commends love so often, as though it alone were to be commanded, without which other good things cannot profit, and which cannot be possessed without the other good things by which a human being is made good.

The same, sermon III on the Epistle of John (I John II, 27): “That you may know that the anointing which we have received from him remains in us.” [Note: [Col. 1577D] Cous.: “in you.”] That invisible anointing is charity; wherever it is, it will be like a root in that person, and it cannot wither even beneath the burning sun. Everything [Col. 1577C] which is rooted is nourished by the sun’s heat and does not wither. The same, sermon V: If anyone is prepared to die even for the brethren, charity is perfect in him. But is it utterly perfect as soon as it is born? It is born in order to be perfected; when it has been born, it is nourished; when nourished, it is strengthened; when strengthened, it is perfected; when it has reached perfection, what does it say? “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain; I desired to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 21).

Likewise, sermon VII: Therefore this brief command is given to you once for all: love, and do what you wish; let the root of love be within. Nothing but good can arise from this root. The same, sermon VIII: Charity has taken root: be secure; no evil can proceed from it. Love could not have been commended more highly than by being called God: “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (I John IV, 16). You dwell in God so that you may be held fast; God dwells in you so that he may hold you fast, lest you fall.

Likewise, sermon IX: God remains in you in order to hold you fast; you remain in God lest you fall, because the Apostle says of charity itself: “Charity never falls.” How can one fall whom God holds fast? In this love of God is made perfect in us, that we may have confidence on the day of judgment. Likewise: Beloved, if our heart has not judged us adversely, let us have confidence toward God. The heart has not judged adversely because brotherly [Col. 1578A] love is in us—genuine, not feigned—seeking a brother’s salvation and expecting no gain from the brother except his salvation. Likewise: Therefore whoever possesses brotherly charity, and whose heart, examined under a just scrutiny, gives no answer except that the genuine root of charity is there, from which good fruits arise, has confidence before God.

The same, on Psalm CIII, on the passage, “Who coverest its upper parts with waters”: In all the Scriptures charity holds the most eminent place; the evil do not share it with us. For it is the peculiar fountain of the good, the peculiar fountain of the saints, of which it is said: “Let no stranger share with thee.” Who are strangers? All who will hear: “I do not know you.” The same, to Count Julian: Charity which can be abandoned was never true.

Gregory, *Morals*, Book X: Love is strong as death, because it utterly kills from love of the world the mind which it has once captured and renders it insensible to terrors. From Leviticus (VI, 12): “The fire on the altar shall always burn; the priest shall feed it, placing wood upon it every morning, day by day.” Likewise: This fire is perpetual because it shall never fail from the altar.

Gregory, *Morals*, Book XXV: The altar of God is our heart, upon which we must continually kindle the flame of charity for God; lest the flame of charity fail within it, one must not cease to pile up both examples of predecessors and testimonies of sacred Scripture. For because our inward newness itself grows old every day through the conduct of this life, this fire must be fed. Likewise: For this fire upon the Lord’s altar—that is, in [Col. 1578C] our heart—is quickly extinguished unless it is restored by the diligent application of examples of the Fathers and the Lord’s testimonies. Likewise: But because this same charity remains unquenchable in the hearts of the elect, it is aptly added: “This is a perpetual fire, which shall never fail from the altar,” because even after this life the ardour of charity increases in their minds, [Note: [Col. 1577D] Cous.: “powers.”] so that God is loved more abundantly the more he is seen.

Ambrose, in the *Apology of David*: Paul rightly glories in weaknesses. For he knew that an abundance of strength had caused even many saints to fall without remedy. [Note: [Col. 1578D] Monac.: *coarctavisse*, “to have constrained.”] Jerome on Ezekiel: For we are judged not from the past but from the present; we must take heed and always fear lest the storm of one hour overthrow former glory and solid steadfastness.

Prosper’s Replies to Rufinus, chapter III: There is no doubt that very many pass from holiness to impurity, from justice to iniquity, from faith to impiety; and it is altogether certain that such persons do not belong to the predestination of the sons of God, coheirs of Christ. Likewise, chapter VII: Many examples, alas, prove that some of those regenerated in Christ Jesus, abandoning faith and pious conduct, apostatize from God and end their impious life in their turning away.

Gregory, homily XXXVIII: My father had three sisters, all three of whom were holy virgins. One was called Tharsilla, another Gordiana, another Emiliana. All were converted with one ardour [Col. 1579A] and consecrated at one and the same time; living under the discipline of a rule, they led a communal life in their own house, etc. Likewise: But Gordiana, forgetting the fear of the Lord, forgetting modesty and reverence, forgetting her consecration, later took as her husband the steward of her estates. Behold, all three were first converted with one ardour, but they did not remain in one and the same diligence; because, according to the Lord’s saying, many are called, but few are chosen. I have said this, therefore, lest anyone who is now engaged in a good work attribute the strength of good work to himself, lest anyone trust in his own action; for although he knows what he is today, he does not yet know what he will be tomorrow. Let no one, therefore, rejoice securely in his works already done, [Note: [Col. 1579D] Cous.: “rejoices.”] since in the uncertainty of this life one does not know what end awaits him.

The same, in the *Pastoral Rule*, chapter III: David became cruelly severe in the death of a man because he had weakly yielded in desire for a woman. His fault would surely have dragged him far from the number of the elect, unless chastisements had recalled him to pardon. The same, in the homily on the Gospel reading, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word,” etc. (John XIV, 23): The Spirit himself is love; hence John also says, “God is charity.” Therefore whoever desires God with an undivided mind [Note: [Col. 1580D] Cous.: “strength.”] surely already possesses the one whom he loves. Nor could anyone love God unless he possessed the one whom he loves. But if, behold, each one of you were asked whether he loves the Lord and answered, “I love him,” you heard at the beginning of the reading what Truth said: [Col. 1579C] “If anyone loves,” etc. The proof of love, therefore, is the performance of a deed. Thus John says in his Epistle: “Whoever says, ‘I love God,’ and does not keep his commandments, is a liar.” For we truly love if we keep his commandments; for whoever still flows away through unlawful desires surely does not love God, because in his own will he opposes him. Likewise: The love of God is never idle; if it exists, it accomplishes great things; but if it refuses to act, it is not love.

The same, *Morals*, Book XXIX: We see many every day who shine with the light of justice and yet are held in the darkness of wickedness at their end. Likewise: Who can discern either who will persist in evil, or who will persevere in good, or who will be converted from the lowest things to the highest, or who will return from the highest to the lowest? The thief passed from the cross to the kingdom. Judas fell from the glory of apostleship into hell.

*On the Use of Names*, chapter LXXXI: “You shall not show partiality nor accept gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the just” (Deut. XVI, 19).

Augustine, on the Epistle of John, sermon II: Those who have charity have been born of God; those who do not have it are not of God. Have whatever else you wish; unless you have this one thing, nothing profits you. If you lack other things, have this, and you have fulfilled the law. For “he who loves another has fulfilled the law” (Rom. XIII, 8), says the Apostle, and “charity is the fullness of the law” (ibid., 10).

The same, in the book *On Charity*, on this chapter: “Everyone who [Col. 1580A] is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God.” Perhaps he said this with reference to a particular sin, not every sin; and this sin is such that, if anyone commits it, he confirms the rest, while if he does not commit it, he dissolves the rest. What is this sin? To act against the commandment. What is the commandment? “A new commandment I give you” (John XIII, 34).

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, Book II, chapter III: Love of God is compared with death, Solomon saying: “Love is strong as death” (Song VIII, 6); because, just as death violently separates the soul from the body, so love of God separates a human being from worldly and carnal love. Whoever despises God’s commandments does not love God; for we do not love a king if we hate his law.

From the Gospel: “For the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me.” Likewise: “Thou knowest, Lord, that I love thee.” Likewise: “If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice.”

Augustine on John: “If you seek me, let these go,” so that the saying which he spoke might be fulfilled: “Of those whom thou hast given me I have lost none.” Why then would he lose them if they died at that time, unless because they did not yet believe in him as all who do not perish believe? The same, *Questions on the Old and New Law*: Even Mary, through whom the mystery of the incarnation was accomplished, doubted at the Lord’s death, so that she might be confirmed at the Lord’s resurrection. For all doubted at the Lord’s death; and because every uncertainty was to depart at the Lord’s resurrection, he said that a sword would [Col. 1580C] pass through.

The same, in *On Rebuke and Grace*: I received faith which works through love, but I did not receive in it perseverance unto the end. Likewise: Faith which works through love either does not fail at all or, if there are persons whose faith fails, is restored before this life ends; and, once the iniquity which intervened has been blotted out, perseverance unto the end is reckoned to them. But those who will not persevere are undoubtedly not to be counted in their number even at the time when they have lived well and piously. Likewise: If I am asked why God did not give perseverance to those to whom he gave the love by which they might live as Christians, I answer that I do not know. Likewise: It is indeed wonderful, and greatly wonderful, that God does not give perseverance to some of his children [Col. 1580D] whom he has regenerated in Christ and given faith, hope, and love, while he remits so many crimes to alien children and by grace bestowed makes them his children.

The same, in the same work: It must be believed that some of the children of perdition, not having received the gift of perseverance unto the end of life in faith which works through love, begin to live and for a time live faithfully and justly, but afterwards fall; nor are they taken from this life before this happens to them. Likewise: If the just person turns away from his justice and dies in his impiety, he shall go into punishments, and his former justice will not profit him. But if he had died when he was just, he would then have found rest.

The same, in the same work: God made the human being upright at the beginning of human creation. Falling by his own evil will from the uprightness in which God first made him, he became crooked. But if one already regenerated and justified relapses by his own will into an evil life, certainly he cannot say, “I did not receive,” since he lost by his free choice directed toward evil the grace of God which he had received. Likewise: Can even such a person, unwilling to be rebuked, say, “What did I do, who did not receive?”—though it is clear that he received and by his own fault lost what he had received? “I can,” he says, “I can indeed, when he rebukes me because I have fallen by my own will from a good life into an evil one, still say: ‘What did I do, who did not receive?’ For I received faith which works through love, but I did not receive in it perseverance unto the end.” [Col. 1581B]

Likewise: The Apostle speaks to those who are called according to purpose—not their own purpose but God’s, concerning which he says elsewhere, “that the purpose of God according to election might remain.” Their faith, which works through love, either does not fail at all or, if it fails in any, is restored. But those who will not persevere and will thus fall from Christian faith and conduct, so that the end of this life finds them such, are undoubtedly not to be counted among these even during the time when they live well and piously. Yet who would deny that they are called elect when they believe, are baptized, and live according to God? Clearly, they are called elect by persons who do not know what they will become, not [Col. 1581C] by him who knows that they lack the perseverance which brings the elect to the blessed life.

Likewise: “They went out from us, but they were not of the number of the children” (I John II, 19): this is God’s voice. John says that, had they been of us, they would certainly have remained with us. What else is said except this: they were not children, even when they were in the profession and name of children—not because they feigned justice, but because they did not remain in it. For he does not say, “For if they had been of us, they would certainly have held true and unfeigned justice with us,” but, “they would certainly have remained with us.” Undoubtedly, he meant that they should remain in the good. Therefore they were in the good, but they did not remain in it.

The same, *City* [Note: [Col. 1581D] Cous.: *Trinity of God*. Cf. Maurists VII, 297.] *of God*: The number seven is often used for the whole, as in (Prov. XXIV, 16): “The just man falls seven times and rises,” that is, whenever he falls, he shall not perish. This, however, he intended to be understood not of iniquities but of tribulations that lead to humility.

The same, homily XI: When the prince of all vices saw Adam formed from the clay of the earth in God’s image, armed with chastity, ordered by temperance, and resplendent with charity, he envied that this earthly human had received what he himself, while an angel, had lost through pride; and he stripped the first parents of those gifts and such great goods, and likewise [Note: [Col. 1581D] Cous. omits *pariter*, “likewise.”] destroyed them. For when he had taken faith, chastity, and continence from the human being, he subjected him to his own dominion. [Col. 1582A] Likewise: Having lost temperance, he became intemperate; having lost charity, he was found evil.

The same, in the book *On Faith to Peter*, speaking of human spirits, says: While they are in bodies, they are not present by parts; but as they are whole in whole bodies, so they are whole in the parts of the same bodies. Yet the variety of thoughts shows in them the diversity of temporal change: now they do not know something, now they know; now they will, now they will not; now they are wise, now foolish; now they become unjust from being just, now just from being unjust; now they are illuminated by the light of piety, now they are corrupted by the dark error of impiety.

Jerome, to Rusticus: The justice of the just person shall not deliver him on whatever day he sins; and the iniquity of the wicked person shall not harm him on whatever [Col. 1582B] day he is converted. God judges each person as he finds him; he does not consider the past but the present, provided only that old crimes are changed by a new conversion.

Gregory, in the homilies *On the Angels*: Through the prophet the Lord says that, on whatever day the just person sins, all his acts of righteousness will be forgotten before me (Ezek. XXXIII, 13). You are just: fear wrath, lest you fall. The same, *Morals*, Book VIII: The human being, created such that he possessed an innate firmness for standing, immediately fell in himself from the love of his Creator when he moved the foot of his will toward sin.

### CXXXIX. That the grace of God precedes our good will, and the contrary

[Note: [Col. 1581D] Cous.: “does not precede.”]

[Col. 1582C] Chrysostom, in the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews, sermon XII: For if we wish to stand firm and immovable, we shall not be moved. What then? Is nothing God’s? All things indeed are God’s, but not in such a way that free choice is injured. “If all things,” he says, “are God’s, why does he blame us?” [Note: [Col. 1582D] Cous.: “why are we blamed?”] I said this so that our free choice may not be injured; for we must first choose what is good, and then he introduces what is from himself. He does not go before our wills, lest our freedom of choice be injured; when [Note: [Col. 1582D] Cous.: “for if we choose the good,” etc.] we have chosen, he then supplies abundant assistance.

How, Paul says, is it “not of him that wills nor of him that runs, but of God that shows mercy” (Rom. IX, 16)? First, he did not introduce this as his own judgment, but drew it as a conclusion from what had been set forth. For he said, “It is written: ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy’” (ibid., 15). Therefore, it is not of him who wills nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. Yet it must be said in another sense that, because the one whose share is greater is said to possess the whole, Paul called the whole God’s. For ours is only to choose and to will; God’s is to accomplish and bring to perfection. Therefore, because his part is greater, he called the whole his. For example, we see a house built and say that it is wholly the builder’s, although not all the work is his, but also belongs to the labourers and to the one who supplies the material. Likewise, in a crowd where very many are present, we say that all are there; where [Col. 1583A] few are present, that none are there. Truth says: “You did not choose me, but,” etc. (John XV, 16).

Augustine, to Julian: Nor indeed is the error of those small who think that we have from ourselves whatever justice is in us a small one, defining God’s grace and help merely as that by which we live justly. In order to possess a good will—the very thing in which we live justly—they do not wish us to be aided by God, but say that by our own free choice we suffice for ourselves in these matters. Let this error not seem slight to us; for unless free choice itself is helped by God’s grace, even good will cannot exist in a human being. For, says the Apostle, “It is God who works in us both to will and to act for good will” (Phil. II, 3).

From the decrees of Pope Celestine: God so works in human hearts and in free choice itself that holy thought, pious counsel, and every motion of a good will come from God, without whom we can do nothing good.

Augustine, *On the Baptism of Infants*, Book II [Maurists X, 54]: Human beings do not wish to do what is just either because it is hidden whether it is just or because it gives no delight. For we will each thing more strongly insofar as we see more certainly how good it is and take more ardent delight in it. But that what was hidden may become known and what did not delight may become pleasant is God’s grace, which aids human wills. The reason why they are not aided by it lies likewise in themselves, not in God—whether they are predestined to condemnation because of the iniquity of pride, or are to be judged against [Col. 1583C] that same pride of theirs so that they may become instructed children of mercy. Therefore attribute no cause of human fault to the Lord; for pride is the cause of all human vices. The humble God descended in order to convict and remove it.

Likewise: A good work delights more the more God is loved, God the supreme good and author of every good of whatever kind. But that God may be loved, his charity is poured out into our hearts, not through ourselves but through the Holy Spirit given to us (Rom. V, 5). Yet people labour to discover in our will what good is ours and what in us is not from God; and I do not know how this can be discovered. Therefore, unless we maintain not only that free choice of the will, which bends freely this way and that, but also that good will cannot exist in us except from God, I do not know how we can defend the saying (I Cor. IV, 7): “For what do you have that you did not receive?” For if a certain free will is from God, which may still be either good or evil, but good will is from ourselves, then what is from us is better than what is from him.

The same, in the *Enchiridion* [Maurists VI, 208]: Lest anyone, even if not from works, should glory in free choice of the will itself as though merit began from himself, let him hear the same herald of grace saying (Phil. II, 13): “For it is God who works in us both to will and to act for good will.” [Col. 1584A] Human good will precedes many gifts of God, but not all; among those which it does not precede is itself. For both are read: “His mercy shall go before me” (Ps. LVIII, 11), and “His mercy shall follow me” (Ps. XXII, 6). It goes before one unwilling, so that he may will; it follows one willing, lest he will in vain.

The same, *On Rebuke and Grace*: But God’s grace is always good; through it a person who was formerly of evil will becomes a person of good will. Likewise: A person did not receive grace in such a manner as to lose his own will. Yet, lest that will itself be thought able to do anything good without God’s grace, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (I Cor. XV, 10), that is, not I alone; and therefore neither God’s grace alone nor I alone.

### CXL. That the commandments of the law are not as perfect as those of the Gospel, and the contrary

[Note: [Col. 1583] Questions CXL–CXLIII, absent from the Munich manuscript, have been transcribed from Cousin’s edition.]

[Col. 1584B]

From the Gospel according to Matthew [V, 20]: “Unless your righteousness exceeds,” etc. Likewise: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients,” etc. Paul in the Epistle to the Hebrews [VII, 18]: “There is a setting aside of the former commandment because of its weakness and uselessness, for the law brought nothing to perfection; but there is the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God.”

From the Gospel according to Luke [X, 25]: “Master, what must I do to possess eternal life?” And he said: “What is written in the law? How do you read?” He answered: “You shall love [Col. 1584C] the Lord your God,” etc., “and your neighbour as yourself.” And he said to him: “You have answered rightly; do this and you shall live.” Paul in the Epistle to the Romans [XIII, 8]: “For whoever loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law. For: ‘You shall not commit adultery,’” etc., “and if there is any other commandment,” etc. Therefore charity is the fullness of the law.

### CXLI. That works of mercy do not profit unbelievers, and the contrary
Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book XII: Works of mercy are of no benefit to pagans, Jews, heretics, or schismatics. The same author, in the book of Prosper’s *Sentences*: The whole life of unbelievers is sin, and nothing is good without the highest good. For where recognition of eternal and immutable truth is lacking, [Col. 1584D] false virtue exists even amid the best morals. The same author, from Tractate XX on the Gospel according to John: There are works which seem good without faith in Christ, yet are not good, because they are not directed to that end from which they are good; for Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes. Therefore he did not wish to distinguish faith from work, but called faith itself a work. For it is faith itself that works through love; nor did he say, “This is your work,” but, “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent” (John 6:29), so that whoever boasts may boast in the Lord (1 Cor. 1:31).

Jerome, in his second book against Jovinian: Cornelius the centurion, in order to receive the Holy Spirit before baptism, [Col. 1585A] earned this by alms and frequent fasts. The same author, to Heliodorus: Ecclesiastical rank does not make one a Christian: Cornelius the centurion, still a heathen, is cleansed by the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Gregory, at the end of his work on Ezekiel, Homily VII: For one does not attain faith through virtues, but virtues through faith. Cornelius the centurion, whose alms before baptism were praised, as the angel attests, did not come to faith through works, but came to works through faith. For the angel says to him: “Your prayers and alms have ascended before God” (Acts 10:4). For if, before baptism, he had not believed in the true God, whom was he praying to? Or how had God heard him, if he was not asking to be perfected in good things by God himself? He therefore knew God, the creator of all things, but did not know that his Son had been made [Col. 1585B] incarnate. For he could not do good unless he had first believed. For it is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God.” He therefore had faith, since his prayers and alms could please God. Yet by good action he deserved to know God perfectly and to believe the mystery of his incarnation, so that he might come to the sacraments of baptism. Thus he came to works through faith, but was strengthened in faith by work.

John Chrysostom, on Matthew: Hear the mystery which Peter expounded in Clement: If a believer performs a good work, it benefits him, delivering him from evils and enabling him in that age to receive the heavenly kingdom. But if an unbeliever performs a good work, that work benefits him, and God repays him for his work. [Col. 1585C] But in that age his work benefits him nothing. For he is not placed among the other believers because of his work; and rightly so, because, moved by natural good, he performed the good work not for God’s sake. Therefore he received in his body the bodily reward, not in his soul.

Gospel according to Luke (17:7): “Which of you, having a servant ploughing or tending sheep, when he returns from the field, will say to him: ‘Come at once and recline at table’? Rather, will he not say to him: ‘Prepare something for me to dine upon; gird yourself and serve me until I eat and drink; and afterwards you shall eat and drink’? Does he thank that servant because he did what he was commanded? I think not. So you also, when you have done all that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done.’”

CXLII. That the works of saints do not justify a human being, and the contrary.

[Col. 1585D]

Paul the Apostle, in the Epistle to the Romans (3:26): That he himself may be just and the justifier of the one who is of the faith of Jesus Christ. Where then is your boasting? It is excluded. By what law? By that of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we judge that a human being is justified by faith apart from works of the law.

Likewise (4:2): For if Abraham was justified by works of the law, he has glory, but not before God. For what does Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned [Col. 1586A] to him as righteousness.” But to the one who works, wages are not reckoned according to grace but according to debt; whereas to the one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness according to the purpose of God’s grace.

The same author, further on (13:8): Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for whoever loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law. For: “You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet”; and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself.” Love does no harm to a neighbour. Therefore love is the fulfilment of the law.

Likewise (10:10): With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.

Ambrose, on [Col. 1586B] the same Epistle: “For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” It is true that God’s grace seeks neither groaning nor lamentation nor any work, but only the confession of the heart.

Truth (Luke 11:41): “Give alms, and all things are clean for you.”

John Chrysostom, on Matthew: Before God, the will is rewarded, not the work; for the will proceeds from our free choice, but the work is brought to completion by God’s grace.

Augustine, in a sermon for the first Sunday of Lent: But when we speak of alms, let narrow poverty not be distressed; for the person who did whatever he could has fulfilled all things, because the perfect will to act will be reckoned as the deed itself. But this can be fulfilled by one who has wished to regard every poor person as himself, [Col. 1586C] were he himself in such need. Whoever does this has fulfilled the precepts of the New and Old Testaments, fulfilling that evangelical saying (Matt. 7:12): “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them.”

The same author, on Psalm 31: When the Apostle commended the righteousness that is from faith against those who boast of the righteousness that is from works, he said: “For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not from God” (Rom. 4:2). You find many pagans unwilling to become Christians for this reason: they think their good life is sufficient for them.

Likewise: On what ground does Scripture say that Abraham was justified? “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” You see, then, that he was justified by faith, not by [Col. 1586D] works. “Then I shall do whatever I wish, because even if I have no good works, provided I believe in God, it is reckoned to me as righteousness.” I answer, against this reading of the Apostle concerning Abraham, from what we find in the Epistle of another Apostle, who wished to correct people who had misunderstood this Apostle. For James, opposing those who did not wish to work well because they presumed upon faith alone, commended the works of that same Abraham whose faith Paul had preferred. He recounts the work known to all: Abraham offered his son to God to be sacrificed. I praise the fruit of the good work, but in faith I recognize the root. If he had done this apart from right faith, whatever the work might have been, it would have profited him nothing.

The same author, to Armentarius [Col. 1587A] and Paulina:

[Note: [Col. 1587D] Cousin notes here: From this point until the passages from Ambrose, *On Repentance*, the passages cited in the Abrincatensian manuscript are lacking in the Turonensis manuscript. In their place the Turonensis has the following, which the Abrincatensian in turn omits: “In the Gospel: ‘Produce fruits worthy of repentance,’ etc. Likewise: ‘What must I do to possess eternal life?’ Jesus says to him: ‘Keep the commandments.’ Likewise: ‘Whoever has left father or mother or sister or brother or son for my sake shall receive a hundredfold [Col. 1588D] in this age, and moreover shall possess eternal life.’ Paul the Apostle in the Epistle to the Romans: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness; with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.’ The same author in the same Epistle: ‘Who renders to each according to his works.’ The same author to the Corinthians: ‘But each shall receive his own reward according to his own labour.’ Truth in the Gospel: ‘Give alms, and all things are clean for you.’]

But a just life is present when we will it, because to will it fully is itself righteousness; nor does righteousness require anything more than a perfect will in order to act. See whether there is labour where willing is enough. Hence it was said (Luke 2:14): “Peace on earth to people of good will.” Where there is peace, there is rest; where there is rest, there is the end of striving and no reason for labour.

The same author, to the presbyter Deogratias (*Maur.* II, 282): Concerning what is written, “With what measure you have measured” (Matt. 7:2): Why Christ said this, Paul has made sufficiently clear above: “Do not judge,” he says, “and you shall not be judged; for with the judgment by which you judge, you shall be judged.” Will they be judged with an unjust judgment if they judge unjustly? Far from it! Rather, it is said as though it were said: “According to the will with which you have done good or evil, [Col. 1587B] in that same will you shall be delivered or punished.” For in his own will a good person measures his good deeds, and in it blessedness is measured out to him. Likewise, in his own will an evil person measures his evil works, and in it misery is measured out to him. For where each person is good, when he wills well, there also he is evil, when he wills badly; and accordingly there too he becomes blessed or miserable—that is, in the disposition of his own will, which is the measure of all deeds and merits. For right actions and sins are measured by the qualities of wills, not by lengths of time. Thus, in the same measure, eternal punishments are measured back for non-eternal evil deeds, so that one who wished to enjoy sin eternally may find eternal severity in punishment.

[Col. 1587C]

The same author, in book XX of *The City of God*: “For, as it is written, there shall be an examination of the thoughts of the ungodly” (Wisdom 1:9). And the Apostle says (Rom. 2:15): “Their thoughts accusing or even excusing them on the day when God judges the hidden things of human beings.”

The same author, on Psalm 118: All works, whether good or evil, proceed from thought. In thought each person is innocent; in thought each is guilty. Hence it is written: “A holy thought will keep you.” And elsewhere: “There shall be an examination of the thoughts of the ungodly.” And the Apostle says, “their thoughts accusing,” etc.

The same author, in Sermon X on the Epistle of John: Faith without works does not save. But the work of faith is love itself, as the Apostle says (Gal. 5:6): Faith works through love.

[Col. 1587D]

Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book I: The one who believes has his grace; he has another grace if his faith is crowned by sufferings. For Peter was not without grace before he suffered; but when he suffered, he gained another.

Jerome, to Paulinus: Paul, last in rank, is first in merits, because he laboured more than all.

CXLIII. That sin is an act, not a thing, and the contrary.

[Col. 1588A]

Augustine, to the bishops Eutropius and James, against Caelestius’s objections concerning the perfection of human righteousness: We must inquire what sin is: an act or a thing? If it is a thing, it must necessarily have an author; and if it is said to have an author, another author of some thing besides God will already seem to be introduced. We shall answer that sin is called—and is—an act, not a thing. But by the same reasoning, lameness in the body is an act, not a thing; for the thing is the foot itself, or the body, or the human being who limps because of a defective foot.

Likewise: The defect itself by which a person limps is neither the foot, nor the body, nor limping itself, which indeed is absent when he is not walking, although [Col. 1588B] the defect by which limping occurs when he walks is present. Let him therefore ask what name he wishes to give that defect: whether he wishes to call it a thing or an act, or rather an evil quality of a thing, by which a defective act occurs. So too, in the inner human being, the mind is a thing; robbery is an act; greed is a defect—that is, a quality by which the mind is evil even when it does nothing.

Likewise: I wonder that he dared to cite the testimony where it is said (Job 1:1), “abstaining himself from every evil thing,” when he wished this to be understood as “from every sin,” although above he had said that sin is an act, not a thing. Let him remember, therefore, that even if it is an act, it may be called a thing.

The same author, *On Nature and Grace*: You hear one confessing; what do you seek from one disputing? “Heal my soul,” he says (Ps. 40:10). Ask him whence [Col. 1588C] that which he asks to be healed has been damaged. And hear what follows: “for I have sinned against you.” This man asks him: “You who cry, ‘Heal my soul; for I have sinned against you’: what is sin? Is it some substance, or a name wholly lacking substance, by which is expressed not a thing, not an existent entity, not a body, but merely the act of doing wrong?” He replies: “It is as you say: sin is not some substance, but merely the act of doing wrong is expressed by this name.” The other replies: “How could that which lacks substance violate your soul?” Do we not observe, to omit other instances, that not eating is also not a substance? For one withdraws from substance, since food is a substance; but abstaining from food is not a substance. Yet if food is wholly withheld, the substance of the body languishes, weakens, and is broken down so greatly that, if it somehow remains alive, it can scarcely be restored to that same food; indeed, it has been harmed by abstaining. So sin is not a substance; but God, the highest [Col. 1588D] being, is substance, and by withdrawing from him through disobedience you hear how he says: “I have been struck,” etc. (Ps. 101:5).

[Col. 1589A]

Seneca, in his *Proverbs*: Every sin is an action; every action, whether honourable or shameful, is voluntary; therefore every sin is voluntary. Set aside excuses: no one sins unwillingly.

From Jerome’s writings, his sayings for widows or monks: There are two kinds of sins: one depends on deliberate purpose, the other on negligence.

Likewise: Many refrain through fear, not innocence. Such people are timid, not innocent.

Augustine, to Orosius in the book in dialogue form: Whence comes evil? We must distinguish what doing evil is.

Likewise: Perhaps, then, lust in adultery is evil. For, that you may understand that lust in adultery is evil: if someone does not have an opportunity to lie with another’s wife, yet it is nevertheless in some manner [Col. 1589B] clear that he desires this and would do it if he had the power, he is no less guilty than if he were caught in the very deed.

Orosius: Nothing at all is clearer; it is now plain that nothing other than lust is condemned in the whole class of evil-doing.

Augustine: Do you know that this lust is called by another name, covetousness?

Orosius: I know.

The same author, *On Faith and Works*: If a virgin unwittingly marries another’s husband, and always remains unaware of it, she will never on that account be an adulteress.

The same author, book I of *The City of God* (*Maur.* VII, 18): Certainly they extol Lucretia, that noble Roman matron of old, with great praises for chastity. When the son of King Tarquin had violently overpowered her body and possessed her lustfully, she disclosed the crime of that utterly wicked young man [Col. 1589C] to her husband Collatinus and her kinsman Brutus, men most distinguished and brave, and bound them to vengeance. Finally, distressed and unable to bear the foul deed committed against her, she killed herself. What shall we say? Is she to be judged an adulteress or chaste? Someone declaiming excellently and truthfully on this subject said: “Wonderful to say: there were two, and one committed adultery.” Splendidly and most truly said. For, observing in the union of two bodies the utterly impure lust of one and the utterly chaste will of the other, and attending not to what occurred by the joining of limbs but to what occurred by the difference of minds, he said: “There were two, and one committed adultery.” She was ashamed of another’s disgrace committed against her, though not with her; and, a Roman woman excessively desirous of praise, she feared lest it be thought that what she had suffered by force while alive she had suffered willingly had she continued to live.

[Col. 1589D]

The same author, book III of *On Christian Doctrine*: Scripture commands nothing but charity and condemns or reproves nothing but covetousness. By charity I mean the movement of the mind to enjoy God for his own sake, and oneself and one’s neighbour for God’s sake; by covetousness, the movement of the mind to enjoy oneself, one’s neighbour, or any body not for God’s sake. What unrestrained covetousness does in order to corrupt its own mind and body is called a disgraceful offence (*flagitium*); what it does in order to harm another is called a crime (*facinus*). These are the two kinds of sins.

The same author, on the Epistle of John: The children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil only by charity.

[Col. 1590A]

Likewise: If you have nothing else, have this, and you have fulfilled the law.

The same author, *On the Good of Marriage*: Continence is a virtue not of the body but of the mind. But the virtues of the mind, etc.

Jerome, against Helvidius: “She who is unmarried thinks of the things of the Lord, that she may be holy in spirit and body” (1 Cor. 7:34). The definition of a virgin says that she is holy in body and spirit, because it benefits nothing to have virgin flesh if someone has married in mind.

The same author, on the Epistle to the Romans, book I: It cannot happen that a person can commit adultery in body unless he has first committed adultery in heart.

Ambrose, *On the Fall of a Consecrated Virgin*: Truly the flesh cannot first be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted.

Augustine, on the Epistle of John: What a human being does is not to be considered, but with what disposition he does it. In the same act we find God the Father [Col. 1590B] and Judas: the handing-over was done by the Father; it was done by the Son; it was done by Judas. Different intentions made the acts different. Though one thing arises from different intentions, if we evaluate it, one is to be loved and the other condemned.

Likewise: Goodwill alone is sufficient for one who loves, even if there is nothing that we can bestow.

The same author, in the book of *Questions on the Old and New Law*: No nature is proved to be evil; it is the will [that is evil].

Likewise, chapter III: We know that some people, suddenly insane, have even killed others; when captured and brought before courts, they were by no means judged guilty, because they had acted unknowingly, not by will but under the impulse of some force I know not what. For how is one established as guilty who does not know what he has done? Likewise, if the devil does not know the good, why is he judged worthy of [Col. 1590C] condemnation for not doing what he does not know?

Likewise, chapter XCII: Not everyone who is ignorant is free from punishment. For one who could have learned and did not apply himself has made himself guilty.

Isidore, *Synonyms*, book II: The body cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted.

Likewise: Flesh clean from the thought of the mind does not sin.

Chrysostom, on Matthew: Before God, the will is rewarded, not the work; for the will proceeds from our free choice, but the work is brought to completion by God’s grace.

CXLIV. That one is a sinner only if one is habitual in sins, and the contrary.

Origen, on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, book V: When he says that all have sinned, it is one thing to have sinned, [Col. 1590D] another to be a sinner. A sinner is said to be one who has arrived at a habit and practice of sinning, just as a righteous person is not one who has done some righteous act once or twice, but one who possesses righteousness in use and habit. For if a person is unjust in almost all other respects, yet has performed a just work once or twice, he will be said to have acted justly [Note: [Col. 1589D] Cousin: “would be said” (*diceretur*).]; so also a righteous person will indeed be said to have sinned [Note: [Col. 1590D] Cousin: “is said” (*dicitur*).] if he has at some time committed something unlawful, but he will not on that account be called a sinner if he does not maintain the practice of sinning—just as one is called a physician who possesses the practice, training, and discipline of healing. It may be that all have sinned, even if they have been saints, [Col. 1591A] because no one is clean from defilement, not even if his life has lasted one day.

Aristotle, in the treatise *On Quality* (Buhle edition VI, 487): A habit differs from a disposition in that it is more permanent and enduring. Such are forms of knowledge and virtues. For knowledge seems to belong to what is permanent and difficult to move, as when someone has acquired knowledge perfectly or even moderately, unless perhaps a great alteration has occurred through illness or something of that sort. Virtue likewise—such as justice or chastity, and each of the like—does not seem able easily to be moved or altered.

Boethius, in his commentary on this passage: For virtue [Note: [Col. 1591D] Cousin: “unless” (*nisi*).], where it is difficult [to change], is not unstable [Note: [Col. 1591D] Cousin: “changeable” (*mutabilis*).]. For one who judges justly once is not thereby just, nor is one who has committed adultery once thereby an adulterer, but only when this [Col. 1591B] will and thought have remained.

For Aristotle does not regard virtues as forms of knowledge, as Socrates does.

The same author, in the book *Divisions*: Let the division be converted into itself like a definition. For the definition is converted thus: “Virtue is the best habit of the mind”; and again: “The best habit of the mind is virtue.” [Note: The source reads *mentis*; Cousin gives *intus*, “within.”]

The same author, in the second book of the *Topics*: Let the question be whether virtue is a habit of a mind rightly constituted. It is a question concerning definition, etc.

Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book I: The Lord indeed came to the sinner, though he himself had no sin, and he wished to be baptized, though he had no need to be cleansed.

Augustine, on John (8:35): “But the servant does not remain in the house for ever.” It is one thing to sin, another to be a slave of sin. For no one can avoid being a sinner; [Col. 1591C] [but to be] a sinner in sin is to be a slave of sin.

The same author, to Paulinus: It is asked whether a human being ought to be without sin. If he ought, then he can, because if he cannot, he ought not. And if he ought not to be without sin, he ought to be with sin, and sin will no longer be sin. But if that is absurd, one must confess that a human being ought to be without sin; and it is clear that he ought to do nothing other than what he can do.

Likewise: By freedom of choice it came about that the human being was with sin; but the penal defect that followed from freedom has made necessity. Hence even the defect cries out to the Lord: “Deliver me from my necessities, O Lord” (Ps. 24:17). [Note: [Col. 1592D] Cousin: “faith” (*fides*) for “defect” (*vitiositas*).]

The same author, in Sermon I on the Epistle of John: So long as a person bears flesh, he cannot be without even slight sins. But do not despise [Col. 1591D] these slight sins: many slight things make one great thing. Many drops fill a river.

CXLV. That we sometimes sin unwillingly, and the contrary.

Paul the Apostle, in the Epistle to the Romans (7:15): “For I do not do the good that I will; but the evil that I hate, that I do. But if I do what I do not will, I agree with the law that it is good,” etc.

Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, book II, chapter XXII: Many sin not by will but by necessity alone: fearing temporal want, and while fleeing the necessities of the present age, they are deprived of future goods.

From Jerome’s writings, his sayings for widows or monks: Every sin is an action; and every action is voluntary, etc.

Augustine, *On True Religion*: Sin is voluntary evil to such an extent that it is not sin at all if it is not voluntary; and this is so evident that no small number of learned persons and no multitude of unlearned persons disagrees with it. Therefore either one must deny that sin is committed, or one must admit that it is committed voluntarily.

Likewise: Therefore sin is committed voluntarily; and since it is beyond doubt that sin is committed, it must likewise not be doubted that souls have freedom of choice in God. For God judged his servants better if they served him freely, which could not happen at all if they served not by will but by necessity. Therefore they serve God freely, [Col. 1592B] and this benefits not God but themselves.

The same author, recalling and revising this statement in book I of the *Retractations*, says (*Maur.* I, 20): “Sin is voluntary evil to such an extent,” I said, “that it is not sin at all if it is not voluntary.” This definition may appear false; but if it is carefully examined, it is found most true. For one must think here of the sin which is sin only, not of that which is also a punishment of sin. Yet even those things not without reason called involuntary sins, which are committed by the ignorant or by persons under compulsion, cannot in every way be committed without will. For one who sins in ignorance sins by will, certainly, because he thinks that what ought not to be done [Col. 1592C] ought to be done. And the one who, because the flesh lusts against the spirit, does not do the things he wills, lusts unwillingly and in that respect does not do what he wills; but if he is conquered, he willingly consents to lust, and in that respect, because he does only what he wills, he is free from righteousness and a slave to sin.

And what is called original sin in infants, although they do not yet use free choice, is not absurdly called voluntary as well, because, contracted from the evil will of the first human being, it has become in some way hereditary—so that sin is not sin at all if it is not voluntary.

The same author, in the same work: What I said, that sin exists nowhere except in the will, Pelagians may think was said on their behalf because of infants, whom they deny to have sin—as though the sin which we say they draw [Col. 1592D] originally from Adam, that is, by which they are implicated in his guilt and are therefore held liable to punishment, could have existed anywhere but in the will, since it was committed by will when transgression of the divine command was made. This statement may also be considered false because the Apostle said (Rom. 7:16): “But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.” But that of which the Apostle spoke in this way is called sin because it was made, by sin, a punishment of sin; since this is said concerning the lust of the flesh, as he makes clear in what follows: “I know that no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh; for willing is present with me, but accomplishing [Col. 1593A] the good is not.” For the perfection of good is that even this lust for sin should not be in a human being. When one lives well, the will does not consent to it; nevertheless, one does not accomplish the good, because lust remains within, against which the will struggles. The guilt of this lust is removed in baptism, but weakness remains [Note: [Col. 1593D] Monacensis omits “is removed, but weakness remains.”], and one who makes good progress struggles against it.

But the sin which exists nowhere except in the will must be understood especially as that to which just condemnation has followed. For this entered the world through one human being. Although even that sin by which one consents to sinful lust is committed only by will. For this reason I also said elsewhere: “Therefore one sins only by will.”

Likewise: I defined will by saying: “Will is a [Col. 1593B] movement of the mind, with no one compelling it, either to admit or not admit something, or to obtain it.” This was said so that the intention might be referred to those who first, in Paradise, brought about the origin of evil for the human race by sinning under no compulsion—that is, by free will—because knowingly they acted against the command: the tempter persuaded them but did not compel them. For one who sinned unknowingly can not inappropriately be said to have sinned unwillingly, although he nevertheless did willingly what he did unknowingly. This will is certainly thus defined: “a movement of the mind,” etc. Thus even such a sin could not exist without will, but by will in respect of the act, not in respect of the sin. Yet that act was sin, for what was done ought not to have been done.

But one who sins knowingly, if able to resist without sin a person compelling him to sin, yet does not do so, [Col. 1593C] plainly sins willingly; for one who can resist is not compelled to yield. But one who cannot resist a compelling desire by a good will, and therefore acts contrary to the command, has a sin which is also a punishment of sin. Therefore it is most true that sin cannot exist without will.

Likewise, the definition of sin which we gave—“sin is the will to retain or obtain what justice forbids and from which one is free to abstain”—is true because it defines that which is sin only, not that which is also a punishment of sin. For when it is such that it is both sin and punishment of sin, how great is the power of the will under ruling lust, unless perhaps it is devout enough to pray for help? For it is free only insofar as it has been freed, and only so far is it called will; [Col. 1593D] otherwise it should properly be called both desire and will. But if anyone says that desire itself is nothing other than will, yet a will made defective and enslaved by sin, he need not be opposed; when the matter is clear, there should be no dispute about words. For even so it is shown that no sin, whether in deed or in origin, exists without will.

Likewise: We answer that by “nature” in these words of mine I meant the nature properly so called, in which we were created without defect. And again, in the statement that it is the height of injustice and wrong for anyone to be held guilty of sin because he did not do what he could not do: “Why, then,” they ask, “are infants held guilty?” The answer is: because they are held guilty [Col. 1594A] from the origin of him who did not do what he could do—namely, keep the divine command. But what I said—that whatever souls do, if they do it by nature and not by will, that is, if they lack a free movement of mind both to do and not to do it, and if finally no power of refraining from their act is granted to them—we cannot hold their sin against them: the question concerning infants does not disturb this, because they are held guilty from the origin of him who sinned by will, when he had the fullest power to refrain from the act.

The same author, in the same work: I say, then, that there is no sin if it is not sinned by one’s own will; here I intended “sin” to mean that which is not [Col. 1594B] also a punishment of sin. For concerning such punishment I said elsewhere in the same discussion what had to be said.

CXLVI. That God does not punish the same sin here and in the future.

Origines, Homilies on the Old Testament, Homily XLIV: “If a man,” he says, “has cursed God, he shall bear his sin. But whoever names the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death” (Lev. 24:15). What does this mean? He who has cursed [Note: Col. 1593D, Cous.: “curses.”] God does not receive the penalty of death, but he who has named the name of the Lord? Is it not much more serious to curse God than to name him, even if it is said that he named him in vain? Likewise: They think that he who curses the name of the Lord ought immediately to be punished, whereas it should suffice for him who names the name—that is, names it needlessly and in vain—to bear his sin. Yet we cannot doubt that the sin in which God is cursed is greater than that in which he is named. It remains for us to show that bearing sin and having it with oneself is far more serious than being punished by death. Death inflicted as a penalty for sin is a cleansing of the very sin for which it is commanded to be inflicted. Therefore sin is absolved by the penalty of death, and nothing remains for the day of judgment and the punishment of eternal fire to discover for this crime. But when someone bears sin, has it with himself, and it remains with him, without being washed away by any punishment or penalty, it passes with him even after death; and he who has not paid temporal penalties here pays eternal punishments there. You see, therefore, how much more serious it is to bear sin than to be punished by death; for here death is given as retribution, and before the Lord, the righteous judge, one is not judged twice for the same thing, as the prophet said (Nah. 1:9, according to the LXX). But where retribution has not been exacted [Note: Col. 1594D, Cous.: “customary” (*solita*).], sin remains to be demanded by eternal fires.

I can bring you witnesses from the divine books: Reuben and Judah speaking to their father Jacob when they wished to take Benjamin with them to Egypt. Reuben indeed said to his father: “Put both my sons to death if I do not bring Benjamin back to you” (Gen. 42:37). But Judah said: “I shall be guilty of sin against you if I do not bring him back to you” (Gen. 43:9). Jacob, knowing that what Judah had promised was far more serious, did not entrust his son to Reuben, as one who had chosen the lighter penalty, but entrusted him to Judah, knowing that he had chosen the graver thing.

Do you also wish to learn from the Gospels that one who receives his evils in this life does not receive them there, whereas for one who has not received them here all things are reserved there? “Remember, son, that you received your good things in life,” etc.; “but now you indeed are tormented, while he rests here” (Luke 16:25). And people, ignorant of the judgments of God because they are an abyss, are accustomed to complain much against God and say: Why do wicked people suffer no adversity in this life, while hardships come upon those who worship God?

Jerome on the prophet Nahum (1:9): “What do you devise against the Lord? He himself will make an end. Affliction shall not rise up a second time.” God says this: “I afflicted you, and I shall afflict you no more” [Nah. 1:9, according to the LXX]. If God seems cruel because he destroyed the human race by the flood, overwhelmed Sodom and Gomorrah with fire and sulphur, overthrew the Egyptians in the sea and the Israelites in the wilderness, know that he punishes for a time in the present, lest he punish eternally in the future. God will not judge twice for the same thing. Therefore those who have been punished will not afterward be punished; otherwise the prophet lies, which it is impious to say. Thus those who perished in the flood, the Sodomites, the Egyptians, and the Israelites in the wilderness received their evils in their lifetime.

Someone may ask: if a believer is caught in adultery and beheaded, what will happen to him? Either he will be punished, and this statement—“God will not judge twice for the same thing”—is false; or he will not be punished, and adulterers ought to desire to die in this way. I answer that God, as he knows the measures of all things, so also knows the measures of punishments; his sentence is not forestalled, nor is his power to inflict thereafter punishment upon the sinner taken away from him. A great sin is washed away by great and prolonged torments. But if someone has been punished—as the man in the Law who cursed an Israelite, and the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath—such persons are not punished afterward, because a light fault has been compensated by present punishment.

Likewise: There is a similar passage in Ezekiel, book VI, where it is said: “My eye spared them, lest I should kill and destroy them.” The question is asked how he spared those whose corpses lay in the wilderness, and of whom, apart from Joshua son of Nun and Caleb, none entered the land of promise. From this we understand that they live, are not reserved for eternal punishments, and have not been erased from the book of the living.

Gregory, *Morals*, book IX: “Show why you judge me thus” (Job 10:2). God judges a human being in this life in two ways: either, through present evils, he already begins to inflict the torments that follow; or he extinguishes the torments that follow by present scourges. For unless the righteous judge struck some persons both now and afterward, when their sins require it, Jude [5] would not have said: “He destroyed a second time those who did not believe”; nor would the Psalmist have said of the wicked (Ps. 108:29 [Vulgate]): “Let them be clothed with their confusion as with a double garment.” We call a *diplois* a double garment. Thus those are clothed with confusion as with a double garment who, according to the merit of their guilt, are struck by both temporal and everlasting punishment. Punishment frees from punishment only those whom it changes. For present evils lead onward to later evils those whom they do not correct.

The same, book XVIII, on Job’s words concerning the wicked rich man: “And like a whirlwind it shall carry him away from his place” (Job 27:21). The place of the perverse is delight in temporal life and pleasure of the flesh. “He shall send upon him and shall not spare.” Whenever God corrects a sinner by striking him, he sends the scourge in order that he may spare him. [Note: Col. 1595D, Munich manuscript omits “But when … in order not to spare.”]

But when he ends, by striking, the life of one persisting in sin, he sends the scourge but by no means spares him. For he who sent the scourge in order to spare sometimes sends it in order not to spare. In this life the Lord is so much the more intent upon sparing as he scourges more while waiting, as he himself says through the angel to John: “Those whom I love I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3:19); and as it is elsewhere said: “Whom God loves he chastises; he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). Conversely, concerning the scourge of condemnation, the Lord says through Jeremiah (30:14): “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel chastisement. Why do you cry out over your ruin? Your pain is incurable.”

Every divine striking, then, is either a purification in us during the present life or the beginning of the punishment to come. On account of those who profit from the scourge, it is said (Ps. 93:20): “You who fashion pain in the commandment”; for, when the wicked person who would not hear the commandment is scourged and corrected, he hears pain. Pain, therefore, is fashioned into a commandment for the person who is restrained from evil works by pain as though by a commandment. But of those whom scourges condemn rather than free, it is said (Jer. 5:3): “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to receive discipline.” For these, scourges begin in this life and endure in eternal striking. Hence the Lord says through Moses (Deut. 32:22): “A fire has been kindled by my wrath”; and with reference to eternal condemnation he adds: “And it shall burn even to the lowest hell.”

Although some are accustomed to cite what is written, “God does not judge twice for the same thing,” those who say this of the wicked do not heed: “Crush them, O Lord, with a double destruction” (Jer. 17:18); and what is elsewhere written (Jude 5): “Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, destroyed a second time those who did not believe.” Yet, if we grant them that no fault can be struck twice, this must be understood of those struck because of sin and dying in their sin: their striking, begun here, is completed there, so that for the uncorrected it is one scourge, beginning temporally but consummated in eternal punishments. Thus for those who wholly refuse correction, the striking of present scourges is already the beginning of the torments to come.

The same, *Dialogues*, book III: The Lord rained fire and sulphur upon the Sodomites. Because they had burned with unlawful love of corruptible flesh, they perished together by burning and stench, so that in their punishment they might recognize that, by delight in their own stench, they had surrendered themselves to eternal death.

### CXLVII. That Cain was not condemned, and the contrary

Jerome to Damasus: Thus, since Cain’s sin was dissolved in the seventh generation, the Lord will not judge twice for the same thing; and one who has once received evils in his life will not suffer in death the same torments that he suffered in life, etc.

Gregory, *Morals*, book VI: “I saw the fool firmly rooted, and immediately I cursed his beauty” (Job 5:3). Cain is recorded as having first built a city, in order that it might plainly be shown that he laid a foundation upon earth who was estranged from the solidity of the heavenly homeland.

[Note: Col. 1597D. After this brief question concerning Cain, the Munich manuscript, under a new division but, contrary to its usual practice, without a heading, repeated a great many passages that we have already read above in Question XXXI, pp. 81–85. It was not worth while to repeat them here yet again. Omitting a few passages from Augustine, Jerome, and the Book of Kings, found on pp. 83 and 84, it added before the sayings of Rufinus and Gregory the following new passage among the others:

Chrysostom on Matthew (22:2): “The kingdom of heaven is like a man, a king, who made a wedding for his son,” and the remainder. Every evil is without substance and is nothing. Likewise: No thing can arise from evil. But since evil itself is nothing, how can it make any thing exist? Yet it can destroy something in which evil is present: the good withdraws because of the evil dwelling within, and so the thing goes toward nothingness. Therefore, a thing in which there is good alone is living and immortal. But man was created from good and evil so that, despising evil, he might follow good and thereby have the reward of choice.]

### CXLVIII. That what God forgives he does not exact afterward, and the contrary

[Col. 1597B]

The Apostle Paul, in the Epistle to the Romans (11:29): “For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.”

Augustine on Genesis: When we read the Lord saying, “I repent” (Gen. 6:7), let us consider what the work of repenting ordinarily is in all cases. Without doubt, a will to change is found in it, but in a human being it arises from grief of soul.

Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, book II, chapter XXXI: God’s swearing is that providence by which he decrees not to overturn what has been decreed. Repentance is change; not to repent is not to revoke what has been decreed, as in the statement: “God has sworn and will not repent” (Ps. 109:4 [Vulgate]), that is, he will not change what he has sworn.

Prosper’s *Responses to Rufinus*, chapter II (Augustine, Maurist edition X, appendix, p. 198): For one who departs from Christ and ends this life estranged from grace—into what does he fall but perdition? Yet he does not fall back into what has been forgiven, nor will one be condemned in original sin; nevertheless, because of his final [Note: Col. 1598D, editions: “last” (*postrema*).] crimes he will be afflicted with that death which was due to him because of those things that were forgiven.

Augustine, *On Baptism*, book I: The Lord teaches most plainly in the Gospel that forgiven sins return where brotherly charity is absent, in the case of that fellow-servant whom, because he had not shown mercy, the lord commanded to repay what he had forgiven him.

Gregory, *Dialogues*, final chapter: Because the servant did not forgive his fellow-servant’s debt, he was commanded to pay what had already been forgiven him. From these statements it is plainly established that, if we do not forgive what is committed against us, that which we had rejoiced had already been forgiven us through repentance is again exacted from us.

Rabanus: “He handed him over to the torturers” (Matt. 18:34), that is, to evil spirits, until he should repay the entire debt. He will always repay; he will always be tormented in punishments for all his sins. It must be noted that he says “the entire debt,” because not only sins committed by a person after baptism will be reckoned against him for punishment, but also original sins, which were forgiven in baptism.

### CXLIX. That it is more serious to sin openly than secretly, and the contrary

[Note: Col. 1598D, Cous.: omits “than secretly.”]

Isidore, *On the Highest Good*, book II, chapter XX: It is a greater fault to sin openly than secretly. For one who sins publicly is guilty in two ways, because he both acts and teaches. Of such persons Isaiah says (3:9): “They proclaimed their sins like Sodom; they did not conceal them.”

Likewise: To commit sin is criminal wrongdoing; to proclaim sin is an outcry, concerning which the Apostle also says (Eph. 4:31): “Let all outcry be removed from you with all malice,” that is, together with the sins themselves.

From Augustine’s sermon *On the Life and Conduct of Clerics*, which begins, “For this reason I have wished”: “Those who wish to possess something of their own, for whom God and the Church are not enough, may remain wherever they wish; I do not take clerical status from them. I do not wish to have hypocrites. For it is evil to fall away from one’s purpose; but it is worse to feign a purpose.”

From the books of Prosper’s *Sentences*: Equity is not feigned; rather, it is a doubled sin, in which there are both iniquity and pretence.

Jerome on Ezekiel, book VI: In the cooperation of two sinners, it is a lighter sin to sin openly than to simulate and feign holiness.

### CL. That adultery, after heresy, is more serious than other sins, and that it is not

Clement, in the First Epistle to James: What among all sins is more serious than adultery? It is second in punishments, the first place being held by those who go astray, even if they have lived soberly. Likewise: The poison of adultery is more destructive than all evils.

Bede: “Herod the tetrarch heard the report of Jesus,” etc. (Matt. 14:1). Herod feared John and gladly listened to him, but love of the woman prevailed. Likewise: Because he was unwilling to restrain lust, he sank into the guilt of a murderer; and the lesser sin was the cause of the greater sin for him. By God’s distinct judgment it happened that, because of his desire for an adulteress whom he knew to be detestable, he shed the blood of a prophet whom he knew to be acceptable to God.

Ambrose, in the book *On Virgins*: Certainly this was the cause of that suffering: “It is not lawful for you,” he says, “to have her as wife.” If this was said concerning another man’s wife, how much more concerning a consecrated virgin.

### CLI. That sins are not forgiven without confession, and the contrary

Augustine, *On Repentance*, book I: No one can be justified from sin unless he has first confessed the sin. Hence the Lord says: “Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26).

Hilary on Psalm 134: Outside forgiveness is the one who knows sin and does not confess what he knows. But confession must always be made—not because one must always sin, so that one must always confess, but because untiring confession of old and ancient sin is beneficial.

From the decrees of Pope Calixtus: If the sick are in sins, have confessed this to the priests of the Church, and have sufficiently shown that with a perfected heart they abandon and amend those sins, they are forgiven; for they cannot be forgiven without confession of amendment. Hence it is rightly added: “Confess your sins to one another,” etc. (Jas. 5:16).

Gregory to Abbot Eusebius: Never doubt that anyone whom you see washing away sins with tears obtains mercy before the sight of the Godhead, because he who came to redeem sinners by his blood despises no sinner who returns.

[Note: Col. 1599D. This passage is not found in the printed edition of the letter to Abbot Eusebius. Cf. Gregory, *Works*, II, 599.]

Bede, in a homily on the ten lepers (*Works*, Giles edition V, 97): If anyone has been delivered by God’s grace from Jewish unbelief, heretical perversity, Gentile superstition, or fraternal schism, he must come to the Church and show the true color of faith that he receives. But God himself remits all other [Note: Col. 1599D, Munich manuscript: “all” (*cuncta*).] sins in the conscience.

John Chrysostom on Psalm 50: Speak your sins, that you may blot them out. If you are ashamed to tell them to someone, tell them to God, who heals them; if you weep, they are blotted out.

Maximus, in Sermon II for Easter Monday: Peter burst into tears; he asks for nothing in words. I find that he wept; I do not find what he said. I read of his tears; I do not read of a formal satisfaction. What is customarily bewailed is not customarily excused, and what cannot be defended can be washed away. For tears wash away the fault which shame prevents one from confessing with the voice; tears provide both for modesty and salvation. They ask forgiveness and obtain it; they do not state the case, yet they receive mercy. Speech sometimes does not disclose the whole matter; tears always reveal the whole affection. Therefore Peter no longer uses the speech by which he had deceived, sinned, and lost faith, lest by the very means he used for denial he should not be believed when confessing. I find another reason why Peter was silent: lest a petition for pardon made so quickly should through shamelessness offend more than it obtained. For one usually merits pardon more quickly because [Note: Col. 1599D, Cous.: “who” (*qui*).] one entreats more modestly.

Ambrose on Luke (Maurist edition IV, 247): It is not enough that the answer of one confessing Jesus should be veiled [Note: Col. 1599D, Cous.: “in the will” (*in voluntate*).], but confession must be open. What benefit is it to wrap up one’s words if you wish to appear to have denied? Therefore Peter is represented as having answered so not deliberately, because afterward he remembered and nevertheless wept. For he preferred to accuse his own sin, so that he might be justified by confessing, rather than be weighed down by denying. “The righteous person is the first accuser of himself” (Prov. 18:17). He grieved and wept because he had erred as a human being. I do not find what he said; I find that he wept. I read of his tears; I do not read of a formal satisfaction. Tears wash away the fault which shame prevents one from confessing with the voice, and weeping provides for forgiveness and modesty. Tears speak of guilt without horror; they confess the crime without offence to modesty.

[Note: Col. 1599D. The words “I read of his tears … without offence to modesty,” which occur in the Munich and Tours manuscripts, were not admitted by Cousin into the text.]

His tears do not ask forgiveness, yet they merit it. I find why Peter was silent: lest a request for pardon made so quickly should offend more. One must first weep, and then pray. Peter first denied and did not weep, because the Lord had not looked upon him. Look upon us, Lord Jesus, so that we may know how to bewail our sin.

### CLII. That fear of God remains in the saints, and that it does not

From Psalm 33 [10]: “Fear the Lord, all his saints, because,” etc.

From Proverbs (28:14): “Blessed is the man who is always fearful; but he who is hard of heart shall fall into evil.”

Ecclesiasticus, chapter 1 [17]: “The fear of the Lord drives out sin; for one who is without fear cannot be justified.”

Truth himself, through himself (Matt. 10:28): “Do not fear those who kill the body but have nothing they can do to the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both body and soul in Gehenna.”

From Paul’s Epistle to the Romans (11:20): “But you stand by faith; do not be high-minded, but fear.”

[Note: Col. 1600D, Cousin omits the words “But you stand by faith … are led by the Spirit of God.”]

The same, above (8:14): “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God. For you have not received again the spirit of slavery in fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry: Abba, Father.”
