From the First Epistle of John (4:16): “God is charity, and he who remains in him,” etc. “In this charity has been made perfect with us, that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as he is, so also are we in this world. There is no fear” [Note: Col. 1600D, Cous.: omits “no.”] “in charity, but perfect charity casts fear out, because fear has punishment. But one who fears is not perfect in charity.”

### CLIII. That one ought not [Note: Col. 1600D, Cous.: omits “not.”] to pray for all people, and the contrary

Paul the Apostle, in the First Epistle to Timothy (2:1): “I urge, therefore, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are established in high position, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity. For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book I: But they will say: It is written (1 Sam. 2:25), “If a man sins against a man, one shall pray for him; but if he sins against God, who shall pray for him?” It is not written, “no one,” but “who?” And elsewhere (Hos. 14:10): “Who is wise, and shall understand this?” Will no one understand? And, “Who is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord has appointed,” etc.? In the same way “who shall pray for him?” must be understood: that is, some person of exceptional life ought to pray for one who has sinned against the Lord. The greater the fault, the greater the aids that must be sought.

Likewise: “There is a sin unto death; not concerning that do I say that anyone should pray.” He was not speaking to Moses and Jeremiah, but to the people, who ought to present another sinner for their own sins. It is enough for such a person to pray to God for lighter offences, while he should think that forgiveness for graver ones must be reserved for the prayers of the righteous. Did not John himself know that Stephen had prayed for his persecutors, who could not bear to hear Christ’s name? We see the effect of that prayer in the Apostle who guarded the garments of those throwing stones.

Likewise: Finally, Paul teaches that those who have committed sin unto death are not to be abandoned.

Bede on the Epistle of John (5:16): “If anyone knows his brother to be sinning a sin not unto death, let him ask, and life shall be given him.” He speaks of daily and light sins, which, as they are difficult to avoid, are also easily cured. But James makes clearer the order in which this mutual petition for sins is to be performed, saying: “Confess to one another,” etc. Therefore, if perhaps you have sinned in word, thought, forgetfulness, or ignorance, go to your brother, confess to him, and by piously interceding wash away his errors in turn. But if you have committed something more serious, bring in the priests of the Church and correct yourself under their examination.

“There is a sin unto death; not concerning that do I say that anyone should pray.” John shows us that there are certain brothers for whom we are not commanded to pray, although the Lord commands us to pray even for persecutors. This cannot be resolved otherwise than by confessing that there are certain sins among brothers more serious than the persecution of enemies. A brother’s sin unto death is when, after recognition of God given through Christ’s grace, someone attacks brotherhood and is stirred by the fires of envy against the very grace by which he has been reconciled to God. But sin not unto death is when someone has not withdrawn love from a brother, but through some weakness of mind [Note: Col. 1601D, Cousin omits: “of mind.”] has failed to render the services owed to brotherhood. Therefore the Lord also says: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” Not yet made participants in the grace of the Holy Spirit, because they had not yet believed in Christ, they were not fighting against that common grace.

Sin unto death, for which he forbids anyone to pray, may also be understood as sin not corrected in this life, because forgiveness for it is sought in vain after death. “We know that everyone born of God does not sin.” There are sins unto death, such as those of which the Apostle says: “Those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.” One born of God does not sin sin unto death; this may be understood of every capital crime, and especially of that by which charity is violated, as we have explained. But we have also said that sin unto death may be understood as sin prolonged until the time of death [Note: Col. 1601D, Cous.: “handled” (*pertractum*).] (*Works*, Giles edition XII, 317).

### CLIV. That it is lawful to lie, and the contrary

[Note: Col. 1602D, Cous.: “That it is lawful to lie for no cause, and the contrary.”]

Augustine, *On Lying*: The sixth kind of lie is that which harms no one and benefits someone, as when a person who knows where another’s money, about to be unjustly taken, is located lies that he does not know. The seventh is that which harms no one and benefits someone, as when a person, unwilling to betray someone sought for death, lies.

Likewise: One must not lie in the sixth kind; for not even the truth of testimony may rightly be corrupted for anyone’s temporal advantage and safety; and no one is to be led to eternal salvation with lying assistance. Nor must one lie in the seventh kind; for another person’s temporal advantage or safety is not to be preferred to faith, nor is anyone so wrongly moved by our right actions that he becomes worse in mind and further removed from piety.

The same, on Psalm 5: Let no one suppose that a perfect and spiritual person ought to lie, whether for his own sake or another’s, for this temporal life, in whose death the soul is killed. But since lying is one thing and concealing truth another—for to speak what is false is one thing and to keep silence about what is true another—if perhaps someone does not wish to betray a person even to the said visible death, he ought to be ready to conceal the truth, not to speak falsehood, so that he neither betrays nor lies, nor kills his own soul for another’s body.

Likewise: There are two kinds of lies in which the fault is not great, though they are not without fault. When we joke, or lie for a neighbor, the first—joking—is not harmful because it does not deceive; for the person to whom it is said knows that it was said in jest. The second is milder because it retains some benevolence. But that which does not have a double heart ought not even to be called a lie. For example, if a sword is entrusted to someone and he promises to return it when the person who entrusted it asks for it, but that person asks for his sword while insane, it is plainly not to be returned, lest he kill himself or others, until health is restored to him. The person has no double heart because, when the sword was entrusted to him and he promised to return it to its owner upon request, he did not think that the owner could demand it back while insane. It is plain that one is not to be blamed for sometimes keeping truth silent; but that falsehood may be spoken is nowhere found to have been permitted to the saints.

Isidore, *Sentences*, II, chapter XXX, no. 6: Sometimes it is worse to deliberate a lie than to speak one. For sometimes an unwary person is accustomed to utter a lie precipitately; but he cannot deliberate one except by intention. Likewise, because it is written: “A lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11), and: “You will destroy all who speak lies” (Ps. 5:7 [Vulgate]). Perfect men particularly avoid even this kind of lie, so that neither another person’s life may be defended by their deception nor they harm their own souls while striving to provide safety to another’s flesh, although we believe that this very kind of sin is most easily forgiven.

Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter CXLV (Maurist edition III, 413): The meaning of Joseph’s words to his brothers (Gen. 44:15), “Did you not know that a man such as I am is not without augury?” is commonly questioned. Since, as the outcome showed, this was spoken not seriously but in jest, is it not to be considered a lie? For lies are seriously enacted by liars, not in jest; but when things that are not so are said as though in jest, they are not counted as lies.

Hilary on Psalm 14: A lie is often necessary, and falsehood is sometimes useful: when we lie to an attacker concerning one who is hiding, frustrate testimony on behalf of one in danger, or deceive a sick person because treatment is difficult. For, according to the Apostle’s teaching, our speech ought to be seasoned with salt.

### CLV. That it is lawful for a person to lay hands upon himself for certain reasons, and the contrary

[Col. 1603C]

Jerome on the Prophet Jonah (1:12): “Take me up and cast me into the sea, and the sea will cease from troubling you.” For it is not ours to seize upon death, but willingly to accept it when it is inflicted. Hence, even in persecutions, it is not lawful to perish by one’s own hand, except where chastity is endangered.

Ecclesiastical History, book VI, chapter XXXI: But when they seized a remarkable virgin of advanced age, named Apollonia, they first knocked out all her teeth; then, having piled up wood, they built a pyre, threatening to burn her alive unless she uttered impious words with them. But when she saw the pyre kindled, she suddenly tore herself from the hands of the impious men [Col. 1603D] and voluntarily leapt into the fire, so that the very authors of the cruelty were terrified, because the woman was found readier for death than the persecutor for punishment.

Augustine, *The City of God*, book I (Maur. VII, 20): It remains for us to understand what was said: “You shall not kill”—not another person, therefore not yourself either. For one who kills himself kills nothing other than a human being.

Likewise: “You shall not kill,” excepting those whom God commands to be killed, whether by a law given for a particular time or by an express command directed to a particular person. Nor does the person himself kill who renders service to one commanding, just as a sword is an instrument for its user.

Likewise: It is asked whether Jephthah’s killing of the daughter who met him is to be regarded as done at God’s command, since he had vowed to sacrifice to God whatever should first meet him as he returned victorious from battle. Nor is Samson otherwise excused for crushing himself together with his enemies beneath the fall of the house, except because the Spirit, who worked miracles through him, had secretly commanded this.

Likewise: Whoever have perpetrated this upon themselves are perhaps to be admired for greatness of spirit, but not praised for soundness of wisdom. Indeed, if one examines the reasoning more carefully, not even that greatness of spirit can properly be so called where someone, unable to endure either hardships of whatever kind or the sins of others, has killed himself. For the mind is shown to be weaker when it cannot bear either the severe harshness of its own body or the foolish opinion of the crowd.

Likewise: If it is thought to be done with great spirit when a man brings death upon himself, then Cleombrotus [Note: [Col. 1603] Cous.: *Theobrotus*; Monac.: *te obrutus* (“buried you”). Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.34, calls him Cleombrotus of Ambracia.] is especially found eminent in this greatness. It is said that, after reading Plato’s book in which the immortality of the soul was discussed, he threw himself headlong from a wall and thus departed this life for the one which he believed to be better. Yet Plato himself, whom he had read, could testify that this was a great act rather than a good one; for Plato would certainly himself have done this above all things, or even prescribed it, unless he had judged, with that same mind by which he perceived the soul’s immortality, that it must by no means be done, indeed that it must be forbidden.

Likewise: Yet, apart from Lucretia, they do not easily find anyone by whose authority they may support their position, except that Cato [Col. 1604C] who killed himself at Utica—not because he alone did this, but because he was considered a learned and upright man.

Likewise: If it was shameful to live under Caesar’s victory, why was he the author of this shame for his son, whom he instructed to hope for everything from Caesar’s kindness? Why did he not compel him too to die with him?

Likewise: One reason remains, of which I had begun to speak: that it is thought useful for a person to kill himself, namely, lest he fall into sin, whether through the enticement of pleasure or the savagery of pain. If we admit this reason, it will advance so far that people ought to be exhorted to kill themselves immediately after they have been washed in the laver of regeneration and received forgiveness of all their sins. For then is the time to guard against all future sins, when all past sins have been wiped away.

Likewise: O deranged minds [Col. 1604D]! What is this great thing if not error, indeed madness? “But,” they say, “some holy women, in time of persecution, in order to escape persecutors of their chastity, threw themselves into a river that would carry them off and kill them; and their martyrdoms are celebrated with most renowned veneration in the Catholic Church.” Concerning these women I dare make no rash judgment. For I do not know whether divine authority, through some trustworthy testimonies, persuaded the Church to honor their memory in this way; and it may be so. For what if they did this not through human deception, but by divine commission—not in error, but in obedience? Concerning Samson we are permitted to believe no other thing. But when God commands and unmistakably declares that he commands, who would charge obedience with crime? Who would accuse the submission of piety? For even a soldier, when he kills a man in obedience to the authority under which he has been lawfully established, is guilty of homicide under no law of his state; indeed, unless he does it, he is guilty of deserting and despising authority. If this is so when an emperor commands, how much more when the Creator commands!

The same, to Laetus: Likewise, the command by which we are ordered to lose our soul does not mean that each person should kill himself—which is an unforgivable crime—but it does mean that he should kill within himself the carnal inclination of the soul.

Macrobius, book I, chapter 13, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*: “I ask you, most holy and excellent father,” I said, “since this is life, as I hear Africanus say, [Col. 1605B] why do I linger on earth? Why do I not hasten to come here to you?”—“It is not so,” he replied. “For unless God releases you from these bodily guards, the way hither cannot lie open to you. Therefore, both you, Publius, and all the devout must retain the soul in the body’s custody, nor must you depart human life without the command of him from whom it was given to you, lest you seem to have fled the task assigned to you by God himself.”

This is Plato’s school and teaching: in the *Phaedo* he determines that a person must not die of his own accord; yet in the same dialogue he says that death ought to be desired by philosophers, and that philosophy itself is a meditation upon dying. But Plato knew that human beings have two deaths. Nor do I now repeat what was said above, that there are two deaths, one of the soul and the other of the living being; rather, he also asserts that the living being itself—that is, the human being—has two deaths, one supplied by nature, the other by virtues. For a man dies when the soul leaves the body, released [Note: [Col. 1605D] Cous.: *solum* (“alone”).] by the law of nature; he is also said to die when, though his soul remains in the body, he scorns bodily allurements under philosophy’s instruction and casts off the sweet snares of desires and all other passions. Plato therefore says that the wise should seek this death; but he forbids the other, which nature has appointed for all, to be forced, inflicted, or summoned, teaching that nature must be awaited.

He added also that we are under God’s dominion, governed by his protection and providence; and that, against the Lord’s will, nothing that he possesses should be removed from that place [Col. 1605D] in which he had placed it. Just as one who forcibly takes life from another’s slave will not be free from guilt, so one who seeks his own end while the Lord has not yet commanded it will attain not acquittal but guilt.

Plotinus develops these seeds of Plato’s school more deeply. “Since it is agreed,” he says, “that recompense is to be given there to souls according to the degree of perfection which each has attained in this life, the end of life must not be hastened, when an increase in progress may still be possible.” [Note: [Col. 1605D] Editions: *cum* (“when”).] “Then,” you will say, “one who has been perfectly purified ought to lay hands upon himself, since he has no reason to remain, because one who has reached the heights requires no further progress.” But precisely in summoning for himself a swift end through hope of enjoying blessedness, he becomes entangled in the snare of passion; for hope, like fear, is a passion. And this is why Paul forbids and turns away his son, hurrying to come to him in hope of a truer life: “For unless God,” he says, “releases you from these bodily guards, the way hither cannot lie open to you.” Nor does he say [Note: [Col. 1605D] Cous.: “For unless the Lord, he says, releases you from these bodily [Col. 1606D] . . . . nor does he say that,” etc.] that you cannot die unless natural death comes, but that you cannot come here. With equal constancy, death neither ought to be feared when it comes through nature nor compelled contrary to nature’s order.

### CLVI. That Christians may for no reason kill anyone, and the contrary

[Note: [Col. 1606D] Cous.: “kill a human being.”]

[Col. 1606B] Augustine, to Macedonius (Maur. II, 530): No one is good through fear of punishment, but through love of justice. Nevertheless, human laws usefully restrain audacity through fear, so that innocence may be safe among the wicked and, among the wicked themselves, while the power to act is checked by dread of punishment, the will may be healed by calling upon God. Episcopal intercessions are not contrary to this ordering of human affairs; indeed, there would be neither reason nor place at all for intercession if these things did not exist. For the benefits bestowed by those who intercede and spare are so much more welcome as the punishments of sinners are more just.

Nor, as I understand it, did the harsher vengeance of the Law rage in the Old Testament for any reason except to show that punishments were rightly appointed for the unjust, so that when we are admonished by the indulgence of the New Testament to spare them, either there may be a remedy of salvation by which our own sins too are forgiven, or there may be a commendation of gentleness [Note: [Col. 1606D] Cous.: *magnitudinis*, “greatness.”], so that through those who spare, the truth preached may not only be feared but also loved.

Likewise: Discipline must not be extended to death, so that there may be someone whom it can benefit.

Likewise: When we intercede for a sinner who is to be condemned, consequences sometimes follow which we do not wish: either in the person who is freed through our intercession, so that an audacity unpunished may rage more savagely, subjected to desire and ungrateful for leniency, and one person rescued from death may kill many; or another person, seeing that through our benefit he has changed for the better and been corrected in conduct, may perish by living badly himself, and, taking this impunity as a precedent, commit such acts or worse. Yet I think that these evils should not be charged against us when we intercede for you; rather, those goods should be credited which, when we do this, we behold and desire: namely, the commendation of gentleness, to reconcile people to love for the word of truth, and that those delivered from temporal death may so live that they do not fall into eternal death, from which they can never be delivered.

Likewise: Let nothing be done from a desire to harm, but from the charity that seeks another’s good; and let nothing be done cruelly, nothing inhumanely. Thus the punishment imposed by the judge will be feared without contempt for the religious intercession of the advocate, because both in punishing and in pardoning this alone is rightly done: [Col. 1607A] that human life may be corrected. If perversity and impiety are so great that neither discipline nor pardon can benefit their correction, nevertheless, whether through severity or gentleness, good persons fulfill only the duty of love, according to the intention and conscience which God sees.

The same, to Boniface (Maur. II, 699): Therefore let necessity kill the enemy who fights, not the will. As violence is returned to one who rebels and resists, so mercy is now owed to one defeated or captured.

The same, *Questions on the New and Old Testament*, chapter XXX (Maur. III, Appendix, p. 100): Why, then, was the sentence given that whoever takes up the sword shall perish by the sword, except because no one except a judge may kill anyone with the sword? But Peter the apostle was permitted only so far as to inflict pain, not to kill. For by hearing, “Do not strike again,” he learned further that Christians, once made such, are not permitted to kill. For those who are placed under mercy may not harshly employ the law of worldly right entrusted to them.

### CLVII. That it is lawful to kill people, and not lawful

[Note: [Col. 1607D] Cous.: “a human being.”]

Jerome on Isaiah, book V: One who slays a cruel person is not cruel.

The same, on the Epistle to the Galatians: One who strikes evil people insofar as they are evil, has a cause for killing, and kills the worst, is a minister of the Lord.

The same, on Jeremiah: To punish murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners [Col. 1607C] is not shedding blood, but the ministry of the laws.

Cyprian, in the ninth kind of abuse: A king ought to restrain the strong, punish adulteries, remove the impious from the earth, and not permit parricides and perjurers to live.

Augustine, *On Free Will* (Maur. I, 572): Although killing a human being is homicide, a person may sometimes be killed without sin. For a soldier who kills an enemy, and a judge or his officer who kills an offender, and someone from whose hand a weapon happens to fly unintentionally and unwittingly, do not seem to me to sin when they kill a human being [Note: [Col. 1607D] Cous.: *tantum*, “only.”] [Note: [Col. 1608D] Cous.: *occidere*, “to kill.”].

Likewise: A soldier is commanded by law to kill an enemy; if he refrains from that killing, he suffers punishment from the commander. Shall we dare to call such laws unjust—or rather, no laws at all? For a law that is not just does not seem to me to be a law.

The same, on Exodus, chapter XXVII: The Israelites did not commit theft by despoiling the Egyptians, but rendered service to God who commanded it; just as when a judge’s officer kills someone whom the law ordered to be killed, he is certainly a murderer if he does it of his own accord, even if he knows that the person killed ought to have been put to death by the judge.

The same, on Leviticus, chapter LXXV: When a person is justly killed, the law kills him, not you.

The same, *The City of God*, book I (Maur. VII, 21): “You shall not kill,” excepting those whom God commands to be killed, whether by a law given [or] by an express command directed for a time to a particular person. Nor does the person himself kill who owes service to the one commanding, just as a sword is an instrument to its user.

Likewise: When a soldier, obedient to the authority under which he has been lawfully established, kills a man, he is guilty of homicide under no law of his state; indeed, unless he does it, he is guilty of deserting and despising authority. But if he had done it by his own will and authority, he would have incurred the crime of shedding human blood. Thus, for the very reason that he is punished if he does it without command, he will be punished if he fails to do it when commanded.

The same, to Publicola: I do not approve the policy of killing people lest one be killed by them, unless perhaps one is a soldier or holds public office, so that one does this not for oneself but for others and for the state, having received lawful authority, if it befit the person concerned.

Likewise: It was said (Matthew 5:39), “Let us not resist evil,” not so that we may neglect the correction of people, but lest vengeance delight us—that vengeance which feeds the mind upon another’s evil [Col. 1608B].

The same, to Marcella: If this earthly commonwealth observed Christian precepts, even wars themselves would not be waged without benevolence. For wars would be waged mercifully, if possible, by good people, so that, once lawless desires had been subdued, those vices might be destroyed which under just government ought either to be eradicated or punished. For if Christian teaching condemned all wars, the Gospel would rather have advised soldiers seeking salvation to cast away their weapons and withdraw completely from military service. But it was said to them (Luke 3:14): “Do violence to no one; make no false accusations against anyone; be content with your wages.” By commanding them to be content with their own wages, it certainly did not forbid them military service.

The same [Col. 1608C], to Count Boniface: I shall give you and your people useful advice: take up arms in your hands; let prayer strike the ears of the Creator, because, when battle is fought, God watches from open heavens, and to the side he sees as just he gives the victory.

Likewise: Whether God or some lawful authority commands it, wars are undertaken by us. Otherwise, when soldiers came to John for baptism and said to him, “And what shall we do?” he would have answered: “Throw down your weapons; abandon this military service; strike no one; cast no one down.” But because he knew that in serving as soldiers they did these things not as murderers but as ministers of the law, not as avengers of their own injuries but as defenders of public safety, he answered them: “Do violence to no one,” and so forth.

Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVIII, chapter III: A just war is one waged after a formal declaration, either to recover property or to repel enemies.

Pope Nicholas, in reply to the questions of the Bulgarians: If no necessity presses, one must abstain from battles not only during Lent but at every time. But if unavoidable necessity presses, then even during Lent no doubt must preparation for war be neglected in defense alike of oneself, one’s country, or ancestral laws, lest the saying seem applicable: “A man tries [*tentare*; the construction is uncertain] if he has something he can do, yet does not endeavor to provide for his own safety [Col. 1609A] and that of others, nor to avert harm to holy religion.”

### CLVIII. That the punishment of unbaptized infants is the mildest in comparison with the other punishments of the damned, and the contrary

Augustine, *Enchiridion*: Certainly the mildest punishment of all will be that of those who, besides the sin which they contracted by origin, added no further sin.

John Chrysostom, *On the Restoration of the Fallen*: To be excluded from the good things prepared for the saints produces such torment and pain that, even if no external punishment tortured one, this alone would suffice. Therefore, to be deprived of the good things which it was in one’s power to enjoy surpasses every torment of Gehenna.

Likewise: Some of the unlearned think it sufficient for themselves if they are merely free from Gehenna. But I say that to be removed and cast out from that glory is a suffering far heavier than the torments of Gehenna; nor do I think the punishments of Gehenna as bitter as those by which one is tortured who happens [Note: [Col. 1609A] Cous.: *cum*, “when.”] to be excluded [Note: [Col. 1609A] Cous.: *contigit*, “happened.”] from Christ’s presence. Believe me: this is more grievous than every punishment; this alone surpasses even Gehenna.

Ambrose, *On Repentance*, book II: Nothing causes such supreme pain as when each person, held captive under sin, remembers from where he has fallen and from where he has descended, because he has flowed away [to] bodily and earthly things from that beautiful and fair intention of divine knowledge [Note: [Col. 1609A] Cous.: *cogitationes*, “thoughts.”] [Note: [Col. 1609A] Editions: *deflexerit*, “has turned aside.” — Here the work ends in the Munich manuscript and, according to Cousin’s testimony, also in the Avranches codex [Col. 1610A]. The Munich manuscript, indeed, contrary to its custom, omitted to indicate the end of the book with any distinct notice; yet the agreement of the two codices seems to confirm that nothing is missing.].

[Col. 1609]

# PETER ABAELARD’S DIALOGUE BETWEEN A PHILOSOPHER, A JEW, AND A CHRISTIAN

(First edited from manuscripts of the Imperial Library at Vienna by Frid. Henr. Rheinwald, Doctor of Philosophy, Licentiate in Theology, and Extraordinary Public Professor in the Royal Frederick William University, in the collection entitled *Anecdota Pertaining to Ecclesiastical History*, part 1, Berlin, 1831, octavo.)

## PREFACE

We now publish the first fascicle of *Anecdota Pertaining to Ecclesiastical History*, and hope that it will not prove unwelcome to learned men accustomed kindly to receive even the smallest remnants that may be recovered from antiquity.

I was led to become acquainted with the excellent little work which I first offer here by S. R. Neander, a teacher to be revered with the greatest devotion. Through the singular goodwill with which he regards me, when he admitted me to his company on a journey to the metropolitan city of Vienna in 1827, he gave me the opportunity, under his guidance, to examine the most eminent treasures of the Palatine Library and, among others, to inspect this manuscript as well. The book immediately pleased me; on being read again it pleased me still more, and seemed more worthy than the rest to be brought to light. S. V. Neander agreed. In carrying out this undertaking, the most noble Kopitar, prefect of the Imperial Library, assisted me with such goodwill that I can scarcely praise worthily enough the humanity and generosity of that most learned man, long celebrated by the common praise of all.

Our manuscript is marked no. DXXI (otherwise 666) in the very extensive collection of manuscripts of the Vienna Library, and is assigned by Denis to the section of books called polemical. [Note: [Col. 1609] M. Denis, *Codices Manuscripti Theologici Bibliothecae Palatinae Vindobonensis Latini*, vol. I, part II, Vienna, 1794, folio, p. 1996 ff.] It is written on parchment, contains sixty-one quarto leaves, and, according to Denis, is to be assigned to the beginning of the thirteenth century; it is not written throughout with equal polish and care. Quite a few errors occur in the manuscript. Where it was clear that these had been committed by the scribe’s pen, we corrected them; but where there was room for doubt, we took care to print the book letter for letter, and attempted to restore the genuine reading by conjectures either inserted into or placed beneath the text. We enclosed in square brackets what seemed to require removal from the text, and in curved brackets what needed addition.

A somewhat later hand has labeled the manuscript: “Dialogue of Peter Baiolard.” [Note: [Col. 1609] Da Chesne teaches in the apologetic preface on behalf of Peter that Abaelard’s name was pronounced in various ways: “Abaelardus or Bailardus, to speak with Accursius and Alciatus; or Balardus, with Genebrardus; or, if you prefer, Abailard, from the French name of the bee; or ab Abailardum, for I found this latter form in the Chronicle of John Crispin, just as among our countrymen it is common usage to employ *ab* instead of *de* in names of peoples,” etc. Compare also Denis, cited above. Having rejected certain ridiculous derivations of this name, he himself says: “I think the name Baiolard arose from Abailard, with the beginning of the word truncated, as is customary in the proper names of many peoples.”] That is, it bears the name Abaelard according to the pronunciation now more commonly used. That the book is rightly so titled you will learn from the dialogue itself, whether you consider the subject treated or the character of its discourse.

[Col. 1611] For you will observe everywhere keenness of mind and the happy abundance of an intellect well trained in the treatment of divine matters. Although Abaelard was far superior to his contemporaries in this respect, he was by no means puffed up with the rash pride of reason and did not attempt to wander beyond the limits set for the weakness of human nature.

Then, from the dialogue’s very course of reasoning, from its argumentation and method by which the proposed question is handled and brought to its conclusion, you may readily be led to suppose that the book’s author both studied and imitated the Platonic dialogues. For in a similar manner the decision of the question is drawn out; in a similar manner an end is imposed upon the debate of the three speakers—so that a certain and definite verdict of the arbiter is wanted by the reader who only glances through it, yet can readily be understood by one who is knowledgeable and discerning. This suits Abaelard well. There is no reason for us to doubt that our Peter devoted the most diligent effort to studying the Platonic dialogues [Note: [Col. 1611] It seems highly probable that Abaelard acquired knowledge of Plato not only from Augustine, but also by examining Plato’s own writings. Compare S. V. Schlosser, *Dulcin und Abaelard* (Gotha, 1807, octavo), pp. 115 ff., 123 ff. For little force lies in the possible objection that Latin translations of Plato had not yet existed in that period, since we know for certain that he knew Greek well and taught others the language (Abaelard, letter to the virgins of the Paraclete, above, col. 333: “You have as your superior in your mother, Heloise, one who is not only versed in Latin literature, but also not unacquainted with Hebrew and Greek, and who alone at this time appears to have attained proficiency in all three languages”).] and was moved by sufficiently weighty reasons to choose, following Plato’s example, this method of setting forth his own opinion.

Indeed, scarcely any other form could be found better suited to defend and conceal his opinion from the rage of enemies everywhere seeking grounds for the suspicion of “heresies” (*τῶν αἱρέσεων*), while making it intelligible to the discernment of friends initiated into philosophical teaching. Finally, the elegance of Latin style by which our dialogue, no less than Peter’s other writings [Note: [Col. 1611] Compare above all Abaelard’s sermon on Saint John the Evangelist, sermon 25, above, col. 536.], stands out among the books both of the scholastics who wrote at that time and of philosophers who lived later, appears to indicate that Abaelard had spent much time with Roman books.

This is what we had to say concerning the character and completeness of the manuscript. We have not wished to investigate and explain the connection by which the doctrines set forth in our treatise are joined with Abaelard’s teaching, since it may be hoped that S. V. Neander will soon perform this task [Note: [Col. 1611] In the excellent book now being reissued, entitled *Saint Bernard and His Age*, Berlin, 1813, octavo.]. We are sufficiently content to have brought out of darkness [Note: [Col. 1611] None of those who wrote Peter’s life mentioned the *Dialogue*, except the authors of the celebrated work *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XII (Paris, 1763, quarto), p. 132. They say in the section on Abaelard’s unpublished theological works: “Two conferences or disputes, one of a philosopher with a Jew, the other of a philosopher with a Christian. These two pieces are among the manuscripts of Thomas Barlow, Bishop of Lincoln, and those of Thomas Gale. The second is in the Jacobean Library.”] a document that seems capable of contributing something to the illumination of the mind of “a man often and always to be named with honor, the servant and truly Christian philosopher.”

Given at Berlin, on the very day of Saint Albinus, 1831.

# PETER ABAELARD’S DIALOGUE BETWEEN A PHILOSOPHER, A JEW, AND A CHRISTIAN

[Col. 1611]

[Col. 1611A] I was looking in a vision of the night, and behold, three men, coming by different paths, stood before me. I immediately asked them, in accordance with the manner of the vision, what profession they followed and why they had come to me.

“We are men,” they said, “relying upon different sects of faith. We all alike profess to be worshipers of one God, yet we serve him by differing faith and manner of life. One of us is a pagan, one of those called philosophers, content with the natural law. [Col. 1612A] The other two possess Scriptures: one is a Jew, and the other is called a Christian. Having long discussed and disputed among ourselves concerning the differing sects of our faith, we have at last submitted ourselves to your judgment.”

Greatly astonished at this, I asked what had led or gathered them into this matter, and especially why they had chosen me as their judge. The philosopher replied:

“This undertaking,” he said, “was begun through my efforts, because the highest aim of philosophers is to investigate truth by rational arguments and in all things to follow not human opinion but the guidance of reason. Thus, applying my heart to the schools of my people and instructed both by their arguments and by their authorities, I finally turned to moral philosophy, which is the end of all disciplines and for whose sake I judged that all else should be preliminarily studied. Having learned there, as far as I could, concerning the highest good and highest evil and those things which make a person happy or miserable, I immediately began carefully to examine for myself the different sects of faith into which the world is now divided. Having inspected them all and compared them with one another, I resolved to follow that which was more consistent with reason.

“I therefore turned also to the teaching [Col. 1613B] of the Jews and Christians and examined the faith and laws—or arguments—of both. I discovered the Jews to be foolish and the Christians mad, if I may say these things without offending you, who are called a Christian (fol. 1v). I conferred long with both parties, and, although the contention of our discussion has not yet reached an end, we have resolved to entrust the rationale of our respective positions to your judgment. For we know that neither the force of philosophical arguments nor the defenses of either law are unknown to you. The Christian profession rests upon its own law, which they call the New Testament, in such a way that it nevertheless does not presume to reject the Old, but devotes the greatest study to the reading of both. We had to choose some judge so that our dispute might reach an end, and we could find no one except within one of these three sects.”

Then, as though selling the oil of flattery and soothing my head with this ointment, he immediately added:

“The more greatly you are said to excel in keenness of intellect and knowledge of every kind of Scripture, the more capable you plainly are, in this judgment, to favor or defend, and to answer the objections of whichever of us rebels. And what your intellectual keenness is, how abundantly the treasury of your memory is supplied with philosophical and divine opinions, a sure proof has made clear to us, apart from the customary pursuits of your schools by which you are known to have flourished above all teachers in both branches of learning—even above your own masters and the writers of those sciences themselves [Col. 1613D]: that marvelous work of theology which envy could neither endure nor destroy, but which persecution made more glorious.”

Then I said: “I do not seek the favor of this honor which you have reserved for me: that, namely, passing over wise men, you should appoint a fool as judge. For I too, like yourselves, am accustomed to the vain disputes of this world, and shall not find it burdensome to hear things in which I have been accustomed to take delight.

“But you, philosopher, who profess no law and yield to reason alone, should not consider it a great achievement if you seem to prevail in this contest. For you have two swords for battle, while the others are armed against you with only one. You can proceed against them with both writing and reason (fol. 2r); [Col. 1614A] but they, because you follow no law, can make no objection to you from the law, and are so much less able to contend against you through arguments as you are more practiced and possess the fuller armor of philosophy.

“Yet because you have established this by agreement and unanimous consent, and because I see that each of you is confident in his own strength, I shall not, recoiling through embarrassment, shrink from your venture—especially since I believe I may gain some instruction from it. For, as one of our writers observes, no teaching is so false that it does not mingle some truths with it; and I think that no dispute is so frivolous that it contains no lesson. Hence that greatest of sages, at the very beginning of his Proverbs, preparing his reader to be attentive, says: ‘The wise hearer will become wiser, and the discerning person will possess guidance’ (Proverbs 1:5). And the apostle James says: ‘Let every person be quick to hear, but slow to speak’ (James 1:19).”

They agree, rejoicing at my assent.

**THE PHILOSOPHER.** “It belongs to me,” he says, “to question the others first, since I am content with the natural law, which is first. I gathered you together for this purpose: to inquire about the writings subsequently added. I say that it is first not only in time but also in nature. For everything simpler is naturally prior to what is more complex. The natural law, however, in the science of morals which we call ethics, consists solely in moral teachings. But the teaching of your laws has added certain precepts concerning external signs, which seem to us wholly superfluous; concerning these, too, we must discuss in their proper place.”

Both assent that the philosopher should have the first place in the encounter of this contest.

Then he says: “First, I ask you both together that which I see applies equally to you, who chiefly rely on writing: namely, whether some reason led you into these sects of faith, or whether here you follow only human opinion and attachment to your own people. If the former is the case, it is most commendable; if the latter, wholly blameworthy. Yet I believe that no discerning person’s conscience can deny that the latter is true. For love of one’s own people and of those with whom one is brought up is so deeply implanted in every human being that they recoil from whatever is said against that people’s faith; and, turning custom into nature, they zealously retain as adults whatever they learned to be holy [as children], and before they can understand what is said, they affirm that they believe it—as the poet too recalls:

> The jar will long preserve the scent  
> With which, when new, it was once imbued.

(HORACE, *Epistles*, Book I, Epistle 2, verse 69.)

[Source locations: cols. 1615A–1623A, continuously; fol. 3R at “nor conceived in the mind”; 3V at “May the Lord himself”; 4R at “isolate myself”; 4V at “How could anyone govern”; 5R at “Whoever judges”; 5V at “The rulers themselves”; 6R at “From this it is plainly clear”; 6V at “shown by manifest deeds”; 7R at “And after he was circumcised”; 7V at “Either, therefore”; 8R in the Mosaic quotation; 8V at “yet no mention is made”; 9R at “you have lost the land of promise.”] This is precisely what one philosopher rebukes when he says: “Let nothing acquired in childish instruction be judged inviolable; for later philosophical study often removes things suited to immature ears.” For what is remarkable if, through the succession of ages and the passage of time, human understanding grows in all created things, while in faith—where error entails the gravest danger—there is no progress? Rather, the young and old alike, the unlettered and the learned alike, are said to hold the same opinion on this matter; and he is called most steadfast in faith who does not exceed the common understanding of the people. This certainly happens because no one among his own people is permitted to inquire what ought to be believed, or safely to doubt what is said by all. People are ashamed to be questioned about matters for which they cannot provide an answer. For no one who distrusts his own strength willingly comes forward, and one who hopes for the glory of victory runs voluntarily to battle. They often break out into such madness that they are not ashamed to profess belief in what they confess themselves unable to understand—as though faith consisted more in uttering words than in the mind’s comprehension, and belonged more to the mouth than to the heart. They especially glory in this very point: that they appear to believe such great things as can neither be explained in speech nor conceived in the mind. The distinctiveness of their own sect likewise makes them so presumptuous and proud that, whenever they see persons divided from themselves in faith, they declare them alien to God’s mercy and, condemning all others, proclaim themselves alone blessed.

Therefore, as I long considered this blindness and pride of the human race, I turned to divine mercy, imploring it humbly and continually to deign to draw me from so great a whirlpool of errors and from this most miserable Charybdis, and to guide me through such storms to the gate of salvation. Concerning this I am still anxious, as you see; and I am listening with the keenest attention, like a pupil, to the instruction of your replies.

**THE JEW.** You have questioned two persons at once; but it is not fitting for two persons to answer at once, lest the multitude of speakers impede understanding. If you please, I shall answer first, because we came first to the worship of God, or received the first instruction of the Law. This brother, who professes himself a Christian, will supply what is lacking for my inadequacy whenever he sees that I fail or am insufficient—he who, as it were, bears two horns in the two Testaments, armed with which he can resist and fight the enemy more powerfully.

**THE PHILOSOPHER.** I agree.

**THE JEW.** But before the contest of our disputation, I wish to warn you in advance of this: if perhaps you seem to overcome my simplicity by the truth of philosophical arguments, do not boast that you have therefore defeated our people; do not turn the weakness of one insignificant man into a disgrace for the whole people; do not rebuke the faith because of a man’s fault; and do not slander it as erroneous because I am less able to expound it.

**THE PHILOSOPHER.** This too seems quite prudently said; but it was not necessary to state it beforehand, since you surely do not doubt that I labour for the investigation of truth, not for a display of arrogance; that I examine arguments not to wrangle like a sophist but as a philosopher; and—what is greatest—that I revere the salvation of my soul.

**THE JEW.** May the Lord himself, who seems to have inspired in you this zeal to seek him with such concern for your soul’s salvation, grant us this disputation, through which you may healthfully find him. It remains for me now to answer the questions, insofar as he himself permits.

**THE PHILOSOPHER.** Indeed, this accords with the purpose of our agreed arrangement.

**THE JEW.** While all people are children and have not yet reached the age of discernment, it is evident that they follow the faith or custom of those among whom they live, especially of those whom they love more greatly. But once they are grown and can be governed by their own judgment, they ought to entrust themselves not to another’s judgment but to their own; and it is fitting that they investigate truth rather than follow mere opinion. I have said this beforehand because perhaps at first an affection arising from fleshly descent and the custom first known to us led us into this faith. But now reason rather than opinion holds us fast in it.

**THE PHILOSOPHER.** I beg you, disclose this reason to us; that is enough.

**THE JEW.** If this Law that we follow was given to us by God, as we believe, we are not to be reproached for obeying it; indeed, we ought to be rewarded for obedience, while those who despise it err grievously. But if we cannot compel you to acknowledge that it was given by God, neither can you refute this. Let us take an example from ordinary human life. Give me, I beg you, advice. I am the servant of a certain master; I greatly fear offending him; and I have many fellow-servants troubled by the same fear. They tell me that, in my absence, our master commanded all his servants to do something which I do not know, which they themselves do, and which they urge me to do with them. What do you advise me to do if I doubt a command at which I was not present? I do not think that you or anyone else would advise me, disregarding the counsel of all the servants, to follow my own opinion and isolate myself from what they do in common and what they all testify that the master commanded—especially when the command appears such that no argument can refute it. Why must I risk danger when I can remain secure? If the master commanded what is confirmed by the testimony of many and has great reason behind it, I am wholly without excuse if I do not obey. But if, deceived by the counsel, exhortation, and example of my fellow-servants, I do what was not commanded, then—even if it ought not to have been done—the blame belongs rather to them than to me, since reverence for my master drew me to it.

**THE PHILOSOPHER.** Certainly you yourself have disclosed the counsel that you sought, and no discerning person would think otherwise. But apply the example of the proposed comparison to the point toward which we are tending.

**THE JEW.** As you know, many generations have passed since our people, obediently observing this Testament which they affirm was given them by God, instructed their descendants, all alike, concerning its observance both by word and by example. Nearly the whole world agrees that this Law was given to us by God. Although perhaps we cannot compel certain unbelievers to believe it, there is nevertheless no one who can refute by any argument what we believe. For it is pious, wholly consonant with reason, and fitting both to divine goodness and to human salvation, to hold that God takes such care for humankind that he deigned also to instruct them by a written Law and at least restrain our wickedness through fear of punishments. For if the laws of secular rulers were beneficially established for this purpose, who would deny that the highest and kindest ruler of all likewise undertook such care?

How could anyone govern a subject people without a law, if each person, left to his own choice, follows whatever he chooses? Or how does he justly restrain the wickedness of evil persons by punishing them unless a law has first been established forbidding evil deeds? By this reasoning I believe it clear that divine Law preceded human laws, so that the world, when it wished to restrain wickedness by establishing laws, might derive the origin and authority of this good also from God. Otherwise it could easily seem that God does not care for human affairs, and that the order of the world is governed by chance rather than by providence.

If any law is believed to have been given by God to the world, about which is it more appropriate to agree than ours, which has gained such authority from its antiquity and from the common opinion of humanity? Let it finally be doubtful to me, as it is to you, that God established this Law; nevertheless, since it is confirmed by so many testimonies and by reason, you are compelled, by the application of the proposed comparison, to advise me to obey it—especially since my own conscience invites me to do so. I share with you faith in the truth of the one God; perhaps I love him equally with you; and moreover I show this by works which you do not possess. How do these works harm me if they do not benefit me, even if they were not commanded, since they are not forbidden? Who can accuse me if, though bound by no command, I labour more for the Lord? Who could accuse a faith which, as has been said, especially commends divine goodness and greatly kindles our love for him—him who is so concerned for our salvation that he deigns to instruct us even by the written Law? Therefore either find fault with something in this Law, or cease asking why we follow it!

Whoever judges that the perseverance of our zeal, which bears so much, is devoid of reward, asserts that God is most cruel. For no nation is known or believed ever to have endured so much for God as we endure continually for his sake; and no rust of sin can exist which one ought not to grant is consumed by the furnace of this affliction. Are we not scattered among all nations and, alone without earthly king or prince, burdened by such exactions that on almost every day of our wretched lives we pay an intolerable ransom for life? We are deemed worthy of such contempt and hatred by all that whoever inflicts any injury upon us believes it to be the highest justice and the supreme sacrifice offered to God. They hold that this calamity of such captivity could have happened to us only because of God’s utmost hatred, and they regard whatever cruelty both pagans and Christians exercise against us as just retribution.

The pagans, remembering the ancient oppressions by which we first possessed their land and afterward wore them down and destroyed them through long persecutions, count whatever they inflict upon us as due vengeance. Christians, however, seem to have a greater cause for persecution against us because, as they say, we killed their God. See among whom our exile wanders and from whose protection we must seek refuge! We entrust our lives to our bitterest enemies, and we are compelled to put faith in the faithfulness of unbelievers. Sleep itself, which especially cherishes and restores relaxed nature, disturbs us with such anxiety that even while sleeping we may think only of danger to our throats. No entrance is safe for us except that into heaven, since even our place of dwelling is dangerous. When we are about to go to any nearby place, we hire at no small price an escort in whom we have little confidence.

The rulers themselves who govern us, and whose protection we buy dearly, desire our death all the more because they seize more freely what we possess. Although thus bound and oppressed, as though the world had conspired against us alone, it is itself remarkable if we are permitted to live. We are allowed neither fields nor vineyards nor any earthly possessions, because there is no one able to protect them for us from open or secret attack. Hence our chief remaining means of profit is to lend at interest to foreigners, and thereby sustain this wretched life—a practice that makes us especially hateful to them, since they judge themselves greatly burdened by it. But our condition itself speaks more sufficiently to everyone than the tongue can of the extreme misery of our life and of the dangers in which we labour continually.

Nor is anyone who has encountered the Law unaware how difficult its commandments are, so that we are afflicted intolerably both by human oppression and by the yoke of the Law. Who would not shrink from or tremble at receiving the sacrament of our circumcision, both from shame and from pain? What part of the human body is more tender than that upon which the Law inflicts this wound even in infants? What bitterness is so great as that of the wild lettuces which we eat as a condiment at the Paschal sacrifice? Who does not see that almost all refined foods—and especially those easiest to obtain—are forbidden us? Any meat tasted by these persons is unclean to us; every carcass or strangled animal is prohibited. We may not eat even beasts unless we ourselves have slaughtered them and carefully cleansed them of fat and veins, which burdens us considerably, especially when we cannot afford to buy an entire animal. For just as we shun meats slaughtered by pagans, so they shun those prepared by us. We all likewise abstain from wine prepared by them. From this it is plainly clear how difficult our pilgrimage among them for God’s sake is.

Finally, who would not shrink not merely from enduring the severity of legal punishments, but even from inflicting them upon offenders? Who would take from his brother tooth for tooth, eye for eye, and life for life—not even consenting to endure these things in himself, lest he be found opposed to the Law? From these things, indeed, and from innumerable other observances, it is clear that every one of us who obeys the Law may rightly profess to God with the Psalmist: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” (Psalm XVII:4).

**THE PHILOSOPHER.** Truly, this zeal which you seem to have for God endures many and great things, with whatever intention it may be held. But it matters greatly whether that intention is right or erroneous. For there is no sect of faith which does not believe that it serves God and does for his sake what it thinks pleases him. Yet you do not thereby approve the sects of all, since you defend only your own or strive to prefer it far above all others. I want you to consider how contrary this is to reason, and to be challenged by the very written text of the Law which you follow.

**THE JEW.** I willingly accept this as well.

**THE PHILOSOPHER.** It is evident that before the giving of the Law itself, or the observance of the legal sacraments, very many persons—content with the natural law, which consists in the love of God and justice toward one’s neighbour—were pleasing to God: Abel, Enoch, Noah and his sons, Abraham, Lot, and Melchizedek, whom your own Law recalls and highly commends. Enoch, indeed, is reported to have pleased God so greatly that the Lord is said to have taken him alive into Paradise, as one of your own writers affirms in these words: “Enoch pleased God and was translated into Paradise, that he might give repentance to the nations” (Ecclesiasticus XLIV:16).

And how greatly Noah loved the Lord is shown by manifest deeds, since, as it is written, he was “a just and perfect man in his generations” (Genesis VI:9), and, when all others were submerged by the flood, God preserved him alone and his household as the seed of the human race. Add to these your illustrious patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, in whom and in whose seed the blessing of all nations is promised. They too preceded the Law; and consider how much more excellent is their prerogative than that of those who came after the Law. Hence God is called especially their God, and the lawgiver reconciles the Lord, angry with the people, through their merits and through the promises made to them. For it is written:

> Moses prayed to the Lord, saying: “Let your anger cease, and be merciful concerning the wickedness of your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: ‘I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven; and all this land of which I have spoken I will give to your seed, and you shall possess it forever.’” And the Lord was appeased, so that he did not do the evil which he had spoken.  
> —Exodus XXXII:11–14

From this it is plainly inferred how acceptable to God were the gratuitous acts of obedience of the earlier Fathers, to which no Law yet bound them, whereas we still serve him without such freedom. But if you say that the Law somehow began in Abraham, namely because of the sacrament of circumcision, you will certainly find that he obtained no reward from God on this account, lest you should have any ground for glorying in the Law, nor that he attained any justification thereby. For it is written that, still uncircumcised, he was justified by faith like the earlier Fathers: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Genesis XV:6). His religion had already received the promise of the land and of future multiplication, both for himself and for his seed. And after he was circumcised, when he hears from the Lord that all nations are to be blessed in him or in his seed, he deserved this not through circumcision but through that obedience by which he was willing to sacrifice his son.

Finally, if you review the entire history of your Testament, you will find no reward promised for circumcision. The Lord merely established that whoever from Abraham’s seed was not circumcised should not be numbered among his people—that is, among Abraham’s children. For the Lord says to Abraham:

> “I will establish my covenant between me and you, and your seed after you,” etc. “This is the covenant which you shall keep. Every male among you shall be circumcised; an infant of eight days shall be circumcised among you. The male whose foreskin’s flesh is not circumcised, that soul shall perish from among his people,” etc.  
> —Genesis XVII:10–14

If you say that this “perishing” must also be understood as the condemnation of the soul, then the institution of circumcision has all the less reason, the more dangerous it is not to possess it, whereas previously its absence did no harm. This interpretation also bars the kingdom of heaven to infants dying before the eighth day, although they have as yet committed no fault deserving condemnation.

Consider also carefully what reward the Lord promises and sets forth for observing the whole Law. Certainly you can expect from him nothing but earthly prosperity, since you see that nothing else is promised there. And since he does not even show whether you obtain this prosperity—though by your own judgment you are afflicted above all mortals—it is no small wonder on what hope you endure so many and such great things in obedience to the Law, since you are especially deprived of that benefit which, by the very obligation of the promise, you should expect. Either, therefore, you do not fulfil the Law and thereby incur the Law’s curse and condemnation; or he who promised these things to those fulfilling the Law is not truthful in his promises. Whichever of these you choose, I see that you have no confidence to place in the Law, and that it earns little toward blessedness.

What, I ask, happened that, when by its reward God invited us to observe the Law, he promised what is least and altogether passed over what is greatest? He certainly did not argue discerningly if he knew that each was sufficient to induce obedience to the Law, yet wholly omitted what had the greatest persuasive force. For, as has been said, nothing at all is mentioned there concerning true and eternal blessedness as a reward; earthly prosperity alone is announced, so that this alone is made the reason for obedience. It is repeatedly commended in order that its answer may be judged sufficient for every subsequent inquiry. Thus it is written, with the lawgiver Moses himself instructing the people against every attack upon the Law and saying:

> “Hear, Israel: keep the commandments of the Lord your God, and the testimonies and ceremonies which he has commanded; and do what is pleasing and good in the sight of the Lord, that it may go well with you, and that, having entered in, you may possess the excellent land concerning which he swore to your fathers, and may destroy all your enemies before you, as he has spoken. When tomorrow your son asks you, saying, ‘What do these testimonies, ceremonies, and judgments which the Lord our God has commanded us mean?’ you shall say to him: ‘We were Pharaoh’s servants in Egypt, and the Lord brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand. He wrought signs, wonders, great and grievous things in Egypt against Pharaoh and all his house before our eyes; and he brought us out from there in order that, having brought us in, he might give us the land concerning which he swore to our fathers. And the Lord commanded us to do all these statutes and fear the Lord our God, that it might go well with us all the days of our life, as it is today.’”  
> —Deuteronomy VII:3

Again:

> “The Lord your God has chosen you to be his peculiar people out of all the peoples who are upon the earth. Therefore keep the commandments, ceremonies, and judgments which I command you today to do. If you keep and do them, the Lord your God will keep for you the covenant and mercy which he swore to your fathers; he will love you and multiply you; and he will bless the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your land—grain, vintage, oil, herds, and flocks of your sheep—upon the land which he swore to your fathers that he would give you. You shall be blessed above all peoples; that is, there shall be no barren person of either sex among you, whether human beings or your herds. He will remove every sickness from you and the grievous infirmities of Egypt; he will not bring them upon you, but upon all your enemies. You shall devour all the peoples whom the Lord your God will give you.”  
> —Deuteronomy VII:6–16

And again:

> “He will give the early and latter rain to your land, so that you may gather grain, wine, and oil; grass from the fields for feeding your beasts; and so that you yourselves may eat and be satisfied.”  
> —Deuteronomy XI:14–15

> “All these blessings shall come upon you and overtake you, if only you hear his commandments. Blessed are you in the city, and blessed in the field. Blessed is the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your land, the fruit of your beasts, the herds of your cattle, and the folds of your sheep. Blessed are your storehouses and your reserves. Blessed shall you be when entering and when departing. He will bless all the works of your hands; you shall lend at interest to many nations, and you yourself shall receive no loan from anyone.”  
> —Deuteronomy XXVIII:2–12

See: as the reward for fulfilling the Law, blessing is promised for human beings, for the offspring of your beasts, for your herds of cattle, and for your sheepfolds; yet no mention is made of any spiritual blessing for the soul, nor is anything concerning salvation or condemnation of the soul promised to those who obey or transgress. Earthly advantages or disadvantages alone are mentioned, while what is greatest is wholly passed over.

I ask also whether, even now after the Law was given to you, the natural law may, as before, suffice for some persons’ salvation without those external and distinctive works of the Law. You cannot deny this by any argument, since this Law was plainly given only to you and not to other peoples, and circumcision was imposed only upon Abraham and his seed. To that seed belong only those who are born from Isaac, the Lord saying to Abraham: “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Genesis XXI:12). And after establishing the covenant of circumcision, he further added: “But I will establish my covenant with Isaac” (Genesis XVII:21).

You do not doubt that Job, a Gentile, lived after Abraham and without the Law. Yet the Lord commended him so highly that he said: “There is none like him upon the earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil” (Job I:8). Explaining to us in his own words the justice that we should imitate, he mentions nothing of those works of the Law, but only works of the natural law which natural reason itself persuades every person to perform: “If I have walked in vanity, or my foot has hastened to deceit; if I denied what the poor desired, or made the eyes of the widow wait,” etc. (Job XXXI:6–16). By these words and examples he established this as a law for us Gentiles.

But if these things sufficed for salvation before the Law, or even suffice now for certain people, what need was there to add the yoke of the Law and, by multiplying commandments, increase transgressions? For where there is no law, neither can its violation occur. How did he establish a peculiar people by giving the Law, and for what reason does he call Israel his firstborn, whom he burdens without cause with such a load? Who can excuse you from the Law’s curse, when, through the sins you yourselves acknowledge, you have lost the land of promise, outside which you are in no way able to fulfil the Law? You are not permitted to exercise the penalties of your judgments; nor may you celebrate the sacrifices or offerings established for cleansing sins; nor may you even render the songs of divine praise. You yourselves confess this in saying: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Psalm XII:4).

Thus it is clear that you have lost both the works and the words of the Law, together with its reward; and that now, deprived alike of priesthood and temple, you and your wives cannot be cleansed or consecrated to the Lord by sacrifices or offerings which have been lost. You have not even the consolation of earthly dignity, though you never ask anything from the Lord except earthly things, nor, as has been said, received a promise of reward except in earthly matters.

JEW. You have raised many objections in succession; it is not easy to remember them all so as to answer each in order. Yet I shall try to reply as they occur to me. Even if we granted that, now too, as in the manner of the earlier saints, human beings can be saved by the natural law alone—without circumcision, that is, or the other bodily observances of the written law [Col. 1623B]—we must not therefore grant that these additions were superfluous. Rather, they are of very great usefulness for enlarging or more securely safeguarding religion, and for restraining wickedness more fully.

Take, then, from the very points which you yourself have introduced, several reasons for this. So long as the faithful lived scattered and intermingled with unbelievers, and the Lord had not yet granted them a land of their own, they were not separated by any observance of the law from those among whom they were compelled to live, lest this very difference of life produce hostilities. But after the Lord led Abraham out from his land and kindred, in order to give him and his seed a land as an inheritance whereby they might be separated from the nations, he determined also to separate them completely by the bodily works of the law, so that the faithful might be less able to be corrupted by unbelievers [Col. 1623C] (fol. 9v), in proportion as they were more divided from them both in place and in their bodies.

Therefore, once this promise of a land had been made to Abraham and his seed—a land in which the Lord would gather a people to himself and establish his own city—he began to institute the law according to which they were to live there, beginning with circumcision. For the Lord knew that our people would be stiff-necked and readily inclined to idolatry and the corrupt customs of the Gentiles, as was indeed proved later. He therefore decided, by setting legal observances between them as a kind of wall, to divide their rites in such a manner that they might be joined in no association of intercourse or intimacy; indeed, that they might thereby conceive perpetual hostilities against one another [Col. 1623D].

Now the marriage bond and fellowship at table usually create the greatest intimacy among people. Therefore, especially to remove these, the Lord instituted circumcision and forbade the eating of choice foods. For the sign of circumcision appears so abominable to the Gentiles that, if we sought their women, they would by no means consent to us in this. Hence, even if there were other reasons, I believe these are sufficient for the present.

But as for your effort to nullify or diminish the merit of circumcision or of the law by the authority of Scripture itself: I believe that you can be refuted by that same authority, if you carefully attend to those things which, by keeping silent, you seem to have stolen away from the sequence of Scripture—things which, I believe, you saw would harm your case. For when the Lord established with him the covenant—namely, that made through circumcision—he said to Abraham: “I will establish my covenant between me and you and your seed after you throughout their generations, an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed” (Gen. 17:7) [Col. 1624A].

When he says, “an everlasting covenant, that I may be your God and the God of your seed,” he plainly teaches that through circumcision we are to be covenanted to God perpetually, and that by these means we obtain him as our God, so that we are not separated from him either in this life or, certainly, in the life to come. Repeating this also, that he might commend it more strongly to memory, he added: “My covenant shall be in your flesh as an everlasting covenant” (Exod. 6:7). Thus, just as circumcision once performed in the flesh can no longer be erased, so neither can we thereafter be separated from him, who, strengthening us spiritually [or “specially”], says: “You shall be my people, and I will be your God” (Gen. 17:13) [Col. 1624B].

Hence he calls himself especially the God of the Hebrews, not merely the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Indeed, through circumcision God is indicated to become the God of the sons [or “his sons”], since before circumcision he is not said to be the God either of these persons or of human beings.

He appropriately instituted circumcision as the sign of the covenant between himself and us, so that those who are generated by that member—which is especially consecrated after the obedience of circumcision has been undertaken—may be admonished to sanctify themselves to the Lord by the very instrument of their generation. Thus they are inwardly to be circumcised from vices in heart, just as they are already outwardly circumcised in flesh; and they are to cut themselves off in their conduct from their former Chaldean [un]believing origin [Col. 1624C], just as they have removed from themselves the first part of that member. They are to depart from those people not so much in body with Abraham as in mind, as David recalls when inviting the faithful soul: “Forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. 44:11), and so forth.

Thus too, when the Lord compares his people to a chosen vineyard, he complains that he expected it to bear grapes, but it bore wild grapes (Isa. 5:2). As his whole people is compared to a vineyard, so individual believers are fittingly compared to vines, and their genitals to layers [or “shoots”]. But a vine-shoot, unless it is cut back, bears wild grapes rather than grapes and remains so. In accordance with this likeness, therefore, the foreskin cut away signifies the careful divine cultivation of us, from which God begins to cultivate us.

If you also review the beginnings of human guilt in the first parents and the Lord’s sentence of punishment pronounced upon the woman—when he says to her, “In pain you shall bear children” (Gen. 3:16)—will you not see that the man too, as a participant in sin, is rightly made a sharer in punishment especially in the generative member? [Col. 1624D] That is, he rightly suffers in that member through which he begets children destined to die in the exile of this present life, having by his own transgression cast himself and us alike from paradise into the miseries of this life. For the woman, labouring in childbirth, rightly suffers in the member by which she conceives and gives birth; and in childbirth she is punished for the pleasure of concupiscence which she has in conception, and moreover pays the penalty which she acquired by sinning.

Since she sinned first and afterwards drew the man into sin, she appropriately preceded him also in this punishment. Yet God did not altogether delay punishing the man himself. He was at once placed under punishment, and the Lord said to him: “Cursed is the earth in your work; in labours you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you,” and so forth (ibid., vv. 17–18) [Col. 1625A].

But when we obtained the abundance of the promised land, which no longer produced thorns and thistles, that diminution of punishment was appropriately compensated by circumcision. Yet circumcision was begun at once by the patriarchs after the promise of that land, before the land itself was obtained, in order that they might transmit firmer authority to their descendants. I think this sufficient for the present concerning circumcision.

But you who endeavour to prove from Scripture that it was imposed only upon those descended from Abraham’s seed do not notice that the same passage is written also concerning those who are not of that stock. For after the Lord had said: “Every male among you, eight days old, shall be circumcised throughout your generations, both one born in the house and one bought” (Gen. 17:12; fol. 11r), he immediately added: “and whoever is not of your stock.” Therefore, consider how discordant is your assertion that Isaac alone and his seed belong to circumcision, and correct yourself from Abraham’s own action.

He too is recorded, by the Lord’s command, to have circumcised with himself Ishmael as well as every male of his household—those born in the house, those purchased, and foreigners alike [Col. 1625B]—immediately on that same day, as Scripture says, before Isaac had yet been born. You should therefore know that you received it from us, and so claim it for yourselves as something more natural to you.

Let us now, if you please, set down the very words of Scripture, which are as follows: “Abraham took Ishmael his son and all those born in his household, and circumcised the flesh of their foreskin immediately on that same day, as the Lord had commanded him” (ibid., v. 23). And again: “On that same day Abraham was circumcised, and Ishmael his son, and all the men of his household, both those born in the house and those bought; and foreigners were circumcised together” (ibid., vv. 26–27) [Col. 1625C].

As for the passage you also adduced, “But I will establish my covenant with Isaac” (ibid., v. 21), note that this should be understood only of the covenant of circumcision, not of earthly promises. Nor does it hinder this, as was stated a little earlier: “I will establish my covenant with him as an everlasting covenant, and with his seed after him.” For although Ishmael too was circumcised by the Lord’s command, the Lord did not establish circumcision in him, since it did not persist in his posterity.

As for the Gentile Job, whom you introduced as an example, you cannot prove either that he was uncircumcised or that he lived after circumcision had been instituted. For just as Ishmael was circumcised by Abraham, so Esau by Jacob; and it is agreed that the rejected sons, no less than the chosen, were circumcised by the patriarchs according to the Lord’s command [Col. 1625D]. Thus their descendants also, if any adhered to God, might take the example of circumcision from them.
