And this you yourselves observe to the present day: imitating Ishmael, your father, you receive circumcision in the twelfth year.

We know also that our people had many proselytes from among the Gentiles converted to the law, not so much through imitation of their parents as through a kindred virtue. This too could have happened in Job’s case, whom we see, in our manner, offering sacrifices accepted by God both for his children and for his friends.

The objection that no reward was promised for observing the whole law except one temporal and earthly, and that the Lord would not have spoken carefully in commending or condemning the law if the fulfilment of legal commandments did not merit eternal life, is easily refuted. For by circumcision itself [Col. 1626A], which the law commands, we have, as I said, been joined in covenant with the Lord forever.

Moreover, why did he choose us out of all nations as his own people and give us a law by which we might become holy, if, from the additional observance of the law, only the delights of this present life were owed to us—delights possessed more by the reprobate than by the elect? If holiness procures for you or for any people a blessed and immortal life, it is plain that this especially is owed to us through the law, if its observance sanctifies you.

And it certainly sanctifies us, as the Lord himself speaks to us through Moses: “If therefore you hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my peculiar possession from among all peoples—for all the earth is mine—and you shall be to me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation” (Exod. 19:6–7) [Col. 1626B]. How, then, does he choose us as his peculiar people (fol. 12r), his own people, and sanctify us by the law, if he makes you or others more blessed?

And after some words, exhorting us to obedience to the law, he says: “I am your God, showing mercy unto thousands to those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exod. 20:6). What is “showing mercy unto thousands” except showing perfect and consummate mercy, beyond which none can be extended—just as no new names of numbers exceed a thousand? And elsewhere: “Be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Lev. 19:2). Again, below: “Sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am holy, the Lord your God. Keep my commandments [Col. 1626C] and do them. I am the Lord who sanctifies you” (Lev. 20:7–8). And after some words: “You shall be holy to me, for I the Lord am holy, and I have separated you from other peoples that you might be mine” (ibid., v. 24). And again: “I am the Lord who sanctifies you and brought you out of the land of Egypt, that I might be your God” (Lev. 11:45). And once more: “If you walk in my commandments, I will place my tabernacle in your midst, and my soul will not cast you off” (Lev. 26:11). Elsewhere: “Who will grant,” he says, “that they may have such a mind as to fear me and keep all my commandments at every time, that it may be well with them and with their children forever?” (Deut. 5:29).

The Lord plainly declares to Eve an everlasting reward from obedience to the laws, not a reward which has an end. Moses too, after that earthly reward which you mentioned above [Col. 1627A], added that mercy would moreover be fulfilled for those who keep the law, plainly promising us a reward other than an earthly one. For after saying, “that it may be well with you all the days of your life, as it is today” (Deut. 6:24), he immediately added: “And he will be merciful to us if we keep and do all his commandments, as he commanded us.” And after certain intervening words, when he had said, “The Lord has chosen you to be his peculiar people out of all peoples” (Deut. 7:6), he added below: “And you shall know that the Lord your God is the faithful and mighty God, keeping the covenant and mercy for those who love him and keep his commandments unto a thousand generations” (ibid., v. 9; fol. 12v).

I do not think you are unaware how perfectly the law itself commands the love of God and neighbour, in which you say the natural law consists. For Moses, completing the law at its end, says: “And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you except that you fear your God and walk in his ways and love him, and serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and keep the commandments of the Lord and his ordinances, which I command you today, that it may be well with you? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens, the earth and all that are in them, belong to the Lord your God; yet the Lord was joined to your fathers and loved them, and chose their seed after them—that is, us—from among all peoples, as is proved today” (Deut. 10:12–15) [Col. 1627B].

The law carefully expresses and amplifies love of God to such an extent, in order that it may be perfect, that it commands God to be loved with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole strength. We are commanded to love our neighbour as ourselves, so that the love of God, extended even above ourselves, may be bounded by no measure. We are also commanded to love the strangers dwelling among us as ourselves; and the law itself so widens the embrace of love that its benefits are not to be withheld even from enemies or those who injure us.

Let us now cite some passages concerning them: “If you encounter the ox or stray ass of your enemy, bring it back to him. If you see the ass of one who hates you lying beneath its burden, you shall not pass by, but shall lift it up with him. You shall not oppress the stranger, for you yourselves were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Exod. 33:4) [Col. 1627C]. “Do not seek vengeance, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens. If a stranger lives in your land and dwells among you” (fol. 13r), “do not reproach him, but let him be among you as a native-born person, and you shall love him as yourself; for you too were strangers in the land of Egypt. I am the Lord your God” (Lev. 19:18–33). And elsewhere: “The poor will not be lacking in the land where you dwell; therefore I command you to open your hand to your brother, to the needy, and to the poor who live with you in the land” (Deut. 15:11).

From these things, I beg you, consider how far the law extends the affection of love both toward human beings and toward God, so that you may recognize that your own law, which you call natural, is contained within ours. Thus, even if the other commandments ceased, these commandments of perfect love would suffice for our salvation as for yours. You do not deny that our earlier fathers were saved by these [Col. 1628A]; so our security is all the greater, because the other commandments of the law, added besides, instituted for us a stricter life.

This addition seems to me to belong not so much to the religion of holy conduct as to its more secure protection. True love of God and human beings is sufficient for every virtue of the soul. Even if good works are absent, a good and perfect will is by no means diminished in merit. But just as the Lord wished to separate us from unbelievers in place, so that we might not be corrupted by them, so too he determined that it should be done by the rites of our works, as I said.

Since, then, the perfection of love suffices to obtain true blessedness, the added commandments of a stricter life surely ought to procure something further, at least in this life. Thus, by the consolation of an earthly benefit as well [Col. 1628B], we might become more eager and secure toward God; and as his gifts toward us increased, our devotion toward him might grow; and the foreign people of unbelievers, seeing these things, might more readily be invited by our advantages to the worship of God (fol. 13v).

That the Lord seems more often or more openly to mention earthly rather than eternal benefits in the reward of the law, you will understand to have occurred especially because of the people who were still carnal and rebellious. He was leading them from the abundance of Egypt, about which they continually murmured, into an extremely harsh wilderness. Moreover, it seemed superfluous to mention in the promise eternal blessedness, since it was clear that the earlier persons had obtained it even without the giving of the law.

Then consider the perfection of the law from this single conclusion, which Moses writes in these final words: “And now, Israel, hear the commandments and judgments which I teach you,” and so forth: “You shall not add to the word which I speak to you, nor take away from it” (Deut. 4:1–2) [Col. 1628C]. And again: “What I command you, that alone do to the Lord; add nothing and diminish nothing” (Deut. 12:32). For that is perfect to which nothing is to be added. Or, if anything necessary for perfection were lacking, this prohibition would be evil, since it would forbid what is lacking and block for us the path to blessedness.

What, moreover, does the law command to be done through sacrifices or other observances for our purification, cleansing, and forgiveness of sins, if this has no bearing on true blessedness? For nothing excludes from blessedness those whose sins are forgiven. Otherwise, neither could it be hoped for by you. Why, too, does it forbid us sins through the law, except in order to reserve for us that which sins, if absent, confer, and, if present, impede?

PHILOSOPHER. I am astonished that you, skilled in the Law, speak so thoughtlessly as to exalt circumcision to the point of not fearing to lie—by saying, namely, that only after circumcision, and not before, is God called the God of men, and only of those who have already been circumcised, as he is called the God of Abraham (fol. 14r), Isaac, and Jacob. The very Scripture of the Law plainly rebukes you for this, since Noah long before said: “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem; let Canaan be his servant” (Gen. 9:26). Behold: Noah calls God the God of Shem. [Col. 1629A] Thus, when he is called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, or of Jacob, it is not inappropriate also to add “the God of our fathers.” And if you weigh the divine benefits in which you especially glory as his peculiar people: Enoch was more happily translated into Paradise than you were brought into the land of Canaan; and he is said to have deserved this when it is said: “Enoch walked with God, and was seen no more, because God took him” (Gen. 5:22). But Moses altogether denies that you obtained that land by your merits, saying: “Do not say in your heart, when the Lord has destroyed them: ‘Because of my righteousness the Lord brought me in to possess this land,’ whereas these nations have been destroyed because of their impieties, that he might fulfill the word which he promised to your fathers. Know, therefore, that God did not give you this excellent land because of your righteousness, since you are a people of the stiffest neck” (Deut. 9:5–6).

Noah, however, because of his righteousness, after all human beings except his household had been overthrown, was made lord of all things on earth and sea; and everything except blood was granted him for food. Thus, in comparison with the earthly benefits of God which you desired, the life of the earlier faithful was so much happier as it was freer and ruled all the creatures of the earthly dwelling-place. And in proportion as the life of Noah and his people was freer than yours—not yet oppressed by the yoke of your Law—so too is our life freer: that more ancient life which you cannot prove to have been constrained by any outward works of a harsh Law (fol. 14v). [Col. 1629C] Let us consider that life carefully, beginning with Noah himself, to whom the first law concerning abstinence from blood was given.

Yet I know that certain precepts of the Law extend even to foreigners: namely, only to those whom you possessed as household-born persons or slaves, or who dwelt with you within your gates or in your land. Scripture carefully specifies these people in many places; and you yourself above showed from a precept of the Law that they were to be treated mercifully as natives. In many observances the Law also joins them to you and plainly distinguishes them from other foreign sojourners. Thus, when it says in one place: “In the seventh year you shall make a remission, which is observed in this manner: anyone to whom something is owed by a friend, neighbor, or brother shall not be able to demand it, because it is the year of the Lord’s remission; from a foreigner and stranger you shall exact it” (Deut. 15:23), it plainly teaches that the foreigner and stranger is not to be treated as mercifully as the native.

It similarly understood “foreigner” where it says: “Eat everything that is clean; let no one eat anything that has died of itself. Give it to the foreigner who is within your gates to eat, or sell it to him, because you are a holy people of the Lord your God” (Deut. 14:20–21). Long before, indeed, another book says of the stranger who sojourns among you by dwelling there rather than merely passing through—as the immediately preceding matters there indicate [Col. 1630A]—that he too is forbidden to eat carrion, as you are: “The person who eats what has died of itself or has been taken by a beast, whether among natives or strangers, shall wash his garments and himself with water, and shall be unclean until evening; and in this manner he shall become clean. But if he does not wash his garments and body, he shall bear his iniquity” (Lev. 17:15–16; fol. 15r).

The one whom in one place it calls a foreigner and stranger, elsewhere it sometimes calls an outsider; as when it says: “You shall not lend to your brother at interest, whether money, grain, or any other thing, but to an outsider” (Deut. 23:19). But concerning those strangers who sojourn among you, not you among them, it is written elsewhere: “Any man of the house of Israel and of the strangers who sojourn [Col. 1630B] among you, if he eats blood, I shall set my face against that person and scatter him from among his people” (Lev. 17:10–11). You will find no other stranger included in any precept of the Law except one who lives among you and is therefore subject to your authority and discipline.

Accordingly, by the providence of divine grace, which has entirely taken from you every possession of land, so that no one now sojourns among you but you sojourn among all peoples, you know yourselves bound by none of your legal ordinances. But as for your attempt to press us toward circumcision by the precept concerning it and by Abraham’s example, so as to include in the sacrament of the Law those to whom you nevertheless concede that the Law was by no means given, or that the promise of the land established in the covenant of circumcision was made—see how weak your objection is.

For when the Lord had first said: “Every male among you shall be circumcised throughout your generations, both the household-born and the purchased servant, and whoever is not of your stock” (Gen. 17:27), surely by the words “among you” he includes not only Abraham and his descendants, but also all who belonged to their household and possession, so that they might have authority over them and compel them to circumcision.

> [Note: The words in brackets are read in the margin at Col. 1629D.]

Thus, after saying “among you,” and then adding “throughout your generations, both the household-born and the purchased servant,” and afterward, “and whoever is not of your stock,” by saying “throughout your generations” and “whoever is not of your stock” [Col. 1630D], he carefully expressed what he had included above in saying “among you”: not only the generations of his own descendants, but also the household of foreigners which they possess (fol. 15v).

> [Note: [Col. 1630D] The same.]

In saying, “My covenant shall be in your flesh,” he spoke generally, “in your flesh,” just as before he had said “among you.” Otherwise it would be very incongruous to promise that God’s covenant would not appear in their flesh unless the others too were circumcised. Therefore it is evident from the phrase “in your flesh” that these strangers too are included. And the final added statement completes the point: “The male whose foreskin has not been circumcised—that person shall perish from among his people, because he has broken my covenant” [Col. 1631A]. How can this refer to what precedes, where strangers have already been included, unless his covenant is also with the strangers—at least where it says, “Every male among you shall be circumcised,” and so forth?

But your effort to establish that eternal blessedness of souls is promised to you through your legal observances can be shown from the Law itself to rest on a most worthless inference. Because it is said “with an everlasting covenant” or “as an eternal covenant,” you understand those who are circumcised at God’s command to be so bound to him forever that they cannot be separated from his grace even in the future. Hence, one must not doubt that Israel, Esau, and most of the reprobate will be saved. [Col. 1631B] I am astonished also that you do not observe that “eternal” or “everlasting” is frequently used in the Law in a sense that does not exceed continuance during the present life.

For even in the covenant of circumcision itself, when it says: “I will give to you and to your seed the land of your sojourning, and all the land of Canaan, as an everlasting possession” (Gen. 17:8), I do not think you are so mad as to include, under the word “everlasting,” the blessedness of the future life—about which it would be superfluous to prescribe anything here. As you know, the Law often adds even regarding observances celebrated only in this life: “It shall be an everlasting ordinance for us throughout all your generations and dwellings.” Thus, to cite one instance among many, concerning the celebration of the Feast of Tabernacles it added: after first saying, “On the first day you shall take for yourselves the fruit of the most beautiful tree, palm branches, boughs of trees with varied foliage, and willows from the brook; and rejoice before the Lord your God; and celebrate his feast seven days in the year” (Lev. 23:40–41), [Col. 1631C] it immediately added, “It shall be an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations.”

Likewise, establishing the seventh-day celebration of the Sabbath, it says in one place: “It is an everlasting covenant between me and the children of Israel, and a perpetual sign” (Exod. 31:17). Again, when the Lord says concerning the Hebrew slave who does not wish to leave free that he “shall be a slave forever” (Exod. 21:6), he includes only the period of that man’s life. Hebrew slaves, after all, are not transmitted to descendants under the Law, as are those taken from the nations. Hence: “Your slave and maidservant shall be from the nations round about you, and from the strangers who sojourn among you, or who have been born from them in your land; these you shall have as servants, and you shall transmit them to your descendants by hereditary right and possess them forever. But do not oppress your brothers, the children of Israel, by force” (Lev. 25:44–46). It was enough for the Lord, in rewarding a carnal people who knew only earthly things, to adapt that reward merely to the time of this present life.

But when, commending the perfection of the Law, you asserted that only what Moses commanded ought to be done, I wonder that you have forgotten that above you yourself commendably maintained that many precepts are added by grace. [Col. 1632A] This is plainly most true for everyone. You yourselves have received certain primary traditions after the Law, which you judge most useful. Thus, following Daniel’s example in rejecting royal food and wine lest he be defiled by them, you also abstain from our wine. Moreover, the Rechabites, abstaining permanently from wine at the command of their father Jonadab, went beyond both Moses’ precepts and all the traditions of your fathers. Jeremiah too, sent to them by the Lord to induce them to drink wine, was not heard by them. Therefore their obedience is commended so highly by the Lord’s voice that he promises them: “Because you obeyed the command of Jonadab your father and kept all his commands, there shall not fail from the stock of Jonadab son of Rechab a man standing before me all days” (Jer. 35:18–19; fol. 16v).

Was King Hezekiah then a transgressor of the Law when he broke the bronze serpent (4 Kings 18:4), commendably destroying without a command what had usefully been made by command? David also, when he composed psalms in God’s honor, solemnly brought the ark of the Lord to Jerusalem, or Solomon built and dedicated the Lord’s temple, certainly did what Moses had by no means commanded. All prophecies too were written apart from any command of Moses or the Law handed down to him. Countless things after Moses were done by holy fathers either at the Lord’s command or because of evident usefulness, though they are never contained in Moses’ precepts. [Col. 1632C] In matters of manifest usefulness one need not wait for the Lord’s commands; nor is it a sin to do what has not been commanded, but to do what is contrary to a command.

Otherwise you could not spend even one day of this present life or carry out household care for a single day, since we must do many things—buying, trading, passing from one place to another, and finally eating or sleeping (fol. 17r)—which are not found in a command. Besides, who does not see that, if one must do neither more nor less than Moses commanded, all who keep the Law possess equal merit, and none can be better than another, since their merits cannot be unequal? Therefore it is clear from what has been said that you cannot in any way commend the Law’s perfection by maintaining that an act contrary to the Law occurs if something not commanded in it is added.

Nor should you think that you sufficiently excuse the Lord because, when he urged obedience to the Law, he omitted, as I have said, especially that matter in its reward—if he judged that obedience sufficient also for earning that reward. But when you trust that spiritual good, namely purification from sins, is attained through sacrifices or any outward works of the Law, I wonder whether, as you yourself confessed and as evident truth holds, your love of God and neighbor suffices for the justification of holiness. [Col. 1632D] For without these, the others would avail nothing with respect to salvation of the soul; nor is there doubt that, when these have made anyone righteous, he is no longer under guilt of sin so as to need spiritual purification.

Hence you have written concerning the penitent sinner: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God,” and so forth (Ps. 50:19); and again: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31:5). See how he commends this sacrifice of a contrite heart, when elsewhere, speaking in the person of the Lord, he altogether rejects the outward sacrifice: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine and its fullness. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats? Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise; pay your vows to the Most High; call upon me in your day of tribulation, and I shall deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49:9–15; fol. 17v).

The Lord hungers for the sacrifice of the heart, not of animals; he is refreshed by the former. When he finds it, he does not seek the latter; and when he does not find it, the latter is wholly superfluous—so far, I say, as the justification of the soul is concerned, not as regards the curtailment of legal penalties, according to which sins are nevertheless said to be forgiven you. [Col. 1633B] Your Law, which pays out the merits of its fulfillment or transgression only in this life, and has its recompense here alone in either case, so accommodates all things to this bodily life that it judges nothing clean or unclean according to the soul, nor refers any purifications to the uncleanness of souls, which we properly call sins.

For it calls foods clean or unclean in the same way as it calls persons, beds, seats, the whole furniture of a house, garments, and many other inanimate things unclean or polluted. If you count the uncleannesses of human beings, for which purifications have been instituted, among those who are defiled by sins, do you judge that a woman cleansed by sacrifice after childbirth has incurred sin merely by giving birth—although you yourselves judge cursed rather the woman who has not left seed in Israel? And what, I ask, does the man who suffers a flow of semen contract by this? Yet the Law regards him as so abominable that the bed on which he sleeps is unclean, as is wherever he sits. The earthen vessel that he touches shall be broken; the wooden one washed. If anyone touches his bed or sits where he sat, [Col. 1633D] he shall wash his garments, and he too, washed with water, shall remain unclean until evening (Lev. 15; fol. 18r).

Likewise, when a woman naturally suffers the flux of menstruation, she is judged so unclean that even that on which she sleeps or sits is again polluted; by her touch she pollutes whatever she touches, just as was said above concerning the man suffering a flow of semen. What, I beg you, do these things have to do with defilement of the soul—that even the bed touched by someone should be polluted? What are these uncleannesses or pollutions, I ask? Certainly the same kind as those of foods: just as the latter are to be avoided in eating, so the former in touching; and just as foods are unclean because not to be eaten, so these things are unclean or polluted because not to be touched. Those who touch them, even if compelled or acting unknowingly, are likewise pronounced unclean, because they are to be avoided in ordinary association until the appointed time of purification. [Col. 1634A]

But manifest sins, such as murder, adultery, and the like, are punished by death rather than expiated by sacrifices; nor is any remedy of such purifications allowed to those who have committed them, by which they might be saved. From this you should understand that these purifications are adapted more to a certain propriety of present life than to salvation of the soul. And when the sins of such people are said to be forgiven, it is evident that the bodily penalties instituted for them are remitted to those who are separated from the common community by conversion. For what else is it to understand that a sin is forgiven than that the penalty owed for it is remitted, whether that penalty is bodily or eternal?

But the soul’s guilt, because it is committed through its own will, is immediately forgiven through its contrite heart and true compunction of repentance, so that it is in no way further condemned for it, as was said: “I said, ‘I will confess against myself.’” For after a repentant sinner resolves within himself to accuse himself of it through confession, then, in that very fact that he lacks the fault of the perverse will through which he had sinned, the guilt of the deed and its eternal punishment are forgiven—although a temporal punishment may still be retained for correction. [Col. 1634B] As your Prophet says elsewhere: “The Lord chastening chastened me, and did not deliver me to death” (Ps. 117:18; fol. 18v).

Nor do I think I have sufficiently consulted you concerning the salvation of my soul by inquiring into your faith or my own. In this conference of our inquiry, I perceive that the result has been that you cannot know, by your Law’s authority—even if you receive it as given by God—that I ought to submit myself to its burden, as though it were necessary to add anything to that Law which he prescribes for us by the example of his Job, or to that moral discipline which our prophets have left to posterity concerning virtues sufficient for blessedness. It remains now to hear the judgment of the present judge, or for me to transfer the labor of our inquiry to the Christian.

JUDGE. Both declare that they await the judgment of our court. But I, more eager to learn than to judge, reply that I wish first to hear everyone’s reasons [Col. 1634D], so that I may be more discerning in judgment as I become wiser through hearing, according to the saying I mentioned above, from the proverb of the highest sage: “The wise hearer shall become wiser, and the intelligent shall possess the rudders” (Wis. 1:5). To this all alike assented, inflamed with the same desire to learn (fol. 19r).

PHILOSOPHER. Come now, Christian, I address you, that you may answer my inquiry according to the terms of our undertaking. The law of him whose recompense is higher must be more perfect, and his doctrine more reasonable, inasmuch as it is later. For earlier laws would be written for a people in vain unless something were added to them for the perfection of doctrine. One of our people, carefully considering this in the second book of his *Rhetoric* when he was framing a case concerning conflicting laws, instructed that one should consider which law was given later. “For,” he says, “whatever is latest is most weighty.”

CHRISTIAN. I am astonished that you so shamelessly contradict what you professed at the beginning. After you had stated that your investigations had found the Jews foolish and Christians insane, you afterward said that you were not striving for contention but engaging in a search for truth. On what ground, then, do you now expect the doctrine of truth from those whom you have found insane? Do you now judge that their insanity has ceased after your inquiries, so that they can suffice for your instruction? Certainly, if you regard the Christian faith as insanity and count those who follow this sect insane, consider, philosopher, what is to be thought of those greatest Greek philosophers who, through the crude and uncultivated preaching of simple men—the apostles—were all converted to this faith and became utterly insane. [Col. 1635B] Indeed, this insanity of ours, as you call it, has taken root and been confirmed among the Greeks to such an extent that both evangelical and apostolic teaching was written there and afterward great councils were held; from there it filled the whole world and suppressed all heresies (fol. 19v).

PHILOSOPHER. Sometimes people are more easily provoked by insults and reproaches than they are moved by entreaties and supplications; and those provoked in this manner labor more eagerly for combat than those moved by gracious requests.

CHRISTIAN. You should be forgiven if you did this with that intention. Yet, lest I seem to postpone this contest from distrust, both you and I must pray that the Lord himself may inspire what you should seek and what I should answer—the Lord who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of himself. Now, then, if you please, since you are ignorant of the perfection of our Law, both evangelical and apostolic teaching, let us first examine it and compare it with all other doctrines, so that, if you find it more perfect in those commands and exhortations which justify, you may choose it as you ought. This is also what your rhetorician, as you said, advises concerning conflicting laws: “If two or more laws cannot be observed because they conflict with one another, that one should chiefly be preserved which appears to concern the greatest matters.” [Col. 1635D]

PHILOSOPHER. Nothing is more plausible than this counsel, and nothing more foolish than to depart from ancient for new laws unless the doctrine is superior. Those who composed new laws could write them more cautiously and perfectly in proportion as they had already been instructed by the discipline of earlier laws and by experience itself of necessary matters, and could easily add from their own intelligence what was lacking—as also happens in the other disciplines of prophecy [or philosophy]. But confidence in the perfection of later writers is especially appropriate if modern writers can equal the ancients in ability. What if one may even hope that they greatly surpass them? This is certainly not doubted concerning the lawgiver, Christ, whom you call the very Wisdom of God. You also assert that our Job had previously sung of him: “Behold, God in his strength, and none is like him among lawgivers” (Job 36:22). [Col. 1636A]

Your Apostle too, preferring his teaching and openly professing the imperfection of the first Law, says: “God, who formerly spoke to the fathers in many portions and in many ways through the prophets, in these last days has spoken to us in his Son,” and so forth (Heb. 1:1). And further below, distinguishing the old and new Laws, he says: “There is a setting aside of the former commandment because of its weakness and uselessness; for the Law brought nothing to perfection. But there is the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God” (Heb. 7:18–19).

CHRISTIAN. Certainly, as I see it, you are condemned not by ignorance of our faith but rather by the obstinacy of your unbelief. You have learned the perfection of our Law from its own writings and still inquire what you should follow, as though you did not possess there a perfect and more excellent teaching than all others concerning the virtues which you do not doubt are sufficient for blessedness. When the Lord himself gave the New Testament, completing what was lacking in his old one, he immediately began by saying to his disciples concerning this perfection: “Unless your righteousness shall exceed,” and so forth (Matt. 5:20). Then, setting out point by point the abundance of the new Law, [Col. 1636C] he carefully expressed what was lacking in moral perfection and completed true ethics—that is, ethics in comparison with which, if we carefully compare these things with what preceded, it will readily be shown that all that had been handed down both by ancient fathers and by prophets concerning moral discipline and the distinction of virtues is nothing.

PHILOSOPHER. As you know, these comparisons alone brought me here, and we have assembled with this purpose.

CHRISTIAN. Now indeed, as I understand, we are proceeding to the goal and completion of every discipline. What you are accustomed to call ethics—that is, moral philosophy—we call divinity. We name it from that which we strive to comprehend, namely God; you name it from the means by which one comes there, namely good morals, which you call virtues. [Col. 1636D]

PHILOSOPHER. I assent to what is clear, and I approve no little this new designation of your term. Since you regard that to which one arrives as worthier than the means by which one arrives, and arrival as happier than the journey, your designation is more distinguished, drawing the reader greatly through the origin of its proper meaning, “divination.” If it excels in teaching as it does in name, I judge that no discipline is comparable with it.

CHRISTIAN. Now then, if you please, we wish you to define in what the sum of true ethics consists, what we ought to seek from this discipline, and at what point, when attained, its purpose is completed. The whole sum of this discipline, I think, is gathered into this: that it reveals what the highest good is and by what path we may reach it. [Col. 1637A]

PHILOSOPHER. I strongly approve that the sum of so great a matter is expressed in so few words and the purpose of all ethics so carefully comprehended. These words concerning its purpose immediately draw the hearer to themselves and commend the study of this discipline, so that the teachings of all arts become worthless by comparison. For since the highest good surpasses all other things, and true blessedness consists in its enjoyment, its doctrine plainly surpasses all others by far both in usefulness and in dignity. The pursuits of other disciplines remain far beneath the highest good; they do not attain the height of blessedness, and no fruit appears in them except insofar as they serve this highest philosophy, like handmaids occupied about their mistress.

What has the study of grammar, dialectic, or other arts to do with the search for true human blessedness? All lie far below this height and cannot raise themselves to so lofty a summit. They set forth certain kinds of expression or exercise certain natures of things, as though preparing steps toward this height, when we must discourse about it or bring forward some natures of things by way of example or likeness; [Col. 1637C] so that, guided as it were by these handmaids, we may attain the mistress, finding in them a passage for our progress but in this discipline rest and the end of our labor.

CHRISTIAN. I rejoice that you have so carefully grasped the excellence of this philosophy and distinguished it from the others, since I understand that you are chiefly engaged in its study.

PHILOSOPHER. Rightly engaged, I say. For this alone is the natural discipline, which accords with philosophers in moral precepts all the more because they are known to employ law and adhere to rational arguments, as that learned man observes. “For,” he says, “the Jews seek signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom” (1 Cor. 1:22). Since Jews are merely animal and sensual, untrained in philosophy by which they can examine reasons, they are moved to faith only by miracles of outward works, as though performing such things belonged to God alone and no demonic deception could occur in them. [Col. 1637D] How foolish this belief is, the magicians in Egypt taught, and Christ especially instructed you, when warning you about the pseudo-philosophers of Antichrist. He testifies that in deceiving people they will work miracles so great that, “if possible, even the elect shall be led into error” (Matt. 24:24).

Thus, since to seek such signs is foolishness, the Apostle mentioned the contrary when he added: “and the Greeks seek wisdom”—that is, they demand reasons from preachers, which are the sure instruments of wisdom. Therefore your preaching, that is, Christian preaching, is especially commended because it could convert to faith those who relied greatly and abundantly upon reasons, trained in all studies of the liberal arts and armed with rational arguments (fol. 22r). They were not only investigators but inventors of those arts, and streams flowed from their springs into the whole world. Therefore we now especially trust your discipline: strengthened and established as it has now become more fully, it may be greatly powerful in conflict. [Col. 1638A]

CHRISTIAN. Rather, after the conversion of so many philosophers, neither you nor those after you may doubt our faith, nor does such a contest now seem necessary, since in secular disciplines you believe everything on their authority and are not urged to faith by their examples, saying with the Prophet: “We are not better than our fathers” (1 Kings 19:4).

PHILOSOPHER. Yet we do not yield so far to their authority that we do not examine their sayings by reason before approving them. Otherwise we would cease philosophizing, if, setting aside the investigation of reasons, we made much use of the arguments from authority, which are called inartificial and are wholly separated from the matter itself, resting in opinion rather than truth. Nor would we believe that our own elders were led to confession of your faith so much by reason as conquered by force, as your histories themselves agree. [Col. 1638B] Before emperors or rulers were converted to your faith through miracles, as you say, your purification won few wise persons, or none at all—although peoples might then easily have been torn from the most manifest errors of idolatry and transferred to any worship of one God.

Therefore your Paul, wisely taking an occasion for his attack upon the Athenians, began thus: “Men of Athens, I see that in every respect you are superstitious,” and so forth (Acts 17:22). For already at that time the knowledge of natural law and divine worship had vanished, and the multitude of the erring had wholly destroyed or oppressed the small number of wise persons. Yet, to speak from our own conviction and acknowledge no small fruit of Christian preaching, we do not doubt that idolatry was then chiefly destroyed in the world through it. [Col. 1638C]

CHRISTIAN. Add also what is evident: that the natural law was restored, and perfect moral discipline—on which alone, as you say, you rely and which you believe sufficient for salvation—was handed down only by him from whom, as true *sophia*, that is, God’s wisdom, all who have been instructed are rightly called true philosophers. [Col. 1638D]

PHILOSOPHER. If only you could prove these things as you say, so that, from that supreme Wisdom itself which you call in Greek *Logos* and in Latin the Word of God, you might show yourselves truly *logici*, equipped with the rational arguments of words! And do not presume to present to me, wretched man that I am, that refuge of your Gregory: “Faith,” he says, “has no merit where human reason provides proof.” Because among you they cannot adequately argue for the faith they assert, they immediately take up this Gregorian saying as consolation for their ignorance. According to their opinion, what does it accomplish except that we should assent equally to every preaching of faith, however foolish or sound? If faith is not to be examined by reason lest it lose its merit, and the mind’s judgment is not to consider what ought to be believed, but one must immediately assent to whatever is preached, then it makes no difference what errors preaching sows, because where reason may not be applied, nothing may lawfully be refuted by reason.

Let idolatry say of a stone, wood, or any creature, “This is the true God, Creator of heaven and earth” (fol. 23r), or let it preach any manifest abomination: who can refute it if nothing concerning faith is to be examined by reason? At once, when challenged, it will object to the Christian especially what was said above: “Faith has no merit,” and so forth. The Christian will immediately be confounded by his own defense, saying that no arguments at all are to be heard in such matters where he himself wholly forbids them to be introduced, and not allowing anyone to be rightly challenged by arguments concerning faith.

CHRISTIAN. As that greatest of sages says, so too arguments often merely appear to be such—that is, things are spoken rationally and plausibly when in fact they are not.

PHILOSOPHER. What of the very things that are held as authorities? Is not error very frequent even in them? Otherwise there would not be so many different sects of faith, if all made use of the same authorities. Rather, as each person deliberates by his own reason, individuals choose the authorities which they follow. Otherwise the pronouncements of all Scriptures would have to be accepted indiscriminately, unless reason, which is naturally prior to them, first had to judge concerning them. For those who wrote themselves deserved authority—that is, the dignity of being believed immediately—only from the reason with which their statements appear to abound. Indeed, reason is so far preferred to authority even in their own judgment that, as your Antony recalls, since human understanding invented letters, letters are by no means necessary to one whose understanding is sound. In every philosophical disputation authority is thought to hold the last place, or none at all [Col. 1639D], so that those who, confident in their own powers, disdain recourse to outside assistance, would be ashamed to introduce arguments drawn from the judgment of another—that is, from authority.

Accordingly philosophers rightly judged the loci of such arguments, to which an orator rather than a philosopher is compelled to resort, to be wholly external, disconnected from the matter, and deprived of every force: since they rest on opinion rather than truth, and he who introduces them produces none of his own arguments by any art of intellect, but uses not his own words but another’s. Hence your Boethius also, in his *Topics*, embracing both the Themistian and Tullian classification of loci, says: “Arguments from the judgment of a matter [Col. 1640A] offer, as it were, testimony; they are non-artificial loci, wholly disconnected, and follow opinion rather than the matter itself.” Again, the same writer says, following Tully: “There remains,” he says, “the locus which he called assumed from without. This rests upon judgment and authority and is wholly probable, containing nothing necessary.” And after some intervening matter: “This locus is said to be established from without, because it is not taken from the terms which have been predicated or subjected, but comes from an externally posited judgment.” Hence, he says, it is also called non-artificial and unprovided with art, because the orator does not construct an argument for himself from it, but uses testimonies already prepared and set forth.

But what you said—that one sometimes errs even in discerning or recognizing arguments—is certainly true and plain. Yet this happens to persons who lack skill in rational philosophy and discrimination among arguments: such as the Jews profess themselves to be, who seek signs instead of arguments, and all who place their support in another’s sayings; as though it were easier to judge from the authority or writing of one absent than from the reasoning or opinion of one present, and as though the meaning of the former could be investigated better than that of the latter.

But while, so far as we can, we seek God with concern for our own salvation, his grace certainly supplies what our effort does not suffice to provide; and he helps those who are willing so that they may be able, he himself also inspiring them to will. He often draws the unwilling; he does not reject the willing [Col. 1640C]; and he extends his right hand to one striving—he whose negligence no one can accuse. Concerning him, Christ, making you secure by the very truth which you claim, added this fitting comparison: “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and he who seeks finds, and to him who knocks it shall be opened” (Matt. 7:7–8). I recall that Augustine, expounding these preceding words in a certain treatise *On Mercy*, says: “Ask by praying, seek by disputing, knock by acting.”

Hence, preferring the art of disputation to the other disciplines in the second book of *On Order*, and commending it as though it alone knows, or makes people knowing, he says: “The discipline of disciplines, which they call dialectic. This teaches how to teach; this teaches how to learn. In it reason itself shows what it is and what it wills; it alone knows. And it not only wills to make people knowing, but is also able to do so.” In the second book of *On Christian Doctrine*, likewise showing it to be especially necessary for sacred reading, he says: “There remain those things which pertain not to bodily senses but to reason, where the disciplines of disputation and number hold sway.” But the discipline of disputation is exceedingly useful for penetrating every kind of question found in the sacred writings. Yet there must be guarded against in it a lust for wrangling and a childish [fol. 24 V.] display of deceiving one’s adversary. For there are many things called sophisms: false conclusions of arguments, often imitating true ones, so as to deceive not only the slow-witted but even intelligent persons who are insufficiently attentive. Scripture, I think, condemns this kind of captious conclusion in the passage where it says: “He who speaks sophistically is hateful” (Ecclus. 37:23).

CHRISTIAN. Certainly no discerning person forbids our faith to be pursued and examined by arguments; nor is rational assent given to doubtful matters unless a reason has first been supplied why assent ought to be given. When that reason produces certainty concerning a doubtful matter, it itself becomes what you call an argument. In every discipline controversy arises concerning both a writing and an opinion; and in every conflict of disputation the truth of a stronger reason is produced rather than authority displayed. For, in establishing belief, the question is not what is true in the reality of the matter, but what may enter into opinion; and very many questions arise from the words of authority itself, so that one must judge concerning them before judging through them.

Once a reason has been supplied, however, even if it is not truly a reason but only appears to be one, no question remains, because no doubt remains. Yet one must argue with you from authority all the less because you rely more upon reason and acknowledge the authority of Scripture less. For no one can be argued against except from concessions, nor convicted except through what he accepts; and one must contend with you differently than with us. We know that what Gregory or our other teachers assert, even what Christ himself or Moses asserts, does not yet concern you, so that you might be compelled to belief from their sayings [Col. 1641C]. Such things have force among us who accept them; and especially the matter of sometimes establishing or defending faith by arguments. Against those who deny that faith is to be pursued by arguments, the second book of Christian theology, as I recall, argues more fully—by the force of arguments as well as the authority of writings—and refutes the rebellious. But now, if you please, let us return to the subject.

PHILOSOPHER. Indeed, since it pleases you—and above all ought to please you—let us strive, so far as we can, and endeavor to demand the natural law by means of the teachings of truer ethics. We believe that this will be rightly and orderly completed if, following the summary of ethics which you set forth above, we examine what the highest good is and by what path one must arrive at it; so that our ethical treatise may be divided into these two parts.

CHRISTIAN. I approve what you approve. But because, in accordance with the agreed plan of our earlier proposal, our views must be compared with yours so that we may choose the more weighty, and because you have claimed the first place for yourself on account of the antiquity of the natural law, it is for you—who, as you say, are content with the earlier law, that is, the natural law, and employ only it—to put forward your own views, or those of your people, on this matter; afterwards, if we differ on any point, you are to hear our reasons.

PHILOSOPHER. The highest good, or end of good—that is, its completion or perfection—our predecessors have defined, as most of them recall, as that at which each person, when he has arrived, is blessed; just as, conversely, the highest evil is that whose attainment makes one wretched. We earn both by our character. Character, moreover, is plainly called virtues or the vices contrary to them. Some of us, however, as Augustine recalls in Book Eight of *The City of God*, have called virtue itself the highest good; others, pleasure [fol. 25 V.].

CHRISTIAN. What, I ask, did they understand by pleasure?

PHILOSOPHER. Not the shameful and disgraceful delight of fleshly enticements, as most suppose, but a certain inward tranquillity of the soul, by which it remains at rest amid adversity and prosperity and is content with its own goods, while no consciousness of sin gnaws at it. Far be it from philosophers—the greatest despisers of earthly happiness and foremost tamers of the flesh—to have located the highest good amid the disgraces of this life, as many ignorantly impute to Epicurus and his followers, the Epicureans; for they do not understand what, as we have said, those people called pleasure. Otherwise Seneca, that greatest builder of character and a man of the most restrained life, as you yourselves confess, would certainly not so frequently have introduced the opinions of Epicurus as his master for moral instruction, if Epicurus had departed, as is alleged, from the path of sobriety and honour.

CHRISTIAN. Let it be as you think; but explain this, I pray: in understanding pleasure in this way, do they differ in meaning as well as in words from those who name virtue?

PHILOSOPHER. There is no difference between them, or only a slight one, as regards the substance of the view. To excel in virtues is itself to possess this tranquillity of soul, and conversely.

CHRISTIAN. Thus both have one view about the highest good, though the designation differs; and so the two views which appeared to concern the highest good have been reduced to one.

PHILOSOPHER. So I judge.

CHRISTIAN. And what path did they establish for reaching this highest good—that is, virtue?

PHILOSOPHER. Certainly the study of moral instruction itself, or the exercise of subduing the flesh, so that a good will, strengthened into a settled habit, may be called virtue.

CHRISTIAN. And whom do they define as blessed?

PHILOSOPHER. They call the blessed person one who is, as it were, well fitted—that is, one who conducts himself well and easily in all things—so that to be blessed is the same thing as to excel in good character, that is, virtues.

CHRISTIAN. Do they hold anything concerning the immortality of the soul and some blessedness of the future life, and do they expect it according to their merits?

PHILOSOPHER. Certainly; but what follows from that?

CHRISTIAN. Do they judge that the blessedness of that life is greater, where those received into it are afflicted by no pain of suffering, so that we should expect the highest human good and true blessedness there rather than here [Col. 1643A]?

PHILOSOPHER. The rest of that life is indeed supreme, immune from every suffering, as you said; but when affliction ceases, they say that blessedness is by no means increased unless virtue increases. No one, in their view, becomes more blessed unless he becomes better in virtue; for, as I said, they define blessedness itself as possessing virtues. Hence, anyone who suffers for justice’s sake and is said to merit more by suffering is equally blessed amid torments as before, because equally good. Although his virtue now appears greater than before, it has not increased because of the torment; rather, through the torment it has appeared to be as great as it was.

Far be it from us to think that anything pertaining to bodily rest or affliction increases or diminishes our blessedness, if virtue preserves the mind in the same purpose. Did your Christ himself diminish his blessedness by suffering, or increase it by rising again? Therefore, do not judge that we shall be more blessed there merely because these bodily afflictions cease there, if we are not to be better.

CHRISTIAN. What if we are?

PHILOSOPHER. Then certainly we shall be more blessed, because better.

CHRISTIAN. You said that you expect that life, as something due in return for merits: as though here there is conflict with vices, and there the crown of victory.

PHILOSOPHER. Yes; this is plain to everyone.

CHRISTIAN. In what manner, then, is the reward of these struggles to be received there, if life there is not to be happier, and if that life is not better and more blessed than the present? But if that life is more blessed than this, then surely those who enjoy it are more blessed than they appear to be here.

PHILOSOPHER. Certainly more blessed, as I said, if better. We do not accept it otherwise. For one who has gained a crown is not thereby endowed with greater virtue than he possessed during the contest; nor has his courage been made greater, though it may have been more proved or known than ever before—indeed, perhaps diminished by the very burden of the struggle. Nor is the life of the victor better than that of the combatant, though it is more pleasant.

CHRISTIAN. Both your teachers and ours, together with all people alike, count poverty, sickness, death, and the other troubles of adversities or sufferings among evils; and likewise there are many vices of both soul and body, because they are contrary to virtues, which must nevertheless be counted among evils, such as bodily lameness or blindness, dullness of mind, or forgetfulness. Aristotle, indeed, discussing contraries in his *Categories*, says: “The contrary of the good is necessarily evil; and this is evident by the opposition of particular cases: sickness to health, injustice to justice, weakness to courage. Likewise also in other cases. But sometimes the contrary of evil is good, and sometimes evil. For to poverty, which is an evil, excess is contrary, and this itself is an evil. But one will observe such a case only in a few instances. In most cases evil is always contrary to good.” And Tully, assigning the locus from contraries in his *Topics*, says: “If health is good, sickness is evil.”

The Lord himself says through the prophet, concerning the peace which he grants to the obedient and the persecutions which he sends upon the rebellious: “I am the Lord, making good and creating evil” (Isa. 45:7). And in the Gospel the Lord says to the rich man concerning earthly goods and evils: “You received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things” (Luke 16:25). Augustine too—yours first, and afterwards ours—maintains that death is evil. “Just as the law,” he says, “is not evil because it increases the desire of those who sin, so death is not good because it increases the glory of those who suffer and makes martyrs.” The law is good because it is a prohibition of sin. Death, however, is evil because it is the wage of sin. But just as the unjust use good things badly, so the just use evil things well. Hence evil persons use the law badly, although the law is good; and good persons die well, although death is evil.

PHILOSOPHER. To what end, I ask, is this?

CHRISTIAN. That you may understand that the life which is manifestly entirely immune from these evils, and so completely removed from sin that there not only is no sinning but sinning is impossible, is better. Unless that life is better than the present [Col. 1644C], or more pleasing, it is set forth in vain as a recompense. But if it is more pleasing and not better, it is irrationally preferred to this life, and those who desire it act without judgment.

PHILOSOPHER. Certainly, to confess the truth, I now find you a philosopher for the first time; and it does not suit one to oppose such manifest reasoning shamelessly. Thus, according to the reasoning you have set forth, the highest human good must be expected there rather than here. Perhaps this was Epicurus’s view when he called the highest good pleasure: namely, because the soul’s tranquillity is so great that neither outward bodily affliction disturbs it, nor any consciousness of sin inwardly troubles the mind, nor any vice obstructs it, so that its best will is altogether fulfilled. For so long as anything opposes or is lacking to our will, there is by no means true blessedness.

This always happens while one lives here: the soul, weighed down by the mass of the earthly body and confined, as it were, in a prison, does not enjoy true freedom. Who, for instance, does not sometimes desire warmth when excessively cold, or conversely; or clear weather when oppressed by rain; or food or clothing, often in greater quantity than he possesses? There are countless other things which, unless we resist manifest truth, are thrust upon us unwillingly or withheld when we desire them. But if, as reason requires, we must judge the good of the future life to be our highest good, I think that the path by which one arrives there is the virtues by which we are adorned here. We must discuss these more carefully later [Col. 1645A].

CHRISTIAN. Behold, our disputation has brought us to this: that we set the highest human good—or, as was said, the end of good itself—in the blessedness of the future life, and the virtues as the path by which one arrives there. But first I wish to compare our teaching, that is, the Christian teaching, with yours concerning this highest good, so that that which has the richer doctrine or exhortation concerning this good may be judged more perfect and obeyed more fully. And concerning the old law, in which the Jews glory, you rightly think that you have shown that no reward of this blessedness was promised there, and no exhortation to it was employed there.

But when the Lord Jesus delivered the New Testament, at its very beginning he laid down such a foundation for his teaching as would at once incite both contempt for the world and desire for this blessedness, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3); and after some intervening sayings: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid., 10). If we attend carefully to these words, all his precepts and exhortations are directed to this: that by hope of that heavenly and eternal life all prosperous things may be despised and adverse things endured. I do not think that your teachers attained this, or equally invited your minds toward this end of good. If they did, set it forth by reviewing all the doctrines of your ethics. If you cannot set it forth, confess that Christ’s teaching is more perfect and better by as much as it exhorts us to virtues with a better cause or hope; whereas you judge that virtues, or their contraries, ought to be sought or avoided more for their own sake than for anything else.

Accordingly, you judge that the former ought to be called honourable and the latter dishonourable. For you call honourable that which pleases in itself and ought to be sought for its own sake, not for another end; and conversely dishonourable that which is to be avoided because of its own ugliness. Those things which are to be sought or avoided for another end you call useful or useless rather.

PHILOSOPHER. This indeed seemed right to our elders, as Marcus Tullius sets it forth more fully in the second book of his *Rhetoric*. But when it is said that virtue is to be sought for its own sake and not for another, the reward of merits is not entirely excluded; rather, the intention toward earthly advantages is removed. Otherwise we would not rightly establish blessedness as the end of virtues—that is, their final cause—as your Boethius, following Themistius, recalls in the second book of his *Topics*. For there, when he gives an example under the locus “related”: “If,” he says, “being blessed is good, and justice is good. For,” he says, “this is the end of justice: that, if someone lives according to justice, he may be brought to blessedness.” Here he plainly shows that blessedness is set as the recompense of a just life, and that our purpose in living justly is to arrive at it. This blessedness, I think, Epicurus calls pleasure and your Christ calls the kingdom of heaven. What difference does it make by what name it is called, provided that the reality remains the same, and there is no different blessedness nor a different purpose in living justly proposed for philosophers and Christians? For just as you, so we, arrange to live justly here in order to be glorified there; and we fight against vices in order to be crowned there with the merits of virtues, having attained that highest good as our reward.

CHRISTIAN. On the contrary, as I understand it, our purpose and yours differ greatly, as do the merits; and we differ not a little also concerning the highest good itself.

PHILOSOPHER. Explain that, I pray, if you can.

CHRISTIAN. No one rightly calls that the highest good above which something greater is found. For what is inferior or lesser than something else cannot in any way be called supreme or highest. Yet every human blessedness or glory is certainly surpassed by the divine, far beyond measure and beyond expression. Therefore no good except that divine good is rightly called highest; apart from it nothing is rightly called the highest good.

PHILOSOPHER. Here we do not mean the highest good absolutely, but the highest human good.

CHRISTIAN. Yet neither do we rightly call that the highest human good above which a greater human good is found.

PHILOSOPHER. That is certainly clear.

CHRISTIAN. I ask, therefore, whether in that blessedness one person is more blessed than another, just as here one person may be more just or holier than another; that is, whether the recompense differs according to the diversity of merits.

PHILOSOPHER. What if it does?

CHRISTIAN. Indeed, since it does, you must concede that one human being becomes more blessed there than another, and that consequently the lesser blessedness of that person cannot be called the highest human good. Hence neither should one who is less blessed than another be called blessed at all. For you defined the highest good as that at which each person, when he has arrived, is blessed. Therefore you must either concede that the person who is lesser there than another has attained the highest good, or concede that he is not blessed at all, but only the one than whom no one there is more blessed. For if what he has attained makes him blessed, then, according to the definition set forth above, it must surely be called the highest good.

PHILOSOPHER. Wait a little, I pray, and attend to what I added to my latest question—since it is permissible also to correct an ill-considered concession when we confer for the investigation of truth, not for display of ingenuity, as has been said.

CHRISTIAN. I approve and concede what you say. For when we are wholly occupied with investigating truth, we ought not, after the childish manner or that of an importunate declaimer, to quarrel over words. If things are conceded with insufficient foresight, no one intending either to learn or teach should take from this an occasion for bringing shame upon another, when it is sometimes permissible, even for the sake of argument, to concede false things. We therefore grant complete permission either to withdraw a statement altogether or to correct it.

PHILOSOPHER. Remember, I say, what I said, and recall the condition I added: namely, “What if it does?” For it has seemed to many philosophers that all virtues are simultaneously present in every good person, and that no one is in any way to be judged good if any virtue is lacking to him; and consequently that there is no difference among all good people, either in the merits of life or in the recompense of blessedness. If perhaps this is so, the same blessedness is rendered to all, and all alike, having attained the highest good, become blessed.

Tully plainly professes this view in these words in the second book of *On Duties*: “Although justice without prudence possesses enough authority, prudence without justice is of no avail for producing confidence. For the more shrewd and crafty a man is, the more hateful and suspect he is when the reputation of uprightness has been removed. Therefore intelligence joined with justice will have as much power as it wishes for producing confidence. Justice without prudence will have great power; prudence without justice will have no power. But lest anyone wonder why, when it is agreed among all philosophers, and has often been argued by me myself, that whoever has one virtue has them all, I now separate them as though anyone who is not likewise prudent could be just: that subtlety is one thing when truth itself is refined in disputation; another when all speech is adapted to common opinion. Therefore we speak here as the multitude does, calling some brave, others good men, others prudent. For when we speak of popular opinion, we must use popular and customary words.”  
[Note: [Col. 1647D] This Ciceronian passage, very corrupt and defective in the Muscr. manuscript, has been corrected from Orelli’s edition [Col. 1648D] of Tully’s works; what needed supplementation has been added.]

He also, in the *Paradoxes*, so equates bad people not only in vices but even in sins that he maintains all sins to be equal.

CHRISTIAN. Now for the first time I see you as importunate and more intent on wrangling than philosophizing. For, lest you seem compelled to acknowledge manifest truth, you turn to the madness of patent falsehood: namely, that all good persons are equally good, all guilty persons equally guilty, and all alike worthy of the same glory or punishment.

PHILOSOPHER. Yet the matter rests in reality, not in human opinion; for people judge and recompense the intention manifested in deeds more than the quality of character, and according to what appears to be done outwardly they judge some more just, stronger, better, or worse than others. Nor do I think you are far from this view, if you carefully consider your teaching. For all virtues, as Augustine—that greatest philosopher—maintains, are included under the one name *charity* (*caritas*), which alone, as he himself says, distinguishes the children of God from the children of the devil. Hence he fittingly says somewhere: “Where charity is, what can be lacking?” For “love is the fulfilment of the law.” The Apostle who says this (Rom. 13:10), pursuing that fulfilment and both excluding evils from it and including goods within it, says: “Charity is patient, is kind; charity does not envy, does not act perversely,” and so forth (1 Cor. 13:4).

And of charity it is also said, among other things, that it “bears all things” or “endures all things,” and therefore death as well. But Christ says: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Therefore no one abounds in charity more than another, since charity contains and brings with it all these things. But if no one surpasses another in charity, then certainly neither in virtues nor merits, since, as you say, charity embraces every virtue.

CHRISTIAN. Truly, if virtue is understood properly—namely, that which obtains merit before God—charity alone is to be called virtue. Since it makes one just, courageous, or temperate, it is rightly called justice, courage, or temperance. But just as not all who possess charity are equally inflamed by it, and not all prudent persons understand equally, so not all just persons are equally just, nor are all equally courageous or temperate.

Although, according to the earlier distinction, we concede that all virtues are present in certain persons—since each of them is just, courageous, and temperate—we nevertheless do not grant that they are equal in virtues or merits, since one may be more just, courageous, or restrained than another. Although we hold that individuals agree in the aforesaid species of virtues, there is nevertheless a great difference among the individuals within those species: the justice, courage, or temperance of this person is greater than that of another. And although charity bestows all that you have named, it does not bestow everything in equal measure on each person in whom it resides. For just as nature gives all bodily advantages, but not every advantage to everyone, so too with goods of soul or virtues: not all are enriched equally with all of them.

I therefore want you to notice how feeble—indeed, how worthless—a sophism is the argument by which the aforesaid philosopher, following another’s opinion, introduces the paradox that virtues, like vices, are equal in everyone. He says that no one is better than a good man, more temperate than a temperate man, stronger than a strong man, or wiser than a wise man. Even if no one is better than a good man, however, one may be better than some good man. For what else is it to say of someone that he is better than a good man than that he is better than whatever good man is being referred to? For when we call God better than a human being, we understand nothing other than that he surpasses all human beings.

Likewise, when we say that a good man is better than a good man—namely, than a good man is, or than some man is good—it seems that this can only be understood as placing him above all good men generally. That is altogether false, since he himself is also one among good men. For if he is better than a good man, or than any good man is, it seems to follow that neither a good man nor any good man is so good; rather, if anyone is good, he is less good than that man. Thus it makes a great difference whether someone is said to be better than some good man, or better than any good man is.

This snare of sophism may occur in every comparison. Thus, just as they attempt to prove that all good people are equally good because no good person is better than a good person in the simple and general sense, they may likewise prove all beautiful persons equally beautiful because no beautiful person is more beautiful than “a beautiful person” in that same simple and general sense—although he may be more beautiful than another beautiful person.

Finally, who does not understand how utterly insane it is to say that all sins are equal? Whether you place sin in the will or in action, it is clear that among wicked people one has a more depraved will than another, and does greater harm or acts worse. For the will leads to action, and when the power to harm is granted, one person harms more than another or persecutes a just person more violently, because he hates him more and desires more keenly to afflict him. Likewise, not all good people benefit others equally, or desire equally to benefit them. From this it is plain that neither good persons nor bad persons are equal among themselves, nor ought their merits to be equal, so that their recompense too may be understood as equal.

Moreover, if, setting aside the opinion of fools, you consider the doctrines concerning virtues of philosophers of proven excellence, and carefully attend to the eloquent Plotinus’s fourfold distinction of virtues—calling some political, others purificatory, others virtues of the purified soul, and others exemplary—you will be compelled at once by the very names and descriptions to confess that human beings differ greatly in virtues. The Apostle himself, whom you cited against us, does not pass over this difference. Speaking of continence and the concession of marriage, he says: “I wish all people were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Cor. 7). He also distinguishes the rewards of the future life according to the quality of virtues or merits: “Star differs from star in glory; so also will be the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:41). And elsewhere: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Cor. 9:6).

But when he said that charity is the fulfilment of the law, that is, that the law is fulfilled through charity, he did not prove that all are equal in charity, since charity extends beyond the commandment. Hence comes that exhortation of Truth: “When you have done all that has been commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do’” (Luke 17:10). That is: consider it a small thing if you fulfil only what you are obliged to do by commandment, unless you add from grace something beyond the obligation of the commandment; and this is what the phrase means: “We have done what we were obliged to do.” It is as if he said: “Because in fulfilling the commandments we pay only what is owed, and perform works that are, as it were, necessary, not gratuitous.”

But when someone advances to the excellence of virginity, he certainly goes beyond a commandment, to which he is not compelled by commandment. Hence the Apostle says: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7:25). But even among those who fulfil the law without going beyond it, charity can be unequal, because in the same work the affection of charity may be greater in this person than in that. As for the objection drawn from Augustine’s saying, “Where charity is, what can be lacking?” no one can suppose that he understood it so as to make all people equal in all virtues and merits—something which, following both the Lord and the Apostle, he contradicts almost everywhere. Its meaning is that nothing which can be lacking for salvation can be lacking where charity is, not that nothing can be lacking for perfection in virtues. No one perishes while possessing charity, but not all are equal in it.

PHILOSOPHER. Do not be troubled that we introduce many views or opinions, so that from all of them we may draw out the truth of the arguments. Those who seek a place which they do not yet know must explore many paths in order to choose the more direct one. Thus I am compelled now to do this in investigating the highest good, setting forth, at your invitation, the opinions of our elders or my own.

CHRISTIAN. It would not trouble me if something were advanced as an opinion which, even if it were not true, possessed at least some appearance of soundness. For what is plainly false needs no refutation by argument.

PHILOSOPHER. What if we call the supreme good of man that state of the future life, by comparison with the goods of the present life? For when you say that two ends have been set before us by God—the supreme good in heaven and the supreme evil in hell—you understand this only in relation to the good or evil condition of the present life. Reason indeed suggests to us six states of human beings: three in this life, and correspondingly three others in the future life. The first state of a human being is that in which he is born, while reason has not yet been awakened in him and he has not attained free choice, so that, according to what he chooses, he may be called a good or an evil man, although he himself is a good thing, or a good substance or creature. From this first state of man, when he has been brought to the age of discernment and knowingly inclined himself toward good or evil, he is now made a good or evil man and has entered upon a good or evil human condition. The first state of man is, as it were, indifferent, and is to be called neither good nor evil [fol. 33v]. The second is good if he rises toward virtues, evil if he descends toward vices. Likewise the future life has three states: one, as it were, indifferent, neither properly blessed nor miserable—namely, the state of those whose condition in this life too was indifferent, as we said, since they were altogether devoid of merits, reason not yet having been awakened in them [Col. 1651A]; another best according to merits, and another worst. I think that these latter two, in comparison with the two corresponding states of the present life of those who merit them, are called the supreme good and the supreme evil, because no adversity or prosperity is mixed with them; whereas the other two are plainly mixed with such things, so that no equality either of good or of evil belongs to them.

CHRISTIAN. Behold: according to you, the supreme good is to be understood as that rest of the heavenly life, just as, conversely, the supreme evil is that future condemnation of the wicked. As you recalled, we ourselves acquire both through our merits, by which, as by certain paths, one arrives there.

PHILOSOPHER. So I think, and it is plain. For among those who embrace the natural law no position is held more firmly than that virtue suffices for blessedness, and that virtues alone make one blessed; by no other path does anyone attain that name. Conversely, it is established that no one becomes truly miserable except through vices. Thus, as virtues are paths to the supreme good, so vices are paths to the supreme evil.

CHRISTIAN.
