Since you now seem to have come somewhat near to the supreme good of man, as also to his supreme evil, and have moreover touched upon their paths, I should like to loosen the reins of your objections a little for the course, so that you may reach the goal of your undertaking more quickly and may be judged more truly and perfectly concerning the completion of your work [fol. 34r]. Having therefore shown what you call the supreme good or supreme evil of man, it remains for you carefully to define and distinguish these paths of theirs which you mentioned—namely virtues and vices—so that they may be sought or avoided the more effectively as they are better known.

PHILOSOPHER. Virtue, they say, is the best habit of the soul; and conversely I judge vice to be the worst habit of the soul. By this habit we mean that which Aristotle distinguished in the *Categories*, when he comprehended the first species of quality under “habit” and “disposition.” A habit, therefore, is a quality of a thing not naturally implanted, but acquired through application and deliberation, and difficult to change. Therefore we do not count among virtues what some call natural chastity in certain persons—arising, that is, from bodily coldness or some natural constitution that never endures any struggle of concupiscence over which it might triumph, and therefore obtains no merit—nor any qualities of soul that are easily changed. For where there is no battle of resistance, there is no crown of conquering virtue, according also to that saying of your great philosopher: “He who has not contended lawfully shall not be crowned” [II Tim. 2:5]. Hence too that statement of Philosophy herself to Boethius in Book IV of the *Consolation*: “Virtue is so called because, relying on its own powers, it is not overcome by adversities.” Here too, asserting that every virtue is difficult to change, when expounding Aristotle in the aforesaid treatment of quality and placing the sciences and virtues among habits, she says [fol. 34v]: “For virtue, unless it is difficult to change, is not virtue. For one who judges justly once is not just, nor is one who commits adultery once an adulterer, but only when this will and thought has persisted.”

The best habit of the soul is that which forms us for the merit of true blessedness. Such are the individual species of virtue, of which some have posited more and others fewer. Socrates, through whom the study of moral discipline first, or especially, gained strength, distinguishes four species of virtue: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. Some, however, call prudence or discernment the mother or origin of the virtues rather than a virtue. Prudence, indeed, is this very knowledge of morals, which, as ethical treatise teaches, is called knowledge of good and evil things—that is, the very discernment of goods and evils which are properly called good or evil in themselves. For some things are properly and, as it were, substantially called good or evil in themselves, such as the virtues and vices themselves; others are so called accidentally and through something else. For example, the actions of our deeds, though indifferent in themselves, are nevertheless called good or evil from the intention out of which they proceed. Hence it often happens that when the same thing is done by different persons, or by the same person at different times, the same deed is called good or evil according to the differing intentions. But things called good or evil substantially and by their own nature remain permanently unmixed, so that what is once good can never become evil, or conversely. The discernment, then, of such goods and evils is called prudence [Col. 1652C].

This discernment, because it can belong equally to wicked and good persons and possesses no merit, is rightly called neither a virtue nor the best habit of the soul. Hence Aristotle, distinguishing sciences from virtues, when he gave examples under “habit” in the aforesaid treatment of quality, says: “Such are sciences or virtues.” Explaining this passage, Boethius says: “For Aristotle does not consider virtues to be sciences, as Socrates does.” Likewise Augustine—who, as I have already recalled above, was first ours and afterward yours—sometimes extends the name of virtue even to faith and hope, and sometimes restricts it to charity alone, which is proper and special to the good, whereas the other two are common to both reprobate and elect. For it is written: “Faith without works is idle.”

> Note: [Col. 1651] James 2:17: faith without works is called **νεκρὰ καθ’ ἑαυτήν**, “dead in itself.”

And “the hope of the wicked shall perish” [Prov. 10:28]. Just as faith or hope without works becomes useless—or rather harmful—to us, so too does prudence. For we are more guilty when knowingly we avoid what ought to be done, or do what ought not to be done, than if this occurred through ignorance, which might offer some excuse. Hence too is the saying you know: “The servant who knows and does not do his master’s will shall be beaten with many stripes” [Luke 12:47]. And elsewhere: “It would have been better not to know the way of truth than, after knowing it, to turn back.” Prudence, therefore, like faith and hope, which belong to evil persons as much as to good, should be called not so much virtues as a kind of guidance or inducement toward virtues [fol. 35v].

CHRISTIAN. I think that this is enough for the moment about prudence. It remains now to proceed to the remaining virtues, as Socrates holds.

PHILOSOPHER. Justice, then, is a virtue which, with the common advantage safeguarded, gives each person his due rank. This is the virtue by which we will that each person should have what he deserves, provided this does no injury to the common good. For it often happens that, while we render to someone what is his according to his merits, something done individually in one person inflicts common injury. Therefore, lest the part prejudice the whole and what is individual prejudice the community, the phrase “with the common advantage safeguarded” has been added. For all that we do ought rightly to be directed to this end: that in all things each person attend not so much to his own good as to the common good, provide not so much for his household as for the state, and live not so much for himself as for his country.

Hence Socrates, that first and greatest teacher of moral philosophy, judged that all things ought to be brought into common ownership and applied to the common benefit. Thus he instituted that wives should be common, so that no one would recognize children as his own; that is, they should believe the children to have been born not so much for themselves as for their country, so that this community of wives is understood not in carnal intercourse but in the fruit of offspring. Aulus left this as an example to posterity both in word and deed by killing his own son, saying that he had begotten him not for Catiline against his country, but for his country against Catiline [fol. 36r]. Inflamed with zeal for justice, and seeing in his son not his own son but an enemy of his country, he displayed the aforesaid definition of justice not so much with his mouth as with his hand.

Whoever, therefore, is constant in this will of which we have spoken, so that he cannot easily be moved from it, possesses justice as a virtue, even if he is not yet perfected in fortitude and temperance. But because those things which are difficult to lose may nevertheless sometimes be abandoned under the pressure of some great intervening cause, just as this good will called justice disappears through some fear or desire, fortitude is necessary against fear and temperance against desire. For fear of something we do not want, or desire for something we do want, if they are so great as to prevail over reason, easily draw the mind away from one purpose and lead it into the opposite. Therefore fortitude takes up a shield against fear, and temperance a bridle against desire, so that, strengthened by these, we may be able, insofar as lies in us, to accomplish what we now will through the virtue of justice. Accordingly, we call each of these a certain firmness and constancy of soul, by which we are made capable of fulfilling what we will through justice.

Their opposites are rightly called certain weaknesses of soul and incapacities for resisting vices: cowardice or faint-heartedness, which make a person slack, and intemperance, which loosens us into shameful pleasures or disgraceful desires [Col. 1654A]. Fortitude is considered—that is, rational—endurance of labours and undertaking of dangers. It is the virtue that makes us ready to undertake dangers or endure labours as occasion requires. This depends chiefly upon love of justice, which we call good zeal in repelling or avenging evils. Temperance is the firm and moderated rule of reason over lust and other unrighteous impulses of the soul. For we often exceed the measure while seeming to ourselves temperate, and so transgress the bounds of temperance: when, while pursuing sobriety, we afflict ourselves with excessive fasts; and while wishing to subdue vice, we extinguish nature itself; and thus, by excess in many things, we establish as virtues vices adjacent to them. Hence, rightly, after “firm” was said, “moderated” was added.

Over this reason, certainly, the reason of prudence itself must preside, which, as we have said, they call the mother of virtues—that is, their origin and nurse. Unless through it we know the virtues beforehand and can carefully distinguish them not only from contrary and manifest vices but even from neighbouring ones, we shall never apply ourselves to acquiring or preserving virtues which we do not know. Hence whoever is perfected in these virtues must possess prudence, through which justice, which dispenses deserts, knows what is due to each person. Fortitude has discernment in undertaking dangers or enduring labours; temperance, as has been said, has moderation in restraining desires [Col. 1654C]. It is established, therefore, that a person is made complete and perfected in goodness by these three virtues which we have named and in which prudence cannot be lacking. It remains now to distinguish their species or parts, so that we may know them more carefully and, pursuing their teaching item by item, judge it more truly.

CHRISTIAN. Indeed, since this pleases you and ought to please you, we desire that it be done.

PHILOSOPHER. To justice, then, which preserves for each person what is his, belong, to speak briefly, reverence, beneficence, truthfulness, and vindication.

[Col. 1654D] **What reverence is**

We call reverence that part of justice by which we are disposed willingly to render due veneration to all: to God, which is called religion, and to human beings worthy by authority or some merit, which is called observance. The virtue of obedience is plainly included here: by complying with the commands of superiors, we also pay them honour, because we do not despise their reasonable ordinances.

**What beneficence is**

Beneficence is that by which we are ready to give due aid in human relationships: either by giving necessities to those in need, which is called generosity—though wastefulness consists in superfluities—or by freeing those violently oppressed, which is called clemency [Col. 1655A].

But our elders called mercy, so named from the miserable, a vice or a certain weakness of soul rather than a virtue: by it we desire to assist others merely because we naturally suffer with them in their affliction. Clemency, however, is directed to assisting some persons only by rational affection; it attends not so much to their suffering as to their suffering unjustly, so that, by opposing injustice, it obeys justice. Otherwise, when we assist others, these are not works of justice unless we render to each person what is his. Moreover, since virtue is a habit of the soul acquired, as is clear from what has been said above, through application or study rather than by nature, such natural compassion must by no means be referred to the virtues. By it we endeavour to assist even persons guilty of crimes when they are afflicted, out of a certain human or carnal rather than rational feeling, thereby opposing justice instead, lest penalties due to them be rendered.

Finally, to subject the soul to grief belongs rather to weakness than virtue, to misery rather than blessedness, and to a troubled rather than tranquil mind. Since nothing happens without a cause, while God disposes all things most excellently, what can occur by reason of which a just person ought to be sad or grieve, and thus, insofar as he can, oppose God’s best ordering, as though he judged it needed correction?

**What truthfulness is**

Truthfulness is that by which we strive to keep those things for which, by promising, we make ourselves debtors [fol. 38r]. For if we promise what ought not to be promised, we do not become guilty by failing to fulfil it; an evil promise has not made us debtors for it. For the person who carries out what ought not to have been promised doubles his disposition toward evil action, since he joins a perverse deed to a perverse promise, and does not choose to correct the evil promise by refraining from the deed.

**What vindication is**

Vindication is the constant disposition by which due punishment is inflicted for evils committed. In each of these four parts of justice, however, what we placed beforehand in the definition—namely, “with the common advantage safeguarded”—is plainly to be understood. For, as we also recalled above, this ought to be the end of our works: that each person seek not so much private as common advantages, and live not so much for himself as for all, in accordance with what Lucan sings in praise of Cato:

> For he alone, free from partisan pursuits and devoid of hatreds,  
> Has leisure to mourn the human race . . . . . .
>
> . . . . . Such were the manners, this the fixed school  
> Of stern Cato: to preserve moderation and hold to the end,  
> To follow nature, to devote life to his country,  
> And to believe himself born not for himself but for the whole world. And after some lines:
>
> . . . . . He is father to the city, and husband to the city  
> . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  
> Good for the common good.

> Note: [Col. 1655D] Lucan, *Pharsalia*, Book II, verses 377 ff., 388 ff.; Leiden, 1740, quarto.

For to attend to one’s own advantages belongs to weak nature; to attend to those of others, to outstanding virtue. He who cares only for himself, is content with his own advantages, and earns neither gratitude nor praise from others ought to value his own life little [fol. 38v]. Each person ought, according to his own measure, to imitate God, who, though he needs no one, takes no care for himself but for all; he supplies not what is necessary for himself but for all, as the administrator of the entire fabric of the world, as though of one great commonwealth.

There are those who distinguish the parts of justice by a larger number, not of things but of names; they divide into several names most of what we have included under one term, distinguishing into parts what is contained in the whole: filial devotion toward parents; friendship, that is, benevolence toward those who love us, more for their own sake than in hope of some advantage, when their will toward us is equal; and gratitude, in the repayment of benefits. But these three plainly fall under beneficence, through which the soul is ready to render whatever beneficence is due, both to parents and to others.

**On natural and positive justice**

In matters pertaining to justice, one must not exceed the path of either natural or positive justice. For one law is called natural and another positive. Natural law is what the reason naturally present in all persuades us must be fulfilled in action, and therefore remains among all peoples: for example, worshipping God, loving parents, punishing the wicked, and whatever observance is necessary for everyone, without which no merits can ever suffice [Col. 1656C].

Positive justice, however, is that which, instituted by human beings in order more securely to defend or enlarge utility or honour, rests either upon custom alone or upon the authority of written law. Such are the penalties of punishments or judicial decisions in examining accusations: among some peoples there is the practice of duels or of heated iron; among others an oath is the end of every controversy, and every inquiry is conducted by witnesses. Hence it follows that we must observe, among whatever people we live, the institutions we have mentioned as well as natural laws.

Even the laws which you call divine—the Old and New Testaments—hand down some natural precepts, which you call moral: to love God or one’s neighbour, not to commit adultery, not to steal, not to become a murderer. But others are, as it were, of positive justice, adapted to certain persons according to circumstances: circumcision for the Jews and baptism for you, and many other things whose precepts you call figurative. Roman pontiffs likewise, or synodal assemblies, daily establish new decrees or grant certain dispensations, by which you maintain that things formerly lawful become unlawful, or conversely—as though God had placed it in their power or permissions to make good or evil things which previously were not so, and as though their authority could prejudice our law.

> Editorial note: “I have corrected the passage from Burman’s edition.”

It remains now, after considering justice, to turn the pen to the other two species of virtue.

**On the parts of fortitude**

Fortitude, then, seems to us to be comprised of two parts: magnanimity and endurance.

Magnanimity is that by which, for the sake of a rational being, we are prepared to undertake any arduous task. Endurance is that by which we persevere steadfastly in what we have begun with this purpose [fol. 39v].

**On the parts of temperance**

The parts of temperance, in my view—and I do not think you disapprove—are these: humility, frugality, gentleness, chastity, and sobriety.

Humility is that by which we so restrain ourselves from the desire for empty glory that we do not desire to appear greater than we are.

Frugality is the bridle of superfluous expenditure, by which we refuse to possess more things than are necessary. Likewise gentleness is the bridle of anger, chastity of lust, and sobriety of gluttony.

And it should be noted that, whereas justice is the constant will of the soul that preserves for each person what is his, fortitude and temperance are certain powers and strength of soul by which, as we recalled above, the good will of justice is confirmed. For since their opposites are incapacities, these plainly must be powers. Weakness of soul, opposed to fortitude, is a certain infirmity and incapacity of it, which we may call cowardice or faint-heartedness. Intemperance too, opposed to temperance, is a certain weakness and incapacity of soul, unable to resist the assaults of its irrational motions. By these, as though by certain attendants, the weak mind is drawn into the wretched captivity of vices and becomes the slave of those over which it ought to rule [Col. 1657C].

Now, just as justice is that good will of which we have spoken, injustice is the contrary will. Justice makes a person good, whereas fortitude and temperance make him upright, because what through justice we will, through these we are strong enough to accomplish. You think, moreover, that I have at present distinguished the species or parts of virtue so that all the degrees by which one reaches blessedness and attains the supreme good according to merits are included in them. Now, if it seems good to your prudence, we are ready to receive what you have decided to approve or disapprove in these matters, or what perhaps you judge should be added for perfection.

CHRISTIAN. That is indeed fitting. But before we come to those degrees of the supreme good which you have set forth, let us return to the interrupted, not abandoned, dispute about the supreme good or supreme evil, and determine what is called simply the supreme good or supreme evil, and whether the supreme good is something other than the supreme good of man, or the supreme evil something other than the supreme evil of man.

**Return to the interrupted inquiry concerning the supreme good**

PHILOSOPHER. Among all who philosophize rightly, the supreme good is undeniably and rightly said and believed to be nothing other than God. His incorporeal and ineffable blessedness, knowing neither beginning nor end, can neither increase nor decrease. But I judge the supreme evil to be the greatest misery or torment of punishment belonging to any being whatever, whether a human being or another creature. The supreme good or supreme evil of man, however, I understand—as I have already recalled and defined above—to be the rest or eternal punishment of his future life. I think, therefore, that this is the difference between the supreme good and the supreme good of man: as is clear from what has been said, the supreme good is God himself, or the supreme tranquillity of his blessedness, which we nevertheless judge to be nothing other than himself [Col. 1658B], who is blessed from himself and not from elsewhere. But the supreme good of man is that perpetual rest or joy which each person receives after this life according to merits, whether, as you say, in the very vision or knowledge of God, or in whatever other way it occurs. The supreme evil, as I have said, is the greatest misery or punishment which any creature undergoes according to merits. But the supreme evil of man is whatever torments human beings undergo there according to merits.

**On the supreme evil**

CHRISTIAN. As I understand you, you mean by both the supreme evil and the supreme evil of man nothing except the punishments of the future age, rendered according to merits?

PHILOSOPHER. Certainly.

CHRISTIAN. But those punishments imposed according to merits are surely just, because it is just that those who deserved them should be punished thus. Whatever is just is evidently good. Therefore those punishments which you call the supreme evil or the supreme evil of man are without doubt good. Consider, then, whether you appear to concede that what is good rather than evil is the supreme evil. For I do not see on what reasoning you can call the supreme evil, or the supreme evil of man, something that is in no way evil.

PHILOSOPHER. You ought to remember that you yourself showed above, by the testimonies of both our writers and yours, that every affliction is evil rather than good. Yet I do not think that one must therefore concede that every affliction is evil in the feminine sense [*mala*]. For a change of grammatical gender in adjectives often changes the meaning: it is one thing to say that a punishment is good [*poenam esse bonam*], and another to say that a punishment is a good thing [*poenam esse bonum*], that is, a good object.

Thus it is one thing to say that this bronze statue is everlasting, which is false; another that it is an everlasting thing, that is, some thing that is everlasting, which is true—for example, bronze itself, whose nature is enduring and unfailing. Likewise, although every proposition is something composite, we do not call every proposition “composite,” but only one that has propositions among its parts—that is, a hypothetical proposition [fol. 41r]. Nor do we call every word “composite” which we know to be a composite thing, nor shall we concede that everything we call “simple” is a simple thing.

Accordingly, when we say that some punishment is just or good, because it is just or good that the person being tortured should be afflicted, we are not thereby compelled to concede that the punishment is itself a just or good thing. You likewise maintain that every creature is good because nothing created by God is not good; and you do not deny that a human being is a creature, and therefore concede that a wicked person is a good thing. Yet you do not therefore accept that he is a good human being. For no human being is to be called good unless he is adorned with good morals. But even an irrational and inanimate thing can be called a good thing or good creature.

When God is said to have created all things good, and this little human being or horse has already been created by him, although he was created a good thing, he was not thereby created a good human being or a good horse. Nor did God create this little one, who will be perverse, either a good or evil human being; rather, he made him a good thing, a substance of good nature. Nor did he ever create as a good horse the horse that will never be good, though he may appear to create some defective horses, which are said to acquire some defect in their very creation, so that later they become useless or of little use.

It is also evident that human beings themselves naturally acquire certain defects from the composition of the elements in their very creation, so that they become naturally irascible, lustful, or ensnared in other vices [fol. 41v]. Nor, perhaps, did he create as a good angel or good spirit that angel set above the others as, so to speak, Lucifer, whom you say afterward apostatized, and whom you say never stood in the truth—

> Note: [Col. 1659] John 8:44: **ἐν τῇ ἀληθείᾳ οὐκ ἕστηκεν**, “he has not stood in the truth.” Compare I John 3:8.

—and in the love of God, since most of you deny that charity once possessed can ever be lost. For no angel, spirit, or human being alien from the love of God and true charity is rightly called good, just as neither is he called evil so long as he is free from sin. Therefore, if that angel was created neither with sin nor with the charity of God, how can he be said to have been created as yet either a good or an evil angel?

Likewise, individual human beings, when they are created and do not yet possess the use of reason, are not to be called good or evil human beings by reason of their creation, since by their creation itself they have not received the condition of being good or evil human beings. Some of them are naturally born sickly or foolish and are born afflicted by various defects both of soul and body; and all human beings without exception are created mortal. Thus the substance of human nature, good by virtue of its creation, shares in many evils through that very creation.

For, as Aristotle recalls and manifest truth maintains, nothing can be contrary to good except evil. It is clear, then, that mortality and the other things just mentioned with which we are born must be counted as evils, since no one doubts that their contraries are good; and that certain defects or evils naturally belong, by creation itself, to certain good substances—for example, mortality to a human being and irrationality to a horse. Although mortality is not called a defect of a human being, since no one is worse than another by reason of it and all share it equally, it is nevertheless a defect of nature in the human being, because in this respect human nature is worse or weaker than immortal nature [Col. 1660A].

Therefore, just as we concede that any human being, however much he may be disfigured by defects, is a good thing, yet do not thereby grant that he is a good human being, so conversely we declare that any punishment is an evil thing, although we maintain that some punishment is good. See, then, that it does not follow that, if we establish that a good and just punishment is the supreme evil of man, we therefore believe that what is good is his supreme evil. For even if, as has been said, that punishment is good, it must not on that account be called simply good—that is, a good thing.

CHRISTIAN. Let it be so for the moment: as you say, you cannot be charged, from what has been conceded, with allowing that what is good is the supreme evil of man, although you do not deny that the punishment which is good and just is that supreme evil. But I ask again: since both the preceding fault and the punishment resulting from it are evil, which of these ought to be called the worse and greater evil of man—his fault, which makes him evil, or punishment, which, imposed by God, carries out a just judgment upon him?

PHILOSOPHER. Certainly, in my judgment, a person’s fault is a worse evil than his punishment. For among any evils, no one doubts that one is greater than another when it displeases God more and is more deserving of punishment. Who, then, would doubt that fault is worse than the punishment for fault? By fault a person displeases God, and from it he is called evil; not from punishment, which is imposed for fault. For the former is injustice; the latter is the due effect of justice and proceeds rightly from intention. It is plain, therefore, that in a person what makes him guilty is worse than what, by punishing, carries out just judgment upon him.

CHRISTIAN. Since, then, a human being’s fault is a greater evil of man than his punishment, how do you call his punishment his supreme evil, when, as has been said, fault is a greater evil?

PHILOSOPHER. If you disapprove our opinion on this matter, I should be pleased to hear your own judgment: what do you consider should be called the supreme evil of man?

CHRISTIAN. That which can make him worse, just as conversely his supreme good is that by which he is made better.

PHILOSOPHER. And what, I ask, are these things?

CHRISTIAN. His greatest hatred and his greatest love for God [Col. 1661A]. By these two, a person is known to displease more or please more the one who is simply and properly called the supreme good. Both, indeed, follow after this life. For those tortured by everlasting and most severe punishments, the more heavily they feel themselves burdened by them, the more they burn with greater hatred against him by whose judgment they are punished, from despair of pardon itself. They would wish him not to exist at all, so that they might thus at least be free from punishment; and there they are far worse through hatred than they were here through contempt.

Conversely, whoever enjoy that vision of God of which the Psalmist says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” [Ps. 17:5], that is, “after you have made known to me through yourself the majesty of your divinity, I shall seek nothing further, needing nothing”—these then become better in proportion as they love more deeply him whom they behold more truly in himself. Thus that greatest love, that enjoyment of the supreme good, which is true blessedness, is rightly called the supreme good of man. For so great is the glory of that divine majesty that no one can behold it without immediately becoming blessed in that very vision. Hence it is also said: “Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God” [Isa. 26:10, according to the Septuagint]. When his faithful ones, who loved him above all things, have beheld such blessedness as they could in no way estimate by faith, their highest exultation will be their everlasting blessedness.

PHILOSOPHER. It pleases me, then, that the supreme good or evil of man should be understood as that by which a person is made better or worse, as you say. But if it happens in the future life that we become better or worse there than we are here, then we seem also to merit something more there than here. For by whatever we become better or worse than before, we are judged worthy of a greater punishment or reward. And if there too the disposition becomes better, so that, the more we know God, the more we love him, and our love of God grows together with the reward itself, so that we are continually made better, then the increase of our blessedness is extended to infinity, so that it is never complete, because it always receives increase.

CHRISTIAN. Do you not know that in this life alone there is time for meriting, and in the other for receiving recompense—here, that is, for sowing; there, for gathering? Although, therefore, by the reward of merits we are made better there than we had been here by our merits, it does not follow that we must again merit anything there. Indeed, the very fact that we are made better there than here is the recompense of merits acquired here; and this recompense, bestowed for merits, makes us better, but does not itself deserve a further reward, since it has been established solely as the reward of merits, not as something by which merit may again be acquired. For among us too, when someone receives from a friend a recompense for friendship and loves him more because of it, he is not judged to deserve a further reward from him because of this greater love, which has arisen from the reward bestowed, so that merit should extend thus to infinity. For although love is increased by the constraint of obligation and by the repayment of a reward, and thus seems not so much voluntary as necessary, such an affection is naturally implanted in everyone: the repayment of reward itself brings with it some increase of love and kindles us to love the giver, by a kind of necessity—or rather by self-love than by virtue or love of the one rewarding us. If, then, among human beings a friend receives a reward from a friend and is compelled by the reward itself to love him more, yet is not said thereby to merit again from this increase of love, what wonder is it if in the other life, loving God more because of the reward received, we do not turn that reward itself again into merit? Or finally, what prevents us from granting that the glory of the divine majesty is so great that there may always be some progress in its vision, so that the longer we behold it and the more fully it makes itself known to us, the more blessed it makes us? For this continual increase of blessedness is worth more than a greater blessedness that keeps only one measure and advances in no increase.

PHILOSOPHER. How, I ask, can there be any progress in that vision of God, or any difference among those who see him, since that highest good is wholly simple and can never be seen unless it can be seen in its entirety, nor can one person see anything that another does not see?

CHRISTIAN. The difference is certainly not in the thing seen, but in the manner of seeing it, so that the better God is understood, the more our blessedness is increased in his vision. For in understanding any soul or spirit, we do not all understand it equally, although the parts of an incorporeal nature are said not to possess quantity in the magnitude of their essence. And when some body, or a part of it, is viewed simultaneously by several persons, it is known better by one person than by another and understood more perfectly; though the object understood is the same, they do not perceive its nature equally. Thus God grants to this person a more perfect and better knowledge of himself than to that one, in accordance with merits, and reveals himself more fully. It may happen that, although this person knows everything that the other knows, he nevertheless knows each thing better and more perfectly than the other; and although as many things are known by this person as by that, one does not have as many kinds of knowledge concerning the same things as the other, or does not know the same things as well.

PHILOSOPHER. Did the angels whom you say fell never possess that vision of God in which true blessedness consists? Or at least did not the chief among them, who in comparison with the rest is likened to Lucifer?

CHRISTIAN. Certainly one must believe that neither any of those who fell, nor even those who did not fall, possessed it until, after the fall of the others, they received this vision as the recompense of their humility—the vision through which they were at once made blessed and confirmed, so that they could fall no more. For all angels, like human beings, were created such that they could act well or badly. Otherwise those who did not sin would have no merit from the very fact that they did not consent to sin with the others. That Lucifer was endowed with the privilege of a certain excellence came not so much from blessedness as from keenness of knowledge: namely, because, being more eminent than the rest in the light of knowledge, he was created more subtle in understanding whatever natures of things there might be. Reflecting upon this within himself, he swelled with pride through the very greatness of his knowledge, by which he saw himself set above the rest; and he presumed to aspire to greater things than he could hope for—namely, because he knew himself superior to the rest, he thought himself capable of becoming equal to God and of obtaining a kingdom as God does.

PHILOSOPHER. I beg you also to determine whether this highest good of man—I mean that highest love of God which a human being receives from the vision of God—should be called an accident of man; and whether it is fitting in turn to call an accident the highest good, as though it were to be preferred to substance itself.

CHRISTIAN. You turn to “accidents,” “substances subject to them,” and the terms of philosophical teaching, and measure only what belongs to earthly, not heavenly, life. For this secular and earthly discipline has been content with those teachings alone that are suited to the condition of the present life, not to the character of that future life, to which neither these terms nor any human teaching of the arts has applied its rules in investigating the natures of things. Rather, as it is written: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth” (John 3:31). If, therefore, you strive to ascend to that height of heavenly life which far surpasses every earthly discipline, do not rely too heavily upon the rules of earthly philosophy, by which earthly matters themselves have not yet been fully comprehended and defined—much less heavenly things.

But whether that love which is said to be possessed in heavenly life is an accident or some kind of quality brings no usefulness in determining it, since it cannot truly be known except by experiencing it, because it far surpasses every capacity of earthly knowledge. And what does it matter for blessedness whether we hold it to be an accident, a substance, or neither, since whatever we say or suppose, it is not thereby changed nor does it diminish our blessedness? Indeed, if you carefully consider what your philosophers have said about accidents and substantial forms, you will see it to be neither substantial, because it is not present in all, nor accidental, because once present it cannot be absent. Your own definition of an accident is that which can be present and absent.

What also prevents us from allowing that the love to exist there, like the love we have here in the present, is an accident? Although our substance is reckoned better or more worthy than any of its accidents, nevertheless the highest good of man seems not improperly to be called that which, by participation in itself, makes the human being supremely good and most worthy. Or, to speak more truly and more plausibly, let us establish God himself—who alone is properly and absolutely called the highest good—as also the highest good of man. By participation in that vision of himself which we have mentioned, we become truly blessed. For from the very one whom we see in him, that highest love of him flows into us; and therefore it is more correct to call him himself, who is not from another and makes us thus blessed, the highest good of man.

PHILOSOPHER. Indeed, that opinion concerning the highest good pleases me; nor is it unknown to our prophetic teaching. But if, as you say, this vision of God which makes people blessed is open only to the eyes of the mind and not of the body, why is it necessary, as you say, for holy souls finally to resume their bodies, as though their glory or blessedness were thereby increased? For if, as you say, “the measure of man is the measure of an angel,” what benefit does the resumption of bodies bring to your blessedness, when their absence from angels in no way hinders or diminishes their blessedness?

CHRISTIAN. God directs all that he does not so much to our blessedness as to his own glory, even those things that are harmful to some. Thus Solomon says: “God made all things for himself, even the wicked for the evil day” (Prov. 16:4). Even the punishment by which God punishes the wicked person’s iniquity commends God’s justice and thus glorifies him. Therefore, even if we held that the resumption of bodies contributed nothing to the blessedness of holy souls, we would not judge it superfluous, since it greatly serves the praise of divine power. For the weaker and more subject to suffering we have known them to be before, the more it afterward shows God to be glorified. And when we see them made so strong and indissoluble that no suffering can arise for us from them and no dissolution can occur in them, souls seem thereby also to gain something of blessedness, because the more fully they experience the greatness of divine power, the more fully they love him; and it must not be denied that they are made more blessed.

PHILOSOPHER. I beg you also to explain clearly whether that vision of God in which blessedness consists can be increased or diminished by a difference of place; whether it can be displayed to all in every place; or whether some definite place has been assigned to it, to which those who are to enjoy that vision must necessarily come.

CHRISTIAN. Those who do not doubt that God is everywhere through the greatness of his power believe all places to be present to him, so that in all of them he can do whatever he wills, and that both the places themselves and all things in them are governed or ordered by his operation. Such persons ought not to be troubled by this question. For he is the one who, even now, existing without local position as he existed before times, is not so much to be said to be in a place—since he is in no way local—as to contain all places in himself, holding even the heavens, as Scripture says, in the span of his hand (Isa. 40:12). He who existed before all things without place, who made places not for his own limitation but for ours, whose blessedness can neither be diminished nor increased nor undergo any variation, and who has no local position or any perfection to acquire, since his wholly simple and incorporeal eternity endures.

Therefore, although he is nowhere locally—that is, enclosed by local position—he is nevertheless said to be everywhere in all places through the power of his operation upon all places. For in every place nothing occurs unless he orders it; and thus all places are present to him, or he to them, so that whatever he wills to occur there must occur. Thus, as has been said, he is everywhere through the greatness of his power. Hence he speaks through the prophet concerning himself: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24). And the Psalmist, considering that he could nowhere escape the power of the angry God, said: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present,” and so forth (Ps. 139:7–8).

But just as he is said to be in all places, or within all things, by the operation or ordering of his power, because all things there must be ordered by him, so also, as enclosing places, he is likewise said to be around them: that is, to hold them so in his power that nothing can occur in them without him or his ordering. Since, therefore, God is by his power, as stated, both within and outside all things, and penetrates all things, however solid they may be, by his own power, what place can hinder him from imparting his knowledge equally wherever he wills to all whom he wills? For in the manner in which he is said to be in or over every place by power and not by local position, he is able everywhere to impart knowledge of himself to whomever he wills; and the highest spiritual power, for which all existing places are passable, cannot be impeded by any solidity or quality.

For when the brightness of the sun penetrates the most solid glass so that it sheds its illumination upon us even through it, and when we believe that our bodies after the resurrection will possess such subtlety that, having in some manner become spiritual, no material can obstruct them—whence the Lord’s body, born before his death while the womb was closed, after the resurrection, immortal and incapable of suffering, entered to the disciples though the doors were shut—how much more must we believe that the vision of that supreme divine brightness can be hindered by no obstacle or assisted in illuminating by nearness of place? You also say that fire, which is subtler than the other elements, is not subject to cutting, because its parts cannot be divided by any body placed between them. Much less, then, is a spiritual substance, far subtler than every body, obstructed by a bodily barrier.

But if divinity is of such subtlety that, in comparison with it, every other nature is judged bodily and it alone is judged incorporeal in relation to the others, how can its supreme brightness, which comprehends all things by knowing them, have any obstacle? Those who enjoy this brightness, when they see all things, do not fail to know whatever they ought to know, however remote it may be. Otherwise those enjoying paradise would not behold the torments of hell, so that they might love God more as they see that through his grace they have escaped greater evils.

The Lord Jesus clearly intimates that this paradise consists everywhere in the vision of God itself when, on the very day on which his soul, having suffered in the flesh, descended to hell in order to free his own from there, he said to the thief who confessed him: “Truly I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Nor was the soul of Christ then excluded from that paradise, even when, as has been said, it descended into hell.

Accordingly, by this faith and evident reasoning of ours, wherever a faithful soul may be, because it finds God everywhere present, as has been said, and because it is hindered by no obstacle, it remains everywhere equally in its blessedness—a blessedness which we attain from the vision of God infused into us by him, not seized by our own powers. For we do not ascend in order to grasp the brightness of the bodily sun; rather, it pours itself into us so that we may enjoy it. Thus both we draw near to God and he to us, as though pouring down upon us his brightness and the warmth of his love. If we are said somehow to draw near to him, who is nowhere locally situated, this must be understood to occur not by places but by merits: namely, insofar as we are made more like him in goodness or more fully agree with his will. Conversely, we must understand ourselves to withdraw from him.

The venerable teacher Augustine, highly skilled also in your teachings, carefully explains this: “With God, who is everywhere, we are near or far not by places but by morals.” Hence, although after the resurrection the bodies of the saints will be so capable of movement that they are believed to be wherever their souls will, no departure of theirs will obstruct the vision of God so as to prevent their souls from being blessed; nor can any quality of place be punitive for those in whom there will be nothing to punish, just as before sin nothing could be harmful to the first human beings.

Thus, when holy angels sent to us carry out God’s commands, they are not deprived or emptied of the vision in which they are blessed by any quality or distance of place. Nor are demons dwelling in the air, and therefore called “birds of heaven,” to be said to draw nearer to God than we do merely because they appear, by their local position, to be above us. God is superior to every nature by the dignity proper to his nature. Thus Satan, coming among the sons of God, standing in the Lord’s presence, and conversing reciprocally, as is written in the book of Job (Job 1), is not by this coming relieved of his misery so as to become more blessed. By falling from the highest of the heavens, he openly showed that the dignity of a place contributes nothing to blessedness.

For it is not because, coming among the sons of God—that is, among the holy angels—he stood in the presence of God, that the Lord came into his sight so as to be seen by him; rather, he is seen by the Lord, like a blind person standing in the sunlight among people who see, differing from them not by position of place but by the benefit of light. What the condition of bodies accomplishes in the vision of the bodily sun, the quality of merits accomplishes in the vision of the spiritual sun. And just as here there is no difference of powers in the quality of bodies or places, so there is no difference there in recompenses. The vision of divine glory by which people are made blessed appears all the more wonderful because it can neither be hindered nor aided in this by any quality or diversity of place; for even among those who are not separated by place, it acts so as to make some blessed by enlightening them and leave others miserable in their blindness, just as it does not cease to act in this life by imparting its grace.

Thus God is said to be everywhere by power, while nevertheless he is said to be present somewhere by grace and absent somewhere. Therefore, in whatever way the grace of divinity is said to be present or absent, to come or to depart, this does not happen locally or bodily, but rather spiritually or through some efficacy of his operation. For if he were everywhere locally, where could he come locally, or from where could he depart? He is sometimes said to descend to us either through some gift of his grace bestowed upon us, or through some manifestation in a visible sign, or when he performs something unusual upon the earth. Thus this sun too is said to descend to us or fill the world, not locally but effectively: that is, not by its local position but by the operation of its illumination.

PHILOSOPHER. I am surprised that you produce, in the arguments by which you seek to refute me, those authorities from your Scriptures by which you do not doubt that I am in no way compelled.

CHRISTIAN. As you know, my purpose is not to bring forward my own opinions to you, but to explain to you the common faith or teaching of our elders. The testimonies I bring from our writings, therefore, are not intended to compel you by them, but so that you may understand that these things belong more to others than were invented by myself.

PHILOSOPHER. Certainly I do not disapprove even of that, if such is your intention. But now let us hasten to the remaining matters. If, then, as you maintain, the power of the divine vision is so great that wherever souls may be it can make them equally blessed by participation in itself, why, I ask, is the kingdom of heaven assigned spiritually to God and to holy souls, so that they are said especially to be in heaven, as though they were more blessed there? Christ himself also presented this by his own example to such an extent that he bodily ascended into heaven in the sight of his followers; and there, as Scripture says, sitting at the right hand of the Father, he is promised to come from there for judgment to meet those who come to meet him in the air (Col. 3:1; 1 Thess. 4:17).

Since, therefore, no region of the world except heaven is assigned as the divine dwelling-place, if God, existing everywhere as you say, enjoys his blessedness equally everywhere, and the brightness of his vision, pouring itself equally wherever he wills into whomever he wills, makes them equally blessed everywhere, needing no help from any quality or nearness of place for this, but being wholly sufficient in itself—since, I say, the Lord exists everywhere by power and yet, as though enclosing the dwelling of his majesty in one place, says, “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1), and all writers of both the New and Old Testaments assign no other part of the world but heaven to his habitation—it may not unreasonably seem that the serenity of that higher place contributes something to their or our blessedness. Therefore Isaiah promises, for the fullness of this blessedness, that the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun and that the light of the sun shall shine sevenfold, and also that heaven and earth shall be newly created (Isa. 30:26), so that happiness may be increased even in the very nature of things.

> **Note: [Col. 1667D]** Either *nomine* should be rejected from the text, or read conjecturally: *omni* (“every”).

CHRISTIAN. If you knew how to prophesy rather than to Judaize in the letter, and knew that things said of God under a bodily image must be understood not bodily and literally, but mystically through allegory, you would not receive what is said as the common crowd does. If you follow their common opinion and your understanding does not rise above the faith of those who conceive in their minds nothing but bodily things, or things very like bodily things, you will certainly again fall into the error of being unable to understand God as anything other than a bodily thing composed of certain parts—namely, head, hands, feet, and other limbs—especially since almost all the parts of a human body are assigned to him in the Scriptures under some likeness. What uneducated or simple person could bear to hear you preach that God has neither eyes nor ears nor the other limbs that seem necessary to us? He will immediately object that one who has no such eyes cannot see, and likewise cannot hear or act if he lacks ears and hands.

Therefore, just as you judge that everything belonging to a body must be understood of God only parabolically, so do not doubt that whatever is said of divinity concerning a bodily position in place must be understood in the same manner. When, then, you hear Isaiah saying: “Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and earth the footstool of my feet. What is this house that you will build for me, and what is this place of my rest? My hand made all these things,” and so forth (Isa. 66:1–2), just as you do not understand him to be bodily, so do not understand heaven as his bodily throne, earth as the bodily footstool of his feet, or any local position of his by which he may be thought to sit.

> **Note: [Col. 1668D]** Conjecture: *quae sedes* (“what throne?”), or *qua sedere* (“by which he may sit”).

Far be it that his majesty should have any weakness such that it needs support from some throne or footstool. Therefore by “heaven” and “earth” in this place good and evil souls are distinguished, as superior and inferior according to their merits. Good souls, then, are called his temple or heaven, according to the Psalmist: “The Lord is in his holy temple; the Lord, his throne is in heaven” (Ps. 11:4), because he presides over those who are higher in merits and dwells in them by grace, as though in his own house and temple sanctified to himself. But carnal souls, namely those that pursue earthly and low desires, he tramples as a footstool, because those whom he despises and does not mercifully raise to himself, he presses down as left below, crushes by trampling, and reduces, as it were, to dust.

Therefore, says the Lord, since I do not dwell in things made by hand, and have so exalted a throne in holy souls while I hold carnal and earthly people in such contempt, why do you seek to build me a house of earthly construction as though I needed it, instead of building for me within yourselves a spiritual house? Otherwise the signification of the visible temple is empty if the invisible one is absent.

> **Note: [Col. 1669D]** Conjecture: *habitem* (“I may dwell”) or *habeam* (“I may have”).

When, therefore, you hear heaven or the kingdom of heaven called the future blessedness, understand the sublimity of the future life rather than the bodily position of heaven. That blessedness is also sometimes signified by the name “earth,” on account of its stability, just as it is called “heaven” because of its dignity. Thus the Psalmist says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 27:13). And through Ezekiel the Lord himself, promising future blessedness to his elect after the resurrection, says: “Behold, I will open your tombs and bring you out from your graves, my people; and I will bring you into the land of Israel, and I will make you rest upon your soil” (Ezek. 37:11–12).

That our Lord Christ bodily and visibly ascended the bodily heavens served not his own glory—in whom the fullness of divinity dwells bodily—but our faith. For he had previously shown, by entering to the disciples through closed doors, the subtlety of resurrected bodies, through which they can penetrate all things, in his own resurrection; afterward, in his ascension, he showed that their future lightness would be so great that they would no longer be hindered from ascending anywhere by the mass of earthliness by which they had previously been weighed down, as it is written: “A corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15), but would immediately be transported without any difficulty wherever their souls wished.

> **Note: [Col. 1669D]** Perhaps read: *non propediantur* (“are not hindered”), or *nusquam ulterius* (“no longer anywhere”); see [Col. 1670D], p. [uncertain].

Yet the statement that he ascended upward to the right hand of the Father does not mean that the Father’s right hand is bodily, nor that this sitting by which the Father sits is a local position. Rather, it expresses the power of ruling together with the Father and equal dignity, when he is said to have sat beside him at the right hand. Since sitting at the right hand cannot literally and bodily be standing, the preceding statement about his bodily ascension, though it was in fact bodily accomplished, nevertheless signifies a better ascent of his in the minds of believers. Concerning this ascent he had already said to Mary: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17). For Christ is then, as it were, lifted in a cloud from human sight into heaven, to sit at the right hand of the Father, when through the preaching of the saints he is withdrawn from the sight of his laborious life and is proclaimed as exalted in glory, reigning with the Father over all things, ruling all things as an equal substance or Son.

As for your assertion that the brightness of moon or sun will be multiplied bodily for future blessedness, it is easy to refute it both from the authority of the prophet himself who said it and from evident reason. For the Lord later speaks through the same Isaiah to Jerusalem, promising it the brightness of the future life: “You shall no longer have the sun for light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illumine you; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God your glory. Your sun shall no longer set, and your moon shall not diminish for you; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be fulfilled. But your people, all righteous, shall inherit the land,” and so forth (Isa. 60:19–21).

What is this land to be inherited by those who are righteous forever, and illuminated by the presence of divine brightness as by a sun that never sets, if not the eternity of future blessedness? Since that brightness is so great that it needs no assistance for illuminating, this sun is rightly said to cease from its office of further illumination, once we experience that which was stated before: “the measure of man, which is the measure of an angel,” no longer animal but spiritual. Who does not know that lesser lights, when greater light is added, are immediately obscured or lose their power of illuminating? What office of illumination, then, can bodily light have where the presence of divine brightness will so illuminate the hidden things of darkness that it also reveals the counsels of hearts?

“For now,” says the Apostle, “we see through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know as I am known” (1 Cor. 13:12). For then all things are known perfectly and most truly by us, as by angels, through the eyes of the heart, where the functions of all senses and of all administrations will cease, when God is all in all. His vision will so satisfy all our desires in every respect that it will itself bestow on us all things necessary for true blessedness. That vision of divine majesty will be for us unfailing light, highest holiness, perpetual rest, peace surpassing all understanding—in short, every good, every virtue, every joy.

When, therefore, God is all in all, it is clear that then, as the same Apostle says, every principality and power will be abolished, since then the sole ruling power will be that which exists principally through itself and which, as stated, supplies every good to all the elect through the presence of its vision.

> **Note: [Col. 1670D]** Colossians 2:15: “Despoiling principalities.”

No angelic or human principality will then preside over us in any administration, and no power in any government, because nothing can be lacking where God is all in all; where, when that which is perfect has come, that which is partial will be abolished. For nothing now benefits us except partially; nothing suffices to bestow all things necessary upon us. Whatever now benefits us in teaching, in some virtue, or in some administration, acts imperfectly, because God alone can do all things. Therefore whatever is done imperfectly will cease when he who can do all things is sufficient through himself.

That we shall there resume the eyes of the flesh along with the other members of the body will certainly not be for functions which we need, but in order to glorify God, as we have said. In them we shall experience his power all the more fully in proportion as we perceive them to be stronger in performing their functions, should there be need, and see them to have attained a condition far stronger and better. But even if we understand bodily, and not only mystically, the multiplication of the light of sun and moon, it should be referred to the glory of the Creator rather than to a necessity of their function. So too the whole condition of the world is to be changed for the better, in order that God may be manifestly made known to us by the assistance or transformation of the heavenly lights and of the world: namely, that its former lesser state did not arise from the Creator’s impotence, but from the condition of mortal and weak life, which could neither endure such great things nor was worthy to use such great benefits.

Yet it is easy to understand mystically that the moon will then shine as the sun: that is, that the Church of the elect, like its sun, God, will possess unfailing light; and that then the light of this moon will be surpassed by its sun so completely that perfection of light will be in him alone, signified by the number seven.

PHILOSOPHER. As far as I can see, if these things are as you say, God seems to owe much to your faith, whose glory you especially proclaim in all things. It remains now for you carefully to explain what ought also to be thought concerning hell. For just as the highest good of man is to be desired more the more it is known, so, conversely, the highest evil will be more to be avoided the less it is unknown.

CHRISTIAN. Here among us, as among you, there has long been a diversity of opinion. Some consider hell to be a certain bodily place beneath the earth, called *infernum* from that very local position, since it is lower than the other parts of the world. Others consider hell to be not so much a bodily torment as a spiritual one: just as by the name of heaven, which is the upper part of the world, we distinguish the highest blessedness of souls, so by the name of hell we distinguish the utmost misery, said to lie so much lower as it is known to stand farther from that highest blessedness and to be more contrary to it. For as what is better is called high because of the excellence of its dignity [Col. 1672A], so conversely what is worse is called lowest because of its abasement.

Both the Old and New Testaments indeed relate many things concerning the punishments of hell which seem by no means capable of being taken literally. For what is the literal meaning of what the Lord says through Isaiah concerning the righteous and the ungodly: “They shall go forth and see the corpses of those who have transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24)? What bodily going forth is this on the part of the saints, that they may behold the punishments of the ungodly? Or what bodily worms are those in the bodies of the reprobate, whose bodies, like those of the saints, are all to rise again whole? What gnawing by worms will there be there, where there shall equally be immortality of all bodies without any defect [Col. 1672B]?

The Lord also relates in the Gospel concerning the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16) after their death. How can this stand literally, since the soul of that rich man cannot have a bodily burial in hell? Or what is that bodily bosom of Abraham, into which Lazarus’s soul is said to have been carried by angels? What tongue does the rich man’s soul have there? Or what finger does Lazarus’s soul have? Or what bodily water is there, whose drop, poured upon the burning tongue, could extinguish or lessen its burning? Therefore, since these things cannot in any way happen literally to souls already stripped of flesh—just as neither can that which is elsewhere said: “Bind him hand and foot; cast him into the outer darkness. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 22:13) [Col. 1672C]—both the Old and the New Testament seem to indicate that what they have said concerning hell should be understood more mystically than bodily.

Thus, just as that bosom of Abraham, into which Lazarus’s soul was received, is to be understood spiritually, not bodily, so hell is that spiritual affliction in which the rich man’s soul is remembered as buried. So long as souls lack bodies, by which they might be borne or moved locally, or confined, as it were, within the compass of a body—souls which are by no means local and by their own nature are far subtler than every body—it cannot easily be explained or understood what bodily power of the elements, whether fire or the others, could touch or torment them without bodies. [Col. 1672D]

Hence demons after their fall are said to have been cast down into certain airy bodies, so that they might also suffer bodily; these they have received as a kind of prison. Accordingly they are called powers of the air, because they are especially powerful in that element into which they have been embodied, just as men who rule on earth are called earthly powers. But if the prophet is said to have understood by the worms of souls a certain inward gnawing of them, by which they are already tormented through consciousness of their guilt, despair of pardon, and the increase of their future punishment (52v), and afterwards by fire the punishment by which they will be tormented when they have resumed their bodies, it is easy to define hell as both spiritual and bodily torment: namely, in comparison with other punishments, since these, as the lowest or final ones, are so called, whether they are said to be inflicted [Col. 1673A] under the earth or elsewhere.

For since it is established that the earth rests upon waters, how can any bodily fire be said to exist beneath the earth, unless perhaps “beneath the earth” means any depth of the earth beyond the surface of the earth on which we stand? But again, since the number of the reprobate will be infinite, while according to the assertion of Truth that of the elect will be small, it may perhaps not readily be admitted that there is anywhere such a vast cavity of earth as could contain so many bodies. Therefore, if anyone thinks the power of divine judgment so great that God can punish equally in all places where he wills, and that the qualities of places contribute nothing to punishment, just as they contribute nothing to glory, I do not doubt that this will find readier assent in proportion as it more highly commends divine power and seems closer [Col. 1673B] to reason.

For, to follow the common opinion of nearly all, those who say that persons placed in the same fire are tormented more or less according to their merits, not according to the quantity of the fire: I do not see how such a moderation of one and the same fire can be effected by divine power in punishment, and why God could not instead afflict with different torments persons placed in different locations, or torment anyone, wherever they may be, by whatever punishments he wills, and turn all the elements against them into whatever punishments he wills, as it is written: “I shall fight for God against the senseless ones of the earth” (Wis. 5:21).

For even according to their view, in the very ethereal heaven, where the purer the fire, the more sharply and violently it burns and shines (fol. 53r), the common faith maintains that blessed bodies remain without any injury [Col. 1673C]; and it asserts that this has been granted them after the resurrection for glory—something which the weakness of our souls could in no wise endure. So indeed light refreshes healthy eyes and burdens diseased ones. Who, moreover, does not daily experience such diverse natures of animals, that what sustains the life of some extinguishes that of others, and, owing to the different constitution of bodies, what benefits one impedes another—both animate and inanimate things? Human beings die beneath water; fish die in the open air. The salamander is known to live in fire, which brings certain destruction to other living creatures. Poison is life to the serpent and death to the human being; the same things afford necessary nourishment to some animals and a deadly one to others. There is absolutely nothing [Col. 1673D] that can suit all natures.

Those born from the same womb and begotten by the same father do not at all live by the same habits, nor are they alike delighted or offended by the same things, nor, while remaining in the same heat or cold, are they tormented alike. This diversity of sufferings does not, certainly, arise from the quality of those punishing, but of those punished. What wonder, then, if divine justice so regulates resurrected bodies, standing in the same place or in different places according to the merits of each, for punishment, that wherever they are, all things may be equally punitive to them? He certainly considered this carefully who confessed that he could nowhere escape God’s vengeance, saying: “Where shall I go from your spirit, or where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Ps. 138 [139]:7–8). [Col. 1674A]

Finally, who judges the souls of wicked human beings in hell to be more tormented than the spiritual wickednesses dwelling in the air, who carry their own torments with them wherever they go? It is certainly established that these are worthy of a greater torment in proportion as they are beyond doubt more wicked. Who in the same way would deny that the souls of the impious, after resuming their bodies, carry their torments with them wherever they move, even if no external torment is imposed? For we see that many sufferings are inflicted upon a soul still remaining in the body, either inwardly or externally through some disturbance or bodily disorder [Col. 1674B], and, once acquired, cannot be removed by any change of place.

To omit other sufferings: what remedy does it provide for pain to place a dying person, or one labouring under extreme suffering, in any location, if that suffering cannot be alleviated by a change of place? Or since, as blessed Augustine recalls, there is now in us who are dying such great suffering in bodily death that the soul is compelled to leave the body, who, as it seems, would not judge that in bodies resumed and already made immortal this same suffering—by which we are dissolved here in dying—would suffice for damnation if it were perpetual, even if no greater suffering could exist without an externally imposed torment? [Note: [Col. 1673D] Read, apparently: “who.”]

For what better accords with justice than that souls should especially resume for torment those bodies which they have used badly for pleasure? It is certain, moreover, that there is such great suffering in the dissolution of death that, even if a punishment, however brief, has been inflicted for any sin [Note: [Col. 1674D] Supply: “punishment” [?]], it is believed sufficient for purging that sin, provided it was not worthy of eternal damnation. Hence, as blessed Jerome declares, comes the saying of the prophet: “The Lord will not judge twice in the same matter, and a double tribulation shall not arise” (Nah. 1:9, according to the Septuagint).

We also read that certain souls of the departed, condemned, refused to be restored to this present life in order that they might be saved by good works, if they were compelled again to end it through the intervention of death. Elsewhere we find written that certain souls of dying saints, through fear of the punishment of their dissolution, wholly refused at the time of death to depart for the blessedness prepared for them (fol. 54r) [Col. 1674D], until the Lord commanded that they be received by angels without pain. From this it is clear how great is the suffering of this death, since, as we have said, through fear of it one person was unwilling to return to salvation and another trembled to depart for blessedness.

Yet it is established that divine power can wholly remove this suffering from whomever it wills, just as the aforesaid teacher asserts in saying that the apostle John was exempt both from the pain of death and from the corruption of the flesh. Therefore, he who can so completely remove the suffering of death in death itself seems able to do the same anywhere, for whomever he wills [Col. 1675A]. For a passible nature is more prone to incur suffering than to be free from it.

From all these considerations, I think it is now clear that the quality of place contributes nothing to the punishment of the damned, just as it contributes nothing to the glory of the blessed. Rather, to be tormented in hell or delivered to everlasting fire is to be tortured by those supreme punishments which are especially compared to fire, because the torment of that element seems more acute. It also seems greatly to commend the glory of divine power if he himself grants equally in all places both the punishment of damnation and the glory of blessedness—he whose power is not doubted to be absent anywhere. [Note: [Col. 1675D] “Scripture” seems to have been omitted.]

PHILOSOPHER. As I see, you endeavour to turn the punishment of the damned, no less than the glory of the elect, to the praise of divine power [Col. 1675B], so that even amid the greatest evils you proclaim his goodness.

CHRISTIAN. And this is certainly fitting, because none of his works are other than magnificent and full of wonder. I judge it superfluous, however, to determine in which places these things occur, provided that we may attain the one or avoid the other.

PHILOSOPHER. And this still remains to be discussed: since our highest good and, as you have held, our highest evil have been described, you must no less diligently explain, in accordance with our purpose, by what means you think we may attain them, so that we may hold the one more securely or avoid the other in proportion as we know more about them. I also desire, if you can define it, to know what the highest good or highest evil is, and what is to be called good or evil generally [Col. 1675C]. For we know many species of these things; yet we do not sufficiently understand or can explain in what respect things are to be called good or evil. Our authorities, indeed, who say that some things are good, some evil, and some indifferent, have not at all distinguished these by definitions, but have been content with certain examples to demonstrate them.

CHRISTIAN. In my judgment, they considered difficult to define things whose names scarcely ever seem to retain one meaning. For when one says “a good man,” “a good craftsman,” “a good horse,” and the like, who does not know that the word “good” derives a different sense from what is joined with it: a good man from his morals, a craftsman from skill, a horse from strength and speed, or from whatever pertains to its use? Indeed, the meaning of “good” varies so greatly according to its adjuncts that we do not hesitate even to join it to the names of vices, saying, for example, “a good” or “an excellent thief,” because he is clever or cunning in carrying out that wickedness. [Col. 1675D]

We apply the term “good” not only to things themselves, but also to what is said about things—that is, to the very statements of propositions—in such a way that we even say that “it is good for evil to exist,” although we by no means concede that “evil is good.” For it is one thing to say “evil is good,” which is entirely false; another to say “for evil to exist is good,” which cannot at all be denied. Why then should it be surprising if we, like them, are unable to define a meaning (fol. 55r) [Col. 1676A] so inconstant?

Still, as far as occurs to me now, I think that good in the simple sense—that is, a good thing—is something fitted to some use, yet through which no one’s advantage or dignity need be hindered. An indifferent thing, that is, something which is neither good nor evil, I take to be that through whose existence no good need either be conferred or hindered, such as an accidental motion of the finger or any actions of that kind. For actions are judged good or evil only according to the root of intention; all actions in themselves are indifferent. And, if we examine closely, those things which are not in themselves good or evil contribute nothing to merit, since they belong equally to the reprobate and the elect. [Col. 1676B]

PHILOSOPHER. I think we must pause and dwell here a little, in case what you have said can stand as definitions.

CHRISTIAN. It is indeed exceedingly difficult to circumscribe everything by proper definitions so that it may be separated from all else, especially now, when the time available does not permit us delay for devising definitions. Through the use of reason we have learned to what things most names apply; yet we cannot at all assign their meaning or intelligible content. We find many things whose designation, just as their meanings, we cannot determine by definition. Even if we do not fail to know the natures of things, their terms are not in use; and often the mind is readier to understand than the tongue is to utter or explain what we perceive. [Col. 1676C]

Consider: from the use of everyday speech we all know what things are called stones. Yet I believe that we are not yet able to assign by any word the proper differentiae of stone, or the property of this species, by which some distinction or description of stone can be accomplished (55v). Nor should you think it remarkable if you see me fail in matters in which those great teachers whom you boast of as philosophers are known not to have succeeded. Nevertheless, as far as I can, I shall attempt to answer your objections concerning what I have stated.

PHILOSOPHER. What you now say seems sufficiently supported by both reason and proof.
