Yet indeed, unless what is said is understood, it is uttered in vain; nor can it teach others unless it can be explained. Now, if it pleases you—or rather, since you have already consented to this—I want you to unfold a little what you have said. Why, then, I ask, when you defined a good thing, did it not seem enough to say: “that which is suited to some use,” that is, useful for some advantage? [Col. 1677A]

CHRISTIAN. It is a common and plausible proverb that scarcely any good exists which does no harm, and no evil which brings no benefit. For example, someone has long exercised himself so diligently in good works that, being frequently praised for them or trusting in his own virtues, he becomes puffed up in pride; or another is thereby inflamed with envy. Thus it is established that evil arises from good, and that evil is frequently even the cause of good. For our vices or sins, which are properly called evils, can exist only in a soul or in good creatures; nor can corruption arise except from good. Conversely, who does not see that people often rise stronger or better after great falls into sin, through humility or repentance, than they were before?

Repentance for sin itself, moreover, because it is an affliction of the mind and cannot coexist with perfect blessedness because it brings pain, is evidently evil rather than good [Col. 1677B]; nevertheless no one doubts that it is necessary for forgiveness of sins (fol. 56r). Who also does not know that the supreme goodness of God, which permits nothing to occur without cause, orders even evils well and makes the best use even of them—so that it is good for evil to exist, although evil is by no means good?

For just as the supreme wickedness of the devil often makes the worst use even of good things, turning them into causes of the worst effects and producing certain most evil things through what is good, so conversely God makes the best use of those things which the devil contrives most wickedly. A tyrant and rulers, for example, may use the same sword badly and well: the former for violence, the latter for punishment. And I believe there are no instruments, nor any things suited to our uses, which we cannot use as badly as well according to the quality of our intentions; plainly, it matters not what is done, but with what disposition it is done. [Col. 1677C]

Hence any person, good as well as perverse, is a cause of both good and bad things; through them both good and evil may occur. A good person does not seem to differ from a bad one in doing what is good, but rather in doing it well. Although current usage treats *bene facere* (“to do well”) and *bonum facere* (“to do a good thing”) as equivalent, the force and proper sense of the expressions perhaps do not say the same. Just as something is often called good, though it is not done well—that is, with a good intention—so it seems that a good thing can be done, though it is not done well.

For the same thing often happens to be done by different persons, such that according to their intentions one does it well and another badly. For example, if two men hang someone guilty of a crime, one merely because he hates him and the other because it falls to him to administer justice: this hanging, though just, is carried out justly by the latter because of his right intention, but unjustly by the former because he acts not from love of justice but from zeal of hatred or anger. [Col. 1677D]

Sometimes evil men, or even the devil himself, are said in the same act to cooperate with God, so that the same thing is said to be done both by God and by them. Behold: we see the possessions of Job taken away by Satan, yet Job himself confesses that God has taken them from him, saying: “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away” (Job 1:21).

Let us therefore come to a matter more dear to the minds of Christians, even though it may seem ridiculous to you or those like you. The handing over of the Lord Jesus into the hands of the Jews is remembered as performed by Jesus himself, by God the Father, and by Judas the betrayer. For the Father is said to have handed over the Son, the Son himself, and Judas the same person; nevertheless in such matters the devil or Judas did the very thing that God did. Even if they may seem for that reason to have done some good, they should still not be said to have acted well. Or if they did, or wished to do, what God wills to be done, or have in doing it some will identical with God’s, are they for that reason to be said to do good because they do what God wills to be done, or to have a good will because they will what God wills? Certainly not. [Col. 1678A]

For although they do, or wish to do, what God wills to be done, they do not do it, or will to do it, because they believe that God wills it to be done; nor is their intention in the same act the same as God’s. Although their will and God’s may be called the same because they will the same thing, their will is nevertheless evil and God’s good, because they will its occurrence for different reasons.

Thus, when different persons perform the same action because they do the same thing, nevertheless because of the difference of intention one person’s action is good and the other’s evil. Although they perform the same act, one does it well and the other badly. And—what is astonishing to say—sometimes even the will is good when someone wishes evil to be done by another, because he wills it with a good intention. [Col. 1678B]

For the Lord has often decreed through the devil or some tyrant to afflict persons who are innocent, or who have not deserved that affliction: namely, for the purging of some sin of those afflicted, for the increase of merit, as an example to others, or for any reasonable cause, though hidden from us. Therefore Job remembers concerning that which the devil had wickedly done, but which the Lord had rightly permitted: “As the Lord pleased, so it has been done” (ibid.). Because he did not doubt that the Lord had permitted it rightly, he shows this by giving thanks to him and adding: “Blessed be the name of the Lord.”

The Third Book of Kings likewise teaches that a lying spirit was sent by the Lord to deceive the impious Ahab. For when the Lord said, “Who will deceive Ahab?” a lying spirit came forth and stood before the Lord, saying: “I will deceive him.” The Lord said to him: “By what means?” And he said: “I shall go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” And the Lord said: “You shall deceive him and prevail; go out and do so” (3 Kings 22:20–22). [Col. 1678D] When the prophet Micaiah had declared before Ahab himself that this had been revealed to him, he added: “Now therefore, behold, the Lord has put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these your prophets, and has spoken evil against you” (ibid., 23).

Whether the Lord permits the devil to rage against saints or against the impious, it is certainly established that the Lord permits only rightly what is good to permit, while the devil acts only wickedly in doing that which is nevertheless good to be done; and there is a reasonable, though unknown, cause why it is done. For as that great philosopher of yours recalls in his *Timaeus*, when proving that God makes all things in the best way: “Everything that comes to be comes to be from some necessary cause. For nothing happens whose origin is not preceded by a lawful cause and reason.” [Col. 1679A]

This plainly shows that, whatever is done by whomever, because it occurs by the dispensation of the best divine providence, it happens reasonably and well as it happens, because it has a reasonable cause why it occurs—even though the person doing it does not himself do it reasonably or well, nor consider in doing it the cause which God considers. Therefore, since it is established that nothing occurs except by God’s permission, because nothing can occur against his will or resistance, and since it is further certain that God permits nothing without cause and does nothing except reasonably—so that both his permission and his action are reasonable—then, because he sees why he permits each event to occur, he cannot be ignorant why it ought itself to occur, even if it is evil or is done wickedly. [Col. 1679B]

For it would not be good for such things to be permitted unless it were good for them to occur; nor would he be perfectly good who, though able, did not prevent what would not be good to happen. Indeed, he would plainly be blameworthy for consenting that what was not good should happen. It is therefore evident that whatever happens has a reasonable cause why it happens or does not happen. Consequently, it is good for it to happen, or good for it not to happen, even if it occurs through someone who does not do it well, or does not occur through someone who fails wickedly to do it—that is, who allows it to happen from an evil intention. [Col. 1679C]

Hence it is good even for evils to exist or to occur, although evils themselves are by no means good. Truth itself openly declares this when it says: “It must needs be that scandals come; but woe to that man through whom the scandal comes!” (Matt. 18:7). It is as though he said plainly: It is expedient and fitting for human salvation that some people, being offended or angered, should thereby incur a scandal of their souls—that is, damnation—so that through the wickedness of certain persons that may be accomplished by which all who are predestined to be healed are saved. Yet woe to that person: that is, condemnation shall be his, by whose counsel or persuasion this scandal is stirred.

Therefore scandal is evil, but it is good that scandal should exist. Likewise, it is good for any evil whatsoever to exist, though no evil is good. Augustine, that great disciple of truth, observed this and considered how excellently God orders even evils; thus he speaks of God’s goodness and the devil’s wickedness: “God, as he is the best creator of good natures, is likewise the most just disposer of evil wills; so that, while the devil makes evil use of good natures, God makes good use even of evil wills.” [Col. 1679D]

The same writer says of the devil: “When God created him, he was not ignorant of his future malice and foresaw what good he would make from his evils.” Again, after some intervening remarks: “God would not, I do not say, have created any angel or human being whom he foreknew would be evil, unless he knew at the same time to what good uses he would assign them.” Again, elsewhere: “Individual things are good; but all things together are very good, because from all of them consists the lovable beauty of the universe.” Again: “That which is called evil, when rightly ordered and set in its place, more eminently commends goods, so that they are more pleasing and more praiseworthy, while it cooperates with goods. For God almighty, being supremely good, would in no way permit any evil to exist in his works, unless he were so almighty and good that he could make good even from evil.” [Col. 1680A]

Again: “It must not be doubted that God acts well even by permitting whatever evils occur to occur. For he permits this only by a just judgment, and certainly what is just is good.” Therefore, although things which are evil, insofar as they are evil, are not good, nevertheless it is good that there should be not only good things but also evil things. For if it were not good that evils should exist, they would by no means be permitted by the omnipotent Good; and without doubt it is as easy for him not to permit what he does not will to exist as it is to bring about what he wills. He is truly called omnipotent for no other reason than that he can do whatever he wills, and the effect of his omnipotent will is not hindered by the will of any creature.

You have heard, then, a clear argument demonstrating that it is good for evil to exist, although it is in no way true that evil is good. It is one thing to say, “evil is good,” another to say, “for evil to exist is good.” In the former, “good” is applied to an evil thing; in the latter, to an evil thing’s existing—that is, in the former to the thing, in the latter to the event of the thing. [Col. 1680B]

Now, as has been said, a thing is called good when it is suited to someone’s use and no advantage or dignity of any thing need be hindered or diminished through it. Such advantage or dignity would necessarily be hindered or diminished if, through its opposite or absence, that dignity or advantage could not necessarily remain. For example, immortal life, joy, health, knowledge, and chastity are such things that, since they have some dignity or advantage, it is certain that this does not remain when their opposites supervene.

Likewise, all substances must be called good things, because although they can confer some usefulness [Col. 1680C], no dignity or advantage need be impeded through them. For even a perverse person, whose life is corrupt or corrupting, could be such that he was not perverse; and therefore through him something would necessarily become worse. [Note: [Col. 1679] The apodosis must either be restored from the preceding sense, or supply: “this is possible.”]

This, however, I think sufficient at present for the description of a good thing. But when we apply the term “good” to the outcomes of things—that is, to what is asserted by propositions and proposed by them as occurring—so as to say that this being or not being is good, it is as if we said that it is necessary for the completion of some most excellent divine ordering, though that ordering may be wholly hidden from us. [Col. 1681A]

For it is not good that even someone should act rightly, if his doing so does not accord with, but rather obstructs, some divine ordination; nor can something occur which has no reasonable cause why it occurs. It has no reasonable cause why it occurs when something ordered by God would necessarily be obstructed if that event happened. Therefore we are often deceived when we say that it is good for us to do this or that which everyone thinks should be done. But when we disagree with divine ordering, we speak falsely through error, though in thinking as we say we are not guilty of the thing called lying.

Likewise, through error we often ask in prayer for many things which are denied to us by God, who knows better than we do what is necessary for us (59v) [Col. 1682A]. Hence it is most important to say thus: “Your will be done.” This is enough for me to have said at present, in order to show how the name “good” should be understood when it is taken simply for a good thing, and when it is also applied to outcomes of things or to what is asserted by propositions. Since this depended upon the inquiry into the highest good, if you think anything remains to be asked further concerning it, you may add it, or hasten on to the rest. [lacuna]

EXHORTATION OF THE MASTER TO THE DISCIPLE CONCERNING THE INQUIRY INTO THE HIGHEST GOOD.

[Note: [Col. 1681D] This word in the manuscript is found rewritten over another erased heading in red.]

[Col. 1681]

[Col. 1681B] My dearest son, your zeal delights me: you investigate the writings of the wise by reading and understanding them for yourself, and seek from me and other elders those things which you do not understand. For that schoolroom exercise, in which gifted pupils advance while trembling under the rod and dull pupils fail, is scarcely suited to adolescents of good disposition except as infant food. We have often seen such food chewed by midwives or nurses and put into the mouths of wailing, toothless little children, who resist it and sometimes reject in disgust the morsels contaminated by another’s saliva.

Therefore, once their jaws have acquired their first teeth and they can chew for themselves, they no longer accept what others have chewed. Indeed, as the disciples, passing through abundant grainfields, pluck and rub ripe ears with their own hands, then eat the grains they have extracted and test them by experience, so we find them taking the greatest delight in those scholarly exercises, yet not finding the flavour of wisdom until after the time of their weaning. [Col. 1681C]

Hence we read that the patriarch Abraham made a great feast on the day of Isaac’s weaning, plainly rejoicing with paternal affection at the progress of so great a son. In contrast, there is much weeping and wailing when Rachel weeps for her sons slain by Herod before the time of weaning. At that time the Church also laments and refuses consolation, because those children of hers whom the sword of Antichrist slays have not been weaned: they are below the age of two, not attaining the fruit of a twofold understanding and action.

Wretched man that I am, how many little ones thus snatched away must I mourn, because after schoolroom exercises I see them either grow lukewarm into a childish and animal-minded understanding, which does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, or grow wholly cold into a reprobate and unapproved understanding, so that they not only do things unbecoming to their profession but even persecute what belongs to the Spirit of God! [Col. 1681D–1682B]

But you, most beloved son, as I hope in God’s mercy, will advance even beyond the age of two, so that you need not fear the sword of Antichrist, which is the deceitful speech of heretics or false brethren. For unless you advanced in this way, unless you had now been weaned and hungered intensely for solid food concerning the highest good, as you inquire, you would not inquire.

The occasion of this inquiry, as you say, arose because, while reading the dialogue composed by Master Peter as a disputation among a Christian, a Jew, and a philosopher concerning the highest good, you found there something investigated, but not sufficiently made clear: what that highest good itself is, where it is, and by what path one ought most rightly to proceed toward it. Therefore receive this little work entitled *On the Inquiry into the Highest Good* in such a way that, if you find anything good said of this good (60v) [Col. 1682C], you do not doubt that it has either trickled forth from that very good—if it is little—or flowed forth—if it is sufficient. I call it sufficient not in proportion to the worth of the matter under discussion, but in proportion to the hunger of the reader and inquirer. For the matter itself, of which we nevertheless desire somehow to speak, is ineffable, as far as we shall be able with its own aid.

Having read this most excellent present philosophy,

It will bestow upon everyone a threefold honour of learning.

[Note: [Col. 1681D] Denisius says in the passage cited: “This exhortation is interrupted by a red couplet. It would more properly have been placed at the end of the dialogue: “the” (τὸ); for it seems to allude to the threefold doctrine of the three speakers.” [Col. 1682D] —The observation is approved. The argument of the couplet, compared with both exhortations, seems to suggest nearly the same thing.]

[Note: [Col. 1682D] The following exhortation in the manuscript codex was written by a different hand, apparently of the same period.]

I think, moreover, that if you have carefully examined Augustine’s little work entitled *On the Highest Good*, you will there be abundantly instructed that the highest good is that from which, through which, and in which exist all goods, great, intermediate, and least; and that it is itself such that nothing better can be conceived—indeed, it is better than any creature can conceive. For unless it transcended every thought alike of angels and of human beings, it would not surpass all understanding nor dwell in inaccessible light; nor would that be truly called incomprehensible which someone could attain or comprehend by thought or intellect. He perceived this who said: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord?” (Rom. 11:33–34.)

Yet those through whom the canonical Scripture of the Old and New Testaments was administered knew that highest good in part and also prophesied in part. In Scripture, as through a mirror and in an enigma, there appears the beauty of the highest good, the highest justice, the highest life, the highest power, the highest joy, the highest love, and the highest brightness. All these things, and things like them, predicated of the highest good, are not many things, but the one causal and primordial principle or foundation of all things which are good through it and after it in the order of things. Although these things are all good in their own nature, since they have being from the highest good, it is good for them to exist and to be used well, but evil to be used badly.

Holy Scripture, and especially that of the New Testament, teaches how a human being should use lower goods in order to attain the highest good. Its eternal fruit, like the daily denarius, will be paid to those who, by making good use of lower goods, labor in the vineyard—that is, the present, pilgrim Church. Those standing idle in the marketplace of this world—pagans, or Jews engaged in trade, or false Christians worse than they—will not be able to possess the denarius. It is known to be given only to those laboring well in the vineyard, or, where they have no time for labor, to infants who bear Christ’s sacraments; for they have received the teaching of truth not from philosophers, nor from Jews ignorant of or rejecting Christ, but from Christ himself.

“Listen to him,” says the heavenly Father (Matt. 17:5). “Listen to him,” I too say, to all of you, my disciples or children, who hear me. Listen to him rather than to a pagan philosophizing or a Hebrew practicing Judaism. Listen to him, who not only teaches what is right but also justifies the ungodly—not through the wisdom of this world or through works of the law, but through faith, by which his teaching is believed and kept. As he himself says: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11:28). In keeping it there is great reward.

Truly this reward is great: it has no end, but is itself the end and consummation of those who participate in the highest good, enjoy the highest joy, and are wise with the highest wisdom, which is Christ. Listen to him. He is counsellor: listen to him. He is teacher: listen to him. If you cannot receive his counsel, namely that, denying yourselves, you should follow him, at least keep the commandment; and in knowing both, listen to him. First, if possible, listen to him in order to preserve innocence. Second, when you have lost innocence, at least listen to him in order to do penance. If you have the means to do good works, listen to him; if you lack even the capacity to will good things, listen to him.

If you wish to know what the highest good is, or by what path one must advance toward it, listen to him saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). For he himself is both the way by which one travels and the truth and life to which one travels: listen to him. If perhaps, while walking on this way, you are sad like the disciples going to Emmaus, listen to him walking with you and consoling you, so that at last you, stirred up though foolish and slow of heart, may say: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32). He is the one who opens the Scriptures to those walking in him as way and truth: listen to him. He opens and no one shuts: listen to him!

To those walking, he says: “Make your ways and your pursuits good”: listen to him. To those arriving, he says: “I shall dwell with you”: listen to him. He teaches the natural law defended by the pagan philosopher: listen to him. He came to fulfill, not abolish, the law of Moses: listen to him. The law, indeed, announcing and revealing infirmity, was given through Moses; but grace and truth, healing that same infirmity, came through Jesus Christ: listen to him. He promised the highest good as a reward to those following and obeying him; he granted them other, lower goods for use, so that all things might work together for their good through good use. By this use they are taught to use not only good things but even evil things for good—provided that they listen to him.

Therefore listen to him! And let anyone who teaches otherwise than the word of his evangelical teaching be anathema to us: that teaching is full of truth, with grace arousing and strengthening the will, truth enlightening reason, grace preceding and following the will, and truth directing and leading reason into the way of peace, toward the homeland of eternal light. There the highest good will be seen clearly and tasted: the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one and triune God. To him be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1683D] Denisius rightly observes concerning this appendix, in the cited place: “This entire exhortation seems to be an indirect criticism of Abaelard’s preceding dialogue and a forewarning to the disciple. For, after many things had opportunely been drawn from Augustine’s little work *On the Highest Good*, the anonymous master adds: ‘Let such persons listen, who have received not from philosophers,’ etc.; and then, making apt use of many passages of Scripture, concludes: ‘Therefore listen to him,’ etc.”]

[Col. 1685]

# PETER ABAELARD’S EPITOME OF CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY

(First published from the manuscript codices of the monastery of St. Emmeram at Regensburg, preserved in the Royal Library at Munich, by Friedrich Heinrich Rheinwald, doctor of theology and philosophy, etc., in the collection entitled *Anecdota Pertaining to Ecclesiastical History*, Part II, Berlin, 1835, octavo.)

# PREFACE

[Col. 1685A] During the theological leisure which I happened to spend in the city of Munich, I visited the Royal Library, the foremost of all others, very frequently, and never returned without some new increase both of knowledge and pleasure. I took especial delight in reading and rereading the books of the library of St. Emmeram, transferred here from the Regensburg monastery dedicated to St. Emmeram. For besides seeing it most splendidly furnished with various kinds of theological writings, and especially with books pertaining to historical theology, I found that external aids for attaining a more inward knowledge of it had also been so arranged that my interest daily increased and was kindled.

Let me gratefully recall the memory of the man who deserved so well of this library of St. Emmeram: he arranged it well, compiled an excellent catalogue, added unpublished materials to the catalogue, and furnished it generously with excellent notices pertaining to literary history. [Col. 1685B] I mean Coloman Sanftl, monk of the Regensburg monastery (d. 1809), to whom I know and deeply feel that I owe very much both in every kind of historical study and especially in the work of which I shall shortly speak more fully. We have before our eyes in him a new testimony to that indefatigable labor—examples of which we now seek in vain—by which the Benedictine order once, according to a most salutary principle, advanced, sustained, and assisted learning.

As I was passing through this library, certain codices caught my eye, upon whose title-page I read the name of a man which I have never heard without a certain feeling of reverence. I examined them more carefully and almost leapt for joy when I seemed to have come upon a work whose subject, although not entirely unknown, had, so far as I know, not come to the attention of other theologians.

[Col. 1686A] The book just mentioned bears in the Emmeram library the title *Sentences of Peter Abaelard*. These are arranged in thirty-seven chapters. On reading the first chapter, one may indeed observe a very great agreement with Abaelard’s *Introduction* [Note: [Col. 1685B] Above, cols. 979–1110.]: the opening words are altogether the same.

[Note: [Col. 1685B] From this fact Mabillon, who only cursorily inspected our codex during his journey through Bavaria, inferred that Peter’s *Introduction* and our book were one and the same. What Mabillon had proposed (*German Journey*, p. 10), the authors of the *Literary History of France*, in their dissertations on Abaelard’s life and writings, rashly repeat (*Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. XII, p. 118 n.). Compare also André Duchesne’s notes on Abaelard’s works, and Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of St. Benedict*, vol. V, p. 357.]

Traces of this agreement are found down to the middle of chapter 15.

[Note: [Col. 1685C] *Introduction*, above, col. 981.]

Yet chapters 1–15 of Book I of the *Introduction* are represented in chapters 1–11 of our codex not word for word, as those who seem to have inspected these books only cursorily supposed, although they agree with each other in various ways. What is further present in the *Introduction* is reported no longer exactly, but only in summary, so that both the words and the argument itself are entirely different. The thread of the discussion in *Introduction*, Book III, chapter 7, is demonstrably broken off in mid-course. But our codex, continuing further the matter treated by Peter in the *Introduction*, both adds what is lacking in the *Introduction* concerning the attributes of God and also touches upon other dogmatic questions.

These remarks in general concern the subject of our codex and its relation to Master Peter’s *Introduction*.

Now, in order to see by what right this book can be claimed for Abaelard, the first question seems to be whether traces of some book of *Sentences* attributed to Abaelard can be sought in Abaelard’s own time, whether in his writings or in those of another man living in his time. And this is indeed so. Bernard of Clairvaux, in certain letters, enumerated among Abaelard’s writings a *Book of Sentences* and even cites a passage from it.

[Note: [Col. 1685C] St. Bernard, Letter 188, to the bishops and cardinals of the curia (*Works*, ed. Mabillon, vol. I, p. 182 [*Patrology*, vol. CLXXXII]): “Read, if you please, the book of Peter Abaelard which he calls *Theology*, for it is at hand. Read also another, which they call his *Sentences* [Col. 1686B], and likewise the one entitled *Know Thyself*; and observe how great a crop of sacrileges and errors flourishes there too: what he thinks about Christ’s soul, Christ’s person, Christ’s descent into hell, the sacrament of the altar, the power of binding and loosing, original sin, concupiscences, the sin of pleasure, the sin of weakness, the sin of ignorance, the act of sin, the will to sin,” and so forth.—His Letter 190 to Pope Innocent: “The mystery of our redemption, as I read in a certain book of his *Sentences* and likewise in a certain exposition of his Epistle to the Romans, this rash investigator of majesty undertakes; and at the very beginning of his disputation he says that all ecclesiastical teachers hold one opinion on the matter, sets it forth, rejects it, and boasts that he has a better one.”]

[Col. 1687A]

[Note: [Col. 1687C] Letter 190: “It must be known,” he says, “that all our teachers, following the apostles, agree in this: that the devil has dominion and power over humankind, and possessed humanity by right, namely because the human being, by the freedom of choice which he had, voluntarily consented to the devil. For they say that if someone conquers another, the conquered is by right made the victor’s slave. Therefore, he says, as the teachers say, the Son of God was incarnate out of this necessity, so that the human being, who could not otherwise be freed, might by the death of an innocent man be rightfully freed from the devil’s yoke. But, as it seems to us,” he says, “the devil never had any right over humanity, unless perhaps by God’s permission, as a jailer; nor did the Son of God assume flesh in order to free humanity.”]

Moreover, Walter of St. Victor mentions a certain treatise circulated under the title *Sentences* and attributed to Abaelard. Walter reports the opening words of this treatise.

[Note: [Col. 1687D] Walter, in his book *Against the Four Labyrinths of France*, concerning which excerpts are found in C. E. Bulæus, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. II, p. 200.]

[Note: [Col. 1687D] Bulæus, cited work: “He acts particularly against Abaelard because of a certain treatise whose title was: ‘Here begin the Sentences of Divinity’; and whose opening was: ‘All you who thirst, come to the waters and drink, friends; be intoxicated, most beloved,’ etc. It contained many heresies and profane novelties of expression,” and so forth.]

These words, however, are such that they differ entirely from those which our codex presents. Nor is it possible from what Walter discusses concerning the subject of the whole book to prove that our treatise is one and the same as the book he mentions; rather, one may infer the contrary. For the few things Walter adduces are far removed from the simple style in which Peter opens his treatises. One would judge that this lofty style, borrowed from rhetorical schools, these polysyllabic words, came from a vain and garrulous man—Tanquelm or some similar sophist—rather than from Abaelard, the genuine and chaste foster-child of the Muses.

The matter stands otherwise with Bernard’s testimony. [Col. 1687B] For what he brings forward from the book of *Sentences* and the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans (in Letter 190) is not read word for word in our book, but the same matters are presented to us in sense.

[Note: [Col. 1687D] Compare chapter 23 of our codex and chapter 28 near the end. These passages should be compared with Abaelard’s *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans* (above, cols. 783–978). [Col. 1688C] Abaelard adds approximately these words to his exposition of redemption accomplished through Christ: “These matters we shall expound more fully in their proper place. But for now, insofar as the brevity of exposition requires, let what seems sufficient to us concerning the manner of our redemption suffice; if anything is lacking for completeness, we reserve it for the treatise of our *Theology*.”]

But there is a difficulty. Abaelard himself seems to rise against the witness just mentioned, when he says somewhere:

[Note: [Col. 1688C] Abaelard, *Confession of Faith*, above, col. 107.]

“What concerns the fact that our friend concluded the chapters written against me with the following statement: ‘These chapters have been found partly in the book called the *Theology* of Master Peter, partly in his book of *Sentences*, and partly in the book entitled *Know Thyself*’—I received it with the greatest astonishment, since no book called *Sentences* is ever found to have been written by me. But like all the other chapters against me, this too was advanced through malice or ignorance.”

But who does not see that both Peter and Bernard could rightly and truthfully have said these things? Abaelard could maintain with complete confidence that he had never composed such a book, if he had never given such a title to a book written by himself; Bernard, on the other hand, could without error attribute to Abaelard a certain treatise which had been given the title *Sentences* not by Peter but by someone else. Added to this is the fact that Bernard, in those passages where the title of the book is at issue, speaks insufficiently clearly and definitely (see note no. 76).

[Col. 1688A] Since, then, external testimonies do not refute the claim that Abaelard composed the book which became known to his opponents and to other learned men under the title *Sentences*, one must next inquire whether internal evidence proves and requires this, or whether there are explicit indications in it that this book came from Abaelard’s hand.

In resolving this question, attention must first of all be paid to a passage

[Note: [Col. 1688C] Chapter 24.]

in which the author of our little book names and describes himself more precisely. For he says: “Because I have carefully set this forth in the Epistle to the Romans, on the passage ‘Jacob I loved,’ etc., I judge that I should pass it over as already known.”

[Note: [Col. 1688D] Abaelard, *Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*, above, col. 783.]

These words indicate quite clearly that the author of our writing does not differ from the author of the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans. That Commentary, moreover, is beyond all doubt a genuine work of Abaelard. Therefore, unless one falls under the suspicion that some clever interpolator contrived this with sufficient dexterity, one must also attribute to Abaelard the book which is called the *Sentences*.

This is further supported by the end and subject of the whole book, especially when a comparison is made with the *Introduction to Theology*.

[Note: [Col. 1688D] If one considers the end and subject, one may also compare Abaelard’s book entitled *Christian Theology*, above, col. 1113.]

For the author of the *Introduction* observes immediately at the beginning that he will treat his subject in three divisions: first faith, then love, and finally the sacraments. Yet the *Introduction*, as it has come down to posterity, does not complete even the first part, on faith; rather, it leaves unfinished in mid-course a subject begun in its discussion of God’s attributes. Abaelard, namely, says in *Introduction*, Book III, chapter 3, that he wishes now to explain more carefully the three attributes of the divine nature: power, wisdom, and goodness. He begins with power and passes from it to wisdom; but in the middle of his exposition of this divine attribute—indeed, in the middle of a sentence—he abandons his subject. Of goodness, however, not a word is read. Thus the *Introduction* offers nothing further concerning the second and third parts, namely love and the sacraments.

Our little book, however, as has been said, presents exactly the same subject as the *Introduction* down to the article on wisdom.

[Note: [Col. 1688D] Sanftl likewise thinks that from the agreement of the subject set forth in our treatise with that of the *Introduction*, one should infer not the spuriousness (*νοθεία*) but rather the authenticity (*αὐθεντία*) of our book. For he says: “Nor is this book to be denied to Abaelard because a great part of it is excerpted from the same man’s *Introduction to Theology*. Anyone who compares his *Christian Theology* with his *Introduction to Theology* will be certainly persuaded that this was by no means unusual for Abaelard. For he will discover that the first and fifth books of the *Theology* occur in the *Introduction* almost word for word. Speaking of this matter, William, abbot of St. Thierry, says in his letter to Geoffrey of Chartres and Bernard: ‘There were two little books of Abaelard, containing almost the same thing, except that somewhat more was found in one and somewhat less in the other.’”]

But where the *Introduction* ceases in treating its subject, our codex continues, and it also completes the begun material in accordance with the arrangement proposed in the *Introduction*. [Col. 1689A] Chapter 22 discusses divine goodness. Chapters 23–37 add the two remaining parts, the treatises on love and the sacraments. Thus our book pursues a certain end which Peter professes as his own in the *Introduction*; and this may have considerable weight in defending the authenticity (*αὐθεντία*) of our book, provided that the manner in which it is done appears worthy of Abaelard.

Indeed, the subject of our book may be judged not unworthy of Peter. For, if we compare the *Introduction* with our book,

[Note: [Col. 1689D] Compare, for example, *Introduction*, Book I, chapter 2, with chapter 28 of our book.]

we find the same man: a clever and often daring interpreter of Holy Scripture, free from all human authority;

[Note: [Col. 1689D] Chapter 25 of our book: “But let Augustine state his own opinion; we state ours,” etc.]

a careful and diligent investigator of antiquity; and no less a man possessing a perfect knowledge of his age and of the various opinions which carried authority within it. The same will hold if we compare our treatise with Abaelard’s other writings, [Col. 1689B] especially with *Christian Theology*, the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, and fragments of his writings which survive in his opponents.

[Note: [Col. 1689D] If anyone is troubled by the contradiction encountered when the words of the *Confession*—“I profess that the Son of God alone was incarnate in order to free us from the slavery of sin and the yoke of the devil, and to open to us by his death the entrance of the heavenly life” (above, col. 107)—are compared with the words of our book (chapter 23), let him consider that the same contradiction is found in the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans (chapter 3; compare note 8). Moreover, other things too are explicitly denied in the *Confession* as though they had never been uttered or written by Peter, though they are nevertheless read in his books. You have an excellent illustration of this in the *Confession*: “Therefore, what has been maliciously imputed to me, namely that I wrote, ‘the Father is full power, the Son a certain power, the Holy Spirit no power’—these words I abhor, detest, and, as is altogether just, condemn together with their author, not merely as heretical but as diabolical. If anyone finds them in my writings, I declare myself not only a heretic but even a heresiarch.” Martène rightly observes (in the preface to vol. V of the *New Treasury of Anecdotes*) that Abaelard in these words, as it were, kills himself with his own sword and applauds Bernard, the censor of his writings. Yet we do not wish to subscribe to the opinion which Martène adds shortly afterwards: “And certainly,” he says, “anyone who has once recognized Peter Abaelard’s genius easily observes that the man was so constituted by nature that he could without difficulty teach propositions opposed to one another.”]

This is the more noteworthy because a genius such as Abaelard’s is the less capable of being reproduced by imitation. Finally, the external and internal form of expression, the character of the language, and the style prove Abaelard to be the author of our book. For one encounters Latin prose which gives pleasure, entirely different from the speech that had prevailed in those times of barbarism. Our little book abundantly demonstrates that its author, like Abaelard, was continually engaged in studying and turning over the writers of antiquity—Cicero, Horace, and others.

If from these things one may conclude that our book was truly written by Abaelard, one must next investigate about what time it appeared in public. Since, as we have shown above, there is the greatest resemblance between our book and the *Introduction*, [Col. 1689C] the decisive question is whether we should judge our book to have been written earlier or later than the *Introduction*. In this matter one might, with great appearance of truth, say that our treatise came first and contains the outlines of Abaelardian theology, or his theology reduced to a compendium; that the *Introduction* was written and intended to be written as a fuller exposition of it; and that Abaelard’s *Christian Theology* finally completed its defense and expansion. For there seems nothing rash or absurd in the opinion that Peter wished to treat the same subject in three ways, slightly differing from one another, gradually rising from a less complete to a more complete work.

But a passage of our book, read in chapter [Col. 1690A] 34, explicitly contradicts this view. In it the author refers to the Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans. Since the Commentary clearly indicates that the *Introduction* was written before it, there can be no doubt that our little book must be placed after the *Introduction*. Beyond that, nothing certain can be determined about the time. It seems that it must be left wholly uncertain whether our book appeared before or after *Christian Theology* and the book entitled *Know Thyself*. In support of our opinion, that it occupies a middle place between the Commentary and *Christian Theology*, only this can be advanced: after publishing *Christian Theology*, Peter would scarcely—indeed, hardly at all—have repeated so precisely the subject of the *Introduction*, already published earlier, as we see done in our book. Before fuller theological commentaries, such repetition may cause less surprise. But leaving these points aside, one may assert with certainty that the book was composed before the year 1140. [Col. 1690B] It would not be easy to proceed beyond this year.

Closely related to this question is another: did Peter bring the *Introduction* to an end, or did he leave it incomplete and mutilated as we have it in the Paris edition? We wish only to touch upon this question, since others too have touched upon it, and not to pursue it more fully. The controversy cannot be settled a priori. For sufficiently weighty reasons can be enumerated for either opinion: that Abaelard gave the book its final hand, or that he did not complete the work he had begun. Either opinion has its difficulties.

The blessed Sanftl takes Mabillon’s side,

[Note: [Col. 1690D] Mabillon, note on Bernard’s Letter 190 (*Works*, vol. I, p. 642 [*Patrology*, vol. CLXXXII]).]

who, without a lengthy enumeration of reasons, maintains—or rather conjectures—that the *Introduction* came from Abaelard’s hand complete. Whatever is lacking, he says, was cut out by later persons because of scattered errors. But it is difficult to understand why the man who undertook this critic’s task only severely cut out objectionable material in the middle of the book, [Col. 1690C] and why he did not do the same in the earlier chapters; indeed, why, if he wished to be consistent, he did not destroy the whole copy which came into his hands and burn it, according to the practice customary at that time.

Two considerations, on the other hand, seem to favor the view that Peter never completed the *Introduction*, but was prevented by some circumstance from finishing the studies he had begun. First, this easily explains why the discourse ceases in the middle of a proposition. Second, perhaps, the form of *Christian Theology* also has in common with the *Introduction* the greatest resemblance insofar as the same matter occurs in both treatises.

[Note: [Col. 1690D] Yet I am not unaware that this reason is in some way uncertain. For if we wish to infer that the *Introduction* is incomplete from the fact that the *Theology* is incomplete, it must first be proved that the latter too was really incomplete, if one wishes to avoid a circle in the proof. Indeed, the *Introduction* might have survived complete even if Abaelard was never able—or never wished—to complete the *Theology* entirely.]

Moreover, one may ask why Abaelard, who, having already written the more complete work of the *Introduction*, intended to add an even more complete work—namely the *Theology*—composed a book bearing the form of a compendium. [Col. 1691A] If conjecture is permitted, one may suppose that our Peter did this for the use of the schools which, together with his most beloved teacher, withdrawing into solitude, he maintained at the Paraclete before a faithful company of disciples. Just as in the case of the *Introduction*,

[Note: [Col. 1691C] Compare Abaelard’s preface to the *Introduction*: “Insofar as we can satisfy the request of our students, we have written some Summary of sacred learning, as though an introduction to divine Scripture.” Compare *History of My Calamities*, chapter 9, above.]

who does not see that the disciples could have asked this of Abaelard and that he could have assented to their wishes? Those to whom this is less pleasing may suppose that it was done for the benefit of people who ardently desired thoroughly to know his system reduced to the form of a little compendium. Since this system was now extolled with the highest praises and now heaped with every kind of insult, it seems not contrary to probability that sincere friends of truth could have sought such a book for a fair consideration of the matter. From them, it must then be supposed, the book passed into the hands of others less favorably disposed toward Master Peter. [Col. 1691B]

Whichever of the two opinions—earlier or later—you may prefer, benevolent reader, another opinion may also be invoked in support.

It does not seem unlikely that Abaelard did not himself commit to writing what is read in our book, but that some other learned person did so. If we add our vote to the conjecture of those who judge that the *Introduction* once existed complete, this view strongly recommends itself. The more unworthy of Peter you judge the role of abbreviator or excerptor—if the word may be permitted!—the more readily we may attribute it to his admirer and disciple. The brief treatment of historical matters found in chapter 12 of our treatise, though these matters are more fully expounded in the *Introduction* (Book I, chapter 15; Book II, chapter 7), seems to indicate someone who, in excerpting the book, valued matters concerning the history of philosophy less highly, but Abaelardian demonstration more highly.

[Col. 1691C] Nor does this view seem less capable of defense if we agree with those who maintain that the *Introduction* was not completed. For if we suppose that someone who attended Abaelard’s philosophical-theological schools, during or after those schools,

[Note: [Col. 1691C] Compare chapter 23 near the beginning.]

briefly noted their subject for himself, consulted the *Introduction* in various places, and by its assistance completed his notes or submitted them to Abaelard’s criticism, then both the similarity and dissimilarity between Peter’s *Introduction* and our book can be explained, as can the aphoristic form of the whole book, which appears here and there. The openings of individual chapters would likewise admit of an easier interpretation.

Nonetheless, authenticity (*αὐθεντία*) may be claimed for our book if we retain the broader notion of authenticity which we see accepted in our time, both in other fields of literature and in theology, especially in the critical history of the New Testament. Even if the material received orally was committed to writing by another, it nevertheless owes its origin to Abaelard.

Finally, on the same hypothesis (*ὑπόθεσις*), what has been said above concerning the existence and title of the book can be reconciled very easily. Both the abbot of Clairvaux and Master Peter stated the truth. Some friend and admirer of Abaelard gave our book, composed by himself, the title *Sentences*, under which title Bernard received the book. Abaelard, however, had neither written such a book [Col. 1692B] nor furnished it with such a title.

But let us set aside these and other small questions, which can be resolved only by historical investigation. If, however, Oudinus is to be believed,

[Note: [Col. 1691D] C. Oudinus, *Commentary on Ancient Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. II, pp. 1169–70: “Among the manuscript codices of the Bodleian Library, codex 8615, in Langbaine’s notebooks, codex 2, no. 6: a supplement to Book III of P. Abaelard’s *Introduction to Theology*, p. 148.” And shortly afterwards: “Among the manuscripts of Oxford University, no. 458; in the manuscript codices of Balliol College, R. 5: three books of P. Abaelard’s *Theology*, of which the third is complete, not mutilated and incomplete as in the printed editions.” In the libraries of France, codices of this kind do not seem to have been complete. For Martène says, in the preliminary observations to Abaelard’s *Christian Theology* (*Treasury of New Anecdotes*, vol. V, p. 1148): “Abaelard’s *Introduction* is mutilated in the printed editions, nor have we found it complete in manuscripts.”]

then, as soon as some Oxford theologian wishes to devote his theological leisure to deciding this matter, it may be done.

Meanwhile, the book seemed to us well worthy of being brought to light. For besides those reasons for which we pursue every monument of antiquity with reverence and make it common property, other considerations also prompted us: above all, we hoped that the book might assist in recounting the history of dogma—especially the history of soteriology and ethics during the earlier period of what is called scholasticism—and might make possible a better understanding of the part which Abelard played in forming the theology of Peter Lombard. [Note: [Col. 1691D] John of Cornwall, in the *Eulogium*: “Master Peter Abelard argues thus in his *Theology*: What is it to say that God becomes man, except that the divine substance, which is spiritual, unites to itself in one person the human substance, which is corporeal?—That Master Peter Lombard received this opinion from Master Peter [Col. 1692C] Abelard I have suspected all the more because he frequently had that book at hand and perhaps did not examine every point with sufficient care, being one who possessed skill in disputation more through practice than through method.”] We further judged that the connection among Abelard’s several doctrines, together with the history of Master Peter, might be illuminated by a new light. For a more exact acquaintance with this part of his theology seems especially well suited to elucidating various difficulties, to weighing in a fair balance the stratagems of Abelard’s opponents, to examining the truth or falsity of the reproaches made against him, and to making a just assessment of the defenses issued by Abelard himself [Note: [Col. 1692D] *Confession* (= *Apology*): “To all the children of the Holy Church, Peter Abelard, one among them but the least among them” (above, col. 107); letter to G., bishop of Paris; *History of My Calamities*, chs. 9–11; letter to his Heloise.] or undertaken on his behalf. [Col. 1693A] [Note: [Col. 1693C] Berengar the Scholastic’s *Apologeticus against Bernard*; compare with it his letters to the bishop of Mende and against the Carthusians (below, in the Appendix). See also Otto of Freising, *The Deeds of Emperor Frederick I*, bk. I, ch. 47.] But Augustus Neander, our most beloved and highly revered teacher, in his forthcoming short *Life of Bernard*, and other learned men bound to us by the ties of friendship—Bernard Hundeshagen, Albert Liebner, Karl Meier, and Ludwig Pelt—will set forth these matters more fully in the works which they have prepared or are preparing on the scholastic age.

[Note: [Col. 1692C] William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, in his letter to Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, and Bernard of Clairvaux (*Works of Bernard*, vol. I, p. 303; *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII); Bernard of Clairvaux: letter to the bishops summoned at Sens, [Col. 1692D] letter to the bishops and cardinals of the curia, letter to Pope Innocent, “Fourteen Heads of the Heresies of Peter Abelard,” letter to Guido of Castello, letter to Master Ivo the cardinal (*Works of Bernard*, vol. I, pp. 181–186 and 646–664); letter of Samson, archbishop of Reims, and others to Pope Innocent (*Works of Bernard*, vol. I, p. 184); rescripts of Pope Innocent against the heresies of Peter Abelard (*Works of Bernard*, vol. I, p. 186); Walter of Maurienne, bishop of Laon, letter to Peter Abelard (Dachery, *Spicilegium of Ancient Writers*, vol. III, p. 224 ff.); Robert Pullen, observations against Abelard in book I of the *Sentences*, art. 7, on God’s omnipotence (ed. D. H. Mathoud, Paris, 1655; *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI).]

It remains to add something concerning the manuscript’s outward form. It is written in folio, though it fills a smaller extent than is usual for that format. The material employed, commonly called parchment, has been preserved excellently. On every page there are two columns, each containing thirty or thirty-one lines. The numbers placed over the chapters are in red and adorned with varied ornament; the initial letters have their decorations. The writing is somewhat faded; the letter-forms, abbreviated in many ways, appear to date from Abelard’s age. The whole book consists of XXXIX folios, or LXXVII [Col. 1693B] pages. We have corrected what seemed to require correction here and there; what we thought should be removed from the text we enclosed in crescent-shaped brackets; what should be added, in square brackets; and we have added a few conjectures.

To what has already been said about the subject, we add the following. At the beginning of the manuscript is read an encomium of Abelard, already published by Pez. [Note: [Col. 1693C] In the *Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. III, introductory dissertation, [Col. 1693D] p. XXII.—Since Pez published from the same Emmeram manuscript, in which both this encomium of Abelard and our book are found, Peter’s book entitled *Know Thyself*, we cannot but believe that he too held Mabillon’s opinion concerning our book (see above, note 74), and therefore did not examine it further.] Then follow the titles of thirty-seven chapters, and finally the chapters themselves. It seemed appropriate to present complete and entire a manuscript which is not in itself of great extent. For although chapters 1–11 agree with the *Introduction* in many places, in other places they depart from it. Our manuscript presents entirely new propositions which throw light upon passages of the *Introduction* and can remedy its exceedingly corrupt text. Yet even apart from this consideration, it seemed already necessary that the whole work should be printed, because the relation between the *Introduction* and our book could be clearly understood and judged only on this condition.

[Col. 1693C] As for the title which we have given our book, we did not wish to retain that found in our manuscript, because Peter declared in explicit words that he had never written a book marked by this title. Those words cannot be disbelieved. Besides, it is easy to understand how our book acquired the title *Sentences*, whatever one may hold to be true concerning its origin. For the word *Sentences* was customary, both before and after our Peter, for distinguishing books of this kind by title. [Note: [Col. 1693D] Likewise Abelard’s book *Yes and No* is entitled in manuscripts: “Collection of the Sentences of Peter Abelard.”—There also circulated a *Book of Sentences* to which the name of St Bernard had been prefixed. The editors relegated it to the end of Bernard’s *Works*.] [Col. 1694A] Thus, if Abelard’s book came into someone’s hands without a title, he gave the book this title. Under this name the book then became known. Thus it also came to the abbot of Clairvaux. [Note: [Col. 1693D] Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, twelfth century, diss. 7, art. 6: “The holiness of St Bernard prevents one from believing that he invented that passage. It was therefore taken from a book so called, perhaps because it [Col. 1694C] lacked an inscription and nevertheless contained opinions on theological matters.”] Moreover, it should be recalled that the titles of Abelard’s works vary greatly. Thus, to omit other examples, Peter calls the *Introduction* itself at one time a work *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity*, at another his *Theology*, at another a theological treatise *On the Divine Unity and Trinity*, at another a book *On the Trinity* (*History of My Calamities*, ch. 9); similarly, his opponents speak indifferently of the *Theology*, the book *On the Trinity*, and so forth. Hence we decided that the manuscript title should not be much regarded, but that one should choose a title close to those of Abelard’s works akin to ours in subject matter, while at the same time indicating what was distinctive to the book.

But enough of this. It remains for me to offer and express the greatest thanks in my power to the director and custodians of the court library, for the extraordinary liberality and kindness with which they have aided my studies, and for the [Col. 1694B] generous instruction which I received from them about the subject, history, administration, and organization of the royal library. From these gentlemen I also learned that another book of Abelard, entitled *Yes and No*, well known from monastic libraries, had come to Munich [Note: [Col. 1694C] This manuscript passed in 1804 from the Tegernsee Benedictine library to the royal library at Munich. In the Tegernsee manuscript collection it was designated C. T. Lat. 926. It is written on parchment, fols. XC. 8. Imperial folio. Its prologue begins with these words: “Since in so great a multitude of books there are certain things,” etc. The book is divided into 156 chapters, of which the first bears the title: “That the limits of human reason are not to be established.”] and was still preserved here. I saw this book and read it in part, but returned it to its place because I knew that Victor Cousin, the Parisian philosopher, a man distinguished on many grounds, intended to publish it. [Note: [Col. 1694D] Victor Cousin, therefore, will render void the lamentable judgment once held in the Parisian assembly of Benedictines a century ago, concerning which Martène (at the cited place) relates approximately the following: “We possess another book of the same Abelard in which, indulging his genius, he turns all the mysteries of the Christian religion to both sides, denying what he had affirmed and affirming what he had denied. Our Achéry once intended to make this work public; but when it had been seriously examined, he judged, on the counsel of learned men, that it deserved eternal darkness rather than light.” Compare *Histoire littéraire de la France*, cited place, p. 131.] It is among my highest wishes that the book may soon appear and, together with our book and the fragments previously published from the Imperial Library at Vienna, may once again awaken study of Abelard among his contemporaries. From this it will finally come about that, when all Abelard’s works have been collected and published together, a monument worthy of so great a man may be erected. While we hope and long for this, we append at the end the words of an admirer of Abelard, who, carried away by the greatest [Col. 1694C] reverence for him, dared in a sorrowful time to utter these words:

> “Hail and farewell, my Abelard restored to life: a phoenix to yourself and to your ashes, and one dug out into the light by truth, the daughter of time! Receive this saying spoken to your memory:
>
> But the honour which the envious crowd had taken from me while I lived  
> Will after my death repay me with double interest!”

Given at Munich, on the very Vigil of Holy Easter, 1835.

# PETER ABELARD’S EPITOME OF CHRISTIAN THEOLOGY

[Col. 1695]

## CHAPTER I. That faith, charity, and the sacraments constitute the sum of our salvation, and what each of these is

[Col. 1695A]

There are, I think, three things in which the sum of human salvation consists: namely faith, charity, and the sacraments. I consider hope to be included within faith, as a species within its genus. For faith is an estimation of things not apparent—that is, not subject to bodily senses. Hope, however, is the expectation of attaining some good, when someone believes that he will obtain some good thing. Faith therefore concerns both good and bad things, and present things as well as past and future things, as blessed Augustine explains at the beginning of the *Enchiridion*. Hope, however, concerns only [Col. 1695B] good things and future things. For the expectation of some misfortune is to be called not so much hope as despair, that is, distrust of good.

Charity is honourable love: love, that is, directed to that to which it ought to be directed, so that we love God himself for his own sake and our neighbour for God’s sake. For nothing ought to be loved, and absolutely nothing done, except for God’s sake, so that we establish in God the end of all things. Hence he himself is called Α and Ω, that is, the beginning and the end (Rev. 1:8): the supreme beginning, from whom are all things; and the end—that is, the final and supreme cause—for whose sake are all things. For I ought not to eat, sleep, take a wife, or do anything whatever except for Christ’s sake. Otherwise we would live like beasts, devoted solely to our own pleasures. We ought, however, to eat for his sake, so that we may furnish to the body, which is his and entrusted to us for service, the necessities by which it may be sustained in his obedience. Likewise, we should restore it by sleeping, so that we may be able, when necessary, to keep watch in his praises. A wife also ought to be taken by one who is incontinent, not only to beget children, but lest he offend Christ through fornication. Thus it is clear that all other things too must be done for his sake. Otherwise we would vainly expect a reward if we did not do what we do for his sake. Carefully attending to this, the Apostle says in the Letter to the Corinthians: “Therefore, whether you eat or drink, or do anything else, do all things for the glory [Col. 1695D] of God” (1 Cor. 10:31).

A sacrament is a visible sign of invisible grace. Thus, when someone is baptized, that outward washing of the body which we see is a sign of the inward washing of the soul. As the inward person is cleansed of sins, so the outward person is washed of bodily defilements.

## CHAPTER II. On faith, which naturally comes first

[Col. 1696A]

Now that the three matters set out above have been briefly identified and defined, let us discuss each more carefully, insofar as seems relevant to the sum of human salvation set out above, and especially those matters that appear entangled in greater questions. First, then, faith, which naturally precedes the rest as the foundation of all goods. For how can what is hoped for be loved as hoped for unless it is first believed? Yet it can be believed even if it is not loved or hoped for. Hope therefore arises from faith, when we trust through God’s mercy that we shall obtain the good which we believe [Col. 1696B] we shall receive. Hence the Apostle: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for” (Heb. 11:4), that is, the foundation and origin by which we are led to hope for something: namely, by first believing that these things exist, so that we may afterward hope for them; “the evidence of things not apparent,” that is, proof that things not apparent exist. For since no one doubts that faith exists, it follows that he believes some things not apparent to exist, because, as has been said, faith is properly spoken only of things that have not yet appeared.

Hence, when according to the Apostle three things are now said to remain—faith, hope, and charity (1 Cor. 13:13)—charity alone never fails (ibid. 8), remaining both here and in the future. For this reason it is rightly called greater, both because of the dignity of its endurance and because it deserves reward, since it alone, in my judgment, is worthy of reward. But if anyone says that faith is also held concerning apparent things, he uses the name “faith” improperly. Faith is nevertheless found to be spoken of concerning apparent things as well as non-apparent things. We have examples of both before us.

Gregory, Homily 26 on the second book of the Gospels: “Since the Apostle says, ‘Faith is the substance,’ etc., it is surely clear that faith is the evidence of those things which cannot appear. For things that are apparent do not have faith but knowledge.” The same, *Dialogues*, book IV, ch. 7: “When Paul says, ‘Faith is the substance of things hoped for,’ etc., that which cannot be seen must truly be believed. For what can be seen [Col. 1696D] can no longer be believed.” Augustine on John: “‘And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened you may believe’” (John 14:29). “What does this mean, when what ought to be believed is rather to be believed before it happens? For this is the praise of faith: that what is believed is not seen. Is it a great thing if what is seen is believed? According to that saying of the Lord, by which he rebukes the disciple, saying: ‘Because you have seen me, you have believed. Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed’” (John 20:29). “But he saw one thing and believed another. For deity could not be seen by a mortal human being. He therefore saw the man and confessed the Lord, saying: ‘My God and my Lord’” (ibid. 28). “For faith itself is thus defined: ‘Faith is the substance,’ etc. Why then does he say, ‘that when it has happened you may believe’? For the person to whom it was said, ‘Because you have seen me,’ etc., did not believe what he saw; he beheld flesh and believed God hidden in the flesh. But if we say that things which are seen are believed, as everyone says that he has believed his own eyes, still this is not the faith that builds us up; rather, from the things which we see, it comes about in us that we believe those things which we do not see.”

From these and many other testimonies which we might adduce, it is clear that “faith” is used sometimes properly and sometimes improperly, since faith is spoken not only of hidden things but also of manifest things. There are also many matters relating to God which make no difference to us whether they are believed or not; for, whether they are believed or not, we incur no danger. For example, whether we believe that God will give rain tomorrow or not, or will grant mercy to this person or not; or whether we believe that Christ was of this or that stature, or preached in this city or not.

Therefore, for one speaking about faith for edification, it is sufficient to discuss and teach [Col. 1697C] only those matters which, if not believed, produce condemnation. These are precisely the matters that pertain to Catholic faith. Catholic faith—that is, universal faith—is so necessary for all that no person of discernment can be saved without it. Or faith is called Catholic, that is, universal, because it makes us one, or because it unites us to God. Hence Athanasius, after beginning, “This is the Catholic faith,” immediately explains why it is called Catholic by adding, “Which unless each person,” etc. Some also wish Catholic faith to be so called in distinction from the faith of heretics, which does not spread everywhere with the Church but lies hidden, as it were, in a corner.

## CHAPTER III. The matters in which Catholic faith consists

[Col. 1697D]

Catholic faith consists partly in the nature of the Godhead itself, and partly in divine benefits and in all God’s most righteous dispensations or ordinances, which have been carefully expressed for us in the creed of the apostles or holy fathers. First let us discuss what pertains to the divine nature: namely, how three persons are believed to exist in one and altogether the same divine substance, and what rationality or usefulness this distinction of persons has in the one God. Let us therefore first set forth this summary of faith, concerning divine unity and trinity; then let us discuss what has been set forth, as the Lord grants.

## CHAPTER IV. That the summary of faith lies in divine unity and trinity

The religion of Christian faith therefore holds that there is only one God: one God of all, one Creator of all, one substance or essence, wholly immutable and simple, in which no part or anything that is not, or has not been, that very substance itself can inhere; and it preaches that this substance is altogether one according to unity, with the sole exception of the plurality belonging to persons. To this utterly simple and indivisible substance it truly confesses three persons, coeternal and coequal with one another in every respect, distinguished not by number but by properties: God [Col. 1698B] the Father, God his Son, and the Holy Spirit proceeding from both.

One person is not another, although each is the very same thing that the other is. For he who is Father is not Son or Holy Spirit, nor is he who is Son Father or Holy Spirit. But what the Father is, the Son and Holy Spirit are also; and conversely. For the same God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. They are altogether one in nature, one both in number and substance; but according to their properties they are personally distinguished, so that this one is other than that one, though not another thing. Hence Sedulius: “Not because he who is the supreme Father is this Son, but because what the supreme Father is, that the Son is also.”

The Father’s proper characteristic is to be unbegotten—that is, to exist from himself and not from another. As the Son’s proper characteristic is to be called begotten from the Father alone, not made or created, so the Holy Spirit’s is to proceed from both, not to be created or made. For what subsists eternally and has no beginning should be called neither created nor made. Thus we say that the Father alone is unbegotten, that is, exists from himself and not from another.

Hence Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VI: “The Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called unbegotten. It is one thing, then, to call the Father unbegotten, and another to call him not begotten; just as it is one thing to call something unjust, and another not just. For what is unjust must necessarily be not just, but not conversely. A stone, for example, is not just, yet it is not unjust. So too, when the Father is called [Col. 1698D] unbegotten, it is certainly clear that he is not begotten—that is, he is not the Son. The Holy Spirit too is not begotten, since he is not begotten—that is, he is not the Son—yet he is not altogether unbegotten, since he is from another, proceeding from both the Father and the Son. Thus the Father alone is called unbegotten, as the Son alone is called begotten. The Holy Spirit, however, is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but, as has been said, not begotten.”

Hence Augustine, *To Orosius*, chapter 5: “Certain faith declares the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten; for if we say unbegotten, we shall appear to affirm two Fathers, while if we say begotten, we are accused of believing in two Sons.” The same [Note: [Col. 1697D] Namely, Gennadius.] in *On Orthodox Faith and Ecclesiastical Doctrines*, ch. 1: “The Father, then, is the beginning of the Godhead, from whom the Son is born, from whom the Holy Spirit is not born, because he is not the Son, nor unbegotten, because he is not the Father.” Blessed Gregory, following him, also states in the creed prefixed to his letters: “We believe that the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but coeternal, proceeding from the Father and the Son.”

Although each of these persons is God, Lord, and Creator, and one person is not another, there are not therefore as many gods, lords, or creators as there are persons. For when we say “gods,” “lords,” or “creators,” we indicate a certain number of things, each of which is a god, lord, or creator; but in the Godhead [Col. 1699B] there can be no multiplicity of things. Hence we call the Trinity indivisible. But when we confess many persons in God, we indicate a plurality of properties, not of things. Certain terms, then, are said of individual persons only: “unbegotten” of the Father alone; “begotten” or “incarnate” of the Son alone; and “proceeding from both” of the Holy Spirit alone. Certain terms are said jointly only, and not separately: for example, “Trinity,” said jointly of the three persons. Certain terms are equally said of them both jointly and separately: God, Creator, Lord, omnipotent, wisdom, power, and so forth. Yet only this name, “person,” is uttered in the plural, because we profess several persons, not several gods or lords, nor admit any plurality in the other terms. Hence Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book VII, ch. 6: “The Father is called a person in relation to himself, not in relation to the Son or the Holy Spirit. Again, this name alone, although said of each separately in relation to itself, is taken plurally rather than singly in the highest reality. For we say: the Father is a person, the Son is a person, the Holy Spirit is a person; yet the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not one person, but three.”

## CHAPTER V. He sets forth what he himself thinks concerning unity and trinity, and defends it by reason and authority

Having briefly set forth this summary of faith concerning divine unity and Trinity, it remains to defend and establish it against the inquiries of doubters by suitable illustrative comparisons. [Col. 1699D] For what use is it to speak in teaching if what we say cannot be explained so as to be understood? Blessed Augustine carefully observed this when he wished to explain that most difficult passage on the Trinity with which the Evangelist John began: “In the beginning,” etc. “The natural man,” he says, “does not perceive this. What then, brothers, shall we be silent about it? Why is it written if it is to be silent, or why heard if it is not explained? But why is it explained if it is not understood?”

The first thing requiring our discussion, therefore, is what this division or distinction of persons means in the one nature of the Godhead: that the Father is the same, the Son the same, and the Holy Spirit the same, although by this distinction of the Trinity we understand the supreme good and all things. For by the name Father is designated the power of divine [Col. 1700A] majesty: that he can accomplish whatever he wills. Hence Augustine in the *Enchiridion*: “He is not truly called omnipotent unless he can do whatever he wills.” The same, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*: “He cannot do unjust things, because he himself is supreme justice and goodness. But he is omnipotent not because he can do all things, but because he can accomplish whatever he wills.” That is, all things are so placed under his power that, among all that he himself wills to ordain or do, there is no one who can impede his will.

As the power of divine majesty is expressed especially by the name Father, so by the designation Son or Word is signified God’s begotten wisdom, by which he can so discern all things that he can be deceived in absolutely nothing. But by the name Holy Spirit is understood his very charity or goodness, proceeding from both: namely, that he wills everything to happen in the way in which it can happen best. For one is not perfect in all respects if found powerless in some respect; nor is one perfectly blessed if capable of deception in some respect; nor altogether good if he does not will all things to be done and ordered in the best way. But where these three concur—where, that is, one is perfect in power, wisdom, and good will—there is no good lacking from that person’s fullness. Thus, to profess God as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is equivalent to proclaiming, as has been said, that he is the supreme good, lacking nothing as the fullness of all goods.

This distinction of the Trinity, moreover, is suitable not only for describing the perfection of the supreme good, as has been said, [Col. 1700C] but also greatly assists in persuading human beings toward the perfection of divine worship [“religion”], so that God’s wisdom incarnate rightly ordained above all to adopt it in his preaching. For there are two things that make us entirely subject to the Lord: fear and love. Power and wisdom especially inspire fear, when we perceive him to be judge, know that he can punish whatever he wills, and recognize that nothing is hidden from him. Goodness, however, belongs to love, so that we love most of all him whom we know to be most good. From this one may also see that he wills to avenge in righteousness: for the more equity pleases him, the more iniquity displeases him. Hence: “You loved justice and hated iniquity” (Ps. [Col. 1700D] 44:8).
