Yet this distinction of the Trinity is necessary not only for instilling fear or love of God in human beings; it also has great force for commending all his works, so that whatever he does is believed to be excellently done, since he can accomplish whatever he wills, knows how to observe measure in all things, and wills all things to be done or to proceed in the best way. Therefore, when we implore divine grace for accomplishing something, we rightly make mention of the Trinity, saying, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” or, “In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity,” so that, by recalling divine power, wisdom, and goodness, we may show that whatever God accomplishes is excellently done.

Thus Moses too, [Col. 1701A] when treating the universe of the world, immediately mentions God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit at the very beginning of Genesis, so that whatever he narrates as made by God may be believed excellently made. For when he says, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” and afterward adds, “And the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters,” he carefully expresses the divine Trinity: in God the Creator, indeed, implying the Father—that is, recalling divine power, by which he could create all things from nothing. This is not unfittingly suggested by the proper interpretation of the name “God” itself, as though from *Theos* [Θεός], that is, “fear,” because the reverence of fear is especially shown toward power.

By the name “beginning,” however, he designates the Son: that is, divine reason or wisdom, in which all things first had, as it were, their subsistence through providence. Hence the Evangelist, speaking of the Word of the Father, says: “In him was life” (John 1:3). Thus Macrobius too, following Plato, reports that the mind of God—which the Greeks call *noun* [νοῦν]—contains the original forms of things, called ideas, before, as Priscian says, they came forth into bodies; that is, before they emerged as the completed effects of works. By “the Spirit of the Lord,” however, Moses plainly indicates the Holy Spirit, that is, the goodness of divine grace.

With the same careful consideration, when he came to the excellent creation of the human being, wisely setting this work before the others and commending it as surpassing them, he plainly makes the distinction of the Trinity, where the Lord says “Let us make,” rather than “I shall make,” “in our image,” he says, “and likeness” (Gen. 1:26): the man, indeed, in God’s image, the woman in likeness. For according to the Apostle, the man is the image of God, not the woman. But as the man is the image of God, so the woman is the image of the man. For an image is called the exact likeness of a thing; “likeness,” however, may be said even if it does not express very closely that of which it is a likeness.

That divine power is especially expressed by the name Father, divine wisdom by the name Son or Word, and divine goodness or charity by the name Holy Spirit, is not concealed from us either by authority or by reason. Haymo especially understands power by the name Father in his explanation of the Letter to the Ephesians, where it says, [Col. 1701D] “Giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God and the Father.” Haymo says: “‘To God and the Father,’ that is, to God the omnipotent Father.” Maximus the bishop also, in his exposition of the creed: “Do you believe in God the omnipotent Father? In ‘God’ the unbegotten nature is shown; in ‘Father,’ the truth of the Only-Begotten; in ‘omnipotent,’ the fullness of truth. For he is omnipotent through unbegotten deity, Father through power.” In this place he calls “unbegotten” uncreated. By “unbegotten deity” he means God—that is, he professes that only he among the three persons is unbegotten, since he alone is not from another, whereas the other persons are from him. But when it is said that he is omnipotent through unbegotten deity and Father through omnipotence, it plainly implies that power pertains especially to the property of the Father alone, [Col. 1702A] although each person, together with the Father, is of the same substance and altogether the same power.

## CHAPTER VI. That certain things belong to one person and not another, while certain things are said of one but understood of all

According to the properties of the three persons, certain things belong especially to one which do not belong to another; and certain things are customarily said and understood of one which, because of the identity of their nature, we do not doubt belong to each individually. Thus wisdom is especially attributed to the Son and charity to the Holy Spirit, although the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—and indeed the whole Trinity—are wisdom; likewise the Father himself as well as the Son can be called charity.

So too, according to the properties [Col. 1702B] of the persons, certain works are especially attributed to a particular person, although the works of the whole Trinity are proclaimed undivided, and whatever is done by one of them is certainly done by each. The assumption of flesh, indeed, is ascribed to the Son alone; one is said to be regenerated by water and the Holy Spirit alone, not by water and the Father or Son—although the working of the whole Trinity was present in these things. Yet what concerns power is to be assigned to the Father, what concerns wisdom to the Son, and what concerns goodness to the Holy Spirit.

The works of the three persons are called indivisible, that is, common, because whatever is effected by power is regulated by wisdom and fashioned by goodness. Thus, in those things which we do or ask God to do, we make commemoration of the Trinity, saying, “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” so that, as the operation of the three persons is undivided, so their invocation may be inseparable; and thus both faith itself may be confirmed by the benefits sought and the effectiveness of the divine work may be commended. For it is readily believed that he will accomplish the good which is requested if he is known to be most good and able to do it as he wills.

But when the remembrance of wisdom is added—which is expressed by the name Son, and by which he wills to observe measure in all things—the effect is shown to be excellent. When, moreover, we recall goodness, denoted by the name Spirit, the effect is designated best. Thus, by such an invocation, an effect is shown to occur which proceeds from one who can do [Col. 1702D] whatever he wills, knows how to observe measure in all he does, and wills all things to occur in the best way.

## CHAPTER VII. That any one of the persons does the same as another, but does not possess itself in the same manner as another
Nevertheless, it must be understood that, although each of these persons is called omnipotent, because whatever any one of them may will to accomplish, he can bring to completion, it does not follow that one is in every respect constituted in the same manner as another, since they are distinguished from one another by their own properties. For the Father alone is unbegotten; the Son alone is begotten or incarnate; the Holy Spirit alone proceeds. Therefore, whatever one can do, the others can also do, and for this reason each is called omnipotent [Col. 1703A]; but whatever one can be, another cannot also be. As Jerome says: “The Father is found to have this more than the Son: that he alone is from himself; whereas the Son is not from himself, but is from the Father as begotten.” Therefore, when Bishop Maximus says that the Father is by omnipotence, he plainly indicates that the Father is called omnipotent not because he alone is omnipotent—as has been said, that is, able to accomplish all that he wills—but because he has this ability from himself, just as he has being from himself and not from another. Hence the Son himself says: “I can do nothing of myself” (John 5:39). And elsewhere: “I do nothing of myself” (John 8:28), or “I do not speak of myself” (John 14:10).

## CHAPTER VIII. He proves by evangelical and apostolic authority that the Father is specially designated by omnipotence, the Son by wisdom, and the Holy Spirit by goodness.

[Col. 1703B]

We now maintain, on both evangelical and apostolic authority, that divine power is assigned by the title Father; then it will become incontrovertibly clear, both by reason and by the authority of the saints, that what we say is true. For the Son says: “Which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1:7)—not because the Son or the Holy Spirit lacks it, although the power of the three persons is the same. And elsewhere: “As,” he says, “my Father has appointed for me” (Luke 22:29). Whenever the humanity of the Son himself implores the aid of the divinity united to it, or pours forth any prayers, it uses the title Father alone, namely commemorating [Col. 1703C] that power by which he is able to accomplish what is asked: as when it is said, “Holy Father, preserve them” (John 17:11); “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46); and similar words belonging to prayer. The Church still observes this practice in those special prayers made at the altar during the celebration of Mass, which direct their address to the Father alone.

Thus the Apostle says that Christ rose from the dead through the grace of the Father—that is, through the strength of divine power—or that the Father raised the Son from the dead, or will give life to our bodies, or that the Son sent the Spirit, or obeyed the Father. When, I say, he speaks in this way, he seems to attribute specially and properly to the Father those things which appear to belong to power. Thus also [Col. 1703D] those things which belong to power seem to be assigned to the person of the Father, in accordance with his property, as was said; just as those things which pertain to reason or wisdom are assigned to the Son—for example, judging, which belongs to discernment. As it is written: “The Father has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), because in discernment power yields to wisdom, where equity is more to be examined, although power also must be exercised.

Moreover, the statement added—that judgment especially depends on the Son of Man—is made clear according to what the Son himself declared: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” [Col. 1704A] (John 15:22). It is as though he said that the ungodly justly incur the greatest condemnation because they proved ungrateful and without excuse for so great a benefit, rejecting even the Son sent by the Father. To this also belongs the title of the Psalm, “For the hidden things of the Son” (Psalm 9), namely his judgments, of which it is said: “Your judgments are a great deep” (Psalm 35:7). For, as has been said, it belongs to wisdom to judge—that is, to recognize what is due to each person according to justice.

The Apostle calls Christ “the power and wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24): wisdom, through which he knows all things completely; power, through which he accomplishes the effective fulfillment of all good things. Hence it is written: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3); and elsewhere: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24). Therefore he is called the right hand or hand [Col. 1704B] of the Father, through whom the Father works all things. He is also rightly called the mind of the Father, or reason, or the Angel of Counsel, because in this wisdom the Father rationally orders all things, whether by creating the world or by restoring it after its fall; and in this the Father gave true counsel to our ignorance when his incarnation visited us.

Accordingly, when the Son of God is called *Logos*, that is, “Word,” the term is taken in the sense in which λόγος (*logos*) among the Greeks signifies the very conception of the mind, or reason, not an utterance of the voice. Hence Boethius, in the *Categories*: “Because in Greek speech λόγος is called both the thought of the mind and inward reasoning [Note: [Col. 1703] *Introduction to Theology* reads: ‘reasoning, and λόγος also means speech, lest anyone,’ etc.], lest anyone should think that Aristotle, when he said that λόγος—that is, [o] [Col. 1704C] reason—is a quantity, was speaking of that λόγος which each person arranges in thought, he added: ‘which is produced with the voice.’”

Blessed Augustine also mentions this in book 81, chapter 44, of the *Questions*: “In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word, which in Greek is called λόγος, while in Latin it signifies both reason and word. But in this place ‘word’ is better understood, so that it may signify not only a relation to the Father, but also those things which were made through the Word.” John is called the voice of this Word, because the Word precedes him in being born, in preaching, and in dying. Concerning him it is said, “The voice of one crying,” etc.; for just as an audible word precedes an intelligible word in the hearer, because the voice first sounds and afterward the meaning is conceived by the understanding, so John’s preaching went before, announcing the coming.

Therefore “Word” denotes the conception of the mind and a certain utterance of intelligence formed in the mind. In likeness to this, the only-begotten Word of God is called the Word, and as it were a certain intellectual and eternal utterance of God, in whose providence the preordained ordering of all things has stood from eternity. Hence, when Moses prefaces the creation of different things with “God said,” and immediately adds the result to the saying—“And it was so” (Genesis 1)—he shows that God created all things in the Word, that is, in his wisdom, rationally. Of this the Psalm also says: “And they were made” (Psalm 32:9), that is, he created or ordered all things by reason.

Elsewhere, making the nature of this Word clearer, [Col. 1705A] he says that it is not audible or passing, but intelligible and permanent: “Who made the heavens in understanding” (Psalm 135). That is, he made them according to that pattern by which he first ordered them in the word of the mind—that is, in the conception or perpetual intelligence which foresees all things.

Now, just as what pertains to power is specially attributed to the Father, and what pertains to wisdom to the Son, so what concerns the working of divine grace and the goodness of divine love is attributed to the Holy Spirit: such as the remission of sins and the distribution of whatever gifts proceed from his goodness alone, not from our merits. Such are regeneration in baptism for the forgiveness of sins, and confirmation by the bishop’s laying on of hands, for the giving of spiritual armor, [etc.]. So too the other [Col. 1705B] sacraments administered in the Church are to be attributed to the Holy Spirit through the goodness of God.

From this it is plainly evident that the affection and sweetness of divine power or goodness are expressed by the title Holy Spirit. For through the spirit of our mouth, that is, our breath, the affections of the mind are especially manifested: namely, when we sigh from love or groan under the pressure of pain or toil. Hence in this place the Holy Spirit is set for good affection, according to that saying of Wisdom: “The spirit of wisdom is gracious,” etc. (Wisdom 1:6), and that of the Psalm: “Your good Spirit will lead me” (Psalm 142:10); and the Apostle: “God is love” (1 John 4:8), because, according to Gregory’s testimony, the Spirit himself is love—the love by which, according to John, the Father loves the Son. Hence Augustine, in the book *On the City [of God]*: “The Holy Spirit is a certain [Col. 1705C] communion of the Father and the Son; and perhaps for this reason he is so called, because the same designation can belong to the Father and the Son.” Therefore, in order that the communion of both may be signified by a name fitting both, the Holy Spirit is called the gift of both.

## CHAPTER IX. Proof from the Law.

I consider it clear, then, from the testimonies already given, that divine power, as we have said, is expressed by the title Father; that the Son is understood as divine wisdom; and that the goodness of divine grace is called the Holy Spirit. The modes, however, of this generation and procession, as the Lord grants, we shall explain in what follows. But now, in support of our faith against both Jews and Gentiles, let us bring forward testimonies from their Scriptures, so that they may understand that this distinction of the Trinity was announced to all—revealed by divine inspiration through the prophets to the Jews and through the apostles [Note: [Col. 1705D] Perhaps “philosophers” should be read. Cf. chapter 11.] to the Gentiles.

First there occur the very beginnings of the Law, where Moses the legislator sets forth the Catholic faith concerning unity together with Trinity as the foundation of all goods. For when it is said, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1), the Hebrew truth uses *Eloy* in place of what we call “God”; this is the plural of the singular *Hel*. Why then is not *Hel*, meaning “God,” used, but *Eloy*, interpreted “gods” or “judges,” unless this is adapted to the plurality of divine persons? Thus plurality in God is intimated in the same way as Trinity, and God is in some sense called manifold, as he is threefold—not according to diversity of substance, but according to the properties of the persons. Thus *Eloy* means, as it were, not many things but many persons, each one of whom is God. Otherwise we should say that there are several gods, whereas there is only one.

Hence Augustine also says: “God is indeed one, but not solitary.” Yet the legislator also carefully provided there for showing the unity of substance, where it is said “created,” not “created [plural],” preserving the singular number in [Col. 1706B] the verb according to the unity of substance, although in form of sound and inflection *Eloy* is plural. Thus conversely, when it is said, “the crowd rush,” a plural verb is applied to a singular noun, according to the understanding of the things substantially signified by the noun. Therefore, “*Eloy* created” is as if one said, “The Trinity created,” that is, acted jointly. Immediately afterward he also attaches an expression of the persons, as though to show that *Eloy* is said in the plural to determine this point.

For the paternity of the Holy Spirit is shown when it is said: “The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters” (ibid., 2). But the Word, that is, the Son, and the Father [Note: [Col. 1705D] *Introduction*: “that is, the Son, is at the same time clearly intimated,” [Col. 1706D] etc.] are intimated when it is said: “God said: Let there be” (ibid., 3): that is, in his utterance or Word—in his coeternal wisdom—the Father ordered what was to be made [Col. 1706C]. This cannot be understood as bodily speech.

Likewise, in what is written: “And God saw that it was good” (ibid., 10), it is as though one said: Understanding that the work he had made was good, he loved it because it was good. From this he is also plainly shown to be good. And what could be clearer for teaching the Trinity than what is afterward added in the creation of man, when the Lord says: “Let us make man,” etc. (ibid., 26)? Why is “let us make” said in the plural except to express the cooperation of the Trinity? For whom was God exhorting to create man, when he alone was to make him? For it is written: “Who has helped the Spirit of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Isaiah 40:13).

Man is rightly said to be made in the image and likeness of the Trinity—that is, in a certain expressed likeness of the three persons—so that he may imitate the Father through the power he has over other creatures; the Son through reason; and the Spirit through the graciousness of innocence, which he afterward lost through sin. This plurality of persons is also said to be relevant to what the serpent said later: “You shall be as gods” (Genesis 3:5), which, as was said above, in Hebrew sounds *Eloy*: that is, divine persons rather than different gods. Nor is that rebuke of the Lord irrelevant [Note: [Col. 1706D] Read: “and likewise that one.”]: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” [Col. 1707A] (Genesis 3:22). And again what the Lord says: “Let us go down and confuse their languages” (Genesis 11:4), although God alone accomplished this. Hence it is added: “And he scattered them” (ibid., 8).

## CHAPTER X. Proof from the Prophets.

Let us now pass from the Law to the testimonies of the prophets. Thus says David, that greatest of prophets and kings, who, preferring his understanding to that of others, says: “I have understood above all who teach me” (Psalm 118:99); and again: “I have understood above the aged” (ibid., 100). He says, I say, openly declaring the distinction of the Trinity: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Psalm 32:6). Elsewhere he also intimates unity together [Col. 1707B] with Trinity, saying: “May God bless us, our God; may God bless us” (ibid., Psalm 66:8). For the threefold confession of God expresses the Trinity of persons: namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

He fittingly added “our,” designating the Son of God, as though showing him to share our nature and to have been given to us by the Father, since through the incarnation of the Word Wisdom enlightened us. Of him the Apostle also says: “God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8:32). The Spirit, however, reveals in the same passage the unity of the divine substance: after the threefold utterance of the divine name, understanding one God in three persons, he did not add “may they bless” in the plural, but “may he bless” in the singular.

Isaiah agrees with this when he says that he saw the Seraphim and heard them crying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth” (Isaiah 6:3). He rightly used the title “Lord” to designate power, since it belongs to lords to rule. This power is frequently denoted by the name God, because Θεός (*Theos*), that is, “God,” is interpreted, according to Isidore’s testimony, as “fear”; and every power is a fear to subjects.

That the Word of God is wisdom itself is clearly shown in Ecclesiasticus in these words: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has been with him always, and is before the age” (Ecclesiasticus 1:1). “Who has investigated the wisdom of God, preceding all things? Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence from eternity. The source of wisdom is the Word of God in the heights.”

David also plainly intimates the eternal generation of the Son from God the Father when he introduces the person of the Son speaking thus: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son,” etc.; “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2:7–8). What he says, “I have begotten you today,” means: “You are eternally from my substance.” For since in eternity there is nothing past or future, but only the present moment, he used the adverb of present time for eternity, saying “today” for “eternally.” He aptly added “I have begotten” to “today,” joining a past tense to the present, in order to signify that the generation is always present through “today” and perfected through “I have begotten” [Col. 1708A]—that it neither ceases nor has begun. For things past have already been completed and perfected. Therefore he used the perfect past tense [Note: [Col. 1707D] *Introduction*: “He used the past as though for the sake of perfection.”] to signify perfection, showing that the Son is always begotten from the Father and always begotten.

Elsewhere David declares the eternity of the Son more plainly: “He shall remain with the sun and before the moon,” etc. (Psalm 71:5). Isaiah too, marveling at this ineffable generation, both eternal and temporal—each of which is wondrous—says: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8). That is, he says openly: It is not a matter for human genius to explain, but for God alone; yet his Spirit speaks of these things in those faithful persons whom he wills, as he himself testifies when he says: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

[Col. 1708B] Jerome, commenting on Ecclesiastes at the passage, “Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of men ascends upward, and whether the spirit of cattle descends downward into the earth?” (Ecclesiastes 3:21), takes the saying, “Who shall declare his generations?” (Isaiah 53:8), as an example of what is difficult, not impossible. Adding “who,” he says, was intended to demonstrate the difficulty of the matter. For in Holy Scripture this word “who” is always understood not of what is impossible, but of what is difficult: as, “Who shall declare his generation?”—that is, Christ’s.

This coeternity of Wisdom with the Father is also plainly shown in Proverbs in these words: “I, Wisdom, dwell in counsel. The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways, before he made anything from the beginning. I was ordained from eternity; before the hills I was brought forth; he had not yet made the earth and the foundations of the world. When he prepared the heavens, I was present; when he weighed out the foundation of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things; and I delighted day by day, playing before him at all times” (Proverbs 8:22–32).

For what could speak more plainly of the eternal generation of the Word than the declaration of eternal Wisdom that she was conceived and brought forth before the foundation of the world, remaining eternally with the Father and always playing before him? For when what is conceived is brought forth, it is certainly in the one by whom it is generated; and Wisdom is in the very substance or essence of power, since it is itself a certain power, as we shall show later. Therefore, for Wisdom to be conceived and brought forth by God is as though it were said that Wisdom is begotten from the substance of the Father, in which it exists.

Likewise, for Wisdom to play before the Father and arrange all things with him is as though he said that divine power disposes all things for itself in Wisdom according to the decision of its goodness, so that in that play we may understand the affection of goodness in the Spirit. Of this it is written: “By the Spirit [Col. 1708D] of his mouth is all their power” (Psalm 32:6). But when he says that Wisdom always stands before God the Father, this means that omnipotence accomplishes nothing except with Wisdom supplying reason and guidance [Note: [Col. 1708D] *Introduction*: “Omnipotence itself accomplishes nothing except with the reason and guidance of Wisdom going before.”].

Again, in the same Proverbs he writes most clearly concerning the Son of God and the ineffable name of that Son, as though introducing the person of a certain wondrous prophet, proclaiming and marveling at this inexpressible generation. For the vision says thus: “The words spoken by the man with whom God is, and who, strengthened by God abiding with him, says: Who has raised up all the ends of the earth? What is his name, and what is the name of his son?” (Proverbs 30:4).

What firm and open testimony to our faith occurs in Ecclesiasticus, where the Wisdom of God says that she is firstborn before all things according to the nature of divinity, and afterward created according to the assumption of our nature, since she visited Israel, at the command of the Father, by the garment of incarnation. For it is written there: [Col. 1709B] “Wisdom shall have praise among the elect in the multitude, and among the blessed she shall be blessed, saying: I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, firstborn before every creature. I caused unfailing light to arise in the heavens, and like a mist I covered the whole earth. I dwell in the highest places, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud. I alone traversed the circuit of heaven,” etc. (Ecclesiasticus 24:4–8). And a little later: “Then the Creator of all commanded and said to me; and he who created me rested in my tabernacle, and said to me: Dwell in Jacob, inherit in Israel, and put down roots among my elect” (ibid., 12–13).

In the same book it is also stated most plainly that forgiveness of sins rests upon the incarnation of divine Wisdom, who is Christ; divine Wisdom prophesies, declaring that David’s sins were cleansed through Christ. For when many things had been said there in praise of David, the sum of all his praise is gathered into this one point, which follows: “Christ [the Lord] cleansed his sins, and exalted his horn forever; and gave him a covenant of kings and a throne of glory in Israel” (Ecclesiasticus 47:13).

Micah also says concerning this eternal generation of the Word from the Father, together with his temporal generation from a mother: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrathah, are by no means small among the thousands of Judah; for from you there shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Micah 5:2).

Let rebellious and unbelieving Jews say of whom to be born in Bethlehem this was said: namely, that his going forth was from the beginning, from the days of eternity. For that is eternal which lacks an origin. But if [Col. 1709D] they refer this to the Messiah—that greatest prophet whom, they say, they expect, and who according to them will be merely a pure man, not also God—let them show what his eternal going forth is, or from where he proceeds eternally. If they say that he proceeds eternally from Bethlehem because his birth in that place was eternally foreseen and predestined by God, then the birth of every human being or of every thing is eternal in this way, because it was foreseen from eternity.

Let them therefore affirm the eternal generation which they read written, which they profess while reading, and which, while professing, they do not believe. Let them also answer me when they hear the Prophet say: “By the Word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6). What do they understand by the Word of the Lord, by his mouth, or by his Spirit? It is acknowledged that God is the principle of all other things; and everything that exists either is God, and therefore eternal, or flows from that eternal principle as a creature.

Furthermore it is written: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1). Hence they hold that nothing was created before these. Therefore that Word by which the heavens were established, and which is prior to those whom it established, is not created; indeed, it is the Creator himself, who is God, by whom the heavens were established. But if they call this Word a passing utterance, like the word of a human being—because it is written, “He spoke and they were made” (Psalm 32:9)—and thus say that God, like a human being, sometimes speaks when he says, “Let there be light” (Genesis 1:3), and sometimes is silent, then the eternity of divinity is plainly mutable, since he does not always say, “Let there be light,” or the other things which now all exist.

Moreover, what need was there for an audible word before creation, when there was not yet anyone to whom he might speak or anyone who could hear? Did he utter an empty word [not] if there was no need for a word, especially when will alone would have sufficed and there was not yet anyone to be instructed by hearing the word? Into what place could he emit words to be uttered, when no place had yet been created, nor any air formed out of which words might be shaped? By what instruments could he form words, when neither a mouth nor any part could belong to one who is altogether simple and indivisible? For everything made up of parts is naturally later than those things of which it consists and by whose combination it is completed, since it derives its being from those things out of which it is constituted. And Plato says: “Everything joined together by nature is dissoluble.”

But if they understand the Spirit of the Lord as wind, as they wish to understand it in the saying, “The Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters” (ibid., 2), because, they say, wind appears especially upon waters which it stirs, how can the Spirit be called the breath of the Lord’s mouth, when he has neither mouth nor any part, as has been said? How too does the power of heaven and earth subsist through wind? Let them understand, therefore, that this is the Spirit of the Lord whose sevenfold grace Isaiah describes, saying: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding,” [Col. 1710D] etc. (Isaiah 11:2). And elsewhere: “And now the Lord and his Spirit have sent me” (Isaiah 48:16); and again: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to announce to the meek” (Isaiah 61:1).

Of him it is also said in the book of Wisdom: “The spirit of discipline will flee deceit, for the spirit of wisdom is gracious,” etc. (Wisdom 1:5–6). And when it is added concerning him, “That which contains all things has knowledge of speech,” the Spirit himself is plainly declared to be God, since he is said to contain all things. Again Wisdom, speaking to God, says: “Who has known your counsel? . . . and you sent your Holy Spirit from the highest places” (Wisdom 9:17). And again: “How good and sweet is your Spirit within us!” (Wisdom 12:1).

Likewise, when the Spirit of Wisdom is described, he is plainly proclaimed to be the true God, since among other things it is written of him in Wisdom: “Having all power, beholding all things, and comprehending all spirits” [Col. 1711A] (Wisdom 7:23). Elihu in the book of Job professes him to be Creator, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord made me, and the breath of the Almighty gave me life” (Job 33:4). The Son himself also, in the Gospel, assigning to the Spirit dignity equal to himself and the Father, says: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

The Apostle likewise, according to Augustine’s testimony, when he calls believers the temple of the Holy Spirit, openly declares that the Spirit is God, since a temple is said to belong to God alone. For it is written in the Apostle: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16). Here he plainly intimates that the God whose temple it is and the Spirit of God whom he says dwells therein are the same.

So too blessed Peter, in the Acts of the Apostles, professes the Holy Spirit to be God, saying: “Why have you lied to the Holy Spirit, Ananias? You have not lied to human beings, but to God” [Col. 1711B] (Acts 5:4). Concerning the same Spirit the Acts also contain these words spoken by the Spirit in command: “Set apart for me Barnabas and Paul” (Acts 13:2); and again: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us” (Acts 15:28). The Psalmist declares the Spirit of God to be everywhere, as uncircumscribed, saying: “Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your face?” (Psalm 138:7).

Immediately afterward, in order to intimate that the Spirit of God whom he professes to be everywhere is the same as the God to whom he speaks, he plainly shows this by assigning the Spirit’s presence everywhere through God himself, whom he asserts to be everywhere: “If I ascend into heaven, you are there,” etc. (ibid., 8). But when Truth itself declares that sin against the Spirit is unforgivable, while saying that sin against the Father or the Son is forgivable (Matthew 12:32), does he not plainly intimate that the Spirit himself is not less than the Father or Son, and therefore is fully God, as the Father himself and the Son are?

It is certainly clear from what has been set forth above that both the Word of God and his Spirit are God, just as he himself is God whose Word and Spirit they are. Let them understand, therefore, as has been said, that this Word of the Lord—that is, the Son of God—is not a passing word, not audible, but intellectual: that is, reason or wisdom coeternal with God. It is fitting that this be called all-wisdom, just as we speak of omnipotence. Hence it is written: “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and has always been with him” (Ecclesiasticus 1:1).

He is also called in the book of Wisdom the true Son of God and is shown to be substantial, in distinction from adoptive sons, whom God acquired through his preaching; of these it is written: “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” [Col. 1711D] (John 1:12). Thus, when his passion was plainly prophesied in Wisdom, the ungodly said among other things: “For if he is the true Son of God, he will receive him and deliver him from the hand of his enemies” [Col. 1712A] (Wisdom 2:18). The holy soul delivered by God also openly professes this kinship when it says in Ecclesiasticus: “I called upon God, the Father of my Lord, that he might not abandon me in the day of my tribulation.”

## CHAPTER XI. He proves that philosophers were not without either salvation or knowledge of the Trinity.

Now, after the testimonies of the prophets concerning faith in the Holy Trinity, it is pleasing to add also the testimonies of the philosophers. Philosophy’s own reasoning led them to an understanding of the one God, so that, according to the Apostle, “the invisible things of God are clearly perceived, being understood through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world” [Col. 1712B] (Rom. 1:20); and the sobriety of their self-restrained life itself acquired this through a certain merit. For it was fitting that God should then also signify in them, by some gift of more abundant grace, how much more acceptable to him is one who lives soberly and withdraws himself from this world’s allurements by despising it, than one who, devoted to its pleasures, plunges himself into every impurity.

Holy teachers also report how great the philosophers’ abstinence and self-restraint were. They adduce their lives to rebuke us, and draw many things from their moral teachings or testimonies of faith for our edification. Whoever does not know this should at least read Jerome Against Jovinianus, and will see [Col. 1712C] how much he recounts concerning their virtues, or those of other pagans—namely, to crush the shamelessness of that heretic. Above all, it is fitting for us too to employ in this work the testimonies or arguments of philosophers, since we are especially arguing against those who strive to attack our faith by philosophical teachings—particularly since no one ought to be refuted or convicted except through the things he accepts [Note: [Col. 1711] Introduction: “particularly since no one is to be refuted except through the things he accepts”]; and the man who is defeated by the very means through which he sought to conquer is crushed with excessive confusion.

That philosophers recognized only one God is attested by one of them, Tully, in the first book of the *Rhetorics*, when he says that those who devote themselves to philosophy do not suppose that there are gods. It is as if he plainly said: indeed, that there is one God, not many. Paul the Apostle also clearly indicates, in the Epistle to the Romans, how, God revealing it, they rose to a divine knowledge [Col. 1712D] of the Trinity itself, saying:

> What is known of God is manifest among them, for God has made it manifest to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly perceived through the things that have been made—his eternal power and divinity also—so that they are without excuse; because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks, but became vain in their reasonings, etc.  
> (Rom. 1:19–21)

Hence Claudianus, writing to the patrician Prefect about the state of the soul, recalls these words:

> And because it has been granted to the human race to seek hidden things more eagerly, to desire denied things more intensely, [Col. 1713A] and, having acquired them more slowly, to love them more greatly, truth is apprehended more ardently the longer it is desired, the more laboriously it is sought, or the more slowly it is found. Hence it happened that philosophers also, of outstanding intellects, seeking truth through a long age, have always existed from Pythagoras of Italy or Thales of Ionia onward; and, although others disagreed, they perceived something worthy of so great an investigation, whether in the whole work or in part.

Therefore the Doctor of the Gentiles accuses philosophers not so much of ignorance of the truth as of contempt for truth known, saying: “The invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are clearly perceived through the things that have been made,” etc.

Hence too is that passage from Augustine’s *City of God*, Book VIII:

> A Christian man instructed only in ecclesiastical writings avoids those who philosophize according to the elements of this world [Col. 1713B]. He is also warned by the apostolic command: “Take care lest anyone deceive you through philosophy and empty deception according to the elements of the world” (Col. 2:8). Yet, lest he suppose that all such persons are of this sort, he hears from the same Apostle concerning certain persons that “what is known of God is manifest among them,” etc. And when, speaking to the Athenians, he had said a great thing concerning God, something which few could understand—“in him we live, move, and are” (Acts 17:28)—he added: “As certain of your own have said.”

The same writer, in *On the Spirit and the Letter*:

> The wise Life which made the world is understood by contemplating the world. Question the world: the adornment of heaven; the fruitful earth, full of grasses, trees, and animals; the sea, full of so many swimming creatures; the air [Col. 1713C], full of so many flying creatures. Question all things, and see whether in their appearance they do not answer you as though with a voice: “God made us.” Noble philosophers sought this, and from the work they knew the craftsman.

Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, Book I, chapter 4:

> As praise for a work directs praise back to its maker, so the Creator of things is praised through his creation and shown, by the condition of the work itself, to be how much more excellent he is. Likewise, invisible things praise God through us, while we contemplate them, etc.

[Note: [Col. 1713D] Supplement: “we praise God.”]

The ancients say that nothing exists which does not have a sense directed toward God. Therefore let no one wonder if we introduce testimonies from philosophers also, who, through the assertions of the saints, rose to knowledge of divinity, the Lord himself also revealing it. Although very many of them [Col. 1713D] are severely rebuked even by the Apostle, because, in accordance with what he himself says, “knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1), they became reprobate through pride in the privilege of divine knowledge. We do not take them here as examples for living, but for teaching or believing, just as we frequently do Solomon.

Yet Solomon, though the excellence of his wisdom was to be preferred to all others even by the Lord’s own testimony, was overcome by desire and carnal pleasures, consented to idolatry, and abandoned the divine worship which he taught and proclaimed in his writings. He himself built, by God’s command, the Temple for the magnification of that worship, though his righteous father had been forbidden to do so. God [Col. 1714A] sometimes distributes very great gifts to reprobate and unbelieving people when he sees that these will be necessary for the instruction or use of others. He also works many miracles through the reprobate, concerning whom Truth says in the Gospel:

> Many will say to me on that day: “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, perform many mighty works in your name, and cast out demons in your name?” And then I shall confess to them: “I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity.”  
> (Matt. 7:22–23)

When God displays miracles through reprobate persons, speaks prophecies, or performs any great works, this is done not for the benefit of those whom he uses as instruments, but rather for the benefit of others whom he intends to instruct through them. Not abandoning the gift of his grace even through unworthy ministers, he daily effects spiritually the sacraments of the Church at the invocation of his name for the salvation of believers [Col. 1714B].

God fittingly performs very great works even through the unworthy or unbelieving—he who taught a prophet through the words of an ass—lest, if he performed such great works through great men, they should be ascribed more to human virtues and merits than to divine grace. Yet, lest anyone despair of the salvation of all philosophers, or judge the lives of all those who preceded the Lord’s incarnation to have been reprobate, let him hear blessed Jerome expounding the Gospel of Matthew. Among other things he says:

> From the fact that the wicked servant dared to say, “You reap where you did not sow, and gather where you did not scatter” (Matt. 25:24), let us understand that God accepts even the good life of Gentile philosophers, and deals differently with those who act justly and with those who act unjustly.

For if we examine the cause stated above by the Apostle—namely, that he remembered certain of them to have been handed over to a reprobate mind through the divine knowledge which they followed, when they became vain in their reasonings and said that they were wise, that is, attributed their wisdom to their own study and intellect rather than assigning it to the gift of divine grace—we shall find that those most highly esteemed, especially Socrates and Plato, attributed all philosophy especially to divine grace.

Blessed Augustine praises Socrates in such terms in Book VIII of *The City of God*:

> Socrates, Plato’s teacher, is remembered as having turned the whole of philosophy toward the correction and ordering of morals [Col. 1714D]. He directed his attention to the one thing necessary for a happy life; for the sake of that one thing the industry of all philosophers seems to have kept watch and labored.

## CHAPTER XII. How philosophers recognized that God is one and three.

For the present, then, let it suffice to investigate how they recognized that God is one and three, and three. They recognized him as one from the creation of the world, that is, through things which human beings make within creation. For example, gold is in this object, since it is a creature of God; a human being works it and makes from it either a ring or some such [Col. 1715A] thing. This ring is this gold, and this gold is this ring. Therefore this gold and this ring are numerically the same, though they differ in definition, because to be this gold is one thing and to be this ring another.

For we say that all those things are numerically the same of which no counting or distinction from one another can be made. Such things are those which are of the same essence, such as this white thing [Note: [Col. 1715D] Perhaps read “this tall thing,” or something similar.] and this seated thing; or such things of which one is contained in the other as a part or as constituted from a part. For this white thing and this seated thing are numerically the same, but differ in definition, because being white is one thing and being seated another: one thing belongs to it insofar as it is white, another insofar as it is seated. Likewise, this wall and this house are numerically the same. Yet being this is one thing, and being that another.

In the same way we reason concerning God. For although the same substance which is the Father is the Son, and the same is the Holy Spirit, and these are divided by properties—because being Father is one thing, being Son another, and being Holy Spirit another—yet, although this is so, those three persons are numerically the same, because they are one and the same essence. Likewise, God is omnipotent, all-wise, and all-benign. Yet omnipotent, all-wise, and all-benign are numerically the same, although being omnipotent is one thing, being all-wise another, and being all-benign another.

Therefore, if it is said, “The Father is the same as the Son and the Holy Spirit,” and conversely, this is false, because the three persons would then be one person. But if it is said, “The Father is the same thing as [Col. 1715C] the Son and the Holy Spirit,” and conversely, this is true, because the essence of the three persons is one and the same.

They recognized him as three from creation. In order, then, that what we say may become somewhat clearer in general, let us consider the familiar example from the preceding subject matter. First, then, there is gold; when it is taken up, it is engraved and becomes a seal; afterwards it is impressed upon wax and becomes something sealing. Thus, although it is numerically the same, because it is one and the same essence, it is nevertheless three things differing in property: for being this gold is one thing and being this sealable thing another.

Accordingly, from this trinity in creatures they could easily infer a trinity in the divine substance. For when they clearly discerned, in the one and same divinity, power in creating, wisdom in governing created things [Col. 1715D], and benevolence in bringing them to the best outcome, from the effects of that same love, they perceived there the holy divine Trinity: one and the same in unity of substance, three things divided by property. For being powerful is one thing, being wise another, and being benevolent another.

## CHAPTER XIII. How “person” is understood in the Trinity.

Since, therefore, we have said that these three things divided by property designate again and again the person of the Father, the person of the Son, and the person of the Holy Spirit, we judge that it must be explained how “person” is used here. So that what we intend to show may be clearer [Col. 1716A], let us offer different definitions according to different senses of the term. Reason persuades us to begin somewhat higher up.

For “person” is understood differently in grammar, differently in rhetoric, differently among human beings, and differently also in the divine essence. Every utterance must have three elements: that through which it is made, that to which it is made, and that concerning which it is made. That through which it is made is the speaker; that to which it is made is the hearer; and that concerning which it is made is the thing, namely that about which the speech is made. The speaker is called the first person, the hearer the second, and that of which speech is made the third, existing between speaker and hearer.

Thus in grammar the same thing is first, second, and third person, because the same human being at one time speaks to another, at another time speech is directed to him, and at another time speech is made about him. Thus grammar defines person: it is one who speaks, or one to whom another speaks, or one about whom someone speaks. In rhetoric, however, a person is one whose definite saying or action is brought forward in a controversy. In a human being, person is an individual rational substance.

Thus Boethius, in his book *On the Two Natures in Christ*, against certain heretics, Nestorius and Eutyches, who said that there are two persons in Christ, defined person: “Person is an individual rational substance.” But Christ is one individual rational substance; therefore Christ is one person. In God, however, a person is one who begets, one who is begotten, or one who proceeds from both.

Thus one person is the same thing as first, second, and third person; yet the first is not the second or third, nor conversely [Col. 1716C]. So one and the same divine substance is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; such that the Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Father or Holy Spirit, nor the Holy Spirit the Father or the Son.

## CHAPTER XIV. That some names of the divine essence are natural and others personal.

The names of this essence, then, are partly personal and partly natural. Natural names, as we have already explained above, are these: God, omnipotent, eternal, and the other names of this kind. Therefore they belong equally and individually to all the persons. Personal names are those which belong individually to each person and not to all, nor in the same way: namely, Father, Son, and Holy [Col. 1716D] Spirit.

Thus in other things also some names are natural and others personal. For “human being” is a natural name, while “Socrates” is personal, because the former is common to this nature, the latter proper to this person. For nature is the same likeness of those begotten.

## CHAPTER XV. On the begetting of the Son and the procession of the Holy Spirit.

Since we have sufficiently explained above these names, let us briefly define the begetting of the Son from the Father and the procession of the Spirit. To understand this, one must know that all these names—Father, Son, Holy Spirit—are transferred metaphorically. For wisdom and knowledge are powers of the soul, and thus power is a genus of wisdom [Col. 1717A] and knowledge. Every wisdom is a power of the soul, but not conversely. Likewise, every knowledge is a power of the soul, but not conversely.

In the same way, divine power contains wisdom; for divine power is the power of making the world, of creating a human being or a horse, and so forth. Wisdom, however, is the faculty and power of discerning. Thus power contains the power of creating and the power of governing and discerning, which is wisdom. This can readily be seen also from the analogy of genus to species, or matter to that which is formed from matter.

For philosophers say that a genus is divided, as it were, into certain progenies of its own. They call these progenies species, as though they were begotten by the genus, because it contains them under itself and enters into their definition, but not conversely. Thus animal contains human being as genus contains species, because whatever is a human being is an animal, but not conversely [Col. 1717B]. Therefore animal does not require a human being in order to exist, but a human being requires animal. In the same way, this ring consists of bronze and form; yet bronze does not require the ring in order to exist, while the ring requires bronze.

As these things stand, so divine power, although it contains the wisdom of discernment, does not require it in order to exist. But the wisdom of discernment wholly requires power in order to exist; and thus divine power begets wisdom from itself, as genus begets species, or matter that which is formed from matter. But because it could not be said, “This power is matter; wisdom is that which is formed from matter,” since power is eternal and wisdom coeternal, the name Father was metaphorically transferred to signify divine power, and Son to signify wisdom. For, as we said, the wisdom of discernment is from that power, but power is not from wisdom—just as the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son.

But because there are many who are able and know, and yet do not will, and therefore such power and such knowledge attain no effect, a will coeternal with that divine essence is also present. Since will is not power, it neither contains wisdom nor is contained by power. Therefore it does not beget wisdom from itself and thus is not Father; nor is it begotten by power and thus is not Son. Rather, this will proceeds from power and wisdom, because God wills all that he does because he is able and knows, but is not able because he knows or wills [Col. 1717D].

This procession arises because this will—which is goodness, or benevolence, or more properly love—comes forth from omnipotence and all-wisdom. For God, being wholly sufficient to himself and needing nothing, cannot benefit himself in any respect. But love, as Gregory says, is reciprocal, because it cannot exist among fewer than two; hence Christ sent the apostles out two by two. Since God himself, as stated, cannot show mercy to or benefit himself, it was fitting that this love should be exercised toward his creatures [Note: [Col. 1717D] Perhaps read: “he ought to exercise it”], distributing his gifts to each according to the choice of his freedom, bestowing this gift upon that one and that gift upon this one according to the measure of suitability.

This effect of divinity toward creatures is therefore called “spirit,” *spiritus*, as though from breathing (*spiramen*), because, as we said above, the dispositions of our mind are made especially evident by the spirit of our mouth, that is, by breath, when we sigh from love or groan from pain. Thus this divine disposition is called Spirit from love. And note that, although the Son proceeds from the Father, and proceeding from the Father is nothing other than being begotten by the Father, and although the Spirit also proceeds from the Father, the Spirit is nevertheless not begotten by the Father. For the Son proceeds as born; the Holy Spirit does not, but as given.

## CHAPTER XVI. How one may answer the Greeks, who say that it ought not be granted that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son.

[Col. 1718B] Concerning this procession of the Spirit from both, there is great disagreement between us and the Greeks. They say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, but not from the Son; and they confirm this by the authority of the Gospels and other apostolic Scriptures. Since no mention of this occurs in them, they say that nothing else ought to be added, nor ought anything to be said which is not contained in them.

They also firmly establish this by the authority of the fourth [Note: [Col. 1718D] Perhaps read “fourth”] of the councils, where their doctors discussed the Catholic faith before the emperor Constantine and set forth something approved by all, in which they made no mention of the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son. At its conclusion they struck with anathema anyone who should add anything other than what is contained in this creed, or alter anything. Therefore, seeing that the Romans both believe and proclaim that this procession is also from the Son, they often came to Rome, especially in the time of Paschasius, saying that they were prepared to prove by arguments and authorities that the Romans were excommunicated and heretics.

When the pope gave them a delay so that on the following day they might meet prepared to prove this, and they returned on the next day ready for this purpose in accordance with the apostolic counsel, the aforesaid bishop refused to hear that controversy, fearing that the Romans might be overcome by the cunning and subtlety of the Greeks and that from this a very great danger might perhaps arise in the Church. Yet the Greeks may readily be answered on this point, and it can be demonstrated from the authorities of the saints that it is so.

If the Greek authors in that excommunication used “other” in the sense of distinct rather than contrary, it follows that all who preach in the Church about the life of blessed Martin or another saint are excommunicated. Christ himself would likewise be struck by this anathema, since he said: “It was said to those of old, ‘You shall not kill’; but I say to you, whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’ etc.” (Matt. 5:22). For Paul says to the Galatians: “If anyone preaches to you another Gospel than that which I preach—even if he be an angel from heaven—let him be anathema” (Gal. 2:2). And Moses says in Deuteronomy: “Whoever adds another word or [Col. 1719A] alters it, let him be accursed” (Deut. 4:2).

Therefore, if “other” is used not for what is contrary but for what is distinct, then holy preachers and Christ himself are liable to this curse; or, at least, we may say that they excommunicated not human beings but God. For whenever such an addition or alteration occurs, it is not a human being who does this, but God through a human being.

## CHAPTER XVII. He proves by authority that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, as from the Father.

Having shown, then, how the Greeks may be answered, let us demonstrate, relying on authorities, that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son. Let us first introduce the unassailable authority of Truth itself. For when he breathed upon the apostles, he said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Unless the Spirit also proceeded from him, he would not have given them the Spirit by breathing upon them.

Didymus, one of the Greek authorities, also plainly shows this when, in a certain treatise of his, as an edition made from it reports, he says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son. Likewise Chrysostom, who was also Greek. Athanasius likewise says: “The Spirit is from the Father and the Son, not made, not begotten, but proceeding.” This should be understood as follows: the Spirit is not made by the Father and the Son, namely, he is not begotten by the Father and the Son; this applies alike to both. But he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Otherwise he would not have joined the phrases properly [Col. 1719C].

Nevertheless, it should be noted that our authorities did not say this without reason. Augustine, and again Jerome, say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son and the Father, but principally from the Father. Hilary also, who long preceded them and was therefore still closer to the Greeks, said that the Spirit proceeds from the Father through the Son. And this is fitting: just as water is said to proceed from a spring and to go through a channel, so the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, and through the Son—not from the source, but from him who is the source—because whatever grace he confers on us through the Son, he does so through him as mediator.

It may also be said that, just as water proceeds secondarily from the channel, so the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, who is also from the Father, not principally but secondarily [Col. 1719D]. We, however, say without doubt that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, either because he belongs to the Father and the Son, or because God wills to order all things because he knows and is able, but not conversely.

The Holy Spirit, as we said above, is neither begotten nor unbegotten, because, in order for him to be begotten, it would be necessary for will to be omnipotence, from which wisdom also comes. He is therefore not begotten; that is, he is will in such a way that he is not wisdom from power. For the Holy Spirit is of the same substance as the Son, yet he is not from the same substance as the Son. For, as we have said, being not begotten is not the same as being unbegotten, just as being not pious is not the same as being impious: every impious person is not pious, but not conversely [Col. 1720A].

Let us now consider the predication of names: what names are predicated of what. One should know that some names belong to God substantially, others relatively—that is, by the properties of the persons. The names which belong substantially are those which we called substantial above: omnipotent, wise, benevolent, eternal, immeasurable, and so forth. For these are said of each individual person: the Father is omnipotent, the Son is omnipotent, the Holy Spirit is omnipotent; the Father is wise, the Son is wise, the Holy Spirit is wise; the Father is benevolent, the Son is benevolent, the Holy Spirit is benevolent; and so with the rest.

But the names of the persons are not said in this way. For although one says, “The Father is Father; the Son is Son,” we cannot say, “The Father is the Son,” or “God’s Wisdom is not the Son,” or “God’s Wisdom is the Father”; for then it would be necessary that the Father be Father of himself, and likewise that the Son be Son of himself. It would also be necessary that the Holy Spirit be spirit of himself, that is, proceed from himself, as may be seen in the preceding analogy.

For these propositions are indeed true: “This bronze is a seal, and this seal is bronze; and this sealable thing is a seal or even bronze; and this seal or this bronze is sealable.” But if I use names of relatives or relations and say, “This matter is materialized,” or “This materialized thing is matter,” these statements [Col. 1720C] are false. For in order that the statement “Matter is materialized” should be true, this bronze would have to be a seal in such a way as to be matter of itself. Likewise, for the other statement, “This materialized thing is matter,” to be true, it would be necessary that this seal be made from itself as seal, which is false.

For although this bronze and this seal are the same thing, many things can be said of this bronze that cannot be said of this seal, and conversely. It is said of this bronze that it is a creature of God and that it is the matter of this seal; neither of these can be said of this seal. Likewise, it is said of this seal that it is a human work and that it is the materialized product of this bronze; neither can be said of this bronze. In the same way, one may reason concerning the Father and [Col. 1720D] the Son.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That philosophers designated the Holy Spirit by the world-soul.

It remains to consider what philosophers thought concerning the Holy Spirit, because they seem to have represented the Spirit as less than the Father and Son and as created. Plato called *to agathon* (τὸ ἀγαθόν, “the Good”) the supreme Father, and *nous* (νοῦς, “mind”) the divine mind, that is, wisdom, because he asserted that *to agathon* was coeternal. But he said that the soul of the world—by which he understood the Spirit giving life to all things—was a creature infused into the world.

Since the Apostle adduces them as an authority for proving that the Gentiles knew God, if they said that the Holy Spirit was lesser, they did not know God properly. Thus the Apostle seems inappropriately to have said that what was known of God was manifest among them—that is, through them—because what they understood they taught to others. Let us therefore examine their meaning, so that we may finally recognize that he spoke rightly.

As we have already said sufficiently, the goodness of God is called the Holy Spirit. We have also explained why the Holy Spirit is called his goodness. It should be noted, therefore, that this same Holy Spirit—namely, he who, in himself according to affection, is coeternal with the Father and the Son—has distinct effects. Hence Solomon says: “The Holy Spirit is one, manifold, stable, discerning.” Insofar as he is one in himself and simple [Col. 1721B], he is the third person in the Trinity, coeternal with the Father and Son; but insofar as he effects something in individual creatures, he is mobile and discerning. Hence the Holy Spirit is called one and simple Spirit.

Thus John says in the Apocalypse: “And to the seven spirits which are before the throne of God” (Rev. 1:4). Accordingly, in respect of this sevenfold effect—by which is designated the whole array of effects produced in creatures—the Holy Spirit is called the soul of the world, because soul is reckoned as created, and because the Spirit himself gives life to creatures. Therefore the same substance is called both Holy Spirit and soul: spirit from goodness, soul from giving life; Holy Spirit from disposition, soul from effect; Spirit in his eternity, soul in temporal administration.

Nor is it incongruous if the Holy Spirit is called eternal according to effect, and the world-soul, giving life to all things, according to disposition. Thus the same divine essence is called God and is called Lord: God from eternity, but Lord in time. Hence also comes that symbolic covering, that Plato placed it in the middle in order that it might give life to all things, animate and vivify what was fitting, because the grace of the Holy Spirit is available to all, conferring gifts upon each according to each person’s suitability. For Jews, Gentiles, and all human beings whatsoever have certain gifts. Even if they do not have faith or hope or such things, they nevertheless have kinds of tongues and healing of infirmities, and so forth.

Thus Plato, although he did not assign an eternal procession, did assign a temporal one: namely, how the Spirit proceeds in order to give life to all things. This procession is from both Father and Son, though in different ways. For procession is twofold: one eternal, discussed above, and the other temporal. Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “I shall go to the Father, and I shall send the Paraclete Spirit” (John 15:26). And elsewhere: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father, he will teach you all things” (ibid.). Here, indeed, the discussion is of temporal procession.

Thus Bede, commenting on this passage, says: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father, that is, is sent. For the Spirit’s proceeding from the Father is the same as his being sent.” And elsewhere: “The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world,” etc. (Wis. 1:7). This mission or procession occurs daily among different people; different gifts are conferred daily. Hence the Apostle says: “Dividing to each individually as he wills” [Col. 1722A] (1 Cor. 12:11). Some of these goods are stable and continuous; others are intermittent and variable. Thus certain gifts granted to Peter were stable and permanent in him, such as faith, hope, and love; others were not permanent, such as the working of miracles. The prophets likewise at one time had the spirit of prophecy, and at another lacked it.

## CHAPTER XIX. What belongs to divine power, what to wisdom, and what to goodness.

Having considered generation and procession, let us return to that description of the supreme good which Christ himself, as was said before, gave. And since many other things are said of God—eternal, immeasurable, unchangeable, and so forth—let us consider whether all these are contained within those three [attributes]. [Col. 1722B] Otherwise, that divine designation of the supreme good is found to be less perfect. Let us therefore see what belongs to power, what to wisdom, and what to divine goodness.

That he is called invariable, immutable, unfailing, eternal, and so forth belongs to power. For the ability to change, the ability to fail, and so forth, belong to weakness. Again, that he is called foreseeing and foreknowing belongs to wisdom. For to know things only from their outcomes or effects belongs to human ignorance. But when he is called just, merciful, compassionate, and so forth, this pertains to goodness—although he is called “compassionate” more from the bestowal of mercy than from goodness itself.

Thus we said above that, although those three persons are plainly distinct from one another, [Col. 1722C] nevertheless the operation of the whole Trinity is one and the same. For the Father does nothing which the Son or the Holy Spirit does not [also do]. That is: God does nothing that he cannot do, does not know, or does not will. Yet many can do what they do not know how to do, and therefore what they do lacks an elegant result. Again, some can and know how, but are unwilling; therefore they do not act in the way from which the best result might arise.

It is therefore as though one said: God can act in such a way that none can resist him; he acts so wisely that no more elegant result can arise from it; he acts so graciously that no better result can come from it. Yet although, as has been said, the operation of the three persons is thus common, it does not follow that, if the Son was incarnate, the Father was also; [Col. 1722D] nor does it follow, if all things belonging to the Son belong to the Father—as he himself says in the Gospel—that the flesh of the Son is the flesh of the Father.

For this is how the saying, “All mine are yours” (John 17:10), is to be understood: whatever I possess, you also possess, O Father, and conversely. So one says, “Whatever belongs to the king belongs to the queen”; yet it is false to infer, “therefore the king’s limbs are the queen’s limbs.” Rather, it means: whatever is in the king’s possession is in the queen’s possession. Likewise, something belongs to the Spirit which does not belong to the Father or the Son: namely, that one is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, not from water and the Son and the Father.

For God forgives sins by grace, which belongs to goodness, not to power or wisdom. He does not forgive because he is powerful or wise, but because he is good. But since, as we said, wisdom was incarnate—[Col. 1723A] that is, since “the Word was made flesh,” as the Evangelist proclaimed—it seems that the Word was made something which it had not been from eternity. This we readily grant; yet it was not “made” in the proper sense. Thus, “The Lord has become my salvation” (Ps. 117:14), and yet he was not made.

“The Word was made flesh” (John 1:14) is as though one said, “God was made man”; this occurred without any change of nature being visible. For no change occurred there, since that is not properly said to be changed which remains in its own nature. Thus, flesh and soul become one without any mixture of the natures; so God was made man, without the divine nature being converted into the human, or the human into the divine. This could not occur unless each nature lost its own substantial difference.

Therefore God is called man because of the other nature which he assumed; man is called God because of the other nature by which he was assumed. Thus man is called rational because of the soul, whose distinguishing characteristic is rationality, since the soul alone discerns and not the body. He is also called mortal because of the body, since the body alone dies and not the soul.

Let us therefore consider what is meant by saying that the Son of God descended. They say, of course, that God is everywhere, and this is true. Yet Augustine says that he is not *somewhere*, and by this he proves that he is not a body either. [Note: [Col. 1723D] Perhaps read: “that he is not a body.”] His argument is as follows: God is not a body. Whatever is somewhere is a body. But God is not somewhere; therefore he is not a body. Thus he is both everywhere and not somewhere.

For he is everywhere by power, because he acts everywhere. Every place [Col. 1723C] is present to him, and likewise every time. He is also everywhere by essence, because he acts everywhere through himself, without need of intermediaries. For although a king is present by power throughout his kingdom—hence, “Do you not know that kings have long hands?”—nevertheless he is not everywhere throughout the kingdom by essence, since he cannot act throughout the whole kingdom at once without the assistance of ministers.

Therefore, when God is said to have descended into the Virgin’s womb, it means that he humbled himself in order to assume humanity. But where Augustine proves that God is not somewhere because he is not a body, he evidently seems also to establish that a created spirit is not somewhere, since no spirit is a body. For if God is not somewhere because he is not a body, then a created spirit, since it is not a body, ought not to be somewhere either.

That a created spirit is not somewhere, Augustine shows in these words in his commentary on Genesis: “A bodily creature moves through times and places; a spiritual creature through times only.” Again, in the same work: “Bodily things move in time and place; the Creator Spirit moves neither in time nor place; but the created spirit moves in time, not place.” Thus the created spirit is, as it were, a middle thing between the Creator and bodily creation. In moving through time it agrees with the body; in not receiving local motion it agrees with the Creator.

But if one finds in an authority that created spirits are locally circumscribed, [Col. 1724A] this must be understood according to operation or assumption of a body: when it acts here, it is not there. Thus Christ’s soul is said to have descended into hell, not by a change of place but by the efficacy of despoiling hell; and this spoiling is rightly attributed to the soul, because the soul suffered in the body.

## CHAPTER XX. Whether God can make more things, or otherwise, or better, than he does make.

Having dealt with everything pertaining both to the unity of the divine essence and to the properties of the persons, before we proceed to the benefits [bestowed on us], it seems necessary to ask whether God can make more things, or otherwise than he does. Therefore, that we may discuss this more fully and clearly, [Col. 1724B] let us begin somewhat higher up.

That God is the creator and governor of all things, and yet is one and not many, is easily known from creatures, as not only Augustine but also other saints and philosophers have taught. Cicero alone proves that all these things are well governed because they are governed by one, the wisest of all, by whom they are foreseen; and therefore they are well ruled. For things foreseen with pious care are governed better than things not foreseen and therefore not well [Note: [Col. 1723D] Supply: “governed.”] governed. The world is governed by providence; human beings are a part of the world; and so forth.

They especially discern this most orderly governance from the diversity of the things constituting this structure, seeing that the world is compacted from natures so diverse and discordant with one another. Thus they readily recognized both that it was something other [Note: [Col. 1724D] Perhaps read: “something.”] that had made this and its inestimable wisdom in governing these things. For he creates and governs all things so powerfully and so wisely that nothing can resist him and that he permits nothing to happen without a reason. Hence Job: “Not even a leaf falls from a tree without a reason” (Job 5:6). Plato likewise says that nothing happens without a rational cause.

Therefore, since among creatures, as was said, they could in no way find something that could do this, they observed that there is something above this universe which does it; and they called it the Creator and ruler of all things, and wise. From the fact that nothing could resist it, they judged it omnipotent; from the fact that it brought all things to an elegant result, all-wise; [Col. 1724D] and from the fact that it causes all things to turn out in the manner in which they can turn out best, they judged it wholly gracious.

They also knew from this that it is one alone and not many. For if there were two, either one would be equal to the other in all things or not. If unequal, then one would be insufficient in itself, since it would need something for its fullness, just as one which was not supreme would. But if one were equal to the other, then, since each alone would suffice for creating all things and governing what had been created, the other would plainly be superfluous. It remains, therefore, that one God alone is the creator and governor of all things.

It is commonly asked whether he can make more things than he makes. Some say [Col. 1725A] that he can make more and differently from what he does: that he can save those whom he condemns, and conversely; that he can make a human being from this stone, and otherwise than he does; and the like. They introduce examples: Balaam’s ass, the five loaves, Lot’s wife, and water made wine. They also rely on several authorities.
