Thus Augustine says: “Another mode was possible for God, but none more suited to our misery.” Again, the same author: “He who raised Lazarus in body could have raised Judas in mind.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Can I not ask my Father, and he will furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26:53). But, as it seems to me, they have understood neither God’s wisdom nor the authorities.

For since, as has been said, God is plainly all-wise, he is more rational than all creatures. Therefore he wisely and rationally foresees what ought or ought not to be done. He sees the rational cause why it is fitting or unfitting that this be done or not done. He sees that Jacob should be chosen and Esau rejected, because, just as it was suitable for the former to be chosen in order to suffer from his brother, so it was suitable for the latter to be rejected, in order that he might be the furnace and persecution of his brother. For just as it is good—that is, useful—for good to exist, so it is good—that is, useful—for evil to exist.

Hence Augustine says: “The supremely good [God] would not permit any evils to occur unless he brought some good from them.” He is the one for whom evils are goods. Therefore, since the rational cause of every event is present and certain to him, [Col. 1725C] he wisely administers to each person what he sees is fitting for that person. Thus he bestowed more on John than on Peter, because he saw that it was fitting for more to be given to the former than to the latter. But if Peter had possessed more than he did possess, he would not thereby have been better, because that additional amount would have been irrational.

For if it were rational that he should have more, and [Note: [Col. 1725D] Perhaps read: “and.”] God had not bestowed it on him, God would plainly not seem supremely good. Hence Augustine: “If the Father could have begotten his Son equal to himself and did not do so, he would be envious.” Likewise Plato, discussing the sensible world, says that “the Best made the best,” because all envy is banished from him.

The saints say, therefore, that God made all things in such a way that he could not have made them better. Yet we do not dare deny that he could have made a human being better than he made him. But this comparison must be referred to the thing, not to God himself. Thus someone makes a golden cup and a glass cup: he does not make the golden one better than the glass one, but makes a better one, because the golden cup is better than the glass.

Since, therefore, whatever he makes he makes as he sees it ought to be made, and makes as many things as it is fitting to make, then if he made otherwise, or made more or fewer things than he makes, this would be unfitting, and he would act against his reason and wisdom [Col. 1726A] [“would act”]. But this would be impossible, because, since his wisdom is altogether immutable and invariable, it can neither increase nor diminish. Therefore he cannot make more things, or otherwise than he makes.

We reason similarly concerning foreknowledge or providence, and likewise concerning predestination. Yet one may doubt whether Peter could have been more just than he was; this we readily grant. But one asks: by whom? We say that he could have been more just than he was by God and through God, and yet God could not make him better or more just, because, as we said, he would have acted otherwise [Note: [Col. 1726D] Supply: “than was fitting.”] than was fitting.

Thus this field can be cultivated by that boy and through him—that is, it is suited for this—yet he cannot cultivate it. I can receive a hundred solidi from you, and you cannot give them to me.

The aforesaid authorities must be understood so that possibility is referred to things, not to God. Thus we say: “A chimera is thinkable,” that is, people can think a chimera. Similarly: “God could have raised Judas in mind, who raised Lazarus in body.” This ability is referred to Judas’s nature, not to God himself; and the rest should be explained similarly.

There are, however, some who are accustomed to determine such questions thus: “God could do this or that, if he wished.” They subordinate the rational outcome of things to will, rather than to reason or wisdom, as if God first willed that this or that occur, and then afterward deliberated within himself whether this or that would happen fittingly. Such people plainly err concerning God and attempt improperly to confuse in God the order of deliberating and willing.

For the mind must first observe what utility and what appropriateness follows from a thing; then the will must be applied to its being or not being. These people altogether misunderstand Origen and Jerome. Jerome says: “To speak now in a rustic manner: just as someone first considers and thinks about a thing, whether it ought to be done or not, before either doing or leaving it undone; and, if he sees that it ought to be done, does it, but otherwise leaves it undone—so, I say, God foresees what ought or ought not to be done, and then wills or does not will to do or leave those things undone.” Thus the usefulness of a thing precedes in his knowledge.

Therefore he does the things he does because they ought to be done, not because he wills to do them. Accordingly it is beyond doubt that all things, both good and evil, occur by a most ordered dispensation, because they happen fittingly and cannot happen more fittingly. Hence Augustine: “God is so good that he would not permit evils to occur unless it were good for evils to exist.”

For by the same reason by which he wills good things to exist—because it is fitting that they exist—he also wills evil things to exist. For just as whatever he does not permit to exist, he rationally does not permit, so whatever he permits, he rationally permits to exist or even ordains. All this pertains to his greater glory. Thus a painting is sometimes made more beautiful and commendable by the addition of some inferior colour than it would be if it were of one colour and uniform. [Col. 1727A] Thus this commonwealth is made more beautiful and commendable by the admixture of evils. For when good people often see others fall who were nevertheless thought more steadfast, they then take greater thought for their own weakness, recognize themselves, and realize that they ought to be more indebted to God’s grace.

There is another cause of this rational diversity: if all were good, they would understand God’s grace less and would in some manner ascribe their salvation to their own good nature. A third cause, which [Note: [Col. 1727D] Perhaps read: “they do not except this cause either.”] they do not omit, is that evils provide the good with material for exercising virtue. Thus both reason and the authority of the saints confirm that this is so.

But if this is so—indeed, since it is so—why do we sympathize with the wretched? Why do we grieve for those who die? Why does Rachel weep? What, too, is the meaning of the Apostle’s words, “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15)? We already know that Stephen’s stoning and Lawrence’s burning happen fittingly, [Col. 1727B] both for their own benefit and for God’s glory. [Note: [Col. 1727D] Perhaps read: “that Stephen’s stoning and Lawrence’s burning are fitting”; or: “Lawrence’s burning.”] Therefore, since all these things occur, as has been said, by an irrefutable reason, such griefs and tears seem irrational. This indeed cannot be denied, both because we strive against God’s disposition and because we cannot accomplish what we undertake. Whoever undertakes what he cannot accomplish acts irrationally by that very fact.

What then? Does the Apostle not command us to weep with those who weep and rejoice with those who rejoice? Certainly he does not command this kind of weeping or rejoicing. For, as Augustine says, Scripture forbids only what is blameworthy and commands only what is rational. The Apostle, I say, does not command this, but commands us to have an affection of charity toward our neighbours. From the perfection of this charity we are often accustomed to burst forth into what is irrational. Hence Gregory says: “Charity is impatient; it has no measure.” The same is also read in the Life of blessed Martin concerning the grieving disciples.

It would surely be more fitting to rejoice, if the force of grief admitted reason. What then shall we say? Is it sin? It certainly is not sin, but it is irrational. Therefore one ought rather to confess as Christ taught, that all things should be attributed to God’s will. It would indeed be safer, in whatever events occur, for each of us to say: “Father, may your will be done” (Matt. 6). Thus in the passion the Son taught us, when, transforming his weak members into himself, he said: “Nevertheless, not my will but yours be done” (Luke 22). Likewise blessed Job: “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away” (Job 1). This is the one remedy and complete consolation in every event.

But what shall we say about repentance, when we know that it is good for evil to exist by nature? Yet it is one thing for evil to exist, another thing to be evil. Although it is good for evil [Col. 1728A] to exist—for a good effect is drawn from it—evil nevertheless displeases the Lord, as is evident when he punishes it. Therefore, what pleases God should please us in the same manner as it pleases him, who, for whom the existence of evil is good, draws good from every evil. But what displeases him—our evil will and the works which proceed from it—should also displease us.

Let us therefore attend to his goodness: that he bears with us in this way; that he has bestowed these and those goods upon us; that he prohibited this or that act. Thus, by doing that, we show his goodness, which [Note: [Col. 1728D] Read perhaps: “which in every way”; or: “by doing those things.”] we ought to love in every way and before all things. Therefore, because of his love, which we have embittered by sinning, we ought to repent and grieve—not because we are to be punished for it. For one who repents of something because he is to be punished for it is not to be called repentant. Just as one who wishes his son to be imprisoned in order that he himself may leave prison is not said to wish his son to be imprisoned.

## CHAPTER XXI. Matters pertaining to wisdom.

Having considered power and its effects, let us now discuss wisdom briefly. Wisdom therefore contains providence—or, what is the same thing, foreknowledge—and predestination. By his wisdom he foreknows and foresees all things before they happen or exist; and this providence can in no way be deceived. For what has been foreseen cannot fail to happen.

From this, some people, understanding badly, have thought that all things happen by necessity. But they are refuted both by reason and by the authority of philosophers. For a false simple proposition does not follow from a true [Note: [Col. 1728D] The passage appears corrupt. Cf. Introduction, book III, chapter 7.] determination. Thus, when this is true, “This has been foreseen by God,” it cannot necessarily be inferred: “Therefore this will necessarily happen.”

It is easy for us likewise to be mistaken in this: “While I see a chariot being driven, the chariot is necessarily being driven.” For it does not follow that, if it cannot simultaneously be the case that I see a chariot being driven and that the chariot is not being driven, then there is necessity in the event. Providence imposes no necessity on the events of things; rather, things are foreseen to be as they are in relation to either possibility.

This providence, or foreknowledge if you prefer, is altogether immutable. God does not know something new which he did not know from eternity, nor will he know in the future anything which he does not now know. For from eternity he knew that I would read now or today [“that I would read today”]; and to eternity he will know that I read today.

Note that adverbs of this kind, uttered at the same time, signify different things. Thus if I now say, “I read yesterday; I read today; I shall read tomorrow,” “that I read yesterday,” “that I read today,” and “that I shall read tomorrow” are different. But uttered at different times, they signify the same thing. Thus one who says, “Hermann will read tomorrow,” and another who says, “Hermann reads today,” signifies the same thing as if I were to say today, “I shall read.” For it is the same thing that yesterday I was going to read today, that I read today, and that tomorrow I shall have read today. [Col. 1729A] The words or tenses themselves have changed, but the same truth remains.

Therefore, since he is one for whom no change of time is an obstacle—for there is nothing between his eternity and the last moment of time—since, I say, whatever was, is, or will be is wholly present to him, note that divine providence or foreknowledge and disposition extend both to good and evil; predestination, however, only to good. Augustine nevertheless sometimes uses “predestination” in place of “foreknowledge.”

It should also be noted that *fate* (*fatum*) derives from *disposition*, as passion from action. For since fate is the divine disposition inhering in mutable things, it is nothing other than disposition, an action belonging to the one who disposes—except that disposition acts immutably. But the things disposed undergo some change. Hence to be fated is nothing other than to be disposed.

Because many fell into error from the word *fate*, thinking that fate was a constellation, the saints therefore refused to use the word. Fate is, then, as Boethius says, the disposition of things in God’s hand. It depends upon divine disposition as passion upon action. Predestination, as we said, concerns good things alone. When Augustine says that there is predestination also of evils, he takes it in the sense of foreknowledge.

Predestination is the preparation of grace. It begins from the very kind of gifts, proceeds through the succession of divine goods, and then through gifts bestowed, as far as the end of the present [Col. 1729C] life. Thus this preparation occurs temporally. But if predestination is said to exist from eternity, as providence or disposition also is—when we say, for example, “From eternity he predestined this person to life”—this is as though one said: “From eternity he foresees that he will give some good to this person through which he will be saved.”

Whether he can dispose more things than he disposes, or can know more things, or can predestine more people to life, is sufficiently evident.

## CHAPTER XXII. Things pertaining to divine goodness.

Having spoken thus far about power and wisdom, something should briefly be added concerning goodness. God, as we said, is gracious, merciful, and compassionate. [Col. 1729D] Since he needs nothing, being wholly sufficient to himself in every respect, he exercises the effect of this goodness in his creatures. Therefore, while he is gracious in disposition in himself alone, he brings about in creatures alone what it is established should be brought about by such goodness.

But from him who is supremely good every envy is banished; likewise every anger and every fury are removed from him. What then of the saying, “Lest your furious anger be kindled against us” (Exod. 32:10)? And what does the Prophet pray: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury” (Ps. 37:2)? We use the names of such affections metaphorically when speaking of God, so that they are understood of him according to their effect, not according to an affection. Thus “God is angry,” or “God is appeased,” is as though one said: “God punishes that person,” or “God spares that person.” For no such affection and no movement falls upon him who acts in tranquillity.

Therefore he is called merciful in himself, as he is gracious, but compassionate in the bestowal [of mercy]. Thus if there were no one upon whom he might have mercy, he would not be compassionate. Here it is commonly asked whether he can be more gracious or more compassionate. For he could bestow gifts on more people and save them; he could have mercy on and spare more people. Thus he could be more gracious and more compassionate, or less so, or not compassionate at all, since it was also possible that there should have been no one upon whom he might have mercy. But what can be answered here too may be learned from what has gone before: for the reason assigned above, he cannot bestow good things on more people, have mercy on more people, or act otherwise than he does.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Why God became man.

[Col. 1730B]

Having spoken of the other part of faith, which consists in the knowledge of God—namely, the unity of the divine substance and the Trinity of persons, and those matters pertaining to each, as far as memory suggests—let us now briefly set forth the other part, namely the benefits bestowed upon us by him. The highest and greatest of these was that the wisdom of God, by assuming flesh from the Virgin, enlightened us by its light and showed us its love.

For in this he showed how great was his love toward us: he laid down for us the soul which he assumed. Hence he himself says: “No one has greater love than this: that one lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). For the love which he had toward us, he assumed flesh in order to redeem us from the yoke of sin.

Reason persuades us that we should inquire carefully from whom he redeemed us and how that redemption was accomplished. Some say that we were redeemed from the devil’s power: that, by deceiving the human being, the devil subjected him to himself and acquired over him a power which he had not previously possessed. Therefore, they say, the Son of God was sent so that, although he could have taken the human being away from the devil by power, he might instead deal with him through justice and humility. Otherwise he would seem to inflict an injury upon the devil, since the devil possessed by right the human being who had made himself the devil’s slave.

But I say the contrary, and prove by irrefutable reason that the devil had no right whatever over the human being. [Col. 1730D] For one who, by deceiving him, alienated him from subjection to his Lord ought not to acquire any power over him; rather, if he possessed any before, he ought to lose it. Whoever abuses a power granted to him deserves to lose his privilege.

For example, suppose there were three servants of one lord, and that the lord had given one of them precedence over the others. If that servant attempted to withdraw them from their lord and from subjection to him, he would not acquire any power over them from the lord; rather, through his wickedness he would lose the power previously granted. There is another reason why the devil had no right over the human being: the human being could not enslave himself to him. Although a servant may flee from his lord, he cannot lawfully give himself to another as that other’s servant.

Therefore, since a servant cannot make an emancipation of himself, whereas the human being made this emancipation, it is clear that the human being was not under the devil’s power and was not redeemed from his servitude. Thus the Son of God came not to redeem the human being from the devil’s power—[“was not”] [Col. 1731A]—since the devil himself would receive no price for this, indeed would never wish the human being to be reconciled to God; rather, he came to redeem him from the servitude of sin by infusing his love into him, offering and paying himself as the price and pure sacrifice to the Father.

He could indeed have done this in many other ways, but in none so fitting. Yet I think it has been more than sufficiently determined to what this possibility must be referred. Since it is sufficient for us to act well, it is not fitting or proper that he who is supremely good should do anything except in the manner by which the best result can occur. But this redemption could not have been accomplished in any better, or even equally good, way than by the Son of God becoming man.

For since humanity was to be freed from sin, there had to be preaching in words and demonstration in deeds. These could not be accomplished so fittingly unless the Son of God, having become man, instructed humanity. Thus humanity would become better; and the devil would suffer more, since the better a human being he sees, the more he envies, and the more he envies, the more he ought to be punished.

There is another rational cause, namely humility. For, as is found in Ezekiel, “a voice sounding above the firmament causes the outstretched wings to bend” (Ezek. 1:25). If the martyrs had not had the example of Christ’s death, they would have thought that they had done something so great for God by their death that no one could possibly do more for God; therefore such humility would not exist.

But they see Christ, who held all things in his hand, endure every kind of insult: seized by night; led before Annas, Caiaphas, Pilate, and Herod; his face veiled; spat upon; bound; scourged; mocked; crowned with thorns; clothed in purple; finally condemned to a most disgraceful death; reckoned among the wicked. And they guarded him not only in death but also after death, and wished to extinguish his reputation both in himself and in others. That this passion was more difficult than all the rest, he himself testifies through Jeremiah, saying: “O all you who pass by the way, consider whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1:12).

Therefore, compared with this passion, all the torments of the martyrs will seem almost nothing; and no one can make himself equal to him in suffering. All this was clearly done in order to show how great was his love for humanity, and to kindle humanity more strongly toward love of himself. Hence: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). And the Apostle: “Why did Christ, while we were still weak, die at the appointed time for the ungodly?” (Rom. 5:6). And elsewhere: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16).

For, as Hilary says, he loved humanity more than [Col. 1732A] the other creatures. Therefore he made the world for humanity’s sake, along with all that belongs to the world’s adornment; he placed humanity in the midst as lord and possessor, and assigned angels to its service. When humanity sinned, it was separated from its Lord by sin. Therefore the Son of God came, that, as a fitting mediator, he might free humanity from sin and instil his love into it.

He accomplishes this by offering to the Father the human being whom he assumed—that is, by giving a human being as the price for humanity. Yet he is called a price metaphorically. This, then, is the certain and proper cause of redemption, taught both by the Apostle in Romans and by Christ in the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the union of two natures in one person.

[Col. 1732B] We must now consider the union of the two natures into one person. To signify it, we can adduce no more expressive likeness than that notable and Catholic one brought forward by Athanasius: “As flesh and a rational soul are one human being, so God and man are one Christ.” For as flesh and soul meet in one person, so in Christ the divine and human natures meet. Although the Word is there—the third person in the Trinity—he is nevertheless not there as a person by himself; for then person would already be in person, and thus there would be two persons in Christ. Just as a soul separated from the body is a person, yet, joined to the body, cannot be called a person, because it meets with the body to constitute one person.

That there are not two persons in Christ is demonstrated by reason and confirmed by authority: “He assumed nature, not person.” Boethius also, as we have already said, disputing against Eutyches and Nestorius, who said that there were two persons there and consequently two Christs, showed that there is only one person there, according to the definition applicable to a human being—namely: “A person is an individual rational substance.” Christ, therefore, is one person. Here they take “individual” not in the sense of what can be predicated of one thing only, but in the sense of what is distinct and separate from others. Therefore, because the Word is not there distinct and separate from the human being, but rather, together with the human being, makes one person distinct and separated from others, this shows, I say, that Christ is one person only.

But since God is said to be in holy persons, and to be in them so as to fill and dwell in them, it is commonly asked how the Word was present there more fully by union than in other holy persons. For the Holy Spirit was in the Blessed Virgin so as wholly to fill her; and in many others, from whose spirit and the Spirit of God, as the Apostle says, one [spirit] is made. Thus the Holy Spirit seems to be united in them as in Christ. Yet although the Holy Spirit is said to fill and dwell in holy people, it can by no means be said that he is united with them, since he does not meet with them to constitute one person; and, though he may remain for a time, he withdraws from them. That he withdraws was clearly apparent in the prophets, who had him at one time and were certainly without him at another.

But when the Apostle says that the Spirit of God becomes one with their spirit, he means one in will—yet in such a way that they may will and desire whatever else [they will], even contrary to what the Holy Spirit counsels them to will or not to will. The Word, therefore, was otherwise in Christ: he was so united to that human being as to meet with him in one person. And just as flesh is subject to the soul, so that it can have no movement or operation except from the soul, so that soul was subject to the Word, so that it could attribute no movement to that body except insofar as the Word inspired it.

And it must be known that this union was effected in such a manner that, as blessed Ambrose says, neither of those natures was changed into the other. This too can clearly be shown in the human being. For soul and body meet in one person in such a way that neither is turned into the other. The soul does not thereby become flesh, nor does flesh become soul. In the same way, in Christ divine and human nature meet in one person, so that neither passes into the other. For, as Augustine says, if the Word passed into a human being, or a human being into the Word, there would then be there only a human being or only the Word.

It is also usually disputed whether these two natures ought to be called parts of that person. Yet unless they are parts of that person, Athanasius’s likeness seems to have been introduced to no purpose. Again, if they were not parts, they would not meet to constitute something; but they meet in one person. It is therefore necessary that they be parts. This is compelled not only by this reasoning and by Athanasius’s likeness, but authority too is found to assert the same. Jerome says: “Christ is in part man and in part God.”

Augustine, however, was unwilling to approve this, perhaps because of their mutual predication of one another. We should therefore carefully inquire whether such predication is true or not. For all these expressions are found in authoritative writings: “God is man”; “man is God”; “Christ is Son of Man”; “Christ is Son of God”; “Christ is God and man.” Of these, none except one seems proper. For if the expression “God is man” is proper, then what is eternal is temporal, what is simple is composite, and the Creator is a creature; and likewise with the others. They are therefore improper expressions, in which a part is taken for the whole.

For it often happens that the whole is taken for the part and the part for the whole. Thus the soul, though it is part of a human being, is used for the human being, as in: “All flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Luke 3:6). In the same way, when we say “God is man,” it is true with respect to a part, and the sense is: God is uniting a human being to himself. Again, “Man is God” is meaningful, and means: the human being is united to God. Likewise, these must be referred to a part: “This Christ is man,” and “Christ is God.” Therefore only this statement is proper: “Christ is God and man,” that is, Christ is the Word possessing a human being; and “Christ is man and God,” that is, a human being possessing the Word.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the will of the assumed human being

Having thus dealt with the union of the two natures in one person, it remains to inquire concerning the will of the assumed human being: whether it was the same as the will of the Father. That it was not the same is shown quite plainly not only by reason but also by the Gospel. For Christ says in the Gospel: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you [will]” (Matt. 26:39). This is as though he said: “If the human race can be saved without my death, I shall not die, since I cannot will to die; but if not, I place my will beneath yours.”

Here it is openly shown that the will of that human being was other and different. Augustine, however, and certain others say that he did not say this on his own behalf, but on behalf of the weak members whom he transformed into himself, in order to instruct them what should be done in sufferings: when one can no longer avoid suffering, one should place God’s will before one’s own and say, “May your will be done.” Likewise when he said, “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (ibid., v. 38), and when he began to be afraid and distressed. In all these things, they say, he made a transformation of his members into himself.

And indeed it can quite soundly be expounded in this way, because, as Augustine himself says, when some expound a verse in one way and others differently, the expositions may be good and fitting although diverse; for though the writer may have understood it in only one sense, the Holy Spirit nevertheless knew that it could suitably be expounded in many and very different ways.

But let Augustine call it his own will; we, however, say that, just as he assumed true humanity, so he had the genuine weaknesses of human frailty—which the saints unanimously affirm. Pope Leo says: “The Lord Jesus Christ assumed all that is ours except sin.” Augustine likewise says: “He assumed our will and sorrow; I confidently say sorrow, because I proclaim the cross.” He therefore had true sorrow and real pains, not simulated ones.

[Note: [Col. 1733D] Read: “had therefore.”]

For Hilary is charged with error when he says that Christ felt the nails driven into his feet and hands no differently than if they had been driven into wax. For unless there were suffering there, there would be nothing contrary to the will. Hence in the future life, where there will be no suffering, nothing will happen contrary to the will. For will is never present except with delight: what delights us, we will; what troubles us, we usually abhor.

He therefore endured those pains and discomforts against his will; otherwise there would have been no merit in them. He suffered, then, not because he willed to suffer in death—for he feared it—but because he loved the Father, whom he knew to will this, and because he desired that the salvation of his neighbour should come about through his death. Nor does it follow: if for this reason he willed to suffer, therefore he willed suffering. This may be seen in the case of a sick person who cannot be cured unless he is cut or cauterized. He wills to be cut in order to be cured, yet he does not will to be cut; rather, he fears the incision.

The same may be said of someone imprisoned, who cannot otherwise escape prison unless he himself places his son in prison. He therefore wills to put his son in prison in order that he himself may escape; yet he does not will his son to be imprisoned, but rather grieves over it. But where there is pain or suffering, there is no will, as we have said.

Nor was it ever otherwise in Christ than in the martyrs. They did not wish to suffer, and therefore fled their persecutors as much as they could; yet they willed to suffer because of love for Christ. But to will to be stoned or burned, if this were possible, would have no merit. To suffer for Christ, to will to be mutilated for love of God, has merit. Where Christ is made the foundation, where God is established as the highest and greater cause, there alone is merit.

For we say that martyrdom does not give love or good will, but displays the love already possessed and sometimes increases it. That martyrdom is not in itself voluntary for anyone is evident because it is not pleasant. Jerome shows that it is not pleasant in his commentary on “Behold, how good and how pleasant” (Ps. 132:1), where he says: “There is something good that is not pleasant, such as martyrdom.” The Lord also plainly disclosed this to Peter when he said: “And he will lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18).

If it is objected, “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53:7), we say that “he willed it” means that he approved or judged necessary the death that was necessary. So too the Apostle says: “For what I will, this I do not do; but what I do not will, that I do” (Rom. 7:19). “What I will,” he says, means what I approve as needing to be done; “what I do not will” means what I do not approve.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the will of God

Since we have mentioned God’s will, let us pause briefly to examine it. The will of God is spoken of in two ways. When I say, “God wills this or that,” it may be explained in two ways: “He wills this,” that is, he ordains it; or “he wills this,” that is, he counsels it. In divine Scripture the will of God is found to be understood only in these two ways: as in, “He has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113:3), that is, what he ordained; and elsewhere, “Who has resisted his will?” (Rom. 9:19), that is, his ordinance. Or otherwise, as in, “He wills all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4), that is, he counsels or approves it.

We often resist this will when we do not do what he counsels us to do. We also resist his ordinance, insofar as lies in us, when we strive against it, though we cannot hinder it. This sometimes happens culpably and sometimes without fault. It is culpable when we oppose the contrary not from good zeal or some affection of love, but rather from envy or some wickedness—for example, when God grants someone some good which, from envy or malice, we hinder as much as we can, so that he may not have it.

We strive without fault in two ways. Sometimes, when we see things occurring that seem to us unfitting, we do not think they are ordained by God; and therefore we oppose them and desire that they not occur. Ignorance excuses this. We also do the same from an affection of charity or some natural affection: for example, when one sees one’s father dying, knows that this is in God’s ordinance, and yet wills that he not die and grieves that he is dying.

Here it should be noted that at times a human being’s good will disagrees with God’s will, while at times an evil will agrees with it. Augustine plainly shows this in the *Enchiridion*. The Church also does this: when she sees a martyr being slaughtered or stoned, she knows well that this is in God’s good pleasure and that it is good for that person also, so that through that martyrdom he may be transferred from this misery to blessedness; and yet she grieves and weeps that he is so afflicted.

Such weeping and sorrows, as said above, are irrational, because they rest on error. For whoever undertakes what they cannot accomplish is mistaken. Yet they are without fault, because they proceed from an affection of charity or love. Therefore, from the fact that will is understood as ordinance, it may plainly be inferred that God commands many things which he does not will to be done, and prohibits many things which he ordains to be done.

For he commanded Abraham to sacrifice his son, whom nevertheless he did not will to be sacrificed. This is evident from the fact that he was not sacrificed. Yet God both commanded well and did not will it well. He commanded in order to make Abraham’s obedience known; but he did not will it because there was no rational reason for Abraham to sacrifice his son.

He prohibited the cleansed lepers from making themselves known; yet he willed them to do so, and he knew well that it would not be concealed. He rightly prohibited it, namely in order to offer all an example of humility. He also rightly willed it to be made known, so that God might thereby be glorified. They too did well in not obeying him in this matter; they were not thereby disobedient, but rather humble.

It is like the case where someone stands before a bishop with bended knee and the bishop forbids it: each does what belongs to him—the person, by showing deference, for deference ought to be shown to superiors; and the bishop, by forbidding it, because an example of humility ought to be given by all. Hence Solomon: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20).

God commands everyone without exception: “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:5), and he knows well that some will not obey. But lest anyone say, “He commanded them and not me; therefore I do not know in what I ought to obey him,” or, “I am not guilty if I do not do this, because I have not been commanded to do it, and so I am excusable”—lest anyone, I say, should say this, he commands all, in order to remove every excuse.

Yet he does not will all to obey, because just as it is rational that some obey, so it is rational that others do not obey. The same reasoning may be applied to prohibitions. To see this more clearly, take the example of Peter and Judas. He gave both the commandment of love. Peter obeyed; Judas did not, because he did not will Judas to obey. And just as there was a rational reason why he willed Peter to obey, so there was a rational reason why he did not will Judas to obey and be condemned.

Note: he does not ordain evils to exist, but permits them to exist; nevertheless, he orders well concerning evils—that is, concerning them. Nor does it follow that he ordains and wills [evils], for for him to will something is nothing other than for it to please him and for him to reward it.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Was that union divided in Christ’s death?

It is further asked whether that union was divided in death. Some authorities hold that the Word never deserted the human being; and it is true that he did not desert human nature. Augustine also says that he did not desert even the flesh from the time he assumed it. Ambrose, however, seems to hold that in death the divinity was separated from the flesh, for he says in his commentary on Luke: “The flesh about to die cries out at the separation of divinity.”

It seems more reasonable, indeed, that it was separated from the body. For just as it could not be joined except through the mediation of the soul, so it ought not to remain in it when the soul was separated. Augustine says that it could not be joined except through the mediation of the soul. Thus, even if the union remained with the soul, it did not remain with both soul and body.

It is also asked whether that soul had the same knowledge as the Word had. Some say that it did, and thus that creature knew as much as the Creator. It was therefore as perfect in knowledge as God. Consequently that creature was equal to its Creator in this respect, which seems irrational. Therefore we do not say that it had the same knowledge. Ambrose also shows this in commenting on the passage, “No one knows the things of God,” etc., “no one knows the things of a human being except the human spirit.” Here, Ambrose says, the Apostle shows against certain heretics that [the Spirit] is not a creature. But if this soul has the same knowledge as the Word of God, the Apostle’s statement is null, since this soul is created.

Although it did not know as much, it nevertheless saw God most perfectly. But it is objected that God said to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33:20). We reply that this was said concerning animal life. By animal life we mean that animation and movement which flesh has from the [vital] soul, because the body can in no way be moved except through the soul. But Christ’s life was not of this kind; rather, as we have already said, what the soul does for the body, the Word did for that soul, because no movement could be imparted to the body except through the Word.

There is no objection based on natural affections such as pain and the rest, because they were naturally present in that soul. But if anyone says that it was likewise natural to that soul to provide motion to the body, we grant this; but he removed one thing by which a human being usually sins, and left the other in place so that he might remain a true human being.

It may also be disputed whether, since the Word is everywhere by essence, he has any diversity in his mode of being. He seems to. For since the Word was in that human being by union, where that human being was not, there the united Word was not; where that human being was not, there was not the mediator between God and human beings. Thus he admitted diversity in his existence. In this way it may be said that he is otherwise here and otherwise in heaven.

But, as we said above, God is everywhere in such a way that he is not somewhere. Blessed Augustine stated this plainly when he proved that God is not a body, because he is not somewhere. Therefore he is everywhere by power, since he can act everywhere. He is everywhere by essence, because all places are so present to him through his governance that he needs no place to serve as his substitute. In every place he administers what is fitting. Blessed Gregory describes him as everywhere in this way: “He is above all things, ruling them; beneath all things, sustaining them; and within all things, disposing them.”

He is therefore united to the human being in such a way that he is not in any place, just as the soul is united to the body in such a way that it is not in a place. But just as the soul’s being in the body is nothing other than moving the body, so the Word’s being in that human being was nothing other than moving him in such a way that he could have no movement from himself; indeed, he could not even move a finger except insofar as the Word inspired him. Thus all the objections are disposed of—“he is otherwise here, otherwise there,” that is, “he is united there [but] not united [here],” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the sacrament of baptism

Having shown thus far concerning the greatest of benefits, let us turn to the benefit of the sacraments. For just as his coming was necessary, so after his departure he left necessary sacraments. For it was fitting that a new King should leave behind new laws for himself, as is still customary when kings are installed.

Of these sacraments, some are spiritual and some are not. The spiritual ones are the greater, namely those which avail for salvation. Yet one of them does not pertain to salvation, though it is the sacrament of a great matter—namely marriage. For taking a wife is not in itself meritorious for salvation, but is permitted because of an impediment to salvation. A sacrament is a visible form of invisible grace, or a sign of a sacred thing—that is, of some secret reality.

The first of them is baptism, which takes the place of circumcision. For, as blessed Gregory says, baptism does for us what circumcision formerly did for those who were of Abraham’s race; for others, sacrifices, or, in the case of infants, the faith of their parents. Some nevertheless say that they differ in this: access to heaven is now open to the baptized, but it was not then. But we say that baptism does not accomplish this, but the Passion added to it; if this had been added to circumcision, it too would have accomplished it. This can be seen from two coins: when we receive more for two than for one, it does not follow that one is worth more than the other.

But someone will say: Why then was circumcision changed? Because the new King had to establish a new law; because enmities between Jews and Gentiles had to be dissolved; and because Jewish pride had to be checked. Since, because of the legal observances, Jews were hostile to Gentiles and Gentiles in turn to Jews, the Gentiles would never have accepted those observances. Again, if they had accepted them, the Jews would have become proud and boasted, as though saying, “Whether you wish it or not, you have now come to our sacraments.” It was therefore fitting that those observances should be abolished and that others, which would certainly be common to all, should be established.

For this reason baptism also took the place of circumcision: circumcision was an imperfect sacrament, since it applied to males alone, whereas baptism is a perfect sacrament because it is suited to both sexes. It is commonly asked why baptism is performed in water rather than another liquid. Several answers may be given. First, this was done for the fitting beauty of the sacrament. No liquid is so effective for washing as water; and therefore it was fitting and proper that, just as the cleansing of the soul is better than every other cleansing, it should be signified by washing in the liquid most effective for washing.

Again, it was done so that it might be more readily available, so that all, poor as well as rich, could have it and could not excuse themselves on grounds of poverty. If it were performed in some other liquid, not everyone could obtain it so easily.

In this sacrament, as in the others, there are two things: the sacrament itself and its reality. The sacrament is the outward washing itself; the reality of this sacrament is inward washing. This sacrament, like the sacrament of the altar, is received by some unto life and by others unto death. Those who approach truly receive both the reality and the sacrament; those who approach deceitfully receive the sacrament only. Therefore, if they repent, they are not baptized afterward, because they have received the sacrament.

Augustine nevertheless advances a certain opinion concerning them, because it does not seem consistent that the Holy Spirit should not always retain his efficacy. He therefore says that, if remission of sins is granted to them, it passes away for a time. This is what he says: “Not even the grace of baptism is hindered by brotherly hatred; for yesterday is dissolved,” etc.

This washing was signified in the prophet Ezekiel: “She is washed with water, anointed with oil, clothed in many-coloured garments”; that is, the faithful soul, in order to be worthy of royal embrace, is cleansed from the filth of sin, anointed with the grace of oil—that is, made a member of Christ. For Christ is said to be anointed with chrism; she is clothed in many-coloured garments, that is, adorned with diverse virtues.

Concerning this sacrament, as concerning the others, it must be considered that it makes no difference from what minister it is given, because the minister ministers, but Christ baptizes. Hence: “This is he who baptizes” (John 1:33). Therefore, whether it is given by heretics, laypersons, or even women when necessity is pressing, it must never be repeated.

It is commonly asked whose words those are—whether the child’s or the sponsor’s. Whoever owns those words, the person who answers certainly appears to lie. If the person answers on his own behalf, “I wish to be baptized,” he lies, because he does not in his own conscience desire to wish to be baptized. If he speaks on behalf of the child, neither can he be entirely excused from lying. For he undoubtedly knows that the child does not have this will, since the child has command of no will at all. That the child does not wish this, I say, may easily be inferred from the fact that it resists as much as it can.

But we say that the sponsor speaks in his own person. When he says, “I believe,” it is as though he said: “I have such faith that this child may be saved through it.” Likewise, when he answers, “I wish to be baptized,” the meaning is: “I wish this child to be baptized in my faith.” Nevertheless, the child’s own words are retained, so that from the identity of the words, the sponsor’s identification with the child may be noted.

It must be known that this form must everywhere be observed. Blessed Ambrose nevertheless says that baptism can be performed in the name of Christ, because the Trinity is understood there: “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”—that is, by invocation of him whom nothing can resist, who does all things wisely, who brings it about concerning all things that the outcome is the best that can result.

After this sacrament follows another, greater indeed with respect to the dignity of its ministers; for it is conferred by the highest pontiffs, just as it was conferred only by the apostles. First there is anointing; afterward comes confirmation. There sin is forgiven; here gifts of grace are given. For here is undoubtedly given that grace by which one fights, if not always, then at least sometimes, against each particular vice. This grace is a kind of armour by which, after the crossing of baptism, we fight against vices in this desert.

For just as, after the Egyptians pursuing the children of Israel from behind had been submerged, other enemies attacked them through the desert, so, after the devil who formerly pursued us has been submerged in baptism, many vices resist us through the desert of this life. Against them we are fortified, as with armour and a defensive stronghold, by the grace given in this sacrament.

Therefore it must undoubtedly be known that, however unworthy a bishop may be, this power is nevertheless bestowed on him in consecration, so that this grace is given through his ministry. It is recorded concerning Caiaphas that, since he was high priest that year (John 11:49), the grace of prophecy was given not to his person but to his office. For though he was not worthy in himself, he nevertheless prophesied by virtue of his office and said by the Holy Spirit: “It is expedient for you that one [man should die],” etc. (John 18:14).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the sacrament of the altar

[Col. 1740D]

Next follows the sacrament of the altar. The purpose of this sacrament is the remembrance of Christ’s death and Passion. Christ himself made this purpose clear to all when he consecrated this sacrament at supper, saying: “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). For the memory of our friends is accustomed greatly to awaken their love within us. Therefore, in order that there might be greater love for himself, he instituted that this sacrament should be performed in remembrance of himself.

For in the sacrament we ought to have Christ before our eyes as one led to the Passion, suffering and crucified for us. This representation makes us mindful of the love that he showed us. Hence we are kindled with greater love to embrace him and to suffer for him; and this reciprocal love joins him to us and us to him.

This sacrament is celebrated in bread and wine. It should therefore be noted that before consecration the bread is bread and the wine likewise wine; but after consecration, the bread is Christ’s body and the wine is his blood. Thus it is the true body of Christ—indeed, Christ himself.

This body is the sacrament of that body of Christ which is the Church. For just as this body which he assumed from the Virgin has diverse members, some of which were mutually necessary to others, so too does this body which is the Church. Thus the Apostle describes the Church as a kind of living creature having as its head Christ himself; spiritual eyes, the prelates, who provide foresight for the others; hands, the workers themselves; and feet, the lesser members necessary for carrying the body. They need one another’s assistance in turn, so that greater and lesser alike must mutually supply one another. For in the human body we see that eyes should serve hands and hands eyes, and hands feet and feet hands.

The blood, however, is the sacrament of the Church’s spirit, which gives it life and works in it through sevenfold grace. For as Augustine says, the soul is the life of the body, so God is the life of the soul. This life-giving grace is fittingly signified by blood because the soul has greater power and efficacy in the blood than in any other fluid. Hence Moses says: “The life of every flesh is in the blood” (Lev. 17:11).

That reception and incorporation which occurs in receiving this sacrament is [the sign] of the union and incorporation of the members with the head. For when someone approaches to receive it, he shows not that he is then united to Christ, but that he has already been perfected, that love has been united, and that it has passed into his members. Concerning the reality of this sacrament our Lord said: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me” (John 6:57). He did not say this of the sacrament, because many are of his body who do not receive this sacrament, and many receive it who are not his members. Judas received this sacrament as Peter did; but one received it unto salvation, the other unto death.

It is commonly asked why he wished to confer this sacrament in bread and wine rather than in other foods. But it is clear that bread is more substantial food than all other foods and supports [the body] more. No complete meal or abundance of the table can exist without bread. Hence too the Prophet says: “Bread strengthens the human heart” (Ps. 103:15). Therefore he chose to give his body under the form of bread rather than another food, in order to make it plainly understood that, just as this food excels in providing bodily sustenance, so this sacrament excels above the others in increasing within us the love of God, which is the soul’s sustenance. For in none of the other [sacraments] are we so affected by love for him as in this one.

He also preferred to give his blood in wine rather than in another drink, because wine signifies joy. Hence: “Wine gladdens the human heart” (ibid.). By this he also plainly showed the inestimable joy that would come to the Church through his Passion, a joy that the saints who lived before his coming did not at all possess, because by dying they did not pass into life, but were held in hell. Hence their birthdays are not celebrated in the Church.

We do not read that Christ added water to this sacrament. Why, then, is it mixed with wine? We say that the water signifies the people of the Gentiles. Hence: “Many waters [are] many peoples” (Rev. 17:15). For just as water is always in flux and motion, so that people were held in the flux of the flesh and a certain instability. For, restrained by no yoke of law or prophets, they were carried hither and thither among groves and altars of demons.

Therefore, since before Christ’s death this people had not entered the Church, it was not fitting that water—which expresses joy at their entrance—should be added. But when they afterward entered, the Church, rejoicing in their entrance and fellowship, added water.

It is likewise commonly disputed whether the breaking which appears there truly happens to Christ’s body, just as it is truly present there. We say that just as bread appears to be present and is not, and wine likewise appears to be present although it is not wine, so it appears to be broken although it undergoes no breaking and receives no division of parts. Nor is that appearance therefore phantasmal, because it is not for deception or error of faith, but for the commendation of the sacrament.

But though it is easy to answer concerning the breaking that occurs at the altar, it seems difficult to resolve the breaking which Christ performed at supper, concerning which the Evangelist says: “He broke [it] and gave [it] to his disciples” (Luke 22:19)—namely, whether he truly broke his body and gave it to his disciples divided into parts. To this it seems that the answer should be that, whole, entire, and perfect, just as he derived it from the Virgin, so he gave it whole and entire to each disciple. So too it is received at the altar by every faithful person.

What the Evangelist said—“He broke and gave to his disciples”—must plainly be understood thus: “He broke,” that is, he disclosed and opened to the disciples what this sacrament signified: namely, that the body figured the Church and that the blood figured the joy which the Church has in its redemption. Hence those who do not know this receive it unbroken—that is, unrevealed according to its signification.

Jeremiah shows that it may soundly and fittingly be expounded in this way: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4). This bread is Scripture. The weak little ones before Christ’s coming asked that this bread—that is, this Scripture—be broken for them, that is, opened and expounded; and there was none to break it for them until Christ came, who opened the Scriptures to them. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “And no one was able to open the book and loose its seals,” etc. (Rev. 5:2).

Scripture is rightly called bread because the inner human being is refreshed and sustained by it as by spiritual food, just as the outer human being is by bodily food. It must be broken—that is, expounded—because, just as the crust of hard bread must be broken in order that we may come to the marrow and crumb within, so the bark and shell of the letter must be broken—that is, the sequence of the letter must be expounded—so that we may be able to reach the marrow, that is, the inward meaning.

It is also customary to ask in what condition he gave it to the disciples: namely, passible or impassible. To this we say that we have no authoritative determination on the matter. Yet we may safely answer that he gave it such as he willed. For if he willed to give them an immortal body, he could indeed at that time assume for himself impassibility, just as in death he adorned himself with the beauty of immortal life. [Col. 1743B] But if he wished to give it passible, he could certainly do this also, provided that, though it were ground by their teeth, he would feel nothing from it and would undergo no diminution in himself; just as he gave blessed Vincent such firmness of body that he felt little of the torments inflicted on him. For if anyone who did not possess the same power in his body had suffered even a tenth part of those punishments, he could never afterward have lived. Similarly, if Christ had willed it, he would have laid aside all other bodily weaknesses as well as affections of the mind.

There is likewise doubt concerning whose appearance that of the bread and wine is. To this the sound answer is that the body itself, because of the horror of receiving it, takes those forms into itself. For if it is objected that, since [Col. 1743C] that body assumed its own form, it has never laid that form aside and therefore cannot have another form while that one remains, we say that, just as it belongs to the singularity of that body that it was conceived of the Holy Spirit, entered and came forth while the womb was closed, walked upon the waters, entered among the disciples when the doors were shut, and is possessed simultaneously and at the same time in different places—just as, I say, all these things belong to the singularity of that body—so also does this: that it has diverse forms at once. For if this is astonishing, each of the others is no less clearly wondrous, since all things concerning it are to be marveled at.

It also plainly indicated that manna was a sacrament of this true bread. For when manna rained down upon the children of Israel, they wondered what [Col. 1743D] it was and asked one another: *Manhu*, that is, “What is this?” (Exod. 16:15). In the same way it may always be asked here: “What is this?” For neither human intelligence nor speech suffices fully to express what it is. If we do not wish to say that this form belongs to that body, we may sufficiently say that the form remains in the air, reserved for concealment of the flesh and blood for the reason stated above; just as a human form is in the air when an angel appears in human form.

A question is commonly raised concerning what happens through the negligence of ministers: namely, that mice appear to gnaw and carry that body in their mouths. [Col. 1744A] But we say that God does not leave it there to be handled by so base an animal; rather, the form remains there to correct the negligence of the ministers.

Let us now consider the efficacy of this sacrament. Its efficacy is greater and stronger than that of any other, because it confirms so fully that one who receives it devoutly, so long as he does not reject it from himself through his own weakness, suffers no temptation of the devil; for through reception of this Eucharist the devil is conquered and bound. And although such a person always has in himself [Note: [Col. 1743D] Read perhaps: “has the Holy Spirit.”], nevertheless he always receives it and makes in it a dwelling-place.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the sacrament of anointing

[Col. 1744B] It remains to consider the sacrament of anointing. One must know, therefore, that this sacrament is a sacrament of the same reality as the sacrament of the altar, because it signifies that anointing of head and members which is signified by the sacrament of the altar. For as this anointing preceded threefold in the head, so it follows in the members as well. But because this sacrament is the last of all and, as it were, their consummation, it is by a certain prerogative rightly called the sacrament of anointing, although anointing is contained in the others; and it indeed preceded threefold in our head, Christ, as has been said. Hence he was called Christ, that is, one anointed with chrism. For he was anointed with spiritual oil from his very conception. Hence also Christ says: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because [Col. 1744C] he has anointed me; he sent me to proclaim good news to the meek, to heal the broken-hearted,” etc. (Isa. 61:1). Likewise the Psalmist says: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God has anointed you,” etc. (Ps. 44:8).

Afterward Mary anointed his feet in the house of Simon the leper; then she anointed his head, when she poured the alabaster vessel over his head. He received these two anointings because he was king and priest. Likewise two persons are anointed in the Church: king and priest, one greater and the other lesser. The lesser is blessed by the greater, as the Apostle says. Thus in the anointing of the feet the lesser person, that is, the priest, is represented; in the anointing of the head, the greater person, that is, the king.

David also, who went before as a figure of Christ, [Col. 1744D] is read to have been anointed first in his father’s house by Samuel, second over part of Israel, and third over the whole. In the same way every Christian is anointed three times: first at the beginning, namely in baptism, where sins are forgiven; second in confirmation, where the gifts of grace are bestowed; third at departure, where either all sins, if any remain, or the greater part of them, are blotted out.

It must therefore be considered what the reality of this sacrament is, and what its efficacy is: whether reality and efficacy are the same or rather distinct from one another. To this it must be said that certain sacraments agree in this, namely that their efficacy is one thing and their reality another. [Col. 1745A] Others differ in this respect; baptism, for example, has reality and effect as the same thing. But the sacrament of the altar is not so constituted. For although its reality and what it effects are the same, nevertheless the sacrament of the altar effects one thing—concerning which efficacy we have shown enough above—and its reality is another. Likewise, in this sacrament too, the reality is one thing and the efficacy another; its reality is the same as that of the sacrament of the altar. For this sacrament does not make [Note: [Col. 1745] Supply: “make.”] that which it signifies, but shows that it has been made. For a person becomes a member of Christ in baptism before approaching consecration at the altar. Similarly, one is a member of Christ before being thus anointed.

Moreover, this anointing ought to be performed upon each of the senses, so that whatever has been committed through the senses may be forgiven wholly or for the most part. Concerning its repetition, [Col. 1745B] let it be done according to the differing customs of the churches. For when James says, “Is anyone among you sick? Let him bring in the presbyters of the Church, and let them anoint him, and he shall be well” (Jas. 5:14), he does not seem to forbid its repetition. For concerning the greater sacraments—baptism, confirmation, and the sacrament of the altar—it has been said that no sacrament is to be repeated. Nor is the same offering consecrated twice, although the same body is frequently received by the same person.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the sacrament of marriage, and that it confers no gift as the others do. Also on charity

Now we must speak of marriage. It is indeed a sacrament, but it confers no gift as the others do; nevertheless, it is a remedy for evil. [Col. 1745C] For it is given to restrain incontinence; hence it belongs more to indulgence. It is defined thus: Marriage is the lawful covenant of a man and a woman, by reason of which they may unite without fault.

Now one covenant concerns contracting marriage, as when a man promises that he will take her as his wife; another is the covenant of marriage itself, as when he says: “I give myself to you for the use of my flesh, so that, as long as you live, I shall not join myself to another.” This covenant especially makes a marriage.

It should be known, however, that in this sacrament many things were formerly permitted which are now not permitted. For in the Old Testament one man was permitted to have many wives, so that the people of God might increase; but a woman was not permitted to have many husbands, because many women can be made fruitful by one man, but one woman not by many. [Col. 1745D] Now this is not permitted, because the people of God has increased. Even then kings were not permitted to have many wives, but one, so that they might be able to provide for their subjects. For if they had many, their minds would be hindered by concern for them, and thus they would provide less well. That David and Solomon had many wives, therefore, was plainly contrary to the law.

But our marriage has been reduced to the marriage of kings, because we are kings, of whom Peter says: “We are an elect race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9). This sacrament, as has been said, is a remedy for evil, even if it confers no gift. Hence: “Let him who can receive it, receive it” (Matt. 19:[Col. 1746A] 12); that is, let him who can be continent remain continent; he who cannot may take a wife. And the Apostle says: “Let each have his own wife, to avoid fornication” (1 Cor. 7:2).

It is commonly asked whether clerics may contract marriage. Priests who have not done so [i.e., made a vow] may do so. But if someone belongs to a church that has taken a vow, though he himself has not made a vow, he may marry; but he will not exercise office in that church—that is, he will not hold a parish. Greek priests, however, because they have not taken a vow, may properly take wives. When they are consecrated, they receive wives and virgins from the bishop’s hand; if these wives die, they do not take others, nor do the wives themselves take other husbands. [Note: [Col. 1745] At this point several sentences seem to have dropped out, perhaps through a copyist’s negligence.]

It was also commanded that each man take a wife from his own tribe, [Col. 1746B] lest the tribes be mingled and the possession of one tribe pass into that of another, because the land was divided by tribes. But this is not now permitted: rather, one may marry from another people, a practice which the Church received from the Romans for the propagation of charity. For when the Romans wished to establish friendship with other cities, they took wives from them to form a covenant of friendship. Similarly, the Church ordained that a person should take a wife not from his own but from another lineage, because it did not judge this sufficient for the extension of charity, since through the wife he takes, he loves her entire kindred.

[Col. 1746C] Many things impede marriage: kinship, vow, orders, frigidity. Some secretly vow continence. If they cannot remain continent, let them repent of the vow and take wives. But those who make a public vow, such as a monk and a priest, cannot contract marriage. Orders are an impediment; nevertheless, men may marry up to the rank of acolyte, but they must relinquish their benefices. Those ordained above acolyte may not marry. Gregory nevertheless permitted it to the English, because, if it were prohibited [to them], being newly converted to the faith, they might easily fall back. Slavery too is an impediment. If anyone unknowingly marries another’s maidservant, then, if he does not wish to be reduced to slavery, he must either redeem her or dismiss her.

Likewise, if a frigid man takes a wife and cannot have her, Pope Leo says that he may dismiss her. But Gregory says that there is a marriage, even if he cannot have [Col. 1746D] her as a wife: let him have her as a sister, and it will be no less a marriage, like the marriage of Mary and Joseph. But if the woman cannot remain continent and says so, she is not to be separated for this reason, because she must remain continent.

Hence Jerome and Theophrastus say: “No wise man should take a wife.” For in other cases we can test what things are like before possessing them—for example, a horse before buying it—but we are not permitted to test a woman until after taking her as a wife. Again, a woman is either chaste or unchaste. If chaste, she is proud; if unchaste, she will never be free from suspicion.

Marriage is also called servitude. Hence the Apostle says: “Were you called as a slave?” [Col. 1747A] etc. (1 Cor. 7:21), that is, in marriage make use of servitude: even if you have an opportunity to leave, do not leave. But if free—that is, without marriage—do not take a wife, if you wish to be free.

There are three goods of marriage: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament. Fidelity is not Catholic faith, but the marital agreement that, as long as he lives, he does not unite with another. Offspring means that a child who is born should be raised religiously; and it serves as an adornment, so that what has there been committed through sin may be compensated by the fruit of children. The sacrament is that of Christ and the Church: for as a wife belongs to one husband and a husband to one wife, so Christ is bridegroom of one bride, that is, the Church, and the Church is bride of one bridegroom, that is, Christ.

It is asked whether marriage can exist among unbelievers. [Col. 1747B] Certainly it can. Hence John the Baptist says: “It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife” (Matt. 14:4). John says that it was adultery, and therefore there was a marriage. But it is objected: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). Yet this must be understood as meaning “not from faith,” that is, contrary to conscience. What conscience testifies to be evil is sin if it is done. Augustine says that marriage is a natural good, diffused among all people, even unbelievers. Likewise, marriage exists between believers and unbelievers. Hence the Apostle says: “If any believer has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her” (1 Cor. 7:12). A Christian could also marry a Jewish woman if some recompense were to result from it.

[Col. 1747C] We have said above that the sum of salvation consists in these three things: faith, sacrament, and charity. Having now sufficiently dealt with two of them, faith and sacrament, let us henceforth discuss the third, charity. Charity, as we said above, is honorable love, that is, love directed to the end to which it ought to be directed. Love is good will toward someone for that person’s own sake. For if I love someone for some advantage, my love is not for that person but for my own advantage. Thus, if I wish eternal life for someone not for that person’s sake but in order to be free of him, I should already wish him to be in paradise; I do not love him, but desire some benefit to myself from his death. Such love, then, is not honorable, that is, it does not tend [Col. 1747D] to the end to which it should tend, namely God himself.

Although there may be many and diverse ends in love or in some undertaking—for example, in building a house for the poor, the poor are a cause—yet the end, that is, the final and supreme cause, namely God, is one. Therefore, although I love someone for that person’s own sake, I should not make that person the end of my love, but God himself; and then love is referred to its first end, to which it ought to be referred.

This twofold love consists, indeed, in love of God and of neighbor. For we cannot love God unless we love our neighbor. Yet this inability should be referred not to nature but to the institution of the commandment; for it could be that no human being existed apart from me, and I could love God well. [Col. 1748A] John’s saying concerning the obstinate must also be understood in this way: “He who does not love the neighbor whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20). It is as though he said: one so hardened against the neighbor whom he sees that he can in no way be recalled to love of that neighbor, while he remains such cannot love God; for this is now nothing other than hating one’s neighbor, and one who hates a neighbor does not love God.

## CHAPTER XXXII. In what ways God loves us, and in what ways we ought to love God or neighbor

It now seems proper to state in what ways God loves us and in what ways we ought to love God or our neighbor, so that the order which should be observed in charity [Col. 1748B] may clearly appear. For God to love someone is nothing other than to dispose well concerning that person from eternity, and, through the succession of times, to prepare that person by the gifts of his grace for eternal life. Thus, when I say, “God loves him,” the meaning is: “From eternity he has disposed concerning his salvation, namely that in the present life he may bestow upon him some good through which he may be saved.”

For there is no movement in God toward loving us such as there is in us toward loving him. When we love God, we have such a movement of soul toward him. For charity, as Augustine says, is a movement of the soul toward loving God for his own sake and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. Here it is commonly asked whether God now loves someone whom he has not always loved. But we say: not at all. It is also asked whether [Col. 1748C] God loves all who love him. No. If it is objected that he says, “I love those who love me” (Prov. 8:17), and similar texts, we say that this is said of persevering love.

But it should be noted that no measure, indeed no limit, has been set for love of God. In love of neighbor, however, there is a measure. For it is said: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart,” etc. (Matt. 22:37). One loves with the whole heart who is prepared to obey him to the extent of one’s ability. The rest that follows is emphatic repetition; it is as though it said: “For fulfilling his service, stretch forth all your attention.” But in the love of neighbor there is a measure where it is said: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (ibid., [Col. 1748D] 39). It does not say “as much as,” but “as.” Thus the meaning is: the good which you would wish done to yourself if you were in that person’s rank, wish for that person in the rank in which that person stands. Hence elsewhere: “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7:12). We ought indeed to do for others everything we would wish done for ourselves if we were in the same rank and dignity. “Whatever you wish,” that is, approve. For if I wish a prostitute brought to me, I do not approve this. Hence it is also said: “What you do not wish done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. 4:16). One of these principles is natural, namely this latter one; the other is positive, namely “Whatever you wish men to do,” etc.

God and neighbor must be loved in this way, so that our charity may be ordered. For as God is good above human beings, so he must be loved above [Col. 1749A] all things; and as he must be loved before all things, so honor and reverence must be rendered to him more than to all others. After him, the same must be done toward each person according to that person’s rank. For if I see someone more worthy of good than I am, I ought to desire good for that person more than for myself. Thus the order of charity is preserved: according to the merits and fittingness of each person, we love them more or less in differing degrees.

It should nevertheless be noted that, although we ought to maintain such an order in love that I ought to love a religious person more than my father, who is not so religious, the practice of charity must certainly be different. For if I cannot provide for both, I shall withhold from that person and give to my father. [Col. 1749B] For in practice I ought to extend myself more to those whose care I bear; nevertheless, I do not on this account love my father as much as I love that person.

Here it should be noted that if, overcome by some weakness, I fall into fornication or homicide, or into some other sin, provided that I have Christ as my foundation, it is not thereby true that I do not love God. For I can well despise my Lord in some respect for a time and still love him above all things and esteem him above others. David, when he sinned, had charity because he had Christ as his foundation. To have Christ as foundation is to love him in such a way that, if a choice were offered, one would rather permit oneself to be killed than deny him. When a person sins in such matters, the stone is moved, [Col. 1749C] not torn out. “Let the righteous fall, let the righteous stumble, let the righteous rise again: he will be better.” For all things work together for good to the saints (Rom. 8:28).

Since charity is the highest of virtues, and every virtue other than charity itself rests upon it, let us inquire more fully concerning virtues and vices. But first let us consider this point about charity: Augustine seems to wish every virtue to be charity. For when charity makes one brave, courage is charity; when it makes one humble, humility is charity; when it makes one patient, patience is charity; and likewise with the others. Hence the Apostle says: “Charity bears all things, endures all things,” etc. (1 Cor. 13:7).

Some, however, explain Augustine’s authority—“Every virtue is charity”—thus: every virtue is charity [Col. 1749D] or comes from charity. This is because of those virtues which are not acts of will but rather powers, as will appear more clearly below. We must therefore understand how virtue is defined and into how many principal parts it is divided. Virtue, as the philosophers say, is the best disposition of the mind, or the disposition of a well-ordered mind.
