It should be noted that the saints did not alter the definitions of virtues given by the philosophers, or their divisions into species, but carefully expounded and retained what they had received from them. Let us therefore see how the definition is to be understood. Virtue is a disposition of the mind—that is, a good will of the mind, by application of the soul so transformed into a settled disposition that it can scarcely or never be separated from it. [Col. 1750A] For this is indicated by the phrase “disposition of the mind.” Some people, though they presently have the will to render to each person what is that person’s due, are nevertheless easily changed from it. The same may be seen in other cases: someone now endeavors to restrain the will of the flesh, yet indulges it somewhat more fully. For a thing to be virtue, it must arise from application of the soul. Hence Aristotle: “For such are the sciences and the virtues.”

But because some have an inclination toward the virtues of continence or even piety toward others, yet not for God’s sake, it does not avail them for salvation. Therefore the definition adds: “best,” that is, such as contributes to the best life, or in which merit consists. Note that David, when he lay with Bathsheba, did not have love [Col. 1750B] of neighbor in practice. For it is written: “Love of neighbor does no evil” (Rom. 13:9–10), namely, “You shall not commit adultery,” etc. Preserving the authority of this text, therefore, we shall say that he loved Uriah in affection, but not in effect. This authority concerns love as put into effect.

Let us now consider the species of virtue, which some have set at a greater and others at a lesser number. Socrates, placing prudence under virtue, taught that there are four species of virtue: prudence, justice, courage, and temperance. For he said that prudence is the discernment of good and evil things joined with the adornment of character. He called such prudence knowledge or wisdom. Rhetoric has much eloquence concerning this, but little knowledge or wisdom. [Col. 1750C] Aristotle, however, separated it from the virtues when he said: “Such are the sciences and the virtues.” Aristotle did not wish, or did not even think, that what is equally compatible with good and evil persons was a virtue. According to Aristotle, therefore, there are three species of virtue: justice, temperance, and courage.

The philosophers define justice thus: “Justice is a disposition of mind rendering to each person what is that person’s due, with the common good preserved.” Justinian likewise indicated this in his definition when he said: “Justice is the constant and perpetual will,” etc. For by saying “constant and perpetual will,” he indicated a quality of mind arising from application and difficult to move. By saying “rendering to each person his own right,” he indicated the best quality. [Col. 1750D] “One’s own” can be referred either to the recipient or to the giver. If it is referred to the recipient, then “with the common good preserved” must be added. For it belongs to justice to refer all things to the common good.

Thus in a commonwealth it ought to be done in this manner: when someone has deserved to be rewarded so greatly or punished so severely, deliberation should take place as to whether, if such a reward were given or such a penalty imposed, the commonwealth would be harmed. For someone could be rewarded or even punished so greatly that the commonwealth would suffer great detriment. As it is in the commonwealth, so it should be in the Church. Thus every discerning judge, both secular and ecclesiastical, ought to refer everything he does to the common good of the commonwealth or also of his own parish. [Col. 1751A] Thus he preserves the common good in his judgment: by rewarding this person in this way and punishing that person in that way, he renders others more liable to divine [Note: [Col. 1751D] Supply: “justice.”] justice.

But if “one’s own” is referred to the giver, no addition is needed. For the judge punishes and rewards in a manner fitting to himself and according to what is owed to himself; namely, justice ought neither to be cruelty nor laxity, as it would be if he either did not remit in part or remitted entirely. An earthly judge also owes this to himself: that by this he may be rendered more commendable and possess greater authority for doing justice. Similarly, when God punishes one person less than he deserves or rewards another more than merit requires, this belongs to his justice, that is, it pertains to the justice of himself as the giver.

[Col. 1751B] Because this good will may be hindered by some worldly fear or some worldly desire to such a degree that justice is impaired in some respect, it needs, as it were, two supports and buttresses. For if there is someone whom I ought to honor and to whom I ought to give of my possessions, because the person is wise and such that I owe this by justice; but someone says, “Do not do this; do not associate with him, because he is the king’s enemy, and you will therefore easily incur the king’s hostility”—I can certainly be drawn away from the justice I owe him by that fear. Then courage is necessary. Courage is the virtue directed against adversities, which prevents us from abandoning justice through fear or anything similar.

[Col. 1751C] Likewise, when I ought to give someone of my possessions because that person is in need, but I desire to retain what I have because I consider it useful to myself or because I would not easily recover it, then temperance is necessary against prosperities. By restraining desire, it preserves justice uninjured. This will of the mind, supported by these two, as it were by braces, is justice.

It should be noted, however, that although justice is a will of the mind, courage and temperance must be powers, since their opposites are incapacities. For intemperance and weakness, which are their opposites, appear to be incapacities. These supports, therefore, are from charity, not charity itself. When Augustine said that every virtue is charity, he meant that everything was either charity or an effect of charity: charity, as all those [Note: [Col. 1752D] Read perhaps: “all things.”] which consist in will; effects, as whatever are powers. This I say if we wish to assent to the opinion [Col. 1751D] that courage and temperance, and those contained under them, are powers of the mind. On this account we rightly say that many are saved without virtue, because many are saved without perfect charity: when they die, they have the will that, if a choice were offered, they would die; yet they do not have that will as something difficult to change, because, if they lived, that will would change, and therefore it is not virtue.

But if we wish to say that every virtue is good will, we may say that every virtue is charity; and so charity will be the genus of all virtues. We have said that there are three species of virtue: justice, courage, and temperance. [Col. 1752A] We must now inquire how all virtues are reduced to these three, and which are reduced to which.

First, then, let us see what is reduced to justice. All those virtues which concern rendering to each person what is that person’s due pertain to justice. The virtue that concerns rendering to God what is his due, namely religion, belongs to justice. Likewise, the virtue that renders parents what is their due, namely filial piety; the virtue that renders to superiors, inferiors, or equals what is their due; and the virtue that gives to the poor what is their due—all these, I say, are referred to justice as integral parts. Hence: “Unless your justice exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees” [Col. 1752B] (Matt. 5:20). And David says of almsgiving: “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor; his justice remains for ever and ever” (Ps. 3:9). All these things constitute justice as the sciences of discovery and judgment constitute logic. They cannot be called species of justice, because none of them by itself makes a person just—that is, one rendering to each person what is due—but just as a house is made by the union of wall, roof, and foundation, so a just person is made by the union of these virtues.

Having seen what is reduced to justice, it remains to see what is referred to courage and what to temperance. Courage and temperance, as was said, are powers, because their opposites appear to be certain incapacities; yet for this reason they do not cease to be dispositions. [Col. 1752C] Natural power and disposition are opposed. But powers that arise through application of the subject are dispositions. Therefore temperance, being the power to restrain illicit movements, plainly has referred to it everything pertaining to restraining illicit movements: continence, which restrains lust; chastity, which restrains sexual desire; sobriety, which restrains gluttony. These virtues are necessary in prosperity. Courage, however, is the power that makes the mind steadfast against adversities.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On vices contrary to virtues

Let us now likewise discuss the vices contrary to these virtues. Every virtue has a vice contrary to it: injustice is contrary to justice, intemperance to temperance, weakness to courage, [Col. 1752D] because evil is necessarily contrary to good. For if something is good, its contrary is necessarily evil; but the converse does not hold, since evil may be contrary to evil.

Injustice is a vice of the mind by which one does not render to each person what is that person’s own and what is owed. Thus such an evil will is injustice, just as a good will is justice. Intemperance is the incapacity to resist illicit movements, as lust is contrary to chastity and gluttony to sobriety. Weakness of mind is contrary to courage; and, as stated above, courage is necessary in adversities, temperance in prosperities.

[Col. 1753A] Note, however, that powers of this sort are not the natural powers which are not presently active, or which, even if present, are easily moved; rather, they are those possessed through application of the soul. Thus a man is called a runner, not because he naturally has that power, but because he has trained himself for it. Many unbelievers have these natural powers, yet lack the virtues, since they do not apply themselves to them out of love. For every virtue, as we have said, is either charity, where it is a will, or from charity, where it is such a power arising from love. For a person is not called brave, sober, just, humble, or such like, unless charity makes that person brave, sober, or such.

Having seen what virtue is, let us now see what vice is, what sin is, and what difference there is between them. [Col. 1753B] Vice, then, is such a corruption of nature as renders a person incapable of resisting an illicit movement, or unwilling to render to each person what is due, such as irascibility, lust, gluttony, and so forth. Sin, however, is willing to be angry, willing to indulge lust. Thus it may easily be seen that many have sin without vice and vice without sin.

For example, someone easily moved to anger may restrain himself so fully that he does not break out into the heat of evil will against another; or perhaps he has no occasion for being moved against another. The same may be inferred concerning a lustful person. There are many who, though inclined to this, nevertheless restrain their will. Hence it is found that their merit is the greater to such a degree that they become victors in the struggle. There are also others who have no external material for it and, although naturally inclined to it, are not moved to it—for example, many cloistered men, solitaries, and the like. The same can easily be considered in the other cases.

There is also sin in someone without vice, as in a person who does not possess this or that power yet, because some great cause intervenes, is moved to anger or irascibility. Thus vices consist in corruption of nature, but sins in the will; and for this reason vices for the most part arise from one bodily constitution or another. Hence they are also called carnal. There are some, however, that belong only to the soul, such as pride, envy, and so forth.

Sin is nothing other than fault itself, which, as we have shown, may exist in many without vice. Fault is nothing other than contempt for the Creator: it consists in either willing, against conscience, what we know displeases him and is forbidden by him, or not willing what we know pleases him and is commanded by him. Hence no fault is found in children or in those naturally lacking understanding, because they do nothing against knowledge. It should be noted, however, that punishment itself is figuratively called sin, as when it is said: “God forgives him sin,” that is, remits eternal punishment.

Some of these sins are venial, others mortal. A sin is called venial when it is not by itself sufficient for damnation—for example, anything which, while it is being done, does not come to mind as displeasing to God. Yet it cannot be said not to be against conscience [Col. 1754A]; for, although it may then be separated from memory, when we recall it we do not approve it in conscience. A mortal sin, however, is one sufficient by itself for death: namely, every sin committed against conscience through deliberate intention. Therefore, however slight a sin may be in itself, as Augustine says, when it is pleasing and deliberately committed, it is mortal. However grave it may be, when it displeases and is not done through deliberate intention, it is venial.

Among mortal sins, some are criminal and some are not. Criminal is that which makes a person conspicuous and infamous. Criminal is that which is most worthy of accusation; and sins are especially criminal when they occur in open habitual practice and corrupt the brethren. Hence those who are such—that is, notorious for some crime [Col. 1754B]—are cut off from communion with the Church unless they are willing to repent. Any such act—for example drunkenness, rapacity, and so forth—is criminal when it is readily practised and habitual. It therefore seems necessary to observe that Adam’s sin, though mortal, was nevertheless not criminal. Since he desired what was forbidden against conscience—for he knew that it was forbidden—it was mortal. But because he did not do this habitually, indeed acted as though unwillingly, thinking that he could make satisfaction through penance, and therefore wished to comply with his wife, it was not criminal. It is thus clear that some sin far more grievously than Adam sinned; but God chose to punish that first sin so severely in order to show that sin displeases him and to instil into all descendants [Col. 1754C] a horror of sinning.

## Chapter XXXIV. On merits: where they reside

Having considered virtues and vices, having also distinguished sins from vices and shown the diversity among sins themselves, it remains now to consider where merits reside. Therefore, just as every sin resides in the will alone, so does merit. Merit is nothing other than that which we merit by a good will—that is, eternal life. Since we merit good things by diverse wills, according to which one star differs from another there in glory, we therefore speak of diverse and multiple merits. The good will itself by which we merit is also called merit.

That merit resides in the will alone Augustine proves in many ways and by examples [Col. 1754D]: for instance, concerning the disciples of John, who fasted, and the disciples of the Lord, who ate, though wisdom was justified by both. Thus the Lord says: “John came fasting, and you said, ‘He has a demon.’ But the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you say that he is a glutton, a drinker of wine, and a friend of tax collectors. Yet wisdom has been justified by her children.” Likewise, concerning the widow who placed two small coins in the treasury, the Lord says that she offered more than the rich. Hence Jerome: “God does not weigh the amount, but the disposition.”

He also says concerning King Josiah that, when he went out to fight for God’s people against their enemies, he did not thereby merit more than previously [Col. 1755A], when he already possessed this in his will; rather, he did it in order to give other kings and princes an example of fighting for God’s people against enemies. Similarly, we say of the martyrs that their outward instruments of suffering did not make them better, but showed them to be such as loved Christ. So too we rightly maintain concerning Christ that, when he was led to his passion and fastened to the wood, he did not merit more than he had from his very conception. For his disposition was no better then than it had been from his very childhood, since from that time he loved God with his whole heart.

Thus every merit resides in the will, not in works, which are shared by good and evil alike [Col. 1755B]. For often some hypocrite fasts more and afflicts himself more severely than some saint. That merit resides in the will alone may also be inferred from the fact that God is called the searcher of hearts and reins, and is said to see in secret—that is, in the will. Hence the Apostle says: “He will judge the hidden things of human beings according to my Gospel” (Rom. 2:16), that is, according to my preaching. This is as if he said: He does not concern himself with works which are indifferent in themselves, but demands purity of intention. Isaiah attests the same when he says: “He shall not judge according to the sight of his eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of his ears” (Isa. 11:3).

For if someone is more pleasing to God because he builds a house for the poor—and does so because he is able—than one who has the same will but does not build because he is poor, it cannot be denied that the former is more pleasing to God precisely because he is rich [Col. 1755C]. Again, if Hermann has the same will as his master Peter, and each has set aside money to build a house for the poor, but one builds because his money remains, while the other does not because his money has been taken away, the one who builds ought not to have greater merit before God than the one who does not. Otherwise there is no reason why thieves should not diminish a person’s merit before God—how unreasonable this is, let us leave to everyone’s judgment.

We do not deny, however, that some temporal merit may sometimes follow outward acts: either that we may be more inflamed with love for God, or that by being seen to receive a reward we may offer others an example of doing good. Yet when we discuss merits, they seem almost not to exist, because grace seems so opposed to merits that, since all things are from grace, merits do not exist. Hence the Apostle: “If it is from merits, it is no longer from grace” (Rom. 11:6).

[Col. 1755D] For it seems that we can do no good of ourselves. Our condition is like that of a physician and a sick man. The physician has prepared a medicine and says to the sick man: “See, this medicine will restore your health if you rise and take it.” But since the sick man cannot rise, the medicine is of no use to him; and because he cannot rise by himself, he needs the physician’s help in rising, so that he may take the medicine and benefit from having taken it. Therefore, unless we say that a human being possesses from himself, even through free choice and by his own nature, the ability to love and cleave to God, we cannot avoid demonstrating that grace prejudices our merits [Col. 1756A]. Since I have carefully explained this in my Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans, on the passage “Jacob I loved,” etc. (Rom. 9:13), I judge it should be passed over here as known.

But if a creature made in the image and likeness of God were by its own nature more inclined toward evil than toward good, it would not be good in its nature. To will the good, however, is natural to every person. Hence the Apostle: “The willing is present with me” (Rom. 7:18).

## Chapter XXXV. On the remission of sins

Let us now consider the remission of sins. In the reconciliation of a sinner to God three things are necessary: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and satisfaction in works. Contrition or groaning of heart [Col. 1756B] occurs when the sinner grieves over his sins and is inwardly troubled: that is, when sin and iniquity displease him, not from fear of punishment but from love of justice. Otherwise it is not contrition of heart unto salvation, but consternation of mind unto damnation. For thus the wicked also will grieve in the future: not over the sin by which they offended God, but over sin insofar as they will be punished for it. Those who groan for sins in this fashion do not find their sins displeasing because of God, but because of punishment. Such contrition therefore has no merit before God.

But of the contrition arising from love of God and love of justice, it is said also through the prophet: “In whatever hour the sinner shall turn,” etc. (Ezek. 33:9). [Col. 1756C] Observe that he did not say “day,” “month,” or “year,” because with God nothing is slow or absent: as soon as someone truly repents, so soon is God himself present to forgive. Hence David says: “I said, I will confess against myself my injustice to the Lord” (Ps. 31:5); that is, I resolved in my heart that what I did by despising God should displease me because of God. It is therefore plain and manifest that, from the moment someone truly groans over sin, that sin is forgiven him by God. Nor is God’s forgiving sins anything other than remitting the eternal punishment due for them.

## Chapter XXXVI. On the confession of sins

It should also be known that confession is very useful [Col. 1756D]. It was instituted, indeed, for a greater display of humility. Hence: “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5:16). Since a human being, placed in his own power, departed from God, it was fitting that he should return, placed under another, with humility and devotion. Therefore God instituted the priest as his vicar and, as it were, physician, to whom [his] sins should be entrusted like wounds for healing, so that a person might receive from another, rather than from himself, the measure of satisfaction, for the sake of greater humility.

Yet it should be observed that, if a person does not confess when an urgent necessity is imminent, he will not for that reason be punished eternally. But if he has refrained through contempt or negligence, we maintain that he must be punished eternally for this. For he does not appear to have had true contrition of heart; and even if he did have it, nevertheless, because he despises an institution of the Church, he is proved worthy of eternal punishment. But if, as we have said, some obstacle prevents him from approaching a lesser priest [Col. 1757A], let him approach a greater one, of whom Ecclesiasticus says: “Behold the great priest,” etc. (Ecclus. 50:1). And the Apostle: “They became many priests,” etc. (Heb. 7:23). For one who lacks a visible priest does not lack the invisible one; indeed, one who wishes to confess and cannot is never denied by the invisible priest what the visible priest would administer.

It should certainly be observed that someone may also refrain from confession by dispensation and is not thereby liable to greater punishment. This is readily evident in Peter. For when Peter was in the primitive Church, where all were still weak [Col. 1757B], he kept silent about his denial by dispensation, because if others had known that this chief architect of the Church had fallen so grievously, they would have been greatly scandalized by it. The Lord himself showed that they were weak and prone to scandal when he said: “Let them go, that the Scripture may be fulfilled: ‘Of those whom the Father gave me, I have lost none’” (John 18:8–9). On this passage Augustine says: “They were not of such faith as could save them; and therefore, if they had died then, they would have been eternally damned.”

That Peter did not confess we have on authority; for Pope Leo says: “I have read of Peter’s tears; I do not find his confession. Therefore tears blot out sins which it is shameful to confess.” Ambrose likewise confirms this same point there in his work *On the Sacraments* [Col. 1757C]. Gregory too expresses this opinion on the matter: there is no clearer indication of the remission of sin than tears, because when someone breaks into tears from excessive grief over sin, it is certain that his sin has been forgiven.

Yet observe that, if this shame is referred to one’s own person, it is pride; but if it is referred to the Church, it is a salutary dispensation. Hence, if someone had sinned with a prince’s wife, or had done something such that, if the Church knew of it, it would suffer scandal; and if his conscience testified to him that, should he tell his parish priest—or even anyone else—the matter could not remain concealed, then, if he kept silent by this dispensation, he would not for that reason be punished eternally. But if he did it for his own person’s sake, so as not to become infamous and contemptible in the eyes of others, it would indeed be pride and very damnable [Col. 1757D].

## Chapter XXXVII. On satisfaction through works

Having considered contrition of heart and confession of mouth, let us consider satisfaction through works. This is especially useful because of the temporal punishment which remains. For, once eternal punishment has been remitted, temporal punishment will be left [Note: [Col. 1757D] Read perhaps: “remains” (*relinquitur*)], so that what the soul committed in unlawful delight or even carnal pleasure may worthily be cleansed by the bitterness of satisfaction. Hence [Col. 1758A] John says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3:8). We produce fruits worthy of repentance when what was wrongly committed in the present is expiated in such a way that nothing remains to be expiated in the future.

However small future punishment may be, it is nevertheless asserted to be more grievous than any punishment, however severe, in this life. How necessary satisfaction in this life is, therefore, I consider fully demonstrated by what has been said. That, after the punishment of Gehenna is remitted, temporal punishment remains is plainly apparent in baptism: although Gehenna, which was due to original sin, is forgiven there, dissolution of the body still remains, as does a countless multitude of defects. Hence Augustine says in *On the Origin of Sin*: “It passes away in guilt; it remains in act” [Col. 1758B]. This happens not only for the reason already stated, but also, as Augustine says, because this punishment becomes material for the exercise of virtue. For every virtue is perfected in weakness.

It remains also for this reason, as the same Augustine says: lest anyone should approach the sacrament of baptism in order to gain immortality in the present life, and not for God; and thus neither possess this present life worthily nor attain eternal life. It should also be known, concerning whether sins once forgiven later return—as seems doubtful to many—that some try to affirm this from that parabolic comparison: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all the debt.” On this passage Jerome says: “If we do not forgive from the heart what is committed against us, that which had been forgiven through repentance is exacted from us” [Col. 1758C]. Blessed Gregory says the same in a certain homily.

But what they say about the return of sin should be understood thus: the sinner becomes as he formerly was and is rendered more guilty because of ingratitude for the mercy shown him. This is what is meant in that parable: “Ought you not also to have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?”—as if he said: “You have proved ungrateful for the mercy bestowed upon you; therefore you shall not leave here until you pay the whole debt.” By “the whole debt” he means not what had already been forgiven, but rather the mercy which the servant ought to have shown to others because he had received mercy from the Lord. Hence elsewhere: “With the measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Luke 6:38). For this parable concerns mercy. Thus it is as though he said: “If you are unwilling to show mercy to others, as God showed mercy by forgiving sins, then your heavenly Father will exact this debt from you.”

Some commentators say that the statement that what was forgiven through repentance is exacted from us was spoken as a warning. That “the whole debt” must be understood as we have said is also plainly proved by the fact that he does not say “until the first,” but “until the last farthing” (Matt. 5:26); for a person is severely punished for having become harsh and obstinate toward his neighbour after sin was forgiven [Col. 1758D].

# Part Four of the Works of Peter Abelard: Poems and Miscellanies

[Col. 1759]

VIII, fol. 18r, by Thomas Wright and James Orchard Halliwell, in the book entitled: *Reliquiae antiquae, Scraps from Ancient Manuscripts, Illustrating Chiefly Early English Literature and the English Language*; London, 1841, 2 vols., octavo; vol. I, p. 15.)

[Col. 1759A] The teaching of Master Peter Abelard.

[Note: [Col. 1759]

Line 13, *fructuque non* (“and not by fruit” [context uncertain]), B. Line 24, *fugit* (“flees”), B. Line 39, *doctis* (“learned [men]”), C. Line 48, *ciat* (“causes/sets in motion” [uncertain]), C. Line 61, *discute* (“examine”), C. Line 64, *exequitur* (“carries out”), B.

[Col. 1761] Line 69, *is atque* (“he and”), C. Line 90, *quod* (“that”), C. Line 104, *qui differt* (“the person who delays”), C. Line 110, *ne se* (“lest he consider himself [good]”), C. Line 112, *data sint* (“may have been given”), B. Line 127: in C, *precem* (“prayer”) was written first and changed to *preces* (“prayers”). Line 143, *subveniat* (“may help”), B. Line 145, *parvo pretio* (“at a small price”), C.

[Col. 1763] Line 160: in both manuscripts *haec* (“this”) is explained in a gloss as *fortuna* (“fortune”), and in B *quos* (“whom”) is similarly explained as *amicos* (“friends”). Line 161, *ulli* (“to anyone”), C. Line 164, *set* (“but”), B; *et* (“and”), C. Line 174, *via* (“way”), C. Line 179, *quidquam* (“anything”), C. Line 180, *fortis in hoc* (“strong in this”), B. Line 181, *supponit* (“subjects/places under”), C. Line 196, *Corde* (“heart”), B. Line 201, *conjunx* (“spouse”), B. Line 202, *quislibet* (“anyone”), B. Astralabe, my son, sweetness of your father’s life,  
I leave you these few things, in devotion to your instruction.  
Let your concern for learning be greater than your concern for teaching:  
by the latter you benefit others; by the former, yourself.  
When there is nothing left for you to learn, cease learning;  
but do not say that you must cease before then.  
Learn long, and teach steadily and slowly;  
do not rush hastily into writing.  
Let your concern be not who speaks, but what is said:  
well-spoken words give their author a name.  
Do not swear allegiance to the words of a beloved master,  
nor let love for your teacher detain you.  
Everyone feeds upon fruit, not leaves, of trees;  
meaning must be preferred to words.

[Col. 1759B] Let persuasion capture minds by adorned words;  
plainness is more properly due to instruction.  
Where there is abundance of words, there is no abundance of meaning;  
and it is clear that it multiplies paths for one who wanders.  
When you see that someone’s teaching disagrees with itself,  
take it as certain that it contains nothing sure.  
The fool changes like the unstable moon;  
the wise person, like the sun, remains himself.  
Now here, now there, the blind mind of the fool wanders;  
the provident mind fixes a firm step everywhere.  
It looks far ahead to see what it can rightly say,  
lest it disgracefully become its own judge.

[Col. 1759C] I do not want your teaching to resemble that of a sudden-made master,  
who is still compelled to invent what he is to teach.  
Let no one grant you the title to one who has not yet attained a name;  
if you wish to test him, do so only after many years.

A wise son is his parents’ great blessing;  
a foolish one is their disgrace and sorrow.

[Col. 1760A] An ignorant king is an ass endowed with a diadem;  
he is destructive both to himself and to all.  
A ruler who persists in being ignorant of Scripture  
is often compelled to disclose his secret.  
The wise person considers the setting; the fool, the rising:  
for the end of a thing holds songs of praise.  
Attend to the sayings of teachers and the deeds of the good;  
let your breast always burn with this avarice.  
No one becomes wise through great sharpness of intellect;  
rather, character and a good life create this person.  
Wisdom declares itself by deeds, not words;  
so great a grace has been granted only to the good.  
He believes the minds of the wise inhuman  
who thinks that their hearts feel no pain.

[Col. 1760B] The mind of virtue is not so iron and hard  
that its inward parts know no compassion.  
Let concern for doing good come first, then concern for teaching it,  
lest you yourself be at variance with yourself.  
I beg you, read Holy Scripture frequently;  
if you read any other things, read them all for its sake.  
It is proper to the just to wish to render to everyone what is his;  
to the courageous, not to tremble amid their own adversities;  
to the temperate, to restrain illicit impulses of the mind,  
especially when prosperity attends them.  
Just as virtue is held to be a wall in adversity,  
so prosperity needs the tempering of this virtue.  
Nor does that former virtue remain unless supported by these,  
[60] [Col. 1760C] lest it be broken by evils or relaxed by good things.

Prudent man, learn what vice is and what virtue is:  
if you lose this, you cease to be what you are.  
The philosopher discerns the hidden causes of things;  
the practical man carries out the effects of deeds.  
Let honour in divine worship be your chief concern,  
[Col. 1761A] and let fear and love always subject you to God.  
No one will fear or love God as is fitting  
unless he knows him as is fitting—  
how just and powerful he is, how good he is,  
[70] how much he bears with us, how severely he strikes!

The better God is than all, the more he ought to be loved;  
and after him each person according to his rank of goodness.  
The better anyone is, the more love he deserves;  
and as he is dearer to God, so let him be dearer to you.  
For whom ought we to love except for God’s sake?  
Let this be the single end of everything you do:  
may not your glory but the Lord’s be sought through you;  
[Col. 1761B] live not for yourself but for all—indeed, for God.  
Above all, guard against harms to your reputation,  
that you may benefit many people and yourself.  
What has gone before compels new crimes to be believed;  
your earlier life will testify to the later.  
Strive to avoid human scandals as much as you can,  
provided you incur no scandal against God.  
Let your manner of life always shun infamous people,  
and rejoice in having a companion better than yourself.  
It is better to be the companion than the kinsman of the good:  
from the former virtue arises; from the latter, lineage stands out.  
Son, never presume to put God to the test;  
[90] strive as far as you can to deserve his help.

[Col. 1761C] The supreme goodness of God, rightly disposing all things,  
orders both good and evil things well.  
Hence the just person lacks no consolations in adversity,  
since he knows that even evils are good.  
Commands of earthly power must be examined;  
know that those of heavenly power must at once be performed.  
If anyone commands what is contrary to divine commands,  
let no agreement draw you against the Lord.  
Only by despising God does anyone sin;  
[100] nor does anything but contempt make one guilty.  
He is not a despiser who does not know what ought to be done,  
[Col. 1761D] provided that he is not ignorant of this through his own fault.  
Yet greater still than that madness is the folly  
which delays reconciling oneself to him.  
It is supreme madness to offend the all-powerful;  
what the person who presumes this fears, I do not know.  
Whoever seeks to be justified before the Lord  
must not know any justice of his own.  
Let him acknowledge, accuse, and correct his faults;  
[110] let him not judge himself good in heart and evil in speech.  
But let this be reckoned to him as justice:  
[Col. 1762A] that the good things he bestows are rendered back, not given.

Do not do to anyone what you do not wish done to yourself;  
what you wish done to yourself, do likewise to others.  
A true friend surpasses all God’s gifts;  
he is to be preferred to all riches.  
No one endowed with this treasure will be poor;  
the rarer it is, the more precious it is.  
There are many brothers, but a friend among them is rare:  
nature creates the former; grace provides the latter.  
Grace is freedom; nature is a kind of compulsion,  
while everyone clings in love to his own family.  
Even beasts are drawn by nature’s law,  
and no grace remains in their affection.

[Col. 1762B] If anyone asks or does something that harms honour,  
he crosses the bounds and law of friendship.  
To grant the request of a friend who asks what is dishonourable  
is to withdraw from the path of friendship.  
Yet the one who forces another to such things by asking  
offends more than the person who, overcome by entreaty, consents.  
No master compels you to love anyone more than yourself;  
nor does anyone who asks shameful things of you love you.  
Do not commit shameful deeds, but avoid them for a friend’s sake,  
if you wish to be truly precious to him.  
He shamefully excuses an offence who is not ashamed  
to say that it was committed by him for a friend’s sake.  
If I commit anything base for friendship’s sake,  
I make the beautiful ugly and the good evil by a base deed.  
Things given to a friend as what is owed are more than gifts,  
[140] yet there is nothing for which love does not deserve more.  
When you see people seeking profit for themselves in friendship,  
know that they feign what they wish to have called friendship.  
If you do not help a friend until he begs you,  
consider that what you think you give, you are rather selling.  
The shame of a petitioner is not to be valued cheaply,  
by which he buys under compulsion what you call gifts.  
Whoever is loved receives more than he gives in gifts:  
for what can be dearer than friendship?  
We deserve greater thanks for a greater gift;  
[150] everyone gives more by giving himself than by giving his possessions.

[Col. 1762D] Unless you are another self, you are not my true friend;  
unless you are to me as I am, you will not be another self.  
A good person despises loss for a friend’s sake;  
for in this way, if he has a friend, he has one by whom he may be betrayed.  
You are not a friend if you quickly believe accusations against him;  
thus the last to know the evils of his own household is properly each person.  
A rich man cannot know his own friends—  
whether they belong, that is, to fortune or to the man.

[Col. 1763A] The poor man is fortunate in this: he is free from that error;  
[160] when fortune perishes, those whom it gave you perish.  
Do not entrust yourself to one whom you have wronged:  
when the injury has passed, the injured person’s anger remains.  
Boasting is considered worse than the loss occasioned by an evil person,  
though that loss is usually more grievous to anyone injured.  
If you wish to be good among friends, be foremost yourself,  
and you will not remember your status toward such a person.  
You will restrain him, when raised up, with goads and a whip,  
lest he direct his heel against your face.  
You will be ashamed to serve not a man but a vice;  
[170] since the mind is free, think nothing shameful for yourself.  
One whom gifts can corrupt is not faithful;  
a betrayer of another will not be faithful to you.

[Col. 1763B] Every prostitute and betrayer prevails by compliance;  
this is the one means by which they please others.  
Nothing is better than a good woman; nothing worse than a bad one:  
the former surpasses all good things, the latter all evils.  
Whatever species of bird is accustomed to rapine,  
a woman is stronger in these things to the extent that she can do more.  
Nothing seizes human souls more than a woman;  
[180] in these things she is stronger than any enemy.  
She who freely submits herself to lust as its companion  
is counted a prostitute, as is she who does this for a price.  
Yet in this vice she seems more ardent  
who receives from it nothing beyond its filth.

[Col. 1763C] A husband ought to love his wife rationally,  
and not for intercourse, as if she were an adulteress.  
As impetuous appetite drags beasts wherever it wills,  
so lustful love drives men.  
If, after conception, the sated desire of beasts  
does not wish to endure the male, what does a woman do—what drives her?  
Does she think that she alone was created for lust?  
Will all other females bear the fruit of intercourse?  
A humble prostitute is more pleasing than a proud chaste woman,  
and the latter more often disturbs her household.  
The former pollutes the house; the latter more often sets it ablaze;  
[Col. 1763D] flame can harm a house more than filth.  
The anger of a serpent is gentler than that of a sharp-tongued wife;  
he who has her does not lack a serpent in his bosom.  
A sharp-tongued woman is far worse than a prostitute:  
the latter may please someone; the former can please no one.  
A sharp-tongued wife is the greatest conflagration of a household;  
every fire is lighter than this flame.  
Though the tongue is a small member, it is a mighty fire;  
[Col. 1764A] not so many have perished by the sword as by it.  
He prevails through speech who is not strong in arms;  
in this contest no one has greater power than a prostitute.  
The cowardly and the bold differ chiefly in this:  
the latter prevails by deeds, the former by threats.  
If warfare of the tongue were stronger than warfare of arms,  
[210] Thersites would be greater than Achilles at Troy.  
Always rejoice to have been timid in words;  
be bold in deeds, whenever occasion permits.  
Nothing offends a powerful person more than wicked speech;  
a free man fears insults more than losses.

[Col. 1764B] A gentle answer calms inflamed anger;  
a harsh one rather increases it and creates new anger.  
I do not wish you to tell a man of the offence of his beloved wife:  
for him, knowing it is more grievous than its occurrence.  
No one willingly lends his ear to his own reproaches;  
neither you nor anyone wishes to know such things.  
To every chaste man his own wife seems chaste,  
and he will always be suspicious of incest.  
Do not be so blinded by love for your daughters  
that you think they cannot be corrupted.  
Hasten to give them in marriage as soon as it is lawful;  
a woman quickly loses value through suspicion.  
Nor can a clever man be kept safe by a shining appearance,  
nor can a woman be precious to everyone.

[Col. 1764C] Those who give a girl in marriage should endeavour to adorn her;  
a wise husband quickly deprives her of adornment.  
You labour in vain to preserve an unchaste woman as chaste;  
you cannot preserve the former, and need not preserve the latter.  
You compel a woman to love the man for whom you blamed her,  
and often create a true charge from a false accusation.  
Do not doubt that she distrusts her own beauty,  
nor does she strive to deceive men by good deeds.  
The more fragile the female sex is held to be,  
the more its virtue excels in merits.  
The harsher she was toward the lover whom she later married,  
[240] the more pleasing she will be to her husband.  
Having scorned a man, she pleases him through her very refusal,  
[Col. 1764D] and by her harshness makes him gentle.  
I wonder whether any woman loves a stepson,  
except in the manner in which Phaedra is said to have loved hers.  
I wonder whether a wife loves a servant whom her husband loves;  
she always fears that he is lying in wait for her.  
The pleasure of lust is too pleasing to a woman  
if she loves a husband more than a brother.  
If any man’s wife is dearer to him than his mother,  
[250] it is clear that nature yields to lust.  
No grace can reconcile you  
to one whom nature does not compel to love his own parents.  
Let one who is bad toward his father be thought good toward no one;  
do not ask on behalf of one for whom his own parent does not ask.  
Do not torment your parents by bringing in a wife;  
bury them first, if you can survive them.  
A parent’s curse is God’s swift vengeance;  
no one but a madman can endure it.  
Let your rebuke be gentle, that it may benefit more;  
[260] harsh rebuke does not contain the perverse but rather provokes them.

[Col. 1766A] Rebuke the fault of a boy, and whip a youth;  
exhort an old man and admonish him with kindness.  
When an elder rebukes you, bear it patiently,  
and return thanks as for great benefits bestowed.  
Fearing blame, he tries to cut off fault,

[lacuna]

Whoever will not patiently obey one who commands  
is fit to be set over no command.

# Hymns and Sequences for the Whole Course of the Year, for the Use of the Virgins of the Monastery of the Paraclete

## Notice

[Col. 1765] It is entirely certain that the ninety-three poems which we are now about to publish were composed by Abelard, and that he did so about the year 1130, shortly before he brought out the book of *Sermons*. For in the letter which he prefixed to those *Sermons* in place of a preface, he wrote to Heloise that not long before he had sent her a little book of Hymns or Sequences which the nuns of the Paraclete might sing while celebrating the divine offices.

This writing did not escape Henry of Ghent—or whoever it was that appended an Appendix to Henry of Ghent’s *Ecclesiastical Writers* [Note: [Col. 1765] In Fabricius, *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*, part XI, p. 128.]—nor most others who subsequently published commentaries on literary history.

But it may be doubted whether any of them saw those poems of Abelard, or whether they knew them solely from the prologue to the *Sermons*. Ambaesius, however, saw them and discovered—as he himself testifies in the Preface to Abelard’s apologetic works—“a great radiance of Catholic piety shining forth in them, whether read or sung.” The fact that they remained in obscurity was rightly and deservedly wondered at by Victor Cousin, the most recent editor of Abelard’s works.

Thereafter, as happens, every trace of those Hymns and Sequences vanished, so completely that Dom Clement listed them among Abelard’s lost works [Note: [Col. 1765] *Histoire littéraire de France*, vol. XII, p. 135.]. Indeed, no Sequences have yet been discovered, but ninety-three Hymns together with the beginning of the next one have been found.

These were concealed in a quincuncial manuscript, composed for the most part in the thirteenth century and containing works of various kinds.

That this book is Belgian in origin is clear; but where precisely it was written is highly uncertain. A genealogical fragment added to the lower margins of folios 75v and 76v contains the names of villages situated between the Sambre and the Meuse; and at the upper margin of folio 17 there is a German or Flemish verse: “*Scone en ghi hebet mi ghevaen, ich . . .*” (“Beautiful one, and you have captured me, I . . .”). These words seem to belong to the Limburg dialect. Thus, if one said that this volume was once written and preserved in the diocese of Liège, one would run no risk of error; but otherwise, should one wish to determine the book’s homeland more precisely, one would do so at risk.

When Belgium was occupied by the troops of the French Republic, the manuscript was brought to Paris and kept there until the reign of Napoleon I endured. When he fell, the parchment leaves returned to Belgium, marked with the seal of the Republic and imperial emblems, and thereafter destined to bear the pressmark of the Burgundian Library at Brussels. The works inscribed in these parchment leaves are listed in the general catalogue of the Burgundian Library [Note: [Col. 1765] *Catalogue des manuscrits de la Bibliothèque royale de Bourgogne*, vol. I, pp. 203–204.] under nos. 10147–10158.

Now it happened by chance that Oehler, a German by birth, came upon the final booklet of this manuscript, containing the greater part of Abelard’s hymns. Without delay, he published the first eight songs [Col. 1767] and transcribed the rest in his own hand. He subsequently sold that copy for a fair price to Victor Cousin.

Meanwhile Émile Gachet, a Belgian who had pursued palaeographical study with no little success, described all the parts of that manuscript and was the first to share with scholars the beginning of Abelard’s letter prefixed to the hymns [Note: [Col. 1767] *Compte-rendu des séances de la Commission royale d’histoire*, vol. V (3 July 1841–6 August 1842), p. 164 ff.]. At the same time he announced that Victor Cousin had requested from the Belgian government the Brussels parchment leaves against which he might collate Oehler’s copy.

For, when Cousin was preparing a new edition of Abelard’s works, “he considered it his duty to reproduce as faithfully as possible a kind of image of the Brussels manuscript, since that work had not yet been published.”

This edition has now been published for several years and, if its preface is to be believed, was prepared with the greatest care from the Brussels manuscript: “We have altered only very few things,” says the distinguished editor, “where obvious faults of writing occurred, and have added variant readings at the foot of some pages.”

Nor have we laid down different rules for ourselves; but we shall take care to observe them in another manner. Accordingly, since the Brussels manuscript everywhere has *caelum*, *caelestis*, etc., we shall not alter these to *coelum*, *coelestis*. To be sure, several dictionaries teach that *coelum* ought to be written, as though the root of this word were the Greek κοῖλον, “hollow”; but I do not think their authority so great as to prevail over the most ancient monuments in stone and parchment—not only Latin, but Greek as well—in which, for example, to avoid itacism, Κελεστίνος is written for the Roman *Caelestinus*.

Similarly, I do not think it necessary to change the word *ceteri* (as it is always written in the manuscript) into *caeteri*; for what grammarians still dispute cannot be called an obvious scribal error. I would say the same of the word *seculum*, which M. V. Cousin thought should be changed to *saeculum*. Certainly the ancient Romans more commonly said *saeculum*, and the Greeks likewise wrote σαικουλον; nevertheless, there were those who argued for *seculum*, believing the word derived from *senescere*, “to grow old,” or from *secare*, “to cut”: a ridiculous derivation indeed. Yet the question here is not that derivation, but the spelling of *seculum*.

Moreover, throughout the Brussels manuscript one reads *sollemnitas*, *sollemnis*, which M. V. Cousin thought should be changed to *solemnitas*, *solemnis*. For my part, I would again not venture to assert that *sollemnitas*, *sollemnis* are obvious scribal errors. For, as is clear from the senatorial decree concerning the Bacchanalia and from other very ancient monuments, the ancient Romans did not customarily double consonants. Later another usage gradually prevailed, though no fixed rules were observed. Thus some doubled consonants in these words, others in those. There has been much dispute over the word *sollemnis*; nevertheless, analogy favors this form, and the most learned grammarians generally defend it.

Finally, to pass over many other matters, the conjunction *cum* cannot be classed among obvious scribal errors, although M. V. Cousin judged that *quum* should everywhere be written, contrary to the evidence of the manuscript. This again is an ancient controversy among grammarians. Certainly *quum* has the same origin as *quando*, *qui*, *quis*, etc.; but this is no conclusive argument, since we all write *sicubi*, *alicubi*, *alicunde*, etc. And so in ancient inscriptions *cum* is found no less than *quum*. Quintilian testifies that certain excessively subtle grammarians devised three forms—*qm*, *cum*, and *quum*—the first to signify time, the second accompaniment, the third cause. Yet Quintilian himself, like the Brussels manuscript, did not employ that distinction, writing *cum* everywhere. “Other refinements are still more frigid,” says the same grammarian, “such as that whatever had a fourth-letter C should be so written lest we seem to ask a question twice; and *quotidie*, not *cotidie*, so that it may mean ‘on how many days.’ But these things have now vanished among sheer absurdities.”

This also makes clear how long the grammatical controversy between *quotidie* and *cotidie* has endured. We mention it last because, whereas the Brussels manuscript everywhere reads *cottidie*, *cottidianus*, M. V. Cousin thought these should be changed to *quotidie*, *quotidianus*. Not quite rightly. Let *cottidianus*, if one wishes, be reckoned among sheer absurdities—we shall not object, although Quintilian applied that censure to the other form—but to class it among obvious scribal errors would be a harsher judgment. Nor should the double *t* be more severely condemned, since Catullus sang, following a sufficiently familiar metrical law:

> He burned with the daily fault of his wife.

But enough and more than enough of these grammatical trifles.

It is vexing to add that the learned editor has sometimes stumbled in matters of greater importance: occasionally omitting words, sometimes reversing the order of words, and even of verses, substituting one word for another, and so forth. We shall indicate these blemishes at the foot of the page whenever it seems worth the trouble.

We approve almost all his other changes. Since in the Brussels manuscript the diphthong *ae* is commonly written with tailed *e*, the diphthong has rightly been retained where the scribe omitted that tail. Moreover, the manuscript knows no diphthong *oe*, but everywhere has *fedus*, *pena*, *cepit*, etc.; M. V. Cousin chose everywhere to write *foedus*, *poena*, *coepit*, and so have we. Of another sort is the treatment of the letter *y*, which occurs in a few words, for example *hymnus* or *ymnus*, while elsewhere its place is occupied by the Latin element *i*. The learned editor preferred to write *mysteria*, *martyr*, etc.; we do not disapprove. Nevertheless, we preferred, with the manuscript, to say *misteria*, *martir*, etc., because here again an entire grammatical system lies concealed. Read what recent grammarians have written about certain Greek words granted the rights of Latin, for example στυλος, *stylus*, *stilus*.

In marks of aspiration the manuscript is most inconsistent. M. V. Cousin everywhere followed the usage now prevailing in France; we have done nearly the same, except that we have written *hymnus* in one place and *ymnus* in another, because the scribe himself seems deliberately to have gone both ways; and except that we have noted in the margin whatever we corrected in aspiration. Peculiar to the Brussels manuscript are *eicio* for *ejicio*, *prodigi* for *prodii*, and conversely *prodii* for *prodigi*; these are to be explained largely by the rules of Teutonic aspiration. These observations are offered to account for the labor of our predecessors in the same field and to prevent our new edition from being thought wholly useless.

As to the reasons for the work undertaken by Abelard, he himself explains them in the first part of his letter or preface. In the second he touches upon the same subject and declares the method he followed in these words:

> “In the preceding booklet we included the daily hymns for weekdays, sufficient for the whole week. You are to understand that they were so composed that their chant, like their rhythm, is divided in two: one melody, and likewise one rhythm, is common to all the nocturnal offices, and another to the daytime offices. Nor have we omitted the hymn of thanksgiving to be rendered after meals, in accordance with what is written in the Gospel: ‘Having sung a hymn, they went out.’ The other hymns set above these we arranged on this principle: those for the night contain the works proper to their respective weekdays; those for the day offer an allegorical or moral exposition of those works. Thus the obscurity of history is reserved for the night, but the light of exposition for the day.”

When he had written the second booklet of Hymns, he likewise explained its rationale in the appended letter—or, if one prefers, third preface:

> “What is lacking in the ornament of eloquence we have made up by the multitude of hymns, composing, namely, for the nocturns of each individual feast its own proper hymns; whereas until now only one hymn had been sung before the nocturns on feasts as on weekdays. We therefore appointed four hymns for each feast, so that in each of the three nocturns a proper hymn should be sung, and that the morning praises should also have their own. Of these four we further ordained that two be joined at the vigil as one hymn and the other two similarly recited at vespers on the feast-day itself; or that they be divided two and two at the individual vespers, so that one psalm be sung with the first two and another with the remaining two. Concerning the Cross, I remember that five hymns were composed: the first is to be set before each Hour, inviting the deacon to take the Cross from the altar and bring it into the middle of the choir, and there to set it up as though to be adored and greeted, so that in its presence too the whole solemnity may be performed throughout the several Hours.”

But why do we pause here over matters which will recur below in their order? Namely, that the principle of this new edition may be plainly evident. Since the Brussels manuscript nowhere has titles, and many inconveniences arise from this defect, these words especially shone before us continually like a most brilliant torch. In accordance with them, we have been able not only to add indications beneath the individual hymns, but also to illuminate certain obscurities and recognize an order sometimes thrown into confusion.

Yet we have not wished to alter the order, both that the Brussels manuscript may appear in its genuine form and because this kind of alteration—especially since another edition has already preceded ours—would produce little benefit for readers and generally much confusion: some finding this order in their books, others that one in theirs. Read the letters of Saints Cyprian, Jerome, and Augustine: how many different numbers are assigned to them in various editions?

From the time when those hymns began to emerge from obscurity, many conjectures have been made about them. It is not worth recording these, except one: namely, that the attached letter and the hymns themselves show that Abelard’s purpose was to alter the sacred liturgy. This opinion must be rejected. Those who embraced it appear to have believed that the same rules then prevailed as those which the Church now commands to be observed. Certainly, if anyone today laid hands on the Breviary and substituted unfamiliar hymns for the customary ones, he would not escape punishment. But in the twelfth century the same strictness did not exist, and much was entrusted to the authority and religious judgment of bishops, provosts, abbots, and other eminent persons—especially in matters concerning hymns and sequences, since some churches omitted them, others employed them, and those that employed them used very diverse ones. But I do not wish to expound at greater length matters set forth everywhere in books on liturgy.

In any event, everything in this collection of hymns is thoroughly Catholic. Although Abelard’s mind was less tranquil at the time when he wrote them, he has scarcely impressed upon them any trace of his contentiousness. Indeed, as some passages are quite poetic, so others are truly devout, especially in the second booklet.

Yet no one should suppose that a treasure of the highest value has at last been discovered. It is not so. The hymns of the Roman Breviary and of other ancient books generally far surpass Abelard’s in devotion, rhythm, choice of words, and thought; nor do Abelard’s attempts possess the merit of novelty, since for the most part he does nothing but bind into some kind of rhythm matters already long expounded by others in prose. We could readily indicate whence the writer drew all his material, but this edition would thereby grow without limit. Moreover, in recent times several antiquaries—above all the Rev. Fr. Charles Cahier, in his work *On the Painted Windows of Bourges*—have explained nearly all the symbols and mystical interpretations of Holy Scripture occurring in Abelard’s three books of hymns; and several Oxford theologians, in a collection of treatises suited to the present age, have most successfully made clear the origins and history of these matters. Thus scarcely anything has been left for gleaners. No longer preface seems necessary.

# FIRST BOOKLET: HYMNS FOR WEEKDAYS

[Col. 1771]

## PREFACE: ON THE REASONS FOR UNDERTAKING THE WORK

At the urgent request of your prayers, sister Heloise—once dear to me in the world, now dearest in Christ—I have composed hymns, called in Greek *hymnoi*, in Hebrew *tillim*.

[Note: [Col. 1771] Read *tehillim*.]

Since both you and the women of holy profession dwelling with you repeatedly urged me to write them, I asked what your intention in this matter was. For I thought it superfluous to compose new ones for you when you possessed an abundance of ancient hymns—

[Note: [Col. 1771] M. V. Cousin wrongly reads *habeatis*, “you possess.”]

—and almost sacrilegious to prefer or equate new songs of sinners with the ancient songs of saints. But while different answers were given me by different persons, you, among other remarks, added, as I remember, this argument:

“We know,” you said, “that the Latin Church, and especially the Gallican Church, follows custom rather than authority in hymns as in psalms. For we still do not know whose translation of the Psalter is used by our Church, that is, the Gallican Church.

[Note: [Col. 1771] At that time the Gallican Church followed the same Psalter as now: namely, the Old Latin version made from the Greek text of the Seventy Interpreters and corrected by St. Jerome. Abelard wished to replace it with the version made by St. Jerome according to the Hebrew text, which the holy doctor himself had not wished to substitute.]

If we wished to judge it from the statements of those who have disclosed to us the differences among translations, it would differ widely from all interpretations and, I think, would possess no dignity of authority. Yet the practice of so ancient a custom has now prevailed to such a degree that, although in other matters we retain the corrected texts of blessed Jerome, in the Psalter which we use most frequently we follow apocryphal writings.”

[Note: [Col. 1771] By the same right the translation of the Gospel is apocryphal.]

“The confusion of the hymns now in use is so great that no, or only rare, title-headings distinguish which hymns belong to whom. And if some seem to have definite authors—Hilary and Ambrose believed to have been the first among them, then Prudentius and very many others—there is often such inequality of syllables that they can scarcely receive a melody of song, without which a hymn cannot exist at all, its definition being ‘the praise of God with song.’

“You further added that proper hymns are lacking for very many feasts—for instance, those of the Innocents and the Evangelists, or of those holy women who were neither virgins nor martyrs. Finally, you maintained that there are some hymns in which those who sing them must sometimes speak falsely, whether because of the needs of time or because falsehood has been inserted. For by some circumstance or dispensation the faithful are often hindered in such a way that they either anticipate the appointed Hours or are anticipated by them, and thus are compelled to speak falsely at least regarding the time itself, when they sing nocturnal hymns by day or daytime hymns by night.

“For according to prophetic authority and ecclesiastical institution, the night itself is not to be without the praise of God, as it is written: ‘I remembered by night the name of the Lord,’”

[Note: [Col. 1771] “Thy name, O Lord.” Psalm 118:55.]

“and again: ‘At midnight I arose to confess to thee,’”

[Note: [Col. 1771] “At midnight I arose to give thanks unto thee.” Psalm 118:62.]

“that is, to praise you; nor are the remaining seven praises, of which the Prophet himself speaks—‘Seven times in the day I have praised thee’—

[Note: [Col. 1771] “I have praised thee.” Psalm 118:164.]

to be rendered except by day. The first of these, called the morning praises, concerning which it is written in the same Prophet, ‘In the mornings, O Lord, I will meditate upon thee,’”

[Note: [Col. 1771] “In the mornings, O Lord, I will meditate upon thee.” Psalm 62:7.]

“must be said immediately at the beginning of day, when dawn or the morning star begins to shine. This is also marked in many hymns. For when one says, ‘Rising by night, let us all keep watch,’”

[Note: [Col. 1771] “Rising by night, let us all keep watch.” Gregorian hymn in the Roman Breviary, Sunday at Matins.]

“and again, ‘By singing we break the night,’”

[Note: [Col. 1771] “By singing we break the night.” Ambrosian hymn in the Roman Breviary, Tuesday at Matins.]

“or, ‘We rise to give thanks and break the delays of night,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “And break the delays of night.” Ambrosian hymn in the Roman Breviary, Wednesday at Matins.]

“and elsewhere, ‘Black night covers all the colors of the earth,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “The colors of the whole earth.” Ambrosian hymn in the Roman Breviary, Thursday at Matins.]

“or, ‘For we rise from bed in the quiet time of night,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “In the quiet time of night.” Ambrosian hymn in the Roman Breviary, Friday at Matins.]

“and again, ‘That we may now break the hours of night by singing,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “Now break them by singing.” Ambrosian hymn in the Roman Breviary, Saturday at Matins.]

“and similar expressions, the hymns themselves bear witness that they are nocturnal. Thus the morning hymns too sometimes declare the rule concerning the time at which they should be said. For example: ‘Behold, now the shadow of night grows thin,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “Behold, now the shadow of night grows thin.” Gregorian hymn in the Roman Breviary, Sunday at Lauds.]

“and again, ‘Behold, the golden light rises,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “Behold, the golden light rises.” Hymn of Prudentius in the Roman Breviary, Thursday at Lauds.]

“or, ‘Now dawn scatters across the sky,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “Now dawn scatters across the sky.” Ambrosian hymn in the Roman Breviary, Saturday at Lauds.]

“or, ‘The dawn of light glows red,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “The dawn of light glows red.” Ambrosian hymn in the Roman Breviary in Eastertide at Lauds, but with this opening: “Dawn makes the heavens purple.”]

“and elsewhere, ‘The bird, herald of the day, proclaims the approaching light,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “Proclaims the approaching light.” Hymn of Prudentius in the Roman Breviary, Tuesday at Lauds.]

“or, ‘The rising morning star shines,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] The manuscript and M. V. Cousin read *Ortum*, “the rising.”]

“and any others of this sort. The hymns themselves teach us at what time they are to be sung, so that, if we do not observe their proper times, we are found false in their very utterance.

“Yet this observance is commonly set aside not so much through negligence as because of some necessity or dispensation—something which must happen daily, especially in parochial or smaller churches, because of the occupations of the people, where almost everything is performed, and nearly continuously, during the day. Nor does failure to observe the times alone entail falsehood. The composers of certain hymns too, whether reflecting the compunction of their own souls as that of others, or seeking through an imprudent zeal of devotion to exalt saints, have in some cases exceeded measure so far that we often utter things wholly alien to truth and contrary to our own conscience.

“For very few can worthily sing, weeping and groaning with the ardor of contemplation or the compunction of their sins: ‘We pour forth groaning prayers; forgive what we have sinned,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “We pour forth groaning prayers; forgive what we have sinned.” Ambrosian hymn in the Roman Breviary, Wednesday at Matins.—But if this reasoning were valid, one would have to abstain from the Psalms of David.]

“and again, ‘Graciously receive our tears with songs,’”

[Note: [Col. 1773] “Graciously receive [our tears].” Ambrosian hymn in the Roman Breviary, Saturday at Matins.]

“and similar words which suit the elect as they suit only a few. By what presumption, likewise, do we not fear every year to sing, ‘Martin, equal to the apostles’?”

[Note: [Col. 1773] This hymn has for many centuries been removed from most monastic breviaries, and still more from others. It seems fitting to recite it here from the Breviary of St. Maximinus of Trier, printed in 1600:

[Col. 1773]

> Christ the King, glory of Martin,  
> Here is thy praise; thou art his.  
> Grant that in honoring thee in this man  
> We may be joined to thee thyself.
>
> Thou who grantest throughout earth’s quarters  
> That the jewel of bishops shines forth,  
> Grant that those heavily burdened by sins  
> May be released through his great merit.
>
> Behold: poor and humble,  
> He enters heaven rich;  
> Heavenly choirs meet him,  
> Tongues, tribes, and nations rejoice.
>
> As his life shines, so is his passage  
> Splendid in heaven and on earth.  
> It is fitting that all rejoice;  
> May this day be salvation to all.

**DIVISION**

> Martin, equal to the apostles,  
> Foster us who keep thy feast;  
> Thou who wouldst live or die  
> For thy disciples, look upon us.
>
> Do now what thou didst of old:  
> Glorify bishops now,  
> Increase the splendor of the Church,  
> Put Satan’s deceits to flight.
>
> Four times thou didst conquer chaos:  
> Raise those sunk in guilt,  
> And, as thou didst divide thy cloak,  
> Clothe us in righteousness.
>
> That thou mayest remember  
> Thy spiritual glory of old,  
> Aid now the monastic order,  
> Which has almost fallen away.
>
> Glory be to the Trinity,  
> As Martin confessed it;  
> May he himself strengthen in us  
> By his works the faith which was his.
>
> **AMEN.**]

Or when, excessively glorifying individual confessors for miracles, we say: “At his sacred tomb the limbs of the sick are often restored to health,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1773] This is drawn from the ancient hymn *Iste confessor*. Since the time of Urban VIII it reads:

> Because of his outstanding merit,  
> Sick limbs which lay everywhere  
> Are often restored to health,  
> The powers of disease having been overcome.]

“Let your discernment judge.”

By these and similar persuasions of your reasoning, the holiness of your reverence compelled my mind to write hymns through the whole yearly cycle.

[Note: [Col. 1773] The manuscript reads *reverentiae sanctitatis*, “of your reverent holiness.” M. V. Cousin reads *reverentia sanctitatis*, “the reverence of holiness.”]

Therefore, as you, brides or handmaids of Christ, entreat me in this matter, so we in turn entreat you: lift by the hands of your prayers the burden which you have placed upon our shoulders, so that the one who sows and the one who reaps, laboring together, may rejoice together.

# NOCTURNAL HYMNS

[Col. 1775]

## I. SUNDAY AT MATINS: IN THE FIRST NOCTURN

[Col. 1775A]

> Creator of all things,  
> Ordainer of created things,  
> All creatures praise thee;  
> All things ordained glorify thee.
>
> Needing no instrument,  
> Nor expounding a theme,  
> By command alone thou accomplisheth all things:  
> Thou sayest, “Let them be,” and at once they are.
>
> Thou art the highest Author,  
> Almighty, without rival;  
> Therefore all that thou makest  
> Thou makest as excellently as is fitting.

[Col. 1775B]

> For whose judgment  
> Does not acknowledge as just that sovereignty  
> Which knowingly withholds an advantage  
> That neither burdens nor at length diminishes?

[Note: [Col. 1775D] The manuscript reads *minuitur*, “is diminished.”]

> Therefore the world is made most good  
> And perfect in all respects;  
> It is made by weight, measure, and number,  
> So that reason may not waver in anything.
>
> A work worthy of its maker,  
> Beautiful and indissoluble,  
> It is made according to a most perfect pattern,  
> Comprehending all things in the likeness of the highest good.
>
> It is ordered by no lesser goodness  
> Than that by which it is created:  
> Whatever wickedness does wrongly,  
> highest justice orders well.

[Note: [Col. 1775D] In almost this entire hymn anyone may see a certain philosophical optimism being urged. In the three books of hymns no other distinctive opinions of Abelard are to be found.]

[Col. 1775C]

> Let everlasting glory be to God,  
> From whom are all things that are.  
> Let all things proclaim him through whom they are;  
> In him, in whom they are, let them ever rejoice.
>
> **AMEN.**

## II. IN THE SECOND NOCTURN

> O God, who instructest thine own  
> By the pages of the Testaments,  
> From their understanding  
> Thou fashionest our songs with sweetness.
>
> May what we render from thy praises  
> Be acceptable to thee  
> And become useful to us,  
> If we understand what we sing.

[Col. 1775D]

> A threefold understanding  
> Provides diverse dishes.  
> The fruitful table of Sacred Scripture  
> Abounds in varied delights.

[Col. 1776A]

> Historical meanings nourish children;  
> Mystical meanings feed adults;  
> Moral reading is received  
> By the ardent zeal of the perfect.

[Note: [Col. 1775D] Thus the manuscript. M. V. Cousin reads *ferimenti*, “of leaven.”]

> By the first faith is built up;  
> From the second its fruit is gathered;  
> This fruit and consummation  
> Is instruction in morals—grant it to us.
>
> Thy grace, O God, has prepared  
> These dishes for us,  
> That by them our pilgrimage  
> May be sustained as by provisions for the way.
>
> Let everlasting glory be to God.

[Note: [Col. 1776D] In several places the Brussels manuscript has *etc.* signs, but they were commonly omitted, as they are even now in liturgical books. M. V. Cousin inserted them everywhere. We preferred to follow the manuscript.]

## III. IN THE THIRD NOCTURN

> At the origin of the sensible world,  
> The intelligible world,  
> Heaven and earth having been created together,  
> Now proceeds from the divine mind.

[Col. 1776B]

> Heaven was at once adorned  
> With spiritual citizens;  
> These, praising their Creator,  
> Are those morning stars.
>
> The earth, empty and void,  
> Lay covered by waters;  
> The face of the deep abyss  
> Was darkened by spreading shadows.
>
> Over the water brooded  
> The life-giving Spirit,

[Note: [Col. 1776D] Thus the manuscript. One should read *aquam*, “the water,” or *aquae*, “of water.”]

> So that even then the waters might conceive  
> That from which they now bear sacred offspring.
>
> The grace of light also beautified  
> The beginnings of the world.

[Col. 1776C]

> God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made;  
> Then it was divided from darkness.
>
> Let everlasting glory be to God.

## IV. MONDAY: AT MATINS

> In the coeternal Word the Most High Lord said:  
> “Let a firmament be placed between,  
> That it may divide the midst of the waters.”
>
> The effect follows the word;  
> An abyss lies between.  
> While the waters lie below,  
> The waters above are suspended.

[Col. 1776D]

> For what uses he reserves these waters,  
> The Lord knows.  
> But it is certain that these, and all other things,  
> Were created for us, not for himself.

[Col. 1777A]

> In all things provision is made  
> For our necessities;  
> For each benefit, from us to the Lord  
> Thanksgiving is owed.
>
> Let everlasting glory be to God.

## V. TUESDAY: AT MATINS

> The works of the third day  
> Summon us to praise:  
> The lower waters having been gathered together,  
> The Lord uncovered the earth.
>
> The uncovered earth puts forth shoots;

[Note: [Col. 1777D] Thus the manuscript.]

> It produces grass and trees.  
> Every kind of herb comes forth;  
> Every kind of tree is sent out.

[Col. 1777B]

> About to place upon earth  
> Man, the ruler of the earth,  
> God prepares by adorning  
> The place required by the use of our life.
>
> We are accused in all things  
> If we scorn our Maker;  
> He who made all things for us  
> Requires an account for all things.
>
> The world argues against us,  
> Made and adorned for our sake,  
> If grace does not subject us to God,  
> To whom he subjected all things.
>
> We please him by praises  
> Whom we anger by deeds.  
> The teaching of the Psalms shows us  
> How great is the sacrifice of praise.
>
> Let everlasting glory be to God.

## VI. WEDNESDAY: AT MATINS

[Col. 1777C]

> Plants adorned the earth;  
> Now the heavenly lights adorn the sky.  
> It is painted with sun, moon, and stars,  
> Whose great usefulness is known.
>
> They distinguish times by their light;  
> They are most certain signs.

[Note: [Col. 1777D] Thus the manuscript, not *insignia*, “distinctions,” as M. V. Cousin reads.]

> The natural science of the planets provides  
> Nearly every benefit of earthly things.
>
> Consider also, O man,  
> That these things above were created for thee,  
> And that the region of heaven confesses itself  
> To be in service to these.

> In winter, he who lacks the service of fire  
> Is warmed by the sun.

[Col. 1777D]

> In place of a night-lamp,  
> The poor man has moon and stars.
>
> The rich man lies on ivory couches;  
> The poor man lies on beds of leaves.  
> Here songs of birds delight him;  
> There the fragrance of flowers breathes forth.

[Note: [Col. 1778D] The manuscript wrongly has *flagrantia*, “burning.”]

> With excessive expenditure, rich man,  
> You build a house destined to fall;  
> With a false sun you paint your ceiling  
> To resemble the sky, with false stars.
>
> In the most beautiful chamber of the true sky  
> The poor man lies.

[Col. 1778A]

> With true sun and true stars  
> The Lord painted it for him.
>
> The work of nature is more excellent  
> Than the work of men:  
> It is prepared neither by labor nor expense,  
> Nor does age dissolve it and scatter it.
>
> A man serves the rich;  
> An angel, however, the poor;  
> Thus it may also be clear  
> How heavenly things are subjected to us by God.
>
> Let everlasting glory be to God.

## VII. THURSDAY: AT MATINS

> The upper regions  
> Of the world having been adorned with light,

[Col. 1778B]

> It remains to adorn the lower places,  
> From which light has now been created.

[Note: [Col. 1778D] Thus the manuscript. *Ex* appears superfluous.]

> The waters bring forth creeping things  
> And produce winged creatures;  
> At one command fishes and birds  
> Came forth in their kinds.
>
> Great whales together with small oysters came to be;  
> In one brief moment the greatest griffin
