> And the little sparrow were made complete.
>
> For he spoke, and they were made;  
> He commanded, and they were created.  
> He accomplishes great and small together,  
> To whom all things are equally easy.
>
> Let everlasting glory be to God.

## VIII. FRIDAY: AT MATINS

[Col. 1778C]

> Praise is due to the sixth day,  
> For which the others are owed,  
> On which man is formed last,  
> All things now having been prepared for him.
>
> On this day earthly living creatures  
> Are created;  
> Every creeping thing of earth comes from earth;  
> Every kind of beast is brought forth.
>
> Last of all is made  
> Man, who rules over all things;  
> All things looked toward this end,  
> As though to the one end of all things.

[Col. 1778D]

> The supreme Creator of all things—  
> In whom the summit of the works stands—  
> In this end fulfills  
> The plan of the divine counsel.
>
> This one noble creature,  
> In whom thou shinest forth, O Lord:  
> The honor of thine image  
> And glory of thy likeness.
>
> First man, then woman,  
> Made from the man’s rib,  
> After sleep is sent upon the man—  
> A great sacrament is thereby enacted.
>
> The other living creatures  
> Are given into their power.

[Col. 1779A]

> For their dwellings they possess  
> The most delightful temple of Paradise.

[Note: [Col. 1779D] The manuscript reads *tempore*, “time.”]

> Let everlasting glory be to God.

## IX. SATURDAY: AT MATINS

> When God had completed and inspected  
> All his works,

[Note: [Col. 1779D] We supplied *et*, “and,” which is lacking in the manuscript.]

> Being supremely good, he sees and approves  
> All that he had made as very good.
>
> All things are completed in the sixfold  
> Number of days,  
> So that the power of number may bear witness  
> To the perfect work of the days.

[Col. 1780A]

> He rested on the seventh day,  
> Not weary in any respect;  
> God himself is eternal rest,  
> In whom are all the joys of rest.
>
> Therefore he sanctifies the day  
> On which he had rested by ceasing;  
> In the mystery of the true Sabbath  
> He blesses the seventh day—

[Note: [Col. 1779D] The manuscript reads *die*, “day.”]

> That Sabbath, I mean,  
> Which knows no end,  
> In which true peace and highest tranquility  
> Keep the unceasing festival of feasts.
>
> Let everlasting glory be to God.

# DAYTIME HYMNS

## X. SUNDAY: AT LAUDS

[Col. 1779B]

> Truth has come; the shadow has passed away;  
> After night, the brightness of day has arisen.  
> At the rising of the heavenly light  
> The mysteries of the Law, full of darkness, shine red.
>
> Let Moses’ nocturnal proclamation yield place;  
> A daytime song befits the day.  
> With Christ all things emerge from hiding,  
> Nor does so great a light leave a place for darkness.
>
> Mystical figures lay aside their veil;  
> Truth is in the reality, no longer in the figure.  
> Clearly fulfilling the prophetic promises,  
> It allows nothing, even to the least point, to remain unfulfilled.
>
> When the mournful evening of death has passed,  
> Morning gives back the joy of life;  
> The Lord rises, angels appear,

[Col. 1779C]

> And the guards flee, terrified by the splendor.
>
> Very many saints who had already slept  
> By rising proclaim the glory of the Risen One.  
> In witness to the risen Lord,  
> The dead ascend and angels descend.
>
> To the everlasting Lord be everlasting glory,  
> From whom, through whom, and in whom are all things.  
> He from whom they are is the Father; he through whom they are, the Son;  
> He in whom they are, the Spirit of Father and Son.
>
> **AMEN.**

## XI. EVERY DAY: AT PRIME

> The morning star goes before the dawn; the sun follows.  
> The dawn is understood as the light of faith,  
> Which the true morning star bestowed by rising,

[Col. 1779D]

> When the Lord’s flesh flowered anew.
>
> This same morning star will shine like the sun  
> When he comes for the common judgment;  
> The light of his presence will be so great  
> That each conscience will speak its own deeds.
>
> The visible sun which we behold announces  
> Him whom we understand as the invisible Sun;  
> And the visible effect of works  
> Praises the invisible Author of all things.
>
> O man, do not be silent while all things praise,  
> Since you owe praises to the Lord for all things.

[Col. 1780B]

> You are urged by every benefit  
> To render continual thanks in praise.
>
> To the everlasting Lord be everlasting glory.

## XII. AT TERCE

> The path of the sun has now been raised on high,  
> And the warmth by which the world is nourished increases.  
> Light is poured in first, then warmth,  
> As love follows faith in us.
>
> The true Sun brought this light of faith  
> When the Word visited us in flesh;  
> At this hour the Spirit whom the Word sent  
> Brought the strongest heaven of love.
>
> Thus rightly the Spirit was seen in fire  
> Above the apostles, when he gave this gift;  
> For fire is love, animating minds  
> As fire hardens a clay vessel.

[Col. 1780C]

> To the everlasting Lord be everlasting glory.

## XIII. AT SEXT

> At full noon the sun’s light shines,  
> And full is the heat by which the world burns.  
> This is the perfection of blessedness,  
> When the vision of God itself kindles us.
>
> The greater one’s knowledge of him,  
> The greater will be love in each person;  
> To behold him will be nothing else  
> Than to enjoy true blessedness.
>
> Happy eyes, blessed lights,  
> To whom it has been granted to enjoy this glory.  
> We beseech thee, O Lord:  
> Grant us even the lowest places in that court.

[Col. 1780D]

> To the everlasting Lord be everlasting glory.

## XIV. HYMN OF THANKSGIVING AFTER MEALS

> O God, who createst bodies and souls  
> And restorest both with their proper foods,  
> May bodies as well as souls sing praise to thee,  
> Who grantest them being and life.
>
> Forgive, O Lord, our excesses,  
> If we have indulged the appetite more than was fitting;  
> Rather, most merciful one, because we have done so,  
> Forgive, we ask, this and all else.

[Col. 1781A]

> By this fault our first parents are exiled  
> And entangle their descendants in repeated miseries.  
> This is naturally implanted in us  
> And, as it were, hereditary in children.

[Note: [Col. 1781D] Thus the manuscript. M. V. Cousin changed it to *haereditarium*. This is unnecessary, since the ancient grammarians do not agree.]

> And if at meals more unrestrained talkativeness  
> Has added any fault,  
> It is thine also to forgive thine own,  
> For thou reservest for us time for pardon.
>
> It is thine to grant grace to suppliants,  
> By which each may restrain himself from these and like things.  
> It is thine to set a limit upon all things—

[Note: [Col. 1781D] The manuscript has *in omnibus*, “in all things”; but this is marked with an obelus or critical sign.]

> And to govern precipitous nature.
>
> Give us pilgrims necessary provisions;  
> Remove what is superfluous.  
> Let our small baggage not burden us,  
> Lest our homeland come late to meet fugitives.
>
> Who in exile seeks delights?

[Col. 1781B]

> Would that he might at last depart hence even naked!  
> And may rocks receive the shipwrecked man, naked,  
> Clinging to a plank on the stony shore.
>
> He who prepares himself with spiritual food  
> Does not seek what may make excrement.  
> He who fattens his soul with heavenly bread  
> Does not prepare fine flour for the roarings of his belly.
>
> O he whom the cup of the true vine intoxicates,

[Note: [Col. 1781D] M. V. Cousin omitted the *O!*]

> Does not stir his throat with the sweetness of wine.  
> These are the concerns of nations,  
> The delights of kings, not of Christ’s poor.
>
> These think earthly, not heavenly things;  
> They make exile their homeland;  
> Here they make their lot with beasts  
> And miserably choose such companions.
>
> They seek the easy descent to hell  
> And shun the steep path of heaven.

[Col. 1781C]

> Creeping wholly with belly and breast,  
> They are now unable at all to raise themselves.  
> As nature made beasts prone in body,  
> So gluttony has made these prone in soul.
>
> Constant attendants at the temples of Bacchus or Ceres,
In ceremonial observances they are prodigal of the belly.  
[Note: Col. 1781D: The manuscript has *prodii*.]

But you, Lord, lead us back through abstinence,  
whom gluttony has made exiles;  
and abandon none of your own in need—  
you who clothe the lily and feed the sparrow.

Let no one be oppressed by the necessity of want,  
but let there be the frugality of sufficiency.  
Let there be what can suffice for nature,  
not what supplies fuel to indulgence.

To the everlasting Lord be [glory].

XV. At None.

[Col. 1781D]

The seven [hours] which we perform with daytime praises,  
with eight added at night we complete;  
of these assign four to evening  
[Note: Col. 1781D: We have retained *vespere* (“in the evening”), since immediately afterward Abelard also uses *mane* (“in the morning”) as though it were a dative: Col. 1782D, likewise in the fourth stanza.]  
and four to morning, and so complete the day.  
[Note: Col. 1782D: Abelard’s four evening hours are None, Vespers, Compline, and Matins; his four morning hours are Lauds, Prime, Terce, and Sext.]

[Col. 1782A] We know that evening begins from None,  
when the sun has begun to sink beneath the earth;  
conversely, one may rightly assign morning  
to the time after midnight when the sun has risen.

Our substance is made up of eight,  
which the glory of the eighth finally perfects;  
we know that the body consists of four [elements],  
and that minds are adorned by as many virtues.

Therefore we have ordained that thanks be rendered  
to the Lord for us in eight offices:  
in evening offering the body’s weariness,  
in morning assigning the vigor of the soul.

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XVI. SUNDAY. At Vespers.

In the Psalms we read, under the title “For the Eighth,”  
[Col. 1782B] of the glory of the life to come, as they sing,  
when the everlasting light of the faithful  
shall follow the sevenfold course of this present age.

We know that this has already been fulfilled in its head,  
when the Lord rose again in this light,  
so that he may thus grant to his own members  
the most certain hope of that same blessedness.

Therefore this day is deservedly honored by Christ’s worshippers  
above all others in this mystery.  
For they long for eternal, not temporal,  
goods, whose fountain is the Lord.  
[Note: Col. 1782D: The manuscript has *iniant*.]

And lest, for those who follow so steep a path,  
their spirit grow lukewarm through distrust,  
on this very day the Lord sent  
the Paraclete Spirit into the air to the disciples.  
[Note: Col. 1782D: Cousin’s edition reads *Dominus die* (“the Lord on the day”).]

Add to the glory of this day that by which  
you may rightly perceive the Lord’s Day:  
[Note: Col. 1782D: The manuscript reads *additae . . . diei dominicam*.]  
[Col. 1782C] that bodily, in this light, the Lord  
was received as king and royal heir.

Entering at once into his own palace,  
he displays the power of a mighty king:  
casting out the wicked, he enlightens the blind,  
and thus reconciles the house of the Lord.  
[Note: Col. 1782D: The manuscript has corrupt readings: *exibet . . . eitiens . . . eitiens*.]

Jesus enacts the mystery of the eighth,  
on which he sits as judge of all,  
enlightening his own by his presence,  
casting the wicked out from the glory of the kingdom.

Nor do we believe it devoid of mystery  
that this day alone is granted to the gentiles;  
let them too consecrate it by name,  
since the Sun of Justice claims it for himself.  
[Note: Col. 1782D: The manuscript has *Ipsi quoque* (“they too”).]

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XVII. DAILY. At Compline.

[Col. 1782D]

We know, Lord, that everywhere and always  
we ought to devote ourselves to your praises—  
you who fashion for us places and times,  
night for rest, day for work.

[Col. 1783A] And since our frailty cannot bear this,  
[Note: Col. 1783D: Cousin’s edition reads “And since our frailty cannot bear this.”]  
you established hours and fixed churches,  
so that places themselves may remind us of these things,  
and times may invite us or rebuke us when sluggish.

Now that the seventh hour of the day is completed,  
we ask for rest—the week of praises.  
[Note: Col. 1783D: Thus the manuscript. Cousin’s edition has *Hebdomada*. The sense is: “Now that the seventh hour of the day is complete, we ask for rest, namely the week of praises, or heaven.”]

Lord, bless our Sabbath,  
and may rest renew those whom your service restores.

May your right hand sanctify this house  
and bind the most savage lion;  
thus refresh the body with peaceful sleep,  
that the ever-sober mind may remain watchful in you.

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XVIII. MONDAY. At Lauds.

[Note: Col. 1783D: The subject of this first hymn belongs to Sunday; but since Abelard had already written above a hymn on Sunday for Lauds, he treated at Lauds on Monday the theme of the first age of the world and humanity, and at Vespers of the same weekday the second age. While Abelard was staying at Saint-Denis, he had encountered the works of the Venerable Bede; perhaps from these—namely chapters XVI and following of *On Times*—he drew this material.]

[Col. 1783B]

The divine number of works prefigures  
the ages of time and of our own body;  
we know in this the sixfold number of days,  
and there are six ages of the world or humankind.

In Noah occurs the end of the first age,  
which we rightly compare to infancy;  
by a certain similarity, the first light  
contains separately the mysteries of these things.

Then the unformed matter had been made,  
[Note: Col. 1784D: Cousin’s edition printed *Tunc*, “then.”]  
which was thereafter to be formed into shapes;  
and the rough age did not know the law,  
nor did earthly life consider what was right.  
[Note: Col. 1784D: The manuscript has *eterrena*.]

The former age was destroyed by the flood;  
so forgetfulness destroys infancy.  
On the first day light is said to have been created,  
and infancy begins this light.  
[Note: Col. 1784D: The manuscript has *infantiam*.]

[Col. 1783C] There is also a certain lesser light of faith,  
which we first received as little children.  
This too appearance itself will dissolve,  
when what we now believe begins to be seen.

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XIX. At Vespers.

The second age ends in Abraham,  
as though childhood had now been reached.  
The flood did not wash away this age,  
since everyone remembers childhood.

On this day the firmament was created,  
to divide the waters by being placed between them;  
[Note: Col. 1784D: The manuscript has *aqua*.]  
from waters pouring down and flooding,  
[Col. 1783D] the ark provided for the faithful.

This age did not beget the people of God,  
since instruction in the law had not yet been given;  
nor are the powers of begetting available to a child,  
even though memory now grows firm in the mind.

After the light of faith, hope strengthens us  
and now encourages the believer toward difficult things,  
[Col. 1784A] so that in hope of heavenly things and true glory  
he may now endure every misery of this life.

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XX. TUESDAY. At Lauds.

The third age is brought down to David.  
Adolescence resembles it.  
The wise interpreter rightly compares  
both ages to the third day.

This light removes the waters from the dry land,  
and the law given restrains the shifting world,  
lest, as lusts press us downward,  
the mind plunge into desires.

This age begot a people through the law,  
and made Abraham the father of many;  
[Col. 1784B] and as though this were the earth’s first offspring,  
today trees are born together with herbs.

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XXI. At Vespers.

After faith and hope, fear is instilled,  
by which the hireling or slave is driven,  
while hoped-for benefits trouble the former,  
or appointed scourges urge the latter on.

This fear possessed the ancient people,  
subject to the promises and threats of the law:  
while the law promised goods to those who desired them,  
it afflicted the guilty with most grievous punishments.

We know that plants live from the earth,  
which we read were created today;  
and Israel led an earthly life,  
[Col. 1784C] whose promise was earthly.

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XXII. WEDNESDAY. At Lauds.

The fourth light adorns heaven with stars,  
whose abiding strength is fiery;  
love, which claims the heavenly seats for itself,  
is thus ardent and never declines.

The Gospel, whose law is fourfold,  
corresponds to the number of four days;  
the squared body has great firmness,  
and unconquered love sustains all things.

Love is the fulfillment of virtues;  
maturity is the perfection of powers.  
As this fills a human body with strength,  
[Col. 1784D] so love perfects the mind in character.

XXIII. At Vespers.

Theologians place the beginning  
of the world’s fourth age in David’s kingdom;  
let its evening be the Babylonian captivity  
of Israel.

[Col. 1785A] In David the love of the perfect is known,  
which embraces savage [lacuna] and enemies.  
[Note: Col. 1785D: A word has fallen out here.]  
He spared Saul, whom he mourned when dead,  
promptly punishing by death the lying messenger.

Love restrains the hostile robber,  
and with it there will be no captivity of the soul;  
where it is lacking, salvation is lost,  
and the city of our breast is handed over to the enemy.

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XXIV. THURSDAY. At Lauds.

Many hand down that the world’s fifth age  
extends to the times of Christ:  
in the world’s old age, the New Man was sent to the old  
in order to renew him.

[Col. 1785B] Old age suffers failing strength,  
and this is rightly called the world’s old age,  
in which the power of the Most High came  
to aid the failure of every good thing.

The religion of the fathers had already passed away,  
the prophets were lacking, anointing had failed,  
when divine grace anointed him  
who would restore all things spiritually.  
[Note: Col. 1785D: The manuscript has *injuxerit*; Cousin’s edition, *injunxerit*.]

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XXV. At Vespers.

The truth of Scripture teaches  
that living souls were brought forth today from the waters,  
because, when baptismal washing is absent,  
instruction in morals is not enough.

[Col. 1785C] Here mother Grace buries the old man;  
here the pious people receives the new man.  
He who first administered this sacrament,  
the Baptist, preceded the coming of the Lord.

He is sent in the time of the fifth age  
to disclose the mystery of the fifth weekday.  
He who gives new washings at the end of the old things  
is as though bringing forth living creatures from them.

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XXVI. FRIDAY. At Lauds.

The sixth age alike of humanity and of time  
is the boundary or end of all ages;  
Christ, who suffered in the world’s sixth age,  
is the end that perfects good things.

[Col. 1785D] His passion, our redemption,  
is the consummation of all good things;  
[Note: Col. 1785D: Cousin considers *est* to be deleted; nevertheless the final syllable of *omnium* is elided twice elsewhere also.]  
the other things are aids to salvation—  
this sacrificial offering is salvation’s completion.

On this day the created human being lost himself;  
on the same day the Creator restored him,  
who, undergoing the suspension of the cross for his sake,  
gave himself as the price to redeem the slave.

[Col. 1786A] At Vespers.  
[Note: Col. 1785D: The manuscript makes no division; yet a new hymn certainly begins here. We did not, however, alter the numbers, as we said in the preliminary notice.]

From the side of the sleeping man comes woman:  
in this mystery Christ’s bride is his Church.  
[Note: Col. 1786D: The manuscript has *Christus*. The sense is: “In which mystery Christ’s bride is his Church.”]  
Christ’s death is sleep; from his side  
flow water and blood that cleanse us.

We call an expressed likeness  
the image of any thing;  
but a gift which represents any thing  
does not reject the name “likeness.”

We know that the man presides over the woman,  
whom the Lord took from his body.  
Therefore we call man the image of God  
and woman his likeness.

For the greater is the man’s eminence  
and the more his rank surpasses in power,  
the more is man like God,  
since reason too sets him before all else.

[Col. 1786B] To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XXVII. SATURDAY. At Lauds.

The prize of blessedness brings the end  
and rest of all labors.  
[Note: Col. 1786D: Thus the manuscript, and rightly. Cousin printed *brachium*, “arm.”]

This is attained through the preceding things,  
which signify the works of the six days:  
faith, hope, fear, love,  
the grace of baptism, and Christ’s passion.  
After the blessed steps of this sixfold course,  
the entrance of blessedness follows.

Lead us, Lord, through each step,  
that the members may attain you, their head,  
[Note: Col. 1786D: The manuscript has *apprehendere*.]  
[Col. 1786C] in the everlasting glory of the true Sabbath,  
whose joys overflow every heart.

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

XXVIII. At Vespers.

O how great, how splendid are those Sabbaths  
which the heavenly court celebrates forever!  
What rest for the weary, what reward for the strong,  
when God shall be all in all!

Truly Jerusalem is the city there  
whose unbroken peace is highest delight,  
where desire does not precede the thing,  
nor is the reward less than the desire.

What a king! What a court! What a palace!  
[Col. 1786D] What peace! What rest! What an assembly is that!  
Let those who share that glory expound it,  
if they can express as much as they feel.  
[Note: Col. 1786D: The construction *exponant si possint* is Greek, but was also used by ancient Romans.]

Meanwhile it is ours to lift up the mind  
and seek our homeland with every longing,  
and at last return to Jerusalem from Babylon  
after long exiles.

There, once all troubles have ended,  
we shall securely sing the songs of Zion;  
[Col. 1787A] and the blessed people will render you, Lord,  
unending thanks for the gifts of grace.  
[Note: Col. 1787A: The manuscript has *Domine*; Cousin printed *[Domine?]*, as though he had added it himself.]

There Sabbath will succeed Sabbath—  
the perpetual joy of those who keep Sabbath;  
[Col. 1788A] nor will the ineffable jubilees cease,  
which we and the angels shall sing.

To the everlasting Lord [be glory].

## SECOND BOOK

[Col. 1787]

### PREFACE: ON THE PLAN OF THE PRECEDING BOOK

The office of divine worship is threefold. The Doctor of the Gentiles set it in order in the Epistle to the Ephesians, saying: “And do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery; but be filled with the Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.”  
[Note: Col. 1787A: Ephesians 5:18–19.] And again he says to the Colossians: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you abundantly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing in grace in your hearts to the Lord.”  
[Note: Col. 1787A: Colossians 3:16.]

Psalms and songs, however, because they have long been provided from the canonical Scriptures, need neither our effort nor anyone else’s in order to be composed now.

But concerning hymns, since nothing is distinguished in the Scriptures cited above, although certain psalms also bear in their titles the name of hymns or sacred songs, many were afterward written everywhere; and particular hymns were composed for various times, hours, or feasts. These we now properly call hymns, although in ancient usage some called hymns and psalms alike any songs of divine praise composed in rhythm or meter.

Hence Eusebius of Caesarea, in chapter XVII of the second book of his *Ecclesiastical History*, recounting the praises of the most eloquent Jew Philo concerning the Alexandrian church under Mark, added among other things:  
[Note: Col. 1787A: Cousin’s edition omitted *secundi*, “second.”]  
[Note: Col. 1787A: Thus the manuscript, and rightly. Cousin printed XIX.]

“After a little while, again, concerning the fact that they make new psalms, he wrote thus: ‘Therefore they not only understand the subtle hymns of the ancients, but they themselves make new ones to God, setting them to music in every meter and melody with a composition sufficiently noble and sweet.’”  
[Note: Col. 1788A: Here Cousin appended the following note: “The words of Eusebius are lacking in the manuscript.” Nothing is lacking. The words from “After . . . wrote” are Eusebius’s; “Therefore . . . setting them to music” are Philo’s. Abelard cited everything accurately from Rufinus’s translation.]

Perhaps it is not inappropriate for all psalms composed in Hebrew in meter or rhythm, and fashioned with melodic sweetness, also to be called hymns, according to the very definition of hymns which we gave in the first preface. But since psalms translated from Hebrew into another language are now freed from the law of rhythm or meter, the Apostle, writing to the Ephesians, who are Greeks, properly distinguished hymns separately from psalms, just as he did songs.

Concerning these, therefore, dearest daughters of Christ, since you have often pressed my modest talent with many prayers, adding besides the reasons why this seemed necessary to you, we have now complied in part with your request, as the Lord has granted. In the preceding little book we included the daily hymns for weekdays, sufficient for the whole week. You should understand that they are so composed that their chant, like their rhythm, is divided in two: one melody common to all nocturns and another to the daytime offices, just as there are two rhythms. Nor did we omit the hymn of thanksgiving to be rendered after meals, according to what is written in the Gospel: “When a hymn had been sung, they went out.”  
[Note: Col. 1788A: The manuscript has *sic*, with the abbreviation mark omitted.]  
[Note: Col. 1788A: Matthew 26:30; Mark 14:26.]

We arranged the remaining hymns set above with this plan: the nocturnal hymns contain the works of their respective weekdays, whereas the daytime hymns present an allegorical or moral interpretation of those works. Thus the obscurity of history is reserved for night, and the light of interpretation for day. It remains, moreover, that I be assisted by your prayers, so that I may send you the little gift you desire.

## HYMNS FOR DIVINE SOLEMNITIES

[Col. 1789]

[Col. 1789A] ### AT THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD

#### XXIX. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

The Virgin, conceiving the Word by the Word,  
from you the true East has arisen,  
from whom true brightness, poured abroad,  
has driven away the encompassing shadows.

Happy day, glory of days,  
which saw the joys of this birth!  
Happy mother, who bore God!  
Happy star, who bore the sun!

O truly blessed poor woman in childbirth,  
whose giving birth enriched all things—  
poor, I say, yet lofty in lineage,  
of the blood of priests and kings.

She bore the Way of Life upon the way;  
[Col. 1789B] she had lodging, not a home.  
The offspring of kings and lady of heaven  
entered a stable instead of chambers.

Midwives were absent at the birth,  
but angels were present in their place,  
whose choir at once brought forth  
the no small joys of this birth.

Baths perhaps were lacking,  
but there was no stain for them to wash.  
There was no pain for them to relieve,  
nor tearing for them to repair.

“Glory to God in the highest,  
and bonds of peace on earth”:  
such are the angelic voices  
known to have sung today concerning these things.

Amen.

#### XXX. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

[Col. 1789C]

The only Son of God the Father and his mother,  
laid in a manger instead of a cradle,  
endures the narrowness of a manger—  
he whom the expanse of heaven cannot contain.

He is received in a lowly hut  
who presides over heaven’s palace.  
Who would not be astonished at this?  
Whose mind would this not move?  
[Note: Col. 1789D: Thus the manuscript, and rightly. Cousin’s edition has *commoneat*.]

God is poor—indeed, poorest of all—  
thus made for the sake of us all.  
What thanks, what recompense  
do we owe the Lord for these things?

He cries in a manger like a little child,  
who shakes heaven with thunder;  
[Note: Col. 1789D: The manuscript has *tonitruis*, also a good Latin form. But *tonitrubus* is preferable, for the rhyme.]  
[Col. 1789D] his bed is the remnants of hay,  
though he bestows purple upon kings.

He is placed as food for beasts,  
he who is himself the refreshment of angels.  
[Col. 1790A] Here a herd of animals stands near;  
there angels offer service.

Glory to God in the highest.

#### XXXI. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

How blessed is this bed of straw  
which pressed the side of so great a Virgin,  
where the newborn little one is received,  
whose palm encloses heaven!  
[Note: Col. 1789D: Thus the manuscript. Cousin printed *palma*. We preferred to follow the manuscript, since Vitruvius wrote: “This [giving of gifts] is always performed by the palm of the hand.”]

Other queens are accustomed to give birth  
on silks and in utmost pain.  
The happy little bed of lowly straw  
was free from every pain.

For royal children to be nourished,  
nurses’ breasts are made ready.  
[Col. 1790B] He is fed with virginal milk,  
which a virgin poured forth from her closed womb.

To no king among so many banquets,  
among such great and many delights,  
has it been granted that any one  
of his little children be fed with virgin’s milk.

The poor Virgin perhaps goes hungry,  
she who nourishes this little one with milk.  
The heavens marvel, the angels wonder,  
diligent in their service to the nursing mother.

Glory to God in the highest.

#### XXXII. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS

Rejoice, Virgin, glory of virgins,  
honor and mother of mothers, exult—  
you who deserved to bestow  
the common joy of all the saints.

The Lord promised you as daughter  
to holy patriarchs and kings;  
the riddles of the law prefigure you,  
the oracles of prophets sing of you.  
[Note: Col. 1790D: The manuscript has *fugantur*.]

The prayers of the faithful seek you;  
the hearts of all sigh toward you.  
You are our sole hope after God,  
appointed as our advocate.

Those fleeing a judge’s anger  
take refuge with the judge’s mother.  
She is compelled to plead for them,  
she who is made mother for the accused.  
[Note: Col. 1790D: Thus the manuscript. Delete *quae*, “who,” at the beginning of the line.]

O merciful [lacuna]ness! The Son  
[Col. 1790D] begets for this purpose, and is begotten for this purpose,  
that servants may be saved through grace!  
[Note: Col. 1790D: We have supplied *gratiam* (“grace”) conjecturally.]

How great [is the joy] which this day displays!

Glory to God in the highest.

[Col. 1791A] ### AT THE EPIPHANY OF THE LORD

#### XXXIII. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

The King of heaven and earth,  
whether soon to be born or already born,  
both realms proclaimed  
by wondrous signs worthy of him.

For, Augustus, while you flourished,  
a halo encircled the sun;  
oil flowed from the shop  
which had been commanded to flow.  
[Note: Col. 1791D: Thus the manuscript, and rightly. Cousin printed *mundavit*.]

At the Redeemer’s coming,  
freedom is granted to slaves;  
you remove the yoke of slavery  
and prefigure one whom you do not know.  
[Note: Col. 1791D: The manuscript has *tollit*, “removes.”]

You forbid and do not permit  
yourself to be called Lord,  
[Col. 1791B] so that this honor may be reserved  
for Christ who is to come.

The gates of Janus remain shut;  
peace, sent beforehand by Christ,  
which was once promised  
to the world by the prophet’s voice.

Peace on earth; in the highest  
let there be glory, supreme glory,  
to the highest King—the Father, the Word,  
and the Spirit—for ever.

Amen.

#### XXXIV. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

The shepherds, warned by the angels’ song,  
stand amazed;  
a new star leads the Magi;  
[Col. 1791C] Herod languishes in fear.

He gives the Magi foolish commands,  
speaking deceitfully to them;  
but deceit was deceived,  
the deceiver defrauded.

They hold to their begun way,  
find him whom they seek,  
and by three gifts offered  
describe who he is.

They are warned in sleep  
not to return to Herod,  
and by divine instruction  
are taught what they should do.

Peace on earth.

#### XXXV. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

[Col. 1791D]

He enters the waters to sanctify them,  
baptized by a servant—  
he who takes away our sins,  
he who has no need of baptism.

He who truly baptizes with his own baptism  
is baptized;  
at once the heavens are opened,  
which sin had shut.

The Spirit’s descent in a dove  
was revealed;  
[Col. 1792A] grace was shown  
to those being baptized and reborn.

The Father’s voice was heard,  
attesting the Son;  
and that gift makes the reborn  
true children.

What a gentle, mild voice,  
which shows God appeased,  
nor does any equal voice represent  
the pattern of divine grace.  
[Note: Col. 1791D: The manuscript has *quis*. The passage appears corrupt in Cousin’s edition. The sense seems to be: “No equal or similar voice presents to anyone the pattern of divine grace,” that is, so manifests divine grace.]

Peace on earth.

#### XXXVI. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS

He who sanctified the waters  
for us by his baptism  
turned them into pure wine  
[Col. 1792B] and refreshed the guests.

Hence this glorious day  
shines with a threefold deed,  
because through so many signs  
the salvation of the world appears.  
[Note: Col. 1792D: Thus the manuscript and Cousin’s edition.]  
[Note: Col. 1792D: The manuscript has *tanta*, “so great.”]

Yet after signs so great or greater  
the Jew does not believe—  
he whom the Chaldean at once sought  
because of a single star.

All the elements recognize  
their own creator.  
Do neither signs nor the law itself  
move you, wretch, to faith?

If you judge that neither signs  
nor prophets are to be believed,  
at least, an exile under long punishment,  
learn your guilt.

[Col. 1792C] Peace on earth.

### AT THE PURIFICATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

#### XXXVII. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

Adorn your bridal chamber, Zion,  
you who await the Lord;  
receive the bridegroom and bride  
with the light of candles.

You prudent virgins,  
trim your lamps;  
and let young maidens arise  
to meet their Lady.

Let servants kindle torches,  
and let the house, with all its masters,  
[Col. 1792D] go out with lights  
to meet the true light of the world.  
[Note: Col. 1792D: Here again there is elision.]  
[Note: Col. 1792D: We have deleted *cum* (“with”), which is superfluous in the manuscript.]

Blessed old man, hasten;  
fulfill the promised joys  
and reveal to all peoples  
the light that is to be revealed.

Devout widow,  
dedicated to God and his temple,  
with equal prophetic joy  
confess the Lord.

To God the Father with the Son,  
with the Paraclete Spirit:  
as there is one substance,  
so may there be one glory.

Amen.

#### XXXVIII. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

Christ’s parents bear him;  
in the temple they offer the Temple.  
He chose to obey the law  
who owed the law nothing.

Offer, Blessed One, your little child,  
your own and the Father’s only Son;  
offer him through whom we are offered,  
the price by which we are redeemed.

Come forth, royal Virgin;  
bring forth your son with the offering.  
[Col. 1793B] Let the mystical birds be taken,  
fitting for you or for him.

Let the dove show the simple one;  
let the turtledove designate the Virgin.  
The offering is indeed poor,  
but the mysteries are great.  
[Note: Col. 1793C: *Est* is absent from the manuscript.]

This was indeed the offering of the poor,  
though the lamb was for the rich;  
but the offering of the true Lamb  
has no need of a mystical lamb.  
[Note: Col. 1793C: The manuscript has *esse*.]

To God the Father with the Son,  
with the Paraclete Spirit.

#### XXXIX. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

He who commends poverty  
[Col. 1793C] first displays it in himself:  
God, rich in all things,  
became poorest in order to enrich us.

He first displayed in deeds  
what he afterward taught in words,  
beginning at once from the cradle  
and anticipating speech by action.

[Col. 1794A] This is the little cord,  
of linen in the hand of a man:  
the subtle word of evangelical law  
in deed.

This is the measuring reed  
which the little child bears in his hand,  
that he may measure the building  
placed upon the mountain.

For the measuring reed  
is the book of the Gospel,  
which he is said to bear in his hand  
who fulfills in action what is written.

The Church, placed upon this very thing,  
is measured,  
while each person thereby perceives  
how much he grows or falls short.

To God the Father [be glory].

#### XL. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS

[Col. 1794B]

Let every sex and every age  
clap and rejoice.  
He who comes, the salvation of all,  
summons everyone to joy.

Rejoice, man; rejoice, woman,  
happy in the shared glory.  
A woman ignorant of man  
gave birth to the man whom God clothed.

Virgin, rejoice with the Virgin!  
She is mother of the Most High.  
Let the married woman rejoice with the married woman,  
who at once proclaims the one conceived.

Still enclosed in the womb,  
with what mighty joy does the child  
who has sensed the Life of the world  
[Col. 1794B] announce him at once to the world!

Here an old man, there a widow,  
confessing Christ in prophetic praise,  
made manifest  
the Lord’s presence.

To God the Father [be glory].

### AT THE RESURRECTION OF THE LORD

#### XLI. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

Christians, clap your hands:  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

The prince of death defeated,  
Christ reigns.  
Meet the victor,  
who frees us.

The Devil overcome,  
[Note: Col. 1793C: For *diabolo*, “devil”; an ancient change of *di* into *z*. In Roman cemeteries *zabulus* and similar forms are not infrequent.]  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

Hell despoiled,  
he brought out his own;  
attended by an angelic  
company, he returned.

Deceit is deceived by the hook  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

when it feeds on flesh  
placed around it;  
it is pierced by the power  
inherent in that flesh.

[Col. 1793] Hell taken captive,  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

and the heights enriched,  
heaven rejoices;  
earth resounds  
with hymns, psalms, and songs.

Glory to God the Father,  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

salvation and victory  
to Christ the Lord;  
equal honor through the ages  
be to the Spirit.

Amen.

#### XLII. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

Give Mary a timbrel:  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

singing, let her summon  
the Hebrew women to song;  
let Jacob offer  
whole burnt offerings of poems.

Overthrowing the Egyptians,  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

God filled the channels  
of the Red Sea with enemies,  
whom the sea engulfed,  
buried beneath its waves.

Let the timbrel-player say:  
“The Lord has risen!”  
That other woman indeed  
saw first, in reality and not in name,  
the risen Lord, as she deserved.

Let her sing a sweeter song:  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

joined with the other faithful women,  
while she herself, with them,  
tells these things  
to the disciples.

To God the Father with the Son,  
with the Paraclete Spirit.

#### XLIII. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

[Col. 1795]

Goliath has been cast down:  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

the enemy himself has been slain by his own sword;  
[Note: Col. 1795: Thus the manuscript, and rightly. Cousin’s edition reads: “Goliath has been cast down, slain with the sword; the Lord has risen, by his own enemy”—which makes no sense.]

that Pharaoh  
was drowned with his own people.

Let the daughters of Zion say:  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

coming forth to meet the true David,  
let them bring out choirs  
[Note: Col. 1795: The manuscript has *proferantur*; but *ur* is marked with critical signs.]  
and sing praises  
to the victor of victory.

Our mighty Samson,  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

surrounded by enemies,  
lifted up the gates.  
The foreigner, the enemy, was frustrated  
[Note: Col. 1795: Cousin printed *Alophilus* as though a proper name; but it signifies “a foreign man,” an enemy, from Greek *ἀλλόφυλος*, “of another tribe.”]  
and groans in astonishment.

Like a lion’s cub,  
(“The Lord has risen!”)

whom his father’s life-giving roar  
raises on the third day,  
as natural science testifies.

To God the Father [be glory].

#### XLIV. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS

In the welcome season of spring,  
the Lord has risen.

When the world is already beginning  
to come back to life,  
it was fitting that the creator  
of the world should rise.

While all things rejoice,  
the Lord has risen;

as herbs are reborn,  
the trees put forth leaves  
and give forth many fragrances  
and flowers.

Winter now passed,  
the Lord has risen

into those joys  
of everlasting life  
which know  
no affliction.

[Col. 1795] To restore all things,  
the Lord has risen.  
[Note: Col. 1795: *Ut*, “in order that,” supplied conjecturally; the manuscript is erased here.]

The world was as though it felt  
these joys  
when, with the Lord’s flesh,  
it now flowered again.

To God the Father [be glory].

### AT THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD

#### XLV. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

Leaping upon mountains here,  
coming over hills,  
he calls his bride from the mountaintop:  
“Arise, sister, and now follow me.”  
[Note: Col. 1795: Cousin read *Montium*, “of mountains”; the manuscript has *montibus*, incorrectly; *montis* should be read.]  
[Note: Col. 1795: The manuscript has *sorori*, incorrectly; the copyist himself marked the end of the word with a critical sign.]

Ascending to the paternal palace,  
to the Father’s throne,  
he calls to his bride: “Beloved, hasten;  
sit with me at the Father’s right hand.”  
[Note: Col. 1795: A new elision.]

All the multitude of citizens,  
your paternal kingdom awaits you.  
The whole court with the Father  
seeks the joy of your presence.

What befits a king’s bride,  
what suits a queen,  
here you will don gold-woven robes  
with purple garments set with gems.

Glory be to Christ most high,  
who, ascending above the stars,  
with the Spirit and the Father, one God,  
rules things above and below.

Amen.

#### XLVI. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

By stages, as it were, the Son  
of the heavenly Father  
came down from above to earthly things  
and now returns, having despoiled Tartarus.

He came from the Father’s bosom,  
received in his mother’s womb;  
laid from the cross in the tomb,  
he rose, through whom we rise.

A bright cloud received him  
as he ascended into heaven;  
[Col. 1796] he was borne with uplifted hands,  
blessing those who stood by.  
[Note: Col. 1795: Thus the manuscript, and rightly; Cousin’s edition has *Terebatur*.]

As they watched him ascending  
and marveled at this,  
angels stood there in white,  
bright in face as well as clothing.

“Why,” they said, “do you stand amazed  
and gaze thus into heaven?  
The one whom you see going into heaven  
will come thus in the form of a judge.”

To the highest [be glory].

#### XLVII. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

While still placed on earth,  
Christ daily calls his bride,  
the Church, upward to himself,  
and urges her to ascend in mind.

Let her say: “Draw me after you;  
[Note: Col. 1795: The manuscript does not have *Citat*, as Cousin has, but simply *icat*, the red letter D having been omitted.]  
[Note: Col. 1795: The manuscript has *thrae*, by transposition of the aspiration.]  
stretch out your right hand to one who strives.  
You fly upon the wings of the winds—  
who will follow unless you grant wings?”  
[Note: Col. 1795: The manuscript plainly has *nisi*, “unless,” and the rhythm indeed requires it. Cousin nevertheless changed it to *ni*.]

Let her ask for a dove’s wings  
that she may hasten to rest.  
Let her seek the wings of a mighty eagle,  
by which she may ascend to the heights.

Together with wings he will give eyes  
that, with unturned gaze,  
she may behold the rays of the true sun—  
than which nothing is happier.  
[Note: Col. 1796: The manuscript has *veri*; Cousin read and printed *mihi*, which confuses the sense.]  
[Note: Col. 1796: Cousin read *in reflexis*; the manuscript has *irreflexit*, with the final letter marked by a critical sign.]

That heavenly place is fitting for winged creatures,  
according to the merits of virtues,  
to whom God has given these wings.

Glory to Christ most high.  
[Note: Col. 1796: The hymn for Lauds and Vespers appears below, no. LI.]

### ON THE FEAST OF THE INVENTION OF THE HOLY CROSS

#### XLVIII. AT THE FIRST OR SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS

[Note: Col. 1796: From what Abelard states in the prologue to the third book, it is clear that he wrote five hymns on the Cross: one inviting the deacon to take the cross from the altar and bring it into the middle of the choir; three for the three Nocturns; and a fifth for Lauds. The first hymn is certainly missing, for only the beginning of the doxology is written at the end of the surviving hymns. I would not venture to assert that a hymn for the first or second Nocturn is missing; indeed, I think that the copyist combined two hymns into one. Certainly “Hail, banner of the heavenly king,” etc., appears to be the opening of the remaining poem, and it can readily be divided after the words “is restrained.” Recall that hymn XXVI likewise consists of two joined hymns. Yet the same ending of the third verse throughout the hymn somewhat opposes this conclusion.]

Hail, banner  
of the heavenly king;  
hail, holy cross,

by which, when the grim robber  
was despoiled,  
his prey was recovered.

The gates of hell  
lie shattered,  
their bars broken.

Blessed Tau—  
[Col. 1797] by which, when penitents’ foreheads  
are signed,  
the cruel wrath  
of the slayer  
is restrained.  
[Note: Col. 1797: See Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under “Tau.” One should read “O Tau,” or “Taü,” lest a syllable be lacking. In more recent times many have spoken of this symbol of the cross.]

See: once you were  
the punishment  
of thieves;

now, impressed upon  
the foreheads of kings,  
you are a glorious sign.  
[Note: Col. 1797: Cousin asserts that the Brussels manuscript reads *Fide* (“Trust”); incorrectly. Only the red letter *v* has been omitted.]

You are the tree of life,  
upon which the King himself  
ascended as a palm [reading uncertain],  
that by your fruit  
he might restore the losses  
caused by the deadly fruit.

For the blessed sailor,
Whoever, as though in a ship,

Enjoys life—[Note: [Col. 1797] The manuscript reads: *quae quasi nave fruendo vita* (“who/which, as though by a ship, enjoying life”); the words have absolutely no sense.]

Must sail across

This great sea

Toward the things above.

To the triune Persons—[Note: [Col. 1797] The complete doxology, as we noted, is found nowhere in the manuscript. It is perhaps: “To the three Persons, to God most high, be everlasting praise.”]

XLIX. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

The uplifted serpent

Heals the bites of serpents

By its sight.

Christ, suspended,

Cures the venom

Of the ancient serpent.

The Father’s Wisdom

From itself supplies

Healing to all.

The prophet’s rod—

The rock struck twice—

Overflows with water.

Christ, hung upon

Two pieces of wood,

Gives us drink from himself.

The Jew drinks,

But the Christian

Stands refreshed.

To the Persons.

L. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1797]

The wood cast into them

Sweetens the bitter waters.

All conflicts

Are sweet to the saints

Through the Crucified One.

The glorious cup

Is the draught of death

For them through him.

Every torture also

Is welcome to them

Through this example.

“There is no sorrow

Like my sorrow”:

They heed what is written.

For he who bears

All sins

Knows no sin.

With him who suffered for all,

All are universally bound

To suffer in sympathy.

To the triune Persons.

ON THE FEAST OF THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD. [Note: [Col. 1797] Above, at Hymn XLVII, we noted that this Hymn LI has been moved from its proper place.]

LI. AT LAUDS AND VESPERS.

When God ascended on high,

And drew with him

The triumphant majesty of the Lord,

Those set free stood round the victor.

The heavenly city of the King

Brings forth splendid processions to meet him—[Note: [Col. 1798] The manuscript reads *ovias*.]

“Rejoice!” [Note: [Col. 1798] Χαῖρε, “Rejoice!”]

The angels sing to the victor,

And “Hosanna!” the people who have been saved.

To those who seem to be asking

And wondering about this,

Others reply, and in alternating song

So soften the chant with these words:

“Who is this King of glory?

What is this glory of victory?

Who is this coming from Edom,

Shining in a purple garment?”

“The Lord, strong and mighty,

Triumphant over conquered enemies,

Returns victorious from battle,

Having subdued Zabulus.”

To Christ most high.

ON THE FEAST OF PENTECOST.

LII. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

By the coming of the Holy Spirit,

[Col. 1798]

O God, adorning the altars

Of our hearts with virtues,

Dedicate them as temples for yourself

With that sevenfold grace which you possess,

Against those seven demons—[Note: [Col. 1798] M. Victor Cousin reverses the order of the verses, writing: “Whose gifts are all good / Against those seven demons.”]

Whose gifts are all good.

Through the fear of the Lord

He first frees us from evil,

So that one poor in this world

May enter heaven rich.

Grant us this grace, Lord:

Do not repay the guilty with their due punishment,

But give glory to your name.

Grant bowels of mercy,

Lest temptation prevail;

This grace makes gentle those

Whose possession is the earth.

And grant us this, Lord, etc.

You add also knowledge,

By which we recognize what must be wept for;

You comfort us through pardon

When we have first done this.

And grant this, etc.

You strengthen us with fortitude

For hunger after righteousness.

The fullness of the true bread

Is the provision for the soul’s journey.

And grant this, etc.

You give that highest counsel

Concerning mercy,

So that you may give the same reward—[Note: [Col. 1798] The manuscript adds *vel bravium* (“or prize”), thus giving Abelard a choice between *praemium* (“reward”) and *bravium* (“prize”).]

You desire this, not sacrifices.

And grant this, etc.

You are the Spirit of understanding,

By whom divinity is seen

By the enlightened eyes of the heart;

This is the sublimity of the kingdom. [Note: [Col. 1798] The manuscript reads: “This is the sublimity of the kingdom of the Spirit”; *spiritus* is redundant.]

And grant this, etc.

At last you give wisdom,

Through which they become peacemakers,

Sanctifying the Father’s name,

In whom they are God’s children.

And grant this, Lord, etc.

By the prayers of the peoples

Whom you consecrate on this day,

Strengthen with those same gifts

Those whom you regenerate. [Note: [Col. 1798] I think one should read: “O you whom the prayers of the peoples consecrate on this day, strengthen with those same gifts those whom you regenerate.”]

With that sevenfold grace, and so forth.

LIII. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

The fiftieth light

Marks the number of remission,

By which the jubilee year

Cancels everyone’s debts.

To God, the highest King, be highest glory:

By whose grace all things subsist,

From whom, through whom, and in whom are all things.

[Col. 1799]

Under this number of days,

The Spirit of remission

Came from the throne of the highest Father,

Whom the Son sent.

Highest glory, etc.

For we call the divine Spirit

His love,

By which we know him merciful to the guilty,

By which we know him gentle.

Highest glory, etc.

Today the world is kindled

By the flame of that love:

Christ came to send him

Into the earth; fire is sent.

Highest glory, etc.

Showing him today

In fiery tongues above the apostles,

He marked these messengers beforehand

As belonging to the fiery law.

Highest glory, etc.

The old law, as if cold,

Held servants in check through fear;

In Christ, mother Grace

Bore children for God.

To God, the highest King, be highest glory, etc.

LIV. [Note: [Col. 1799] From the appearance of the manuscript, the following verses ought to be joined to the preceding ones. Nevertheless, they must certainly be separated, so that there are two hymns: first, the subject of each is different; second, otherwise there would be only three hymns, although there ought to be four; third, the repetition, more extensive than usual, of words from the doxology—“To God, the highest King, be highest glory,” etc.—indicates some division.] AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

When the Lord gave the law, [Note: [Col. 1799] The manuscript and M. Victor Cousin read *tradentem*, “giving.”]

A trembling mind brought fear;

The Spirit received in the upper room

Removed it.

Highest glory, etc.

There lightning flashed;

The mountain smoked in darkness;

Here is a manifold flame,

Not burning but illuminating.

Highest glory, etc.

There the people feared

The sound of the dreadful trumpet;

Here the sound is the Spirit

Of understanding.

Highest glory, etc.

There the smoke signifies

The darkness of the obscure letter;

Here receive the appearance

Of shining fire as the sign of the clear one. [Note: [Col. 1799] The manuscript reads: “Receive here into the appearance of shining fire / the clear sign.” M. Victor Cousin printed: “Receive here the appearance of shining fire / as the clear sign.” The sense seems to be: “Receive here the appearance of shining fire as [Col. 1800] the sign of the clear letter.”]

Highest glory, etc.

There everything is full

Of terror and darkness;

Here the Paraclete heals

Contraries by contraries.

Highest glory, etc.

Divine consolation removes

All troubles;

[Col. 1799]

It inscribes the tablets of the heart,

So that reason may be restored.

To God, the highest King, be highest glory, etc.

LV. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

The divine Spirit, filling

The breasts of the apostles,

Enriches their hearts with understanding

And their tongues with every language.

Highest glory, etc.

As the division of tongues

Once scattered the proud,

So now the gathering

Of diverse tongues unites the humble.

Highest glory, etc.

He who created these things and all things

Had to be praised in every tongue

And proclaimed

In every region of the world.

Highest glory, etc.

We know that the testimony of Joel

Has been fulfilled,

Which Peter brings forward against

Those barking slanderers.

Highest glory, etc.

This feast is the fulfillment

Of the divine feasts;

Let it be the bestowal completing

The divine promise—

He who may teach all truth,

Who was promised to suggest all things [Note: [Col. 1800] The passage is corrupt. It should read: “This promised Spirit is he / who suggests to us all things / which the Son spoke to his own / who teaches every truth.”]

Which the Son spoke to his own.

Highest glory, etc.

ON THE FEAST OF THE DEDICATION OF A CHURCH.

LVI. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

At Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1800] Against the authority of the manuscript and the metre, M. Victor Cousin printed *Hierosolymis*.]

Sacred dedications were made,

When the Light was celebrated

In the Lord’s presence.

May he himself, we ask,

Be present at our festivals today—

The proper Basileon [Note: [Col. 1800] *Basileon* in place of *Basileus*, “king.” From this and elsewhere it is clear that Greek was wholly unknown to Abelard.]

Of this present basilica.

May he consecrate for himself

The temple of our breast,

And join inward realities

To outward signs.

May he himself fulfill within

What is done outwardly—

He who dwells in the inner chambers

Of the heart.

[Col. 1800]

Glory to God the Father;

Equal honor to the Son;

Equal thanksgiving

To the Spirit.

Amen.

LVII. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

This visible temple

Is a spiritual sign,

And all that is done in it

Is done mystically in this. [Note: [Col. 1800] Thus the manuscript. M. Victor Cousin substitutes *sit*, “is.”]

Water is blessed;

A mixture of salt is made;

The church is sprinkled with these,

Being carried around it three times.

Meanwhile lights are lit

Within,

Twelve in number,

Arranged in a circle.

While sprinkling, the bishop

Goes around the church three times.

He strikes the front of the doors

Above three times with his staff.

He orders them opened,

So that the King of glory may enter;

When he has done this three times,

The doors are opened.

Having entered the basilica,

He offers prayers to the Lord:

First an offering for himself,

Then for the people.

While he traces the forms

Of a double alphabet

With intersecting lines,

He expresses the sign of the cross.

What is done outwardly, etc.

Glory to God the Father.

LVIII. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

The bishop prepares himself

To consecrate the altar;

He mixes water, salt, ashes,

And earth.

With his finger dipped twice,

Along the horns of the altar,

The consecrator’s right hand

Traces the sign of the cross.

Then, holding

A sprinkler of hyssop,

He sprinkles seven times

Around the altar.

[Col. 1801]

After the inner walls

Have been sprinkled [Note: [Col. 1801] The manuscript and M. Victor Cousin read *Ligatis*, “bound”; it seems one should substitute *Rigatis*, i.e. “sprinkled.” There are frequent errors in the red letters.]

Three times in succession,

He prays that the Lord may hear

Everyone there—[Note: [Col. 1801] Above *quosque* (“everyone”) the manuscript writes *vel vota*, “or prayers.” M. Victor Cousin preferred *vota*, without mentioning the original reading.]

At the altar the prelate,

After these things have been done,

Turns; the psalm is said

With the antiphon leading. [Note: [Col. 1801] The manuscript reads *pereunte*, marked with an obelus on *per*.]

The remaining water is poured

At the altar’s base;

A clean cloth is at hand,

By which it should be wiped. [Note: [Col. 1801] The manuscript correctly reads *debeat*, “should”; although M. Victor Cousin asserts that it reads *debeatur*, which he corrected [Col. 1802] to *debetur*, so that the endings of the first and third verses may rhyme.]

The bishop burns incense

To the Lord upon it;

Both it and its corners [Note: [Col. 1802] Thus the manuscript, not *angeli*, “angels,” as M. Victor Cousin printed.]

Are marked with oil.

The altar is anointed

With chrism,

And at the same time

The antiphon to be sung is begun.

Then twelve crosses

On the walls are anointed;

The altar is covered,

And the sacrifice takes place.

What is done outwardly, etc.

Glory to God the Father.

LIX. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

Behold the house of the Lord;

Behold the faithful people,

Devoting themselves to psalms, hymns,

And spiritual songs.

May Christ, whose house it is,

Protect it for himself,

And may the shepherd fortify

The sheepfold of his own flock.

May he employ the protection

Of spiritual powers;

May he drive invisible wolves

Away from them.

May the guardianship of angels,

Presiding here always,

Watch over

The defenses of the faithful people.

May Michael be sent

To crush proud Zabulus;

May Raphael be sent

To heal the wounded.

May Gabriel [Note: [Col. 1802] Thus the manuscript.]

Strengthen wavering hearts,

And may he likewise help those standing firm

To persevere.

[Col. 1802]

Since this is the palace

Of the heavenly King,

It ought never to be empty

Of heavenly ministers. [Note: [Col. 1802] M. Victor Cousin reads *nocuum*, “harmful.”]

By their ministry may all things

Be ordered—

They who know what things

Are or are not pleasing to the Lord.

May they offer to Christ

The prayers of the people;

And may they teach them

What he himself vows and prays for.

Let the faithful here ask

Nothing with vain prayers,

Nothing with futile vows [Note: [Col. 1802] The manuscript reads *vocis*, “of speech”; incorrectly.]

Either for themselves or for others. [Note: [Col. 1802] M. Victor Cousin reads *Hinc*, “hence”; the manuscript reads otherwise.]

Whoever of the faithful here [Note: [Col. 1802] The manuscript reads *Quis hic*, “Who here?”; M. Victor Cousin, *Quis autem*, “But who?”]

Pours out prayers to God,

May rejoice that he has obtained

Whatever he asked.

Let no Jezebel here,

No simoniac,

Corrupt Christ’s flock

With heretical plagues.

Whoever brings back those

Whom he himself has expelled

From his own house

May feel his wrath.

BOOK THREE: HYMNS FOR THE FEASTS OF THE SAINTS.

[Col. 1801]

PREFACE: ON THE PLAN OF THE PRECEDING BOOK.

In the preceding two books we arranged the daily hymns for weekdays and those proper to the divine solemnities. Now there remains, for the glory of the heavenly King and the common exhortation of the faithful, to extol as best we can with the due praises of hymns that court also of the heavenly palace. In this work, may those especially assist me by their merits, to whose glorious memory I desire to pay such small offerings of praise as I can; as it is written: “The memory of the righteous is with praise” [Note: [Col. 1802] Proverbs 10:7.], and again: “Let us praise glorious men,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1802] Ecclesiasticus 44:1.]

[Col. 1803]

I also entreat you, dearest sisters, dedicated to Christ, by whose prayers [Note: [Col. 1803] Thus the manuscript. M. Victor Cousin printed *quorum*, “by whose [masculine].”] I have undertaken this work above all, add the devotion of your prayers, remembering that most blessed lawgiver who accomplished more by praying than the people could accomplish [Note: [Col. 1803] The manuscript reads *populis potuit*, “could [with/by] peoples.”] by fighting. And, that I may find your charity generous in abundance of prayers, consider carefully how lavish a demand your request makes upon my resources. For while we have endeavoured to pursue the praises of divine grace according to the ability of our little talent—[Note: [Col. 1803] Here some word is missing; M. Victor Cousin suggests *virtute*, “strength.” I myself would rather think *parvitate*, “smallness,” *imbecillitate*, “weakness,” etc.]—we have compensated for what was lacking in the ornament of eloquence by a multitude of hymns: composing, namely, hymns proper to each nocturn of each solemnity, whereas until now only a single hymn was sung before the nocturns on feasts as well as on weekdays.

Accordingly, we have ordained four hymns for each feast, so that a proper hymn may be sung at each of the three nocturns, and that the morning praises may also have their own. Of these four we have further arranged that two may be joined during the vigil as one hymn, and the remaining two similarly recited at vespers on the solemn day; or that they may be divided two and two at each vespers, so that one is sung with the first two psalms and another with the remaining two. Concerning the Cross, however, five hymns have been written. The first is to be prefixed at every hour, inviting the deacon to remove the cross from the altar, bring it into the middle of the choir, and set it there as though to be adored and greeted, so that the whole solemnity may be performed in its presence through every hour.

ON THE FEASTS OF BLESSED MARY.

LX. AT MATINS AND VESPERS.

God’s Word,

Coeternal

With the Father,

Mind born from God,

Not created. [Note: [Col. 1803] Thus the manuscript. Perhaps one should read: “But not created.”]

Through whom the world was made,

Through whom restored,

Attend to the prayers

Of your suppliant servants. [Note: [Col. 1804] The manuscript reads *supplicantium*, “of those supplicating.”]

Christ, our judge,

Have mercy on us;

Forgive now in goodness,

Lest you condemn in justice.

Be for us one born,

Be for us one who suffered,

You who give us hope of salvation

In both respects.

Let birth not be vain;

Let suffering not be fruitless; [Note: [Col. 1804] The manuscript reads *Nescit*, “does not know,” in both places.]

Let not the enemy insult us

Who put our trust in you.

[Col. 1803]

Mother of mercy,

Be graciously present to us;

Do not disappoint in their hope

Those who presume upon you.

Through you God’s descent

To us took place;

Through you we must ascend

To him.

Through you may we who confess you

Be led back—

You, his gate to us,

And ours to him.

To him, and to the triune God,

Be everlasting honor:

From whom, through whom are all things,

In whom they were created.

Amen.

LXI. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

Mother of the Saviour,

See what you are called;

Consider the singular honor

Of your name.

Fulfil what is spoken by the deed,

Yet with no labour,

Although a single prayer

Absolves the guilty. [Note: [Col. 1804] M. Victor Cousin printed *Quam vos*, “although you [plural].”]

For whatever you ask

With a mother’s ear [Note: [Col. 1804] Thus the manuscript. Perhaps *ore*, “with a mother’s mouth.”]

You will obtain

From so kind a Son. [Note: [Col. 1804] The manuscript reads *postulabit*, “will ask.”]

A just Son

Will not offend his holy mother,

Nor will your prayers

Suffer any refusal.

The power of holiness

And the authority of a mother

Will obtain

Whatever great gift they seek.

He will not despise

The prayers of his suppliant mother,

Who commands obedience

To father or mother.

To him be.

[Col. 1803]

COMMON OF THE APOSTLES.

LXII. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

The height of the apostolic order

Renews the world with new joys,

Which it gladdens with annual feasts.

These are the standard-bearers of the Church. [Note: [Col. 1804] The manuscript incorrectly reads *Alii*, “Others.”]

They are leaders in the Lord’s battle-line;

After them comes the praise of the martyrs’ army.

Like infantry, the remaining saints,

Devoted to long abstinence,

Do not fail in the Lord’s camp.

Everlasting glory to the everlasting King,

Christ, prince of hosts,

And equally to the Father and Spirit.

Amen.

LXIII. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

With fitting apostolic praises

The world resounds in all its parts,

Through those by whom God has become known to all.

Formerly known among Israel,

The Lord’s name has now through them gone forth [Note: [Col. 1804] The manuscript reads *prodigit*.]

To every region of the world.

[Col. 1805A]

For this purpose they were endowed with every tongue

And were radiant with miracles,

Great alike in word and deed.

Everlasting glory.

LXIV. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

They subject beneath the Lord’s yoke

The thrones of kings and the lofty chairs

Of philosophical teaching. [Note: [Col. 1805D] The manuscript has *modo*, “only,” incorrectly inserted.]

If a feeble populace subdues military things,

A rustic tongue eloquence,

A small band subdues the world.

On one side kings fight with swords;

On the other philosophers thunder with words;

But, conquered by miracles, they beg.

Everlasting glory to the everlasting King.

LXV. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1805B]

Christ, the wisdom choosing

The foolish things of the age and the lowly things of the world,

Also crushes lofty things.

Here rhetorical refinement counts for nothing,

And the verbosity of logic has no force; [Note: [Col. 1805D] We have supplied *valet*, “has force,” which the sense and verse require.]

But the simplicity of sacred faith does.

Tully’s eloquence has yielded;

Aristotle has been told to be silent;

Rustics issue laws to the world.

Everlasting glory.

ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL.

LXVI. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1805C]

The fisherman’s lines [Note: [Col. 1805D] M. Victor Cousin printed *Piscatoria*, against the authority of the manuscript and the demands of metre.]

Now often make an emperor’s knees

Bow down in supplication to God.

Paul, not unequal in the merit of his life,

Possesses a double diadem:

White as a virgin, red as a martyr. [Note: [Col. 1805D] The manuscript clearly reads *rubeo*, “red,” although M. Victor Cousin wrote that *rube* was read there.]

This day has sent to those above

The most blessed princes of the world,

Comrades in battle and companions in death.

Everlasting glory.

LXVII. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

Prince of the apostolic summit,

Shepherd of the sheep of the Lord’s flock,

Guard these with watchful protection.

Using your former art to better purpose,

Cast nets to draw in human beings,

Thus fulfilling the Lord’s promises.

Mighty key-bearer [Note: [Col. 1805D] The manuscript reads *Clavier*.]

Of the heavenly court,

Open the doors; extend your hand;

Receive those whom you lead to the Lord.

Everlasting glory.

LXVIII. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1806A]

Greatest trumpet of the Lord, Paul,

Giving thunder from heavenly things,

Scatter the enemies; gather the citizens.

You are the chief teacher of the nations,

A vessel made a cup for all,

Full of draughts of wisdom. [Note: [Col. 1806D] The manuscript reads *austibus*.]

In the morning Benjamin seized prey;

In the evening he distributes generous food;

With dishes of life he refreshes the world.

He is like an untamed rhinoceros,

Whom the Lord, binding to the plough,

Immediately breaks the clods of the valleys.

Now he praises the steward of wickedness,

Whom he calls endowed with prudence

[Col. 1806B]

And provident for the children of light.

Everlasting glory. [Note: [Col. 1806D] The hymn for Lauds and the fourth hymn for Vespers are plainly to be taken from the Common of the Apostles; and therefore the doxology “Everlasting glory” has properly been retained.]

ON THE FEAST OF SAINT JOHN THE EVANGELIST.

LXIX. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

The eagle, flying higher than heaven,

Has brought the hidden dwelling-place

Of its nest to the Lord’s bosom.

There, beholding the rays of the sun

With its most blessed, highest splendour,

It restores its sight and feeds its eyes.

From the fiery substance of the sun

Proceeding heat and begotten light

Provide supreme delights.

Everlasting. [Note: [Col. 1806D] The remaining hymns are to be taken from the Common of the Apostles, as the doxology shows.]

[Col. 1806C]

COMMON OF THE EVANGELISTS.

LXX. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

The chariot of Christ carries

The Lord’s winepress,

By which the pressed cluster, in the cup,

Refreshes the hearts of the faithful.

Understand the body of the chariot as

The vessel of the Lord’s Scripture,

By which countless churches hold

The Word of God brought to them.

The wheels of the chariot [Note: [Col. 1806D] The manuscript reads *roctae*, with the *c* marked by an obelus.]

Are the four books of the Gospels,

Whose writers have deserved

Most splendid solemnities.

[Col. 1806D]

Glory to the Father and the Son,

And to the Paraclete Spirit,

To one God as well as Lord,

Though there are three Persons in number.

Amen.

LXXI. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

The winepress is the Lord’s cross;

Consider Christ here as the cluster.

Mystical history prefigured him

Hanging from a pole.

Those carrying him to the people,

A sign of fertility,

Are those who reveal the mystery of the cross,

The salvation of the world.

The first, who does not see what he bears,

Signifies Christ’s prophets.

He who follows, so as to see,

Denotes those who tell of what they have seen.

Glory to the Father.

LXXII. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

These are the four living creatures,

Distinct in their various forms.

Prophetic vision and mystical Apocalypse

Relate them.

On the right a man is understood,

And a lion is joined to him;

A calf is assigned to the left,

And an eagle is raised above.

[Col. 1808]

Each is endowed with four wings

Or with faces;

Their bodies are full of eyes,

So that even their backs are not empty.

Glory to the Father.

LXXIII. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

They go [Note: [Col. 1807] The one who applied the red letters wrote *S* in place of *E*. Hence the manuscript reads *Sunt*, “They are.”]

When those beings go,

And the wheels stand when they stand;

They are lifted when they are lifted,

For the spirit of life is in them.

Their feet are straight feet,

And the sole of the foot is like a calf’s;

Sparks seemed to go forth

As though from glowing bronze.

They have the likeness of burning coals,

Of shining lamps

Seeming to flash;

They go and return like lightning flashes.

Glory to the Father.

[Col. 1807]

ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY INNOCENTS.

LXXIV. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

At the rising

Of the heavenly King,

The earthly king

Fears that the right

Of his sovereignty

Will be taken from him.

When they report

The unheard-of sign

Of the star,

The Magi disturb

The city

And its king.

Then the wicked king,

Stirred up against the children,

In order to destroy

One among the children,

Destroys many.

For one, many

Were slain for Christ;

But through one, all

Were crowned by Christ.

LXXV. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

The king, surpassing

All tyrants,

And more inhuman

Than even

The beasts,

Musters an army

Against children

As against enemies,

And turns arms

Against none

But his own.

The fury of his wrath,

Not comparable even

To that of wild beasts,

Destroys those

Whom the wolf,

Having seized them,

Cherishes.

At the general command

Given by the king—[Note: [Col. 1807] The rest is missing in the Brussels manuscript; Macrobius, however, inserts the following: “Macrobius, in Book II of the *Saturnalia*, concerning Augustus and his jokes: When he heard that among the boys under the age of two whom Herod, king of the Jews, had ordered killed in Syria, his own son also had been slain, he said: ‘It is better to be Herod’s pig than his son; not even his own infant is safe from slaughter.’ Rather, continue in the manuscript:] [lacuna]

Brought to Augustus,

This caused laughter,

And the gentle king

Wittily mocked

The cruel one.

“It is an evil,” he said,

“To be born

Of Herod;

It profits one more

To be the pig

Of such a king.”

LXXVI. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

To the bosoms

Of nursing mothers, [Note: [Col. 1807] The manuscript reads *Lactandum*, “of those to be nursed.”]

As to battle-lines,

All the armed populace

Rushes upon nursing infants. [Note: [Col. 1808] The manuscript reads *Lactantes*, “nursing.”]

The child, joyful [Note: [Col. 1808] Thus the manuscript, and correctly, although M. Victor Cousin substituted *lactabundus*, a word unknown to the Romans.]

At the flashing sword,

Laughs at the enemy

Rushing upon him

To kill him.

What is so astounding

To say or hear?

What is so far removed

From human nature? [Note: [Col. 1808] The manuscript has the words reversed: “What from human nature?”]

Why, Herod,

Do you languish in fear

Over Christ?

“My kingdom,” he says,

“Is not of this world.” [Note: [Col. 1808] The manuscript reads: “Not mine, he says, / is the kingdom / of this world.” M. Victor Cousin thought one should read: “Mine, he says, / is not the kingdom / of this world”; but the rhyme fails.]

He reigns among eternal,

Not passing, things;

He neither takes nor desires

These things,

Who gives them.

LXXVII. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

In Ramah

A voice is heard—

Rachel weeping,

[Col. 1809]

Wailing over

Her slaughtered

Children. [Note: [Col. 1809C] The manuscript reads *Ejullantis*, with the second *l* marked by an obelus.]

The torn limbs

Of little children lie,

And with milk

As much as with blood

They water the ground.

The bereaved mother bends over them,

Wailing, [Note: [Col. 1809C] The manuscript reads *Ejullando*, with the same obelus.]

And in vain gathers them,

Cherishing them

In her loving bosom. [Note: [Col. 1809C] The manuscript reads *Sic cupio*, “thus I desire.”]

Blind frenzy beats the breast,

Tears the bosom, [Note: [Col. 1809C] The manuscript reads: “The bosoms he tears.”]

Which maternal

And human love

Produces.

They were killed unwillingly,

But though their merit

Was nothing,

Their recompense

Was great.

[Col. 1809]

The reward itself

Was the life

Which they too,

By dying,

Not by speaking,

Confessed.

COMMON OF MARTYRS.

LXXVIII. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

O God, shield of all

And crown of martyrs,

Both cause of their contests

And palm of the contenders,

You fight through the unarmed

And overcome the armed.

Within, you fashion weapons

With which charity fights.

Trusting in these, virtue

Boldly offers its bare breast to the enemy;

These, from right

And left,

Fortify it

And protect it

From every wound.

However great the battles

That rage against it,

Hope makes it secure

And faith makes it certain.

[Col. 1810]

Through this, the martyr’s breast,

A tower of strength,

Remains unmoved

In every danger.

Countless engines

Are raised on this side and that;

Masses of stone

Are hurled at it from every direction.

The world fights without on couches, [Note: [Col. 1809C] Thus the manuscript.]

The one God saves within.

The enemy rages

With sword and flames;

Within they know

What protecting strength is.

He makes frequent blows,

Violent assaults;

But within,

God’s strength

Prevails.

Many and great

Are the battles against the saints;

But few or small,

Compared with the rewards.

To the King whose gifts these are,

Be glory.

Amen.

LXXIX. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1809A]

Every kind of torture

Is sought out,

So that the martyrs’ greatest

Constancy may be tested.

A furnace refines gold

And thus makes it pure;

Mustard receives its strength

When someone crushes it. [Note: [Col. 1810C] The manuscript reads *eas*; it also reads *Ut sinapis*, “as mustard,” instead of *dum quis eam*, “when someone [crushes] it.”]

Tools are employed;

They prepare all things for their own ruin.

Stones are consumed while they are struck; [Note: [Col. 1810C] The manuscript reads *tontuntur*.]

Trees are blunted while they are hewn.

Compare the wicked to those, the good to these,

When you see [Note: [Col. 1810C] The manuscript reads *videns*, “seeing.”] Christ’s soldiers afflicted.

Insults, prison, chains,

Scourgings, spectacles,

[Col. 1809B]

Nakedness, hunger,

Are preludes to punishments.

With fire, water, sword,

Claws, rack,

And every kind of gibbet,

The final struggle is fought.

But as the punishment is prolonged,

The end of punishment—death—is delayed.

The martyrs, long tortured, desire to die;

But the rulers who kill them forbid them to die.

Delicate maidens joined with men

Are companions in punishment, as in victory.

Many and great.

LXXX. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

The princes of the world fight,

[Col. 1810A]

The satellites of demons;

Christ’s soldiers conquer,

Attaining their desire.

Nor are women absent

From this warfare,

This great victory,

And the glory of its reward.

As the strong sex fights and triumphs,

So does the weak;

So that the armies of the highest King

May have their Amazons alongside men,

Whose palms are the more admirable

Because by nature they are weaker.

Men stand in the encounters of war

With their wives,

Brothers with sisters,

Sons with mothers.

A wife encourages her husband,

A mother strengthens her children,

And regenerates for heaven

Those whom she bore for earth.

About to follow them at once,

A sister, made Christ’s whole burnt-offering,

Urges her brother to fight,

And exhorts him in both word and example.

What are young men to do but fight,

When they behold maidens fighting?

Many and great.
