LXXXI. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

This Davidic tower

Gives them sure defenses;

They have shields

And ramparts for protection.

This whole armour

Of the strong is for all,

To repel the attack

Of enemies of whatever kind.

Here Christ’s athletes fight,

And safely mock their enemies.

Diamond is stronger than bitumen:

Neither axe nor hammer breaks it.

This soldier, surrounded by enemies,

Mocks their futile assaults.

With this tower too, Lord,

Always protect us;

Fortify us on every side

With your wall and rampart,

Lest any entrance be open

By which the enemy may strike.

Whoever here calls upon you [Note: [Col. 1811D] M. Victor Cousin incorrectly printed *Hinc*, “hence.”]

May sleep safely;

And because we are more cowardly,

Fortify us with greater aid.

[Col. 1811B]

If we do not prevail with the palm,

May we in some fashion stand in the place of our foot-soldiers;

If we do not deserve the prize of the victors, [Note: [Col. 1811D] Following a Greek glossary, M. Victor Cousin substitutes *brabium*.]

May it suffice to have escaped danger.

Many and great.

COMMON OF CONFESSORS.

LXXXII. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

Mother Church, rejoicing, celebrates

The memory of the righteous, worthy of praise,

With psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs;

Trusting, she asks for their intercessions.

Highest Father, to you thanksgiving and solemn offerings

Of grace are rendered for the gifts you have bestowed,

Through whom all who are righteous are righteous,

Through whom all who are blessed are blessed. [Note: [Col. 1811D] These words are written above: “Or: Without whom none are blessed.”]

[Col. 1811C]

Their good things are gifts of your grace;

Their praises in hymns are your glory.

Whoever praises them praises truly

You in them, and them in you alike.

The highest purpose in celebrating their feasts

Is none other than to recount

Your benefits,

Through whom all who are righteous are righteous.

Glory to God, wonderful in his saints,

From whom, through whom, and in whom are all things;

Whose power accomplishes whatever it wills,

And whose wisdom orders all things most excellently.

His supreme goodness does not permit doubt

That he wills all things to come about and be ordered well. [Note: [Col. 1811D] This strophe is placed in the manuscript so that it can be referred equally to the preceding or to the following hymn. [Col. 1812D]]

LXXXIII. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

You who give abstinence,

Which tames the flesh;

You who give continence,

Which adorns the flesh;

You instill in them the will for what is good,

And grant them the accomplishment itself.

They are your instruments,

Through whom you work marvels,

And move human hearts

By signs and wonders;

Through whom.

[Col. 1812A]

They free the possessed

From demons;

They boldly [Note: [Col. 1812D] The manuscript reads *Audacter*, “boldly.”]

Command every sickness;

They give help by words of consolation;

Prayer supplies a remedy for leprosy.

They restore sight to the blind,

Steps to the lame,

Life to the dead;

Whatever they ask,

They can do through you,

Who accomplish what you command;

Through whom.

In the saints.

LXXXIV. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

Their present life was Friday,

In which they suffered with Christ through abstinence.

[Col. 1812B]

As he himself commands one to take up the cross,

And Paul declares himself crucified [Note: [Col. 1812D] The manuscript reads *crucifixus*, “crucified.”]

After this comes the soul’s rest, as though a Sabbath;

At last, on the eighth day, you will restore to them the robe of the body.

Through whom.

The persecutor’s sword was absent from them,

But their ready spirit was present. [Note: [Col. 1812D] The manuscript reads: “But a ready spirit had was present.” M. Victor Cousin omitted *habuit*, adding that “something seems lacking for the metre.”]

If the body did not receive sword-blows,

The mind nevertheless possesses the martyr’s palm.

Let the executioner cease; let every kind of torture cease.

You who are the examiner of hearts, assign rewards according to this.

Through whom.

God wonderful in the saints.

LXXXV. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1812C]

The funerals of the righteous call for praise;

The deaths of the impious bring grief.

Death lifts these to eternal life;

A double death crushes those in death.

This grievous life is prison and chains for the saints.

When these are broken, the soul, delivered from here, flees to you.

Through whom.

When the blessed soul has come to you,

Who can adequately recount its joys?

What is that majesty which it beholds?

What surrounding court—who can describe it?

No miserable person can behold that glory

In which you rejoice with the elect; draw us also to it.

Through whom all who are righteous are righteous.

In the saints.

COMMON OF HOLY WOMEN.

LXXXVI. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1812D]

From each sex we received the wound;

From each sex we received healing.

God clothed himself as a man in a virgin,

So that both men [Note: [Col. 1812D] The manuscript reads *vitae*, “lives.”] and women might be saved.

Salvation arose from a woman;

From where guilt began, grace began.

The more this sex, after guilt, had been lower

And more abject by nature,

The more divine mercy

[Col. 1813A]

Raised it by greater grace. [Note: [Col. 1813D] The manuscript reads *majora*, “greater [neuter plural].”]

Observe this step by step

From his virgin mother.

Who can number the choirs of holy virgin women

Who emulate her?

After them, who does not know that innumerable widows

Embrace the sacred vow?

Nor are there lacking from marriage

Those who burn with this desire.

After all these, if I look upon prostitutes,

[an Egyptian woman] anointing a Magdalen [the syntax is uncertain],

Where guilt had first abounded,

I see that power afterwards sets free. [Note: [Col. 1813D] The manuscript reads *post exliberat*.]

Honor to Christ, glory to him,

Who performs so many wonders.

LXXXVII. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1813B]

After the singular honor of the virgin,

Who has such power that she is God-bearer,

With what virtue or honor

Are the individual ranks of this sex endowed,

By the manifold form of things?

Sacred histories teach us.

The first inhabitant of Paradise, Adam, was made outside; woman, within, so that the very place itself [Note: [Col. 1813D] Manuscript: *ex*.] might indicate how excellent is the creation of women, who, formed from the rib of man, should be strong as though made of bone.

This strength has shown itself in many women, when the courage of men had failed. [Note: [Col. 1813D] Cousin emends *exaruerit* to *exaruit*, contrary to the authority of the manuscript and the laws of the rhythm.]

As an example stands the judge Deborah, and the widow who laid Holofernes low [Note: [Col. 1814D] Cousin: Judith.], and the illustrious mother of seven brothers, celebrated for her merits in solemn Mass.

[Col. 1813C] Jephthah’s daughter, born to a victor, encouraged her father’s own right hand against her throat, choosing rather to die than that her father should be deprived of the favour granted him in fulfilment of his vow.

Glory of Christ.

LXXXVIII. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

If women may contend with men in the virtue of steadfastness, what man could be matched, in strength of mind, with Jephthah’s daughter, who, lest her father be guilty regarding his vow, offered herself to her father as a victim?

What would she have done in the contest of the martyrs, if she had been compelled to deny the Lord?

Whence does the virgin possess so great a steadfastness? [Col. 1813D] From a certain spiritual grace, so that the solemn hymns of virgins may celebrate a virgin’s death.

Many men, by outstanding deeds, freed the faithful from enemies; Esther alone, by delivering the people, deserved from this a festal proclamation [Note: [Col. 1814D] Cousin prints *festinum*, “hasty.”], so that it may be clear how greatly the virtue of women excels.

[Col. 1814A] Indeed, the more fragile this sex is, the more wonderful is its virtue, raising a greater proclamation of praise into a title to be exalted on high.

Glory of Christ.

LXXXIX. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

To come to our own times: who, considering the grace that God has poured forth, will not be able to gather from many instances that women excel, when he looks upon Anne after Mary, and also beholds Elizabeth?

A woman anointed Christ’s head; a woman made him Christ in the flesh. It is established that he received the mysteries of priest and king from a woman. [Note: [Col. 1814D] The manuscript has *Mistericia*, with the letters *ci* marked by an obelus.]

[Col. 1814B] And the sex which bore him also handed on the sacraments. And bearing spices to him when buried, this sex [Note: [Col. 1814D] Cousin reads *hinc*, “thence.” *Hic* refers to *sexus*, “sex.”] first saw the joys of his resurrection; and woman, made more vile through sin, surpassed all others in this grace, so that it may be clear how great a joy is the conversion of sinners.

COMMON OF VIRGINS.

XC. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

Bride of Christ, both virgin and mother, whose palm of victory is celebrated by this day: the present feast doubles the palm; as virgin she overcomes the flesh, as martyr the enemy.

Therefore let psalms resound here, and lessons ring out there.

[Col. 1814C] This twofold palm is rarer in men; in women it shines more abundantly. As their sex is weaker, so their virtue is more wonderful; and their sacrifice is so much the more pleasing, the purer it is.

Whole both in spirit and body, the virgin becomes a true holocaust. Refer to the burning of this sacrifice the type of the red and tender heifer. There is shadow there, but truth here, if you compare the realities properly with their signs.

She who had consecrated her heart to God by herself now offers her body also through the executioner. The soul first consecrated to God fearlessly exposes its body to the enemy.

Glory of Christ.

XCI. AT THE SECOND NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1814D]

Since God is wonderful in his saints [Note: [Col. 1814D] Thus the manuscript; Cousin: “Since God is wonderful.”], he is pre-eminent in the merits of victories. But when he grants victory to women, who would not rank such grace before all others? The frailer the sex, the more wonderful its virtue.

[Col. 1815A] The steadfastness of women overcomes exquisite kinds of tortures. Either their courage is wonderful, or the punishment of these contests is easy; but we believe, by God’s ordering, that both are brought about for the better.

Love is strong as death, and this fire has no extinction. Many waters cannot extinguish the flame of invincible charity; nor is the sex ever weak [Note: [Col. 1815C] Thus the manuscript; perhaps one should read *numquam*, “never.”] in the presence of this love, however fragile it may be.

What will bearded young men say when delicate virgins endure such things? Let the stronger sex blush at this, where the weaker bears so much.

Glory of Christ.

XCII. AT THE THIRD NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1815B]

How faithful she was to her bridegroom, both her life and her death have taught. The one preserved her body whole; the other offered it as a holocaust. The virgin is bride; the virgin is bridegroom. The bride is mother; the bridegroom is martyr.

Such a bridegroom befitted such a bride, who followed him wherever he went, whom neither the beauty of sacred flesh divided nor unequal love revealed in death.

The other women follow the bridegroom; she proceeds at his joined side [Note: [Col. 1815C] Manuscript: *jucto*; Cousin: *victo*, “conquered.”]. And the bridegroom’s queen, holding his right hand, has the remaining crowd following her.

She shines in gilded raiment, [Col. 1815C] she who possesses the crowns mentioned above. This is the best of the other women’s adornment: it is incorruptible and radiant.

A garland woven of roses and lilies is the distinction of martyr and virgin, most sweet in fragrance to Christ. [Col. 1816A] The martyr offers a rose; the virgin, a lily.

Garments give their tokens: shining linen [Note: [Col. 1815C] Cousin: *cadens*, “falling”; the manuscript is stained at this point.], crimson purple. Her steps are beautiful [Note: [Col. 1815C] Cousin: *pulchri*; the correction is unnecessary, since in Cicero’s time the letter *h* had not yet been inserted there.] in sandals, and the bridegroom praises them in the songs.

What her adornment is has been said; what her progress is must be told.

Glory of Christ.

XCIII. AT LAUDS AND AT VESPERS.

She advances, rising like the dawn, she who is joined to the bridal chamber of the heavenly bridegroom. [Note: [Col. 1816C] Manuscript: *junguntur*, “are joined.”] As the betrothed bride had made a covenant in faith, there she now dwells as wife. Thus, covenants made in faith become there an everlasting union in reality.

There she has angels as bridal attendants [Note: [Col. 1816C] Manuscript: *habent*, “have.”], [Col. 1816B] whom we have here as our own guardians. An angelic procession conducts her to the heavenly joys of the bridal chamber.

Here the virgin meets virgins [Note: [Col. 1816C] Manuscript: *oviam*, not *aviam*, as Cousin writes.]; there the mother has martyrs.

When she has thus been brought to the bridegroom and rested in his embrace, who could say what glory she enjoys? What mind could conceive such joys? Certainly no one is equal to this—unless perhaps when one has experienced these things.

These are the things which no eye has seen [Note: [Col. 1816C] Manuscript: *oculos*, “eyes.”], nor can they be grasped by human hearts, which God offers to those who love him, prepared from eternal ages.

Glory of Christ.

ON THE FEAST OF ST MARY MAGDALENE.

XCIV. AT THE FIRST NOCTURN AND AT VESPERS.

[Col. 1816C]

The solemnity of the blessed sinful woman brings especial joy to sinners.

[Note: [Col. 1816C] The remaining leaves have long since perished, as is clear from the worn final leaf. Besides several hymns, they contained sequences, as we observed at the beginning.] [lacuna]

HYMN FOR THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY.

(Daniel, *Thesaurus hymnologicus*, II, 59.)

[Col. 1815C]

He sends to the virgin  
Not just any angel,  
But his own strength—  
The archangel—  
The lover of humankind.

Let him dispatch  
A mighty messenger for us;  
Let him bring about  
Nature’s exception  
In a virgin’s childbirth.

[Col. 1815]

The King of glory, once born,  
Surpasses nature;  
He reigns and rules  
And removes from the midst  
The leaven of dross.

May he crush the heights  
Of the proud,  
Tread upon the necks  
Of the lofty by his own strength,  
Mighty in battle.

[Col. 1816C]

May he cast out  
The ruler of the world  
And make his mother  
A participant with him  
In the Father’s sovereignty.

Go forth, you who are sent;  
Set forth these gifts;  
Reveal the veil  
Of the ancient letter  
By the power of the messenger.

[Col. 1817]

Draw near, messenger;  
Say, “Hail,” close by;  
Say, “Full of grace”;  
Say, “The Lord is with you”;  
And say, “Do not fear.”

The virgin, receiving  
God’s deposit,  
May in it fulfil  
Her chaste purpose  
And maintain her vow.

The maiden hears  
And receives the message;  
[Col. 1817] she believes and conceives  
And bears a son—  
Yet a wondrous one:

The counsellor  
Of humankind,  
The God of the mighty,  
The Father of those to come,  
Steadfast in faith.

May his steadfastness  
Make us steadfast,  
Lest worldly instability  
Cast us, made unstable,  
[Col. 1818] down with itself.

But may the giver of pardon,  
Pardon having been granted,  
Grace having been obtained  
Through the mother of grace,  
Dwell in us.

May he grant us  
Forgiveness of sin,  
Wash away guilt,  
And give us a homeland  
In the height of the stars.

[Note: [Col. 1817] Two admirers of this outstanding sequence come to mind; both the authority of the indexes and the judgment itself, suited to the poem’s genius, advise that their eulogies be repeated here. I mean Clichtoveus in the *Elucidatorium*: “This prose is elegantly and gracefully composed according to rhythmic law. Its author is said to have been P. A., a man distinguished in his own age by the brilliance and renown of virtue and learning. Certainly, the elegance and charm of this melody readily reveal him to have been most fully endowed with every kind of learning.”

Add Rambach, *Anthologie*, I, 264: “A. first wrote several church songs for the use of the monastery of the Paraclete (Henry of Ghent, *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, appendix, ch. 3), among which the following may also belong. Despite the evil reputation into which the branding of its author as a heretic had brought it, it found extraordinary approval both in France and in other countries, and was still frequently sung in Protestant churches long after the Reformation, on the Feast of the Annunciation and during Advent. An imitation of it is the song of the Bohemian Brethren, formerly not unknown among us: ‘When the gracious God …’ (Wackernagel, p. 301).”

John of Salisbury had already rendered it into German: “The lover of mankind sent to the maiden” (Hoffmann, *D. K.*, p. 143). “In the reprinted edition here, three—more correctly two, stanzas 11 and 12—superfluous and partly objectionable stanzas have been omitted.”

And indeed it was granted to the learned man to have a nose: he detected what codex Munich 10 confirms on sufficiently ancient authority; codices Fr., Nb., and Lud. also agree. For all of them omit those stanzas as spurious and alien to Abelard’s genius. The sequence was sung either on the Feast of the Annunciation, during Advent, or in the Mass for the Sunday after Advent; nevertheless, it is not especially frequent in German missals.]

RHYTHM ON THE HOLY TRINITY.

(See *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXI, col. 1411, among the miscellaneous poems of the Venerable Hildebert. It begins: “Alpha and Omega,” etc.)

VARIOUS LAMENTS.

(Greith, *Spicilegium Vaticanum*, Frauenfeld, 1838, octavo, p. 123.)

[Col. 1817]

I. PETER ABAELARD’S LAMENT OF DINAH, DAUGHTER OF JACOB.

Offspring of Abraham, daughter of Israel,  
Illustrious by the blood of the patriarchs,  
By the rape of an uncircumcised man  
I became the prey of a baseborn man.

The greatest stain upon a holy race,  
Mocked in the sport of an enemy people!

Woe to me, miserable woman,  
Ruined by my own self!

What good was it to me  
To look upon foreigners?  
How miserably was I known,  
Because I wished to know them!

Woe to me, miserable woman,  
Ruined by my own self!

Shechem, to the destruction  
Of your own race,  
You have become an everlasting reproach  
To our descendants!

Woe to you, miserable man,  
Ruined by your own self!

In vain did circumcision  
Make you a proselyte,  
When you did not wish  
To remove the foreskin of disgrace.

Woe to you, miserable man,  
Ruined by your own self!

[Col. 1817]

Though compelled to seize me,  
Seized by my beauty,  
You would not have been beyond pardon  
Before any judge.

You did not judge so,  
Simeon and Levi—  
In the same deed  
Too cruel and too righteous.

You equated the innocent  
With the guilty in punishment;  
indeed, you disturbed your father also,  
and for this are to be cursed.

The impulse of love,  
The sanctification of guilt—  
what are these in judgment  
but a diminution of guilt?

Youthful age, lighter  
And less discerning,  
ought to have been borne less harshly  
by those more discerning in punishment.

The brothers’ anger should have been softened  
by the honour  
which the ruler of the land bestowed on them  
because he had taken a foreign woman.

Woe to me!  
Woe to you,  
Pitiful young man!

You fall in the common slaughter  
Of so great a people!

II. JACOB’S LAMENT OVER HIS SONS.

[Col. 1818]

Unhappy sons,  
Born to an unhappy father:  
such vengeance is given  
for my new crime.

For what offence  
is so great a loss the punishment?  
By what sin have I deserved  
to be struck by this sword?

Joseph, glory of the race,  
Splendour of sons,  
Devoured by beasts,  
Has fallen by a most wretched death.

Simeon in chains  
Pays for my crimes;  
after the mother and Benjamin,  
now I have lost my joys.

Joseph, by the envy of your brothers  
Mighty through divine grace,  
what portents, my son,  
were those dreams?

What did the sun, what the moon, my son,  
what the stars, what the sheaves—  
which I long pondered with you—  
bear within themselves of mystery?

[Col. 1819]

Last-born among your brothers,  
First of all to them in love,  
whom your dying mother called Benoni,  
but your rejoicing father called Benjamin:

By your endearments you revealed to your wretched father his old age,  
giving back to me the likeness of your brother  
and the face of your beautiful mother.

Your childish prattle,  
sweeter than all songs,  
was sweet to the old man  
desolate in misery.

Your tender words,  
unformed in expression,  
surpassed every honeycomb  
of eloquence.

You bore in yourself the greatest solace  
for two whom I had lost, my son:  
with equal beauty representing them both,  
you thus gave me back myself.

Thus I lost them with you,  
and, my son, I held this soul  
beyond what was right.

You, small in age,  
were greatest in sorrow,  
as to your mother, so to your father.

God, whom I serve,  
make us be joined to one another in your presence.

III. LAMENT OF THE VIRGINS OF ISRAEL OVER THE DAUGHTER OF JEPHTHAH THE GILEADITE.

Come, virgins, unmarried as custom requires,  
to the festal dances as custom requires!  
Let the songs be mournful,  
and let lamentations be celebrated as songs.

Let the faces be unadorned, sad,  
like those who mourn and weep;  
let gilded robes be far away,  
and rich adornments be kept at a distance.

The Gileadite virgin, Jephthah’s daughter,  
pitiably made her father’s victim,  
requires every year  
the virgins’ elegies  
and the measures of a pious song  
due to a virgin’s courage.

O virgin more astonishing than lamentable!  
O man scarcely to be found worthy to resemble her!

Lest her father’s vow be void  
and he defraud the Lord of what he promised—  
the vow by which he saved the people—  
she urges it upon her own throat.

When this victor returns  
from battle with the people,  
she is the first, out of joy,  
to run forward with a timbrel.

Seeing her and groaning, her anxious father, conscious of his vow, turns applause into lamentation. The people turn triumph into mourning.

“You have deceived me, my daughter,”  
says the leader, “my only one—  
you who have been deceived,  
whose loss destroys  
the joys granted us  
by the Lord through this victory.”

[Col. 1819]

She replies: “Would that my ignorance might make me so gentle a victim for so great a matter.

Abraham, desiring to sacrifice his son, did not receive from the Lord this grace: that he would have the boy himself as victim. He who rejected the boy thus receives the girl.

Understand what an honour this is to my sex; behold the fruit of your womb. For what glory is this to you? Be a man in spirit as in sex, I beg you now.

Do not oppose either my soul or your own, if you wish to prefer me to your own soul. Let not misguided affection permit you to harm all men by a bad example. Offer me to the Lord, lest you alone offend the Lord together with the people, and therefore lose his favour.

This is cruelty here, but piety toward the Lord, who would not have given victory if he had not wished a victim.

Therefore, father, pay the debt and appease the Lord, lest perhaps, when it is pleasing, it may no longer be lawful.

What the tender virgin does not tremble to endure, let a man’s right hand sustain itself in inflicting. The pledge of the vow itself binds you.

But grant me the space of two months, so that, wandering through valleys and hills with my companions and raising my voice in lamentations and tears, I may mourn that the Lord thus deprives me of offspring.

And let my curse be the sanction of the law: let the sacrifice of my undefiled flesh, which knew no pollution or stain, have no remedy.”

When these things had been done, the only daughter returned to her father. Entering the recesses of a private chamber, she laid aside the coverings of her mournful dress.

Immediately, entering the bath amid the surrounding choir of virgins, she refreshed herself a little, weary as she was; the bath cleansed and revived her body, squalid with dust, and her limbs weakened by travel.

The boxes of her beloved ointments contain varied kinds of perfume, which the weeping virgins bring. Some anoint her with them; the rest arrange her hair, to prepare her for the Lord.

[Col. 1820]

A little later, the virgin, washed from the bath, sends word to her father to build an altar and hasten the fire, while she in the meantime prepares the victim—a victim fitting for God and becoming to a ruler.

Oh, with what lamentation from everyone is this message received! The leader presses the people to hasten these things, and the virgins to prepare her adornment, that she may prepare herself for death as though for a wedding.

One offers linen moistened with her own tears; another purple damp with her weeping. A necklace varied with gold, gems, and pearls adorns her breast, and adorns it still more by doing so. Earrings and rings, with golden bracelets, weigh upon the tender little body of the virgin.

No longer bearing the delay caused by the weight and adornment of things, the virgin rises from the bed and pushes away what remained, saying: “These are enough for a bride; they are far too much for one about to perish.”

At once she took up the bare sword which she had brought to her father. What more, what further can we say? Why do we utter tears, why make lamentations? Yet we bring what we have undertaken to its end, lamenting and weeping.

With garments gathered about her, upon the steps of the kindled altar, the sword is handed over by the maiden herself; on bended knees he killed her.

O mind bereft of reason in the judge! O mad zeal in the ruler! O father, yet enemy of his race, who washed away his guilt by the death of his only daughter!

Hebrew virgins, speak! Remember the distinguished virgin, the illustrious maiden of Israel, ennobled by this most noble virgin!

IV. ISRAEL’S LAMENT OVER SAMSON.

Truly your judgments, O God, are a deep abyss: the more dreadful because they are more hidden, and because every power is weaker in proportion as it approaches them.

The strongest of men, announced by an angel, the renowned Nazarite, Israel’s shield—let not a heart of stone fail to weep for him thus lost.

[Col. 1821]

Delilah first deprived him of his sacred hair; afterward his enemies deprived him of sight.

His strength exhausted,  
his eyes taken away,  
the noble athlete  
is given over to the mill.

Shut in prison and now deprived of the light of his eyes, he sweats at the mill as though oppressed by twin darknesses. His limbs, formerly accustomed to martial contests, are broken.

What, impious Delilah, what do you gain by these things? What have you done? What rewards do you seek through so many crimes?

No favour endures long for a traitor.

A scanty meal barely sustains him, which even a beast of burden, worn out by harsh and unaccustomed labour, receives only rarely—driven by frequent goads and hostile men like an animal.

When his strength has returned and his rights have been restored, he is led to slaughter before his trembling enemies, so that by death he may put an end to all sufferings.

His mind, long roused, is turned from games to serious action; with both left and right hand pressed against the columns, he mingles the deaths of enemies with his own.

O woman, ever the greatest ruin of the strong, created for destruction! She immediately cast down the father of all, and offers the cup of death to everyone.

Who is thought holier than David, wiser than Solomon? Or who is found more foolish through her? Who among the strong is weakened like Samson, strongest of men?

Noble Adam, the creature of God’s right hand, she quickly overthrew; the one whom he had received as his own help, he found an enemy.

From that time woman fashioned the greatest weapons against men.

Open your breast to an asp or fire, whoever you are who are wise, rather than entrust yourself to feminine allurements, [Col. 1821] unless you prefer to hasten with those mentioned above to most certain ruin.

V. DAVID’S LAMENT OVER ABNER, SON OF NER, WHOM JOAB KILLED.

Most faithful Abner,  
Most valiant in war,  
Love and delight  
Of military glory:

What force could not prevail against,  
Deceit accomplished against you.  
May he through whom you perish, himself ruined,  
Meet a like end.

Worthy of no tears is he  
whom your abominable treachery  
gives to all men.

Your pitiable fall compels even an enemy to continual tears, and pity melts hearts of adamant.

While you were the open enemy of the kingdom, you were always exalted by brilliant triumphs.

You punished us with many losses, suffering none: mighty in arms, mighty in judgment, a perfect man, a strong wall of Israel. Therefore you were at once my enemy and my greatest friend!

At last, yielding to our wishes, you make a treaty in these things [manuscript perhaps: *inis*] and, in hope of peace, lay down arms—fatally unguarded—while you believed that you had provided against every danger.

Trusting in our faith, you fell, because, truthful man, you judged ours by your own. He who feared the name of Abner when armed prevailed over you, Abner, when unarmed.

Not daring to meet you on the road, through this crime he defiled the gates of the city.

Soldiers of the army, weeping, lament so great a leader thus laid low! Princes of justice, take up zeal to avenge so abominable a deed.

VI. DAVID’S LAMENT OVER SAUL AND JONATHAN.

Comfort of sorrows,  
Remedy for labours,  
My lyre—  
Now, since the pain is greater  
And the grief more just,  
You are more necessary.

The great slaughter of the people,  
The death of king and son,  
The enemies’ victory,  
The desolation of commanders,  
The despair of the multitude  
Fill all things with mourning.

[Col. 1822]

Amalek prevails while Israel falls; faithless Philistia rejoices while Judaea wastes itself in lamentation.

The faithless people insults the faithful; the opposing nation is divided in the greatest honour and made a mockery before all.

The king whom it first made available to them falls defeated. Such an election is a cause of mockery; such is the anointing of the great prophet.

Those who mock say: “Behold him of whom they boast: how the highest God has destroyed them, while the Lord lies overthrown, slain by many.”

Saul, strongest of kings; Jonathan, unconquered courage: he whom none could conquer was permitted to kill you.

As though he had not been consecrated with the Lord’s oil, a wicked hand cuts his throat with the sword in battle.

Jonathan, dearer to me than a brother, one soul with me: what sins, what crimes have torn apart our hearts?

Mountains of Gilboa, be without dew and rain; let not the first fruits of your fields aid your inhabitants.

Woe, woe to you, earth wet with royal blood! Why, Jonathan, did an impious hand strike you down? Where are the Lord’s anointed and glorious Israel, who have perished miserably with their own people?

Now, Jonathan, you are to me more to be mourned than all else; amid every joy, tears will be everlasting.

Daughters of Zion, take up lamentation over Saul, by whose lavish generosity purple garments adorned you.

Alas! Why did I yield to most evil counsel, so that I was not your support in battle? Or that, pierced together with you, I might happily have died, since what love can do has nothing greater than this?

To live after you is continually to die; nor is half a soul sufficient for life.

[Col. 1823]

At that time of utmost distress, I ought to have returned to you even one service of friendship: a participant in triumph or companion in ruin, that I might either rescue you or fall with you, ending for you the life which you saved so often, [Col. 1823] so that even death might join us more than separate us.

Meanwhile, having gained an ill-fated victory, how vain, how brief were the joys I received here! How swiftly there followed the harshest messenger, whom pride spoke in his own soul!

[Col. 1824]

The death he announces gathers the dead together, so that the messenger of grief may be a companion of grief.

I give rest to the strings; would that I could do the same to lamentations and tears! With hands exhausted by striking and voices hoarse from lamenting, even the spirit fails.

APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF PETER ABAELARD.

[Col. 1823]

BOOK AGAINST HERESIES.

(Edition of the Works, 1616, from an old manuscript of François d’Amboise.)

CHAPTER ONE.

[Col. 1823A]

Heretics say and believe that this world and all that are seen in it—namely, the heaven which we see, the sun, moon, stars, earth, all animals, human beings, and the things seen upon it; the sea, fish, and all things seen or existing in it, in its hidden places—were not made by almighty God, but by the prince of evil spirits.

Against these heretics and their malicious error stand very many authorities of the New Testament. In the Gospel of blessed John (chapter 1), who wrote against heretics affirming such an error, it is recorded that he says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

From this it is clear that almighty God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—created and made all visible and invisible things.

And the blessed apostle Paul testifies in the Epistle to the Hebrews (chapter 11), saying: “By faith we understand that the ages were framed by the word of God.” Likewise, in the same epistle [Col. 1823B] (chapter 3): “God is he who created all things.”

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 4), it is found that all the apostles and disciples, gathered together in one place, raised their voices unanimously, saying: “Lord God, you made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them,” etc.

Likewise John says in the Apocalypse (chapter 10): “The angel whom I saw standing upon the sea and upon the earth raised his hand to heaven, and swore by him who lives for ages of ages, who created heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them,” etc.

Likewise, in the same book (chapter 14): “Fear the Lord and give him honour, because the hour of his judgment has come; and worship him who made heaven, earth, the sea, all things in them, and fountains of waters.”

Likewise Paul said in the Epistle to the Hebrews (chapter 1): “And you, Lord, in the beginning founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands.”

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew (chapter 11): “I confess to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth.”

Likewise [Col. 1823C] John (chapter 1) says concerning the same: “And the world was made through him.”

Let these New Testament authorities suffice for you, although many authorities in the New and Old Testaments and in the prophets are found testifying likewise that God created and made all visible [Col. 1824A] and invisible things.

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 14), Paul and Barnabas say: “Brothers, we announce to you that you should turn from these vain things to the living and true God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all things in them, giving rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.”

CHAPTER II.

In saying that there are two gods, one almighty and the other evil, the heretics think contrary to all divine Scripture; for all divinely inspired Scripture—namely, that of the New and Old Testaments and all the prophets—affirms one God alone.

For blessed Paul says: “There is one God and Father of all, who is above all and in all of us” (Eph. 4).

Likewise Mark records in the Gospel (chapter 12) that one of the scribes asked the Lord Jesus which was the first commandment of all. Jesus answered him: “The first commandment of all is: Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one God. And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.” And the scribe said to him: “Well, master, you have spoken truly, because God is one, and there is no other besides him.”

CHAPTER III.

Heretics say that the law of Moses, which we call the Old Law, was not given by almighty God but by the prince of evil spirits. Very many authorities of divine Scripture contradict this error.

For the Lord says in the Gospel according to Matthew (chapter 5): “Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets. I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfil it.” He who is the Son of God would not have said that he came to fulfil the law if it had been given by the devil; rather, he would have destroyed it.

Likewise, according to Luke (chapter 2): “When the days of Mary’s purification according to the law of Moses had been completed, they brought Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord,” etc.; and “to offer a sacrifice, according to what is written [Col. 1824C] in the law of the Lord.” And again (ibid.): “When they had completed all things according to the law of the Lord, they returned to their city of Galilee, Nazareth.”

This is certain and beyond doubt: Christ, who is true God and true man, would not permit the precepts of a diabolical law to be observed or fulfilled in himself.

Likewise, in the Gospel according to John, the Lord says (chapter 5): “Do not think that I shall accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses,” etc. “For if you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”

It is as though he said: Whoever does not believe the words of the old law, and in his faith does not receive the words of the Gospel, cannot believe or receive them for his salvation.

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Luke (chapter 10), the Lord said to a lawyer who asked him what he should do to possess eternal life, asking him what was written in the law. The lawyer answered him: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” etc. Jesus said to him: “You have answered correctly; do this, and you shall live.” For if the law of Moses had not been given by God, Christ would never have promised life for keeping it.

Likewise, the Lord testifies in the same Gospel (chapter 16): “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.” This shows that observance of the law and prophets does not permit a person to go to the places of infernal punishments.

Likewise, in the same Gospel (chapter 24), after Christ had risen from the dead, appearing to two disciples going to the village of Emmaus and testifying to the law, he said: “Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” And beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

For if the law had been given to Moses by the devil, Christ would never have taught and interpreted it to his disciples.

Likewise, Truth said in the same Gospel: “It is necessary that all things written about me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms be fulfilled.”

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew, when the Pharisees asked why his disciples transgressed the traditions of the elders, the Lord says (chapter 15): “And why do you transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition? For God said: ‘Honour your father and your mother’; and ‘Whoever curses father or mother shall surely die.’”

It is certain that this testimony comes from the law of Moses; Christ said that this testimony was spoken and given by God. Therefore the law was given by God.

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles Paul says (chapter 14): “I proclaim to you God, who made heaven, the world, and all things in it. He is Lord of heaven and earth.”

Likewise Paul, in the same book, defending himself before Felix, governor of Caesarea, against the charges brought by the Jews, says (chapter 24): “I confess this to you: according to the sect which the Jews call a heresy, I now serve the Father, believing all things written in the law and the prophets.”

Likewise Paul, in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 8: “Do you say in ignorance, ‘Is the law sin?’ By no means! The law indeed is holy and good, and the commandment holy, just, and good.”

CHAPTER IV.

There are also certain heretics who assert that Moses was a magician [Col. 1825D] and that almighty God did not speak to him or give him the law.

Against this error Paul wrote in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying (chapter 1): “In many ways and by many means God formerly spoke to the fathers in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son.” But Moses is one of the prophets to whom God spoke. He is also called faithful in the Lord, to whom God spoke.

Likewise, in the same epistle (chapter 3): “Every house is built by someone; but God is he who created all things. Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, for a testimony of those words which were to be spoken; but Christ as a son in his own house. We are that house, if we hold firm to the end the confidence and glory of hope.”

The apostle testifies not that Moses was a magician, but that he was a faithful servant in God’s house.

Likewise, in many writings of the New and Old Testaments and of the prophets, Moses is called God’s friend and faithful servant. As blessed Paul recalled concerning him in the Epistle to the Hebrews, [Col. 1826A] saying (chapter 11): “By faith Moses, when he had grown great, denied that he was the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be afflicted with the people of God than to have the pleasure of temporary sin; reckoning the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasure of the Egyptians. He looked to God’s recompense.”

This makes it wholly clear that blessed Paul did not distrust Moses, Moses’ law, or the God of the Hebrews. Rather, in words he asserted, and in his heart believed, that Moses was holy and good, the law holy and good, and the God of the Hebrews almighty God.

CHAPTER V.

Heretics following the heretic Tatian, who condemned marriage, say and believe that no marriage of a man and woman joined together can in any way be saved. But many testimonies of the divine Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments oppose this error. It is found in the [Col. 1826B] Gospel according to Matthew that the Lord, when the Pharisees questioned him, said (ch. XIX): “Is it lawful for a man to dismiss his wife for any cause whatever?” He answered them: “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’? Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let no man separate,” and likewise a woman. But everything that prevents a human being from eternal life is evil; yet if marriage were evil, Christ would never forbid its dissolution, nor would he consent to it, since he consents to no evil.

Likewise, Mark says concerning the same matter (ch. X): “From the beginning of creation God made them male and female,” etc. Likewise, in Luke (ch. I): “In the days of Herod, king of Judaea, there was a certain priest named Zacharias, of the division of Abia,” etc. “And they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the [Col. 1826C] commandments and ordinances of the Lord.” It follows: Thus, since they were righteous, they were being saved; and they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both had advanced in their days.

It should be noted that it was not owing to the husband that he did not have a child, but to the woman, because she was barren. And the angel of the Lord, appearing to Zacharias in the Temple, said to him (ibid.): “Do not fear, Zacharias; for your wife shall bear you a son, and you shall call his name John,” etc. “For he shall be great before the Lord,” etc. Likewise (ibid.): “How shall I know this? For I am old, and my wife has advanced in her days.” Note that he said this because he did not believe the angel’s words on account of his wife’s old age, since she herself had passed the age of conception. Likewise: “They made signs to his father what name he wished him to be called.” The Evangelist would not call him father unless he had a son. For no one can be a natural father unless he has a natural son. Likewise: “Zacharias, his father, was filled with the Holy Spirit.” [Col. 1826D] Behold a threefold affirmation of fatherhood. The Gospel does not deny that both were righteous before God because of the begetting of a son, provided that they walk in all the commandments of the Lord; nor does either the Old Testament or the New.

Likewise, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, the Apostle, giving counsel to faithful Christians, said (ch. VII): “On account of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. Let the husband render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. A woman does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; and likewise a husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not defraud one another, except perhaps by agreement for a time, that you may be free for prayer”—that is: Do not practise continence when the other is unwilling. Likewise, in the same place (ibid.): “I say to the unmarried and widows: let them remain as I am. But if they do not practise continence, let them marry. It is better to marry than to burn. But to those joined in marriage I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband. But if she departs, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband.” It follows: “If anyone therefore has an [Col. 1827A] unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not dismiss her,” etc. “For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and conversely,” etc. “Otherwise your children would be unclean; but now they are clean.” The Apostle did not believe that believing husbands and wives lose their holiness by rendering the marital due, if their other works are good.

Likewise, the Apostle says in the same place: “If you take a wife, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.” Likewise, the Apostle says in the same place: “He who joins his virgin in marriage does well; and he who does not join her in marriage does better.” The Apostle would not give his disciples these aforesaid commands or write these words to them if he believed that they were to be damned on account of this marital act. Likewise, the Apostle says in the First Epistle to Timothy (ch. IV): “The Spirit expressly says that in the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, speaking falsehood in hypocrisy, forbidding marriage.”

[Col. 1827B] Note that the Holy Spirit openly declared that some would depart from the faith, cling to doctrines of demons, and speak falsehood in hypocrisy; and such persons forbid marriage. Likewise, in the same epistle (ch. V): “I desire younger women to marry, bear children, manage households, and give the adversary no occasion for reproach.” Note that the Apostle did not believe that this act supplied married people with any occasion of condemnation.

Likewise, we have this in the First Epistle of blessed Peter. Blessed Peter the Apostle, who was appointed by God prince of all the apostles and likewise head of the whole Church—as Christ says in the Gospel: “You shall be called Cephas” (John I); and again: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI)—after writing his teaching to faithful Christian men, wrote to women concerning how they should be subject to their own husbands, preserving humility and modesty, saying: “Likewise let women be subject to [Col. 1827C] their husbands, so that, if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives. Thus also formerly holy women hoping in God adorned themselves for their husbands, as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord. You are her daughters if you do good” (I Pet. III), etc.

Here blessed Peter indicates that husbands should not depart from wives, nor wives from husbands, because Abraham did not depart from Sarah his wife except through death, but knew her by divine prompting and begot a son, as Elkanah [knew] Susanna, and Joachin Anna. Likewise, blessed Paul says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (ch. XI): “I wish you to know that the head of every man is Christ, the head of woman is man, and the head of Christ is God. Man is not from woman, but woman from man. For man was not created for woman, but woman for man. Nevertheless, in the Lord neither is man without woman nor woman without man.”

Likewise, it is found in John that Jesus our Saviour, his mother, and his disciples were invited and came to a wedding; [Col. 1827D] and at that wedding, before his disciples, he performed the beginning of his signs—namely, making wine from water. Therefore it is altogether certain that weddings are good, because it is not to be believed that Christ would have come, or performed so great a miracle, unless they were good. Likewise, Paul says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (ch. VII): “A woman is bound by the law to her husband as long as her husband lives. But if her husband sleeps, she is released from the law of her husband and may marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord.” Likewise Paul says to Timothy (ch. II): “A woman shall be saved through the bearing of children, if she continues in faith, love, and sanctification with sobriety.”

## CHAPTER VI

Likewise, they say that John the Baptist was announced not by a good angel but by a demonic one, and they do not believe him to have been good. But many testimonies in the Gospels are found against this error. Thus, in the Gospel of blessed John, John himself wrote, saying (ch. I): “There was a man sent from God, whose name was [Col. 1828A] John. He came as a witness,” etc. Likewise, in the same place he bore witness concerning Christ (ibid.): “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.” Likewise, John bore witness concerning him: “He who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit of God descending and remaining, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit,’” etc. Likewise, in the same Gospel (ch. III): “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears,” etc. “Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.”

In the Gospel according to Matthew Christ himself commends John, saying (ch. XI): “Amen I say to you: among those born of women there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist.” Likewise (ibid.): “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A prophet? Yes, I say to you, and more than a prophet. For this is he of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who shall prepare your way before you.’” Whoever thinks wrongly or perversely concerning John is opposed to Christ, to the apostles, and to the Catholic faith.

We have in the Gospel that John the Baptist himself [Col. 1828B] baptized Christ in the river Jordan, saw the Holy Spirit descending upon him in the form of a dove, and heard the Father’s voice saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII). If he had been announced by an evil spirit, as the heretics say, Christ would never have permitted himself to be baptized by him, nor would he have wished so great a sacrament to be initiated by him. Likewise, in Matthew Christ himself approves him, saying to the Pharisees (ch. XXI): “Amen, amen, I say to you: tax collectors and prostitutes shall go before you into the kingdom of God. For John the Baptist came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him. Tax collectors, sinners, and prostitutes believed him. But you, when you saw him, did not afterward repent so as to believe him.” Behold: Christ declares concerning John the Baptist that John himself walked in, and preached, the way of righteousness by which one goes to the kingdom of God. He would not have done this if he had been evil or announced by an evil spirit.

Likewise, in the [Col. 1828C] Gospel according to John, concerning the commendation of John the Baptist (ch. V): “You sent to John, and he bears witness to the truth. Yet I do not receive testimony from a human being; but I say these things so that you may be saved. He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing for a time to rejoice in his light.”

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning Christ’s Incarnation, there are certain heretics among these who follow the Condonian heresy, who say that Christ was not born of a woman, did not have true flesh, did not truly die, and suffered nothing, but only feigned the Passion. They do not believe that he ate or drank; they say that he had, as it were, a phantom body; nor do they believe that he rose again.

Against this error of the heretics, who do not believe that Christ was born of a true virgin woman, we have testimony in Matthew (ch. II): “When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judaea,” etc. “When the magi saw the star, they rejoiced with exceedingly great joy. And entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother,” etc. Likewise, in the same place (ibid.): “An angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: ‘Rise, and take the child with Mary his mother.’” Likewise, in the Gospel according to Luke (ch. II): “Joseph went up from Galilee to Bethlehem, the city, that he might be registered there with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was pregnant. And the days were fulfilled for her to give birth, and she gave birth to her firstborn son.” Likewise, in the same place, the angel of the Lord announced his birth to the shepherds, saying (ibid.): “Behold, I proclaim to you great joy, because a Saviour has been born to you today, who is Christ in the flesh of David; and this shall be a sign to you: you will find the child Jesus laid in a manger.” Likewise, in the same place: “When eight days had been completed for the child to be circumcised, his name was called Jesus”—the name which had been called by the angel before he was conceived in the womb. Likewise, in the same place: “When Jesus had become twelve years old, as they went up [Col. 1829A] to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day, and when the days were completed and they returned, the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it,” etc. “And Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, grace, and the Holy Spirit before God and men.”

Likewise, Paul testifies in the Epistle to the Galatians that Christ was born of a woman when he says (ch. IV): “But when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, made under the law, in order that he might redeem those who were under the law.” Heretic, behold many testimonies concerning Christ’s conception, birth, circumcision, childhood, age, youth, and also that Christ was born of a woman and made under the law. Likewise, John says of Christ’s birth (ch. XVIII): “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world: that I might bear witness to the truth.”

Testimonies concerning Christ’s Incarnation against heretics who do not believe that Christ had true flesh but say that he assumed an aerial body. [Col. 1829B] But against this error John wrote his Gospel, saying (ch. I): “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.” Likewise, in the same Gospel (ch. XIX): “The Jews asked Pilate, because it was the Preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the Sabbath, and that their legs should be broken. Therefore the soldiers broke the legs of the first thief and of the other who was crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs; but one of the soldiers opened his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out. And he who saw it bore witness, and his witness is true.”

Likewise John says in the First Epistle (ch. IV): “Every spirit which confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit which dissolves Christ is not from God”—that is, which denies that he is a human being of flesh—“and this is Antichrist.” Likewise, in the same place (ch. V): “And we know that the Son of God came, put on flesh for us, [Col. 1829C] died, and rose from the dead for us.” Likewise John says in the Second Epistle (ch. I): “For many deceivers have gone out into the world, who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. This is the deceiver and Antichrist. Everyone who goes ahead and does not remain in the doctrine of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in the doctrine”—that is, apostolic doctrine—“has both the Son and the Father. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, but denies that Christ came in the flesh, do not receive him into your house or say ‘Greetings’ to him. For whoever says ‘Greetings’ to him shares in his evil works.”

Likewise Paul says in the Epistle to the Romans (ch. I): “What he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the Holy Spirit, saying: ‘Who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh; who was predestined Son of God in the Word.’” Likewise Peter says in the First Epistle (ch. IV): “Therefore, since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought. For he who has suffered in the flesh has ceased from sins.”

[Col. 1829D] Likewise, against the same heretics who do not believe that Christ suffered or was dead: Matthew wrote in the Gospel, saying (ch. XXVII): “Pilate handed Jesus, after he had been scourged, over to the Jews to be crucified. Then the governor’s soldiers, taking Jesus into the praetorium, stripped him and put a scarlet cloak around him; and, plaiting a crown of thorns, they put it on his head, and a reed in his right hand; and, bending the knee, they mocked him, saying: ‘Hail, King of the Jews.’ And spitting upon him, they took the reed and struck his head,” etc. Likewise, in the same place (ibid.): “Then they crucified him,” etc. Likewise, in the same place: “Then one of the soldiers, taking a spear, pierced his side, and blood and water came out. But Jesus, crying again with a loud voice, gave up the spirit.” These things concern Christ’s Passion and his death. The other Evangelists bear witness to the same matters in their Gospels.

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, Peter, standing with all the apostles among the Jews, said to them (ch. II): “Men [Col. 1830A] of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved by God also by words, mighty works, wonders, and signs which God performed through him in your midst, as you know. Him, delivered up by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God, you afflicted and killed through the hands of the wicked; but God raised him up, having loosed the pains of hell.” This is testimony to Christ’s Passion, death, and resurrection, which all the apostles who remained in the same place bore witness to.

Likewise, Peter says concerning Christ’s Passion in the First Epistle (ch. II): “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his steps,” etc. “When he suffered, he did not threaten; he himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree; by whose death we have been healed.” Likewise, Paul says of his death in Romans (ch. V): “For while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” Likewise, in the same epistle (ch. XIV): “Christ Jesus, who died for us—indeed, who also rose again.” And many further testimonies on these matters are found.

Concerning Christ’s resurrection against heretics who do not believe that Christ rose from the dead: Matthew says in the Gospel concerning Christ’s resurrection (ch. XXVIII): The angel said to the women: “Do not fear. I know that you seek Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, for he has risen, as he told you.” Mark and Luke bear witness to the same in their Gospels (ch. XVI; ch. XXIV). Likewise John says in his Gospel (ch. II): “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall raise it up.” But he was speaking of the temple of his body. Therefore, when he had risen from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, etc. Likewise, in the Gospel according to Luke, affirming by testimony that Christ possessed human flesh (ch. XXIV): “See my hands and my feet, that I myself am he. Touch and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see me to have.” And when he had said this, he showed them his hands, feet, and side. Likewise John [Col. 1830C] says in the Gospel concerning the resurrection of the flesh (ch. XX): “Jesus came, the doors being shut, and stood in the midst of the disciples and said to them: ‘Peace to you.’ Then he said to Thomas: ‘Put your finger here and see my hands; bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing.’”

There are certain heretics who do not believe that Christ ate and drank while he was with his disciples before the Passion. But to destroy this error, we have testimony in the Gospel according to Matthew, which Christ himself, who is Truth, uttered, saying (ch. XI): “For John the Baptist came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and they say: ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating, and they say: ‘Behold, he is a glutton and a drinker of wine, a friend of tax collectors and sinners.’” Likewise Luke bears witness in the Gospel that he ate, saying (ch. VII): “A certain Pharisee asked him to eat with him.” It is altogether certain that he ate; otherwise no one would invite him to eat.

Likewise, Luke says in the same place (ibid.): “A certain Pharisee asked him to dine at his house. And he entered and reclined.” Likewise, he testifies in the same Gospel (ch. XIV): “It happened, when Jesus entered the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees on the Sabbath, to eat bread.” Likewise John says in the Gospel (ch. IV): “Rabbi, eat.” His disciples said this to him when they came from Samaria, bringing food that they had bought, and found him speaking with the Samaritan woman. If someone objects that he said to them: “I have other food to eat which you do not know” (ibid.), it is true that Christ himself used two kinds of food, namely bodily and spiritual. He said this of the spiritual food. Nevertheless, it should no less be believed that the other Evangelists testify that he used temporal food.

Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew, when his disciples asked him: “Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?” [Col. 1831A] (Matt. XXVI), they said *for you*, not that they themselves were to prepare the Passover; this establishes that he ate temporal food while he was with them. Likewise, in the same testimony, Christ himself said (ibid.): “He who dips his hand with me in the dish, he shall betray me.” It is not to be believed that Christ himself dipped his hand in the dish unless he ate. Mark and Luke bear witness to the same in their Gospels. These are testimonies concerning Christ’s eating before he suffered.

But after his Passion Luke testifies in the Gospel that he ate before his disciples, saying (ch. XXIV): “Have you here anything to eat?” But they offered him a portion of broiled fish and a honeycomb. And when he had eaten before them, taking what remained, he gave it to them. The same Luke bears witness in the Acts of the Apostles, saying (ch. I): “And eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem.” Thus it is altogether certain and firm that, before he suffered, he made use of every human activity except sin. Paul also bears witness in the Epistle to the Philippians, saying [Col. 1831B] (ch. II): “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as robbery, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and was found as a man. He humbled himself unto death.” And let these things concerning Christ’s humanity suffice.

## CHAPTER VIII

Concerning the institutions of churches, it is read that the Lord showed Moses on the mountain a tabernacle not made by human hands, saying: “Go and make a tabernacle not made by human hands like this one, in which I may dwell among them when I speak with you; in which gifts, libations, sacrifices, victims, and offerings brought with the Israelite people may be offered by priests” (Heb. IX). Then Moses faithfully carried this out according to the Lord’s command; and after Moses, when the people of Israel entered the promised land, they carried it with them to Shiloh. In it was the ark of the covenant, within which was a golden vessel containing manna, the tablets of the [Col. 1831C] covenant, and Aaron’s rod that had budded.

Then, after a long time, Solomon son of David, at the Lord’s command, built a temple made by human hands in Jerusalem, in which the whole Israelite people assembled to pray and sacrifice. As their fathers had customarily come to the former tabernacle, so they observed the legal commands of the Lord until Christ’s coming. But when Christ came, not wishing to destroy the law but to fulfil it, he wished to be presented in it by his parents, and, as was customary, to be offered according to the law given by God. After this, he is found to have come to the Temple in his youth with his parents, when he was twelve years old. But after thirty years of his age he came to Jerusalem, as is found in the Gospel according to Matthew, entered the Temple, and drove all buyers and sellers out of the Temple, saying (ch. XXI): “It is written: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer.’” Thus Christ himself testified that the Temple [Col. 1831D] is God’s house of prayer.

Likewise Mark gives the same testimony in the same words in his Gospel (ch. XI): “He also prevented anyone from carrying a vessel through the Temple.” Likewise Luke bears witness in his Gospel with these words. Likewise John wrote in his Gospel, saying (ch. II): “Jesus found in the Temple those selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and money-changers sitting there. And having made, as it were, a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the Temple, together with the sheep and oxen; he poured out the money-changers’ coins and overturned their tables. And to those who sold doves he said: ‘Take these things away from here; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.’ His disciples remembered that it was written: ‘Zeal for your house has consumed me.’”

It is found in the Gospels that Christ came many times to the Temple, taught the people there, and worked in it many signs and miracles in healings of the sick, as Matthew the Evangelist relates (ch. XXI): “The blind and the lame came to Jesus in the Temple, and he healed [Col. 1832A] them.” We have in the Gospels that, when Jesus travelled through the Israelite towns preaching, he especially entered the synagogues of the Jews, where he taught the people about God’s kingdom and performed many signs and wonders, as Matthew says (ch. IX): “Jesus went around all the cities and villages, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel, and healing every disease and every infirmity.” Likewise, in the Gospel of Matthew he himself testifies, saying to you [the plural is incongruous in the Latin] (ch. XXVI): “Every day I sat with you in the Temple teaching.” Luke testifies in the Gospel in the same words. Likewise John testifies in the Gospel (ch. XVIII): “I always taught in the synagogue and in the Temple, where all the Jews gather, and I said nothing in secret.”

If you object to us that he preached more often in other places than in the Temple or synagogues, that is true. But because of the crowds that came, lest they hinder the ministers of the Temple and synagogues from rendering their vows and performing the duties imposed upon them, he withdrew to mountains and other places.

[Col. 1832B] But after his Ascension, his disciples, wishing to imitate Christ their Teacher and Saviour, as long as they remained in Jerusalem came daily to the Temple to pray, as is found in the Acts of the Apostles, which says (ch. II): “The apostles continued daily, persevering and praying with one accord in the Temple.” And again (ch. III): “Peter and John went up to the Temple to pray at the ninth hour of prayer.” Likewise, in the same book (ch. V): “When Annas the high priest and all who were with him laid hands on the apostles and put them in public custody, an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night, led them out, and said: ‘Go, stand, and speak in the Temple to the people all the words of this life.’” From this arose the beginning of the house of prayer made by human hands, which we call a church.

## CHAPTER IX

When the apostles and their disciples had been expelled from Jerusalem [Col. 1832C] and, by God’s will, scattered through the various regions of the world; and when in all cities of the Jews they had seen buildings of synagogues; then, passing to the Gentiles and finding in their cities various temples of idols, in which they continually assembled to offer their vows and sacrifices to demonic idols, the Apostles, by counsel of the Holy Spirit, decided that, in order more easily to uproot them from such great error and wickedness and free them from diabolical bonds, houses made by human hands should be ordered to be built in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and that they should be shown how to build them after the pattern of the Temple. In these the faithful people might assemble faithfully and devoutly for baptism, prayer, sacrifice, hearing the word of God, and receiving all the sacraments of Christianity.

In these houses, which we call churches because the people assemble in them, the apostles appointed ministers—namely bishops, presbyters, and deacons—to perform Christ’s mystery, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. XIV): “When they had appointed presbyters in each church and had prayed with fastings, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed.” And we have this: that in the Church of God presbyters were first ordained deacons by the apostles. [Col. 1832D]

We have in the First Epistle to the Corinthians that the Apostle, rebuking them, called the house in which the faithful were gathered a church, saying (ch. XI): “Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink? Or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I praise you? In this I do not praise you.” Likewise Paul says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (ch. XIV): “Let women be silent in the churches. For it is not permitted to them to speak, but to be subject, as the law says. But if they wish to say anything, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.” In this and many other passages the Apostle makes it understood that every house established where believers [Col. 1833A] are gathered to participate in Christ’s sacraments is called the Church of God.

Likewise, John wrote threatening Diotrephes in the Third Epistle, saying (ch. I): “For this reason, if I come, I shall call to mind his deeds which he does, babbling maliciously against us. And, as though these things were not enough for him, he himself does not receive the brethren; and he forbids those who do receive them and drives them out of the church,” etc. Likewise Paul says in the First Epistle to Timothy (ch. III): “But if I delay, that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of the Lord, which is the Church of the living God.” In these aforementioned testimonies of the apostles, and in many others not written in this treatise, it is plainly shown that the house of God—the house of prayer—is called and understood to be a church made by human hands, in which Christ’s sacraments are performed by ordained ministers for the salvation of faithful Christians.

## CHAPTER X

Because heretics treat as nothing the church made by human hands, the altars in it, the sacraments performed in them by God’s ministers, and all ecclesiastical ornaments; say that they contribute nothing to the salvation of souls; and despise them: to destroy this great and utterly wicked error, we shall briefly set forth testimonies. First, concerning the altar, without which there ought not to be a church made by human hands, and upon which gifts, offerings, and victims for sins are offered.

We have in the Gospel according to Matthew that Truth itself teaches the one making an offering and instructs him how he ought to offer, saying (ch. V): “If you offer your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother; then, when you come, you shall offer your gift.” Here Christ himself indicates that believers should have altars in churches on which to offer gifts.

Again, in the Gospel according to Luke, when Christ wished to be offered by his parents in the Temple according to the law [Col. 1833C] of the Lord, and sacrifices were offered on his behalf at the altar in the Temple—namely a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons—it is thereby understood that, just as Christ wished to be offered and for a sacrifice to be given on his behalf, so all the faithful in every region of the world should have altars on which gifts and offerings for their sins may be offered to God.

Likewise Paul, instructing his disciples in the First Epistle to the Corinthians to have altars, serve God at them, and become participants in the gifts of the altars while serving God, wrote (ch. IX): “Those who serve at the altar partake with the altar.” Likewise Paul, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. XXI), offered in the Temple sacrifices at the altar for himself and for the others who had been purified with him; he was unwilling to despise altars or treat them as nothing, but gave an example.

Likewise John testifies in the Apocalypse (ch. V) that he saw an altar in heaven on which an angel offered much incense, which is the prayers of the saints. [Col. 1833D] Therefore blessed John, because he saw a golden altar before God in heaven, wished that on earth a handmade altar, clean and purified, should be built in churches made by human hands.

Against the aforementioned errors we might bring forward, as it were, a very great cloud of witnesses from the Old Testament—namely the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. But because heretics refuse to answer or give a reason in response to testimonies from the Old Testament, the Law, and the Prophets which are put before them—because, namely, they are ignorant and would immediately be convicted—we do not wish to labour over these, except only over the testimonies which we have drawn from the books of the New Testament. To these they can give no answer or explanation, nor have they any just excuse.

Likewise, heretics disapprove of the Church’s chant and the praises which clerics offer to their Creator from the New and Old Testaments. Against this error we set forth Paul’s testimony in the Epistle to the Ephesians (ch. V): “Be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking [Col. 1834A] among yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing in your hearts to the Lord, always giving thanks for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God the Father.” Likewise Paul says on the same subject to the Colossians (ch. III): “Let the word of Christ dwell abundantly in you in all wisdom, admonishing yourselves with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing to the Lord in your hearts with grace.”

Likewise John saw in the Apocalypse twenty-four elders, and they fell before the Lamb, each having harps and golden bowls full of perfumes, which are the prayers of the saints, and they sang, as it were, a new song, saying (ch. V): “You are worthy, Lord, to open the book and loose its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us to God by your blood.” Likewise John says in the same book (ch. XIV): “And the voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing their harps; and they sang, as it were, a new song before the throne.” And elsewhere (ch. XV): “Having harps of God, and singing the song of Moses, servant of God,” [Col. 1834B] etc. Likewise John says in the same book (ch. XIX): “I heard the great voice of many crowds in heaven saying: *Alleluia*: praise, glory, and power belong to our God, because his judgments are true and just.”

## CHAPTER XI
After touching on some—not all—of the testimonies that occur to us concerning the house of the Lord, which is the Church, let us now, against the perversity of heretics, set forth divine authority regarding the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, which is more worthy than all sacraments, from which and whose consecration is celebrated in the house of the Lord, the Church of the living God, as Paul testifies.

Christ, seeing that death was imminent for him, and wishing to commend to us the sacrament of his body and blood, took bread; and, giving thanks, blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, and likewise the cup. Thus the Evangelist Matthew says (ch. XXVI): “While they were at supper, Jesus took bread [Col. 1834C], blessed and broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body.’ And taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, saying: ‘Drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be shed for many for the remission of sins.’”

Likewise Mark says of the same matter (ch. XIV): “While they were eating, Jesus took bread; and, blessing it, broke it and gave it to them, and said: ‘Take; this is my body.’ And, taking the cup, he gave thanks and gave it to them, and they all drank from it. And he said to them: ‘This is my blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many.’”

Likewise Luke says (ch. XXII): “And taking bread, he gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to them, saying: ‘This is my body, which is given for you; do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup after supper, saying: ‘For this is the cup of the new covenant in my blood, which shall be shed for you.’”

The Evangelists indeed affirm that the Lord took bread, blessed it, and gave it to his disciples [Col. 1834D], saying: “This is my body.” Observe each point: he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it. The Gospel does not state that the Lord took his own body, blessed it, broke it, or gave it to his disciples; rather, the Evangelists testify that he took bread and, blessing it, broke it and gave it to them, saying: “This is my body”; and: “This is the cup of the new covenant, in my blood, which is shed for you.”

But heretics say that this demonstrative pronoun does not refer to the bread which he held in his hands, blessed, broke, and distributed to his disciples, but refers to his body, which performed all these things. Their most wicked error has its origin and beginning in their ignorance that the pronoun *hoc* (“this”), being a noun-pronoun, cannot be referred relatively except to things already mentioned. Yet, in the handing over of this sacrament, no mention of his body had then been made. Therefore what they assert is utterly false.
