[Col. 1835A] But just as flour, water, and salt, when mixed and baked together in such a way that they are no longer flour, water, or what they had previously been, are truly pure bread and are called bread: so the bread which Jesus Christ took in his hands after supper, after he blessed and broke it, is understood and believed to be Christ’s body, not bread. Christ the Saviour and Redeemer gave it to his disciples at supper, saying: “Take and eat; this is my body.” We say the same concerning the cup, over which he gave thanks and which he gave to his disciples, saying also: “Drink from this, all of you; for this is my blood of the new covenant, which shall be shed for many for the redemption of sins.” And he added: “As often as you do this, do it in remembrance of me.”

These words spoken by Christ over this sacrament at supper ought especially to be noted as though they were his final testament. But when he said, “As often as you do this, do it in [Col. 1835B] remembrance of me,” these words indicate that Christ did not wish this so great and holy sacrament to end there. Rather, he commanded the apostles, as his co-heirs, and their successors, to perform this sacrament for ever after his passion, resurrection, and ascension, in remembrance of his passion and in hope of eternal salvation.

When the Lord Jesus Christ had gathered his disciples, he promised that he would give them his flesh under the form of bread and his blood under the form of wine, as is contained in the Gospel of blessed John; and he says (ch. VI): “The bread which I shall give you is my flesh for the life of the world.” But when the Jews heard this, they disputed among themselves, saying (ibid.): “How can he give us his flesh to eat?” Because of this dispute, and because he understood that they did not possess spiritual understanding, he said to them with a definite assertion: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves; [Col. 1835C] and he who eats my flesh and drinks my blood shall have eternal life, and I shall raise him up on the last day.”

In these words it should be noted that no one can have eternal life unless he has eaten Christ’s flesh and drunk his blood, according to what he himself said. But Christ himself did not wish to deceive his disciples or render his promise void. At the Last Supper he gave his flesh and blood to his disciples under the forms of bread and wine, for them to eat without revulsion of the mouth.

Whatever words Christ spoke are most certain and most true; they deceive in no respect. For he said many things which are true, but which, if another had said them, would neither appear true nor be believed. He said: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he shall be saved. I am the good shepherd” (John X); “I am the bread” (John VI), etc.; “I am the true vine, and you are the branches” (John XV); “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). So great is the force and power of God’s word [Col. 1835D] that all things whatsoever he has said are never false and never pass away, as the Psalmist said: “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. XXXII).

It should also be noted that the Evangelist used not the past tense but the present, although he wrote after Christ’s passion, understanding and believing that what Christ said he is, he is and always will be. Thus those words which Christ uttered at supper before his disciples, and taught them, retain in themselves what force they possessed among the apostles in the sacrament of bread and wine—namely, the Lord’s body and blood—and they will retain the same force, power, and efficacy in God’s ministers until the end of the age.

After our Lord Jesus Christ heard the Jews’ dispute concerning his flesh, he said to them: “Unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, they shall not have eternal life; but those who eat and drink his blood shall have life and eternal resurrection.” The promise of eating his sacrament [Col. 1836A] should not seem difficult and useless to anyone, but certain, most useful, and capable of being received in the present time under the forms of bread and wine, which he gave them at supper and which, in distributing it, he declared to be his body. He adds: “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John VI).

But there are certain heretics who believe that by hearing the word of God they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood—as though Christ, who knows all things, did not know how to say: “My word is truly food, and my blood is truly drink,” substituting one word for another. But when he said, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink,” he did not say, “My flesh is truly hearing and understanding”; rather, through the operation of spiritual grace, “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Christ said this properly. And it is most certain concerning the sacrament of bread and wine which he bestowed at his supper.

Every day this sacrament is consecrated upon the altar in the Church of God by ordained ministers of God [Col. 1836B], in remembrance of him. But because he wished to show those who receive it worthily the power of eating this sacrament and its benefit, he added (ibid.): “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. And he who eats me shall live because of me.” This is the power of the sacrament and the benefit obtained by the faithful recipient: namely, that he abides in God and God in him. Such a person bears much fruit, as John testifies (ch. XV): “For without me,” says Truth itself, “you can do nothing.”

The blessed Apostle Paul, having heard and known the power and benefit of this great and most certain sacrament, wished to instruct his disciples by word and deed, withholding nothing useful for their salvation, so that it might always be held in memory by those who followed them. He wrote in the First Epistle sent to the Corinthians, saying (ch. XI): “For I received from the Lord what I also handed on to you: that our Lord Jesus Christ, on the night in which he was betrayed, took bread, and, giving thanks, [Col. 1836C] broke it and said: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which shall be handed over for you; do this in remembrance of me.’”

It should be noted that Christ commanded his disciples to perform this sacrament in memory of him, and that they should hand it on to their disciples, just as they themselves received it from him, so that the memory of his passion might be preserved among the faithful through this sacrament for ever and ever.

Likewise: “Similarly also the cup after supper, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.’ For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Therefore whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the Lord’s body and blood” (ibid.).

But if, as the heretics say, consecrated bread and wine possessed no dignity, why would the Apostle state that one who unworthily receives the consecrated bread [Col. 1836D] is guilty of the Lord’s body and blood? For if someone eats ordinary bread, he is not said or believed to be guilty of the Lord’s body and blood. Therefore the Apostle says that whoever wishes to receive this sacrament—namely, that of bread and wine—should examine himself, that is, cleanse himself from his sins, and then eat of that bread and drink of the cup.

Likewise, the Apostle himself gives the reason why the recipient ought to be cleansed from sins, when he says: “For he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord.” Likewise, it is not through the merit of the consecrator, but through the power and truth of the Holy Spirit—the Spirit approving and confirming that this sacrament of bread and wine is the Lord’s body—which he had demonstrated to the Corinthians in word and deed when he wrote in the First Epistle sent to them, saying (ch. X): “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a participation in Christ’s blood? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the Lord’s body [Col. 1837A]? Since there is one bread, we who are many are one body, all who partake [read: *we partake*] of the one bread.”

In this chapter the Apostle Paul makes manifest that he himself performed the sacrament which he had received from the Lord. Likewise did the other apostles.

Likewise the Apostle Paul says in the same epistle (ch. XI): “When you come together in one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s supper. For each one takes his own supper first to eat; one indeed is hungry, while another is drunk.” But to assemble together, consume one’s own food, distribute nothing to others, and become drunk—these actions are not to eat the Lord’s supper. Rebuking the Corinthians, the Apostle asks (ibid.): “Do you not have houses for eating and drinking?”—that is, ordinary food—“or do you despise the Church of God and shame those who have nothing?”

“I praise you for this, that you come together in one place in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; I do not praise you for this, that you eat your own food and shame those who have nothing [Col. 1837B] but are hungry. For they have nothing to eat.”

From this it is plainly evident that the apostles’ disciples, imitating them, carried out from memory the handing down of this sacrament throughout the entire world. We say and believe—and the whole Roman Church, first founded by blessed Peter and Paul, says and believes—that every person who does not have faith in this sacrament and in the other apostolic traditions, such as baptism, confession, penance, and the other apostolic institutions performed in the present Church, is alien from the unity of the holy Church and the Catholic faith, separated from the fellowship of the holy faithful—both those who have gone before and those dwelling here [read: *here*]—and is condemned for ever and ever.

[Col. 1837C]

## CHAPTER XII

After treating, though unworthily, of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, universally celebrated in the Catholic Church extended throughout the whole world, let us begin concerning baptism. Against the errors of heretics who corrupt the sacrament of water-baptism, let us bring forward the authorities of the New Testament—testimonies supplied to us by the Holy Spirit—in order to overthrow them.

For certain heretics say that this sacrament of water-baptism, without their laying on of hands, is of no benefit to adults receiving it for the attainment of everlasting salvation, nor even to infants. This error is the greatest among their other errors.

We have in John’s Gospel that John the Baptist, in order that he might be Christ’s forerunner and true herald, was sent by almighty God to baptize in water, as the Baptist himself testifies, saying (ch. I): “He who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘He upon whom you see the Spirit of God descending and remaining like a dove, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’”

Likewise, at Christ’s baptism the heavens were opened, the Father’s voice was heard, and the Holy Spirit appeared [Col. 1837D]. See the great sacrament of divine mercy. For the whole Trinity acted and deigned to be present in Christ’s baptism: the Father is heard, the Son is baptized, and the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove. When the Son of God was baptized, the heavens were opened.

Because the institution and sacrament of baptism are of such great dignity, the Lord said to Nicodemus, as John testifies in his Gospel (ch. III): “A man cannot receive anything unless it has been given him from heaven. Amen, amen, I say to you: unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. What is born from flesh is flesh; and what is born from the Holy Spirit is spirit.”

Listen, heretic. We must have two births, namely a carnal and a spiritual birth, as divine utterance testifies. Whoever lacks spiritual birth cannot see the kingdom of God or enter it. But spiritual birth cannot be had unless carnal birth has been had. How, then, do you say that carnal birth is evil, when [Col. 1838A] spiritual birth follows it, a birth which grants the sight and entrance of God’s kingdom, whereas spiritual birth cannot be had without carnal birth? For no one can ever be born again.

We have in the Gospels that John the Baptist, inspired by the Holy Spirit, went into the desert and preached and taught repentance and water-baptism to those who came to him. Therefore Christ, wishing to sanctify and confirm the water through John the Baptist, came to him and deigned to receive water-baptism in himself from him. Thus he gave all believers an example that the sacrament of water-baptism ought to be received for the attainment of the salvation of souls; in it they are cleansed of every sin, both original and actual. The universal Church’s faith is that anyone who despises this sacrament and refuses to receive it can in no way merit or attain eternal life, as our Saviour Jesus Christ testifies in the Gospel of blessed John, saying (ch. III): “Unless one is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter [Col. 1838B] the kingdom of God.”

We have in the Gospel that, before his passion and at his command, his disciples baptized those who believed in the Son of God. It says: “When Jesus heard that the Pharisees were saying, ‘He makes more disciples than John, and they baptize’—although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did—he left Judaea” (John IV), etc.

But it should be known that John the Baptist baptized in the name of the Lord who sent him. Our Lord Jesus Christ, however, who was sent from heaven by the Father and brought eternal salvation with him to the human race, taught his disciples the form of this sacrament of baptism. Sending them throughout the world, he commanded them to preach the kingdom of God and to baptize, adding: “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (ch. XXVIII), as is found at the end of the Gospel of blessed Matthew. Appearing to his disciples on a mountain, he said to them: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” etc.; and he added: “He who believes [Col. 1838C] and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark XVI). From this authority we may understand that unbelief in this sacrament of baptism benefits no one for salvation, even if that person receives it.

The heretics also say that it can benefit no one unless he requests this sacrament with his own mouth and heart. From this they advance the error that water-baptism is of no benefit to infants. But we have in the Gospel of blessed Mark that after his resurrection the Lord Jesus Christ appeared to his disciples and said: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.” In this passage he made no exception of adults or children, males or females, when he said “to every creature: He who believes and is baptized shall be saved.”

Therefore the faith of the Catholic Church throughout the world, in every place where Christ’s name is celebrated and believed, is that whether they are infants or adults, men or women, if they receive this sacrament of baptism, they are without doubt saved and are cleansed and purified from all sins, original and actual, through the cooperating grace of the Holy Spirit—unless, after the washing of baptism and before dying, they fall into the corruption of sin [Col. 1838D].

Against what the heretics say—that infants cannot be saved in baptism—the blessed Paul says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (ch. VII): “If a believing brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, he should not dismiss her. And if a believing woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, she should not dismiss him. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife through the believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean; but now they are holy.”

The Apostle says that the children of believing parents are clean and holy. All the more must it be believed [Col. 1839A] that infants baptized in the faith of their sponsors are cleansed and saved when ministers perform immersion in water and invoke the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Thus we have in the Gospel of Matthew (ch. XV) that the daughter of the Canaanite woman was made well through her mother’s faith. Likewise, we have in the Gospel that certain persons carrying a paralytic lying on a bed to Jesus could not approach him because of the crowd; they lowered the paralytic through the tiles before him so that he might heal him. Looking upon those who lowered the paralytic, he restored health to the sick man through their faith (Matt. IX). Likewise, the power of the devil is expelled.

And it is found in the Gospel of blessed Matthew concerning a certain centurion who came for the health of his servant, that he heard from the Lord (ch. VIII): “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” And his servant was healed from that hour. Likewise, the dead daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was raised by the Lord at her father’s request (Matt. IX). Likewise, when the son of a certain widow was being carried outside the city gate [Col. 1839B] for burial, the Lord, moved by his mother’s weeping and lamentation, raised him and restored him to his mother (Luke VII).

For this reason, on the basis of these Gospel authorities and very many other testimonies contained in the apostolic Scriptures, the universal Church throughout the world believes and holds that, through the faith of sponsors and the invocation of the Holy Trinity by ministers of the Church, spiritual grace is bestowed in baptism by almighty God upon infants and children. As Paul testifies, saying: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase. Therefore neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase” (I Cor. III).

And because the Apostle said, “God gives the increase,” every believer ought to believe that, whatever the character of the one who baptizes, once the invocation has been made—namely, “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”—God gives the increase, namely, spiritual increase, to the one receiving this sacrament, whether infant or adult. Thus Peter said in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. II): “Let [Col. 1839C] every one of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

Likewise, you say, heretic, that a sinner cannot baptize. How, then, did the apostles baptize, who were sinners, as John testifies in saying: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I)? Likewise, you say that the Holy Spirit is not given through a priest’s ministry, although you falsely claim to give him. And how do you say that you give the Holy Spirit, when you oppose the Holy Spirit as far as you can, and when giving the Holy Spirit belongs to God alone?

Likewise, it is recorded in the Acts of the Apostles (ch. VIII) that the apostles laid hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit. It is not said that they gave him; rather, through their laying on of hands people received the Holy Spirit. Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles [Col. 1839D] (ibid.): “Both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water. And he baptized him, and the Holy Spirit came down upon him.”

Likewise, concerning infants or little children, we find in the Gospels that our God Jesus Christ approved such an age of little children that he said to the disciples, when they were forbidding those who brought little children to him: “Allow the little children to come to me; for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Mark X). Therefore whoever does not believe that the baptism of little children and infants avails for the salvation of eternal life believes contrary to the Gospel and is like one who prevents little children from coming to Christ.

Likewise, in the First Epistle of blessed Paul to the Corinthians (ch. XV), we have that in the primitive Church the apostles’ disciples were baptized on behalf of the dead, believing that they conferred upon them the salvation of their souls. The Apostle also says (ibid.): “If the dead do not rise, why are they also baptized on their behalf? Why are we also endangered [Col. 1840A] every hour?”

Therefore, if it was the faith of the primitive Church that the baptism of the living on behalf of the dead conferred eternal salvation upon those dead persons—who had neither heard nor received it, and for whom they were therefore baptized—how much more ought believers now to believe that little children baptized in the faith of sponsors obtain eternal salvation and spiritual grace in baptism?

> **[Note: Col. 1839D]** Here he is mistaken; for the Church does not hold this.

And let these things concerning baptism suffice.

## CHAPTER XIII

We have spoken of the sacrament of baptism, which is the first plank after shipwreck, that is, after immersion in sins. And because penance is the second plank after shipwreck, we must therefore speak in the second place, after baptism, of penance, which we ought authoritatively to confirm against heretical perversity.

John’s preaching begins with repentance; for he says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near” (Matt. III). And Peter said in the Acts of the Apostles to those whose hearts had been pierced by his preaching [Col. 1840B] (ch. II): “Repent, and let every one of you be baptized.” Likewise Peter: “Repent, therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts III).

But because inward contrition of heart, confession by the mouth, and worthy satisfaction imposed by a priest are necessary in penance, let us bring forward examples of each.

That inward contrition of heart is necessary is shown by the authority of Joel, where it is said (ch. II): “Rend your hearts, and not your garments.” It is also shown by the authority of the Psalmist saying: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. L). For contrition is compunction of heart, born from recollection of past evils, as in the Gospel: “And Peter remembered the word of Jesus, who had said: ‘Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.’ And he went out and wept bitterly” (Matt. XXVI). See how he was pierced in heart: remembering past evil, he had recourse to tears.

[Col. 1840C] Likewise, confession by the mouth is necessary, and it is spoken of in two ways: namely, confession of God and confession of sins. Confession of God is that of which the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “Whoever confesses me before men, I too will confess him before my Father” (Matt. X). Confession of sins is that of which David says in the Psalm: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures for ever” (Ps. CV). He called the Lord good and merciful because, if anyone confesses, he is ready to show mercy. For he foresaw his mercies from afar through the Holy Spirit, when he said: “I shall sing to you for ever of the mercies of the Lord, O Lord” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Likewise: “Your mercies are many, O Lord” (II Kings XXIV). Likewise David: “I said: I shall confess against myself my injustice” (Ps. XXXI).

For confession is the condemnation of one’s own act together with self-accusation. Hence: “The righteous man is the first accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. XVIII). And James says in the Catholic Epistle (ch. V): “Confess [Col. 1840D] your sins to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be saved.” And the Apostle Paul: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X).

See: from the authority of James we have that we should confess our sins. He did not say “to God alone,” as the heretic says, but “confess to one another.” And that we ought to confess to priests, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go, show yourself to the priest” (Luke V). And James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him,” etc. (James V).

That satisfaction is likewise necessary is found in the Gospel, where Luke says (ch. III): “Bring forth fruits worthy of repentance.” For “bring forth fruits worthy of repentance” means nothing other than performing worthy satisfaction imposed by a priest. Satisfaction is the sentence or judgment that a priest gives to a penitent concerning sin. This is the judgment of which it was said: “The Lord will not judge twice in the same matter” [Col. 1841A] (Nahum I according to the Septuagint). And Paul says: “If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged” (I Cor. XI). And Peter: “For the time has come for judgment to begin from the house of the Lord” (I Peter IV).

This is the authority which the Lord gave to all: the power of binding and loosing. Truth itself says: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX). For just as lepers in the Old Testament were commanded to show themselves to priests so that they might discern who was clean and who unclean (Lev. XIV), so now, in accordance with his office, the priest, when he hears the various kinds of sins, should know who is to be bound and who is to be loosed.

Likewise, after Christ raised Lazarus, he said to the disciples: “Loose him” (John XI). The Lord wished them to loose the man whom he had raised and show him loosed . . . God forgives sins through ministers. For although God forgives sins and human beings forgive them, God does so in one way and human beings in another. God forgives sins from himself, because he forgives them through himself [Col. 1841B] whenever he wills; human beings do not do so from themselves, but through grace working in them and through them.

Thus it is true that God alone forgives sins, as the Lord himself says in the prophet: “I alone blot out the iniquities and sins of the people” (Isa. XLIII). Likewise: “You alone perform wonders” (Ps. LXXI). Yet it is not denied that human beings also perform wonders, but not from themselves as God does. Likewise: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke XVIII), because he is good from himself. Yet we do not deny that there are good human beings. Thus human beings forgive sins not from themselves, but God forgives through their ministry.

But you say that someone can be saved without confession, and you object with the authority which says: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. XXXIII). To this it must be said that the true universal priest, namely God, absolves from the debt of eternal punishment through contrition of heart one who wishes to confess but cannot. But, so long as he is able, unless he confesses by mouth he is not absolved. [Col. 1841C] For it is certain that one who has a contrite heart wishes to confess. Yet he can abandon this good will. For while a human being is in this life, he cannot will something which he cannot cease to will. If, having lost this will, he should not wish to confess and then die, there is no doubt that he is then condemned for that sin which he refused to confess. No sin goes unpunished: either a human being punishes it, or God does.

It is therefore evident that God alone forgives sins by giving life inwardly through grace, and that the priest forgives not by giving life inwardly, but by absolving from the debt of eternal punishment through the satisfaction which he imposes. As for what you say concerning sinners—“At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved”—this was said of those who, with the danger of death imminent, cannot have time for satisfaction. It is as though he said: “At whatever hour a sinner truly repents, he shall not perish in the life to come.” Or it may be said of all: “At whatever hour he groans, he shall be saved,” because the sinner’s salvation begins then.

But after speaking of the matters to be considered [Col. 1841D] in penance, we must say what penance is. Penance is to lament evils that have been committed and not to commit again those that ought to be lamented. For one who so bewails deeds already done that he nevertheless commits others either does not know how to do penance or pretends to do it. Likewise, the person who does not repent is a mocker, who still does what he has repented of; he does not seem to seek God in submission, but to mock him in pride.

Isaiah said to sinners: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. I). The person who is washed and clean laments the past and does not again commit what ought to be lamented. This is true penance, concerning which the Lord says in the Gospel: “There is greater joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous persons who do not need penance” (Matt. XVIII)—not because anyone is so righteous as not to need penance, but because “who do not need” means those who think they do not need it. This is what the heretics still retain from the arrogance of the Pharisees. They are those of whom Solomon says: “They rejoice [Col. 1842A] when they have done evil, and exult in most wicked things” (Prov. II).

Let what we have said concerning penance suffice for the present matter.

## CHAPTER XIV
After the Treatise on Penance follows a discussion of the laying on of hands, because heretics presume to perform the laying on of hands, which they call the *consolamentum*, contrary to the Lord’s precepts and the ordinances of the apostles. How, and by what persons, it is performed, and what they think of it . . . . . must first be stated. The manner of the *consolamentum* is as follows: . . . . . among the people, either a bishop or a deacon, is designated as ruler over the other heretics subject to him. When they wish to confer the *consolamentum* upon a man or a woman, the one who is called greater and ordained, having washed his hands—and likewise all who wish to be present, after washing their hands—holds the book of the Gospels in his hands and admonishes the person or persons who come to receive the *consolamentum* to place, in that *consolamentum*, all [Col. 1842B] their faith and hope for the salvation of their souls in God and in that *consolamentum*. Then, with the book placed upon their heads, they say the Lord’s Prayer seven times. Afterward, beginning the Gospel of blessed John (chapter 1) with “In the beginning,” he recites aloud, before all those present, as far as this place in the Gospel: “Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ”; and thus that *consolamentum* is concluded.

Let us say by what persons it is performed: namely, by those who among them are called ordained. If these are lacking, it is supplied by others who are called consoled; and if men are not present, women alone perform it for the sick. Let us say what they think of it. For in it all those to be saved generally place their faith and hope, and they believe that by it they obtain forgiveness of all their sins and cleansing from all their offences without any satisfaction, if they immediately die. They believe that through it forgiveness is given them not only for the venial sins they have committed, but also for the grave sins they have perpetrated. They also say that no great or small [Col. 1842C] man or woman can attain the heavenly kingdom and fellowship with the angels by any work, benefaction, religious contemplation, or even martyrdom, unless he or she has received that *consolamentum* from those whom they call consoled; indeed, even if such a person should abstain from all sins and offences—which is impossible.

They also believe that, if the person administering that *consolamentum* has fallen into any of the sins which they themselves call grave—such as eating meat, an egg, or cheese; killing a bird or any animal other than reptiles; or even into those sins named by the Roman Church, such as homicide, adultery, fornication, impurity, theft, false witness, perjury, and robbery—the *consolamentum* is of no benefit to those who receive it. For they say that a person who has thus fallen does not have the Holy Spirit; and they believe that one who does not possess it cannot give it to anyone else. Indeed, they believe that such a person himself must receive that *consolamentum* again from another, if he desires to be saved. And [Col. 1842D] they hold that this must be done universally for all who have fallen, both men and women, as has been stated.

But the Roman Apostolic Church judges all these aforementioned practices performed by heretics to be very evil and deadly errors, on many authorities, because they are not performed by the persons by whom they ought to be performed. For it was neither instituted by Jesus Christ, nor by the apostles, nor performed in their time. We have also in the Gospels that the Lord Jesus Christ and our Saviour laid his hands upon little children brought to him, and also upon the sick; he blessed them, and they were healed (Matt. 19; Mark 6; Luke 13). And this . . . . . we do not find that he gave to any of the disciples before his Passion, until he rose from the dead; but after the resurrection he gave only to the apostles authority to baptize and to lay hands in the name of the Lord (Mark 16), and . . . . . when they had been ordained, they should have the same authority to baptize and lay [Col. 1843A] on hands: that is, those whom God had chosen and whom they themselves had judged worthy.

Accordingly, we have in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 8) that blessed Peter, when Simon Magus offered him money and asked that the Holy Spirit and such authority might be given him that whomever he laid hands upon should receive the Holy Spirit, answered: “You have neither lot nor part in this matter, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money. But pray to the Lord and repent of this great wickedness of yours, which has arisen in your heart.” Thus he judged him unworthy and to be rejected from this divine office.

We have also in the same book (chapter 14) that the apostles ordained presbyters and deacons in all the cities in which the name of our Lord Jesus Christ was celebrated and faithful Christians persevered, to perform these same sacraments for them: for example, “when they had appointed presbyters in every church.” Likewise, in the same book (chapter 20), when Paul, passing through the churches [Col. 1843B] in which he had ordained presbyters and bishops, wished to go from Asia to Jerusalem, he came to Miletus; and, sending to Ephesus, he summoned the elders of the Church and said to them: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired by his blood.”

And after our Lord Jesus Christ chose the apostles, after his Ascension the people throughout all the Churches established bishops, presbyters, and also deacons for the performance of all divine mysteries; and they granted to those ordained by them the same authority and tradition which they themselves had received from Christ. Whoever acts or believes contrary to this apostolic . . . . . errs greatly and works death for himself. Hence James also says (chapter 2): “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all.” Likewise Paul: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5). And these things suffice against the persons of the heretics.

Likewise, against their manner of *consolamentum*. Heretics [Col. 1843C] give that *consolamentum* both to the great and to the small, to men and women alike. This was never done by the apostles, nor among their disciples, nor is it found to have been commanded by them, because the apostles laid hands only upon those whom they wished to ordain as preachers, presbyters, or deacons over the people. Concerning others we find nothing in divine Scripture, except that they preached and baptized them with the invocation of the Holy Spirit, as our Lord Jesus Christ taught and commanded them, when he said: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”; and he gave them the form and manner which is retained continuously in the Church to this day.

Therefore it is greatly to be wondered from whom such a custom of the heretics’ *consolamentum* took its beginning or derived its origin, since it appears to have had its beginning neither from the prophets, nor from Christ, nor from the apostles, nor from apostolic men, successors of the apostles; for it differs greatly [Col. 1843D] from the sayings, deeds, and writings of all these. Therefore it must be believed that they are among those of whom the apostle Paul wrote in the Second Epistle to Timothy (chapter 4): “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound teaching, but, according to their own desires, will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears, and . . . . . will turn away their hearing from the truth.” For these persons obey neither the sayings of the prophets, nor the traditions of the apostles, nor the practices of apostolic men, nor even the writings of the saints . . . . .

These heretics judge all persons who . . . . . have not received that *consolamentum* from them . . . . . and in this they contradict the word of our Lord Jesus Christ, who . . . . . said: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Matt. 7). Therefore they may be among those concerning whom he added: “With the judgment with which you judge, you shall be judged; and with the measure with which you measure, it shall be measured back to you.” Since they judge and condemn all others who are not of . . . . ., their condemnation and judgment, God willing, [Col. 1844A] shall be upon their own heads. For they neither heed nor obey the counsels of the blessed apostle Paul, who says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4); and elsewhere: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2).

## CHAPTER XV

It is the belief of all heretics that no one, after receiving his *consolamentum*, can be saved if he eats meat, cheese, or eggs, unless he receives penance from them and is afterward reconsoled by them. But let us endeavour to oppose and destroy so great an error by testimonies from the Gospels, the Epistles of the Apostles, and the Acts.

For in the Gospel the Lord said to his disciples: “Into whatever house you enter, remain there, eating and drinking what is set before you” (Luke 10). He made no exception of foods—meat or other kinds of food—but said universally: [Col. 1844B] “Eat whatever is set before you.” Likewise, in the Gospel according to Matthew (chapter 15), he is found to have said: “Not what enters the mouth defiles a person,” because from the heart proceed such things as murders, adulteries, thefts, false witness, and so forth.

Likewise, we have in the Gospels that the Lord Jesus Christ, at supper with his disciples, ate the flesh of the Paschal lamb, as Luke writes plainly in his Gospel (chapter 22): “The day of Unleavened Bread came, on which the Passover had to be sacrificed. And he sent Peter and John, saying: ‘Go and prepare the Passover for us, that we may eat it.’ But they said: ‘Where do you wish us to prepare for you to eat the Passover?’” And so forth. “The Master says to you: ‘Where is the guest room where I may eat the Passover with my disciples?’” And so forth. “So they went and found it as he had told them, and they prepared the Passover. And when the hour had come, he reclined at table, and the twelve with him, and he said to them: ‘I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer. For I tell you that from this time I shall not eat it until it is fulfilled [Col. 1844C] in the kingdom of God.’” The other evangelists also wrote words similar to these: that Christ ate the Passover; and that Passover which had to be sacrificed was the Paschal lamb, concerning which the Lord had commanded Moses (Exod. 12). Christ ate the Paschal lamb; that lamb was flesh; therefore Christ ate flesh.

Likewise, the Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians (chapter 10): “Eat whatever is sold in the market, asking no questions for conscience’ sake. If any unbeliever invites you to supper and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for conscience’ sake. But if someone says to you, ‘This has been sacrificed to idols,’ do not eat it, for the sake of the person who informed you and for conscience’ sake—not your own conscience, but that of the other person.” Likewise the Apostle says to Timothy: “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (1 Tim. 4).

We know and believe [Col. 1844D] that Christ, who is the Word and Wisdom of God the Father, came into the world, taking flesh from the womb of the Virgin, for no other purpose than the salvation of souls. He would not have done, nor commanded to be done, the things written above if the eating of these things were judgment and condemnation for the souls of the faithful. Nor would . . . . . the apostles, endowed with spiritual wisdom and imitators of Christ, . . . . . have written or eaten the eating of meat . . . . . foods, if they knew eating to be a damnable sin.

Likewise, Paul says to the Romans (chapters 14–15): “Receive the weak in faith, not for disputes about opinions. One person believes that he may eat all things, but the one who is weak eats vegetables. Let not the one who eats despise the one who does not eat; and let not the one who does not eat judge the one who eats. For God has received him. Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls to his own master. Yet he shall stand, for God is able to make him stand. One person judges one day above another; another judges every day alike. Let each be fully assured in his own mind. The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord; and the one who [Col. 1845A] eats, eats for the Lord, for I give thanks to God. For none of us lives to himself, and none dies to himself. For whether we live, we live to the Lord; and whether we die, we die to the Lord. Therefore, whether we die or live, we are the Lord’s. For Christ died and rose again for this reason: that he might rule both over the dead and over the living. But why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God,” and so forth.

“For I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean through itself; but to the person who thinks anything unclean, to that person it is unclean. For if your brother is grieved because of your food, you are no longer walking according to love. Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died. Therefore do not let your good be spoken of as evil. For the kingdom of God is not . . . . . but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. For whoever in this . . . . . pleases God and is approved by all. Therefore let us pursue the things that make for peace, and let us keep between ourselves the things that make for edification. Do not [Col. 1845B] destroy the work of God for food’s sake. All things indeed are clean, but it is evil for the person who eats in a way that gives offence. It is good not to eat meat, nor drink wine, nor do anything by which your brother is offended, scandalized, or made weak. Keep the faith that you have within yourself before God. Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves. But the one who doubts, if he eats, is condemned, because he does not act from faith. But whatever is not from faith is sin. We who are stronger, however, ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak, and not to please ourselves.”

The Apostle calls weak in faith the person who judges and condemns one who eats meat and drinks wine; and it is a most evil error to judge the servant of God, when God says: “Do not judge, and you shall not be judged; do not condemn, and you shall not be condemned” (Matt. 7), and the Apostle in his Epistle says: “Do not judge before the time,” and so forth (1 Cor. 4). But when he says, “It is good not to eat meat [Col. 1845C] and not to drink wine,” this is not a command but counsel given to those who wish to afflict their flesh, lest they fall into the temptations of demons—provided that they do not believe people are damned by eating flesh.

Again the Apostle says to the Colossians (chapter 2): “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink,” and so forth. Again the Apostle says to Titus (chapter 1): “All things are clean to the clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean, because both their mind and conscience are defiled.” Mark says (chapter 7): “Hear me, all of you, and understand. There is nothing outside a person entering into him that can defile him . . . . . those things which proceed from the person are what defile the person.”

## CHAPTER XVI

After speaking of the eating of foods, let us now speak of the resurrection of the dead. For heretics, imitating the error of the Sadducees, do not believe in the resurrection of the bodies of dead human beings. [Col. 1845D] Christ destroyed this error when speaking with the Sadducees about the resurrection of the dead, saying: “You are mistaken, knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven. But concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22).

Likewise, in the same Matthew (chapter 27): “The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose; and, coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many.” You hear, heretic, that bodies rose. Likewise the Lord says in the Gospel according to John (chapter 5): “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear the voice of the Son of God; and [Col. 1846A] those who have done good shall come forth to the resurrection of life, while those who have done evil shall come forth to the resurrection of judgment.”

Likewise, in the same: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty; and all nations shall be gathered before him, and he shall separate them from one another as one separates sheep from goats” (Matt. 25). The resurrection of the dead is confirmed not only by Gospel testimonies; Paul also spoke at length in his Epistles, disputing with the Corinthians about the resurrection: “Now if Christ is preached as having risen from the dead, how do some among you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not risen. And if Christ has not risen, then our preaching is empty and your faith also is empty” (1 Cor. 11).

But this is what the heretics object: “Flesh and blood shall not inherit the kingdom of God” (ibid.). The Apostle did not say this concerning the substance of flesh and blood, but concerning the works of flesh and blood. The Apostle explains this in what follows, saying: “Nor shall corruption inherit incorruption.” Seeing that the Corinthians had been led astray by this error, the Apostle, wishing to correct them regarding the resurrection, wrote: “It is sown in corruption; it shall rise in incorruption. It is sown in dishonour; it shall rise in glory. It is sown in weakness; it shall rise in power. It is sown a natural body; it shall rise a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body,” and so forth (ibid.).

Likewise Paul says to the Thessalonians: “We do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For this we say to you in the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who sleep. For Christ, at the command and voice of an angel [Col. 1846C] and with the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven, and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first” (1 Thess. 4).

“. . . . . But I tell you that many shall come from East and West and shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the children of this kingdom shall be cast out into the outer darkness. There shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8). If there is weeping of the eyes, which belongs to flesh, . . . . . and gnashing of teeth, which indicates bones, then the resurrection of those same bodies that had fallen is true.

## CHAPTER XVII

Against the perverse opinion of certain heretics, who maintain that the saints and their prayers are of no benefit to those still living in the world and contending for Christ, and that the departed are not relieved by the benefits and prayers of the living, let us fortify ourselves with our faith and with the authorities of all Catholic teachers of the Church of God.

At times the living pray for the departed, and the dead [Col. 1846D] for the living, as is found in the Gospel according to Luke (chapter 16). Thus the rich man says to Abraham: “Therefore I ask you, Father, to send him to my father’s house. For I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, lest they also come into this place of torments.” This rich man was buried in hell, and yet he prayed for the living. What then should be said of the saints who have obtained mercy, and who desire not their own salvation but that of others, and rejoice in the salvation of the elect who are yet to come?

And John says in the Apocalypse (chapter 8): “Another angel came and stood before the altar, holding a golden censer in his hand; and much incense was given to him, that he might offer it with the prayers of all the saints upon the golden altar which is before the throne.”

The remainder of the manuscript is worn away and torn.

[Col. 1847]

[Col. 1847]

Heloise, Abbess of the Paraclete, grants the place called Pomerium to the Countess of Blois for the construction of an abbey.

[Col. 1847C] I, HUGH, by the grace of God Archbishop of Sens, wish it to be known to all present and future that Heloise, Abbess of the Paraclete, through the intervention of religious men, granted to the Countess of Blois, with the approval and consent of her entire chapter, the place called Pomerium for the construction of an abbey, certain agreements having been established between them which we have thought proper to record.

It was therefore determined and agreed that the first abbess of Pomerium, who has now been appointed—Lady Gertrude, a noble and honourable woman, canonically elected at the Paraclete from among the ladies of that same church—and the others who, after this first abbess, are appointed in the same place, shall be canonically elected according to the custom of other churches, and shall be taken from that church if they can be found there. But if not, they shall go to the Church of the Paraclete and take an abbess for themselves from it; and they shall not be permitted to transfer by election to another church, because they may observe no rule other than that of the Paraclete.

The Abbess of the Paraclete shall go to Pomerium once a year, and, sitting in chapter, shall correct whatever needs correction concerning the rule or anything pertaining to the rule. For the grant of the aforesaid place, the countess gave the Church of the Paraclete three measures of grain each year from her mill at Provins, below Crèvecœur, with the approval of her sons, Counts Henry, Theobald, and Stephen; and she promised lawfully to warrant the property. This was done with the consent of the Abbess of the Paraclete and her entire chapter.

The Abbess of the Paraclete and the countess each promised that what had been done should not in any way be altered through the lord pope or anyone else; moreover, that the conditions designated above between the two churches should not be abolished by either party. The abbess and the countess made me mediator of these agreements; and, at the gracious request of both parties, I received the matter into my hand, so that what had been simply and devoutly concluded, with the Lord’s help, might remain in force to the end. And so that it may be held firm and valid by the present generation and by posterity to come, we caused it to be confirmed by the authority of our seal, under division of the chirograph.

[Col. 1849]

# SUCCESSION OF ABBESSES OF THE NUNNERY OF THE HOLY SPIRIT OF THE PARACLETE

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. 12, p. 572.)

[Col. 1849A] I. Heloise, who in some places is called Heloissa, Helvidis, and Helwisa . . .

II. M . . . . a certain woman resigned to the monastery of Rivotier in 1179. Perhaps she is Melisende, who obtained from Lucius III, Supreme Pontiff, around 1182, confirmation of all the possessions of the monastery of the Paraclete. In 1185 she made an agreement with Guibert, Abbot of Cantumverula. From A. Garnier, Bishop of Troyes, she obtained the parish church of Saint Albin in 1193. She was also granted several [benefices?] by the same bishop in the following year, when the Church of the Paraclete was dedicated and the nuns were introduced into it. Melisende was still alive in 1202; she is commemorated in the calendar of the Paraclete on 19 October.

III. J. . . in the year 1203. Perhaps Ida, who occurs in 1209 in the charters of Vallis Lucens.

IV. Ermengard, perhaps identical with E. who is found in 1210 in the charters of Vallis Lucens. In 1214 she reached an agreement with Hemeric of Lesmes concerning certain tithes. She is mentioned in December of the same year, [Col. 1849B] as also in 1215 and 1219 in the cartulary of Saint Quiriacus, and in 1220 in a charter of Joigny. In August 1228 she issued letters in which she mentions a certain sale made by Louis IX to the prioress of Borenc. Peter, Bishop of Meaux, commanded by the Supreme Pontiff and with Ermengard’s consent, ordered that there should be no more than twenty-five nuns at the priory of Neauphort near Meaux, in October 1229.

In May 1233 she entered into an arbitration agreement with Theobald, Count of Champagne, concerning a certain dispute. With the same count, in August of the same year, she made a settlement concerning the usufruct of the wood on Mount Morvei and of the wood called Aschampenois; in that same year she acknowledged that satisfaction had been made to her by the count. She is also found in 1234 and 1239, in which latter year she sold twelve deniers of rent to Peter of Châtillon, lord of the Castle. In May 1244 she reduced the number of nuns in the priory of Bosrenc; she also fixed the number of nuns at Triangle [Col. 1849C] at twenty-five. In September 1245 she reports that she had received from the Count of Champagne 160 *jugera* of woodland in the park of Pons. Finally, she occurs in 1248. According to the calendar, she died on 29 August. She lies in the choir.

V. Mary I, sister of Odo, Archbishop of Rouen, began to govern around 1249. From Innocent IV, in the eleventh year of his pontificate, on 25 April 1254, she obtained permission that, if in the event of illness she were compelled to resign the abbey, she might retain for life the place she had previously occupied in the monastery. The same pope also granted her permission to admit one suitable woman as a nun in the monastery of the Paraclete itself, notwithstanding the statute concerning a fixed number of nuns, the oath of the same monastery, confirmation by the Apostolic See, or any other sanction whatsoever. The day of her death is recorded in the calendar of the Paraclete as 3 September.

VI. Heloise II is shown by a charter of the Paraclete to have been in charge [Col. 1849D] in 1266.

VII. Mary II issued letters in 1278 concerning the testament of the noble Lady Mary of Esternay, who chose burial for herself at the Paraclete. She sold a certain house in 1280. She also occurs in 1282. She [Col. 1850A] seems to be identical with M. who, according to the charters of the Paraclete, governed in 1295 and 1298.

VIII. Catherine I exchanged certain things with Giles, Abbot of Saint-Denis, in November 1320, according to the records of Saint-Denis, where other letters given in the same month and year are found. The day of her death is noted in the calendar as 23 November.

IX. Alix des Barres settled a dispute with Guy, Abbot of Vallis Lucens, in 1337. She exchanged certain things with the monastery of Celle in 1339. She occurs in a charter of the Paraclete in 1347, and in a charter of Saint Thomas of the Valley in 1348, on the Monday before Christmas.

X. Elisendis des Barres, in a charter of the Paraclete in 1371.

XI. Joanna I des Barres reached an agreement with Theobald, Abbot of Saint James of Provins, in 1403.

XII. Joanna II de la Borde, in the charters of Mont-Royal in 1415.

[Col. 1850B] XIII. Catherine II des Barres, 1420.

XIV. Guillemette I de la Mothe, according to the calendar, died on 1 January 1431. Buried before the high altar.

XV. Guillemette II de la Mothe was in charge in 1457 and 1474, according to charters of the Paraclete. According to the necrology of Neauphort, she died on 14 December.

XVI. Catherine III de Courcelles, daughter of John de Courcelles, knight and lord of Saint-Theobald, was already Abbess of the Paraclete in 1482, when she obtained bulls dated 12 October for the Abbey of Saint Mary of Troyes. She built the cloister, refectory, dormitory, and other buildings. On 2 May 1497, with permission from James, Bishop of Troyes, she transferred the bones of Peter Abaelard and Heloise from the Chapel of Saint Denis, commonly called *le petit Moustier*, into the choir of the church: Abaelard on the right and Heloise on the left. But having long since been removed from there, they rest in an underground vault beneath the altar of the Holy Trinity [Col. 1850C] which is behind the nuns’ choir. Catherine died on 9 July 1519. During her tenure, James Raguier, Bishop of Troyes, reformed this monastery in its walls and grilles in 1509.

XVII. Charlotte de Coligny, by Catherine’s resignation, obtained bulls from Pope Leo X on 13 October 1513. In 1531 she conferred the priory of Mont-Saint-Denis near Meaux upon Sister Herberte de Melun. Thus she is commemorated in the calendar: “On 23 April, our Abbess Charlotte de Coligny, of blessed memory, died in the year of the Lord 1533.”

XVIII. Antoinette de Bonneval, upon the death of Charlotte de Coligny, obtained bulls on 14 May 1533. In that same year, on 6 November, she conferred the priory of Saint Thomas of the Valley upon Sister Herberte de Melun, then prioress of Mont-Saint-Denis near Meaux. The day of her death is thus recorded in the calendar on 20 May: “On this Friday, the day after the Ascension of [Col. 1850D] the Lord, in 1547, died the wise and prudent Lady Antoinette de Bonneval, Abbess of this monastery.”

XIX. Renée de la Tour, daughter of Francis, Viscount of Turenne, and Anne de la Tour of Boulogne, a nun of the monastery [Col. 1851A] of Pissy, did not come to the Paraclete, because she was carried off by untimely death on 20 April 1548.

XX. Edmunda, or Emedia, de la Chastre obtained bulls on 4 May 1548 upon the death of Renée de la Tour.

XXI. Léonarde, otherwise Bernarde, de Turenne occurs in a charter of Saint Thomas of the Valley on 9 June 1556. She died on 1 September 1583.

XXII. Joanna III Chabot, of an ancient and distinguished family, daughter of Philip Chabot, Count of Buzançais and Charny, Admiral of France and royal governor of Burgundy, by Françoise de Longwy-Givry, niece of the Cardinal of Givry, a nun at Jouarre, obtained bulls from Pius IV in 1560, on 12 October, perhaps through the resignation of her predecessor. She took possession on 29 December of the following year; afterward she abandoned religious life and died on 25 June 1593.

XXIII. Mary III de la Rochefoucauld, otherwise [Col. 1851B] de Chaumont, called “of Jesus,” daughter of Antoine de La Rochefoucauld, lord of Calvimont on the Loire, and Cécile de Montmirail, sister of Antoine, Bishop of Angoulême, obtained bulls on 27 August 1598 after the death of Joanna Chabot. She was blessed at Paris by René Potier, Bishop of Beauvais, in the Church of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, on 12 September 1599. She built the chapel and the novices’ quarters, and repaired and renewed the other buildings of the abbey house. She caused the bones of Abaelard and Heloise to be transferred beneath the tomb of the high altar. She presided for forty-five years and two months. She died on 19 February 1639.

XXIV. Anne Mary de la Rochefoucauld de Langeac, called “of the Holy Spirit,” niece of the preceding abbess through her brother James, lord of Langeac, and Françoise de Langeac in Auvergne, heiress of that lordship, a nun of the Paraclete, received bulls on 15 October 1624. [Col. 1852A] On 3 August 1641 she gave her consent for Margaret Thiersaut to transfer the priory of Saint Thomas of the Valley to Madeleine Miron. She is also mentioned on 25 March 1642, when she consents to the transfer of the priory of Saint Thomas to the town of Lagny. She governed for seven years and three months. She died on 28 May 1646.

XXV. Gabrielle Mary de la Rochefoucauld, daughter of Francis, Duke of La Rochefoucauld, Prince of Marcillac, Knight of the Collar, Viceroy of Poitou, by Gabrielle du Plessis-Liancourt; born 13 December 1624; sister of Francis, Duke of La Rochefoucauld, and Louis, Bishop of Lectoure; a nun of Blessed Mary of Saintes; succeeded Anne Mary from being coadjutrix in 1644. She afterward became Abbess of Blessed Mary of Soissons upon the death of Armande de Lorraine, who died on 19 May 1684.

XXVI. Catherine IV de la Rochefoucauld, born 25 October 1619, sister of the preceding, first Abbess of Carentoir in 1674 and then transferred to the Paraclete [Col. 1852B] in 1675. She resigned in favour of the following abbess.

XXVII. Mary IV de Roye de la Rochefoucauld de Roucy, daughter of Frederick Charles, Count of Roye, and Elizabeth de Durfort, a nun of Blessed Mary of Soissons, obtained bulls dated 1 October 1705 and took possession on 9 February 1706. Into her hands Elizabeth Le Coq resigned the priory of Saint Thomas of the Valley on 25 July 1727.

Besides these, the following are found in the calendar without dates:

Aelipdis, 28 February. Jacoba, 8 March. Agneta de Bordis, 19 May. Isabella, 30 August. Joanna, 4 October. Helisendis, 8 October. Joanna, 25 December.

# HILARY AND BERENGAR, DISCIPLES OF ABAELARD

[Col. 1851]

# HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, vol. 12, p. 251.)

## I. THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF HILARY
Hilary, according to Dom Mabillon [Note: [Col. 1851] *Annals*, book LXVIII, no. 69], was English by birth. While still very young he left his country to come to France and attend Abelard’s lectures, at the time when the latter was teaching at the Paraclete—that is, about the year 1125. When his master became abbot of Saint-Gildas de Rhuys during the course of his studies, Hilary went to complete them at the school of Angers. The remainder of his life has been forgotten.

While studying at the Paraclete, he composed a rhymed prose in the form of an elegy, the occasion and object of which have not hitherto been properly explained. Here is the key to the piece. Abelard’s servant having informed him of certain secret disorders among his pupils, he was so angered that he wished to cease teaching altogether. Neither the prayers nor the tears of the young men could move him, except on condition that they abandon the lodgings which they had made for themselves at the Paraclete and go to reside in the nearby village of Quincey. Hilary’s piece concerns this event, and not, as Dom Gervaise maintains [Note: [Col. 1851] *Life of Abelard*, vol. II, p. 27], following Du Boulay, Abelard’s departure for Saint-Gildas.

From the refrain in the vernacular found at the end of every stanza, a modern critic [Note: [Col. 1851] *Poetry of the King of Navarre*, vol. I, p. 212] has wished to conclude—but wrongly, in our opinion—that twelfth-century usage admitted only Latin in songs and other poems, and scarcely allowed a French verse to be inserted from time to time.

There are two editions of this piece: one among Abelard’s Works, the other in the second volume of the *History of the University of Paris*.

While at the school of Angers, Hilary composed a second rhymed prose whose subject is the life of Blessed Eve, an anchoress of Anjou who died toward the end of the eleventh century. Like Hilary, she was from England, where she had embraced the religious life in the monastery of Clington. But, hearing of the reputation of a holy man named Hervé, who lived as a recluse at Calone near Angers, she crossed the sea to place herself under his direction and to practise the same kind of life with him. They lived together near the church of that place, dedicated to St Eutropius. Hilary expresses this in the following terms:

> At last she chose for herself a place at Saint Eutropius,  
> which she saw would be for her the beginning of every good.  
> There, in a certain enclosure, she remained devoted to Christ,  
> and this path of living rightly pleased her greatly,  
> on which, by God’s gift, she avoided every unlawful thing.  
> There Eve lived for a long time with Hervé as her companion.  
> You who hear this, I perceive that you are troubled at the report.  
> Flee, brother, from suspicion; let this suspicion not arise:  
> this love was not in the world, but in Christ.

These two persons, being of different sexes, must doubtless have taken suitable precautions to shield themselves from all suspicion, since Geoffrey of Vendôme—so zealous, as is known, for good discipline—made no reproach on this account to Hervé in the letters he wrote to him. Hervé survived Eve, whose funeral was celebrated with a great gathering of devout people:

> Clerics committed her body to the earth according to custom;  
> nuns were present, monks, and canons.

This piece is known only through the extracts which Dom Mabillon inserted in his *Benedictine Annals*. That learned man did not think fit to tell us the repository in which the original exists; and it is solely on his authority that we assign it to our author.

We do not have the same grounds for assigning to him the glosses of a Hilary on the ecclesiastical hymns. There are three editions of this work: the first two [Note: [Col. 1853] Lipenius, *Bibliotheca theologica*], quarto editions printed at Paris in 1480 and 1488 by Pierre Levet; the last [Note: [Col. 1853] Royal Library, vol. I, no. 226; Lipenius, ibid.], at Rouen in 1505. All three bear this title: *Book of Hymns, or Golden Exposition of the Hymns together with the Text, by the study and labour of a certain Hilary*. From so vague an indication it is impossible to say precisely who this Hilary was. Three Hilarys are known in the twelfth century, the period in which the glosses seem to have been composed: namely, the subject of this notice; Hilary, a professor at Orléans; and Hilary of Poitiers, the teacher of Gilbert de la Porrée. Perhaps there was a fourth, of whom history says nothing, to whom the work in fact belongs.

The same difficulty arises concerning the author of a discourse entitled *Hilary’s Sermon on the Body and Blood of the Lord*, found at the abbey of Saint-Amand and at the cathedral of Saint-Omer [Note: [Col. 1853] Sanderus, *Belgian Manuscripts*, part I, pp. 33–319]. What is certain is that it does not belong to the great St Hilary, bishop of Poitiers. The proof is drawn from the words with which it begins: “Those,” says Augustine, in *On Care for the Dead*.

## THE LIFE AND WRITINGS OF PETER BERENGARIUS, SCHOOLMASTER

Peter Berengarius of Poitiers, one of Abelard’s last disciples in chronological order, bears the title “Schoolmaster” at the head of his works. It cannot positively be said in what part of France he exercised that office. But the most probable supposition is that it was in his native country. He had scarcely entered upon it when he learned of the censure pronounced against his master in 1140 at the Council of Sens. At this news, carried away by blind zeal, he took up his pen to avenge him. His work, to which he gave the title *Apology for Abelard*, was to have had two parts. But the poor reception of the first part, which he hastened to publish as soon as it was finished, prevented him from working on the second. In that part, according to his plan, he would have examined the substance of the case, whereas in the first he touches only upon its formalities.

This *Apology* is addressed to St Bernard as Abelard’s accuser and the instigator of his condemnation. St Bernard possessed too much nobility of soul and elevation of feeling to lower himself to refute such a work, which could dishonour only its author. But honest men did not share his indifference. On every side people rose against Abelard’s shameless apologist; even the solitaries of the Grande Chartreuse broke their silence to express their displeasure. Berengarius wished for some time to withstand the flood of public indignation. He even wrote a letter to the Carthusians in which, mingling praise of their order with personal reproaches, he accused them of having fallen away from their primitive holiness by presuming to speak indiscriminately of persons unknown to them.

To escape the storm gathering over his head, Berengarius chose exile. After wandering here and there, he settled in the Cévennes Mountains. From there he wrote to the bishop of Mende—William, who governed that church from 1109 until 1150—to implore his protection. This letter, published by Duchesne along with the two preceding writings among Abelard’s Works, and by Du Boulay in his *History of the University of Paris*, presents an extremely equivocal retraction. It displays the embarrassment of a proud offender who will acknowledge his fault only so far as necessary to escape punishment. He says first that, although he had fallen among a barbarous people and thieves, his life was nevertheless safe; but his mind was not at peace, being assailed as it was by the insulting words of a great many persons whose virtue he could not help respecting. He begs the prelate to defend him from the bites of these sheep, which inflict wounds more painful than if he were being torn by wolves. He pays homage to the holiness of the abbot of Clairvaux, admitting that he shines in the Church as a bright and burning lamp. “But,” he says, “this lamp is enclosed in an earthen vessel; and with all his merit, the abbot of Clairvaux is a man subject, like others, to the infirmities of nature.” He excuses having written against Bernard with too much vehemence on the ground that, being then in the first heat of youth and newly out of school, he breathed nothing but disputation and sought only an occasion to measure himself against some professional scholar. Yet he dares to challenge learned men to show anything which he rashly advanced against St Bernard in his *Apology for Abelard*:

> Let learned men read the *Apology* which I published; and, if I did not justly accuse the lord abbot, let them freely rebuke me.

Nevertheless, a few lines later—so little is he consistent with himself—he is willing to blot out that work, provided that everything he said to the disadvantage of the man of God be read not seriously but as mere jest:

> I shall condemn it on this condition: that, if I said anything against the person of the man of God, it may be read as a joke, not seriously.

He goes further, declaring that, having become wiser with age, he embraces with his whole heart the opinion of the abbot of Clairvaux, abandons Abelard’s party, and no longer wishes to defend his articles—not, however, because they are bad in themselves, but because they are harsh and ill-sounding:

> As time passed, my understanding increased, and, as they say, I went over with both feet to the abbot’s opinion. I did not wish to be the advocate of the propositions brought against Abelard, because, although they had a sound meaning, they did not sound sound.

Coming next to the invectives he had hurled against the Carthusians, he admits that these good anchorites amassed great spiritual riches. But, seeing, he adds, that they put them into a pierced bag by the liberty they allowed themselves of opening their mouths on every occasion, I wished to close the hole in the bag by imposing silence upon them, so as to preserve the pure flour of religion. He also tries to justify himself concerning a monk of Marseille whom he had attacked in a writing which has not come down to us. His defence is that this monk, in distinguishing the supreme God from the Creator of the universe—as, he says, the letter which the monk wrote to him attests—deserved the rebuke Berengarius gave him.

Finally, he was reproached with insulting the monastic order in general by this satirical line:

> Among religious men, a dish is a psalm, and a fat meal is an alleluia.

(Duchesne says that this line occurs in the prologue to Berengarius’s treatise on the Incarnation, dedicated to a canon named Benedict. He would have done well to indicate the repository in which this work is preserved, for we have made fruitless searches to discover it.) Berengarius’s answer is that he spoke only in general terms, without naming anyone in particular. He ends by asking forgiveness from those whom he had wounded, being willing to acknowledge himself guilty, though rather out of complaisance than conviction:

> I ask pardon as an innocent man; and, if it please you more, I seek pardon as a guilty one.

Such is Berengarius’s alleged retraction. Our ignorance of everything concerning him after this letter does not allow us to say what came of it. Yet among the defects of judgment, integrity, and charity which swarm in the writings just reviewed, one cannot fail to recognize a great fire of imagination, lively flashes of wit, and a fairly wide reading of sacred and profane authors, especially the poets, whom Berengarius sometimes applies happily. It is a pity that he corrupted such fine literary gifts by the unworthy use he made of them.

[Col. 1855]

## ELEGY IN WHICH HILARY, DISCIPLE OF PETER ABELARD, LAMENTS HIS MASTER’S DEPARTURE FROM THE PARACLETE

[Col. 1855A]

> The tongue of a servant, the tongue of treachery,  
> the mover of quarrels, the seed of discord—  
> today we feel how wicked it is,  
> as we lie under a grievous sentence.  
>
> Our master has wrongfully abandoned us.  
> *Tort avers nos li mestre.*
>
> The servant’s tongue has stirred Peter’s anger  
> into hostility against us;  
> it deserves the avenging sword,  
> because it has extinguished our studies.  
>
> Our master has wrongfully abandoned us.  
> *Tort avers nos li mestre.*
>
> That peasant is to be detested,  
> through whom the cleric withdrew from the school;  
> it is a grievous pain that a certain common fellow  
> brought it about that the logician should cease.  
>
> Our master has wrongfully abandoned us.  
> *Tort avers nos li mestre.*
>
> It is to be lamented that the tongue of a little servant,  
> the cause to us of great peril,  
> whispered in the ear of one too ready to believe,  
> [Col. 1855B]  
> and through it his pupils cease [their studies].  
>
> Our master has wrongfully abandoned us.  
> *Tort avers nos li mestre.*
>
> O how hard I find our master,  
> if, at the report of his oxherd—  
> a worthless fellow of no value—  
> his teaching is denied us.  
>
> Our master has wrongfully abandoned us.  
> *Tort avers nos li mestre.*

[Col. 1856A]

> Alas! How cruel is this announcement,  
> saying: “Brothers, depart quickly!  
> Let Quincey be your dwelling-place;  
> otherwise the monk will not lecture.”  
>
> Our master has wrongfully abandoned us.  
> *Tort avers nos li mestre.*
>
> What, Hilary—why then do you hesitate?  
> Why do you not go and dwell in the village?  
> But the shortness of the day restrains you,  
> the long journey, and your burden.  
>
> Our master has wrongfully abandoned us.  
> *Tort avers nos li mestre.*
>
> From different places many of us assembled  
> where the spring of logic was most abundant;  
> but let greatest and least depart,  
> for what we sought here is denied us.  
>
> Our master has wrongfully abandoned us.  
> *Tort avers nos li mestre.*
>
> The rushing wind of logic  
> drew us together, everywhere and openly.  
> [Col. 1856B]  
> Look upon us in our desolation, master,  
> and restore our hope, which is failing.  
>
> Our master has wrongfully abandoned us.  
> *Tort avers nos li mestre.*
>
> If, through a deceiver, through one who misleads,  
> you are willing to deny us help,  
> this place will not bear the name  
> of an oratory, but of a place of weeping.  
>
> Our master has wrongfully abandoned us.  
> *Tort avers nos li mestre.*

[Col. 1857]

## APOLOGY OF BERENGARIUS THE SCHOOLMASTER AGAINST BLESSED BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, AND OTHERS WHO CONDEMNED PETER ABELARD

So that you may laugh, reader, see; indeed, see in order that you may laugh at the ridiculous things which will occur to you. And, as Berengarius himself advises you in the following letter, if he said anything against the person of the man of God—that is, Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux—read it as a joke, not seriously.

[Col. 1857A]

Your writings, Bernard, are made widely famous by celebrated report. Nor is it surprising that your writings are set upon the platform of renown, since it is evident that, whatever they may be, they are approved by the leading men of this age. Men marvel that in you, unacquainted with the liberal arts, there should be such abundance of eloquence, because your utterances have now covered the whole face of the earth. To them one must reply from Scripture: “Great are the works of the Lord” (Ps. 110); and: “This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76). But there is no reason why they should be struck with amazement. Rather, it would be more astonishing if you suffered from dryness of speech, since we have heard that from almost the first rudiments of adolescence you composed little mime-songs and polished tunes. Nor do we speak on uncertain hearsay; the native land of our language, which fostered you, is witness.

[Col. 1857B]

Is it not also deeply impressed upon your memory that you always strove to surpass your brothers in contests of rhythm and in the ingenuity of sharp invention? You thought it a grave and bitter injury to find anyone who answered with equal boldness. From the corroborating testimony of credible witnesses, I might insert in this little work something about your trifles; but I fear that the page may be corrupted by the insertion of a shameful tale. Besides, matters known to all need no witness. You therefore often bring that habit of composing and trifling into the service of the divine instrument; and the unlearned assert that what you pour forth abundantly and eloquently is spoken loftily and grandly.
