But necessary reason proves that this is not so. For truth is often uttered plainly and without polish, while falsehood is commended by the pleasing grace of plausible speech.

[Col. 1857C]

And, as Augustine says, plainness of speech and eloquence are like rustic and refined vessels, while falsehood and truth are like cheap and precious dishes. Either kind of dish may be served in either kind of vessel. I do not say this in order to render you conspicuous and suspect, but in order to maintain simply that truth is not found in everyone’s eloquence. But enough on this matter; let us pass rather to the rest.

Long ago winged fame scattered abroad through the world the fragrance of your holiness, proclaimed your merits, and declaimed your miracles. We called our age blessed, adorned with the brightness of so radiant a star; and we thought that a world already due to perish was preserved by your merits.

[Col. 1858A]

We hoped that at the discretion of your tongue lay heaven’s mercy, the temperateness of the air, the abundance of the earth, and the blessing of its fruits. Your head touched the clouds, and, according to the common proverb, the shadows of your branches rose above the mountains. So long did you live, so did you shape the Church by chaste institutions, that we thought demons roared at your waistcloths, and we counted ourselves blessed to boast of so great a patron.

But now, alas! what was hidden has been disclosed, and at length you have awakened the stings of the sleeping serpent. Passing over everything else, you set Peter Abelard up as though he were a target for the arrow, that you might vomit upon him the poison of your bitterness, remove him from the land of the living, and place him among the dead.

[Col. 1858B]

Having assembled bishops from every quarter, you pronounced him a heretic at the Council of Sens; you cut him off from the womb of Mother Church as though he were an untimely birth. As he walked in Christ’s way, you came forth secretly like an assassin and stripped him of the seamless tunic. You preached to the people that they should offer prayer to God for him, while inwardly you planned to proscribe him from the Christian world. What could the common people do? What could they pray, when they did not know for whom prayer was to be made? You, man of God, who had performed miracles, who sat with Mary at Jesus’ feet (Luke 10), who kept all these words in your heart (Luke 2), ought to have burned the purest incense of holy prayer before the gaze of heaven, that your accused man Peter might repent and become such that no suspicion could defile him.

[Col. 1858C]

But perhaps you preferred him such as he was, so that you might find a suitable occasion for reproach. Finally, after dinner Peter’s book was brought in, and someone was ordered to recite Peter’s little works in a loud voice. But he, animated by hatred of Peter and irrigated by the shoot of the vine—not that vine which said, “I am the true vine” (John 15), but the vine of him who laid the patriarch naked on the threshing-floor (Gen. 9)—shouted more loudly than he had been asked to do. After a while you might have seen the bishops jeering, clapping foot against foot, laughing, and fooling about, so that anyone would easily judge that they were paying vows not to Christ but to Bacchus. Meanwhile cups were saluted, drinking-vessels were celebrated, wines praised, and the bishops’ throats drenched.

[Col. 1859A]

Then someone might have played with Horatian wit:

> “No tree, Varus, plant before the sacred vine.”

For the words which the same poet promises in another poem—

> “Now is the time for drinking; now with free foot  
> the ground must be struck . . .”

—were there carefully put into practice. How much more wholesome it would have been to hear the pleasing judgment of the Gallic poet, wrought out in very polished verses. For he says:

> I approve wines if drunk in moderation, and they ought to be approved;  
> if they are not drunk in moderation, I think wines are poisons.

But the drink of Lethean juice had already buried the hearts of the bishops. Behold, says the satirist:

> “. . . amid their cups  
> satiated bishops ask what the divine poems tell.”

[Col. 1859B]

Finally, whenever anything subtle and divine sounded forth, something unfamiliar to episcopal ears, all who heard were cut to the heart and gnashed their teeth at Peter. And, having the eyes of a mole fixed upon the philosopher, they said: “Should we allow this monster to live?” Shaking their heads like the Jews, they said: “Ha! behold the one who destroys the temple of God” (Matt. 27). Thus the blind judge the words of light; thus drunkards condemn a sober man; thus eloquent cups argue against the instrument of the Trinity. Thus horned men dispute against the simple. Thus dogs [attack] a holy man; thus swine gnaw pearls. Thus the salt of the earth loses its savour. Thus the trumpet of the law is stopped up. The wise man preaches: “He who touches pitch shall be defiled by it” (Ecclus. 13); and we may render this in another verse: “He who touches wine shall be defiled by it.”

[Col. 1859C]

The sobriety of the bishops had drunk the wholly unmixed blood of the grape, whose purity water had not deflowered, because, according to Martial:

> It is a very great crime to murder sacred Falernian wine,  
> nor does Bacchus endure marriage with water.

The philosophic rulers of the world had filled their casks of the throat [variant: “their casks”] with wine upon wine. Its heat had so invaded their brains that the eyes of all were loosened into lethargic sleep. Meanwhile the reader sounds aloud and the hearer snores. One leans on his elbow to give sleep to his eyes. Another seeks sleep for his eyelids upon a soft pillow. Another, resting his head upon his knees, dozes.

[Col. 1859D]

Whenever the reader found some sufficiently sharp point in Peter, he cried to the deaf ears of the bishops: “Do you condemn [it]?” Then certain men, scarcely awakened at the final syllable, with sleepy voice and nodding head, said: “We condemn.” Others, roused by the tumult of those condemning, with the first syllable cut off, said: “. . . demn [we do].” Truly you are “born,” but your swimming is a storm, your swimming is a sinking [variant: “an immersion”]. Thus sleeping soldiers bear witness: “While we slept, the apostles came and took away the body” (Matt. 28). He who had kept watch over the law of the Lord day and night is now condemned by priests of Bacchus. Thus a sick man treats a physician. Thus a shipwrecked man condemns one standing on the shore. Thus a man being led to the gallows to be hanged accuses innocence.

[Col. 1860A]

What are we doing, my soul? Where are we turning? Have the precepts of the rhetoricians slipped from your mind, and, occupied with grief and hindered by sobs, do you fail to preserve the order of speech? Do you think that, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith upon the earth? (Luke 18.) Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests, but Peter has nowhere to lay his head (Matt. 8). Thus the accused sit in the judge’s seat; in the avenger’s place sit the persecutors of innocence. With such judges and such plaintiffs, all things are perverted:

> One, stuffed with food, prefers to swell with a little sleep;  
> another, with lips stretched out, inflates his words.  
> One talks too much, another is silent; one walks, one stands;  
> one loves tears, another to burst out in laughter.  
> Peace is madness to them all, in their different ways.

What did such men do? What did these legal experts decree?

[Col. 1860B]

The Gospel reading consoles us: “The chief priests and Pharisees gathered a council and said, ‘What are we doing? For this man performs many signs. If we let him go on thus, all will believe in him.’ But one of them, named Bernard the abbot, being high priest of that council, prophesied, saying: ‘It is expedient for us that one man be destroyed from among the people, and that not the whole nation perish’” (John 11). From that day, therefore, they planned to condemn him, saying those words of Solomon: “Let us lay snares for the righteous man; let us overthrow the grace of his lips” (Wis. 2); “Let us find a root of speech against the just man” (Job 19). You did what you set out to do, and you drew your viperous tongues against Abelard. Overthrown, you overthrew; and you swallowed wine as one who devours the poor in secret.

[Col. 1860C]

Meanwhile Peter prayed: “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. 100:2). At times he diligently pondered the Psalmist’s words: “Many calves surrounded me; fat bulls besieged me. They opened their mouth against me” (Ps. 21). Truly fat, their necks thickened with folds of fat and sweating liquidly toward ruin [perhaps *aruinam*, “destruction”]. Nor is this surprising. For those of the household of neither faith visited tears neither in mercy nor in charity. Yet there sat in the council of vanity—against the decree of Psalm 25—a certain bishop of celebrated memory, to whose authority the assent of very many claimed allegiance. Belching out the previous day’s drunkenness, he vomited forth the following address to the assembly:

[Col. 1860D]

> “Brothers, sharers in the Christian religion, provide for the danger of all [variant: “the common danger”]. Let not faith be disturbed within you; let not the pure eye of the dove be covered by a swelling blemish. For the possession of other virtues avails nothing where faith is lacking, according to that saying of the Apostle: ‘If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, it profits me nothing’” (1 Cor. 13).

O charm of Minerva! O Attic wit! O Ciceronian eloquence! Surely this donkey does not want such a tail. Such an end does not fit such a head. Hence even those who approved confessed their shame with downcast brow. And deservedly we may assign this shadow of a great name to the flock of whom it is said: “They conceived wind and wove spiders’ webs” (Isa. 59).

[Col. 1861A]

The aforesaid bishop, adding also the following to what he had said:

> “Peter,” he says, “always troubles the Church; he is always devising novelty. O times! O manners!”

Thus a blind man judges of the sun. Thus a man without hands paints upon ivory. Thus a donkey appraises a city. Thus animal bishops judge; thus they debate cases; thus they examine arguments. Thus the sons of his mother fight against him. Thus fat swine grunt against one who is silent.

Therefore, caught in so many and such great straits, Abelard fled to the sanctuary of Roman judgment. “I am,” he said, “a son of the Roman Church. I wish my case to be judged as that of an accused man: I appeal to Caesar” (Acts 25). But Abbot Bernard, in whose arm the multitude of prelates trusted, did not say, as the governor who held Paul in chains said: “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go” (ibid.); but: “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall not go.”

[Col. 1861B]

For he reported what had been done to the Apostolic See, and immediately from the Roman See letters of condemnation against Peter flew through the Gallican Church. Thus was condemned that mouth, treasury-house of reason, trumpet of faith, dwelling-place of the Trinity. Condemned, alas, in his absence, unheard and unconvicted. What shall I say—or what shall I not say, Bernard?

> There is no need for war: we ask pardon and peace;  
> we stretch out our joined hands to your reins.  
> The laws of things will fall; the authority of laws will be overturned,  
> if you wish it, if you command it, if you decree that it be done thus—  
> you in whose hands lie decision, power, and the rule of speech.

Good Jesus, whose guilt ever had judges so blind that they did not examine the sides of the case on both sides, that they did not determine toward which side justice inclined most strongly?

[Col. 1861C]

These men, with closed eyes, feel their way around the matter; and, as though they were clear-sighted judges of affairs, suddenly shoot the poison of iniquity from a drawn bow. Whatever the inward fury of hatreds might whirl against Peter, whatever the tempest of implacable madness, whatever unjust envy might forge, the sober sharpness of apostolic censure ought never to sleep. But he easily deviates from justice who fears man more than God in a cause. And true is that utterance sounding through the prophetic instrument: “Every head is sick; from the sole of the foot to the neck there is no health in it” (Isa. 1).

“But,” say the abbot’s supporters, “he wished to correct Peter.” If, good man, you intended to recall Peter to the sound state of faith, why did you stamp upon him before the people the mark of eternal blasphemy?

[Col. 1861D]

And again, if you took from Peter the people’s affection, how did you intend to correct him? From this combination the conclusion follows that you burned against Peter, not from love of correction, but from desire for your own revenge. The Prophet spoke excellently: “Let the righteous man correct me in mercy” (Ps. 140). For where mercy is absent, there is not correction by a righteous man, but the uncultivated barbarity of a tyrant. His letter addressed to Pope Innocent also testifies to the rancour of his mind, in which he fumes thus: “He who attacks Peter’s faith ought not to find refuge at Peter’s See.” Spare us, spare us, renowned warrior. It does not befit a monk to fight thus. Believe Solomon: “Do not be too righteous, lest perhaps you become stupefied” (Eccles. 7).

[Col. 1862A]

He does not attack Peter’s faith who affirms Peter’s faith. Therefore he ought to find refuge at Peter’s See. Allow, I beg you, Peter to be a Christian with you. And if you wish, he will be a Catholic with you. And if you do not wish it, he will nevertheless be a Catholic. For God is common, not private.

But if this judgment pleases your heart, let us consider together how Peter attacks Peter’s faith. Peter writes to the handmaid of God Heloise, excellently instructed in sacred letters, a rather familiar letter which, among other things, contains even the following words:

> “My sister Heloise, once dear to me in the world, now most dear in Christ,” etc.

See above, at the beginning of the volume.

[Col. 1862B]

I thought these words should be extracted word for word from Peter’s letter, so that it might become clear how Peter attacked Peter’s faith. Now, stern censor, be present and weigh Peter’s faith with sincere judgment. You said: “He who attacks Peter’s faith ought not to find refuge at Peter’s See.” Taken by itself, this would be a lofty and generally true statement. But because you said it personally concerning Peter, I prove that you hold things contrary to truth. For Peter does not challenge the faith to whose rule he directs his life; nor is he alien from Christ’s portion, whose name he has so humbly marked upon himself. He ought, therefore, to have found refuge at Peter’s See, had not the enticement of your speech shut the bowels of mercy in the Roman Church. But, while you close to Peter the door of mercy, you clearly reveal the force of the madness you have conceived.

[Col. 1862C]

Here perhaps you will say: “Excessive wrong is inflicted upon me. Zeal for God’s house consumed me, because the leprosy of insane doctrine stained the body of the Church. I thought that it must be opposed at once in the very seed of its wickedness, lest the force of the poison spread widely. Did I not act cautiously and judiciously in compiling that foul and sacrilegious doctrine into a sort of manual index, so that those wishing briefly to grasp the substance of the matter might not be burdened with traversing the broad forests of Abelard’s volumes?”

To this I reply: “I praise you, Father, but I do not praise you in this. We have seen the index, in which we read not Peter’s doctrines but the propositions of a wicked fabrication: namely, that the Father is omnipotence, the Son a certain power, and the Holy Spirit no power; that the Holy Spirit, although of the same substance as the Son, is nevertheless not from the same substance; that a human being can act without new grace; that God cannot do more than he does, nor do better than he does, nor act otherwise than he does; that Christ’s soul did not descend into hell.

[Col. 1862D]

“These and other matters are contained in your index. Some of them, I admit, Peter both said and wrote; but others he neither uttered nor wrote. Which things he did say, which he did not say, and with what Catholic mind he understood those things which he did say, the second treatise of the work I have undertaken will ardently and diligently declare through Christian disputation. For these matters are such as must be dissolved and refuted; not without reason, therefore, they are reserved for a separate volume.”

[Col. 1863A]

It must now be vigorously pursued why a holy man, most celebrated in the mouth of fame, should charge Peter Abelard with the crime of heresy when he had committed to his own writings certain things that ought to be buried in perpetual silence. For it is an established report, promulgated from ancient times as though by the laws of nature, that no one can convict another of a like crime. Since you did this, you acted both imprudently and shamelessly.

Peter had erred: granted. Why did you err? You erred either knowingly or unknowingly. If knowingly, you are proved an enemy of the Church; if unknowingly, how are you a defender of the Church, who cannot distinguish error? You certainly erred when you asserted that the origin of souls is from heaven. How you maintain this in your book, I shall set out again from its higher starting-point for the discerning reader, since it is useful and easy to ascertain.

[Col. 1863B] There is a book which the Hebrew calls *Firasirim* [materially uncertain; apparently “Song of Songs”], and the Latin calls the *Song of Songs*, whose letter, for wakeful minds, sweats forth the secret of a certain divine understanding. Bernard applies his hand of exposition to this book, in order to draw the crop of outstanding meaning from the shaggy little works of the letter; he indeed employs a moderate and restrained style of speech. Yet I should like to ask briefly why Bernard, after the labours of so many distinguished men who devoted their talents to the aforesaid work, attempted to bring into the light a volume of such immense majesty. For if our elders have fully and sufficiently brought this book’s hidden places into the sun, I wonder with what face you dared to extend your hands to a work polished to the fingernail. But if certain mysteries have been revealed to you

[Col. 1863C] which escaped their knowledge, I do not begrudge it; indeed, I warmly applaud the labour. Yet when I turn over their expositions and your commentary with studious hands, I find that you have said nothing new; rather, I discover another’s meaning clothed in your words. Your explanation therefore appears superfluous.

And lest anyone think that I have uttered improbabilities, I shall produce a four-horse team of commentators on this book: namely Origen the Greek, Ambrose of Milan, Retius of Autun, and Bede the Englishman. The first, although, as Jerome says, he surpassed himself in his other books, surpassed himself in the *Song of Songs*. The second, in plausible and learned speech, established the love of Bridegroom and Bride. The third

[Col. 1863D] discussed the complexity of the volume in lofty utterance. The fourth dispelled the obscurities of the same book in seven books. After such industrious men, then, Bernard ploughs as though our elders had left something unattempted.

We might indeed rest content with the midnight labours of an eloquent man, were he not seen to weave tragedy rather than commentary. For, after some portion of the work has been laid open, he suddenly introduces the death of his brother, and in pursuing that funeral he consumes nearly two quaternions. How discordant and incongruous this is there, I shall explain briefly. That book of Solomon, forged in the workshop of the Holy Spirit, joins in marriage the embraces of Christ and the Church under the figure of Bridegroom and Bride. Joy properly accords with weddings. But Bernard, either overcome by weariness at obscure matters,

[Col. 1864A] or disregarding the Apostle’s saying that urges us to rejoice with those who rejoice (Rom. 12), brings his dead man to a wedding, although it is written: “God is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Mark 12). Thus, while the Bridegroom reclines in the Bride’s bosom, and the young men of the Bridegroom and the maidens of the Bride applaud in reciprocal delight, a funeral trumpet suddenly sounds. The feast turns to mourning; the instruments are turned to a funeral. Tragedy brings forth laughter amid the wedding. Were you not an undiscerning and inelegant lyre-player, presenting funeral melodies at a royal banquet? Who ever dreamed of such a monstrosity?

We are accustomed to laugh at pictures which begin with a human being and end in an ass. Review, I beg you, the monuments of ancient genius on this book, and you will find no one who joined sad things to joyful ones in such a subject.

[Col. 1864B] Hence the golden Muse of Retius of Autun speaks thus:

> “The propriety of a noble subject must be observed: let the festive dances of Bridegroom and Bride leap to the trumpet. For it is not lawful for the mind to be drawn away to funerals, since the cheerfulness of the guests invites us to expound the song of weddings. But because in us the capacity for so great a task is either nonexistent or exceedingly deficient, I shall rely upon the grace of him who says through his Gospel: ‘Without me you can do nothing’ (John 15). Nor indeed will a passing word fail me, since I believe in the Word who was in the beginning with God” (John 1).

O utterance worthy of a Catholic teacher! O faithful confessor of grace! The wise man rightly marked out the plumb-line of his judgment, separating grief from joy by so great an interval.

[Col. 1864C] But you, transgressing the boundaries set by your fathers, have, by a miserable fate, turned songs into elegies and poems into dirges. Even if the authoritative decisions of ecclesiastical judgment failed you, you could have recalled the precepts of pagan wisdom as well. For when Zeuxis, the outstanding painter, painted an image of Helen, he did not attach a monkey’s arms to her, nor a chimera’s belly, nor a fish’s tail; rather, he displayed her, perfected by the refinement of human limbs, for public use [read: public viewing]; otherwise the picture would have been indecent and ridiculous. Hence Horace in the *Art of Poetry*:

> If a painter chose to join a horse’s neck  
> To a human head, and add varied feathers,  
> Bringing limbs together from all sides, so that a lovely woman above  
> Ended shamefully in a black fish—  
> Would you, my friends, when admitted to view it, refrain from laughing?

[Col. 1864D] Art allows you to begin whatever you wish, but not to assign any random ending to what you have begun. Hence the same poet wrote shortly afterwards:

> [lacuna] To painters and poets  
> There has always been an equal power of daring anything;  
> But not so that the gentle may be joined with the savage, nor so that  
> Serpents be coupled with birds, lambs with tigers.

Like the dreams of a sick man, the empty images of your work are fashioned,

> [lacuna] so that neither foot nor head  
> Is restored to a single form …

> One purple patch, gleaming broadly,  
> Is sewn on, and another [lacuna]

But lest any of your supporters object:

> We know how to set aside what is uncouth with a graceful phrase,  
> And are skilled in proper sound by hand and ear.

[Col. 1865A] What more is needed? The whole *Art of Poetry* has undertaken sworn warfare against you. You truly ought, in accordance with the teaching of that same poet, to keep the offspring of your genius until its ninth year, so that it might be lawful to return a badly turned work to the anvil, and to take care that the labour of the file did not offend you. You should certainly have delayed the haste of publication, since it is written:

> [lacuna] a word once sent out does not know how to return.

We praise in you, Father, the vein of genius, but we blame your ignorance of art. Hence the ancients defined genius as maimed unless it calls art to its aid. Lucilius’s wit is praised, and yet he is criticized because he runs with an uncomposed foot:

> Ennius, rich in genius and crude in art, composes verses  
> Imposed upon him and lacking artistry.

[Col. 1865B] Among these is the line:

> All mortals desire to be praised.

But since it is clear even to the bleary-eyed and barbers that you did not rightly join lamentations to an epithalamium, I should like to consider something of that tragic bellowing itself. Among other things, if I am not mistaken, the mournful Muse of our orator thus reckons:

> “My brother has departed from life—or rather, to speak more correctly, he has left death for life. My brother, I say, has departed: the tenor of continence, the mirror of morals, the bond of religion. Who henceforth will strengthen me for labour? Who further will soothe me in my grief?”

And after some words:

> “The ox seeks the ox; thinking itself alone, it bears witness to its dutiful affection by frequent lowing. The ox, I say, seeks the ox with whom it was accustomed to draw ploughs with its neck.”

What Bernard says is indeed beautiful and ringing;

[Col. 1865C] but he hunts for the reward and reputation belonging to another’s labour. For Ambrose set down these very words, syllable for syllable, in the lament which he fashioned in polished and brightened style over the death of his friend Satyrus. Thus Bernard is so vehement, so persistent, so vivid in this lament that every reader is firmly convinced that he does not utter genuine tears, but pours out words by which genuine complaints may be expressed.

Yet some foolish people say, deceived by the seductive moderation of his tongue—people who love the body of words but despise the soul of reason—that he employs such exalted eloquence in those lamentations that no power of modern eloquence can equal him. O false judges of eloquence, whom the wind of speech casts away like dust from the face of the earth! What force of thoughts is there? What draughts of reasoning?

[Col. 1865D] He surges wholly in words, and the death of a ridiculous syllogism turns in a circle. Hence the poet says of the lyre-player:

> “He is laughed at who always strays upon the same strings.”

The luxuriant grasses of words sown there choke the thoughts. Or perhaps, in saying the same thing repeatedly, he wished to imitate Ulysses, of whom it is written:

> “He often used to tell the same thing to another.”

But the dead man is not raised by such instruments, nor is life procured for the dead by the tricks of eloquence. Hence a certain couplet finely resounds:

[Col. 1866A]

> Why are beautiful poems given vainly in place of psalms?  
> “Have mercy on me” said three times would help him more.

But if he did not wish to release his grief through the soothing ornaments of eloquence and the remedy of verse, why did he not at least compose a separate little work on this subject? Nor did he lack models from which he might borrow an example for such material. Socrates bears witness to the death of his Alcibiades with the abundance of philosophical vigour. Plato escorts the boy Alexis, for whom he had composed little love songs, to the tomb under a distinguished title. I pass over Pythagoras, Demetrius, Carneades, Posidonius, and the rest in whose excellence Greece takes pride, who, as Jerome testifies, in different ages and different books attempted to lessen the lamentations of different persons. I pass over also the ever-praised saying of Anaxagoras, who, when he was told

[Col. 1866B] that his son had died, restrained his tears and said: “I knew that I had begotten a mortal.”

And, leaving foreign examples to come to our own: Cicero, the greatest author of Roman eloquence, published a book of consolation on the death of his daughter, in which he set the splendid memorials of great men like gleaming stars. Jerome heals with persuasive eloquence the grief he conceived at the death of Nepotian. Ambrose, of whom I have spoken above, treats in two books, with sweet style, of the death of his beloved Satyrus. You ought to have woven your lament according to their model, not forgetting that common proverb:

> You ought to fashion your own beard after your neighbour’s.

But since we have discussed this sufficiently and abundantly, it is timely to examine that chapter in the same book

[Col. 1866C] in which you fabulously assert that the origin of souls is from heaven. There I recall you saying: “The Apostle rightly said: ‘Our citizenship is in heaven’” (Phil. 3). When closely examined, these words of yours taste of heresy to the palate of a Christian mind. For if you establish that the soul’s origin is from heaven because it will one day be blessed in heaven, by the same reasoning the body’s origin will be in heaven, because it too will one day be blessed in heaven. But such words are not suited to signify this.

Or if you ascribe a heavenly origin to souls because they once arose—that is, were made—in heaven, which is indeed the apparent intent of such words, you incur the perversity of Origen, who in the books *Periarchon*, following the Pythagorean and Platonic doctrine, assigns to souls their original dwelling in heaven.

[Col. 1866D] But since mention of the soul has intruded, it is not absurd to recall what variety of controversy has occupied men concerning the origin of souls. The philosophers, whose leaders are Plato and Pythagoras, and with whom you too agree in the greatest part, say that souls were formerly made and created from the beginning in the treasuries of God; and that, because of the contagion of an ancient life, they fell into the prison-house of bodies, but will return, if they have governed the body justly, in the vehicle of merit to the countenance of their ancient honour.

Heretics also maintained that the soul is a part of the divine substance, seizing an occasion for this fable from what is written in Genesis: “And God breathed into his face”—that is, Adam’s—“the breath

[Col. 1867A] of life” (Gen. 2). Against them Augustine thunders briefly:

> “That breath by which the man was animated is said to have been made by him, not from him; for a man’s breath is not a part of the man, nor does a man make it from himself, but from an airy breath that is taken in and breathed out.”

There were likewise certain men wrapped in the thick darkness of ignorance who madly imagined that souls come by propagation; to refute them is, in a way, to reinforce their absurdities. Once these three trifles (*naeniis*; read: “knots,” *nodis*), as it were opposed to reason, have been cut away by the sword of orthodox truth, the holy Fathers assert that newly created souls are daily infused into newly created bodies, according to the Gospel: “My Father works until now, and I work” (John 5).

You, therefore, straying from the path of wholesome teaching, rush upon the rocks of the philosophers. And while you boast of the soul’s dignity,

[Col. 1867B] you market its stellar origin with the barren flower of your speech. Had you found this madness in Peter’s little works, there is no doubt that you would have placed it among the monstrous propositions which you produced.

From here the discussion must turn to other fruits of your genius. A man swollen with Roman pride asks you what is to be loved, and how. You reply to him thus: “Aimeric, you used to ask me for prayers, not questions”; and a little later: “You ask what is to be loved. I answer briefly: God.” The Roman man, a coarse camel hunchbacked with Gallic argument, leaps across the Alps to inquire what is to be loved, as though he did not have near him someone to instil in him knowledge of this matter. Our philosopher instructs him that virtue is not to be loved, as Chrysippus taught; nor pleasure, as Aristippus taught; but God, as a Christian teaches. A rather sharp answer indeed, and worthy of a learned man.

[Col. 1867C] But what lowly old woman, what utterly unlearned man, does not know this? Old women philosophize thus in workshops. Thus we are accustomed, laughingly, to marvel at Dagan’s propositions. I shall insert a few of them by way of example:

> “I am my mother’s son. A cake is bread. My head is larger than my fist. When it is noon, it is daytime.”

Who, on hearing truth so ridiculous, does not have his lips shaken with laughter? Similarly, when Bernard said that God is to be loved, he indeed said what is entirely true and venerable; but to say this he opened his mouth to no purpose. No one doubts it. The Roman expected to hear something secret, and our archimandrite thunders something which any rustic could answer. Yet, while secretly declaring that God is to be loved, he strikes the Roman, who had learned in the papal court to love not God but gold.

He next proceeds to the manner of loving:

[Col. 1867D] “The manner,” he says, “is to love without measure.” You fed Aimeric—for that is the name of the man to whom you write—as though with milky food when you openly declared that God is to be loved. Now, suddenly lifting him to higher matters (*subrigens*; read: *suberigens*), you say that the manner of loving God is to love without measure. He had asked what was to be loved—a matter about which not even the poorest Christian would hesitate. How will he be able to understand this subtlety, that the manner of loving God is to love without measure? In this you seem to promise something impossible. For since it is stable and fixed that God is endowed with such magnificence that our love for him can by no means adequately correspond to his dignity, how shall we love without measure when we cannot love him even with measure?

[Col. 1868A] How, I ask, will love be extended beyond measure when it always remains short of measure? Or if you understood “to love without measure” thus—namely, to love in such a way that one does not attain the fitting measure of love—your dream displays a ridiculous interpretation. Thus, while you wished to play the rhetorician, you produced both obscurity and something impoverished and impossible, when you taught that God must be loved without measure.

[Col. 1868B] How much more rightly does he speak here who undertakes nothing ineptly—namely Jesus Christ, who, expressing the manner of loving through his Gospel, says: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, and with your whole mind, and with all your strength” (Matt. 22). Here there is no cosmetic of eloquence, but only pure truth expressed in simple and unqualified speech. Here let the Roman lend his ear. Here let the camel lay aside the swelling of pride, for Jesus here pronounces nothing impossible. Jesus, I say, does not wrap the light of his thought in the darkness of speech, as Bernard does, who veils the majesty of a venerable matter with a certain elaborate adulteration of words. The wise man Horace says:

[Col. 1868C]

> “Not to give smoke from light, but to give light from smoke  
> He thinks [lacuna].”

Bernard attended to this badly: what Jesus says with naked and open speech, he excludes from the path of understanding by a cloud of language. You have poured a heaped and compacted measure of these and similar trifles into the bosom of your little books, Bernard. Anyone whom learning has made clear-sighted could readily criticize them. If I wished to pursue them to the fingernail, the length of the composition would certainly repel even a diligent reader.

Since you utter such great beams, why do you endeavour to turn Abelard’s specks into beams? It is not the task of a merciful man to enlarge a fault, but to lessen it. Hence, when the Psalmist was about to say, “I will sing to you of mercy

[Col. 1868D] and judgment, O Lord” (Ps. 100), he fittingly placed mercy before judgment, as though saying: “Immense God, I know that you are merciful and just; but in the one lies my salvation, in the other my condemnation; and I more willingly desire the song of mercy first.” It is written in Isaiah: “They shall turn their swords into ploughshares” (Isa. 2). Swords must be turned into ploughshares, not ploughshares into swords, because evil men must be drawn to the good of peace by the gentleness of correction, and good men must not be summoned to discord by the harshness of attack.

Persuaded by these and other examples, if Peter had been wounded by error you ought to have placed him upon your beast and thus brought him back to the stable of universal faith. Many Catholics have said things deserving blame, yet have not thereby

[Col. 1869A] been enrolled in the company of heretics. Hilary, the conqueror of error and defender of the Church, made two statements in which the sobriety of the Church does not follow him. First, he asserted that Christ felt no pain in the Passion. Against him Claudianus, a presbyter of Lyons, a most Christian man, as subtle in disputation as he was skilful in speech, thus declares:

> “If Christ felt no pain in the Passion, he did not truly suffer; and if he did not truly suffer—”

[Note: [Col. 1869D] Something is lacking here.]

Second, Hilary said that no incorporeal thing was created. “Therefore,” Claudianus says, “the soul, being incorporeal, is not created. But if it was not created, it is not a creature of God.” Yet, as the same Claudianus says, the learning of the teacher does not lose the merit of the confessor on this account, because the Church indulged in her good son what human opinion had argued with insufficient caution.

[Col. 1869B] Without doubt, had Peter said these things, the severity of your strictness would have decreed that he be stoned.

Blessed Jerome too, in his book *Against Jovinian*, discusses certain matters concerning marriage. Especially in the place where he adduces the Apostle’s statement: “It is good not to touch a woman” (1 Cor. 7). Jerome adds:

> “If it is good not to touch a woman, then it is evil to touch her. For nothing is contrary to good except evil.”

Anyone who professes to have been trained in the discipline of disputation knows this argument to be frivolous. For likewise it is good not to eat flesh and not to drink wine; yet it does not therefore follow that eating flesh and drinking wine is evil. Those who asserted this were received among the heretics.

Yet let it be conceded briefly that, according to Jerome, touching a woman is evil. The chain of reasoning itself shows how great an absurdity follows. For if it is evil to touch a woman, it is evil to have intercourse with a woman. It cannot happen that intercourse is good if touch is evil. And if it is evil to have intercourse with a woman, whoever has intercourse with a woman acts evilly.

[Col. 1869C] Therefore married persons sin in lawfully employing marital intercourse, for even in intercourse they touch a woman. Thus, lest husbands act wrongly, they must abstain from their wives. Or, if intercourse is necessary, let them have intercourse in such a way that they do not touch the woman. But this is impossible. Therefore the good of marriage suffers shipwreck—a good which divine providence prepared as a remedy for mortal lust. For if marriage does not excuse intercourse, let husbands go and compete in doing penance because they have at some time had intercourse with their wives.

Elsewhere in the same book Jerome argues more inhumanely concerning marriage upon the Apostle’s text: “It is better to marry than to burn” (ibid.). But if marrying is good,

[Col. 1869D] why is it compared to evil? No one reasonably compares evil with good. To burn is certainly evil, and marriage is good in comparison with this evil. But what is good in relation to evil is not simply good. From these words of Jerome we distinctly infer that marriage is not absolutely good.

[Col. 1870A] Therefore the good of marriage perishes. For, according to Jerome, the good of marriage is not good except because burning is a greater evil than marriage itself. This harsh and savage argument scandalized many faithful men, including the senator Pammachius, and they testified to their grief in letters written to Jerome on this subject. Had Peter declaimed so cruelly against marriage, Bernard would surely have armed cohorts of married people for his destruction.

[Col. 1870B] Augustine, an enemy to his own errors, entrusts them to be purged in the book of his *Retractations*. Lactantius—of whom Augustine himself declares that he came out of Egypt laden with much gold—while with thunderous speech he defends Christ against the pagans, later dreams certain discordant things concerning the doctrines of the Church. It would take too long to list the writings of the ancient treatise-writers which have not been so thoroughly purified that many things are not found in them worthy of the rod of correction. For the Apostle James’s statement is true: “We all stumble in many things. But if anyone does not stumble in speech, he is a perfect man” (Jas. 3).

Thus, if Peter had stumbled in speech, when judged by you he ought rather to have felt

[Col. 1870C] the gentle touch of mercy than the spur of anger. It was fitting that you should recall what the prophet Habakkuk sings to God, saying: “When you are angry, you will remember mercy” (Hab. 3). See how far God’s anger differs from human anger. When a man is angry, the thought of clemency is banished from his breast. But when God is angry, through the abundance of his inborn goodness he remembers mercy—he remembers—not without forgetfulness—who is angry without disturbance. Great is our Lord, who so governs the highest things that he does not neglect care for the lower.

You ought to have imitated this image, embraced these footsteps with all your efforts, so that with the coal which the angel took from the altar with tongs you might cleanse the fault of Peter’s lips. Nor ought you to have been unaware that you are a human being, whom the slipperiness of fault might draw to punishment, and whom healing grace might restore to pardon.

[Col. 1870D] Having thus run through these matters, the length of the discourse commands silence. And since the wearied voice now seeks the harbour of refreshment, a due end shall be set to the first volume, so that we may apply ourselves more dutifully to the struggle of a second labour, to unravel what we have promised.

[Note: [Col. 1869D] The second book is not extant here and was not written by Berengar, as is clear from the following letter.]

[Col. 1871]

## LETTER OF THE SAME BERENGAR TO THE BISHOP OF MENDE

[Col. 1871A] To his father and lord G., bishop of Mende, full of days: Berengar wishes that his youth may be renewed like the eagle’s.

In a barbarous place my body is quite free from robbers, but my spirit is endangered among you in a holy place. Therefore, before the sight of the whole world, I extend to you the staff of my defence, so that the teeth of holy men may not dare to bite one whom the savagery of swords permits to feed on the breath of life. Be therefore the Ulysses of my cause, so that Circe, although daughter of the Sun, may not dare to alter my right by magical murmur, and so that envy may not darken the star of my conscience. I should certainly grieve less if a wolf’s jaws drank my blood than if I were torn to pieces by the teeth of sheep.

Correct, therefore, good shepherd,

[Col. 1871B] your sheep, lest they bleat against me, for I am not a wolf lying in wait but a dog protecting the sheep. Relying at last upon your favour, I shall raise the sails of speech and, amid the Scyllas of barking tongues, sail by the oarage of firm reason.

A religious band heaps many dreadful charges upon my person and honours the head of an innocent man with the sacred diadem of accusations. They say that my tongue is an unruly evil, and that envy of mind has vomited forth a book against the abbot of Clairvaux. They affirm that he is a man of such holiness that, already near heaven, he has passed beyond human opinions. Those who say this, though they may be white with the fleece of religion, nevertheless corrupt their tongue with folly when they wish to be doves without the serpent.

Is not the abbot a man? Does he not sail with us upon this great and wide sea,

[Col. 1871C] wherein are creeping things without number? (Ps. 104.) Although his ship may be carried by a more favourable voyage, the severity of the sea remains uncertain.

For the south wind has not yet pledged him not to shake his vessel; nor has he himself trodden the north wind beneath his feet; nor escaped the threats of east and west winds; nor extorted a truce from Aeolus, king of the winds. What wine can dwell in pitch and not have its flavour changed? Hence the Apostle Paul wished his wine to be removed from companionship with pitch and transferred into a vessel of glory, when he said: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Rom. 7). It is as though he spoke more openly: “I am God’s wine, and I am in pitch; but unless I leave the fellowship of pitch, I fear that I shall taste of pitch to my Creator.”

[Col. 1871D] Therefore the abbot can both be borne aloft like fire and fall downward like earth. He is not yet the sun; he is not yet fixed in the firmament; it is enough if he is the moon. Let no one suppose that I draw my stylus across wax in order to injure him; in my judgment he is the Martin of our times. I speak simply and without fox-like cunning to your candid heart. This is how I judge the abbot:

[Col. 1872A] he is a lamp burning and shining, yet he is in an earthen vessel. What disgrace is attached to gold when, while it is praised, its dross is criticized? You praise the abbot; I praise him still more. Why, then, do you write so harshly against him, of whom you think so well? Offer open ears that they may drink in the reason.

He had condemned Abelard, my teacher: a man who was a trumpet of faith, an armoury of the law, walking with kingly foot in the path of morals. He had condemned Abelard, I say, and had strangled his voice without a hearing. At that time I was a young man, and the clouds of down had not yet shaded my immature cheeks; and, like a schoolman, my mind was accustomed frequently to turn aside into unfeigned subject matter. When therefore the vein of a contest for truth smiled upon me, I set myself to cleanse Abelard and refute the abbot’s audacity.

[Col. 1872B] “But,” they say, “it was not fitting for you to criticize such a theologian. You are a beast and must not touch the mountain.” More sparingly with such things, brothers. Remember that you are throwing this reproach at a man. In what does the abbot dare? He dares in letters; so do I. He dares in theology; so do I. He dares in faith; so do I. He dares in holiness; here I do not dare. What sin, then, have I committed if I, a believer, rebuked a believer; a lesser man, a greater; a secular, a religious? I bit, I confess, not the contemplative but the philosopher; not the confessor but the writer; not the mind but the tongue; not the inmost feelings but the pen; not the man’s meditations but his dream.

Let learned men read the *Apologeticus* which I published; and, if I did not justly criticize the lord abbot, let them freely criticize me. Search through the entire series of writings from the rising of the sun to its setting,

[Col. 1872C] and you will see that in the field of philosophy it has always been permitted for one person to rebuke another on just grounds. Colotes, notable for talkativeness, gnaws at Plato, prince of philosophy, because, while treating divine matters, he mingled in fables. And certainly Colotes is a mouse in comparison with Plato’s elephant. Lucilius tears apart Ennius, Horace Lucilius. I shall pass over the smoke of the pagans and adorn this little parchment with the luminaries of the Church. Augustine and Jerome, presbyter and bishop, tear at one another with reciprocal beaks. Fulgentius marks a certain king of Africa as a heretic, not fearing royal power because he loves truth. Julian attacks Augustine boldly: “No fuller’s herb,” he says, “will cleanse you of the infection of heresy.”

[Col. 1872D] Ambrose alone is free from every stain of suspicion, whom Pelagius, although a heretic, crowned with outstanding praise, saying: “Ambrose shone forth like a certain flower among Latin writers.” Not even an enemy dares criticize his most pure understanding of the Scriptures.

Therefore, if the abbot wrote—wrote—something that should have remained unspoken,

[Col. 1873A] what sin did truth commit in my mouth when it noted that it ought to be uprooted? Justice ought not tremble before the face of the sword, nor should truth put on the cloak of flattery before a powerful man. Hence Seneca, addressing Caesar: “Caesar,” he says, “those who dare speak against you do not know your greatness; those who do not dare do not know that you are a man.” Socrates also, whom Apollo’s oracle sang to be wisest, was of supreme authority; yet Aristotle nobly dared to say: “Socrates is a friend, but truth is a greater friend.”

“But,” they say, “why, after completing the first volume, do you not weave the second, as you promised?” Because in the course of time my judgment increased, and I came round, as the saying goes, to the abbot’s opinion. I did not wish to be the defender of the propositions charged against Abelard, because, though they might mean soundly, they did not sound sound.

[Col. 1873B] “Since therefore,” they say, “your hand grew numb after the second book, why did you not erase the first?” “I would have done so,” I say, “had the effort not been vain. For living copies would remain, which have already spread throughout all France and Italy.” “If, therefore,” they say, “you cannot kill that apology, condemn it at least while it is alive. Brand its forehead with the mark of the matter, so that everyone who reads it may know that you sinned through age, not malice.” “I shall condemn it,” I say, “on this condition: that, if I said anything against the person of the man of God, it be read as a joke, not seriously.”

“They say: “We do not refute your arguments; you carefully unload the little ass sufficiently. But why did you disturb the Carthusian hermits, a chosen race, a people for possession” (1 Pet.

[Col. 1873C] 2)? “Why did you anoint them with invective? Why did you draw them away from their cells?”

Hear my defence here calmly. The prophet reproaches those who gather wages and put them into a bag with holes (Hag. 1). The holy Carthusian anchorites gathered the wages of righteousness, but had a bag with holes. I took care to stop the hole in the bag, lest the flour of religion should run out through open cracks. I wished to cut away in them the immoderate licence of tongue by which, like certain geometers, they measured the whole world. Why is my piety here accused of cruelty? Why is the diligent tailor called a destroyer?

“But,” they say, “you lean here on pillars of firm reason. Yet why did you wound that monk of Marseilles

[Col. 1873D] to the soul?” Because he was wounding the ring of Christ’s Bride and threatening shipwreck to the purity of the ancient faith. For he introduced, besides God, another Creator, as the letter written by him to me declares.

“But,” they say, “wherever we pursue you, you oppose the weapons of defence. Answer concerning your members, because you poured out the poison of your tongue.” “When,” I ask, “was this word spoken?” “Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you my friends, because humiliation has touched me” (Job 19). Where did I harm you? Where did I wound your majesty?

[Note: [Col. 1873] This is found in the prologue of a certain treatise which he made on the incarnation of Christ, addressed to Benedict the canon.]

Then, they say, did you not strike when

[Col. 1874A] you said: “Among religious people a psalm is a little dish, and an *alleluia* is a rich meal?” Brothers, forgive me: I harmed none of you. I spoke indeterminately. I babbled without specification. I flogged no one in particular. Like Apollo, I issued an empty oracle, as though striking the air. But, as I see, whatever I say will either be or not be. Why have you imposed another’s burden upon yourselves? Why have you wounded your purity with a dart not aimed at you?

I said: “Among religious people a psalm is a little dish, and an *alleluia* a rich meal.” What is that to you? The religious of Maguelonne are religious too, and so are the canons of Saint-Ruf. Apollo hurled the sky (*coelum*; read: “dart,” *jaculum*) into the air, and lest it fall fruitlessly, you willingly offer yourselves to the wound. Who has ever seen someone open his mouth to receive an arrow? I, brothers, had aimed my bow elsewhere, but you

[Col. 1874B] caught the flying iron. I refused; I wished to bear it, but you, moved by charity, draw its wounds into your own health. Believe me, I was not so full of *agave*, that is, frenzy, as to shoot the daughter of my quiver at you. Therefore pardon an innocent man.

And they say something else: “Why have we hired Cyclopes to forge thunderbolts for your head?” “What, I ask?” “Then,” they say, “you said: ‘Your bishop is bishop not of the people of Mende, but of mimes.’” I should like to cry out with the prophet Jeremiah: “Woe to you, my mother: why have you borne me, a man of strife and pain in the whole earth?” (Jer. 15). Where and when, I ask, did I belch out such things? Perhaps when I held markets outside the world I was stamping such blasphemies upon your bishop. For I truly confess that I uttered no such slanders against him.

[Col. 1874C] “There is another matter,” they say: “why should we make you drunk with our vinegar?” “What is it?” “You said of us: ‘Your Donatus is a mob.’” You terrify me, brothers, with your novelties; and against the monsters you invent I shall sign my brow with the cross: In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. What is this that you say?

> I should like to flee hence beyond the Sauromatians and the icy…

Oceanus . . . . Certainly that prophecy is true: “Fiction will send truth into exile.” Could you, brothers, have fabricated this? Yet, so that these tales may gain greater authority in public ears, you make me their inventor. Shall I swear that I did not say it? But you will laugh, as though a mountain had brought forth a mouse. Shall I acknowledge it? But I shall immediately experience the power of the cross. What then shall I do? Innocent, I beg pardon; and, if it pleases you more, guilty, I ask pardon. Moreover, to complete my satisfaction, I offer you a sextary of my blood. Spare me therefore, brothers, spare me; and do not defile your mouths by accusing my poor person. For my tongue serves your praises, and everywhere I am a devout preacher of your church. This humility I send you while absent in this present page; when present, I shall display it in a single living voice—and, if life accompanies me, in person.

[Col. 1875]

## LETTER OF THE SAME BERENGAR AGAINST THE CARTHUSIANS

[Col. 1875A] B. to the brothers bound by profession to the Carthusian order: may you have eternal rest with Lazarus, once poor.

I shall speak to my lords, though I am dust and ashes (Gen. 18). Yet I have become like a beast of burden before you (Ps. 72), and nevertheless, “You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 35). God has multiplied his mercy, who gathered you from the four winds of heaven, that you might recline with Abraham in the kingdom of his Father. He who was faithful in all the house of Egypt drew you out of your Egypt with a mighty hand and uplifted arm, so that, spewing out the pots of meat, you might cry in the wilderness, “Manhu? What is this?” (Exod. 16).

This voice is the voice of the wilderness. It marvels at the rain of heavenly food, which the throat of Egypt cannot bear to utter [Col. 1875B]. Therefore, lest you should smell again of Pharaoh’s garlic, you approached the hyssop of the cross; and instead of the Egyptian groan, with longing for the heavenly bird you cry: “What is this?” From the land of the wilderness manna comes to travelers in the wilderness, and rightly you say: “What is this?” What, I say, is that which drives hunger away, satisfies desire, and, while satisfying it, kindles it?

That hand of inexhaustible mercy snatched clay from clay and, in Solomon’s diadem, with which his mother crowned him (Cant. 3), made you golden out of clay. But I do not know by what means gold has now returned to clay, and the coinage of a golden age has degenerated into the worthlessness of iron. You raised your bodies onto the mountains, but your minds remained in the valleys. Whence, then, will help come to you? We hoped that on the mountain summits you would forge wings that might carry you [Col. 1875C] to the Father’s right hand. A deceptive expectation misled us; and, what we deeply lament, now that the oarage of wings has been stripped away, the weight of bodily feathers sinks you down.

We thought that God was God only of the mountains; but “the valleys too shall abound with grain” (Ps. 64). You ought to have received peace for the people, but you have hurled the darts of your tongue not against the people but against God. The worship of righteousness, as the prophet testifies, is silence (Isa. 32). How weighty is this judgment when weighed in the balance of the Holy Spirit: “of disputes” [read: “silence”]. For folly and lust fall away or fail: they leap beyond the mark or lie short of it unless governed by the bridle of silence. You have broken the joints of this bridle, shattered its nails, and, with the charioteer weakened, like unbridled horses you perceive the precipices before [Col. 1875D] you gain the prize.

He indeed said: “The worship of righteousness is silence.” But you, interpreting otherwise, say: [Col. 1876A] “The worship of righteousness is much speaking.” For what marketplaces, what law courts, burn with such fierce litigation of cases as the cloister of mountainous Chartreuse? There the accuser does not bring charges, nor does the advocate wipe away the charges brought; nor, according to your judgment, does anyone uniformly condemn or acquit what is lawful and unlawful. You eagles fly above the clouds, and at last, with wings slackened, lower your beaks to tear at your own carcass. You abstain from the flesh of animals, yet without salt devour human flesh.

For you say: “This woman is pregnant, not by her husband’s seed; that woman keeps many lovers; those canons stuff their bellies with meat three times a day; that man pollutes the air with the belch of spiced drink; that one drains his bowl to the point of vomiting.” You have leisure, and therefore you belch such things. Truly, “the worship of righteousness is silence.” What has not yet [Col. 1876B] reached your tongue is already established among you as having been done. What is doubtful to us is sworn truth with you: “the worship of righteousness is silence.”

O merciful physicians, who strive not to cure the sick by remedies but to take upon themselves their wounds, so that they may be sick together with them! What good is it, brothers, to go out into the desert and to retain an Egyptian heart in the desert? What good is it to avoid Egypt’s frogs and croak with obscene detractions? Behold: you who languished under Pharaoh expired under the hand of Moses. The smoke of your tongue is evidence against you: though you drink from the spring in the privacy of your cell, detraction is conceived in the cells and vomited forth in the cloisters.

Chartreuse is not heaven; Chartreuse is not paradise. Chartreuse is still among the rivers of Babylon. In heaven there was an apostate; in paradise, [Col. 1876C] a transgressor. What is a slanderer doing in Chartreuse? After the purity of dross, after tears of compunction, one goes to the marketplace of the cloister, and the door of the tongue is not opened but broken down. Whoever has not entered through that door is not touched but believed; not healed but judged; not refreshed but slaughtered; and, to say it briefly, among you no one is without guilt.

> **[Note: Col. 1875]** This dialogue seems to be by another author, perhaps Abelard, and to have nothing to do with Berengar’s letter.

A. said to P.; P. said to A. The same man said to the same man: “Since, Peter, Christ is God, from whom Christians take their name, our people alone, I think, is distinguished by the appellation of a divine name.”

P. Glory to him who granted the glory of so great a name to so frail a creature, so that, joined even by this very designation [Col. 1876D] to that head whose members we are, we may be admonished by the very interpretation of the name to preserve what we are called [Col. 1877A]. For *Christus* is called in Greek from *chrisma*, that is, “anointing,” and in Latin is interpreted “anointed”; this is what *Messias* signifies in Hebrew. Both kings and priests customarily were anointed. Hence, by the name of anointing he is shown to be both king and priest: king, indeed, through the power by which he can rescue his own from dangers and protect them; priest, through the sacrifice of his own body, by which he reconciles to God those whom he rescues from the devil.

Thus from Christ Christians are called, as Messianites from the Messiah—that is, from that supreme King or Priest—as kings or priests. Blessed Peter expresses this when he calls us “a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2), recalling what we ought to be: namely, governing the impulses of our flesh and, after slaying fleshly desires, offering ourselves to God as a sacrifice [Col. 1877B]. Therefore, once Christ’s grace had been spread abroad in us, in accordance with that saying of the Apostle, “Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5), it was fitting that the name also should be spread abroad, as is likewise said in the Song of Songs: “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Cant. 1). As though it said: Your name, O Christ, which signifies ointment, that is, anointing, has been poured out—that is, spread abroad—and distributed among many, who for that reason are called Christians.

A. B. But also, according to the Apostle, since Christ is Wisdom itself (1 Cor. 1), which the Greeks call *sophia* (σοφία), I think that none are more rightly called philosophers than those who are lovers [Col. 1877C] of this highest and perfect Wisdom.

P. This is certainly required by the etymology itself of the term “philosopher”; and it is especially evident that both the doctrine of faith and the discipline or life of morals agree with the philosophers of the Gentiles. For they discussed the faith of the Trinity so openly that it is astonishing that in many matters they expounded the whole sum of this faith more carefully even than the prophets themselves. Their followers even dared to break out into such madness as to say that the Lord Jesus himself learned from philosophers the things which he preached concerning the faith of the Trinity.

Hence blessed Augustine, in Book VIII of *The City of God*, says: “Some are astonished,” he says, “when they hear or read that Plato held such opinions about God as are recognized to agree greatly with the truth of our religion, joined to us in Christ’s grace” [Col. 1877D]. The same author says in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*: “Certain readers and lovers of Plato have dared to break out into such madness as to say that all the sayings of our Lord Jesus Christ which they are compelled to admire and utter, he learned from Plato’s books.”

And if we weigh also the life of the philosophers and their discipline of morals, we shall judge that no Christians, or few Christians, are to be preferred to them in contempt for the world or in moral discipline. They maintain that a *sophus*, or philosopher, ought to be so called more from life than from consciousness. But concerning the philosophers’ faith and life, and likewise their discipline [Col. 1878A] of morals, I think we have sufficiently set forth our position in our exhortation to our brothers and fellow-monks. Whoever reads that exhortation will see that philosophers are associated with Christians above all not so much in name as in reality. For grace, armed with so many philosophical arguments, would not so quickly have made necks submit to the yoke of evangelical preaching, unless it had first been prepared for this through the writings of philosophers, just as Judaea was prepared through the prophets.

A. B. We likewise say that the Word of God, which the Greeks call *logos* (λόγον), is Christ alone. Hence Augustine, in Book 44 of the *Eighty-Three Questions*, says: “‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John 1), which in Greek is called *logos* (λόγος).” Thus, according to the etymology of the name, whoever cleave to this true and perfect Word through teaching and love [Col. 1878B] are truly *logicians* and ought to be called philosophers; and no discipline ought more truly to be called logic than Christian doctrine.

P. Although ordinary usage of speech does not permit us in this way either to call Christians specifically philosophers, or to call their knowledge of Christ, or the doctrine handed down by Christ, logic, we nevertheless acknowledge that the etymologies of the names wholly agree with what you say.

A. B. Indeed, the things themselves also testify to it very strongly. For as philosophical disciplines are pre-eminent among the Gentiles, so evangelical discipline, which Christ handed down, is pre-eminent above all sacred learning by as much or much more. The manifested coming of the Holy Spirit in tongues of fire shows how great an abundance of speech he gave to his own [Col. 1878C], for he taught them most perfectly the varieties of every language and every kind of discourse. Hence it is written: “There are no tongues nor speeches whose voices are not heard” (Ps. 18). It is as though it were plainly said: There are no varieties of readings, or ornaments and kinds of eloquence, which he did not give to his own. To them he had also promised, saying that when that Spirit of truth came, he would teach them all truth (John 16), so that he might make them perfect both in words and in knowledge, so that they could fully expound what they perfectly knew.

How much more perfect a knowledge of God those taught by God’s Only-Begotten himself obtained than the ancient Fathers did, Gregory declares in expounding Homily 3 at the end of his work on Ezekiel: “Through the increase of times, the knowledge of God came among the Fathers. Hence Daniel [chapter 12 says]: ‘Many shall pass through, and knowledge shall be multiplied.’”

P. We gladly accept this also, since it is true and commends the profession of our faith. For how could Christ, through the preaching of a few simple people, have gained so many people in all regions of the world, unless he filled them inwardly with wonderful wisdom and distinguished them outwardly with the force of words and the grace of eloquence? For, as Tully himself recalls in rhetorical fiction, no one except a person endowed with wisdom and eloquence could turn human beings away from their pleasant custom—especially once, through age, it had acquired the force of nature [Col. 1879A]—and lead them over to different ways of life. And the more difficult and perfect Christ’s precepts appear, the greater discernment and eloquence had to be bestowed upon his preachers.

A. B. Certainly nothing is truer or more consonant with reason than that those whose preaching was appointed by the Lord to win the whole world should be equipped with the best weapons of both knowledge and eloquence [Col. 1880A], so that with confidence they might preach the word to all. When he sends them, he himself strengthens them, saying: “When you stand before kings and governors, do not think about how or what you are to speak. For in that hour what you are to say will be given to you” (Matt. 10).

## Back Matter of the Volume

[Col. 1879]

### A

**ALCUIN.**—To Charles, 1446.  
**ALEXANDER II.**—1538.
